en: | | Homage to Śrī Gaṇeśa! | | Homage to the Blessed One Vāsudeva!
Now begins the first chapter.
Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and to Nara, the best of men,
as well as to the goddess Sarasvatī, one should then utter the word "Victory.
Victorious is Vyāsa, the son of Parāśara and the delighter of Satyavatī’s heart.

I bow to that Mādhava, the supreme bliss, by whose grace the world drinks the nectar of speech falling from his lotus-like mouth; he who makes the mute eloquent and enables the lame to traverse the mountain.
The stainless lotus of the words of Pārāśarya (Vyāsa), intense with the fragrance of the meaning of the Gītā,
its filaments being various narratives awakened by the awakening of the stories of Hari—
this is drunk with joy day after day by the bees that are the virtuous in this world.
May the lotus of the Bhārata, which destroys the impurities of the Kali age, lead to our ultimate welfare—
[that Bhārata] by which one who gives a hundred cows with horns made of gold to a Brahmin who is learned in the Vedas and possessed of great erudition [attains such merit].
Whoever should hear this entire meritorious and auspicious narrative,
his merit shall be equal to that very person's [merit].
Having composed all these various Purāṇas which bring happiness, the son of Parāśara—

Therein, for the sake of his own future welfare, Vyāsa recorded everything concerning the events that would occur in the Kali age. Furthermore, he concisely explained the future by means of the meanings found in the Smṛtis, the Dharmāgamas, and the Saṃhitās composed by the foremost of all excellent sages, such as Parāśara and other munis.
Having observed that the people of the world are short-lived, devoid of knowledge, and behave like beasts despite their outwardly virtuous conduct,
Vyāsa composed the celebrated Purāṇa for their welfare and enlightenment.
Victorious is the Sun, the maker of the world and the lamp of the universe!
Victorious is Murāri, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow with his dark-blue body;
victorious is Rudra, known by that name and bearing the moon upon his crest;
and victorious is that god Bhānumān, the one of variegated radiance.
All the great-souled maharṣis— Bhṛgu, Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu— approached the immensely powerful King Śatānīka, who was surrounded by splendor, in order to see him.
Parāśara, as well as Vyāsa, Sumantu, and Jaimini;
the sage Paila, Yājñavalkya, and Gautama of great austerity;
the wise sage Bhāradvāja, as well as Nārada and Parvata.
Seeing those sages who had arrived— the high-souled Vaiśampāyana, Śaunaka of great austerity, Dakṣa, Aṅgiras, Garga, and the highly ascetic Gālava— Śatānīka, the lord of the earth, [welcomed them].
The high-minded one, having approached him, honored him according to the prescribed rites;
placing the family priest at the forefront, he offered the guest-offering (arghya), a cow, and words of welcome.
Having thus honored them all, he then bowed his head deeply before them.
Then the king, having become prostrate and raising his right arm, spoke to those best of beings who were seated at ease, free from anxiety, and relieved of fatigue:
"O most excellent ones on earth, I now consider my birth to have borne fruit."
O tigers among the twice-born, my very self, as well as my fame, glory, and strength, have been purified;
I am blessed and a performer of meritorious deeds, since you have come to see me—
by the mere remembrance of whom a man is sanctified.
"I wish to hear some unsurpassed teaching on dharma;
relying upon compassion, O mighty ones, please speak it,
so that having heard this treatise on dharma, I may attain the supreme goal."
Just as my father had heard the Bhārata in the past,
so were those Brahmins addressed by that king from all sides; having assembled together and deliberated deeply upon it at that time, they spoke.
Having worshipped Vyāsa, they then spoke these words:
"O Lord, propitiate Vyāsa; he will tell this to you.
O mighty-armed one, as long as he remains present, we are unable to speak."
O high-minded one, how can a disciple speak while the Guru is present? [He should say:
"This Guru is always our manifest Nārāyaṇa;
he is likewise compassionate and a knower of divine ordinances."
For the purification of the four great classes,
he has declared this treatise on Dharma, which is fully endowed with righteousness and other virtues;
for people fear this profound scripture as the world fears disease from medicine.
The sage himself has declared the extent of the Bhārata;
just as a physician would administer medicine that is both palatable and wholesome,
so too has the sage composed the Bhārata, which is both delightful and a sacred scripture.
This *Bhārata* is said to be the ascending staircase to faith;
having heard it, people behold heaven and hell directly.
Through the *Bhārata* alone is there certainty regarding the gods, sacred fords, and ascetic penances.
Even by the Mīmāṃsakas, his atheism is not produced;
for the wise, auspicious devotion toward Viṣṇu, the gods, the Vedas, the gurus, and the Brāhmaṇas arises from the Bhārata alone.
Indeed, the accomplishment of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa comes from the Bhārata;
the path of the Bhārata is straight for those going to the state of nirvāṇa.
The manifold exposition of mokṣa, dharma, artha, and kāma has been set forth in the Bhārata.
They become scorched by the heat of impermanence for the sake of liberation from it;
having heard of the misfortunes of the Vṛṣṇis and Pāṇḍavas and their ultimate end in suffering from the *Bhārata*, O King of kings, the wise man should take refuge in merit.
The great-souled one by whom this Bhārata was thus proclaimed is that very Nārāyaṇa himself, the great sage in the form of Vyāsa. Having heard their words, that powerful lord of the earth—
He propitiated the sage Vyāsa, who was proficient in the scriptures.
Śatānīka said:
"O Brahmin, this salutation with joined palms and head bowed is made at your feet."
Speak to me the Dharmaśāstra by which I may attain purity;
deliver me from this worldly existence by reciting an auspicious narrative,
just as my father formerly attained [liberation] by reciting the Bhārata.
Vyāsa said: Having heard these words of his, Vyāsa spoke these words:
"O Lord, this disciple of mine, Sumantu, will relate it to you."
O mighty-armed tiger among the Bharatas, if you desire that which is delightful, wonderful, auspicious, worthy of being heard, and the remover of all sins and fears—
just as it was formerly spoken by Vaiśampāyana to your father.
The exposition of the Mahābhārata dispels even the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Then all the sages said this to the king:
"Well spoken, O mighty-armed one, by Vyāsa of immeasurable intellect!"
"O royal sage, ask Sumantu, who is proficient in all the scriptures;
O Indra among kings, our minds also turn toward listening to him.
Then the highly effulgent Vyāsa spoke to the sage Sumantu.
"O dear one, tell him those stories by hearing which the king rejoices—
those such as the narratives of the Mahābhārata and others— in which his mind finds delight.
Having heard the intention of that high-minded one, he too, possessed of great splendor,"
O tiger among the twice-born,

that high-minded one resolved in his mind to speak on behalf of Vyāsa and all the sages as well; O brahmin, by the command of Vyāsa and indeed of all the sages, he set his heart upon it for the sake of the king.
Then the king of great splendor, Ājamīḍha, having bowed his head most deeply to the best of the twice-born, began to speak. Śatānīka said:
"O Brahmin, recite for me the narrative of merit for my purification;
having heard it, O best of Brahmins, may I be released from all sin.
Sumantu said:
O Bhārata, there are various kinds of scriptures that are like flowers;
having heard them, O King, a man is liberated from all sins.
O mighty-armed one, what do you wish to hear? Tell me what I shall speak to you.
"But regarding the stories of Bhārata and others in which Dharma and the rest are established—
" Śatānīka said:
"O best of Brahmins, O observer of noble vows, what are considered the authoritative treatises on Dharma?"
"O Brahmin, by hearing which a man is liberated from all sins.
Sumantu said:
"Listen to the treatises on Dharma: Manu, Viṣṇu, Yama, Aṅgiras..."
Vasiṣṭha, Dakṣa, Saṃvarta, Śātātapa, and Parāśara;
Āpastamba, Uśanas, Kātyāyana, and Bṛhaspati; Gautama, Śaṅkha and Likhita, Hārīta, and also Atri.
"O Bhārata, having heard and understood these treatises on Dharma, one goes to the city of the gods and rejoices; of this there is no doubt. Śatānīka said:
"O you of excellent vows, O best of Brahmins, I do not wish to hear these treatises on dharma that have been spoken by you; for these, O twice-born one, have already been heard [by me],
even as they were proclaimed by the learned for the sake of the three castes."

But for the Śūdras, it does not lead to the highest good; listen to my words regarding this. O tiger among the twice-born, O observer of noble vows, hear those [teachings] which exist in the three worlds for the welfare of the four castes here.
Especially for the fourth caste, O best of the twice-born;
the Vedas were established among the three castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas,
as well as the treatises of Manu and others, and all the auxiliary sciences (aṅgas) throughout.
O Lord of the twice-born, the Śūdras appear exceedingly wretched;
how could they be praised for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa on this earth?
For they are indeed bereft of the sacred scriptures—alas, what a tragedy! This is my opinion.
"And what is their traditional source said to have been by the ancient wise Brahmins,
O Brahmin, for the attainment of the three aims of life and likewise for the welfare of both worlds?
Sumantu replied:

Excellent, excellent, O mighty-armed one! Listen to my supreme word. O Indra among kings, O best of monarchs, listen to those treatises on dharma which have been proclaimed for the welfare of all four castes.
Furthermore, O tiger among the Kurus, the wise have declared that for Śūdras,
the eighteen Purāṇas and the life-story of Rāghava— namely,
that of Rāma— are the means of purification for the attainment of dharma, artha, and kāma.
Thus it was said, O hero, by the wise son of Parāśara in the Bhārata:
"O Lord, having combined the entire meaning of the Vedas with the Dharmaśāstras,
this scripture was composed by the compassionate one for the welfare of the four [orders] in this world."
For the sake of the social classes submerged in worldly existence, he indeed created this unsurpassed boat:
having mastered the eighteen Purāṇas and the eight grammars,
the son of Satyavatī composed the Bhārata-saṃhitā.
O King, by hearing which a man is released from the sin of killing a Brahmin:
first is proclaimed that of Brahmā, the second is said to be that of Indra;
then that of Yama, followed by that of Rudra, as well as those of Vāyu and Varuṇa.
The Sāvitra has been declared, as well as the eighth, the Vaiṣṇava. Learn from me these ancient grammars (Vyākaraṇas) and Purāṇas:
the Brāhma, the Pādma, the Vaiṣṇava, the Śaiva, and likewise the Bhāgavata.
Likewise, O hero, the Nāradīya is another, and the Mārkaṇḍeya is the seventh; the Āgneya is the eighth, and the Bhaviṣya is remembered as the ninth;
the Brahmavaivarta is the tenth, and the Laiṅga is remembered as the eleventh.
The twelfth is declared to be the Vārāha, and the thirteenth is the Skānda;
the fourteenth is the Vāmana, and the fifteenth is remembered as the Kaurma;
then follow the Mātsya, the Gāruḍa, and after that, the Brahmāṇḍa.
O tiger among the Kurus, these treatises on dharma have been proclaimed by the wise as common to all castes for their perpetual welfare;
O Indra among kings, O observer of noble vows, they ought to be heard here by all four.
"What do you wish to hear, O mighty-armed one, regarding these [lineages], O best of kings?
Śatānīka said:
"O Brahmin, I have heard the Bhārata while seated on my father's lap."
"O Brahmin, I have heard the life-story of Rāma in its entirety, as well as the Purāṇas, O lord of sages; however, O observer of noble vows, I have not heard the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa.
Tell me that Bhaviṣya Purāṇa, O lord of sages, for I have a great curiosity."
Sumantu said: "Excellent, excellent, O mighty-armed one! Well have I been questioned by you, O giver of honor.
Listen, O King, as I speak of this great, new Purāṇa."
O King, by hearing this, a man is liberated from all sins;
having obtained the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice, he shall go to the Sun—of this there is no doubt.
This unsurpassed treatise on Dharma was indeed proclaimed by Brahmā.
This must be studied with diligent effort by a learned Brāhmaṇa,
and it must indeed be taught to disciples belonging to all four varṇas;
however, it must not be studied by anyone other than a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya.

It must certainly be heard by a Śūdra, but it must never be studied. O best of kings, having placed it before the image of a deity, it must be heard by Brāhmaṇas, as well as by Śūdras and other twice-born castes.
O best of kings, both the Śrauta and Smārta Dharma have indeed been proclaimed herein;
therefore, this must never be heard by Śūdras in the absence of Brāhmaṇas.
A Brāhmaṇa of firm vows who studies this scripture—
One is never smeared by the defects of karma born of mind, speech, or body.
O King, those who listen with devotion, such as the Brāhmaṇas and others,
are liberated from all sins and go to heaven, O Lord.

O best of kings, that Brahmin who causes all the social orders to hear [the sacred texts] is declared here, my dear, to be the Guru of all the orders in every respect. He is to be honored at all times by all the social orders, O lord of men.
Even he alone deserves this entire earth.
This is the most excellent means of securing well-being; this increases the intellect;
this constantly brings fame; and this is the supreme state of ultimate bliss.
In this [work], Dharma has been declared in its entirety, as well as the merits and defects of actions,
the eternal conduct of all four castes,
and, O best of men, conduct is the primary Dharma as declared in the Śruti.
Therefore, a twice-born man who possesses self-control should always be devoted to this;
a Brahmin fallen from right conduct does not enjoy the fruit of the Vedas,
whereas one endowed with right conduct is declared to be a partaker of the full fruit.
Having thus observed the course of Dharma through conduct, the sages took up conduct as the supreme root of all austerity;
and other men as well, O King, have always relied upon conduct.
Thus, O Indra among kings, in this Purāṇa the glorification of right conduct (ācāra) is recounted, as well as various historical narratives (vṛttāntas) spoken by the wise; furthermore,
the origin of the three worlds and the supreme procedure for the sacraments (saṃskāra-vidhi) are described.
O King, the method for hearing this history is being described;
likewise, O King, the greatness of the reciter is told herein,
as well as the conduct of vows, the duties of the stages of life, and the supreme rule for the *snātaka*.
The approach to wives and so forth, the characteristics of marriages,
the characteristics of men, and those of women are described here;
as well as the procedure for the great sacrifices and the eternal ritual manual of the scriptures.
O dear one, [I shall explain] the characteristics of the earth, the auspicious marks of a deity’s image,
the characteristics of livelihoods, the vows of a snātaka,
what may and may not be eaten, purity, and the purification of ritual substances.
The duties of women, the practice of asceticism, liberation, and renunciation; the entire duty of kings and the adjudication of legal cases;
and the majesty of the Sun as well as that of sacred fords, O lord of the people, are all described herein.
The majesty of Nārāyaṇa and likewise that of Rudra is told;
the great fortune of the brahmins, the majesty of the book,
and also that of the goddess Durgā and of Truth, O high-minded one, have been declared.
He also taught the summary of legal procedures and the law concerning men and women, the division of property, lawful gambling, the purification of storytellers,
the conduct of Vaiśyas and Śūdras, and the origin of the mixed castes.
O King, [he taught] the duties for times of distress for the various social classes, as well as the rules for penance,
the ritual for the twilight prayers, the purification after death, the rules for bathing and libations,
the ritual for the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, and likewise the rules regarding what may be eaten.
The characteristics of the tooth-stick, the supreme *caraṇavyūha*, the journey through *saṃsāra*, the threefold origin of action (*karman*),
the liberation from actions, and the examination of their merits and defects.
The characteristics of wives have been declared, as well as the examination of worthy recipients;
likewise, O King, the birth of the embryo and the fruits of actions;
and the duties of castes, the duties of families, and the duties of the Vedas, O Ruler of the Earth.
O best of the Kuru lineage, the Lord Brahmā likewise spoke this to the high-souled Śaṅkara for those who observe the Vaitāna vow;
and O joy of the Kurus, it was likewise told by Śaṅkara to Viṣṇu.
O lord of the earth, it was proclaimed again by Viṣṇu to Nārada;
Śakra received it from Nārada, and Parāśara from Śakra.
From Parāśara it went to Vyāsa, and from Vyāsa, O Lord, it was obtained by me.

Thus, O Indra among kings, listen also from me to this supreme Purāṇa, which has been handed down through tradition and is the highest good. O bull among men, all [other] Purāṇas indeed should be understood as being included herein.

O bull among men, O descendant of Kuru, the wise have stated that there were originally twelve thousand verses here; however, they have again increased through various narratives, just as it is with the Skānda Purāṇa, so too is this Bhaviṣya Purāṇa.
The *Skānda* Purāṇa consists of one hundred thousand verses and is indeed well known among the worlds; this *Bhaviṣya* Purāṇa was composed by the sage in fifty thousand verses.
Having heard it with devotion, a person shall obtain this fruit.
"Supernatural power, prosperity, and likewise fortune will certainly belong to him.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Introduction to the Narrative," in the Brāhma Parvan of the Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, in the Saṃhitā consisting of fifty thousand verses.
Now begins the second chapter.

Sumantu said: "Listen, O mighty-armed one, to this Purāṇa characterized by five features, which contains a description of creation and a description of the origin from the mouth of Brahmā as the fifth."
O King, by hearing which a person is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin;
furthermore, five sacred days (parvans) have been proclaimed here by the Self-born One:
the first is called Brāhma, and the second is remembered as Vaiṣṇava.
The third is declared to be the Śaiva, while the fourth is called the Tvaṣṭra;
the fifth is named Pratisarga, which is highly honored by all the worlds.
O dear one, learn from me the characteristics of these sections (parvas).
Primary creation, secondary creation, genealogy, the periods of the Manvantaras,
and the history of the dynasties— thus the Purāṇa has five characteristics. It is adorned, O descendant of Kuru, with the fourteen branches of knowledge.
The auxiliary sciences, the four Vedas, Mīmāṃsā, the extensive Nyāya,
the Purāṇa, and the Dharmaśāstra— these indeed are the fourteen branches of knowledge.
Āyurveda, Dhanurveda, and Gāndharvaveda are the three [additional ones].
The science of polity (Arthaśāstra) is the fourth; indeed, those sciences are eighteen in number.
First, the creation of all beings here is described in its entirety;
having heard this, one is liberated from sin and attains supreme peace.
In the beginning, O dear one, the world was enveloped in darkness, devoid of distinguishing marks,
unknowable, inconceivable, and as if entirely asleep.
Then the Blessed Lord, the Unmanifest, made this manifest.
He whose vital energy has arisen as the great elements, who is indestructible,
who is beyond the senses, ungraspable, subtle, unmanifest, eternal,
composed of all beings, and inconceivable— he himself has now risen up.
O mighty-armed one, he who is called the Twenty-sixth in the world, as well as Puruṣottama, Bhāskara, and the Supreme Brahman— he,
desiring to emit various creatures, meditated upon his own body.
For this very reason, he first created them and cast his seed into them—
that from which everything arises, including gods, asuras, and humans.
That seed is called *śukra*, as well as *reta*, *ugra*, and *vīrya*.
These names of vigor were proclaimed by the Self-Existent One. Then, O Lord, that golden egg came into being, filled with garlands of flames,
within which Brahmā himself was born, the grandfather of all the worlds.
Surajyeṣṭha, Caturvakra, Parameṣṭhin, Pitāmaha,
Kṣetrajña, Puruṣa, Vedhās, Śambhu, and likewise Nārāyaṇa—
by these synonymous terms, indeed, Brahmā is celebrated.
O dear one, the wise have always declared that Virañci is likewise born from the lotus (kañjaja).
Water is called "nārāḥ," for water is indeed the offspring of Nara;
since it was his primary abode (ayana), he is therefore remembered as Nārāyaṇa.
The word "ara" was established by the seers as a term for swiftness;

because those waters became the ocean and flowed very swiftly, those men [were called] "arṇava. That which is the unmanifest cause, eternal, and consisting of both being and non-being—[that is the source].

The person emitted by him is celebrated in the world as Brahmā. Having thus established the very principle within the egg, O king of kings, that Blessed Lord entered into meditation and divided that egg into two parts.
And from two fragments, O Indra among kings, he fashioned heaven and earth;
the intermediate space, the eight directions, and indeed the realm of Varuṇa.
Having ascended high above, O King, he pervaded all sides for the welfare of the worlds.
From that [unmanifest] arises the Great Principle (mahat), and from that, the ego (ahaṃkāra); and from that, the three qualities (guṇas) as well.
These three qualities, O Bhārata, are indeed extremely subtle and are perceivable only by the intellect (buddhi).
They are, O King, the causal basis for the production of the great elements (bhūtas).

O King, the Lord, the omnipresent one, gradually took up their five sense organs as well as the subtle constituent parts of those six beings of immeasurable splendor, and placed them within his own portions.
O dear one, he created all the elements according to the prescribed rules;
these six are the substrata for the subtle constituent parts of his form.
Therefore, the wise call that form of his "the body" (śarīra).
Then those great beings enter the omnipresent Lord,
O King of kings, along with their actions and their qualities as well as the [five] qualities.
This, however, is the [creation] of those seven persons of great power.
From the subtle, imperishable, and non-dual material constituents (mūrti-mātrās),
O dear one, there arises the Great Principle (mahat), which is the source of the elements and by which this entire world is pervaded.
From that as well, O mighty-armed one, indeed proceed the five classes of beings.
Some wise men, O dear one, desire this supreme creation;
others also, O mighty-armed one, speak thus:
that Supreme Self, O dear one, creates a body at the beginning of the kalpa.
And he, O mighty-armed one, desiring to emit various creatures, was Prajāpati;
by him, O King, the individual soul (pudgala) was created, and it enters into Pradhāna.
By that [soul], Pradhāna is agitated and produces many transformations.
From that, O descendant of Kuru, the Great One (Mahat) arises; from Mahat, indeed, the Origin of Elements (Bhūtādi) arises; from the Origin of Elements, the Vast (Viśāla) arises;
from the Vast, my dear, comes Hari; and from Hari likewise come the Wolves (Vṛka).

O King, the wise rob [the senses] with wolves; therefore, O ruler of men, everything should be [understood] thus. Furthermore, O Indra among kings, O tiger of the Kurus, immediately thereafter, the awakening of the elements (mātrās) occurs for them with great force.
Therefore, O best of kings, the various sense organs [arose];
thus has this creation been described from the perspective of the one to be worshipped, O joy of the Kurus.
Listen further, O lord of kings, to the detailed account of beings here.
O Lord of the Earth, all elements,
beginning with space, possess an increasing number of qualities;
indeed, they have one, two, three, four, and five respectively.
Then that Lord Brahmā, the sovereign seated upon his lotus-throne,
created in the beginning the names and the distinct activities of all beings, as well as their various stations, from the very words of the Vedas.
The Lord created for embodied beings the class of Tuṣita gods who arise from karma, O King,
as well as the eternal sacrifice;
and having bestowed the secret, eternal Brahman upon those of equal status, O Hero.
For the sake of accomplishing the sacrifice, O King, he milked the Vedas characterized as Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman; likewise, he milked time, the divisions of time, the planets, and the seasons;
as well as rivers, oceans, mountains, and both level and uneven terrains.
O best of the Kurus,
O king of kings, desiring to create various progeny, he likewise created desire, anger, speech, and pleasure; for the sake of discerning between actions, he also created both dharma and adharma.
He joined these creatures with pairs such as pleasure and pain. Those subtle, imperishable particles which are known as the five [elements],
by means of them, O hero, all this comes into being in due succession.
O King, whatever action was performed in the past by him while he was still under constraint,
that very same thing he experienced himself as he was being created again and again—
whether it be violent or non-violent, gentle or cruel, righteous or unrighteous, true or false.
Whatever was produced at its creation, that entered into it of its own accord; and just as the seasonal signs recur in their proper turn by themselves,
so too do the actions of embodied beings follow them.

O best of kings, for the sake of the prosperity of the world in this realm, [the Lord] created the Brahmin, the Kṣatriya, as well as both the Vaiśya and the Śūdra from his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet. From those four mouths, the Vedas issued forth.
O dear one, O mighty-armed one, listen to how the Ṛgveda-saṃhitā was [revealed] by the high-souled Vasiṣṭha from his eastern and southern faces; and likewise,
O great king, hear how the Yajurveda was [revealed] together with Yājñavalkya.
O dear one, O king of kings, the Sāman hymns emerged from the west, and the great seer Gautama [emerged] from the north;
likewise, O king, the Atharvaveda issued from the mouth,
and the seer Śaunaka, honored by the world, [emerged] from the north.
O mighty-armed one, descendant of the Kuru lineage, that fifth face which is world-renowned—
from that mouth issued forth the eighteen Purāṇas along with the Itihāsas, O Bhārata.
Likewise, there are other Smṛtis as well, such as those concerning Yama, which are honored by the world.
Then that Blessed Lord caused his body to become twofold;
having divided his own body into two, he became a male with one half.
With half of himself, the Lord created a woman, and in her he produced Virāj;
having performed penance, that Puruṣa himself became Virāj. O King, desiring to create various offspring, he performed austerities.
In the beginning, he created ten great sages as the lords of progeny:
Nārada, Bhṛgu, Ka, Pracetas,
Pulaha, Kratu, Pulastya, Atri, and likewise Aṅgiras, O dear one.
O king of kings, he also created Marīci, who was the first Prajāpati;
and these and others of great splendor he created, O king of kings. Then, O descendant of Kuru, he created the gods, the ṛṣis, and the Daityas.
O Bhārata, O mighty-armed one, he created various hosts of Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Piśācas, Gandharvas, Apsarases, and Asuras, as well as those of humans, Pitṛs, and serpents, and of Nāgas.
He saw flashes of light like thunderbolts, red clouds, and rainbows;
likewise, comets and meteors emerging from the hosts of luminous bodies;
as well as humans, kinnaras, fish, boars, and birds.
O Bhārata, [he created] elephants, horses, cattle, deer, and wild beasts;
worms, insects, moths, lice, nits, and bedbugs;
all gadflies and mosquitoes, as well as various kinds of stationary beings.
Thus did that god Bhāskara create the three worlds. Whatever kind of karma is proclaimed here for living beings, I shall describe all of that, as well as the sequential order of their birth.
O dear one, elephants, predatory beasts, deer, and various kinds of cattle;
Piśācas, humans, and Rākṣasas—these are born from the womb (jarāyuja);
as well as birds, serpents, crocodiles, fish, and tortoises.
Such are the beings here that are born from land and from water;
those born from moisture, such as gadflies, mosquitoes, lice, nit-eggs, and bedbugs;
and whatever else is of this same nature, which arises through heat.
All stationary beings that sprout from the soil, whether growing from seeds or from stems, are called *udbhijja*.
Herbs (*oṣadhi*) are those that bear various kinds of fruit and perish at the ripening of their fruit.
Those that bear fruit without flowers are known as forest trees (*vanaspati*).
Trees are traditionally held to be of two kinds: those that flower and those that bear fruit;
likewise, there are various types of shrubs and bushes, as well as species of grasses, plants that grow from seeds or from stems, and spreading creepers and climbing vines.
Enveloped by manifold darkness caused by their past actions,
these beings possess internal consciousness and are endowed with pleasure and pain.
O descendant of Kuru, such are the destinies that have arisen.
From that radiant and high-souled god, like the sun,
[all things arise] in this terrible, ever-moving cycle of worldly existence, O dear one.
Having thus created all this, O King, he [became] the supreme teacher of the world.
Having become concealed, that elemental self oppresses time with time;
when that god is awake, then this world moves;
when he, the peaceful-souled one, sleeps, then everything closes its eyes.
O Indra among kings, while that [Supreme Self] sleeps, living beings bound by their karma cease from their respective actions and the mind falls into exhaustion;
yet when they all dissolve simultaneously into that Great Self, [they find rest].
Then, O Bhārata, this Self of all beings sleeps happily;
when, having resorted to darkness, it remains for a long time with its senses,
it does not perform new action and then departs from the body.
When he, having become identified with the ego (ahaṃmātrika), enters the seed— both the stationary and the moving—
in union, he then casts off his form.
Thus, through waking and dreaming, the Lord [creates] this entire world.
The Imperishable One constantly revives and causes destruction;
O dear one, at the beginning of a kalpa he creates, and at the end of the kalpa he withdraws all.
That which is his day, O dear one, is called the end of a kalpa.
Now hear, O Bhārata, the calculation of time for that kalpa:
eighteen nimeṣas of the eye are said to be one kāṣṭhā;
thirty kāṣṭhās they call a kalā, and thirty kalās are known as a kṣaṇa.
Then, the experts in moments (mauhūrtas) say that twelve kṣaṇas constitute one muhūrta;
thirty muhūrtas are designated as a day and night by the wise;
thirty days and nights make a month; and two months each are recorded as a season (ṛtu).
Three seasons constitute an *ayana*, and two *ayanās* make a year.
The sun divides the human and divine day and night:
the night is for the sleep of living beings, and the day is for the performance of actions.
For the ancestors, a month constitutes a day and a night; its division consists of two fortnights.
Among their activities, the dark fortnight is the day and the bright fortnight is the night for sleep.
For the gods, a year constitutes a day and a night; their division is as follows.
O Lord of the Earth, the night of Brahmā is the northern course (udagayana) and his day is the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana). Now,
learn from me the duration of each of the Yugas in their proper sequence.

They say that four thousand years constitute the Kṛta Yuga; its dawn (sandhyā) lasts for as many hundreds of years, and its twilight (sandhyāṃśa) is of the same duration. The wise know the Tretā Yuga to consist of three thousand years.
O Indra among kings, six hundred years each are proclaimed for the dawn and the twilight of the Dvāpara age; however, the wise say that two thousand years constitute the Dvāpara itself,
while four hundred years each are said to be its dawn and twilight.
One thousand years, together with two hundred, were declared for the Tiṣya [age].
O best of kings, this is the number of the entire cycle of four ages (caturyuga) that has been proclaimed;
this very calculation constitutes one caturyuga from the beginning.
This period of twelve thousand [years] is called a *yuga* of the gods; however,
by a count of one thousand such divine *yugas*,
a single day of Brahmā is to be known, and his night is said to be of equal duration.

Those people who know day and night understand that the holy day of Brahmā ends after a thousand such yugas, and his night is of exactly the same duration. Then, at the end of the yuga, he who was asleep awakens.
But once awakened, it emits the mind, which consists of both the existent and the non-existent;
impelled by the desire to create, the mind transforms its own creation, and from that, the vast [element] is born; they know sound to be its quality.

From the transformation of the vast [space], the pure and powerful wind, which carries all fragrances, is born; it is indeed considered to have touch as its quality. From the further transformation of the wind, that which is radiant and dispels darkness [is produced].
It produces variegated rays; the wise know its quality to be form (rūpa).
From that [element] as well, undergoing transformation, water is born, so it is remembered by the learned.
Its quality should be known as taste (rasa), which brings about the nourishment of all the world.
From water arises earth, whose quality is fragrance; such is the creation from the beginning.
That period of twelve thousand years previously described as the Saumanasa Yuga is here called a Manvantara when multiplied by seventy-one.
The Manvantaras, as well as the creation and the dissolution, are indeed innumerable;
nevertheless, O tiger among the Kurus, the fourteen Manus of Brahmā are always enumerated by the wise.
In this world, six other Manu lineages followed that of Svāyambhuva Manu;
those great-souled ones of immense power each created their own respective progeny:
Sāvarṇeya, Pañca-Bhautya, and likewise the other, Raucya.
O best of kings, these seven future Manus have been described;
each, during his own interval, protects all this world of moving and non-moving beings.
Such is a single day of that high-souled Viriñci.
At its conclusion, he brings about creation just as has been described to you;
O lord of men, the Supreme Lord performs this as if in sport.
In the Kṛta age, Dharma is complete in all four quarters, as is Truth.
No acquisition whatsoever occurs for human beings through unrighteousness; rather,
O dear one, descendant of Kuru, acquisitions and righteousness among others proceed in such a manner that they do not decline,
as the blessed Manu has declared.
O King of immeasurable splendor, due to theft, falsehood, and deceit,
dharma indeed declines by one quarter in each successive age beginning with Tretā.
[In that age, people] were free from disease, accomplished in all their aims, and lived for four hundred years.

In the Kṛta, Tretā, and subsequent ages, O joy of the Kurus, the lifespan and the vigor of these mortals diminish by a quarter in each age. The lifespan prescribed in the Vedas and the vitality of mortals,
O dear one, as well as the fruits of their actions, always bear fruit according to the respective yuga.
And likewise, the power of embodied beings bears fruit in this world;
the religious duties of men differ according to the nature of each age— others in the Kṛta Yuga, others in the Tretā and Dvāpara, and others in the Kali Yuga.

Austerity is supreme in the Kṛta age; knowledge is said to be so in the Tretā; sacrifice, they say, is the path in the Dvāpara; and charity alone is the means in the Kali age. O King of great luster, this is for the sake of protecting the entire creation.
He assigned distinct functions to the mouth, the arms, the thighs, and the feet.
He ordained for the Brāhmaṇas teaching, studying, sacrificing, officiating at sacrifices, giving gifts, and receiving gifts.
O King, for the Kṣatriya, there is the protection of subjects, as well as giving, study,
attachment to the objects of the senses, and likewise sacrifice; while for the Vaiśya,
there is the protection of cattle, giving, sacrifice, and study.
Trade, moneylending, and agriculture are the duties of the Vaiśya;
however, only one duty is proclaimed in this world for the Śūdra:
namely, serving these very castes in their proper order.
O best of kings, for a man, the region above the navel is always the most excellent;
even more pure than that, O dear one, is the face of the Self-born.
From that mouth the twice-born was born—such is the Vedic revelation.
O bull of the Kuru lineage, the Brāhmaṇa is the master of this entire dharma by virtue of his very nature;
he was created by Brahmā in the beginning after performing austerities,
for the protection of all— the offerings to the gods, the offerings to the ancestors, and indeed everything else.

The gods consume his sacrificial offerings (havya) with his mouth, and the ancestors likewise consume his ancestral offerings (kavya); what could be superior to that? Among beings, the living creatures are the best; among living creatures, those who live by their intellect are the best.
Among the intelligent, men are considered the best; among men, the Brāhmaṇas;
among Brāhmaṇas, the learned; among the learned, those whose intellects are perfected;
among those with perfected intellects, the performers of duty; and among the performers, those who know Brahman.
O Indra among kings, the birth of a Brahmin is described here as being for the sake of dharma;
once born, O King, he goes to the abode of Brahmā for the sake of attaining all perfections.
And he, while being born, is indeed born here upon this earth.
For the very sake of the prosperity of beings and for the protection of the treasury of Dharma,
everything whatsoever that exists upon the earth belongs to the Brāhmaṇa; indeed,
by virtue of his supreme birth, the Brāhmaṇa deserves all this.
O one of noble vows, the Brāhmaṇa eats his own [portion] and bestows it [upon others];
while he exercises compassion, other people eat as well. Indeed, for the existence or non-existence of the other three castes in this world, the twice-born is the cause.

O King, there is no doubt that when a twice-born man is pleased, he leads to prosperity; when he is angry, he leads to ruin. Therefore, he is indeed most worthy of worship. O King, while a Brāhmaṇa exists, no one else possesses sovereignty.
O best of kings, he performs action out of desire and moves according to his will;
from there he goes to the city of the gods, and from there again to the Maharloka,
and from Maharloka to Janoloka and Brahmaloka.
"O mighty-armed one, a Brahmin attains the status of Brahmā; of this there is no doubt.
Śatānīka said:
"O observer of noble vows, that which is called the status of Brahmā is difficult to attain even within the worlds of Brahmā."
O Brahmin, what is the nature of the state of Brahmahood, and how does one go to the world of Brahmā?
Is a Brahmin merely a matter of name, or is he always the very essence of Brahmā? O Brahmin, tell me: what are the qualities that lead to the attainment of Brahman?
Sumantu said: "Excellent, excellent, O mighty-armed one! Listen to my supreme words regarding those purificatory rites (saṃskāras) for a Brāhmaṇa which have been declared in the Vedic scriptures."
O King, O giver of honor, that man for whom the forty-eight purificatory rites (saṃskāras), beginning with conception (garbhādhāna) and performed according to the scriptures,
have been accomplished, attains the state of Brahman and the status of a Brāhmaṇa.
"Rites of passage (*saṃskāra*) are in every way the cause for the state of being a Brahmin; there is no doubt in this matter.
Śatānīka said: "O Brahmin, what are considered the rites of passage for a Brāhmaṇa regarding his status as a Brahmin?"
"Tell me, O tiger among the twice-born, for my curiosity is great.
Sumantu said: "Excellent, excellent, O mighty-armed one! Listen to my supreme words."
O mighty-armed one, listen in their entirety to all those purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) for a Brāhmaṇa that have been proclaimed by the wise in the Vedic scriptures: namely,
the rite of conception (*garbhādhāna*), the rite for a male child (*puṃsavana*), and likewise the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*).
O King, [the rites are] the birth-ceremony, the first feeding of solid food, the tonsure, and the initiation;
then the four vows of Vedic study, followed by the ceremonial bath,
the union with a lawful wife, and the performance of sacrifices, O giver of honor.
O King, they say that the duty of the five is for the sake of one’s own welfare:
[the service] of the gods, the ancestors, human beings, living creatures, and likewise the Brahmins.
For these, there is indeed the performance of the Aṣṭakā rites and the Parvaṇa Śrāddha.
O King, the Śrāvaṇī, Āgrahāyaṇī, Caitrī, and likewise the Āśvayujī—
the seven pākayajñas— as well as the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādhāna) with due rites,
the agnihotra, and the darśa sacrifice at the waning of the moon.
O king of kings, there are indeed the Paurṇamāsa sacrifice, the Cāturmāsya sacrifices,
the Nirūpaṇa, the animal sacrifice (Paśuvadha), as well as the Sautrāmaṇī;
these are the seven Haviryajñas, and their proper performance is likewise required.
The Agniṣṭoma, the Atirātra, the Ukthya, the Ṣoḍaśin,
the Vājapeya, the Atirātra, and the Āptoryāma—
these seven Soma sacrifices are traditionally known, O scion of the Kuru lineage, as being established among the purificatory rites (saṃskāras).
Thus, O best of kings, these are the forty sacraments for the twice-born;
and now, O dear one, hear also of the eight qualities of the self, O Bhārata:
freedom from malice, compassion, patience, lack of exertion, and auspiciousness.
O best of the Kurus, freedom from miserliness, purity, and lack of longing—
these, O dear one, are the eight qualities proclaimed by the wise. O hero, listen to the definition of each of these in their entirety and without omission.
Not disparaging the virtues of the virtuous, nor praising one's own virtues,
and not rejoicing in the faults of others— this is proclaimed as freedom from envy (*anasūyā*).
Whether toward others, among kinsmen, or toward a friend or an enemy, it is always thus.

That which consists in behaving as one would toward oneself is proclaimed to be compassion (*dayā*). When one neither becomes angry nor feels displeasure in speech, mind, or body, even when provoked by suffering, that is proclaimed to be forbearance (*kṣamā*).
Abstaining from forbidden food, associating with those who are blameless,
and remaining steadfast in right conduct— this is proclaimed as purity.
Even by that auspicious action by which the body is afflicted, [that too is considered pure].

One should not do that to an extreme extent; that is called freedom from exertion. Constant practice of what is praiseworthy and the avoidance of what is blameworthy—this indeed is declared as auspiciousness by the sages who discourse on Brahman.

One should give even a small amount with a heart free from dejection; whatever is given day after day without stinginess is called "non-miserliness. Furthermore, one should be content with whatever has arisen, even if it be a very small thing.
Non-coveting the property of others through non-violence is proclaimed as *aspṛhā*.
One whose body has been refined by these purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) becomes a twice-born (*dvija*);
having attained the state of Brahman in this world, he goes to the realm of Brahmā.

The purifying refinement of the body for the twice-born must be performed through meritorious Vedic rites beginning with the *niṣeka* (conception rite), which brings sanctity both in this world and after death.
Having thereby attained purity of the womb and the dharma characterized by the stages of life (*āśrama*), [one should proceed].
O best of kings, there is no doubt that one attains liberation through this Purāṇa; O tiger among the Kurus, the Brāhmaṇas desire this, and there is no uncertainty here,
especially for those who take refuge [in it] and are always utterers of blessings.
O King, if one abandons Brahmins who are standing nearby and worships other Brahmins instead, the sin resulting from that insult is already accomplished; it cannot even be described.
Therefore, O King, those who are always nearby should be worshipped according to the prescribed rites.
Likewise, one should honor guests by giving them food, drink, and other necessities.
A Brāhmaṇa is the eldest, the best, and likewise the most excellent among all social classes.
Thus, in this Purāṇa, [the author] describes the purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) of a Brāhmaṇa.
Whoever hears it, whoever knows it, and whoever always recites it shall obtain here supernatural power, prosperity, fame, and supreme fortune;
as well as wealth, grain, glory, sons, kinsmen, and a beautiful form.
"Having reached the world of Savitṛ, one shall attain the world of Brahmā.
Thus ends the second chapter in the Brāhma Parvan of the Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, in the Saṃhitā consisting of fifty thousand verses.
Now begins the third chapter.

Śatānīka spoke, requesting a concise description of all the purificatory rites (saṃskāras) beginning from conception, as well as the description of the rules for sipping water (ācamana) and other rituals,
and the purificatory rites such as the birth ceremony (jātakarma) for the social classes (varṇas) in their proper sequence.
"O best of the twice-born, tell me also the dharma of the stages of life (āśramas).
Sumantu said: "The rite for conception (garbhādhāna), the rite for a male child (puṃsavana), and likewise the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana)..."
The birth-rite, the first feeding of solid food, the tonsure,
and the tying of the girdle remove the taints of seed and womb for the twice-born;
[these taints are removed] by Vedic study, by vows, by burnt offerings, by the threefold knowledge, by sacrifice, and by sacred learning.
This body is made Brahmic through the great sacrifices and other rites;
listen with a focused mind, O King, how that body is so made.
Before the cutting of the umbilical cord, the birth-rite (jātakarman) is prescribed for the male child.
And there is the ritual consumption by him of gold, honey, and clarified butter accompanied by mantras.
O King, some desire the naming ceremony on the tenth day;
others, O King, on the twelfth day; and still others when the month is complete.
On the eighteenth day, other wise men likewise say:
"O King, on an auspicious lunar day, at a favorable moment, and under a constellation endowed with excellence,
the auspicious name of the Brahmin, O dear one, shall be Śivaśarman."
For a Kṣatriya, however, it is specifically called Induvarman;
for a Vaiśya, it is joined with *dhana* (wealth); and for a Śūdra, it is contemptible.
For a Vaiśya, it is *Dhanavardhana*, while for one of low birth, it is *Sarvadāsa*.
And Manu has likewise declared the excellent characteristics of names: the name of a Brāhmaṇa should end in *śarman*, that of a Kṣatriya should be endowed with *rakṣas*,
that of a Vaiśya should be joined with *puṣṭi*, and that of a Śūdra should be joined with *preṣya*.

O Indra among kings, on the twelfth day, the child’s departure from the house should be performed with a name for women that is easy to pronounce, not harsh, clear in meaning, and pleasing; it should be auspicious, end in a long vowel, and consist of words of benediction.
O Lord, it is the opinion of others that this should be performed in the fourth month;
the first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana) takes place in the sixth month, according to the auspicious custom of the family.
For all the twice-born, the tonsure ceremony (cūḍākarma) is to be performed in due order.
O joy of the Kurus, it should be performed in the first or the third year;
one should perform the initiation (upanayana) of a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year from conception,
and for a Kṣatriya, O King, one should prescribe it in the eleventh year from conception.
One should prescribe the vow for a Vaiśya in the twelfth year from conception;
it should be performed by a Brāhmaṇa desiring spiritual luster in the fifth year,
and likewise by a Kṣatriya seeking strength in the sixth year.
O joy of the Kurus, for a Vaiśya desiring wealth, [the initiation] should take place in the eighth year;
for a Brāhmaṇa, the Sāvitrī does not expire until the sixteenth year;
for a Kṣatriya, until the twenty-second; and for a Vaiśya, until the twenty-fourth.
But those Kṣatriyas who, after this time, remain uninitiated at the proper age,
are fallen from the Sāvitrī and become Vātyas; and with these impure men, one must never associate even in times of distress, except through the Vrātyastoma sacrifice.
One should cultivate a relationship through marriage and kinship with Brāhmaṇas.
O King, there are three kinds of skins for those observing vows:
those of the black antelope, the Ruru deer, and the goat, belonging respectively to the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, and the Vaiśya, O ruler of men.
O King, they should also gradually provide various garments— namely,
those made of hemp, linen, and so forth— for the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas.
The girdle of a Brahmin should be made of Muñja grass, triple-stranded, even, and smooth.
The bowstring of a Kṣatriya should be made of mūrvā fiber, and that of a Vaiśya of hemp fibers.
In the absence of Muñja grass, however, it should be made from Kuśa, Aśmantaka, or Balvaja grass;
it should be triple-stranded and provided with one, three, or five knots.
The sacred thread (*upavīta*) of a Brāhmaṇa should be made of cotton, twisted upwards and triple-stranded;
that of a Kṣatriya should consist of hempen threads, and that of a Vaiśya of woolen threads. Furthermore, their loops (*puṣkara*) likewise become threefold.
O King, for a Brāhmaṇa, [staffs] made of bilva and palāśa wood are prescribed, and the third is that born from the plakṣa tree;
for a Kṣatriya, those of vāṭa and khadira, as well as another made from vetasa;
and for a Vaiśya, those of pīlu and udumbara, as indeed also that born from the aśvattha tree.
O mighty-armed one, these staffs deserve to be carried according to dharma:
the staff of a Brāhmaṇa should be measured so as to reach the hairline;
that of a Kṣatriya should reach the forehead; and that of a Vaiśya should reach the tip of the nose.
All those Brahmins should be upright and gentle in appearance;
they should not cause distress to people, should have unblemished skin, and should not be scarred by fire.
Having taken up their desired staffs and having stood facing the sun, [they should proceed].
Having duly honored the preceptor, he should practice begging for alms according to the prescribed rule.
An initiated member of the highest twice-born class (the Brāhmaṇa) should practice begging by placing the word "bhavat" at the beginning;
a Kṣatriya should place it in the middle, and a Vaiśya should place it at the end.
He should first beg for alms from his mother, or his sister, or his own maternal aunt— whichever among these will not treat him with contempt. She shall place gold, silver, or food into his bowl.
Then, having collected as much almsfood as required without guile, he should offer it to his guru; then, having sipped water (ācamana) and being pure, he should eat while facing the east.
One who eats facing the east gains longevity; one who eats facing the south gains fame.
Facing west, he eats for the sake of prosperity; facing north, he eats for the sake of truth.
Having sipped water, O King, the twice-born man should eat his food with a concentrated mind.
After eating, he should properly sip water again and touch the cavities of his head with water.
In this manner, one should always honor the food and eat it without disparaging it;
O Bhārata, one should indeed rejoice at the sight of it and be gratified by it.
Having welcomed it, one should then eat; thus Manu has declared.
Food that is always honored bestows strength and vigor;
however, when eaten without being honored, it destroys both. One should not give the remnants of one's meal to anyone, nor should one eat between the prescribed meals.
O best of kings, that man who, out of greed, eats food by placing another person in between goes to destruction both in this world and in the next;
just as there was formerly a Vaiśya known by the name Dhanavardhana.
Śatānīka said:
O best of the twice-born, how did that interval regarding food first come about?
What is the nature of that interval of food, and how was it brought about?
Sumantu said: O King, in former times, during the Kṛta Yuga, there lived in Puṣkara a Vaiśya named Dhanavardhana,
who was prosperous in wealth and grain.
O Indra among kings, having performed the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice during the summer season,
he partakes of a meal consisting of various kinds of hard and soft foods together with his sons, brothers, friends, and kinsmen, O King.
Then, O tiger among the Kurus, as he was eating that food, a great and piteous sound arose; thereupon,
abandoning his meal, he rushed out from the house.
Then, O King, when the sound had vanished, he returned home;
taking that very vessel,
O mighty-armed one, he took his meal, eating the food that remained after [the previous guest] had eaten.
Having eaten, O King, he was born again in a hundred ways at that very moment.
Therefore, O Indra among kings, one should never eat food between [meals],
nor should one overeat, nor should one ever go anywhere while still impure from food.
From overeating, one becomes attached to taste; from attachment to taste, disease arises.
O bull of the Bharatas, when such attachment to taste has arisen, bathing, giving gifts, recitation, fire-offerings, and the worship of ancestors and gods no longer bear fruit for men.

Excessive eating is detrimental to health, longevity, and the attainment of heaven; it is meritless and loathed by the world. Therefore, one should avoid it, O best of kings, for it belongs to the yakṣas, bhūtas, piśācas, and rākṣasas.
O Brahmin, one who is impure becomes unfit for social interaction; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, one should maintain purity, for through purity one rejoices in the higher realms (diti) and delights here in this world with happiness—such is the Vedic revelation.
Śatānīka said:
"O Brahmin, how does one attain purity, and how does one attain impurity? Tell me this, O best of Brahmins; it is my greatest curiosity."
Sumantu said: "O bull of the Bharatas, by performing the ritual sipping of water (upaspṛśya), a Brahmin becomes pure;
O tiger among the Kurus, he should therefore be devoted to the prescribed rules and act according to them."
Śatānīka said: O Brahmin, tell me the entire procedure for ritual sipping (upasparśa),
by which a twice-born Brāhmaṇa, having performed the ācamana, attains purity.
Sumantu said:
"Well asked, O Indra among kings! Listen, O Brahmin, tiger among the Bharatas, to how one may become pure according to the prescribed rule, O Lord."
Having washed his hands and feet, facing either east or north,
he should sit in a clean place, O mighty-armed one, placing his right arm between his knees and wearing the sacred thread (brahmasūtra).
Having made his two feet perfectly even and likewise having tied his topknot, O King,
he should not stand, nor engage in conversation, nor look about;
nor should he hurry, nor be angry, having left [the place] at a great distance, O King.
Having sipped clear water, one attains purity;
not with water that is hot, nor frothy, nor turbid,
nor lacking in color, taste, and smell, O Bhārata.
O King, a wise man should likewise not rinse his mouth with water containing bubbles.
O giver of honor, it is heard that there are five sacred sites (*tīrthas*) on the right hand of a Brahmin:
the site of the gods (*devatīrtha*), the site of the ancestors (*pitṛtīrtha*), and the site of Brahmā (*brahmatīrtha*).
Likewise, another is called *prājāpatya*, and another is called *saumya*.
O Lord of the Earth, that line which is found above the base of the thumb—
Vasiṣṭha and other foremost of the twice-born declare this to be the *brāhma* tīrtha.
The *kāyatīrtha* is at the base of the little finger; the *daivata* at the tips of the fingers;
the *pitrya* is said to be between the index finger and the thumb;
and the *saumya* is situated in the middle of the palm, which is recommended for rites dedicated to the gods.
O best of the Kuru lineage, one should perform the worship of the gods, the offering of bali,
and the scattering [of food] using the *devatīrtha*;
likewise, O King, the distribution of food and the sipping of water (*ācamana*), O ruler of men.

O gentle one, O king of kings, a wise man should always perform the oblation of parched grain (lājāhoma) and the rite for Prajāpati; likewise, he should always perform the touching of the water-pot (kamaṇḍalu-upasparśana) and the consumption of curd (dadhi-prāśana) using the Saumya-tīrtha.
The wise man should perform the libation for the ancestors using the *pitṛ-tīrtha*;
he may also use the *brāhma-tīrtha*, though contact with it is considered secondary.
Having joined his fingers closely together, the twice-born man, one-pointed and well-disposed, [should proceed].
Listen to the fruit that one obtains and how he gratifies the gods, who drinks water three times while avoiding the sound of his mouth:
by the first draught of water he satisfies the *Ṛgveda*.
O Bhārata, that which is the second [wipe] is the Yajurveda; by it he gratifies [the gods].
O Bhārata, that which is the third is the Sāmaveda; by it he gratifies [the gods].
That first wipe which he makes on the mouth from the base of the right thumb—
O King, there is no doubt that the Atharvaveda brings satisfaction through this;
for the twice-born man cleanses that which is the second [part],
and indeed, O Indra among kings, he consecrates that which is the head.
By touching the tuft of hair (śikhā), one indeed pleases Rudra;
by touching the two eyes, one indeed pleases the Sun (Ravi).
By touching the nose, one certainly pleases Vāyu—of this there is no doubt.
When a Brahmin touches his ear, he indeed pleases the quarters;
when he touches his arm, he indeed pleases Yama, Kubera, Varuṇa, Vāsava, and Agni.
"O King of kings, by touching the navel and the knot of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*), one gratifies [the deity]; such is the Vedic revelation (*śruti*).
By sprinkling water upon his feet, one indeed gratifies Viṣṇu."
O giver of honor, descendant of Bharata, by releasing the water that covers the earth, he gratifies the Nāgas headed by Vāsuki;
and those drops which fall here upon the surface of the earth, O lord of men, [gratify the ancestors].
Then, O King, one should gratify the fourfold collection of beings here;
one should touch the eyes with the thumb and the forefinger, O King,
and one should touch the nose with the ring finger and the thumb, O King.
O bull among the Bharatas, one should touch the mouth with the middle finger and the thumb;
O King, one touches the ears with the little finger and the thumb;
likewise, one touches the arms with all the fingers, and the auspicious [forehead] with the thumb.
O best of the Kuru lineage, one should touch the navel with all the fingers together, and the head likewise;
O mighty-armed one, the thumb is said to be Agni, the forefinger Vāyu,
the ring finger Sūrya, and the little finger Mādhava, O Lord.
O best of the Bharatas, Prajāpati is to be known as the middle [sip]; therefore, O dear one,
by sipping water in this manner, a Brahmin constantly gratifies the entire world,
all the deities, and even the worlds themselves— of this there is no doubt.

Therefore, a Brahmin is always to be honored, for he embodies all the gods. He should constantly perform his ritual sipping (upaspṛśet) using the Brāhma or the Vipra-tīrtha, never using the Kāya, Traidaśika, or Pitrya tīrthas.
A Brahmin is purified by water reaching the heart; a Kshatriya, by water reaching the throat;
a Vaishya, by water that is merely sipped; and a Shudra, by water touched at the extremity [of the lips].
When the right hand is raised, one is called a wise man wearing the sacred thread (upavītin).

Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī) with the left hand, and then wearing it around the neck (nivītī), the knower of the mantras should discard the girdle, the antelope skin, the staff, the sacrificial thread,
and the water-pot when they are worn out, saying "May they be [discarded]," and take up others.
O Lord of the Earth, one should always sip water while wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder and with the hands between the knees.
O Bhārata, it is in this manner that a Brahmin, having sipped water, attains purity.
Furthermore, O Bhārata, regarding those lines which are found in the middle of a Brahmin’s palm—
O best of the Bharatas, know that all the rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā are present there;
and know indeed that the mountains are the joints upon the fingers.
O King, the right hand of a Brahmin is composed of all the gods.
The ritual for sipping water with the hands has been declared to you, O Lord of the Earth;
by performing this rite in all these worlds, one shall go to heaven.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for Sipping Water," in the Brāhma Parvan of the Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty thousand verses.
Now begins the fourth chapter, containing the description of the meaning of the *praṇava*, the majesty of the *sāvitrī*, and the rules for the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*). Sumantu said:
"The tonsure ceremony (*keśānta*) is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa in his sixteenth year."
O Lord of the Earth, for a kṣatriya the tonsure ceremony should always be performed without mantras at the twenty-second year, and for a vaiśya three years after that; likewise, for women,
it should be performed at the appropriate time according to their respective divisions, for the sake of purifying the body.
The marriage rite for women is recorded in the sacred scriptures as their consecration (saṃskāra).
Alternatively, she may reside either with her teacher or in her own home while performing the fire-rituals.
Thus, O King, has this procedure for the initiation ceremony been described to you.
O mighty-armed one, he is the supreme indicator of the origin of the twice-born.
Now, O one of great strength, I shall describe to you the yoga of action:
having initiated the disciple, the teacher should first instruct him in purity.
Having sipped water according to the rules (ācamana),

facing north, and with hands joined in the Brahmāñjali gesture, he who has conquered his senses should always teach good disciples the conduct, the fire-ritual (agnikārya), and the twilight worship (sandhyopāsana). He should be taught [the Veda] while maintaining this posture.

Wearing light clothing, with a one-pointed mind, cheerful and well-composed, one should always worship the feet of the teacher at both the beginning and the conclusion of the Vedic recitation. One should study with hands joined together; this, indeed, is known as the *brahmāñjali*.
The clasping of the teacher’s feet should be performed with crossed hands:
the left foot is to be touched with the left hand, and the right foot with the right hand.
Furthermore, the teacher, always remaining vigilant, [should address] the student who is about to study.
One should say, "Please teach, sir," and one should signal the end by saying, "May there be a pause.
One should always utter the Praṇava (Oṃ) at the beginning and at the end of the Veda;
for that which is not preceded by Oṃ flows away, and that which is not followed by it falls apart.
Listen also, O Indra among kings, as to how a twice-born man is entitled to the syllable Om:
seated upon grass-blades with their tips pointing eastward, purified by sacred purifiers (pavitra),
and cleansed by three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), he then becomes worthy of the syllable Om.

And listen also, O joy of the Kurus, to the characteristics of the syllable *oṃ*. Having extracted the letters *a*, *u*, and *m* from the three Vedas, as well as the words *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svaḥ*, Prajāpati [formed it].

From the three Vedas alone, Parameṣṭhin Prajāpati milked out foot by foot that syllable "tat" of this Sāvitrī verse. Reciting this syllable and this [verse] preceded by the vyāhṛtis, one attains success.
By performing the two twilights, a Brahmin is joined with merit;
but by practicing this triad outside [the village] a thousand times,
a twice-born man is released from even great sin within a month, like a snake from its skin.
Deprived of this *ṛc* and of his own timely ritual action,
one born of the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, or Vaiśya castes incurs censure among the virtuous.
Listen with a focused mind, O King, to the supreme mouth of Brahman.
The three imperishable Great Utterances preceded by the syllable *Oṃ*,
together with the three-footed *Sāvitrī*, should be known as the mouth of Brahman.
He who studies these daily for three years without indolence [attains that goal].
Becoming like the wind and possessing the form of space, he attains the supreme Brahman;
O scorcher of foes, prāṇāyāma is the supreme single syllable Brahman.
There is nothing higher than the Sāvitrī, and truth excels silence.

O King, the performance of austerity, the performance of fire-offerings, and likewise the performance of giving are always inexhaustible in their results, O Rājanya, just as the Blessed Manu has said:
"The Imperishable (Akṣara) is to be known as the lower, and Brahmā as Prajāpati."

O King, O best of monarchs, the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña) always excels the ritual sacrifice (vidhiyajña) due to its various described qualities that are subtle in nature. It is traditionally held that the physical sacrifice is worth a hundred thousandfold, while the mental sacrifice is worth a thousandfold.

The four types of cooked sacrifices (pākayajña), together with those performed according to ritual injunctions (vidhiyajña)—all these are not worth even a sixteenth part of the sacrifice of silent recitation (japayajña). Through recitation alone a Brahmin attains perfection; there is no doubt in this matter.

Whether he performs other rites or does not perform them, a Brahmin who is friendly toward all is so called. He should stand reciting the Sāvitrī during the morning twilight until the sun appears; but during the evening twilight, he should remain seated until the stars are clearly visible.
At the beginning of the day there is the former [sandhyā], and likewise at the beginning of the night there is the latter.
The latter is to be known as that which possesses the stars; the former is that which possesses the sun.
Standing and reciting during the latter sandhyā, one destroys the sin committed during the night.

But by sitting for the latter [prayer], one destroys the impurity created during the day. O King, he who does not attend the morning prayer and does not perform the evening worship should be excluded from all the duties of the twice-born, like a Śūdra.
Restrained and composed, O King, one should go to the forest and, established in the daily rule, recite even the Sāvitrī near water; likewise,
one should engage in the study of the Vedas and the daily recitation of the sacred texts.
O Lord, there is no fault here regarding the *anadhyāya* days for those performing oblations or reciting mantras;
for in the daily rites (*nityaka*), there is no *anadhyāya*, since that is performed as a "Brahma-sacrifice.
It is nourishing when offered with the oblation of the Veda, even if it is accompanied by the *vaṣaṭ* call on a day of *anadhyāya*.
If a twice-born man, being self-restrained, studies even a single verse according to the prescribed rule,
this [study] constantly yields for him pure milk, clarified butter, and honey.
He should perform service to the sacred fire, live on alms, and sleep on the ground, which is beneficial to his teacher.
A twice-born man who has undergone initiation should, until his formal return home (from Vedic study),
perform service to the son of his teacher— provided he is a giver of knowledge, righteous, pure,
trustworthy, capable, generous, virtuous, and devoted to the study of his own Veda; these ten are to be taught according to the Dharma.
One should not speak to anyone unless asked, nor to one who asks in an improper manner;
for even if he knows the truth, a wise man should conduct himself among the world like one who is dull-witted.
He who speaks unrighteously and he who asks unrighteously—[both are at fault].
One of those two will perish or fall into enmity,
where neither dharma nor artha exists, nor even such service as that;
there knowledge should not be sown, just as good seed is not sown in barren soil.
A knower of Brahman should die together with his knowledge alone;
even in the midst of terrible calamity, he must never sow it in barren soil.
Knowledge says to the Brahmin: "I am your treasure; protect me."
"Do not give this to one who is censorious; in that way, I shall become most powerful.
Some here desire only worldly pleasure and happiness, while others declare it to be knowledge.
Because he indeed maintains both of these, he is therefore called a *śevadhi* (a treasure-house)."
But speak of me to that Brahmin whom you know to be pure, self-restrained, and a celibate student— a guardian of the treasure who is free from negligence.
For he who should obtain the Veda from one who recites it without having been authorized to do so, [incurs sin].
Whether it be worldly, Vedic, or even pertaining to the inner self (adhyātmika),
he goes to the terrible Raurava hell, which is fearsome to behold.
The body, consisting of the subtle essence, is traditionally known as "half of sixteen" (the sixteen-fold subtle body).
One should first salute him from whom one receives knowledge.
A Brahmin who is well-restrained is better, even if he knows only the essence of the Sāvitrī,
than one who is unrestrained, even if he knows the three Vedas, eats all kinds of food, and sells all kinds of goods.
One should not occupy a bed or seat frequented by a superior;
rather, while remaining on one's own bed or seat, one should rise to meet him and offer salutation.
For the vital breaths of a young man rise upward when an elder approaches.

By rising to greet them and by saluting them, one regains those very qualities. For one who is habitually inclined to salutation and who constantly serves the elders, four things increase correctly: lifespan, wisdom, fame, and strength.
A Brahmin intent on respectful salutation should greet one who is senior, proclaiming his own name, saying: "I am so-and-so by name.
For those who do not understand the proper form of greeting when a name is mentioned, [one should say: "I salute you."
A wise man should address all those people and likewise all women as "I am so-and-so.
At the end of one's own name when offering a salutation, he should utter the word "bhoḥ. For the sages have declared that the word "bhoḥ" represents the essential nature of a name.
When greeting a Brahmin, one should say, "May you be long-lived, O gentle one.
At the end of his name, the initial vowel should be pronounced with a protracted (pluta) accent.
A Brahmin who does not know how to respond to a greeting [is considered as one who has not been properly greeted].
He is not to be saluted by a learned man; he is exactly like a Śūdra.
O tiger among the Kurus, he who does not return a greeting when one has been offered fails to bestow a blessing and certainly goes to hell.
"Abhi," says the Blessed One Viṣṇu; "Ārvādayāmi," says Śaṅkara. Thus, by one who performs the salutation, both [deities] are indeed worshipped.
One should ask a Brāhmaṇa about his welfare (*kuśala*) and a member of the Kṣatriya caste about his health (*anāmaya*).
Having approached a Vaiśya, one should inquire after his welfare (*kṣema*); however, toward a Śūdra, one should inquire only after his health (*ārogya*).
A consecrated person (*dīkṣita*), even if he be younger, must not be addressed by name;
rather, he should be addressed with the words "Bho" or "Bhavat" placed first—thus Svāyambhuva declared.
But as for another's wife, O King, who is not related by birth,
she should be addressed simply as "lady" (bhavatī) or "fortunate one" (subhage), or even "sister" (bhaginī).
[One should likewise address] paternal uncles, maternal uncles, O King, fathers-in-law, officiating priests, and gurus.
The younger brother should rise and say, "I am so-and-so.
A mother’s sister, a maternal uncle’s wife, a mother-in-law, and a father’s sister are to be honored; they are equal to the wife of one's guru, for they are all like the guru’s own wife.

O King, a Brahmin who, being self-restrained, honors day after day the wife of his elder brother of the same caste, goes to the abode of Viṣṇu. Upon returning from a journey, one should honor the women of one's kinsmen and relatives.
O King,

O lord of the people, O best of the Bharatas, descendant of the Kuru lineage, one should always behave toward a father’s sister, a mother’s sister, and one’s own elder sister as toward one’s own mother.
Therefore, O lord of men, a mother is to be known as more venerable than those two;
indeed, sons, friends, and nephews should be regarded as equal to oneself. Friendship among citizens lasts for ten years, while that among artists lasts for five years.
Among those learned in the Vedas,
even one who is a hundred years old is considered a son by one of ten years, provided he is of the same lineage; yet among these two, the Brāhmaṇa is the father.

Thus, the wise have declared that even for a Vaiśya, a Kṣatriya may be his father, and for a Śūdra, he may be his grandfather and great-grandfather. Wealth, kinship, age, ritual action, and learning as the fifth— these [are the bases of respect].
These are the grounds for respect, each subsequent one being weightier than the preceding;
among the five classes, those who possess more of these qualities and are superior in virtue deserve honor here, even a Śūdra who has reached the tenth decade of life.
The way must be yielded to one who holds a wheel, to one who stands in his tenth decade, to the sick, to one burdened with a load, to a woman, to a *snātaka*, to a king, and to a bridegroom.
O dear one, when these meet, the *snātaka* and the king are to be honored.
O King, upon the union of these two, the Snātaka receives honor from the monarch.

That twice-born man who, having performed the initiation (upanayana), teaches a disciple the Veda along with its secret doctrines (rahasya) and its ritual manuals (kalpa), O best of the Bharatas, [is entitled to such honor].
O mighty-armed one, the wise declare him to be an *ācārya*. But he who teaches even a single portion of the Veda, or even the Vedāṅgas, for the sake of his livelihood, is called an *upādhyāya*.
O best of kings, that brahmin who performs the rites beginning with the impregnation ceremony (niṣeka),
and who teaches [the Veda] by means of another, is called a guru.
[He also performs] the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya), the domestic sacrifices (pākayajña), and the great sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma.
He who performs the rites for one who has chosen him is called that person's officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) here.
He who truly fills both ears with the Veda is to be known as both mother and father; one should never act treacherously toward him.
Ten preceptors equal one teacher; a father exceeds a hundred teachers in honor;
a mother exceeds a thousand fathers in honor.
Between the biological progenitor and the giver of the Veda, the father who gives the Veda is the more venerable.
For the birth of a Brahmin from the Veda is eternal both in this world and after death.
One should understand that his birth from his mother and father, when they procreate him through mutual desire, is merely his physical origin within a womb.

The teacher, who has mastered the Vedas, produces that birth for him through the Sāvitrī; it is true, and it is free from old age and death. Those who are said by you to be worthy of worship, beginning with the sub-teacher (upādhyāya), [are now described].

O mighty-armed one, he is remembered as the great preceptor, superior to all; this is the opinion that he is equivalent to a hundred thousand teachers. He is called the great preceptor for all four castes.
Śatānīka said:
"All these twice-born ones whom you have mentioned, beginning with the preceptor, are indeed already known to me; however, he alone is my great guru."
Sumantu said:
"The Brahmin who subsists on [teaching] victory is called a great preceptor (mahāguru).
[He knows] the eighteen Purāṇas as well as the life-story of Rāma."
O Bhārata, O lord of the earth, there are the Viṣṇu-dharma and other religious systems, as well as the Śiva-dharma;
and that which is known as the Mahābhārata is the fifth Veda belonging to Kṛṣṇa.
Furthermore, O king of kings, there are the Śrauta dharmas spoken by Nārada.
The wise proclaim "Jaya" as their name;
thus, he who upholds this assembly of Brahmins is remembered as the most excellent.
He who here finds all these Purāṇas [is likewise so honored].
O mighty-armed one, that Bhārata is considered by men to be omniscient;
therefore, O Indra among kings, it should always be honored by the castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas.
Have you not heard the words spoken by the all-pervading Blessed Lord?
One who benefits another with even a little or much of what has been heard should be known here as a teacher (guru) by virtue of that service through sacred learning;
likewise is he who effects one's birth into the Vedic lineage and is the instructor of one's own duty.
"Even a young Brahmin becomes the father of an elder according to dharma.
The child Kavi, the son of Aṅgiras, taught his ancestors;
having embraced them with knowledge, he said, 'O my sons!'"
With their anger aroused, they questioned the gods about that matter.
And the gods, having assembled, said to them: "What the child has said is indeed just.
For a boy is truly ignorant, while he who imparts the sacred mantras is a father."
They say that the ignorant one is a "child," but they call the giver of mantras "Father.
They said, "O Grandfather," and "Victory-giver" to him; thus the gods spoke.
Victory, the mantras, and likewise the Vedas—these three are the single body divided into three parts.
"Neither by bathing, nor by grey hair, nor by friends, nor by kinsmen did the seers establish dharma; he who is learned in the Vedas is great to us,
O lord of the people, among the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras."
O Indra among kings, listen indeed to how they honor the eldest:
