according to knowledge, heroism, wealth, birth, and likewise according to character—
those who are preeminent in these respects are considered by me to be the foremost.
One does not become an elder merely because one's head is gray;
rather, even if he is young, the gods recognize him as an elder who is truly learned.
As is an elephant made of wood, or a deer made of leather, so is one who possesses learning but lacks conduct.
And that brahmin who has not studied— these three merely bear the name [of their kind].
Just as a woman who bears no fruit is among women, as a cow who yields no milk is among cows,
as a gift given to an ignorant man is fruitless, so too is a brahmin who knows no Ṛgveda verses fruitless.
Those who are devoid of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice and shunned by the rites of hospitality—
though they have acquired the Vedas, all such twice-born men are to be known as Śūdras.
One does not become a Brāhmaṇa by the Ṛgveda alone, nor by being a merchant, nor by being an actor.
A Śūdra who performs service, one who is not a thief, and one who is not a physician—
wherever such twice-born men live as those who do not observe vows, do not study the Vedas, and subsist on alms,
the king should punish that village; for it provides sustenance to thieves.

O descendant of Kuru, wherever a Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires is indeed contented, there the Vedas attain fulfillment; for thus it has been spoken by the gods. O hero, this is exactly as stated in the Vedas regarding the approach to the Eldest of the Gods.
The Brahmins tremble on the ground and practice their recitations without fire;
why do those fools suffer in this way, desiring the fruits of actions that are devoid of actual performance while they practice upon the earth?
"O Lord, affliction alone is the fruit of our practice, not anything else;
O Supreme God, our constant practice is for Your sake.
Thus, O tiger among kings, the Vedas spoke to the Creator.
Therefore, after the study of the Vedas, the performance of ritual practice is considered supreme.
Whatever four or even three who have mastered the Vedas may declare—
that should be known as Dharma, and not that of thousands of others.
Whatever those deluded by darkness, fools who do not know the Dharma, speak— that sin becomes a hundredfold and follows after the speakers themselves.
[This applies] to a Brahmin devoid of purity, fallen from his vows, and abandoned by the Vedas.
"O King,

descendant of Bharata, when food was being given to one who lived by recitation and he saw his own self [as the recipient], he raised his hands and danced, crying out, 'What evil deed have I committed!'"
When a Brahmin endowed with both knowledge and austerity arrives at one's home,
all the medicinal herbs rejoice, thinking, "We shall go to the supreme goal.
O Bhārata, [this is true] even for those who have not observed vows, who lack mantras, and who do not recite prayers.
One should not accept gifts, nor does one gift cross over by means of another gift.
Oblations to the gods and ancestors must always be given only to one learned in the Vedas;
when given to one who is not learned in the Vedas, they reach neither the ancestors nor the deities.

Whether a fool resides in one’s own house or a man of great learning lives far away, the gift should be given to the man of great learning; there is no bypassing of the learned. There is no bypassing of a Brahmin who is a fool only so long as he is devoid of recitation.
For one does not offer oblations into ashes after setting aside a blazing fire;
nor do the ancestors and the deities consider it so,
whether a Brahmin possesses qualities or is devoid of them, for he is the supreme deity.
One should not bypass a Brāhmaṇa seated in his house while he is engaged in his priestly duties;
by bypassing him, O mighty-armed Bhārata, one goes to the Raurava hell.
Even a Brāhmaṇa whose essence consists of nothing more than the Gāyatrī has attained a state worthy of honor.
One who dwells excessively near a household does not become fallen;
however, a village devoid of grain, a well without water,
and a Brahmin who has not studied— these three are merely bearers of names.
But if one gives unequally at a single row [of guests] out of affection, fear, or for the sake of wealth—
the sages declare that act to be equivalent to the killing of a Brahmin, as seen in the Vedas and sung by the seers.
By non-violence alone toward all beings should the teaching of what is beneficial be practiced.
One who desires to attain dharma should employ speech that is sweet and gentle;
O Bhārata, he whose speech and mind are pure and protected by truth indeed attains the entire fruit taught in the Vedānta.
One should not be a wounder of others, even when afflicted; one should not have a mind intent on deeds that harm others.
One should not utter that speech by which the world is provoked to resentment. That which is spoken by the wise through speech is auspicious.
Listen, O tiger among the Kurus, and always speak likewise:
neither the moon, nor water, nor sandalwood paste,
nor cool shade gladdens a person as much as speech that speaks sweetly.
A Brahmin should always tremble at honor as if it were poison;
he should always long for contempt as if it were nectar.
For one who is held in contempt sleeps in happiness and wakes in happiness.
One who treats others with contempt perishes in this world;
yet, O King, a twice-born man whose self is refined by this method,
dwelling with his teacher, should gradually accumulate this austerity for the attainment of Brahman.
The entire Veda, along with its secret portions, must be mastered by the twice-born through various specific austerities and diverse prescribed vows.
The best of the twice-born should constantly practice the Veda itself as his austerity.

Indeed, the study of the Vedas is said here to be the supreme austerity for a Brahmin. That twice-born man who, even while sleeping, recites his own portion of the Veda daily to the best of his ability, truly performs the highest austerity down to the very tips of his nails.
The twice-born who, without having studied the Veda, exerts himself in other pursuits,
quickly falls to the status of a Śūdra while still living, along with his lineage—
O Lord of the People, he who possesses neither the Veda, nor the muttering of prayers, nor sacred knowledge.
"The Lord, the All-pervading One, has declared that he must be considered a Śūdra alone.
Birth from the mother is the first; the second is the tying of the girdle of Muñja grass;
and the third is the initiation for sacrifice—this is the rule proclaimed for the twice-born."
In that stage where his Brahman-birth is marked by the tying of the girdle of muñja grass,
Sāvitrī is said to be his mother and the Ācārya his father;
for Manu has declared that the Ācārya is his father because of the imparting of the Veda.
Indeed, no ritual action whatsoever exists for him prior to the binding of the girdle of muñja grass;
nor should he utter the Veda, except for the offering of the *svadhā* oblation.
He remains equal to a Śūdra as long as he is not born into the Veda.
For one who has undergone the initiation ceremony (upanayana), the instruction in the observances (vratādeśana) is prescribed,
as well as the sequential acquisition of the Veda according to the rules;
likewise, whatever sacred thread (sūtra), skin (carma), and girdle (mekhalā) he possesses.
Furthermore, whatever punishment is prescribed for wearing clothes [inappropriately], that indeed applies to him even regarding his vows.
While living with his teacher as a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī), he should observe these restraints,
fully controlling the collection of his senses for the sake of increasing his own austerity.
O mighty-armed one, having bathed with diligence, one should indeed perform the libation (tarpaṇa) for the gods, the ancestors,
and men; as well as [offer] flowers, water, fruit, and the placing of sacrificial fuel.
He should avoid various kinds of wood, as well as clay and *kuśa* grass;
he should avoid honey, meat, perfumes, garlands, vehicles, women,
all white objects, and the harming of living beings.
Anointing the body, applying collyrium to the eyes, wearing shoes, carrying an umbrella,
forming intentions born of desire, anger, greed, singing,
playing musical instruments, dancing, as well as gambling, idle gossip, and falsehood;
O Lord, one should avoid slander from afar;
likewise, O joy of the Kurus, one should not gaze upon or touch the wives of others, nor wear another's sacred thread, and one should not associate with unchaste women.
One should always sleep alone and never let semen spill;
for by spilling semen out of desire, one indeed destroys his vow.
A twice-born student who emits semen while sleeping unintentionally [must perform penance].
Having bathed and worshipped the Sun, one should then mutter the verse beginning with "punar mām.
Furthermore, the supreme word of Manu is heard in this regard:
[one should provide] a water-pot, flowers, cow-dung, earth, and *kuśa* grass.
One should indeed always collect as much alms as is required;
O best of kings, hear from me about those households from which it should be taken—
those who are devoted to their own duties and likewise devoted to the Vedas.
O Indra among kings, those who are devoted to sacrifices and established in faith,
as well as celibate students, should daily collect alms from houses with self-restraint;
however, one should not beg for alms within the family of one's teacher, nor among one's own paternal kinsmen or maternal relatives.
If those of other lineages are not available, one should avoid each preceding one in turn.

If even those previously mentioned are unavailable, O mighty-armed one, one may wander through the entire village, excluding only the lowest castes; thus spoke the Blessed Lord, the All-pervading One.
Restraining his speech and remaining self-controlled, he should avoid fire and weapons.
O descendant of Kuru, he should wander for alms among the four castes; if nothing is obtained, he may collect sacrificial fuel from afar and place it above the house.
One should, however, unweariedly offer oblations into the fire with those [verses] every morning and evening; but if,
without having gone out for alms, one fails to kindle that fire while not being ill for seven nights, one must perform the penance of an *avakīrṇin*.
The wise declare that his livelihood should be by means of alms;
therefore, a renunciant should always subsist on alms and must not eat the food of a single person. For one observing the vow, subsistence through alms is considered equal to fasting.
O King, at a rite for the gods one should eat like one observing a vow, and at a rite for the ancestors like a seer;
if invited, one may eat at will, and his vow is not thereby violated.
O mighty-armed one, this is the duty that has been proclaimed for a Brāhmaṇa.
O descendant of Kuru, the wise have declared that this [duty] applies to both the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya:
whether urged by the teacher or not,
he should always apply himself to his studies and to the welfare of his preceptor.
Having restrained the organs of perception along with the mind, as well as the body and speech,
he should stand with palms joined in reverence, gazing at the face of his teacher.
He should always keep his right hand uplifted, maintain virtuous conduct, and remain self-controlled.
When told, "Be seated," he should sit facing the teacher. In the presence of the teacher, he should be deficient in his dress, ornaments, and food.
He should rise before him and be the last to lie down.
One lying on a bed should not engage in replying or conversation;
nor should one do so while sitting, eating, standing, or with one's face turned away. One should stand when responding to one who is seated, and go toward him when responding to one who stands.
He should go out to meet one who is coming, run after one who is walking,
stand facing one who has his back turned, and approach one who is at a distance;
having paid homage to one who is lying down, he should always remain at his command.
In the presence of his teacher, he should always use a low bed and seat;
within the range of the teacher's vision, he should not sit as he pleases. O observer of noble vows, he should never utter the teacher’s name even when he is out of sight.
One should not imitate him in his gait, speech, or gestures.
Where there is gossip or disparagement of the guru,
one should cover one's ears or depart from that place to another.
One who utters slander becomes a donkey; a reviler, a dog;
one who consumes another's property becomes a worm; and one who is envious becomes an insect. One should not worship him while standing at a distance, nor when angry, nor in the presence of a woman.
O King, one should descend from a vehicle or seat to offer salutation. One should not sit together with a guru on an equal or opposing seat.
O King, when the guru is not listening, one should not speak anything at all.
He should sit together with his teacher on vehicles drawn by oxen, horses, or camels, on palanquins, on stone slabs, on mats, on rocks, on wooden planks, or in boats.
When the teacher’s own teacher is present, he should behave toward him as he would toward his own teacher.
Among the teacher’s sons who are noble, and among the teacher’s own kinsmen— even if they are younger,
of equal age, or superior in sacrificial rites—
the son of the teacher deserves honor just like the teacher himself when he is teaching.
O King, one should avoid massaging the limbs, bathing, eating the leftovers [of food],
and washing the feet for the sons of a guru;
however, wives of the same caste as the guru should be honored like the guru himself.
Those of a different caste, however, are to be honored by rising from one's seat and by salutation.
Anointing the body, bathing, massaging the limbs,
and the dressing of the hair— these should not be performed for the wife of one's guru.
A young wife of the guru, however, one who has completed twenty years of age and understands virtues and faults, should not be saluted at the feet. Indeed,
it is the very nature of women here to be a source of corruption for men.
Therefore, having explained this matter, the wise do not become negligent;
for in this world, women are capable of leading astray both the ignorant and even the learned who has fallen under the sway of desire and anger.
One should not sit in a secluded place with one's mother, sister, or daughter;
for the powerful collection of the senses drags away even a wise man. O Indra among kings, on this earth, a youth [is drawn] toward the young wives of his elders.
He should perform the salutation according to the prescribed rule, saying, "I am so-and-so.
A Brahmin should daily grasp the feet of his teacher and offer salutations to the teacher's wife, recollecting the dharma of the virtuous.
Just as a man obtains water by digging with a spade,
so too does one who desires to listen acquire knowledge residing in the teacher.
Whether he be shaven-headed, or wear matted hair, or have a single lock of hair on his crown and matted locks.

The sun should never set while he is in a village, nor should it ever rise while he is there. If the sun should rise or set while he is sleeping out of his own volition, or even if he is unaware of it, he shall fast for the day while reciting prayers.
For he who is abandoned by the sun while lying down, or upon whom it has risen while he is still asleep,
and who fails to perform the penance, becomes joined with great sin; yet, O Great King, by performing the ritual ablution at both twilights with a concentrated mind, one is purified.

In a clean place, one should perform the recitation of the mantra to be recited according to the prescribed rule. If a woman or a junior person should perform some virtuous act, one should practice all of that with diligence; or rather, one should do whatever the mind finds delight in.

Some say that dharma and artha constitute the highest good; others, kama and artha, or dharma alone; some say that artha alone is the highest good here, while the established tradition holds that the triad [of dharma, artha, and kama] is so.
O joy of the Kurus, father, mother, brother, and teachers—
One must not treat with contempt even one who is destitute, especially a Brāhmaṇa.
The teacher is the embodiment of Brahman; the father is the embodiment of Prajāpati;
the mother is the embodiment of Aditi; and the brother is the embodiment of one's own self.
The suffering that a mother and father endure during the birth of human beings cannot be repaid even in hundreds of years;
therefore, O Bhārata, one should always do what is pleasing to them and to the teacher.
For when those three are satisfied, all austerity is completed;
service to these three is said to be the highest austerity.
Without being permitted by them, one should not practice any other dharma.

For these indeed are the three worlds; these indeed are the three stages of life (āśramas); these indeed are the three Vedas; and these indeed are said to be the three sacred fires. The mother is indeed the Gārhapatya fire, and the father is remembered as the Dakṣiṇa fire.
The guru is the Āhavanīya fire; thus, this triad of fires is most venerable.
When these three are satisfied, the householder conquers the three worlds;
blazing with his own body, he rejoices in heaven like a god.
Through devotion to one's father one attains this world; through devotion to one's mother, the middle world;
and through service to one's teacher, one goes to the same world as Śakra.
He by whom these three are honored has honored all dharmas.
But for one by whom these are disregarded, all [other duties] are fruitless.
As long as those three live, he should not perform any other [duty];
he should constantly practice service toward them alone, devoted to their pleasure and welfare.
Whatever one may do separately without causing them any obstruction,
that very thing one should report to them through thought, word, and deed;
for it is within these three that a person’s duty is fully accomplished.
This is the supreme Dharma directly perceived; any other is called a secondary dharma (upadharma).
One who possesses faith may acquire auspicious knowledge even from a lowly person; one may learn the highest Dharma even from the lowest caste, and a jewel of a woman even from a base family.
Nectar should be taken even from poison; well-spoken words even from a child;
virtuous conduct even from an enemy; and gold even from filth.
Women, jewels, policy, knowledge, righteousness, purity, and eloquent speech [are to be accepted from anyone].
And various crafts are to be acquired from all sources.
In times of distress, study from one who is not a Brahmin is permitted;
likewise, following and serving the teacher is required for as long as the study lasts.
A disciple should not dwell for life with a teacher who is not a Brahmin,
nor with a Brahmin who has not mastered the Vedas, if he desires the supreme goal.
However, if dwelling for life in the family of a teacher is pleasing to him, [he may do so].

One should attend upon him with devotion until the release from the body. That Brahmin who serves his guru until the completion of his physical existence goes straightway and immediately to the eternal state.
One who knows the Dharma should not provide anything to the teacher beforehand;
however, when commanded by the teacher to perform the ritual bath, he should procure items for the teacher’s benefit according to his ability—
be they a field, gold, a cow, a horse, or even a parasol and sandals.

One should bring grain, clothing, or vegetables that please the guru. O best of the Bharatas, O King, when the guru has passed away, one should offer a cow to the guru’s son who possesses good qualities, or else to the guru’s wife.

One should behave toward a sapinda relative of the guru and toward the guru himself as one would toward the guru. When these are not available, remaining steady in standing, sitting, and moving about, one should perfect the body through self-restraint while performing service to the sacred fire.
By performing service to a hero, one attains the same world as that hero.
Indeed, the Brahmin who thus practices the vow of celibacy without violation goes to the abode of Brahmā and rejoices together with Brahmā.
Thus has been declared the duty of the first stage, that of the religious student (brahmacārin).
Now listen, O Indra among kings, to the duty of the householder (gṛhastha) in its entirety.
Having reached the proper time for marriage, O Brahmin, O Bhārata, through the union of the seasons according to the vow...
O Lord, one who observes this vow goes to the same world as Brahmā.
The initiation ceremony (upanayana) is always recommended for a Brāhmaṇa in the spring, while for a Kṣatriya it is recommended in the summer; so Manu has declared.
"In autumn, for a Vaiśya, initiation is always the best option.
Thus has this threefold time been described for the undertaking of the vow.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual of Initiation," in the Brāhma Parvan of the Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, in the Saṃhitā consisting of fifty thousand verses.
Now begins the fifth chapter:
the description of the auspicious and inauspicious characteristics of women.
Sumantu said:

The vow pertaining to the three Vedas consists of practicing service under a guru for thirty-six years; or it may be half of that, or a quarter, or even until the [Vedas] have been mastered. Having studied the Vedas—whether all of them, two of them, or even one alone, O best of kings—
Having lived the life of a student with his vow of celibacy unbroken, he should enter the stage of the householder.
When he is recognized for his adherence to his own duty as one who has inherited the Veda from his father,
one should first honor him while seated upon his couch, adorned with a garland, by presenting him with a cow.
"Having been duly permitted by his teacher upon returning home,
a twice-born man should marry a wife of the same caste who possesses auspicious marks.
Śatānīka said:
"O tiger among the twice-born, O great sage, tell me the characteristics of women.
Endowed with what kind of characteristics would a maiden be a source of happiness for a king? Sumantu said:

O mighty-armed King, listen with a one-pointed mind as I relate to you that which was previously declared by the Brahmins regarding the unsurpassed characteristics of women— those signs which bestow auspicious or inauspicious fruits for the welfare of all the worlds.
By means of that learning through which you know the maiden of auspicious marks—
formerly, having approached the preeminent god as he sat at ease, the great seers asked about the characteristics of women, concerning which I have now been questioned by you.
Bowing their heads to the Lord, they spoke these words:
"O Blessed One, for the welfare of all the worlds, tell us the entire supreme science of the characteristics of women,
which bestows both auspicious and inauspicious fruits."
"By what means do we know whether a maiden is auspicious or inauspicious?
Having heard those words of theirs, Viriñca spoke this speech:
"Listen, O tigers among the twice-born; I shall tell you everything."
The soles of her feet are well-settled and possess a luster equal to a perfectly blooming lotus;
such blessed feet increase the enjoyments of women.
[In contrast, those with] hands that are formidable, excessively fleshless, rough, and possessed of half-visible veins—
They undoubtedly encounter poverty and misfortune;
however, women whose fingers are joined, rounded, smooth, and possessed of fine nails, bring about supreme sovereignty and the status of royalty.
Short lines portend a short life; sparse lines lead to the loss of wealth;
broad lines indicate subsistence on the roots of poverty and servitude; while lines that are thin, knotted, and overlapping one another likewise foretell misfortune.
O twice-born ones, even after killing many husbands, she indeed becomes a slave.
Fingers whose joints are elevated by the thumb, with high tips and endowed with softness, lead to the acquisition of jewels and gold; the opposite leads to misfortune.
Good fortune comes from glossy nails, and wealth from those that are slightly copper-colored. High-set nails indicate sons, while very fine nails indicate sovereignty.
Pale, cracked, rough, dark blue, smoky, or harsh nails, however, portend the opposite.
If women have no ankles, they will become destitute; if they drink [liquor] or eat what is forbidden, they will suffer.
If their ankles are smooth, rounded, and with veins not protruding, they will wear anklets and obtain wealth from kinsmen and others.
Shins that are veinless, resembling stalks of reeds, well-rounded,
and sparsely hairy bring good fortune and travel by means of elephants and horses.
A woman with hairy shins suffers, while one with elevated ankle-bones wanders about.

A woman with legs like those of a crow kills her husband; so too do those who are talkative or have reddish-brown hair. However, by having knees that resemble those of a cat or a lion, women attain prosperity, good fortune, and likewise obtain sons.

Women who are travelers will have pot-shaped breasts; unchaste women will have fleshless ones; violent women will have veiny breasts; and those devoid of wealth will have breasts that are separated [from one another].
Furthermore, those with breasts that are extremely crooked, rough, cracked at the tips, and the color of molasses [will suffer misfortune].
A woman whose body hairs and likewise her hair are excessively reddish-brown due to many births is certainly like poison; within seven days, this sinful woman will kill her husband, without a doubt.
Women constantly experience the pleasure born of the god of love through thighs that resemble the trunks of elephants, which are like plantain trees and comparable to the forearms of young camels;
whereas misfortune results from thighs that are overly fleshy, and bondage from those that are hairy.
They say that a slender waist indicates a lack of power; however,
O twice-born one, a woman’s broad hips— which have a color like the twilight, are even and beautiful, and are covered with fine hair— are praised as bringing pleasure in sexual union.

She whose vulva is fragrant, symmetrical, well-knit, and properly shaped becomes the wife of a king, even if she is born of a low family. Likewise, one that resembles the leaf of the *aśvattha* tree and is elevated like the back of a tortoise [is auspicious].
The female organ (bhaga) that resembles the orb of the moon or likewise has the shape of a water-pot is most auspicious for women, increasing pleasure and good fortune;
so too is one that resembles a sesame flower or, at its tip, resembles a horse's hoof.
Both of these perform service for others and bring about poverty;
they cause grief like mortars, with gaping mouths resembling death,
deformed, foul-smelling and fleshless, and covered in hair like that of an elephant.
One incurs immorality, misfortune, and poverty.
O twice-born ones, a woman who is plump, free from wrinkles, and resembles a wood-apple fruit is praised; otherwise, she is censured.
The waist of women, bent by the weight of their breasts, heavy with the movement of the three folds,
adorned with a line of hair, and auspicious,
is like a small drum (*paṇava*), a large drum (*mṛdaṅga*), or resembles a barley grain in its center.
Through such [deeds], they encounter fear, dwelling in affliction, and moral corruption;
whereas [this state] possesses a back that is straight, not protruding, hairless,
and beyond reproach, providing supreme pleasure through various rugs and couches.
If a woman’s back is humped, depressed in the middle, and hairy,
she has no happiness even in her dreams and she shall kill her husband.
With broad and delicate abdomens, women give birth to many children.
A woman whose belly resembles that of a frog gives birth to a king;

those with prominent folds [on the abdomen] are to be executed, while women with well-rounded ones are unchaste. Such women will be devoted to the affairs of paramours and will eventually take up the life of a wandering ascetic.
A woman with elevated [breasts] but sunken [areoles] is of low character; one with uneven [breasts] has an uneven disposition. A wife endowed with long life and sovereignty possesses even hearts.
[Her breasts] are well-rounded, elevated, full, not too high, and broad.

This pair of breasts is auspicious; any other brings unhappiness. In the first pregnancy, if the elevation of one of the two is greater—on the left side a daughter is born, but on the right side it shall be a son.
A woman whose nipples are elongated is a cunning woman who is fond of sexual pleasure;
however, she whose nipples are well-rounded always hates her husband.
Furthermore, those with breasts shaped like the hoods of snakes or like the tongues of dogs [are likewise ill-omened].
Women who adopt the behavior of men fall into poverty;
likewise, O twice-born ones, they become like overturned water-jars.
A head that is perfectly level, fleshy, beautiful, and hairless—
If a woman’s chest is [well-formed], she enjoys pleasures according to her desire;
if it is crooked, she becomes predatory; if it is hairy, she is of bad character; if it is fleshless, she will be widowed; and if it is broad, she is fond of quarreling.

If a woman has four lines on her hand that are red, deep, and glossy, she attains happiness; if they are broken, she lacks mastery. Those lines which extend from the base of the little finger to the forefinger [indicate her fortune].

If three [of these] are successively prominent, her lifespan shall be one hundred years. A woman whose fingers are rounded, have even joints, sharp tips, and soft skin, and are all equal in length, increases her enjoyments.

O twice-born ones, through high nails red as the bandhujīva flower, one attains sovereignty; through nails that are rough, crooked, discolored, or white, there is lack of power. Through nails that are red and soft, and fingers that are without gaps, one attains sovereignty.
Those with hands that are cracked, uneven, and rough shall experience suffering; however,
for those women whose joints of the thumbs and fingers possess even lines and barley-shaped marks,
there will indeed be abundant happiness, as well as inexhaustible wealth and grain.
A wrist that is continuous and adorned with three lines bestows,
before long, enjoyment as well as inexhaustible longevity.
[It is further auspicious] when marked by the Śrīvatsa, a banner, a lotus-seed, an elephant, a horse, or a palace.
The wives of the king held in their hands signs resembling a wheel, a svastika, a vajra, a sword, and a full pitcher;
as well as hooks, palaces, umbrellas, crowns, necklaces, armlets, and earrings;
and conch shells, archways, and gate-turrets.
She on whose palm red sacrificial posts, water-pots,

and ritual jars are seen, and on whose feet [these are found], she becomes the wife of a sacrificer. Women [are to be known] by their streets, marketplaces, weights and measures, as well as by their seals and so forth.

The wives of merchants who possess jewels and gold become [prosperous]; the women of the farming folk become rich in wealth and grain through the gifts of sickles, yokes, pairs of oxen, mortars, pestles, and plows.
The pair of arms of women is auspicious when the veins and joints are not prominent, when it is plump and hairless, and shaped like a cow’s tail; likewise,
her elbows should have hidden ligaments and be devoid of hair.
Indeed, those arms of a woman which are graceful, praiseworthy, rounded and tender,
slightly elevated and slightly curved, neither too thick nor hairy,
always bestow happiness upon women and increase their good fortune and health.
If the shoulder is thick, she will carry heavy burdens; if it is hairy, she will be diseased.
If the shoulder is crooked, she will be barren; if the face is prominent, she will be unchaste. She on whose neck there are clearly three lines extending four finger-breadths [is auspicious].
She wears ornaments enriched with gems, gold, and pearls;
yet a woman who is destitute has a thin neck, a harlot has a long neck,
one whose children have died has a short neck, and a sorrowful woman has a thick neck.

She whose nape of the neck is not protruding and is even-fleshed and level shall have very long life, and her husband shall live for a long time. Likewise, one who is fleshless, or has excessive flesh, or is veiny, or hairy [is inauspicious].
A jaw that is crooked, deformed, or overly broad is not praised;
nor one that is excessively thick, too thin, curved, or hairy.
A jaw of this description is auspicious; any other is not commended.
A woman with a square face is cunning; one with a circular face is auspicious. A woman with a horse-like face is childless, and one with a large mouth is unfortunate.
Furthermore, those women whose faces resemble those of a dog, a boar, a wolf, an owl, or a monkey [are likewise ill-fated].
Cruel, performers of evil deeds, and deprived of children and kin;
though their faces possess the fragrance of jasmine, bakula, lotus, and blue water-lily,
they do not release it through drinking betel, wine, or fine food.
If a woman’s lower lip has a copper-like luster, is slightly fleshy, is free from both excessive thickness and thinness, and is elevated, it always bestows enjoyment.
If it is thick, she will be quarrelsome; if it is discolored, she will be exceedingly miserable.
A woman with a sharp upper lip is exceedingly irascible. A tongue that is very thin, curved, copper-colored, and long is praised;
one that is thick, short, discolored, crooked, or split is censured.
With teeth as white as a conch shell, a kunda flower, or the moon, glossy, prominent,
without gaps, and not protruding, one obtains sweet food and drink; whereas with teeth that are fine, excessively thin, short, cracked, or sparse, one does not.

A woman with a rough face will always be miserable and deformed. The face of excellent women, which resembles a well-polished mirror, a lotus, or the full orb of the moon, is said to bestow desired fruits.
She whose nose is neither thick nor thin, not crooked, not excessively long, and well-elevated— such a woman is blessed and brings auspiciousness.
Furthermore, that which is elevated, soft, marked with a pure line, and not joined [to the upper lip] is auspicious.
A woman whose eyebrows are curved like a bow and fine brings happiness;
those resembling a bow bring good fortune, while those with long hairs lead to barrenness. Those that are reddish-brown, uneven, and short undoubtedly lead to poverty.
With these eyes of hers, resembling the petals of a blue lotus, slightly reddish,
and possessed of beautiful lashes, this woman— whether with eyes like a wagtail, a deer, or a boar— is a noble lady who partakes in the fortune of enjoyment and good luck.
Wherever they are born, they enjoy great prosperity;
with eyes that are not deep-set, not too closely set, adorned with many lines,
and honey-brown in hue, women become queens in this world.
The eyes of women that have the shape of a crow, with long outer corners,
being clear and beautiful, indeed lead to prosperity;
whereas those that are deep and tawny make them sorrowful, though they may be long-lived.
A woman whose eyes are protruding should abandon her life-breaths in the prime of her youth; likewise,
a woman with blood-red eyes, uneven eyes, smoky-colored eyes, ghost-like eyes,
or dog-like eyes should always be avoided from afar.
Here, the women have eyes with variegated, wildly tossing hands;
they are constantly fond of wine and meat, fickle in every way,
and possess terrifying forms with ears that stand out, emitting sounds from the sky.
Women whose ears are tawny like those of a donkey, a camel, a mongoose, or an owl carry ornaments of gold and jewels that possess a radiant luster;
they generally encounter great suffering and frequently enter into the life of a wandering ascetic.

That which is slightly pale on the cheeks, well-rounded, and possesses joints here during the full moon is praiseworthy; any other is censurable, being marred by hair-pores. That which has the expansive curve resembling a half-moon and is devoid of hair is well-proportioned.
The forehead of excellent women brings about wealth and health;
it is ordained that such a forehead be twice as broad [as the face].
A head is praiseworthy for women, whereas those with heads like an elephant's trunk are unfortunate.

The hair of women that is fine, black, soft, glossy, and curled at the tips leads to prosperity; otherwise, it brings about suffering and grief. Women whose voices resemble those of the swan, the cuckoo, the lute, the bee, the peacock, or the flute [attain fortune].
They obtain many enjoyments and command servants;
however, a woman whose voice is like the sound of cracked bell-metal, or who has the voice of a donkey or a crow,
encounters disease, illness, fear, sorrow, and poverty.
A woman who walks with the gait of a swan, a bull, a chakravaka bird, or a rutting elephant,
brings glory to her own family and becomes a queen to a king.
One whose gait is like that of a dog or a jackal is censurable, as is she who moves like a crow.

A woman with the gait of a doe is a female slave, and one who moves with a hurried pace is unchaste. A complexion that possesses the luster of *phalinī*, *rocanā*, gold, or saffron brings good fortune to women; likewise, a complexion resembling the sprout of *dūrvā* grass is auspicious for women.
Those women whose limbs are soft, covered with fine hair, not excessively perspiring, and fragrant are to be honored.
One should not marry a girl who is tawny-haired, nor one with extra limbs, nor one who is diseased.
One should not [marry] a woman who is hairless, nor one who is too short, nor one who is talkative, nor one with reddish-brown eyes;

nor one whose name is that of a constellation, a tree, or a river; nor one whose name is that of a low-caste person or a mountain; nor one whose name is that of a bird, a serpent, or a servant; nor one whose name is terrifying.

One should marry a woman whose limbs are unimpaired, who has an auspicious name, whose gait is like that of a swan or an elephant, and whose body hair, hair, and teeth are fine; she should be gentle in nature. Even great and abundant wealth consisting of cattle, goats, sheep, grain, and riches—
In matters concerning marriage, one should avoid these ten types of families:
those deficient in sacred rites, those lacking male progeny, those devoid of Vedic study, and those afflicted with excessive body hair,
hemorrhoids, consumption, chronic disease, epilepsy, vitiligo, and leprosy.
First are the feet with beautiful ankles, well-established; second are the shanks with well-formed kneecaps;
third are the penis, thighs, and private parts; they say the fourth consists of the navel and the waist;
they describe the fifth as the abdomen; and the sixth is the heart together with the breasts.
Now, the seventh [digit] is said to be the shoulders; the eighth, the lips and neck;
the ninth, the eyes together with the eyebrows; and the tenth, the head including the forehead.
In the case of unfavorable [planets], the results of the periods (daśā) are inauspicious; however, for those starting from the feet, the results are auspicious.
O twice-born ones, that high-souled and majestic preceptor spoke this concerning Śacī;
having been questioned by Śakra, he explained the most excellent and distinctive characteristics of a choice woman.
Furthermore, having heard from me the characteristics of a man as well, [Śakra departed].
O best of the twice-born, just as you have now heard from me that the virtuous conduct of women is more praiseworthy than their physical marks,
so too a woman who possesses virtuous conduct is truly praiseworthy, regardless of her physical marks.
Whoever marries a Sukanyā endowed with such characteristics as these,
prosperity, growth, and fame shall abide there eternally.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Characteristics of Women," in the Brāhma Parvan of the Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty thousand verses.
Now begins the sixth chapter,
describing the characteristics and virtuous conduct of women. Śatānīka said:
"I wish to hear in great detail about the virtuous conduct of celestial women,
and how they behave toward those who are superior, inferior, or equal in relation to women.
Sumantu said:
O mighty-armed Śatānīka, in the world of Brahmā, the Grandfather (Brahmā),
having described the characteristics of women, spoke again concerning their virtuous conduct,
exactly as it was told to those Brahmins and Ṛṣis, O joy of the Kurus.
Having heard those pleasing words, Brahmā spoke these words:
"Listen, O tigers among the twice-born, to the virtuous conduct of women from the very beginning;
I shall indeed declare it to you in its entirety out of a desire to favor the world."

For the attainment of the three aims of life, I shall describe the conduct of women for householders. Having first acquired knowledge and the other [requirements], and having obtained wealth through them in due order, one should obtain a suitable wife by means of the rites prescribed in the scriptures.
For the householder’s life for those who possess nothing is indeed a great mockery;
therefore, one who desires a home must first acquire wealth.
It would be better for a man to endure the intense agonies of hell than [to live as a pauper].
But never indeed have I seen in my home a son or wife afflicted by hunger;
seeing a child weeping and full of longing when food was unavailable,
I consider my heart to be made of the essence of a diamond, since it does not shatter.
"Having seen my virtuous and beloved wife in soiled raiment, emaciated by hunger,
there is no happiness that can equal this sorrow.
[I see her] coarse, discolored, famished, and sleeping upon the bare ground."
Seeing their own wives and sons, what could men not do?
O twice-born ones, seeing one's son emaciated by hunger, with his arms as his only upper garment and a dejected face,
death itself is a festival for men, while life is a calamity.
Seeing his beloved with her children languishing, he became dejected in countenance;
yet those whose bodies are as firm as adamant do not shatter into a thousand pieces.
Therefore, for a man devoid of wealth, the taking of a wife [is a source of misery].
How can there be the accomplishment of the three aims of life for one who is merely subject to torment? For just as one without a wife has no entitlement to the second stage of life (āśrama),
likewise those devoid of wealth have no entitlement in any matter whatsoever.

Some, however, say that offspring alone is the means for attaining the three aims of life (trivarga) for men; others who are experts in policy know that wealth and a wife are the means. Furthermore, dharma is also twofold, consisting as it does of the performance of *iṣṭa* (sacrificial rites) and *pūrta* (charitable works).
And that [wealth], consisting of wives and so forth, is the sole means for accomplishing all objects of knowledge;
yet even by his own impoverished kinsman, a man feels ashamed,
for even a stranger becomes like one's own kin to people through the possession of power.
People do not notice even a poor man standing right beside them,
yet they honor with respect one who is wealthy, even if he stands far away.
Therefore, one should first strive diligently to secure wealth.
For he is the root of the three aims of life, of virtues, and of dignity.
Indeed, all the qualities of men—learning, noble birth, character, and so forth—exist in him when he is present;
they do not exist even if they were present when he is absent.

Scripture, craft, the arts, labor, and whatever other activity there may be—all these are the means for achieving worldly ends (*artha*). Worldly ends are themselves the means for achieving dharma and the other goals of life.
For human beings, there is this triad of goals (*trivarga*) as the purpose of all means; without it, they are merely [human] beings.
Just like the fleshy protuberance on a camel's neck, the arising of wealth is for the sake of its own destruction.

Through prior merits, vast prosperity arises as a cause for dharma, desire, and so forth; yet through that very [pursuit of worldly ends], it is lost again here and in the next world—such is the sequence.
For this is indeed called the "Single Wheel," wherein each part is the cause of the other.
Having understood that the upper, lower, and middle [powers] arise from the eastern and western arms,
the wise man who thus pursues the threefold aim (trivarga) attains success.

Through means joined with hundreds of such calculations, one attains ever-increasing success. One who lacks a wife, or one who is destitute, has no authority regarding the three aims of life; therefore, before anything else, one should first secure wealth.
Therefore, endowed with wealth acquired through inheritance or obtained by himself, capable and competent for ritual action,
he should take a wife born into a suitable family [in terms of] learning, wealth, conduct, and so forth.

A man shall obtain a blameless maiden who is pleasing to the mind and a means for the practice of dharma; for as long as he does not have a wife, he is only half a man. Therefore, at the proper time and in due order, he should take a wife.

Just as a chariot with a single wheel or a bird with a single wing, so too a man without a wife is unfit for all undertakings. Through the acceptance of a wife, there is dharma; likewise, through abundant gain, there is artha.
Through the union of true affection, even desire is known by the wise as being threefold in this [matter].
The connection of marriage is of three kinds: with those who are inferior, equal, or superior.
With equals, it is the best for all of them; the other two [unions] are considered low and middling.
Because he is censured by the unequals, treated with contempt by the best,
and praised by his equals, he is therefore considered the most virtuous;
for even after establishing a superior relationship, he experiences only insult.
One should not bow down to them, nor should one endure being treated with inferiority;
even a superior alliance with the lowly leads to equality with them.
Therefore, a wise person should avoid that which is censured by the equal and the superior.
The wise do not desire association with those of a different class;
for by such association, both fall, just as a parrot does by associating with a cuckoo.
Consequently, he appears excluded from the noble family and will certainly suffer contempt.
Furthermore, because it is impossible to practice, even the highest [type of relationship] is not praised.
Some [of those with the highest type] must be avoided, while others actually do avoid them.
Therefore, both the lowest and the highest types of relationships are undesirable.
That relationship is designated as "bond" (sambandha) wherein mutual affection increases daily through services such as sharing a single vessel and the like;
it is that in which there are reciprocal obligations toward one another during occasions such as bringing home a bride or giving her in marriage.
The wise know that relationship to be one based on rivalry alone;
whereas that relationship among those who share a single course of action through both adversity and prosperity, even at the cost of their lives and wealth, is the highest.
For men, there are only two touchstones for the manifestation of affection:
likewise, for gratitude, they are the occurrence of misfortune and the arrival of prosperity.
And that affection among men is generally seen only toward equals.
One should also seek equality in terms of wealth, character, lineage,

and so forth; therefore, one should form marriage alliances with those who are similar, for such unions bring about singular success, but not with those who are superior, even if they are themselves unsurpassed.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Characteristics and Good Conduct of Women," in the Brāhma Parvan of the Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty thousand verses.
Now begins the seventh chapter:
"Description of the Laws of Marriage."
Brahmā said:
A woman who is not a sapinda of one's mother and not of the same gotra as one's father is recommended for the twice-born in the rite of marriage for sexual union.

A wise man should not marry a girl who has no brother and whose father is unknown, for fear of the practice of *putrikā* (an appointed daughter). For Brahmins, a wife of the same caste (*savarṇā*) is recommended for the rites of marriage.
But for those who have entered [the life-stages] out of desire, these [wives] are inferior in successive order.
O best of the twice-born, even for a Kṣatriya, the wife of his own caste (savarṇā) is the first;
likewise, two others are declared as inferior when taken out of desire, but not according to dharma.

For a Vaiśya, one wife of his own caste is declared lawful; likewise, a second of a lower caste may be taken out of desire, but not as a matter of dharma. Manu has declared that for a Śūdra, only a Śūdra woman is a wife according to dharma.
The best of the twice-born may marry women from all four castes;
however, for a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya, even when standing in distress,
a Śūdra woman is never prescribed as a wife in any traditional account whatsoever.
Twice-born men who, out of delusion, marry women of low birth quickly lead their own families, along with their offspring, to the status of Śūdras. Indeed,
Utathya became an outcast by marrying a Śūdra woman upon the sacrificial altar.
Utathya incurred the state of being fallen due to the birth of a son;
having obtained a son from a Śūdra woman, Śaunaka likewise fell into the status of a Śūdra.
Bhṛgu and others as well would have incurred the same state of being fallen in this very manner.
A Brāhmaṇa who places a Śūdra woman upon his bed goes to a low state;
by procreating a son with her, he falls away from Brāhmaṇahood itself. But for him whose rites for the gods, ancestors, and guests are primarily performed through her...
The ancestors and the gods do not eat [the offerings] of one who has drunk the foam from a *vṛṣalī*, nor does he go to heaven; for one who is struck by her breath and procreated by her,
no atonement is prescribed.
O best of Brahmins, I shall briefly describe the eightfold marriage, which is excellent and brings benefit or harm both in this world and after death:
the Kāla, Daiva, Ārṣa, Prājāpatya, and Asura [forms].
The Gāndharva, the Rākṣasa, and the Paiśāca, which is the eighth and lowest;
hear, O best of the twice-born, what duties belong to each caste, what their respective merits and defects are, and the qualities and faults regarding their offspring.
One should know that for a Brahmin there are four [marriages] preceded by the Rākṣasa rite; for a Kṣatriya, four following it; and for a Vaiśya and a Śūdra, only three, excluding the Rākṣasa rites.
The wise know the first four to be the most praiseworthy for a Brāhmaṇa.
The Rākṣasa form is prescribed for a Kṣatriya, and the Āsura for Vaiśyas and Śūdras.
Among these, three are considered lawful for Kṣatriyas, while two are recorded here as unlawful;
the Paiśāca and the Āsura must never be performed under any circumstances.
Either separately or combined, the two forms of marriage previously mentioned—
the Gāndharva and the Rākṣasa— are recorded as lawful for the Kṣatriya.
Having clothed and honored a man of learning and good character himself, [he should give his daughter].
Giving a daughter after being invited is proclaimed as the *bāhya* (external) rite;
likewise, when a sacrifice is being performed and the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) is engaged in the ritual,
the giving of a daughter after she has been adorned is declared the *daiva* rite.

Having accepted one or two pairs of cattle according to the law from the bridegroom, the giving away of the daughter according to the prescribed rule is called the Ārṣa rite. Having addressed the words, "May you both perform your duty together," [the gift is made].
The giving of a daughter after honoring [the groom] is recorded as the Prājāpatya rite.
Giving wealth to the kinsmen and to the girl herself according to one's ability,
while the giving of the daughter is done at her own will, is called the Āsura dharma.
The mutual union of a maiden and a suitor through their own desire is to be known as the Gāndharva rite; it is carnal and born of passion.
[It occurs] after killing, cutting, and piercing [the way out], while she is crying out and weeping from her home.
The forcible abduction of a maiden is called the Rākṣasa rite.
When one approaches a woman in secret while she is asleep, intoxicated, or mentally deranged,
that is declared the eighth and most sinful of marriages, the Paiśāca.
The giving away of a daughter to the foremost of the twice-born is praised when preceded by water;
for the other castes, however, it occurs through mutual desire.
Whatever merit has been proclaimed for each of these various forms of marriage, [that merit accrues to the one who performs it].
Listen to that, O Brahmins, as I proclaim it correctly:
he surely liberates ten preceding generations of his lineage as well as ten others, and himself as well, from sin.
O Brahmins, hear that the son born of a woman wedded according to the Daiva rite is a "Son of Brahma" who performs meritorious deeds;

the son born of a woman wedded by the Daiva rite delivers seven generations of ancestors and seven of descendants. O twice-born ones, the son born of a woman wedded by the Ārṣa rite delivers ten generations of women and men.
In the four forms of marriage beginning with the Brāhma, sons are born in successive order who possess Vedic luster, are esteemed by the learned,
and are endowed with beauty, character, and virtue, as well as wealth and fame.
Those who have sons live for a hundred years, being most righteous;
but understand this regarding others: from ill-contracted marriages are born sons who are cruel, speakers of falsehood, and haters of Brahman and dharma.
Through blameless marriages with women, one's offspring become blameless; through blameworthy ones, they become blameworthy for men. Therefore, one should avoid those that are blameworthy.
Indeed, the sacraments beginning with the taking of the hand (marriage) occur only among those of equal caste.
This rule for the rite of marriage with women of a different caste should be known:
by a Kṣatriya woman, an arrow is to be grasped; by a Vaiśya maiden, a goad;
and by a Śūdra woman in marrying a man of higher caste, the hem of the garment is to be grasped.
A wise father shall not accept even the slightest bride-price for his daughter;
for by accepting a bride-price out of greed, a man becomes a seller of his offspring.
And those kinsmen who, out of delusion, live off a woman’s property...
Those wicked men who go about with women as their vehicles or for the sake of clothing fall to a low state.
As for the claim made by some that a pair of cattle is the bride-price according to the Rishis' tradition—that is indeed false;
whether it be small or great, it remains nothing other than a sale.
When the kinsmen do not take a bride-price for them, that is not a sale;
it is merely a token of honor for the maidens and an act of pure benevolence.
Having thus obtained a wife, he should dwell in an excellent region.
"O tiger among the twice-born, what [should a] Brāhmaṇa do if he desires extensive fame?
The sages said:
"O Brahman, what region is supreme, and which one is considered meritorious by you?"
"O best of Brahmins, O lotus-born one, where does one who travels abroad obtain glory?
Brahmā said:
"O twice-born ones, that place where Dharma, with its four feet, remains entirely unimpaired."
O Brahmins, that region is supreme and is considered meritorious by me;
that country in which dharma practiced by the learned prevails,
O best of Brahmins— even as prescribed in the scriptures— is considered supreme.
The sages said:
O best of gods, O supreme among deities, tell us of the dharma practiced by the wise and prescribed in the scriptures; for our curiosity is indeed great.
Brahmā said:
Understand that dharma which is practiced by the wise and the virtuous who are always free from hatred and passion, and which is approved by the heart.
A nature of self-centered desire is not praised, nor indeed is a total lack of desire here;
for the acquisition of the Vedas and the Vedic application of ritual action are both objects of desire.
Desire arises from volition, as do sacrifices and all other such acts in their entirety.
All vows, observances, and duties are traditionally held to be born of mental resolve (*saṅkalpa*).
Never is anyone seen here performing an action without desire;
for whatever anyone does, that is the movement of desire.
The *nigama* (Vedic revelation) is the root of Dharma, as are tradition (*smṛti*) and virtuous conduct (*śīla*),
as well as the practice of the righteous and self-satisfaction.
One should examine all these with the eye of knowledge to reach a definitive conclusion.

A learned man should indeed abide in his own duty by prioritizing the revealed scriptures (śruti). A person who always practices the dharma proclaimed in the śruti and smṛti attains supreme fame in this world and goes to the same world as Śakra.
The Veda is to be known as Śruti, while the Dharmaśāstra is indeed Smṛti. Both of these are to be investigated in all matters, for from them Dharma has shone forth.
That twice-born man who, relying on the treatises of logic (hetuśāstra), would hold both of these in contempt—
That atheist who reviles the Veda must be expelled by the virtuous.
O Brahmins, the Veda, the Smṛti, the conduct of the righteous, and what is pleasing to oneself— this fourfold is the manifest definition of Dharma.

O Brahmins, for those who are unattached to wealth and desire and who seek to know the Dharma, knowledge of the Dharma arises from the supreme authority of the Vedic scriptures (Naigama). That Dharma is the procedure ordained by mantras, beginning with the rite of impregnation (niṣeka) and ending at the cremation ground (śmaśāna).
He shall have the right to study the Vedas and to perform their recitation.
That region which lies between the two divine rivers, the Sarasvatī and the Dṛṣadvatī,
is declared to be Brahmāvarta, a land specially created.

In whatever region a particular custom has been handed down through successive tradition among the social classes (varṇas) and the intermediate castes (antarālas), that is called right conduct (sadācāra).
[Such regions include] Kurukṣetra, Matsya, Pañcāla, and Śūrasena.
This is indeed the land of the Brahman-sages, immediately following Brahmāvarta.
From the presence of a twice-born man born in this country,
all men on earth learn their respective duties.
That region which lies between the Himavat and Vindhya mountains, east of Vinaśana and west of Prayāga, is celebrated as Madhyadeśa (the Middle Country).
It extends from the eastern ocean to the western ocean.
The wise know that Āryāvarta lies between those very two mountains;
where the black cow and the deer roam constantly by their very nature,
that region should be known as the land fit for sacrifice (yājñika), while beyond that is the land of the Mlecchas.

The best of the twice-born should always resort to these auspicious regions; however, in whatever place he may dwell, even if he is a foot-born outcaste oppressed by lack of livelihood— O best of the twice-born, this has been proclaimed by the wise as the source of dharma.
"And the origin of all this has been told in brief, but not in detail.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Laws of Marriage," in the Brāhma-parvan of the Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, in the Saṃhitā consisting of fifty thousand verses.
Now begins the eighth chapter.
Regarding the duties of marriage and the conduct of men toward women,
Brahmā said:
"Now learn that which must be performed by a householder."
O tiger among the twice-born, having spoken thus at length according to the scriptures,
one should perform the domestic rites (*gṛhyakarma*) according to the rules in the nuptial fire; likewise,
the wife who brings auspiciousness should reside with her husband in the home.
Since protection and other such duties cannot be accomplished apart from one’s own support—
just as [the protection] of wealth [requires] wives— therefore, that [support] is prescribed. For, O Manu, the causes of the three aims of life are their opposites.
Because they would otherwise fall into ruin, it is considered necessary to protect them;
for women must indeed be guarded due to their innate nature, their lack of contentment with men, their tendency to deliberate upon virtues and faults, and also because of association with the wicked.
They say that the abode of men consists of three types of dwellings:

for the purpose of protecting existing wealth and for the acquisition of new wealth. [Such a person should be] of noble birth, possessed of statesmanship, wise, true to his word, and firm in his vows.
One who is disciplined, righteous, and generous should be known as a person worthy of refuge. He may reside in a city, a town, a hamlet, or even a village that has come down by tradition,
or he may dwell wherever there is a community of righteous people and the like, for the sake of his livelihood.
Having obtained permission from his teacher, or from the village headmen and others there,
he should construct a pure dwelling without causing distress to his neighbors and the like,
[ensuring space] for gates, courtyards, halls, and the dwellings of all craftsmen.

One’s livelihood, appropriate to one’s wealth, should be maintained in great secrecy from afar from those who live by gambling, slaughter, liquor, acting, and kingship; from heretics, temples, and streets; and from the royal highway and its surrounding families.
It should have a single outlet with a lid, its back surface clean on all sides;
it should be crowded with virtuous, upright people and have neighbors who are not wicked;
and it should be situated in a region sloping toward the east or north, according to the rules of the science of architecture (vāstuvidyā).
It was distinguished by its various functional requirements, enchanting in all seasons,
and equipped with temples for worship, bathing areas, water-houses, storehouses, and kitchens,
as well as stables for cattle and horses, and dwellings for servants and attendants.
The inner apartments, containing women and provided with all necessary furnishings,
were arranged with designated sleeping quarters and supervised by trustworthy elders;
for through the failure to protect one's wives, there arise offspring resulting from the confusion of castes and other such evils.
For many faults have been observed; therefore, women must always be guarded.
One should not grant them freedom of movement, nor independence, nor place trust in them.
Yet, one should behave as if trusting them and administer reasonable reprimands when necessary.
One should not grant them authority anywhere except for tasks such as cooking;
for women, when well-governed, are fit for enjoyment like village women. They must be kept constantly occupied with those duties without interruption.
Thus, because [the mind] is always pervaded in this way, ignorance would be without a basis; likewise,
poverty, a distorted form of mind, association with the wicked, independence,
a fondness for drinking, eating, and social chatter, and a lack of inclination toward spiritual practice [would all follow].

[One should avoid] those who are deceitful, glancing women, shaven-headed women, female mendicants, women recently delivered, and so forth; likewise, one should avoid cowherds, the wicked, ascetics, beggars, and artisans;
as well as [occasions such as] massaging, garden parties, processions, and invitations to gardens.
There is the necessity of traveling on pilgrimages and the exposure of one's religious duties;
constant separation from the husband, the destitution of his kinsmen and family, lack of sweetness of character, miserliness, and being severely censured by men.
Excessive cruelty, excessive patience, extreme fearlessness,
and being utterly overcome by women— these are indeed faults;
yet it is the man himself who is censured because of his total dependence on women.
For the unworthiness of servants is indeed the dullness of the master himself;
therefore, these [servants] should be guarded against such lapses through commands and beatings,
and one should treat them with beatings at the proper time and in the proper manner.
Having taken many wives, he should be impartial toward them with appropriate services;
he should perform his duties in due order through acts of giving and honoring.
Noble birth, righteousness, capability, and having excellent sons are the primary requirements.
In this context, wealth enters into women, and likewise, pride is its cause.
Therefore, pride should not be cultivated, nor should that which is produced by it;
for whether in matters of weightiness or lightness, the conduct of the virtuous is the binding authority.
A discerning person, when employing honor or contempt without cause,
incurs only insignificance due to acting impulsively;
for just as one might employ honor or insult without any justification, so too does he suffer the loss of dignity.
Dependent upon that [lineage], people strive for the renunciation of their own birth;
indeed, this alone should be known as the cause of honor for offspring:
that the preeminent fitness of the family exists on account of one's own progeny.
From union with that [object] comes happiness for men, and from separation comes great suffering;
therefore, for the sake of one's own true interest alone, even those things which are dear must be abandoned so as to attain that [liberation].
Thus, it is determined that this entire world is solely intent upon its own self-interest.
The establishment of that [truth] occurs through the measurement of the setting [of the sun], which brings about the cessation of delusion.
Therefore, wives, servants, and likewise the twice-born should be governed in such a way that one may attain ever-increasing welfare both in this world and the next.

One should not practice excessive deception regarding the dharma, artha, and kāma of women; for by deceiving them in these matters, one becomes deceived oneself. Indeed, for men, the wife is half of the body in the accomplishment of dharma and the other goals of life.
Therefore, one should not cause them any distress nor act in any way contrary to their interests.
During sacrifices, festivals, and the like, one should not treat any among them with special distinction;
one should be impartial in the distribution of gifts such as clothing and betel-leaf.
For distinction between the beloved and the unbeloved arises from private desire;

however, when treated with equal conduct through services and words, such equality is praised. Furthermore, during her fertile period, all women should be approached as if they were one's own beloved.
One who has previously acquired the knowledge of the meaning of the Dharma and possesses sons should,
during her menses, always follow the prescribed rule of ascending and descending;
maintaining a consistent conduct and not interrupting her respective residence at the proper times.
The wise know that the departure of the vital breaths is the end of those who dwell in the cycle of constant rebirth;
likewise, there is the suffering of the seasons and the joy previously encountered.
Furthermore, whatever suffering—whether real or unreal—one experiences in secret with another woman.
Whatever longing one feels for co-wives should not dwell within;
whatever is connected to another or spoken privately in a different manner,
one should ensure no resentment arises from it and should reflect upon it by oneself alone.
One should not even reproach them with words by recounting their mutual jealousies; rather,
having personally discerned their virtues and faults,
one should provide them with clothing, ornaments, food, and the like, in due order, according to their children.
Disregarding the faults of the mother, a father should maintain an equal regard for all;
indeed, it is not consistent with sound policy to find fault in one person on account of the defects belonging to another.
Furthermore, whatever offspring they may have belongs equally to both.
One should always ascertain through servants and secret agents the affection, hatred, intentions, and the movements regarding purity and impurity of others, both externally and internally;
and one should likewise know oneself as being no master over the fluctuations of the mind.
How can one trust women, who are the abodes of all immodesty?
Old female servants inherited through lineage, nurses, attendants,
their own mothers and fathers, and elderly eunuchs are considered suitable spies.
By means of various narrations and stories involving those of similar character and endowed with compassion,
employed at the appropriate time, one should enter their inner disposition and understand it;
while those various topics of discourse are being told, one should observe [their reactions].

One should discern the intention residing in the mind through signs such as facial expressions and the like; likewise, one should know the internal state from behavior through accounts of the conduct of Sītā, Arundhatī, Śakuntalā, and others, both virtuous and non-virtuous.
From this, there arises affection for the virtuous among the wicked and for others among the good,
as well as friendship toward men through the composition of stories; thus,
by means of scripture and inference, [the truth] is known in reality.

Having understood the intentions of women, one should act quickly as is appropriate; for it has been observed that kings have even deprived rebellious women of their lives, and therefore one should protect them with great effort.
King Śubhadhvaja was slain by a weapon hidden in his braid;
King Sauvīra by the jewel from the queen’s girdle;
and Bhadrasena was struck down by his own brother, who was instigated by the queen.
Likewise, Kārūṣa was slain by his own son with a sword that had been polished on a mirror;
and two kings of Kāśī, though they were worthy of honor and of purified souls, were brought to their death by the woman of Ānandapura through the administration of poison.

When even such highly fortunate kings and brahmins are brought to ruin by women, what need is there to mention others here? Therefore, one must always remain vigilant and constantly protect one's wife.
One should attend to them appropriately according to their specific qualities and defects;
for through irregularities in treatment, disorders arising from no apparent cause,
and especially when accompanied by a co-wife or by sudden pains, [the condition may be aggravated].
Furthermore, due to the lack of association and the harshness of verbal abuse,
women develop hatred and even open hostility toward their husbands;
consequently, they reach old age while their husbands become their enemies.
Therefore, one should not employ those [practices] which cause faults that lead to the destruction of the wife;
nor do these women immediately disregard their own family traditions or even unrighteousness,
for they do not neglect virtues by their very nature, much less when they are tormented.
Generally, three causes for the chastity of women are observed:
lack of attraction to other men, affection for their husband, and a desire for self-protection.
Therefore, they should always be well-guarded by appropriate measures.

Women should always be kept well-supported in their constant duties. One should win over a superior woman through conciliation and gifts; a middling woman through both of these; and an inferior woman by means of both of the latter two.
Even after employing division and punishment with regard to their children and others,
one should subsequently win over those remaining under their influence through conciliation and gifts;
however, as for those whose conduct has been ruined and who act to the detriment of their husband—
Thus, virtuous women who resemble the *kālakūṭa* poison must be abandoned by the good; however,
those who are beloved, born of noble lineage, chaste, humble,
and devoted to their husbands should always be won over through successive traditional practices.

In this very way, he who practices the conduct of a wife as it has been prescribed attains the complete threefold aim (trivarga) arising from the world. Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Conduct of Men Regarding Women," in the section on the Duties of Marriage within the Brāhma Parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty thousand verses.
Now begins the ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Praise of the Āgamas.
Brahmā said:
Thus has the conduct of men toward women been described in brief;
now, the conduct of women toward men is being taught. Through the proper propitiation of men, women attain both pleasure and their livelihood.
Sons and the unseen rewards such as heaven—therefore, the performance of that rite is indeed desired. Whatever is to be done whatsoever depends upon a prescribed rule;
otherwise, even that which has been commenced results in futility.

All undertakings depend upon injunctions; even those that appear fruitless are, especially when undertaken on a grand scale, causes for the attainment of the three goals of human life (trivarga). Knowledge of all that is to be accomplished is based solely upon the traditional scriptures (āgama).
The object to be accomplished through injunctions and prohibitions is twofold: the seen and the unseen.
Women have no authority over the scriptures, nor do they possess the capacity for retaining their texts.
Therefore, others here consider that teaching [of the Veda] to them to be useless.

Women also possess the right [to perform rituals] when engaged in actions based solely on scripture (*āgama*). This is stated in the Smṛtis, such as: "A woman becomes virtuous (*sādhvī*) when her husband has died," and so forth. Therefore, having determined from scripture what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, the master [should act].
The king properly instructs them regarding virtues and faults, just as he does his subjects;
for while some women indeed possess a specialized mastery of the scriptures,
their authority over the treatises would otherwise be rendered meaningless.
Some Brahmins learned in the Vedas are intent upon ritual acts and the performance of dress and ceremonies;
nevertheless, it is they alone who are entitled here by virtue of their birth alone.
Ritual applications pertaining both to the scriptures and to the world are performed by those who know the Vedic treatises.
Even though it is not far from them, the scripture alone is their authority;
for even among hunters, fishermen, cowherds, and others,
the avoidance of days such as Viṣṭi, Ārdrā, and Saurya is observed.
This established order of regulated conduct concerning who may be approached and who may not, and so forth,
is the very life-breath of the scriptures and of people, being bound to one's own desired goals.
Therefore, it applies in every respect to all four castes and stages of life.
The eligibility for the scripture should be understood through the distinctions of primary and secondary [meanings] and so forth;
however, it is impossible to determine the relative priority between worldly convention and the scripture.
Therefore, that [scripture] alone must be accepted as authoritative, just like ritual action and the physical body.
In both the Āgamas and the Purāṇas, one should, with an undistracted mind, follow the twofold path practiced by the great ones, which is free from the stubborn grasp of nihilism;
for virtuous wives are the very root of the duties of householders.
"Therefore, I shall proclaim for them the method for propitiating their husband.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "Praise of the Arrival," in the Brāhma Parvan of the Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, in the Saṃhitā consisting of fifty thousand verses.
Now begins the tenth chapter.
Description of the Wicked Conduct of Women.
Brahmā said:
This indeed is the rule for the propitiation of all those who are to be propitiated.
Conformity with her thoughts and knowledge, and always wishing for her welfare—these are the qualities of the three types of women: the maiden, the remarried woman, and the courtesan;
likewise, there are those who are beloved, those who are indifferent, and those who are unloved, as well as those who are suitable, mediocre, and otherwise.
It is again threefold—equal, excellent, and inferior;

furthermore, as before, the conduct toward the superior and inferior [partners] is considered pleasant or unpleasant through their expression or non-expression. In this context, the relationship between husband and wife, and so forth, is regarded as that between the inferior and the unpleasant.
Regarding those things prohibited, such as forbidden foods and the like, they are indeed prescribed with great effort.

O best of the twice-born, the various distinctions concerning singularity, duality, plurality, and so forth have been illustrated in the first chapter; we shall now describe all of them in detail in the section on the conduct of the eldest brother and others.
The conduct of women is twofold: external and internal.
That which occurs toward anyone other than her husband is external; that which pertains to her own body is internal.
Furthermore, the external is divided again into two types based on the distinction between kinsmen and others.

The worshipful, the equal, and the junior—each of these is again threefold: secret, public, and physical. This should be practiced appropriately according to what is suitable for each, in accordance with the disposition of the husband.
Mother, father, sister, brother, paternal uncle, teacher, maternal uncle,
wife, sister, husband, husband’s mother, husband’s father, husband’s sister,
nurse, elderly women, and whoever else is there who is an equal person— [all these are to be honored].
The first wife and the co-wife constitute the most venerable class among women.
Their children and so forth, as well as their sisters and brothers,
and the younger wives of the husband and others, are considered equal to one's own kin.
There is no one else there who is inferior or in need of instruction,
as long as her fitness— established through the excellence of her son— is not yet firmly established;
even in that case, it depends entirely upon the constant favor of her elders and husbands.
The conduct of women is praised when it does not conflict with the practice of honoring [elders]; likewise,
one should avoid staying in secluded places and engaging in jesting with brothers-in-law or friends of the husband who are prone to ridicule.
For generally, the causes of the destruction of the virtue of noble women are:
improper association, constant secrecy, independence,
excessive joking, haste in the company of the wicked, and inappropriate jesting with young men.
One should worship in secret for the sake of the independence and success of those who are fearless;
one should avoid men whose gestures and appearances are wicked, being motivated by evil intentions, regarding them instead as one would a brother or a father.
