For a man, there are the grasping of another’s garlands, smiles, and sidelong glances; the binding, receiving, and giving away of objects with the hand;
standing at the gateway, and looking out upon the royal road.
One should avoid visiting gardens and such places, as well as staying in a region where many people congregate; one should also avoid restlessness of sight, speech, and body,
spitting, whistling, loud laughter, and idle chatter.
Association with those who possess [only] signs, with corrupt women, with those who are gluttonous, fickle, and so forth;
attachment to the initiation of mantras and mandalas, and to living together [with such people];
such evil conduct as this is generally characteristic of wicked persons.
"She should avoid [such conduct], guarding against the reproach of the three families.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "Description of Women’s Evil Conduct," in the Brāhma Parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of fifty thousand verses.
Now begins the eleventh chapter.
The Description of the Duties of Householders for Women.
Brahmā said:
She who regards her husband as a deity through the actions of mind, speech, and body;
As if born from half of his own body, he should always act for her benefit;
he should look upon her beloved as if he were his own beloved, and always look upon those she hates as if they were his own enemies.
He should refrain from anything unbecoming that might lead to unrighteousness or misfortune.
"O twice-born ones, having understood what is pleasing to him, what is beneficial for him, and how his equanimity may be maintained, one should never be negligent toward any servant.
[One should likewise attend] to the rites for the gods and ancestors, and to the master’s bathing, eating, and other such needs."
One should not fail to honor guests who have arrived according to their merit;
for the household of housewives is twofold— the dwelling and the body—
and both must be diligently maintained, the former even more so than the latter.
Having thoroughly cleansed the dwelling and performed worship according to the three periods of the day,
one should appropriately prepare the food for those who have completed their work and are ready to eat;
this should be done in the morning, at midday, and in the afternoon, both outside and within the house.
Having swept the house, one should not discard the refuse at night;
rather, the dung and other such waste from the stables of cows, buffaloes, and so forth,
should be diligently removed using a broom for cleaning.
One should know the rules for the maintenance and the employment in tasks of slaves, laborers, and others, whether they move within or outside [the household],
as well as those of vegetables, roots, fruits, creepers, and medicinal herbs.
The collection of all seeds according to the season and according to their strength;
and the gathering of vessels made of copper, bell-metal, iron, and so forth, as well as those made of wood, bamboo, and various kinds of clay.
Water-tubs such as basins, jars, and ladles;
numerous vessels for vegetables, oils, and cow's milk;
a pestle, a mortar, a mechanical press, and a sifter for flour.
The milking vessel, the net, the churning-stick, the rings, the tongs, the water-pot,
the spikes, the cloth-strainer, the grinding stone, the ladle,
the hand-broom, the spoon, the frying pan, and the small baskets.
One should always take great care to maintain scales, measures such as the prastha, brooms, baskets, and all such items. Furthermore,
one should keep asafoetida and other spices, cumin, long pepper, and black pepper.
Black mustard, coriander, ginger, the three and four spices (trijātaka and caturjātaka),
salt, the group of alkaline substances, fermented gruel (sauvīraka), parūṣaka,
split pulses, myrobalan, tamarind, and all varieties of oily substances.
Dried wood, dried meat, fermented liquors, preparations of flour and black gram,
various products of milk,
and diverse kinds of bulbous roots [are used] for the performance of daily and occasional rites.
Everything and so forth should be collected appropriately according to one's means;
whatever is not seen available at the time of performing the rites,
that one should diligently collect beforehand as required.

One should observe the decrease or increase in grains that have been ground, pounded, crushed, or damaged, as well as those that are very dry, moist, or cooked. Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "Description of Domestic Duties," in the Brāhma Parvan of the Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, in the Saṃhitā consisting of fifty thousand verses.
Now begins the twelfth chapter,
the description of the duties of women.
Brahmā said:
The noble *udāraka* possesses the essential quality (*sāradharma*) of both rice (*vrīhi*) and *kodrava*;
the *varaṭa* should be known as having five parts of *kaṅgu* and *kodrava*.
There are five parts of *priyaṅgu*, and three and eight [parts] of *śāli*.
They know that three parts of chickpeas (caṇaka) should be well-ground together;
likewise, the four grains—water, barley, wheat, and flour—are to be understood as being equal in measure. So too are mung beans, black gram, sesame seeds, and barley.
Wheat that has been ground with one-fifth [of water] and likewise barley-meal,
as well as boiled grain, flour-meat, and properly prepared half-portions and so forth;
that very same thing when cooked becomes double [in quantity], as does *punnāka* and *yāvaka*.
One should know that the cooked food of *kaṅgu*, *kodrava*, chickpeas (*caṇaka*), and *udāraka* is double [the volume of the raw grain]; that of *cīnaka* is double; that of *vrīhi* rice is fourfold;
and that of *śāli* rice is fivefold; however, in the case of aged grain, it exceeds these proportions.
Regarding the specific results of the ripening of actions, it is taught that there is indeed growth;
from the excellent food which is the cause, that growth becomes twofold.
Therefore, for that which has further sprouted, a fourth part increases.

Parched grains, seeds, and peas increase twofold when roasted; for other items that must be roasted, an increase of one-fifth is considered appropriate. For flattened grains and flour products, those made from peas are reduced by one-quarter.
For mung beans, black gram, and lentils, the reduction shall be half a quarter (one-eighth).
For various cooked or dry grains, a decrease or increase is specifically prescribed.
By that same half-measure, the quantity of *āḍhakī*, mung beans, and black gram to be subtracted is determined.
One should know that there is a loss of one-fifth for lentils;
for linseed oil, white mustard, and wood-apple, there is a loss of one-sixth;
likewise, for neem, kadamba, and similar items, one should know there is a loss of one-fifth.
One should know that oil is one-fourth [the weight] of sesame, *iṅgudī*, *madhūka*, *naktamāla*, and *kusumbha*; the remainder is called *khala*.
Due to variations in field, time, processing, and so forth, there is deviation from the expected yield through loss and other factors.
Having perceived these directly, one should determine them correctly through inference:

those who know the subject matter understand that for cows, the yield of milk is one *prastha*; for buffaloes, it is a *prastha* plus a quarter; and for goats and sheep, they know the production to be greater still.
The increase of milk and clarified butter depends upon the quality of the ground, the grass, and the season;
therefore, their determination must indeed be made through inference.
Having observed this with effort over the course of a fortnight or a month, one should reach a conclusion accordingly.
One should determine the origin of cows and other animals by their products, such as milk.
The weaving of cotton, silk, linen, wool,
and flax should be caused to be done by women who are crippled, lame, blind, widows, or barren.
Whatever must necessarily be done for children, the elderly, the blind, and the destitute,
he should perform it all with kindness and conciliation.
During intervals between his own duties, and even when his husband is away on a journey, [he should attend to these].
This indeed should be performed by oneself, provided it does not conflict with the obligatory duties (*nitya*).
Having considered the grossness or subtlety, the multiplicity, and the expendable or inexhaustible nature [of the materials],
one should apply distinctions in the conscious realizations.
One should have garments, grain, and other goods managed by trustworthy and experienced men;
the decrease, increase, and wages of the Śūdras should be closely monitored.
One should know that the thread for linen and cotton consists of five parts.
However, due to the division by place, time, and other factors, the determination is made through direct perception itself:
"By the threshing of cotton, a twentieth part is destroyed;
likewise, they declare that wool is [subject to loss] when covered or pervaded by the wind."
One should calculate a reduction of one-fiftieth according to the [original] measurement in the Sūtra;
however, through contact with the *maṇḍa*, there shall be an increase of one-tenth for each subsequent tenth.
For fine and medium threads, this increase shall be respectively half and equal [to the original].
For coarse objects, however, the price for one with immature discernment is reduced by one-quarter.
Because of the great variety of actions due to differences in place and time,
the determination regarding those with immature discernment must be understood from those who are experts in that matter.

The coarse [method] should be applied for three days, the medium for three nights, and the subtle, refined [method] for a fortnight; its preparatory ritual is completed within a month. Whatever concerns the increase of the *kṣatra* and so forth have been demonstrated here by way of illustration.
Even deviation is observed due to differences such as the agent of time (kālakartṛ) and so forth:
"There are many beds and seats, blankets with four corners, conch-shells, and unhusked grains; there are many middling ones and red ones."

The husband, for the sake of their enjoyment, should provide various articles for his gurus, children, the elderly, and guests; as well as whatever bedding and other necessities have been prepared for his father-in-law and the rest.

She should not cause her husband’s specific garments, garlands, or ornaments— once worn by him or by his elder brothers and others— to be worn by anyone else. She should not wear them herself, nor should she step upon their beds or seats.
One should avoid oil-cakes, pounded sesame seeds, and anything that is black or harsh;
one should discard stale food and the like, and instead utilize it as fodder for cows, especially for families with many milch cows or for those who live by managing herds under a cow-herd.
One should collect the butter for the sake of food from those who sell inspissated milk, cow-milk, and so forth;
one should milk the cows but not squeeze the calves.
[The cows should be milked] twice during the rainy season, autumn, and spring, and once at other times.
Or he may employ buttermilk for the nourishment of dogs, pigs, and other such animals;
or he may use it for moistening oil-cakes, or sell it as is appropriate.
He should provide for the livelihood of cowherds and others with grain and gold.
For out of greed, they would destroy the offspring of those cows who observe the milk-vow;
O twice-born ones, the cowherds would neglect the milking time of the cows,
and the churners would neglect the churning of the water and the curd-mixture.

For one month she should constantly feed [the child] breast milk; for one month she should feed from both breasts; thereafter, she should feed from one breast at a time. [She should also provide nourishment] with balls made of sesame paste, with grass, and with salt.

And one should nourish the calves with water at the proper time. One should provide fodder to the herd by dividing it into five equal portions for the following: the aged cow, the pregnant cow, the cow with a calf, and the heifer.
One cowherd was for those three, or perhaps for two;
and for five there was one calf. These excellent ones were each separate, for the purpose of bringing back the grazing herds and for frightening away wild beasts.

They should attach bells to the ears [of the cattle] for the sake of beauty and protection. One should always establish the cow-pen in a forest that is suitable for cattle, free from predators, abundant in grass and water, and where no harm has occurred.
One should always keep goats and sheep living in well-guarded forest enclosures.
Twice a year—in the months of Caitra and Āśvayuja—one should collect their wool.
In a herd of ten of these animals, there should be four or five cows.
He should ensure that horses, camels, and buffaloes are well-cared for;
he should know the application of farmers and others in their agricultural labors,
as well as the provision of food and wages in accordance with the requirements of the work and the time.
One should observe the application of activity at every moment among the servants performing work in the fields, meadows, and enclosures, as well as in the threshing floors; for,
having recognized the exceptional competence of someone in their respective tasks, one should [employ them accordingly].
One should provide him special treatment with food, clothing, and head-anointing.
There should be a collection of all seeds— such as lotus stalks, vegetables, and those produced from bulbs and seeds— and their sowing at the proper time in fertile soils.
The protection of those already born, the gathering together of those properly protected,
and the appropriate distribution of those gathered;
women are the root of the household, and grain is the root of the householder's life.
Therefore, one should not practice open-handed generosity with grains that have been consumed;
rather, grain should always be accumulated and the expenditure of food should be measured. Open-handedness at the end [of the year] is not praised for housewives.
O twice-born ones, one should certainly not show contempt for food simply because it is small,
having observed the growth of honey and anthills, as well as the depletion of collyrium.
Whatever activities appropriate for men are prescribed here—
By establishing the unity of the couple, in connection with the granting of that [gift],
it should be understood that there is no fault on the grounds that there are indeed thousands of men in the world for whom women are the primary authority, since it is they who direct those women.
Thus, endowed with fitness, good fortune, and diligence,
she should properly serve her husband and bring him under her influence right there.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "Description of the Duties of Women," in the Brāhmaṇa Parvan of the Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty thousand verses.
Now begins the thirteenth chapter,
the Description of the Duties of Women.
Brahmā said:
She should wake first, engage in her own duties,
and afterwards eat and sleep, even while the servants are still at work. A woman separated from her husband, especially when away from her parents-in-law, [should act thus].
She should not overstep the threshold even when there is great cause for retaliation.
Having risen first, she should not go out without her husband's knowledge,
whether at night when the night still remains, or during the beginning of the day.
Having slowly summoned the workmen to that very residence, he should assign them all to their respective tasks here and there; then,
once the master has awakened, he should perform the necessary daily rites.
She should perform all household duties without negligence;
having set aside her bedding and ornaments and having donned attire suitable for work,
she should carry out her timely obligations in their proper order.
The kitchen was well-swept, with the hearth and other implements duly honored;
it was equipped with all necessary utensils, spacious, and free from disorder;
it was neither too secluded nor too exposed, being arranged so as to facilitate distinct activities.
In a place for her husband that is crowded with trusted attendants, secluded, and free from servants and the like,
she should have cooking vessels and other utensils prepared both inside and out,
their stains and dirt washed away with powders of oyster shells, bark, and similar substances.
At night one should prepare the smoke-flame; during the day, the vessels should be purified by the heat of the sun. One should always prepare curd-pots that have been kept out of the way.
When the milk has been properly prepared and purified by the heat of the sun during the day...

Having prepared clarified butter, milk, cooked rice, and other such items, ensuring they are pure and having personally supervised the husband’s cooking process with full confidence, she herself should attend to the ritual of preparing food using vessels that have been slightly handled and spoken over.
"What is beneficial, what is fiery, and what among the six tastes is internal?
What is wholesome and what is unwholesome, and how may his health be maintained?"—
one should diligently understand these things and practice accordingly.

One should provide constant affection, honor, and well-tested food to trustworthy people who have come through hereditary succession, such as those in the kitchen; however, one should exclude enemies, heirs, relatives, and those who are angry, afraid, or insulted.

Or she should provide food, drink, and other necessities for her husband, having ensured they are not tainted by what is unfit to be spoken; she should do so repeatedly, having established them securely, kept secret, and personally supervised, without negligence.
Having completed the cooking for her mothers-in-law and performed the rite of fomentation and wiping,
she should take a small amount of perfume, betel, garlands, and so forth,
and at that time, according to propriety, attend to her husband with humility and zeal.
One should provide food that is extremely congenial to that particular time;
those who know [the science] have declared that all food, drink, and so forth should always be employed in a manner contrary to the times of one's natural constitution and disease.

In whatever way a husband regards his children— as inferior, equal, or superior— he should likewise regard them as superior in their conduct according to justice. He should look upon his children born of rival wives with even greater distinction than toward his own.

One should treat one's sisters-in-law and their wives like one's own kinswomen. Without providing food, clothing, oil for the head, bathing materials, ornaments, and so forth to one's co-wives, one should not even perform such acts for oneself.
For the sake of treating those who are ill, he should diligently provide medicine and other necessities for them,
as well as for himself and all the people dependent upon them.
He should take sorrow at their grief and bring joy in their satisfaction.
She should share equally in the sorrows and joys of her servants, kinsmen, and co-wives. Having found an opportunity, she should sleep at night only after they have risen from sleep in succession.
She should privately admonish her husband whenever he spends money on other things.
Whatever fault she has against her co-wives, she should not speak of that herself to him;
however, she should secretly inform him of any harmful conduct, such as immorality. Likewise, she should report if a wife is unfortunate, childless, or excessively mistreated by her husband.
Having properly consoled one who is not at fault, he should win her over with that;
likewise, having consoled people oppressed by their master with harshness of speech or punishment,
he should make them compliant, for that would not lead to any fault.
Realizing that he was childless and that much time had passed,
he offered himself for the sake of obtaining progeny and other such matters;
furthermore, he understood whatever else his master might desire to accomplish.
As if not knowing, she should demonstrate to him as if it were already accomplished;
having performed the entire marriage rite for her husband with great haste,
she should look upon her once-married husband always as if he were a younger sister.

With a very joyful heart, he should perform the worship of her circle of relatives, as well as auspicious rites and blessings for his newly wedded bride. Free from envy, he should instruct her in household duties as if she were his own mother.
Or she herself should diligently perform for her [the husband] the partial rites;

in this way, she should carry out everything according to the husband's intention. Or, even setting aside her own pleasure, she should act for his sake, for among women, the husband is the presiding deity.
The husband is the presiding deity of the wife; the social classes have the Veda as their deity;
the Brahmins indeed have Agni as their deity; and the subjects have the Kshatriya as their deity.
For the successful accomplishment of their threefold aims of life, two causes have been prescribed.
Neither youth, nor beauty, nor ornament in this world is as effective as being well-disposed toward one's husband and possessing an unimpaired character;
for such devotion to a beloved is eternally established as a medicine that requires no other drug.
Unfortunate women are seen who have stolen away youth, beauty, and other qualities; likewise, many beloved women possess inferior forms once their youth has faded.
Therefore, being dear to the world has as its primary cause excellence of character.
Without her, all other virtues are barren, or even lead to misfortune.
Therefore, one should strive with every effort to cultivate self-worthiness;
for in this world, the knowledge of others' minds is the root of all successful actions.
Knowing that he is coming from outside, she should sweep the ground,
prepare a seat, and remain waiting, intent on carrying out his command. Having raised her handmaid, she herself should wash his feet.
One should remove [the disciple's] heat and perspiration with palm-leaf fans and the like.
Whenever one perceives a longing for food, bathing, drinking, or other such things,
one who understands signs should truly offer him that which has been prepared.
A wife should act toward her husband’s kinsmen and relatives in a manner that accords with her husband’s wishes,
but she should not behave in that same way toward her own kinsmen.
Having ascertained his mind regarding them and herself, she should seek to please him.
Nevertheless, even if she does not attend to the conduct of her own kinsmen,
a woman living in her husband's family who honors her husband's wishes does not incur reproach from her own relatives because of that.
For a woman’s relationship is indeed to be honored in all circumstances;
what man of noble birth would seek even a fraction of benefit from her?
Having honored his own daughter, he bestows her upon him according to the prescribed rites.

Therefore, he desires her name; what could be more improper than this? For those who provide for their own livelihood by giving away a daughter, this is the path of slaves, petty traders, actors, and the like, not that of the great-souled.
Therefore, women and kinsmen should always maintain a conduct toward their relatives that is based solely on affection and is consistent with their social ties;
they should protect her affection for her husband and guard against public censure.
Even those of virtuous conduct might engage in false speech regarding themselves;
having understood this, a woman should always behave with such good character that she remains esteemed by her husband and his retinue.
Though she was beloved, virtuous in conduct, and of renowned lineage,
Sītā met with a most terrible calamity due to public scandal;
for everyone is like a baited hook, being ignorant of the distinction between virtue and fault.
Generally, because of their lack of discipline and propriety, the conduct of women is indeed difficult to maintain;
for their mental dispositions are ungraspable, they mostly display deceit,
and the world is unrestrained— thus, blameless women are rare.
Due to the influence of fate, lack of self-control, and ignorance of worldly conduct,
women are seen to fall into states of reproach even when their minds are pure. For them, there can be no remedy for such fate other than sexual enjoyment.
They know that conduct and worldly behavior are the remedy for these two:
[the sight of] a young widow, wandering at will, who at night is addicted to games such as the swing and is sporting with libertines.

Who would believe that even a virtuous woman is chaste when she is surrounded by an elderly husband and others, and is addicted to traveling, singing, and such diversions? For even the gestures and facial expressions of such women can establish a doubtful matter.
If the thorough knowledge of reality is the domain of yogins,
then one should perform the prescribed conduct with great self-restraint;
for even a false doctrine, when adhered to, causes that family to tremble.
The three lineages must be protected from censure, and the lineage must be established;
the husband’s attainment of the three aims of life is to be accomplished by women of that family. Through misconduct, they surely cause themselves and the three lineages to fall.
At that very moment, those women whose ornament is their character lift themselves up— those whose unswerving conduct consists in being compliant with the heart of their husbands;
for them, jewels, gold, and the like are merely a burden, not an adornment.
Supreme mastery in worldly knowledge and eternal devotion to her husband—
know this to be the family vow of women of pure lineage.
Therefore, by her, both the world and her husband are perfectly propitiated.
She alone attains dharma, artha, and kāma without any obstacle.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Duties of Women," in the Brāhma Parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty thousand verses.
Now begins the fourteenth chapter.
Regarding the prohibition of women's adornment while residing in another country,
Brahmā said:
When her husband has been sent away, a woman’s ornamentation serves merely as an auspicious rite.
The diligent completion of the work once begun;
the acquisition of wealth through one's bed (or resting place); the avoidance of expenditures;
devotion to vows and fasts; and the pursuit of one’s livelihood.
Consulting astrologers and physicians, supplicating the gods,
constantly hoping for their arrival, and worshipping the deities for the sake of security;
neither wearing excessively brilliant attire nor always carrying oil [on the head].

She should not go to the house of her relatives unless she has a specific purpose for going; even then, she may stay only with the permission of her elders and in the company of her husband’s trusted kinsmen.
Even there, she should not remain for long, nor should she perform acts such as bathing.

Having remained for as long as necessary for a moment, she should then act quickly. When her beloved has returned— having performed the immediate rites, being in his natural state, having discarded his travel-weariness, bathed, and eaten— she should attend to him.
Having adorned herself with special care and filled with joy,
she should first present the offerings for the worship of the deity that have been prepared;
she should regard her younger sister-in-law as her own mother and her elder sister-in-law and her children as herself.

She should always regard his retinue as her own; she should stand before him when he is seated and not address her husband by name. She should carry out all activities in accordance with his intentions.
She should not associate with those who hate him, but should form friendships with those who are dear to him. She should always honor his most trusted people as well as her own husband.
She should carefully guard the wealth, perfumes, and other such items brought from her father’s house.
Having offered it to him as his own self, he should then utilize it for that purpose.
He too, for the sake of pleasing him, should give back something of little value.
One should remain hidden like a mother and utilize that [gift] in exactly the same manner.
Whatever has been undertaken for the sake of pleasing her, or to remove her embarrassment and the like,
one should explain that in detail through the course of conversation.
For this state of rivalry among women is a supreme cause of jealousy.
Therefore, that [fault] must be avoided through most noble conduct.
Thus, having arrayed herself in her chosen finery on the day of her husband's turn, she should go to her husband when dismissed, acting with modesty and bashfulness.
Having gone into private, she should attend upon her husband with special care, employing various gestures appropriate for the occasion and in accordance with his disposition. Then,
having awakened him at the proper time, she should serve him with particular devotion while filled with modesty.

She should especially go to the residence of the eldest wife; she should act without opposition toward her and do what is beneficial for her, except in the case of other women. Then, gradually alienating the husband from her, she should bring him under her own control.

By means of external massage and other such techniques, she should delight her husband— who is secluded with her and possesses a superior intellect— by employing the sixty-four arts. Women should display boldness in private, whereas at other times they should exhibit an excess of modesty.
She should follow the husband’s mind and devote herself entirely to his service. Having thus gratified her husband and having gradually entered the household life,
she must not neglect the respect or the proper conduct due to her elders and others.
In matters of household affairs and the distribution of gifts, she should speak to her husband secretly;

even if she is unwilling, the elder brother should appoint her as he would by force. She too, having perceived that her husband’s mind has been drawn away by the younger wife, [should act accordingly].
She should seek rest for him and attend to him as if he were her own son;
considering it to be her husband’s desire, she should protect her own dignity. Whatever she does to be favorable toward her husband, she should rejoice in that which is pleasing to him.
What can servants do otherwise than that which is intended by their master?
Therein, the foolish person who is dependent on others suffers in vain.
Therefore, in all circumstances, through the actions of mind, speech, and body—
Beneficial conduct and compliance with her husband are especially required of women; moreover,
that wise woman, having always won over both her elder husband and the management of the household through her virtues, should not forget her former state.
She should not display pride on account of her good fortune, nor undergo transformations such as arrogance;
she should always maintain extreme humility, as if out of fear of the ignoble.
In this way, her good fortune increases through her fitness for her husband.
She should thus emulate the noble women of her family by means of humility;
and having thus gratified her husband, she should be diligent in his affairs,
constant in honoring those worthy of worship, and in the maintenance of her servants.
"By the constant acquisition of virtues and by the diligent preservation of moral conduct,
one attains unsurpassed happiness, free from the pairs of opposites, both in this world and after death.

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Duties of a Co-wife among the Duties of Women," in the Brāhma Parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of fifty thousand verses.
Now begins the fifteenth chapter,
the Description of the Duties of Women.
Brahmā said:

Moreover, she will be perpetually unfortunate, constantly devoted to fasting and such practices, and will be especially intent on external duties to her husband. She will find no praise among her co-wives, nor will she receive any blame for herself.
She may display resentment toward her husband, or jealousy, or even affection;
for a woman like me can manifest all these things extensively, yet she attains the ultimate state—
that which entitles her to be designated by the very word "wife" in relation to you.
She should not remain without ornaments, nor should she wear ostentatious ornaments.
On other occasions, perfumes, garlands, and the like should not be accepted except as an offering to her husband;
however, she may accept them in reduced quantities, especially from her beloved.
Ornaments, perfumes, and garlands should remain unnoticed for that duration;
there should be constant wiping away of sweat and the like from congested areas,
as well as the cleansing of the grime from the teeth, nose, and so forth, and the removal of foul odors.

She should observe any sign from her husband that might indicate his preference for one of them; she should not, on that account, exert herself in grooming his body. She should remain consistently attentive toward all her co-wives in every respect.
Adopting the conduct of a reed, especially toward her beloved husband,
she should diligently perform whatever is to be done for others that is not distressing, provided it is not known to the husband and is not contrary to his interests.
Treasury, clothing, food, betel, perfumes, drinks, medicines, and so forth—
all these are forbidden for those who are not authorized, because they involve fault; however,
that which is prescribed as a duty, such as the sweeping of the house and other such tasks, is permitted.
Although women generally have no formal entitlement [to Vedic rites], their duties are mostly described as follows:
she should respectfully perform the husband's oil massage, dry rubbing, bathing, feeding, and adornment, as well as the nursing duties for the children.
She should provide for her other children according to their needs as if they were her own;
she may also adorn them with her own wealth.
As for the husband's wealth, he himself or his children shall enjoy it; the wife has no right to it.
In youth one should delight in [worldly] companionship, and in old age one should apply oneself to [spiritual practice];
whether one engages in both or neither, that [result] arises solely from action.
Furthermore, through virtuous conduct, one should again achieve great renown by means of one's deeds.

No woman is by birth either unfortunate or fortunate; this designation arises from worldly convention, just like the distinction between enemy and friend. It occurs either from a failure to understand the husband's mind or from a failure to act accordingly.

Through conduct that is contrary to worldly norms, women fall into misfortune; yet through mental dispositions that are favorable, even a stranger may become beloved. Through opposition, even one's own husband will quickly turn into an object of hatred.
Therefore, in all circumstances, one should always act agreeably toward her with the deeds of mind, speech, and body, conforming to her wishes.
Toward any other woman whom she desires, one should cause her to be united with that person.

And when some beloved woman is angry, he should strive with effort to appease her; likewise, he should practice supreme skill in the service of her feet, in massaging her limbs according to the traditional methods, and in the gentle pressing of her head.

The pressure—whether mild or moderate—should be applied according to the specific condition of the body parts, using signs such as the face and limbs; it should be administered so as to bring comfort.
[This applies] to the arms, thighs, waist, back, shoulders, head, and feet.
Generally, they desire firm massage elsewhere, though moderate pressure is preferred for fleshy parts,
the base of the navel, and the vital points (marmans).
For the heart region, the cheeks, the temples, and so forth, they desire gentle massage.
In the waking state it is intense; for one who is half-asleep, it is moderate;
and for one who is lightly asleep, it is slightly obstructed or not felt at all.
It is contrary [to the normal state] throughout all the limbs, and especially so in the hair follicles.
Scratching with great enthusiasm, massaging with affectionate oil,
producing horripilation through touch, slowly scratching with the fingernails,
accompanied by the lifting of bristling hair, and scratching the head and sides— these are the acts [of love].
And on those various parts of the body, it should be applied in such a manner as is appropriate for inducing sleep at that time and for inflaming passion—
whether he is standing, sitting, awake, or even sleeping.
They praise massage, which brings about extreme happiness:
the absence of movement, the breaking out of horripilation, the closing of the eyes,
the offering of one's body parts, and the manifestation of some transformation upon awakening.
One should press her hands against the region of the thighs and the root;
where the skillful woman perceives [sensitivity], there one should apply pressure more intensely. Thus indeed, she who follows the conduct of women as it has been prescribed—
"By pleasing her husband, she attains the fulfillment of the three aims of life (trivarga).
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Duties of Women," in the Brāhma Parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium consisting of fifty thousand verses.
Now begins the sixteenth chapter.
Sumantu said: Having thus spoken the description of the characteristics of women in their entirety, the blessed Lord Brahmā [proceeded]. [This is] the description of the ritual procedure.

Having thus heard the entire account of the woman's character and conduct, O Lord of the Earth, Sadvṛtta returned to his own home, and the sages likewise departed for their respective abodes without exception.
O Lord of the Earth, having obtained a wife endowed with such characteristics,
now learn from me what must be performed by a householder:
one should perform the domestic rites according to the rules in the nuptial fire.
A householder should always perform the fivefold sacrifice by means of cooking;
yet because of the householder's five slaughter-houses, he does not go to heaven:
the mortar, the grinding stone, the hearth, the water-jar, and the broom.
For the sake of purifying all these [debts] in due order,
the wise have prescribed five great sacrifices for householders to be performed every day:
teaching is the sacrifice to Brahman (brahmayajña), and the libation of water is the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña).
The sacrifice to men, the sacrifice to the gods, the sacrifice to the earth, as well as another— the honoring of guests—
these five great sacrifices he who does not neglect according to his ability,
even while constantly living in the house, is not tainted by the faults of the senses.
"He who does not offer [oblations] to these five— the gods, guests, dependents, ancestors, and himself— though he breathes, he does not truly live.
Śatānīka said:
He who has no fire in his house is as good as dead; of this there is no doubt.
That best of Brahmins is unable to worship the gods and other deities.
O twice-born one, how can the gods and others [be pleased] with a Brahmin who maintains no sacred fire?
"May they be pleased for his peace; this is my supreme curiosity.
Sumantu said: "I have been well questioned, O Indra among kings; let this supreme word be heard."
But for those Brahmins who are without sacred fires,
their welfare is declared [to be achieved] through vows, fasts, observances, and various gifts, O King;
the gods and others will surely be pleased with them— of this there is no doubt.
"Especially on a lunar day (tithi) observed with fasting, O Lord of the Earth, the gods and others indeed become pleased; such is the case for them, O joy of the Kurus.
Śatānīka said:
O Blessed One, tell me of the lunar days (tithis) and the ritual procedure for those days; tell me also of the consumption of food, the duties of the Grihya tradition, and the rules for fasting,
so that by your grace, O best of the twice-born, we may be liberated from the flood of sins.
"And for the sake of the welfare of the world, O best of Brahmins, [he withdrew] from saṃsāra as well.
Sumantu said:
"Listen, O Kaurava, to the rites based on the secrets of the lunar days (tithis)."
The sacred texts destroy sins, as do the fruits of fasting.
On the first lunar day (pratipad), one should consume milk; on the second, one should avoid salt;
on the third, one should eat food with sesame seeds; and on the fourth and fifth days, one should subsist on milk.
On the sixth day he should always eat fruit; on the seventh, vegetables; on the eighth, he should subsist on *bilva* fruits;
on the ninth, he should eat flour; on the tenth, he should eat food not cooked by fire; on the eleventh, he should eat clarified butter; on the twelfth, he should eat milk-rice (*pāyasa*);
on the thirteenth, he should eat cow’s urine; and on the fourteenth, he should eat barley-gruel.
On the full moon day he shall consume water infused with *kuśa* grass, and on the new moon day he shall subsist on sacrificial food (*haviṣya*).
This is the rule for consuming [the offerings] on the lunar days; and whoever observes this rule for one fortnight obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice multiplied tenfold.
He dwells in heaven for as many Manvantaras as there are months [in the three or four]; being sung of by Apsarases and Gandharvas,
he obtains a hundredfold the merit of the Aśvamedha and Rājasūya sacrifices.
Being sung of by apsarases and gandharvas in heaven, he dwells there for as long as a thousand cycles of four yugas.
Likewise, by breaking his fast on the eighth month, he obtains a thousandfold the fruit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices;
and he dwells in heaven for as long as fourteen manvantaras.
He who, having undertaken such a discipline, lives for one year while being sung to by Apsarases and Gandharvas,
dwells in the world of Savitṛ for the duration of a Manvantara.

O King, he who— whether a celibate student, a householder, a forest-dweller, a woman, a man, or even a Śūdra— being of restrained mind, undertakes these lunar-day vows (tithi-vrata) on the ninth day of Āśvayuja, the seventh of Māgha, the third of Vaiśākha, and the full moon of Kārtika, attains long life and reaches the same world as Savitṛ.
Furthermore, O King, those who in a previous birth performed the rite of fasting on these lunar days according to this method—whether they gave various kinds of gifts to Brahmins or to ascetics;

or those who observed the three-night fast, were devoted to pilgrimages, austerities, and service to their gurus, mothers, and fathers—the signs of the fruition of their merit for those who have returned here from the enjoyment of heavenly realms are seen directly in the world of men.

These are the fruits for those devoted to giving and fasting: elephants, horses, vehicles, draft animals, wealth, jewels, gold, bracelets, armlets, necklaces, waist-bands, ear-ornaments, crowns, excellent garments, beautiful women, and superior ointments; as well as handsome forms, virtuous qualities, and long life, free from mental and physical afflictions. Even today, those who have performed meritorious deeds are seen being awakened here by the sounds of dancing, singing, instrumental music, and auspicious recitations.
Likewise, those who have observed fasts are indeed seen;
and likewise, those who have not given gifts and have not performed merit are seen directly before our very eyes.
"For example, even today one sees men who are one-eyed, leprous, deaf, dull-witted, mute, or deformed, as well as those whose lives are struck down by disease, poverty, calamities, and illness.
Śatānīka said:
"O wise lord of the twice-born, you have described the lunar days (tithis) in brief."
O best of the twice-born, tell me again in detail that secret concerning the lunar days (tithis) and the activities of the gods,
as well as those offerings dear to the gods, the foods to be consumed, and the religious observances (niyamas).
"Tell me those, O knower of dharma, by which I may become purified;
for how, O brahmin, may I be free from the pairs of opposites and obtain the fruits of sacrifice?
Sumantu said:
The secret regarding the lunar days, as well as the food and its specific fruits, the duration and the rules of observance— and especially those concerning women—
all this we shall declare; learn from me that secret.
Indeed, that which I have never before spoken to anyone, even my dearest friend—
that I shall now declare to you: the specific lunar day (tithi) of each deity,
as well as the secrets of the gods, their vows, and their observances.
Listen to those as I speak, O mighty-armed Nārada;
first, I shall describe the creation in brief according to the lunar days.
This universe was indeed composed of darkness, unattainable and inconceivable.
Having arrived, the Brahmā of the world created himself by means of his own self;
having manifested as the Self, he emerged from the midst of the cosmic egg.
Indeed, that Lord, having first created the egg from himself by means of his own self, [proceeded].
That Brahmā, known as Nārāyaṇa, being intent upon performing creation,
fashioned from those two skull-bowls the heavens and the earth,
as well as the cardinal and intermediate directions, the gods and others, and likewise the Dānavas.
O King, the Lord himself then established this first lunar day (tithi);
because it was proclaimed by Brahmā as the foremost of all lunar days,
it is called "Pratipad" (the First), being established at the very beginning.
Since other lunar days (tithis) are proclaimed to be distinct from this specific day,
I shall describe the supreme procedure for fasting at its conclusion:
on the full moon of Kārttika, on the seventh day of Māgha, and on the Yugādi days of Vaiśākha.

One who knows the ritual procedure should first cause [the devotee] to undertake the observance of fasting. O lord of men, learn now that specific rite which is to be performed on whichever lunar day one follows with devotion in order to observe the vow.

But when one should undertake the vow on the first day of the lunar fortnight, O King, having taken food on the fourteenth day, one should form the formal resolve (saṃkalpa). One should not eat on the new moon day and should perform ablutions at the three times of day.

Being purified, one should daily recite the Gāyatrī together with its head (śiras). Having honored the best of the twice-born in the morning with perfumes and garlands, one should offer milk according to one's ability, saying: "May the Lord Brahmā be pleased with me."
Then, O King, one should drink cow's milk according to this procedure.
This very procedure is prescribed for all lunar days, O King;
when a full year has elapsed, this vow is completed.
O lord of men, learn now what the fruit of that vow is at its conclusion:
for that embodied soul, freed from sin and purified in essence, possessing a divine body,
Brahmā, being well-pleased, grants a celestial vehicle of exceeding splendor.
Having sported there for a very long time like a god, together with the deities and accompanied by Kinnaras and Apsarases in his divine state of unimpeded movement,
he shall return here and obtain the status of a Brahmin for ten births.
In the Kṛta Yuga, he is born as one who knows the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, long-lived, highly radiant, an enjoyer of pleasures, a lord of wealth, and a donor;
O Indra among kings, Viśvāmitra, however, desired to conquer the status of a Brāhmaṇa.
He performed extensive austerities to the distress of the inhabitants of heaven;
yet he did not attain the status of a Brāhmaṇa, but encountered numerous obstacles.
Consequently, among those lunar days (tithis), that day became the most excellent due to their observances.
Having observed various fasts on that lunar day beloved by Brahmā,
Brahmā then bestowed upon the wise Viśvāmitra the status of a Brāhmaṇa— so difficult to attain— which he attained in this very body.
This lunar day is indeed the most excellent among lunar days, the supreme of all lunar days.
Whether a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra, they may attain the status of a Brāhmaṇa.
Thus, O King, this lunar day grants all desires and is dear to the Lotus-born One (Brahmā).
I have proclaimed this along with its secret doctrine, which has not been told to anyone else;
here on this very spot, the Haihayas, Tālajaṅghas, Turuṣkas, Yavanas, and Śakas fasted, desiring to attain the status of Brāhmaṇas.

Thus, O King, this [narrative] is supremely meritorious, auspicious, and likewise a destroyer of sins; it is so when recited, practiced, or heard with faith. Furthermore, O King, that man who hears its greatness [shall also attain these benefits].
"Having attained supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), prosperity (*vṛddhi*), as well as fame and auspiciousness, one shall go to heaven.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual for the First Day," in the Brāhma Parvan of the *Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of fifty thousand verses.
Śatānīka said:
"O Brahmin, please tell me in detail and with due respect the duties to be performed on the first lunar day (pratipad),
the procedure for the worship of Brahmā, and whatever fruit indeed results from that worship. Sumantu said:

Listen with a focused mind, O King; I shall relate this which bestows peace. In the past, when the terrible single ocean had arisen and all moving and stationary beings had perished, the self-existent God appeared—the eldest of the gods, the four-faced one.
He created the worlds, the gods, and various beings—
both moving and stationary— by means of body, mind, and speech;
he who is the father of all gods and the grandfather of all beings.
Therefore, he is always to be worshipped, for he is the supreme teacher of the world;
he creates the entire universe, protects it, and likewise withdraws it.
Rudra was born from his mind, and Viṣṇu was born from his chest.
From his mouths [issued] the four Vedas and the Vedāṅgas in their entirety;
the gods, apsarases, gandharvas, along with yakṣas, uragas, and rākṣasas,
always worship Viriñci, the leader of the gods, O hero.
The entire world is composed of Brahman; everything is established in Brahman.
Therefore, one who desires his own welfare should worship Brahman.
He who does not worship with devotion the eldest of the gods, the Lord of the gods—
He who worships Viriñci, the Lord of the World, with devotion, is not merely a recipient of the kingdom of heaven nor of liberation; rather,
he quickly becomes a recipient of both the kingdom of heaven and liberation.
Therefore, O King, having become serene in mind and making a vow for as long as life lasts, a man who always worships the God— even if he has fallen into calamity—
would rather abandon his body than endure the occurrence of hell.
But they never eat without first worshipping the god born from the lotus;
he who always worships the Grandfather with devotion, O hero,
is the Creator himself encased in human skin— of this there is no doubt.
For there is no merit whatsoever greater than the piercing [of the image] through worship;
having understood this, the ritual procedure (vidhi) should always be honored with effort.
He who, out of delusion, hates Brahmā, who is saluted by all the gods—
Even by conversing with such a person, a man would go to hell.
Now listen with a one-pointed mind to the meritorious fruit that one obtains by installing an image of Brahmā according to all efforts and the prescribed injunctions.
Whatever fruit is obtained from all sacrifices, austerities, gifts, sacred fords, and the Vedas,
one shall obtain that fruit multiplied ten million times by performing the consecration of a piercing [of an image].
He who constructs a beautiful hall and installs the Lotus-born [Brahmā] therein, [attains the same merit].

One shall obtain merit arising from every limb, multiplied by millions upon millions. Having delivered twenty-one generations— both those born of one's mother and father, as well as the wife one marries— one is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
Having enjoyed extensive pleasures, when the dissolution of the world has arrived,
he attains the yoga of knowledge and is liberated right there;
or else, if he should desire sovereignty, he is born again in another existence.
He who, having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus, recites the Brahman at the three junctions of the day, shall become the sovereign of the earth with its seven islands and oceans;
hear now the meritorious fruit of that person on the full moon day and the first day of the lunar fortnight.
With this very body, he remains upon the earth as Brahmā,
the destroyer of the sins of all mortals through both sight and touch;
having uplifted twenty-one generations of his lineage, he establishes them in heaven.
Accompanied by those families, O King, he rejoices eternally in the world of the cows.
Even he who worships with devotion even once the Lotus-born Lord,
whether as the lotus-seated one or in embodied form, goes to the world of Brahmā.
Upon the exhaustion of merit, having reached the earth, one may become a great lord of the earth;
or else, one is born as a Brāhmaṇa who knows the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences. Neither by most intense austerities nor by all the great sacrifices does one attain this.
Except for those whose souls are devoted to Him, he shall go to the divine city of Brahmā.
Whoever constructs a house for Brahmā using clay, wood, brick, or stone,
is honored in the world of Brahmā together with twenty-one generations of his lineage.
The fruit obtained from a house made of wood or bricks is ten million times greater than that from one made of clay;
and when a house is constructed of stone, the merit is twice that of a brick-built one.
O King, even if he were merely playing, he who builds a hall for Brahmā [attains this].
In the world of Brahmā, he obtains a celestial palace that fulfills all desires,
encircled by garlands of flowers and adorned with networks of tinkling bells;
it is equipped with swinging cradles and embellished with bells and yak-tail fans.
Adorned with canopies of pearl necklaces, possessing the brilliant splendor of the sun,
crowded with hosts of apsarases, and bestowing all objects of desire and happiness—
having dwelt there, that great enjoyer sports eternally with the gods.
Returning again to this world, O lord of the earth, he becomes a righteous king;
beholding and protecting living beings with gentleness and gradually performing purification, he shall attain the fruit of the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
He who performs the smearing of the floor with water filtered through a cloth,
while observing and avoiding living beings, shall obtain the fruit of the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
He who performs sweeping and worship continuously for a fortnight [attains the same].
For more than a hundred crores of yugas, he is honored in the world of Brahmā.
At the end of that time, possessing knowledge of the four Vedas, handsome and pleasing to behold,
wealthy and endowed with all virtues, he becomes a righteous king.
O giver of great honor, even he who constructs a Brahma-śālā through deceit,
or performs tasks such as its sweeping and maintenance, shall indeed obtain the fruit thereof;
yet they continue to wander in saṃsāra, overwhelmed by suffering, grief, and fear, for that long.

O best of gods, O lord of the earth, as long as the minds of living beings are not attached to the Supreme Brahman in the same way they are attached to the realm of sense objects, who would not be released from bondage? If the mind were thus fixed upon Brahman, who would not be liberated from bondage?
He who indeed performs the repair of what is broken or cracked in a hall, or in gardens, dwellings, and the like, obtains the fruit of a pearl.
There is no god equal to Brahman; there is no teacher equal to Brahman.
There is no knowledge equal to that of Brahmā; there is no austerity equal to piercing [the vital points].

One should perform the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*) for the four-faced God, the eldest of the gods, with the great sounds of conchs, kettledrums, and other instruments accompanied by songs;
O King, one should perform this lustration according to the prescribed rite on every festival day.
For as many thousands of yugas as he performs dance and instrumental music, or song or vocal music, at the time of bathing during the three junctions of the day, he is honored in the world of Brahmā;
hear now the fruit of his merit.
For as many days as one performs singing, dancing, instrumental music, and the like,
for that many thousands of eons one is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
[One should bathe] with the five products of a tawny cow (pañcagavya) mixed with water infused with kuśa grass.
One should bathe [the image] with water purified by mantras; that is indeed remembered as the Brāhma-bath.
O Lord of Men, a bath performed with the five products of a tawny cow (pañcagavya), along with curd, milk, and ghee, should be known to be a hundred times more efficacious than others.
One should always bring a tawny cow for the purpose of the divine fire-ritual;
indeed, this applies to Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas, but never to a Śūdra.
If a Śūdra should drink the milk of a tawny cow prepared for the sake of a divine rite, [he incurs sin].
He would be cooked for a very long time in the most terrible ocean of hell; however,
by anointing oneself with the ghee of the eldest of the gods (the *surajyeṣṭha*), whatever sin has been accumulated over thousands of millions of years will be burned away— of this there is no doubt.
Whatever sin has been accumulated over thousands of millions of kalpas,
a single bath with ghee offered to the Grandfather (Brahmā) on the first day of the lunar fortnight burns it away, just as fire consumes fuel.
By performing this ghee-bath even once on the first day, one is released from the debt born of one's ancestors.

Having delivered twenty-one generations of one's family, he is honored in the world of Viṣṇu. Whatever fruit is obtained by one who, with devotion, gives ten thousand cows— endowed with garments, gold, and other gifts— to those who have mastered the Vedas, that same fruit is attained through the ritual bathing [of the image] with milk.
He who bathes [the deity] once with clarified butter and milk shall travel by a vehicle made of the Ganges to the same world as Brahmā.
O Hero, having bathed the Lotus-born Viṣṇu once with curds, one shall attain Viṣṇu.
Having bathed [the image] with honey, one is glorified in the world of heroes;
he who performs the bathing of Viriñci here with sugarcane juice goes to the world of Savitṛ, illuminating the sky with his splendor.
He who, with devotion, bathes the Lotus-born Lord with pure water,
having cast off the mire of sin, surely attains residence in the same world [as the Lord].
He who bathes the All-pervading Lord even once with water filtered through a cloth—

He whose soul is ever-contented shall attain mastery over the world. He who bathes the Lotus-born Lord with devotion using all medicinal herbs is glorified in the world of Brahmā, traveling in a golden celestial chariot.
Whoever bathes the Lotus-born One with water scented with sandalwood attains the world of Rudra, radiant like gold.
[One should always offer] *pāṭala*, blue lotus, red lotus, and *karavīra* flowers.
At the time of bathing, one should employ substances that are stable and fragrant.
Having performed the bath with devotion using even one of these for Brahmā,
one shakes off the mire of sin and is glorified in the world of the Creator.
He who bathes the Lotus-born One with water scented with camphor and agallochum becomes purified of all sins and is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
[One should bathe] the Lord with pure water over which the Gāyatrī has been recited a hundred times.
Having bathed [the Lord] once with devotion, one shall attain the world of Brahmā;
then, having bathed the All-pervading One with cool water and subsequently with warm flowing milk,
and thereafter performing a bath with ghee, one is liberated from sins.
Having performed these three baths and having worshipped with devotion,
a person obtains the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices.
A bath with earthen jars or copper jars shall yield a hundredfold merit.
It is said that [the merit] with silver is one hundred thousandfold, while with gold it becomes ten millionfold.
Seeing Brahmā is meritorious; touching him is superior to seeing him;
worshipping him is better than touching him; and bathing him with ghee is even more excellent than that.
Since the lotus-born Brahmā destroys verbal and mental sins of embodied beings through a bath with ghee, one should therefore perform that bath; having bathed [the deity],
one should worship with devotion— listen to how this is done, O Bhārata.
Wearing clean garments, having bathed, and having performed the ritual placement of mantras (nyāsa), O Bhārata,
one should draw a four-handed lotus divided into four parts;
in its center, one should draw a wheel adorned with twelve petals.
Then, having placed the syllables around the lotuses on all sides,
another syllable is prescribed to be inscribed upon the portion of the petals;
one should write them in successive order through the combination of various colors.
The center should be intensely black, while the other [parts] should be yellow and red;
the pure white portion should be made circular in the middle part.
One should surround the Lord of the Wheel (cakranāyaka) with outer circles of light and earrings.
Having thus drawn [the diagram] with effort, one should then place the root mantra.

The wise practitioner should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *praṇava* from the crown of the head down to the soles of the feet. One should place it in the form of sound (*nāda*) until the emptiness of that sound is reached.
One should place the syllable *ta* on the head, the syllable *sa* on the circle of the face,
the syllable *vi* in the region of the throat, and the syllable *tu* at all the joints;
the syllable *va* in the center of the heart, and the syllable *re* on both sides.

One should place the syllable *ṇa* on the right side of the abdomen and the syllable *ya* on that which is called the left. One should place the syllable *bha* at the navel of the hips and the syllable *rgo* on the joints of the knees.
Having placed the syllable *de* on the two shanks, one should place the syllable *va* on the two lotus-feet.
Having placed the syllable *sy* on the two thumbs, one should place the syllable *dhī* on the chest;
the syllable *ma* on the region of the knees, and the syllable *hi* residing in the private parts.
Having placed the syllable *dhi* on the heart, one should place the syllable *yo* on the two lips.
One should place the syllable *na* on the tip of the nose, the syllable *pra* supported by the eyes,
the syllable *co* between the eyebrows, and the syllable *da* supported by the vital breath (*prāṇa*). One should assign the syllable *yā* to the head and the syllable *ta* supported by the hair.
O King, having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon one's own body, one should likewise perform it upon the deity;
having provided all the ritual offerings (*upacāra*),
one should gaze intently [upon the deity] who is blended with saffron, agallochum, camphor, and sandalwood.
Having prepared scented water with the Gāyatrī and the Praṇava, one should sprinkle all the ritual substances; thereafter, one should perform the worship.
One should place the Praṇava within all the knots of the thread.
Having further uttered the *praṇava* (Oṃ), which faces in all directions,
one should place it in the center of the lotus for the purpose of accomplishing the pedestal (*pīṭha*). The earth is to be known as the seat, considered the supporter of all beings.
She is considered to reside in the short *oṃkāra*, while in the long *oṃkāra* she is the King of the Gods (*devarāj*).

But in the protracted (*pluta*) form, she pervades the state that bestows liberation and consists of nectar. A yogi who is intent on effort and devoted to the vital breath (*prāṇa*) shall not turn back.
Then one should perform the invocation with the supreme syllable;
having invoked Him whose form is light, one should then install the excellent mantras.
Thereafter, one should visualize the God, four-faced and seated upon a lotus.
Having honored the creator of all worlds, who is the source of Viṣṇu and Rudra,
one should prepare all the requisite materials, such as perfumes and flowers, in their proper order;
reciting the Gāyatrī mantra, one should perform all the ritual acts.
Flowers, incense, as well as lamps and most enchanting food offerings— namely, candied sugar, *laḍḍukas*, *śrīveṣṭakas*, *kāsāras*, *aśokavartikas*,
*svastikas*, *ullopikās*, milk-based sweets, sesame cakes, and *tilāḍhikās*.
One should also give ripe fruits with pieces of molasses attached,
as well as various other items and diverse kinds of cakes;
O King, one should cause all such things to be given according to one's capacity.

Then, one should visualize the body of the deity by means of the root mantra; I shall now tell you the procedure by which one should also worship him. Having performed three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma) for the purification of the body, indeed—
Then one should invoke Ananta, who always upholds the Word;
having meditated upon Ananta, one should then meditate upon Rudra situated in the midst of the filaments of the lotus,
and thereafter meditate upon the god Viṣṇu, born from the interior of that lotus, and install him there.
O King, one should worship with the root mantra the lotus-born [Brahmā] seated upon the three deities in the center of the lotus;
one should also worship the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, and the Sāmaveda.
O King, a wise person should worship Knowledge, Dispassion,
Sovereignty, and Dharma in all directions and intermediate points, beginning with the northeast (Īśāna) and proceeding in order.
Likewise, one should worship the Śikṣā, Kalpa, Vyākaraṇa, Nirukta, and Chandas.
O mighty-armed one, he also taught astronomy and all the Upavedas,
as well as the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, in their proper order and according to what was appropriate; and always in the presence of the Lord, he taught phonetics, ritual manuals, and grammar.

Then, O King, one should worship according to the prescribed rite all the other Kalpas and so forth, located in the cardinal and intermediate directions, together with all the Mahāvyāhṛtis accompanied by the Praṇava, following the sequence starting from the east.
These powers of Brahman, which exist in the form of the worlds,
are themselves established as mantras and should be worshipped with diligence.
One should also worship the six oceans situated within the spokes.
The constellations, the planets, and especially the zodiac signs,
all established at the forefront of the gods, are to be worshipped according to the prescribed rule;
likewise, the Nāgas and Garuḍa are to be worshipped in the front.
The deities, the sages, and the principal mountain ranges—
all of whom are abodes of that splendor— should be worshipped with diligent effort.
First, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the rules, using water purified by mantras.
One should install the limbs, beginning with the heart, in their entirety upon the heart and other parts;
likewise, O bull among the Bharatas, one should worship the tuft, the eyes, the armor, and the weapon,
as well as these directions beginning with that of Mahendra, according to the prescribed rite, O King.
The heart is to be worshipped in front, and the head of the God behind;
one should first worship the God in his entirety with the root mantra.
Then, O bull among the Bharatas, one should perform the dismissal after displaying the mudrā.
O tiger among men, one should employ the goad for summoning and the lotus for the initial invocation.
He who thus worships the God on every first lunar day (pratipad),
having fasted on the fifteenth day (the full moon), attains the supreme state.
Sumantu said:
This mantra, "āpo hi ṣṭhā," is proclaimed as the heart;
"ṛtaṃ satyam" is declared the crest-lock (śikhā); and one should designate "ud u tyaṃ" as the eye.
"Citraṃ devānām udagāt" is renowned throughout all the worlds;
with this I cover your armor, which is called "kavaca.
Likewise, "bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ" is proclaimed for the head.
The practitioner who has the Gāyatrī as the root of his tantra for all rites should worship the Deity with the Gāyatrī consecrated by the syllable Oṃ;
he should worship all others, such as the Ṛgveda and the rest, with the Praṇava.
O Hero, at the time of invocation, worship, and the dismissal of Brahmā,
the Gāyatrī is the supreme mantra, the mother of the Vedas, and the radiant one.
He who worships the deity with the essential principles of the syllables of the Gāyatrī [attains success].
"He shall go to the abode of Brahmā, which is difficult to attain and hard for the wicked to reach.

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Worship of Brahmā," in the Brāhma Parvan of the Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the Saṃhitā consisting of fifty thousand verses, in the section on the Pratipat Kalpa.
Now begins the eighteenth chapter.
The Description of the Completion of the Ritual Practice. Sumantu said: O lord of men, having observed the fast on the full moon day with devotion, [one should proceed].
O mighty-armed one, the man who worships Viriñci according to this rite on the first day of the lunar fortnight shall go to the abode of Brahmā;
specifically with *ṛg* verses, he should worship the Goddess, Viriñci, and the deities of the site.
In the month of Kārttika, the chariot procession (rathayātrā) of the Lord is proclaimed;
by performing it with devotion, a human being attains the same world as Brahmā.
O King of kings, on the full moon day of the month of Kārttika, [one should worship] the Four-faced One.

O scorcher of enemies, he should cause the entire city to be circumambulated along with the skin, the bowstring, and Sāvitrī, accompanied by various musical instruments. Having thus circumambulated it, O King, he should establish it within the city in the presence of the people.
Having first fed a Brāhmaṇa and worshipped Śāṇḍileya,
one should place the Lord upon the chariot amidst the sounds of auspicious musical instruments;
having worshipped the son of Śāṇḍilī at the front of the chariot according to the prescribed rites.
Having caused the Brahmins to recite the benedictions and performed the auspicious *puṇyāha* rite,
he should place the deity upon the chariot and keep a vigil (*prajāgara*) with various kinds of spectacles and abundant Vedic chants.
Having thus kept a vigil, O King, at dawn he should feed the Brahmins according to his ability with various kinds of foods, both hard and soft;
and having honored the people, O hero, O King, he should worship Vajra according to the prescribed rites.
O mighty-armed king, having caused the Brahmins to recite the benedictions according to the prescribed ritual with seeds, milk, and milk-rice,
and having proclaimed the "Auspicious Day," one should cause the chariot to be paraded through the city.
Brahmins who are learned in the four Vedas should cause the chariot of Brahmā to be wheeled around;
likewise, with the recitations of the Bahvṛcas, Atharvaṇas, Chandogas, and Adhvaryus,
they should cause that chariot of the God of gods, the eldest of the Suras, to be wheeled around.
The entire city should be circumambulated by a very smooth path;
O hero, the chariot must not be drawn by a Śūdra who desires auspiciousness.
O King, a wise man should not mount the chariot, with the sole exception of the Bhojaka.
O King, one should place Sāvitrī on the right side of Brahmā,
the Bhojaka on the left side, and the lotus-born Brahmā in front.
Thus, amidst the sounds of musical instruments and the abundant blasts of conch shells, [the rite proceeds].
Having caused the chariot to circumambulate the entire city, O King,
the wise man should perform the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*) and place it back in its original position.
Whoever performs this procession with devotion, or even merely beholds it, [attains great merit].
He who draws the chariot shall go to the abode of Brahmā;
he who offers a lamp in the hall of Brahmā on the new moon day of the month of Kārttika shall go to the abode of Brahmā.
On the first day of the lunar fortnight (pratipad), he who honors Brahmins with lamps mixed with molasses and with unwashed garments shall go to the abode of Brahmā; likewise,
he who worships himself with perfumes, flowers, and new clothes [shall attain the same].
On that first lunar day (pratipadā), he shall go to the abode of Brahmā.
This is a highly meritorious lunar day, marking the commencement of King Bali’s reign;
it is eternally dear to Brahmā and is celebrated as the Bāleyā.
Having honored the Brahmins on this day, and especially himself,
he goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu, whose splendor is immeasurable.
O mighty-armed one, in the month of Caitra, the first lunar day (pratipad) is supremely auspicious.

O best of men, O King, O tiger among the Kurus, whoever bathes after touching a *śvapaca* (outcaste) in that [river], for him there shall be no sin whatsoever, nor mental afflictions, nor physical diseases; therefore, one should perform a bath there.
That divine *nīrājana* rite indeed destroys all diseases;
O King, one should adorn everything there— cows, buffaloes, and so forth—
with oil, weapons, and the like, and lead them beneath the archway (*toraṇa*).
O perpetuator of the Kuru lineage, one should likewise provide food for the Brahmins.
For these three lunar days are declared to be supreme, O joy of the Kurus:
those in the months of Kārttika, Āśvayuja, and Caitra, O Bhārata.
"O King, whatever lunar day occurs in the month of Kārttika, bathing and giving gifts on that day yield a hundredfold merit;
it bestows the happiness of attaining the kingdom of Bali and destroys the impurities of the dust.

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Conclusion of the Pratipat Kalpa," in the Brāhma Parvan of the Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, in the Saṃhitā consisting of fifty thousand verses.
Now begins the nineteenth chapter, the description of Puṣpadvitīyā within the narrative of Śaryāti. Sumantu said:
"But on the second day, O Indra among kings, the two Aśvins, who drink the Soma,
were made [such] by Cyavana at the sacrifice even as Maghavan looked on.
Śatānīka said:
How did those two become drinkers of Soma while Indra looked on? Tell me that, as Cyavana performed it even as the gods were watching.
Oh, how great was the ascetic power of that high-souled Cyavana!
"Since both were brought to the state of divinity solely through the power of Indra," Sumantu said:
"O lord of men, this occurred in the transition between the ancient yugas, during the final period."
Having adopted the practice of yoga, Cyavana lived for a long time on the bank of the Gaṅgā.
There, Śaryāti arrived with his harem to bathe;
having bathed and worshipped the ancestors and the gods, he prepared to depart.
There, the king beheld a bewildered people struggling on the path,
obstructed by the discharge of excrement and urine, their movements paralyzed as if struck by a celestial light;
seeing them wandering aimlessly here and there, he [encountered] his army.
The king, dejected in mind, spoke to his ministers who were before him:
"This is indeed the hermitage of Cyavana; surely no one has committed an offense.
When no one said anything in reply as the king was thus questioning them, he continued:
Then his daughter Sukanyā spoke these words to her father: "O father, listen;
I shall tell you of a wonderful marvel that I saw with my companions. Hear it, O father, for it is most marvelous."
In this forest, I heard the faint, indistinct notes of cuckoos, as well as the abundant tinkling sounds of waist-bands, anklets, and girdles— sounds of women singing, lamenting,
and sporting there.
"O fair maiden, come here! Come here!"—thus a voice issued from the anthill.
"O dear one, having gone there, we shall surely behold a marvel: two fires with motionless flames, like two lamps. Then the maiden spoke again.

And out of curiosity, O father, and without understanding what it was, I struck them with the tips of darbha-grass needles; thereupon, his splendor subsided. Hearing that, the king, seized with terror, quickly came to that forest.
Where the descendant of Bhṛgu, that sage who had entered within an anthill, was dwelling in distress, he went there, prostrated himself before that best of the twice-born, and said:
"O Lord, I have committed an offense; forgive it, for salutations be unto you."
He said to that king: "O lord of men, I have understood;
O King, give me Sukanyā, for I am seeking a wife. By bestowing Sukanyā upon me in due order, O King, become happy."
Thus addressed, the king gave away Sukanyā without hesitation.
Then, having returned to his own city, he dwelt there for a very long time in happiness.
Having obtained a husband, Sukanyā too was well-pleased and then devoted herself to his service.
Having renounced the glory of sovereignty and donned bark garments and deerskins,
after a long time had passed and spring had arrived,
she— whose every limb was illuminated by asceticism and who was endowed with the virtues of beauty and nobility— [appeared].
To his wife, who had just bathed, Cyavana spoke in sweet words:
"Come, come, auspicious lady; may you be blessed. Come to the bed;
today give birth to offspring who shall increase both lineages."
Thus addressed, the maiden spoke with joined palms to her husband:
"O most auspicious one, you ought not to have union with me today upon this uneven ground.
Do what is pleasing to me now, and then summon me."
Just as you used to stay in your father’s house upon a well-prepared bed,
variegated with many colors such as red ochre, white, yellow, and crimson,
and adorned with garments, ornaments, perfumes, and the like— do you likewise do so now.
"May I behold myself endowed with youth, possessed of beauty and great luster, richly adorned with garments, ornaments, and perfumes, and regarded with respect.
Having heard the words of Sukanyā, Cyavana spoke, dejected in spirit.
"I have no wealth, O auspicious lady; your father has as much as he has in the forest.
How then shall I adorn myself today, and how shall I appear handsome? Tell me.
She, smiling and with palms joined in reverence, spoke again to her husband:
Vittala gave wealth, Vairocana gave his form,
and Cyavana said to his wife, "I shall not cause the depletion of my ascetic merit.
Having spoken thus, he then performed severe penance for a very long time.
Then, as time passed, the two heroic Aśvins arrived there and beheld Sukanyā, who, by her radiance, was indeed like a goddess.
Approaching her, they both said to her: "Who are you, O beautiful one, endowed with such form?"
"For what purpose do you stand here alone? Who is your support?
That slender-limbed woman replied to them both: "I am indeed the daughter of Śaryāti, and Cyavana is my husband; who are you two? Let that be told to me."
And the two Aśvin deities said: "O daughter of a king, know us to be the Aśvins.
What will you do with one who is both aged and emaciated?
