Choose one of us as your husband, whichever you desire."
But she replied, "O dwellers of heaven, you ought not to speak thus to me;
for my heart is devoted to my husband, just as Svāhā is to Vibhāvasu.
The two Aśvins said:
"Let Cyavana come and enter the Vaiṣṇava water today;
then, choose one of us two who stands between you, or whichever other you desire.
They both said, "Go and ask your own husband about Sukanyā."
"Having questioned him, return here again to our presence;
we two shall remain right here until your arrival.
She went and told her husband what the two Aśvins had said.
"We shall make you a husband endowed with beauty, whichever one you desire;
then, from among these three, you may choose one as your husband.
"So be it," Cyavana said quickly to his wife.
Taking him, she went quickly to where both those physicians were. She said to them, "O Aśvins, perform exactly as was spoken by Cyavana; for Sukanyā has chosen you as her desired husbands."
Having taken hold of him, the two entered the Gaṅgā with the sage;
after a moment, rising up endowed with beauty and splendor,
those mighty-armed ones, possessed of ascetic power, shone like lotuses that have burst through the water.
O lotus-eyed one, just as at the beginning of the kalpa the sky arose for Brahmā from the water within the jar,
so all of them emerged from that [water] with identical forms;
then Sukanyā beheld her husband, who possessed a divine form.
Filled with great joy, O Bhārata, she did not recognize him;
seeing those who were identical in body, identical in age, identical in form, and identical in splendor,
all alike in their dress and ornaments, she fell into deep reflection for a long time.
Having reflected for a very long time, she said to the physicians and the gods:
"Even though Bībhatsu has been rejected by me, he was never truly abandoned.
How could I, having rejected one who is like yourselves, choose another?"
"Therefore, O dwellers of heaven, bestow him alone as her husband.
Then, having been requested with great respect by her with palms joined in reverence, those two—
bearing their own divine marks and being well-honored— consented.
But Sukanyā, having gazed intently at the two of them, was overwhelmed;
for they were indeed free from dust, free from blinking, and their feet did not touch the ground.
This one, however, is covered in dust, withered, and stands resting upon the earth.
Having understood that very moment [of his choice], Cyavana was indeed chosen;
when Cyavana was chosen by Sukanyā, a rain of flowers fell,
and celestial drums were sounded many times over.
Then Cyavana, pleased and assuming a divine form, spoke to the two Aśvins with great joy: "What shall I do for you?
Your wife has been restored, and your beauty has been made such that it is difficult even for the gods to attain."
He who does not perform a supreme service for one who has rendered him a service shall indeed go in succession through twenty-one hells;
therefore, I shall certainly perform a most excellent, superhuman service.
"Out of joy, I shall certainly perform a service for you both;
I shall grant the fruit of a share in the sacrifice, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain.
Having spoken thus, the great sage dismissed the two lords of the gods.
Accompanied by his wife, he arrived at the holy hermitage filled with joy.
Then Śaryāti heard that Cyavana possessed a divine form;
and the self-controlled king of great splendor went to see that best of sages.
Having seen him, he first prostrated and honored him as was fitting;
then, having seen Sukanyā, he prostrated, greeted her with joy,
embraced her, smelled the crown of her head, and then took her onto his lap.
Overwhelmed with tears of joy, she embraced her out of love. Having settled her there with delight, the king, together with his wife,
spoke once more to the highly gratified Cyavana, that lord of men.
"Prepare the requisites for the sacrifice, O lord of men; I shall officiate as the priest.
Having been addressed thus, the king prostrated before the great sage and, filled with joy, departed for his own city and applied himself to the efforts required for the sacrifice.
Dispatching his messengers, he quickly gathered the materials for the sacrifice;
he summoned the ministers, the family priest, and the preceptors with all haste.
O Bhārata, when all those materials had been brought together, [he performed the rites].
The pure-souled Cyavana arrived together with his wife;
having been duly honored, he heard of the great and powerful renunciation [of Śibi],
along with many others, including Atri, Aṅgiras, and Bhārgava.
When the great sacrifice had been inaugurated by that best of kings as he performed the duties of the patron,
and while the oblations were being poured into the sacrificial fire,
all the inhabitants of heaven were summoned and arrived, welcomingly, for the sake of their shares.
When the sacrificial portion had been set forth according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures,
the two Aśvins arrived there, having been summoned by Cyavana.
O King, while the invitation was being made to the two Aśvins at that time—
Then Indra said to Cyavana, "Do not grant these two their shares;
they are the physicians of the gods, not entitled to a portion, nor are they deities.
Cyavana, however, replied to Indra, "For both of these are indeed gods."
"These two have been my benefactors; I shall give them a share, of this there is no doubt.
Thereupon, Śakra spoke with anger and wrath to Cyavana:
"O Brahmin-sage, I shall strike you if you grant them a share!"
Thus addressed, the brahmin-sage said nothing at all;
yet, raising the sacrificial ladle with the sacred mantra, he offered two portions to the Aśvins.
Then, having raised the thunderbolt, the Lord of Heaven desired to hurl it.
Then, O lord of men, Indra was paralyzed by Cyavana along with his thunderbolt;
having thus paralyzed Indra and granted a share to the two Aśvins,
he then completed the sacrificial rite according to the prescribed rules.
Then Kañjaja arrived quickly and said to Cyavana at that time,
"Let this written document be suspended, and let there be a share here for the two Aśvins.
Then Indra, with a pleased mind, spoke thus to Cyavana.
"I know your supreme power of asceticism here, O Cyavana.
Indeed, this was done by me for the purpose of making your asceticism known.
From this day forward, let there be a share [of the sacrifice] and likewise divinity for the two Aśvins."
Listen now to the meritorious fruit for that pure-souled person who shall either read or even hear this account of your ascetic power:
having gone to the abode of Virocana, and likewise having gone to the abode of Puṣpa.
Then, at that time, Vāmadeva’s assembly hall was filled with Muñjakeśas;
he remained there engaged in play, endowed with youth—of this there is no doubt.
Having spoken thus, the self-controlled god quickly departed for his own abode.
Cyavana, accompanied by his wife, having recovered from his illness, returned to his hermitage.
There he beheld a mansion built by the gods, resembling a celestial chariot,
furnished with excellent beds and seats, and endowed with the fulfillment of every desire.
Adorned with gardens and ponds, brought there by the Lord of the Gods, that house— resembling a mass of cow-herbs (or a cluster of clouds)— shone forth, being difficult to find on earth;
it was filled with great, divine ornaments, rich in jewels.
The great sage, together with his wife, received all of that— dustless garments and divine robes—
and attained the highest joy; he then praised Śakra.
Thus, O King, this second lunar day (dvitīyā) of the month of Āśvina is so esteemed;
it is here, O Bhārata, that the two Aśvins attained divinity and their share of the sacrifice.
Listen, O lord of men, to the ritual procedure by which it should be observed as a fast.
O lord of men, he who desires beautiful form should,
on the second day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, O lord of men,
remain self-restrained and subsist on flowers for one year.
O lord of men, one should eat those sacrificial flowers that are available in season after having given them to the Brahmins; likewise,
one may give flowers made of gold or silver, or even those born in water.
At the conclusion of his vow, the two gods, the Aśvins, being well-pleased with him,
granted him a divine, exceedingly radiant celestial chariot that travels at will;
for a very long time, he delighted in heaven among women in the world of the Aśvins.
Having come here at the end of the kalpa, he was born as a preeminent brahmin;
for seven successive births,
he was born as a learned brahmin who knew the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences during the Kṛta Yuga.
A donor, a lord of sacrifice, eloquent, and free from mental and physical ailments,
surrounded by sons and grandsons, he shall dwell for a long time with his wife;
in the Middle Country, in a beautiful city, he shall become a righteous ruler of the kingdom.
Thus has this second [kalpa], known as Puṣpa, been recounted to you.
O Muñjakeśinī, there shall indeed be another known as Phala;
it is exceedingly meritorious, a destroyer of sins, and dear to Viṣṭaraśravas.

O joy of the Kurus, she is renowned in the world as Aśūnyaśayanā. By fasting upon her, O King, a man who is endowed with faith and devotion rejoices together with his wife in prosperity, growth, and fortune.

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Puṣpadvitīyā" within the narrative of Śaryāti, in the Brāhma Parvan of the Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty thousand verses, in the second Kalpa.
Now begins the twentieth chapter:
"The Greatness of the Second Lunar Day Known as Aśūnyaśayanā."
Śatānīka said:
"O tiger among the twice-born, tell me of the second [fast], known as Phala,
by fasting upon which neither man nor woman undergoes separation in this world."
O best of sages, how may a man with his wife, and a wife with her husband,
ensure that she does not become a widow? O noble one, I wish to hear about that fast which a man, together with his wife, should observe.
"Tell me that, O best of the twice-born, for the sake of the welfare of men and women,
by hearing which, O Brahmin, my curiosity spreads forth as it has never done before.
Sumantra said:
O Bhārata, listen now to the second [vow], named Aśūnyaśayanā,
by fasting upon which a woman never falls into widowhood, O lord of men,
and a man is never born separated from his wife.
O King, when Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the Universe, sleeps together with Śrī,
that lunar day should indeed be observed as Aśūnyaśayanā (the Day of the Unempty Bed),
O Bhārata, on the second day of the dark fortnight in the month of Śrāvaṇa.
Having bathed and bowed to the Lord of the universe, one should recite this after worshipping with devotion the God who bears the Śrīvatsa mark, together with Śrī:
"O bearer of the Śrīvatsa! O beloved of Śrī! O Śrīvatsa! O imperishable Lord of Śrī!"
May my household life, which yields virtue, wealth, and pleasure, not go to ruin;
may my cattle not perish, and may my people not perish;
may my female relatives not perish through the alienation of their marriages from me.
"O Lord, just as you are never separated from Lakṣmī,
so may my connection with my wife never be severed;
O Giver of Boons, let your bed never be empty of Lakṣmī."
"O Madhusūdana, may my bed likewise never be empty.
Having thus made this prayer and performed the worship of Lakṣmī and Hari,
one should offer desired fruits in the shade to the Lord of the World.
Having bowed at the temple at night, one should eat the sacrificial offering while restraining one's speech;
on the second day, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brāhmaṇa according to one’s ability.
Śatānīka said:
O Brahmin, please tell me which desired fruits are to be offered upon the bed of Keśava, the God of gods;
and what gift should be given to the Brāhmaṇa on the second day?
"O best of the twice-born, by devotees of the God of gods, according to their capacity...
Sumantu said: "O mighty-armed one, whatever fruits are available there at that time,"
O best of kings, O monarch, on the day of the funeral couch, offerings should be given according to one's own capacity— neither excessively sweet nor indeed bitter. By offering sweet things,
a man shall attain popularity.
And a woman, O tiger among the Kurus, attains the favor of her husband;
therefore, one should avoid pungent and bitter things that are feminine in name,
such as dates, citrons, and white garlic.
O tiger among the Kurus, fruits should be given according to one's ability upon the bed of Muñjakeśin, who receives a share of the sacrifice from the king;
however, for a Brahmin, these same items, together with [images of] Gaṅgeya, should be provided.
On the second day, O Bhārata, one should devoutly give gifts according to one's capacity,
including the gift of clothing along with gifts of grain and fruit;
indeed, they declare that the gift of grain is especially meritorious for the son of Gaṅgā.
O Hero, for the man who performs this correctly for four months, there shall be no destruction of his home for three lifetimes;
he shall never sleep on an empty bed and shall accomplish the goals of dharma, desire, and wealth.
A man becomes one whose sovereignty is unimpeded; of this there is no doubt.
And a woman who knows the dharma, O King, who performs this vow according to the prescribed rule, does not become an object of grief for her circle of kinsmen.
O best of men, O descendant of Kuru, by performing this great vow, one does not incur widowhood, misfortune, or abandonment by a husband in a future birth,
provided that one does not eat pungent fruits here without first giving them away.
O Indra among kings, having given dates, citrons, large-fruited sirīṣas,
and other supreme sweets to the twice-born,
one should therefore diligently offer sweet things according to one's own capacity.
Thus has been described this most excellent lunar day, the second of Kṛṣṇa;
by fasting upon it, O King, a man shall attain prosperity as well as growth.
Śatānīka said:

"O tiger among the twice-born, this second lunar day has indeed been described by you as most excellent. How is it that Janārdana, together with Padmā, is to be worshipped on this day known as Phala-saṃjñā?"
"O twice-born one, a very great curiosity arises in me regarding this.
Sumantra said: "It is exactly so, there is no doubt; you speak thus, O Bhārata."
"This lunar day indeed belongs to the Aśvins; however, listen to my words.
It has been given to Viṣṇu of immeasurable splendor as the Aśūnyaśayana (the vow of the non-empty bed).
O tiger among men, perform it for the pleasure of Muñjakeśin [Viṣṇu] through the two Aśvins."
O tiger among the Kurus, O lord of the earth, those two alone are worshipped here:
the two Nāsatyas, the Lord Viṣṇu, and Datta; and Śrī is likewise perceived [therein].
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, at the conclusion of the second Kalpa, in the Brāhma Parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, in the Saṃhitā consisting of fifty thousand verses.
Now begins the twenty-first chapter:
The Greatness of the Vow of the Third Lunar Day. Sumantu said:
A devoted wife, whose very life is her husband, who delights in serving her husband—
even such a woman, when described as pure, beautiful,
and virtuous, should observe a fast on the third lunar day and strictly avoid salt.
She indeed undertakes this vow with devotion until the end of her life;
and Gaurī, being well-pleased, grants beauty, good fortune,
loveliness, grace, charm, and that which is praiseworthy and delightful to men.

O King, by the observance of the Gaurī-vrata and by abstaining from salt, a woman becomes pleasing to her husband and a husband becomes pleasing to his wife. O Lord, listen to this vow as Dharmarāja hears it.
Listen to me as I relate the words spoken by Umā in the past:
"I have created this vow which brings about good fortune for men;
and whatever mortal woman, being self-restrained, shall perform this vow."
She shall rejoice together with her husband, just as my husband Hara does;
and whatever virtuous maiden, though beautiful, does not find a husband,
she should observe this vow while subsisting on food that is free from salt.
With her mind fixed on me and her thoughts absorbed in me, my devotee who has accepted me as her own should establish an image of Gaurī made of gold, adorned with perfumes and ornaments,
clothed in garments and finery, and decorated with a circle of flowers.
O descendant of Bharata, one should offer salt, molasses, ghee, and oil to the Goddess according to one's ability; likewise, O King, one should offer pungent pieces, cumin, leafy vegetables,
sweetmeats mixed with molasses and ghee, and pastries filled with sugar-candy.
One should give it to a Brāhmaṇa who is perfected in his vows and deeply learned in the scriptures.
It should always be given during the bright fortnight according to one's ability, preferably made of gold;
however, O King, for one who lacks wealth, it may be made of honey-wood (madhuvṛkṣa) out of devotion.
Gaurī is always worthy of worship there due to her constant presence; of this there is no doubt.
Restraining her speech, she eats at night food that is neither pungent nor salty.
Gaurī is eternally present there, sleeping upon a bed of grass spread on the ground.
O mighty-armed one, listen as I describe that which was proclaimed by the Goddess for one who is thus disciplined— a teaching of great fruit:
a maiden shall obtain as a husband the one she desires in her heart, who follows her wishes.
Having sported here for a very long time with her husband, and having established progeny, she goes together with him to the world of Heli,
the world of Candra, and the world of Citraśikhaṇḍin.
O King, descendant of Bharata, having gone there, she went to the assembly hall of Vāmadeva.
But when the queen was a widow, O King, she remained devoted to her vows,
constantly self-restrained toward her husband and always intent on his worship.
And here, having cast off her own body and beholding her beloved in the city of Hari,
she shall snatch herself away from the messengers of Yama and rejoice in heaven with her husband for ten times ten million years; having rejoiced there, she shall return here.
Together with her husband, she obtained the desired fruit mentioned previously.
O lord of men, even Indrāṇī, desiring a son, performed this vow;
at the conclusion of the vow, she obtained a son named Jayanta.
Arundhatī likewise practiced [austerities] out of desire for Vasiṣṭha;
she is seen even today in the sky in the vicinity of Vasiṣṭha.
By Rohiṇī’s renunciation of salt, there was the crushing of the host of her co-wives.
"By the grace of the Goddess, I have obtained imperishable good fortune in heaven.
Thus is this lunar day known as the third, honored by the world;
it is especially meritorious whenever it occurs in the month of Vaiśākha.

It is meritorious in the month of Bhādrapada, and likewise in Māgha; of this there is no doubt. For women, it is declared to be auspicious in both Māgha and Bhādrapada, O Bhārata; however, in Vaiśākha, it is common to all people.
O King, on the third day of the month of Māgha, the giving of molasses and salt brings great merit to both women and men;
Datta is pleased by molasses, while Viśvabhū is pleased by salt.
Likewise, balls of molasses (guḍapūpa) should be given in the month of Bhādrapada;
and on the third day of Māgha, for the pleasure of Vāmadeva,
the gift of water and sweetmeats (modaka) is highly praised, O Bhārata.
O King of kings, on the third lunar day of the month of Vaiśākha, Brahmā is pleased by water mixed with sandalwood, while Bhīma is indeed pleased by sweetmeats (modakas).
By the gift of sandalwood here, the Lotus-born One is gratified; of this there is no doubt.
O tiger among the Kurus, this lunar day that occurs in the month of Vaiśākha is indeed inexhaustible in the world and is celebrated by the gods;
O mighty-armed one, when it arrives, those devoted to their vows offer abundant oblations to the moon.

Gold, as well as food and especially ghee—whatever is given there becomes inexhaustible; for this reason, it is remembered as "Inexhaustible" (Akṣayā). Whatever gift is given, whether it be small or large, [it becomes inexhaustible].

All that indeed becomes inexhaustible; for this reason, it is known as the Inexhaustible (Akṣayā). O Hero, the man who gives water-pots filled with water and seeds on this day goes to the world of Hemamālin.
Thus, O Hero, has this third lunar day (tithi), the most excellent, been described;
by fasting upon which, O King, a man shall enjoy prosperity, growth, and fortune.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual for the Third Day," in the Brāhma Parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, consisting of fifty thousand verses.
Now begins the twenty-second chapter:
The Greatness of the Vow of the Fourth Lunar Day. Sumantu said:
On the fourth day, O King, always observing the vow of fasting,
he gives sesame-rice to a Brahmin and then eats sesame-rice himself. When the completion of the vow occurs at the end of two years—
Vināyaka, being pleased with him, grants his desired fruit;
he indeed becomes an abode of fortune, sports with great splendors,
and upon returning here at the end of his merit, he possesses a divine body and glory.
Intelligent, steadfast, eloquent, fortunate, and acting according to his own will,
he can accomplish even the most difficult and great tasks in an instant; indeed,
aided by his sons and accompanied by horses and chariots, he destroys all opposition.
"That king shall be long-lived for seven births;
thus does the gratified Vināyaka, the destroyer of obstacles, grant [this boon].
Śatānīka said:
"By whom was this obstacle created by him, such that he is known as Vighnavināyaka?
O Lord of Obstacles, tell me today the cause of this obstacle.
Sumantu said:
When the auspicious marks of men and women had been performed by the youth,
Vināyaka, the Lord of Obstacles, created an impediment for Gāṅgeya;
and perceiving that obstacle, Kārttikeya was filled with wrath.
Having pulled out a tooth from his mouth, he prepared to kill him;
but the Lord of Gods restrained him and asked, "Why should you harbor such anger?
He then explained to his father that he had indeed performed the characteristic mark of a Pūruṣa.
"In that matter, no woman has been able to create an obstacle for me, nor have they possessed my characteristic.
Then Mahādeva, laughing, said to his son:
"My son, tell me, what characteristic of mine do you perceive?"
He said, "Place this skull, marked with the sign of a twice-born, in your hand without hesitation; for that reason, you shall be called Kapālī.
Taking that token, he cast it into the ocean in a rage.
Then, while the assembly of the gods was indeed convened, a dispute arose between Brahmā and Rudra, each saying, "I am the elder, I am the elder. [Rudra said:
"You know the origin of this world, but no one knows me."
When Śiva had spoken thus, the fifth head of Brahmā, letting out a loud, liberated laugh, replied: "May I become your knower.
Thus did the great Hayashiras speak to Rudra on behalf of Brahmā.
Cut off by the tip of his claw, it remained in his very hand;
with that [claw] still held in his hand, he went to where Hari was.
At that time, the self-controlled Lord was performing austerities on Mount Meru.
When that horse-head had been cut off, another man emerged from that place of Brahmā out of anger; he was white-eared,
wearing armor, with a helmet, and equipped with an arrow and a bow.
"His form is indescribable and he wears a garland; what shall I do? He replied.
Then Brahmā said in anger, "Let that evil-minded one be slain!
But he [the demon] approached Rudra's path swiftly out of rage.

Rudra, too, entered and was presided over by the splendors of Viṣṇu. Having entered, he then beheld the supreme Lord Nārāyaṇa, the unconquered Vaikuṇṭha, performing intense penance. Hara [beheld] the divine Nārāyaṇa.
Then, seeing that Hara had arrived and reflecting upon his purpose,
the god said to the wielder of the trident, "Pierce my arm with your trident.
Thereupon, the immensely radiant Hara pierced that arm with his trident.
From the piercing by the trident, blood rose upward, pervading heaven and earth;
then, turning back, it fell upon a skull-cup.
Having fallen into the skull-cup, the blood increased in volume through the forefinger.
For when there was to be a cessation regarding the god's blood,
he then assumed the form of Varuṇa and discharged water;
and as that blood became water, it flowed upon the skull where that head lay.
With his index finger on the skull, Rudra created from the blood a man clad in armor, red, and with red earrings.
Then he said to the god Bhava, "O giver of honor, what shall I do?"
He, too, then created a man with white earrings;
those two, wielding excellent bows,
fought together like the powerful Kujā and Ketu at the end of a Yuga, O King.
As those two were thus fighting, the period of Saṃvarta passed away;
yet, at that time, victory was not seen for either of them.
Then, seeing them in the sky, an incorporeal voice spoke from the atmosphere:
"Indeed, an incarnation of both you and myself shall take place together;
for the sake of the earth, the removal of its burden must be accomplished along with the gods.
Then, a marvel shall indeed occur for the fulfillment of the purpose of the divine mission."
"Having shaken off his state as an inhabitant of the mortal world, he shall go once more to the abode of the gods.
Having spoken thus, Vaikuṇṭha then gave one [son] to Ravi;
Ravi joyfully accepted that proud youth, Śvetakuṇḍalin.
After that, he gave the red-eared one even to Indra;
and Indra, filled with joy, accepted him and went to his own city. Having seized those two men born of wrath, the Sun and the Moon departed.
Then the lotus-seated Lord spoke to Rudra:
"Go you also, O Kāpālin, to practice the vow of the skull-bearing rite;
an incarnation of this vow shall take place in the world of mortals."
"And those men who shall indeed uphold your vow—
for them nothing whatsoever will be difficult to attain, both in this world and in the next.
Having spoken thus at length and having greeted Sumukha with joy, [he departed].
Having summoned the ocean, he replied without hesitation:
"Create ornaments for women that possess extraordinary characteristics;
speak of that which was proclaimed by Kārttikeya without any deliberation."
And he said, "Let this mark of a man belong to me by my name;
that which was promised by Your Majesty shall surely come to pass.
Speak without hesitation whatever has been declared by Kārttikeya."
"Give him indeed that tusk which has now been extracted by you;
for that must certainly have belonged to someone else,
having come into his possession through the turn of fate and not by his own will— save for Vināyaka."
"Accept this *sāmudra* which has been proclaimed by you—
the excellent characteristics of men and women known as *sāmudrika*.
And indeed, fashion this Devavināyaka with its tusks."
Then Bāhuleya, filled with resentment, said to the Lord of the Gods:
"I shall give him my horn at your word; of this there is no doubt.
But when he has cast off this horn and wanders about..."
"Then, being freed from the tusk, he will reduce this to ashes.
Having said "So be it" to him,
the Lord of Gods, abiding by the opinion of Kārtikeya, placed that tusk in his hand.
O King, even today an image with horns on its hands is seen,
intended to create an obstacle for the high-souled and mighty-armed son of Bhīma.
This secret of the gods has been declared by me to you.
Where even the God does not know that which is difficult for the gods to obtain on earth—
this secret has been declared by me, being pleased with you.
This nectar of the narrative of Vināyaka has been told in connection with the lunar day (tithi).
For the wise man who causes this to be heard by Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas,
by Kshatriyas established in their own duties, and by Vaishyas and Shudras endowed with virtue—
nothing whatsoever is difficult for him to attain, both in this world and in the next.
He shall not fall into an evil state of existence, nor shall he suffer defeat;
he will accomplish all his undertakings without obstacle— of this there is no doubt—
and he shall obtain supernatural power, prosperity, and glory, O best of the Bharatas.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Fourth Kalpa," in the Brāhma Parvan of the Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty thousand verses.
[Now follows] the description of the story of Vighna-Vināyaka.
Śatānīka said:
"O Brahmin, by whom was this son of Bhīma made the lord of the Pramathas? And how did he shine as the master and the presiding authority over obstacles?
Sumantu said:
"I have been well questioned, O Indra among kings, regarding this Vināyaka who causes obstacles, and also those means by which even Vināyaka is employed to create obstacles.
I shall tell you that, O mighty-armed one; listen now with a one-pointed mind."
O hero, O descendant of Bharata, in the first Kṛta Yuga, he indeed undertook the creation of beings; having seen that actions were accomplished without obstacle,
and seeing the entire population free from affliction and full of pride, O King.
O Lord of the Earth, after reflecting many times upon this matter,
Vināyaka was appointed by the lotus-born Brahmā and the Sāttvatas for the prosperity of all creatures,
and Bhīma was likewise appointed to the lordship over the Gaṇas.
Now, learn from me the symptoms of one who is possessed by that [spirit]:
he plunges excessively into water in his dreams, sees shaven-headed men,
those dressed in saffron robes, and mounts upon carnivorous beasts.
He dwells together with outcasts, donkeys, and camels;
likewise, while walking, he imagines himself followed by others.
Dejected and with his undertakings fruitless, he sinks down without apparent cause.

O tiger among the Kurus, O King, at the end of his sleep he sees himself mounted upon Karada, likewise immersed in the waters, surrounded by foot soldiers, and proceeding toward the confluence; of this there is no doubt.
And the mind becomes distorted in form and adorned with oleanders;
one possessed by that [spirit] does not obtain the kingdom inherited from his ancestors.
Likewise, a maiden finds no husband, and a pregnant woman finds no offspring.

O Lord of the Earth, he does not obtain the status of a teacher nor the learning of a Vedic scholar, nor do his disciples obtain their studies; likewise, a merchant does not obtain profit and a farmer does not obtain success from his cultivation. For him, a ceremonial bath (snapana) must be performed on an auspicious day.
O King, having rubbed [the body] with a paste of white mustard seeds mixed with clarified butter on the fourth day of the bright fortnight, on the day of Jupiter (Thursday),
under the asterism Tiṣya (Puṣya) and the Vīra-lagna, one should perform [this] in front of that very [deity].
With his head anointed with all medicinal herbs and all fragrant substances,
seated upon an auspicious throne, and having caused the auspicious twice-born ones to pronounce blessings,
he should worship Vyomakeśa, Pārvatī, and likewise the son of Bhīma.
O dear one, descendant of Bharata, [he saw] Kṛṣṇa with his father, as well as Pavamāna, Śita, Dhiṣaṇa, the son of the Moon (Budha), Koṇa, Ketu,
Vidhuntuda, Bāhuleya, and the bearer of Nandaka.

One should cast into the waters earth from a horse-stable, an elephant-stable, an anthill, a confluence, and a lake, as well as yellow pigment (rocanā), perfumes, and guggulu resin. Indeed, these should be brought by four individuals of a single caste using jars drawn from a lake.
Likewise, let the auspicious throne be placed upon a red bull-hide;
with that which has a thousand eyes and a hundred streams, purified by the sages—I sprinkle you with it; may the purifying verses (pāvamānyas) cleanse you.
May King Varuṇa grant you fortune; may Sūrya and Bṛhaspati grant you fortune;
may Indra and Vāyu grant you fortune, and may the Seven Seers grant you fortune.
Whatever misfortune is in your hair, at your parting, or upon your head—
May those waters always destroy [impurities] on your forehead, ears, and eyes.
Having bathed, one should offer mustard oil with a ladle made of udumbara wood,
while holding kusha grass with the left hand, upon the head.
O best of kings, Mitra, Sammita, Śālakaṇṭaka, and Kūṣmāṇḍa— these are the fires accompanied by Svāhā;
[one should offer] with their names, with mantras for the bali offering, and with salutations.
At a crossroads, having spread *kuśa* grass on all sides upon a winnowing basket,
one should offer both husked and unhusked rice, as well as rice mixed with sesame paste,
cooked fish and likewise raw fish, and meat in equal measure.

Variegated and fragrant flowers, as well as the three kinds of liquor; radishes, fried cakes, bread-rolls, and likewise garlands of *uṇḍerika*; curd, milk-porridge, rice, sweetmeat balls, and *modakas*.
Then one should worship Ambikā, the mother of Vināyaka, after offering three handfuls of flowers consisting of *dūrvā* grass, mustard seeds, and flowers, [with the prayer]:
"O Blessed One, grant me beauty; grant me fame; grant me fortune."
"Grant me sons; grant me wealth; grant me all my desires.
Grant me unwavering intellect and renown upon the earth.
Then, wearing white garments and adorned with white garlands and unguents, [he spoke].
One should feed the Brāhmaṇas and give a pair of garments even to the Guru. Having thus worshipped Vināyaka and the planets according to the prescribed rule,
one obtains the fruit of one's actions and attains unsurpassed prosperity.

"By always performing worship of the Sun, as well as the tilaka of one's Lord and of Vināyakapati, one shall obtain all success. Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Caturthī-kalpa," in the Brāhma-parvan of the Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, in the Saṃhitā consisting of fifty thousand verses.
Now begins the twenty-fourth chapter:
the description of the characteristics of men in the fourth kalpa.
Śatānīka said:

O best of Brahmins, those characteristics of men and women which were proclaimed by the son of Vyomakeśa— those which were cast into the great ocean by the enraged Īśvara— have been declared, O Mahāmati.
O best of Brahmins, O observer of noble vows, tell me how those [jewels] were again offered by the Ocean at the word of Kṛṣṇa, and how they were obtained by that son of Bahulā.
Sumantu said:
O Indra among kings, O tiger among the Kurus, I shall indeed relate to you exactly how the characteristics of women and men were described by Guha.
When Krauñca had been slain by the son of Vyomakeśa through the descent of divine power (śaktipāta),
Brahmā was pleased and said to him, "O sinless one, choose a boon from me.
Then that one of great splendor, bowing his head to the Lord, replied:

He spoke thus to the Grandfather: "O Lord, tell me the characteristics of men and young women; I have a great curiosity regarding that which was previously spoken by you, O God, and cast into the salt ocean."
"O Lord of the gods, tell me in its entirety how my father previously obtained that [knowledge] while filled with wrath, yet subsequently forgot it. Brahmā said:
"Excellent, O Lord of Gods, increaser of Bhīma's joy!
Listen now to the characteristics of men in their entirety—
those low, superior, and middling ones whom the Ocean obtained."
On an auspicious day, under a favorable lunar mansion, with gentle planets, a propitious sun,
and during the forenoon accompanied by auspicious omens, the discerning physician should examine the patient's proportions,
compactness, complexion, gait, and the characteristics of all the limbs.
The wise man should first examine the teeth, hair, nails, and beard;
he should first investigate the lifespan and only afterwards indicate the physical marks.
For when the lifespan of mortals is exhausted, what is the use of physical marks?
The inferior [length] is said to be ninety [aṅgulas], while the middling is one hundred aṅgulas;
that which measures one hundred and eight is the characteristic of the superior. Thus has the measurement and the auspicious or inauspicious characteristics been declared by Samudra.
O best of gods, that which was previously told to you by me,
beyond that I shall now declare the characteristics of the limbs of the body:
with feet that are fleshy, smooth, red, gentle, and very beautiful.
O King, that man whose soles are elevated, free from perspiration, and devoid of visible veins,
and upon whose sole a line appears like a goad—
there is no doubt that such a person shall possess constant happiness.
O son of Vyomakeśa, his feet are free from perspiration, soft-soled, and resemble the interior of a lotus; O son of Bhīma, his fingers are closely joined with copper-colored nails,
his heels are well-formed, and his ankles are warm and hidden from view.
The feet of a king are renowned for being elevated like those of a tortoise;
however, O mighty-armed one, those that are shaped like winnowing baskets, rough, with white nails,
crooked, covered in prominent veins, withered, and having widely spaced toes [belong to others].
O son of Bhīma, O tiger among gods, know that his two feet are like ripe clay— capable of bestowing both poverty and suffering;
they are stained black, always devoted to drinking and to approaching women who should not be approached.
O best of army commanders, those whose two big toes are white should be known as eaters of forbidden food.
Those men whose big toes are broad are bereft of fortune;
with deformed big toes, those men suffer and must travel on foot.
Those with thumbs that are flattened, deformed, or broken are highly censured;
likewise, those with thumbs that are crooked, bent, or short are partakers of suffering.
Those with thumbs shaped like winnowing baskets, deformed, broken, crooked, or covered in visible veins [are also so].
Those whose feet are excessively censured for being sweaty, pale, and rough;
and he whose forefinger is long enough to extend beyond the thumb—such a man constantly enjoys the company of women; of this there is no doubt.
O Guha, he whose little finger is long and who possesses gold,
yet whose other fingers are flat, sparse, and dry,
shall indeed be perpetually miserable and destitute of wealth.
Men with white and rough nails lead lives of suffering;
those with deformed nails should be known as being of bad character and deprived of sensual enjoyments;
and those with disfigured, cracked, and rough nails share in poverty.
Men with greenish nails commit the murder of a Brahmin;
they are separated from their kinsmen and are destroyers of their lineage. Kings are said to have nails resembling the color of the *indragopaka* insect.
A king possesses nails resembling the spiral of a conch shell;
likewise, one with copper-colored nails attains sovereignty. Fortunate men have lotus-like nails; with red nails, one attains sovereignty, and with flower-like (convex) nails, one becomes handsome.
Kings are said to have nails that are fine, well-proportioned, and copper-colored;
those with hairy shanks share in suffering and poverty.
One should indicate imprisonment for those with short shanks, and sovereignty for those with long ones.
Kings with legs like those of deer are born; of this there is no doubt.
Those with long legs and thick legs are always devoid of fortune.
Men with legs like those of jackals are always devoid of fortune.
Those men whose shanks resemble those of a crow are destined to experience suffering;
likewise, those with thick shanks undoubtedly attain sovereignty.
Those whose shanks are like those of a lion or a tiger are proclaimed to be wealthy.
O Great-minded One, for kings there shall be but a single hair in each pore; for learned Vedic scholars, two hairs each should be known;
likewise, those men who are destitute and partakers of suffering shall have three hairs each.
O mighty-armed son of Śiva, one whose hair is both reviled and honored,
and who has fleshless knees, dies while away from home;
little good fortune is said to come from such traits, while deformity likewise brings poverty.

Those with depressed [limbs] should be known as those conquered by their own wives; those with even-fleshed [limbs] are sharers in sovereignty. He whose gait is equal to that of a swan, a vulture, or a parrot shall become a king worthy of worship, according to the words of Samudra.
The auspicious gait of other excellent birds is also favorable;
the gait of the bull, the lion, and the lordly elephant increases one's enjoyment.
That which resembles a wave of water, as well as that which is like a crow or an owl, [is inauspicious].
The destination of those destitute of wealth is terrifying with suffering, grief, and fear;
it is like that of dogs, camels, buffaloes, donkeys, and pigs.
Those men who are equal to sheep are devoid of fortune.

Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Characteristics of Men," in the Caturthī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan, within the Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty thousand verses.
Now begins the twenty-fifth chapter:
Description of the Characteristics of Men.
Brahmā said:
By means of a clockwise-rotating liṅga, a man indeed becomes possessed of sons;
likewise, by means of a counter-clockwise-rotating liṅga, a man begets daughters.
One should predict poverty from signs that are thick, veiny, and irregular;
men with straight, circular-shaped [genitals] possess sons.
When seated on a low seat, the penis touches the ground.

One should know that man to be suffering; there is no doubt about this. When the penis touches the two ankles of one sitting with his feet on the ground, one should know him to be a lord and a favorite among women.

He whose penis is short and resembles that of a lion or a tiger should be known as a man of enjoyment, endowed with every kind of pleasure. Indeed, he upon whose penis a jewel-shaped line shines resplendent [is likewise so endowed].
That king, however, should be known as one who acts according to the words of the ocean:
he becomes a sovereign through gems that resemble gold and silver, possess a luster equal to jewels and pearls, and are as smooth and beautiful as coral.
One who possesses white, soiled, rough, or long-spreading gems will go forth in all directions; likewise, one who possesses even, elevated,
and very lustrous gems becomes a protector of wealth and an enjoyer of women.
O mighty-armed one, by gems that are sunken in the middle, those ancestors indeed become destitute; by those that are not prominent, even if they belong to young women,
they become wealthy men and heroes.
If a single stream of urine falls, coiled toward the right, he shall become a sovereign of the earth, according to the word of Samudra; likewise,
if there are two streams that are smooth, he is declared to be wealthy and possessed of enjoyments.
Those whose semen has many streams, is rough, and is accompanied by sound are the lowest of men.
That which has the scent of fish indicates one will possess wealth and sons;
that which has the scent of sacrificial oblation (havis) is said to belong to one who is wealthy and learned in the Vedas (śrotriya).
A daughter will have the smell of a mouse; a king is said to have the smell of a lotus.
He who has the smell of lac will father many daughters;
he who has the smell of liquor will be a warrior; and he who has the smell of alkaline ash will be poor.
O tiger among gods, he who engages in sexual intercourse quickly lives long; otherwise, he should be known as short-lived—of this there is no doubt.
One with scant semen begets daughters, while one who smells of meat is a man of enjoyment.
If the color of the lotus is red, that man shall be wealthy;
however, he whose blood is somewhat reddish-black should be known as inferior, always a vessel for nothing but suffering.
O Guha, one whose blood is glossy and resembles a young sprout should be known as a king, the sovereign of the seven continents.
A bladder that is broad, fleshy, and glossy is praised in men.
Those whose bladders are fleshless, misshapen, and parched are not auspicious.
A man whose [bladder] resembles that of a jackal, a dog, a camel, or a buffalo will be constantly miserable; of this there is no doubt.
O dear one, he who has only one testicle and gives up his life in water,

as well as one who is fickle toward women, is said to rule over an unstable kingdom. One with upward-pointing [testicles] has a short lifespan, while one with pendulous testicles lives for a hundred years.
Moreover, men with reddish buttocks indeed become wealthy;
one with thick buttocks is secure; one who possesses flesh on his buttocks is endowed with riches;
one with buttocks like those of a tiger becomes a king; and one with buttocks like those of a frog becomes a lord of men.

O mighty-armed one, having two circles [on the buttocks] and having buttocks like those of a lion are signs of universal sovereignty. O high-minded son of Bhīma, he who has buttocks resembling those of a camel or a monkey should be known as one devoid of wealth and grain.
A man with a belly like that of a deer is fortunate, as is one with a belly like a peacock;
one with a belly like a tiger becomes a lord of men, and one with a belly like a lion becomes a king.
As for the man whose belly resembles a frog...
He shall become a king through prosperity, just as the words of the ocean [foretell].
Kings are said to have sides that are fleshy, straight, and rounded;
one with a tiger-like back is a lord and indeed a leader of an army.
One should predict bondage for that man whose back is like a lion's;
however, kings whose backs are like those of a tortoise partake in wealth and good fortune.
Those whose chest is broad, fleshy, hairy, and even [are likewise blessed].
One should know that such a person will live for a hundred years, enjoying pleasures and possessing great wealth. However, if the fingers on the hand appear sparse, withered, and rough,
that man will be constantly miserable and a vessel for poverty.
He whose lines are like fish has success in his undertakings;
that man should be known as wealthy and possessed of many sons. Furthermore, he in whose palm a balance or a sacrificial altar is seen [is likewise blessed].
The trade of that man succeeds without a doubt;
especially for a twice-born man who has a gentle [saumya] mark on the palm of his hand,
that person shall always be a performer of sacrifices and possess great wealth.
If a mountain or a tree is seen in the middle of the hand,
one attains unshakable prosperity, accompanied by many servants.
Likewise, lines resembling a spear, a javelin, an arrow, a sword, or a bow [indicate similar fortune].
O mighty-armed Guha, he in whose hand a banner appears, or else a conch is seen in the middle of his palm, shall conquer his enemies in battle;
he shall be a traveler upon the ocean and shall always be wealthy.
One should recognize that king as the destroyer of enemy armies, upon whose hand the Śrīvatsa, or a lotus, or a thunderbolt, or a discus, or even a chariot or a water-pot appears.
If a barley grain is seen on the thumb of the right hand, he shall indeed become a proclaimer of all branches of knowledge; of this there is no doubt.
He upon whose palm a line rises from the base of the little finger [attains great fortune].
"If it has reached the middle of the index finger, he shall live for a hundred autumns.

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Characteristics of Men," in the *Caturthī-kalpa* of the *Brāhma-parvan*, within the *Śatārdha-sāhasrī-saṃhitā* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya-mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the twenty-sixth chapter.
Regarding the description of the characteristics of men,
Brahmā said:
One with a level belly will be an enjoyer of pleasures, while one with a sunken belly is a destroyer of wealth.
One with a crooked belly is deceitful, treacherous, and always a practitioner of trickery.
A king with a sunken belly becomes a sovereign ruler of the whole earth and possesses great strength.
O observer of noble vows, those with bellies like a serpent become impoverished and gluttonous.
With navels that are broad, circular, and elevated,
heroic men become happy and endowed with wealth and grain;
however, those with navels that are depressed or very small indeed become partakers of suffering.
O Lord, a line that passes through the middle of the palm, being uneven and especially so,
constantly produces loss of wealth as well as colic;
however, the wise know that one which turns counter-clockwise always brings peace.
O Lord of Heaven, wisdom is produced when [the mark] is turned toward the right;
when it extends along the side, it is known by the wise that it grants long life; and when directed upward, it bestows sovereignty; while when it points downward, it brings abundance of cattle.
O Great-minded One, he whose navel has the luster of the pericarp of a hundred-petaled lotus will undoubtedly attain lordship over the earth;
one with a level belly becomes an enjoyer of pleasures, while one with an uneven belly remains destitute.
He will have a slender belly, be eloquent, and endowed with great wealth;
the hero will meet his end by a weapon and likewise obtain the enjoyment of women;
and the teacher will have many sons—one should point these out according to their respective order.

"O tiger among gods," said that ocean, "those who approach women who should not be approached are to be known by their uneven lines; of this there is no doubt. One who possesses upright lines will enjoy wealth and be a censurer of others' wives."

One with fleshy and soft sides will be a king; of this there is no doubt. Those whose chins are not recessed are indeed fortunate, while those with uneven or long chins become poor in this world, O Suvīraja.
O Bhīmāṅgasambhava, kings who possess shoulders that are thick, well-developed, and slightly depressed become happy in this world; of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, a heart that is level, elevated, even, and broad [brings the same result].
O best of Ṛbhus, there is no doubt that the hearts of kings are steady and fleshy; however, the hearts of the poor are specifically covered with coarse hair and marked by prominent veins.
Those with broad chests are known by the wise to be endowed with wealth; those with broad chests are considered by the learned to be heroes.
Those with thin chests will be destitute of possessions, and those with uneven chests shall be utterly penniless;
they shall even be slain by the sword—of this there is no doubt.
O Hero, a man with uneven jaws will be devoid of noble birth;

he whose jaw is elevated shall be an enjoyer of pleasures, of this there is no doubt. O Hero, one with fleshless and uneven jaws is declared to be destitute, while one with sunken jaws is likewise described as poor.
A man with full [cheeks] shall be wealthy and endowed with happiness and enjoyments;
one with uneven [cheeks] shall be destitute of wealth and always a partaker of suffering. O Guha, one with a flat neck is considered wicked in the world.

One with a buffalo-like neck will be a hero; one with a deer-like neck will be afflicted by fear. One with a conch-like neck will be a king, while one with a pendulous throat possesses the foremost marks of excellence.
Furthermore, one with a short neck is wealthy, very happy, and likewise enjoys great pleasures.
O son of Vyomakeśa, shoulders that are fleshless, hairy, broken, or especially small are known to belong to a poor man. O son of Bhīma, the backs of the wealthy are hairless.

O Lord of the Forces, O Six-faced One, the armpits of those who are destitute are hairless, crooked, perspiring, elevated, and thin; whereas the armpits of those endowed with wealth should be known to have hair, to be fragrant, and to be even, smooth, and fleshy.
O Lord of the Gods, O increaser of the joy of the Mountain-born, such shoulders as these— uninterrupted, well-knit, and broad— belong to heroes.
He whose arms are so long that he can seize his victim for slaughter or capture is truly a hero.
A king should have long arms, according to the words of Samudra;
a man with pendulous arms is to be known as one endowed with all virtues;
one with short arms will be a servant or a messenger for others.
The Ocean said: "He whose arms curl to the left, whose arms are long and extended, and whose forearms are full, shall be a king;
likewise, his neck should be circular in shape and adorned with lines like those of a conch shell."
He shall become a king on earth, a destroyer of all the wicked.
Those men who have long necks, crane-like necks, parrot-like necks,
camel-like necks, or elephant-like necks are all considered to be destitute.
O observer of good vows, O best of gods, the arms of kings are undoubtedly round, symmetrical, fleshy, resembling the trunk of an elephant, and reaching down to the knees;
whereas the arms of the poor are known to be hairy and short.
O observer of noble vows,
O tiger among men, he whose palms are uneven, thick, and thin, and whose palms are depressed, will certainly not possess paternal wealth; likewise, such a man is a coward.
One with a palm that is well-rounded, thin, and slightly depressed is wealthy;
one with an upturned palm is a giver—of this there is no doubt.
Those with uneven palms will be troubled, especially those that are deeply depressed.

O tiger among gods, lords who possess palms as red as lac are remembered as [bestowers of] power; those with yellow palms are said to lead to forbidden sexual intercourse, while those with rough palms lead to poverty. Indeed, those with blue or black palms always engage in the drinking of what should not be drunk.
O Guha, the lines on the palms of men that are deep and glossy belong to the wealthy,
not to the poor— so said the Ocean.
Those whose fingers are widely spaced are declared to be poor.
O mighty-armed one, those men who have thick fingers are wealthy;
he whose face is round should be designated as virtuous in character.
But those men who have trunks-like faces are unfortunate, of this there is no doubt.

Those with the faces of tigers, those with distorted faces, those with deformed mouths, those with broken jaws, and those with gaping maws— all such men are known as thieves. Kings, however, have full faces, as well as faces resembling those of elephants and lions.
Those whose faces resemble those of a goat or a monkey are proclaimed to be wealthy.
A man whose cheeks are well-filled and possess a luster like that of a lotus petal shall always be a sharer in the fruits of agriculture and will possess abundant riches.
If his cheek is like that of a lion, a tiger, or a lordly elephant,
he should be known as one of great fortune and the leader of an army;
indeed, his face is even, smooth, gentle, and well-proportioned.
O mighty-armed one, for kings, the opposite [of what has been described] brings suffering;
O Lord of Gods, a large mouth bestows misfortune;
a woman's face leads to the destruction of sons; and a circular face leads to happiness.
Indeed, a long [shape] leads to the destruction of wealth, as well as to sin and fear;
a square one belongs to rogues, O Lord of Devas, and listen, it causes the loss of sons. A face that is sunken likewise results in the loss of sons.
A short chin indicates a miserly person, while one that is full and beautiful belongs to those who enjoy pleasures. A king has red lips, and one who possesses wealth has lips like lotuses.
Those with thick lips and the base of the jaw are prosperous, whereas those with thin and sharp lips are miserable.
O Guha, a king’s beard that is smooth at the tips, glossy, curved, soft,
full, and always well-kept is praised;
O son of Bhīma, one with sparse, red, and rough beards is not so.

Men indeed become thieves as well as those addicted to the wives of others. He whose ears are devoid of flesh perishes in battle; with flat ears one becomes diseased, and short ears belong to a miser.
One with spike-like ears becomes a lord of the earth, striking fear into all enemies;
and a king with long, thick,
and abundant hair shall always be an enjoyer of pleasures and a worshipper of the gods and Brahmins.
O Vyomakeśaja, the ears of a cruel person are bound by veins and especially pendulous; those that are fleshy should be known as givers of happiness.
One with a prominent jaw becomes an enjoyer of pleasures, while one with full cheeks becomes a minister.
One who possesses a beautiful nose is fortunate, while one with a long life has a dry nose.
A king has teeth that are radiant and resemble jasmine buds or earrings;
those with teeth like those of bears or monkeys are constantly afflicted by hunger.
Those with teeth like elephant tusks, donkey tusks, or smooth teeth are endowed with virtues;
those with jagged, sparse, or rough teeth live in misery.
A king has thirty-two teeth, and one with thirty-one is a possessor of enjoyments.

Men who always have thirty teeth share in both happiness and suffering; those with fewer than thirty teeth are partakers of misery. One with a black tongue will be a servant, while one with a wrinkled tongue will likewise be so.
Indeed, those who are prone to anger are generally coarse and rough-tongued;
men with white tongues should be known as being endowed with purity and good conduct.
A tongue that resembles a lotus petal—subtle, long, and very beautiful—is auspicious.
Those lords of men whose tongues are thick yet not broad,
and if their tongues are depressed, smooth, short, and red-tipped,
they become expounders of all branches of knowledge; of this there is no doubt.
A man whose palate is black shall be a destroyer of his lineage;
one with a yellow palate is a lord of men, partaking of happiness;
however, a palate that is deformed, cracked, or parched is not praised.
A king shall have a palate like a lion’s, and likewise one with a palate like an elephant’s;
a king shall have a palate like a lotus, while one with a palate like a conch-shell is a lord of wealth.
Men who possess voices like swans are fortunate, and those whose resonance is as deep as a thundercloud are likewise blessed.
Kings with the cry of cranes are enjoyers of pleasures and possess great wealth;
kings with the cry of ruddy geese are blessed and devoted to dharma;
a king with the sound of a water-jar or the sound of a drum likewise [attains his desires].
Those with harsh and long-continued voices are cruel, resembling beasts;
men endowed with a deep, guttural sound are partakers of suffering.
Those with the cry of a blue jay are possessed of good fortune, as are those with a voice like cracked bell-metal.
Those whose voices are feeble or broken are proclaimed to be inferior. Kings have thin noses, while those with long noses are possessors of enjoyments.
But those men who have short noses are considered to be of virtuous character.
For those men who have noses like those of elephants, horses, or lions, or who have needle-like noses,
trade succeeds as well as the sale of horses.
However, for one whose nose is deformed, thick at the tip, and lacking beauty, [trade does not succeed].

He should be known as one of evil deeds, according to the words of the ocean. O Guha, he whose eyes resemble the pomegranate flower should be known as a lord of the earth, a sovereign of the seven continents.
Those with eyes like tigers should be known as wrathful; those with eyes like crabs are fond of strife.
Those with eyes like cats or swans are the lowest of men. And those men whose eyes are like those of a monkey or a mongoose are considered middling.
Fortune does not abandon the omniscient person who is honey-tawny;
kings with tawny eyes are endowed with all enjoyments.
Those who are tawny like yellow pigment, orpiment, lac, or guñjā seeds become lords of wealth.

Those endowed with strength, courage, and virtue who rule the earth as universal monarchs live forever relying on the Supreme, their gaze fixed upon the two measures (dvimātra). Men who flow with the three measures (trimātra) should be known as partakers of happiness.
Those whose eyes blink four times [in the duration of a breath] are known as lords;
they are long-lived, devoted to dharma, and blink five times.
Those men who have short ears are highly fortunate, as are those who have large ears.
Those with spiraled ears are wealthy; likewise, those with smooth ears are also so.
Those with oyster-shell-shaped ears are long-lived, and those with conch-shell-shaped ears possess great wealth.
Those with long ears are long-lived, while those with hanging ears are ascetics.
Those with a half-moon mark on the forehead become lords of the earth;
one with a broad forehead is said to be a great master of wealth;
while a man with a small forehead is said to be devoted to righteousness.
If there are five lines on the forehead of either a woman or a man,
he lives for a hundred years and attains sovereignty;
with four lines, eighty years, and with three, seventy years.

With two lines, one should know [the lifespan] to be sixty; likewise with one, forty; and with a forehead devoid of lines, twenty-five. Men are to be known as inferior, middling, or superior according to the breaks in their lines.
Those who have short lifespans and are afflicted by few diseases,
and upon whose forehead a trident or a sharp-edged spear is seen— he should be known as a lord, an enjoyer of pleasures, and one established in fame.

A head that is elevated and depressed, or even slightly injured, is auspicious for kings; it is remembered as being shaped like the moon and rich in cattle. A head that is uneven belongs to the poor, while a long head belongs to those who suffer.

The king’s elephant, resembling the frontal globes of a serpent, has coils that are uniform in all parts. Men with hair and beards that are tawny, cracked, rough, and coarse at the tips should be known as miserable.
Those whose hair is coarse, discolored, lusterless, rough, and thick,
and who have neither too few nor too many hairs on their heads, are partakers of suffering.
Conversely, those whose hair is sparse, soft, glossy, and possesses the luster of bees or collyrium, [are partakers of happiness].
"He whose hair is seen [in this manner] shall become a lord of the earth.

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Characteristics of Men," in the *Caturthī-kalpa* of the *Brāhma-parvan*, within the *Śatārddhasāhasrī-saṃhitā* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya-mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the twenty-seventh chapter.
Regarding the description of the characteristics of a man,
Kārtikeya said: "O Lord, please tell me briefly the characteristics of a king."
"O best among speakers, tell me of the auspicious bodily marks.
Brahmā said:
"Listen, I shall describe the auspicious bodily marks of a king."
O mighty-armed one, that man among men by whom the earth is known from its middle portion— who possesses three broad parts,
six elevated parts, and indeed three deep parts— is a king.
O Lord, he whose four [parts] are short, or seven are red;
or whose five are long and subtle;
and whose three—namely the navel, the joints, and the voice—are indeed deep.
O hero, that man whose face, forehead, and chest—these three—are broad, shall be a king; of this there is no doubt. Now hear also concerning those who are elevated.
O mighty-armed one, the wise know these six to be short: the back of the neck, the mouth, the nails, the chest, the nose, and the armpits;
likewise, O observer of noble vows, the penis, the back, the neck, and the shanks are also short.
O best of gods,

O high-minded one, O most excellent of the Ṛbhus: the corners of the eyes, the hands, the feet, the palate, and the lips— these seven, as well as the tongue, the nails, the skin, the fingernails, the hair, and the teeth, are red.
O Guha, the wise also know these five to be subtle:
the nose, the eyes, the two arms, the space between the breasts, and the jaw.
Thus, O King, this set of five has been declared as the "long" [proportions] for rulers of the earth.

O son of Śiva, the wise know that a single, double, or triple sneeze, as well as a roar or a cry, uttered by kings, signifies long life; and they understand a laugh to be likewise indicative of longevity.
O son of Śiva, eyes resembling lotus petals belong to the wealthy.
He whose eyes are red at the corners shall obtain the daughter of Bhṛgu;
O Lord of the Gods, those great-souled men whose eyes are honey-tawny are to be known as such,
while those who are timid and have thin eyes are thieves, as are those with circular or wheel-shaped eyes.

Horses with reddish-brown eyes bring wealth; those with deep-colored eyes bring abundance of meaning; those resembling blue lotuses belong to the knowers of the Vedas; likewise, those that are very black bring fulfillment of desires.
Those who know them say on earth that horses with large, beautiful eyes lead to the office of a minister.
Those with dark eyes should be known as fortunate; with sunken eyes, there is poverty. With wide eyes, O Guha, one is a possessor of enjoyments; likewise, with large eyes, one is excellent.
With very prominent eyes, one has a short life; with broad eyes, one shall be happy.
O best of gods, one with uneven eyebrows should be known as poor;
O best of sages, those with eyebrows resembling the crescent moon are wealthy;
O observer of noble vows, one with long eyebrows is to be known as destitute, while those with joined eyebrows are prosperous.
O best of gods, men with sunken temples should be known as destitute and lacking wealth;
those whose brows are arched in the middle are devoted to the wives of others. Those with sparse and prominent temples are fortunate; of this there is no doubt.
O best of gods, those with depressed brows are addicted to praising others for their own gain, while those with elevated brows are lords of men; those with uneven foreheads shall always be destitute.
Men with brows resembling oyster shells will become teachers; of this there is no doubt.
O Guha, men with elevated heads should always be known as noble;
heroic men with sunken foreheads are destined for slaughter and imprisonment;
those with excessively high foreheads are fools, and likewise, those with depressed ones are miserly.
Listen as to how the face of humans brings about auspiciousness:
it should be undepressed, gentle, and especially endowed with a smile;
whereas, O Guha, a face that is tearful, dejected, harsh, or ungentle is censured.
O Guha, the tearless smile of men should be known as impossible; it is the destroyer of mountains for men. O best of gods, the smile of a sinner should be known as one with closed eyes.
A man whose head is shaped like a mandala shall become wealthy in cattle;
a man whose head is shaped like an umbrella shall become a king;
but a man whose head is flattened shall indeed kill his parents.
A man who repeatedly practices the resonance of the head (śirodhvani) in the shape of a bell attains excellence from birth; however, O best of men, a depressed head brings misfortune to people.
Likewise, with jaggery that is oily, black, and with uncracked tips, [the same result follows].
A king shall not have hair that is excessively thick, though it may be soft; rather,
the hair of the poor is thick, tawny, coarse, uneven,
cracked, rough, short, and overly curled.
Thus has been described the auspicious and inauspicious characteristics of men.
Now, O son of Bhīma, I shall tell you the characteristics of women.

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Characteristics of Men," in the *Caturthī-kalpa* of the *Brāhma-parvan*, within the *Śatārddhasāhasrī-saṃhitā* of the glorious *Mahāpurāṇa Bhaviṣya*.
Now begins the twenty-eighth chapter,
the Description of the Characteristics of Women.
Brahmā said:
Listen now, O mighty-armed one, to the unsurpassed characteristics of women,
which were previously told by me, O hero, to the high-souled Nārada;
by means of which that which is auspicious and inauspicious as it exists may be discerned.

I shall describe the characteristics of women, both those that are censured and those that are praised. One should examine two types of women as one would test two images, according to the word of Samudra: the mother and the father, as well as the brother and the maternal uncle.
When the hour is auspicious, the lunar day is favorable, and the asterism is highly honored,
the knower of the scriptures, having approached together with the twice-born, should examine the girl;
he should inspect her hands, feet, fingers, and even her nails.
The hands, the shanks, the hips, and the thighs; the loins, the belly, and the back; the breasts, the ears, and likewise the arms;
the tongue, the lips, the teeth, the cheeks, and likewise the throat.
The eyes, nose, forehead, head, and likewise the hair; the line of body hair, voice, complexion, and furthermore the whorls;
she whose lines are on the neck and whose eyes have reddish corners—[such a woman is auspicious].

Whichever woman should come to one's house, that house shall prosper in happiness. She on whose forehead the trident fashioned by the gods is seen should be designated as the mistress of many thousands of women.
That deer-eyed girl who has the gait of a royal swan, possesses the color of a deer,
and has teeth that are even and white at the tips— they know her to be an excellent maiden.
A girl whose belly is shaped like a frog and whose body is as well-proportioned as a banyan tree [is likewise auspicious].
She shall give birth to one son, and he too will become a king.
As for the girl with the voice of a swan, soft speech, and honey-brown eyes,
she shall give birth to eight sons who increase wealth and grain.
She whose ears are long, whose nose is well-formed,
and whose eyebrows are shaped like a rainbow, shall partake of extreme happiness.
She who is slender, dark-complexioned, yet blackish, with smooth limbs and gentle speech— she too shall be so.
She whose teeth are like a conch shell, a kunda flower, or the moon shall possess sovereign power;
she whose hips are broad and whose waist is like the middle of a sacrificial altar shall become a queen; and she whose eyes are long and large shall likewise become a king’s consort.
She on whose left breast, hand, ear,
or even neck there is a mole or a freckle will first give birth to a son;
she who has hidden ankles, fingers, and veins, small heels, and a beautiful waist.
One whose eyes are red and whose feet are red is destined for extreme happiness; however,
one should avoid that girl whose nails are shaped like the back of a tortoise, who lacks a glossy luster, and whose feet have crooked toes and soles.

One should know that woman whose flesh increases in any part whatsoever to be like a female donkey; she does not deserve prosperity. She whose forefoot exceeds the big toe [in length] is likewise [unfortunate].

One should know such a girl to be immoral and unfortunate; one should avoid her. If the middle toe of her foot does not touch the ground, she will not find pleasure in youth, being self-willed and acting according to her own desires.
If the ring finger of her foot does not touch the ground,
she has killed a second man and is established upon a third.
If the little toe of her foot does not touch the ground, [she has likewise slain].
Having killed a second man, she is established in the third;
one should avoid that girl who is not a goddess, nor wealthy, nor named after a grain, and who bears the name of a thicket or a tree.
When a woman shares the name of a person such as Indra or Candra, or those who bear the names of constellations, they do not remain devoted to their husbands. Furthermore,
she whose hair-whorl on the back reaches down toward her navel [is also so described].
One should predict that her offspring will be short of stature and short-lived.
A cow with a curl on her back kills her husband; one with a curl at the navel is devoted to her husband;
but one with a curl on the hip is independent and never becomes disaffected.

She whose cheek becomes hollow when she laughs does not find pleasure in youth; she acts according to her own whims. She whose shanks quiver like a *ṭiṭṭibhā* bird when she walks [is likewise fickle].

One should determine that such a girl is intended to be made a son; there is no doubt in this matter. Furthermore, a wise man should designate as a slave-girl any maiden who has thick feet, is hairy over her entire body, and has thick hands.
She whose heels are prominent, whose face is deformed,
and who has hair on her upper lip, will quickly devour her husband.
She from whom three things hang down— the forehead, the belly, and the buttocks— [will likewise do so].

She consumes three: her brother-in-law, her father-in-law, and her husband. Endowed with adorned conduct, devoted to her elders, faithful to her husband, and devoted to the gods and Brahmins—one should designate her as a human woman.
One who is constantly bathed and well-scented, always speaks kindly, eats little, and is free from malice— such a woman one should designate as a goddess;
yet she commits evil deeds in secret and guards her reputation against slander.
If the heart is difficult to grasp, one should designate it as "mārjārī";
if she laughs, plays, becomes angry, and then becomes gracious,
and always delights in base things, one should designate her as "rāsabhī."
One who is constantly antagonistic toward her kinsmen and her husband, who acts according to her own whims, and who is merely charming in appearance— her one should designate as *āsuri*. Furthermore,
she who eats excessively, speaks much, and is always a speaker of unpleasant words [is likewise so designated].
One who harms her own husband should be designated as a *rākṣasī*;
one who has fallen away from purity and proper conduct, who is disfigured, terrifying,
and covered in sweat and filth, should be designated as a *piśācī*.
One should designate her as a Gāndharvī who is constantly bathed, fragrant, fond of meat and wine, eating at all times, and devoted to trees and gardens;
she is fickle and restless, and likewise gazes constantly toward the quarters of the sky.
One should identify that woman as a Vānarī who is fickle by nature and greedy; however,
the wise man should know her to be a Vidyādharī who has a moon-like face, auspicious limbs, the gait of an elephant in rut, and hands with reddish nails.
"One should designate that [goddess] as Gāndharvī when she is intent upon flowers and incense, accompanied by the sound of lute music and the resonance of flute and song.
Sumantu said:
Having spoken thus, that high-souled Creator indeed departed for his own abode,
O Hero, after describing those characteristics of women and men, O King, which are honored by the world.

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Characteristics of Women," in the *Caturthī-kalpa* of the *Brāhma-parvan*, within the *Śatārddhasāhasrī-saṃhitā* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya-mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the twenty-ninth chapter,
the Description of the Ritual Manual of Gaṇapati. Śatānīka said:
"Tell me the method of propitiation for the great-souled Gaṇeśa, the deity of the syllable *ga*, together with its ancillaries and accompanied by the mantra.
Sumantu said:
Neither a lunar day nor a constellation is prescribed, nor is fasting enjoined;
for one who acts as he pleases, success that fulfills every desire occurs at all times.
Having taken the root of the white *arka* plant, the wise man should fashion an image of Gaṇapati.
The size of a thumb-joint, seated in the lotus posture,
with four arms and three eyes, adorned with all ornaments,
his body having a serpent for a sacred thread, and the moon as his crest-ornament.
One should place a tusk in the left hand, a rosary in the second,
an axe in the third, and a sweetmeat (modaka) should be placed in the fourth.
Saffron and sandalwood are said to be the unguents for anointing.
One should worship the Gaṇa with garments, red ornaments, and garlands;
one should also honor him with fragrant incense and sweetmeats (modakas). Having worshipped in this manner before him, the wise man should feed a Brāhmaṇa.
One should feed a dwarf and a hunchbacked person before the twice-born;
then, having received a blessing from them, one shall attain success.
O best of the Kuru lineage, listen now to the words of the mantra with devotion.
Gaṃ Svāhā—this is the root mantra (mūlamantra) conjoined with the syllable Om.
Gāṃ Namaḥ is to be known as the heart; Gīṃ is proclaimed as the head;
Gūṃ Namaḥ is to be known as the crest-lock (śikhā); and Gaiṃ Namaḥ is remembered as the armor (kavaca).
*Gauṃ* is declared as the *netra-mantra*; *gaḥ phaṭ* is called the *kāmāstra-mantra*.
"Oṃ āgaccha ulkāmukhāya" is indeed this mantra for invocation (*āvāhana*).
*Gaṃ gaṇeśāya namaḥ* is proclaimed as the mantra for the incense (*gandha*).
"Salutation to Puṣpolkā"—this is proclaimed as the mantra for flowers. "Salutation to Dhūpolkā"—this is proclaimed as the mantra for incense.
"Salutation to Dīpolkā"—this is proclaimed as the mantra for the lamp.
Oṃ Gaṃ, homage to Maholkā; this is proclaimed as the bali-mantra.
Oṃ Saṃsiddholkāya, homage; this is the mantra for dismissal.
Oṃ, may we know Mahākarnā, may we meditate upon Vakratuṇḍa.
May that Dantī inspire us. First, there is the recitation of the Gāyatrī;
always to the south, "Mahāgaṇapataye Vīrasvāhā";
to the west, "Maholkāya"; and to the north, "Kūśmāṇḍāya."
One should designate the one with a single tusk, the destroyer of Tripura, as being in the southeast, O Hero.
"Oṃ, to Śivadatta, the one with a terrifying laugh, to Prāṇa, svāhā" is for the southwest.
"To Tulambana, the one with extremely immovable tusks, svāhā" is for the northwest.
The wise one should perform the fire offering (homa) in the northeast for Padmadaṃṣṭra Narāyaṇa with the mantra *huṃ phaṭ huṃ phaṭ*. Then, making the sound of hand-claps,
laughing and leaping, and dancing upon the clay, he should perform the oblation while assuming the mudrā of the Lord Gaṇapati.
When she does not become submissive, one should offer eight thousand oblations of black sesame seeds; within three nights, the king becomes submissive.
By an offering of sesame and barley, all the people of the realm become submissive.

An exceedingly beautiful maiden follows one who is departing. By offering oblations of *caṇaka* pulse and rice, one becomes unconquerable. With oils mixed with equal parts of neem leaves, one effects enmity.
During a lunar eclipse, having entered into the midst of water, one should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times;
one will remain undefeated in battle.
(Oṃ, homage to Lamba-rājñī.)
Facing the sun, one should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times;
the Sun will become a granter of boons.
Having fasted on the fourth day of the bright fortnight and performed worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should offer oblations of sesame seeds and rice.
By wearing these on his head, one becomes unconquerable by them.
Having kindled a fire with *apāmārga* fuel-sticks, if one offers twenty-one oblations,
one destroys the enemy within three nights.
Now I shall explain the subsequent mantra:
Having collected lampblack at the root of a tree and consecrated it seven times with the mantra, one should apply it to the eyes; whoever one looks upon becomes submissive.
Having consecrated a flower, fruit, or root eight thousand times with the mantra, whoever one gives it to becomes submissive.
Whatever one performs with the root mantra, that succeeds;
all the planetary spirits (grahas) become well-pleased.
