Having gone to the city gate, one should gaze at the gate eight thousand times.
The city is captured through its gate; one who sacrifices facing the east causes [an enemy] to be expelled;
one who recites facing the opponent puts the thieves to flight;
he mows down the grass and cuts down the wood.

One fights with the king of elephants. One should recite the mantra for seven nights in the midst of water; it causes rain out of season and dries up wells and ponds. One makes an image dance, attracts, and paralyzes. One attracts women and men from a distance of a hundred *yojanas*.
Having consecrated cow bezoar (*gorocanā*) one thousand times and bound it upon the hand, one can travel a hundred thousand *yojanas* and return again.
Now, if one desires to kill [an enemy], having fashioned a stake of *khadira* wood and visualizing the man or woman, one should drive it into the heart; in an instant, they die.

One becomes liberated from all sins. One possesses the brilliance of fire and remains unconquered by all. *Oṃ vakatuṇḍāya svāhā*. *Oṃ ekadaṃṣṭrāya svāhā*. *Oṃ kṛtakṛṣṇāya svāhā*. *Oṃ gajakarṇāya svāhā*.
Oṃ, svāhā to Lambodara! Oṃ, svāhā to Vikaṭa! Oṃ, svāhā to Dhūmravarṇa! Oṃ, svāhā to Gaganakūja!
Oṃ, svāhā to Vināyaka! Oṃ, svāhā to Gaṇapati! Oṃ, svāhā to Hastimukha!

Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual for Gaṇapati," in the Caturthī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan, within the *Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of fifty thousand verses.
Now begins the thirtieth chapter,
describing the ritual for the worship of Vināyaka. Sumantu said:

Having fashioned an image of Gaṇapati from nimba wood the size of a thumb-joint, and having worshipped it daily with incense, perfumes, and other offerings, one should go about after binding it secretly upon one's head;

one will become beloved by all people. Having fashioned an image of Gaṇapati from the root of white arka wood the size of a thumb, and having worshipped it with incense and other offerings, one brings all castes under one's control.

Having fashioned an image of Gaṇapati from white sandalwood the size of a thumb, and having worshipped it with flowers, perfumes, and other offerings, one should offer a *bali* sacrifice on the fourth or eighth day of the bright fortnight and perform eight thousand oblations with curd and milk-rice (*pāyasa*); this brings a king under one's control.

Having fashioned an image of Gaṇapati made of red sandalwood the size of a thumb, one should offer a material *bali* oblation; by offering oblations of curd, honey, and ghee eight thousand times to Gaṇapati, one brings under control offspring who come to one’s own side. One should have an image of Gaṇapati made from the root of the red *karavīra* flower, the size of a thumb-joint.
One should offer a *bali* with red flowers and perfumes; by offering oblations of sesame, salt, and ghee eight thousand times, one brings ten villages under control.

Having fashioned an image of Gaṇapati the size of a thumb-joint from white *karavīra* wood, one should offer eight thousand oblations mixed with sesame flour, curd, ghee, milk, and turmeric; this brings a courtesan under one's control.

Having fashioned an image of Gaṇapati the size of a thumb-joint from the root of an *aśvattha* tree, and having offered perfumes, flowers, incense, and a sacrificial bali, one should offer a hundred oblations; this brings an enemy under one's control.
Having fashioned an image of Gaṇapati from the root of the *arka* tree, the size of a thumb-joint, one should offer perfumes, flowers, incense, and oblations.

By offering one hundred sticks of *tinduka* wood as a sacrificial oblation, one brings an enemy under one's control. Having fashioned an image of Gaṇapati from the root of the *bilva* tree, the size of a thumb-joint, and having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and incense, one should offer eight thousand oblations smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*); this brings kings and ministers under one's control.
Having held incense to one's head, one should go to the king’s gate; victory will be achieved in battle.
One should have an image of Gaṇapati made from ivory or clay, the size of a thumb-joint.
Having honored it with perfumes, flowers, and incense, one should worship it naked on the fourth lunar day of the dark fortnight.
If one recites [the mantra] seven times daily, one becomes beloved by women.
One should fashion an image of Gaṇapati from the earth found at the tip of a bull's horn, the size of a thumb;
having worshipped it with perfumes and flowers, one should offer incense of guggulu, and thus brings the Lord of the Ghoṣas under one's control.
Alternatively, one should have an image of Gaṇapati made from anthill clay, measuring the size of a thumb-joint.
One should smear the image with mustard oil.

Having kindled a fire with wood from the *unmattaka* tree, one should offer eight thousand oblations mixed with sesame and mustard seeds. One should offer all types of incense and smear [the image] with the three pungent spices (*trikaṭuka*).
If one offers aloe-wood incense, it brings kings under one's control; one also becomes beloved by others. If one perfumes oneself with red sandalwood, one becomes handsome.

Oṃ, to Gaṇapati, the one with the curved trunk, the one with the elephant’s tusk, who utters the sound "gulugulu ninin," the four-armed, the three-eyed, who holds a mace, a noose, and a vajra in his hands, the subduer of all spirits, the bringer of all worlds under control, the producer of the destruction of all the wicked, the crusher of all enemies, the seeker of all kingdoms: bring the king here under control! Strike, strike! Cook, cook! O Gaṇeśa, with the vajra-goad, phaṭ svāhā!
Oṃ gāṃ gīṃ gūṃ gaiṃ gauṃ gaḥ svāhā, namaḥ—this is the heart-mantra of the root mantra.

Oṃ kaḥ, the head; Oṃ khaḥ, the crest-lock (śikhā); Oṃ gaḥ, the heart; Oṃ guḥ, the face; Oṃ gaiṃ, the eyes. Oṃ ghaḥ, the armor (kavaca). Oṃ ṅa, the invocation (āvāhana) of the heart; these are the limbs of the invocation. Oṃ namaḥ, the heart, is the root mantra (mūlamantra). Oṃ gāḥ, the head; Oṃ gaiḥ, obeisance to the crest-lock; Oṃ gauḥ, obeisance to the armor; Oṃ gaṃ, obeisance to the eyes; Oṃ gaḥ phaṭ, the weapon (astra). Oṃ aṅguṣṭholkāya svāhā, the invocation of the heart; svāhā, the dismissal (visarjana) of the heart; Oṃ gandholkāya svāhā.

The incense mantra: *Oṃ dharmabhūtolkāya svāhā*. The flower mantra: *Durjayāya* (to Durjaya) in the east; *Oṃ dhūrjaṭaye* (to Dhūrjaṭi) in the south; *Oṃ lambodarāya* (to Lambodara) in the west; *Oṃ gaṇapataye* (to Gaṇapati) in the north; *Oṃ gaṇādhipataye* (to Gaṇādhipati) in the northeast (*aiśānī*); *Oṃ mahāgaṇapataye* (to Mahāgaṇapati) in the southeast (*āgneyī*); *Oṃ kūśmāṇḍāya* (to Kūśmāṇḍa) in the southwest (*nairṛtī*);

*Oṃ ekadantatripuraghātinetrinetrāya* (to the one with one tusk, the destroyer of the three cities, and the three-eyed one) in the northwest (*vāyavī*). *Oṃ mahāgaṇapataye vidmahe vakratuṇḍāya dhīmahi*.
May that Dantī inspire us. [This is] the Gāyatrī.
Having displayed the eight mudrās—the lotus, the tusk, the garland, the drawing-in, the axe, the goad, the noose, and the drum—one should then perform the rites.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of black sesame seeds; thus one shall bring the king under one's control.

One should display the eleven mudrās, beginning with the invocation (āvāhana) and ending with the food offering (naivedya), in their proper sequence. O King, by whatever rite one worships Hara— the three-eyed wielder of the trident— one should worship the Lord Vighneśa, Gaṇapa, by that very same rite.
That very same maṇḍala belongs to him, and likewise the ritual placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa);
for here, everything is indeed identical except for the mantra-words.
He who worships Vighneśa—the one-tusked son of Umā—[attains success].
His obstacles perish, and no misfortune ever befalls him—
that man who, having observed a fast on the fourth lunar day, performs worship;
all his undertakings shall succeed, of this there is no doubt.
O delighter of the lineage of Śiva and Śivā, for one to whom Vighneśa is favorable,
everything in this world shall indeed be favorable in all undertakings.
Therefore, one should worship him, endowed with devotion and faith.

One should worship according to this rite on the fourth day of the bright fortnight with saffron, agallochum incense, as well as garlands of *uṇḍīraka*, cakes of minced meat, and *jātī* and *unmattaka* flowers.

When the one-toothed Lord of the World, Gaṇeśa, has been propitiated, all his actions succeed without obstacle; of this there is no doubt. O Bhārata, when he is pleased, the ancestors, gods, humans, and all others are likewise pleased.
Therefore, O Lord of the Earth, one should always propitiate him with devotion;
for the destruction of obstacles, one should constantly worship the elephant-faced god with ear-wax, betel-nuts, and sweetmeats.

Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Worship of Vināyaka," in the Caturthī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan, within the Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty thousand verses.
Now begins the thirty-first chapter:
The Worship of Śivā-caturthī.
Sumantu said: O King, the fourth lunar day is remembered as being threefold—Śivā, Śāntā, and Sukhā.
The bright (śukla) fourth day in the month of Bhādrapada is honored as Śivā throughout the worlds.

O King, bathing, giving gifts, fasting, and chanting performed there, by the grace of the Elephant-faced One (Gaṇeśa), yield a hundredfold merit. Furthermore, the giving of molasses, salt, and ghee is remembered as bringing auspicious results.
O hero,
tiger among men, on that day women who always honor their mother-in-law and father-in-law with offerings of molasses, salt, and cakes perform a meritorious feeding of Brahmins.
All of them shall become fortunate through rejoicing in the Lord of Obstacles;
however, a maiden should especially worship Him according to this rite.
(Thus ends the Śivākalpa.)
Sumantu said:
O Lord of the Earth, that fourth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Māgha is eternally peaceful and bestows peace; it indeed always brings about tranquility.

O Lord, whatever rite such as bathing or giving charity is performed on this day becomes multiplied a thousandfold by the grace of that elephant. Whoever observes a fast on this day and worships Vināyaka, [attains great merit].
O King, his ritual acts such as the fire-oblation (homa) shall be a thousandfold;
and by devotedly giving salt, molasses, vegetables, and molasses-cakes to the Brahmins, O Bhārata, he shall enjoy a thousandfold fruit.
Especially for women, O King, those who honor their guru with jaggery, salt, and ghee, O Hero, shall always be endowed with good fortune. (Thus ends the Śāntā-kalpa.)
Sumantu said:
O tiger among the Kurus, the fourth [tithi] is auspicious, bringing happiness, exceedingly pleasant, the supreme bestower of good fortune, and the giver of beauty and charm.
O Hero, this vow is easy to perform, brings great merit, bestows beauty and fortune;
it is extremely subtle, auspicious, and brings merit and happiness in this world,
while yielding fruit and granting divine form in the hereafter.
Her laughter, her graceful speech, and her pleasant gestures;
her playful movement of the arms and her auspicious walking—
all these brought happiness to everyone through her vow of bliss, O scion of the Kuru lineage.

When the Lord of Obstacles (Vighneśa), the son of Śiva and Śivā, is worshipped with offerings on the fourth lunar day of the bright fortnight, and it happens to be a Tuesday, then that fourth day should be known as "Sukhā" and indeed as "Sukhā Caturthī."
O mighty-armed one, in former times, while Bhīma and Mā were standing on the Himālaya mountains engaged in sexual union, a drop of blood fell to the earth;
it was caught with effort by this woman upon the ground for her own comfort.
"O hero, that son of yours, born from her, is red and produced from blood;
since he was born from my own body (aṅga), he is indeed Aṅgāraka.
He shall be known as Aṅgada and Aṅgopakāra, for he is the bestower of limbs (aṅga) upon men."
Because he bestows good fortune and other blessings, he is therefore known as Aṅgāraka.
O King, whatever man or woman, endowed with faith and single-minded devotion, shall observe a fast on the fourth lunar day by eating only at night;
One should worship Kuja with devotion using red flowers and ointments. Endowed with faith, one should first worship Gaṇeśa with devotion;
when he is pleased, he bestows good fortune and the perfection of beauty.
Having previously formed this resolve and having bathed according to the prescribed rite,
O Bhārata, one should take up earth and worship it with this mantra:
"In this world, you were indeed worshipped in the past by Kṛṣṇa when he was lifting [Govardhana]."
"Therefore, burn away my evil that has been accumulated by me in the past.
Reciting this mantra, O hero, one should offer it to the Sun;
[the water] purified by the rays of the Sun and sprinkled with droplets of the Ganges water.
Having placed that clay upon his head, he should apply it to all his limbs;
then he should perform his bath and consecrate the water again with this mantra:
"O Waters, you are the source of origin for all the Daityas, Dānavas, and celestial beings."
Salutations to the Lord of sweat-born beings, egg-born beings, those born from the earth, and of fluids.
I have bathed in all sacred fords,
in all springs, in all ponds, and in lakes such as Mānasa.
In rivers, in natural pools, at excellent sacred fords, or indeed in lakes,
one should wander while meditating on this mantra and then perform the ritual bath.
Having bathed there and become pure, one should then return home and touch [the prescribed objects].

Having touched dūrvā grass, the aśvattha tree, the śamī tree, and a cow while knowing the mantra, one who knows the mantra should pay homage to the dūrvā grass that has grown upon pure ground with this mantra:
"O Dūrvā, you are named Amṛta; you are saluted by all the gods."
Having saluted you, I offer all that evil which has been committed by me.
O Lord of the Earth, listen as I proclaim the *śamī* mantra:
"O Kāśyapī, you are celebrated in the Vedas as the most purifying among all purifiers."
O Śamī tree, pacify my sin; you surely know the mountains.
O hero, listen to this mantra of mine for the touching of the Aśvattha tree:
[it removes] the suffering born from the twitching of the eyes and the like, as well as bad dreams and evil thoughts.
"O Aśvattha, forgive my exertion on behalf of those who are capable.
Reciting this mantra, O hero, the wise man should perform the touching [of the tree];
then, having circumambulated it, he should give a cow to the Goddess, O hero.
Having touched [the image] with his hand, he should then utter this mantra:
"O Goddess, you who consist of all the gods and are well-worshipped by the sages;
therefore, I touch and salute you; being saluted, become the destroyer of my sins."
O hero, O descendant of Kuru, that man who, reciting this mantra with devotion and endowed with faith,
performs a circumambulation of Arjuna,
has undoubtedly circumambulated the entire earth.
Having thus arrived in silence, one should then proceed to the fire-chamber;
having washed one's feet with earth and sipped water for purification (ācamana), one should enter the fire-chamber.
There, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with these excellent mantra-words.
To Śarva, to the son of Śarva, and to him who was born from the lap of the Earth;
to Kuja, to Lalitāṅga, and likewise to Lohitāṅga—
with mantras preceded by Oṃ and accompanied by the utterance of Svāhā.
O Hero, O King, one may perform [the rite] one hundred and eight times, or half of that, or even half of that again;
with these mantra-words, whether out of devotion, according to one's capacity, or by desire,
using well-prepared fuel-sticks of *khadira* wood, along with clarified butter, milk, barley, and sesame seeds.
Endowed with various kinds of edible foods and other offerings according to his ability and devotion, O Hero, having offered oblations, he should then establish the deity upon the ground—
either in gold, silver, or, according to his means, in wood, O King.
It may also be made of devadāru wood or even of śrīkhaṇḍa sandalwood;
[it should be offered] in a vessel of copper or silver, with ghee, saffron, and kesara,
or with other red flowers, leaves, or fruits.
O hero, one should worship with various kinds of blood, or otherwise according to one's ability; O hero, if a wealthy person gives wealth out of devotion,
his merit increases a hundred-thousandfold for the sake of the donor.

Other men, according to their capacity, worship it in a vessel made of copper, bamboo, or even clay; having fashioned a vessel in the form of a human being, they should worship it with these mantras using saffron filaments.
Having worshipped according to the rules with the mantra "Agnirmūrdhā" and likewise with perfumes, flowers, and incense, [the gift] is bestowed upon a Brāhmaṇa:
jaggery-rice, clarified butter, milk, wheat, and husked śāli rice.
Having considered one's capacity, one should indeed give, whether poor or wealthy.
O King, one must not practice stinginess regarding wealth when resources are available;
for he who practices stinginess with his wealth shall not possess strength in the world hereafter.
Śatānīka said:
When the fourth lunar day (caturthī) coincides with Tuesday (Aṅgāraka),
on how many occasions should it be observed by fasting and eating only at night, or is it to be done only once?
Sumantu said:
That fourth lunar day is indeed the fourth; when it is joined with Mars, one should fast on that very day and offer molasses according to the prescribed rite.
O Lord, having observed the fast at night for four Mondays,
listen to the procedure as it is for each fourth lunar day:
having respectfully fashioned an image of Mars along with Vināyaka out of gold.
The principal [image] should weigh ten *sauvarṇikas*, and the others half of that, or even half of that again.
These should be placed with devotion in vessels made of gold, silver, or even copper;
the vessels should weigh twenty *palas* or ten *palas*.
O Hero, one should prepare twenty *karṣas*, or even ten, five, or two and a half; or a *pala* measured in silver, or even half a *pala*,
according to one's capacity, wealth, and devotion, even if it be in a vessel made of copper.
Having installed the Lord of Planets (the Sun),
well-wrapped in cloths and accompanied by various red flowers,
one should always give him to a Brāhmaṇa along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), O King.
"O mighty-armed King, [this was told] to the eloquent, virtuous Śreya;
thus, O descendant of Bharata, has this meritorious and most excellent of lunar days been described to you, by fasting upon which a man attains divine form."
O King, having attained such a form— heroic like Kātyātreyas in luster, resembling the sun in brilliance,
equal to the sun in radiance, and endowed with the strength of the wind—
one goes here to the abode of Bhauma.
O King, by the grace of Vighnanātha and likewise Gaṇapati,
the sins of those who read, listen, and especially those who perform [this], such as the killing of a Brahmin, are destroyed; of this there is no doubt.
One obtains supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), prosperity (*vṛddhi*), and likewise fortune (*lakṣmī*); there is no doubt in this matter.

Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Sukhāvaha-Aṅgāraka-Caturthī Vow," in the *Caturthī-kalpa* within the *Brāhma-parvan* of the *Śrī-Bhaviṣya-Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of fifty thousand verses.
(And here concludes this *Caturthī-kalpa*).
Now begins the thirty-second chapter:
The Worship of Nāgapañcamī. Sumantu said:
O King, the fifth lunar day is beloved by the Nāgas and increases their joy;
indeed, on the fifth day, a great festival for the Nāgas takes place.
Vāsuki, Takṣaka, Kāliya, and Maṇibhadraka [participate].
Airāvata, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Karkoṭaka, and Dhanañjaya—
these grant fearlessness to living beings who sustain their lives.
Those men who bathe these nāgas with milk here on the fifth lunar day [attain this].
In their families, they bestow the gift of life and fearlessness;
when the nāgas, cursed by their mother, are burning day and night,
they extinguish [the fire] with ablutions mixed with cow’s milk.
"It is certain that for those who bathe the nāgas with devotion and endowed with faith,
there shall be no fear of serpents in their family.
Śatānīka said:
"How were the Nāgas cursed by Mātṛkā? With what purpose and for what reason? And how did that which causes joy arise from her grace? Sumantu said:
Uccaiḥśravas, the jewel among horses, was born white, produced from the nectar of immortality.
Seeing him, Kadrū, the mother of the Nāgas, said to her sister:
"I behold this white jewel among horses, born of the nectar."
"You see black hairs, yet the entire sky is white.
Vinatā said, "This excellent horse is entirely white; it has no black nor any red."
"How do you see Kṛṣṇa? Vinatā asked her sister.
Kadrū replied, "I, who am one-eyed, see him accompanied by a black child."
"O two-eyed one, you do not see; Vinata, make a wager!
Vinatā said:
"I shall become your slave, O Kṛṣṇā, once my hair has been shown [to be black]."
"If you do not show them to me, you shall become my slave.
Having thus made this wager, Kadrū departed filled with rage, while Vinatā remained asleep upon her bed; then Kadrū thought a devious thought.
Having summoned her sons, she said: "Remaining as children upon this excellent horse, stay in the marketplace; I shall defeat Vinatā, who is greedy for victory.
But the Nāgas, grasping their mother’s intention, spoke to that woman of crooked mind.
"This is unrighteous, O mother; we shall not carry out your command.
At this, Kadrū cursed them in her wrath: "The fire shall consume you!
After a long period of time had passed, Janamejaya, the son of Pāṇḍu, [arose].
"He shall indeed perform on earth a snake-sacrifice, which is very difficult for others to accomplish;
at that sacrifice, the fierce-rayed Fire shall consume you.
Having cursed them thus in her wrath, Kadrū said nothing further.
The Nāgas, having been cursed by their mother, did not know what ought to be done.
Perceiving Vāsuki to be distressed, Brahmā spoke to him, consoling him:
"Do not grieve excessively, O Vāsuki; hear my supreme word."
At that time, there will be born in a family of Yāyāvaras a twice-born named Jaratkāru, a man of great splendor and a treasury of asceticism;
you shall give your sister Jaratkāru to him in marriage.
He shall have a son renowned as Āstīka; that wise one will indeed bring to an end that great, expanded sacrifice which was so terrifying to the Nāgas,
by means of his supreme words.
Therefore, O King, you shall give this sister of yours back to him;
you should unhesitatingly bestow Jaratkāru upon Jaratkāru.
Whatever he may request when he seeks her in the forest, you must grant it.
"If you desire your own welfare, that must be done without hesitation.
Having heard the words of the Grandfather and having prostrated himself, Vāsuki acted accordingly as he was told, exerting the utmost effort.
Having heard that, all the serpents, those best of snakes, with eyes wide open in great joy,
considered themselves as if born again;
for there, O mighty-armed one, a sacrificial session was commenced by your father.
For that [act], which is difficult to perform in all the worlds,
was previously declared by Viṣṇu to the wise son of Dharma (Yudhiṣṭhira) along with the officiating priests;
it will certainly bring about fear among the Nāgas.
Therefore, O King, when more than a hundred years have passed from that time,
there will occur a terrible sacrificial session that brings about the destruction of the Nāgas;
the venomous serpents, filled with unrighteousness, shall depart.
"O Great King, by the tens of millions, they shall fall day and night into that unprecedented, terrible, and fierce ocean of fire. For those submerged therein,
Āstīka will become their boat in that ocean of flames."
Having heard that the king and his officiating priests would immediately thereafter cause the sacrifice— which was intended to utterly delude the Nāgas— to be turned back,
Brahmā spoke to Lelihāna on the fifth day.
Therefore, O mighty-armed one, this fifth [daughter],
who always brings joy to the Nāgas, was given by Brahmā in the past;
she was given after first providing food for the Brāhmaṇas according to their desire.
Having released them, let the nāgas be gratified— those who dwell anywhere upon the surface of the earth,
those who abide in the rays of the sun, those situated in the intermediate space of the sky,
those great nāgas in the rivers, and those who frequent the Sarasvatī.
And having honored all those nāgas and brahmins at all those step-wells and ponds with salutations, and having dismissed them according to the proper rite,
O lord of men, one should thereafter eat together with one's servants.
One should first eat something sweet and thereafter eat according to one's desire;
learn from me the fruit that belongs to one who observes this rule:
upon death, he goes to the city of the Nāgas, being honored by hosts of Apsarases.
Mounted upon an excellent celestial chariot (vimāna), he enjoys himself for as long as he desires.
Then, having returned here, that king shall become the best among ten thousand rulers;
he will be enriched with all kinds of jewels and born into great abundance of vehicles.
In each Dvāpara age, that king shall be born for five lifetimes,
free from mental and physical ailments, and accompanied by his wife and sons.
Therefore, they should be honored and protected with offerings of ghee, milk-rice, and guggulu resin.
Śatānīka said:
"O Brahmin, what happens to that man who is bitten by serpents filled with rage? Tell me in detail, O twice-born one."
Sumantu said:
O King, a man bitten by a snake who meets his death goes downward;
by going downward, he becomes a snake devoid of poison—of this there is no doubt.
Śatānīka said: "If one's father, or brother, or even daughter,
or mother, son, or wife has been bitten by a snake, tell me what should be done."
"O best of Brahmins, tell me that gift, vow, or fast for his liberation, O tiger among the twice-born, by which I may indeed perform it. Sumantu said:
O King, the fifth lunar day (Pañcamī) should be observed as a fast; it increases the prosperity of the Nāgas.
O Indra among kings, O Bhārata, listen now to this single ordinance:
it is that which occurs in the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, O Lord of the Earth.
O Lord of the Earth, that [day] is declared to be of great merit and is indeed to be observed;
O bull of the Bharatas, one should know that there are twelve fifth days in a year.
On the fourth day, however, eating only once is prescribed, while on that [fifth day], eating at night is proclaimed.
O King, having fashioned images of serpents on the ground made of cloth, or of gold,
or even of wood, or of clay,
one should worship the five serpents with devotion on the fifth lunar day, O King.
O observer of noble vows, having worshipped the supreme group of five with *karavīra*, *śatapatra*, and *jātī* flowers, as well as with perfumes and incense,
one should afterwards feed a Brāhmaṇa with ghee, milk-rice, and sweetmeats.
Ananta, Vāsuki, Śaṅkha, Padma, and Kambala;
likewise the Nāga Karkoṭaka, O King, and the Nāga Aśvatara;
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Śaṅkhapāla, Kāliya, and Takṣaka.
And likewise, the serpent Piṅgala is proclaimed [to be worshipped] month by month;
at the end of the year, there should be a breaking of the fast, and one should feed many Brāhmaṇas.
O King, an image of the Nāga made with red ochre should be given to one who knows the Itihāsas.
In that manner, O lord of the earth, worship should be offered to the reciter.
This is indeed the rite for Nāgapañcamī proclaimed by the wise, O King;
it was performed by your father for the sake of his own liberation, O Bhārata.
O hero, O bull among the Bharatas, by giving one *bhāra* of gold fashioned into an elephant, as well as a cow, to Vyāsa on the fifth lunar day,
you shall indeed attain freedom from debt to your father, O tiger among the Kurus.
O King, O hero, your father’s grandfather indeed performed this worship on the fifth day;
having abandoned the Nāgata assembly,
he went to the Puṣpottara assembly, and likewise to the Puṣpasad assembly, O King.
Having gone to the assembly of Sunāsīra, he then went to the assembly of Bharga;
having gone from there to the assembly of Svabhū, he went to the assembly of Kañjaja.
Others as well who shall perform this unsurpassed vow [shall likewise attain these states].
The one bitten shall be liberated, and he shall attain an auspicious state.
And that man who constantly hears this, endowed with faith,
will never experience fear of the nāgas anywhere within his lineage.

Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Nāga-Pañcamī Vow," in the Pañcamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan, within the Śrī-Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty thousand verses.
Now begins the thirty-third chapter: "The Classification of Serpents."
Śatānīka said:
How many forms do snakes have? What are their colors and what are their characteristics?
What is their lineage, and from which wombs or families do they originate?
Sumantu said:
Long ago, on Meru, the best of mountains, Gautama bowed his head with devotion to Kaśyapa, the treasure-house of asceticism, and spoke these words.
O Prajāpati, tell me everything: how many forms do snakes have, what are their signs, and what are their characteristics? Tell me their species, lineages, and colors.
Furthermore, O Lord, how is a snake born, and how does it release its poison?
How many stages of the poison's onset (*viṣavega*) are said to exist, and how many poison-channels (*viṣanāḍikā*) are there?
How many kinds of fangs (*daṃṣṭrā*) are said to be, and what is the measure at the arrival of the poison?
When does it take up the embryo, and how is it born here in this world?
"What kind of woman is she, what kind of man is he, and what kind of eunuch?
What is the name of this tooth? Tell me this, O you of excellent vows.
Having heard those words of his, Kaśyapa replied:
Listen, O Gautama, to the true characteristics of serpents here:
in the months of Āṣāḍha and Jyeṣṭha, the snakes become intoxicated;
then the male nāga and the female nāgī engage in sexual union.
The female serpent bore the embryo for four months of the rainy season;
then, in the month of Kārttika, she gave birth to the eggs. It should be known that there were two hundred and twenty eggs.
She alone should eat them, yet she might abandon even that single enjoyment out of disgust.
From that egg, which has the color of gold or the sun, a male is born;
the serpent eats those very [eggs] for twenty days and nights.
O best of Brahmins, from that egg which has the luster of the color of a golden ketaka flower and resembles a long lotus, a female indeed is born;
from an egg with the luster of the color of a śirīṣa flower, a neuter being arises.
Then, O Gautama, after six months, he breaks the eggs;
thereafter, through the bond of affection, those young ones develop love for him.
Then, after seven nights, that serpent becomes black.
The lifespan of serpents is recorded as one hundred and twenty years;
furthermore, death is known to be of eight kinds—listen now to them in their proper order:
[death] from peacocks, humans, cakora birds, and likewise from the hooves of cattle.
If one should survive an encounter with a cat, a mongoose, a boar,
or a scorpion, he shall live for one hundred and twenty years;
however, when that seven-day period is complete, there occurs the eruption of the fangs.
One should repeatedly introduce poison there;
having understood this according to its true nature, one should indeed undertake the rite of poison.
Within twenty-one nights, a fang capable of producing poison will truly arise.
A young serpent that curls its body like the side of a female elephant is so described;
it becomes fatal within twenty-five nights. However, one born only six months ago sheds its slough immediately.
Furthermore, it should be known that there are two hundred and twenty joints in the feet;
these joints, resembling cow-hair, enter and move [within].
Likewise, it should be known that there are two hundred and twenty joints in [the rest of] his body.
Their fingers should also be known to number two hundred and twenty.
Those snakes that are born out of season are proclaimed to be non-venomous;
their lifespan is said to be seventy-five years.
Those with red, yellow, or white teeth, those that are not blue, and those that are slow-moving are known to have short lifespans; others are recorded as being timid.
Furthermore, it is proclaimed that such a snake may have one mouth or even two tongues.
It is said that snakes have thirty-two fangs, of this there is no doubt.
Among those, four fangs are carriers of potent venom:
Makarī, Karālī, Kālarātrī, and likewise Yamadūtī.
And for all the fangs, the presiding deities have been proclaimed:
the first has Brahmā as its deity, the second has Viṣṇu as its deity,
the third has Rudra as its deity, and the fourth has Yama as its deity.
But that which is deficient in size rests upon the left eye;
in this case, no mantras should be employed, nor any herb or medicine.
The physician turns his back and departs; death results from the scraping of that [eye].
The wise should not attempt medical treatment, for his life ends with that [onset].
One should know Makarī to be monthly, Karālī two-monthly,
Kālarātrī three-monthly, and Yamadūtī four-monthly.
One should give molasses-rice to Makarī; astringent food to Karālikā;
pungent food to Kālarātrī; and for Dūtī, food prepared with a combination of all three humors (sānnipātika).
One should know that Makarī is the weapon-bearing [deity] and Karālī is the crow-footed one.
The one with the form of a hand is known as Kālarātri; the one with the form of a tortoise is remembered as Yāmyā.
Makarī should be known as Vātalā, and Karālī is remembered as Paittikī.
Kālarātrī consists of phlegm (kapha), while Yamadūtī is of the nature of the combination of all three humors (sānnipātika).
Makarī should be known as white; Karālī is like the color of blood;
Kālarātrī should be yellow, and Yamadūtikā is black.
Vāmā is white and black, while Dakṣiṇā is red and yellow.
I shall now describe them briefly according to their colors as they are traditionally recorded:
the Brāhmaṇī is to be known as white, the Kṣatriyā is recorded as red,
the Vaiśyā is to be known as yellow, and the Śūdrā is said to be black.
Hereafter, I shall explain the characteristics of the venom in the fangs.
Indeed, there is no venom in the fangs of a serpent at all times;
rather, the serpent's venom resides having reached the right eye.
When a serpent is enraged here, its poison goes to its head;
from the head it enters the vessels, and from there it passes into the channels. From the channels it descends to the fangs, and there the poison is discharged.
I shall relate all of that exactly and in due order.
A snake bites for eight reasons; there is no doubt about this.
First, it bites when it has been stepped upon; second, it bites an old enemy.
He bites the third out of fear, the fourth out of pride and arrogance,
the fifth when overcome by hunger, and the sixth here because of his intense venom.
He bites the seventh for the sake of protecting his city, and the eighth when impelled by Time.
One should diagnose as fatal that case where a snake, having bitten, coils itself around the abdomen with its fangs bent by force and pressed against the body;
likewise, one whose wound from a snake-bite appears deep.
One should recognize a bite inflicted with enmity according to the words of Kaśyapa; that which has a single tooth-mark, indistinct and not well-formed,
one should recognize as a bite inflicted out of fear, just as the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) declared.

One should recognize that a person has been bitten by me if, when bitten by a snake, the marks of my fangs appear; this is according to the word of Kaśyapa. Furthermore, if two fang-marks are seen and there is a large wound, [one should know it was my bite].
One should recognize it as being possessed by hunger, just as Prajāpati has said:
"If two fangs are seen anywhere amidst a mass of blood, one should know that bite to be full of virulent poison; of this there is no doubt."
One should know him without doubt as being for the protection of his offspring; however,
that which has the shape of a crow's foot and is marked by three teeth is called a "great serpent" (mahānāga), and one should designate it as the "staff of death" (kāladaṇḍa).
The symptoms produced by those born from the bite [of a snake] have been declared to be threefold.
According to the word of Kaśyapa, one should recognize that which is "drunk" (consumed) by the bitten person:
a third part of the serpent's poison may transfer there [to the victim].

One who exposes his belly should be designated as "arrogant"; one whose vomit is driven by the force of poison becomes a snake free from venom. Furthermore, one bitten by the four fangs should be known as incurable.
If there is a slight contraction of the neck and the bite is slightly constricted due to the influence of the poison,
yet the area from this bite to that one is clear, it is proclaimed as a *vyantara* (intermediate) bite.

Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Snake’s Fangs," in the *Pañcamī-kalpa* of the *Brāhma-parvan*, within the *Śatārdhasāhasrī-saṃhitā* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya-mahāpurāṇa*.
Kaśyapa said: Hereafter, I shall explain the characteristics of one bitten by Time (Kāla).
Listen, Gautama, to the truth concerning the nature of such a man:
there is a drooping of the tongue, pain in the heart, and he does not see with his eyes;
the bite appears as if burnt, resembling a ripe jambu fruit.
There is discoloration of the teeth, which become dark in hue;
there is looseness in all the limbs and diarrhea.
With shoulders, hips, and neck broken, he gazes upward with his face turned downward.
He burns, trembles, and falls asleep again and again;
though being cut with a weapon, blood does not flow,
and though being struck with a staff, the marks of the staff do not appear.
If the bite is a deep black spot like a crow's foot, repeatedly resembling the jambū fruit, dense, swollen, and profusely moist with blood, and if there is difficulty in restraining the venom;

if there is hiccup, labored breathing, constriction of the throat, and the skin appears very pale while the limbs become dry—the experts in the scriptures declare such a person to be bitten by a "fatal" (tatkāla) snake.

Furthermore, if there is swelling at the site of the bite, or a moving, wrinkled, or deep blue circular mark; if there is perspiration, breaking pain in the limbs, and the patient speaks with a nasal tone while blood flows [from the mouth]—[these are signs of imminent death].

There is a separation of the teeth and lips, and the heart wanders while experiencing intense constriction; know this to be the bite of a celestial serpent, vast as a mountain plateau, and one bitten by such a one is marked by Time.
He repeatedly touches his teeth with his teeth, his gaze is distressed with exhaustion, and from the thick bite, blood flows from one squinting eye.
He breathes incessantly as if rebuked, speaks with a nasal twang, and utters all that is wicked; they call him one struck by the Staff of Time.
When intense pain causes trembling and the eyes become bloodshot,
when there is a contraction of the neck and the navel becomes unstable, one should declare that person to be bitten by Kāla.
Furthermore, if one does not see one's own reflection in a mirror or in water, [one is marked for death].
When the sun’s rays have become faint and the day-maker has lost its brilliance,
the living being trembles, terrified by agony, and his eyes turn red;
such a person goes to his death— one should declare this to be the staff of Time (Kāladaṇḍa).
On the eighth and ninth days of the dark fortnight, on the fourteenth,
and on the fifth day known as Nāgapañcamī— for these eight [periods] there is danger to one's life,
especially under the asterisms of Ārdrā, Āśleṣā, Maghā, Bharaṇī, and Kṛttikā.
Those bitten by a snake under the asterisms of Viśākhā, the three Pūrvas, Mūla, Svātī, and Śatabhiṣaj, as well as those who have drunk poison, do not survive; likewise,
[those bitten] in an empty house, a cremation ground, or under a withered tree [do not survive].
Men bitten on a lunar mansion (nakṣatra) conjoined with an inauspicious lunar day (tithi) do not survive.
It is declared that there are one hundred and eight vital points (marmas) in living beings; among those, twelve vital points are specifically proclaimed.
In the temples, the eyes, between the eyebrows, the two testicles, above the scrotum,
the armpits, the shoulders, the heart, the center of the palate, the chin, and the anus—
one who is bitten by [venomous creatures] or struck with a weapon in these twelve vital points (marmas) [perishes].

A man does not live in this world; one should declare that the rod of Death has been cast upon him. They say that among the letters *a, ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, ya, śa*, if these are uttered [in the name] and he does not live therein, then if he falters when pronouncing the letter *ga*, his time has arrived.
Furthermore, if the messenger is of lower status than the superior person, or if the messenger is of higher status than the inferior person;

or if he first mentions the name of the one who was bitten and later speaks of the other; or if there is a disparity in their complexions, yet the messenger arrives at the same time as the appointed hour;

or if the messenger has a staff in his hand, or likewise holds a pair of nooses; or if he wears red or black clothing, or has it draped over his face and head, or if the messenger is clad in a single garment—[these are signs of the messenger].
Likewise, he who goes with anointed oil, with hurried gait, and with disheveled hair, or who utters a terrible sound with his hands and feet, is a messenger of one whose time has arrived.
I shall now declare the arising of the Nāgas as spoken by Īśāna;
for in ancient times, Brahmā created many Nāgas as planetary deities.
One should know Ananta as the Sun; one should know Soma as Vāsuki;
Takṣaka as the son of the Earth (Mars); and Karkoṭa as Mercury.
One should know Padma as Jupiter; and Mahāpadma as Venus.
Kulika and Śaṅkhapāla—these two are indeed Śanaiścara.
Śaṅkhapāla is the first quarter, and Kulika is the second;
they are always present in the assigned portion, as well as during day and night.
Venus and the Moon [are dominant] at midday, while the son of Earth (Mars) is at sunrise;
Saturn is in the eighth part of the day. Thus the distribution for day and night is stated here;
the planets consume [their portions], and the remainder is the characteristic of the [remaining] part.
On Sunday, one should always know the feet to be ten and fourteen;
on Monday, eight and twelve; likewise on Tuesday, ten and six;
on Wednesday, at the ninth foot; and on Saturday, at the day's [ninth foot].
One should avoid the second and sixth [lunar days] of the Guru (Jupiter), as well as the sixteenth;
on the day of the Sun (Sunday), the fourth, tenth, and eighth are declared [to be avoided];
and on the day of Saturn (Saturday), one should abandon the most dreadful quarter [of the day].
One should avoid the second and the twelfth [muhūrtas] of the sixteenth [tithi].
Beyond a muhūrta and a ghaṭikā, a ghaṭikā is a fourth part; twenty [of these] constitute a kuhū, a suta, a budbuda, and a nimeṣa—such is the definition of time.

Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Messenger Bitten by a Scorpion," in the *Pañcamī-kalpa* of the *Brāhma-parvan*, within the *Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of fifty thousand verses.
[Now follows] the characteristics of the messengers of Yama;
Kaśyapa said:
The messenger of Yama indeed dwells between the two venomous fangs;
therefore, the wise should not attempt medical treatment, for one who has reached that state is declared dead.
For half a watch each, day and night, they consume [the victim] from the outside.
When the first and second [lines] are equal, as well as the sixteenth,
and the Nāgodaya occurs— knowing this to be the "Kāladaṣṭa" (Time-Bitten) according to the word of Kaśyapa, one should recognize that the person aimed at has been killed, pierced, or torn apart.
However much of a drop, even as small as the tip of a hair raised from water,
falls [into the mouth], that much of the serpent’s dreadful venom flows through its fangs;
when the hundreds of channels are filled, the poison spreads throughout the body.
As long as one shifts the arm or extends it while it is bent,
by this mere moment the poison goes to the head; then,
during the onset of the poison's force, the person trembles hundreds and thousands of times.
Having reached the blood, it increases like a fire fanned by winds;
it grows with great force like a drop of oil upon reaching water;
like a peacock, having found its refuge and being impelled by the wind.
Then, having reached a hundred locations, its movement within the skin is observed;
one should know it to be twofold in the skins, fourfold in the bloods,
threefold in the bile, and indeed sixteenfold in the phlegm.
When the wind has thirtyfold [power] and the marrow likewise sixtyfold,
and when the vital breath (prāṇa) has become a single ocean, one should join all the limbs together.
But when the sense of hearing is being obstructed, the bitten person passes into a state beyond cure.

Then that living being dies, deprived of inhalation and exhalation. When the life-force has departed and the elements have reached their dissolution into the fivefold state, those elements go each to its own respective destination according to its nature.
Earth, water, fire, air, and space—
this very collection of these is designated as the body. Earth dissolves into earth, and water dissolves into waters.
The fire-element goes to the sun, and the wind-element proceeds to the wind;
likewise, the space-element goes into space along with that very [wind].
Thus, joined together with one another, they each attain their own respective abodes.
O you of noble vows, no one who has arrived here in this life shall fail to survive;
one must not neglect a person afflicted by poison, but should treat them with haste.
There is but one poison in the world, and a second is found only through its application.
Just as there are various kinds of stationary [poisons], so too is it with the first onset of poison:
horripilation arises;
in the second onset of poison, perspiration arises on the limbs.
In the third stage of the poison's onset, trembling arises in the limbs;
in the fourth stage of the poison's onset, it causes the obstruction of the ears;
and in the fifth stage of the poison's onset, hiccups arise in the limbs.
In the sixth stage of the poison's onset, one is even deprived of life.
These [stages] that carry the seven bodily constituents were indeed spoken by Vainateya;
now hear from me the symptoms when the poison has reached the location of the skin.
The limbs become dim-sighted and repeatedly burn;
he in whom these signs appear has poison located in his skin. I shall declare the remedy for it, by which well-being is attained.
Having mixed together the roots of *arka*, *apāmārga*, *priyaṅgu*, and *tagara*, this should be administered; thereby happiness is attained.
O Brahmin, even if the poison does not recede once that has been done, [the remedy remains effective].
Having pierced the location of the skin, it then rushes to the location of the blood.
Listen to me regarding the symptoms when the poison has reached the blood:
he feels a burning sensation, becomes delirious, and excessively craves cold things.
The poison residing in the blood belongs to one who possesses these symptoms. I shall now declare the antidote by which well-being is attained:
*uśīra*, sandalwood, *kuṣṭha*, blue lotus, and likewise *tagara*.
The roots of Mahākāla and the Sinduvāra tree,
along with cinnabar and black pepper, should be administered during the first stage;
likewise, the roots of Bṛhatī, Vṛścikā, Kālī, and Indravāruṇī.
The second [preparation] is proclaimed as Saptagandhaghṛta;
likewise, a wise person should prepare Sinduvāra and Hiṅgu for the third.
One should employ it as a drink, as well as an ointment and an external application.
By this very treatment, one then attains well-being.
From that place of blood, it then rushes to the place of bile.
O Brahmin, hear from me the symptoms of poison when it has reached the seat of bile.
One rises up, falls down, is burned, and likewise becomes deluded;
indeed, there is yellowness in the limbs, and one perceives the directions as yellow.
There is intense fainting, and one does not recognize oneself.
One should administer an anti-venom treatment for him so that he attains well-being;
[the venom] passes beyond the seat of bile and reaches the seat of phlegm.
Long pepper, licorice, honey, sugar, and likewise clarified butter [are to be used].
One should grind together madhusāra, alābu, jātī, śaṅkhavālukā,
and the root of indravāruṇikā with cow’s urine;
one should then employ this as a nasal drop (nasya), as well as for drinking, external application, and as a collyrium (añjana).
By this very treatment, one then attains well-being.
Now listen to me regarding the symptoms that arise when it reaches the seat of phlegm (kapha):
his limbs become rigid and he is unable to breathe.
Saliva flows from his mouth and his throat makes a rattling sound;
he whose symptoms are these has poison located in the phlegm (kapha).
I shall now declare the remedy for it, by which he attains well-being.
One should grind equal parts of trikuṭakī, śleṣmātaka, lodhra, and madhusāraka with cow’s urine;
one should then employ this as a drink, an ointment, and likewise as an external application.
By this very treatment, one then attains well-being;
having passed beyond the seat of phlegm, the poison goes to the seat of wind.
There I shall describe the symptoms when the poison has reached the seat of wind.
The abdomen distends and he no longer sees his kinsmen;
he assumes such a form and the cessation of rain occurs.
These are the symptoms of one whose poison has entered the wind (*vāyu*).
I shall prescribe for him a medicine by which well-being is attained:
the root of śoṇa, priyāla, red gajapippalī,
bhārṅgī, vacā, pippalī, devadāru, and madhūka.
One should grind together the essence of *madhūka*, *sinduvāra*, and *hiṅgu* to form pills;
by administering these as collyrium, ointment, and so forth, this medicine destroys the poisons of snakes.
One should quickly administer both collyrium and nasal drops when [the victim] is afflicted by poison.
Then, leaving the seat of the wind, it rushes to the seat of the marrow;
O Brahmin, hear from me the symptoms when the poison has reached the marrow:
his vision fails him and his limbs utterly give way.
If these symptoms appear, the poison has reached the marrow.
I shall now describe the remedy by which one attains well-being:
uśīra and sandalwood combined with ghee, honey, and sugar.
O observer of noble vows, having mixed these together, this should be administered as a drink or as a nasal drop (*nasya*).
Thereby suffering is destroyed and happiness is attained;
once this application has been performed, his poison is neutralized.
Having reached the site of the marrow, the poison then rushes to the vital points (marmas).
Listen now to what happens when the poison has reached a vital point:
the person becomes motionless, falls to the ground, and becomes deaf in both ears.
When being sprinkled with water, no horripilation arises;
when being struck with a staff, no bruise-mark appears;
and when being cut by a weapon, blood does not flow.
When the hair is being plucked out, if one does not feel the hair itself,
and if his ears, sides, hands, feet,
and joints become slack in this world, the sacred tradition declares that he has lost his life.
O Gautama, if these signs appear in a perverted manner,
one should not recognize the person as dead, according to the words of Kaśyapa;
physicians who are poorly trained do not perceive this.
But those who are discerning, being endowed with mantras and medicinal herbs, perceive it;
I shall declare its remedy, spoken by Rudra himself:
peacock bile, cat bile, and the root of *gandhanāḍī*.
One should grind equal parts of saffron, tagara, kuṣṭha, the bark of kāsamarda,
and the filaments of the blue lotus, the lotus,
and the water lily with cow’s urine.
This is the antidote; whoever has it in their hand does not die even when bitten by the black serpent (Kālāhi). One who is bitten by that serpent quickly becomes free of poison.
This life-restoring medicine must be administered with great speed.
"A wise physician should quickly administer both collyrium and nasal drops.

Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Treatment for Poison Residing in the Dhātus," in the *Pañcamī-kalpa* of the *Brāhma-parvan*, within the *Śatārddhasāhasrī-saṃhitā* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya-mahāpurāṇa*.
Gautama said:
What is the appearance of one bitten by a male snake, and what would it be for one bitten by a female snake?
What would one bitten by a youth be like, and likewise for one stung by a woman who has recently given birth? And what is the form here of one bitten by a eunuch or by a *vyaṃtara* spirit?
"Tell me all of this—the symptoms of one bitten by these [snakes].
Kaśyapa said:
"Henceforth, I shall declare the physical characteristics of the nāgas."
And likewise, O bull among the twice-born, for one bitten by a snake:
now, in the case of one bitten by a snake, an upward gaze arises;
and in the case of one bitten by a female snake, a downward gaze arises.
O best among the foremost of the twice-born, if bitten by a virgin, the gaze will be directed to the left;
likewise, if bitten by a young boy, it occurs on the right. Furthermore, if bitten by a pregnant woman, perspiration arises.
Horripilation and trembling also arise in the case of a woman who has recently given birth.
In one bitten by a *napuṃsaka* [neuter] snake, aching in the limbs occurs.
Female snakes are most potent at night, while during the day, the male snake possesses the greater venom.
But regarding one who is neuter, it was stated by Kaśyapa:
"If one bitten in the twilight, or in darkness, or in deep water, or in a dense forest,
or while asleep, or if distracted, does not see the snake..."
Indeed, not knowing the forms of those who have bitten, how can there be medical treatment?
For the high-souled one has declared that serpents here are of four kinds:
the hooded (darvīkara), the circular-spotted (maṇḍalin), the striped (rājila), and the intermediate (vyantara).

The *darvīkara* snakes are known to have poisonous venom characterized by *vāta*; the *maṇḍala* snakes are considered to have *pitta*-dominated venom; the *rājila* snakes should be known as having *śleṣman*-dominated venom; and the *vyantara* snakes have venom resulting from the combination of all three (*sānnipātika*).
One should examine the blood of these snakes individually.
In the case of the *darvīkara* snakes, a black, intense, and not insignificant bite occurs;
in the *maṇḍalī* species, blood is drawn thickly and copiously;
in the *rājila* species, it is slimy and slight; and the same applies to the *vyaṃtaraka* species.
The serpents are to be known as four; a fifth is not found.
They are the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra as the fourth.
To the Brāhmaṇa one should give what is sweet, and likewise to the latter (the Kṣatriya), one should give what is bitter.
To a Vaiśya, one should give the fruit of the *karṣa* plant, and to a Śūdra, the *tristhūṇa* plant.
When bitten by a Brāhmaṇa [snake], a burning sensation arises in the limbs;
there is indeed intense fainting, and he does not recognize himself.
The face becomes dark-complexioned and a stiffness of the marrow arises;
one should provide a remedy for that by which happiness is attained.
[The remedy consists of] aśvagandhā, apāmārga, sinduvāra, and liquor.
This clarified butter (sarpir), combined with these [medicines], should be administered both as a drink and as nasal drops (nasya). By this very treatment, the person becomes comfortable.
However, in one bitten by a Kṣatriya [snake], trembling arises in the limbs.
Fainting and delusion likewise occur; he does not recognize himself.
Pain arises for him, and he gazes upward.
One should provide a remedy for him by which he may attain comfort.

One should administer the root of *arka*, *apāmārga*, *priyaṅgu*, and *indravāruṇī* combined with clarified butter as both a drink and an errhine (*nasya*). By this very treatment, a person becomes comfortable.
Now hear also the symptoms of one who has been bitten by a Vaiśya:
there is an aggravation of phlegm and saliva, and he does not maintain consciousness;
furthermore, he suffers from intense fainting and takes no pleasure in himself.
One should provide a remedy for that by which well-being is attained:
Ashvagandhā with cow's urine, house-soot with guggulu, and Śirīṣa, Arka, Palāśa, Śvetā, and Girikarṇikā.
One should administer it as a drink and as nasal drops combined with cow urine;
this is proclaimed as the antidote for those bitten by a Vaiśya.
Now hear, O Gautama, the truth regarding one who has been bitten even by a Śūdra.
The body shivers and trembles, fever arises along with coldness, and the limbs throb;
these are the symptoms of one bitten by a Śūdra snake.
In that regard, I shall declare the antidote (agada) by which well-being is attained.
Take lotus, *lodhraka*, honey, the filaments of the lotus, the essence of *madhūka*, liquorice, and white *girikarṇikā*. Grind these in equal parts with cold water.
A person becomes comfortable through drinking, ointments, collyrium, and nasal drops.
A Brahmin should practice [the observance] in the forenoon, a Kṣatriya in the midday,
a Vaiśya in the afternoon, and a Śūdra should practice it during the twilight.
O best of the twice-born, the wise know that the food of Brahmins is the flowers of the wind; the food of Kṣatriyas is mice;
Vaiśyas subsist on frogs, while Śūdras are eaters of all things.
The Brahmin bites on the front, the Kṣatriya on the right side,
the Vaiśya always on the left side, and the Śūdra should bite from behind.
When the time of rut has arrived, these highly venomous snakes are provoked by being tormented.
Indeed, at the improper time, serpents bite those afflicted by sexual desire.
O Brahmins, those with the scent of flowers are known as Brahmins; those who bear the scent of sandalwood are Kṣatriyas;
those with the scent of ghee are Vaiśyas; and those who have the scent of fish are Śūdras.
I shall describe their dwelling places correctly and in due order:
Brahmins dwell by ponds, wells, and tanks, as well as at mountain springs; serpents dwell at the village gate and at crossroads.
Kṣatriyas always dwell in sacred groves and pure sanctuaries, at gateways and by lakes;
they also reside in cremation grounds, in huts of ashes, upon straw mats, and on riverbanks.
O Brahmin, Vaiśyas dwell in cow-pens, on roads, and at the foot of trees;
they also dwell in unsecluded places, in lonely forests, in empty houses, and in cremation grounds. O Brahmin, Śūdras likewise dwell in these same places.
Those serpents that are white and tawny, possessing the brilliance of fire,
who are high-minded and characterized by the quality of goodness (sattva), are remembered by the wise as Brāhmaṇas.
Those of red color, with a golden luster, resembling coral and gems—
O Brahmin, those serpents who possess the luster of the sun are Kṣatriyas; those resembling the color of flax and adorned with various wonderful stripes are Vaiśya serpents;
and those having the hue of the Bāṇa flower are indeed Vaiśya serpents.
Those who resemble the belly of a black cobra, those who resemble collyrium,
those with the color of crows, and those with a smoky hue are proclaimed to be Śūdras.
[Furthermore,] when one bitten by a serpent has a bite-mark between the thumb and [the forefinger]...
One should recognize a bite by a child according to the word of Kaśyapa:
for one bitten by a snake, if the distance between the two puncture marks is two finger-breadths,
this is the characteristic of one bitten by a youth.

One should recognize a bite as "old" when the interval between the fangs and the wound is two finger-breadths; this is according to the word of Kaśyapa. Ananta looks first, while Vāsuki is on the left side.
Takṣaka moves here on the right, and Karkoṭaka likewise behind;
Padma wanders about, Mahāpadma sinks down,
and Śaṅkhapāla remains repeatedly unconscious.

The Kulika, the best of serpents, assumes the form of all of them. The eastern direction belongs to Ananta; that of Vāsuki is the south-east; the southern is said to belong to Takṣaka, and the south-west to Karkoṭaka.
The western [lotus] belongs to Padmanābha, while that of Mahāpadma is born of the wind;
the northern belongs to Śaṅkhapāla, and the northeastern to Kambala.
The lotus belongs to Ananta, and likewise the blue water-lily (utpala) belongs to Vāsuki.
The svastika is said for Takṣaka; for Karkoṭa, however, it is the lotus (paṅkaja).
For Padma, there should be a lotus; for one other than Padma, a trident (śūla).
For Śaṅkhapāla, there should be an umbrella (chattra); for Kulika, a crescent moon (ardhacandraka).
The two Brahmins are Ananta and Kapila; Śaṅkha and Vāsuki are the two Kṣatriyas;
Mahāpadma and Takṣaka are proclaimed as the two Vaiśyas, O Brāhmaṇa;
and Padma and Karkoṭaka are always to be known as the two Śūdras by the wise.
Ananta and Kulika are fair in complexion and born from Brahmā;
Vāsuki and Śaṅkhapāla are red, for they were born from Agni;
Takṣaka and Mahāpadma became slightly yellowish.
O Brahmin, the two serpents Padma and Karkoṭaka became black.
Having produced these— the horse, the vehicle, the bull, the umbrella, the king, the fire,
and the earth— they are known as those who bestow success when maintained.
A full water-pot, a banner, gold, and likewise jewels;
a *śirīṣa* flower, a ruby on the neck, and a *jīvajīvaka* bird— O observer of good vows, the sight of these is most auspicious, as is a maiden who has borne but one child.
Sixty-four are declared to be the serpents who possess enjoyments;
among them, thirty-six are invisible, thirty are visible as earth-dwellers,
twenty are said to wear garlands, and seven are the coiled ones (maṇḍalins).
Ten are said to be *rājīvantas*, and sixteen and five are *darvyas*.
Also, *dundubha*, *ḍuṇḍubha*, *ceṭabha*, and *indravāhana*—
those snakes which have the color of *nāgapuṣpa* flowers are known as *nirviṣas* (non-venomous).
In this very manner, one hundred and ninety-two types of snakes are recorded.
Having ground together varāhakarṇī, gajapippalī, gāndhārikā, pippalī, devadāru,
the essence of madhūka, sahasrā, sinduvāra, and hiṅgu, a pill should be prepared.
Sumantu said:
O hero, in ancient times the Prajāpati Gautama spoke thus regarding the characteristics of all the nāgas, as well as their forms, colors, and poisons.
Therefore, one should always worship the Nāgas with devotion,
especially on the fifth lunar day with milk and milk-rice (pāyasa).
O lord of men, [this should be done] on the fifth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Śrāvaṇa.
On both sides of the door, one should draw fierce venomous serpents with cow dung.
One should worship the door according to the rules with curd, dūrvā grass, unbroken rice, and kuśa grass,
as well as with offerings of fragrances, flowers, and by gratifying the Brāhmaṇas.
"But those who here worship the Nāgas in this [rite], preceded by devotion—
O Hero, for them there shall never be any fear from any quarter whatsoever.

Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Śrāvaṇika Nāga-Pañcamī Vow," in the Pañcamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan, within the Śatārddha-sāhasrī Saṃhitā of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa.
Sumantu said:
Likewise, in the month of Bhādrapada, on the fifth lunar day,
a man endowed with faith should then paint the Nāgas using pigments of black and other colors.
One should worship with perfumes, flowers, clarified butter, milk-rice, and guggulu incense;
then Takṣaka and the other serpents will attain satisfaction toward him.
For seven generations of his lineage, there shall be no fear from the Nāgas.

Therefore, a wise person should worship the Nāgas with every effort. Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Bhādrapada Nāga-pañcamī Vow," in the Pañcamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan, within the Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of one hundred thousand verses.
Sumantu said:
Likewise, O joy of the Kurus, on the fifth day of the month of Āśvayuja,
having fashioned serpents out of *kuśa* grass, one should worship them with perfumes and other offerings;
O lord of the people, one should bathe them with ghee, water, and milk.

O tiger among the Kurus, O King, he who— pure and endowed with devotion— worships the Nāgas on this day according to the rules with wheat, milk-boiled rice, and various kinds of foods, for him Śeṣa and the other [Nāgas] grant their favor.
O Lord, the Nāgas become pleased here, or he attains peace;
having reached the world of peace, he rejoices for eternal years.
Thus, O Hero, this excellent ritual of the fifth day has been described.
In this regard, the mantra that repels all serpents is recited as follows:

*Oṃ kurukulle phaṭ svāhā*. Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Conclusion," in the *Pañcamī-kalpa* of the *Brāhma-parvan*, within the *Śatārdha-sāhasrī-saṃhitā* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya-mahāpurāṇa*.
Sumantu said: O King, one who subsists on fruits on the sixth lunar day, especially during the month of Kārtika,
shall regain his own kingdom without delay, even if he has been deprived of it.
The sixth lunar day, O Great King, always grants all desires;
it should be observed with diligent effort at all times by one seeking victory.
This great lunar day, the sixth, is beloved by Kārttikeya.
For the high-souled Skanda attained the leadership of the divine army on this very day;
since Skanda, endowed with excellence, is the foremost leader,
one who eats only at night on the sixth lunar day shall always obtain their heart's desire.
Having offered the *arghya* to Kārttikeya while standing facing south,
O observer of noble vows, [one should worship] with curd, ghee, water, and flowers, using this mantra:
"O Skanda, son of the wives of the Seven Sages, born from Svāhāpati!"
O Lord, born of Rudra, Aryaman, and Agni, O you who are the womb of the Gaṅgā, salutations be unto you!
May the Commander of the Divine Army be pleased; may he fulfill that which is in [our] hearts.
Having given one's own self, food, and whatever else exists to the Brahmin, [may it be so].
He eats afterwards at night, having made the ground his vessel.
Thus, out of affection, Skanda diligently proclaimed this vow on the sixth day;
listen to that in its entirety, O Great King, as it is being told by me.
He who, on the sixth lunar day, subsists on fruits or observes the night-meal (nakta),
being self-restrained, celibate, and composed throughout both the bright and dark fortnights—
for him there shall be accomplishment, fortitude, contentment, sovereignty, long life, and freedom from disease.

Skanda bestows both benefits for the next world and for this one; of this there is no doubt. For he who observes a fast during the night becomes a practitioner of the *nakta* vow, and he attains supreme renown exceedingly both in this world and the next.
He attains a certain residence in heaven; of this there is no doubt.
Returning here at the end of time, he shall enjoy the fruits as described.
He will become one who is worthy of worship even by the gods, and he shall be a king among kings.
"And he who shall hear this Kalpa of the Ṣaṣṭhī, O scion of the Kuru lineage,
for him there shall be success, as well as contentment and fortitude arising from renown.
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ṣaṣṭhī-kalpa," in the Brāhma-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya-mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of fifty thousand verses.
Now begins the fortieth chapter, the Description of Kārttikeya.
Śatānīka said:
"Alas! What a great and painful vow; doubt dwells within my heart.
O twice-born one of noble vows, having heard of the majesty and the birth of Kārttikeya, who was born here through many previous lives."
"O Brahmin, how is this very great majesty to be understood? Is birth the superior factor, O hero, or is action the better? A great doubt has arisen here in me upon seeing the son of the Kṛttikās."
"Tell me this after having determined it with certainty, so that no doubt remains;
tell me which is superior, birth or action.
Sumantu said:

In former times, Brahmā was asked about this very matter by his wise disciples; what he said to them, I shall now tell you—learn it from me. Having approached the eldest of the gods as he sat at ease, the great sages [inquired].
And having bowed down, O mighty-armed one, and having seen Viśvāmitra’s state of being a Brahmin,
they were filled with wonder and curiosity;
placing devotion and faith before them, they bowed with their necks bent low.
The sages said:

O Brahmin, tell us what constitutes Brahminhood in the Ādikalpa; for if the distinctions between birth, study, body, self-purification, conduct, and ritual action—whether external or internal, general or specific—are merely artificial, [then what is the true nature of Brahminhood]?
Those things consisting of mental, vocal, and bodily actions, as well as genus, substance, and quality—
which are established as causing distinctions between classes, yet are either non-existent or not determined by indirect means of knowledge— must be abandoned.
"If the rule regarding the distinction of human castes is established through an unmanifest tradition,
this mere conjecture does not nourish the strength of your intellect.
Brahmā said:
"It is exactly as you say here; there is no doubt. Listen, O yogins, to these words full of reasoning for the welfare of the disciple.
Thus spoke the Lord of Yoga.
Since the two means of valid cognition are established as having distinct objective domains,
perception is first observed to have as its object a clear and perceptible entity;
whereas the tenet [of the opponent] is accepted as grasping a universal that is beyond the senses.
If it is argued that this Blessed One alone is the sole authority, that is not so;
for, O fortunate one, you find yourself in a double-bind:
on the one hand, the Veda is held to be of human origin, while on the other, its eternal nature as a genus is being asserted.

The specific [phonetic] operations prescribed by the Vedas must be performed; it is not right that the word remain unproduced. For [the word] is heard immediately after the operation of the articulatory organs such as the palate, and because there is a specific prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) of that [word] following the operation.
The conformity to the existence of that [word] is established through positive and negative concomitance;

therefore, the relationship between the word and its object stands as one of cause and effect, like smoke and fire. Nor can this be explained otherwise by means of an intermediate operation (*vyāpāra*).
If there exists a caste such as Brahminhood that follows individual persons,
it is because it is characterized by perceptible objects through the distinction between the two castes;
just as a horse standing in the midst of a herd of cows is identified by those who are wise due to their keen discernment.
Just as [the distinction between castes] does not differ from the human state itself, so too the twice-born is not distinct from the classes of Śūdras.
There is no further distinction belonging to the human species that can be postulated as applying to all men;
rather, it is the specific performance of rites accompanied by sacramental consecration (*saṃskāra*) that constitutes the basis for distinguishing the twice-born from the Śūdras.

Those men who, being ignorant of the truth, declare that even the individual soul (jīva) is a Brāhmaṇa, fall away from their status as Brāhmaṇas; yet through association with true Brāhmaṇas, they may be reborn [into it].
[The world] is crowded with families of corrupt grāhakas, beset by the afflictions of old age and the transitions between births.
[The ocean of saṃsāra] is crowded with the waves of suffering from births as humans, animals, and low-born śūdras;
it is filled with whirlpools consisting of the masses of people afflicted by misfortune, disease, and grief;
and its body is composed of dogs, pigs, caṇḍālas, worms, tortoises, and the like.
"How indeed can that living being, a Brahmin, who is submerged and tossed about in the terrible ocean of saṃsāra, and overwhelmed by the burden of manifold sins, [attain liberation]?
Brahmā said:
O Brahmins, the story of the seven hunters was proclaimed by Manu;
having heard it, O best of the Yadus, one should forever abandon the state of birth [as a hunter].
"The seven hunters were deer in Daśārṇa, on the Kālañjara mountain."
The cakravāka birds on the river-islands and the swans in Lake Mānasa—
even they have been born in Kurukṣetra as brahmins who have mastered the Vedas;
having set out upon the long journey toward death, why do you despair?

Therefore, we do not perceive Brahminhood in any way whatsoever within the living being (jīva). For just as in this world there is a clear distinction made by the characteristics of limbs, colors, and duties among elephants, horses, cattle, goats, camels, donkeys, and so forth— each belonging to a specific caste such as the Bhārgava and others who possess weapons and other attributes— so it is here.

Therefore, it must not be modified by that [objection], for among men there is no such thing as a genus called "Brāhmaṇa-ness. A permanent form does not exist without a differentiated nature, so that a supreme distinction might be established here.
Since white and other colors possess a common form in their specific characteristics, there is no eternal difference in color among the limbs [of the body].
This status of a Brahmin is indeed unstable because it is artificial; it becomes non-artificial only through association with conventional rules.
These distinctions of caste are merely conventional, obtained through a specific residue of merit, just like the various professions of merchants and physicians.
Are those who abandon their merit still Brahmins? And are those who fail to protect the world still Kṣatriyas?
For likewise, Vaiśyas are devoid of their own specific duties, and Śūdras are deprived of their own primary functions;

therefore, there is no distinction of caste among embodied beings such as that between cows and horses. Rather, the conventional designation [of caste] would be artificial, based solely on the capacity for performing specific tasks.

Thus, when conventional reality is being refuted by means of valid cognitions, that wretched person of deluded mind does not realize that he is undermining his own established position through his own arguments. [He fails to see:
"The lord of cows, buffaloes, goats, horses, camels, wild animals, sheep, and elephants..."
Those twice-born ones whose minds are intent on the work of servants, usurers, and laborers; those occupied with the crafts of merchants and artisans;
and even those who are like gods [in appearance]—they should be known as ruined, as well as carnivorous beasts and actors.
Those who eat onions and garlic; those who drink the milk of deer, female camels, or women; those who buy or sell meat, all kinds of savory juices, or milk;
and those who consort with remarried women, Śūdra women, prostitutes, or Cāṇḍāla women.
Their limbs nourished by the essence of a Śūdra’s food, they eat the clothing and food of the deceased;
they consume food, drink, and other sustenance obtained during periods of death-impurity or birth-impurity;
and they are excluded from the community of Brahmins, gods, ancestors, spirits, and men.
Those twice-born who are characterized by stinginess, pride, hatred, craving, desire, and delusion, and who follow inferior conduct— whether they be others or even those who are treacherous—
all of them perish through these many ways; it cannot be otherwise.
Thus, those men who have strayed from the path of reasoning taught in the scriptures—
even if they possess the entirety of the refinements and purificatory rites of a distinguished lineage,
and even if they study the Vedas according to the traditional sequence of the Śruti— [are nonetheless lost].

Those who practice evil conduct fall away from their status as Brahmins; therefore, there is no single, immutable essence of being within a caste. And regarding this perishability, the following verses from the *Manava* [Dharmaśāstra] are studied: "By performing forbidden acts, by neglecting prescribed duties, and by failing to maintain the sacred fires, the three castes become Śūdras, as does a Brāhmaṇa. "By the loss of Vedic study, by the failure to perform sacrifices, and by the abandonment of the sacred fires, one falls from one's own caste and enters the state of a Śūdra. "By committing these and other such acts, the three castes become Śūdras; likewise, a Brāhmaṇa becomes a Śūdra through the omission of his specific duties. "Even though they may have been born into a high caste, those who are devoid of good conduct and are intent on evil deeds sink to the level of a Śūdra in this very life. "Therefore, there is no caste that is eternal; for all castes are subject to destruction. "And regarding this, the following verses from the *Manava* are recited: "By the non-performance of rites, by the abandonment of the sacred fires, and by the neglect of Vedic study, even a Brāhmaṇa becomes a Śūdra within three generations. "By performing forbidden acts and by neglecting his own duties, a man of high birth quickly sinks to the level of a Śūdra. "By the loss of Vedic knowledge, by the failure to offer oblations, and by the neglect of the sacred fires, one falls from his own caste and enters the state of a Śūdra. "By these and other such causes, the three castes become Śūdras; and a Brāhmaṇa becomes a Śūdra by the omission of his specific duties. "Therefore, there is no caste that is eternal; for all castes are subject to destruction. "By the performance of forbidden acts and by the neglect of prescribed duties, even those of high birth quickly sink to the level of a Śūdra. "By the loss of Vedic study, by the failure to perform sacrifices, and by the abandonment of the sacred fires, one falls from his own caste and enters the state of a Śūdra. "By committing these and other such acts, the three castes become Śūdras; likewise, a Brāhmaṇa becomes a Śūdra through the omission of his specific duties. "Therefore, there is no single, immutable essence of being within a caste. "And regarding this perishability, the following verses from the *Manava* are studied."
One falls immediately by selling meat, lac, or salt;
a Brāhmaṇa who sells milk becomes a Śūdra within three days.
[Likewise, those who] tend cattle, those who trade, as well as artisans and actors—
Manu has declared that those who employ servants and usurers are Śūdras;
