a Śūdra attains the status of a Brāhmaṇa, and a Brāhmaṇa falls to the state of a Śūdra. One should know that a Kṣatriya likewise becomes a Brāhmaṇa, as does a Vaiśya.

Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Description of Castes," within the "Description of Kārttikeya" in the *Ṣaṣṭhī-kalpa* of the *Brāhma-parvan*, in the *Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of fifty thousand verses.
Now begins the forty-first chapter:
"The Description of the Discernment of Brāhmaṇas."
Brahmā said:
Even this study of the Vedas leads to the status of a Brāhmaṇa; for like a Brahmin, the Vaiśyas, the Kṣatriyas, and even the Rākṣasas such as Rāvaṇa and others [attain it].
Dog-eaters, Cāṇḍālas, slaves, hunters, Ābhīras, and fishermen—
whatever other Śūdras there may be— they too study the Vedas when,
having gone to another country, they have resorted to the status of Brāhmaṇas or Kṣatriyas.

Men born of pure Brahmin lineage, having studied the Vedas— either all three, two, or even one— in due order, marry auspicious brides according to [prescribed] rites, despite the various activities, forms, and states imagined by those who are like sophists.
Alternatively, men of the Kṣatriya or Vaiśya castes who, having studied the Vedas,
have adopted a Gauḍa or a Dākṣiṇātya caste out of their own desire,
attain Brāhmaṇahood because their Śūdra status is not recognized.
Therefore, it is not understood that any distinction [between them] is produced by the act of studying the Veda;
for so it has been stated by the authors of the treatises who follow the path of logic. Having heard this well-reasoned opinion, the virtuous, being free from envy, remain [in agreement].
The Vedas do not purify those devoid of right conduct, even if they have been studied along with the six auxiliary sciences (*ṣaḍaṅga*).
For the study of the Vedas is merely a craft for the twice-born; rather, virtuous conduct is remembered as the true characteristic of a Brāhmaṇa.
Even after studying the four Vedas, if one does not abide in right conduct...
No purpose is served by that [initiation], just as a eunuch gains nothing from a jewel of a woman.
The rites of the topknot and the *praṇava*, the twilight devotions, the girdle,
the staff, the deerskin, the purifier (*pavitra*), and so forth, are practiced without restraint even among Śūdras.
For even the association of Śūdras cannot be prevented;
indeed, men turn back from it by themselves through the three supreme deities.
Therefore, these [Śūdras] are not perceived as distinct from non-debtors (anṛṇas).
The consecration of the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), the girdle, the top-knot (*cūlikā*), and so forth—
by means of spells for malevolent rites (*ābhicārika*) or by speaking of their difficulty to obtain and the like—
if the Brāhmaṇa possesses the power [to perform them], by whom can that power be destroyed?
Through the greatness of austerity, truth, and other virtues, the recollection of the deities' conventions and the power of mantras exist within all these men; indeed,
they are able to deceive even one who speaks harshly.
Therefore, there is no difference whatsoever between a Śūdra and a Brāhmaṇa;
the capacity to bestow curses or favors, as well as the distinction of power, does not exist [between them].
This applies even when men are struck by thieves, beggars, kings, or wicked people.

A Śūdra is not capable of protecting his own kind from the arising of suffering and its removal; likewise, a Brāhmaṇa is indeed not capable of doing so. May this never happen in the Kali age, nor in this land, that a twice-born man should fail to perform his duty.
It may be that for certain eminent twice-born ones, there exists in other places, times, and so forth,
the power to curse or favor, or something else pertaining to the inner self;
for some declare this to be a sign of the means to attain Brahman.

Those whose minds are stained by attachment to cyclic existence and who are shrouded by the blinding darkness of delusion fall into the pits of the wrong path, like moths into a fire. By nature, they possess some slight distinction arising from contact with sacred learning.

The sacramental rite (*saṃskāra*), whether accomplished through birth or produced by a collection of causal factors, is unestablished among those of the Śūdra caste but well-known among those of the Brāhmaṇa caste;
it confers upon them a quality of excellence that transcends the common nature shared with Śūdras.
Scholars should conceive of a fivefold division among Brahmins;
however, no distinction based on birth or the Vedic triad is tenable, as it is contradicted by reason.
Successive or simultaneous actions do not belong to an eternal entity.
That which is eternal cannot be a cause because it is devoid of activity; it could only be a cause by virtue of a specific distinction within the Veda.
Since it is coextensive with that [Veda] due to its constant presence therein, it is entirely improper for it to be observed as having "lapsed time" (kālātyayāpadiṣṭa).
That which arises from the application of scripture, abiding within one's own heart and functioning through the body—
Its nature, unknown through any other means of knowledge, is not apprehended by others;
for if it were a property resulting from specific study, its connection with Brahman would be artificial.
If that which possesses excellence does not depend on anything else, then nothing else can serve as its substratum.
Is this Brahminhood intended to have a visible nature, or rather an invisible form?
For if it were of a visible form, it would be perceived by everyone; otherwise, there could be no understanding of it at all.
O non-gods (asuras), you fail to perceive that supreme distinction residing in the body of a god on earth (a Brahmin) due to the absence of the necessary causal complex.
Therefore, it is incorrect to say that they remember merit and demerit within themselves "just as [others do].
Since Śūdras possess all the qualities resulting from the performance of the complete ritual requirements and are thus equal to the twice-born,
there is no distinction between the names "twice-born" and "Śūdra," whether based on the inner self or on external causes.
If that excellence were due to refinement (*saṃskāra*), then it would belong to every person who is highly refined;
for there is no equality between him who is refined and stands as the preeminent among the host of Brahmins and others like Vyāsa, and [anyone else].
Causality does not apply to these factors such as birth (*jāti*) and the rest, because they are impossible [as causes of excellence].
Furthermore, because the universal (jāti) is uncreated, it does not undergo specific modification;
nor does it reach another state due to an excellence of refinement (saṃskāra), as others maintain.
Moreover, because the body is material (bhautika), it cannot exist as a composite of all its parts taken individually.
Furthermore, among other people such as atheists, barbarians, and Yavanas—
evil-minded individuals whose conduct is manifestly wicked and contrary to what is declared in the Vedas—
an excess of righteousness is observed even in those who are cruel and reckless.
Therefore, among Brahmins, that [distinction] does not arise from a collection of factors such as birth;
consequently, there is no distinction at all— neither externally nor within the self—
with respect to happiness and the like, nor in sovereignty, nor in ignorance, nor even in fearlessness.
Neither in vigor, nor in form, nor in eyesight, nor in activity, nor in lifespan;
neither in the nourishment of the limbs, nor in weakness, nor in stability, nor even in fickleness;
neither in wisdom, nor in dispassion, nor in righteousness, nor in prowess.
Neither in the three aims of life, nor in skill, nor in beauty and such, nor in medicine;
neither in a woman’s womb, nor in sexual intercourse, nor in the washing away of bodily impurities;
neither in a porous unstable vessel, nor in affection, nor in the means of valid cognition, nor in body hair.
Even when sought with great effort, the distinction between a Śūdra and a Brāhmaṇa is not perceived in any of their duties, even by the gods acting in concert;
such is the non-differentiation declared by those who employ the method of inquiry.
This speech, which cannot be assailed even by the lords of the ancient gods, is as follows:
"There are no Brāhmaṇas here white as the rays of the moon; no Kṣatriyas with the color of the Kiṃśuka flower;
no Vaiśyas resembling yellow orpiment; and no Śūdras with a complexion like charcoal."
How indeed do they become fourfold, being equal in their movement of the feet, the color of the body and hair, in pleasure and pain, and in blood; as well as in skin, flesh, fat, bone, and marrow;
and in complexion, stature, form, dwelling in the womb, speech, intellect, the organs of action, and life? [In these respects, they are all alike.]
Among the medicines for the three-fold afflictions of strength, no distinction based on caste exists. He alone is the lord of all creatures here; how then can there be a division based on caste?
When examined through the methods of valid cognition, illustration, and reasoning, such a notion falls apart.

Four sons belong to one father, and indeed the birth of those sons is one and the same. Thus, for all progeny there is but one father; because of this single paternity, there is no distinction of caste.
Just as fruits produced from the *udumbara* tree—whether they arise from the top, the middle, or the base—are of the same origin.
They are equal in color, form, touch, and taste; likewise, their birth is altogether inconceivable.
There are those of the Kauśika, Kāśyapa, Gautama, Kauṇḍinya, Māṇḍavya, and Vaśiṣṭha lineages;
those of the Ātreya, Kautsa, Aṅgiras, Garga, Maudgalya, Kātyāyana, and Bhārgava lineages.
There are various lineages and diverse castes, as well as the states of brother, son-in-law, sexual union, and son;

there is the rite of marriage, yet no distinction of caste—these are all their crafts. Furthermore, those other wise men who declare that the Brahminhood of men consists in the body [are also included].
Having removed the cataract of their false views and having shown them compassion,
we shall— by means of the divine medicinal ointment of right reasoning, which brings about ultimate happiness— carefully restore their clear vision.

Because it is subject to death, it is perishable; because it is perishable, like any other remnant of matter, the status of being a Brahmin cannot be attributed to those things that reside as the support for the body. Not even a single one of their individual parts partakes in the status of being a Brahmin.
Nor [can it be defined] as a collection of many [factors], because that would lead to an over-extension in every respect;
for it would follow that all beings possess Brāhmaṇahood by virtue of their bodies, due to the specific transformations of earth, water, air, and fire.

Those who, being ignorant of the truth, imagine that the status of a Brahmin belongs to the body, would themselves lack the state of being Brahman, for their own bodies are subject to consecration. Even when sought with great effort, that [status] is not found within the body.

Therefore, brahminhood does not reside in the body, nor can it have the body as its essence; for if you were to accept that the body itself possesses the status of a Brahmin, it would follow that outcasts, Cāṇḍālas, dogs, and the like would also be Brahmins.
When the powers and qualities of the body have decayed, it takes on forms such as bodily ashes;
therefore, this Brahminhood does not consist of the body, nor is it born of ritual action.

Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Discernment of Brahminhood," in the *Brāhma* section of the *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the compendium of fifty thousand verses, in the *Ṣaṣṭhī-kalpa*.
Now begins the forty-second chapter: A Description of the Distinction Between the Sacraments of the Brāhmaṇas.
Brahmā said:
Listen to these well-spoken words which were uttered by other wise men of great being, endowed with virtuous conduct and yoga:
"By citing the species of many trees, conchs, ants, bees, and elephants..."

Driven by karma through the various states of existence, a living being wanders constantly like an actor, failing to attain right vision. If, though armored with beauty, sovereignty, knowledge, noble birth, and power, you abandon the path of Dharma, I shall not speak to you as you wander through the worlds; therefore, let the intoxication of self be reduced to ashes.
Blinded by the intoxication of birth, lineage, beauty, youth, complexion, and manifold learning, these eunuchs do not perceive what is beneficial for themselves, either in this world or the next.
Having understood that within hundreds of thousands of millions of births throughout the cycle of existence, [such states recur].

What wise person would take pride in birth, considering its states as inferior, superior, or middling? One goes through various specific births, all of which are preceded by the cessation of the senses and governed by karma; in this world, whose birth is eternal?
Even he who, in an assembly of the learned, claims that one becomes a Brāhmaṇa through sacramental rites (saṃskāra) must be refuted by those skilled in logic with arguments consistent with reason.
[The rites include] Garbhādhāna, Puṃsavana, and Sīmantonnayana.
The birth-rite, the naming ceremony, as well as the first feeding of solid food; the tonsure, the initiation, and likewise the instruction in vows;
the return home after study, and also the taking of the hand in marriage.
Those who have been thoroughly purified by such rites as these,
and whose desires have ceased through continuous practice— they alone are Brāhmaṇas.
For indeed, Brāhmaṇas were born from Brāhmaṇas who had performed the purificatory rites.
Indeed, no clear distinction in lifespan, power, or radiance exists between them;
nor do those two men— one born of a Brahmin body and consecrated by rites, the other not—
differ from one another in terms of attaining or failing to attain what is desired or undesired.
Even when the application of purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) is present, a man does not differ from a Śūdra if he lacks knowledge, study, inquiry, observances, and restraint of the senses;
furthermore, the purificatory rite being performed does not apply to a Śūdra.
One who possesses refined limbs does not fail to see and turns away from evils. Like those intoxicated by wine, such as playful women, serpents, and the like,
people become utterly deluded regarding right conduct and fall from their status as Brahmins.
Even a man refined by sacraments goes to hell if he is of evil conduct;
whereas one who lacks such refinement, if he is of good conduct, shall always be the best among Brahmins.
Even one endowed with the purification of self through the consecration of mantras does not float [on the surface] if he lacks right conduct.
That man who, having been previously free from conceptual construction regarding his Brahminhood, subsequently commits evil conduct,
will certainly fall from that Brahminhood by virtue of that [transgression];
this is the view of the best of men concerning those individuals who are attached to difficult practices.
"Has this been seen anywhere before, or is it born of mere rivalry?
Tell me, are you capable of performing even that which has never been seen?
For the most excellent sages, such as Vyāsa and others, were performers of traditional conduct."
Clearly, many of the best of Brahmins, though devoid of the entire series of sacraments beginning with conception (garbhādhāna),
have attained prosperity and are honored by all the world;
hear now of some of those who are being mentioned.
Vyāsa was born of a fisherwoman, and Parāśara of a dog-cooker woman;
Śuka was born of a female parrot, and the one named Kaṇāda likewise became the son of an owl-woman.
Ṛṣyaśṛṅga was born of a deer, and Vasiṣṭha was the son of a courtesan.
Mandapāla, the best of sages, is said to be the offspring of a boatwoman;
Māṇḍavya, the king of sages, was born from the womb of Maṇḍūkī.
Many others as well, who were twice-born in former times, attained the status of Brahmins.
And having reflected upon these words uttered by him whose conduct was worthy of praise,
the great sage Ṛṣyaśṛṅga— who was born from the womb of a doe— practiced them with intensity, his splendor augmented by his virtuous conduct.

A Brahmin is born through austerity; therefore, spiritual refinement is the cause [of his status]. O King, Vyāsa’s father was born from the womb of a dog-cooker, yet he became a Brahmin through austerity; therefore, spiritual refinement is the cause.

The great sage named Kaṇāda, though born from the womb of an owl, became a Brāhmaṇa through austerity; thus, the purificatory rite (saṃskāra) is the cause. And the great sage Vasiṣṭha was born from the womb of a courtesan.

A Brāhmaṇa is born through austerity; therefore, spiritual refinement is the cause. Though born from the womb of a fisherwoman, the great sage Mandapāla became a Brāhmaṇa through austerity; therefore, spiritual refinement is the cause.
Even for those skilled in the entire collection of purificatory rites born of the Vedas and Tantras,
a superior fruit is obtained through the power of knowledge and asceticism;
yet there are men who, despite having bodies refined by such rites, remain great sinners.
"Because Brahman ceases [to be designated] from that [name], therefore they know it to be conventional (sāṅketika).

Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Discernment of the Saṃskāras of Brāhmaṇas," in the *Brahma-parvan* of the *Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the compendium (*saṃhitā*) consisting of fifty thousand verses, in the section on the *Ṣaṣṭhī-kalpa*.
Now begins the forty-third chapter.
Regarding the description of the system of castes, Brahmā said:
"Furthermore, what else [remains]? You people are knowers of the Vedic mantras."
One must ask: in whose refinement does excellence arise? Is it the body, which remains naturally impure, born of semen and blood like a worm produced from filth?
Through various extensive rites beginning with conception and ending at the cremation ground,
some human beings attain a state of excellence. Yet,
for those whose minds, bodies, and speech are secretly corrupted, their outwardly virtuous deeds are in vain.
I am now refuting this position held by unrestrained men:
that the twice-born, who constitute the very essence of all Vedic sacraments,
surpass all Śūdras who perform every kind of labor.
One who performs violent deeds, one who persists in forbidden acts, a killer of a Brahmin, a violator of the Guru’s bed,
a thief, a killer of a cow, a drinker of intoxicants, one who delights in the company of others’ wives,
a speaker of falsehoods, one intoxicated by pride, an atheist, and a reviler of the Vedas.
The village priest and the naked ascetic (nirgrantha) are full of many faults and difficult to approach; likewise,
one who practices forbidden conduct, a thief, a flatterer, one arrogant with pride,
a rogue, an actor, a deceiver, a sinner, a glutton who eats everything, and a seller of all things.

Those lowest of Brahmins who have been slain by the evils born of speech, mind, and body do not attain purification in this world even through hundreds of sacrifices. Whatever undesirable things occur to Shudras by their very nature, [they do not incur sin].
Even for Brahmins, those very same [acts] do not become free from obstacles;
therefore, neither mantra, nor the Agnihotra sacrifice, nor even the slaughter of animals on the altar are causes for Brahminhood, just as such acts cannot be performed by Śūdras.
And those living beings who, bound by the fetters of karma,
languish with their minds distressed by the heat of the fire of saṃsāra—
they, thirsting for the nectar of happiness in the wilderness of birth and death, [seek refuge].
Wandering for refuge with the miserly, they find no peace at all.
Those men of the four castes who are the lowest of men due to their respective lack of vigor— among them, a total confusion of all duties is observed through every means.

Śūdras, Brahmins, and others do not differ from one another in their origin; since all are equal in terms of dharma, rituals such as initiatory consecrations (*saṃskāra*) and the like are purposeless. This is because [the distinctions between castes] are merely due to differences in the performance of those rituals, and because death and other factors dissolve such distinctions.

Through the service of those who should not be served and other such acts, Śūdras, Brahmins, and others become equal in terms of intellect, capacity, innate nature, duties, caste and so forth, prosperity,
and the merits and demerits that must be performed, all of which gradually permeate the entire body.

Through bondages, confinements, and various forms of torture by means of diverse instruments; through punishments and the infliction of unjust penalties, as well as despair and lamentation; and through virtuous acts such as counter-measures against injustice, or through passionate acts involving various deceptive stratagems.
Tormented again and again by the qualities of darkness (tamas) such as suffering and delusion,
by phlegm, wind, bile, and the like— which are most loathsome to behold—
and by the occurrence or non-occurrence of actions that are respectively immortal or mortal, beneficial or harmful;
Through the employment of ornaments, through the activities of Love and other [passions],
through the casting down of multitudes of beings out of hope for the acquisition of wealth,
and through various kinds of mental longings, one attains the state of supernatural power (*siddhi*).
Through the protection of wealth acquired by self-attachment, hatred for others, and extreme intoxication;
through agitation, hunger, emaciation, and diseases;
as well as through the means of torture, malice, and the absence of tranquility.
The years in which there are beasts of prey nearby due to ignoble practices; in which living beings are harmful and speak sinful and false words;
and in which people are slanderers of the virtuous, thieves, merciless, and adulterers.
Engaged in base occupations, eating all kinds of food like Piśācas,
born of low lineage and of wicked conduct, they live off kings;
they perform the work of Brahmins while remaining fixed in improper acts— wealthy yet evil-minded.
Just as hunters, having killed deer, take up residence in the forest and eat them,
so too do many malicious people, under the influence of the wheel of action,
study the declarations of the Vedas while praising the slaughter of living beings.
These lowest of men, who sell the Vedas, nourish their wealth through deceits;
they are deceitful, consumed by envy, greedy, deluded, arrogant with pride,
flatterers, wandering beggars, cruel, miserly, and fond of quarreling.
Garrulous and wicked unchaste women wander about with hired men;
arrogant soldiers, full of rage, are great plunderers;
wandering mercenaries live by their lives, uttering verses that are mere thorns.
For those lowest of men, devoid of remorse, sell what should not be sold and consume forbidden substances; they perform the duties of Śūdras and subsist by undertaking service,
teaching, trade, agriculture, and other such pursuits.
Those who take away external riches such as goods, grain, and wealth,
as well as internal defects such as anger and evil desires,
yet do not abandon their own excellence, are the best among the "hair-pressers."
The twice-born always wear garments that should not be worn;
they discard what should not be discarded. How can such men be gurus on this earth?
They are like Dantikas, Diṇḍikas, and Bhaṇḍas—vicious men with the conduct of outcasts.
Like lions slaying deer and cattle,

those cavillers strike down the Nirgrantha sage when they behold him, perceiving him to be merely arrogant; they stand there treating him with contempt— fie on those empty men who are their own enemies!
Therefore, worldly beings are defiled by the stains of mental afflictions;
because they are bound by fetters of a similar nature— such as immorality and dejection—
a Brahmin finds pleasure in sexual union with a Śūdra woman who is likewise possessed of passion.
Upon the cessation of desire, she conceives when they come together;
however, for those women who are afflicted by the longing for pleasure, Śūdra men are pleasing to them.
Even they bring them happiness in regard to sexual union, despite their Brāhmaṇa status.
However, those such as cows, horses, camels, and elephants, which are distinct by birth and other factors,
do not even conceive offspring with those of a different species, even when seeking pleasure; rather,
it is only the ox that, in union with the cow, fulfills its desire.
And stallions take full delight with mares;
having obtained a young male elephant as her mate, a female camel rejoices with joy;
and having found an elephant as her husband, a female elephant dwells in happiness.
For even when a woman of human birth engages in sexual intercourse with an animal,
it does not cause her to conceive, nor does it provide her with pleasure;
likewise, a human woman who engages in sexual intercourse with an animal [does not conceive].
She does not conceive a child begotten by him, nor is sexual union appropriate for the two of them.
There is no such distinction at all in sexual intercourse between a woman and a man,
by which the difference between the twice-born and the Śūdra would clearly be diminished.
Under the pretext of reciting the Vedas, he does not attain [the goal] through ritual actions;
for on this day, which is no different from a mere collection of many inert things,
both the body and that impure embodied soul therein are unstable.
When the assembly— its mind whirling like a potter's wheel in the ocean of sensory objects, excessively tormented by defects such as passion and hatred,
overwhelmed by the fear of terrible suffering, and lacking a sovereign self— is thus afflicted;
In one tormented by the fires of birth, death, old age, sorrow, and union with the undesired,
no distinction is perceived within the body and so forth of those whose strength is diminished.
Therefore, this differentiation among humans is constructed through the power of convention.
A Brahmin woman, through her association with Brahmins, attains the status of a Brahmin;
yet, abandoning her husband out of a longing for the taste of his face and a craving for intoxication,
she becomes an unchaste woman who, having gone to a paramour, is served even by servants.

"Others who commit great sins fall away from their Brahminhood; therefore, this conceptualization of caste and so forth is merely a false construction. Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "Description of the System of Castes," in the *Brahma-parvan* of the *Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the *Ṣaṣṭhī-kalpa*, in the compendium of fifty thousand verses.
Now begins the forty-fourth chapter:
A Description of the Discernment of the Classification of Castes.
Brahmā said:
Those who know the truth regarding what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, who have abandoned paths and traditions that are contrary to logic,
whose senses, minds, and speech are conquered, who are devoted to virtuous conduct,
who abide by the practice of observances and right behavior, and who are intent on seeking the welfare of others.
Their minds were intent on the practice of means for protecting the world from saṃsāra;

they were endowed with right vision, established in meditative concentration, and had destroyed their anger. Their hearts were devoted to sacred study, they were free from attachment, and devoid of envy.
Free from sorrow, free from intoxication, peaceful, and desiring the welfare of all living beings; viewing pleasure and pain with equanimity, they dwell in secluded places;
with all their limbs dedicated to their vows, they are righteous and fearful of sin.
Free from possessiveness and free from egoism, heroic in generosity and devoted to compassion,
they were knowers of the Truth and Brahman, peaceful, and firmly established in all the scriptures;
[they were created] by the Self-Existent One, who is engaged in means for the welfare of all the worlds.
By the god Vāgīśvara, the son of Nabhi, the destroyer of worldly existence,
and by Brahmā, the boundaries were established; thus are they known as Brāhmaṇas—
noble ones whose wealth is great austerity, who grant fearlessness to all living beings.

For the sake of the welfare of the entire world, [the system] is skillful and well-established. Because of its vastness, the Blessed One Brahmā is called Nābheya; those people who are devoted with faith and have sought refuge in him are proclaimed as Brāhmaṇas.
The Kṣatriyas are so called because they protect from injury (kṣata-trāṇa); the Vaiśyas because they enter into the means of livelihood (vārtā-praveśana);

and those who have attained the melting away (druti) of the Veda are celebrated here as Śūdras. Furthermore, those devoted to right conduct are declared by the exponents of Brahman to possess the nature of Brāhmaṇas.
They, however, praise that fruit which is always desired by the mind:
forbearance, self-control, compassion, charity, truthfulness, purity,
fortitude, pity, gentleness, straightforwardness, contentment, freedom from egoism, austerity, and tranquility.
Dharma consists of knowledge, absence of backbiting, celibacy, freedom from delusion,
meditation, faith, lack of hatred, detachment, and a tranquil nature;
as well as fear of evil, non-stealing, lack of envy, and freedom from craving.
Freedom from attachment, service to the teacher, and restraint of mind, speech, and body—
those men who practice such conduct as this find their Brahminhood constantly and fully increasing.
They were of great majesty, whose conduct was praised for its relish in their own philosophical systems;
they had purified their minds through non-contradiction with all the scriptures;
they were esteemed by the virtuous, wise, and learned in the Purāṇas and Āgamas.
The authors of the Smṛtis, who are masters of the traditions of song and scripture,
declare: "In all Manvantaras, according to the divisions of the four Yugas,
the unsurpassed action performed through the conduct of the castes and stages of life attains perfection."
When their livelihood was fully established, the Lord himself then fixed the boundaries for them as they had mutually undertaken;
those who were indeed accepted [as protectors] were superior in strength and courage.
He established the other Kṣatriyas as protectors of the wounded;
those who always approach them with supplications are indeed the Narmadās.
But those who speak of truth, sacred knowledge, and eternal reality are the Brāhmaṇas.
And those others who were weak, established in the occupation of a Vaiśya,
diligently destroyed the stakes upon the earth;
he called those very Vaiśyas, who had adopted that livelihood, "Kīnāśas."
He declared those men who grieve and run about performing services, who are lacking in luster and of little prowess, to be Śūdras.
He [defined] the mutual relations among Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras.
Actions are divided according to the qualities born of one's own nature.
Tranquility, austerity, self-control, purity, forbearance, and uprightness;
knowledge, realization, and faith—these are the duties of a Brahmin, born of his own nature.
Heroism, majesty, firmness, dexterity, and not fleeing in battle,
as well as generosity and lordliness— these are the duties of the kṣatriya, born of his own nature.
Agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade are the duties of the vaiśya, born of his own nature.
Service is the action born of one's own nature even for the Śūdra.
Yoga, austerity, compassion, charity, truthfulness, hearing the Dharma, modesty,
knowledge, realized wisdom, and faith— this is the characteristic of a Brāhmaṇa.
He whose topknot consists of knowledge and whose sacred thread consists of austerity—his Brahminhood is complete; so declared Svāyambhuva Manu.
Whether in that caste or another, whether high, low, or middling—
He who has desisted from evil deeds is ordained as a Brāhmaṇa;
even a Śūdra endowed with virtuous conduct may be superior to a Brāhmaṇa,
whereas a Brāhmaṇa devoid of proper conduct is inferior to a Śūdra.
He who does not mix liquor in shops or in houses,
nor sells it likewise— he is indeed called a true Śūdra.
If one caste is clearly evident, then the other is distinct from it by virtue of its actions.
Or rather, since the sacred utterance (vyāhṛti) has attained oneness, and since it has entered into other attributes—
pervading the destruction, origination, and subsistence of every single thing and of the whole—
is it not possible for it to come within the range of human comprehension through grammatical case-inflection?

In the Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium consisting of fifty thousand verses, in the Brāhma Parvan, in the Ṣaṣṭhī Kalpa, this is the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Discernment of the Division of Castes.
Now begins the forty-fifth chapter: "The Description of Kārttikeya."
Brahmā said:
Listen to these words spoken by me, preceded by reasoning,
now that a doubt has arisen among you regarding caste and ritual action.
I shall speak again; listen, not in detail but in summary:
human beings attain perfection through the accumulation of birth and action;
one should achieve success in whatever task is undertaken through the accumulation of destiny and action.
"In this way, a person attains perfection regarding birth and action.
Thus did the Lord of Yoga, possessed of great splendor, speak previously for the sake of instructing his disciples, summarily and not in detail.
Sumantu said:
Thus questioned in the past, O Bhārata, Brahmā spoke these words full of deliberation to the sages regarding birth and action, O brahmin-sage.

Therefore, O mighty-armed King, you should not feel any astonishment regarding Kārttikeya; the course of the gods is always difficult to comprehend. Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Kārttikeya," in the *Ṣaṣṭhī-kalpa* within the *Brāhma-parvan* of the *Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium consisting of fifty thousand verses.
Now begins the forty-sixth chapter, the Description of the Brahma-parvan. Sumantu said:
O bull among the Bharatas, this sixth lunar day in the month of Bhādrapada is exceedingly meritorious, a destroyer of sins, auspicious, peaceful, and dear to Guha; on this day,
all acts such as ritual bathing and giving of gifts are said to be inexhaustible.

Those who behold Kārttikeya, the son of Gaṅgā, residing here in the southern region, are liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa; of this there is no doubt. Therefore, O best of kings, one should always behold Kārttikeya at this place.
Those men who, endowed with devotion, worship Guha on this [day],
having obtained here all their desired pleasures, go to the same world as Indra.
Furthermore, he who causes a very firm and well-established temple to be built—
Endowed with devotion and faith, one who has ascended a vehicle made of wood or stone fashioned for Gaṅgeya shall indeed go to the abode of Gaṅgeya; likewise,
the man who performs acts such as sweeping in the temple of Guha [attains the same].
O King, he who performs the hoisting of the banner shall indeed go to the abode of Rudra;
and he who worships Guha with sandalwood, agallochum,
and camphor attains the command of an army, enriched with elephants, horses, chariots, and vehicles.
O lord of the earth, it is said that Kārttikeya is always to be worshipped by kings;
they declare that there is no one else to be worshipped by kings except Kārttikeya.
He who, when going forth to battle, worships the son of the Kṛttikās—
O hero, he conquers his enemy just as Indra conquered the Dānavas in battle;
therefore, with every effort, one should worship the son of Śaṅkara.
O King, by worshipping him with devotion using various campaka flowers, one attains success.
He is liberated from all sins and shall then go to the abode of Śiva.
O joy of the Kurus, one should not consume oil on the sixth lunar day, nor during the daytime.
O bull of the Bharatas, that man who observes the *nakta* fast on the sixth day [is likewise blessed].
Released from all sins, he shall go to the abode of Gaṅgeya; he who,
endowed with faith, goes to the southern direction three times and worships the Lord of the God of Gods, shall go to the temple of peace.
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Kārttikeya," in the Sixth Kalpa of the Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty thousand verses.
Herein concludes the Sixth Kalpa.
Now begins the Forty-seventh Chapter.
The Description of the Śākasaptamī Vow.
Sumantu said: On the seventh lunar day, one should observe a fast, or otherwise take food only at night.
On the seventh [day], the God of gods respectfully regained his own form. Born indeed together with the cosmic egg, he attained consciousness while remaining within the egg.
While he was still within the egg, Dakṣa gave him his own daughter as a wife.

By name she is Rūpā, and by form no other woman could be so; thus, while still dwelling for a long time within the egg, he became Mārtaṇḍa. Then, at the command of Dakṣa, Viśvakarman manifested his body.
O lord of men, from that time forth he became known by the name Prakāśat;
while still remaining within the egg, Yāmuna and Yama were born to him.
His wife was the slender-waisted daughter of Dakṣa, who, out of world-weariness, [renounced her body].
That goddess, having fallen into despondency due to her grief, reflected:
"Alas! The beloved's radiant form is full of splendor and beautiful;
yet, I cannot see any part of his body, for it is bewildered by his own brilliance."
"My auspicious form, which was like gold, lovely and exceedingly beautiful,
has now turned dark, scorched by his splendor.
Therefore, I shall go to the Northern Kurus and perform austerities."
Having cast her own shadow there out of fear of the curse, she assumed a physical form;
having deposited it, she said to that young girl, "Do not speak of this to him.
Having made this resolve, she departed for the Northern Kurus.
Having cast off her own form there and assuming the shape of a mare,
she wandered with the deer for many groups of years, O King.
And that Mārtaṇḍa also regarded his shadow-self as his wife.
He begot two offspring, Śani and Tapatī;
then the son of Chāyā (Svarbhānu) would protect his own children with great affection,
yet he did not look upon Yamunā and Yama with such excessive fondness.
Then a dispute arose between those two daughters of Āditya;
both of them, arguing with one another in disagreement,
became the two rivers Yamunā and Tapatī.
Yama, the brother of Yamunā, having been struck violently by Chāyā,
raised his foot and stood directly in front of her.
Out of rage, Chāyā cursed him because he had raised his foot against her.

Therefore, O fool, that loathsome deed of yours—the destruction of the lives of living beings—will endure for a long time, as long as the moon and sun exist; of this there is no doubt. And if you set even one foot upon this earth, [the same shall happen].
Worms will devour [the body] fouled by my urine;
as they were thus disputing, Mārtaṇḍa arrived there.
Then Yama spoke to the high-souled Mārtaṇḍa, the purifier of the world:
"Father, she always looks upon me with a cruel disposition;
it is evident that her gaze toward us is not at all favorable.
Then the Sun, becoming exceedingly angry, spoke to that Shadow.
"O fool, why do you not perceive equality when the offspring is the same?
Yama said to his father: 'Father, this is not my mother;
this is but a sinful shadow of my mother. I have been cursed by her, Father.'"
Yamunā related the entire account of Tapatī;
then Mārtaṇḍa said: "Let not your foot remain upon the surface of the earth;
let worms go into the ground, taking away the flesh and blood."
And the water of the Yamunā shall become equal to the Gaṅgā;
O twice-born one, it shall indeed be equal in merit to the Narmadā and the Tapatī.
Here, to the south of the Vindhya mountains, the Tapatī shall flow.
Through union with that [power], the beautiful Gaṅgā will proceed for a full year;
having reached the Yamunā, the Gaṅgā herself shall become that very [river].
Both the solar and the lunar [streams] are meritorious and destroyers of all sins.
Both the solar and the Vaiṣṇava [mantras] remove the fear of great sins.
O son, honoring the command of Brahmā, you shall hold the office of a world-protector (lokapāla). From this day forward, I shall remain as your shadow, residing within your own body.
Having thus settled his wife and likewise his offspring,
he indeed came into the presence of Dakṣa and explained the reason.
Dakṣa, having understood all of that, spoke this to Mārtaṇḍa:
"Your wife Uttara has departed; she does not see your form.
I shall reveal my form to you if you can endure the pain.
He replied, "I shall be able to do so; manifest your body to me."
Then he remembered the carpenter, and as soon as he was remembered, the carpenter arrived.
Dakṣa said to the carpenter, "Make Mārtaṇḍa manifest.
The carpenter replied to Mārtaṇḍa, "Will you be able to endure the pain?"
Urged by Dakṣa, he said to the carpenter, "May you be able to endure it.
Then the carpenter indeed fashioned his form in the fire,
from the mouth down to the feet, using his own carving tools.
As his limbs were repeatedly pierced by the rays [of the sun],
Mārtaṇḍa, afflicted by the pain, fainted moment after moment.
Out of fear of his curse, Takṣaka [cut] his feet from the ankles upward.
Then he made his fingers shapeless so that they did not reveal [the work];
"This carpentry work is finished; my pain is afflicting me.
The carpenter said to Mārtaṇḍa, "O Lord of Light, dispel my pain."
"Anoint your limbs, born of the body, beginning from the hands, with karavīra flowers and red sandalwood. When he had done exactly as instructed, Ravi was freed from his pain.
Therefore, O King, these are desired here for Mārtaṇḍa:
the flowers of the karavīra and likewise red sandalwood.
For the Lord formerly spoke thus in the presence of Anūra, O King.
Whoever offers me with devotion the flowers of the *karavīra*, red sandalwood,
and likewise *guggulu* resin along with the *itihāsas* and *purāṇas*,
he bestows his very life-breaths upon me.
Therefore, O Bhārata, one who knows this should not give anything else to me with devotion; for it is said that the Sun, having taken the egg-born splendor from the Egg of Brahmā,
fashioned the indestructible thunderbolt which destroys the ranks of enemies.
Mārtaṇḍa became thoroughly satisfied; having regained his form and been freed from distress, he went swiftly toward the Kurus, eager for a sight of his wife.
Seeing her in the midst of the deer, assuming the form of a mare, he pursued her.
Then, having assumed the form of a horse and mounting his own wife,
he emitted his vital energy with speed, leaping like a horse.
Fearing that he might be another man, she stood facing the god.
Then, from both nostrils, the seed fell simultaneously like a flash of lightning;
from that were born the two divine physicians known as the Nāsatyas and Aśvins.
At the conclusion of the emission of the seed, however, there was the great Revanta, the son of Virocana.
O descendant of Bharata, they know that Tapatī, Śani, and Sāvarṇi were the offspring of Chāyā;
likewise, Yamunā and Yama were the two children born of Saṃjñā as previously mentioned.
Furthermore, O Bhārata, she obtained a divine form as her wife, as well as sons.
Since all this [universe] proceeds from the God of gods on the seventh day,
for that reason the seventh day is always desired by the Lord.
That man who, having fasted on the seventh day, eats only at night—
Having observed a fast on the sixth day and eating only once on the fifth,
one should offer well-prepared vegetables along with various kinds of hard and soft foods to the deity and to the Brahmins; then, remaining silent, one should eat at night.
If a man should observe this vow for as long as he lives,
his prosperity, victory, and even the three aims of life (trivarga) will increase;
and upon death, he goes to heaven, seated upon an excellent celestial chariot.
He rejoices in the world of the Sun for many series of Manvantaras;
and having returned here at the end of time, that king,
endowed with peace and surrounded by sons and grandsons, shall remain a donor and a ruler for a long time.
O King,

tiger among men, those men who, remaining undefeated by their enemies in battle, fast on the seventh lunar day with a diet of vegetables and attain that ancestral tirtha known as Rājasa, indeed enjoy the earth.
By your ancestor Kuru, through his subsistence on vegetables on the seventh lunar day,
that field of dharma, Kurukṣetra, was made sacred by Vivasvat;
O King, [so too were] the seventh, ninth, sixth, third, and fifth days.
For these lunar days (tithis) indeed grant desires to men and women right here in this world:
the seventh day in the month of Māgha, the ninth in Āśvayuja,
the sixth in Bhādrapada, and the third in Vaiśākha are considered auspicious.
The fifth lunar day of the month of Bhādrapada is declared meritorious as Nāgapañcamī.
These specific lunar days are remembered as particularly auspicious during those months.
Whoever, endowed with devotion, prepares well-prepared vegetable dishes [and offers them], [attains great merit].
Having given according to his ability to a Brahmin, the observer of the vow eats afterwards at night.
O descendant of Kuru, this [vow] should be undertaken during the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika;
the first breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) is prescribed after four months.
In this rite, the worship of the Fire-god should be performed with Agasti flowers;
the unguent should be saffron, the incense should be Aparājita,
and the bath should be with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), after which one should consume that very same substance.
In this rite, milk-rice (pāyasa) is proclaimed as the food offering for the God of gods;
that very same offering should be given to the Brahmins, while one may eat vegetables oneself—
vegetables that are auspicious, accompanied by various kinds of edibles and drinks.
On the second breaking of the fast, O King, one should offer to the Lord flowers that possess auspicious fragrances, as well as white sandalwood,
agallochum as incense, and offerings of jaggery cakes.
In this [rite], bathing with water containing *kuśa* grass and the consumption of cow dung are prescribed;
on the third day, *karavīra* flowers and red sandalwood are used,
and among incenses, *guggulu* is always dear to the God.
O Great-minded One, the wise man should offer as an oblation boiled rice mixed with curd;
O Lord, he should likewise give that same offering to the Brahmins, accompanied by foods to be chewed and licked,
and combined with black pot-herbs.
The wise know that bathing here with a paste of white mustard seeds is prescribed;
likewise, the consumption of that same paste is auspicious, meritorious, and a remover of all sins.
At the conclusion of the third fast, there should be a great feast for the Brahmins.
Hearing and reciting the Purāṇa is likewise praised,
O dear one, in the presence of the deities as well as before Brāhmaṇas.
It should be heard from a Brāhmaṇa reciter, and not from one born of another caste.
Then one should honor all those Brahmins with devotion and according to one's capacity.
O King, one should present two spotless garments to the reciter;
when the reciter is honored, the god Bhāskara is always pleased.
Karavīra flowers are dear to him as he desires; likewise red sandalwood is dear to him as he desires;

guggulu resin is always dear to him as he desires; milk-rice (pāyasa) is always dear to him as he desires; sweetmeat balls (modaka) are dear to him as he desires; and indeed, a copper vessel is dear to him as he desires.
O descendant of Kuru, for him there is always as much ghee as he desires, a reciter as he desires,
and indeed the Purāṇa as he desires from the Sun;
such is this meritorious seventh day, called Śākā, belonging eternally to the Lord of Rays.
"By fasting upon this [day] with devotion, a man becomes fortunate.

Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Śāka-saptamī Vow," in the Saptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan, within the Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty thousand verses.
Now begins the forty-eighth chapter.
Description of the Greatness of Āditya:
Śatānīka said,
"O best of Brahmins, describe in detail the excellent Saptamī-kalpa."
And [regarding] the great majesty of the high-souled god Bhāskara,
Sumantu said:
"In this very context, the high-souled ones have related a most excellent and meritorious dialogue."
O Lord of the Earth, together with his son Sattva,
Śāmba duly prostrated with devotion before Vāsudeva, the teacher of the world,
and inquired about the supreme knowledge that brings welfare both in this world and the next.
O Madhusūdana, how is it that a being born here in this world is not afflicted by the sufferings of birth? And how does he obtain various desires,
as well as attain heaven and manifold pleasures in the next world?
Having experienced this for the appropriate duration, how can one attain liberation?
O Janārdana, seeing this, despondency has arisen within me like a disease;
even the hope for life no longer pleases me for a single moment upon seeing this.
"But this is why my purpose remains unfulfilled, that my life-breaths do not depart;
I shall not fall again into this cycle of existence, fraught with old age and disease.
O you of noble vows, show me favor today by telling me the means by which this may be so."
"Tell me how I may become free from mental and physical afflictions, just as I am now.
Vāsudeva said:
"The grace of the deity is considered by all to be the supreme [means] for everything else."
It is my firm conviction that the means [of liberation] is eternal and constant;
it has been correctly established by me through inference, scripture, and other means.
No one anywhere could ever alter this at any time.
Faith arises in him when that [rite] is performed with proper propitiation by one who knows it;
for a distinguished deity is properly worshipped only by a distinguished embodied being.
When propitiated, she bestows the desired and distinguished fruit.
Śamba said:
There is no doubt for some regarding the existence of a deity.
"Others are certain that [the self] does not exist, yet you deliver distinguished discourses on it.
Vāsudeva said:
"The existence of the deity is established in many scriptures."
For one for whom scripture is the means of valid cognition, its existence is established;
or else, its existence is today proven by inference. For one who possesses this means of valid cognition, its existence here is established.
Furthermore, the existence of the deity is established even by direct perception;
and that [perception] is necessarily a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for all embodied beings,
even those belonging to the animal realm, provided they are free from mental obscurations.
"It does not arise, for conventional usage exists just as it stands.
Śamba said:
"If the deities are indeed properly perceived through direct observation,"
"And there is no need for that purpose through inference or scripture.
Vāsudeva said:
"Not all deities are perceived anywhere by direct perception."
"There are thousands of others that are to be known through inference and scripture.
Śamba said:
"And there is one which is within the range of the senses and bestows distinguished, desired fruits."
"First tell me that very one; afterwards you shall speak of the others.
Vāsudeva said:
"The Sun-god, the maker of day and the eye of the world, is a deity manifest before our eyes."
Therefore, there is no eternal deity whatsoever superior to him,
from whom this world was born and into whom it shall go to its dissolution;
Time, characterized by the Kṛta age and the others, is known as the Sun himself in visible form.
The planets, lunar mansions, and yogas, as well as the zodiac signs and the karaṇas;
the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, the two Aśvins, Vāyu, and Anala;
Śakra, Prajāpati, and all the worlds of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ.
All the worlds, the mountains, the serpents, the rivers, and likewise the oceans—
the Sun is himself the cause of the entire multitude of living beings.
By his will, the entire universe, with all its moving and unmoving things, has come into being.
It remains steadfast, it proceeds, and it continues to function for its own sake;
through its grace, this world is seen to be active. When it has risen, everything rises; when it has set, everything sets.
"Why do you say that he has 'set' when he has merely become invisible?
Therefore, there is nothing beyond this; it has not existed, nor will it ever exist—that which is indeed celebrated in all the Vedas as the Supreme Self."
In the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, he is celebrated as the "inner self" (antarātman). Abiding in the Suṣumṇā, he is the "outer self" (bāhyātman) when situated in the waking state or dreaming state.
Why do I say that he "sets" (astaṃ yāti) through the unseen (adṛṣṭa)?

Therefore, there is nothing beyond this; there has been none, nor will there ever be, who is not known as "I," the impeller of all embodied beings. There is no being, whether moving or stationary, that exists devoid of this.
That which can be described here in detail by the Vedas and those who know the Vedas even in hundreds of years cannot be described by me in brief.
Therefore, this Sun is renowned everywhere as a mine of virtues.
He is the Lord of all, the creator of all, the sustainer of all, and the imperishable.
Fishes and other beings were born from Maheśvara and attained their proper state;
moreover, I know from the perspective of ultimate reality that he is distinct from the cosmic sphere.
Likewise, whoever approaches this [deity] after having prepared its mandala—
at dawn, at dusk, and at midday— attains the supreme goal;
how much more so for one who recites [the mantra] while situated within the mandala according to the ultimate truth?

Various accomplishments come to him; this is not surprising. He who, being undeluded, perceives the deity residing in the mandala and established within his own body through his own intellect—he truly sees.
Whoever meditates thus, worships, recites [mantras], and offers oblations,
shall attain all desires and likewise go to Dharmadhvaja. Therefore, if you wish to bring an end to your sufferings here, [you must do so].
To obtain the enjoyment of riches both here and hereafter, as well as eternal liberation,
one should worship the Sun residing within the Sun by means of mantras directed toward that Self.
This should be done while surrounded by the ancillary limbs (*aṅga*) and in a place enclosed and purified according to the scripture.
When you are girded with the armor and protected on all sides by the weapon-mantra,
you shall thus obtain through effort the desired fruit at all times;
there will be no suffering here, whether of a spiritual (ādhyātmika) or physical (ādhibhautika) nature.
The most fierce afflictions caused by divine powers shall never befall you.
No fear exists for those who have taken refuge in the Sun;
for them, uninterrupted happiness arises—happiness both in this world and the next.
This supreme knowledge was directly taught to me by the Sun,
who was propitiated according to the prescribed rites over a long period of time;
through this, the highest state is attained, where Dharmadhvaja resides.
This has been briefly indicated as the supreme means for swift accomplishment;
indeed, Tūrya himself declared that there is nothing else like it.
Thus, this method has been explained to you here in summary.
"Because there is no means for the welfare of embodied beings superior to this.

Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Sun," in the *Saptamī-kalpa* within the *Brāhma-parvan* of the *Śrī-Bhaviṣya-Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of fifty thousand verses.
Now begins the forty-ninth chapter.
Description of the Majesty of the Sun.
Vāsudeva said:
Now I shall describe the unsurpassed procedure for the worship of Dharmaketu (the Sun).
This merit-bestowing rite grants all desires, destroys obstacles, and removes misfortune.
Having first bathed with the mantras of the Sun, one should worship Bhāskara with those very same mantras. Therefore, I shall now describe the procedure for the initial bath in brief.
O son, descendant of my lineage, having sipped water and reproached him, and having performed the lustration with a pure and stainless mudrā,
you should then purify the water with a mantra purified by the heart-mantra after bathing.
Having risen and sipped water, and having put on two garments with that same [mantra],
he should then sip water twice and sprinkle his body with the seven-syllable mantra.
Having risen and sipped water again, he should likewise offer the *arghya* oblation to the Sun.
Having given [the offering], having muttered that [mantra], and having meditated upon himself as the Sun within his heart,
he should go to a bright sanctuary and worship the form of the Sun;
being composed, he should perform inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and exhalation (recaka).
Having performed [the recitation] with the syllable *oṃ*, one should destroy the defects arising from the body and so forth;
for the sake of one's own success, one should destroy sin through the Vāyavya, Āgneya, Māhendra, and Vāruṇī [mantras], respectively, and by means of the waters of Varuṇa.
When drying, burning, stiffening,
and flooding have been performed respectively by the concentrations (dhāraṇās) known as Vāyu, Agni, Indra, and Jana,
one should meditate upon the self as purified and bow to the Sun situated therein.
Having thus meditated upon the supreme body composed of the five elements,
both subtle and gross, and having likewise established the senses in their respective places,
one should assign the elements beginning with space (ether) to the limbs, and the [mantras] beginning with the Heart to the heart and other parts.
*Kha svāhā* is the heart of the Sun; *kham arkāya* is likewise the head.
*Ulka svāhā* is the crest-lock (*śikhā*) of the Sun; *yai ca hūṃ* is the supreme armor (*kavaca*).
*Khāṃ phaṭ* is the weapon (*astra*), and the *praṇava* (Oṃ) is placed at the beginning of each of these mantras of withdrawal.
First, for the sake of accomplishing the mantra-rites of the *praṇava*,
he should recite these [mantras] over water three times; then, having sprinkled the bathing substances with that water,
he should worship the Sun with auspicious perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Then, during the night, one should worship within the fire in all the forms; indeed,
in the morning, evening, and at night, facing east, west, north, or toward the front,
having meditated upon that mantra consisting of seven syllables as being in the pericarp of a lotus.
One should visualize the body situated within the solar disc;
having meditated upon that body as before, standing in the midst of a circle of light,
complete with all auspicious marks and blazing with a thousand rays.
With red perfumes, flowers, sacrificial porridges (caru),
and offerings (bali), or with garments and auspicious coverings mixed with red sandalwood;
one should perform the rites beginning with invocation (āvāhana) and provide protection by means of the Heart-mantra.
Having understood the sequence of ritual actions, the wise one, with a focused mind, should always perform them:
having performed the invocation with mantras, he should then effect the stabilization [of the deity] in one place,
and maintain its presence there until the conclusion of the sacrifice.
Having offered worship beginning with water for the feet (pādya) according to one's capacity, and having presented the water for the guest-offering (arghya),
and having performed the recitation (japa) and meditation (dhyāna) according to the rules, one should then dismiss the Goddess.
This sequence of ritual action has been declared as the procedure for the worship of all [deities].
I shall now describe the place for recitation (japa) within the enclosure of Padmeśa:

the Sun is situated upon the pericarp (karṇikā), and the limbs (aṅgas) are on the petals starting from the east; likewise, the planets beginning with the Moon and ending with Rāhu are placed starting from the north.

Then, for the sake of protection, one should worship the world-protectors in embodied form within the enclosures in their proper order, as well as their weapons, using their respective mantras sequentially,
joined with the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ), their names in the dative case, and the word "namas" (obeisance).

The mantras for all [deities] have been declared; now I shall describe the mudrās: Vyomamudrā, Rati, Padmā, Mahāśvetā, and the Astra-mudrā—these five mudrās are fully proclaimed for the successful accomplishment of all rites.
Having placed the two hands palm-upward, the fingers are to be joined in sequence until they reach the index fingers; these two [hands] remain level or facing downward,
with the index fingers positioned over the tips of the middle fingers or the thumbs.
This mudrā among all mudrās is celebrated as the "Space Mudrā" (Vyoma-mudrā).
This yoga is applicable for all rites; likewise, it prepares the locus.
All [fingers] extended like a lotus are known as Mahāśvetā of the Sun.
The Sun is traditionally remembered as being constantly mounted upon his chariot.
Having raised both hands with the palms facing upward and joined them with the left thumb,
this mudrā should be employed for the purification of substances and especially for protection.
By means of this mudrā, everything becomes protected and purified.
It should be employed after offering the *arghya*, especially at the conclusion of the worship,
as well as at the end of recitation and meditation, if one desires one's own spiritual accomplishment (*siddhi*).
By this method, one should constantly recite for a year without weariness;
he shall obtain his desired objects both in this world and the next, of this there is no doubt.
One afflicted by disease is freed from disease, and one destitute of wealth shall obtain wealth.
One fallen from his kingdom shall regain his kingdom; one without a son shall obtain a son; a human being shall attain abundance of wisdom and intellect and live for a long time;
and a man shall certainly obtain a beautiful daughter of noble birth.
"Even an unworthy woman obtains good fortune, and an unlearned maiden attains knowledge from the Supreme Person; thus was it said by the Sun in the past.
Indeed, this is remembered as the eternal sacrifice (nityayāga), which brings wealth, grain, and happiness."
Even for one who is free from desire, there arises an increase in progeny and cattle;
such a person alone is praised in heaven and proclaimed as the best among men. That man who worships him with devotion is always most meritorious.
"Having indeed attained his desire here, one should then go to the abode of Manu;
by his grace, the twice-born becomes like Mercury in splendor.
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Sun," in the Saptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan, within the Śatārdhasāhasrī-saṃhitā of the glorious *Bhaviṣya-mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the fiftieth chapter, describing the greatness of the seventh [tithi].
Vāsudeva said:
Next, I shall briefly describe the occasional [rites] (*naimittika*), knowing which one will [attain success],

specifically on the seventh lunar day, during eclipses, and at the transits of the sun; having once partaken of the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) on the seventh day of the bright fortnight during the daytime.
Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) at the twilight, having prostrated to Varuṇa,
and having restrained the senses, one should meditate upon what has been done and sleep on the ground.
Having gone to a bed of darbha grass at night, one should bathe in the morning and remain well-restrained.

Then, having performed the twilight worship (sandhyā), one should mutter the previously mentioned mantra and offer oblations into the fire after mentally conceiving it as the Sun-fire. I shall now describe briefly the ritual of conceiving the Sun as fire and the libation (tarpaṇa).
Having delineated the sanctum of worship and entered it, one should worship the people with the people;
then, having cast down and spread out *darbha* grass, and having consecrated the vessels and other implements in due order,
one should prepare the *pavitra* from two *kuśa* blades, complete with tips and measuring a span (*prādeśa*).
Having sprinkled the vessels with water, purified them, and inspected their interiors,
and having placed the vessels with their openings facing north,
he should then kindle a firebrand and perform the circumambulation by fire (paryagnikaraṇa) as well as the threefold waving of light (ājyotvaṇa).
Then, having wiped the *sruva* ladle and other implements with *darbha* grass, one should sprinkle them with water;

having sprinkled them, one should offer oblations into the fire. Thereupon, one should proceed as before with the *arka* [oblation], using a vessel placed on the ground and held in the hand upon a sacrificial seat (*viṣṭara*).
O tiger among the Yadus, by means of this gift, [one is not obstructed] anywhere in the sky or on the earth.
Holding the sacrificial ladle with his right hand, the wise man should offer oblations into the fire.
All the rites previously enjoined should be performed with the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
Beginning with the sun, one should offer oblations silently while standing for the sake of the ritual name.
On the seventh day of the month of Māgha, one should worship Varuṇa with a hundred offerings.
Furthermore, according to one's capacity, one should give pieces of sugar-candy and cakes to the Brahmins.

And one should give a sacrificial fee according to one's ability; thus one obtains the fruit requested. In this manner, one should worship the Sun in Phālguna, Dhātṛ in Caitra, and Indra in Vaiśākha; and in the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should worship Ravi.
In the month of Āṣāḍha one should worship Śravaṇa, in Śrāvaṇa Nabhas, in Bhādrapada Yama,
likewise in Āśvayuja Parjanya, and in Kārttika one should worship Tvaṣṭṛ.
If one worships Mitra in Mārgaśīrṣa and Viṣṇu in Pauṣa, [one attains the desired fruit].
Whatever desired fruit is said to be obtained day by day throughout the year,
the observer of the vow, endowed with devotion and faith, shall quickly attain all of that.
Thus, when the year is complete, having fashioned a golden chariot—
Yoked with seven horses, adorned with various jewels,
and featuring a beautiful image of the Sun in the center made of pure gold;
having fashioned it thus, adorned with gems, and placed it upon a golden lotus.
Having placed that excellent chariot there with the charioteer standing at the front,
and having surrounded himself with twelve Brahmins who are the embodiments of the presiding deities of the months,
he placed his own preceptor in the center and honored him according to the sacred tradition.
Having intentionally honored those who possess the luster of the sun with garments, jewels, and other such gifts,
and having thus worshipped the Brahmins who are the lords of the months,
one should then present to the preceptor a chariot, an umbrella, a village, cows, and auspicious land.
One should offer horses to the twelve lords of the months;
thus, with devotion and according to one's capacity, having given ornaments such as gold and jewels,
and having bowed to him, one should announce that the vow is complete.
From this point forward, there is no fault here even if the vows are not performed.
Saying "So be it," the preceptor, together with the lords of the brahmins, repeatedly bestows many blessings and should say, "May [the deity] be pleased."
May Āditya, for whatever desire you have propitiated him with these vows, grant that desire to you; may your vow be fulfilled.
The Sun himself has entered into the preceptors in the form of Brahmins.
The Sun himself declared:

"He shall indeed perform the supreme rite by giving according to his capacity as sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to virtuous Brahmins, especially to those who are destitute, and to the poor, the blind, and the wretched."
Having fed the Brāhmaṇas, one should complete this vow. By performing this for seven years, a man becomes a righteous king,
and a woman becomes the beloved of such kings.
He enjoys for more than a hundred years, in happiness, a perfected mandala extending a hundred yojanas, free from rivals and thorns;
even one devoid of wealth who, out of devotion, has fashioned a chariot made of copper.
At the conclusion of the vow, having performed everything as prescribed,
that king shall enjoy a vast realm extending eighty yojanas;
even so, O man, does he who, though lacking wealth, makes [the image] out of flour.
Long-lived, free from disease, and happy, he enjoys [the earth] for sixty yojanas;
and having remained in the world of the Sun until the end of the kalpa, he shall attain this.
Moreover, he who, unwearied and with devotion, worships the Sun even in his mind—
In all circumstances, even he is here completely liberated from diseases;
calamities do not touch him, just as mists do not touch the sun—
how much more so one who is perfected by vows, devoted, and protected by mantras!
Therefore, having understood the procedure enjoined in the ritual manual (kalpa) in this way,
one should perform everything without exception for the sake of easily attaining the fruit.
O Sāmba, this auspicious [teaching] was told to me by the Sun in the past.
This kalpa has always been kept secret by me since the first kalpa.
O child, if one desires the highest fruit, one should quickly propitiate the Sun according to this rite with a pure inner self.
"By his very grace alone, thousands of sons were obtained by me;
the asuras were utterly defeated, and all the gods were brought under my control.
You too must preserve this Kalpa, which is esteemed by the Sun."
By the grace of this eon, the sun is always present;
for by him the gods, along with the asuras, humans, and serpents, were conquered upon this discus.
If this discus were not itself presided over by the rays of the sun, [it could not prevail].
How could it ever be obstructed, since it is eternally endowed with radiance?
By constantly reciting this, worshipping, and meditating upon it according to my ability,
I have become worthy of honor and preeminent in splendor among all who possess their desires.
Having practiced this with your mind, speech, or even through action,
perform devotion according to this very rule for the sake of attaining the fruit.
Any man who listens, endowed with devotion and possessed of faith, [shall likewise attain it].
O son, he who performs the rite from the beginning on the seventh lunar day,
having obtained here every desire, as well as health and victory,
and being endowed with supreme fortune, shall go to the assembly of Vairocana.

Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Seventh Day (Saptamī)," in the Saptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan, within the Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty thousand verses.
Now begins the fifty-first chapter:
"Description of the Mahāsaptamī Vow."
Vāsudeva said:
O upholder of my lineage, on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, a single meal is prescribed;
on the sixth day, eating only at night is declared.
O observer of good vows, some desire the fast on the seventh day, while others here say that the breaking of the fast occurs on the seventh after the sixth;
having fasted on the sixth, the wise man should worship the Sun.
O observer of noble vows, O mighty-armed one, with *karavīra* flowers mixed with red sandalwood, and with *guggulu* resin and *saṃyāva* cakes, O observer of noble vows,
one should worship Śaṅkara, the Lord of the Gods of gods, the Sun, Ravi.
In this manner, one should worship the Sun for four months beginning with Māgha;
for the sake of one's own purification,
one should consume cow dung and perform a bath with cow dung here on earth for the sake of self-purification.
One should also feed Brahmins, both celestial and terrestrial, according to one's capacity.
Furthermore, during the months beginning with Jyeṣṭha, white sandalwood is prescribed,
as well as white flowers endowed with auspicious fragrance.
Black agallochum is likewise prescribed as incense, and milk-rice (pāyasa) is known as the food offering;

with that very [milk-rice], O great-minded one, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas until they are satisfied. Furthermore, O son, one should consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and perform the bath with that same [substance].
O tiger among men, it is taught that during the months beginning with Kārttika, one should worship [the deity] with Agasti flowers and incense made from Aparājita;
the food offering (naivedya) is prescribed to consist of jaggery cakes and sugarcane juice.
O dear one, with that very [money], feed the Brahmins according to your ability;
you should consume water with *kuśa* grass and perform a bath for the sake of purification.
O high-minded one, at the end of the third fast, there shall be the breaking of the fast in the month of Māgha.
In that place, food and the gift [of alms] are declared to be twofold [in merit].
The wise should perform the worship of the God of gods according to their ability.
O observer of noble vows, there should also be the gift of a chariot and the chariot procession.

When one possesses the means, a gift of a golden chariot should indeed be made here as a cause for attaining the vow, according to what has been prescribed when wealth is available. Thus, O son, this auspicious seventh lunar day called Rathasaptamī has been described.
The Mahāsaptamī is renowned as greatly meritorious and of great prosperity; by fasting upon it, one may obtain wealth, sons, fame, and knowledge,
as well as the entire world, which is like the moon in its splendor.
Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Mahāsaptamī Vow," in the Saptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan, within the Śatārdhasāhasrī Saṃhitā of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa.
Now begins the fifty-second chapter:
"Description of the Worship of the Sun."
Sumantu said:
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord, the God who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace,
vanished while the hero Śāmba was looking on.
Śāmbo, too, having duly observed the Ratha-saptamī vow on the seventh lunar day,
was liberated from mental and physical ailments and quickly returned to his own abode.
Śatānīka said:
"How should the chariot procession be performed? How is the chariot of the Sun to be made?
By whom was this chariot procession first inaugurated here in the worlds of mortals?
Sumantu said:
O tiger among the Kurus, in former times, while seated on the Golden Mountain, the lotus-born Prajāpati was questioned by Rudra regarding this very matter as he sat comfortably upon his lotus-seat.
Having bowed his head, the god Rudra uttered these words.
Śrī Rudra said:
"This Blessed Lord, the god Bhāskara, the illuminator of the worlds—"
"How does this pure god always move while stationed upon his chariot?
Brahmā said:
"O dear one, just as the sun always moves in the sky while mounted upon its chariot."
O Three-eyed One, I shall describe his chariot to you:
it is a beautiful golden chariot with a single wheel, five spokes, three hubs, eight bands, and a single rim.
With his radiant wheel, the Sun moves through the sky;
its width is said to be ten thousand yojanas,
and its circumference is three times that, measured from the base of the chariot.
Its yoke was broad, with Aruṇa as the charioteer;
it had a divine golden pole and was yoked to horses swift as the wind,
which stood positioned wherever the wheel moved, taking the form of Vedic meters.
By means of that radiant chariot, the Lord of Day traverses the sky; now,
these constituent parts of the Sun's chariot have been fashioned in due order from the components of the year.
The three spokes of its wheel are proclaimed to be the three divisions of time;
its five spokes are the five seasons, and its felloes are known as the six seasons.
Its two chariot-seats are remembered as the southern and northern solstices.
The muhūrtas are known as its arrows; its yoke-pins are remembered as the kalās.
Its kāṣṭhās are remembered as the corners; the moments (kṣaṇas) are remembered as the axle-shaft.
The winks of the eyes (nimeṣas) are its weights (karṣas); the lavas are remembered as the pole-axle.

Night is its fender, and Dharma is its banner established aloft; both Artha and Kāma are known as its two poles at the ends of the yoke. The Vedic meters, in the form of horses, draw it on the left side of the pole.
The Gāyatrī, the Triṣṭubh, the Jagatī, the Anuṣṭubh,
the Paṅkti, the Bṛhatī, and the Uṣṇih as the seventh;
the wheel is fixed upon the axle, and the axle is secured within the hub (dhruva).
The wheel revolves together with the axle, and that axle revolves within the hub;
the axle revolves together with the wheel while remaining fixed in the hub.
Such is the arrangement of that chariot according to the nature of its axle.
Thus, the chariot of the Sun is perfectly constructed through its state of conjunction;
by means of it, the divine Ravi always traverses the sky.
Furthermore, two reins of the chariot are fastened to the ends of the axle of the yoke.
The two poles of its axle do not rotate,
yet the two shafts of this chariot of the Sun revolve; as it moves,
its orb travels in every direction like a potter’s wheel.
The two ends of its axle are fixed at the southern pole of that chariot;
held by the Ṛg and Yajur Vedas, it revolves upon the Dhruva pole with its wheels and horses.
Its two reins shorten within their respective orbits during the northern course.
Then, as it moved in circles upon the prosperous southern path,
the two poles of its axle turned;
and the wheel moved in circles in every direction, both in contact and detached.
O observer of noble vows, when [the pole-star] is drawn here by Dhruva, it remains level with him;
then the deity revolves within the circles.
But when it is released by Dhruva from that pair of rays, indeed—
In the same way, the sun revolves externally through its orbits;
it traverses one hundred and eighty orbits between the two solstices (kāṣṭhā),
moving together with the ṛṣis while presided over by the gods in its chariot.
The Gandharvas, Apsarases, Sarpas, Grāmaṇīs, and Rākṣasas—
by these [deities] the Sun indeed dwells for two months each in succession:
Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Pulastya, and Pulaha, the Prajāpati.
Khaṇḍaka and Vāsuki, Sakarṇa and Raśmi,
as well as Tumburu and Nārada, the two best of Gandharvas who sing;
and the Apsaras Kratusthalā and she who is Puñjikasthalā.
Grāmaṇī, Rathakṛtsna, both Rathaujas and Aśvatara,
Rakṣas, Heti, Praheti, and those two Yātudhānas—
this is the group that dwells in the sun during the months of Madhu and Mādhava.
Likewise, during the two months of summer, there are Mitra and Varuṇa;
the sages Atri and Vasiṣṭha; Takṣaka and Ananta; and Menakā, Sahajanyā, and the Gandharvas Hāhā and Hūhū.
Rathasvana and Rathacitra,
both of them leaders of hosts, as well as Pauruṣeya and Vadha—
these two mighty Yātudhānas dwell in the sun during the two months of Śuci and Śukra.
