Indra, Vivasvat, Aṅgiras, and Bhṛgu;
Elāparṇa, Sarpa, and Śaṅkhapāla the serpents;
Pramlocā and Dundukā, and the two Gandharvas Bhānu and Dardura.
The two Yātudhānas, as well as the serpent and the Brāhma—
these two dwell in the sun during the months of Nabhas and Nabhasya.
In the autumn, these deities dwell again in their radiant forms.
Parjanya and Pūṣan, Bhāradvāja along with Gautama,
the Gandharva Citrasena and he who is Vasuruci,
as well as Viśvācī and Ghṛtācī— both of them possessed of auspicious marks.
The elephant Airāvata and the famous Dhanañjaya,
Senajit, Suṣeṇa, Senānī, and Grāmaṇī;
and these two, Āpa and Vāta, are proclaimed as the Yātudhānas.
These two indeed dwell in the Sun during the months of Iṣa and Ūrja through the revolution of time;
and these two, Aṃśu and Bhaga, as well as Kaśyapa and Kratu, dwell in the Maker of Day during the two months of the winter season.
The serpent Mahāpadma and the snake Karkoṭaka,
as well as these two— Āpa and Vāta— are proclaimed to be Yātudhānas;
and both Citrāṅgada and Aruṇāyu are Gandharvas.
During the months of Sahas and Sahasya, these dwell with the Sun:
Pūṣan, Jiṣṇu, Jamadagni, and likewise Viśvāmitra;
as well as both great Nāgas of Kadrū’s lineage, Kambala and Aśvatara.
The Gandharvas Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Sūryavarcas— both of them—
as well as Tilottamā and Rambhā, who are renowned throughout all the worlds;
and Grāmaṇī, Senajit, and Satyajit of great ascetic merit.
The Rakṣasa Brahmopeta, Yajña, and likewise Yajña—
these dwell in the sun for the sake of performing penance.
Furthermore, I shall describe to you those other Mandeha lords of the Rākṣasas who have been appointed by all the gods, including ourselves, for the protection of the most secret deity of deities.
Rudra said:
"Speak, O Brahman, the divine narrative for which I have come to ask;
tell me that very thing in detail and quickly, O Lord."
"Having seen the Sun-god situated in heaven, by what rite should one bow to him? O Lord, what fruit is obtained for him when the ritual action is completed?
Brahmā said:
Listen, O Rudra, to the ritual of salutation to Bhāskara in brief;
by performing it, those afflicted by disease and suffering are liberated from their accumulation of sins.
Having prepared a mandala on a sacrificial mound measuring twelve finger-breadths in size,
Immediately after smearing that very spot with cow dung, one should invoke the Sun;
and having worshipped Gaṇeśa and the others, as well as Vāsudeva, Sātyaki,
Satyabhāmā, Lakṣmī, Umā, and Lord Śaṅkara.
Then, one who knows the Vedic mantras should circumambulate those previously mentioned persons standing near the maṇḍala; having done so, he should prostrate himself like a staff once,
or a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, or a hundred thousand times, according to the gravity of his own sins.
Having seen the Śakti and having prostrated before it with a mind ever restrained,
one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brahmin while remaining breath-controlled and composed—
whether it be two raktikās of gold, or a hundred, or even a thousand.
One should bestow four thousand and ten times ten thousand māṣakas;
it is declared that ten times that amount should be given to the right side for the sake of liberation from disease.
When this is done, O Virūpākṣa, one is liberated from all diseases.
Whatever man should hear this supreme secret,
his diseases are destroyed by the grace of Mārtaṇḍa.
Furthermore, O Lord of Umā, I shall declare to you that which has not been asked.
Listen to that which has been declared by me concerning the controller of the chariot-driver.
Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Sun," in the Saptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan, within the Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty thousand verses.
Now begins the fifty-third chapter.
Brahmā spoke in praise of the Sun:
"There, Aruṇa was previously appointed by me to the office of charioteer."
Indra appointed one named Māṭhara; Vāyu, Kalmāṣa;
and Vainateya Tārkṣya, who went before them with his claws and beak as weapons, was appointed as Vimala.
By Kāla, Daṇḍa was appointed, armed with the great staff; and by you, Śeṣa was made the lord of the great hosts.
By King Vaiśākha, Vasu and Bhidā were given the weapons of Aṅgārika; by Agni, Piṅgala; by you, Śeṣa became the great leader of the Gaṇas with the Mahādaṇḍa weapon;
by Yama, Hasta was given the noose; and by the Lord of Waters, Samindhana.
Viṣṇu was [conquered] by the Lord of Alakā;
Kāla and Upakāla, the foremost among the Vākṣas, by the two Aśvins;
and Kṣāra and Dhāra, as well as Dhiṣaṇa and Kṛṣṇa, by Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
The Viśvedevas granted the protection of the quarters and intermediate directions to Vairāja, Śaṅkhapāla, Parjanya, and Rajas.
These seven, the mothers of the world, gave all the Maruts.
Oṃkāra, Vaṣaṭkāra, the sound of the Vedas, Pinākin, Vināyaka, Śeṣa, Ananta, and Vāsuki follow the chariot of the Sun with a thousand serpents equal to themselves.

Both Gāyatrī and Sāvitrī are stationed upon the chariot; that deity who never departs from the solar disc is always present there to support the Blessed One of a thousand rays. This orb, indeed, belongs to all the deities; it is the sacrifice for the proclaimer of Brahman and for the one who proclaims the Brahma-sacrifice.

To the devotees of the Blessed One, he is Viṣṇu, the Supreme Āditya; to the devotees of Maheśvara, he is Śiva. O Bull-bannered Lord, these deities who preside over the various stations always nourish the Sun, the highest light among all lights.
The sages praised the Sun with their own composed words;
the Gandharvas and Apsarases worshipped him with songs and dances;
and by circling through the sky, they provided protection for the constellation of the Arrow (iṣugraha).
The serpents indeed carry the sun, and the Yātudhānas follow him;
the Vālakhilyas bow down to this sun as he rises from the mountain of sunrise.
Both Divaspati and Svabhū are the two leaders at the front of his journey across the yojana.
Bharga is on the right side, and the lotus-born Brahmā stands on the left;
all those planets worshipped in the worlds are to be known as being behind [the deity]. Both Upagraha and Śikhin are in front; of this there is no doubt.
O Kṛṣṇa, the human laws arise from the south and the north of the wise; likewise, these two are always at the forefront. Vītihotra is on the left, while Hari is always behind.
The chariot seat is to be known as the earth, and the space within it as the sky;
resting upon the splendor born of the chariot, the void stands as the abode of heaven.
The flagpole is to be understood as the banner-staff, and at the tip of the banner is the bull itself.
O beloved of Pārvatī, there were Ṛddhi, Vṛddhi, and Śrī as banners at the tip of the flagstaff;
upon that staff was Garuḍa, and ahead of him was the ocean.
Maināka was the handle of the parasol, while Himavat is said to be the parasol itself.
O Mahāmati, some others here in this world speak thus:
"The handle of the umbrella is likewise affliction; the wise know affliction to be the umbrella.
For these very gods, their ascetic power is exactly like their heroic vigor.
According to their fitness, so is their being; according to their being, so is their power.
Thus that perfected Sun blazes with his own splendor for them.
These [suns] scorch, rain down, move, and create the universe.
When recited, they dispel the inauspicious karma of living beings;
these, together with their followers, revolve in the sky along with the sun.
Indeed, O twice-born ones, they heat, they chant, and they bring delight.
Out of compassion for them, they indeed protect all beings here;
the Sun, having increased the gods with nectar through the Soma and the hymns, satisfies them with the bright,
full moon as the days progress, which the deities drink during the dark fortnight.
For when the moon in its dark fortnight has two digits remaining and is blazing with rays after having drunk the Soma,
the Pitṛs— the Ūrjas and the Saumyas, as well as the Kalpas— drink that nectar of immortality;
and it is again released by the sun through waters enriched by its rays.
Likewise, they constantly drink from medicinal herbs and overcome hunger with excessive drinking.
Satisfying them for half a month is considered [the merit of] these waters; for a month, the ancestors are satisfied by *svadhā*.
Through food, a mortal perpetually sustains himself, and by means of cattle, he supports this entire world.
Traversing day and night on his single-wheeled chariot,

together with seven horses that were the very Vedas (*chandas*) in the form of steeds, he circled the earth bounded by the seven continents and oceans, with those horses stationed wherever the wheel was located.
With horses that can assume any form at will, endowed with instantaneous speed, swift as thought,
imperishable, obedient, and free from hunger and fatigue,
they traverse one hundred and eighty-two mandalas in a single year.
The mandala, both external and internal, proceeds according to the sequence of days;
joined together at the beginning of the kalpa, they flow until the dissolution of all beings.
Enclosed by those Bālakhilyas, they revolve throughout those days.
Being praised by the great sages with their own composed words,
he is attended by Gandharvas and hosts of Apsarases with dance and song;
like the sun among birds, he dwells in the sky, causing it to revolve.
He travels along the foremost path like the moon among the stars.
When the sun is situated in the middle of Amarāvatī,
it is then seen rising in the Vaivasvata realm of Saṃyamana.
When the sun sets in Vaivasvata Saṃyamana at midnight, it rises in Sukhā and Vāruṇī when it is at the meridian. When it rises in Sukhā, it is seen in Vāruṇī.
When the sun sets in Amarāvatī, the city of the gods, it is midnight in the city of Yama;
when Aryaman is at the meridian in Vibhā, the city of Soma,
the sun rises in Amarāvatī, the city of Mahendra.
At midnight he sets in Saṃyamana, and at sunset in Vāruṇī;
thus, performing his circumambulation of Meru on its four sides,
he rises again and again at sunrise and sunset.

In the forenoon and in the afternoon, two celestial abodes each are heated; however, at midday, he alone heats [the world] with those very same rays. Having risen, the Sun heats [the world] with rays that increase until midday.
After that,
when the rays diminish and the sun goes to its setting, that place where the sun is seen rising is known as their sunrise; and where it goes to its disappearance is called their sunset.
Thus, when the sun then glides through the middle of Puṣkara,
it traverses a thirtieth part of the earth in a single muhūrta.
Listen now to my reckoning of the number of yojanas covered by him in that muhūrta.
O Three-eyed One, a full hundred-thousandth part of a thousand,
as well as fifty and some additional thousands—
this is prescribed as the speed of the sun during one muhūrta.
In the space of a mere blink of an eye, the sun traverses two thousand, two hundred, and two yojanas across the sky;
that Maker of Light moves so swiftly that he revolves like a whirling firebrand.
Wandering indeed among the wandering stars, he moves through them;
Indra worships the Sun as he rises day by day,
Yama at midday, and the Lord of Waters as he sets in the west.
Soma always worships Ravi at midnight;
Viṣṇu, you, I, and Rudra worship him at the end of the night.
Likewise do Agni, Nirṛti, Vāyu, and Īśāna.

"O tiger among gods, for the sake of their welfare, all the deities, beginning with Brahmā, worship the Sun as he revolves in due order. Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Sun's Motion," in the *Rathasaptamī-kalpa* of the *Brāhma-parvan*, within the *Śatārddhasāhasrī-saṃhitā* of the glorious *Mahābhārata*. (Note: The text identifies this as part of the *Bhaviṣya-mahāpurāṇa*, though it is traditionally known as the *Mārkaṇḍeya-purāṇa*).
Now begins the fifty-fourth chapter:
A Description of the Greatness of the Sun.
Rudra said:
"Aho! The greatness of the swan has been described by you in such a manner.
Let this greatness of the Sun (Bhāskara) be told once again.
Brahmā said:
The entire mantra of the Sun, the three worlds with all that is moving and unmoving,
and this whole universe— including gods, asuras, and humans— comes into being from it.
It is the source of Rudra, Indra, Upendra, and Candra, as well as of the lords of brahmins and the inhabitants of heaven.
The entire splendor belonging to all those of great luster throughout the world— this Sun is the soul of all, the lord of all worlds, the god of gods, the progenitor of creatures,
and the supreme deity who is the root of the three worlds.
An oblation properly cast into the fire reaches the sun;
from the sun rain is born, from rain comes food, and from that, living beings.
Everything is produced from the sun, and into it alone everything is dissolved.
Indeed, existence and non-existence for all people issued forth from the Sun in ancient times.
This is the meditation of those who meditate, and this is the liberation for those seeking liberation.
Here they go to nirvāṇa; from here, living beings are born again.
Moments, hours, days, nights, fortnights,
months, years, seasons, and even the ages (yugas)—
this enumeration of time does not exist at all without the Sun.
Without time, there would be no regulation, no fire, and no act of offering.
Since there would be no division of the seasons, whence could flowers, roots, and fruits come?
Whence could the production of grain be, and whence the multitude of grasses and medicinal herbs?
There would be an absence of all worldly activities for living beings, both in heaven and here on earth,
were it not for the Sun, who heats the world and draws up the waters.
The Sun does not scorch without rain, nor is he encompassed by rain.

The sun does not undergo transformation due to drought; rather, it blazes with water. In spring the sun is tawny, in summer it has the luster of gold, in the rainy season it is white in color, and in autumn the maker of light is pale.
In the winter the sun is copper-colored, and in the cool season it is red; thus the colors have been fully described. Listen, O Hara, to the results of these colors:
a black sun portends misfortune for both worlds, while a copper-colored one destroys the commander-in-chief.
A yellow halo portends the death of the king’s son, while a white one kills the domestic priest. Furthermore, a variegated or smoky halo causes great distress by agitating the sun's rays;
it brings about the falling of thieves' weapons unless water is quickly poured [as a rite].

Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Sun," in the Rathasaptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan, within the Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty thousand verses.
Now begins the fifty-fifth chapter: "Description of the Procession of the Sun’s Chariot."
Rudra said:
How should the chariot procession of the Sun be performed here by men in this world,
and what fruit shall accrue to those who undertake the pilgrimage of Ravi?

O Supreme among Gods, by what rite should it be performed and at what time? And how, O Lord, should one cause the Sun-god mounted upon his chariot to circumambulate? For those who, out of devotion, cause the chariot of the God to circumambulate or carry it— [The answer follows: By the rite prescribed in the *Saura Purāṇa*, O best of gods, this festival should be performed on the seventh lunar day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa. One should cause the Lord, the Sun, mounted upon his chariot, to circumambulate the city clockwise. Those who, with devotion, cause the chariot of the God to circumambulate or carry it, attain the world of the Sun and are never again born in this mortal realm. They shall dwell for ten thousand kalpas in the abode of the Sun, enjoying every celestial pleasure. After that, they shall become sovereign kings on earth, possessing great power and long life. Therefore, O King, you should perform this rite with all your heart, for it is a source of supreme merit and destroys all sins. Thus ends the description of the Rathayātrā festival.
And what fruit is proclaimed for those men who act as dancers,
who wander about devoted to dance and song,
and who keep a vigil with devotion and endowed with faith?
And what fruit is declared for those who offer a chariot to the Sun,
and those who devotedly present offerings, food, and meals for the snakes?
O Foremost of the Gods, tell me all of this in full detail.
"O God, for the welfare of the worlds, my curiosity is indeed great.
Brahmā said:
"Well asked by me, O Lord of Beings; you are Gaṇeśa, O Three-eyed One."

Listen with a focused mind as I speak at length according to your question. O Rudra, I have thus described to you both this chariot procession of the high-souled god Bhāskara and likewise the festival of Indra.
O one worshipped by the worlds, in whatever land these two great festivals of the gods are celebrated for the sake of peace among the people in the world of mortals,
there are no calamities arising from kings or thieves.
Therefore, O Hara, for the sake of pacifying this famine, these two rites must be performed with devotion here. On the seventh day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada,
one should indeed anoint the Lord with clarified butter produced from five purified limbs.
He who, endowed with faith, daily anoints Maheśa— the Lord of the World— who has entered into the pigment along with the sun,
shall go mounted upon a vehicle made of red chalk and adorned with tinkling bells.

Whoever offers daily to the Sun-god Vaiśvānara divine Vaiśvānara-city, adorned with Gandharvas and Apsarases, along with rice-porridge mixed with sugar-candy, a thunderbolt accompanied by a diamond, and portions of various colors;
Having ascended that auspicious celestial chariot, which is filled with garlands of flames,
O God, he shall go to my city while being praised by the great sages.
Therefore, O Śiva, a man should [worship] the Sun with every effort.
Colorful food should be offered; for one who has entered here, the following should be provided:
cakes filled with ghee, sweets wrapped in sugar-candy, *kāsāra*, *modaka* sweets, milk, rice with curd, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), *saṃyāva* cakes, and sweetmeat buns.
Those men who offer cosmetic ointment here to the god Bhāskara go to my abode; of this there is no doubt.
He who offers it to Bhāskara with devotion day after day—
Ghee should be given for the purpose of anointing; he goes to the supreme goal.
Likewise, he who daily and with devotion gives food according to [the recipient's] caste, having obtained auspicious desires in this world, shall go to the abode of Bhava.
He who offers auspicious powder for the ritual anointing of the Sun here goes to the supreme abode where the divine Maker of Day resides.
Then, in the month of Pauṣa, one should bathe that deity according to the prescribed rite.
Listen with a one-pointed mind to [the rites for] the seventh day of the bright fortnight:
having brought water from a sacred ford (tīrtha) or other auspicious water,
the wise man should install the image according to the procedure prescribed in the Vedas.
For the wise man should perform sacrifice while mentally recollecting the names of sacred fords (tīrthas):
Prayāga, Puṣkara, Deva, Kurukṣetra, Naimiṣa,
Pṛthūdaka, Candrabhāgā, Śaura, and Gokarṇa.
Brahmāvarta, Kuśāvarta, Bilvaka, and the Nīla mountain;
likewise the meritorious Gaṅgādvāra and the confluence of the Gaṅgā with the ocean; Kālapriya, Mitravana, and Śuṇḍīrasvāmin.
Likewise, the meritorious Cakratīrtha and the auspicious Rāmatīrtha; the Vitastā, Harṣapaṃthā, and the Devikā is remembered as such;
as well as the Gaṅgā, Sarasvatī, Sindhu, Candrabhāgā, and the Narmadā.
The Vipāśā, Yamunā, Tāpī, Śivā, Vetravatī,
as well as the Godāvarī, Payoṣṇī, Kṛṣṇā, and Veṇyā rivers;
the Śatarudrā, Puṣkariṇī, Kauśikī, and Sarayū likewise.
Likewise, let the other oceans indeed provide their presence;
as well as the most meritorious hermitages and divine sanctuaries.
Having thus performed the ritual of bathing, and having worshipped and prostrated, [one should proceed].
Having offered incense and the arghya water, one should perform the consecration (adhivāsa) of the image for three nights,
seven nights, a month, or even half a month; meanwhile,
the person should worship with devotion the Lord who remains in the bathing chamber.

O Destroyer of Tripura, on the seventh day of the dark fortnight of Māgha, one should smear a square altar made of auspicious materials at the crossroads, adorned with white jars in the four directions and graced by an excellent canopy.
Having performed the fire-ritual according to the rules and having provided a meal for the Brahmins,
[he should proceed] with the sounding of conchs and kettledrums, with abundant Vedic chants,
and with various proclamations of "Auspicious Day," after having caused the Brahmins to pronounce blessings.
Then, with supreme devotion, the Sun-god, the Supreme Self,
should cause the deity to be circumambulated on a beautiful chariot adorned with garlands of tinkling bells,
preceded by a great festival.
In the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, one should have the Sun mounted upon a chariot,
having performed the fire-oblation according to the rules as well as the feeding of Brahmins,
and having gratified all the people with sacrificial fees, food, and other gifts.
Having worshipped the divine Brahmins as well as those on earth who are excellent reciters—
specifically the best of Brahmins who serve as reciters through the Itihāsas and Purāṇas—
the deity and the chosen priest (iṣṭa) should then be worshipped with great effort.
On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, one should observe a single meal;
on the fourth, an unasked meal (ayācita); and on the sixth, a night-meal (nakta) is prescribed.
On the seventh day, however, one should fast and cause the chariot to be brought from the hermitage.
O Śiva, lord of beings, having performed the fire-ritual (agnikārya) in front of the chariot on the sixth night, one should perform the consecration (adhivāsana) of the chariot here,
after feeding the Brahmins, both celestial and terrestrial, as well as the reciters.
On the seventh lunar day of the bright fortnight in the month of Māgha, one should place the Lord, the creator of all beings, upon a chariot in front of His temple;
while the Lord remains there, one should perform a night vigil.
One should devoutly perform a night vigil before the deity, adorned with various spectacles and lamp-trees, accompanied by the sounds of conchs and trumpets, and the abundant chanting of the Vedas.
Then, on the eighth day, one should diligently lead the deity mounted upon his chariot to the northern gate of the city, which resounds with the blare of conchs and kettledrums; thereafter,
likewise to the eastern and southern gates, and finally to the other [western] gate.
When this pilgrimage is performed in this manner for the duration of a year,
human beings prosper in happiness, the king conquers his enemies,
all people become free from disease, and likewise, there shall be peace for the cattle.
Indeed, even the makers of the journey attain a share of heaven;
and likewise, O child, the bearers surely worship the world of the Sun.
Rudra said:
"O Brahman, how can that intuitive insight (pratibhā) which has been established once be moved?
Tell me this, O Lord of Gods, for my doubt is indeed very great.
Brahmā said:
Long ago, for the sake of the high-souled Thousand-rayed One,
I fashioned his chariot according to the divisions of the year; indeed,
that chariot is remembered as the foremost of all chariots.
Having seen that, O son, other chariots were then fashioned by Viśvakarman for all the gods, beginning with Soma, in great numbers;
and having obtained the chariot made by Viśvakarman, the god [set forth].
O upholder of a noble lineage, that which was given to Manu for the sake of his own worship—
Manu having given it to Ikṣvāku— it was said, "Let the Sun be worshipped by mortals.
Therefore, the movement of the Sun by means of a chariot-vehicle was ordained.

Therefore, there is no fault in its movement; rather, it is the Sun himself who moves, since Bhāskara traverses this earth by means of his chariot. Thus, as he goes, this orb of the Sun is not perceived [as stationary].
O beloved of Pārvatī, because that which is unseen moves,
it is for this reason that the movement of the Sun is observed by the wise during chariot processions;
however, O beloved of Pārvatī, the movement of other deities is not desired.
Since the images of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others have been installed according to the prescribed rites,
the procession of the Lord by chariot must therefore be performed according to the rules every year for the sake of the peace of the subjects here.
Whether made of gold, silver, or even of solid wood,
a chariot should be constructed with strong axles, yokes, and wheels, and well-equipped with a mechanism.
Upon that most excellent, noble, and beautifully fashioned chariot—
Having carefully mounted the image,
one should yoke auspicious horses that possess the characteristics of Hari, with beautiful faces,
well-behaved, anointed with saffron, and adorned with chowries and garlands.
Having yoked excellent horses to the chariot and offered the *arghya* water,
and having honored the gods with incense, garlands, and ointments,
he also fed the best of the twice-born with various kinds of food.
Having satisfied all those who are distressed, blind, or miserable according to his ability,
he should not turn anyone away— whether they be superior, inferior, or middling.
Thus have the wise declared regarding the performance of the Sūrya sacrifice when it is fully extended.
He who, with his hopes shattered and tormented by hunger and wind, thinks [of food],
causes even his ancestors residing in heaven to fall, for he has failed to give.
A sacrifice devoid of sacrificial fees is not praised by the Sun-god.
Therefore, having honored all these people with various kinds of desires, including foods to be chewed and licked, one should recite this mantra:
"May the gods, the Ādityas, and likewise the Vasus, accept my offering."

May the great sages of the celestial realms grant welfare to the world!
May there be no obstacle for me, may there be no sin for me, and may there be no adversaries for me.
May the gods and the hosts of spirits likewise be gracious, satisfied, and well-disposed.

One should recite the Vāmadevya hymns, the purificatory (pavitra) verses, the Mānastoka, the Rathantara, and the single verse beginning with "ākṛṣṇena rajasā. Then, with the proclamation of a "holy day" (puṇyāha) and the sounding of musical instruments, [the rite is concluded].
One should prepare a chariot-track with a perfectly level path;
it should be drawn by men endowed with devotion to the Sun,
or else by well-trained, tamed oxen with well-fashioned reins.
Just as there would be fatigue for one traveling on a rugged path,
so it is for Brahmins who observe fasts— whether celestial or terrestrial— and who are firm in their vows,
when they [construct] an image of the Sun-god with thirty or sixteen [components].

O Rudra, having moved it from its place, one should indeed slowly mount the chariot. O Rudra, the two wives of that high-souled one— Rājñī and Nikṣubhā— one should slowly mount them on both sides of the chariot.
Nikṣubhā is on the right side and Rājñī likewise on the left;
on both sides of that [chariot] are two Brahmins, one divine and one earthly.
Furthermore, the earthly Brahmakalpa is situated above the pole (kūbara).
One should depict Garuḍa leaping behind him,
as well as a white parasol with an incomparable golden handle,
variegated with golden spots and radiant with jewels and pearls.
Then, he who destroys all desires should fashion for him a flawless banner with a golden staff, resembling a rainbow and adorned with seven pennants of various colors belonging to the Lord of Beings.
The sky above the banner should be presided over by Aruṇa;
one should lead the excellent chariot of the Sun, with the Brahmins seated upon the front of the chariot.
Rudra should indeed perform the role of charioteer for his own perpetual welfare.

One who desires his own welfare should not mount the chariot without faith; for him who mounts the chariot without faith, his progeny goes to destruction. That chariot of the God of gods must always be borne by Brahmins.
It may indeed be carried by Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, but never by Śūdras;
nor by those who are devotees of other deities, nor by those who promote the use of intoxicants— it must not be borne by these Śūdras, but is always borne by others.

O Rudra, beloved of Pārvatī, you who are dear to those observing the vow of fasting must be carried; having departed from your own place, you should proceed to the eastern gate. There you shall dwell for one day, being honored indeed by the king.
With various spectacles, by listening to the Purāṇas,
with diverse Vedic recitations, and with the satiation of Brāhmaṇas,
one should remain there until the end of the eighth day; on the ninth day, one sets out again.
O Three-eyed One, O Destroyer of Andhaka, proceed to the southern gate of the city;
stay there for one day,
being honored by them just as you were by the king and the other monarchs.
Therefore, O auspicious one, he should move from there to the western gate, and from there further north.
There too, O Priyadarśana, he is to be worshipped by the Śūdras according to the prescribed rites. And from there, O Rudra, he should proceed to the center of the city.
There, the Brahmins, filled with faith, worshipped him who was stationed there,
with the sounding of conchs and musical instruments, with excellent spectacles,
with various Vedic chants, and with auspicious lamps on all sides.
O Destroyer of Tripura, having satisfied the Brahmins with various kinds of gifts of wealth and offerings, and having gratified the poor, the blind, and the wretched,
he should depart from the center of the city and remain upon reaching his own palace.
Having arrived in this manner, the Lord stands before the temple;
stationed there, he is to be worshipped by all the citizens in their entirety.
Being thus honored day and night, he remains mounted upon his chariot.
On the following day,
O Trilocana, one should proceed with reverence to that ancient site on the fourteenth day after the thirteenth has passed.
In this manner, one should always cause the Lord, the Master of Planets who removes all evils, to be circumambulated.
"O Rudra, [worship] the Supreme Lord together with his retinue and his followers.

Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Chariot Procession," in the Rathasaptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan, within the Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty thousand verses.
Now begins the fifty-sixth chapter.
Description of the Procession of Sūryaratha.
Śrī Rudra said:
O Brahman, how should one cause that Sun, who bestows immortality, to move while stationed upon his chariot?
And how do his followers come to be, and who are those followers in their proper order?
O Best of Gods, for my own welfare, tell me all this in detail again and again; O Lord of the World, for my curiosity is great.
Brahmā said:
"O Rudra, you should lead the chariot slowly along a perfectly level path,
so that there may be no jolting as it travels upon uneven ground."
First, one should lead the chariot of the doorkeeper for the purification of the path;
immediately after that, O Rudra, one should respectfully lead the staff-bearer (Daṇḍanāyaka);
and thereafter, one should respectfully lead Piṅgala following behind him.
Since the two gatekeepers were mounted upon chariots behind him,
and likewise Diṇḍi was mounted upon a chariot standing before the Lord,
for that reason also, O Rudra, the scribe who is dear to Bhāskara [was likewise placed].
"O Rudra, O Three-eyed One, you must lead the chariot of the God very slowly and with great care, so that there may be no breaking of the yoke, the axle, or the wheels.
If the pole breaks, there is danger to the Brahmins; if the axle breaks, there is the destruction of the Kshatriyas."
If the balance-beam breaks, there will be the destruction of Vaiśyas and the loss of beds for Śūdras;
if the yoke breaks, there will be drought; if the pedestal breaks, there is danger to the subjects;
and if the wheel of the chariot breaks, one should know that an enemy army is approaching.
One should predict the defeat of the king even upon the falling of the banner;
however, when the image is mutilated, one should foretell the death of the king. O Rudra, from the breaking of the parasol, one should predict danger for the crown prince.
When such portents and inauspicious omens have arisen,
one should again perform the bali-offering and likewise the śānti-homa;
one should further cause the Brāhmaṇas to recite blessings and indeed bestow gifts.
In the north-eastern quarter of the chariot, one should prepare the fire;
one should offer oblations to Jātavedas with fuel-sticks smeared with clarified butter,
correctly pronouncing the word "svāhā" for the deities in their proper order.
One should offer oblations, addressing them by name, to the planets and to the progeny;
first, indeed, an oblation to Agni, Svāhā, and then to Soma, Svāhā,
and to Prajāpati, Svāhā— the offerings should be given in this sequence.
May there be well-being here for the Brahmins, and likewise well-being for the king;
may there be well-being for the cows and for the subjects, and may there indeed be peace for the world. May there always be auspiciousness for us bipeds, and may there be peace for our quadrupeds.
May there be well-being for all creatures, and likewise may there be well-being always within the self.
O Lord of Gods, may there be peace for Bhūḥ, and likewise peace for Bhuvaḥ;
may there be peace for Svaḥ as well, and may there be peace everywhere from the Sun.
O Lord, you alone are indeed the creator and the sustainer of the world;
O protector of subjects, lord of the planets, lord of heaven, grant us peace!
And I shall say this other thing, which is the supreme cause of peace.
Having ascertained that the planets are unfavorable for the person whose birth caused the undertaking of the journey, one should perform the pacification of the planets (grahaśānti). Furthermore,
the sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh) should be made according to the prescribed measurement, measuring one span (prādeśa) in length.
The sticks for the Sun should be made of Arka wood; those for the Moon are prescribed as being of Palāśa wood; those for Mars should be of Khadira wood; those for Mercury of Āpāmārga wood;
then those for Jupiter of Aśvattha wood, and for Venus of Udumbara wood.
For Saturn, [the offering] should be made of śamī wood, and for Rāhu, of dūrvā grass; for Ketu, however, kuśa grass should be used. Now hear also regarding the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās):
one should give a beautiful cow to the Sun, and a conch shell to the Moon.
A red bull should be given to Bhauma; gold to the son of Soma;
two garments should be given to Jīva; take a white horse for Śukra;
a dark-blue cow for Śanaiścara; and a vessel of milk-porridge for Rāhu.
One should give a goat to Ketu; hear also their respective foods:
rice with jaggery for Sūrya, milk-porridge with ghee for Soma, sacrificial food (haviṣya) for Bhauma, and rice with milk for Budha.
One should offer curd-rice to Jupiter, and ghee-food to Venus;
one should cause sesame-flour and black gram to be given to Saturn;
one should cause meat to be given to Rāhu, and variegated rice to Ketu.
Sauvīra, māranāla, steamed seeds, and kāñjika—
just as armor is known to be the warder-off of arrow-wounds,
so too does propitiatory rite (śānti) become the warder-off of calamities sent by fate.
For one who is non-violent, self-controlled, who has acquired wealth through righteous means,
and who is constantly established in his observances, the planets are always gracious. O Rudra, those who desire extensive fame should always worship the planets.
One who desires prosperity, or one who desires peace, should perform the sacrifice to the planets;

likewise, one who desires rain, long life, or nourishment, or even one performing malevolent magic (abhicāra). Furthermore, a woman who is childless, or one whose offspring are difficult to sustain, [should do so].
For those whose children die in infancy, for women who give birth only to daughters,
for kings fallen from their kingdom, and for those afflicted by chronic disease—
the wise have prescribed the *grahayajña* (sacrifice to the planets) for such men.
Therefore, O Hara, one who knows what is beneficial should always perform this rite for the sake of prosperity:
Dattapuṣpa, Krūradṛk, Puṣpaja, and likewise Dhiṣaṇa; as well as Sitāsita, Rudra, Uparāga, and Śikhin.
O mighty-armed one, these planets are always worshipped by the learned. The planetary images should be diligently fashioned from copper, crystal, red sandalwood, gold, silver, iron, or lead.

O Maheśvara, [the deity] should be depicted either on gold or on cloth according to the scriptures. Garments, flowers, and perfumes should be offered according to their respective colors, as well as oblations and incense made of guggulu resin.

Sacrificial oblations accompanied by mantras should be prepared for each respective deity. These verses are proclaimed in their proper sequence: "ākṛṣṇena," "imaṃ devāḥ," "agnirmūrdhā divaḥ kakut," and "udbudhyasva."
"Bṛhaspate atiyat aryaḥ," "tathaivānnāt parisrutaḥ," "śaṃ no devī," "tathā kāṇḍāt," and "ketuṃ kṛṇvan"
— these previously mentioned verses are to be used in sequence for the fuel-sticks (samidh) here; one should offer them into the fire according to the scriptures.
For each [deity], one hundred and eight or indeed twenty-eight oblations should be offered, combined with honey, clarified butter, and curd. Furthermore,
one should present to the Brahmins the aforementioned meal.
Or, according to one's ability and as things are obtained, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given according to the prescribed rule.
Whoever is in distress at any time should honor that person with effort;
for this boon has been granted by me: "When you have been honored, you shall in turn honor others."
The rise and fall of kings, as well as the existence and non-existence of the world, are dependent upon the planets; therefore, the planets are most worthy of worship.
So too are the planets, cows, kings, teachers, and Brahmins.
When honored, they honor [one] in return; when insulted, they consume one with fire.
Just as a machine that has been activated is struck down by another machine, so too should one pacify affliction once it has arisen through the propitiation of the planets.
For those who perform sacrifices, who speak the truth, who observe constant fasts,
and who are devoted to recitation and fire-offerings, all that is evil is pacified.
Having thus brought peace to the subjects and having performed the rite for auspiciousness, [he should proceed].
O Hara, having again made the chariot ready, one should perform the procession;
having led the Sun along the remaining path, one should lead him to the temple.
Then, after worshipping the deities of the chariot who were previously mentioned, one should proceed.
"O Three-eyed One, just as all the planets are to be worshipped during portents,
so too must the deities of the chariot be worshipped who reside supported upon the chariot.

Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Sun," in the *Saptamī-kalpa* of the *Brāhma-parvan*, within the *Brahmā-saṃhitā* of one hundred thousand verses, in the glorious *Mahāpurāṇa Bhaviṣya*.
Now begins the fifty-seventh chapter,
the Description of the Chariot Procession.
Brahmā said:

Milk and barley gruel should be offered to Brahmā; O Three-eyed One, fine rice (paramānna) should be given to Kārttikeya for the pleasure of the Lord of Beings (Bhūteśa). O observer of noble vows, one should likewise offer honey, meat, and wine to Vivasvat.
One should offer edible foods to Puruhūta along with his followers.
The oblation for Agni should be cooked grain, and likewise, the first portion of food should be for Viṣṇu.
O Hara, one should give maireya wine and meat-rice to the Rākṣasas.
O Destroyer of Tripura, one should offer refined food and meat to Revatī;
one should give sesame-rice to the King of the Ancestors (Yama);
cakes to the two Aśvins; and meat with boiled rice to the Vasus.
One should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) mixed with ghee and honey to the ancestors;
likewise, one should give gruel (yavāgū) to Kātyāyanī, curd to Śrī,
the "three sweets" (trimadhura) to Sarasvatī, and rice cooked with sugarcane juice to Varuṇa.
Thus, one should offer the food of the Khāṇḍava forest to Dhanapati (Kubera) and likewise to Trilocana (Śiva).
It is prescribed that the Maruts be gratified with affectionate buttermilk;
and one should indeed present meat, cooked rice, and soups to the Mātṛs.
O Destroyer of Tripura, offer water to the spirits (bhūtas) and to the Sun; O Lord of the Gaṇas, one should give sweetmeats (modakas) to the Lord of the Gaṇas;
and O Leader of the Gaṇas, fried cakes (śaṣkulis) should be given to Nairṛta.
All kinds of edible foods should be offered everywhere to the Viśvedevas;
rice cooked with milk should be given to the Ṛṣis, and milk indeed to the Nāgas.
One should present an offering to the chariot of the Sun and perform the Sārvabhautika rite.
O Bhārata, one should give unguents, wine, and meat to those who carry it;
likewise, one should give clarified butter to Brahmā and sesame seeds to Tryambaka.
O Destroyer of Tripura, parched grain (lājā) should indeed be given to the Son of Svāhā.
O Three-eyed One, one should always offer the *kovidāra* tree to Bhāskara;
likewise, the *rājavṛkṣa* to Indra, and sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) to Pāvaka;
seven kinds of grain to the Wielder of the Discus (Viṣṇu), and fish-rice to Garuḍa.
One should offer various foods to the Yakṣas and resin to Revatī.
O Rudra, garlands of *vaikaṅkata* wood are prescribed for Yama.
And, O Bull-bannered One, the *karṇikāra* flower should be given to the two Aśvins.
Lotuses should be given to Śrī, and excellent sandalwood to Caṇḍikā;
fresh butter to Sarasvatī, and likewise meat to Vinatā;
flowers to the Apsarases, O Rudra, and the Mālatī flower is prescribed for her.
O Destroyer of Tripura, one should give a fire-drill to Varuṇa, fruit and root to Nirṛti, a bilva fruit to Kubera, and likewise a kapittha fruit to the Maruts;
and one should give an āragvadha tree to the Gandharvas.
One should give camphor to the Vasus, wood to the Lord of the Gaṇas;
one should offer rice-balls and roots to the ancestors, and the Bibhītaka fruit to the spirits; one should indeed give barley to the cows, O Hara, and unbroken grains (akṣata) to the Mothers.
Guggulu should be offered to Vighnapati; boiled rice is to be given to the Viśvedevas;
the Brahma-tree to the Ṛṣis; and the finest poison to the Nāgas.
O Lord of Gaṇas, all these things are to be offered here to Bhāskara.
O Three-eyed One, O Hara, one should likewise offer honey, clarified butter, and red ochre;
or, O Rudra, with devotion, one should present the fruit of the Nyagrodha tree to his mounts at dawn,
at dusk, and at midday, always with a one-pointed mind.
The wise one should burn incense for all [the deities] according to their capacity and with devotion, O tiger among gods, using the specific mantra prescribed here for each. Furthermore,
for the sake of pacification, the wise one should give sesame seeds to the Brahmins.
Or rather, O Hara, offer them together with clarified butter into the Vaiśvānara fire;
for these are indeed the nectar of the gods and the immortal *svadhā* of the ancestors,
and the wise always know them to be the refuge of the Brahmins.
"O Hara, these are indeed the sons of Kaśyapa and are likewise purifying;
they are supreme for bathing, giving, burnt offerings, libations, and eating.
Having thus worshipped the gods and the planets with great effort,"
Having brought him down from the chariot, one should place him again within the mandala;
having diligently performed the ārārtika with lamps, water, barley, and unbroken rice,
as well as with cotton seeds, salt, and husks, for the pacification of defective vision.
O observer of noble vows, he should thereafter cause [the deity] to ascend the altar together with his two wives;
O Hara, he should worship the Lord while He remains there for ten days.
This worship, O Hara, is renowned on earth as the "Ten-Day" (daśāhikā) rite.
With that [mixture], O Hara, one should worship the God on the fourth day;
indeed, on the fourth day, the ceremonial bathing of the Sun must be performed with effort,
accompanied by massages, food offerings, and circles of worshipful honors.
Having worshipped the Sun-god for ten days according to this procedure,
one should then lead him to that supreme abode which was previously established as his own sanctuary.

Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Sun," in the Rathasaptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan, within the Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty thousand verses.
Now begins the fifty-eighth chapter,
the Description of the Chariot Procession.
Brahmā said:
Whoever, according to this rite,
should perform or cause to be performed a pilgrimage to the Blessed Sun of immeasurable splendor with devotion,
shall be honored in the world of the Sun for a period of a hundred million years.
He who offers clarified butter for anointing to the Sun, having applied the sectarian mark with sesame seeds, shall not be born poor or even diseased in his family;
he shall go to the city of Surabhi.
O Three-eyed One, whoever brings with devotion water from sacred fords as well as water from the Gaṅgā for the purpose of bathing the Sun-god,
and whoever offers the three castes with devotion to the Sun-god, O Three-eyed One—
Having fulfilled all desires here, he shall attain the abode of Varuṇa.
O Rudra, he who gives a red-colored vessel containing sacrificial food and rice cooked with jaggery shall go, radiant, to the excellent city of the world of the Sun.
O Rudra, one should go to that best of cities where the god Prajāpati resides;
whoever bathes there with devotion and likewise worships the Sun,
he, O radiant Rudra, shall go to the world of the Sun— of this there is no doubt.
He who places a chariot [on the track] and cleanses the path for the chariot goes to the world of Vāta, possessing prowess equal to the wind;
he who creates a beautiful circle on the path as the chariot passes.

He shall attain the meritorious world of Māruta; of this there is no doubt. He who would prepare a well-rounded path for the moving sun—he who prepares that path with devotion—shall attain a meritorious world.
Richly adorned with heaps of flowers, decorated with auspicious archways,
filled with the sounds of conchs and trumpets, and accompanied by performances,
he goes to that supreme abode where the god Vibhāvasu dwells.

He who, together with the Lord, performs a great festival with devotion— dancing, singing, and likewise worshipping— he goes to the supreme state. He who keeps a vigil while the Sun has mounted his chariot for the deity [attains the same].
That meritorious man, being happy, rejoices eternally for everlasting years;
the person who gives everything, including servants and slaves,
to the Sun, having attained all desires here in this world, shall reach the realm of the Sun.
O tiger among gods, it is difficult to obtain a sight of the sun as it revolves mounted upon its chariot,
especially when one is walking ahead of it as it moves toward the north or likewise toward the south.
The fortunate person beholds the Lord of Gods, Bhāskara, who is affectionate toward his devotees;
provided that when the year has arrived, on the day of the Sun's festival,
the procession of the chariot has not been obstructed in any way.
Therefore, one who desires prosperity must perform [the rite] in the twelfth year;
likewise for the raising of Indra’s banner, if it has not been performed.
Thus, it must indeed be done in the twelfth year, and not again in the interval.
O Bull-bannered One, those who cause the obstruction of the procession should be known as the Rākṣasas named Mandehas; of this there is no doubt.
Likewise, those men who perform the procession for Dharmadhvaja [are likewise blessed].

Indra and the other gods are to be known as having attained the supreme state. Now I shall describe to you briefly this procedure for the return journey, by hearing which one is liberated from all sins; there is no doubt in this matter.
When the month of Māgha has arrived, while the chariot is occupied by the hosts of gods,
he should be mentally established upon that very chariot;
just as the heaven and earth, existing as a dual form, were previously established.
In the same way, the queen Dyau (Sky) is to be known, and Nikṣubhā is remembered as the Earth (Pṛthivī).
Just as it was for the Sun, so too for these two goddesses, and likewise for Diṇḍin,
Piṅgala, and the others, the broad arrangement of the chariot must be constructed.
One should mentally contemplate another deity in their respective places;
indeed, one should mentally visualize the guardians of the directions and the guardians of the worlds.
For this deity is composed of the Vedas and likewise consists of all the gods.
The Maṇḍala is said to consist of the Ṛgveda, and the Vedic meters are proclaimed to be its mouth:
Gāyatrī, Triṣṭubh, Jagatī,
Anuṣṭubh, Paṅkti, Bṛhatī, and Uṣṇih as the seventh.
Because he consists of the gods and because of the arrangement of the meters,
and because he consists of the Vedas, Taraṇi is honored by the world.
Because he sets the chariot in motion, Sūrya must be borne by those who discourse on Brahman.
O Three-eyed One, a Śūdra should not mount the chariot of the Sun-god, even if he is devoted to fasting and has mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences;
for by mounting the vehicle of the Sun, a Śūdra would surely go to a downward state.
O Rudra, by performing what has been prescribed, peace shall always prevail for men.
Moreover, the Sun, the leader of all the gods,
should be installed within the chariots and in the temples of the deities.
Then, one should first worship the Sun with offerings of incense;
one should also worship the deities of the directions and their attendants, for thus one is honored by Prosperity. But he who worships others without first worshipping the Sun [is not so honored].
The deities do not accept the water for washing the feet (pādya) offered by various beings;
however, when the time for the journey has arrived, those men who behold the consecrated body of the Sun with devotion shall become free from sin.
Beholding [the deity] on the full moon day and the new moon day is remembered as bestowing merit;
likewise on the seventh and sixth lunar days, and on the day of that Sun.
The lunar days of Āṣāḍhī, Kārttikī, and Māghī are remembered as most meritorious.

The great fortune and merit of this lunar day are sung of in the scriptures; indeed, the Kārttikī is especially distinguished as the "Great Kārttikī. Thus, through the conjunction of time, the period for the pilgrimage is rendered preeminent.
Beholding [the deity] is of great merit and shall remove all sins;
he who, intent on fasting and restrained in his vows at that time,
worships the Sun with devotion, shall go to the supreme goal.
This divine Lord of Sacrifice, desiring to bestow grace upon the worlds,
has assumed the form of an image and accepts worship out of his benevolence;
[he does so] through bathing, giving, recitation, burnt offerings, ritual union, and the performance of divine rites.
By the shaving of the *kūrca* hair, a man becomes initiated (*dīkṣita*).
Men who are devotees of the Sun should always have their hair (*kaca*) shaved;
thus, being pure during the solar sacrifice, the man becomes initiated.

For all four castes, those who here shall always act thus with devotion toward the Sun— those high-souled men, being perpetually initiated and having fulfilled their vows, shall go to the supreme goal.
Thus, O Rudra, this chariot procession of the Lord of Heaven has been described;
by hearing or reciting it, one is liberated from all diseases. And having performed it with devotion according to the prescribed rules, a person goes to the abode of the Sun.
O Rudra, the auspicious seventh [tithi] known as Rathasaptamī has been described by me in brief.
Listen further, O Rudra, as I speak of the Saptamī.

Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Chariot Procession," in the Saptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan, within the Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty thousand verses.
Now begins the fifty-ninth chapter,
the Description of the Greatness of Rathasaptamī.
Brahmā said:
O God, likewise in the month of Māgha, during the bright fortnight, one who has conquered his senses,
having fasted on the sixth day and worshipped the Maker of Day with offerings of perfumes and flowers, should sleep at night in front of Him.
Then, having awakened on the seventh day, one should worship the Sun with devotion;
afterwards, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas, avoiding any stinginess regarding wealth,
[offering] sugar-candy sweets, modakas, and likewise cakes made of sugarcane and molasses.

Then, when a year has been completed, on the seventh day, O Hara, the wise one should perform the festival procession of the God of gods according to the previously mentioned ritual. Having performed this during the dark fortnight, he should mount the Sun upon his chariot.
He who beholds the Lord of the World with devotion attains the supreme goal.
On the third day, one meal is prescribed; on the fourth, eating only at night is declared;
on the fifth, it should be food obtained unasked; and on the sixth, likewise, a fast is observed.
On the seventh day, one should break the fast after beholding the God seated upon His chariot;
having worshipped Him according to the prescribed rite with devotion and according to one's means, O Three-eyed Lord,
one should fashion a golden chariot resting upon a copper vessel.
O Hara, one should place the honored void (ākāśa) in the center of the chariot;
one should place a ruby in the middle, a pearl to the east,
an sapphire to the south, and an emerald to the west, O Hara.
O Rudra, the wise one should place coral in the north along with the vajra;
and O Destroyer of Andhaka, white, yellow, black, and red—
these, my dear, are the cloths he should place in all the directions.
O Rudra, having adorned the chariot on all sides with banners in the shape of flags and decorated with bells and ornaments, and having embellished it with flowers and garlands,
one should worship it according to the prescribed rule and offer it to Bhāskara.
Or, having fed the Brahmins, one should present it to the teacher;
he who studies the Saptamī-kalpa along with its narratives, O Bhārata,
is to be known as a twice-born teacher for all the social orders in their proper sequence.
O beloved of Pārvatī, for those who follow Sūrya, Viṣṇu, or Śiva,
one should prescribe a silver chariot in the absence of gold;
and in the absence of that, one should have a copper chariot and a celestial canopy made.

O Mahādeva, even in the absence of copper, a chariot made of flour is prescribed; it should be accompanied by gold and placed upon a copper vessel. One should present this, together with a pair of silk garments, to a Brāhmaṇa.

O Mahādeva, O Virūpākṣa, one should offer to that high-souled reciter previously mentioned an image endowed with the five jewels and perfumed with auspicious fragrances; one should act according to one's own capacity and avoid any stinginess regarding wealth.

O Hara, O Rudra, this meritorious and sin-destroying seventh day known as Rathasaptamī has been described by me to you; it is celebrated as a great festival. O Hara, bathing, giving gifts, fire-offerings, and the worship of the Lord of Planets [should be performed].
A hundred thousand [merits] of this earth-bearing [rite] are obtained by her;
thus is this most meritorious seventh day (Saptamī) declared for the month of Māgha,
by fasting upon which with devotion a man becomes an attendant of the Sun.
A Brāhmaṇa attains the status of a deity, and a Kṣatriya may attain the state of a Brāhmaṇa;
a Vaiśya attains the status of a Kṣatriya, and a Śūdra attains the status of a Vaiśya. A maiden shall obtain as her husband one who is endowed with learning and humility.
A sonless woman shall obtain a son and good fortune, O Lord of the Gaṇas;
and even a widow, having fasted on this seventh lunar day, O Destroyer of Tripura,
shall not encounter widowhood in future births, O Beloved of Pārvatī.

Having many sons and much wealth, such a woman shall attain the affection of her husband for as long as seven births— both women and men alike. Thus has this seventh [tithi] been described to you, O Bull-bannered One.
"Having heard this with devotion, a man is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin.

Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Rathasaptamī," in the Saptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan, within the Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty thousand verses.
Now begins the sixtieth chapter.
Sumantu said: Having spoken thus, he quickly went to the three-eyed one, the eldest of the gods, for the description of the chariot procession.
"O mighty-armed one, this is the chariot procession of the Sun of immeasurable splendor.
Śatānīka said:
"Having propitiated that Lord of the World, my ancestors..."
For the satisfaction of the Brahmins, he provided four kinds of food;
and I have heard many times the majesty of that deity,
who is praised day after day by gods, sages, perfected beings, and men.
Who is capable of praising that Unborn One, from whose awakening this world of moving and unmoving beings arises—
he who is immutable and immeasurable?
He, the Lord of Gods, from whose two hands [emerge] Kavi and Viṣṇu, who are worshipped by the worlds.
O tiger among the twice-born, when the Destroyer of Tripura was born from the forehead of that god,
who is capable of describing all his manifestations? O twice-born one, I desire to know all about that god with my whole being.
I wish to hear the means of propitiation by which I may cross the ocean of existence—
whether by means of mantras, secret doctrines, or ritual service;
or by gifts, fasts, burnt offerings, or even recitations.
When propitiated, it brings about the destruction of all afflictions;
for that alone is the true knowledge among all forms of learning by which the Creator of All is pleased.
Even among those things heard, that merit belongs to where the praise of the Sun is proclaimed.
That by which the Haṃsa is propitiated is the secret of secrets;
it is the one most excellent mantra, that single supreme vow.
And that is the best fast by which the Sun is propitiated.
That single tongue is blessed which always praises the Sun;
that single mind is pure which is constantly fixed upon the Sun.
Both of these are praiseworthy, even among the praiseworthy, in this world and in the next.
O tiger among the twice-born, that body alone among all living beings is truly blessed whose hands are always engaged in the worship of the Sun;
for it alone is radiant with horripilation when chanting the names of the Sun.
That tongue, or perhaps the throat, the palate, or even the uvula—
otherwise, it is merely another disease— that does not speak of the qualities of the Sun;
O best of men, there are nine gates in this city.
The wise know that those efforts made on all sides to enclose [the mind] with ramparts are in vain; for when one pays attention to sound even without the praise of the Sun,
human exertion does not lead to the attainment of the highest goods.
Service rendered by taking refuge in the Sun is not fruitless in this life;
for those rushing through the shoreless wilderness of difficult worldly existence,
a single salutation to the Sun is the savior from the ocean of saṃsāra.
Meru is the source of jewels; the sky is composed of all wonders;
the Gaṅgā is the refuge of holy fords; and the Sun is the refuge of the gods.
Such are the qualities of the enjoyment of the Sun, who possesses immeasurable splendor.
I have heard him many times being sung of by the Siddhas and likewise by the immortals; therefore, I desire to behold that God, the refuge of the seven worlds,
the Sun who dwells within the hearts of the entire universe.
"To propitiate the Lord of Lords, the Sun of immeasurable splendor,
Mārtaṇḍa, the support of the worlds, who destroys all sins upon being remembered.
Thus ends the sixtieth chapter, titled "Description of the Service of the Sun," in the Saptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan, within the Śatārddhasāhasrī Saṃhitā of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa.
Now begins the sixty-first chapter,
"Description of the Majesty of the Sun. Sumantu said:
O King, having prostrated before the Sun, that single-syllabled abode which is the great reality beyond both being and non-being, and which abides in the nature of both difference and non-difference,
I shall speak as it was formerly told by the high-souled Viriñca.
O lord of men, understand that which was previously told to the sages:
how the high-souled Lord, born from the lotus, taught the supreme yoga of Brahman to the great seers for the sake of propitiating the Sun.
Because it brings about the cessation of all mental fluctuations, it leads to liberation.
Then the Lord Brahmā, the Master of the World, having prostrated himself along with all the great sages,
spoke to the Blessed One, the Self-born, for the welfare of all creatures.
O Lord of the world, this yoga consisting of the cessation of mental fluctuations which has been proclaimed by the Blessed One can be attained only after many births;
for sense objects, O Master, are difficult for men to conquer as they drag away the senses.
The mental fluctuations of the mind, though it is flickering and difficult to restrain—
such as passion and the rest— how could they be conquered even in hundreds of years?
The mind does not become fit for yoga as long as these have not been conquered.
O Brahman, these men are short-lived even in the Kṛta Yuga;
how much more so in the Tretā and Dvāpara, let alone when the Kali Yuga has arrived?
O Blessed One, you should graciously speak to us who are devoted to your service.
O Brahman, just as men submerged in the waters of suffering might cross the ocean of existence by obtaining a great boat,
so too should you consider how we may cross the ocean of existence without effort.
Thus addressed, Brahmā then explained the yoga of action for those great-souled ones,
out of a desire for the welfare of those sages and men:
"Worship the Lord of All, the Sun, with unwearied devotion."
Dependent upon external objects, they [worship] that unborn Lord of the world day and night with sacrifices, offerings, prostrations,
and service, as well as with various vows, fasts, and the gratification of Brahmins.
With whatever desired objects bring satisfaction to the mind,
worship the Sun, whose majesty is immeasurable;
being devoted to him, with your intellect fixed on him, performing his rites, and taking refuge in him.

With their vision fixed on Him and their minds absorbed in Him, remain established in Him who dwells within all. Then, renounce all actions within that Self, the Self of all; He shall be your doer, bringing about the destruction of all veils.
This is that Imperishable Brahman, from which both Pradhāna and Puruṣa proceed,
in which they both abide, and by which they both pervade all things;
he is the supreme among the supreme, the highest, the one who is beyond even the most excellent minds.
Since all this— whatever moves and whatever does not move— is distinct from that [Ultimate],

one is liberated by propitiating the Lord of the World through the yoga of action (kriyā-yoga), [thereby realizing] the Unmanifest, which is the cause of liberation, inconceivable, and without possession.
Having thus heard this secret from Brahmā, those best of sages composed numerous treatises on Yoga for the benefit of humanity—
works devoted to Kriyāyoga that bring about liberation in this world.
The Lord of the World is propitiated by those intent upon the performance of those rites.
He is the Supreme Self, the Sun, the Lord of All, and the Creator of All.
O descendant of Kuru, those [teachings] which were previously spoken by that Brahmā—
O tiger among the Kurus, I shall now declare to you those [mantras] which remove all sins;
listen today to this supreme secret for those submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra and whose minds are overcome by sense-objects.
There is no other refuge whatsoever except for the young swan (the *haṃsapota*).
While rising, contemplate the Sun; while walking, contemplate the Lord of Rays;
while eating, contemplate Mārtaṇḍa; and while sleeping, contemplate Bhāskara.
Thus, with a one-pointed mind, you shall constantly take refuge in the Sun;
you will cross the waters of saṃsāra, which have birth and death as its great crocodiles—
[taking refuge in] the Lord of planets, the Sovereign, the Giver of boons, the Ancient One, the Creator of the world, the Unborn, and the Eternal.
"For those who have taken refuge in the Sun, the Lord, and who partake in liberation, there is no further rebirth.

Thus ends the sixty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Yoga of the Sun," in the *Saptamī-kalpa* of the *Brāhma-parvan*, within the *Śatārddha-sāhasrī Saṃhitā* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the sixty-second chapter.
Sumantu said: Now I shall tell you in its entirety another dialogue, together with its secret doctrine, concerning Sūrya and Diṇḍi.
Together with Diṇḍi, Sūrya performed that which destroys all sins.
Overcome by the sin of killing a Brahmin,
the great ascetic Diṇḍi composed a hymn for the propitiation of the high-souled God.
Having heard that hymn in its true sense, the Blessed Lord Ravi was pleased.
The God of gods spoke to that leader of the Gaṇas, Diṇḍin:
Āditya said:
"Ah! O sinless one, I am pleased with your devotion and your hymn of praise.
O knower of dharma, choose a boon, whatever dwells in your heart.
Diṇḍi said:
This alone is a praiseworthy boon that you have come into my presence;
for the sight of you is difficult to obtain even in dreams for those devoid of merit.
Just as this slaughter of a Brahmin, which is censured by the world, has come upon me.
"O Lord of all, you know everything that resides within the hearts of all embodied beings.
By your grace, O Lord, let my destruction come quickly;
likewise, let all my evil deeds and whatever else is censured by the world perish."
"O Lord of Heaven, let all that I desire be so;
by this very inference, O Blessed One,
it is known by me that you are pleased, for when the Sun is not pleased, there are no manifestations of power."
Thus, although you, O Radiant One, abide amidst all pleasure and delight,
you ought to uplift me who am submerged in the bottomless ocean of saṃsāra;
for those pleasures end in suffering, and that which ends in suffering is not true happiness.
But when suffering is approaching, or indeed because of being devoured by someone, O Lord, O Master of the worlds, grant me your grace,
so that by the gift of knowledge I may thus cross over the ocean of existence.
Thus addressed by him, Mārtaṇḍa, the knower of yoga,
explained the seedless yoga (nirbīja-yoga), which is the supreme medicine for the conjunction with suffering.
Having heard that seedless and partless yoga, Diṇḍi shone forth.
Having prostrated himself, the one of great splendor spoke these words:
"O God of gods, O destroyer of darkness, this yoga which has been proclaimed by you cannot be attained by me, nor by other men who have not conquered their senses."
Objects of the senses, which constantly attract the organs, are difficult for men to conquer;
yet the mastery of the senses is appropriate—what [powerful being] will not achieve it? The sense of "I" and "mine" is well-known, and the flickering mind is difficult to conquer.
If passion and the like can be abandoned through successive births,
then, O Lord of Gods, I desire— through your grace—
to attain immortality while remaining unconquered by passion and the rest, my defilements having been utterly destroyed.
The Sun said:
"O Lord of the Gaṇas, if you thus desire liberation, listen to that Kriyāyoga which brings about the destruction of all afflictions."
Fix your mind on Me, be devoted to Me, sacrifice to Me, and bow down to Me.
Thus, with your self disciplined and making Me your supreme goal, you shall come to Me alone.
Those who meditate on Me, who sacrifice to Me, who are devoted to Me, and who make Me their supreme goal—[attain Me].
And those men who offer worship to me go to dissolution in me;
seeing Me, the Lord, abiding in all beings,
by what [action] will you act, and thus how will you cast off these faults?
When the moving and the unmoving are known to be attached to Me on all sides,
the state of having accomplished all that was to be done will come about through the destruction of passion, greed, and the like;
provided, however, that the mind— due to its fickleness— is not [distracted] even by devotion and intense affection.
"Directing your mind toward me once more, fashion a body in my likeness.
Then, with gold, silver, and other materials, create a carving of the Three-eyed One from stone, clay, or wood, and worship him with various offerings and oblations."
Entering into that which is supported by her, always and with your whole being,
she alone has been worshipped by you with devotion; and she, the benefactress, has been meditated upon—
whether you were walking, standing, sleeping, or eating— with her alone before you and behind you.
Contemplating [the deity] above, below, and likewise on all sides, becoming truly absorbed in that state,
he should worship with pleasing baths of sacred waters, flowers, fragrant ointments,
garments, ornaments, edible offerings, and delightful songs and instrumental music.
"O best of the Gaṇas, whatever food or anything else is dear to you, being bowed with devotion, please yourself with my offering.
O father, if you are drawn toward the Gandharvas by passion,"
Having focused your intellect upon me, you should sing those stories that concern me;
if your heart finds delight in my narration,
then you should listen with a sense of devotion to the stories that arise from my true nature.
Thus, having surrendered your mind, abandon all those supports of the consciousness that are to be discarded; by renouncing them entirely, be happy.
Even one whose passion and hatred are not yet extinguished is my most supreme beloved.
You shall attain the goal; do not fear. Let your mind be offered unto me.
Having surrendered everything to me, be diligent.
Perform actions for my sake, and do not transgress dharma.
Thus, having cast off all acts of violence, you shall be liberated from worldly existence through Brahman.
By this very instruction, everything has been explained to you.
Having established yourself in the yoga of action, let your mind be offered unto Me.
Diṇḍi said:
O Lord of the World, for my benefit, please explain to me in detail the nectar of Kriyā-yoga; for you, being gracious, are the destroyer of suffering.
"O Teacher of the World, no one else besides you is capable of speaking that;
it is secret and purifying. Speak it to me; be gracious unto me.
The Sun replied:
"O Lord of the Gaṇas, all that which is free from conceptual construction shall be told.
Having spoken thus, the God, the illuminator of all worlds, vanished;
and that Diṇḍi, possessed of great splendor, quickly ascended into the sky.

Thus ends the sixty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Dialogue between Diṇḍi and Āditya," in the Brāhma Parvan of the Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, in the Saṃhitā consisting of fifty thousand verses.
Now begins the sixty-third chapter: "Description of the Majesty of Āditya."
Sumantu said:
Having bowed his head to the four-faced god, the eldest of the deities,
the highly effulgent Diṇḍila spoke with reverence to the Lord of the World.
"I have been commanded by you, the high-souled God of gods:
'You shall indeed explain the entire nectar of Kriyā-yoga.
Therefore, O Brahmin, I ask you about Kriyā-yoga in its entirety."
"You ought to speak so that I may satisfy you properly.
Brahmā said:
"Come, come to my presence, O Lord of the Gaṇas, near me!"
The sin of killing a Brahmin was destroyed for you by the mere sight of him.
O Lord of Beings, you are worthy of favor from the Sun-god of immeasurable luster;
O Lord of Beings, if your mind is inclined toward his propitiation, [then do so].
If you wish to propitiate Bhānu, the Lord of the Gods,
who is the Blessed One without beginning or end, then become endowed with the virtues of initiation (dīkṣā).
For Bhānu cannot be known or praised in accordance with reality by those who have not received initiation.
It cannot even be seen by the deluded; how much less can they enter it?
O Blessed One, only those men whose minds are fixed upon that [reality], who have been purified through many births, and who possess the qualities of initiation, become devotees of the Sun.
As long as the accumulation of sins gathered through the cycle of many births has not been exhausted, men do not develop a mind directed toward the Sun;
they harbor hatred for the Sun, and they revile the twice-born and the Vedas.
One should recognize that man as being born from the seed of evil who finds delight in heretical doctrines and conforms to the arguments of rationalists;
such a state arises for wicked-souled men who have fallen into the waters of Viṣṇu’s Māyā.
When the evil of men has been exhausted, then unshakable faith arises toward the Vedas, the twice-born, and others, as well as toward the Sun, the Lord of the gods of gods;
this occurs when the accumulation of men's sins remains only in a small residue.
Then all shall partake of the virtues of initiation; of this there is no doubt.
For men wandering here in this cycle of existence, which is difficult to traverse due to sin, the Sun alone, pleased by devotion, serves as a supporting hand.
"Having become a devotee of all [the gods], one should worship with devotion here that Sun, the remover of all sins; the Maker of Light will attain satisfaction.
Diṇḍi said:
"O Padmasambhava, what are the characteristics of men who are worthy of initiation?
And what must be performed by those endowed with initiation? Tell me that, O Lotus-born One.
Brahmā said:
He who does not harm living beings through action, mind, or speech, and who possesses devotion in heart toward Mārtaṇḍa, is endowed with the qualities of initiation;
he also constantly bows down before Brāhmaṇas and the gods.
He who does not seek to harm another in debate worships the Sun;
he knows that the Sun is all the gods and all the worlds. That man, realizing that the Self is not other than these, attains the state of Saura.
Whether it be a god, a human, or another being—beasts, birds, or ants; trees, stones, or wood; earth, water, sky, or the directions;
even one's own self—one should regard these as distinct from the Lord of Gods, the Maker of Day.
He who does not know [the faults] among ascetics shall indeed partake of the virtues of initiation;
he who harbors no evil intention toward any living being by deed, thought, or word is truly worthy of initiation.
Men do not attain that goal by means of well-performed austerities here with abundant sacrificial fees, which those who have taken refuge in the Sun have attained— [the goal] for which one has,
with their whole being and with devotion, fixed their heart upon the Sun.
That man who worships the Sun with a spirit of devotion is praiseworthy, for he has achieved his life's purpose; indeed, such a person is born as a blessed purifier of his lineage within our family.
The man who has an image of the Sun made, which serves as a focal point for his heart, attains residence in the same world as the Sun once his impurities have been shaken off.
Furthermore, he who certainly causes a temple of the Sun to be built out of devotion [attains the same].
That man leads seven generations of his lineage to the world of the Sun;
for as many years as the image of the Sun remains in the temple,
for that many thousands of years he is glorified in the world of the Sun.

In whose house there is an image of the deity endowed with the proper characteristics, and in whom the ritual is performed continuously and the mind is free from desire, that person attains equality with the Imperishable. Furthermore, the man who [offers] fragrant and pleasing flowers...
With a mind always disciplined, that man daily offers various kinds of incense and fragrant unguents to the thousand-rayed Sun;
he thus performs a sacrifice as an act of worship to Ravi.
The Lord Pūṣan, the master of sacrifice, is always worshipped with rituals;
yet sacrifices require many implements and an extensive array of various materials.
These, O Diṇḍin, cannot be obtained by men who possess only meager resources.
Indeed, even if worship is performed by men with devotion using only dūrvā grass sprouts,
it yields for the Sun a fruit that is very difficult to obtain through all other sacrifices.
Whatever flowers are pleasing, as well as incense, perfumes, and ointments—
Give whatever ornaments are dear to you, as well as garments that bring you joy;
and whatever foods, snacks, and fruits there may be—
offer these to Mārtaṇḍa, and remain single-mindedly focused upon him.
Propitiate that primordial support of the worlds according to your ability;
by worshipping that God, a person attains dissolution into Him alone,
[using] flowers, water from sacred fords, perfumes, honey, and likewise clarified butter.

One should bathe the Sun— the lord of planets, the master of rays, and the traveler through the sky— with milk. Thereafter, O best of the Gaṇas, he who pours forth honey shall go to the meritorious worlds consisting of lakes of curd and milk, and attain a unique state of liberation.
Worship the Sun-god with hymns, songs, musical instruments, and the gratification of Brahmins,
as well as through the yoga of the mind.
Having worshipped him, the Lord of the World, I set this creation in motion.
Having propitiated that Sun-god, Viṣṇu protects the worlds;
Rudra obtained the goddess Bhavānī through his grace;
and even the sages shine brightly by propitiating that Sun-god.
"Therefore, through these methods and fasts, you must propitiate the Sun for one year;
for when he is pleased, that Bhānu bestows the pacification of all dualities.

Thus ends the sixty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Yoga of Rituals Dedicated to Āditya," in the dialogue between Brahmā and Diṇḍi within the Saptamī-kalpa, in the Brāhma-parvan of the Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty thousand verses.
Now begins the sixty-fourth chapter,
the Description of Phalasaptamī.
Diṇḍi said:
O best of gods, how is Bhāskara pleased by fasts?
Tell me likewise the exceptions, as well as those things that must be avoided by those observing the fast.
And whatever is to be done, and in what manner, by men in the worship of Bhāskara.
"O Brahman, you should relate all of that in detail and exactly as it is.
Brahmā said:
"The Sun-god, when remembered and respectfully honored with incense, flowers, and food offerings,"
