What need is there to speak of those who observe fasts for the benefit of those who enjoy worldly pleasures? That which is known as fasting is the dwelling together with virtuous qualities by one who has turned away from sins, being entirely devoid of all enjoyments.
Whether for one night, two nights, or three nights, or even by night alone,
that man who meditates upon the Sun with devotion,
chanting His name, intent on His rites, and with his mind absorbed in Him;

A person free from desire who fasts at Diṇḍi shall attain the supreme Brahman. And whatever desire one contemplates while fasting with a mind dedicated to Māskara, all that is obtained when the Lord of Birds is pleased.
Diṇḍi said:
O Lotus-born One, how may Brahmans, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and women attain a good rebirth when they are stuck in the mire within the pit of saṃsāra?
Brahmā said:
Without having propitiated the Lord of the World, the Master of Rays who destroys darkness,
who can attain the state of the righteous with a sincere heart?

How can that man, whose mind grasps at sense objects and is not fixed upon the Sun, go to a happy rebirth while smeared with the mire of sin? If you are afflicted by the suffering of saṃsāra and desire to attain a happy state, [then fix your mind upon the Sun].
Therefore, devoted to fasting, worship Bhāskara, the Lord of all and the Master of luminaries,
with fragrant and pleasing flowers, incense mixed with agallochum and sandalwood,
garments, ornaments, and edible offerings.
If, out of weariness with saṃsāra, you desire the auspicious state,
then propitiate Mārtaṇḍa with a mind inclined toward devotion.
If flowers are not available to you, [use] the tender leaves of excellent trees.
In the absence of those, one should worship Āryaman even with blades of dūrvā grass;
or with flowers, leaves, water, and incense according to one's own means. Thus honored, he attains incomparable satisfaction through devotion with a single-minded heart.

He who performs the act of sweeping in the temple of the Sun always goes to the highest station and casts off all sin. As many particles of dust as are swept away in the abode of the Maker of Light, [so many years shall he dwell in heaven].
A man remains in heaven for as many days as he has swept an area the size of a cow-hide within the abode of the Sun;
O Leader of the Gaṇas, whatever sin he commits day after day,
that he destroys by sweeping that space.
And whatever man should apply anointment in the temple of the Sun,
he too, having attained that world, rejoices together with Haṃsa.
Whether with clay, mineral derivatives, pigments, or cow dung—
One who applies ointment to the sun’s path while mounted on a vehicle goes to my city;
and he who always performs the ritual sprinkling of water for the sun in his home also goes to where the Blessed Lord, the Lord of the Waters, resides.
A person who, having anointed themselves, offers a profusion of exceedingly fragrant flowers at the abode of the Sun, shall not fall into an evil state of existence;
they shall instead attain a celestial chariot (vimāna) richly adorned with splendor and graced by the pleasures of all seasons.
A man obtains that same fruit by giving a lamp in the abode of the Sun,
as well as by a man who, for a full year, gives a vessel of sesame seeds and offers a banner to the Sun.
O King, a gift made out of ignorance destroys the sin committed by the donor in the house of the recipient, whether by day or by night, just as wind shakes off dust.
He who worships the Sun, the dispeller of darkness, with songs, musical instruments, and other offerings, [is freed from all evil].
Seated in his celestial chariot, he is attended by Gandharvas with dance and song;
O tiger among the Gaṇas, having performed the recitation of this book, he attains the memory of past births, intelligence, and likewise, mindfulness at the time of death.
Thus, he who has worshipped the Sun with devotion becomes a lord of birds; he attains whatever praiseworthy state he desires in his heart—
whether divinity by some men, or likewise the state of a Gandharva by others.
Others have attained the status of Vidyādharas by propitiating the Sun here;
Śakra, having propitiated the Lord, the Master of the Luminaries, with a hundred sacrifices, attained the sovereignty of the gods. Therefore, there is nothing else more worthy of worship anywhere.

O Lord of the Gaṇas, for those in the stages of studenthood, householdership, and forest-dwelling, there is no other worthy of worship than the divine Sun; likewise, for women, there is none other than the god Divākara.
Even among the high-souled wandering mendicants, the thousand-rayed one is supreme.
Those who have conquered their selves enter that Sun, the gateway to liberation;
thus, the thousand-rayed one is indeed the supreme refuge for all stages of life (āśramas) and the ultimate goal for all social classes (varṇas), for he is the Lord of the Planets.
Listen as I speak of other optional fasts;
listen, O Diṇḍi, to this supreme seventh-day rite (Saptamī), which yields great merit, is auspicious,
removes all sins, and is for the propitiation of the Sun.

By fasting with devotion on this day, a person is liberated from all sins and likewise attains the world of the Sun of immeasurable splendor. Now, when the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada has arrived...
O dear one, having first observed that fast, listen indeed to the procedure for it:
on the fourth day one should eat only what is unasked for, and on the fifth day one should take a single meal;
on the sixth day, intent upon fasting, one should have conquered anger and subdued the senses.
Having worshipped the Sun with offerings of perfumes and incense,
O son, you should sleep at night on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) before the deity,
meditating in your mind upon the God who destroys the suffering of all beings.
It pacifies all defects and destroys all sins. Having awakened on the seventh lunar day, one should feed the Brahmins after worshipping the Sun with flowers, incense, and ointments.
"O dear one, they say that the fruits offered as naivedya to the Lord are indeed dates,
coconuts, mangoes, and citrons;
so it has been declared by the wise."
With these one should feed the Brahmins and eat them oneself;
likewise, O observer of good vows, listen to other [substitutes] in the absence of these:
one should have flour made from rice and wheat, O leader of the Gaṇas.
One should purify these items, which have molasses as their core, by cooking them in ghee;
mixed with four parts of barley-gruel, one should offer them to Āditya.
Then, having performed the fire-ritual, one should feed the Brahmins.
In this manner, one should perform this unsurpassed vow for twelve months.
Month by month, one should subsist on fruit, offer fruit as a gift, and worship with fruit.
At the end of the year, moreover, one should provide a feast for Brahmins according to one's capacity.

O observer of noble vows, listen also to the procedure for the ritual bath and the consumption [of the five products]. O observer of noble vows, [the ingredients are]: cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, water with *kuśa* grass, a paste of sesame and mustard seeds, and white clay.
A paste of *dūrvā* grass, clarified butter, water washed from a cow’s horn,
and the resinous exudation of the *jāti* bush are recommended for the act of bathing;
furthermore, when consumed, these indeed remove all sins.
Starting from the month of Bhādrapada, the wise know [the sequence] according to their respective order.
Having thus reached the final month of the year and having fed the best of the twice-born,
one should then offer divine enjoyments to them, O Mahādeva.
O Lord of the Gaṇas, O dear one, according to one's capacity, [one may give] golden fruits,
or a milch cow with her calf, or land endowed with crops,
or a temple built upon the earth and furnished with all kinds of grain.
One should give white garments, a copper vessel with coral, and these items for one who possesses wealth; but hear from me what is for the poor:
fruits and flour-cakes mixed with sesame powder.
Having fed the twice-born, one should give silver fruits;
O Mahādeva, one should present a pair of garments dyed with safflower to the preceptor,
together with gold and endowed with the five jewels.
In this manner, dear one, the annual fast is concluded.
This indeed is the most meritorious Saptamī, which destroys all sins;
by fasting upon it, all men attain the same world as the Sun.
Constantly worshipped by the gods and the hosts of gandharvas and apsarases,
a human being should always worship the Sun with this [hymn].
Freed from poverty, suffering, and sins, he goes to the Maker of Day.

A Brāhmaṇa attains liberation, and a Kṣatriya shall go to the state of Indra; a Vaiśya reaches the world of Kubera, and a Śūdra shall obtain the status of a Brāhmaṇa. One without a son obtains a son, and an unfortunate woman becomes fortunate.
O giver of honor, that woman who, having fasted on this seventh lunar day honored by the world,
worships the Sun with devotion— whether she be a widow or a virtuous wife—
shall not encounter widowhood in another birth.
"Indeed, this Phala-saptamī should be known as equal to a wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi);
for those who recite it or listen to it, O Diṇḍi, it is remembered as the bestower of all desires.

Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Phala-saptamī," in the Saptamī-kalpa within the Dialogue between Brahmā and Diṇḍi, in the Brāhma-parvan of the Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty thousand verses.
Now begins the sixty-fifth chapter:
A Description of the Majesty of Āditya.
Brahmā said:
Henceforth, I shall proclaim the seventh [vow] named Rahasyā;
by merely performing this seventh [vow], it delivers men from existence—
seven ancestors and seven descendants as well, without a doubt.
He who observes the seventh vow (Saptamī) cuts through diseases that are difficult to cure, conquers enemies that are hard to defeat, and attains wealth that is difficult to acquire;
one seeking a daughter obtains a daughter, and one seeking wealth obtains wealth.
One desiring sons shall obtain sons; one desiring dharma shall attain dharma. A wise man, observing all these conventions, should perform this rite.
O Lord of Beings, listen to these conventions for your own welfare as I speak them.

O Leader of the Gaṇas, a person devoted to the Sun should practice universal friendliness on the seventh lunar day, or else meditate upon the Maker of Light. On the seventh day, one should not touch oil nor wear blue clothing.
"One should not bathe with *āmālaka* fruits, nor should one ever engage in a quarrel.
Diṇḍi said: "O Lotus-born One, for what reason should one not touch oil on the seventh lunar day?"
"And what fault would there be, O Lord, from wearing blue garments?
Brahmā said:
"Listen, O mighty-armed Diṇḍi, regarding the wearing of blue garments."
O tiger among the assembly, listen to me as I describe in its entirety the defilement [of a Brahmin] through protecting,
selling, or making a livelihood from [forbidden things]. A Brahmin who has fallen becomes purified by three *kṛcchra* penances.
Whatever rite a twice-born man performs while wearing a garment dyed with indigo—
whether it be bathing, giving gifts, recitation, burnt offerings, Vedic study, or libations to the ancestors—
all his great sacrifices become fruitless by virtue of wearing that blue thread.
If a Brahmin wears a garment dyed with indigo on his body,
he becomes pure by fasting for a day and night and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
If the red dye of indigo should enter even a single hair follicle, [he must likewise purify himself].
A Brahmin who has fallen becomes purified by three *kṛcchra* penances. If a Brahmin should ever enter the midst of indigo-dyeing by mistake,
he becomes pure by fasting for a day and night and consuming the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
If one should break indigo wood against the body of a Brāhmaṇa,
or wherever blood is seen, the twice-born should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
likewise, he who performs the cleaning of his teeth with indigo out of ignorance [must do the same].
By performing two *kṛcchra* penances, one becomes purified on the *diṇḍa*; of this there is no doubt.
Wherever one sows indigo, that ground becomes impure;
for twelve years it remains so, and only after that time does it become pure again.
If one touches oil on the seventh lunar day, a beloved wife perishes.
Thus have I described to you this defect regarding indigo-dyed oil.
Furthermore, a wise man should neither eat meats nor drink intoxicants.
One should not harbor malice toward anyone, nor should one practice harshness.
One should not speak with a *caṇḍāla*, nor indeed with a woman in her courses. Nor should one touch a low-caste person, nor look upon a corpse.
One should not snap one's fingers, nor laugh excessively, nor sing songs;
one should not dance with excessive passion, nor play musical instruments;
one should not sleep with a woman, nor indulge in gambling.
One should not weep by shedding tears, nor should one utter words of grief;
one should not pull lice from the head, nor engage in idle talk.
One should avoid speaking ill of others and excessive lamentation.
One should not strike any living being, nor should one eat excessively;
one must avoid sleeping during the day, as well as hypocrisy and deceit.
Furthermore, one should diligently avoid wandering about in the streets.
Now, O Destroyer of Tripura, hear another rite concerning this:
the Saptamī known as Sarvadā should always be observed beginning from the month of Caitra.
In the month of Caitra, the Sun-god is to be worshipped under the name "Dhāta."
Āryaman is [the deity] in Vaiśākha, and Mitra is proclaimed in Jyeṣṭha;
Varuṇa is to be known in Āṣāḍha, and Indra is said to be in Nabhas (Śrāvaṇa);
Vivasvat is in Nabhasya (Bhādrapada), and Parjanya is remembered in Aśvayuj (Aśvin).
Pūṣan is to be honored in the month of Kārttika, while Āśura is said to be the deity in Mārgaśīrṣa; Bhaga should be worshipped in Pauṣa, and Tvaṣṭṛ is praised in Māgha;
furthermore, Viṣṇu is to be worshipped in the month of Phālguna, and the Sun-god (Bhāskara) is to be saluted.
On every seventh day, the wise man should feed those who prepare the food;
having fed them according to the prescribed rite,
he should give a gold māṣaka as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to each of those brahmin cooks.
Food accompanied by ghee and indeed red garments should be given;
in the absence of those who would eat it, O Lord, the best of the twice-born should be honored with sacrificial fees and likewise fed with supreme faith.
Especially so is the Brāhmaṇa who knows the ritual manuals (kalpa) and is always an expounder of the sacred word.
Thus has this seventh [vow] been described to you, O Lord of the Gaṇas;
when heard, it removes sins and bestows the world of the Sun.

Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Seventh Day," within the "Description of the Greatness of the Sun" in the dialogue between Brahmā and Diṇḍi, in the Brāhma Parvan of the Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty thousand verses.
Now begins the sixty-sixth chapter: "The Description of Yājñavalkya."
Sumantu said:
Having spoken thus, the blessed Brahmā vanished from the sight of the Lord.
Diṇḍi propitiated the Sun and became an attendant of the Sun.
Śatānīka said:
O best of brahmins, O observer of noble vows, tell me further of the majesty of the Sun;
for me, there is no satiety in hearing it, just as there is none in drinking nectar.
Sumantu said: Listen attentively, O King, to the dialogue between the twice-born and Śaṅkha;
having heard it, O monarch, a human being is liberated from all sins.
A twice-born man went to see Śaṅkha as he sat in the hermitage—
a place crowded with clusters of trees whose shadows were bent low by the weight of their fruit,
and filled with deer scratching one another against their horns.
In that place where the forest trees provided a carpet for the enjoyment of the roots of the sacred bathing-places;
where it resounded with the humming of bees drawn by the fragrance of abundant flowers;
and where the waters were frequented by Siddhas, celestial rishis, and Gandharvas at their holy sites.
In that hermitage adorned with shaven-headed ascetics, those with matted hair, and other forest-dwellers, he approached the best of sages named Śaṅkha, who was seated at ease—
devoted to him and intent upon him— to praise the Thousand-rayed One (the Sun) with hymns.
Then, having gathered together suddenly, those princes of the Bhojas approached him with humility,
saluted him according to custom, and sat down upon their seats; once they were seated, they spoke to him as he sat.
"O Blessed One, cut through our great doubt regarding all the Vedas. Then the Sage, with a pleased mind, spoke the four beginningless Vedas to the princes who were endowed with humility.
While they were thus reciting,
O King, a preeminent sage, a twice-born man of immeasurable splendor, arrived at that hermitage by chance; he was duly honored by Śaṅkha.
Having been saluted by those princes, Śaṅkha became pleased in his mind;
then he spoke to those Bhojaka youths:
"According to the traditional scriptures, this is a day unfit for study (anadhyāya); let it be observed."
"Let it be as you command," the princes then said to the sage.
He questioned them: "Who are these givers of perfection, and what do they recite?
Śaṅkha replied: "O Great King, these are princes, the sons of Bhojaka."
O Brahmin, he studied the four Vedas along with their Sūtras and Kalpas; likewise, in the seventh Kalpa, he mastered the ritual service of the Sun,
the rules for fire-rituals, and the Kalpa for consecrations from the very beginning.
The Brahmin said: "O twice-born one, tell me the characteristics of Adhyaṅga, as well as the ritual procedure for the chariot procession;
how should the sequence of the ritual for worshipping Kambha be performed on the seventh lunar day?"
What is the fruit of offering perfumes, flowers, and lamps in the abode of the Sun?
By what gift, vow, or observance is he pleased?
And what should be offered to Vivasvat—incense, flowers, oblations, and so forth?
"I desire to hear this; tell it to me, O one rich in asceticism!
Specifically, tell me of the majesty of Bhāskara.
Śaṅkha said:
Just as Sāmba was formerly questioned by Vasiṣṭha regarding this matter, he spoke it to Vasiṣṭha; that I shall relate to you. In this most holy hermitage, the best of sacred fords, the Lord—

Approaching with humility, he paid homage to Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages, whose self was disciplined; he prostrated at the feet of the sage. To Sāmba, who had offered his salutation with his face bowed low in devotion, [the sage spoke].
Beholding him, the sage was greatly pleased and then asked him:
"Your body is cracked all over by a great leprosy of terrible form and intense severity; how has that been removed from you?"
"And how is it that her fortune is so great, her form so exceedingly captivating, her splendor so immense, and likewise her tenderness? Sāmba said:
The Lord of the World, the Sun, having been praised with a thousand names,
appeared before me in person and granted me boons.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O delighter of the Yadavas, how was the Sun propitiated by you? By what vows, austerities, and gifts did the Blessed One grant you his vision?
Samba replied:
Listen attentively, O Brahmin,
to how the Lord Sūrya was propitiated by me through a specific rite, O observer of noble vows;
and how the wrathful sage Durvāsas was mocked by me out of delusion.
Then, by his curse, I contracted leprosy.
Afflicted by this leprous condition, I went to my father;
out of excessive pride and feeling ashamed, I then spoke these words.
"Father, my limbs are sinking and my voice is failing;
this body, afflicted by a terrible and great disease, seeks to destroy me.
I am tormented by the sovereign of all diseases, whose actions are cruel."
Neither by physicians nor by medicinal herbs is any peace found for me.
Therefore, permitted by you, I wish to renounce my life;
or if I am worthy of your favor, then you ought to grant me leave.
Having spoken these words, that father, oppressed by grief for his son, meditated for a moment and then addressed me with this speech:
"O son, take recourse in fortitude; do not set your mind on sorrow."
"Disease destroys one afflicted by grief, just as fire consumes dry grass;
therefore, my son, be devoted to the propitiation of the gods and do not grieve.
When this was said by me, he replied, "Whom shall I propitiate?"
"O father, by propitiating whom shall I be liberated from diseases on all sides?
When I had spoken thus, the Blessed One, my father, said to me:
"In former times, the eternal Lotus-born One was questioned regarding this very matter."

O son, having become pure, listen for the sake of your own welfare to that which was spoken by the great-souled seer Yājñavalkya, the lord of yogis and possessor of great splendor, to that descendant of Yadu.
To the Grandfather Prajāpati, the lotus-born one, who was seated comfortably as the supreme lord,
the highly resplendent Yājñavalkya addressed this question:
"O Blessed One, I desire to hear something that has arisen in my mind."
Having propitiated the Lord, O All-pervading One, a man shall indeed be liberated from worldly existence.
Whether he be a householder, a student, a forest-dweller, or a mendicant—
whoever desires to attain liberation, which deity should he worship?
For whence can he have a certain heaven, and whence the bliss of ultimate liberation?
And having reached heaven, what could he do by which he would not fall from there again?
Among the gods, who is the God, and among the ancestors, who is the Father?
Therefore, O Grandfather, tell me that which is even higher than this.
By whom was this universe, with its moving and non-moving beings, created, O Brahman? And into whom does it enter at the time of dissolution? You ought to explain this to me.
Brahmā said:
"I have been well questioned by you, O high-minded one, and I am pleased.
Having bowed my head to the God who is most meritorious and unsurpassed—"
I shall speak, O best of the twice-born; listen now with a one-pointed mind.
For your own welfare, O Brahmin, being pure and composed, listen as this sun rises and dispels the darkness of the world with its rays.
There is no god higher than this; what else shall I tell you?
For this Puruṣa is without beginning or end, eternal and immutable.
He indeed illumines the three worlds with his intense rays, just as the sun does.
For he is the soul of all the gods, who by his ascetic power causes the rays [of the sun] to heat;
he is the lord of the entire world, the witness of the auspicious and inauspicious deeds of all.
He destroys living beings and likewise emits them once again.
He shines and blazes; he increases with his rays.
He is the Ordainer and the Disposer, Pūṣan, the creator of primordial nature.
Indeed, he never undergoes decay, for his orb is eternally imperishable.
For he is the father of the ancestors and the deity of the deities;
he is indeed remembered as the eternal abode and likewise the support of the world.
At all times, the entire universe is brought forth from the Sun.
And at the time of dissolution, he enters that Sun of blazing splendor;
here, the yogins, having abandoned their bodies and homes,
enter this solar mass of light, becoming one with the wind.
Upon its thousands of rays, like birds upon branches,
dwell perfected sages together with the deities; likewise,
Janaka and other kings who were householders remained devoted to the practice of yoga.
The Vālakhilyas and other sages who were celibate students,
Vyāsa and others who were forest-dwellers, and likewise the mendicant Pañcaśikha—
all these, having established themselves in yoga, entered the solar orb.
The illustrious Śuka, son of Vyāsa, having attained the dharma of yoga and drinking in the rays of the sun, did not undergo rebirth again.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others are merely sounds that are pleasant to hear.
This god Sūrya, the destroyer of darkness, is traditionally known as being directly perceptible.
Therefore, one who desires auspiciousness should not direct devotion toward any other vow;
for it is through joy that the unseen fruit is indeed constantly accomplished.
"Therefore, O Brahmin, the Sun-god must be constantly worshipped by you.
Yājñavalkya said:
"Aha! This Bhāskara whom you have described to me—"
This which arises among all the gods is not false;
I have heard many times of the majesty of that great-souled deity,
who is praised here by divine sages, perfected beings, and men.
Who praises that unborn deity from whom this world of moving and non-moving beings arises,
who is imperishable and immeasurable,
and from whose right ray the blessed Lord Hari was born?

O Lotus-born One, you were indeed born from a ray of light from his left side, while Rudra was born from his forehead; what deity is equal to him? Who is capable of describing the full extent of that god’s qualities?
Therefore, I desire to hear of the means for propitiating that Lord, the Soul of All, by which I may cross over the ocean of worldly existence—
whether by what method, by mantras, by secret rites, or by ritual service.
"O Lord of Creatures, tell me how the Sun, who when propitiated through gifts, vows, fasts, burnt offerings, or even recitations,
grants the destruction of all afflictions,
can be fully worshipped."
For men striving to attain virtue, wealth, and pleasure,
that alone is a true action in this life which is directed toward the Sun;
for it is [the only refuge] for those running through the shoreless wilderness of the difficult cycle of existence.
A single salutation to the Sun is the guide to the path of liberation. Therefore, O Lord, I desire that God, the ultimate refuge of the seven worlds,
who is the vehicle of Time and resides within the hearts of the entire universe.
Desiring to propitiate Śaṅkara— the protector of the world, the lamp of the universe, the lord of planets of immeasurable splendor, and the destroyer of sins the mere thought of whom is remembered—
he wished to please that beginningless and most excellent of gods.
"You ought to show favor by granting me instruction.
Having heard these words of the one who bore devotion toward the Sun,
that lotus-born being of great asceticism attained supreme satisfaction.
Brahmā said: O best of the twice-born, listen now with a focused mind to that which you ask regarding the propitiation of the Sun— concerning vows, fasts, silent recitations, and so forth.
That which is beginningless, the supreme Brahman, devoid of all that is to be abandoned;
which, pervading all beings, abides as the reality beyond both the existent and the non-existent;
from which proceeds the agitation of these two—the Pradhāna and the Puruṣa.
Because He agitates those two great souls— which are eternal, all-pervading, and present at the beginning of the universe—
the stainless Parameśvara,
though Himself causeless and the Self of all, becomes the cause of the creation of the cosmic egg.
And likewise, through the play of the Lord, he attains the state of Pradhāna and Puruṣa;
and from that, the Lord, by his own will, attains the state of Brahmā.
Then, for the maintenance [of the world], he becomes Viṣṇu, the protector; and at the destruction of the universe, [he becomes Śiva].
The Sun, the Lord of the World, assumes the state of Rudra by his own will;
having prostrated before that one imperishable Abode, who is saluted by all the gods and whose nature consists of both difference and non-difference, [one should worship] that Divākara.
O Brahmin, I shall describe the entire mode of worship of that very Sun,
as well as his secret [rites]; listen indeed to this which was formerly told to me by the gratified Bhāskara.

Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Sun," in the Saptamī-kalpa of the Dialogue between Yājñavalkya and Brahmā, within the Brāhma-parvan of the Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty thousand verses.
Now begins the sixty-seventh chapter:
Description of the Dialogue between Brahmā and Yājñavalkya.
Brahmā said:
At dawn, the high-minded god was previously praised by me for the sake of obtaining a form,
while another god, bowing with devotion, was performing sacrifice.
Then, having become manifest, he spoke this secret to me;
and I, seeing the Sun-god directly before my eyes, posed a question:
"You are praised in the Vedas and the Purāṇas, along with their limbs and sub-limbs."
You are the unborn, eternal Creator, the unsurpassed Great Being;
this entire world, consisting of the past and the future, is established in you.
O Lord, all four stages of life have the householder’s state as their foundation.
Day after day, people resorting to various forms worship you;
for you are indeed the father and mother of all, the eternal deity. Yet we do not know which god you yourself worship.
"O Lord of Gods, let it be told to me, for my curiosity is indeed great.
Thus addressed by me, the Blessed One spoke these words:
"This must not be spoken; it is to be told as the eternal secret of the Self."
O Brahmin, because you are devoted, I shall explain this to you here exactly as it is:
that which is subtle, unknowable, unmanifest, immovable, and eternal;
which is devoid of the senses, the objects of the senses, and all elemental beings.
For he is called the inner self (antarātman) of all beings and the knower of the field (kṣetrajña);
he is called the Puruṣa as he is distinct from the three qualities (guṇas).
That blessed Hiraṇyagarbha is likewise remembered as the intellect (buddhi).
He is called "the Great" among yogas and is described as "the Foremost.
In the Sāṃkhya scripture, he is always recited under many names:
Viśvaga (all-pervading), Viśvabhūta (become the universe), Viśvātman (the soul of the universe), and Viśvasambhava (the source of the universe).
He by whom this triple world is sustained through his own self—
bodiless among bodies, he is not tainted by actions.
He is my inner self, yours, and that of all others who are designated as "bodies."
He is the witness of all; he acts, yet he is not tainted. Viṣṇu is both with attributes and without attributes, for he is remembered as being accessible through knowledge.
His hands and feet are everywhere; his eyes, heads, and faces are on every side.
Endowed with ears everywhere, he stands pervading all;
having the universe as his head, the universe as his arms, and the universe as his feet, eyes, and nose,
he moves alone through the fields, wandering at will according to his pleasure.
His fields are his bodies, and the seed is both auspicious and inauspicious;
because that self of yoga knows them, he is called the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña).
Because he dwells in the city of the unmanifest, he is known as the Person (puruṣa).
The universe is to be known as manifold, and He exists everywhere;
therefore, because of His many forms, He is remembered as Viśvarūpa (the Universal Form). Indeed, this Eternal One bears the title Mahāpuruṣa (the Great Person).

Having undergone transformation, he indeed creates himself by means of himself; just as water fallen from the sky acquires a different taste through the specific quality of the earth, so too does he [acquire different states] under the influence of the *guṇas*.
Just as the single wind resides within the body in five ways,
so too its unity and its diversity are beyond doubt;
just as fire attains a superior state through the distinction of different locations.
He is indeed remembered as the God who manifests consciousness within forest fires and other such phenomena;
just as a single lamp produces thousands of lamps,
so too does that One alone produce thousands of forms.
When he realizes himself, then he becomes solitary;
his state is one of unity during dissolution, while multiplicity occurs during manifestation.
Indeed, there is no being—whether stationary or moving—that exists eternally in this world.
The one most true Lord, the Puruṣa known as the Seed,
is imperishable, immeasurable, eternal, and is called Heaven.
From him the Unmanifest was produced, which possesses the three qualities and is the cause of all.
That which exists in the state of both the unmanifest and the manifest is called *prakṛti*.
Know that to be the womb of Brahman, who is of the nature of both being and non-being. Indeed, there is no other higher than Him; He is the Father, He is Prajāpati.

"He is to be known as my very self; therefore, I worship him. And whatever embodied beings, even those who have gone to heaven, bow down to him, they go to the supreme goal by his grace, directed by him."
Both gods and asuras, relying on various doctrines, worship that primordial one with devotion; he grants them their respective goals.
For he is said to be all-pervading and yet devoid of qualities (nirguṇa).
"Knowing him thus, I worship that eternal Self—
the Sun, the Lord of the gods, the Lord of all beings, the infallible one.
Brahmā said:
Thus did the divine Sun-god formerly speak when questioned by me:
"Worship that Great-Souled One who is performing vast ascetic penance.

Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Sun," in the *Saptamī-kalpa* within the dialogue between Brahmā and Yājñavalkya, in the Brāhma-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of fifty thousand verses.
Now begins the sixty-eighth chapter,
the description of the Siddhārtha-saptamī vow.
Brahmā said:
I shall tell you of the Supreme God, worshipped by all the gods—
He whom Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara always propitiate;
[Brahmā worships Him] in the form of a lotus with lotuses and guggulu incense.
O best of the twice-born, Mahādeva worships the Sun-god, the eternal deity whose form is like space,
with *jāti* flowers and with *vijaya* incense; and likewise, O Brahmin,
with *vṛṣaṇa*, *sihlaka*, *śrīkhaṇḍa*, and *agaru*.
O twice-born one, camphor, mustā, sugar, and cinnamon—
this is the Vijaya incense, fashioned by the Lord himself.
Keśava, moreover, should always worship the Sun in the form of the Discus.
Dark as the petal of a blue lotus, surrounded by clusters of blue lotuses,
and endowed with devotion and faith, he— being questioned by me for the very purpose of propitiating that Lord of Gods— was honored with incense known as aguru.
Which flowers are always desired for the worship of the Sun?
Listen to me as I describe those very flowers that were spoken of by him:
by means of the blossoms of the *mallikā*, a man becomes possessed of enjoyments.
By worshipping the Sun with white lotuses (*puṇḍarīka*), one indeed attains eternal good fortune;
by worshipping him with *gandhakuṭajaka* flowers, one enjoys supreme sovereignty.
For one who constantly worships the Sun, these rewards become inexhaustible and absolute.
Worship with mandāra flowers destroys all forms of leprosy;
with bilva leaves and blossoms, one attains great prosperity;
and with a garland of arka flowers, one obtains wealth that grants the fruit of all desires.
One should give a girl adorned with a garland of *bakula* flowers;
the Sun-god, when worshipped with *kiṃśuka* flowers, does not cause affliction,
and when honored with *agastya* blossoms, he bestows favorability.
O best of Brahmins, by worshipping the Sun with *karavīra* flowers, one becomes an attendant of the Sun;
likewise, by worshipping the Maker of Day with *mudgara* flowers,
one shall go to the same world as the Sun (*sālokya*) in a vehicle drawn by swans.
With a hundred thousand *śatapuṣpa* flowers, one shall go to the same world as Pūṣan;
with *baka* flowers, O best of the twice-born, one goes to the world of the Sun.
Having worshipped the Maker of Day with a fragrance consisting of the four ingredients, [one attains the same].
One shall attain the abode of the five elements; of this there is no doubt. He who, with devotion, sweeps and smears a temple of the gods, is quickly freed from diseases and obtains wealth.
One should devoutly smear its pedestal with red ochre;
thus one shall attain great fortune and be liberated from diseases.
Here in this world, the eighteen types of leprosy and whatever other ailments there are for men [shall be cured].
If one were to smear it with clay, they would all go to destruction.
Among all ointments, red sandalwood is the most excellent;
among flowers, karavīra blossoms are declared to be the most praised.
There is nothing superior to this for bringing satisfaction to the Radiant One;
what could he not attain in this world who worships the Sun with these [flowers]? He who, endowed with faith, honors Bhāskara with *karavīra* flowers—
He who has all his desires fulfilled shall attain the sun's desire;
he who makes a beautiful mandala as a plastered sanctuary,
having reached the world of the Sun, rejoices for eternal years.
With one [recitation] he shall obtain wealth; with two, he enjoys freedom from disease;
with three, his lineage remains unbroken; with four, he attains the fortune of Bhārgava;
with five, abundant grain; and with six, long life, strength, and fame.
A man who performs the seven-fold mandala becomes the lord of a mandala;
endowed with long life, wealth, and sons, he is honored in the world of the Sun.
By the gift of a ghee lamp, a man becomes possessed of keen vision.
By the gift of pungent oil, that man conquers his enemies;
by the gift of sesame oil, he is glorified in the world of the Sun;
and by the gift of Madhūka oil, he shall attain supreme good fortune.

Having worshipped the God according to the prescribed rules with flowers, incense, and other offerings, the wise man should thereafter devoutly present an offering of food (naivedya) according to his capacity.
Among flowers, the jasmine (jātī) is the most excellent; among incenses, the vijaya is supreme.
Among fragrances, saffron is the best; among ointments, red sandalwood is supreme.
For the offering of lamps, ghee is best; for the food offering, the sweetmeat (modaka) is foremost.
By these, the Lord of Gods is pleased and attains his presence.
Having thus worshipped according to the rules and performed a circumambulation,
he should bow his head to the god, the Sun, the god of gods;
then, seated comfortably and facing the Sun, he should gaze upon him.
O Brahmin, having placed a single white mustard seed in his hand along with water,
and having fixed his desire for whatever he wishes upon his heart,
a man should drink that water once, without letting it touch his teeth.
On the second and seventh [days], O observer of good vows, one should take two;
on the third and seventh, all three should be taken;
they should be known as four on the fourth, and exactly five on the fifth.
"One should drink six [mouthfuls] on the sixth day; such is the Vedic revelation (śruti).
On the seventh, however, a man should drink seven [mouthfuls] on each seventh day.
This mantra is to be understood as being used for the consecration (abhimantraṇa) from the very beginning."
"Just as you are indeed heard of everywhere in the world as Siddhārthaka,
so may the Sun make me also successful in my purpose.
Then, having touched the oblation, one should perform the recitation as desired.
And one should offer oblations into the fire according to the rite prescribed by rule.
In this very manner, the seven subsequent seventh-day rites should always be performed;
beginning with the first, that is always known as the Udaka-saptamī.
One [ball] together with water, two combined with ghee,
three likewise with honey, four with curd,
five joined with milk-rice, and six combined with cow dung.

O twice-born one, he should drink seven [grains] of white mustard seeds with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). He who performs the Saptamī of White Mustard according to this rite shall always have many sons, great wealth, and his goals accomplished.

"In this world, O Brahmin, a man goes to the sun after death; therefore, one should worship the god Bhāskara according to this rite. Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Siddhārtha-Saptamī Vow," in the Saptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan, within the Śatārdhasāhasrī-saṃhitā of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa.
Now begins the sixty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Vision in Dreams.
Brahmā said:
On the seventh [lunar day], the Brahmin who has stayed there is said to have a vision in a dream.
When such a dream is seen on the seventh day, the man of firm vows,
having duly completed all the rites such as recitation and fire-offerings in their proper sequence, [attains his goal].
Having worshipped the Lord of Day according to one's own means,
one should then lie down upon a bed while meditating upon the God of gods. When, in deep sleep, one beholds the sun rising, [one attains success].
Likewise, Śakra’s banner, the moon, all his prosperities, visible people, power, garlands, garments, the sound of flutes,
white lotuses, chowries, mirrors, golden swords, and the birth of a son— [all these he saw].
The flowing, sprinkling, and drinking of blood bestows sovereignty;
the sight of the white *pañcapūtā* cow brings about prosperity;
and the sight of Prajāpati smeared with clarified butter is remembered as granting sons.
Climbing auspicious trees swiftly brings about sovereignty; likewise,
milking a buffalo, a lioness, a cow, or a female buffalo at one's own mouth [is auspicious],
as is the swift discharge from the center of bows and arrows.
He may strike down lions and likewise serpents, and he may eat them himself;
the Goddess Śrī stands before him whose own body and head are offered into the fire—
that twice-born man who eats milk-rice (pāyasa) from a golden vessel.
O Brahmin, as a lotus leaf remains unsoiled upon water, so shall the strength of that living being be;
for victory in gambling, debate, or battle brings true happiness.
Furthermore, O Brahmin, the consumption of fire is the fiery rite that causes prosperity.
O Brahmin, the burning of one's limbs and the piercing of the head are for prosperity;
likewise, the constant acquisition of garlands, garments, and auspicious white-winged birds, as well as being smeared with excrement, is praised.
The cutting off of one's own limb, verbal abuse, traveling by chariot, and the arrival of offspring;
likewise, having various heads and arms, and the hands bestowing prosperity;
as well as approaching women who should not be approached, grief, and study—these are the results.
Whatever gods, twice-born men, teachers, preceptors, elders, and ascetics say,
all that one should indeed declare as the truth.
Furthermore, an auspicious vision is the consecration for royal glory.
A kingdom might be obtained through the severing of one's head, yet it may shatter in many ways;
one might weep upon attaining joy, or find a kingdom in the bondage of fetters.
[One sees] a horse, a bull, a lotus, kings, and a white elephant.
Whoever ascends [this mountain], even if fearful, attains great sovereignty;
swallowing the planets and stars, revolving the earth,
and uprooting the mountains, he shall obtain the acquisition of a kingdom.
The departure from the body, the intestines being coiled around a tree,
the falling of oceans and rivers, sovereign powers, and pleasures;
or crossing over the ocean or a river and reaching the further shore.
If one crosses over a mountain, there will be success in wealth and long life;
a radiant woman shall enter one's lap, and women intent on bestowing blessings shall appear.
Wealth will arrive swiftly if [the letter] is devoured by worms.
Recognizing a dream as a dream, as well as recounting what has been seen, the auspicious sight of all things that bring good fortune,
and union with those who are auspicious, bring about health and wealth.

If a dream is described as leading to the attainment of sovereignty and a kingdom, those who see it will be freed from their diseases; of this there is no doubt. Having seen an auspicious dream, one should not sleep again, and one should recount it in the morning.
"A pure man [should give] to kings, Bhojakas, and Brahmins who are themselves pure.

Thus ends the sixty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Vision of Dreams," in the *Saptamī-kalpa* of the *Brāhma-parvan*, within the *Śrī-Bhaviṣya-Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of fifty thousand verses.
Now begins the seventieth chapter.
Description of Sarṣapa-saptamī.
Brahmā said:
Then, at the time of midday, having bathed with a restrained mind, [one should proceed].
In that same manner, having worshipped the gods according to the prescribed rules and as is pleasing,
the man— having properly performed his recitation, remaining silent, and having offered oblations into the fire—
should depart from the temple and then feed the bhojakas.
Likewise, O observer of noble vows, [one should honor] Brahmins who are learned in the Purāṇas, those learned in the Itihāsas,
and those learned in the Vedas— both celestial and terrestrial—
as well as red garments, cows, fragrant garlands, and sacrificial food.
Furthermore, a milch cow should be given to the *bhojaka*, as well as whatever else may be dear to him.
O Brahmins, if there is no such gain from the *bhojakas*, then those who subsist on victory [the *jayins*] deserve it—
those Brahmins who are knowers of the mantras and reciters, and those who are devoted to the study of the Sāman hymns.
First, the *bhojakas* (those who enjoy) should be fed along with those learned in the Purāṇas;
after them, the twice-born who know the mantras as well as those who know the Vedas.
Having thus performed this on the seventh [day] seven times, a man endowed with devotion—
One who is faithful and free from malice shall attain infinite happiness.
Whatever fruit a person might obtain from performing ten horse-sacrifices,
that same fruit a human being attains by performing the Saptamī vow seven times.
There is nothing in this world difficult to obtain that cannot be gained through this;
nor is there any disease in this world that is not cured by it.
Furthermore, even all forms of leprosy, however difficult they may be to eradicate, are certainly overcome.
Just as serpents flee, tormented by fear of the Garuḍa,
so too does a man of virtuous character, having duly observed seven sets of the seventh-day rites here through vows, restraints, and austerities,
go to that eternal world of the Sun, endowed with sacred learning, wealth, sons, fortune, health, and merit.

O best of the twice-born, having heard and performed this rite, a person will especially [attain] the Thousand-rayed One; there is no need for deliberation on this matter. This has been heard by gods, sages, and those who know the Purāṇas.
All of them worship the Supreme Self, the Sun. This narrative concerning the seers which I have related to you must be given to one who is devoted to the Sun, and never to anyone else.
The man who constantly causes this to be heard and he who hears it shall enter the deity of a thousand rays; of this there is no doubt.
Likewise, one who is afflicted shall be freed from disease by hearing this narrative from the beginning.
One who desires knowledge attains their desires; a devotee attains the path of the sun. He who recites this while on a journey travels his way in safety.
Whatever desire one prays for, that one certainly obtains.

Having attained this supreme secret and become one who observes the vow of the Sun, a man who has entered into solitude and is well-composed in that solitary place attains the highest abode of the Great-Souled Bhāskara.
A pregnant woman whose fetus is dead shall be delivered, and a woman with child shall give birth to a son;
a barren woman shall obtain offspring endowed with sons and grandsons.
Thus was this declared to me by Bhāskara of immeasurable splendor.
O twice-born one, I have also declared this to you out of devotion:
Bhānu is to be worshipped by you for the pacification of all sins;
for he is indeed the creator and the non-creator, the teacher of the entire world.
"May that Lord of Gods, the twelve-fold soul, the son of Aditi, who constantly dispels the darkness of the world with his rays, be pleased with you.

Thus ends the seventieth chapter, titled "The Description of Sarṣapa-saptamī," in the Āditya-māhātmya within the Saptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan, in the Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty thousand verses.
Now begins the seventy-first chapter:
The Description of the Names of the Sun as Spoken by Brahmā.
Brahmā said:
I shall proclaim to you those names by which the god Arka is praised and with which he is fully satisfied, according to their proper order and as they truly are:
"Obeisance to Sūrya, to the eternal, to Ravi, to Kārya, and to Bhānu."
Salutations to you, Bhāskara, Mataṅga, Mārtaṇḍa, Vivasvat,
Āditya, the primordial god, the one garlanded with rays;
to Divākara, the radiant one, to Agni, and to Mihira.
Salutations to you, Prabhākara, Mitra, O you who are born of Aditi!
Salutations always to Gopati and salutations to the Lord of the Quarters!
Salutations to Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, to Aryaman and Varuṇa!
Salutation to Pūṣan, Bhaga, Mitra, Parjanya, and Aṃśu;
salutation to Dharma, the eternal benefactor and the scorching sun;
salutation to Hari, the one with green horses, the lord of the universe.

Salutations always to Viṣṇu, to Brahmā, and likewise to Tryambaka and to the Self; salutations to you, O Lord of the seven worlds; salutations to you, the creator of the seven worlds. Salutations indeed to you alone, the possessor of the single-wheeled chariot.
Salutations eternally to the Lord of the luminaries, the sustainer of all living beings;
salutations to the benefactor of all creatures, to Śiva, and to the remover of suffering;
salutations to the awakener of the lotus, salutations to the embodiment of the source of the Vedas.
Salutations to you who are born from Kā, and salutations to the son of Tārā;
salutations to you who are born of Bhīmā, and indeed salutations to Pāvaka. Constant salutations to Dhiṣaṇa, and perpetual salutations to Kṛṣṇa.
"Salutations to the son of Aditi; salutations eternally to Lakṣya.
These names of the Sun have indeed been proclaimed by me previously for the propitiation of the God, O observer of noble vows, for the sake of every desire."
Whoever, having become pure and being well-composed, recites this in the evening and in the morning,
shall obtain all desires, just as I obtained them in the past through the grace of that high-souled deity, Bhāskara.
One desiring fortune shall obtain fortune; one seeking dharma shall obtain dharma.
The afflicted is released from disease, and the bound is released from bondage.
One desiring a kingdom obtains a kingdom, and one desiring pleasure obtains pleasure.
"This is the secret to be recited, as well as the very ritual of the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana).
By this mere recitation, a person is liberated from sin.

Thus ends the seventy-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Names of the Sun Spoken by Brahmā," in the Saptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan, within the Śatārddhasāhasrī Saṃhitā of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa.
Now begins the seventy-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Release from Durvāsas’s Curse. Sumantu said:

Having thus heard the words of Brahmā, O King, the yogin worshipped Divākara, who is of the nature of space, and attained the same world as the Sun. In the same way, O Indra among kings, you too, having worshipped Vibhāvasu, [shall attain that state].
"You shall go to the supreme abode, which is difficult even for the gods to attain.
Śatānīka said:
"O great sage, where in Jambūdvīpa is that primordial abode of the Sun?"
"Wherever that Sun-god accepts the worship performed according to the prescribed rites.
Sumantu said:
"There are three places of the divine Bhāskara on this continent."

First is that named Indravana, and likewise Muṇḍīra is mentioned; Kālapriya is the third, renowned throughout the three worlds. Furthermore, I shall tell you of another which was spoken of in the past by Brahmā.
On the bank of the Candrabhāgā, there is a city named Sāmba;
on this island is the eternal abode where the sun is ever-present. Out of affection for Sāmba and for the sake of bestowing grace upon the people, the Sun resides there.
There, at the twelfth division, Mitra always remains for the sake of the world's welfare, beholding the entire universe with a friendly eye;
he himself accepts the worship offered according to the prescribed rites.
Śatānīka said:
Who is this Sāmba? Whose son is he? O Divākara, with whom was he pleased, that the thousand-rayed Sun became the granter of boons to this man of meritorious deeds?
Sumantu said: "Of these twelve Ādityas who shine forth with great power,
he who is known by the name Viṣṇu is renowned throughout all the worlds."
Here, the all-pervading Lord attained the state of Vāsudeva;
from him was born a son named Sāmba of great strength by Jāmbavatī.
However, having been severely cursed by his father, he contracted the disease of leprosy.
Therefore, he established this Sūrya and built a city after his own name.
Śatānīka asked:
"For what reason was this son of his father praised by him?"
"O Brahmin, the reason for which he cursed his son was certainly no small matter.
Sumantu said:
"Listen attentively, O King, to the cause of that curse."
The venerable sage named Durvāsas, who was born from a portion of Rudra,
wandered about as he traveled through the three worlds.
Then, he arrived at Dvāravatī, which had formerly been known by the name Madhu.
Seeing that the sage had arrived, Samba, arrogant in his own beauty, made him—
who was tawny-eyed, hungry, coarse, deformed, and very emaciated—
an object of ridicule in both his appearance and his gait.
Seeing his face, Samba likewise distorted his own;
O best of the Kuru lineage, he did so out of pride in his youth.
Then the most excellent of sages, Durvasas, possessed of great splendor, became enraged.
Shaking his own face, the Blessed One said to Samba:
"Since, upon seeing my deformed appearance,
you were proud of your own form and acted with imitation toward me in both your gait and your gaze."
"Therefore, you shall soon fall ill with leprosy.

Thus ends the seventy-second chapter, titled "The Pronouncement of the Curse upon Sāmba by Durvāsas," in the *Saptamī-kalpa* of the *Brāhma-parvan*, within the *Bhaviṣya-mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of fifty thousand verses.
Now begins the seventy-third chapter.
Sumantu said: At that very time, the venerable sage Nārada [arrived]. [This is followed by] the description of Sāmba’s propitiation of the Sun.
The mind-born son of Brahmā, renowned throughout the three worlds,
was then wandering everywhere;
he went constantly to the city of Dvāravatī in order to behold Vāsudeva.
The best of sages, filled with wrath, arrived together with the other seers. As he approached, all the Yadu princes, headed by Pradyumna, stood there bowed and humble.
Having offered salutations with water for the hands and feet, they performed worship from all sides.
However, because that curse was destined to come to pass,
Sāmba constantly showed contempt for the high-souled Nārada.
Constantly devoted to amusements and proud of his beauty and youth,
Nārada, seeing him so ill-behaved, reflected:
"I shall bring about the auspicious discipline of this undisciplined man."
Having reflected thus, he then spoke to Vāsudeva:
"O best of the Yādavas, O Lord, these sixteen thousand women always maintain their affection for Sāmba."
"Sāmba is peerless in beauty in this world of the moving and the unmoving;
indeed, women always desire a sight of him.
Having heard these words from Nārada, Keśava reflected upon them.
What else could there be here other than what was said by Nārada?

In the world, it is heard that fickleness exists in women; and these two verses were sung of old by brahmins who knew the hearts of women: "Even when a woman is being constantly watched over by her mother, her father, her husband, or her brother, she finds a way to stray. "Women are not easily restrained by words, nor by staffs, nor by tears, nor even by binding them with ropes; rather, they are subdued by the power of wealth alone."

Due to their proclivity for men, their fickle-mindedness, and their natural lack of affection, these women, even when guarded on all sides, act perversely toward their husbands. They do not examine beauty, nor do they have any certainty regarding age.
Whether handsome or ugly, they enjoy her simply as a man;
even while reflecting thus in his mind, Kṛṣṇa said to Nārada:
"Indeed, I do not believe this which has been spoken by you."
While the god was speaking thus, Nārada addressed these words to him:
"I shall do exactly that so that you will have faith.
Having spoken thus, Nārada departed for heaven just as he had come.
Then, after a few days, he returned again to Dvārakā. On that day, the Lord also, having enjoyed water-sports with the women of the inner apartments, indulged in drinking in private.
In the delightful Raivataka garden, adorned with various trees,
eternally perfumed by the flowers of all seasons throughout the entire grove,
and embellished with long ponds filled with various blossoming lotuses.
Resounding with the cries of swans and cranes and graced by ruddy geese,
the god then delights there, surrounded by women adorned with ornaments such as necklaces, anklets, armlets, and girdles.
Especially for those beautifully adorned and lovely-limbed excellent women,
a drink endowed with auspicious fragrance and auspiciousness was consumed by them. In the meantime, the women became aware of the drinking of liquor.
Nārada said to Sāmba, "Sāmba, rise up, O youth!
The Lord is summoning you; it is not proper for you to remain here.
Thus urged by Nārada, yet failing to understand the meaning of his words, Sāmba then [prepared to depart].
Having gone there quickly, Samba performed a prostration before the Lord; Samba offered a full eight-limbed obeisance according to the prescribed rites to Hari and his beloved wife.
In the meantime, those women there who were indeed of a weak sattvic nature—
Upon seeing that handsome Sāmba,
all those women who had never before seen him while residing in the inner apartments were agitated;
this was due to the defect of their intoxication, O King, which had caused them to lose their memory.
The hips of women of little virtue naturally discharged their fluids;
moreover, this verse, renowned in the Purāṇas, is heard upon the earth:
"It is indeed heard that even for a virtuous woman who remains in celibacy," [the discharge occurs].

For upon seeing a man who pleases the heart, a woman’s womb becomes moistened. This is indeed observed even in the world: through excessive indulgence in liquor, even modest women cast off shame and become fearless.
Through meals containing meat, unctuous foods, vehicles, and spirits such as *sīdhu*, *surā*, and *āsava*;
through fragrant perfumes, beautiful garments, and desire for women, lust expands.
It was constantly and effectively employed by Śukra, who desired to win over [the king].
"A wise man must not drink intoxicants to excess.
Then Nārada, having dispatched Sāmba, returned there with great haste, following right upon Sāmba's heels.
Seeing their beloved, the sage Saumanasa, approaching,
all those women, overwhelmed with passion, rose up suddenly.
And as they were rising, Vāsudeva looked on.
Having torn through their bright garments, they fell upon the leaves;
seeing them, Hari became enraged and cursed all those women:
"Since your hearts have gone elsewhere, leaving me behind, O women!"
Therefore, at the end of your lives, you shall not go to the worlds won by your husbands;
having fallen away from the world of your husbands as well as from the path to heaven,
you will become helpless and fall into the hands of bandits.
Sumantu said: Then, due to the fault of that curse, after Hari had ascended to heaven,
those women were carried off by the Pañcanada thieves while Arjuna was looking on.
But those women who possess little strength of character and lack self-restraint are a source of corruption;
however, Rukmiṇī, Satyabhāmā, and likewise my beloved Jāmbavatī—
these did not fall into the hands of bandits, for they were protected by their own inner strength.
Having thus cursed those women, Kṛṣṇa then cursed Sāmba as well:
"Since all these women became agitated upon seeing your exceedingly beautiful form, therefore you shall contract the disease of leprosy."
O descendant of Bharata, having heard those words of Kṛṣṇa, Sāmba laughed and said, "O King,
O dear one, I am free from any fault of character and have no motive."
"Durvāsas was not angry with me here; he would not have spoken otherwise.
Sumantu said: "When he had been cursed by his father for no reason, this son of Jāmbavatī—"
O Bhārata, he attained leprosy and deformity;
furthermore, the sage Durvāsas was provoked to anger by Sāmba,
and by that curse a club was produced, by which his lineage was destroyed.
O Lord of the Earth, having heard of the faults arising from lack of discipline as described by Sāmba,
one should always remain humble toward teachers, gods, and the twice-born;
and one should speak pleasant words, O Lord, which bring joy to all.
Have you not heard the two verses spoken by the Creator in the past,
O Bhārata, concerning the hearing of the God of gods, Vyomakeśa?
"He who is virtuous in conduct, who has conquered pride and anger, who is disciplined by learning, and who does not oppress others..."

Content with his own wife and avoiding the wives of others, he has no fear whatsoever in this world. Neither cool water, nor sandalwood paste, nor cool shade gladdens a person as much as a sweet-spoken word.
Then, having propitiated the Sun-god perfectly while overcome by a curse,
Samba regained his health as well as his supreme form; thus,
having obtained both his beauty and his health from the Sun, the son of Hari [was restored].
"O Lord of the lords of the earth, the Sun has been installed by you with devotion under your own name.

Thus ends the seventy-third chapter, titled "Description of Sāmba’s Worship of the Sun," in the *Saptamī-kalpa* of the *Brāhma-parvan*, within the *Śatārdhasāhasrī-saṃhitā* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya-mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the seventy-fourth chapter.
Description of the Twelve Forms of Āditya.
Śatānīka said: "If Sūrya was installed by Sāmba on the bank of the Candrasarit river..."
"Therefore, this place is not as you describe it.
Sumantu said: "O descendant of Bharata, this is the original station of the Sun; later, it was occupied by Samba."
Listen to me as I relate this first account in detail.
In this regard, O King, that first Lord of the World, the Sun-god who wears a garland of rays,
formerly performed austerities while established in the state of friendship.
Brahmā is without beginning or end, eternal and indeed imperishable.
Having created the Lords of Creatures (Prajāpatis) and having created various beings,
Brahmā first emitted from his mouth the god who resembles a lotus.
Then, O King, from his chest he created the god Kañjaja;
from his forehead, O tiger among the Kurus, he created the lotus-eyed one clad in the directions as his garment.
All the Ṛbhus were likewise created by that Great-Souled One from his feet.
Then the unmanifest Puruṣa himself, possessing a hundred thousand rays,
divided himself twelvefold and was born from Aditi:
Indra, Dhātṛ, Parjanya, Pūṣan, Tvaṣṭṛ, Aryaman, and Bhaga.
Vivasvat, Aṃśu, Viṣṇu, Varuṇa, and Mitra—
by these twelve, along with that high-souled Āditya,
this entire world is pervaded by their forms, O lord of men.
Of him, that first form which is named Indra,
established in the sovereignty of the gods, is the destroyer of Dānavas and Asuras. And his second form is celebrated by the name Dhātṛ.
Abiding in the state of Prajāpati, she, as the Ordainer (Vidhātrī), creates all beings. His third form, renowned as Parjanya,
abides within his hands and indeed pours down the nectar of rain.
His fourth form, O Bhārata, is renowned by the name Pūṣan; established in the mantras, he nourishes all creatures. His fifth form is renowned by the name Tvaṣṭṛ.
That sixth form of his, which is renowned as Aryaman, is eternally established among the lords of the forest and the medicinal herbs;
for the sake of protecting progeny, it always resides within cities.
O Bhārata, that seventh form of the Sun which is known by the name Bhaga is established upon the earth and among the mountains;
and his eighth form is designated as Vivasvat.
Established in fire, she indeed digests the food of embodied beings.
That ninth form of Citrabhānu, known as Aṃśu,
situated in the moon, O hero, truly nourishes the world.
The tenth form of his is designated as Viṣṇu;
it manifests eternally as the destroyer of the enemies of the gods.
The eleventh form, however, is that of the Sun, known by the name Varuṇa.
For she, having taken refuge therein, indeed sustains the entire world with life.
The ocean is the abode of the waters, and Varuṇa is established there;
therefore, O hero, it is called the Sāgara, the dwelling place of Varuṇa.
That form of the Sun known by the name Mitrā, which is the twelfth,
remained on the bank of the Candrasarit for the sake of the welfare of the worlds;
subsisting on air, she performed penance, endowed with a friendly gaze.
Constantly favoring his devotees with various kinds of boons,
this primordial and meritorious place is known as Mitrapada;
it is called Mitrapada because Mitra resides there.
O mighty-armed one, having propitiated him with Samba of immeasurable splendor,
the installation of that [liṅga] was indeed performed by that high-souled Bhāskara through his grace and by his command, together with these twelve [forms].
O lord of men, this entire world is pervaded by his forms;
therefore, he is to be honored and saluted in all twelve of his manifestations.
Those men who, endowed with devotion, pay homage to Āditya, [attain the highest state].
They shall go to the supreme abode where the Lord of the Lotus dwells;
thus, whoever worships the Sun as the twelvefold Āditya,
being liberated from all sins, attains the world of Heli.

Thus ends the seventy-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Twelve Forms of the Sun," in the Saptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan, within the Śatārdhasāhasrī Saṃhitā of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa.
Now begins the seventy-fifth chapter:
"Description of Nārada’s Arrival."
Śatānīka said: How did Sāmba take refuge in the Sun, or by whom was he instructed?
And having received that terrible curse, what did he say to his father?
Sumantu said:
O hero, O great king, it has already been told how that Yādava, Sāmba, was cursed by his father, the lotus-bearing Hari.
Then Samba, overcome by the curse, spoke to his father;
bowing with humility and joining his palms, he stood with his head bowed low:
"O Lord, what wrong have I committed that I have been cursed by you?"
"O Lord, I have come here in haste at your command.
Why has this curse been cast upon me, who have done you no harm?
I truly know nothing; be gracious, O Lord of the World!"

"Restrain this curse of mine, O God; grant me your grace, O Lord, so that I, who am overwhelmed by dejection, may be released from this sin. Then Kṛṣṇa, having understood that Sāmba was indeed innocent, spoke to him.
"O son, I am no longer capable of removing this disease. O son, only this Lord of the world, the twelve-fold Divākara,
the thousand-rayed Āditya, is capable of removing it."
"I have now understood how you were sent to my presence by the high-souled Nārada out of anger;
therefore, having propitiated that most excellent of sages, you should ask him yourself."
"He will tell you of the god who shall remove the curse from you.
Then, O Bhārata, having heard these words of his father, the son of Jāmbavatī became dejected, his soul overwhelmed with grief, and reflected upon it.
Once, having approached with humility Viṣṇu who was staying in Dvāravatī and had come there to see him, Sāmba questioned Nārada:
"O Blessed One, son of Brahmā, knower of all worlds, observer of noble vows!"
"O wise Brahmin, show favor to me who am prostrate before you!
O observer of noble vows, teach me that yoga by which my body may become free from disease and my impurity may perish."
Nārada said: "He who is worthy of praise by all the gods, and indeed worthy of salutation and worship—
by quickly worshipping that deity, you shall then be freed from your ailment."
Sāmba said:
Who among all the gods is worthy of praise, who is to be saluted, and who indeed is to be worshipped?
Who is omnipresent and everywhere, and whom shall I take as my refuge?
"O great sage, being consumed by the fire of my father's curse,
which deity should I seek as a refuge for the sake of its pacification?
Having heard these words of Sāmba, which were full of compassion, [the sage replied:]

But having abandoned those words born of desire, O hero, Nārada spoke these words: "O tiger among the Yadus, O sinless one, the Sun-god is always to be praised, saluted, honored, bowed to, and lauded by Brahmā and the other gods."

Thus ends the seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Sāmba’s Meeting with Nārada," within the account of Sāmba in the Brāhma Parvan of the Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty thousand verses, concerning Kṛṣṇa’s curse upon Sāmba.
Now begins the seventy-sixth chapter:
"The Description of the Sun’s Retinue" in the dialogue between Nārada and Sāmba.
Nārada said: Once, while wandering through the worlds, I went to the world of the Sun;
there I beheld the Sun surrounded by all the hosts of gods.
By Gandharvas, Apsarases, Nāgas, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas;
there the Gandharvas sing and the Apsarases likewise dance,
while the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Pannagas guard it with uplifted weapons.
The Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāman Vedas stand here in personified form in every way;
the seers praise the Sun with various hymns composed by them.
There, the three auspicious twilights stand in embodied form with beautiful countenances.
Having grasped their vajra-arrows, they stood surrounding the sun. The first twilight was red in color, the middle one resembled the moon, and the third was proclaimed to be like the earth.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Maruts, and likewise the two Aśvins,
as well as other dwellers of heaven, worship the Sun at the three junctions of the day;
and Indra himself stands right there, uttering shouts of victory.
The poet, however, [says] that the three-eyed god is indeed worshipped at the three junctions of the day:
at the beginning of the day, one should worship the lotus-seated one in the form of a lotus;
at midday, one should always worship him in the form of a wheel, as a flame of ghee.
One should always worship with devotion the god Ravi— who is of the nature of abundant clarified butter— along with his attendants at night, wearing a lotus as half of his crest-ornament;
the elder brother of the bird (Garuḍa) always performs the role of his charioteer.
He was driving a divine chariot constructed from the constituent parts of Time,
yoked with seven green horses in the form of Vedic meters;
by his two sides were his two wives, known as Rājñī and Nikṣubhā.
Likewise, other gods stood surrounding the Sun;
there was Piṅgala the scribe, another who was the chief of the staff,
and two royal messengers standing at the gate, birds with speckled wings.
Then, O twice-born one, the god Vyoman appeared, possessing four peaks and characteristics similar to Mount Meru;
Dindi stood before him, while other deities were stationed in the various directions.
Thus did the all-pervading god blaze forth in the world.
"Go for refuge to the Sun, the Lord of the planets and the Sovereign of the worlds, the best of bulls among the gods, who is praised by Brahmā and the other deities. Sāmba said:
I wish to hear this according to the truth: how is it that the Sun is omnipresent?
How many are his rays, and how many are his forms remembered to be?
Who is the queen Nikṣubhā, and who is this Daṇḍanāyaka?
And who is Piṅgala there, and what does he always write? O King, whom did you hear of there, and who are those two birds with speckled wings?
And to which deity does that sky belong, which possesses characteristics similar to Mount Meru?
Who was Diṇḍi there at the forefront, and who were the gods stationed in the various directions?
Tell me this in detail according to the truth and through the sacred scriptures,
O twice-born one, so that having known it in its true essence, I may go for refuge.

Thus ends the seventy-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Sun’s Retinue," in the dialogue between Nārada and Sāmba within the Legend of Sāmba, in the *Saptamī-kalpa* section of the *Brāhma-parvan*, in the *Śrībhaviṣya-mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of fifty thousand verses.
Now begins the seventy-seventh chapter:
"Description of the Sun" in the Legend of Sāmba.
Nārada said:
Listen as I describe the Sun in detail and in proper sequence;
thereafter, having paid homage to Vivasvat, I shall proclaim the remaining [deities].
That which is the unmanifest cause is eternal, consisting of both being and non-being;
that which the seekers of truth call Pradhāna and Prakṛti is devoid of odors,
colors, and tastes, and is free from sound and touch.
The source of the world, the great being, the supreme, eternal Brahman—
the unmanifest, which is indeed the restrainer of all beings,
without beginning or end, unborn, subtle, composed of the three qualities, and the origin and dissolution [of all].
They call that Supreme Person formless and unknowable;
this entire world is pervaded by the self of that Great-Souled One.
The likeness of that Lord is characterized by knowledge and dispassion.
The intellect of that [Lord], which possesses the conceit of being Brahmā, is characterized by sovereignty over the dharma;
from the Unmanifest, whatever he desires arises through his mind.
In his state as the four-faced Brahmā, he becomes the bringer of the end in the form of Time.
The Puruṣa has a thousand heads; there are three states of the Self-born (Svayambhū):
Sattva and Rajas in his state as Brahmā, Rajas and Tamas in his state as Kāla, and the quality of Sattva in his state as Puruṣa—such is the operation of the qualities of the Self-born.
In the state of Brahmā he creates the worlds; in the state of Kāla he withdraws them;
and in the state of Puruṣa he remains indifferent. These are the three conditions of Prajāpati; having divided himself threefold, he proceeds through the three periods of time.
He himself creates, devours, and beholds by means of these three;
first, Hiraṇyagarbha manifested from the Self-born (Svayambhū).
Because he is the primordial deity of the Sun and because he is unborn, he is known as the Unborn (Aja).
Among the gods, he is remembered as the great god, Mahādeva;
because he is the lord of all the world and its supreme ruler, he is Īśvara;
because of his vastness, he is remembered as Brahmā; and because of his existence, he is called Bhava.
Because he protects all creatures, he is therefore remembered as Prajāpati;
and because he lies within the city (the body), he is called Puruṣa.
Because he is not produced and is without prior cause, he is renowned as Svayambhū, the Self-Existent.
Since the Lord of Planets, the Master of the Day, resides within the golden egg,
he is therefore Hiraṇyagarbha, the God of gods, the Maker of Day.
Water is called *nārā* by the seers who perceive the truth.
Those waters were his vehicle (ayana); therefore he is remembered as Nārāyaṇa.
The particle *ara* is recorded by the wise as having the sense of "swift";
however, those waters, having become the ocean (*arṇava*), were not swift; therefore they are called *nara*.
In ancient times, when that world had become a single ocean and all things mobile and immobile had perished,
the Person named Nārāyaṇa then slept upon the waters;
he was thousand-headed, benevolent, thousand-eyed, and thousand-footed.
The first Lord of Creatures, the thousand-armed one who is declared the Puruṣa on the path of the three Vedas;
he is the color of the sun, the protector of the world, the peerless, singular, ancient Puruṣa.
That Great-Souled Hiraṇyagarbha indeed comes into being beyond darkness.

Thus ends the seventy-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Sun," in the Sāmbopākhyāna of the Saptamī-kalpa, within the Brāhma-parvan of the Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of fifty thousand verses.
Now begins the seventy-eighth chapter:
"Description of the Majesty of the Sun."
Nārada said: Having passed a period of night equal to a thousand yugas,
at the end of that night he assumes the state of Brahmā for the purpose of creation.
Seeing the earth submerged in water and reflecting upon his task,
that Lord, becoming a boar indeed, entered the waters;
having thus resolved, the Lord of Gods was capable of lifting up the earth.

He began to lift up the earth submerged in the great ocean. As that Great Boar, whose flanks were wet with water, rose up supporting the earth and shaking his body composed of the Vedas, the sages dwelling within his pores perform their silent recitations.
Having lifted the earth from the waters, he fashioned the creation of beings;
by his mind, he generated auspicious sons equal to himself:
Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Atri, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu.
Having created the nine Prajāpatis— Marīci, Dakṣa, and Vasiṣṭha as the ninth—
that Puruṣottama then manifested as the son of Aditi, desiring the welfare of all creatures.
From Marīci, the Creator produced in the waters a son named Kaśyapa,
the tenth among the Prajāpatis, who was equal to Brahmā in splendor;
his wife was the daughter of the trees, Aditi by name.
She produced an egg composed of the three worlds: Bhūr, Bhuvas, and Svar.
Therein was born the thousand-rayed Sun, the twelve-fold Divākara;
the extent of this great-souled one is nine thousand yojanas.
The circumference of this fire is three times its diameter;
just as the *kadamba* tree is surrounded on all sides by its filaments according to its merit,
even so the sphere of light is surrounded on all sides by its rays.
The Puruṣa with a thousand heads, proclaiming the yoga of Brahman,
is situated in the midst of the fiery sphere;
he draws [light] from all sides with a thousand rays.
When the sun has set, the solar radiance of the deity enters the waters from rivers and oceans, as well as from lakes and wells;
it enters the fire at night, and therefore it shines from afar.
Then, when the sun had risen, the fiery energy entered him;
from that foot of the fire of energy, the sun shines.
Thus, luminosity as well as heat are proclaimed to reside in both the sun and the fire.
Through their mutual interpenetration, they nourish one another day and night.
Now learn from me the pervasiveness of the rays and their names:
*hetayas*, *kiraṇās*, *gāvas*, *raśmayaḥ*, and *gabhastayaḥ*.
The *abhīṣavas*, the *ghanas*, the *usrās*, the *vasus*, and the *marīcis*;
the *nāḍīs*, the *dīdhitayas*, the *sādhyas*, the *mayūkhas*, the *bhānavas*, and the *aṃśavas*; the *saptārcis*, the *suparṇas*, and likewise the *karas* and the *pādas*.

Twenty synonyms for these names of the rays are recorded. O dear one, I shall state their individual names, beginning with "Sandalwood" (Candana) and others; a thousand such names have been proclaimed, which produce cool, rainy, and hot sounds respectively.
Four hundred of those rays, possessing diverse forms, pour down rain;
they are named Candana, Mandā, Kautanāmanu,
and Amṛta— all of them being the causes of rain.
Furthermore, there are three hundred other rays there known as the "snow-bearers";
