they are all named after the moon, and those rays are yellow in color.
They are the lords of the moon, the leftward-flowing ones, the gladdening ones, and the producers of snow.
The Śuklas, the Kakubhas, and the Viśvabhrts—
these three hundred, known by those names, are the creators of Dharma.
They all equally sustain both human beings and the gods.
With herbs they satisfied the humans, with *svadhā* the ancestors, and with nectar all the gods; thus, in three ways, they gratified the three classes.
And in both spring and summer, he torments [the world] with three hundred [rays].
In the rainy season and autumn, Īśa blazes and pours forth rain;
in the early winter and late winter, he releases snow with three [rays].
He bestows strength upon the plants and, moreover, places the funeral offering (svadhā) within the ancestral oblation (svadhā).

Among mortals, the Sun bestows immortality; he ordains the triad within the three worlds. Time, Fire, the Year, and Prajāpati, whose self is twelvefold—he, the foremost of gods, heats these three worlds with their mobile and immobile beings.
He is Brahmā, and likewise Viṣṇu; he alone is Maheśvara.
He alone is the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman Vedas—of this there is no doubt.
He is praised by the Ṛg verses in the morning, and always by the Yajus verses at midday.
In the afternoon hours, Maheśāna is worshipped with Sāman hymns.
Being constantly worshipped, this Lord of the Day indeed blazes forth;
he is always a mass of splendor, radiant, and the one who pervades all worlds.
He heats [all things] from the sides, above, and below, on every side;
he is eternally worshipped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśāna.
He remains pervading all, like the wind that blows everywhere.
In the same way, the thousand-rayed Sun, the king of planets and lord of the day,
illuminates the entire world in every direction with his rays;
three hundred of his rays indeed illuminate the earthly realm (bhūrloka).
Likewise, three and three others, as well as two more worlds, are heated;
furthermore, they heat even the hundred nether regions of Pātāla below.
This is the white, radiant orb known by the name of the Sun.
He is indeed the foundation and the source of the lunar mansions, the planets, and the moon.
All the moons, stars, and planets are to be known as originating from the sun. As for the thousand rays of the sun that were previously described by me—
Among them, moreover, seven rays are preeminent and are designated as planets:
Suṣumṇa, Harikeśa, and likewise Viśvakarman;
and another ray is Sūrya, who is remembered by the name Viṣṇu.
Accompanied by his progeny and all his kinsmen, he indeed sustains the world;
among them, the first-born was Saptaja, then Kañjaja,
and another there was Tāreya, as well as Guru, the preceptor of the wise.
Ugrāhva was the fifth among them; another son of Vanamālin was Kaśeṣa, who was the seventh. These indeed are the seven rays.
The entire three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile, have the Sun as their root.
From him arises this entire world, including the gods, asuras, and humans;
O best of Brahmins, it is the entire great and radiant splendor of Rudra, Indra, Upendra, Candra, and all the inhabitants of heaven that belongs to the whole world.
The soul of all, the lord of all worlds, the god of gods, the progenitor of creatures—
the Sun alone is the root and the supreme deity of the three worlds.
An oblation duly cast into the fire reaches the Sun.
From the sun rain is born; from rain comes food, and from that, living beings.
Everything is produced from the sun, and into him alone it is dissolved.
Indeed, the existence and non-existence of the worlds have issued forth from the sun since ancient times.
This indeed is the meditation of meditators, and it is liberation for those seeking liberation.
Herein beings go to Nirvana, and from this, living creatures are born again. Moments, hours, days, nights, and fortnights arise from it perpetually.
The months, the years, the seasons, and the yugas— indeed,
without the sun, no reckoning of time exists for these.
Without time, there are no religious observances, nor the ritual act of tending the sacred fires.

Without the sun, who heats the world and draws up the waters, how could there be the seasonal divisions of flowers, roots, and fruits? There would be an absence of all worldly activities for living beings both in heaven and here on earth.
The sun does not scorch because of drought, nor is it surrounded by a halo because of drought.
There are twelve names of Āditya that are common here;
I shall explain those same twelve in their distinct forms many times over.
Āditya, Savitṛ, Sūrya, Mihira, Arka, Pratāpana,
Mārtaṇḍa, Bhāskara, Bhānu, Citrabhānu, Divākara,
and Ravi— these twelve should be known as his general names.
Viṣṇu, Dhātṛ, Bhaga, Pūṣan, Mitra, Indra, Varuṇa, Aryaman,
Vivasvat, Aṃśumat, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Parjanya are recorded as the twelve;
thus these twelve Ādityas are proclaimed individually.
For these indeed always arise in succession over twelve months:
Viṣṇu blazes in Caitra, and likewise Aryaman in Vaiśākha;
Vivasvat in the month of Jyeṣṭha, and likewise Aṃśumat in Āṣāḍha.
Parjanya blazes in the month of Śrāvaṇa, Varuṇa in the month known as Proṣṭhapada;
Indra in the month of Āśvayuja, and Dhātṛ in Kārttika.
Likewise, Mitra in Mārgaśīrṣa, and Pūṣan, the maker of day, in Pauṣa.
In the month of Māgha, Bhaga is to be known; Tvaṣṭṛ blazes in Phālguna.
By these twelve [months], Viṣṇu is always illuminated by his rays.
Aryaman blazes with a thousand cows and three hundred [rays].
Vivasvān [reigned] for fourteen [years], Aṃśumān for fifteen,
Vivasvān like Parjanya, Varuṇa like Aryaman,
Indra for twelve [years], and Dhātṛ for eleven hundred [years].
The Lord of Light, Mitra, with his eight hundred and one rays,
always increases in intensity as the sun begins its northern course; as it begins its southern course, the rays of the sun diminish even further.
Just as the thousand sunbeams that accomplish the welfare of the world are divided into many thousands by means of seasons and months,
so too has this twenty-fourfold enumeration of names been proclaimed for each [deity].
Furthermore, a thousand [verses] have been proclaimed in detail in this manner;
those of divergent views declare these with supreme effort,
for they indeed cite illustrative examples due to the delusion of their intellects arising from *tamas*.
Some say Brahmā is the cause, some say the Sun;
some say Bhava is the supreme, and others likewise say Viṣṇu.
Indeed, these best of gods are remembered as the causes for various purposes.
He alone, though one, is renowned as the Self-born (Svayambhū) due to his manifold nature;
he who wears a garland of forest flowers, the fierce Lord, who is like the eye in the sky and like Death itself.
He is called Svayambhū, possessing the form of Garuḍa, incomparable and peerless.
Just as a crystal gem is colored by various hues,
so too does the Self-Existent One undergo coloring through the power of qualities.
Just as a single cloud, having become one, establishes itself in a state of diversity.

Just as water fallen from the sky assumes different tastes according to the specific quality of the earth, so too does he [the soul] assume various qualities by virtue of his own attributes, in accordance with color,
form, and excellence.
Just as fire, though one, appears manifold through the power of fuel— differing in color and form— so too does that [Self] appear through the power of its qualities;
and just as wind, though one, becomes distinct through the particularity of substances.
Whether it be fragrant or foul-smelling, it becomes so by virtue of its qualities;
just as the domestic fire (gārhapatya) may take on other designations such as the southern fire (dakṣiṇāgni) or the offertorial fire (āhavanīya), even so does this [Self] among Brahmā and the others.
This illustration has been declared regarding both unity and diversity;
therefore, devotion should always be offered to this god, the Sun.
He is indeed the one born from the egg, he is Adhiga, and he is likewise Bhṛgu.
He is indeed Rajas and Tamas, and likewise He is the quality of Sattva;
He is the Vedas and the sacrifices, and everything else without a doubt.
This entire world, both moving and stationary, is pervaded by the Sun.
Here, this Sun, who consists of the vehicles (yāna), is sacrificed to and worshipped;
everywhere, the god Savitṛ dwells with his various forms and names—
even in fire, as well as in wind, in space, and likewise in water, O Lord.
For such as this is the Sun, he who knows him should always worship him;
he who understands the Āditya in this way merges into him alone.
Even he who knows but a single name of the Sun, along with its root-meaning and scriptural authority, [attains the same].
He is freed from all diseases and is instantly liberated from sin.
Indeed, O Sāmba, devotion to the Sun does not arise for those who have committed evil deeds;
therefore, you should take refuge in the Maker of Day with supreme devotion.
By which you shall be liberated from disease and attain all desires—
just as your father, O Samba, and just as Brahmā and Hara;
just as the gratification of the Self-born One occurs through the influence of his qualities.
"Just as a cloud, having become one,
establishes itself in diversity according to its color and form, so too does he [the Sun] by the power of his qualities.

Thus ends the seventy-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Sun," in the *Saptamī-kalpa* of the *Brāhma-parvan*, within the *Śrī-Bhaviṣya-Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of fifty thousand verses.
Now begins the seventy-ninth chapter,
the Description of the Greatness of Āditya. Sumantu said:
Having heard this in its entirety, the son of Jāmbavatī was delighted;
his curiosity aroused once more, he questioned Nārada further.
Sāmba said:
"Oh, how the majesty of the Sun has been described, increasing my joy! By this, supreme devotion has arisen in me toward this radiant deity.
Then, O great sage, [he spoke] to the highly fortunate queen Nikṣubhā.
"O Sage, tell me about Diṇḍin, Piṅgala, and all the others.
Nārada said:
"Previously mentioned were the two wives of Arka, known as Rājñī and Nikṣubhā."
Of those two, the sky is to be known as the queen (Rājñī), and the earth is remembered as Nikṣubhā.
On the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the Sun is joined with Dyau;
on the seventh day of the dark fortnight of Māgha, the Sun shall be with Mahī.
The earth and the divine sun likewise come together;
there, having bathed after her season, the earth conceives a fetus from the sun.
And here on the surface of the earth, the sky gives birth to water as its fetus during the rainy season.
Then, for the sake of the prosperity of the three worlds, the earth produces crops;
delighted by the consumption of those crops, the twice-born offer oblations;
and with the utterances of *svāhā* and *svadhā*, they worship the ancestors and the deities.
Because she gives birth to food, medicinal herbs, nectar, and ambrosia for mortals, ancestors, and gods, this earth is known as Nikṣubhā;
and just as the queen was divided in two, she is considered her daughter.
And I shall describe her offspring in their entirety:
Marīci was the son of Brahmā, and Kaśyapa was the son of Marīci;
from him [was born] Hiraṇyakaśipu, and Prahlāda was his son.
Prahlāda’s son was known by the name Virocana. The auspicious mother of Saṃjñā was the daughter of Hiraṇyakaśipu and the granddaughter of Diti.
She is the daughter of Viśvakarman, known by the wise as the daughter of Prahlāda;
she is the auspicious daughter of Marīci named Surūpā,
and she is indeed the daughter of Aṅgiras and the mother of Bṛhaspati.
The sister of Bṛhaspati was renowned as a teacher of the Veda;
she became the wife of Prabhāsa, the eighth of the Vasus,
and gave birth to Viśvakarman, the most excellent creator of all crafts.
He was indeed known by the name Tvaṣṭṛ, the architect of the thirty gods;
and this beautiful woman is the daughter of that Viśvakarman,
renowned throughout the three worlds as Sureṇu.
The queen Saṃjñā, the daughter of Tvaṣṭṛ, was perceived as light itself;
however, the shadow of her body that fell upon the earth became Nikṣubhā, who was of earthly nature.
She became the wife of the high-souled Lord Mārtaṇḍa.
The goddess was virtuous, devoted to her husband, and endowed with beauty and youth;
yet in former times, the Sun did not approach her in human form,
for his appearance here was obscured by his own great splendor.
On his limbs that were not yet formed, it did not appear particularly beautiful.
Seeing him as a mere globe while his limbs were still unevolved, the Grandfather said, "Become distressed (mārta) and fierce (caṇḍa);
therefore, he is remembered as Mārtaṇḍa."
Because he was the first among the gods, he is remembered as Āditya.
Hereafter, I shall declare the progeny of that high-souled one:
the Sun indeed begot three offspring upon Saṃjñā.
Having lived for a thousand years in her father’s house,
she was told again and again by her father, "Go to the presence of your husband.
Thereupon, the illustrious lady abandoned her form and became a mare.
Having gone to the Northern Kurus, she indeed grazed upon the grass.
She who was Saṃjñā, the wife who had gone to her father’s side by his command,
remained with the Sun while Chāyā assumed the form of Saṃjñā.
While reflecting on the second designation, "the one to be designated," Āditya begot two sons and a beautiful daughter;
both of them were equal to his elder brother Manu in their resemblance to him.
Śrutaśravas, the knower of dharma, and likewise Śrutakarma;
from those two shall come Manu Sāvarṇi, who is known as Śrutaśravas,
and he who is the planet Śanaiścara is to be known as Śrutakarma.
And there was a daughter named Tapatī, peerless in beauty; however,
she did not show the same affection toward her elder brothers as Saṃjñā, the daughter of the Earth, had shown toward them.
Manu forgave her, but Yama did not forgive her.
Though he was repeatedly driven away by his father’s wife, he was deeply distressed;
yet, out of anger, childishness, and the force of destiny, he indeed [departed].
Yama, the son of Vivasvat, threatened Saṃjñā with his foot;
thereupon, out of anger, that earthly Saṃjñā cursed him severely:
"Since you threaten me with your foot, the weighty wife of your father..."
"Therefore, this foot of yours shall fall; of this there is no doubt.
Yama, his mind deeply afflicted by that curse, reported everything to his mother's father along with Manu.
"O King, our mother does not behave toward us with equal affection;
for, devoid of love, she desires to have her younger son superior to us, her elder brothers.
Although I raised my foot against her, O King, I did not actually strike her down."
Whether out of childishness or through delusion, you ought to forgive me for this.
O Lord of the World, best among those who radiate heat, I have been cursed by my mother;
may your feet protect me from this great fear through your grace.
Ravi said: "Without doubt, my son, there must be a great cause for this,
by which anger has taken possession of you, who are a knower of dharma and endowed with righteousness."
A remedy exists for all curses whatsoever;
however, for those cursed by their own mother, there can never be liberation in this world.
It is not possible for me to make your mother’s word false.
Out of paternal affection, I shall grant you a favor:
worms shall take the flesh and depart to the surface of the earth;
thus her word will be made true, and you shall be saved.
Sumantu said: Āditya then spoke to Chāyā: "For what reason do you show greater affection toward one of these two sons when they are equal?"
She did not reveal her former existence to Vivasvat;
concentrating her mind, she looked at him as he prepared to speak.
Then the Blessed One, desiring to curse her, rose up in anger.
Then Chāyā related everything as it had happened to Vivasvat.
Upon hearing that his father-in-law had arrived, Vivasvat became enraged;
she, however, honored the Sun-god according to the prescribed rites.
Desiring to burn him with his wrath, he slowly pacified him.
Viśvakarman said:
"This form of yours, permeated by excessive brilliance, is very difficult to endure."
But Saṃjñā, unable to endure it, wanders in the forest upon the grassy meadows;
today you shall see her,
your own self, moving auspiciously through the woods, performing great penance for the sake of your form.

"O Lord, if it pleases you, O All-pervading One, I shall assume a form at the word of Brahmā for the welfare of the world, O Indra, O Master. Being satisfied by those words, that one of great asceticism held them in high regard.
Thereupon, he gave permission to Tvaṣṭṛ for the fashioning of his form;
for Viśvakarman, being thus authorized, placed Vivasvat's splendor upon a lathe in Śākadvīpa and whetted it away.
He was skillfully carved up to the knees by Viśvakarman;
however, he did not approve of the carving, and so he was stopped by him. Thereupon, his form shone with its innate splendor.
Having become more beautiful than the most beautiful, he then shone forth even more brilliantly.
Resorting to yoga, he beheld his own wife Vaḍavā,
who was invisible to all beings, enveloped by her own splendor.
In the form of a horse, Mārtaṇḍa approached her with his mouth;
she, fearing another man, made an effort for sexual union. She held that seed of Vivasvat within her two nostrils.
From her were born two gods, the Aśvins, the best among physicians;
they are known by name as Nāsatya and Dasra, and thus they are called the Aśvins.
Thereafter, the Sun-god revealed his own true form.
Having seen that, Saṃjñā was both delighted and bewildered;
then she gave birth to a beautiful son of the Sun,
equal to herself in form, known by the name Revanta.
As soon as he was born, he fled toward the horse that had been seized by Pīṭha;
having mounted it but once, he would not let go of that horse.
Then Daṇḍanāyaka and Piṅgala were commanded by Arka.
"You two should bring back my horse, but do not take it by force through a vulnerability of his.
Stand at his side, watching for a flaw in the horse;
yet even to this day, those two have found no flaw in that great-souled one."
Because he goes leaping (*plavaṅga*) and bestows peace (*śānti*) upon his mother, he is her son;
furthermore, since the verbal roots *revṛ* and *gati* [are involved], he is remembered as Revanta. Manu, Yama, Yamī, Sāvarṇi, and Śanaiścara are also his [offspring].
Tapatī, the two Aśvins, and Revanta were the sons of Ravi.
Thus, this second Saṃjñā was known in ancient times as Pārthivī;
she who was Saṃjñā is remembered as the queen, while she who was Chāyā is Nikṣubhā.
The verbal root *rāj* is traditionally understood in the sense of "shining"; because he always shines, he is called a *rājā*.
Furthermore, the sun shines more intensely than all other beings;
and because he shines preeminently, he is therefore called a *rājā*.
Because she was the wife of the king, she is therefore celebrated as Rājñī;
since the root *kṣubh* means "to move," she is Niḥkṣubhā because she is immovable.
Alternatively, because those belonging to heaven (*svargīyāḥ*) are free from hunger (*kṣut*), she is [called] Kṣubhā.
He entered that divine shadow; therefore, she is remembered as Nikṣubhā.
O dear one, seeing people whose minds were always deeply afflicted, he delighted them through righteousness (dharma); thus he is remembered as Dharmarāja.
O dear one, through pure and auspicious deeds, he of supreme luster attained sovereignty over the ancestors and the status of a world-protector;
he who now exists in the world as Manu, O high-minded one.
In whose lineage was born the wielder of the conch, discus, and mace;
and she who was the sister of Yama, the illustrious maiden Yamī,
became the Yamunā, the best of rivers and the purifier of the world.
This Manu Sāvarṇi, the Prajāpati of great renown, will become the eighth Manu, O dear one; he is thus celebrated.
Even today, that lord continues to perform divine austerities upon the summit of Mount Meru.
His brother Śanaiścara attained the status of a planet;
their eldest daughter, named Tapatī,
became the auspicious wife of King Saṃvaraṇa.
This river named Tāpī, flowing with eternally meritorious waters toward the western ocean, has issued forth from the foot of the Vindhya mountains;
joined by the Saumyā, it removes the fear of all sins.
O hero, best of the Yadus, just as Vaivasvatī was united with Śiva’s beloved,
so too did the two Aśvins obtain the status of divine physicians;
in this world, physicians always subsist upon their professional practice.
The son named Revanta, who is equal to the Sun in form,
was appointed by Bhānu to the lordship over horses;
he travels his path with safety for whoever honors him on the road.
O perpetuator of the Yadu lineage, you are always easily propitiated by mortals;
and by your splendor, Tvaṣṭṛ likewise, at the command of Mārtaṇḍa himself,
O observer of true vows, brought forth the Bhojas for your worship.

Whoever hears or recites this account of the birth of the god [Kṛṣṇa] shall be liberated from all sins and attain the same world as the Sun, among all the sons of Vivasvat who possess immeasurable splendor.
"In this world, he shall indeed become a king upon returning; of this there is no doubt.

Thus ends the seventy-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Sun," in the *Saptamī-kalpa* of the *Brāhma-parvan*, within the *Śrī-Bhaviṣya-Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of fifty thousand verses.
Now begins the eightieth chapter.
Sumantu said: Having thus heard this divine narrative concerning the greatness of the Sun, [the sages asked:]
Sāmba questioned Nārada, the best of sages, once again.
Sāmba said: "Tell me the fruit of the worship of the Sun and whatever great fruit there is from giving gifts."
O best of the twice-born, tell me fully what fruit is obtained from prostration and what fruit is obtained from singing and instrumental music to the Sun;
by means of which I may always worship Bhānu, who is ever adored by the gods.
Nārada said:
O tiger among the Yadus, listen with a one-pointed mind to this matter which was asked of Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, by Diṇḍi in ancient times.
Having bowed his head to the Grandfather, the God who is the eldest of the Suras, as he sat there comfortably, Diṇḍi spoke these words.
Diṇḍi said:
Tell me the fruit of worshipping the Sun, and likewise tell me the fruit of giving gifts;
O Lord, tell me the fruit that is said to come from prostration, as well as from the performance of the three types of musical arts,
and from having the Itihāsas and Purāṇas recited for one's hearing.

O Grandfather of the worlds, tell me what fruit would accrue from sweeping and smearing the temple of the God of gods, Bhāskara; speak of that which results from such acts performed for the sake of the Sun-god.
Brahmā said: By means of praise, recitation, offerings, and worship of the Sun,
and by fasting on the sixth lunar day, a man is liberated from all sins.
Placing his head upon the ground and intent on prostrating before the Sun, he is liberated from all sins at that very moment; there is no doubt about this.
Furthermore, the man who, endowed with devotion, performs a circumambulation of the Sun—
By him the earth with its seven islands has been circumambulated;
he shall go to the world of the Sun and be liberated from diseases in this life. However, having cast off his sandals, he would otherwise go to hell.
O Lord, that man who, wearing shoes, should ascend to the temple of the Sun,
goes to the terrible hell known as Asipatravana. He who, having placed the Sun in his mind, performs a circumambulation of the sky [is likewise fallen].
Indeed, by him all the gods are circumambulated;
and they all, being thoroughly pleased, bestow an auspicious state. O mighty-armed scorcher of foes, all the gods grant whatever is desired.
O mighty-armed one, the man who, eating but once a day, worships the Sun on the sixth or the seventh lunar day, goes to the world of the Sun; likewise,
he who, fasting for a full day and night, worships Bhāskara.
On either the seventh or the sixth lunar day, he shall attain the supreme goal.
He who, on the seventh day of the dark fortnight, fasting and with senses subdued,
worships the Sun with all kinds of red offerings, [attains that same state].
O best of Gaṇas, he who is always devoted to fasting on the seventh day of the bright fortnight goes to the world of the Sun by means of lotuses, karavīra flowers, saffron, sweetmeats,
and sandalwood.
Whoever would worship the Sun with an offering of all-white items—
with *jātī* flowers, *mudgaraka* fruits, clusters of white lotuses and *kadamba* blossoms—
and likewise worship the Lord Ravi with milk-rice (*pāyasa*) together with a thunderbolt (*vajra*).
With his soul purified of all sins, he becomes like the moon in splendor; of this there is no doubt.
By means of a vehicle drawn by swans, he attains the world of the swans.
Diṇḍi said:
"O God, tell me in detail about the supreme Saptamī-kalpa,
by fasting on which Saptamī I shall go for refuge to the Sun.
Brahmā said:
I have been well questioned by you regarding the supreme seventh kalpa,
just as the thousand-rayed Sun was formerly questioned by Aruṇa.
These seven Saptamīs were narrated by Bhānu for the welfare of human beings.
O best of the Gaṇas, while Aruṇa was questioning for some other reason,
after a certain time had passed, Aruṇa spoke these words to the Sun, the God of gods, as he stood absorbed in meditation.
"For what purpose, O God of gods, do you remain absorbed in meditation? The day does not pass, O Lord of gods; let the reason be told to me.
Perform your circumambulation, O God, carrying [me], O Lord of heaven."
Thus questioned, the Blessed One spoke these words:
"Listen, O tiger among the twice-born, to the purpose for which you have undertaken this meditation.
That best of the twice-born, Arvāvasu, O foremost of birds, is childless."
"O best of birds, this man, desiring a son, constantly propitiates me with offerings of perfumes and flowers; yet he does not know how I,
when worshipped according to the prescribed rite, become the giver of sons, O bird."
Listen, all of you, to the ritual by which men may become dear to me;
this supreme among rituals is indeed known as the Saptamī-kalpa. To him who worships me constantly, I grant sons.
"Go and take the Saptamī-kalpa and speak it to that best of the twice-born,
O bird, so that I may grant him the state of having many sons. Having heard this from the Sun, that best of birds departed in an instant.
O best of birds, he related all those words of Bhānu from the beginning;
and having heard them, that most excellent of the twice-born performed the Saptamī ritual exactly as it had been described by the bird.
Having attained supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), prosperity, health, and abundant sons,
he went to the world of the Sun and became equal to him in splendor.
Thus ends the eightieth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Saptamī-kalpa," in the Brāhma-parvan of the *Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of fifty thousand verses.
Now begins the eighty-first chapter,
the Description of Vijayā-saptamī.
Brahmā said:
Jayā, Vijayā, Jayantī, Aparājitā,
Mahājavā, Nandā, Bhadrā, and another are proclaimed [as the names of the seventh days].
If the seventh day of the bright fortnight should fall on a Sunday, [it is known as Jayantī].

The seventh [tithi] is named Vijayā; what is given there yields great fruit. Bathing, giving gifts, likewise fire-offerings, and likewise fasting—all these on Vijayā-saptamī destroy even the greatest sins.
On the fifth day there should be a single meal; on the sixth, they prescribe eating only at night;
on the seventh, however, there is a fast; and on the eighth, the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) occurs.
O Lord of the Gaṇas, some indeed desire [the worship] of the God [on the eighth], while others say "no."
"O best of assemblies, my intention is that there shall be a fast on the sixth day;
one should prescribe a single meal on the fourth, and a night-meal on the fifth.
There shall be a fast on the sixth, and the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) should take place on the seventh."

Devoted to fasting on the sixth lunar day, the wise man should worship the Lord of the Year with perfumes, flowers, and offerings, endowed with devotion and faith. Having performed the worship upon the ground, he should sleep before the deity.
While reciting the Gāyatrī, or the Saura-sūkta,
or the Mahāśveta syllable, or even the six-syllabled mantra, one should remain awakened; then, O Lord of Gaṇas, having performed the ritual bath on the seventh lunar day, one should proceed.
Having worshipped the Lord of Planets (Graheśa) and performed the fire-oblation (homa) according to the prescribed rules,
O Leader of the Gaṇas, one should devoutly feed the Brāhmaṇas according to one’s capacity with rice cooked in milk,
cakes, and sugar-coated sweets, as far as possible.
One should offer milk-rice with ghee to the Brahmins according to one's ability;
having given them a sacrificial fee with devotion, one should then dismiss the Brahmins.
Thus, O God, has this meritorious Vijaya-saptamī been described.
By fasting on this day, a person may go to the supreme abode of Vairocana.
Red *karavīra* flowers, saffron as an ointment,
and *vijaya* incense are indeed pleasing to the Sun-god on this occasion.
This place is meritorious, a remover of sin, and a destroyer of great transgressions;
O Lord of the Gaṇas, whatever is given or offered as an oblation here is never exhausted.
Likewise, bathing, giving gifts, performing fire-sacrifices, and the worship of the ancestors and the gods [yield inexhaustible fruit].
On the Vijaya-saptamī, everything destroys great sins;
when joined with a Sunday, it is known as Vijaya-saptamī.
Thus, O Hero, this has been described as the bestower of all desires.

"O Destroyer of Tripura, it is proclaimed that [this rite] bestows wealth, fame, and long life; likewise, its hearing and its remembrance grant merit. Thus ends the eighty-first chapter, titled "The Description of Vijaya-saptamī," in the Saptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan, within the Śatārdha-sāhasrī Saṃhitā of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa.
Now begins the eighty-second chapter: The Description of Nanda.
Diṇḍi said:

O Brahman, tell me: what would be the fruit for those who worship the Sun on the day of Āditya by performing ablutions, giving gifts, and so forth? O Grandfather, that seventh lunar day is declared to be meritorious when joined with that [weekday].
"Let its merit be described by the name 'Vijaya'.
Brahmā said: "O Brahmin, those men who perform a śrāddha on a Sunday—"
Those men who, remaining steadfast, perform the night rite there while reciting the supreme mantra to be recited, the *Ādityahṛdaya*, shall be born for seven lifetimes free from disease.
Having attained health in this world, they indeed go to the realm of the Sun;
and those who always observe a fast on the day of the Sun and recite the Mahāśvetā mantra obtain whatever they desire.
By reciting [the mantra] of Mahāśvetā for a day and night, for a single night, or by observing the rule of three nights, one obtains the desired fruit;
especially so, O Lord of Gaṇas, when reciting it on a Sunday.
Likewise, by reciting the six-syllable mantra, one shall go to the white realm of Vairocana.
Here, twelve lunar days (vāra) of the high-souled Āditya are recorded:
Nanda, Bhadra, Saumya, Kāmada, and Putrada.
Jaya, Jayanta, Vijaya, Ādityābhimukha-sthita,
Hṛdaya, Rogahā, and another, Mahāśvetapriya—
O Lord of Gaṇas, [these are worshipped] on the sixth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Māgha.
Whoever performs this shall become a king who removes the fear of all sins.

In this regard, the meritorious practice of fasting at night (*nakta*) is prescribed, as is the bathing of the Sun with clarified butter (*ghṛta*). Furthermore, *agasti* flowers here bring great satisfaction to the Sun.
The unguent should be fragrant, with white sandalwood being the most excellent;
the incense should be the finest guggulu resin, and the food offering should indeed be a cake.
Having given the cake to a Brahmin, one should then eat while maintaining silence.
O giver of honor, some desire that the night begins from the appearance of the stars;
some wise men proclaim that it is the day minus one muhūrta.
O Lord of the Gaṇas, I consider the night to begin from the appearance of the stars.

One should prepare an excellent cake made of wheat measuring one *prastha*, or one made from barley; it should be mixed with jaggery and clarified butter. This, along with gold, should be given to a Brāhmaṇa well-versed in the Itihāsas.
Whether on earth or in the divine realm, one should offer it or place it before the Sun;
this [offering] must indeed be given with the mantra, and the *maṇḍaka* must certainly be accepted.
Having become devoted to the Sun, one should indeed pay homage to Āditya.
"O Brahmin, please accept this excellent cake for my welfare; it is produced from the splendor of the sun, fashioned by the hand of the queen,
and bestows desires, happiness, merit, wealth, and likewise sons."
"May it always be yours; I accept this *maṇḍaka*, which is dear to the Sun.
These two great mantras for giving and receiving the *apūpa* are dear to Ravi, O best of the Gaṇas; they lead to spiritual welfare, of this there is no doubt.
O Lord, this procedure for Nanda has been proclaimed for the welfare of men.
Whatever man worships the Sun according to this rite,
being liberated from all sins, is glorified in the world of the Sun.

In the family of that great-souled one who worships the Sun with this [rite], there shall be neither poverty nor disease; likewise, there shall be no decline in his lineage. Having descended from the world of the Sun, he becomes a king upon the earth.
Endowed with many jewels and resembling fire in brilliance,
O Destroyer of Tripura, this ritual procedure grants to those who recite or hear it an unshakable divine abode as well as the goddess Ambujā.
Thus ends the eighty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Nanda Rite," in the Ādityavāra-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan within the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa.
Now begins the eighty-third chapter:
"Description of the Bhadra Rite."
Brahmā said:
O hero, O best of the Gaṇa clans, he who occurs on the sixth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada is celebrated as Bhadra.
In that regard, he who performs a fast during the night, or even observes a day of fasting,
ascends the vehicle of the swans and attains the same world as the swans.
Likewise, [he who offers] jasmine flowers here and white sandalwood—
O destroyer of the three cities (Śiva), one should perform the worship of the Sun here with victory-incense and the supreme milk-rice offering (pāyasa) at midday,
having thus fully worshipped the Lord of Gods, the master of the day.
Having given a sacrificial fee according to one's ability, one should then eat while restraining one's speech—
milk-rice with jaggery and ghee, O tiger among hosts.
Any man who thus worships with devotion this dispeller of darkness, [attains the highest goal].
One obtains all desires, such as sons, wives, wealth, and the like;
liberated from all sins, one goes to the world of the Sun.
O Lord of the Gaṇas, this procedure for Bhadrā has been declared by me to you.
"By hearing and by performing [this], a man on earth is liberated from sin.
Thus ends the eighty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Rite of Bhadra," in the Ādityavāra-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan within the glorious *Bhaviṣya-mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the eighty-fourth chapter.
Brahmā spoke on the description of the gentle rite:
"O Hero, when the lunar mansion Rohiṇī falls on its own day,"
That hero attains gentleness; he is proclaimed as gentle (Saumya).
Bathing, giving gifts, recitation, burnt offerings, and libations to the ancestors, gods, and others—these shall become inexhaustible on this day of the Great-Souled One; of this there is no doubt.
The man who, resorting to the night here, worships the Sun, goes to the world of the god Bhāskara; of this there is no doubt. Indeed, red lotuses and likewise red sandalwood are to be found there.
There should also be fragrant incense, as well as an offering of milk-rice (pāyasa);
this should be given to a Brāhmaṇa and likewise eaten by oneself.
Whoever thus worships Citrabhānu, the Lord of Rays, O gentle one—
"Being thus liberated from sins, he shall attain the splendor of Tvaṣṭṛ’s daughter.
Thus ends the eighty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Saumya Rite," in the Ādityavāra-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan within the glorious *Mahāpurāṇa* *Bhaviṣya*.
Now begins the eighty-fifth chapter.
The Description of the Kāmada Vow.
Brahmā said:
He who, when the month of Mārgaśīrṣa has arrived, [observes it] on the sixth day of the bright fortnight...
That day should be known as the "Wish-granting" (Kāmada) day, which is always beloved by the Sun;
whoever worships the Sun there with devotion and endowed with faith,
being liberated from all sins, attains the Lord of Nandana.
O observer of noble vows, one should offer karavīra flowers mixed with red sandalwood to Bhāskara; O hero, one should also employ incense and oblations of clarified butter.
Furthermore, the food offering (naivedya) should consist of fragrant and pungent kṛśara.
O Destroyer of Tripura, having observed either a fast or a night-meal,
the Sun, the illuminator of the world, being thus worshipped here,
indeed grants all desires; therefore, he is remembered as the "Giver of Desires" (Kāmada).
O Lord, the Sun, being fully worshipped with mantras, grants a son to one desiring a son, wealth to one desiring wealth,
auspicious knowledge to one seeking knowledge, health to the sick,
and various other desires as well.
O tiger among hosts, he who gives this [offering] is remembered as a granter of desires.
He who gives a *maṇḍaka* here becomes an ornament of the lineage of the Lord of Cows (Gopati);
equal in splendor to the protector of the lineage, he shall go to the city-gate (*gopura*) of Gopati.
Thus ends the eighty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for Kāmada," in the Ādityavāra-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan within the glorious *Śrībhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the eighty-sixth chapter:
"Description of the Jayavāra-tithi."
Brahmā said: O Bull-bannered One, when a constellation consisting of five stars occurs on the day of the God of gods,
that day is remembered as one that bestows sons.
There, one should observe a fast, and likewise a *śrāddha* ceremony should be performed;
it is proclaimed that the consumption of the middle *piṇḍa* should also take place.
He who, observing a fast, worships the Lord of Cows (*Gopati*) there with devotion—

Having thus worshipped Vivasvat with offerings of incense and garlands endowed with divine fragrance, O hero of great intelligence, he sleeps upon the ground at night while reciting the Śvetā Upaniṣad in his very presence.
Having risen early in the morning and performed his ablutions, and having offered the most excellent *arghya*,
he worshipped the Lord of the Gaṇas, the three-eyed Aṃśumat, with *karavīra* flowers mixed with red sandalwood, O Lord of Beings.
Having worshipped Vīra, one should then perform the Śrāddha ceremony,
O God of excellent vows, with five Brāhmaṇas— both celestial and terrestrial.
Among them, one should designate two Brāhmaṇas known as Magas as the celestial ones.
O slayer of Andhaka, having first envisioned three formidable Brahmins here,
one should then perform the Pārvaṇa Śrāddha, which is dear to the Sun;
and when the Śrāddha is completed, one should offer the middle piṇḍa.
Standing before the God of gods, O observer of noble vows, with this mantra:
"O Lord of Gods, this is that very *piṇḍa* which has always been desired by you;
I eat it while looking at you, and through that, may my lineage flourish."
"O Lord of Gods, my mind has been convinced by your grace that Bhāskara, when worshipped here in this manner, shall indeed grant sons. Therefore,
this day of the Lord is proclaimed as 'Putrada' (the son-granting day)."
Thus, the man who always worships Bhāskara here,
being devoted to fasting during the Śrāddha ceremony, certainly obtains a son,
as well as wealth, grain, gold, and health that bestows happiness.
And having reached the world of the Sun, he shall thereafter become a king among men;
in splendor he resembles a twice-born brahmin, in beauty he is like a lotus,
in valor he is equal to the Lord of Rays (the Sun), and in profundity he is comparable to the ocean.
(Thus ends the description of the rite for obtaining a son.
Brahmā said:
That which occurs during the southern solstice is proclaimed as Jaya.
In this regard, O Lord, fasting, eating only at night, bathing, giving gifts, and likewise the recitation of mantras—
when performed for the pleasure of the Sun-god, these become a hundredfold more meritorious.
Therefore, O All-pervading One, one should perform such acts as eating at night, which result in a hundredfold merit.
Thus ends the eighty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Jayavāra Tithi," in the Ādityavāra-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan within the glorious *Śrībhaviṣyamahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the eighty-seventh chapter:
"The Description of the Jayantī Rite."
Brahmā said:
O Lord of the Gaṇas, Jayanta is indeed to be known as occurring during the northern course (of the sun);
on whichever day of the week it falls, the Sun-god (Divākara) should be worshipped there.
O tiger among gods, when the Lord of Devas is worshipped there, he bestows a thousandfold fruit for acts such as bathing and giving gifts;
there, bathing with ghee, milk, or sugarcane juice [yields great merit].
Saffron ointment is highly recommended and dear to the Sun;
incense should be made with guggulu, and sweetmeat (modaka) is prescribed for the food offering.
Having thus worshipped the Lord of Gods, one should then perform a fire sacrifice (homa) with sesame seeds.
Afterwards, one should feed the Brahmins with sweetmeats, sesame cakes, and fried pastries.
O Lord of the Gaṇas, the God indeed bestows upon him who worships the Sun in this manner with the mantra a fruit multiplied a thousandfold.
O Lord, [this concerns] bathing, giving gifts, recitation, and indeed fasting.
Thus ends the eighty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Jayantī Rite," in the Ādityavāra-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan within the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the eighty-eighth chapter.
Description of the Ritual for Vijayā Sunday.
Brahmā said:
When the seventh lunar day of the bright fortnight is conjoined with the Rohiṇī asterism, [it is known as Vijayā].

That place should be known as Vijaya, which removes all sins and fears. There, the Blessed Lord, the God who is the sovereign of Candana, when worshipped, bestows ten millionfold the fruit of every meritorious deed.
Bathing, giving gifts, recitation, fire-offerings, worship of the ancestors and gods, as well as eating at night or fasting— all these acts performed here, O Maker of Day,
become ten millionfold when the Lord of Rays (the Sun) is worshipped here.
Therefore, a devoted person should always worship the God here—
the Lord of all, the Lord of the seven continents, whose vehicle is drawn by seven horses,
who arises from the seven primordial elements— by propitiating Him on the seventh lunar day.
"By means of the seven rays, one attains sovereignty over the seven worlds.
Thus ends the eighty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for Vijaya-vāra," in the Ādityavāra-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan within the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa.
Now begins the eighty-ninth chapter.
A description of the rite for facing the sun.
Brahmā said:
"He who [performs it] on the seventh day of the dark fortnight in the month of Māgha..."

He should be known as facing the sun; hear now its supreme procedure, O Destroyer of Tripura: having observed a single meal on the day of Kṛṣṇa, one should then perform the morning bath and worship the Sun.
Facing the sun, O observer of noble vows, one should stand until the setting of the sun, reciting the Mahāśvetā mantra while maintaining a sense of spiritual attainment.
[The staff should be] four cubits long, straight, smooth, free of blemishes, perfectly even, and firm.
O Lord of the Gaṇas, having fashioned a pillar from red sandalwood and taking refuge in it with great devotion, one should remain gazing at the Sun, the God of gods,
while reciting the Śvetā mantra until the setting of the sun.
Having worshipped the Sun with offerings of perfumes and flowers,
and having given a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brāhmaṇa, one should then eat while maintaining silence.
The man who performs this rite in such a manner for the propitiation of Āditya [attains his goal].

Bhānumān will be pleased with him; indeed, being pleased, he grants everything—wealth, grain, as well as a son, health, and fame, O Bhārgava. Therefore, one should worship the Lord of the Gods here, O Hara.
Thus ends the eighty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for Facing the Sun," in the Ādityavāra-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan within the glorious *Śrī-Bhaviṣya-Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the ninetieth chapter: "Description of the Ritual for Hṛdayavāra."
Brahmā said:
O Lord of Gaṇas, that day on which the Sun’s transit occurs and it falls on a Sunday is known as Hṛdaya; it is dear to Ādityahṛdaya.
There, having resorted to the night and worshipped the God with devotion,
and having gone to the abode of the Sun and stood facing the Āditya,
the wise one should recite the Ādityahṛdaya eight hundred times.
Or else, O Śiva, one should meditate upon the setting sun within the heart until it has vanished;
then, having returned home, O Hero, the wise man should feed the Brahmins according to his capacity,
and after eating milk-rice (pāyasa), he should sleep upon the ground.
Whoever here worships the Sun with devotion, endowed with faith, obtains all desires residing within the heart from Bhāskara;
he becomes equal in splendor, fame, and radiance to these great-souled ones.
"O Lord of Cows, the eyes of the bull of the Cowherd [are like] those of the Śakragopa insect.
Thus ends the ninetieth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Heart-Day," in the Ādityavāra-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan within the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the ninety-first chapter.
The Description of the Ritual for Removing Disease.
Brahmā said:
When the lunar mansion of Puṣya coincides with the asterism presided over by Bhaga, [that is the time].
That day is declared to be great, removing the fear of all diseases;
he who worships the Sun here with auspicious perfumes and ointments,
being liberated from all diseases, goes to the world of the Sun.
O observer of noble vows, the wise man who, having prepared a vessel from *arka* leaves, places *arka* flowers before the deity at night with devotion,
and having worshipped the Sun— who is ever dear to the *arka*— with *arka* flowers;

O Hero, having caused [the devotee] to eat arka flowers and having given a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brahmin, he should sleep devotedly on the ground at night with milk-rice (pāyasa). He who worships the Sun here according to this rite—
Released from all diseases, he shall go to the abode of the Sun;
from there, he shall proceed to the world of the one whose weapon is the sound of the *phuṃkāra*.
Thus ends the ninety-first chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for Removing Diseases," in the Āditya-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan within the glorious *Bhaviṣya-mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the ninety-second chapter,
the description of the ritual procedure for the Great White Thursday (Mahāśvetavāra).
Brahmā said:
O observer of noble vows, he who honors the Sun, the beloved of birds, on this day of the Āditya-graha—
which is declared praiseworthy, dear to the world, and renowned as "Gośrutibhūṣaṇa"—
[attains great merit].
By means of offerings of perfumes and flowers, he goes to the world of the Sun; likewise,
O best of the Gaṇas, one who is fasting and pure during a solar eclipse,
reciting the Mahāśvetā or the Khapoṣa or Śiva [mantras], [attains the same].
One should worship the Lord of the worlds, the destroyer of darkness, who moves swiftly;
having worshipped him, one should then recite the *mahāśvetā* [mantra] for the nourishment of one's own body.
Having worshipped *mahāśvetā*, one should likewise honor the divine Sun.
Having installed Mahāśvetā and worshipped her well with perfumes and flowers,
one who is well-composed should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) outside of that very [shrine] on a pure portion of ground; there, having carefully established the Hero (Vīra).
Having bathed, one should perform a fire sacrifice with sesame seeds and especially with clarified butter;
O high-minded one, at the time of the solar eclipse, one should recite the Śvetā [Upaniṣad].
After the sun has been released [from the eclipse], one should then bathe with a concentrated mind.
Having worshipped Mahāśvetā and Khagolka, the lord of the planets,
and having caused the Brahmins to recite auspicious prayers, one should then eat while restraining one's speech,
O Destroyer of Tripura, on this day joined with the planet Āditya.

Whatever meritorious deed is performed, all of that shall be auspicious. O Bull-bannered One, for acts such as bathing, giving gifts, and recitation, their fruit is indeed infinite; of this there is no doubt.
O best of the Gaṇas, according to the words of Bhāskara,
the twice-born who are skilled in meritorious deeds should perform a single meal, eating at night, or fasting; O Lord of the Gaṇas, this is what must be done.
Those who perform [this rite] on Sunday go to the supreme state.
It is righteous, meritorious, conducive to fame, beneficial for obtaining sons, and likewise a granter of desires.
On that day, the gift of a cake becomes equal to the gift of a cow.
O mighty-armed one, these twelve [names] of the high-souled Vīrabhānu have been declared to you as bestowers of satisfaction, which remove all sins and fears—
especially for those who recite them, listen to them, or perform them, my dear.
O Bull-bannered Lord, having duly performed one of these [rites],
and having reached the triad beginning with Vṛṣa as well as the immovable daughter of Atri,
you shall then go to the supreme world of that Great-Souled One.
In brilliance he resembles a lotus, in splendor he is like a bird (the sun),
equal to a feathered weapon in heroism, and in luster he possesses a radiance like the moon.
Thus ends the ninety-second chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Great White Day," in the Ādityavāra-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan within the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the ninety-third chapter:
The Description of the Majesty of the Sun.
Brahmā said:
In the families of those who always perform all their religious rites dedicated to the Sun, neither a poor person nor even one afflicted by disease is born. Furthermore,
the ground of a temple should be smeared with cow dung.
The man who performs this with devotion is immediately liberated from sin. Indeed, the one who applies the plaster— whether with white, red, or even yellow clay— obtains the fruit he has desired.
He who, while fasting, worships Citrabhānu with fragrant flowers offered by Virañci shall obtain his desired objects; likewise,
he who lights a lamp for the Sun with ghee or sesame oil [shall attain the same].
He goes to the world of the Sun surrounded by hundreds of millions of lamps;
by the gift of lamp oil, a man does not go to hell.
Lamp oil and sesame seeds are indeed destroyers of even the greatest sins.
He who constantly offers a lamp in the temples of the Sun,
at crossroads, or at sacred fords (tīrthas), is born endowed with beauty and vigor.
Furthermore, he who causes a lamp to be made for the Sun, filled with devotion, [attains the same].
Having obtained his desired objects of desire, he shall go to the city of the gods;
he who anoints the Sun with sandalwood, agallochum,
and saffron, mixed with camphor and combined with musk.
Having dwelt for a hundred times ten million auspicious eons in the abode of existence,
he is born once again on earth as a king of kings, without a doubt;
his soul is enriched with all desires, and he is honored by all the worlds.
Having offered arghya to the Sun with flowers mixed with sandalwood water,
one is honored in the heavenly world together with one's sons, grandsons, and wife.
Having offered arghya to the Sun with flowers mixed with fragrant water...
Having dwelt for a long time in the world of the gods, he becomes a king on earth;
with gold, or with water colored red by vermilion,
he is honored in the heavenly world for a hundred million years.
Having performed worship with lotuses, a man goes to heaven;
there he dwells for years surrounded by hundreds of lotus-like women.
By offering guggulu resin with clarified butter while endowed with devotion to the Sun, [he attains the same].
At that very moment, one is liberated from all sins; there is no doubt about this.
By offering guggulu resin for a fortnight, one is released from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
O Śiva, by doing so for a year, one obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Through incense one attains heaven, and through fragrant turuṣka;
by means of camphor and aguru incense, one obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
That man who, with devotion and faith, worships the Sun in the forenoon—
He obtains that fruit which is gained by giving a hundred tawny cows;
he who, with a restrained mind and controlled senses, worships the Sun at midday,
attains the fruit of both a gift of land and a gift of a hundred cows.
The man who worships the Sun during the evening twilight,
being pure and wearing white garments and a turban, shall obtain the fruit of a thousand cows. Furthermore, the man who with devotion fully worships the Sun at midnight—
He who worships the Sun at the time of twilight during the night, O hero, attains the memory of his past births and is born into a family endowed with righteousness;
having gone there, he shall swiftly sport in the abode of Saumanasa.
At the time of the staff-bearer (the sun), at dawn,
having again worshipped the Sun with devotion, one should proceed to the abode of Animiṣa (Śiva).
In this manner, a human being [should worship] at all times, both during the prescribed hours and at other times.

He who, with a concentrated mind and devotion, worships the Sun with *arka* flowers, is indeed honored in the world of the Sun, possessing a splendor equal to that of the Aditya. This applies whether during the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*) or the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*) of the Sun.
He who indeed worships with devotion shall go to the abode of the Lotus-born;
staying there, he is honored by all the gods as well as by celestial flowers,
just as the Lord of Cows (Indra) is honored by the gods headed by Gopati.
Having worshipped the Sun with devotion during the equinoxes, eclipses, and the six *aśītimukha* periods, a man does not grieve for himself;
whether he learns of it from another or knows it himself, he who pays homage to the Sun [attains this].
The Sun-god, being pleased, grants him his desired goal. By offering an oblation to Sūrya consisting of kṛśara, milk-rice, cakes, meat-mince, and sweetmeats, one shall obtain all desires.
O observer of noble vows, by the offering of sweetmeats (modaka) and milk-rice (pāyasa),
as well as with honey, meat, and juices, the Sun is exceedingly pleased. By performing a libation with clarified butter (ghṛta), a man shall always remain radiant.
By satisfying [the deity] with meat, one is immediately released from sin;
by performing a bath with ghee on the day of the sun's rising,
one enjoys the fruit of giving a hundred thousand cows.
By satisfying [the deity] with cow’s milk, one obtains the fruit of the Puṇḍarīka sacrifice;
by bathing the deity with meat-broth (rasa), one obtains the fruit of the Aśvamedha sacrifice.
He who gives a single young cow to the Sun—
Having reached Kañjajāmacalā, one shall go again to the city of the gods (Lekhapura).
O Destroyer of Tripura, for as many hairs as there are on the body of a cow,
for that many tens of millions of years one is glorified in the world of the gods.
By giving a hundred cows to the Sun, one obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice;
he who bestows a thousand [cows] obtains the fruit of the Aśvamedha.
One should constantly burn guggulu and devadāru wood while dripping with clarified butter.
Indeed, the smoke of clarified butter is always naturally dear to the gods.
Those who offer drums and other musical instruments, as well as conchs, flutes, and the like,
to the Sun go to the abode of Haṃsa.
He who, endowed with devotion to the Sun, brings a vajra,
or another who brings water from a sacred ford (tīrtha), goes to the abode of the gods;
having sported for a long time in celestial chariots crowded with hundreds of women, that man [attains liberation].
Having attained human birth, such a person becomes a righteous king. That man who is devoted to the Sun should indeed offer umbrellas, banners, canopies, flags, and chowries with golden handles.
By means of a divine celestial chariot adorned with garlands of tinkling bells,
he goes from here to the world of the sun and becomes the lord of the apsarases.
Having dwelt there for a very long time, he returns once again from heaven.
Having given garments and likewise ornaments to the Sun, he is born as a king among men, saluted by all kings; residing in Janaloka,
he sports until the dissolution of all beings (ābhūtasaṃplava).
One should keep a vigil for the Sun with songs, instrumental music, and dances;
such a person sports for a very long time in the midst of Gandharvas and Apsarases.
Likewise, one may worship with perfumes, flowers, leaves, and various hymns of praise.
Those who praise the Sun with devotion go to the abode of the birds;
those who always praise the Sun at dawn and sing hymns to him,
as well as reciters and bards— all of them go to heaven.
Whoever should give to the Sun a chariot yoked with teams of horses—
whether made of gold or silver, auspicious and adorned with gems and jewels—
he, by means of that sun-colored vehicle garlanded with networks of tiny bells, [attains the celestial realm].
Having gone from here to the heavenly world, he sports with an apsaras;
but he who would make an unsurpassed chariot for the Sun out of wood goes to the solar orb by means of a celestial vehicle (vimāna) having the color of the sun.
O best of the Gaṇas, listen to the fruit of the merit of those men who undertake a pilgrimage to the Sun even once a year or every six months;
they attain that very goal which meditators and yogins reach in this world.
Those men who, endowed with devotion, draw the chariot of the Sun as it traverses the solar path, attain that destination; in birth after birth, they remain free from disease and free from poverty.
Those men who perform the chariot procession of the Sun, having reached the world of Bhānu, sport there according to their pleasure.
But that man who, out of delusion or anger, causes an obstruction to the procession—
Those men who offer wealth, grain, gold, or various garments to the Sun should be known as Mandehas, Rākṣasas who perform evil deeds; yet those who bestow these upon the Sun attain the supreme goal.
Listen to the meritorious fruit for one who bestows cows, or even buffalo-cows, as well as splendid elephants and horses upon the Sun:
he shall obtain the inexhaustible fruit of the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha), which fulfills all desires.
And that gift of his stands multiplied a thousandfold.
He who gives to the Sun auspicious, fertile land that has been ploughed,
truly delivers ten ancestors and ten descendants of his lineage.
By means of a divine celestial chariot, that wise man shall go to the gateway of the Lord of Rays (the Sun) and sport in the midst of the Apsarases like an elephant among a herd of female elephants,
he who with devotion gives a village to the Sun.

He goes by means of a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun to the supreme goal. Those who, endowed with devotion, bestow gardens provided with leaves, flowers, and fruits upon the Sun, they too go to the supreme goal.
Whatever evil deed has been committed through mind, speech, or action—
all that, without exception, perishes by the grace of the Sun.
Whether one is afflicted, diseased, impoverished, or even suffering;
Having gone for refuge to Āditya, a man does not grieve for himself;
the fruit that is obtained from the worship of Bhānu in even a single day is indeed that same supreme fruit obtained by performing hundreds of sacrifices.
Having performed a beautiful spectacle for the Sun in a divine temple,
one obtains the imperishable fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice, which fulfills all desires.
Furthermore, he who with devotion offers a group of courtesans to the Sun, [obtains the same reward].
He shall go to the supreme abode where the Sun-god dwells;
O Lord of the Gaṇas, by giving a manuscript of the Mahābhārata to the Sun,
one whose soul is liberated from all sins is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
O Destroyer of Tripura, by giving a manuscript of the Rāmāyaṇa,
one attains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice and shall go to the city of the Lord of Rays (the Sun). Or, by giving a manuscript of the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa known as the Sāmba to the Sun;
A person obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices;
he attains all desires and goes to the same world as the Sun.
Having remained in the world of the Sun for a long time, he shall then proceed to the world of Brahmā.
Having remained there for a hundred kalpas, that man becomes a king upon the earth;
and he who constructs a water-station at the temple of the Sun, O Lord of the Gaṇas,
goes to the supreme, divine realm of Saumanasa.
In the cold season, one should give thick [clothing] to men to dispel the cold;
O God, at the temple of the Sun, one obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
The recitation of books from the Itihāsas and Purāṇas is meritorious.
One who constantly engages in performing a thousand horse-sacrifices does not obtain that fruit which one obtains from this rite;
therefore, with every effort, the recitation of the book should be performed.
In the auspicious temple of the Sun, there is nothing superior to the Itihāsas and Purāṇas for bringing nourishment to the Sun,
nor anything else so supremely pleasing to him;
indeed, the Sun is as pleased by meritorious narratives and stories as he is by these.
Thus ends the ninety-third chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Sun," in the *Saptamī-kalpa* of the *Brāhma-parvan* within the glorious *Śrī-Bhaviṣya-Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the ninety-fourth chapter:
"Description of the Greatness of Hearing the Meritorious [Narrative]."
Brahmā said: O bull among the Gaṇas, in this regard they here desire to hear the sacred,
merit-bestowing, and auspicious dialogue between the Grandfather and Kumāra.
Having bowed his head to the Grandfather, the creator of all worlds, who was seated comfortably, Kumāra— that tiger among gods— endowed with faith and devotion, addressed these words to the Lord:
"O Blessed One, today I went to see the divine Sun;
having circumambulated him, that god Ravi was worshipped by me,
O Lord, bowing my head with devotion and supreme faith."
Then, permitted by him, I remained seated comfortably;
while sitting there, I beheld a wonderful and marvelous sight:
a golden celestial chariot adorned with a network of small bells.
O best of men, seeing the man arrive there with a magnificent altar made of lapis lazuli and variegated with jewels and pearls, the god Divākara rose hastily from his very seat.
Taking that man by his right hand and bringing him before him,
the Lord of Gods, Ravi, smelled the crown of his head and indeed honored him. Once he was seated, Bhānu spoke these words to him:
"Welcome, noble one! We are delighted by you, who bring us happiness.
Remain near me until the dissolution of all beings;
then you shall go again to that place where Brahmā himself resides."
In the meantime, another divine person, seated upon an excellent celestial chariot, arrived where the Sun-god was staying; and that man,
O Lord, was likewise honored by Bhānu at that time.
Having been addressed thus with conciliation, he stood there bowed down with humility.
O tiger among gods, curiosity arose in me upon seeing the worship performed for those two; I then questioned Bhānu, who had been questioned by me.
"O Lord, what has been done by this man who previously came here, that you have become so pleased with him, such as you are? For indeed,
you yourself performed worship for him."
In this matter, curiosity has arisen within me, and especially wonder;
for in the same manner, worship was performed for this second man as well.
In every respect, these two are the best among men, performers of meritorious deeds.
"The Blessed One is always worshipped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others;
yet you, O best of gods, have performed worship that surpasses even theirs. Tell me, O Lord of Gods, what deeds did these two perform?"
"Since they have obtained such a supreme, divine, and meritorious fruit," having heard those words, the god spoke these words. Sūrya said:

"Excellent! I have been well-asked by you regarding the supreme determination of karma. O best of sages, O high-minded one, listen now to what karma was performed by this man who has come here to the sun."
This city named Ayodhyā, which is renowned upon the surface of the earth and has always been protected by kings born from my own lineage—
therein lived one of the Vaiśya caste known as Dhanapāla.
O best of the twice-born, he established a divine sanctuary in that city;
in that divine sanctuary, having taken refuge in the meaning of the Vedas and honored a multitude of distinguished Brahmins, he resided.
Having especially honored the reciter— who is the best of the twice-born, the best of sages, and a great ascetic— by means of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas,
and having also worshipped the book with perfumes, flowers, and offerings;
Having arranged it before that assembly of Brahmins and Vyāsa,
this best of reciters, a twice-born man, was addressed by him:
"O Lord of Gods, here stands the thousand-rayed Sun."
"Or rather, let this assembly of the four castes who desire to hear remain here, O best of the twice-born, and perform the reading from the book,
so that the Sun may indeed become the granter of boons to me for seven births."
"O Brahmin, for as long as a year, I shall provide you with excellent sustenance;
O Brahmin, thereafter I will give you another hundred gold *niṣkas*.
When the year is complete, O best of the twice-born, I shall do so for the sake of my own spiritual welfare."
When that meritorious recitation of the book had thus proceeded,
O best of gods, after only six months had passed,
he likewise met his end in the interim.
"And I have sent a celestial chariot for him as he performs his vow;
such is my satisfaction with this deed, honored by the recitation of his meritorious life-story,
which is not produced for me even by offerings of perfumes and flowers."
O best of gods, O supreme one, my joy in hearing the Purāṇas is such that even the gift of cattle,
gold, silver, and all kinds of garments,
as well as villages and cities, does not bring me such pleasure.
"O best of gods, O Guha,

commander of the celestial army, the hearing of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas is not so pleasing to me as when those who perform a śrāddha for me with various kinds of foods, both solid and soft, [hear them]."
O best of gods, the joy I derive from the recitation of a book is not equaled by any other pleasure;
nor does the joy I feel at a *śrāddha* performed for the ears (*karṇa-śrāddha*) arise in the same way from a *śrāddha* consisting of food offerings.
Now, what is the use of speaking at length? O Lord, there is nothing else that brings me such joy as a meritorious narrative; this secret has been proclaimed.
And as for this other brahmin, the best of men, who has arrived here—
This best of the twice-born lived in that very same excellent city.
Once, O best of the twice-born, he went with devotion and filled with supreme faith to hear the most excellent discourse on Dharma.
Having heard that unsurpassed and meritorious narrative there with devotion,
and having performed a circumambulation of that high-souled reciter,
this brahmin, O best of the immortals, gave a gold māṣaka.
Having given a sacrificial fee to that reciter of immeasurable splendor,
the brahmin attained bliss as if he had obtained gold;
for this alone was his fruitful deed, and he performed no other.

Whatever worship has been performed by him for the high-souled reciter, the fruit of that very action is indeed this: that I myself have been worshipped. Whoever, endowed with faith and devotion, worships the reciter—
By that, I am indeed honored; for who else is Viṣṇu or Śaṅkara?
He who feeds the reciter with devotion shall feed me with the most excellent offerings;
by him I am truly honored for fifteen years.
Neither Yama nor Yamī, nor Manda nor Manu,
nor even Tapatī was sought after by me as much as my messenger;
for when the messenger is honored and fed, O Lord, O Commander of the Divine Armies, [the mission is accomplished].
“O Lord, my satisfaction lasts for two hundred years.
Not only does joy arise for me when the reciter is fed,
but it likewise arises for all the deities, beginning with Indra.”
"He is the most excellent designator of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others for me;
when he is pleased, all the deities are pleased—of this there is no doubt.
Thus was everything told to these two by that one of great power.
They performed no other deed with their wheel; what else do you wish to hear?
Having seen this marvel, I have come here into your presence. O Lord of Gods, tell me the truth of this matter; I am filled with curiosity.
Having heard the words of the youth, Brahmā, the Grandfather of all the worlds, said:
"Ah! O noble one, you are virtuous; there is no other equal to you."
For those two who were seen by you are indeed highly meritorious doers of virtuous deeds;
O child, what was spoken by Bhānu shall be exactly so and not otherwise.
O son, that face of mine which was first honored by the world— [it has now become thus].
Therefore, all these Itihāsas and Purāṇas have issued forth from me on every side out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds;
O high-minded one, just as these Purāṇas are dear to me.

O Great-minded One, neither the knower of the four Vedas nor one skilled in the auxiliary sciences attains such [merit] as those who constantly listen to these [teachings] with devotion and endowed with faith; indeed,
having provided a livelihood for the reciter, they go to the supreme state.
O observer of noble vows, the Itihāsas and Purāṇas were created by me for the supreme clarification of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa;
for these four Vedas are always considered to have their meanings hidden.
Therefore, O Mahāmati, these were created for the sake of their awakening;
he who constantly causes the supreme hearing of the Dharma to be performed,
having reached the Sun from the Ādityas, goes to that highest state.
Having given a sacrificial fee there, one shall go to the city of Āditya.
O best of gods, what wonder is there? For that is the supreme vessel for gifts; just as the scribe is the foremost among gods, and just as the thunderbolt is the supreme weapon.

Likewise, the reciter is the most excellent among Brāhmaṇas; there is no doubt in this matter. Just as fire is the foremost among radiant things and the ocean is the foremost among bodies of water, so too is the reciter remembered as the most preeminent among all the twice-born.
The man who worships the reciter with devotion has, in this world, worshipped everything; of this there is no doubt.
O upholder of my lineage, what has been spoken by the Sun is the truth, without a shadow of doubt.
"The vessel shall never at any time be anything other than equal to the reciter.
Having heard those words of Brahmā, Kumāra spoke these words:
"Oh, how blessed is he who causes the merit of this [text] to be heard!"
"Indeed, for one who gives a gift to the reciter, there is great merit.
Brahmā said:
"O Diṇḍi, he who always [acts] thus in the temple of the God of gods..."
"By listening to the Dharma, he shall attain the supreme goal.

Thus ends the ninety-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Listening to the Meritorious [Text]," in the *Saptamī-kalpa* of the *Brāhma-parvan* within the glorious *Bhaviṣya-mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the ninety-fifth chapter.
Description of the Greatness of the Abode of the Sun.
Brahmā said:
He who, having performed three circumambulations, bows down to the Sun;
He who goes with his head touching the ground attains the supreme goal.
But that man who ascends a temple while wearing shoes goes to the terrible hell known by the name Tāmisra.
He who indeed voids phlegm, urine,
or excrement in the temple of the Sun-god shall go to hell in succession.
[Likewise, one who spills] ghee, honey, milk, water, or excellent sugarcane juice...
O Bull-bannered Lord, those men who give here for the purpose of bathing the God attain all their desires in this world and then go to the solar orb;
and those who behold the Sun being bathed with devotion, O Vṛṣadhvaja, [attain the same].
Having obtained the fruit of the horse sacrifice, they attain dissolution in the one whose banner is the bull.
And those who perform the ablution of the Sun endowed with devotion,
O Bhīma, obtain that fruit of both the Rājasūya and the Aśvamedha sacrifices.

Just as no one should ever transgress the ritual bath of the Sun, so too must this [observance] be performed with great effort; for its transgression brings misery. One who transgresses it goes to the Tāmisra hell and to the Raurava hells.
Therefore, with every effort, the ritual bathing should be performed first.
By bathing the Lord with ghee, a human being attains a lotus-like state;
with honey, he attains what is dear; and even with water, he attains the abode of Ghr̥taka (the Milky Ocean).

Having bathed the one whose banner is the lotus (Viṣṇu) with sugarcane juice and milk, one should likewise bathe the Sun with these [substances]; thus one shall obtain the desired fruit. Thus ends the ninety-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Abode of Āditya," in the Saptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan within the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the ninety-sixth chapter,
the description of the seventh day named Jayā.
Diṇḍi said:
O Lord, these seven groups of seven that have been described by you to me—
of those, the first has been told in detail. O tiger among gods, please tell me all the others as well.
"Having fasted on that [seventh day], I shall then go to the house of Helī in Vraja.
Brahmā said:
"On the seventh day of the bright fortnight, when the constellation consists of five stars..."

When that [seventh lunar day] occurs, it should be known as the seventh named Jayā. On that day, whatever is given, offered in sacrifice, recited, used for libations, or performed as worship of the gods— even worship of the Sun— is declared to be a hundredfold more meritorious.
This seventh lunar day, which destroys sins, is indeed dear to Bhāskara;
it bestows wealth, fame, sons, and desired objects, and brings about the birth of lotuses.
This lunar day, which belongs to me, should be observed according to this rite.

Listen to that procedure from me, by performing which one attains one's purpose. O Śaṅkara, having fasted on this white seventh day (Śukla-saptamī) in the month of Haṃsa (Bhādrapada), known as Haṃsī, it should be observed according to this rite.
The third day shall be the breaking of the fast; this was declared by the one who rides upon the bull.
The wise have stated that the first breaking of the fast occurs after four months. O observer of noble vows, the flowers prescribed for this occasion are those of the *karavīra*.
One should offer red sandalwood and the finest guggulu resin for incense,
as well as well-cooked kāsāra as an offering to the Sun;
having thus worshipped Mārtaṇḍa, the lord of the wise, according to this rite.
O Bhīma, one should worship the brāhmaṇas with various kinds of food and edibles according to the prescribed rules.
On this day of breaking the fast, the wise man should feed the brāhmaṇas at Kāsāra.
Likewise, he himself should eat, being pure and observing silence.

On the fifth day, one should eat only one meal; on the sixth, the practice of eating only at night begins. Having observed a fast on the seventh, the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) should take place on the eighth.
This eighth day must never be performed joined with the sixth; it must always be joined with the seventh.
Just as the wise declare that one has fasted on the sixth day for the sake of fasting, and as they observe a fast on the eleventh day,
so too is this [twelfth day] proclaimed for the purpose of fasting.
The mantra for bathing with *siddhārthaka* (white mustard seeds) is: "May the Sun be pleased with me here. Likewise, there is the consumption of cow dung and a tooth-stick made from the *arka* plant.
Thus, O dear one, this procedure has been described for the first breaking of the fast.
O Bhīma, hear the second method of breaking the fast as I describe it:
one should offer jasmine flowers and sandalwood paste here,
and for the Sun, one should prescribe milk-rice as the food offering and the Vijaya incense.
O Lord, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas or likewise eat oneself;
here one should proclaim the name of the deity, saying, "May Ravi be pleased with me.
One should consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and use Khadira wood for cleaning the teeth.
O Hero, the procedure for the second breaking of the fast has now been declared by me;
listen to me as I describe the third breaking of the fast as well.
On this occasion, the wise man should worship the Sun with Agasti flowers.
Anointing with sandalwood and flowers is prescribed,
as well as incense of *sihlaka*, which is said to be supremely pleasing to the Sun;
the food offering (*naivedya*) should consist of *śāli* rice accompanied by *rasāla*.
One should give [food] to the Brāhmaṇas and likewise eat it oneself;
one should consume water with Kuśa grass and use Badarī wood for cleaning the teeth, while reciting the name of the deity: "May Vikartana be pleased with me."
During the rainy season, the worship of the God of gods should be performed according to the prescribed rites with offerings of perfumes, flowers, and various spectacles,
as well as by gifts of cows, gifts of land, and the gratification of Brahmins.

Having thus worshipped the Lord of Gods, he should stand before the deity and cause the recitation of the book— which is supremely meritorious and auspicious— to be performed; thereafter, he should honor the reciter with garments, perfumes, and incense.
Standing before the deity, one should then recite this mantra:
"O God of gods, Lord of the world, destroyer of all diseases and afflictions;
Lord of the planets, eye of the worlds, sun, dispeller of darkness!"

"O Lord of the Gods, this seventh day has been performed by me under your grace; it is named Jayā, auspicious, blessed, and the destroyer of sins. O Hero, whoever shall observe this seventh day according to this rite,"
