O Lord, for one who performs this Saptamī vow, O Hero, all his acts— bathing and the rest— become a hundredfold more efficacious. By performing this, a person shall obtain fame,
wealth, grain, gold, sons, noble strength, and prosperity.
Having attained this, O tiger among gods, he goes to the world of the Sun;

returning from there to earth once more, that wise man becomes a king of kings. Thus has been described, O hero, this seventh [day] called Jayā; when performed, remembered, or heard, it bestows the world of Hari.
Thus ends the ninety-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Saptamī named Jayā," in the Saptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan within the glorious *Bhaviṣya-mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the ninety-seventh chapter,
"Description of the Jayantī-kalpa."
Brahmā said:
O Three-eyed One, that seventh day in the bright fortnight of Māgha is called Jayantī; it is declared to be meritorious, sin-destroying, and auspicious.
O beloved of Pārvatī, listen to the procedure by which that [vow] is to be observed.
The learned have declared four concluding meals (pāraṇas) here:
a single meal on the fifth day and a night-meal (nakta) on the sixth is proclaimed.
The fast should be observed on the seventh day, and the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) should take place on the eighth;
likewise in the months of Māgha, Phālguna, and Caitra, O observer of good vows.
One should offer beautiful *baka* flowers and use saffron as an unguent.
The food offering here consists of sweetmeats (modaka), and clarified butter is prescribed as the incense.
The consumption of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) is the supreme means of purification.
O Lord of Gaṇas, one should feed the Brahmins with sweetmeats according to one's capacity.
O Lord of Beings, one should indeed give śāli-rice to the twice-born according to one's capacity.
O Hero, he who thus worships Bhāskara, who is honored by the world, shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice at every completion of the fast.
On the second breaking of the fast, having performed worship, one obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
O observer of good vows, in the months of Vaiśākha, Āṣāḍha, Jyeṣṭha, and Śrāvaṇa,
one should offer hundred-petaled lotuses for the worship of the Sun.
O Bhīma, white sandalwood is prescribed, and the incense is said to be guggulu;
the food offering consists of jaggery-cakes, while the substance for consumption is cow dung.
Furthermore, for the meal of the Brahmins, jaggery-cakes are proclaimed.
This second fast, which destroys sins, has been described;
it yields the fruit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices and is dear to the Sun-god.
Now hear about the third [fast] for the purpose of worshipping the divine Bhāskara.
O Hero, O Lord, one should prescribe red sandalwood in the months of Bhādrapada, likewise in Āśvayuja,
and also in the month of Kārttika;
here, Mālatī flowers and the incense called Vijaya are prescribed.
The food offering consists of ghee-filled cakes, and the meal for the twice-born is likewise;
the consumption of water infused with *kuśa* grass is the supreme means for purifying the body. This third fast, known as *pāraṇa*, is proclaimed to be the destroyer of sins.

I shall now describe to you the fourth fast, which grants the fruits of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices, is dear to the Sun-god, and destroys all sins. It grants the fruits of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices and is dear to the Sun-god.
Therefore, O tiger among gods, listen now for the sake of your welfare regarding this breaking of the fast:
O hero, in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, and likewise in Pauṣa, O Śiva,
and in Māgha, O tiger among gods— listen to the merits in their entirety.
Red oleanders (karavīra), red sandalwood,
incense known as amṛta, and the supreme food offering of milk-rice (pāyasa) are to be procured; likewise,
buttermilk is prescribed as the supreme substance for consumption.
Agallochum, sandalwood, nut-grass, storax, and likewise the three pungents (ginger, black pepper, and long pepper) should be prepared in equal parts; this is called Amṛta.
Herein, the names of the great-souled Bhāskara have been declared.
"Citrabhānu, Bhānu, Āditya, and likewise Bhāskara—may they be pleased. One should prescribe this ritual for every breaking of the fast.
Whoever performs the worship of Vibhāvasu according to this rite, [attains the fruit].
On that lunar day, O God of gods, he attains the supreme state.
Having thus observed the Saptamī, O Bhīma, one obtains all desires;
he who seeks a son obtains sons, and he who seeks wealth obtains wealth.

One who is afflicted by disease is liberated from diseases and attains abundant auspiciousness. O Bhīma, when the year is complete, a worship of the Sun-god must be performed with offerings of perfumes, flowers, and the gratification of Brāhmaṇas.
With various kinds of spectacles and by honoring the reciter,
having thus worshipped the Lord of Gods and honored the Brahmins,
and having honored the twice-born reciter, one should utter this speech:
"O King, may victory always be mine in all matters of dharma, in all matters of wealth,
and in all matters of pleasure.
Then he should dismiss the brahmins and the reciter, the best of the twice-born."
Whoever performs this in this manner shall obtain the fruit of victory;
with his soul purified of all sins, he goes to the world of the Sun,
mounted upon an excellent celestial chariot to the supreme abode born of the Lotus-born One.
In splendor he resembles the sun; in radiance he is like Garuda.
Thus ends the ninety-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Jayantī Kalpa," in the Saptamī Kalpa of the Brāhma Parvan within the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the ninety-eighth chapter.
Brahmā said: O Lord of the Gaṇas, that which is the seventh day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada is Aparājitā.
She is renowned as Aparājitā, the destroyer of great sins. One should prescribe a single meal on the fourth day, a night-meal on the fifth,
a fast on the sixth, and the breaking of the fast on the seventh.
In this regard, the wise have declared four types of concluding offerings (pāraṇā):
flowers of the *karavīra*, red sandalwood,
the preparation of incense with *guggulu*, and an offering of food consisting of molasses cakes.
This procedure has been proclaimed for the months beginning with Bhādrapada:
white and formidable flowers, as well as white sandalwood;
clarified butter is declared here as the incense, and milk-rice (pāyasa) is the food offering for the Sun.
This procedure has been proclaimed for the months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa.
Thereafter, the flowers of Agastya and saffron are for the unguent;
storax is prescribed for incense, or else the color of the sun (red sandalwood).
In the months beginning with Phālguna, the food offering (naivedya) should consist of flavorful rice cooked with śāli grains;
likewise, O Lord of Beings, red lotuses, agallochum,
and sandalwood are prescribed as incense for Ananta, while the food offering consists of sweet cakes made with sugar.
Śrīkhaṇḍa, aguru with knots, sihlaka, mustā, indra, and sugar, O Lord of Beings, are taken for three days. Thus,
O best of gods, this infinite incense has been described.
The wise have likewise declared this procedure for the months beginning with Jyeṣṭha.
Listen, O observer of good vows, to the names of the deity and the substances to be consumed:
Sudhāṃśu, Aryaman, Savitṛ, and Tripurāntaka.
At every conclusion of the fasts, one should proclaim, "May [the deity] be pleased.
A man who performs this seventh [observance] according to this rule— [offering] cow-urine, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), warm ghee, milk, and curd— [attains the desired fruit].
He shall always be unconquered by enemies in battle;
having conquered the enemy, he shall also attain the three aims of life—of this there is no doubt.
Having attained the three aims of life, he then enjoys the city of Svarbhānu.
Then, when the months are complete, one should worship the Sky-goer (Viṣṇu) according to one's ability with perfumes, flowers, and offerings, as well as by listening to the Purāṇas,
by the gift of a horse to the Lord, and by the gratification of the Brāhmaṇas.
Having worshipped the reciter, who is always dear to Bhāskara,
one should offer banners adorned with various jewels to Bhāskara;
O hero, he who thus always observes the Saptamī with diligence [attains the fruit].

Having truly conquered his enemy, he goes to the same world as the *haṃsa* birds by means of a vehicle drawn by white horses, which is watery and adorned with banners. Resembling the lord of the waters, he becomes a follower of the waters.
Thus ends the ninety-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of Aparājitā," in the Saptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan within the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa.
Now begins the ninety-ninth chapter: "The Description of the Mahājayā-kalpa."
Brahmā said:
When the sun enters [a new zodiac sign] on the seventh day of the bright fortnight,
that seventh day is indeed Mahājayā, beloved of the Sun.
Bathing, giving gifts, recitation, fire-offerings, and the worship of the ancestors and the gods—
all these are said to be multiplied ten millionfold, according to the word of Bhāskara. That man who, with devotion, bathes the Sun with clarified butter on that day [attains this merit].
Having obtained the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice, he shall attain the heavenly world.
That devoted man who bathes the Sun with milk,
being liberated from all sins, goes to the same realm as the Sun.
Adorned with a garland of networks of tinkling bells, he travels in a celestial chariot made of camphor;
resembling Hari in splendor and equal to the sun in brilliance,
the king remains there for a long time and quickly attains sovereignty.
O Destroyer of Tripura, this seventh [day] has been declared as the Mahājaya;
by fasting upon it with devotion, a man goes to the world of the Sun,
and from there he proceeds to the Supreme Brahman, reaching which he does not grieve.
Thus ends the ninety-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Mahājayā Kalpa," in the Saptamī Kalpa of the Brāhma Parvan within the glorious *Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the hundredth chapter:
"The Description of the Nandā Saptamī."
Brahmā said:
O hero, that seventh lunar day (saptamī) which falls in the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa is called Nandā; it is auspicious and bestows joy upon all.
On the fifth day, a single meal is prescribed; on the sixth, eating at night is proclaimed;
and on the seventh, the wise declare that one should observe a fast.
In this regard, the wise here praise three occasions for breaking the fast.
One should offer here *mālatī* flowers, fragrant sandalwood,
and incense blended with camphor and agallochum;
as for the food offering dear to the Sun, it should consist of curd-rice mixed with sugar.
One should give that very [food] to the Brahmins and eat it oneself thereafter.
This is the rule for the first breaking of the fast regarding incense for the Sun-god;
O Lord, Palāśa flowers are the incense that is indeed possible to obtain.
Camphor, sandalwood, costus, aloe-wood, and likewise storax;
along with granthiparṇa, vṛṣaṇa, bhīma, saffron, and likewise garlic;
and also myrobalan, O Bhīma—this is called the *pakṣaka* [incense].
Incense is prescribed for awakening, as is the food offering of sugar-candies and sweetmeats;
likewise black agallochum, white lotus, bālaka, and vṛṣaṇa.
Sandalwood, tagara, and mustā, combined with sugar, constitute the awakening [incense].
O Lord of the Gaṇas, one should also feed the Brāhmaṇas with sweets and solid foods;
then, having consumed a neem leaf, one should eat while remaining silent.
This is proclaimed as the rule for the second breaking of the fast.
One should bring blue lotuses, white flowers, and guggulu incense;
milk-rice (pāyasa) should be offered as the food-oblation for the pleasure of the Sun.
Sandalwood paste is the unguent; now the rule for the consumption [of the remnants] is stated.
O Hero, this supreme rite has been declared for you as well;
listen to the names of the God which always purify men:
"May Viṣṇu, Bhaga, and Dhātṛ be pleased"—thus one should indeed utter them.
He who performs this rite with a disciplined mind,
having attained his desires in this world, rejoices for eternal years;
thereafter, having gone to the abode of the Sun, he rejoices, O increaser of joy.
O Śiva, this Nandajanani has been described to you by me;
having fasted upon her and then eaten, one indeed rejoices after attaining Haṃsa.
Thus ends the hundredth chapter, titled "The Description of the Seventh Day Named Nandā," in the Saptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan within the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the one hundred and first chapter, the Description of the Bhadrakalpa.
Brahmā said:
When the constellation of the Sun occurs on the seventh lunar day of the bright fortnight,
and it happens for the first time, then indeed one attains auspiciousness. On that occasion, the wise have prescribed a ceremonial bath for the God with clarified butter.
O Hero, having likewise bathed the Lord of Gods with milk and then with sugarcane juice, one should anoint him with sandalwood paste; then,
having burned guggulu resin, one should offer auspicious incense before him.
Scattering pure wheat flour, which resembles the moon,
together with diamonds and molasses, and adorned with red flowers;
one should place a pearl upon that horn of his which faces the northeast (Īśāna).
One should place a ruby or a red gem there in the southeast;
one should provide a crocodile in the southwest and a ruby in the northwest;
finally, the wise man should place gold according to his capacity.
On the fourth day, one should observe eating only once a day; on the fifth, one should prescribe eating only at night;
on the sixth, it is declared that one should eat only what is unasked for (ayācita); and after this, indeed, comes the fast (upavāsa).
One should avoid heretics, those engaged in improper acts, those who act like cats (vaiḍālavratika), and outcasts.
On the seventh [day], the wise man should observe the vow and avoid sleeping during the day.
For whoever performs the Bhadrasaptamī according to this rite,
the Ṛbhus always bestow all auspicious things upon him.
He who bestows auspiciousness upon this [tithi] shall have a son named Bhadra;
having attained auspiciousness, O Lord of Beings, he always abides in prosperity.
Diṇḍi said:

"Who is this one called 'Bhadra'? How is the ornament to be made? What fruit does one know comes from giving it, and by what rite is it bestowed? Brahmā said: [The following is the response: "This Bhadra is the son of Viśvakarman; he is the foremost among artisans. One should fashion him with gold, silver, copper, iron, or even clay. Having fashioned him according to the prescribed rule, one should worship him with fragrant flowers and incense. Then, having circumambulated him three times, one should give him as a gift. By giving him, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices. He who gives Bhadra according to this rite attains the highest state. Brahmā said: [The following is the response: "This Bhadra is the son of Viśvakarman; he is the foremost among artisans. One should fashion him with gold, silver, copper, iron, or even clay. Having fashioned him according to the prescribed rule, one should worship him with fragrant flowers and incense. Then, having circumambulated him three times, one should give him as a gift. By giving him, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices. He who gives Bhadra according to this rite attains the highest state. Brahmā said: [The following is the response: "This Bhadra is the son of Viśvakarman; he is the foremost among artisans. One should fashion him with gold, silver, copper, iron, or even clay. Having fashioned him according to the prescribed rule, one should worship him with fragrant flowers and incense. Then, having circumambulated him three times, one should give him as a gift. By giving him, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices. He who gives Bhadra according to this rite attains the highest state. Brahmā said: [The following is the response: "This Bhadra is the son of Viśvakarman; he is the foremost among artisans. One should fashion him with gold, silver, copper, iron, or even clay. Having fashioned him according to the prescribed rule, one should worship him with fragrant flowers and incense. Then, having circumambulated him three times, one should give him as a gift. By giving him, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices. He who gives Bhadra according to this rite attains the highest state. Having fashioned him according to the prescribed rule, one should worship him with fragrant flowers and incense. Then, having circumambulated him three times, one should give him as a gift. By giving him, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices. He who gives Bhadra according to this rite attains the highest state. Brahmā said: [The following is the response: "This Bhadra is the son of Viśvakarman; he is the foremost among artisans. One should fashion him with gold, silver, copper, iron, or even clay. Having fashioned him according to the prescribed rule, one should worship him with fragrant flowers and incense. Then, having circumambulated him three times, one should give him as a gift. By giving him, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices. He who gives Bhadra according to this rite attains the highest state. Brahmā said: [The following is the response: "This Bhadra is the son of Viśvakarman; he is the foremost among artisans. One should fashion him with gold, silver, copper, iron, or even clay. Having fashioned him according to the prescribed rule, one should worship him with fragrant flowers and incense. Then, having circumambulated him three times, one should give him as a gift. By giving him, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices. He who gives Bhadra according to this rite attains the highest state. Brahmā said: [The following is the response: "This Bhadra is the son of Viśvakarman; he is the foremost among artisans. One should fashion him with gold, silver, copper, iron, or even clay. Having fashioned him according to the prescribed rule, one should worship him with fragrant flowers and incense. Then, having circumambulated him three times, one should give him as a gift. By giving him, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices. He who gives Bhadra according to this rite attains the highest state. Brahmā said: [The following is the response: "This Bhadra is the son of Viśvakarman; he is the foremost among artisans. One should fashion him with gold, silver
The sky is declared to be auspicious, the incomparable emblem of the gods;
by wearing it here, a man is released from all sins.
It should be made from a mass of rice, four-cornered and incomparable.
O Lord of the Gaṇas, it should be prepared with cow's ghee, mixed with candied sugar,
filled with the four spices (cāturjātaka), and especially with grapes and coconut fruits, and made fragrant.
The wise man should place a medium-sized indranīla gem at the center of the Bhadra [pavilion] according to his capacity;
likewise, he should place a puṣparāga, a marakata, a padmarāga,
and an incomparable māṇikya in the corners in due order.
Or he may give it to the reciter, or even to the one who feeds him himself;
whoever, having performed this rite according to this rule, bestows auspiciousness,
shall indeed attain blessings and go to the abode of the Lord of Cows.
Then, mounted upon a celestial vehicle, he shall go to the world of Brahmā without a doubt;
in brilliance he will be like a bull, in luster likewise equal to a bull,
in splendor equal to the Lord of Cows (the Sun), and in vigor equal to the Supreme Bull.

"Therefore, O hero, having returned to earth through the grace of Gopati—who is worshipped by the lords of all-knowing ones—he shall become a lord of cattle; of this there is no doubt. Thus, O Bhīma, has been told this seventh [vow] called Bhadrā."
O Bhīma, by fasting on this day, a man may attain the world of Brahmā;
O Lord of Gaṇas, those who hear it here, those who recite it, and those who perform it—
having all attained auspiciousness, they go to that eternal Brahman.
Sumantu said:
Thus did Brahmā formerly describe the Saptamī vow to Diṇḍin;
and by me, O Lord, it has been told to you exactly as it was known and as it was heard.
Any man on earth who, having undertaken the Saptamī-kalpa, should abandon it out of desire or even fear, is to be known as a fallen fool.
Therefore, O hero, observe that vow; the Saptamī-vrata must not be abandoned.
A man who abandons [this practice] becomes a hero fallen from his high station.
But he who, with devotion, causes this Saptamī-kalpa to be heard from the beginning,
attains the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice and thereafter goes to the supreme state.
Thus ends the one hundred and first chapter, titled "The Description of the Bhadrakalpa," in the Saptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan within the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the one hundred and second chapter:
"The Description of the Ritual for the Worship of the Constellations."
Sumantu said: Thus is the seventh [tithi] of the Sun, the God of gods;
just as among many wives, one may become the beloved of her husband.
"Indeed, O Bhārata, all lunar days (tithis) are dear to this Sun;
therefore, on this day, the Maker of Day should be worshipped by a man here.
Śatānīka said:
"If the Sun is declared to be the lord of all lunar days (tithis),
for what reason is his sacrifice performed by the wise on the seventh day alone?
Sumantu said:

O tiger among the Kurus, O lord, listen with a one-pointed mind as I relate to you in its entirety all that which was asked regarding this matter in the past by Viṣṇu from the Eldest of the Gods while he was stationed in heaven, and how it was answered to Hari.
O God, having bowed his head to the Grandfather, the divine Lord who was seated comfortably, Kṛṣṇa spoke these words:
"If this god Bhānumat is remembered as the lord of the lunar days (tithis)..."
"For what purpose, O Brahman, is [he] worshipped on the seventh day? Tell me, O Lord.
Thus addressed by the powerful Viṣṇu, the blessed Lord, the eldest of the gods, smiled and spoke these words.
Brahmā said:
All the lunar days (tithis) were granted to the gods by the high-souled Bhāskara,
with the exception of the seventh alone, provided they are properly propitiated.
On whichever day a deity is given [an offering], he is traditionally held to be the lord of that very day;
therefore, when worshipped on his own day with his own mantras, he becomes the bestower of boons.
Viṣṇu said:
Which day was given to whom by the high-souled Arka?
When this [day] is worshipped on its own day with its own mantras, it certainly bears fruit.
Brahmā said:
The first [day] is given to Agni; likewise, the second to Brahmā;
the third to the King of Yakṣas; and the fourth also to Gaṇeśa. The fifth is for the King of Nāgas, and the sixth also for Kārttikeya.
The seventh was established for her own sake; the eighth was given to Rudra;
the ninth was given to Durgā; the tenth herself was given to Yama;
and the eleventh was always given to the Viśvedevas.
The twelfth day was given to Viṣṇu; the thirteenth to Madana;
the fourteenth to Śaṅkara; and the full moon to Soma.
The meritorious fifteenth day was always given by Bhānu to the ancestors.
These fifteen lunar days (tithis) are proclaimed to belong to the moon; in the dark fortnight, it is drunk by these aforementioned deities,
while in the bright fortnight, it is replenished along with the sixteenth digit.
Each of those [rays] is eternally imperishable, and the Sun is directly present therein;
for it is he who causes waning and waxing, and thus he is remembered as their lord.
Established in mere meditation, the Sun bestows an undecaying state.
Others indeed grant desired objects according to one's wishes with ease;
I shall explain all that to you, O Kṛṣṇa, so listen in brief:
having worshipped and offered oblations into the fire, one obtains immortality and clarified butter.
By offering oblations of all types of grain, one shall obtain immeasurable wealth;
and by worshipping Brahmā as a celibate student on the second lunar day and feeding him, one shall become a master of all branches of knowledge.
On the third lunar day, one becomes certainly rich in wealth;
in transactions such as buying and selling, profit shall be manifold.
On the fourth lunar day, one should perform the worship of Gaṇeśa in all undertakings.
He shall undoubtedly create obstacles for his enemies and remove his own;
and by worshipping the Nāgas on the fifth lunar day, he is not overcome by poisons.
He obtains a wife and sons, and shall attain supreme prosperity.
By worshipping Kārttikeya on the sixth lunar day, one becomes preeminent,
intelligent, endowed with beauty, long-lived, and an increaser of fame.
By worshipping Citrabhānu, the Sun, the Lord of the Planets, on the seventh day, one attains these same qualities.
On the eighth day, when worshipped, Lord Hara, who is adorned with a bull,
bestows vast knowledge as well as great splendor. When fully honored, he is the destroyer of death, the giver of knowledge, and the severer of bonds.

Having fully worshipped Durgā on the ninth day with the desire to cross over difficulties, one always attains victory in battle and in worldly affairs. On the tenth day, one should worship Yama; this certainly removes all diseases.
Furthermore, it delivers a man from hell and death;
when the Viśvedevas are worshipped as prescribed on the Ekādaśī day,
they bestow progeny, cattle, wealth, grain, and likewise land.

By worshipping Viṣṇu on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī), one shall always be victorious here and become worthy of honor by all the worlds, just like the Lord of Cows (Indra). By worshipping Kāmadeva on the thirteenth lunar day (trayodaśī), one will certainly be born with a beautiful form.
One shall obtain a beloved and beautiful wife and abundant fulfillment of desires;
having beheld the Lord on the fourteenth day, one will be endowed with all sovereignty,
possess many sons, and have great wealth— of this there is no doubt.
The man who, full of devotion, worships Soma on the full moon day shall possess complete sovereignty that never diminishes.
On their own day, the ancestors, being beheld by him, always grant him blessings.
The increase of progeny, wealth, protection, longevity, and strength— these,
even without fasting, bestow the aforementioned fruits when they are always gratified with devotion through worship, recitation, and burnt offerings.
The Lords of the Lunar Days (Tithīśvaras) are proclaimed by means of their root mantras, their names, and their partial mantras; they should be placed in the center of the lotus as before,
and worshipped with offerings of perfume, flowers, and other gifts according to one's capacity.
Even worship performed according to external rites yields fruit; likewise,
an oblation consisting of streams of clarified butter, sacrificial fuel, curd, milk, cooked rice,
and honey grants the results as prescribed, provided the recitation is performed with a tranquil mind.
The root mantras and the limb mantras have been proclaimed by their respective names.
Having performed twelve sacrifices with devotion,
one shall obtain these fruits exactly as described, and even more besides.
In this world, because a knower of mantras who dwells in another's abode and remains there happily for as many lunar days as he stays,
burns away the misfortunes of those [inhabitants], a man born from that [practice] becomes of such a nature.
Handsome, endowed with righteousness, and having destroyed his enemies, he becomes a lord of the earth;
whether woman or eunuch, he is born as the best of men.
These lunar days (tithis), O Kṛṣṇa, which I have described to you, [are thus concluded].
All the deities of the lunar mansions are established within those constellations;
O Mountain, I shall describe to you those who grant desired boons.
In whichever lunar mansion the Moon is always situated for great prosperity—
When the sacrifice to the deities has been thus described, it will then become fruitful.
I shall now declare the deities of the lunar mansions (nakṣatras) in their proper order;
likewise, all the lunar mansions and the sacrifices associated with each one individually.
Having worshipped the two Aśvins under the asterism Aśvinī, a man becomes long-lived;
one who is excessively afflicted by diseases is quickly liberated from them.
Under Bharaṇī, Yama is indicated with auspicious black flowers.

Likewise, with pure perfumes and other offerings, one may release [the person] from untimely death. Anala, when supremely worshipped here on the Kṛttikā day with red garlands and other offerings, will certainly bestow the fruit through the performance of oblations.

O tiger among gods, O lord of cattle, when Prajāpati is worshipped and pleased during the asterism Rohiṇī, he likewise bestows cattle here in this world. During Mṛgaśīrṣa, Soma always grants knowledge and health.
O twice-born one, by worshipping Śiva under the asterism Ārdrā, one subsequently attains Yama;
honored with divine offerings such as lotuses and the like, he bestows well-being.
Likewise, Aditi is always worshipped in heaven under the asterism Punarvasu.
When the Gurus are gratified, they protect one like a mother;
Jupiter, when in Puṣya, bestows vast and auspicious intelligence;
and the Nāgas, when worshipped with songs, perfumes, and other offerings in Āśleṣā, grant their favor.
O giver of honor, when they have been duly gratified with sweet and white foods,
as well as with various offerings such as meat and protection, the ancestors bestow their favor; for on the Maghā day, all the ancestors are worshipped with *havya* and *kavya* offerings.

They bestow wealth, grain, servants, sons, and likewise cattle. Furthermore, when Pūṣan is worshipped with auspicious flowers and other offerings on the Phālgunī day—specifically on the Pūrvā-phālgunī—he grants victory; likewise, on the Uttarā-phālgunī, he grants fortune.
One should give a desired husband to the maiden, or her to the man; thus, in this very birth, she shall be endowed with beauty and wealth.
The Sun, the repository of universal splendor, is always honored in the hand.
By means of perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one bestows all manner of abundant wealth.

Tvaṣṭṛ, being pleased, gratified, and delighted by offerings made under Citrā, bestows a kingdom free from rivals. Vāyu, likewise satisfied and gladdened by offerings under Svātī, grants supreme strength.
Having worshipped Indra and Agni with red flowers under the Viśākhā asterism,
one shall obtain wealth and grain in this world and may always dwell as one possessed of splendor.
Likewise, having worshipped Mitra with red flowers under the Anurādhā asterisms with devotion, [one attains the same].
Prosperity attends everyone [who acts thus], and they live long at all times. By worshipping Śakra under the Jyeṣṭhā constellation as previously described, one shall obtain nourishment;
and one becomes the eldest among all in terms of virtues, deeds, and wealth.
Having worshipped all the gods and ancestors at the root with devotion as before,
one obtains the fruit as before and shall certainly abide in the heavenly realm.
Indeed, having worshipped the waters in Pūrvāṣāḍhā and offered oblations there in the same manner as before, [one attains the same result].
One is swiftly liberated from both physical and mental suffering.
By worshipping Viśveśa with flowers and other offerings during the Āṣāḍhās and through the conjunction with Uttarāṣāḍhā, a human being attains everything.

By worshiping Viṣṇu with devotion during the Śravaṇa asterism using white, yellow, and blue offerings, one attains prosperity as well as supreme victory. By making offerings to the Vasus during the Dhaniṣṭhā asterism, one never encounters fear anywhere.
Even from great fear, by means of these auspicious perfumes, flowers,
and other offerings during the Śatabhiṣā constellation, one is certainly freed from diseases;
the afflicted person attains nourishment, health, and even sovereign power.
By worshipping Aja, who resembles pure crystal, on Bhādrapadā,
one attains devotion as well as supreme victory. By worshipping Ahirbudhnya on Uttarā, one shall obtain ultimate peace.
When Pūṣan is worshipped under the asterism Revatī, he constantly bestows auspiciousness;
with white flowers, he grants stability, fortitude, and victory as well.
These sacrifices have been described by me to you in brief.
Indeed, for the benefit of practitioners and the deities of the constellations,
they always grant results when worshipped with devotion according to one's means;
whether one desires to attain the infinite or has already commenced a ritual action.
Having performed a sacrifice to the deity of the lunar mansion, one should carry out all of that;
for when this is done, one shall obtain the entire fruit of the journey and the complete fruit of the ritual— so it was said by the Sun himself.
Through sacrifice he shall achieve victory and perform whatever rite he desires;

or else, having meditated upon the Sun— the treasury of universal splendor— within the wheel of time (kālacakra) or within the wheel of the zodiac (rāśicakra) as the essence of the digits (kalā), he may accomplish everything according to his wish.
This manifestation (vibhūti) has been described; it is certainly accomplished through ritual actions.
When these [actions] are performed with effort according to the yoga of liberation, liberation itself is attained;
indeed, liberation is also obtained through the propitiation of the Sun.
Therefore, O Madhusūdana, propitiate the Sun with devotion day and night through sacrifices, worship, prostrations,
and service; by means of various vows and fasts, and by the gratification of the Brāhmaṇas.
"The man who causes an image of the Sun— the support of the heart— to be made,
attains the same world as the Sun (bhānusālokya), his sins having been destroyed.

Thus ends the one hundred and second chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Worship of the Constellations," in the *Saptamī-kalpa* of the *Brāhma-parvan* within the glorious *Bhaviṣya-mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the one hundred and third chapter:
A Description of the Greatness of the Worship of the Sun.
Brahmā said:
That man who, with devotion, causes a permanent temple to be built for the Sun,
leads seven generations of his lineage to the worlds of the Sun.
For as many years as the image of the Sun remains in that temple, [so long does he enjoy those realms].
For as many thousands of years as there are images of the gods endowed with auspicious marks in his house, provided that the ritual is performed continuously, he rejoices in the world of the Sun;
or, if his mind is free from desire, he attains equality with the Sun.
That person who, with a mind fully absorbed in that state of being, offers to the Lord of Gods flowers that are exceedingly fragrant and pleasing,
as well as various kinds of incense and richly scented unguents;
Through this worship of the Sun, a man daily obtains the fruits of sacrifices— such as offerings of lamps and oblations— as well as whatever is desired by himself;
for the Lord Sun, the master of sacrifice, is gratified even by these sacrificial rites.
Sacrifices requiring many implements and extensive collections of various materials are obtained by those men who possess wealth and gather vast resources;
however, even worship performed with devotion by men using merely sprouts of *dūrvā* grass [is efficacious].
For the Sun indeed bestows the fruit that is very difficult to obtain through all other sacrifices:
whatever flowers, edibles, incense, perfumes, ointments,
beloved ornaments, and even two red garments [one may offer].
O Lord of Gods, offer those oblations, edible foods, and fruits; and remain single-mindedly intent upon Him. Propitiate that primordial Lord of Sacrifice according to your ability.
Having propitiated the deity, he installed him in that very temple;
one should bathe the god Citrabhānu, the maker of day, with flowers, water from sacred fords, perfumes, honey, clarified butter, and likewise with milk.
O best of the Yadus, he shall go to lakes of curd and milk, and to the heavenly worlds dripping with honey;
or else,
through hymns, songs, musical instruments, and the gratification of Brahmins, he shall attain eternal bliss.
And by attaining one-pointedness of mind, worship Vibhāvasu;
having worshipped him, seventy-seven men of the Videhas and fifty of the Haihayas attained immortality.
"Therefore, satisfy that Bhāskara with these types of fasts;
for when he is pleased, the Sun becomes a bestower of peace.
Kṛṣṇa said:
How is it that Citrabhānu becomes pleased by fasts? How should service be performed, and what specifically must be done by one observing a fast?
What is to be done, and at what time, for the propitiation of Bhānu by men?
"O Brahman, you ought to relate all of that in detail and exactly as it is.
Brahmā said:
"That Sun-god, when remembered and worshipped with incense, flowers, and other offerings, is always [gracious]."

What need is there to mention its benefit for those who observe fasts? Indeed, that which is known as fasting (upavāsa) consists of turning away from sins along with the qualities of worldly attachment, being entirely devoid of all enjoyments.
O Hari, that man who, fasting for one night, two nights, or even three nights,
meditates upon the Sun with devotion—
sacrificing to His name, delighting in His rites, and having his mind fixed upon Him— [attains the supreme goal].
One who worships him free from desire attains the Supreme Brahman;
and he who, having meditated upon a specific desire with his mind fixed on the Sun,
observes a fast, obtains that [desire] when the Bull-bannered Lord is pleased.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Lord, how may those situated in the mire of the pit of worldly existence— whether Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, or women— attain a good destination?
Brahmā said:
"Then, having propitiated the Lord of the World, the Sun who dispels darkness,
with a sincere heart, he shall attain the state of the righteous."
The mind is not the grasping of sense objects nor the unevenness [of passions], but is the offering to the Sun;
how then can that man, being a doer of evil, attain a good rebirth?
If you, afflicted by the suffering of saṃsāra, desire to go to a good rebirth, [then practice this].
Therefore, devoted to fasting, worship the Lord of All, the Master of the Planets, who is honored by the world,
with fragrant and pleasing flowers, incense containing aguru and sandalwood,
garments, ornaments, and edible offerings.
If, out of weariness with saṃsāra, you desire the auspicious state,
then propitiate Kāleśa with whatever is desired by your heart. If flowers are not available, it is better to use the sprouts of trees.
O Kṛṣṇa, in the absence of those [materials], one should worship the Sun even with blades of dūrvā grass;
with flowers, leaves, water, and incense, according to one's means and with devotion, the Lord, being thus worshipped, attains incomparable satisfaction for those of single-minded focus.
The man who performs the sweeping of the Sun’s abode in the sacred precinct is liberated from all sins resulting from contact with the dust of his body.
As many particles of dust as are swept away in the temple of the Sun-god, [so many merits does he gain].
For as many divine days as there are in heaven, that man rejoices,
who sweeps the dwelling of the Sun both inside and out;
his body, both external and internal, shall become free from all stain.
And whatever man should apply anointment in the temple of the Sun,
he, having reached the world of Hari, rejoices when Hari has gone to the cows (i.e., at the time of his departure).
Whether with clay, or with products of clay, or with pigments, or with cow-dung—
A man who anoints [the image] with devotion shall obtain the status of a lord of cattle;
likewise, O Kṛṣṇa, that man who performs the ritual sprinkling of water upon the Sun shall go to the imperishable realm where the Lord of Cattle dwells forever.
A man who, having anointed himself, offers an exceedingly fragrant heap of flowers at the abode of Bhāskara shall go to the supreme house of Pūṣan;
he ascends an excellent celestial chariot composed of all kinds of jewels in the sky.
A man who gives a lamp at the abode of the Sun attains [great merit]; likewise,
the man who for a full year provides a vessel of sesame seeds and offers a banner to the Sun shall obtain an equal fruit in this world.
The sun shakes off, day and night, without a doubt, the sin committed through ignorance by the donor within the donor’s own house;
this applies to one who worships the god Vibhāvasu with songs, musical instruments, and other offerings.
Seated in a celestial chariot, he is attended by the dances and instrumental music of Gandharvas; moreover,
one who recounts meritorious narratives in the temple of Heli attains the memory of past lives, prosperity, and thereafter the supreme goal.
Therefore, one should make an effort to honor the reciter;

indeed, there is nothing anywhere that brings such pleasure to the Sun as the meritorious narration [of his deeds]. Even a single prostration made to the Lord of Rays is equal to the final purificatory bath of ten horse-sacrifices.
One who has performed ten horse-sacrifices returns to birth, but one who bows to the Sun does not return to existence.
Thus, he by whom the Lord of Gods, the Sun, is worshipped with devotion,
attains the praiseworthy state that his heart desires.
"By propitiating him, O sinless one, I attained the status of Brahmā, honored by the worlds; and you, O ancient one, have likewise obtained from Sūrya whatever you desired.
Yet Hara was overcome by the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa, though he wore earrings made of cow-horns."
Having propitiated the Sun with devotion, he was liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Indeed, some men attained the state of gods, others that of Gandharvas,
and still others that of Vidyādharas, through Divākara.

Lekha, having propitiated this Lord Divākara with a hundred sacrifices, attained the status of Indra; therefore, there is none other more worthy of worship than Divākara. Furthermore, for a religious student (brahmacārin), his own guru is to be honored even more than the gods.
Therefore, that sacrificial Puruṣa, Vivasvat, is indeed worthy of worship;
and for a woman, apart from her husband, the Sun is most worthy of worship;
and for a householder who is a husband, the Moon, the Lord of Rays, is worthy of worship.
The god Vibhāvasu, who does not perish, is to be propitiated by Vaiśyas through austerities and is always to be meditated upon by wandering mendicants;
for thus Citrabhānu is the supreme refuge of all stages of life.
"By worshipping him, one may attain the goal [of liberation] for all the social classes (varṇas).
Thus ends the one hundred and third chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Worship of the Sun," in the Saptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan within the glorious *Bhaviṣya-mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the one hundred and fourth chapter.
Listen with self-restraint to the description of the Trivarga-saptamī vow, as well as other optional fasts;
by resorting to those various [vows], one whose mind is intent on desire may accomplish his desired objects.
On the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Phālguna, a person here, being pure, should worship the deity and recite with devotion the name of the god "Helī" again and again,
performing this one hundred and eight times.
Having bathed at the time of departure, or upon rising, stumbling, or sneezing, one should not speak with heretics, the fallen, or those who act unjustly; likewise,
one should worship the sun endowed with faith.
And with the mind fixed upon that [sun], being intent on it, one should recite this:
"O Haṃsa, O Haṃsa, you are compassionate; be the refuge of those who have no refuge. Be the savior of those submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra, O Maker of Day!"
Having thus become serene and observed the fast with a restrained mind,
one should partake of water for rinsing the mouth only once during the forenoon; then,
having bathed and performed worship, one should again proclaim the name "Haṃsa."
One should likewise cast three vajra-streams at the feet of the deity during the months of Caitra and Vaiśākha,
and similarly while performing worship in Jyeṣṭha;
O Kṛṣṇa, such a man indeed attains the highest state in the mortal world.

Having departed, O Kṛṣṇa, he shall go to the auspicious and divine abode of the swans, endowed with the splendor of Indra through the grace of the bull-bannered Lord. This applies to those who die in the months of Āṣāḍha, Śrāvaṇa, and likewise Bhādrapada.
In the same manner, in the month of Āśvayuja, a man who fasts according to this rite,
worships, and likewise recites "Mārtaṇḍa," being purified by the consumption of cow's urine, shall become wealthy and go to the City of Wealth.
O Kṛṣṇa, at the time of death, one should likewise obtain the remembrance of the Sun, the imperishable soul and Lord of the worlds who has been propitiated,
as well as the drinking of milk and the performance of the rite exactly as prescribed.
One should perform [the rites] during the four months beginning with Kārttika according to the rule;
by that very procedure, O Kṛṣṇa, one should recite "Bhāskara.
He goes to the world of Bhānu and remembers Bhāskara at the time of death.
Every month, one should give gifts to the twice-born as desired;
and when the Cāturmāsya period is complete, having performed the recitation of the book,
one should here [perform] the narration of the story of the Sun-god, or even a musical performance.

The hearing of the Dharma is always desired by one who bears the banner of righteousness; therefore, having honored the reciter, a wise man should perform the Śrāddha rite with another cooked offering,
provided that the reciter is a twice-born brahmin.
Just as the sun attains its desired goal through its own inherent power,
so too, O Kṛṣṇa, a man shall always attain the threefold, supreme state of the gods— known as the three worlds— by constantly reciting this [account].
It has been told to you how, by that first breaking of the fast consisting of the gift of a cow,
a human being thereafter attains lordship as well as enjoyments;
likewise, by the second, a man shall obtain the enjoyments of the Lord of Cows (Kṛṣṇa).

By the third fast-breaking meal, one shall likewise attain the world of the Sun. Thus has been fully declared, O tiger among gods, this supreme procedure for attaining the goal, which was described regarding the Saptamī vow.

The man who observes Śvetasaptamī with faith, as does the woman with devotion, attains a happy rebirth and indeed the threefold goal. This lunar day, when constantly observed, is auspicious and removes all sins.
O Mountain, when this [work] is recited or even heard by those who seek to propitiate the Sun, it removes all sins and fear;
likewise, it is always auspicious, meritorious, and bestows the desired fruits of the three aims of life and more.
Thus ends the one hundred and fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Trivarga-saptamī Vow," in the Saptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan within the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the one hundred and fifth chapter:
"The Description of the Kāmadā-saptamī Vow."
Brahmā said: O imperishable one, on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Phālguna,
a man or a woman, having fasted and worshipped the Dispeller of Darkness (the Sun), [attains the fruit].
Chanting the name of Sūrya with devotion, eating moderately, and having conquered his senses,
he should glorify Sūrya alone while rising and while sleeping.
Then, when the next day, the eighth lunar day, has arrived, being self-restrained, he should worship Ravi.
Having bathed and worshipped the deity, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brahmin;
having performed the rite of an oblation of ghee in the fire dedicated to the Sun,
and having prostrated before the Lord of the World, one should utter these words:
"May that Lord of Gods, Vibhāvasu, by propitiating whom in the past the goddess Sāvitrī indeed obtained all her desires, grant all my desires as well—
having worshipped him, I have obtained all my desires exactly as I wished."
"The Lord of the Day, being pleased with me, grants all desires. Having worshipped him, the Lord of the Gods regained his kingdom even after it had been lost; may he grant my desire."
Having thus honored and completed the worship of Vivasvat here,
O bird-bannered one, one should eat the sacrificial food (haviṣya) properly while remaining self-restrained.
This [rite] concludes in the months of Phālguna, Caitra, Vaiśākha, or Jyeṣṭha.
The breaking of the fast should be accomplished with these four months.
For four months, one should worship the Sun with devotion using *karavīra* flowers;
one should burn black agallochum as incense and consume water produced from a cow's horn.
One should also offer sweetmeat balls (khaṇḍaveṣṭa) as an oblation to the Brahmins.
Now, listen to another practice regarding the months beginning with Āṣāḍha:
jasmine flowers are recommended, and guggulu incense is prescribed.
One should consume well water and consider milk-rice (pāyasa) as the food offering (naivedya).
One should eat that same [offering] oneself and perform the remaining rites as previously described.
During the months beginning with Kārttika, cow’s urine serves for the purification of the body.
The incense prescribed is mahāṅga, and likewise the worship is performed with red lotuses.
A lake of milk-rice (kāsāra) is to be offered here as the food-oblation (naivedya) to the Sun-god.
Furthermore, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given to a Brahmin every month.
Camphor, sandalwood, musta, agallochum, and likewise tagara;
long pepper, sugar, black fragrant resin, and likewise sihla—
this is known as the Mahāṅga incense, which is always dear to the God.
When the fast has been completed, one should please the Sun with offerings according to one's ability and as is appropriate; one must avoid deceit regarding wealth,
since the Seven-Horsed One (the Sun) is pleased only when worshipped with sincerity.

At the conclusion of the fast, when the Sun has been worshipped and bathed according to one's ability, he, being gratified, O Hari, shall grant all desired objects without fail. This meritorious seventh lunar day (Saptamī) is the destroyer of sins and the bestower of all desires.
O Garuḍadhvaja, by fasting on this day one obtains all desired objects;
indeed, in ancient times, Indra attained the three worlds by observing this fast,
Sāvitrī obtained a son, and likewise Aditi obtained sons.
The Yadavas obtained their desires, Dhaumya acquired the Veda,
and you, O Krishna, attained the daughter of Bhrigu; Shankara attained purity,
and by his grace, O Janardana, I have attained the status of the Grandfather.
Others have attained their desires by propitiating him, without a doubt—
whether they be Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, or even women.
Whatever desire one contemplates, that very thing one obtains through fasting.
For by worshipping the Sun, a person undoubtedly attains their desire:
one without a son obtains a son, and even from illness one finds joy;
the one overcome by disease gains health, and a maiden finds a virtuous husband.
Having arrived and fasted there, one who has gone abroad shall obtain this;
he attains all desires and rejoices even when dwelling among cattle.
Neither is he childless, nor poor, nor undesirable, nor devoid of compassion.
Having observed this vow, whether a mortal man or a woman, one is born [again] and,
having reached the world of Gohelila, rejoices for eternal years,
mounted upon a white vehicle and radiant as the sun.
"O Kṛṣṇa, having returned to the earth, that man shall become a king equal to a rain-cloud;
by the grace of the Lord of the Cowherds (Gopati), he shall remain upon the surface of the earth—of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Kāmadā-saptamī Vow," in the Saptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan within the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the one hundred and sixth chapter,
the description of the ritual procedure for the Pāpanāśinī vow.
Brahmā said:
Furthermore, O highly fortunate one, listen as I speak;
this supreme majesty of the lunar days (tithis) was proclaimed by the bird to the gods.
Viṣṇu said:
O best of chariot-warriors, I have heard from you of Vijayā, Atijayā, Jayantī, and the great lunar day (Mahātithi) which destroys sin;
now tell me of that which is likewise auspicious for the worship of the Sun during the northern course (Uttarāyaṇa).
"Tell me with effort, as I have asked with devotion, that place where the Sun, when fully worshipped, becomes the destroyer of all sins, and which yields imperishable fruit. Brahmā said:
On the seventh day of the bright fortnight, whichever lunar mansion coincides with the sun,
then that seventh day becomes highly meritorious and destructive of sins;
on that day, one should worship the Lord of Gods, Citrabhānu, the Teacher of the World.
One is liberated from the sins committed over seven lifetimes; there is no doubt about this.
And he who observes a fast on that day with a restrained mind, his soul being freed from all sin, is glorified in the world of the Sun.
Whatever gift is given with the Sun in view,
or whatever oblation is performed there, all that shall become inexhaustible.
Furthermore, if even a single verse of the Rigveda is recited in front [of him] by one filled with faith, [the merit is likewise infinite].
The Sun bestows the certain and excellent fruit that belongs to the entire Ṛgveda;
the Sāman yields the fruit of the Sāmaveda, the Yajus the fruit of the Yajurveda,
and Atharvan bestows the whole fruit of the Atharvāṅgirasa.
Shining day and night, they gleam like stars;
and having worshipped the Sun, the God of gods, on the seventh lunar day—
at which place the Maker of Light destroys every single sin.
O Kṛṣṇa, that Saptamī which destroys sins has been described by him;
by worshipping the Sun on this day,
a man ascends an excellent celestial chariot made of camphor and goes to the city of the Sun.
In splendor like a poet, in radiance resembling the sun,
in beauty equal to the son of Atri (Dhanvantari), and always in valor like Hari, O Kṛṣṇa,
he rejoices there for a very long time together with hosts of gods.
"O Kṛṣṇa, having returned to earth, he shall indeed become the sovereign of the lords of the earth.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Pāpanāśinī Vrata," in the Saptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan within the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the one hundred and seventh chapter.
The Description of the Vow of the Two Feet of the Sun.
Brahmā said:
O knower of dharma, listen further as I speak of another [vow].

O Kṛṣṇa, those two feet of the Lord of the World, the God of gods, the Lord of Light— those very two feet which form a single footstool were placed there by the Sun himself out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
O Kṛṣṇa, the northern foot of Vāmana is to be known as the *uttarāyaṇa*, while the southern foot,
which is worshipped by all the gods and others, is the *dakṣiṇāyana*.
O Kṛṣṇa, both you and I always worship the southern foot.
Hari and Īśa, endowed with faith, worship the left [side] of the Sun;
the man who daily performs the proper propitiation of the God of gods toward that [side] shall always be pleasing to Bhānumat.
Viṣṇu said:
"O tiger among gods, how is the propitiation of that God of gods, the Lord of the Cows, performed? You ought to explain that to me."
Brahmā said: O Kṛṣṇa, during the northern solstice, one who has bathed with a restrained mind should bathe the God, the dispeller of darkness, with ghee, milk, and other such substances.
Having properly worshipped with offerings of beautiful garments, flowers, incense, and ointments, and having likewise satisfied the Brahmins with libations,
one who is devoted to the Sun should undertake the vow of the two feet.

One should worship Citrabhānu after bathing, and likewise when eating food, when walking toward Citrabhānu, when sleeping, when waking, when bowing, when performing oblations, and when offering worship— O Garuḍadhvaja— to him, Citrabhānu.
I shall perform the chanting of the names of Citrabhānu every day,
from this very day until the commencement of the southern solstice (dakṣiṇāyana) arrives in due course;
and always at the start of the Vedas, when the breath moves, or when the sound "huṃ" is uttered.
I shall speak of Citrabhānu for as long as the sun moves northward; and whatever I have done throughout my life, whether knowingly or unknowingly,
I shall likewise perform and proclaim that Lord.
Whenever I shall speak anything untrue, then I shall utter these words:
"Whether out of ignorance or through knowledge, I shall proclaim that Supreme Lord,
the effulgent Citrabhānu, with a single-minded focus for six months."
Remembering him at the time of death, may that same destination be mine.
If my death should occur within six months from now,
then I have here offered myself to the Sun-god.
"Brahman consists of the Supreme Self; the supreme Sun consists of light. I shall remember Yama; he is my sun, my ultimate goal.
Whether at dawn, at evening, or at midday, if I recite this, [may it be so]."
Within six months, I have performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) consisting of my vow.
O Lord of the World, you who are devoted to the heavenly realm, act in such a way that you,
O Citrabhānu, may become my refuge according to my capacity.

Having thus undertaken this vow consisting of the worship of Citrabhānu for six months, one should fulfill it until the completion of the sun's southern course (dakṣiṇāyana). Thereafter, one should perform a propitiatory rite for Vibhāvasu according to one's capacity.
One should feed divine and terrestrial Brāhmaṇas with ritual fees (dakṣiṇā);
likewise, one should recount meritorious narratives in the presence of Mārtaṇḍa,
and worship the reciter with devotion as well as the scribe according to one's ability.
O Kṛṣṇa, tiger among gods, the man who observes this vow in this very life is liberated from all sins;
and if his death should occur within six months, [he attains the supreme state].
One undoubtedly attains that fruit which has been described for fasting; moreover,
the two feet of the Lord, when worshipped with perfect devotion,
become [fulfilled]— this is what Bhānu proclaimed in the past to Candra when he questioned him.
Thus ends the one hundred and seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Bhānupādadvaya Vow," in the Saptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan within the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the one hundred and eighth chapter,
"The Description of the Sarvārthāvāpti-saptamī."
Brahmā said:
Listen now to the account of the Sarvāpti Saptamī in the dark fortnight of Māgha,
by fasting upon which one attains all desires as well as the supreme goal.
One devoted to the Sun should not engage in conversation with heretics and the like;
rather, with a single-pointed mind, one should worship the auspicious Lord while remaining prostrate.
The breaking of the fast after six months, beginning from the month of Māgha, is known as the *Sāṃkrāntika* rite.
Mārtaṇḍa is the first name, Ka is proclaimed as the second; Citrabhānu is the third, and Vibhāvasu follows after that. Bhaga should be known as the fifth, and Haṃsa is said to be the sixth.
When six months have been completed, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) are prescribed;
it is commended for both bathing and consumption, as it destroys sin.
Having performed prostration to the God of gods and worship according to the rules, [one should partake of it].
One who possesses faith should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brahmin according to one's ability;
and at the conclusion of the fast, one should perform the propitiation of the Lord with devotion.
Through such devotion, performed according to the rules, one is accepted by the Sun-god.
Likewise, O Viṣṇu, eating only at night and avoiding oil and alkaline substances,
one should perform a vigil for Kṛṣṇa at night on the seventh lunar day, or during the day;
having fasted on this [day], the knower of dharma should be intent upon pleasing Haṃsa.
One obtains all desires and is liberated from all sins;
since one attains everything that one wishes for with the mind,
this day is therefore renowned in the worlds as Sarvārthāvāptisaptamī.
For this [devotion], when undertaken by those intent on righteousness,
fulfills all desires both when it is heard day after day and when it has been performed as desired;
therefore, O Garuḍadhvaja, worship that Sun.
Just as the Lord of the Constellations (Brahmā) propitiated the Sun in ancient times.
Thus ends the one hundred and eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Sarvārthāvāptisaptamī," in the Brāhma Parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the Saptamī Kalpa.
Now begins the one hundred and ninth chapter.
Description of Mārtaṇḍasaptamī.
Brahmā said:
O sinless Kṛṣṇa, I have described to you the Mārtaṇḍasaptamī just as it is.
Listen with a one-pointed mind, O hero, as I relate this auspicious [vow],
by the perfect performance of which one attains the desired fruit.
Having fasted on the seventh day of the bright fortnight in the month of Pauṣa, [one should proceed].
Having worshipped the Sun perfectly, one should indeed mutter "Mārtaṇḍa, Mārtaṇḍa.
Endowed with supreme faith and devotion, one should worship Kutapa with incense,
flowers, offerings, and the like, remaining composed through fasting.
Chanting the name "Mārtaṇḍa" with his mind fixed upon Him,
O bird-bannered one, he should give a sacrificial fee to a Brahmin according to his ability;
whether sleeping or waking, or even when stumbling, he should utter "Mārtaṇḍa."

One should avoid conversation with those who follow heretical paths or engage in improper occupations. For the sake of self-purification, one should consume cow’s urine, cow’s milk, curd, or even cow’s milk itself— all produced from the body of a cow.
On the second day, having bathed again and performed the worship of the Sun in the same manner,
and having offered a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to a Brahmin under that very name,
he should then eat together with him food prepared from the milk of a cow.
In this very manner, having fasted throughout all the months, being self-restrained and pure,
one should give cows and other gifts to Brahmins every month according to one's capacity.
Furthermore, if [the vow] was maintained for a year, one should likewise give cows and other gifts according to one's ability.
Having further given [a gift] to the Sun, hear now what fruit one enjoys:
by giving a cow with golden horns on the fifth lunar day and a bull on the sixth, to the twice-born every month, whatever fruit a man enjoys— [hear that].
One who observes this vow with complete purity attains all of that;
he reaches that world where Mārtaṇḍa dwells,
and he becomes equal to Śāṇḍileya in splendor, O Kṛṣṇa— of this there is no doubt.
"O Mountain, even today these hosts are seen shining in the sky by people who have observed this Mārtaṇḍasaptamī fast.
Therefore, you [should worship] the Sun, Ravi, the Lord of the Primordial Deity and Lord of the Planets."
"O Govinda, worship the Lord of the Cows (Gopati), who resembles a mountain of gold, with this [hymn].
Thus ends the one hundred and ninth chapter, titled "The Description of Mārtaṇḍasaptamī," in the Saptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan within the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the one hundred and tenth chapter.
In the seventh chapter, the description of the Anantara-saptamī vow:
Brahmā said,
"O Acyuta, on the seventh day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada..."
Having bowed his head to the Sun, O Hero, he should worship the one with seven steeds with flowers,
incense, and other offerings, as well as with libations of *kutapa* garments;
remaining self-controlled, he should avoid conversation with heretics and the like.
Having given a sacrificial fee to a Brahmin, one should eat at night while restraining one's speech;
whether standing, walking, or setting out on a journey, and in cases such as hunger or stumbling,
one should likewise perform the recollection and the utterance of the names of Āditya.
By this very procedure, having fasted for twelve months in succession,
and having fully worshipped the Teacher of the World on the completion of the breaking of the fast during the auspicious month of Śrāvaṇa,
one attains nourishment while pleasing Him here in this world.
Since it is declared here that the fruit of listening [to this] is infinite,
by worshipping the Sun in that manner, one obtains that very same fruit.
Thus, the pure person who should perform the propitiation of the Sun—
Having obtained here abundant enjoyment, as well as dharma and imperishable wealth,
one goes to the world beyond— a celestial realm filled with songs in the sky.
Or a woman, having reached heaven, indeed enjoys infinite fruit.
Thus ends the one hundred and tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Anantarasaptamī Vow," in the *Saptakalpa* section of the *Brāhma Parvan* within the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the one hundred and eleventh chapter:
"The Description of the Abhyaṅgasaptamī in the Saptamī-kalpa."

Brahmā said: In the month of Śrāvaṇa, on the seventh day of the bright fortnight, one who is pure should worship the foremost of gods, the seven-horsed one (the Sun), with flowers, incense, and other offerings.

Restraining his speech and maintaining self-control, he should not engage in conversation with heretics and the like; having given a sacrificial fee to a Brahmin, he should eat at night while remaining silent.
He should perform the ritual oil-anointing of the God of gods once every year.
On the seventh day, food that is foremost, auspicious, pure, and fresh is prescribed;
likewise, among other available riches, musical instruments are known to be essential.
Furthermore, in this month of the Lord, anointing the body with oil is highly extolled.
But that man who, O Acyuta, should worship the Sun with devotion,
having performed an oil massage according to the rules and to the best of his ability, and having fed the Brahmins amidst the sounding of conchs and trumpets and the abundant chanting of the Vedas;

Mounted upon a divine vehicle, he comes to the world with ease. By this very procedure, having fasted for twelve months in succession, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brahmin when the breaking of the fast is complete.
"The man who, being pure, performs this vow of worshiping the Sun shall go to the supreme world of the Divine One who wears a garland of forest flowers.
Thus ends the one hundred and eleventh chapter, titled "Description of the Abhyaṅga-saptamī Vow," in the Saptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan within the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the one hundred and twelfth chapter,
the description of the Tṛtīyā-pada-vrata.
Brahmā said:

In this way, O Kṛṣṇa, the Sun-god always bestows rewards difficult to attain upon men who worship him with devotion according to the prescribed rites, even when he is honored merely with water. Neither by the gift of living beings, nor by flowers, nor likewise by fruits does the Sun grant such results.
He is propitiated solely through fair combat and by the heart alone;
the heart free from passion, speech free from falsehood and the like,
and action devoid of violence— these three constitute the worship of the Sun.
When the mind is defiled by passion and the like, the motionless one who removes the darkness does not shine;
the swan sometimes becomes bound within that man, as if in muddy water.
Indeed, the crescent of the moon is always capable of destroying the darkness.

How can an action defiled by violence and other such faults lead to the worship of Keśava? Indeed, due to the lack of clarity in one's mind, a person does not obtain that which removes the darkness [of ignorance].
Therefore, O Acyuta, through a nature of truth and truthful speech, [one attains this].
Even by one who practices non-violence, the Sun is gratified simply through natural disposition; whereas one of crooked intent, even if he were to give his entire possessions to the god,
would not thus propitiate the Sun, the God of gods.
"Make your heart free from passion and offer it to Bhāskara;
then you shall attain Bhāskara, who is otherwise difficult to reach, without any effort at all.
Viṣṇu said:
"O Lord of Gods, this Bhāskara has been fully described by you as one who grants all desires. I ask you again about the entire procedure for his propitiation; please tell me that.
Furthermore, birth in a noble family, health, and the increase of wealth are difficult to attain."
"O Lord of the World, tell me that by which this triad is attained.
Brahmā said:
"On the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, when the moon is in conjunction with the asterism Hasta, [one attains] the birth of the world."
Having worshipped the Sun according to the prescribed rite while observing a fast, with fragrant incense, food offerings, and excellent gifts,
and having performed the worship with flowers, a householder should observe this vow for one year, joined with acts such as giving charity.
O wise one, listen attentively as I describe that gift which should be given to the foremost of sages.
One should offer, in successive order, a vajra, sesame seeds, rice, barley, gold, barley-food, water, a water-pot, sandals, an umbrella, and molasses enriched with cream;
having worshipped the Teacher of the World on whichever lunar day this [rite] is prescribed according to the injunctions for that year.
Understand these substances for consuming here as causes for the purification of the self:

cow’s urine, water, vegetable juice, greens, *dūrvā* grass, curd, rice, sesame seeds, barley, and water heated by the sun’s rays; O lotus-eyed one, milk as well—these are to be employed in succession over the months.

In a preeminent family, filled with wealth and grain, adorned with lotuses, and where all suffering has ceased, one obtains birth with unimpaired senses; one becomes free from disease, wise, and happy.
Therefore, you too, O you of unfailing vigor, should perform this propitiation of the Sun without negligence.
"Exert your power by propitiating the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign; attain all your desires!
Thus ends the one hundred and twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of the Tṛtīyapada Vow," in the Saptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan within the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the one hundred and thirteenth chapter.
[This is] a description of the worship, sweeping, and other rites at the abode of Āditya.
Viṣṇu said: "O eldest of the gods, speak again of that which I asked from the beginning."
Whatever fruit one attains by having a temple built for the Sun,
and whatever merit a person enjoys by having an image of a deity made,
as well as the fruit obtained by worshipping it according to the rules and by anointing it with unguents; [all that is attained by this].
Which garlands are recommended, and which does the Sun not deserve?
Which incenses are dear to the Sun, and which are to be avoided by the Lord of the World?
What would be the fruit of ritual service, and what the fruit of song and instrumental music?

O Father, tell me in its entirety the fruit that is obtained when the Sun is bathed with ghee, milk, and so forth, as well as the fruit from the smearing [of the temple] and other rites, compared to merely sprinkling it with water in the abode of the Maker of Day.
Brahmā said:
"Excellent, my child, that you ask here about this meritorious rule for the service of Mārtaṇḍa; listen now with a one-pointed mind."
Now hear the fruit of merit for one who causes a temple for the Sun to be built, whether of wood, stone, or even of clay:
the great fruit that belongs to one who performs sacrifice day after day with a ritual.
He who causes a temple to be built for the Sun attains that fruit:
he who causes the abode of the Blessed One to be built shall lead a hundred future lineages and a hundred past lineages to the world of the Sun.
Whatever sin has been committed over seven lifetimes, whether it be small or great,
perishes from the very commencement of the construction of a temple for the Sun.
For him who builds a house for the Sun, who consists of the seven worlds, [that sin is destroyed].
That man attains a firm foundation throughout the seven worlds. By having a praiseworthy temple for the Sun constructed on a praiseworthy portion of land, that man reaches imperishable worlds.
For as many years as the arrangement of the brick-pile remains standing,
for that many thousands of years does its maker abide in heaven;
so too for the man who has a well-characterized image fashioned.
He attains that imperishable world of Divākara;
for sixty thousand times a thousand years,
O Hero Madhusūdana, he rejoices in each of the worlds of the Sumanasas.
Having installed the image of the Sun in a highly auspicious dwelling,
a man has fulfilled his purpose and does not experience the fruit of any fault;
this applies to all those who will be and those who have been in his family throughout the duration of the kalpa.
By establishing an image of the Sun-god, one causes those very beings to cross over.
O Kṛṣṇa, in ancient times, the servants of Yama were indeed instructed by Yama himself; with nooses and staffs in their hands, they were intent on restraining living beings.
Yama said:
"May you sport according to your pleasure; let my command be observed. Living beings shall never anywhere disobey your orders."

Only those who have taken refuge in Vivasvat, the root of the world, must be avoided by you; they have no place here at all. But those in this world who belong to Vaivasvata, whose minds are fixed on him, and for whom he is their supreme goal— [they are to be honored].
Those who always worship the Sun should be avoided from afar; however,
he who— whether standing, sleeping, walking, rising, or upon stumbling or sneezing—
constantly glorifies the Lord, he is not to be avoided from afar.
O gods, those who worship the Sun with regular and occasional rites are not to be looked upon by you, for their meditation destroys your progress—
those who [worship] with flowers, incense, garments, ornaments, and other beloved offerings.
Those who worship [the sun] are not to be accepted as the dependents of my father;
those who perform the smearing [of the floor] and those who perform the sweeping in the temple of the Sun—
their lineage for three generations must be abandoned.
Furthermore, that man born of the same lineage who caused the temple of the Sun to be built must certainly not be looked upon by you with evil eyes,
for he has devoutly commissioned this auspicious image of the Lord for the sake of my father.
O heroes, that clan among men must always be avoided from afar,
where, as you wander under the seal of taking refuge in the Sun,
no man anywhere shall ever violate your command.
Thus addressed by that great-souled Yama,
the *kiṅkaras* did not heed his words, O observer of noble vows, and went instead to Satrājit, for they were all overcome by the splendor of that devotee of the Sun, Kṛṣṇa.

"Deluded, they fell to the ground like birds from a mountain. O mighty-armed one, this is the account of that man who causes this worship of the Sun— which yields great fruit— to be performed, as well as the account of him who causes a temple to be built."
Sacrifices are the destroyers of the flood of men's sins and the granters of all desires;
likewise, the Sun, the light of the world, is desired as the embodiment of all sacrifices.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Veneration, Cleansing, and Other Rites for the Temple of Āditya," in the *Saptamī-kalpa* of the *Brāhma-parvan* within the glorious *Bhaviṣya-mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the one hundred and fourteenth chapter:
The Description of the Yoga for Bathing the Sun.
Brahmā said:
Having properly worshipped an installed image of the Sun,
a person undoubtedly attains whatever desire they pray for.
He who bathes the image of the divine Ravi with ghee [attains great merit].
In every *prastha* of land belonging to the foremost of the twice-born, he gives a hundred cows;
whatever fruit may accrue from giving a hundred cows to Brahmins,
that same fruit belongs to Bāna for his bath with a *prastha* of ghee offered to the *snātaka*-yogins.
The earth with its seven islands was obtained by Bhūridyumna;
it is said that he bathed the image of the Sun with water from a jar. On the eighth day of the dark fortnight, he likewise bathed the image of the Lord of the World with clarified butter.

Having bathed [the Sun], O Kṛṣṇa, one is liberated from all sins. Furthermore, a bath for the Sun with cow-derived oblation on either the seventh or the sixth lunar day is most excellent and destroys even the greatest of transgressions.
Whatever sin a man commits, whether knowingly or unknowingly,
he washes it away by bathing the Sun with ghee during the twilight rite;
for the Sun consists of all sacrifices, and ghee is the supreme oblation.
The meeting with those two shall be the washer away of all their sins.
In those worlds where rivers flow with milk and lakes have milk-porridge for mud, he who bathes the Sun in milk rejoices.
Another donor of milk to the Sun obtains joy, a state of liberation, health, and a beautiful form for seven births;
just as curds and other derivatives originate from milk.
Just as pure milk brings about tranquility,
so too stainless knowledge arises without a doubt;
it brings favor from the planets, nourishment, and belovedness among all people.

The Lord Sun, gratified by the bathing with milk, bestows radiance upon all; he becomes gracious at the mere sight [of his devotee]. O Lord of Gods, when the Dispeller of Darkness is bathed with ghee and milk, he grants his favor.
Thus ends the one hundred and fourteenth chapter, titled “Description of the Yoga for the Bathing of the Sun,” in the *Saptamī-kalpa* of the *Brāhma-parvan* within the glorious *Bhaviṣya-mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the one hundred and fifteenth chapter, titled “Description of the Ritual for the Worship of the Sun.”
Brahmā said:
The high-souled ones praise this dialogue concerning the Sun,
which took place between Gautamī and Kauśalyā Sumanā in the abode of the gods.
Having seen Kausalyā looking exceedingly beautiful in heaven together with her husband,
a Brahmin woman named Gautamī, filled with wonder, questioned her.
Gautamī said:
In Kośala there are hundreds of gods dwelling in heaven,
as well as these wives of the gods, the Siddhas, and the wives of the Siddhas;
yet they possess neither such fragrance, nor such luster, nor such beauty of form.
Neither their two beautiful garments nor their various ornaments shone as they did when with their husband, nor indeed did they shine as yours and your husband’s do,
nor even as those of the inhabitants of heaven.

Even the power of asceticism, or charity, or the fire-oblation known as ritual action— which is free from the fluctuations of increase and decrease even for the lords of the gods beginning with Brahmā— is surpassed by the mere garment of you two who are well-bathed.
"O lady of excellent complexion, tell me everything that you both have related,
