by which my mind may be inclined toward valor, and by which men are united with it.
Kauśalyā said:
The Lord of Sacrifice, Bhānu, was indeed gratified by us through sacrifice;
this attainment of heaven is the supreme fruit of that deed.
From that comes our beautiful form, our joy, and our lovely attire as we behold [him].
O illustrious lady, I shall tell you that which you ask regarding them:
because the Sun was bathed with waters from sacred fords and with fragrant perfumes, he possesses this eternal splendor that surpasses even the gods who are lords of the three worlds.

Clarity of mind, gentleness, those who are at peace in their bodies, and whatever state of belovedness there may be— all that is the fruit of bathing with ghee. Whatever garments are desired and whatever ornaments are desired [are likewise obtained].
Whatever jewels were desired, whatever unguents were pleasing,
whatever garlands he wore, and whatever things were always dear to my husband while he was ruling his kingdom— [all those have vanished].

All these have been offered to the Omniscient One, the Protector of All, the Sun; this quality consisting of fragrant incense has arisen from that. And those beloved foods, which are pure, have been presented as an offering.
The satisfaction of the Sun, the creator of the three worlds, arises from his own qualities.
O lady of auspicious appearance, this was performed by my husband, who desires heaven, and by me; yet through this very act, the destruction of our worldly existence has been achieved.
"But those men who perform that correctly without desire, O beautiful one,
to them the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign of All, the Master, grants liberation.
Brahmā said:
Having thus worshipped Mārtaṇḍa, Arka, the Lord of Gods, and my Guru, I,
Kṛṣṇa, have obtained my desired objects for eternal years,
[anointing him] with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, saffron, ushira, and padmaka.
Anointed with devotion by men, he bestows that which arises from the ocean;
offer me the *kāleyaka*, the *turuṣka*, and the red sandalwood—
whatever things are most dear to yourself are recommended for this purpose.
O Knower of Dharma, O Acyuta, all auspicious fragrances and incenses that bring about victory should always be offered to the Sun;
one should not offer the resin of the sallakī tree, nor anything gathered with the mouth.
O knower of dharma, one intent on worship should offer incense to the Sun;
likewise, *mālatī*, *mallikā*, *yūthikā*, *atimuktika*,
*pāṭalā*, *karavīra*, *japā*, and *sevantī* flowers.
Saffron, tagara, karṇikāra with its filaments, campaka, ketakī, kunda, bāṇa, barbaramālikā,
aśoka, tilaka, lodhra, and likewise aṭarūṣaka.
Hundred-petaled lotuses are auspicious, and those called *baka* are especially so;
likewise, the *agasti* and *kiṃśuka* flowers are for the worship of the Sun.
These varieties of flowers are recommended for the worship of the Sun.
O Hari, the *bilva* leaf, the *śamī* leaf, or the leaf of the *bhṛṅgara*,
as well as the *tamāla* leaf, are always dear to the Blessed One.
So too are the *tulasī*, the black *tulasī*, and red sandalwood.
The leaf and flower of the *ketakī* bring immediate satisfaction to the Sun. O Acyuta,
lotuses, water-lilies, the red lotus, the blue lotus,
and the white lotus are always beloved by Bhānu.
One should likewise offer the lovely *girimallikā* and the intoxicating *kṛṣṇalokanmat-taka* to the Sun; however, one should not present the *karṇikārikā* flower,
nor the *kuṭaja*, the *śālmalī* flower, or any other flower that is devoid of fragrance.
It bestows fear, disease, and poverty upon those for whom there is no prohibition. Flowers endowed with fragrance and color should be offered to the Sun, the illuminator of the world.
One should worship the Wreath-Bearer (Vanamālī) with fragrant substances such as *mura*, *māṃsī*, camphor, *agaru*, and sandalwood, as well as with other auspicious materials;
and with garments made of fine silk (*dukūla*), woven cloth (*paṭṭa*), silk (*kauśeya*), bark, cotton, and the like.
One should worship the Sun with garments that are dear to oneself;
whatever foods one desires, whatever delicacies one prefers,
and whatever fruit is beloved— that should be offered to the Maker of Day.
O Acyuta, one should offer gold, gems, pearls, silver,
various sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), and whatever else is dear here,
regarding oneself as the Sun, and dedicate the sacrifice to him.
One should offer [the oblation] to the Sun-god, who possesses those various unmanifest forms.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Worship of Sūrya," in the *Ādityamāhātmya* section of the *Saptamī-kalpa* within the *Brāhma-parvan* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya-mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the one hundred and sixteenth chapter.
Description of the Ritual for the Worship of the Sun.
Brahmā said:
O Kṛṣṇa, there was once a great king born in the lineage of Yayāti.
The world-renowned universal monarch Satrājit was possessed of great strength;
he was endowed with majesty, splendor, beauty, and patience, as well as physical power.
He was perfected in fortitude and profundity, generous, and distinguished by his fame.
Endowed with intellect and skill in valor, he was highly esteemed by Brahmins;
being accomplished, a poet, and likewise a hero, he was not surpassed by those called "six-footed" (bees).
Always devoted to the five [objects of sense], he was not surpassed by the wealthy.

O Acyuta, O Lord Kṛṣṇa, he who was born from the Vasus as Rudra was endowed with the essence of beings and faith; he was indeed the vessel for the water of Ambujā, just as [the waters] are for the lotus-born Brahmā and likewise for the son of Atri.
O Kṛṣṇa, as the hermitage of Paulastya was equal to the strength of Gāṅgeya,
so too was that of Dhiṣaṇa equal to Gāṅgeya’s;
and as he was always devoted to the twice-born like Vālmīki, so was he beloved by Hari.
O tiger among gods, that mighty-armed king, endowed with many virtues of Vyāsa or the powerful son of Jamadagni,
ruled the earth consisting of seven islands upon the surface of the world, O Lord.
Regarding that mighty-armed Satrājit, who took refuge with Kṛṣṇa as his protector, those people who are knowers of the Purāṇas sing this verse:
"As long as the sun rises and as long as it sets..."
That entire territory is called Satrājita. In former times, that mighty universal monarch ruled the earth, consisting of seven continents and endowed with all jewels, according to righteousness.
Neither did he act unjustly, nor was he powerless; rather, he was generous and exceedingly powerful.
That king, who governed in accordance with righteousness, had four ministers.
Indeed, those were the four ministers of that King Satrājit.
The winds blew forever unimpeded for that King Bala; indeed, he possessed an innate devotion from birth toward Divākara,
the light of the world, who was garlanded with red sandalwood.
Beholding that sovereign’s exalted greatness, not only the people but the king himself was filled with wonder; thus,
amazed by such prosperity, the monarch began to reflect.
"How might this prosperity of mine be attained once again in another birth?
Thus, O Kṛṣṇa, that highly illustrious king reflected many times,
yet even while contemplating, he did not discover its root, despite being possessed of firm resolve.
When that king, the beloved of Bhārgava’s daughter, reached no certain conclusion, he,
remaining in the secluded inner apartments, questioned the assembled Brahmins who were learned in dharma and all those who were there for his welfare, O hero.
Having prostrated himself, the mighty-armed one said:
"O best of beings, you possess a mind characterized by trust and grace toward me;
therefore, I wish to ask something, and you ought to speak it."
O best among the knowers of the Vedas, if I am to be favored by you whose inner selves have been thoroughly cleansed by the complete knowledge of the six sciences, then may you,
being well-disposed toward me, answer what I have asked according to the truth.
"O learned ones, you who are beneficial to all, please speak.
Brahmā said:
"O lord of the earth, ask today whatever doubt is in your mind."
We shall speak according to what is right, whatever is in our minds;
for we have been gratified by you, O tiger among kings,
who protects your subjects properly and always provides us with food.
A contented Brahmin should eat, or he should resolve his doubts regarding the Dharma;
he should instruct others in what is beneficial or turn them away from what is harmful.
Then, O King, the wife of that very wise man spoke to him as he was about to speak.
With prostration, humility, and affection, she spoke this:
"O Protector of the Earth, it is not fitting for women here to speak in such a manner.
Nevertheless, O King, I shall say this, for such prosperity is exceedingly difficult to attain."
"O King, you are indeed capable of questioning the sages further regarding my doubts;
for I, O tiger among men, am one who always moves within the inner apartments.
Therefore, O ruler of the earth, if you would grant me your favor,"
"Therefore, O King, you ought to ask my sages about this doubt.
Satrājit said:
"O fair-browed one, tell me what you think should be asked of the twice-born by me."
"O best of the twice-born, I shall ask these further questions regarding my own doubts.
Vimalavatī said:
"O protector of the earth, those kings who are of ancient times are indeed heard of."

"O protector of the earth, by what ripening of karma did you come to possess such prosperity as you now have? O lord of the world, let the great seers explain how you became the abode of such complete abundance."
And I am your wife, the most excellent of all women; because of my past deeds, I have a great curiosity regarding that knowledge. For even the abundance of prosperity is found among others as well.

"O Lord of Men, because it is free from all excellence, your own conduct in another birth was surely not accomplished by a small deed. Ask the sages about that which was performed by you and by me in the past."
Brahmā said:
Thus addressed by his wife, the king, his mind filled with wonder,
spoke these words in the presence of the sages, praising her illusory power (māyā).
"Excellent, O Goddess, is this resolve of mine which has been expressed by you.
Truly, the word of the sages must be followed by men, and likewise by their wives.
Therefore, O highly blessed one, I shall ask these great sages about this."
"There is nothing in the three worlds unknown to them.
Having spoken thus to his beloved and having prostrated before those sages, the king,
the upholder of the earth, questioned them about all this exactly as it was.
The king said:
"O venerable ones, with your minds filled with grace toward me, please relate everything exactly as it happened regarding whatever meritorious deed was performed by me."
"O Brahmins, who was I in the past, and what deed was performed by me?
Or what has been done by this wife of mine, O twice-born ones,
that we possess this splendor which is so difficult to attain in the world of mortals?"
Four unassailable ministers accompany me as I go; all kings are under my control, and there is no end to my wealth. My power is likewise irresistible, and my body is free from ailment.

"O twice-born ones, the entire world appears to me as my wife because of her splendor; yet no one can endure the radiance of my own body. Therefore, I desire to know that [truth], and likewise this blameless woman."
"His own entire performance of rites has this whole world as its fruit.
Brahmā said:
"Thus questioned by the lord of men, all those ascetics..."
Then they said to Parāvasu, "Let the lineage of this king be told.
Thus urged by those who know the dharma, that great hero and high-minded man, having established himself in yoga for a very long time, exerted himself with a disciplined mind according to the rule.
Having understood the king's former deeds in a previous life,
that sage spoke to that high-minded monarch who desired knowledge— namely,
the noble Satrājit, the wise one who had conquered his enemies.
Parāvasu said to the highly intelligent and truthful Brahmins who were accompanied by their wives:
"O protector of the earth, listen to the entirety of that action of which this is the fruit."
O lord of the earth, this woman of beautiful brows was once your wife, and you possessed a kingdom and such;
yet you were of the Śūdra caste, devoted to harming others,
afflicted by leprosy, cruel in your punishments, and devoid of affection for any living being.
And your wife, O long-eyed one, was likewise so even before;
she was always devoted to your heart and delighted in serving you.
That illustrious woman, faithful to her husband, remained so even when harshly rebuked.
O hero, though intent upon all your words and deeds,
that wealth which had been accumulated by our great-grandfathers has gone to ruin— wealth belonging to one who, through lack of sovereignty and being abandoned by his kinsmen, is left without allies.
When that was exhausted, O Lord of the Earth, you became devoted to agriculture;
yet even that agriculture, through the ripening of karma, came to fruitionlessness.
Consequently, being destitute, utterly depleted, and reduced to servitude under others—
"O King, this virtuous woman did not leave you even though she was being abandoned;
for with this virtuous lady, you performed service in the abode of the Sun with proper conduct and devotion, including sweeping and other such tasks."

Free from attachment to all desires, absorbed in that [the Sun] and offering yourself to him, O hero, you have performed great service day after day with full confidence in that abode of the Sun in the city of Kānyakubja.
O King, you have constantly performed the sweeping of the Sun’s abode,
as well as its sprinkling and daily anointing; and likewise,
O Monarch, this wife of yours, who conforms to your will, has done the same.
O King, having given the ring formerly bestowed by your father to the reciter, you have caused the merit of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas to be heard;
and whatever ritual acts you two perform day after day, O monarch—
Right there, through total absorption in him, the destruction of his sins occurred.
"The task of the Sun must be performed by me; likewise, supreme service must be rendered.
Whether it was not yet dawn or already dawn, he thought of this alone throughout the night.
At that time, your mind was such that you thought: "Thus this sense-base is delightful," and "Thus it brings happiness";
"And this shall be just like the sun," and likewise, "The action of yogis bestows happiness, and that too is happiness."

Day and night, your mind was devoted to the practice of yoga there. O King, for one whose mind is thus applied with effort, who perceives the elements through inference, and who performs his duties correctly and even more than prescribed— The original Sanskrit text is as follows: bhavaccittamabhūttatra yogakarmaṇyaharniśam | evaṃ tanmanasastatra kṛtodyogasya pārthiva | bhūtānumāninaḥ samyagyathoktādhikakāriṇaḥ ||
For you, whose mind is firm, your sin has been entirely pacified by constantly remembering the Lord of Light even with your thoughts and by attending upon the sun;
furthermore, the anointing of that former house was even more efficacious than that.
Having abandoned all means of livelihood and relying solely on dharma, she and her husband repeatedly performed the sweeping [of the temple];
by this woman, the meritorious act of listening [to the scriptures] was constantly caused to be performed through a reciter.
Formerly, you performed anointing with devotion in the temple of the gods using cow dung and clay, which were modifications of various elements;
then, King Kuvalāśva indeed arrived there.
Seeing that army of Saṃkrandana, which was accompanied by a great host, possessed numerous elephants for mounts,
endowed with every prosperity, adorned with all ornaments,
and surrounded by a thousand wives;
You conceived a longing for that king of the beautiful crown;
you performed an action devoted to the Sun that grants all desires,
and by that, you have obtained this entire kingdom and the whole earth without exception.
O King, listen likewise to that superior splendor which you possess;
I shall relate to you in its entirety how it was obtained through the power of yoga.
In that very dwelling, the lamp had gone out due to the exhaustion of its oil.
O hero, it was rekindled by you with the oil from your own food, and further augmented by another wick made from your upper garment; then,
having been lit by your wife herself, its radiance became even greater than before.
O King, even for you, whose splendor once again agitates the minds of all monarchs,
what need is there to mention worshipping the Sun?
Thus, O King, because of his status as a Śūdra, he was devoted solely to the service of the Sun.
He has attained unsurpassed greatness by becoming one with That;
how much more so the man who, devoted to constant service with devotion,
always performs worship without desire and with no other thought in mind?
Having attained all this prosperity, the Great Lord of all the worlds,
having worshipped the Sun— the Lord of lords—
and having propitiated him with flowers, incense, or other offerings, as well as lamps, garments, and ointments, does not come to grief.
Propitiate the Sun by constantly sweeping his abode and performing other such services;
for by giving whatever is most dear to one, or even that which is otherwise difficult to obtain,
to Bhāskara, the sustainer of the world, one does not suffer.
With fragrant agallochum, camphor, sandalwood, aloe-wood, and saffron; with various garments, incenses, flowers, garlands, chowries, and banners;
and with various other offerings, having performed the consecration with milk.

O King, please the Sun with devotion through songs, instrumental music, dance, and the like; on meritorious nights, honor Mārtaṇḍa with radiant dances and songs. Always remaining pure, you should perform fire-offerings (homa) with devotion during the ritual vigils.
Especially by listening to the Itihāsas and Purāṇas,
and likewise by the meritorious sounds of the Vedas— the Ṛg, Sāman, and Yajus— O King,
the Blessed One, the destroyer of worldly existence, is thus gratified through devotion.
Becoming once again Vaivasvata, the Lord Bhānu, the Sun who dwells in the hearts of beings,
being propitiated by men, bestows their desired fruit upon those living creatures who are capable of performing divine rites through the arising of their memory.
When propitiated, the Blessed One, the Maker of Day, bestows all desires;
he is not pleased by rituals, nor by heaps of jewels, nor by flowers, incense, and ointments.
It is only when remembered with true sincerity that Mārtaṇḍa attains satisfaction.
"By you, with a one-pointed mind, having performed such a small task as the sweeping of the house, this kingdom— difficult for others to obtain— has been attained.
By her, through causing the meritorious hearing [of the scripture] at the home of the Sun, [this result was achieved]."
Having performed such worship for the reciter when this prosperity has been attained,
he who satisfies that one-pointed-minded Bird with the necessary requisites—
even Indra himself is nowhere equal to you.
"Therefore, O best among the upholders of dharma, you should make an effort to worship the Sun-god together with this exceedingly humble goddess.
Brahmā said:
O hero, having heard these words of the sage, that lord of men,
accompanied by his wife, then experienced the hair on his body standing on end;
he then felt as though his purpose had already been accomplished.
Having bowed down, King Satrājit spoke to Acyuta.
Satrājit said:
"Just as [Indra] attained immortality, and just as Vāyu possesses supreme strength..."

Thus, by your word, I have attained supreme Nirvāṇa; having accomplished my purpose, sitting at ease, I have reached the highest bliss. For you have held up a lamp for me when I was shrouded in the darkness of ignorance.
O Brahmin, both this slender-limbed woman and I— fearful of the loss of our prosperity— have today acquired wealth through your word. O Sage, you have explained to us the seed of all riches.
O best of the twice-born, for the words issuing from your mouth have indeed been understood by me.
The Lord of the World, the Maker of Day, cannot be propitiated with jewels, nor with floods of wealth, nor with flowers and ointments by those devoid of true devotion.
And by those who are independent of external objects, the movement of the mind is achieved through the mind alone;
thus the Sun-god, the Lord of all lords, is propitiated even by the destitute.
O great sage, all this that you have spoken has been understood by me.
And that which I ask, please answer me with a face gracious with favor:
how is the Sun-god propitiated by men and women? O best of Brahmins, O great sage, tell me how he attains satisfaction.
"Tell me also the secrets of the God that are always pleasing to Him, as well as other matters in their entirety, for I am desirous of worshipping the Sun. Parāvasu said:
Listen, O protector of the earth, to those by whom the Sun is worshipped in their homes—
by men and by women who have fallen into this most terrible ocean of worldly existence—
having propitiated the Lord of the World, the God Aka, with meditative concentration.
He who eats but one meal himself during the month of Kārttika and offers a second to a Brāhmaṇa for the pleasure of the Sun,
whether he does so intentionally or unintentionally during his early life with great effort, [attains the highest goal].
Therefore, evil conduct is destroyed; of this there is no doubt.
By this very procedure, he who again worships an emerald in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa and bestows it upon the Brahmins, [attains the supreme goal].
Listen to me regarding the fruit that comes from pleasing the Blessed One:
whatever sin has been committed by a woman or a man in the middle stage of life, liberation from it is proclaimed by the Supreme Self.
And likewise, O Lord of the Earth, he who, having worshipped the Sun, gives a single meal to a Brahmin in the month of Pauṣa,
that very act pleases the Sun as much as if it had been performed with a hundred thousand offerings.
O King, whether it be a man or even a woman,
whoever performs this three-month vow, O lord of men,
is liberated from minor sins through the propitiation of the Sun.

O King, in the second year one is liberated from minor sins (upapātaka), and likewise, when performed in the third year, it destroys even the great sins (mahāpātaka). This vow, when observed by men and women for three months, [yields these results].
O King, through three years it bestows fruit upon men;
through three months of practice, it delivers one from the three kinds of sins;
and by means of the annual rites, the three names of the Lord grant liberation.
Therefore, this various vow has been proclaimed as the supreme means for propitiating the Sun-god, which pacifies all sins.
Satrājit said:
"To which brahmin, O Sage, should it be given with devotion?
O tiger among the twice-born, tell me everything regarding the second [day].
Parāvasu said:
It should be given to one who knows the Purāṇas, O best of Brahmins, and to a garment as well. Listen also to the words spoken by Bhāskara in the past,
O mighty-armed King, when he was questioned by Aruṇa.
Having bowed his head to the Sun, the dispeller of darkness, as he had ascended the mountain of sunrise, he indeed spoke these words:
"O Lord, what things are always dear to you for the purpose of worship?"
Bhāskara said: "In the ritual of propitiation with all [offerings] such as flowers,
and always during eclipses and the like, as well as regarding garments and so forth, it is the same for Brāhmaṇas and for me,
O Sun."
Among flowers, karavīra is dear, as is red sandalwood;
among incenses, guggulu is preferred, and sweetmeats (modaka) are beloved as an offering of food.
A priest who performs the worship and one who serves the meal are dear, as is a lamp fed with ghee.
O best of birds, a gift is given to the reciter as something pleasing;
and whatever gift is given by men on earth with me in mind,
that should be given to the reciter for my own satisfaction, O bird.

O best of birds, that Brāhmaṇa reciter who is well-versed in the Itihāsas and Purāṇas should be honored for my pleasure. When this Brāhmaṇa is always worshiped, I am worshiped; of this there is no doubt.
O tiger among birds, because he is always dear to me,
O best of birds, my delight upon hearing him is not equaled by the Vedas, lutes, drums, nor by excellent perfumes and ointments.
"The Itihāsas and Purāṇas being recited by reciters—
for this reason, the reciter is dear to me, as well as the one who performs worship and the one who offers food.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Worship of the Sun," in the account of Satrājit within the Saptamī-kalpa, in the Brāhma-parvan of the *Bhaviṣya-mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the one hundred and seventeenth chapter, describing the greatness of smearing and bathing;
Aruṇa said:

"O Lord of Gods, tell me why the *bhojaka* is dear to you; why indeed are other castes, such as the Brahmins, not [so] in the temples? And who is this *bhojaka*, O God—whose son is he, and what is his nature?"
"Tell me its color and its function in every respect.
Āditya said:
"I have been well questioned by you; may it be well with you, O high-minded Vainateya!"
Listen with a one-pointed mind to everything as I speak, O sky-traveler!
O son of Kaśyapa, those other castes such as the Brahmins and others always worship me, endowed with devotion and faith.
"O Bird, those Brahmins who worship me with affection in temples,
yet act as attendants to other deities, are indeed *devalakas*.
For this reason, the *bhojaka* (temple-priest) is always dear to me."
If this man is a Brahmin by caste and devoted to his own prescribed duties, he should not be abandoned;
for one who is devoid of the performance of duty undoubtedly goes to hell.
Therefore, the Bhojakas should never abandon their own duty.
O bird, he was indeed previously created by me through my own splendor for the sake of my own worship; his deeds have certainly been proclaimed.
He is the high-minded King Priyavrata’s son in Śākadvīpa.

By him, for my sake, was constructed a divine house resembling a celestial chariot (*vimāna*) on that island of his own— a vast structure made of divine stone. Having caused an image of me to be fashioned there, golden and endowed with all auspicious marks, he established it.
Indeed, for the sake of consecrating it, he of noble vows reflected:
"An excellent temple has been built by him, and this image was fashioned;
who indeed shall consecrate the divine Sun in this auspicious abode?"
Having reflected thus, he came to me for refuge. O bird, considering his devotion, I went into the presence of that king, and I said to him: "O bird..."
"What are you thinking about, O Indra among kings? From where has this anxiety come upon you? Tell me what profound cause for worry has arisen in your heart;
I shall accomplish all of it. Do not be despondent, O King."
"I shall perform even that which is exceedingly difficult; of this there is no doubt.
When addressed thus by me, the king spoke these words:
"On this island, you have constructed a temple for the God of gods."
"O Lord of the World, this image has been fashioned by me with devotion.
O Bird, whoever should perform the consecration of this image in your temple—
wherein the three castes, beginning with the Kṣatriyas, reside on this island— "
When I spoke to them, they did not perform the consecration for you in its entirety, nor, O Lord of the World, was there any image here, nor was a Brahmin present.
Because of that, this anxiety has come upon me; it has been driven into my heart like a thorn.
Then I spoke these auspicious words to that king, O Vainateya:
"It is exactly as you have said, O lord of men; there is no doubt about this.
There are three castes beginning with the Kṣatriyas on this island; of this there is no uncertainty."
And they do not deserve my worship or a place of installation at any time. Therefore, O King, for their own welfare as well as for my own,
I first create a class known as the Bhaga, which is incomparable.
Having spoken thus to that king, O hero, best of birds,
I fell into deep reflection for the sake of accomplishing his task.
Then, as I was reflecting, [certain beings] emerged from my own body.
Resembling the moon, the kunda flower, and the moon in luster, these eight of great strength recite the four Vedas along with their auxiliary sciences and Upaniṣads, O bird;
all are clad in saffron robes and carry water-pots and lotuses.
Two from the surface of his forehead, two others likewise from his chest,
two from his two feet, and two from his two toes, O bird;
then all those great-souled ones, with their necks bowed in reverence.
Regarding me as their father, they spoke these words:
"O Father, O Father, Great God, Lord of the World, Master of the Universe!
For what purpose have we been created by you from the body of the God?"
"Speak, we shall carry out every single command of yours;
you are our father, a god, and we are your sons—of this there is no doubt.
When they had all spoken thus, I addressed those beings born of the gods.
"O bird, you shall do as this son of Priyavrata says;
for that king, the lord of Śākadvīpa, has also been addressed by me:
'O King, these sons of mine are worthy of honor and are the best of Brāhmaṇas.'"
O Lord of the Earth, let them all perform my consecration;
having performed the consecration of my image, O ruler of men,
subsequently entrust the entire temple to them for the purpose of worship.

These are worthy for my worship and for all types of consecrations; once the work is completed, one must never strike the patrons. Furthermore, whatever houses, fields, and so forth belong to the temple, they are for the sake of the sanctuary alone.

O King, whatever wealth, grain, and so forth may come into my sanctuary, all of that must be given to the officiating priests; of this there is no doubt. Whatever wealth, grain, gold, and the like, as well as houses, fields, and so on, [should be given].

O Indra among kings, whatever belongs to me— whether in a village or anywhere in a city— all of that which is mine is subject to my authority on every side; O King, all the Bhojakas are my lords, and no others, such as the Brahmins and so forth.

"Just as a son who possesses the right of inheritance becomes the master of his father's wealth, so too shall they be the enjoyers of my riches; of this there is no doubt. When I, the king, had spoken thus, everything was carried out accordingly.
Having caused the consecration to be performed and having given away all his possessions to the Bhojakas,
O best of birds, he then attained great joy.
Thus, O elder brother of Garuḍa, were these Bhojakas created by me.

For I am their very self; therefore, all these well-disposed ones should be known as equal to my own son, and always as beneficial to me. Consequently, one should give to them and never take from them at any time.

He who, out of greed or even out of hatred, seizes the property of a village chief, goes to the terrible Tāmisra hell for eternal years. Therefore, whatever property such as a village or other assets belongs to me—
All of that is indeed my ancestral property as a *bhojaka*;
O Lord of Birds, I shall tell you what kind of person a *bhojaka* should be:
he who always abides by his own duty must uphold my command.
First comes the study of the Vedas, and likewise the taking of a wife;
daily anointing with oil and bathing at the three periods of the day are prescribed. Indeed, I am always to be worshipped five times a day, both by night and by day.
One must never, under any circumstances, engage in the censure of the gods, the Brahmins, or the Vedas.
Furthermore, the Bhojaka must not perform the installation of other deities,
nor should he ever perform even mine alone by himself at any time.
A consumer should never eat any food that has not been offered;
O elder brother of Garuḍa, one should not go to the house of a Śūdra to eat.
Indeed, food remaining from the leavings of a Śūdra must always be avoided with great effort by those who consume [the offerings].
"O sky-walker, how will those cooks who constantly eat the food of Śūdras in the house of a Śūdra ever obtain the fruit of their worship?
Having gone to the house of a Śūdra, one must never eat."
And food from a Śūdra that has come into the house must likewise be abandoned;
furthermore, a lotus must always be blown [as a conch] in front of me by the one who feeds me.
Indeed, when the conch is sounded even once, my delight is born.
There is no doubt that by listening to the Purāṇas in this manner for six months, [one attains the same fruit].
Therefore, the conch must always be sounded with great effort by the Bhojaka;
this is his supreme livelihood: the food offering (naivedya) that belongs to me.
Because they do not eat what is unfit to be eaten, they are considered Bhojakas; because they meditate upon the Maga, they are known as Magadhas;
and because they constantly cause me to be fed, they are known as Bhojakas.
Anointing the body with oil is a supreme means of purification that should be practiced with diligence;
for one who eats without having anointed himself is indeed impure, of this there is no doubt.
O Hero, O Bird, he who would worship me without such anointing [is likewise impure].
His lineage would surely not endure, nor would I be pleased.
Therefore, one should perform the shaving of the head while carefully preserving a tuft of hair (śikhā).
One should likewise observe this on the day of the Sun (Sunday) and on the sixth lunar day (ṣaṣṭhī), even at night.
O elder brother of Garuḍa, on the seventh lunar day and likewise on my transit, a fast must be observed by the sacrificer for my pleasure;
furthermore, he should recite the Gāyatrī mantra with his voice three times a day before me.
Having carefully covered his mouth, I should be worshipped with reverence;
one should diligently maintain silence and cast anger far away.
He who, out of greed or desire, bestows [this] upon Śūdras or Vaiśyas, [incurs sin].

O child, that person who sells my floral offerings certainly goes to hell. O Lord of Birds, O sky-ranger, that wicked-souled one who, out of greed, offers my flowers to another without having dedicated them to me; The result for him is that he shall dwell in the Raurava hell for sixty thousand years. Therefore, O bird, you must never sell my flowers. By selling them, O best of birds, one surely goes to hell. Thus have I spoken. O son, you must not sell my flowers under any circumstances. He should be known as my supreme enemy; he is not worthy to worship me.
Indeed, among men such as Brahmins and others, he should be given my discarded flower offerings (nirmālya), and he must always consume whatever food offering (naivedya) belongs to me.
By that act, he is constantly purified, just as if he had partaken of sacrificial food (haviṣyānna).
Whoever should immediately pluck even a single flower from my body, my own offering (naivedya) must not be given to anyone else; one should cast it into the water.

In my opinion, there is no doubt that such a person is equal to the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). Whatever scent or flower has come into contact with my body should never be given to a Vaiśya or a Śūdra.
One should take it for oneself; it must never be sold. Whoever in this world takes away my flowers without having first placed unblemished blossoms upon me shall certainly go to hell.
O bird, that man who should transgress my ablution and my sacred remains, which are purifying, goes to the terrible Raurava hell.
My worshiper must always perform my ablution with great effort.
O Lord of Birds,

if the one who feeds me were to perform my bathing without great care, someone might leap over me, or even a dog might devour me; for indeed, O Lord of Birds, my mind would be vulnerable to being leaped upon or being eaten.
He goes to the terrible hell known by the name Tāmisra.
One must always eat only one meal a day and indeed perform ablutions at the three periods of the day.
One should change one's clothes three times; this must be done day after day.
At the time of worship and at the time of offering the *arghya*, anger must be abandoned with effort.
One should not speak anything inauspicious; rather, one should speak what is auspicious at that time, thinking:
"Such a person as this is my beloved patron, always performing worship for me."
Just as I am one who is to be honored and worshipped by the Brahmins and others,
whoever treats me with contempt in the form of my livelihood as a patron— against him I shall quickly become enraged and destroy his entire lineage on all sides.
"O son of Vinatā, this cook is always as dear to me as you are—
he who performs the plastering and is ever intent on sweeping.
Parāvasu said:
Having spoken thus, the Lord Sun, mounted upon his chariot, set forth;
and Aruṇa likewise, O King, hearing this, was filled with supreme joy.
Therefore, O Great King, O Lord of the Earth, the Bhojaka is worthy of worship.
"Therefore, O King, a second meal should be given by men to the reciter.
Brahmā said:
Having thus heard [this], that king [realized] the fruit of his own action.
The mighty-armed lord of the earth experienced great joy regarding the ancient [shrines]; whatever sanctuary of the Sun the king beheld upon the earth,
in each of those he had a plastering performed with devotion.
O lady of beautiful hips, his wife also, having respectfully given a fee to the reciter for the merit of hearing [the scripture],
[worshipped] in the temple of the divine Bhānu;
thus the king, together with his wife, worshipped the Sun-god with devotion.
"Both have attained supreme joy as well as the unsurpassed goal.
Thus ends the one hundred and seventeenth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Smearing and Bathing," in the Saptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan within the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
The narrative of Satrājit is complete.
Now begins the one hundred and eighteenth chapter,
titled "Description of the Fruit of Offering Lamps.
Brahmā said:
The man who offers a lamp in the temple of the Sun becomes radiant as the sun himself and obtains the fruit of all sacrifices;
this is especially true when a lamp is offered during the month of Kārttika, the month of Kaumāra.
By giving, one obtains a fruit that cannot be attained by any other means.
O Kṛṣṇa, O Kṛṣṇa, I shall now tell you this sin-destroying dialogue between the high-souled Brāhmaṇa Bhadra and his brothers.
In this world, there was formerly a beautiful city named Māhiṣmatī.
In it, O Kṛṣṇa, there lived a twice-born man renowned as Nāgaśarman.
By the grace of the Sun-god, a hundred sons were born to him.
Among them, Bhadra was the youngest and the most discerning of those sons;
he was constantly devoted to providing wicks for the lamps of the radiant God of gods, the Sustainer of the World, and was ever intent on bringing oil and other necessities.
In that temple of the Sun, a thousand lamps dear to the descendant of Bhṛgu blazed day and night without fail;
they were surpassed by his brilliance and eclipsed by his beauty.
All those brothers respectfully asked this:
"O brother, speak! May it ever be well with you, O twice-born one.
We are all filled with curiosity; let that which we ask be told."
Having heard those words of theirs, Bhadra spoke these words:
"If there is a matter to be said by me, let it be stated here;
for I am indeed not possessed of envy, nor am I corrupted by passion or other such defects."
"Sirs, you are all indeed my brothers and likewise my elders;
how could I not speak to you, who are like sons to me?
Therefore, let all my brothers tell me what they wish to say."
The brothers said:
"We do not see such great effort among you regarding flowers and incense, nor in the worship of the twice-born;
rather, we observe it most intensely at the temple of the Sun."

"Just as it was by day, so it was by night; just as it was by night, so it was by day. O auspicious one, tell us the truth regarding that constant exertion of yours for the offering of lamps; indeed, our curiosity is great."
"O one of great strength, tell us in detail that very fruit of the gift of lamps which has been understood by you.
Thus addressed and urged with joy by those brothers, he then spoke.
O observer of noble vows, he did not say anything at all regarding his brothers;
however, being urged again and again by those brothers with joy,
Bhadra, whose very essence was courtesy, related everything in full.
"You have such great curiosity even regarding this very small matter;
therefore, O you of noble vows, I shall today tell you what my vow is.
In ancient times, Vasiṣṭha was the family priest of King Ikṣvāku."
And by him, that twice-born man, a shrine for the Sun was constructed on the bank of the Sarayū;
there, day after day, he performed service with flowers, incense, and ointments,
as well as with the offering of lamps and other such rites.

Because a lamp was offered with devotion by him during the month of Kārtika, he indeed attained eternal nirvāṇa; yet that very lamp went out at night before the image of the deity. Consequently, I dwelt in the temple, feeling extremely distressed.
O observer of noble vows, pus and blood were constantly flowing from his body;
his nose was decayed and he made a harsh sound, fallen into a foul odor,
and always possessed of a wicked mind toward the Sun, the seven-horsed god.

O best of the twice-born, whenever I offer lamps with wicks and other materials into the fire by chance, I always attain satisfaction after consuming each of those offerings. Once, however, I went to that temple of the Sun.
At night, I saw there some devotees who had come for a vigil;
they requested shelter, and being filled with compassion, they granted it to me, thinking the auspicious thought: "This man is diseased and very wretched."
Then,
O best of the twice-born, resorting to a wicked intent and seeking out a vulnerability, I took refuge in the fire and stood near them, desiring to seize the divine ornament of Vivasvat, the Sun.
"I shall remain here, O herdsmen; if they fall asleep, I will take away this beautiful ornament from the sun as if he were my enemy.
Then those herdsmen fell asleep, deluded by slumber.
The lamps were also extinguished; then, rising up in haste and filled with supreme joy, I went toward the sacrificial fire. Having carefully ignited the flame, I then placed the lamp-wick [into it].
Having indeed prepared the lamp and held it before the Sun,
O observer of noble vows, those Bhojakas— all of them elderly sons of the god— desiring to take away the ornament of the divine Bhānu.
O best of the twice-born, I was indeed seen there by them standing before the fire with a lamp in hand; they seized me here,
and then I was bewildered by the splendor of the high-souled Sun.
Lamenting piteously, I fell to the ground at their feet;
and they too, moved by compassion, then released me from the hands of the executioners.
I was seized by the king’s men and questioned on all sides.
"O evil-minded one, what is this that you have begun in the temple of the God of Gods? Having lit the lamp, speak; do not delay!
Having spoken thus, he was then surrounded by them, weapons in hand.

Then, O best of the twice-born, afflicted by disease and fear, I abandoned my life-breaths and went to where the divine Vibhāvasu himself resides. Having stayed there for a kalpa, I subsequently attained the state of being your brother.
Such is the power of the lamp offered in the month of Kārttika, O observers of noble vows,
for this is the supreme fruit of one given in the abode of the Sun.
Yet, as for the lighting of the lamp that was performed by me with a wicked intention—
This is the fruit being experienced by me for that lamp at the abode of Bhaga; overcome by hunger, I lit a lamp before the God of gods, the Sun, as an ornament for him.
Then, through the recollection of his former births, he attained a final birth in the house of a Brahmin;
even though born as a leper Śūdra, he achieved the highest status of a Brahmin and mastered various scriptures along with the Vedas and their auxiliary branches.
"O best of the twice-born, this most wonderful fruit was obtained by me from a lamp held with a wicked intention; how much more so, then, for those who actually give lamps!
For this reason, I [offer] lamps in this manner day and night."
I bestow this knowledge within the abode of the Sun, for its fruit is indeed known.
This which has been spoken to you out of affection is the truth, there is no doubt;
such is the power of the lamp in the month of Kārttika, O you of excellent vows.
As Bhadra previously declared regarding the lamp for the abode of the Sun: "He who,
being composed, recites the name of the Sun day after day and offers a lamp at the temple of the Sun during the month of Kārttika, [attains great merit]."

The man who gives a lamp attains, without a doubt, the memory of past births, wisdom, renown among all beings, and unimpeded faculties; at all times, he is endowed with sight and possesses great intelligence.

He is born even in hell and does not perceive that which is known as darkness— that man who diligently offers a lamp on the sixth or the seventh lunar day of every fortnight; learn from me the fruit thereof.
He ascends a divine celestial chariot (vimāna), made of gold, adorned with jewels, enchanting, exceedingly beautiful, and filled with rows of lamps.
Therefore, O Acyuta, one should always offer lamps in that temple of the Sun.
Having given them, one must not harm them, nor deprive them of oil;
for one who steals a lamp is born as a blind rat.
Therefore, a man seeking his own welfare should give a lamp and never take one away.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Fruit of Offering Lamps at the Abode of the Sun" within the Narrative of Bhadra, in the Saptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan, in the glorious *Bhaviṣya-mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the one hundred and nineteenth chapter:
Description of the Offering of Lamps.
Brahmā said:
To those who were crying out in distress and agitated, having fallen into a hell of blinding, impassable darkness, the servant of Yama spoke.
Enough with these lamentations! What fruit is there in your wailing?
For this self was previously neglected through negligence and other such faults.
Why was this not considered before, so that it might have been otherwise at the end?
"Now endure your torment; why do you lament?
This body lasts but a few days, and sense-objects are exceedingly fragile. Who does not know this, such that you remain so heedless?"
If a living being, after thousands of births, should at last obtain a single human birth,
why does that person, remaining utterly deluded even there, rush headlong after sensual enjoyments? They are constantly exerting themselves for the sake of children, wife, home, fields, and wealth.
Therefore, those fools do not recognize even the slightest benefit for themselves; deluded, they think, "I have been deceived," or "I have gained this," or "This has come to me.
No man, being thus infatuated, realizes that he is already departing for hell.
One does not perceive the sun, the moon, and so forth, nor time, nor even the self;
for [the self] is the witness of all that is auspicious and inauspicious here.
Other births arise for embodied beings such as sons, wives, and others.
For whatever purpose and for whomsoever an action was performed, its consequences follow through hundreds of births!
Oh, how great is the power of delusion— that even while being tormented in hells,
one still cries out for mother and father, despite being the perpetrator oneself!
For those whose minds are thus drawn away by objects that provide such delicious gratification,
the intellect that perceives the ultimate truth does not arise;
likewise, their mind remains incessantly attached to sense objects.
For what burden is there for the tongue in proclaiming the name of the Sun?
Since even when oil is of little value, ghee is obtained in exchange for the wick, which of these two is the greater gain? What concern could there then be?
Since he did not give the lamp— which removes one from hell and yields great fruit— into the long hands [of the needy] while he had the freedom to do so during the month of Bhānu (Kārttika),
the man now laments slightly as the fruit of his action is seen.
For those who lament over their lack of independence while being proud of their independence,
life inevitably falls away day and night; even the living soul,
desiring sense objects, receives what has been given to experience.
Today I have beheld this place joined with the results of evil deeds;
now, what is the use of lamentation? Endure that which has come upon you. If this suffering that has arisen is undesirable to you, [then so be it].

Therefore, one of wondrous intellect should never commit a sinful act; even if a sinful deed has been committed through ignorance, one must constantly perform the uninterrupted worship of the Sun, which destroys all evil.
Brahmā said:
Having heard those words, the denizens of hell, their throats emaciated by hunger and their palates split open by the heat of thirst, spoke to him in extreme distress.
"O good sir, tell us what deed was committed by us,
for which this most terrible retribution is being experienced while we remain in hell. The servant replied:
Formerly, out of greed for ghee, you— deluded by the intoxication of youth and devoid of discernment— stole a lamp from the house of Mārtaṇḍa;
because of that, you are now tormented by hunger and thirst in this terrible hell.
"O sirs, you have fallen, pierced by the piercing cold wind.
Brahmā said:
"This is the result of giving a lamp and of stealing a lamp."
"O Acyuta, merit and demerit have been described;
indeed, O Kṛṣṇa, the offering of a lamp is praised everywhere,
but especially in the abode of Bhāskara, the sustainer of the world."

O Hero of the Vṛṣṇis! Those who are blind, mute, deaf, devoid of discrimination, and lacking in various means for giving—by them, O Kṛṣṇa, lamps offered by virtuous people have been taken from the temple to other places.
Thus ends the one hundred and nineteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Offering Lamps," in the Saptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan within the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the one hundred and twentieth chapter, describing the worship of Āditya.
Viṣṇu said:
O Blessed One, all living beings are at all times afflicted by calamities such as poisons and diseases, by the malevolent influences of evil planets,
by sorcery and magical rites, and by dreadful contagious diseases.
O Lotus-born One, they remain constantly tormented;
you ought to explain to me accurately by what ripening of karma afflictions such as poison and disease arise for human beings.
Brahmā said:
O tiger among gods, those men who have not propitiated the Sun with vows and fasts in another birth shall be subject to planetary afflictions, diseases, and other such misfortunes.
Those men by whom their minds have never been made inclined toward Him at any time,
O Kṛṣṇa, those people are the recipients of poison, planetary afflictions, and fevers;
yet whatever they desire in their minds, such as health or supreme prosperity, [they obtain].
By pleasing the Sun, one undoubtedly attains all those things in the hereafter;
one incurs neither mental afflictions nor diseases, nor the bondage of grasping at sense objects,
nor even the fear of being struck by malevolent spells when the Dispeller of Darkness has been propitiated.
For him all malevolent planets are always equal, and for him all benign planets are ever so; he who is honored even by the gods is one with whom the Sun is pleased—
he who is impartial toward all beings, regarding their welfare just as he does his own.
By means of fasting and other such practices, the Dispeller of Darkness is propitiated;
when this Lord of Creatures is pleased, men have their desires fulfilled,
remaining forever free from disease, happy, and endowed with manifold merit and bliss.

Neither enemies nor any malevolent rites against the body and so forth, nor even planetary afflictions, diseases, and the like, arise as evil consequences for them. The god’s masses of wealth remain unimpeded for that man.
"By whomsoever the Lord of Śveta has been worshipped, he protects them from all calamities.
Viṣṇu said:
"Those men who have not propitiated Mārtaṇḍa are partakers of suffering."
"How may they be free from disease, free from fever, and cleansed of all taint?
Brahmā said:
"Let them worship the Lord of Gods with this incomparable flower."
To Bhāskara, the Lord of the World, the supreme teacher of all the gods,
Viṣṇu said:
"How can there be worship of the Sun by those whose bodies are overcome by defects?"
"O Lord of Gods, tell me what must be done for my own welfare out of devotion;
if I am worthy of your grace because of this devotion of mine,
then you must instruct me in the great worship of the Sun."
"O Lord, with your permission, I wish to propitiate the infinite and undecaying God who destroys wicked doubts,
so that by your grace I may become exceedingly valorous."
Brahmā said: "O Viṣṇu,
you are surely destined to be favored by the Lord whose birth is unmanifest,
since this mind of yours is so intent upon his worship."
If you wish to propitiate Bhānu, the lord of the gods,
and the Blessed One who is without beginning, then become a son of Vivasvat, O Acyuta;
for Bhānu cannot be known or praised by those who are not sons of Vivasvat.
It cannot even be seen by the deluded, much less entered;
yet purified men who have petitioned for devotion to Him, whose minds are fixed on that devotion,
become like the sons of Vivasvat and thus enter into Vivasvat himself.
As long as the accumulation of sins gathered through the cycle of many births has not been exhausted, men do not develop an inclination toward the Sun;
they harbor hatred for the Sun, and they revile the twice-born and the Vedas.
One should recognize that man as born from a portion of the Asuras,
for among those fallen wretches who are submerged in the waters of hypocrisy and deceit, there arises a delight in heretical sects and an inclination toward rationalistic arguments.

When the evil of men is exhausted, then unswerving faith arises toward the Vedas, the twice-born, the sun, and the Lord of Sacrifice. When, however, the accumulation of sin remaining for men is very slight, [then faith arises].
At that time, while the Bhojakas and Brahmins perform worship to the Sun,
the Sun-god alone— delighted by devotion— grants a hand to hold for men wandering here in this worldly existence, which is difficult to traverse due to their karma.
Therefore, you, as Vaivasvata, should worship Hari—who removes all sins—with equal devotion for the sake of prosperity; thus the Sun-god will attain satisfaction.
Viṣṇu said:
"O Lotus-born One, what are the characteristics of these men belonging to the Vaivasvata age by virtue of their qualities?
And tell me what the duty of the Vaivasvata age is.
Brahmā said:
He who does not harm living beings by deed, thought, or word,
and who is devoted in his inner being to Mārtaṇḍa and Kṛṣṇa— he is indeed Vaivasvata. He who constantly bows down to the Bhojaka brahmins as gods [is likewise].
Nor is he the enjoyer of the property of others, for he is Viṣṇu Vaivasvata;
he knows all the gods as Ravi (the Sun), and all the worlds as Bhāskara (the Light-maker).
And he knows himself to be non-different from them, O Kṛṣṇa, for he is indeed Vaivasvata.
Whether it be a god, a human, or another being—be it an animal, a bird, or an ant; whether trees, stones, wood, and so forth, or the earth, the ocean, and likewise heaven;
even the self itself, by the grace of the Lord, is distinct from the Maker of Day.
One who does not know this, O Kṛṣṇa, should know him to be the man belonging to Vaivasvata;
for he who truly understands that "every portion belongs to Vaivasvata— whatever has been and whatever exists," he indeed is the man belonging to Vaivasvata.

When meditated upon with a spirit of devotion, he removes the fear of worldly existence; he who is the light (vivasvān) is the man known as Vaivasvata. He, however, who does not harbor any evil intent toward any living being, [is truly devoted].
That man who, through action, mind, and speech,
performs the ritual of Vivasvat with devotion— being independent of external objects—
and accomplishes it with true feeling, he indeed should be known as Vaivasvata himself.
He whose enemies are neither affectionate nor subject to divisive conduct,
and who perceives all this as the sun [perceives it], is indeed Vaivasvata;
for he has attained this through intensely practiced austerity or through sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
Men do not go to that destination which Vaivasvata has gone to— namely,
for one who has with his whole soul fixed his devotion upon the Sun;
for, O best of gods, because he has achieved his purpose, such a person is indeed praiseworthy even to Vaivasvata himself.
May there be born in our lineage one who is blessed and a purifier of the family,
who shall worship the Sun with a spirit of devotion,
and who shall have an image of the Sun fashioned that rests within his heart.
That man attains the sun, which is the incomparable banner of dharma;
and that person who, with devotion, causes a permanent temple to be built for the Sun,
leads seven generations of his family to the worlds of the Sun.
For as many years as an image of the Lord remains in a temple,
for that many thousands of years shall one dwell in the abode of Puṣpottara;
so too for one whose house possesses the characteristics of a divine image and where the ritual is performed continuously.
He whose mind is free from desire attains equality with the Imperishable.
That man who offers exceedingly fragrant and pleasing flowers to the Lord of the World, the seven-horsed Sun, the lord of the luminaries;
He goes to the supreme abode where the eternal light resides. Whatever place is devoid of this, or whatever is lacking it— there,
one should offer various kinds of incense and fragrant, excellent ointments.
A man who daily performs sacrifices consisting of lamps, wicks, and offerings— whatever is desired by himself— through the worship of the Sun,
satisfies the Lord Sun, the master of sacrifice, with those very oblations.
Sacrifices requiring many implements and extensive collections of various materials are achieved only by men possessed of wealth, not by those with meager stores;
yet worship performed by men with devotion, even with mere sprouts of *dūrvā* grass, [is efficacious].
For Ravi bestows the fruit that is very difficult to obtain through all other sacrifices:
whatever flowers are pleasing, incense, perfumes, and ointments;
whatever ornaments are dear, as well as two garments of red cloth.
O Mārtaṇḍa, offer whatever foods, edibles, and fruits there may be; remain focused on him alone,
and propitiate that primordial Lord of Sacrifice with devotion.
Having propitiated that God, who is remembered as the Supreme Brahman, one goes to Him;
one should bathe the Lord Acyuta, the Master of the worlds, with holy waters from sacred fords, with flowers, honey, clarified butter, and likewise with milk.

O best of the Yadus, through these heart-warming hymns, musical instruments, and the satiation of Brahmins, you shall go from here to the meritorious lakes of curd and milk where honey flows, and you shall attain divine bliss.
And by attaining one-pointedness of mind, worship the Sun;
it is he who is to be worshipped that Mahādeva obtained the title "Mahat," and I too am the creator of all the worlds.
Having propitiated Vivasvat, O Janārdana,
you too— by his grace, O Hṛṣīkeśa, there is no doubt—
will always be capable of destroying the Daityas, the enemies of the gods.
I am born from that southern ray of the god Vivasvat, which is equal to the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas;
whereas the northern ray, O Kṛṣṇa, is always filled with a garland of dark rays.
From him, O Acyuta, was born Īśa, the beloved of Pārvatī;
from your chest was born he who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Likewise, the goddess whose hand holds a lotus and who is beloved by the lotus-faced one [Lakṣmī] was born.
"Having propitiated Bala, I have obtained fame and prosperity;
likewise, O Indra among kings, by propitiating that Sun,
you too shall obtain all whatever desires you wish for."
Whoever should constantly hear this dialogue between Vidhi and Kṛṣṇa,
he too, having attained the foremost desires, shall thereafter attain the higher world,
mounted upon a red vehicle yoked with elephants and horses.
O King, he was like a lotus in brilliance, resembling a bird [the sun] in radiance,
and equal to the moon in beauty; he was surrounded by hosts of gods,
while being sung to by Gandharvas and throngs of Apsarases.
Thus ends the one hundred and twentieth chapter, titled "Description of the Worship of Āditya," in the Saptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan within the glorious Śrī-Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa.
Now begins the one hundred and twenty-first chapter:
"Description of the Dimming of the Sun’s Radiance by Viśvakarman."
Śatānīka said:
You have described the marking of the body for the Sun in brief;
I wish to hear it in detail—explain that to me, O observer of noble vows.
Sumantu said:
O descendant of Kuru, when Saṃjñā had gone to her father’s house, the Sun-god reflected: "Saṃjñā has assumed my own form."
In the meantime, Brahmā arrived there and spoke sweet, auspicious words that brought joy to Ravi:
"You are the primordial god of the gods; this entire world is pervaded by you."
"Your father-in-law, Viśvakarman, will fashion your form.
Having spoken thus to Ravi, Brahmā said to Viśvakarman:
"Fashion for Mārtaṇḍa a most beautiful form of his own."
Then, at the command of Brahmā, Viśvakarman placed the sun upon a lathe and gradually fashioned his form. Thereupon,
Brahmā, together with all the hosts of gods, offered praise to him.
With various secret hymns by those who have mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences:
"May it be well with you, O Lord of the World, O showerer of Dharma, O maker of the moon!
O God of gods, O Maker of Day, may there be peace for all the worlds!"
Then Rudra, Viṣṇu, and the others praised that Sun-god:
"O Lord, O Master of Heaven, may your splendor increase even as you are being drawn.
Then Indra, having arrived, praised that god while he was being depicted.
"Victory, O God! Be victorious! they cried; "O Lord of the World, you are the giver of truth.
Then the seven sages, led by Viśvāmitra, praised him with various hymns, uttering words of "May there be well-being! May there be well-being!"
Then the Vālakhilyas praised him with blessings declared in the Vedas:
"O Lord, you are the liberation of those seeking liberation; you are the object of meditation for meditators as well.
You are the refuge of all beings; everything is established in you."

O Lord of gods, may there be welfare for us and for all creatures; O Lord of the world, from you indeed the universe constantly arises, and into you it is dissolved. You alone are one, and you are indeed twofold and threefold—of this there is no doubt.
By you alone the world was created; by you alone it was awakened.
Then all the hosts of Vidyādharas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Pannagas, with palms joined in reverence, bowed their heads toward the Sun.
They spoke such words as these, which brought pleasure to the mind and the ear:
"O Creator of beings, may your splendor be bearable for all creatures.
Then Hāhā, Hūhū, Tumburu, and likewise Nārada [spoke].
Skilled in the high-pitched cry of the cow, they began to approach it,
being experts in the three scales (*grāma*) of *ṣaḍja*, *madhyama*, and *gāndhāra*,
as well as in the melodic modulations (*mūrcchanā*) and the *dhaivata* and *pañcama* notes.
With various deep-toned melodies and likewise with half-deep tones,
accompanied by the rhythms of musical instruments according to the three methods of performance,
Viśvācī, Ghṛtācī, Urvaśī, and Tilottamā [sang].
Menakā, Sahajanyā, and Rambhā, the foremost of the Apsarases,
performed many dramatic gestures with coquettish movements, emotional expressions, and playful charms;
then, exceedingly melodious and sweet singing proceeded.
O observer of noble vows, then the lutes, flutes, and other instruments were played there, providing delight to the minds and ears of all the hosts of gods;
likewise, the *paṇavas*, *puṣkaras*, *mṛdaṅgas*, and *paṭahas* were sounded.
Divine drums and conchs by the hundreds and thousands were sounded;
with Gandharvas singing and throngs of Apsaras dancing,
and with the sounds of musical instruments and cymbals, everything was filled with a tumultuous roar.
Then, with their hands joined in hollowed cups resembling lotus buds placed upon their foreheads, all the deities prostrated themselves.
Then, amidst that clamor at the assembly of all the gods, [the Lord spoke].

Viśvakarman gradually performed the whetting of his brilliance. Having heard of the Sun’s inscription upon that [stone]— which is praised by Hara, Kamalāsana, and Viṣṇu for its cause being the seasons of snow, water, and heat— one goes to the world of the Sun at the end of one's life.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-first chapter, titled "The Dimming of the Sun’s Radiance by Viśvakarman," in the Saptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan within the glorious *Śrī-Bhaviṣya-Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the one hundred and twenty-second chapter, "Description of the Hymn to Āditya."
Śatānīka said:
Tell me how the Lord of the Day (the Sun), having ascended at that time while being depicted,
was indeed praised by the gods beginning with Brahmā.
Sumantu said:
Listen with a focused mind, O King,
to how in ancient times the Lord of Heaven was praised by Brahmā and the other gods, as well as by the sages, O sinless one.
Homage to the one who, through his very nature, reveals the world to those who bow down with effort and are compassionate toward their welfare;
homage to the Lord of Heaven, who awakens the lotus-clan and completely dispels the veil of darkness!
Homage to the one whose meritorious deeds possess the highest sanctity, and who bestows the power of manifold desires!
Homage to the one garlanded with radiant and stainless rays, who brings benefit to all the worlds;
homage to the unborn, the creator of the three worlds, the soul of all beings, the lord of rays, and the beloved;
homage to the Sun, the supreme among the greatly compassionate, the illuminator of the three worlds.
Salutations to Vivasvat, whose inner self is defined by knowledge, who is the foundation of the world and desires the welfare of the world;
salutations to the Self-existent One, the eye of the entire universe, the supreme among gods, possessed of immeasurable splendor.
For your own arising, O jewel upon the crests of the hosts of gods, you are honored by the worlds, you who heat with a thousand broad rays of light.

"O Lord of the world, you who purify the world from the darkness of ignorance through the drinking of the nectar of the forest of knowledge, you assume a deeply crimson form out of intoxication; you are fierce, utterly destroying the blindness [of the world] with the masses of light-rays that illuminate the three worlds.
Having mounted your chariot, you ever wander for the benefit of the universe.
Thus was the god Bhāskara praised by the Creator (Brahmā) in ancient times.
"And by the deities, O mighty-armed King, such as Śiva, Viṣṇu, and others.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-second chapter, titled "The Hymn to the Sun," in the *Saptamī-kalpa* of the *Brāhma-parvan* within the glorious *Bhaviṣya-mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the one hundred and twenty-third chapter.
Regarding the description of the parilekha,
Śatānīka said: "Tell me once more this story concerning the Sun."
"O Sage, I do not reach satiety while listening to this story. Sumantu said:
"This is the meritorious story of Bhāskara, which destroys all sins."
I shall relate what was previously told by Brahmā, the creator of the worlds:
the sages, tormented by the rays of the sun and utterly bewildered by its brilliance, questioned the Grandfather in the world of Brahmā.
The sages said:
"Who is this blazing one of great splendor, whose radiance is equal to a mass of sacrificial oblations?
We wish to know this; O Lord, from where does his power come?"
Brahmā said:
When the worlds had become enveloped in darkness and all things mobile and immobile had perished,
primordial intellect (buddhi) first arose from the causal operation of the guṇas.
From that, the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) was born, which sets the great elements into motion;
from it arose wind, fire, water, space, and earth, and from those the cosmic egg was produced.
Within that egg, these seven worlds are firmly established.
The earth, with its seven continents and also its seven oceans—
there indeed I remained as Viṣṇu, the Great Lord (Maheśvara). All were utterly bewildered by darkness, yet they meditated upon the Supreme Lord.
Then, as that great splendor which dispels darkness manifested,
it was perceived by us through the yoga of meditation to be the Sun himself;
and having thus recognized the Supreme Self, we all [stood] individually.
They began to praise the God with divine hymns:
"You are the primordial god of the gods; you are the Lord of lords.
You are the original creator of all beings, O eternal God of gods."
You are the life of all beings—of gods, gandharvas, and rākṣasas;
of sages, kinnaras, and siddhas, as well as of serpents and birds.
You are Brahmā, you are Mahādeva, you are Viṣṇu, and you are Prajāpati.
You are Vāyu, Indra, Soma, Vivasvat, and likewise Varuṇa;
you are Time, the creator of the universe, the destroyer, the protector, and the Lord.
You are the rivers, the oceans, the mountains, the lightning, and the rainbows.
Dissolution and manifestation, the manifest and the unmanifest, the eternal—
knowledge is beyond the Lord, and Śiva is beyond knowledge; O Supreme Lord,
you alone are the deity who is even beyond Śiva.
You have hands and feet everywhere; you have eyes, heads, and faces on all sides. O God, you are the thousand-rayed one, as well as the one with a thousand beams.
You are Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ, and likewise Mahas, Janaḥ, Tapaḥ, and Satya.
Salutations to that form of yours which is blazing, eternally radiant, illuminating all the worlds,
and difficult even for the lords of the gods to behold;
which is frequented by hosts of gods and Siddhas, such as Bhṛgu, Atri, and Pulaha.
Homage to you, whose form is supremely auspicious and undisturbed;
that which abides beyond the five, indeed as ten and eleven,
and having transcended half a month, it resides within the solar orb.
To that form of yours, O God, all the deities are bowed down;
salutation to you whose form is the creator of the universe, the source of the universe, and the one worshipped by Viśvānara and the gods;
salutation to that inconceivable form which abides within the universe.
Salutations to that form of yours which is beyond sacrifice, beyond the gods, beyond the worlds, and beyond heaven;
which is known as "difficult to transcend," and even beyond that which is higher than the high,
renowned as the Supreme Self (Paramātman).
Salutation to that form of yours, the God who is unknowable and inconceivable, inward-turned, imperishable, and without beginning or end.
Salutations again and again to the cause of all causes; salutations again and again to the destroyer of evil.
Homage, homage to the one worthy of being saluted; homage, homage to the destroyer of disease.
Homage, homage to the bestower of all boons; homage, homage to the bestower of all strength.
Homage, homage to the eternal treasury of knowledge; homage, homage to the one whose nature consists of fifteen aspects.
Thus praised, the Blessed One, having assumed a form of splendors, spoke these auspicious words: "What boon shall be granted to you?
O Lord, no one can endure your form of such exceeding brilliance."
"O Lord, may this be endured for the welfare of the world.
Having said "So be it" to the Earth, the Blessed One, the doer of all, himself—
who provides heat, rain, and snow— acted for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the worlds.
Therefore, the Sāṃkhyas, the Yogins, and others who desire liberation,
constantly meditate as meditators upon the Sun residing within the heart;
even one devoid of all auspicious marks, or one joined with all sins.
One who takes refuge in the service of the Divine indeed transcends all evil.

The Agnihotra fire-sacrifice, the Vedas, and sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of a single salutation offered with devotion to the Sun.
I take refuge in that Divākara, the supreme sanctuary among sanctuaries, the auspiciousness among auspicious things, and the purity among purifiers;
those gods led by Brahmā who praise him and take refuge in Bhāskara [attain their goal].
Freed from all sins, they go to the abode of the Sun;
just as the Lord of the Day is to be propitiated in the Veda through ritual services and other means,
so too is the divine Sun-god for all people in this world.
Śatānīka said:
O observer of noble vows, tell me how the scraping of the body was indeed established for the Sun by the gods or even by the sages.
Sumantu said:
Those gods, asuras, and sages, having approached Brahmā as he sat comfortably in the world of Brahmā, spoke these words with composed minds.

"O Blessed One, that son of a deity who shines there in the sky has cut away the darkness; indeed, he blazes intensely. By his splendors, the entire world—both the stationary and the moving—is illuminated."
O Lord of Gods, it perishes like a riverbank eroded by distress;
we all are tormented and bewildered by his splendor,
and even this lotus, which is your very source, O Lord, has withered.
"In heaven, on earth, and in the intermediate space, we find no refuge.
O Foremost of Gods, act in such a way that this splendor is pacified.
Thus addressed, the Blessed One, the lotus-born Prajāpati, [replied].
The blessed Brahmā spoke to the gods, headed by Viṣṇu,
who were accompanied by Mahādeva and the high-souled Indra: "Together, let us all go for refuge to that very god."
Then all those gods, including Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the others,
having gone together for refuge to Bhāskara, the illuminator of the world,
began to praise him from all sides, bowing with devotion.
All the deities, beginning with Keśa, filled with a spirit of devotion, said:
"O best of gods, salutations again and again to you of fierce splendor; O best of gods, salutations again and again to you who are indeed praised by the gods."

You always make those who are dull-witted, blind, mute, deaf, afflicted with leprosy, possessed of white leucoderma, sightless, or covered with various ulcers, new again; therefore, salutations to You, the Greatly Compassionate One. That light which is Your belly is exceedingly swift and great, yet it is but a small radiance even for the eyes here on earth.
Whatever has been removed or deposited here in these sacrifices, that very form of yours exists manifoldly.
Those enemies of the gods who dwell in the waters of the ocean, possessing fierce nooses, swords, and axes as weapons—
those evil-minded ones raised high upon the earth— go to their destruction at the sight of you, O Lord.

Since you, O Blessed One, are eternally established in sacrifices and possess the entire fruit of all holy fords (tīrtha), salutations to you! There is no doubt in this matter; you are always impartial and the bringer of peace to men.
Furthermore, that which is called "penance" (tapas) by the wise in the world—that, the learned declare, is your great splendor (mahātejas).
O Lord of the Earth, having been thus praised by the gods headed by Prajāpati, that Blessed One then directed his attention toward his two ears; thereafter,
those gods, led by Śiva and Viṣṇu, began to praise him once more.
Placing me before them, let everyone bow down from all sides with devotion:
"Salutations, salutations to the bestower of prosperity upon the three worlds; salutations, salutations to the one who grants the true fruits of sacrificial rites;
salutations, salutations to the witness of daily actions; salutations, salutations to the one of a thousand rays."
Salutations again and again to You who are joined with seven horses, who are intent on destruction, and who are bound by the single ray of Dhruva.

O God, always praised by the Vālakhilyas, Apsarases, Kinnaras, and Uragas; by the Siddhas, Gandharvas, Piśācas, and humans; and by the hosts of Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and the highest Guhyakas—salutations, salutations to You!
Since you withdraw the fluids of embodied beings with your rays— which are like the outpourings of cold water from a cloud—
and since you constantly dry up the world, you are known in the world as the "Drier of the World. Brahmā said:
Having understood their intention, the Blessed One spoke these words.
Then, having received his permission, all the gods, with delighted hearts,
honored Tvaṣṭṛ through the actions of their mind, speech, and body.
"By your command, let Viśvakarman create your gentleness.
Then Viśvakarman, who was skilled in the performance of all tasks, placed the mass of splendor, Vibhāvasu, upon the lathe.
Then, as the all-pervading Sun was being consecrated with nectar,
Viśvakarman gradually diminished his brilliance; he,
who is worshipped by both gods and demons, was thus scraped down to his knees.
Thereupon, O King, he did not approve of anything beyond that scraping.
From that time forward, the feet of the god remained constantly covered;
heating and withering them, he then possessed a disciplined splendor.
And from the splendor that was severed from him, the discus was fashioned,
by which Viṣṇu always slays the fierce Daityas and Dānavas,
as well as their spears, javelins, maces, thunderbolts, bows, and axes.

Having fashioned it for the deities, the high-minded Viśvakarman gave it to them. A person who recites this hymn composed by the three gods during both twilights purifies his lineage and is not afflicted by diseases.
Possessing progeny and having his deeds accomplished, he shall live for a full hundred autumns;
endowed with sons and wealth, and undefeated everywhere,
he shall leave behind this city composed of the elements and go to the city composed of the sun.
Furthermore, the gods and the celestial sages,
having assembled from the entire three worlds, praised the Sun with these words.
The gods said:
Salutations to you who are the Sun and the Formless; salutations to you who are the form of the Moon.
Salutations to you whose very nature is the Yajurveda; salutations to Atharvan and to Aṅgiras.
Salutations to the one who has become the sole abode of knowledge and from whom all darkness has been dispelled.
Salutations to the one whose nature is pure light, who is beyond the principles (tattvas), whose essence is stainless, whose form is the self;
salutations to the embodiment of the Self that pervades the entire universe,
the cause of all things, and the ultimate goal for those whose minds are fixed on knowledge.
Homage be to you who are the form of all that is knowable, whose nature is luminosity;
