homage to you, the Sun, and likewise homage to the creator of sound. Homage to the cause of worldly existence, and homage to the maker of twilight and moonlight.
O Blessed One, this entire world indeed revolves because of you;
the whole universe, including all that is moving and unmoving, is set in motion by you.
This entire world, joined with your rays, becomes pure.
The purification of water and other substances is brought about by the touch of your hand;
yet religious acts such as fire-offerings and charity do not result in benefit so long as you, O Pure One, have not come into contact with this world.
For the morning sacrifice is indeed praised when it arises while you have risen;
for you, O Lord of the World, are all these Rig-verses, the Yajus-formulas,
and all the Saman-chants, as you thus eternally heat the universe.
O Lord of the World, you consist of the *Ṛgveda*; you alone consist of the *Yajurveda*, and likewise, O Lord, you consist of the *Sāmaveda*, and thus you consist of the three Vedas (*trayī*).
You alone are the form of Brahman, both the supreme and the non-supreme.
Manifest and unmanifest, subtle and existing in a gross form,
consisting of moments, *kāṣṭhās*, and so forth, you are the form of time, whose nature is decay.
Be gracious and, by your own will, manifest a form composed of your own splendor.
Thus being praised by the gods and the celestial sages,
that imperishable mass of splendor then released his own energy;
by that energy of his which consists of the Rigveda, the earth shall come into being.
The sun himself, consisting of the Sāma Veda,
[took] fifteen portions of that very splendor of Śarva;
by him, the high-souled one, the trident was fashioned.
The discus of Viṣṇu, the terrible weapon of the Vasus and of Śaṅkara,
the spear of the six-faced one, the palanquin of the Giver of Wealth,
and whatever other fierce weapons belong to the enemies of the Asuras— [all these were there].
The creator of all things fashioned those [discs] for the Yakṣas and Vidyādharas; furthermore,
the blessed Sun bears a sixteenth part of that splendor,
while fifteen parts of it were diminished by Viśvakarman.
Thereupon, Surūpadṛgbhānu went to the northern Kurus;
there he beheld Saṃjñā, who had assumed the form of a mare.
O best of sages, this entire account of Bhānu has thus been told.
"The man who listens with devotion shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-third chapter, titled "The Description of Parilekha," in the dialogue between the Brahmanical Sages within the Saptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan in the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said:
I shall tell you once more, O Diṇḍi, about that which is the most excellent and preeminent among all things pertaining to the Sun:
he who stands beyond the sky, yet remains immersed therein, is liberated; here too, O Diṇḍi, is Rudra.
In ancient times, it is said, he stood having seized that very skull of Brahmā’s head.
Then, when Śiva was naked in the forest of wood, seeing that lord of the gods wandering for alms among the sages in that most excellent hermitage abounding in water, flowers, and fruits,
all the sons of the women became agitated; yet those sages, being well-pleased, went toward Hara.
Being struck by the assembly of eminent sages with clods of earth and the wooden staffs of the ṛṣis, Diṇḍi abandoned those celestial seers and then departed for the world of the Sun.
As he was approaching, the Pramathas said to him: "O Lord of the Gods, why do you wander about constantly?"
He said to them, "I wander through sacred fords and the abodes of the gods for the sake of liberation from sin.
Those Pramathas spoke to him again: "Stay right here in front of the Sun;
he will bring about your purification, and once purified, you shall go to the world of Rudra."
Thus addressed by the Pramathas, Rudra remained right there to please Ravi;
naked, with matted hair, carrying a fist and a skull-bowl in his hands, and possessing a form incomparable in the three worlds.
Then he was addressed by the gratified Savitṛ: "O God, I am pleased with you because of your arrival."
"By the mere sight of me, you shall be purified and shall become known in the world by the name Diṇḍi.
These eighteen Pramathas, as well as the fourteen others stationed on the chariot of Ravi,
O Goddess, and the two preeminent sages, and likewise the Gandharva and the Serpent— all these [shall be yours]."

The two Yakṣas, the two Siddhas, the two night-stalkers, the two sons of the Sun, and the two foremost of the Apsarases—these indeed dwell within the sun at its setting and rising; their number is eighty-four. All these preeminent among the gods are established through words that signify the functions of the elements.
The sages said:
"O Brahmin, tell me in detail about the most excellent words derived from the root *dhātu*,
for a great curiosity arises within us here, O Brahmin."
Brahmā said:
I shall further describe to you Daṇḍanāyaka and Piṅgala,
as well as the other guardians of the directions, such as Rauṣa and others, together with Diṇḍin.
In the past, the gods deliberated together with me:
"This compassionate Sūrya is fighting with the Dānavas.
Yet those ministers and others, having obtained boons, act with constant disregard.
Thinking him to be the sun, they prepared to kill him as he was scorching;
therefore, for the sake of thwarting them, we have become preeminent. Blocked by us, they shall not see the maker of day.
Having thus deliberated, Skanda then took his place on the left side of the Sun;
he is the lord of all the worlds, known as Daṇḍanāyaka. And at that time, he was addressed by the Sun: "You are the leader of the punishment of living beings."

Because you administer the rod of punishment, you are therefore the Leader of Punishment (Daṇḍanāyaka). He who records the good deeds and the evil deeds of living beings is Agni; because he is tawny (piṅgala) on his right side, he is Piṅgala.
The two Aśvins also stood on both sides of Sūrya;
because they were born from the form of horses, those two gods are called the Aśvins. They are remembered as the gatekeepers of that king, most excellent and possessed of great strength.
Kārttikeya is remembered as the king, and Hara is also remembered as the most excellent.
The verbal root *rāj* is known to mean "to shine," and *na* is its suffix;
because he always shines by virtue of being the commander-in-chief of the divine army.
Therefore, he is remembered by the name Kārtikeya, the son of the King (Kumāra). The verbal root *gam* is traditionally known as "sugati," and its suffix is traditionally known as *pratyaya*.
Because he goes (*gacchati*) in secret (*rahas*), he is called Śrausa by way of that synonym.
O best of the twice-born, at the first gate, which is supported by both Dharma and Artha, these two gods, who are worshipped by the world, are stationed;
and in the second enclosure, the two invincible ones are established.
The lords of birds and spirits are known by the names Kalmāṣapakṣin (the Spotted-winged One).
Because of the variegated color of his body, Yama is called Kalmāṣa;
and the bird whose wings are such is celebrated as Garuḍa.
To his south stood one endowed with a staff in hand;
and to the north of the Sun stood Kubera and Vināyaka.
Kubera is to be known as the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada), and Vināyaka has the form of an elephant.
Cursed by Kutsa in his anger, he was born with a deformed body (kuśarīra).
Because of his deformed body, Kubera is known by that name; as the giver of wealth, he is remembered as Dhanada.
Since he is the leader of all beings, he is called Nāyaka.
Because he leads [them] in various ways, he is therefore called Vināyaka. Raivata and Diṇḍi are situated to the east of Ravi; of these, Diṇḍi is remembered as Rudra, the son of Revatī and Ravi.
Because he, who is honored by all the worlds, goes by leaping (pluta), and since the verbal roots *revṛ* and *plu* both mean "to leap," he is therefore remembered as Revata. Furthermore,
from the root *ḍīṅ*, meaning "to fly," the word *ḍiṇḍi* is derived as an irregular form (nipātyate).
"He always flies (ḍayate), therefore he is celebrated as Diṇḍi.
Thus have these auspicious etymological meanings been declared by the Naigamas as the *pravara* lineages.
Furthermore, I shall indeed tell you their number in brief.
Then those two Aśvins are to be known as Daṇḍanāyaka and Piṅgala;
they are to be known as the gatekeepers of the Sun, and from them the two royal eunuchs (srauṣas) are remembered.
Revata and Diṇḍi—these are the foremost ones described by me.
"Thus, eighteen names have been declared by me in brief according to their number.
With these names, other Dānavas, desiring to slay him and equipped with various weapons and missiles, stood surrounding the Sun."
Those of similar form, those of different forms, and those of diverse forms— capable of assuming any shape at will— stood surrounding the Sun, as did the mighty Garuḍa.
The root *dhātu* is indeed said to mean "to play," and thus he is called *Divi*.
Because they indeed sport in heaven, they are known as the deities (daivatas).
Those Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman verses which have been mentioned here by me exist everywhere around the Sun, manifesting in various forms.
Sumantu said:
Having spoken thus in the past to the sages who were questioning him, Brahmā departed;
and they, having heard this and propitiated the Lord of Gods, attained perfection and dwell in heaven.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Pravaras," in the dialogue between the Brahmanical Sages within the *Saptamī-kalpa* of the *Brāhma-parvan* in the glorious *Śrī-Bhaviṣya-Mahāpurāṇa*.
Śatānīka said:
"O twice-born one, this sky which is seen here in front of the sun—"
"That which is called the Self—what is its nature? Let it be told. Sumantu said:
"Indeed, I shall describe the auspicious *Vyoman*, the weapon of the Sun."
Indeed, that which has been described as the nature of the Sun, and how the deities dwell within it—
that abode of the Sun in the sky has four peaks in front;
it is called "Vyoma" (the Sky), possesses four peaks, and consists of all the gods.

That which was produced from the ocean of red chalk (gairika) and took refuge within its interior—from that this sky was born; the sky of the Kali age is known as the earth. Just as the noose belongs to Varuṇa, so is the syllable "huṃ" to the Creator (Brahmā).
Just as Viṣṇu has his discus and Tryambaka his trident,
and just as Indra has his thunderbolt, so is the sky (vyoman) known as the [weapon] of the Sun.
Within that sky, the thirty-three sacrificial deities sport.
Hara, Varṣaśuddha, Tryambaka, Aparājita,
Vṛṣākapi, Śambhu, Kapardin, Raivata,
Īśvara, and Bhuvana— these are remembered as the eleven Rudras.
And let the names of the Ādityas and of Viṣṇu’s discus be given:
Aryaman, as well as Mitra, Bhaga, and Varuṇa;
Vivasvat, Savitṛ, Pūṣan, and likewise Tvaṣṭṛ.
Aṃśu, Bhaga, and Atitejas— these are remembered as the twelve Ādityas.
Dhruva, Dhara, Soma, Āpa, Anila, Anala,
Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāsa are proclaimed as the eight Vasus.
Both Nāsatya and Dasra are remembered as the two Aśvins.
I shall now declare the Viśvedevas by name; learn of them.
They are Kratu, Dakṣa, Vasu, Satya, Kāla, Kāma, Dhṛti, and Kuru.
Śaṅku, Mātra, Vāmana, and the Viśvedevas—these ten are remembered as the present gods. Now hear of those who will be in the next interval:
Yama, the Tuṣitas, the Vasus, and the Vaśavartins.
The Satyas, the Bhūtarajas, and the Sādhyas immediately following them—
thus, in six Manvantaras, there were twelve gods each.
Furthermore, the Pārāvatas and others likewise existed together with the Tuṣitas.
I shall declare the deities who are to be propitiated; learn them from me by name:
Manas, Anumantṛ, Prāṇa, Nara, and likewise Nārāyaṇa; Vṛttilambha, Manu, Sama, and the heroic Dharma.
Vittasvāmī and Prabhu— these are proclaimed as the twelve Sādhyas.
These gods, who partake in sacrifices and are worshipped in all the worlds,
O wise one, are remembered as the sons of Kaśyapa born from Aditi.
The Viśvedevas and the Vasus are to be known as the Sādhyas, the sons of Dharma.
Thus, Soma is considered the third son of Dharma;
indeed, it is established in the Purāṇa that Dharma himself is the son of Brahmā.
Now, learn from me the names of the Indras and the Vasus as well.
First was Svāyambhuva Manu, and after him Svārociṣa is recorded;
then Uttama, Tāmasa, Raivata, and likewise Cākṣuṣa.
Thus these six have passed away; the seventh is the present Manu, to be known as Vaivasvata. There will be seven others yet to come.
Of these, the first were Arkasāvarṇi and Brahmasāvarṇi.
From him [came] Bhavasa-varṇi and Dharmasa-varṇi;
the fifth is Dakṣasa-varṇi—these five are celebrated as the Sāvarṇis.
Raucya and Bhauvya are the two others; these are remembered as the Manus.
Indra shall be known as Viṣṇubhuj; after him, Vidyuti;
then Vibhu, Prabhu, Śikhin, and likewise Manojava;
Ojasvin is the Indra of the present time, and thereafter Bali shall be the future one.
Adbhuta, Tridiva, and the tenth is said to be Indra; Susāttvika, Cakrin, Kīrtimat, Śatadhāman, and Divaspati—
thus the fourteen Indras, both past and future, are to be known.
Kaśyapa, Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Bharadvāja, Gautama,
Viśvāmitra, and Jamadagni— these seven are remembered as the sages (ṛṣis). Hereafter, I shall proclaim the Maruts who are the attendants of Agni.
Pravaha, Avaha, Udvaha, Samvaha,
Vivaha, Nivaha, and likewise Parivaha—
these move through the intermediate space, spreading out along their respective paths.

Sūrya, Agni, and Śuci are known by name as Vaidyuta and Pāvaka; Nirmathya and Pavamāna—these three are declared to be the fires. Furthermore, the sons and grandsons of these fires number exactly forty.
It should be known that for all the Maruts there are seven groups of seven.
For him (Dakṣa), the seasons, the year, and Agni were born;
and his sons from the seasons were five—such is the eternal creation.
The first is the Saṃvatsara, the second is the Parivatsara,
the third is the Idvatsara, and the fourth is the Anuvatsara;
the fifth among them is the Vatsara— thus are those five remembered.
Among them, Agni is indeed Saṃvatsara, while Sūrya is Parivatsara; Soma is Idvatsara, and Vāyu is Anuvatsara;
Rudra, however, is to be known as Vatsara—these five are the deities of the Yuga.
The ancestors known as the Ārtavas are those born from the seasons (Ṛtusūnavas). The grandfathers are to be known as the five-year-old sons of Brahmā.
These three groups are the Saumyas, the Barhiṣads, and the Agniṣvāttas.
These indeed are the ancestors of those men whose fathers are still living:
Āditya, Soma, Lohitāṅga, Budha,
Bṛhaspati, Śukra, and he who is the son of Helī (Śani).
Uparāga and Śikhin—these nine are traditionally known as the planets;
they are the eternal indicators of the existence and non-existence of the three worlds.
Both Āditya and Soma are these two planetary orbs.
Among them, Rāhu is the shadow-grasper (chāyā-graha), while the others are known as the star-planets (tārā-grahas).
Soma is the lord of the lunar mansions (nakṣatras), and the Sun is the king of the planets;
moreover, Agni is recited as the Āditya, and the Moon is remembered as water.

The Sun is recited as Brahmā, Viṣṇu is among them, and the Moon is Maheśvara; the third is to be known as the stellar planet (Tārakagraha). Sūrya is the son of Kaśyapa, while Soma is remembered as the son of Dharma.

These two great planets, Śukra and Bṛhaspati, are by name the preceptors of the gods and the asuras; both are sons of Prajāpati. The illustrious Budha is known as the son of Soma, and Śani is remembered as the son of Ravi.
Rāhu is the son of Siṃhikā, while Ketu is the son of Brahmā.
Indeed, the Sun moves below all the planets;
far beyond that, it is said, lies the lunar mansion and the circle of stars.
From the constellations [come] Mars and Mercury; after that, the one called Śveta;
above him, Māheśvara; after that, Dhiṣaṇa;
above him, Kṛṣṇa; and after that, from him, the one born of Citraśikhaṇḍin.
The sequence of these very [planets] has been declared; they are unattached and fixed in the third heaven.
Rāhu sometimes occupies the path of the Sun and sometimes the path of the Moon. However, Śikhin (the Fire-planet), situated within the solar orb, always glides along.
The diameter of Bhārgava’s [Venus] sphere is nine thousand yojanas;
the diameter of Śani [Saturn] is recorded as twice that of the Sun’s diameter.
The stellar sphere (nākṣatra) is to be known as three times the diameter of the Moon.
There, Bṛhaspati is one-quarter less than the circle of the constellations;
Śukra and Aṅgāraka are indeed each one-quarter less than Bṛhaspati;
and Budha’s extent is one-quarter less than those two circles.
The constellations are equal in size to the Buddha; indeed, all the constellations are half a *yojana* in measure, and nothing is found smaller than they.
Rāhu is the same size as the sun, and at times he resembles the moon.
O lord of men, the comet is known to be unstable;
its course is unascertainable due to its flickering nature.
Thus, though its form is not clearly defined, it indeed assumes many forms.

The *bhūrloka* is declared to be the earth (*pṛthivī*), and the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) is remembered as *bhuvaḥ*. The *svarloka* is to be known as the third heaven (*tridiva*); that which remains above these is to be understood in due order.
Furthermore, because the lord of the earth (*bhūpati*) is always Agni, he is therefore remembered as *bhūpati*.
Vāyu is the lord of the sky, and likewise Sūrya is the lord of the day;
as are the Gandharvas, Apsarases, Guhyakas, Siddhas, and Rākṣasas.
All those who dwell in the world of earth—now hear of those who move in the intermediate space.
The Maruts are on the seventh ridge, as are the Rudras and the two Aśvins;
all the Ādityas and Vasus, as well as the herds of cows, likewise reside there.
However, in the fourth world, Maharloka, dwell those who live for an entire kalpa.
Accompanied by all the Lords of Creatures (Prajāpatis), O descendant of Kuru,
those who have given land always dwell in the fifth world,
Janaloka; there reside Ṛtu, Sanatkumāra, and others, taking refuge with the brothers of Vairāja.
In the seventh world,

O descendant of Kuru, is the realm of Brahmā, known as the world of truth for those who travel the path of non-returning; it is characterized by the absence of obstruction, where those who know the Itihāsas sport.
And those who always listen to the Purāṇas, O son of Bhīma,
[hear that] the Sun is a hundred thousand yojanas above the surface of the earth,
while Dhruva is situated a hundred million yojanas above the earth.
Beyond that, the height of the three worlds is said to be twenty lakhs [of yojanas];
then, at two hundred thousand yojanas,
the space between the worlds (lokāntara) is likewise ordained above the Pole Star (dhruva).
Gods, Dānavas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Pannagas,
Bhūtas, and Vidyādharas— these are the eight divine origins (devayonis). In that very sky these seven worlds are firmly established.

For these Maruts are indeed the Pitṛs; they are the fires and the vessels within that very [space]. Moreover, those eight divine origins which have been enumerated by me—both those with form and those without form—all of them are established in the ether.
This sky is of such a nature that it is remembered as consisting of all skies,
as consisting of all gods, and likewise as consisting of all planets.
Therefore, whoever worships the sky has indeed worshipped all the deities.
Therefore, one who desires auspicious results should worship the sky with every effort.
O King, he who always worships the sky with devotion and endowed with faith shall go to the abode of the Bull-bannered Lord; of this there is no doubt.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Cosmic Egg (Bhuvanakośa)" within the "Greatness of the Sky" (Vyoma-māhātmya) section of the Saptamī-kalpa in the Brāhma-parvan of the glorious *Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the one hundred and twenty-sixth chapter:
"Description of the Greatness of the Sky."
Sumantu said:
Ākāśa, kha, the quarters, vyoman, antarikṣa, nabhah, ambaram,
puṣkara, gagana, meru, vipula, and likewise bila.
Āpa, chidra, likewise śūnya, tamaḥ, and rodasī—
these, O lord of the earth, are proclaimed as the names of the sky (vyoman).
Furthermore, there are the oceans of salt, milk, curd, sour [liquor], clarified butter, honey, and molasses.
These seven oceans are proclaimed to be filled with sweet water;
and Himavān, Hemakūṭa, Niṣadha, Nīla,
Śveta, and Śṛṅgavān— these six are the mountain ranges that divide the regions.
Situated in the midst of these is the Mahārājata mountain;
likewise, there are the regions of Māhendrī, Āgneyī, Yāmyā, Nairṛtī,
Vāruṇī, Vāyavyā, Saumyā, and Aiśānī.
These cities of the gods are likewise situated above;
O hero, the Lokāloka mountain stands upon the earth,
and beyond that is Caṇḍakapāla, and further than that is what lies beyond it.
From that [the intellect] arise fire, wind, and space; from that, the originator of the elements (bhūtādi) is said to proceed.
From that comes the Great One (mahat), then the ego (ahaṅkāra), then primordial nature (prakṛti), and then the person (puruṣa).
From the person arises the Lord (īśvara), who is the supreme good; by the Lord the entire world is pervaded.
The Lord Bhānu, the Blessed One, has filled this world;
he is the thousand-rayed one of great splendor, four-armed and of mighty strength.
Furthermore, there are worlds above those which were previously described by me.
Furthermore, I shall fully describe those who form the enclosures of the cosmic egg:
Bhūrloka, Bhuvarloka, and the third is proclaimed as Maharloka; along with Janarloka, Taparloka, and Satyaloka, these are celebrated as the seven worlds.
From that comes the egg-shell, and beyond that, heat (tapaḥ).

From that, fire, air, and space; from that, the origin of the elements (bhūtādi) is said to arise. From that, the Great One (mahat) and the Primal Matter (pradhāna); and from that, Nature (prakṛti) and Spirit (puruṣa).
The Supreme Lord is to be known as Puruṣa; the universe is pervaded by the Lord. Listen now to the seven worlds situated beneath the earth that are well-known:
Tala, Sutala, Pātāla, Talātala, and likewise Atala.
And Vitala, O best of the Kurus, is the seventh netherworld (rasātala).

Beyond that are fire, wind, and space; beyond those is the source of the elements (bhūtādi); beyond that is the Great One (mahat) and the Primal Matter (pradhāna), which is Nature (prakṛti); and beyond that is the Spirit (puruṣa).
Puruṣa is to be known as the Lord; the world is enveloped by the Lord.
Thus has the entire measurement of Meru been proclaimed:
that auspicious Meru is golden, four-cornered, and possesses four peaks.
Situated in the midst of the earth and frequented by Siddhas and Gandharvas,
it seems to scrape the very heavens with its four divine golden peaks;
it rises eighty-four thousand yojanas in height.
It enters sixteen [yojanas] below and extends twenty-eight [yojanas] across;
its circumference is known to be three times its width.
Of that mountain, there is one golden peak named Saumanasa.
The second is named Jyotiṣka, with the luster of a ruby;
the third is auspiciously named Citra, consisting of all the gods;
and the fourth is known as Rājata, white and possessing the splendor of the moon.
That peak of the Gaṅgā which is called Saumanasa is indeed named Udaya, where the sun is seen rising;
having circled Jambūdvīpa to the north, the maker of day [emerges there].

Established upon the peak of the golden mountain, he becomes visible to all beings; and because the splendor of the sun has been withdrawn, both the eastern and western twilights shine with a coppery hue.
On the Saumanasa peak, the sun rises during its northern course;
it is at Jyotiṣa during its southern course, and exactly between those two at the equinox.
Īśa and Indra are on Mount Udra in the northeast, while Agni is there in the southeast.
Then, one should know that Nairṛta is in the southwest and likewise Marut in the northwest;
in the center, however, is the Lotus-born One himself, as well as the planets and the luminaries.
The Sun is established in that sky in that very form.
This [space] is known as consisting of the gods, and likewise as consisting of the worlds;
O Lord of the Earth, Śukra is situated on the peak located in the eastern corner,
while the son of the Sun (Saturn) is to be known in another, and the Lord of Wealth (Venus) in yet another.
O lord of men, Soma is also situated on the fourth peak;
O King, Keśa is stationed in the middle, as is the Huṅkāra of the wielder of the Pināka bow;
O King, the god is stationed on the northeastern peak at the time of the waning moon.
Then Mahādeva, the Lord of Rays (Gopati), worshipped by the world, remained there;
on the peak situated in the southeast stood the son Śāṇḍila;
and then the highly effulgent Kīnāśa, the son of Heli, remained there.
The mighty Virūpākṣa indeed stands on the western peak;
immediately adjacent to him stands the god who is the lord of aquatic creatures.
Beyond that stands the highly effulgent and very powerful Vīramitra.
Taking his stand upon the Vāyavya peak, which is saluted by all the gods,
the Daśabala (the One of Ten Powers) then mounted the Nara [pillar], O Bhārata;
the god Brahmā stood in the middle, and Ananta indeed at the very bottom.
The two gods Upendra and Śaṅkara are stationed together at the end of Brahmā.
This is Meru, as well as the sky; this is also recited as Dharma.
This Meru consists of all the gods and is remembered as the sky.
Likewise, it is also recited as being composed of the Vedas; there is no doubt about this.
The wise know that its four peaks are the four Vedas, beginning with the eastern peak.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Vyoma," in the Saptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan within the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa.
Now begins the one hundred and twenty-seventh chapter,
"Description of the Grace of the Sun.
Śatānīka said:
"How was the Sun propitiated by Sāmba of immeasurable splendor?
And how was he freed from his diseases? Tell me, O best of the twice-born.
Sumantu said:
"I have been well questioned, O Indra among kings; listen now to the ancient story of Sāmba.
I shall relate to you in full detail this entire narrative that liberates one from sin.
Formerly, having heard the majesty of the Sun-god from Nārada..."
Approaching his father with humility, he spoke these words:
"O Acyuta, I am overwhelmed by a dejection born of impurity and disease;
even through physicians and medicinal herbs, no relief is found for me."
"I am going to the forest, O Blessed One; you should grant me permission.
With auspiciousness, O lotus-eyed one, meditate upon me, O Supreme Person.
Having been thus permitted by Kṛṣṇa, he [departed] from the northern shore of the ocean.
Having gone there, he crossed the great river Candrabhāgā;
then, having gone to Mitravana, a sacred ford renowned throughout the three worlds, Sāmba remained intent on fasting, emaciated and with his veins standing out.
For the sake of propitiating the Sun, he recited a secret hymn equal to the four Vedas and augmented by the Purāṇas:
"That which is this white orb, divine, indeed undecaying and imperishable..."
He is yoked with horses swift as thought, tawny-hued and exponents of the Veda;
for he is the first of all beings, known by the name Āditya.
He is indeed the eye of the three worlds, the Supreme Self, and the Lord of Creatures.
Indeed, this great Person shines within this mandala;
he is Viṣṇu of inconceivable nature, and he is Brahmā, the Grandfather;
he is Rudra, Mahendra, Varuṇa, ether, earth, and water.
Vāyu, Śaśāṅka, Parjanya, Dhanādhyakṣa, and Vibhāvasu—
this great person who shines within this orb is indeed the one Great God himself,
always resembling the splendor of Vṛtra.
For this mighty-armed one is Time itself, characterized by the manifestation of creation;
he who, filling the earth with his splendors within this very circle,
revolves incessantly, driven by the winds, and is characterized by immortality.
There exists nothing anywhere superior to him in brilliance;
he alone nourishes all beings with the nectar of immortality—
beings dwelling within, those of barbarian descent, and even those belonging to the animal realm.

Out of compassion, O Vibhāvasu, you protect all beings; likewise, O Lord, you who are affectionate toward those who seek refuge, O God, render even those afflicted with vitiligo, leprosy, blindness, deafness,
and lameness free from disease.

O Lord, you who perceive all directly, effortlessly uplift those with deficient wheels, those lacking limbs, the destitute, and the short-lived. What power do I have to praise you with hymns? I am but a wretched man, tormented by disease.
You are constantly praised by the gods, beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva;
by Mahendra, the Siddhas, Gandharvas, Apsarases, and Guhyakas.
O Lord, what need is there for other purifying hymns uttered in your praise?
You, whose triad of Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāman resides within the Maṇḍala,
are the supreme meditation for those who meditate and the gateway to liberation for those seeking liberation;
you are indeed unshakeable by infinite splendor, inconceivable, unmanifest, and partless.
"Since the Lord of the World has been interrupted in this hymn of praise,
you ought to understand all of that, having perceived my distress and my devotion.
Then Sūrya spoke with affection to the son of Jāmbavatī:
"I am pleased with your asceticism, my child; tell me what you desire.
Samba said:
"If the Blessed One is pleased, this itself is the boon for me."
"O eternal God, may I have supreme devotion toward you.
Śrī Sūrya said: "I am pleased with you once more; may it be well with you. Choose a boon, O observer of noble vows."
He then requested a second boon from the omnipresent Lord, the bestower of boons:
"O Lord of Light, by your grace, may the impurity residing within my body perish,
so that my entire form may become pure."
Sumantu said:
Having been told "So be it" by that high-souled Bhāskara,
Sāmba released that pain from his body, just as a snake sheds its skin.
Then, by means of his divine form, he became possessed of beauty once again;
bowing his head to the God, he stood before him.
Śrīsūrya said:
Furthermore, O Sāmba, listen to what I say to you out of satisfaction;
from this day forward, O observer of noble vows, those who shall establish my shrines upon the earth under your name will attain eternal worlds.
Establish me indeed on this auspicious bank of the Candrabhāgā;
by your name, this Sāmaveda shall attain supreme renown.
O observer of noble vows, your fame shall become inexhaustible in the world and achieve great celebrity.
"Furthermore, I shall grant you a vision in dreams every day.
Sumantu said: Having thus granted that boon and another to that lion of the Vṛṣṇis, [the Lord departed].
Having granted a direct vision, Hari vanished right there.
A devoted person who recites this hymn at the three times of day,
or performs a fire-oblation (homa) seventy-three times for seven nights, [attains the goal].
One who desires a kingdom shall obtain a kingdom; one who desires wealth shall obtain wealth.
One afflicted by disease is liberated from disease, just as Sāmba was;
likewise, by worshipping the Sun with devotion, one shall even go to the world of the Sun.
And thus he rejoices therein, surrounded by the gods.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Grace of the Sun," in the *Sāmbopākhyāna* within the *Saptamī-kalpa* of the *Brāhma-parvan* in the glorious *Mahāpurāṇa Bhaviṣya*.
Now begins the one hundred and twenty-eighth chapter.
Sumantu said: Then Samba, emaciated and covered with visible veins, offered this hymn of praise.
Then, seeing the son of Kṛṣṇa wearying himself with the Thousand Names of the thousand-rayed Sun,
Sūrya appeared to him in a dream and spoke these words again:
The illustrious Sūrya said:
"O Sāmba, Sāmba, O you of mighty arms, son of Jāmbavatī, listen!
Enough with the thousand names; recite this auspicious hymn."
I shall proclaim those secret names which are purifying and auspicious; listen attentively as I recite them with care:
Vaikartana, Vivasvat, Mārtaṇḍa, Bhāskara, and Ravi.
The illuminator of the world, the glorious one, the eye of the world, the lord of the planets,
the witness of the world, the lord of the three worlds, the creator, the destroyer, the dispeller of darkness,
the burner, the scorcher, the pure one, whose vehicle is drawn by seven horses.
Gabhastihasta, Brahmā, and he who is saluted by all the gods—
this hymn of twenty-one verses is always dear to me;
it bestows physical health, increases wealth, and brings about fame.

Known as the King of Hymns, it is renowned throughout the three worlds. O mighty-armed one, whoever, having bowed down, praises me with this at both twilights— at sunset and at sunrise— is liberated from all sins.
Whatever evil deed has been committed— whether mental, verbal, or physical—
all of that perishes before me by means of a single recitation.
This [mantra] is for recitation, for fire-offerings (homa), and likewise for the twilight worship (sandhyopāsana).
The mantra for the bali offering, the mantra for the arghya water, and likewise the mantra for incense;
when this great, auspicious mantra— which removes all sins— is employed during the giving of food, bathing, prostration, and circumambulation, it becomes fully empowered through worship.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One Bhāskara, the Lord of the worlds,
took leave of the son of Kṛṣṇa and vanished on the spot.
Sāmba, too, having praised the one whose vehicle is seven horses with this king of hymns—
With a joyful soul, free from disease and endowed with splendor, he was liberated from that illness.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Hymn to Sāmba," in the *Saptamī-kalpa* of the *Brāhma-parvan* within the glorious *Bhaviṣya-mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the one hundred and twenty-ninth chapter.
The Description of the Installation of the Sāmba-Aditya Image.
Sumantu said: Now, having obtained the boon, Sāmba, having received that ancient favor...
Considering that a marvel, with a heart full of joy, he went—
not very far— to the river Candrabhāgā for the purpose of bathing, together with other ascetics and with that same former habit.
Having fashioned the form of his own maṇḍala, full of faith day after day, he bathed and reflected: "What form shall I establish?
Having bathed, he then immediately prostrated before Prabhāvatī.
Seeing that image being carried by the flood of water directly toward the sun,
this thought arose in that hero:
"Without a doubt, this is exactly what was commanded by the Lord."
Having rescued her from the water and brought her there, O lord of the earth,
he then established her in that region of Mitravana;
having set up images of that high-souled one in the world, Sāmba remained there.
Having installed Mitra according to the prescribed rites in the beautiful Mitravana grove,
he then bowed down and questioned that very image of the Sun:
"O Lord, by whom was this auspicious form of yours fashioned?"
Then the image spoke to him: "Listen, Sāmba, I shall speak for myself.
By whomsoever this anthropomorphic form of mine was fashioned, my ancient form had previously been permeated by supreme splendor."
"Because it was unbearable for all beings, I was then worshipped by the gods with the words:
'May your form become bearable to all living creatures.
Thereupon, I commanded Viśvakarman, who is possessed of great ascetic power."
"Diminishing the brilliance [of all things], fashion my form.
Then, by my command,
he skillfully fashioned my form by making a lathe in Śākadvīpa at that very time.
Out of affection for them, this elaborate display was once again caused to be made by me;
therefore, this [city] was fashioned from the Kalpa-tree by Viśvakarman after he had previously constructed it on the slopes of the Himavat mountain, which are frequented by the Siddhas.
For your sake, she was then brought down by him into the Candrabhāgā river; indeed,
for the purpose of your liberation, this auspicious and beautiful place shall always remain here, where my presence, along with Ambā, will abide.
My presence shall be seen by people daily at the excellent shore in the forenoon,
at Kālapriya at midday, and in the afternoon as well.
In the forenoon Brahmā shall worship me, and at midday the wielder of the discus himself.
"Śaṅkara, moreover, always worships me in the afternoon.
Having been addressed thus by the Blessed One Bhāskara, O mighty-armed one, that Yādava attained great joy; thereafter, Bhāskara vanished.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Installation of the Solar Image by Sāmba," in the Sāmba-episode of the *Saptamī-kalpa* within the *Brāhma-parvan* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya-mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the one hundred and thirtieth chapter,
"Description of the Characteristics of Grace."
Śatānīka said:
O best of Brahmins, how was the installation of the Sun performed by Sāmba?
And at whose word did he have the temple of the Sun constructed?
Sumantu said:
O Indra among kings, I shall tell you here how the wise Sāmba caused the installation of the Sun-god and obtained his grace, O lord of the earth.
Having obtained an image of the Sun, he thought of Nārada;
and being thus thought of, Nārada arrived where the son of Jāmbavatī was.
Beholding that best of sages, Nārada, who had arrived—
Having worshipped Nārada together with Ambā according to the prescribed rites, Sāmba spoke these words:
"O twice-born one, O divine sage, what is the fruit for that man who causes a temple to be built for the Sun-god, and who also performs its consecration?"
Nārada said:
O tiger among men, he who causes a temple to be built for the Sun in a beautiful location goes to the world of the Sun; of this there is no doubt.
Sāmba said:
O best of the twice-born, how should one construct a temple, and in what location?
And of what nature, O twice-born one, should the temple of the God of gods be?
Nārada said:
Where there is abundant water both at the beginning and at the end [of the rainy season],
one should construct a temple for the deities for the sake of increasing fame and merit.
Through sacrifices and charitable works, one attains those worlds that are adorned;
there, the abode of the gods is to be constructed, where two things are seen:
water and the like, and groves within the established sanctuaries.
In these places the deities manifest their presence:
in lakes covered with lotus beds that block out the rays of the sun,
where the waters are pure and the rows of white water-lilies are gathered together by swans.
Resounding with the cries of swans, *kāraṇḍava* ducks, cranes, and ruddy geese,
where people rest in the pure shadows at the edges,
and where the girdles of cranes murmur sweetly and the melodious calls of swans ring out.
There, the rivers have water for their garments, shoals of fish for their girdles,
and flowering, excellent trees for their dwellings; they possess the circular hips of their confluences, high breasts in the form of sandbanks, and laughter in the form of their flowing currents.
The deities always delight in the regions near forests, rivers, and mountains, as well as in cities provided with gardens;
these are the grounds for the Brahmins and others that have been prescribed in the science of architecture (vāstu).
These very [measures] are thus recommended for them even in the temples of the deities. One should always construct a temple with sixty-four squares;
in that [layout], a central door is highly commended when aligned with the cardinal directions.
Whatever its width may be, its height should be double that;
the elevation should be one-third of that, and the base should be equal to it.
For a structure with a divided womb (bhinnayoni), the inner sanctum (garbha) should be half the width on all sides.

The door should be one-quarter of a *garbha* in width and twice that in height. The *śākhā* (the side-lintel) should be one-quarter of the height in width; likewise for the *udumbarī* (the cross-beam).
The thickness of the remaining two (the *śākhā* and *udumbarī*) is recorded as being one-quarter of their own width.
The king is praised with nine branches;
then, one should place two door-keepers at the fourth part of the branches,
adorned with mountains, auspicious birds, *śrīvṛkṣa* trees, svastikas, and jars.
The image together with its pedestal should be one-eighth of the height;
therein, the image occupies two parts and the pedestal the third part. O mighty-armed one, Meru is to the east and Kailāsa likewise to the west.
And there are others, O Hero, such as the Vimānacchadana,
as well as the Samudra, Padma, Garuḍa, Nandivardhana, and Kuñjara;
the Gṛharāja, Vṛṣa, Haṃsa, Sarvatobhadra, and Ghaṭa.
The Siṃha, the Vṛṣa, the Catuṣkoṇa, and likewise the Ṣoḍaśa and Aṣṭāśraya—
these twenty types of temples have been declared, O delighter of the Yadus.
I shall now describe their characteristics to you in the very order previously mentioned.
Mount Meru is thirty-nine units high, possesses twelve stories, and contains various caves;
it is provided with four gates and is thirty-two cubits wide.
Mount Mandara is thirty cubits long, has ten stories, and consists of seven [peaks].

Kailāsa, though possessing peaks, has twenty-eight peaks and eight stories; it is endowed with lattice windows, is known as a *vimāna*, and measures twenty-one in length. The terrestrial [garden] called Nandana, however, possesses thirty-two [features] and is endowed with sixteen limbs.
This [structure] named Samudga is circular and lotus-shaped, and it has eight [parts].
It should have one peak (śṛṅga) and one base (bhūmikā).
Garuḍa is shaped like Garuḍa, while Nandī is indeed sixty [units] in width.
The body is adorned with seven stories and twenty-seven constituent parts.
"Kuñjara" refers to the back of the elephant; it is sixteen *hasta*s in height at its center.
The "king of houses" (*gṛharāja*) consists of sixteen [parts], and there should be a *valabhī* (pinnacle) with three circular halls.
The *vṛṣa* (bull) has horns like those of a deer and is twenty-eight cubits in height; it is elevated and circular.
The *haṃsa* (swan) is shaped like a swan; the *ghaṭa* (pot) has the form of eight thousand jars.
Endowed with four doors and many spires, it becomes the *sarvatobhadra* (auspicious on all sides).
The Bahurucira has a moon-chamber (*candraśālā*) and a ground area of twenty-seven parts;
the Siṃha is twelve-cornered in the shape of a lion and measures eight cubits;
and three thousand [other types] have been described by Viśvakarman.
"In this matter, the wise say that there is one opinion of those who establish [the truth];
therefore, it attains equality with the *kapotapālinī*.
Sāmba said:
O Brahmin, regarding these twenty temples you have described, which temple among them should be constructed for Sūrya, the Maker of Light? Furthermore,
O best of the twice-born, what are the locations that have been prescribed for his temple?
"You have indeed told them that their city is filled with men subject to decay;
in that region, an excellent temple for the Sun must be built.
O best of the twice-born, tell us in which direction it should be situated; please speak further."
Nārada said:
Having occupied the center of the city, one should construct a temple for Ravi;
or else, in the eastern quarter of the directions, near the eastern gate.
Having first examined the ground, one should then construct the sanctuary;
a ground endowed with desirable fragrance and taste, which is not low-lying, is praised,
provided it is free from gravel, husks, hair, bones, salt, and charcoal.
Resounding like the thunder of clouds and causing all seeds to sprout,
the earth is said to be white, red, yellow, and black,
respectively for those born of the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra lineages.
Once that [ground] has been examined, one should smear an area in its center measuring four cubits on all sides according to the prescribed dimensions;
having made it one cubit deep at the bottom, one should leave a space of ten finger-breadths in its middle.
Having dug a pit, one should fill it back with that very same earth.
If the ground is level, the qualities [of the site] should be known as average; if it is lower, the qualities will be inferior;
but if the earth rises up, the ground will bring about prosperity.

The house should always be properly situated facing the sun, or occasionally facing west, by means of the calculation of the eastern-facing position. To the right side of the residence, there should be a bathhouse for the sun.
The auspicious Agnihotra house should be constructed to the north of the Sun;
the house of Śambhu and that of the Mothers should face the north.
Brahmā should be installed in the west, and likewise Viṣṇu in the north.
Nimba is proclaimed to be on the right side, and Rājñī on the left;
Piṅgala is the leader of the guards for the Sun-god on the left,
while the place of Śrī and Mahāśvetā is in front of the Radiant One (Aṃśumālin).
Then, outside the temple of the previous deity, the station of the Aśvins was established;
in the second enclosure, the two horses of the King were stationed;
and in the third enclosure, the two variegated birds were stationed.
Jaṇḍa and Kāmacara are to be stationed, taking recourse to the southern direction;
Kubera, honored by the world, is to be placed in the north;
and to the north of him is Revata together with Vināyaka.
Or wherever a place exists among all the directions, such as caves and so forth;
two mandalas should be prepared for the purpose of offering the *arghya*, one on the left and one on the right.
At the time of sunrise, one should offer the *arghya* to the Sun on the southern [mandala].
At sunset, one should offer the *arghya* oblation upon the northern mandala;
likewise, O Hero, one should duly install an image of the Sun-god in the form of a wheel within another [mandala] using four auspicious jars.
In the third mandala, the Sun-god (Divākara) should indeed be worshipped with the sounds of various musical instruments and the abundant blasts of conchs.
In front of the temple of the deity, one should construct a square celestial abode (vyoma) with four peaks.
A mandala should be constructed in the center of this [site] using a cord for the sake of the image.
A staff (diṇḍī) should be placed before it, standing facing the sun.
This which has been described by me as the sky consists of all the gods.
O best of the Yadus, at midday, the arghya offering should be given to him here;
or else, having established another mandala, the third of which is equal in size to the wheel,
the Lord of Gods should be installed and the arghya offered by the most learned ones.
The task should be performed before the deity, in a place near the sky (an open space),
or at the location for reading the scripture, or wherever one finds it pleasing.
This is declared to be the rule for the locations of the deities in their proper sequence.
"Then there is Gṛharāja and Rudra; these two are dear to Bhāskara.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirtieth chapter, titled "Description of the Characteristics of Temples," in the Sāmbopākhyāna of the Saptamī-kalpa within the Brāhma-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the one hundred and thirty-first chapter.
Description of the Examination of Wood.
Nārada said:
Now I shall fully explain to you the detailed procedure for the making of images.
For all the gods, and especially for Āditya,
seven kinds of images are prescribed for the increase of the welfare of devotees:
those made of gold, silver, copper, earth, and stone are traditionally taught.
The wooden [image], the painted one, and so forth— these are indeed the seven types of physical forms (mūrtisthāna).
O Hero, I shall describe to you in their entirety the procedure for the wooden image on a day favorable to the artisan, purified by the [astrological] year.
One should enter the forest accompanied by auspicious omens, favorable portents, and auspicious departures.
All milky trees are to be avoided, for they are naturally weak;
likewise, those known as *putraka* trees at crossroads should not be accepted.
Those situated in temples of deities, as well as those arising from anthills; those upon which carved deities are found, and those known as sacred trees (caitya-vṛkṣas);
those born on cremation grounds, and those that are the nests of birds.
Those trees that have hollows, those whose tops are withered,

those elephants slain by weapons, as well as those made into pillars, those afflicted by the Sāma and other [magical] powers, those suffering from disease, and likewise those struck down by pestilence;

Those trees that have blossomed out of season, as well as those whose blossoms have fallen prematurely; those with withered leaves, frequented by rākṣasas and crows; those with only a single branch, or excessive branches, or three branches—these are likewise base.
Madhūka, Devadāru, Vṛkṣarāja, and Candana;
Bilva, Āmrātaka, Khadira, and likewise Añjana;
Nimba, Śrīparṇa tree, Panasa, Sarala, and Arjuna.
The best trees for images are those ending with red sandalwood;
two trees are proclaimed for each of the castes in their respective order.
Trees beginning with the neem are remembered as common to all castes.
Listen further, O hero, as I describe other [trees] in detail:
the suradāru, the śamī, the madhūka, and likewise the candana. These trees, my dear, are remembered as auspicious for Brāhmaṇas.
Likewise, for the Kṣatriyas, there should be the Ariṣṭa, Khadira, Tinduka, Aśvattha, Sāmba, Druma, and the auspicious Karakata tree.
For the Vaiśyas, it should be the same: the Khadira and the Candana.
And these trees are meritorious and likewise bestowers of auspiciousness:
the Kesara, the Sarjaka, the mango, the Śāla tree, and others as well. These indeed are the meritorious trees that grant auspicious results to Śūdras.
Having thus installed the *liṅga* and the image according to the prescribed rule,
one should go to a desired tree and worship it with offerings and flowers in a pure,
secluded place, free from hair and charcoal.
In a region sloping toward the northeast, free from the hardships of the world,
there stands a tree with broad trunks and branches, possessing leaves, growing straight and tall,
free from disease, independent, and endowed with auspicious foliage.
Those trees that have fallen by themselves, as well as those felled by elephants,
those that are white, those burnt by fire, and those shunned by birds—
these trees are to be avoided; auspicious trees are to be selected.
Those trees which are glossy in appearance, possessed of leaves, flowers, and likewise fruits—
their selection should take place during the eight months beginning with Kārttika.
Having chosen them on an auspicious day, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) while observing a fast.
Then, having smeared the ground beneath it on all sides,
and having sprinkled water purified by the Gāyatrī mantra all around,
he should put on two garments that are white and well-washed.
One should worship with perfumes, garlands, incense, and offerings of bali;
then, having strewn kusha grass around the fire and offered oblations into it with fuel-sticks of devadaru wood near that [image], the knower of reality should act with this mantra.
With "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ," one should then worship the tree:

"Oṃ! To Prajāpati, the truly existent, the eternal, the most excellent inner self, the soul of all that moves and is stationary—O God, manifest your presence in this tree; enter the solar orb surrounded by rays. Homage!"
Nārada said:
"Having thus honored him and consoled him with these words,
go to the auspicious abode of the gods for the sake of bringing peace to the world of trees."
"O Deva, you shall remain there, free from being cut or burned;
at the proper time, through the offering of incense, flowers, and ritual oblations,
people will worship you, and thereby you shall attain liberation."
Having worshipped the axe at the foot of a tree with incense and garlands,
it should be carefully placed there with its blade facing eastward,
along with various foods such as *paramānna*, sweetmeats, boiled rice, meat, cakes, and other edibles.
Having worshipped the tree with liquors, flowers, incense, and perfumes,
and having performed worship to the gods, ancestors, piśācas, rākṣasas, serpents, hosts of deities, Vināyaka, and others, one should touch the tree at night and say:
O God of gods, you have been installed by the deities within these images.
Homage to you! May this worship be accepted according to the prescribed rite.
Whatever beings dwell here, may they accept this oblation offered according to the ritual.
"May they arrange their residence elsewhere; may they forgive us today; homage be to them!
Then, when the night has turned to dawn, having again worshipped that mountain and having given sacrificial fees to the Brahmins and the cooks,"

One should have trees cut down by those who are experts in them, after they have performed the ritual recitation of auspicious prayers (*svastivācana*). One should cut them down in the eastern direction, or in the northeast, or likewise in the north; but not otherwise.
A fall in the three directions of Indra (East), Īśāna (Northeast), and Udīcī (North) is commended;
a fall in the directions of Nairṛti (Southwest), Agni (Southeast), and Yāmya (South) is not auspicious;
and its fall in Vāyavyā (Northwest) and Vāruṇī (West) is middling.
That tree whose branches extend outward in the four directions and which,
standing first to the east of the site (vāstu), subsequently stands to the west,
is praised for its falling— provided it falls without snagging and without making a sound.
One should avoid that tree from which a split appears, or whose sap is sweet, or from which ghee and oil exude.
O tiger among the Yadus, listen as I describe what brings auspiciousness; hear it, O pure one.
In the morning, having watered a tree and cut it down toward the northeast direction,
one should strike it so that it falls clockwise toward the northwestern quarter;
when it falls in the northwestern portion of the direction, it shall bring about prosperity.
In the sequence of the south-eastern corner (Āgneya), there is fire, burning, fierce and terrible diseases, and the loss of great wealth.
In the direction of Garuḍa (the south-west), there is stone, pigeons, and house-lizards;
the water should be known as white in color, and the worm would be the size of a thumb.
"Free from these defects, one should joyfully extract the [proper] time.
Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Examination of Wood," in the *Saptamī-kalpa* of the *Brāhma-parvan* within the glorious *Śrī-Bhaviṣya-Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the one hundred and thirty-second chapter.
Description of the Characteristics of the Auspicious Image of the Sun.
Nārada said: "Ah! I shall now describe to you the supreme characteristics of the images of all the gods."
I shall tell you specifically regarding the image of the Sun, O tiger among the Yadus:
the auspicious image of Savitṛ may be one cubit, two cubits, three cubits, or even three and a half cubits in measurement.
The measurement is likewise prescribed according to the Prasāda or the entrance;
one who desires constant auspiciousness should always proceed in that manner.
A [shrine] of one cubit is gentle, while one of two cubits bestows wealth and grain.
An image of the Sun three cubits in height is remembered as the bestower of all desires;
an image measuring three and a half cubits brings about abundance and security.
An image that is uniform in its front, middle, and base is auspicious in every respect.

That [type] is to be known as Gāndharvī; it is traditionally held to bring wealth and grain. From the door of the temple, rising up by one-eighth part, the pedestals (piṇḍikās) should be made with [certain] divisions, and two parts shall be for the image.
The image should be made with eighty-four finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in both width and length;
the face should be twelve finger-breadths.
The chin, the forehead, and the nose should each be one-third of the face.
The ears should be equal to the nose, and the two feet should be of no fixed proportion to them.
The two eyes should be two *aṅgulas* [in length], and the pupil (*tārakā*) should be one-third of that. From one-third of the portion of the pupil, the wise artist should fashion the gaze.
One should make the elevation of the forehead and the crown of the head equal to that [measurement];
the circumference of the head should be twenty-two finger-breadths (aṅgulas).
The neck should be equal to the nose, and the space from the mouth to the heart should be equal to the face.
The navel should be equal in measure to the mouth, and immediately following that, the penis.
The chest is said to be equal to the width of the mouth, and half of that is the waist.
The two arms are equal to the length of the stream [of the altar], and the thighs and shanks are the same as those.
Below the ankle, the foot should be four *aṅgulas* in height;
its width should be six *aṅgulas*, and the big toe three *aṅgulas*. The forefinger (second toe) is equal to that, while the remaining toes are smaller and provided with nails.
The foot is proclaimed to be fourteen finger-breadths in length;
an image endowed with such characteristics should always be worshipped.
Likewise, the shoulders, the thighs, and the forehead together with the nose [should be proportionate].
One should fashion the eyes well-set, the cheeks prominent,
and the face with large, white, curved eyelashes and long eyes;
likewise, the lotus-face should be accompanied by a smile and beautiful bimba-like lips.
Wearing a crown, bracelets, armlets, and necklaces resplendent with jewels,
even his union with the limbs of the goddess— whose feet and other parts were flawless— was beautiful.
He was of radiant luster, adorned with a charming mandala, and possessed wonderful jeweled earrings.
Carrying a golden lotus garland in his two hands—
one endowed with such auspicious marks— one should have [the image] fashioned; it bestows desired objects,
and the Sun always grants to all creatures welfare, health, and fearlessness.
If she has missing limbs, there is fear of the king; if she has deformed limbs, there is lack of ritual fitness.
If she has a sunken belly, there is suffering from hunger; if she is emaciated, there is poverty.
If she has sores, there is danger from weapons; if her skin is cracked, it brings about death.
If it inclines toward the south, there will be a constant decline in life;
if it inclines toward the north, separation is certain.
A form that is neither visible nor invisible is praised as worthy of protection.
Therefore, one who is devoted to the Sun and desires the welfare of both worlds should show reverence to His form, for all prosperity is dependent upon Him.
[This applies even when afflicted] by headaches, swellings on the cheeks, facial ailments, or any other part of the body.
Thus, an auspicious image becomes complete in its characteristics when it is endowed with a well-proportioned nose,
forehead, shanks, thighs, and chest;
likewise, one should fashion it in the likeness of the Sun, with hidden feet and belly.
Resembling the luster of the interior of a lotus, protected by a tunic, with a serene countenance and a halo with the radiance of a red lotus, the Sun brings prosperity to the maker.
With a face adorned by earrings and wearing long pendants, he is established in his own abode.

If the woman is deformed, there is fear of the king; if she has missing limbs, it indicates the failure of the undertaking for the doer. If she has a protruding belly, there is fear of hunger and loss of wealth;
if she is emaciated, death by the stroke of a weapon should be predicted for the doer.
If the reflection is elevated on the left side, it destroys the wife; if depressed on the right, it destroys longevity.
An upward gaze causes blindness, while a downward gaze produces anxiety.
Thus has the auspicious and inauspicious been declared by Bhāskara regarding all reflected images.
Brahmā has a water-pot in his hand, four faces, and is seated upon a lotus;
Skanda has the form of a youth, holds a spear, and has a peacock for his emblem;
Mahendra’s elephant is white with four tusks, and Indra possesses the thunderbolt in his hand.
"The third eye, as a mark, is situated horizontally upon the forehead.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Characteristics of the Image of the Auspicious Sun," in the *Sāmbopākhyāna* (Account of Sāmba) within the *Saptamī-kalpa* of the *Brāhma-parvan* in the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the one hundred and thirty-third chapter.
Description of the Universal Form.
Nārada said:
Thereafter, one should perform the consecration (adhivāsana) according to the ritual procedure prescribed by rule.
One should construct the consecration pavilion in the northeastern direction;
it should be provided with four archways, adorned with all ornaments,
and decorated with banners in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
In the southeastern direction they should be red; in the southern and southwestern directions they should be black;
in the western direction they should be white, and in the northwestern direction they should be pale yellow.
In the northern direction they should be variegated, and likewise in the northeastern direction they should be yellow.
O best of the Yadus, O hero, that image made of clay, when consecrated, undoubtedly bestows prosperity, long life, victory, strength, and fame; it becomes a source of well-being for all the worlds.
All [images] made of jewels always bestow abundance and security;
one made of gold bestows nourishment; one made of silver indeed promotes fame;
and one made of copper constantly brings about an increase in progeny—of this there is no doubt.
An image made of stone always brings about the acquisition of vast land;
one made of tin or iron always destroys the principal person.
Thus, one should diligently fashion the image of the one who embodies all the gods.
Sāmba said:
"Tell me, indeed, how the Sun-god possesses the nature of all the gods;
for how, O Nārada, is it said that he is composed of all the gods?"
Nārada said:
"Excellent, O mighty-armed Sāmba! Listen to my supreme words:
Budha and Soma are remembered as the eyes, and Īśvara resides in the forehead."
Surajyeṣṭha was his head, and Bṛhaspati was upon his skull;
likewise, the Rudras resided in his neck,
while the lunar mansions and the planets were situated in his teeth.
Both merit and demerit reside within the god's lips;
the goddess Sarasvatī, who embodies all the scriptures, dwells upon his tongue;
and all the cardinal and intermediate directions are situated within his ears.
Brahmā and Indra reside in the region of the palate, honored by the gods;
the twelve Ādityas, O Lord, are situated within the eyebrows;
the sages dwell in the pores of the skin, and the oceans are located in the belly.
The Yakṣas, Kinnaras, Gandharvas, Piśācas, Dānavas,
and Rākṣasas— all these hosts abide within the heart of the Sun;
the rivers are situated in his arms, and the mountains reside within the folds of his armpits.
Meru is situated in the middle of the back; Kuja is between the breasts. His son, Dharmarāja, is indeed situated in the region of the navel.
Earth and the other elements are in the region of the hips; the creation is supported by the *liṅga*.
The two Aśvinī deities are known as his knees, and the immovable mountains are his thighs;
the seven netherworlds (pātāla) are situated within the hollows of his nails,
while the earth, together with its oceans and forests, exists within the space between his feet.
The god Kālāgnirudra, who is stationed at the tips of the teeth;
the Sun, who consists of all the gods and likewise has the nature of all the gods;
and the winds within the limbs—these pervade the world and the non-world, the moving and the unmoving.
The body of action of that all-pervading Lord is indeed pervaded by the wind;
he is this very Blessed Sun, established in the favoring of all beings.
This is your supreme knowledge; this is your supreme state.
"I shall explain to you all that regarding the installation of images according to the division of their locations, as it was told by Brahmā in the past.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Universal Form," in the *Pratimā-pratiṣṭhā-kalpa* (the Ritual for the Installation of Images) within the *Sāmbopākhyāna* (the Narrative of Sāmba) of the *Saptamī-kalpa*, in the *Brāhma-parvan* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the one hundred and thirty-fourth chapter, describing the ritual procedure for the mandala.
Nārada said:
The second, fourth, fifth,
tenth, thirteenth, and the full moon day are likewise proclaimed as days of practice;
and [the planets] Soma, Bṛhaspati, Śukra, and Budha are likewise [to be honored].
These are declared to be the auspicious planets for the rites of consecration and sacrifice:
in the three Uttarās, in Revatī, in Aśvinī, and likewise in the asterism of Brahmā (Rohiṇī);
as well as in the two Punarvasūs, in Hasta, in Dhaniṣṭhā, or in Śravaṇa.
The installation of the Sun under the constellation Bharaṇī is most excellent;
having purified the ground, making it free from husks and hair,
and having thoroughly cleansed it so that it is devoid of sand, charcoal, stones, and bones.
The altar for the Sun should measure four cubits in width;
the pavilion, however, should be ten cubits on all sides. One should construct the mandala with branches of trees according to the prescribed ritual.
One should bring earth raised from the banks at the confluence of rivers;
having smeared the ground with it, one should then have an excellent sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) constructed.
First, one should have the pit made square and endowed with beauty.
In the south there should be a half-moon, and in the western direction a circle;
the wise one should indeed make it lotus-shaped in the north. Then, O observer of noble vows, he should construct arches five cubits in height.
Nyagrodha, Udumbara, Bilva, Pālāśa,
Aśvattha, Śamī, and Candana are thus proclaimed.
[The image] is provided with white cloth and endowed with a multicolored silk band.
Equipped with a rosary, the wise practitioner should construct the archways.
He should worship the eastern archway with the mantra "agnimīle" and the southern archway with the mantra "iṣetvorje".
One should worship the western arch with the mantra "agna āyāhi," and one should worship the northern arch with the mantra "śaṃ no devī. Then,
taking up the water-pots (kalaśas) which contain gold within them, [one should proceed].

One should set down the water jars while reciting the mantra, [visualizing them] adorned with swastikas on their necks made from white sandalwood paste, and containing barley, rice, bowls of food, new cloth, ornaments, and images.
One should wrap the pillar and the garland with *dukūla* cloths and variegated silks;
[one should adorn it] with banners, mirrors, flags, chowries, and canopies,
accompanied by the sounding of conchs and bells, and by songs and auspicious recitations.
One should cause a great festival to be celebrated with the sounds of trumpets and kettledrums accompanied by the chanting of the Vedas, and with meritorious shouts of "Victory!",
adorned with variegated banners and offerings of worship and garlands.
Richly adorned with various garlands and canopies, and strewn with flowers and sprouts, the wise man should place the image of the deity upon a seat of *kuśa* grass in the center of that area.
He should cause a yellow-colored banner to be offered to Śakra in the east.
One should cause [the offering] to be presented in the southeast to those with a reddish luster, resembling Yama in the southern direction,
appearing like blue collyrium in the southwest,
white-colored in the west, and black in the domain of the northwest.
To the north-east, for the Yakṣa king Harita,
one should then draw a lotus of all colors using white and red powders.
The touching of the altar should be performed with the mantra "vaidyā vedī."
Having carefully spread out kusha grass with its tips pointing eastward and northward,
the spreading of the kusha grass should be performed with the mantra "Yoge yoge.
There, a bed provided with a divine covering should be prepared.
The wise man should place two variegated bowls in their midst;
he should provide them with garlands of various lamps, along with various kinds of foods, snacks, meals, and drinks,
as well as many varieties of cakes and sweetmeats.
One should place milk-rice (*pāyasa*), rice mixed with sesame (*kṛśara*), and rice accompanied by curd;
one should also set down curd as bright as the moon and an auspicious umbrella.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Mandala Ritual in the Installation of the Sun," in the *Sāmbopākhyāna* within the *Saptamī-kalpa* of the *Brāhma-parvan* in the glorious *Mahāpurāṇa Bhaviṣya*.
Now begins the one hundred and thirty-fifth chapter,
describing the ritual for the installation bath (*pratiṣṭhā-snāna*).
Nārada said:
Henceforth, O best of the Yadus, I shall explain to you the ritual procedure for the bath;
the officiating priest, however, should be a man of great wisdom, a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas,
well-versed in the Saura scriptures, and named Aruṇa.
The Bhojaka, surrounded by other Bhojakas and likewise by Brāhmaṇas,
should duly place a blessed throne (bhadrapīṭha) measuring one cubit in size in the northeast corner of the mandala.
One should bring the Lord to the temple with an elephant, a cart, a palanquin, or a Brahma-chariot, accompanied by auspicious objects and the chanting of the Vedas;
and taking up the auspicious throne with the mantra "Bhadra karṇebhiḥ."
The Sūtradhāra, likewise described as pure and clad in white garments,
should take a water-pot and bathe the god of gods, Vibhāvasu;
he should do so having brought water from the ocean, as well as from the Ganges and the Yamunā.
The water of the Sarasvatī is meritorious, as is that of the Candrabhāgā and the Saindhava;
the water of Puṣkara is excellent, as is water from mountain springs.
Moreover, any other pure water originating from rivers, streams, or tanks is likewise beneficial.
Having brought offerings according to their capacity with jars made of gold and other materials,
the eight officiating priests indeed bathe the Sun with those jars;
thereafter, they likewise [offer] gems, jewels, all types of seeds, and medicinal herbs.
And fragrant garlands, both those grown on land and lotuses born in water;
the finest sandalwoods and likewise various perfumes;
as well as brāhmī, suvarcalā, mustā, viṣṇukrāntā, and śatāvarī.
Having gathered these materials— dūrvā grass, śibipuṣpī, priyaṅgu, rajanī, and vacā— one who understands the divisions of the bathing rite [should proceed] with the sprouts of balā,
aśvattha, and śirīṣa, together with kuśa grass.
Having placed [the vessel] upon a pitcher, one should always offer the arghya to the Sun with pitchers made of gold,
silver, copper,
or clay, filled with unbroken grains, gold, and all medicinal herbs.
One should bathe the Sun with sixteen [vessels] purified by the Gāyatrī mantra. Then, having constructed an altar made of baked bricks with Kuśa grass spread upon it,
one should place [the image] upon that altar and clothe it in two garments.
One who has observed a fast should diligently consecrate the image by placing all medicinal herbs and likewise *āmalaka* fruits upon its head;
one should also apply clay with the mantra and water with the mantra.
O Goddess, you are worshipped by all the gods, as well as by all the Daityas and Dānavas;
therefore, for the sake of the God’s purity, you have been established upon my head by me. You are ordained in every way as the presiding deity of all beings and of all the gods.
"An invocation has been made by me to you, the Lord of the Rasas,
with these Puranic mantras and especially with Vedic ones. O descendant of Yadu, the Varuna-bath for the God must indeed be performed."
The wise man should utter these words and perform the bath:
"May the gods— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others— along with the celestial Gaṅgā, consecrate you with this full second pitcher."
O best of gods, let Śakra and the other world-protectors, the most excellent of deities, consecrate him with a full pitcher of Sarasvatī’s water;
and with the fourth pitcher, filled with the waters of the ocean.
Let the Nāgas consecrate [him] with the fifth vessel, filled with water fragrant as lotus petals;
and let those beginning with Himavat and Hemakūṭa consecrate him with water.
May the seven excellent sages consecrate [the king] with the sixth jar, which belongs to Nairṛta and is filled with water,
and with the seventh, which is filled with the waters of all sacred fords (tīrtha) and perfumed with the pollen of lotuses.
And may the Vasus consecrate you with the eighth pitcher, endowed with the eight auspicious signs; O God of gods, salutations be unto you!
Then, one should commence the rite of bathing with divine pitchers.
One who utters this mantra, "Go to the ocean," and recites the mantra beginning with "Hiraṇyagarbha," should wash [the vessel] with clay while reciting the mantra "Samudrajyeṣṭhā."
One should offer earth from an anthill with the mantra "sinīvālī";
and one should offer the five astringent decoctions— of *śamī*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, *nyagrodha*, and *palāśa*— with the mantra "yajñaṃ yajña".
One should bring the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) as a purifying substance in a copper vessel:
cow’s urine with the Gāyatrī mantra, cow dung with "gandhadvārām," milk with "āpyāyasva," and curd with "dadhikrāvṇo."

With the mantra "tejo'si," one offers clarified butter; likewise, with "devasya tvā," one offers water with *kuśa* grass. Thus, the *pañcagavya* (five products of the cow) is proclaimed as being accompanied by such rites.
Then, one performs a bath with medicinal herbs in sequence, using the mantra "yā oṣadhī."
Furthermore, a wise person should perform an oil massage for him with *drupadā* mantras;
then he should provide a head bath consecrated with the *mānastoka* mantra,
and he should offer auspicious fragrant water with the *viṣṇorarāṭam* mantra.
Then, one should wash [the image] with pure water originating from a river,
using water filtered through a cloth while reciting the *jātavedas* mantra.
Thereafter, one should invoke the auspicious deity, who is adorned with red garlands and garments.
"Come, come, O Blessed Sun, you who bestow grace upon the worlds!
Accept this portion of the sacrifice and this water offering (arghya); O Divine Sun, salutations be unto you!
One should cause the arghya to be offered to the deity using a vessel made of gold.
With the mantra "idaṃ viṣṇurvicakrame," one should offer the arghya water.
O Hero, the wise man should first bathe the Sun-god with earthen jars,
and thereafter with those made of udumbara wood and silver.
Then, O Śaṅkara, the descendant of Yadu should bathe the Lord with golden [vessels],
using water from all sacred fords (tīrthas) combined with all medicinal herbs;
then, taking up a conch shell, he should place it upon the head of the God.
Having carefully offered flowers upon the head of the Lord,
the wise practitioner should then perform the ritual bathing by diligently sprinkling water;
O descendant of Yadu, he should first bathe the Lord with water.
Then, O King, with milk, with milk-rice (pāyasa),
or indeed with clarified butter, honey, or even sugarcane juice,
[one obtains the fruit] of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice and the Gomedha sacrifice, O observer of noble vows.

O Indra among kings, O Lord, he who causes a bath to be performed, or he who beholds it with devotion, obtains the fruit of the Jyotiṣṭoma, the Vājapeya, the Rājasūya, and the Aśvamedha sacrifices, as well as the merit of offerings such as clarified butter.
O scion of Yadu’s lineage, the fruit of all these sacrifices that have been described is obtained in due order by seeing the bathing of the God being performed;
and indeed, O tiger among the Kurus, one obtains that same fruit by beholding His image.
O observer of noble vows, the bathing of the God of gods must be performed with great care,
so that no one may obstruct the ablution of the Lord;
lest those birds condemned by the world, like crows, should defile the sacred site.
O descendant of Yadu, if the water used for the bathing of the deity, or even milk itself,
falls upon the ground and one consumes it,
the performer of the act will surely incur disease, and the one who caused it to be done will likewise suffer misery.
Therefore, the bathing of the omnipresent Lord must be performed with great effort.
Having bathed him in this manner according to the sequence,
the one who knows the ritual procedure should then take the pouring vessel and release a stream of water.
Reciting "Ācamasva" three times before the sun,
he should cause the sacred thread (upavīta) to be put on with the mantra "Ve dosī.
He should cause a pair of garments to be given with the mantra "Bṛhaspate."
Performing the sequence of ritual efforts, one should cause a flower garland to be offered;
with the mantra "dhūr asi," one should offer incense containing guggulu;
and with the mantra for kindled fuel, one should cause collyrium to be offered.
With the mantra beginning "yuñjāna," one should cause him to offer the *rocanā* (yellow pigment);
and for the sake of long life and splendor, one should indeed perform the *ārārtika* rite.
This is declared to be the ritual of bathing for the high-souled Bhāskara.
The Bhojakas and Brahmins should perform the rites with great care;
likewise the Bahvṛcas, Atharvaṇas, Chandogas, and Adhvaryus,
as well as those who bear the marks of the Snāpaka and those who are Mūrtidharas.
O Lord, listen with a single-minded focus as I shall describe them:
one who is complete in limb, intelligent, learned in the scriptures, pleasing in appearance,
of noble birth, endowed with faith, and born in a holy land.
One who is neither stout nor lean, neither tall nor short, and is proficient in the solar scriptures (Saura-śāstra);
who is disciplined, self-controlled, devoted to the guru, has conquered his senses,
and knows the twenty-five principles (tattvas)— such a person is declared to be a consecrator (sthāpaka).
I shall now describe those who are to be avoided, with whom one should not have the ritual performed:
one with missing limbs, one with extra limbs, a dwarf, and likewise one who is deformed;
one who is neither too fair nor too dark—one should employ such persons for the purpose of bathing.
A Cārvāka, a sacrificial priest, one who constantly practices the "cow-mouth" deception,
one joined with impure vows, one with black teeth,
or one who is envious, wrathful, and of wicked character— whether young or even old.

One who has white leprosy, one with skin disease, one who is diseased, one who is blind, and likewise one who is wicked-minded; one of mixed caste, one devoid of caste, as well as the husband of a *vṛṣalī*;
one who is hunchbacked, one who is deformed, one who is bald, and one whose sense organs are impaired.
One who is undisciplined, evil-minded, deformed, or even a cripple;
