one who, O Lord, points out the conjunctions of lunar days, asterisms, and weekdays for the sake of a livelihood; and he who teaches for a fee—these are likewise excluded.
One should diligently avoid all such bathers.
Therefore, the wise should examine the bathers with every effort.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Installation and Bathing of the Sun," in the Sāmba-episode of the Saptamī-kalpa within the Brāhma-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the one hundred and thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Installation of the Sun.
Nārada said:
Hereafter, I shall explain the supreme consecration (adhivāsana).
The Thousand-headed Puruṣa should enter the pavilion with care;
then others [should do so] in a pure place, smeared with unadulterated plaster.
One should draw a square mandala with five colors,
adorned with banners, arches, umbrellas, flags, garlands, and the like;
it should be enriched with a variegated and excellent canopy and strewn with heaps of scattered flowers.
In its center, upon a bed of *kuśa* grass, an image of Vivasvat should be installed.
Having performed the invocation (*āvāhana*) there, one should offer the respectful water (*arghya*) to Vivasvat.
Then, having performed the rites with gold, honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), and so forth according to the prescribed rule, [one should proceed].
One should show a beautiful, reddish-brown cow with her calf to the deity, saying:
"Salutations to you, the Lord of Cattle; O thousand-rayed one, be gracious to me.
Having thus consecrated the water-offering (arghya) and put on two garments, [one should proceed].
Every year, one should provide him with a sacred thread, hospitality, and likewise an oil massage;
for that indeed constitutes his purificatory rite (*pavitra*) in the month of Śrāvaṇa, O Indra among kings.
O tiger among the Yadus, having fed the Brahmins year after year,
one should perform the rite for the Sun-god in the month of Śrāvaṇa; one who is free from physical defects should be anointed with all perfumes— sandalwood, agallochum, and saffron.
Having adorned [the image] with ornaments, fragrant flowers,
and various garlands fastened in many ways,
one should then quickly and diligently offer incense before the image.
One should cause the thousand-headed Puruṣa to enter the pavilion;
with the mantra "Namaḥ śambhave," one should place him upon the bed.
With the verse "Viśvataścakṣuḥ," one should fashion the stainless lotus.
Furthermore, I shall again explain the auspicious *saṅkalīkaraṇa*.
Just as the supreme ritual placement (*nyāsa*) should be performed upon one's own body during the consecration bath,
so too should it be performed upon the image, just as the wise man performs the touching (*ālambhana*).
"Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to Khaṣolkā—this is proclaimed as the root mantra.
This Sun himself is the deity, augmented by the syllables.
One should place the syllable Oṃ on the head and the syllable Hūṃ above the nose."
One should place the letter *kha* on the forehead and the letter *ṣa* on the face;
the letter *la* on the throat and the letter *ka* on the heart;
the letter *ya* on the left arm and the letter *na* on the right arm.
One should place the letter *ma* on the left side of the abdomen and the *visarga* on the right;
one should always meditate upon the syllable *oṃ*, which is filled with garlands of flames,
and upon the syllable *huṃ*, which has the luster of a pure color and emits abundant auspiciousness.
The wise one should contemplate the syllable *kha*, possessing a luster like crushed collyrium;
the learned one should contemplate the syllable *kha* as having the hue of the rising sun;
and the mighty-armed one should contemplate the syllable *ṣo* as being golden in color.
The wise one should contemplate the syllable *A*, which has the appearance of a white lotus;
the syllable *Hrīṃ*, which resembles a *jātī* flower and contains all phonemes;
and the wise one should constantly contemplate the syllable *Sa*, which is the color of milk.
The wise one should constantly contemplate the syllable *na* as white as snow or a jasmine flower, the syllable *ma* as the immortal syllable,
the syllable *hrīṃ* as resembling lightning, the syllable *hrīṃ* as containing all colors,
and the syllable *sa* as the color of milk.
One should visualize the letter *Na* as having the luster of gold and the letter *Ma* as having the radiance of refined gold;
then, one should place upon the bed the Great-Souled Deity, the Sun with its thousand rays, the God who is inclined toward bestowing grace.
Then the twice-born should perform the fire-ritual in the sacrificial pits;
having produced fire from the friction-sticks or using common fire,
the wise one should kindle the fire according to the rules and perform the oblation.
The Bahvṛca should perform [the rites] in the eastern sections, the Madhyandina likewise in the south;
the Chandoga in the west, and the Atharvaṇa is held to be in the north.
And the Bhojaka should perform the most excellent oblation (homa) in the center during the sacrifice.
Indeed, [the wood of] śamī, pālāśa, udumbara, and likewise apāmārga—
twelve thousand, eight, four,
two, three thousand, or even just one thousand [recitations].
The touching of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) should be performed with the mantra "Agnirmūrdhā";

having scraped it and sprinkled it with water using that same [mantra], one should perform the rite of impregnation (*garbhādhāna*) with the mantra "Agniṃ dūtam" and "Sambudhyasvāgne," as they are traditionally taught.
Furthermore, one should perform the *sīmantonnayana* there by means of the great mantra;
likewise, the *jātakarman* is prescribed, and the wise know *prāṇāyāma* [to be performed].
And the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*) is performed with the mantra "Namaḥ svāhā."
One should prescribe the first feeding of solid food with the *annaprāśana* mantra; the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍā*) and the initiation ceremony (*upakarma*) with the *jyeṣṭhamagra* mantra;
and one should prescribe the binding of the vows (*vratabandha*) with the *vratabandha* mantra.
One should perform the *samāvartana* (the return ceremony) and offer oblations with the verse beginning "ākṛṣṇena. One should personally arrange the *patnīsaṃyājana* (the ritual union with the wife),
as well as the *agnihotra* and other such rites, and whatever sacrificial acts there may be.
One should offer oblations on all sides with the Mahāvyāhṛti mantra;
one should cause the bali-offering to be presented for the Mothers who constitute the sacrifice.
For the sake of the fulfillment of all desires, one should perform the consecration ceremony (adhivāsana).
For three nights, five nights, or even for a single day and night,
one should then perform the consecration (adhivāsana) of the image— which has been bathed, adorned with jewels and gems, and protected with great care.
Then, having constructed a divine pavilion in the northeastern quarter of the temple,
he prepared a white bed with its head toward the east, covered with a fine spread and strewn with *kuśa* grass, and draped over with a white cloth.
One should properly cause [the deity] to enter it and bring forth Mahāśveta.
Nikṣubhā is proclaimed to be on the right side, and Rājñī on the left.
Daṇḍa and Piṅgala stand at its feet, having entered them.
When that night had passed and he had entered the image of the Sun,
he should dwell there for that night while being praised from all four directions by Brahmins, bards, and likewise by singers and *cāraṇas* skilled in song.
One should keep a vigil there together with those endowed with devotion to the Sun. When the night has turned to dawn, one should awaken [the deity] according to the prescribed ritual,
as well as the Brāhmaṇas who desire to eat sacrificial food (haviṣya) and the officiating priests.
Having honored them with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās) and having had the recitation of benedictions (svastivācana) performed by them,
he should then place a golden chariot drawn by seven horses there according to the prescribed rites, having first established a pedestal (piṇḍikā) in the center of the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha).

Having placed all types of seeds and medicinal herbs there according to the prescribed rite, the patron of the sacrifice, accompanied by his assistants, should offer the *arghya* water and establish [the vessel] there amidst the sounding of conchs and kettledrums, along with streams of water and unbroken grains (*akṣata*).
Having caused the proclamation of "an auspicious day" (puṇyāha) to be made, the wise man should install the image in the temple after circumambulating it clockwise,
on a day with an auspicious conjunction of the lunar mansion (nakṣatra), during the forenoon at a favorable moment for the sun,
and under an auspicious hour of the sun.

One should install this image neither with its face downward, nor upward, nor likewise tilted to the side; rather, it should be placed level and facing forward. Then, one should properly position his two wives on either side.
Nikṣubhā is on the right side and Rave-rājñī is on the left.
Then, for the purpose of that offering, he brought together the previously mentioned materials,
consisting of sweetmeats (*modaka*), *āyūṣikā*, cakes (*apūpa*), fried pastries (*śaṣkulī*), and *bhūtaśīrṣaka*.
One should scatter an offering of *kṛsara* mixed with milk-rice in all directions:
"To Indra, the lord of the gods, the powerful one who wields the thunderbolt,
the sovereign of a hundred sacrifices— to that Indra, homage to you!"
The invocation of Indra should be performed with the mantra "trātāram indram.
[One should offer oblations] to Agni, who has red eyes, who is indeed honored by garlands of flames,
who holds a spear in his hand, who is fierce, and who likewise has goats as his vehicle.
The invocation of Agni is prescribed with the Āgneyī mantra:
"Obeisance indeed to the god Dharmarāja, the son of the Sun, who holds a staff in his hand, who is dark-hued, and who is borne by a magnificent buffalo."
The mudrās for him alone are proclaimed with the mantra "yamāya tvā.
To the one in the southwest, who holds a sword in his hand and has a dark-blue and red body,
and who is the sovereign of all that is external— to Virūpākṣa, indeed, obeisance!
One should perform the ritual in the southwest with the mantra "āyaṃ gauḥ";
in the west, one should perform it for Varuṇa, who holds a noose, with the mantra "varuṇāya".
One should know that the invocation is performed with the mantra "pañcanadyaḥ sarasvatīm".
Salutations to the one whose nature is breath, to the smoke, to the flawless one, and to Anila;
salutations to the one with the banner in hand, to Bhīma, and to the bearer of fragrance.
One should also know his invocation [by the mantra]: "O God, that which is the offense against the gods..."
Salutations to Soma who holds a mace in his hand, who is powerful and moves among men;
salutations indeed to Somarāja, who holds a mace and a spear in his hands.
The *Īśāvāsya* is indeed declared to be the secret mantra of Soma.
Salutations to the four-faced god seated upon a lotus throne,
who rests upon a black antelope skin; salutations to the pot-bellied one,
O Lord, the leader of the hosts, the blue-throated wielder of the trident.
Homage to Virūpākṣa, to Rudra, the sovereign of the three worlds!
One should offer the mantra "Abhi tvā śūra no" to Īśāna.
Homage to the king of all nāgas, the white-colored serpent.
"Salutations again and again to Ananta, who possesses a thousand hoods, eternally;
let there be salutation to the serpents"—this is the mantra proclaimed.
Indeed, the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the limbs (aṅganyāsa) is performed according to the Pañcarātra and other traditions.
Likewise, one should worship the Sun with offerings of milk and drinks, and with hymns and praises; then one should give sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to the Brahmins and the cooks.
One should never perform the highly meritorious Sūrya-sacrifice without a sacrificial fee.
By this rite, the image which is installed by its devotees shall always bring about prosperity and shall remain eternally present;
indeed, for seven lifetimes, no diseases shall afflict them.

Those who observe a three-night vigil at the conclusion of the sun’s journey, honoring it with perfumes, garlands, and offerings, go to the world of the Sun. Whether it be their own or that of another, the installation of an image of the Sun [is likewise meritorious].
The man who beholds [the deity] with devotion shall attain the world of the Sun;
by installing the Maker of Day, a person obtains the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices and a hundred Vājapeya sacrifices.

O best of the Yadus, for as long as the fame of the merit-earner remains established in the place of the Sun, so long is he honored in the world of the Sun. And the mantra for its installation, which is revered throughout the worlds, has been proclaimed.
Firm is the sky, firm is the earth, and firm is this entire world;
for the welfare of the sacrificer, may you likewise attain firmness.
Having established the Sun with devotion through the rite prescribed by the rules, [may you attain stability].

Month after month, they obtain the fruit of a seasonal sacrifice; of this there is no doubt. Yet the fruit that is obtained by worshipping the Sun for even a single day cannot be attained on earth, O hero, by men through hundreds of sacrifices.
Even after committing a very great sin, he who subsequently worships the Sun goes to the world of the Sun, his impurities entirely removed;
yet there shall be no melting of bricks when measured against the earth.
The builder of a divine temple is honored in heaven for as long as that [merit lasts];
the fruit obtained by repairing what is broken or dilapidated is a supreme fruit that cannot be attained even through thousands of sacrifices.
"Even he who might build a house upon the sands of fire would go to the beloved assembly of the Lord of Cows (the Sun) and receive the boon of the Lord of Cows.
Thus spoke that best of gods, Bhānu, the cause of the maintenance, abode, and birth of all beings.
"The man who builds a temple becomes a possessor of fortune and dwells in the world of the Sun for a hundred kalpas.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Installation of the Sun," in the Sāmbopākhyāna of the Saptamī-kalpa within the Brāhma-parvan of the glorious *Śrī-Bhaviṣya-Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the one hundred and thirty-seventh chapter.
Description of the Ritual for Consecration.
Nārada said:
That man who, being a devotee of the Sun, diligently and with devotion constructs a temple for the deities, should immediately perform the consecration ceremony therein.
He always obtains divine enjoyments according to his desire, immeasurable in extent; having enjoyed them, he shall once again become a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) upon the earth.

Those men who construct temples for the forms of the gods—structures that delight the eyes of virtuous people—even when their bodies, composed of non-ultimate reality, have perished, their fame-endowed body wanders through the world.
Thus has this been told to you: the installation and the foundational rite of Savitṛ, who is worthy of worship by the gods.
Now hear, O Hero, the common procedure for the consecration of the deities.
Having bathed, eaten, and adorned himself with garments, flowers, and perfumes, he should perform the installation of the image upon a prepared bed.

While she sleeps, having properly performed the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) with dances, songs, and vigils, he should perform the installation (*saṃsthāpana*) at the time prescribed by the astrologer.

Having worshipped [the image] with flowers, perfumes, and ointments, and with the sounding of conchs and trumpets, he should lead it around the temple with great care in a clockwise direction. Having offered the sacrificial oblation (*bali*), worshipped the image, and given gifts to virtuous Brahmins, he should place a golden pitcher according to the rite into the center of the pedestal within a well-dug pit. Having specially and thoroughly worshipped the installer, the astrologer, and the twice-born, one becomes an enjoyer of pleasures here until the end of the eon and happy in the next world.
The devotees of Viṣṇu are considered [his followers], as are the twice-born smeared with ashes for Śambhu, and the Brahmins who know the circle of the Mothers for the Mothers;

likewise, those who wear white garments for the Buddha and those who wear red robes—whatever deity they have taken refuge in according to the proper rule, by them his ritual must be performed. This common procedure for the consecration of the deities has been described by me.
Seeing this installation of the deities being performed,
a man who acts with devotion attains his desires in this world and becomes a recipient of heaven.
Thus, O King, has this installation been described to you from the beginning.
Having performed this bath of Savitṛ, a person attains the state of mind;
thus should a wise man perform the installation of Savitṛ with devotion,
and a wise man should cause the installation of Savitṛ to be performed before him with devotion.
Listening to the Itihāsas and Purāṇas destroys sin;
for by listening to those two, O Hero, the Sun-god comes into one's presence.
And when that sanctuary has been established, whatever other deities [are present there as well].
Therefore, O hero, the wise should always first listen to the Dharma;
having honored the reciter and likewise worshipped the Brahmins,
they should cause the recitation to be performed before the book in the presence of the Sun.
One should give one's entire possessions to the officiating priest, or whatever has come into the house;
or else, one should give the gift of a cow and thus gladden his heart.
Thus, O Hero, has this ritual for consecration been described from the beginning.
"Whatever a man may obtain by performing, seeing, or hearing [this], he shall attain the Sun.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for Installation" in the Sāmba-episode within the Saptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan in the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the one hundred and thirty-eighth chapter.
Description of the Ritual for Hoisting the Banner.
Nārada said:
"Behold, I shall describe to you the supreme ritual for hoisting the banner."
O Lord of Ṛṣabhas, that which was previously spoken by Brahmā in the presence [of the assembly]:
"In former times, during the war between the gods and the asuras, whatever emblems, vehicles, and banners were employed by the gods desiring victory."

He is celebrated here by synonymous names such as *lakṣma*, *cihna*, *dhvaja*, and *ketu*; now listen as I describe its dimensions. The banner-pole (*dhvaja*) of the lineage should be made of bamboo, unblemished, straight, and without flaws.
The measurements for the *mañjarī*,

the pinnacle (*kalaśa*), and other elements of the temple are said to correspond to the width of the temple building; alternatively, the flagstaff (*dhvajadaṇḍa*) is proclaimed to be of that same measurement.
O best of the Yadus, the width of the hall (prasāda) should be equal to the width of the altar (vedī) of the inner chamber as determined by the measuring line;
or else, it should be equal to the width of the inner chamber according to the primary measuring line.
The width of the temple has thus been declared to you here; of this there is no doubt.
The banner-pole (ketu) should be excellent, of good lineage, neither sunken nor straight.
Likewise, there should be the leaf, the pair on the banner, the tube, and the man.
O son of Kṛṣṇa, these are praised when they are four cubits long;
however, a staff measuring eight cubits, according to the measurement of twenty-five [aṅgulas],
is considered the standard flagstaff (dhvajadaṇḍa) common to all.
The flagstaff known as Daṇḍapāṇidhvaja is prescribed as being sixteen cubits long;
for the Sun (Ravi), a staff longer than twenty cubits must not be made under any circumstances.
Wise men should ensure that the flagstaff is of even cubits.
It should be four finger-breadths wide, well-rounded, and two finger-breadths above [the base];
it must not be too thin nor too thick, and its joints should not be bent. It should be made with even joints, very firm, and indeed quite slender.

A curved mark on the hand leads to the destruction of sons; one with a wound destroys wealth. A mark resembling a disease brings endless suffering when it appears on both hands. Furthermore, a mark that is deficient in its proportions causes the loss of dharma.
Vaiṣamya, Asamaparvan, Dadyāt, Kṛcchra, Madhonnata;
Jaya, Jayanta, Jaitreya, Śatruhantā, and Jayāvaha;
as well as Nanda and Upananda, who are likewise declared to be Indra and Upendra.
These ten varieties of the banner (dhvaja) have been proclaimed, equal in measure to the Ānanda staff.
The Jaya staff is twelve cubits long; the Jayanta is considered to be double that length.
The Jaitreya is twelve cubits long, and the Śatruhantṛ is provided with a kalā.
Jayāvaha is the tenth, Nanda resembles the sun;
Upananda is said to be the fourteenth, and Indra is called the sixteenth.
Upendra is declared the eighteenth, and likewise Indra is remembered as the twentieth.
A staff that is broken, crooked, or unrefined must certainly not be used;

rather, O mighty-armed one, the flagstaff should be made according to the root mantra or measured according to the dimensions of the site (vāstu). Specifically, it should be constructed for the inner chamber in detail. Alternatively, it may be measured according to the proportions of the dwelling.
O Lord, the auspicious banner should be made either the size of the *mañjarī*, or half of that;
it should hang from the staff of the flagpole and measure one-third of the height of the temple's spire.
O Hero, she is said to be tenfold according to her measures:
the sprout, the leaf, the trunk, and likewise the branch;
the banner, the plantain tree, O Hero, the standard, the mark, and victory.
The tenth is declared to be the banner (dhvaja), which is imperishable and composed of all the gods.
The sprout (aṅkura) is said to be two finger-breadths (aṅgulas) long; the leaf (pallava) is four finger-breadths;
the trunk (skandha) is said to be six finger-breadths; and the branch (śākhā) is considered to be eight finger-breadths.

The eleventh is the banner (patākā), the fourteenth is the plantain (kadalī), the sixteenth is declared to be the flag-staff (ketu), and the eighteenth is called the mark (lakṣma). Jayā is indeed said to be the twentieth; such, then, are the finger-breadths (aṅgula).
O delighter of the Yadus, that bright broom of the temple-jar should be known as the banner called Aṅkurā;
the broom of the second [jar] is proclaimed as Pallavā.
The trunk of the third [tree] is three parts; the branch is indeed for the fifth;
the banner is prescribed for the sixth; the plantain tree is for the seventh;
likewise, the flagpole is for the eighth, and the mark is for the ninth.
Then, O delighter of the Yadus, the tenth is declared to be Jayanta;
his station is the bull, and he is proclaimed to have the banner of a flagstaff.
[The others are] the elephant, the ram, the buffalo, the headless trunk, and likewise the bull.
Furthermore, O best of men, one should designate these positions for the banner when it is deployed: the deer, the man, and again the man;
these should be assigned in order, starting from the eastern direction.
Thus, the ten kinds of banners have been described by the seers of reality. O lord of men, listen as I explain how they are to be made according to the traditional rule:
they should be made of white cloth, variegated, equipped with bells, and most beautiful.
Adorned with various chowries and decorated with a network of small bells,
a banner should be placed at the top of the pole, indicating the deity’s emblem;
it may be made of gold, silver, or even composed of jewels and gems.
Or else, O joy of the Yadus, a banner-staff shaped like that vehicle should be placed here and painted with colors;
for the banner of Viṣṇu is Garuḍa, while the banner of the Lord [Śiva] is the bull.

The lotus is the emblem of Brahmā; the banner of the Sun is recorded as the Dharma (the Bull); the swan is said to be the emblem of Varuṇa, the lord of waters; the banner of Soma is the Nara (the Moon); Kāla (Time) is the emblem of Baladeva; and the Makara-bannered one is the emblem of Kāma.
O descendant of Yadu, the lion is proclaimed as the emblem of Durgā;
the iguana is the emblem of the goddess Umā, and the horse is recorded as that of Raivata.
The tortoise is said to belong to Varuṇa, and the deer is considered the emblem of Vāta.
Likewise, for Pāvaka, a ram is considered the mount of Gaṇapati;
Kuśa is declared the mount of the Brahmarṣis—such is the arrangement of the banners. Whatever vehicle is declared for a deity, that is said to be his banner.
On Viṣṇu’s banner, the wise man should fashion a golden staff;
the flag near Garuḍa should also be yellow.
O descendant of Yadu, on Īśvara’s banner, the staff should be silver.
There should also be a white banner near the bull.
For the banner of the Grandfather (Brahmā), the staff is prescribed by the wise to be made of copper.
There should be a lotus-colored banner near the lotus.
O King, the staff on the banner of Āditya is proclaimed to be made of gold;
the five-colored flag of Dharma should hang below it,
equipped with a network of small bells and resembling a cluster of lotus buds.
Adorned with garlands of flowers and surrounded by various musical instruments,
O delighter of the Yadus, the staff of Indra’s banner is said to be made of gold;
there should be a multi-colored flag positioned near the elephant.
Furthermore, the staff of Yama is declared by the wise to be made of iron;
its banner, positioned near the buffalo, is black in color.
The staff of Varuṇa, the lord of waters, is proclaimed to be made of silver.
The banner on all sides is white, and it is described as variegated;
moreover, the staff of Kubera’s banner is said to be made of jewels,
and its red banner is situated near the foot of the man.

O delighter of the Yadus, on the banner of Baladeva, the staff is made of silver; its flag is known to be white in color and positioned below the palm tree. O upholder of the Yadu clan, on the banner of Kāma, the staff should be made of three metals.
There, Rohiṇī is the banner situated near the Makara;
the peacock is celebrated in the worlds as the emblem of Kārttikeya,
mounted upon a triple-metal staff and adorned with many jewels.
The wise have declared that the banner should be variegated with many colors;
O King, one should make the staff of Gaṇapati out of ivory.
It should be mounted upon a copper staff, thoroughly purified, and duly consecrated.
O Lord of the Earth, a white banner of proper dimensions should be made;
likewise, the wise should fashion for the Mothers a multi-formed flag,
adorned with many banners and various jewels.
O lord of men, O delighter of the Yadus, a horse-standard should also be made for Revata;
there too, a red banner should be fashioned.
In the temple of Cāmuṇḍā, a standard adorned with a garland of heads should be prepared.

A blue banner should be made, and likewise a staff made of iron; one should have those for the Mothers and for Revata made of brass. For Gaurī, the flagpole shall be made of copper, and the banner should resemble the color of a cow.
O descendant of Yadu, the hero's banner should have a golden staff topped with a ram,
and its pennon should be adorned with many jewels;
the banner of Vāta is said to have a staff made of iron.
The banner of black color belongs to the deer that is near the Blessed One;
the staff of the Goddess’s banner is said to consist of all kinds of jewels,
O King, while the three-colored banner is attached below the lion.
Having thus fashioned this banner, marked with the auspicious signs, and having consecrated it, O King, the wise man should then hoist it; thereafter,
he should diligently bathe it with all medicinal herbs.
O King, having anointed it, one should tie the *pratisarā* cords in the middle;
having prepared an auspicious altar adorned with water-jars,
one should place the [image] upon that altar and perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) for that night.
One should hang a garland variegated with various flowers upon it;
having worshipped it with great care, one should offer incense to it.
Then, having performed the bali-rite with kṛśara, cakes, and other such offerings.
One should offer an oblation (bali) intended for the world-protectors (lokapālas), including straw cakes, curd, milk-rice, and soups, as well as portions for the crows; then,
having had the Brāhmaṇas recite auspicious blessings and performed the rite for a holy day (puṇyāha), one should proceed.

On an auspicious day, at a favorable moment (lagna) and under a propitious asterism (ṛkṣa), the wise man should hoist the banner upon water that resounds with the playing of musical instruments, is endowed with consecrated rites, is filled with various bubbles, and is encircled by a new cloth.
Having placed a golden pitcher upon the king of pillars of the flagstaff,
whoever thus hoists the banner atop the temple shall increase in prosperity eternally and attain the supreme goal.
The Asuras desire to dwell in a celestial abode that is devoid of a banner;
therefore, a wise man should not cause a temple to be built without a banner.
Furthermore, the experts in ritual procedure have prescribed a specific mantra for the installation of the banner.
Come, come, O Blessed One, O God whose vehicle is drawn by gods, O You who move through the sky!
You are the bringer of prosperity and the abode of Śrī; victory to You, adorned with the splendor of victory!
O You whose form is the ether, O You of the great form, O righteous-souled one, You are indeed the very essence of movement.
Be present in this staff and remain as its steadfast witness.
O beloved of the Sun, always grant prosperity to the builder of this temple!

Oṃ, come, come, O Blessed One, fashioned by the Lord, following the path of Upāricara Vāyu, Abode of Śrī, Destroyer of Enemies, Dwelling of Yakṣas, you who are dear to all the gods! Grant your presence; grant me peace, well-being, and fearlessness; may all obstacles depart!
O King of kings, with this mantra one should place a staff in a pit;
O Lord, facing east in the established posture, the king should first fix a banner with the previous mantra,
and then, from the pinnacle of the temple, cast it upward into the sky.
Then, O delighter of the Yadus, the sacrificer should observe the banner;
if the banner should fall down in front of the temple,
then the performer shall indeed enter the world of Indra, O delighter of the Yadus.
In the southeast one reaches the world of Agni, while in the south one shall partake of the abode of Yama;
in the southwest one goes to the world of Nirṛti, and in the west one shall go to the realm of Varuṇa.
O scion of the Yadu clan, whichever deity’s residence has been constructed in each direction, [one reaches that domain].
If the builder of the temple stands upon the bull-position (Vṛṣasthāna), he attains that world;
in the northwest he attains Vāyu, in the north he shall attain Soma, and in the northeast he attains Īśa. Indeed, such is the fate of the one who constructs a divine abode.
Whoever should thus devoutly perform the hoisting of the banner for the Sun,
having enjoyed supreme pleasures, is indeed glorified in the world of the Sun;
radiant with splendor like a lotus and resembling a lotus in beauty.
"He is equal to a twice-born in splendor and in valor, O Lord of Cows.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for Raising the Banner," in the Sāmbopākhyāna of the Saptamī-kalpa within the Brāhma-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the one hundred and thirty-ninth chapter.
The Description of the Summoning of the Bhojakas.
Samba said:
"By your grace, I have obtained this ancient form."
Having obtained all this, including the direct vision of the high-souled Bhāskara,
my mind is again overwhelmed with anxiety:
"Who will carry out the maintenance of the service to the God?"

"O Brahmin, by my very grace, you ought to explain [the duties of] a twice-born man who is endowed with virtues, somewhat capable of protection, and devoted to me. Thus addressed by Sāmba, Nārada replied to him.
The twice-born do not accept wealth already appropriated by the god;
for while wealth exists here, this acceptance constitutes a merit.
However, no Vedic rite can be performed with materials that have come into the possession of the deity.

Those twice-born ones who, deluded by greed, perform rituals with contempt, become excluded from the company of the righteous in this world; they are indeed temple-priests (devalakas). He who, out of greed, lives off the property of the gods or the status of a Brahmin [is likewise fallen].
That evil-minded man lives in this world on the leftovers of vultures;
consequently, no Brahmin will perform the service of the gods,
nor one who is knowledgeable in the ritual rules, possessed of wisdom, and capable of such service.
"Only the King can explain that; therefore, go to him for refuge.
Alternatively, O tiger among the Yadus, go to Gauramukha, the priest of Ugrasena, and ask him; he will fulfill your desire."
O King, having been addressed thus by Nārada, the heroic Sāmba, son of Jāmbavatī, [approached] the hero Gauramukha, the priest of Ugrasena, who was seated comfortably in his home,
O King, and had already performed his morning rites.
Having approached with humility, Sāmba then spoke these words:
"By the grace of the Sun, I have caused a vast mansion to be built,
which stands firm upon the earth as the most excellent on the face of the world, together with my wife and my army."
Everything has been given by me to him, and the mandala of the embodied form has been prepared.
Therefore, having performed the sacrifice, the gift intended for the distinguished ones should be bestowed.
O great sage, please accept all of that with my full pleasure.
Having heard these words of Sāmba, the great sage replied;
Gauramukha said:
"I shall speak to you in its entirety, exactly as it is, and in due order."
I am a Brahmin and you are a king, and he is the husband of a goddess;
thus, such a mutual union is contrary to my understanding.
For the twice-born perform their own duties as directed by the knowledge of Brahman.
Those who act otherwise, with corrupted conduct, do not escape [the consequences].
O delight of the Yadus, patience, teaching, recitation, and truth—
these are the duties of Brahmins, not the acceptance of wealth for the sake of the gods.

If the giving of wealth were for the sake of the gods, then those twice-born who serve the gods would covet divine property, and their status as Brahmins would be lost. Furthermore, whatever gift one bestows upon a Brahmin at the gateway of a temple [is likewise affected].
These two men are evildoers through their own fault,
O Vārṣṇeya: the one who accepts gifts for the sake of the gods, and the twice-born who,
having accepted them, offers or gives them away at a śrāddha or a sacrificial session.

A twice-born man of corrupt conduct and sinful nature is reborn as a Rākṣasa. O Lord of the Earth, wherever a twice-born man who is a temple-priest (devalaka) eats in a row, that lowly row defiles the food and commits sin.
The twice-born man who performs the sacramental rites for a *devalaka* causes all his ancestors to fall headlong into ruin;
how can he, having caused himself to fall, uplift others?

The notion that he will thereby uplift himself is the lowest of conceptions. He who, out of sheer force or fear, adopts the livelihood of one outside the Vedic fold, though born a Brahmin, becomes an outcast.
A twice-born man accepts a gift by reciting the mantra for receiving a gift;
however, there is no Vedic injunction regarding the acceptance of gifts on behalf of the gods.
Therefore, a king should never, under any circumstances, give a gift to a Brahmin for the sake of the gods.
"Let it go, thinking, 'I shall depart after cutting through this sacred thread (brahmasūtra).
Sāmba said:
'If it is not to be accepted by the twice-born, to whom then should I give this?'"
"Whether it has been heard of or seen before, you ought to explain that to me.
Gauramukha said:
"O Lord, bestow this auspicious city upon Maga."
"He has the right to partake of the food of the gods and to perform the worship of the deities.
Sāmba said: "Who is this one called 'Magā' by you? O Lord, where does he dwell?"
"Whose son is he, O best of the twice-born? What is his conduct and what is his appearance?
Gauramukha replied:
"O best of the twice-born, this one who is called Māga is indeed the divine Māga."
In Nikṣubhā, the son is called the heroic Ādityātmaja.
Sāmba said:
"How is he the son of Nikṣubhā, and likewise how is he the son of Vīra?"
"And how was this descendant of the Sun called 'Maga', O sinless one?
Gauramukha said:
"O Yādava, it is said that the goddess Nikṣubhā attained human form."
Having received a curse here from the Sun, she who was honored by the world departed;
they call his lineage "Mihira," and he bestowed supreme Brahminhood upon him.
O sinless one, in ancient times there was a righteous son of a seer named Sujihva.
To him was born a daughter, that excellent woman Nikṣubhā;
she was peerless in beauty in the world and was known as Hāralīlā. By her father’s command, that maiden would sport in the sacrificial fire.
While they were dwelling there according to the proper rule near the kindled fire,
the Lord of the Gods, the one garlanded with rays, beheld them;
endowed as they were with beauty and youth, he then fell under the sway of desire.
The Lord of Gods reflected: "How indeed shall I enjoy her?
This Agni, who is worshipped by the gods, has been led away by her;
having entered the forest, I shall enjoy that slender-limbed woman who is honored by the world."
Having reflected thus, O hero, the Lord of Gods, the thousand-rayed Sun, the lord of day, entered the fire; he then became his son.
Thereupon, she was endowed with grace, beauty, form, and youth.
Having leaped across the blazing fire, the large-eyed maiden departed;
but seeing the girl, the Fire-god became enraged, assumed his own form, and being tormented by her,
seized her hand with his hand.
The tiger among the Yadus spoke, unprompted by the Sun:
"Since you have transgressed the Vedic injunctions as I instructed,
no son shall be born to you from me."
He is known by the name Jara, the increaser of the lineage's fame.
Those born from the fire-lineage are called Magas; those born from the soma-lineage are the twice-born (dvijātayas);
and those born from the Bhojakāditya-lineage are indeed proclaimed as the divine ones.
Having spoken thus to her, the Lord Āditya then vanished within; meanwhile,
the seer, possessing great splendor, a tongue of *Ṛg*-verses, and supreme intelligence, having ascertained through the yoga of meditation that progeny had been produced, fell down.
Raising a curse, the radiant Ṛgjihva spoke these words:
"O illustrious lady, because this child was conceived by you through your own transgression, he shall be one who is not to be honored."

Tormented by grief for her son, the young woman, her eyes distraught and afflicted by sorrow, meditated upon that one being of fiery form. Then, [she realized] he was born from my own womb, the source of the most excellent of gods.
"This great curse has been bestowed; you ought to fulfill it.
O Lord of Gods, let my son indeed be worthy of worship; act accordingly.
While the Blessed One Aryaman was thus reflecting, [the following occurred].
Resorting to a fiery form, he spoke these words:
"Gentle, with a deep resonance, peaceful and free from fever,
straightforward in speech and possessed of great splendor, he practices righteousness with firm vows."
Therefore, I cannot alter this great curse that has been released;
however, because of the gravity of my own duty, I shall make your son worthy, supreme, and one who has mastered the Vedas, though he remains beyond ordinary veneration.
And his lineage shall dwell upon the earth as a very great one;
the high-souled descendants of Vasiṣṭha, exponents of the Veda,
shall be my singers, my sacrificers, my devotees, and those who have me as their supreme goal.
Those who serve me and observe my vows,
perceiving the true meaning of the Veda, will— being devoted and always permeated by my nature— honor both you and me according to what is right.
By performing my rites, by regarding my limbs as their own, and by fixing their being upon me, they shall become free from passion through my grace and will undoubtedly come to me alone—
those who always wear matted hair and beards, and who are ever devoted to me as their supreme goal.
Knowing the ritual procedure for the five times, the sacrificer of the Hero’s Time—
pure and self-restrained— holding the armor in his right hand which was full of water,
and covering his face with the cloth given by his wife, [proceeded].

Having first offered the vital breath (*prāṇa*) to the great ones, one should then eat while restraining one's speech. Those who worship me from this point on with distracted senses and mind, and who perform the rite devoid of ritual rules and mantras, [shall not attain success].
Having fallen from heaven and being weary, they too shall take delight in the vicinity of the sun;
such will be your sons upon the earth—
high-souled men in the lineage of Māgha, who have mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
Having thus consoled that queen, the sun-god Bhāskara, the stealer of waters, vanished;
and that lady of great splendor attained joy.
Thus, O son of Kṛṣṇa, were these Bhojakas born.
Likewise, the Ādityas, honored by the world, were born from Viṣṇu’s splendor;
grant this city to them, for they are sufficient for the acceptance of this gift of yours,
O hero, as well as for the worship of the Sun.
Having heard these words of Gauramukha, that Yādava,
Sāmba— the son of Jāmbavatī— bowed his head and said:
"Where do these high-souled sons of the Sun reside?"
"O tiger among the twice-born, I shall bring them by means of the herdsmen.
Gauramukha said:
"O mighty-armed one, I do not know where the deer dwell during the springtime."
"O hero, the Sun knows them; therefore, go to him for refuge.
When Samba was thus addressed by the Brahmin, he bowed his head to the Sun and said to Bhaskara: "Who will perform worship for you?"
Thus addressed by Sāmba, the image spoke to him:
"O sinless one, [these people] are not fit for my service in Jambūdvīpa.
Go to Śākadvīpa and bring here someone who performs my worship."
On the opposite shore beyond the Salt Ocean, surrounded by the Ocean of Milk,
lies that which is known as Śākadvīpa, situated beyond Jambūdvīpa. There, the regions are meritorious and endowed with the four social orders (varṇas).
The Magas, the Magagas, the Gānagas, and likewise the Mandagas;
among them, the Magas are known to consist mostly of Brāhmaṇas, the Magagas are considered Kṣatriyas,
the Gānagas are to be known as Vaiśyas, and the Mandagas are their Śūdras.
There is no confusion whatsoever among them regarding their respective bases of dharma;
for by this investigation of dharma, the subjects are made happy in every way.
They have been fashioned from my own splendor by Viśvakarman.
To them, I have declared the four Vedas along with their secret Upanishads;
and by means of various hymns proclaimed in the Vedas— both supreme and secret— which were composed by me,
they meditate upon me alone and worship me constantly.
Those whose minds are fixed on me, who are my worshippers,
devoted to me, and intent upon me; those who serve me, who observe my vows, and who wear the unimpaired [emblems] according to the rites prescribed by rule.
My followers always perform auspicious worship for me;
likewise, the gods along with the gandharvas, siddhas,
and cāraṇas sport and take delight while being seen together with them.
In Jambūdvīpa, I am Viṣṇu, worshipped by the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas;
in Śālmalīdvīpa, I am Śakra; and in Krauñcadvīpa, I am indeed Bhaga.
In Plakṣadvīpa, I am Bhānu, and in Śākadvīpa, I am Divākara.
"Brahmā is remembered as being in Puṣkara, and from there I am Maheśvara. O Sāmba, mount Garuḍa and go quickly without hesitation; bring those deer here from Śākadvīpa for the sake of my worship."
Having accepted that command of the Sun with the words "So be it," the son of Jāmbavatī,
endowed with extraordinary splendor, returned once more to Dvāravatī and related to his father everything regarding his vision of the God.
Having obtained a Garuḍa from him, Sāmba mounted it and departed;
reaching Śākadvīpa with his hair standing on end in joy,
he beheld there the radiant Magas exactly as they had been described.
Worshipping Vivasvān with auspicious incense, lamps, and other offerings,
he first saluted them, performed circumambulation around them,
and inquired after their well-being with words of praise and hymns.
For you are performers of meritorious deeds, seekers of auspiciousness for the sake of what is to be seen;
you who are devoted to the worship of the Sun, and to whom he is indeed the bestower of boons—
know me to be the son of Viṣṇu, renowned by the name Sāmba.
"And on the banks of the Candrabhāgā, the Sun was established by me;
by him I have been sent here. 'Arise, let us go!
they said to him, and he replied to them with Ambā: 'It is even so, there is no doubt.'"
Indeed, it was previously explained by Your Majesty that eighteen clans of Magas who are exponents of the Vedas shall go here along with you,
just as Your Majesty has spoken.
Then, having placed those eighteen families here on all sides upon Garuḍa, Sāmba quickly returned;
and in a very short time, he reached Mitravana from there.
Having received the command of the Sun, Sāmba reported everything accordingly.
The Sun, being pleased, said "Excellent! and spoke to Sāmba:
"Indeed, these shall be the performers of my worship and the bringers of peace to all living beings."
"O best of the Yadus, they shall perform my worship according to the prescribed rites;
because of that, no further anxiety shall remain for you.
Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Bringing of the Bhojakas," in the Sāmbopākhyāna of the Saptamī-kalpa within the Brāhma-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the one hundred and fortieth chapter, the description of the origin of the Bhojakas. Sumantu said:
O lord of the earth, having thus brought the monkeys there,
that great-souled Samba, in former times, established a city on the bank of the river Candrabhāgā after installing the Sun-god.

Having made it prosperous with wealth, he presented that city of the Sun— which is meritorious and renowned throughout the three worlds— to the Bhojakas. Since it was caused to be built by Sāmba, it is known as Sāmbapura.
In that city, situated in its center, the god Divākara was established;
all [the gods] were installed with due honor in the city marked with their own names. Furthermore, the conduct of the Magas was always consistent with the traditional practices of their lineage.
Having served the god with song and through the rites prescribed by the Vedas,
Samba, having accomplished his purpose and obtained the boon, became young once again;
he then prostrated before the Adidiva, the eldest of the gods, the Sun.
Immediately thereafter, having prostrated before and saluted all the Magas,
the stainless Sāmba then set out for the city of Dvāravatī;
he had been requested by the descendants of the Bhoja lineage for the sake of the Magas.
The high-souled descendant of Vasudeva, a member of the same lineage,
performed the gift of these maidens to those Bhojas, the best of the Magas;
all those maidens were together, adorned with coral and gems.
Having worshipped all of them, they were sent to the abode of Savitṛ;
then, having returned, the god Divākara was questioned by Sāmba:
"Tell me the knowledge of the Ma-gas and the Vedas in their entirety."
Having heard Sāmba’s words, Bhāskara spoke these words:
"Go and ask Nārada; he will tell you everything.
Thus addressed, Sāmba then went toward Nārada.
Having gone there, he reported all of this to him;
and he then said to Sāmba,
"O best of the Yadus, I do not possess that supreme knowledge which the great sage Vyāsa knows regarding the Bhojas."
"Go to him and, having bowed your head to the sage, question him;
out of regard for Kṛṣṇa, he will tell you everything, there is no doubt.
Thus addressed by Nārada, Sāmba, the son of Jāmbavatī, [departed].
Having gone to Vyāsa’s hermitage and bowed his head to the sage,
he joined his palms in reverence and spoke these words:
"I went to Śākadvīpa and brought back the foremost of the Magas."
The sons of the best lineage, endowed with youth, settled there;
having honored and worshipped them, the city was entrusted to them.
Having indeed obtained the city, they were established as the eldest, the middle, and the youngest.
Having chosen maidens born of the Bhoja lineage and adorned with ornaments,
they performed the auspicious rite of bestowing them upon the Brahmins.
Oh, how fortunate, praiseworthy, and ever meritorious they are!
For those who are devoted to the worship of the Sun, and for whom he is the bestower of boons— for them,
every fruit pertaining to this world and the next is fully attained.
Indeed, while human existence is impermanent, those who are intent on the worship of the gods [secure their welfare].
But as I reflect upon them— having considered the Sun and the Bhojakas—
I have a doubt in my heart regarding their knowledge:
how is it that these are worshippers, and who are the Magas and who are the Bhojakas?
What is their supreme knowledge, and what indeed is their object of knowledge?
Why are they called "divya"? For what purpose is the wearing of the *kūrca* [tuft of hair]? For what purpose is the solar vow (*sauravrata*)? And how are they remembered as the reciters (*vācaka*)?
For what purpose do they sing the Vedāṅgas with splendor, and how is that so?
Furthermore, O dear one, what is the measure of the body of the daily ritual (āhnika-kañcuka), and to whom does it belong?
What is declared to be its name, how was it produced, and how is it remembered?
How do they sing to the gods, and how do they perform sacrifice?
What is their *agnihotra*, and what are the five "swings" (*dolā*) remembered to be? Tell me all this—the conduct of the *bhojakas*.

Having heard the words of Sāmba, the sage Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, the son of Kālī and possessor of great splendor, spoke these supreme words: "Excellent, excellent, O best of the Yadus! Well asked, O you of noble vows."
There is no doubt that the conduct of herdsmen is somewhat difficult to understand;
however, by the grace of the Sun, it has come to my memory.
Just as it was told by Vasiṣṭha, I shall relate it to you in its entirety.
O son of Kṛṣṇa, listen to the supreme conduct of the deer;
for they are knowers of wisdom who have taken refuge in the yoga of action.
It is heard that all the sages remain established in their vows through silence.
Moreover, all those supreme ṛṣis who dwell in Śākadvīpa eat in silence, for they have adopted the conduct of sages;
therefore, one who does not desire the presence of sensory qualities should eat in silence.
Speech is declared to be like the sun, and likewise, it is the supreme cause;
those who constantly worship within that [speech] are remembered as *arcakas*.
Because they were born from the daughter of a *Bhoja*, they are therefore remembered as *Bhojakas*.
Just as it has been declared that there are four Vedas for the Brāhmaṇas—
the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, and the Atharvaveda—
so too, O observer of noble vows, were the Vedas spoken by Brahmā for the Magas.
But their Vedas are proclaimed to be the reverse of those.
The Veda, the Viśvamada, the Vidvadvahni, and likewise the Rasa—
these are indeed the Vedas of the Magas, which Prajāpati spoke of in the past.
The sages study this Veda; therefore, it is known as the Vedāṅga.
Indeed, the illustrious Śeṣa, who brings happiness to all living beings, having mounted the chariot of the Sun, pours down rain along with the other charioteers.
Furthermore, that which is its release is indeed the great arrow of the Sun;
it should be constantly saluted by those who seek the path with the weapon-mantra (astramantra),
just as a garland is offered to the twice-born at the time of worship.

Just as *darbha* grass is proclaimed to be the purifier among the twice-born in all sacrifices of ritual action (*saṃskāra*), so too is Dharma the purifier for the Magas. By means of these [practices], the lords of the Magas in that island achieve the greatest victory.
O tiger among the Yadus, O delighter of the Yadus, the Bhojakas are learned, of noble lineage, endowed with purity and proper conduct,
devoted to sacrifices, and reciting mantras from the beginning;
they are indeed dear to me.
The mantra is indeed recited as the weapon of the Veda;
for all Brāhmaṇas, however, the Sāvitrī is prescribed.
But for us, O best of the Yadus, it is preceded by the Mahāvyāhṛtis.
Then, one should enjoy the celestial mansion with freedom from delusion and through silence as is appropriate;
nor should one touch anything that causes forgetfulness, nor indeed should one touch that very thing here.
Even while breathing involuntarily, one should circumambulate it and always bow to one's desired sun.
Just as a sacrifice is accomplished through the rite of action accompanied by mantras proclaimed in the Vedas, so too,
because their oblation is perfected by being preceded by ritual rules and mantras,
they are remembered as performers of sacrifice.

Just as the Agnihotra is renowned among the twice-born, so is the Adhvahotra prescribed for the Magas. "Accha" is indeed the name of that Adhvahotra; such are the words of the sage, and there is no doubt in this matter.
Five types of incense should be offered, for its accomplishment is always assured here.
"The two Dandanayaka-Velas belong to the Sun during the three junctions of the day.

Thus ends the one hundred and fortieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of the Bhojakas," in the Sāmbopākhyāna of the Saptamī-kalpa within the Brāhma-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya-mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the one hundred and forty-first chapter.
Regarding the description of the Bhojaka caste,
Sāmba said: "As for what you have said concerning the Bhojakas— that the Avyaṅga is the purifier of the body— "
"But this vow-binding has been declared for them; what is their caste remembered to be?
Vyāsa said:
"All those young boys of the Bhojakas were questioned by you."
"What was told by them? Tell that in its entirety.
Samba said:
"I have described to you the settlements of the Bhojakas on all sides."
"Tell me the truth of this: what is his caste here, and how does he stand?
Then the Blessed One, skilled in speech, spoke these words:
"O Sāmba, those young Bhojakas who were mentioned by you and heard [by us]—"

"These eight Magas are to be known as mine alone; these Śūdras are born from my own body. Having understood these words and having bowed his head to the Sun, the daughter of the Bhoja clan gave ten maidens to the ten [Magas].
Then eight maidens were indeed given even to the Mandakas;
thereafter, O Samba, remember that a city was established for them by me.
As for the eight servant-maidens and the ten Bhoja maidens, [they were likewise settled].
These eighteen sons of those princes are to be known;
there, the sons begotten by the twice-born upon the Bhoja maidens were called Bhojakas,
while the Brāhmaṇas were designated as Divyas.
Those born of the daughters of slaves by those known as the slow-moving (Mandaga) and the last (Antya) are to be known as the Madaṅgas, the attendants of the Sun; and they,
in that city of the Brahmins, were surrounded by their sons and wives who were auspicious.

O best of sages, in Śākadvīpa, the Sun is worshipped with various Vedic mantras by mortals who observe their own specific duties and maintain the integrity of all their limbs; thus, having begun their sacrifices according to their respective dharmas,
they honor the Lord of Day.
Seeing their physical deformity, Sāmba, filled with curiosity,
paid homage once more to the son of Satyavatī and said:
"O best of sages, why was this bridegroom described as being without deformity?"
From where has this arisen, and why is it considered pure? When is it to be bound, and for what purpose is it maintained?
What is its measure, O Blessed One, and why is it called "deficient in limb"?
Sumantu said:
O tiger among the Kurus, having heard these words of Jāmbavatī and her son, Vyāsa spoke; and he, the son of Kālī, spoke to Sāmba.
Vyāsa said: "And as you have told me this, there is no doubt that this is their birth;
listen as I speak of the characteristics of one who is free from physical defects."

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Bhojaka Caste," in the Sāmbopākhyāna of the Saptamī-kalpa within the Brāhma-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the one hundred and forty-second chapter,
titled "The Description of the Origin of the Vyaḍa."
Vyāsa said:
The deities, sages, nāgas, and hosts of gandharvas and apsarases,
as well as yakṣas and rākṣasas, dwell in the sun in accordance with the sequence of the seasons.
Thereupon Vāsuki, having swiftly paid homage to the Sun, quickly returned to his own abode from the chariot of the rising sun with speed;
he indeed offered the unimpaired [serpent] to Sūrya for the sake of his pleasure.
He bound that divine, auspicious, and slightly reddish-white ornament made of Ganges gold around his own waist out of affection for him;
for it was produced from the body of a serpent-king and had been worn by the Sun himself.
Therefore, it should be worn according to the prescribed rite and in accordance with reality by one who desires devotion to Him and wishes to please the Sun; thus the wearer becomes pure.
And through its constant wearing, the Maker of Day shall be pleased.
But those priests who do not maintain such [knowledge] regarding the Sun, though they may be sacrificers and worshippers, are devoid of solar [power];
they are unfit for sacrifice and are like leavings—of this there is no doubt.
For they are fallen from the Smṛti and right conduct, and thus they are unworthy to worship the Sun.
Indeed, those who worship the Sun while laughing or rising [from their seats] go to the Raurava hell;
they must not laugh nor rise as long as they have not completed the worship.
Knowing this, there is no doubt that the Sun is not pleased without a limbless [complete] offering.
Indeed, having been touched by the Nāga king, he was remembered by Āra;
he should be made of a single color and likewise a bringer of success in one's undertakings,
measuring exactly one hundred and more than one hundred finger-breadths (aṅgulas).
This [measure] is the best by standard; the middling is twenty more;
the short is one hundred and eight, but there is no shorter than that. This form was fashioned and created by Viśvakarman.
Among the Bhojakas, however, it is declared that there are more than a hundred [initiations] in the middle [category].
Even one who has been consecrated does not become pure without it;
therefore, O Hero, by wearing this [amulet], he indeed becomes pure at that time.
All his auspicious rites, such as the *havir-homa* and others, become successful.
O Lord of the Earth, he who is free from defects and whose limbs are not fallen is indeed "Avyaṅga.
This essence, which is delightful, is to be known by the names of "Jaya."
For he was born from the limb (aṅga) of Ahi, and thus he is remembered as Avyaṅga;
because his limb (aṅga) came from Ahi, he is therefore called Avyaṅga.
Furthermore, the suffix -ṇvul is prescribed after the root *arh* in the sense of "worship" (*pūjā*).
Because he is honored and pure, he is therefore remembered as the Arhaka.
The form "sāra" is known to mean the essence; that which is the primary essence is called Sāra.
Since the verbal root *ṣaṇ* is known to mean devotion, he is therefore remembered as Sārasana.
Because he has been thus honored with gold, gems, and pearls, he should be known as one whose limbs have fallen away, yet who is sustained by constant sacrifices. Thus,
O hero, these have been described as those who are themselves free from defects but who consume those who possess defects.
He is the eternal bestower of supernatural power and prosperity, as well as the purifier of the body;
he consists of all the Vedas, and likewise consists of all the gods;
O Sāmba, he consists of all beings and likewise consists of all the worlds.
O high-minded one, Brahmā is situated in its middle, Viṣṇu at its base,
and the Moon-crested Lord (Śiva) is stationed at its end, O descendant of Yadu.
The Ṛgveda is situated at its base, and the Yajurveda occupies its middle.
O sinless one, the Sāmaveda stands at the top as the knot of the Aṅgiras;
O best of the Yadus, the Earth stands supported by the root;
O Sāmba, the waters are the food of the root, and in the middle is the god Vibhāvasu (Fire).
Immediately following those, wind and space were established at the top;
Bhūrloka was situated at the base, Bhuvarloka in the middle,
and Svarloka rested at the top, extending as far as the tip of the body.
Thus, O best of the Yadus, this great [form] consisting of the gods and likewise consisting of the worlds must be worn with devotion by the worshiper for the pleasure of Ravi;
indeed, those who worship Ravi without this, O best of the Yadus, [do not truly worship].
They shall have no fruit from their worship and will indeed go to hell;
likewise, for them there shall always be an unimpaired officiating priest (bhojaka) at all other times, O best of the Yadus— this has been told to you.
"O Hero, O observer of noble vows, what is the cause of this bondage, and what are these ornaments?
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-second chapter, titled "The Origin of Vyaṅga," in the Sāmbopākhyāna of the Saptamī-kalpa within the Brāhma-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the one hundred and forty-third chapter.
Sumantu spoke: Having thus heard from Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī, this very description of the various rites for incense and other offerings, Sāmba [acted accordingly].
The high-minded one returned once more to see the birth of the one who was free from physical defects. Then, having arrived at the hermitage again,
the highly effulgent Samba spoke these words to the mighty-armed Narada.
O Sage, how did the Bhojakas offer incense,
perform ablutions and sipping of water, and present the respectful offering (arghya) to the Great-Souled One,
the Sun? Having heard these words of Samba, Narada, the best of sages, [proceeded].
O tiger among the Kurus, he spoke to Samba, the son of Jambavati:
"Indeed, I shall describe to you the sequence of the ritual for offering incense to the Sun,
as well as the rules for bathing, sipping water (ācamana), and likewise the gift of gold."
Having sipped water three times and bathed, one should put on two clean, auspicious,
and dry garments, and having donned these pure clothes,
one should carefully sip water while facing either north or east.
Standing in water, one should not perform the ritual sipping (ācamana); having emerged from the water, one should do so with care.
For within the waters reside the Sun, Agni, and the Goddess Mother Sarasvatī;
therefore, one should sip water after emerging, but not while remaining in the reservoir.

Having sat down in a clean place, self-restrained and facing either the east or the north, he should wash his feet and hands; then, with his hands between his knees, he should perform the ritual sipping (ācamana). Being pure and well-composed, he should drink water three times from the palms of his hands.
One should perform the wiping twice and the sprinkling with water three times; then,
having touched the head, the sense-orifices, and the self in successive order,
one who has sipped water and paid homage to the sun attains purity through these acts of purification.

If an atheist performs a rite here out of delusion without having sipped water for purification, all his rites become fruitless; of this there is no doubt. For the gods desire purity; thus it has been declared by the Vedas.

All the gods, having been worshipped with effort, praise purity alone; for it is through the constituent parts of purity that [the rite] is ordained. Having sipped water and observed silence, one should then proceed to the temple of the deity.
For the purpose of restraining the breath,
one should cover the mouth with a cloth and carefully wrap the head to prevent water from touching the hair;
thereafter, one should perform worship of the Sun with various kinds of auspicious flowers.
The sacrificer should diligently recite the Gāyatrī together with its Śiras;
then he should offer incense to Agni, first offering oblations of guggulu.
Thereafter, taking a handful of flowers, he should diligently place it upon the [fire’s] crest.
One should place that upon the head of the sun while reciting the mantra of the deity:
"Oṃ! That which the observers of vows avoid—whether gods, humans, or all the ancestors—we meditate upon that radiance of the Sun, which shines forth first by its splendor."
The five periods for incense are traditionally prescribed for the five types of incense;
likewise, I shall protect the five rites beginning with the fire-oblation.
Furthermore, the period of the Daṇḍanāyaka begins at dawn upon the appearance of the stars.
For one who understands the true nature of duty, the time of twilight is not the time for ignorance;
rather, worship of the Sun must be performed at the three junctions of the day by beholding the Sun.
When the all-pervading Sun has half-risen in the forenoon, it is then that he is half-set.
In the forenoon, one should offer with the word "Helaya," and at midday, for the sake of the Fire;
likewise, in the evening, it should be given to the Fire within the mandala.
These offerings should be mixed with sandalwood water and endowed with fragrant water.
Having placed lotuses, karavīra flowers, as well as red utpala lotuses,
kuraṇṭaka flowers, and divine perfumes and other offerings mixed with water and flowers into a copper vessel.
O hero, having offered incense to the fire with diligent effort, an oblation of guggulu,
and then taking the vessel of water for the guest-offering (arghyapātra), one should perform the invocation (āvāhana) of the Sun:
"Come, O Sūrya, thousand-rayed one, mass of splendor, Lord of the World!"
"O Lord, having compassion for me, O Maker of Day, accept this water offering (arghya). Having performed the invocation with these words, he knelt upon the ground;
then, reciting the Āditya-hṛdaya, he presented the arghya to the Sun.
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Āditya, the All-pervading, the Lord of the Sky, the Brahman who is the creator of the worlds;
homage to you, the Sovereign, the Ancient, the Thousand-eyed;
homage to Soma, who is the Ṛg, Yajur, and Atharva Vedas.
Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ mahaḥ oṃ janaḥ oṃ tapaḥ oṃ satyam. To Brahmā, to Muṇḍa, in the middle, and in front:
obeisance to Āditya. Nārada said:
And according to the supreme *Sāvitrī-tantra*, for the sake of the protector of the three worlds,
one should then take hold of the incense vessel from all sides and lift it up; thereafter,
having offered the incense, one should utter this speech:
You alone are the ancient one among the Rudras and the Vasus;
you, the eternal, are praised on all sides by the hymns of the gods in heaven.
By you, as the former [Agni], the morning was brought about, and by another, as the latter [Sūrya], the midday.
Oṃ, salutations to the Blessed One, the Self of Knowledge, and to you as well.
"The wise always behold that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
At sunset, one should offer the arghya with this mantra: Oṃ.
Homage to Varuṇa, the source of bliss! Oṃ! Moving through the dark expanse, establishing both the immortal and the mortal, the divine Savitṛ comes upon his golden chariot, beholding all beings.
Having offered incense to the Sun according to this rite,
the priest should raise it with the incense and then enter the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha).
Having entered, he should present the incense for the sake of the image.
With the mantra "Salutation to Mihira, salutation to Nikṣubhā," one should [worship] constantly; then "Salutation to the King" and "Salutation to Nikṣubhā";
and then indeed "Salutation to the one known as Daṇḍanāyaka and to Piṅgala."
Likewise, [one should offer] to Rājñī, Srauṣā, Īśā, and Garutmān;
then, performing a circumambulation, one should announce [the offering] to the deities of the directions.
O best of the Yadus, one should then give [offerings] to Diṇḍin and Hemanta.
O Yādava, one should likewise offer [oblations] to Maheśvara and to Vyoman.
(Salutations to the Viśvedevas; salutations to the Rudras.
Oṃ, repeated salutations to Brahmā, the Lord of the Mundas, to Āditya, to Puruṣeśvara, and to Sūrya.
Oṃ, having bowed to Ananta, Śeṣa, Vāsuki, Takṣaka, Karkoṭaka, Padma, Śaṅkha, and Kulika—to the Nāga kings, salutations!
To the Daityas, Dānavas, and Piśācas dwelling in Talātala, Pātāla, Atala, Vitala, Rasātala, and the other regions, salutations!
Then one should perform circumambulation, saying "Salutations again and again to the Mātṛkās" (Oṃ, salutations to the Planets).
Oṃ, homage to Daṇḍanāyaka! Oṃ, homage to Mārtaṇḍa! Oṃ, homage to Vināyaka!
Having thus addressed these names and offered incense, O fair-faced one, wherever that incense rises up, release it right there once again.
Having been thus praised by the Sūryaguptas and having understood this, they then said:
"O Vibhāvasu, you have been worshipped by me according to my ability and with devotion;
O Lord, tell me how to achieve success in my undertakings pertaining to both this world and the next."
Thus, having bathed at the three sessions of the day, he who worships the Sun with devotion according to the prescribed rite shall obtain the fruit of a horse-sacrifice;
and he who daily performs the extensive offering of incense as described.
Possessing sons and free from disease, he dies and merges into the Sun;
indeed, all undertakings performed with diligence according to the prescribed injunctions become successful and bear fruit.
If the best flower is not available, one should offer leaves;
if there are no leaves, then incense; if there is no incense, then water. And when nothing at all is available, one should worship with prostration.

One who is unable to perform prostration should worship the Sun with the mind alone; this rule is proclaimed for when ritual materials are unavailable. However, when materials are available, one should offer everything.

He who, joined with the ritual through mantras, offers incense to Mitra— by the mere utterance of those [mantras], Ravi becomes pleased by the incense. Having carefully and thoroughly covered his head, nose, and mouth, [he should offer it].
One should worship the Sun, O hero, and never allow oneself to become lax.
By means of a lotus, O king of kings, a man goes to the Maker of Day;
therefore, one should always act with diligence, for thus the Maker of Day is worshipped.
Having obtained the fruit of the horse sacrifice, they indeed go to the world of the Sun;
O Yādava, those men who behold [the deity] being worshipped with incense go to the supreme abode which even the wise do not perceive.
Those men who behold the Sun being worshipped in this manner with devotion,
having attained all their desires in this world, go to the supreme state.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-third chapter, titled "Description of Various Offerings such as Incense," in the Sāmba-episode of the Saptamī-kalpa within the Brāhma-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the one hundred and forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of the Bhojaka. Sumantu said:

Then the blessed Vyāsa arrived at the city of Dvāravatī to see the god Nārāyaṇa, who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace. O lord of the people, upon seeing that the sage had arrived, Vāsudeva [honored him].
Rising up, O Bhārata, the one of great splendor personally offered him a seat,
as well as water for his feet and the guest-offering;
then, becoming composed, he questioned Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī.
"O Brahmin, these Bhojaka Brahmins who have indeed been brought here by my son—
having gone from here to Śākadvīpa, they are wise and destined for liberation;
having seen them, O Brahmin, both by their appearance and by their conduct and entry [into that state]."
Curiosity has arisen within me, and my joy is supreme:
how is it that these people remain on the surface of the earth for even a moment,
they for whom the Sun is always worshiped, and for whom liberation shall dwell forever?
"Indeed, no one attains liberation without first becoming a *bhojakatva* (an enjoyer).
O Brahmin, this is what truly manifests in my mind at all times.
Vyāsa said:
Just as you have said, O wielder of the conch, discus, and mace,
these high-souled Bhojakas are blessed; of this there is no doubt,
for they constantly worship the radiant Sun, the maker of day.
The wise and those established in action always proceed toward liberation;
they constantly worship the Sun with offerings of flowers, fruits,
food, medicinal herbs, and entirely with oblations of clarified butter.
Having performed the eternal *homa* and thereafter resorted to the supreme *homa*, they— purified in soul and free from stain through the performance of the supreme *homa*—
enter the supreme, divine, solar, and radiant digit.
One [power] is established in the means of action and therein in fire;
the second is situated in the path of the wind and illuminates within the ether;
beyond that, the third is remembered as being in the solar orb.
And that maṇḍala of the Sun is indeed divine, undecaying, and imperishable.
Within it resides that Person who consists of both the existent and the non-existent;
he is to be known as both the perishable and the imperishable, and likewise as the Great Sun.
Both the partless (niṣkala) and the with-parts (sakala) are conceived as his two forms.
The imperishable (akṣara) is indeed the with-parts, abiding within all beings;
that which possesses the principles (tattva) is called the with-parts, while that which is devoid of the principles is the partless.
He carries away the grasses, shrubs, creepers, trees, wild beasts, lions, and lords of birds, as well as gods, siddhas, and humans— both those born on land and those born in water;
for he is established everywhere within the inner self of all beings.
When he, who is of the nature of the cosmic age (kalpa), assumes a second body,
he should always be known as being partless (niṣkala) while abiding in his radiant (taijasa) portion;
he perpetually brings about cold, heat, and rain throughout the three worlds.
The second body of his is the Imperishable, that supreme state;
it is established upon the path of the gods (devayāna) through the yoga of action (karmayoga).
Those who know Sāṅkhya and Yoga, as well as those perfected by the Sun (āditya-siddha), [follow this path].
They go to that place; that is proclaimed as liberation.
Free from dualities and free from departure, having gone there, one does not grieve.
In the Vedas, those who know reality speak of Brahman and meditate upon it.
O Supreme Person, they meditate in reality upon the syllable *a*,
as well as the three-syllabled *oṃkāra* which abides in three morae (*mātrās*). They say that the consonantal syllable *ma* resides in the half-mora.
Those who meditate upon this knowledge beginning with the letter *ma* are indeed of the nature of the eternal Self.
The Lord God Bhāskara is proclaimed to be the letter *ma*;
and because of their yoga of meditation on the letter *ma*, these are celebrated as the *magas*.
"Furthermore, because they feed the Thousand-rayed One (the Sun) with incense, garlands, and likewise with offerings,
they are known as Bhojakas.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of the Bhojaka," in the Sāmbopākhyāna of the Saptamī-kalpa within the Brāhma-parvan of the glorious *Mahāpurāṇa* *Bhaviṣya*.
Now begins the one hundred and forty-fifth chapter,
titled "The Description of the Knowledge of the Bhojakas.
Vāsudeva said:
"O best of Brahmins, O great sage, tell me the truth regarding the attainment of knowledge by the Bhojakas; O foremost of the twice-born, I have a supreme curiosity. Vyāsa said:
Now, listen as I speak regarding this realization of knowledge:
[the body] is a framework of bones bound together by sinews, smeared with flesh and blood,
covered with skin, and filled with the foul stench of urine and excrement.
One should abandon this abode of the elements, which is possessed by old age and sorrow, a dwelling place for disease, afflicted, full of passion, and impermanent.
[One should seek] a skull, the roots of trees, ragged garments, and solitude.
Equanimity toward all beings is thus the characteristic of one who is liberated. Just as oil is in sesame seeds, milk in cows, and the continuity of fire in wood,
a wise and composed person should contemplate the means for this with their intellect.
The embodied self, having restrained with effort the turbulent and flickering mind and having controlled the sense organs like birds in a cage,
finds satisfaction through the senses when they are disciplined, as if by steady streams of water.
O Janārdana of great intelligence,
one should constantly burn away defects through breath-control (prāṇāyāma), sins through concentration (dhāraṇā),
attachments through withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), and qualities that are not divine through meditation (dhyāna).
Just as the defects of one who meditates are consumed at the end by [the fire of wisdom] as if by fire,
so too are the defects produced by the senses consumed by the restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Having purified the mind with the mind, one should purify one's disposition with that disposition.
The mind should be purified by the mind, and one should purify the intellect by means of the intellect.
Through the extreme clarity of the consciousness (citta), both auspicious and inauspicious karma shines forth.
One who is liberated from the auspicious and the inauspicious is free from dualities and devoid of possessiveness.
Free from possessiveness and free from egoism, one then attains the supreme goal.
In the forenoon, the first form is red and is known to consist of the Ṛgveda;
the second, at midday, is white and is known to consist of the Yajurveda.

The third form, Kṛṣṇa, appeared in the evening; that was the form of the Sāman. O Lord, the first is remembered as Rājasa, the second as Sāttvika, and the third as Tāmasa; thus his threefold nature (traiguṇya) was fashioned.

Distinct from these three is the fourth solar orb, a subtle light that illuminates; it is declared to be the stainless deity. Thus do the knowers of the Vedas and those who understand the Sūryasiddhānta describe the fourth.
Endowed with the syllable *oṃ* and the *praṇava*, their defilements purified through meditation,
those heroes sat in the lotus posture (*padmāsana*) with their hands placed at their navels,
[purifying] the path of the *suṣumnā* channel by means of *kumbhaka*, *recaka*, and *pūraka*.
