Having purified those five vital airs located within the body by means of the three [methods],
one should, while pressing the big toes of the feet, gradually draw them upward once they are heated.
Then, having beheld that healthy god Agni in the region of the navel—
Then, having seen the Soma in the heart and the crest of fire in the head,
one who is established in yoga reaches that supreme orb by means of the rays of wind, and having pierced it,
proceeds further to the solar orb.
Having gone there, they do not grieve; that is the supreme solar station.
O mighty-armed slayer of Keśin, the worship of the gods has been proclaimed:
the first place is the heart, and the second is that which rests in fire.

The third is situated at the navel, and the fourth is the solar orb; those who know the truth declare that the supreme station of the Sun, the Lord of the Gods, is established in the Supreme Self. That is to be known as liberation for men, and it is therefore the state that brings about the cessation of saṃsāra.
This, which is like nectar, is the supreme object of knowledge; it is the deathless state for others, beneficial to all people.
Having understood the conduct of the seers—the essence of reality—those whose minds are free from delusion proceed to liberation.
This conduct of the Magas, joined with the most excellent vehicle, has been proclaimed by me to you.
Having known this, those who know liberation speak of it, and the perfected ones (siddhas) attain that state.
This knowledge which has been declared by me should be given to men who possess faith;
it should not be given to atheists or the unintelligent by one who desires prosperity.
Sumantu said:
Having thus spoken this supreme knowledge of the Bhojakas regarding Nārāyaṇa, O mighty-armed one, the blessed Vyāsa departed for the abode of Hari.
"O Hero, that hermitage of Nara and Nārāyaṇa is renowned throughout the three worlds; it was gratified by the Gaṅgā and adorned by Badarī.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Knowledge of the Bhojakas," in the Brāhma Parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the Saptamī-kalpa.
Now begins the one hundred and forty-sixth chapter:
The Description of the Bhojakas.
Śatānīka said:
These who have been described as the *bhojakas*, the worshippers of the God of gods—
these must never, under any circumstances, be fed by Brāhmaṇas with food other than [that prescribed].
For they are beloved of Bhāskara, and they have likewise attained a state of being worthy of worship.
O Brahmins, these are remembered as divine, born from the waters of the sun;
how did they come to be unfit for consumption? Tell me that. Furthermore, tell me what action they must perform to become fit for consumption.
Sumantu said:
O lord of the earth, in former times Vāsudeva was questioned regarding this very matter by Kṛtavarman, O King, as well as by the mighty Sāmba.
O hero, having thus gone to Sāmbapura, Nārada and Parvata likewise ate in the house of the high-souled Bhojaka Ādityakarman,
who had attained fame as a deity in the world.
They were all honored by him with devotion through various kinds of foods.
O Hero, they arrived at the holy city of Dvāravatī, the abode of the Lord.
O King, those two sages, Nārada and Parvata, ascended to heaven.
The son of Hṛdika, possessed of great splendor, addressed these words to Vāsudeva:
"O Brahmin,
Janārdana, how is it that you two have eaten the food of these Bhojas, who are worshippers of the Sun?"
"Those two sages who are known as Nārada and Parvata—
these, indeed, O Janārdana, are unfit to be eaten by Brāhmaṇas.
Vāsudeva said:
"O mighty-armed one, those Bhojas are never to be fed;
yet they are always to be honored with effort, O high-minded one, just like the sun. By performing that specific rite, they attain the status of being worthy of being fed."
Listen to that, O best of the Yadus, and also what must be done by them, O Lord;
listen here with a focused mind, O mighty-armed one, as they strive.
For he whose wife is a *vṛṣalī* and he who does not wear the *avyaṅga* mark—

He should be known as unfit to be fed, and the one who feeds him is likewise so; of this there is no doubt. O tiger among the Yadus, O Lord, he who worships the Sun without having bathed and likewise without having applied oil, does not follow the prescribed rite.

He who is a servant or a cook, he by whom the food of a Śūdra is eaten, he who practices agriculture, and he who avoids even the worship of the gods; he for whom the purificatory rites (saṃskāras), such as the birth-ceremony and others, have not been performed, O Lord— Please note: The provided text contains a grammatical inconsistency (the relative pronoun *yaḥ* is used with masculine nouns while the demonstrative *yasya* is used with neuter nouns). The translation above reflects the intended meaning of the Sanskrit verse as it stands. If you would like the translation adjusted for grammatical consistency, please provide the corrected Sanskrit text.
If one does not recite the Sāvitrī mantra with the Āruṇeya mantras,
a twice-born man who eats in that person's house is purified by a quarter-kṛcchra penance;
this applies also to those who fail to honor the ancestors, the gods, men, living beings, and the Sun.
He who eats without having performed the worship according to the prescribed rule is a destroyer of dharma.
He who is devoid of oil massage, as well as he who is without the conch-shell [mark],
and he who wears his hair on his head— such a person is to be known as the lowest of cooks.
For a Brahmin who performs the worship of the gods, fire-offerings, ritual bathing, libations,
giving of gifts, and the honoring of Brahmins,
yet is devoid of an oil massage (abhyaṅga), all of it becomes fruitless.
For this oil massage, O tiger among the Yadus, consists of all the gods and likewise all the Vedas; it is remembered as the most supreme purifier.
O best of the Yadus, Hari resides at its very root for those who offer the oblations.
In the center was Brahmā of great splendor, adorned at his foreheads with the ears of cows;
the Ṛgveda stood at his base, all the Sāman hymns in the middle,
and the most excellent Yajurveda together with the Atharvaveda stood [at the top].
O King, just as the three fires and the three worlds are established in their respective order,
so too is the sacred anointing of the Bhojaka.
That Bhojaka who is devoid of this is the lowest of Bhojakas.

He should be known as unfit for food and impure; of this there is no doubt. Those cooks who offer the remains of offerings (nirmālya), sacrificial food (naivedya), or saffron belonging to those who have offended the deity to Śūdras, or who sell them to them, [are likewise to be avoided].
Those who seize the property of the gods should be known as the lowest of Bhojakas;
they do not worship the Lord of Gods, yet they squander the property of the gods.
O dear one, those who do not honor the Lord of Gods should be known as the lowest of Bhojakas, for they are not beloved by the God.
O giver of honor, if the one who eats the food offering (*naivedya*) eats it before it has been offered,
that food leads him to hell and not to peace;
therefore, a person should always feed the *naivedya* to the Sun-god.
O tiger among the Yadus, first there is that purification of the body:
just as the *puroḍāśa* cake is the purifier of the body for Brahmins,
so too, O hero, the *naivedya* offering is the purifier of the body for the Bhojakas.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Bhojakas," in the *Sāmbopākhyāna* within the *Saptamī-kalpa* of the *Brāhma-parvan* in the glorious *Śrī-Bhaviṣya-Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the one hundred and forty-seventh chapter:
"The Description of the Bhojaka Brāhmaṇas."
Vāsudeva said: "In this regard, O mighty-armed one, when the god Bhāskara, who is worshipped by the gods, was questioned by Aruṇa as to who the dear Bhojakas were,"
"Who are worthy of worship in your ritual, and who are not?
Thus questioned by Aruṇa, O mighty-armed one, listen with a focused mind to that which the Blessed Lord, the Maker of Day, spoke.
Bhāskara said:
Those householders who do not harm another's wife or another's property,
and those who do not revile the deities— they are indeed always dear to me.
Those who engage in trade, agriculture, or service, as well as those who revile the Vedas—
all such Bhojakas should be known as my enemies; likewise,
those who take wives and those who practice cultivation [are also my enemies].
O best of birds, those who serve kings should be known as fallen;
and those who eat the food of Śūdras should be known as my enemies.
Whatever worship or respectful offering (arghya) has been performed by them, O supreme bird—
Furthermore, O sky-walker, I do not accept that worship nor the water offering (arghya).
O hero, those [offerings] which have been mentioned, as well as those devoid of the conch,
my own remains of offerings (nirmālya), the food offering (naivedya), and likewise the saffron— [I do not accept these].
O Bird, those who bestow [offerings] upon a Śūdra, those who scatter them [indiscriminately],
and those who give them to a Vaiśya— those patrons of mine are not dear to me. Nor are those dear to me who worship Sāvitrī or Mahāśvetā, the cow of the Lord of Cows.
O Hero, O Bird, those who do not know my mudrās and the names of the servants— these Bhojakas whom I have mentioned—
are not capable of worshipping these Bhojakas who are dear to me.
Listen to that, O best of birds, with a one-pointed mind:
those who worship the gods, the twice-born, human beings, and the ancestors, are indeed always dear to me; they are capable of worshipping the Sun.
Those whose heads are perpetually shaven, those who are provided with oil massages,
and those who blow the conch shell— these are considered divine Bhojakas.
Furthermore, those who always worship me at the three junctions of the day, being well-bathed and free from anger, [are likewise so regarded].
O best of birds, those Bhojakas who worship me on my day,
and those who perform a night vigil on the sixth lunar day,
as well as those who observe a fast on the seventh and likewise during my transit (saṅkramaṇa), are dear to me.
Those Brahmins who worship me should be known as divine; those devotees of mine who are intent on me and who worship the Brahmins are my constant favorites, O Bhojaka, O elder brother of Garuḍa.
They do not show devotion to me, nor do they honor the Brāhmaṇas;
those who always hate me are neither worthy of worship nor of salutation.
O elder brother of Garuḍa, those performers of great sacrifices are my enjoyers.

O bird, for the sake of honoring the ancestors, gods, and men, you are always dear to the Bhojakas, O hero, as are those who are most excellent. Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the five great sacrifices.
O son of Kaśyapa, those who always subsist on a single meal and do not eat at night are dear to me;
and likewise, O hero Keśava, those who [fast] on my day and on the sixth lunar day are dear to me.
O bird, those wise Magas who do not eat at night are dear to me;
O elder brother of Garuḍa, those who do not offer [food] on the anniversary of their father's or mother's death are dear to me for that reason.
Such are the officiants for the seventh day of the month of Māgha:
*karavīra* flowers, red sandalwood,
a reciter of the Vedas, Brāhmaṇas, and likewise sweetmeat offerings (*modaka*) as the sacrificial food.
Offerings of clarified butter, guggulu incense, and likewise bathing with milk;
the sound of musical instruments and conchs, as well as dancing and dramatic performance—these are my preference.
Banners of five colors and a white parasol are dear to me.

O bird, worship performed by those of other castes does not please me as much as worship performed by a Bhojaka always does; furthermore, a Bhojaka must never perform the consecration of another deity.
Vāsudeva said:
Having spoken thus to Aruṇa in former times, O sinless one, the Blessed Lord then described the characteristics of the Bhojakas and subsequently ascended Mount Meru.
Thus, those who eat and those who feed others are never unfit to be fed; however,
those who are devoid of religious observances are not fit to be fed,
even if they are Brahmins born of the earth and yet lacking in such observances.

They too become unfit to be fed in this world, especially those who persist in improper occupations. Among the four castes here, there is nothing more worthy of honor, auspicious, or purifying than the excellent patron who provides the meal.
O hero, descendant of Yadu, when a Bhojaka is honored, Āditya becomes honored. Indeed, O delighter of the Yadus, in whose house the Bhojakas eat,
there Bhānu himself, as well as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, partake.
Just as the sun stands as the foremost among all beings here,
so too is the consumer [of offerings] said to be the most worshipful among all creatures;
just as Kurukṣetra is among sacred fords and the ocean is among lakes.
Likewise, O Lord, he who feeds others should be known as the most worthy of worship among those who are themselves worthy of worship;
specifically, one who feeds the devotees of the Sun is said to be especially venerable.
Just as a husband is to be honored by women, so too is a teacher to be honored by his disciples.
O son of Hṛdika, the Bhojaka is likewise to be honored by the devotees of the Sun;
for when the Bhojaka eats after being worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings,
Bhānu himself, as well as the ancestors and the deities, eat from him.
O son of Hṛdika, those who are worshippers of the Sun and who eat the food of the Bhojaka without hesitation are likewise worthy of worship and of being fed;
all such people, liberated from sin, attain the same world as the Sun.
Wherever it has been declared who is to be fed, how they are to be fed, and who is to be excluded from the meal—now, what is the use of speaking at length? Listen to my words:
there is no scripture superior to the Veda, and there is no river equal to the Gaṅgā.
There is no merit equal to the horse sacrifice; there is no happiness equal to that of a son;
there is no god equal to the Sun; there is no refuge equal to a mother.
O best of the Yadus, all these are supreme in this way.
Thus, the Bhojaka has been declared as the highest by Bhāskara.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Characteristics of the Bhojaka," in the Sāmbopākhyāna of the Saptamī-kalpa within the Brāhma-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the one hundred and forty-eighth chapter.
Sumantu spoke this description of the Kālacakra: "Then the highly resplendent Sāmba, seeing the discus in his father's hand..."
Sāmba, filled with devotion and faith, questioned his father regarding that which was formidable with garlands of flames and endowed with great splendor:
"O father, from where did you obtain this discus, which resembles the sun?"
"For what purpose, O Lord, do you carry this supreme, divine weapon?
Tell me all of this, for I desire to hear it out of curiosity.
Vāsudeva said:
"Excellent, excellent, O mighty-armed one! I have been well questioned by you.
Listen with a focused mind, my son, to the determination of the rules for the *cakra*.
Having propitiated the Sun-god with faith for a thousand divine years..."
Therefore, the wheel was obtained by me from that Bhāskara, who is worshipped by the world;
he stands manifest as the Sun, moving through the sky and mounted upon his fivefold form,
within whose navel-mandala the planets, beginning with Soma, are situated.
The twelve Ādityas are likewise situated in order upon the spokes;
and the principles (tattvas), beginning with earth, are said to reside in the paths.
This supreme wheel, whose nature is Time, is completely pervaded by these principles.
"In brief, I have described this to you as another wheel that has been bestowed.
Samba said:
"O Lord, how is it that this wheel consisting of Time is called a lotus?"
"First, tell me this; I wish to know it according to reality.
Vāsudeva said:
"The lotus indeed has six petals corresponding to the six seasons and is supported by the imperishable."
For that [wheel] is presided over by the Puruṣa; therein the Sun stands with all its parts. That which is the threefold time in the world is called the three naves.
The months, O mighty-armed one, are the spokes, and the fortnights are known as the rim.
The two solstices, southern and northern, are called the "Rims" (Nemi);
the conjunctions at the Pathins and Nabhis are known as the "Junctions" (Yoga), along with the Tapanas and others.
It is traditionally held that the lunar mansions and the planets are always situated here.

This wheel is pervaded by these [divisions] through their gross and subtle distinctions. Within this, those times beginning from the Yugas and ending with the Kalpas, which were not specifically mentioned by me to you, are also situated here in their proper sequence.
This wheel of yours, which is of the nature of Time, has been described by me in brief; it emerged from the blazing solar orb. For the sake of slaying the Asuras, I obtained this from the Sun.
Having propitiated Sūrya, the teacher of the world, through austerity in a former kalpa,
he who is devoted and full of faith always worships this Arka, who is surrounded by the planets and the principles (tattvas),
situated within the wheel.
Resplendent with a brilliance like that of the sun, he shall go to the city of Puṣpottara;
therefore, I constantly worship with devotion that Lord, the joy of my lineage and my friend,
who is surrounded by the planets and the principles (tattvas) through his own mantras.
On the seventh [lunar day], having drawn a wheel, those who worship the Sun with fragrant saffron filled with red sandalwood,
or with flour, perfumes, and so forth, mixed with red pigments;
With pure red lotuses, fragrant karavīra flowers,
or other fresh wild blossoms free from insects,
as well as with auspicious and blessed petals that are not stale and without holes.
With ripe fruits and medicinal herbs, as well as with sprouts of dūrvā grass, kuśa grass,
various incenses, fragrances, garments, and ornaments;
and with foods to be chewed, eaten, drunk, sucked, and licked, according to one's ability.
Adorned with Palāśa leaves fashioned into the beauty of canopies,
and decorated with umbrellas, chowries, bells, ornaments, mirrors, and the like;
accompanied by dancing, instrumental music, singing, the Vedas, and the sounds of meritorious recitations.
Those who worship [the deity] when it is everywhere filled with shouts of victory obtain all various desires in their entirety and without obstacles;
and one's own circle also increases without hindrance, O observer of noble vows.
Wherever this is worshipped even once, the enemy's army is destroyed.
O Sāmba, for one who writes this down and recites it during a solar or lunar transit or an eclipse,
the planets will certainly become gracious toward them.
Free from all diseases and devoid of all suffering,
the righteous-souled one lives for a long time, endowed with all forms of sovereignty.
This, indeed, O child, is the Cakrayoga that has been described by me to you.
The Arkahoma is the most excellent of all sacrifices, bestowing great success;
it is meritorious, conducive to righteousness, nourishing, and especially destructive of enemies.
It is further divided according to its colors: white, red, yellow, and black.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Kālacakra," in the Sāmbopākhyāna of the Saptamī-kalpa within the Brāhma-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the one hundred and forty-ninth chapter,
"The Description of the Solar Initiation" (*Sūryadīkṣā-varṇanam*).
Sāmba said:
What should be the measurement for drawing the wheel, and what should the lotus there be like? How is the division of the rim, the spokes, and the hub to be made?
Vāsudeva said:
Having fashioned a circular disc sixty-four finger-breadths in measurement,
its rim should always be eight finger-breadths wide, according to one's means.
The navel-field should be likewise, and the lotus there should be three times that size;
the field of the spokes, as well as the pericarp and the filaments of the lotus, should be [proportioned],
and one should fashion the remaining petals by a quarter of the filament.
The junction of the petals and the foot-parts are likewise divided there in sequence;
one should make that lotus elevated at the navel, without a doubt. The filaments should be made thick and well-distributed in due order.
The base of the spokes should be one finger-breadth thick, and their tips should be three times that thickness.
The ground outside is to be known as yellow, as are the pericarp and the filaments. The central navel-area there should be white; one should fashion the doors therein.
It should be one cubit in size, with its dimensions resembling those of a door;
the remainder is specified as red. The joints of the petals are closely joined, and between the hub and the rim there are white lines measuring one finger-breadth in width.
The cheek and the lotus at the door should be fashioned so as to be adorned on all sides by white, red, and white [lotuses];
thus there shall be four doors, and one should fashion the eastern door.
Then, in the afternoon or at dawn, one should always invoke Varuṇa;
having closed these doors, one should worship according to the prescribed rule all the aforementioned deities with devotion, using their respective mantras alone.
"Thus has the Cakra been described by me to you for the purpose of sacrifice.
Bound by this sacrifice and initiated within the solar orb—
this was previously told to me by Bhānu, O fair-faced one."
Sāmba said:
Which mantras are proclaimed for the deities in this Cakra-sacrifice?
What is declared to be the sequence of the sacrifice, and what are their respective forms?
Vāsudeva said:
One should worship Khaṣolka, the presiding deity of the heart, in the previously mentioned lotus;
likewise, one should worship the limbs, beginning with the heart, in the pericarp and the petals.
The name-mantras are in the dative case; their number is as previously stated.

The word "namaskāra" (salutation) is used everywhere; this indeed is remembered as the rule. At the time of the fire-oblation (*homa*), they end with "svāhā," and in other rites, they are again [as before].
In brief, the ritual applications should be performed according to the conclusion of the rites:
*Oṃ, may we know Khaṣolka; may we meditate upon Divākara;
may Sūrya inspire us.*
And the Sāvitrī, O mighty-armed one, is considered to consist of twenty-four syllables;
it comprises all principles, is meritorious, belongs to the lineage of Brahmā, and is the beloved of the Sun.
Thus, these mantras should be employed in all rites by those who are unwearied.
Otherwise, ritual action would be fruitless both in this world and the next.
Therefore, having understood the mantras as well as the procedure with every effort,
one should perform that rite correctly and accomplish the desired result.
Sāmba said:
"In the solar orb, for whom is initiation to be performed, and how is it done?
When, by whom, and for what purpose? Tell me all of this."
Vāsudeva said:
One may initiate a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or even a Śūdra—
whether a man or a woman— into the solar orb.
Being himself endowed with devotion, having likewise prostrated before the guru,
the brahmin guru— knowing the ritual manuals, truthful in speech, and pure— should initiate him.
Having established the fire on the sixth lunar day according to the sequence of the previously mentioned procedure, he should proceed.
Having worshipped the Sun and likewise offered oblations of clarified butter into the fire for Ravi,
he should then touch the limbs of the disciple— who has bathed, sipped water (ācamana), and whose body has the form of a meteor—
on his various parts with darbha grass and unbroken grains (akṣata).
Having worshipped the limbs with flowers, an offering (bali) should likewise be presented.
Āditya, Varuṇa, Arka, and Agni are to be propitiated with the heart-mantra;
it should consist of ghee, molasses, milk, and rice in the prescribed measure.
Having offered three handfuls of water into the fire for the deity,
and having likewise given the remainder to the preceptor, he should finally give him a tooth-stick made from a tree,
twelve finger-breadths in length, along with milk.
When the twig held between the teeth has been removed by him, he should then cast it toward the east;
he should then cast his mouth and the tooth-cleansing twig upon that [ground].
[The directions are] Maitra (east), Vāruṇa (west), Īśāna (north-east), and Vaktra (mouth) situated in the north (Saumya).
The end of the tooth-stick is auspicious, while its other part is censured.
Whichever direction the end of the tooth-stick points toward, one should worship that presiding deity;
by doing so, peace shall be attained—thus was it spoken by the Sun himself.
Having again heard those words, and having touched his limbs in sequence,
having worshipped there at the eyes, having meditated upon them, and having performed the recitation;
and having likewise made a formal resolve (saṅkalpa) and restrained the senses.
Having heard the excellent [instruction], one should remain composed;
having sipped water (ācamana), performed the protection ritual (rakṣā), and consecrated the ritual materials (dravya-adhivāsana), one should,
after bathing in the morning and offering oblations into the fire, bow with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya).
One should ask about the dream exactly as it was seen and confirm its auspiciousness;
however, if something inauspicious is seen, one should perform a hundred-fold oblation (śatahomam) with the heart-mantra.
In such a dream, one may see the palaces of the deities or the sacrificial fire.
If one sees in a dream delightful rivers, gardens, and groves; or lotuses rich with leaves, flowers, and fruit; or silver; or a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas.
If one should instruct a king endowed with heroism, a wealthy man, or the best of Kṣatriyas— who are devoted to service— regarding the true meaning [of the teachings],
such speech is considered praiseworthy according to the circumstances.
Touching these [objects] is excellent, and ascending them is even better; having ascended these praised vehicles, as well as a palace, a boat,
and a mountain, one should resort to the vast Bhārgavī.
Having drunk wine, and having consumed the ocean, as well as curd, clarified butter, and milk;
having eaten *soma*, meat, and sacrificial oblations, a man attains the earth (*kāśyapī*).
Having obtained garments, jewels, and various ornaments, [he likewise attains the earth].
One shall obtain vehicles, land, cattle, grain, and implements; such is a slightly auspicious vision among dreams. Whatever conforms to virtuous action is all declared to be auspicious.
Therefore, something undesirable might otherwise occur; hence, a remedial action is appropriate.
Having drawn [the mandala] in sequence and worshipped the Sun there on the seventh lunar day, having satiated the twice-born and bowed to the Guru as before, one should proceed.

It should be performed according to the order of emanation for the sake of service and liberation, and not otherwise. Having worshipped the Sun, a person should then duly apply that [mantra] to all the planets and principles (tattvas) in their proper sequence.
Having meditated upon that which is pure within the pure, like the sun, one should then gradually apply it everywhere, beginning from the earth;
one should apply the entirely liberated, pure solar orb.
Having thus meditated with the mind, one should offer that [oblation] a hundred times;
in this manner, with all the mantras in sequence, the initiation (dīkṣā) is declared as both superior and inferior.
Having performed the "falling of the flower" upon that solar orb, [one should proceed].

Having tied a flower in his joined palms and empowered it with mantra, one should cast it for the sake of determining the purity of the lineage and especially for the sake of the name. Wherever that auspicious flower falls, one should designate that as his lineage.
And the name "Aditya-samyukta" was spoken by Bhānu himself;
having worshipped [the deity], one should cause [the disciple] to hear there the rules (samayas) proclaimed by Arka.
Standing facing the Sun at dawn, at evening, and at midday.
A person should always perform attendance and always offer worship;
one should not eat without having seen the Sun by day, nor the Fire by night. Having seen that which is called the Sun, one may eat, but one should never eat [without seeing it].
One should not touch the footpath, nor likewise should one avoid sitting upon it.
One must not step over the shadow of an image, nor should one ever step over lunar days (tithis),
constellations (nakṣatras), planets, astrological conjunctions (yogas), months, or the presiding deities of the months.
The solstices, the seasons, as well as the fortnights and the days,
time itself, the year, and whatever else is called time—
all that is to be saluted, revered, and indeed worshipped.
Therefore, the Sun is proclaimed as the Lord of Time, being himself Time;
he who is celebrated as the Self of all— the entire host of luminaries, both the stationary and the moving, and even the conscious and the unconscious.
"O King, you must always praise, honor, and worship him in every way.
One should abandon the reviling of the deity in thought, deed, and speech.
Having offered the remains of the floral offerings (*nirmālya*) to him, one should then present them to the horses."
Having washed both hands and feet, one should pay homage to the Sun.
Thus, this supreme initiation has been described by me to you in brief;
it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and has been explained according to its divisions.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Sun’s Initiation," in the *Sāmbopākhyāna* within the *Saptamī-kalpa* of the *Brāhma-parvan* in the glorious *Śrī-Bhaviṣya-Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the one hundred and fiftieth chapter: "The Description of the Ritual for the Worship of Āditya."
Vāsudeva said:
Hereafter I shall explain how the Sun-god is to be worshipped upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), O tiger among the Yadus; listen with a one-pointed mind.
The auspicious wheel, whose nature is Time, should be constructed with eight mandalas;
in its center is a lotus-shaped wheel endowed with twelve spokes.
In the middle of that, a lotus is prescribed, provided with eight petals.
The all-pervading, complete God Khaṣolka,
blazing with rays and armed with a thousand rays, should always be worshipped in the center;
O mighty-armed one, he is endowed with four arms and is to be invoked with the syllable Om.
A wise person should always worship the auspicious Aruṇa, the elder brother of the gods;
one should worship the goddess Nikṣubhā to the right of Bhāskara,
Revata on the right side, and Piṅgala always on the left.
O tiger among the Yadus, a wise man should always perform the ritual of *saṃjñā* for his own welfare;
O hero, he should worship the scribe in the southeast, the two Aśvins in the southwest,
and the powerful Lord Manu, son of Vivasvat, in the northwest.
In the northeast, one should worship the goddess Yamunā, the purifier of the world.
O Hero, in the second enclosure, one should worship Viyat in the east;
then the goddess in the south, and likewise Garuḍa in the west.
In the north, one should worship the auspicious Airāvata, the son of the Naga king;
likewise, one should worship Helī in the southeast, Prahelī in the southwest,
the goddess Urvaśī in the northwest, and Vinatā in the northeast.
In the third enclosure, one should worship the Guru with devotion in the east;
in the west, the son of the Sun (Saturn); likewise in the north, Dhiṣaṇa (Jupiter);
in the northeast, the son of the Moon (Mercury); and Soma (the Moon) in the southeast mandala.
One should worship Rāhu with devotion in the southern corner and in the southwest;
O Hero, the wise one should constantly worship Vikaca in the northwest.
O God, one should worship the deity Lekha with devotion in the fourth enclosure.
A person should constantly worship Śāṇḍilīputra in the southeast, Dakṣiṇādhipa in the south,
the god Virūpākṣa in the southwest, Jaleśa likewise in the west,
and Vāyuputra in the northwest.
In the northeast, the wise one should constantly worship the god Īśāna;
in the north, the wise one should worship Kubera, the king of the Yakṣas;
O twice-born ones, O hero, he should always worship [him] in the fifth enclosure.
To the east, the high-minded one [worships] the supreme goddess Mahāśvetā,
as well as Śrī, Ṛddhi, Vibhūti, Dhṛti, and likewise Unnati;
O tiger among the Yadus, he also worships Pṛthivī and Mahākīrti.
One should worship Indra, Viṣṇu, Aryaman, Bhaga, Parjanya,
as well as Vivasvat, Arka, and Tvaṣṭṛ who is radiant with rays;
and one should likewise worship Varuṇa on the sixth day— thus these sun-gods.
O best of the Yadus, the wise man should worship the head, the eyes, the armor, and the weapon on the sixth day; O hero, he should worship Aruṇa along with his chariot on the seventh.
Likewise, O tiger among the Yadus, the wise man should always worship the horses during the protective rite.
O son, one should first worship the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Gandharvas, months, fortnights, days, and likewise the year; indeed,
that man who thus constantly worships the god Bhāskara [attains his goal].
He shall go to the supreme state, having gone to which he does not grieve. (Oṃ Khaṣolkāya Namaḥ).
Here, the syllables of the root mantra are declared to be the limbs.
"Whoever worships the Sun constantly according to this rite,
especially on both the seventh lunar days (saptamī), shall go to the supreme state.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord, the Sun-god, quickly departed for his own abode.

Thus ends the one hundred and fiftieth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Worship of the Sun," in the Sāmbopākhyāna within the Saptamīkalpa of the Brāhma Parvan in the glorious *Śrībhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the one hundred and fifty-first chapter: "Description of the Duties Pertaining to the Sun."
Sūta said:
Then the highly resplendent King Śatānīka, having bowed his head with devotion to Sumantu, the best of the twice-born, spoke these words.
"Oh, how great is the majesty of the god Bhāskara of immeasurable splendor!
You have recounted it to me as the destroyer of all sins.
Therefore, O observer of noble vows, I see no deity in this world equal to the Sun."
Nor, O Brahmin, does a stable course of existence exist for him within the worlds. At the time of creation, the universe proceeds from the Sun;
during the period of maintenance, he protects it, and at the end of the kalpa, he withdraws it once again.
Having heard this majesty of the god Bhāskara of immeasurable luster,
which has been recounted by you to me as being superior to a hundred horse-sacrifices,
yet a very great doubt remains in my heart, O Brahman.
O best of Brahmins, by what means is one liberated from the ocean of worldly existence?
Through the grace of Divākara, who is indeed well-pleased and whose emblem is the bull—
by what dharma does the Lord always become satisfied?
I have heard many doctrines proclaimed in the Śrutis and Smṛtis;
likewise, the Vaiṣṇava and Śaiva doctrines, as well as those derived from the Purāṇas, have been heard by me.
O Brahmin, I am indeed desirous of hearing the incomparable doctrine of the Sun.
O Blessed One, most blessed are those who are devoted to the solar dharma.
Tell me the incomparable dharma of Bhanu, the God of gods;
for me, there is no satiety in hearing it, just as there is none in drinking nectar.
Sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha involve extensive preparations and many requisites; since they cannot be performed by twice-born men of limited wealth, therefore,
please describe an easy means that accomplishes virtue, pleasure, and wealth.
For the welfare of all mortals, [this discourse] removes the fear of all sins;
it is devoted to the dharma of the Sun, meritorious, purifying, and destructive of evil.
Having heard these words of the king, the great sage, the disciple of Vyāsa, [spoke].
Having bowed his head to Vyāsa, he spoke these words. Sumantu said:
"Listen; I shall declare a means that is easy to practice and yields great fruit."
O lord of the people, O hero, the Sun previously declared to Aruṇa that which is the supreme among all phenomena, the incomparable nature of all phenomena:
it is found neither in Kṛṣṇa, nor in Brahmā, nor in Śaṅkara.
This glorious Sauradharma has arisen for the welfare of the world, for the benefit of all living beings submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra;
it is intended for those devotees of the Sun who possess peaceful hearts and seek spiritual prosperity.

The supreme dharma is practiced by him; he belongs to the Sun, of this there is no doubt. O Bhārata, those who remember the Sun with devotion—even but once—at one time, twice, thrice, or constantly, [attain the highest goal].
They are liberated from all sins, even those committed over seven lifetimes;
those who always praise the Sun are not ordinary humans.
Having descended from the heavenly world, they should be known as suns upon this earth.
One who is not devoted to the Sun does not truly remember the Sun; one who is not devoted to the Sun cannot properly worship the Sun;
one who is not devoted to the Sun cannot praise the Sun; and one who is not devoted to the Sun cannot attain the Sun.
This unwavering devotion to Sūrya is the very essence of the Saura Dharma.
And that [observance] was proclaimed here by the Sun for the dwellers of heaven as consisting of sixteen limbs:
morning bathing, recitation, fire-offerings, likewise worship of the gods, O King,
the devout honoring of the twice-born, and the worship of the cow and the holy fig tree.

O tiger among kings, listening to the Itihāsas and Purāṇas with devotion and faith, as well as the study of the Vedas; affection for people through devotion to me, and rejoicing in my worship— these are the means.

O gods, one should personally worship with devotion the supreme reciter before me; for the book is always excellent and exceedingly dear to me. One should constantly listen to my stories, which cause transformations of voice, eyes, and limbs.
Constant remembrance of me, performed with devotion and preceded by faith—
this is the sixteen-fold devotion. Even if it exists in a barbarian,
he is a lord of Brahmins, a sage, a glorious one, of noble birth, and a scholar.
To me, the four Vedas are not distinct from my devotee, even if he be a dog-eater (śvapaca).
To him gifts should be given, from him they should be accepted, and he is to be honored just as I am.
Whoever offers me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water—
I am never lost to him, nor is he ever lost to me—
he who sees Me as all-pervading and sees everything established in Me.
I am eternally established in him, and he is eternally established in Me.
O mighty-armed one, having blocked the eighteen half-stages with eight further births, and likewise by means of the boat of knowledge,
one should quickly conquer the invincible Durgapāla, who is like the half-disk of the sun.
And having conquered the kings of cities, that man of incomparable great splendor who meditates upon me with an unwavering mind and devotion— I constantly think of that very person as my own self.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Duties of the Sun," in the Saptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan within the glorious *Śrī-Bhaviṣya-Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the one hundred and fifty-second chapter:
"Description of the Questions Regarding the Duties of the Sun."
Sumantu said:
Devotion to the Sun is difficult to attain, and the worship of the Sun is difficult to achieve;
giving gifts to the Sun is difficult, and the fire-oblation to the Sun is likewise difficult to perform.
The knowledge of Ravi is very difficult to attain, and even its practice is difficult to find.
The supreme knowledge of Khaṣolka is to be known as even more difficult to attain;
indeed, the knowledge of Bhāskara is always exceedingly rare.
With devotion, they indeed performed circumambulation at the temple of the Sun;
those two hands attained praise which performed the worship of Ravi,
and that alone is a blessed tongue which offers a hymn of praise to Ravi.
"O King, that mind has attained merit which, having abandoned sense objects,
is as steady as the play of the sun— fearless and free from anger.
Śatānīka said:

O best of the twice-born, by your grace I wish to hear in truth the procedure for the worship of the Sun; my curiosity is indeed great regarding the merit that accrues when the Sun is installed and when a temple for the Sun is constructed.
Whatever merit lies in sweeping, whatever merit in smearing [the ground],
whatever merit in preparing a place for the deity, and likewise in performing the lustration ceremony (nīrājana);
by scattering blue herbs, and with dances and auspicious musical instruments—
Whatever merit is gained by the offering of *arghya*, whatever may arise from bathing with water,
the fruit of bathing with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and bathing with curd,
and whatever is proclaimed as the fruit of the oil massage with the discus (*cakrābhyaṅga*) and bathing with the thunderbolt (*vajrasnāna*).
During the bath with honey, the bath with milk, and the bath with sugarcane juice,
one should perform the rubbing of the body in a pure place with water containing *kuśa* grass and flowers,
as well as with water containing gold and gems, and with waters scented with sandalwood.
Whatever fruit is obtained by means of clear water scented with camphor and agallochum,
one obtains that same fruit for the application of richly fragrant ointments. Furthermore,
there is the fruit of offering palm leaves and the offering of a fly-whisk.
Whatever merit comes from worshipping with red flowers, from adoration with garlands,
from hanging flower garlands in a pavilion of beautiful blossoms,
and from the specific acts of devotion in worship such as hanging garlands around the house; [all that is attained by this].
Whatever fruit is obtained through the specific offering of flowers, incense, and lamps,
as well as from the gift of garments and ornaments, from hearing and reciting the sacred texts,
and from the gift of the Veda to one who is free from physical defects, O Lord of Cows—

O best of Brahmins, by my grace, whatever fruit is obtained from the salutation and worship of the sages, as well as the fruit of worshipping Vyoma and Aruṇa, and whatever else has been mentioned through ignorance— [may all that be yours].
"O Brahmin, out of compassion for your devotees, tell me all of that.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Questions regarding the Duties of the Sun," in the Brāhma Parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the one hundred and fifty-third chapter.
Sumantu said: O high-minded son of Pāṇḍu, Sumati was also a devotee of the Sun.

Therefore, O Hero, I shall tell you everything; listen with a one-pointed mind, O King. At the beginning of the Kalpa, as Brahmā was creating various beings, there arose the Great Ego (Mahat), which thought: "There is nothing in the world superior to me."
O hero, lord of the earth, while Keśava was thus protecting and Tryambaka was thus destroying, pride arose [in them]. Then those gods and Keśava reflected upon this, O ruler of men.
Driven by mutual rivalry and hostile toward one another, O mighty-armed one,
a great dispute arose among the inhabitants of the lotus, the water, and the mountain,
each relying solely upon his own mind.
"I am the creator, I am the transformer, I am the protector, and I am the Lord of the universe"—
thus spoke the Blessed Brahmā when Kṛṣṇa and Bhīma were being worshipped.
Then Śaṅkara arrived in a rage, saying, "Who on earth is capable [of this] except for me?"
Indeed,
even Nārāyaṇa, when possessed by even a slight degree of anger,
is likewise unable to create, destroy, or protect this world in such a manner.
As they were thus speaking and becoming angry with one another,
O Lord, ignorance consisting of darkness and delusion then entered them;
with their intellects overwhelmed by that, they all could no longer see one another.
Having fallen into extreme delusion, they knew nothing here;
not seeing one another, O Lord, they sat upon the surface of the earth.
But those others who were engaged in their own activities remained established in the sun.

All were deluded by darkness, their consciousness overcome by sleep; assailed by a mere glimmer of knowledge, they were bewildered as to what they should do. Then the god, the lord of beings, shone with ornaments of cow-horn.
O Lord, his beauty enhanced by the crescent moon and purified by cool rays,
the hero fell into a state of extreme distress; deluded by darkness and unable to see, he spoke to the god Mādhava, the supporter of the earth, Hari.
Mahādeva said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, O mighty-armed one, where have you gone, O high-minded one?
And where has Brahmā gone, O hero? I do not see either of you anywhere."
I am indeed deluded by great ignorance and darkness;
what shall I do, where shall I go, and where am I situated now?
[I see] the mountains, the earth, the trees, and the gods, gandharvas, and dānavas.
"I do not see anything at all beyond the vast ocean and the rivers;
by what means might I behold the world of the moving and the stationary?
Tell me, O tiger among gods, for a great sense of shame arises within me."
Having heard the words of Śaṅkara, Hari spoke these words with a voice faltering from grief, O King, for he was deluded by darkness. Viṣṇu said:
O Bhīma, O Bhīma, I do not know where you are now;
my mind too has been deluded by this intense darkness, O Śaṅkara.
Where shall I go? Where shall I stay? How can that [darkness] come to an end?
O Supreme Lord, the entire world is indeed filled with darkness;
if this god, the eldest of the gods, born from the lotus, is seen,
let us question that high-souled one, O Hara, if it pleases you.
"Abandoning pride and egoism, and remaining solely equanimous—
[behold] the lotus-faced one, born from a lotus, whose eyes resemble lotus petals.
Such were the words spoken by Viṣṇu of immeasurable splendor.
Having heard this, the omnipresent Brahmā said to Gaṅgādharas and Mahīdharas:
"O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, O mighty-armed one! O Bhīma, Bhīma, O high-minded one!
Where are you two? Tell me; what did you two say to one another?"
My mind and intellect have fallen completely under the sway of darkness;
overcome by the delusion of sleep, I neither hear nor see.
Alas! This entire world, including gods, asuras, and humans—
"O gods, enveloped as we are by darkness, I do not know where that great light has gone.
Then, while Brahmā and the other inhabitants of heaven were thus speaking—
afflicted by pride, anger, and fear, their minds overwhelmed by darkness—
O King, for the purpose of removing their pride and for the sake of awakening the Lord of the Cows (Indra),
there emerged from him a form of splendor consisting of eight incomparable peaks—
a great void, invisible due to the darkness of sin.
O Hero, it shines with many forms, enveloped in garlands of flames;
extending for a hundred yojanas, it rises upward and whirls about like the pericarp of a lotus in the midst of its petals, O Great King.
O King, O Hero, by his splendor this entire world was illuminated,
just as the interior of a lotus is always lit by its rays.
Seeing one another, they all reacted with outbursts such as the sound "hum."
O King, this entire world was bewildered by his splendor;
O lord of men, even the great ether was bewildered by his splendor.
Then, O King, having witnessed that manifestation of power, he sat there filled with wonder.
Beholding the great radiance in the sky, they spoke these words to one another:
"O King, a brilliance has been manifested for our welfare and for the illumination of the worlds; what indeed is this that we all behold?"
Brahmā went upward toward the sky, and Tripurāntaka went downward;
the Lord of Gods, the wielder of the discus, lotus, and mace, moved across horizontally. Having failed to find his limit, all those lords of the mountains [stood there].
With eyes wide open in wonder, all the gods, beginning with Kañja, approached one another and spoke these words:
"Who is this? Of what nature is he? What is this treasury of splendors?"
"Aha! By the sight of him, we have all become possessors of knowledge.
Therefore, let us all bow down to this one of wondrous appearance and offer praise. With palms joined in reverence, all the inhabitants of heaven offered their hymns of praise.
Then, as they were offering praise, the thousand-rayed Sun,
moved by supreme compassion, revealed himself to them,
O mighty-armed one, having recognized the great devotion of Brahmā and the others.
Then they beheld in the sky the Lord of Gods, the Supreme Lord,
the sovereign of the world of Khaṣolka, blazing with a thousand rays;
he was untouched by the Kṛttikās, or rather, he was established in the month of Kārttika.
It was difficult to conquer, lacking one of the Kṛttikās,
likewise deprived of Hasta, and likewise devoid of the Seven Sages;
it was the God deprived of the year and the months, and bereft of the seven musical notes.
Having seen him who is both with parts and without parts, whose form is eternally of a single nature,
and who likewise possesses many heads, many feet,
many bellies, many arms, and many shoulders, adorned with many ornaments;

Having thus beheld the form of the Great-Souled Bhānu, the God of Gods, which possesses many faces, is unwinking, thousand-eyed, incomparable, endowed with many colors and forms, and radiant with many crowns;
With eyes wide with wonder, they praised the Sun;
then Brahmā, joining his palms in reverence, began to offer hymns of praise.
Bowing his head to the Sun, he spoke these words:
Brahmā said:
Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods, blazing with a thousand rays!
Salutations to you, the lamp of the world; salutations to you, the beloved of the corners [of the directions].
Salutations eternally to Bhāskara; salutations again and again to Khaṣolka. Salutations to Viṣṇu, to Kālacakra, to Soma, and to the one of immeasurable splendor.
Salutations to you, the five-fold time, to Indra, and to the one whose seed is wealth.
Salutations to the Lord of the World, to the one who possesses the single-wheeled chariot,
to the God who acts for the welfare of the world, to Śiva of immeasurable splendor;
salutations to the destroyer of darkness, to the one of beautiful form, to the treasury of all radiant energies.
Salutations again and again to the one who is for the sake of purpose, who can assume any form at will, who is the Dharma, and who possesses immeasurable splendor;
salutations to the one who is liberation itself, whose form is liberation, and who is the Sun; salutations to the one free from anger and greed, the cause of the stability of the worlds.

Salutations indeed to you who are auspicious, whose form is auspicious, who bestows auspiciousness, whose self is auspicious; salutations to the peaceful one, whose form is peaceful, and who is peace itself within us.
Salutations to you whose form is Brahman; repeated salutations to the Brāhmaṇa.
"O God, O Lord of the Universe, grant your grace indeed to Brahmā, who is the god Brahmā, whose form is Brahman, who is the Supreme Self,
and who is Brahman.
Having thus praised the Sun with supreme faith, O Lord, Brahmā—

The illustrious one remained silent with a joyful inner soul. After Brahmā, Rudra— the enemy of Tripura and possessor of great splendor— having bowed his head to the Sun, composed a hymn of praise for Vibhāvasu.
Mahādeva said: Victory to you, O Bhava! Victory to the unconquerable one! Victory to the Swan, the Maker of Day!
Victory to you, O Śambhu, O mighty-armed one, O mover in the sky, O supporter of the earth!
Victory to you, O lamp of the world! Victory, O Bhānu, Lord of the universe!
Victory, O Kāla! Victory, O Ananta! Victory, O auspicious-faced Saṃvatsara!
Victory, O son of Aditi and Kaśyapa, who increases the joy of Kaśyapa!
O Destroyer of Darkness, victory! O Lord of the Seven, victory! O You whose vehicle is the seven-horsed chariot, victory!
O Great Lord, victory! O Lord of Splendor, victory! O Śaṅkara, Lord of Time, victory! O Lord of Wealth and Desire, Lord of Dharma, victory! O Bestower of Bliss, Lord of Liberation, victory!
Victory to you who are the embodiment of the Vedāṅgas; salutations indeed to you who are the form of the planets!
Victory to the Truth, to the one whose nature is truth, to the one of beautiful form, and to the auspicious one!
Victory indeed to the destroyer of anger and greed, and the destroyer of desire!
Victory to Śambhu, who has the form of a speckled bird and the form of an ascetic;
victory to the All-pervading One, whose form is the universe, and who is indeed the architect of the universe! Victory, O Oṃkāra, Vaṣaṭkāra, Svāhākāra, and embodiment of Svadhā!
Salutations to the one whose form is the horse-sacrifice (Aśvamedha) and who is Agni in the form of Aryaman;
to the one who has swallowed the ocean of saṃsāra and who bestows the gateway to liberation;
O Lord, Master of the Universe, [be gracious] to me who am submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra.
"O Lord, O wonderful Master of the Cows, be my support with your hand!
Having thus praised the Sun, whose limbs were not diminished, even though he was the Supreme Lord, O Great King, Īśa ceased his recitation and bowed his head to Ravi with great effort.
Then Viṣṇu, of great splendor, with palms joined in reverence,
spoke to the Sun with devotion and full faith, O tiger among kings.
Viṣṇu said:
I bow to the Lord of the gods of gods, the imperishable creator of all beings;
to Divākara, Ravi, Bhānu, Mārtaṇḍa, Bhāskara, and Bhaga;
to Indra, Viṣṇu, Hari, Haṃsa, Arka, the Teacher of the World, the All-pervading One.

Salutation always to the three-eyed one, who possesses three syllables, three limbs, three forms, and three states; salutation again and again to the auspicious six-faced one. Salutation to the one with twenty-four feet and twelve hands.
Salutations to you, O Lord of Beings; salutations to the Lord of the Worlds.
Salutations eternally to the Lord of the Gods; salutations to the Lord of the Castes.
You are Brahmā, you are the Lord of the Universe, you are Rudra, and you are Prajāpati.
You are Soma, you are likewise Āditya, and you are indeed the syllable Oṃ;
you are Bṛhaspati, you are Budha, you are Śukra, and you are Vibhāvasu;
you are Yama, you are Varuṇa—salutations to you, O son of Kaśyapa!
By you all this world, both moving and unmoving, has been pervaded;
from you alone have arisen the gods, asuras, and humans. O Lord of the World, Brahmā, I, and Rudra have all emerged from you.
O sinless God, in the beginning of the aeon, for the sake of the stability of the world, salutations to you who are the form of the Vedas; salutations indeed to you whose form is day;
salutations to you whose form is knowledge, and repeated salutations to you as the sacrifice.
Be gracious toward us, O Lord of Gods, O Lord of Beings, radiant with rays!
O Lord of the Cow (Gopati), grant your favor to those submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra.
Eternal salutations to the Vedānta, and salutations to the essence of sacrifice.
Sumantu said: O best of the Bharatas, having thus praised the Sun with devotion, Viṣṇu,
O tiger among kings, meditated upon Ravi with his mind fixed entirely on him.
"Thus, O tiger among men, those gods led by Brahmā, O sinless one,
praise that high-souled Sun of a thousand rays. While those great-souled ones were thus praising the Sun with devotion,"
Then the Lord of the World, the all-pervading Sun of great splendor, being pleased with Brahmā and the others,
and perceiving their supreme devotion and supreme faith,
spoke with a joyful inner soul.
The lord of the planets, having ascended the sky and blazing the quarters with his splendor,
addressed Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśāna, O lord of the people;
and seeing them all prostrate with their heads touching the earth, he spoke.
"I am pleased with you, O eldest of the gods, four-faced one, Lord of the world!
Choose a boon—blessings be upon you—for whatever you desire in your mind.
Having spoken these words to Bhānu, O King, Brahmā, the teacher of the worlds, [responded].
He went down to the ground with his head bowed and spoke with palms joined in reverence.
Brahmā said:
"O Lord of Gods, I have accomplished my purpose; O Sovereign of Birds, I am purified."

I am blessed, I am favored; I have attained the supreme goal, since you, O Lord of Gods, have come into my sight like the thousand-rayed sun. And because I did not see you, O Lord of Gods, my mind remained in delusion.
O Blessed One, be gracious toward me, O Vibhāvasu!
Grant me strength and devotion to yourself, O Lord of the Cowherds,
as I lie prostrate upon the earth with my eight limbs and my head bowed.
"O Lord of the Cows, having heard this petition with devotion, grant your favor!
Having heard the words of Brahmā, the divine Pūṣan, the lord of the world,
said "So be it," O Great King Virāṭ, filled with humility.
O King, having granted a boon to Brahmā,
the divine Sun-god spoke to the three-eyed god whose crest is adorned with the moon:
"Choose a boon, O Lord of Beings, O sinless one born from the mountain!"
"O Mahādeva, I shall give you here everything that you desire.
Hearing these words of Bhāskara, Īśvara, the destroyer of Tripura,
went and prostrated with his head upon the ground and spoke to Bhāskara.
Mahādeva said:
"I am meritorious, I am a performer of meritorious deeds; there is none more blessed than I.
I have attained supreme perfection and I have reached the highest goal."
"O Lord of Gods, there is nothing unattainable for me, nor is there anything whatsoever that cannot be accomplished,
since the Blessed Lord remains inclined toward me with grace.
By you, this entire world— both the stationary and the moving— is pervaded."
"From you alone it has arisen, and into you it shall go to its dissolution.
O Lord, if you are pleased with me, and if I am worthy of your grace,
grant me unwavering devotion and lead me to your own feet."
Having heard the words of Vyomakeśa, the divine Pūṣan, the maker of day, said "So be it" to Hara, O hero; then he spoke to Hari:
"O Nārāyaṇa of mighty arms, O upholder of the earth, choose a boon."
"I am well-pleased with you, O God; choose whatever you desire, O one of great power.
Having heard the words of the Sun, Hari, the progenitor of Kīlāla, bowed his head in supreme devotion and spoke to Ravi.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Victory, O God, Lord of the World! Victory, O God, Teacher, Sun!
Be gracious to me, O Lord of Gods; grant devotion to yourself, O Sun!
O Lord of the World, grant that through devotion to you I may become the foremost of all gods,
and likewise, O God, invincible to the Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas,
my strength augmented and endowed with great splendor.
Therefore, O Lord, by your command, I must perform a great task:
the protection of subjects, O God, and of the gods, O Lord of Planets;
as well as that of the castes and stages of life, and of the duties of the castes, O All-pervading One.
"O sinless one, I was created by you in the past at the beginning of the Kalpa for the destruction of wicked Daityas and for the protection of the worlds; indeed,
there is no man with whom you might ever be angry."
Disease, physical suffering, mental anguish, poverty, the extinction of one's lineage,
and likewise various anxieties— these befall him in this world.
Therefore, O Lord, you should always be praised by the wise.
"Thus, O Lord of the Rays (Gopati), endowed with devotion and faith, I desire to worship you;
therefore, show me your grace.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Solar Splendor," in the Sauradharma section of the *Saptamī-kalpa* within the Brāhma-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the one hundred and fifty-fourth chapter,
the description of the narrative of Trayī. Sumantu said:
Having heard the words of Viṣṇu of immeasurable splendor,
O tiger among the Kurus, the Sun-god, filled with compassion, spoke.
The Sun-god said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, O mighty-armed one, hear my supreme word.
For whatever purpose you have been entreated, O Kṛṣṇa, all that shall be yours—
[even] among the gods, dānavas, yakṣas, gandharvas, uragas, and rākṣasas."
O mighty-armed one, you shall be invincible, of this there is no doubt;
you shall be capable of protecting the entire world,
and your devotion toward me shall remain unshakable.
By my grace, Brahmā shall also be perpetually capable of creating the world, and Śaṅkara likewise shall be capable of destroying it. By my grace, you all shall attain the supreme station of the wise.
"They will go [to heaven], there is no doubt, by the grace of my worship.
Having heard the words of the Sun, O Lord, Gośrutābharaṇa,
the lord of cows, spoke to the lord of cows, whose banner bears the bull.
"Having propitiated you, we shall all become the foremost of the gods.
How indeed, endowed with faith, may we propitiate you?
O God, for our ultimate welfare, tell us the truth concerning yourself."
Indeed, we do not perceive your supremely worshipful form;
we perceive only a radiance, like the water cast off by the ocean,
filled with garlands of flames, possessing many shapes, and wondrous.
Furthermore, an object of focus devoid of form cannot exist for the mind;
O Lord, without an object of focus, there is nowhere any delight for the consciousness.
When the consciousness finds no delight, devotion never arises in men.
Without devotion, the dwellers of heaven cannot be worshipped;
for it is through your worship, O Lord, that men attain dharma and the other goals of life. Therefore, reveal that form of yours which is considered supreme.
"By worshipping you, may we indeed become perfected.
The Sun said:
"Excellent, excellent, O Mahādeva! You have asked me well, O observer of noble vows."
Listen with a one-pointed mind to everything as I speak, O giver of honor!
I, the Lord, exist pervading the universe in four forms,
eternally the creator of the beginning, middle, and end, for the welfare of all worlds.
One of my royal forms is celebrated as Brahmā;
O All-pervading Lord, she constantly effects the creation of the worlds at the beginning of every kalpa.
The second is declared to be the Sāttvika form, which is proclaimed as the Supreme (Parā).
She, the destroyer of wicked Daityas, shall eternally protect the world;
she is to be known as the third [form], Tāmasī, celebrated as Īśā.
At the end of the kalpa, she who holds the trident in her hand shall indeed withdraw the three worlds.
But the fourth is unsurpassed, yet devoid of qualities such as truth and the rest;
it is impossible to perceive it anywhere, for it remains eternally as it is.
By it all this is pervaded, even that which is my destination, the Udgītha.
She is both partless and whole; she possesses beautiful form and is yet devoid of form.
She has entered within all worlds, yet she does not partake in the fruits of karma.
Though dwelling [within them], she remains unstained, like a lotus leaf by water.
She is eternally undecaying, established beyond the seven by means of the six;
she has four breasts, is called the Fourth (Turyā) beyond the six, and is highly honored. She cannot be touched by you, nor by Hari, nor even by Brahmā.
O Lord of Beings, O Three-eyed One, without having propitiated me— who am of the nature of space—
this [teaching] has appeared for your enlightenment, O God,
because you were deluded by egoism and enveloped in darkness.
And for the illumination of the worlds, it stands filled with garlands of flames like the pericarp of the entire lotus of the earth, O Lord;
by the mere sight of which, you all have been awakened.
Then the entire world became illuminated by rays of light.
Therefore, worship him who is untouched and beyond comparison;
by doing so, O Three-eyed One, you shall behold that divine form of mine.
That which was born as the first Lord is proclaimed as Vyoman (the Ether).
Indeed, at the end of the kalpa, all the deities dissolve into this Vyoman;
Brahmā dissolves on the right side, and Janārdana on his left.
O Destroyer of Tripura, you always dissolve into the hair-tuft;
Gāyatrī dissolves into his heart,
and the Vedas, along with the six auxiliary limbs and the Pada and Krama recitations, dissolve indeed into his head.
The entire world, both stationary and moving, dissolves into his belly;
indeed, from him arises once again everything, including Brahmā and all that is mobile and immobile.
They call him Ākāśa and Vyoman, and the Earth is considered Nikṣubhā.
"O Three-eyed One, I am the space that is the ultimate welfare of all beings, and Nikṣubhā is my beloved. O Trilocana, the entire world is pervaded by me and by Nikṣubhā;
therefore, you, as well as Brahmā and Keśava, should worship the void."
"O Three-eyed One, having worshipped that form of mine in the great void for a thousand divine years on Mount Gandhamādana,
you shall then attain the supreme, auspicious perfection consisting of six limbs."
Residing in Kalāpagrāma, may Janārdana, the bearer of the conch, discus, and mace, worship me with devotion in my form as space;
[and likewise] Puṣkara, the world-purifying holy site situated in the intermediate region.
"Having gone there, let Viriñca always worship my form as space.
In this way, you too, having constantly propitiated me, the Lord of the World,
with three thousand excellent divine years, [shall attain your goal] with devotion."
Then you shall behold my supreme form, which the wise know to be like a cluster of Kadamba flowers, filled with garlands of rays, and most exalted.
Then the god Nārāyaṇa, bowing his head to the Sun, [spoke].
With palms joined in reverence, he spoke these words.
Viṣṇu said:
"If you consider my supreme form to be the incomparable void (ākāśa),..."
"Having propitiated him, we shall all attain the highest perfection.
What is the nature of space? And who am I, Brahmā, and Hara, the destroyer of Tripura?
O Lord, we worship you with devotion for the sake of our own spiritual welfare."
"By worshipping that Sun-god, we shall attain success;
therefore, O most worshipful one, tell us the characteristics of the sky.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Trayī within the Saura-dharma," in the Saptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the one hundred and fifty-fifth chapter: The Description of the Duties of the Sun-worshipper.
Āditya said:
"Excellent, excellent, O best of gods! Excellent, O upholder of the earth, you have questioned me well.
Listen with a one-pointed mind, O Kṛṣṇa, as I tell you everything.
This god shall worship my form, which is incomparable."
The supreme sky is a four-cornered wonder, radiant with red chalk;
having reverently worshipped you, who are marked by the discus, Śaṅkara,
the three-eyed one, constantly [attained] Brahman at the beginning of sound and at the beginning of the ocean.
"O God, you must always worship me with devotion at midday;
indeed, let all the Ṛbhus worship me with devotion according to their desire.
Then the gods, headed by Brahmā, having heard these words of Vibhāvasu, [acted accordingly].
Bowing their heads, they all spoke these words:
"O Lord, we are all blessed and likewise have fulfilled our purpose;
we have questioned the Blessed One, who blazes with splendor."
Through the vision of you, the Knower, we have all become awakened;
thus, darkness, delusion, and lethargy have all vanished in an instant. We are all your very forms, encompassed by your splendor.

"O Eldest of the Gods, by your command all the world-protectors remain entirely established for the sake of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the worlds. Now, let us proceed here to perform the worship of the Sky."
Having thus heard their words, Bhāskara, the stealer of the waters,
spoke these words preceded by Sāman chants to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa.
Āditya said:
It is exactly so, there is no doubt, as you say, O you of excellent vows:
you are all my very forms, for I am indeed you yourselves. O gods, this vision of mine is the supreme authority.
O tigers among gods, understand the cause of this white mass, filled with garlands of flames, which has been cast off like a flash of lightning:
it belongs to those who are deluded by egoism and who quarrel with one another.
Indeed, for the sake of your awakening and for the destruction of darkness,
and for the purpose of setting all actions in motion, this has been revealed.
Therefore, having understood this, you should never harbor egoism.
O best of gods, those who desire prosperity should always act thus:
having first cast far away pride, arrogance, and egoism,
they should constantly worship me with devotion, endowed with faith.
"Then you shall behold my form, both with parts and without parts;
by the mere sight of which, you all shall attain perfection.
Having spoken thus, O Great King, the omnipresent Lord of a thousand rays—
O Bhārata, he vanished from their sight even as they were looking on.
Then all of them— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the wielder of the Pināka bow— were struck with wonder by the splendor of that god, the sun of great majesty.
Then, O King, they said to one another in amazement:
"Aha! This is the Great-Souled God, the son of Aditi, the Lord of Day;
he is the one of vast radiance, of great splendor, the lamp of the world, the source of light."
Let us all go to every single place and propitiate him by whom we have all been saved while he was destroying the vast darkness,
so that through his grace we may all attain perfection.
Having worshipped that sky with supreme faith toward the Lord,
they all took leave of one another and departed respectfully for the sake of worship;
Brahmā went to Puṣkara, and Janārdana went to Śālagrāma.
O hero, the bull-bannered god has gone to Mount Gandhamādana;
having abandoned pride and ego,
they perform supreme penance and worship that deity Bhāskara, the drawer of waters.
Having fashioned a square in the sky, Brahmā worshipped it constantly;
Hari always worshipped the sky properly as marked with discs;
and Hara too, O hero, [worshipped] that which was perpetually like fire in its splendor.
Endowed with devotion, he constantly honored Vyoman according to his conduct.
At the end of a thousand divine years, while they were worshipping the Sun-god with perfumes,
garlands, offerings, and with dances, songs, and instrumental music, [he continued his service].

Performing supreme austerity with unwavering devotion and a steady mind, they gratified the high-souled Vivasvat, the unsurpassed lord. Then, O great king, the Lord of the World was pleased with them.

The Soul of the World, the radiant one, manifested himself simultaneously in four ways through his yogic power, O sinless one; he who is the essence of Kṛṣṇa and possesses great splendor went by one form to the best of the gods and spoke these supreme words.
In one form he was thought to be Śaṅkara, in another Garuḍadhvaja,
and in yet another he always scorched the heavens while mounted upon his chariot;
thus, by the power of yoga, the Sun performed a great marvel.
O Great King, seeing the four-faced one engaged in fierce austerity and worshipping the great ether with his lotus-like faces turned toward the earth,
Bhāskara spoke to that four-faced one.
"Behold, behold, O best of gods, me, the giver of boons, who have arrived!
Upon hearing these words of Bhānu, Viriñca then looked at him;
having seen him, he prostrated himself upon the ground with his lotus-like faces.
With eyes wide open in joy, he rose again and, standing with palms joined in reverence, spoke these supreme words to the Sun.
Brahmā said:
Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods; salutations to you, the dispeller of darkness.
Salutations to you, the Lord of the past and the future, the source of all beings, the creator of all beings.
O God, show me favor; may you, the Maker of Day, be gracious to me.
"O Lord, O All-pervading One, no other refuge exists for me but you.
The Sun-god said: "It is exactly as you have said; there is no doubt in this matter."
"You were born as my first-born son long ago for a specific purpose. Choose a boon—blessings be upon you—for I stand before you as the giver of boons.
O eldest of the gods, choose whatever you desire; do not harbor any doubt, O Lord."
Brahmā said:
"O Lord of Cows, if the Blessed One is pleased with me and grants me this supreme boon, then by your grace I shall be able to perform the work of creation."
"For my creation, O Lord, whether accomplished or unaccomplished, does not succeed here.
The Sun said:
"O four-faced God, I have not attained the status of being your son."
"I shall enter into your lineage as a son to Marīci;
from him, O Four-faced One, your entire creation will attain perfection. This shall surely come to pass through my grace, O Lord of the World—of this there is no doubt."
O Lord of the Earth, having been addressed thus by Ravi, Viriñci—
having bowed his head to the Sun, the Lord of the World and Master of the Universe who was indeed naked and about to depart— spoke again to that foremost of the gods.
"O Lord of the World, O Lord of Heaven, where will my dwelling be?
Āditya said:
"That form of mine which is the great sky, with its unsurpassed back and peaks—"
There you shall dwell eternally among the hosts of gods:
Indra in the eastern quarter, the son of Śāṇḍilī in the south-eastern (Āgneyī),
Yama always in the southern, and Nirṛti in the south-western (Nairṛtī).
In the west is Varuṇa, and in the northwest is Sadāgati;
in the northern quarter of the directions dwells Dhanada;
in the northeast is the god Śaṅkara, and in the center you are together with Viṣṇu.
Having heard these words of Bhānu, the Creator spoke to him with affection;
and O lord of men, he considered himself to have accomplished his purpose and performed everything exactly as spoken by the Sun, without exception.
And that hero attained perfection through the grace of the Sun; O sinless one, the Sun-god, who is devoted to Brahman, having granted a boon to Brahmā,
departed for Mount Gandhamādana along with the Lord.
There he beheld the Lord of Beings, who had undertaken intense austerity—
the one with matted hair, the wielder of the trident, whose crest is formed by the moon and sun,
who worships the supreme ether, who is firm in his vows, and endowed with splendor.
Having worshipped the Great Space with offerings of perfumes and garlands, with dance, song, and instrumental music,
with many kinds of mouth-instruments, and with the chanting of the *praṇava* and hymns of praise,
he touched the earth with his head.
Having seen Hara thus worshipping the Destroyer of Tripura, the Sun-god of great splendor, adorned with earrings shaped like cow-ears, was pleased and said:
"O Bhīma, my child, I am pleased with you; choose indeed a boon from me."
"I have come into your presence, O giver of boons, dweller on the mountain.
Upon hearing these words of Bhānu, O lord of the earth,
Mahādeva beheld that supreme Lord of the World, blazing with light.
Bowing down and prostrating with his eight limbs upon the ground, he said:
"Salutations, salutations to you, O Lord of Gods, O Prabhākara, O Divākara!
O Abode of Auspiciousness, O Support of Auspiciousness, O Vikartana, O One of Auspicious Countenance!"
"Be gracious, O Lord of Gods; be pleased, O Maker of Light!
Be a boat for me who am submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra, O Lord of the World!
O God, I am your son, born from your own body, and I am dear to you."
"O Mahādeva, do that for your son which a father should do for his son.
Āditya said:
"It is exactly so, O Śaṅkara; there is no doubt regarding what you say."
"O best among those who possess sons, you have been born from my forehead;
choose a boon—blessings be upon you—whatever you desire in your mind.
O handsome one, destroyer of Tripura, I shall grant it to you, even if it is difficult to give."
Mahādeva said: "O Lord, if you are pleased with me, and if I am worthy of your grace, O Bhānu, grant me a boon; bestow upon me unwavering devotion."
"O Lord, just as I have conquered the hosts of gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas, and shall likewise withdraw all creatures at the end of the age,
so grant me, O All-pervading Lord, a supreme station."
"By which means, O Lord of the World, may I conquer all the gods?
Āditya said:
'The gods, Dānavas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Pannagas...'"
And at the end of the age, O Destroyer of Tripura, you shall consume the world as well.
This supreme trident, which is my own form and is eternally honored by me,
shall become your weapon.
"And likewise, in the northeastern quarter, there shall be a dwelling in the sky.
Mahādeva said:
"O God, let it be so; this favor has been granted by you to me."
"I have accomplished my purpose, O Lord of Gods, since the God has granted me this boon.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Narrative of Traisura," in the *Sauradharmnirūpaṇa* (Description of Solar Duties) within the *Saptamī-kalpa* of the *Brāhma-parvan* in the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sumantu said:
O lord of people, O king, having thus granted the boon to the Lord,
Bhānu went quickly to Śālagrāma to bestow the boon upon Hari.
There he beheld Hari performing supreme austerity;
wearing a black antelope skin, peaceful, yet blazing with his own splendor,
he was worshipping the great, incomparable, discus-shaped firmament.
Having thus worshipped that sky with perfumes, garlands, offerings, and with dance, song, and instrumental music, he, endowed with devotion and faith,
touched the ground with his head while meditating on the Sun-god within his heart.
Seeing Viṣṇu prostrate before him, the god Vibhāvasu was pleased;
addressing Viṣṇu, he said, "O Hari, behold me who have come.
Having heard those words, Keśava touched the earth with his head.

Salutations to you, Lord of all gods; salutations to you, traveler of the sky. Salutations be to you, O Lord of the world; salutations to the Lord of the planets. Salutations to you, destroyer of poverty, disease, and suffering; salutations to the annihilator of worldly existence.
O Āditya, Arka, Ravi, Bhānu, Bhaga, Pūrṇa, Divākara!
Homage to you, O knower of all principles, who are free from all sins!
Be gracious to me, O Lord of the World, O sinless Haṃsa, O Lord of Heaven!
"O God whose banner is the bull, save those submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra!
O Lord of Gods, O sinless one, I am your second son, a Brāhmaṇa.
O Sun, O Lord of the World, grant my desires just as a father grants those of his son."
Having heard the words of Viṣṇu and attained great joy, O tiger among the Kurus, Divākara spoke with a voice faltering with delight:
"Excellent, O Kṛṣṇa, O mighty-armed Keśava! I am well-pleased with you."
"O Puruṣottama, having perceived your supreme devotion and faith,
choose therefore a boon, my child, whatever you desire in your mind.
O sinless one, I have arrived as a granter of boons, overcome by your devotion."
Having heard the words of Bhānu, Viṣṇu, filled with devotion and with palms joined in reverence, spoke these words:
