"O Lord of Gods, I have accomplished my purpose; there is no one more blessed than I."
O Blessed One, since you yourself have come to me as a giver of boons, being pleased with me—
if the Lord is pleased with my devotion, and if I have purchased him,
then grant me unwavering devotion so that I may conquer the enemy.
Likewise, grant me this boon: the destruction of all enemies;
a supreme abode for me, honored by all the worlds;
and the means, strength, heroism, fame, and happiness required for the protection of the worlds.
Thus addressed with devotion by Viṣṇu, O tiger among the Kurus, Ravi spoke these excellent words, roaring as if making the earth resound:
"Excellent, excellent, O mighty-armed one! You are the youngest-born of Brahmā."
He is the elder brother of Hara and is saluted by all the gods;
he is exceedingly devoted to me and is always virtuous and devoted to Brahman.
Therefore, your devotion toward me shall be unwavering.
This very great void shall become your discus,
O hero— the best of all weapons, the destroyer of all enemies—
and likewise your supreme abode, honored by all the worlds.
Having thus obtained the boon from Bhānu, the god Hari, the Lord of the World, said, "This is a great favor," and touched the earth with his head;
Bhāskara, for his part, having granted the boon to Keśava of immeasurable luster, departed.
O great king, the lord of the gods quickly departed for his own city,
having bestowed upon Kṛṣṇa the power, strength, heroism, fame, and happiness required for the protection of the worlds, as well as whatever else was desired.

Thus, having worshipped the Sun-god, the gods beginning with Brahmā became empowered for the undertaking of creation and other cosmic functions. Thus has been told to you this meritorious narrative that destroys all sins.
This narrative concerning the three deities and the three asuras is honored by the world;
it is joined with three hymns of praise and serves as a means for achieving dharma, kāma, and artha. It is righteous, leads to heaven, is meritorious, and bestows health, wealth, and grain.
Whoever should constantly hear this, and whoever should recite these three hymns, he ascends the solar vehicle and goes to the supreme abode of the Sun.
One without a son obtains a son; one without wealth attains wealth.
A seeker of knowledge obtains knowledge through the grace of the Sun;
resembling the sun in brilliance and like a speckled stone in luster,
he rejoices for a very long time and becomes the best among the wise.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Narrative of Traisura," within the Sauradharma section of the Saptamī-kalpa, in the Brāhma-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
[Now follows] the introduction to the story of the incarnations of the Sun.
Śatānīka said:

This is my curiosity, O Brahmin: why did the Sun grant a boon to Brahmā that you would become his son in the lineage of Kaśyapa? O tiger among the twice-born, I shall go there, for I am the dispeller of the darkness of those who have sought refuge.

This is a great marvel to me; tell me how he could go to the earth—he who is the leader of the gods and others, the pervasive source of all that is born upon the earth. How can he, who is like the sky, undergo the state of birth on the surface of the world?

For what purpose will he, who alone sets in motion the delightful wheel [of sovereignty] for Brahmā and the other gods, employ his divine self for the sake of birth? O best of the wise, how did he form such a meritorious intention regarding birth?
He who performs the protection of the entire world for all people,
he who, as the Sun himself, sustains everything by means of his rays (gobhiḥ),
and he who, as the Soul of Beings, created and maintains the great elements.
How could that omnipresent Lord, who is himself without a womb, request a womb within a belly—
he by whom the fourteen worlds, O Brahmin, were pervaded by rays of light,
and by whom the three paths of the world, preeminent as the triple aggregate (trivarga), were established?
He who at the time of the end, having swallowed the world and assumed a body made of adamant,
turned the universe into a single ocean, is seen through his own karma;
he who is the ancient Self in the Purāṇas has taken on the form of all splendors.
O best of the twice-born, even after creating [the world], he who created the earth and who,
immutable, fashioned these three worlds in ancient times—
that best of gods, having prepared it, gave the earth to the deities.
He who, remaining steady, has drunk fire for a year; he who, situated in Pātāla, [drank] the excellent liquor and the oblation consisting of the middle waters;
[he who beheld] the thousand-headed god with a thousand eyes in thousands of ways.
They say that in age after age, Brahman is the thousand-footed one;
from whose mouth the Creator, the Grandfather of the worlds, was born,
and from whose chest Hari arose, and from whose forehead Śaṅkara.
By him those Daityas known by the name Mandehas were slain—
he who is unassailable even by Brahmā and the other gods, and who is the eternal destroyer of obstacles;
having fashioned a body composed of all the gods and bearing all weapons.
Mounted upon a chariot with a single wheel, having the elder brother of Garuḍa as his charioteer,
he who holds the entire world— including the Dānavas and Rākṣasas— in the palm of his hand;
O twice-born one, whose body is eternally luminous and untouched by darkness.
He who, having gone to the eastern direction, constantly ascends the mountain of sunrise,
perpetually destroys the darkness of the world for its peace;
and having destroyed that darkness, he sets all activities in motion.
Having consecrated the sacrificial girdles, the southern fire, the pestle and mortar,
as well as the Āhavanīya fire, the altar, the *kuśa* grass, and the offering-ladle, according to the procedure for the Gārhapatya fire and likewise by means of the ritual act of maintaining it.
He likewise performed the *prokṣaṇīya* vow and the *avabhṛtha* bath;
he was the one who, at the beginning of the sacrifice, presented all these gods as recipients of the sacrificial oblations (*havya*),
and offered the oblations to the gods who consume them (*havyād*) and to the ancestors who consume the ancestral offerings (*kavya*).
For the sake of his share, he fashioned Madhudhāna for the performance of the sacrifice,
as well as Pūṣan, the pressed Soma, the strainer, and the fire-drill;
he also fashioned the sacrificial implements, the sacrifices themselves, and the officiating priests.

In ancient times, he who acted in accordance with the age, having fashioned the worlds in successive order, distributed everything— including the members of the assembly, the sacrificers, and the most eminent sages— through his supreme, sovereign ritual action.
Moments, minutes, and hours, as well as the deficiency of time;
muhūrtas, lunar days, months, fortnights, and likewise years;
the seasons and the conjunctions of time—the various measures [of duration] among men.
He who ordained the lifespans, the fields, and their respective decreases and increases;
by whom, through the path of knowledge, the three infinite worlds were created;
and by that Soul of all beings, the hosts of all creatures were eternally brought forth.
He who delights in the yoga preceded by the three prostrations,
who is the protector using the boat of going and returning— he is the Lord of the World.
He is the refuge for those joined with virtue, and he is the refuge for those whose actions are free from evil.
The power of the four castes is the body that protects the Hotṛ priest;
he who knows the science of elements and medicine, who takes refuge in the four stages of life, who is experienced as the sky-clad (Digambara), is Vāyu, the manifestor of the wind.
The Lord of Yogis, the destroyer of night, is the light whose essence is Agni and Soma;
he who is heard of as the supreme light, he who is heard of as the supreme austerity,
whom they call the supreme, the highest, the imperishable Supreme Self.

The Lord who is praised by Brahmā and the others, the all-pervading one who brings an end to the Daityas; he who is without pain at the ends of the ages, and who is the supreme destroyer of the worlds;
he who is the bridge among all bridges of the world, and who stands in the midst of all intermediate actions.
He who is the knower among the knowers of the Vedas, the lord of the powerful;
he who has become the moon among gentle beings, and has become fire among those with the luster of fire;
he who has become the mind among human beings, and has become asceticism among the ascetics.
He is the discipline for those who follow the path of right conduct, the splendor even of the splendid;
he is the disputation of disputants and the goal of those who possess a goal.
He is the wind born from space, the wind that is life-breath, and the fire that is the sacrificial oblation.
He is the extinguisher of the fire of life that is intent on offering oblations to the gods;
for from essence (rasa) blood arises, from blood flesh is said to be born,
from flesh the marrow and fat are produced, and from the birth of the marrow, bones arise.
From the marrow, semen indeed came into being; one should designate that as the primary [element].
From semen, the embryo was produced through action rooted in essence (rasa).
Therein, water is the first constituent; that is called the lunar mass (saumyo rāśiḥ).
From that, the second aggregate is said to be known as the earth-born (kṣmāsaṃbhava).
One should know semen to be of the nature of the moon; that which consists of the self is the form of the self.
Among these, existence (bhava) is of the nature of fluid (rasa), and their potency is like the moon and fire.
Semen arises from the category of *kapha*, and blood from the category of *pitta*.
The seat of *kapha* is the earth element, while *pitta* is established in the navel.
The middle of the heart is known as the seat of the deity, the mind.
Within the interior of the navel-cavity resides the deity Divākara (the Sun);
the mind is to be known as Prajāpati, and phlegm is perceived as Soma;
bile is remembered as Agni, for the world consists of the nature of Agni and Soma.
When the embryo has thus begun to develop and has grown to resemble a cloud,
the wind, united with the Supreme Self, enters it;
then, circulating it, it emits and sustains the limbs.
Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna—
prāṇa is its first station, and it circulates while increasing [it]. Apāna is in the posterior part of the body, and udāna moves upward within the body.
Then the pervasive *vyāna* [vital air] remains in the body, and the *samāna* returns;
thereafter, his attainment of the elements occurs within the range of the senses:
earth, wind, space, water, and light as the fifth.
His sense organs, being ground down, each proceeded toward its own corresponding element:
they called the body "earthen" (pārthiva) and the vital breath (prāṇa) "of the nature of wind" (māruta).
For sleep has space as its source and functions within that which rests in water.
Light is his eye; his birth is from that [eye], and he is remembered as the portion of Tamas.
The villages and the sense-objects are the power (vīrya) set forth by him.
Thus, he creates the worlds together with the gods, asuras, and humans.
"How will that radiant Lord of the Gods enter a womb, just as he himself entered the womb of Aditi in the past?
O Brahmin, this is my doubt; it is a great wonder to me."
"O best of the twice-born, how did Ravi enter the state of being in the womb?
I ask you about this supreme wonder concerning the Sun;
the wondrous origin of Bhānu revolves within my heart."

"O great sage, relate this wonderful narrative; tell us of the strength and valor of the Sun of immeasurable splendor. Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Introduction to the Story of the Sun’s Incarnation," within the Sauradharma section of the Saptamī-kalpa, in the Brāhma-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Regarding the description of the origin of the Sun among the solar duties, Sumantu said:
"O dear one, you have posed a great burden of questions concerning the One Adorned with Rays."

I shall speak according to my ability; let the solar glory be heard, since your mind has been inclined toward hearing the power of the Sun. Indeed, listen now to the divine account of the Sun's activity as it is narrated by me.
To that Lord who has a thousand faces, a thousand eyes, and a thousand rays;
who has a thousand heads, a thousand arms, and is imperishable;
who has a thousand tongues, is radiant, and wears a thousand crowns.
He is the giver of thousands, the enemy of thousands, the thousand-armed, and the imperishable; he is the sacrifice, the place of sacrifice, the oblation, and the priest;
he has transcended the sacrificial vessels, the Vedic initiation, and the auspicious *caru* offering.
A Vedic scholar, a winnowing basket and pestle, the sprinkling water, the southern solstice, the Adhvaryu priest, a Sāma-singing Brahmin, the Sadasya, the sacrificial hall,
as well as the sacrificial post, fuel, the dipping-spoon, the ladle, and the pestle and mortar.
The sacrificial hall, Jayabhūti, the Hotṛ priest, and the piling of the fire-altar;
the secret doctrines, the authoritative measures, the stationary and moving beings, as well as the established firmness, the sacrificial mounds, and the Kuśa grass.
He who carries the mantras and sacrifices, the portion of fire, and indeed the descendant of Bhṛgu;
he who is proclaimed as the foremost among those who consume the Soma in the three worlds—
the eternal, all-pervading Lord, the knowers of Āyurveda worship him.
O hero, they say that thousands of existences of that Bhānu, the lord of gods who wears a garland of sandalwood,
have passed away many times;
furthermore, they will come into being again and perish day after day.
O Great King, as you ask for this meritorious, divine, and auspicious narrative—
concerning the purpose for which the Blessed Sun became the son of Kaśyapa—
I shall relate it to you; listen to it all in its entirety.
For the benefit of all mortals and for the prosperity of the worlds,
the Self of all beings manifests himself many times;
thus was the Lord born as the son of Kaśyapa and Aditi.
O hero, O Bhārata, being pleased, he granted a boon to the high-souled Virañci:
"Whichever son Aditi may bear from the lord Kaśyapa,
each one shall indeed meet his destruction at that very moment."
Seeing her sons perishing, Aditi, overcome with grief for her children,
approached Kaśyapa with eyes agitated by sorrow;
she beheld that son of Marīci, the radiant sage who was a treasure-house of asceticism.
The first was a divine brahmin, the preceptor of the gods,
who resembled fire in his splendor and possessed the brilliance of a wolf;
he was endowed with the glory of one who has laid down the staff of worldly life, and wore a black antelope skin as his garment.
Clad in bark garments and deerskins, blazing with the splendor of sacred knowledge,
he was like a flaming fire or like the scorching sun. Then Aditi, upon seeing her husband of immeasurable luster in this state, [was filled with joy].
With a voice faltering from grief, he spoke these words:
"For what reason does the divine Lord remain inactive?
For every son born to me perishes immediately."
Having heard her words, Kaśyapa, the best of sages,
O Lord, set his mind on departing for the world of Brahmā.
Having gone to the abode of Brahmā, which was endowed with various wonders, he—
Having heard all those words spoken by his wife,
as well as the speech of Kaśyapa, the lotus-born Brahmā spoke these words:
"O son, let us go to the abode of the Sun, which is exceedingly difficult to attain."
Having spoken thus, the lotus-eyed Creator ascended the fiery vehicle and went to the abode of the high-souled Āditya;
Aditi, Kaśyapa, and Brahmā followed, taking refuge in that vast [splendor].
In a mere moment, O descendant of Kuru, they reached the brilliantly radiant world of the Sun by means of celestial vehicles that travel according to one's desire; there,
they desired to question Āditya, the supreme mass of splendors, as was fitting for each.
And as they went, they reached the vast, supreme assembly hall of Āditya,

which resounded with the humming of bees and was filled with the auspicious voices of those who had attained fortune; there, the sacrificial rites, headed by the Ṛgveda, were being proclaimed with holy syllables.
They praised that tiger among men during the performance of the extensive rites; likewise,
at the junction of the sacrifice, all there was made to resound with the chanting of the supreme sages— those who know the Vedas as well as the *pada* and *krama* recitations.
By twice-born ones who were experts in the praise of sacrifice and likewise in the rules of phonetics,
who knew the eighteen Purāṇas and were proficient in all branches of knowledge, who understood the Mīmāṃsā and the logic of reasoning, and were skilled in all philosophical doctrines.

The leaders of the Lokāyatikas praised the Sun as he was invoked; and here and there, Kaśyapa and the others beheld the best of Brahmins, who were self-restrained, firm in their vows, and devoted to the practice of recitation and burnt offerings.
In that assembly sat the sun-god, garlanded with rays;
the glorious preceptor of gods and asuras shone there through his power, O hero,
while the lords of creatures waited upon the Lord right there.
Dakṣa, Pracetas, Pulaha, and Marīci, the best of the twice-born;
Bhṛgu, Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Gautama, and likewise Nārada;
as well as the heavens, the self, the intermediate space, wind, fire, strength, and earth.
Sound, touch, form, as well as taste and smell; the primary nature (prakṛti) and its transformations (vikāras), and whatever other great cause there may be;
likewise, O Lord of the World, the four Vedas with all their limbs and sub-limbs.

The lunar days (tithis), the seasons, as well as the mental resolves (saṃkalpas) and the sacred syllable Om (praṇava)— these and many others worship the Sun. Furthermore, material prosperity (artha), righteousness (dharma), desire (kāma), and liberation (mokṣa) especially worship him.
Dveṣa, Harṣa, Moha, Matsara, and Māna;
Vṛka, the son of Viṣṇu, Puṣpaja, and Dhiṣaṇa;
likewise Māheśvara, Saurya, Viṭapa, and Vikaca.
Māruta, Viśvakarman, and the two Aśvins, whose vehicle is the wind—
having been thus addressed with these excellent words by the powerful Bhānu,
O hero, Kaśyapa went to his own hermitage together with the Ādityas.
Aditi, the mother of the gods, herself deposited that embryo—
the great-souled one who is the self of all beings— for a thousand divine years.
When the thousand years were complete, that supreme embryo began to move.
The god who is the refuge of the gods and the destroyer of the asuras likewise protected his son while he was still in the womb;
indeed, O lord of men, he took away the splendors of the three worlds.
When that Lord of Gods was born— bringing happiness to the three worlds,
striking down the hosts of Daityas, and increasing the roar of the gods—
supreme bliss arose among all who stood there.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Origin of the Sun," within the Sauradharma section of the Saptamī-kalpa, in the Brāhma-parvan of the glorious *Śrībhaviṣyamahāpurāṇa*.
Sumantu said: [Now follows] the description of the incarnations of the Sun.
Dakṣa, the lord of progeny, indeed offered his salutation;
shining with a radiant body and adorned with all ornaments,
he approached the Lord of Gods, Bhānu, together with hosts of sages.
Then, O lord of the earth, while the leaders of the Gandharvas sounded forth in the sky and many Gandharvas sang together,
those gods and Gandharvas thus approached with devotion.
He was born as the twelvefold Bhāskara, the maker of light who draws up the waters:
Indra, Vivasvat, Pūṣan, Tvaṣṭṛ, Savitṛ,
Bharga, Aṃśumat, Aryaman, Arka, Pṛśni, and Mārtaṇḍa.
Thus these are indeed eleven; the twelfth is said to be Viṣṇu.
When he had thus manifested in twelve forms, most wonderful and radiant, all the deities praised him and swiftly departed to the earth.
Mṛgavyādha, Śarva, Mṛgāṅka, the highly illustrious Aṅka,
Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Pati, Kāca, Paraṃtapa,
Damana, Īśvara, and Kapālī, O lord of the people.
Sthāṇu, Bhaga, and the blessed Rudras stood there;
the two Aśvins, the eight Vasus, and the mighty Garuḍa,
as well as the Viśvedevas and the Sādhyas, stood with palms joined in reverence, O King.
The Naga king Vāsuki, O Great King, stood with palms joined in reverence;
so too did many other Nagas and mighty Rākṣasas,
as well as Tārkṣya, Ariṣṭanemi, and the exceedingly powerful Garuḍa.
Aruṇa and Aruṇi stood there with palms joined in reverence;
and the blessed Grandfather himself, the creator of the worlds, having arrived in person,
spoke to the illustrious preceptor of the gods along with all the deities and great sages.
"Since the eternal and powerful one gazes upon everything,
let him therefore become the illustrious Vivasvat, the Lord of the World,
for the sake of the gods, dānavas, yakṣas, gandharvas, uragas, and rākṣasas."
"Since he is the primordial god, he is indeed Āditya himself.
Having spoken thus, the Lord, the Master, together with the celestial sages,
paid homage and performed a thorough worship, and then departed toward his abode.
That destination which belongs to those whose nature is sacrifice, that destination which belongs to those of meritorious deeds,
that destination which belongs to those perfected in yoga, and that destination which belongs to the high-souled ones—
[he attained] that state in which the eightfold sovereignty arose for him, O best of gods.
Having attained which, O Brahmins, they do not return to the ocean of existence;
which the Vālakhilyas and others, who dwell in all stages of life,
serve with self-restraint, having undertaken vows difficult to perform.
He who is like Ananta among the Nāgas, for whom all those yogins—
Śeṣa and the other supreme ones— are but a thousand heads;
he who is worshipped as Yajña by the best of Brahmins seeking well-being.

And Kaśyapa, having obtained that most excellent son who is the twelve-fold self, whom all those who have restrained their vital breaths meditate upon as the embodiment of Brahman, whom the knowers of the Vedas sing as the knower of the sacrifice and the giver of the sacrificial fee— him [he obtained].
O Lord, he obtained youth along with the Ādityas and supreme happiness;
all the worlds rejoiced, while the Rākṣasas fell into fear.
Madhupiṅgala, the mighty-armed one with a neck like a conch shell, appeared as if smiling.
Wearing a crown bound with *iṅgudī* wood and as if setting the quarters of the sky ablaze,
that one of great splendor said to Kaśyapa, the best of sages:
"I am here, having entered into the state of being your son for the sake of the perfection of the fetus."
"O Brahmin, having formerly granted a boon to the high-souled Virañci, [I said]:
'Therefore, O tiger among sages, perform a peerless act of creation.
Having thus propitiated the Lord of Gods, Brahmā obtained the power of creation."
Having propitiated the Sun, Kaśyapa also obtained a son.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Incarnation of Sūrya," in the *Ubhayasaptamī-mahātmya* within the *Saptamī-kalpa* of the *Brāhma-parvan* in the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Description of the Incarnation of Sūrya.
Śatānīka said:
"Oh, how wonderful is the conduct of the divine Bhāskara that you have described—
He whom even Brahmā and the other gods constantly worship according to the prescribed rites!"
O Brahman, having propitiated that Sun-god, Brahmā, Viṣṇu,
and the gods beheld his form, which was most wonderful. Sumantu said:
O tiger among the Kurus, having propitiated the Lord Īśāna, Bhāskara, Sūti, and Vācaka, as well as Kavi and Viṣṇu, those two went to the Himālaya mountain,
O hero, being greatly delighted at the sight of the All-pervading One near the Lord of the Cows (Śiva).
O King, like heroes, both the lotus-born Brahmā and Acyuta Viṣṇu beheld that high-souled one, who resembled a jasmine flower or the moon, who wore the crescent moon as his crest-jewel,
and who was worshipping the sun-god Vivasvat.
The two great-souled ones, Kavi and Viṣṇu, praised that three-eyed Lord.
"O Bhīma, O best of gods, behold us; we have arrived here.
Having heard the words of the lotus-born Brahmā and Acyuta, he spoke.
Having prostrated with his head upon the ground and performed worship according to the prescribed rite,
he spoke sweet words endowed with the syllables of instruction,
making the quarters of the sky resound as if with a voice faltering with joy.
"O gods, tell me everything: having propitiated whom have you obtained the all-pervading Ravi, the best of all deities? I am filled with supreme curiosity.
Have you seen any other supreme form of the god Śaṅkara?"
O hero, having heard the words of the high-souled Śaṅkara— the imperishable, immeasurable Sun of infinite splendor—
those two great-souled ones, Kavi and Viṣṇu, the best of gods, spoke.
We do not see that form which is supreme and most wonderful; indeed, we have come into his presence solely to propitiate him.
Therefore, let us together propitiate the Fire-god.
O hero, O mighty-armed one, having heard the words of the lotus-born Brahmā and Acyuta, Hara went to the sacred Udayagiri mountain, which blazes with gold;
and with eyes wide open from joy, he said, "So be it."
Then, O tiger among kings, those men whose minds were free from worldly attachment, O monarch,
quickly went to that best of mountains, the Udayācala.
Having reached that holy mountain adorned with three peaks, they arrived there.
With their limbs bound by various minerals and adorned with various minerals,
they exerted themselves according to the prescribed rites for the propitiation of Vibhāvasu; praising, worshipping, and meditating upon Vibhāvasu.
At the end of a thousand divine years, they remained performing austerities on the mountain.
Brahmā sat in the lotus posture meditating upon the Sun,
while the Three-eyed Lord stood upon the ground like a pillar with his arms raised upward.
Practicing the five-fire penance, Viṣṇu remained standing with his head downwards;
thus, at the end of a thousand years, they performed most severe austerities,
worshipping Gopati Putramālin according to the prescribed rites.
Then, while Brahmā, Śiva, and Viṣṇu were performing supreme austerity,
the Lord Bhānu was pleased and said, O King:
"O Brahmā, Śambhu, and Hari, tell me what you desire from me."
"I am pleased with you; I have come here myself to grant you a boon.
Sumantu said:
Having heard these words of the Sun—calm, heart-pleasing, and delightful—
Bowing their heads with their hair, they spoke these words:
"O Lord of the Cowherds, by your grace we have all achieved our purpose;
having propitiated you in the past, O God, we obtained from you an auspicious boon."

O Divākara, by your grace we are all indeed capable, when united here, of bringing about the creation, maintenance, and destruction [of the world]; of this there is no doubt. However, O Lord of the gods, O All-pervading One, we desire one boon.

O Lord of the World, O Acyuta, show us that supreme form of yours which is so difficult to attain and difficult to behold; show that form of yours which consists of all the gods, as was previously described by you, O Sinless One.
Having heard those words spoken by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa,
he revealed that wondrous form honored by the worlds—
a form with many faces and heads, and many marvelous sights.
It is divine, consisting of all the gods, and likewise consists of all the worlds;
the earth is its feet and the sky its head, while fire is considered its two eyes;
the piśācas are its toes and the guhyakas its fingers.
The hosts of all the gods, the most excellent of deities, are remembered as his thighs;
the Yakṣas are merged within his flanks, and the throngs of Apsarases are his hair.
His wide-open eyes are known as the rays of the heroes, and his hair is said to be the rays of the sun.
The stars were his body hairs, O great sages, and his hair;
his arms were the intermediate directions and his ears the cardinal directions, O lord of men;
the two Aśvins were his sense of hearing, and the mighty Vāyu was his nose.
His grace was forbearance, and his mind was likewise righteousness;
his speech became truth, and his tongue was the goddess Sarasvatī.
His neck was the great goddess Aditi, and his palate was the powerful Rudra.
The gateway to heaven was indeed his navel; Mitra and Tvaṣṭṛ were his belly.
Vaiśvānara was his mouth, and Bhaga was then his testicles. The Lord Brahmā was his heart, and the sage Kaśyapa was his stomach.
On his back dwell the Vasu deities, and the Maruts in all his joints;
all the Vedic meters are in his teeth, and the pure lights are his radiance.
Rudra Mahādeva is his vital breath, and the great oceans are in his belly.
In his belly are the Gandharvas and the mighty serpents;
Lakṣmī, Medhā, Dhṛti, Kānti, and all the sciences are indeed in his waist.
The forehead of this Supreme Self is the supreme abode of youth.
Know that all the luminaries and the wheel of austerity belong to the King of Gods;
for this, they say, is within the body of the Great-Souled Primordial God.
The Vedas are his two breasts and his two sides, and the sacrifices are remembered as his testicles.
O King,
having beheld the form of the Sun, which embodies all the gods, the twice-born who were performing animal sacrifices and those engaged in Vedic rites,
as well as Brahmā, Hara, Hari, and the other deities, were struck with supreme wonder.
Bowing their heads to the god and trembling, they fell to the ground and spoke these words with voices faltering from fear:
"O God, having beheld your terrible form, filled with blazing flames..."
We are terrified by this form with its many faces, arms, thighs, and feet;
our sense of direction has been lost. Be gracious, O Lord of the Universe!
Withdraw [this form], O Soul of the Universe, for we are not able to behold it.
Having heard these words of theirs, the Lord of Gods, the Sun,
the Blessed One, being pleased, spoke these words to them while smiling:
Āditya said:
O sinless ones, this supreme merit, wonderful and a source of blessing for the world—
which you have beheld, O lords of the gods, as my own self pervading the entire universe—
has been revealed by me, being well-pleased, for your welfare.
The Great Abode (Mahālaya) which was shown here by the honored yogi has been revealed.
Brahmā, Īśa, and Acyuta said:
"It is exactly so, there is no doubt, just as you have spoken, O Lord of Heaven."
O Lord of Gods, even for yogins, a vision of him is indeed difficult to obtain.
Having propitiated you, the Lord of the World, there is nothing unattainable here;
therefore, no one else among the gods is found to be more worthy of worship in this world.
Having spoken thus, the Sun, the son of Aditi, vanished from sight;
and Brahmā and the other gods also attained great joy from the vision of the Lord.
Thus, having worshipped the Maker of Day, the gods led by Brahmā [departed].
"Those Gandharvas and Ṛṣis have likewise attained supreme perfection.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixtieth chapter, titled "Description of the Vision of the Sun’s Form by Brahmā and Others," within the Saura-dharmas of the Saptamī-kalpa in the Brāhma-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
[This is followed by] the "Description of the Question Regarding the Fruit of Sun-Worship."
Śatānīka said:
"It is exactly as you have said; Bhāskara is the supreme deity.
There is no god equal to Āditya, and there is no destiny equal to Āditya."

The entire three worlds have the Sun as their root; of this there is no doubt. From him arises the whole universe, including gods, asuras, and humans—O best of brahmins, including Rudra, Indra, Upendra, and the lords of the dwellers of heaven.
Splendor is the entirety of those who possess splendor, and radiance is that which belongs to all the worlds.
Mahādeva, the Lord of All, the Sovereign of All Worlds, and the Progenitor of Creatures,
is indeed the Sun— the root and supreme deity of the three worlds.
From that everything is born, and into that very same place it dissolves.
Indeed, existence and non-existence for the world emerged of old from the Sun.
O Brahmin, the Sun is the blazing planet, the eldest in the universe, and the source of all.
There they go to their destruction and are born again and again;
passing through moments, muhūrtas, days, nights, and entire fortnights,
as well as months, years, seasons, and the ages (yugas).
He is indeed Time, he is Fire, the twelve-fold Prajāpati;
O best of Brahmins, he illuminates the three worlds with all their moving and unmoving beings.
Therefore, O foremost of the twice-born, whatever fruit may arise from his worship—
"Tell me that with diligence; be inclined toward showing me favor.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Inquiry Regarding the Fruit of Sun-Worship," in the *Sauradharma* section of the *Brāhma-parvan* within the *Saptamī-kalpa* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*. [This concludes] the description of the *Sauradharma*.
Sumantu said:
O hero, by installing the omnipresent Bhānu, who embodies all the gods,
a man attains immortality, becoming equal to the sun in splendor.
The man who, out of delusion, hates the Sun who is saluted by all the gods,
shall go to hell— even from merely conversing with him.
Having installed the beloved Sun according to the prescribed rites and with every effort, [one should worship Him].
Listen with a one-pointed mind to the fruit of merit that he obtains:
whatever fruit is found in all sacrifices, austerities, gifts, sacred fords, and deities—
a man shall obtain that fruit multiplied ten millionfold by installing the Sun-god.
O lord of men, the man who installs the image of Bhānu with devotion according to the prescribed rites shall obtain ten million times the merit of all the limbs of that rite. Furthermore,
he redeems those born of his mother and those born of his father, as well as the wife whom he marries.
Having uplifted his three lineages, he is glorified in the world of Śakra;
having enjoyed vast pleasures, when the dissolution of the universe has arrived,
he attains the yoga of knowledge and is liberated right there.
Alternatively, if he should desire sovereignty, it shall arise for him in another birth;
he shall become the lord of the earth with its seven islands and oceans.
Having performed that [rite], he shall worship all the gods as kings in the sky.
By that act, the entire three worlds, along with their roots, become worshipped.
In this very life he becomes wealthy and illustrious, and at the end he attains the state of the Sun.
Having fashioned an earthen image, one should recite [the mantra] in the sky during the three junctions of the day.
Listen now to the fruit of his merit up to eleven hundred [times]:
he remains on earth in this very body as the Sun,
destroying the sins of all mortals through both sight and touch.
Having established it, he shall uplift twenty-one generations of his lineage;
accompanied by the gods, he rejoices eternally in heaven like the Sun.
Even one who [offers] a sky made of flour, adorned with every fragrance—
O King, it was adorned with highly fragrant flowers and various fruits, as well as foods to be chewed, licked, and tasted, along with prepared lamps;
it was endowed with manifold flavors and possessed diverse fragrances.
The wise one should place agallochum on its right side;
he should indeed offer auspicious śrīkhaṇḍa sandalwood on the western part;
he should offer sandalwood on the north and red [sandalwood] on the east.
Having thus performed the extensive display of wealth according to one's means,
one should offer it to the Sun on the seventh day of the dark fortnight;
O best of the Bharatas, he who performs this even once attains the celestial realm.
Listen as I declare what fruit shall indeed accrue from that:
liberated from all sins and freed from all sufferings,
becoming partless and omnipresent, one shall enter the supreme, imperishable state.
Resplendent with brilliance like the sun and possessing a radiance equal to the sun,
he who, while playing in the dust, makes the sky appear darkened— O King, he shall become a king over all the mountains.
Of all vessels indeed, the supreme vessel is fire;
for it delivers one from the ocean of hell most effectively. One should declare the greatness of that vessel to be certain and inexhaustible.
Therefore, those who desire immeasurable fruit should always give to him; whatever is offered to the Sun— whether as a burnt oblation, recitation, a sacrificial offering, or worship—
is declared by the foremost of the gods, beginning with Brahmā, to yield infinite results.
He who builds a temple for the Sun with devotion according to his means shall ascend a celestial vehicle of fire and rejoice together with the Sun;
whereas he who, despite possessing great wealth, builds one devoid of devotion, [shall suffer].
Whether the rite be small or great, the fruit is equal for both the wealthy and the poor. That man who, though possessing wealth, performs it with stinginess regarding his resources—
his mind overcome by greed— he does not obtain the fruit.
Therefore, one should set aside one-third of one's wealth for the purpose of livelihood,
and two parts for the sake of dharma, because life is transient. Even a man of meager means should perform his duties, impelled by devotion.
Even one who possesses the essence of great wealth would not [attain merit] if he is devoid of devotion.
Even if one were to give away all his possessions to the Sun while being bereft of devotion, he would not partake in the fruit of dharma; in this matter, devotion alone is the cause.
O King, neither through fierce austerities nor through all the great sacrifices does one go to that single divine city; rather, he who, endowed with devotion to the Sun,
constructs a beautiful temple for Ravi made of auspicious stone, shall attain it.
Accompanied by seven times three generations of his lineage, he shall attain the world of the Sun.

O Daughter of the Mountain, the wise know that the merit earned through the desire for a specific rite performed with me as the object— even if multiplied ten million times— is surpassed by this [merit], which is increased by two parārdhas.
The merit of the wealthy and the poor should be known as equal to that of [a temple made of] clay or stone.
Wherever one may go, one should perform meritorious acts with devotion;
[the shrine] should be made of stone, bricks, or be firm and auspiciously constructed of wood.

He who, adorned with ornaments, should construct a temple for the Sun while playing even in his childhood, shall ascend a vehicle made of red chalk and go to the supreme abode of the Sun of immeasurable splendor.
Seated upon an excellent celestial chariot, he attains the world of Arka—
a divine realm filled with flower garlands, perfumed with the scent of incense and other fragrances,
crowded with hosts of Apsarases, and bestowing the fulfillment of all desires.
Having resided there, O Great King, for an excellent year in the city of Bhāskara while being honored by the deities,
he who is established therein eventually returns to this world and becomes a righteous king.
O lord of men, one who is endowed with virtue, wealth, and pleasure, and possessed of fame,
should sweep while observing living beings and avoiding them with a soft, fine broom;
by sweeping slowly in this manner, he shall obtain the fruit of the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
One should perform worship for the sake of obtaining a son— especially for a barren woman whose body is worn out—
and for the sake of health for beings afflicted by disease;
taking pure cow dung that has fallen in an auspicious place.
Having repeatedly discarded [the old] and applied fresh, living-creature-free cow-dung purified by a cloth as a plastering agent,
he who beholds happy living beings shall obtain the merit of a hundred Cāndrāyaṇa fasts.
He who performs all his duties with water filtered through a cloth is a sage, he is a great saint, and he shall go to the supreme goal.
All gifts, sacrifices, fire-offerings, and ritual oblations eventually perish.

The imperishable syllable is indeed a great gift that bestows happiness upon all embodied beings. He who performs its sweeping and worship continuously for a fortnight is honored in the world of the gods for one hundred divine years.
And at its conclusion, there arises a righteous king, the first of his kind, endowed with all virtues, beautiful in form and pleasing to behold, who possesses the four Vedas;
even by mere contact with him, a man may perform deeds that lead to the abode of the Blessed One.
He too, having gone to the city of Saumanasa, sports there eternally;
meanwhile, all embodied beings wander in saṃsāra, overwhelmed by suffering and grief,
as long as they do not worship the Sun with devotion.

If the Sun were not Your Majesty, who could release the mind of a living being— so deeply attached to the realm of sense objects— from its bondage? He who can make the ground as smooth as the surface of a mirror.
Variegated with diverse colors and radiant with various flowers,
in some places arranged with water-jars and adorned with lotuses—
delightful, enchanting, and serene— it stood in the assembly of the Sun’s abode.
As many thousands of yugas as there are *daṇḍas* of land that are beautifully adorned on all sides, for so long is one honored in the world of the gods;
one should have paintings executed in the temple of the Sun by those skilled in the science of painting.
Having mounted a variegated vehicle, he shall go to the abode of Citrabhānu;
for as many thousands of yugas as he causes divine forms and planetary forms to be painted, for that long he is glorified in the heavenly world.
If one should construct a temple to the Sun on level ground,
as well as groves, dwellings, and so forth, he shall obtain a priceless reward.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Duties of the Sun," in the Sauradharma section of the Brāhma Parvan within the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Description of Flower Worship among the Duties of the Sun.
Sumantu said:
O mighty-armed one, [listen] regarding the Sun, Bhāskara, who possesses immeasurable splendor.

At the time of bathing, one should perform auspicious rites such as the utterance of the word "Victory" (jaya). O best of the twice-born, one should fashion the lotus, the svastika, the conch, and the śrīvatsa upon vessels made of gold, silver, or other materials, using cow dung and similar substances.
With unbroken grains of rice and sesame seeds mixed with various colors,
and with clear substances mixed with curd, filling [the vessels] as beautifully as possible;
and with lamps upon pedestals made of materials and the sprouts of the *bhūta* tree, the *aśvattha*, and other such trees.
With purifying herbs and all kinds of seeds, such as barley and others,
one should produce a most beautiful sound of musical instruments, including conchs, kettledrums, and so forth, on all the seventh lunar days and especially on the sixth and subsequent days.
One should cause the sound of the Vedas to resound at the three junctions of the day for the sake of the highest fruit;

one should also perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) with auspicious conch shells and musical instruments. As long as one performs the lustration according to the rules on the solar festivals, [the merit is secured].
For as many thousands of yugas as there are [drops], he is honored in the world of the heroes (Sūraloka).
Indeed, one should bathe [the deity] with the five products of a tawny cow (kapilā-pañcagavya) mixed with kuśa-water purified by mantras; for that is remembered as the "Brahma-bath" (brahmasnāna).
He who bestows even a single Brahma-bath throughout all the years is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of the Sun.
[One should perform it] with the five products of a tawny cow (kapilā-pañcagavya) combined with curd and milk.
O lord of men, one should know that bathing [there] yields tenfold merit and great spiritual reward.
For the sake of the hero and for eternal purification of the body,
one should daily bring a tawny cow produced by the sages, gods, and fire.
The Śūdra who drinks the Kāpila [milk] prepared for the purpose of a rite for the gods is cooked for a very long time in the most terrible ocean of hell;
whatever sin has been accumulated over a thousand crores of years [he must endure].

By anointing oneself with clarified butter, one would burn away everything belonging to the Sun; of this there is no doubt. Whatever sin has been accumulated over thousands of millions of kalpas, all that is consumed by the Vajra-bath, just as fire consumes fuel.

On the seventh [lunar day], having performed his ablutions, a man should worship the Sun even once; having uplifted seven generations of his lineage here on earth, he is glorified in the world of the Sun. A bath with milk, provided it is accompanied by wealth, gold, and other offerings, is equal in merit to that [bath].
The man who bathes the Sun once with a *droṇa* of milk is honored in the world of the Sun by means of a silver celestial chariot (*vimāna*).
Having bathed the Sun once with curds, he is honored throughout the three worlds.
Having bathed him with honey, he is honored in the world of Śukra;
having raised him up with rice-flour paste, he is honored in the worlds of Vāyu;
and he who performs the bath here with sugarcane juice even once, [is honored] in the world of Sūrya.
That man who bathes the Sun once with fruit and water, endowed with all his desires, shall go to Gopati-pura;
casting off the mire of his sins, he is glorified in the world of the ancestors.
O lord of men, having bathed the Sun-god even once with sandalwood water,

a person becomes as pure as a moonbeam and, endowed with splendor, may wander in the abode of Ātreya. If one should bathe the Sun even once with water filtered through a cloth, [the same result follows].
With his soul satisfied by all desires, he shall go to the city of the Lord of Rākā;
O Bhārata, by muttering the hymn "Āpo hi ṣṭhā" and by means of Ganges water and red chalk,
he is glorified in the world of Brahmā in a celestial chariot.
He who bathes the Sun even once with water scented with camphor and agallochum,
having fasted on the seventh lunar day and bathed the Lord of Light once with mantras,
shall deliver twenty-one generations of his lineage and attain the realm of the Sun.
He who bathes the Sun with cool water for the sake of his ancestors—
those ancestors, even if they are in hell, quickly go to heaven satisfied.
Having bathed the Sun with cool water along with a stream of warm milk, [he attains great merit].
Having bathed the Lord with the Vrata thereafter, one is glorified in the world of Agni.
O Bhārata, by performing these three baths and worshipping [the Lord],
a human being obtains the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices.
A bath with copper jars is considered a hundred times more meritorious than one with earthen jars;
with silver ones, the merit is four times greater; seeing [the image] is superior to touching it, and worship is better than touching it; and a bath with ghee is even more excellent than that.
Sin committed here or in the hereafter is destroyed by a bath with ghee;
however, sin committed over seven lifetimes is destroyed by listening to the Purāṇas.
One may forgive ten offenses with water, but a hundred with milk.
A thousand [faults] are forgiven by [offering] curd, and ten thousand are forgiven even by ghee;
he who performs a bath with ghee continuously for a month shall lead eleven generations of his lineage here to the abode of the Sun.
It is known from the sacred tradition that a bath requires one hundred palas, an anointing twenty-five palas,
and a great bath (mahāsnāna) two thousand palas.
O best of the twice-born, one should perform the anointing and the bath with ghee for the Sun.
Whatever fruit one obtains by giving ten thousand cows along with decoctions of wheat flour measured by the *darbha* grass,
that entire fruit is obtained when an ointment of *arka* is applied.
He who offers the *arghya* accompanied by flowers and fruits to the Sun is worthy of honor in all worlds and rejoices in heaven like the Sun himself.
[One should offer] water mixed with fragrant substances, increased twelvefold over the original amount.

O King, having filled a vessel with the eightfold ingredients and offering water for honor (arghya) mixed with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya)— which is a hundred times more efficacious— one should present it upon the head of the Sun;
such a person rejoices in the abode of the Sun for ten thousand years.
Water, milk, tips of *kuśa* grass, clarified butter, curd, as well as honey,
red *karavīra* flowers, and red sandalwood—
this is indeed the eightfold *argha* proclaimed by Brahmā.
O King, that which constantly generates joy for the Sun—
whatever fruit may accrue from a donor giving the *arghya* offering with a bamboo vessel,
a hundred times more merit than that, O King, is gained by using an earthen vessel.
By the gift of a copper vessel for the arghya offering, merit is considered to be a hundredfold;
one obtains the same fruit as with palāśa or lotus leaves when using a copper vessel.
With a silver vessel, it should be known that the arghya is worth a hundred thousandfold; of this there is no doubt.
An *arghya* offered placed in a golden vessel becomes ten million times more meritorious.
In this same manner, regarding the bath, *arghya*, food offerings (*naivedya*), sacrificial oblations (*bali*), incense (*dhūpa*), and so forth,
the fruit increases progressively according to the specific excellence of the vessels used.
Whatever merit there is for one who has mastered the Vedas from the gift of a silver vessel,
a hundred times that merit is obtained from the gift of a copper vessel to the Sun;
and he who gives the fruit of ten million gold pieces to one who has mastered the Vedas [obtains even greater merit].
The merit from giving a silver vessel to the Sun would be even greater than that;
O Lord of the Earth, it is impossible to describe the merit of one who gives a golden vessel to Bhāskara, owing to the excellence of the recipient vessel.
The fruit is declared to be exactly the same for both the wealthy and the poor;
yet, between them, the superior result belongs to that person who possesses greater devotion toward the Sun.
He who, despite having wealth, fails out of delusion to perform the elaborate rites, [obtains no such merit].
One whose mind is overcome by greed does not obtain that fruit at all.
Therefore, it should be understood with effort that through mantras, fruits, waters, sandalwood, and so forth, that fruit is infinite; devotion alone is the cause in this matter.
One is honored in the world of the Sun for a hundred divine crores of years.
The merit of anointing with fragrant unguents is double that of sandalwood;
O King, it should be known that the merit of flowers is four times that of fragrance and eight times that of [sandalwood].
One should declare that the fruit of black agallochum (kṛṣṇāguru) is especially twofold;
from that, the merit of saffron (kuṅkuma) is ordained to be a hundredfold greater.
[Anointing should be done] with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and saffron, finely ground together.
Having completely anointed Bhānu, he shall dwell in heaven for ten million kalpas;
anointed with the fragrances of merit, he shall sport there with hosts of gods.
O Hero, he shall dwell in the city of Mitravana for ten thousand years.
O lord of men, by devotedly offering a palm-leaf fan to the Sun,
one is honored in the world of heroes for ten thousand years;
likewise, by giving a most beautiful peacock-feather fan to the Sun.
One shall dwell for a full hundred million years in the city of Prabhañjana,
offering flowers grown in the forest or leaves produced on the mountains— flowers that are not stale, free from holes, gathered while fresh, and devoid of living organisms.
One should worship the Sun with flowers grown in self-reliant (unplowed) soil;
through a specific variety of such flowers, the merit obtained will be even greater.
This is said regarding a twice-born who is endowed with austerity, virtue, and good qualities, and who knows the *Hāsa* [Purāṇa].
Having given ten niṣkas of gold, one obtains that fruit;
O hero, one should offer a karavīra flower to Arka,
and one obtains that same fruit, just as the Blessed Lord Ravi has said.
In this way, through a particular flower, the fruit becomes even greater;
understand that the merit is to be known by one who knows the taste—listen to me as to how that may be.
Among all the thousands of flowers, the *karavīra* is always preeminent.
O lord of men, a single lotus is superior to a thousand bilva leaves;
a bakapuṣpa flower is superior to a thousand lotus flowers;
and the mudgara flower is said to be superior to a thousand bakapuṣpa flowers.
A leaf of the *śamī* tree is superior to a thousand leaves of the *kuśa* grass;
O King, the blue lotus is supreme over a thousand *śamī* flowers.
Among all species of flowers, the blue lotus is the most excellent.
Whoever worships the Sun with a thousand red lotuses, a hundred blue lotuses,
and red *karavīra* flowers,
[remains so] for thousands of millions of *kalpas* and hundreds of millions of *kalpas*.
The illustrious one, whose prowess is equal to the sun, shall dwell in the city of Arka;
according to the fruit that is proclaimed for the remaining varieties of flowers,
he is glorified in the world of the Sun.
The flower of the śamī and the blossom of the bṛhatī are said to be equal. The jātī, vijayā, and pāṭalā are to be known as equal to the karavīra.
The white mandāra flower and the white-flowered [lotus] are likewise equal to that.
The *nala*, *caṃpaka*, *puṇṇāga*, and *mudgara* flowers are considered equal [in merit].
One should avoid flowers that are fragrant yet impure;
however, even a flower devoid of fragrance is acceptable if it is pure, such as *kuśa* grass and the like.
For that flower which is *sāttvika* is indeed pure, while that which is *tāmasa* is impure.
*Mudgara* and *kadaṃba* flowers should be offered to the wise one at night;
during the day, one should discard all other flowers as well as those that are withered.
One should worship the Sun with buds, but one must not offer unripe fruit.
One should carefully avoid fruit that is overcooked or pierced, even if it is ripe.
Indeed, in the absence of flowers, one may even offer leaves.
If even leaves are not available, one should offer fruits;
if fruits are also unavailable, one may offer grasses, shrubs, or medicinal herbs. In the absence of even these herbs, one becomes worshipped through devotion alone.
For each individual flower offered, the fruit is ten gold pieces;
he who properly worships the Sun with fragrant, offered flowers,
being well-disposed even during the dark fortnight of Māgha, enjoys infinite fruit.
O Great King, one who worships the Sun with *karavīra* flowers,
being liberated from all sins, is glorified in the world of the Sun. He who, out of devotion, worships the Sun even once with *agastya* flowers [attains the same].
Having obtained the fruit of the gift of ten million cows, one shall go to heaven;
likewise, with jasmine, blue lotuses, lotuses, *jāti*, *punnāga*, and *campaka* flowers,
as well as with *aśoka*, white *mandāra*, *karṇikāra*, and *andhuka* flowers.

O lord of men, whatever man worships the Sun with karavīra, arka, kahlāra, śamī, tagara, keśara, agasti, baka flowers, or śatapatra— whichever of these flowers are available— he shall [attain his goal].
Listen with one-pointed mind as he attains that fruit:
[he travels] in celestial chariots that resemble ten million suns, which fulfill all desires,
are adorned with garlands of flowers, and resound with the music of singing and instrumental演奏.
O King, with the sweet sounds of lutes and musical instruments,
moving at his own will amidst the daughters of the Sun-god— a sight difficult even for the gods to obtain—
he was fanned with yak-tail whisks and praised by both gods and asuras.
He shall go to the divine city of the Sun,
where he will be honored; O King, by worshipping the Sun with whatever flowers— whether aquatic or terrestrial— with faith, one is glorified in the world of the Sun.
One should fashion a beautiful flower-mandala above the sun,
adorned with garlands and wreaths of flowers hanging down as far as the pedestal;
it is further graced by most wonderful great vehicles and embellished with divine flowers.
And he shall dwell happily above all others in the city of the Sun;
for he who, on the occasion of a festival, constructs a house with fragrant flowers of many colors, radiant with various blossoms.
By means of the Puṣpaka chariot, which is strewn with flower garlands,
he undoubtedly resorts to the divine city of Puṣpetara; there,
his commands unchallenged, he rejoices for an imperishable duration of time.
"He goes to whichever world among all those beginning with that of the Sun he desires.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-third chapter, titled "Description of Flower Worship" within the Saura Dharmas of the Saptamī Kalpa, in the Brāhma Parva of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
[This is followed by] the "Description of the Sūrya-Ṣaṣṭhī Vow."
Śatānīka said:
O best of the twice-born, tell me once more what fruit has been declared for the worship of the Sun-god, the god of gods, who possesses great splendor.
Sumantu said:
Listen, O Great King, to that which bestows all things and is honored by the world—
the [merit] belonging to all three, namely Brahmā, Īśa, and Upendra, O Bhārata.
Having bowed their heads to the ground before the four-faced one, the eldest of the gods, who was seated comfortably on Mount Manovatī, Viṣṇu and Īśa spoke these words:
"This blessed deity, the thousand-rayed Sun..."
"Tell us the merit that is obtained from his worship.
Brahmā said:
"Excellent, excellent, O Lord of the World! You have asked me well here."

Therefore, listen with one-pointed attention to everything as I speak: Ravi himself, out of devotion to him, constantly accepts those very offerings from one who, having personally prepared them, nourishes himself and worships the Sun.
He who would establish a grove for the Sun, adorned with mangoes, bilvas, and other trees;
with jasmine, vijaya, rājārka, karavīra, and saffron;
with punnāga, nāga, bakula, aśoka, sesame, and campaka;
Listen to the meritorious fruit of one who offers sections of Agasti and plantain trees:
for as many leaves, flowers, seeds, and fruits as there are,
for that many thousands of years he is honored in the world of the gods.
O King, one should likewise offer guggulu resin with clarified butter, or kanduru resin;
such a person attains birth in the house of one who knows the four Vedas and remains perpetually happy.
One should also offer black agallochum and camphor incense to the Sun-god.
O King, hear now the fruit of merit for one who performs this without interruption:
having enjoyed pleasures in the City of the Sun for thousands of millions and hundreds of millions of kalpas, he shall at the end of that time become a lord of the earth.
A Yakṣa who makes a sound seizes one who has taken guggulu mixed with clarified butter;
by giving a gift named after the Yakṣa, one is glorified in that world.
He who burns guggulu with clarified butter on the seventh lunar day of the dark fortnight [is likewise honored].
Having reached that solar region after ten billion years,
and having burned Devadāru, Nameru, Śrīvāsa, Kunduru,
and Śrīphala mixed with clarified butter as his fuel, he shall attain a refuge.
In this way, saugandhika incense is six thousand times superior;
agaru incense is ten thousand times superior; and when combined with ghee, it becomes twenty thousand times superior.
This divine substance, beginning with kunduruka, always bestows infinite fruit.
Having burned two thousand palas of pure Mahiṣākṣa guggulu resin, one becomes equal to the sun;
there is no doubt that he shall purify a person tainted by sin.
One should burn incense made of black agallochum, which is like gold in a cool fire,
and should smear the inner apartments with fragrant perfumes,
including the doors, panels, walls, and so forth, both horizontally and vertically, along with the pedestals.
One should cause it to be perfumed with flower garlands and fragrant incenses;
I shall describe to you both, in its entirety and exactly as it is, the merit of that act which fills all directions with various scents.

For a hundred divine millions of aeons, blazing with splendor like fire and radiant like Śakra, that deity is honored in the world of the Sun. At the end of that period, by the remainder of his merit, he becomes the sovereign of the three worlds.
He who thus makes the abode of the vulva one hundredfold with perfumes shall be endowed with all happiness and possess prowess equal to the Sun;
honored by you both, he shall dwell as a god in the world of the Sun.
Likewise, by giving a sacred thread (upavīta) made of white silk threads to the Sun, one becomes a master of the Vedāṅgas;
and by giving various beautiful garments, one is honored in the world of the gods.
I shall now declare the merit of one who offers even a fragment of woolen cloth together with a lotus upon the head of the Sun;
such a person shall sit upon half of Indra’s throne for as long as fourteen Indras endure.
Thus, everything should be understood in brief according to one's wealth:
for all the golden vessels and crowns in their entirety,
there should be a powder made from arka leaves combined with madhuparṇī.
He who offers this to the Sun shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
One should prepare well-prepared food from a prastha measure of śāli rice and,
especially on the seventh lunar day, offer a caru oblation to Sūrya.
Samyāva, kṛśara, pūpa, pāyasa, and likewise yāvaka;
curd-rice, rasālā-food, sweetmeats, and molasses-cakes—
however many grains of rice there are in that offering by count.
For that many thousands of years, he is honored in the world of the gods.
By offering foodstuffs made of jaggery and sugar-candy,
drenched in ghee, one obtains a hundredfold fruit.
Among foods such as *rasāla* and other delicacies, fruit is desired;
one should also offer half of that amount of scented water.
Furthermore, various kinds of edible foods obtained according to the season [should be presented].
By offering oblations to the Sun and performing worship, one attains the supreme abode.
Having lit a beautiful lamp of ghee in the temple of Bhāskara,
one ascends a fiery vehicle and goes to the city of Saumanasa.
Whoever should create a beautiful row of lamps in the month of Kārttika,
whether on the seventh, the sixth, or even on the new moon day,
shall illuminate the quarters with splendor, resembling ten thousand suns.
Endowed with divine ornaments and having uplifted his entire lineage,
he who has awakened [the lamp] by filling it with ghee according to the number of lamps shall be honored in the world of the Sun for as many thousands of years.
Furthermore, by kindling a lamp-tree at sacred shrines on the auspicious festival days (parvan), one obtains twice the merit compared to the previous [act]; of this there is no doubt.
O, by kindling a lamp-tree at the shrines of the Sun (Bhāskara), [one gains great merit].
O hero, one who is made of all metals is honored in the world of the Sun;
one should carry a lamp on the head before the Sun at night,
as well as on the forehead with both hands, and likewise diligently upon the chest.
Resplendent like ten thousand suns and traveling in celestial chariots resembling the sun,
he is honored in the world of the Sun for a hundred times ten thousand kalpas. But he who gives food, O hero, is honored in the world of heroes.
Having placed a pure and auspicious mirror before Bhāskara,
and having adorned the couch with white garlands and sandalwood paste,
[he beholds] the glorious one, stainless as the sun and fire, wearing divine ornaments and assuming a celestial form.
A man who, full of faith and devotion, performs a circumambulation of the Sun, is honored in the world of heroes for ten thousand times ten thousand kalpas;
he easily obtains the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices.
Whoever performs a circumambulation and offers a salutation obtains the entire fruit of both the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices.
Salutation is remembered as a sacrifice, the most excellent among all sacrifices.

Having paid homage to the Thousand-rayed One (the Sun), one obtains the fruit of the horse sacrifice. He who worships by prostrating himself on the ground like a staff— such a destination as he attains cannot be reached even by hundreds of sacrifices.
Whatever fruit is obtained from all sacrifices, fasts, and all sacred fords,
one enjoys that fruit through worship accompanied by an offering and an announcement.
Having fashioned a white banner with a great emblem and having prepared a bow and a colored arena, one attains the same reward.
That man who, endowed with supreme faith, gives to Āditya a chariot resounding with the tinkling of a network of small bells and adorned with a peacock-feather parasol,
shall travel in a hundred celestial chariots, honored by all the gods.
O God,
he who makes the temple of the Blessed One crowded with rows of banners at its extremities,
and who offers eight great banners in the cardinal and intermediate directions, rejoices in heaven like a god for a hundred manvantaras.
With a thousand celestial chariots adorned with rows of banners,
he rejoices like a hero in heaven for a hundred times ten thousand divine eons,
in a vehicle as stainless as the rays of a hundred moons and graced by strings of pearls.
Or he may give a parasol made of jewels or one made of gold and other precious materials;
being seated upon an excellent celestial chariot and with a parasol held over him, adorned with a golden handle, he rejoices in the world of the Sun.
Then, having fallen from that world,
he comes to earth by the force of his nature and enjoys the earth bounded by the oceans under a single umbrella—
[he who gave] a great bell with a loud sound, joined with a chain.
Or one may fix [an image] made of bell-metal or iron in the vulva;
such a man becomes handsome, prosperous, and exceedingly dear to the Bhaga.
Having attained strength equal to the sun, he is glorified in the world of the sun.
He who offers for the sake of the Lord the sounds of kettledrums, clay drums, war-drums, jharjharīs, mardalas, and so forth— ten types of musical instruments such as bronze cymbals and the like—
he, by means of magnificent celestial chariots resounding with the music of flutes and lutes, [attains the divine realm].
He is honored in the world of Bhaga for a hundred divine ages at the end of the eon;
especially by the gift of excellent music accompanied by instruments,
he rejoices as he desires in the world of the Sun for imperishable time.
Having sounded a pair of conchs with a great, great roar at the abode of Bhaga,
one is glorified in the world of Bhaga for a hundred times ten million divine yugas;
[one obtains] a celestial chariot of many-colored luster, adorned in its center with a lotus.
Whether multicolored or of a single hue, fashioned from fine cloth, provided with a network of small bells, adorned with pigments,
radiant as a garland of flowers, and decorated with bells and chowries.
Whoever should place upon the Bhaga one adorned with all kinds of jewels,
or cloths such as fine linen, silk, or divine raiment, endowed with various colors—
whatever may be the total number of threads in those silken and other fabrics;
For as many thousands of yugas as there are, he is honored in the world of the gods;
by the oblation into the womb, the entire universe is sustained through the gateway of creation. Agni’s path is declared to be in speech, for fire is eternally his own offspring.
O Indra among kings, he who daily performs the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) according to the rules in the abode of Bhaga, dedicating it to Bhaga, attains the supreme goal.
He who daily observes the prescribed rule, offering all kinds of food mixed with barley-meal (*yāvaka*), [attains the same].
Provided with flowers, incense, and water, especially at the appropriate times,
whoever— even if only once— performs this offering of *bali* in all directions for the Mothers such as Mahāśvetā and for all the three Kalpas, [attains the supreme goal].
That man shall dwell for thousands of years in the city of Śāṇḍileya;
having constantly offered the solar twilight-oblation (saurasaṃdhyābali) to the Sun at the end of each day,
he is glorified in the world of Bhaga for more than a hundred thousand years.

One should carry on one's head a vessel filled with curd, rice, and milk, covered [with a lid], honored with flowers and incense, and beautified by a canopy above; then, one should proceed slowly in a clockwise circumambulation.
At the edge of the solar abode, adorned with the sounds of conchs, lutes, and other instruments,
with mirrors, incense, and garlands, and graced by song, dance, and the like—
the fruit of the merit of one who is devoted to the remembrance of the Sun, listen now.
Whether he has performed great austerities for a thousand divine years or likewise for a hundred divine years, there is no doubt that it shall be so;
even if he be a doer of evil, his soul becomes gratified by devotion to Bhaga.
Having attained the state of a constant attendant of Bhaga, he shall dwell eternally in the world of Bhaga.
Furthermore, he who observes the sixth lunar day of the dark fortnight with a fast and the seventh lunar day of the dark fortnight by eating only at night,
attains enjoyments in this world and an auspicious destination in the hereafter.
A man who observes this for one year should eat only at night on the day of Bhaga;
remaining celibate, with anger subdued, and devoted to the worship of Bhaga, he should practice eating at night rather than begging for food; therefore, he should subsist by means of the night-meal.
The gods eat at midday, the sages likewise in the forenoon,
the ancestors in the afternoon, and the Guhyakas and others at twilight;
however, having bypassed all these times, the meal of the Sauras is supreme.
Eating at night while being devoted to the worship of the Sun,
a person of noble mind who observes the Sumanā-vrata attains the world of Bhaga;
having enjoyed the worlds of the Sumanas, he becomes a king upon the earth.
One who observes the fast at night should eat sacrificial food (haviṣya), bathe, consume light food,
perform fire-rituals, sleep on the ground,
and practice these observances diligently, having performed the nocturnal rite according to the rules on the sixth day of the dark fortnight.
In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, a man should worship [the deity] as Aṃśumān according to the prescribed rite;
having consumed cow's urine and fasting through the night, he should sleep.
Such a person obtains the fruit of the Atirātra sacrifice.
Likewise, during the month of Puṣya, they desire the thousand-rayed, resplendent Sun;
having attained the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice and consumed clarified butter,
a man [should worship] the one named Divākara on the sixth day of the dark fortnight in Māgha, O best of men.
Having drunk cow’s milk at night, one obtains the fruit of a horse-sacrifice (gomedha).
Having worshipped Mārtaṇḍa in the month of Phālguna and then drinking cow’s milk, one rejoices in the world of the Sun for ten million times ten thousand years.
In the month of Caitra, one who is full of devotion, having worshipped Vivasvat while subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya),
rejoices in the world of the Sun together with celestial nymphs (apsarases).
And in Vaiśākha, one should worship the fierce-rayed Sun while observing a vow of milk.
Having worshipped the Lord of the Day (the Sun) during the month of Jyeṣṭha, one who drinks water from the horns of cows shall rejoice in the presence of the Sun for more than ten thousand years;
he shall obtain the entire fruit of the gift of ten million cows.
Having worshipped the one named Arka in the month of Āṣāḍha and consumed cow-dung,
one goes to the world of the Sun for a hundred times a hundred years. Having honored the one named Aryaman in the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should drink milk.
For more than ten thousand years, he rejoices in the abode of the Sun.
On the sixth day of the month of Bhādrapada, one should worship the deity named Bhāskara;
by offering Bhāskara the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices.
In the month of Āśvayuja, on the sixth day, one should worship the deity named Bhaga;
subsisting only on meat and cow’s urine, one obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
In the month of Kārttika, on the sixth day, one should worship the deity named Śakra.

Having consumed a single sprout of dūrvā grass once, one obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice. At the end of the year, one should feed Brahmins who are devoted to the Sun with milk-rice mixed with honey and sprinkled with ghee.
According to one's capacity, one should offer gold and garments to them with devotion;
and one should also offer a black, milk-yielding cow to the Sun.
Thus, he who should pass a single year before the Lord without interruption—
Listen to the meritorious fruit of that person who observes the Kṛṣṇa-ṣaṣṭhī vow with devotion:
liberated from all sins and endowed with all desires,
that man rejoices in the world of the Sun for eternal years.
"O Bird, on all meritorious days— such as the equinoxes, lunar eclipses, and so forth— acts such as giving gifts, fasting, and offering oblations become inexhaustible. Sumantu said:
Thus, O lord of the people, did Bhānu formerly speak to Aruṇa regarding the meritorious Kṛṣṇa-ṣaṣṭhī vow, which removes the fear of all sins.
By performing this with devotion for the sake of the high-souled Bhāskara, a person [attains his goal].
"He goes to the supreme abode of the Sun of immeasurable splendor.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Sūrya-Ṣaṣṭhī Vow," in the Saptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan within the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
[Now follows] the description of the Ubhayasaptamī.
Sumantu said: I shall fully declare to you the supreme vow of the Sun,
which is the highest means for the attainment of dharma, desire, wealth, and liberation.
When the month of Pauṣa has arrived, he who observes the practice of eating only at night—
having conquered his senses and speaking the truth— and who diligently passes the seventh day of both fortnights in fasting, subsisting on rice, wheat, and dairy products; |||
O observer of excellent vows, descendant of Śāṇḍilī, one should worship the Sun at the three junctions of the day;
one should always sleep on the ground, renouncing all enjoyments.
Then, O subduer of enemies, when the month is complete, on the seventh lunar day, one should worship with ghee and other offerings.
Having performed his bath and a great worship of the Sun-god,

he should offer a prastha of sweetmeats (modaka) as a food offering, along with prepared milk. He should also feed eight Brahmins and perform the worship of the vulva (bhaga) which possesses auspicious characteristics.
O Great King, having given a tawny cow to the Sun,
whoever performs this meritorious and supreme vow of the Sun—
for him I shall declare the fruit of merit, endowed with the fulfillment of all desires.
With celestial palaces resembling ten million suns, fulfilling all desires,
crowded with throngs of apsaras, endowed with great splendor,
and graced by hosts of gandharvas with songs, dances, instrumental music, and the like;
Fanned by chowries and praised by gods and asuras,
possessing a brilliance like that of a thousand rays, he goes together with the sun-gods to the supreme abode where the radiant Sun dwells.
For as many thousands of yugas as there are hairs on his body and those born in his lineage, he is honored in the world of the gods;
having enjoyed desired pleasures together with the members of twenty-one generations of his kin.
Having attained the yoga of knowledge, one is liberated once again;
through yoga one reaches the end of suffering, and the yoga of knowledge proceeds from it.
Knowledge arises from the solar dharma, and the solar dharma results from the worship of Bhaga.
Thus has been fully explained to you this means for crossing the ocean of existence— the solar method for attaining liberation through devotion to the Sun.
Furthermore, whoever should observe the practice of eating only at night when the month of Māgha has arrived, [shall attain the same].

Eating oil-cake mixed with ghee, that man of subdued senses should observe a fast on the seventh day of both fortnights. O lord of men, on the eighth day he should perform an ablution of the Sun with ghee.
One should also give a young cow, dark blue in color,
to the Lord of the Day (the Sun). Having gone to the beautiful city of the Sun by means of celestial chariots resembling sapphire and accompanied by peacocks, one enjoys desired pleasures.

O Indra among kings, that man who, having conquered anger and subdued his senses, observes the practice of eating only at night during the month of Phālguna, subsisting on śyāmāka grain, milk, and wild rice (nīvāra)—
or else, O King, a man intent on fasting on the sixth or the seventh lunar day— [attains great merit].
On the eighth day, one should perform a great ablution with the five products of the cow, ghee, and so forth;
with earth from anthills and the like, as well as cow-urine, cow-dung, and so forth;
and having bathed [the image] with the barks of milk-exuding trees, one should wipe it clean.
Then, one should give a reddish-brown cow adorned with a red garland to a recipient;
having gone to the beautiful city of the Sun by means of celestial chariots resembling rubies and accompanied by elephants, he rejoices there for eternal years.
When the month of Caitra has arrived, O King, he who observes the practice of eating only at night,
consuming rice mixed with milk-porridge while his senses are subdued,
should offer a young *pāṭala* tree to the Sun, the Lord of Viṣṇu.
Traveling in vehicles possessing the luster of topaz and drawn by various swans and other birds,

he shall go to the beautiful city of the Sun and rejoice for eternal years. Furthermore, he who observes the practice of eating only at night during the month of Vaiśākha, the month of heroes, [attains this same reward].

O King of auspicious countenance, one should offer a single oblation to the Sun mixed with honey and clarified butter; one should also give a cow to Bhāskara. Furthermore, one should perform the general procedure that I have prescribed for you.
Endowed with the powers of *aṇimā* and the other superhuman qualities, he shall travel through the sky like the sun in vehicles resembling pure crystal and drawn by peacocks.
He who observes the practice of eating only at night when the month of Śrāvaṇa has arrived [attains this].
Devoted to the welfare of all beings, one should offer milk-rice made with sixty-day rice and a yellow-colored cow to the high-souled Bhāskara;
one should perform the entire ritual procedure exactly as it has been proclaimed.
