Traveling on various magnificent Mahāyāna vehicles that move like swans and cranes, that glorious one goes to the City of the Sun and attains the fruit previously described.
O Hero, he who observes the practice of eating only at night (*naktabhojana*) in the month of Bhādrapada [attains this].
Eating only the remnants of the sacrificial oblation, taking refuge at the foot of a tree,
he should sleep at night in a sanctuary, showing compassion toward all living beings;
he should give an excellent red cow to the high-souled Bhāskara.
Having traveled in celestial chariots that resemble the rays of the moon, are like diamonds and lapis lazuli, are adorned with ruddy geese, and fulfill all desires,
he goes to the beautiful city of the Sun, which is well-honored by gods and asuras alike.
That illustrious and fortunate man,
who in the month of Āśvayuja observes the practice of eating only at night,
consuming measured food while having conquered anger and subdued his senses, rejoices until the dissolution of all beings.
One should give a cow, possessing the luster of a lotus, to the Sun of immeasurable splendor—
a young, milch cow adorned with divine ornaments,
[and decorated] with pearls resembling the *svastika* and embellished with sapphires.
That self-controlled person, enjoying himself, shall go to the world of the Sun in celestial chariots that fulfill all desires and are joined with living beings;
he should give a cow to the Maker of Day that possesses a radiance equal to fire and the sun.
And by performing the previously mentioned rite, a man shall become equal to the Sun;
he rejoices happily like the Sun, traveling in great celestial vehicles that resemble mountains, which possess crests like the flames of the fire of time and are mounted upon great lions.
In the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa, he who observes the practice of eating only at night,
consuming food mixed with milk while his senses are subdued,
and likewise bestows a red cow adorned with various ornaments, [attains great merit].

O tiger among the Kurus, one should also perform the ritual for Sūrya. Endowed with supreme splendor, he goes to that delightful city by means of vehicles resembling white lotuses, yoked with chariots drawn by white horses.
Non-violence, truthful speech, non-stealing, forbearance, and straightforwardness;

performing the fire-sacrifice at the three periods of the day, sleeping on the ground, and eating only at night— on both fortnights, O joy of the Kurus, one should observe these on the seventh lunar day during the path.
Relying upon these virtues and performing this supreme vow known as the Saptamī of both [fortnights], which removes the fear of all sins,
pacifies all diseases, and bestows the fruits of all desires—
One who desires the vast abode of the Sun of immeasurable splendor should always observe these and other such rules as a practitioner of the Sūryavrata.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Ubhayasaptamī," in the Saptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan within the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Description of the Nikṣubhā Vow within the Saura Dharma.
Sumantu said: "Any woman who is devoted to the Sun will certainly become a man."
O hero, if that woman desires an excellent son, listen to that vow known as Nikṣubhārka; it is said to always increase affection, prevent separation, and accomplish virtue, desire, and wealth.
On the seventh or the sixth lunar day, or on the sun’s transit (saṃkrānti) or on a Sunday,
one who observes a fast should perform an oblation of clarified butter with clarified butter.
Having fashioned an auspicious *nikṣubhā* made of bell-metal and adorned with gold, [he should offer it].
One should bathe the image made of silver or gold with clarified butter and other substances;
having adorned it with perfumes, garlands, and beautiful pairs of garments,
one should honor it with all kinds of food— both solid and soft— as well as canopies, banners, and chowries.

One should feed those devoted to the Sun, draped in white garments; having prepared them within the sanctuary, one should arrange an image there. Placing that vessel upon the head, it should be adorned with a canopy and a parasol.
One should lead the image of Bhaga to its sanctuary with the splendor of banners, conchs, and other ornaments.
On the day of the Sun, one should offer this vow to Nikṣubhārka;
then, one should place the vessel, adorned with decorations, upon his pedestal.
Having circumambulated the Sun and prostrated before him, one should ask for forgiveness;
having completed that meritorious vow, one hears [the teaching] and attains the fruit.
By means of great celestial vehicles resembling mountains and shining like twelve suns, [one proceeds].
He rejoices as he pleases with the solar deities in the world of Bhānu for thousands of crores and hundreds of crores of years.
O fortunate one, he delights and is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Then, by virtue of that specific merit, having reached the world of Brahmā which is endowed with all desirable things, he shall attain supreme happiness;
and when he eventually falls from the world of Brahmā, he will be illustrious and highly honored by the gods.
Honored by gods and asuras, he attains Prajāpati;
having enjoyed the worlds here for a long time, he is glorified in the world of Soma. From Soma’s world, he reaches the world of Indra once more and becomes the lord of Indra.

Having reached the world of the Gandharvas from the world of Indra, he rejoices there; then, by the remainder of that merit, he becomes an inhabitant of the realm of the Sun. Through the exertion of his own karmic impressions, he again undertakes auspicious deeds.
From the auspicious state, he returns here again and goes forth by the thousands;
as long as death is not attained, he wanders on by the power of karma.
Through profound world-weariness arises dispassion, and from dispassion arises the birth of knowledge.
"From knowledge yoga proceeds; from yoga one attains the end of suffering.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Nikṣubhā Vrata," within the Sauradharma section of the Saptamī-kalpa in the Brāhma-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa. [This is followed by:
"Description of the Nikṣubhārka Vrata."
Sumantu said:
Furthermore, she who, self-restrained and observing celibacy, does not eat for one year on the sixth and seventh lunar days out of a desire for great fortune, [attains her goal].
Having fashioned an image known as Nikṣubhā,
one who performs the prescribed rites such as bathing obtains the aforementioned merit;
[he shall travel] in vehicles made of gold and adorned with four gates.
Having gone to the delightful city of the Sun, she obtains the fruit in its entirety;
after enjoying all desired pleasures in the worlds of the Sun and others,
she returns in due course to this world and shall obtain a king as her husband.
That noble woman who thus observes the fast on the single seventh day of the dark fortnight shall go to the supreme abode of the Sun of immeasurable splendor;
at the end of the year, she should fashion an auspicious image made of rice-flour.
One should worship with yellow unguents, garlands, and yellow garments;
having performed everything previously mentioned, one should offer it to Bhāskara.
[The deity ascends] upon seven formidable great vehicles, possessing the luster of ivory and gold.
For more than a full hundred million years, she is honored in the world of the Sun;
having enjoyed pleasures in the worlds beginning with that of the Sun, O lord of men,
she returns in due course to this world and finds a husband according to her desire.
On the seventh day of the dark fortnight, a woman of firm vows who possesses all auspicious marks and is endowed with wealth and grain should,
at the end of the year, offer a *nikṣubhārka* tree richly laden with all kinds of perfumes.
Having fed a woman of the Maga clan with gold, jewels, and pearls,
she indeed dwells in the world of the gods for thousands of yugas, O lord of men, in magnificent celestial vehicles adorned with divine Gandharvas.
Having enjoyed all pleasures at will in the world of the Sun,
she gradually returns to this world and finds a king as her husband.
O King, she who performs this vow, which removes the fear of sin, attains such a result.
O mighty-armed one, she who for one year remains endowed with supreme faith and recites this *Nikṣubhārka* merit goes to the highest station. O hero,
at the end of the year, she should indeed feed a married couple among those who provide the food.
O descendant of Kuru, having fed the couple with great quantities of delicious foods,
one should honor them with perfumes, garlands, and garments;
and having prepared a copper vessel adorned with diamonds, it should be filled [with the offerings].
Having given a golden *nikṣubhā* and an *arka* tree to those two according to one's ability—
knowing that the *nikṣubhā* is the nourisher (*bhojikā*) and the *arka* is proclaimed to be the nourisher (*bhojaka*)—
one should therefore worship them with faith, like the Lord of the Sun.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Nikṣubhārka Vow," within the Sauradharma section of the Saptamī-kalpa in the Brāhma-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
[This concludes] the description of the vow for women that grants all desires.
Sumantu said:
O King, that woman who passes the month of Kārttika eating but one meal a day—
self-controlled through observances such as forbearance and non-violence, remaining celibate,
and offering rice mixed with molasses and ghee to the Sun-god;
O dear one, endowed with supreme faith during both fortnights,
one should offer *karavīra* flowers along with *guggulu* resin mixed with clarified butter.
O dear one, on the seventh and the sixth lunar days, one should indeed take delight in fasting.
In celestial chariots resembling sapphire and fulfilling all desires,
he is honored in the world of the gods for more than a hundred thousand years;
and likewise, having diligently attained enjoyments in all the worlds.
"Having come in due course to this world, she shall find a husband according to her desire.
Thus is the rule proclaimed as identical for all sacrifices;
and the fruit of fasting with a single meal shall be equal [to that of these].
Forgiveness, truthfulness, compassion, charity, purity, restraint of the senses,
worship of the sun, offering oblations into the fire, contentment, and avoidance of theft—
this tenfold duty is recorded as common to all vows.
I shall describe in its entirety, month by month, the observance for each month.
In the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa,
having adorned the incomparable face of the sky with perfumes and garlands, one should worship that which is established upon the vault of heaven.
With vessels of copper and the like, served by hosts of apsarases,
he is glorified on Mount Sumeru for ten thousand years in the world of the Sun;
having attained stainless splendor among all the multitudes of gods.
Having arrived in this world in due course, she shall obtain a king as her husband.
Having adorned him with flowers, she should offer him to the Sun;
having adorned that one of auspicious countenance and incomparable beauty with perfumes and garlands.
Having fashioned a vessel of copper or bell-metal, one should offer [the gift] therein;
by means of a great flower-chariot that wafts divine fragrances,
one is honored in the world of the Sun for ten thousand years on Mount Sumeru.
Having enjoyed abundant pleasures in all the worlds, O Bhārata,
she reaches this world in due course and obtains a husband according to her desire.
In the month of Māgha, she should offer a chariot adorned with lamps and garlands on the day of Aśvayuj.
Having prepared a dwelling-place smeared with flour-paste, one should lead [the image] there;
by means of vehicles resembling great chariots and yoked with excellent white horses,
one is honored in the world of the Sun for more than a hundred thousand years.
Having enjoyed all desired pleasures in the worlds of all the immortals,
she shall eventually return to this world and obtain a husband according to her wish. To achieve this, one should fashion an image of the Sun out of flour in the month of Phālguna.
Having adorned it with perfumes and garlands, one should place it in the abode of the Sun;
[the donor] is honored in Sumeru for ten thousand years and in the world of the Sun by means of incomparable, divine vehicles filled with the sound of singing.
Having obtained all desired enjoyments according to her wishes in this world,
she returns again to this world and finds a husband as she desires;
likewise, having fashioned an image of Aruṇa in the month of Caitra and adorned it with perfumes and garlands.
Having placed [the offering] in the vessel as prescribed, one should present it to the Sun-god.
With celestial chariots resembling the autumnal moon and fulfilling all desires,
he is honored in the world of the Sun for more than a hundred thousand years.
Upon the exhaustion of her karma, having returned here and obtained a beloved husband along with sons and grandsons, she shall attain enjoyments that are very difficult to obtain.
Having fashioned Mount Meru from a measure (āḍhaka) of rice flour—
Joined with Nikṣubhā and Arka, adorned with all the elements,
endowed with various ornaments, decorated with various garlands,
and furnished with all kinds of jewels, one should place it in the abode of the Sun.

Indeed, he who observes this great vow of the vast sky (mahadvyomavrata) in the month of Vaiśākha is honored in the world of the Sun by means of various kinds of celestial vehicles. Having enjoyed all pleasures without exception in the worlds of the Sun and others, he [attains liberation].
Having arrived in this world in due course, she shall obtain a king as her husband.
Likewise, in the month of Āṣāḍha, she should prepare a second excellent lotus made of flour,
white in appearance and filled with the juices of all seeds.
O King, by means of these golden vehicles— rich with the fragrance of various filaments and adorned with all kinds of jewels—
and endowed with every enjoyment,
one is glorified in the world of the Sun for more than a hundred million years.
Having enjoyed vast pleasures in all the worlds in succession,
she obtains as her husband a youthful man enriched with every enjoyment,
endowed with all the bodily constituents, and adorned with various banners.
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should offer a mountain of sesame seeds to the Sun;
[thereby], by means of vehicles that move at will and are adorned with various colors,
one is honored in the world of the Sun for more than a hundred crores of years.
Having enjoyed various pleasures endowed with many wonders,
and having reached this world in due course, she finds a king as her husband,
O King, by making an offering of rice in the sky during the month of Bhādrapada.
Adorned with canopies, banners, and parasols, and decorated with various garlands,
he is honored in the world of the Sun for thousands of millions of years by means of magnificent great vehicles that resemble the rays of the rising sun.
Having experienced all various enjoyments arising from every moment,
she eventually comes to this world and finds a king as her husband;
having fashioned a vast mountain of grain in the month of Āśvayuja.
One should offer [a gift] rich in gold, garments, and perfumes to the Sun;
by means of celestial vehicles belonging to Savitṛ, endowed with excellent enjoyments,
one is honored in the world of the Sun for thousands of millions of years.
Having enjoyed desired pleasures in worlds such as that of the Sun,
she returns to this world and finds a king as her husband,
endowed with the beauty, splendor, and radiance of the Moon, Fire, and Sun.
Whatever desire men, women, or eunuchs have in mind,
when they worship the Sun with devotion, they indeed obtain all of that.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Vow of Women for the Fulfillment of Desires," within the Saura-dharmas of the Saptamī-kalpa, in the Brāhma-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Description of the Sūryavrata. Sumantu said:
[The image of the Sun] may be made of clay, wood, stone, or even baked brick.
Having constructed a monastery or even a house according to one's available means,
equipped with all necessary utensils and provided with all kinds of grain—
one should thus give this house to the Sun; thereby, one shall attain all desires.
Having observed the practice of eating only one meal a day with diligence during the month of Māgha in the winter season,
at the end of the month he should have a chariot constructed,
adorned with variegated cloths and yoked to four white horses, all beautifully decorated.
O lord of men, having fashioned an image of the Sun out of a measure (āḍhaka) of ground rice, adorned with white banners, flags, umbrellas, chowries, and mirrors,
and having placed it upon the seat of the chariot along with Saṃjñā, O king.
Having paraded him slowly through the royal highway at night with the sounding of conchs, kettledrums, and other instruments, he should afterwards enter the temple of the Sun;
there, he should perform vigils and worship adorned by rows of lamps.
Having passed the night gradually with spectacles and gifts,
and having performed the ritual bath at dawn with honey, milk, and ghee,
one should give food and a sacrificial fee according to one's ability to the poor, the blind, and the miserable.
One should offer a chariot equipped with a carriage to the Sun;
having eaten together with one's kinsmen and bowed down, one should go to the temple of the Sun.
This is always the most excellent of all vows, endowed with the dharma of mantras.

This vow is named the Sūryavrata, for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals. O King, whatever merit is found in all vows and whatever fruit is found in all sacrifices— all that merit one obtains here by means of the Sūryaratha vow.
Together with those born of twenty-one generations of his lineage, he is honored in the world of the Sun by means of celestial palaces that resemble ten thousand suns and fulfill all desires;
having enjoyed vast pleasures in all the worlds in succession.
Then, for more than a full hundred thousand aeons, he shall become a king upon the earth.
One should designate the Sun as being endowed with the five-fold strength, composed of the six soft substances, and provided with all necessary implements.

One should offer [the oblation] accompanied by the goddess Saṃjñā and enriched with flour-cakes (piṣṭa-śāḍhya). Having worshipped the preceptor— who is endowed with rising splendor and who knows the reality of the meaning of solar knowledge— with perfumes, flowers, garments, ornaments, and chowries.
Then, having offered all kinds of food and edibles, one should present a bed;
for as many thousands of years as there are threads of wool or cotton in that bed, one is honored in the world of the Sun.
Having enjoyed all pleasures without exception in all the worlds beginning with that of the gods,
he returns to this world out of desire and becomes a righteous king.
A bull together with ten cows is traditionally known as "the eleven consisting of a bull" (*vṛṣaikādaśa*).
Listen now to the fruit one obtains by offering here to Sūrya:
his soul becomes equal to the twelve Ādityas, endowed with the qualities of *aṇimā* and the rest;
he rejoices everywhere, O King, and becomes an attendant of the Sun.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Sūryavrata," in the Saptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan within the glorious Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa.
[Chapter 169] **Description of the Gift of Cows** Sumantu said:
O lord of men, listen to the fruit that one obtains by giving a hundred cows along with a bull to the Sun-god, together with those born of twenty-one generations of his lineage—
[a reward] resembling ten million excellent [celestial vehicles] and endowed with all objects of desire.
Accompanied by innumerable Mahāyāna deities worshipped by gods and asuras,
resembling twelve suns like another sun itself,
he goes to the delightful city of the Sun and sports in the pavilion of the solar orb.
Having enjoyed vast pleasures until the dissolution of all embodied beings,
he casts off the cloak of delusion and enters the solar orb;
omniscient, supreme like the sun, pure, and established in his own self.
Being all-pervasive due to its perfection, it becomes radiant like the sun.
He who gives a cow with two faces to the Sun shall obtain that fruit which is gained by giving the earth with its seven continents.
"Two feet and half a head, together with the mountains, forests, and groves.
Thus ends the one hundred and seventieth chapter, titled "Description of the Gift of a Cow," in the Saptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan within the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
[Now follows] the description of the performance of the feeding of the Bhojakas.
Śatānīka said:
"Tell me the dharma of the Magas, both in brief and in detail;
and what, O Brahmin, would be the fruit from practicing the dharma of the Magas?"
Sumantu said:
"O sinless one, that which has been declared by me to you as the 'Dharma of Sūrya' is indeed the 'Dharma of Maga,' which removes the fear of all sins."
For all castes alike, the practice of the Magadha dharma is prescribed;
and this Magadha dharma is proclaimed for their liberation from worldly existence.
Whether they be Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, women, or Śūdras, they may be followers of the Maga stage of life.
He who worships Mārtaṇḍa attains the supreme goal.
One should worship the Sun at the three junctions of the day and perform the fire-ritual according to one's ability.
O mighty-armed one, a man should diligently cover his face while doing so.
One should worship the Sun with faith at the three junctions of the day or at least once;
never, out of delusion, should one eat without having worshipped the Sun. This is to be known as the supreme duty; otherwise, a person remains merely a mortal.
One who eats without having first offered worship indeed eats excrement, like a dog.
This worship must always be performed by the three [classes] who have taken refuge in the Divine.
A yogi should worship with his mind, using flowers gathered from the forest.
If one kills for the sake of the gods or for the sake of flowers, he is not a killer;
however, if one should kill even a small amount for one's own sake, then he is indeed a killer.
One who is devoted to the deer, ever intent on the sacred fire, dedicated to that [practice], and a worshiper of guests—[is not a killer].
A householder belonging to the stage of life of the house-dweller (gṛhastha) should be illustrious and refrain from sexual intercourse [with others' wives].
He cooks food for the sake of the gods, the sacred fire, his own kin, and guests;
however, he who out of delusion cooks for his own sake alone—that householder shall go to hell.
For those whose cooking is for the sake of the gods, whose sexual union is for the sake of progeny,
and whose wealth is designated for the purpose of giving— hell indeed awaits them in the opposite case.
One should not perform worship even when one-third of the day has passed.
Since life is always [at risk] when acquiring wealth, one should spend half of it on that purpose;
one should possess wealth acquired through righteous means and avoid unrighteousness.
For by performing [deeds] with wealth acquired through unrighteous means, one would attain hell.
One who is a celibate student (brahmacārī) devoted to the meaning of the Veda, intent upon the worship of the Sun and the sacred fire,
who has conquered his senses and is peaceful— whether he be a lifelong student (naiṣṭhika) or one belonging to the stage of a householder (bhautika)—
being free from all perfumes and subsisting on bulbs, roots, and fruits;
My Vaikhanasa should be known as one intent on the worship of the Sun and the sacred fire;
having withdrawn from social gatherings, he is always devoted to meditation on the Sun.
He should be known as a leader among the Saura ascetics, dedicated to worship and having his senses subdued.
One who is shaven-headed, initiated, free from physical defects, and clad in white garments—this is to be known as the place for his worship; this must be performed with great care.
Furthermore, O Great King, if the Bhojaka priest is free from defects, he should maintain [the ritual].
He goes to the world of the Sun, which is inaccessible to all other beings;
it is the destruction of all the wicked and the remover of the fear of all sins.
The Maker of Day should be constantly worshipped by one whose disposition is pure.
Even one devoid of the application of perfumes does not incur fault if his inner disposition is pure; he should practice purification regarding his thoughts, drink water filtered through a cloth,
set down his foot purified by sight, and speak words purified by truth.
Devoted to the meditation on the Sun, peaceful, and dedicated to the dharma of the Sun—
all stages of life (āśramas) should be known as originating from the body of the Sun.
The incomparable vow of the eight-fold Bhoja should be observed as declared by the Sun.
The supreme and unsurpassed abode of Dharma among all vows is this: for a devotee of the Sun,
there is always forbearance, non-violence, constant tranquility,
contentment, truthfulness, non-stealing, and celibacy as the eighth.
One should always practice devotion to the Sun through worship according to one's capacity, by means of action, mind, and speech—
especially toward those who officiate the rites.
For the wise person should protect those officiants as if they were no different from his own body.
One should indeed do what is pleasing for them [the Brahmins] regarding fear, poverty, and disease.
O King, what can men truly do for the full sun? Whatever is done for the *bhojakas* is indeed done for the Sun.
Even if one must travel a very great distance, one should certainly go where there is a community of deer;
for the Sun is present there, and he should be beheld with effort by a devotee who is a *bhojaka* and is devoted to the worship of the Sun.
Having performed the command according to the rule, one obtains the fruit of the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*).
O King, having gone to a divine hermitage, one should worship the image of the deity with devotion,
following the sequence of welcome, a seat, water for the feet (*pādya*), the guest-offering (*arghya*), and the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*).
Having fed them according to the rule, one is glorified in the world of the Sun;
by providing shelter, O Bhārata, one becomes a king;
likewise, by giving a place for purification, one attains the world of Varuṇa.
One who fans with a palm-leaf fan a person whose limbs are covered in white spots, who is emaciated by the fatigue of meditation,
or likewise one who is afflicted by hunger and thirst, exhausted, soiled, or diseased, is honored in the world of Vāyu.

Having protected [them] according to one's ability, one shall obtain all desires. Out of compassion for all beings— including those who have fallen from their status, those who are censured, those of mixed caste, Caṇḍālas, and so forth— one should give food to birds according to one's own capacity.
Even a very small gift, when given out of compassion, becomes inexhaustible;
therefore, compassion toward all beings is said to be the highest form of devotion to the Divine.
In the absence [of other resources], one should give grass, ground, food, leaves, wealth, or fruits.
Having given [a gift] to one who has arrived, he goes to heaven by bowing down or with pleasant words;
for there is nothing like pleasant speech in this world for traveling to heaven. Those whose speech is sweet shall find happiness both here and in the hereafter.
Having spoken words that are like a stream of nectar, cool with the touch of sandalwood,
and non-contradictory to the Dharma, one shall attain imperishable happiness. O Indra among kings, enough with giving, or with worship and teaching!
This beloved speech is the immovable staircase to heaven;
honoring, addressing, and looking upon others—each of these is a cause for attaining heaven.
One should inquire with devotion and respectful attention after the welfare of a guest who has arrived.
When he departs, one should say: "May your paths be auspicious;
may you always have happiness that effectively accomplishes all your undertakings. This word of blessing should be uttered at all times and on every occasion.
In utterances such as salutations, in the recitation of auspicious blessings,
and in all ritual acts, one should say, "May there be constant welfare for you.
Having thus performed such verbal conduct, the resident of an ashrama should always remain steadfast.
Freed from all sins without exception, he is glorified in the world of the Sun.
Whatever devotion is practiced by virtuous men toward a devotee of the Sun,
that same devotion is constantly performed toward the devotee, equal to the devotion shown to the Sun himself.
Whether reviled or even struck, he who does not revile in return nor strike back—
being composed and self-possessed through his speech— is liberated from suffering.
Among all holy places (tīrthas), forbearance is most highly honored.
Therefore, one should first diligently practice forbearance in all actions.
Since knowledge, yoga, austerity, sacrifice, charity,
and virtuous deeds are all in vain for one who is prone to anger, one should therefore avoid anger.
Unpleasant speech burns the vital points, the bones, the life-force, and the heart. Therefore, one should never speak unpleasant words, especially toward those who provide food.
Forgiveness, generosity, splendor, truth, and non-violence—all these originate from the Sun.
"It is not possible to describe this in detail even in hundreds of years.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-first chapter, titled "Description of the Performance of Feeding the Bhojaka," within the Saura-dharma section of the Saptamī-kalpa in the Brāhma-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*. [This concludes] the Description of the Saura-dharma.
Sumantu said:
Listen again, O great king, to the dharma approved by Āditya— the eternal dharma of the Sun, dear to Sūrya, purifying, and the destroyer of sins.
Whenever, while traveling somewhere, he should see the worship of an image of the Sun, he should go toward that place where the worship is taking place; there is no doubt that it is the Sun himself.
[He should do so] with baths, food offerings, garments, and various ornaments and decorations.
Relying on one's means,
having seen the sacred site (āyatana), one should approach it, pay homage to the Sun with prostrations and other forms of praise, and then proceed.
On the path, one may encounter a river, a mountain, or a Bhojaka priest passing by.
Having heard this and gone to the ground, the wise man should honor the Bhojaka.
O King, having descended from his chariot, horse, elephant, or carriage,
he should provide food for the Magas with devotion and offer gifts according to his capacity.
O Bhārata, taking with him ten ancestors and ten descendants along with himself,
he shall go to the abode of the Sun of immeasurable splendor on auspicious festival days dedicated to the gods,
at a śrāddha ceremony, or on other holy days.

Having worshipped the Sun according to the prescribed rites, one should then feed the officiating priests. Since the ancestors of all the gods abide depending upon the Sun, when the Sun is pleased, they all become pleased; of this there is no doubt.
And when the worship of the Sun is performed with devotion and constancy,
O King, one should feed the officiating priest (*bhojaka*) with devotion according to the rules during the *śrāddha* rites.
O Great King, whatever fruit is obtained by the priest even in a single day—
It is not possible for him to attain this even in hundreds of years—
he who perceives with a serene soul, who neither hates nor desires,
and who is known as one who has conquered his senses because he does not indulge in the enjoyment of sounds and other objects.
One who is perfected in both knowledge and discernment, endowed with devotion to the Sun,
and liberated from the yoga of heresy— he indeed is called a *bhojaka*.
From the dharma of the Sun comes knowledge, and from knowledge arises detachment.
For one endowed with knowledge and dispassion, the yoga of the sun proceeds.
Through the yoga of the sun, he becomes omniscient, perfectly fulfilled, and utterly tranquil;
established in the self, pure, he rejoices in the sky like the sun.
The Puruṣa is remembered as the supreme among all beings;
the twice-born (dvija) is superior to ordinary men, and the one who has mastered the scriptures is superior to the twice-born.
Those who know the Vedas are superior to those who merely master the texts, and those who contemplate the meaning of reality are superior to them.
One awakened to the meaning of knowledge is superior to those who merely know the meaning; yogins are considered more excellent than millions upon millions of such seekers of knowledge;
and the patron who feeds them is the most excellent of all, even compared to millions upon millions of yogins.

The ancestors who possess yogic knowledge, who are established in yoga, and who are born of yoga—all of them become pleased when the host has fed [the guests]; of this there is no doubt. Whatever fruit is obtained through all forms of knowledge, austerity, and charity performed or bestowed, [that fruit is attained by feeding the guests].
One obtains the entire fruit of that which consists of the food, the eater,
the sacrificial materials, the ritual fees, the oblation, and the officiating priests,
as well as the application of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas; this is proclaimed as the sacrifice to the gods (devayajña) performed according to the rules.
Celibacy, austerity, silence, forbearance, and moderation in diet—
this is the form of austerities, firm and characterized by five marks.
Furthermore, whatever is ordained, excellent, and obtained through right means;
"To one who possesses such-and-such virtues, this is the definition of a gift:
one should give land endowed with water, which increases thousands [of crops] and causes all grains to sprout; that is called the gift of land."
Having brought the earth under a single umbrella, one should bestow it upon the twice-born;
that which is complete with its mountains and forests is called the gift of land.
O lord of men, one should give a decorated maiden to a man who is destitute.

The giving of a daughter to a twice-born man who is learned in the Vedas is called *kanyādāna*. She should be free from all defects, suitable for the family, and adorned with new garments of middling and superior quality.

This, in brief, should be known as the characteristic of the gift of clothing. One who is devoted to the splendor and virtue that exceed even those of Brahmā and Viṣṇu should not eat for a day and night; this indeed is the characteristic of fasting.
Two hundred and forty morsels of food,
taken at will according to one's desire within a month,
is known as the *Ādrāyaṇa* penance by the sages who know all the scriptures, who are devoted to austerity, and whose senses are conquered.
That water which is resorted to by the gods on earth is called a *tīrtha*.
One should point out the holy fields (*puṇyakṣetra*) situated within the solar orb;
for embodied beings who die in those solar fields, there is the attainment of the state of the Sun.
One should perform acts of charity, build dwellings, establish gardens, and construct temples for the gods. He who constructs these at sacred fords (tīrthas) obtains inexhaustible fruit.
Patience, lack of covetousness, truthfulness, charity, good conduct, austerity, and sacred learning—these are [the virtues].

This is declared to be the supreme eightfold characteristic of a worthy recipient (pātra). By feeding such recipients with devotion, one obtains in its entirety the fruits of sacrifices, vows, gifts, austerities, and pilgrimages.
Devotion to the Sun, forbearance, truthfulness, restraint of the ten senses,
and friendliness toward those who are happy— these are the characteristics of the Sun’s dharma.
Whoever, with devotion, feeds a twice-born devotee of the Sun at śrāddha ceremonies, [attains great merit].
Having uplifted seven generations of his lineage, he is glorified in the world of the Sun. What need is there for much speaking on this matter? One should feed a devotee of the Sun;
O King, that which is eaten by a devotee of the Sun becomes a refuge for the name of Bhānu.
That fruit is not obtained here even by ten million knowers of the Vedas;
yet, O King, one obtains that very fruit by offering food and clarified butter according to the prescribed rites.
Therefore, especially at a śrāddha and on auspicious days, [one should do so].
O best of Brahmins, O King, one should feed a Brahmin in honor of the Sun;
for whether he be unrestrained or self-controlled, even if he has fallen into any state whatsoever,
if he is a devotee of Ravi, he is indeed worthy of worship like the Sun himself.
Even if one causes a *bhojaka* to eat out of social association or greed,
he shall attain a destination that cannot be reached even by hundreds of sacrifices.
Therefore, such a person is always to be honored, worshipped, and protected.
O tiger among the Kurus, the Bhojaka priest was approached by Saura, who desired a way [to attain his goal].
"If even one who makes an effort merely in name were to become a Bhojaka priest of the Sun,
he should indeed be regarded like the Sun himself and worshipped, O Bhārata."
The merit that comes from performing a *śrāddha* at home is increased a hundredfold in the forest;
in the hermitages of the Sun (*saura-āśrama*), that merit should be known to be increased ten-thousandfold.
Having given a pleasant seat along with its furnishings to the officiant (*bhojaka*), O gentle one...
O Lord of the Earth,
by giving two stainless garments to a cook, a king on this earth becomes possessed of teeth made of precious gems;
having offered a hundred thousand [coins], he is glorified in the world of the Sun.
O King, having given a large, auspicious cow with hairy coats to a Bhojaka,
one obtains the fruit of gold given for every single hair.
Likewise, he who gives a conch shell and divine sandals with devotion [obtains great merit].
He who causes a manuscript of a Purāṇa to be written with devotion attains the world of the Sun, resembling the Sun in splendor;
he is glorified in the world of the Sun for a hundred divine crores of yugas.

One who builds a house for the Sun would become glorious, wealthy in happiness, and a master of the Vedas; that location shall be most excellent. Here, the Sun is the patron (bhojaka), for indeed, the patron is the Sun himself.
Therefore, it is said that a gift given to Brahmins who are cattle-herders is inexhaustible.
Whatever may be useful to anyone, that should be given to them with diligence;
for the Sun is always intent on utility toward both of these [classes].
O gods, having performed the exposition of the solar dharma, one should place a large *āmalaka* fruit,
adorned with flowers, leaves, and the like, upon that seat;
it is the great means for the propitiation of the Sun, beautified with garlands and perfumes.
Having established the preceptor before him, one should always worship him;
these two statements regarding the Saura Dharma are equal, like the sun itself. Whoever speaks the Saura Dharma according to this principle and whoever listens to it [attains the highest goal].
Having obtained longevity, knowledge, glory, and fame, one should recite the *Ravi-mantra*.
Some say it, others drink [its essence]; all of them partake in the fruit.
Therefore, the wise know that such is the nature of dharma for those who recite.

"One who desires extensive fame should worship at its conclusion with devotion. Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Duties of the Sun," in the Saura-dharma section of the Brāhma-parvan within the glorious *Bhaviṣya-mahāpurāṇa*.
Śatānīka said:
O best of Brahmins, tell me again the unsurpassed dharma of the Sun;
though it has been spoken in brief, O Brahmin, proclaim it in detail.
Sumantu said: "Excellent, excellent, O mighty-armed one! Well have I been questioned by you, O Bhārata.
There is no one equal to you in this world, O best of kings, who possesses such solar knowledge."
O King, O lord of men, I shall now proclaim that meritorious dialogue between Garuḍa and Aruṇa which destroys all sins— an account of events from the past.
Long ago, O King, Aruṇa, the charioteer of the Sun, was seated comfortably.
Having approached, O mighty-armed one, Garuḍa spoke these words:
"O sinless one, best of birds, tell me in its entirety the solar dharma— the supreme among all dharmas— which destroys all sins."
Aruṇa said:
"Excellent, my child! You are a great soul, blessed and free from sin.
Since you desire to hear, O son, the unsurpassed dharma of Sūrya,"
Listen, I shall proclaim this easy means of great fruit,
the supreme among all dharmas, the unsurpassed dharma of the Sun;
it is for all living beings who are submerged in the ocean of ignorance.
For this glorious solar dharma indeed bestows the further shore;
O bird, those who remember the Sun with devotion, those who glorify him,
and those who worship him constantly, have gone to the supreme state.
O Lord of Birds, he who has been born in this world but has not worshipped Ravi, the thousand-rayed Lord of Gods, has committed an act of self-betrayal;
he wanders for a very long time in this sorrow-inducing ocean of worldly existence.
In this great crocodile-infested ocean of old age, where others are tossed about by the surging waves of craving,
those who, having attained this rare human birth, worship the Sun—
their life is indeed fruitful; they are the best of men, having accomplished their purpose.
Those who are devoted to the Sun, whose minds are fixed upon him,
and those who always remember the Sun— they shall not partake of suffering.
[They shall possess] various charming things and women adorned with diverse ornaments.
Those who desire wealth with its visible limits as the fruit of the ritual for worshipping the Sun;
or those who long for great enjoyments, or sovereignty in the abode of the thirty gods;
or good fortune, incomparable luster, enjoyment, renunciation, fame, and prosperity—[for them, this is the means].
O wise son, it is traditionally taught that beauty, renown, fame, righteousness, and other such qualities are indeed the fruits of the practice of devotion to the Sun;
therefore, one should worship the Sun, who is honored by all the hosts of gods.
Devotion to the Sun is difficult to attain, and his worship is likewise difficult to achieve;
giving gifts to him is rare, and the performance of oblations for him is exceedingly rare. Knowledge of him is difficult to obtain, and even the practice thereof is hard to find.
The supreme propitiation of them should be known as exceedingly difficult to attain;
for those men who have gone for refuge to the Sun, there is no greed.
Their minds are constantly fixed here upon the Lord Bhanu, the Sun.

The two syllables "Ravi" (the Sun), preceded by the salutation "Namaḥ" and so forth, abide on the tip of the tongue of whoever possesses them; for him, his entire life is fruitful. Whoever thus worships the Sun, endowed with supreme faith, [attains all success].
That man is liberated from all sins; there is no doubt about this.
Dākinīs of various forms, Rākṣasas along with Piśācas, and other terrifying beings do not cause him any affliction.
Enemies shall meet their destruction, and he shall attain victory in battle.
The hero shall not be afflicted by diseases, nor shall calamities touch him.
Indeed, wealth, longevity, fame, knowledge, and incomparable power shall be his.
"Through auspiciousness, they always attain prosperity, their desires ever fulfilled.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-third chapter, titled "Description of the Solar Duties," within the dialogue between Garuḍa and Aruṇa in the *Saptamī-kalpa* of the *Brāhma-parvan* in the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
[This is followed by] the "Description of the Praise of the Sun."
Aruṇa said:
By worshipping the Sun with devotion, Brahmā attained the state of Brahmā;
and the Lord of Gods, Viṣṇu, also attained the state of Viṣṇu through that very adoration.
Śaṅkara, the Lord of the World, having worshipped the Sun,
attained the state of Mahādeva through his grace, O Lord of Birds.
Even Indra, the thousand-eyed Lord of the Gods, [worshipped] Bhānu, the dispeller of darkness.
Having worshipped the Sun, the god attained the status of Indra.
The Mothers, gods, Gandharvas, Piśācas, Uragas,
and Rākṣasas always worship Bhānu, the Lord and leader of the gods.
This entire world is eternal and is established in the divine Sun;
therefore, one who desires imperishable heaven should worship the Sun.
He who does not worship Sūrya, the Maker of Light, the Destroyer of Darkness—
A man would not be a fit vessel for dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa;
therefore, that meditation must indeed be practiced with a vow for as long as one lives.
O bird, even when one has fallen into calamity, one should always worship the Sun.
But for one who always persists without the worship of the Sun—
better is the abandonment of life or even the cutting off of the head;
having fully worshipped the Sun, the Lord of the Thirty-three Gods, one should eat.
He whose worship of Him continues in this manner for as long as he lives—he, though bound in human skin, is the Sun himself; of this there is no doubt.
Indeed, there can be no merit greater than the worship of the Sun.
Having understood this, worship the Sun with diligence.
Those who are devoted to the scriptures on the Sun, intent upon the worship of the Sun,
self-controlled, and endowed with righteousness, accomplish dharma and other goals.
These heroes endure all dualities; their minds are intent on the principles of ethics and right conduct.
They are devoted to helping others and delight in serving their gurus.
Free from pride, possessed of wisdom, they do not compete with the unmanifest and are devoid of worldly longing.
They were peaceful, inwardly composed, auspicious, and always spoke with a welcoming greeting; they were of few words, well-disposed, heroic, and proficient in the scriptures;
they were perfectly endowed with purity and right conduct, and were characterized by compassion and courtesy.
Free from hypocrisy and envy, devoid of craving and greed, they are said to be devoted to sharing; they are neither deceitful nor contemptible.
Even amidst sense objects, they remain unstained, like a lotus leaf by water.

Those of purified soul are neither dejected nor arrogant, nor are they subject to the power of disease; they are exceedingly gentle and devoted to the service of the virtuous. They take no delight in their hands, feet, speech, eyes, ears, genitals, or stomach.
Free from all attachments, they do not act with fickleness;
devoted to the seat of the Sun, peaceful, and with the six-syllabled mantra dwelling in their minds—
such are the men on earth who are endowed with this conduct.

Resorting to exclusive devotion for the sake of attaining dharma, kāma, and artha, one should worship the Sun daily; for he abides in these very virtues. Of all worthy recipients, the Maker of Day is the most excellent recipient.
Because it saves one who is falling from the exceedingly deep ocean of hell,
even a tiny gift given to such a worthy recipient (pātrātipātra) is of great majesty;
by this, the fruit is ordained both in this world and in the next.
For even that man who performs an act in that temple with material wealth shall,
upon the dissolution of the body, attain knowledge and reach peace; indeed,
someone among the entire assembly of the twice-born shall obtain knowledge.
Someone who, having obtained this divine knowledge of mine, abandons it,
continues to wander in saṃsāra, overwhelmed by suffering and grief,
as long as all embodied beings do not become devotees of the Sun.
Anointing with *sūrya* incense yields merit, while that of sandalwood (*candana*) is twice as great.
The merit from *agaru* is known to be eight times greater than that of sandalwood;
specifically, the fruit from black *agaru* is held to be double that amount.
Therefore, a hundredfold merit is ordained for saffron.
Having prepared even a small or large set of implements for the Sun-sacrifice,
according to one's devotion and means, one is glorified in the world of the Sun.
Whatever comes by way of destiny, whether desirable or undesirable,
that should be offered with true devotion to the Sun by one who seeks infinite fruit. He who performs that worship even with difficulty, yet without deceit in his actions, [attains the goal].
That twice-born man also goes to heaven, freed from sin by his actions;
having renounced everything else, he who desires his own welfare should always be single-minded toward the Sun and perform the ritual for the worship of the Sun.
Life passes swiftly, and youth likewise passes swiftly;
even disease approaches swiftly. Therefore, one should constantly resort to the Sun while death has not yet arrived and while old age has not yet overtaken one.
"As long as there is no impairment of the senses, so long should one worship the Maker of Day;
for there is no other dharma in the three worlds equal to the worship of the Sun.
Having understood this, worship Divākara, the Lord of Gods."
Those who, with devotion, worship the Lord of the gods of gods, the peaceful, unborn, and sovereign Sūrya,
having attained happiness in this world, have gone to the supreme state,
after having honored the Lord of Rays with a joyful inner self.
Having joined his palms in reverence, Brahmā spoke this in the past.
Brahmā said:
"To the Blessed One, the bestower of fortune, whose mind is tranquil and who is unsurpassed—"
I am forever bowed down to the Sun, the guide upon the path of the gods;
the eternal, beautiful, pure, and multiformed lord of day. I am bowed down to the Maker of Light, the Lord of the gods of gods, the Sovereign of lords.

I bow eternally to Vibhāvasu, the god who removes all suffering, the sun who removes all suffering; he of the excellent countenance and excellent limbs, the one of excellent station who bestows boons, the most worthy one, the giver of boons.
I bow down to Arka, Aryaman, Indra, Viṣṇu, Īśa, Divākara, Deveśvara, Devarata, and Vibhāvasu. Whoever should daily hear this supreme hymn spoken by Brahmā, [shall attain the highest state].
"Having attained supreme fame, he shall indeed go again to the city of the Sun.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-fourth chapter, titled "The Praise of the Sun," in the dialogue between Garuḍa and Aruṇa within the Saptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan in the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
[This section] describes the rites of the Sun and Fire.
Garuḍa said:
Those men who are struck by all diseases, possessed of mental and physical ailments,
and afflicted by various planetary oppressions;
"O sinless one, what should be done for the welfare of those who are oppressed by enemies and those who have been slain by their leaders?
Aruṇa said:
For those struck by various diseases as well as those afflicted by enemies,
there is no other supreme means of securing welfare than the propitiation of Āditya.
Therefore, one should constantly worship him, who is the destroyer of all diseases.
[It is] the destroyer of planetary afflictions and the eradicator of royal calamities.
Garuḍa said:
[Grant it to me] entirely devoid of leaves and free from all diseases.
"Behold my body, O best of the twice-born, [as it is] by the curse of the knower of Brahman.
O father, what task remains for me who am thus intoxicated? By what action might I become fit once again to possess leaves?"
"Tell that to me, O best of birds, O lord of birds, for I have sought refuge in you: what act must I perform so that, having attained perfection, I may worship the Sun?
Aruṇa said:
Worship Bhāskara, the Lord of the World, who dispels darkness;
with a pure mind, constantly perform the fire-ritual (agnikārya) dedicated to the Sun.
This is renowned as the bringer of great peace and the destroyer of all calamities.
[He is] the destroyer of planetary afflictions and the supreme performer of auspicious deeds.
Garuḍa said:
"I am indeed not capable of performing the worship of the Sun."
"Having become incapacitated, I am unable to perform the fire-ritual (agnikārya).
Therefore, O Lord of Birds, perform the fire-ritual for my sake to bring about peace;
O observer of noble vows, it is known as 'Mahāśānti' for the sake of my pacification."
Aruṇa said:
"O Vainateya, lord of birds, it is exactly as you say;
being afflicted by a great disease, you are incapable and unable [to carry me]."
"O son, for your peace, I shall perform the worship of the Fire-god,
which was formerly performed by Arka for me with devotion as a bestower of tranquility—
a meritorious rite that removes all sins and destroys great obstacles."
The procedure for the Lakṣahoma is remembered as bringing great prosperity and providing protection;
O Hero, it removes untimely death, is supreme in curing all diseases,
crushes the armies of enemies, and always increases victory.

Having smeared the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) with cow dung in the south-eastern direction according to the rules, one should then awaken the fire for the temple, which grants satisfaction to all the gods and is most beloved by the Sun.
O Hero, one should perform a hundred-thousand-fold oblation (lakṣahoma) with the Mahāvyāhṛtis:
"Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā," accompanied by the Praṇava (Om),
for the Great Soul whose body and form are reddish and whose eyes are red.
One should offer the first oblation with "Svāhā" to the mountain-bearer, the peaceful one, the thousand-eyed and thousand-headed, the downward-facing,
and the white one; and to the four-faced, the peaceful one, seated upon the lotus throne.
One should offer an oblation with the utterance "Svāhā" here to the lotus-colored Creator who holds a water-pot and has a second face turned upward;
and to the golden-hued body seated upon Airāvata.
One should offer the utterance "Svāhā" to the thousand-eyed one, to him who faces the eastern direction,
to Indra the lord of gods, to the dexterous one, to the auspicious one,
and indeed to the one with three faces.
To the radiant one, whose body is manifest, who is surrounded by garlands of flames,
whose body has the luster of a sapphire, who bestows all health,
to Yama, the King of Dharma, whose face is turned toward the southern quarter.
One should offer a *svāhā* oblation here to the one who wears black garments;
to the one with the color of a dark blue cloud, who wears red garments,
whose body is like a pearl, who has tawny eyes, and who is the Great Soul.
To the one clad in white garments, to the yellow one, and to the bearer of the divine noose;
likewise to the one characterized by the utterance of "svāhā," and to the one facing westward;
to the one with dark-brown eyes, and to the one facing the northwest.
The wise man should here offer an oblation with the cry "Svāhā! to Nīladhvaja, to Vīra, as well as to Indra, to Vedhas, and to Pavana;
and [an oblation] to Sūrya, who holds a mace in his hand and is adorned with variegated garlands.
To Mahodara, to Śānta, and likewise to Svāhādhipati;
to him who faces north here, and to the beloved of Mahādeva;
to Śveta, to the one of white complexion, to Citrākṣa, and to the Great Soul.

O sinless tiger among birds, one should offer an oblation here to Īśa, who is peaceful, whose form is peaceful, who bears the excellent Pināka bow, and who faces the northeast; one should release [the offering] according to the rules for the sake of spiritual welfare.
O bird, one should thus honor the high-souled god Pāvaka according to the prescribed rites;
O best of birds, that which must be performed for the Sun-god is as follows:
having performed the Lakṣahoma sacrifice according to the rules, one should perform the propitiatory rite (śāntika).
"Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ Svāhā"—this is recorded as the procedure for a hundred-thousand-fold oblation (*lakṣahoma*).
In a great oblation (*mahāhoma*) dedicated to the Sun, this indeed is the supreme rule.
Having thus performed the fire-rite, the one who feeds the guests should indeed [offer] to Bhāskara.

Then, for the sake of the peace of all the worlds, one should perform the rite of pacification (śāntika). The deity has the luster of vermilion, a seat, and red light; his eyes have the brilliance of a red lotus; he is the thousand-rayed god whose vehicle is a chariot drawn by seven horses.
May the Blessed One, garlanded with rays and saluted by all the gods,
grant you great peace that wards off the afflictions of the planets—
he who is mounted upon a triple-wheeled chariot made of the essence of the waters.
May the god Soma— the ten-horse-drawn, descendant of Atri, the flowing nectar,
the cool-rayed one, whose essence is immortality, and who is endowed with waning and waxing—
dispel the affliction caused by the planets through his gentle nature.
May Aṅgāraka, who resembles a ruby, whose eyes are tawny like honey,
and who is like fire itself, dispel the affliction caused by the planets.
He is entirely tawny here with a body resembling a topaz.
May Budha, wearing yellow garlands and garments, dispel my suffering.
Resembling molten red chalk, proficient in all scriptures,
the teacher of all gods, the Brahmin sage who is the foremost of the Atharvans.
May he who is renowned as Bṛhaspati and is devoted to the science of statecraft (Arthaśāstra),
with a tranquil mind and being perfectly composed,
conquer the affliction of the planets and perform for you the rite of pacification.

Constantly devoted to the worship of the Sun, by the grace of Bhāskara he became as radiant as snow, the kunda flower, and the moon; then that wise and high-minded Maheśvara became a great devotee of Sūrya, honored by Daityas and Dānavas.
May Śukra, who is constantly devoted to the worship of the Sun, who then appears with a white luster,

and who is eternally intent upon the science of ethics (nītiśāstra), remove the affliction caused by the planets. He who assumes various forms, who is unmanifest, and whose course is unknown— may he [grant protection].
He whose birth does not occur even when afflicted by the rising [of obstacles]—
he who has one crest, two crests, three peaks, or five crests;
who possesses a form with a thousand heads, standing like the moon-bannered one (Śiva).
The son of the Sun, the son of Fire, whose nature is that of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva,
the comet with its many crests— may he remove all affliction from you.
These high-souled planets are always devoted to the worship of the Sun.
"May they, being delighted and ever intent on our welfare, grant us peace.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Duties of the Sun," within the section on the rites of the Sun and Fire, in the Saura-dharma of the Brāhma-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, in the Saptamī-kalpa.
Sumantu said:
Seated upon a lotus, lotus-colored, with eyes like lotus petals,
holding a water-pot, glorious, and worshipped by gods and gandharvas.
May Brahmā— the four-faced lord of gods, ever devoted to the worship of the Sun,
the eldest of the deities, possessed of great splendor, and the progenitor of all the worlds—
grant you peace through his divine name, "Brahman."
The god Krama, who always delights in Ātreyī, wears yellow garments;
he is dark-complexioned, four-armed, and holds a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands.
He is the embodiment of sacrifice and is eternally beloved by Ātreyī.
May Viṣṇu—the Mādhava, the slayer of Madhu, who holds the conch, discus, and mace in his hands;
who is eternally accompanied by the devotees of the Sun; who is free from death and free from the three qualities (guṇas);
and who is perpetually intent on meditation upon the Sun—grant you peace.
Resembling the moon, the kunda flower, and the moon in brilliance, adorned here with renowned ornaments,
four-armed and of great splendor, with a crest formed by half a flower;
four-faced, wearing ashes, and eternally dwelling in the cremation ground.
The enemy of the mountain, the abode of the universe, and likewise the destroyer of the sacrifice;
the excellent one, the most worthy of choice, the giver of boons, the God of gods, Maheśvara,
who is born from the body of Āditya— may he indeed grant you peace.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for Fire-Sacrifice," in the Sauradharma section of the Saptamī-kalpa within the Brāhma-parvan of the glorious *Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*. Aruṇa said:
The goddess Padmarāgaprabhā has four lotus-like faces;
her auspicious hands hold a rosary and a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu);
Brahmāṇī, with a gentle countenance, is devoted to the worship of the Sun.

O bird, may she, who is ever beloved by the Sun, renowned as Mahāśvetā, who resembles snow, the kunda flower, and the moon, and who rides upon a great bull— may she, being well-pleased and intent on bestowing blessings, grant peace.
Holding a trident in her hand, adorned with renowned ornaments,
virtuous, four-armed, four-faced, and three-eyed, she is the destroyer of sins;
devoted to the worship of the bull-bannered Lord, may Rudrāṇī be the bestower of peace.
The goddess has a peacock for her vehicle; her body is crimson like vermilion;
she holds a spear in her hand, possesses a massive form, and is adorned with all ornaments. She is devoted to the Sun, endowed with great heroism, and is ever intent upon the worship of the Sun.

May the goddess Kaumārī, the bestower of boons, swiftly grant you peace. O bird, that goddess Vaiṣṇavī is dark-complexioned, wears yellow garments, holds a mace and a discus, possesses four arms, and is indeed worshipped by the gods.
Constantly devoted to the worship of the Sun, with her mind solely fixed on the Sun,
may she who crushes all asuras grant you perpetual peace;
she who is mounted upon the elephant Airāvata, holds a thunderbolt in her hand, and possesses great strength.
May the goddess Locanā, who is everywhere, who is variegated and reddish in hue,
who is saluted by Siddhas and Gandharvas, and who is adorned with all ornaments—
may that goddess Indrāṇī always quickly grant you peace.
The goddess whose snout is like that of a boar, who is formidable, and who rides upon an excellent boar; she who is dark yet radiant, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace;
she who illumines the moments and always worships the Sun.
May the goddess Vārāhī, the bestower of boons, truly grant you peace.
Ardhakośā, emaciated at the waist, devoid of flesh due to the binding of her sinews,
Karālavanā, the terrible Khaḍgaghaṇṭodgatā, being virtuous— may she protect you.
Wearing a garland of skulls, cruel, and holding a khaṭvāṅga as her supreme weapon;
reddish-brown in hue with tawny eyes, she is draped in an elephant hide. Adorned with ornaments of cow-horns, the Goddess dwells in the abode of the departed spirits.
In her terrible form as Śivā, she who is fearsome even to the form of Śiva,
may Cāmuṇḍā, in her fierce form, always grant you peace.
May the Goddess, who holds Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa in her hands, being the virtuous one residing within the body of Muṇḍa, [grant you peace].
The goddess Kapālamālinī, who is cruel and holds a sword (khaḍga) as her excellent weapon;
the Ākāśamātṛ goddesses, as well as others who are the Lokamātṛs;
all the Bhūtamātṛs, and likewise others who are the Pitṛmātṛs.
Those goddesses who are worshipped by the wise during the Vṛddhi-śrāddhas—
namely Mātṛ, Pramātṛ, and Tanmātṛ, as well as those headed by the Mothers (Mātṛmukhās)— as also Pitāmahī, her mother (Tanmātā), and the elder Pitāmahī.
Thus, these grandmothers on the father’s side,
your paternal mothers, all the great goddesses of the mothers, with their own weapons held busily in their hands,
pervading the world, remain established there, desiring offerings and possessing great majesty.
May those Śāntis, who are ever devoted to the worship of the Sun,
bestow peace upon you with peaceful minds; they are the givers of peace,
possessing beautiful waists and limbs where every part is preeminent.
Yellowish-dark and gentle, she was radiant with a glossy complexion;
adorned with a tilaka on her forehead and bearing the crescent of the moon,
the goddess wore variegated garments and was embellished with every ornament.
The supreme goddess Umā, the bestower of boons, who is the very embodiment of the beauty and perfect excellence of all forms of excellent women, and who is content with mere contemplation,
has arrived in person with a tranquil form and immeasurable splendor.
"May the Adityas, pleased and devoted to bestowing prosperity, grant you peace.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of Solar Duties," within the section on the Ritual of Fire-offerings (*agnikārya-vidhi*) concerning the Ten-faced One (*daśamukha*) in the *Sauradharma* (Duties of the Sun) of the *Saptamī-kalpa*, in the *Brāhma-parvan* of the glorious *Mahāpurāṇa Bhaviṣya*.
Aruṇa said:
The glorious one with three points, who possesses a trident and a spear, appears in the east in the form of a child, though he is not weak; he has a skull-topped staff and a peacock for his vehicle.
Born from the limbs of Kṛttikā and Rudra, honored by the gods,
the immensely radiant Kārtikeya— who is endowed with the splendor of the Sun and the boon of Āditya—
may he grant you constant peace, strength, happiness, and luster through his brilliance.
O Lord of Birds, the son of Atri is powerful, healthy,
and radiant like gold; he wears white garments, possesses three eyes,
holds a trident in his hand, is endowed with great wisdom, is the lord of rivers, and is propitiated by the Sun.
May the peaceful one grant you peace and the highest resolve toward the Dharma;
may he, who is eternal and immovable, bestow both the Dharma and its opposite.
Mahodara, of massive body and a luster like smooth collyrium—
The god with a single tusk is fierce, elephant-faced, and possessed of great strength;
he is adorned with a serpent as a sacred thread and various ornaments.
He is the extractor of all goals and attainments, the leader of the Gaṇas, and the bestower of boons.
May the divine son of Bhīma, the leader and Vināyaka,
who is devoted to the worship of the Sun, grant you great peace;
he who resembles a sapphire, possesses three eyes, and holds aloft his blazing trident weapon.
Clad in red garments, glorious, with a dark-blue body, adorned with serpents,
the remover of incomparable sin, invisible, and the destroyer of impurity—
may he, being pleased, grant you great peace with a gracious heart.
Clad in excellent garments and adorned with various ornaments,
she is the mother of the thirty gods, meritorious, and honored by the worlds;
the goddess who grants all perfections is the supreme abode of grace.
May your mother, the crusher of the great buffalo, bring you peace, O Lord of Birds! She is of a glossy, dark-blue complexion,
armed with a bow and a discus, and bearing a sword and a paṭṭiśa.
May Durgā, Bhavānī, and likewise Śivā— who has hands extended with the index fingers raised and who destroys all calamities— grant you peace.
For the great Bhṛṅgirīṭi, though possessing three eyes, is exceedingly subtle and free from excessive anger.
May the Great Hero, whose essence is the Sun, whose mind is solely intent upon the Sun,
and who constantly practices devotion to the Sun, bestow auspiciousness upon you.
May he, the Lord of the fierce army of attendants, who bears the great bell and the akṣa beads, grant you well-being.
May the excellent Akṣacaṇḍeśvara, whose hand is joined with a rosary,
who eternally destroys fierce sins and annihilates the murder of a Brahmin,
grant you perpetual peace as he remains devoted to the worship of the Sun.
And the great yogi effects a succession of auspicious deeds.
The divine mothers of space, as well as other mothers of the gods—
goddesses devoted to the path of the sun— remain pervading the entire world.

May the Mothers, who are worshipped by the gods, grant me constant peace. Those Rudras of fierce deeds who dwell in terrible abodes, the Mothers who possess the forms of Rudras, and those who are the lords of the Gaṇas— may they grant me peace.
Likewise, others who have become obstacles and who dwell in the cardinal and intermediate directions—
may they all, with pleased minds, accept my bali offering;
may they grant me success constantly and protect me from fears on every side.
Those hosts led by Indra, who hold thunderbolts in their hands and possess great strength;
who resemble snow, the kunda flower, and the moon, yet have limbs that are dark blue and red;
who dwell in heaven, the intermediate space, on earth, and in the depths of the netherworld.

May those belonging to Indra bring about peace and auspiciousness again and again. All those who are stationed in the south-eastern quarter, associated with the destruction of Dhruva, devoted to the Sun, possessing a red luster like that of the Japā flower; may they likewise grant peace.
The divine Bhāskara and the others in the south-east, whose redness is passionless,
who are intent on the propitiation of Āditya and whose minds are fixed upon Āditya—
may they grant me constant peace and accept my offering.
Those who are like the sun in brilliance, who constantly hold staffs in their hands,
and are devoted to the worship of the Sun— what can they ever grant? But those who abide in the northeast, peaceful and bearing tridents in their hands— [what can they grant?]
With their bodies smeared with ashes, blue-throated and crimson-hued,
they dwell in the heavens, the atmosphere, on earth, and in the depths of the netherworld;
they are constant worshippers of the Sun, having offered worship to the one garlanded with rays.
Then, with minds well-pleased, accompanied by the world-protectors (Lokapālas),
may they, being duly honored, grant me constant peace and bestow happiness.
In the eastern quarter is situated the city named Amarāvatī.
Crowded with hosts of Vidyādharas and frequented by Siddhas and Gandharvas,
it was beautiful with jeweled walls and adorned with great gems;
there dwelt the glorious Lord of the Gods, the mighty Vajrapāṇi.
Gopati shines with a thousand resplendent cows;
mounted upon the elephant Airāvata, possessing the hue of red chalk and great luster,
the lord of the gods is ever joyful and devoted to the worship of the Sun.
May Sūryapraṇāma— who is solely devoted to the knowledge of the Sun and endowed with devotion to the Sun—
grant you supreme peace today.
In the region of the southeast, there is the auspicious city Tejasvatī.
Crowded with various hosts of gods and adorned with diverse jewels,
there dwells the god Agni— the burner, the consumer of cities, the destroyer of sins— surrounded by flames and possessing a radiance like glowing embers.
Devoted to the worship of the Sun, with his mind fixed upon the Sun,
may that deity grant you peace as well as the complete destruction of your sins.
To the south of that Great-Souled One lies the beautiful city of Vaivasvata.
Crowded with hundreds of gods and demons and adorned with various jewels,
[he saw] there one who resembled a jasmine flower or the moon, with tawny-yellow eyes,
mounted upon a great buffalo, and wearing black garlands, garments, and ornaments.

Now, Antaka, of great splendor, who is devoted to the dharma of the Sun and intent upon the propitiation of Āditya, may he grant you security and health. In the southwestern quarter of the directions, there is a city renowned as Kṛṣṇā.
It was crowded with hosts of demons of delusion, impurity, piśācas, and pretas;
therein stood the god, resembling a jasmine flower, adorned with red garlands, garments, and ornaments,
holding a sword in his hand, possessed of great splendor, and radiant with a formidable countenance.
The lord of the Rakṣasas dwells there eternally, devoted to the worship of the Sun;
may he always grant me peace and bestow upon me wealth and grain.
In the western quarter, there is the city Śuddhavatī forever.
Crowded with various bhujangas and frequented by diverse kinnaras,
may he who resembles the kunda flower and the moon, whose eyes are tawny like a lion,
being pleased, peaceful, and with a tranquil mind, grant me peace.
The beautiful city of Yaśovatī is situated in the northeastern direction;
it is filled with various hosts of attendants and contains many auspicious dwellings of diverse forms.
Encircled by a wall of splendor, it is incomparable and eternally radiant.
Therein, may the supreme Lord Īśāna— who resembles a kunda flower or the moon, whose eyes are like lotuses, who is adorned,
who possesses three eyes, whose nature is peaceful, and who holds a rosary—
grant eternal peace.
May those who always dwell in the world of Bhūḥ and the world of Bhuvaḥ—
the gods among gods, endowed with auspiciousness— grant peace forever. And may those who have gone to Maharloka, Janoloka, and the world beyond likewise grant peace.
May all those joyful gods grant you peace forever.
May Sarasvatī, the devotee of the Sun, bestow peace upon me—
she who dwells in beautiful gold and whose hands are like tender lotus petals.
May the Goddess, who is devoted to the Sun, bestow prosperity upon you.
Adorned with a girdle of shining gold by the most wonderful Hara,
may Aparājitā, the devotee of the Sun, grant you victory.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Duties of the Sun," in the Sauradharma section of the Brāhma Parvan within the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa. [The Description of the Duties of the Sun.
Aruṇa said:
Kṛttikā is the supreme goddess, and Rohiṇī is fair-faced;
Mṛgaśiras is glorious and auspicious, and Ārdrā is likewise radiant.
So too are Punarvasu, Puṣya, and Āśleṣā, O Lord.
Constantly devoted to the worship of the Sun and permeated by the nature of the Sun,
these Mothers of the Constellations, adorned with garlands of light, always worship the god Āditya in the celestial realm.
Maghā, endowed with all virtues, as well as Pūrvaphalgunī,
Svātī, and Viśākhā— the bestowers of boons— residing in the southern direction,
always worship the god Āditya, who is honored by the gods.
May these stars, risen in the sky, also bring you peace and radiance:
Anurādhā, Jyeṣṭhā, Mūla preceded by the Sun (Pūrvāṣāḍhā),
the highly powerful Pūrvāṣāḍhā, and likewise Uttarāṣāḍhā.
The constellation named Abhijit and Śravaṇa, which is rich in sacred learning—
these shine resplendently in the west, following the forms [of the sun].
Well-cultivated, they worship the Sun at all times.
May they always grant peace and great, magnificent prosperity—
Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣā, Pūrvabhādrapadā,
as well as Uttarabhādrapadā, Revatī, and Aśvinī, O high-minded one.
And the great goddess Bharaṇī, eternally stationed to the north,
constantly devoted to the worship of the Sun with her mind fixed upon Āditya,
may she grant you perpetual peace and great, prosperous power.
The Ram, the lion who is the lord of beasts, and the Archer, the best among the luminaries—
may these auspicious ones, intent on union with the Sun, illuminate the eastern quarter;
may they grant peace eternally through devotion to the lotus feet of the Sun.
Taurus, Virgo, Capricorn,
and Sagittarius— these always worship the Sun in the southern direction with supreme devotion; may they always grant you peace.
Gemini, Libra, and Aquarius are situated in the west;
these always chant to Āditya for the protection of the planets.
May they, who are devoted to the command of Khakholka, constantly grant peace.
May those seven renowned sages, who are constantly remembered by the wise as Satapa, Datta, and Puṣpa, and who are brilliantly radiant and culminate in Dhruva,
having attained perfection through the grace of the Sun, always bestow peace.
Kaśyapa, Gālava, Gārgya, the great sage Viśvāmitra, the sage Dakṣa, Vasiṣṭha, Mārkaṇḍeya, Pulaha, Kratu,
Nārada, Bhṛgu, Ātreya, and the sage Bhāradvāja.
Vālmīki, Kauśika, Vātsya, Śākalya, Punarvasu,
and Śālaṅkāyana— may these sages of great asceticism,
who are solely devoted to meditation upon the Sun, grant you peace at all times.
May the highly fortunate daughters of the Munis, the daughters of the Rishis, and the young maidens,

who are ever devoted to the worship of the Sun, grant you perpetual peace. May the Siddhas, those whose austerities are perfected, and all others who are great ascetics, likewise bestow peace upon you.
The high-souled Vidyādharas and Garuḍa, together with you—
these who are indeed supreme to the Ādityas and devoted to the propitiation of the Ādityas—
may they, intent upon bestowing blessings, grant you success.
Namuci, the lord of the Daityas, Śaṅkukarṇa of great strength,
Mahānātha, and the famous Daitya of supreme heroism—
all were constantly devoted to the worship of the god who is the lord of the planets.
"May they proclaim your strength, your heroism, your supernatural power, and your health!
[There are] the very wealthy Hayagrīva, Prahlāda who is endowed with splendor,
the Daitya Tānaka, Agnimukha, and the mighty Kālanemi."

May these high-souled Daityas, the enemies of the gods, who have been conceived as the nature of the sun, grant contentment, strength, and likewise health— Vairocana, Hiraṇyākṣa, Turvasu, and Sulocana.
Mucakuṇḍa, Mukunda, and the Daitya Raivataka likewise worship this Sun constantly with supreme devotion;
may those of auspicious nature always grant them prosperity forever.
May the illustrious lords of the Daityas, the auspicious daughters of the Daityas,
and those who are the sons of the Daityas always grant peace.
With bodies of deep red hue, they possess large eyes with reddish corners.
May the highly fortunate ones, Śaṅkha and the others, who are full of majesty and endowed with auspicious marks,
and Ananta, the lord of the serpent kings, who is devoted to the worship of the Sun—
having destroyed the poison of great sins, may they swiftly grant you peace.
With a body of intense blue, possessing a wealth of shimmering coils,
and marked with the auspicious svastika sign by his exceedingly radiant splendor,
the glorious Takṣaka, king of the nāgas, was present together with ten million attendants.
May he grant you great peace, which removes all defects and poisons—
he who is exceedingly dark in complexion, with a prominent forehead and head,
endowed with three lines on his neck, and raising weapons of terrible fangs.
May the great Naga Karkoṭaka, endowed with the power of poison and pride,
destroy the torment of poison, weapons, and fire, and grant you peace.
He is lotus-colored, possesses the luster of a lotus, and has eyes as long as blooming lotuses.
The great Naga Padma is renowned as one who constantly worships the Sun;
may he swiftly bestow upon you peace, auspiciousness, and immovability.
With his dark-hued body and glorious lotus-like eyes, [may he grant this].
Intoxicated by the pride and power of his venom, marked with lines upon his neck,
radiant with the splendor of Śaṅkhapāla, and a worshiper of the sun’s lotus feet—
may he, having destroyed the great poison, the most excellent of poisons, grant you peace.
With a body of exceeding whiteness and the crescent moon as his crest-ornament,
making a majestic display in the region of the lamp, marked with auspicious characteristics,
