he is the lord of serpents named Kulika, who is eternally devoted to the Sun.
Having removed the terrible poison, may they grant you peace!
Those nāgas who are in the atmosphere, those nāgas who dwell in heaven,
and those nāgas who reside on earth in mountain caves and difficult terrains— may they grant you peace!
May all those Nāgas who dwell in Pātāla,
gathered together there and intent upon the worship of the Sun’s rays, always grant peace.
May the Nāginīs, the Nāga maidens, and likewise the Nāga youths [grant peace].

May those who are devoted to the Sun and well-disposed always grant you peace. Those who recite or likewise hear this collection of names shall never be harmed by serpents, nor shall poison ever take hold of them.
Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of Solar Duties," in the Saptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan within the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
[Now follows] the description of propitiatory rites:
The Gaṅgā is the meritorious Great Goddess; so too are the Yamunā and the Narmadā rivers.
Gautamī, Kāverī, Varuṇā, and likewise Devikā—
these rivers, permeated by the true nature of the Sun, always worship the Lord who is the master of all planets, the ruler of the world, and the leader of the world.
May they, whose minds are solely intent on meditation upon the Sun, grant you eternal peace.
There is the river named Nirañjanā, the great river Śoṇa,
the supreme Mandākinī, and likewise the auspicious Sannihitā.
May these and many other rivers on earth, in heaven, and in the intermediate space,
who are devoted to the worship of the Sun, perform your propitiation.
May the god Mahāvaiśravaṇa, the king of Yakṣas and great sage, [grant you peace].
Surrounded by a retinue of ten million yakṣas and joined by countless yakṣas,
he was endowed with great majesty and devoted to the worship of the Sun’s feet.
He was solely intent on meditation upon the Sun and was permeated by the very nature of the Sun.
May the great yakṣa Māṇibhadra, adorned with jewels and gems, bring you peace when pleased; he whose eyes are as broad as lotus petals shines with a captivating necklace resting upon his neck.
With his form surrounded by yakṣiṇīs and yakṣa maidens,
and intent upon the worship of the Sun,
may the lord of yakṣas named Sucira, adorned with jeweled earrings, grant you peace.
Adorned on his forehead with a bound plate of gold,
surrounded by many yakṣas, and with his body bowed down by yakṣas,
he who is devoted to the worship of the Sun and is disciplined— may he grant you peace.
The lord of yakṣas named Pāñcika was adorned with a necklace;
he was surrounded by a multitude of yakṣas and accompanied by ten million yakṣas, and carried a variegated cock embellished with many jewels.
May the glorious Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who worships the sun, perform peace for you—
he of great splendor, the lord of various yakṣas,
O bird, wearing a divine turban and a white parasol, adorned with jewels and gold.
Devoted to the Sun, delighting in the Sun, and dedicated to the worship of the Sun—
endowed with the grace of the Sun, may he perform your pacification.
And Virūpākṣa, the lord of Yakṣas, clad in white garments and possessed of great splendor.
With his neck adorned by various golden garlands,
devoted to the worship of the Sun, lotus-eyed and resembling a lotus,
possessing a splendor like that of the sun— may he grant you peace.
The yakṣas who dwell in the intermediate regions, those yakṣas who go to heaven,
the yakṣas who assume various forms, those devoted to the Sun and firm in their vows—
those who are devoted to him, whose minds are set on reaching him, and who are eager for the worship of the Sun.
May those joyful ones— peaceful, devoted to peace— grant you tranquility;
as well as the Yakṣiṇīs of various forms, the Yakṣa youths,
and the highly fortunate Yakṣa maidens who are intent upon the worship of the Sun.

May all the mountains on every side and all the trees of great supernatural power, being ever perfectly composed, grant peace, prosperity, security, strength, supreme auspiciousness, and swift success.
May all those who are ever devoted to the Sun grant you perpetual peace.
May all the oceans on every side, and all the houses and forests in their entirety,
being intent upon the worship of the Sun, perform your pacification.
All the Rākṣasas everywhere— those of terrible form and great strength, whether they dwell on land, move through the atmosphere,
or reside in the netherworld (pātāla)— are constantly devoted to the worship of the Sun.
May they all, eternally illuminated by their own splendor, grant peace:
all the *pretas* and the hosts of *pretas*, those *pretas* who face in every direction,
those *pretas* who are exceedingly radiant, and those *pretas* who feed upon blood.
Those hungry ghosts (pretas) who dwell in the intermediate space, as well as those who reside in heaven;
those hungry ghosts who, capable of assuming any form at will, dwell in the netherworld (pātāla) or upon the earth;
he whose chariot has but a single wheel, and that god whose banner bears the bull—[to them all, I offer this].

May those who are Piśācas of great heroism, prosperous, and possessed of great strength— those who all assume various forms and are all exceedingly virtuous— always bring peace through the splendor of that deity.
Those Piśācas in the atmosphere, those of great strength in heaven,
those on the surface of the earth in the netherworld, and those of many forms who are as swift as thought—
O hero, for whom I am always the charioteer and for whom you are the horse.
By the splendor of that deity, may they all swiftly bring about peace:
all the *apasmāra* spirits and all the *jvara* spirits;
all those who dwell in heaven and all those excellent *grahas* who move upon the earth.
Whatever planets are in the netherworld (pātāla) and whatever planets have gone everywhere,
[they all abide] in the southern ray of that Sun, in whom Hari resides on the right,
Hara always on the left, and the Lotus-born (Brahmā) is situated on the forehead.
"By the splendor of that deity, may they always grant peace.
Thus, all the gods and others who perform the Sūrya-sacrifice shall always bring peace to the world and to the devotees of the Sun.
Victory to the divine Sūrya, the destroyer of darkness, the radiant Vivasvat!
Homage be to you, Sūrya Bhāskara, the bestower of victory!
Victory to the supreme deity, the bringer of auspiciousness!
Victory to you who causes the lotus to bloom; salutations to you who possess the form of a wise sage.
Victory to the bestower of radiance; victory to the ordainer of peace.
Salutations again and again to the unconquered one, the conqueror who destroys darkness.

Victory, O Sun! Victory, O Lord of Radiance! You who blaze with a thousand rays, victory to you! You are the creator of the worlds; salutations, repeated salutations to the Unconquered One! Salutations to the one whose body is Gāyatrī, and to the beloved of Sāvitrī!
"Salutations again and again to Dharādhara, to Sūrya, to Mārtaṇḍa.
Sumantu said:
"O lord of the earth, while Aruṇa was thus performing this propitiatory rite..."
For the welfare of the high-souled Garuḍa, the son of Vinatā,
at that very time Suparṇa became possessed of wings;
he was like Budha in splendor and equal to Hari in strength.
With all his limbs restored, the king became as he was before,
through the grace of the high-souled Bhāskara, the god of gods.
O lord of kings, other men who were diseased likewise [were healed].
Indeed, when the fire-ritual is performed by me, their ailments are surely dispelled.
Therefore, O Indra among kings, the fire-ritual must be performed with effort according to the prescribed rules; it should also be performed by men who are afflicted by disease.
When this fire-ritual has been performed, all afflictions indeed cease;
likewise in cases of planetary seizure, destruction, famine, and all types of portents.
When the rain-god fails to send rain, one should perform this accompanied by a hundred-thousand-fold oblation.
Having worshipped with the *prasūkta* and having meditated upon the Hero with diligence,
the wise practitioner should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) with the *vāruṇa* hymns,
using clarified butter together with honey, with a perfectly serene mind.

One should prepare this propitiatory rite (śāntika) with milk-rice mixed with sesame and barley, as well as honey; one should diligently offer the bali-oblation. When this is done, the gods shower prosperity upon men and fulfill their desires.
Thus, whoever should recite or even hear this chapter on pacification (śāntikādhyāya) according to the prescribed rite,
while meditating upon the Sun who illumines all the worlds,
shall conquer his enemy in battle and attain supreme honor.
He rejoices for an inexhaustible time, his commands remaining unopposed; he shall not be overcome by diseases, and being established with sons and grandsons,
he becomes like the sun in brilliance and splendor.
O Hero, the man on earth who recites this for the sake of others is not afflicted by those diseases consisting of wind, bile, and phlegm;
he does not meet with untimely death, nor is he bitten by serpents.
Poison does not affect his body; there is no dullness, blindness, or muteness.

He has no fear of birth, nor shall there be any harm arising from malevolent magic. Whatever diseases, whatever great portents, and whatever serpents with potent venom [may exist], they do not affect him.
O Bhārata, all those [afflictions] come to rest through hearing this;
one obtains ten million times the merit of all sacred fords, especially the Gaṅgā and others, by means of hearing and other such acts.
By performing ten Rājasūya sacrifices and especially others,
one shall live for more than a hundred years, free from all diseases;
even a cow-killer, an ungrateful person, a slayer of a Brahmin, or one who violates the teacher’s bed [is purified].
One who betrays those who have come for refuge, the wretched, the distressed, friends, or those who trust him;
one who is wicked, of sinful conduct, a slayer of his father, or likewise a slayer of his mother—by hearing of this [sacred site], one is liberated from sins; there is no doubt in this matter.

O hero, one should not give this meritorious history, this unsurpassed ritual of the fire-oblation, to anyone who is a fool or of a defiled soul. It was told of old by Sūrya himself that it should always be given to a devotee of Sūrya.
O mighty-armed lord of the earth, in ancient times Garuḍa spoke to Aruṇa, and Aruṇa [spoke] to the high-souled Bhojas—
Sūryaśarman and the others— in Śākadvīpa.
And they also recounted the meritorious [account] of the wise sage Vyāsa;
he too recounted that merit which removes the fear of all sins.

Thus ends the one hundred and eightieth chapter, titled "The Description of Peace," in the dialogue between Garuḍa and Aruṇa within the Saptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan in the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Description of the divisions of Smṛti. Śatānīka said:
"Tell me, in due order, the fivefold Dharma according to the Smṛtis."
"O Brahmin, ask whatever curiosity you have, whether in brief or in detail. Sumantu said:
"O King, listen to Dharma as it has been described in five ways, in summary."
As it was told here by Bhāskara regarding the high-souled Aruṇa:
having bowed his head to the thousand-rayed Sun, the god Divākara, who stands at the point of rising, the elder brother of Garuḍa spoke.
"O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods of gods, radiant with a thousand rays,
you ought to speak to me who asks about the true nature of the dharma of mindfulness as it really is.
Thus questioned by Aruṇa, O Lord of Birds, the Blessed One—
Having honored him with supreme affection, O lord of the earth,
Bhāskara said:
"O elder brother of Garuḍa, listen to the Dharma of Smṛti, which is rooted in the Vedas."
Meditation previously experienced, and the recollection thereof, is memory (smṛti).
Dharma is defined as action, characterized by the attainment of prosperity and the highest good;
it is declared to be fivefold, eternal, and rooted in the Vedas.
"From the performance of this sound, heaven and liberation arise;
as well as abundant happiness and sovereignty in this world, O Lord of Birds.
Anūru said:
"How indeed is this eternal Dharma said to be fivefold?
Of what are those five the divisions? Tell me, O best of gods.
Bhāskara said:

The Vedic dharma is traditionally held to be one, dedicated to those [in the first] stages of life (āśrama); the third, however, is the dharma of the social classes and stages of life (varṇāśrama), which is contingent upon qualities (guṇa) and circumstances (naimittika). Relying upon the single status of being a member of a class (varṇatva), it proceeds with respect to the qualification for ritual duties.
The staff, alms-bowl, and so forth, which belong to the specific caste and stage of life,
as well as that which proceeds by taking the state of caste and stage of life as its basis—
this is the dharma of caste and stage of life, such as the staff, the girdle, and the rest.
That which proceeds by virtue of its quality is called a *dharma*;
for example, the supreme protection of the subjects by one who has been consecrated as a king.
That *dharma* which proceeds by relying upon a single cause—
That [action] which depends on genus, substance, and quality is to be known as occasional (naimittika).
This, however, is said to be of two kinds in brief according to its specific distinctions;
it is to be understood as occasional, such as the rule for expiation (prāyaścitta).
It should be examined in four ways— by its essential nature, its fruit, its means,
and its source of knowledge (pramāṇa)— both individually and collectively, in due order.
However, in case of conflict with Śruti, it is sublated, except insofar as it concerns a different subject matter.
An effort should be made to examine [the matter] through systematic arrangement and by way of contradiction;
likewise, the establishment of the *Arthaśāstra* is determined by its contradiction with the *Smṛti*.
However, when there is mutual contradiction between them, the authority belongs to the *Arthaśāstra*.
Conceptual construction regarding an unseen purpose occurs when a systematic arrangement is possible;
conceptual construction regarding the treatises on recollection occurs when there is a fulfillment of expectancy. This performance, being an action, is established as having its root in the Veda.
Thus, the rule for what is possible to perform is established by logic;
however, O Lord of Birds, the scripture is twofold, consisting of both prohibitions and injunctions.
Some say it has a single form, while others say it has many forms.
O Bird, the fivefold types of memory are thus established in the disciple:
as threefold, fourfold, twofold, singlefold, or manifold.
Some memory has a perceived object, while another has an unperceived object.
Recollection based on tradition is another; the fifth, however, is that which concerns both the seen and the unseen.
All these have been declared by the sages themselves to be rooted in the Vedas.
Aruṇa said:
O best of beings, please state in brief the characteristics of these Smṛtis which you have proclaimed for the protection of the world-folds.
O Lord, which among them is considered to have a visible purpose, and which might have an invisible purpose?
"What [Smṛti] has its nature based on what is seen? What would be rooted in logic (nyāya)? Which Smṛti would be a mere restatement (anuvāda)? And which would have both a seen and an unseen basis?
Thus addressed, the highly resplendent Bhāskara, the stealer of waters, [replied].
He spoke to that heroic bird who was bowed down with humility;
Āditya said:
"The true nature of the six qualities [of statecraft], however, depends upon their application and the gravity of the task at hand."

O elder brother of Garuḍa, this Smṛti, which has visible worldly purposes, has been proclaimed by the sages as the application of oaths and expedients both in detail and in summary, as well as the appointment of supervisors and the description of the instruments of administration.
One should perform the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsti) and likewise must not eat the flesh of a dog;
such a Smṛti rule was declared by Manu to have an invisible purpose (adṛṣṭārtha), O son of Vinatā.
The wise know that one should carry a staff made of Palāśa wood as having both purposes (ubhayārtha).
But where there is a contradiction, there should be an option, just as between a sacrifice and an oblation;

if what is seen in the Śruti is to be performed, and the Smṛti is of that same nature, then it is merely a restatement of what has been said— just as renunciation from the householder's life is likewise [an option].
Thus Ravi spoke: "Dharma has been explained in brief, along with the technical terminology pertaining to it, as well as its means of accomplishment, such as the [sacred] regions and so forth.
Brahmāvarta is the supreme region, while that which is praised by the sages is next best."

Beyond that is the Middle Country (Madhyadeśa), and immediately adjacent to it is Āryāvarta. That land where the black antelope naturally roams is fit for sacrifice; beyond that is the land of the Mlecchas.

O sky-walker, Manu has declared that the three [castes] are the eternal means for the accomplishment of all the gods beginning with Brahmā, as well as for the Brahmins and others, and indeed for the entire multitude of living beings; this is rooted in the Veda.
For the sake of perfecting the sacrifice of illumination,
that very seer, having perceived the truth of that which is beyond sound, has shown this:
"Dharma, which consists of the correct means of accomplishment, must be practiced by the qualified person."
O Hero, he who is always free from desire yet endowed with desirable qualities,
who is disciplined in conduct, full of faith, a knower of the Vedas, a contemplator of the supreme self,
and one whose wealth is earned through righteous means— such a person attains the fruit of his actions.
Aruṇa said:
"O Vibhāvasu, O Lord of Devas, O Sovereign of the Planets, please describe the divisions of all the regions, beginning with Brahmāvarta."
The Sun said:
"The region between the two divine rivers, the Sarasvatī and the Dṛṣadvatī,
that land created by the gods is called Brahmāvarta."
That region which lies between the Himavat and Vindhya mountains,
extending westward from Prayāga, is proclaimed as Madhyadeśa (the Middle Land).
It extends from the eastern ocean to the western ocean.
The wise know the region between those two mountains to be Āryāvarta. Having identified these as the virtuous lands, one should diligently take refuge in them.
However, a Śūdra who is distressed for a livelihood may dwell in any place whatsoever.
"This light of Dharma has indeed been described to you in brief.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Various Smṛtis," within the dialogue between Aruṇa and Āditya concerning the Saura Dharmas, in the Saptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan in the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
[Now follows] the description of the marriage rites.
The Sun said:
"The eternal nature of dharma, along with its specific applications, has been declared.
Hereafter, O bird, I shall proclaim the dharma of those belonging to the various stages of life (āśramas)."
The student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and the mendicant—
these are declared to be the four stages of life (āśramas), yet they constitute a single state in its fourfold form.
The first is the Gāyatra student, while the second is the Prājāpatya.

Devavrata is the third, while Naiṣṭhika is the fourth; these four stages of life (āśramas) have been declared, along with their respective Vedas and common duties. Hereafter, I shall explain the purificatory rites (saṃskāras) for the accomplishment of dharma.

The *garbhādhāna* (conception rite) should be performed during the fertile period when both [the couple] are joyful, accompanied by mantras. The *puṃsavana* (rite for ensuring a male child) should be performed for the mother in the third month with the appropriate mantras.
The *sīmantonnayana* (parting of the hair) should be performed in the seventh month of pregnancy, or in the sixth, or even in the seventh.
The three sacraments beginning with *garbhādhāna* (conception) are desired for the purification of the vessel [the body];
however, all the sacraments beginning with *jātakarma* (birth-rite) belong to the person.
Among these, the *prāśana* (feeding) of gold and other substances performed with mantras is for one who has been born.

That which is called the *jātakarman* (birth-rite) is indeed the secret name; however, on the eleventh day, a meaningful public name should be given. O Bird, the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*), accompanied by recitations from the Dharmaśāstras and other texts, should take place in the sixth month.
The rite of tonsure (cūḍākarma) is prescribed for the first or the third year;
the initiation (upanayana) of a Brāhmaṇa occurs in the eighth or the tenth year,
as does that of a man of other castes, according to their specific distinctions.

The rite for the consecration of the Vedas for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas should be performed in the eleventh or twelfth year; I shall now describe that which they consider to be the initiation (upānayana),
as well as another [rite] for a man, and I shall speak of both.
The Sāvitra, the Vaidika, the Mahānāmnī and Mahāvrata, as well as the Aupaniṣada for a year, the Godāna, and the Suvarṇaka—
these are the vows for the purpose of receiving the Veda; such is the opinion of Manu.
The detailed exposition regarding the recitation of a portion of the Veda has been stated in the Gṛhya-sūtra;

likewise, service to the teacher, which is the means for accomplishing both visible and invisible goals, has been described. Furthermore, there are other duties pertaining to both [the student and the teacher], according to what is proper and as it has been heard in the tradition.
One should know that even toward the guru it is thus; that meditation is remembered as being threefold:
mutual satisfaction. This much is the summary of dharma: the entire Veda is to be mastered by one who performs his own duty.
Having mastered the Veda along with its texts and meanings according to the rules, the student—
whether a lifelong celibate (naiṣṭhika) or one following the prescribed rite until the time of impotence—
should, at the conclusion of his studies, give the desired gift; then, being permitted by his teacher, he may become a householder.
Just as a householder would perform his departure from the teacher's house,
so too should the lifelong student (naiṣṭhika) perform his ceremonial bath (snāna) properly according to the rules.
Thereafter, he should indeed marry a wife of the same caste who is endowed with auspicious marks.
O best of birds, one whose celibacy has not been violated is qualified;
however, other excellent twice-born ones desire qualification even for those who are independent [in this matter],
provided they are fifth or seventh in descent from their father or mother.

A twice-born man should marry a wife who is not born of the same *ṛṣi* or *gotra*. Regarding the number of wives prescribed in the rules for marriage, the mention of *gotra* should be understood as optional; for the various scriptural traditions of the sages present diverse views.

The Vedic revelation states that there are eight forms of marriage for the social classes, known as sacraments (saṃskāra). However, the king himself shall impose a fine of ninety-six paṇas upon him who gives away a defective maiden without disclosing her faults.
If an unmarried girl sees her menses while still in her father’s house,
her ancestors fall and she herself becomes a *vṛṣalī*.
Any Brāhmaṇa, weak in knowledge, who should marry such a girl [is likewise fallen].
One should know that husband of a *vṛṣalī* to be unworthy of receiving gifts at a funeral feast (*aśrāddheya*) and excluded from the ritual row (*apāṅkteya*).
Having publicly proclaimed all the faults of the woman or the man— or having proclaimed the faults of both— one may then enter into a relationship with him.
The Gaurī maiden is indeed the foremost; the Kanyakā is remembered as the middling;
Rohiṇī should be known as equal to her; but the Rajasvalā is the lowest.
Anūru said:
"O Lord of the World, what maiden is considered Gaurī, and who is Rohiṇī?
Who is the Rajasvalā, the Nagnikā, and who is the Devakanyā?
Bhāskara said:
One who has not yet reached puberty is Gaurī; once puberty has been reached, she is Rohiṇī.
A girl who lacks secondary sexual characteristics is a Kanyā, and one who lacks breasts is a Nagnikā. One of seven years is called Gaurī, while one of ten years is a Nagnikā.
In the twelfth year, however, she becomes a maiden; beyond that, she is a woman of menses.
Indeed, Soma enjoys the maiden when she is endowed with the primary sexual characteristics;
the Gandharvas [enjoy her] in her breasts, and Agni is proclaimed to be present in her menses.
One destroys one's sons with [excessive] facial features, destroys one's lineage with [excessive] breasts,
and likewise destroys the father’s desired goal and his worlds with [excessive] menses.
Therefore, [one should marry] a girl who is not possessed of [excessive] facial features and whose breasts are free from menses.
A father should not give his daughter in marriage to one who has already been enjoyed by others, such as Soma and the rest;
one must not eat his food, for that is remembered as a "vain cooking" (vṛthāpāka).
Having eaten the food of one whose cooking is vain, one should perform an expiation.
By practicing breath control (prāṇāyāma) three times and consuming clarified butter, one becomes purified.
O Bird, if one should marry a woman of the same lineage (gotra) or the same ancestral rite (pravara),
having performed emission with her, the atikṛcchra penance is the means of purification.
One should marry a daughter who is of the same lineage (sagotra) and even the daughter of one's maternal uncle;
such a twice-born man who acts thus is equal to a sage and shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
A woman who is not a sapinda of one's mother and not of the same lineage as one's father [is eligible for marriage].
"She is praised for the sexual act of marriage among the twice-born.
Aruṇa said:
"What indeed is meant by this 'act of marriage' that has been mentioned by you?"
"She is highly praised for the sexual union that constitutes marriage among the twice-born.
Āditya said:
"O son of Vinatā, whatever Vedic rites there are, such as the Agnihotra and others—"

Thus it is said: "The act of giving a daughter [in marriage] is performed through two [means]; however, regarding sexual union, one should not marry a girl who is tawny (kapilā), nor one with extra limbs, nor one who is diseased, nor one without body hair, nor one with excessive body hair, nor one with a crooked nose, nor one who is reddish-brown (piṅgalā)."
One should not name a girl after a bear, a tree, or a river, nor after another mountain; nor after a Yakṣa, a serpent, or a servant, nor after anything extremely terrifying.
Furthermore, she whose brother does not exist and whose father is indeed unknown [should not be named].
A wise man should not approach her for fear of violating the law regarding daughters;
yet one who desires a household, O best of birds, may choose such a maiden— one with the voice of a swan, uniform in complexion, and with eyes tawny like honey.

He who enters into the union of marriage and the *agnihotra* while his elder brother remains [unmarried] is to be known as a *parivettṛ*; the elder brother, however, is a *parivitti*. Both the *parivitti* and the *parivettṛ*, as well as the woman through whom he is so wedded, [are all fallen].

All of them go to hell— the giver, the officiating priest, and the fifth, the one who permits the marriage. However, there is no fault in superseding a marriage if the husband is impotent, resides in another country, has fallen from his caste, has gone away, or is devoted to the practice of Yoga.
There is no fault in superseding one who is lame, dwarfed, humpbacked, stammering, or mentally dull; nor in the case of one who is blind from birth, deaf, or mute.
However, one should not perform a *śrāddha* for a younger brother, nor give a daughter in marriage to one of low lineage.
Furthermore, a groom who is deficient in lineage and character shall never be purified;
in that case, neither the mantras nor the fact that the girl was chosen serves as a cause [for purification].
However, a girl who has been married but has not yet engaged in sexual intercourse [is purified].
Just as a maiden returns to her husband, so too does she;
O Lord of Birds, there is no fault if a father, having considered a maiden of unblemished womb, gives her to one of noble birth and character.
Anūru said:
"O Lord of the World, these eight forms of marriage have been declared;
O Dispeller of Darkness, tell me their characteristics in brief."
Āditya said:
"Adorning a maiden who is auspicious, endowed with the proper marks, and possessed of noble lineage, character, and virtues,
and giving her to a worthy suitor— this is called the Brāhma marriage."
The gift of a daughter, adorned with ornaments, for the purpose of performing religious rites together and bound by a formal agreement, is called the Prājāpatya rite.
Where the giving of the daughter is accompanied by the gift of a pair of cattle, [that is the Ārṣa rite].

The sages know that [the marriage] with a woman of the same caste (savarṇā) and the same lineage (sagotrā) is the Ārṣa form. That which consists of giving a maiden adorned with gold to the officiating priest (ṛtvij) after bringing her within the sacrificial altar (antarvedi) is the marriage known as Daiva.
These four forms of marriage bestow virtue, pleasure, and wealth;
they were declared by Brahmā to be without bride-price and they deliver both families. Whatever son is born of a woman wedded according to these four [forms], [he sanctifies the lineage].
It purifies the ancestors of both the giver and the receiver up to the seventh generation.
That union of a man and a woman in a secluded place,
which is the cause of mutual pleasure, is considered the fifth form of marriage, the Gāndharva.
The forcible abduction of a maiden from her home while she cries out and weeps— after killing,
cutting, and piercing [her relatives]— is called the Rākṣasa marriage. The abduction of a maiden after giving a bride-price, even in times of distress, is also [a form of marriage].
Thus, this seventh [form], pertaining to the asuras, has been described as a cause for [merely] pleasure.
When one approaches a woman in secret while she is asleep, intoxicated, or distracted, that is the most sinful of marriages; it is the eighth, the lowest, known as the paiśāca.
These four types of marriage, involving a bride-price and common to all [classes], are known;
however, the Rākṣasa form occurs only for a Kṣatriya after his prowess has been displayed.
When the aforementioned marriages have been obtained, the auspicious marriage rite is performed.
The marriage contract must be made by the three castes with fire as witness according to the established rule.
However, if a girl with defects is given in marriage, the fine for the giver shall be ninety-six paṇas;
the same applies in the case of receiving a bride-price or the abandonment of the bride.
Aversion to the path leading to liberation, the withholding of women and wealth,
longing, and the obstruction of sacred fords are said to be the causes of renunciation.
Liberation for both woman and man is traditionally held to arise from their mutual connection.
Neither of them should be pleased by even immediate anger.
If the husband oppresses his wife, that is known as hatred (*dveṣa*).
Her maintenance, ornaments, the nuptial fee (*śulka*), and her acquisitions shall constitute the woman’s property (*strīdhana*).
If he himself were the enjoyer, it would constitute a violation of his own vow;
liberation would be in vain, and he might as well give wealth with interest to a woman.
Only when a time of calamity has arisen does one deserve to enjoy a woman’s property.
A husband may wait for eight years for the birth of a child from his wife;
even if no sons are born despite great effort,
he who desires a son may, in accordance with dharma, take a woman of good family.
For one desiring offspring, there is indeed nothing in this world superior to obtaining a son.
Having enjoyed that [first wife] for her dowry, if he wishes to take another,
he should satisfy all [his wives] with wealth and then marry a Sūryoḍhā as his supreme [consort].

A Śūdra may have one wife, a Vaiśya two, a Kṣatriya three, and a Brāhmaṇa four; for a king, however, there may be as many wives as he desires. By a man’s failure to visit sacred sites (tīrtha) and by a woman’s bathing at such a site [without her husband], [their merit is lost].
There would be a loss of dharma for both, especially regarding their own respective duties.
However, if the sacred sites (tīrthas) are simultaneous, one should proceed according to the order of marriage;
or else, if they are equal, according to the order of the living sons, or even the order of initiation.
O Lord of Birds, those two were consecrated by means of the Brahma and other forms of marriage;
for the castes, O Vainateya, they indeed prescribe eight types of marriage:
the Brahma, the Daiva, the Arsha, and the Prajapatya, O Lord of Birds.
The Gāndharva, Āsura, Rākṣasa, Paiśāca, and the eighth, the lowest, [are for others].
For Kṣatriyas and the other castes, these are recommended; however, for Brāhmaṇas and the others, according to their rank, marriages such as the Brāhma and so forth are prescribed.
As for the acceptance of gifts and other matters, they are restricted for the Brāhmaṇa alone.
A Kṣatriya woman may also be given [in marriage], provided she is exempt from accepting gifts. Some desire that a woman’s [duty] be active engagement, while others say it is giving;
however, they declare that marriage is the means of purification for men.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Marriage Rite," in the Dialogue between Sūrya and Aruṇa, within the Brāhma Parvan of the Seventh Kalpa of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
[Now follows] the description of the narrative on the rite of Śrāddha.
Bhāskara said:
He is entitled to perform the five great sacrifices (pañcamahāyajña) for the spirits,
ancestors, gods, Brahman, and humans according to the prescribed rules;
others, however, remain intent on performing constant acts of charity for the sake of their rewards.
Others say that the fruit [of these acts] follows as a consequence, whether it be permanent or impermanent.
Service is prescribed for the sake of satisfying the guest; while the unseen merit arises from the observance of the rule, the avoidance [of unwholesome things] results in health as its ultimate end.
Three Aṣṭakās are to be performed, with the fourth occurring in the middle;
the fourth is performed with vegetables, milk-porridge, and cakes,
while that which is performed on the first lunar day (pratipad) is called the fourfold Pārvaṇa.
That [rite] is proclaimed according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Gṛhya-sūtra;

it is to be known as the daily (nitya), the occasional (naimittika), the optional (kāmya), the prosperity-śrāddha (vṛddhi-śrāddha), the sapinda-śrāddha, and the pārvaṇa— this last being the most excellent for the purification of the cow-pen (goṣṭha).
The ninth is declared to be the Karmāṅga, and the tenth is remembered as the Vaidika.
Anūru said:
"O Lord, this Śrāddha which has been described by you as being twelvefold—"
Tell me the specific characteristics of each of those individually:
what is called the "regular" (nitya) śrāddha, and what might be the "occasional" (naimittika)?
O Lord of the Gods, tell me the characteristics of these, such as the "optional" (kāmya) and others.

Āditya said: "O bird, that śrāddha which is performed day after day is declared to be *nitya* (obligatory). However, when one is unable [to perform it with food], it may be done with water, though it is devoid of the Vaiśvadeva offering."
The *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha is called occasional (*naimittika*);
it should always be performed, and one should feed an odd number of twice-born men.
Indeed, that which is joined with a specific desire is called *kāmya*, for the sake of accomplishing a desired object.
O Lord of Birds, that too has been described according to the Pārvaṇa rite;
the Śrāddha which is performed on an occasion of prosperity (vṛddhi) is called Vṛddhi-Śrāddha.
Everything should be performed in a clockwise direction during the forenoon by one wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (upavītī).

One should prepare four vessels filled with scented water and sesame seeds for the purpose of the *argha* offering; one should then pour the vessel of the deceased (*preta*) into the vessels of the ancestors (*pitṛ*). This rite, performed with the two verses beginning "ye samānāḥ," is to be known as the *sapiṇḍana*.

The remaining rites for a woman should be equal to those of the perpetual (nitya) offerings; even for her, the ekoddiṣṭa rite is performed. That which is performed on the new moon day (darśa) is declared to be pārvaṇa;
and that which is performed on a festival day (parvan) is pārvaṇa—this is the established rule.
When a Śrāddha is performed for cows, it is called a Goṣṭha-śrāddha. Furthermore,

when food is provided for the sake of the prosperity and happiness of many learned men, for the satisfaction of the ancestors, and indeed for the purification of the Brāhmaṇas, [it is likewise so designated].

O Vainateya, that [rite] has been declared by the wise to be for the purpose of purification. At the time of conception, during the Soma sacrifice, and likewise at the Simantonnayana, the Puṃsavana Śrāddha is to be known; and it is indeed an integral part of the ritual act.
Whatever is performed with effort on the seventh lunar day and subsequent days for the sake of the deity,
he who is traveling to another country should perform a *śrāddha* with clarified butter;
it is declared that this is for the purpose of his success, and one should bestow it— of this there is no doubt.

The Śrāddha performed for the nourishment of the body and specifically for the increase of horses is to be understood as being for the sake of growth; it is called "auxiliary" (aupacārika). Among all Śrāddhas, that which is performed annually is considered the most excellent.
O best of birds, that which is performed by the wise together on the anniversary of death—
yet he who does not perform the śrāddha with devotion on the anniversary of death,
O tiger among birds, as well as for his mother at the end of the year on her anniversary of death; [he incurs sin].
"O best of birds, neither I, nor Hari, nor Brahmā, nor Rudra, nor any other hosts of deities accept his worship. Therefore,
one must diligently perform [this rite] every year on the anniversary of his death."
O tiger among birds, this applies especially to a man who is a *bhojaka*;
for that *bhojaka*, O lord of birds, who does not perform the *śrāddha* for his mother and father on their anniversary of death every year.
He goes to a terrible hell known by the name Tāmisra;
thereafter, O bird, he becomes a wicked-souled hog in a city.
Anūra said:
O Lord of the Wise, how can that man who does not know the day nor the month when his parents died perform the *śrāddha* for them according to the rules throughout the year, O highly intelligent one?
Āditya said: "O son of Vinatā, O best of birds, that man who does not know the month and the day of the death of his ancestors, O most excellent of winged creatures, [does not perform their rites]."
Listen, O best of birds, to how one should perform it entirely and in brief:
O son of Vinatā, that man who does not know the anniversary of the day of death must perform the annual *śrāddha* on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), O bird.
O Hero, O Bird, he who always worships me according to the rules with special offerings of food during the months of Mārgaśīrṣa or Māgha—
by him my ancestors are indeed always worshipped for my own pleasure.
"O observer of noble vows, my ancestors, the cows, and the Brahmins are always dear to me;
therefore, they must always be honored, especially by my devotee.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Śrāddha Rite," in the Sauradharma section of the *Saptamī-kalpa* within the Brāhma-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Description of the rules for the duties of a Brāhmaṇa:
Accepting gifts preceded by questioning based on reputation alone;
sacrificing for others, teaching, and engaging in debate—these six constitute the sale of the Veda.
O Lord of Birds, wealth designated for the sale of the Vedas, that acquired by a woman, and that which comes from a eunuch should not be given to the ancestors or the gods; likewise,
one should not give a gift to a Brāhmaṇa through the practice of extortion.
O Brahmins, he first goes to hell, and immediately after that [he suffers further].
For as many syllables of the Veda as are employed for the sake of worldly gain, so many instances of killing an embryo does one indeed incur through the sale of the Veda.

Those who are devoid of the Vaiśvadeva rite and the ritual of the Āditya, even if they are Brāhmaṇas who have acquired the Vedas, should all be known as Śūdras. This applies to those who lack Vedic study and to anyone who maintains no sacred fires.
Those families among whom there are none learned in the Vedas (śrotriya) all follow the dharma of Śūdras. O bird, he who eats without having first performed the Vaiśvadeva rite is ignorant;
by that food cooked in vain, he shall go to the womb of Yama.
Whether he be beloved or hateful, a fool or even a scholar,
when the Vaiśvadeva rite has arrived, such a guest is a bridge to heaven.
However, one who lives in the same village, nor likewise a Brahmin who is merely a relative, is not considered a guest.
Because he arrives unexpectedly, he is called a guest (*atithi*). He who has arrived for the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice is indeed "unexpected" by name;
one should recognize him as a guest, but not one who has come previously.
O Bird, they know that as much food as a twice-born Snātaka may obtain after having made his formal resolve (kṛtāśī) is called *hantakāra*, which is one-fourth part of that meal.
A single morsel constitutes a *bhikṣā*; four times that amount is for four meals.

And four *puṣkala* offerings are prescribed as the *haṃtakāra*. Know this, O Lord of Birds: he who, having ascended to the lifelong vow (*naiṣṭhika-dharma*), falls away from it again, shall perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance for one month.

O bird, know that these two are outcasts (cāṇḍālas): a Brāhmaṇa woman whose husband has died after she had married another, and one who has been approached by a Śūdra; and furthermore, he who knows [her] becomes so as well. O bird, a Brāhmaṇa woman who is unchaste always abandons her own husband.
O Lord of Birds, O high-minded one, when a man enters the house of another Brāhmaṇa,
the son who is born of that woman by that Brāhmaṇa is declared to be a great Caṇḍāla, indeed a Mahācaṇḍāla.
But he who, having become a renunciant, again indulges in sexual intercourse,
is born as a worm in excrement for sixty thousand years;
purification comes through the five products of the cow— thus said the Creator of my body.
The food of a Brāhmaṇa invited by a Śūdra is unfit to be eaten; likewise, the food of a Śūdra invited by a Brāhmaṇa is unfit.
A Śūdra giving the food of a Brāhmaṇa, and a Brāhmaṇa giving the food of a Śūdra, [render it unfit].
Both of these are persons whose food should not be eaten; having eaten it, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
If a twice-born man cooks the food of a Śūdra under the pretext of a deposit, that food becomes unfit to be eaten, as does that Brāhmaṇa who acts as his domestic priest.
Food from a Śūdra, contact with a Śūdra, dwelling together with a Śūdra,

or even the acquisition of some knowledge from a Śūdra— these may cause one to fall, even if one is blazing with spiritual power. Brahmins corrupted by the food of a Śūdra become agitated and lustful.

What can those who are angry do? They are like venomless serpents. However, salt, condiments, and other such items that are given with affection by hand do not affect the giver; yet the eater indeed incurs the sin.
If food is offered in an iron vessel,
the eater consumes excrement and the giver goes to hell. Likewise, [eating with] a finger, using a tooth-stick, or consuming salt in its raw state [is forbidden].
Eating clay is indeed equal to eating beef;
as long as the mouth remains stale, a twice-born man is perpetually impure.
Therefore, he should consume a tooth-stick, whether dry or moist.
Flowers, ornaments, garments, perfumes, garlands, and ointments—these do not cause a transgression during a fast; likewise, the cleansing of teeth and the application of collyrium are permitted.
A fool may dwell within one's house, while a virtuous person remains far away.

A gift should be given to one endowed with virtues; there is no bypassing of a fool. There is no bypassing of a Brahmin who is devoid of Vedic knowledge, for one does not offer oblations into ashes after setting aside a blazing fire.
"He who bypasses a Brāhmaṇa studying nearby by refusing him food or gifts burns his family down to the seventh generation.
Anūru said:

In this very way, O Lord of the World, God of Gods, Master of the Universe! However, O Lord, Sovereign of the Wise, listen to those words which you previously heard from the high-souled Nārada as he was speaking.
O best of gods, as I speak of this righteous matter that brings happiness—
regarding a twice-born man who is devoted to truth, of pure birth, and pleasant of speech,
even if he be a fool, a heretic, or devoid of proper conduct.

O bird, by transgressing [this rule], a man would cause himself, along with seven descendants and seven ancestors, to fall into a terrible hell. Therefore, a king should not bypass a Brāhmaṇa who is his neighbor.
O Lord of Planets,

O Lord of the Cowherds, a man should not bypass these— namely a daughter’s son who is likewise closely related by kinship, a sister’s son especially, and a paternal kinsman— even if they are utterly foolish.
Having passed beyond it, one would go to the most terrible Raurava hell.
Āditya said: "It is exactly so, O sky-walker; there is no doubt regarding what you say."
O hero, it has also been understood by me that one should not examine a Brahmin.
A Brahmin embodies all the gods and likewise embodies all the worlds;
therefore, one should worship him and not consider his personal qualities.
O son of Vinatā, one should consider only the birth [of a guest] and not his qualities;
therefore, a wise man should first invite a Brāhmaṇa who is nearby.
He who, bypassing a nearby Brāhmaṇa—provided he is not an outcast—[commits a fault].
A fool who worships those who are distant from him, even if they are rich in virtues, shall go to hell.
By the destruction of rites for the gods, by the seizing of the property of a Brāhmaṇa,
and by [misappropriating] the property of the gods, the food of the twice-born, and the wealth acquired by a Brāhmaṇa— [one incurs great sin].
He who casts [an embryo] into a womb other than its own, he who enters a womb other than his own,
or he who says "do not give" regarding cows, fire, or Brahmins—
having passed through a hundred animal births, he is born among the Cāṇḍālas.
Whatever action has been promised by word but not fulfilled by deed is a debt connected with dharma, both in this world and in the next.
When a *śrotriya*— one who has completed his Vedic studies and vows and has performed the ceremonial bath— arrives at one's house, [one must honor him].
"All the medicinal herbs are playing: 'We shall go to the supreme goal.
A twice-born man who sells any one of these—honey, meat, liquor, soma, lac, or salt—must perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance."
Having sold molasses, sesame, indigo, hair, wheat, barley,
or a cow, a Brāhmaṇa shall perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra penance.
Likewise for consuming camel’s milk or sheep’s milk, or food [eaten] during the impurity caused by death or birth.

Having eaten the food of a thief or at a funeral rite (śrāddha) for the dead, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. One bitten by a dog becomes pure by bathing in water from a cow's horn, at the confluence of great rivers,
or even by beholding the ocean.
O bird, a twice-born man who has completed his studies of the Vedas and the observances of his vow, if bitten by a dog,
becomes pure by consuming ghee mixed with gold and water; likewise,
O bird, a twice-born man bitten by a dog while standing or walking [is purified in the same way].
By consuming the *vajra* (cow’s urine), one indeed becomes pure, as the Blessed Manu has declared. For one observing a vow who has been bitten by a snake, a fast of three nights is prescribed;
thereafter, having eaten with ghee, he should complete the remainder of his vow.
If a Brāhmaṇī woman is bitten by a dog while the moon is visible, she should perform the rite prescribed for when the moon is seen.
When the moon is not visible, how should the expiation be performed?
She should gaze toward whichever direction the moon has gone.
That former [sin] is purified by the five-fold Soma-path; however,
when pus and blood arise at the Brahma-door of a Brāhmaṇa and he is bitten by worms, I shall tell you the expiation for that.
One should perform a bath three times a day using the dung of cows;
having drunk curd, milk, and ghee, one bitten by a worm is purified.
Now, O son of Vinatā, regarding one bitten from the navel down to the feet:
O Lord of Birds, O Hero, the wise should prescribe this atonement:
when a worm arises within the space between the navel and the throat,
the learned have declared that the atonement lasts for six nights.
O son of Vinatā, O son of Kaśyapa, when worms bite the head, then a wise man should perform the Kṛcchra penance for the sake of purification.
Furthermore, any Brāhmaṇa who should eat food belonging to the deceased, honey, or meat [must likewise do so].
"He should fast for three days and dwell in water for one day.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Duties of Brāhmaṇas," in the dialogue between Anūru and Āditya within the Saptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan in the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
[This is followed by] the "Description of the Ritual for the Śrāddha for Mothers."
The Sun said:
"One should not perform a *śrāddha* at night, for it is declared to belong to the *rākṣasas*. Nor, O hero, during either of the two twilights, nor when the sun has set."
"If one serves the śrāddha meal without first performing the sacrifice to the Mothers,
they desire for his father a terrible violence accompanied by wrath.
Anūru said:
"How should the śrāddha for the mothers be performed, and who are those remembered as the mothers?
And how may the Nāndīmukha ancestors receive worship?
Āditya said:
"Behold, O bird, I shall fully explain to you the ritual for the *śrāddha* of the Mothers.
Listen, O tiger among birds, as I speak it in its entirety.
In the forenoon, one should feed eight Brahmins, all of whom are circumambulated."
Likewise, O Lord of Birds, having duly given nine other upright Brahmins four handfuls each, O Bird, according to the rite with truthfulness,
and having substituted barley for sesame seeds mixed with curd in due order;
One should perform circumambulation of the Brahmins while offering all things such as perfumes and flowers;
then, O Bird, one should give sweet food to the Brahmins,
O best of birds— excellent rice mixed with molasses and accompanied by clothing.
One should offer sweetmeats of various flavors, but not those that are pungent;
when the Brahmins have thus eaten, O Lord of Birds, one should, with a concentrated mind, offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) mixed with curd, unbroken rice, and jujube fruits.

O hero, O best of birds, having constructed a square pavilion and circumambulated it clockwise, and having likewise laid down *kuśa* grass with its tips pointing eastward along with a profusion of flowers, one should perform the rite according to the rules with the right hand, O hero.
Facing the east,
one should offer to the mother’s mother (the great-grandmother) and her mother;
O Bird, the wise man should likewise duly offer another to the father’s mother and her mother, as well as to the elder great-grandmother.
Having thus designated the Mothers, O bird, one should offer six rice-balls (piṇḍas).
O hero, lord of birds, one should feed eight twice-born men at the Mātṛ-śrāddha;
O bird, one should duly feed a ninth guest intended for all the deities.
One should feed five excellent brahmins, intended for those ancestors known as the Nāndīmukhas,

according to the rules during a Vṛddhi-śrāddha, with the offerings presented in a clockwise direction. O son of Kaśyapa, one should perform these two types of śrāddhas in this manner at a time of prosperity.
Likewise, I shall tell you another supreme procedure for the Śrāddha rite for you.
Now, one should feed [the guests] at the Śrāddha in this manner, but first one must perform that preliminary rite;
otherwise, the gods, asuras, and humans will cause it to fail.
In the absence of fire, however, one should place the food directly into the hand of the Brahmin;
for that twice-born man is said by the seers of the mantras to be the very fire itself.
Whatever food is already in the vessel and whatever food has been prepared—
One should eat together with him alone; no separation is prescribed.
For the rite to the gods (daiva), one should seat two Atharvan Brahmins facing east;
for the rite to the ancestors (pitrya), three facing north; and at a rite for prosperity (vṛddhi), those who have studied the Adhvaryu [Yajurveda].
Three things are purifying at a Śrāddha: a daughter’s son, the Kutupa vessel, and sesame seeds.
And three things are praised here: purity, freedom from anger, and lack of haste.
A daughter’s son is called Khaṇḍa by Prajāpati for the sake of the forehead.
In that regard, the vessel belonging to Śṛṅga is known as the dauhitra-vessel.
One who has slipped from the left shoulder and settled at the region of the navel,
wearing but a single garment— such a person one should recognize and exclude from rites for the gods and the ancestors.
The worship and feeding of the ancestors, gods,

and humans must not be performed without an upper garment (uttarīya), for if done so, it becomes fruitless. A householder who worships the ancestors while wearing the garment over his shoulder [is at fault].
He does not obtain that fruit,
O best of birds, as one who is covered by a yoga-band; for the sake of the success of their actions, O great-minded hero, the yoga-band is prescribed for forest-dwellers and ascetics.
The foolish man who, having washed his hands, drinks the water used for rinsing the mouth (gaṇḍūṣa),
destroys the offerings to the gods, the ancestors, and himself.
Those twice-born ones who remain present at meals and pronounce blessings [are to be honored].
That śrāddha becomes demonic; it does not reach the ancestors.
[May] the givers prosper, as well as the Vedas and the virtuous!
May faith not depart from us, and may we have much to give!

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Śrāddha to the Mothers," in the dialogue between Aruṇāditya and [the Sun] within the Sauradharma of the Saptamī-kalpa, in the Brāhma-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa.
The Description of the Section on Purity.
Bhāskara said:
On the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, an offering to the serpents (sarpa-bali) should be performed according to the mantras;
likewise, by one desiring happiness, the rites for their going to sleep and ascending [to their resting place] should be performed.
There is no doubt that the rite of their descent (pratyavaroha) should be performed on the full moon day of Mārgaśīrṣa.
The performance of obligatory rites (*nitya*) is clearly intended to be without fruit;

however, the performance of optional rites (*kāmya*) is for the sake of obtaining a result, and that of occasional rites (*naimittika*) is for the sake of avoiding a fault. Thus, the fruit of the three types of action is threefold.
Some declare that the fruit is the destruction of accumulated evil;

others likewise maintain it is the non-arising [of future evil], having accepted this through reasoning. Others say that the scriptural statement regarding the fruit of obligatory rites follows as a secondary consequence.
The establishment of the sacred fires (Agnyādheya), as well as the New Moon (Darśa) and Full Moon (Paurṇamāsa) sacrifices as the second pair,
the Cāturmāsya, the Agnihotra, the Animal Sacrifice (Paśubandha), and the Nirūḍha offerings—
these are the forms of the Havis sacrifice proclaimed in the Śruti, including the Sautrāmaṇī as their concluding rites.
The Agniṣṭoma, Atirātra, Ukthya, Ṣoḍaśin,
Vājapeya, Atirātra, and Āptoryāma are heard of in the Śruti.
Compassion toward all beings, freedom from malice, and auspiciousness— these are [the qualities].
Forbearance, compassion, lack of exertion, purity, freedom from desire, and the observance of vows—
these are rightly declared to be the purificatory rites (saṃskāras) that cause the attainment of Brahman.
Immediately thereafter, I shall proclaim the auspicious modes of livelihood for the Brāhmaṇas.

For Brahmins, there are the modes of life known as *ṛta*, *amṛta*, *ṛta-amṛta*, and *pramṛta*; among these, each subsequent one is inferior to the preceding. These various means of livelihood (*ājīvikā-vṛttayaḥ*) were thus established.
Among them, one should live according to any one [of these] and conduct oneself according to the rule:
always pure, fragrant, habituated to bathing, and speaking kindly;
worthy of honor, one should worship the gods and perform one's duties personally.

One should not look at the sun, nor at a naked woman, nor at one who has engaged in sexual intercourse; nor should one void urine or feces in water, nor look at the stars at night while impure. Furthermore, one must observe those restraints prescribed by the scriptures as well as the vows that have not been specifically mentioned.
One who possesses the capacity should accomplish these for the sake of heaven, as well as mentally;
some desire them to be obligatory (*nitya*), while others likewise consider them optional (*kāmya*).
When there is engagement in optional rites or attachment to them, an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is prescribed.

The mental vow is that which is formed by the mind with a firm resolve; the sages have proclaimed that its fruit is realized internally. One should personally and properly avoid non-study periods as a means for attaining that fruit.
When one is impure, or likewise when the place is defiled by the presence of a corpse;
when there are inauspicious omens, portents, or deformities;
on the sacred festival days (parvan); and when there is impurity of mind—this is traditionally known as a time unfit for study (anadhyāya).

"O Lord of Birds, my vision of *adhyāna* (meditative absorption) is threefold: there are those *anadhyāyas* (periods when study is forbidden) that have a visible purpose, others that have an invisible purpose, and yet others which consist solely of the study of the Vedas. Furthermore, O Lord of Birds, the ritual impurity following a death (*śāvāśauca*) is forbidden for all social classes."

In that very way, the purity of the substance would be maintained; otherwise, it would be inconsistent. [Substances] are considered impure by reason of their species, by the defect of the action, by the defect of the time, by association, by the nature of their receptacle, or by their inherent nature.
One should not eat garlic, leeks, onions, mushrooms,
eggplant, coconut, radish, or anything naturally impure;
nor should one eat food that is ritually defiled, or that has been separately prepared by outcasts.
That which is spoiled by time should be known as causing loss [of merit] when it has been kept for a long duration;
this applies to curd and its various preparations, with the exception of honey.
It is likewise held to be so when touched by liquor or garlic, or when mixed with the milk of a cow that has recently calved (peyūṣa), and so forth.
O Lord of Birds, this food is indeed defiled by association; it is like the leavings of a dog.
It should be known as corrupted by its source when it is attached to a Śūdra or attached to a Khaṇḍa (outcaste). Furthermore, that food regarding which doubt arises in the heart [is likewise unfit].
That feces should be known as having a foul odor by its very nature;
furthermore, it has been shown that when the *rasa* (nutrient fluid) is vitiated, a disorder of the *rasa* also occurs.
Likewise, milk-porridge (*pāyasa*) and other preparations cooked in milk [are spoiled] on that very same day.

O best of birds, one should determine what is fit and unfit to be eaten according to the scriptures. One incurs no fault by eating meat when life is at risk, when it has been consecrated for sacrifice, when it is part of a śrāddha rite, or when requested by a twice-born guest, provided that one first offers it to the ancestors and the gods.
When one dies among the sapindas,
the impurity for the deceased lasts ten days, twelve days, a fortnight, or a month; however,
these periods of ten days and so forth do not apply according to the specific caste divisions within those three groups.
In cases of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) or death-impurity (*āśauca*), those [who have heard the news] may eat after ten days;
however, if the news is heard after the ten days have passed, purification occurs after one day.
But when a full year has elapsed, one becomes pure simply by bathing.
The status of *samānodaka* (distant kinsmen) is declared to exist when there is no recollection of either birth or name;

the *sapiṇḍas* extend to seven generations—this is the illustration found in the scriptures. [Impurity] is immediate until the eruption of teeth, and until the *cūḍā* ceremony it is considered total (*naiṣṭhikī*).
In the case of the death of sapinda relatives, impurity lasts for three nights until the instruction for the vow;

for them as well, that same period applies, though it must be considered in relation to their age and stage of life. One becomes pure after three nights upon the birth or death of a samānodaka relative.

A woman who has given birth is purified after three nights, as is a woman in her menses; likewise, one is purified from the death of countless births by the remainder of that [period]. This same rule applies to the twice-born for the sake of their father or mother.
It is established that immediate purification (sadyaḥśauca) is to be understood for the purpose of performing the Agnihotra sacrifice;
however, in the case of one who is not a sapinda relative, a man must observe three nights of impurity after carrying out the funeral procession.
O Lord of Birds, it should be known that immediate purification applies when following the corpse of that very same person.
A twice-born man is purified in ten days by birth or death occurring among those of his own caste;
however, for those born of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes, he is purified in six, three, or one day respectively.
Thus has the purification of the body been declared according to the rule by the seers of truth.
The procedure for the purification of substances is now described correctly:
O Hero, purification by water is prescribed for metallic and earthen objects;
however, in the case of contact, it is indeed by wiping free of stains and washing, or by sprinkling.
"O Sky-walker, there is indeed no substance whatsoever that is inherently impure;
however, O Sky-walker, purity and impurity of substances exist here in this world.
Therefore, after the purification of the substances, one must perform ritual bathing and cleansing."
The morning bath should be performed daily; it is also to be done for specific desires during an eclipse.
The occasional bath (*naimittika*) following a haircut or impurity purifies one from sin.
O Bird, this purification which has been described should be understood as that which causes the destruction of faults.

It should be known that it consists of six types in brief, including the ritual action (karmāṅga). Thus one should understand the sipping of water (ācamana) as specifically intended for the twice-born; for those who have died, it should be done likewise, while for others, it may be according to their convenience.
A father should duly arrange for the cessation of his daughter's dependence through sons;
he should cause her to acquire all the arts and crafts for her satisfaction. A wife should serve her husband so that he may attain complete contentment.
The eternal duty of women is the satisfaction of their elders.
If an elderly woman dies without a son, she passes to her husband in his absence;
likewise does one who has died after her children, one who has no offspring, or an elderly woman whose children have passed away, provided she remains devoted to her husband.
Whether her husband has departed or is still present, she should remain unsatisfied [with worldly life];

by adhering to this righteous and steadfast conclusion, she shall attain the world of her husband. A virtuous woman who practices dharma, when deceased, should likewise be cremated with the sacred fires.
Furthermore, the taking of a wife from one who is contrary [to the prescribed order] is likewise forbidden;
for women, the practice of *niyoga* (levirate) is ordained, as is lifelong celibacy until death.
And that which accords with *dharma* must be attained, for it bestows both visible and invisible fruits.
"Therefore, one should always practice dharma; by practicing it, one shall attain heaven.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Section on Purity" within the *Sauradharma* (Duties toward the Sun) in the *Saptamī-kalpa* of the *Brāhma-parvan* in the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
[Now begins] the description of the greatness of the cow (*dhenu-māhātmya*) within the *Sauradharma*.
Anūru said:
"What meritorious deeds must men perform here so that,
having been born in the world of mortals, they go to the supreme heavenly realm?"
The sacrifice of action, the sacrifice of austerity, the study of sacred texts, that which consists of meditation,
and the sacrifice of knowledge— these five are proclaimed as the great sacrifices.
Among these very sacrifices, which one is remembered as the most excellent?
What is the fruit of these fruits of sacrifice, and what is its destiny?
How many distinctions between dharma and adharma have been proclaimed? Tell me how many are their means of accomplishment and what their destinies are like.
What are the signs that arise for those men who were hell-beings and have returned again to the earth due to the remainder of their karma,
after they have emerged from the terrible great ocean of existence which is filled with both merit and demerit?
"How can embodied beings be liberated from this mass of foam consisting of the sufferings of the womb and so forth?
Thus addressed with respect regarding the meaning of all these questions, the Blessed Sun,
possessed of great splendor, replied in both concise and detailed form.
The Sun said:
O Śūra, listen as I speak of that meritorious dharma which bestows the fruits of heaven and liberation, provides a crossing over the ocean of hell, and removes all sin.
Dharma is always preceded by faith, established in the beginning, middle, and end of faith;
Dharma has faith as its goal and its foundation—thus is faith proclaimed.
The subtle essences of the Vedas and mantras, as well as Pradhāna, Puruṣa, and Īśvara, [are likewise rooted in faith].
The subtle Dharma is attained through faith alone, and not by another means;
it is not reached through manifold bodily austerities nor by heaps of wealth—
even by the gods, if they are devoid of faith.
Faith is the supreme, subtle Dharma; faith is the oblation offered in sacrifice and austerity;
faith is liberation and heaven; faith is this entire world.
Even if one should give away all one's possessions or even one's very life, if it is done without faith—
He would not obtain any fruit at all; therefore, one should be devoted to faith.
Thus, all my teachings have been proclaimed as consisting of faith.
A person should worship with faith, and he who is to be meditated upon is to be worshipped with faith.
For the sake of attaining authority and bestowing liberation of great essence,
this wonderful speech of mine has been spoken; it is sometimes expressed for the ignorant or with ambiguity,
yet it is divine, brings about various accomplishments, and delights the hearts of the world.
"Listen to my words, which are profound and convey a well-ascertained meaning; they are pleasing to my mind. For the wise know this two-legged one to be the ocean of my heart.
O bird, he is renowned as Khaṣolka; may his realm be auspicious."
Transcending the qualities of the three deities, omniscient, all-knowing, and sovereign—
He who abides in the single-syllable mantra "Om" is my Supreme Lord.
Just as this terrible ocean of worldly existence has proceeded from beginningless time, so too does He abide.
Khaṣolka likewise is beginningless and the purifier of the ocean of saṃsāra;
like medicine for diseases by virtue of its nature as their antidote,
he is the cause of liberation for those seeking release, perfected, and the accomplisher of all goals.
This mantra is my name, and it is always remembered as the object of that name;
I am both the name and the named, O sky-walker, perfected through the mantra.
Herein, within the six-syllabled mantra situated in the mind's reach, lies the Veda.
Or rather, he who is liberated by the single syllable "Akṣara" is remembered in this world as one possessing five syllables.
What need has he for many mantras or for scriptures of great extent,
if this mantra "Oṃ Namaḥ Khaṣolkāya" is established within his heart?
By him everything has been studied, by him everything has been heard, and by him everything has been practiced—by him who [has mastered] my six-syllable utterance: "Oṃ namaḥ Khaṣolke.
This entire statement of mine is a formal injunction; it is not a mere figurative or hyperbolic expression.
"I shall explain to you in its entirety this supreme meaning of my words.
O high-minded Vainateya, quickly ask this after bowing down.
Sumantu said:
Having heard the words of Bhānu, the mighty Vainateya,
O Bhārata, bowed with devotion to Saptāśvatilaka and spoke.
Anūru said:
"Speak to me, O tiger among gods, that which I ask, O high-minded one!
What kind of speech is this? Tell me the meaning of the Sun's words, O Lord!
Saptāśvatilaka said:
That stainless speech which was uttered by the Blessed One, the omniscient one who is free from all defects, is authoritative; of this there is no doubt.
For this reason, he is called "Mārtaṇḍa" by the wise.
One obtains merit according to the truth, but falls downward through lack of faith;
one should worship like the Sun the Guru who speaks the words of the Sun,
he who lifts up a person submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra.
Who would not worship that Guru, who— like a vessel filled with the water of the solar dharma—
gradually extinguishes the heat of the fire of ignorance in his devotees with the nectar of knowledge?
Neither by a great kingdom nor by heaps of wealth is that pacification of ignorance attained which brings happiness in the next world;
yet that which has been spoken for the sake of attaining heaven and liberation is truly excellent.
That speech of yours, which was well-spoken by the God of Gods, should be understood as such; however,
for those who follow passion, hatred, intolerance, anger, desire, and craving,
their speech is called ill-spoken because it is a cause for hell.
Of what use is that Sanskrit which is attached to soft-sounding speech,
the talk of those who delight in ignorance, and the cause of the afflictions of saṃsāra—
[that Sanskrit] by hearing which merit is born and the destruction of passion and the other defilements occurs?
Even that speech which appears deformed should be understood as exceedingly beautiful;
for the Smṛtis, the Bhārata, the Vedas,
and the great Śāstras are intended solely for the exhaustion of one’s own lifespan through the complete exposition of Dharma and Artha.
For men of deluded minds, there is attachment to the cycle of worldly existence consisting of sons, wives, and so forth;
however, for those who understand the nature of saṃsāra, this scripture—which has issued from the mouth of the beginningless—is the means [of liberation].
You desire to know all of this: "This is the best," "This is to be known."
Even one with a lifespan of a thousand years does not reach the end of all treatises;
realizing that life is a mere collection of syllables and is utterly deceptive,
one should abandon all scriptures and attend to the world beyond.
Of what use is that wisdom or that capability to embodied beings which is unable to bear the burden of merit pertaining to the next world?
Even a wise man is a fool, and one endowed with power is powerless, if he lacks this capacity.
He who is unable to utter the greatness of the knowledge of the Sun is not a scholar; he alone is capable, he is an ascetic, and he has conquered his senses,
who is intent upon contemplating the true nature of the knowledge of the Sun.
Even if a king were to bestow upon him the entire earth, wealth, and gold,
the teacher should not instruct him if he asks anything out of improper motives.
But he who listens to the Dharma of the Sun and speaks it according to justice— [to him the teacher should teach].
From that, one goes to a good state; in the opposite case, one goes to hell.
By means of the ritual of the six-syllable mantra, the Sun, who arises from the milking of the cow, is fully worshipped; thus, for men, equality with him is swiftly and thoroughly attained.
In ancient times, from the Ocean of Milk (Kṣīroda) while it was being churned by the gods and demons,
five cows were born, the mothers of all the worlds:
Nandā, Subhadrā, Surabhī, Sumanā, and Śobhanāvatī.
Cows, equal to the sun in brilliance, have arisen and attained their manifest form for the sake of benefiting all the worlds and for the satiation of the gods;
these cows remain taking refuge in me for the purpose of bathing the Sun.

O best of birds, understand that their limbs are meritorious and consist of the six flavors; they remain constant throughout all the species of birds and other creatures. The cow-dung, gallstone, urine, milk, curd, and ghee of cows—these are the six products.
The six limbs are pure and bestow all accomplishments.
The glorious Bilva tree, beloved of the Sun, arises from cow dung;
Śrī, with a lotus in her hand, resides there, and for that reason it is known as the Vṛkṣa (the Tree).
Blue and red lotuses are born again from mud;
and from cow dung comes gorocana, which is auspicious, purifying, and grants all desires.
From cow urine is born guggulu, fragrant and pleasing to behold.
Food is the sustenance for all the gods, and for the Sun-god especially;
whatever seed exists in the world should be known as originating from milk. All auspicious things born from curd lead to the accomplishment of one's goals.
Amṛta was produced from ghee, which is exceedingly dear to the immortals;
therefore, he who bathes the Sun with ghee, milk, and curd,
should at the end of that rite cleanse him with warm water and decoctions.
Having bathed [the image] with cool water, one should subsequently mark the Sun with yellow pigment (rocanā).
One should worship with bilva leaves, lotuses, and blue water-lilies;
thereafter, O Bird, one should offer the arghya oblation consisting of guggulu resin together with a vajra.
One should offer milk-rice, curd-rice, and the *vajra* together with honey,
as well as various kinds of edible foods, with true devotion.
Having performed a circumambulation and prostrated thereafter, one should ask for forgiveness.
By this method, he who worships the Sun, the Lord of Day, with the six-limbed rite,
attains all desires both in this world and in the next; indeed,
having thus worshipped the Sun with the six-limbed ritual, he becomes well-disposed in mind.
The wise man shall lead twenty-one generations of his lineage to heaven;
having established them in heaven, he himself shall go to that state known as Jyautiṣa.
O Hero, the Bhojakas have been appointed by a portion [of the merit] for the sake of the gods' work.
Together with their lord, they go to the supreme light, the glorious Sun;
having enjoyed abundant pleasures, the Bhojaka, equal in enjoyment,
returns here again after time and becomes a sole ruler upon the earth.

Whatever flowers, leaves, fruits, or water have been offered in the worship of the Sun, and even the cows belonging to the Sun, go to the world of the Sun; of this there is no doubt. He who drinks the milk of a cow that has not been given to the Sun at his meal [commits a fault].
If he does not perform the libation for the Sun, he shall go to a terrible hell. He should drink the milk of cows at one time for the sake of the Maker of Light;
O best of birds, with this milk he should bathe the Lord.
O elder brother of Garuḍa, one should bathe the Sun with all the milk that cows produce at dawn;
for whatever portion of the world one enjoys, one should not offer it to the deity.
O Lord of Birds, for as many thousands of years as there are pores on the body of a cow,
so long shall one who hears of the Sun— whether he has already worshipped him or is currently worshipping him— be cooked in hell.
He who hears this and rejoices partakes in the fruit of sacrifice;
by seeing the Sun-god worshipped, one is liberated from all sins;
and by bowing to Bhānu with joy, one is glorified in his world.
O bird, that man who beholds the Sun being worshipped with devotion shall obtain the entire fruit of a sacrifice; of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, he who hears of the Sun being worshipped and rejoices in it [attains the same].
One obtains all that fruit through the grace of the Sun.
A gift offered with devotion, which follows one for a single lifetime,
is said to yield results for a thousand lifetimes for those who are devoid of the sacrifice of recitation (japa-yajña).
O Lord of Birds, for those who subsist on recitation, a gift that endures until the dissolution of all beings—
even if it be exceedingly small—
provides enjoyment for the donor until the great final dissolution.
For those who possess discernment, no gift whatsoever is small or insignificant;
that which is joined with the proper place, time, ritual procedure, faith, and a worthy recipient is inexhaustible.
That which is given to a worthy recipient, in a suitable place, at the right time, according to the prescribed rite, and with faith—

Whatever is given, offered in sacrifice, or performed, that shall yield infinite fruit. O Hero, even if only half a sesame seed is given with faith to a worthy recipient by a twice-born man, according to the rules and with devotion, it shall fulfill all desires.
That bath which is performed with the waters of knowledge and wiped clean with the ashes of virtuous conduct—
