that bath is proclaimed to be the most excellent among all vessels of merit.
For men, the recitation of mantras, self-restraint, and discipline are the saviors from the ocean of saṃsāra.
That [teaching] is considered the supreme vessel for those who are ignorant and led by evil;
yet the scripture, when equipped with the raft of knowledge, truly carries the ignorant across the great ocean of sin— how could a stone ever carry another stone?
Whatever fruit is obtained by twice-born men learned in the Vedas from sharing their food with others at their waist,
that same fruit belongs to one who lives by recitation (japa) through the offering of *hantakāra*.
Furthermore, he in whose house a living being comes and eats, having been honored with hospitality, [attains that same merit].
He shall deliver his family from its immersion in the ocean of hell.
Whatever fruit is proclaimed to come from sacrifices, fire-offerings, and sacred fords,
one obtains that entire fruit by giving food to a practitioner of recitation.
By giving food even once with faith to one who is self-restrained, peaceful in mind, and devoted to meditation, one is liberated from all sins; likewise,
by giving to those who chant prayers, who are endowed with tranquility, and whose minds are dedicated to the Sun.
Having fed [the guest] with single-minded devotion even once, one shall obtain all desires.
And whoever, while meditating upon the *sūkta* of the Sun, should constantly feed [the guest],
then by that very act, food has been eaten in the direct presence of the Sun himself.
"The man who, at a *śrāddha* ceremony dedicated to the ancestors, feeds a priest (*bhojaka*),
undoubtedly attains the solar realm.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Cow" within the *Sauradharma*, in the *Saptamī-kalpa* of the *Brāhma-parvan* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
The Description of the Honoring of the Feeder.
Saptāśva said:
Having offered all cooked food to the Sun, one should perform oblations in the fire.

Having offered it into the fire, O hero, one should cast the bali-offering in all directions. That man who eats cooked food daily without first offering it to the Sun, the Fire, his Guru, and the Brahmins, eats only sin.
In agriculture, animal husbandry, and trade, the sins of men increase through anger, falsehood, and exhaustion, as well as by the five defects of the slaughterhouse:
the mortar, the grinding stone, the hearth, the water-jar, and the broom.
A householder has five slaughterhouses; because of them, he does not go to heaven.
By worshipping the sun, fire, and the guru, he is not tainted by these sins, nor by other terrible transgressions; therefore, he should always worship them.
For as many grains of rice as there are in the food offering made to the Sun, Agni,
and the Guru, for that many thousands of years shall the donor dwell in the City of the Sun.
If these offerings are sprinkled with ghee and accompanied by honey-cakes, the merit is ten times greater.
O bird, an offering endowed with the qualities of appetizers yields a hundredfold merit;
an offering of sixty-day rice (*ṣaṣṭika-odana*) yields a thousandfold fruit;
and an offering of fragrant *śāli* rice should be known to yield ten thousand times more.
Gifts of food, drink, and edibles, as well as their respective fruits—
whatever it may be— should always be given to the Sun, fire, the Guru, and the virtuous.
By offering the aforementioned edible foods, one obtains inexhaustible fruit.
Thus, whoever offers devotion to the Sun, the God of gods,
shall uplift his ancestors from all sins and lead them to heaven;
by the mere sight of the Sun, one obtains this meritorious merit of bathing in the Gaṅgā.
O bird, by bowing down one obtains the merit of bathing at all sacred fords;
by prostrating with the head before the Sun, one is liberated from all sins.
Furthermore, by attending upon him during the twilight, one is glorified in the world of the Sun.
When Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are worshipped by him simultaneously,
as well as the ancestors and all the gods, they become as if worshipped on that day of the Sun;
his ancestors are gratified just as farmers are by a bountiful harvest.
O Lord of Birds, would he who, out of devotion, feeds at a *śrāddha* a Brāhmaṇa who subsists by recitation, uplift even one person in our lineage? He who,
having fully honored the Sun, feeds at a *śrāddha* one who subsists by recitation— [would he not do so]?
His ancestors are satisfied and his grandfathers sing:
"Today, that wise man in our lineage will feed the reciter;
having seen the knower of the Purāṇas approaching, they stand together [in joy]."
"All the medicinal herbs are playing: 'We shall go to the imperishable heaven.
For the sake of favoring the worlds and for the testing of faith, the ancestors and likewise the deities wander in the form of guests."
Therefore, one should go forward with palms joined in reverence to meet a guest who has arrived,
honoring him with a welcome, a seat, water for the feet, the arghya offering, a bath, food, a bed, and so forth—
whether he be handsome or ugly, or even if he be soiled and dressed in dirty clothes.
When a guest arrives at the proper time, a wise man should not hesitate;
for the Sun is eternally present within the bodies of those who serve food.
Those other cooks who reject him are established in all manner of sins.
With their faces downward and feet upward, they fall into the fires of hell;
their mouths pierced by worms and tormented by fire,
they are afflicted by fierce weapons for as long as the reign of fourteen Indras.
And those deluded ones who indeed hear slander against the Brāhmaṇas are especially cooked in the hells by my will.
Among all worthy recipients, the reciter (jāpaka) is the supreme vessel.

"Therefore, with all effort and being well-composed, one should worship [the Sun]. Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-eighth chapter, titled 'Description of the Honoring of the Bhojaka,' within the Saura-dharma section of the Saptamī-kalpa in the Brāhma-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya-mahāpurāṇa*. [Next: The Dialogue with the Seven Horses regarding the Saura-dharma."
Saptāśvatilaka said:
Just as juices in an unbaked clay vessel perish when that vessel is destroyed,
so too do recitation, meditation, and charity perish along with the unworthy recipient.
Just as a good seed sown in saline soil becomes fruitless,
and just as an oblation poured into ashes is fruitless for the sacrificer,
so too is a gift given to a Brahmin devoid of recitation (japa) rendered useless.
Just as a eunuch is fruitless with women, and just as a cow is fruitless with another cow,
so the birth of a Brahmin who is devoid of recitation is fruitless. Just as one crossing in a boat made of iron sinks in the water, so it is for him.
Both the giver and the receiver fall into blind darkness; however,
O bird, that gift which is bestowed out of compassion for all beings and with faith should be known as the supreme gift that fulfills all desires.
O best of birds, whatever is given to the poor, the blind, and the wretched, and to children, the elderly, and the sick, its fruit shall be infinite;
for the virtuous do not accept gifts with their own self-interest in mind.
The ears and other senses accepted [the gift] solely for the benefit of the giver;
the suppliant speaks only for the benefit of the giver, saying, "Give to me.
For it is because of this that the giver ascends upward, while the receiver remains below.
The suppliant who speaks so eloquently, "Give," seems as if he were awakening the wealth itself, saying:
"That which I requested this morning has indeed borne the fruit of non-giving.
Miserly people do not awaken [their wealth] by begging; they simply say, "Give."
Such is the state of one who does not give: he must beg from house to house.
But what person would not honor a supplicant who comes to his home?
Who could fail to honor this seeker who begs day after day?
By whose power they compel even those who are unwilling to take refuge in men;
for day after day they beg and show themselves to the donor.
One stands below, while another stands above.
The distinction between the giver and the beggar is indicated by the hands themselves:
he who, having received a petitioner, abandons the gift and gazes instead at the recipient,
is not a giver in the ultimate sense, because he remains occupied with all worldly activities.
If there were no people who sought [gifts], how could the dharma of giving exist?
Therefore, one should give to those seekers; "Welcome, welcome" is dear.
Following them with water for their feet constitutes the sevenfold staircase to heaven.
When will the anxiety that conforms to one's thoughts ever perish?
It is proper to give even half a morsel of food to those who constantly seek it;
the wise say that a gift devoid of kindness is as good as lost.
Therefore, one who desires infinite fruit should give with reverence;
even a refusal that is tender with affection is better than a gift defiled by disrespect and harshness.
No boon was granted to supplicants by me with a mind full of anger;

neither that wealth, nor joy, nor righteousness exists when deprived of what is dear [to others]. Giving, the practice of vows, sacrifice, meditation, oblation, and austerity—[all these are fruitless without it].
"O bird, even if everything is done with great effort, anger renders it fruitless for him.
He who gives what has been honored with faith, and he who receives it with honor—both of them go to heaven; by the opposite of this, they go to hell."

Generosity toward a teacher yields great fruit for the donor through five qualities: magnanimity, hospitality, friendliness, compassion, and the absence of envy. [Likewise, giving at] Vārāṇasī, Kurukṣetra, Prayāga, and the Puṣkara lakes [yields great merit].
Gātaṭa and the ocean, as well as the Naimiṣa forest;
Mūlasthāna, which is highly meritorious, and likewise Puṇḍīrasvāmika;
Kālapriya, O best of birds, and the abode of Kṣīrikā.
Thus have these regions been proclaimed, frequented by gods and Siddhas;
all the hermitages of the Sun are meritorious, as are all rivers and mountains. Furthermore, those regions where cows, Siddhas, and sages dwell are celebrated as sacred.
Whatever small amount is given at the Sūryāyatana site,
it should be known as having infinite fruit due to the power of that sacred field; likewise,
an eclipse of the moon or sun and the commencement of the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa) are most excellent occasions.
The equinox, the Savyatīpāta, the Ṣaḍaśītimukha,
the intercalary days (dinacchidra), the Saṃkrānti, and the meritorious Viṣupada— O Bird,
these times are declared to increase the merit of men.
Devotion, supreme affection, righteousness, the singular contemplation of dharma,
and practice— these are to be known as the five synonyms of faith.
That which is offered according to rule into a worthy recipient by means of faith is most excellent.
Therefore, one who desires imperishable results should establish faith and give;
that gift which is bestowed according to rule upon a worthy recipient with faith should be known as having infinite fruit, even if it is merely the weight of a burden.

He who, with faith, gives even a small amount to those who are distressed, the lowly, or endowed with virtue, attains all his desires and reaches the higher worlds; the knowers of truth declare that faith itself is the gift. Faith is to be known as the supreme gift, and faith alone is the supreme austerity.
In this world, people desire faith as their sacrifice; faith is the highest nourishment.
Furthermore, non-violence, patience, truthfulness, modesty, faith, restraint of the senses, charity, sacrifice, austerity, and meditation—this tenfold set is the means for achieving dharma.
Whether slain by all of them individually or collectively, or through the performance of the solar duties (*sūryadharma*),
a single destiny is proclaimed for those who have attained the abode of the Sun.
Just as the earth is traditionally held to be the supreme peace for all living beings.
Therefore, a wise person desiring my world should perform great merit;
likewise, one who forms a purposeful intention regarding another's wife or property,
or toward a guru who is distressed, incapacitated, or about to depart for a foreign land.
One who is overcome by enemies, as well as a doer of evil who abandons [them],
and he who shows contempt for their wife, friends, or sons—
this should be known as a sin equal to the reviling of one's guru.
The slayer of a Brahmin, the drinker of intoxicants, the thief, and the violator of the Guru’s bed—
these are the great sinners (mahāpātakins), and the fifth is he who associates with them.
He who speaks ill of a Brahmin out of anger, hatred, fear, or greed [is also a sinner].

He who commits a great offense resulting in the loss of life is declared a slayer of a Brahmin (brahmahā). And he who, having summoned a Brahmin who is begging and destitute, says "I have nothing," is declared a Cāṇḍāla.
He who seizes land previously given to the gods, the twice-born,
or cows— even if it has been lost over time— is called a slayer of a Brahmin.
That dull-witted man who, having studied the knowledge of the Sun, abandons it, is likewise condemned.
O observer of noble vows, his sin should be known as equal to that of a drinker of *surā* liquor:
the abandonment of the *agnihotra* fire and the five daily sacrifices;
the desertion of one’s mother and father; giving false testimony; and the killing of a friend.
It is unpleasant for the devotees of the Sun, as is the eating of forbidden food;
likewise, it is the slaughter of innocent living beings.
They possess no sovereignty over this supreme city of the gods.
The Lord of all beings bestows sovereignty over one's own world;
yet, some men devoted to the yoga of knowledge are liberated right here,
while others, intent on worldly enjoyments, revolve again in saṃsāra.
Therefore, one seeking liberation should abandon attachment to enjoyments;
being dispassionate and having a peaceful mind and self, one shall attain the world of the Sun.
And even those with unattached hearts who recite this incidentally—
Among them, one speaks according to his own experience:
"To those who, having once eaten the remnants of another's meal, do not worship the Sun,
the Sun grants enjoyments in the world of the Piśācas."
For those cruel ones with eyes full of rage who mutter [the name of] the Sun twice,
the Sun bestows great fortune upon them in the world of the Rākṣasas.
For those men devoted to liquor and meat who worship the Sun three times [a day], [he grants the same].
In the world of the ṛṣis, Ravi bestows divine enjoyments upon those who,
by chance, perform dance and song three or four times; O bird, they go before the Sun to the abode of the Gandharvas.
People worship the Lord of Rays (the Sun) with the desire for fame;
for them, the Sun bestows all their desires in the abode of Śakra.
He who worships the Sun with a mind attached to sensual pleasures—
O Lord of Birds,
for one who worships Citrabhānu nine times during the Prājāpatya [period], Ravi bestows enjoyments in his world; he goes to the realm of Viṣṇu and rejoices together with Viṣṇu.
Beyond that is another station, enchanting to all beings,
filled with divine celestial chariots possessing immeasurable qualities that fulfill every desire,
and pervaded by countless objects variegated with red ochre and crimson.
O best of birds, those who go to that place— which is filled with various dwellings and possesses a splendor equal to ten million suns— and who honor the twice-born,
reside and sport there in that world.
Therefore, even beyond that, the solar realm is called the "Luminous" station.
Thus, by the power of the sun, even through inferior action,
men attain various stations in accordance with their faith and disposition.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-ninth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between the Seven Horses and Anūru," in the Sauradharma section of the *Saptamī-kalpa* within the *Brāhma-parvan* of the glorious *Śrī-Bhaviṣya-Mahāpurāṇa*.
[This is] the description of the dialogue between Sūrya and Anūru among the Sauradharmas.
Saptāśvatilaka said:
There are also millions of celestial chariots in the form of stars;
whoever offers salutation to them shall obtain that very fruit.
Thus have been described these great destinies for those who follow the solar dharma.

Therefore, one who desires happiness should always practice the dharma of the Sun. Now, the gross accumulations of sin that cause rebirth in hell are being described in brief, according to their means: mind, speech, and body.
The theft of cattle on a path, or of fire in a forest, city, or village—
these sins here are equal to the drinking of liquor;
as is the seizing of everything in a forest, including men, women, elephants, and horses.
O sky-walker, the theft of medicinal herbs grown near cattle or land,
as well as the theft of sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, musk,
and fine cloth by means of placing one's hand upon them, is recorded as being equal to the theft of gold.
The improper seduction of marriageable maidens,
sexual intercourse with one’s own son, friend, or wife, as well as with sisters;
the heinous violation of virgins, and consorting with women of the lowest castes.
Sexual intercourse with a woman of the same caste is recorded as equal to violating the Guru’s bed.
Those sins which have been described as equal to the great crimes (mahāpātaka) are designated as "pātaka," while we shall now describe those that are minor offenses (upapātaka).
O twice-born one, he who, having promised wealth for the sake of a Brahmin, does not give it;
he who abandons virtuous wives, holy kinsmen, and ascetics;
and he who makes a deliberate effort to steal cows, land, gold, and garments—[these are great sins].
A very great injury has been committed against those whose intellects are dedicated to the Lord.

For whoever should inflict even the slightest harm upon one established in a stage of life— that person who is already overcome by his own servants and deprived of cattle, grain, and wealth— [he incurs a grave sin].
Stealing water-pots, grain, or cattle; officiating at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice; the sale of a sacrifice, a grove, a tank, a wife, or a child;
and [the neglect] of pilgrimages, fasts, vows, and the practice of recitation—these are [offenses].
Those people who, through sinful deeds, misappropriate women's property;
those who fail to protect women; those who consort with women who drink liquor; those who fail to give to the sages; and those who practice usury on grain—[these are the ones who fall].
The disparagement of gods, fire, virtuous men, and virtuous women, as well as of cows and Brahmins—
whether done in their presence or in their absence— even toward regional kings;
and those who have abandoned their ancestors and deities, as well as those who have forsaken their own duties.

Those who are immoral, nihilistic, and wicked, who propound that existence and non-existence are both void— when desire has thus arisen, they engage in sexual intercourse with those of improper birth, with animals,
or with women during their menses or in non-vaginal openings.
Those who destroy the pleasure gardens of women, sons, and friends;
those who speak unpleasantly to people and subvert their intentions;
and those who breach tanks, embankments, bridges, and reservoirs.
"And he who causes a breach in the row of those seated in a single line—
by these sins, men are known as *upapātakin* (secondary sinners).

Thus ends the one hundred and ninetieth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Sūrya and Anūru on Solar Duties," in the *Sauradharma* section of the *Brahma-parvan* within the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, in the seventh kalpa.
The Dialogue between Saptāśvatilaka and Karuṇa.
Saptāśvatilaka said:
"Those who [cause harm] to cows, Brahmins, crops, virtuous people, or ascetics..."
Moreover, those men who act as corrupters go to hell; likewise,
those others who are informers against him suffer through their own exhaustion,
as do those who take pleasure in the wives of others and those who defile virgins.

Those men who constantly delight in drinking liquor and taking pleasure in singing and instrumental music, and who void their excrement in cow-pens, near fires, in water, in pleasant places, under the shade of trees, on mountains, in gardens, or in temples— [they fall into hell].
Possessed by lust, anger, and pride, intent on seeking out vulnerabilities,
joined with heretical doctrines, and delighting in idle chatter,
they obstruct the paths and seize the boundaries of others.
Men who forge official decrees, those who perform fraudulent acts,
he who is a maker of bows, craftsmen's tools, or weapons, he who is a seller [of such items],
one who is merciless toward his servants, and he who is a tamer of animals— [These are the ones who go to the Raurava hell.]

He who listens with feigned attention to the words of one speaking falsely; he who betrays his master, friends, and teachers; he who is deceitful, fickle, and treacherous; and those who [abandon] their wife, sons, and friends, as well as children, the elderly, and the afflicted— (The remainder of the verse follows: ...these, O King, go to the Raurava hell. || 106 || The wicked man who, having promised "I shall give," does not give when asked for wealth; he who, having promised "I shall do it," does not do it when asked to perform a task—such a person goes to the Tāmisra hell. || 107 || One who steals gold, one who drinks liquor, one who violates the bed of his guru, and one who associates with them—all these four fall into the Kumbhīpāka hell. || 108 || A woman who kills her husband, a Brahmin woman who drinks liquor, and a woman who violates the bed of her guru—all these fall into the Asipatravana hell. || 109 || One who steals grain, one who steals land, one who steals water, one who steals fruit, and one who steals fire—all these go to the Mahāraurava hell. || 110 || One who steals clothes, one who steals cows, one who steals food, one who steals flowers, and one who steals roots—all these go to the Saṃjīvana hell. || 111 || One who steals cotton, one who steals salt, one who steals ghee, one who steals oil, and one who steals honey—all these go to the Vaitaraṇī hell. || 112 || One who steals gems, pearls, corals, conch-shells, silver, copper, iron, or lead—all these go to the Lohasaṃvartana hell. || 113 || One who steals silk, one who steals wool, one who steals linen, one who steals jute, and one who steals cotton—all these go to the Śālmalī hell. || 114 || One who steals molasses, one who steals sugar, one who steals salt, one who steals curd, and one who steals milk—all these go to the Andhatāmisra hell. || 115 || One who steals vegetables, one who steals greens, one who steals cooked food, one who steals uncooked food, and one who steals fuel—all these go to the Kālasūtra hell. || 116 || One who steals a vehicle, one who steals a bed, one who steals a seat, one who steals a house, and one who steals a field—all these go to the Mahāpadma hell. || 117 || One who steals a slave, one who steals a horse, one who steals a goat, one who steals a sheep, and one who steals a bird—all these go to the Padma hell. || 118 || One who steals a deer, one who steals a dog, one who steals a cat, one who steals a rat, and one who steals a snake—all these go to the Mahāpadma hell. || 119 || One who steals a monkey, one who steals a bear, one who steals a tiger, one who steals a leopard, and one who steals a boar—all these go to the Padma hell. || 120 || One who steals a buffalo, one who steals an elephant, one who steals a cow, one who steals a bull, and one who steals a calf—all these go to the Mahāpadma hell. || 121 || One who steals a goat, one who steals a sheep, one who steals a chicken, one who steals a duck, and one who steals a crane—all these go to the Padma hell. || 122 || One who steals a frog, one who steals a tortoise, one who steals a fish, one who steals a crab, and one who steals a lizard—all these go to the Mahāpadma hell. || 123 || One who steals a snake, one who steals a scorpion, one who steals a centipede, one who steals a spider, and one who steals a fly—all these go to the Padma hell. || 124 || One who steals a bee, one who steals a wasp, one who steals a mosquito, one who steals a gnat, and one who steals a louse—all these go to the Mahāpadma hell. || 125 || One who steals a flea, one who steals a mite, one who steals a hair, one who steals a
He who eats cooked food himself while neglecting his servants, guests, and kinsmen who are hungry,
and who does not give food to a Brahmin—
his cooking is known to be in vain and is censured among those who discourse on the Veda.
Those who, having voluntarily taken up a religious vow, abandon it because their senses are unsubdued;
those who have fallen from the life of renunciation; those who reveal secrets;
and those fools who beat cows or repeatedly terrify them.
They do not nourish the weak, nor do they seek out lost cattle;
they oppress them with excessive burdens and force them to carry what is beyond their endurance. Indeed, other most wicked men even cause the testicles of bulls to be drained.
Those most sinful and lowest of men drive even a barren cow; those fools who show no compassion for the helpless, the destitute, the young, the old, and the emaciated—
those men go to hell.
Goats and sheep, owners of buffaloes, and the husbands of *vṛṣalī* women; Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who have always fallen away from their own duties;
artisans, craftsmen, courtesans, and those who bear the banners of kings for the sake of security.
Dancers and those who strike at the light—all these go to hell.
[They consume] drinks of ghee and oil, honey, meat, juices, and fermented liquors;
as well as molasses, sugarcane, milk, vegetables, curd, roots, and fruits.
Grass, wood, flowers, seeds, and unsurpassed medicinal herbs;
sandals, an umbrella, a cart, a seat, a bed, and earth;
copper, lead, tin, bell-metal, and that which originates from water such as conch shells and the like.
Whether made of wood or bamboo, as well as household utensils,
or those produced from wool, cotton, silk, or hemp—
whatever items, coarse or fine, deluded people indeed steal; [for them, there is no atonement].
A man who forcibly seizes various other such diverse substances will certainly go to the hells;
whether it be this or that, even if it is as small as a mustard seed, it remains a hidden transgression.
Having stolen [these], a man goes to hell; there is no doubt about this.
Through such sins as these, immediately after departing from the body, a man obtains a body corresponding to his previous form for the purpose of experiencing physical torment.
Thus, by the command of Yama, he shall go to the world of Yama with his very body,
being led by the most terrible messengers of Yama and filled with great suffering—
those beings, whether divine or human, whose souls were devoted to unrighteousness.

The Teacher is remembered as the King of Dharma; for those who are devoid of discipline and whose selves have strayed through negligence, sin is brought to destruction by means of various kinds of expiations, even through most terrible and diverse forms of execution.
The lord of the earth is declared to be the punisher of adulterers, thieves, and those who act unjustly, while the King of Dharma (Yama) is the punisher of those who act in secret.
Therefore, one should perform the expiation for any sin committed.
There is no destruction of what has not been experienced, even in hundreds of millions of eons.
He who performs a virtuous deed, causes it to be performed, or rejoices in its performance—
whether by body, mind, or speech— he shall attain supreme happiness.
Thus, in brief, the threefold destiny has been declared according to the divisions of sin.
Likewise, other diverse destinies are now described according to the divisions of karma.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-first chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Saptāśva and Tilakāruṇa regarding the Duties of the Sun" (*sauradharma*), within the *Saptamī-kalpa* of the *Brāhma-parvan* in the glorious *Bhaviṣya-mahāpurāṇa*.
The description of the dialogue between Saptāśvatilaka and Ūru.
Saptāśvatilaka said:
[It was] a terrible thing that produced terror for sinners who commit evil deeds.
Among all living beings— those dwelling in the womb, those being born, the young, the middle-aged, women, men, eunuchs, and the elderly— one must depart;
likewise, embodied beings must experience there the fruits of their auspicious and inauspicious deeds.

Whatever auspicious or inauspicious deeds had been performed were indeed reported by Citragupta and all the other judges of dharma, who speak the truth, in the presence of the King of Dharma; for once a deed has been committed and deliberated upon, it must necessarily be experienced.
In that regard, those men who perform auspicious deeds, whose minds are gentle, and who are endowed with compassion, go to the abode of Yama by a pleasant path.
He who gives sandals, wooden shoes, or an umbrella to the foremost of the twice-born [attains this].
And he goes happily to the abode of Yama by means of that great merit.
But the man who enters a temple while wearing shoes,
especially the inner sanctum, experiences great terror.
Gifts of sandals, and especially food—
by such specific acts of giving, a man goes to the city of Dharmarāja with ease; therefore, one should practice righteousness.
Furthermore, O bird, those men who perform cruel deeds and are devoted to sin travel by that terrible southern path to the abode of Yama,
which measures eighty-eight thousand and eighty yojanas.
The city of Vaivasvata is known to exist in various forms;
it appears as if situated nearby to men of virtuous conduct,
yet it remains exceedingly distant for those who proceed with fierce wickedness.
In some places it was filled with sharp thorns and strewn with gravel;
in others, it was covered with stones as hard as razor edges and swords,
and in some parts, it was scorched by the great sun and by bottomless chasms.
Pierced by iron spikes and struck by swords,
they proceed along a path lined with a wall of hungry ghosts, distressed as they pass beneath falling mountains covered in trees and adorned with stainless peaks.
In some places it was filled with uneven chasms, in others with slippery clods of earth,
with scorching sands, and likewise with sharp spikes;
and in some places it was pervaded by bamboo groves formed of many interlacing branches.
With great difficulty, he clung to a most dreadful path through the darkness;
it was strewn in some places with sharp-pointed thorns, in others with forest fires,
in some places with heated rocks, and in others covered with snow.
In some places he should cause him to enter what is filled with sand up to his neck;
in some places it is filled with foul water, and in some places with the fire of chaff;
in some places with lions, in some places with tigers, gadflies, and dreadful insects.
In some places there were great leeches, and in others vipers;
in some places fierce flies, and in others serpents with virulent venom;
and in others, young lordly elephants, intoxicated by their strength and intent on destruction.
With great bulls possessing sharp horns that scraped the path,
with buffaloes and camels having massive horns,
and with intoxicated, rutting [animals], as well as with fierce ḍākinīs and terrifying rākṣasas.
Indeed, being tormented by most terrible diseases, they proceed,
being struck by a great and fierce wind mixed with mighty nooses and by a rain of massive stones, left utterly without refuge.
In some places they indeed go forth being torn apart by the falling of lightning;
by the crashing of masses of thunderbolts and by terrible falls of meteors;
and they indeed go forth being consumed by a rain of blazing coals.
Indeed, they proceed being afflicted by a great blinding darkness and by the brilliance of the planet Venus;
they are repeatedly terrified by the terrible roars of massive clouds,
while being filled on all sides with sharp stones.
Indeed, they proceed while being assailed by great torrents of sharp swords;
they are repeatedly terrified by the terrible roars of massive clouds,
and by a wind that is exceedingly cold, piercing, and harsh.
Thus, by means of a path that was fierce, devoid of provisions,
without support, difficult to traverse, utterly desolate on all sides,
vast and without rest, and hard to withstand due to its many dangers;
"All embodied beings who are deluded and performers of evil deeds are led [to their destination].
Knowing this, a person should perform merit and avoid sin;
through merit one attains divinity, and through sin one goes to hell.
O Bird, those by whom the Sun, the Lord of Gods, has been worshipped even slightly in their minds, shall never behold the face of Yama; however,
due to their most terrible sins, they remain [in this state] for some time by your command.
Those who do not worship the Sun on earth with their whole being become kings of the pretas and then go to the city of Ravi;
however, those who again worship Bhāskara on earth with their entire being are not smeared by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
Therefore, a person should indeed constantly practice devotion toward the Sun;
he who desires abundant wealth should worship Bhānu with faith.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-second chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Saptāśva and Tilakānūru regarding the Duties of the Sun in the Saptamī-kalpa," in the Brāhma-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Description of the Ritual for the Tooth-stick.
Saptāśvatilaka said:
On the solstices, the equinoxes, on [auspicious] days, at the transition of the sun (saṃkrānti), and likewise during eclipses;
One should worship the Sun constantly, especially on the seventh lunar day.
O Vainateya, learn from me the procedure for the Saptamī vow;
for this is the supreme secret, the highest means of propitiating the Sun.
The first [Saptamī] should be performed with *siddhārthaka* seeds, the second with *arka* flowers, the third with black pepper, and the fourth with sesame; the seventh,
O Hero, is proclaimed as the *odana-saptamī*.
These seven seventh days (Saptamīs) should be observed by one desiring prosperity;
accordingly, I shall describe their characteristics in order.
The bright seventh day (Śukla-saptamī) should be performed in either the month of Māgha or Mārgaśīrṣa.
For one who is afflicted by illness, however, there shall be no restriction regarding the fortnight or the month.
When half a watch (three hours) remains [of the day], one should indeed perform the cleaning of the teeth.
Regarding that, I shall now declare those trees which are desired on the fifth lunar day.
Through *madhūka* there shall be the attainment of a son; *mārkava* shall be the destroyer of suffering.
Through *badarī* and *bṛhatī*, one is swiftly liberated from disease.
Through *bilva* there shall be sovereignty, and through *khadira*, the accumulation of wealth.
The destruction of enemies occurs through *kadaṃba* flowers; the acquisition of wealth through *atimuktaka*;
one attains preeminence everywhere through those originating from the *āṭarūṣaka*;
one attains prominence among kinsmen through the *aśvattha*, which bestows fame.
From the *karavīra* flower, one’s knowledge becomes unshakable; of this there is no doubt. By placing the *śirīṣa*, one attains abundant prosperity.
By using the *priyaṅgu*, supreme good fortune shall arise.

Then, seated comfortably and restraining his speech, the wise man should form the object of his desire within his heart; having consecrated it with this mantra, he should use the tooth-stick for cleansing his teeth. *Oṃ namo bhagavate ratnatrayāya, sarvabuddhabodhisattvebhyaḥ, sarvatathāgatātmabhāvāya vajradantakāṣṭhābhimukhāya svāhā.* Having thus recited this mantra, the intelligent one should eat the tooth-stick for the sake of accomplishing his desired aims.
"O Lord of the Forest, you who grant desires, having granted this boon, recognize me;
O tooth-stick, grant me constant success—salutations be to you!
Having recited this three times, one should chew the tooth-cleansing stick.
Afterwards, having washed the wooden stick, one should discard it in a clean place.
Success is achieved if it falls facing upwards or remains facing the practitioner;
otherwise, if it falls differently, one should bring it back and cast it out again.

If the brushing of the teeth should be performed with the face turned away [from the sun], one should know that it is ineffective; furthermore, that seventh [day] is not to be accepted. On that night, the religious student (brahmacārī) should sleep while attending to auspicious rites.
Wearing an unwashed garment and being pure, endowed with proper conduct,
O bird, when that night has passed, the wise man should rise in the morning, wash his face, and perform the cleansing of his teeth before eating.
Having sat down and become pure, having bowed his head to the Sun,
and having performed the recitation (japa) as desired, he should then offer oblations into the fire.
Then, at the time of afternoon, having bathed with clay, cow dung, and water.
Having performed the ritual observances according to rule, remaining silent, dressed in white garments, and pure,
one should worship the God of gods, the Sun, with devotion according to the prescribed rite; then,
intent on the recitation of the Gāyatrī, one should sleep before the deity.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-third chapter, titled "Description of the Rules for the Tooth-stick," in the *Sauradharma* section of the *Saptamī-kalpa* within the *Brāhma-parvan* of the glorious *Mahāpurāṇa Bhaviṣya*.
In the dialogue between Sūrya and Aruṇa, [this is] the description of dreams. Saptāśvatilaka said:
Hereafter, I shall declare by which [dreams] seen on the seventh lunar day a man of restrained vows obtains various fruits,
having duly completed all rites such as recitation and fire-offerings.

Having established oneself on a bed upon the ground, one should meditate upon the God of gods. Alas, if a sleeping man should see the sun, the banner of Indra, or the moon in a dream, for him all prosperities are assured.
A water-pot, a yak-tail whisk, a mirror, and golden ornaments;
the flowing of blood and the falling of hair—these bring about sovereignty.
Furthermore, climbing a tree in a dream brings swift sovereignty in battle.
Milking a buffalo, a lioness, or a cow in one's own hand; their binding; the acquisition of a kingdom; touching the navel; being of wicked mind;
killing a sheep and eating it oneself; and [killing] a lion or a lotus—[these are the omens].
O Lord of Birds, for a man who consumes liquor, his own body's bones become fire;
yet for that man who eats milk-rice (pāyasa) from a vessel made of gold or silver,
or even from a lotus leaf, his sovereignty shall be equal [to that of the gods].
For victory in gambling or in battle brings happiness;
the burning of one's own body and the binding of the head lead to prosperity,
as do white garlands, garments, horses, cattle, and birds.
They always praise gain and the smearing of excrement.
Traveling by horse brings swift success, while traveling by chariot brings an increase in progeny.
Having various heads and arms bestows the prosperity of a householder.
Sexual union with a forbidden woman is auspicious, as is the supreme study of the Vedas;
whatever these— gods, the best of the twice-born, heroes, gurus, elders, and ascetics—
say to a man in a dream, he knows that to be indeed the truth.
O Lord of Birds, their sight is auspicious and their blessing brings prosperity;
sovereignty is gained even by the cutting off of one's own head, great wealth comes from the killing of many,
the acquisition of food results from weeping, and kingship is attained through imprisonment.
Indeed, he who, displaying valor, mounts a mountain, a horse, a lion, a bull, or even an elephant, attains great sovereignty;
seizing the planets and stars, he revolves like a ray of light.
The king uproots even the mountains upon the earth;
O Lord of Birds, there is the emergence of all the entrails from the body,
and the drinking of the rivers of the ocean, which brings about the happiness of sovereignty.
O Hero, O Lord of Birds, for one who reaches the further shore of the ocean of strength or even a sacred ford, his offspring shall be firm;
wealth shall come swiftly, even if a worm should devour him.
In that dream which is thus described, there is the acquisition of beautiful limbs and the very sight of them;
as well as union with auspicious things, health, wealth,
sovereignty, and the attainment of a kingdom.
There is no doubt that with seven [recitations] one attains these; with four, the highest learning is heard;
with five, abundance of sons; with six, long life, sons, and wealth;
with seven, various desires; and with eight, manifold fame.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Dreams," in the dialogue between Sūrya and Aruṇa within the Saptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan in the glorious *Bhaviṣya-mahāpurāṇa*.
In the dialogue between Sūrya and Aruṇa regarding the description of dreams,
Anūru said:
"O Blessed One, I wish to hear the supreme method for all seven [saptamīs] that correspond to one another; please tell me, O Great Sage. Saptāśvatilaka said:
Listen, O hero, best of birds, to the supreme rite of the seventh days.
I shall proclaim it all to you exactly as requested,
for it is indeed equal, O best of birds, to that which was declared by Vivasvat.
On a Sunday during the bright fortnight, when the sun has entered its northern course (uttarāyaṇa),
one should undertake the Saptamī vow for the sake of sons, wife, wealth, and fields—
[a vow] praised by sages endowed with knowledge who bestow the fruits of all desires.
Seven [types of] *saptamīs* have been described; hear their names from me:
the first is with *arkasaṃpuṭaka* flowers, the second likewise with black pepper (*marica*), the third with neem leaves (*nimba-patra*), and the fourth with the fruit of the *saptamī*.
The seventh is named Kāmikā; learn from me the rule for these [fasts]:
on the fifth day, one should take only a single meal with a restrained mind;
one should not eat a small amount of food, and one should avoid sexual intercourse from afar.

O Lord of Birds, one should avoid honey, meat, and what is excessively sour. At dawn on the sixth lunar day, having prepared rice cooked with ghee in individual leaf-cups, one should eat it according to the prescribed rite.
One who does not eat any other food should take a meal on the seventh day.
O Lord of Birds, he who dwells [in this practice] should increase his intake by one [meal] at a time;
otherwise, he may consume black pepper and neem leaves thereafter.

Thus, those who have obtained the fruits in both fortnights should, with effort, avoid eating food; this is known as *anodana*. Having worshipped the Fire-god according to the rules, one should perform the practice with devotion.
For a day and night, subsisting only on air, one should perform the Vijaya-saptamī vow;
in this very rite, one should duly observe each of the seven Saptamīs for seven days. Having written their names individually on separate leaves, one should proceed accordingly.
Having inscribed all those names with a well-concentrated mind,
[one should place them] upon one whose limbs are smeared with white sandalwood paste and adorned with garlands of flowers,
who is enriched with the seven kinds of grain and gold, and who resembles the moon, a kunda flower, or the moon itself.

One should worship with devotion for that purpose [the deity] upon a vessel rich with leaves of the *aśvattha* and *aśoka* trees and provided with curd-rice; there is no doubt that one will see various auspicious sights. Having seen a beautiful dream, however, one should not sleep again.
And in the morning, O Lord of Birds, one should recount the dream exactly as it was seen to wise men, Bhojakas, Brahmins, and friends; then,
at the time of midday, having bathed with a restrained mind.
Having worshipped that very god, the Sun, according to the prescribed rites,
the man— having properly performed his recitation, observing silence, and having offered oblations into the fire—
should depart from the temple and announce it to the officiating priest.
If there should be no gain for the officiating priests, then the Brahmins who are knowers of the Purāṇas deserve it—

those who, being certain in their mastery of the branches of the Mantra-Veda, would go to heaven after having worshipped the All-pervading Lord. Having thus performed the seven Saptamīs, a man endowed with devotion [attains his goal].
How could even one who merely has faith not obtain the fruit of the Sun?
Whatever fruit may come from ten performed horse-sacrifices,
a person obtains that same fruit by performing the Saptamī vow seven times with devotion.
O Hero, there is nothing difficult to obtain on the seventh [day] that is not consumed;
nor is there any disease in this world that is not pacified by these [mantras]. Even those leprosies which are terrible and difficult for physicians to cure—
All those [dreams] are led away by him, just as serpents are by Garuḍa.

Endowed with sons, wealth, family, enjoyments, happiness, and merit, he who honors that one—who is revered by all the gods, self-luminous, consecrated for the granting of desired fruits to people, and worthy of great worship—goes to a certain beautiful, eternal body of the Sun of fierce rays.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-fifth chapter, titled "Description of Dreams," in the Sauradharma section of the Sūryāruṇa-saṃvāda within the Saptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan in the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Description of the Ritual for Worship by Name.
Saptāśvavatilaka said: "O elder brother of Garuḍa, having passed over [the previous days], on the seventh day a person [should perform worship] after having eaten."
One should practice loving-kindness toward all and avoid harming any living being.
On the seventh lunar day, one should not touch oil, nor wear blue clothing;
one should not sleep with a woman, nor engage in gambling.
One should not weep by shedding tears, nor should one meditate upon *piśācas*. One should not pull lice from one's head, nor engage in idle talk.
One should avoid speaking of what is undesirable for others and refrain from excessive speech.
One should never strike any living being, nor should one ever enter [the sun's abode];
by entering the house of the Sun, one incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Thus, O elder brother of Garuḍa, these rules have been declared for the followers of the Sun.
O sinless one, O tiger among birds, in former times I specifically told the Bhojakas:
"O hero, that Bhojaka who, out of greed, would relinquish wealth for the sake of constant interest shall certainly go to hell."
O Lord of Birds, when even a few hundred distinguished individuals desire [to worship],
yet the Bhojaka employs only five hundred,
he becomes liable for penance, O Hero, and is not worthy to perform the worship of the Sun.
Having performed the Sāṃtapana Kṛcchra penance, he should there worship the Sun;
however, no installation of another deity should be performed by a Bhojaka.
O best of birds, having done so, a man becomes liable to expiation.
Therefore, O best of birds,
the priest must certainly not perform that [offering] for any deity other than the god Bhāskara;
having established the seats for the gods beginning with Brahmā, O lord of birds, he should offer nothing else.
A cook shall not touch the sun; he must perform the *kṛcchra* penance for purification.
O Lord of Birds, having performed the *kṛcchra* according to the rules as a cause for purity, a man thereafter becomes qualified to worship the sun.

One who desires prosperity should not offer a garland that is unknown, nor one that is withered, nor one that is defiled, nor one that is stale. He who hangs such a garland over the deity out of greed for flowers is indeed a rogue.
And fragrant flowers, but not others;
the host who, deluded by greed, serves such [meat], incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Having reached the Mahāraurava hell, he is cooked there for eternal years.
Come now, I shall proclaim to you the supreme ritual for offering incense,
and the fruit that results from which incense when offered to the God of gods.
By means of sandalwood incense, the Sun-god always makes his presence manifest.

Whatever a person desires in their mind, that indeed he should offer; likewise, with aguru incense, one should grant the desired boon. Or, desiring health or seeking a wife, one should constantly burn guggulu.
The Sun always bestows auspiciousness through the offering of incense;
he grants health and a wife, and supreme happiness shall prevail.
Through the constant offering of saffron incense, a man attains good fortune.
By means of the incense of *śrīvāsaka*, trade shall become fruitful;
for one who offers *rasa* endowed with all flavors, the acquisition of wealth is certain;
and for one who burns *devadāru*, there shall be inexhaustible food.
Anointing with saffron bestows the fruits of all desires;
having become happy in this world, the donor shall attain heaven.
By the gift of sandalwood, one finds prosperity and long life.
By the gift of red sandalwood, the Sun-god bestows everything;
even those seized by hundreds of diseases shall quickly attain health. Through the offering of wicks and fragrant perfumes, a person attains supreme fragrance.
By applying ointments of musk, one obtains incomparable sovereignty;
by using perfumes blended with camphor, one becomes the overlord of kings.
What can a man obtain that is equal to the perfume known as *catuḥsama*?
I consider that man who, out of devotion, smears the temple of the gods,
to be quickly freed from diseases and to become possessed of enjoyments;
for the eighteen types of leprosy and whatever other ailments there are among men in this world [shall depart].
If one were to smear it with clay, they would all go to destruction.
Among all types of ointments, red sandalwood is the most excellent;
there is nothing superior to this for bringing supreme satisfaction to the Sun.
What world would not belong to him who should smear [the temple] with this?
He, enriched with all desires, is glorified in the world of the Sun. Having smeared the abode of the Sun, he should further draw a mandala.
Then, by one [recitation], a man—whether a child or any other person—attains good fortune and supreme health. By three or seven [recitations], his lineage remains unbroken;
therefore, one should cause the gods to be offered [the oblation] by him, and one should not prevent them from doing so.

One should perform this rite according to this procedure for as many as seven seventh-days. Indeed, the man who performs these seven seventh-days with devotion, as they have been proclaimed by Vivasvat, is liberated from all sins.
One obtains wealth through *arkasaṃpuṭaka* flowers, union with a beloved through black pepper (*marica*),
the destruction of disease through neem leaves (*nimba-patra*), and desired sons through its fruits;
thereafter, one should offer wealth, grain, and gold to the Sun-god (*Vivasvat*).
O sky-walker, by performing this everywhere, one attains vast victory;
and being one who desires, one shall obtain all desires— of this there is no doubt—
whether it be a man or a woman who observes the Saptamī vow as prescribed.

O best of birds, he who performs this goes to the supreme state. For those who, observant of vows and with senses restrained, worship the Lord of the World with devotion, there is nothing in the three worlds that is difficult for them to attain.
The fruit of all sacrifices as proclaimed in the Vedas shall belong to them;
by this, Brahmā, Indra, and Viṣṇu are worshipped—of this there is no doubt.
They shall not be blind, nor leprous, nor impotent, nor maimed, nor destitute.
And perhaps there may be someone who performs the Saptamī vow;
desiring sons, he shall obtain sons endowed with Vedic learning and long life.
For them, nothing whatsoever in the three worlds is difficult to attain.
O observer of good vows, one who desires enjoyments obtains those enjoyments through this vow.
Should a breach of the vow occur due to anger, negligence, or greed,
one becomes a practitioner of the vow once again by performing this expiation.
O bird, as soon as the seven [days] up to the seventh have been completed by the preceptor,
a man who worships the Sun in those [days] with garlands, incense, and other offerings,
and feeds the twice-born according to his ability, shall attain imperishable heaven.

O Lord of Birds, O Hero, he who gives food to the foremost of Brahmins on the seventh lunar day shall find that [merit] to be inexhaustible for him, and he shall go to the abode of the Sun. Thus has this supreme Saptamī vow been proclaimed to you.

I shall speak further; listen to me as I speak, O sinless one, regarding that power of the vow by which one enjoys the fruit of one's desires. O tiger among birds, it concerns the seventh [tithi] of the bright fortnight known by twelve names.
Subsisting on cow urine and cow dung, or indeed subsisting on the six products of the cow;
or else subsisting on barley-gruel, or even eating only withered leaves;
or subsisting on milk, or eating only once a day, or furthermore, subsisting on a single mouthful of food.
Alternatively, the wise man, subsisting only on water, should worship the Sun with various offerings of flowers— lotuses, fragrant *saugandhika* lilies, and blue lotuses—
as well as with diverse perfumes and incenses such as *guggulu* and sandalwood.
O best of the twice-born, having honored [the deity] with kṛsara, milk-rice, various ornaments, and with foodstuffs, garments, and other finery,
one attains the fruit of all religious observances and thereafter proceeds to the world of the Sun.
At the conclusion of his ascetic penance, O hero, he is then born into a great family.
One should recite his names with effort in due order:
in the month of Māgha, Phālguna, and Caitra, O elder brother of Garuḍa.
O Hero, O Bird, one should constantly worship the Sun in the months of Vaiśākha, Jyeṣṭha, Āṣāḍha, Śrāvaṇa, Bhādrapada, Āśvayuja,
Mārgaśīrṣa, and Pauṣa.

O best of birds, O lord of winged creatures, these are the names of the deity during these months: Vibhāvasu, Vivasvat, Bhāskara, Vikartana, Pataṅga, and Sahasrāṃśu. O sky-ranger, [these are his names] in these respective months.
One should worship the Lord of the gods of gods, who is difficult even for the gods to attain;
thus, in due order, one should fully worship the Sun (Tīkṣṇāṃśu) with these names.
Thus has this secret been fully declared to you by me, O bird.
It must not be given to one who is not a devotee, nor under any circumstances to one who is not a disciple,
nor to a doer of evil, O hero, son of Vinatā.
It should be given to a brahmin of noble vows for the purpose of destroying disease.
"O Bird, by giving [this] one attains heaven, and by hearing it according to the prescribed rite, one likewise attains it.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for Worshiping by Name," within the Sauradharma section of the *Brahma-parvan* in the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
[This is followed by] the "Description of the Cowrie Shell."
Saptāśvatilaka said: Hereafter, I shall explain the various offerings such as flowers, incense,
and so forth, by which specific gift one may obtain their respective fruit.
Worship with *mālatī* flowers brings about divine presence; with *karavīra* flowers, one attains health and eternal wealth,
as well as incomparable sovereignty and vast fame.
One should stand before the Blessed One with *mallikā* flowers;
by means of white lotuses (*puṇḍarīka*), one shall attain good fortune and supreme sovereignty.
Through *kamala*, *utpala*, and *kunda* flowers, there shall be fame, knowledge, and strength.
By quickly offering various kinds of beautiful flowers, one is liberated from disease;
and for one who constantly worships the Sun, food becomes inexhaustible.
Worship with mandāra flowers wards off all forms of leprosy.
With the leaves and flowers of the *bilva* tree, one shall attain great prosperity;
with a garland of *arka* flowers, the Lord becomes like the Sun, always granting boons;
and when worshipped with a garland of *bakula* flowers, he shall bestow a beautiful maiden.
When worshipped with *kiṃśuka* flowers, the Sun-god does not cause affliction;
when worshipped with *agastya* blossoms, he bestows success and favor.
When worshipped with a garland of *campaka* flowers, he himself grants a beautiful wife.

He who worships the god Divākara with Aśoka flowers shall always be free from agitation, even when honored with garlands of flowers; for the flower of the Āmrātaka tree is regarded as no better than discarded remains.
Because it is not accepted externally, one should therefore avoid it.
By nine [verses] one attains unshakable fame; by ten, supreme happiness;
and by eleven, enjoyments in this world—of this there is no doubt.
By the twelfth [recitation], one shall obtain an immovable kingdom known as the "Twelve.
A person should first worship with devotion the form of Bhūḥ and always bow down;
then the second is Bhuvaḥ, and the third, a man should worship Svaḥ.
The fourth is Maharnava, while the fifth is Jana;
the sixth is Tapa, and the seventh is Satya;
the eighth is Bhurbhuvah, and the ninth, O best of birds, is Khah.
The tenth [mantra] is "Oṃ namaḥ ṣaḍato vīra," and likewise the next is "namo 'lkāya. The twelfth is "khaṣolkāya"; O Khaga, one should worship with "Oṃ namaḥ.
Thus, the performer of the maṇḍala shall obtain the fruit in this very sequence.
By the offering of a ghee lamp, a man becomes endowed with sight;
by a lamp of pungent oil (kaṭutaila), he shall become a refuge for his enemies;
and by a lamp of madhūka oil, he shall obtain supreme good fortune.
Having worshipped the God according to the rules with flowers, incense, and other offerings,
a person should thereafter present an offering of food (naivedya) according to his capacity.
Among flowers, the jasmine (jātī) is the most excellent, and among incenses, sandalwood is the best.
Among fragrances, saffron is the best, and sweetmeats (modakas) are excellent for the offering;
by these, the Lord of Gods is pleased and attains a presence [in the worshipper]. He grants the most excellent desired objects and likewise the attainment of heaven to the giver.
Having thus worshipped according to the prescribed rites and performed circumambulation,
and having bowed his head to the god Bhāskara, the dispeller of darkness,
he ascends a magnificent celestial chariot and goes to the same world as the Sun.
Having worshipped the Lord of Gods once again, one should perform the recitation (japa) as desired;
and one should offer oblations into the fire according to the ritual procedure prescribed by rule.
In this manner, seven seventh-days (saptamīs) should always be observed, one by one.
O Hero, that seventh [day] which is observed after drinking a handful of water is always to be known as the "Water-Seventh" (Udakasaptamī), which bestows happiness.
Whatever Seventh [day] has not been mentioned, I shall describe it to you at all times.
Whatever may be obtained in the course of time, such as a single cowrie shell, one should eat it;
with whatever has been acquired at this price, one should consume it—
whether it be edible or inedible, no deliberation on this point should be made.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Cowrie-Shell," within the Sauradharma section of the Saptamī-kalpa in the Brāhma-parvan of the glorious *Śrī-Bhaviṣya-Mahāpurāṇa*.
[This concludes] the description of the dialogue between Vyāsa and Bhīṣma. Śatānīka said:
What is the one deity in the world, or what is the one supreme refuge? Praising whom and worshipping whom do human beings obtain auspiciousness?
What is the dharma among all dharmas, and who, in your view, is worthy of worship?
"Whom do Brahmā and the others worship, and who is the foremost among the inhabitants of heaven?
Sumantu said:
"In this regard, I shall relate to you a conversation that destroys all sin."

O tiger among men, having seen the great Vyāsa, the best of the twice-born, seated comfortably on the bank of the Gaṅgā— Bhīṣma and the high-souled Vyāsa beheld him, possessed of immense splendor, blazing like a fire.
O hero, having bowed my head to the supreme Lord Nārāyaṇa himself, who is radiant like the sun, the abode of all scriptures,
the author of the Mahābhārata, and the supreme touchstone for the meaning of the Vedas.

O Bhārata, that tiger among the Kurus, endowed with devotion toward the twice-born, questioned the preceptor of the supreme sages and the royal sages— the founder of the Kuru lineage and my own supreme deity.
The greatness of the Sun, the god of gods, was established in his mind.
That high-souled and highly resplendent Bhīṣma [inquired] of the sage as before.
Bhīṣma said:
O Blessed One, tiger among the twice-born, O high-minded son of Parāśara,
you have explained to me the entirety of all speech, including everything moving and unmoving.
Yet, O best of sages, a doubt still persists regarding the Sun.
First,
tell me truly and with its underlying cause why he is saluted first, and why Brahmā and the others are saluted by Rudra and the rest immediately thereafter.
O Brahmin, who is this Bhāskara, from where was he born, and what is he called?
"Relate it according to the truth, for my curiosity is great;
you are indeed skilled in this world, therefore you ought to speak.
Vyāsa said:
"Alas! Your suffering is great; you have surely been deluded, there is no doubt.
Even the Siddhas and the gods, beginning with Brahmā, praise him with their worship.
Āditya is said to be the origin of all the gods."
He destroys all darkness situated in the cardinal and intermediate directions;
he is the Dharma among all dharmas and is considered the most worthy of worship. Brahmā and the others worship him, and he is the primordial source of the inhabitants of heaven.
Aditi was the wife of Kaśyapa, and for that reason he is called Āditya;
or else, because he is the primordial creator (ādikartā), he is therefore called Āditya. From him, this entire world proceeds.
Together with the gods, asuras, and gandharvas, along with the yakṣas, uragas, and rākṣasas;
likewise Rudra and Upendra, as well as Indra, Brahmā, Dakṣa, and Kaśyapa;
all the Āditya deities, and similarly all other gods and dānavas.
Viriñci was born from his mouth, and then Rudra from his chest;
Upendra from his right hand, and likewise Dhātṛ from his left hand;
Dakṣa from the sole of his left foot, and Kaśyapa from his right.
Thus were others born— the gods, asuras, humans, and birds—
and for that reason, this god Āditya is worshipped among all the gods.
Bhīṣma said:
O hero, if it is thus proclaimed in all directions and intermediate points that this is the power of that Sun, the son of Parāśara and Lord of the World,
then for what reason is he being humiliated by the Rākṣasas at the three junctions of the day?
"It is further protected by the twice-born and revolves again like a wheel;
it is seized by Rāhu, though it is unseizable. For what reason is this so, O best of the twice-born? Vyāsa said:
The Piśācas, Uragas, Rākṣasas, as well as the Ḍākinīs and Dānavas,
the Dakṣiṇāgni shall burn out of wrath; the Sun-god overcomes him,
and at the three junctions of the day, the three gods abide in the solar disc.
This is the power of the *muhūrta*: even when a matter is difficult to accomplish, it becomes so when [the time] is observed.
With reference to that single [moment], dharma proceeds in the world.
When it is saluted and praised, all the gods are saluted.
The Sun is saluted three times at the three junctions of the day by the gods of the earth;
Rāhu remains beneath the solar disc, there is no doubt.
Desiring nectar, he stays in his celestial chariot as long as the nectar flows down.
One should predict an eclipse when the solar disc is obscured by a celestial mansion (vimāna);
no one is able to rejoice [at its occurrence], for the Sun surely burns.
The Sun proceeds through the days, nights, and muhūrtas for the sake of providing knowledge.
Without the sun there is no night, no day, and no libation;
neither unrighteousness nor righteousness exists. By him the world of moving and unmoving things is perceived. Indeed, the sun protects everything; the sun creates it eternally.

"All this that was asked of me by you has been fully explained. Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Dialogue between Bhīṣma and Vyāsa," within the Sauradharma section of the Saptamī-kalpa in the Brāhma-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Bhīṣma said: "O Brahmin, I wish to hear from you in truth that by which Āditya may become a bestower of boons upon me before long; tell it to me."
Vyāsa said: Having performed the entire mandala, as well as its initiation and the prescribed ritual timing, together with worship, recitation, burnt offerings, meditation, and concentration.
O Hero, for one who, having obtained [this], worships with devotion with a mind fixed upon Him, the Sun will soon become the bestower of boons;
he shall obtain strength, success, great heroism, majesty, and his own body.
O giver of honor, for one with whom the Sun is pleased, he bestows wealth, grain, gold, beauty, the perfection of good fortune,
health, long life, renown, fame, and sons;
of this there is no doubt.

When pleased, the Sun bestows upon men dharma, artha, kāma, knowledge, as well as liberation and prosperity; of this there is no doubt. O dear one, having worshipped the Maker of Day according to the ritual prescribed by Sauri, [one obtains these fruits].
"O King, one obtains all desires as well as the abode of the Sun.
Bhīṣma said:
"O high-minded one, tell me the procedure for the solar bath (saurasnāna), together with its secret teachings."
By means of which a man, having bathed and become stainless, goes to worship the Sun.
Vyāsa said:
"Indeed, I shall fully describe to you that bathing which destroys all sins."
Having gathered earth from a pure and pleasant place with the Astra-mantra—

[the mantra] consisting of the *saṃdhi-saṃgha* [the letter *ha*], joined with the *ṭa*-class, *repha* [the letter *ra*], and the *upadhmānīya* [the letter *ḥ*]— and having taken it with this Astra-mantra, one should then perform the ritual bath.
Thereafter, one should perform the impurity-bath (malasnāna) with the remaining half [of the earth].
One should take three parts and a half, free from grass and stones;
having consecrated one part with the Weapon-mantra (astra), and likewise the other with the Bhāskara-mantra.

Having consecrated one's own limb with the third mantra once each time, and having recited the Astra-mantra, one should scatter [water] in all directions; thus the water will become free from obstacles.
At the Sūryatīrtha, one should consecrate [the water] with the second mantra once each time.
Having shaved his head, a man should then bathe at sacred fords (tīrthas),
meditating upon the divine Sun amidst the sounding of musical instruments and conchs;
having bathed with royal honors, he should again perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) with diligence.
Then, O Bhīṣma, having performed the bath accompanied by the King of Mantras:
the letter *ha* joined with *repha* (r) and the bindu (m), and likewise another [letter] with a long vowel;
the letter *ha* joined with *repha* (r) and the bindu (m).
The king of mantras is said to be this [syllable] with the letter *sa* and the *visarga*.
Thereafter, one should satisfy all those mantras with [water] from the tips of the fingers;
the gods [are satisfied] from above the joints of the right hand, and likewise the sages with the left.
One should satisfy the ancestors with that seed-syllable while using the apasavya method;
that which is sung by the wise as the most excellent among syllables in the world,
joined with the bindu, is declared to be the heart-seed (hṛdbīja)— of this there is no doubt.

Having performed this with his left hand and meditated upon it, the wise man who knows the ritual procedure should bathe according to the rules and perform the twilight worship (saṃdhyā) according to the rules. Thereafter, the learned man should offer a handful of water to the Sun.

And one should recite the three-syllabled mantra or the six-faced mantra as desired. O King, that which was previously described by me to you as the "King of Mantras," after withdrawing the mantras into the sacred site (tīrtha), one should then place them in the heart.
Having unified oneself through mantras, one should indeed cause the arghya offering to be presented.
Having bathed cleanly, one should draw a mandala on the surface of the earth with red sandalwood and perfumes, remaining there with a focused mind and wealth at hand.
Having taken karavīra flowers and placed them in a copper vessel,
one should prepare that arghya by adding sesame seeds and rice, along with kuśa grass and scented water,
and perfuming it with red sandalwood incense.
Placing that vessel upon his head and kneeling upon the ground,
he should offer the *arghya*— conjoined with the previously mentioned mantra— to the Sun.
Indeed, he who makes this offering in such a manner is liberated from all sins.
Whatever fruit is obtained at Jyeṣṭha-puṣkara by [the merit of] a thousand Yugas, a hundred Vyatīpātas,
a thousand solstices (ayanas), a lunar eclipse,
or a hundred thousand cows— [that fruit is attained here].
O best of the Kuru lineage, by giving that [offering], one obtains its fruit;
even one devoid of initiation and mantras, O hero, obtains the fruit through the arghya-offering with devotion within a year— of this there is no doubt.

Furthermore, that wise man who, having been initiated, offers the arghya according to the prescribed rite, is not born again upon this earth; he attains dissolution in the Sun. In this very life, he attains good fortune, long life, health, and prosperity.
O hero, before long you shall become a partaker of the happiness of having a wife.
This procedure for bathing has been declared by me to you in brief;
it is for the benefit of the lords of men and is the destroyer of all sins.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Saura Dharmas," in the dialogue between Bhīṣma and Vyāsa, within the Saura Dharmas of the Saptamī-kalpa, in the Brāhma Parva of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Bhīṣma said:
"O Brāhmaṇa, you have indeed described to me the procedure for bathing that removes sin;
now I shall properly perform the rite of worshipping Brahmā by which I may truly offer worship.
Vyāsa said:
Come, I shall fully explain to you the procedure for the worship of Āditya.
In a secluded, victorious, serene, and most beautiful place,
the practitioner, with his body made straight, should worship Bhāskara with mantras.

Seated upon a *bhadrāsana* and facing the east, the most excellent practitioner should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on his own limbs with the weapon-seed mantra (*astrabīja*). Beginning with the thumb and ending with the little finger, he should perform the placement well.
One should always place those [mantras], beginning with the heart and ending with *phaṭ*, in their proper sequence.
O Hero, having placed [the mantras] on the eyes and the palms of the hands, the knower of mantras should perform the *arghya* offering and other rites.
Regarding the *ya*-group, the fourth letter, joined with the ear-dot (*bindu*), [is used].
The seed-syllable of the eyes is said to be the form of light; of this there is no doubt.
Afterwards, the wise one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the three-syllabled Sūrya-kavaca.
O Hero, as you asked, I have thus described to you this king of mantras.
Then one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma), first exhaling the seed-syllable;
having offered oblations in the Viraja fire according to the remaining sequence with the power of Bhīṣma,
the purification of the self is thereby accomplished through those very three terrible [syllables].
Having thus purified oneself, one should place the Sun in the proximity of all;
having placed the Heart-mantra in the heart, one should place the Head-mantra on the head.
This is proclaimed as the twenty-first syllable of the Mātṛkā.
That which is renowned as the seed-syllable of the heart (hṛdbīja) is the incomparable abode of Brahmā.
Worship with the head [mantra] is indeed called "the Sun in the world" (lokerka).
One should place the crest-mantra (śikhā) upon the crest and place the armor-mantra (kavaca) upon the body.
One should place the Netra-mantra on the two eyes and the Astra-mantra on the two hands.
O King, the Mahāvyāhṛtis are likewise for the armor (kavaca), as is the Arjvālinī for the crest-lock (śikhā).
The syllables *ha*, *ra*, and *ku*, together with the nasal bindu, [constitute the seed-syllable].
The pledges (samayas) for these as well as the armor (kavaca) are now fully described.
One should place the Eye-mantra upon the eyes and the Weapon-mantra upon the two hands.
Having thus placed the limbs [of the mantra-body], one cannot be overcome by anyone.
Enemies become friends, and in times of loss one obtains gain;
having realized oneself to be the Sun as described by the seers of truth,
one should then duly worship the Sun upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) according to the prescribed rites.
Having placed a divine flower-basket on the right side,
and having placed [a vessel] filled with copper-colored water on the beautifully adorned left side—
[the latter] being full and washed with the Astra-mantra— one should likewise [perform the rite] with the remaining waters using mantras.
Then, having consecrated it with mantras and established it while veiling it with the *kavaca* mantra,
the wise practitioner should sprinkle all the materials prepared for worship upon the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*), as well as the *arghya* vessel, with water.
Thereafter, the knower of mantras should recite the mantra with a one-pointed mind.
Bhīṣma said:
This is the procedure described by the wise through mantras accompanied by the Purāṇas.
I have learned that entire [teaching] and have heard it recounted many times by various twice-born ones;
just as the Sun is worshipped with the diverse mantras declared in the Vedas,
so tell me in its entirety that most excellent Vedic procedure.

Thus ends the two-hundredth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for Worshipping the Deity in the Solar Orb," in the Sauradharma section of the Brāhma-parvan within the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Vyāsa said:
Now, O Bhārata, I shall relate to you this dialogue which increases righteousness, between the elder of the gods, the deity Keśava,
and the four-faced one seated comfortably on Mount Manovatī.
Bowing his head, Viṣṇu spoke these words:
Viṣṇu said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, eldest of the deities, four-faced one!"
Tell me the procedure for propitiating the high-souled Bhāskara. How should one worship Bhānu, the lord of the day, who resides within the solar orb?
O God, tell me of the host [of deities] therein, so that I may worship the All-pervading Lord.
"Excellent, excellent, O mighty-armed one! I have been well questioned by you, O upholder of the earth.
Listen with a single-minded focus, O Lord, to the procedure for the propitiation of Bhāskara.
Having worshipped the stainless god Vibhāvasu, who possesses the radiance of a meteor,"
One should sequentially assign [the deities] to the east, the center, the southeast, Virūpākṣa, and Prabhāñjana, up to Īśānī, using the seed-syllable in the heart;
this is the Khaṣolkā seat which has been established by the best of men.
Then, above that,
he should visualize with his heart a most wonderful five-colored garment, joined by seven enclosures, possessing eight petals and a pericarp, adorned with filaments and presiding deities.
Having performed the ritual according to the rules prescribed in the scriptures for the stage of examination,
the mantra-practitioner should place the eight Śaktis— beginning from the southeast (Dīptā) and extending as far as the northeast— starting from the center and facing in all directions.
Dīptā, Sūkṣmā, Jayā, Bhadrā, Vibhūti, Vimalā,
Amoghā, Vidyutā, and the ninth, Sarvatomukhī.
Then one should invoke the Sun and establish him upon the pericarp.
O observer of noble vows, having performed the ritual attendance with this mantra—
namely the mantra proclaimed as "udutyaṃ jātavedasam"— and with this mantra "agniṃ dūtena," O observer of universal vows, [one should proceed].
One should worship with the mantra "ākṛṣṇena rajasā," and one should worship the Sun with the mantra "haṃsaḥ śuciṣat.
One should worship the goddess Tārakā with the mantra "apaptat."
One should worship the subtle goddess with the mantra "adṛśram asya ketavaḥ.
One should constantly achieve victory with the mantra "taraṇir viśvadarsati. One should worship the auspicious goddess with the mantra "pratyag devānām viśa."
O observer of noble vows, one should always worship Vibhūti with this mantra: "By that which has fire as its eye, may I obtain knowledge";
and one should always worship the pure and unfailing [Vidyā] with this very mantra.

One should constantly worship the ninth goddess, Sarvatomukhī, with this mantra of Kṛṣṇa: "udvayantam" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.4.43). One should then proceed to the first syllable of the "udyannadya mitram" oblation (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 2.1.2).
One should worship Kṛṣṇa with the second [verse] during the light fortnights, and Hari in battle;
"udagādayamādityaḥ" is used for the third,
and "tatsaviturvareṇyam" is proclaimed as the fourth.
One should recite the five verses beginning with "mahito mahito ya.
The sixth seed-syllable is proclaimed as "hiraṇyagarbhaḥ samavartata.
O best of gods, the seventh is "savitā paścātāt purastāt."
Having thus deposited the seed-syllables, the twice-born should establish Āditya;
the wise one should meditate upon Āditya and worship him for the sake of all.
O tiger among gods, [he should place] Indra and the others on the outside in every direction.
Red in color and possessing great splendor, he stands upon a white lotus;
endowed with all auspicious marks and adorned with every ornament,
he has two arms and a single wheel, is gentle in appearance, and holds a lotus and a bow in his hands.

Circular, situated in the center by means of that disc, and possessing supreme brilliance— this is the form of the Sun worshipped in all the worlds. Having meditated upon it, one should constantly worship the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) resting within the mandala.

Thus ends the two hundred and first chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for Worshipping the Deity of the Solar Orb" within the Saura-dharma section of the Saptamī-kalpa, in the Brāhma-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
[Now follows] the description of the ritual for the worship of Āditya;
Viṣṇu said:

O best of gods, tell me that ritual procedure by which a human being may worship the Sun, the lotus-born Bhāskara, who resides within the mandala, with devotion. Tell me that ritual procedure by which one should worship Bhāskara according to the rules.
To the omnipresent God who resides within the form and is worshipped by both gods and demons, Brahmā said:
