"Excellent, O Kṛṣṇa of mighty arms! Excellent, O you of noble vows; I have been well questioned."
Listen with a one-pointed mind to how one should formerly worship the deity residing in the image:
one should always worship the head with the mantra "iṣe tvā," and one should worship the right hand with the mantra "agnim īle."
One should worship the feet of the God with the mantra "agna āyāhi";
one should worship [the deity] with a garland of flowers with the mantra "ājighra";
and one should cast an offering of loose flowers with the mantra "yogayogeti."
One should bathe the Sun with the mantra "Go to the ocean," which has been proclaimed by him; and with the mantra "This is mine, O Gaṅgā," which has also been proclaimed, O Supporter of the Earth,
one should adorn [the image] with decoctions using the "Samudrajyeṣṭhā" mantra.
O Kṛṣṇa, one should bathe [the Sun] with milk using the mantra "Āpyāyasva";
one should bathe the Sun with curd using the mantra "Dadhikrāvṇo akāriṣam," making it like curd;
and the supreme bathing is with ghee using the mantra "Tejo 'si śukram."
Bathing with medicinal herbs is prescribed with the mantra "yā auṣadhīḥ";
then, O Lord of the Gods, one should rub the body with two-footed verses. One should perform the simultaneous bathing with the mantra "mā nas toke".
One should bathe [the deity] with fragrant water while reciting the *viṣṇorarāṭam* mantra;
one should offer the *arghya* and *pādya* with the *sauvarṇa* mantra;
and one should cause the *arghya* to be presented with the *idaṃ viṣṇurvicakrame* mantra.
One should cause the sacred thread to be offered with the mantra "vedo'si";
one should give garments to the Sun with the mantra "bṛhaspate";
and one should offer a flower garland with the mantra "yena śriyam prakurvāṇām".
One should offer incense containing guggulu with the mantra "dhūrasi";
one offers collyrium with the "samiddha" mantra;
and one should worship the sun with the "yuñjāna" mantra and the "rocanā" hymn.
A wise man should indeed make it slightly reddish for the sake of long life.
He should worship the thousand-headed Puruṣa as the Sun in the lake,
and he should touch the lotus-eyed one with the mantra beginning with "saṃbhāvaya."
One should touch the body of the Sun with the mantra "viśvataścakṣuḥ" and worship Him with this mantra: "śrīśca te lakṣmīśca.

Thus ends the two hundred and second chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Worship of Āditya," within the Saura Dharma of the Brāhma Parvan in the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, in the section on the seventh lunar day (Saptamī-kalpa).
Description of the Ritual for the Worship of Bhāskara.
Viṣṇu said:
O Four-faced One, tell me briefly the procedure for the worship of the Sky (Vyoma).
"How should one worship the eight-peaked sky of the Sun?
Brahmā said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, learn from me as I speak the ritual procedure for the worship of the sky."
Just as the wise worship the sky as having eight peaks, so too,
O mighty-armed one, should one worship the mountain with eight peaks by making it of gold, silver, copper, or likewise stone, according to this ritual procedure.
O observer of noble vows, one should first worship the Sun in the center with the mantra "mahiṣā vo mahāya," using clusters of various flowers; then,
one should always worship Indra, the protector of all peaks, with the mantra "trātāram indram."
Then, one should worship with the mantra "udīratām avaraḥ," or else worship the horn of the Nairṛta [direction] with the mantra "āyaṃ gauḥ.
One should worship the destroyer of the Asuras, the horse who slays the Rakṣases, with the mantra "rakṣohaṇaṃ vājinam."

O Acyuta, one should indeed worship Indra, Soma, and Antaka with this [mantra]; then one should worship Īśāna with "abhitvā śūra nonumaḥ" and Śṛṅga. In this manner, they always worship Bhānu as well on all sides.
One should indeed worship with the thought, "By whom this world was created," or else with this [mantra].
One should always worship Vyomapīṭha with the words, "Salutation to all sins.
Those men constantly attain their desires; of this there is no doubt.
"You alone [are the leader] of the Rudras and the Vasus"—with this [verse], one should worship in the forenoon;
"That supreme step of Viṣṇu" and "The swan dwelling in purity"—with these [verses], one should always worship in the afternoon.
O Lord of the Assembly, thus they worship the Sun together with the planets.
They obtain all various kinds of desires without a doubt,
O Kṛṣṇa, by giving two spotless garments along with purifying threads to the preceptor,
as well as sandals and a golden ring.
Whoever, observing a fast, should worship the Sun according to this rite with various fragrant flowers and manifold kinds of food and edibles,
that man shall become possessed of many sons, great wealth, and noble character.
He who, during the northern course of the sun, worships Ravi while observing a fast,
shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice and be born with many sons.
Furthermore, he who, having observed a fast on the equinox (Vishuva), worships Ravi—
Having observed a fast according to the rules during an eclipse of the moon or the sun, one is born with many sons, great wealth, and renown;
by worshipping the Sun with devotion, he goes to the world of Brahmā.
Thus, O Viṣṇu, I have described to you the procedure for the worship of Bhāskara,
by hearing which a person is glorified in my world through devotion.
Returning again to the earth, O Kṛṣṇa, he becomes a king upon the surface of the world.
"He shall have many sons, great wealth, and remain unconquered in battles.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Worship of the Sun" within the Saura-dharma of the *Saptamī-kalpa*, in the Brāhma-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya-mahāpurāṇa*. [This is followed by:
"Description of the Ritual for the Worship of Vyoman."
Sumantu said:
Hereafter I shall proclaim the most highly honored ritual for the consecration of the jeweled sky-vault, according to which one should worship the Sun.
O Lord, having worshipped Prakṛti with perfumes, flowers,
and unbroken grains (akṣata), one should invoke the omnipresent Mahādeva Khaṣolka Bhāskara with a handful (añjali) of water, or together with flowers and unbroken grains.
O tiger among the Kurus, with this mantra one should indeed cause Khaṣolka to become manifest:
"Oṃ, I invoke Khaṣolka; Oṃ Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svar Oṃ. This is the mantra for the worship of Āditya.
Having consecrated the ground with the Sāvitrī verse, O Lord, one should offer a portion to the earth.
The verse beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," which has been proclaimed, is always useless for the sun;
rather, having washed it according to rule, one should fill it from another source,
and the wise man should wash it with the verse beginning "hiraṇyagarbhaḥ samavartata."
"Savitar from behind— Savitar indeed shall fill [this] with her";
having thus filled [the vessel] with water, flowers, and unbroken rice, the wise man,
taking a vessel made of udumbara wood, should show the entire [vessel] to the Sun.
With the mantra "ud u tyaṃ jātavedasam," one should project [the deity] into the sky;
with "haṃsaḥ śuciṣat," the wise practitioner should offer water for the feet.
One should then extinguish the "khaṣolka" fire with milk and subsequently bathe [the deity].
O hero, O descendant of Kuru, O lord of men, the seven [verses] beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā" are proclaimed in their entirety for Agni,
and those beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇā" are likewise used in sequence, four by four.

O King, having consecrated water with the three Rigvedic verses beginning with "kṛṇuṣva pājaḥ," one should pour it out while circumambulating the sun. "tyamūṣu vājinam" is proclaimed as the first of the hymns.
"Patimiṃdrastavācāma" is proclaimed as the second [verse].
"Patimiṃdrastu śuddho na āgahi" is proclaimed as the third.
One should worship Bhānu with fragrant substances while reciting "sidhye vṛtrāṇi jighne."

O tiger among the Bharatas, one should worship the Sun with unbroken grains using this verse, "asya vāmasya"; and one should constantly worship that destroyer of darkness with flowers using this verse, "sapta yuñjanti ratham."
With the verse "Who has seen? one should first offer incense;
with "I ask about the cooked food," one should present sandalwood;
and with "O Fire, may you shine forth," one should give a lamp to the Lord of Light.
Having worshipped with saffron and offered milk as a circular libation,
one should present the food offering (naivedya) with the mantra "yuktā mātāsī";
likewise, one should offer two white garments with the mantra "gaurīrmimāya".
With the verse beginning "tasyāḥ samudre," one should offer the sacred thread (upavīta).
Having thus worshipped the Lord of Gods, one should then perform a supreme hymn of praise with five Rigvedic verses; listen, my dear, with single-minded attention.
The first [verse] is proclaimed as "ukṣāṇaṃ pṛśniḥ";
the second is proclaimed as "catvāri vāk";
and the third, beginning with "indraṃ mitram," is proclaimed for the purpose of increasing one's boons.
Likewise, the fourth [verse], "kṛṣṇaṃ niyānam," is proclaimed;
with this verse, "yo ratnavāhī," one should place the crown upon the Sun. With the verse "gatehanām," one should install the unimpaired Bhāskara.

O Acyuta, having first performed worship with the verse beginning "iyamadadādrabhasamṛṇacyutam," one should then duly worship the eight powers of the God in sequence with the eight verses beginning with "iti."

Thus, O mighty-armed one, this procedure for the worship of the image has been recounted to you by me— the very same that was previously declared by Brahmā to Viṣṇu. Whoever should constantly worship the Sun according to this rite, [attains the highest goal].
He attains all desires in this world and in the next:
one seeking sons obtains sons, one seeking wealth obtains wealth,
one seeking a daughter obtains a daughter, and one seeking the Vedas becomes a knower of the Vedas.
The man who worships without desire shall attain liberation;
having worshipped according to this rite, that Vaiṣṇava indeed attained perfection.
Likewise, Brahmā and the other gods, having worshipped the god Vibhāvasu, [attained their goals].
By worshipping according to this rite, the virtuous have attained supreme perfection.
Thus ends the two hundred and fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for Worshipping Vyoman," in the Saptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan within the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
[Now follows] the description of the ritual for worshipping Mahādeva.
Vyāsa said:
Listen again to me, Bhīṣma, as I describe the supreme rite by which one constantly worships Mahādeva, the maker of day.
Having propitiated the abundant and stainless splendor for the sake of supreme bliss,
one should sequentially place the seed-syllable in the heart, starting from the east, then the southeast, the southwest, the abode of the wind (the northwest), and finally up to the northeast.
This seat of the Sun (Bhāskara) should be deposited by those who perceive the ultimate reality;
above that, one should place a lotus with eight petals and filaments, possessing five-colored filaments, using the Hṛdaya-mantra.
Beginning from Dīptā and extending as far as Mahādevagocarī,
one should install the eight Śaktis with their mantras starting from the beginning at Sarvatomukhī.
One should then worship them in due order upon the tips of the filaments with their seed-syllables (abījas).
Then one should invoke Bhānu and establish him upon the pericarp.
Having offered that [oblation] to him, another is to be understood as the "sky-flower" (khapuṣkara).
By means of that very [flower], one should perform the invocation, the worship, the installation, and the offering of water (arghya).
Water for the feet, water for sipping, a seat, garments, perfumes, and other ornaments,
as well as hero-flowers, food offerings, and incense, should be presented according to the prescribed rite with faith and devotion; in this way, Bhāskara is pleased.
Even those who have committed great sins quickly obtain their desired fruit.
Having worshipped Āditya, one should then worship the limbs:
having placed the Heart-mantra upon Dīptā, one should place that of Bhavānī upon the head.
One should assign the Weapon-mantra (astra) to the cardinal and intermediate directions, starting from Indra’s direction (the east) and ending with the north.
One should assign the Eye-mantra (netra) to the pericarp (karṇikā), or one should worship it with its own seed-syllable (bīja).
Then, one should worship the Heart-mantras (hṛdaya) in sequence with flowers, perfumes, and incense.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite, the knower of mantras should thereafter worship Mandi in the east outside the womb, Budha likewise in the south,
Viṣāṇa in the west, and Bhārgava in the north.
Having worshipped Kuja in the southeast and the son of the Sun (Saturn) in the southwest,
one should worship Kṛṣṇa in the northwest and Vikaca in the northeast, O King;
thereafter, the wise man should worship the eight world-protectors, beginning with Indra.

O best of the Kuru lineage, he who desires his own welfare should worship the Sun, together with the world-protectors and the planets, in due order using various fragrant flowers and delightful incenses, while reciting the sacred mantras.
Wherever the Sun-god is worshipped according to this rite,
there is no fear of thieves or fire, nor is there any fear of hell;
and there, no fear exists from rain-stones, poison, or other such dangers.
Happiness, health, bliss, abundance, and unshakable prosperity—

these are attained by practitioners who should constantly worship the Sun, who in the highest sense resides within the center of the solar orb; neither the chariot nor the horses are to be worshipped.
Thus, O Bhīṣma, this entire procedure has been declared by me,
by which one constantly worships Mahādeva as the Sun.
Having thus worshipped Vivasvat, one should dismiss him with the seed-syllable of the heart.
"He who thus worships the Sun attains the supreme goal.

Thus ends the two hundred and fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Worship of Mahādeva," within the *Sauradharma* section of the *Bhīṣma-Vyāsa-saṃvāda* in the *Saptamī-kalpa* of the *Brāhma-parvan* in the glorious *Mahāpurāṇa Bhaviṣya*;
herein is the description of the majesty of the worship of the Sun.
Bhīṣma said:
"Tell me the supreme extraction of mantras, endowed with the power of mudrās,
equal in form and color, and unsurpassed according to the Purāṇas."
Vyāsa said: Listen, O mighty-armed Bhīṣma, O sinless one, as I shall explain to you the extraction of the Puranic mantras, apart from those of the Vedas.
Joined with the letter *ra* and adorned with coral,
it is indeed the last of the semivowels (*anta-sthāna*) and is said to have Brahmā as its presiding deity;
likewise, joined with the nasal dot (*bindu*) and the letter *ra*, and with a long vowel measure, [it is so].
The first syllable of initiation has been declared; the second has Viṣṇu as its presiding deity.
Likewise, O lord of men, the third is said to be accompanied by the visarga;
that third one is indeed declared by the wise to have Rudra as its presiding deity.
This Bhāskara is the Great One, the manifest embodiment of the three-syllabled mantra;
he is difficult to attain, supremely secret, the triple deity worshipped by the gods.
Whoever recites this with devotion attains the supreme goal.
Next, I shall describe the mudrā which is the supreme cause for [the deity's] presence:
having formed the hands into the shape of a lotus with the two middle fingers joined together, one should sprinkle water upon them; this is called the Vimudrā.
O King, by binding this [mantra], one becomes dear to the Sun;
it protects like a mother in all great dangers.
Its heart should be known as that which is remembered as the supreme syllable.
O Bhārata, that which is covered with coral, situated in the heart and always present there, is declared to be the Sun upon the head of the God of gods;
likewise, the three Great Utterances (Mahāvyāhṛtis) and the Arajvālinī are the crest-lock (śikhā).
This eight-syllabled vidyā belongs to the great-souled Āditya;
the practitioner who remembers it is not oppressed by anything.
It is joined with the letter *a*, and endowed with the bindu and the letter *ra*.
The syllable *ha* has Agni as its deity; it is armor, beloved by the Sun.
This single syllable is proclaimed to be impenetrable. Whoever remembers this, there is no doubt that it destroys even the most wicked obstacles.
The letter *ra* with the *visarga* is known as the single-syllable weapon (*astra*).
It destroys the evil deeds of the practitioner; of this there is no doubt.
Having brought the two hands face-to-face, they should be joined with the fingers interlaced.
One should join the little finger with the ring finger and likewise the two index fingers with the middle fingers;
this mudrā, involving the heart, head, crest, and shield, is known as Vyoma (Space).
One should form a fist with the left hand and raise the index finger.
The mudrā of the Astra-mantra is indeed proclaimed as beginning with the word *māla*;
it is renowned by the name Trāsanī, which causes fear to all enemies.
O Great-minded One, the fourth [syllable] is joined with the bindu of the ear (*yaṃ*).
This eye of Bhāskara is said to have Agni as its presiding deity;
for the foremost of practitioners, it is certainly Smara (the God of Love) when used for destruction.
The middle finger and the index finger of the right hand should likewise be raised.
Having contracted the little and ring fingers, one should then proceed with the thumbs;
one should touch this [mudrā] with both eyes—this is proclaimed as the Netra-mudrā.
Known by the name Govṛṣā, one should display it to the divine sphere.
*Rāṃ* is the Radiant Enemy; thereafter, *Sūkṣmārī* is called *Jayā* and *Bhīṣma*.
*Ubhāhvārūṃ* is *Vibhūti*, and *Reṃ* is proclaimed as *Vimalā*.
*Aghahā*, O mighty-armed one, and *Rauṃ* is proclaimed as *Vidyutā*.
Govṛṣā, Raṃ, Sarva, and Vīrabhadrakarī—
these are the Śaktis described as being in the form of seed-syllables (bīja).
Having placed the hands palms-upward and then contracted the fingers of the left hand...
One should place the two thumbs on top and move them repeatedly;
one should display these mudrās for all the Śaktis. By name and by its lightning-like brilliance, the ninth is indeed Sarvatomukhī.

These names of the Śaktis have been told by me in brief, along with their seed-syllables (bījas), out of affection for you, O mighty-armed Bhārata. Now hear from me as I speak the seed-syllables and the forms of the Planets (grahas).
O bearer of the lotus and curiosity, in every case, *bhaṃ*,
*thaḥ*, and *khaṃ* are all illuminated by the syllable *oṃ* and joined with a concluding salutation (*namaḥ*).
These are to be employed at the time of worship as well as at the time of recitation.
At the time of the fire sacrifice (homa), the mantra should end with "svāhā" and be joined with the six syllables [namaḥ].
O Bhīṣma, all [the mantras] are endowed with the bindu, and the crest-mantra (śikhā) is adorned with the bindu.
Thus indeed are the planets proclaimed, beginning with Soma and ending with Ketu.
I shall now describe these mudrās, which bestow all accomplishments:
having placed the two hands with palms facing upward, joined and extended,
this mudrā is used for salutation and brings about the presence of the planets.
O King, the extraction of the mantra has been declared to you; it is a secret and difficult to obtain.
Now listen to the form of the deities when the time for meditation has arrived:
[the deity] of great splendor, colored like a hibiscus flower, seated upon a white lotus.
Endowed with all the auspicious marks and adorned with every ornament,
he has one face and two arms, with the moon as his crest-jewel and a lotus at his throat;
his form is situated in the center of a mandala, and he is clothed in red garments.
O Bhīma, he who— pure, bathed, with senses subdued, and established in single-minded concentration— recalls this form of Mārtaṇḍa at the three times of day,
will before long become like Kubera, the lord of wealth, in riches within this world.
One is liberated from all enjoyments and becomes radiant and powerful.
The heart, the head, the crest-lock, and the face—
these are red in color, yet dark-hued, and adorned with all ornaments.
The practitioner should meditate upon her with hands granting boons and fearlessness;
her weapon is like a mass of lightning, fierce, and as formidable as the rays of the moon. Indeed, this specific form is described as being capable of assuming any shape by its very nature.
My Śaktis should be meditated upon as blazing and having the form of flaming crests.
One should remember Soma as white in color, and Kuja as red in color;
Saumya as resembling a checkerboard (white), and Guru as yellow in color.
One should meditate upon Rāhu as white like a conch or milk, one-eyed and resembling collyrium; smoky-colored, with disheveled hair, and resembling *rajāvarta* stone;
with both left hands placed on his hips and the right hands granting the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*).
"O best of kings, those who meditate upon Bhānu together with the planets— [Bhānu] whose eyebrows, eyes, and face are red, and who has half his body joined in *añjali*—
they shall attain great siddhi before long; of this there is no doubt."
O Bhīṣma, you have described this entire discourse on the planets,
by hearing which men on earth are liberated from all sins.
O Bhīṣma, one should always [worship] the divine Sun according to this rite.
O Hero, one endowed with faith should worship [the Sun] with devotion three times a day.
By worshipping the Sun, the lord of all gods, in this manner,
one is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin and shall attain the state of Mahādeva.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Worship of the Sun," within the Sauradharma section of the Saptamī-kalpa in the Brāhma-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
[Now follows] the description of the ritual procedure for the worship of Āditya.
Bhīṣma said:
"Aha! You have proclaimed the majesty of the divine Bhāskara;
for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others always worship him.
Vyāsa said:
It is exactly so, there is no doubt, just as you say, O Bhārata:
there is no deity equal to the Sun; there is no goal equal to the Sun;
there is no Brahman equal to the Sun; there is no oblation equal to the Sun.
There is no dharma equal to the sun; there is no wealth equal to the sun.
There is no desire apart from the sun; there is no state apart from the sun.
There is no kinsman equal to the sun; there is no friend equal to the sun.
There is no mother equal to the Sun; there is no teacher equal to the Sun.
There is no sacred ford equal to the Sun, and nothing more purifying than that.
One should know him alone as the deity, being solely devoted to the Sun.
O Bhārata, those who worship and praise Him— the Lord of the worlds, the gods, and the ancestors— attain the supreme goal;
those who have taken refuge in Him with devotion are liberated from the ocean of worldly existence.
Kings, thieves, planets, serpents, poverty, and the multitude of miseries—
none of these are able to cause affliction when the Sun is pleased.
Vyāsa said:
Thus, O dear one of mighty arms, the divine Sun is devoted to that [task];
he is to be worshipped, he is to be saluted, and he is indeed to be meditated upon. For this God of gods is the manifest deity; [he should be honored] with reverence.
Now, what is the use of much speaking? Listen to what I shall say:
even a sinful son should worship [the Sun] on the days of the Sun (Sunday) and so forth;
indeed, those men who do worship attain the supreme goal.

When a Sunday arrives, a man who, with devotion and faith, worships the Sun and observes the *nakta* fast, goes to the world of the immortals. He who first [offers] to the Sun with devotion [an image] endowed with five jewels...
By offering with the mantra, he goes to the world of the immortals.
O Hero, he who performs a śrāddha according to the rules for the pleasure of Mārtaṇḍa during a saṃkrānti or an ayana goes to the world of the Sun.
That man who, having observed a fast on the sixth day, performs a śrāddha according to the rules on the seventh day with the thought,
"May the Sun be pleased," is liberated from all defects and is glorified in the world of the Sun.

O lord of men, whatever man or woman worships the Sun-god, Bhānu, according to the prescribed rites on the seventh lunar day— especially on that specific day or during an eclipse— they shall attain all their desires.
Thus understand, O Bhīṣma: there is no deity dearer than the Sun.
Among the gods of gods, Āditya alone is worshipped as supreme, just as kings on earth ascend the mountain of jewels.
Just as beings proceed according to their nature to receive their full share of jewels,
so too do men, by propitiating the Sun, obtain their fruit:
one seeking wealth shall obtain wealth, and one seeking a son shall obtain a son.

One who seeks liberation attains liberation, or else one may attain immortality. Now, what is the use of much speaking? Listen to my words, O Bhārata: having propitiated the Sun, the hosts of gods beginning with Brahmā [attained their goals].
Those highly fortunate ones attained divine, heart-stealing,
and eternal abodes in heaven that remove all sins.
Sumantu said:
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Vyāsa vanished on that very spot.
Bhīṣma also worshipped the Sun with devotion according to the prescribed rites.
Therefore, O Indra among kings, you too should worship this Maker of Day.
Having worshipped the Sun with devotion, you shall go to the eternal abode,
just as the blessed Vyāsa and Bhīṣma,
O giver of honor, departed after worshipping the divine Maker of Day with devotion on the seventh lunar day even once.

Thus ends the two hundred and seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Worship of Āditya," in the dialogue between Vyāsa and Bhīṣma within the Saptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan in the glorious *Śrī-Bhaviṣya-Mahāpurāṇa*.
[Now follows] the description of the Saptamī-vrata. Śatānīka said:
"Tell me again, O best of the twice-born, regarding the practice for the seventh [lunar day] for the pleasure of the Sun; how does a man here become one who has fasted? Sumantu said:
Furthermore, O Mahāmati, these seven Saptamīs have been described;
yet there are many more, O tiger among the Kurus. Listen again to me as I speak of those which were previously recounted by the Sun himself, O Lord of Birds.
O mighty-armed one, seven Saptamīs of Aruṇa are honored:
the first with *arkapuṭaka* flowers, the second likewise with black pepper (*marica*),
the third with neem leaves, and the fourth with the fruit-Saptamī.

The fifth is Anodanā, the sixth is Vijayā, and the seventh is known as Kāmikā; learn from me the ritual procedure for them. On a Sunday during the bright fortnight, under the southern solstice, or during the northern course of the sun—
During an eclipse of the sun in the constellation of Puṣya, one should observe the vow for seven seventh-days (saptamīs).
He should be a true celibate student, endowed with purity, with his senses conquered,
devoted to the worship of the Sun, self-controlled, and likewise intent on recitation and burnt offerings.
On the fifth day itself, the man should always practice celibacy;
on the sixth day, he should not engage in sexual intercourse and should avoid honey and meat.
He should spend one night with *arkasaṃpuṭaka* flowers and another with black pepper.

Likewise, on the other [day], known as Phalā, one should perform the rite with *nimba* leaves and fruit; subsisting on no cooked food and deprived of solid food, one should observe the vow according to the rules,
consuming only air for a day and night during the Vijayā-saptamī.

Likewise, having observed one seventh day each month, the wise man should joyfully perform it according to the prescribed rule; thereafter, he may perform the optional rites. Having written the names of these days separately on individual slips of paper:
One should place all those leaves into a new jar;
even if a man does not know its purpose or is an outcast from society,
he should extract one leaf from it without making any deliberation.

Whoever performs that same penance every month for as long as seven seventh-days (fortnights), that is to be known as the Kāmikā. Thus these seven seventh-days have been proclaimed by Vivasvat himself.
O King, the man who performs this with devotion goes to the abode of the Sun.
By means of *arkasaṃpuṭaka* offerings, he obtains stable wealth for seven generations; through black pepper, he shall indeed always have union with beloved ones, such as sons and others.
All diseases perish by means of nimba leaves; of this there is no doubt.
By its fruits, one obtains sons, grandsons, and abundant daughters' sons.
From this [tree] likewise come wealth, wealth, grain, gold, and silver.

Likewise, O King, one who fasts on Vijayā day constantly obtains cattle, gold, and good health; O Monarch, he always conquers his enemies. When properly observed according to the rules, she fulfills all desires and grants one's wishes.
One desiring a son shall obtain a son; one desiring wealth shall obtain inexhaustible wealth;
one desiring knowledge shall obtain knowledge; and one seeking a kingdom shall attain a kingdom.
This [goddess] grants all desires; she is the Giver of Desires, O joy of the Kurus.
Whether it be a man or a woman, whoever performs the Saptamī vow as prescribed with a self-controlled mind indeed attains the supreme goal;
for them, nothing whatsoever in the three worlds is difficult to obtain.
O Hero, those who, observant of vows and firm in their ascetic discipline, worship the Lord of the World with devotion—
neither by various rites nor by extremely difficult austerities,
nor even by sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees, do they obtain that fruit.

O best of kings, whatever fruit is obtained through ablutions at sacred fords, or likewise through gifts, fire-offerings, and worship, as well as the fruit of worshipping [the Sun] on the seventh lunar day which grants liberation— that fruit is attained by one seeking liberation, just as the Blessed Lord Ravi has declared.
Having observed the fast on a Sunday, a person endowed with faith and devotion should worship the Sun; such a person attains an immovable station,
and his residence in the world of the Sun is certain— of this there is no doubt.
But that man who worships the Sun with devotion on the seventh lunar day attains unimpeded passage through the worlds of Brahmā, Indra, and Rudra;
he shall not be blind, nor leprous, nor impotent, nor maimed, nor destitute.
O Hero, in whose family one who observes the Saptamī vow may be born,
he shall obtain knowledge if he seeks knowledge, and he who seeks wealth shall attain wealth;
O Bhārata, he who seeks a wife shall obtain a woman endowed with beauty, as well as sons.
If a breach of the vow should occur through greed, negligence, or delusion,
then one should not eat for three nights, or else have one's hair shaved. Having performed this expiation, one becomes a practitioner of the vow once again.
O Lord of Birds, as long as there are seven [cycles] of the seventh days,
a man who worships on the Sūrya-saptamī with garlands, incense, and other offerings,
and feeds the twice-born according to his ability, shall attain imperishable heaven.
"He who bestows gold upon the foremost of Brahmins on the seventh lunar day attains that which is inexhaustible and goes to the world of the Sun.
Thus, O hero, has this supreme Saptamī vow been proclaimed."
"I shall speak further; listen with a one-pointed mind, O King.

Thus ends the two hundred and eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Saptasaptamī Vow," in the *Sauradharma* section of the *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the *Brāhma Parvan*, during the *Saptamī-kalpa*, in the dialogue between Sūrya and Aruṇa.
(This concludes) the description of the Saptamī vow.
Sumantu said:
He who, subsisting on cow dung, should pass twelve seventh days of the bright fortnight,
or else subsisting on barley-gruel, or even eating only withered leaves;
Subsisting on milk, or eating only once a day, or again subsisting on alms, or even subsisting only on water, the wise man,
having worshipped the Sun with various offerings of flowers— lotuses, fragrant lilies, and blue water-lilies— [attains his goal].

Having worshipped the most excellent twice-born with various kinds of perfumes, incense such as guggulu and sandalwood, with black aloe-wood, milk-rice, and other diverse offerings, and with fine ornaments, as well as with gold, food, and other gifts, a man [attains his goal].
O hero, he obtains that fruit which is attained here by means of sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees;
having ascended an excellent celestial chariot, he is glorified in the world of the Sun.
Then, O King, upon the exhaustion of his merit, he is born into a great family.
Thus, with devotion and a concentrated mind, one should worship Vivasvat month by month according to the prescribed rite and recite his names with devotion.
In the month of Caitra, Viṣṇu resides; indeed, in Mādhava, he is Aryaman.
In the bright fortnight of the month of Vaiśākha, he is Vivasvat; and in the month of Śuci, he is Divākara.
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, he is Parjanya; likewise, in Nabhasya, he is Varuṇa.
He is to be known as Mārtaṇḍa during the month of Kārttika;
furthermore, in Mārgaśīrṣa, he is always celebrated by the wise as Mitra. In the month of Pauṣa, however, he should be worshipped with diligence as Pūṣan.
In the month of Māgha he is to be known as Bhaga, and in Phālguna as Tvaṣṭṛ;
thus one should recite the names in sequence for the pleasure of the Sun.
With a well-concentrated mind, one should perform this rite of incense and worship on the seventh lunar day.
The man who performs this with devotion attains the supreme goal.
Thus, O Lord, everything that is most secret regarding the All-pervading One has been told to you.
This must never be given to one who is not a disciple, nor to one who lacks devotion.
It should not be given to one who has committed evil, nor should it be given to an atheist;
O hero, it should not be given to an ungrateful person, an atheist, or one of cruel deeds.
He who constantly hears this supreme Saptamī vow [shall attain his goal].
Whoever recites this with self-restraint and endowed with supreme faith,
having attained happiness in this world, is glorified in the world of the Sun;
and upon the exhaustion of his merit, returning here to the earth, he becomes a king.

Thus ends the two hundred and ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Monthly Seventh-Day Vow," within the Dialogue between Sūrya and Aruṇa in the Saptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan in the glorious *Śrī-Bhaviṣya-Mahāpurāṇa*.
[Now follows] the Description of the Worship of Sūrya. Sumantu said:
Thus, this seventh kalpa has been described to you in brief.
O Lord, listen with a single-minded focus as I speak of it again in detail.
One should observe a fast on the sixth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Phālguna.
Having bathed, O mighty-armed one, one should worship the Sun with perfumes, flowers, and ointments—
with *arka* flowers, fragrant *guggulu*,
white *karavīra*, and sandalwood— to the Lord of Day.
Having offered an oblation of molasses-water for the pleasure of the Sun,
and having thus worshipped the Sun during the day, the wise man should sleep at night before Him,
constantly reciting the supreme mantra of Mars while remaining awake.
Śatānīka said: What is that supreme, unsurpassed mantra to be recited which is dear to the Blessed One—
the mantra which other men should devoutly recite in his presence?
"Tell me that, as well as the mantras, especially those for incense and lamps,
by which I may worship the Sun-god while reciting that which is to be recited.
Sumantu said:
I shall tell you, O best of the Bharatas, in brief and not in detail:
with a concentrated mind, one should perform all [rites]—recitation, fire-offering, and worship—with the six-syllable mantra; always using that which has been recited a hundred times.
Having first performed the recitation of the Sāvitrī mantra one hundred thousand times, one should thereafter perform all other rites, such as further recitations, with an undisturbed mind.
Oṃ! O Sāvitrī, we meditate upon the Sun, the possessor of a thousand rays.
"May the Sun impel that [mantra] for me.
Recitation itself is declared to be supreme on the seventh lunar day by the Sun himself;
having recited it even once, a human being becomes purified—of this there is no doubt.
Then, on the morning of the seventh day, O King, with a restrained mind and chanting, one should worship the Maker of Light (the Sun) with devotion according to the previously mentioned rite;
and with faith, O King, one should also feed the Brahmins according to one's capacity.
One should offer divine enjoyments, including various kinds of food and edibles, according to the prescribed rites;
one must not practice stinginess regarding wealth and should feed those who officiate the meal.
Likewise, one should not feed non-Śauras, but should diligently feed those who are Śauras.
Śatānīka said: O best among the knowers of Brahman, which Brāhmaṇas are worthy of being fed and which are not?
On whose minds does the Sun, the God of gods, reside on the seventh lunar day?
O King, that brahmin who eats from a water-pot (ghaṭī), he who observes the seventh lunar day (saptamī),
he who does not eat during the solar eclipses, and he who eats while the sun is visible—
these, in brief, are the twice-born who may be fed by the Sun.

O best of the Kuru lineage, those who have been described [as unfit for company] have been told; now listen indeed to those whose food should not be eaten: he who lives with his wife and children yet is afflicted by leprosy, he who is a devotee of another deity, and likewise one who serves as a predictor of the stars.
"He who delights in slandering others and likewise the temple-priest (devalaka)— these are persons whose food should not be eaten, as was considered by the Creator himself,
the Lord. Śatānīka said:
"Tell me, with a concentrated mind, the characteristics of all those Brahmins who are declared fit to be fed and those who are unfit to be fed, O best of the twice-born. Sumantu replied:
"I have been well questioned, O Indra among kings; I shall indeed recount it in its entirety.
While a multitude of Brahmins was reciting the triple Vedic knowledge (trayī-vidyā), O King, she was addressed as 'Ghaṭā' by the Sun-god himself."
O Hero, he who possesses that jar is called "one with a jar" by the twice-born. O assembly of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras,
listen as the meritorious recitation of the book is performed according to rule with devotion.
Thus, O tiger among the Kurus, the Sun himself, who travels through the sky, spoke regarding the oblation prescribed for each month:
"Whoever may be the performer of this [rite], he shall be considered my attendant."
That brahmin, O tiger among kings, was a favorite of the Sun;
Vyāsa lived by the profession of a bard, as did Jīvaka, who was his equal.
These are the Purāṇas along with the Itihāsas, O Bhārata.

"Victory!"— these words were spoken here by the radiant Lord himself. O King, he who dwells in one place and subsists upon a Brāhmaṇa should be known as a *jayopajīvī* (one who lives by "victory"), and likewise as a *vācaka* (reciter).

O best of kings, that brahmin who knows the Saura scriptures, such as the *Āruṇeya* and others, as well as the *Saptāśvatilaka*, is a true knower of the reality of the Sun. He who constantly worships Bhāskara is likewise a knower of that truth.
Likewise, one who feeds the Brahmins as if they were the divine Sun himself should be known as a devotee of the Sun; he must be diligently provided with food.
This indeed is the characteristic of those whose food may be eaten; now hear from me regarding those whose food must not be eaten.
That Brāhmaṇa whose wife is indeed a Vṛṣalī, especially if she is the wife of another,
is a husband of another's wife; he is the lowest of Brāhmaṇas,
struck down by fate as a leper, a Brāhmaṇa who is a slayer of the Veda (Brahman).
O descendant of Kuru, that Brahmin who eats [at the temple] but does not likewise honor him should be known as a devotee of another deity;
one should know the Bhojaka to be Āditya himself, born from the body of the Sun.
O King, he who does not worship the Sun should never be fed; likewise, that man in whose house a *bhojaka*— whether shaven-headed, deformed, fair-skinned, or bearing a conch-shell and flowers—
enters, [should not be fed].
The gods, the ancestors,
the Rākṣasas, the Bhūtas, the Piśācas, and even the Yoginīs flee from the house of that householder in whom a Bhojaka eats but once.
The Sun remains satisfied for as long as seven years;
therefore, a wise man should always feed those divine Bhojakas.
However, that Brahmin who censures them should never be fed.
She who, having abandoned her own husband, goes elsewhere at will, is indeed called a wanton woman (svairiṇī); she is most sinful and a defiler of her family.
That woman who, due to the faults of her husband, finds pleasure in a secret lover, O King, [is likewise condemned].
O King, she should be known as a wanton woman who brings ruin to her family;
any Brahmin who takes pleasure in her should be known as one devoted to a wanton woman. So too are the actor, the storyteller, and the common dancer.
O Indra among kings, one who lives by painting and one who is a great beggar—
O King, these two names are proclaimed for the storyteller. O descendant of Kuru, such was the arrogant man he became because of this deed.

O Bhārata, that wise man who sings a hymn of praise loudly in an assembly of people is called a *raṅgopajīvī* (one who lives by the stage); this is proclaimed as the second [type]. In all the scriptures, O Bhārata, "hinting" (*sūcanam*) is said to be "telling" (*kathanam*).
"He who indicates the constellations is indeed a pointer of the stars.
Śatānīka said:
"Alas! What great misery you have toward these twice-born ones!"
The science of astronomy (jyotiḥśāstra) is declared by the wise to be the sixth auxiliary limb (vedāṅga).
A twice-born man devoid of it would not truly possess the six limbs;
for a Brāhmaṇa who studies that [science] is like one who recites from a forbidden source.
The Brahmin went to Bhojya with an unbroken [vessel], yet he received nothing from that which was purposeless.
Having reflected, [the king said: "Tell me, O Brahmin; I have a great doubt in this matter. Sumantu said:
"I have been well questioned by you; hear now the decision on this matter:
that by which a Brahmin’s livelihood is to be known as his proper means of subsistence is through the annual science of astrology, which indicates the knowledge of the lunar mansions."
He should not be fed by a king; this would be his livelihood. To proclaim the faults of others behind their backs without cause, while concealing their virtues—he is one devoted to slander.
O Indra among kings, O scorcher of foes, that Brāhmaṇa who indeed performs labor for a livelihood,
as well as the worship of the gods here in a temple,
and the exercise of authority over and the eating of the food offerings (naivedya), [is considered fallen].
O King, that Brāhmaṇa should be known as a mere Devala, the lowest of Brāhmaṇas.
For Brāhmaṇas who subsist on the earth, there is no authority to perform the worship of gods,
O tiger among the Bharatas, especially regarding the office of lordship.
But that Brāhmaṇa who, O best of the Kuru lineage, worships the Goddess out of greed for wealth or for the sake of a livelihood, certainly goes to hell, O observer of noble vows; likewise,
he who performs the fire-ritual in all temples [without qualification].
O King, O Lord, he who, out of greed for wealth, performs the worship of the gods or the fire-rituals in all temples except that of Śiva, shall fall into a low state of existence.
O King, there is no doubt that the office of the Bhojakas is traditionally recognized [as such];
for by worshipping the gods, they attain the supreme goal. Since they consume the food offerings (naivedya) and cause the Sun to partake of them, they are called Bhojakas.
Having gone there, they worship the gods according to the divine ritual;
and having worshipped the gods, they partake of the food offerings and edibles of the Lord,
and go to that supreme abode where the god Divākara dwells.
And the Brahmin should say to him, O high-minded one, while he is still fierce:
"O Lord, for the sake of my own welfare and yours, I shall do so.
Having thus addressed him, O joy of the Kurus, he should then go to his own home.
Likewise, on the following day, O King, having worshipped the god Divākara with devotion and having established the sacred fire,
one should then feed the Brahmins rice cooked with *śāli* grains,
as well as fragrant mung beans and indeed mung bean soup.
O King, best of men, with cakes and jaggery-cakes, as well as milk and curd,
the Sun attains satisfaction through these offerings.
O best of the Bharatas, listen as I speak of those things that must be avoided.
One who desires his own welfare should not offer these to the Sun: horse-gram, lentils, flat beans and the like, as well as peas and other such pulses, and likewise kidney beans.
O King, one should not give to the Sun rice that is foul-smelling, pungent, or too small in quantity, nor indeed rice that is mixed with other grains;
having thus fed the twice-born, one should then have him consume the *arka*-saṃpuṭa.
Having prostrated with his head before the Lord accompanied by water,
he who accepts the sacred emblem and then resorts to another worldly path—
neither his ancestors, nor the gods, nor human beings will eat [the offerings] of that person.
Having departed from the city, O King, and having gone toward the northeast direction,
the mighty-armed one, O best of birds, saw the supreme sun born in a pure place that was neither too high nor too low, and he worshipped it.
O King, its branches extend toward the east and the north;
at the tip of such a branch, one should take two very fine leaves resting upon a vessel—
well-joined and not separated— and having honored them, one should return home.
O best of birds, having bathed and worshipped the Sun with *arka* flowers,
and having fed the Brahmins while saying, "May the Sun be pleased with me," one should then consume the *arka*-cup with the mantra and thereafter eat.
Restraining his speech, O Hero, he should not touch the vessel with his teeth while before the deity:
"Oṃ! O Arkasaṃpuṭa, may it be well with you; may it always be well with you, O Arka.
Grant me also prosperity and become the bestower of expiation."
O King, O high-minded one, reciting this mantra while remembering the Sun,
and standing facing the east, O King, he who consumes water mixed with *brahmakūrca* and then eats, attains the supreme goal.
O Hero, that vessel known as Arka should not be touched with the teeth;
by this rite and with devotion, the Saptamī should always be observed with faith for the pleasure of the Sun throughout the year, O mighty-armed one.
And that man who performs this seventh [observance] while pleasing the Sun,
his wealth shall become inexhaustible, stable, and extend to seven generations;
likewise, gold, silver, copper, and precious metal shall never diminish.
Having achieved this success, Kauthumi departed suddenly;
King Jayastoma was indeed liberated from leprosy,
as were Bṛhadbala, Dhvajaka, Kopī, Yājñavalkya, and Kṛṣṇaja.
Having propitiated the Sun, they thereafter attained equality with the Sun. O King,
this seventh lunar day is most auspicious, meritorious, and destructive of sins,
especially for those who recite it, listen to it, or perform its rites.
Therefore, O sinless one, this should always be performed according to the rules for the sake of the highest good.
Śatānīka said:
Just as Janaka and others attained perfection by worshipping the Sun.

I have heard this many times, yet I have not heard how Kauthumi attained perfection by propitiating the Sun and was freed from leprosy, O observer of noble vows. Who was that Brahmin Kauthumi, and how did he contract leprosy?
"O twice-born one, how did he propitiate Bhānu, the lord of the gods?
O Brahmin, recount all of this to me in brief.

Thus ends the two hundred and tenth chapter, titled "Description of the Worship of the Sun and Other Duties," within the Sauradharma section of the Saptamī-kalpa, in the Brāhma-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Description of Arkasampuṭikā.
Sumantu said:
"O Indra among kings, I have been well questioned; listen as I speak."
In former times, there was a great scholar, a Brāhmaṇa named Sthāṇugautama.
That twice-born man went, accompanied by his son, to the hermitage of Janaka.
There, O best of kings, a debate took place between them and other Brāhmaṇas.
O mighty-armed one, a brahmin there was indeed slain by Kauthumin while he was possessed by anger;
seeing that the brahmin had been killed, Kauthumin was abandoned by his father,
as well as by his brothers and all his other elders.
Rebuked by them all, he was overcome with grief and sorrow;
he then traveled to sacred fords and divine shrines,
yet that brahmin was not suddenly released from the sin of killing a brahmin.
When she was not released, another severe affliction arose for the brahmin:
deprived of his ears and nose, with pus and blood flowing from them,
he wandered over the entire earth and returned once more to his father’s house.
With his heart stricken by grief, he spoke these words to his father:
"Father, I have traveled to sacred fords and holy shrines;
yet, O dear one, I am not liberated from this cruel Brahman-slaughter."
"O sinless father, even though an expiation has been performed for me, what shall I do and where shall I go? O Lord, my pains are exceedingly great;
tell me of some deed that might be done with little effort."
"O scorcher of enemies, may this Brahman-murder and this disease perish!
Speak, my dear father, do not delay; bring about my ultimate welfare.
Having heard these words of his son, the brahmin Hiraṇyanābha—
Overwhelmed by grief and sorrow, he spoke these words to his son.
Hiraṇyanābha said:
"O son, the suffering you have endured while wandering over the earth is known to me."
"O child, though you visit sacred fords while performing penances,
the sin of killing a Brahmin will not leave you, O upholder of my lineage.
I shall tell you one means by which you will obtain liberation."
"Listen, my son, as I speak to you with little effort.
Kaushumbhi said:
"O Lord, whom among the gods beginning with Brahmā do I worship, and how?"
"I am deprived of a body by the cause of all my actions.
Hiraṇyanābha said:
"They attain satisfaction through action joined with the continuity of spiritual perfection (siddhi)."

"O best of the twice-born, even the gods— including Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Mahādeva, Varuṇa, and likewise Kubera— worship this Sun alone with offerings of ointments and cleansing; thus have the wise declared."
"O son, relying upon Bhānu, they all rejoice in heaven;
therefore, I do not see any deity whatsoever who is equal to Bhānu. Thus, Bhānu is now honored by all as the granter of every desire."
"O dear one, there is no doubt that he is the father and mother of all men.
Worship him indeed with devotion while reciting this unsurpassed mantra;
and, endowed with faith, listen to the Itihāsas and Purāṇas."
"O high-minded one, by propitiating the Sun with devotion while chanting the Sāman and the Purāṇas,
you shall thereafter attain liberation in this world, my son.
Kauthumi said:
O dear one, O high-minded one, the Sāman chants are indeed preeminent;
the Udgītha has the syllable Om as its excellence, and there is the fourfold Prasthāna.
Here, the fifth is the Parihāra, and they call the sixth the Adbhuta.
The seventh of the Sāmans is known as Nidhana, and it is remembered as the "Sevenfold" (Sāptavidhya).
This Sevenfold nature is indeed proclaimed in the Hiṅkāras and Praṇavas.
The eighth is your Śāṭhya, and the ninth is Vāmadevika.
The tenth Sāman is the Jyeṣṭha, which is dear to the Creator and leads to supreme liberation.
O dear one, among these Sāmans, this is considered the supreme to be recited from the throat.
Having recited it according to my capacity, I shall go to the highest state.
Hiraṇyanābha said:
"Excellent, my son! Your lineage has been purified by a son such as you.
Even though you have met with such a fate, O son, your memory of your duty has been restored."

Thus it is, dear father; there is no doubt that these Sāmans, my son, are indeed common [to all], for they were proclaimed by Brahmā himself. Yet, even among these, two supreme Sāmans are declared to be unsurpassed.
"Therefore, let that one supreme mantra be recited, which removes all sins and fear.
Kauthumi said:
"O father, tell me quickly what those two supreme Sāmans are."
"O dear one, among these *sāmans*, there is nothing else that should be chanted.
Hiraṇyanābha said:
"Listen as I speak of the first, which is the supreme *Jyeṣṭhasāman*, and the second."
Then, by one desiring liberation, the third [Veda] which is to be heard must be recited.
And thereafter, the supreme [Veda] was proclaimed by the Sun-god himself;
it was personally ordained by the Deity as the highest vow among all sacred meters.
It is always dear to Hiraṇyagarbha and dear to Sūrya.
Learn from me its recitation, its application, and its characteristics:
by means of truth, one is absorbed into the Supreme; this is remembered by the wise as beginning with the word "Śūkara."
The seasons, existence, as well as dharma, adharma, and the performer of truth; likewise,
both dharma and adharma as effects, and the experience of dharma—
whatever is sung by these twice-born ones in beautiful words according to their conventions.
That supreme recitation was proclaimed by the Sun-god himself;
indeed, one who performs this recitation does not return to rebirth,
but being liberated from all diseases, is freed even from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Having recited this mantra, worship the Sun;
O son, listen to the Puranic Sāman proclaimed for you.
O son, I shall indeed describe to you the characteristics of the Jyeṣṭha-Sāman as well.

The *jyeṣṭhasāman* is also characterized by the [verse] beginning with "ādyāyādājyadoha"; O son, you should always listen to and recite this for the sake of your eldest brother, while constantly worshipping the Sun as if he were your own son.
"By thus propitiating the Lord of Gods, you shall thereafter cast off your sorrow. Sumantu said:
"Then, having heard his father's words, the singer of the Sāman hymns, Kauthumi, likewise [acted]."
Endowed with faith, he propitiated the Sun with devotion;
then, O King, while reciting the Śrāvya at the three times of day before the Sun,
as he listened to the Purāṇas, his sin of Brahman-slaughter was then removed.
And this, O tiger among the Kurus, is indeed the fruit of sacred learning:
that which is the fruit for one who mutters prayers while worshipping the God, O King, has been attained by him as well, O Ravi; listen with a focused mind, O monarch.
That embodied Brahmin, through the grace of the Sun,
entered the orb of the Sun, that supreme station of the All-pervading Lord;
yet even today he does not return, for he has gone to the highest state.
Thus it has been told to you, O King: that great twice-born man attained perfection.
By fasting on this seventh lunar day, O hero, one goes to the Sun;
so it was for Kauthumi, O tiger among men, through the grace of the Sun-god.
While he was indeed engaged in recitation as well as listening to the Purāṇas—
thus, O King, has been described this first Saptamī,
the meritorious Arkapuṭikā, which bestows wealth and is dear to the Sun.

Thus ends the two hundred and eleventh chapter, titled "Description of the Saptamī Vow named Arkasaṃpuṭikā" within the Saura-dharma of the Saptamī-kalpa, in the Brāhma-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
[Now follows] the description of the ritual for the worship of the Sun. Sumantu said:
Thus, O hero, this Arkasaṃpuṭikā has been described to you;
now listen as I speak of the second, which is made with black pepper.
Having fasted properly on the sixth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, one should proceed.
One should worship the Sun with devotion according to the ordinances of the Saura-dharma.
Śatānīka said:
O Brahmin, tell me all the meritorious mantras, especially those that are distinguished.
And likewise the heart-mantras of the Sun and others, together with the placement of the head-mantras. Sumantu said:
O Lord, I shall declare to you this supreme secret.
O high-minded one, listen to that which was previously spoken by Brahmā with devotion to the great-souled Bhānu, for the sake of destroying all sins—
the meritorious Aditya hymn, which removes all evil and is honored by the world.
Adorned with a crest-jewel, this is the supreme nectar of the syllable *vaṃ*:
*oṃ vaṃ phaṭ*.
*Oṃ*, this is the Sun himself, my dear, the embodiment of the mantra, possessed of great power.
By constantly recollecting this, the practitioner of mantra, always consuming sweet food,
beholds the Lord of Gods, Bāṇu himself, within a year.
Freed from disease and death, he goes to the world of the Sun.
O King, that best among those who know mantras, constantly muttering [the mantra] with his mind, actions, and speech— whether through cursing or bestowing grace—
subsisting on milk, observing silence, dwelling in solitude, and having his senses restrained.
Having recited it twelve hundred thousand times, one shall go to heaven in one's own body;
O King, one wanders through the three worlds at will like a wish-fulfilling gem.
Now hear this supreme Vāma-hṛdaya of the Sun.
O Bhārata, this heart-mantra is proclaimed as that which should always be meditated upon by the pure, which removes all sins and fears,
which is joined with the letter *ṛ* and conjoined with the moon (*u*),
and which is illuminated by the syllable *oṃ*.

The letter *ya* joined with the nasal bindu is declared by the wise to be Vaiśākha. O King, the letter *ya*, the letter *va*, the vowel-mātrā, and likewise the bindu—this is taught as the beloved armor; now listen to me as I describe the weapon.
The syllable *du*, preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ) and accompanied by the anusvāra, as well as *kaṭa*—this, O King, is known as the weapon (*astra*). Now learn from me the nectar (*amṛta*):
the letter *va* joined with the bindu and the moon is known as the nectar.
Oṃ! Brahmā is the weapon, Amṛta is the Gāyatrī, and the Cow is proclaimed to be the disease.
One should designate the letter *ya* and the letter *va* as the two eyes and the thunderbolt.
These are the limbs of the Sun of immeasurable splendor, who is three-eyed.
Having placed the Āditya-mantra upon the head, one should place the Hṛdaya-mantra upon the heart;
one should place the Sāvitrī-mantra in the region of the throat, and one should contemplate the Aśeṣa-mantra upon the head.
This placement of the Sun (arkanyāsa) has been declared by me; the wise man should perform this ritual placement.
O King, listen to the supreme method of worship for the One-Syllabled Sun. First, having bound the *kiṃkiṇī* mudrā at the heart,
one should likewise perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) accompanied by the *parivīra*.

One who understands the single syllable with devotion for the sake of self-purification shall again obtain you, the one to be slain, through the letter *va* as the Self. Having performed this, one becomes equal to the sun; of this there is no doubt.
O lord of the earth, having formed the mudrā and applied the Astra-mantra to the temple,
it shall indeed become beautiful, O bull of the Bharatas; having performed that,
one who possesses the armor [mantra] like the sun should perform the rite of consecration (vardhanakriyā) to wash away the enemy.
Then, O King, one should worship the arghya vessel with flowers according to the rules;
one should bathe the Lord with the *hṛdaya-mantra* and thereafter perform the worship.
One should place the lotus-mudrā, containing flowers within it, upon the head of the Lord.
In this manner, the Sun, the God of gods, is invoked.
O Bhārata, perform the worship accompanied by the *arghya* offering with the Heart-mantra;
and the food offering (*naivedya*) for the Lord should be given according to one's capacity with the Heart-mantra.
One who is firm in his vows should perform recitation according to his capacity, with speech and senses restrained.
By this method, O King, one shall accomplish all undertakings;
there shall be no obstacle anywhere, nor shall any evil occur.
Having bound the supreme *vyomamudrā* and having performed a circumambulation,
one should then dismiss the deity with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, O Lord of the Earth.

Thus ends the two hundred and twelfth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Worship of the Sun," in the *Sauradharma* section of the *Saptamī-kalpa* within the *Brāhma-parvan* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Description of the Ritual for Worshipping the Sun. Sumantu said: Having beheld the divine Fire-god and the Sun situated within that Fire, [one should proceed].
One should recite the syllable "ghū" along with its retinue;
when this is done, there is no doubt that the purification of the fire is accomplished.
Then, one should cast it into the heart-fire within the interior of a lotus.
The God of gods will be invoked in person; of this there is no doubt.
With the syllable *oṃ* and through the meditative absorption on the collyrium of the eyes, one should offer a hundred oblations.
Then, O King, one should offer five oblations for the gratification of the limbs [of the deity].
Then the wise one should perform the ritual dismissal (visarjana) with the *hṛdaya-mantra*.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Worship of the Sun" in the Saurārcanavidhi section of the Saptamī-kalpa within the Brāhma-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
[This is followed by] the description of the Marica-saptamī vow.
Sumantu said:
"Padminī, and likewise another named Madhyamā,
as well as Arkiṇī, Jvālinī, Tejanī, and Gabhastinī."
The conch mudrā is the tenth, and likewise the sun-faced [mudrā] is another;
the thousand-rayed mudrā is indeed proclaimed as the twelfth.
A wise person should offer the arghya with the lotus [mudrā], and having formed the sky [mudrā], should recite the mantra.
Udayāśrayā is for summoning; Madhyamā destroys disease.
If one is established in the ritual procedure, one should gaze at the sun with Arkīṇī;
having bound Jvālinī in order to approach [the deity], one should recite the mantra facing the sun.
Within seven days he beholds the Sun, and thereafter he himself attains perfection.
Having descended into the cluster of lotuses and facing the Sun,
a man who recites [the mantra] one hundred thousand times indeed obtains an inexhaustible treasure.

Listen to this procedure for the solar wheel, beginning with the conch mudrā and so forth. Having fasted for a day and night, O King, a man facing the sun should sit in the lotus posture and recite the mantra ten thousand times.

One who beholds the sun after three days shall attain mental perfection (*mānasī siddhi*). Having fixed [the gaze] upon the thousand-rayed sun while standing in water reaching the navel, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times with the mind focused entirely upon that.
He beholds the supreme light, the thousand-rayed god surrounded by rays;
he shall attain abundant perfection and become the bestower of both curses and favors upon all living beings.
Having cast off the sheath from all sides, one indeed becomes free from fever.
Placing the two feet together with the heels joined and the hands likewise joined to each other,
one should press the right little toe with the left ring finger.
The left [hand] with the right, and likewise the right with the left—
this mudrā is indeed of great merit and is proclaimed as the Vyoma-mudrā.
By binding this, the diseases of men are instantly destroyed.
No practitioner devoid of this attains accomplishment;
for everywhere this is considered the supreme secret of mantras. It is the Heart of the Sun, renowned as the *Arka-mudrā*.
One should constantly bind [the thread] with mantras for the increase of longevity and health. Standing before the solar disc at sunrise,
the practitioner, facing the sun, should recite the mantra.
For three days, the meditator, devoted to the recitation of mantras, should gaze upon it;
having seen it, he does not meet death nor suffer misery— of this there is no doubt—
and he attains the supreme abode where the god Divākara dwells.
Having placed the two hands palm-upward with their backs joined to one another,
and having bound all the fingers so that they are well-spread out, there is no doubt [this is the mudrā].
Then, one should press the bases of the fingers with the two thumbs in their proper order.
This mudrā is named Udayā; one should bind it at sunrise.
From that day, he beholds the sun for twelve days, without a doubt.
It removes all sins and destroys all evil.
Without rising, one should cast that [wind] from the left and from the center;
it is renowned as the "Middle" (madhyamā), and one should contemplate it when the sun is in the middle.
By that method of the Middle, the practitioner, having bound the mudrā, [should proceed].
One should join both thumbs together with the other fingers according to the prescribed rite;
this auspicious mudrā is indeed the "Sunset" (astamanī), the sovereign of all tantras. Having bound this mudrā at the setting of the sun, one should begin the recitation.
Having formed the mudrā, the wise man should recite [the mantra] even a thousand or a hundred times;
though joined with all manner of sins, he becomes radiant within seven days.
The two hands are joined together, and the thumbs are positioned pointing upwards.

Both thumbs raised and joined together, positioned at the crown of the head—this is indeed the Mālinī mudrā; it shall burn away the cage of sins. Whatever sin there may be, such as the killing of a Brahmin, when this mudrā is applied to the head, it destroys it.
Having slightly separated all the fingers, with the middle and index fingers likewise [extended],
and their two thumbs positioned upwards— this is known as the Tarjanī mudrā.
It is the goddess who removes all diseases and destroys all enemies.
Having bound this highly meritorious [mudrā], one paralyzes all enemies.
Having extended both hands, they are positioned with the middle fingers joined;
then the remaining fingers are bent, and likewise the tips of the thumbs are brought together in sequence.
The mudrā named Gabhastinī is the supreme heart-mantra of the Sun;
indeed, when bound at sunrise, it is auspicious and destroys death.
One should bind it at the time of offering the arghya water and worship the sacrificial fire.
And at the time of recitation, one should bind the mantras; of this there is no doubt.
It should be done with the right little finger and likewise with the two index fingers.
Furthermore, the two thumbs should be joined together with the two index fingers.
He who performs this recitation daily becomes purified within three months.
Having formed the hands into a hollowed cup (*saṃpuṭa*) and bent the two index fingers,
this is indeed the *Sahasrakiraṇā* mudrā, the sovereign of all lords of mudrās.
The practitioner should bind this at the head of the mantra during the three junctions of the day;
it destroys all sins just as the sun destroys a mass of darkness.
Having first bound the *mudraka-kumbha* mudrā, one should then recite the mantra.
"One shall destroy leprosy in one month; in three months, there is no doubt.
Thus, O King, he who worships the Sun together with the *mudrā* and the limbs according to this ritual is like Brahmā himself worshipping the Sun.
Therefore, O Indra among kings, you too should worship the Sun with this [rite].
Having thus attained Sūrya here, he goes to the world of the Sun. Whoever worships that Sun according to this procedure, [attains the same reward].
He goes to the supreme abode where the Sun-god dwells.
O King, having thus worshipped the Lord of Gods according to this rite,
one should feed the Brāhmaṇas according to one's ability and in accordance with the rules.

On the seventh day, one should likewise consume black pepper according to the mantra. O King, it is traditionally taught that one should take a single, firm, unblemished peppercorn and consume it with water while reciting this mantra.
Having worshipped the Sun according to the prescribed rite and having thus consumed black pepper, one should then eat while remaining silent;
one obtains union with a beloved at that very moment, and not otherwise.
Thus, this seventh meritorious [day] bestows reunion with loved ones;
by performing it once, one attains all desires within a year,
O best of men, and again achieves union with sons and other kin.
Therefore, O mighty-armed one, you yourself should perform this rite that bestows what is dear;
having fasted according to the rules on the seventh day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, O hero, Indra duly entered into union with Śacī.
Having observed this fast, the mighty Nala together with Damayantī,
and Rāma together with Sītā, went forth, O lord of men, having observed this fast.
Thus ends the two hundred and fourteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Marica-saptamī Vow," in the Saptamī-kalpa of the Brāhma-parvan within the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Description of the Extraction of the Sun Mantra. Sumantu said:
O hero, listen as I speak of the third and the seventh [mantras].
It is taught that worship with neem leaves is the supreme destroyer of disease;
furthermore, there is another method of worship by which one worships Ravi—
the God of gods, who holds the Śārṅga bow and bears the conch, discus, and mace.
Now I shall declare the procedure for worship; learn from me the extraction of the mantras.
*Oṃ khaṣolkāya namaḥ* is the root mantra (*mūlamantra*).
*Oṃ viṭi* is the head (*śiras*).
Oṃ, the weapon for Sahasraraśmi.
Oṃ, the upward-binding for Sahasrakiraṇa.
"Oṃ, obeisance to Ghanā, the progenitor of beings"—thus is the binding of beings.
Oṃ, blaze, burn brightly, O mass of fire!
Oṃ, may we know Āditya; may we meditate upon the one who possesses all light;
may that Sūrya inspire us.
This is the Gāyatrī-saṃkalīkaraṇa. Oṃ, salutation to Dharmātman in the northeast; Oṃ, salutation to Dakṣiṇa in the southeast.
Oṃ, homage to the infinite Vajrapāṇi in the north;
Oṃ, homage to Śyāmapiṅgala in the northeast;
Oṃ, homage to Amṛta in the southeast.
Oṃ, salutation to Budha, the son of Soma, in the south;
Oṃ, salutation to Vāgīśvara, the lord of all sciences, in the southwest;
Oṃ, salutation to Śukra, the great seer and a being, in the west.
Oṃ, obeisance to Īśvara, whose nature is the Sun, in the northwest;
Oṃ, obeisance to Kṛtavan, in the north;
Oṃ, obeisance to Rāhu, in the northeast.
Oṃ, obeisance to Antarāya, whose self is the Sun; in the east.
Oṃ, obeisance to Dhruva; in the northeast.

Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, Pūṣanmālin, Lord of the entire universe, whose vehicle is the seven horses, O Sovereign of the earth, who has reached the pinnacle of supreme perfection! Accept this form of splendor, O you of infinite flames! This is the invocation mantra.

"Oṃ, salutations to the Blessed One, the Sun, the possessor of a thousand rays; for your return at your pleasure. Thus ends the two hundred and fifteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Extraction of the Solar Mantra," within the *Sauradharma* section of the *Saptamī-kalpa* in the *Brāhma-parvan* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
[Now follows] the description of the rules for listening to the Purāṇas. Sumantu said:

Listen, O King, to the procedure for worship: with water purified by mantras, one who knows the mantras should carefully perform the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) while being well-composed; then, having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the mantra upon the limbs beginning with the heart.
Having meditated upon himself as the Sun-god, accompanied by his retinue,
he should perform the *saṃmārjanī* mudrā and the awakening of the directions;
likewise, the purification of the netherworld (*pātāla*), the earth, and the sky is prescribed.
This method of worship bestows all desired objects upon everyone;
O Hero, it has been proclaimed as the "Lotus" by all the wise.
One should draw an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp in a clean place.
Then, having formed the *āvāhanī* mudrā, one should invoke the Sun;
there, one should bathe Khaṣolka, whose form bestows desire. One should establish and bathe the one whose body is mantra with mantras.
A person should place the heart of the deity in the southeastern direction;
having placed the head in the northeastern direction, one should install the crest-lock (śikhā) in the southwestern direction;
one should place the two eyes in the eastern direction, for he is the single-hearted one.
Having invoked the single armor (kavaca) in the west and the weapon (astra) itself,
one should establish Soma in the northeast, Lohita in the east,
Somatapani in the southeast, and Bṛhaspati in the south.
In the southwest [he placed] the Dānava Śukra, in the west Śanaiścara,
in the northwest likewise Ketu, and in the north Rāhu;
and in the second enclosure, those born from the splendor of the gods.
One should install the twelve Ādityas, the descendants of Kaśyapa who possess great power:
Bhaga, Sūrya, Yama, Mitra, Varuṇa,
Savitṛ, Dhātṛ, and the mighty Vivasvat.
Tvaṣṭṛ, Pūṣan, and likewise Rudra; the twelfth is said to be Viṣṇu.

[One should offer] to Indra in the east, to Yama in the south, to Varuṇa in the west, to Kubera in the north, to Īśvara in the northeast (aiśānī), to the deity Agni in the southeast (āgneyī), to the Pitṛ-devas in the southwest (nairṛtī), and to Vāyu in the northwest (vāyavī).
Also [the goddesses] Jayā, Vijayā, Jayantī, and Aparājitā.
And Śeṣa and Vāsuki, Revatī and Vināyaka,
the great goddess Mahāśvetā and Queen Suvarcalā—
likewise, there were various other hosts of deities here and there.
Likewise, another yoga renowned in the world has been taught in the Dakṣiṇa [Tantra]:
"The wise man should place Siddhi, Vṛddhi, Smṛti, the goddess Śrī, and Utpalamālinī in the eastern radiant location."
O Hero, one should place on one's own right side, all around, those worthy of worship by the world: Prājñāvatī, Kṣudhā, Vīrā, Hārītā, and Buddhi;
and Buddhimatī should always be placed there by those desiring prosperity, or [the images of] Vivasvat.
Ṛddhi, Visṛṣṭi, Paurṇamāsī, and Vibhāvarī—
these divine powers (devaśaktayaḥ) are to be established on one's own northern side. Then,
with the recitation of mantras, [one should offer] a lamp, food, ornaments, clothing, and flowers.

These offerings should be given to the God of gods, together with his attendants and his manifest form. He who constantly worships the Sun according to this rite shall attain his supreme desires and thereafter go to the abode of the Sun.
O King, he who should feed the Sun-god according to this rite [should say]:
"O Nimba tree, you are bitter by nature and likewise the abode of Āditya;
being the remover of all diseases and peaceful, may you always be my food."
Having thus consumed [the offering], O King, one should mutter prayers on the ground before the deity;
then, having fed the Brāhmaṇas and given them sacrificial fees according to one's ability,
one should afterwards eat sweet food, avoiding alkaline substances, while remaining silent.
Thus, this Saptamī vow should be performed for as long as a year.
One who performs this Saptamī is liberated from all diseases;
being freed from all diseases, he goes to the world of the Sun.
Sumantu said:
Then, O lord of the earth, in the month of Bhādrapada, during the bright fortnight,
having observed a fast on the seventh day, one should worship the Sun according to the prescribed rites.
One should worship the Sun here according to the ritual prescribed for Maheśvara;
then, having bathed again on the eighth day and worshipped the Maker of Day,
one should give fruits to the Brahmins, saying, "May Mārtaṇḍa be pleased."
Having offered dates, coconuts, citrons,
and likewise mango fruits before the God—
thus, O King, I have described to you from the beginning the fruit of the Saptamī vow.
O lord of the people, this is the great and most excellent account of Bhāskara,
hearing which, O King, a human being is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin;
likewise, this supreme section has been told, known by the name of Brahma.
O King, by hearing which men are liberated from all sins;
which yields the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices, a hundred Vājapeya sacrifices,
visiting all sacred fords, and the study of the Vedas.
A man shall obtain all that fruit which results from the gift of the earth;
that human being finds the fruit of a thousand Rājasūya sacrifices, a hundred Vājapeya sacrifices, and the gift of a hundred thousand [cows].
A Brāhmaṇa may become a scribe, a Kṣatriya may attain the status of a Brāhmaṇa,

a Vaiśya likewise attains the status of a Kṣatriya, and a Śūdra attains the status of a Vaiśya. This also applies to the Sūtas, Māgadhas, Bandīs, and others who are born from the intermixture of castes.
O Lord, they too go to the supreme abode by hearing the Purāṇas.
There is nothing more purifying for men than the Itihāsas and Purāṇas,
by the mere hearing of which one is liberated from all sins.

O tiger among kings, there is indeed no doubt that the fruit which has been declared for those who listen according to the prescribed rule, as well as for those who recite it, shall be attained; so it is said, O lord of the people. Śatānīka said:

"O Blessed One, by what method should men listen to the Bhārata, the life-story of Rāmabhadra, and especially the Purāṇas? And how indeed are the Vaiṣṇava and Śiva duties to be practiced in their entirety?"
O best of Brahmins, let the ritual for the *śravaṇa* of the solar [Purāṇas] also be told;
and how, O most excellent of the twice-born, should the reciter be addressed?
Furthermore, describe to me the characteristics of that high-souled reciter.
O twice-born one, tell me the true nature of this great-souled Khaṣolka,
and what fruit would result from worshipping him according to the rules?
How should the reciter be honored by the lay devotees at each and every conclusion of the fast?

"O Blessed One, when this is completed, what should be given to the reciter on the festival day? And is there anything that has not been accomplished which must be achieved at every festival? Sumantu said:

I have been duly questioned, O Indra among kings, regarding the Itihāsas and Purāṇas. Listen, O mighty-armed one, to what was previously heard by me when the highly effulgent and venerable Guru, Viriñca, spoke as he was questioned.
"Come, I shall tell you the rule for listening to the Purāṇas:
by listening with devotion, especially to the Itihāsas and Purāṇas,
O Lord, one is liberated from all sins, including the killing of a Brahmin."

He who listens, having become pure, in the evening, in the morning, and likewise at night— Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Śaṅkara are pleased with him. At dawn the Lord Brahmā is pleased, and at the end of the day, Hari is pleased.
