Likewise, O tiger among kings, listen to the fruit that accrues to those who perform the breaking of the fast on the tenth days; for the omnipresent Mahādeva is pleased with those who listen during the night. Some indeed perform those very fast-breaking rites on the tenth days. Listen, O best of kings, to what the fruit of theirs shall be.
O Lord of the People, listen now to the procedure for the reciter and those who hear here:
having come from one's home dressed in pure garments, one should go clockwise to that place which is prepared according to the rules; for he who is there is indeed the God himself.
Therefore, O King, he who seeks awakening should always use a seat that is neither too high nor too low; such a seat,
O joy of the Kurus, should be honored and worshipped by his listeners.
That is declared to be the seat of Vyāsa; one should designate it as the seat of the Guru.
Therefore, O King, listeners must not sit upon the seat of the reciter, just as servants do not sit upon the king's throne, nor sons upon their father's, O King.
O Hero, just as a child is regarded by them as their teacher, so too is the teacher;
having placed the worship of the gods before him, and especially the worship of the Brahmins,
the lay follower (śrāvaka) should then sit down and listen, O King.
Having brought all future [readings] together, one should then take up the book;
O lord of the people, having bowed one's head to that book,
the reciter should loosen the knot, O joy of the Kurus.

One should bind that thread again, or having released it, one should recite it at some point. One should know the book to be threefold: the thread is said to be Vāsuki, the leaves are the Lord Brahmā, and the syllables are Janārdana.
Śaṅkara likewise [is in] the thread, as are the rows of all the deities;
and Pāvaka likewise [is] in the thread, while Bhānu is situated in the middle.
All the planets are stationed at the front, O Lord, as are the directions.

Meru is always remembered as the peg (śaṅku), and the void is called the aperture (chidra). The two wooden instruments mentioned above and below are likewise called the conch (śaṅkha) and the moon between heaven and earth.
Thus, this book is indeed composed of the divine and is worshipped by the gods;
it is to be saluted and honored, and should be placed in the home for the sake of prosperity.
That best of men who, having made its thread broad, offers it [is likewise blessed].
O Indra among kings,
having identified a worthy recipient and holding him with both hands, the reciter,
having bowed his head to all beginning with Brahmā and to Vyāsa as well, goes to the supreme abode where the Sun-god dwells.
O King, O delighter of the Kurus, having likewise offered salutations to Vālmīki, as well as to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the Sun, the reciter,
filled with faith, should then address the Brahmins.

O Lord of the People, at various times [he sang] that which was sustained, not rigid, wonderful, heroic, and powerful; with syllables and words unattached [to one another], endowed with aesthetic flavor (rasa) and emotion (bhāva), and joined with the seven musical notes.
O King, the reciter should speak, manifesting all the aesthetic sentiments (rasas).
Having heard such words from the learned Brahmin, one endowed with faith [should listen to] the Itihāsas,
the Purāṇas, and likewise the life-story of Rāma.
One who stands firm in his observances and is pure shall hear [this] and obtain its fruit.
A Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, and especially a Śūdra as well,
obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and attains all desires.

One is liberated from all diseases and attains great merit; one may even go to the supreme, wondrous, and most excellent abode of the God. Having bathed and returned home, the listeners of the reciter [shall likewise attain these fruits].
O King, having bowed his head with faith to the brahmin reciter,
he should take his seat and remain facing the reciter,
O tiger among kings, with speech restrained and mind well-composed.
O King, when the reciter has performed his salutation to Vyāsa,
O mighty-armed one, the listeners should not speak except out of doubt.
When a doubt arises, the reciter should be questioned after having been propitiated.
And since he is their guru, he is called their kinsman according to dharma;
therefore, O King, even by the reciter (vācaka), that which serves as instruction for them must be spoken for the benefit of all without exception. Thus, all gurus are [to be regarded as] such.

O tiger among kings, O lord of the earth, the salutations and other rites should be performed audibly, and it is declared that "May there be auspiciousness" should be uttered by all the castes while restraining their speech. Vaiśyas [should stand] in front of Śūdras, and likewise Kṣatriyas in front of Vaiśyas.
Then, O King, standing in the midst of all, the reciter should speak.
And those men who are born of mixed castes, O King, should stand behind the Śūdras. One should know the Brāhmaṇa to be the reciter; one should not respect a reciter born of any other caste.
"Having heard the words from one of a different caste or from a reciter, one would go to hell.
Thus, O King, descendant of Kuru, for those listening to these castes in their proper order, there shall be a breaking of the fast month by month."
O King, for the sake of his own welfare, a wise man should honor the reciter;
O best of the twice-born, when the month is complete, a gold *māṣaka* should be given.
O mighty-armed one, two [gold *māṣakas*] should be given by a Brāhmaṇa, but for a Kṣatriya, two [are required].
O best of the twice-born, three gold *māṣakas* should likewise be given to the reciter by a Vaiśya,
and four should be given by a Śūdra; O best of the twice-born, these should be given with faith to the reciter month after month.
O King, at the first breaking of the fast, by honoring the reciter according to one's capacity,
a person obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice;
this continues from the beginning of Kārttika until the month of Kārttika, O Acyuta.
O King, O Lord, he who would perform the Agniṣṭoma, the Gosava, and likewise the Jyotiṣṭoma;
the Sautrāmaṇi, the Vājapeya, and the Vaiṣṇava sacrifice;
as well as the Māheśvara, the Brāhma, and the Puṇḍarīka—[he attains the highest state].

O Indra among kings, by means of these twelve months in succession, one obtains the fruit of the Āditya sacrifice, as well as that of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices. Having thus attained the fruit of such sacrifices, one goes to the highest worlds.
O King, having ascended a celestial chariot (vimāna) adorned with jeweled gems and provided with a vajra-enclosure, he rejoices in the abode of Śakra;
thereafter, he dwells in the palace of Candra and then in the palace of Varuṇa.
Having gone to the abode of Śociṣkeśa, one should go to the house of Cailavila;
having gone to the house of Dhiṣaṇa, then to that of Citraśikhaṇḍin;
and having reached Vṛddhaśravas, one should go to the temple of the Lotus-born (Brahmā).
In this very way, O best of kings, no doubt should be entertained here;
this fruit has been declared for men who listen constantly.
O King, this fruit is attained by one who listens according to the prescribed rule for the duration of a year.
These quantities indeed accrue over the course of a year for those who listen or give to the reciter, O tiger among kings—
namely one, two, three, and four, O lord of the people.

O lord of men, O best of kings, gifts should be given here month after month to the reciter by those of the Brāhmaṇa and other castes, according to the divisions of their respective classes; likewise,
when the festival is concluded, one should again honor the reciter.
One should honor both the reciter and the Brahmin with all desired objects—
with divine perfumes, garlands, and various kinds of garments.
Having given [the rewards] to the reciter, one should then honor the Brahmins.
By giving gold, silver, ornaments, and cows with bronze milking vessels to the reciter here on earth, one obtains the fruit of the sacred learning heard;
it is just as when food accompanied by ritual fees is proclaimed at the time of a Śrāddha ceremony.
Thus it has been heard, O best of kings, that [the scripture] is declared to be accompanied by sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
One should worship the reciter first, and afterwards the worship of the scribe;
at the conclusion of the section (parvan), O Lord, one should especially perform the worship.
"By him who honors the reciter, the deities are honored;
when the reciter is satisfied, my own supreme pleasure is attained.
Thus Brahmā always spoke in the presence of the gods in ancient times.
When he is satisfied, the entire world is perpetually satisfied;
therefore, O best of kings, one should worship the reciter, O Brahmin.
There exists nothing equal to the gift given to such a worthy recipient in this world.
O lord of the earth, he upon whose tongue-tip the scriptures reside— who,
my dear, has ever beheld his like among the twice-born? Indeed,
there is no recipient among men on this earth who is equal to him.
Therefore, the wise know that food should always be given to him first; O King,
when a reciter endowed with faith eats at one's Śrāddha,
his ancestors remain satisfied for a hundred years.
Just as the Sun is remembered here as the most excellent among all the gods,
so too [is this speech]— clear, wonderful, peaceful, with distinct syllables and words,
endowed with beautiful tones, and possessed of aesthetic flavor and emotion.
O King, always and most thoroughly understanding the entire meaning of the texts, one should cause the meaning of the texts to be recited among the castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas. O King,
that Brāhmaṇa who causes this to be recited is called Vyāsa.

Otherwise, he who speaks in a different manner should be known as one merely called a "speaker. O King, that country or city in which such a reciter, resembling Vyāsa himself, may dwell, is remembered as the most excellent.
They are blessed, they are great-souled, and they have achieved their life's purpose; of this there is no doubt.
That land in which they dwell with diligence is considered the most excellent.
O Hero, a city never shines when it is devoid of Vyāsa.
Just as a day bereft of the sun, or a night devoid of the moon,
or as a lake without its lotuses does not shine, O King,
so too a city never shines when it is deprived of Vyāsa.
O descendant of Kuru, that fruit which is obtained by men through devotion when bowing to the reciter cannot be attained even by a thousand sacrifices;
just as all the planets on one side are outweighed by the sun alone on the other.
Just as all the twice-born together on one side are not equal to that single reciter on the other— just as there is no scripture whatsoever on earth equal to the Veda—
so too there is no brahmin on earth equal to Vyāsa.
They declare that there is no second sacred site equal to Kurukṣetra;
no river is equal to the Gaṅgā; no deity is superior to the Sun;
there is no merit equal to the horse-sacrifice, and no sin equal to the killing of a Brahmin.
O King, just as there is no happiness equal to the joy of a son's birth,
so too a Brahmin equal to Vyāsa is not found anywhere;
he is the supreme purifier for men in rites for the gods and the ancestors.
"There is no one superior to Vyāsa"—this is the Vedic revelation.
Yet, among thousands of brahmins, this brahmin is declared the most excellent;
for when Vyāsa sits down to eat within the circle of brahmins, he does so indeed as such.
"O dear one, O tiger among kings, those things declared by Brahmā in the past as pure for the *śrāddha*— listen to them according to the rule:
honey, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), black vegetables (*kālaśāka*), sesame seeds, and the *kutapa* blanket."

Furthermore, when silver vessels are used for the Brahmins at rites for the gods or the ancestors, that reciter should be known as a "purifier of the assembly. This applies to the reciter, the ascetic,
and likewise to one who knows the six Vedāṅgas.
O best of kings, all these should be known as purifiers of the assembly (paṅktipāvanas).
These two names of the reciter are for the sake of the peak (śṛṅga);
indeed, the Itihāsas and Purāṇas are known as "Jaya."
O King, because this twice-born man subsists by means of recitation,
he has attained the reputation of being a "vācaka" (reciter), one who lives by his voice;
for he recites this [text] which is clearly articulated, wonderful, peaceful, and composed of distinct syllables.

O King, one who is thoroughly engaged in the meaning of the text while fighting with great intensity— endowed with the proper tone (*kala-svara*) and possessed of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and emotion (*bhāva*)—
should likewise offer that meaning of the text to the social classes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas.
The Brahmin who recites in this manner is called Vyāsa;
one who recites otherwise shall never attain the status of Vyāsa.
One should know that the reciter is of three kinds, according to the constant distinction of their qualities.
O mighty-armed one, the *śrāvaka* is of three kinds according to the distinction of its qualities;
listen as I describe these two that are being mentioned:
the *abhidruta*, the *aspaṣṭa*, and the *vistara* which is devoid of musical modulation (*svaravarjita*).

O Lord of Kings, that reciter who reads such a text— one devoid of word-segments, likewise lacking in proper intonation (*bhāva*), failing to comprehend the meaning of the work, and bereft of the desired enthusiasm— is [unfit].

One who is prone to anger, speaks unpleasantly, and out of ignorance corrupts the text; who does not perceive the work even with great effort—he should be known as the lowest of reciters. [But that which is] clear, wonderful, peaceful, and endowed with aesthetic flavor (rasa) and emotion (bhāva)...
O King, that reciter who recites without understanding the meaning of the text should be known as *rājasa*; now hear about the *sāttvika*.
[He is one who recites] clearly, wonderfully, peacefully, and with distinct syllables and words.
O King, thoroughly understanding the entire meaning of the text— endowed with proper phonetics and combined with aesthetic flavor and emotion—
the teacher shall act according to the prescribed rules among the castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, O King.
O King, he who recites this in such a manner should be known by the wise as one of sattvic nature; whereas he who is devoid of faith and devotion, excessively greedy, harsh,
intent on rationalistic argumentation, and possessed of malice— O King, [he is known] as one of such a [tāmasa] nature.
O King, O mighty-armed one, that reciter who accepts regular, occasional, or optional sacrificial fees,
as well as the man who listens to him—
he should be known as tāmasa, O King, and so too is the human listener.
O Hero, one who is truly wise should certainly not recite this before him;
for he who listens incidentally, devoid of faith and devotion,
O King, should be known as a vessel of mere curiosity and one of a rajasic nature.
Having abandoned all other activities,
he who constantly worships the reciter with devotion, endowed with faith and joy,
as well as the gurus and the deities, during obligatory, occasional, and optional rites; |||
O Hero, he who listens in this manner should be known by the wise as one of a sattvic nature.
O King, just as Vyāsa is to be honored by the disciples, so too is the word of Vyāsa;
therefore, O best of kings, there is no other more worthy of honor for the disciples than that.
For he, O King, is indeed their teacher and the perpetual giver of knowledge;
among the four castes here, no other is declared to be their kinsman except for Vyāsa,
O best of kings— such is the Vedic revelation.
Therefore, one should always worship the reciter with every effort;
he is the guru, he is the father, he is the mother, he is the kinsman, and likewise the friend—
for the reciter, O tiger among kings, is [the source] for Brahmins and all others without exception.
In this way, Vyāsa is to be known as the Guru; he is to be worshipped and honored by the twice-born.
O King, those men who listen to him are said to have him as their Guru.
This time for his worship has been declared for his disciples.
O best of kings, those who hear [this] give one gold māṣaka to each reciter individually, month after month,
on the twelfth lunar day, on the new moon day, or during the sun’s transit.
That is the eternal sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for her;

and whatever gift one gives according to one's ability for the sake of one's own welfare during the solstices, the equinoxes, during lunar or solar eclipses, or when the dark fortnight has arrived, it is for her.
O Father, O King, that [gift] should be given by the disciples (śrāvakas) to him alone and not from anyone else;
for the sake of their own welfare, the disciples should always give to him first.
If the disciples bestow it upon another without having given to him, [they incur fault].

O King, an insult has been committed by them against the reciter. Now, O fair-faced one, hear from me what fruit is obtained by all those people, beginning with the Brahmins, who have thus committed that insult.
A Brāhmaṇa falls to the state of a Śūdra, and a Kṣatriya becomes a crow;
likewise, a Vaiśya is born [in such a state], and a Śūdra sinks to the condition of a Caṇḍāla.
Therefore, O best of kings, the reciter (vācaka) must first be honored by the wise.
In times of distress and during one's prosperity, since he is remembered as the Guru,
O hero of noble vows, he should be worshipped first on the full moon of Vaiśākha, at the solstice, on the third lunar day, and likewise on the full moons of Kārttika and Mārgaśīrṣa.
O Lord, on other festival days as well, he is traditionally remembered as worthy of worship according to dharma;
likewise, gold, fine gold, wealth, grain,
as well as cooked food and meat, O descendant of Kuru.
O best of kings, the disciples must first give to him so that the reciter may always abide in happiness, O lord of men; he should be treated in such a way,
O fair-faced one, that he is not afflicted by the pairs of opposites.
O best of men, during the winter one should give woolen garments, an umbrella during the rainy season,
and sandals at the appropriate time;
and likewise, one who is free from the pairs of opposites (dvaṃdva) should be the reciter for those [who offer these gifts], O King.

Those disciples in the world are blessed; they have attained the supreme state. O Hero, how could a wise man desire happiness for himself when his teacher, the king, is in distress? For such a person is considered a true teacher.
Therefore, O lord of men, one should prevent any conflict between the reciter and the śrāvakas;
the śrāvakas must also exert effort for the sake of the reciter.
Thus, O King, Vyāsa should always be honored first for the sake of one's ultimate welfare.
O Lord of the Earth, just as a husband is indeed to be honored by all women,
so too, O King, is the reciter said to be worthy of honor among the disciples;
and just as the Blessed Hari is to his disciples, so is the preceptor.
Just as Bhānu is to the followers of the Sun and Śaṅkara is to the followers of Śiva,
so too, O lord of men, is the reciter to be honored by the lay disciples.
One who desires prosperity should always listen while offering a sacrificial fee.
O lord of men, when he is unable to give that aforementioned *māṣaka* of gold to the reciter,
then, O King, a *māṣaka* of silver should be given for his spiritual welfare.
In the absence of that, gold should be given, avoiding any stinginess regarding wealth;
even clay indeed should be given, for one thereby obtains the auspicious and excellent fruit.
Thus, O King, this sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is obligatory month after month.

O King, there should be those who perform rites on the festival days such as the lunar eclipses; O Lord, one desiring prosperity should give two clean garments, perfumes, garlands, and ornaments once the festival is concluded.
Having understood that all [duties] are fulfilled therein, the disciple should certainly perform worship—
even by selling himself— if he desires his learning to bear fruit.
He should do so without withholding the occasional and regular sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
And for one who always listens [to it], that hearing is fruitless;
just as one does not enjoy the fruit from a sacrifice devoid of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), so too, O Indra among kings, hearing is traditionally held to be fruitless when deprived of dakṣiṇā.
"O Lord, the sacrificial fee for a Kṣatriya should always be fourfold;
this is said by the Blessed Lord Śiva when the festival is concluded, O Lord.
Thus, O King, has this rule for listening to the Purāṇas been described.

For when a rite is devoid of its prescribed rule, the fruit of that action does not arise. O subduer of the Kurus, bathing, giving, recitation, fire-offerings, and the worship of ancestors and gods are known to be effective only when performed according to the rules; this is how it should be understood here.
O tiger among kings, the hearing of the Purāṇas is likewise fruit-bearing, just as this hearing was described by me to you according to the prescribed rule, exactly as it was spoken,
exactly as it exists, and exactly as it was declared by the expounder of Brahman.
That Brahmin, O Great King, is honored in all the worlds.
O mighty-armed one, this has been recounted to you exactly as it was heard:
the majesty of the Sun and the majesty of the reciter.
And thus, the seventh ritual manual removes all sins and fears.
Whatever man constantly worships according to this procedure,
having reached the world of Bhaga, he is celebrated throughout the three worlds.
Then, having reached the world of Arka, one should go to the world of Citraśikhaṇḍin;
from there as well, O mighty-armed one, one should go to the world of Divākara.
Having gone from the world of Arka, one thereafter attains Goloka.
From there one should go to Ṛtasya, and after that to Kañjajasya;
by hearing [the names] of these, one obtains the fruit of ten Rājasūya sacrifices and a hundred Agniṣṭomas, according to the word of Pitāmaha.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Rules for Hearing the Purāṇa and the Majesty of the Reciter," within the Sauradharma section of the Seventh Kalpa in the Brāhma Parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa.
This first half is complete.
May it be offered unto the glorious Nārāyaṇa.
Thus ends the first section, the Brāhma-parvan, in the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa.
Description of Pātāla. Salutations to the glorious Gaṇeśa.

Oṃ, salutations to Śrī Rāmacandra, who is as delightful as a lotus petal. This [work], pure and white as the moon, has foam produced by the agitation of the sea-monsters that are the hands of poets; it is served by the foremost of Brahmins devoted to vows and observances through the well-spoken verses arising from their chests.

May the *Pauṣkara* [Purāṇa], purified by the gaze of Brahmā—the preceptor of the three worlds who is adorned with the syllable *Oṃ*, accessible through the fullness of divine enjoyment, and the remover of the impurities of living beings—purify you!
Victorious is the Sun, the maker of the world and the lamp of the universe; victorious is the enemy of Mura, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, whose body is dark blue.
Victorious is the one named Rudra, who bears the moon upon his crest; victorious is the Sun, the source of all crowns, the possessor of light, the manifold radiance.
Having paid homage to the immeasurable God who has the form of Brahmā,
I shall fully proclaim the Purāṇa as it was spoken by the Brahman-yogin.
[The sages] questioned Romaharṣaṇa regarding this meritorious compendium of the Purāṇas.
"You ought to speak for us, O expert in the meaning of the Purāṇas.
Having heard the words of the sages, Sūta, the best of Paurāṇikas,
bowed mentally to his guru, the son of Satyavatī, and spoke.
Sūta said:
Having paid homage to Hari, the source of the universe who assumes the form of Brahmā,
I shall relate the divine narrative of the Purāṇas, which destroys all sins.
O twice-born ones, listen now to this meritorious, purifying, and life-prolonging account, which, upon hearing, even a doer of evil deeds may attain the supreme goal—
the entire Bhaviṣya Purāṇa that Gadādhara proclaimed.
Now, in this middle section, I shall indeed declare the determination regarding installation and other rites;
herein is the praise of dharma, the praise of the Brāhmaṇas and others,
the exposition of the duties in times of distress, and the enhancement of the majesty of knowledge.
Furthermore, the making of images, the characteristics of their installation and painting,
the determination of time, the accounts of primary creation and secondary dissolution,
the characteristics of the Purāṇas, and the definitive description of the terrestrial globe.
The determination of lunar days, the ritual resolve for the *śrāddha* ceremony, the duties even for one about to die, the greatness of giving,
as well as the past, present, and future, and the instruction on the duties of the ages (*yuga-dharma*).
It contains various high and low observances as well as expiatory rites (prāyaścitta) and so forth,
consisting of nine hundred and eight hundred and sixty verses;
it is joined with the Pañcatantra, and there are twenty [verses] for each tantra.
O best of the twice-born, there are fifty-one chapters in this Purāṇa.
Among the three stages of life, the householder is said to be the source;
others indeed depend upon him for their livelihood, and therefore the householder stage is the most excellent.
The householder’s life is the single stage of life; it is the manifestation of the three [other stages].
Therefore, the householder state alone should be understood as the sole ordinance of Dharma. One should abandon wealth and pleasure if they are devoid of Dharma.
One should not practice even the Dharma if it is contrary to the whole world.
In the vicinity of a reservoir, one should avoid using that reservoir;
at the site of a water-shed, a water-shed should be avoided; and at the site of a monastery, one should abandon that monastery.
For from Dharma wealth is born; from Dharma desire is produced;
and from Dharma alone comes this liberation. Therefore, one should take refuge in Dharma.
Dharma, wealth, and desire are considered the threefold aggregate (trivarga), consisting of three strands.

There are the qualities of goodness (sattva), passion (rajas), and darkness (tamas); therefore, one should take refuge in righteousness (dharma). Those established in goodness go upward; those characterized by passion remain in the middle; and those established in the conduct of the lowest quality, the tamasic, go downward.
In that dharma wherein righteousness is joined with wealth and pleasure,
one becomes happy in this world and, after death, is fit for the infinite.
Therefore, having combined wealth and pleasure, one should take refuge in dharma.
From dharma arises desire, and from dharma wealth is born;
thus, in the midst of dharma, this fourfold set is demonstrated.
And in this way, for the sake of dharma, pleasure, and wealth, a human being [attains] even liberation.
One should also practice the greatness [of dharma], for that leads to infinity.
Therefore, having set aside wealth and pleasure, one should practice dharma;
the exponents of Brahman say that everything arises from dharma.
By dharma, the entire world—both the stationary and the moving—is sustained.
This power of Brahmā, O best of the twice-born, is without beginning or end.
Dharma is attained through action and through knowledge; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, one should practice the yoga of action accompanied by knowledge.
Vedic action is of two kinds: engagement and withdrawal.
Withdrawal is preceded by knowledge, whereas engagement proceeds otherwise.
But one who practices renunciation attains that supreme state;
therefore, renunciation is to be cultivated, for otherwise one wanders again in saṃsāra.
Tranquility, self-control, compassion, charity, non-greed, and indeed renunciation—
Rectitude, freedom from envy, as well as visiting sacred fords; truthfulness, contentment, faith in the scriptures, devotion, restraint of the senses,
worship of the deities, and especially the honoring of Brahmins.
The Sage declared that non-violence, truthfulness, absence of backbiting, good conduct, purity of behavior, and compassion toward all classes constitute dharma.
Dharmas are said to be preceded by faith, established in the midst of faith, and [concluded] with faith.
Faith is proclaimed as the foundation and the very basis of all dharmas; it is faith itself that is so extolled.
The station of Prajāpati is for Brahmins who possess Vedic learning and perform their duties;
the station of Indra is for Kṣatriyas who do not flee from battle.
The immortal realm belongs to the Vaiśyas who follow their own duty;
the Gāndharva realm belongs to those Śūdras who live by service;
and [the realm] of the eighty-eight thousand sages of perpetual celibacy...

The station that is remembered as the station of the Seven Sages is indeed the station for those dwelling with their preceptors; the station heard of as belonging to the Seven Sages is for forest-dwellers.
The Prājāpatya station was declared by the Self-born One to be for householders.

That very station of Hiraṇyagarbha, which belongs to the ascetics whose minds are restrained and to those dwelling in the forest— from that place one does not return again. It is the immortal station of the yogis, known as Vyoman, the supreme source.
"Bliss is the name of the Lord; that is the ultimate limit, the supreme goal.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "Description of Creation," in the first part of the Madhyama Parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said:
Now I shall describe in detail the divisions and the divine form,
according to the sequence of the Kalpas and following the hundreds of Manvantaras.
All was composed of darkness, unknown and without characteristics;
therein there was one Great Rudra, the supreme cause.
Having meditated upon himself by himself through his own self, the Lord, the all-pervading one, [arose].
The mind first creates the ego,
and from the ego it perceives the five great elements.
These eight are declared to be the primary natures (prakṛtis), as well as the sixteen transformations (vikāras).
Sound, touch, form, taste, and likewise smell; prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna;
as well as sattva, rajas, and tamas—these three are declared to be the qualities (guṇas).
From him Brahmā, the devotee of the Lord, was born; from him Viṣṇu was born.
Then Śambhu appeared by his splendor for the purpose of deluding both Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
Indeed, Vāsudeva is bodiless, unborn, and not produced from a womb.
Having deluded all that [was before him], he bewildered the entire world with his splendor. There is nothing higher than him; indeed, there is nothing higher than him.
Both Brahmā and Viṣṇu—these two—were born as the sons of the Blessed One.
In every kalpa, he indeed creates all that— the people and the world—
and likewise withdraws them from every side, including all diverse beings.
Seventy-two yugas are traditionally known as a single manvantara.

Fourteen such kalpas are called a single day of Brahmā; likewise, the night is said to be of the same duration as a kalpa. O twice-born ones, in this manner, there are months and years, and his lifespan is eight hundred such years.
Thus,
the twinkling of this Viṣṇu’s eye is known as the measure for all from Brahmā down to a blade of grass;
indeed, the entire universe of moving and non-moving beings in all worlds has its life-span measured by that very twinkling of Dhruva’s eye.
The Bhūrloka, Bhuvarloka, and Svarloka are proclaimed;
then Janaloka, Tapoloka, Satyaloka, and Brahmālōka as the seventh.
Furthermore, there are Pātāla, Vitala, Atala, and Tala.
Know the fifth to be Sutala and the seventh to be Rasātala.
Among these, seven are renowned as the inhabitants of the subterranean Pātālas.
Rudra is proclaimed to be at their beginning, in their midst, and at their end.
Maheśvara devours and gives birth to the worlds for the sake of sport.
For those desiring to reach the world of Brahmā, the upward path is proclaimed;
[so too are] the earth, the intermediate space, the cardinal directions, and the intermediate points.
Listen now to the enumeration of the oceans and mountains below and across, as well as the extent and measurement of the oceans,
the stationary mountains, and the gods who dwell in heaven.
"For those with four feet and likewise for bipeds who speak only the Dharma, [the merit] is declared to be a thousandfold;
for stationary beings, it is proclaimed to be a thousandfold.
And their virtue is a thousandfold," so said the Blessed One, the Sage.
The Rishi, first performing that which is called Prakṛti by name,
[beheld] from that Prakṛti Brahmā born together with Viṣṇu;
from that, O twice-born ones, he effects the occasional creation through his intellect.
Therefore, Brahmā, the Self-Existent, fashioned the Brāhmaṇas;
he fashioned the Kṣatriyas with one foot less, and the Vaiśyas as inferior even to them;
and the fourth [the Śūdras] he made with yet another foot less, excluded from ritual practices.
He fashioned the earth, the intermediate space, and the directions;
likewise, he established the configuration of the world-system, the islands, the oceans,
the rivers, the seas, the sacred fords, and the shrines.
Thundering clouds, rainbows,
meteors, thunderclaps, comets, celestial lights, and sacred abodes—
these, once arisen within his bodies, shall again afflict him with time.
Thus ends the second chapter in the first part of the Madhyama-parvan within the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa.
Description of Pātāla. Sūta said:

Above Dhruva is Maharloka, extending for ten million yojanas; there, O best of the twice-born, the inhabitants remain until the end of the kalpa. Janaloka is likewise situated above Maharloka, measuring twenty million yojanas.

The sons of Brahmā, Sanandana and the others, are established there. From Janaloka, Tapoloka is situated at a distance of thirty million [yojanas]; indeed, the gods reside there, shining brilliantly and free from the affliction of heat.
From the realm of Prajāpati, however, the Bhūrloka is joined by six crores [of yojanas].
There, the world of Brahmā is known as Sanatkumāra;
in that world resides the Guru, Brahmā, the soul of the universe, whose face is turned in every direction.
He sits there, having drunk that Yoga which transcends death and is attained by yogis. Indeed,
ascetics, believers, exponents of Brahman, yogis, ascetics, perfected ones, and reciters of prayers sing this song of praise to the Supreme Lord.
But there is one gate for yogins going to the supreme state;
having gone there, they do not grieve—that is Viṣṇu and that is Śaṅkara.
His city is difficult to approach and resembles ten million suns.
It is impossible for me to describe that place, which is filled with garlands of flames;
there, within the city of Brahmā, is the abode of Nārāyaṇa.
Upon Śeṣa lies the glorious Hari, the Supreme One, accompanied by Māyā.
He is Viṣṇu, as proclaimed by the world, and is free from rebirth.
Those great-souled ones who have taken refuge in Janārdana go upward,
beyond the seat of Brahmā, to the supreme, auspicious, and effulgent light.
Thrown into the fire, the Blessed Lord Bhava remains there;
Mahādeva, together with the Goddess, is meditated upon by the wise,
surrounded by hundreds of thousands of yogis who are absorbed in the state of oneness.
There, those twice-born ones who are devoted to the discourse on Brahman go, being disciplined;
they are ascetics devoted to Mahādeva,
the Supreme Lord, free from the sense of "mine," devoid of egoism, and abandoned by desire and anger.
Those joined with Brahmā shall behold it; that indeed is remembered as the world of Rudra.
These seven Maharlokas are proclaimed to be upon the earth;
and below the surface of the earth, O twice-born ones, there are the netherworlds (pātālas).
Mahātala has a golden surface and is adorned with every kind of color;
it is filled with various bright palaces and temples of the deities,
and is inhabited by the infinite and wise Mucukunda.

O brahmins, the powerful king, though a dweller of heaven, drank up Pātāla, Śaila, Rasātala— the latter being the realm of Śaṅkara— and that which is called Sutala; Vitala was said to have the luster of coral.
For Vitala is said to be white, and Tala is indeed its opposite;
O best of sages, Rasātala is renowned as being auspicious, endowed with all splendors, [adorned] with gold and likewise by Vāsuki.
It was likewise shattered by Vainateya and others led by Kālanemi, as well as by Śaṅkukarṇa and Namuci at their head,
and by various other nāgas, including the exceedingly beautiful Tala.
Beneath them lie the hells, Raurava and others, numbering in the tens of millions;
sinners are cast into these, for they are not capable of bowing down.
And at the very end, below the Pātālas, is the Vaiṣṇava body known as Śeṣa.
Mādhava, who is Nārasiṃha, the soul of the yoga of Kālāgnirudra;
and that Lord Janārdana who is recited as Ananta in the form of a serpent—
upon him this entire universe rests, supported by all the fires.
Entering him, the Great Yogin Kāla— whose mouth is fire,
who is like the flame of poison, and who is infinite— the Supreme Lord himself, whose nature is Time, being the Tāmasī form of Śambhu, destroys the universe.
"Taking recourse in the womb itself, he constantly brings forth light.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "Description of Pātāla," in the first part of the Madhyama-parvan within the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
[Now follows] the Description of the Celestial Sphere (*Jyotiścakra*).
Sūta said:
This great fourfold cosmic egg has been described.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the definitive account of the Bhūrloka.
The principal islands of that [world] are Jambū, Plakṣa, Śālmala,
Kuśa, Krauñca, Śāka, and Puṣkara as the seventh.
These seven great islands are surrounded by seven oceans.
Each successive continent is said to be larger than the preceding one, and each successive ocean is likewise larger than the preceding one.
These oceans are the Ocean of Milk, the Ocean of Sugarcane Juice, the Salt Ocean, the Ocean of Clarified Butter,
the Ocean of Curdled Milk, the Ocean of Fresh Water, and the Ocean of Alcohol.
It is recorded as being fifty crores in extent, encircled by the ocean,
and endowed with seven islands, measured in yojanas.
Among all the islands, Jambūdvīpa is auspicious, situated in the center.
In its center stands the renowned Mount Meru, with the luster of gold;
its height is eighty-four thousand yojanas,
sixteen thousand of which are submerged below, while thirty-two thousand extend above the surface.
At its base, its extent is sixteen thousand [yojanas] on all sides;
this mountain, beginning with Bhū, stands as the Kali age itself.
To its south are Himavat, Himakūṭa, and Niṣadha.
Nīla, Śveta, and Śṛṅgin are the mountain ranges in the north;
two of them in the middle are one hundred thousand [yojanas] in measure, while the others are ten less than that.
They are two thousand [yojanas] in length and as many in breadth.

O twice-born ones, Bhārata is the southern region (varṣa), and beyond that is known as Kiṃpuruṣa; likewise, Harivarṣa is another region to the south of Meru. To the north is the region of Campaka, and similarly, Aśvahiraṇmaya.
The Uttarakurus are just like these Bhāratas;
each of these regions, O best of the twice-born, measures nine thousand [yojanas].
Ilāvṛta is in their center, and in its center stands the lofty Mount Meru.
There, on the four sides of Meru, lies Ilāvṛta, extending nine thousand yojanas;
O fortunate ones, there are four mountains there which serve as the buttresses for Meru,
rising ten thousand yojanas high.
To the east is the mountain named Mandara, and to the south is Gandhamādana;
Vipula is situated in the western part, and Supārśva stands in the north.
Among these Kadamba trees are the rivers Pippalī and Vaṭī.
O great sages, that tree is named Jambū for this very reason:
its fruits, as large as great elephants,
fall upon the back of the mountain, shattering in every direction.
And because of its flavor, that river is known as the Jambūnadī;
it flows there and is drunk by those who dwell on its banks.
There is no fatigue, nor foul odor, nor old age, nor the decay of the senses.
Men of pure mind indeed arise there;
having reached the level riverbank and been dried by the wind,
it becomes the gold known as Jāmbūnada, the ornament of the Siddhas.

Bhadrāśva is on the eastern side of Meru, and Ketumāla is on the western side; O best of sages, between those two regions lies Ilāvṛta. Above Meru, O lords of Brahmins, is the supreme abode of Brahmā.
Above that is the abode of Vāsava, and above that is that of Śaṅkara;
above that is the world of Viṣṇu, and above that is the world of Brahmā. Beyond that is the supreme station, consisting of light, formless, and golden.
Above that is the station of the devotee, and there indeed resides the divine Lord Ravi;
situated in the wheel of light, he is the pure, immovable Supreme Lord who revolves upon Mount Meru within the wheel of the zodiac, O best of men.

The chariot-wheel [of the body] revolves day and night at the navel, which is the seat of the sixfold *biṃba*, being fixed upon the support of the Pole Star (*dhruva*) by means of the tethering-ropes of the vital winds (*vāta*). Therein reside the guardians of the directions and other planets; from that point begins the southern and northern solstices (*dakṣiṇāyana* and *uttarāyaṇa*).
The path traversed each month involves the decrease of days due to the waxing and waning [of the moon];
the lunar month overtaken by the sun is known as *malimluca* (the intercalary month).
When the Lord Sun reaches his twelfth [station], for the devotee who serves him daily, [the fruit is attained].
Having established the Lord, who consists of stars, throughout the three days and nights—
both at every watch and in every region—
the Sun moves by day and the Moon moves by night.
The constellations [are established] by day, and the solar disc is established by night;
from that place comes the arrival of food for the regions, and thus it became day.
Where there is the waning of the moon, and where the sun proceeds, [there it becomes night].
One should know that day and night are established upon the wheel of light;
for the stars in particular, there is no rising or setting.
That constellation which occupies a particular region is considered their "rising."
In that regard, the eight [planets]— Jīva, Śukra, and all those beginning with Sūrya—
are to be employed at that time for the rites of Bhārgava and others.
Sūrya, Soma, Budha, Candra, and the swift Bhārgava [are to be used].
When the sun, possessing rays, moves while established in its southern course,
then that sun glides beneath all the planets;
having made his orb wide, the moon moves above him.
The entire circle of constellations extends upward from Soma;
above the constellations is Budha, and above Budha is Bhārgava;
above Bhārgava is Candra, and above Candra is Śanaiścara.
Above that planet Śanaiścara (Saturn) is the constellation of the Seven Sages (Saptarṣimaṇḍala),
and above the Seven Sages is established Dhruva.
On the wheel consisting of the wheel of time (Kālacakra), the Sun is always present.
Where the motion of the lunar days is recorded as half a zodiacal sign,
there the days are known to be stationary, moving swiftly, or even decreasing;
and therein the setting of the quarters of Venus and its great setting are observed.
The *pāda* [of the sun's movement] lasts for only a fortnight; the *māha* [or *mahā*] lasts for only a watch (*yāma*);
the *cakra* lasts for half a month; and the *aticāra* lasts for eight days.
It is not counted according to the difference of location, nor is it counted by means of the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*).
O best of the twice-born, when Venus is situated in the sign of a child or an old man, or in the constellation of a group (Gaṇa),
the childhood and old age of a Kṣatriya are never taken into account by the wise; however,
for a Vaiśya, O excellent Brahmins, [the period] above the foot is indeed great.
The remaining half belongs to Bhārgava; however, it is censured for Śūdras.
It is not prescribed for a Śūdra in the performance of malevolent rites (*abhicāra*) or in the making of a wheel.
"One should avoid [these] seven days," so says the *Atharvaṇa* Śruti.

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Determination of Manifestation According to Karma," in the first part of the Jyotiścakra within the Madhyama Parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*. Sūta said:
By birth alone, the Brāhmaṇa is the lord of the three castes.
Formerly, those best of the twice-born, being mixed Brāhmaṇas,
performed austerities for the protection of the oblations to the gods, the oblations to the ancestors, and indeed everything else in this world.

The gods of the triple heaven eat his sacrificial offerings (havya) from his mouth, and the ancestors eat his ancestral offerings (kavya); what being could be greater than he? Furthermore, by birth alone, this Brāhmaṇa is the highest and deserves worship from all.
The Brāhmaṇa eats his own food and performs his duties, O best of the twice-born;
for the sake of the existence or non-existence of the other three castes in this world, the twice-born Brāhmaṇa exists—
of this there is no doubt— and when satisfied, he indeed brings about their well-being.
One should be angry with non-existence; therefore, he should indeed always be honored.
O best of the twice-born, those for whom the forty-eight purificatory rites (saṃskāras), beginning with conception (garbhādhāna) and so forth, have been performed here according to the scriptures—
Endowed with the status of a Brahmin, he goes to the abode of Brahmā. Purified by sacraments is the first; purified by the Vedas is the second;
purified by knowledge is the third; and thereafter, purified by sacred fords.
O twice-born ones, having recognized that which is purified by the sacred field, one should worship that which is thoroughly purified;
it bestows the fruits of heaven and liberation, whereas otherwise one would meet with exhaustion.
It is the most supremely pure among the pure and the supreme teacher among teachers.
In ancient times, a Brahmin endowed with all the qualities of sentient beings was created by Brahmā.
By honoring the twice-born, the gods enjoy imperishable heaven;
and even humans, having gone to their respective kingdoms, attain divinity through him.
Viṣṇu is pleased with him with whom the Brahmins are pleased;
therefore, Viṣṇu is satisfied at that very moment by the worship of Brahmins.
For, O twice-born ones, in ancient times the Brahmin was born from the mouth of Viṣṇu.
The Vedas, which are the causes of creation and dissolution, were born from that very source; indeed,
they were placed within the mouth of the Brahmin by the Supreme Person for the sake of honoring the worlds of Brahmā and certainly for the purpose of attaining all knowledge.
In ancestral rites, marriages, fire-sacrifices, and propitiatory ceremonies,
as well as in all rites for auspiciousness, Brāhmaṇas are always highly praised.
The gods partake of the sacrificial offerings (havya), while the spirits of the deceased and the Asuras partake of the oblations (bali).
The ancestors certainly receive the *havya* and *kavya* offerings from the mouth of the Brahmin alone.
Whatever one gives to the gods and the ancestors during sacrificial rites—
whether a gift, an oblation, or a ritual offering— is fruitless without a Brahmin.
Any religious act performed without a Brahmin yields nothing but the fruit of mere physical exertion;
in such cases, it is the asuras, pretas, bhūtas, and rākṣasas who consume the merit.
Therefore, one should invite a Brahmin and cause him to perform the worship.
At the proper time, place, and to a worthy recipient, [the merit] becomes a hundred thousand-fold or ten million-fold.
Upon seeing a twice-born man, one should offer salutation with faith;
by his word, a person becomes long-lived and lives for a long time.
For those who do not offer salutations to Brahmins out of hatred or even lack of faith,
the lifespan of men shall diminish, the earth shall perish, and they shall fall into miserable states.
[By conversing with them, however,] there is an increase in lifespan, an increase in fame, and an increase in knowledge and wealth.

By honoring the best of the twice-born, one shall attain [this merit]; there is no doubt in this matter. Those houses which lack the mud of the water from the feet of Brahmins, which do not resound with the Vedas and Shastras, and which are devoid of the sounds of Svaha, Svadha, and Svasti, are equal to cremation grounds.
Men who fear hell say there are twenty-six defects [in villages];
therefore, one should dwell in a sacred place (tīrtha), or in a village, a town, or a forest, having abandoned those [defects].
They remain established in heaven, in the world of the ancestors, and in the worlds of Brahmā.
Otherwise, one should not wear clothing; therefore, a thief should not protect it.
[The following are names of types of thieves: Adharma, Viṣama, Paśu, Piśuna, Pāpiṣṭha, Naṣṭa, Kaṣṭa, Ruṣṭa, Duṣṭa, and Muktaka.
Delighted, dull-witted, blind, and likewise one-eyed;
fierce, fragmented, talkative, and likewise a stealer of what has been given;
base, wicked, loquacious, miserly, and likewise fickle.
These defiling defects of yours are considered to be twenty-six;
O best of Brahmins, their total number is also said to be eighty-five.
Listen, O tigers among the twice-born, as I speak of them in order according to this scripture.
In this context, the lowest type is threefold due to ignorance; the uneven type is as prescribed for the twice-born; the *paśu* (animal-like) is fourfold; the wretched (*kṛpaṇa*) is indeed twofold;
the most sinful is also twofold; and the ruined (*naṣṭa*) is recorded as being sevenfold.
O twice-born ones, *kaṣṭa* (distressed) is to be known as fivefold; *ruṣṭa* (angry) is also twofold;
*duṣṭa* (vicious) is to be known as sixfold; *puṣṭa* (nourished) is likewise twofold;
*hṛṣṭa* (delighted) is said to be eightfold; and *kuṇṭha* (dull) is declared to be threefold.
The blind and the one-eyed—these two pairs may each possess qualities or be devoid of them;
the two fierce ones and the fickle one form one group, while the eunuch and the fierce one form another;
the staff-bearer and the wise man are likewise known as a pair, and the wicked and the base constitute the fourth pair.

One is described as talkative (*vācāla*) by the first three [qualities], and stingy (*kadarya*) by the next three; one should know that the "stained" (*malīmasa*) is characterized by being both stingy and fickle (*capala*). There are two types of the "clever" (*catura*), and the thief (*steyin*) is of only one kind.
O best of the twice-born, listen to their individual characteristics,
by the thorough knowledge of which a man may attain divinity:
one who carries shoes and an umbrella while walking before his guru or the gods.

O best of Brahmins, he who occupies a high seat in the presence of his guru, or travels on a journey while mounted upon a vehicle, is likewise considered the lowest of men. Even if he bathes in a sacred ford according to the prescribed rites, yet lives according to the ways of the vulgar, he remains base.

The second is declared to be the lowest and is proclaimed as censurable. Sweet and gentle in speech, yet possessing the *hālāhala* poison in his heart—he who says one thing and does another; these two are considered equally dangerous.

He who, having bypassed the contemplation of liberation, exerts himself in other thoughts, and he who is devoid of service to Hari— he is a beast by birth, even a beast. He who performs his ritual bath elsewhere, even while Prayāga is present [nearby], [is likewise].

He who abandons the visible God to resort to the invisible does so for the sake of exhausting his lifespan; this is the teaching approved by the sages. Therefore, he who abandons the practice of yoga is the third type of person, the lowest of beasts.
Though there are many books here and various treatises, he does not know their essence; he alone is a beast, a jackal.
[He relies on] force, deceitful guile, and stratagems for his binding.
He too shall be known as a slanderer, or perhaps a second [slanderer] due to his intimacy; that evil-minded man who, having set out sweet food for the rites of the gods and ancestors,
instead serves stale or bitter food.
He should be known as a miser who neither attains heaven nor partakes in liberation.
He who performs sacrifice while being a base giver, devoid of joy, and full of anger—
he alone is renowned as a miser, excluded from all dharma.
One who abandons virtue without fault, one who sells away auspicious deeds,
one who forsakes father, mother, and teacher, and one who is devoid of purity and right conduct—
who eats in the presence of his parents— is remembered as the most sinful of all.

One who serves a son abandoned by his living father, or one who does not serve him at all; the second is even more sinful, while the third is a neglecter of the fire-sacrifice (homa). Furthermore, he conceals the son's virtuous conduct and displays only his faults.
He should be known as lost, for his sexual union was purchased by purchase;
he who lives by the livelihood of a temple-priest, or who lives by the sale of his wife,
or who lives by the bride-price or by his wife's wealth at any time.
These six alone are lost according to the scripture and do not partake of heaven or liberation:
he whose mind is always angry; he who becomes enraged upon seeing someone inferior;
he who is frowning with a knitted brow; he who is wrathful; and he who is furious—thus the angry man is said to be of five kinds.
He who constantly wanders about in improper conduct, who is not established in dharma and artha,
who is prone to sleep, addicted to vices, a drunkard, devoted to women,
and always conversing with the wicked— he is considered wicked in seven ways.
Alone he eats sweets, a deceiver who reviles the virtuous;
he is proclaimed to be as well-nourished as a fattened pig.
That twice-born man who does not teach the Nigamas, Agamas, and Tantras—
The evil-minded man who does not listen is called wicked;
for the Śruti and Smṛti have been fashioned as the two eyes of the Brahmins—
one who is deficient in one is called one-eyed (kāṇa), and one who lacks both is proclaimed blind.
One who quarrels with his siblings, speaks what is displeasing to his parents,
or is a slanderer, a backbiter to the king, or a servant of a Śūdra— such a person is to be known as the lowest of the twice-born; he is fierce and censured by the scriptures.
A Brahmin who approaches a Śūdra woman is a Caṇḍāla, the lowest of the twice-born;
he who eats cooked food even once in the house of a Śūdra,
or dwells in the house of a Śūdra for five nights, is called a Caṇḍāla.

One afflicted with the eight types of leprosy, one who suffers from the three types of leprosy, and one censured by the scriptures— one who constantly converses with these becomes their equal, the lowest of men.
He whose wandering is like that of a worm is a false scholar engaged in wicked pursuits.
Out of ignorance, one who speaks of Dharma while rushing after worldly pursuits,
or who abandons Avimukta and dwells in another land for a long time— he is considered by the Siddhas to be a contemptible beast, like a pig, in two ways.
Indeed, he who, with his face contorted by a frown and joined by a grimace,
punishes like a king is declared to be *daṇḍa* (punishment). Having seized the property of a Brahmin, O King, as well as one's own [property], [one incurs this].
He who eats that wealth himself, or who gives it away to another god or even to Brahmins,
is a donkey— the worst of animals— condemned in all the Vedas.
One who is intent on the mechanical repetition of syllables recites indeed but does not understand;
abandoned by the science of words, he is a beast, without a doubt—
since he says one thing while doing another in the presence of his guru and the gods.
He should be known as base, for he is likewise devoid of proper conduct. A wicked person seeks out the faults of a virtuous man adorned with the six excellences,
just as a locust seeks out thorns in a forest filled with flowers and fruit.

He who, deprived by fate, utters improper speech and is devoid of shame is known as "vācāla" (a loquacious chatterer). He who engages in conversation with outcasts and is devoted to the rearing of birds [is likewise so characterized].
He who eats even what has been offered by cats, he who performs the rites prescribed by crows,
he who cuts grass, he who crushes clods of earth, he who eats meat in vain,
and he who is fickle— such a person should be known as one who delights in the wives of others.
He who is devoid of oil-massage and ointment, who lacks perfumes and sandalwood paste,
and who does not perform his daily rites, is perpetually defiled.
He acquires a house through unjust means and acquires wealth for his home through unjust means.
One who takes a domestic mantra other than that prescribed by the scriptures is a thief and a slayer of Brahmins.
One who steals the books of the gods, jewels, gems, pearls, horses,
cattle, land, or gold is declared to be a thief.
A god may practice this meditation afterwards, and so too a human being; of this there is no doubt.
One should practice mutual meditation; he who does not meditate is a thief.
Through the grace of the Guru, and also through the grace of one's parents, one attains victory.
He acts according to what is appropriate and is honored in heaven; however,
that evil-minded person who does not support [those dependent on him] is remembered as another kind of thief—
one who, having encountered a benefactor, fails to perform a service in return.
He lies in the Tapana hell and falls headlong into blood;
for among all those of the same caste, the Brāhmaṇa is the master according to dharma.
The king, the protector of the earth, is declared to have dharma as his eye.
As stated in the *Horātantra*, [the science] emerged from the mouth of Prajāpati;
those other Brahmins who are experts in calculation declare it thus:
"A land devoid of the Gaṅgā is ruined, just as a ritual act devoid of a Brahmin is ruined."
That country which is bereft of astrological counsel is overwhelmed by calamities;
just as a night without a lamp or a sky without the sun,
so too a king without an astrologer wanders like a blind man upon a path.
One should establish the Brahmin according to the Dharma and cultivate him for the increase of ritual merit.

A twice-born man endowed with a beard is worthy of worship; indeed, a Brahmin with a beard is like the sun. By looking upon him facing westward for three days, one gains merit that destroys all impurities.
Upon seeing the sun, one is purified after beholding a Vrātya Brahmin.
One should not treat a Sūrya-Brahmin as a Vrātya for the sake of accomplishing a sacrifice.
Indeed, O twice-born ones, the Sūrya-Brahmin alone possesses the authority over the Jyotirveda.
There are four divisions of castes: the Bhojaka, the Kathaka, the Śivavipra, and the Sūryavipra is enumerated as the fourth.
Among them, the Kathaka is middling, while the Sūryavipra is the best.
A Śiva-brahmin who is devoted to the worship of the Śivaliṅga is censured;
one should banish him, along with his sons, cattle, and kinsmen, using an unbroken grain (akṣata) [as a ritual symbol], as well as a Sūrya-brahmin, an ordinary brahmin, a physician, and a king.
The king, who is inviolable in all the worlds, should protect his kingdom with wealth,
garments, perfumes, and various kinds of garlands.
Those who know the wheel of the country (deśacakra) are worthy of honor, while those who know the wheel of the horā (horācakra) are supreme.
Those who know the solar cycle (sūryacakra) are worthy of worship; one should never treat them with contempt.

He who desires the increase of accomplishments, the abundance of wealth, and a long life [should honor them]. It is declared that an astrologer is as worthy of worship as a member of a religious assembly or a Brahmin.
When a child is born and must be examined, one should determine the ascendant and the planets.
O best of men, he who is a Sūryavipra,
having mastered the two Mātrikās, shall obtain the fruit of all the Vedas.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Preceptor," in the first part of the Madhyama-parvan within the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said:
"O best of the twice-born, it is declared in the traditional scripture (naigamī smṛti) that for all four castes, there is no other kinsman than the father. Furthermore,
although three [other] elders are excellent, the mother is the supreme elder among them."
Those brothers who are elder and most excellent, being increasingly venerable,
should be honored on the twelfth lunar day, on the new moon day, or during the sun’s transit;
garments, sacrificial fees, gems, and pearls should be given according to one's inclination.
During the solstices, the equinoxes, and likewise during lunar and solar eclipses,
as well as when the dark fortnight has arrived, one should feed [the guests] according to one's ability.
Afterwards, O best of men, one should salute their feet with this mantra:
By merely offering obeisance according to the prescribed rite, one obtains the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrthas).
I bow to the Father, the singular, primordial essence of Brahman, who bestows both heaven and liberation;
since he perceives the world as a beautiful form, we satisfy him with water mixed with sesame seeds.
The ancestors procreate here, and the ancestors protect;
for the ancestors are indeed the very form of Brahman—salutations again and again to them.
Since the world prevails, therefore dharma proceeds.
Salutations to you, O Father, the manifest form of Brahman; salutations be to you!
I bow to the divine Mother, the supreme embodiment of primordial nature (Prakṛti), who, having placed [the child] within the cavity of her womb, herself protects it from all sides.

Just as I was carried in your womb by the Goddess with great hardship, so too, O Mother, have I beheld the world through your grace; salutations be ever unto you! Whatever holy places exist upon the earth, such as the oceans and all others in every direction—

I bow to that Mother who dwells there for the sake of prosperity. Glory to Him whose form is Śiva, the bridge across the ocean of saṃsāra, by whose grace the fame-bringing knowledge has been obtained.
O first-born one, salutations to you, in whom the truth of the Vedas, the Vedāṅgas, and the Śāstras is established; you are the support of all beings,
for the Brāhmaṇa is the supreme purifier and the sacred ford of the worlds.
"O Earth-god, take away my sin; O you who possess the form of Viṣṇu, salutations be unto you!
One should first bow down to the Grandfather (Brahmā), then to one's mother and preceptor, followed by the maternal grandfather, the teacher, and the officiating priest."
First, one should bow with a spirit of devotion using the mantras dedicated to the mothers.
O best of the twice-born, just as one's elder brother, so too is an eldest paternal uncle;
whether seen or unseen, he is a guru, as is one's mother, who is likewise a guru.
The visible, the invisible, and the third, which is the Sun, Fire, and the Moon;
the teacher who imparts the mantra is renowned as the seventh;
and the teacher of the Kabbhājana is the most excellent, being the cause of both heaven and liberation.

O twice-born ones, that evil-souled man who, having abandoned one whose divinity is visible, devotes himself to one whose divinity is invisible, goes to the state of an animal; he is the foremost among the wicked. Just as there is a father, an elder brother, and a younger brother, so it is with these two classes of Brahmins.
The eldest brother is equal to a father and is to be honored through the duty of hospitality.
The teacher is the embodiment of Brahman; the father is the embodiment of Prajāpati;
the mother is the embodiment of the Earth; and brothers are the embodiment of one's own self.
One’s father shall be like Mount Meru, a supreme sage, the eternal embodiment of Dharma;
he too shall have beheld the gods and must strictly observe his commands.
Furthermore, one should gratify the Grandfather (Brahmā) before the father with offerings to the gods (havya) and the ancestors (kavya).
He goes to the abode of Brahmā, from which he does not return again.
By bathing with the water that has washed his feet, the Gaṅgā alone is not equal to him;
likewise, what need is there for hundreds of jyotirliṅgas by the mere sight of him?
Whatever fruit is obtained by touching the thirty-two sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), ten million times that same fruit is obtained by circumambulating the Grandfather (Brahmā). Furthermore,
one who nourishes his grandmother is superior even to a hundred mothers.
"O Brahmins, by beholding those virtues, one shall not enter into saṃsāra again.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Teacher's Qualities," in the first part of the Madhyama Parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*. [This concludes] the description of the teacher.
Sūta said:
O best of Brahmins, I shall here relate this ancient history;
O virtuous soul, listen to that which was heard by me in the past, even as it is being heard.
Being thus questioned, the illustrious Lord Viriñca, of great splendor, replied:
"Indeed, I shall tell you the procedure for hearing the Purāṇas.
O best of the twice-born, having heard the Itihāsas and Purāṇas with devotion..."
He who, having become pure, listens [to this] every evening, morning, and at night, is liberated from all sins, even from a hundred murders of Brahmins;
likewise, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Śaṅkara are pleased with him.
For men who listen and recite it, Lord Brahmā is pleased at dawn, Hari at the end of the day,
and Mahādeva likewise at night.
[The reciter] should wear white garments and sit upon a seat of cloth, deerskin, and kuśa grass.
One should perform three circumambulations of that deity and the guru; thereafter,
one takes a seat that is neither too high nor too low,
having paid homage to the guardians of the directions as well as those presided over by the syllable *Oṃ*.
The book is the eternal locus of Dharma for the treatises on righteousness;
Śiva is the deity of the Āgamas, and Śāradā is that of the Tantras and so forth;
Gaṇapati is the lord of the Jāmalas, and Śatakratu (Indra) is that of the Ḍāmaras.
Nārāyaṇa is the deity of the Mahābhārata and likewise of the Rāmāyaṇa;
Vāsudeva shall be the deity of the seven [Purāṇas], O best of beings—listen:
Āditya, Vāsudeva, Mādhava, Rāma, and Keśava.
The eternal Śiva, the great god wearing a forest garland, is to be known as the author of the seven [works] beginning with the Viṣṇudharma during their respective seven sections; furthermore,
Viriñci is proclaimed as the author of the Ādipurāṇa.

One should offer pure rice, barley-milk, milk-rice, and likewise *kṛśara*; or one may offer *kṛśara*-food; these are known as the sequence of the group of offerings (*baligaṇa*). One should also offer *śāli* rice along with wheat, mixed with sesame seeds and unbroken grains (*akṣata*).
Cow-products and fruits should indeed be offered, and this sacrificial oblation (bali) should be given to them;
one should place each separately in vessels of bell-metal in the cardinal directions and in the center.
One should also recite according to the prescribed rule; that sacrifice is the supreme sixfold (ṣaṇmaya).

Cold water, honey, milk, the juice of white sugarcane, and molasses—this is known as the "with-essence" (sagarbha) offering; another oblation consists of these six items. One *prastha* of *śāli* rice, or half of that, or half of that again [is prescribed].
This is known as *yavakṣīra*, prepared by mixing it with milk.
One should take eight parts of milk and seven parts of water;
then one should cook a sacrificial oblation (*caru*) of winter white rice.
Then, one should obtain the perfected [preparation] measured at eighty palas;
subsequently, one should add half a portion of either honey or sugar.
If one gives it mixed with jaggery (guḍa), a certain chemical transformation (saṃparka) occurs.
A wise man should also give sugarcane juice mixed with honey.
O best of the twice-born, listen:
a pure beggar who receives it, or one who listens while studying, should place the book in his hand.
Having risen, one should take [the vessel] and, having bowed, present it. Standing to the east, the renowned Brahmin disciple should remain to its right,
facing the western direction with his index finger joined with the thumb.
The wise should always perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) either with a grass mat or with the hand;
it should never be done otherwise. Having performed the placement, one should attain [the fruit]; O Brahmins, one should place [the mantras] repeatedly and mutter the Pāvamānī verses over water.
This is the rule for the Vedānta scriptures and the Vedānta teachings as remembered by the wise:
the listener should face the south and the speaker should face the north;
this indeed is the procedure declared for the Purāṇas and the narrations of the Mahābhārata.
O best of the twice-born, it should be understood through the reverse method in the Rāmāyaṇa, the Dharmaśāstra, and the Harivaṃśa, O virtuous ones;
for otherwise, the Yātudhānas plunder the fruit.
Therefore, one should listen to or recite this according to the prescribed injunctions.
But he who, having heard this sacred knowledge, should nevertheless eat meat—
even if it were from an animal that died in the act of mating— goes to the womb of a donkey.
If one should cause this to be recited or listen to it in a temple or at a sacred ford (tīrtha)—
specifically the description of whichever deity’s shrine or whichever sacred ford it concerns—
one shall obtain the fruit of gifting a cow merely by hearing its greatness.
One should not recount the greatness of the Great Guru in the presence of one's parents.
It is the greatness of the father that should be spoken of by sons in an assembly on festive occasions;
likewise, after Vāsudeva, the description of the greatness of Rudra [is to be told].
The chanting of Vāsudeva’s names in front of Rudra increases merit; likewise, the recitation of the glories of Viṣṇu in front of Durgā or Śiva-Sūrya—
if a person of deluded soul performs these [reversals], he shall enter the womb of a donkey.
With the permission of one's guru, one should perform salutation to one's parents;
likewise, with the permission of one's parents, one should perform circumambulation of Hari.
Neither Viṣṇu, nor Brahmā, nor Rudra, nor the Lord of Śacī [is equal to them].
Equal to all the Vedas, devoted to all dharmas,
consisting of all knowledge, and equal to the Omniscient One—
therefore, O twice-born one, through service to one's parents, the eternal Brahman is attained.
Salutation to the gurus is in vain for one who does not offer libations to his father;
if he does not satisfy the primary [deity] while living, nor even at the Ganges upon death,
there is no satisfaction for either, and though living, he does not truly live.
The hearing of the Purāṇas is meritorious, provided the Bhāgavata is not absent;
O Brahmins, the Bhāgavata is useless if it is devoid of the Nārasiṃha [section].
Likewise, one should not uphold that which is called the Mahābhārata if it is lacking the Ādi-parvan.
O Brahmins, one should not uphold the Mokṣadharma without the Aśvamedhika section, without the Ānanam, and devoid of the rites of giving; likewise,
one who recites the Bhārata at dawn and other times shall attain excellence.

Without having heard the Vāyu Purāṇa and without the Yoga scripture, the family of his body is devoid of vital breath; it is useless and does not sustain him. Likewise, that Vāyu Purāṇa which is devoid of other things worthy of being heard [is likewise useless].
Just as one would not preserve the Āraṇyakakāṇḍa without the Sundarakāṇḍa,
nor should one write down and preserve the Ādikāṇḍa without Laṅkā; likewise,
one would not preserve Vyāsa without Pārāśara, nor the sacrifice without Yājñavalkya.
Without Dakṣa there is no Śaṅkha, and without Śaṅkha there is no Bṛhaspati;
nor can one provide the proper application without Vahnīya and Śravaṇādi,
nor is there anything [attained] by Rākṣasas without the formal installation (saṃsthāpana).
One should not give [the book] to supplicants and the like, nor should one sell it under any circumstances;
nor should one take away a book, nor should one steal even six syllables.
From the theft of a syllable of Brahman, one does not return from the Raurava hell.
By stealing the first letter [of a mantra], one becomes afflicted with copper-colored leprosy in this world;
by stealing the "mouth-circle" (mukhavṛtta), for as long as the moon and stars endure,
he falls here into the Kuvale and Asipatra hells— of this there is no doubt.
Whatever [sin] there is in stealing one's own letter or even in stealing one's own mother,
one who steals a mere book would incur that same hell. This applies to the *Bhārata*, the *Purāṇas*, and those works in the form of hymns.
One may have those Vedas, Āgamas, and so forth recited even from books;

however, one should not cause that place where a book of the Vedas has been written to be read. Likewise, one should not cause that place where mantras proclaimed in the Tantras have been written to be read.
Having clearly composed a compendium of the explanations of the Vedic mantras and placed it before [the teacher], as long as that work continues to circulate,
he shall remain in a terrible hell and in the state of a preta birth after birth.
The expounder should not cause [the text] to be recited, nor should the reciter cause it to be recited;

for in the *Pauṣkara*, there is a verse stating that at every step one incurs the sin of a horse-sacrifice. Since he causes the meaning of the Veda to be recited, one who speaks contrary to it is a false reciter (*apavācaka*).
Both of those should be known as fallen; one should recite the *pāvamānī* verses a hundred times.
One should place the *praṇava* at the beginning, middle, and end of the mantra. With offerings of food, perfumes, and flowers, one should honor the book created by the gods.
One should know that the book contains the three gods; the thread is said to be Vāsuki.
There is a fault in making it measureless, therefore one should not omit it.
The leaves are the Lord Brahmā, and those which are long from top to bottom.

Janārdana is the letters, while the syllabic measure (mātrā) is the imperishable Prakṛti. Maheśa is the script and its stylistic variation (bhaṅgī); Sarasvatī is its measure (mātrā). The single line is the single Self, and from the foot comes the movement of the feet.

O best of the twice-born, in the *Bhārata*, the *Itihāsas*, and the *Purāṇas*, it is said that a pair [of verses] within a four-line stanza, or a pair at the end of the middle [line], brings about misfortune; whereas in an uneven sequence, it is the means for attaining heaven.
O best of men, in an odd-numbered row there is heaven, while in an even-numbered row one enters hell;
this applies when the name of the speaker is joined with the name of the person addressed according to the distinction of the rows,
along with the appropriate measure (mātrā) in the Kali age.
One should uphold the collection of Dharma through the purification of one's own self;
otherwise, a fault would arise, therefore one should avoid that.
[The protectors are] Ripu, Sūrya, Tayārāma, Yakṣa, Ananta, and Sarasvatī.
Brāhmī and Yakṣiṇī are the [first] two, and Gāyatrī is remembered as the ninth.
Liberation occurs at the end of Viṣṇu, while the falling away from one's station occurs at the end of Sūrya.
For him, it becomes a source of enemies; if it falls upon a Yakṣa, one should predict misfortune.
Through Anantā, one gains vast fame; through Sarasvatī, the arrival of wealth;
through Brāhmī, one attains the state of Brahmā; through Yakṣiṇī, a mansion of Yakṣas;
and through Gāyatrī, one attains liberation—such is the arising of the fruit of these five lines.
The book composed of the Dharma should be divided into four parts:
the Brahma, Indra, Vaiṣṇava, and Śaiva sections, O Maheśvarī; and the Śāktika section.
The form of Brahmā consists of the Itihāsas, while that of Indra consists of the Rāmāyaṇa.
The supreme Vaiṣṇava deity is located on its forehead, which belongs to Śiva;
likewise, Agni is at its base, and Indra is in the middle portion.
All the planets, the lords of the directions, and the twice-born (Brahmins) are situated at its tip.
Meru is designated as Sumeru, and he is called Saṅgava and Kāma.
Heaven and earth, along with the netherworld (Pātāla), are declared to be within him.
He is the book containing the narratives of the Purāṇas, worshipped by the gods.

A man who provides a livelihood for a Brahmin, even if he be a Śūdra, is not merely praiseworthy but worthy of honor; he should be established in the home. That man goes to the abode of Brahmā, whose floors are paved with jeweled paths and the like.
A person who is not praiseworthy nor worthy of worship should not be placed within the house.
One should make a perfectly circular perforation at the tip of the petals;
by merely hearing of it there, a circular lotus [is formed] therein.
If one performs a piercing that is confused regarding the *saṃhitās*, *āgamas*, and *tantras*, it causes distress to the mind; through that, one shall go to the city of Śakra.
A piercing in the center takes away his lifespan, while a piercing on the side destroys his auspiciousness.
In the case of a double-piercing, one shall grant victory; in the case of a single-piercing, Bali shall prevail.
This is the supreme secret place of Prakṛti, fashioned by the gods;
one should fill it with a liṅga made of copper or of bell-metal.
If one is unable [to obtain other materials], one may use wood from the *bilva* or *śrīparṇika* trees;
however, one should never employ fresh wood, nor should one ever employ iron.
Prior to the commencement, one should indeed write out a hundred verses from the *Dharmaśāstra*.
In the ancient Saṃhitā, that [work] consists of half a Yugma-kalpa;
one should not write it down through the vow of celibacy (brahmacarya) out of delusion regarding Brahman.
Nevertheless, from the transcription of the entire Vyāsa, there occurs a decline in progeny.
O best of men, one should not write the *Anāmātva*, the *Hemayutā*, the *Balāka*, or the *Citta*;
nor should one write the *Khilabhāga* of the *Harivaṃśa*. Furthermore, one should not write the *Madhyatantra* of the *Garuḍa* and the *Skanda* Purāṇas.
One established in vows and endowed with restraints may transcribe the *Harivaṃśa*,
but a householder should not write this book, except for the *Mathurā* section. In the transcription of the *Pārijāta* section, one should depict a consumer of fish and meat.

And likewise, when writing the Vālmīki-saṃhitā, O Brahmins, one should write only the hymns; one who has not taken vows should never write it. That which is written by a non-Brahmin is proclaimed to be fruitless.
