A woman never writes anything, even if she is fallen or a heretic; nor should one who is of evil intent, has a wicked wife, or is of corrupt mind write the Dharmaśāstras, the Purāṇas, or the collections of hymns.
And while attaining that,
the practitioner of mantras (mantrī) should make gold and silver dark with soot,
using resin consecrated with mantras and combined with the juices of living beings that are greedy for jewels and mud.
One should know that through the *vaṃguṇya* [configuration], or even with ten thousand primary [planets], or likewise through yellow yogas,
wind is produced in the black [color] and there is a decrease of wind in the yellow.
In the red [color] one obtains nourishment, and in the black there is the arrival of prosperity.
Listen as I describe what one should write from the mouth of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas:
one should inscribe the wooden board (kāṣṭhaveda) facing the northwest and so forth;
facing the east brings loss of wealth, while facing the north brings prosperity.
Death occurs if [the lines] face south, and loss of wealth if they face west.
One should not draw [the diagram] during a Pitṛmedha rite, an earthquake, one's own birthday,
a period of impurity due to death, a birth, the new moon, or the sun’s transit (saṃkrānti).

In this regard, writing [a letter] on such a day leads to poverty, as well as the destruction of one's sons, and the decline of strength and merit; therefore, one should avoid it with great effort. Writing on the day of the ancestral śrāddha causes the ruin of the family.
If there is an earthquake for one night, there will be loss of wealth in that region;
even during a period of impurity, one becomes poor, and on the anniversary of one's birth, there is a decline in lifespan.
One who knows scripts, prosody, and grammar, being young, wise, and having mastered his posture [in yoga], [attains success].
The scribe who writes with speed and brilliance,
whose characters are uniform and progressively higher without being crowded together,
and who is endowed with both correct script and proper composition— he alone is a scribe of the Āgamas.

Whether written by Nāndīnāgaraka scribes, or by pure Nāgarakas, or even by those from Kāmarūpa— indeed, for as long as the collection of the Saṃhitās exists and for as long as it continues to circulate, even when written by one who is insentient.

As many syllables as there are in the composition, for so long shall he be honored in heaven. But that evil-minded man who, having written it, causes it to be read without being asked, must pay the fee for the Dharmaśāstra according to the number of syllables.

He is cooked in hell for that duration of time; there is no doubt about this. Even if one should accept a salary for the sake of maintaining a family, that evil-minded person does not truly live, even though he is possessed of wealth, clothing, and fruits.
A householder should not wear that which has been written by outcasts, those of the lowest castes, barbarians, or those afflicted with leprosy, consumption,
elephantiasis, or even by one who is mute,
unless he is firmly established in dharma.
Since it causes a loss of lifespan, one should therefore avoid it;
likewise, an image with missing limbs or a manuscript lacking the proper measurements—
one should not keep these on one's person in the Kali age, for they cause a loss of lifespan.

The best manuscript should be made thirty-two finger-breadths in length; it is indeed known as Nārāyaṇa, for by its mere retention one is fully protected from all dangers. That which is twenty-four finger-breadths long is called Svadhana.
He should be known as Śaṅkara, the bestower of the fruits of dharma and desire.
That which measures eight finger-breadths is here called the smallest;
it should be understood as consisting of Brahman and yielding the fruits of the three aims of life.
It should be struck upon a lotus leaf or else upon the bark of aguru;
for these [materials], there is a prescribed measurement for the leaf, but no such measurement exists for birch-bark (bhūrja).
That which is made of birch-bark, teḍa, and so forth, should be twelve finger-breadths in length.
By that same measure of finger-breadths, the book of knowledge placed in his hand becomes a source of longevity;
for every thousand [verses] of the Dharmaśāstra, this is the fee for the Dharmaśāstra.
In the land of Bhārata, one gains half the merit of traveling the path to heaven;
in the Harivaṃśa, it is worth a thousand gold pieces when weighed. In each successive age, one should practice the Dharma as desired, though it is diminished by one quarter in each.
Having bowed his head to all those who have heard the Saṃhitās, beginning with Vyāsa,
and then to Jaimini, Vyāsa, Śaṅkara, and likewise Hari—
he offers salutation to them at the beginning, the middle, and the end.
Then a Brahmin, learned in the meaning of the Dharmaśāstras, should cause [the text] to be recited;
with an unobserved mind, he should pronounce its form clearly,
with syllables and words unjoined and provided with distinct divisions.

Endowed with the seven musical notes and adorned with the seven sounds, one should recite the Sāman verses according to their melodic modes (*rāga*), following the internal intervals. Whatever wealth may belong to Maṇivāra, Gaura, Andha, and Saṃtika— [that shall be his].
Śrīrāga, Hillola-rāga, and likewise Vājāvika—
by proceeding in this manner, one should listen to the compendiums of Dharma,
especially as a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or even a Śūdra.
He obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice, he shall attain all his desires,
he is liberated from all sins, and he acquires great religious merit. Indeed,
a Vaiśya is superior to Śūdras, and a Kṣatriya is superior to Vaiśyas.
Likewise, Brahmins should always listen in the presence of Kṣatriyas;
however, a Śūdra should not speak of the Dharmas, nor of austerity or instruction.
He shall obtain neither worldly benefit nor the hereafter, neither auspiciousness nor the supreme goal.
There is no distinction in the characteristics of speech acquired by a Śūdra;
for he was made a slave of the twice-born by Brahmā, whose origin is unmanifest.
Just as the milk of a dog, a jackal, or a she-ass is indeed unfit to be drunk, so too is that [speech].
Thus, the Dharma should not be accepted from the mouth of a Śūdra, even if it is refined by grammar;
for while impurity is cleansed by water, a Śūdra listener is indeed purified.
Likewise, a Śūdra would remain impure even if he were a knower of the meaning of grammar.
Any Śūdra who should expound the Dharma, as well as the Vedic scriptures, must indeed be executed by the king; he should have his tongue cut off with a discus.
For he always understands the meaning and the entire significance of the texts.
He who speaks thus is truly a Brahmin and is called Vyāsa;
he shall dwell in a city or village and is proclaimed as one belonging to a holy land.
They are blessed, they are perfected in soul, and they have achieved their life's purpose—of this there is no doubt.
O twice-born ones, that city where the expounder resided was inhabited by many;
yet, just as a day without the sun or a night without the moon,
the assembly did not shine when it was bereft of Vyāsa.
In whose house children did not shine at all, nor did the home ever gleam;
just as on one side all the planets are gathered and on the other side the sun alone,
even so was the sight of Puṣkara seen in his brother’s house.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the first part of the Madhyama-parvan in the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa;
titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Aṅka. Sūta said:
Listen, O assemblies of Brahmins, to this Purāṇa esteemed by the gods,
hearing which a person is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
The third is declared to be the Śaiva, and after that, the supreme Bhāgavata.
The fifth is likewise the Matsya, and the sixth is said to be the Bhaviṣya;
when there is incapacity [to perform other rites], the Vaiṣṇava and the Bhaviṣyaka mentioned in the Matsya are prescribed,
as well as the Śānti and Bhaiṣmīyaka parvas in the Mahābhārata.
One should study the domestic ritual manual of Parāśara, those [texts] spoken by Gobhila,
and the other [manual] spoken by Kātyāyana, beginning from the Nigama. One should never teach the scripture to a mortal who has arrived in the interval [between lessons].
When a mortal has died, [the impurity lasts] for one night; for a goat or a ram, three nights;
for a frog, five nights; for a snake, four nights;
for a horse, one year; and for an elephant, twelve years.

For one month [the impurity lasts] when [a dog dies] in a donkey or a crow; because of the abandonment of its place, it is said to be for no longer than that. For a crane or for the sun (the sky), they declare it to be a day and night. Even for three nights [is it declared] in the case of a cat, a mongoose, a mouse, or a donkey.
When the sun is in the zodiac sign of Haṃsa (Leo), there is no suspension of study; nor is there any fault regarding small insects.
One should teach the son of the guru who is wise, righteous, pure, devoted, peaceful, a Vaiṣṇava, and one who has conquered anger and subdued the senses.
One should teach these internally: the deceitful, the one who has committed a sin, the enemy,
the one who gives a hundred [coins] through unjust means, the hypocrite, the enemy,
the useless one, the sluggish one, the one who desires to hear [the truth], and the non-sacrificer.
One should avoid from afar one who is impotent, crooked, angry, miserable, seeking out calamities,
a reviler, and one ignorant of the rules. One should speak without concealment, except regarding one's sons, grandsons, and so forth.
"One must die with one's knowledge; one should not give it to an ordinary person.
Therefore, Knowledge speaks thus to the best of the twice-born who imparts her:
"Do not give me to one devoid of devotion, to a wicked man, or to one of evil soul."
O best of beings, give [this] to one who is heedful, wise, pure, a celibate student,
purposeful, knowledgeable in the ritual rules, and virtuous; for if one were to give this unsurpassed wealth of knowledge to one who is prohibited [from receiving it], [it would be a grave error].
Of those two, one shall before long go to the abode of Yama; he who,
by unjust means, causes another to study the science for his own pleasure is said to be one who has discarded the science,
and he goes to a terrible hell.
Having first bowed to the authority— whether it be internal, Vedic, or even supramundane— one who is firm in his vows should then study;
without that [authority], one should not practice the ritual section of the Jyotiṣa.
Through the habitual practice of the *cūta* portion, one is born poor;
through the habitual practice of the *vāda* portion, it leads to the destruction of wealth;
and through the habitual practice of the *nidhi* portion, one is born into a family destined for hell.
One should not study those scriptures that have not been mentioned, nor those that are to be honored yet are spoken by barbarians, such as the *Mahimnas*; one should avoid them from afar.
He who compiles a compendium of Dharma for the sake of increasing the knowledge of the world [should do so according to these principles].
Having set [the wheel] in motion, he becomes a guru, a father who bestows knowledge;
as the giver of knowledge to the worlds, the Dharma proceeds among them—
of the Nigamas, the Jyotiṣas, the Vedas, and the Nāṭaka.
Having composed a compendium of commentaries, she shall meet her destruction in the Kali age;
likewise, for the Vedas, the Dharmaśāstras, the Purāṇas,
as well as for Mīmāṃsā, Jyotiṣa, and the Nāṭakas, she is the destroyer, O Virañcinī.
At the conclusion of each section, there is indeed a Purāṇa chapter;
furthermore, there are the Puṣpaka, the Pariccheda, the Khaṇḍa, and the Pratikhaṇḍaka.
There are also legal procedures, the treatise on statecraft (Arthaśāstra), and likewise the treatise on horses (Aśvaśāstra).
Indeed, that very [meter] which is to be employed at the conclusion of a section must also be employed by the poet in its summary;
for if the summary does not proceed according to the instruction given here, it fails.

For those who have counted the syllables [of the mantra], there is no falling from the world of Brahmā, nor shall they be subject to worldly attachment. One should avoid [the use of] Tantric mantras within Vedic mantras.
By performing a fire sacrifice and giving a cow out of delusion, purification will occur.

Having composed a work in the form of a narrative concerning the Dharmaśāstra and the judicial procedure (vyavahāra) that is to be understood, he who compiles this during the Kali age while Keśava is asleep shall go to heaven.
As long as the world continues to exist, one is honored in heaven for that long.
One should not undertake any collection [of alms] during the months of Siṃha, Pauṣa, or Caitra;
likewise, O twice-born ones, one should not do so in the morning or at midday.
At the end of a lunar fortnight, during an earthquake, a conflagration, an earth tremor, or at the end of a day;
especially during an intercalary month and at the two twilights—one should avoid [writing].
Likewise, one should avoid a leaf smeared with impurities or adorned with written characters.
O Brahmins, by means of the four or five-syllable mantra, one becomes pure at that very moment;
likewise, through the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the Nārasiṃha mantra, one becomes pure instantly,
even when the body of great sin has been cast off through the manifestation of Māyā.
Within half a muhūrta, they attain purity and reach the supreme goal. Whether they be women, the censured, or even Mlecchas, they go to the supreme goal.
Even a fool who perceives fault in this should practice its purification.
He shall enter the womb of a female donkey; of this there is no doubt.
Brahman is one alone in essence, yet that duality consists of Prakṛti.
Bhairava is ninefold, and Janārdana is the tenth.
Rudra is indeed the eleventh, and Arkārka is the twelfth;
Bhūtātman is in the twenty-third, and Manu is declared in the twenty-sixth.
The fifteenth consists of the lunar days (tithis), while the sixteenth is called the supreme digit (kalā).
The seventeenth mantra is of the nature of Vāta;
the eighteenth mantra is indeed of the nature of the Purāṇas.
The nineteenth is Candra, and the twentieth is the form of Nārāyaṇa.
The twenty-first [chapter] consists of light; in the twenty-second is the worship of Keśava;
the constellations (nakṣatras) are in the twenty-third; the musical scales (tānaka) are in the twenty-fourth;
the sacred fords (tīrthas) are in the twenty-fifth; and Tryambaka is in the twenty-sixth.
In the twenty-eighth [digit] is Dhaneśa, and in the twenty-ninth is Sarasvatī;
Śiva is said to be in the thirtieth yoga, and Pātāla in the thirty-first;
Ahorātra is in the thirty-second, and Jāhnavī in the thirty-fourth.
Within a hundred [years], at its end, he becomes the Sun;
in a thousand, he is to be known as Śiva; in ten thousand, he is called Meru;
in a hundred thousand (lakṣa), he is Brahmā; and in ten million (koṭi), he is the supreme Lord Nārāyaṇa.
And another [form] consists of the male principle (puṃprakṛti) and the alphabet of Śāradā;
it is eternally composed of pure Brahman, consisting of the nature of knowledge, supreme and great,
in which there is no distress whatsoever, whether in a pure place or even in an impure location.
"In an instant, one attains the nature of Brahman," so said the Blessed Manu.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Greatness of the Number One," in the first part of the Madhyama-parvan within the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa;
followed by the description of the determination regarding works of public utility (pūrta).
Sūta said:
I shall describe the *antarvedī* (inner altar) as spoken by Brahmā in another age,
and likewise the *bahirvedī* (outer altar), which is recommended for the Dvāpara and Kali ages.
That ritual action which is to be accomplished through knowledge is said to take place within the altar (antarvedi).
The installation of deities and their worship are declared to take place outside the altar (bahirvedi).
Furthermore, the construction of water-stations and wells, as well as the gratification of Brahmins, [are likewise included].

Service to the gurus is considered to be of two kinds: that performed outside the sacrificial altar (bahirvedī) and that performed within the sacrificial altar (antarvedī). An action performed without desire, as well as actions such as those arising from addiction, is said to be "within the altar"; the opposite is "outside the altar."
The king is the cause of Dharma; therefore, the king himself shall be this Dharma.
Consequently, by relying upon the king, one becomes "outside the sacrificial altar" (bahirvedi).
Among these, the "outside the sacrificial altar" consists of eighty-seven [types], and the third of these is the dog-eater (sārameya).
The installation of deities, the construction of a temple, and the third, the digging of a tank—these are the [first] three; the fourth is not [required].
The fifth is the worship of the ancestors, preceded by the worship of the guru.

The consecration, the installation, and the non-alteration of the deities; likewise, the fashioning of images and the planting of trees—this [practice] is declared to be threefold: namely, the superior and the middling.
The youngest [method] is the remaining ritual; this is the rule for all undertakings.
Everywhere, the procedure for consecration and other rites is considered to be threefold:
by means of worship, fire-offerings, and gifts, according to three proportions.
By means of the ritual procedure to be accomplished in three days, the twenty-eight deities are worshipped;
the rite for installation and so forth is considered to be performed in three ways everywhere. There, sixteen reciters (jāpaka) should perform worship every day.
This entire procedure is supreme, for it bestows the fruit of the horse sacrifice (Aśvamedha).
Therein are four officiating priests and twenty-three deities:
Brahmā, the Guardians of the Quarters, Varuṇa, the Earth, and likewise Śiva.
Worship performed in a single day alone is declared the middling procedure.
Where one worships Gaṇeśa, the planets, the guardians of the directions, Varuṇa, and likewise Śiva,
that is remembered as the lowest procedure.
A single tree, minor deities in the form of images of uniform appearance, lotus ponds, oblong ponds, wells, large tanks, water-stalls,
and the like— among these, during the rites of consecration, there is the embellishment of the images.
Then, having performed the fire-ritual (agnikārya), one should not engage in elaborate procedures.

One should worship Gaṇeśa, the planets, and the guardians of the directions with the ritual offerings (upacāra). Thereafter, one should pour Ganges water into the step-well, the lotus pond, and so forth.
One should never perform the consecration of dilapidated structures, even if they consist of two mortars; this applies to temples, embankments, step-wells, and likewise tanks and other such works.
Temples, embankments, and similarly tanks and so forth—[these should not be restored if ruined].
Those worthy of consecration are distinguished by three types of measures; for the aged, however, they are measured by their [physical] height.
Sages desire such measurement, for no other measure is seen.
Therefore, I shall explain the measurement and what kind of fruit it yields.
That which is declared by Vāraṇa is measured at sixty cubits;
they know a temple measuring sixty-one cubits to be the best.
The middle one should be known as half of that, and the smallest is recorded as being beyond that [half].
Alternatively, one desiring prosperity should construct it according to divine measurement.
Whoever builds a new tank, or brings an old one back to a state of newness,
having uplifted his entire lineage, is glorified in the heavenly world.
Ponds, wells, tanks, gardens, and flowing streams must be renovated again and again; thus one obtains the fruit of pearls,
according to the measure and proportion of their qualities.
Whether by two hundred or even by one hundred [cubits], this is the determination for the palace:
it should be one thousand cubits in width and eight more in length. One should know that to be the tank; this is declared as the first measurement.
The medium [size] is four hundred minus ten *prasthas*;
the smallest is three hundred minus twenty *prasthas*. In the Kali age, it should be known as half of that, and half of that again.
The measurement of a pond (taḍāga) should be understood as that which bestows the fruits of the three aims of life (trivarga).
Now, in the case of a lotus-pond (puṣkariṇī), two hundred [cubits] is the supreme measurement;
for a pond, the embankment (nemi) is double that, and the pit (garta) is said to be half the measurement.
That field is the station of Varuṇa; that which is outside it is known as Tryudita.
The fourth is indeed Gāndharva, and they know the fifth to be Paiśāca.
The station of the Yakṣas is in the [next] portion; thus indeed are all the sequences.
A *maṇi* is said to be a *nalinī* measuring eighty cubits;
those who know the measurements understand that in the case of a *prastāva*, it is five less than that.
A *nalinī* is sixty cubits, and in the case of a *prastāva*, it is four less.
The oblong pond (dīrghikā) is proclaimed to be sixty-four cubits in length;
in the case of the square (prastāva), it is reduced by a quarter, while for the pit (garta), there is no fixed measurement.
If [the pit] is in the southeast, disease occurs; in the south, the destruction of kinsmen; and in the southwest (rākṣasa), a terrible death is encountered.
Terrible fear is encountered in the Vāyavya [direction]; therefore, these [places] should be avoided with effort.
One should perform [the rite] in the assembly of deities such as the Brahmins, or at Meru, or wherever else [is suitable].
One should avoid the bank of a river, a cremation ground, a pond, hermitages, and the like of people.
When a fool of evil mind does not perform consecration for temples, ponds, and the like,
he encounters terrible fear and indeed incurs the fate of being killed by a snake at his own feet.
But when [consecration] has been performed for long lakes, tanks, ponds, temples, wells, and so forth—
Furthermore, when they perform other sacrifices, these do not yield any fruit for him at all. It is said that the fruit one obtains from establishing water-troughs, temples, wells, groves,
and so forth in locations that are already established, is but a very small fraction of the fruit obtained from those [previously mentioned] acts.
Therefore, a self-restrained person should perform the consecration of water and other elements according to the prescribed ritual as desired,
at the proper time, by means of wealth acquired through merit and with a virtuous intention achieved through one's own resources.
O twice-born ones, this meritorious rite for a temple made of clay has thus been described by me.
Therefore, it is declared that [the merit] for one made of grass or wood is fourfold;
for one made of grass it is a hundredfold, and half of that for one made of fresh bark. For one made of wood when prepared with care, it is said to be ten times that.
Ten times that merit is said for one constructed with auspicious bricks;
a hundred times that for one made of stone; a thousand times that for one of copper or silver; and a hundred thousand times that, O best of the twice-born, for one made of gold.
Likewise, one who has a temple of Hari constructed out of jewels and other precious materials obtains infinite fruit;
such a person swiftly leads ten thousand generations of his lineage— both those past and those yet to come—
to the world of Viṣṇu.
Having caused a temple of Hari to be built as small, medium, or large,
one attains the world of Viṣṇu and liberation in succession;
this applies from a temple measuring sixteen cubits down to one that is devoid of cubits (i.e., very small).
The middle [size] for a measure made of grass or bamboo should be twelve cubits;
the smallest should be eleven cubits, the best twenty-five, and the most excellent thirty-two. A square [shape] yields great fruit.
The city gate should be made square and symmetrical;
it should not be made octagonal, nor should there be a triple-gated city in the Kali Yuga.
O best of the twice-born, as many atoms as there are in the abode of the gods, [so many...]
For that many thousands of years he is honored in the heavenly world. It is said that the protector of the drinking hall receives ten times the merit of the builder;
and he who rescues those who have fallen [into the hell] enjoys the full fruit of all [merits].
Having rescued one that has fallen, one that is falling, or likewise one that is half-crushed,
one obtains double the merit by bringing it to the temple of Hara.
Furthermore, he who is the restorer of what has fallen is the protector of what was falling.
A human being who constructs a temple for Viṣṇu,
or for a Jyotirliṅga anywhere,
or even for Sūrya, Viriñci, Durgā, or Śrīdhara, shall surely partake of heaven.
Having himself uplifted his own lineage, he shall dwell in heaven for ten million eons;
when fallen from heaven, he shall become a king, or a wealthy man, or one most worthy of honor.
By constructing a temple for the gods at the Liṅgas of the Goddesses or at a Yoni, a man [attains these rewards].
One shall attain remembrance [of the deity] in this world and be honored forever in heaven.
Water present during the rainy season yields the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice;
water present during the autumn season is superior even to the waters of a sacrificial rite.

He who has water remaining in his reservoir during the heat of the summer season shall go to heaven; he shall never fall into hell. O best of the twice-born, even a single day’s supply of water remaining on the earth [yields such merit].
It shall deliver his family—seven generations before him and seven after him;
likewise, O twice-born ones, seven in the paternal line and seven in the maternal line.
This is to be known as the "fourteen-fold" [rite]; now hear from me of the "hundred-fold" inscription.

One should know that the lineage of the father extends twenty generations upward, and likewise the lineage of the mother; similarly, one should know the lineage of the wife to extend five generations,
as well as five generations on the side of the mother and five on the side of the maternal grandfather's family.
One should know five each for the mother and the maternal grandfather;
five in the father’s lineage and likewise in his mother’s lineage;
two in the teacher’s lineage, and ten in the royal family.
In the maternal grandfather’s family of the king, five families are proclaimed;
indeed, one hundred and one families are enumerated.
O best of Brahmins, it is traditionally held that the liberation [of these] includes oneself as well.
One should perform the worship of the deity at the holy ford of Svavimukta in Daśārṇa;
listen, O twice-born one, he shall uplift a hundred generations— twenty each for his own lineage,
for his parents, and for his father’s maternal grandfather.
The pair consisting of the mother and the maternal grandfather has been declared;

likewise, the pair for the lineage of the preceptor, as well as for the Yādava and Sāttvata lineages. For the opposing faction, there shall be one [pair]; thus, the family [lineage] proceeds in sequence up to the twenty-first.
This entire triple world, with all its moving and non-moving beings, is water;
there is never any subsistence in the world without water.
As much as a portion of a flower falls into the water while it remains in the vessel, [so much is the world].

For that duration of time he shall dwell in heaven, and at the end, he shall attain the state of Brahmā. Therefore, one should avoid building a house upon water or upon a temple; for that water which is indeed touched by the rays of the sun is to be condemned.
That which is devoid of the moon's rays does not lead to immortality;
therefore, the merit in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is ten times greater than that, and in a lake it is ten times greater still.
One should perform the installation of the deities there, which yields the auspicious fruit of Avimukta.
One should not move a Śiva-liṅga, whether it be well-established or poorly situated;
by moving it, one goes to the Raurava hell, neither attaining heaven nor being a partaker of its merit.
[This prohibition does not apply] in the case of a ruined city or village, when abandoning a site, or during a calamity.
Furthermore,
O best of men, one should establish an image of Viṣṇu or another deity according to worldly custom without over-analyzing;
once established, one should not move it, nor should one move a tree planted by a Brāhmaṇa.
One should never plant the Keśava, Harivṛkṣa, Madhūka, or Kiṃśuka trees out of season; by moving them, one becomes a slayer of a Brahmin.
O twice-born ones, one should construct a lotus pond in front of a temple.

In an assembly of Brahmins, at the king’s gate, or at a crossroads—for the sake of the gods and for the sake of Brahmins—one should direct the face in every direction. However, if one desires prosperity, the face should be directed toward the west; if one desires all objects of desire, it should be directed toward the north.

One should not perform one's own self-interest in the southern direction; however, in the corner, there would be hell. One should fashion the entrance in the middle; some say one may perform the northern crossing.
But one should do so in the southeast, measuring twelve cubits.
In the case of a pond (taḍāga), one should gradually reduce the depth by one cubit (hasta) for each elephant;
however, in the case of a lotus-pond (nalinī) and similar bodies of water, one should not make it less than three cubits.
For a pit (garta) or a grassy area, a depth of one-sixteenth of a cubit (kalāhasta) is prescribed here for a pond.

In an inferior [performance], one should make it even more inferior; one should reduce it by the measure of a cubit. Likewise, the sacrificial post (yūpa) should be made of khadira wood, or of śrīparṇika, or produced from dhātrī wood.
Its measurement should likewise be sixteen cubits, joined with gems, along with the gaṇḍī, the pair, and the kāma.
When the central part is broken at the base, it should be twenty finger-breadths thick; that which is in the middle should be double that thickness.

It should be made with the middle portion reduced by finger-breadths, for such a sacrificial post (*yūpa*) for a pond will always bestow auspicious results. Likewise, it should be sixteen cubits in length at its midpoint.
In the case of a well, the sacrificial post (yūpa) is one cubit in measure; thereafter, it is proclaimed to be four cubits.
In the case of a garden-enclosure as well as a pavilion, the sacrificial post should be made four cubits in measure.
This measurement is declared for a full [circumference]; however, those who know the tradition state that if it is less, the measurement should be proportionately less.
In a pond, two cubits should be provided; in a lotus-pool, one and a half cubits for the planting.
For the planting of a sacrificial post (yūpa) in a well, the measurement is indeed one span or one cubit.
O best of men, one should never place the sacrificial post submerged in water in any case whatsoever.
One should also establish [the image] upon water in a pond or a grove;
it should be given according to this measurement of one cubit, half a cubit, or half of that again.
In a tank, a pit, or a lotus-pool, one should make it level with the water.
As long as the number of grains of dust clinging to the city gates does not reach old age,
so long indeed shall the Lord of the Gods, dwelling in the world of the Suras, never fail to construct palaces.
What more need be said of the power of the lotus pond, which brings from the world of Brahmā the very creator of the western quarter?
As long as the gaze is raised to the height of one's own arm and does not ever turn back, it is called "the gaze.

The best [meditation] consists of a single *mātrā* of the *ārāma* measure; the middling is half of that, and the smallest measure is half of that again—or rather, the sages say that even half of that is excellent and not otherwise.
"One should make [the vessel] devoid of *arjuna*, *badara*, and *śailuka* fruits, and lacking *śāṇala* and *pātila* fruits.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Determination of Pūrtadharma," in the first part of the Madhyama-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Description of the Determination of Pūrtadharma.
Sūta said:
O twice-born ones, having first purified the ground and measured it out,
one should do so with a staff ten cubits long or again five cubits long.

One should always have the land for the sake of a pond ploughed by bulls; likewise, the land for a temple should be ploughed by white bulls. One should not even touch with draft animals that land intended for the sacrifice to the planets.
O Brahmins, for the sake of a grove, one should cause black bulls to plow and have the ground excavated;
one should then sow five kinds of grain for three days.
When establishing a grove on land belonging to a deity, the merit is sevenfold.
Mudga, māṣa, dhānya, sesame, and śyāmāka as the fifth;
masūra and kalāya are recorded as the group of seven grains (saptavrīhigaṇa).
Sarṣapa, kalāya, mudga, and māṣa as the fourth.
The three types of rice, mung beans, black gram, śyāmāka grain, and buffalo constitute the group [of offerings]. Gold and earth should be accepted according to the sequence of the castes.
On the day of the banner (adhvaja), one should fashion this [image] from bilva trees, along with sacrificial posts and stakes.
A staff of one *aratni* is to be known as the most excellent;
having fashioned a figure made of woolen thread, one should prepare four [such figures].
They should be twelve finger-breadths in length and provided with pits for milky wood.
One should kindle [the fire] with sesame oil or with saffron. Success is attained when [the flame] points toward the eastern direction; movement toward the western quarter is auspicious.
If it points toward the south at the time of death, there will be loss; if it remains in the north, there is well-being.

One should know that [the rite] is destructive in the *kalpa* and likewise when the direction is unfavorable; having kindled the fire with the *Nārasiṃha-mantra*, one should cause it to be offered. One should perform the acquisition of the ground for one month in the month of *Ghaṭa*.
O best of the twice-born, one should subsequently mark out the lines and drive in the stakes according to the great measurement;
then one should offer the *vāstu-bali* and worship the spade.
One should dig in the central region with the mantra beginning "From Brahmā... (ā brahman).
One should smear one limb with clarified butter mixed with honey;
having bathed with water containing gold and likewise with water containing jewels, one should smear it.
The wise know that, in the case of a well, this should be done while facing the northeast.
If one should construct a tank without performing the Vāstuyāga sacrifice,
King Vaivasvata cuts away half of his merit.
This applies equally to a palace, a grove, and likewise to a large well.
O best of Brahmins, at the commencement of building a house, one should then offer the Vāstu-bali;
in the Kali age, a sacrificial post (yūpa) made of Śāla, Khadira, Palāśa, Keśara,
Bilva, or Bakula wood is recommended.
A dog-shaped mark made by the belly [of the earth] indicates two banners on that side;
a snake-like shape occurs at a pond, and a jar-like shape at a well. In a grove, it has the luster of a lotus flower, while in a sacred circle (maṇḍala), it takes the form of an umbrella.
One should fashion the form of a dog at a bridge, the form of a mace in the temple of Viṣṇu,
the form of a horse in an Aśvamedha sacrifice, and the form of a man in a Naramedha sacrifice; likewise,
the form of a bull in a Goyāga and the form of a banner in a Gṛhayāga.

For the purpose of grazing cattle in the cremation ground, the excellent sites for a shrine-tree (caityavṛkṣa) are those shaped like a wheel for a *lakṣahoma* and shaped like a plow for a *koṭihoma*. Likewise, the Mūla asterism is recommended for the planting of trees.
Having thus acquired a site praised for its crops, pure and sloping toward the east, one should worship the deity Vanapāla Śikhidhvaja and Soma,
the king of the Nāgas; thereafter, one should thoroughly purify the seed.
One should bring it forth, hold it, and subsequently heat it with fierce fire. After an interval of two days, one should consecrate it thoroughly with mantras.
Then, while reciting the Viṣṇu-mantra three times, one should perform the rite of impregnation (garbhādhāna).
Having recited the mantra "evam asya" three times, one should perform the purification (vimārjana). Then,
having sprinkled [the water] ten times with the mantra "dehi me," it is thus consecrated five times by one who has not yet grasped the [final] mantra.
Then, with the mantra "tryambakam," one should plant the seed;
O best of men, having bathed on the fifth day after her menses,
he should place his wife upon his lap, kiss her, and then recite the mantra over her.
In this way, even during the consecration of the tree, he follows it;
by that, he attains the status of a son—no doubt should be entertained here.
Having taken a seed of Tulasī on a day [conducive] for a Vaiṣṇava tree, the twice-born man...
One should cause it to be eaten, or sprinkle it with drops of cow's urine and water;
by this one attains heaven. One should place it in a white jar, leave it for one night, and then set it upon the ground.

In the digging of wells, ponds, and the like that are not properly constructed, some results may occasionally be produced; however, those lowest of men who plant mango trees and such [in such places] do not obtain fruit here, but rather descend to a lower state.
By planting a *tulasī* tree on a riverbank, in a cremation ground, or to the south of one’s own house,
the planter goes to the abode of Yama;
for even the contact with the dust and pollen of its leaves, flowers, and fruits [is sufficient].
They nourish their father daily with every service;
moreover, he who plants a tree that provides shade, flowers, and fruit,
along a path or even at a temple, delivers his ancestors from sin.
And fame, as well as the auspicious fruit [of merit], returns to him in the world of men;
therefore, O twice-born ones, the planter of trees shall rescue his ancestors of the past and future from hell once he has gone to heaven. For this reason, one should plant a tree.
For in this world, trees indeed act as sons for one who has no son;
therefore, O best of Brahmins, plant an aśvattha tree with great effort.
Among hundreds and thousands of sons, even one such [tree] is distinguished as superior.
O Brahmins, one should plant [the seed] according to one's desire, numbering one, two, or three;
it is the cause of liberation for thousands, hundreds of thousands, and tens of millions. The *aśvattha* tree brings wealth, and the *aśoka* tree destroys grief.

The Plakṣa tree is known as the giver of a wife, and the Bilva is remembered as the bestower of longevity. The Jambu tree grants wealth, while the Plakṣa tree is the giver of Brahman-knowledge. From the Tiṃduka tree there shall be an increase in one's lineage, and the Dāḍima tree is the bestower of a beloved wife.
The Bakula and Vañjula trees destroy sin and bestow strength and intelligence;
the Dhātakī tree grants heaven; the Vaṭa tree is the bestower of liberation; the Sahakāra (mango) grants desires; and the Guvāka (betel nut) indicates the attainment of perfection.

*Sarvaśasya* is for strength; likewise *madhuka* and *arjuna* are for strength. *Kadamba* brings extensive fame; *tiṃtiḍī* is a defiler of dharma. Through *jīvantī* there shall be the pacification of disease; *keśara* is the crusher of enemies.
The *vaṭa* tree bestows wealth, as does the white *vaṭa*. Under the *panasa* tree one becomes dull-witted; the *kalivṛkṣa* tree takes away fortune.
The *śākhoṭa* and the *udarāvartaka* are likewise *kalivṛkṣas*.
Likewise, from planting *markaṭī* and *nīpa*, there is the destruction of one's lineage;
however, by planting *śiṃśapā*, *arjuna*, *jayantī*, *hayamāraka*,
*śrīvṛkṣa*, and *kiṃśuka*, one should point toward heaven.
One should never plant a thorny tree as the first sacrificial fuel;

by planting *kuśa* grass or lotuses among water-born plants, one goes to a miserable state of existence. By planting a *mandāra* tree, there will be the destruction of the family; by a *śālmali* tree, one becomes as foolish as a parrot.
If a *niṃba* tree appears, there will be the destruction of livestock; if a *chatrāka*, one who brings disgrace to the family.
When such a tree arises, there shall be the downfall of the lineage and the ruin of the very cattle.
In the case of a *kākanāda*, there is an increase of enemies; in a *balapūga*, one's prosperity is destroyed.
O best of the twice-born, [the meat of] a lion is not forbidden except during a sacrifice;
for during a sacrifice it would be forbidden, and one would incur the form of hell.
Two *dhātaki* trees are superior to a thousand *sahakāra* trees.
Indeed, a single *pāṭalā* flower is superior to those very thousands;
after a hundred *pāṭalās*, there may be one red *vaṭa*;
and for two thousand *vaṭas*, five *nāgakeśaras* [are required].
Therefore, the Śrīvṛkṣa is the most excellent, and the Jambū tree is praised;
from that Himavat mountain, the Śrīparṇī tree is to be known as the best.
There should be three of the Tiṇduka and five of the Jambū tree.
Having spoken thus regarding the triad of the kadamba, arjuna, and coconut trees,
that righteous soul should cause such a force to be prepared;
for thousands of millions of kalpas and hundreds of millions of kalpas [he shall enjoy its fruit].
By planting trees according to the prescribed rites, one enjoys the pleasures of heaven;
having destroyed sins accumulated over three births and more, one shall attain heaven.
One who plants a hundred trees attains the state of Brahmā, and one who plants a thousand attains the state of Viṣṇu.
By planting *tulasī* in the month of Caitra, one becomes afflicted with mental anguish and physical disease;
in Vaiśākha, one attains fame; but in Jyeṣṭha, one meets death.
In Āṣāḍha, one attains fame, and in Śrāvaṇa, the supreme goal.
In the month of Bhādrapada there is indeed the arrival of wealth, while in Āśvina and Kārtika there is loss.
In this world, Tulasī is of three kinds; in the Kṛta age, the white variety is praised. Furthermore, whoever should make even a slight cut in an Aśvattha or a Vaṭa tree [incurs sin].
O best of Brahmins, he who cuts down a Śrīvṛkṣa tree becomes a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa.
By cutting it at the root, O best of Brahmins, the downfall of his entire lineage follows.
The one who cuts the tree shall become mute and shall suffer hundreds of mental agonies and physical diseases.
In the evening and in the morning, at the end of the hot season and during the cold season on alternate days,
one should offer fruits, raw kulattha, masha, mudga, sesame, and barley;
and one should be a giver of dance, song, water, hair, fruit, and flowers.
One should cause the powder of *avikāka-sakṛt* (the dung of the *avikāka* bird), whatever powders of barley there may be,
beef, and water to remain for seven nights;
that single [mixture] bestows the growth of fruits, flowers, and so forth upon all trees.
One should place the bile of the Rohita fish and coriander (dhānyāka) therein;
when sprinkling with water and other liquids is performed with that, one may indeed predict growth.
Taking the seeds of the Titiḍī tree, one should grind them with a stalk of sugarcane.
By that, there shall be watering for the *aśoka* tree, which brings about the growth of the *sahakāra* (mango);
one should also sprinkle coconut water mixed with honey.
This is the "longing" (*dohada*) treatment for all trees, especially for betel-nut palms and others.
One lives through the consecration (abhiṣeka) joined with the seed-syllable of the Ten-Headed One (Rāvaṇa).
If the birth of cows and other animals, goats, buffaloes, and so forth, occurs prematurely,
one should, without hesitation, place water upon the tips of trees during the months of the rains.
There is no doubt that the fruit of another mango tree will appear here.
One should collect the juice of the *vitāla* plant and barley-gruel;
then, one should fill [the vessel] with *māsa* beans and mustard seeds and subsequently crush them.
O Lord, one should grind and rub the *guvāka* tree with these three;
even one who is dead will quickly be restored to life, and even one who is dying shall live.
[One should also use] *nimba* leaves, *yogapatra*, *śatāvarī*, and *punarnavā*.
One should provide smoke for three days using leaves of *kṣīrikā* and copper;
by means of the root of the *sahakāra* tree, the obstruction of insects does not arise.
Thereafter, I shall describe primarily the *dohada* (longing) of trees, otherwise [known as] their specific requirements.
The growth of mango trees is desired when they are sprinkled with fish-water;
ripe mangoes and blood are likewise recommended for pomegranates;
and barley-water mixed with beef is recommended for ketaki flowers.

In milk, there is an increase in strength; likewise with *tiṇḍuka*, *karamardaka*, meat, putrid substances, broth, marrow, *śoka*, *tāla*, and *guvāka*. [The meat] of the *rohit* fish from a coconut, along with putrid meat and ghee, [is also beneficial].
By sprinkling with water infused with licorice (madhuyaṣṭī), the common [pests] shall be eliminated.
One should sprinkle kapittha and bilva trees with molasses-water;
likewise for jasmine (jātī), mallikā, kunda, and rantiaka.
Having established scented water, white rice, incense of sloughed snake-skins,
tortoise meat, savory food,
and the flowers of *viḍaṅga* upon a roadside tree, it thereafter becomes fruitful.

One should place the slough of a wind-snake and that of a *tagara-aja-gava* among the grain as incense; thus, an increase in grain occurs. Furthermore, one should take a peacock feather along with seven hairs from a goat.
At the onset of night, one should offer incense prepared with a mixture of castor oil;
combined with asafoetida and flowers, it should be applied to ward off mice. One should collect elephant dung and the dung of a *mṛga* (deer) under the asterism Kṛttikā.
Sprinkling with water from the night [well] would remove the root of that *kṣatriya* [sin].
An area of ten cubits at the foot of an *aśvattha* tree is sacred to Puruṣottama;
indeed, in the midst of the shade and water of the *aśvattha*, it is especially like the Gaṅgā at the triple-junction (*tripatha*).
One who knows the Dharma should plant a mango tree at a distance of twenty cubits;
likewise, the dhātrī, bakula, and vañjula trees should be planted at a distance of one cubit, as should the śrīparṇika and punnāga.
The śrīvṛkṣa should be planted at twice the distance from a tree.
The supreme measurement is declared for [shrines] made of stone measuring four cubits;
this applies to ponds and the like, wells, and those consisting of a single tree and so forth, when constructed of stone, brick, or similar materials.
One should worship Śrī Viṣṇu on the tree, Varuṇa at the well,
Gaṇeśa at the water-pot, and especially the guardians of the directions;
one should perform the fire-rite without [the usual restrictions] and follow the path of the virtuous.
Having heard of this rite according to the prescribed rules, or likewise the origin of others,
one should establish the Lord of Forests (Vanaspati) in another tree, in a grove of Tulasī, or in a water-pot; then one should worship Him and perform fire-oblations.
Having consecrated trees with this [mantra], one should envelop them with garments;
this should be known as pure, whether it originates from others or indeed from the Tulasī,
the Sahakāra, and the Brahmavṛkṣa.
"Then one should pierce [the image] into the state of gold, whether it be of the Aśvattha or the Vaṭa tree.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the first part of the Madhyama-parvan in the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*. Description of the Installation according to the Tantras.
Sūta said:
Now I shall describe the ritual procedure for the Tantra, which is also sung of in the Purāṇas; one should perform the consecration according to the Tantra on a most auspicious day.
One should abandon [the ritual] at a bridge when there are one hundred trees and small shrubs, or ten or twelve trees within the range of vision;
however, one should never abandon the well-ritual for the sake of the tree-ritual under any circumstances.
During the Tulasi-vanayāga, one should not perform any other sacrifice;
likewise, during a Taḍāgayāga, one should never perform a Setuyāga or others in an ārāma.
During a Devayāga, however, one should neither construct a Setu nor dedicate a Taḍāga.
In this Tantra, there is no separate Śrāddha; it would become separate only if the performer were different.
In the installation of a Śiva-liṅga, there is no installation of another deity.
One should avoid that [other deity] in one's own place, for it is ordained by its own independent rule.
Even when the rite is performed incorrectly, it is recorded in the Smṛti that there is merely a depletion of one's lifespan.
O best of the twice-born, whether in the case of a pond, a lotus-pool, or even a grove,
there is no fault provided it is ten cubits in measurement, whether lacking in sanctity or full of it.
O twice-born ones, one should perform the installation ceremony there where there are more than two thousand [trees],
or in a grove of ten or twelve trees as previously described;
likewise for the *bilva* tree, though otherwise there is the piercing of the ear.
One should perform the granting of the pregnancy-longing (dohada), including the act of churning and so forth;
immediately thereafter, parched grain (lāja) and unbroken rice (akṣata) and other items should be offered upon the head.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the first part of the Madhyama-parvan within the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa.
Description of the Characteristics of an Image.
Sūta said:
O twice-born ones, I shall describe the characteristics of an image according to the tenets of the scriptures.
One should never worship an image that is devoid of the [proper] characteristics, even if it has been acquired.
An image made of stone, wood, copper, or clay grants all desires;
it may be one cubit, two cubits, or even one and a half cubits in height.
Furthermore, a wise person should not worship [the deity] in a house with a temple measuring eight fingers in height, nor with all its characteristic features. Rather,
[it should be placed] at a distance of eight fingers from the door of the temple.

The pedestal (piṇḍikā) should be made with three parts, and the image should consist of two parts. The increase in measurement should indeed be one finger-breadth (aṅgula) for each eighty-four [units].
The face should be made twelve aṅgulas in width according to the measurement.
The chin, the forehead, and the nose should each occupy one-third of the face;
the two ears should be equal to the neck or fixed at that same measurement. The two eyes should be two digits wide, and the pupil should be one-third of that.
The wise man, having observed an auspicious aspect in the third part of the asterism,
should fashion the forehead, head, and neck;
the circumference of the head, moreover, should be thirty-two finger-breadths.
The neck is equal to the nose, and the interior of the chest is equal to the face;
then the row of measurements for the width is such that the hips are always half of that.
The two arms are equal to the arms, and the thighs, shanks, and the tail (jaghana) are likewise measured.
The foot, including the ankle bone, should be four finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in thickness;
its width should be six finger-breadths, with the big toe being equal [to that].
The second toe (pradeśinī) is equal to it, while the remaining toes are shorter, each being one finger-breadth less than the preceding nail.
The length of the foot is proclaimed to be fourteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas).
A beautiful image endowed with such characteristics is worthy of worship;
likewise [the proportions of] the lower lip, the thighs, the eyebrows, the forehead, and the intellect (the cranial region) [should be measured accordingly].
One should certainly fashion a *gaṇḍa* on the body where there is a protrusion of the limbs;
[the deity] has wide eyes, copper-colored feet, and elongated eyes,
like a beautiful Vidyādhara with the wings of the sun and fire.
He wears the Atimukuṭa crown proclaimed by Vatsa, along with bracelets, armlets, and necklaces;
he is generally adorned with ointments, foot-bindings, and the like.
He possesses a beautiful, radiant halo and lovely, variegated jeweled earrings.

One should have fashioned this [image], endowed with such characteristics, holding a golden garland in her two hands and [arranging] her locks of hair; she should be very glossy, bestowing boons, and gentle toward those in the second stage of life (the householder). She should be offered according to the prescribed rites.
Viṣṇu should be nine tālas, Vāsudeva three tālas;
Nṛsiṃha should be five tālas, and Hayagrīva is the fifth [at five tālas];
Nārāyaṇa is eight tālas, and Maheśa is five tālas.
Durgā should be nine *tālas* in height, and Lakṣmī three *tālas*.
One should know Vāṇī to be three *tālas*, and Savitṛ seven *tālas*.
On the right hand of Vāsudeva, the discus is established.
Below that, on its left side, there should be a conch, and below that indeed a mace;
and below that should be a lotus adorned with the Śrīvatsa. On the right side, there is a three-eyed face of Tāraka, which possesses the nature of both.
One should place Nalina and Siṃha on the two sides, Subhadrā on the right,
and Rukmiṇī on the left; below them, Divīndraka,
as well as Nārada and Kapila, with their hands joined in the gesture of reverence (añjali).
Both Dharma and Adharma should be depicted on the two sides as the most excellent among those wearing garlands.
One should understand that the fierce [aspect] belongs to Vāsudeva and likewise to Nārāyaṇa;
one should know the reverse for the Mādhavas as well.
A wise person should install [the image] at a sacred ford (tīrtha), on a mountain, by a pond,
in the midst of a city or village, or in the assembly of Brahmins;
especially in Avimukta, in Siddhakṣetra, or in Daśārṇaka.

O best of Brahmins, three thousand and sixty-five families were formerly uplifted; it is not otherwise. In the Kali age, an image made of wood should be fashioned, or else one made of clay for those who are incapable.
One should fashion [the image] from sandalwood, agallochum, bilva, and śrīparṇika wood;
likewise, for Vāma, it should be made of lotus wood.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the first part of the Madhyama-parvan in the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa.
Description of the Procedure for Constructing the Fire-pit (Kuṇḍa).
Sūta said:
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the definitive rules regarding the fire-pits.
O best of the twice-born, listen now to its extraction and refinement:
it is square, circular, half-a-foot [in measure], half-moon shaped,
womb-shaped, crescent-shaped, and fifthly, semi-octagonal.
The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is declared to be of seven-and-a-half, nine-and-a-half, or ten [units] in measure.
Having purified the ground according to the rules, removing husks, hair, and other debris,
one should carefully sweep away the ashes and charcoal from its surface.
The wise man should perform the rite of sowing sprouts within seven days itself;
he should soften the site by digging it up and drenching it with water,
and having measured it to the height of a *puṣṭihasta*, he should trace out its boundaries.
One should prepare a square measuring twelve finger-breadths (arkāṅgula) by means of a cord;
then, one [finger] should be set aside from the eighteen-finger field.
By that measurement, one should measure out a brilliant pit (kuṇḍa) consisting of three circles.
One should divide the field as before and place one part in front;
one should exclude the three circles beginning with Kālikā on the outside.
This is declared to be the lotus-shaped sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), which is enchanting to the eyes.
One should divide the field tenfold by two finger-breadths each, upward and downward;
one should rotate the thread and cut it according to that measurement.
Or, when the field has been divided fivefold, the wise man may divide it as he desires.

One should first place the limbs [of the deity] at the front, according to the measurement of half of a quarter of the corner. Having established the location of the *yoni* in the shape of a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree, one should then apply two threads so that the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) becomes properly measured.
O best of the twice-born, having drawn out a square by means of the application of the cord according to rule, one should cast it toward each direction;
the wise [should know] the triangle, the double-petaled lotus, the hexagon, and the three sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas).
Just as in the case of reservoirs, groves, wells, and permanent dwellings,
the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be quadrangular during the sacramental rites for the twice-born;
likewise, it is the fourth [type] for the installation of deities, sacrifices, and the consecration of a house-site.
One should prescribe the lotus for the Vasuṃdharā-yoga-bheda, for worldly expansion, for the Soma sacrifice, for the Naramedha and Aśvamedha sacrifices,
for the rite of sowing seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa), and for Vaiṣṇava sacrificial rites.

On the eighth lunar day (Aṣṭamī), there is the birth of Śiva and the Goddess; on the half-moon day (Amāvāsyā), [there is] the rite for prosperity involving a cat, as well as for enmity, for beauty, and likewise for pacification (Śāntika). Furthermore, during rites for peace, installation, sacrifice, and the optional rites (Kāmyakarman) of the Śākta practitioners.
For those desiring the preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa), for the liberation from fevers and other ailments,
and in such tasks as these, the Yoni-kunda is recommended;
likewise for journeys to deities and sacred fords, and when entering a great battle.
In rites for subduing, pacifying, and nourishing, the excellent six-fortress *kuṇḍa* is supreme;
likewise for killing, expulsion, and the alleviation of disease,
as well as for the *koṭihoma* of Vaiṣṇavas and for the intense mourning of kings.
The fire-pit for the accomplishment of treasures should be eight-cornered and lotus-shaped, while for the accomplishment of a king it should be seven-cornered;
for the attainment of a maiden, it should be five-cornered and three-cornered.
Its depth should be exactly equal to its width.
The wise should construct the girdle (mekhalā) all around in proportion to the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
In homas of ten thousand oblations and more, the intelligent practitioner should likewise apply the girdle;
even here, at the lower measurement, one should leave a space of one and a half finger-breadths at the base.
The measurement should be according to the requirements in sequence, [determined] by the corners and the tastes (six).
In a *muṣṭi* or *hasta*-sized [pit], the height is one and a half finger-breadths;
however, in a pit of one *aratni*, it is three fingers, increasing by one finger in sequence.
In a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one cubit, the measurements for the seven girdles (mekhalā) are four, three, and two finger-breadths (aṅgula);
such a configuration is not recommended for a Lakṣahoma.
Alternatively, for a Lakṣa or Koṭi homa, one should employ a pit with five girdles.
The wise man should increase the circumference by one finger-width and so forth;
in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring four cubits, there are that many "virtuous" finger-widths (guṇāṅgula).
In an eight-cubit pit, there is a row of twelve [finger-widths], and even when decreased by two, they follow that sequence respectively.
In the *grahamakhā* sacrifice, all the girdles (*mekhalā*) are equal, numbering one thousand;

there, the wise practitioner should join those girdles on the sides in their proper sequence. According to the measurement beginning with one and a half finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), the wise one should increase the circumference (*nemi*).
One should unite [the practitioner] with the sacrifice of the single girdle through the state of Śakti.
When there is an excess in the fire-oblation (homa), the fruit is great; if it is deficient, it will not be greater than that.
One should know the form of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) to be the supreme body of Prakṛti.

The fruit obtained from a sacrificial fire-offering (homa) is a hundredfold greater than that from a ritual site (sthaṇḍila), though the latter yields a small result. One should fashion the altar so that it possesses the qualities of six, four, or eight units in its length, width, and height;
the tip of the yoni should be one finger-breadth wide and slightly downturned.

O best of the twice-born, one should increase the yoni by one finger-breadth for each of the empty sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas). That yoni, which is well-characterized and possesses a middle altar (mekhalā) of equal proportions, should be established at the corners of the pit.
One should fashion the navel of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) clearly resembling a lotus;
it should be proportionate to the pit, very distinct, and beautiful.
However, in the case of a yoni-shaped pit, one should omit the yoni, and in the case of a lotus-shaped pit, one should omit the navel.
Up to the measure of two [units], one should increase the navel by a sequence of half-fingers outward, according to the form of the various sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas).
In each of those places, there should be a pit; however, one should not perform the fire-oblation (homa) in a pit that lacks the central image (biṃba).

Since desire arises from the union of Śiva and Śakti, the well is known as the goddess Umā and the reflection as Sadāśiva. One should not perform [the rite] lacking even one of these; otherwise, it shall lead to death.
Having left aside thirteen finger-breadths, or even one cubit,
in a great sacred ford (mahātīrtha), a field of accomplishment (siddhakṣetra), or wherever there is a temple of Śambhu within a lineage,
one should draw a mandala on its southern side, directly in front.
In that place, worship should be performed, and one should rely upon the previously mentioned measurement;
one should construct [the structure] at a distance of one cubit from the sun, or with a hundred [bricks], up to the end of a hundred.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the first part of the Madhyama-parvan in the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa.
Description of the Measurements for Sacrifices.
Sūta said:
One should employ the specific measurement belonging to whichever sacrifice it may be.
A sacrifice performed without the proper measure is ruined; therefore, one should not neglect the measurement.
First is the measure of fifty, then a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, and likewise a hundred thousand; beyond that is the *koṭi-homa*.
Beyond this, O best of the twice-born, neither a king nor anyone else who possesses wealth attains perfection;
he merely becomes a partaker of the fruit of non-sacrifice.
A man always experiences the full ripening of all his actions.
It is said that from this, a person always obtains both auspicious and inauspicious results;
moreover, the planets are constantly engaged therein in rites for pacification and prosperity.
Therefore, one should always perform worship with effort and devotion according to the prescribed rules.
Likewise, one endowed with devotion should perform a propitiatory rite (*śānti*) for a portentous event (*adbhuta*);
therefore, indeed, the auspicious or inauspicious results produced by the planets [are pacified] through all such portents.
A person should have ten thousand recitations (*ayuta-japa*) performed for all portents.
In rites for nourishment (*pauṣṭika*) or in rites for specific desires (*kāmyakarman*),
a king should perform the *lakṣahoma* or *koṭihoma* according to the prescribed rules;
others, if they possess the means, should perform one of a hundred or ten thousand oblations.

In the Kali age, a householder should not perform the hundred-thousand-fold oblation (lakṣahoma) or the ten-million-fold oblation (koṭihoma) for the planets, nor the treasure-oblation (nidhihoma) or malevolent rites (abhicāra). Wherever a recitation (japa) or an oblation (homa) is to be performed, it should be done in any such place.
One must certainly not practice pride, and one should place the eight [deities] beginning with Pride.
One should not perform a rite involving a pair, for from a pair danger is foretold.
In a *lakṣa*-homa, the number is seventy *tālas*, and in a *koṭi*-homa, it is twenty.

Or even within thirty-one days, one should never cause a transgression. The first undertaking consists of three thousand [recitations], the second of eight thousand, and the third of one thousand; this is the procedure prescribed for subduing the planets.
When the five-day rite is commenced, the wise one should offer a thousand oblations;
on the second day, two thousand; on the third, a thousand;
on the fourth, a thousand plus three hundred; and the remainder is prescribed for the fifth day.
During the nine-day period, one should perform one hundred thousand oblations daily for each constituent part;
likewise, on the fifth and sixth days, two additional parts should be assigned to the lineage.
For the *koṭihoma*, one should assign a part equal to the lunar day (tithi) and calculate the remainder by means of a hundredth part.
This measurement has been declared as neither deficient nor excessive.
One should offer it daily once; one should not perform it separately every day.
He should always recite the *pañcatāra* mantra for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering within the assembly.
In the case of ten thousand, one hundred thousand, or ten million oblations,
one should always perform the installation of the deities on the first day;
likewise, on the second day, during the great festival, one should offer the bali-oblation.
In a rite to be completed in three days (tryaha) or a three-night (trirātra) period, one should perform the final rites and dismiss [the deity] once it is finished.
In a five-day rite, however, the offering of the bali-oblation is recommended on the third day;
likewise in a seven-day, eight-day, or nine-day rite, it is performed on the fifth day.
"On the fifth day, the twelfth day, the thirty-second day, or the sixteenth day;
otherwise than this one should not perform [the rite], for in that case one would not obtain the fruit of the sacrifice.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the first part of the Madhyama-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa.
Description of the Consecration of the Kuṇḍas. Sūta said:
Now I shall describe the consecration of the kuṇḍas according to the doctrine of the scriptures.

Since there would be a loss of purpose regarding the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), one should therefore perform the consecration and offer the oblation. Eighteen consecrations for the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) are shown therein:
one should inspect the site with the Tāra mantra and sprinkle it with water mixed with kuśa grass.
After performing the "three-thread" measurement, one should subsequently lay down the circle-line.
One should place the peg with the *Vāra* mantra and the bud with the *Nārasiṃha* mantra.
Thereafter, one should fashion the tongue and from that, one should bring forth the fire.

One should avoid taking fire from the house of a barbarian (mleccha), nor ever from the dwelling of a Śūdra, nor from a river, a mountain, or a hall; one should avoid taking it from the hand of a woman. Having consecrated it, one should take hold of it and lift it up after dividing it into three parts.

The wise one should receive that fire facing toward himself; he should sprinkle it with the seed-syllable of Fire (Raṃ) and the seed-syllable of Śiva (Hauṃ). He should contemplate Vāgīśvarī, who has bathed after her menses, united with Vāgīśvara.
Having meditated, one should offer the breath; from that, desire arises.
One should cast fire into the womb in the northeast with the seed-syllable of Time (Kāla).
Afterwards, one should offer water for sipping (ācamanīya) to both the God and the Goddess.
"Pitṛpiṅgala dahadaha," having uttered these five pairs,

"sarvajñājñāpaya svāhā"— this is the mantra for the worship of Fire. The letters beginning with 'sa' and ending with 'ya', joined with the fire-syllable (ra) and the sacrificial grass-syllable (ha), and accompanied by the bindu, [are used].
The mantras of the fire have been fully described, and the mantra for the twice-born has been proclaimed.
O best of men, those tongues are said to be of three kinds by Yajñadatta:
one should offer oblations with a self-controlled mind using the Hiraṇyā tongue during offerings of clarified butter.
There, one should perform the oblation with those [offerings] smeared with the three sweets (trimadhu) in the pericarp;
from Kanakāsyā comes Kṛṣṇāsyā, and likewise Hiraṇyā and Śubhratā,
as well as Bahurūpā and Atirūpā, who are sattvic in yogic rites.
Viśvamūrti, Sphuliṅginī, Dhūmravarṇā, Manojavā,
Lohitāsyā, Karālāsyā, and Kālībhāsā—
these seven should be employed in rites of a cruel nature; they are to be thus known.
One should join those tongues which are in the various fuel-sticks with that very [substance]. One who is free from pride should offer the clarified butter oblation into the golden [tongue];
and one should perform the oblation with the three sweets (trimadhu) applied [to the sticks] into the pericarp.
In the daily rites, radiance is recorded as being produced by pure milk poured into a red vessel;
it is multiform in a flower-homa, black with cooked rice and milk-rice (pāyasa),
ruby-red in a sugarcane-homa, and golden in a lotus-homa.
Lohitā is present during the lotus-homa, while Śvetā is indeed present when using bilva leaves;
Dhūminī is present during the sesame-homa, and Karālikā during the wood-homa.
Lohitāsyā is known to be present during the ancestral (pitṛ) homa, and thereafter Manojavā is to be understood as present.
O best of beings, one should offer oblations into the fire from the mouth [of the deity], for Vaiśvānara is present during the *samit-homa*,
seated during the *ājya-homa*, and situated within all remaining substances;
thus one should offer the oblation into the fire for the fulfillment of all rites.
In the case of an oblation in the ear, disease occurs; in the eye, both of those are said to happen.
In the nose, there is mental anguish; in the head, there is travel—of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, it brings about a son who causes misfortune; therefore, one should not perform the oblation there.
Now I shall describe that which is common; the tongues of the Fire have been proclaimed.
I will explain the entire procedure; furthermore, hear what its specific distinction is:
in an oblation of clarified butter, the tongue is named Hiraṇyā; from the offering with the hand, it is Gaganā.

Vakrā is renowned for the great fire-sacrifice (mahāhoma), while she who has a black luster is considered [the deity] for the ritual (kratu). Suprabhā is for the rite of sweetmeats (modaka); Bahurūpā and Atirūpikā are proclaimed as the tongues of the fire in the fire-sacrifice involving flowers and leaves.
Alternatively, one should not conceive of a difference in the shape of the *kuṇḍa* based on the caste of the Śūdra [performer].
The *indrakoṣṭha* (Indra’s square) shall be the head; the two squares in the northeast and southeast shall also be the head.
On either side of that [head], the two squares are the two eyes, and the two [squares] following them in sequence are the two hands.
The tail should be undifferentiated, and the arising of the belly should be in the middle.
One should offer nourishment into the belly, as well as milk-rice (*pāyasa*);
having offered there a collection of grains, one should offer a flower-oblation into the ear.
A wise practitioner should offer the lotus and other items into the left ear and the left eye;
likewise, the sugarcane piece is offered into the right ear and the right eye.
This is recommended for malevolent rites (abhicāra) when performed on the left foot and the left hand.
In the rite of killing (*māraṇa*), one should offer flowers at the designated spot and never offer anything else;
know that [any other offering] brings misfortune, for the sound [of such an offering] causes total destruction.
[The auspicious scent] resembles sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, *pāṭalā*, and *yūthikā*.
The fragrance of the fire spreads on all sides with great intensity;
when the flame is clockwise, steady, shaped like an umbrella, and not flickering,
it bestows auspiciousness upon the sacrificer and especially upon his kingdom.
If the flames are cut off, one should know that death or the loss of wealth will occur;
likewise, in a fire filled with thick smoke, one should know that extinction signifies death. When such defects arise, one should perform an expiation.
Having offered twenty-eight oblations, one should then feed the Brahmins;
one should offer twenty-five oblations with clarified butter using the root mantra.
A great ceremonial bath should be performed, and the worship of Hari should be conducted at the three times of day.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the first part of the Madhyama-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa;
titled "The Description of the Ritual for Worship at the Conclusion of the Sacrifice. Sūta said:
One should recite the sixteen services at the beginning of the daily (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) rites, as well as upon their completion; at the conclusion of the fire-oblation (homa),
one should offer the breath (samīraṇa) and perform the worship of the pedestal (pīṭhapūjā).
Having taken a red flower, one should meditate upon the Fire-god according to the prescribed rule:

one should meditate on Agni as having three eyes, wearing a crown of matted locks, adorned with golden ornaments, seated upon a lotus, and holding in his long arms a desired object, a spear, the svastika, and the gesture of fearlessness, while bestowing boons.
In the locations of the eastern and other doors, one should properly worship Kāmadeva, Śatakratu (Indra), Varāha, and Ṣaṇmukha with perfumes and other offerings;
having invoked them, one should then establish them and display the eight mudrās.
Having offered a seat and a welcome, one should present the three items beginning with water for the feet (pādya).
Then, within the vessels starting from the east, [one should visualize] the sacrificial fire—
pure, golden-colored, fully kindled, and facing in all directions.
One should worship Mahodara and Mahājihva as being of the nature of space.
Upon the completion [of the ritual], one should worship Tāraka and the others with various kinds of perfumes and flowers.
Right there, preceded by the mantra, one should meditate upon the three types of tongues.
Immediately thereafter, with the ritual services and the mantra to be recited:
"You are the beginning of all beings, the deliverer from the ocean of saṃsāra;
you are the form of the supreme light; make this seat fruitful."
One should offer a seat with these three clusters of flowers;
then, having formed the añjali-gesture with hollowed palms, one should inquire after [the deity's] welfare, beginning with:
"O Vaiśvānara, homage be to you; homage be to you, O Havyavāhana."
Welcome, O best of gods; grant peace, salutations be unto you!
Salutations to you, O Blessed Lord, O God whose essence is the waters and Nārāyaṇa;
for the sake of the welfare of all the worlds, please accept this water for washing the feet.
O Nārāyaṇa, supreme abode, eternal one in the form of light;
accept this water-offering given by me, O Viśvarūpa, salutations be unto you!
You who always illumine the world with the form of the Sun.
Salutations to you, Jātavedas, whose nature is light;
salutations to you, Dhanañjaya, the destroyer of all sins.
This bath-water has been offered by me to you for the fulfillment of all desires and aims.
O Hutāśana, O mighty-armed one, O eternal God of gods, I seek refuge in you; grant me the supreme state. You are the form of light among all lights, O Acyuta, without beginning or end.
Adorn yourself with this ornament given by me; homage be to you!
Through the perfect union with you, the goddesses and gods attain joy.
For the sake of pacifying all defects, please accept this fragrance.
You are Viṣṇu, you are indeed Brahmā, and you are the Lord who is the refuge of all luminaries.
O Lord of Gods, accept this flower along with the unguent,
for it shall become the sole, eternal happiness of the deities and the ancestors.
"O Lord of the gods, O Dhanañjaya, let this incense be accepted from me.
You alone, among all beings—both stationary and moving—are the Supreme Self, the ultimate form; let this lamp be accepted."
Salutations be to the Lord of Sacrifice, the Source, Jātavedas!
For the sake of the welfare of all worlds, may you accept this food offering.
O Consumer of Oblations, salutations to you; salutations to you, whose vehicle is gold.
"O Lord of the World, homage be to you; homage be to you, O Jātavedas.
With this mantra, one should offer even a divine gift, including one's entire property, the sacrificial thread, and rice-milk with honey.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "Description of Fire," in the first part of the Madhyama-parvan within the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa. Sūta said:
I shall describe the classification of sacrifice and its three divisions according to the doctrine of the scriptures,
in accordance with the Vedas and as applied to the specific ritual procedures.
In fifty [verses] Vahni is declared, and in fifty Kāśyapa is remembered.
In the offering of a ghee lamp, Viṣṇu is present; in a sacrifice of sesame seeds, he is the Lord of Forests (Vanaspati).
In a thousand-fold rite, he is called Brāhmaṇa; in ten-thousand-fold, he is called Hari.
In a hundred-thousand-fold homa, he is Vahni; in a ten-million-fold homa, he is Hutāśana.

Varuṇa is to be known for rites of pacification (śāntika), while Aruṇa is remembered for rites of killing (māraṇa). In the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma) he is named Anala, and in expiatory rites (prāyaścitta) he is Hutāśana. And Lohita is the one who presides over the sacrifice of food (annayajña), according to the successive order of the planets.
In the sacrifice for the installation of a deity, Lohita is proclaimed;
Prajāpati is for the Vāstu-sacrifice, as well as in the lotus-shaped pavilion;
in the water-shed (prapā), the one named Nāga; and in the great gift (mahādāna), Havirbhuj.
In the gift of a cow one becomes Rudra; in the gift of a maiden, one becomes Gojaka;
and in the gift of the Tulāpuruṣa, one is proclaimed as Dhātāgni.
In the ritual release of a bull one becomes Sūrya, and at the conclusion of the rite, one is remembered as Ravi.
Pāvaka is in the Vaiśvadeva rite; Janārdana is in the fortnight of initiation (dīkṣā);
Kāla is in the act of terrifying; Kravyāda is in the burning of the body;
Yama by name is in the burning of leaves; and Śikhaṇḍika is in the burning of bones.
