In the rite of conception (garbhādhāna), the Maruts are presiding; at the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana), Piṅgala is traditionally taught; at the rite for a male child (puṃsavana), Indra is proclaimed as the deity, being highly praised in the sacrificial act;
likewise, in the naming ceremony (nāmakaraṇa) and the rite of first feeding (annaprāśana), O King, Pārthiva is the presiding deity.
Niṣkāma at the [birth] ceremony, Hāṭaka at the first feeding, Śuci at the tonsure, Ṣaḍānana at the initiation of vows, Samudbhava at the sacred thread ceremony,
Vītihotra at the return home from study, and Dhanañjaya at the graduation ceremony.
In the belly is the digestive fire (jaṭharāgni), and in the ocean is the submarine fire (vaḍavānala).
In the crest-lock (śikhā) is to be known the pervasive lord (vibhu), and in the vital breath (svara) is the serpent-fire (sarīsṛpa).
The horse-fire is named Manthara, and the chariot-fire is Jātavedas.
Gajāgni is Mandara, while Sūryāgni is known as Vindhya;
Toyāgni is named Varuṇa, and Brāhmaṇāgni is Havirbhuj;
Parvatāgni is Kratubhuj, and Dāvāgni is said to be Sūrya.
The lamp-fire is named Pāvaka; the domestic fire is Dharaṇīpati;
the clarified-butter fire is Nala; the wind-fire is Vāyu; and the birth-fire is Rākṣasa.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "Description of the Names of the Fires," in the first part of the Madhyama-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa.
The Description of Homa Substances.
Sūta said:
Now, therefore, the measurement of the substances for the *homa* sacrifice is being declared.
In both the case of the prescribed measure and the absence of a measure, [the result] certainly becomes fruitless.
One *karṣa* of clarified butter is prescribed for the *homa*; a *śukti* of milk is likewise recorded;
and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*)—curds, milk, and honey—are equal to that.
Puffed rice (*pṛthuka*) and parched grain (*lāja*) should be measured by a handful (*muṣṭi*);
sugar (*śarkarā*) is likewise a handful in measure, though some know sugar to be one *tolaka*.
One should know jaggery (*guḍa*) to be three *tolakas*, and for sugarcane products, the rule is according to the joint (*parva*).
One should not offer each leaf or flower individually, nor should one offer three handfuls of *śālūka* at once; one should never offer them separately.
One should offer a *japā* flower together with its stalk, and likewise the filaments together with their stalks.
And for each of the water-born lotuses,
as well as for the flour-cakes, there was a number equal to the measure of Jīvantī fruits;
and for the *modaka* sweets, the measure was that of a *vasantaka* sweetmeat.
Each fruit [should be divided] individually; the citron and the trikheda should be divided into three parts each.
The coconut should be divided into eight parts, and the jackfruit into ten.
The pumpkin should be divided into eight parts, according to the size of a lotus seed.

The *urvāruka* is divided into eight parts, and the *guḍūcī*, *caturaṅgula*, and *pūga* are measured by weight; there, meat is seen along with jaggery (*guḍa*). Elsewhere, the *badarī* is measured by weight and the *tiṇduka* is divided into three parts.
One should take a piece of wood one span (prādeśa) in length, dūrvā grass consisting of three leaflets,
a birch leaf, and a śamī branch one span in length;
the rice should be a single handful, and the mustard seeds should be measured by a śukti.
Black pepper should be used with *vimāna*, as well as lotus stalk and radish; the eggplant (*vārtāka*) should be cut into seven pieces, and the *tripuṣṭa* is declared to be of three kinds.
Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, musk, and saffron are also [to be offered].
The teachers have prescribed that when three parts of sesame seeds are immersed along with the fuel sticks,
ten thousand [immersions] are equal to one hundred thousand immersions of *tittiḍī* seeds.
Likewise, for the sprinkling of rice, for a small wooden staff,
for soft flowers, and similarly for creepers and the like;
and for milk-rice, ordinary food, sweetmeats, and flour-cakes as well.
One should offer oblations with rice that is not stuck together; if there is a reversal [in the quality], the result will be reversed.
One should cause the *bilva* leaf to float while setting aside its stalk;
for by floating it with the stalk attached, the *rākṣasa* seizes the fruit.
One should employ it by taking only the eastern half of a bilva leaf.
Likewise, in a fire-oblation (*homa*), three leaves are required; if they are broken or split, it is a great defect.
One should not perform the floating [of the vessel] two or three times; having done so, one goes to the netherworld (*rasātala*).
Therefore, having turned toward the eastern direction, the son, disciples, and other Brahmins learned in the truth should purify [the site] in due order;
one should not perform it deficiently or excessively, and for the rite of pacification (śānti), one should face the north.
One should carefully avoid offering milk-rice (pāyasa) to other deities;
one should not cause it to be offered into the fire, but should present it to these [deities] with effort.
Having reached the little finger, one should perform the decoration of the joints.
O wise ones,
the downward movement [of the thread] should be measured by the length of the cord, at two, three, or four finger-breadths, according to the sequence of the leaf-offerings (*patra-homa*).
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the first part of the Madhyama-parvan within the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Description of the Determination of the *Sruva* and *Darvī* Ladsles.
Sūta said:
"The *Śrīparṇī*, the *Śiṃśapā*, the milky tree (*kṣīrī*), the *Bilva*, and the *Khadira* [are suitable for these ladles]."
For the *sruva* ladle, trees that are praised grant success in sacrificial rites.
For the installation (*pratiṣṭhā*), the *dhātrī*, *khadira*, and *keśara* are praised;
for the consecration (*saṃskāra*), the two [trees] distinct from the moon [are used], and the *dhātrī* was fashioned by the Creator himself.
The *sruva* ladle that was described for the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the sacrificial implement is intended for the act of consuming;
however, those who know the scriptures have stated that other types are prescribed for the rite of installation (*pratiṣṭhā*).
Now I shall describe the *sruva* and the *sruc*, upon which everything else depends.
In the sacrifice, the *sarvaka* should not be held, and there is an exchange with the *akṣara*. First, I shall describe its *sruva* spoon—its measurement and its base.
Having taken a piece of wood from a *bilva* tree on a lunar day other than the *riktā* and so forth, [one should proceed].
Having observed the fast, one should prepare the sacrificial offerings and not recall [worldly desires];
one should avoid sexual intercourse during the construction of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles.
Having taken a piece of wood, one should then divide it into thirty parts.

A wise person should fashion a *sruva* ladle measuring twenty finger-breadths in length, with a belly equal in size to the altar of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), and a hollowed-out base shaped like a cauldron;
it should be as beautiful as the fruit of the *dhātrī* tree, with a well-formed cavity for the *svadhā* offering.
One should fashion the altar in the shape of a winnowing basket and arrange the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas).
Alternatively, one may draw them with the hand in the form of a swan, having three folds;
and one should certainly construct the *sruva* ladle out of twenty-four parts.

The measurement for the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) when not used for the gods is said to be thirty-two [aṅgulas]; its width is four aṅgulas, and from that, the tip of the sruva ladle is one karṣa. One should draw the form of a deer in the mud with two aṅgulas.
At the base of the staff, one should be a staff-bearer adorned with bracelets;
a ladle should be made of gold or copper according to the prescribed measure. It should be produced from the wood of a tree belonging to the three higher castes, or from the Indu tree.

Produced from a milky tree (kṣīravṛkṣa) and measuring twelve finger-breadths in length, its bowl is two finger-breadths wide; this ladle (darvī) is used for the accomplishment of sacrifice. It should be made of copper and weigh forty tolakas.
The mandala should be five finger-breadths [in size], and the staff eight cubits long;
in the preparation of food, milk-rice, and the like, the sacrificial ladle (darvī) is used as an instrument for the sacrifice,
and that ladle is declared to measure ten tolakas.
For the purpose of purifying the clarified butter (ājya), however,
one should use a vessel made of copper measuring sixteen finger-breadths; in the absence of all these, one may rely on a vessel made of peepal wood, or one made of ghee, or even one made of clay.
"Alternatively, it may be made of copper, but one should not employ it there.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Sruva and Darvī," in the first part of the Madhyama Parvan within the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
[It contains] the description of the complete ritual procedure.
Sūta said:
Now I shall describe the rite of completion (pūrṇavidhi) for those who seek to know the meaning of the Moon;
by the perfect performance of which, it is established that [the ritual] becomes complete.
At the conclusion of the *homa*, the ritual for liberation (*mokṣakalpa*) is performed, and at the end of the worship, the *arghya* offering is prescribed.
Now, if that [offering] is incomplete, one’s prosperity is destroyed and the sacrifice fails.
Therefore, with every effort, one should place the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) beneath the *sruva* ladle.
Having offered the full *arghya* to Savitṛ, one should then feed the Brāhmaṇas;
having entered the house thereafter, one should perform the family worship (*kulapūjā*) in due order with the verses: "O Seven, give me the full" and "May it purify."
One should employ [these mantras] in the installation ceremony, as well as in the daily and occasional rites; listen now.
The first is proclaimed as the full [offering] with the verse beginning "punātu";
the second is "saptate"; and the third is "dehi me."

The fourth [offering] should be the full ladle (*pūrṇā*); having established [the vessel] in the family line, the preceptor (*deśika*), having risen, should offer the full [oblation], and never while remaining seated. And in the sacrifice to the planets (*grahayāga*), [it is offered] upon the golden tongue that is red.
In the fire-oblation for the planets (graha-homa), one *pūrṇā* offering is prescribed at the end of a hundred;
at the end of a thousand, one should give a pair (*yuga*); at the end of ten thousand, two pairs;
and at the end of a thousand [in the case of a flower-homa], O best of beings, one should give one.
One desiring the fruit of a sacrifice should offer one thousand *pūrṇāhuti*s;
however, for a single offering made with soft flowers or for a simple oblation of sugarcane juice, there is one;
and for the rites of conception (*garbhādhāna*) and the first feeding (*annaprāśana*), there are two hundred and two.
In the Sīmantonnayana rite, in the performance of expiatory rites (prāyaścitta),
and in the daily Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, one full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) alone is prescribed. Having thus made the two ladles (srucau) level, one should place them one above the other.
O best of men,

having heard the seers, meters, and so forth pertaining to each mantra, one should perform the fire-oblation after renouncing [all else], so that it is not exhausted once performed and one does not engage in conceptualization; otherwise, the fruit will be very slight.

"Saptate" is said to have the Brāhmaṇa Kauṇḍinya as its seer (ṛṣi); Jagatī is its meter (chandas), and Agni is proclaimed as its deity. Furthermore, for the mantra "Dehi me," Prajāpati is remembered as the seer.
The meter of this [verse] is Anuṣṭubh, and its deity is Prajāpati.
For the mantra "pūrṇā darvī," Śatakratu is recorded as the seer (ṛṣi);
the meter is declared to be Anuṣṭubh, and Vahni is the deity here.

Furthermore, O best of the twice-born, for the mantra beginning with "punātu," Pavana is remembered as the seer (ṛṣi); Jagatī is known as the meter (chandas), and Agni is proclaimed as the deity (devatā). O Nakula, this [mantra] is used during the fourth full-moon sacrifice in the midst of the ritual.
Neither in the midst of the sacrifice nor during the consecration or the libation should the officiating priest touch the sacrificial formula,
nor the right limb of the patron,
nor even the patron himself together with his wife, who is preceded by a great festival.
The wise Viśvāmitra should perform ten thousand oblations there;
the lavalī, badarī, picumanda, kacchatraka,
nāgaraṅga, and dhātakī are recommended, yet one should avoid them on the full moon day.
If the number is not counted, there occurs a loss of the recitation and a failure of the fire-oblation.
Therefore, one should count them beforehand while they still contain sesame seeds and set them aside separately; or else, one may count them all at once, but never by means of a finger-joint (aṅga).
One desiring success should perform the counting with the fruits of *dhātakī*,
or with the fruits of *badarī* and *lavali* for the accomplishment of all aims;
likewise, one may use the fruits of *nāgaraṅga*, *dhātakī*, and *bakula*.
Since it causes the destruction of the sacrifice, one should therefore avoid it;
for the success of the sacrifice, O twice-born ones, one should prepare the Holi-pile with camphor and sandalwood,
or else with the clay of the Gaṅgā mixed with dog-dung.
One desiring nourishment should employ red guñjā fruits for counting;
likewise, one may be the offerer [of oblations] at five hundred, a hundred, or even a thousand [recitations],
or even at ten thousand (ayuta) in a single day, according to the number of the Vedas.
In a rite for the repayment of debts, there should be three officiating priests, the best of the twice-born;
in a *lakṣahoma*, however, six officiating priests are prescribed;
and in a *koṭihoma*, the Brahmins should be praised as being ten in number.
There should be nine, five, ten, ten, or even twenty-five officiating priests (ṛtvij),
who are free from desire and anger and possess tranquil minds. In the sacrifice to the nine planets (navagrahamakha), there should be four Brahmins who are knowers of the Vedas.

Alternatively, two peaceful priests alone are prescribed; they should perform the ten-thousand-fold oblation (ayutahoma), for one should not be entangled in excessive elaboration. Likewise, in the nine-fold oblation (navahoma), there are eight or ten priests.
Likewise, four [Brahmins] should be honored according to one's capacity, free from envy;
Brahmā should worship that very person, or two or three, according to the rule.
Even among a thousand, Brahmā should honor at least one Brahmin.
One who possesses little wealth should perform the rite with effort by means of sacrificial fees;
however, when wealth is available, a Lakṣahoma should be performed,
for by doing so according to the prescribed rules for one's desires, one obtains everything.

He is honored in the world of Śiva by the Vasus, Ādityas, and the hosts of Maruts for eight hundred kalpas, and at the end of that time, he shall attain liberation. He who, free from desire, performs this Lakṣahoma according to the prescribed rite [attains these fruits].
One obtains a hundred desires and attains an infinite state;
one seeking a son obtains a son, one seeking wealth obtains wealth,
one seeking a wife obtains a wife, and a maiden obtains an auspicious husband.
One whose kingdom has been lost shall regain his kingdom; one who desires prosperity shall obtain prosperity. Whatever desire one may cherish, one attains it all in its full abundance.
But he who performs this without desire attains the supreme Brahman.
Therefore, the Koṭihoma has been declared by the Self-born One to be a hundred times more efficacious.
In the absence of other Brāhmaṇas, the Ācārya himself shall be the Hotṛ;
however, one should not employ only a single person for the rite of ten thousand oblations (Ayutahoma).
Therefore, one should not [sit] on a seat of darbha grass, nor on kuśa grass, nor on straw, nor even on a leaf or bark;
nor on stone, nor on earth, nor ever on a cloth seat.
In that regard, the twice-born who follows the traditional scriptures (āgama) should make [the seat] out of wood.

One should give a gift at the conclusion of the *homa* and at the *pūrṇāhuti* and other rites; likewise, a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is given during the purificatory ceremonies for the twice-born, as well as at the *pūrṇāhuti* and other rites,
during the practice of mantras, and in the Soma sacrifice and the horse sacrifice.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "Description of the Mandala Rite," in the first part of the Madhyama-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said:
Now, therefore, I shall describe the mandala as it is declared in the Purāṇas;
since spiritual success (siddhi) depends upon it, one should construct it with a concentrated mind.
The gods will reside and dwell within it, seated upon lotus-thrones.
One should not worship the Goddess without a lotus; if she is worshipped [without one], the Yakṣiṇī will take it away.

Therefore, because the interruption of the maṇḍala would result in a tenfold [reduction], the merit is a hundredfold when accomplished with colored powders (rajas), and double the fruit when done alone.
When the goal is worship, three hundred [prostrations] are required; for a thousand [prostrations], there is the "eightfold dust" (rajo’ṣṭaka).
With sixteen measures of dust, one attains a hundred, a hundred, and then infinity—whether at a yantra, a gem, a śālagrāma, or especially before an image.

One should avoid that which is stained with dust, even if it is superior, when drawing [a yantra] upon a Mahālaya, a Mahāyoni, or a red liṅga for the purpose of worship and for the sake of prosperity; since the fruit of the ritual depends upon this, one must therefore strictly avoid such [defilement].
The quadrangular, the ninefold array, the *krauñca-prāṇa* of four kinds,
the seed-syllable of desire (*kāmabīja*), the diamond-navel (*vajranābha*), the king of obstacles (*vighnarāja*), the one called elephant (*gajāhvaya*),
the *pārijāta*, the lunar orb (*candrabimba*), the sun-lover (*sūryakānta*), and the crest-jewel (*śekhara*).
The hundred-petaled, the thousand-spoked, the nine-naved, and the fist-shaped;
the five-lotus, the Maināka, the Kāmarāja, and the Puṣkara;
the eight-sided, the Śrībiṃba, as well as the six-sided and the three-sided.
In the Vaiṣṇava sacrificial rite, the square altar arranged with nine divisions is prescribed, numbering forty-five in total; furthermore,
the Krauñca and Ghrāṇa altars, each of four types, are also commended for the Gomedha sacrifice.
The Subhadra, the Aśvamedha, and the Naramedha; the Narāsana;
everywhere the Sarvatobhadra, which is quadrangular and auspicious;
likewise the Kāmarāja, which is triangular, octagonal, and hexagonal.
For those who are capable, there is the great fivefold lion-throne on the side of desire;

the summit of Mount Meru for one fixed in the mountain of meditation; and likewise upon mountains of gems and pearls, as well as a thousand lotuses for the gift of food and a mountain of sesame seeds.
Harivallabha is praised at the Rājasūya and Soma sacrifices;
Subhadra and Sarvatobhadra are for consecration;
and Vighnarāja is commended for the consecration of reservoirs of water.
For the rite of placing the water-jar (ghaṭaprasthāpana), one should use an elephant-shaped seat;
for a hundred thousand oblations (lakṣahoma), a lotus-seat; and for ten thousand (ayuta), a square seat.
Whatever the form of the sacrifice may be, one should employ that very same form [for the seat].

Otherwise, there would be a fault; for those who act contrarily, there is rebirth in the lower realms. The altar (vedikā) is proclaimed to be two cubits square, and its height should be measured at either four or six finger-breadths.
The expert in sacrifice should increase the dimensions by six finger-breadths in the Navavyūha;
it should be made with a height of one finger-breadth by those who are well-composed.
In the Krauñcaprāṇa, it should be four cubits high, or raised to the height of a fist.

O best of the twice-born, one should make the middle pair inferior by three finger-breadths, and the smallest by two; they should be made progressively smaller in height according to the sequence of two and three [finger-breadths].
The crest-jewels should be made of pārijāta, moonstone, and sun-crystal.

In rites for nourishment (pauṣṭika) pertaining to the planets, and in the accomplishment of external villages and the like, one should employ three mandalas of altars (vedikā-cakra) in each respective case.
In the first [mandala], the hand should be in the fist-position; when it is complete, the remaining measurements are used.
In the absence of a boat, a three-hand span five-petalled lotus is prescribed;
furthermore, the *variṣṭhā*, *lavalī*, *bhitti*, and *vedikā* types should be understood,
O tigers among the twice-born, and employed according to one's preference.

There is a fault in the inversion of the proportions; therefore, one should accomplish it with effort. At ten cubits, eight cubits, and sixteen cubits [in length], one should increase the fist, the forearm, and the span by a sixteenth part.
The height should be made equal to the length of the hand; if it is deficient, one should decrease it further.
One should make it mirror-shaped for the sacrificial rite and for rites of pacification (śānti).
For the ritual of circumambulation (paristava), one should carefully make it in the form of a rampart.
One should smear the altar with night-soil and cow-dung,
and consecrate it with water containing gold and gems, as well as with water infused with *kuśa* grass.
Furthermore, one should avoid the dung of cows that are weak or barren, as well as the dung of a *dhenukā*.
One should carefully smear the sacrificial pit and the mandala with the dung of a tawny cow;
one should diligently avoid doing so on altars during all sacrifices.
Without using cords and stakes, one must not draw lines upon the mandala at all.
Therefore, one should diligently prepare the thread and the peg.
The thread should measure twelve cubits (arkahasta), be soft, and made of lac;
likewise, there should be a garland of yellow *kārya* flowers, and the peg should be fashioned from gold.

O best of the twice-born, one should make [the vessel] out of silver or copper for the Vaiṣṇava sacrificial rite; it is highly recommended for the leader of the Gaṇas (Gaṇeśa), and likewise for the Śaiva, the Āmārga,
the planets, the Lord (Īśa), and the Tortoise.
"And on the sixteenth [digit] and the solar hand (arkahasta), there shall be that which is joined with the rim (nemi).
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the first part of the Madhyamaparvan in the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Herein concludes the first part of the Madhyamaparvan.
Now begins the second middle section:
the description of the arrangement of the deities in the mandala.
Sūta said:
Now I shall explain the extraction [of measurements] for the square and other shapes.
One should fashion a square field measuring twelve *aṅgulas*.
A wise person should increase it by three *aṅgulas* in each direction.
One should make it square and equal, measuring eighteen finger-breadths for the desired [area];
at the tip of the cord for the two-cubit [measure], there are three finger-breadths on all sides. Once it has been made square, it likewise becomes two cubits in size.
In this manner, one should personally increase [the size] up to sixteen cubits in due order;
O Brahmins, the wise man should prepare the mandala with a measurement of one cubit.
In the mandala for the "honey-cubit" (madhuhasta), it should be fashioned with twelve finger-breadths (aṅgula) and two kalpas.

In a space of two cubits, there should be one cubit [for the center]; in a four-cubit area, however, the measurement of the lotus is fourfold. One should make it circular on all sides. In the first [section] the pericarp (karṇikā) should be made, and the filaments (kesarāṇi) in the second.
One should draw the junctions of the petals in the third [circle] and the tips of the petals in the fourth;
the pericarp and the lotus should be drawn with pure yellow pigment.
The filaments are said to be of three kinds, according to their locations at the base, the middle, and the tip.
At the base they are white and reddish, in the middle yellow, and established at the tip;
the junction of the vessels should be dark blue, and one should color the corners with red.
One should draw the weapons of the deities on the exterior, in the middle of the city, and in the corner.
Measuring eight finger-breadths and according to their respective colors,
they are Śambhu, Gaurī, Brahmā, Rāma, and Kṛṣṇa, in that order.
One should join them with a boundary line one finger-breadth in height, using half of each respective measurement.
In the great sacrifice (mahāyāga) of Śiva and Viṣṇu, one should cause [the offerings] to be given starting from Śambhu;
in the installation (pratiṣṭhā), ending with Rāma; and in the case of a reservoir of water, ending with Kṛṣṇa.
In the sacrifice of Durgā, according to the Śrī-pakṣa, one should arrange [the deities] beginning with Brahmā.
In the sacrifice to the planets (grahayāga), one should employ yellow and other colors, and not otherwise.
Now I shall describe the Ninefold Array (navavyūha) as approved by the Purāṇas. The wise man should perform everything as before and draw a lotus well.
One should encircle [the mandala] with threads corresponding to that number, starting from the first step,
using white and red, as well as yellow, and also yellow,
red, and white; thus, according to its own nature, in each respective section.
At its end is the *kalāyantra*, and by means of the tip of the secret petals,
it measures sixteen and twenty [units]; with the *liṅga* and eight petals,
one should thus avoid the mantras of the mandala according to the ultimate truth.
Likewise, one should fashion filaments at the roots and in the corners;
it should have the form of ten staffs, be colored with three hues,
and one should provide ten spokes at the tips, each measuring one finger-breadth in size.
With yellow [pigment], one should draw a circle everywhere, and in its center, a red-beaked [deity];
this is declared to be the Ninefold Array (Navavyūha), which bestows dharma, kāma, and artha.
A Śūdra should not construct a maṇḍala, nor should one who merely calls himself a Brāhmaṇa (Brāhmaṇabruva).
One should perform [this] at a confluence, a sacred ford (tīrtha), or in temples;
however, he who does not worship after having drawn [the image], being devoid of the fire-rite (agnikārya),
is born as one pierced by [the consequences of that act] in birth after birth.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of Krauñcamāna," in the second part of the Madhyama-parvan within the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa. Sūta said:
I shall now describe the Krauñca measurement as it is accepted by those who expound the meaning of the Vedas;
it is esteemed in all Tantras and should be guarded with great effort.
One should calculate it as being twice the measure of one's own aratni (cubit).
One should rotate that thread over the pegs with an increase in the middle;
one should lay down four circles according to the superior, middling, and inferior [capacities].
The pericarp is on the first circle, and then the filaments on the second.

In the third [square] one should draw lotus petals, and in the fourth, sixteen-petaled [lotuses]. One should fashion the primary and secondary ornaments within the even and auspicious square. One should well-draw two side-wings on both sides, with their tips pointing toward the south.
There, one should fashion a pair of lotuses with an interval of one finger-breadth in the center;
the eight colors are enumerated as white, yellow, red, black, crimson-like, copper-colored,
and dark green.
White [color] is known to arise from rice powder; yellow from *niśā* (turmeric);
red from the application of *niśā* along with conch powder and other substances;
black from burning *pulaka* and similar materials; and red from the application of *pītāsya* (yellow-berried leadwort).
Powdered color (rajas) is prescribed as follows: that which has the luster of saffron is pale yellow; it is produced from red and white [pigments];
copper-colored powder is made with safflower; and black powder is made from bilva leaves through the application of flour of barley, wheat, and so forth.

One should divide the white [color] across all the lines, but yellow in the center; one should apply pure white to the pericarp and the filaments. Following the sequence starting from the east, one should employ white and the other colors accordingly.
One should divide the powder at the junction of the petals according to the sequence of the intervals between sprinklings.
Then, upon the sixteen petals, starting from the east in due order,
there should be white, yellow, copper-colored, and then that which is numbered [the fourth].
Dark, saffron-colored, red, white, black, yellow, and copper—these are enumerated;
one should offer the dark, saffron, and red [colors] in this manner. The twice-born should meditate upon them, starting from the east and ending with the northeast (Īśāna).
The head of the *krauñca* bird should be red, measuring four finger-breadths;
the beak portion should be yellow, and the neck white. On the tail there are twenty feathers, beginning with five in the sequence of colors.

One should fashion the egg-portion within six finger-breadths using yellow pigment; specifically, the neck should be prepared with white powder. Therein, the yellow and other colors should be applied exactly as previously described.
One should apply white and the other colors individually and separately upon the receptacles:
yellow on the foot four finger-breadths high above the knee,
and red for the same distance of four finger-breadths below that.
It should be dark blue by two finger-breadths; one should also apply it upon the fingers.
In this way, one should draw both wings and contemplate them as white.
On the foot, it is pure; on the fingers, one should contemplate it as red and dark blue.
In the eastern and western directions, the area starting from the doorway should be white;
one should designate the southern and northern sides as red in color.
This is to be known as Mahākrauñca; now hear about this Madhyakrauñca.
The youngest among all sacrifices, and the seventh among the sciences, is supreme.
Now I shall further proclaim, in due order, the doctrine of the Sarvatantra.
One should make four tails, red and yellow, with red and yellow [threads].
In the sequence beginning from the east,
one should well-draw four external corners joined to the base at the edge of the petals upon the surface of the earth;
one should form eight segments for the little finger and make the tail fourfold.
Thereafter, one should encircle it three times with white, red, and black [lines] in sequence;
this certainly destroys the sins accumulated over hundreds of births.
O Brahmins, or one may draw it in yellow, and all calamities will perish.
Therefore, the outer wheel and the field are to be observed individually;
they certainly destroy the sin accumulated over a hundred kalpas.
[One should likewise observe] the peacock, the bull, the lion, the curlew, and the monkey.
O twice-born ones, whether by negligence at home, in a field, or even at the top of a tree, one should rise and perform salutation; it burns away the sin of a hundred Brahman-murders.
Through its nourishment one attains fame, and through the mere sight of it, there is liberation from sin.
From seeing [these images], prosperity increases and the extension of life arises.
The peacock is the form of Brahmā, and the bull is Sadāśiva;
Durgā is manifested in the lion, and the one who is Viṣṇu is said to be Vidhi (Brahmā).
If one bathes and daily beholds the Krauñca, the god Nārāyaṇa, the tiger, Tripurasundarī,
Kālikā, the black tiger, Lakṣmī, and the variegated pigeon,
the affliction of the planets shall not arise.
Therefore, having exerted effort, one should maintain and nourish [the deity] in the home.
Hereafter, I shall explain the measurement of the colored powders (*rajas*) for each and every mandala, as well as the avoidance of effort as it has been taught.

One should avoid planting vermilion (mākṣika) produced from rice or barley under Capricorn; likewise, one should always avoid cinnabar, sulfur, yellow orpiment, and realgar that were produced during the month of Śrāvaṇa in one's childhood, for these always cause obstacles.

O twice-born ones, that which originates from the Himalayas, as well as white stone (sitapāṣāṇa), and the variety known as Kāñcanī— these are praised for their white qualities. [Likewise are] śephālī,
vṛtta, niśā, and the flowers of the linseed plant (atasī).

The flowers of the *kiṃśuka* tree are auspicious; yellow pigment (*guṇa*) is beneficial. Likewise, red ochre derived from serpents (*nāgaja-gairika*), safflower blossoms, *kuśīta*, *guḍaka*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, and the five-colored pigments (*pañcaraṅgaka*).
Vijayā leaves, bilva leaves,
and likewise the leaves of punarnavā, keśara,
and baka; black stone (kṛṣṇapāṣāṇaka), black cloud (kṛṣṇābhra), and samayūthaka.
One should avoid nāgapāṣāṇaka, punnāga, dagdhapañcaka, powdered conch-shell, iron excrement, and snake excrement; however,
one should resort to camphor, saffron, gorocanā, and aruṇā.
The wise man should cause [the cloth] to be dyed white with barley and *śālīyaka*.
If he should take lac, he should give it after it has been parched.
[He should offer] Ākāśa, Pṛthivī, Bhauma, Rāma, and likewise Śani.
One should divide the ground into five parts outside the site of the dwelling;
having first drawn a lotus, one should then draw the pericarp. With a composed mind, one should divide the previously arisen [space] using the tips of the index and middle fingers.
Or, by joining the index finger and thumb, one may begin with a blade of grass;
or, in the case of a general [rite], beginning with grass, or starting from the middle finger;
for the installation of Rākṣasas and others, or in the case of the planets, beginning with fire.

One should divide [the space] at the tip of the finger for the sake of accomplishing all desired aims; however, one should avoid it during consecrations, sacrifices to the planets, and rites performed for specific desires. I shall now describe the auspicious Maṇḍala, which bestows welfare and should be declared as auspicious.
Therefore, the Subhadra [mandala] is prescribed as bestowing both heaven and liberation.
One should construct the excellent mandala with a measurement of one and a half cubits;
one should specify that a cubit consists of twenty-four finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in all respects.
The middle finger of a maker who possesses an average thousand [of years] is measured at its middle joint;
this length of the middle finger is known as the *mānāṅgula*.
Furthermore, that space between two lines which does not depend upon the root-line [is also defined].
Having fixed a peg in the middle at the measurement of a fist or a forearm,
one should cause three circles to be made in the center— largest, intermediate, and smallest— using either the pair of grown thumb-nails or the mānāṅgula as the measure.
Having fashioned the pericarp and other parts, one should draw an eight-petalled lotus in the center; outside that, one should make a twelve-petalled lotus according to the sequence of the letters.
One should make a third enclosure outside with white color.

One should make it white, yellow, and reddish, and subsequently, at an interval of four finger-breadths (vedāṅgula), one should encircle it with white color; in the center, one should draw a *kalpalatā* (wish-fulfilling creeper).
Before the *subhadra* mandala, listen now to the description of the *sarvatobhadra*.
In all undertakings and in sacrifices, one shall obtain every auspiciousness.
The Sarvatobhadra mandala bestows nourishment in all sacrifices;
it was spoken by the Lord himself for the benefit of practitioners.
The first hand should be twenty-four finger-breadths long;
one should then lay down two threads at the corners and again two threads in the middle.
Thereafter, the practitioner should fashion the "fish" figures and lay down the threads along the diagonals.
One should lay down four threads according to the division of east and west;
again one should give four threads, and then again give the diagonal (karṇa) threads.
Thus, there shall be two hundred and fifty-six squares.
One should likewise drop the thread so that it becomes the seventeenth;
there shall be a pair of squares in the upper row, and at the side of the door, four squares in the first row, extending as far as three squares in the row of teeth.
The best of those fit for sacrifice should draw all the lines with white;
in the Vaiṣṇava sacrificial rite, the lotus should be white.
In the Śakti-yoga it should be red, and in the Śaiva rite, one should specify it as yellow.
In all types of consecrations, white alone is praised.
The pericarp should be made yellow, measuring one-fourth [of the total size]. Having heated it at the location of the cakora bird, the wise practitioner should perform the auspicious rite.
Starting from the base of the pericarp, one should fashion sixteen lines.
At the base of each line it should be white; in the middle, one should apply red;
and at the tip it should be yellow—having thus performed the encircling of the lotus.
One should provide that with a white color and yellow everywhere;
it should be red in the center, and thus one should arrange sixteen [squares].
One should place red in the corners and indicate the lotuses within the fields.

One should fashion the limbs of the pedestal with white; at the three points in the corners of the pedestal, one should arrange them in two rows of two using yellow pigment. One should fashion the feet with pure [white], and again with colors such as yellow and the rest.
A wonderful and beautiful work should be executed there, wherein one should place a *kalpalatā* (wish-fulfilling creeper).
The measurement of the *kalpalatā* is proclaimed to be two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
Two [revolutions] are recommended, and three revolutions in the manner of a conch-shell spiral are also praised.
One should visualize the clusters of branches bearing flowers and fruits of various colors;
it is joined by various herds of animals and flocks of birds.
For a Vaiṣṇava [temple], a Garuḍa is recommended, while for a Śaiva one, one should depict a monkey and a bull.

One should draw a tiger in the Śākta [direction] and a śarabha in the Aiśa [direction], adorned with yellow garlands. One should fashion the primary ornament (*śobhā*) with yellow and the secondary ornament (*upaśobhā*) with yellowish hues. In the corners, one should use black color; outside, there should be three enclosures (*veṣṭana*).
The delightful mandala should be made with white, yellow, and red [pigments].
Another is the Sarvatobhadra, which bestows all accomplishments;
it consists of all knowledge, is pure, and grants dharma, desire, and wealth.
O twice-born ones, having made it a perfect square, one should cast twelve lines from each of the directions;
therein a hundred squares are seen,
of which the first consists of forty-four and the lotus of thirty-six.
One should fashion the inner chamber (koṣṭha), the pedestal (pīṭha), and the pathway (vīthikā) here in rows;
the door-ornaments (dvāraśobhe) and the secondary ornaments (upaśobha) are to be arranged as before.
With the remaining good squares, the knower of mantras should construct the threads (tantrāṇi).

One should perform the remainder as before; thus the mandala shall be formed. O wise ones, in the previously described mandala, there should be a dwelling on the earth outside, and in the center, a wish-fulfilling creeper (kalpalatā) should be fashioned, O best of men, in the outer corners.
With the color of *gulālītūrya*, it is known as *mahāmatta*.
One should fashion the primary ornament (*śobhāgra*) with both primary and secondary ornaments (*śobhopaśobhe*); thus indeed shall the mandala come to be.
This is the *sarvatobhadra*; hereafter follows that which is joined with the heaps (*rāśi*).
The *śatapatra* has a diamond-like navel; the *biṃbanābha* has a thousand [petals];
the *gajāhva* is shaped like an elephant and is beautifully adorned in its center;
and that which has four moons is declared to be the *candrabimba*, which is as lovely as the moon.
It is proclaimed as "Sūryākānta" when surrounded by twelve suns on the outside;
then follow, in sequence, Śekharī, Tripuṭa, and Śatapatra.
O best of Brahmins, it is called "Sahasra" when there is a svastika at the end of the lotus.
O Brahmins, that [arrangement] is known as the Svastika; the Puṣkara is considered to be like a thunderbolt (vajra); the Cintāmaṇi consists of a portion of saffron; the Khāta is dear to Hari;
and that which is situated upon five lion-thrones is known as the Pañcasiṃhāsana.
In the same way, one should know the bull-throne (vṛṣāsana), the form of the peacock (śikhirūpa), and the one with the peacock-banner (śikhidhvaja);
likewise there should be the man-lion (nārasiṃha), the lotus-womb (padmagarbha), and the dove-faced (kapotāsya).
There is also the eagle-form (gāruḍa), the Meru-womb (merugarbha), the blue-throated (nīlakaṇṭha), and the human-shaped (narākṛti).
Śatakratu is mounted upon an elephant, adorned with the fresh thread of the Śrī-bimba;
it is octagonal, beginning with eight corners, with a forest of lotuses created on the outside,
encased by two *kāma* syllables, and surrounded by a thousand lotuses.
The lotus with three triangular centers is proclaimed to be triangular;
its petals are eight, and Meru is Sumeru in its inverted form.
The summit of the great Mahāmeru is surrounded by three hundred petals.
O twice-born ones, I shall explain the manifestation of the apertures according to measurement:
[the body] consists of eight, ten, twenty, forty, and fifty [units].
It is endowed with staffs and ears; the space is measured by the Vasus [eight].
Immediately thereafter, one should fill in two hundred and ten petals;
the bimba-like lips should be completed with white, red, and eight other colors.
Therein, one should first make a white lotus, and afterwards perform a triple encircling.
Now I shall describe the Śatapatra, which is called Bimbarāja.
On the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) and with kuśa grass in hand, one should encircle it in sequence as before;
the eight [petals] are the five kalās, and from that leaf [it consists of] twenty-five.
Thereafter, there should be forty, and then one hundred and eight.

White, red, yellow, and then dark-blue and white; the joints of the petals are in reverse order. In the Śākta system there is the six-city [arrangement], while in the Śaiva system there is the sixfold [structure].
One should encircle it on all sides with five colors, beginning with white;
having strewn the corners with red and yellow, one should fill them with white.
On the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila), one should prepare an area of eight cubits using a cord of ten cubits.

The maṇḍala of Bimbarāja is surrounded by one hundred and eight petals; it may have eight, five, twenty, forty, or fifty petals. It should be perfectly circular, provided with three seasonal petals, and endowed with a circular enclosure containing bilva leaves.
Forty-two [units] are covered by the sky;
one hundred, one hundred and twenty, two hundred and twenty are the superior [measurements].
One should increase by three hundred steps at each shoulder of the enclosure.
Now I shall describe the Lavalyābha [mandala], measuring one and a half cubits;
one should fashion nineteen [parts] and cast four lines.
Know that it is exactly the same from south to north.
When yellow [is used], white is visualized in the center, surrounded by semen;
when yellow is used for the planets and fortnights, red is established in the center.
All lines are white in rites for nourishment (pauṣṭika), while one should prescribe yellow as the primary color.
One should not employ it in rites for pacification; one should designate it as being attached to desire.
In the center, however, there is a red lotus; in the pair, there is a lotus of the Moon.
One should make that white in color, having cast aside the yellow color.
In the northeast and the northern quarter is the yellow lotus of Guru;
in the eastern direction is the white-colored lotus of Śukra;
in the western quarter is the black lotus of Śani, and in the southwest is the smoke-colored one.
One should fashion that [lotus] for Rāhu and likewise employ it for Ketu;
having joined them in the northwestern direction (vāyavyā), one should then draw a lotus.
Thereafter, the wise practitioner should fill in the junctions of the petals in reverse order.
On the exterior, it should be constructed with five colors and adorned with a youthful fortress (yuvadurga).
In the eastern and western directions, the area of the gateway should be white;
in the southern and northern directions, red is indeed recommended.
In the three locations and at the center, starting from a twelve-finger step,
one should increase it by one finger up to two cubits according to that division.
The five-lotus maṇḍala is to be known as adorned with four svastikas.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Statement of Values," in the second part of the Middle Section of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*. Sūta said:

One should not perform a sacrifice lacking sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), nor should one cause it to be performed lacking honor (māna). A sacrifice destroyed by a lack of honor is ruined; therefore, honor is highly praised.
Whatever the prescribed measure for a particular sacrifice may be, one should employ that very measure for it.

If all [officiants] act without measuring [the qualifications], they shall again go to hell. If in one's sacrifice a sinful person of low birth should cause the Preceptor (ācārya), the Hotṛ, the Brahman, or the assistant officiant— who must know the ritual rules— to enter [the rite], [the sacrifice is ruined].
Eighty cowries (varāṭas) are called one paṇa;
sixteen of those are known as one purāṇa, and with seven of those [silver purāṇas],
or eight silver [purāṇas], gold is prescribed as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for sacrifices and other rites.
At Mahārāma, two gold pieces are prescribed; at a well, half a gold piece;
at the Tulasī and Āmalakī sacrifices, one gold piece is declared;
at Yakṛlloka, one gold piece; and at Lakṣa, four gold pieces.
In the case of nine crores of oblations, the installation of deities,
and the consecration of a temple, eighteen gold pieces are prescribed;
for a tank or a lotus pond, half of that amount is proclaimed.
O best of men, during a great gift, an initiation, or the rite of releasing a bull;
likewise, when one releases a bull while still living, or performs a śrāddha at Gayā—
one should perform a sacrifice in the Kali age that does not require wealth for its accomplishment.
For a husband and wife, a single measure is prescribed for the rite of releasing a bull (vṛṣotsarga).
Even when performed by many most excellent persons, the sacrifice remains one.
Likewise, it applies to the king’s collection of taxes, his initiation (dīkṣā), and acts of giving.
Eighty rattis of gold are prescribed for the Śravaṇa sacrifice and for the Bharata sacrifice;
for the installation of a deity during a planetary sacrifice, one hundred rattis of gold are required;
and this same measure is ordained for the Lakṣahoma, the Ayutahoma, and the Koṭihoma.
The gift that has been prepared for the gods and the Brahmins must be given to them alone, complete with all its constituent parts and accompanied by a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Nothing at all should be given to anyone else, because otherwise there would be a violation of the ritual integrity.
Whatever gift a householder gives, he thereby becomes a debtor to that [deity].
Whatever substance— be it wood, clarified butter, or the like— is used in sacrifices and fire-offerings,
they say that substance is prepared for the worship of the Leader (Nāyaka).
In the worship of the beginningless deity, in rites such as ritual bathing and offerings,
whatever substance is used for honoring that deity shall belong to that deity alone. In sacrifices, gifts, vows, and the like, one should give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) directly.

One should never perform a rite without a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), nor should one perform it with a meager fee; rather, that which was given in the past, that which was given before, and that which is to be given now—
whatever is given by those whose minds are noble toward the property of others— that indeed shall be the true sacrificial fee.
Indeed, whatever divine gifts— such as female and male slaves, cattle, and so forth— have been duly given by men, even those which were merely intended in the mind at any time,
one should certainly cause them to be exchanged, even if they ought to have been given.

One person may give many gifts at once, or one may offer them individually. One should perform the formal selection (*varaṇa*) at some point and offer the ritual fee (*dakṣiṇā*) within the Tantra. As the ritual fee for a jewel, gold is prescribed.
For gold, silver should be given; for silver, one should offer gold. For land, land is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā); for clothing, clothing is the dakṣiṇā.
For water, water indeed; for rice, rice is the dakṣiṇā.
A goat is said to be the sacrificial fee for an elephant, and a sheep for a horse;
for all four-footed animals, the sacrificial fee for the deity is one-fourth. It is proclaimed that the sacrifice of a human being is sixfold, or twice that amount.
The sacrificer shall give one share to the preceptor alone;
immediately thereafter, one share for the wives of the wicked [officiants];
and three shares are prescribed for the vessels, the officiating priests, and others.
Out of respect for what remains, one should set aside a very small portion for every living being;
from the teacher's share, someone whose wealth is exhausted may collect it.
That which becomes the square root of the value of the priceless [mantra] shall indeed be the supreme sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
But when one is unable to perform sacrifices, whatever must be given for the successful completion of the sacrifice—
divinities, books, jewels, cows, grain, sesame seeds,
as well as *nameru* fruits and flowers— all these should be given in every respect.
He who is marked with four wheels, who is solid and circular, is Janārdana; likewise, there are images of deities and the like, as well as the head and the navel,
and the white liṅga, the jewel-liṅga, and those made of sapphire and other gems.
A right-spiraling conch, the Harivaṃśa, and the Khila;
a tawny bull, a blue bull, and likewise grain for the Soma sacrifice—
these they say are priceless, and by giving them, one obtains infinite fruit.
The price for a Śālagrāma should be one gold coin as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
For a small liṅga, the price is half a gold coin, and the same applies to the Śrīdhara. For the Ananta-liṅga, it is said to be "infinite," while for the Bāṇaliṅga, it is half a gold coin.
Just as gold is required for half a foot-measure merely by means of a book,
so too is half a *jyotis* of gold [required] for silver in the case of a bull;
and in the *Harivaṃśa*, one *suvarṇa* is proclaimed for a hundred verses.
For a transgression involving the Dharmaśāstra, three silver coins (rajata) are prescribed;
for a *kapilā* cow, half a gold coin (*suvarṇa*); and for a mere cow, one *purāṇa*. In the rules for expiation (*prāyaścitta*), it should be understood that "mere cow" refers to one *purāṇa*.
Others say that there should be three Purāṇas when [the bull] is devoid of vigor;
two when it is Kṛṣṇa; six Purāṇas when it is white; nine Purāṇas when it is Śveta;
and likewise thirty-two Purāṇas when the bull is blue.
In the Praticakra of Nameru, twelve gold rattikās are the price;
even for a mere *śrīphala*, it would be three *purāṇas*.
Even for a single row [of fruits], it would be four, due to the arrangement of *paṇas* in the Kali age.
For each *dhātrī* fruit, there shall be one-sixteenth of a silver *māṣaka*.
These are said to be the recommended values; however, they know that for the root [of the plant], the price is higher.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of Prices," in the second part of the Middle Section of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Description of the Payment of Fees.
Sūta said:
Now I shall describe the *pūrṇapātra* (the vessel of fullness), which is used both in sacrifices and in ordinary rites.
In the *kāmahoma*, a handful (*muṣṭi*) should be used; eight handfuls constitute a *kuñcikā*.
One should always fashion the vessels according to the measure of each *kuñcikā*.
Having prepared the vessels separately, one should place them at the entrance.
One should offer [the oblation] to each of the perfected sword-edge [deities] there itself, day by day; not elsewhere, and one should never perform a transposition.
Listen now to the manner in which the piercing of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) and the buds (kuḍmalas) is to be performed.
In the Kali age, half a silver coin is required for the Caturasra-pada;
two silver coins for the Sarvatobhadra; a fourth part for the Krauñcaghra;
five for the Mahasimhasana; and half of that for the Dasapatra.
On the thousand-spoked Meru summit, there is more than four thousand silver [units] on the bull;
on the bull's neck, there is a bull [of gold], and for the remainder, there are a thousand silver [units].
In the construction of the square [mandala] during the Kali Yuga, there is one quarter of gold.
In a large circular pit (*mahākuṇḍa*), one should offer double [the usual amount] in silver;
in a lotus-shaped pit (*padmakuṇḍa*), a bull; and in a crescent-shaped pit (*ardhacandra*), silver.
In a womb-shaped pit (*yonikuṇḍa*), one should give a cow made of eight and a half gold *māṣakas*.

In a six-cornered [mandala], it should be half of that; in a sacrifice, it should be two *māṣas*. In the Śaiva tradition, for both the rite of consecration (*udyāpana*) and every day thereafter, it should be one gold *māṣaka*.
For the rite of splitting (*dāraṇa*), it should be one cubit in measure, and it should consist of one *kṛṣṇala* of gold.
For the manufacture of bricks, there shall be a fine of two paṇas every day;
for a broken brick, ten varāṭakas; and for a large-sized one, one kākiṇī.
This applies to the first stage of digging a tank or a lotus pond.
In a sacrificial pit measuring seven cubits, once it has been completed and the foundation is secured,

one part of the total cost is proclaimed as the fee for the ancient [image]. One should increase the payment by one paṇa for each additional depth and for each leaf [of the pedestal], according to the sequence.
For the construction of a large well, two paṇas per day should be known [as the wage]; for stonework, one rattikā of gold; for housework, one and a half paṇas;
and for work involving painting and the like, one paṇa.
For the planting of trees, one should pay half a māṣaka every day;
for the construction of a bridge and for a muddy embankment, two paṇas and one kākiṇī;
and for every paṇa of copper, one should pay four paṇas.
For the smelting of bell-metal and lead, three paṇas are prescribed;
alternatively, for a number of days, one paṇa plus one kākiṇī.
For gold, however, one purāṇa is charged per paṇa when it is set in a jeweled inlay.
For silver, it should be half of that; for the cleaving of crystal, it is two paṇas for each day's count. For gems, the price is a pair of paṇas per day;
furthermore, for a gem with a perforation, the value is known to be one kākiṇī.
For piercing gems such as crystal, four varāṭakas are required;
for the manufacture of a bronze cymbal, three paṇas are charged,
while for the production of lac, half of that amount is prescribed.
For milking cows, at a water-station (varāṭa), and for the fourth wage, the fee is one-fourth;
for the manufacture of cloth, it is three hand-paṇas per piece.
For the manufacture of clothing for one who has no clothes, the charge is ten kākiṇīs per chariot-load.
For the manufacture of cloth for covers, a fine of three *paṇas* is proclaimed;
ten *kākiṇīs* shall be the wage for the sale of that [cloth] from top to bottom.
For one who lives by bamboo, half a *paṇa* plus one *kākiṇī* is the daily wage.
The wages for the barber and likewise for the blacksmith,
when shaving his head, should be known as ten *kākiṇīs*;
but when measuring the beard and nails, he should give two *kākiṇīs*.
Now, for the purification rites of women, for the decoration of the nails and so forth,
and for the breasts, one should give a *kākiṇī* and a *paṇa* to the Sun;
likewise, for the *sīmanta* ceremony and the application of collyrium, one should give a quarter of a *paṇa*.
In the case of footprints, however, it shall be one and a half [paṇas] for the concealment of the neck and the private parts;
likewise, for the planting of grains, the wage is one paṇa per day;
and the same should be given for the planting of salt and for the planting of jackfruit trees.
For the preparation of *daṇḍapatra* and likewise for black pepper,
the price shall be two *varāṭas* and ten more;
for *halehala*, it shall be one *paṇa* and one additional *kākiṇī*.
For buffaloes used for drawing a cart, the fine is three *paṇas* plus one additional *paṇa*;
for men used as carriers, it is one *paṇa* and ten *kākiṇīs*;
and for female slaves and donkeys, it is more than two *kākiṇīs*.
In the washing of cloth, provided it is free from oil and alkaline substances, one should pay one *paṇa* for each garment;
for long cloth, even if it is a *prastha* in measure, the fee should be increased.
Even for immediate washing, the fee is half a *paṇa*, but it becomes greater at the beginning of the day and so forth.

In the case of white cloth, there should be a reduction; in the case of fine cloth, one should increase the rate. The wage for the extraction of clay, for using a spade, for pressing sugarcane, and for the preparation of flowers, shall be ten thousand *kākini*s.
When strung with a cord, a *kākiṇī* necklace is double that length;
when unstrung, it is proclaimed as a *muṇḍamālā* (skull garland) extending up to two finger-breadths beyond the neck.
A *kaṇṭhamālā* (necklace) reaches three cubits, while one reaching down to the navel is called a *kamalā*.
O best of the twice-born, three *kākiṇī*s are required for the creation of *mālatī*,
*tulasī*, *jāti*, and *yūthī*; O excellent ones,
half of that again for *maruta*, and half of that again for *damana* and *bakula*.
One should increase the wages for the lamp-oil and the clarified butter;
at every watch (yāma), a silver māṣa [should be given], and for the oil, a kākiṇī.
The wise know that the wick of cloth should be of the measure of one and a half finger-breadths.
O best of the twice-born, its length should be six finger-breadths, neither less nor more; it should be made with twenty-five threads by one who is well-composed,
according to the measurement of five finger-breadths.
One should give [the gift] at the height of a cubit; however, for a fist-sized hand, it is middling.
For a three-cubit or four-cubit [height], the best measurement is declared. In a vessel of gold, the king is slain; in silver, it grants all desires.

A lamp-stand made of copper causes the exhaustion of one's lifespan, while one made of iron leads to an evil rebirth. A stand made of the excellent *karamarda* fruit is said to be most auspicious. Likewise, those made of bell-metal (*kāṃsya*) or tin (*ārīti*) are also recommended.
In the absence of an earthen vessel, one may use an earthen [container] free from human defects.
For a ten-ingredient incense (*daśāṅga-dhūpa*) worth twenty [units], the price is three *paṇas*.
One should prepare a wick half the size for the incense even when it is twelve finger-breadths long.

One should prepare a wick with cloths measuring five *hasta*s in length, or even with twenty-five; such a person is said to possess a "great wick" (*mahāvarti*). Thus ends the fourth chapter in the second part of the Madhyama-parvan in the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Description of the Determination of the Vessels.
Sūta said:
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the determination regarding the vessels (kalaśas).
When auspicious objects are offered into it, success in the expedition is achieved; however,
that success is not attained if the vessel is known to contain only its seven constituent parts— or even its five— when filled with mere water.
Then, having invoked the deity into unblemished flowers, one should worship him;
for it is proclaimed that worshipping the deities elsewhere is fruitless.
[This applies to] the banyan tree, the holy fig tree, the dhātakī, and the bilva.

One should place upon the pitcher the five-fold sprouts as prescribed. The pitchers are said to be made of gold, silver, copper, and so forth, or likewise of clay, in due order according to one's means.
The *plakṣa* trees should be indivisible, beautiful, all of them prime, well-filled, without gaps, and straight; the irrigation channels should have a single cultivator.
One should make [the channel] thirty-one finger-breadths wide at the mouth and double that, one hundred [finger-breadths], in length.

Its mouth should be eight finger-breadths wide, and for one who seeks the highest goal, it should be two finger-breadths [deep]. One should have the measurement made with metallic materials; however, for an earthen vessel, the following measurement is prescribed.
In the preparation of the water from the pitcher, one must certainly not employ an incorrect measurement.
I shall describe the installation of the water-pot (kalaśa), wherein the gods are present;
for if it is arranged out of order, a demon (yātudhāna) will surely carry it away. I shall explain the general procedure for the sacrifice according to my understanding.
When laying out the complete [mandala] upon a svastika according to the half-measure,
the wise one should divide the square further by equal vertical and horizontal measures,
drawing four lines and five eastern foundations.
One should sweep [the ground] into the shape of a svastika so that it measures four finger-breadths;
thus a svastika arises there as the seat for the water-pots (kalaśas).
One should perform the demarcation of the site with the mantra "syonā pṛthivī."
One should place [the mantra] with the middle and ring fingers facing toward Pātāla.
Nārāyaṇa is its seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is its meter, and the Sun is its deity.
Its application (viniyoga) is for installation as well as for the formal acquisition of the ground.
One should recite the Dhānya-sūkta with the mantra "dhānyamasi.
For this mantra, Gautama is proclaimed as the seer (ṛṣi); the meter (chandas) is Anuṣṭubh, and its deity is remembered as Guru.
Having smelled the jar, one should then place the jar upon the ground;
having released the little finger and the thumb,
the ritual placement (nyāsa) should be performed at the front and the belly of the pitcher with the Brahma-mudrā over a space of three finger-breadths.
The seer (ṛṣi) of this mantra is declared to be Bharga;
Paṅkti is specified as the meter (chandas), and the deity is the imperishable Viṣṇu.
One should employ it both in the ritual installation of the water-pot (kalaśa) and in the Soma sacrifice.
Then, one should sprinkle Gaṅgā water with the mantra beginning "pañcanadya.
The deity is the supreme Triṣṭubh, and its presiding deity is Soma;
its application (viniyoga) is proclaimed as being for the purpose of ritual placement upon the sprouts (pallava).
One should offer unbroken rice grains along with fruit using the mantra "yāḥ phalinī.
Regarding this mantra "yāḥ phalinī," the seer (ṛṣi) is known as Kamala,
the meter (chanda) is Triṣṭubh, and Gaṇapati is proclaimed as the deity (devatā).
One should avoid these fruits: the jujube (badara), the citron (nāgara), the emblic myrobalan (dhātrī), the neem (picumardaka), the jīvantī, and the pīvara.
One should deposit five gems with the verse beginning "hiraṇyagarbha."
The seer of this [verse] is Hiraṇyagarbha, its meter is declared to be Triṣṭubh, and its deity is Savitṛ; one should apply it to the "depositing of jewels" (ratnanyāsa).
One should perform the "rendering immortal" (amṛtīkaraṇa) as well as the "divine lead" (daivaśulbana).
With the mantra "Varuṇasya tvā," one should join the rishi within the interior of Varuṇa;
with the mantra "Śrīśca te," one should offer a flower together with sandalwood paste;
and with the mantra "Gandhadvārā," one should offer well-blended perfume.
Furthermore, one should offer *dūrvā* grass and unbroken rice with the mantra beginning "kāṇḍāt";
and with the mantra beginning "vrīhayaśca," one should deposit five types of grain:
sesame, black gram, mung bean, *śyāmāka*, and *śāli* rice are traditionally recorded as these.
"The group of five grains is proclaimed as the destroyer of all misfortunes.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Months," in the second part of the Madhyama Parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said:
Now, in order to perform the rites pertaining to the months, the definition of the month is set forth;
according to its various types, the month is fourfold in number.

The lunar, solar, civil, and likewise another, the sidereal; that which begins from the first day of the bright fortnight until the new moon is the lunar month. That period during which the sun remains within a single zodiacal sign is called the solar month.

A month consisting of thirty days is proclaimed as the *sāvana* (civil) month; the *nākṣatra* (sidereal) month is well known as beginning with Aśvinī and ending with Revatī. That which goes from sunrise to sunrise is the *sāvana* day of the sun.
The time consisting of one-thirtieth part of a lunar day is a single solar day;

likewise, the time consisting of one-thirtieth part of a zodiac sign is the duration of one solar day. However, that [calculation] does not apply to the solar day when measured by its own specific divisions.
A full day and night (ahorātra) is obtained for the primary duration of the practice according to the solar measure;
however, in the lunar measure, the two auxiliary periods are not seen within the thirty parts. Therefore, in the time and household of the sages, the civil days (sāvana) are to be accepted.
In the determination of shares, in the performance of penances,
in the practice of mantras and worship, in the feeding of an infant,
in the taking of the hand [in marriage], in royal legal proceedings, and in the months [of the lunar cycle].
In sacrifices, the solar month is to be adopted for the calculation of days;
however, the *sāvana* (lunar) month is used for marriages and other such rites when accepted by the ancients.
It is also employed in sacrifices, religious observances, and prescribed acts of ritual bathing.
The lunar month (cāndra) is to be accepted for the Pārvaṇa rites, the annual rites, and the Aṣṭakās;
it is used for Śrāddhas, matters concerning lunar days (tithi), and vows prescribed for specific lunar days.
The sidereal month (nākṣatra) is used for the calculation of the portions of the Āryas and others, such as the Soma-drinkers.
In the matter of collecting taxes from the subjects, this [lunar month] does not possess the form of all months for kings;
likewise, the rites prescribed for the months beginning with Caitra and for specific lunar days (tithis) are observed,
yet those must be performed according to the lunar month, for it is that which is designated as Caitra and the others.
When the king has spoken, the Sāvana [month] is declared for the purpose of dividing the lunar days (tithis);
therein, the Saura [month] should be stated because of the application of the term "saura.
That full moon day associated with the Citrā constellation is known as Caitrī.
The month characterized by that [full moon] is called Caitra.
That month, consisting of lunar days (tithis), is the lunar month; it is marked by the sun being in Śravaṇā.
The lunar month ending with the full moon of Caitrī is the primary one, designated as beginning with Caitra.
This [lunar month] is considered secondary because it is extended in accordance with the beginning of the Yugas and other such cycles;
the primary month, defined by the characteristic of ending on the new moon of the bright fortnight and so forth, is regarded as technical (lākṣaṇika).
Furthermore, those twelve lunar months beginning with Caitra are established through conjunction (yoga).
But those [months] joined with the full moon do not attain the status of a lunar mansion (nakṣatra) month,
whether they fall under Viśākhā and the following [asterisms] or under Bhādrapada;
that month in which there is no conjunction with the full moon shall be destructive.
Although this [yoga] may be found even as a constant state in Caitra and other months,
just as it occurs in the solar month, this yoga is exceedingly difficult to achieve;
nevertheless, by means of this yoga, it may occur somewhere within any month whatsoever.
If, at the end of a thousand years, that very lunar mansion is joined with the full moon,
there occurs the destruction of the kingdom;
for the sun and the moon always take their meal upon the lunar day.

One should never eat when two *daṇḍas* remain of the previous meal; nor should one eat after having passed the next lunar day (*tithi*) upon which both [the previous and current days] overlap. Since there are twenty *daṇḍas* in a lunar day, one [unit] should be accumulated from that.
Indeed, by thirty lunar months, one [solar] month is increased by the moon;
because that month is an extra one, it is called an *adhimāsaka* (intercalary month).
Having made night and day equal, one reaches the city of Vaivasvata.
As long as the radiant sun travels from one zodiac sign to another,
he increases the lunar days (tithis) that have previously accumulated;
the lunar days continue to increase until the maker of day reaches Libra.
But in the six signs beginning with Libra, it never increases at all,
because the sun transits them with its natural, even motion; whereas in the [other] six signs, each month increases by one day due to the accumulation [of the sun's transit].
Furthermore, O son of Sūrya, even during the nights, there may be three [tithis] in a single day;
when a month consists of exactly thirty lunar days,
that is the impure (malina) lunar month, as desired by the followers of Koṇapa and others.
When the moon, having been eclipsed by the sun for that month, transits while remaining untouched by the sun's rays,
then that month is to be known as *malimluca* (intercalary).
Thus, when two and a half years are completed, the moon falls [into such a state].
Furthermore, all those lunar days that have been omitted and those that have occurred out of sequence must be applied; there shall be no man who fills [the gap].
For the sake of welfare, the comet Jalaketu proceeds toward the southwest.
The month that is devoid of the *mama* (possessive) suffix and is considered impure (*malina*) is for the benefit of the *pretas*.

Therefore, O best of the twice-born, all rites for the deceased (*pretakriyā*) should be performed even during the intercalary month (*malimluca*). Furthermore, those actions which ought to be done and those which ought not to be done during the impure month shall now be stated.
I shall now declare that śrāddha pertaining to the deceased which was mentioned in passing, up until the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa;
that must be performed even during an intercalary month (malamāsa), for the sapiṇḍana does not perish.
But when the twelfth month happens to be an intercalary month due to fate,
the annual rite for the deceased must be performed with effort in that very month;
even if another month falls within it, [the rite is still performed] in that same intercalary month.
Then, in the thirteenth month, that sapindikarana should be performed;
however, in that thirteenth month, one monthly śrāddha must be omitted.
Even now, a śrāddha is considered to increase [in frequency] by thirty ghaṭikās.

One should diligently perform the annual śrāddha rite even during an intercalary month (malimluca), and one should also perform occasional rites (naimittika); however, there is no authority for those two [types of rites] [to be performed at that time].
Bathing at sacred fords (tīrtha) and the first visit to a deity are likewise unattainable [during such a period].
One should perform the rites of fasting and so forth, as well as the *sīmantonnayana*,
the *puṃsavana*— excluding the period of menstruation— and the first sight of the face of a son and other such ceremonies,
even during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*) or when Venus has set.
One may perform the coronation of kings even during an intercalary month (malamāsa),
as well as the commencement of vows, consecrations, the tonsure ceremony, the investiture of the sacred girdle,
the secret practice of mantras, and highly auspicious great gifts.
One should not perform marriage, the construction of a house, the entry into a new dwelling,
the acquisition of cattle and other livestock, the transition to another stage of life (āśrama),
long sacrificial rites, pilgrimages, or the consecration of wells during the long mātrās.

A learned man should avoid in an intercalary month (mala-māsa) the rites for increasing prosperity, the ritual release of a bull (vṛṣotsarga), the marriage of a daughter, the second initiation (upanayana), and sacrifices performed for specific desires. Likewise, when Venus has set, or during its periods of old age and infancy, one should likewise renounce these.
Its setting (asta) is of two kinds: partial (pādāsta) and total (mahāsta).
Of this [planet], the total setting occurs to the east for seventy-two days;
the partial setting on the earth itself lasts for twelve years.
For two hundred and forty-nine days,
the planet Venus (Kāvya), having risen in the west, is visible at all times;
it remains so as long as it stays in the same lunar mansion as Jupiter.
Just as during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*), they say all ritual acts are to be abandoned in every respect;

likewise, if there is a conjunction of these two [the Sun and Moon] within a single zodiac sign despite a difference in constellations, or even in the case of Jupiter or Rāhu, the wise man should abandon [the rites], without a doubt.
When the Sun is situated in the sign of Leo and Jupiter has set,
those actions which are to be abandoned and forbidden during the intercalary month (malimluca) [should be avoided]. When the Sun is in Gemini, this intercalary month falls.

The month known as "Double Āṣāḍha" is so called because of the figurative application of the term. Furthermore, for one performing the funeral rites (aurdhvadehika) for a deceased person during this time, the invocation of the name "Āṣāḍha" must be performed; the same applies even in other years.
Likewise, when there are two full-moon days connected with the two Āṣāḍhas,
and the two zodiac signs of Gemini and Cancer [occur], then it shall be a double Āṣāḍha. That secondary double Āṣāḍha occurs precisely when conjoined with that same sign.
When the first triad [of months] has passed, the Blessed Lord Hari makes his bed in Cancer; he will come forth again in the subsequent triad.
While the Sun is in Cancer and Hari is asleep, the worship of Indra should take place in the month of Āśvina.
"In the scale [of the year], at the rising of Durgā, Viṣṇu abandons his sleep.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Rules for Lunar Days," in the second part of the Madhyama-parvan within the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said:
Whether it be the action pertaining to the gods or that pertaining to the ancestors, it proceeds depending upon time;
it is at the proper time that those very actions yield fruit for those who perform them.

In childhood, the fruit of action is not found even at the three times; nor does expenditure primarily yield fruit for those characterized by their actions. Time, however, exists as a subordinate factor, for every action is dependent upon time.
Nothing whatsoever in the three worlds arises without time;
therefore, I shall here explain Time as the instrumental cause of actions.
For although the Blessed One is indeed one and formless, he exists as Time alone.
Nevertheless, it is differentiated by the distinctions of limiting adjuncts (upādhi) according to the divisions of time—

such as lunar days, asterisms, and weekdays— as well as the conjunctions with night and so forth; these temporal factors also apply within the intervals of fortnights, months, zodiac signs, and years.

These means of accomplishment do not belong to anyone independently; they are the primary operation of either dharma or adharma. For that which is prohibited or enjoined with respect to times such as lunar days and so forth is indeed established [as such].
By protecting [the earth], one attains heaven; by abandoning it, one reaches a downward state.
Even while accomplishing their respective tasks, they look toward one another;
for even those who are the instruments of action are powerless against the portion of time.
One should perform Vedic rites on a lunar day that extends into the forenoon;
one should indeed perform the Ekoddiṣṭa rite on a lunar day that extends into midday;
and having reached a lunar day that extends into the afternoon, one should perform the Pārvaṇa rite.

However, one should not perform rites such as those dedicated to the gods at inappropriate times during the forenoon, midday, or afternoon; rather, one should perform such secondary rites as the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* and others at the single time of morning.
It does not require assistance on the specific lunar days, equinoxes, and so forth;
for Brahmā granted the forenoon together with the lunar days to the gods,
while the afternoon was granted to the ancestors, except for the Pārvaṇa rite.
When the [lunar day] arrives at the very beginning of the forenoon (pūrvāhṇa), one should then worship the gods;
even when it merely touches the forenoon, one should offer it according to the division of the lunar day (tithi).
For the lunar day is of three kinds: Kharvā, Darpā, and Hiṃsrā.
One should overcome Kharvā and the others when they are equal; Darpā becomes increased.
Hiṃsrā, however, should be known as arising from decay and is seized according to the distinction of time.
Kharvā and Darpā are to be seized later, while Hiṃsrā is to be seized earlier.

In the bright fortnight, the later [tithi] should be accepted; in the dark fortnight, the earlier is praised. This application regarding the conjunction with a weekday (viṣayoga) is demonstrated for bathing, giving gifts, and vows, whether the sun rises during the tithi or at any point within its duration.
That same lunar day (tithi) should be understood to persist throughout that entire day and night;
whichever tithi the sun remains upon for ten ghaṭikās or more,
that tithi alone is to be designated for that day and night, and no other.
