Whether in the bright or the dark fortnight, whichever lunar day (tithi) is short or full, that day on which the sun sets is the one for the ancestral rites (pitṛkārya). Even if the Kutapa period occurs during both days, one should rely upon the lunar day that ends at sunset.
Wherever the time for the *śrāddha* and so forth occurs, there the *śrāddha* is prescribed;
likewise in the case of a vow or an occasion of prosperity (*vṛddhi*), it is performed when the sun rises.
And in the *pārvaṇa* *śrāddha* on the new moon day, that lunar date is used for the worship of the ancestors.
Wherever the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha for the deceased occurs on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*),
that lunar day which ends at sunset is the "abode of the ancestors" (*pitṛmandira*).
One should perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite there, but never when it does not rise [at sunrise].
In both the bright and dark fortnights, whichever lunar day (tithi) falls on the yoga of the previous or the following day,
and which extends across the three junctions (saṃdhyās) either on the preceding or the succeeding day— that tithi is to be honored in one's own religious rites during both fortnights.
Indeed, those who know the Dharma should observe these meritorious lunar days (tithis) after abandoning the individual first and eleventh days,
as well as the second day joined with the third, and the fourth day joined with the fifth.
These are the days to be fasted upon.
But these [days], when mixed with others, destroy even previously accumulated merits:
the sixth day pierced by the fifth (Bāṇa), the eighth pierced by the seventh (Muni),
the eleventh pierced by the tenth, and the fourteenth pierced by the thirteenth.
The new moon day (amāvāsyā) that is pierced by the fourteenth day (bhūta) should not be observed as a fast even by a sage;
if one does observe a fast on such a day, it destroys one's sons, wife, and wealth.
Those [days] which are pierced should not be censured, for they are praised by those who are disciplined.
When there is a possibility of separation, the pair becomes pierced in every respect;
having reached each respective lunar day (tithi), the pairs attain non-worshipability.
The pairs should be accepted when joined with the daytime; there is censure for those that are separated.
In the case of observances such as the *nakta-vrata*, one should avoid the conjunction with the sun during the day;
however, the conjunction occurring at night on the two [consecutive] fourth days is specifically preferred.
Even without the nocturnal conjunction, the vow of the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) and others may still be observed.
Keeping a vigil at night is indeed commended even when there is no conjunction with the twelfth day;

however, one should observe the fast on the eleventh day only if it is conjoined with the twelfth. If there is a conjunction during the daytime, one should reject that which is complete [only by day], whether it precedes or follows both days.
When conjoined with night, that Ekādaśī is always to be fully observed.

Even the seventh day (Saptamī) of the bright fortnight is to be honored when it is joined with the sixth (Ṣaṣṭhī). But when the sixth occurs at night and the seventh and ninth occur during the day, [the latter are to be observed].
Having fasted on the sixth day alone, a man should propitiate the Sun;
likewise, O twice-born ones, having fasted on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight according to the prescribed rule,
one who propitiates only the Lord of Pārvatī [attains the same merit].
If the fourteenth day (caturdaśī) is joined with the thirteenth day during the daytime, it should be observed as a fast;
however, one should not perform the fast on the subsequent fourteenth day if it does not include the new moon (amāvāsyā).
If, having reached a time that pervades the three junctions (trisandhyā), one should perform the fast.
One should break the fast on the day of Sinīvālī, the fourteenth lunar day;
for by breaking the fast after passing the fourteenth day,
his vows are destroyed, as is the merit of the ordinary fourteenth-day observance.
The seventh [tithi] is Lalitā; in Bhādrapada, there is Śaktyutthāna and Vāruṇī.
These supreme [tithis] should be worshipped even when they extend across the three junctions (saṃdhyās).
If [the tithi] extending across the three junctions occurs earlier and then increases further, [the one occurring earlier is to be taken].
When there is a conjunction with the asterism Ṛkṣā, it is [the time for the rite]; in the absence of Ṛkṣā, the next [conjunction] is joined [to the rite].
Even when the three twilights (saṃdhyā) overlap, the next one should be accepted in the absence of Ṛkṣā.
Moreover, in the first quarter of the month of Śrāvaṇa, it is highly recommended for the worship of Indra (Śakra).
In its absence, Uttarāṣāḍhā and Dhaniṣṭhā are especially distinguished.
Whether it lasts for half a daṇḍa, one daṇḍa, half of that, or even a single pala, that lunar day (tithi) joined with the rising [of the asterism] should be accepted; it is most excellent.
Excluding the [eighth day] that extends across the three junctions (trisaṃdhyā), the subsequent white eighth day (śuklāṣṭamī) is to be worshipped;
it should be accepted by the Lord of the Solar Wheel (Ravicakravartin) even if it occurs on the chariot-day (ratha-tithi).
However, that which extends across the three junctions but exists for only a single pala on the following day [is not to be taken].
Furthermore, one should everywhere avoid driving oxen;
on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight, on the new moon, on the day of a solar transit (saṃkrānti), and on the day of a śrāddha ceremony,
one becomes a sinner by driving men, horses, cattle, elephants, and so forth.
The master shall not cause his oxen, buffaloes, donkeys, camels, or mules to be driven by male or female slaves; there is no fault in using them as vehicles.
This applies likewise during long-duration sacrifices and sacrificial śrāddha ceremonies.

There is no fault in [riding] between villages, nor in the sky, nor even across a river. Also, regarding the monthly *śrāddha* which occurs during the obligatory daily *śrāddha* when water-jars are used, there is no defect in using cattle, buffaloes, and the like for transport.
One should perform the water-pot *śrāddha* (aṃbughaṭa-śrāddha) without any restriction regarding time;
one should not impose restrictions on the food, and one must avoid using stone vessels. The vessel may be made of metal or fashioned from tree leaves.

One should not employ earthenware for Śūdras; the rule regarding earthenware applies [only] to them. At the end of the month, one should offer the earthen vessel at the foot of a tree. One should have another person strike it, but never with a cloth under any circumstances.
One should avoid the *daivalaka* at a *parva-śrāddha*, as well as one who has entered the stage of a widower (*raṇḍāśrama*).
One who abandons his mother and father, or one who sells oil, sacrificial offerings (*havya*), and the like—
if such a person should perform forty-eight festivals, [the merit is lost].

A certain man is liberated from his wife; he is considered to be one who has entered the stage of the *raṇḍāśramī*. As long as the age of forty-eight years is not completed, one who is separated from son and wife has no entitlement to perform sacrifices.
The lunar day (tithi) upon reaching which the sun rises is considered complete for the purposes of ritual bathing, study, and giving;
however, in the dark fortnight, that lunar day is complete by which the sun sets.

In rites such as ritual bathing and giving for the ancestors, all [days] should be known [as suitable], provided they are not interrupted by other lunar days (khaṇḍitā) according to one’s desire— specifically, the seventh day of the bright fortnight occurring in the first part of the sun [day] while conjoined with the sixth, or occurring at the end of the [sixth] while conjoined with the eighth.
If she remains unbroken, she should then be known as Bhavātmikā;
likewise, by means of the month of Māgha, she is Pūrvā Ravitoṣiṇī,
while by the subsequent [month] she is Manvantarā during acts such as bathing and drinking.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the second part of the Madhyama-parvan within the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa.
Description of the Determination of the Most Excellent Tithis.
Sūta said:
Since this has been proclaimed by Brahmā as the most excellent of lunar days (tithis),
it is established in the subsequent and preceding [periods]; having been established, it is now being declared anew—
especially during the months of Kārttika, Āśvayuja, Caitra, and Māgha.

Bathing, giving gifts, and the worship of Śiva and Viṣṇu yield tenfold merit. Having performed the fire sacrifice on the first day of the lunar fortnight (pratipad), it is traditionally taught that one obtains all kinds of grain and desired wealth through oblations.

Having performed the ritual worship on the second day of the bright fortnight under the constellation Bṛhaspati (Jyeṣṭhā), one should eat only at night; thus one obtains the desired prosperity. Furthermore, during the months of Mithuna and Karkaṭa, after the subduing of cows and Brahmins, [one should perform the rite].
O best of Brahmins, having fasted on that second lunar day, one should worship Hari;
by fasting on this day, a woman never falls into widowhood—of this there is no doubt.
For the month of Amūlyaśayana, the couple should perform worship.

By bathing in the waters of the Gaṅgā on the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, and likewise honoring her with garments, perfumes, flowers, and various kinds of diverse foods, a person is liberated from all sins.
Especially on the third lunar day conjoined with the asterism Svāti in the month of Vaiśākha,
or when it is conjoined with Rohiṇī in Māgha, or likewise in Taurus during Āśvayuja—
whatever is given on that day is declared to be inexhaustible.
The wise especially praise the gift of sacrificial food (haviṣya) combined with sweetmeats (modaka) and the like, as well as the gift of water;
one who gives [water] mixed with jaggery and camphor is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
If the third lunar day (tṛtīyā) is found conjoined with the asterism Śravaṇa and the weekday Wednesday,
bathing, fasting, and other such rites performed on that day are proclaimed to be inexhaustible.
When the fourth lunar day (caturthī) coincides with the asterism Bharaṇī, it becomes a "moving" day (caradina).
By worshipping the god Yama at that time, one is liberated from all sins.
The fourth lunar day is remembered as being of three kinds: Śivā, Śāntā, and Sukhā;
that [Sukhā] occurring in the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada is highly honored in the world of Śiva.
In the month of Kārttika there is the Śāyā-tithi, and likewise it is proclaimed in Māgha;
on that day, bathing, austerity, charity, fasting,
and japa become multiplied a thousandfold, and a śrāddha becomes inexhaustible.
One should respectfully perform the worship of Gaṇeśa with sweetmeats (modaka) and other offerings on the fourth lunar day for the destruction of obstacles and the fulfillment of all desires;
especially so on the fifth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Śrāvaṇa.
One should bathe nine elephants with fragrant scented waters;
they grant fearlessness and protection of life to those in their lineage,
especially on both twelfth lunar days (Dvādaśīs) when one bathes them with cow-dung.

One should worship with devotion using curds, milk, vermilion, and other offerings. When Janārdana is asleep on the fifth day of the dark fortnight (Kṛṣṇapañcamī), one should mentally worship the Goddess Vāmā, who resides in the Snuhī plant, within the courtyard of the temple.

A man who places the leaves of the *picumanda* tree within his house and worships the Goddess shall not encounter the fear of serpents. O best of the twice-born, this is the sixth lunar day (*ṣaṣṭhī*) that occurs in the month of Bhādrapada.
All acts such as bathing and giving charity performed on that day are said to be inexhaustible.
O Brahmins, one who subsists on fruit on the sixth lunar day— especially during the months of Māgha and Kārtika—
attains preeminent and supreme renown both in this world and the next.
When the sun transits on the seventh day of the bright fortnight,
that seventh day is indeed Mahājayā, beloved of the Sun;
while the seventh day of Bhādrapada is Aparājitā, which destroys even the greatest sins.
Lalitā alone should be known as the one who increases sons and grandsons;
whether it be the sixth or the seventh lunar day,
if it falls on a Sunday, that date is remembered as most meritorious.
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina, one should worship her who has eighteen arms;
or else, during the bright fortnight of Kārttika, with extensive and magnificent offerings.
And on the eighth day of the bright fortnight in the months of Āṣāḍha or Śrāvaṇa, one should worship Caṇḍikā.
Having bathed in the morning, O twice-born ones, one should worship with devotion; at night, one should perform the ritual bathing.

On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra, O twice-born ones, one should worship the earthen image of the Goddess with Aśoka flowers for the sake of freedom from sorrow at all times.
Or, the eighth lunar day conjoined with the Rohiṇī asterism occurring during the eighth muhūrta of the day is also praised when the sun is in Leo in the month of Śrāvaṇa;
by this, one obtains the fruit of performing the vows of ten million Ekādaśīs.
Therefore, it is declared that by performing this [rite], one obtains ten times the fruit.
Even one who is unable to perform other rites, by undertaking a fast alone,
is liberated from sin— the best among those who have performed the sevenfold duty.
There is no restriction regarding time there, nor any restriction regarding the day of the week;
there is no defect in the lunar mansion (nakṣatra), nor is the defect of the weekday taken into account.
One should worship the God three times a day, especially by day and at night.

Especially at midnight, one should perform the vow with various kinds of flowers. However, if the lunar day (tithi) is not present during the day, one should not perform the vow according to the rules;
it may be performed at night only if the eighth day (aṣṭamī) extends into the night.
If the seventh lunar day (saptamī) extends for one and a half watches (yāmas), or if Rohiṇī does not touch it at all,
the observer of the vow (vratī) should make his formal resolve (saṃkalpa) during that time, and never at night.
One who observes the vow should perform the commencement before the [lunar] intercalary month (adhimāsa) has exceeded its limit.
One should first avoid visiting Viśvanātha and other such deities;

one should observe a fast wherever one may be and perform the eight-watch vow (yāmāṣṭaka-vrata). After half a watch has passed, the observer of the vow should then proceed with the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) during the [next] watch.
A householder who is intent on that [observance] should not break his fast with food obtained from others;
during the conjunction of a lunar mansion or an eclipse, he should worship the Supreme Lord.
A householder should perform recitation, fire-offerings, and so forth, but he should never fast.
On the eighth day of the lunar fortnight, or during the Muhūrta joined with the Prajāpati constellation,
one should likewise perform the daytime rites and then observe the vow;
even at the end of the Muhūrta, at the end of the month, or on the eighth day when Rohiṇī is present.
Regarding the fault that may arise from fasting, worship and fire-offerings (homa) are highly commended.
On the ninth day, twice-born ones should always worship ten thousand images every month;
one should likewise undertake a vow so that the ritual yields its fruit.
On the tenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika,
Brahmins who partake of a restricted diet shall attain the world of Brahmā;
if that tenth day occurs in the month of Jyeṣṭha, it is remembered as Daśaharā.
The Ekādaśī in the month of Āśvina is known as Mahāpuṇyā, while in Kārttika it is remembered as Vijayā. Devoted to the vow, it destroys all sins;
thus do men act, becoming completely liberated from all evil.
On the tenth day, one should eat only one meal, remaining self-controlled and with senses subdued.
Having fasted on the eleventh day, one should then break the fast on the twelfth day.
A wise person should act in this manner, for [otherwise] they would destroy twelve sets of twelve lunar days.
If the eleventh day (Ekādaśī) is complete on the previous day and increases on the following day,
while the twelfth day (Dvādaśī) does not increase, then the rule is as follows:
one who dwells in the forest (a forest-dweller) should observe the later day, whereas one in the householder stage (a householder) should observe the earlier day.
If both lunar days increase, the previous Ekādaśī should be abandoned;
rather, the fast should be observed on the subsequent lunar day, namely the Dvādaśī.
However, when the Dvādaśī does not remain available for the Pāraṇā (the ritual breaking of the fast), [one should observe the fast on the Ekādaśī].
In that case, the previous [Ekādaśī] alone should be observed, and the increased [Dvādaśī] should be abandoned on the following day.

If the Ekādaśī is joined with even a single moment (kalā) and the Dvādaśī is complete, the merit therein is equal to a sacrifice; however, the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) should take place on the Trayodaśī.
If the Ekādaśī and Dvādaśī are not found on the following day,
that [Ekādaśī] should not be observed as a fast, for it carries great fault due to the destruction of sons, grandsons, and wealth.
When the Ekādaśī is pierced by the Daśamī and there is even a single *liptikā* of Dvādaśī [on the next day].
If the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) is unfit for breaking the fast and increases on the following day,

then it must be abandoned on both days, and the breaking of the fast must be performed according to rule after observing the sixteenth lunar digit (ṣoḍaśī). In such a case, the twelfth day is considered one where the breaking of the fast is omitted.

If the guest is fierce, it destroys even the merit previously performed; likewise, breaking the fast on the thirteenth day does not bestow merit. Furthermore, one who lives as a householder should not observe the vow when there is a conjunction (kṣaya) of the tenth or twelfth lunar days.
Even if the sun’s transit occurs on the tenth day, which is as fierce as ten Rudras,
one should nevertheless completely abandon it and observe the fast on the twelfth day;
for if the tenth day should enter [the twelfth] even by the mere glance of a lightning bolt, [it renders the fast invalid].

The eleventh day (Ekādaśī) must not be observed as a fast; rather, the following eleventh day is the one to be kept. If, however, that [following] Ekādaśī is pierced by the tenth day (Daśamī), it should still be observed as a fast without fault.
That best of men who performs the fast on the twelfth day (Dvādaśī) [is likewise virtuous].
He goes to the supreme abode where Viṣṇu is free from all affliction. But the man who, out of delusion, fasts on the eleventh day while the tenth has not yet passed,
goes to hell after death due to the destruction of his lineage of dharma.
On a Sunday, a Friday, at a solar transit (saṃkrānti), or on the day of the conjunction of the moon and a lunar mansion (dinakṣaya),
one should observe a fast and avoid breaking the fast;
this applies whether it falls in the bright or the dark fortnight, even if it was previously intended for another day.
One should always observe Ekādaśī, but never the one following Kṛṣṇā (the twelfth) under any circumstances.
It is the settled conclusion of the scriptures that one should pass the Kṛṣṇā [Ekādaśī] by eating only at night.
Whenever Ekādaśī occurs in the bright fortnight of a month—
In that regard, one should perform it during the dark fortnight; the later lunar day is not accepted.

When the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa coincides with the constellation Bhadra-pada and the moon is in the sign of Leo (Harau), a person, having fasted there, should worship Hṛṣīkeśa according to the prescribed rites.
On the twelfth day (dvādaśī) in the months of Śrāvaṇa and Āśvina,
when it is conjoined with the asterism Śravaṇā, it is proclaimed as "Mahatī" (the Great).
When the twelfth day in Phālguna is joined with the asterism Puṣya, it is known as "Vijayā" (the Victorious).
If it is to be abandoned in Kārttika, one would become a denizen of hell in Māgha.
That which is called Vijayā in Bhādrapada, conjoined with the Śravaṇa asterism—its specific details are now told; therein one should perform the vow exactly as prescribed.
If the twelfth day (dvādaśī) follows the eleventh (ekādaśī) on the northern side [of the lunar month] and is joined with the daytime,
and if the twelfth day is full at night and also conjoined with the Śravaṇa asterism,
that twelfth day should be known as fruitful; it must be observed as a fast and yields great rewards.
On the twelfth day (dvādaśī) pierced by Viṣṇu [the eleventh day], one should worship Vāsudeva;
however, on a dark (kṛṣṇa) [twelfth day], one should perform the vow, for otherwise one would experience great suffering.
If the twelfth day is pierced by Kāma [the tenth day], one should not even consider fasting.
One should destroy previously accumulated merit by fasting on the thirteenth day. Bathing at every watch of the night is prescribed;
the observer of the vow should perform worship and fire-rituals during these six periods.
If the Śravaṇa nakṣatra reaches both the Ekādaśī and the Dvādaśī,
one should fast on the Ekādaśī and likewise observe the fast on the Dvādaśī;
however, the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) should take place on the Trayodaśī if the Dvādaśī is not available.
One should not eat meat; the breaking of the fast should be done with sacrificial food (haviṣya).
When a Dvādaśī suitable for breaking the fast is obtained, then it is not proper to let that day pass; in its absence, the Trayodaśī may be used.
When the eleventh and twelfth lunar days are conjoined with the Śravaṇa asterism on a Wednesday,
it is known as Viṣṇuśṛṅkhala and is especially distinguished.
Having remained self-restrained on the tenth day, one should do so again at dawn on the eleventh day.
Having performed a bath at the confluence at every watch of the day, O twice-born ones,
and having observed this supreme vow on the Vijayā day according to this rite,
a man shall bring all his sins to an end and dwell in the world of Viṣṇu.
For as long as he bears the form of Viṣṇu throughout the four divine yugas,
for that long indeed shall that man be a sovereign ruler everywhere.
O twice-born ones, during the Tretā age, he shall have ten births in the Middle Country.

And thereafter, in the land of Bhārata, he is born for ten lifetimes as the best of Brahmins during the Tretā age— one who knows the essence of the Vedas and Vedāntas, endowed with sons, grandsons, and wealth, a giver of hundreds of thousands, and equal to a king.
Accompanied by his wife, long-lived, and honored in the performance of righteous deeds,

he should rouse the lord of the earth against his enemy on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada, during the forenoon, at an auspicious lunar mansion and a favorable moment.
Of the Śalya, Śālmali, Saptaparṇī, or any one of these trees— whether it be a Campaka, an Arjuna,
or a large Kadamba tree— one should [measure] with forty-two finger-breadths.
Alternatively, there are two measurements: either thirty-two finger-breadths or three *vyāyāmas*.
The first [measurement] is twenty-two cubits;
for a householder with sixteen wives, eighteen cubits is specifically recommended.
The height for a Brahmin shall be twelve cubits, for a Kṣatriya twelve as well,
for a Vaiśya eight cubits, and for a Śūdra five cubits.
Above the clouds, there shall be a white umbrella and a banner in every city.

A man who is firm in devotion should perform the worship with great steadiness, having placed [the image] upon a pedestal, joined with camphor, adorned with camphor ornaments, covered with red cloth, and decorated with flower garlands.
The knower of mantras should perform worship for seven nights with the Aindra mantra.
He should never touch crows and the like, especially those belonging to the enemy's side. If the banner falls, one should predict the ruin of the kingdom.
If the banner is displaced or broken, it portends the destruction of buffaloes;
if a pillar falls or is broken, one should predict the loss of horses. Furthermore, there will be thieves in his family, and he should perform an expiation.
With the mantra "tad viṣṇoḥ," one should offer ten thousand oblations of *pippala* wood dedicated to Viṣṇu, accompanied by a hundred lotuses;
and the wise man should offer ten thousand oblations for the planets, using one-third of that amount.

O twice-born ones, this is the wonderful portent of the Sun when a bird falls; one should indicate the portents of Venus when a pigeon falls, and those of Mars when a crow or similar bird falls. One should indicate the wonderful portent of Jupiter when an earthquake occurs.
O Brahmins, if a wound caused by an insect occurs on the Moon [in the lunar mansion], one should predict a portent for Candra;
if the banner is blown out or broken, one should predict a portent for Rāhu;
and if jackals howl or a monkey touches the Moon [in the lunar mansion], one should likewise predict a portent.
O twice-born ones, regarding the Ketu rite prescribed for an earthquake:
having reached the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight, one should worship Kāmadeva with various kinds of flowers and most enchanting perfumes and other offerings.
If, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Caitra, there should be a Saturday conjoined with the Śatabhiṣā nakṣatra,
and if this occurs at the Gaṅgā, it is equal to a hundred solar eclipses.
This very thirteenth day of the dark fortnight is renowned as Mahāvāruṇī.
Bathing, giving gifts, and performing ancestral rites (śrāddha) in this [tirtha] are said to yield inexhaustible merit.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Madhu, there is the Dambhabhañjī Caturdaśī;
on that day, one should worship the imperishable Kāma at the root of the Madana tree.
By the power of Madana, he goes to the supreme abode;
for Manobhava was perfectly pleased by his contemptuous words.
I shall now describe the vow of Ananta, which destroys all sins.
The man who, full of devotion,

performs worship on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) to Śakra, to the flagstaff, or to the sacrificial posts, shall attain infinite bliss; thereafter, on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, he should worship Hari as Ananta.
Having fashioned an image of Ananta out of *darbha* grass and provided it with water and grain,
one should worship it with sandalwood paste, fragrances, and various kinds of food offerings,
as well as with fourteen fruits, roots, and aquatic flowers.
Having prepared a cake called *pūpa* from the flour of barley, wheat, or rice— using only one of these— he should give one to him who has heard [the teaching], as prescribed by the scriptures;
he himself should eat one, and he should tie a cord of the sacrificial grass (*satra*) around [the recipient's] arm.
A thread made of fourteen strands of cotton, smeared with saffron and provided with fourteen knots;
then, on the fourteenth day of the fortnight of the deceased, having fed those whose wealth is austerity (tapodhana), [one should perform the rite].
Having given gifts to the twice-born, one does not go to the world of Yama.
Then, having heard the discourse on the departed (pretas), one should subsist on vegetables at night for the fourteenth,
twelfth, seventh, or even the fifth [day].
Having performed even a mere prostration and so forth, one is liberated from all sins.
Who could fail to purify their own sin by drinking the water of the banyan tree in the month of Māgha?
Having bathed there on the fourteenth day at the time when the stars appear, [one attains liberation].

That fourteenth day of the dark fortnight which occurs in the month of Phālguna is renowned as Śivarātri; it grants all desires for the entire world. If it is not obtained during the day, one should observe the vow when it coincides with the night.
One should avoid that vow on the fourteenth day when it is pierced by the new moon (amāvāsyā).
When the lunar day is joined with the night and is complete, one should perform the vow.
That [fourteenth day] pierced by desire (kāma) is also to be honored; the observer of the vow should perform it when there is conjunction with the night.

At every watch of the day, having bathed oneself, one should cause Śiva to bathe according to the rules with devotion, and perform the fire-oblation (homa) according to the prescribed rite. Now I shall describe how the full moon occurs in the months beginning with Caitra.

If the full moon is conjoined with the Citrā nakṣatra while Jupiter is present, that full-moon day is known as Mahācaitrī; it bestows inexhaustible merit. When the full moon moves through the various divisions beginning with Viśākhā while Jupiter is present, [the same applies].
The twelve full-moon days beginning with Mahāvaiśākhī are traditionally recorded;
this Mahājyaiṣṭhī is a special occasion, occurring when the sun is in the constellation Prājāpatya (Rohiṇī) and Jupiter and the full moon are in Jyeṣṭhā— that is remembered as Mahājyaiṣṭhī.
Even without the moon being in conjunction with the Guru (Jupiter), when the full moon occurs in Kṛttikā,
that lunar day becomes the most meritorious Mahākārttikī; likewise,
when the moon is situated in Rohiṇī on the full moon day of Kārttika, it is so.
Likewise, the Mahākārttikī, whether it be Citrā or Pūrṇā, when the lunar day is the full moon, is difficult to obtain even in the heavenly world;
so too is the Mahācaitrī, which bestows the fruit of a horse sacrifice.

When the full moon on a Sunday occurs in conjunction with the Kṛttikā constellation, it is known as Mahācaitrī; likewise, even if it falls on another day, it renders whatever is given inexhaustible. Similarly, when the full moon on a Thursday occurs in conjunction with Jupiter (Guru), it is proclaimed as Mahācaitrī.
There, bathing, giving gifts, recitation, and even the observance of vows—
all these become inexhaustible, and their fruit is equal to that of a horse sacrifice.
The ancestors, being gratified, go to the imperishable world of Viṣṇu.
If the full moon day occurs under the constellation Bharaṇī in the month of Kārttika,
it is known as the great Vaiśākhī at Gaṅgādvāra, bestowing great merit. At Śālagrāma, that same lunar day is the great Caitrī, a high festival through which merit is secured.
At Gaṅgādvāra, the great Vaiśākhī is remembered as bestowing merit;
at Puruṣottama, the great Jyaiṣṭhī; at Śṛṅkhala, the great Āṣāḍhī;
and at Kedāra, the great Śrāvaṇī is considered most meritorious.
At Badarī, there is Mahābhadrī, and likewise a man becomes Kuja;
at Puṣkara, there is Mahākārttikī, and similarly Uttara at Kānyakubja;
and in Mārgaśīrṣa, there is Mahatī at Ayodhyā, as well as Uttara.

The Mahāpauṣī is most meritorious, as is the Mahāmāghī at Prayāga; the Mahāphālgunī at Naimiṣa is likewise declared to yield great fruit. Whatever action is performed here, whether auspicious or inauspicious, [it becomes so].
Everything becomes inexhaustible, and the fruit increases even further.
The full moon day of the month of Āśvina is celebrated as Kaumudī;
on this day, at the rising of the moon, a person should worship Lakṣmī according to the prescribed rites.
That twice-born man who does not perform the ancestral *śrāddha* at dawn on the new moon day month after month must undergo penance.
On the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvina, he should perform it according to the prescribed rule.
Having performed the rites such as bathing and observing a fast, one should pass the day;
then, at the time of dusk, having worshipped Lakṣmī according to the prescribed rules,
one should set out lamps on trees and other plants for the pleasure of Lakṣmī.

One should cause them to be placed on a riverbank, on a mountain, in a cow-pen, in a cremation ground, at the foot of a tree, at a crossroads, in one’s own house, or in a marketplace. One should never eat a second meal on the new moon day (amāvāsyā).
"And especially on the night of the new moon in the months of Māgha and Phālguna, [this should be performed] by men.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Consideration of Pravaras," in the second part of the Madhyama-parvan within the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said:
O twice-born ones, I shall describe the lineage of the Pravaras in their proper order; for without this, there would be a confusion, and therefore I speak according to the scriptures.
The three *pravara* lineages of Kāśyapa are certainly those of the Kāśyapas and Āśvalāyanas;
those of Gautama today are Pañcāśva, Gautama, and Cyavana;
and likewise Cyavana, Jāmadagnya, and Āplavāyana.
From the commentary of Mokunī-Aṅgiras comes the Jāmadagnya-Āplavāyana;
likewise, the three *pravara* lineages of Śāṇḍilya, Asita, and Daivala,
as well as Parāśara’s own Śāmbava and Śiṣṭhaka.
Indeed, the lineage of the teacher Ātreya is preeminent from childhood;
Vātsya, Vāsyāyana, and Urukaṇṭhaka,
as well as Arthakṣīra and Mitrāvaruṇa, are proclaimed as the fifth.
One should know that Autathya has three [schools]: Vālmīki is indeed the lowest;
furthermore, the Vāśiṣṭha, the Aindra, and the Krauñcāyana belong to Autathya.
That which is known as Autathya also includes the Māhiṣya and the Cyavana.
One should know the three Urukaṇṭhas and likewise the three Kauśikas;
O twice-born ones, that which is known as Gāla, Devarāja, and those beginning with Kuśika—
Viśvāmitra, Devarāja, and himself are considered the triad.
From Ghṛtakauśika came the Kuśikas, from Viśvāmitra came the Aghamarṣaṇas,
and likewise from Caṇḍakauśika came the Devarātas; furthermore,
the lineage of Sumantu is indeed renowned as belonging to Viśvāmitra.
Taruṇa Śākaṭāyana himself [declared] three *pravara*s;
Jaimini’s own two *bhrama*s, as well as Vāsiṣṭha itself;
and the triad of Śaṅkha, Āṅgirasa, and Cyavana is considered the *pravara* for Śaṅkha-bha.
The son of Vātsya was named Cyavana, and likewise Āplavāyanaka.
Of Sāvarṇya, however, there were Sāvarṇi, Cyavana, Jamadagni, Bhārgava, and Āplavāyana; O best of men, these are the readings for Pāṭhīna, though some maintain that there is only one.
The *kṛṣṇājina* of Kṛṣṇājina, the *jaimina* of Viśvāmitra,
the three [recensions] of Kātyāyana— namely Kātyāyana, Gārgya, and Āyana—
as well as the one renowned as Vātsyāyana, and the fifth belonging to Kuśika.
Viśvāmitra, Jāmadagnya,
Āplavāyana, Gārgya, and likewise Aṅgiras,
as well as Bārhaspatya and Bharadvāja— these five are proclaimed.
The lineage of Vasiṣṭha is that of the Vāsiṣṭhas, and likewise that of Aṅgiras;
it is proclaimed as being joined with Mitrāvaruṇa. Jāhvakarṇa and Bhavakarṇa are proclaimed as his two principal ancestors (pravaras).
Upamanyu, Upamanyu, and likewise Indra;
"Taduttama"—these three belong to Mitrāvaruṇa, and there are indeed three pravaras:
Ātreya, Gautama, and Āṅgirasa.
Kamaṇḍalu, Utpala, Mitrāmitra, and Varuṇa,
as well as Kamaṇḍalu— this triad is indeed the three *pravara*s of Cyavana;
likewise, Ūrvacyavana and Āplavāyana are to be known [as his].
Now, he belongs to the lineage of Kasyapa, Angiras, and Bṛhaspati;
and to that of Agastya— namely Agasti, Māha, and Cyavana—
and likewise to Viśvāmitra, Devarāta, and Autathya.
"O Kāśyapa, those things which have not been spoken and those which are even unknown have been declared to the world.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Vāstuyāga," in the second part of the Middle Section of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said:
Now I shall describe the Vāstu sacrifice, preceded by the offering of oblations (*bali*) and the ritual planting of sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*); one should construct the mandala in the center.
A square pedestal (piṇḍikā) measuring three cubits and overflowing with water on all sides should be made;
its height should be one span (prādeśa), and it should be as smooth as the surface of a mirror. In the center, the wise man should sweep away the nine lines (pādas) in their proper order.
In the corners, a four-square [pattern] is to be known; in the cardinal directions, a three-square [pattern] in sequence;
then, beyond that, a five-square [pattern] with double steps in the four directions.
Having established a four-square [pattern] in the corner, one should visualize it within the four corners.
One should draw a square on the outside and also four [lines] at the corners;
there would be thirty-two [deities] on the exterior, and thirteen more from that [interior],
making forty-five Vāstu deities in total when combined.
Śikhin, Parjanya, Jayanta, Kuliśāyudha,
Sūrya, Satya, Vṛṣa, Ākāśa, Vāyu,
Pūṣan, Vitatha, Guha, Aja, and likewise Yama.
Gandharva, Mṛgarāja, and the hosts of Pitṛs; then Dauvārika, Sugrīva, Puṣpadanta, and Jalādhipa;
as well as Asura, Paśu, Pāśa, Roga, and Mokṣa.
Bhallāṭa, Soma, Sarpa, Aditi, and Diti—
these twelve external deities, beginning with Īśāna,
should be worshipped by the wise one in their proper order, situated in the four corners starting from Īśāna.
Āpa, Sāvitra, Jaya, and likewise Rudra;
Aryaman, Savitṛ, Vivasvat the lord of the gods;
Mitra, Rājayakṣman, and the seventh, Pṛthivīdhara.
The eighth is Āpavatsa, who is remembered as belonging to Brahmā on the enclosing-stick (paridhi).
Likewise, they should be worshipped with various kinds of perfumes and flowers in the directions starting from the east.
This constitutes forty-five [deities], and the fourth belongs to Carakī.
O Brahmins, one should not employ fewer than forty-nine supreme deities of the site (vāstudevatā), especially in the case of a temple; however,
one may place Carakī and the others, as well as Caraka and Vidārī, in the outer corner.
And thereafter, one should worship Pūtanā and the evil Rākṣasī in the northwest (vāyavya) with their respective mantras, using perfumes, flowers, and other offerings; furthermore,
one should present the bali-offering as prescribed, or else with milk-rice (pāyasa).

One should visualize the lotus with white lines everywhere; one should color it with red pigment, and its exterior with five-colored powder. Now, I shall describe the colors of the deities exactly as they have been described.
Rakta, Gaura, Śoṇa, Sitarakta, and Sita;
Pīta, Śukla, Dharma, and Rakta are proclaimed as Pūṣan;
and Śyāma, Śukra, Kṛṣṇa, Pīta, and Śukla follow in due order.
Yellow, bumblebee-colored, white, black, and likewise white;
red, white, crimson, and likewise black-red;
smoky-yellow, reddish-yellow, white, black, and dark-brown.
By means of the color red, thirty-two colors are proclaimed.
Furthermore, white and red is proclaimed as the color sindūra;
pale yellow is like saffron, while red is to be known as yellow.
White-yellow, yellow, white, and fair—these are the eight colors;
yellow, red, dark-blue, and fair—these are the four.
On the musical instrument, [the colors] begin with the color of Śambhu (white) and proceed in order.
One should color the gates white, as well as the central city gate;
in the center and at the ends, there are forty-nine [sections] in all for the work of the site (vāstuka),
and there are also forty sections including the gates for the house and the temple of the deity.
Likewise, Śveta is praised in the Mahākūpa and elsewhere;
in a well-smeared and pure place measuring one and a half cubits,
there should be ten lines extending eastward and ten extending northward.
One should form the square for the eleventh [deity] with lines and a grid;
through the division of the entire site-plan (*vāstu*), nine groups of nine should be understood.
One should worship thirty-five deities situated within those squares.
Thirty-two [deities] are to be worshipped on the outside; thirteen are to be worshipped in the hall of worship (pūjyāgāra);
in the center, Brahmā occupies nine squares, with eight others situated near him.
In the four directions, there are squares of six, three, and four [units].
A single square in the four corners— this is the determination of the site (vāstu).
Having then set aside the forty-five [squares] beginning with Carakī,
I shall describe another mandala correctly and in due order.
By means of the application of nine lines, one should arrange nine squares;
then, one should worship Āryaman with two squares in each of the directions,
followed by Vivasvat, then Mitra, and after that Mahīdhara.
In the corners and in the pairs of cells, starting from the exterior as previously described,
[one should place] Sāvitra and Savitṛ, Śakra and Indra, Jaya again,
Rudra and Rudrajaya, Vāyu and Jṛmbhaka.
The wise one [should worship] Pilipiccha, Vidārī, and likewise Pūtanā; then,
extending in order up to Īśāna, Jayanta, Śakra, and Bhāskara,
as well as Satya, Vṛṣa, and Antarikṣa, are stationed in the eastern direction.
Agni, Pūṣan, Vitatha, Yama the guardian of the house,
Gṛdhra, Bhṛṅgarāja, and Mṛga are stationed on the southern side.
Then come Nirṛti, Dauvārika, Sugrīva, and Varuṇa.
Puṣpadanta and Svara, as well as Śoṣa and Roga, are situated in the western direction. Prāṇavāyu, Nāga, Soma, Bhallāṭa,
the one named Mudgala, Diti, and Aditi are situated in the direction of Kubera (the north).
Having combined these, one should offer an oblation (bali) to the fifty-three [deities] previously mentioned,
using either oil-cakes, fine rice-pudding, or the aforementioned items, in their proper order.
One should meditate upon Aryaman as being red in color and surrounded by four or many [attendants].
[One should meditate upon] the divine [deity] whose vehicle is a white horse, adorned with his own crowns;
for the mantra beginning with "ākṛṣṇena," the seer is Svarṇa, the meter is Jagatī, and the application is for the propitiation of Savitṛ and Aryaman.
[He is] Vivasvat, yellow-colored, wearing yellow garments, and auspicious.
[One should meditate on] Mitra, who is situated in Aries, possesses a massive body, and is served by gods and Gandharvas.
For the mantra "etā taviṣīm," Kardama is the seer (ṛṣi), Paṅkti is the meter (chandaḥ), Kamalā is the deity (devatā), and the application (viniyoga) is for the propitiation of Vivasvat.
One should meditate on Mitra as being white in color, seated upon a white swan.

One should meditate upon the pleased Mahīdhara (Śiva), who has three eyes, possesses three faces, wears white garments, and is auspicious; [this is for] the mantra *Kayā naścī*, where Jayanta is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Gāyatrī is the meter (*chandaḥ*), Śaṅkara is the deity (*devatā*), and the application (*viniyoga*) is for the propitiation of Mitra. One should meditate on him seated upon his bull.
[One should meditate on] the three-eyed [Lord], who has a triangle, holds a lotus in his hand, and wears a serpent as a sacred thread.
For the mantra "tryambakam," Garga is the seer (ṛṣi), Triṣṭubh is the meter (chandaḥ), Hara is the deity (devatā), and its application (viniyoga) is for the propitiation of Mahīdhara.
[One should meditate on] Sāvitrī, white in color and endowed with all auspicious marks.
[She is] two-armed, wearing yellow garments, seated upon a white lion-throne;
she wears red robes, is red in complexion, and is adorned with a red garland.
For the mantra "tad varṣam," Gautama is the seer (ṛṣi), Virāṭ is the meter (chandaḥ), Sūrya is the deity (devatā), and its application (viniyoga) is for the propitiation of Savitṛ.
One should meditate upon Śakra, yellow in color, seated upon the white elephant Airāvata,
being praised by all the gods, having two arms, and wearing yellow garments.

For the mantra beginning with "Trātāram," Bhārgava is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Triṣṭubh is the meter (*chanda*), Narasiṃha is the deity (*devatā*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is for the propitiation of Indrajaya.
One should meditate upon Rudra as white in complexion, with a form mounted upon a bull,
wearing a serpent as a sacred thread (yajñopavīta), and endowed with all auspicious marks.
For the mantra "namaste rudra," the meter (chanda) is Gāyatrī, the deity (devatā) is Tryambaka, and its application (viniyoga) is for the propitiation of Rudra.
One should meditate upon Rudra Jaya as red in complexion, seated upon a red lotus,
wearing red and dark-blue garments, having two arms, and clad in red robes.
For the mantra "Tryambakam," the meter is Gāyatrī, the deity is Maheśa, and the application is for the propitiation of Rudra Jaya.
Then one should meditate upon the Supreme White One, who bestows boons and fearlessness,
endowed with all auspicious marks, and seated upon a white lotus.
For the mantra "Īśāna," Marīci is the seer (ṛṣi), Paṅkti is the meter (chandas), Vāyu is the deity (devatā), and its application (viniyoga) is for the propitiation of the waters.
[One should meditate upon] the supreme [deity] Āpavatsa, yellow in color, mounted on a ram, four-armed,
holding a lotus and a conch in his left hands, and displaying the gestures of granting boons (*varada*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*).

O best of men, for the mantra "Varuṇasyottaṃbhanam asi," Narottama is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Virāṭ is the meter (*chandaḥ*), Varuṇa is the deity (*devatā*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is for the propitiation of the waters (*āvayaḥ*).
Furthermore, on both sides of the diagonal line within the two white squares,
one should meditate upon Śarva, red in color, seated upon a bull,
having two arms and three eyes, and adorned with a mass of matted hair.
For the mantra *mālā svāhā*, Bhārgava is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Gāyatrī is the meter (*chanda*), Mahādeva is the deity (*devatā*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is for the propitiation of Śarva.
One should meditate upon Guha as yellow in complexion, seated upon a yellow lotus throne,
enriched with the splendor of various ornaments, and adorned with earrings and other finery.
For the mantra "sa bodha," Agastya is the seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is the meter (chandaḥ), Hara is the deity (devatā), and its application (viniyoga) is for the propitiation of Guha.
[One should meditate on] Aryaman as two-armed, red in color, adorned with red garlands,
seated upon a red lotus throne, and served by gods and Gandharvas.
"Vāto vāreti"— O Kāśyapa, the seer of this mantra is Ṛṣi, the meter is Anuṣṭubh, the deity is Vāyu, and its application is for the propitiation of Aryaman.
One should meditate upon Jambhaka as white, two-armed, with a crooked face,
a terrifying countenance, and fierce, seated upon a boar.

For the mantra beginning with "kuvidogavaya," Viśvāmitra is the seer (ṛṣi), Jagatī is the meter (chandaḥ), Soma is the deity (devatā), and its application (viniyoga) is for the propitiation of Jambhaka.
[One should meditate on him as] having a plum-colored body, adorned with red garlands,
seated upon a red lotus throne, and beautified by red ornaments.
For the mantra *devasya hetih*, the meter is *Paṅkti*, the deity is Śacī, and the application (*viniyoga*) is for the propitiation of Pilapiñcha.
One should meditate upon Carakī as yellow in color, adorned with red garlands,
possessing a very beautiful face, auspicious, and graced by a necklace of *guñjā* berries.
For the mantra beginning with "tad varṣam," Jaṭila is the seer (ṛṣi), Bṛhatī is the meter (chandaḥ), Bhava is the deity (devatā), and its application (viniyoga) is for the propitiation of Carakī.
One should meditate upon the goddess Vidārī as dark-complexioned, three-eyed, four-armed,
accompanied by various hosts, and holding two lotuses.
For the mantra beginning with "śrīśca te," Varuṇa is the seer (ṛṣi), Nṛsiṃha is the deity (devatā), and its application (viniyoga) is for the propitiation of Vidārikā.
One should meditate upon Pūtanā as red in color, seated upon a lotus, exceedingly beautiful,
endowed with all ornaments, and adorned with every finery.
For the mantra "mayi gṛhṇāmi," Vivasvān is the seer (ṛṣi), Nārāyaṇa is the deity (devatā), and its application (viniyoga) is for the propitiation of Pūtanā.
In all directions, beginning with the east, and at the middle and final points of each,
one should meditate upon Īśāna— matted-haired, white, holding a trident in his hand, and possessing great arms.
One should meditate upon the three-eyed Parjanya, mounted on a bull, adorned with a necklace of serpents.

For the mantra "Āyuḥ śīrṣāṇi," Vāmadeva is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Bṛhatī is the meter (*chanda*), Dharaṇīdhara (the Earth-bearer) is the deity (*devatā*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is for the propitiation of Īśāna.
One should meditate upon him as red in color, two-armed, and clad in yellow garments.
One should meditate on an axe in the right [hand], and likewise on the syllable *oṃ* in the other.
For the mantra "kayā naḥ," Dharma is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Bṛhatī is the meter (*chandaḥ*), Bhava is the deity (*devatā*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is for the propitiation of Parjanya.
Having meditated upon Jayanta, who is white and mounted upon a white bull.
For the mantra *mānastoke*, Śakti is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Triṣṭubh is the meter (*chandas*), Śaṅkara is the deity (*devatā*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is for the propitiation of Jayanta.
Having meditated upon [Jayanta] as white and yellow, two-armed, seated on Airāvata, and holding a thunderbolt, one should establish him with the root seed-syllable (*mūlabīja*).
Having meditated upon Bhāskara as red and two-armed, seated upon a red horse, one should worship him with the *māyā* seed-syllable.
One should worship Satya, who is two-armed, white, three-eyed, and clad in yellow garments, with the seed-syllable of the moon (*maṃ*).
One should worship Vṛṣa, who is yellow and mounted upon a bull, with the seed-syllable of space (*haṃ*).
One should worship Ṛkṣa, who is blue, four-armed, and mounted upon a buffalo.
For the mantra "ācchīma," the Hotṛ is the seer, Triṣṭubh is the meter, Śaṃkara is the deity, and its application is for the propitiation of the stars.
One should worship beginning with Agni;
having meditated upon Agni as red, seven-tongued, clad in red garments, and tawny-eyed.
For the mantra *agnidūtam*, Bharadvāja is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Triṣṭubh is the meter (*chandaḥ*), Śaṅkara is the deity (*devatā*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is for the propitiation of Agni.
Having meditated upon Vitatha—red in color, mounted on a goat, and possessing two arms—one should worship him with the Gāyatrī.
For the Gāyatrī, Viśvāmitra is the seer, Gāyatrī is the meter, Savitṛ is the deity, and its application is for the propitiation of Vitatha.
One should meditate upon Yama, who is dark-complexioned, mounted upon a buffalo, and holding a staff in his hand.
For the mantra *acchiya*, the meter is *triṣṭubh*, the deity is Bhavānī, and its application (*viniyoga*) is for the propitiation of Yama.
Having meditated upon him as having a house, a field, red hair standing erect, mighty arms, and red garments, one should worship him with the seed-syllable of fire (*vahni-bīja*).

Having meditated upon the white Gandharva, two-armed and seated upon a lotus throne, one should worship him with the seed-syllable of Yama. One should meditate upon Bhṛṅgarāja as mounted upon a red lion-throne and wearing a divine sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*).

For the mantra beginning with *hotā yakṣat*, Bhārgava is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Gāyatrī is the meter (*chandas*), Yaśas is the deity (*devatā*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is for the propitiation of Bhṛṅgarāja.

Having meditated upon a yellow deer, mounted by a deer and clad in yellow garments, [one recites] the mantra beginning with "kadācana. Vāmadeva is the seer (ṛṣi), Bṛhatī is the meter (chandaḥ), Vāmadeva is the deity (devatā), and its application (viniyoga) is for the propitiation of the deer.
It is also [recited] at the half-footed steps of Nairṛta.
Having meditated upon Nirṛti as yellow and white, seated upon a lotus throne;
[one should know that] for the mantra *kaidācana*, the meter is *paṅkti*, the deity is Savitṛ, and its application (*viniyoga*) is for the propitiation of Nirṛti.
And in the southern half-sections, one should meditate upon Dauvārika, who is mounted upon a white Śarabha, has three eyes, and is adorned with all ornaments.
For the mantra *hotasva*, Narasiṃha is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Bṛhatī is the meter (*chandas*), Gaṇeśa is the deity (*devatā*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is for the propitiation of Dauvārika.
Having meditated upon him as dark-complexioned, with a beautiful neck, black, mounted upon a ram, and clad in yellow garments;
for the mantra *svādityā*, Triṣṭubh is the meter, Vāmana is the deity, and its application is for the propitiation of Sugrīva.
For the mantra *sumitriyā naḥ*, Kandarpa is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the Paṅkti meter (*chandas*), and Sūrya is the deity (*devatā*); its application (*viniyoga*) is for the propitiation of Varuṇa.
Having meditated upon Puṣpadanta as yellow, mounted upon a ram, and clad in yellow garments;
for the mantra *yā oṣadhīḥ*, Manmatha is the seer, the Jagatī meter, and Vāyu is the deity; its application is for the propitiation of Puṣpadanta.
Having fashioned the Asura Kṛṣṇa adorned with black garlands,

one should meditate upon the black Asura, endowed with snake-garlands and seated upon a lotus throne. For the mantra beginning with "Ā kṛṣṇena," Hiraṇyavarṇa is the seer (ṛṣi), Jagatī is the meter (chandaḥ), Savitṛ is the deity (devatā), and its application (viniyoga) is for the propitiation of the Asura.
For the mantra *ā brahman*, Nalina is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Triṣṭubh is the meter (*chandas*), Bhavānī is the deity (*devatā*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is for the propitiation of Soma.

Having meditated upon the black disease as wearing a blue lotus and mounted upon a white bull, [one recites] the mantra *namaste rudra*; for this, Nārada is the seer, Paṅkti is the meter, Śrī is the deity, and its application is for the propitiation of disease.
One should perform worship beginning from the northwest (vāyukoṇa).
Having meditated upon Vāyu, who is smoke-colored, holds a banner in his hand, and is mounted on a deer;
for the mantra "devā," the meter is Bṛhatī, the deity is Yama, and the application is for the propitiation of the Nāgas.

Having meditated upon Śveta Soma, white in color and seated upon a white-colored throne, one should worship him with the seed-syllable *Bhadrā*. Having meditated upon Rakta Bhallāṭa, yellow-robed, one should worship him with the seed-syllable of Fire (*Rak*).
One should worship [the deity] clad in yellow garments, mounted on a goat, and adorned with necklaces and armlets, using the seed-syllable of Wind (*Ya*) along with Mandara and the others.
Having meditated upon Diti as red in complexion, adorned with a necklace of serpents, and seated upon a red lotus throne,
one should worship her with the mantra beginning "mānārthaṃ.
For the mantra "māno tvā," Bhārgava is the seer (*ṛṣi*), *paṅkti* is the meter (*chandaḥ*), Pṛthivī is the deity (*devatā*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is for the propitiation of Diti.
Having meditated upon Aditi as yellow-complexioned, mounted upon a lion, and wearing yellow garments; [one should perform the ritual].
For the mantra beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇa," Janārdana is the seer (ṛṣi), Bṛhatī is the meter (chandaḥ), Soma is the deity (devatā), and its application (viniyoga) is for the propitiation of Aditi.
Having thus performed [the meditation] according to the rules, one should then perform the fire-oblation (homa) according to the prescribed rite.
At the conclusion of the *homa*, one should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consisting of gold combined with refined metal;
however, in the case of a tank-consecration sacrifice (*taḍāgayāga*), it should be gold or even half of that.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the second part of the Middle Section of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Description of the Sequence of Worship.
Sūta said:
Now I shall describe the sequence of worship as enjoined by the Purāṇas and the Smṛtis.
One should perform it in the north, the west, or even the east;
on a riverbank or at the edge of a wheel-track, O Brahmins, one should prepare a mandala numbering ten or twelve, provided with two types of sacrificial porridge (caru).

One should divide the field into three parts; with two of the middle parts, one should construct a three-cubit altar (vedikā) that is as high as a palm tree and slopes toward the north. Between the northern and southern [sections], at a distance of one cubit, there should also be [a space] of one aratni.
One should fashion a pedestal with three girdles, measuring one cubit [in height],
provided with cords and a sacrificial altar; at its base, there should likewise be a white girdle,
and one should arrange a four-finger-wide altar that is elevated in the middle.

One should place the vulva (yoni), measuring six or seven finger-breadths, upon the western edge of the girdle (mekhalā) so that it is joined with the navel; in this manner one should fashion the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
One should perform the Śrāddha rite characterized by prosperity and carry out the mental resolve (saṃkalpa).

One should not make a formal resolve (saṃkalpa) for the purpose of a Śrāddha, nor likewise for the sight of the deity; this applies also to a Śrāddha for Gayā and a Śrāddha for the eight holy sites (tīrthas). One should worship the Lord Gaṇanāyaka in a water-pot (kalaśa) located in the northeast.
In the central pit, one should worship the great Lord Viṣṇu, the lords of the directions,
and Brahmā in the fire-pit with their respective mantras.
Then, having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should carry out the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
One should meditate upon the Lord of the Forest (Vāṭavīśa), endowed with all auspicious marks:
white-complexioned, four-armed, peaceful, adorned with earrings and other ornaments,
holding a book and a rosary, and granting boons and fearlessness.
Endowed with the fire of the ancestors (pitṛvaiśvānara) and adorned with curved eyebrows,
his face was formidable, with arms reaching down to his knees;
having established the fire in his head, the vital air (vāyu) was concentrated in his mouth.
One should worship Pṛthvīdhara and Uryamā, as well as those stationed in the eight forests; one should worship Aparā Saṃdhyā on the chest according to the prescribed rite,
and Diti and Parjanya in the eyes, and Diti and Ijyaputraka in the ears.
One should visualize the two lords of serpents seated on the left and right;
there, truth, the moon, and fire—five each for Rāhu—are situated.
Rudra and consumption (rājayakṣman) are established in the left hand.
Likewise, on the right side is Viratha and Mahārṣaka;
both Gandharva and Puṣpaka are to be known as being at the two knees;
Bhṛṅga and Sugrīva are at the shanks; and the group of Daivārika is at the buttocks.

One should meditate thus and place flowers on the penis as Jaya and Śakra, and on the two feet as the Pitṛs; one should not contemplate it otherwise regarding Soma. With the syllable *mandara* joined with the long vowel, one should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*).

Having exerted such vigor, one should perform the ritual bathing with this mantra: "Oṃ, we know the Praṇava as Brahman; may Viṣṇu, the Lord of the Site, inspire us. With this, one should sprinkle the articles of worship.
One should first worship the seat according to the Dharma and according to one's own capacity;

at the outset, one should worship the Sun, Bhāskara, the Lord of Śacī (Indra), and the Lord of the Gaṇas (Gaṇeśa). Therein, one should worship the Support-Power (Ādhāraśakti), the Earth, and the lotus.

It is said that this is the "Bandī-Āsana"; one should then worship the seat with white sandalwood paste while holding white flowers. Thereafter, one should perform meditation on Hari and place Him within the central mandala.
Having invoked [the deity], one should offer a seat, and then the triad beginning with water for the feet (pādya);
thereafter, one should offer the honey-mixture (madhuparka) to Vāstoṣpati, the Lord.
Regarding this mantra, the seer (ṛṣi) is stated to be [Vasiṣṭha] and the meter (chandas) is Gāyatrī.
And Brahmā shall be the presiding deity; one should assign Aśvamedhaka,
Mandara, Vijaya, Soma, Mahādeva, Mādhava,
Rudra, Hara, Jaya, and Bhaṃ to the bases of the petals starting from the east.
One should meditate upon Jayā, Vijayā, Satyā, Māyā, Śivāmbikā,
Hāsinī, and Kāminī at the bases of the petals;
one should also offer three handfuls of flowers with the mantra "vāstoṣpataye."

One desiring prosperity should worship with perfumes and other offerings using the *arghya* mantra. Having meditated with the mantra "O Lord of the Dwelling, be favorable to me," one should worship with the mantra "ṛtaṃ ca. Nārāyaṇa is proclaimed as the seer (*ṛṣi*) and Gāyatrī as the meter (*chanda*).
The deity known as Sūrya is pleased, as is the wielder of the thunderbolt (Indra).
One should visualize Sūrya seated upon a red throne, with two arms and clad in red garments;
he holds a pair of red lotuses and is beautifully adorned with earrings and other ornaments.
Having meditated thus upon the Lord Haṃsa together with his mantra,
[one should know that] for this mantra "Haṃsasya," the seer (ṛṣi) is said to be Autathya,
the meter (chandas) is Paṅkti, the deity is the Lord himself, and the application (viniyoga) is for the sake of propitiation.
Holding a pair of blue lotuses, the embodiment of truth, seated upon Death,
wearing pure white garments, bestowing boons, and affectionate toward his devotees—
one should worship him with white sandalwood and flowers using the mantra: "svam madāt tvam."
One should worship with supreme devotion using garments, ornaments, and decorations;
then one should worship with black flowers while reciting the mantra "uddharṣaṇa.
Satyavrata is its seer (ṛṣi), Triṣṭubh is its meter (chandas), and [the deity] is its presiding divinity (devatā).
He should meditate upon Savitṛ, who is to be known for the pleasure of the Bull (Vṛṣa),
as having a golden complexion, being praised by hosts of Ṛṣis and showers,
seated upon a pitcher, two-armed, and bearing a mace and a lotus.

Reciting "śanno devī," one should worship with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. O Brahmins, Kardama is the seer (ṛṣi), the meter (chandas) is Jāgatika, and Agni is the deity; one should perform this placement for the propitiation of Ākāśa.
Having meditated upon Vāyu— who has a banner in his hand, possesses mighty arms, is served by the Maruts,
has two arms, and is smoke-colored—
one should worship him with the mantra "O Kings" using white rice grains.
The seer is Nārāyaṇa, the meter is Gāyatrī, and the deity, O twice-born ones, is Vāyu; one should employ this for his propitiation. Pūṣan is red, two-armed, and seated upon a red lotus throne.

One should worship with the verse beginning "rājānaḥ" using perfumes and sandalwood paste. Gobhila is its seer (ṛṣi), Paṅkti is its meter (chandaḥ), and Vāyu is remembered as the deity; one should employ it for the sake of propitiation.
The kings sent for me a messenger who was deformed, dark-complexioned, and possessed four arms;
he held a deer, a noose, a khaṭvāṅga staff, and a trident in his hands,
was mounted upon a ram, and had large eyes.
Likewise, Gṛhakṣata and Śukla, mounted upon four donkeys,
bearing a trident, a staff, and a khaḍvāṅga, riding on a bull,
wearing yellow garments, and adorned with a crown of matted locks— [these are the deities].
One should worship with perfumes and sandalwood using the mantra "āśuḥ śiśānaḥ.
Puṣpadanta is proclaimed as the seer (ṛṣi) and Triṣṭubh as the meter (chanda);
it should be employed for the propitiation of the deity Īśvara.
One should meditate upon Yama as being black in color, seated upon a buffalo, possessing two arms,
holding a staff and a noose, and adorned with armlets and other ornaments.
One should worship him with flowers and other offerings using the mantra beginning with "Īśāna."
Vāmadeva is the seer, Paṅkti is the meter, and Kāla is its deity. One should meditate upon the six-faced Gandharva as yellow in color and four-armed,
wearing yellow garments and adorned with various ornaments.

One should worship with flowers and other offerings using the mantra beginning with "yaddeva. Hārīta is declared to be its seer (ṛṣi), Jagatī is said to be its meter (chandas), and Hiraṇyagarbha is its deity; one should employ it for the sake of his propitiation.
One should worship Bhṛṅgarāja— who is mounted upon matted locks, pure, clad in yellow garments, and auspicious—
with the mantra "cakṣuḥ pīta," using perfumes and sandalwood paste.
Agasti is declared to be the seer (ṛṣi), and Triṣṭubh is proclaimed as the meter (chanda).
For the propitiation of Bhṛṅgarāja, the Viśvedevas are the presiding deities.
One should worship him— who is yellow, mounted upon a deer, and adorned with a crown of matted locks—
with offerings of oblations and milk-rice, reciting the mantra "paro devāḥ."

The sage is declared to be Kapila, the meter is said to be Gāyatrī, and Varuṇa is its deity; one should employ this for the sake of propitiation. One should meditate upon the assembly of ancestors as brilliant white, endowed with four arms.

One should worship with flowers and other offerings using the mantra "pitṛbhyaḥ. Its seer (ṛṣi) is Śunaḥśepa, its meter (chandas) is Triṣṭubh, and its deity (devatā) is declared to be the Viśvedevas; one should worship them through the Pitṛmedha rite.
One should visualize the doorkeeper as having eight arms and a black complexion,
wearing red garments, with tawny eyes, and standing upon a black tiger.
Devoted to worship, one should honor him with the mantra "yo naḥ pitā."
Vaiśvānara is its seer (ṛṣi), and Gāyatrī is declared to be its meter (chandas). Its deity is Śakti, and its application (viniyoga) is in worship.
[One should meditate on the Lord] as having the luster of a conch shell, with beautiful necks, two arms, and holding a discus.
One should meditate upon [the deity] mounted on a swan, possessing a massive body, the cause of the consciousness of Bali,
holding a conch and a lotus, and seated upon a buffalo;
one should worship him with red ornaments using the mantra "sa iṣuhasta."
The seer is Śaṅkha, the meter is Paṅkti, and the deity is Soma.
One should meditate upon the white Lord of Waters, surrounded by Gandharvas and others;
one should meditate on him seated upon the seat of the seer and worship him with white fragrances.
With devotion, one should recite the mantra "Bṛhaspate paridīya";
its seer is Tryambaka, its meter is Triṣṭubh, and its deity is the Lord of Waters (Varuṇa).
One should meditate upon the Asura as being red, formidable, and having a man as his vehicle.
One should worship [the deity] endowed with ten arms, dressed in black garments and smeared with black unguents,
with black flowers while reciting the mantra "śanno devī".
The seer (ṛṣi) is said to be Vaiśvānara and the meter (chandas) is called Virāṭ.
One should employ the deity Vaiśvānarottara for his gratification;
as for the remainder, one should meditate upon the six-faced one (Kārttikeya) as dark and honey-tawny,
seated upon a ram, adorned with earrings, and wearing a serpent as a sacred thread.
One desiring prosperity should worship with the mantra "udvarṣa.
One should contemplate [the deity] as red, three-eyed, and red at the extremities;
one should likewise contemplate him as bearing red moustaches and having hands in the boon-granting gesture.
One should worship with black flowers using the mantra "siddho vīra.
O twice-born ones, [one worships] Yama and Kṛkarākṣa while contracting the hair on the head;
Kapila is proclaimed as its seer (ṛṣi) and Anuṣṭubh as its meter (chandas).

One should employ the deity and the renowned glory for the sake of joy. One should meditate upon Yama, who has reddish-brown eyes, whose hair is curled by the earth, who is mounted on a donkey, and who has two arms; then one should recite this mantra:
Vāsuki shall be its seer (ṛṣi), the Paṅkti its metre (chandas), and Hiraṇyagarbha is said to be its deity; one should employ [this mantra] for his propitiation.
[The form of the deity is] half-drunk, two-armed, with red eyes, or indeed smoky-colored.
It is endowed with the deities, and Vāta is its presiding deity;
the seer is Vāyu, the meter is Gāyatrī, and Vāyu is the deity.
It is pale red in color and likewise holds the conch, discus, mace, and lotus.
One should worship [the deity] clad in yellow garments, seated upon a serpent, and adorned with necklaces and armlets,
using the mantra "avasṛṣṭā parāpata.
Agni is declared to be its seer (ṛṣi), Soma its metre (chandas), and Soma its deity (devatā).
One should meditate upon the yellow Bhallāṭaka seated upon a lotus, adorned with red ornaments, two-armed, and holding a lotus in his hand; one should contemplate the deity in this manner.
One should worship him with white rice using the mantra beginning with "yanmātuḥ."

Jambhaka is the seer (ṛṣi) of this [mantra], Gāyatrī is declared to be its meter (chandas), and Kumbha is the deity; it is employed for the sake of propitiation. One should meditate upon Soma as having a white form, seated upon a lotus throne, and supreme.
One should worship with perfumes and other offerings while reciting the mantra "marmāṇite," [visualizing the deity] as endowed with various ornaments and wearing an excellent crown.
The seer (ṛṣi) is Svārtha, the Veda is the Yajurveda, and the meter (chandas) is declared to be Jagatī.
The deity shall be Soma; one should please him and employ him [in the rite].
O best of the twice-born, one should meditate upon Darpa as being black in color, wearing black garments, with a serpent as his sacred thread, and possessing a crest like a pillar.
One should worship with perfumes and other offerings using the mantra "Paścadīśa. Its seer (ṛṣi) is said to be Pañcāyatanī,
its meter (chandas) is declared to be Paṅkti, and its deity is remembered as the five-faced one (Pañcānana).
One should meditate upon Diti as being dark-complexioned, two-armed, and yellow-bodied;
she is endowed with all auspicious marks and adorned with every ornament.
One should worship her with yellow sandalwood paste while reciting the mantra "Suparṇo 'si."
The sage is Nārāyaṇa, the meter is proclaimed to be Jagatī, and the deity is Bhārgava; one should worship for the fulfillment of desired aims.
One should meditate upon Aditi, who has a reddish luster and is adorned with all ornaments.
One should worship with perfumes and other offerings while reciting the mantra beginning with "śukrām̐bhāri.
Its seer (ṛṣi) is Vāmadeva; one should worship with perfumes and other offerings, knowing the deity to be Śukra, and employ it in the act of praise.
Being well-composed, one should worship those situated in the corners beginning with the northeast.
One should meditate upon Āpaṃ, white in color and adorned with earrings and other ornaments;
one should worship him with the mantra "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ" using the three fragrances.

The seer is Kardama, the meter is said to be Virāj, and the deity is declared to be Soma; one should employ this for the sake of propitiation. [One should visualize] the river as two-armed, red in color, and clad in red and white garments.
One should worship with the mantra "payasā śuklaḥ" using [offerings] such as lotuses.
Nārāyaṇa is proclaimed as its seer (ṛṣi) and the Paṅkti as its meter (chandas).
One should employ this for the propitiation of the Lord Nārāyaṇa himself.
One should meditate upon Jaya, who is yellow in color, two-armed, with a hand in the gesture of granting boons, a deity endowed with a crown and adorned with all ornaments;
having visualized him, one should worship him with this mantra: "O you who have been heard."
The seer is Nārāyaṇa, the meter is Paṅkti, and the deity is Soma.
One should meditate upon Rudra as red-colored, with the moon as his crest-ornament, two-armed, and holding a trident and a hand-drum (ḍamaru). One shall thus overcome all adversaries.
By the mantra "divo mūrdhan," the sages are proclaimed;
the seer is Kāśyapa, and the meter is designated as Virāṭ.
The deity himself is the application (viniyoga), and one should employ it in praise.

One should worship him with supreme devotion using red garlands, sandalwood paste, and so forth, with the mantra "His crown... [and the rest]; he is two-armed, holding a pair of lotuses upon a red lotus, and the sage is declared to be Nīla.
The Triṣṭubh meter and Hradas are proclaimed as its deities.
One should meditate upon the Lord Savitṛ, seated upon a lotus, possessing two arms,
adorned with various ornaments, and graced by a chariot drawn by seven horses.
One should worship [the deity] with perfumes and other offerings while reciting the mantra "yad devāḥ.
For the sake of propitiation, one should apply the sage known as Autathya.
One should meditate upon Vivasvat, who is red in color, two-armed, and whose form is a lotus.

One should worship with the mantra "Avidyā" using perfumes and sandalwood. Gandha is declared to be the seer (ṛṣi), Triṣṭubh is said to be the meter (chandas), and Soma is the deity; one should employ this in the act of praise.
Then one should meditate upon the Lord of the Gods (Śiva), who is yellow in complexion, mounted upon a bull,
four-armed, holding a staff in one hand and a rosary in another,
three-eyed, clad in red garments, and adorned with a crown and other ornaments.

The sage is said to be Hārīta, the meter is declared to be Jagatī, and the deity is Śakti; one should employ this for the sake of propitiation. One should meditate upon Mitra as supreme, white in color, and holding the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
One should worship him, who is situated in Aries, three-eyed, and adorned with an excellent crown,
with curd and milk-pudding using the mantra "Dhanākaraḥ.
It is said that Autathya is the seer (ṛṣi) and Jagatī is declared to be the meter (chanda).
One should employ the deity Yakṣmā for the sake of propitiation;
one should contemplate him as having a yellow face, formidable, and afflicted with consumption (rājayakṣman).
One should worship him thoroughly with perfumes and other offerings using the mantra "Yaśo rūpam."
Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa is declared as the seer (ṛṣi), the Gāyatrī as the meter (chandas), and Yakṣman as the deity; these should be employed in the recitation of the hymn.
One should meditate upon [the deity] wearing white garments, having two arms, and having the peacock as his vehicle.
One should worship Yama with devotion, intent upon the mantra "yamaṃ vineti.
Nārada is declared to be the seer (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh is proclaimed as the meter (chandas), and Vivasvat is the deity; one should employ this in the ritual sacrifice.
Having thus meditated upon Vivasvat, who has a massive body and a vast belly,
one should worship him with perfumes and other offerings using the *abhinnarūpa* mantra.
Kāśyapa is his seer (*ṛṣi*), the *triṣṭubh* is its meter (*chandas*), and the Lord of Śacī (Indra) is its deity.
One should worship the deities and others in the outer northeast corners;
one should honor them with *kūṣmāṇḍa*, *varaṇa* flowers, or *śauraka* flowers.
One should meditate upon the yellow Karālikā, Carakī of excellent complexion.
One desiring prosperity should worship her, who stands upon a white lotus, has two arms, and is adorned with a necklace of *guñjā* berries,
by means of the *pītivarṇa* mantra.
Baladeva is its seer (*ṛṣi*), Gāyatrī is its meter (*chandas*), and Gaurī is its deity (*devatā*).
One should meditate upon Vidārikā, who is red in color and endowed with fresh youth;
one should worship her with this mantra: "Pavitreṇa punīhi.
Garga is declared to be the seer (ṛṣi), Triṣṭubh the meter (chandas), and she is the deity (devatā).
Rudra is also fully described; one should employ him in the hymn of praise.
One should meditate upon the Rākṣasī Pāpā, seated upon a bull, and worship her with perfumes and sandalwood using the mantra "Kayā na."

The seer (ṛṣi) is proclaimed as Suvarṇa, the meter (chandas) is celebrated as Paṅkti, and the deity is Mahādeva; one should employ this for the fulfillment of desired aims. A wise person should install it according to the rules between the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and the altar (vedi).
As well as earth from a mountain peak and earth from an elephant’s tusk; earth from an anthill and from a confluence of rivers; from a royal gate and a crossroads;
and earth from the roots of *kuśa* grass and from a sacrificial tree.
A surrounding enclosure should be made with the leaves of indravallī, ākrāntā, amṛtā,
and trapuṣa, as well as mālatī, campaka, urvāruka,
and pāribhadra.
One should fashion five-peaked [lingas] around the mouth, provided with hoods;
[one should place] a bilva fruit, a citron, a coconut, a pomegranate, an emblic myrobalan, and a rose-apple fruit. Otherwise, one should prescribe a defect.
One should cast five red flowers and gold, and worship Varuṇa;
one should worship him according to the rule with the five types of offerings, beginning with perfumes and flowers.
One should worship Varuṇa again with the mantra beginning with "udvartana."

The seer (ṛṣi) of this mantra is Viṣṇu, and its meter (chandas) is declared to be Gāyatrī; one should employ it for the propitiation of the deity Pāśī. Then, having cast five fragrances and placed the hand [over them], one should recite it.
May all the oceans, rivers, lakes, and great ponds come forth—
those destroyers of all sins and bringers of happiness to all the worlds. May all the rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā, all sacred bathing places, water-givers, and streams arrive.
"May they come, the destroyers of the sacrificer's misfortunes;
may the Vāstoṣpatis, who perform the eight oblations of clarified butter, also come—
either a hundred, or specifically a thousand, accompanied by eight."
Or a Brahmin should offer fifty oblations with sesame seeds together with rice;
he may likewise perform the rite with leaves of the Palāśa, Pippala, or Udumbara trees.
It is especially distinguished when performed with milk, curd, and so forth, or with honey and clarified butter.
And for others, by means of the vow alone, one should offer either a single oblation for each deity,
or twenty-eight for each, or eight times eight, or five times five;
and for Carakī and the others, with seats made of flour or with *vaṭaka* cakes.

When one has diligently recited the *Vāstoṣpati* mantra many times with a red flower or leaf smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*), one should then duly worship the Lord of the Site (*Vāstupati*) with the five types of offerings, together with all his limbs and sub-limbs.
One should subsequently present the bali offering and give it one by one in sequence;
with the Brahmins, one should always offer ghee mixed with honey.
One should give rice from the *śāli* paddy to Śikhin, as well as blue lotuses.
A wise man should offer rice with blue lotuses to Parjanya;
a cake of flour should be prepared for Jaya; ghee and sweetmeats for Indra;
flour-based food for Sūrya; and barley-buns for Satya.
One should offer fish, meat, and rice to Bhrama;
likewise, fried cakes and flour-cakes to Vāyu; similarly, parched grain flour (saktu) to Pūṣan; and indeed, cakes to Vitatha; and food with chickpeas and honey to Gṛhakṣa.
One should offer kṛśara-rice and śāli-rice to Pūṣan;
to Gandharva, musk-rice (kastūrikānna); to Bhṛṅgarāja, kṛśara;
to Mṛga, barley-gruel (yāvakānna); and to the Pitṛs, mung-bean milk-porridge (mudgapāyasa).
