One should give *kṛsara* to Dauvārika, a *pūpaka* to Anaḍuha,
*pāyasa* to Puṣpadanta, and flour-cakes (*piṣṭaka*) to Varuṇa;
one should give sweetmeats (*modaka*) to Asura and liquor (*surā*) at the end of the Āpika rite.
One should offer rice cooked with ghee to Soma, and groats to Yakṣman;
to Roga, ghee-laddukas along with milk-rice and jaggery-rice;
and likewise various kinds of food to Akṣa and to Bhallāṭa.
One should offer honeyed rice to Soma, jaggery-flour cakes to Nāga,
and wheat cooked in ghee to Aditi.
Likewise, one should give milk with white sugar to Diti.
Milk-rice is for Pūṣan, and curd is indeed for Āpavatsa;
sweetmeat balls (laḍḍukas) are for Sāvitrī, and rice with jaggery for Savitṛ;
ghee-rice is for Jaya, and sweet food for Vivasvat.
One should give that [offering] to Virūpa, and likewise yellow rice (haridrānna) to Citra; ghee-rice to Rudra, and milk-porridge with ghee (ghṛtapāyasa) to Yakṣman;
meat-rice to Yakṣman, and kṛśara to Varuṇa.

One should offer four sugar-cake balls (*śarkarāpūpa*) outside for Aryaman. Furthermore, for each deity, one should place milk mixed with ghee and milk upon the offerings: variegated rice with meat, fish, food, and molasses-cakes.
One should offer [the vessel] joined with water from sacred fords (tīrtha) and endowed with fragrance,
along with a banner of divine color, to Brahmā and the others in due order;
one should mutter the mantra according to one's capacity and recite hymns of praise according to one's capacity.
For this *Puruṣastava*, Sūrya is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Jagatī is the meter (*chandaḥ*),
Savitṛ is the deity (*devatā*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is in the praise for the ripening of the soma.
Śaṅkara said:
Viṣṇu, the Victorious, the All-pervading, the Sacrifice, the Worthy of Sacrifice, the Protector of Sacrifice;
Nārāyaṇa, Nara, Haṃsa, Viṣvaksena, the Consumer of Oblations;
Lord of Sacrifice, the Lotus-eyed, Kṛṣṇa, the Sun, worshipped by the gods.
The primordial god, the creator of the universe, the lord of the mandala, the upholder of the earth;
Padmanābha, Hṛṣīkeśa, the giver, Dāmodara, Hari;
Trivikrama, the lord of the three worlds, the increaser of Brahmā’s joy.
He is beloved by his devotees, infallible, truthful, one whose word is truth, steadfast, pure,
an ascetic, a knower of the reality of the scriptures, and the embodiment of fifty-three qualities.
He is Vidārī, modest, peaceful, an ascetic, and possesses the brilliance of lightning.
You are indeed the sacrifice, you are the *vaṣaṭ* call, and you are the *oṃ* call; you are the sacred fires.
You are *svadhā*, you are *svāhā*, and you are *sudhā*, O Supreme Person.
Salutations to Viṣṇu, the God of gods, the eternal one.
O you whose banner is Garuḍa, salutations to you who are infinite and immeasurable!
This hymn of Brahmā, spoken and proclaimed by Mahādeva,
he who recites it daily with diligence attains immortality.
Those who constantly meditate upon the infinite, infallible One, who is himself established within the center of the heart-lotus—
the sole Lord and Master of all worshippers— they indeed attain the supreme Vaiṣṇava perfection.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the second part of the Madhyama-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa.
Description of the Procedure for Offering the Arghya.
Sūta said:
Then, amidst the sounding of kettledrums and other instruments, the sacrificer, facing north, [proceeded].
One should smear [the ground] with golden water and fragrance using the tip of a *mudgala* stalk.
One should worship, being well-composed, either in the northeast or in the center; for one should fashion it into a circular shape while reciting the mantra according to one's desire.
The seer (ṛṣi) is Kaṇṭha, and the meter (chandas) is said to be Gāyatrī; the deity (devatā) is Pṛthivī herself—one should employ these in the hymn of praise.
In the cavity, one should worship the ritual action, as well as Brahmā and Dharādhara.
Having adorned the earth with perfumes, flowers, and various kinds of food offerings,
one should draw an eight-petaled lotus in front and then place a water-pot there,
having fixed gold upon its mouth or fashioned it from silver.

One should worship that which resembles a pearl-oyster shell or originates from Viśvāmitra with the water of sacred fords (tīrtha), along with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), and so forth;
it should be stirred with *viṣṇukrāntā*, *vacā*, *kuṣṭha*, and sandalwood.
One should prepare the *arghya* offering consisting of milk, citron, and *sāvitra* [grain] along with *durvā* grass,
as well as curd mixed with unbroken rice and honey;
likewise, one should offer white sandalwood, garments, and various kinds of *śāli* rice.
Having prepared a flawless water-pot endowed with five colors,
one should devoutly invoke the Ocean with this mantra:
"Come, O Blessed Lord, O God whose form is water, O Lord of Waters!"
"Obeisance to you; this water for the guest-offering (arghya), consisting of the syllables of the heart-mantra, is given by me for your satisfaction.
[The mantras] 'To Soma from the houses,' 'To Tvaṣṭṛ,' and 'To the Trident-bearer'—and beginning with 'imaṃ me varuṇa'—each should constitute a triad of movements."

Then, the sacrifice-offerer, together with his wife, having placed the water-pot upon his lap, should perform the offering of the *arghya* according to the rules with milk, clarified butter, and honey. Regarding the mantra beginning with "Hiraṇyagarbha," Bharadvāja is traditionally remembered as the seer (*ṛṣi*).
The meter is known as Jagatī and the deity is the Lord of Waters (Varuṇa).
One should offer the water-pitcher with the mantra "varuṇasyottaṃbhanam";
for this mantra, the sage (ṛṣi) is proclaimed to be Nārada.
The Virāṭ meter and the deity Īśāna are proclaimed [for this].
One should release a pair of fish and likewise a pair of rams;
when available, one may also release a pair of birds, such as a water-fowl or a ruddy sheldrake.
One should release a pair of nāgas for the sake of increasing longevity;
one should place *jīvantikā* plants in the cardinal directions and offer a sacrificial oblation (*bali*) to the *rākṣasas*.
This [oblation] should be prepared with black-gram flour and adorned with red flowers.
Kṣātraka, Lakṣmaṇa, and Maṇibhadra, the lord of the Gaṇas,
together with Sabinduka and Haṃta, are stationed in the cardinal and intermediate directions in due order.
Those who have been, those yet to be, and those who have already become [liberated], as well as those who dwell within them, [are likewise present].
"May they joyfully grant me auspiciousness by accepting this offering.
Having spoken thus, one should present the offering and thereafter perform prostrations;
one should especially give a milch cow to the preceptor.
For others, one should give gold and a cow to a twice-born man; then one should offer the two *vyāhṛtis*, followed by the five *vāruṇa* oblations,
the *prājāpatya*, and the *sviṣṭakṛt* thereafter.
There is no *sviṣṭakṛt* offering with clarified butter, nor with juices and extracts;
[one should offer] lotuses, blue lotuses, citron fruits, jackfruits, pomegranates, *madhūka* flowers, *viśva* flowers, as well as *āmrātaka* and *kāśa* flowers.

Then one should perform the consecration while reciting the mantra "Svasti," and according to the prescribed rule, one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and present the water-offering (arghya) to the Sun. Having set aside the five defects and with the consent of the Brahmins, [one should proceed].
Having entered his home, he should then feed the Brahmins;
he should also give to the poor, the blind, and the wretched according to his means.
He should eat together with his kinsmen, avoiding curd, milk, and meat.
Neither milk nor decoctions, nor fried vegetables;
neither stalks nor flowers, nor bamboo shoots at any time; nor boiled rice, nor radishes, nor fruits such as the jackfruit and the mango.
One should know that mastu, honey, ghee, jaggery, mātuliṅga with rock salt,
jujube, dhātakī fruit, kunda flower, and likewise sesame—
these are recommended, especially black pepper.
Then, having abandoned [the site] for three nights or seven days at the threshing floor (*khala*),
one should thereafter perform the five-limbed rite (*pañcāṅgaka*) and install the pair beginning with *na*. The first [line] is twelve cubits long, and the second is ten cubits.
At one *vitasti* there shall be a hundred [units], and immediately thereafter twice that;
then fifty thereafter, and sixty *hasta*s immediately after.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Offering the Arghya," in the second part of the Madhyama-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Description of the Procedure for the Agnihotra.
Sūta said:
O best of beings, I shall describe the rules for the domestic fire (gṛhya-agni) according to the various types of yoga.
What is spoken by another according to the ritual rule brings fear and destroys one's reputation.
Sons, daughters, grandsons, and other offspring are designated as "household members" (gṛhya); they are the heirs of the sacrificer.
In their ritual sacrifices and in the performance of pacifying rites,
the procedure ordained by the Teacher is therefore remembered as the *cakṣa*. He takes hold of the triple blade of kuśa grass and then makes it firm.
The seer is Dakṣa, the metre is Jagatī, and the deity is Viṣṇu;
"Kaśyapa may be satisfied" and "Thou art the earth" (bhūrasi) constitute the purification. The seer is Suvarṇa, and the metres are held to be Gāyatrī and Jagatī.
And the deity should be Sūrya; one should place him during the purification of the earth,
proceeding with effort in a clockwise direction starting from the northeast (aiśānī) in due order,
while reciting the mantra "yat pavitram" and using the index finger and thumb.
One should also rotate [the grass] in the shape of a circle using three bundles of *kuśa* grass;
this is called "sweeping" (*parisamūhana*). O best of beings, listen now to the ritual bathing (*snapana*).
One should perform the consecration (*saṃskāra*) beginning with Īśāna and the sweeping.
In the sacrifice, one should perform the taking up of the directions starting from Nairṛti during the *pratiṣṭhā*;
the sweeping (*parisamūhana*) belongs to Indra. Parvata is remembered as its seer (*ṛṣi*), the *paṅkti* meter is prescribed, and Indrāṇī is its deity.
One should not smear cow dung, the three fragrances, or even the five medicinal herbs on the deity’s image, having excluded the *kaniṣṭha* and *guhyaka* types. Furthermore,
the Viśvedevas should be worshipped with the verse beginning with *mā nastoke*.
The seer is Kāśyapa, and Viśvedeva is proclaimed as the metre.
O best of men, having tied the jar, the wise man should join and smear it,
beginning with the *kuśa* grass on the right side using the middle and index fingers.
O best of men, by means of the mantra beginning with "yajvabhiḥ," the sacrificers make the field four-cornered and likewise the face one cubit in measure; thus Sūrya is pleased.
Having abandoned one and a half finger-breadths on the right, one should likewise abandon it on the west.
One should draw a line with its tip pointing north; otherwise, it would be inauspicious.
For the mantra "āpyāyasva," Dhanvantari is remembered as the seer (ṛṣi), Triṣṭubh is declared to be the meter (chandas), and Savitṛ is the deity (devatā) here.
One [line] is joined at the right, measuring twelve finger-breadths in its eastern half;
another is separated by one finger-breadth, and from that, it becomes seven finger-breadths wide. It may be made with the root of *kuśa* grass, gold, or silver for the consecration ceremony.
Chanting the mantra "saṃjyotiḥ" with the thumb and ring finger,
one should meditate upon Mitra and Varuṇa; the seer is named Autathya,
the meter is Paṅkti, and the deity is Śiva— one should then apply it to the line.
With that very [mantra], one should raise both hands once each on the right and left;
one should cast [the offering] into the fire for "Bhāsvarāya" (to the Radiant One), and thereafter, the combat is prescribed.
Sadasampad is declared to be the Ṛṣi, and Karṇa is called the Virāj.

O best of men, with water containing *kuśa* grass and flowers, using the *devatīrtha*, as well as with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and water containing the five jewels, the wise man [should perform the rite]. May Indra be the deity, and may the Earth be the deity.
Especially in the Mahāyoga, [this rite] is performed with water from five sprouts;
furthermore, this mantra is proclaimed to be the most excellent. Its meter is the goddess Gāyatrī, and its deity is Gaṇanāyaka.
Reciting, "Taking the fire from the monkey, I accept it for myself," the seer (ṛṣi) of the mantra "I accept it for myself" is said to be Gautama;
its meter (chandas) is declared to be Anuṣṭubh, and Vāmadeva is the deity (devatā).

Having abandoned the *kravyād* fire and invoking the *kravyād* fire with this mantra, the wise man should cast it toward the south. Hārīta is the seer (*ṛṣi*) of this mantra, and its meter (*chandas*) is prescribed [as follows].
The deity is Vāmadeva; one should also employ this [mantra] even in the rite of cremation.
Then one should perform the invocation while muttering the mantra "saṃsara kṣa.
For the mantra "saṃsara kṣa," Nīla is declared to be the seer (ṛṣi).
The Virāj is to be known as the metre, and Śatakratu (Indra) as the deity.
The installation of the fire is declared by means of the verse beginning with "vaiśvānara. One who recites this mantra is gratified; the seer is remembered as Kāśyapa.
The meter shall be Anuṣṭubh and the deity Havyavāhana;
with the mantra beginning "badhnāsi," one should circumambulate the fire.
The seer is declared to be Svayaṃbhū, and the meter is cited as Virāṭ.

One should join the deities and the Supreme Self with a salutation. Then, in the southern part [of the site], upon two cubit-long seats made of folded kuśa grass with tips pointing eastward, one should place the hand and foot seats.
One should seat the Brahman priest with the words, "O Brahman, please sit here," using the verse,
"The cow that milks for the sacrifice of Brahman" (RV 10.109.3),
and with these two mantras; this is the entry of the Brahman.
"May Śakra protect him"—listen, O twice-born sages, to these two verses.
Prajāpati is the seer, the Triṣṭubh is the meter, and Śaṅkara is the deity.
Nārada is the seer, the Triṣṭubh is the meter, and the Lord of Śacī is the deity.
To the north of the fire, at a distance of one cubit,
one should place the *praṇītā* water-vessel while reciting the mantra "ehy ehi" (Come,
come). For this mantra, Vāmadeva is proclaimed as the seer (*ṛṣi*) and the meter (*chandas*).
The meter is Jagatī and the deity is Śatakratu (Indra).
Specifically for Varuṇa, [the vessel] is made from Śrīparṇī and Sahakāra wood,
with a width of six aṅgulas and a length of twenty aṅgulas.
In length, it should be four well-known finger-breadths (aṅgulas) according to measurement;
for the rites of the gods, the height of the base should be two finger-breadths.
For malevolent rites (abhicāra), it should be made of bell-metal (kāṃsya), and for rites of pacification (śāntika), it should be of copper (tāmra).
At the time of consecration, one should fill the *praṇītā* vessel— made of clay, measuring eight fingers,
or else made of metal with a width of twelve fingers and devoid of human-made marks—
with the verse "imaṃ me varuṇa".
Then one should perform the meditation thus: "May the oceans be pleased.
With a single unbroken blade of darbha grass, one should spread [the grass] around in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
In the Nairṛta direction and likewise in the Vaiśvadeva direction, there should be a boundary-line (sīta).
O best of beings, one propitiates the Naga with the verse beginning "Kayā naścitra.
For this mantra, Bharadvāja is declared to be the seer (ṛṣi),
the Anuṣṭubh the meter (chandas), and Īśāna is proclaimed to be the deity (devatā).
One should then obtain the materials for the purpose and so forth in due order,
from the south to the north, with the verse beginning "dhruvāsas.
Nārada is the seer (ṛṣi), the meter (chandas) is Anuṣṭubh, and the deity is as follows.
And one should satisfy Śatakratu; then, with due respect, one should join [the ritual elements]. One should place a piece of wood in the west while offering it from the west.
In front [of the fire], there should be food, the five grains, sesame seeds, and mustard seeds.
On the right side, there should be a cake and likewise a bhr̥ṅgarāja leaf;
on the left side, fruit and leaves, flour-cakes, curd, and milk;
as well as a jackfruit, coconut, sweetmeat (modaka), and a ball-sweet (laḍḍuka).

One should place the *praṇītā* water in the cardinal and intermediate directions without hesitation. O Brahmins, one should never touch the *praṇītā* at any time during the *homa*, nor the bathing pitcher, for as long as the sacrifice proceeds.
One should place the uccīraka, the mātuliṅga, dūrvā grass, and dhātrī fruits,
as well as tulasī, mālatī, jātī, and especially water-born flowers,
along with everything made of kāñcanāra wood, in the northeast.
This is the specific detail regarding the southwest:
that which is made of *vikaṅkata* wood and *śamī* wood should all be taken according to the requirements, as well as its leaves.
When boiling milk, one should bring the *caru*-pot at the end of the milk-cooking process.
One should cut the *pavitra* into finger-breadth sections using *kuśa* grass blades.
Having cut it, one should place the *pavitra* in the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, and with the *balabhit* mantra, one should cut the tip of the *āmra* leaf.
One should then cut the front portion [of the *pavitra*] with the *viṣṇo rarāṭam* mantra.
One should never crush it with thick milk-rice,
nor with juice, nor with black pigment, nor ever with anything hard;
rather, one who is restrained in speech should do so with copper ash or with mother-of-pearl and conch-shell.
The preceptor should then cut the piñjulī grass and the pavitra blades;
Hārīta is remembered as the seer (ṛṣi) of the mantra "viṣṇo rarāṭam," paṅkti is its meter (chandas), and one should employ it in the rite of consecration (saṃskāra).

Taking the vessel for the *praṇītā* water, one should fill it with the three [substances] using the *kāya-tīrtha*; one may also do so using the *devatīrtha*. Afterwards, one should place the *prokṣaṇī* vessel upon the palm of the left hand.

With the middle fingers and the thumbs [joined] by means of *apāmārga* stalks while reciting the mantras, one should hold that sacred thread (*pavitra*) with the palm facing upward, muttering the mantra "pavitraṃ te.
Gautama is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the *dharmarāja* [verse] is the meter (*chanda*), and the Lord of Justice (*dharmarāja*) is the deity (*devatā*).
Then, one should sprinkle the established materials and arrange them in sequence:
once with three wooden sticks over each material, and three times with mantra-empowered flowers.
This should be done in a stable location to the south of the Praṇītā vessel that has been brought forward.
One should place the vessel for clarified butter (ājyasthālī) at a distance of one span;
having prepared a mandala in front, one should establish the fire upon the Brahmin.
One should then quickly remove the gambling pieces, having examined them in the proper sequence.
The act of placing the vessel over the fire is declared to be performed with the mantra "Īśāna.

Nārāyaṇa is the seer (ṛṣi), Paṅkti is the meter (chandas), and Īśa is the deity (devatā). Then, one should respectfully perform both the rite of carrying fire around the vessel (paryagnikaraṇa) as well as the subsequent rites.
Having gazed [at the fire] starting from the Lord (Īśa) and proceeding in a clockwise direction, while recollecting the seer, meter, and other details of the *kulāyanī* mantra, one should,
with a concentrated mind, circumambulate the vessel of clarified butter either three times or once.
In the rite "May the ancestors be satisfied," the Mothers are remembered;
Jamadagni is the seer, Gāyatrī is declared the meter, and Pinākin is the deity; one should employ this in the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.

And likewise for ghee, [one should say]: "O Brahmā, may you indeed be satisfied. Then, having taken a *sruva* ladle six finger-breadths long and heated it over the fire, O best of beings, [it should be used] three times during the *mahāyoga* rite, but only once elsewhere.

One should sweep [the area] even with *kuśa* grass; one should sprinkle from the root to the tip, and again from the tip to the root, worshipping repeatedly. Immediately thereafter, one should sprinkle that [area] three times each with water from the *praṇīta* vessel.
Then, having heated the ground again, one should place the *prokṣaṇī* vessel to the north.
Having set down the vessel of clarified butter (*ājya*), one should take up the *pavitra* strainer;
one should grasp that *pavitra* with the two thumbs and the two ring fingers.
Having made eight finger-widths of space in the center, one should perform the purification of the ghee three times.

One should likewise gaze at the clarified butter three times in the nether world (pātāla) and three times in the sky; then, with the three [mantras], the preceptor should perform the sprinkling in the *prokṣaṇī* vessel and likewise sprinkle below.
Then, having taken the milk-rice (pāyasa) and risen with the mantra,
one should offer it silently into the fire according to the true procedure;
taking the *prokṣaṇī* vessel along with the *pavitra* grass in the right hand.
At the base, which measures eight finger-breadths, one should sprinkle water starting from the northeast (Īśāna) and proceeding clockwise around the fire; then,
having placed the *pavitra* strainer and the *prokṣaṇī* sprinkling-vessel into the *praṇītā* vessel.
And for the sake of the *saṃyāva* offering, O Brahmins,
the preceptor there should meditate upon Agni as being red in color, with three arms,
holding a *sruva* ladle in one hand and a *kamaṇḍalu* water-pot in his other hand, while the third is the right hand.
Taking up the *sruva* ladle, one should offer oblations silently while remaining composed;
at the end, designating the deity as Prajāpati,
one should offer them everywhere with the *praṇava* (Om) at the conclusion, O best of the twice-born.
Starting from the northwest corner and ending at the southeast corner,
one should offer an unbroken stream of ghee to Indra; immediately thereafter,
one should offer oblations consisting of Agni and Soma, beginning from the southwest (the direction of the Rākṣasas).

Then one should perform the occasional rite (naimittika) up to the northeast corner (aiśānakoṇa). After that, one should offer the sviṣṭakṛt oblation, and likewise offer with the [mantras] beginning with "mati". Having performed the fivefold rite of Varuṇa (vāruṇapañcaka), one should then obtain the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Regarding the mantra known as *udvāha*, the seer (*ṛṣi*) is traditionally held to be Atharvaṇa;
the meter (*chaṃdas*) is the goddess Gāyatrī, and the deity (*devatā*) is Varuṇa. The practitioner of mantra should employ it in ritual application and likewise employ it in praise.
The seer (ṛṣi) of the mantra "tvanno agne" is known as Vāśiṣṭha; its meter (chandas) is called Bṛhatī, and Agni himself is proclaimed as its deity.
The seer of the mantra "iḍo gataṃ" is the one known as Ko Guhya.

The meter is known as Jagatī, and the deity is proclaimed to be Viṣṇu. Who indeed is proclaimed as the Ṛṣi of the mantra "udvartana"? The meter is the goddess Gāyatrī, and Varuṇa is the presiding deity.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for Sacrifices," in the second part of the Madhyama-parvan within the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said:
Then, at every sacrifice, one should choose a Brahmin as the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*).
Having performed the *kuśakaṇḍī* rite according to one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra*, one should thereafter worship the fire.
[The offerings consist of] the two *āghāra* libations, the two *ājyabhāga* portions, and the three *mahāvyāhṛti*s.
Everything designated as *prāyaścitta* and the *prājāpatya* [offering], as well as the *sviṣṭakṛt*,
one should always prescribe for every homa rite;
and in the *prājāpatya*, [the offerings] to Indra— these two are known as the *āghāra*.
The two portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāgau) are prescribed for Agni and Soma;
likewise, the three great utterances (mahāvyāhṛtayaḥ)—bhūr, bhuvaḥ, and svaḥ—are traditionally remembered. Furthermore, there is the verse "ayāścāgne," as well as "ye te śatam" which is unsurpassed.
These five mantras are indeed known as the "universal expiations" (sarvaprāyaścitta).
One oblation to Prajāpati is prescribed, and another is remembered as the Sviṣṭakṛt.
These fourteen rites, designated as "constant" (nitya), are to be offered.
Having first made a single dedication to the deity, one should subsequently perform the fire-oblation (homa).
In the Soma sacrifice, the cow-sacrifice, the human sacrifice, and the horse sacrifice,
the wise practitioner should otherwise offer with the mantra ending in "svāhā" in the reverse order.
Without the occasional rite (*naimittika*), the daily rite (*nitya*) becomes fruitless; it is not otherwise.
In the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice, as well as in sacrifices lasting three days or more, the daily rite should be excluded by half;
O twice-born ones, hear now the specific instruction regarding this.
On a single-day rite (*ekāha*), having performed the *āghāra* and *ājyabhāga* offerings and the occasional (*naimittika*) rites,
one should know that the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering follows, as well as the *ākṛti* and subsequent offerings.
However, specifically in the three-day rite (*tryaha*) and others, the *āghāra* and *ājyabhāga* offerings come first.
Thereafter, one should perform the occasional rite (naimittika) on the day of completion as well;
preceded by the pouring of clarified butter (āghāra) and the oblation of ghee (ājya), one should then perform the occasional rite,
including the Sviṣṭakṛt, the Vyāhṛtis, and likewise the six beginning with those dedicated to Varuṇa.
Where a twice-born man has fallen from his caste, one should perform two, three, or four [offerings] on a single day during a Soma sacrifice or in childhood;
however, at the marriage of the twice-born, the daily obligatory rite (nityaka) shall take place first.
On a single day, one should perform the fire-ritual separately for each [deity];
one should offer one [oblation] daily, and never perform it separately on a daily basis.
Where a twice-born man has fallen from his caste, one should offer two, three, or four [oblations] for each.
One may perform [the rites] on a single day; even then, one should not omit the daily (nitya) obligation.
In the *homa* sacrifice, Brahmā is present; in the hymn of praise (*stuti*), Viṣṇu; and in the *sruva* ladle, Maheśvara.
In the offering of the *aja* goat, Indra is present; and in the placing of the vessel upon the fire (*adhiśrayaṇa*), Vivasvat.

In the rite of circumambulation with fire and in the marriage ceremony, the Mothers are traditionally invoked; in the drawing out of water and the inspection of the site, the Moon and Sun; likewise, in the sprinkling and the installation, the Quarters;
in the vessel for sprinkling, Durgā; and in the act of establishment, Lakṣmī.
O best of the twice-born, one should perform the fire-sacrifice (homa) with a concentrated mind and follow the prescribed rite.
These deities have been declared for the benefit of the twice-born;
one should worship them during well-prepared animal sacrifices, at the time of purificatory rites (saṃskāra), and on sacred festival days (parvan).
All these deities should be known by those concentrated in mind during the sacrifice.
One should know them through their presiding deities (adhidaiva), since there are five fruits on the *karavallī* plant;
therefore, one should install the deity with every effort.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Meditation on the Deity," in the second part of the Madhyama-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
Now I shall truly declare the supreme meditation upon these deities;
through thorough knowledge of this sacrifice, the tongue bestows the full fruit [of the rite].
First is the golden-colored tongue of fire, possessed of great splendor.
For the attainment of desired success in rites known as *hiraṇya*, we praise the goddess Kanakā,
who is rich in gold, two-armed, white in complexion, holding *darbha* grass and a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) in her two hands,
and bestowing accomplishment upon the practitioner.
I bow to her who resembles the rising moon, who is red in hue, and who holds a conch, a discus, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons with her four sprout-like arms;
she who has the appearance of a mass of crushed collyrium and bears a golden jar on her left side.
I bow to her who holds a beautiful red lotus in her right hand;
she who possesses the luster of a radiant halo, with her two hands joined in *añjali*,
seated in the *padmāsana* posture, and clothed in silken garments— may she be gracious to me.
O friend, she who resembles the hibiscus flower and possesses many forms shall be the bestower of auspiciousness upon me; she is white with her arms, wielding a thousand supreme weapons.
O Goddess, you who resemble a blue lotus and whose supreme splendor is the color of fire!
"O you who always wear the hibiscus flower, O virtuous one, be gracious to me!
With the root mantra, one should gaze upon the site; digging is considered to be performed with the mantra.
One should perform the "three-threading" and then cast down the "four-threads."
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Method for Meditating upon the Deity," in the second part of the middle section of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
On the day preceding the consecration, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) of the deity,
as well as the consecration of the grain and the sacrificial post (yūpa) according to the prescribed rules.
At night, one should place Gaṇanāyaka upon the root and the tip of the vessel.
Having worshipped, according to the prescribed rite, the lords of the directions as well as the planets; having worshipped Brahmā at the reservoirs, Varuṇa at the sacrifice for peace (śāntiyāga),
Soma at the maṇḍala, and likewise Sūrya and Viṣṇu at the foot [of the pillar].
In a Śiva temple, one should worship Śiva; likewise, at a water-shed (prapā), one should worship Varuṇa;
and in a grove, one should worship Brahmā with water for the feet and other offerings.
A wise person should first bathe [the deity] with the mantra beginning with "drupadādī".
Thereafter, one should apply the unguent with the Gāyatrī mantra and then with the mantra "gandhadvārām";
it is especially distinguished by these two mantras. One should offer flowers with the mantra "śrīśca te" and fruit with the mantra "phalinī".
Then, with the mantra "kāṇḍāt," one should offer a hundred blades of dūrvā grass;
with "siṃdoriva," vermilion (sindūra); and with "viśvā," the ritual sprinkling (mārjana). Reciting "samit" and "surāsurāḥ," one should apply collyrium (añjana) for those who are in distress.
Having recited the *mānastoke* mantra over the sandalwood,
one should especially place it with its tip pointing north upon the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).
Then, with that same mantra, one should immediately establish it with water.
First, reciting the Gāyatrī and "āpo hi ṣṭhā," and then the "śanno devī" and the Drupadā verse, he should perform the ritual bath; thereafter,
having consecrated [the water] with the mantra "brahma," he should utter that mantra for three nights.

Having recited the *Yoga* and *Yogadṛḍha* mantras, one should then place the purifying thread (*pavitra*). Then, with the two mantras "Tvaṃ Gandharva" and "Subhābha," as well as the *Śrīsūkta*, one should apply oil and perfume, and likewise offer flowers.

One should offer incense with the mantra "dhūrasi," a lamp with the mantras "āsrajyotiḥ" and "bhirdīpakam," and then offer dūrvā grass and unbroken rice (akṣata) with the mantra "anumīmaha iti. Furthermore,
one should offer water for washing the feet with "viśvāmī" and again unbroken rice with "nimnyaṃtakāṇḍāt."
With "Like Sindhu" (siṃdoriva), one offers vermilion; with "The fuel is kindled" (samidheti), likewise collyrium;
with "This foot of his" (pādo’sya), then food is offered; with "Those which are fruitful" (yāḥ phalinī), again fruit;
with "Not form" (rūpaṃ na), one burns the image; and with "He does not grieve" (na sociti), there is worship.
With the mantra "yuvā suvāsā," [he offers] a garment; with "nāgagandha," sandalwood paste.
Then, having taken refuge in another pavilion outside the house of Yama, he should utter the words "sunāti" and thereafter invoke the Lord.
Therein, one should perform the ritual acceptance (*adhivāsana*) and protect [the site] with well-guarded sentries.
The preceptor (*ācārya*), the patron (*yajamāna*), and the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) should partake of a meal;
they should consume food that is free from pungent salts and abstain from all curd and sesame seeds.
I shall describe the common consecration (*adhivāsa*) according to that [tradition]:
one should utter the words "Well-bathed" (*sunātā*) and offer oil with three [mantras] to Śivā;
together with five Brahmins, one should recollect [the mantra] "The Gandharvas" (*gandharvā*).
One should again offer perfume mixed with oil with the verse beginning "gandhadvārām"; then fruit with the verse "yāḥ phalinīḥ"; and betel nuts and leaves with the verse "pūgatāmbūlavarjanam";
and one should offer an extremely sharp sword with the verse "kauśikīruttamāsīḥ."
One should offer the mallet with the mantra "rūpeṇa vā," and while reciting "śrīśca te" for the flower and "viśvāni" [the hymn],
the act of churning should then be performed; this is the general procedure.

Therefore, one should perform the rite in a location where the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) has been carried out. O Brahmins, if one performs the installation (pratiṣṭhā) without the preliminary consecration, one does not obtain its fruit; it would be like providing refuge at a marriage ceremony.

Therefore, with great effort, one should construct the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and the pavilion (maṇḍapa) during the forenoon or at night; one should have them prepared for the daily (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and optional (kāmya) rites,
whether on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) measuring one cubit or even one made of sand.
O Brahmins, [the measurement] increases by one finger-breadth for every cubit, whether it be in a hand-sized pit or even in a two-cubit pit; there is no doubt regarding this rule for the pedestal.
And in the case of a pit of nine or five cubits, or even for a hundred thousand [offerings] and so forth, there may be uncertainty.
Next, O twice-born ones, hear about the ten-fold [offering] in the ten-fingered rite:
wood, leaves, flowers, sweetmeats, flour-cakes,
as well as cooked food, milk-rice, ghee, and sesame seeds.
Indeed, in the Gṛha-pakṣa and Viṣṇu-pakṣa, [the offering] should begin with sesame seeds;
in the Śaiva [pakṣa], it should begin with barley; in the Śākta [pakṣa], it should begin with flowers;
in the Sūrya-pakṣa, it should begin with flour-cakes (piṣṭaka); and in the Gopāla [pakṣa], it should begin with kṛśara.
In the Kṛṣṇa [mantra], the Karavīra and others; in the Traipura, the Śrīphala fruits; and in the Sārasvata, the Śrīvṛkṣa is prescribed for one desiring liberation.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the second part of the Madhyama-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa.
Description of the Meditation on the Deity.
Sūta said:
Eight officiating priests (hotṛs), eight gatekeepers, and eight Brahmins who are to act as sacrificial priests must be appointed.
All [the officiants] should be pure and distinguished by their auspicious marks and other qualities; one great-souled person among them should be appointed as the reciter (jāpaka).

O Brahmins, oil should be prepared with divine perfumes, fragrant garlands, and gold. Twenty-five Brahmins should be employed, and they should be honored twice as much with superior offerings, divine garments, worship, and sacrificial fees.
No one should cause a leaf-offering to be placed [before a guest] without having honored him as prescribed;
if one offers it to unworthy Brahmins, one shall not obtain the full fruit. In all rites such as consecrations and the like, one should duly honor the Brahmins.

One should duly offer the guest-water (arghya) and a seat (viṣṭara) made of kuśa grass to the twice-born in every case; thereafter, one should present the vessel. If that honoring is performed without the guest-water, one is cooked in hell.

At the sacrifice, each of the Brahmins who have mastered the Vedic mantras should be chosen by the preceptor for his duties; if ten such groups of cows are required, he should do so. Even in the absence of distinguished individuals, one may employ Brahmins made of kuśa grass.

Even when using a substitute made of *kuśa* grass, one should not perform the ritual assignment of the feet nor the striking together [of the hands] without mentioning one's own lineage (*gotra*) and one's own name; likewise,
at the conclusion of the recitation of the lineage and so forth, one should utter the mention of one's own name.
In the gift of the Tulāpuruṣa, as well as at the Hāṭakācala,
in the giving away of a daughter, and likewise at the time of a ritual libation (utsarga), one should recite the lineage of ancestors (pravara) and so forth.
One should not offer a vessel for the sake of a mere image, nor should it be empty or contain water alone.

One whose wife has died and who remains without a wife; one who is childless and whose sons have died; one who performs the consecratory rites for a Śūdra; a miser; one who officiates at sacrifices for a multitude;
one who has undertaken a penance; a priest for a king; and a slanderer.
One who dwells in the house of a Śūdra, one who incites a Śūdra, one with a very thin neck, a dwarf, one who is the husband of a Śūdra woman,
as well as one who hates kinsmen, one who hates his guru, and likewise one who hates his wife.
One who is deficient in a limb, one with redundant limbs, one with broken teeth, a hypocrite, a receiver of gifts, one with deformed nails, an adulterer,
one afflicted with vitiligo, one with leprosy, one born of a low family, one who is excessively sleepy, and one who is addicted to vices and devoid of purpose.
One who is uninitiated, a miser, one afflicted by a violent disease, one with oozing sores,
one with large ulcers, and one with abdominal dropsy— one should not have them prepare the sacrificial vessels.
O twice-born, listen now to the mantras for the worship of the vessels at the conclusion of the selection.
The most excellent knower of mantras should worship with perfumes and other offerings while reciting the *pratimantra*:
"O Preceptor, you are the embodiment of Brahman; protect me from the cycle of existence, O All-pervading Lord!
By your grace, O Guru, I have attained this sacrifice which was desired by me."
May my eternal fame endure for as long as the worlds of moving and unmoving beings exist.
Be gracious, O Great Lord, for the successful completion of this rite of installation.
You are the origin of all beings and the one who delivers them across the ocean of saṃsāra.
O Yajurveda, teacher who bestows the nectar of knowledge, salutations be unto you!
O Yajurveda, born from Brahmā himself, who has illuminated the quarters of space,
and who resembles pure gold, salutations be unto you!
O you who possess the luster of molten gold, illuminating the surface of the earth with your radiance;
O you whose form is established through the proclamation of mantras, O Yajurveda, homage be to you!
O you who possess the brilliance of a full-blown golden flower, adorned by radiant deities!
O knower of the procedures for the collection of scattered mantras, I bow to you!
O knower of the Vedas and their six auxiliary limbs, O officiating priest, grant me liberation!
Having entered the mandala, O Brahmins, one should install [the deities] in their respective places in due order.
The wise one should station the Ācārya on the western side of the Vedyā;
Brahmā in front of the Kuṇḍa, specifically to the west of the Maṇḍala;
and the Hotṛ, who is knowledgeable in the ritual rules, there to the north.
Having made each pair of them indicators, as well as the bearer of the sword,
one should then diligently station the door-keepers at every door in succession, one by one,
with the mantra that is about to be recited.
One should worship with perfumes, flowers, and the like, as well as with a pair of garments.
"O Puruṣa who is always worshipped in this sacrifice as the Sun,
in the form of Nārāyaṇa, make my sacrifice fruitful."
Witness in all sacrifices, knower of the true essence of the Yajurveda,
knower of the truth of the Ṛgveda’s meaning, O you who are the form of Indra, salutations be unto you!
By whom the mantras were extensively elaborated in all the most excellent sacrifices.
O knower of the true essence of the Yajurveda, O embodiment of Brahman, salutations be unto you! Among all the most excellent sacrifices, this alone is remembered as the prescribed rule;
it is eternally auspicious for all rites, omniscient, and the very form of knowledge.
For the success of my sacrifice, I bow to you who possess the form of Śiva.
Protect all the cardinal and intermediate directions, as well as this [place];
I bow to this Brahmin in the form of a guardian of the quarters for the sake of the completion of the sacrifice.
One should not perform a sacrifice, a vow, or the worship of the gods with a mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*).
Desire indeed has its root in resolve; sacrifices are born from resolve.
O Brahmins, whatever a man does without resolve is [fruitless].
The fruit of that dharma is meager, and it results in the destruction of half [one's merit].
Therefore, with every effort, the wise person should resolve upon performing a sacrifice. Neither the pursuit of desire nor even the state of being free from desire is truly auspicious.

Therefore, one should not practice dharma consisting of desire without [the pursuit of] liberation. That man who practices dharma without intention (saṃkalpa) does not obtain the fruit of either the obligatory or the occasional rites.

One should not perform the installation [of the deity] there; rather, one should indeed do so within the mandala. Taking a vessel made of udumbara wood, filled with water and endowed with auspicious qualities, one should face the eastern direction during the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for a reservoir, a grove, or a well.

In common rites, however, one should face north; but in the sacrifice to the planets (grahayajña), one faces the deity directly. In the Mahāvrata and in consecrations (pratiṣṭhā), a vessel made of copper, gold, silver, or stone, complete with its parts, is praised for use in sacrifices.
The vessel for sacrificial offerings is prescribed to be held in the hand;
one should pour water to the northeast during the consecration (pratiṣṭhā), and to the east during the installation.
One should cast [the vessel] into the air during a sacrifice (yāga), a vow (vrata), or a daily rite (nitya) performed for Īśa.
In the Pitṛmedha, the Goyāga, and the Dakṣiṇa Naramedha,

one must never perform the formal ritual resolve (saṃkalpa) with vessels made of mother-of-pearl, bell-metal, and the like, nor with those made of copper, silver, and so forth, nor ever with those made of clay.
Having first uttered the Praṇava, one should worship and remember the Lord of Sacrifice;
likewise, Gaṅgā, the Sun, the Moon, heaven, earth, night and day,
Sūrya, Soma, Yama, Kāla, and the five great elements.
"These nine are the witnesses here in this world of auspicious and inauspicious actions.
Having uttered this, one should invoke Dharma, meditate upon him, and offer a handful of flowers.
Then, having consecrated the water in the ritual vessel as nectar, one should designate it with "Oṃ Tatsat."
May that Dharma—who possesses a radiant form, wears white garments, stands upon a bull in the upper region, and constantly bears the supreme form granting fearlessness and boons with both hands;
who brings happiness to all living beings and is the sole cause of liberation for those of disciplined intellect—protect the worlds forever and may he always lead the virtuous to prosperity.
Furthermore, one should engage the Brahmins associated with the sacrifice in a single day alone.

"Whatever sacrificial materials (havirdravya) there may be, even within the interval of the eight sacrifices, these should be offered again and again; the Brāhmaṇas are the sacrificial offerings and the fires. Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the second part of the Madhyama-parvan in the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa.
A description of the installation of Yoga and the consecration of deities.
Sūta said:
The installation of Yoga, as prescribed by the sages, should also be performed during the six months beginning with Māgha.
They say that the installation of the gods and others should take place here as long as Madhusūdana is not asleep.
On the days of Venus, Jupiter, Mercury, and the Moon, all [such rites] become auspicious.
Furthermore, the consecration of reservoirs of water should be performed when an auspicious planet is situated in the ascendant or when it aspects the ascendant.
O Brahmins, the second, the third, and likewise the thirteenth;
furthermore, the seventh, the full moon day (paurṇamāsī), the tenth, and also the fifth—
these lunar days are recommended for the consecration of life-force (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) in reservoirs of water and the like.
Without having attained these auspicious times— the two equinoxes,
the two solstices at sixty-four [days], the two transits of the sun, the beginnings of the Yugas, and other meritorious days—
one should perform the consecration of a reservoir of water, such as a pond, either to the east or to the north.
O Surata, on a slightly sloping site that is very beautiful, there should be a well-rounded pavilion sixteen cubits in size;
it should be provided with four renowned doors and possess four entrances.
O Lord of the Gods, at the four doors starting from the east, there should be archways (toraṇas) made of Plakṣa and other trees.
Likewise, the Plakṣa, Udumbara, Pippala, and Nyagrodha trees were placed in their proper order;
and those pillars, reaching up to the height of the hands and adorned with various garlands, garments, and ornaments,
as well as these arches on the ground, became pleasing to the eye.

Indeed, in every sacrifice, white banners should be erected upon the pavilion in the cardinal and intermediate directions; they should be provided with flags colored according to the guardians of the quarters, and in the center, they must be provided with a blue flag. Where the banners measure ten cubits, the flags there should also be five cubits long.
If they are only one *aratni* in length at their base, they should be fixed and concealed with five finger-breadths at the tip.

At that door, plantain trees (raṃbhā) should be arranged, along with beautiful flowers and pleasant grassy plots; likewise, there should be five-cubit-high arches (toraṇa) made of vacā wood, each having five branches. The sacrificial pavilion (yāgamaṇḍapa) should be bound and encircled on both sides with well-dyed munja grass, kusha grass, or lotus sprouts, and also with stalks of sugarcane.

Likewise, an altar (vedi) should be constructed in the middle of the pavilion (maṇḍapa), situated in the corners and free from stones and other debris; it should be one cubit high, adorned with beautiful lines, and measure four cubits in extent.
On the altar, having set aside ten finger-breadths from the northeast corner, and likewise three others [from the other directions].
One should provide a single square pit, situated with a girdle three finger-breadths wide and radiant;
and likewise, in the case of a temple, a pond, or a great grove,
one should diligently cause the Sarvatobhadra mandala to be constructed.
One should also construct the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with an inner girdle (mekhalā),
white in color, free from decorative patterns, and aligned with straight lines, extending outward to the womb-shape (yoni).
In the case of nine pits, one should likewise construct them on the altar (vedi) at the intermediate directions (vidiś), elevated and properly aligned.

All [the altars] everywhere are encircled by girdles; they may have six or five girdles, or be formed with eight corners, a lotus, or a triangle, as well as a half-moon or a square shape. To the northeast of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), a jar smeared beautifully with sandalwood paste should be placed.
"With its full waters covered by garlands and garments, possessing well-formed leaves and a golden interior.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the second part of the Madhyama-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa;
titled "Description of the Ritual for Worshipping the Planets of the Gods."
Sūta said:
Having departed from the sacrificial hall and taken refuge in another mandala,
the sacrificer likewise performed his daily rites according to the prescribed rules.
Having paid homage to the five deities as well as Hari, the Lord of Sacrifice,
and having then made a formal resolve (saṃkalpa) with the permission of the Brāhmaṇas, [he should declare]:
"In this meritorious place, such is my fruit, my lineage, and Yama [is the witness]."
O twice-born ones, in accordance with the injunctions shown in the scriptures composed by Vedavyāsa and others,
and exactly as set forth in my own Tantra, I shall duly perform this meritorious rite called Puṇyāraṇya for the consecration of the reservoir of water.

O twice-born ones, I shall duly perform the consecration of the water reservoir according to the rules, just as it is prescribed in the Kalpas, according to the specifications for the sacrificial pit, and with the preliminary perfuming rites performed by a single person who is a purifier and knower of the forest rituals.
Having made this resolve, one should perform the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*;
having placed the sacrifice to the Mothers (*mātṛ-yāga*) at the forefront, one should complete the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*.
Amidst the auspicious sounding of kettledrums and other instruments, one should here inscribe the sixteen-syllable verse.
One should indeed brandish the excellent weapons of the world-protectors, Indra and the others, stationed in their respective directions.
One should honor all of them, but especially the Preceptor (Ācārya),
with a pair of golden earrings as well as vessels made of copper and other metals.

The wise man should choose the preceptor with various jewels and garments, with pairs of golden ornaments and diverse clothes; according to his means, according to his ability, and according to how he wishes to honor him.
"May there certainly be well-being for you," thus was it composed by the sacrificer.
Then, with all medicinal herbs, the progenitors caused the sacrificer and his wife to bathe with the mantra beginning "āpo hi ṣṭhā."
Barley, wheat, nīvāra, sesame, śyāmāka, rice,
priyaṅgu, and vrīhi— these eight are remembered as the group of all medicinal herbs (sarvauṣadhigaṇa).
Then, wearing white garments and adorned with white garlands and unguents, [he should proceed].
Having bathed in water infused with all medicinal herbs and been consecrated by the preeminent among Veda-knowers,
he was authorized by the Brahmins and preceded by his family priest amidst the sounding of various auspicious chants and the resonance of kettledrums and drums.
The sacrificer, together with his wife and accompanied by his sons and grandsons,
having approached the western door, should enter the sacrificial pavilion.
In the Caraka [hall], he should worship Vighna (Gaṇeśa), as well as Gaṅgā and Yamunā.
On both sides, one should worship Lakṣmī and the female door-keepers (pratihārīs) in succession;
having circumambulated the altar clockwise, one should offer salutations according to the prescribed rite.
Then, seated there with the permission of the Brāhmaṇas, one should remain steady.

Then, having recited the benediction (*svasti-vācana*), one should worship the five deities. Next, having performed the expulsion of obstructing spirits (*bhūtotsādana*), one should scatter the *vikira* offerings upon the ground:
"May those beings depart who cause disturbance here."
Since they do not abide in our names, let the sacrifice proceed in its simple form;
thereafter, one should worship one's own seat with flowers and sandalwood, saying:
"Salutation to the Seat of Ananta, and likewise to the Lotus Seat."
"Salutations again and again to Vimalāsana, and salutations to Sārāsana;
salutations to Yogāsana, and also salutations to the Earth.
Then, having placed his left hand upon the surface of the ground, a man should recite this.
"O Earth, by you the worlds are supported; O Goddess, you are supported by Viṣṇu.
You, in turn, support me eternally; make this pure seat.
Then, having offered the *arghya* to the Sun and bowed to the Guru with palms joined in reverence:
Having brought the deity into the heart-lotus, one should perform three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Then, one should worship the Lord of Obstacles (Vighnarāja) upon the water-pot in the northeast,
with perfumes, flowers, garments, and various kinds of food offerings.
Immediately thereafter, one should worship Brahmā with the mantra "gaṇānāṃ tvā," and then,
while recollecting Vāsudeva with the verses "ā brahman" and "tad viṣṇoḥ," one should subsequently honor him with offerings of unguents, sandalwood paste, and other oblations.
Then, having occupied the body of the deity for nine months and thirty days,

[the officiant] should place all [the deities] around the sacrificial altar, each in its own respective place according to the sequence. Then, the sovereign king should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
Then, in the midst of the bubble, [he beholds the Lord] seated upon a white lotus throne,
resembling pure crystal, with the luster of a conch, a kunda flower, and the moon;
adorned with a crown and earrings, white, and holding a white lotus.
Clad in white garlands and garments, white with white perfumes and unguents,
seated upon a snake-head throne, holding a noose in his hand, and possessed of great strength;
he was being praised by hosts of gods and attended by Siddhas and Gandharvas.
The god with the beautiful face, adorned with a garland of lotuses,
with eyes like lotus petals, eternally gracing the world of the Nagas,
surrounded by various aquatic creatures such as crocodiles, sharks, and tortoises.
One should meditate upon the Lord residing in the reservoir of water, reclining upon the waters;
then one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa), adorned with its five limbs.
Thereafter, one should prepare the vessel for the offering (arghyapātra), filled with water divided into three parts.
Having recited the root mantra eight times, he should sprinkle the seat and the sacrificial materials with that water, [chanting]:
"We know Aruṇa; we meditate upon the destroyer of darkness."
One should perform the ritual bath with the mantra "tanno aruṇaḥ pracodayāt. Then, one should worship Gaṇeśa in the northeast (aiśānī) and the sandals of the Guru in the southeast (āgneyī).
Thereafter, one should worship all the principles, beginning with dharma and adharma, as well as sattva and the others.
The orbs of the sun, moon, water, and so forth, in their respective order;
in the center, Śakti, the Ocean of Milk, Ananta, and likewise the Earth;
the Tortoise, the Supportive Power (Ādhāra-śakti), Sumeru, and Mandara.
Having worshipped the five principles (pañcatattva) together with their limbs and ancillaries,
and thereafter taking white flowers along with unbroken grains (akṣata) through the power of yoga-illusion,
one should place them upon the water-pot (kalaśa) in the same location as before.
Then, having performed the invocation with this mantra, the knower of mantras [should say]:
"Come, come, O Lord Varuṇa! This sacrifice is proceeding;
accept this portion of the sacrifice; I invoke you alone."
Having thus invoked Lokeśvara, one should display the eight mudrās;
then, having bathed him with the Gāyatrī mantra, one should offer the triad beginning with water for the feet (pādya).
Thereafter, the preceptor, having offered a handful of flowers with the root mantra, [should proceed].
At the base of the petals in the east and other directions, the wise one should worship Dharma and the others;
there he should also worship Sattva and the rest, as well as their respective excellent consorts:
Jñāna, Dharma, Soma, Rajas, Sattva, and Tamas.

One should worship the eight planets in the middle of the petals starting from the east; likewise, one should worship the weapons of the world-protectors, beginning with Agni, at the tips of the petals. Furthermore, one should worship the Lord of Śacī (Indra) first to the right of the pericarp, and also on the left.
On the eastern petal, one should worship Brahmā with white lotuses;
then Varuṇa in the southwest, and one should worship Ananta in the center.
Among the pedestal mantras, one should likewise worship Brahmā in the east and Śiva [in the center].
One should also worship Viṣṇu, Gaṇeśa, and the Earth with fragrant sandalwood paste;
the wise person should mutter the mantra one hundred and eight times or recite it a thousand times. Then, kneeling upon the ground, one should recite the hymn known as the Vijaya.
In the corners of the seats beginning with Īśāna, [one should place] Kamalā and Ambikā;
Viśvakarman in the southwest (Nairṛtya), and Sarasvatī in the northwest (Vāyavya).
At the doorways starting from the east, one should place Marut and the others, beginning with Āvaha.
One should place Āvaha and Pravaha, as well as Udvaha and Saṃvaha,
at the western gate;
one should place Nivaha and Parīvaha at the northern gate, as well as Maruta and Parābhava.
Then one should conquer the outer seat (bahiṣpīṭha) in the corners beginning with the southeast,
[subduing] respectively the Piśācas, Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, and Vetālas.
[The deities there are] Kṣobhaka, Kāmarūpa, Saubhadra, and Maruta.
Gomukha, Nandabhadra, Dvijihva, Malina,
Hastikarṇa, and the one named Viśāla are known as the group of seven Rākṣasas.
Bhūmida, Varada, Jayanta, and Kṣobhaka likewise [are among them].
Vivasvanta and Sudadanta— these are remembered as the hosts of Bhūtas. Aṅgada, Nīlakaṇa, Vasanta, and likewise Yāvaka,
who are of terrible form and massive body, are proclaimed to be the Vetālas.

All the gods, the planets, and the rest, along with their devotees, should be worshipped with effort using perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata), according to the colors prescribed for their respective meditations.
One should meditate upon the Sun as being deep red, seated upon a red lotus throne.
Clad in red garments, red in hue, adorned with red garlands and unguents,
resembling barley or coral, and possessing a luster as crimson as vermilion—
one should place [the deity] upon the water-pot with the mantra beginning "ākṛṣṇena."

Having invoked him with the words "Come here," one should worship him according to the prescribed rite with devotion, using various kinds of water for the feet (pādya) and guest-offerings (arghya), as well as perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. One should also present a blood sacrifice (bali), along with milk-rice (pāyasa), curd, and sugar-candies.
[One should offer] boiled rice smeared with ghee and a red-colored banner;
[and worship] the mighty God who wears white garments, is white in complexion, is anointed with white perfumes,
has two arms, grants boons, and holds a mace in his hand.
Adorned with various ornaments and attended by Siddhas and Gandharvas,
one should present a horse seated upon a white lotus throne and decorated with white trappings;
one should install it on the petal of the eastern direction with the mantra beginning "imaṃ devāḥ."
One should offer white garments, flowers, white garlands, and unguents;
one should present milk-rice, white sacrificial offerings, and rice with curd,
along with incense, white banners, and various kinds of food offerings.
The god is red in color, wearing red garlands and garments, adorned with red ornaments;
he has beautiful red eyes, sits upon a red lotus throne,
wears a crown and earrings, has a ram's neck, and possesses four arms.

One should meditate with supreme devotion upon the auspicious son of the Earth— the bestower of boons, the destroyer of sacrifices, the wielder of the trident, spear, and mace, the god who grants all desires, and one who is served by the Siddhas and Gandharvas.
One should establish the fire in the petal of the southeast direction with the mantra "Agnimīle" and worship it with red flowers, red garlands, and unguents;
with incense, red banners, and offerings of molasses and cooked rice.
Resembling the flax flower and possessing a luster like the karṇikāra,
the son of Rohiṇī is of massive body and has eyes as dark as a blue lotus;
he is a deity with a serene countenance, clad in yellow garments, and endowed with four arms.
Likewise, [one should meditate on] the God holding a sword and shield, and bearing a mace and an axe;
seated upon a lotus posture, resting on a yellow lotus seat;
adorned with various ornaments, and having the king of beasts as his excellent vehicle.
With the mantra "Udbudhyasva," one should install the wise [deity] upon a lotus;
one should worship him with perfumes, flowers, and the like, with yellow fragrant ointments,
with garments and yellow banners, and with offerings including *kṛśara* (rice and peas).
One should meditate upon the Guru as being yellow in color, seated upon a yellow lotus throne,
endowed with yellow ornaments and yellow garments, and possessing four arms;
he grants boons, holds a staff in one hand, and carries a rosary and a water-pot.
Being worshipped by Gandharvas and even by the hosts of gods led by Indra,
he is situated in the south-western direction with the mantra "To Bṛhaspati.
He is adorned with yellow sandalwood perfumes and yellow garments and ornaments.
One should worship the priest of Purandara with incense, yellow banners, and offerings of yellow water with supreme devotion;
one should meditate upon Śukra, the son of Bhṛgu, seated upon a white lotus throne.
Four-armed and of massive form, granting boons and wielding a staff;
long-armed and large-eyed, carrying a rosary and a water-pot;
being praised by the best of sages and attended by the foremost of the Daityas.
The god was seated upon a lion-throne, his eyes like blue lotuses,
adorned with garlands of shimmering white lotuses,
and repeatedly instructing the sons of various lords of the Daityas.

Having thus meditated upon the best of the Bhṛgus, who is skilled in various weapons and missiles and proficient in various scriptures, one should— while reciting the *parisrut* mantra with a mind full of devotion—
place him on the western petal.
One should worship with the highest devotion using white sandalwood, garments, incense, garlands, and ointments;
with incense, white banners, and parched grain mixed with milk,
as well as with white lotuses.
One should meditate upon Sauri, who has four arms, holds a trident in his hand, and bestows boons;
he is dark-complexioned like a sapphire, wields a divine bow and arrow,
sits upon a blue lotus seat, and possesses the radiant splendor of a supreme lotus.

One should place [the deity] in the northwestern direction with the mantra "Śanno devī," who wears blue garments, is adorned with a garland of blue lotuses, possesses a formidable form and a massive body, and brings joy to the heart through his shadow.
With black sandalwood, garments, black garlands, and ointments;
with incense, blue banners, and offerings mixed with black gram (māṣa)—
one should always worship the smoke-colored Ketu, who holds a mace in his hand and bestows boons.
One should install [the deity] in the northeastern direction with the mantra "ketuṃ kṛṇvan," [visualizing him] as two-armed, of terrifying form, smoke-colored, and clothed in smoky garments;
[one should worship him] with smoke-colored garlands and with incense and unguents of a smoky hue.

One should worship Ketu, the bestower of all success, with supreme devotion using offerings mixed with black gram (māṣa) and smoke-colored banners. I shall now describe the world-protectors (lokapālas), who grant all accomplishments.
When these alone have been worshipped, there is nothing anywhere that remains unattainable.
Thereafter, one should meditate upon the King of Gods (Indra), who possesses the radiance of a multitude of flower-arrows;
he has two arms, is yellowish in hue, and has eyes like blue lotuses.
One should likewise meditate on Indrāṇī on the left, holding a red lotus, clad in yellow garments,
adorned by precious maidens with chowries in their hands,
and bearing two lotuses.
Thus one should worship with devotion the King of the Gods, the Lord of the World.
With the mantra "trātāram," one should establish him in the northern petal of the pericarp.
One should worship him with supreme devotion using incense, perfumes, and unguents.
With various kinds of offerings, banners, and flags,
one should present an oblation accompanied by milk, as well as sweetmeats and white sugar.
One should [visualize] the four-armed Vītihotra (Agni), who resembles molten gold.

Seated upon a half-moon, with a goat as his excellent vehicle, he is reddened by a canopy of flames and possesses seven crests upon his head. He bestows boons and dispels fear; in his right hands, he holds a garland, a thread, and a water-pot.

One should bathe [the deity] on the petal in the southeast direction with the mantra "Agnijihve," [visualizing him] as three-eyed, with red eyes, adorned with a crown of matted hair, endowed with various ornaments, and attended by Siddhas and Gandharvas.
One should worship him with red flowers, red garlands, and unguents;
with incense, red banners, offerings, and even milk-rice (pāyasa).
He resembles a mass of blue collyrium and is seated upon a blue lion-throne.
The Lord was mounted upon a great buffalo, wielding a staff and a noose;
he had a formidable face, was terrifying, with eyes whirling with flames,
and was surrounded by hosts of servants made fearsome by their terrible fangs.
One should meditate on Mahiṣa on the left and Citragupta on the right;
with the mantra "Acchīyase," one should establish [the deity] on the Yamadi-petals and worship Dharmarāja, the teacher of the world, with supreme devotion.
The lord of the waters was of gigantic body, black in complexion, and possessed two arms;
he was adorned with various ornaments, held a sword in his hand, and was endowed with great strength. Seated upon an excellent palanquin made of pearls, he was of terrible appearance.
With the mantra "eṣa te," one should place [the image] in the south-western direction (Nairṛti),
adorned with black sandalwood, black garments, black garlands, and ointments;
with incense, black banners, and offerings mixed with black gram (māṣa).

One should install [the deity] on the western petal with the mantra of Varuṇa: resembling pure crystal, possessing the luster of a conch, a jasmine flower, or the moon, two-armed, holding a noose in his hand, with beautiful limbs, and bestowing boons.
With white sandalwood incense, banners, and flags,
[he worshipped] the Wind-god— who resembles the color of a noble elephant, who is mounted upon a deer, who has two arms and two eyes,
who carries a single banner-cloth and blue garments, and who is surrounded by masses of clouds.
One should worship with supreme devotion using blue sandalwood, garments, blue garlands, and ointments; also with banners, flags,
incense, blue pennants, offerings, and milk-rice.
One should meditate upon the Lord of Wealth (Dhanada), who has two eyes and two arms, wears yellow garments, is borne by a man (Naravāhana),
holds a mace, and bestows boons upon his devotees; one should then invoke him onto the northern petal of the lotus with perfumes, sandalwood paste, garments, and yellow garlands and unguents.
With incenses, yellow banners, offerings, and even milk-rice oblations,
[one worships him who is] resembling smooth camphor, possessing the luster of the moon,
holding a trident and a tumburu fruit, and likewise bestowing the gestures of fearlessness and boons.

Having thus meditated upon Maheśāna— mounted upon a tall bull, three-eyed, adorned with ashes, wearing a garland of skulls, and likewise crowned with a crescent moon— one should install him on the petal in the northeast direction.
One should worship with supreme devotion using various kinds of foods to be chewed and eaten,
with white banners and flags, with offerings such as milk-rice (pāyasa), and so forth,
while reciting the mantra "Thou art Īśāna," proclaiming the seer and the meter.
Brahmā is reddish-white in complexion, with a luster equal to a crimson lotus;
he has lotus-eyes and a radiance like the interior of a lotus.
He is seated upon a lotus throne, wears white garments, and possesses four arms.
The four-faced one, the best of gods, with a voice as deep as a thundercloud,
seated upon an excellent celestial chariot drawn by royal swans;
holding a *sruk* and *sruva* ladle in his right hands, and a staff and water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) in his left.
He appeared as if creating the three worlds, frequented by Siddhas and Gandharvas;
likewise, there was a vessel of clarified butter before him, along with Kuśa grass and sacrificial fuel.
On his left side was Sāvitrī, and on his right was Sarasvatī.
With the mantra "O Brahman," one should establish [the deity] on the petal in the eastern direction;
one should worship with various kinds of edible offerings, perfumes, sandalwood,
incense, white banners, oblations, clarified butter, and milk-rice porridge.
[He is] the Lord of the World, possessing an infinite luster of white color, wearing yellow garments, four-armed,
and bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus;
he is the foundation of all worlds, wearing a golden sacred thread.
Adorned with various ornaments and endowed with a hundred hoods,
one should install [the image] within the Varuṇa [mandala] with the mantra "Oṃ namo'stu.
One should worship it with various kinds of food and drink, as well as with lamps, perfumes, and unguents.

Then, to the east of the mandala, one should worship Brahmā, who is clothed in yellow garments, four-armed and four-faced, holding a *sruva* ladle in his hand and granting boons. [He is to be honored] with incenses, white banners, and offerings prepared for him.
Likewise, one should worship him who bears the sacred knowledge as well as the staff and water-pot,
with perfumes and sandalwood while reciting the mantra "O Brahman.
One should meditate on Tryambaka to the right, bearing the trident and the skull-topped staff.
The God who grants boons, holding a damaru drum, wearing a sacred thread of serpents,
with the crescent moon bound in his matted locks, resembling pure crystal,
wearing a garland of skulls, and adorned with ornaments of snakes.
One should worship with honeyed milk-rice using the mantra "Tryambakam," [visualizing] the three-eyed one, resembling a kunda flower, surrounded by hosts of bhūtas and pretas;
[and then] the one resembling an atasī flower, adorned with necklaces and armlets.

Adorned with various ornaments and clad in yellow garments, he has four arms; in his right hands he holds a mace and a discus, and in his left hands a conch and a lotus. He is accompanied by Śrī on his right and Sarasvatī on his left.
Then, one should install [the deity] in the west with the mantra "tad viṣṇoḥ";
one should worship him with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, as well as with milk-rice and ghee.
Gaṇeśa, however, has four arms and wears a serpent as his sacred thread.

One should meditate upon the god who has the face of a lordly elephant, clad in white garments, possessing four arms; holding an axe and a club in his left hands, and a staff and a lotus in his right hands;
seated upon a mouse, of massive body, and radiant like a conch shell, a kunda flower, or the moon.

One should firmly install the one-tusked deity, who removes fear, who is endowed with various ornaments, and who destroys all calamities, in the north using the mantra "gaṇānāṃ tvā". This is appropriate for both right and wrong intellects.
One should [worship] the auspicious Lakṣmī, resembling refined Jāmbūnada gold, seated upon a lotus throne,
holding a lotus in her left hand and likewise holding a chowrie in her right hand,
outside the mandala in the northeast with the mantra "Śrīśca te".
One should install and worship [the deity] with devotion using white sandalwood paste and lotuses;
one should offer sweetmeats, milk-rice, and barley-milk.
Then, [one should meditate upon] the goddess Ambikā, of divine form, with three eyes, being praised by Brahmā, Indra, and the other gods.
She is seated upon the Lord of Lions, possessing the luster of molten gold, with her matted locks bound by a crescent moon;
she is endowed with divine garments and long, outstretched arms adorned with celestial garlands and ornaments.
Invincible even to Brahmā, Indra, and the other gods, she crushes the buffalo-faced Dānava with her sharp weapons.
She holds a sharp trident, arrows, and two sharp spears in her right hands,
while in her left hands she carries a bow, a noose, a shield, a goad, a bell, and a sharp battle-axe.
She holds the severed head of the king of the Daityas, from which a torso has half-emerged, as well as a sharp sword.

One should meditate upon the radiant Goddess Ambika, shining with various garments and ornaments; she who, having been encircled by Naga-serpents with their coils, strikes him with a trident in the center of his body; she who is praised by the gods led by Indra, and served by Gandharvas and hosts of Siddhas;
and who is honored with cloths, garlands, Yaksha-incense, canopies, and various foods such as eatables, chewables, sweetmeats, and milk-rice.

The goddess Caṇḍikā, the bestower of desired boons, should be worshipped with all kinds of ground meats, including those rich in goat flesh. One should meditate upon the dark-hued Earth, who holds two lotuses, stands upon a frog, and has two arms; one should worship her with the mantra "syonā pṛthivī."
In the southwest, one should meditate upon Viśvakarman, who has two arms and holds a chisel;
he holds a blue lotus in his right hand, stands upon a lotus, and is clad in yellow garments.
Having thus meditated, O Brahmin, one should then worship him with the mantra "brahman".
One should meditate upon Sarasvatī established in her own nature, bestowing boons and fearlessness,
clad in yellow garments, wearing a beautiful crown, and served by gods and gandharvas.
One should worship her with white sandalwood paste using the mantra "yāmadhā."
One should offer the bali-oblation consisting of white caru, kṛśara, and likewise yāvaka;
one should place these on the left side and worship with kunda flowers.
Furthermore, one should worship the hosts of Maruts at the gate-areas starting from the east.
And in the outer corners beginning with the southeast (Agni), one should perform the rites for the external beings:
the Piśācas, Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, Vetālas, and the various species of Kapis;
all of them noseless, fierce, and of deformed appearance.
Then, in the center of the mandala,
one should fill the water-pot according to the previous procedure; therein, O best of men, one should fashion a tortoise in the form of a tortoise out of pure gold or other precious materials.
According to the measurement of the *Bṛhatparvan*, a silver [image] is difficult to obtain;
[one should instead make it] with a foot-measure of one-fourth of that standard, circular in size and measuring one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*).
Likewise, one should fashion a *prauṣṭhīmatsya* and a crab made of copper.
O best of sages, by that same measure, one should fashion a frog on that ground with a length and width of two finger-breadths; likewise,
a crocodile should be properly fashioned from two *tolakas* of material.
They should be three finger-breadths long, according to their proper form; they are to be worshipped on all sides with white sandalwood paste and cloths,
and especially with barley-gruel by those well-versed in many mantras.
Two masters of the Ṛgveda should be stationed in the east for the sake of the Matsyas;
two knowers of the Yajurveda in the south; two with their seats in the west; and two masters of the Atharvaveda are prescribed in the north.
Then, he should indeed address those Hotṛ-priests once again, saying, "Be victorious!"
Having set aside separately in another thread the serpent, the Mother, and the lamp,
as well as the five-limbed Śiva-sūkta for Viṣṇu and Hara,
the Puruṣa-sūkta before Jaya, and the hymn "Born from the Waters" (adbhyaḥ saṃbhūtam).

Beginning with "āśuḥ śiśānaḥ" and "vayaṃ somasya rudra," as well as "yat jāgrataḥ," "agneḥ," "viṣṇoḥ," and "arāṭam," the entire chapter together with the Rudra-hymn is declared to be known by the name Śatarudriya.

For the *Pañcāṅga-Rudra*: Puṣpadanta is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Gāyatrī is the metre (*chanda*), "vedāhameta" is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), "śrīśca te" is the power (*śakti*), "namaste rudra" is the leader (*nāyaka*), and Paramarudra is the deity (*devatā*). Its application (*viniyoga*) is in supreme praise.
For the *Saptāṅga-Rudra*: Puṣpadanta is the seer, Paṅkti is the metre;
for the mantra "tryambakam," [the assignment is] "salutation to the two thumbs" (*aṅguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ*).
"Tripādūrdhvam" (The three feet above) with the two index fingers: svāhā.
"Vedāham" (I know) with the two middle fingers: vaṣaṭ.
"Amīṣāṃ citram" (The wonderful [wealth] of these) with the two ring fingers: huṃ.
"Yavāgūṃ soma" with the two little fingers, *vauṣaṭ*;
"parito dhenum" with the palms and backs of the hands, *astrāya phaṭ*;
and "yajjāgrata" for the heart, *namaḥ*.
"Thousand-headed" (Sahasraśīrṣā) is for the head: Svāhā!
"Born from the waters" (Adbhyaḥ saṃbhūtaḥ) is for the tuft: Vaṣaṭ!
"The swift one, sharpening his weapons" (Āśuḥ śiśānaḥ) is for the two armors: Huṃ! "Salutation to you, O Rudra" (Namaḥ te rudra) is for the three eyes: Vauṣaṭ!
"O Brahmin, [it is] established," [and then recite] *astrāya phaṭ*.
Snap the fingers in the four directions. [Do this] for all limbs. While the fire sacrifice (*homa*) is proceeding, one should indeed recite other hymns (*sūktas*).
One should recite the Vāruṇa Sūkta as well as the Pāla Sūkta;
the Rātri Sūkta, the Raudra Sūkta, and the radiant Pāvamāna Sūkta; and one should also recite the Pauruṣa Sūkta and the Sarvatovara Sūkta separately.
The one who knows the Yajurveda should worship with the Śākta, Raudra, Saumya, Kūṣmāṇḍa, Jātavedasa, and Saura hymns on the south side; [and likewise] with the Vairāja,
Pauruṣa, Sauvarṇa, and Rudrasaṃhitā hymns.
The *Śaiśava*, the *Pañcaniraya*, the *Gāyatrī*, the *Jyeṣṭhasāman*,
the *Vāmadevya*, the *Bṛhatsāman*, and likewise the *Rathaṃtara*—
as well as the *Govrata* and the *Vikarṇa*— are remembered as purifying hymns that destroy the Rākṣasas.
And those Brahmins who, from the eastern gate and the other directions,
chant the five [verses] beginning with "annāt parisrutaḥ" as the Saura-sūkta,
as well as the Rudrādhyāya consisting of five parts, that is designated as the Raudra.
