They declare the four verses beginning with "āpyāyasva" to be the Soma hymn;
the section beginning with "īśāvāsyam" is one's own portion (svāṅga), and the Kauṣmāṇḍa is remembered as the tenth.
The nine hymns beginning with "agre bṛhan" belong to Jātavedas.
The sixteenth is proclaimed as the *Vibhrāḍ*, the great solar hymn (*sūkta*);
the solar hymn beginning with "dhruvo'si" is remembered as auspicious for Maṅgala.
Indeed, the *Rātrisūkta* belongs to Yama, while the hymn beginning with "yajñāgne" is a Śiva-hymn that destroys demons.
Know that the five verses beginning with "gaṇānāṃ tvā" and the triad beginning with "āpo hiṣṭhā" constitute the Pavamāna; indeed, the Pāvamāna consists of sixteen [verses].
This is used in its entirety during divine sacrifices, while at night it is used from that point onward.
Half of that [number] again for the grove, and one *ṛc* for the well;
one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) in each of the sacrificial pits according to the procedure prescribed in one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra*.
Having honored one another, one should consecrate them with the initiatory rites (*īkṣaṇa*) and so forth.
Having kindled the fire according to the prescribed rules, one should immediately perform the *homa* sacrifice.
Having worshipped Vāgīśvara together with Vāgīśvarī—
whatever deity’s sacrifice or installation ceremony it may be.
One should first offer a thousand and likewise a hundred oblations for him with sesame seeds,
clarified butter, milk-rice, or with leaves, flowers, and unbroken grains;
all this should be offered according to the rules to the planets, as well as to Indra and Īśvara.
One should perform the rite according to the rules for the Maruts, the world-protectors, and Viśvakarman,
offering eight oblations each even in one's own home with fuel-sticks of *ūrja* grass.
For Indra, Īśvara, and the Maruts, one should offer oblations of sesame seeds and clarified butter.
One should offer one oblation for each [deity] with their respective mantras in due order;
specifically, eight oblations for each of the lords of the directions.
Then, having offered three oblations of clarified butter with the mantra "viśvakarman," [one should proceed].
One should offer oblations of three twigs each, either of the *palāśa* or of the *aśvattha*, especially with clarified butter;
[offering] to Śiva, Prajāpati, Viṣṇu, Durgā, and Kamalā as well.
And one should offer oblations to Sarasvatī and to the Earth according to the rules with purifying mantras;
likewise, one should give an oblation to the spirits for two months in succession.
For others, one should offer oblations in due order with sesame seeds and parched grain soaked in honey.
One should likewise place Viṣṇu in the northwest, Durgā in the north,
Kamalā in the northeast, and Īśāna along with Bhūta in the northeast;
then, one should perform the oblation according to the prescribed rite in a single, unified sacrificial pit.
In the alternative case, there should be five sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) in order starting from the east;
or, having established the planets in a single pit together with Indra (Balabhid),
one should likewise place the world-protectors (lokeśas) in sequence on the south.
To the west of whichever sacrifice it may be, and to the north of Durgā,
the best of preceptors should offer oblations to Bhūtayakṣman in the northeast;
for the deities beginning with Viṣṇu, the offering is prescribed in the front fire-pit (agratkuṇḍa).
On the first day, one should perform the installation of the deities;
on the second, one should perform worship and offer oblations according to the prescribed rite;
on the third, the offering of bali; and on the fourth, the caturthī-rite.
The Nīrājana rite occurs on the fifth day; this is the procedure for a ritual to be accomplished in five days.
For a ritual to be accomplished in three days, it occurs on the third day, while for a nine-day rite, it occurs on the fifth.
Facing either north or east, one should proceed in order starting from the northeast (Īśāna).
One should perform the sweeping around the sacrificial fire by circumambulating it to the right while reciting mantras;
for those who maintain the sacred fires, this is preceded by mantras, whereas for those without such fires, it is performed with a rite for satisfaction (*tuṣṭika*).
In a great sacrifice, three blades of *kuśa* grass are used, while at marriages and similar rites, two blades are employed.
"In the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, however, there is the rule of using a single vessel; this is the general injunction.
In the Mahāyāgas, one always spreads [the grass] in the cardinal and intermediate directions;
in the Nityaka rites and likewise in the Vaiśvadeva, one spreads it only in the cardinal directions."
If one fails to perform the obligatory rites (*nitya-karma*) constantly, the occasional rites (*naimittika-karma*) will become futile.

Therefore, even by means of fruits and other such offerings, one should perform that occasional rite. This applies specifically to expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*), the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice, and the morning and evening offerings.
In rites of killing, expulsion, and fire-offerings, as well as in those involving imagined forms or in any situation involving a multitude of transgressions,
one should perform the oblation fifty times; however, in those cases where there is no fixed form, one should always avoid it.
Then, having performed the *tūrya-homa* silently, the one who has conquered his senses should mutter prayers to Indra, Agni, and Soma in due order;
thereafter, he should perform the *samidh-homa* followed by the *vyāhṛti* oblations.

"Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ"— thus, O venerable one, listen to the procedure for that [rite] consisting of the five [syllables] beginning with "tatra," at the end of which one should offer the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation;
and in the rites of purification for the twice-born, there is an offering of clarified butter and the *sviṣṭakṛt*.
One should offer the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation with clarified butter, but one should avoid it at the beginning of a sacrifice.
One should perform a bath with water containing all medicinal herbs using warm water from the tusk of an elephant,
as well as from a road, an anthill, a cow-pen, a horse, or a temple.
One should place the three fragrances, the three coolants, and earth from the roots of *kuśa* grass into the bathing jars; then,
having placed the patron at the front, preceded by a tooth-stick, one should install the preceptor and the others.
And at night, having gratified [the deity] with various kinds of food and drink, and having prepared barley and unbroken rice (akṣata),
one should perform worship with a stream of oil according to the prescribed time.
Then, when the dawn is clear, one should perform the ritual bath according to the rules.
The bathing [of the image] should be performed with mantras addressed to the waters, with the Puruṣasūkta,
and with the Vāruṇa-sūkta, while the deities— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara— are invoked in due order, beginning with: "May the gods— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara— consecrate you."
Vāsudeva, the Lord of the World, as well as the powerful Saṃkarṣaṇa;
the divine Ākhaṇḍala (Indra), Agni, Yama, and likewise Nirṛti;
Varuṇa, Pavana, Dhanada (Kubera), and Śiva.
May Śeṣa, together with Brahmā and the guardians of the quarters, protect you always.
Kīrti, Lakṣmī, Dhṛti, Medhā, Puṣṭi, Śraddhā, Kriyā, Mati,
Buddhi, Lajjā, Vapu, Śānti, Tuṣṭi, and Kānti are the Mothers.
May these divine goddesses, composed in mind, consecrate you:
Āditya, Candra, Bhauma, Budha, Jīva, Śukra, and Arkaja—
may the planets, as well as Rāhu and Ketu, being gratified, consecrate you.
The gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and pannagas;
the ṛṣis, the Manus, the deities, and the mothers of the gods;
the wives of the gods, the trees, the nāgas, the daityas, and the hosts of apsarases.
Missiles, all weapons, kings, and vehicles;
medicinal herbs, jewels, and whatever constituent parts of Time there are;
rivers, oceans, mountains, sacred fords, clouds, and streams.
"May these [deities] consecrate you for the attainment of all desires and goals.
Having completed the bath according to the rules, one should anoint oneself with one's own attendants.
[One should then give] one hundred and eight cows, or half of that, or twenty."
One should give [the cow] to a worthy preceptor while honoring him;
then, at the clear light of dawn, one should cause her to enter the water—
she being pure, tawny, a milch-cow, and provided with a jar and a fly-whisk.
Then, one should give to the Sāma-singer a gift accompanied by gold;
having taken up the sacrificial post (yūpa) and established it, one should bathe it while reciting the Vāruṇa mantra,
followed immediately by the Acchāvāka mantra and the Gāyatrī.
With yellow orpiment, the three jewels, and likewise with water from a ritual jar;
with earth from a mountain peak, from water, from a serpent’s mound, and from an anthill; with earth from an elephant’s tusk, and likewise with earth from the base of a riverbank.
With water from a flower, with a conch, and likewise with water containing jewels;
with curd and unbroken grains, with milk, and with a jar of a hundred streams;
having anointed [the image] with fragrant water and the threefold cold water, one should remain composed in meditation.
One should cause a vessel made of bell-metal to be given, or one made of iron;
having adorned it with garlands and garments, one should worship it with perfumes and sandalwood. With the mantra beginning "īśāvā," one should offer three handfuls of flowers.

One should again offer a flower with the mantra "punastvāditi. The measurement of the bronze wheel (*kāṃsyacakra*) is such that its width is one *prādeśa*, it is circular in the middle and six *aṅgulas* [in diameter], while its height is twelve *aṅgulas*.
Above that, one should draw a trident measuring four finger-breadths;
however, one should not have a trident made of iron that is less than a thumb's breadth.
Then, preceded by auspicious rites and with the approval of the twice-born, [one should proceed].
One should abandon the palace and especially the pond;
having taken four blades of *darbha* grass while facing the northeast (*īśāna*), one should thereafter utter this statement: "I hereby renounce [them]."

Om, etc. Desiring the attainment of the fruits mentioned in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa* composed by the venerable Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana Vedavyāsa, I release this powerful water of the pond—delimited by its four corners and the like, honored with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, presided over by the deity Varuṇa—for the purpose of bathing and immersion for all living beings.
Then, with the *Varuṇa Sūkta*, one should cast Varuṇa together with the Nāgas, as well as the Makara and the Tortoise, into the waters.
One should worship the god Varuṇa and especially offer him the arghya water;
having bathed [the image] with that water and with clay from an elephant's tusk,
while reciting the mantra "Śrīśca te," one should apply [the clay] produced from the essence of the white horse.
With the mantra "āpyāyasva," he should take earth from a crossroads;
with the mantra "tad viṣṇoḥ," he should place it using the roots of kuśa grass.
He should likewise [anoint it] with water from sacred fords (tīrtha), with fragrant paste, and with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
The practitioner should bathe the deity with water containing gems while reciting the Gāyatrī;
immediately thereafter, with milk, using the mantra "āpyāyasva";
with curd, using "dadhi krāvṇaḥ"; and with honey, using "madhu vātā".
One should bathe [the deity] with water and *jātī* flowers while reciting the mantra beginning with "sarasvatyāṃ ta.
[For the mantra] "varuṇottama": Nārāyaṇa is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Gāyatrī is the meter (*chanda*), Varuṇa is the deity (*devatā*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is for the propitiation of Varuṇa.
[For the mantra] "śrīśca te": Kardama is the seer, Paṅkti is the meter, the Rivers are the deity, and its application is for bathing with clay from a horse's hoofprint.

For the mantra *āpyāyasva*, Parvata is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Uṣṇik is the meter (*chandaḥ*), Sarasvatī is the deity (*devatā*); its application (*viniyoga*) is for bathing with clay from a crossroads for the propitiation of Varuṇa.
For the mantra *tad viṣṇoḥ*, Maināka is the seer, Triṣṭubh is the meter, Sarasvatī is the deity; its application is for bathing with Kuśa-grass clay for the propitiation of Varuṇa.
For the mantra *kayā naḥ*, Vasiṣṭha is the seer, Anuṣṭubh is the meter, Soma is the deity; its application is for bathing with the scent of serpents (*nāgagandha*) for the propitiation of Varuṇa.

For the mantra *tejo'si*, Garga is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Triṣṭubh is the meter (*chandas*), Vāsava is the deity (*devatā*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is for the propitiation of Varuṇa. For the mantra *sarasvatyai bhaiṣajyena*, Vāmadeva is the seer, Paṅkti is the meter, Viṣṇu is the deity, and its application is for the propitiation of Varuṇa.
This is for the bath with flower-water.
For the mantra *agna āyāhi*, Janārdana is the seer, Jagatī is the meter, Aindrī is the deity, and its application is for the propitiation of Varuṇa.
One should cast five grains of rice while reciting the mantra "iyaṃ ca";
thereafter, one should perform the *nīrājana* rite preceded by the five sounds. [One should also offer] a mirror made of bell-metal and fashioned from *śirīṣa* flowers.
One should prepare a footprint [of the deity] using either gopīcandana, or clay from the Gaṅgā,
or the dung of a black cow, or even a svastika and a conch;
or one may make it from barley or wheat flour.
The wise one should then purify the jar produced from *māṣa* beans, which has arisen from heaven;
the essence of prosperity produced from flowers; the mirror produced from bell-metal;
and the *nandyāvarta* mark produced from sandalwood.
One should offer an oblation of unbroken rice and black-gram flour upon the water for each individual mantra,
using the eight mantras dedicated to Dhruva and his counterparts in their proper sequence,
according to the prescribed rite.
Then, with the Nārāyaṇa-sūkta, one should approach the god Nārāyaṇa;
and for the other deities as well, one should offer thirty-fold bali-offerings.
Thereafter, one should present water for sipping (ācamanīya) and a pair of garments.
O twice-born ones, one should then offer them individually, each according to the sequence and the prescribed rite with the mantra to be recited, even as many as there are,
accompanied by Vedic hymns (sūktas) and provided with sacrificial threads (yajñasūtra).
O God, these two garments of every color have been fashioned for you;
I do not know your body, nor indeed your movements.
Accepting the fragrances offered by me, please anoint yourself.
The wise practitioner should place one hundred and eight lamps around [the deity] in sequence, or half of that, or twenty-five, and worship them with the mantra:
"You are the sun, the moon, and the luminaries; you are likewise the poison."
"You alone are all the lights; please accept this lamp.
Then, one should perform circumambulation five or seven times.
One should offer ten-ingredient incense while reciting the mantra that is about to be described.
This divine incense, the essence of the forest trees, rich in fragrance, sweet-smelling, and pure, has been offered by me with devotion; please accept it.
Likewise, [accept] these ornaments, perfumes, and yellow garments.
One should worship with dūrvā grass, unbroken rice, garlands, and flowers;
thereafter, one should offer five añjalis and again recite the Viṣṇu-sūkta.
Then, having constructed an altar in a very beautiful place, the preceptor [should proceed].
One should install Varuṇa there, as well as the lotus pond;
one should perform the ritual sprinkling and other rites according to the procedure prescribed for marriage.
Then one should offer fragrant flowers and give a cow along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
One should provide a yak-tail whisk, a fan, an umbrella, and likewise vessels of bell-metal and iron;
one should also construct a beautiful silver lotus pond on three legs,
which is four-cornered, perfectly symmetrical, and two thumb-breadths in circumference.
O twice-born ones, one should fashion a golden image with a single face;
or else, one may write upon a gold leaf with saffron on its surface,
the gold leaf being two finger-breadths in size and having the dimensions of a *bāṇa* and a *śakti*.
The wise one should have it made square and place it upon a pedestal;
O best of Brahmins, at the conclusion of the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), he should remember and cross over with the nectar.
Likewise, by one who is unable, it may be done on a single piece of wood or on a leaf of the Pippala tree.
One should inscribe it upon a copper plate with lacquer according to the prescribed rite;
then, one should perform the consecration of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) and present it to Varuṇa. One should maintain the festival for a year, preceded by the chanting of the Vedas.
The aśoka, khadira, śāla, aśvattha, bilvaka,
as well as the dhātrī, kurubaka, bakula, and nāgakeśara—
of these very trees, one should fashion a sacrificial post (yūpa) equal in height to the sacrificer.
Having taken hold of it, established it, and received it with garments and other offerings,
one should cause it to be dug into the ground while reciting the mantra "O sacrificial post, protect!
Then, having placed a hand upon it while reciting the mantra "Be firm," one should thereafter chant as follows:
Likewise, having reached the northeast of the pond and similarly that of the temple,
and then the southern part of the dwelling in the center,
the boat should proceed; thereafter, remaining silent, one should take up the sacrificial post (yūpa).
In the middle of the lake, having likewise crossed to the north,
one should proceed after making preparations; right there, with the verse "āpyāyasva," one should perform the fire-oblation upon a stone and offer three boat-oblations.
With the mantra "Svāhā to Aṅgada" and "Namaḥ to Bhauma," one should perform the counter-homa (pratihoma) with parched grain,
curd, and honey upon the seat.
Then, having said "Namaḥ to Kūrma" and "Namaḥ to Pṛthivī," [one should proceed].
Immediately thereafter, one should offer the *arghya* with the mantra "Svāhā" to Ananta.
One should cause the *arghya* to be presented with the five gems, fragrant scents, and a conch shell.
[The area] should be square, well-spread, and surrounded on the four sides by people who have taken their seats.
One should fashion it and place it there; having placed the hand upon it, one should recite this:
"Be firm! With this mantra, one should worship it with perfumes and flowers.
One should offer the discus along with its mirror, while standing at the head of the serpent-staff.
And here, Vidyut is the agent, beloved for removing the suffering of the planets.
Having thus worshipped the wheel, one should worship the trident and the nāgas. Then, having raised a high banner, one should recite the mantra "O Nāga."
Then, one should recite the mantra "gāyatrasva" at both doors; thereafter,
one should offer an oblation (bali) consisting of black gram rice and rice with jaggery to the guardians of the directions (dikpālas),
having adorned it with red flowers, and after prostrating, one should seek their favor.
One should give a thousand coins as a gift to a Brāhmaṇa who maintains a household;
thereafter, one should provide food with ghee and gold according to the prescribed rite.
One should offer the "Ikṣusvastītikā" gift and worship the Mothers in the water.
Then, one should worship Mantharā, Vasutā, Kāntā, Rākṣasī, Piśācikā,
the Nāginīs, and the sons of the Nāgas in the center.
At the conclusion of the full oblation, one should separately offer parched grain (lāja) and other items mixed with jaggery.
"Indra is powerful; Svāhā is the glory even of the powerful.
This distinction of broad wings exists in the middle and the youngest [sons].
To Bṛhaspati and to Indra—[I offer] your divinity."
One should then offer oblations with the mantra "svāhā" and subsequently move the *praṇītā* water.
In the case of a small temple, a reservoir, or likewise on Mount Mandara,
one should install Viṣvaksena at the archway.
O twice-born ones, there is a fifth distinction regarding the grove and the bridge:
whoever, during the interval between worship, should mutter a thousand mantras,
having completed the hymn of praise according to rule, should recite this mantra.
Having recited, "Even this water drawn up has been offered to all sentient beings," one should take water from the lotus pond in the hand and pour it back into the water.
Then, one should worship the Water Mothers (Jalamātṛs) with the mantra: "Obeisance to the Water Mothers."
Whatever places there are in the three worlds, whether stationary or moving,
this water is released by me for their nourishment;
thus has this been performed for my mother, which brings joy to the entire world.
For the welfare of all beings, always protect this reservoir of water! May all creatures be happy while drinking from it or bathing in it;
this water has been provided by me at all times for the benefit of the entire world.
"O gods, may my fame endure for a long time upon the surface of the earth!
By your grace, O highly fortunate one, O King of Nagas, salutations be unto you!
Whatever beings here meet their end, they are merely consumers of the fruits of their own karma."
May I not be stained by their faults; may each attain their own respective destination.
May Nārāyaṇa, the life-breath of the world and the granter of all desires, be pleased.
May the mothers who are the source of trees for the worlds be worthy of my drink.
O Lord of Waters, O Master of aquatic creatures,
O Sovereign Varuṇa, O Eternal One, salutations to you who sit upon the throne;
may he bestow that water like a treasure-trove as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for the twice-born.

One should give gold and silver, a draft ox, and a milch cow; thereafter, one should give two cows and perform the satiation of Brahmins. Having first performed the worship of the fire, one should then cause [the mixture] to be consumed with the mantra.
One should cause the *arghya* offering to be presented to the ancestors, and then propitiate the deity.
One should display the *bimba-mudrā*, the *padma-mudrā*, and the *nāga-mudrā*.
Having performed the worship with the verse beginning "vaiśvānara," one should conclude the rite.
O twice-born ones, listen: he who, after reciting the life-giving mantras, should then apply sandalwood paste and subsequently perform a circumambulation of the pond,
having placed the Brāhmaṇas in front and uttering the resonance of the Vedas.
The wise man should enter his home preceded by great auspicious rites;
then he should perform the worship of the household deities, provide food for the Brahmins,
and offer the arghya water-oblation to Savitṛ for the sake of the poor and the wretched.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Madhyama-vidhāna," in the second part of the Madhyama-parvan within the glorious *Śrī-Bhaviṣya-Mahāpurāṇa*. Sūta said:
The procedure known as the Saptāgniṣṭoma is declared to be the most excellent;
it yields middling results in the middling [version] and inferior results in the inferior.
Now, I shall describe the middling procedure in accordance with the scriptures.
Whatever ought to be performed by a man according to his means,
having consecrated the sacrificial post and other items through the rite of immediate consecration (*sadyodhivāsa*),
on the very first day, at an auspicious time declared by an astrologer.
Having established the water-pot (kalaśa) for a moment and having taken hold of Gaṇanāyaka,
one should first install the sacrificial post (yūpa) with the mantras beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā. Thereafter, one should apply sandalwood paste with the mantras "śanno devī" and "gandhadvārā."
Then, one should offer flowers and dūrvā grass with unbroken rice (akṣata) using the Śrīsūkta;
thereafter, one should present incense with the mantra beginning "kāṇḍāt";
and then, with the ṛc verse beginning "ye gṛhṇāmi," one should establish the image during the worship.

A wise man should employ the entire procedure for the marriage rite, including the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*), in the case of tanks and other such works. Having thus consecrated the tanks and others, as well as the preceptor (*ācārya*) and all others in every respect, he should proceed.
Having honored [the deity] with perfumes, flowers, and the like, as well as with beautiful incense and lamps,
and having then regularly performed the daily rites according to the scriptures at the time of dawn,
one should then perform the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, preceded by the worship of the Mothers.
Having adorned the preceptor and others according to his ability, the wise man should attend upon them;
he should listen [to the teachings] near the western side of the pavilion.
A sacrificial vessel originating from the central region is highly recommended.
Alternatively, in that [sacrifice], one should indeed appoint a local preceptor or one born of a learned Vedic lineage as the primary assistant to the officiant—
the priest and teacher—
endowed with expertise in the ritual manuals (vaitānakalpa) and devoted to the performance of rites according to his capacity.
One endowed with knowledge of the Vedas is praised as a worthy recipient at a sacrifice.
However, one should completely avoid a person who lacks a wife or a son, one with black teeth or missing teeth, a priest for a multitude, and a eunuch, even if he belongs to one's own lineage.

O best of beings, in secondary sacrifices and in sacrifices consisting of gifts, one should employ a member of one's own lineage for the fire-oblation; there is no doubt about this. Even by means of a substitute made of *kuśa* grass, he then goes to heaven.
Having first purified one's wealth, one should then perform a sacrifice.

The "sprout" (*pallava*) arising from officiating at sacrifices for those unworthy to offer them, as well as that produced by false testimony in legal proceedings and the seizure of property through fraudulent means, must be settled [by expiation].
The property of the gods, the property of Brahmins, wealth obtained from selling iron,
and wealth from selling sacrificial offerings— having sold his son and wife as well, he who sells these things reaps the fruit of whatever was condemned in the Purāṇas for having committed such acts.
One should never feed Brahmins who are not invited to a Śrāddha at the sacrificial hall;
nor should one give them a gift until the rite is fully completed.
O Brahmin, you are the foremost of teachers; O Lord, save me from this cycle of worldly existence!
"O Guru, by your grace, may I obtain my heart's desire in this sacrifice.
May my eternal fame endure for a long time as long as the worlds of moving and unmoving beings exist.
Be gracious, O Maheśāna, for the successful completion of the rite of installation."
You are the origin of all beings and the savior from the ocean of saṃsāra;
O Teacher who bestows the nectar of knowledge, you whose form is Viṣṇu, salutations be to you!
You have arisen from the seat of Brahmā, illuminating the quarters of space.
And you, who resemble Jāmbūnada gold, O Yajurveda, salutations be to you!
You who shine with blossoming lotuses, adorned with radiant garments,
who possess a vast collection of scattered scriptures and know the ritual injunctions— to you I bow down.
"O you who resemble the blazing Vaiśvānara fire, whose face is darkened by a wreath of smoke,
O knower of the six limbs and the truth of the Vedas, O officiating priest, grant me liberation!
Then, amidst the sounding of musical instruments and other music, having placed the best of the twice-born at the forefront—
The sacrificer, together with his wife, should enter the sacrificial pavilion.
He should establish the Brahmins in their respective places within the ritual arena according to the prescribed rules and in due order.
He should honor them with perfumes, garlands, and other such highly pleasing substances, beginning with fragrant scents.

That Puruṣa who is always worshipped in the well-expanded sacrifice is of the very nature of Nārāyaṇa; may He make my sacrifice fruitful. By Him the mantras have been extensively elaborated in all the most excellent sacrifices.
O knower of the true essence of the Yajurveda, whose form is Brahman, salutations be to you!
Witness of all sacrifices, knower of the true essence of the Vedas and the meaning of the Vedas,
knower of the Rigveda, O one of great wisdom, O universal form, salutations be to you!
I bow to the one who is the auspiciousness of all actions, eternally constant, whose form is Brahman,
and who possesses the form of Śiva for the success of my sacrifice;
he who protects all the cardinal directions as well as these intermediate directions.
I bow to the Brahmin who embodies the guardians of the quarters for the successful completion of the sacrifice.
One should cause the right knee to touch the ground and then scatter the *vikira* offerings.
Whatever beings there are in the three worlds, both stationary and moving—

May Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva all indeed provide protection for those [altars]. Having prostrated before the altar (vedi), one should recite the mantra "vedyāvedī" and, having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, should utter this mantra: [The mantra follows: brahmaviṣṇuśivāḥ sarve rakṣāṃ kurvaṃtu tāni vai | vedyāvedīti maṃtreṇa paṭhedvediṃ praṇamya ca || saṃpūjya gandhapuṣpādyairimaṃ maṃtramudāharet ||
Between officiating as a priest and being the patron of a sacrifice, the priest attains the greater merit therein.
"This is the respectful offering (arghya), this is the water for the feet (pādya); let this incense be accepted.
Having thus worshipped the Lord Gaṇanāyaka in the pitcher located in the northeast (aiśānī) direction.
One should worship Brahmā and Vāsudeva in the second pitcher. And indeed, Viṣṇu himself has assumed the form of Dvārakā; with him I worship you today—grant me the attainment of heaven.
Having established three jars each in the directions starting from the east, the wise man should offer a raft made of wood of the same color as the vessel’s base,
together with sprouts and clay from the Ganges.
Having fashioned Mount Mandara from the lineage of the cowherds (gopīs),
and having placed it upon the water-pot (kalaśa), one should worship Mount Mandara with the mantra "syonā pṛthivī" and with various kinds of perfumes and flowers.

(For the mantra "Syonā pṛthivi," Sumanta is the seer, Jagatī is the meter, Hara is the deity, and its application is for the propitiation of Mandara. Thus, in the southern quarter, one should fashion Mount Gandhamādana out of silver, measuring one span in length and nine *tolakas* in weight.
Thereafter, one should at some time worship with a clay image and with a *ṛc* verse.
Regarding the mantra "kadācana": Sūrya is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Triṣṭubh is the meter (*chanda*), Sūrya is the deity (*devatā*), and the application (*viniyoga*) is for the propitiation of Gandhamādana.
[One should place it] two thumb-breadths from the northern archway of the mountain.

With a measure of two *tolakas* of barley flour placed upon the cake— [reciting] the mantra "Āpyāyasva" (May you swell), whose seer is Kardama, meter is Jagatī, and deity is Śacī; its application is for the propitiation of Supārśva—
one should worship Dhātṛ and the other deities in the pitcher at the side, following the sequence starting from the eastern direction.

One should worship the seven Vijayas with the mantra of the Śrīsūkta alone, honoring them with supreme devotion using perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), and other offerings. For the mantra "Ambā Ambike," Nalina is the seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is the meter (chandas), Śambhu is the deity (devatā), and its application (viniyoga) is for the pleasure of Jaya. One should worship the two western jars on the right side with the Gāyatrī mantra.
(For the Gāyatrī: Viśvāmitra is the seer, Savitṛ is the deity; the application is for the pleasure of Vijaya.
A wise person, being self-restrained, should offer both the *Bhadra* and the *Subhadra* [oblations].
(For the mantra "Manonā" in the northern pair of jars: Antaka is the seer, Bṛhatī is the meter, Nirṛti is the deity; the application is for the pleasure of the Bhūtas.)
Then, having performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) according to the rules,
and having prepared the water for libation (arghya) and so forth, one should worship in the maṇḍala of Dharma and the other principles.
In the center, one should worship the foundational powers (ādhāraśakti) and others, and Varuṇa in the middle.
In order from the east and so forth, one should worship Indra and the other deities of the families; on both sides of the pericarp, one should likewise worship Brahmā and Ananta,
with their respective mantras as prescribed, along with offerings of oblations, perfumes, and flowers.
For the mantra of Indra’s consecration (*indrābhiṣeka*), the instrumental music should be in the *gāndhāra* melody;

for the mantra "Thou art the splendor of Agni" (*agneḥ tejo 'si*), the music should be in the *varāṭaka* melody; and for the mantra "The dense thorn" (*ghanakaṇṭaka*), the melody to be sung is *gurjara*.
The battle of the Lord of Rākṣasas is said to be the Vaitāla musical performance;
likewise, hear from me the melody called Nāṭaka belonging to Varuṇa as well.
His musical performance is named Rājyābhiṣeka, and his melody is known as Vasanta.
The musical instrument of Īśa is called Nandighoṣa, and his passion (rāga) is Kāmada;
the wise have declared that the musical instrument of Brahmā is the golden Dundubhi drum, and his passion is the goddess Vasanta. Now learn from me concerning Ananta’s [instruments].

The musical instrument is called Gāndhāratārā, and the melody (rāga) is Aṅgāravātaka. In the sound of Soma, there shall be the instrument of the high-souled Lord of Waters; the great melody known as Mālava shall be upon the tips of the leaves.

Having gathered [the materials] according to their respective properties, one should worship the Earth on the south side with the mantra "Syonā pṛthivi" and various kinds of ritual offerings. One should worship Mahādeva in the northern part of the pavilion.
With the mantra beginning "namo vṛkṣebhyaḥ" and various kinds of food offerings, one should meditate upon Mahādeva—two-armed, holding a *ḍamaru* drum and a trident, accompanied by Umā.
For the mantra "namo vṛkṣebhyaḥ," Brahmā is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Gāyatrī is the meter (*chanda*), and Candra is the deity (*devatā*); its application (*viniyoga*) is for the propitiation of Candra.
One should worship the beings all around with devotion using perfumes, flowers, and other offerings:
"May the vetālas, piśācas, rākṣasas, and reptiles,
as well as any others who cause obstacles, depart from this place of mine."
One should offer milk-rice mixed with honey to Varuṇa;
and the food should be yellow, reddish-brown, black, pure white, dark, smoky,
yellow-white, variegated, and white, respectively.
Now hear of the offerings for the lords of the directions and also for the planets:
milk-rice is prescribed for the Lord of Planets (the Sun), white food for the Moon,
red food for Mars, and milk with *ṣāṣṭika* rice for Mercury.
The food of Venus, the preceptor of the gods, is yellow rice with white grains;
that of Saturn is known to be meat-rice; and that of Rāhu is black cooked rice.
That of Mars is smoky-colored or coppery, consisting of milk and ṣāṣṭika rice.
Flour-based food is prescribed for Śiva, and black-gram rice for the spirits (bhūtas).
Having thus prepared the offering (bali), one should then place a water-pot (kuṃbha) in front;
its circumference should be two finger-breadths [in diameter] and it should be one thousand and eight [aṅgulas] in height.
Having placed many finger-breadths [of cloth] upon the jar one after another, and having wrapped it with threads of the desired color for the night, one should likewise cover it; then,
placing a shallow bowl on top, one should worship the *vardhanī*.
Having meditated upon the Lord Jaleśvara with the mantra "Astrāya Phaṭ," one should worship Him with the Sūkta according to one's capacity and recite it one hundred and eight times.
One should then install the eight Nāgas in the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), starting from the east and proceeding in order.
First, the wise one should worship Ananta, fashioned from gold and measuring exactly one finger-breadth in size, with seven wicks; then,
he should again worship the serpent Vāsuki, made of silver, within another petal.
Even when the vessel is only one foot high, there should be a copper receptacle for the food the size of a thumb;
furthermore, the *karkoṭaka* vessel made of iron should be five finger-breadths wide with a rim,
and it should be sixteen times the size of a large joint when measured by wicks.
One should worship Śaṅkhapāla made of kuśa grass with half a pāda;
the Nāga [Vāsuki] measuring one aṅguṣṭha with blood, and Tālaka measuring one tolaka;
thereafter, one should again worship Padmanāga upon the aṅguṣṭha.
One should properly fashion an image made of stone, measuring half a *tola* in size and endowed with all the correct characteristics,
constructed according to the original proportions of that Great Lotus.
Having meditated upon Ananta, who has four arms and is endowed with seven white hoods;
in his upper right hand is a conch shell upon which a discus is established;
and in his upper left hand is a mace and a lotus, situated in the middle position.
Having meditated thus according to the prescribed rite upon [the deity] adorned with all ornaments,
one should worship with the mantra "sahasraśīrṣā" and offer a bali-oblation consisting of various kinds of parched grain mixed with sesame seeds and milk.
Likewise, one should recite over the fourfold white substance, adorned with all ornaments,
using the verse "āpyāyasva" (VS 1.1);
[the substances are] oil-cake, *nāgajihvā*, resin of the *sarja* tree, and curd.
The offerings for him have been specified: one should worship Takṣaka with red [substances].
Holding a lotus and an axe in his two arms, the best of serpents should be honored with the mantra "Manonnā," while offering clarified butter and Soma as the oblation.
One should worship Karkoṭaka, who has two arms and wears yellow garments, with the verse beginning "pañca nadyaḥ. An offering of Viṣṇukrāntā should be made;
one should worship him as four-armed, wearing yellow garments and holding a thunderbolt.
In the upper portion with two arms, one should meditate on Hari holding a red lotus;
his offering is proclaimed to be sugar and kuṣṭhaka.
And [one should meditate on] Śaṅkhapāla, who has two arms, is conch-like in color, and holds a conch.
One should worship the Lord, who is seated in the lotus posture (padmāsana) and bestows boons with his two lotus-like hands,
separately with the two mantras "dhruvakṣiti" and "dhruvasi. For these two,
there should be a water-pot, cooked rice, the bhr̥ṅgarāja plant, a lotus, and bracelets.
Having established the fire according to the ritual prescribed in one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra* and performed the *kuśaṇḍikā*,
he should prepare the clarified butter (*ājya*) and cook the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) for Varuṇa.
He should indeed offer eight *bilva* fruits with clarified butter to the lords of the directions.
One should offer one oblation for each of the planets, three for each,
using well-prepared fuel-sticks mixed separately with clarified butter, honey, and milk.
Afterwards, one should offer three oblations of *palāśa* fuel-sticks for the installation.
One should offer oblations to Śiva eight times with supreme food (paramānna).
One should offer parched grain (lāja) mixed with honey, clarified butter, and molasses separately.
Then, one should present the parched grain as prescribed, offering each oblation in successive order.
One should again offer individual oblations from the *sthālīpāka*,
dedicating them separately to Varuṇa and to Rudra;
then, with the mantra "To Vāstoṣpati," one should prepare the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
Then, with the mantra "Syonā pṛthivi," he should apply rice-paste; again,
with the mantra "Vṛṣāṇaḥ" and also "Kayā naḥ," he should apply earth from the roots of *kuśa* grass as well as earth from a crossroads.
With the mantra "imā rudra" and again with the verse "śrīśca," one who is well-composed should bathe [the deity] with clay from a lotus-pond;
likewise, with the mantra "tad viṣṇoḥ" and with water mixed with flowers.
With water from sacred fords, with black [substances], with three reds, with three cold [substances],
with five reds, with the earth of the Rakta mountains, with certain waters of Kuśa grass,
and with waters of gold— by means of one hundred and eight jars.
Having established [the vessels] according to one's capacity with twenty-eight made of metal and likewise of clay, and having smeared them with saffron and sandalwood paste,
one should then apply food and offer it with earthen vessels in the proper sequence.
With the verse "surāsura... he should wrap [the banner] with a pair of garments;
with "dhvajaṃ ca dhanu... [he should offer] cow dung; with "gaṃdhadvārā...
incense; and then, with "dhūrasi...", an oblation lamp for the Hotṛ priest.
With the mantra "siṃdho'si" and likewise with vermilion (sindūra), which is naturally red,
and with offerings of jasmine flowers, one should then establish the Nāgas.
This should be done with streams of water, śatapuṣpā flowers, scented water, and so forth.
Alternatively, the wise one, having inscribed [the mantra] upon leaves of the Aśvattha or Vaṭa tree using yellow pigment (rocanā) or saffron, should worship it there; indeed,
he should place pearls therein and cast them into the water-pots (kalaśas).
Having prepared a beautiful bed in the northern part of the pavilion,
one should place upon it a silver image of Varuṇa fashioned to the size of a foot,
and then likewise install a lotus pond measuring a thumb's breadth.
Having worshipped a beautiful, four-sided vessel fashioned with golden feet and measuring the size of a thumb, one should offer it to Varuṇa; thereafter,
according to one's capacity, one should give a cow, or twenty-five if possible.
Having taken gold, silver, grain, clothing, cowries,
and a serpent-staff, as well as some items for the northern direction,
he then offers three oblations of clarified butter to Akṣata and Bhūma.
With a concentrated mind, one should place within the womb parched grain mixed with curd, as well as ghee, honey,
molasses, milk, flour-cakes, fried cakes, incense, and flowers—
the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and the five jewels (pañcaratna).
The preceptor, together with the sacrificer and well-equipped attendants,
having reached the middle of the two banks of the Gaṅgā waters amidst the fivefold sounds, takes up the sacrificial staff and stands firm like a mountain against his enemies.
Then, with the mantra "Dhruva, Dhruva," one should consecrate the sacrificial staff (yaṣṭi) as follows:
"O Goddess, you are dear to sacrifice, the destroyer of all obstacles;
protect me from all sins; may you become firm through your own self."

Having thus addressed [the fire], one should perform the sacrifice and then recite the Gāyatrī; furthermore, one should mutter the mantra "vanaspate" and "vidvān". Then, having returned to that altar and churned [the fire], one should [worship] the Lord Varuṇa.
Likewise, one should cleanse the lotus pond and the Vardhanī vessel with the bellies of water-jars;
having removed the serpents and likewise the jar,
and having made the interior stone-like, one should smear it all over with cow dung.
One should place Varuṇa within the lotus pond in the midst of the water;
with the mantra "Namo'stu," one should offer a bali-oblation of milk-rice (pāyasa). Whatever Nāga is churned forth there, one should install him according to the prescribed rite.
One should cause him to hear this mantra: "Be present here!
O Naga, you are the master here; the people must be protected by you.
Then, one should again cause him to hear the mantra with the Gāyatrī meter.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should place [the vessel] in front in the [northeastern] direction.
Having covered the King of Nagas with the two verses and with threads,
having quickly restrained and established him, one should offer the bali according to the rule.
Having offered parched grain and rice, he should recite the *manas* hymn, "That which [is] for the waking," with the *ṛc* verses;
likewise, having established them in their respective directions with their own various mantras beginning with "Bhūḥ," he should worship them with diligence.
In the eastern part of the lotus pond, having placed a green-colored object together with a vajra by means of the *halagrahīta* mantra,
one should offer parched grain (*lājā*) oblations into the fire while reciting the *trātāram* mantra, and then place a pearl there.
One should recite "agnim īḷe" over realgar and coral;
then, with the Vaiśvānara mantra, one should again offer a ghee oblation.
With the "ye te śataṃ" mantra, one should place a piece of wood in the western direction.
One should offer eighteen oblations with the mantra "kayā na" accompanied by a grain of *śāli* rice, and with the mantra "varuṇasyo.
Likewise, one should offer [oblations] with yellow pigment (*rocanā*), a young girl, and white mustard seeds in the north.
Reciting the Ṛgvedic verse beginning with "kuvidaṅga," one should offer an oblation again using that same mantra, having applied saffron to the tip of the sacrificial ladle (sruva). Then,
reciting "īśāvāsyamidaṃ sarvam," one should offer a gentle oblation in the northeast.
Having established [the deity], one should offer an oblation of clarified butter with the verse beginning "tam īśānaḥ";
then, having seated the Lord Nārāyaṇa, one should worship Him with mantras joined with the [appropriate] ritual formulas.
Then, meditating upon Him as having Varuṇa as His essence, one should recite the *nīrājana* hymn.
Having touched the ground with both knees, one should recite the hymn of praise, the nectar of knowledge (*jñānāmṛta-stava*).
Then, at the conclusion of the ritual offering (*utsarga*), one should perform the *dharma-vaṃśa* (the lineage of righteousness) as prescribed.
Thereafter, having again addressed the Goddess and offered three handfuls of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), [one should conclude].
One should indeed relinquish oneself for the benefit of all sentient beings;
once relinquished to all beings, one is seen as water of great power,
in which all creatures delight through bathing, drinking, and immersion.
Then one should place the god Varuṇa into the lotus pond;
subsequently, one should cast fish and other aquatic creatures into the water with the Varuṇa-mantra,
as well as auspicious birds there, along with frogs, tortoises, and mud.
One should cast *śaivāla* grass into the water, and immediately thereafter,
one should give gold, grain, and gems separately to the preceptor (*ācārya*). One should also give gifts separately to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), according to the extent of one's wealth.

Having completed [the rite] daily according to the rules, he should separately give [gifts] to the Brahmins, the singers, and the Vasus; then, reciting the mantra "hastābhyām," he should again offer the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and present the respectful offering (arghya) to the Sun.
Then, having encircled it with a clockwise-turning stream of milk,
[he should perform the rite] three times with the power of a hundredfold streams upon the temple-wing, the temple, the garden, and then the pavilion, together with the Brahmins.
Having scattered parched grain, flowers, rice, and cowries,
the sacrificer, together with his wife, should then enter his own home again, preceded by Brahmins and accompanied by the great sound of musical instruments.
Then, having performed the worship of the household deities, one should feed the Brahmins,
as well as young girls and boys, and the poor, the blind, and the wretched.
Thereafter, one should devotedly offer [the image of] Nārāyaṇa for the sake of a Brahmin.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the second part of the Madhyama-parvan within the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa.
Thus concludes the second part of the Madhyama-parvan.
Description of the consecration of gardens and other such sites.
Sūta said:
Now I shall describe here the specific details regarding gardens and other such places. Having first caused a square, level, and auspicious mandala to be prepared, |||
One should worship the Lord Nātha there in the pitcher located in the northeast;
thereafter, the worship of the planets is performed in the central pitcher.
Furthermore, at the locations of the doors in their respective directions, specifically at the two western doorways.
One should worship Brahmā and Ananta, and Varuṇa in the middle;
and Varuṇa residing in the water-pot, auspicious upon the branches of the Bhūta-tree. With that [mantra], I invoke you, O All-pervading One; indeed, become [the means] for heaven.
O best of men, having first established Mount Mandara upon the archway and having worshipped Viṣvaksena, one should perform the worship associated with heaven; then,
in the pericarp, [one should place] Vāsudeva, who resembles pure crystal.
Four-armed, adorned with the conch, discus, mace, and lotus;
his chest marked by the Śrīvatsa and the Kaustubha gem, and decorated with a crown and other ornaments; Kamalā is at his right side, and Puṣṭi is stationed at his left.
Being praised by Siddhas, Kinnaras, Yakṣas, and others, as well as by gods and demons,

one should worship [the Lord] with devotion according to the rules using the Ṛgvedic verse "viṣṇorarāṭ asi. Then, on the petals, one should worship Saṃkarṣaṇa and the others, as well as the female deities (nāyikās) beginning with Vimalā.
Having worshipped with incense, lamps, and unsurpassed offerings,
there should be a lamp of ghee for the God, as well as incense of guggulu and sarala;
the offering to the God shall be milk and milk-rice (paramānna) saturated with ghee.
One should meditate upon Soma in the pericarp of the lotus on the right, seated upon a lotus,
white in luster, two-armed, peaceful, adorned with armlets and other ornaments,
highly praised by gods and yakṣas, and holding the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness in his hands.

With the verse beginning "imaṃ devā," he should worship the Lord of the Night with various kinds of offerings and present him with rice cooked in ghee. He should likewise worship Indra, Jayanta, Ākāśa, Varuṇa, and Agni.

One should worship Īśāna and Tatpuruṣa in the directions starting from the east, as well as Vāyu; and on the left side of the pericarp, one should worship Mahādeva, who has two arms, white complexion, and holds the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness in his hands.
One should offer clarified butter and flour with the Tryambaka mantra;
one should offer eight oblations to the divine Vāsudeva,
and twenty-eight oblations of *paramānna* to Saumya.
A wise person should offer two oblations of excellent food (paramānna) to Śiva;
likewise, he should give one oblation of clarified butter (ājya) to Gaṇeśa;
and similarly, one oblation each to Brahmā and Varuṇa.

One should offer a single oblation for each of the planets with the fuel-sticks (samidh) prescribed for them, and separately for each of the lords of the directions, using clarified butter (ājya) in due order:
Karālī, Dhūmalī, Śvetā, Lohitā, and Kanakaprabhā.
The exceedingly red ones, ruby-colored, are proclaimed as Vahnijihvās (Fire-Tongues).
Their mantras, in due order, consist of the letters beginning with *sa* and ending with *va*, accompanied by nasal dots (*bindu*),
situated upon the letter *ya*, and adorned with the eight vowels.
One should offer oblations separately, each sprinkled with ghee, honey, and clarified butter;
being composed, one should give each individual offering to Agniṣoma,
as well as to Indra, Earth, and the Atmosphere.
One should offer oblations with a vessel of cooked food (sthālīpāka) mixed with honey, milk, and barley,

offering each oblation separately while dedicating it to each of them individually; having worshipped [the deity] along with the *parāvaka* using barley-gruel (*yāvaka*), perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
O highly fortunate one, recite with faith and with speech restrained;
as a practitioner of recitation, one should perform the *ruddhaka* there according to this rule.
One should likewise recite the *maṅgala*, the *paramānna*, and the *saurasūkta*.
Then, having cleansed it according to the rule and bathed it according to the ritual,
the wise man, having placed the sacrificial post (yūpa) within the womb [of the altar],
should fix banners at its extremities and offer the Vanaspati Soma.
Having recited "ko'dāt," the piercing of the ears of the trees should be performed with a very sharp needle into two holes, one on the left and one on the right;
likewise, barley gruel and sweetmeat balls should be offered for the satisfaction of the nine planets.
One should also give flour-cakes separately to young girls and children;
having wrapped them with a thread consecrated at night along with powdered substances,
one should likewise offer milk to the trees according to the prescribed ritual.
One should cause those trees to be consumed and recite this mantra:
"Whether fallen from the top of a tree, or fallen while climbing,
whether through death or the breaking of bones, the performer is not stained by sins."
Having circumambulated the preceptor, one should give a cow, gold, and grain;
likewise, one should give gold and silver to the officiating priest (ṛtvij),
and one should give grain, along with food prepared with ghee and sugar, to the Brahman priest.
One should likewise give the desired sacrificial fee to the Sadasyas.

Having brought the Adhika-kalaśa (the surplus pitcher), one should perform the ritual bath according to the prescribed rules. Having performed [the preliminary rites] throughout the night, one should then offer the Pūrṇāhuti oblation.

Having sprinkled the house with water containing all medicinal herbs three times, and having encircled it three or four times with a stream of milk while preceded by the chanting of the Veda, one should then go home; there, together with the Brahmins, one should perform the worship of the house.
I shall state the specific distinction for that [thread] with the verse beginning "Varā evedam.
One should then worship Bala, Kāma, Hayagrīva, Mādhava, Puruṣottama,
Vāsudeva, Dhanādhyakṣa, and thereafter Nārāyaṇa.
One should offer a bali-oblation of curd-rice produced from the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having thus worshipped according to the prescribed rite, one should worship the Earth on the right side—
she who has the luster of pure gold, is auspicious, and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite with the mantra "syonā pṛthivī," [the goddess] who stands upon a frog, has two arms, and is beautiful with all ornaments,
one should offer an oblation of milk-rice mixed with honey and sugar.
To the left, one should worship Viśvakarman— who resembles pure crystal,
who holds a trident and a chisel, and who is peaceful— with ritual offerings;
and with the *ṛc* beginning "viśvan," one should offer him a bali consisting of honey and flour-cakes.
One should give gifts and recite the Kauṣmāṇḍa and Pauruṣa Sūktas;
having performed eight oblations with honey and milk-porridge,
one should subsequently offer each individual oblation in the rite of the Earth-oblation.
Then, having abandoned the bridge, one should recite this mantra:
"For those who have fallen upon the slippery path, through contact with raised limbs;
since the bridge of dharma has been established, may there be dharma for me, not sin."
With supreme faith in this bridge-work,
those living beings who dwell here and provide protection for the bridge shall obtain that merit which is indeed offered through the Vedas and the Agamas.
Having dug a pit, one should place five jewels therein;
then, having erected the sacrificial post (yūpa) and worshipped it according to the prescribed rite,
one should then give the desired and excellent sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor (ācārya).
One should honor a Brahmin couple with parched grains (lāja) as a mark of worship;
then, for the attainment of desired goals, one should offer a mattress and a bed.
Furthermore, one should plant an auspicious banana tree at a bridge where trees may already be standing.
Likewise, on both sides of them, as well as in the grove, [these should be made] separately.
Thus ends the first chapter in the third part of the Middle Section of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*,
titled "Description of the Excellence of the Cow-Pasture."
Sūta said:
I shall speak again of the Gopracāra; hear from me its specific details.
One should worship Viṣṇu together with Lakṣmī with various kinds of ritual services.
And with ritual services, one should worship Brahmā, Rudra, Karālikā,
Varāha, Soma, Sūrya, and Mahādeva in their proper order; and likewise,
for Viṣṇu and Kamalā, there is the triple triad of fire-offerings (homa).

One should offer a single oblation each to the guardians of the field (kṣetrapālas) and others with clarified butter mixed with honey, separately in the parched grains and other materials. Having consecrated the sacrificial post according to the prescribed rite and established it, one should worship it.
One should construct [the base] measuring three cubits and provided with the hoods of a serpent;

one should plant it with a single cubit [of soil] within the womb [of the pit] and perform a fire-oblation (homa) according to the ritual involving parched grain (lāja), while muttering the mantra "viśveṣām."
Likewise, the third [offering] is for Acyuta, the Lord of Nagas;
the fourth is for Bhauma.
Then one should present the sacrificial post (yūpa), having worshipped it with the mantra "mayi gṛbhṇāmi," as having Rudra as its presiding deity.
Having worshipped Rudra with the five-limbed rite, he should give grain, clothing,
and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor (ācārya), as well as to the officiating priest (hotṛ) and others, along with their desired fees.
On the pasture ground for cows, he should set up a sacrificial post (yūpa) made of Śaileya wood, measuring two cubits in length.
One should fashion a sacrificial post (yūpa) five-cubit high, complete with five heads, and plant it; likewise, having touched a Caitra tree, a Kuṇḍalī, a monastery, or a pedestal,
O Brahmins, one becomes pure by sipping water and performing breath control (prāṇāyāma).
It should be measured by a hundred pits, each four cubits in dimension;
the smallest [pit] should be half of that, increased by eight eighths (one).
Having placed a jewel upon the ground, one should recite this mantra:

"The world of Śiva and the cows, who are highly honored by all the gods— this earth is bestowed by me, seeking auspiciousness, upon the cows. Thus should one who is composed announce the pasture ground for the cows.
Released from all sins, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu;
for as many auspicious blades of grass and shrubs as there are upon the earth,
for that many thousands of years he is glorified in the heavenly world.
One should first establish the boundary by planting a tree;
having constructed a dam to the south, one should plant charcoal to the west,
and have a well dug to the north— one must not overstep its boundary.
Then, O Brahmins, one should give a thousand-streamed vessel filled with grain; by doing so, one is liberated from all sins,
whether in a city, a village, or in the east, north, or even the west.
One should not perform an auspicious rite in the south-eastern direction from that [place].
Whoever digs up or causes to be ploughed the pasture ground for cattle,
he quickly causes his family line to fall and incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin.
A cow-skin properly donated along with a sacrificial fee leads one to heaven;
for as many blades of grass as there are upon that ground— counted to the number of seven—
one shall dwell in heaven for that long, never falling from the realm of Viṣṇu.
And he who does not gratify the twice-born at the conclusion of a great sacrifice,
his ritual act is fruitless, resulting in nothing more than mere physical exertion.
O twice-born ones, however, he who bestows land at the conclusion of the rite of releasing a bull—
O Brahmins, one does not go to the state of a preta by being free from envy toward Brahmins;
therefore, O you who have assembled here, listen to the distinct measure regarding this matter.
He who gives without due honor goes to the Raurava hell.
O twice-born ones, where a hundred cows and one bull stand unrestrained, that area is renowned as a *gocarma*; when given away, it destroys all sins.
This applies to the pasture-ground of a deity or of a Brāhmaṇa, O twice-born ones.
As long as the time limit has not expired, there is no sin.
One should worship the pavilion and the Sun together with Vāsudeva;
the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed with sesame and jaggery, eight times each, separately.
With the mantra "dehi me," one should place [the vessel] above the pavilion.
Then, having prepared four white jars with effort,
one should release them and subsequently recite the Saura and Vaiṣṇava hymns.
Having either inscribed [the figures] on a banyan leaf or fashioned them as a painting,

the wise one should install the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) in their respective directions. With palms joined in reverence, he should recite the mantras of Indra and the others in due order.
For the sake of establishing the Dharma and for the manifestation of your own power,
O Mahendra with the thunderbolt in hand, you ought to protect us according to the Dharma.
O Agni, whose vehicle is the ram, you who are adorned with four horns!
For you must protect this helpless pavilion according to the Dharma.
O Yama, Lord of the Southern Quarter, whose vehicle is the great buffalo,
for you must protect this helpless pavilion according to the Dharma.

Seated upon your couch, you are the lord of the Rākṣasas, wielding a sword in hand and possessed of great strength; indeed, it is right for you to protect this protectorless pavilion according to dharma.
You are the king of waters with the serpent as your emblem, and you are the wind-god whose vehicle is the deer.
For you ought to protect this protectorless pavilion according to dharma;
for you are the Lord of Wealth, mace in hand, tawny-eyed, and borne by men—
you ought to protect this protectorless pavilion according to dharma.
You are the primordial god among gods, the creator and destroyer, the Great Lord. You indeed ought to protect this protectorless pavilion according to righteousness.
You are the infinite King of Serpents who stands having lifted up the earth.
Indeed, you ought to consecrate this unprotected pavilion according to the Dharma;
for the sake of the stability of the four castes, of beasts and birds,
and for the pleasure of Vāsudeva, one should thus dedicate the pavilion.

If a pillar is broken or a grass mat becomes worn out, by providing a new grass mat and re-establishing it in that very same manner, its consecration shall remain inexhaustible. If living beings should die due to defects such as injury or decay [of the structure], [the merit remains].
Once the consecration has been performed, may my merit accrue and not my sin.
O Lord, by your grace, may there always be well-being for the humans and animals who dwell here in this pavilion.
Then, having wrapped it seven times with a triple-stranded cord while reciting the verse beginning with "sutrāmāṇe," and having displayed the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),
he should likewise present a pair of sandals and an umbrella to the preceptor.
One should feed the Brahmins in a pavilion and give them whatever they desire;
one should also give separately to the poor. Preceded by Brahmins, one should enter the house to the sound of musical instruments and perform the worship of the home.
In this manner, the specific procedure for the water-shed (*prapā*) should be understood;
one should proceed to Varuṇa together with Vāsudeva, along with all their limbs and sub-limbs, accompanied by ritual fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
The most excellent preceptor should perform the rite according to the rules for the *sthālīpāka* offering.
One should give a house equipped with furnishings to the preceptor;
to the officiating priest (ṛtvij), a copper vessel filled with water and grain.
One should especially worship the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) at the doorway during the ritual of the well (kūpayāga).
One should worship Brahmā, the Nāga kings, and the two gatekeepers in the west;
one should worship these various deities with their respective mantras in due order.
Having performed the offering of the bali according to the rules, one should present it according to the prescribed rite.
I shall now declare, in due order, the true nature of the banners:
Vajrī, Dhūmalī, Kṛṣṇā, Pītā, and Vāruṇī;
Śīghrā, Gaurī, Umā, as well as Pītā and Śuklā are proclaimed.
The wise one should first worship Maheśa in the jars;
then the planets in the central jar, and after that Brahmā.
Then, on the eastern part of the altar, he should worship Śiva in the northern jar.

Having worshipped Viṣṇu in the southern pitcher and Jaleśvara in the pericarp according to the rules with various offerings of devotion, and having drawn the serpents upon a banyan leaf with substances produced from serpents;
I shall now declare those nāgas: Ananta, Vāsuki, Karkoṭaka, Padma, Kulika, Padma,
and Mahāpadma— each with their respective mantras.
O you who possess the luster of the petals of a white lotus, with beautiful eyes reaching to the tips of your ears;
O you endowed with a thousand hoods, whose eyes are fixed upon the conch and the lotus;
O Ananta, Lord of the Naga kings, come here! Homage be to you!
O you who possess the luster of white jasmine and the moon, with a shimmering circle of coils;
O hero among all serpents, marked with the auspicious svastika sign;
O glorious Takṣaka, lord of nāgas, come here! Homage be to you!
O glorious one with lotus-like eyes, dark as a fresh rain-cloud, sole crest upon the necks of those intoxicated by the pride and strength of poison;
you who are renowned as Śaṅkhapāla and await the receptacle of the waters.
O sovereign of the worlds of the Nagas, come here; homage be unto you!
You who possess a complexion like molten gold, whose head is marked with the crescent moon, who display the majesty of your radiant coils, and who are endowed with auspicious marks.
O Kulīra, lord of the serpent kings, who delights in the welfare of all beings;
stay here for the sake of the success of this sacrifice, O you who can assume any form at will—homage be to you!
You who possess a golden complexion and eyes as broad as lotus petals.

O Lord of the Padma-nāgas, you who possess the splendor of the five dots (*pañcabindu*) and wear a single crest upon your neck—homage be to you of fierce form! Homage be to you! [To you] the female nāgas, the nāga maidens, and likewise the nāga youths.
May they all, with joyful minds, always accept my worship.
Having established the sacred fire according to the procedure prescribed in one's own *gṛhya-sūtra*, the wise man,
having consecrated the clarified butter (*ājya*), should offer oblations to the lords of the directions in their proper order.
Then one should offer oblations to the planets beginning with Āditya, to Brahmā, and to Kṛṣṇa;
thereafter, one should offer to Śiva and Varuṇa with honey and flour.
Having sprinkled the sacrificial post (yūpa), which is one span in height and according to its prescribed measurement, [one should proceed].
Having brought the hosts [of serpents], one should worship them within a square diagram marked with tridents;
then, having cast those nāgas into the well, one should subsequently throw in the five jewels.
Then, with the mantra "sutramāṇa," one should encircle it three times with threads.
Having colored the plantain tree, one should dedicate it to Varuṇa with the mantra "trātāram" (the protector), adorning it with cloth and garlands. Then,
having performed the piercing of the ears, one should release [the child] while uttering the appropriate words.

Oṃ. Today, etc., for the sake of attaining the fruits described by Vedavyāsa and others, I, [Name], belonging to the lineage of [Name] Rishi and named Devaśarman, relinquish this well-worshipped grove dedicated to the deity Vanaspati—a garden composed of various principal trees provided with fruit, flowers, leaves, and shade—to all beings.
Then, having performed the great festival, one should recite while standing with palms joined in reverence:
"Whether fallen from the top of a tree, or fallen from climbing it..."
Whether at death or when the bones break, the agent is not stained by sins.
When trees die due to the fault of being struck by a thunderbolt or similar causes,
this [rite] is established for that very tree as well, in order to remove that fault.
Having erected the sacrificial post (yūpa) in the center, one should carefully place it in the four corners as well;
one should offer honey, parched grain, and unbroken rice, as well as collyrium and garlands.
Having wound it with a thread of *niśā* grass, one should set down a plantain leaf.
One should wrap it with a stream of milk and pour a stream of ghee over it;
having provided it with water and a cluster of flowers, one should wrap it and go to one's own home.
Thus ends the second chapter in the third part of the Madhyama-parvan in the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa.
Description of the Installation of a Small Grove.
Sūta said:
O best of the twice-born, I shall indeed describe the installation of a small grove.
In an auspicious place where no mandala has been drawn, or on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) measuring two cubits,
one should place a water-pot there and worship Viṣṇu and Soma;
one should choose only the preceptor and encircle [the area] with night-threads.

Having adorned the tree with garlands, one should decorate it with ornaments and the like; then, one should provide for its longing (*dohada*) and establish it with a stream of a hundred [libations]. One should feed five Brahmins and indeed honor them especially before [the deity].
Then, having performed the piercing of the ears, he should utter the prescribed words.
He should give a sacrificial post (yūpa) in the middle region and plant a plantain tree there;
furthermore, he should plant banana trees in all directions according to the ritual procedure for the *sthālīpāka* offering.
One should offer eight oblations each for the others with clarified butter;
immediately thereafter, one should give a single oblation to Sviṣṭakṛt.
Then, having given the sacrificial fee, one should depart after offering the final full oblation.
O best of the twice-born, I shall now describe the procedure for trees, beginning with a single tree.
Then, having set aside the sacrificial post along with its ritual, the knower of dharma should worship Dharma,
the Earth, and likewise the Vaiśyas at the foot of the tree.
Then he should satisfy the lords of the directions, the Yakṣas, and the preceptor;
he should give a cow as a sacrificial fee, perform the watering of the tree with milk,
and having worshipped the tree according to the proper rite, he should present the *arghya* offering to Savitṛ.
Thus ends the third chapter in the third part of the Middle Section of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Description of the Consecration of Small Groves.
Sūta said:
Now, regarding the consecration of an Aśvattha tree: at its base, to the extent of two arms, one should have an altar prepared and likewise sprinkled with sandalwood paste.
There, one should fashion a lotus and perform the general *arghya* offering.

On the night of the preceding day, one should fill [the vessels] with water while reciting the verse "tad viṣṇoḥ," with fragrant paste while reciting "kayā naḥ," with oil while reciting "gandhadvārām," and with sandalwood paste while reciting "śrīśca te."
In the ritual manual, one should offer *dūrvā* grass and unbroken rice grains, and provide a meal for three Brahmins.
One should cause [the image] to be wrapped with white threads sprinkled with sandalwood paste.
Having worshipped Vināyaka in the primary jar and Brahmā in another jar, [one should proceed].
Having worshipped the lords of the directions in their respective quarters, the nine planets at the base of the tree,
and Śiva within the mandala preceded by the worship of the pedestal (pīṭha-pūjā),
I shall now describe the meditation upon the white bull.

One should visualize [the deity] with two arms, holding a trident in hand, and adorned with all ornaments; one should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) according to one's capacity. Then, having prepared the vessel for the offering (arghyapātra), one should perform the worship of the seat (pīṭhapūjā).
With a concentrated mind, one should worship Gaṇeśa, the feet of the Guru, Jaya, and Bhadra;
in the center, one should worship Ādhāraśakti, Kūrma, and Ananta along with the lotus;
and one should worship the mandalas of the Moon, Sun, Fire, and the others in their proper sequence.
Furthermore, having taken a flower placed in another vessel, the wise one should form the *pāṇikacchapikā* mudrā and likewise meditate upon Varuṇa; then,
according to the previous procedure, he should offer the triad beginning with the vessel.
One should offer the *madhuparka*, a seat, and inquire again after their well-being.
Having displayed the *mudrā* according to the rules, one should perform the ritual worship of the limbs (*aṅgapūjā*).
One should worship Indra and the other deities on the petals starting from the east, and Brahmā in the center.
In front of them is Ananta, and outside of them are their weapons;
in the center are Rudra as the Lord of Waters, Śānta, and Praśāntaka;
and the principles (tattvas) of Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ, and the rest.
One should worship Kāma, Dharma, and Adharma in the cardinal directions, Nārāyaṇa and Śiva, and Durgā in the southwest (nairṛta); and one should worship Śatakratu on both sides,
as well as Vināyaka, Viṣṇu, Gaṅgā, and Pṛthivī-Ṣaṣṭika.

One should especially worship with the sixteen-fold service. On the northern side of the mandala, one should fashion Ananta in the form of a serpent using five black hair-tufts, measuring the size of a large joint.
One should install [the deity] with unbroken grains and the like, white sandalwood, and flowers;
one should worship with supreme devotion and then perform the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*).
One should first offer oblations to Varuṇa with honey or milk-rice (*pāyasa*).

One should offer one hundred and eight oblations to the lords of the directions using sesame seeds and unbroken rice, or with clarified butter, or even with those smeared with the three sweets; indeed,
one should offer each individual oblation with flowers, sesame, and ghee.
At night, one should offer eight oblations each to Nārāyaṇa, Śiva, Durgā, Gaṇeśa, and the planets; these should be made with clarified butter,
and each single offering should be performed with the mantra "brahmāyudhvānam" using milk-rice (pāyasa) for Brahmā.
Then one should offer a single oblation with the three verses beginning "āpo hi ṣṭhā," or else one should offer three oblations of clarified butter (ājya) dedicated to Varuṇa,
either with the verse "imaṃ me varuṇa" or again with the verse "tad vāryam."
With the mantra "varuṇasyottaṃbhanamasi," and likewise with "yenāpāvaka" and "vātasya yama," one should offer five-colored substances in sequence;
thereafter, dedicated to Varuṇa, [one should offer] with ghee together with jaggery.
Then one should offer the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation and present the *bali* offerings in due order;
one should especially give honey, clarified butter, and milk-rice (*pāyasa*) to Varuṇa,
barley-milk to the lords of the directions, and to the others with milk-rice.
One should offer flour-cakes to Nāga and again perform eight oblations of parched grain (lāja).
On the northern bank of the Ananta [river], one should spread lotus leaves;
there, with the measure of sixty-four squares, one should [represent] Varuṇa with silver.
One should construct [the temple] with the first two [sections], using arrows, gems, and gold.
There, in the eastern half, one should construct a square lotus pond;
there one should install Varuṇa as well as the lotus pond itself.
One should release the water-dweller according to the prescribed rite preceded by the formal statement:

"Oṃ, today [and so forth], for the sake of attaining the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice as composed by Vedavyāsa—who is the embodiment of Viṣṇu and compassion and who is praised in the Śruti—I, of such-and-such lineage and named Amukadevaśarmā, do hereby bestow upon you this lotus-pool, made of gold and silver, as prescribed in my own Gṛhya-sūtra, adorned with ornaments and well-consecrated. This is the formula for the ritual release (utsarga).

Oṃ. From today onwards, for the sake of attaining the manifold fruits of the Agniṣṭoma and other sacrifices, I, [Name] Devaśarman of the [Name] Gotra, relinquish this water reservoir dedicated to the deity Varuṇa, well-adorned and accompanied by the four-faced Brahmā, for the enjoyment of bathing, drinking, and other needs by the four classes of beings, to be offered to the foremost Brāhmaṇas. Then, having taken a boat, the officiating priest (ṛtvij) should perform the fire-oblation (homa) from the center of the reservoir, slightly toward the north.
Having erected the sacrificial pillar that stood in its former position according to the prescribed ritual,
one should then, with the Varuṇa-sūkta,
cast a silver image of Varuṇa into the center of the lotus pond between the two serpent-pillars.
In that very place, one should recite this mantra to Anantanāga:
"O you who possess the luster of a lotus petal, with beautiful red-tinted eyes, endowed with a thousand hoods, well-established; obeisance be to you!"
Then one should give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and, having performed the rite of completion (pūrṇāhuti),
one should diligently recite the mantra over the lotuses, blue lotuses, and aquatic moss to release the crocodiles, sharks, fish, tortoises, and other creatures that dwell in the water.
One should perform three circumambulations of the lotus pond, keeping it to the right;
having recited the hymn dedicated to Āditya, one should scatter parched grain and cowrie shells,
and cause a stream of milk to fall by means of a thousand or a hundred [recitations].
The wise man should wrap [the vessel] with a red thread in a fourfold manner.
He should satisfy the poor on the road, and having satisfied them, he should go home.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the third part of the Middle Section of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Description of the Ritual Procedures for the Consecration of Lakes and the Like.
Sūta said:
"O best of the twice-born, [I shall describe] the consecration of lotus ponds, step-wells, and lakes."
