O twice-born ones, listen as I describe the ritual procedure along with its constituent parts. On the preceding day, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) using the measurement of a golden foot,
with the mantra "āpo hi ṣṭhā," as well as with hundreds of weapon-mantras (astra-mantras).
One should enter one's own auspicious maṇḍala facing the east;
there, one should worship Gaṇeśa and Varuṇa in the [central] jar, as well as Śiva.
Likewise, one should worship Vāgīśa and Viṣṇu in the sun-jar (sūryakuṃbha).
One should offer an oblation of milk-rice (pāyasa) to Varuṇa and an oblation of clarified butter (ghṛta);
one should offer a single oblation for each of the others using the *sruva* ladle.
Immediately thereafter, one should perform the offering of the sacrificial portion (*bali*) with milk-rice and then discard that food.
One should subsequently set up the sacrificial post (yūpa) and give a cow as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Having offered a full arghya-oblation to Savitṛ, one should then return to one's own home.
I shall now describe the procedure for a grove (ārāma), along with the detailed ritual for its consecration (pratiṣṭhā).
O twice-born ones, for one who delights in humble things and likewise for one who dwells by a single tree—
specifically in the middle of a forest, or toward the west or north—
one should construct a circular pavilion measuring one aratni (cubit) and one hasta (span) in size.
To the south of that, there should be an auspicious, level, square sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa);
it should be made with four openings and adorned with arches and other ornaments.
Then, having invoked Mandara and the others, one should worship them in due order.
And one should worship Viṣvaksena right there with perfumes and sandalwood paste.
Bhṛgu is mounted upon his ear and adorned with all ornaments.
This is the mantra for Viṣvaksena to be used in worship in every respect.
One should worship the door-keeper Saṃpūrṇa and Gaurī and the others in the water-pots;
one should offer oblations, flowers, unbroken rice, and so forth to the lords of the directions in their respective quarters;
and one should worship Ananta between the regions of Nairṛti and Varuṇa.
One should then visualize Brahmā in the middle between Indra and Īśāna.
Having gone to the side of the altar, one should invoke and worship [the deity] upon the altar;
then, having prepared a seat and performed the general *arghya* offering.
In the northeast pitcher, one should likewise worship Vidyut-Brahmā and the planets with their respective mantras, using perfumes, flowers, and various kinds of food offerings;
as well as Vāsudeva, the Lord of the Mandala, together with his seat and Bṛhaspati.
One should worship with supreme devotion and offer an oblation of milk-rice (pāyasa).
One should meditate upon the omnipresent Lord Vāsudeva, who has two arms and holds a conch and a discus,
seated upon a lotus throne, wearing beautiful yellow garments.
Having meditated upon [the deity] who has the luster of the petals of a blue lotus, who is smeared with yellow sandalwood paste,
who is accompanied by celestial sages and perfected beings, and who is joined by his two consorts—
one should then install the leaders, beginning with Bāla and the others, in this manner.

One should worship Viṣṇu, Śiva, Durgā, and Sarasvatī all around, according to the prescribed rite, with the sixteen principal goddesses beginning with Vimalā and the lords of the directions, each in their distinct forms, by means of sixteen successive handfuls of flowers.
One should meditate upon Soma, who resembles pure crystal, four-faced,
mounted on a horse, possessing a divine form, lotus-eyed, and holding a *puṣpaka* flower;
he is the bestower of boons, served by gods and *gandharvas*, and praised by sages.
One should meditate upon the white Lord of the Forest (Vanaspati), who has two arms, wears yellow garments,
stands upon his own chariot, possesses mighty arms, and holds a conch, a goad, and a shield.
One should also meditate upon the Vidyā to his left and install her with her own mantra.
Water endowed with the ten vowels is its natural state, permeated by *tamas*;
one should employ this mantra in the worship of the God of gods.
[One should place] Nīla, Jaya, and Bhṛṅgin around it in due order.
Then, having performed the *kuśakaṇḍikā* rite, one should prepare the *sthālīpāka* according to the rules;
one hundred and eight oblations for Soma, twelve for Vānaspati, and likewise eight in clarified butter for the others should be offered.
Immediately after the Saptajihvā [mantra], one should offer each oblation individually;
with the mantra "Vāstoṣpataye," one should carry forth two portions of the *sthālīpāka*.
Then, intending for Vanaspati, one should recite this verse addressed to Yama.
First, the wise one should place trees and other objects in the east with the Gāyatrī mantra.
Then, using the mantra "abjairagram," he should place a bell-metal vessel, cloth, and gems in the various directions in due order,
as well as rice and rivers with the mantra "tathā ca saritaśca me."
Likewise, having installed Mitra, the three friends, and Pūṣan with their respective verses,
and having sown rice seeds right there according to the prescribed ritual,
one should pour Ganges water and water infused with all medicinal herbs into the vessel.
Having established the patron with the mantras beginning "The gods [have placed] you," and having installed the preceptor there among the best of the twice-born,
he then completed the daily rites and offered the sacrificial fee to the preceptor.

Having given a cow, an iron vessel, and a desired sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brāhmaṇas according to his ability, he should give a full [gift] and go home. Thus ends the fifth chapter in the third part of the Madhyama-parvan in the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa.
Description of the Consecration of a Small Grove.
Sūta said:
O best of the twice-born, I shall now describe the consecration of a small grove (kṣudrārāma).
In an auspicious place where there is no mandala, upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) measuring two cubits, one should place a water-pot (kalaśa); there, one should worship Soma and Viṣṇu.
One should choose only a preceptor (ācārya) and encircle [the area] with night-threads.
Having adorned the tree with garlands, one should decorate it with ornaments and the like;
then one should provide for its pregnancy-longing (*dohada*) and establish it with a sharp-edged blade.
Furthermore, one should especially feed five Brahmins in front of it at the conclusion.
Then, having performed the piercing of the ears, one should release [the animal] preceded by the recitation of the Vāsa hymn.
One should offer a sacrificial post (yūpa) in the middle region and plant a plantain tree (kadalī);
likewise, one should plant a banana tree (raṃbhā) in the cardinal directions according to the procedure for the sthālīpāka offering.

One should offer eight oblations for each of the others with clarified butter; immediately thereafter, one should give a single oblation to Sviṣṭakṛt. Then one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), offer the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), and go home.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the third part of the Middle Section (*madhyamaparvan*) of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*,
titled "The Description of the Ritual for the Installation of Excellent Trees.
Sūta said:
O best of the twice-born, I shall now describe the ritual for the planting of excellent trees beginning with the number one.
First, one should place a water-pot (kalaśa) on the western side of the tree;
then, having established the tree, one should encircle it with a thread.
From the water-pots, he should offer oblations to Brahmā, Soma, Viṣṇu, and Vanaspati;
then, the knower of dharma, having released the sacrificial post along with the plantain tree, should duly perform eight oblations for each of the eight [deities] using sesame and barley.
At the foot of the tree, one should worship Dharma, the Earth, and likewise the Viśvedevas;
then the lords of the directions, the Yakṣas, and the Preceptor.
Thereafter, one should give a cow as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), offer the "longing" (doḥhada) rite, and perform the worship of the tree.
Having performed [the rite] according to the correct procedure, one should present the *arghya* offering to Savitṛ.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the third part of the Madhyama-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*,
titled "Description of the Procedure for the Installation of the Aśvattha Tree."

Sūta said: Now, regarding the consecration of the Aśvattha tree, one should cause a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) to be prepared at its root, measuring the length of an arm, and marked with sandalwood paste as prescribed.
One should fashion a lotus there and prepare the general *arghya* offering;
on the previous evening at night, one should place [the vessel] full of water with the verse "tad viṣṇoḥ," and [place] the fragrant paste with the verse "kayā naḥ."

One should offer oil with the mantra "gandhadvārām" and sandalwood paste with the mantra "śrīśca te". At dawn, one should present *dūrvā* grass and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), feed three Brahmins,
and wrap the sandalwood with white threads.
Having worshipped Vināyaka in the water-jar (kumbha) and Brahmā in the other jar,
one should worship the lords of the directions in their respective quarters, the nine planets at the foot of the tree,
and Śiva within the mandala, preceded by the worship of the pedestal (pīṭhapūjā).
In the east, Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa; in the south, Nandi and Bhṛṅgin; in the west, Ananta; in the north, Kāma and Gaṇanāyaka;
and in the center, Kārttikeya, preceded by Ādhāraśakti.
The infinite earth itself, threefold and with three circles—
now I shall describe the meditation upon the white bull,
who has two arms, holds a trident in his hand, and is adorned with all ornaments.
One should install [the image] independently and worship Viṣṇu at the base;
likewise, one should worship Śaṅkara in the middle and Brahmā at the front.
Having offered an oblation and flour-cakes, one should cook the sacrificial porridge (caru).
One should offer oblations dedicated to Rudra, numbering eleven (the *rudra-saṃkhyā*) in sequence;
for the others as well, one should diligently perform the *homa* with the *sruva* ladle alone.
One should plant a *kadalī* tree and satisfy the preceptor (*ācārya*).
Having performed the fivefold libation (*pūrṇā-pañcadhārā*) and having also performed a circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇā*),
and having prepared a stream of milk and offered the water of honor (*arghya*), one should return home.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the third part of the Middle Section (*madhyamaparvan*) of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Description of the Ritual for the Installation of the Banyan Tree.
Sūta said:
Now I shall describe the location for the banyan tree; it should be at its root on the southern side.
One should place three water-pots upon a sacrificial altar measuring three cubits;
having worshipped Gaṇeśa, Śiva, and Viṣṇu, one should offer the oblation of cooked rice (caru).
One should first [place] gold, bound with triple-stranded red threads.
One should offer a bali-oblation of barley and milk, uttering the appropriate mantra;
thereafter, one should erect a sacrificial post and offer it at the roots of banyan trees to the yakṣas,
nāgas, gandharvas, siddhas, and the hosts of maruts.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the third part of the Madhyama-parvan within the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa;
titled "Description of the Ritual for the Installation of the Bilva Tree.
Sūta said:
I shall describe the consecration of the Bilva; one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) on the previous day.
One should install it with fragrant water using the mantra "Tryambakam," and offer unbroken rice (akṣata) with the mantras "Sunābhā" and "Me gṛhṇāmi."
Then one should offer incense, clothing, and garlands;
thereafter, one should worship the god Rudra, and in the center, Durgā and the Lord of Wealth (Dhanada).
Then, having risen at dawn, one should daily perform the obligatory rites according to the scriptures.
One should feed seven Brahmins and a Brahmin couple in one's own home.
Having measured two cubits at the root, there shall be a circular altar (*vedikā*).
There, with red ochre or with safflower powder, [one should draw the design].
Or one should fashion a very beautiful eight-petaled [lotus] with red lac;
then, O best of the twice-born, one should perform the encircling of the tree,
wrapping it with five, seven, or nine threads of red silk.

One desiring prosperity should sow rice grains there while facing north; one should worship Śiva, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā. And one should make Śiva the central leader, with the Ādityas at the base of the petals.
And at the foot of the tree, one should worship Śeṣa; in the center, Ananta and Śatakratu; and then Vanapāla, Soma, and Sūrya, and Pṛthivī in sequence.
The fire-oblation (homa) should be performed with sesame seeds and unbroken rice grains, and one should offer the sacrificial gift (bali) with ghee and boiled rice.
For the sake of pleasing the Yakṣas, one should give black-gram rice and twelve woven garments;
for the gratification of the Planets (Grahas), one should offer a gift wrapped in milk,
along with gold, a bell-metal vessel, betel-leaf, and a copper vessel.
One should perform the raising of the sacrificial post (*yūpāropa*), the piercing of the ear, and present the *arghya* offering to Savitṛ.
Now, I shall describe the consecration of the night (*rātripratiṣṭhā*) according to the scriptures;
by performing the ritual for a solitary tree sacred to a Yakṣa, one is not born again on this earth.
On the previous day, however, one should place a water-pot at the foot of a tree;
having worshipped Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Gaṇeśa, one should install it.
Alternatively, one may set up five or seven jars adorned with fragrant oils.
Having diligently performed the wrapping with milk, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and water from a conch shell,
and immediately thereafter with threads, cloths, and garlands,
one should then offer dūrvā grass and unbroken rice grains while reciting the mantra beginning with "kāṇḍāt".

Furthermore, with the Viṣṇu-sūkta, one should offer vermilion, collyrium, and sandalwood, as well as fruit and a lamp; then one should sleep there oneself. One should offer five oblations there, present a sacrificial post (yūpa), and perform the ritual dismissal.
One should perform the ear-piercing ceremony with an offering of milk-rice (pāyasa).
One should surround [the child] with milk-water, and give grain and a cow as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
One should present the respectful water-offering (arghya), perform the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), and feed a Brahmin couple.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Installation of a Good Tree," in the third part of the Middle Section of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*. Sūta said:
Whoever, having prepared a sacrificial site (vāstu) measuring one hundred cubits, adorned with various trees and provided with fruits such as betel nuts and mangoes, performs a sacrifice there,
shall dwell for sixty thousand years in the heavenly world for a long time.
I shall describe its procedure according to the scriptures:
having performed the daily rites according to rule, one should worship five Brahmins;
one should feed them and honor Viṣṇu together with Prajāpati.
Then, having performed the fire-rite (agnikārya), one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brahmin.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the third part of the Madhyama-parvan within the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa;
it is a description of the procedure for the consecration of the pavilion (maṇḍapa-pratiṣṭhā-vidhāna).
Sūta said: O Brāhmaṇas, O Lord, [I shall describe] the consecration of a pavilion made of stone or wood, as well as that of one made of grass and wood, which is like a blade of grass.
On the day prior to the formal acceptance (adhivāsa), one should place a water-pot at an auspicious moment;
one should worship the Sun, the Moon, and likewise Viṣṇu within that jar.
One should then sprinkle it with water from kuśa grass while reciting the verse beginning with "āpo hiṣṭhā."

One should offer perfume with the mantra "āpyāyasva," sandalwood paste with "gaṃdhadvārām," oil with "ākṛṣṇena," and sandalwood with "śrīśca te. One should then offer vermilion, lac-dye, and collyrium along with the previously mentioned [mantra].
Then, at the clear dawn, one should perform an auspicious *śrāddha* ceremony for prosperity;
having installed the guardians of the quarters (*dikpālas*) within the pavilion of auspicious characteristics,
one should draw the mandala with royal figures in the center of the altar.
One should invoke the Sun there, and Soma and Viṣṇu on either side;
one should worship Gaṇeśa, the planets, and the guardians of the directions within the water-pot.
Likewise, one should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) into the fire one hundred and eight times.
Likewise, one should offer twelve oblations to Āditya, Viṣṇu, and Soma,
and present a bali-offering of milk-rice, or else oil or milk. Then, having performed the ritual according to rule, one should utter this statement:
Having knelt upon the ground, one should not move the lips even slightly;
there, one should worship Vāstoṣpati with perfumes and sandalwood,
offer the arghya according to the rules, and perform an oblation into the fire.

(“Oṃ, beginning with ‘Today,’ etc.: for the purpose of pleasing Viṣṇu, I, [Name] Devaśarmā, belonging to the lineage of [Name] Ṛṣi, desiring the attainment of the fruits declared by the Śruti and Smṛti, relinquish this well-adorned pavilion, dedicated to the Sun-god, constructed from stone, brick, and other materials for the sake of all beings, including Brāhmaṇas and others.
Then, O best of men, one should place a white pitcher upon the pavilion, or one should encircle it with a triple thread or with a stream of water consecrated at night.
One should give the sacrificial fee according to the rules and present the *arghya* offering to Sūrya.
Having placed Sūrya together with Vāsudeva in a grass hut,
and having made Gaṇeśa— the bestower of boons and the supreme— reside in a water-pot, one should release [the image].
One should cause a sacrificial post (yūpa) to be placed in the northeast and arrange banners in the cardinal directions.
Having installed a water-pot (kalaśa) atop the pavilion, one should recite the mantra.
In the water-shed (prapā), Varuṇa and Viśvakarman should be worshipped with diligence.
Having worshipped the Earth and Gaṇeśa, one should offer clarified butter (ghṛta) as an oblation.
This statement regarding "everything being excluded" is prescribed merely as a formal declaration (dhvajamātra).
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the third part of the Madhyama-parvan within the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa.
Description of the Construction and Installation of the Great Sacrificial Post (Mahāyūpa).
Sūta said:
The great sacrificial post was four cubits [in girth] and sixteen cubits [in height].
I shall describe that as well as the installation; one should perform the three-night sacrifice at night.
One should worship Varuṇa with a white pitcher to the west of the water-pit.
First, one should bathe [the image] with the Gāyatrī, and then in due order with "āpo hi ṣṭhā" and so forth.
With "Gandhadhārā," one offers perfume; with "Aṃśunā," oil;
with "Manonmanī," flowers; and with "Dhūrasi," incense.
With "Kayā na," one should offer clothing, as well as food offerings (naivedya), lamps, and sandalwood paste.
At the beginning, the Śrāddha rite should not be performed; it is prescribed at the conclusion of the consecration.
One should provide a meal for a married couple and invite a single Brāhmaṇa.
Within an eight-cubit pavilion, one should place a water-pot there.

One should worship the god Varuṇa together with Nārāyaṇa, as well as Śiva and the Earth, each with their respective mantras in the proper order. Then, having performed the *kuśakaṇḍikā* according to the procedure for the *sthālīpāka* sacrifice, [one should proceed].
Having worshipped Varuṇa, one should offer ten oblations;
for the others as well, one should give one oblation each in sequence using the *sruva* ladle.
For Varuṇa, one should recite the mantra "Varuṇam" as previously stated, and after that, "Tattvā yāmi."
With these two mantras, "Thou art the support of Varuṇa" and likewise "The gods [have established]...",
and with "That by which, O purifier, with thy eye... which is declared as the fifth,
and the subsequent one beginning with "The sacrificial post of Rātra," up to the tenth head.

Then, having performed the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, one should offer the *caru* to the Seven-Tongued One (Agni). Then, with the mantra beginning "iha va" and so forth, one should offer five oblations in sequence to Śambhu, to the Earth, and to the Great King.
Having prepared the cooked oblation (caru-pāka), one should present the food offering (naivedya) and the sacrificial bali, including agallochum and rice,
to Śaṅkara, Rudra, Śarva, Paśupati,
Ugra, Aśana, and Bhava, in that order.

Furthermore, for Mahādeva and Īśāna respectively, one should offer the cooked oblation (caru), the food offering (naivedya), and the sacrificial cake (bali) with agallochum (aguru). One should first utter the mantra and then release water; listen now to the procedure for that verbal rite.

(“Oṃ, today [and so forth], for the sake of attaining the fruit arising from the consecration of a well as prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti for my father, named Amukadevaśarman, of the [Amuka] gotra, I, [Amuka]gotra, named Amukadevaśarman, relinquish this well, which has been well-worshipped, properly covered, and dedicated to Varuṇa as its deity.
One should duly give a sacrificial fee and present a milch cow.
O twice-born ones, listen now to the procedure for the consecration of small wells within a pavilion.
The wise man should worship Gaṇeśa and Varuṇa in the water-pot according to the prescribed rites;
he should encircle it with red threads, offer the sacrificial post, and release it.
Then, he should give the priestly fee according to the rules and honor the Brahmins.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Consecration of a Flower Garden," in the third part of the Middle Section of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*. Sūta said:
I shall now describe the consecration of a flower garden; listen indeed, O twice-born ones!

Having constructed an altar three cubits in size in the center, one should place a water-pot there. On the day prior to the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa), the feeding of Brahmins should be performed according to the rules.
Having fashioned Gaṇeśa, Sūrya, Soma, and Hutāśana within a jar,
and having placed Nārāyaṇa upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), one should offer honey and milk-rice (madhupāyasa) as oblation.
Having duly erected the sacrificial post (yūpa), one should cause the wheat to be sprinkled by the preceptor.

One should wrap [the sacrificial post] with red threads and offer a priestly fee (dakṣiṇā). O best of the twice-born, having erected the sacrificial post in the northeast according to the rules, one should offer barley-food with jaggery and milk along with the water from this stream.
Having performed the piercing of the ears, one should bathe [the child] with water infused with kuśa grass.
One should give grain, barley, and wheat as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmin.
O twice-born ones, one should surround [the child] on all sides with water from a hundred streams.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Installation of Tulasī," in the third part of the Middle Section of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*. Sūta said:
In the months of Jyeṣṭha or Āṣāḍha, one should perform the formal installation of Tulasī according to the prescribed rites.
On a pure day, or on the Ekādaśī,
the patron should then place a water-jar at night and worship the Supreme Lord.
One should perform the ceremonial bathing (snapana) of Nārāyaṇa, Śiva, Soma, Brahmā, and Indra with the Gāyatrī mantra as well as with the mantras prescribed for them; likewise,
one should apply perfume with the mantra "kayā na" and oil with the mantra "aśunā".

One should offer a flower with the mantra "tvāṃ gandharve," another flower with "puṣpaṃ maṇḍeśana," a flower with "mā nastoke," sandalwood paste with "śrīścata," and again sandalwood paste with the mantra "vaiśvadevī."
One should offer durvā grass with the *dūrvā* mantra, a mirror with the *rūpeṇa* mantra,
fruit with the *phala* mantra, and collyrium with the *samedha* mantra; then,
one should encircle it with kuśa grass, yellow thread, and the like, while pouring a stream of milk.
One should wrap it with water from a hundred-streamed vessel and proceed to one's own home;

having covered it with a cloth according to the rules, the wise man should place the jar at the proper time with either seven, five, or three [verses], indeed with the Ṛgvedic verse beginning "tad viṣṇoḥ."
Then one should have her bathed by virtuous women, preceded by auspicious rites.
Thereafter, having completed the *śrāddha* ceremony, preceded by the worship of the Mothers (*mātṛpūjā*),
one should first choose the preceptor (*ācārya*) with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
The preceptor himself shall serve as the Hotṛ priest, and there shall be a Brahmā priest and a Sadasya.
Even in a ten-cubit square pavilion, upon circular altars (sthaṇḍila),
one should fashion a thousand mandalas and there worship Nārāyaṇa.

One should worship the planets, the lords of the world, the Ādityas, the hosts of Maruts, the Rudras, and the Vasus in the center and all around the water-pot (kalaśa). Then, having performed the ritual with Kuśa grass (kuśakaṇḍikā), one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with sesame and barley.

One should perform one hundred and eight [oblations]; for others, one should offer according to one's capacity. O best of men, having dedicated [the rite] to Nārāyaṇa and having released [the offering], one should present the sacrificial oblation (bali) consisting of cooked rice (caru) at the center, directed toward the sacrificial post (yūpa).
Having placed plantain trees in all directions, one should plant banners in the various quarters.
One should give gold as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), along with sesame seeds, grain, and flowers;
one should also give a milch cow and surround it with a stream of milk.
O best of the twice-born, [one should avoid the shade] of the Jayantī, the Soma tree, and likewise the Somavaṭa; also of the Panasa, the Kadamba, and the Nimba;
as well as of the Pāṭala, the Kanaka, the Śālmalī, and the Niṃbaka.
One should not perform the installation of a Bimba, Aśoka, or Vaṭa tree;
nor that of a Bhadraka, a Śamī, a Koṇa, a Caṇḍātaka, or a Bakula.
The piercing of the ear should be performed only for a Khadira tree, and one should not have it done otherwise.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Specific Rules for Consecration," in the third part of the Middle Section of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa. Sūta said:

One should perform the installation of trees and other objects in the highest manner for the highest [deities], in the middling manner for the middling, and the lowest manner for the lowest; this is what has been proclaimed. One should make the mandala circular, and that should likewise be done at the head and at the end.
Or one should construct an altar in the center, and in its middle, a circle for the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
On the previous day at night, having established the water-pot (ghaṭa), one should worship it;
then, having worshipped the remainder according to the rules, as well as the Earth and Śiva.
Having worshipped the bridge with fragrant water while reciting the Gāyatrī mantra, one should release it; then,
with the mantra "kayā na" and the verse "āpyāyasva," one should offer perfumes and other articles, and sandalwood paste with the mantra "śrīśca te lakṣmīśca."
One should offer *dūrvā* grass with the *dūrvā* mantra, and fruit with the *phala* mantra; one should present the *kuśa* purifier with the "śanno devī" mantra,
and a pair of garments with the "surāsura" mantra.
Reciting "May this be pleasing to my mind," he should apply collyrium and lac;
on the following day, he should perform the śrāddha preceded by the Vasudhārā rite.
Then, O best of men, he should choose the officiating priest (ācārya) and the reciter (hotṛ).
Two vessels should be prepared for the assembly and for the preceptor;
likewise, they should be prepared at the Setu sacrifice and at the Mountain of Grain (Dhānyācala).
At a thousand-fold oblation (sahasra-homa), however, there should be only one; at a wedding, there are both the Brahmā priest and the officiating priest (ṛtvij).
One should worship this sacrificial pavilion for the sake of the primary sacrifice once it has been prepared.
First, one should invoke the altar (vedi) and then fully honor the pavilion,
as well as the obstructing spirits (vighnas), the planets (grahas), and the guardians of the world (lokapālas), who bestow all accomplishments.
On a *sarvatobhadra* sacrificial diagram, one should represent Śeṣa and Viṣṇu;
right there, one should also represent the renowned and most excellent officiant named Varāha.
One should offer oblations with the *sthālīpāka* twenty-eight times for each of the three [deities].
Five oblations with clarified butter are prescribed for Varāha;
thereafter, one should offer each oblation in sequence with sesame and barley.
One should present the bali offering in its distinct form, leaving the remainder according to the prescribed rule.
One should offer flour-cakes and ghee-rice, or in greater detail, rice with molasses;
for the world of the ancestors, black-gram rice, and for the Earth, the supreme food.
The wise man should utter these offerings preceded by the appropriate words; now hear the sequence of those words.

(“Oṃ, beginning with ‘today,’ etc.: for the sake of attaining the distinguished heaven of the twenty-one families, I duly renounce this bridge, together with its causeway, having Viṣṇu as its deity and worshipped by the gods, for the pleasure of Vāsudeva.
Then, with palms joined in reverence (*añjali*), one should recite the mantra and perform the rite according to the rules.
[This is for] those who have fallen on slippery ground and whose limbs are broken from rising up.
When this bridge of Dharma is established, may there be Dharma for me and no sin;
endowed with supreme faith in this construction of a bridge,
may I be the sustainer of the life-force of all living beings who exist herein.
O Lord, whatever merit is said in the Vedas and Agamas to accrue from the construction of a bridge,
that merit has indeed been offered by me as my travel-provision;
likewise, at the end, one should offer a sacrificial post and banners with the mantra beginning "yūpaṃ dadyāt."
One should duly give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to nine or five families.

Having offered the full oblation to Savitṛ and having presented the water-offering (arghya), one should return to one's own home. One should perform the installation of a small bridge according to the rules in a place free from direct sunlight.
Having first offered [oblations] to Dadhivāsa and provided a meal for Brahmins at dawn,
one should then go to the center of the Setu and duly present perfumes and other offerings.
One should worship Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Agni together within a single sacrificial pit.
There, one should worship Vāstoṣpati and perform a fire-oblation with sesame and barley;
O best of men, the Brahmins should each offer twenty-eight oblations. Having set aside the flag, they should cause incense to be offered, excluding the flag.
"One who has fulfilled his duties is said to eat together with his kinsmen.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the third part of the Madhyama-parvan within the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
[This section contains] a description of the rules for the grazing of cows (*gopracāra*).
Sūta said:
O best of Brahmins, there, within that square enclosure which was equal on all sides,
was a delightful ground measuring sixty cubits, filled to its full extent.
He who, being well-composed, gives cows for the purpose of their roaming,
is honored in the world of Rudra for sixty thousand years;
or he may give half of that, or half of that again, or even half of that.
He who gives away land alone, or a maiden, a female slave, or likewise a bull,
or a cow without ornaments— the fruit of such a gift is proclaimed to be half [of that of a full donation].
This should be done in an auspicious place devoid of gravel and other such impurities, but not in a pavilion.
In the middle of a two-cubit altar, one should construct a pavilion for the bridge;
there, one should worship Bhadra, Brahmā, and the Lord of Śacī (Indra),
as well as Gaṇeśa, Kṣetrapāla, Śeṣa, and the lords of the directions.
One should worship according to the rules with the five types of offerings, such as milk-rice (pāyasa) and the like;
one should offer oblations with the *sthālīpāka* at the conclusion, and finally provide a feast for the Brahmins.
In this sacrifice, excluding the *śrāddha*, one should perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) on the preceding day.
Having established the ground with the Tryambaka mantra, one should worship it;
with the "Tad Viṣṇoḥ" mantra, one should offer scented oil mixed with sandalwood. With the "Asunīte" mantra, one should not establish it again.

Furthermore, with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and the mantra "śrīścate," he prepares the *puṣpaka* offering; likewise, he consecrates the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) with its respective mantra. With the mantra "gandhadvārām" he applies perfume, and with "aṃśunā te" he applies oil.
With the *surāsure* mantra he should offer flowers, and with the *dūrvā* mantra, *dūrvā* grass.

At dawn, he should worship the gods and perform a fire-oblation (*homa*) dedicated to Rudra. According to the prescribed rite using the *sthālīpāka* offering, he should proceed for the other deities as before.
Having set it down, one should establish the lamp with the *ṛc* verse beginning "Be firm.
One should construct the entire structure made according to the ritual manual (*tantra*) measuring three cubits,
specifically reaching one cubit into the middle of the sacred field (*kṣetra*).
One should carefully establish it there with the mantra using the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*): with honey using the mantra *madhuvātā*, with curd using *āpyāyasva*,
and immediately thereafter with water from a jar using the mantra *tad viṣṇoḥ*.

One should worship, in sequence, Pṛthivī, Varāha, Kūrma, the Śaktis of Mādhava, Vāstoṣpati, and Viṣṇu at the sacrificial post (yūpa). One should offer the arghya-water into the cavity of the pit, but one should avoid performing the fire-oblation (homa) there.
O best of men, if the vessel for the *arghya* offering is defiled, one should discard it by hand and recite:

"Om, today [and so forth], for the sake of wandering [for grazing] among cows, Brahmins, and all living beings, I relinquish this well-worshipped ground, whose presiding deity is Viṣṇu, which serves as a pasture for cows, for the attainment of the fruits prescribed by the Śrutis, Smṛtis, and other authorities. "The cows residing in the world of Śiva are highly honored by all the gods.
With these words, the Brahmin, composed in mind, should formally announce the pasture for the cows (*gopracāra*).
Released from all sins, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu;
for as many auspicious blades of grass and shrubs as there are upon the earth, for that many thousands of years he is glorified in the heavenly world.

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for Installation Achievable in a Single Day," in the section on the Rules for Grazing Cows within the third part of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
In the Kali age, a practitioner of the Tantra who possesses little wealth should perform the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) achievable in a single day;
he, the best of tantrikas, should perform the immediate consecration (sadyodhivāsa) with clarified butter (ājya).
This should be done when the sun has moved northward and the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa) has passed.
When the autumn season has passed, one should commence the sacrifice in the spring;
O best of men, [this applies to] the installation of the thirty-two varieties of images, beginning with the forms of Nārāyaṇa, as well as those of Gajāsyā (Ganeśa) and others.
Having performed his daily rites, the wise man should then bring about prosperity;
he should feed the Brahmins or else proceed to the sacrificial hall.
He should worship Gaṇeśa, the planets, and the guardians of the directions within each of the water-pots.
One should worship Viṣṇu upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) and offer sacrifice to his retinue of attendants.
First, one should bathe the Lord with five kinds of water:
with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and also with five lumps of clay.
O best of men, [one may bathe] with sesame oils, fatty substances, or even decoctions;
or else, O best of men, with the water of five flowers or with the "three-footed" [formula].
They say that the leaves of the Tulasī flower constitute the "three-footed."
The five [ingredients] are the five types of mango, śamī, lotus, and karavīra;
likewise, elephant-dung earth, horse-hoof earth,
cow-urine, cow-dung, milk, curd, and ghee as the fifth.
One should perform the consecration of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) and carry out the fire-oblation (*homa*) according to the prescribed rules;
thereafter, one should duly offer the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the third part of the Middle Section of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Description of the Consecration of Deities and Others.
Sūta said:
"O best of Brahmins, hereafter [I shall describe] likewise the consecration of Kālī and the others."
Having accepted the invitation on the previous day for the *śrāddha* consisting of prosperity (*abhyudaya*),
one should first perform a bath with water-born [substances] and subsequently with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
Then, according to the previously mentioned procedure, one should worship Durgā in the water-pot (*kumbha*).
One should worship the Goddess with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and a hundred streams of cow-dung; immediately after offering the life-breath (prāṇa),
one should offer a hundred oblations with bilva leaves or bilva fruits.
O Brahmins, one should give a golden sacrificial fee to each and every one of them;
and having worshipped the images of Kālikā and Tārā separately,
one should perform the rite even with five hundred [offerings] for each, excluding the formal grasping [of the deity].
The deity should feed and bathe [the image] with scented water for three days;
one should worship the Goddess in a copper pitcher for three days, indeed only in the morning. Then, one should provide air and place her within a casket.
Then one should have her bathed with fragrant waters by young maidens and others;
thereafter, on the eighth day, one should perform worship even at night,
offer the gift of an animal, and conduct the fire-ritual with milk-rice oblations.
I shall describe the installation of the Śiva-liṅga according to the Tantric tradition. O Brahmins, one should especially feed three Brahmins after performing the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa).
Having completed the daily rites, one should then perform the rite for prosperity (abhyudaya).
One should choose an Ācārya in the morning and have him bathe according to the previous procedure;
thereafter, one should worship him together with his retinue of attendants.
Afterward, one should offer the wind [as a preliminary] and perform the fire-rite (agnikārya).
One should give a cow made of sesame seeds and gold, and a [real] cow according to the prescribed rite; however,
in the performance of the fire-oblation (homa), one should never mention the name or the lineage (gotra) of others,
especially on the full moon day, and under no circumstances for anyone else.
At the conclusion of the fire sacrifice (homa), having offered a stream of wealth (vasudhārā) into the pitcher according to the prescribed rite,

one should perform the formal installation (pratiṣṭhā) of the śāla, śama, and śilā stones according to the rules, with a body three cubits long for a four-cubit [image] and one cubit for a single-cubit [image].

One should consecrate the deity immediately; then, on the twelfth day (dvādaśī), one should bathe him with water from jewels, perfumes, the three fragrances (trigandha), and the five sprouts (pañcapallava).
Having installed Prajāpati in the pitcher upon a white lotus with nine centers, one should proceed.
One should worship the Supreme Lord according to the path taught in the *Navadurga*;
He is to be understood as being of the nature of the *cakra*, and one should offer the breath (*samīraṇa*).
Having brought [the deity] into a copper vessel, one should worship Him three times a day.

O best of men, one should perform the fire-oblation with milk-rice, blue lotuses, or even white lotuses; one should also present a pair of garments along with gold as a generous sacrificial fee for Śrī Sūrya, Gaṇeśa, and Viriñci as well.
Having gone near a banyan tree, one should then install Varuṇa;
one should worship Sūrya, together with his retinue, upon a red lotus,
having offered twenty-eight [oblations], and thereafter offer the prāṇa-mantra.
Alternatively, having kept it hidden in the open air for one day or three days,
one should perform worship and fire-offerings (homa) again after those three days have passed.
Furthermore, one should feed the Brahmins and give gold as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
One may also install the deities Vārāhī and Tripurā with coconut water according to the prescribed rite, and worship them with vermilion and other offerings;
thereafter, one should offer the breath (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) and perform worship again along with the fire oblation (homa).
And the knowledge of the animal (paśujñāna) should be practiced for six months with five types of sweetmeats (pañcamodaka).
One should feed a young maiden at night and give gold as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
[One should worship] the image of Bhuvaneśī and also Mahāmāyāmbikā.
Then, on the previous day at the time of night, one who knows the ritual procedure should offer eight portions of flour and wood to the goddess Kāmākṣī, Indrākṣī, and Aparājitā; thereafter,
he should fashion eight [images] and present eight sacrificial offerings (bali).
The wise and disciplined practitioner should worship together with the retinue of attendants;
then he should offer the *samīraṇa* (wind) oblation, and again worship Śiva and Sūrya.
He should perform the worship of the syllables (*lipi-pūjana*) for three days, making offerings of milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
One should perform the worship of the Kumārīs and the fire-ritual for three days;
O best of men, the gift of animals should also be made if one has the means.
One should keep a vigil at night, preceded by the festival of the monastery.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Pacification of Planetary Disturbances and Portents," in the third part of the Madhyama-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
Furthermore, O best of sages, listen as I describe the ill omens and the pacification, in due order, of whichever planetary afflictions may belong to whom;
these are proclaimed as threefold: celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial.
Understand from me the celestial and atmospheric phenomena caused by planets, constellations, and so forth:
meteors, the burning of the quarters, and likewise halos;
and the effects upon reservoirs of water are also declared to be terrestrial.

Terrestrial omens should be known to yield little fruit, as do those of the celestial and atmospheric realms; however, a divine omen yields fruit within seven days, and one from the sky yields it instantly.
Furthermore, the laughing of deities, their wrangling, and the flowing of blood [are likewise signs].

Sudden misfortune occurs there where there is a merciless thunderclap, as well as the climbing of snakes and other such things; that too is proclaimed to be the work of fate. Furthermore, if rain produced from a cloud falls upon a rocky surface...

If life is produced within seven days [of conception], it shall be fruitless. When the malefics— Saturn, Mars, and the Sun— are situated in a single sign, the earth will be filled with smoke there, and many people will weep.
When Jupiter has entered the *abhicāra* [sign] and Saturn has not yet arrived there,
O Indra among kings, who will sustain the earth when he beholds such a sight?
There is likewise a pair of eclipses of the sun and a conflagration of the quarters.
The appearance of a comet, the sight of smoke in a star,
an earthquake occurring within a month or even on a single day,
or the appearance of Indra’s bow (a rainbow) on the king’s birthday or during the course of the day;
There will be the sight of harsh winds and the observation of planetary conflicts;
within three months, there will be eclipses and the falling of meteors.
Furthermore, both in the sky and upon the earth, frogs will appear there.
If a shower of turmeric falls upon a stone, or if it takes the form of a lion or a bilva fruit,
there will be famine in the kingdom and the destruction of the king upon its appearance. If, in the month of Caitra, a rapid current is seen in a water-pot (kumbha), there shall be a great upheaval.

This is indeed a marvel of the sun; one should carefully cook the sacrificial porridge (caru) in a ladle with the mantra "Ā kṛṣṇena" or with the solar hymn. There, the temple gateway, the archway, the entrance, the enclosure wall, and the inner chamber [should be prepared].

One should know that the essence of grain, the essence of cows, the sight of a water-jar in a well, and the marvel of the sun are all like a lotus; one should then offer oblations. One may offer a thousand oblations, after which peace will certainly prevail.
Furthermore, if deformed birds, pale pigeons,
white owls, large owls, crows as big as drōṇas, cuckoos, cranes, and female cranes should alight upon one's house; |||
In his house, a great calamity will undoubtedly occur—
either the breaking of a pillar, the snapping of a tethering rope, or even its sprouting;
necklaces will creak, and teeth will grow upon those already born.
When laughing, sweat appears on the bodies of the deities;
or perhaps the birth of snakes and frogs occurs even within the water-pot.
Such omens as these arise in whosever house.
Within six months, even a virtuous housewife shall die.
Know that great danger awaits that house where lightning strikes or a thunderbolt falls upon a tree, and where white sparks of fire appear.
In the case of dates, a navel-like depression in the abdomen, a constricted throat,
and also in the *tinduka* tree which bears fruit, wherever these may arise—
whether in a garden, a temple, one's own home, or at a sacred *caitya* tree.
Or on a Sunday, one should offer ten thousand oblations of sesame and milk-rice;
then peace will quickly be attained. One should also give a cow as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), along with milk-rice, sesame, mung beans, flowers, or a palm-leaf fan.
One should offer oblations of sugarcane, sweetmeats, and oil-cakes while addressing the Sun;
wherever a lion-throne, a chariot, an umbrella, or a banner adorned with chowries is seen suddenly, whether belonging to a king or elsewhere.
They cause the blazing of truth to fade for both women and men;
and upon seeing the very collapse and creaking of the sacred tradition,
this great portent shall come to pass above him.
If the lower lip trembles and makes a cracking sound,
or if even a cuckoo cries out, or if an owl utters an inauspicious cry,
it portends the destruction of the king, his minister, or the king's son, as well as the ruin of the earth.
Elephants intoxicated with rut die there; of this there is no doubt.
Where palm trees, betel-nut trees, and the like stand together with twin trees through negligence, the householder perishes there along with his wife and children.
When a flower or a fruit is seen upon a bound flower,
or when an unbroken grain is seen there, that is a wondrous sight of Soma;
O twice-born ones, one should then offer ten thousand oblations of curd, honey, and ghee.
On the day of Soma (the Moon), one should prepare a caru offering for Soma using palāśa wood,
cooking it with the mantra "imaṃ devāḥ.
In whose house barley and beans sprout in abundance, [that house prospers].
If blood is seen in the cooking of curd, milk, or ghee;
if there is a sudden conflagration of the house as if by fire without fuel; if lightning occurs in a cloudless sky; or if rain falls from a cloudless firmament.

Overwhelmed by disease, all animals and humans perish; likewise, all beings certainly come to ruin when there is no one to act. When the king and his ministers are destroyed, the householder perishes within his own home.
Indeed, these [obstacles] lead to the destruction of the life-force of a Brahmin through the oblation.
Having seen something extremely terrible or inauspicious, one should perform ten thousand oblations in due order with curds,
honey, and ghee, using either a vessel of Khadira or Udumbara wood.
With the mantra "agnirmūrdhā," one should feed three Brahmins the cooked red *caru* offering and give a red sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Then,
with reference to a glowing coal of gold, peace is thereby produced.
Wherever one might drop a flower or likewise a fruit,
or curd-rice mixed with clarified butter, or silver and gold,
or elephants, horses, buffaloes, cows, wives, children, and wealth—
When Aṅgāraka is thus propitiated, let all this be given:
a staff made of Khadira wood joined with unbroken grains, accompanied by the Aṅgāraka mantra;
and furthermore, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brahmin according to one's ability.
And one should offer a red oblation; from that, auspiciousness is attained.
O Brahmins, if cows with upraised tails run of their own accord into the house, or if dogs, pigs, and Brahmins enter the house; [these are signs of prosperity].
In whose house these [omens] appear, his wife perishes;
or else death shall come to all, or a cow gives birth to a barren calf. Furthermore, the householder remains subject to disputes with the king due to false speech.
Alternatively, O best of men, when cows in the house bellow and laugh,
where there is striking the earth and likewise leaping over two [people],
such omens as these arising from cows and horses [are to be known].
In whosever house these things appear, his destruction is certain.
Just as women may give birth to frogs, snakes, and pumpkins,
if these occur suddenly, it is a sign of calamity for the wise man.
I shall now declare the rite of pacification (śānti) by which happiness is attained: one should,
endowed with faith, offer ten thousand oblations of Apāmārga grass smeared with curd, honey, and ghee on a Wednesday.
With the mantra "Ambake," one should cook a sacrificial oblation (caru) for Budha;
one should give gold and a milch cow dedicated to Budha,
as well as gold, a shower of flowers, excellent fruit, and unbroken grains (akṣata).

If, at any time, one should see within the house or the courtyard a woman adorned with ornaments and decorated with all her finery, yet appearing emaciated and hidden from view; or if one should see such a woman in the middle of the house...

A *mālatī* flower may suddenly appear in his house, or he may not be satisfied with the offerings to Soma; all of this is clearly seen. Likewise, wealth, grain, sons, sovereignty, and excellent women [shall be his].
The queens along with their servants will die, there is no doubt;
likewise, on a Wednesday, a wise man should offer a thousand oblations of Apāmārga grass mixed with ghee, using the mantra "śrīścata."
Likewise, one should faithfully give a milch cow together with a pair of garments to a twice-born man; from that, auspiciousness is attained.
Where there is a flow of blood, there a priest (ṛtvij) is produced.
It causes the loss of wealth and brings misfortune to lions, tigers, cattle, and others.
One bull, three cows, seven, eight, or nine elephants—
within a year, even one offspring of his is destroyed again.
Furthermore, repeatedly breaking one's vows and likewise engaging in sexual intercourse at an improper time—
these two are the causes of faults in a place where cows give birth.
So too are grains that have been husked, such as rice, barley, and rice-grains.
If stones, cats,
or frogs scatter the ground with their claws in the courtyard during the breaking of a pillar, or if they sprout there,
or if such creatures are born in one's house, death will surely come to that person; of this there is no doubt.

Within six months, he will certainly go to a cremation ground; there will be quarrels, enmity with kinsmen, and affliction by disease. There will be lamentation, loss of friends, and the sight of what is undesirable among those who are dear.

In these [years], the destruction of one's wife and sons will certainly occur. When one performs the *gṛdhra-bilvaka* rite for a person who is already active in his duties, then there will be confusion among kings as well as the ruin of the household.
And the circles of ministers in the cities of kings who have turned their backs on their kingdom [should act];
one should give a milch cow dedicated to Bṛhaspati,
and [offerings] of honey and sour gruel in a water-pool, a well, and a large pond.
If milk, curd,
and ghee should suddenly appear there, and a tree laden with fruit should grow in the middle of the house, then prosperity follows.
All this is the manifestation of Bṛhaspati when he is pleased. One should offer a white bull as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to Bṛhaspati;
indeed, one should effect the pacification of the inauspicious through auspicious means and perform the fire-oblation (homa).
In that very place where the Rākṣasa Ghaṭaka-Parishoṣaṇa resides,
there stands Keśarī, Śarkarā, Taila, and Rājatāṇḍava;
likewise Māṣabhakta, Dhānya, Suvarṇa, and Rajatāni.
If one indeed has copper, bell-metal, iron, lead,
and brass kept in one's house as if they were permanently installed,
there will be loss of wealth for that person, or even the destruction of heaven.
In such a case, there will certainly arise affliction by disease, as well as terrible calamities from kings, imprisonment,
and the destruction of elephants, horses, cattle, and servants—
whenever these and golden mountains are seen [in dreams].
When [the teeth] have grown together, they become steady and always provide comfort;
however, in the case of *daṃtottara* (overlapping teeth), the teeth remain positioned by overlapping the rows,
and all such [abnormalities], as well as those shaped like wooden splinters (*śalākākṛti*), are likewise producers of defects.
All those who bite [the food] are never at fault in any respect.
Furthermore, when the thundering of clouds is heard from within a vessel or a jar,
or if the sound of armor is heard within a house or upon the rampart wall;
If a householder sees [the planet] blazing in the mouth of a mouse, he shall perish right there; such was the wondrous vision of Śukra.
I shall now declare the propitiatory rite (śānti) by which prosperity is attained.
On the day of Bhārgava (Venus), even a householder’s wife should offer an oblation made of *śamī* leaves mixed with barley, anointed with curd,
honey, and clarified butter; she should also give a pair of white garments and a white, milk-yielding cow.
One should indeed give gold as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brahmin with faith.
When the earth in a temple is seen to be red,
or when it appears covered in blossoms in the world, know that there is great danger therein.
Either the king, or the prince, or even the kingdom itself will perish;
the ministers and the sons of the ministers will die—of this there is no doubt.
Or wherever they are seen in the world, in whosever house they are well-honored...
The pillars of the house, the body, and likewise the water-jar,
as well as elephants, horses, buffaloes, goats, and cows— all these,
when in full bloom, constantly flow forth for the sake of the master’s slaughter.
A swan in the house, water-dwelling frogs gathered properly within the house,
a serpent entering through the door— the visualization of these [omens],
as well as the sudden occurrence of the sound of a jar anywhere at all, [indicate the presence of the deity].
Where women flow [with blood] while their nine-limbed bodies are split asunder,
there the householder perishes along with his sons, cattle, and kinsmen;
likewise when they carry bows and swords at night or during the midday moon.
Likewise, a blazing fire is seen risen in the sky;
there shall be death among the women of men, as well as the upheaval of the kingdom.
Furthermore, substances perfected by alchemy (rasasiddha) and even liquors and the like [will vanish].
Elephants intoxicated with rut and horses that are bold yet harmful—
these always perish when there is the wondrous appearance of Saturn.
Furthermore, enemies arise for him in either the city or the village.
Whether by day or by night, when there is a portentous appearance of Saturn,
or when deer, tigers, and other beasts, as well as cattle and buffaloes,
leap up— then one should predict a portent of Saturn.
I shall proclaim the mantra for treasure, by which auspiciousness is attained.
O twice-born ones, one should properly offer ten thousand oblations of grain and sacrificial fuel on a Saturday for the sake of welfare,
using the mantra "śanno devī".
One should cook a *caru* oblation there, dedicated specifically to Śanaiścara; then one should give a dark-blue cow that has a living calf and yields milk,
as well as a pair of garments, gold, and silver to a Brahmin.
Having properly given the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) with faith while it rests upon the head at the conclusion of the fire-offering (homa), auspiciousness is thereby attained. Furthermore,
if a lizard or a female snail should enter the house through the door, [it portends prosperity].
Then one should know it to be inauspicious; there will be oppression by the king and loss of wealth.
One should perform ten thousand oblations correctly, and thereafter prosperity is attained.
Even without thundering clouds, a shower of stones occurs.
Wherever a pale dust mixed with blood is seen falling,
there clouds are observed appearing even when devoid of wind;
likewise, the banner of Indra, a rainbow, and the falling of flowers are seen.
Formerly, a jackal howled during the day, or an owl that wanders by night;
or a bull, having fallen upon the territory of the descendant of Kakutstha, bellowed at night. In such regions, unrighteousness prevails and the king is averse to dharma.
They will seek to kill one another, as well as cows and Brahmins;
the householder shall perish in his home along with his sons, cattle, and kinsmen. There will be a ruinous fire at his doorway, death, and the upheaval of the kingdom.

The king shall suffer the loss of his kingdom or the death of his mount; indeed, adverse conditions will arise for him in succession. Furthermore, when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu at night or even during the day, [the same results follow].
Like a cluster of stars, he brings about the destruction of kings;
together with their ministers, they perish—those who were once difficult even for the gods to conquer—and these kings are overthrown by a foreign army; of this there is no doubt.
If at any time the shadow of a banner is seen in the sky,
by that very sight the king shall perish along with his kingdom;
likewise, where fire is seen blazing even once within water.
If a thunderbolt strikes his head or body, his life is difficult to preserve;
likewise, if fire or even smoke appears at the edge of a doorway or upon a pillar,
the death of that man will certainly occur right there.

If there is a thunderbolt strike in the sky, or again, if a spear is seen in the hand [of the deity], his death will occur within the year; of this there is no doubt. Furthermore, if smoke arises from fire in the midst of a circle of flames, [death follows].
In the midst of the city, a wondrous sight was seen right there:
either the rising of a corpse being carried away due to negligence,
or likewise, the movement elsewhere of an installed *liṅga*.
There were thunderclaps and earthquakes, the appearance of meteors in a windless sky,
trees flowering out of season, and fruit produced at the wrong time—
all these omens appeared intensely as they drew near from afar.
If there is the destruction of an image of the Bodiless One (Animitta) or one made by Rāhu,
or if men sit upon a seat belonging to cows while speaking in human voices,
these portend the death of his son within the space of a fortnight.
One should diligently offer ten thousand oblations there, dedicated to Rāhu.
I shall now proclaim the propitiatory rite (śānti) by which auspiciousness is attained:
one should likewise prepare dūrvā grass and unbroken grains (akṣata) smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.

On a Sunday, one should offer oblations with the mantra "kalāyu" and cook sacrificial porridge (caru) there for the sake of Rāhu. Then, one should perform the fire sacrifice and give a tawny cow that yields milk.
Alternatively, one should give linseed, sesame, a conch shell, or even a pair of garments as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brahmin with faith, dedicating it to Rāhu;
for the destruction of his misfortune, auspiciousness shall accrue to him.
In the Vāruṇa [lagna], there is curd, honey, ghee, milk, and water;
and a wonder is seen therein by distinguished observers of defects:
the householder there becomes ruined along with his cattle and kinsmen.
There, curlews, jackals, vultures, and crows are seen;
they dance and laugh in a manner that is cruel, terrifying, and dreadful.
Furthermore, if there should be sexual intercourse by anyone while dwelling there—
By the command of the Lord, his death shall come swiftly when the comet,
resembling a blazing fire,
moves from place to place in the sky or falls violently upon the earth.
The king will be abandoned by all his kinsmen and oppressed by foreign armies;
famine and death shall prevail for a long time in the kingdom,
and cows with monkey-like faces will enter the houses of the people.
His cattle perish, as do his wife, children, and wealth;
through negligence, the fault of another enters his house. Within a year, death shall occur, for he will indeed become devoid of passion (viraja).
I shall here proclaim this peace (śānti) by which auspiciousness is attained:
one should give a pavilion equipped with a chariot drawn by seven horses and adorned with a golden umbrella to a Brahmin, or even a bilva leaf.
The twice-born should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with the very mantra dedicated to Indra.
If, unexpectedly, śāla, tāla, akṣa, khadira, utpala,
and seraka trees should grow in the middle of the house, it is a wondrous sight portended by Ketu.
If a swan, a common crow, or a peacock appears above his house,
it is a great portent and a wondrous sight of the Ketu [comet] in his home.
I shall here proclaim the pacification by which prosperity is attained.
One should offer ten thousand oblations of *kuśa* grass smeared with curd, honey, and ghee,
using the mantra "Tryambakam" and likewise offering *caru* to the Ketu deity.
Furthermore, one should give a dark-blue cow that yields much milk along with her calf.
I shall now describe the clay, golden garments, various ornaments,
and the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for which there is no substitute;
likewise, [the rites] performed with reference to the deity through giving, fire-offerings (homa), and the sacrificial oblation (caru).
He who should himself see his own shadow in the southern direction,
or see his own reflection in a sandal-wood footstool as having five heads and two bodies—
whatever is thus severed or remains from that is for his benefit.
One meets with destruction quickly, within seven days; of this there is no doubt.
I shall describe the various [substances], as enjoined by the scripture:
specifically those of the crow, the cat, the porcupine, and especially the pigeon.
Where sexual intercourse is seen, that is a great marvel of Rāhu.
On a Saturday, one should offer ten thousand oblations (ayuta) directed toward Śani;
one should worship him with arka flowers and offer a hundred oblations of cooked rice (caru).
Having performed [the rite] right there, one should behold the wondrous appearance of Saturn;
having prepared the twenty-eighth *caru* offering, peace will then certainly prevail.
Likewise, in the throbbing of the arms, feet, or eyes, one should predict death.
One should know that the lunar miracle occurs on the left and right sides in sequence;
it occurs on the left during the dark fortnight, while in the opposite case, one should declare it a miracle.
Since it indicates what is undesirable, one should therefore perform a propitiatory rite.
For the sake of pacification, one should perform a fire-oblation (homa) directed toward the Sun for fifty times,
according to the procedure for cooking the sacrificial porridge (caru), using barley, sesame seeds, and excellent clarified butter.
Furthermore, the sacrificial thread (yajñasūtra) should be placed in the book, or within the sacrificial vessel or the caru itself.
When Śakra’s garment is consumed by fire, there is a wondrous sight from the sun;
for the attainment of one's desired goal, one should offer into the fire a horse-slayer smeared with the three sweets (trimadhu).
[One should also offer] divine books, jewels, gems, and gold.
One should know that blood is a miraculous sign, as is the purification of a thousand [impurities];
likewise, a monitor lizard, a female conch-snake, a crow, a crane, and two owls may occasionally enter a temple.
If a red-throated pigeon, a dove, a tiger, or even a deer should enter a person's temple, that person should perform ten thousand oblations (homa) for each such instance. Furthermore,
if any deformity of the house or laughter is observed therein, [the same penance applies].
If death is indicated in the house by signs of prosperity, or if there is the sight of suffering amidst wailing,
or if elephants, horses, and vehicles have been destroyed by the loss of the kingdom,
one should offer ten thousand oblations (ayuta) directed toward the Sun for the sake of all success.
If there is trembling due to negligence, there will be loss; if perspiration arises, misfortune shall occur. If milk flows or blood [flows], there is great danger to that kingdom.
Or if a cow, a goat, or a jackal dances upon the roof of the house...

When a jackal howls during the day, destruction will certainly occur. Likewise, if a dog, a jackal, a tiger, or a buffalo runs with all its might toward the northeast, then there will be a calamity in that region.
Regarding a portent concerning Rāhu, one should offer a thousand oblations of sacrificial porridge (caru).
When a portent concerning a tree is observed, one should abandon that [tree].
If the offering goes into houses, one should predict a calamity for the country.
If there is the binding of wild animals in a country, city, or village;
or if a snake appears in a distorted manner, or even a lump of flesh [is seen]; or if death occurs in that very house—one should predict the ruin of the region and so forth.
In the case of a portent occurring during the day, the result is ten thousandfold; at night, it is certainly double that.
At twilight, it is again double, and at midnight, it is fourfold.
In such a time, there will be untimely death, and the death of the householder's wife at an improper time.
One should recognize this as a solar marvel, or [perform] purification in the case of an inauspicious sign;
where there is ten thousand [repetitions] for each [deity], one should offer oblations in that very place,
together with the primary and secondary limbs, or eight times eight oblations.

O best of men, O Brahmins, even when performed on behalf of a householder, one should offer oblations accompanied by the *adhi*, *prati-adhi*, and *saha* mantras; measured by that standard, one should make an offering there as an ornament.
O Brahmins, for each individual, one may offer eight oblations or eight times eight.

One should offer the measure for the presiding deities (adhidevas), the secondary presiding deities (pratyadhidevas), and whatever other limb-deities (aṅgadevatās) there may be. Having offered the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should not perform another homa. I shall now describe the measurement for the sacrifice to the planets (grahamakhā), by which measurement success is attained.
There is a fault in showing disrespect; therefore, one should not abandon honor.
A man should divide [the ritual] fourfold by means of the forty-second [verse] and so forth.
Then, for the sake of the undesirable, he should perform the oblation of sacrificial ghee according to those divisions.
Eight offerings for each of the presiding and secondary deities have indeed been prescribed;
in the Tryambaka and other mantras, three oblations have been prescribed. Likewise, in the Dhanañjaya mantra, one should offer the sacrificial oblation (caru) according to the division.
The wise man should arrange eight additional portions for Āditya;
however, in the case of a hundred-fold oblation (śatahoma), a person should everywhere arrange ten portions for all [deities],
four portions for Aniṣṭa, and one portion for the planets and Aṅganā.
In the same manner, one should assign a limb to the presiding and secondary deities;
one should offer two [limbs] to Tryambaka and likewise to Dhanañjaya.
In all cases, the wise practitioner should perform the fire-oblation (homa) for the central deity.
In a thousand [recitations], one-tenth is for the propitiation of the inauspicious;
with five parts for the planets, and likewise five parts for the barley grains.
Therein, for the inauspicious, there are five hundred [recitations], and half of that for the planets while restraining one's speech.
The measurement for others would be thirty-one, while for the rest it is fourteen;
one should calculate there a pair of oblations exceeding the planets,
and for the sake of non-destruction, the five-fold limb of the lunar day, which is marvelous.
From the planets, one obtains the five-fold [result], and therein the five-fold [result] for others as well;
in each individual limb, the measure shall be six hundred and sixty,
and there shall be an excess of sixty due to the remainder of the tenth part.
In the unfavorable portion, one should give three thousand, three hundred, thirty,
as well as four hundred, and likewise seven hundred and more for the planets;
and for the secondary planets (upagrahas), one hundred and eighty-five.
The portion of the lunar day (tithi) is [calculated] by the remainder; for each planet, there is one [unit] added to seven hundred. Thus, for the Sun and the other planets, there is a yuga.
Whatever portion remains in the planetary division, from that remainder of the portion, there is a pair of yugas.
One should offer that [oblation] to Tryambaka and likewise to Dhanañjaya;
whether for pacification, nourishment, or a specific desire, if one wishes for one's own happiness,
one should perform ten thousand oblations (ayuta-homa) to the planets, to be accomplished over three days.

O twice-born ones, that ritual procedure which was previously described as to be accomplished in three days is now being declared according to its sequential divisions. On the first day, if it is unfavorable, one thousand and three hundred [verses] [are to be recited].
For each of the other planets,
as well as for the presiding and counter-presiding deities (adhipratyadhidevas), fifty oblations are prescribed;
on the first day, one should offer three thousand oblations in total when combined.
On the second day, if the [result] is unfavorable, two thousand is prescribed;
one should give three hundred and eight more to the planets (graha),
and to the sixteen secondary planets (upagraha) in due order.
He diligently gave eighty-one [verses], and for the final two, he gave eighty.
Thus, on the second day, they totaled six thousand;
however, it is held that three hundred were intended for the third day.
For each of the planets, forty-two [offerings] are prescribed;
for each of the presiding and counter-presiding deities, thirty-five. On the third day, one should offer a total of one thousand combined.
One should give one *yuga* to Āditya and one to Tryambaka;
for Dhanañjaya, one *homa* is prescribed, and ten thousand (*ayuta*) is said [for others].
Half of that is for the planets, and half of that again for the other [deities].
One should give three thousand to the planets, one thousand to the five [elements],
the remainder of three thousand to Āditya,
and likewise one thousand to Tryambaka and to Dhanañjaya.
"With a total count of thirty-six thousand and six verses,
the Bhaviṣya [Purāṇa], consisting of nine hundred chapters, shall be complete.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the third part of the Madhyama-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa.
Thus the third part is completed.
Thus ends the Madhyama-parvan in the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa.
May this be an offering to Śrī Veṅkaṭeśvara.
The Narrative of the Kings of the Kṛta Yuga.
Homage to Śrī Gaṇeśa!
Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and to Nara, the best of men...
One should then utter the victory of the goddess Sarasvatī and Vyāsa.
Śaunaka said:
"In the great kalpa called Bhaviṣya, during the half-cycle [parārdha] of Brahmā’s lifespan—"
O sage, when the first year of the twenty-eighth Satya Yuga had arrived within the Vaivasvata Manvantara, who were the kings?
O discerning one, tell me the number of years of their reigns.
Sūta said:
During the Śvetavārāha Kalpa, when three days of Brahmā’s year had passed and the seventh muhūrta had arrived, Vaivasvata Manu came into being.
Having performed divine austerities for a hundred years on the banks of the Sarayū, a son named Ikṣvāku was born from his sacrificial hearth; he became a lord of the earth and,
by virtue of a boon from Brahmā, obtained a celestial vehicle.
Having worshipped Nārāyaṇa and offered the kingdom to Hari,
he then ruled the kingdom for thirty-six thousand years. From him was born Vikukṣi, who ruled for that same number of years minus one hundred.
Having ruled the kingdom, he went to heaven; from him was born Ripuñjaya.
His reign was reduced by one hundred [years], and he is remembered as the son of Kakutstha.
His reign was likewise reduced by one hundred years, and from him was born his son Anenas.
The Kṛta age was diminished by one hundred years; from him was born King Pṛthu. The Kṛta age was diminished by one hundred years; Viṣvagaśva was his son.
The Kṛta age was diminished by one hundred years; from him King Ārdra arose.
Śatahīna ruled the kingdom; his son was Bhadrāśva.
Śatahīna ruled the kingdom; his son was Yuvanāśva.
Śatahīna ruled the kingdom; his son was Śravastha.

And Satyapāda was born as the first [king] in the Bhārata interval. By those kings, who were devoted to statesmanship like gods on earth, the circle of the earth was enjoyed from sunrise to sunset; however, by Śravastha, it was [ruled] upon the surface of the earth.
From him, Bṛhadaśva obtained a kingdom diminished by a hundred [years];
from him, Kuvalayāśvaka obtained a kingdom diminished by a hundred;
and his son Dṛḍhāśva obtained a kingdom diminished by a hundred.
From him was born Nikumbhaka, whose kingdom was less by one thousand;
his son was Saṃkaṭāśva, whose kingdom was likewise less by one thousand;
and from him was born Prasenajit, whose kingdom was again less by one thousand.
Ravaṇāśva, his son, possessed a kingdom diminished by one thousand [years];
Māndhātṛ, his son, likewise possessed that kingdom diminished by one thousand;
and Purukutsa, his son, made the kingdom diminished by one hundred.
The kingdom was reduced by one hundred [years]; his son was Triṃśadaśva, whose chariot was said to be drawn by thirty excellent horses. From him was born Anaraṇya for twenty-eight thousand years.
Indeed, the second quarter of the Satya Yuga is recorded as the reign of Pṛṣadaśva;
having ruled the kingdom on earth for six thousand years,
he then departed for the world of the ancestors.
From him was born King Haryaśva in a family devoted to Viṣṇu;
his son was known as Vasumān, whose kingdom was diminished by one thousand [yojanas].
His son was Tridhanvan, whose kingdom was likewise diminished by one thousand.
That kingdom, diminished by a thousand [villages], was honored by that king.
Thus ends the section on the four quarters of Truth (Satyapāda) within the second interval of the Bharata lineage.
And the son of King Tridhanvan was indeed Trapāraṇya.
Having ruled that kingdom for one thousand years less [one], he departed for heaven. From him was born Triśaṅku, who ruled the kingdom for a thousand years.
His son was Hariścandra, who was born deficient due to a deception.
Rohita, his son, ruled for twenty thousand years;
Hārīta was his son, who likewise ruled a kingdom equal to that of his father; and Cañcubhūpa was his son, who also ruled a kingdom equal to that of his father.
For his kingdom was equal to that of his father; his son was named Vijaya.
His kingdom was indeed equal to that of his father; from him came the son Ruruka.
Sagara became his son, and he likewise ruled a kingdom equal to that of his father.
The kings, ending with Bāhusena, are proclaimed to be Vaiṣṇavas.
The kingdom was properly established by the kings beginning with Vaivasvata;
it abounded in jewels and gold, and possessed much food and much milk.

O Sage, at that time, during the third quarter of the Satya Yuga on this earth, the Dharma was indeed complete. There was a king named Sagara, a devotee of Śiva and of virtuous conduct; his sons are known as the Sāgaras.

That kingdom is recorded by the sages as lasting for thirty thousand years. When the oceans had thus disappeared, Aṃśumat, the son of Asamañjas, reigned; his reign was reduced by one hundred [years], and he became the father of his son.
The kingdom was reduced by a hundred [years]; Dilīpa became his son.
The kingdom was reduced by a hundred [years]; from him was born Bhagīratha. The kingdom was reduced by a hundred [years]; Śrutasena arose after him.
The kingdom was reduced by one hundred [years]; from him came the son Nābhāga. Then Aṃbarīṣa became king; the Śaiva kings ended with Ṣaṭśrutasena, while King Nābhāga was a Vaiṣṇava.
This third section within the Mahābhārata, consisting of the Satyapāda, is completed.
By King Ambarīṣa, one hundred verses were removed from this section;
thus, in its fourth quarter, it consists of eighteen thousand verses.
A hundred years of auspicious reign was known in Bhārata, the land of action;
and for twenty-nine years,
as well as thirty years less a hundred, Siṃdhudvīpa, the son of Ambarīṣa, ruled the kingdom.
From him, the kingdom was reduced by one hundred and became ten thousand horses;
from him, Ṛtuparṇa was his son, and the kingdom was reduced by one hundred;
