from him, King Sarvakāma [ruled], and the kingdom was reduced by one hundred.
King Kalmāṣapāda ruled a kingdom for ninety-nine years;
Sudāsa’s son likewise ruled a kingdom for ninety-nine years. From him was born Aśmaka, the son of Madayantī, begotten by Vasiṣṭha.
The kingdom was reduced by one hundred [years], and thereafter Harivarmā arose.
Seven kings ending with Sudāsa are celebrated as Vaiṣṇavas.
However, due to a preceptor’s curse, Saudāsa offered a limb of his kingdom to the preceptor.
The devotee of the Gokarṇa-liṅga, a follower of Śiva, is called Samaya; Harivarmā, born of the Śamaka family, was a Vaiśya who honored the virtuous,
numbering twenty-nine thousand and seven hundred.
Harivarmā ruled the kingdom; from him, Daśaratha arose.
He governed the kingdom equal to his father’s; from him came the son of Dillīvaya.
King Viśvāsahasta likewise governed the kingdom equal to his father’s.
That king Niyajña was an ordinary ruler over a kingdom of ten thousand villages.
Due to the power of his unrighteousness, a drought occurred at that time;
for a hundred years there was no rain, and it destroyed the entire kingdom.
Having performed a sacrifice, Vasiṣṭha, intent on the queen’s words,
produced Khaṭvāṅga from that sacrifice; bearing the weapon Khaṭvāṅga,
he went to assist Indra for thirty thousand years of kingship.
Having performed [the rites] there and obtained a boon from the gods, he attained liberation.
From Khaṭṭāṅga was born Dīrghabāhu, who ruled for twenty thousand years;
from him was born Sudarśana, who was devoted to the worship of the Goddess.
Those three sons of Daśaratha were renowned for their excellent strength;
Khaṭvāṅga and Dīrghabāhu are celebrated as Vaiṣṇavas.
Sudarśana, the highly wise king, [married] the daughter of the King of Kāśī.
Having uprooted and conquered other kings through the grace of the Goddess's service,
the king righteously established his sovereignty over the entirety of Bharatavarṣa;
that monarch ruled the kingdom for five thousand years.
Indeed, during the midst of a dream, Mahākālī spoke these words to the king:
"O child of great intelligence, together with your beloved wife and accompanied by Vasiṣṭha and the others,
go to the Himālaya mountain and make your dwelling there."
By the power of a great wind, there was destruction in the land of Bharatavarṣa;
the western ocean, the Ratnākara, and its islands were destroyed, as were the eastern ocean, the Mahodadhi, and its islands.
To its south is the Vāḍava ocean, and its islands have gone to destruction;
to its north is the Himābdhi ocean, which was indeed excavated by the sons of Sagara.
Even those islands that were well-known have all likewise met their end.
"This very land of Bhārata shall meet its destruction on the seventh day of the year while still alive; therefore, remain alive. Thinking "So be it," that king went to the Himālaya mountain.
Together with the chief kings, the chief vaiśyas, and the twice-born, he attained [the dissolution];
in five years' time, through the sequence of air, fire, and water,
sugar and the earth were reached, and thereafter living beings went to their destruction.
During the period of five years, the earth became filled with water;
then, having become calm, the wind dried up all that water once more.
Within ten years, the earth was seen to have become dry land again.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Kings of the Kṛta Yuga," in the Pratisarga Parva of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, which is also known as the Caturyuga Khaṇḍa.
Now follows the description of the narrative of the kings of the Tretā Yuga.
Sūta said:
On the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, on a Thursday,
Sudarśana returned to Ayodhyā along with the people;
by the power of Māyādevī, the entire city was enchanting.
Having attained a kingdom endowed with great prosperity, abundant food, and all kinds of jewels, Sudarśana ruled for ten thousand years and reached the eternal world. His son was Dilīpa.
By the granting of the boon of Nandinī, his son Raghu became supreme;
Dilīpa was honored in the kingdom for ten thousand years,
and after Dilīpa’s end, the kingdom was ruled by Raghu in a manner equal to that of his father.
O descendant of Bhṛgu, thereafter the lineage became renowned as the Raghuvaṃśa during the Tretā age;
by the granting of a boon to a Brahmin, his son was known as Aja. Having ruled a kingdom equal to that of his father, from him Daśaratha was born.
He ruled the kingdom equal to his father; therefore, Rāma himself was Hari.
The reign of Rāma is celebrated as lasting eleven thousand years.
His son, named Kuśa, ruled for ten thousand years.
His son was named Atithi, who ruled the kingdom equally with his father;
his son was named Nibandha, who likewise ruled the kingdom equally with his father;
from him was born the one named Nala, who in the Tretā age was a worshiper of Śakti.
Nābha was born as a son who ruled a kingdom equal to his father’s;
Puṇḍarīka was born as a son who ruled a kingdom equal to his father’s;
and Kṣemadhanvan was his son who likewise ruled a kingdom equal to his father’s.
He ruled a kingdom equal to his father's; his son was named Dvāraka.
He ruled a kingdom equal to his father's; from him was born Ahīnaja.
He ruled a kingdom equal to his father's; from him came a son named Kuru.

He established Kurukṣetra in the Kṛta age and Śatayojana in the Tretā; thus this first quarter of the Tretā age was completed within the Bharata interval. He ruled a kingdom equal to that of his father, and Pāriyātra became his son.
Dalapāla, his son, then ruled the kingdom equal to his father;
Chadmakārī, his son, likewise ruled the kingdom equal to his father;
from him was born a son named Uktha, who also ruled the kingdom equal to his father.
Vajranābhi then ruled a kingdom equal to that of his father;
Śaṅkhanābhi then ruled a kingdom equal to that of his father;
and Vyutthanābhi then ruled a kingdom equal to that of his father.
Viśvapāla then ruled the kingdom equal to his father;
Svarṇanābha, his son, likewise ruled the kingdom equal to his father;
and Puṣpasena, his son, likewise ruled the kingdom equal to his father.
Dhruvasandhi, his son, ruled a kingdom equal to that of his father;
Apavarmā, his son, likewise ruled a kingdom equal to that of his father;
and Śīghragantā, his son, likewise ruled a kingdom equal to that of his father.
Marupāla, his son, ruled a kingdom equal to that of his father;
Prasūvaśruta is said to have ruled a kingdom equal to his father’s;
Susandhi was born as a son who ruled a kingdom equal to his father’s.

Thus ends the first section, the Tretāpāda, within the Bhārata-antara. Thereafter, until his reign rose from one prosperity to another, the king ruled with great conciliation; his son Māmarba then governed the kingdom as an equal to his father.
He ruled the kingdom equal to his father and became Mahāśvastana;
then Bṛhadbāla was his son, who likewise ruled the kingdom equal to his father;
and Bṛhadaiśāna indeed followed him, ruling the kingdom equal to his father.
The kingdom was ruled equally with his father, and from him came Urukṣepa;
the kingdom was ruled equally with his father, and his son was Vatsapāla;
the kingdom was ruled equally with his father, and from him came Vatsavyūha.
King Prativyoma then ruled a kingdom equal to his father's;
after him came his son Devakara, who likewise ruled a kingdom equal to his father's;
and after him came Sahadeva, who also ruled a kingdom equal to his father's.
King Bṛhadaśva then ruled a kingdom equal to that of his father;
after him came Bhānuratna, who likewise ruled a kingdom equal to his father's;
and after him came Supratīka, who also ruled a kingdom equal to his father's.
Then Marudeva ruled a kingdom equal to his father's;
after him came Sunakṣatra, who likewise ruled a kingdom equal to his father's;
and after him came his son Keśīnara, who ruled a kingdom equal to his father's.
The kingdom was made equal to his father’s; then the king Antarikṣa ruled. The kingdom was made equal to his father’s; King Suvarṇāṅga became the ruler.
The kingdom was made equal to his father’s; his son was indeed Amitrajit.
From him was born Bṛhadrāja, who ruled a kingdom equal to that of his father;
from him came King Dharmarāja, who likewise governed a kingdom equal to his father's;
and from him was born Kṛtañjaya, who also maintained a kingdom equal to his father's.
A kingdom equal to his father's was established by him; from him was born Raṇañjaya.
A kingdom equal to his father's was established by him; he is remembered as Sañjaya, his son.
A kingdom equal to his father's was established by him; his son was Śākyavardhana.
His son was Krodhadāman, who ruled a kingdom equal to his father's;
from him was born Atulavikrama, who ruled a kingdom equal to his father's;
and from him was born Prasenajit, who likewise ruled a kingdom equal to his father's.
The kingdom was made equal to his father’s; his son was known as Śūdraka. The kingdom was made equal to his father’s; Suratha became his son.
All those born in the lineage of Raghu, however, made their kingdoms half the size of their fathers’.
Sixty-five kings, devoted to the worship of goddesses and all intent on sacrifices involving violence, departed from here for the heavenly realm;
yet those sons who were born as Buddhists were all of mixed caste.
Having attained youth at the commencement of the third quarter of the Tretā age,
the Moon, the lord of Rohiṇī, was sent to earth by Indra;
he ruled the earth in the beautiful city of Prayāga.
Devoted to Viṣṇu and intent upon the worship of Śiva,
Candramas performed a hundred sacrifices for the sake of pleasing Goddess Māyā;
having ruled for eighteen thousand years, he departed for heaven.
His son was named Budha, the offspring of Merudeva; having married Ilā according to dharma, Purūravas was born from him,
and he ruled over the earth for fourteen thousand years.
He too enjoyed the celestial nymph Urvaśī only according to the agreement.
A son named Āyu was born, who was righteous and devoted to Viṣṇu.
Having ruled the kingdom for thirty-six thousand years, Purūravas [departed].
Having reached the world of the Gandharvas, he rejoiced in heaven like a god.
The son of Nahuṣa ruled a kingdom equal to that of his father for the duration of his life;
having ruled a kingdom equal to his father's, he thereafter attained the status of Śakra.
For one thousand years, he brought the three worlds under his control.
Due to the curse of the sage Durvāsas, the king fell into the state of a python.
And of the five sons of Yayāti, three became Mlecchas.

Two attained the state of nobility, since Puru was the elder and Laghu was the younger. By the power of his asceticism, having ruled the kingdom for a hundred thousand years through the grace of Viṣṇu, he then went to Vaikuṇṭha.
The son of Yadu is remembered as Kroṣṭṛ; his reign lasted for sixty thousand years. His son was Vṛjinaghna, whose reign lasted twenty thousand years.
From him came the son Svāhārcana, who ruled for a period equal to that of his father.
From him was born a son named Citraratha, who ruled a kingdom equal to that of his father;
from him came Aravinda, who likewise ruled a kingdom equal to that of his father. Then Śrava was born after him, a radiant soul devoted to Viṣṇu.
The kingdom established for the sake of his father was known as the son of Tamas;
the kingdom established equal to that of his father belonged to the son of Uśanas;
and the kingdom established equal to that of his father was held by King Śītāṃśuka.
Having ruled a kingdom equal to his father's, Kamalāṃśu then arose;
having ruled a kingdom equal to his father's, Pārāvatasuta then arose;
having ruled a kingdom equal to his father's, Jāmagha was born as his son.
Vidarbha became his son, having ruled a kingdom equal to that of his father;
from him came a son named Kratha, who likewise ruled a kingdom equal to his father's;
and Kuntibhoja was his son, who also ruled a kingdom equal to his father's.
Purūravas, the son of the daughter of the Daitya Vṛṣaparvan,
having resided in that city in Pātāla, became a master of the sciences of illusion;
thereafter, he ruled his kingdom in the city of Pratiṣṭhāna at Prayāga.

Having ruled the kingdom for ten thousand years, that king, a devotee of the Goddess, ascended to heaven. His son was Janamejaya, who likewise ruled the kingdom equally with his father. His son was Pracinvan.
The kingdom was ruled equally with his father, and Pravīra became his son;
the kingdom was ruled equally with his father, and Nabhasya became his son;
the kingdom was ruled equally with his father, and he is remembered as his son, Bhavada.
Sudyumna became his son, who ruled a kingdom equal to that of his father;
Bāhuguda is remembered as his son, who ruled a kingdom equal to that of his father;
Saṃyāti became his son, who ruled a kingdom equal to that of his father.
Dhanayāti was born from him, who ruled the kingdom equal to his father;
Aindrāśva was the son who ruled the kingdom equal to his father;
and from him was born the son Raṃtinara, who ruled the kingdom equal to his father.
His son was known as Sutapas, who ruled the kingdom equal to his father;
his son was Saṃvaraṇa, who likewise ruled the kingdom equal to his father,
until he set his mind on performing penance upon the Himalaya mountain.

Then, after a hundred years, the Sun, being pleased, gave a maiden named Tapati to Saṃvaraṇa; the king then departed for the world of the Sun. Thereafter, through the power of illusion, an entire Yuga reached its dissolution.
The four oceans swelled, and Bhārata came to its destruction.
After the earth, together with the mountains, had dwelt within the ocean for two years,
the oceans reached a state of desiccation through the power of a great wind.
Through the spiritual power of Agastya, the earth became visible as dry land;
within five years, the ground was covered with trees, dūrvā grass, and other vegetation.
And by the command of the Sun, Saṃvaraṇa continued to rule together with the sage.
He met with Vasiṣṭha and the leading members of the three social orders.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Kings of the Tretā Age," within the Caturyuga-khaṇḍa (also known as the Pratisarga-parvan) of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*. [Now follows] the description of the narrative of the kings of the Dvāpara age.
Śaunaka said:
O Lomaharṣaṇa, tell me at what time King Saṃvaraṇa appeared,
as well as the kings of the Dvāpara age.
Sūta said:
On the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada, on a Friday,
Saṃvarṇa arrived at Pratiṣṭhāna together with the sages.
A delightful capital was established, five yojanas in length;
a palace half a krośa in height was constructed by Viśvakarman.
King Prasenajit was appointed to the lineage of Buddhi, born of Saktā.
In the Yadu lineage, Sātvata was made the lord of Madhurā;
in the Mleccha lineage, Śmaśrupāla became the king of Marudeśa.
In due course, these kings, together with their subjects, increased in number upon the earth.
Saṃvarṇa is recorded as the king for ten thousand years;
his son was Arcājña, who ruled the kingdom equal to that of his father.
His son was Sūrijāpī, who held half of his father’s kingdom.
Sūryayajña was his son, who was devoted to the sacrifice to the Sun. From him came Ātithyavardhana, by whom the kingdom was reduced by one hundred [years];
his son was Dvādaśātman, by whom the kingdom was likewise reduced by one hundred.
From him was born Divākara, after whom the kingdom was reduced by a hundred [years];
from him was born Prabhākara, after whom the kingdom was reduced by a hundred;
and his son was Bhāsvat, after whom the kingdom was likewise reduced by a hundred.
The son of Vivasvat then ruled the kingdom for ninety-nine years;
after him, Haridaśvārca ruled the kingdom for ninety-nine years;
and from him was born a son, Vaikartana, who likewise ruled the kingdom for ninety-nine years.
The kingdom was reduced by one hundred [years]; from him came the son Arkeṣṭiman.
The kingdom was reduced by one hundred [years]; from him came Mārtaṇḍavatsala.
The kingdom was reduced by one hundred [years]; his son was Mihirārtha.
From him came Aruṇapoṣaṇa, by whom the kingdom was deprived of a hundred [years];
from him came Dyumaṇivatsala, by whom the kingdom was deprived of a hundred; from him came Taraṇiyajñaka, by whom the kingdom was deprived of a hundred.
From him came Maitreṣṭivardhana, by whom the kingdom was reduced by a hundred [years].
From him came Citrabhānu, by whom the kingdom was reduced by a hundred;
from him, Vairocana is remembered, by whom the kingdom was reduced by a hundred.
The kingdom was reduced by one hundred [years]; his son, however, was Haṃsanyāyin.
He ruled a kingdom equal to that of his father; from him came Vedapravardhana.
The kingdom was reduced by one hundred [years] from him; therefore, he is called Sāvitra.
Śatahīna ruled the kingdom; from him was born Dhanapāla.
Śatahīna ruled the kingdom; his son is remembered as Mlecchahantā.
Śatahīna ruled the kingdom; from him came Ānandavardhana.
Then Śatahīna ruled the kingdom; after him, his son Dharmapāla ruled the kingdom; after him, his son Brahmabhakta ruled the kingdom equal to his father; from him came Brahmeṣṭivardhana.
He ruled the kingdom equal to his father; therefore he was known as Ātmaprapūjaka.
His son Parameṣṭhin likewise ruled the kingdom equal to his father.
His son was Hairaṇyavardhana, who also ruled the kingdom equal to his father.

The kingdom was rendered deficient by a hundred [years]; his son, however, was Dhātṛyājī, who ruled a kingdom equal to that of his father and was a worshiper of Vidhātṛ. From him indeed came Druhiṇa Kratu, who likewise ruled a kingdom equal to that of his father.
The kingdom was made equal to that of his father; therefore he is called Vairañca.
His son Kamalāsana ruled for a kingdom reduced by one hundred [years].
His son Śamavartin, however, ruled for a kingdom equal to that of his father.
His son was Śrāddhadeva, who ruled a kingdom equal to his father's;
because he ruled a kingdom equal to his father's, he was indeed called Pitṛvardhana.
His son was Somadatta, who likewise ruled a kingdom equal to his father's.
The son of Somadatta then ruled a kingdom equal to his father's;
from him came Somavardhana, who likewise ruled a kingdom equal to his father's;
and from him was born Avataṃsa, whose son also ruled a kingdom equal to his father's.
The kingdom was ruled like that of his father; then his son Pratansa ruled the kingdom like that of his father.
Then his son Paratansa ruled the kingdom like that of his father;
thereafter Ayatansa became king, ruling the kingdom like that of his father.
His son Samātaṃsa ruled a kingdom equal to that of his father;
Anutaṃsa, his son, likewise ruled a kingdom equal to his father’s;
and from him came Adhitaṃsa, who ruled a kingdom equal to his father’s.
His son was Abhitaṃsa, who ruled the kingdom equal to his father;
then came Samuttaṃsa, who likewise ruled the kingdom equal to his father;
and then there was a son named Taṃsa, who also ruled the kingdom equal to his father.

He ruled the kingdom equal to his father; from him, Duṣyanta was born as a son by Śakuntalā, and from him came the king named Bharata. He too ruled the kingdom equal to his father, and then Duṣyanta attained the celestial realm.
His son was named Bharata, who was devoted to the worship of the gods;
through the power of Mahāmāyā,
his lifespan was extended from thirty-six years to thirty-six thousand years.
The region remembered by his name is renowned as Bhārata;
by him the division of the earth was made and the kingdom was ruled separately for a long time.
He reigned for a hundred divine years, and from him was born one of great strength.
Bharadvāja then held the kingdom for a hundred divine years;
from him, Bhavanamanyumān held the kingdom for a hundred divine years,
during which his reign is celebrated as lasting eighteen thousand years.
From him was born Bṛhatkṣetra, who established a station equal to that of his father; Suhotra was his son, who likewise established a station equal to that of his father.
Vītihotra was his son, and he ruled the kingdom for ten thousand years.
From him was born Yajñahotra, who attained a station equal to his father;
from him was born Śakrahotra, who likewise attained a station equal to his father.
The blessed Lord Indra, being pleased, caused that king to attain heaven.
Then the illustrious lord of Ayodhyā, Pratāpendra, possessed of great strength,
bestowed the land of Bhāratavarṣa for ten thousand years.
His son was Maṇḍalīka, who established a position equal to that of his father.
Vijayendra was his son, who occupied a position equal to his father;
Dhanurdīpta was his son, who likewise occupied a position equal to his father.
By the command of Indra, Śakrahotra [descended] to the earth together with Ghṛtācī.

Having obtained a radiant bow and conquered [the world], he ruled the kingdom. A son named Hastin was born; having mounted the elephant Airāvata’s offspring, he established the city of Hastināpura in the western region.
On the bank of the celestial Gaṅgā, there was a beautiful region ten yojanas in extent;
there he established his residence and ruled for ten thousand years.
His son, named Ajamīḍha, likewise maintained the station equal to that of his father.
From him was born Rakṣapāla, who occupied a position equal to his father;
Suśamyarṇa was his son, who likewise occupied a position equal to his father. His son was named Kuru, who occupied half the position of his father.
By virtue of a boon from Indra, he came to heaven with his physical body.
Then, in this Sāttvata lineage, the exceedingly powerful one named Vṛṣṇi resided in Mathurā and brought the entire kingdom under his own control.
By the boon granted by the Blessed One, Hari of wondrous deeds,
the entire kingdom was brought under his control for five thousand years;
his son, Nirāvṛtti, established a position equal to that of his father.
Daśārī was his son; he attained a position equal to that of his father. Viyāmuna was his son; he attained a position equal to that of his father.
Jīmūta was his son; he attained a position equal to that of his father.

Vikṛti was his son; he attained a station equal to that of his father. From him was born Bhīmaratha; he attained a station equal to that of his father. From him was born Navaratha; he attained a station equal to that of his father.
From him was born Daśaratha, who attained a status equal to his father; from him was born Śakuni, who attained a status equal to his father;
and from him was born Kuśumbha, who attained a status equal to his father.
From him was born Devaratha, who held a position equal to his father;
Devakṣetra was his son, who held a position equal to his father;
his son was named Madhu, who held a position equal to his father.
From him was born a son, Navaratha, who maintained his father's station;
his son was Kuruvatsa, who likewise maintained his father's station; from him was born a son, Anuratha, who also maintained his father's station.
Puruhotra was his son; he attained a station equal to that of his father.
Vicitrāṅga was his son; he attained a station equal to that of his father. From him came the son Sātvatavat; he attained a station equal to that of his father.
Bhajamāna, his son, attained a station equal to that of his father;
Vidūratha, his son, attained a station equal to that of his father;
Surabhakta, his son, attained a station equal to that of his father.
And from him was born a son named Sumanas, who occupied a station equal to his father;
his son was Tati, who occupied a station equal to his father;
and his son was Svāyambhuva, who occupied a station equal to his father.
Haridīpaka alone held that kingdom of my father;
Devamedha was his son, who occupied a position equal to his father's;
then Surapāla was born, who likewise occupied a position equal to his father's.
By the command of Śakra, he became the lord and master of the three divisions of the Kuru land; and when that period had passed,
he came to the Bhārata region, where Kurukṣetra was then established, as the husband of Sukeśī, a celestial nymph.
The wise have declared that this field of merit extends twenty yojanas;
for twelve thousand years, it was brought under the sovereignty of Kuru.
From him was born the son of Jahnu, who established a position equal to his father's.
From him was born Suratha, who held a position equal to his father;
Vidūratha was his son, who held a position equal to his father;
Sārvabhauma was his son, who held a position equal to his father.
Jayasena was his son; he established a position equal to that of his father.
From him, this ocean itself established a position equal to that of his father;
and reaching as far as the four oceans, it established a position equal to that of his father.
Ayutāyu was his son; he ruled the kingdom for ten thousand years.
Akrodhana was his son, who attained a station equal to his father's.
From him was born a son named Ṛkṣa, who likewise attained a station equal to his father's.
Bhīmasena was his son; he attained a station equal to that of his father.
Dilīpa was his son; he attained a station equal to that of his father.
Pratīpa was his son; he ruled the kingdom for five thousand years.
His son Śaṃtanu ruled the kingdom for one thousand years;
his son Vicitravīrya ruled for two hundred years;
and his son Pāṇḍu held the sovereignty for five hundred years.
His son Yudhiṣṭhira ruled the kingdom for fifty years;
after that, Suyodhana held the sovereignty for sixty years.
Subsequently, his death was met by Yudhiṣṭhira on the field of the Kurus.
In a former war between the gods and the asuras, those daityas who were slain by the gods all took birth during the reign of King Śantanu;
their army consisted of one hundred thousand akṣauhiṇīs, and by their weight, the earth was oppressed.
Having obtained the refuge of Śakra and then that of Hari,
he entered into the womb of Devakī through the birth of Vasudeva’s son, Śauri.
Thus Kṛṣṇa, of great prowess, went to the abode of Rohiṇī.
Having dwelt upon the earth for one hundred and thirty-five years,
Kṛṣṇacandra then departed for Goloka;
the birth of Hari is recorded by the wise as occurring at the conclusion of the fourth millennium.
Then Abhimanyu’s son reigned in the midst of Hastināpura for one thousand years; after him came Janamejaya,
who ruled for three thousand years, and then Śatānīka became king.
Then his son Yajñadatta ruled a kingdom equal to that of his father; thereafter, his son Niścakra ruled for five thousand years. Then his son Uṣṭrapāla ruled for one thousand years.
Citraratha was his son, who ruled a kingdom equal to that of his father;
Dhṛtimat was his son, who likewise ruled a kingdom equal to that of his father;
and Suṣeṇa was his son, who also ruled a kingdom equal to that of his father.
Sunītha became the son who ruled the kingdom equal to his father;
Makhapāla became the son who ruled the kingdom equal to his father;
thereafter, Nacakṣu became the son who ruled the kingdom equal to his father.
The kingdom was governed like that of his father, and consequently, it became prosperous;
because the kingdom was governed like that of his father, Pāriplava was born as his son;
the kingdom was governed like that of his father, and Sunaya was born as his son.
Medhāvin became his son, who ruled the kingdom equal to his father;
from him was born Nṛpañjaya, who ruled the kingdom equal to his father;
Mṛdu became his son, who ruled the kingdom equal to his father.
Tigmajyotis ruled a kingdom equal to his father’s;
from him was born Bṛhadratha, who likewise ruled a kingdom equal to his father’s;
from him Vasudāna arose, who also ruled a kingdom equal to his father’s.
The kingdom was ruled by Śatānīka as equally as by his father;
because he ruled the kingdom as equally as his father, he is called Udyāna.
Because he ruled the kingdom as equally as his father, Ahīnara was indeed born from him.
His son was Nirmithra, who ruled the kingdom equal to his father;
his son was Kṣemaka, who likewise ruled the kingdom equal to his father.
Having renounced the kingdom, that wise man took refuge in the village of Kalāpa.
Having met his death at the hands of the Mlecchas, he departed from here to the realm of Yama.
Then, by the instruction of Nārada, his son Pradyota performed a sacrifice for the Mlecchas,
and consequently, the slaughter of the Mlecchas ensued.

Thus ends the third chapter in the *Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the *Pratisarga Parvan*, in the section known as the *Caturyuga Khaṇḍa*, specifically the narrative concerning the kings of the Dvāpara age,
titled "The Description of the Narratives of the Kings of the Dvāpara Yuga.
Śaunaka said:
"O wise one, how was the sacrifice performed by that Pradyota?
O dear father, O great sage who knows the three periods of time, tell me everything.
Sūta said:
Once, while Pradyota, the son of Kṣemaka, was seated in the midst of a discourse in Hastināpura, Nārada arrived there.
Seeing him, the king, who was knowledgeable in dharma, was filled with joy and honored him.
Seated comfortably, that sage said to King Pradyota:
"Your father was slain by the Mlecchas and has therefore gone to the realm of Yama;
yet, by the power of the Mleccha sacrifice, he shall indeed attain the path to heaven."
Having heard that, his eyes copper-red with anger, he summoned Brahmins who were most learned in the Vedas to Kurukṣetra and commenced a sacrifice for the Mlecchas;
the sacrificial pit was four-cornered and sixteen yojanas in extent.
Having performed the ritual preparation and meditated upon the deities, the king should offer oblations to the Mlecchas:
the Hārahūṇas, the Barbaras, the Guruṇḍas, the Śakas, the Khasas,
the Yavanas, the Pallavas, those born of wool, and those produced from donkeys.
Having summoned those dwelling on the islands— such as the inhabitants of Kāmarūpa and China who reside in the midst of the ocean—
he reduced them to ashes by the power of Vedic mantras;
then, having given sacrificial fees to the Brāhmaṇas, he performed his consecration.
The king named Kṣemaka then departed for the heavenly world; his renowned title on earth was "Slayer of Mlecchas. That high-souled one ruled the kingdom for ten thousand years.
Having gone to the heavenly world, his son, known as Vedavān, ruled for two thousand years; then Kali himself became a Mleccha. Having worshipped Nārāyaṇa, he then offered this divine hymn of praise:
Kali said:
Salutations to the infinite and great one, who sets all time in motion;
salutations to you, Vāsudeva, the witness and creator of the four ages.
Salutations to you, O Hari, for your ten incarnations; salutations again and again.
Salutations to you, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, who have descended as powers (śakti);
salutations to the Great One who assumed the form of the Fish and dwelt in the depths of the ocean.
Obeisance to the one who has descended out of devotion and dwells in the field of the kalpa.
O Lord, my abode has been destroyed by King Vedavatā;
the lineage of that Mleccha, who was dear to me, has been destroyed by his father.
Sūta said:
Thus praised by Kali along with the wife of the Mleccha,
the Lord Hari himself, who is affectionate toward his devotees, appeared in person.
That Hari spoke to Kali: "For your sake, having assumed many forms, I shall fulfill your desire by creating an excellent age. There will be a man named Ādama, and his wife will be Havyavatī."
Born from the mire of Viṣṇu, they were the increasers of the Mleccha lineage; Hari then vanished there, and Kali, filled with joy,
reached Mount Nīlācala and dwelt there for some time.
A son was born to Vedavat, a king named Sunanda;
having ruled a kingdom equal to his father's, he died childless.
The lands of the Āryas became depleted, while the Mleccha lineages grew powerful.
"O best of the Bhṛgus, they will come to pass; therefore, having gone to the Snowy Mountain and propitiated Viṣṇu, we shall go to the abode of Hari.
Having heard this, all the twice-born residents of the Naimiṣa forest [acted accordingly].
Those eighty-eight thousand went to the Snowy Mountain;
having reached Viśālā, they recited the hymn to Viṣṇu.
Thus was the speech spoken by Vyāsa, who is skilled in the Kali age.
Having fixed his mind upon the listener, he proclaimed what was to come.
Vyāsa said:
"O Sūta, listen then to the verses concerning the future as they were described by you."
Having heard that completion of the Kali age, bring satisfaction.
Sūta said:
When sixteen thousand years remained of that Dvāpara age...
The land of the Ārya country is celebrated as being of great renown.
In some places Brāhmaṇas are remembered as rulers; in some places they are born of the Rājanya lineage;
in some places Vaiśyas, in some Śūdras, and in others, those of mixed castes.
In the Dvāpara Yuga, when two thousand and eight hundred years remain,
there will be a land of the Mlecchas known as Kīrtimālinī. There, he who has subdued his senses and is devoted to meditation on the Self [shall dwell].

Therefore, she is remembered as the wife Ādamanāmā, the bearer of oblations. To the east of the city of Pradāna, there is a beautiful great forest created by Īśvara, which is said to be four krośas in extent.
Having gone to the foot of a wicked tree, intent on seeing his wife,
Kali arrived there quickly, having indeed assumed the form of a serpent. Deceived by that rogue, the command of Viṣṇu was violated.
Having eaten that delightful fruit which bestows the path to the higher worlds,
the husband [the father] and his two wives subsisted on the leaves of the udumbara tree;
from them were born sons, all of whom became Mlecchas.
His lifespan is proclaimed to be nine hundred and thirty years.
Performing oblations of fruits together with his wife, he ascended to heaven.
From him was born an excellent son, renowned by the name Śveta.
His lifespan is proclaimed to be one hundred and twelve years.
Anuhasta’s son established a realm diminished by one hundred [years].
Kīnāśa was his son, and he attained a status equal to that of his grandfather.
Mahalla was his son; he ruled the kingdom there for one hundred and nine years minus five, and because of that, it is known as Mānagara.
From him Virada was born, who ruled the kingdom for sixty years.
It should be known that he had nine hundred cities built after his own name.
His son was Hanūka, who was devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu;
performing oblations with fruits, he was indeed always victorious through the truth.
It is recorded that he ruled the kingdom for three hundred and sixty-five years;
devoted to the religion of the Mlecchas, he ascended to heaven while still in his physical body.
Right conduct, discernment, the status of the twice-born, and the worship of the gods—[these were abandoned].

These [practices] were indeed established by him alone; therefore, they are called *mlecchas* by the wise. For devotion to Viṣṇu, worship of fire, non-violence, austerity, and self-restraint—these very virtues have been declared for the *mlecchas* by the sages.
Matocchila was his son; he was a Bhārgava of the lineage of Hanu.
His reign is recorded as lasting nine hundred and seventy years.
Lomaka was his son, and his reign lasted seven hundred years.
Seventy-seven years after that, he passed away to heaven. From him was born a son named Nyūha; he indeed emerged as Tūha.
Therefore, he is remembered by the wise as Nyūha, and he ruled the kingdom for five hundred years.
Sīma, Śama, and Bhāva were his three sons.
Nyūha was known as a devotee of Viṣṇu; he was I myself, devoted to meditation. Once, the Lord Viṣṇu appeared to him in a dream.
"O child Nyūha, listen to this: on the seventh day, the dissolution shall occur.
You must quickly board a boat together with the people and sustain life among the devotees; you shall become the most excellent of all."
Thinking "so be it," that sage constructed a well-nourished boat,
three hundred cubits in length, fifty cubits in width,
and thirty cubits in height— charming and equipped with all kinds of living beings.
Having ascended together with his kinsmen, he became intent on meditating upon Viṣṇu. Accompanied by Mahendra, the host of clouds known as Sāṃvartaka caused a great rain for exactly forty days.
Having flooded the entire land of Bhārata with their waters,
all four rivers met at Viśālā, yet they did not enter it;
there, eighty-eight thousand sages who were exponents of the Veda resided.
Nyūha, along with his kinsmen, and all the rest were destroyed.
Then all the sages praised the illusory power (māyā) of Viṣṇu.
The sages said:
Salutations to the Goddess Mahākālī, and repeated salutations to Devakī;
salutations to Mahālakṣmī, the mother of Viṣṇu, and to Goddess Rādhā;
salutations to Revatī, Puṣpavatī, and Svarṇavatī.

Salutations to Kāmākṣā and Māyā; salutations again and again to the Mother. Indeed, through the power of a great wind and the roar of a massive cloud, a terrible fear arose from the fierce torrents of rain.
"Therefore, O Bhairavī, protect us, your servants, from this fear.
Then that goddess became pleased, and by her the water was made calm. Within a year, the entire earth appeared, having become dry land.
Far off from there are the slopes of the mountain named Śiśira;
having ascended a palanquin with his own kinsmen, he remains stationed there,
and reaching the land at the edge of the water, he makes his dwelling there.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Kings of the Dvāpara Age," within the Caturyugakhaṇḍa (also known as the Pratisargaparvan) of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa;
followed by the description of the narrative of the kings of the Kali Yuga. Śaunaka said:
"O Lord of Sages, that which indeed exists now at the end of the dissolution has been known through the power of divine vision; tell me what follows after that.
Sūta said:
A barbarian named Nyūha, who was known as Viṣṇumoha, then brought about delusion;
at that time, the Blessed One was pleased, and his lineage flourished. He created a barbarian language that was turned away from the words of the Vedas.

For the sake of increasing the usage of the Vedic language (brāhmī bhāṣā) and for the purpose of excluding corrupt words (apaśabda), the Lord himself— the master of intellect and the abode of wisdom— composed the *Nyāsa*. Furthermore, he indeed reversed the name of his three sons by means of that *Nyāsa*.
Sima, Hama, and likewise the one renowned by the name Yaqut;
Yaqut had seven sons:
Jumra, Mājuja, Mādī, Yūnān, Tūbal, and Masak.
Likewise, their regions are designated by those names:
Jumra, Daśaka, Nabha, Riphat, and Tajjruma;
and the regions known by those names are remembered as the lands belonging to the sons who are traditionally called the Yūnas and others.
Ilīśa and Taralīśa are said to be Kittīhūda;
these regions were assigned to them by their four names.
From the second son, Dhāman, there were exactly four sons.
Kuśa, Miśra, Kūja, and Kana—by these names the regions of the Mlecchas are well known; six sons are recorded as having descended from Kuśa:
Sa-vā, Havīla, and likewise Sarvatorama.
Likewise, there was one named Savatikā, the daughter of Nirmarūha, who possessed great strength; their sons were Kalana, Siṃnāra,
and Uruka, as well as Akkada and Vāvuna, who were the lords of Rasā.
Having caused the sages to hear this, the Sūta fell under the power of yogic sleep.
After two thousand one hundred years had passed, having regained consciousness, he spoke again:
"I shall now proclaim the lineage of Siṃha; that King Siṃha was the eldest."
That Mleccha reigned for five hundred years; his son Arkansada held the kingdom for thirty-four years. Furthermore, it should be known that Siṃha was his son and reigned for four hundred years.
His reign there is recorded as four hundred and sixty years.
His son should be known as Vṛtasa, who occupied a position equal to his father.
His son was Phalaja, whose reign lasted one hundred and forty-two years.
The kingdom was ruled by him, and from him a son named Raū is remembered;
his reign is proclaimed to have lasted two hundred and thirty-seven years. From him Jūja was born, who established a position equal to that of his father.
Nahusha was his son; he ruled the kingdom for one hundred and sixty years, destroying many enemies.
Tāhura was his son, who occupied the position equal to that of his father.
From him were born three sons: Avirāma, Nahūṣa, and Hārana.
Thus their lineages are remembered; they have been mentioned here by name alone.
Due to the curse of Sarasvatī, they became speakers of the most base Mleccha languages.
Their growth during the Kali age has been proclaimed in brief. Let it be understood that the land of Bhārata is the domain of the Sanskrit language alone;
yet that very same language has spread to other continents, where the Mlecchas indeed rejoice in it.
"Thus, O Brahmin, it has been told to you along with the devotees of Viṣṇu.
Vyāsa said:
"Having heard that, all the sages dwelling in Viśālā..."
Having worshipped the divine Nara-Nārāyaṇa with humility,
they performed meditation with joy for two hundred years.
Thereafter, all those lords of sages, headed by Śaunaka, were awakened.
Having performed their twilight prayers, water-libations, and worship of the gods, and having meditated upon Janārdana,
they approached Lomaharṣaṇa as he sat there and questioned him with great humility:
"O fortunate disciple of Vyāsa, O high-minded one, may you live long!"
"Tell me, O Lord, who is indeed the king reigning at present?
Sūta said:
"O descendant of Bhṛgu, when three thousand years of the Kali age have elapsed..."
In Āvantī, that king named Śaṅkha currently reigns;
meanwhile, in the land of the Mlecchas, the Lord of the Śakas indeed exercises sovereignty.
Listen to the entire cause of this, and how it has increased for him.
When the Kali age has arrived in the second millennium,
the entire earth will be overrun by barbarian lineages and filled with various foreign paths;
yet, except for Brahmāvarta, the auspicious bank of the Sarasvatī there shall remain.
And there was a barbarian teacher named Mūsha; the world was filled with his doctrines. When the Kali Yuga arrived, the Vedic language for the worship of the gods was lost.
Listen to its characteristics, O Sage: the languages of the barbarians are of four kinds.
Vrajabhāṣā, Mahārāṣṭrī, Yāvanī, and Guruṇḍikā—
these consist of four hundred thousand varieties, as do other languages likewise.
Water is known as *pānīya* and *pānī*, while hunger is called *bhūkṣā* and *bhūkha*.
Water is known as *pānīya*, a wicked speech as *bhāṣā*, and food as *kakkana*.
The sound of a pure sacrifice (*iṣṭi*) is proclaimed as *śuddharava*; the female elephant is *masapāvanī*, and the oblation (*āhuti*) is indeed *āju*, for it gives and it bestows.
*Pitṛpaitāmaha-bhrātā*, *bādaraḥ*, *patiḥ*, and *sā*; likewise, the Yāvanī language has *seti*, and furthermore, *aśvaḥ* becomes *aspah*.
In place of the word *jānu* (knee), there is *jainuh*, and similarly, *saptasindhuḥ*.
Saptahindu and Yāvanī should be known as Guruṇḍikā; on Sunday, during the conjunction (saṃḍa), and in the month of Phālguna, one should know it as Pharvarī;
and Ṣaṣṭi and Siksaṭī are to be known—such is the illustration thereof.

In those seven cities which are considered pure, violence indeed prevails; there dwell robbers, Śabaras, Bhills, and men who are fools, though they claim to abide by the Āryan way. In the lands of the Mlecchas, however, even intelligent men follow the customs of the Mlecchas.
All virtues become vices in the land of the Āryas when they fall under the dominion of Mlecchas;
likewise, a kingdom of Mlecchas is recorded to exist in Bhārata and its islands.
Knowing this, O best of sages, O high-minded one, worship Hari.
Having heard that, all the sages wept profusely.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Kings of the Kali Age," within the section on the Kali Yuga, in the Caturyuga-khaṇḍa (also known as the Pratisarga-parvan) of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*. This concludes the description of the narrative concerning the kings of the Kali Age.
Śaunaka said:
"Tell me the reason why the Mlecchas did not reach Brahmāvarta.
Sūta replied: "Listen to this; it is due to the power of the Sarasvatī."
When the Mlecchas had arrived at that place, there was indeed a twice-born man named Kāśyapa;
when the Kali age reached its thousand-year mark, he descended from heaven by the command of the gods.
His wife was Āryāvatī, and they had ten sons free from blemish.
She obtained them from Kāśyapa; hear their names from me:
the Upādhyāya, the Dīkṣita, the Pāṭhaka, the Śukla, the Miśraka, the Agnihotrī, the Dvivedī, the Trivedī, and the Pāṇḍya.
He was called Caturvedī, and his qualities were remembered as being equal to his name;
among them, Kāśyapa was endowed with all-encompassing knowledge. He, too, reached the Mother of the World, Sarasvatī, in Kaśmīra.
Having performed worship with red flowers and unbroken grains (akṣata),
as well as incense, lamps, and food offerings, accompanied by a handful of flowers, he offered praise.
Kāśyapa said:
O Mother, beloved of Śaṅkara, why is there no compassion for me from you? O Mother of the World, are you not the Mother of the Universe; why do you not come to my aid?
O Goddess, for the sake of the gods, you swiftly slay even one who is hostile to dharma, O Mother!
"O Mother, you who possess manifold forms, quickly transform this into the supreme Sanskrit language and delude the barbarians; by the sound 'Hum,' you laugh at Dhūmralocana,
and having slain the terrifying Daitya Durgama, you bring happiness to the worlds."
Having destroyed hypocrisy, delusion, and terrible pride, you always remain in bliss;
O Mother, awaken the wicked of the world and do indeed destroy them.
Then that Goddess became pleased in the mind of that sage.
Having stayed there, the sage went to the land of Miśra and bestowed knowledge upon it;
having deluded all the Mlecchas and then made them twice-born,
he established a multitude of ten thousand twice-born men.
Two thousand were known as Vaiśyas, and the remainder were known as the sons of Śūdras.
Together with them, that best of sages, ever devoted to the duties of a muni, dwelt in the Ārya country by the grace of Sarasvatī.
Due to the boon granted by the Goddess, there was a great increase in those noble assemblies; four crores of men and women were born,
along with their sons and grandsons, and their king was the sage Kāśyapa.
His reign is proclaimed to last for one hundred and twenty years. In the region known as Rājyaputra, there were eight thousand Śūdras;
their king was Āryapṛthu, from whom that Māgadha was born.
Having consecrated his son named Māgadha, the sage departed.
Hearing this, Śaunaka, the best of the Bhṛgus, was filled with joy;
bowing to the Sūta, the knower of the Purāṇas, he became intent on meditation upon Viṣṇu.
And again, at the conclusion of the shower of sacred knowledge, the sages were thus enlightened;
having performed their obligatory and occasional rites, they asked this with reverence:
"O Lomaharṣaṇa, tell us, who were the kings of Magadha?"
"O disciple of Vyāsa, tell us who established the kingdom during the Kali age.
Sūta said:
"In the land of Māgadha, the son of Kaśyapa attained [the throne] as the Māgadha king."
The kingdom of the Pitṛs is remembered as such by him, while the Āryadeśa is distinguished separately.
To the east of Pāñcāla is the region celebrated as Māgadha;
in the south-eastern direction is Kaliṅga, and likewise Avanti is in the south.
The country of Ānarta is in the southwest; the country of Sindh is in the west;
the country of Kaikeya is in the northwest; and likewise the country of Madra is in the north. In the northeast is Koṇinda, and that is what constitutes the Āryadeśa.
The sons of that great-souled Magadha were known by the name Deśa;
after they had been granted their respective portions,
Balabhadra then performed a sacrifice, and being purified by the spirit of the sacrifice, he was filled with joy.
Śiśunāga was born from the sacrifice, originating from a portion of Balabhadra;
he ruled the kingdom for one hundred years, and his son was Kākavarma.
His reign lasted ninety years, after which Kṣemadharmā came to power.
His son was Tatkṣetraujas, who ruled for eighty years. Then came Vedamiśra, whose reign lasted ten years less than that;
after him, his son Ajātaripu ruled for ten years less than his predecessor.
Daśahīna ruled the kingdom, and his son was Darbhaka; Daśahīna ruled the kingdom, and from him Udayāśva arose;
Daśahīna ruled the kingdom, and Nandavardhana was indeed his [successor].
The kingdom was lost for ten years; therefore, the son of Nanda became king.
Born from the womb of a Śūdra woman, he ruled a kingdom equal to that of his father.
And Pranaṇda, born from Nanda, held the throne for ten years.
From him was born Parānanda, who held the office equal to his father’s;
from him was born Samānanda, who held the office for twenty years;
from him was born Priyānanda, who held the office equal to his father’s.
Devānanda was his son; he occupied a position equal to that of his father.
Yajñabhaṅga was his son; he occupied a position half that of his father.
Mauryānanda was his son; he occupied a position equal to that of his father.
Then great joy arose, for a position equal to that of his father was attained.
At that very time, Hari was remembered by Kali;
the god born from Kaśyapa became renowned by the name Gautama.
Having established the Buddha-dharma, Hari arrived in the city;
he ruled for ten years, and therefore he is remembered as Śākyamuni.
He ruled for twenty years, and therefore he became Śuddhodana.
The Śākya-siṃha then reigned for thirty years;
he became king two thousand one hundred years after [the Buddha’s passing].
During the first quarter of the Kali age, the Vedic path was destroyed.
He ruled for sixty years; all men were known as Buddhists.
As the king among men was Viṣṇu, so were his subjects.
In accordance with the power of Viṣṇu, the dharma of the world proceeded.
Those men who have sought refuge in that Hari, the Lord of Māyā—
even those of sinful conduct— are proclaimed to possess liberation.
From Śakya-siṃha came Buddha-siṃha, who established the path for the sake of his father.
Candragupta, the son of that lord of the Pauras,
having likewise married the daughter of Sulūva and being devoted to the Greek and Buddhist doctrines,
ruled for sixty years; after him, Bindusāra became king.
The son Aśoka became king, having made his kingdom equal to that of his father.
At that very time, however, an excellent Brahmin from Kānyakubja,
having reached Mount Arbuda, performed a Brahma-homa sacrifice.
And by the power of Vedic mantras, four Kṣatriyas were born:
Pramara, who was a knower of the Sāmaveda; Capahāni, a knower of the Yajurveda; Trivedī, as well as Śukla; and Utharvā, who was a Parihāraka.
Having mounted separate elephants born in the lineage of Airāvata,
they all brought Aśoka under their own control;
the four hundred thousand Buddhists were remembered as having been struck down by divine weapons.
"In Avanti, King Pramara, having occupied the city named Ambāvatī, which was four yojanas in extent, lived in happiness.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Kings of the Kali Age," within the section on the Kali Yuga, in the Caturyuga-khaṇḍa (also known as the Pratisarga-parvan) of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
In the region of Citrakūṭa mountain, there was a king named Parihāra; his delightful city, Kaliñjara-pura, is remembered as being one krośa in extent.
Having attained the Buddhist state of selflessness (*bauddha-ahaṃtā*), he became powerful and happy.
And in the country called Rājaputra, there was a king named Capahāni;
[he ruled] the beautiful city of Ajmer, endowed with the splendor of divine order.
Having occupied that divine realm inhabited by the four castes, he became happy.
The king named Śukla went to the region of Ānarta;
having occupied the city named Dvārakā, he became happy.
Śaunaka said:
"O highly fortunate one, tell me of those kings who were honored with sovereignty among those born from the fire. Then Sūta spoke these words:
"Go, all you Brahmins, for I am indeed under the influence of yogic sleep.
Having heard that, all the sages performed meditation upon Viṣṇu.
When two thousand years were complete, the Sūta spoke these words:
In the Kali age, when seven hundred and ten years had passed,
a king named Pramara ruled for six years;
thereafter, Mahāmada arose and took possession of half his father's realm.
Devāpi’s son attained a station equal to that of his father;
Devadūta was his son, and his station is remembered as being equal to his father's. From him came Gandharvasena, who held the kingship for fifty years.
Having installed his son Śaṅkha on the throne, he departed for the forest.
Śaṅkha attained that position and ruled the kingdom for thirty years.
At that time, Vīramatī, a celestial nymph, was sent by Śakra.
Having approached Gandharvasena, he begot a jewel of a son.
At the time of the son's birth, showers of flowers fell from the sky,
kettledrums resounded, and pleasant breezes blew.

A twice-born man named Śivadṛṣṭi went to the forest with twenty disciples; having fully accomplished Karmayoga, he became Śiva. When three hundred years had elapsed and the terrifying Kali age had arrived.
For the sake of destroying the Śakas and for the increase of the noble Dharma,
he was born by the command of Śiva from Kailāsa, the abode of the Guhyakas;
having given him the name Vikramāditya, his father rejoiced.
Though but a child, he was possessed of great wisdom and acted for the pleasure of his father and mother;
when he reached the age of five years, he went to the forest for the sake of asceticism,
and there he performed penance with diligence and valor for twelve years.
Afterwards, endowed with splendor, he went to the divine city of Ambāvatī.
There he accepted that beautiful, divine throne, accompanied by thirty-two forms,
which had been sent to him by Śiva.
A Vaitāla was created by Pārvatī for his protection and departed.
Once, that heroic king went to the sacred site of Mahākāleśvara and worshipped the God of gods, the wielder of the Pināka bow.
There, an assembly hall composed of dharma was manifested, vast in its array;
it had pillars fashioned from various elements, adorned with diverse jewels,
filled with various trees and creepers, and provided with flowering vines.
There, O Śaunaka, he had a divine lion-throne placed;
having summoned the chief Brāhmaṇas who were masters of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences,
and having honored them according to the prescribed rites, he then listened to the verses on Dharma.
In the meantime, a deity named Vaitāla,
having assumed the form of a Brahmin and praised him with blessings of victory,
sat upon a seat and spoke thus to the king:
"O King Vikramāditya, if you have faith in hearing it,
I shall describe this great narrative, a compendium of ancient histories.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Kings of the Solar and Lunar Dynasties Born in the Kali Age," in the Caturyuga-khaṇḍa (also known as the Pratisarga-parvan) of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Thus ends the first section.
Om. Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
Sūta said:
Thus addressed, the Vaitāla residing at Mahākāleśvara fixed Śiva in his mind and spoke these words to the king:
"O King Vikramāditya, listen to this enchanting verse."
The city of Vārāṇasī is delightful, where Maheśa resides;
there the subjects consist of the four castes, and King Pratāpamukuṭa rules,
whose queen, the Mahādevī, is devoted to dharma.

His son was Vajramukuṭa, and the sons of the ministers were dear to him like their own children. Then, when he reached his sixteenth year, he went to the forest mounted upon a horse. And there was also the son of a minister, known as Buddhidakṣa.
Mounted on a horse, he went into the forest together with a companion of his own age;
seeing that delightful grove filled with deer and birds,
Vajramukuṭa rejoiced, having fallen under the sway of desire.
There, on its bank, was a divine and beautiful lake resounding with the cries of various birds,
and a sacred abode of Śiva worshipped by throngs of sages;
seeing it, the two heroes went there and attained supreme bliss.
In the meantime, O King, there was the daughter of Dantavakra, the ruler of Karanaṭaka, known by the name Padmāvatī;
she was a passionate woman who could assume any form at will, and she paid homage to Kāmadeva.
The beautiful girl played with her companions in the middle of the lake;
at that time, Vajramukuṭa came out from his palace and saw the young Padmāvatī, who was endowed with equal beauty and virtues.
Having seen her, he indeed fainted and fell upon the ground; she too lost consciousness. Then Vajramukuṭa, regaining his senses, cried out, "Save me, O Śiva, O Śaṅkara!
Having spoken thus, the king's son looked once more at the young girl.
Taking the lotus flower from his head, she placed it upon her ears;
then, holding it again at her feet, she bit it with her teeth. Taking that flower once more, she pressed it against her heart.
Having formed this intention, she went home together with her friends;
meanwhile, having arrived at the forest of Girijā with her father for the sake of visiting sacred sites,
the king was tormented by the arrows of Māra when she had departed.
Having experienced great mental anguish and fallen into a state of delusion,
he became like one possessed; thereafter, abstaining from food and drink,
he meditated upon the young Padmāvatī and undertook a vow of silence.

Then a great clamor arose near Pratāpamukuṭa, with cries of "Alas! Alas! from all sides, as to what state the prince had fallen into. At the end of three days, the minister’s son, who was clever and learned, appeared.
He said to Vajramukuṭa, "O King, tell the truth.
He related the entire cause of what had occurred at the lake. Having heard that, the king, who was skilled in discernment, spoke to the monarch:
With great difficulty, that queen will indeed become your friend;
she is the daughter of Dantavaktra, the king of Karṇāṭaka,
renowned as Padmāvatī, who holds you within her heart.
"Having recognized you by means of your flower-form, I shall lead you to his presence.
Having said this to his father, Pratāpamukuṭa, he said, "O King, give me your permission; I shall go to Kāraṇāṭaka for that purpose."
"If you restore your son to life, that Indra-crowned one will come here before long for the sake of treating your son; there is no doubt in this.
Thinking "So be it," the king gave his son to the minister.
Mounted on horses, they went swiftly to the city of Dantavaktra. An old woman was staying there, and they went to her house;
the wise and learned one, skilled in intellect, gave her much wealth.
They spent that night, shrouded in thick darkness, in that palace.
At dawn, as the old woman was going toward the royal palace, the minister’s son said to her, "Listen, mother, to my words."
And having reached Padmāvatī, speak my words to her in private:
"On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, on a Monday, at the lake,
a beautiful man was seen who has come for your sake."

Having heard this, the old woman departed and reported it to Padma. Enraged, Padmāvatī, whose finger-ring was wet with sandalwood paste, said, "Go, go, O great villainess! and struck her on the chest with her palm.

Having touched her cheeks with his fingers, he went home; that old woman, however, reported the entire situation to him, who was skilled in discernment. To him, who was distressed along with his friend, she said: "Listen, my friend, abandon your grief."
"The daughter of the king says to you: 'O dear one as my own life, listen to these words!
When will my chest, which was struck for your sake, become a friend to you?
Having heard those sweet words, Rajas entered his body."
"O friend, at the end of my menses, I kissed your mouth.
Upon hearing this, the prince experienced supreme bliss. Then, at the end of three days, that old woman reported it to Padmāvatī.
"That king is eager for you, longing for a sight of you;
resort to him today, O fair-hipped one, and make your life fruitful.
Hearing this, she was greatly delighted and [offered] a fish-scale-engraved ring.
Having been cast out through the window and beaten on the ground and on her back,
the old woman approached that minister and spoke these words:
"O friend, you who are gracious and skilled in intellect, listen to what I say."
"O Lord, a window has been constructed for you in the western direction;
having arrived there at midnight, enjoy me while I am overwhelmed by desire.
Hearing this, Vajramukuṭa became eager for the sight of his beloved.

Greatly desirous, he went quickly and delighted that beautiful woman. At the end of the month, his passion having subsided and longing to see his friend, he said to his beloved Padmāvatī: "Listen to my words, O fair-faced one."
O fair-browed one, that friend through whom you—so difficult even for the gods to attain—were obtained by me, and he who is so skilled in counsel, where indeed does he stay now?
Give me your command, my beloved; having seen him, I shall come to your side.
Having heard those harsh words of his, which were like a thunderbolt,
she prepared poisoned sweet food and presented it to the minister.
At that time, however, the one skilled in intellect and the worshiper of Citragupta—
Having understood the entire cause of that matter, he did not eat it himself.
In the meantime, the king arrived with great haste;
seeing his discerning friend, he spoke to him with indignation:
"Why, my friend, did you not eat this food prepared by my beloved?
Laughing, the one skilled in intellect gave it to the dog;
having eaten it, the dog met his death. Seeing this, the king was struck with amazement.
Having understood the conduct of women and having abandoned his affection, he said to him:
"Friend, go home quickly; that sinful woman has been abandoned by me. He replied: "Listen, O King, go quickly to the presence of your beloved."
"Taking that ornament, fashion a trident upon your knee;
abandon her while she sleeps, O friend—do not hesitate!
Having heard this, the king went away, did as he was told, and returned.
Accompanied by his own friend, he went to the cremation ground at the temple of Rudra;
having made that king his disciple, that wise one, appearing in the form of a yogin, gave him to his friend as a piece of jewelry for sale.
Thinking it was his command, Vajramukuṭa went to the city;
but the king's guards, perceiving him to be a thief, bound him and quickly reported it. Dantavaktra then spoke to him.
"O man, tell me where you obtained all these beautiful ornaments.
The matted-haired ascetic replied, "O King, my guru was staying in a cremation ground;
he gave me these gold-plated ornaments for the purpose of selling them."
Having heard this, the king quickly summoned his preceptor Bhūṣaṇa and questioned him; the yogi said, "Listen, O King!
While in the form of a yogi, I performed a mantra-concentration in the cremation ground."
A certain Piśācī was brought before him, and I made a mark upon her;
she indeed gave me an ornament of a trident upon my left knee.
Having learned the cause of that, the king banished his daughter from the house.
Taking her, he who wore a crown of vajras returned home.
Laughing, the Vetāla said: "Listen, King Vikrama!
Tell me now, which among these four has incurred great sin?"
Sūta said:
Having heard these words of his,
the king named Vikrama laughed and said to Bhārgava, "Indeed, sin has overtaken this king."
The minister performed the duty of a friend and the guards performed the duty of their master;
however, O King, Arthasiddha acted as a son toward the monarch. Consequently, he incurred great sin for the king and, because of that, he went to hell.
The man who, upon seeing the daughter Rajovatī, does not marry her,
goes to hell as a sinner for sixty thousand years;
so too does he who performs a Gāndharva marriage with a lustful woman.
He who indeed creates an obstacle for her is a sinner afflicted by Yama;
he who abandons a girl who has no visible fault, without due discernment,
that sinner goes to hell for a duration of one hundred thousand years.

Having heard this verse on dharma uttered by the king, that Vaitāla, with a gladdened heart, spoke to the monarch who was intent upon righteousness. Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Caturyuga-khaṇḍa" (also known as the Pratisarga-parvan), in the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
To the king, who was seated upon the great throne with a tranquil mind,
that best of the twice-born, the Vaitāla, spoke these words with a serene intellect.
Once, on the bank of the Yamunā, there was the auspicious city of Dharmasthalapura,
endowed with wealth and grain and inhabited by the four castes.
There, King Guṇādhipa indeed ruled the kingdom.
The family priest was Hariśarman, who was devoted to ritual bathing and worship;
his wife was Suśīlā, dedicated to her husband;
and a son named Satyaśīla was born, intent upon the study of sacred knowledge.
His younger sister was Madhumatī, endowed with virtue, beauty, and excellent qualities.
When she reached the age of twelve, her father began to wander about for the sake of her marriage,
searching everywhere for a suitable husband for his daughter.
Once, O King, when the prince’s marriage was about to take place,
the twice-born Sattvaśīla went himself to Kāśī for the purpose of study.
In the meantime, another certain twice-born man arrived there.
There was a man renowned by the name Vāmana, endowed with beauty, virtue, and youth;
and upon seeing him, his daughter Madhumatī became afflicted by love.
Distraught, she abandoned food, clothing, drink, and sleep.
Like a female cakora bird distressed by the arrows of love in the absence of the moon,
the young Suśīlā, seeing that dwarfed brahmin,
restrained him with betel leaves accompanied by gifts of gold.
Then Hariśarman, seeing the twice-born Trivikrama—
who was a knower of the truth of the Vedas and Vedānta— in the course of his practice, chose him for the sake of his daughter.
Satyaśīla, however, [chose] Keśava, the son of his preceptor, in Kāśī.
Having chosen him for the sake of his sister, he went home filled with joy.
On the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha, under the planet Venus, an auspicious lagna was prescribed.
At that time, three Brahmins arrived, infatuated by the girl's beauty, seeking her hand in marriage.
At that time, however, that maiden was bitten by a serpent;
she died and, through the power of her past karma, fell into the state of a preta.
Then those brahmins made a supreme effort.
The young girl did not die; she was merely rendered unconscious by the poison.
O King, having performed all those rites according to Vedic injunctions, Hariśarman, infatuated by his daughter's virtues, returned to his home.
Trivikrama, however, having experienced manifold suffering under the sway of love,
became a mendicant carrying a patched garment and wandered from country to country.
Keśava, too, being deeply distressed, took up the bones of his beloved.
Having gone from one sacred ford to another, tormented by the arrows of desire,
Vāmana— clinging to ashes and consumed by the fire of separation—
stood upon the funeral pyre, afflicted by love and intent on meditating upon his wife.
Once, on the bank of the Sarayū at the auspicious city named Lakṣmaṇapura,
Trivikrama arrived at the house of a twice-born for the sake of alms. On that day, Rāmaśarman was entirely devoted to meditation upon Śiva.
O King, she invited the ascetic to her own home for a meal. His wife, Viśālākṣī, having prepared a great variety of food, summoned the ascetic and, taking his vessel, began to serve him.
At that time, the boy died, having fallen under the power of sin;
his maidservant, though large-eyed and even though she had been rebuked,
did not cease her weeping, tormented as she was by the fire of grief for her son.
Then Rāmaśarman arrived and, having recited the auspicious Saṃjīvana mantra and performed the ritual purification (mārjana), he restored the boy to life; at that time,
the Brahmin bowed down with humility before the ascetic.
Having caused him to eat, Trivikrama gave him the Saṃjīvana mantra; having recited that mantra on the bank of the Yamunā,
he reached the place where that woman had been cremated by Hariśarman.
In the meantime, the prince there had met his death;
yet that son, who had been cremated by his father who was then causing him such grief,
regained life through the power of the king's mantra.
The mighty Vīrabāhu, son of King Guṇādhipa, the lord of Dharmasthalī, spoke these words to Trivikrama:
"You have granted me life; choose now a boon for me."

That Brahmin said: "O King, there is a twice-born man named Keśava who has gone to a sacred ford (tīrtha) taking the bone; seek him out without delay. Vīrabāhu, having understood this, set out toward him by way of the messenger's path.
Having reached him, he related how he had indeed regained his life.
Having heard those words of his, Keśava, accompanied by the bones,
went forth and gave all those bones back to that twice-born man.
Having been restored to life once more, the young woman spoke these words to Keśava and the others:
"I shall bestow myself upon that righteous man who is worthy of me according to dharma.
Having heard her speech, the three remained silent.
"Therefore, O Vikramāditya, knower of dharma, tell me:
to whom is that auspicious girl named Madhumatī suitable?
Sūta said:
Smiling, Vikramāditya, with a humble mind, said to the Vetāla:
"Madhumatī is a worthy wife for the dwarf Brahmin;
as for the Brahmin who gave his life, he is like a father, devoted to virtue."
"But that Brahmin who gives bone [for cremation] is equal to a brother and is a knower of the Vedas.
Thus ends the second chapter in the *Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, in the *Pratisarga Parvan*, in the section titled *Caturyuga Khaṇḍa*, otherwise known as the *Kaliyuga Itihāsa Samuccaya*.
Sūta said:
"O most fortunate best of Brahmins, listen to this delightful verse," said the Vaitāla to the excellent king Vikrama once more:
"In the beautiful city of Vardhamāna, frequented by various people..."
There was a protector of the earth named Rūpasena, possessed of great strength.
His learned wife was Mālā, who was devoted to the service of her husband.
Once, there was a certain Kṣatriya known by the name Vīravara.
Accompanied by his wife, sons, and daughters, he approached King Rūpasena for the sake of a livelihood; bowing low with humility,
he gave a thousand pieces of gold every day, O King, after hearing a little [of the king's fame].
Vīrasena, having obtained that wealth, spent it among the twice-born at the sacred site of Vahni;
then, with what remained, he himself enjoyed it among his kinsmen.
Thus, O King, when a year had passed, the royal fortune [restored] by the command of Śiva.
Wailing loudly in the cremation ground for the sake of testing him, she was heard at midnight; then the king, having learned of this, said to his servant:
"Go, Vīravara, indeed, to where that sound is heard."
"Having understood all the causes of that, report them to me quickly.
Hearing this, the powerful Vīravara, skilled in weapons and missiles,
went there to where the auspicious-faced Rājalakṣmī was staying.
Addressing her with gentle words, he said: "For what reason do you stand weeping?
What great suffering has been encountered? O Queen, tell me the cause.
Having heard this, Rājalakṣmī spoke to that Vīrasena.
"Know me to be the royal fortune of King Rūpasena;
I shall meet my destruction at the end of the month, and for that reason, O powerful one, I grieve.
He said, "Listen, O Goddess, he has been declared by you to have a short life."
"Tell me the cause by what merit you have become long-lived. The Goddess said:
"O mighty-armed one, O highly wise one, if indeed [you wish to know] regarding your son..."
"O sinless one, offer this skull to Caṇḍikā;
I shall become long-lived, so accomplish the task of your master.
Having heard this, Vīravara returned to his own home.
With a serene soul, he said to his wife, "Announce the son to the Queen.
Having replied, "So be it," that virtuous woman spoke fearlessly to her son:
"O son, for the sake of the king, protect your body; indeed, do that."
Having understood this, his son, together with his sister and mother,
went to the temple of Caṇḍikā and then said to his father:
"O father, offer my skull to Caṇḍikā."
"By whatever effort long life and royal fortune are attained, perform that.
Having heard this, Vīrasena cut off his head and offered it;
likewise his younger sister died there, as did his mother and his father.
Having seen that form, Sena explained the entire matter from the beginning;
and considering his servant to be true to his word, he offered up his own head.
Then that goddess, being pleased, restored the king to life and spoke to him.
"Choose a boon, O protector of the earth; you shall quickly obtain whatever you desire.
Vīrasena replied, "May my family live on.
Having said, "So be it," that goddess vanished right there.
Rūpasena, his soul filled with faith, gave his daughter Kāmarūpinī to the son of Vaitāla; then, filled with wonder, the king said to him:
"Tell me, among those [four], by whom was the greatest affection shown?"
The King said:
The King displayed supreme affection by giving his own body for the sake of the servant;
Vīravara was devoted to gold, while Dharmapriyā was devoted to her husband.
The affection for a sister is like that for a kinsman, and a son possesses love for his father;
thus great affection was shown by the wise King Rūpasena.

Thus ends the third chapter in the *Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, in the section on the secondary creation (*pratisargaparvan*), within the collection of histories of the Kali Yuga, which is also known as the *Caturyugakhaṇḍa*.
Sūta said:
Having heard this, the Vaitāla spoke thus to the king:
"There is a most wonderful city named Bhogāvatī."
King Rūpavarman indeed ruled there;
he had a parrot, renowned as Cūḍāmaṇi,
who was expert in intellect and resided in his palace within an auspicious cage.

Once, when Rūpavarman was thirty years old and full of vigor, he asked, "O Śuka, is there indeed any excellent woman suitable for me? If she exists, then tell me. Having heard this, Śuka spoke to him.
"The auspicious Candravatī, daughter of the King of Magadha, is indeed worthy of you, O King; accept her now.
Having heard this, that king [spoke to] Gaṇeśa, the best of the twice-born.
Having sent him forth, he gave the wealth and said, "Act so that she may be wed.
Gaṇeśa also went quickly to the auspicious land of Māgadha;
having worshipped Mahādeva, he joyfully offered a hymn of praise.
Salutations to Śiva, the peaceful one, the bestower of all desired objects;
constant salutations to Bhava, to Śaṅkara, and to Rudra;
salutations to Mṛḍa, whose form is bliss, and the remover of all suffering.
When the Brahmin had spoken thus, the auspicious Candravatī,
afflicted by desire, spoke to her who was named Madanamañjarī:
"There is a certain man on this earth who is worthy of me."
"O, that Rūpavarman would be a worthy lord of Bhogāpurī!
Having heard this, the fair-browed queen mentally praised Goddess Durgā, the bestower of desires, by whom this entire world was brought into being.
Salutations again and again, O Mother of the World, who bestows success upon my endeavors!
You are indeed the mother of the three Lingas, the eternal embodiment of the letters.
You are Svāhā, you are Svadhā, and you are Sandhyā; salutations to her, salutations again and again!
"O auspicious lady, make King Rūpavarman my husband!"—
by this praise, the Mother of the World, who is identical with the universe, became pleased;
she then deluded both her father, the Lord of Magadha, and her mother.
At the end of the month, Siddharūpiṇī caused the marriage to be performed;
Rūpavarmā and Candravatī enjoyed supreme happiness.
One day, O King, [he spoke] to Menā Madanamañjarī.
The king said, "O sir, perform the marriage with Suśuka.
Mṛṇakā replied, "O King, if such marriages are considered [appropriate], then men are traditionally known to be of three kinds: superior, inferior, and middling."
In the same way, there are three kinds of women, corresponding to the type of husband who is suitable for them:
the highest woman for the highest man, and the lowest woman for the lowest man.
Listen, O King, to the reason for this as it was seen by me.
In Ilāpura there lived a wealthy Vaiśya, a lord of a hundred thousand, named Devayājī;
he was childless, and his wife was devoted to her husband.
Through great effort, a son was born to him, but he was exceedingly wicked.
Constantly devoted to gambling, always delighting in the drinking of liquor,
visiting prostitutes, a great rogue, and a wicked man who constantly ate meat—
his parents, having observed his conduct, departed for the forest.
Having meditated upon Nara and Nārāyaṇa, they attained the supreme state.
But the son, Madapāla, having exhausted all his wealth,
departed for another land for the sake of a livelihood, destitute of means.
Having reached the beautiful city of Candrapura, where Hemapati resided,
he related the entire account to the merchant Hemapati:
"I am indeed Devayājī’s son, and I have brought back very little wealth."
Having reached another country by way of the sea for the purpose of selling it,
that wealth was submerged in the water by the force of a great wind;
out of shame for that, O noble one, I shall not go before my father.
Having heard this, Hemapati, with a serene mind, spoke these words to his wife Kāmamañjarī: "By destiny, our union has been ordained.
At your command, I shall give my daughter Candrakānti to her husband."
O King, having consulted together, the couple gave the daughter away according to the prescribed rites;
he caused Madapāla, the husband of his daughter, to dwell in his own home. After staying for one month, he, with a humble mind, spoke to his father-in-law:
"Give me your command, O Lord of Wealth; I shall go to my own home, do not delay.
Having heard this, the Lord of Gold gave him his daughter Candrakānti, adorned with golden ornaments, along with a maidservant, and departed for his home.
O King, having dismissed the men who carried his palanquin, that evil-minded and most base Madapāla then killed his maidservant, abandoned his wife who was destitute of wealth,
and returned home all alone.
And after spending that gold on an evil path during the intervening years,
the king, once again hungry, fell into great sorrow;
then that wicked man returned once more to the house of his father-in-law.
Seeing her husband, Candrakānti, with a humble mind, said to him:
"I informed my father that our wealth had been plundered by thieves;
therefore, abandon your grief and dwell for a long time in my house."

Having said, "So be it," the great rogue lived there for several days. Perceiving that his wife was utterly deluded, he killed her at midnight while everything was shrouded in darkness; taking many ornaments, he departed for his own home.
"Therefore, O King, this marriage between Śuka and this woman is improper.
Hearing this, Śuka spoke to the king, that ocean of compassion:
"I will not enter into marriage with a woman who is so base."
"O King, Menakā is a base woman, dark-limbed and ill-favored;
whereas I am an excellent parrot, and a man, O King, may even cast off his body.
Listen, O Ruler of the Earth, to the reason for this, which I have witnessed as most sublime."
