In the city of Kāñcanapura, there was a merchant known as Śaṅkhapati.
His son was the intelligent, virtuous, and wealthy Sindhugupta.
Prabhāvatī was his beloved wife, and their son is remembered as Śrīdatta.
Śrīdatta performed the marriage of his son with Jayalakṣmī, the daughter of Somadatta, in the auspicious city of Jayaśrī; meanwhile,
Śrīdatta himself went to the land of the Kurus for the purpose of trade.
In the twelfth year, however, he returned home with his wealth;
Jayalakṣmī, meanwhile, afflicted by desire in her father’s house,
was infatuated by Homadatta, the son of the minister.
Having reached him by way of a female messenger and having spent much wealth,
that most wicked woman took her pleasure with him.
At the end of three months, Śrīdatta, her husband, was at his father-in-law’s house.
Having arrived there, she saw him and was overcome with great sorrow. At midnight, sent by her mother toward her husband,
Jayalakṣmī arrived, her lower lip quivering with rage.
Out of great respect, she felt affection for her husband and went to his dwelling;
meanwhile, that unchaste woman went to the house of the messenger.
In that empty dwelling, Homadatta was indeed bitten by a serpent.
Having fallen into a deep sleep as if dead, the young woman then approached and passionately enjoyed herself with her paramour, who was utterly infatuated.
And the piśāca, stationed in the pippala tree, beheld that beautiful woman with her lover.
Having reached the corpse, he enjoyed that beautiful woman;
then, having bitten off her nose with his teeth, he went away to the top of a *pippala* tree.
At that time, a thief named Kaphalla saw him and understood the reason for it.
Becoming a follower of the amorous woman, he entered that palace;
then Jayalakṣmī, having obtained her own husband despite being unfortunate,
wept bitterly, and all the people set out.
Seeing his daughter devoid of a nose, the immensely wealthy Somadatta quickly bound his son-in-law and went before the king;
by the king's command, the royal messengers placed him in fetters.
Then Kaphalla approached and reported everything to the king.
Believing his words to be true, [the king] placed the great goddess Jayalakṣmī upon a donkey, having made her take on the form of a miserable woman.
He dispatched her from the city to the forest inhabited by tigers;
therefore, O protector of the earth, listen: "Menā is indeed not a fit match for me.
Having said this, that Vaitāla, with a humble mind, spoke of Vikrama's valor.
"Whether it be a woman who has committed great sin, or likewise a man, tell me how she may dwell [with you].
Vikrama said:
"She is the form of the Māyā of Brahmā, whose nature is beyond qualities (aguṇa) and whose true form is colorless."
Tamas is not to be known as neuter; it is one in all three genders and is indeclinable.
It is the imperishable abode of Brahman, Māyā, whose nature is that of a sign (liṅga).
By her this entire universe was born; salutations again and again to that Mother!
A eunuch is always superior to a woman, and likewise, a man is superior to a woman;
a man free from disease is considered superior, while a woman is considered superior in action.
Ignorance is declared by the ancient sages to be more debilitating than a eunuch.
Karma alone is the bondage of men; knowledge is remembered as freedom from bondage.

Therefore, a woman has greater sin, while a man has less transgression. Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Compendium of Histories of the Kali Age," in the Caturyuga-khaṇḍa (also known as the Pratisarga-parvan) of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said:
O most excellent and illustrious Bhṛgu, having heard those words, that very Vetāla,
with a serene mind, spoke these words to the king who was rich in wisdom.

O Great King, in Ujjayinī there was a wise king of the Lunar dynasty known as Mahābala, who was an expert in the Vedas and the Śāstras. His messenger was a servant of Hari, always performing the tasks of his master.
Devotion was dear to him, and he was devoted to the service of the virtuous.
From her was born a beautiful lotus-eyed daughter,
renowned as Mahādevī, who was proficient in all branches of knowledge.
And she said to Haridāsa, "Listen, dear father, to my words:
O sir, give me to that man who is indeed superior to me.
Having said, "So be it," O King, the father, summoned by the king, went to the assembly hall.
Having bowed to him, the king said: "O servant of Hari, listen!
Go to Hariścandra, the lord of the earth and sovereign of Telangana.
Having ascertained his well-being, report it to me without delay."
Having heard this, the twice-born went to the high-minded Hariścandra and described the welfare of King Mahābala;
hearing this, King Hariścandra became joyful at heart.
The father-in-law of that king was filled with even greater joy;
he asked Haridāsa, "When will the arrival of Kali occur?
Thus addressed, he said to him, "The calculation will be more than sufficient."
When he had ruled the kingdom, that was the time for the arrival of the Kali age.
From the mouth of this Brahmā was born the syllable Om, honored by the truth;
and from his second mouth arose various languages that delude the world.
She was born for the benefit of the Kali age, desiring the welfare of the realm of Yama;
when the Dharma declared in the Vedas is seen to be inverted,
then the reign of Kali is to be known, wherein Mlecchas are remembered as being beloved.
By Kali, the friend of unrighteousness, all the gods were cast out.
Falsehood alone was the wife of sin, and suffering is recorded as their son. Misfortune was his half-sister; then she would dwell in every house.
All kings are enslaved by anger; Brahmins are servants to their desires;
the wealthy are enslaved by greed; and the Śūdras have attained greatness.
Women are devoid of shame, and servants are killers of their masters.
"When the Kali age has arrived, the earth is indeed seen to have become fruitless;
yet all those who have sought refuge in Hari remain joyful in the Kali age.
Having heard this, Hariścandra gave him a generous sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
The king reached his own home, while the brahmin went to the camp. In the meantime, a brahmin there who was skilled in intellect displayed his own learning to the wise Haridāsa.
The goddess gave him a most excellent, swift-moving celestial chariot named Śīghraga,
which was produced through the recitation of mantras, born of desire, and a source of wonder.
In that chariot, the Brahmin, utterly infatuated, then beheld her for the sake of the maiden.
Having chosen him for his daughter, he then returned to his own city.
There, a learned son of Haridāsa named Mukunda,
having completed his studies, said to his teacher, "Please accept a preceptor’s fee."
The Guru said to that disciple, "Mukunda, listen to my words:
give your own sister to my wise son.
Having said, "So be it," Mukunda quickly went to his own home.

At that time, the Great Queen chose the auspicious Vamana, a twice-born disciple of Drona's son, a Brahmin who could pierce a target by sound alone; she honored him according to the prescribed rites with sacrificial fees, betel, and other offerings.
Three Brahmins, experts in the qualities [of men], arrived there for the sake of the daughter.
In the meantime, a lustful Rākṣasa, deluded by fate,
quickly abducted the Great Queen upon reaching the Vindhya mountain range.
Then, becoming sorrowful and tormented by desire, they lamented.
A wise and learned brahmin named Dhīmān, the best of astrologers, said to them:
"The young girl remains on the Vindhya mountain, destined for a flesh-eater."
Having placed those two brahmins upon his own celestial chariot,
the one skilled in archery, who was proficient in the science of sound, reached Mount Vindhya; there,
having fixed an arrow to his bow, he swiftly slew the rākṣasa with that very shaft.
Taking the maiden, they traveled by celestial chariot to Ujjayinī;
driven by passion and disputing among themselves upon seeing the girl, they said, "O King, please tell us out of grace: to whom would this maiden be suitable?"
Sūta said:
Having heard these words of his, the king named Vikrama,
bowing with humility, spoke to the Vetāla, the servant of Rudra.
The twice-born who, having understood [the situation], spoke regarding the maiden was indeed like a father to her;
he who arrived by means of a celestial chariot (vimāna) is remembered as her brother;
and he who slew the heroic Rākṣasa became truly worthy of the maiden.

Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Pratisarga Parva of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, which is an alternative designation for the Caturyuga Khaṇḍa, specifically the Compendium of Histories of the Kali Yuga.
Sūta said: Again that Vetāla spoke: "Listen, O King, to this story."
In the delightful village of Dharmapura, frequented by various people,
there lived a most excellent king of virtuous character,
O Lord of Men; and Lajjādevī was the queen of that monarch.
His minister, named Andhaka, was an expert in the treatises on logic. After some time, that temple of the Goddess was constructed by Dharmaśīla, and there Durgā was installed.
A great festival was held there by the king for the sake of obtaining offspring.
At midnight, Mahāgaurī said to the king, "O, choose [a boon]!
Hearing those words consisting of nectar, the best of kings, who was devoted to righteousness, [responded].
With a humble soul, he offered praise by which Durgā becomes pleased.
Dharmaśīla said:
"There is indeed one eternal primordial nature (prakṛti) who embodies the forms of all castes."

O Blessed Lady, you are that very one; by you all this is pervaded. By your command, the foremost of gods, having fashioned this supreme world, enjoyed stainless happiness together with you, Mahālakṣmī.
O Eternal One, by your devotion the Lord Viṣṇu protects the three worlds created by Brahmā together with you, O Mahālakṣmī;
and by your power, O Great Goddess, the three worlds are protected by Viṣṇu.
Having reduced Mahākālī along with you to ashes, she shines resplendently;
all the gods, as well as the Daityas, the ancestors, humans, and birds,
have come into being through your play, O Mother of the World— salutations to you!
When the king had spoken thus, an incorporeal voice said:
"A son of great strength and great heroism shall be born to you;
being pleased by your praise, I shall grant you various rewards."
Having heard this, that king returned to his own home and, being free from fear,
reported the excellent words of the goddess to the queen.
From that time forth, O Indra among kings, she indeed became manifest in bodily form.
One day, O King, a washerman named Kalibhojana,
accompanied by Kāśīdāsa, went to the village of Dharmapura. There he saw a beautiful maiden, renowned by the name Kāmāṅgī.

As she was walking along the royal road accompanied by her father, afflicted by fatigue, she fainted from the force of passion; then the washerman, whose food was strife, blinded by lust, spoke to Caṇḍikā: "O Mother of the World, O Eternal One!"
"If it shall come to pass for me, O fair-browed one, then I shall give you my head;
for a beautiful daughter born of a washerman is indeed suitable for me.
Having heard these words of the washerman, that goddess—
Having deceived her father, he took her hand in marriage;
having obtained his beloved daughter, he returned home with a joyful heart.
Together with her, he enjoyed various pleasures that bestowed happiness.
Within a year, Śira went to the Goddess and quickly offered his head.
Hearing of this, Kāśidāsa, out of affection, went in haste;
and Kāmāṅgī, due to grief for her husband, gave her own head to the Goddess.
Having offered her head to the Goddess, she attained the form of the Goddess herself.
Then, being pleased, Caṇḍī restored those three to life and said to them:
"Choose a boon today; whatever desire each of you has longed for."
Kāśidāsa, however, said to her, "Surrender me, who am Kāmāṅgī.
Kāmāṅgī then said to him, "Surrender me, who am your own wife.
Then Kalibhojana, with a gracious mind, spoke to the goddess.
"O Mother, salutations, salutations! Give me a beautiful husband.
Having heard their words, Durgā remained silent;
yet, she who possesses a beautiful form granted them a boon according to their desire.
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus, the Vaitāla laughed and said to the king, "O King,
tell me, what was done by that queen for their sake?"
Thus addressed, the king spoke this to the Vaitāla:
"At that time, when the excellent skull was severed from her body, the two of them were made to exchange their portions by their mother; let each receive his own boon."
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Compendium of Histories of the Kali Age," within the Caturyuga-khaṇḍa (also known as the Pratisarga-parvan) of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
At that time, that eminent descendant of Bhṛgu, Vaitāla, became serene in mind.
He recited the famous and supreme verse concerning the king:
"The city of Campā is renowned, and its lord is the monarch Campakeśa;
there dwells a powerful archer, whose queen is Sulocanā."
A daughter named Trilokasundarī was born to her;
her face was like the moon, and her eyebrows were considered equal to bows.
She had eyes like a deer's, a voice like a cuckoo, delicate limbs, and was most excellent.
O King, what need is there for other men when she has been chosen by the gods with their minds?
Then a svayaṃvara took place for her,
and kings of many kinds who were renowned on earth arrived there through her power.
Indra, Yama, Kubera, and Varuṇa, the best of the gods, assumed human forms and arrived for his sake. Addressing Campakeśa, he said: "Listen, O King, to my words."
"Know me to be Indradatta, skilled in all sciences, handsome, and pleasing; bestow your daughter upon me. Then the second one spoke to Dharmadatta, who was likewise pleasing:
"You ought to give your daughter to one who is skilled in the science of archery.
The third said, "O King, [give her] to the illustrious Dhanapāla,
who understands the languages of all living beings and is endowed with virtue and beauty."
"And quickly surrender your own daughter to me; may you be happy.
Then the fourth said: "O King, I am indeed a master in all the arts, O Lord of the Earth, and I am daily engaged with the five precious gems."
For the sake of merit, I have always brought one jewel; for the sake of fire-offerings, a second treasure;
for my own sake, a third jewel; for the sake of my wife, a fourth treasure;
and the remainder is for the sake of excellent food—thus have I constantly procured these jewels.
"You ought to give your daughter to a man such as I.
Having heard these words of theirs, the righteous king was then bewildered and said to his daughter, "To whom shall I give you, my daughter?"
But that queen, hearing these words, was ashamed and bewildered by fate; she, though devoted to righteousness, gave no reply to her father.
Having said this, the Vaitāla laughed and spoke to the king:
"To whom should this maiden, endowed with beauty and youth, be suitable?
Sūta said:
Thus addressed, that king spoke these words to him.
That beautiful maiden is a suitable match for Dharmadatta.
That twice-born man is remembered as being skilled in all the scriptures by virtue of his caste;
he is a knower of languages and a merchant who increases wealth and grain.
For that Śūdra was indeed a knower of the arts and a master of the science of archery; he was a lord of the earth.
O Vaitāla, a maiden is always fit for one of her own caste;
therefore, the young girl was married to the virtuous Dharmadatta.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the *Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, in the *Pratisarga Parvan*, within the *Kaliyuga Itihāsa Samuccaya*, which is also known as the *Caturyuga Khaṇḍa*.
Sūta said:
Having heard this, the Vaitāla spoke thus to the king.
In the land of Videha, there was a city named Mithilāvatī.
There, a king named Guṇādhipa, endowed with wealth and grain, reigned;
he was a certain nobleman known as Ciraṃdeva who had arrived there.
For the sake of his livelihood, he made his residence there in the kingdom of Mithilā.
At the end of the rainy season, that king, accompanied by his fourfold army,
arrived at the forest for the purpose of hunting, where he encountered a magnificent tiger.
Seeing him, the king, his eyes copper-red with rage, slew him in the forest;
then, following the tiger's tracks, the monarch proceeded further into the depths of the woods,
while Ciradeva followed after him into that dense forest.
With his throat parched by hunger and tormented by exhaustion and heat, the king spoke longingly to the deity: "O sir, give me food this very day!
Having heard this, that royal person killed an excellent deer.
Having prepared it, he presented that meat, which was dear to the king, to the monarch.
The king, being pleased, then said, "O best of men, choose a boon;
I shall grant you whatever you desire immediately. He replied to the lord of the earth:
"O King, you have consumed a thousand coins of mine;
O protector of the earth, bring them home and restore them to me without delay. Furthermore, give one hundred coins to me, a householder, at the end of the month."
Having said "So be it," that king quickly returned to his own home. O King, on one day, that monarch Guṇādhipa sent his own servant, Cira, to the ocean.
Having gone to the shore of the ocean, he beheld the form of the Goddess;
he saw the goddess named Kusumadā, situated at the site of Mārkaṇḍeya, the daughter of a Gandharva with beautiful eyebrows. With a serene mind, he worshipped her.
Then the goddess, having arrived, stood before him with palms joined in reverence;
the god said to her, "Choose a boon," and she spoke for a long time, while he said,
"O fair-browed one, take my hand, for I am utterly infatuated by your beauty."
Having heard this, the goddess laughed and said to the lustful man:
"Perform your bath today in my divinely fashioned pool.
Having replied, "So be it," he went into the water, and once bathed, he departed for Mithilā.

Standing there, he spoke to the king regarding a cause that inspired wonder. Having heard that, Guṇādhipa, accompanied by his own servant, arrived at the temple of the Goddess; she, Puṣpadā, spoke to him once again.
"O sovereign of virtues, accept me through the Gāndharva rite of marriage.
Having heard this, the king said: "O Goddess, giver of merit, if you accept my word, then I shall wed you today."
Thinking "so be it," she said to him, "Declare what must be done.
He replied, "Listen, O lady, you who have tremulous eyes: serve my servant Cirasura; O Goddess, make your word true."
Feeling bashful after having spoken thus, the amorous woman said to the king:
"O ocean of compassion, accept me, a loving woman sent by Indra;
having long sought the god, I have come to you, blinded by passion."
"O Puṣpadantī, daughter of the Gandharva, you of beautiful countenance!
You have been sworn by the God of Gods that I am indeed one who must experience human pleasures.
Having heard this, that righteous king, whose very form was his virtuous conduct, [reflected].
"How shall I honor you, O fair-browed one, as if you were a virtuous daughter-in-law?
For this king, who has long been like a god, behaves toward me as if I were his own son;
therefore, O beautiful woman, become now his wife and enjoyer of pleasures."
Then that queen, filled with shame, indeed turned away like a daughter-in-law.
Having spoken thus to the king, the Vaitāla, a servant of Rudra, said:
"O sir, tell me, for whom did truth and righteousness truly arise?"
Sūta said:
The king, smiling, said to him:
"O Vetāla, it is true that truth and righteousness prevail for a long time; hear now the auspicious reason for that."
The supreme duty of kings is recorded as providing all necessary support;
therefore, what is the truthfulness of one who has failed a servant to whom he has rendered assistance?
Listen now as I describe the service performed by that servant.
Remaining at home without a means of livelihood, he performed all forms of service for the virtuous king— service such as was not performed by other men.
Later, when a great crisis had arisen, the king became aware of him.
"And for that reason, Cira is considered superior even to Deva.

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Compendium of Histories of the Kali Age," within the *Caturyugakhaṇḍa*, which is another name for the *Pratisargaparvan* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
"O Śaunaka of great intelligence, the king was told by Vaitāla: 'O King,
in the beautiful city of Kāmapura, there is a monarch named Vīrasiṃha, who is highly proficient.'"
There he ruled the kingdom according to justice and righteousness.
In that very place lived a Vaiśya named Hiraṇyadatta, who was endowed with the gift of wealth;
his daughter was Kāmālasā, distinguished by her beauty and youth.
Always dwelling in happiness, she who was fond of flowers lived there;
once, seeing her going toward the forest— which resounded with the humming of bees— for the sake of gathering blossoms, the powerful son of Dharmadatta observed her.
The one known as Somadatta touched her, who was languid with passion;
but she, full of modesty, spoke to him in that secluded place:
"O great hero, I am a maiden; O sir, abandon me today out of regard for dharma."
"Once the marriage has taken place, I shall enjoy you on the tenth day;
therefore, O ocean of mercy, grant me the instruction for these ten days alone.
Thinking "So be it," he abandoned her and returned to his own home.
But Kāmālasā, having been given by her father to the bridegroom Madapāla—
a Vaiśya who was the son of Maṇigrīva—
went to her father-in-law’s house and thought of her own friend.
On the ninth day, her husband, overcome by passion and filled with intoxication, took that woman by force and embraced his wife. But she,
tormented by the words of her friend, wept.
Then the Vaiśya spoke these words to her with a spirit of peace:
"O beautiful one, filled with joy as you are, why do you weep? Tell me the truth.
Satyavatī then related exactly what had occurred in the forest.
"O Somadatta, best of the wealthy, if I do not come to your side,
then having fallen into widowhood, I shall surely incur that sin.
Bound by these words, I shall go to his presence this very day.

Having heard this, her husband, filled with joy, gave her his command and went to sleep; she, however, overwhelmed by passion, went to his side. Then the thief, seeing her adorned with all her ornaments, [was struck with wonder].
And the greedy-minded one spoke these words: "Where are you going, O beautiful woman? By whom were you expected here at night? Tell the truth, O passionate lady.
Then she, languid with passion and overwhelmed by intoxication, spoke to that thief.
"O sir, I am going toward my friend, protected by the arrows of love.
The thief said to her, "O fair-browed one, O delicate lady, give me your ornaments;
I am a thief who seizes wealth. Having heard these words, she spoke.
"Embracing your paramour, my friend, I shall give you the ornament.
Having said, "So be it," she went with him to Somadatta.
Seeing her, the merchant said, "How have you come here, O you who are languid with passion?"
"Tell me the truth quickly; thereafter, I shall honor you.
Having heard that, Kāmālasā spoke exactly as it had happened.
Upon hearing this, Jñānahṛdaya was enlightened by Lord Viṣṇu.
Recognizing her as a devoted wife, he circumambulated her and let her go.
But the thief, having heard the reason and being enlightened by Lord Viṣṇu,
caused her to enter the house where her husband was staying.
"But that queen, though languid with passion, being devoted to the dharma of fidelity to her husband,
enjoyed the divine objects of sense provided by the God of Gods.
Having said this, the Vaitāla spoke to the learned king:
"Tell me, among those [four], which truth is considered the most excellent?
Sūta said:
Thus addressed, that king spoke this to the Vetāla.
Listen to how the thief’s truthfulness became supreme:
out of fear of the king, that Vaiśya did not enjoy her;
and out of fear of widowhood, that lady went to her friend.
Out of fear of violating the Dharma, her husband did not enjoy his wife;
but the thief, out of fear of untruth, abandoned her and attained joy.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Compendium of Histories of the Kali Age," in the *Caturyugakhaṇḍa*, otherwise known as the *Pratisargaparvan*, within the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
O highly fortunate one, Vaitāla then spoke thus to the king:
"O great king, in the land of Gauḍa there is indeed a city named Vardhana."
There lived a righteous king named Guṇaśekhara;
his minister was Nirbhayānanda, who was devoted to the Jaina dharma.
Once, the king went to the temple of the Lord of Girijā (Śiva).
He worshipped that all-pervading Lord, the Supreme Ruler;
meanwhile, a scorpion arrived there and stung the king in its fury.
From the agony of that sting, the monarch fainted and fell to the ground.
Then Nirbhayānanda, devoted to the Jaina dharma, removed the poison from him and described the king [to his ministers]:
"Listen, O illustrious King, to the six enemies who are the lowest of the mind."
Desire, anger, greed, attachment, violence, and thirst—
these arise from the quality of rajas, and their various distinctions are each distinct.
Delusion, hypocrisy, intoxication, possessiveness, hope, and reproach [arise from tamas].
And from the quality of darkness (tamas) you were born; by these [qualities], this world is filled.
Viṣ� full of desire, as is Rudra; likewise Brahmā is full of anger and greed; Śakra is deceitful, Yama is deluded, and the Lord of Yakṣas himself is intoxicated with pride.
If all those [senses] are under the control of Māyā, then what is the use of worshipping them?
He who has indeed conquered the six enemies is remembered by the sages as a Jina (Victor).
He who is not conquered is not to be known as a Jina; he is the teacher of non-duality, the stainless one.
Through meditation and devotion, men are always possessed of liberation.
O lord of the earth, listen to me regarding that dharma which leads to his grace:
by the worship of cows, the gods indeed always attain satisfaction.
Therefore, the worship of cows is pure, for violence is avoided everywhere.
By drinking intoxicants, the Jina—the soul of all—would incur affliction;
therefore, meat and drink are indeed to be avoided at all times.
"One should feed the hungry with wealth acquired through righteous means;
for the Sun is indeed the very self of the Jina, and one should feed within his light.
Having described this, the minister returned to his home.
Thinking thus, that king adopted the religion of the Jina.
After some time, he indeed transgressed the path of the Vedas;
then the distressed queen sought refuge with Śiva.
By the granting of a boon from Rudra, an exceedingly excellent son was born,
renowned as Dharmarāja, devoted to Vedic vows; yet,
despite being the very crown of virtues, he went to hell at the time of his death.
Then Dharmarāja himself ruled the kingdom according to righteousness;
by the power of his dharma, his father attained heaven. He had three wives who were most excellent, possessing great virtue and beauty.
In the spring season, the king went into the midst of the forest with them and took his pleasure there, which resounded with the humming of bees amidst the flowers.
Exhausted, yet delighted, the monarch remained there together with the queens.
With eyes rolling from intoxication, he bathed [her] in the lake;
taking a lotus flower in his hand, he offered it to the queen.
Indeed, her feet became afflicted with lameness because of that falling flower.
The king, being distressed, sought medical treatment for that queen; however,
when night arrived, she was again deluded by Candraśīla,
and falling into a state of agitation, she dropped her pure foot.
At the sound of her falling, the third became feverish;
then, as her fainting fit subsided, it arose for the second.
Through the touch of the king, that fair-browed woman abandoned the heat of her fever.
When the beautiful dawn had arrived, he returned home with them.
Having spoken thus, the Vaitāla, with a humble mind, said to the king:
"O Great King, which among these is the most excellent Sukumārikā?"
The king said:
"Among them, the third was Sukumārī, the most excellent of all;
she was of a windy temperament and was afflicted by a disease caused by a lotus flower."
The second [woman] fainted from the cool-rayed moon due to her phlegmatic nature;
she in whom a fever was produced by the mere sound [of his voice] is indeed the most excellent.
Laughing, the Lord spoke again to the king, who was devoted to Bhava.
"Tell me, is Jainism the primary dharma or is it the Vedic dharma?
He replied: "The eternal Vedic dharma is indeed the primary one;
for there are eight classes belonging to that very Brahman of unmanifest form."

The Śūdra, the Vaiśya, the Kṣatriya, and the Brāhmaṇa who has practiced celibacy; the householder, the forest-dweller, and the ascetic—these are proclaimed as superior in successive order. That householder who, having entered into the union of marriage, conducts himself like an ascetic [is likewise honored].
That sinner goes to hell until the dissolution of all beings.
The dharma taught in the Jaina scriptures as being for householders like ascetics is considered by the wise to be heresy; it must indeed always be avoided.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the *Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, in the section known as the *Caturyugakhaṇḍa* (also called the *Kaliyugīyetihāsasamuccaya*).
Sūta said:
"O highly fortunate Śaunaka, that Vaitāla is indeed a deity."
He spoke this auspicious verse concerning the inquiry of Dharma to the king:
"O King, in the delightful city of Puṇyapura, frequented by various people,
a monarch named Dharmavallabha formerly ruled his kingdom."
Satyaprakāśa was his minister, and Lakṣmī was the wife of that counselor.
Once, that king, who was a knower of dharma, said to his minister:
"O best of men, tell me: how many kinds of bliss are there in this world?"
He said: "O Great King, happiness is indeed fourfold.
That which is the supreme bliss of Brahman in the stage of the religious student (brahmacarya) is the highest;
the bliss of the objects of the senses in the householder's stage (gārhasthya) is declared by the wise to be middling."
O Great King, among those in the forest-dwelling stage (vānaprastha), he who finds bliss in dharma is the lowest;
he whose bliss is in ritual action (karmakāṇḍa) is remembered as one whose dharma is truth;
but in the stage of renunciation (saṃnyāsa), he who finds bliss in Śiva is indeed the highest of all.
"O King, one who delights in sense-objects is proclaimed to be primarily devoted to women;
O monarch, without a woman there is no happiness in the householder stage of life.
Having heard this, that king departed for another land.

He searched for a wife who was suitable for him and devoted to dharma, yet he did not find a beautiful woman who accorded with his mental disposition. That king said to his minister: "O sir, search for a woman today."
"If I do not give up my life, I speak the truth," he said.
Having heard this, the minister departed from that country for another land;
having reached the Sindhu country, he went toward the ocean.
He mentally praised the auspicious Sindhu, the lord of all sacred fords.
Buddhiprakāśa said:
"O Lord Sindhu, obeisance to you, the abode of all jewels!"
I have come to you for refuge, O you who are compassionate toward those who seek shelter;
I bow to you, the Lord of Waters, the master of the Gaṅgā and other rivers.
Grant me this jewel among women for the sake of the king, otherwise I shall give up my life.
Having heard this, Sāgara, the lord of rivers, with a serene soul,
displayed to his minister a great, divine tree in the water, its trunk of gold, its leaves of coral, and its fruit of pearls.
"O King, a young girl, delicate and beautiful, who was standing upon it,
was born right there in that very tree at the moment of dissolution.
Having witnessed this great marvel, he approached the presence of the king."
Having described all of that together with the king, he concluded;
then, having seen such a sight, the king proceeded to the edge of the ocean.
The lord of the earth himself reached Pātāla along with the young girl.
With a humble soul, he said to that woman: "I have come for your sake;
O fair-faced one, let me obtain you through the Gāndharva form of marriage.
Laughing, she said to that king: "It is the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight."
"O best of kings, I shall come here on that day and honor you.
Having heard this, the king, overwhelmed by the god of love, went with sword in hand on that very day to where the excellent temple of the Goddess was located.

In the meantime, a Rākṣasa riding upon a crane touched that young woman; the king became overcome with anger. Blinded by passion, he slew the Rākṣasa and spoke to his wife, who was now free from fear.
"Who is this that has arrived here? Tell me the reason, O beautiful lady.
She replied, "O King, listen! I am indeed the daughter of a Vidyādhara;
my father’s beloved, Madavatī, I have come to the forest afflicted by love."
"O friend, listen: through meditation my father learned that you had not come at the time of the meal to the house of your parents, and he cursed you, saying:
'Today, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, a Rākṣasa shall devour you.'"
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, you must eat the *aparādha* (the sin).
Then, having wept, I shall say to my father:
"O Lord of excellent vows, tell me the truth: when will there be liberation?"
He said: "O maiden, you shall become one enjoyed by heroes;
then there will be liberation from the curse, and I shall be released by you.
By your command, O King, I shall go to my father's house."
Having heard this, the king said, "Come to my house;
I shall go with you to that home of the Vidyādhara.
Saying "So be it," the goddess went to the king's palace.
At that time, a great festival arose among the people in that city;
but when the minister saw the king accompanied by his divine wife, he suddenly met his death— tell me, for what reason was this?
The king said: "But the minister Buddhiprakāśa, seeing that the queen had arrived and reflecting in his heart upon the king,
was distressed by the fear of the kingdom's ruin."
Listen to the auspicious reason why he abandoned his life and went to heaven: for a king who is addicted to sensual objects suffers the destruction of his kingdom;
having fallen under the intoxication of women, he shall always incur the ruin of his realm.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Compendium of Histories of the Kali Age," within the *Caturyugakhaṇḍa* (also known as the *Pratisargaparvan*) of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
Laughing, that Vaitāla then spoke these words to the king.
O King, in the beautiful city of Cūḍāpura, there was a ruler known as Cūḍāmaṇi.
His preceptor was Devasvāmin, who had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas;
his wife was Viśālākṣī, who was devoted solely to the duties toward her husband.
The woman of excellent complexion propitiated Śiva for the sake of a son;
by the granting of a boon from Rudra, a powerful son equal to Kāmadeva was born,
renowned as Harisvāmī, who possessed a portion of a deity.
Endowed with every prosperity and possessing happiness equal to that of the gods on earth,
he had a wife named Rūpalāvaṇyikā who was indeed a celestial nymph born upon the earth due to the curse of Devala, O King.
Once, during the spring season when the flowers were in full bloom, that beautiful woman, having ascended her bed, slept with great affection alongside her husband in a palace.
At that time, a Gandharva named Sukala was infatuated by her beauty.
Having placed her in his own celestial chariot, he carried her away and went to his own city.
But when he awoke, he searched for that woman in great distress;
failing to find her, he became distraught, abandoned the country, and went to the forest.
Having renounced all sense-objects and being solely devoted to the meditation on Hari,
that affectionate man once reached the house of a brahmin;
having prepared milk-rice (*pāyasa*), he took refuge beneath a banyan tree.
Having quickly placed it upon a tree, he then performed his bath in the river;
thereafter, O King, his food was turned into poison by a serpent.
Then the ascetic arrived, and having eaten, he fell into a state of intoxication.
His body tormented by the poison, he looked at the Brahmin and said:
"O fool, you have given me rice-milk mixed with poison!
I am going to my death, O wicked man; you shall incur the sin of killing a Brahmin."
Having spoken thus, he met his death and went to the world of Śiva;
taking the goddess endowed with beauty and splendor, he attained happiness.
Having said this, the Vetāla spoke thus to the king:
"Tell me, among those [five], to whom did the Brahmin-slaughter accrue?
The King said:
"The serpent was naturally venomous; the poison was produced through ignorance."
Therefore, although he was a serpent, he did not incur the sin of killing a Brahmin;
for that twice-born man, deluded by fate, gave alms to one who was hungry. Consequently, the sin of Brahmin-slaughter did not come upon him, as he was devoted to the duties of his lineage.

The evil committed by oneself must always be experienced by people themselves. Abandoning one’s own self, killing a Brahmin, and insulting a guest—these are to be known as equivalent to the murder of a Brahmin; likewise, it is the same as giving poison.

Sacrificing one's own life is considered to be due to fate; therefore, even he is not a sinner. As for those men by whom it was said that "the killing of a Brahmin was committed by you," that killing of a Brahmin belongs to those men who have fallen from justice.

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Compendium of Histories of the Kali Age," within the section on the Four Yugas (Caturyuga-khaṇḍa), which is another name for the Pratisarga-parvan, in the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
Having accomplished his purpose and being serene in soul, Vaitāla spoke to the king.
In the city of Candrahṛdaya, there was a king named Raṇadhīra.
There lived a wealthy and righteous Vaiśya named Dharmadhvaja. To him was born a daughter, Sundarī, who was destined for happiness.
Once, there was in that city a man devoted to hunting,
who was constantly addicted to the art of gambling and intent upon liquor and meat. There lived a man-eating Rākṣasa named Vāśara.
He gave him liquor and meat every day;
then, becoming a Rakshasa out of favor, he said to that devotee of Yatu:
"Choose a boon that is worthy of me, and you shall obtain everything."
He said, "O man-eater, a boon must be granted to me:
create a hidden pit in the midst of the earth and carry out the investigation of the thief.
Having heard this, he created a pit that bewildered the intellect of men.
The Lord himself remained there, accompanied by his devotee;
by him, during the night, the king’s beautiful female servant was stolen through theft,
cast into a pit, and likewise much wealth was taken.
He had seven wives, women belonging to the four castes;
among them, the king’s female servant was the favorite of that thief.
That Rākṣasa had constructed a dwelling for her that was like a royal fortress.
O King, when various stolen goods were forcibly deposited in pits hidden beneath the earth to delude the intellect of men,
the people became distressed and spoke to the king.
"O King, let us abandon this city which causes you such thievery and obstacles.
Having heard this, the king stationed guards equipped with weapons in that city, intent upon the task of suppressing thieves.

Having issued his command, he went home; and having heard it, those guards did exactly as they were told. At that time, all the guards were deluded by the illusory power of the Rākṣasī, and the thief forcibly seized much wealth from the wealthy men.
Once again they set out, inciting the king who was steadfast in battle.
Having heard this, the king himself arrived at the city in astonishment;
and at midnight, when all was shrouded in darkness, that thief approached the king.
Having understood this, he said to the king, "Who are you that have arrived here?
The king replied, "I am a thief who has come seeking wealth;
I shall go to the houses of the wealthy, so please do as I say."
"Take wealth with me in many ways and be happy.
Thinking thus, the thief took much wealth;
having placed the king outside, he went into the middle of a pit at night and deposited it there.
At that very moment, the king's wife, an excellent woman who was a servant, said to the monarch: "O King, go quickly to your own home;
for this thief, having brought about his own death for your sake, has gone home."
Having spoken thus, she showed the king the way through the different paths.
The king, having reached his own home when the sun had risen in the clear morning,
set out with his army for the place where the thief himself was stationed.

The thief, too, having encountered fear, worshipped the Rākṣasa named Vāśara and described exactly what had happened according to the facts. Laughing, the Rākṣasa said to him: "O friend, you have provided me with my meal."
"Today, impelled by fate, I shall devour all these humans," saying this, that terrible Rākṣasa went toward the king;
he devoured the vast army, while they too fled in the ten directions.
And that king, overcome and rendered distraught by the rākṣasa,
was then addressed by the thief himself in anger:
"Flight is certainly not fitting for a king who is born of righteousness."
Having heard this, the king quickly arrived there;
having meditated upon the goddess Mahākālī and obtained the most excellent mantra,
that pit along with the Rākṣasa was reduced to ashes in an instant.
They quickly bound that thief, the plunderer of the city, with fetters;
then, together with all his wealth and those women,
he arrived at the royal palace, whereupon his downfall occurred.
By the very sound of the beaten drum, they announced in every house the entire judicial decree regarding the execution of that thief; on that day,
he was paraded upon a donkey through that city.
That thief indeed arrived at the door of the house that bore the banner of Dharma;
beholding his form, she who was accustomed to happiness was struck with infatuation.
Afflicted by grief, she said to her father: "Release the thief immediately!"
Having gone there, he said to the king: "Take five hundred thousand pieces of wealth for the sake of releasing this thief; otherwise, my daughter will surely die.
The king laughed and said to him: "This man is indeed a thief who plunders wealth."
"Never indeed shall I abandon this lowest of men on earth"—
hearing this, the thief became hopeless and met his death;
at the moment the arrow was being applied, he first laughed and then wept.
At that very moment, his daughter Devamāyā, deluded by illusion,
assumed the body of a thief and entered the fire-pit;
then Durgā, being pleased, restored them both to life through her grace.
"A divine boon, granting the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation, has been granted to her.
Having spoken thus to the king, he laughed and said to him again:
"For what reason did that thief first laugh and then weep?"
The king said:
"A beautiful woman is ready to give her own life for my sake;
what, then, should be given by me to her, who embodies such affection?"
Therefore, he wept afterwards; now hear the reason for his laughter:
"Blessed is this Lord Kṛṣṇa, whose pastime is such as this!
He is indeed capable of granting the fruit of heaven even to one who is unrighteous."
"Salutations again and again to him, the fruit of whose very nature is hell!
Therefore, he was previously mocked and deluded by the play of Hari.
Having heard this, the Vaitāla said: "The supreme refuge of Hari [is the highest]."
"Because he spoke those words, he was impaled on a stake; therefore, he who desired life became pure.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Compendium of Histories of the Kali Age," in the *Caturyugakhaṇḍa*—also known as the *Pratisargaparvan*—of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
O most excellent and illustrious Bhṛgu, the Vaitāla spoke to the king:
"O King, there is a beautiful city named Puṣpāvatī; there dwells a monarch renowned as Suvicāra, who is devoted to the protection of his subjects."
His wife was Candraprabhā, endowed with beauty and youth.
From her was born a daughter known by the name Candrāvalī.
Once, together with her female companions, she went to a forest filled with blossoming flowers.
She indeed beheld the brahmin Sudeva who had arrived there; the goddess became deluded, and the brahmin also fell to the ground,
suffering the pain of the arrows of love as if his life-breath had departed.
When she had departed from the house, two Brahmins arrived there—
Mūladeva and one named Śaśī— who were both experts in the sciences.
Upon seeing that approaching twice-born man, who was endowed with beauty and youth, they [approached him].
He asked the full reason why he had fallen into such a state of delusion;
having heard this and wept, he reported everything to him. Then the compassionate Mūladeva brought him to his own home.
Having recited the great mantra joined with the seed-syllable of Cāmuṇḍā in his home,
he prepared two pills and presented them to Sudevā.
With one [pill], a beautiful and auspicious girl of twelve years was born.
By means of the second [spell], Mūladeva then became a great old man.
The two went to the king's palace, honored the monarch with blessings, and presented their reason; listen to that, O high-minded one.
O King, in that city of Tāṃtrika, my home, which was like unto a celestial abode,
was forcibly plundered by the king named Vilāpadhvaja.
My son and wife fled, and I have come here to search for them.
"O Great King, this bride is to become my daughter;
until I depart, protect her according to dharma in your own home.
Having heard this, the king then summoned his own daughter.
Having entrusted her to her, that brahmin subsequently returned home.
But at midnight, Sudeva, free from fear, spoke to the woman:
"O friend, why is your mind so agitated? Tell me the truth."
"O friend, that excellent Brahmin Sudeva has always dwelt within my heart;
therefore, I am perpetually distressed by separation from him.
Subhūti then said: "O, if you [desire] that excellent Brahmin..."
"I offer myself to you; tell me, O noble lady among the twice-born, what shall I give? I shall always be your servant," she said.
Having heard this, Sudeva extracted the mechanical device from her mouth.
Having attained the state of his former body, he took pleasure with her.
O King, at that time, the son of a minister, remaining in the womb for four months,
became infatuated with the form of a Brahmin woman.
Then, perceiving that Madanālasa was near death,
the minister, having reflected deeply in his heart out of affection with the aid of wise counselors,
entrusted to him that woman who had been produced by means of a mantra.
"O son of the minister Bhoma, bathe for three months in the circle of sacred fords (tīrthamaṇḍala);
then you will become worthy of me; act accordingly.
Thinking thus, the minister’s son, Madanālasa, with a humble soul, [did as instructed].
Having gone to another sacred ford, that lustful Sudeva embraced his wife,
who possessed the splendor of a queen and was under the sway of passion;
she, indeed, quickly conceived a child from that twice-born man after two months.
Having become a virtuous man, Sudeva went to the house of Mūladeva and reported everything exactly as it had occurred in the royal palace.
Mūladeva, with a gracious mind, [addressed] his friend named Śaśin.
Having made himself appear twenty years younger than he actually was, the handsome man reported everything to the king, saying, "O Lord of the Earth, give me your daughter-in-law.
Then, out of fear, that king spoke to him with gentle words.
The minister’s son, named Rājakara, was languid with passion;
upon seeing your beautiful daughter-in-law, he became infatuated and stood on the verge of death.
And the minister himself became just like that due to the separation from his own son.
"In the same way, O Brahmin, having consulted with the elders, I gave her to him;
therefore, you too should act accordingly so that my lord may be pleased.
Then Mūladeva, vomiting poison, spoke to the king:
"O King, give your daughter to me for the pleasure of my son.
Thinking thus, that king gave his auspicious daughter Candrāvalī,
accompanied by many riches, according to the Vedic rites.
Free from any blemish against the Brahmins, he indeed ruled the kingdom himself.
Meanwhile, Śaśin took the king’s daughter and departed for his own home.
Then Sudeva, filled with grief, spoke to Mūladeva.
"This daughter of the king is my most excellent wife for enjoyment.
Hearing that, Mūladeva was amazed and did exactly so.
Having said this to the king, the Vaitāla, the servant of Rudra, spoke again.
"To whom did the princess go according to dharma? Tell me that.
The king said:
"By the command of her father and mother, the daughter stood before the gods."
She is always worthy, according to the Dharma, for him to whom she has been offered;
for it is declared in the scriptures, O Lord, that a jewel of a woman is always like a seed sown with a mantra in a field renowned upon the earth.
That field belongs neither to the cultivator nor to the giver of the seed;
therefore, the king’s daughter will indeed choose Śaśin,
for Sudeva’s son will attain her fitness.
"Thus it has been told to you, O Lord, as it is spoken in the scriptures.
Tell me exactly what was done by the minister’s son.
Having heard this, he (the sage) said: "That son was Madanālasa."
Having reached auspicious Vṛndāvana, he arrived at Rādhākuṇḍa;
having bathed there on the full-moon day of the month of Bhādrapada, O best of kings, by that merit his sin—
which had caused him to fall into delusion— was reduced to ashes.
Remembering Govinda in his heart, he praised him with gentle words.
Madanālasa said:
"Salutations to you, O Lord Kṛṣṇa, ocean of compassion! By you this entire universe is pervaded, like the form of the ocean."
O God of gods, by you alone, for the sake of sport, this world was indeed hidden along with your beloved consort;
at the time of the world's end, the universe was withdrawn by you in the form of Time—salutations to you, salutations to you!
O Hṛṣīkeśa, O Lord, act quickly so that my intellect may become pure.
Thus, by the power of the hymn, his intellect was liberated from the noose of desire by the God of Gods; that Kṣatriya returned home,
and the king, having embraced his own beloved wife, rejoiced in great delight.
To destroy the fault of his son-in-law, the wise man meditated in his heart and,
having summoned Sudeva, joyfully gave him his own sister;
Sudeva [married] that Kṣatriya’s sister, who was intoxicated with pride.
"Having married according to dharma, he who was a slave to his desires reached his own home.
Thus, O King, I have related to you the life story of that wise Brāhmaṇa Mūladeva; now I shall tell you something else."
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Compendium of Histories of the Kali Age," within the *Caturyugakhaṇḍa*—also known as the *Pratisargaparvan*—of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
Having praised the pure king, Vetāla, the servant of Rudra, [spoke].
O Brahmin, he then related another beautiful narrative:
"In Kanyakubja, O great king, there was a Brahmin named Dānaśīlaka,
who was true to his word and devoted to the worship of the Goddess."
He caused a gift to be performed with whatever wealth he had acquired through acceptance of offerings.
Once, however, during the autumn season, there occurred the vow of Navadurgā;
since no wealth had been obtained from the gift, he then became anxious with worry.
"What must I do today so that I may indeed be possessed of wealth? The girls have been invited today; how shall I feed them?
Thus filled with grief, he then, by the grace of the Goddess—
Then he attained the five mudrās and performed his vow with them. He observed the fast of abstaining from food for nine days;
by the power of that vow, upon death, he attained the state of a deity.
And there was a lord of the Vidyādharas named Jīmūtaketu;
he dwelt for some years on the delightful Himācala mountain, in the auspicious city of the Vidyādharas, enjoying divine pleasures.
There, he constantly worshipped the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpadruma) with devotion.
By the power of that tree, an exceedingly excellent son was born,
skilled in all arts, named Jīmūtavāhana.
O King, in a previous birth, in the most excellent Middle Country,
he was a Kṣatriya ruler of the earth named Śūrasena. Once, that lord of the earth became intent on the sport of hunting.
He reached the forest of Utpala, where Vālmīki resided;
on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, the king performed the festival of Rāma’s birthday according to the prescribed rites, having refrained from taking any life.
In the middle of the night within Vālmīki’s hut, he kept a vigil;
by the power of that merit, he heard the song consisting of Rāma and attained the state of a Vidyādhara, rejoicing there like Śakra.
Indeed, worship was performed by that high-souled one for the Kalpavṛkṣa;
at the end of a year, the tree said, "O best of beings, choose a boon.
He said to that great tree, "My auspicious city—"
"Act in such a way that [this place] becomes endowed with wealth and grain, just as it was before.
When the tree had spoken thus, the city was made equal to that of the king; at that time, there was no one who would consider it to have any dependence on a monarch.
By the grace of the Kalpavṛkṣa, they all became equal to kings;
then those two, father and son,
went to the forest for the sake of penance and performed intense austerity on the most delightful Malaya mountain.
One day, O King, a daughter of King Malayadhvaja,
renowned as Kamalākṣī, arrived at the temple of Śiva accompanied by her female friend, intent upon the worship of Śiva.
And Jīmūtavāhana went to the temple for the purpose of worship;
there he beheld a maiden of divine form, adorned with every ornament.
Merely by the sight of her, he was tormented by the arrows of Kāma.
In his mind, he praised that god of love with gentle words.
Jīmūtavāhana said:
"Salutations to you, Madana; salutations to you, the son of Kṛṣṇa."
Salutations to you, the slayer of Śambara’s life-breath, who possesses the fourfold manifestation (caturvyūha).
Salutations again and again to the five-arrowed Kāma, to Pradyumna.
Make this lotus-faced woman, with beautiful hips, suitable for me as a lover.
Then the Lord, the deity Makaradhvaja, being pleased,
caused his father to be deluded and brought about that marriage;
the son of that king was indeed known as Viśvāvasu.
Together with his sister’s husband, he went to Gandhamādana;
having bowed to Nara and Nārāyaṇa, he arrived upon the lofty Garuḍa.
O King, at that time, the mother of the nāga Śaṅkhacūḍa—
He wept profusely where Jīmūtavāhana was;
that compassionate one, who is kind to the distressed, went there quickly in his grief.
Having comforted the old woman, he asked, "By whom has this suffering been brought upon you?"
"O Lord, this son of mine shall go into the mouth of Garuḍa;
afflicted by the grief of separation from him, I, of noble lineage, lament.
Knowing this, the king approached Garuḍottuṅga.
Garuḍa, having seized him, ascended the path of the sky;
meanwhile, Aṅgada, smeared with blood, placed that [head] there for the beautiful lady.
But the lotus-eyed woman beheld him in the sky, being devoured by Garuḍa.
Beholding her deeply distressed by the grief for her husband,
Garuḍa, terrified, then arrived there in great haste and said to Jīmūtavāhana: "Why have you been devoured by me?"
He said: "O Lord, O high-minded one, listen to my words.
The mother of Śaṅkhacūḍa is afflicted with great sorrow;
for the sake of protecting her son, I have come into your presence."
O protector of the earth, when this was said, the serpent Śaṅkhacūḍa,
distressed by the very suffering of that serpent, approached his enemy and said:
"O ocean of mercy, devour me, who have come for the sake of your food."
"O high-minded one, abandon the human diet and adopt a divine one.
Then Garuḍa, being pleased, granted three boons to Jīmūtavāhana,
the son of a Vidyādhara.
"I shall never eat the family of Śaṅkhacūḍa;
however, you, having attained a most excellent kingdom in the city of the Vidyādharas,
shall enjoy fine food for a hundred thousand years and thereafter go to Vaikuṇṭha."
Having spoken thus, the god vanished; he obtained the kingdom from his father, and after enjoying the pleasures of sovereignty together with his wife, he went to Vaikuṇṭha.
Having said this, the Vaitāla, with a humble mind, spoke to the king.
"O Great King, among them, who has obtained the great fruit?
The king replied,
"Śaṅkhacūḍa has obtained the great fruit of the gift of life."

By the power of the devoted wife and by the gift of life to the king, fate has ordained that Garuḍa’s very nature be one of service to the monarch; he has become satisfied— what then could be the fruit of that?
Fearless, Śaṅkhacūḍa approached his own enemy;
by offering up his body to him, he then attained the great fruit.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the *Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, in the *Pratisarga Parvan*, within the sub-section known as the *Caturyuga Khaṇḍa*, specifically in the *Kaliyugīyetihāsa Samuccaya*.
Sūta said:
Again that Vaitāla spoke to the king, who was skilled in knowledge:
"The city of King Candraśekhara is situated in the south."
There was a Vaiśya named Ratnadatta, who was knowledgeable in the Dharma and possessed of wealth and grain.
To him was born a most excellent daughter, Kāmāvarūthinī.
Having beheld her supreme beauty, that Vaiśya [addressed] the king.
He said, "O Great King, this daughter of mine is highly desired;
O Ocean of Mercy, accept her, for she was fashioned by the Creator as a fit match for you.
Having heard these words, the moon-crested king [replied].
He said to his minister Vidura, "O high-minded one,
you must go and quickly inform me of that form in its proper manner.
Having spoken thus, King Candraśekhara went to his palace.
His wife, named Śyāmalā, learning that the king had arrived,
honored him with incense, lamps, flowers, and other appropriate offerings.
At that very moment, however, a cow was attacked by a tiger.
Distraught with fear, she wailed with a loud cry of "Haṃbhā!
Hearing that, the king approached with sword in hand;
having swiftly slain the tiger, the monarch then rejoiced.
The Dānava named Mukula, having assumed a form from that body,
spoke with a bowed spirit to the Lord of the Earth, the moon-crested one who knows the Dharma:
"O Lord, released by you, I shall go to the abode of Varuṇa."
Due to Prahlāda’s very curse, he had attained the body of a tiger;
having completed his circumambulation, the Daitya went swiftly toward Prahlāda.
The king, having returned home, fell asleep with supreme joy.
At dawn, the king arose and came personally to the assembly hall; directed by the monarch, he went to where the army of Kāma was stationed.
Seeing her composed of divine form, he reflected thus within his own mind:
"By the power of her form, this king will fall into delusion.
Knowing this, she said to the king, "She is certainly not suitable for you.
Thinking thus, the king did not then perform the marriage.
He gave her to Balabhadra, the commander of King Ratnadatta’s army; that woman of excellent complexion became his wife. Once, the king beheld her, who was indeed an army of the god of love.
Deluded by the arrow of desire, he fell to the ground in a swoon.
Then the commander-in-chief quickly raised the king and,
having swiftly set up a palanquin, brought him into the assembly hall.
Then the awakened king joyfully said to the commander-in-chief:
"Whose wife is this beautiful woman? From where was this most excellent lady born?
Hearing that, Balabhadra, with a humble mind, replied to the king.
"This beautiful woman is mine; she is the daughter of Ratnadatta.
Out of fear of the kingdom's ruin, the minister did not describe her beauty to you.
O King, she who is the wife of my servant is always worthy of you."
"I shall fulfill your wish; accept her, O treasure-house of compassion.
Thus addressed, the king, his eyes copper-red with anger, said to him:
"By right, this woman of beautiful form has been obtained by me as your wife."

"If I take that queen, then, O sirs, the servants of Yama will cast me into hell and subject me to great suffering. Having spoken thus, the king, quickly tormented by the fire of separation, [fainted].
"The king has met his death and has gone to the vicinity of the City of Dharma.
Having said this, the Vaitāla spoke to the king: "Listen, O King!
When the king died, his wife was seen to have become a virtuous *satī*."
The commander-in-chief, however, was reduced to ashes right there in an instant.
Having reduced her body to ashes, the goddess Kāmāvarūthinī ascended to heaven;
all of them have gone to heaven—whose merit is considered greater?
The king said to the Vetāla: "The one who is considered superior in righteousness is the one deemed fit for death for the sake of the monarch;
likewise, for a devoted wife, death in the company of her husband is what is fitting."
Sundarī was indeed given by Yatkiṅkara for the sake of the king;
yet, out of fear of dharma, that lustful king did not accept her.
Having thus conquered desire, one must likewise protect dharma; therefore, dharma is held in higher regard than even kingship.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the *Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, in the *Pratisarga Parvan*, within the section known as the *Caturyuga Khaṇḍa*, specifically the *Kaliyugīya Itihāsa Samuccaya*.
Sūta said:
Then the Vetāla, assuming the form of a Brāhmaṇa, spoke again.
Listen, O illustrious king, to this delightful story of yours.
In Ujjayinī, O noble one, there was a king named Mahāsena.
In his kingdom lived a brahmin well-known as Devaśarman.
His son was Guṇākara, who was devoted to liquor and meat;
through gambling, the wealth of that sinful man came to ruin.
Abandoned by his kinsmen, he wandered upon the surface of the earth.
Once, by the turn of fate, a yogi named Kapardin arrived at Siddhāśrama; he worshipped him with food from a skull-bowl,
but knowing it to be food fit for a Piśāca, the [king], though hungry, did not accept it.
For the sake of that hospitality, he summoned the Yakṣiṇī;
by her, that twice-born man obtained great bliss while lying in bed during the night.
But when morning arrived, the Yakṣiṇī departed for Kailāsa.

Due to separation from her, that twice-born man approached the presence of Kapardin (Śiva). At midnight, while standing in the midst of water for forty days, Kapardin bestowed upon him the lore (vidyā) capable of attracting Yakṣiṇīs.
He chanted an auspicious mantra, but she who moves according to her own will did not arrive.
Then, by the command of Yogi, the Brahmin himself, relinquishing his sense of possessiveness,
bowed to his parents and stayed the night in his own home.
Having reached Pratibodhivana, he entered into discipleship under him. Standing in the midst of the five fires, he, being pure, recited his mantra.
When the goddess Yoginī did not appear, he then became distressed with anxiety.
Having spoken thus to the king, who was skilled in knowledge, the Vaitāla spoke again:
"How was the Yakṣiṇī, his beloved queen, not recovered?
O Brahmin, having heard this, the king said to the Vaitāla, the servant of Rudra:
O Brahmin, for the sake of attaining perfection, there are indeed three kinds of action for the practitioner:
action performed through mind and speech bestows happiness in the next world;
furthermore, it should be understood that [action] is produced by the body, as well as by speech and body.
It should be known that when observed in this life, it bestows some degree of accomplishment;
and in the next life, in the world of mortals (bhuvarloka), it is said to produce a physical body.
When produced through the mind and body, it grants sovereignty in the subsequent birth.
Action born of mind, speech, and body bestows accomplishment in this life and indeed grants supreme accomplishment in the next;
therefore, practitioners must certainly perform these three kinds of action in this world.
With wealth obtained from another, that twice-born man performed a rite born of mantras;
consequently, in another birth, that devoted twice-born man attained the state of a yakṣa.
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus, the Vetāla’s face became bright with satisfaction;
saying "Excellent! Excellent! to him, he honored him with these virtuous words.
Then, for the sake of further testing the king, he related another historical narrative.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Compendium of Histories of the Kali Age," within the *Caturyugakhaṇḍa*, also known as the *Pratisargaparvan*, of the glorious *Bhaviṣyamahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
"O Śaunaka, O highly wise one, he indeed spoke thus to that Vaitāla."
There was a king named Sudakṣa dwelling in the city of Vaṃśakaṃbalaka;
he was just, righteous, heroic, generous, and devoted to Śiva. In his kingdom lived a Vaiśya known as Dhanādhyakṣa.
His daughter was the beautiful and auspicious Sundarī, named Dhanavatī;
that excellent woman was given by her father to the Vaiśya Gaurīdatta. After some time, she became his enchanting daughter.
When she was twelve years old, her father passed away;
then Dhanavatī, a widow whose father had died nearby,
arrived at night on a path shrouded in darkness along with her daughter.
A certain twice-born man named Nyāyaśarman, who had stolen the property of a Brahmin, did not meet his death upon a spit because of his habit of speaking untruths.
Suddenly, a woman born of the Vaiśya caste arrived; she touched his hand.
On account of that great sorrow, the twice-born man wept loudly, crying out again and again, "Alas, Rāma! Kṛṣṇa! Pradyumna! Aniruddha!
Hearing this, the distressed Dhanavatī asked, "Who are you?"
The twice-born man said, "I am a Brahmin who has been lying on a spit for three days;
if you will give me your daughter, I shall give you ten million pieces of gold.
Having heard this, Dhanavatī married her enchanting daughter to him.
Having dug up the object situated at the foot of the banyan tree, he returned home.
Mohinī also said to her husband, "You have fallen under the power of death;
tell me, O ocean of compassion, how can a son be born to me?"
The twice-born man said, "Listen, O deformed one: when desire arises in your heart, you must quickly obtain a learned man as a husband and procreate a son.
Having spoken thus, the twice-born man met his death and went to the world of Yama.
She constantly endured the torments of hell born of her censurable deeds.
Yet that woman, Mohinī, endowed with youth, remained in her mother’s house,
repeatedly fixing a time limit within her heart.
"What are enjoyments? What is the wonder? Who is awake? Who should sleep?
From what have sin, disease, and suffering arisen that reside within the heart? When he spoke this verse to the twice-born, the twice-born gave no answer.
A brahmin named Medhāvin, residing in Kaśmīra, arrived there.
With a serene mind, he said to her: "Listen, O beautiful Mohinī!
Fragrance, women, fine garments, song, drink, and food—"
The wise know that bedding and ornaments constitute the eightfold objects of enjoyment.
Day after day, living beings die and are born;
that one should still harbor a sense of "mine" regarding them is considered a marvel by the wise.
He who, having attained discernment, engages in the performance of action,
remains awake as one possessed of discernment within this most terrible darkness of saṃsāra.
He who, recognizing saṃsāra as a serpent, has cultivated dispassion upon this earth—
Indeed, a person who maintains equanimity and meditative absorption sleeps in happiness;
for from volitional thought (saṃkalpa) desire is born, and from that greed arises.
Born from greed and rooted in thirst, that evil leads one to hell.
The taste born from the nature of water undergoes various transformations;
for one born from that taste, there arises in this body an inauspicious disease consisting of karma.
And from Rudra, through Kālī, delusion was produced, which destroys the world within the heart.
He praised Mahādevī, who is worshipped by the gods, for the sake of a wife.
Thereupon, Mithyādṛṣṭi was born and became the beloved of Moha;
from that, affection arose toward his wife, as did Mamatā’s fondness.
Hearing that suffering born from those two, accompanied by grief, that woman of excellent complexion fainted for a moment; [she thought:
"My friend is honorable, heroic, clever, authoritative, and virtuous."
The man who was the woman's protector always brought her under his control;
having given her an embryo, that Brahmin took gold from her.
And that woman obtained daily happiness through that pregnancy.
Once, at the end of ten months, Śiva spoke to Mohinī in a dream, O Great King; she too, having understood this, acted accordingly,
placing her own child along with a thousand pieces of gold in the middle of a swing.
Having placed him at the palace gate, his mother slept soundly; meanwhile,
the king, a worshipper of Rudra seeking a son, was awakened by Śiva and obtained that excellent son born of Mohinī from the Brahmin’s son.
Having performed the birth-rites, he bestowed much wealth;
and he was named Haradatta, proficient in all branches of knowledge. Upon his father's passing, having obtained that kingdom, he caused righteousness to shine forth.
"By him, the Gayā-śrāddha was performed according to the rules on the bank of the Phalgu;
then three hands appeared, and that king was filled with wonder.
Having said this, the Vaitāla spoke to the monarch: "O King!"
"Who indeed is worthy of this alms-offering? Having heard this, the king said:
"A wise man who seeks wealth should be known as one equal to a guru;
to such a thief, this offering is appropriate, for he possesses a woman who is enchanting."
Sūta said: O Brahmin, by the power of that funeral cake (piṇḍa), that thief who had stolen the property of a Brāhmaṇa emerged from hell and arrived in the heavenly world.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Compendium of Histories of the Kali Age," within the Caturyuga-khaṇḍa (also known as the Pratisarga-parvan) of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Furthermore, in Citrakūṭa, there was a king known as Rūpadatta;
on account of pursuing a deer, he entered another part of the forest.
At midday, on the shore of a lake, that son of a sage beheld a woman endowed with beauty and youth as she was gathering lotus flowers;
her eyes and his own eyes met and became one.
In the meantime, a brahmin arrived there and beheld them;
by the mere sight of him, knowledge dawned upon the king. Bowing low with humility, the king questioned him regarding the supreme Dharma.
The wise sage spoke to him, nourishing the dharma of compassion:
"A gift equal to that of one who is fearless has never existed, nor will it ever exist;
one should inflict punishment upon the undeserving and enjoy the fruit of honoring those worthy."
Constant friendship toward the twice-born cows, impartiality in the administration of punishment,
truthfulness in the worship of the gods, self-restraint in the honoring of gurus,
gentleness at the time of giving gifts, and contentment with censurable actions.
Having spoken thus, that sage gave his daughter to him and went home;
the king also lay down at the foot of the banyan tree together with her.
At that time, a certain Rākṣasa, eager to devour her, [arrived].
He awakened King Bali;
and for the sake of giving that flesh-eating demon a Brahmin boy seven years of age,
the king made a solemn agreement and, having done so, went to his own home in truth.
Having obtained the consent of his ministers, he gave a hundred thousand gold pieces to a brahmin;
then, placing the middle son before him, he offered him as a sacrifice to the Rākṣasa.
At the time of death, the son of the brahmin laughed and wept loudly.
"How was laughter made by him, and how did he weep afterwards?
Having heard this, the king said, "Listen, O bard, O twice-born one:
[he laughed] at his eldest son, who was dear to his father, dear to his mother, and most excellent."

Having learned this, the middle son went for refuge to the king; so too did the merciless Rūpasena, who was begging for his wife’s welfare. Recognizing the king with sword in hand, he who was devoted to Śiva laughed.
"My body has been delivered to a Rākṣasa; therefore, she wept.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Compendium of Histories of the Kali Age," in the Caturyuga-khaṇḍa (also known as the Pratisarga-parvan) of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
Having heard this, the Vaitāla spoke again to the king a further tale:
"In the beautiful city of Viśālā, there was a lord of the earth named Vipuleśa.
In his kingdom lived a Vaiśya named Arthadatta, who was devoted to trade."
A charming daughter named Anaṅgamañjarī was born to him;
her father himself gave her in marriage to a Vaiśya named Suvarṇa.
Once, Suvarṇa came from Kamalagrāma to the island.
Desiring to obtain wealth,
that excellent brahmin named Kamalākara lived for a long time in the house of Anaṅgamañjarī; by the turn of fate, he arrived there through the application of his own craft.
At the conclusion of the fire sacrifice, the beautiful daughter went to perform the ritual sprinkling;
seeing her, who was like a blossom of desire, the best of the twice-born was infatuated. The daughter, too, her eyes rolling with intoxication, granted a tryst to the Brahmin.
"Having obtained me at midnight when darkness has arisen, may you be happy.
Having heard these words of hers, the twice-born man then fixed his mind on her;
tormented for a long time by the fire of desire, he fell asleep upon the excellent seat.
At midnight, that woman, intent on the arrival of the twice-born man and tormented by love as she searched for her beloved's path,
met her death when, by fate, that brahmin did not arrive.
Kamalākara himself arrived immediately at the end of the appointed time;
seeing the fair-browed woman under the power of death, he met his own demise. At dawn, Arthadatta, overcome with grief, had her cremated.
Then Suvarṇa arrived and lamented for his beloved;
having been reduced to ashes upon the funeral pyre, she departed for the heavenly realm.
Having said this, the Vaitāla spoke to King Vikrama.
"Whose affection for them was greater, and why did she go to the city of heaven?
The King said:
"Their affection for their husband was greater; among them, neither the middle one nor the woman nor the brahmin [was so]."
Out of affection for the twice-born, that woman died and went to the city of heaven;
for a Brāhmaṇa, who is the very embodiment of Brahman, is always to be honored by those of the Vaiśya caste. Yet even the twice-born did not then attain the woman, nor the path to heaven, nor Hari.
Keeping me in his heart, he indeed met his end and ascended from here to the third heaven.
Suvarṇa, recognizing me in his heart as my beloved and devoted to Brahman,
departed for the celestial realm after abandoning me due to the power of the fire's burning.

Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the *Kaliyugīyetihāsamuccaya*, which is an alternative designation for the *Caturyugakhaṇḍa* within the *Pratisargaparvan* of the glorious *Śrīmad Bhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus, that Vaitāla, with a humble mind, addressed the king.
In the beautiful city of Jayasthala, there was a king named Vardhamāna.
In his village lived a Brahmin, a master of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences,
renowned as Viṣṇusvāmin and devoted solely to Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa.
He had four sons who were devoted to the four [vices]; they were known as Dyūtakarmā, Kulaṭa, Viṣayī, and Nāstika. Once, by the turn of fate, they all fell into poverty.
Filled with humility, they bowed to their father Viṣṇuśarman.
They said, "O dear father, tell us how Lakṣmī was lost.
Having heard that, the father spoke: "Listen to the account of the game of dice."

Gambling causes the loss of wealth, is rooted in evil, and is a great villainy; from it arise sexual misconduct, theft, and cruelty. Through the power of the act of gambling, there shall be the depletion of your own riches.
"O son, by means of wealth, apply your mind to the words of your parents;
through the power of visiting sacred fords and observing vows, your sin shall go to destruction.
O son Kulaṭa, you have indeed engaged in the company of a prostitute, which is most inauspicious."
Having renounced [worldly life] and become devoted to Brahman, fix your mind upon the practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*).
[Do not dwell] in the flesh and wine of sensual objects, which constantly increase sin;
for from that comes the state of a thief, and from that indeed, hell.
Therefore, having offered all the materials to the Lord, the Sovereign, Viṣṇu, the Victorious One, the Master of the World, you yourself should eat while restraining your speech.
Abandoning atheism and reviling the gods, apply your mind [to devotion].
The Self is eternally free from all fear, and Caṇḍikā is the power of the Self.
The gods are the limbs of the Self, dwelling within the secret cave of all living beings.
Knowing them thus, perform their worship for the pacification of sin.
Having heard these words of theirs, they went toward another sacred ford (tīrtha) and propitiated Śiva, who assumes all forms, for the sake of the lore (vidyā).
At the end of a year, Mahādeva granted them the Saṃjīvanī lore.
Having reached the forest and arrived there, they prepared themselves for the test;
he cast excellent water purified by mantras onto the bones of a dead tiger,
and by the power of that mantra, they were transformed into a cage.
Right upon that, the libertine poured water sanctified by mantras;
by that mantra, it became thick flesh and blood. And the sensualist likewise poured auspicious water over it.
By the power of that mantra, the tiger regained its skin and life-force;
recognizing the tiger as being asleep, the atheist nevertheless offered water.
Awakened by the mantra, the tiger devoured those brahmins.
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus, the Vetāla addressed the king in this manner: "O King, which among them was the fool? Having heard this, the king replied as follows.
"The one by whom that tiger was awakened from sleep is considered even more foolish than he.
Having heard this, the best of the twice-born Vaitāla spoke again.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Collection of Histories of the Kali Age," in the Caturyuga-khaṇḍa (also known as the Pratisarga-parvan) of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
The Vetāla said:
"O King, in the village of Bilvatī, situated between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā,
I was formerly in a previous birth a lord of the earth named Kṣatrasiṃha."
In that village lived a Brahmin, a master of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences,
known as Śambhudatta, who was devoted solely to the worship of Rudra. He had two sons, both of whom were proficient in all branches of learning.

The elder brother was known as Viṣṇubhakta, while the powerful one named Līlādhara became a devotee of Śakti. His younger brother was heard to be named Mohana. Once, that lion among Kṣatriyas, desiring to perform a sacrifice for the sake of the sacrificial rite, [set out].
