Having summoned Śambhudatta, who was skilled in dharma and accompanied by his son,
he himself performed the goat sacrifice, which is dear to the gods. Śambhudatta, however, being advanced in years and devoted solely to the worship of Śiva, [proceeded with the rite].
Having established four wheels and a water-pot that grants the accomplishment of one's purpose,
the king joyfully performed a fire-sacrifice with beautifully prepared and delightful oblations;
then, having summoned a goat, the monarch worshipped it according to the prescribed rites.
But Līlādhara, the compassionate, wise devotee of Viṣṇu, seeing that goat on the verge of death, spoke these words with indignation:
"A terrible hell is deserved by this injury to a living being."

Hearing those words of his elder brother, "The Lord Viṣṇu, the ruler of all, is defiled by the sacrifice of violence," Mohana laughed loudly with gentle prelude; then, with a humble mind, he spoke these words.
O brothers, in former times during the Satya Yuga, there were Brahmins devoted to sacrifice who,
having understood the supreme Vedic revelation that "one must indeed sacrifice with a goat," and considering the goat to be superior even to sesame seeds for the oblation, set their minds upon it.
Then Śakra and the other gods, having gathered in the midst of the fire, spoke these sweet words: "Your opinion yields no fruit;
according to the Vedas, the goat is known as 'aja,' therefore one should sacrifice with that."
Having heard these words of theirs, the sages were struck with wonder. In the meantime, Pitṛyoni, who dwells in the Amāvasu constellation,
ascended a supreme celestial chariot and spoke fearlessly to the sages.
"A sacrifice with a goat should be performed for the sake of satisfying the gods.
Having heard these words of his, they did so and went to Śiva.
Therefore, O high-minded one, you too should perform a sacrifice together with me.
Having heard these terrible words, the noble-minded and righteous Līlādhara spoke to Mohana: "In the Tretā Yuga, sacrifice (yajña) came into being;
indeed, the world in the Tretā age became permeated with the quality of passion (rajas)."
"In the Satya Yuga, there was no violence; therein Dharma had four feet. The gods were gratified by sacrificial offerings (havya), not by meat produced from blood.
Having heard this, that lion among Kṣatriyas abandoned the goat, who was overcome with fear.
Then, O King, he performed the final oblations with fruits and other offerings. In the meantime, the goddess Tāmasī, overcome with rage,
set the city ablaze along with its men and women.
By the power of Mahāmāyā, Śambhudatta, who was dear to Śiva, became greatly intoxicated with divine madness; having cast off his body, he went to heaven.
At that time, there was a brahmin named Līlādhara who supported himself by means of ten sons.
He taught the children in the auspicious village of Padmapura.
Then King Kṣatrasiṃha went into the presence of Mohana and obtained the favor and grace of the Mother of the Gods.
Mohana said:
Through the recitation of the seed-mantra (*bījamantra*), Brahmā attained the power of Brāhmī.
Homage to you, O Mother; repeated salutations to the Great Heroine (*Mahāvīrā*).
Having chanted the *Saptaśatī*, Viṣṇu obtained the Vaiṣṇavī power;
therefore, salutations to you, O Mother, salutations again and again to Mahālakṣmī,
whose sons are the Praṇavas and who is beloved by the Fourth Puruṣa.

Salutations to you, O Mother; salutations again and again to you, the Praṇava. Salutations again and again to that Mother, by whom this visible world was born, by whom the universe is indeed protected, and in whose body the entire cosmos resides.
Śacī, Siddhi, Mṛtyu, Prabhā, and the celestial hosts;
Svāhā, Nirṛti, Rātri, Ṛddhi, and Bhukti—all these have originated from you.
You are indeed the beloved of the world-protectors; O Mother of the World, salutations, salutations!

"You are indeed thirst, satisfaction, delight, policy, violence, forbearance, intellect, movement, censure, praise, envy, and shame; salutations, salutations to you! By the power of these eight [verses], the king Kṣattrasiṃha—
A virtuous man who had gone to the world of Śiva attained the state of a vetāla.
Therefore, O Vikramāditya, worship the eternal Durgā;
by the command of Śiva, O lord of the earth, I have come into your presence.
"O protector of the earth, I have thoroughly tested you through this exchange of questions and answers.
My abode shall be upon your two arms; slay all enemies on earth!
The bandits are destroyed; all cities and various fields [are yours]."
O King, establish the agreement according to the authority of the scriptures:
whichever king shall restore all the holy fords (tīrthas),
he indeed shall overturn that which was established by me.
This is the time of the narrative of Vikrama; indeed, he shall practice righteousness once more.
For the Dvāpara age shall proceed for twelve hundred years. At its end, a portion of Kṛṣṇa, possessed of great strength, will appear upon the earth.
For the sake of uprooting the Kali age and for the proliferation of the lineage of the Mlecchas,
all the sages, headed by Sūta, who dwell in the Naimiṣa forest and reside at Cakratīrtha,
assembled at Viśālā.
"O Great King, there will be those who delight in hearing the Purāṇas.
Having spoken thus, the Vetāla vanished right then and there;
King Vikramāditya attained supreme bliss.
Therefore, O best of sages, knowing that the twilight hour has arrived,
worship Śiva, the Lord of All, being fully established in meditative concentration.

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the *Kaliyugīyetihāsasamuccaya* (The Compendium of Histories of the Kali Age), within the *Caturyugakhaṇḍa* (Section on the Four Ages) of the *Pratisargaparvan* (Book on Secondary Creation) in the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard this, the sages residing in the city of Viśālā bathed in the Kedārakuṇḍa and worshipped Śiva mentally.
All of them remained steadfast in their meditative absorption for one full year.
In the meantime, King Vikramāditya, the sovereign,
bowed to the sages established in samādhi and praised them with a voice of supreme devotion.
Having stayed there, those sages went to Sūta and said this:
"This is that king for whose sake the story was thus described;
by your command, let us perform the horse sacrifice for the monarch."
"You indeed, staying at Cakratīrtha, should become intent on meditation.
Having said "So be it," Sūta returned with them and,
according to the prescribed rites, performed the great horse sacrifice (Aśvamedha).
To the east was the abode of Kapila, to the south the Setubandha,
to the west the edge of the Sindhu river, and to the north the Badarī forest;
the horse then proceeded swiftly and reached the Kṣiprā river.
Having cast off his body into the fire, he then went to the heavenly realm.
At the king’s sacrifice, all the gods arrived together with their wives;
however, the Moon did not come there, and the king became despondent.
At the conclusion of the sacrifice, having bestowed various gifts, the king, accompanied by the Vaitālas,
went to the world of the Moon and became as happy as the Moon-god himself.
"O King, O highly fortunate one, when the terrifying Kali age has arrived..."
"There is no place on earth where I can go; therefore, I do not come into your presence.
Having spoken thus, the Moon vanished after offering water consisting of nectar.
Indra, realizing this, arrived there in the guise of a brahmin and made a request.
That nectar was given by the King, and Śakra departed for heaven;
by that act, the fruit thereof arose for him, for his lifespan became equal to a hundred thousand years.
At that time, there was a certain renowned brahmin named Jayanta.
Having attained that fruit through austerity, he went from Śakra to his own celestial abode.
Jayanta, describing it with a hundred thousand pieces of gold, gave it to Bhartṛhari;
having enjoyed it there, Bhartṛhari, established in yoga, departed for the forest.
Vikramāditya himself ruled this kingdom free from all thorns;
filled with joy, he lived for a hundred years and then ascended to heaven upon his death.
The sages, headed by Śaunaka, having learned of the king’s departure to the celestial realm, [proceeded to act].
Having gone there and prostrated before Sūta, they said, "Speak now the foremost Dharma.
To them, Sūta then recited the Purāṇas once more,
joyfully teaching them for a hundred years, consisting of five hundred thousand verses.
Having heard this, all those sages went to their own abodes, filled with joy.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Compendium of Histories of the Kali Age," within the Caturyuga-khaṇḍa (also known as the Pratisarga-parvan) of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Vyāsa said:
Once, in the Naimiṣa forest, the sages headed by Śaunaka indeed questioned Sūta, the knower of the Purāṇas, with humility:
"O Blessed One, speak for the benefit of the worlds regarding the four ages."
Who is worthy of worship and service, and who bestows desired objects? O Brahmin, tell me truly the means by which men may easily and surely attain auspicious fortune and achieve renown.

Sūta said: I ever praise the Lord Satyanārāyaṇa, whose eyes are like fresh lotuses, who is the vessel for the pastimes of Ramā, whose four arms possess limbs as beautiful as gold, who is the cause of the universe's protection, and who reduced Dhūmraketu to ashes in battle.
I salute Śrī Rāma, who is accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa, who is compassionate, who is joined by Sītā,
who is pure in essence, who is like a bee greedy for the lotus-face of Vaidehī, the destroyer of the descendant of Pulastya,
whose lotus-feet are worthy of worship, the best of gods, and the one who shows mercy to his devotees.

O King, listen to this history concerning Rāghava, who was served by Śatrughna, Hanumān, and Bharata; who destroys the impurities of the Kali age; who reveals the fulfillment of desires; who possesses the splendor of the faces of the foremost gods; who is made manifest by the Brahmins; who delights the wise among the learned; who is distinguished by his virtuous conduct; and whose life is the highest example for men.
Once, the yogi Nārada, desiring to bestow grace upon others,
while wandering through various worlds, arrived at the world of mortals. There, he saw all people beset by manifold afflictions.

Thinking in his mind, "By what means can the certain destruction of the suffering of these beings— who are afflicted by mental and physical ailments and being cooked by their own karmas— be brought about?", he then departed for the world of Viṣṇu.
There, one should meditate upon the god Nārāyaṇa, white in complexion and four-armed,
adorned with a conch, a discus, a mace, a lotus, and a forest garland;
his face is serene and peaceful, and he is praised by Sanaka and the other sages.
Having beheld that Lord of the gods of gods, he began to offer praise.
Nārada said:
"Salutations to You whose form transcends speech and mind, and who possesses infinite power."
Salutations again and again to the one who dwells within the middle of the *nāḍīs*, the god who is beyond qualities (*nirguṇa*), the Great Soul (*mahātman*);
to the one who is the primordial source of all, the benefactor of the worlds,
whose measure is boundless, and whose abode is austerity (*tapas*).
Sūta said:
Having heard this hymn of praise, Viṣṇu replied to Nārada:
"For what purpose have you come? What is it that dwells in your mind?"
"Tell me, O illustrious one; I shall tell you all of that.
Having heard this, Nārada spoke to Viṣṇu regarding the cause of everything.
Hearing Nārada’s words, [Viṣṇu] honored him, saying, "Excellent! Excellent!"
Listen, Nārada, I shall describe a single eternal vow:
in the Kṛta and Tretā Yugas it was Viṣṇu; in the Dvāpara Yuga he assumed many forms; but in the Kali age, the omnipresent Lord Satyanārāyaṇa bestows manifest fruit.
For Dharma has four feet, and truth is its means of accomplishment. By truth the world is sustained; upon truth Brahman is established.
Therefore, the Satyanārāyaṇa vow is remembered as the most excellent of all.
Having heard these words of Hari, Nārada spoke again: "O Lord,
O ocean of mercy, please tell me out of compassion all that concerns the fruit and the ritual procedure for the worship of Satyanārāyaṇa."
The Blessed One said:
"The four-faced Brahmā is not capable of describing the fruit of worshipping Nārāyaṇa;
listen, for I shall tell you this briefly before you."
Even one who is destitute shall become wealthy; one without a son shall have sons;
one who has lost his kingdom shall regain it; even the blind shall possess clear vision;
one who is bound shall be released from bondage; and one afflicted by fear shall become fearless.

O Brahmin, whatever one desires in the mind, one obtains that through the prescribed rite; in this very life, one should worship with devotion according to the injunctions. One shall indeed quickly attain that desire; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
Having bathed in the morning and become pure, and having first performed the cleansing of the teeth,
one should hold a sprig of *tulasī* and meditate upon Hari, who dwells in Truth—
Nārāyaṇa, white as a dense cloud, four-armed, and clad in precious yellow garments.
I worship Him whose face is serene, whose eyes are like fresh lotuses, and who is attended by Sanandana and others.
O Lord, I observe this vow for You: the worship of You at the hour of evening.
Having heard Your hymn, I indeed take refuge in Your grace.

Having thus resolved in his mind, he should perform worship in the evening. He should worship the Śālagrāma stone, adorned with five water-pots and a plantain-archway, along with gold, using hymns dedicated to the Self.
Having bathed [the deity] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), one should worship with sandalwood paste and other offerings.
Oṃ, salutation! We meditate upon the Blessed One, the eternally true God;
salutations again and again to You, the bestower of the four aims of life.
One should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times and perform oblations amounting to one-tenth of that number;
having performed the libation and purification, and having heard this narrative of Hari consisting of six chapters, which is headed by the Truth, one should thereafter seek His grace.
Having correctly divided all of that, he should cause it to be given:
the first portion to the teacher, the second to his own family,
the third to the listeners, and the fourth for his own sake.
One should give food to the Brahmins and then eat oneself while maintaining silence.
O divine sage, if one performs the worship of Satyanārāyaṇa according to this rite,
endowed with devotion and faith, [the fruit is attained].
One who observes the vow attains his desired objects in this very life.
Karma performed in this life ripens in a future birth;
likewise, karma performed in a future birth must always be experienced by men.

"Indeed, the Satyanārāyaṇa vow grants all desires in this world; by your command, I shall establish it right here in the midst of the earth. Having spoken thus, the divine Nārada vanished and departed for heaven.
"The Lord Nārāyaṇa himself has arrived in the city of Kāśī.

Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Compendium of Histories of the Kali Age," within the section on the Caturyuga-khaṇḍa (also known as the Pratisarga-parvan) of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:

Out of compassion, he manifested his own history through a Brāhmaṇa; I shall relate this narrative, a dialogue between Hari and a Brāhmaṇa. There is a city renowned as Kāśī, where there lived an excellent Brāhmaṇa.
A householder who was always distressed, yet possessed of sons and a wife,
known as Śatānanda and devoted to the vows of Viṣṇu— once, as he was walking along the road for the sake of alms, the Lord of Śrī [appeared before him].
He became visible to the eyes of the disciplined and exceedingly tranquil one.
Hari, in the guise of an aged brahmin, questioned that brahmin:
"O best of the twice-born, where are you going? Tell me, what is your livelihood according to your desire?"
Śatānanda said:
"O gentle one, for the sake of my wife and children, I live by the life of a mendicant;
I go to the doors of the wealthy to beg for excellent wealth."
Nārāyaṇa said:
"O twice-born one, you have always maintained the practice of begging for alms for a long time;
indeed, this is specifically the means for warding off [suffering] in the Kali age."
O Brahmin, according to my instruction, worship Satyanārāyaṇa;
seek refuge in the lotus-eyed feet of Hari, which pacify poverty and sorrow, remove all affliction, and bestow liberation.
Thus enlightened by Hari, whose nature is compassion, that brahmin asked again: "Who indeed is Satyanārāyaṇa?
The old brahmin said:
Possessing many forms, true to his promise, all-pervading, and stainless,
he has now appeared before your very eyes in the form of a brahmin.
The feet of Hari are the boat for those submerged in the ocean of suffering.

The virtuous go for refuge, not others who are devoted to sense objects. O twice-born one, having gathered the requisites for worship for the welfare of the worlds, honor him while meditating upon him; you must manifest this.
As he was speaking thus, the brahmin beheld Puruṣottama—
dark as a rain cloud, possessing four beautiful arms with the mace and other weapons,
clad in yellow garments, with eyes like fresh lotuses, and smiling.
Hearing that his lotus-feet were being kissed by swarms of bees from the forest garlands,
his body bristling with horripilation and his beautiful eyes filled with love, he fell prostrate upon the ground like a staff, praising Him with a voice faltering with emotion.
I bow to the Lord of the World, the creator of the cause of the world;
the protector of the helpless, the bestower of auspiciousness, the refuge, the sinless and pure one;
the unmanifest who has attained manifestation, and the liberator from the threefold suffering.

Salutations to Satyanārāyaṇa, the creator of this world; salutations to the one of pure being, the sustainer of the universe. Salutations to you, the formidable Time, the destroyer of the universe; salutations to you, the embodiment of the Self, the auspiciousness of the world.
Today I am blessed, today I am successful; today my life has become fruitful.
You, who are beyond the range of speech and mind, have come before my very eyes.
What fortune shall I describe? Or rather, I do not know whose fruit this is:
that this body of mine, so deficient in action and dull-witted, has been made fruitful.
"O Lord of the World, O Consort of Ramā, worship must be performed;
by what rite? Out of compassion, O All-pervading Lord, please command me.
Hari, the Enchanter of the Universe, smiling, spoke sweetly to him.
O best of Brahmins, much wealth is not required for my worship;
worship me with mere faith using what is obtained without effort,
so that you may become free from distress, just as Jābāli was when seized by a crocodile.
Listen to the procedure, O chief of brahmins: one should desire the fruit with the mind and perform the worship according to the rules, having gathered all the necessary materials for the rite.
One should take half a *seṭaka* or similar measure of wheat flour.
That powder, mixed with an equal amount of milk and blended with sugar and other ingredients,
should be offered to Hari along with ghee;
it is dear to Hari when combined with cow's milk, curd, and cow's ghee.
Having bathed the Śālagrāma stone with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta)— which are dear when mixed with honey and Ganges water—
and with fragrant flowers, food offerings, and captivating Vedic hymns;
One should worship with incense, lamps, food offerings, betel leaves, and so forth; likewise,
one intent on devotion should worship with sweet foods and drinks, honors, edibles, and meals, as well as with fruits and flowers that bloom in their respective seasons.
Surrounded by Brahmins and his own kinsmen, and filled with faith,
he shall listen with great reverence to my discourse together with you—
the history of the king, as well as that of these Bhilla merchants.
At the conclusion of the discourse, one should bow with devotion and then distribute the *prasāda*.
Having received the *prasāda*, one should consume it with reverence and without hesitation.
"I find no peace through material offerings and the like as I do through exclusive devotion alone."
O best of Brahmins, those men who worship according to this rite,
being endowed with sons, grandsons, and wealth, and having enjoyed unsurpassed pleasures,
attain my presence at the end and rejoice with me.

"Whatever desire one who observes excellent vows may cherish, that very thing he shall obtain. Having spoken thus, Viṣṇu vanished; and the brahmin, too, having attained happiness, bowed and departed as instructed, his mind filled with curiosity.
"Today, Nārāyaṇa is to be honored by me with alms that are obtained [spontaneously].
Having resolved thus in his mind, he went to the city seeking alms;
and without even the words "give," he obtained vast wealth.
With a mind full of curiosity and agitation, she went to her own home;
she related the entire account, and the Brahmin woman approved with affection. By her husband's command, she respectfully gathered a collection of materials.
Having summoned his kinsmen, friends, and those present there, he said,
"Surrounded by my own attendants, I shall worship the god Satyanārāyaṇa.
Through his devotion, the blessed Lord Satyanārāyaṇa himself was pleased.
At the conclusion of the discourse, the Lord, who is affectionate toward His devotees, appeared, desiring to grant a boon.
The Brahmin chose his heart’s desire: the attainment of happiness in this world and the next, supreme devotion to the Blessed One, and likewise the vow of those associated with Him.
"O Hari, grant me a chariot, an elephant, a beautiful mansion, and a lovely horse made of gold;
grant me wealth, a multitude of male and female servants, cows, land, and bulls that yield fine milk, as well as servitude.
"So be it," said Hari, and then the Lord vanished.
The Brahmin, too, had his purpose accomplished, and all the people were filled with wonder;
bowing prostrate on the ground, they respectfully obtained his favor and returned to their respective abodes, exclaiming, "Blessed! How blessed!"
Thereafter, the worship of Satyanārāyaṇa spread throughout the world;
it bestows the fulfillment of desires, grants liberation and worldly enjoyment, and removes all impurities.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Compendium of Histories of the Kali Age," within the *Caturyugakhaṇḍa* (also known as the *Pratisargaparvan*) of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
There was a certain righteous king named Candracūḍa, renowned in Kedāra-Maṇipūraka, who was devoted to the protection of his subjects.
Peaceful, sweet-spoken, steadfast, and devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa,
he had as his enemies the Mlecchas dwelling in the Vindhya mountains.
A battle took place between him and those exceedingly powerful and cruel foes.
By means of slings, iron clubs, and other projectiles,
the great army of the moon-crested Lord, skilled in the art of *bhuśuṇḍī* combat, was sent to the city of Yama;
likewise, a hundred chariots, a thousand elephants, and as many horses were destroyed.
Five thousand foot soldiers died and went to the city of heaven;
five thousand robbers, who fought with deceit, also died.
That illustrious one was attacked by those barbarians who fought with hypocrisy.
Having abandoned his kingdom and city, he went alone to the forest;
under the pretext of visiting holy places, that king arrived at the city of Kāśī,
where he saw the god Nārāyaṇa, who is worthy of worship in every single house.
He beheld the city, endowed with wealth and grain;
that auspicious city was to be known as just like Dvārāvatī.
And the moon-crested Lord, having seen this unsurpassed wonder, was filled with amazement.
Seeing Lakṣmī restrained by truth and endowed with virtuous conduct and righteousness,
and hearing of that constant joy and the worshiper of the God of Truth,
he fell at his feet and bowed down with great delight.
O King of Birds, salutations to you, O ever-blissful one of great intellect!
Knowing that my kingdom has been lost, please uplift me out of compassion,
so that the Lord Janārdana, the beloved of Lakṣmī, may be pleased with me.
"Tell me likewise what vow is appropriate for the destruction of sin, which pacifies suffering, grief, and the like, and increases wealth and grain.
Sadānanda said:
"It pacifies suffering, grief, and so forth, and increases wealth and grain."

O King, the Satyanārāyaṇa vow brings about good fortune and progeny, grants victory everywhere, and causes the satisfaction of the Lord of Śrī; one should perform it at the onset of night on whichever day one chooses.
One should construct an archway (toraṇa) and other structures adorned with plantain pillars,
provided with five water-pots and equipped with five banners.
In the center of that, the practitioner of the vow should have a beautiful altar constructed by the twice-born.
Having installed there an image of Kṛṣṇa made of stone and endowed with gold,
one should perform worship with perfumes and other offerings while filled with loving devotion. Sleeping on the ground and meditating upon Hari, one should pass seven nights in this manner.
Having heard this, that king worshipped the God in Kāśī.
At night, the gracious Lord gave an excellent sword to the king.
Having obtained that sword which causes the destruction of the enemy faction, the best of kings—
Having bowed to Kedāramaṇi, who is eternal bliss, he departed;
having slain six hundred bandits and seized their great wealth,
he worshipped Hari on the auspicious bank of the Narmadā.
Month after month, on the full moon day, the best of kings,
endowed with loving devotion, worshipped Satyadeva according to the prescribed rite. By the power of that vow, he became the lord of a hundred thousand villages.
Having ruled for sixty years, he went to the city of Viṣṇu at the end [of his life].

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Restoration of Candracūḍa," in the Kali Age History Compendium, which is an alternative section of the Caturyuga-khaṇḍa within the Pratisarga-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
Now hear this ancient history: how the Bhillas, seeking their livelihood,
wandering constantly through the forest as Niṣādas carrying wood,
once went from the forest to the city of Kāśī to sell their timber.
Then, one man, distressed by thirst, went to the hermitage of Viṣṇudāsa.
There he beheld Hari, who possessed vast splendor and was attended by brahmins;
having drunk water, he was struck with wonder, thinking, "Whence comes this wealth for a mendicant?"
"Having reflected in his heart, 'This Brahmin who was seen previously as possessing nothing is now seen today as having great wealth,' he asked that best of the twice-born:
'O Brahmin, from where has this prosperity of yours come, and how did your misfortune depart?'"
"Command me, O illustrious one; I wish to hear this according to the truth.
Sadānanda said:
"What is not obtained by serving the limbs of Satyanārāyaṇa?"
One does not obtain any happiness without compassion for him.
The Niṣāda said:
"Oh, what is this greatness in the worship of Satyanārāyaṇa?"
You ought to instruct me in the ritual procedure along with its attendant services;
for among virtuous, equanimous, and benevolent beings,
there is nothing that should be concealed if it serves to alleviate the suffering of those who are afflicted.
Thus questioned, he spoke this ancient narrative (itihāsa) to explain the ritual procedure:
"O protector of the earth, King Candracūḍa came to my hermitage at Kedāra-Maṇipūraka for the sake of worshipping Satyanārāyaṇa."
Desiring to hear the ritual procedure, he addressed me with respectful words. O son of a Niṣāda, listen to that which was said by me to him:
"Whether a person be free from desire or have some longing in mind, having first formed a mental resolve..."
One should offer as an oblation finely ground wheat flour mixed with half its weight of sugar and other ingredients, prepared with honey, fragrant substances, and ghee, according to one's means.
Having bathed the deity with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), one should worship with sandalwood paste and other offerings.
One should then offer milk-rice, cakes, parched grain, curd, and milk;
and with various fruits, flowers, and delightful incense and lamps,
one should worship with supreme devotion, using extensive offerings if one possesses the means.
The Blessed One, being completely full in every respect, would never accept honor based on mere devotion as He would through the accumulation of material wealth;
thus Janārdana rejected the royal worship offered by Duryodhana.
The Lord accepted hospitality while staying at Vidura’s hermitage;
having eaten Sudāman’s grains of rice— things difficult for mortals to obtain—
Hari joyfully bestowed riches upon him, for devotion alone is required.
Gopa, Gṛdhra, the merchant, the hunter, Hanūmān, and Vibhīṣaṇa—
those others who were evil-minded Daityas, such as Vṛtra, Kāya, Ādha,
and the rest, having reached the presence of Nārāyaṇa, rejoice even today, being under His control.
Having heard this, the king respectfully prepared the materials for worship;
having obtained wealth, he rejoices on the banks of the Narmadā.
O Niṣāda, you too should worship Satyanārāyaṇa with devotion.
"Having attained happiness in this world, may you obtain proximity [to the Divine] at the end.
Having thus prostrated before the bull among the twice-born, the Niṣāda felt his purpose fulfilled;
he then went and told his own people of the greatness of serving Hari.
With joyful minds, they all respectfully made this agreement:
"We shall perform the worship of Satyanārāyaṇa with whatever wood we obtain, according to the ritual for sacred trees, together with our entire families."
Having thus resolved in their minds, they sold the wood and obtained four times the wealth; delighted,
they returned to their respective homes and joyfully related the entire account from the beginning to their wives.

Having heard them, they were delighted in heart and performed worship with reverence. At the conclusion of the discourse, bowing with devotion, they received his grace and gave that excellent powder to their own kin and to others.

O best of the twice-born, through the power of that worship, the Bhillas— along with their sons, wives, and others— obtained wealth upon the earth and the most excellent eye of knowledge; having enjoyed pleasures as they desired, those who were formerly poor and blind [attained this].
They indeed went to the abode of Viṣṇu, which is difficult even for yogins to attain.

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Compendium of Histories of the Kali Age," in the Kaliyuga-section, which is also known as the Caturyuga-khaṇḍa, within the Pratisarga-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said:
Now I shall relate to you this well-composed narrative,
concerning how a virtuous merchant attained his goal through the instruction of a king.
The illustrious King Candracūḍa was the lord of Maṇipura.
Together with his subjects, he worshipped the Lord Satyanārāyaṇa.
Then, a virtuous merchant named Lakṣapati, residing in Ratnapura,
having filled his ships with wealth, was traveling along the riverbank.
He beheld a vast world, delighting in various villages,
adorned with canopies fashioned from jewels and pearls;
and he heard the recitations of the Vedas accompanied by songs and instrumental music.
Having beheld a beautiful place, he commanded the helmsman:
"Bring the ship to anchor here; I wish to see a marvel.
Thus instructed by his master, the helmsman, together with his attendants, did accordingly.
Having ascended from the edge of the bank, those heroic mountain-like pilots, sporting with the grace of wrestlers,
fought with the playful movements of wrestlers.
Having himself ascended, he respectfully questioned the people along with his ministers.
Having observed a highly auspicious site for sacrifice, he went forth with joy.
"What shall be done here by you, O members of the assembly, who are honored by the world?
The members of the assembly all replied: "The Lord Satyanārāyaṇa [is the one]."
He is honored together with his kinsmen by the king who is compassionate toward the world;
through the worship of Satyanārāyaṇa, he has obtained a kingdom free from thorns.
One seeking wealth obtains riches, and one seeking a son obtains an excellent son.
One seeking knowledge obtains vision, and one afflicted by fear becomes fearless;
a man attains all his desires through the worship of the True Sun.
Having heard the ritual procedure from him, he should repeatedly bind a cloth around his neck.
Prostrating himself like a staff, he spoke, delighting the members of the assembly:
"O Blessed One, I am childless; my sovereignty is in vain and my efforts are in vain.
By your grace, may I obtain either a son or a daughter."
"Having fashioned a golden banner, I shall worship the Treasure of Compassion.
Hearing this, the members of the assembly said, "May your desire be fulfilled.
Then, having bowed to Hari, the members of the assembly partook of his grace.

The virtuous man went to his own home, meditating on Hari in his mind. When he had arrived at his house, noble women with auspicious offerings in their hands performed various auspicious rites as was appropriate.
The virtuous one entered the inner apartments amidst great joy and auspicious ceremonies. Having bathed after her menses, the chaste Līlāvatī attended upon her husband;
having conceived, that virtuous woman gave birth at the proper time.
The virtuous man attained supreme joy upon bestowing his daughter— who possessed eyes as tremulous as lotuses and who brought delight to her kinsmen— and he distributed great wealth.
Having summoned Brahmins learned in the Vedas, he caused the auspicious rites to be performed.
Having caused a birth certificate to be written, he gave her the name Kalāvatī. Resembling the digits of the moon, that Kalāvatī grew up;
for Gaurī is eight years old, and Rohiṇī is nine years old.
A girl becomes ten years old, and thereafter she matures and reaches her menses. Seeing that she had matured with time, he thought of marriage.
He heard that in the city of Kāñcanapura there was a merchant named Śaṅkhapati.
A virtuous man of noble birth, endowed with beauty, perfection of form, good character,
and the quality of magnanimity, chose him as a suitable husband for his daughter; and at an auspicious moment, amidst various auspicious rites, he took her hand in the presence of the sacred fire.
To the accompaniment of the sounds of Vedic instruments, the virtuous sage, his mind filled with great joy, gave away the maiden according to the prescribed rites,
and bestowed gems, pearls, corals, garments,
and ornaments for the sake of auspiciousness.
Then, out of love, he settled his son-in-law in his own home;
the virtuous man regarded him as a son, and the wise youth regarded him as a father.
After a great deal of time had passed, there was the worship of Satyanārāyaṇa.
Having forgotten [her], she went forth again for trade along with her son-in-law.
Sūta said:
Then the virtuous man, taking various jewels, departed.
Having moored his ships, he traveled from country to country;
he reached a city on the banks of the Narmadā and took up residence there. Engaging in buying and selling, that high-minded man remained for a long time.
Because he had not practiced truthfulness through deed, mind, or speech,
the merchant soon experienced the heat of the ripening of that karma;
one night, while the king’s palace was shrouded in darkness, [he fell into a pit].
Having learned that everyone had fallen asleep and that great wealth had been stolen by thieves,
at dawn the king was praised by bards, panegyrists, and heralds.
Having performed his morning rites, the king entered the assembly hall.
Then a servant, a favorite of the king, arrived there and spoke these words: "Listen, O lord of the earth!
There are pearl necklaces and various kinds of jewels."
"The thieves who robbed us have all fled; we do not know [where they went], O King.
Thus addressed, the king Puṇyaśloka, the crest-jewel of the virtuous, spoke with eyes copper-red with anger: "Go forth, all of you, without delay!"
"Taking the fourfold army and the wealth, bring them to my side;
otherwise, I shall slay you along with your followers"—thus he commanded his messengers.
Having heard the king's words, those servants departed.
Having failed to purify the goods, which were mixed with stolen property, despite great efforts, he then became consumed by deep anxiety as night fell, thinking:
"Alas! The king will kill me along with my followers; what shall I do, and where can there be happiness?"
"Death here at the hands of the king's punishment would lead to the state of a preta;
however, death on the Narmadā bestows the world of Śiva.
Having thus reached this consensus, they went to the bank of the Narmadā.

The foreign merchant saw his vast wealth; he also saw a pearl necklace that had been snatched from the neck of this merchant. Concluding, "This man is a thief," he bound them both for the sake of his own protection.
He brought Sadhana along with his son-in-law into the presence of the king.
While Hari was thus hostile, the king did not even consider the matter;
instead, he ordered, "Take the wealth into the treasury and bind those two wicked-minded men."
By the king’s command, the messengers bound him in prison with iron chains upon his limbs and feet;
together with his son-in-law, the saint lamented intensely and repeatedly.
"Alas, son! Father! Father! "Son-in-law, where has the wealth gone?
Where are you, daughter and wife? Behold the reversal wrought by Fate!
Plunged into an ocean of sorrow, who shall rescue you two from this calamity?"
Indeed, I must have committed many acts disagreeable to the Dhātṛ in the past;
this is the power of that karma, for I do not know whose fruit it is,
such that both father-in-law and son-in-law are equally despondent over the twelve [months].
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Compendium of Histories of the Kali Age," within the *Caturyugakhaṇḍa* (also known as the *Pratisargaparvan*) of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
"I shall relate to you that auspicious account of Viṣṇu’s deeds, which removes the three-fold afflictions."
The wise who listen to this constantly dwell in the abode of Hari;
those who are hostile toward that Hari shall go to many hells.
His beloved is the goddess Kamalā, and he has four sons.
Dharma, sacrifice, the king, and the thief—all these bring about prosperity for Lakṣmī.
That which is given to Brahmins and to guests is called Dharma;
and that which is offered to the mothers and the deities with the utterances of "svadhā" and "svāhā" is indeed the sacrifice (makha).
The king is traditionally regarded as the protector of both Dharma and the sacrifice (Makha).
Indeed, he who harms these two is a thief; all such persons are servants of Dharma.
Where there is truth, there is Dharma; there, prosperity shall remain steadfast.
The wealth of that virtuous man, which was held by the king, was seized by thieves from one who lacked truthfulness; his wife, being deeply distressed, it is said,
sustained herself by selling her clothes, ornaments, and other possessions.
There was nothing at all to be cooked, and so she fell into great distress.
Then one day, the girl, having gone to the house of a Brahmin without food or clothing, saw the worship of Satyanārāyaṇa being performed.
Seeing the Lord of the World thus entreating her, she prayed to Hari:
"O Satyanārāyaṇa, O Hari! May my father and my husband come home;
I shall worship you," she said, making her request.
"So be it," said the Brahmins, and she then went to the hermitage.
Reprimanded by her mother, she was asked, "O auspicious one, where have you been staying for all this time?
She then related the account of her worship of Satyanārāyaṇa.
"O Mother, I wish to perform that which always yields visible results for men; you ought to grant me permission. It is my desire that Janaka and my lord come to this place."
Having resolved thus in her mind during the night, that Kalāvatī, seeking wealth, arrived at the house of the hidden Śīlapāla at dawn and said:
"O brother, give me some wealth so that the worship of Truth may be accomplished."
Having heard this, Śīlapāla gave five niṣkas of wealth, saying,
"O Kalāvatī, the remainder of your father's debt is now with me.
Having spoken thus and become free from debt, he departed for the performance of the Śrāddha rites at Gayā.

With that wealth, his daughter Līlāvatī also performed auspicious worship of Satya; together with her, she conducted the adoration with devotion. Through that exceptional worship, Nārāyaṇa became highly pleased.
In a city on the banks of the Narmadā, the king slept in his palace;
while the king was sleeping on a fine couch during the remainder of the night,
[someone] spoke in the guise of a Brahmin, awakening him with gentle words.
"Arise, arise, O Indra among kings! Release those two virtuous ones.
They have been bound without any offense; otherwise, death shall not be yours.
Thus was the king awakened by one in the form of a brahmin.

Then Viṣṇu indeed vanished; at that time the king, having awakened, rose up suddenly in amazement and meditated upon the eternal Brahman. In the assembly hall, the king informed his ministers of the cause of his dream.
And the great minister said to the king with truth, "O twice-born one,
I too have had a dream shown to me, as explained by an aged Brahmin;
therefore, O King, bring those two together and question them according to the prescribed rites."
Having brought him near, the king, adhering to the truth, asked the saint:
"From where do you two come? What is your lineage? Where is your residence, and in whose city do you dwell?
The saint replied:
"O Great King, our residence is in the delightful city of Ratnapura, and our birth is in the merchant caste. For the sake of trade, O King, commerce is our livelihood;
we come to your city to sell or purchase gems, pearls, and other such goods."
Having been captured by messengers upon our arrival, we have come into your presence.
When fate is adverse, what man indeed does not fall into such a state?
O Indra among kings, they had us arrested as jewel-thieves, even though we were without fault.
"O Indra among kings, reflect in truth that we two are not thieves. Having heard this and understood their certainty, as well as the reason for their imprisonment,
he cut the firm bonds and caused Lomaśa to be released.
Having had the necessary provisions prepared, the king fed them both;
he honored them throughout the city with garments, ornaments, and vehicles.
Thus honored, the virtuous man spoke to the king with humility:
"Beyond this, I have experienced manifold suffering in prison;
therefore, O Great King, O treasury of compassion, grant me permission to depart for my country.
Having heard these words of the virtuous man, the king spoke to the treasurer:
"By my command, fill the boats immediately with your mudrās!
Accompanied by his son-in-law, the saint has set out for his own country today amidst the auspicious sounds of songs and musical instruments; even now he has not yet performed service to Hari."
The god Satyanārāyaṇa bestows manifest fruit in the Kali age;
he himself, having become an ascetic, performed a mockery of the virtuous.
The ascetic said:
"O virtuous one, what dharma do you have for us that you depart, disregarding me? O good man, give an answer! [The other] replied: "Cast away the boats quickly!
O Master, I have no wealth; they are filled only with creepers, leaves, and such."
"I shall go to my own place by boat; what fruit is there in this conflict?
When addressed thus, the ascetic replied with the words, "So be it," and in an instant, the wealth of the virtuous man vanished, leaving nothing but creepers and leaves.
Thinking that there was no wealth on the boats, the virtuous man became distressed with anxiety:
"What is this? For what reason has my wealth gone, and where has it vanished?
His mind was deeply pained, as if struck by a thunderbolt.
"Where shall I go? Where shall I stay? What shall I do? Whence shall I obtain wealth?
Thus the virtuous man lamented again and again, fallen into a swoon;
later, having been awakened by his son-in-law, he was overcome with remorse.

Taking his garment from his neck, he bowed to the ascetic and asked, "Who are you? The lordly Gandharva said, "I do not know whether you are a god among gods or some other being; I do not know your prowess."
"Command me, O illustrious one, regarding the cause of that mockery.
The ascetic replied:
"The self alone is the enemy of the self; likewise, in this world, there is both the pleasant and the unpleasant."
"Abandon this foolishness, O holy man; do not engage in vain talk.
Thus entreated, the virtuous and very wealthy man did not understand.
Again, out of compassion for his past karma, that ascetic spoke.
O King, when Candracūḍa worshipped Satyanārāyaṇa,
you— who were childless for a long time and desired sons and daughters—
did not remember to pray; now you grieve in vain.
The god Satyanārāyaṇa is all-pervading and the bestower of fruits;
O evil-minded one, how can you attain perfection by disregarding him?
Remembering the boon he had previously received, he called to mind the Lord of the Universe.
He beheld that ascetic, the god Satyanārāyaṇa;
having prostrated on the ground with his body and circumambulated him again and again,
the virtuous man there praised the ascetic with a voice choked with emotion.
The saint said:
I bow to you, O Satya, who are the embodiment of truth, whose promises are true, who are Hari as Satyanārāyaṇa,
and who are the truth by virtue of which the world exists.
Those whose minds are deluded by Your Māyā do not perceive their own welfare;
they are perpetually submerged in the ocean of suffering, yet they imagine happiness within that very misery.
"I am a fool, blinded by the pride of wealth, my vision clouded by intoxication."
I do not know how I, with a deluded mind, failed to see my own welfare;
forgive my wickedness, O Hari, abode of austerity, salutations to You!
Command me to be Your servant, so that I may remember Your two feet.
Having thus offered praise, he deposited a hundred thousand gold coins with his family priest,
saying, "I shall go to my residence and worship the Lord Satyanārāyaṇa.
Nārāyaṇa, being pleased, said, "May your desire be fulfilled."
"Endowed with sons and grandsons, having enjoyed unsurpassed pleasures,
you shall finally attain my presence and rejoice with me.
Having spoken thus, Viṣṇu vanished, and the virtuous man went to his own hermitage.
Protected by Satyadeva, he reached home in seven days;
having arrived near the city, he sent a messenger quickly to the hermitage.
Upon reaching the house, the messenger spoke to Līlāvatī:

The virtuous man arrived together with his son-in-law, having accomplished his purpose; the chaste woman, accompanied by her daughter, remained for the worship of Satyanārāyaṇa. Having entrusted the burden of the worship to her daughter, she went to the vicinity of the boat.
Surrounded by her circle of friends and having performed the auspicious marriage rites,
Kalāvatī, disregarding the favor [of her parents], went in haste to drink from the lotus-face of her husband, like a female cakorī bird at the end of the day.
Then, due to his lack of faith, the ship of Naukāśaṅkhapati sank into the midst of the water at that very moment along with his son-in-law. Seeing his son-in-law submerged, he fainted and lamented.
But Līlāvatī, seeing that, fainted and lamented;
then Kalāvatī, seeing it, fell to the ground in a swoon,
crying out, "O beloved of my beloved!", like Rambhā struck down by the wind.
Alas, O Lord, dear one, knower of dharma, you who are skilled in compassion! Deprived of you as my husband, I have been rendered hopeless by fate.
How is it that half of my husband has departed; how can half of my body remain alive?
Sūta said:
Kalāvatī was skilled in the fine arts; her soles were as tender as red coral;
her lotus-eyes shed drops of water; and her bud-like breasts were adorned with strings of pearls.
"Alas, Satyanārāyaṇa, Ocean of Truth! Lift me up, for I am sinking in separation from her!
Hearing this cry of distress, the Blessed One spoke these words arising from the sky:
"O virtuous one, let Kalāvatī quickly partake of my grace."
"After that, having arrived here, she will obtain a husband; do not grieve.
Hearing these words in the sky, she was amazed and acted accordingly;
by the grace of Nārāyaṇa, Kalāvatī obtained a husband.
Right there, the virtuous man, filled with joy and endowed with supreme devotion,
performed the worship of Satyadeva with one hundred thousand mudrās.
By the power of that vow, he became possessed of sons and grandsons.

Having enjoyed pleasures with joy, he died and went to the city of heaven. Indeed, that man who listens to this history with devotion becomes even more dear to Viṣṇu and shall attain the fulfillment of his desires.
Thus, O Brahmin, has been narrated to you this supreme vow among all vows,
the highest merit in the Kali age, originating from the mouth of Brahmā.

Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Satyanārāyaṇa Vow," in the *Kaliyuga Itihāsa Samuccaya*, which is another name for the *Caturyuga Khaṇḍa* within the *Pratisarga Parvan* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
The sages said:
"O Blessed One, the ancient ones have declared that secret-born action has been proclaimed;
and among all vows, the Nārāyaṇa-vrata is the most excellent."
O Sūta, through your mouth I have heard that which destroys the threefold suffering;
now I desire to hear about the supreme rite born of the Liṅga. Indeed, among all forms of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), what is the highest?
"Tell me that, O one of great wisdom; in my opinion, you are omniscient.
Sūta said:
"In former times, during the Kali age, there was an excellent brahmin named Pitṛśarman."
A knower of the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, yet filled with fear of the realm of Yama,
he perceived that the Kali age was a most terrible time born of unrighteousness;
seeing it as the expansion of Yama’s kingdom, he then became overwhelmed with anxiety.
"By which stage of life (āśrama) or caste (varṇa) would my welfare be secured here?
For in the Kali age, the path of renunciation is shattered by hypocrisy and heresy;
there is no forest-dweller (vānaprastha) in the Kali age, and celibacy (brahmacarya) exists only here and there."
The duty of the householder is said to be the best of all duties.
Therefore, I must take a wife in this terrible Kali age,
provided that she follows the inclinations of my mind.

"Then my birth would be fruitful and my welfare would be secured here. Having thus resolved, he worshipped the supreme Śivā, the bestower of auspiciousness, with sandalwood paste and other offerings, and praised her in his mind.
Pitṛśarman said: Salutations to the Sovereign of All, the embodiment of the universe, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss;
salutations again and again to Prakṛti, the all-encompassing, the absolute liberation.
Salutations again and again to the Fourth State (Turīyā), whose essential nature is the unity of the three qualities;
salutations again and again to the mother of the principle of Mahat and the creator of dualities.
O Mother of Brahmā, grandmother of Ahaṃkāra, salutations to you!

Obeisance, obeisance again and again to the Mother, who possesses distinct qualities and is pure; obeisance to Vidyā, to Śuddhasattvā, to Lakṣmī, and to her who consists of Sattva and Rajas. Obeisance, obeisance again and again to the Mother, to Avidyā, and thereafter to Śuddhi.
Salutations to Kālī, the source of the essence of beings and of darkness; salutations, O Mother, salutations!

Salutations to the Woman whose form is pure passion (rajas); salutations, O dweller in the three worlds! Salutations to Durgā, whose form consists of passion and darkness; salutations again and again!
Having heard this hymn of praise by the Goddess,
she herself then bestowed her grace upon the daughter of the Brahmin Viṣṇuyaśas.
Having married that goddess— who was indeed named Brahmacāriṇī— the twice-born man took her as his wife.
Having personally established righteousness within his heart, he dwelt in Mathurā;
indeed, he offered the seasonal gift (*ṛtudāna*) to his beloved Rajovatī,
and they had four sons who maintained the unity of the four Vedas.
Likewise, Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman, and Atharvaṇa were the four;
and Vyāḍi, an expert in the science of Nyāya, was the son of Ṛc.
Furthermore, Mīmāṃsa, world-renowned, was born as the son of Yajus.
Pāṇini was the son of Sāmanasya, and Śabdapāla was his son;
Vararuci, the most excellent, was the son of Atharvaṇa and a favorite of the king.
They all went to the assembly of Candragupta, the lord of Magadha.
The king honored them with great respect and then asked them,
"O sages, what indeed is the highest form of celibacy?
Vyāḍi replied, "O Great King, it is that man who is intent upon praising [the Lord]."

"According to the principle of logic, I consider him to be a true celibate student (*brahmacārī*) among all the gods. Furthermore, O King, Mīmāṃsaka said: 'That man who is supreme in sacrifice worships the gods through ritual action and honors them with perfumes and other offerings.'"
Having performed the oblation and libation toward the gods beginning with Brahmā, he should indeed accept their grace; he is remembered as a *brahmacārī*.
Having heard this, Pāṇini said: "O Candragupta, listen!"
The Supreme Brahman is threefold through the supreme vowels consisting of pure sound;
likewise, he who, as a celibate student, worships it with the recitation of the Sūtras encompassing the nominal stems, verbal roots, and grammatical classes, attains the Supreme Brahman.
Having heard this, Vararuci said: "Listen, O King of Magadha!
He who, having taken up the sacrificial thread, has come while dwelling in the preceptor’s household;
who maintains his staff, hair, and nails; who seeks alms and is devoted to the Vedas."
"And one who abides by the command of his guru is indeed remembered as a *brahmacārī*.
Having heard these words of theirs, Pitṛśarman spoke this:
"That brahmin who, while living as a householder, is devoted to his ancestors, gods, and guests..."
When his wife had reached her season, he approached her with controlled senses;
for he was indeed a celibate in the primary sense. Having heard this, the king spoke as follows: "O Master, that which has been said by you, who are illustrious and a knower of dharma—"
"When the terrifying Kali age has arrived, that indeed shall be considered my dharma.
Having spoken thus, he became a disciple devoted to the words of his teacher;
then, meeting death in that manner at the end, the king went to the heavenly world.
Pitṛśarman, too, having meditated upon Hari Dāmodara in his mind,
reached the Himālaya mountain and became intent on yogic meditation.

Thus ends the thirtieth chapter in the *Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, in the section on the secondary creation (*pratisarga-parvan*), within the sub-section known as the *Caturyuga-khaṇḍa*, specifically the collection of histories pertaining to the Kali Yuga.
The sages said:
"O Blessed One, among all sacred fords and all acts of giving, which is remembered as supreme? By performing what may one attain ultimate liberation in this terrible Kali age?"
Sūta said:
The son of Sāmana was the eminent and renowned Pāṇini;
he was defeated by the excellent disciples of Kaṇabhuj, who were learned in the scriptures.
Ashamed, Pāṇini went there toward another sacred ford;
having bathed in all the holy sites and offered libations to the ancestors and the gods,
he drank the water of Kedāra and became intent on meditation upon Śiva.
For seven days he subsisted on leaves, and thereafter he became one who lived on water;
then, at the end of ten days, for ten days he subsisted on air.
On the twenty-eighth day, Rudra spoke these words: "Choose a boon."
Having heard these words consisting of nectar, Pāṇini praised with a faltering voice Hara—
the Lord of All, the Lord of all Liṅgas, the beloved of Girijā.
Pāṇini said:
Homage to Rudra, the Great One, the Lord of All, who desires our welfare;
to the God who dwells with Nandin, and who bestows both knowledge and fearlessness;
homage to Bharga, the ender of evil, the infinite Creator.

Salutations to the Lord who took Māyā as his consort; salutations to you, O benefactor of the world! If you are pleased, O Lord of Gods, become the bestower of the root-vidyā. Grant me the supreme sacred site (tīrtha), O Father of the two mothers; salutations!
Sūta said:
Having heard this, Mahādeva joyfully bestowed the Sūtras,
which consist of all the phonemes and begin with the auspicious vowels *a*, *i*, *u*, and *ṛ*.

He who has reached the mental pilgrimage site (mānasa-tīrtha)— a lake of knowledge with truth as its water, which removes the impurities of passion and hatred— shall enjoy the fruit of all pilgrimage sites.
For the mental pilgrimage site is indeed great, bringing about the vision of Brahman.
"O Brahmin Pāṇini, I have given this to you; may you be one who has accomplished his purpose.
Having spoken thus, Rudra vanished, and Pāṇini went to his own home.
[He then composed] the Sūtrapāṭha, the Dhātupāṭha, and likewise the Gaṇapāṭha.
Having likewise fashioned a *liṅga-sūtra*, he attained supreme *nirvāṇa*.
Therefore, O best of the Bhārgavas, practice the mental pilgrimage (*mānasa-tīrtha*),
for it is there that the auspicious Gaṅgā herself, who embodies all holy places, has gone.
"There has never been, nor will there ever be, a sacred site superior to the Gaṅgā-tīrtha.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Compendium of Histories of the Kali Age," in the *Caturyuga-khaṇḍa* (also known as the *Pratisarga-parvan*) of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
In Totadarya, there was a certain twice-born man known as Bopadeva;
he was a devotee of Kṛṣṇa and a master of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.
He went to the beautiful Vṛndāvana, which is frequented by cowherds and cowherd-maidens.
He worshipped Janārdana, the God of gods, with his mind.
At the end of a year, Hari himself bestowed unsurpassed knowledge upon him;
through that knowledge, the narrative of the Bhāgavata was attained within his heart.
Śuka described that eternal narrative, which is the very embodiment of liberation, to the wise Viṣṇurāta. At the conclusion of the narration, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, Janārdana, appeared.
He spoke with affectionate words: "Choose a boon, O high-minded one!
Bopadeva said:
"Salutations to you, O Blessed Viṣṇu, the performer of grace for the worlds."
This entire universe, including gods, animals, and humans, is pervaded by you;
and those afflicted by the sufferings of hell find their purpose fulfilled in the Kali age through your name.
You have bestowed the *Bhāgavata*, composed by the illustrious Vyāsa.
"Tell me its greatness, if a boon has been granted by you.
The Blessed Lord said:
"Once, the Blessed Lord Rudra, Śaṅkara, was together with Bhavānī."
In a Buddhist kingdom filled with hypocrisy and heresy that had spread throughout the world, he beheld Bhūmituṅga at Kāśī and, filled with joy, prostrated himself, saying:
"Victory to you, O All-pervading Lord of Being, Consciousness, and Bliss; O Creator of the world's delight!"
Having heard this, Śivā said, "Which deity is superior to you?
He replied, "O Great Goddess, there is indeed a seven-day sacrifice here;
therefore, O fair-faced one, the purity of the earth has been attained in this place."
Having heard that she herself was the eternal Brahman and superior to all sacred fords (tīrthas), the goddess Śivā arrived at Guhyakālaya.
Accompanied by Rudra, she performed the purification of the ground there.
O twice-born one, Caṇḍīśa, Gaṇeśa, Nandī, and Guha were established there by the God of gods for the sake of protection. O Goddess, listen to this delightful narrative dwelling within my mind.
Having spoken thus, he entered into meditation and described his own form within seven days.
On the eighth day, opening his eyes and seeing that Śivā had fallen asleep,
the Blessed One, the benefactor of the world, awakened her at the conclusion of his discourse.
"How many verses have you heard? the Mother of the World asked upon hearing this.
[The sage replied: "The life-story of Śiva, beginning from the churning of the nectar, was narrated by him;
having heard it while staying within a hollow tree, a parrot attained longevity."
Protected by Pārvatī, that most beautiful parrot remained in the abode of Śiva,
intent on meditation upon me;
by my command, the parrot himself now dwells within your heart.

By him, the Bhāgavata-māhātmya has been obtained, which is difficult to attain. You indeed must go to the banks of the Narmadā and, having approached his father Gaṇdharvasena, King Vikrama, cause him to hear this auspicious narrative.
Indeed, the gift of the greatness of Hari is remembered as the supreme among all gifts;
it should be bestowed upon a worthy recipient who is wise and a devotee of Viṣṇu.
Even the gift of food to the hungry is not equal to that gift.
Having spoken thus, the god Bopadeva, his mind serene, vanished from sight.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Compendium of Histories of the Kali Age," within the *Caturyuga-khaṇḍa*, also known as the *Pratisarga-parvan*, of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
The sages said:
O Sūta, it is traditionally taught that the recitation of the Vedas is an action born of speech; yet,
because of the vastness of all the Vedas, we desire to hear by what hymn one may obtain the fruit of their recitation.
"O wise one, tell me that by which sins go to their dissolution.
Sūta said:
"In the kingdom of Vikramāditya, there was once a certain twice-born man on earth."
Known as Vyādhakarman, he was born to a Brāhmaṇa woman from a Śūdra father.
He was the wife of a twice-born man named Tripāṭhin; she was indeed called Kāminī, for she was constantly desirous of sexual union, her eyes rolling with intoxication.
Once, a twice-born man seeking a livelihood went to read the *Saptaśatī* in a beautiful village inhabited by many Vaiśyas belonging to the Devalaka clan;
there a month passed, yet he did not return to his own home.
Then that wicked woman, possessed of beauty and youth,
seeing the Niṣāda who lived by carrying loads of wood and was accompanied by his strength,
gave him five coins and, tormented by desire, enjoyed him.
Then she conceived a fetus formed by the seed of Vyādhi;
at the end of ten months, a son was born, and his father performed the birth rites.
When twelve years had passed, that rogue remained devoid of Vedic knowledge.
Because he constantly performed the work of a hunter, he indeed became a hunter;
thus, both mother and son, those lowest of the twice-born, were expelled by the twice-born [preceptor].
Tripāṭhī, however, being devoted to dharma, practiced celibacy.
Dwelling on the Vindhya mountain and reciting the Caṇḍikā hymn every day,
he quickly became liberated while yet alive through the grace of the Mother of the Universe. Both of them then went with joy and stayed in the forest at the house of the Niṣāda.
Day after day, under the guise of being a paramour, he accumulated great wealth;
though his livelihood was that of a hunter, he acted as a benefactor to his father and mother.
Once, by the turn of fate, he came to the temple of Śiva.

A rogue devoted to the livelihood of a thief stole the ornaments of a woman. Born among certain people, that thief was highly skilled in many forms of deception. Once, he came upon some cloth belonging to a twice-born man.
Indeed, having heard the primordial narrative from that lover of sound,
his mind turned toward Dharma through the power of the merit of recitation;
then, he gave all the wealth obtained by theft to that reciting Brahmin.
He became a disciple there and indeed chanted the imperishable mantra of Īśa;
by the power of that seed-mantra,
his intense sin emerged from his body in the form of worms of many colors and was consumed by heat.
At the end of three years, that best of the twice-born became free from sin;
having recited the *Akṣaramālā*, he chanted the *Ādicaritra*.
Then, after twelve years had passed, that brahmin went to Kāśī.
With supreme joy, he praised the Great Goddess Annapūrṇā,
who is worshipped with yellow pigment and other offerings, who is served by sages and gods,
who bestows eternal bliss, who grants supreme fearlessness, who is a mine of the jewels of beauty, who purifies by washing away all sins, and who is the sovereign lady of the city of Kāśī.
"O Illuminator of various worlds, Dispeller of great fear, Sustainer of the universe, Beautiful One, O Mother Annapūrṇeśvarī, who provides refuge through compassion, grant me knowledge!
Having thus recited this one hundred and eight times, his eyes motionless in meditation, he slept there joyfully; and in a dream, Śivā appeared before him.
Having imparted the knowledge of the Ṛgveda to him, he indeed vanished once more.
Rising up, that wise brahmin, having obtained that unsurpassed knowledge,
became the officiating priest for the sacrifices of King Vikramāditya.
At the conclusion of the sacrifice, having established himself in yoga, he departed for the Himalayas.
This meritorious account of the primordial deeds has been described to you, O Brahmin,
as to how that Brahmin, becoming one with Brahman, attained unsurpassed perfection.

Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the First Life," in the *Kaliyuga-itihāsa-samuccaya*, which is another name for the *Caturyuga-khaṇḍa* within the *Pratisarga-parvan* of the glorious *Śrī-Bhaviṣya-Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
O Brahmin, in ancient times, there was a Kṣatriya in Ujjayinī who was a perpetrator of violence against all beings.
There was a man famous as Bhīmavarman, who was a consumer of liquor and meat;
that wicked and sinful man, devoted to the company of prostitutes, killed and ate pigs and village cocks out of greed for flesh.
Having abandoned human flesh, that carnivorous being became a consumer of other [meats].
When much time had passed in this manner, the exceedingly wicked Bhīmavarman,
though still young, fell under the power of the fire of cholera and died.
That wicked and timid man had the recitation of the Caṇḍikā performed;
by the power of that merit, he did not go to the hells.
Furthermore, that lord of the earth attained the status of a Kṣatriya in Māgadha.
Renowned as Mahānandin, he was devoted to the science of statecraft;
remembering his past lives, he became dedicated to the Vedic dharma.
He became a disciple of the wise and great Śākta, Kātyāyana.
Having given that middle *caritra* together with its seed-syllables (*sabīja*) to that king, the sage returned and became intent on the *Śakti* in the Vindhya mountains.
The king, for his part, [worshipped] the eternal Goddess Mahālakṣmī every day.
Having worshipped with rocanā and other substances while reciting the *Madhyamacaritra*,
they attained the status of a holy field through the grace of Mahāmāyā;
having abandoned their śūdra nature, they attained the state of kṣatriyas.
Within twelve years, his guru, who was devoted to Śakti,
caused a hundred thousand Caṇḍīs to be performed according to dharma, O King;
then the eternal Goddess, the Mother of the World, appeared.
To the king, he indeed bestowed dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa;
having enjoyed the pleasures desired by the gods, the illustrious Mahānandin finally departed for the supreme world honored by the deities.
"Thus, O Brahmin, has been told to you that destiny of the Yajus which was proclaimed;
indeed, it was attained by the Śūdra king through his conduct in his intermediate life.
In this manner, O Brahmin, has the majesty described by the excellent sage been narrated."
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Compendium of Histories of the Kali Age," in the *Catuḥyugakhaṇḍa* (also known as the *Pratisargaparvan*) of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
On the delightful mountain Citrakūṭa, variegated with various minerals...
There lived the highly wise teacher Patañjali,
who was a knower of the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, devoted to the Gītā-śāstra,
a worshipper of Viṣṇu, true to his word, and an expert in the Bhāṣya-śāstra.
Once that pure-souled one went toward another sacred ford;
in Kāśī, a great debate took place between him and Kātyāyana.
At the end of the year, the brahmin was then defeated by the devotee of the Goddess.
But that righteous-souled one, feeling ashamed, praised Sarasvatī.
Patañjali said:
"Salutations to the Goddess of great form; salutations, salutations to her who is the form of all."
Salutations to you, Śivā, the source of all auspiciousness, and to you, the illusory power (māyā) of Viṣṇu.
You alone are faith and intellect; you are wisdom and the science that brings about auspiciousness.
You alone are peace and speech; O Nārāyaṇī, salutations, salutations!
When the Brahmin had spoken thus, an incorporeal voice said: "O best of Brahmins, recite my life-story with a one-pointed mind;
by the power of that life-story, you shall truly attain knowledge."

"O Patañjali, the brahmin Kātyāyana’s prideful sense of royal status was overcome by his devotion to me; thus he has achieved victory. Having heard these words of the Goddess dwelling in the Vindhya mountains, [he entered] the temple.

Having gone there, he worshipped her and praised her with the recitation of hymns. Having attained knowledge born of divine grace and being devoted to Viṣṇu, the Brahmin defeated Kātyāyana and experienced supreme joy.
Having established the vertical *ūrddhvapuṇḍra*, the *tilaka*, the *tulasī* garland around the neck,
and the mantra of Kṛṣṇa— which bestows auspiciousness— in every house, and likewise having done so for every person, he caused the *Mahābhāṣya* to be proclaimed with great joy.
He attained long life through the grace of Viṣṇu’s Māyā.
Thus, O Brahmin, I have described to you this supreme recitation among all those to be chanted.
What else do the great sages, Śaunaka and the others, wish to hear?
May all behold auspicious things; may no one experience suffering.
Lord Viṣṇu is auspiciousness; the one whose banner is Garuḍa is auspiciousness.
The lotus-eyed one is auspiciousness; Hari, whose abode is auspicious, is auspiciousness.

"Indeed, that man who is always pure and listens to this compendium of histories, seeking virtue, pleasure, and wealth, attains the supreme goal. Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Majesty of the Life of Uttama," within the *Kaliyuga-itihāsasamuccaya* (Compendium of Histories of the Kali Age), which is a sub-section of the *Caturyugakhaṇḍa* (Section on the Four Ages) in the *Pratisargaparvan* (Book of Re-creation) of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
This second section is completed.
Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
The sages said:
O Blessed One, you have described this time known as Vikrama,
which on earth is equal to the Dvāpara age with its twelve hundred-year limit.
O highly fortunate one, it was during this time that the divine pastimes were performed by the Lord.
"Tell us this very story; you are always omniscient.
Sūta said:
"Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and to Nara, the best of men..."
Then one should utter the victory of Goddess Sarasvatī and Vyāsa:
"When the great kalpa named Bhaviṣya had arrived, during the Vaivasvata interval,
at the end of the twenty-eighth Dvāpara age, a battle took place on Kurukṣetra."
All the Kauravas, who were fierce in battle, were utterly defeated by the Pāṇḍavas;
on the eighteenth day, victory belonged to the Pāṇḍavas.
At the end of the day, the Blessed Kṛṣṇa, perceiving the inescapable course of time, [acted].
He mentally praised Śiva, the eternal one whose form is yoga.
Kṛṣṇa said:
"Obeisance to the peaceful Rudra, the protector of beings, the one with matted hair."
"Salutations again and again to the Maker of Time, the Sustainer of the Universe, the Remover of Sins!
O Blessed One, protect the Pāṇḍavas, my devotees who are terrified of all beings.
Having heard this hymn of praise, Rudra remained seated upon the back of Nandin.
For the protection of the camps, Kṛṣṇa, bearing a spear in his hand, then went to Hastināpura at the king’s command; meanwhile,
the five Pāṇḍavas, having gone forth, dwelt on the bank of the Sarasvatī.
At midnight, the son of Droṇa, Bhoja, and Kṛpa arrived there;
they mentally praised Rudra, and Śiva granted them a path. Then the powerful Aśvatthāman took up the sword given by Śiva.
Having seized them, he swiftly struck those led by Dhṛṣṭadyumna;
having slaughtered them at will, the son of Droṇa departed accompanied by those two.
Only the charioteer of Pārṣata remained, surviving the slaughter and overcome with fear.
He described the Pāṇḍavas and how that destruction of men had occurred.
Realizing that Śiva was the perpetrator of the offense, Bhīma and the others were overcome with rage;
they struck the god of gods, the wielder of the Pināka bow, with their own weapons.
Their missiles and weapons entered the body of Śiva;
seeing this, they were all struck with wonder and struck him with their palms and fists.
Then Rudra cursed them: "You shall become worshippers of Kṛṣṇa."
"Therefore, we must indeed guard those who are worthy of death on this earth;
having attained rebirth in the Kali age, he shall experience the fruit of his transgression.
Having spoken thus, the god vanished, and the Pāṇḍavas were then filled with sorrow.
To turn away from their transgression,
all the Pāṇḍavas, accompanied by Kṛṣṇa and divested of their weapons, sought refuge in Hari;
they then praised Rudra with their minds, and Śiva appeared before them.
Having heard this, Kṛṣṇa said, "Choose a boon. [The sage] spoke thus:
"Grant those very weapons and missiles that were indeed destroyed within your body;
give them back to the Pāṇḍavas and show favor toward this curse."
Having heard this, Śiva said: "O Lord Kṛṣṇa, salutations be unto you!
O Master, there was no offense on my part; I was deluded by your command.
Under its influence, O Master, I uttered a terrifying curse."
My word shall not be otherwise; there shall be an incarnation of a portion [of the gods]. Yudhiṣṭhira will become the son of the King of Vatsa, known as Balakhānin, the lord of the city named Śirīṣa.
Bhīma, corrupted by harsh speech, shall be born in the womb of a mleccha;
he will be famous by the name Vīraṇa and will indeed become the lord of forest-dwellers and monkeys.
And the high-minded Arjunāṃśa, my devotee, shall also be born.
The son of Parimala himself is known as Brahmānanda;
indeed, he will become the mighty Nakula in Kānyakubja.
He is truly the son of Ratnabhānu, renowned by the name Lakṣmaṇa.
The powerful Sahadeva will be born as the highly intelligent Devasiṃha; O lion among kings, this son born of Bhīṣma will be known as Devasiṃha,
and he will be born in Ajamera as a partial incarnation of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Pṛthivīrāja will be his [Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s] son, and he is remembered as having Draupadī as his daughter;
she will be famous by the name Velā. Tāraka will indeed become Karṇa, and Rudra will likewise become Raktabīja on the surface of the earth.
"The Kauravas will be experts in the art of illusory warfare,
while all those on the side of the Pāṇḍus will be righteous and powerful.
Sūta said:
Having heard this, Hari smiled and said to the Supreme Lord:
"The Pāṇḍavas must indeed be protected by me through my descent as Śakti.
There is a beautiful city called Mahāvatī, fashioned by Māyādevī."
There, a son of the King of Deśa shall be born as a portion of mine;
he will take birth in the womb of Devakī and is known as Udayasiṃha. Āhlāda, a portion of my own abode, will be born as my preceptor.
"Having slain the kings born of the lineage of Agni, I shall indeed establish the Kali age.
Having heard this, the god Śiva vanished right there.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Narrative of Vikrama," in the *Kaliyuga-Itihāsa-samuccaya* (the Compendium of Histories of the Kali Age), within the *Caturyuga-khaṇḍa* (the Section on the Four Ages) of the *Pratisarga-parvan* (the Book of Re-creation) in the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
When morning had arrived, the Pāṇḍavas, grieving for their son,
performed the funeral rites for him and approached Bhīṣma.

Having heard the duties of kings, the duties of liberation, and the duties of charity in their proper divisions, they performed three horse-sacrifices, which are the highest of rites. Having ruled the kingdom for thirty-six years, they indeed departed for the city of heaven.
"Indeed, portions of him will be born for the further increase of the dharma of the Kali age.
Vyāsa said:
"Having spoken thus to all, that sage [will depart], and then Sūta will speak again."
"Go, all you sages; for I am under the influence of yogic sleep.
Established in samādhi at Cakratīrtha, I shall meditate upon that which transcends the three guṇas.
Having heard this, the sages dwelling in the Naimiṣa forest [departed].
Having established themselves in the perfection of yoga, they shall go into the presence of the Self.
When twelve hundred years have passed, those sages headed by Śaunaka will rise and perform their rites,
such as bathing and meditation, at Devakhāta.
Having done so, they will go to the presence of the Sūta and speak these words again.
The sages said:
"By the command of Śiva, this is the time for the narration of the *Vikrama* in the Dvāpara age."
"O Blessed One, tell me now of those kings who were disciplined on earth.
Sūta said:
"When Vikramāditya had ascended to heaven, many kings arose in various ways."
Likewise, there are eighteen kingdoms; hear their names from me:
at the western edge of the Indus River, at the Setubandha on the south, at the site of Badarī on the north, and near Kapilā on the east.
There were exactly eighteen kingdoms among them:
Indraprastha, Pāñcāla, Kurukṣetra, Kāpila,
Antarvedī, Vraja, Ājamīḍha, and Marudhanva.
Gauḍjar, Mahārāṣṭra, Drāviḍa, Kaliṅgaka,
Āvantya, Coḍupa, Vaṅga, Gauḍa, Māgadha,
and likewise Kauśalya should be known; their kings are each distinct.
Various languages were established there, and many teachers of the Dharma resided;
thus a hundred years passed, after which those Śakas and others,
accompanied by great multitudes, heard of the destruction of the Dharma.
Some, having crossed the river Sindhu, arrived in the Ārya country;
they came by way of the Himālaya mountains and by way of the Sindhu.
Having conquered the Āryas and subdued them, they returned once more to their own land.
Having taken their women, they attained supreme joy. In the meantime, King Śālivāhana,
the grandson of Vikramāditya, took possession of his father’s kingdom there.
Having conquered the invincible Śakas born in the regions of Cīna and Taittiri,
as well as the Bāhlīkas, Kāmarūpas, Romajas, Khurajas, and the deceitful [tribes],
he seized their treasuries and subjected them to punitive fines.
He established separate boundaries for the Mlecchas and the Āryas. It should be known that the region on this side of the Indus is the excellent kingdom of the Āryas,
while the region beyond the Indus was made the domain of the Mlecchas by that high-souled one.
