Once, however, the lord of the Śakas arrived at Himatuṅga;
there, in the midst of the Hūṇa country, the powerful king beheld a beautiful person standing upon the mountain— one with a fair-complexioned body and clad in white garments.
"Who are you? he asked him. Filled with joy, he replied:
"Know me to be the son of the Lord, born from the womb of a maiden, a proclaimer of the Mleccha dharma, and devoted to the vow of truth."
Having heard this, the king asked, "What do you consider to be dharma?
Having heard this, he replied, "O Great King, when the destruction of truth had arrived and the land of the Mlecchas had become lawless, I, Masīh, came here."
"I am the ink of the Dasyus, appearing as a terrifying presence;
having obtained that ink from the Mlecchas, I have attained the state of being ink.
Listen, O King, how I have established the Dharma among the Mlecchas."
Having purified the mind and removed the impurities of good and evil from the body,
a person should resort to the Vedic recitation (*japa*) and chant the supreme, stainless mantra with justice,
truthful speech, and one-pointedness of mind.
One should worship the Lord established within the solar orb through meditation;
for this Lord is directly immovable, yet the sun is always moving. He is the one who draws forth all the moving elements of reality from every side.
Thus, O protector of the earth, through this act, Masīhā has attained dissolution;
the form of the Lord, eternally pure and bestowing auspiciousness, has entered my heart.
And so, my name "Īśāmasīhā" has been established.
Having heard this, that king bowed to the worshipper of the Mlecchas and established him there in that dreadful abode of the Mlecchas;
the king then regained his own kingdom and performed the horse sacrifice.
Having ruled for sixty years, he departed for the heavenly world.
Listen now to what occurred when that king had ascended to heaven.

Thus ends the second chapter, concerning the era of Śālivāhana, within the *Kaliyugīyetihāsasamuccaya* (Compendium of Histories of the Kali Age), which is an alternative designation for the *Caturyugakhaṇḍa* (Section on the Four Ages) in the *Pratisargaparvan* (Book of Secondary Creation) of the glorious *Bhaviṣyamahāpurāṇa*.
The venerable Sūta said:
In the lineage of Śālivāhana there were ten kings;
having ruled for five hundred years, they departed for the other world.

Then, in due course, the established order became dissolved upon the surface of the earth. Seeing that the boundaries of conduct had perished, the powerful king known as Bhojarāja, the tenth ruler, set out on a world-conquest.
Accompanied by an army of ten thousand and joined by Kālidāsa as well as other Brahmins, he reached the far shore of the Indus after defeating the Mlecchas born of Gandhāra,
as well as the deceitful inhabitants of Kāśmīra and Nāra.
Having obtained their great treasury, he caused them to be punished. In the meantime, a Mleccha known as Mahāmada arrived, accompanied by his preceptor and surrounded by his disciples and followers.
And the king, having bathed Mahādeva— who dwells in the desert region—
with the waters of the Gaṅgā mixed with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
and having worshipped him with sandalwood paste and other offerings, praised Hara with his mind.
King Bhoja said:
Salutations to you, O Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain, who dwells in the desert lands;
salutations to the destroyer of the demon Tripura, who employs manifold illusions.
"To you who are protected from the Mlecchas, who are pure, and whose nature is Being-Consciousness-Bliss— know me indeed as your servant, come for the sake of refuge.
Sūta said:
Having heard this hymn of praise, the God spoke these words to the king:
"O Bhojarāja, you must go to the site of Mahākāleśvara;
the land is utterly defiled by Mlecchas and is renowned by the name Vāhīka."
Indeed, the noble Dharma does not exist here in this cruel land of Vāhīka.
That great illusionist who was previously burnt by me— Tripura, who had been sent by the Daitya Bali and has now returned— is here once more.
That increaser of the Daityas,
known as Mahāmada, who was intent on the conduct of a Piśāca, obtained from me that boon through improper means. O King, you must not go to that Piśāca land of rogues.
"O protector of the earth, by my grace, your purification shall be accomplished.
Having heard this, the king returned once more to his own country,
and Mahāmada, together with them, went to the shore of the ocean.
Skilled in the intoxication of illusion, he spoke with affection to the king:
"O Great King, the Lord has entered into the state of my servant;
O King, behold how he may eat the remnants of my food."

Having heard this and seen it thus, the king was struck with great wonder; yet his mind remained set upon the cruel religion of the Mlecchas. Upon hearing that, Kālidāsa, filled with rage and great pride, spoke:
"O rogue, this illusion was created by you for the purpose of deluding the king.
I shall slay that wicked Vāhīka, the lowest of men!
Having spoken thus, that illustrious brāhmaṇa remained intent on the recitation of the nine-syllable mantra.
Having recited the mantra ten thousand times, he performed the fire-oblation with its tenth part;
that master of illusion, having turned to ashes, attained the state of a Mleccha deity.
His disciples, terrified by fear, fled to the land of Vāhīka.
Having taken the sacred ash of their own guru, they attained freedom from intoxication;
they established it in the center of the earth and dwelt there, intent upon that state of being free from intoxication.
Thus the city became "Madahīna" (Free from Intoxication), and it is remembered as a holy site equal to other sacred places.
At night, he who possessed a divine form and was highly skilled in many illusions,
assuming a Piśāca body, spoke to the King of the Bhojas:
"O King, the duty of the noble (Ārya-dharma) is indeed remembered as the highest of all duties for you."
By the command of the Lord, I shall perform the Piśāca rite, which is terrible even to the Dharma.
That person who defiles me shall have his linga cut off, be shorn of his topknot, grow a beard, speak loudly, and become an eater of all things.
Without the Kaula path, they are mere beasts; in my view, they are fit to be devoured. Their consecration will be like that performed with a pestle or with blades of kuśa grass.
Therefore, those castes who possess pestles are indeed corrupters of dharma.
"Thus shall the Paiśāca dharma be established by me.
Having spoken thus, the Lord departed; the king returned to his home.
The Sanskrit language, which bestows heaven, was established within the three-fold [Vedic] speech.
That wise one established the Prakrit language among the Śūdras;
having ruled for a period of fifty years, he ascended to heaven.
He established a code of conduct that was honored by all like the gods themselves.
Āryāvarta is the land of merit, situated between the Vindhya and Himālaya mountains;

there the noble castes (āryavarṇas) reside, while at the edge of the Vindhyas dwell those of mixed castes (varṇasaṃkaras). Furthermore, men known as Musalavantas are established on the far side of the Sindhu river.
"In the land of Tuṣa, among the barbarians, and likewise on various islands,
the Īśāmasīha-dharmas were established by the gods and by kings.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Compendium of Histories of the Kali Age," within the Caturyuga-khaṇḍa (also known as the Pratisarga-parvan) of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
When King Bhoja had ascended to heaven, seven kings were born in his lineage;
they were short-lived and dull-witted, dying within the span of three hundred years.
The land under their sovereignty was indeed possessed by many kings.
King Vīrasiṃha is celebrated as the seventh;
in his lineage, three kings passed away within the span of two hundred years.
And that king who was Gaṅgasiṃha is proclaimed as the tenth;
that monarch righteously ruled his own kingdom in Kalpakṣetra. In Antarvedī and Kānyakubja, Jayacandra was the lord of the earth.
Aṅgapāla, born of the lineage of Tomara, became the ruler of Indraprastha;
many other kings also arose as lords of villages and kingdoms.
Thus, the expansion of the Agnivaṃśa became exceedingly powerful.
To the east, at the site of Kapila; to the west, at the edge of Vāhīka;
to the north, at the border of China; and to the south, at Setubandha—there were sixty lakhs of kings, village lords who were exceedingly powerful.

The performers of the Agnihotra sacrifice were seekers of the welfare of cows and Brahmins; they were experts in religious duties, resembling the Dvāpara age. The time known as Dvāpara prevailed everywhere.
In every house there was wealth, and in every person there was righteousness;
in every village there was a deity, and in every region there was a sacrifice.
Even the Mlecchas became performers of the noble Dharma, facing in all directions.
Having seen this, the formidable and fearful Kali, together with the Mleccha,
reached the Blue Mountain (Nīlādri) and, being wise, went for refuge to Hari.
For a period of twelve years, he became devoted to the yoga of meditation.
Having perceived through meditation the eternal Kṛṣṇa, who is existence, consciousness, and bliss,
he mentally praised Hari there, who is accompanied by Rādhā,
ancient, undecaying, and perpetual, and a resident of Vṛndāvana.
Kali said:
"O Master, O Lord, accept my prostration with all eight limbs like a staff;
protect me, who have come to you for refuge at your feet, O ocean of mercy."
You are indeed the remover of all sins, the Hari who brings about all times;
you are fair-complexioned in the Satya Yuga, red-hued in the Tretā,
yellow-hued in the Dvāpara, and black in my own appointed age (the Kali Yuga).

My sons are remembered as Mlecchas who have attained the state of Ārya-dharma. And my fourfold house— gambling, liquor, gold, and women, along with laughter— has been destroyed by the Kṣatriyas of the Agnivaṃśa lineage.
"O Janārdana, having abandoned my body, my family, and my kingdom,
I stand here taking refuge in you, placing my trust in your lotus feet.
Hearing this, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa laughed and said to him:
"O Kāla, for your protection, I shall take birth here as Mahāvatī.
My portion, having reached the earth, will destroy the mighty kings of the Mleccha dynasty and establish them upon the ground."
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One vanished right there;
and Kali, together with the Mleccha woman, attained supreme bliss.
O Brahmin, hear now what happened in the meantime.
In the village of Vāksara, there was a famous Ābhīrī woman named Vratapā who performed the excellent Navadurgā vow for nine years.
Being pleased, Caṇḍikā said, "O beautiful one, choose a boon."
She said, "O Mother, O Sovereign, if a boon is to be granted by you to me,
may there be two boys in my lineage who shall be equal to Rāma and Kṛṣṇa.
Having said, "So be it," that goddess vanished on the spot.
A king named Vasumān, infatuated by her beauty, married her according to the sacred law and established her in his own home. From her and the king were born two sons; Deśarāja was the elder of them.
Āvārya and Vatsarāja were equal in strength to Śatahasti;
having conquered the Magadha lands, they became kings.
Śatayatta is remembered as a Mleccha, a hero who was the lord of the forest-dwellers.

His son, born by the command of Śiva, was Vīraṇa, who was a portion of Bhīmasena. Indeed, because his upward velocity was equal to the height of a palm tree (tāla), he became famous by the name Tālana; he was created with a hundred *yatta*s.
Between those two kings, a hair-raising battle ensued;
however, the exceedingly powerful Tālana was defeated in that fight.
Then, a friendship was established between them, including Tālana.
Three heroes arrived for the purpose of testing Jayacandra.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Kaliyugīyetihāsamuccaya*, which is an alternative section of the *Caturyugakhaṇḍa* within the *Pratisargaparvan* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
In Indraprastha, King Anaṅgapāla, being childless,
performed a Śaiva sacrifice according to the prescribed rites for the sake of obtaining sons. Then, by the grace of Śiva’s portion, two daughters were born.
Candrakānti was indeed the elder daughter, while Kīrtimālinī was the second.
Her father gave Candrakānti to Devapāla, a pure scion of the Rāṣṭrapāla lineage, who was the sovereign of Kānyakubja.
To Someśvara, the king of the Capahāni clan,
and likewise to the lord of Ajamera, [he gave] Kīrtimālinī.
A certain brahmin named Jayaśarman, established in meditative absorption on the Himalayas—
Having witnessed the delightful festival of the king, he set his mind upon sovereignty;
having cast off his body, that pure-souled one became the son of Candrakānti,
renowned as Jayacandra, mighty-armed and a conqueror of his senses.
And Ratnabhānu was born as his younger brother, a heroic and powerful man.

Having conquered Gauḍa, Vaṅga, and other regions, including the Maru lands that were fierce with intoxication, he brought them under tribute; then, returning home, he became devoted to the commands of his elder brother.

Gaṅgasiṃha’s sister, the auspicious Vīravatī by name, became the queen of Ratnabhānu; she was a woman of excellent complexion. Then, by the command of Śiva, the portion of Nakula was born upon earth from her.
One named Lakṣaṇa was powerful and skilled in sword-fighting;
when seven years had passed, he became equal to his father.
Furthermore, three sons, fierce with pride, were born to Kīrtimālinī.
Dhundhakāra was the first, and after him came Kṛṣṇakumāraka;
he was indeed Pṛthivīrāja, and thereafter he is remembered as Anuja.
Having reached the age of twelve years, he then became Siṃhakhela.
Having heard this, Anaṅgapāla himself gave him the kingdom;
then, having gone to the beautiful Himagiri mountain, he became devoted to yoga and meditation.
In Mathurā was Dhundhakāra, and after that, his younger brother in Ajamera.
There was a king who was skilled in statecraft; by his father's command, those two sons—
Pradyota and Vidyota, both Kṣatriyas born of the lunar dynasty—
became the ministers of that monarch, powerful and fierce with pride.
A powerful son named Parimala was born to Pradyota;
he indeed became the commander of a hundred-thousand-fold army (lakṣasena) and was consecrated by that very king.
Furthermore, from Vidyota was born Bhīṣmasiṃha, who became the commander of an elephant-force (gajasena).
When Anaṅgapāla had ascended to heaven, the king of the earth, the lord of the land,
seeing that all those men were hostile, expelled them from his own kingdom;
these four, beginning with Pradyota, were accompanied by two hundred of their own heroes.
Having reached the city of Kānyakubja, he described Jayacandra:
"O King Jayacandra,
the powerful king who is the son of your maternal aunt has obtained the kingdom of your maternal grandfather and dwells there fearlessly."
"According to justice, we declared that half the kingdom was indeed ordained for you;
how is it that you enjoy the entire kingdom? Having heard this, they were rejected by him, whereupon they said:
"We have come to you for refuge; act accordingly."
Having heard this, King Jayacandra said to them:
"Let your son, the heroic Parimala by name, be the commander of my cavalry; you, however, shall now be my minister."
Likewise, Vidyota was the minister, while Bhīmaka was in charge of the elephant corps.
Indeed, for the sake of your livelihood, I gave you the great city Mahāvatī;
it is the beloved capital of King Mahīpati.
Having heard this, they all agreed with it and rejoiced.
But the powerful lord of the earth, abandoning that city out of grief,
established another city on the earth and made his residence there.
Agamā and Malanā were his two excellent sisters;
Agamā was given by her brother according to the prescribed rites to Bhūmirāja, and the other, Parimalā, to [another], and they both attained supreme joy.
At the conclusion of the wedding, King Bhūpa constructed another fortress;
having built a beautiful city inhabited by the four castes,
he firmly established Dehalī at the gate of the fort at an auspicious moment.
Having reached the end of the *yojana*, she indeed assumed the form of a woman due to the excellence of the time.
The king, becoming amazed, gave her the name Dehalī;
and by the king’s command, it became famous as the village of Dehalīgrāma.
And at the end of three years, O Brahmins, King Jayacandra,
accompanied by an army of one million six hundred thousand, dispatched a letter there [to Pṛthvīrāja],
saying: "For what reason, O Pṛthvīrāja, have you not given me my tribute?"
"Hand over half of your maternal grandfather's inheritance to me;
otherwise, your soldiers shall meet their destruction at my sharp weapons.
Knowing this, the powerful king of the earth, the lord of twenty lakhs, [acted].
The king of kings, intoxicated with pride, dispatched a messenger [to say]:
"O King Jayacandra, listen attentively to this:
when those rogues of the Lunar dynasty were rejected by me..."
From that time forward, you have assembled twenty lakhs of troops,
and sixteen lakhs of battle forces have been gathered by you; indeed,
all the kings of Bhārata are always worthy of being punished by me.
"You are not to be punished; you ought to pay me tribute. Otherwise, my soldiers shall bring about their destruction with my sharp arrows.
Realizing this, a terrible enmity arose between the two on the surface of the earth.
The powerful Bhūmirāja was afflicted by fear of Jayacandra,
and the powerful Jayacandra was fearful of Pṛthivīrāja;
Jayacandra then made the noble land his own half-kingdom.
Pṛthivīrāja himself likewise brought half the kingdom [to his side]. Thus arose that enmity between the two, which led to the destruction of the Agni dynasty.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the *Śrī-Bhaviṣya-Mahāpurāṇa*, in the *Pratisarga-parvan*, within the section titled *Caturyuga-khaṇḍa* (also known as the *Kaliyuga-itihāsa-samuccaya*).
Sūta said:
Once, having conquered the southern quarter protected by the king of the earth, Ratnabhānu indeed brought away their treasuries.
Upon hearing that, Mahīrāja was filled with great wonder;
and the Tilaka of Ratnabhānu became exceedingly extensive. That auspicious woman known as Vīravatī became famous by the name Tilakā.
She was indeed the most excellent among the twelve queens and the mother of Lakṣaṇa.
King Jayacandra had sixteen wives,
yet due to the ripening of past karma, none of them had a son.

The daughter of the King of Gauḍa, named Divyavibhāvarī, was the queen of Jayacandra; Surabhānavī was her maidservant. She was endowed with beauty and youth, and was highly skilled in the arts of love-play.
Seeing her, that king, filled with desire and tormented by the god of love, enjoyed her company.
From her was born a daughter, the auspicious goddess named Saṃyoginī;
having reached the age of twelve years, she became a woman of exquisite beauty.
At her svayaṃvara, the king invited highly auspicious monarchs;
however, the powerful Bhūmirāja, having heard of her supreme beauty,
set his mind on marriage and urged Candrabhaṭṭa to act.
"O dear friend, excellent minister Candrabhaṭṭa,
having reached the city of Kānyakubja, install my image fashioned of gold in the midst of the assembly; tell them the account of what happened to me."
Having heard this, O best of the Bhṛgus, Candrabhaṭṭa, devoted to the worship of Bhavānī, went there and acted exactly as he had been instructed.
And at the svayaṃvara, kings from various lands assembled.
Having abandoned those suitors, Kāmākṣī, deluded by the form of the king,
said to her father: "O King, he whose form is like this one’s and who is endowed with all auspicious marks shall be my husband."
Having heard that, Jayacandra said to Candrabhadra:
"If even the king himself, accompanied by his entire army,
could subdue this Yoginī, then he would be very dear to me."
But Candra-bhaṭṭa, having heard that, described it all:
"This is indeed Pṛthivīrāja; having heard this, he has mobilized his army.
He has one hundred thousand elephants and seven hundred thousand horses."

There were five thousand chariots and one hundred thousand foot soldiers, all skilled in the use of bows and arrows; they were known to be exceedingly powerful. There were exactly three hundred kings who followed in the footsteps of the great sovereigns of the earth.
Accompanied by two of his kinsmen, the king went to Kānyakubja;
they were Dhundhukāra, his relative who was always the commander of the elephant corps,
and Kṛṣṇa Kumāra, the commander of the cavalry, who was exceedingly powerful.
The kings became commanders of the foot soldiers there,
and a great clamor arose as they left the ground empty;
his mighty army remained stationed within a distance of twenty *krośas*.
Jayacandra, having learned of the arrival of Mahīrāja,
arrayed his own army, numbering sixteen hundred thousand:
one hundred thousand elephants and seven hundred thousand foot soldiers.
Eight hundred thousand cavalrymen, all experts in every form of warfare,
and two hundred kings arrived at that assembly;
considering the King of the Earth to be an offender, those scions of the Śukla lineage [prepared for battle].
Seeking battle, they stood there, for the city had indeed committed an offense;
on the opposite bank of the river Īśānī, their palanquin was then stationed,
where they played various delightful musical instruments that produced a great roar.
Ratnabhānu was indeed the leader in the army of elephants and in the army of forms;
he and those two generals were well-protected and exceedingly powerful.
Both Pradyota and Vidyota guarded Ratnabhānu.
Bhīṣma, Parimala, and Lakṣaṇa, born of the Lunar dynasty—
these kings stood in the infantry division, overwhelmed by intoxication.
Between those two [armies] there occurred a great and terrible battle, resulting in the destruction of the troops.
Horses were slain by horses and likewise elephants by elephants;
foot soldiers were slain by foot soldiers, and others died in succession in the battle.
Protected by their kings, they all entered the fray free from fear.
The battle continued as long as the sun remained in the sky.
Thus, for five days, there occurred a war that caused the destruction of heroic men;
ten thousand elephants and one hundred thousand horses were slaughtered.
Five hundred thousand foot soldiers of the lord of the earth were slain there;
likewise, two hundred kings, three hundred chariots,
and nine thousand elephants belonging to the ruler of Kānyakubja perished there.
One thousand chariots, three hundred thousand foot soldiers, and one hundred thousand horses were known to have perished there; having died, they went to the city of heaven.
When the sixth day arrived, he alone remained as the king of the earth.
Distressed in mind, the devoted king praised the god Rudra;
Mahādeva, being well-pleased, then bewildered that army.
The delighted king of the earth then went toward Saṃyoginī.
Upon seeing that beautiful form, the lord of the earth was infatuated;
and seeing the king, Saṃyoginī fainted in an instant.
In the meantime, the king forcibly brought her to the swing.
The king, accompanied by his entire army, proceeded to Dehalī.
When he had traveled for a distance of one yojana, those who were fierce with pride were alerted;
seeing no swing there at all, they rushed forward with even greater speed.
Hearing their clamor, that best of kings, the lord of the earth,
stationed half of his army and went to his home himself,
while those two heroic brothers, accompanied by the other half of the army, remained there.
Having reached Sūkara-kṣetra, they stood ready for battle; in the meantime, all the mighty warriors, headed by Pradyota,
arrived with their own armies and engaged in a great conflict.
Horses clashed with horses, and elephants with elephants;
there was a great, tumultuous, and hair-raising carnage.
At the end of the day, the vast armies of both sides were brought to destruction.
Perceiving that night to be shrouded in darkness,
the other heroes who remained after the slaughter, being terrified by fear, fled;
yet those heroes, Pradyota and the rest, advanced toward Dehalī.
Once again, a great battle occurred between them that caused the hair to stand on end;
Dhundhukāra struck Pradyota in the heart with arrows,
and having fainted from three poison-suffused shafts, he died.
Seeing his brother slain, the mighty Vidyota mounted an elephant and arrived;
he struck Dhundhukāra with three iron javelins (tomaras), and he too fell to the ground unconscious.
Seeing his brother Dhundhukāra, who possessed great strength, fallen unconscious,
that son of Kṛṣṇa then swiftly advanced while mounted on his elephant;
overcome with rage, he struck that hero with a broad-headed arrow (bhalla).
Pierced by that *bhallā* arrow, he died and went to the city of heaven.
When that commander-in-chief of the entire army, Vidyota, had been slain,
the great hero Ratnābhānu fought, accompanied by him.
In the meantime, the king, accompanied by a thousand elephants and joined by Lakṣaṇa and those two [others],
fought furiously against that enraged Bhīṣma Parimala; for the king had been granted a boon by Śiva.
He bewildered the exceedingly powerful Lakṣaṇa with the weapons of Rudra. Observing them to have fainted, Ratnabhānu then struck Dhundhukāra, the king of the earth, with his own Vaiṣṇava arrows.

Kṛṣṇaka and Ratnabhānu fought with one another; both heroes of equal strength stood upon the backs of elephants in the battle. When their elephants had struck each other down, they remained on the surface of the earth with swords in hand.
Those two, who were exceedingly difficult to conquer, fought by employing many maneuvers;
having engaged in combat until the end of their striking power, they both approached death. When that one of great prowess was slain, the people of Kānyakubja became overwhelmed with fear.
Taking the three who had fainted with them, accompanied by five hundred thousand troops,
they abandoned the battlefield and went home, overcome with grief for their king;
and when Ratnabhānu was slain, the lords of the earth lost all their enthusiasm.
Afflicted by fear of the King of the Earth, they each went to their own dwellings;
in every house, they propitiated the gods according to their desire.
But the powerful King of the Earth was accompanied by a force of seven hundred thousand.
Accompanied by Dhundhukāra, Vaṃdhuka performed the funeral rites;
likewise Bhīṣma, Parimala, and Lakṣaṇa,
having gathered on the bank of the Gaṅgā, performed the post-mortem ceremonies for their own father.
The victory of Bhūmirāja and the fame of Jayacandra in battle became renowned throughout the earth, in every house and among every person.
Jayacandra was the lord of the earth in Kānyakubja, while Pṛthivīpati was in Dehali.
Having caused a festival to be celebrated, he attained supreme bliss.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the *Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, in the *Pratisarga Parvan*, within the section titled *Caturyuga Khaṇḍa*, which is an anthology of histories of the Kali Yuga.
Sūta said:
Bhīṣma, established on the bank of the Gaṅgā like a lion, was a worshiper of Śakra;
knowing Śakra to be composed of the Sun, he gratified him through austerity.
At the end of a month, the Lord Indra, perceiving his supreme devotion, [appeared].
"Choose a boon," he said; having heard this, Śūra spoke as follows:
"If you, O Lord, are pleased with me, grant me a divine mare.
Having heard this, he then gave him a beautiful, deer-like mare.
The blessed Indra gave [these gifts] and vanished right there.
At that time, Parimala, who was utterly devoted to grief for his father,
worshipped Mahādeva, the consort of Umā, together with other kings.
To test him, Śiva himself swallowed him with a serpent-disease;
when the fifth month had passed, the king, though deprived of his power and beset by great suffering, did not abandon the great worship.
Accompanied by his wife, the king went to Kāśī to meet his death;
afflicted by disease, he stayed at the foot of a banyan tree during the night.
In the meantime, a certain serpent residing at the root [of the tree] appeared.
Hearing a sweet sound, Rudrāhi arrived;
the serpent spoke to Rudrāhi: "O cruel and dull-witted one, you villain, why do you afflict this king, a devotee of Śiva, every single day?"
"This king is a fool; he would not drink āranāla directly.
Hearing this, that serpent Rudra said, "O lowest of serpents!
I have attained supreme joy every day within the body of the king."
"One's own home must be abandoned out of sorrow; how can I abandon it, O rogue? This king here is a fool indeed, for he did not give me oil that was warm.
Having spoken thus within her body, the virtuous Malanā heard [these words].
The king, afflicted by the disease mentioned by the serpent, performed that [rite];
having filled the hole with hot oil, Satī herself dug it out.
Then there emerged a self-manifested, eternal Liṅga, the size of a thumb.
Seeing the form of light, consisting of consciousness and bliss, endowed with all auspicious marks,
which had attained the state of the sun in every direction when darkness had arisen at midnight,
the king was struck with wonder and worshipped Śaṅkara.
He praised the Lord of Girijā with recitations of the Mahimnaḥ-stava. Then the Blessed One, being pleased, said to him, "Choose a boon.
Having heard this, the king said to the God, "O Maheśvara, if you are pleased..."

"May the Lord of Śrī come to my house and dwell there, performing what is pleasing to me. Having said "So be it," Mahādeva assumed the form of a *liṅga* and produced one *bhāra* of gold from his body every day.
Then Malla, being well-pleased,
reached Mahāvatī along with Bhīmasiṃha and attained supreme joy.
From that time forward, at the end of the year, he went to the city of Jayacandra.
Having seen Parimala, the king attained a sense of fulfillment:
"By good fortune your illness has been cured; by good fortune your face has been revealed to me.
May you reach your own city and be happy without delay."
"When an obstacle arises for me, then you must assist me.
Having heard this, Parimala went and established his residence in that place.
Then the heroic Lakṣaṇa [approached] the Blessed Lord, the husband of Uṣā.

Having approached Jagannātha, he became intent on worshiping him. After only half a fortnight had passed, Viṣṇu, the Lord of the World and husband of Uṣā, spoke these words with joy: "Choose a boon! To which Lakṣmaṇa replied.
Thus addressed, he bowed to that god and spoke with a humble mind:
"Grant me a divine vehicle that destroys all enemies.
Having heard this, the Lord of the World [took] a spear from the elephant Airāvata.
Having brought forth [the elephant], he joyfully gave the divine Airāvatī to him.
Having mounted Airāvatī, King Lakṣaṇa returned to his home;
and that King Parimala went to Mahāvatī.
In the meantime, those heroes, Tāla and the others, intoxicated with pride,
reached the great city of Mahāvatī and beheld that lord of the earth.
Having established a great friendship with him, they took up residence there.
And at the end of the month, those kings, endowed with discipline, said to him:
"O protector of the earth, listen; we are departing for our cities.
Then the king also spoke to all those lords of the earth:
"Having bestowed the authority upon my sons, I shall then come into your presence.
Having been told "So be it" by the king, they returned once more to their own homes;
and Deśarāja, along with his younger brothers, gave his city to the twice-born.
The heroic Tālana gave the city of Vārāṇasī to his sons; their names, in order, were Alikolla, Matis, Kāla, Patrapuṣpodarī, Varī, Karī,
and Narī Sulalita.
Two sons each are recorded for them, equal in prowess to their father.
That hero Tālana, beloved by the Rākṣasas, at the command of his son,
praised the god who consists of Yātudhānas with the worship of the Mlecchas.
Likewise, the two sons of Vasumān, Bhūpati and Deśavatsaja,
having propitiated Śakra and Sūrya, became successful in their purpose.
As for the mare named Siṃhinī, who was given [to them], she was formidable.

Having mounted the great elephant Indradatta, who was pleasing to the mind and produced five sounds, the powerful hero set his mind on departing. King Deśarāja, having mounted him, likewise set his mind on departing.
Having mounted that bird named Papihaka, which was given by the Sun and possessed a human voice,
Vatsarāja set his mind on departing.
Then the three heroes, having come together, [set out for] the city of Mahāvatī.
The high-souled ones dwelt there, honored with great respect;
their army consisted of sixty thousand, and Tālana was their leader. Those two brothers were ministers to the king of the Lunar dynasty.
Protected by those heroes, the king attained the fulfillment of his purpose.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Compendium of Histories of the Kali Age," in the Caturyuga-khaṇḍa (also known as the Pratisarga-parvan) of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
A king named Jambuka, a ruler of the earth who was afflicted by fear,
arrived at the auspicious bank of the Narmadā accompanied by Kāliya;
there he worshipped the God of gods, the wielder of the Pināka bow, along with other kings.
At the end of six months, Mahādeva said to King Jambuka:
"Choose a boon that is desired by you. With palms joined in reverence, the king said: "O ocean of compassion, grant me invincibility against all kings."
Having said "So be it," Mahādeva vanished on the spot. Having obtained that boon from Maheśvara which bewilders all armies, his son Kāliya, the hero, returned to the presence of his father.
With a humble soul, he said to his father, "O Father, grant me your command, which is dear to me;
I shall go with my forces to the auspicious Gaṅgā of pure waters.
Having said, "So be it," the father departed for his own residence.
The powerful one said to his sister, who was desirous of victory: "O beautiful one, what auspicious thing do you desire? Give me your command without delay.
She replied: "A neck-ornament, a necklace adorned with gems and pearls."
"O hero, grant me my beloved! Having said, "So be it," he departed from his home.
Accompanied by one hundred thousand horses, Kāliya went in haste;
reaching the Gaṅgā, which flows to the ocean, he performed his ablutions according to the prescribed rites.
Having bestowed gifts upon the Brahmins, he went to the city of Jayacandra;
though the king was mighty-armed and possessed great strength, he became destitute. In Kanyakubja, he did not obtain even a single high-quality garment of great value.
Then, awakened by that very lord of the earth, the Mahīśa,
the powerful one who had received boons from Śiva went to the beautiful Mahāvatī;
having heard this, the king became afflicted with fear and besieged the entire city.
The wise king went for refuge to Rudra, the matted-haired Śambhu, who is the worthy protector; by the command of Śiva, he went outside the city with sixty thousand troops,
well-guarded by three heroes.
He had a thousand elephants and a regional king as their master;
sixteen thousand horses, with the King of Vatsa as their master;
and the remainder were his foot soldiers, protected by Tālana alone.
The root of their battle was lost through the destruction of the best of heroes;
for the duration of a day and night, a great and terrible conflict raged.
Having slain the enemy host, they repeatedly raised shouts of victory.

Afflicted by fear, the Narmadeyas and the inhabitants of Māhiṣmatī fled in all directions, O Brāhmaṇa; but upon seeing them, King Kāliya consoled them and set out for battle accompanied by half his army.
Placing Mahādeva in his heart and taking up the Mohana-bāṇa arrow,
they were all rendered deluded by the power of the perfected mantra;
then all those remaining enemies advanced to slay their foe.
Free from fear, they struck those exhausted men with skull-topped clubs. Then Bhīṣmasiṃha, seeing this, alerted the soldiers there by means of an arrow given by Sūrya, known as Saṃjñā.
With a spear known as Bhairava, he struck the body of the enemy;
afflicted by the arrow, that hero fell unconscious upon the back of his elephant.
Then the army of Māhiṣmatī rushed out in the ten directions.
Having fallen into a swoon for a moment, Kāliya rose again;
the king struck off his head from his body with a broad-headed arrow. When that one of great prowess was slain, the mighty Tāla and the others [fled].
Having defeated Kāliya and restrained that enemy,
the king, though beset by great hardship, meditated upon Śaṅkara in his mind;
having deluded all his foes, he went to his own abode.
Then King Parimala, accompanied by half his army, saw that those three remaining survivors had likewise been defeated by the enemy;
having embraced those great heroes, he returned once more to his own home.
Having heard that, Jayacandra was filled with great wonder;
he summoned Tālana and appointed him as the commander-in-chief of the army.
When Bhīṣmasiṃha had passed away, five months later, the king—
His wife gave birth to a jewel of a son with a beautiful face;
she, known as Madālasā, the daughter of the Gurjara king,
rejoiced greatly along with her attendants upon beholding that divine son.
Upon hearing of that birth, the king distributed vast wealth;
having summoned wise astrologers, he performed the birth rites (jātakarman).
Indeed, by the command of Śiva, this very portion of Sahadeva had been born upon the earth.
"He was given the name Devasiṃha by the astrologers and thinkers of the scriptures.

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Compendium of Histories of the Kali Age," in the Kaliyuga section of the Pratisarga Parva within the *Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, which is also known as the Caturyuga Khaṇḍa.
Sūta said:
Having defeated Kāliya, those two brothers became servants of the king;
they went to the kingdom of Gopālaka,
where King Dalavāhana was present at a gathering of various kings for a thousandfold oblation to Caṇḍikā.
Those two buffaloes,
who were previously difficult for other kings to conquer and were captured daily by the two princesses,
were duly honored according to the prescribed rites, and he gave the two maidens to them.
By the command of Durgā, the king gave Devakī, who was endowed with beauty and youth, to the King of Deśa, and Brāhmī, her younger sister, to his younger brother;
he also gave a courtesan skilled in song and dance, whose livelihood was supported by a hundred thousand [gold pieces].
And Dalavāhana gave two beautiful maidens who were friends to [his daughter] and were enamored of Meghamalla,
as well as a hundred elephants, five hundred chariots, a thousand horses,
and forty palanquins.
Having married the maiden— who was endowed with abundant wealth and accompanied by male and female servants—
according to the Vedic rites, the two reached Mahāvatī.
Seeing that bride, Malanā gave her a neck-ornament.

The king, filled with supreme joy, gave the beautiful city of Daśapura, inhabited by various people, to the heroic Śūri, who was adorned with sixteen Brahmanical ornaments as well as twelve royal decorations.
Those two heroes, honored by the king and possessed of great strength, dwelt there.
In the meantime, Devasiṃha was born by the command of Hara.
When that boy was born, Devakī conceived a child in her womb.
The goddess Śrutāpatī gave birth to a powerful son,
fair-limbed, lotus-eyed, and radiant with his own splendor;
at that time, the god Śakra was filled with joy along with the hosts of deities.
He raised a loud sound of conchs and the cry of "Victory! again and again;
all the quarters of the sky and the planets in heaven became radiant with blossoms. Many Brahmins, devoted to the Vedas and the Shastras, arrived there.
Knowing that auspicious infant to be a portion of Rāma, they performed his birth rites and naming ceremony accordingly;
on the sixth lunar day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada, on a Monday at dawn.
Born under the asterism Kṛttikā, he brought glory to his paternal lineage;
indeed, on this earth, he became known by the name Āhlāda and was humble in conduct.
When the month had ended and the son was born, Brāhmī gave birth to a son.
Then all the brahmins beheld that child of auspicious countenance, born of a portion of Dharma— fair-complexioned, mighty-armed,
with a broad chest, a serene face, and beautiful feet marked with the sign of the lotus.
By those twice-born ones, that exceedingly powerful one was named Balakhāni.
At the end of the year, he was born among the Vatsas, arising from the junction of Mūla and Gaṇḍa;
he was Cāmuṇḍa, the son of Devakī, who brought terror to his own lineage.
"Therefore, he must be abandoned," said the best of the twice-born.
Yet the king, devoted to compassion, did not abandon his son, even though he was still a child. When three years had passed since that auspicious son Balakhāna was born, [the sage returned].
Born of a Śūdra woman, he was known by the name Rūpaṇa, a portion of Śikhaṇḍin.
Vatsarāja went to the land of Gurjara and,
taking his daughter Madālasā with him, arrived there on that very day.
When that Vatsarāja had arrived, the jackal, surrounded by his own forces numbering seven hundred thousand, being powerful-armed and self-controlled,
reached and besieged the entire city of King Parimala.
Together with three hundred thousand Māhāvatyas, those two departed from the city;
a great battle ensued with seven hundred thousand Māhiṣmatas,
lasting for three nights— terrible, fierce, and increasing the population of Yama’s kingdom.
By the granting of a boon from Śiva, the defeat of the two brothers occurred;
having bound them, King Jambuka plundered Mahāvatī,
along with his courtesan Lakṣārati and that slain elephant of his.
Taking the neck-ornament and the necklace adorned with jewels and gems,
he reduced the entire city to ashes and went home;
those heroes who were hidden beneath the earth remained as his only survivors at that time.
Having joyfully obtained the jewels that were in the difficult-to-reach places, she departed; while that city was being plundered, Devakī, beloved of the gods, bore her excellent womb-child,
a portion of Kṛṣṇa, who was seven months old.

Having learned that her son Cāmuṇḍa was the lowest of his lineage, the virtuous Devakī went to the sacred field of Kalpa and cast him into the Kālindī river. When he had gone a distance of one yojana, the royal priest of Mahīraja [retrieved him].
The vassal, having taken him, went to his father-in-law’s residence;
he was born at the end of ten months, during the night shrouded in thick darkness,
on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada under the Moon, conjoined with the lunar mansion Rohiṇī.
The Lord of the World, the most excellent of beings, appeared within Devakī;
he was dark-limbed, lotus-eyed, and possessed the luster of a sapphire,
while the radiance of thousands of celestial chariots manifested.
Seeing that wonderful child there, his mother was struck with amazement;
and as a great marvel had arisen in the city, everyone gathered together, saying, "Aha!
Has the rising of the gods in the form of the sun occurred?"
To them, who were filled with wonder, an incorporeal voice spoke:
"A portion of Kṛṣṇa has been born upon the earth as the bestower of joy to all;
he is indeed named Udayasiṃha, the destroyer of the splendor of all enemies."
Having heard these words of Ākāśa, they attained supreme joy;
and at the very moment the son was born,
the virtuous Malanā beheld a beautiful dark-bodied infant, endowed with all auspicious marks.
By the command of Śiva, she gave birth to that most noble portion of Phālguna;
at that time, the entire city was filled with joy upon the birth of the son,
who was a mine of the qualities of Brahman-bliss on his sixth day.
Brāhmī gave birth to a son who was a portion of Pārṣada, possessed of great strength,
with a dark-complexioned body, lotus-like eyes, firm shoulders, and long arms;
and then the Brāhmaṇas, having arrived, performed the birth-rites for him.
The best of astrologers, the twice-born, gave them the name Sukhakhāni.
In due course, those children grew up, bringing auspiciousness to all the world;
among them, Kālī was the most excellent and the one who brought joy to her father and mother.
When he had reached his third year and the portion of Kṛṣṇa within him had become exceedingly powerful,
Śakra, desiring a vision of him, went forth mounted upon his horse.
Meanwhile, the portion of Kṛṣṇa was playing with his brothers in the sandalwood forest.
Seeing the thousand-eyed Puruṣa stationed in the sky, she laughed aloud;
then Aśvinī, the divine Hariṇī, having gone near Uccaiḥśravas and taken up the embryo, returned once more to her own home.

In the course of a year, she gave birth to an auspicious son, a pigeon. When he had reached five years of age, they began his education under the Brahmin Śivaśarman, who was proficient in all branches of knowledge.
Having served him with their own devotion, they performed the recitation of the Vedas;
and at the age of eight, Kṛṣṇāṃśa attained preeminence among the boys who were writing out names, lineages, and other such matters.

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Incarnation of a Portion of Kṛṣṇa," in the *Kaliyuga-itihāsa-samuccaya*, which is an alternative section of the *Caturyuga-khaṇḍa* within the *Pratisarga-parvan* of the glorious *Śrīmad Bhāgavatamahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
When he had reached his ninth year, the portion of Kṛṣṇa became exceedingly powerful.
Having studied the science of logic (*anvīkṣikī-vidyā*), as well as the sixty-four arts (*kalās*) and the treatises on dharma (*dharmaśāstra*), he indeed became the most excellent of all.
At that time, O best of the Bhṛgus, there was a king of the earth, the most eminent of monarchs.
He dispatched his army to Mahāvatī for the sake of tribute.
Those great heroes, numbering one hundred thousand and bearing all kinds of weapons and missiles, spoke to King Parimala: "Listen, O descendant of the Lunar dynasty!"
"All the immensely powerful kings in the land of Bhārata indeed pay a sixth part as tax to our king;
you alone are now worthy to be his tribute."
If, from this day forward, he does not pay tribute to that king,
his army shall be destroyed by the fierce weapons of Mahīrāja;
for those kings who have sided with Jayacandra will surely perish out of fear of him.
"Being honored by him, they pay tribute to the king of the earth.
Having heard this, that monarch, filled with affection, took a sixth part as tax and gave it to that high-souled king.
Taking wealth amounting to ten lakhs, they arrived;
King Mahīrāja, with a gracious mind, cast aside their former enmity.
Then those heroes by the lakh proceeded toward Kānyakubja.
Having bowed to Jayacandra, they said, "Listen, O expert in marks (lakṣaṇa)!
The great king Pṛthvīrāja desires punishment from you.
Being addressed thus by them, the Vaiṣṇava Lakṣaṇa spoke to them.
"There are many provincial rulers in the land at present;
let no provincial king exist while I live.
Having said this, he, filled with rage, took up the Vaiṣṇava weapon against them.
Then, terrified by the flames of that weapon, they all fled;
but King Mahīrāja, hearing of this, was seized by great fear when Kṛṣṇāṃśa, who was skilled in wrestling, reached the age of ten years.
Various wrestlers arrived and were honored by that king;
among them, that portion of Kṛṣṇa became preeminent,
for he was a powerful youth of sixteen years, the son of the lord of the earth.
Once, accompanied by a hundred wrestlers, that powerful one named Abhaya arrived;
having bowed to the king, his father’s sister’s husband, he said: "Listen, O protector of the earth, this Kṛṣṇa is intoxicated with pride."
"O best of kings, let there be a wrestling match with him.
Having heard these words, which were like a thunderbolt, the king was overcome with fear.
He spoke with affection to his sister's son, who was himself an expert in combat: "You are skilled in battle."
"This son of mine is eight years old, affectionate, and as dear to me as my own life on this earth.
Where are you, who are like a thunderbolt, and where is this very delicate son?
You are fit to engage in battle with other wrestlers, both mine and others."
Having heard this, the king, the brother-in-law known as Mahīpati, spoke to him while overcome with rage: "This child is exceedingly powerful;
O King, hear the reason why this infant was recognized by me."
Considering his son to have committed an offense against the great king,
Satilaka summoned the learned scholars and joyfully asked them for an auspicious moment.
Among them was one named Gaṇeśa, who was intelligent and an expert in the science of astrology.
He spoke these words regarding the unsurpassed lord of the earth:
"O King, having received boons from Śiva, he is now like Kubera.
This younger son of the regional king is a portion of Kṛṣṇa and is worthy of him."
"O King, there is no other [equal] on the face of the earth; I speak the truth, the absolute truth.
Having heard that, the heroic Lakṣaṇa [conquered] Pūrva-barhiṣmatī in the east, Kalpakṣetra in the south, and Bhūmigrāma in the west.
In the north lies the Naimiṣa forest, which he established as his own kingdom;

therefore, I have heard that this prince is most excellent in Kānyakubja. And during the festival of the Nagas on the fifth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, O protector of the earth...
"The body of the prince is merely an object of sight; therefore, this son is indeed worthy.
Hearing this, that portion of Kṛṣṇa, afflicted by the arrow-like words, quickly took refuge in the arms of Abhaya, for he was powerful in combat.

Having fought for but a moment, he cast him down into the midst of the earth; indeed, Abhaya’s arm was broken there by that strength. Knowing his own son to have fainted, the lord of the earth, sword in hand, [rushed forward].
He dispatched those wrestlers to strike the portion of Kṛṣṇa;
but perceiving them to be possessed by rage, that most powerful portion of Kṛṣṇa threw each one of them down individually and emerged victorious.
When the strength of the wrestler was defeated, the lord of the earth, sword in hand,
set his mind upon death due to the power of Kṛṣṇāṃśa.
Knowing the king to be in such a state, the monarch restrained him.

Having granted him fearlessness and freedom from disease, he affectionately settled him in his home. When the prince was nine years old, Āhlāda and the other sons of Kṛṣṇa’s portion set their minds on hunting; they spoke thus to their dear father, the king: The final output should be the English translation only, formatted as requested. Here it is: Having granted him fearlessness and freedom from disease, he affectionately settled him in his home. When the prince was nine years old, Āhlāda and the other sons of Kṛṣṇa’s portion set their minds on hunting; they spoke thus to their dear father, the king:
"Salutations to you, O dear one, foremost of kings, bestower of all joy!
Grant us the horses; O compassionate one, make them dear to me.
Having heard these words of theirs, the lord of the earth said, "So be it."
The king, filled with joy, gave to them four excellent divine horses born from the womb of a doe that dwelt upon the earth. The sages said:
O Sūta, O Sage, we have heard from your mouth how the mare Vaḍavā reached the lion Bhīṣma from Śakra, the lord of the gods;
now we wish to hear from whence the horses were born.
With divine limbs and adorned with ornaments, they travel through the sky and across the waters.
Sūta said:
"In ancient times, by King Deśarāja, who was indeed endowed with righteousness..."

He performed the service of the Sun-god for twelve years. At the conclusion of his service, the Lord Sūrya said, "Choose a boon. He replied, "O God, salutations to you; if a boon is to be granted by you,"
"Give me a divine horse that traverses the sky and surpasses water.
Having said "So be it," the Sun himself gave him the *papihaka*.
He who protects the worlds is to be known as *Papī*; this is his excellent name.
Therefore, the one named Papīhaka, who possessed the duty of a world-protector,
being a horse intoxicated with passion, enjoyed the divine-natured Hariṇī with the force of love;
from her were born the horses.
Manoratha was yellow-limbed, Karāla was black-hued;
both were born from a single womb as portions of Śaibya and Sugrīva.
On the very day they were born, they emerged from the partial portions of Jiṣṇu and Viṣṇu.
Then, from the doe, Meghapuṣpa and Balāhaka were born;
and Bindula, Suvarṇāṅga, Śvetāṅga, and Harināgara—
these four of divine form were previously born with great strength.
Thereafter, the partial incarnations (*aṃśāvatāras*) of those great-souled ones were born.
Thus it has been told to you, O Brahmin; now hear the auspicious narrative concerning that.
All those horses reached the surface of the earth from the upper realm.
He gave the horse Manoratha to the powerful Devasiṃha;
Karāla to Āhlāda; Bindula to Kṛṣṇāṃśa;
and Harināgara to his son Brahmānanda.
Those four, mounted on horses, went to the forest for the sake of hunting;
Balakhāni mounted a bright, mare-like doe,
and following him, the hero proceeded into the forest frequented by lions.
By joy alone was the tiger, who struck terror into living beings, slain;
by the lion among gods (Śiva) the lion was slain; and by Balakhānin the boar was slain;
and by Brahmānanda the deer was slain there in that great forest.
A hundred deer were killed by them, and taking them, they went home.
In the meantime, the goddess Śāradā, of auspicious countenance,
having become a golden doe, ran before them.
Seeing her, they were all deluded and struck her with their respective arrows;
however, those exceedingly powerful arrows met their destruction upon the body of Mṛgī.
Āhlāda and the other heroes were then filled with astonishment.
At that time, he of the dark limbs struck her with an arrow;
then, the goddess, afflicted and terrified by fear, fled into the forest.
The powerful one, a portion of Kṛṣṇa, his eyes copper-red with rage, followed after her.
Having reached the interior of the forest and resumed her own form, the goddess, with gracious eyes, said to him: "I have tested you;
whenever fear should arise for you, then always remember me."
"I shall accomplish your task, for you are a portion of Kṛṣṇa, O Lord.
Having spoken thus, the goddess Śāradā, the source of all auspiciousness, vanished.
And he, being a portion of Kṛṣṇa, went to his home with them, filled with joy.
Then, having witnessed their prowess, the king became joyful;
and the goddess Lakṣmī entered every single household.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, in the Pratisarga Parvan, within the section titled Caturyuga Khaṇḍa, specifically the collection of histories of the Kali Yuga.
Sūta said:
When Viṣṇu’s incarnation as Śakti had reached the tenth year of his life,
they went to the delightful grove of women during the charming spring season.
They dwelt there, observing their vows during the month of Mādhava, which is dear to Kṛṣṇa;
having bathed in the ocean at dawn,
they worshipped Ambikā according to the prescribed rites with flowers blooming in season, incense, and lamps.
Having recited the Saptaśatī hymn, they meditated upon the auspicious Śivā, the accomplisher of all things;
subsisting on bulbs, roots, and fruits, and abstaining from injury to living beings,
the Mother of the World, having observed their devotion at the end of the month, [appeared].
He granted them a delightful boon; listen to it with concentrated minds:
for the sake of delight, he gave the status of a celestial being and strength to Balakhāni;
to the god, the knowledge of time; and to the king, the knowledge of Brahman.
Having bestowed the state of yoga upon Kṛṣṇāṃśa alone, Śivā vanished;
then, having accomplished their purpose, they indeed returned to their own homes.
When that delightful boon had been obtained by them, Malanā gave birth to a powerful son.
She gave birth to one with a dark body, endowed with auspicious marks, who was a portion of Sātyaki;
he is to be known as the heroic Raṇajit, a benefactor to the kings.
When the month of Āṣāḍha arrived, the portion of Kṛṣṇa, whose vehicle is the horse, appeared.
Having reached the vast city alone, fearless and powerful, that hero—
worshiper of the Brahmins' cows and protector of the twice-born— beheld the beautiful city inhabited by the four castes and went to the residence of a Brahmin.
Having given gold to the twice-born and having gratified the gods and the brahmins,
the exceedingly powerful one went to the beautiful palace of the lord of the earth;
there the wise one bowed to his maternal uncle as well as to the other members of the assembly.
Then, by the king's command, brave men with swords in hand arrived, prepared for his arrest,
like elephants and hares approaching a lion;
having deluded that king, the monarch of evil intent—
Having fashioned an iron net, you placed it over him;
meanwhile, the hero, awakened by the divine illusion and perceiving his enemies as wrongdoers,
stood with sword in hand and struck them down.
Having slain five hundred [enemies], the heroic and mighty one, mounted upon his horse,
reached the city of Urvī and set his mind on drinking water.
Then, he saw auspicious women at a well filling their jars.
He spoke these sweet words: "O beautiful one, give me water.
Seeing his handsome form, they set about to enchant him;
however, having broken their jars, he made the horse drink the water.
Having gone to the forest, the powerful one conquered his enemy and bound him;
having approached the presence of Caṇḍikā, he set his mind on his slaughter.
But hearing her piteous words, he abandoned his own city and departed.
Approaching the king, he described the cause;
having heard it, King Parimala bestowed wealth upon the twice-born. Having smelled the portion belonging to Kṛṣṇa, the king felt his purpose was fulfilled.
When the portion of Kṛṣṇa had reached his eleventh year and was intoxicated by the pride of war,
the king, devoid of enthusiasm and trembling with fear, went toward Dehalī after offering the appropriate tribute to his sister.

He wept many times in grief for his country, his king, and his subjects. His sister, seeing her brother distressed, went to him and described her husband; having heard this, the king spoke as follows.
"Today, having gone there with my own forces to Mahāvatī,
I shall slay that most wicked enemy, the son of the king of the land.
Having spoken thus, he summoned the exceedingly powerful Dhundhukāra.
He commanded an army of seven hundred thousand who were ready to sacrifice their lives.
Some heroes mounted on horses, some of great strength mounted on camels,
others mounted on elephants or chariots, and others as foot soldiers, marched forth together.
But Devasimha, who knew the proper time, having heard of the enemy’s arrival,
approached the presence of the king and reported everything to the monarch.
Upon hearing this, King Parimala became overwhelmed and afflicted with fear.
Rising up, Balakhāni spoke as if filled with joy:
"Today, by your command, I shall conquer Dhundhukāra, the king of the earth, along with his army, and I shall execute the punishment due to him."
Having spoken thus and paid homage to him, O Sage, he became the commander-in-chief.
Then, seeing the king distressed, those fearless heroes,
together with four hundred thousand troops, advanced for battle.
Having then cut down the formidable forest known as Śiṃśapā belonging to their enemy,
they dwelt there in battle, intoxicated and terrifying to all foes; meanwhile,
Dhundhukāra and the other forces were there.
Making a tumultuous noise, they approached for battle;
O best of the Bhṛgus, in the forenoon they set out fully armed, carrying *śataghnīs*.
With three thousand *śataghnīs*, five thousand [warriors] marched forth.
Accompanied by two thousand *śataghnīs*, the descendants of the Lunar dynasty,
along with an army of sixty thousand, departed for their own world;
likewise, half of Mahīrāja’s army was destroyed.
The brave warriors, though fearful, fled in the ten directions from Valakhilya.
In that battle, chariots struck down chariots, and likewise elephants struck down elephants;
horses struck down horses, and camels struck down camels.
When such a tumultuous, dreadful, and hair-raising battle had thus arisen,
and seeing his own mighty troops crying out in lamentation,
O best of the Bhrigus, five heroes arrived in the afternoon.
Brahmānanda sent his enemies to the abode of Yama with arrows;
likewise, Devasiṃha did so with bhalla-shafts, and Āhrāda there with tomara-spears.
Balakhāni used his own sword, and Kṛṣṇāṃśa did exactly the same.
Then, with all his forces, they slew two hundred thousand Kṣatriyas.
Seeing his army defeated, the exceedingly powerful Dhundhukāra,
mounted upon an elephant, struck Āhlāda with a broad-headed arrow.
While Āhlāda was thus rendered unconscious there, the exceedingly powerful Devasiṃha swiftly struck his brother with a broad-headed arrow (bhalla).
Having sustained that sharp wound, he indeed fell into a swoon while still mounted upon his elephant.
Hundred kings of great strength from various lands arrived;
having cut through their weapons and missiles with his sword,
the son of Vatsa struck off their heads with his own blade and cast them to the ground.
When the host of enemies was slain, those who remained fled;
but the powerful Mahīrāja, seeing his own army broken,
arrived mounted upon an elephant— the mighty one who had received a boon from Śiva.
With the Raudra weapon, he struck the enemy Vatsaja in the heart;
likewise, having rendered the great heroes Āhlāda, Vīra, Deva, and Parimalātmaja unconscious, he advanced against the hostile army.
Having honored the *śataghnīs*, he caused a great slaughter;
Ropaṇa, having gone quickly, described everything to the king.
In the meantime, the heroic and mighty Sukhakhāni—
Mounting a pigeon-like horse, he traveled through the path of the sky;
having rendered King Mahīrāja and his kinsmen, along with their mounts, unconscious,
he arrived at the king's presence and prepared for his capture.
Then, having been awakened by Mahādeva, the king of the earth rose up;
filled with wrath, he once again rendered them unconscious with his fierce arrows.
Having bound the heroes, such as Sukhasvānyādi and others, with firm iron chains, he imprisoned them.
Having encountered King Parimala, he provoked him to battle once more; then,
seeing his own army crying out in distress, that Hari Udaya placed the horse on the path of the sky and destroyed those thunderbolts.
Having captured the elephant Mahīrājagaja and bound it with chains,
Bala went to the side of Āhlāda and delivered the king to his brother.
Then Pṛthivīrāja, defeated by him, was filled with shame.
Having given five crores of wealth,
Śūra Balakhāṇi, the son of Vatsa, returned once more to his own home by the command of Devasiṃha;
with those riches, he caused a beautiful and lovely city to be built.

A city named Śirīṣa was indeed established by that hero; it was endowed with all social classes and measured two krośas in length. Therein the hero, the son of Vatsa, resided together with his own kinsmen.
In that very place, within a distance of thirty *kośas*, Balakhānin established a kingdom.
Hearing of this, King Parimala arrived there filled with joy;
having smelled the scent of the brave Vatsaja as well as the son of Deśarāja, he was likewise delighted.
Accompanied by Brahmānanda, he returned once more to his own home.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Compendium of Histories of the Kali Age," within the *Caturyugakhaṇḍa* (also known as the *Pratisargaparvan*) of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
Indeed, listen to how it happened during the twelfth year of Kṛṣṇa’s portion:
on the tenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Īṣa, a gathering of kings took place.
In the most delightful city of Kānyakubja, various monarchs assembled.
O Sage, having heard of the defeat of King Mahīrāja, Lakṣaṇa then felt a desire to see a portion of Kṛṣṇa;
he said to his paternal uncle, the king, "I shall go to see that auspicious one."
"By whom the great king, honored by all the world, has been conquered"—
having heard these words of his, King Jayacandra spoke to his brother’s son who was bowing before him: "Listen, O Śuklayaśaskara!"
"How can you wish to seize the position of the King of Kings?
Having spoken thus, Jayacandra did not grant him permission at all;
and those kings, together with their own armies, surrounded him.
Desiring to see a portion of Kṛṣṇa, they went together to the lord of the earth;
and having learned that the supreme portion of Kṛṣṇa was residing in the city named Śirīṣa,
the kings then arrived, placing the lord of the earth at their head.
They beheld that high-souled one, whose face resembled a lotus;
with serene countenances, they all praised him from every side.
Then the lord of the earth, filled with rage, spoke these words to the kings:
The parents of him for whom this praise was offered by you while living far away have both died in Māhiṣmatī;
he is a king named Jambuka, accompanied by the people of the Narmadā region.
Having bound them and plundered much wealth, he set out for his home;
having placed their bodies upon stone slabs, he crushed them to powder,
severed their heads, and climbed up a banyan tree.
Even now those two heroes remain there, crying out, "Alas, our son!
For him whose parents have become ghosts in their deceased bodies, his great strength is known to be in vain, and his fame, though pleasing, is likewise useless.
Having heard this, that partial incarnation of Kṛṣṇa, with a humble mind, said to the kings:
"My parents have gone together to Gurjara, where indeed there is a battle;
a conflict has taken place between the king and the flesh-eating Mlecchas."

The King of Deśa and the King of Vatsa, having engaged in a terrifying battle, were both slain there by those Mlecchas; this famous account has been heard. Today, their recent death was related by my maternal uncle.
"If his word is true, behold my prowess!
Having said this to them, that portion of Kṛṣṇa quickly spoke to his mother,
describing the reason and the speech of the king.
Having heard those words, which were like a thunderbolt, the mother then wept;
afflicted by grief for her husband, the mother gave no reply.
Having learned of the father's death and having heard that the jackal was a servant of Śiva, she wept.
And that portion of Kṛṣṇa praised the Supreme Goddess in his mind:
"Victory, victory, victory, O Mother of the World! O Bhavānī, you are indeed the source of all worlds, gods, ancestors, and sages.
By you alone is this entire universe, including the moving and the unmoving, pervaded; by you alone has this protection been taken away."
Having meditated thus, that portion of Kṛṣṇa went to sleep in his own abode.
Then the omnipresent Bhagavatī, being pleased, quickly deluded the exceedingly powerful Tālana and dispatched him to his side.
Tālana arrived swiftly with four hundred thousand troops and urged on his own mighty army of one hundred thousand.
Then Balakhāni also arrived, accompanied by a force of one hundred thousand.
Having stationed his younger brother there at the place called Śirīṣa, the mighty King Parimala,
seeing them prepared with their armies in the garden,
became afraid and advanced toward the portion of Kṛṣṇa.
Seeing the king distressed, the portion of Kṛṣṇa joyfully comforted him;
taking his hundred-thousand-strong army, he became its commander.
There were five thousand *śataghnīs* of various colors, well-equipped with excellent mounts.
There were five thousand banners, one thousand carpenters,
ten thousand elephants, five thousand chariots,
three hundred thousand horses, and ten thousand camels.
The remaining soldiers in that fearsome army were to be known as foot-soldiers;
Tālana arrived and became the commander of the entire host,
while Devasiṃha became the lord of all the chariots.
Balakhāni became the lord of all horses,
Āhlāda became the lord of all elephants,
and Kṛṣṇāṃśa became the lord of all foot soldiers.
Having bowed to Mālanā and given manifold gifts,
the king and all those others, accompanied by their forces, set out for the southern direction;
a period of only a fortnight passed while they were on that road seeking battle.
Having cleared that formidable forest filled with various thorns,
those mighty ones fearlessly encamped their army;
at the very word of Devasiṃha, they then became like yogins.
Nartaka, Kṛṣṇāṃśa, Āhlāda who is fond of the hand-drum (ḍamaru),
the god Maḍḍudhārī, Vīṇādhārī, Tālana,
Vatsaja, Kāṃsyadhārī, and the very powerful Balakhāni.
Standing before their mother, they indeed danced, overwhelmed with love;
Devakī was bewildered and did not understand the reason for it.
Seeing their mother thus bewildered, they experienced supreme joy.
Then they said to her, "O lady, we are indeed your sons.
Having bowed to her, they all departed for the auspicious city of Māhiṣmatī;
there, being experts in instrumental music and song, they enchanted the city.
Intent on their mission, they went to the house of the enemy along with the messenger;
devoted to enchanting the king with dance, song, and excellent instrumental music,
the portion of Kṛṣṇa who deludes all rendered the queen unconscious.
He arrived at the place where his daughter, desiring victory, was located.
Seeing that Supreme Person with a beautiful form and a dark-complexioned body,
she became infatuated and fell under his power, intent upon sexual union.

Seeing the woman thus approached, Kṛṣṇāṃśa, with gentle words, questioned the passionate lady, who was overwhelmed by intoxication, regarding the sowing of dissension among the enemies. She said: "O son of Devakī, if you will take my hand in marriage..."
"In that case, I shall tell you of my father's terrible betrayal.
Having said, "So be it," the powerful one took her hand;
and having learned all the enemy's treachery, he comforted her and departed with joy.
In the meantime, the queen, being tormented, said to the yogin:
"Delighted and captivated by his dancing and singing, I shall give you the food favored by the King of the Land, which is worth nine hundred thousand."
Having heard this, the son of Vatsa praised her and accepted it;
he then departed with his kinsmen to where Jambūka was staying. There, the portion of Kṛṣṇa danced and Balakhāni sang.
The god Tālana, who brings delight, joyfully blew various musical instruments;
there, King Kāliya along with his kinsmen became enchanted.
"O limb of Kṛṣṇa, choose whatever boon resides in your heart."
Having heard these words of his enemy, the exceedingly powerful Balakhānin said to him: "O protector of the earth, when that excellent woman, who has performed a hundred thousand circumambulations,
demonstrates her own supernatural power to me, only then shall I attain satisfaction."

Having heard this and reflected thus, the best of kings had his beloved, the princess of Deśa, dance a hundred thousand times in the assembly hall. That courtesan, realizing that her son Āhlāda had attained the state of a yogin, [was filled with joy].
Afflicted by grief, she wept there, shedding tears from her eyes;
seeing her thus weeping, the mighty Āhlāda himself began to cry and struck his own arms for the sake of his beloved.
There, Kṛṣṇāṃśa placed that necklace around her neck;
with eyes copper-red from anger, he comforted her again and again and said:
"I am this Ucchaiḥsiṃha, come here for the sake of my father’s enmity."
"I shall slay the enemy king, along with his sons and his army.
Having heard these words of his, the exceedingly powerful Kāliya,
honoring his father's command, set out accompanied by a hundred battle-arrays.
He firmly shut the door for their very confinement;
then, having given leave to those enemies who held nooses in hand and carried weapons,
those Kṣatriyas drew their respective swords and struck one another.
When Śataśūra was slain by them, Kāliya, overcome with fear,
fled, abandoning his father; they, however, went out from their home and,
quickly reaching their own army, stood ready for battle.
Camps had already been established by those stationed on the banks of the Narmadā;
having constructed a bridge across the Narmadā about a *nalva* in length which provided excellent sustenance,
he ferried his fourfold army across.
Balakhāni, joined by his forces, besieged the entire city,
placing before him hundreds of great-noised *śataghnī* weapons;
he then brought down the palaces of Māhiṣmatī to the ground.
And the men, together with their kinsmen and equipped with their principal resources,
reached a cave in the Vindhya mountain and dwelt there, overcome with fear. Kāliya, however, remained mounted upon Pañcaśabdagaja in the army of elephants.
Ten thousand elephant-riders arrived for battle;
his younger brother Sūryavarman was accompanied by three hundred thousand horses,
and Tuṇḍila, stationed in his chariot, was with a thousand chariots.
Both Raṅkaṇa and Vaṅkaṇa, those two great Mlecchas, set out with four hundred thousand foot soldiers and thousands of Mleccha kings;
placing the village chiefs of the south at their head, they marched forward.
When both armies had encountered one another and stood ready for battle,
a tumultuous and hair-raising conflict ensued between them;
for three watches, a river of their blood flowed swiftly.
Having seen the terrible river Asrajā flowing with mud of flesh, Balakhānin, of immeasurable soul, went forth with sword in hand;
then the god, with *bhalla* arrows in his hand, stood mounted upon the horse of the mind’s desire.
And Kṛṣṇāṃśa, stationed at Biṃdula, slew his enemies with a sword;
Āhlāda, mace in hand, crushed the army;
and a Śūdra named Rūpaṇa, with a spear in hand, struck down his foes.
Tālajaṅgha, with sword in hand, went to Māhiṣmatī.
When such great terror had arisen in that mighty battle, the heroes fled in all directions, crying out, "Protect us! Protect us!"
Seeing his own army shattered, the mighty Kāliya, mounted upon an elephant, struck Bālakhānika with his arrows; meanwhile,
his two wives, Hariṇī and Vaḍavā, perceiving their lord to be in distress, [rushed to his aid].

Mounting upon the elephant, he struck it down with his own feet. When the heroic Kāliya had fallen, the great elephant Pañcaśabda struck those heroes, who were intoxicated with pride, with his chains.
When Pañcaśūra had fainted, Rūpaṇa, trembling with fear,
described Devakī exactly as she had been born by the elephant.
Then the distressed queen quickly mounted a swing.
Having approached that elephant, he explained the reason:
"O King of Elephants, salutations to you, O one of great strength bestowed by Śakra!
O hero, these sons of yours must be protected just as a father would."
Having heard this, the divine elephant, skilled in divine illusions,
sought refuge with Devakī, saying, "Forgive my transgression.
When the king of elephants had spoken thus, the most powerful portion of Kṛṣṇa [manifested].
Abandoning his swoon, he went to where Āhlāda was unconscious;
having raised him with the touch of his hands, accompanied by Balakhāni,
he presented his father’s great rutting elephant to Āhlāda.
Then, with a fierce yet gentle smile, he gave his form to the enemy Kāliya;
having bound that unconscious foe with firm shackles,
the mighty Balakhāni sent him to the edge of the army.
Then Sūryavarman, learning that his kinsman Kāliya had been captured,
advanced toward the enemy army with his lips quivering in rage.
Beholding him approaching, those heroes, intoxicated by the pride of battle, [prepared for combat].

O Sage, as they brandished their respective weapons while standing upon their chariots in circular formations, those weapons became blunted; at that, they were struck with wonder and fell into deep anxiety,
wondering, "How can this one be slain?"
Afflicted by the pain and fear of wounds from his weapons, those great heroes abandoned the battle; yet, returning once more, they fought again and again.
In this manner, that supreme battle continued for several days.
Āhlāda, Vatsaja, Deva, and Tālana were seized by fear;
deluded by that hero, they sought refuge in Kṛṣṇa.
But Kṛṣṇa, seeing them thus, [beheld] the goddess who deludes the entire universe.
The hero praised her mentally while reciting the Rātrisūkta in his heart.
Then Durgā, the sustainer of the world and destroyer of the suffering of the distressed, was pleased;
she deluded that hero and vanished right there.
Seeing him overcome by sleep, the mighty son of Kṛṣṇa bound him with fetters and approached Devakī. Tundila, likewise perceiving this, was overwhelmed with grief for his brother.
Mounted on a horse, sword in hand, and endowed with great strength,
he arrived and struck down many heroes in the midst of the enemy army;
those heroes of Māhiṣmatī were accompanied by Raṅkaṇa.
They shattered that army protected by Tālana;
seeing his own forces fleeing, Tālana, armed with an iron club,
struck off the heads of the Mlecchas one by one.
Having likewise slain Vaṅkaṇa with his sword and Raṅkaṇa as well,
and having bound Tuṇḍila, he went to the camp at the end of the day;
and when the enemy Kāliya was bound and Sūryavarman was securely fettered.
When Tuṇḍila was likewise bound, Raṅkaṇa captured, and Vaṅkaṇa slain,
the thousand Mleccha kings who remained after the slaughter, though possessed of great strength,
fought on all sides for a full fortnight of days and nights.
Every day, the heroic and impatient general Tālana,
who struck terror into the enemy army, swiftly slew sixty kings. Terrified by their foe, those brave kings were slain, their vital energy destroyed.
The survivors of the army, numbering half its original strength, fled to their homes overcome with fear.
Having heard this, Jambuka returned home deeply distressed;
having undertaken a vow of fasting, he lay down at night grieving.
When midnight had arrived, his daughter, desiring victory and dwelling in Vraja,
was to be known as Rādhā, complete in all her digits;
skilled in the arts of illusion, she comforted her father and departed.
Having bewildered the guards of the camps,
she arrived there where her brothers were;
having employed her demonic illusion (rākṣasī māyā), she deluded all five heroes.
He mounted the swing together with his kinsmen, who were without weapons or armor;
having approached his father, he joyfully presented his brothers to him.
At dawn, they were all awakened and performed their rites, such as bathing and meditation.
Having done so, they went to the enemy’s hall, but they did not see them there at that time.
They all became distressed, wondering, "What is this? What is the cause?
Then the god said to them, "The enemy’s daughter has indeed arrived here."
Having employed that Rākṣasa illusion and having carried them away, she returned to her home.
Therefore, you all must go with me to where that preceptor resides,
upon the Vindhya mountains in a great forest frequented by various creatures.
His hut was right there, for he was indeed named Elavila;
endowed with yogic powers, that lustful man was fearless of the Rākṣasas.
There, the daughter of Jambuka lived daily together with her own kinsmen.
And she, being alone at night, gratified that teacher of hers.
This illusion, which deludes men, was created by her from a cloth.
"Having gone to that lowest of men, we shall achieve our purpose."
Having heard this, the four of them went to the forest without Hāhā;
having deluded him that day with song, dance, and instrumental music,
