they took up residence right there with the rogue who was skilled in illusion.
In a previous birth, that great asura named Citra was a Daitya who constantly worshipped Śiva; desiring Uṣā, the daughter of Bāṇa,
he was born as the powerful one named Ailavila, a worshiper of the lunar fortnights.
"If this marriage of mine takes place between those two [brothers],
then I shall serve you, having abandoned my wedded husband;
once that great rogue has been slain at the front of the battle."
Having seen the fortress, they went toward it and ascended;
having slain the heroes stationed there, they took up the śataghnī weapons placed along the moats.
Then the powerful Jambuka, who had received a boon from Śiva, became their king.

Having conquered the five great heroes and bound them with firm fetters, he performed a Śaiva sacrifice, augmented by their names. Rūpaṇa, having likewise learned this, described Devakī [to his father].
Then the virtuous goddess, distressed, quickly went in her mind for refuge to Bhavānī, the remover of fear and the worthy recipient of protection.
Then the Mother of the World, being pleased, spoke to her at the end of a dream and described [the means].
"O auspicious Devakī, abandon now your grief for your son!
When the powerful King Jambuka, having received a boon from Śiva, performs a fire-sacrifice— that evil-minded one— for the sake of an offering to them,"
"Having deluded him at that time and having liberated your sons, I shall grant you victory; do not set your mind on grief.
Having heard this, the virtuous goddess paid homage to Maheśvarī.
He worshipped [them] according to the prescribed rites with incense, lamps, and offerings.
In the meantime, the king, deluded by divine illusion,
fell asleep there at the conclusion of the fire-oblation, and they indeed became free from their bonds.
Bound with those firm iron shackles, the king-jackal was secured;
having bound him, they went quickly and fearlessly toward Devakī.
In the meantime, three sons there, Kāliya and the others—
Taking an army of three hundred thousand, they advanced for battle;
then a terrible battle took place once more between the two armies.
Tāla and the other three brothers, having slain that hostile host, [proceeded].
Having hemmed their three enemies within a courtyard, the powerful warriors struck them with their own weapons.
In this manner, a great battle took place there for several days.
Kāliya, becoming distressed, remembered Hara in his mind.
Having obtained the deluding mantra, he bewildered those enemies.
In the meantime, the goddess Devakī, who held her husband as her deity,
approached her son by virtue of the merit of her devotion to her husband.
Having awakened Kṛṣṇāṃśa, who was seated upon a five-syllabled elephant,
he again praised his mother, who deludes the entire universe. Then the Goddess herself, being pleased, joyfully awakened them.
Then his younger brother, Balakhānin, struck down Sūryavarman, Kāliya, and that Tundila, the son of Jambuka. O Brahmin, in their previous birth, those two— Jarāsandha along with Kāliya— were...
The heroic monkey Dvivida became Sūryavarman here;
Triśiras was born as Tila, and he who was Śṛgāla became Jambuka.
All these kings on the surface of the earth were constant makers of enmity.
Devakī, devoted solely to grief for her husband, threatened the jackal, her enemy among hateful sons of foes, with her sword;
while Kṛṣṇāṃśa, distressed by affection, took hold of his parents' heads.
Overwhelmed with emotion, he placed [the body] upon the heart of the jackal itself.
Then, laughing, those two spoke these pleasing words there:
"Live long indeed, O portion of Kṛṣṇa; perform the Gayā-śrāddha, O high-minded one!"
Thus the conversation between those two powerful ones, whose bodies were like those of the deceased, came to an end.
Then that goddess, sword in hand, having placed her enemy within the stone machine,
urged on her sons with great joy.
The sons, filled with joy, cut that jackal— the lowest of men and enemy of their father— into pieces as small as sesame seeds,
and they crushed his body with oil produced from the *madana* plant.
"I shall bathe," she said, and then the mother wept bitterly.
Having done so, those sons then summoned the queen along with her son,
accompanied by Balakhilyas, and performed that rite there.
Then, O Brahmin sage, seeing her husband afflicted and on the verge of death, Queen Parimala passed away.
Her daughter, having taken up a sword, [rushed] toward the arm of Balakhāni.
Having struck him down and rendered him unconscious, she pursued his partisans—
Tālana, Devasiṃha, and likewise Rāmāṃśa—
and having slain other enemies as well, she returned, though her kinsmen were terrified.
Having quickly deluded Kṛṣṇāṃśa with his illusory power, he seized him;
when that hundred heroes had been slain, the indignant Balakhānin took their heads and cast them onto the funeral pyre.
Then a voice arose: "O Balakhāna, listen!
A woman is always exempt from being killed by you; however, those who are unrighteous may be slain. You must experience the fruit of this sinful deed in your own marriage."
Having heard this, Balakhāni then departed for his city in sorrow;
meanwhile, all the soldiers, filled with great joy,
plundered wealth along with hundreds of camels laden with heavy burdens.
Having attained the state of having fulfilled their purpose, they returned to Mahāvatī;
accompanied by the remnants of their armies, half of whom had been slain, they went home.

Thus ends the twelfth chapter of the *Kaliyugīyetihāsasamuccaya* (The Compendium of Histories of the Kali Age), which is an alternative section of the *Caturyugakhaṇḍa* within the *Pratisargaparvan* of the glorious *Bhaviṣyamahāpurāṇa*.
The sages said:
"In which month did the battle between those two take place, and for how many days?
After that, O Sage, when he returned to his own city, what then happened?"
Sūta said:
The battle between those two lasted for one hundred days during the month of Pauṣa;
then, in the month of Jyeṣṭha, they reached home and blew their various musical instruments many times.
Having heard that his powerful son Jaya had conquered the enemies, King Parimala bestowed gifts upon the Brahmins; happiness arose in every household.
Having heard this, the king of the earth [approached] the exceedingly powerful Balakhāni.
Having arrived there and offered his salutations, he spoke these words with a humble mind:
"O Hero, accept from me wealth amounting to fifty million and be happy;
grant me the kingdom of Māhiṣmatī as well. Salutations to you!"
"O powerful Lord, accept that wealth year after year.
Having heard this and agreed accordingly, Balakhāni went home.
And when the thirteenth year had passed, while the portion of Kṛṣṇa was exceedingly powerful...
O best of the Bhṛgus, hear how the pastimes of Hari unfolded:
on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, Āhlāda set out with his younger brothers for Gayā,
taking with him wealth and a multitude of elephants, horses, and chariots.
Kṛṣṇāṃśa was mounted upon Bindulā; Vatsaja was seated on a deer;
the Lord Papīhaka was mounted on Karālaka, the mine of happiness.
At the end of two days, these four arrived at the sacred field of Gayā.
Having honored those who performed the sixteen śrāddhas at the end of the full moon,
they gave a hundred elephants and a hundred adorned chariots,
as well as a thousand horses decorated with golden garlands.
Having given cows, gold, jewels, and various garments,
they attained excellent fruits and set their minds upon returning to their own homes.
But the courtesan Lakṣāvartī went to Badarikāśrama.
Having cast off her life there, she attained the state of an Apsaras.
And when the moon was eclipsed by Rāhu and enveloped in darkness on the full-moon night,
kings from various lands arrived at Kāśī together with their kinsmen.
On the beautiful Himalaya mountain, variegated with various minerals,
there dwelt a king named Netrasimha, a scion of the Śārdūla lineage.
When the heroic Ratnabhanu was slain, Netrasimha became stricken with fear.
Having reached Navatunga, he gratified Vāsava;
at the end of twelve years, the Lord joyfully gave the Dhaṅkā-nectar to Vāsava,
his devoted servant, which had been prepared by Pārvatī.
He gave the Ḍhakkā-amṛta to the king and spoke these auspicious words again: "O protector of the earth, by its sound you shall revive your army;
your great warriors, the enemies, will swiftly go to their destruction."
When that nectar of the drum was obtained, the mighty Netrasimha caused a city to be built there, filled with all kinds of people,
measuring one yojana across, possessing four gates, and ever impregnable to enemies.

O Sage, that fortress known by the name Netrasiṃhagaḍha, which was built on the border of Kāśmīra in the kingdom of Bhārata and was like a mountain peak, was thereafter protected by Netrasiṃha as if it were his own son.
That village is known as Netrapāla; it is difficult for enemies to access. That king, the very powerful Netrasimha, has also arrived there.
His daughter is Svarṇavatī, who is endowed with a portion of Revatī.
By the granting of a boon from Kāmākṣī, she became proficient in all forms of illusion.
Seeing that beautiful maiden with a face like the young moon,
the kings, infatuated by her beauty and youth, fell into a swoon.
And having seen her thus adorned with every jewel,
a young woman of sixteen years, possessing the form of Rati,
Āhlāda fell to the ground in a swoon; indeed, upon seeing her, he lost consciousness.
Having mounted the swing, her two friends approached the presence of the king;
Āhlāda, however, having risen, fell into a state of great delusion. Seeing his kinsman in such a condition, the partial incarnation of Kṛṣṇa spoke, deeply distressed.
Why have you fallen into delusion, O Lord who are skilled in the knowledge of reality?
Know that passion consists of the quality of *rajas*, and likewise that negligence is born of delusion (*moha*).
O Unconquered One, always sever its head with the sword of wisdom.
Having heard these words of his brother, he abandoned his delusion and went home;
there, having fed a thousand of the best brahmins who were devoted to the Vedas,
he worshipped Durgā by reciting the Madhyamacaritra.

Then, at the end of the month, the blameless goddess, having granted the desired boon that resided in her heart, enchanted that maiden for the sake of marriage. In a dream, the young girl saw the son of Devakī, who is a portion of Rāma.
Having woken up in the morning and reflected deeply, he fell into a state of great delusion;
then, meditating upon Kāmākṣī, the bestower of all desires,
when the month of Pauṣa had arrived, [he saw] a beautiful letter on a parrot’s neck.
Having tied that beloved parrot onto a leaf, he sent him forth.
Having gone to the flower forest situated near the great city of Avanti,
the parrot spoke these words in a human voice to the portion of Kṛṣṇā.
O hero, your younger kinsman named Āhlāda is possessed of great strength;
indeed, a letter conferring benefit was sent to him by Svarṇavatī.
Having learned of that, give her a reply in return that is pleasing to me.
"Or else, having written the letter, deliver it to my neck.
Having heard this, the heroic Udaya took the excellent letter,
learned the news therein, and gave it back with joy.
And the heroic king Jambuka, powerful and granted a boon by Rudra, was invincible to other kings, O hero; yet he has been struck down by you in battle.
Likewise, my father, who was such a foe and had received a boon from Indra—
"Kill him thus in battle; take my hand in marriage.
Having understood this, Āhlāda comforted her as she remained in his heart, and quickly wrote an excellent letter and fastened it around the neck of the parrot.
That parrot, having been previously cursed by Puṇḍarīka,
attained liberation after performing the task of the portion of Revatī.
When that beautiful parrot died, the goddess Svarṇavatī then [departed].
Having cremated him, he gave gifts to the Brahmins for his satisfaction.
And when the month of Māgha arrived, on the fifth day of the dark fortnight,
Āhlāda joyfully set forth together with seven hundred thousand troops.
Those heroes, Tāla and the others, mounted upon their respective vehicles and proceeded for fifteen days while protecting Āhlāda;
having crossed the land of Vaṅga, they quickly reached the Himalayas.
Rūpaṇa spoke to Patrakartṛ, the son of Balakhāni:
"Go, O hero, clad in armor and mounted upon Karālāśva;
equipped with five weapons, bring the king here quickly."
"Having placed the mark of battle upon your body, come to me with haste.
Thinking thus, that Rūpaṇa, who was a portion of Śikhaṇḍin, departed quickly.
He beheld the king’s assembly hall, filled with many heroes.
Accompanied by thousands of exceedingly powerful mountain kings,
he spoke to the mighty Netrasimha, the best of monarchs:
"The very powerful Balakhāni has come for the marriage of your daughter."
Protected by seven hundred thousand forces, he has arrived in your kingdom;
therefore, quickly surrender your daughter for his delight.
O King, give me the bride-price in the form of a most terrible battle.
Having heard these words of his, the king, overwhelmed with rage,
commanded the lord of the city, King Pūrṇabala, and in his fury he had the gates blocked for the purpose of imprisoning him.
Seeing a hundred heroes with nooses in their hands protected by the lord of the city, the heroic Rūpaṇa engaged them in a sword-fight;
having slain them and seized the king's crown, the powerful one ascended into the sky.
Having reached Balakhāni, he presented the token to him.
Hearing this, his soul filled with joy, he— accompanied by seven hundred thousand divisions—
besieged the entire city protected by Netrasiṃha.
The powerful Netrasiṃha, together with the mountain kings,
reached the slopes of Himatuṅga and, seeking battle, challenged them;
he had a thousand elephants and a hundred thousand exceedingly strong horses.
A thousand brave kings with four hundred thousand foot soldiers,
along with Yogasiṃha and his elephants, challenged Balakhāni;
and Bhogasiṃha, together with his horses, challenged Kṛṣṇāṃśa.
Prince Vijaya, along with all the kings,
and likewise Devasiṃha, challenged the Mlecchas and Rūpaṇa.
Between those two, there occurred a great and terrible battle between their armies.
Fearless and heroic, those mountaineers from all sides struck down the enemy army of two hundred thousand men protected by warriors.
Seeing their own forces broken, four who were intoxicated with pride [advanced].
Mounting divine horses, they wrought great slaughter upon the enemy;
yet the entire army was restored to life by the nectar-like sound of the *ḍhakkā* drum.
O best of the Bhrigus, it came again and again to face the battle.
A fierce battle took place among them right there for a full day and night;
thus, when seven days had passed in that war which struck terror into the hearts of cowards,
the heroes waged many battles through numerous stratagems.
Having regained their lives, they struck down those leaders of the enemy army;
yet those heroes, Tāla and the others, became distressed there,
and finding themselves without hope for victory, they sought refuge with the portion of Kṛṣṇa.
Having comforted them, that powerful portion of Kṛṣṇa, stationed upon his divine horse,
traveled through the path of the sky and arrived at the vicinity of Svarṇavatī,
where the Goddess stood atop her palace, endowed with every splendor.
Having bowed, he spoke these gentle words: "O illustrious one, I am your servant here; I have come to you for refuge, O beautiful lady, as Kāmākṣī [seeks her consort].
He related the entire account, including how that great battle had occurred."
"Exhausted by fatigue, the heroes lost all hope for life.
Therefore, O lion among men, you must go to the temple of Kāmākṣī;
as for me, I shall remain intent on worship on the ninth day together with my female companions."
"I shall worship with the sounding of the ḍhakkā drum that grants all desires.
Having heard this, that powerful one returned toward his own army;
and having caused the army, which was reduced to half, to flee from the battle, they retreated.
Having reached the city named Paṭṭana and achieved victory, those of great strength,
together with the sons of Netrasimha, returned home once that enemy had been defeated; thereupon the powerful one bestowed wealth in cattle upon the Brahmins.
Then, on the ninth day, Queen Svarṇavatī said to her father:
"Quickly perform for me a festival of sacrifice by means of serving Kāmākṣī,
through whose grace you have become victorious over those who were difficult to conquer."
Having heard this, the father said: "A dream was seen by me in that same manner;
through worship there will be prosperity for kings, otherwise there will indeed be an obstacle, O beautiful one.
When her father had spoken thus, at night, that daughter, by her father's command, [proceeded].
Accompanied by the sound of the drum of immortality (ḍhakkāmṛta), he went to the house of Kāmākṣī;
having become the wife of a garland-maker, the portion of Kṛṣṇa arrived there,
and taking the ḍhakkāmṛta from the women, he departed in haste.
In the meantime, sixty heroes, accompanied by their mounts and with all their weapons raised, set out quickly for the sake of the drum.
Seeing them approaching, that powerful man took up his sword.
The portion of Kṛṣṇa, having gone quickly to where Rūpaṇa stood, led fifty-five heroes to the abode of Yama;
and having obtained the Ḍhakkā and the nectar, he mounted his horse and went to the assembly hall.
When the divine drum Ḍhakkāmṛta was stolen, Netrasiṃha became afflicted with fear;
having performed the Indra-sacrifice, he became intent upon the oblation.
When morning arrived, those heroes, together with their own forces, [set out].
Mounted upon elephants, camels, and horses, they all proceeded swiftly;
at the end of the day, they reached the place where the great battle had occurred.
Having worshipped him, the powerful portion of Kṛṣṇa blew the Ḍhakkā drum of nectar.
By that word, the fallen heroes were then restored to life;
his army of seven hundred thousand, intoxicated with pride, once again besieged the entire city and blew various musical instruments many times over.
When that city was besieged, Netrasimha, overcome by fear,
offered himself into the fire for the sake of the wise Śakra.
Then the Blessed One, being pleased, spoke to the king:
This [son] is a portion of Rāma and a portion of Kṛṣṇa, born on earth through a single *kalā*.
To that illustrious one, who is a portion of Rāma and worthy of her,
this yoginī Svarṇavatī is an incarnation of a portion of Revatī.
Having spoken thus, the Lord himself took the *ḍhakkā* and the nectar dear to Umā,
cast them into the fire, and presented them to Durgā.
When that lord of the gods had departed, the king, together with the Brahmins, [proceeded].
He set out, intent on meeting the lord of the earth.
Upon seeing the king who had arrived in such a manner, the venerable uncle of Kṛṣṇa— the lord of the earth who was always honored by all his forces— spoke with great joy.

"O King, this powerful Āhrāda, along with his younger brothers, has fallen to a low status in our lineage; that hero did not stand in my row. Have you not heard that their noble mother was an Ābhīrī woman?"
If you intend to give away your daughter, then you shall indeed fall into degradation;
therefore, O sir, listen to these words appropriate for your lineage:
[four lowly boys, accompanied by a cymbal.]
Having deceived them for the sake of their marriage, collect their heads;
having constructed a sacrificial pavilion, offer them to Cāmuṇḍā.
For that Revatī is indeed a heroine summoned by your daughter.
"Afterwards, having yourself slain the maiden, bring about the welfare of the lineage;
otherwise, you will go to destruction along with your kin, just like the jackal.
Having said this, he departed together with him to where Ahrāda’s kinsman was.
Having heard what was spoken by the mouth of Suyodhana, that portion of Śalya said,
"So be it," and having performed a celebration according to the prescribed rites at the edge of the pavilion,
he went into the presence of Āhlāda for the purpose of deceiving him.
Taking his feet in his hands like a staff, the king himself said to him:
"I have learned from the best of gods that you are all partial incarnations;
having honored you five, who are now divested of your weapons, according to the prescribed rites—"
"I shall give my daughter to the portion of Rāma according to family custom. Having thus instructed Āhṛda, the king, resorting to deceit,
went to his home for the festival of Durgā, intent upon her slaughter.
Having stationed a thousand kings with their own forces within the pavilion,
he summoned six brave warriors, including Tāla and others, to the edge of the pavilion.
At the first round of the wedding ceremony, Yogasiṃha drew his excellent sword.
Seizing his tusk and striking it against his head, the powerful one roared in rage.
The wise Tālana said to him, "What you have done is not proper.
Having heard this, Netrasiṃha said to him, "O strong one, this is the custom of our lineage."
"Indeed, our battle is with armed enemies against those who are unarmed.
Having heard this, the portion of Kṛṣṇa mounted that Lion of Yoga (Yogasiṃha),
while Balakhāni likewise dragged away the Serpent-Lion (Bhogasiṃha) and captured him.
In the third turn, Vijaya, a mine of happiness, indeed held back [the enemy];
in the fourth turn, Rūpaṇa quickly seized that wicked king Pūrṇabala, who was full of strength, and fought with his forces.
In the fifth round, Bahurāja and Tālana were subdued;
likewise, in the sixth round, Āhlāda seized Netrasiṃha.
When that tumultuous battle had commenced, many heroes met their destruction.
Deprived of weapons, those six powerful ones, having healed their grievous wounds,
made their respective enemies weaponless— those who were devoted to the worship of Śakti.
In the meantime, the god Kāladarśin arrived.
Coming through the path of the sky, he delivered those horses to them: Bindula and Kṛṣṇāṃśa received the horse Manoratha;
Rūpaṇa received Karālāśva; and Āhlāda received Papīhaka.
Balakhāni, his brother, mounted Hariṇī and went to Harinagara; the heroic Tālana, having mounted Siṃhinī and being intent on battle,
slaughtered that king’s army at night and captured his lord.
Having brought the swing, which was fashioned with seven bells, out from the house,
those even more powerful ones arrived at your army, fearless;
seeing all of them, including Netra, Siṃha, and the others, he cried out, "Save me!"
Having bound those five deceitful kings with shackles on one side,
he confined them in that most terrible prison;
[so too did] Netrasiṃha, the excellent brother, and Sundarāraṇya, the lord of the earth.
Having understood the cause, the illusory Māyāvī arrived swiftly with an army of one hundred thousand;
having reached that place, he was the powerful son of Harānanda, named Tāna.
Then, an army of four hundred thousand belonging to Netrasiṃha also arrived.

A terrible battle took place between them for five days and nights, involving five hundred thousand and seven hundred thousand warriors respectively; that tumultuous conflict lasted for just five days and nights,
and half of the enemy's army fled there, having survived the slaughter.
Filled with wonder, that Hara-ānanda, who was skilled in the illusory powers of Rudra,
recognized them as being endowed with superior strength and became intent on meditating upon Śiva.
Having fashioned an illusory power (*śāmbarī māyā*) capable of assuming various forms, he [acted].
Having rendered all the kings as if they were mere stones,
the mighty one then went home, having fulfilled his purpose and having liberated his eldest brother, King Pūrṇabala, along with his son.
Having bound Āhlāda with fetters and rendered him senseless through illusion,
that powerful Netrasiṃha went forth to his own fortress, prepared for battle;
and the hero, praising his younger brother, bestowed wealth upon the brahmins.
Then Svarṇavatī, distressed upon learning that her own husband was bound,
and seeing those led by Kṛṣṇāṃśa deluded and subject to the power of Śambhu’s māyā,
loudly wept while meditating upon the Goddess who can assume any form at will.
Then the Mother of the World, being pleased, awakened those who had fainted. Having regained consciousness, they all joyfully said to Svarṇavatī:
"O Goddess, where is our friend Āhlāda? Tell us the reason for this."
Just as her husband, the lord himself, had spoken, she did exactly so; saying,
"I shall become a female parrot today, while you remain established as Bindula," she became a female parrot, endowed with a portion of Kṛṣṇa.
She, the passionate woman, went to the place where her husband was bound;
the portion of Kṛṣṇa, mounted upon the horse, also reached that spot through the path of the sky. Assuming the form of an Abhīrī woman, she went toward her lord.
Having comforted him as was appropriate, he described the portion of Kṛṣṇa [the child]:
"The powerful portion of Kṛṣṇa,
having slain the inhabitants of the fortress and killed hundreds of thousands of guards, has come here to his brother."
Knowing that the full moon coincided with the month of Madhu, they all, filled with haste,
quickly arrived at Ayodhyā; having bathed in the Sarayū river,
they swiftly gathered at the confluence (Veṇī) at the time of the Holikā burning.
Having completed their baths, meditations, and other concluding rites, they returned home;
reaching the shore of the ocean and performing a great festival,
they returned once more to their own homes on the fifth day of the dark fortnight of Caitra.
The messengers, mounted upon camels and eager to ensure his welfare,
returned to their own homes on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha;
meanwhile, King Malana held great festivals in every house.
Having caused [the rites] to be performed according to the prescribed rule, he gave wealth to the Brāhmaṇas.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Compendium of Histories of the Kali Age," in the Caturyuga-khaṇḍa (also known as the Pratisarga-parvan) of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
Listen to how it happened in the fourteenth age, during the portion of Kṛṣṇa:
Jayanta, the son of Śakra, deluded by the curse of Jānakī,
attained birth in the Kali age and dwelt within the womb of Svarṇavatī.
On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, at midday on a Thursday,
he was born with a moon-like face, marked with the auspicious signs of royalty.
When that best of sons was born, the gods together with the hosts of sages [then rejoiced].
"He has been born as Indula, the victorious son of Vāsava.
Because they spoke these words, he became known by the name Indula.
Āhlāda, with joy, had the birth rites and other ceremonies performed for the infant.
When his son Indula was born on this earth, at the end of two months, Yogasiṃha arrived and gave a multitude of golden cows, horses, and elephants to the Brāhmaṇas,
as well as wealth to Svarṇavatī.
Seeing her son Netrasiṃha, Malanā, filled with affection,
fed him according to the prescribed rites and inquired after his welfare;
meanwhile, a hundred groups of dancers appeared, endowed with various melodies.
Having arrived there, they danced where the king’s son was staying;
after dwelling there for seven nights, that Yogasiṃha went home.
When six months had passed and a son was born, Devendra became distressed with affection.
Out of affection for his son, he took that son away by means of his own illusory power;
having withdrawn the excellent child, he presented him to Indrāṇī.
The goddess Śacī, overflowing with love, suckled him at her own breast.

Having drunk the milk of the goddess, he indeed became equal to a sixteen-year-old; with his own body, he himself grasped the moon, the abode of nectar. Therefore, he is celebrated by the name Indula and also as Jayanta.
Having studied the science of his father, that boy attained preeminence.
When that boy had perished, Queen Svarṇavatī then wept aloud in her distress:
"Alas, my son! O, where have you gone?"
O Sage, when such joy had arisen in Daśagrāma,
a terrible clamor broke out among the weeping men;
Āhlāda, together with his kinsmen, remained without food and with his senses restrained.
Having sought refuge in Śāradā, he dwelt there for three nights.
Then the Goddess herself, being pleased, spoke an incorporeal voice:
"O son, do not grieve for your son along with your kinsmen."
Jayanta, the son of Indra, has arrived in the heavenly realm;
having studied divine knowledge, he will depart at the end of three years.
For as long as you remain on the earth, he shall likewise dwell upon the earth.

"After that, having attained the heavenly realm, he shall indeed become Jayanta. When these words were spoken by the Goddess, they then became free from grief; reaching the city of Daśagrāma, they dwelt there, devoted to the pursuit of knowledge.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Compendium of Histories of the Kali Age," in the Caturyugakhaṇḍa (also known as the Pratisargaparvan) of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
When Indule had attained heaven, those heroes became overwhelmed with grief.
They worshipped Śāradā, who dwells in all the worlds,
having recited the Saptaśatī hymn with loving devotion at the three junctions of the day;
then, on the seventh hundredth day, they attained bliss through meditation.
And there was a son of a neighboring Brahmin, renowned by the name Cāmuṇḍa;
having reached the age of eight years, he worshipped Caṇḍikā,
and then, when his twelfth year had arrived, through the recitation of the Tricaritra.
"O devotees, this Kuṇḍikā has indeed assumed a manifest form for the purpose of testing you;
I shall fill her up,
but you must apply your minds and devise means to accomplish her filling."
Sukhakhāni filled his water-pot with powerful honey, flowers, and fruits,
yet it did not reach fullness;
likewise Balakhāni [filled it] with meats, while Mūlaśarman [filled it] with blood.
Then Devakī, with offerings of oblations, sandalwood, and other articles of worship, filled the water-pot; yet it did not reach fullness.
Āhṛda himself, with all his limbs, and Udaya with his head, [attempted to fill it].
She then filled the water-pot, and having reached its fullness,
the Goddess, who is affectionate toward her devotees, spoke these words to her devotees:
"O hero, you shall become one who tastes happiness and is beloved by the gods."
The great hero Balakhāni shall meet his death after a long time;
Mūlaśarman, however, will be powerful and possess red seed.
And the goddess Devakī shall remain in her own world for a long duration.
Āhlāda was indeed a portion of Kṛṣṇa; between those two, both were excellent.
One was said to be like a god, while the second possessed superior strength.
This lion among gods was free from desire; upon death, he attained liberation.

Having spoken thus, your mother vanished; they all attained satisfaction. Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Compendium of Histories of the Kali Age," within the *Caturyugakhaṇḍa* (also known as the *Pratisargaparvan*) of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
And when his seventeenth year had arrived, O tiger among sages, listen to what was seen there by that portion of Kṛṣṇa through his yogic vision:
when King Ratnabhānu had died, the lord of Marudhanva [ascended the throne].
O Brahmin, Gajasena, then distressed by fear of Pṛthvīrāja,
worshipped the god Agni through sacrifices, meditation, vows, and ritual offerings;
for twelve years, being of virtuous conduct, he gratified him with loving devotion.
Then the blessed Lord Pāvaka, being pleased, granted him a splendid horse,
both his sons, a daughter, and an elephant;
for those four sons of Pāvaka had indeed been born upon the surface of the earth.
O bull among sages, they were all of the color of fire, great heroes endowed with every auspicious mark, and eighteen years of age;
from the moment of their birth, they were like gods and proficient in all branches of knowledge.
That maiden of excellent complexion, having reached the age of eighteen, obtained a boon from Durgā: "A portion of Dharma shall choose you.
That king of the Śārdūla lineage indeed held a *svayaṃvara*.
Kings from various lands arrived, infatuated by the beauty of his daughter.
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, on a Monday,
her *svayaṃvara* took place, and she went forth toward the kings.
Seeing the face of that restless woman, which had the color of lightning and appeared like a Tathāgata, King Balakhāni Dharmāṃśa was bewildered;
and she too, seeing that hero, Gajamuktikā, was bewildered.
Having understood this, the lady of auspicious countenance gave him the Vaijayantī garland;
meanwhile, Tāraka and the other kings, equipped with all manner of weapons and missiles,
besieged the hero from all sides by force, seeking the maiden.
Seeing those five hundred kings of such a kind,
the powerful Tāraka quickly cast aside his sword and struck off the heads of a hundred kings.
As Balakhāni was being slain on all sides, Tāraka—

He gave the sword with both his arms, and it split his body in two. Seeing the sword thus divided, the eldest son of Mahīrāja, being brave, carried him away from the battlefield; thereafter, those kings departed.
When the king’s army was defeated, the mighty Balakhāni, that powerful man,
took the maiden seated in a palanquin and brought her to his own home.
Seeing his daughter departing, King Gajasena—
Having arrived by the command of the lord of the earth and recognizing him as the lowest of Kṣatriyas,
he deluded that great hero, the slayer of the jackal, through his illusory power;
for when the hero had fallen asleep, he was rendered unconscious by the curse of Durgā.
In a rage, the lord of the earth quickly bound him with firm iron shackles. Having reached the iron fortress that resembled a village, he summoned the cruel Cāṇḍālas who resided there.
He ordered his execution with various punishments.
Those fierce men bound him and beat him violently;
from that beating, his sleep then vanished right there.
Having seen them, he then struck the Caṇḍālas with his strength;
by blows from his palms and fists, the Caṇḍālas met their death.
When five hundred of those fierce ones had died, the survivors fled out of fear.
Having made the door very secure, they approached the presence of the king.
Having understood the cause, that mighty king, bound by the hand,
went there and spoke these words, intent on his duty.
O hero of great strength, you have fallen into captivity by the Cāṇḍālas;
plundered there by bandits, you fell under the power of sleep and entered the forest. By good fortune, my daughter has arrived at your home, and by good fortune, you have returned to life.
"Having married my daughter, you ought to go quickly to your own home.
Having heard these pleasing words, he praised him and did accordingly;
he performed the Vedic rites in a pavilion for the sake of the marriage.
When the worship of the pavilion had been performed, Gajasena, the attendant of Agni, wrote a letter at his command for the sake of bringing joy to his master;
he then summoned a camel-rider and quickly dispatched the letter.
"Having arrived here for the marriage of Balakhāni, you, accompanied by your army,
should obtain suitable provisions and partake of them to your satisfaction.
When this was said, the exceedingly powerful Balakhāni, as night fell, [set out].
There he partook of food provided by the king that was tainted with poison;
though he consumed the venom, he did not die due to a favorable boon.
Then, when the time had arrived, seeing that he had fallen into a state of delusion—
He bound him again with shackles and struck him with cane;
then, as the poison-taint issued forth from all parts of his body through the pores of his skin,
the powerful man, his mind humbled, understood and spoke to the king.
"O King, why has such a thing occurred? Your army is intent on striking.
He replied, "O great hero, such is the custom in my lineage:
having first undergone torment, one may thereafter be elevated."
When the king had spoken thus, the female elephant arrived and addressed these words to her father: "Who is this that has gone to strike him?
The king replied: "O daughter, go quickly to your own quarters."
Hearing these terrible words— "This farmer has come for wealth and has gone to be beaten"— the exceedingly powerful Balakhānin,
sword in hand, arrived there after cutting through those formidable bonds.
Having hemmed him in on all sides with weapons, they struck those five hundred heroes;
but Balakhāni destroyed them all.
Then Sūryadyuti, the eldest son of Gajasena, arrived.
Having bound him again, she threw that powerful man into the middle of a pit.
Seeing her husband in such a state, Gajamuktā was deeply distressed;
at night, the queen went there and gave wealth to the guards.
Crying, she drove her husband out and gave her fan to her husband;
thus she remained night after night until half a month had passed.
In the meantime, O hero, Āhlāda arrived with seven hundred thousand [demons].
Having heard the reason for that very matter, Balakhāni quickly set out with his armies;
he went to the pit and then besieged the city.
Gajasena marched to the battle with sixteen thousand elephants.
Accompanied by three hundred thousand horses, Sūryadyuti arrived;
at that time, Kāntāmala also arrived with three hundred thousand foot soldiers.
Indeed, a great battle took place between those two armies for a full day and night.
When Tālanāda and the others had been protected and Gajasena and his forces were present,
on the arrival of the second day, the mighty Gajasena,
seeing his own army shattered, mounted Pāvakī.
He caused that army, protected by Tālana and others, to be consumed by fire.
Seeing his forces reduced to ashes, Tālana went before the enemy and swiftly struck the king with a broad-headed arrow (bhalla).
Perceiving that the king had fainted, Sūryadyuti approached;
mounting the son of Agni (the fire-weapon), he set the Tāla tree ablaze.
In the meantime, the two heroic gods, Āhlāda and Kṛṣṇaka, arrived.
Overcome with rage, the two bound the subduer of enemies, who possessed the splendor of the sun. Knowing his brother to be securely bound, Kāntāmala mounted the horse and,
having bewildered Devasiṃha, he went toward the portion of Kṛṣṇa.
Having seized that dark portion, he withdrew its splendor;
all its seven-hundred-thousandfold strength then became fire.
Because of his immortality, Āhlāda then restored it to life.
Half of Gajasena’s army was destroyed by all of them;
having achieved victory, the king returned home filled with joy.
But seeing that the portion of Kṛṣṇa had become fire, he was both delighted and deeply distressed.
He praised the goddess Durgā mentally on the front lines of battle.
Then the goddess spoke these words: "O child, your son shall indeed come from heaven and restore them all to life once again."
When these words had been spoken by the Goddess, Indula—
learned in the sciences and having assumed a form equal to that of a twelve-year-old—
arrived there, mounted upon the horse Vaḍavāmṛta at the command of Vāsava.
Then those three, who were like unto gods, emerged from his limbs like clouds on all sides and extinguished the fire;
when the fire had been quenched, Sahaya joyfully [emerged] from his own mouth.
He married Lālā, and by her they were restored to life; then, when seven hundred thousand lives had been saved and the fire was indeed extinguished,
Gajasena departed in all directions along with his two daughters.
But those who remained of the hundred-thousand-strong army, O best of the Bhārgavas, were all overcome with fear; assuming divine forms, they fled—
some becoming renunciants (saṃnyāsins) and some indeed becoming celibate students (brahmacārins).
Some attained the state of being alive, while others likewise met their destruction.
Having bound those three heroes, Gajasena and the rest, along with Tālana,
he— who was joined by a portion of Kṛṣṇa— returned to Indradurga.
Having expelled Balakhāni immediately thereafter,
Tālana questioned him about the entire cause; and having heard the words from his mouth,
he struck those heroes with canes bound to pillars.
O Brahmin, by the command of Gajamukta, the noble-minded Senāpati Tālaṇa abandoned them and arrived for the sake of the wedding;
Balakhāni was mounted on a horse, while Gajamukta was at the pavilion.
Then Gajasena fed them with divine foods;
having settled them in the iron fortress, he secured the gates most firmly.
Having stationed a hundred thousand heroes there, he himself went to Rudrapura.
Having stayed diligently by force during the night at the iron fortresses, they saw that the door was not open at dawn; then he said:
"Open the door quickly, otherwise you shall lose your life."
Having heard this, the commander-in-chief ordered a hundred thousand heroes:
"The terrifying enemies must be slain by various means.
Having heard this, those heroes fixed *śataghnī* weapons against them.

Intent on enmity, they struck down the host one by one in succession. When ten thousand had been slain, a portion of Kṛṣṇa named Bindula mounted a horse and quickly destroyed that great army with his sword.
The survivors of the slaughter, numbering eighty along with their mounts and afflicted by fear,
reported to Indradurga exactly how the destruction of the army had occurred.
Hearing this, the king, overcome with terror, was joined by his two daughters.
Placing an elephant adorned with pearls before him and accompanied by many riches,
he washed away his own sins by giving the girl according to the prescribed rites;
taking sixteen golden camels, that very Ahlāda departed.
Accompanied by his sons and brothers, he went to his own home. When that joy had reached the house, Queen Svarṇavatī herself placed Indula upon her lap and lamented piteously at great length.
"O son, I who was dead have indeed been restored to life by you!
I am blessed and my purpose is fulfilled, O Jayanta, by the sight of you!
Hearing this, the heroic Indula bowed to his mother and spoke with joy.
"O Mother, I have never attained freedom from debt toward you.
When King Parimala, the wise one, arrived home filled with joy,
he had musical instruments played and bestowed wealth upon the Brahmins.

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the *Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, in the *Pratisarga Parvan*, within the section titled *Caturyuga-khaṇḍa* (also known as the *Apaparyāya*), in the collection of histories concerning the Kali Yuga.
Sūta said:
Listen now to exactly what occurred when Kṛṣṇa was in his eighteenth year.

When King Kṛṣṇakumāra had died, Mahīrāja, afflicted by great sorrow, performed the Lakṣacaṇḍī rite along with Ratnabhānu. At the conclusion of the fire-oblation, the Goddess spoke these words to the king:
"Year after year, seven sons shall be born to you from your body;
they will be princes who are portions of the Kauravas, and Draupadī’s sons, O King.
When these words had been spoken, the queen then conceived a child.
And a son named Karṇāṃśa was born, who was exceedingly powerful;
likewise, when the second year had passed, one born from the auspicious portion of Duḥśāsana became renowned as Nṛhari in the third year.
Uddharṣaṃśa was Saradana, while Durmukha’s portion was Mardana;
Vikarṇa’s portion was Sūryakarmā, and Bhīma was the portion of Viviṃśati. Vardhana was the portion of Citrabāṇa, and after that came Velā.
O Sage, she was exactly like Kṛṣṇā in her form, gestures, and qualities. When she was born upon the earth, a terrible earthquake occurred,
and Cāmuṇḍā let out an inauspicious, loud, and boisterous laugh from the sky.
A rain of blood, mixed with gravel-like bones, fell upon the city.
Then the Brāhmaṇas, having assembled and performed the birth-rites and other ceremonies, gave him a name; listen, O protector of the earth, to that syllable.
And Ilā became the mother of Śaśin on earth through her transformation;
therefore, this daughter, endowed with great beauty, became renowned as Ilā.
And when his daughter was born, that father [gave] the highest [gift] to the Brahmins.
Filled with joy, he gave gifts and various garments. When that daughter of excellent complexion reached the age of twelve years, she spoke to her father with humility: "Listen, O Lord of the Earth."
"He who shall bathe me in the pavilion with streams of red liquid,
and who shall give Draupadī’s ornament— he shall become my husband.
Then the king [wrote] on a golden plate a verse originating from the mouth of Velā.
Having written this, he said to Tāraka, "Search for her husband.
Taking three hundred thousand in wealth and accompanied by an army of one hundred thousand,
Tāraka quickly departed for another king at his father's command.
The powerful one went from place to place, from king to king, throughout the land of Sindhu and the Ārya country;
yet that terrible and formidable speech was not accepted by any of the kings.
Having reached his maternal uncle, the lord of the earth, he spoke those words to him.
Having heard this, he said: "O hero, Brahmānanda is possessed of great strength;
he would accept your words only if he were well-protected by Āhlāda and the others.
Is his renowned conduct not already known to you?"
Yourself, along with your six brothers, were married by the portions of Kṛṣṇa and others;
they all came under the control of that wise Brahmānanda.
There is no king on the face of the earth who is equal to him in strength.

Having heard this, Tāraka quickly departed with his own forces; but having recited that verse in their presence, he then found his hands bound. Kṛṣṇāṃśa, however, swiftly seized the verse and spoke these words.
"I shall marry Brahmānanda, the best of kings.
Then everyone remained silent; having performed the consecration along with the twice-born, Tāraka returned once more to his own home.
On the auspicious thirteenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Māgha,
an excellent marriage-muhūrta was determined for the benefit of both the groom and the bride; at that time,
Lakṣaṇa, accompanied by Tālana, set forth together with seven hundred thousand troops.
The powerful Balakhāni, accompanied by Lakṣa’s army and endowed with a portion of Kṛṣṇa, reached the city of Mahāvatī; he was filled with joy and joined by Suṣukhakhāni,
together with a hundred thousand troops and perfumes and other offerings.
Netrasiṃha, endowed with the enjoyment of yoga, possessed an army of one hundred thousand;
Raṇajit, the powerful youth, was joined by an army of two hundred thousand.
Thus, the powerful lord of twelve hundred thousand troops [was born].
Tālana, mounted upon Siṃhinī, set out for Vaḍavā;
accompanied by twelve lakhs of troops, the powerful Tālana arrived at the village of Dehalī, which was protected by King Mahīrāja.
The god Kṛṣṇaka, mounted upon Manoratha and stationed on Viṃdula,
having reached the nectar of Vaḍavā, departed as the son of Svarṇavatī. Rūpaṇa was stationed on Karāla, and Āhlāda was in Papīhaka.
Balakhāni was stationed at Kapota; his younger brother was stationed at Hariṇa.
Then Raṇajit, the son of Malanā, remained in Harinagara. Mounted upon five trumpeting elephants, he departed as the lord of Mahāvati.
Having ascended a magnificent celestial chariot, which was drawn by hundreds of fishermen,
adorned with jewels, pearls, and gold, accompanied by thousands of musical instruments,
tens of thousands of banners, and staff-bearers with attendants;
Accompanied by thousands of palanquins, five thousand chariots,
and five thousand carts carried by buffaloes—
all beautifully adorned and complete with every requisite— he arrived at Brahmānanda.
Hearing their clamor, that best of kings, the lord of the earth,
was struck with wonder; he joyfully provided them with campsites after performing auspicious rites at the gate of the fortress according to the prescribed ordinances.
"Give Draupadī’s ornament to Velā," he said to him;
but Indula went to heaven and spoke to Vāsava:
"O best of gods, give all of Draupadī’s ornaments to me."
Having brought it from Kubera, he gave him divine ornaments;
at the end of the watch, Indula arrived and presented them to his father.
Āhlāda, however, went in person to Velā and gave her the ornaments.
When the Brāhma-muhūrta had arrived, the wedding ceremony took place there;
as the first revolution of the hour began, Tāraka seized his sword,
and Āhlāda, having encountered him, fought with great ease.
Nṛhari, however, held back Kṛṣṇāṃśa in the second encounter;
likewise, Balakhāni opposed the heroic Saradana.
And Sukhakhāni held back Mardana during the fourth turn.
The powerful Rūpaṇa went against the formidable Raṇajit Sūryavarman;
the deity [Vardhana] went against the hero Vardhana at Saptāvarta in due order;
and then [he encountered] the hundred kings bearing swords, Gajasena, and the others.
Lakṣaṇa and the others arrived at the vast pavilion;
seeing the royal army shattered, King Mahīrāja, filled with rage,
mounted his enemy-terrifying elephant and set forth.
Having defeated those lions with eyes like arrows and others, that best of kings, a master of sound-aiming,
quickly approached the elephant named Bauddhinī who stood there as his target.
Fixing his mind on Śiva, he conquered and bound her with great fury.
Taking him by the hand, he led him before the king.
Having heard that he was a portion of Kṛṣṇa, King Parimala, being timid, went forth;
he then related the account of his defeat at the hands of Āhlāda and the others.
And that invincible portion of Kṛṣṇa, the powerful one who bestows joy upon the Yoginīs, went through the path of the sky to the palace and roared;
then the heroic Lakṣaṇa, having cast off his excellent bonds, [emerged].
Having established Viṣṇu in his mind, he went to Mahīrāja;
taking the palanquin, he himself arrived at the camp.
In the meantime, everyone everywhere abandoned their fainting spells.

Having conquered them in a sword-fight and bound those hundred kings along with their lineages with firm shackles, they bathed Draupadī— the most excellent woman who was like the shore itself— with the streams of blood flowing from their slaughter.
And at the conclusion of the wedding, they all returned to their camps;
having dismissed their seven sons, they fed them with excellent food. When those great heroes had finished eating, [the others] along with those thousand sons...
They besieged them on all sides and struck them from every direction with missiles and weapons;
having slain those thousands of heroes and bound those of great strength once more, they—
skilled in mockery— returned to their camps.
Taking ten lakhs of gold and leading his newly wedded bride, Velā, the powerful king went there, bowed down, and said to him:
"O King, son of Pradyota, this [child] is Lakṣaṇa, possessed of great strength."
"He wishes to take my wife and make her his slave.
Having heard this, Parimala, accompanied by all the kings,
was exhorted in many ways, yet at that time the king did not understand.
Then the great chaste lady Velā lamented intensely and repeatedly;
hearing that, the portion of Kṛṣṇa, together with Balakhānin,
consoled Velā and then departed through the path of the sky.
Having threatened Lakṣaṇa and seized him, he returned with joy;
by way of the sky, that portion of Kṛṣṇa crushed him in his palace.
Then, having abandoned those seven sons of the king together, [he departed].
The mighty ones caused an oath to be taken against Dambha;
O Sage, having stayed there for ten nights, they desired to depart.
But the powerful Mahīrāja, grasping the feet of the king, [beseeched him].
With eyes filled with tears, he then said to King Parimala:
"O Great King, this is the twelfth year since your daughter's marriage;
yet this young girl cannot endure the separation from her father and mother."
"Therefore, abandon her and go home; be happy.
When she becomes fit for her husband, he will come for you again.
Having spoken these words, the king affectionately touched her with his hand.
When the fragrance had been reduced to powder, the delighted [demon] became distressed;
he struck Mahīrāja, and that king was likewise reduced to powder. Both kings, their bones shattered, were treated by physicians skilled in the science of fire.
Having returned home full of happiness, they attained a sense of having fulfilled their purpose.
Seeing her son arrived at home married,
Mālinī celebrated various festivities and bestowed wealth upon the Brahmins.
He indeed caused a fire sacrifice to be performed for the propitiation of Caṇḍikā.
In the assembly hall, at the time of the expedition, the heroic Lakṣaṇa said to him:
"I have gone against Jayacandra, thinking that once she was conquered, she would be taken captive."
By the command of Śiva, those two yogins reached me through the path of the sky;
having conquered me, who was deluded by their fierce fear, they departed.
Now I go to my abode; live long, O best of kings!
Having bowed to him who had spoken thus, the kings departed for their own abodes.

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Compendium of Histories of the Kali Yuga," within the *Kaliyugīyetihāsasamuccaya* (Compendium of Histories of the Kali Age), which is another name for the *Caturyugakhaṇḍa* (Section on the Four Ages) in the *Pratisargaparvan* (Book of Re-creation) of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
Listen now to how it happened during the twenty-year period of the portion of Kṛṣṇa:
once, on the shore of the lake named Sāgara, the powerful Indula,
having recited the Saptaśatī hymn, became absorbed in meditation there.
In the meantime, swans descended from the sky to the earth;
by the sound of their cries, he arose from his meditation and spoke these words that are about to be told: "Blessed is this one of divine form!"
Among mountains, the Himalaya is supreme; likewise, among forests, Vṛndāvana;
among cities, Mahāvatī; and among lakes, the ocean.
Among women, the lotus-like woman (Padminī) is supreme; and among men, you, O Moon-like one, are the best.
"O Indula, O one of great wisdom, we who were dwelling in Lake Mānasa heard the words of Śrī and went to the ocean.
There we saw an auspicious woman adorned with all ornaments."
Having seen her, who was accompanied by seven female attendants, beautiful, and skilled in song and dance,
we fell into a state of infatuation and went to another land;
all the men here on this earth have been scrutinized by us.
"Indeed, there is no bridegroom here equal to you who is like a lotus;
therefore, you ought to mount us and behold that goddess.
Having said, "So be it," the son of Śakra mounted the king of swans.
In the beautiful island of Siṃhala, there lived a king named Āryasiṃha. His daughter, named Padminī, was endowed with beauty and youth.
She had seven famous female companions, excellent women who were full of passion.
In the beautiful Nalinī ocean, he beheld the auspicious temple of Girijā;
there, Indula saw the Goddess seated.
She too, seeing him, beautiful and seated upon the body of a swan, [was struck with wonder].
Having deluded him and summoned that god, she sported with him;
enchanted by various pastimes, he spent one year there,
unaware of night or day as he took delight with her.
When Āhlāda was overcome by the pride of devotion, the Mother of the Universe,
the Goddess, seeing him, vanished, her foot having been obstructed by his arrogance.
Great suffering befell that Āhlāda, who had been desiring victory.
That hero was described by certain men in his own palace as being endowed with the beauty of the moon; the Rākṣasas residing in the city of Laṅkā,
having seized him, quickly returned to their own home.
Having heard these terrible words, Sakula lamented aloud;
and a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose from them as they wept, O Sage.
Kṛṣṇāṃśa spoke to the weeping Ahlāda: "O elder brother, please listen."
"Having conquered all the Rākṣasas, accompanied by Tālana and the others, I shall meet you, O Indula; may you remain steadfast in courage. Balakhāni, Kṛṣṇāṃśa, Devasiṃha, and Tālana [are with me]."
Accompanied by seven hundred thousand troops, they went toward Laṅkā with joy. And those kings, village chiefs, and regional governors who had met them on the way,
having offered appropriate and delightful tribute, presented it to him.
Having conquered those kings who were intoxicated with pride, the powerful Tālana bound them and proceeded with them to Setubandha, the sacred site of Śiva; there,
having worshipped Rāmeśa, the auspicious deity established by Rāma.
Then, within six months, he reached Siṃhaladvīpa;
having arrived at Nalinīsāgara, he made his residence there.
Balakhāni also dispatched a letter to the king.
"O noble lion, O illustrious one, deliver your own sons who have crossed over [to safety];
now proceed toward Laṅkā together with your own forces. Otherwise, having conquered you along with your army, I shall bring about the destruction of your kingdom."
Having heard these words of the messenger, the exceedingly powerful king,
protected by the son of Śakra, advanced for battle;
Indula, meanwhile, fixed the paralyzing mantra upon his excellent arrow.

Sukhaśarmā, the son of Āryyasiṃha, together with three hundred thousand of his own troops, brought that army— which was well-protected by means of palm trees and other defenses— to a standstill during the day and engaged in a great battle.
When the onset of night had arrived, the mighty son of Śakra came forth for battle together with a hundred Kṣatriya sons;
their horses were of a golden hue, and they forcibly assumed the guise of ascetics.
He utterly destroyed your great army of a thousand troops;
thereafter, having reached his home, he lived happily with them.
Thus six months passed while the two armies were engaged in battle.
"In this manner, the great army of Balakhānin gradually met its destruction.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Compendium of Histories of the Kali Age," within the *Caturyuga-khaṇḍa* (also known as the *Pratisarga-parvan*) of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
Seeing the slaughter of his army, the mighty Balakhāni was overcome with mental anguish and turned away from the battle;
he summoned the high-minded Devasiṃha, who knew the three periods of time.
He deliberated upon that mantra so that the accomplishment of his purpose might occur.
Having heard it, the great yogi, the exceedingly powerful Devasimha, spoke:
"There is a certain son of Mahendra, skilled in all weapons and missiles."
Having indeed obstructed your army with divine weapons at the break of day,
he comes himself at night and causes the destruction of your forces;
therefore, accompanied by me and joined by Tālana, you [must act].

"Having united with a portion of Kṛṣṇa, O Śakra, become victorious quickly against the fair-faced son; otherwise, we shall go to the abode of Yama. Having heard these words spoken by that lion among gods, [he replied].
Accompanied by his brothers and friends, the powerful one, skilled in warfare, made an effort;
when the twenty-first year of the Dvāpara age had arrived,
he who rides upon horses caused his army to encamp upon the ships.
Having stationed half of his army right there, the mighty one—
Kṛṣṇāṃśa— with the other half of the army set out toward the southern direction;
and all those heroes, mounted upon horses, were fully prepared for battle.
Having firmly flung open the gates, they reached the edge of the city;
having slain all the guards and plundered the beautiful city,
they reached the enemy's fortress and wrought great destruction upon their foe.
Having entered the king’s inner apartments, the exceedingly powerful Kṛṣṇāṃśa beheld a beautiful young maiden, a lotus-eyed Padminī,
who was surrounded by seven female companions, enchanting, and skilled in song and dance.
Having forcibly placed [him] upon a swing and plundered the enemy's house,
he went to that camp where the great battle had taken place;
Balakhāni, moreover, was powerful and accompanied by Devatālana.
He struck down the enemy army protected by Indula with his own weapons.
Having approached Sukhavarmā, the son of the enemy and commander of the forces,
those [warriors], overwhelmed with intoxication, assailed him from all sides with their own missiles.
When that one of great prowess had been slain,
Jayanta, the son of Śakra, overcome with rage, restored his army to life;
having revived his brother-in-law Sukhavarman, he returned to his own home.
There, seeing all the people intent on weeping profusely,
he was struck with wonder and went home just as he had before;
yet, O Sage, he did not see his beloved there, accompanied by her friends.
Having gone to the noble lion’s den, he asked about the cause of everything;
learning that the house had been plundered by enemies skilled in weapons,
the hero wept most bitterly, crying, "Alas, my beloved, who were so intoxicated with joy!"
"Show me your beautiful face today; your husband is longing for you.
Having spoken thus and wept, he stood upon the mare, taking up his bow, his quiver, and his sword that bewilders enemies.
Alone and enraged, he went at night to where his enemy was stationed.
At that moment, the heroic and mighty Balakhānin,
seeing that beautiful young woman, lamented repeatedly and intensely.
"Alas, Indula! O great hero! Alas, my kinsman, you who bring joy!
This auspicious woman, endowed with beauty and youth, is worthy of you.
Grant me a sight of her quickly; take this fair-faced one today!"
Having spoken thus, he fell into a swoon while worshipping Śivā in his mind. At that very moment, the mighty son of Śakra arrived and struck down the enemy army protected by a portion of Kṛṣṇa.
Seeing the destruction of his army, Tālana, the commander of the host,
standing atop his lioness, let out a loud lion’s roar:
"O hero, victory will not be yours through the slaughter of your troops."
"Having slain me, kill my army, O Yogin who has assumed the form of a child!
Hearing these words of his, the terrifying son of Śakra struck him in the heart with arrows, but he [the child] cut them down with his sword.
Then the hero again struck him on the chest with his own spear.
When Indula had fainted, the mare, assuming a divine form,
reached the sky and addressed Jayanta.
Then that boy quickly took up the Kālāstra bow;
by it a great sound was produced, and Tālana died.
When that commander-in-chief had perished, the portion of Kṛṣṇa, overwhelmed with intoxication, [acted].
Having reached him by way of the sky, Indula, his eyes copper-red with rage, roared again and again; then that one of great strength took up an Agneya arrow and,
through his own yogic power, turned the sky itself into fire.
Having quickly performed this, he discharged the Vāyavya weapon at the enemy;
but that portion of Kṛṣṇa, having drunk that supreme Vāyavya by his own yogic power,
returned once more to the side of Hari himself as a single digit.
Seeing his adversary in such a state, the mighty son of Śakra took up the Gandharva weapon and proceeded to bewilder him;
yet, by the power of yoga alone, that weapon was once again brought to exhaustion.
Taking up a Varuṇa arrow, he discharged it at him;
by his own yogic power, the portion of Kṛṣṇa turned all that water into his mouth.
Thus, having drunk every weapon again and again, he swallowed them all.
With a serene mind, the mighty-armed Indula, having restrained his senses, departed quickly. But Indula, then enraged, abandoned Aśvinī and stood upon the ground;
seizing a shield and a sword, he immediately engaged in a sword-fight.
In the meantime, the gods and all the lords of the earth arrived;
they beheld that great battle, which was a cause for universal amazement.
And when morning had arrived, the exceedingly powerful Balakhāni appeared.
The powerful hero, the son of Śakra, emaciated by fatigue, beheld the lovely boy adorned with matted locks and a deerskin;
he himself had previously sworn an oath before his father Balakhāna, his own kinsman.
"O portion of Kṛṣṇa, I shall take off your head with my own sword;
otherwise, my mother named Svarṇavatī, who is a virtuous woman, will be defiled by me.
Having spoken thus, he took up his sword and went forth swiftly, filled with rage.
But Balakhāni, recognizing him and casting aside his weapon, overcome with affection,
approached his son and spoke these words:
"O Indula, illustrious one, who brings glory to your father and mother!"
O hero, you who are like the very life-breath of joy to Svarṇavatyāṅgamānasa,
having previously slain me, as well as your paternal uncle,
and likewise Udayasiṃha, Devasiṃha, and the entire clan.
"Be happy, O great hero, in the house of Sukhavarman.
Having heard these words and recognized his own kin,
the child cast aside his sword, fell at the feet of his paternal uncle, and [remained there].
He wept bitterly to atone for his transgression and spoke these sweet words: "Listen, dear father, to me;
this woman, corrupted by the Vedas, is a bringer of delusion to men."
Whether he be a god, a human, a serpent, or even a Dānava,
he has prepared nets made of noble women for the purpose of binding me—
me, who am pure from birth and the delight of my father.
O Lord, Jayanta, the son of Śakra himself, though born in the home,
did not recognize the delusion produced by Padminī; therefore,
forgive me, your dull-witted servant, for the remainder of my father’s ignorance-born transgression.
Having spoken thus, the child, distressed by affection, wept again;
he revived the army and the mighty Tālana.
Hearing these words of the child, Kṛṣṇāṃśa [replied] with these words:
Having attained supreme bliss, he established that [image] within his heart;
he caused a festival to be celebrated there, among every person in that land.
But Āryasiṃha, having heard of this, arrived accompanied by various materials.
He gave the maiden Padminī to Indula according to the prescribed rites; for the sake of his daughter, the king gave those horses, as well as elephants adorned with pearls and gems,
and many ornaments to his son-in-law.
With his voice faltering from affection, he set out upon their departure;
they all, filled with joy, quickly returned to their own homes.
Having stayed for one month on that terrifying path, they departed.
Having attained the ocean of fame, they celebrated many festivals. Āhlāda, with a delighted soul, seeing his son together with his wife, summoned the brahmins and gave them manifold gifts.
Having arrived at the city named Daśahārā together with his own kinsmen,
the great fame of the portion of Kṛṣṇa spread from person to person throughout the world.
Upon hearing this, Pṛthvīrāja was filled with the utmost wonder.
That woman Padminī, deluded by the curse of Durvāsas,
having herself abandoned her status as an Apsaras, attained the state of a mortal woman on earth;
after dwelling upon the surface of the world for a duration of twelve years, she [departed].
Having met death through consumption (yakṣman), she attained the heavenly world;
she dwelt for nine months in the palace of Āhlāda.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the *Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, in the *Pratisarga Parvan*, within the section titled *Caturyuga Khaṇḍa*, which is also known as the *Kaliyuga Itihāsa Samuccaya*.
Sūta said:
O sage, in the land of Pañcāla there was a king named Balavardhana.
His wife, renowned as Jaladevī, was large-eyed.
The king of the Bisenavaṃśa dynasty, who was highly proficient in the true essence of the Vedas,
worshipped Varuṇa, the lord of aquatic creatures, together with his wife. To him were born two sons who were devoted to the duties of the Kṣatriyas.
Lahara’s eldest son was indeed Mayūradhvaja;
having reached the age of twelve, that very Mayūradhvaja gratified Lord Skanda by the command of his elder brother.
With his senses restrained and observing silence, he became devoted to the forest-dweller’s stage of life;
having undertaken that vow for five years, he became intent upon recitation and meditation.
Then the Lord himself, the commander of the celestial army born from fire, was pleased.
He revealed his own form, endowed with every wonder;
and Mayūradhvaja, beholding that child who consists of all things and is accompanied by Devasenā, praised him with gentle words.
Mayūradhvaja said:
Victorious is your body with its divine form; it always leads the hosts of deities.
It drinks the supreme milk of Māriṣā and always slays the Daityas and Dānavas.
Salutations to you, O Lord of the divine army, crusher of the demon Mahiṣāsura!
O six-faced one of mighty arms, destroyer of Tāraka’s life!
Be gracious, O Soul of all, Guha, wielder of the spear, and imperishable one!
"O you who are compassionate toward those who have come for refuge, protect me, your servant, forever!
Having heard this praise of his, the commander-in-chief indeed said to him:
"O best of kings, what is desired by you? You shall obtain everything from me."
Thus addressed by that god, the king, with a humble mind, said:
"O Blessed One, grant me strength; always be my helper.
Having said "So be it" to him, Skanda then vanished right there once more.
That king, with a delighted soul,
caused a city to be built named Mayūranagara, filled with throngs of men,
measuring two yojanas in length, and protected by the god Skanda.
His kinsman named Lahara, through twelve years of diligent effort,
worshipped Varuṇa along with the rivers and streams.
Then the blessed Varuṇa, the lord of aquatic creatures, was pleased.
"Choose a boon," the Lord of the Waters spoke with affection to the monarch.
Having heard these nectar-like words, King Lahara praised the noose-wielder, the Lord of the Oceans, with gentle speech.
Laharā said:
"Your mind is to be known as great, endowed with austerity and power; therefore, 'Pracetas' shall be your name. Salutations to you, Pracetas!"
"You restrain the flood of waters without being obstructed by anyone;
therefore, you are named Varuṇa. Salutations indeed to you, O Varuṇa!
For the purpose of binding the Daityas and for the sake of the victory of the gods."

"A divine noose has been brought by you; salutations again and again to you, the Holder of the Noose. Thus praised at that time by that wise king, the God caused the excellent city of Lāharī to be built.

The Lord of Waters himself dwelt there for the sake of protecting the village, which was thirty thousand yojanas in extent and inhabited by people of the four castes. By his grace, the king obtained a queen of beautiful countenance.

The most excellent woman named Rāvī, who was like a celestial nymph, should be known [as his wife]. Upon her he begot sixteen principal sons born of Dhārtarāṣṭra, endowed with strength equal to that of elephants.
After that, a daughter was born, named Madanamañjarī.
When his daughter reached the age of twelve, that king,
considering Devasiṃha— the excellent descendant of the Lunar dynasty— to be the most suitable bridegroom,
summoned his eldest son and sent him forth.
The son, brave in battle, powerful, and endowed with a hundred thousand gold coins,
arrived at Mahāvatī accompanied by a thousand Śabaras;
having bowed to King Parimala, he [received] from that illustrious royal family—
He himself described his own lineage for the sake of his sister’s marriage.
Having heard this, King Parimala summoned the highly intelligent Devasiṃha and spoke these words: "Set your mind upon the matter of the marriage."
But the powerful Devasiṃha, with a humble mind, said to his paternal uncle:
"I shall not marry; celibacy is my vow.
Though I have been entreated in many ways by all the groups of twice-born ones,"
The high-minded lion among gods did not abandon his supreme vow.
Then King Parimala spoke these words, firm in battle:
"This boy is a mine of happiness; I speak thus for the sake of his marriage."
Thinking "so be it," that king, steadfast in battle, went home;
there, the one of great vows, Sukhasāni, spoke to his father.
In the meantime, the cunning lord of the earth said to him:
"This marriage is improper here in this most excellent lineage of Agni;
the groom here, O King, is a Śūdra who causes the confusion of castes.
Therefore, you ought to go with your army to conquer them."
"O King, place the monarch in an iron prison;
my fame shall eternally ascend to heaven and endure until the end of the world.
For that king named Netrasimha has been defeated by those jackals."
"Likewise, King Pṛthvīrāja, the lord of elephants and possessor of great strength,
as well as Āryasiṃha and others even more powerful than they, have been conquered.
Having heard these pleasing words, Lahara, the best of kings, [was moved].
On the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, the exceedingly powerful one established an excellent fourfold army,
numbering four hundred thousand and protected by his sixteen sons,
at Balakhāni.
Accompanied by his own kinsmen and endowed with a force of four hundred thousand,
he arrived and stayed in the beautiful city of Laharī in the land of Pañcāla;
there, during the twelfth year of Kṛṣṇa’s incarnation, he made his residence.
By the king's command, the heroes advanced for battle.
But the righteous Balakhāni, seeing the heroes thus arrived,
again commanded his own warriors for the conflict.
A terrible battle, causing the hair to stand on end, took place between those two armies.
When the fifth day arrived during the daytime, the exceedingly powerful Balakhānin,
accompanied by a portion of Kṛṣṇa himself, brought about the slaughter of the enemy.
Those heroes who had been defeated, the survivors of the slaughter, were overcome with fear;
seeing them, the sixteen sons, skilled in the use of bows and arrows, mounted their respective chariots and advanced toward the battle.
Seeing them thus showering volleys of arrows, the powerful Kṛṣṇāṃśa,
wielding sword and shield, advanced swiftly alone;
having severed their bows and bound those warriors who were intoxicated with the pride of battle, he proceeded.
The hero, a portion of Kṛṣṇa skilled in battle, gave [his life] for the joy [of his kin].
Hearing that his sons were being bound, Lahara, the best of kings,
flooded the army of the high-souled Balakhānin.
When the army had thus turned to water, Jayanta, being exceedingly powerful,
dried up all that water in the battle with the Vāyavya weapon;
thereafter, he carried Lahara’s army for many yojanas.
Then the Blessed Lord Varuṇa, the lord of aquatic creatures,
married his daughter to King Lahara.
And Lahara, with a gracious mind, recognized him as a partial incarnation on the surface of the earth.
With supreme joy, he showed devotion to the pure portions [of the deity],
giving away abundant wealth and circumambulating him again and again;
with a tranquil mind, he established [the deity] within his heart for the duration of one month.
Those portions as well, having received the great worship that bestows waves [of grace],
joyfully placed that Goddess upon a swing and departed for their own abodes.
Thus, O Brahmin, has this auspicious account of the deeds of Kṛṣṇa’s portions been told to you.
Upon hearing of the marriage of Sukhakhāni, one shall attain great joy.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Compendium of Histories of the Kali Age," within the *Caturyugakhaṇḍa* (also known as the *Pratisargaparvan*) of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
The Sage said:
"O best of Brahmins, having gone home, what auspicious conduct did those heroes perform? Tell us that truth, for you are indeed considered by us to be omniscient.
Sūta said:
Having returned home, they all went around the king’s assembly hall and reported the news in such a way that a great battle ensued.
Upon hearing that his host of horses had been destroyed, King Parimala—
Having summoned the portion of Kṛṣṇa, he, with a humble mind, spoke these words:
"O powerful one, you must go to the land of Sindhu;
having procured five hundred thousand horses, return once more to our home."
Having heard this, the portion of Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by Devasiṃha,
swiftly departed taking eight thousand camels laden with a thousand bhāras of gold;
he arrived there together with ten thousand brave warriors.
In that city of Mayūra, which was inhabited by the four castes,
when morning had arrived, the daughter of a gardener approached her father’s garden,
seeking flowers for her task.
Then Kṛṣṇāṃśa, filled with joy and embodying the divine, performed worship and went to a beautiful forest during the spring when the trees were laden with blossoms—
a place full of many wonders and resounding with bees intoxicated by the flowers.
Upon seeing her, the son of Kṛṣṇa was infatuated and personally prepared himself for her sake.
In the meantime, Puṣpā, having come there for the sake of flowers,
beheld a man resembling a god, sixteen years of age.
Seeing that auspicious woman, whose face was serene and peaceful, and who possessed the luster of an indranīla gem, Kṛṣṇāṃśa was struck with wonder;
he questioned her with these words: "To whom does this celestial beauty belong?"
"Or have you come here from the heavenly world yourself, O serpent-woman?
Having heard this, the daughter of the gardener replied:
"O mighty-armed one, I am a Śūdra woman who has come here for the sake of flowers."
O protector of the earth, by this flower the king’s daughter was compared;
the queen named Puṣpavatī was like Rādhā, endowed with a multitude of virtues.
That young woman, radiant with beauty and youth, was sought after even by the gods.
O King, because of the fear of Makaranda, the gods were certainly not suitable for her by force.
Listen to the reason for that, O monarch, as to how Makaranda came to be:
a boon was obtained from Guha by King Mayūradhvaja.
On the surface of the earth, you were invincible to others except for those who were portions of Kṛṣṇa.
That friend of yours was Pṛthivīrāja, a king of kings and a beloved of Śiva;
he ruled a kingdom that was a cloud of dharma and dear to Hari.
Then the blessed Lord, the Master of Sacrifice who embodies the sacrifice itself, being pleased,
produced from the fire a couple of beautiful countenance;
the son should be known as Makaranda, and the daughter is considered to be Puṣpavatī.
Having reached the age of five, the very powerful Makaranda,
devoted to the Vedic dharma, propitiated Dharma through his ascetic penance.
When Makaranda, the beloved of the king, had attained the age of twelve years—
The Lord Dharma, being pleased, gave him a great horse made of stone,
possessing immense speed and capable of destroying enemy armies;
having mounted that horse himself, he became happy and worthy of all worship.
"This beautiful, divine forest, worshipped by the gods, belongs to him;
you, O most excellent one, deserve the body of Puṣpavatī.
Having heard these words, the portion of Kṛṣṇa was tormented by love.
Having come to the house of that Mālinī, Devasiṃha, who knew the proper time, gave her much wealth; then, perceiving that she had fallen into delusion,
he awakened her— who was a portion of Kṛṣṇa— with verses arising from the Sāṃkhya philosophy.
Then Kṛṣṇāṃśa, who was absorbed in that [deity], together with Devasiṃha, arrived at the land of Sindhudeśa; having purchased all the horses there,
he returned home at the end of the month and presented them all to the king.
Having meditated upon the auspicious form of Puṣpavatī, the powerful Kṛṣṇāṃśa, impelled by the flowers, was overcome with devotion and praised the Mother of the Universe. Kṛṣṇāṃśa said:
O Goddess of divine illusion, O Great Illusion, whose nature is eternally pure! Protect me, who am afflicted by lust; awaken the one who possesses flowers (the goddess).
