O You who cause the delusion of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, O Destroyer of the demon Mahiṣāsura!
Protect me, who am afflicted by the god of love; O Puṣpavatī, awaken me!
O destroyer of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa in the conflagration of Dhūmralocana, protect me, who am afflicted by the god of love; O Puṣpavatī, awaken me!
O you who have blood-seeds and blood-red-yellow [garments], O you who cause terror to all the Daityas!
Protect me, who am afflicted by the god of love; awaken for the sake of the one possessing flowers (Puṣpavatī)!
O destroyer of the Daitya Niśumbha, O annihilator of the Daitya Śumbha!
"Protect me, who am afflicted by the god of love; awaken Puṣpavatī!
Having thus offered praise, that hero slept upon the supreme seat.
Then the goddess Śāradā appeared to him in a dream.
Day after day, the Goddess, who bestows boons and grants fearlessness, performed [these acts].
O Sage, when four months had thus passed during the rainy season,
the illustrious portion of Kṛṣṇa reached the age of twenty-three years.
In the dark fortnight of the month of Kārtika, accompanied by the gods,
he went to the beautiful city of Mayūra, which was protected by Makaranda;
having arrived at Puṣpāgṛha, he took up residence there.
Once, having taken a beautiful necklace composed of jewels and pearls, adorned with various flowers, and draped with a portion of Kṛṣṇa’s own garment,
Puṣpā went to the palace of Puṣpavatī.
But she, beholding that beloved necklace fashioned as if by Tvaṣṭṛ himself, placed it upon her heart and quickly fainted, for she was a woman whose very form was Rati.
"O friend, O great illusionist, tell me the truth before me! she cried.
"From where did this beautiful neck-ornament, so dear to me, come?
Hearing these words of hers, Puṣpā, distressed by the fear of Makaranda,
offered a handful of flowers and spoke these words to her.
"Grant me the gift of life, and then I shall tell you," she said.
To the maiden who replied, "So be it," my sister said, "O auspicious one,
there is a most beautiful woman named Kṛṣṇā, who enchants all the world."
"In Mahāvatī there is her house; she has come to my home.
By her was fashioned this excellent necklace for Subhū.
Having heard these words, Queen Puṣpavatī herself [acted].
He spoke these words to Mālinī: "Show that night to me;
because of the fear of Makaranda, neither the gods nor other men on earth have access to my presence—I speak the truth."
Having heard these terrible words, Puṣpā, overcome with fear, did not say anything at all, even though she was questioned again and again. Then Puṣpavatī said: "What fear has come upon you?"
If that beautiful sister of mine comes to your house,
and some deluded man should forcibly enjoy her,
then my death must be known to have occurred, for I am devoted to the dharma of my family.
Having heard this, the virtuous Puṣpavatī spoke again:
"Even my father, Mayūradhvaja, is devoted to statesmanship;
those who shall do what is improper will go to the abode of Yama."
"Therefore, take that swing quickly and show that beautiful one to me; then return once more to your own home.
Thinking "So be it," that beautiful Śūdra woman went home.
O Sage,
having heard those delightful words as they were spoken by her, Kṛṣṇāṃśa, becoming exceedingly powerful,
performed the piercing of his own nose and again assumed a female form.
The heroic one ascended the swing and departed together with Puṣpā.
Then, having seen the beautiful Kṛṣṇā, Queen Puṣpavatī spoke these words to Puṣpā: "Listen to my words, O friend."
"Every night at the end of my sleep, I have seen a man as handsome as this auspicious woman, sporting with me;
and that portion of Kṛṣṇa, the excellent son of the King of Deśa, said to her:"
There was a famous man named Udaya, and I am his friend Lalitā. Every day, he would take the necklace I had prepared for the purpose of worship and, having worshipped the Goddess, present it to her.
Once, seeing that hero departing slowly amidst the flowers and remaining indifferent, I approached him and said:
"From where has this delusion come upon you? Tell me who you are; do not delay."
Thus addressed, he said to me at the end of his dream every day:
"O friend, a beautiful woman endowed with form and youth was seen by me;
due to separation from her, my face, afflicted by grief, has become withered."
Having heard this, Puṣpavatī said to that lovely-faced woman: "O fair-faced one, when my marriage with him takes place,
I shall satisfy you with many riches."
"Therefore, go quickly to his side and inform him.
Having heard those words, Puṣpā, filled with love,
placed Kṛṣṇā upon a swing and prepared to go to her own home.
O Bhārgava, when that swing had reached the gate of the fortress,
the powerful Makaranda, of great heroism and twelve years of age,
approached the vicinity of the swing and beheld her of the beautiful countenance.

The powerful hero Govardhanakalāṃśaka was infatuated with Kṛṣṇā, who was dark as a blue lotus, possessed beautiful eyes, and was captivating. Out of love for Govardhana, he said to her: "O lovely-limbed one, O beloved, listen to my words."
"Come quickly to my house and become my wife now.
Having heard this, Kṛṣṇā laughed and spoke these words to the king:
"You are of noble birth, O great hero, born from the sacrificial fire-pit."
"Sixteen years of age, bearing a quiver and equipped with a bow and arrows—such a maiden of the lunar and solar lineages is indeed worthy of you, O King.
But I am a lowly Śūdra woman; how indeed could I be worthy of you here?"
"I am a maiden born of a Śūdra lineage, established in the vow of celibacy.
Having heard these words, Makaranda, the prince,
seized that woman by force and touched her heart himself.

Then Kṛṣṇāṃśa, having inflicted heart-rending pain upon him and deluded the prince, that god departed for his own abode. Makaranda, however, having regained consciousness, was tormented by the fire of love.
Having returned home, she reported everything to Puṣpā.
Then, with gentle words, she addressed the mighty King Makaranda, who was distressed by his affection for her: "Listen, O best of kings."
The beautiful city of Mahāvatī is there, where the auspicious palace of Kṛṣṇā is located;
out of fear of you, that friend has gone to the home of Kṛṣṇā’s portion,
weeping bitterly and intent on censuring you.
The hero of great strength will indeed arrive together with his forces;
therefore, you must prepare all the troops.
By him, your great heroic paternal uncle Lavana was conquered.
"He has arranged the marriage of his kinsman with [my] daughter.
Hearing these terrible words, King Makaranda stationed fearsome *śataghnīs* upon the bastions of the fortress.
Having summoned his own army of three hundred thousand equipped with swords,
he stationed them right there, intent on protecting the kingdom.
Then, having reached home, the partial incarnation of Kṛṣṇa spoke to Balakhāni.
Having heard this, that great hero, accompanied by his brothers and friends,
went to the city of Mayūra together with five hundred thousand troops;
there were five thousand *śataghnīs* and ten thousand elephants.
All one hundred thousand were horses; the remainder were to be known as foot soldiers.
Having stayed for only a fortnight on the road in Pāñcāla at that time, Makaranda, holding a spear like a thunderbolt, stood there upon hearing that.
He commanded his army: "Slay the enemies of great strength!
Hearing this, one hundred thousand foot soldiers took up *śataghnī* weapons and fire;
those seven thousand indeed brought about the destruction of the enemy force.
Then, at the southern gate of the village, they departed mounted on horses;
they were experts in combat with the *bhuśuṇḍī*, the *kṣepaṇī*, the *śakti*, and the sword.
All one hundred thousand horses belonged to King Makaranda.
Then a great and tumultuous battle took place between those two cavalry forces. At that time, twenty thousand elephants at the western gate advanced together with ten thousand enemies.
Forty thousand great heroes who guarded the camels fought together with the Balakhanyas and others in the northern direction;
for a day and a night, there was a tumultuous battle that made the hair stand on end.
Then all those mighty followers of Balakhāni were defeated;
abandoning the battle, they all fled in the ten directions.
Kṛṣṇāṃśa mounted a peacock, while Balakhāni rode upon a pigeon.
The god Manoratha was stationed on a chariot and Āhlāda was mounted upon an elephant;
having gone to the gates in order from the eastward direction, those warriors, intoxicated by battle,
cast aside their scimitars with hilts and wrought a great slaughter of the enemy.
Defeated, those heroes retreated to Makaranda.
But the powerful son of Vahni,
grasping a thunderbolt-like spear in his hand, mounted a stone-made horse and went forth to battle.
And those heroes, Kṛṣṇāṃśa and the others, besieged him from every direction;
the mighty Balakhāni placed his sword at his throat, Devasiṃha struck him with his own spear, and [another] struck him on the shoulder.

Āhlāda held an arrow to his chest, while Kṛṣṇāṃśa held an excellent sword; by the power of their stones and horses, they did not succumb to dejection. Seeing the heroes rendered fruitless, he let out a terrifying roar.
By Śanibhalla’s [missile], they all became unconscious in the battle;
those horses also instantly fell unconscious from the force of Śilāśva’s speed.
But the powerful Makaranda, having bound those who were intoxicated with the pride of war, [remained firm].
With a serene soul, he went home and reported those events to his father.
Seeing the heroes defeated, Rūpaṇa became overwhelmed with fear;
having reached the city of Mahāvatī, he described the situation to the king.
Having heard that, Brahmānanda, accompanied by an army of one hundred thousand and with Indula as his ally, went to the city of Mayūra. Having written a clear letter, he quickly gave it to the king.
"O beloved son of the Earth-king, O bull among men, know me to be [the messenger] of Kṛṣṇa; give me your auspicious daughter named Puṣpavatī as a portion for him.
Otherwise, your soldiers shall meet their destruction by my sharp arrows."
Having heard this, that best of kings, Mayūradhvaja himself,
accompanied by Makaranda and joined by a force of two hundred thousand,
fought a terrifying battle with him for a day and a night.
But the powerful Brahmānanda engaged in a battle of arrows;
struck by Makaranda’s broad-headed shaft, he fell to the ground unconscious.
Then Jayanta, the son of Svarṇavatī and born of Śakra, [advanced].
He displayed his own supernatural power to the wise Makaranda;
by the power of the Vaiṣṇava missile, the stone horse was reduced to ashes.
O best of the Bhṛgus, by means of the Brahmāstra, Śani’s mallet fell to the earth.
Having bound that mighty Makaranda with a serpent-noose, Indula, the powerful one,
caused the marriage of the high-souled portion of Kṛṣṇa and restored his own army to life.
Makaranda had auspicious ceremonies performed in every house;
he gave his daughter away according to the prescribed rites, accompanied by abundant wealth.
King Mayūradhvaja showed her great affection.
Honoring the king’s command, they departed for Mahāvatī together.

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Marriage of Kṛṣṇāṃśa," in the Kali Age History Compendium, which is an alternative designation for the Caturyuga Section within the Pratisarga Parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
When the powerful portion of Kṛṣṇa had arrived at Mahāvatī,
the mighty King Parimala then performed auspicious rites together with that Puṣpavatī, who was skilled in song and dance.
An incarnation of Kṛṣṇa,

the hero Udaya, who was as powerful as Śakra, would daily sport with his friends in the house during the months of Hemanta and Śiśira; indeed, he engaged in secret dalliance just as Śakra does with the Apsarases.
Skilled in all forms of touch, he did not engage in carnal union.
Once, during a dance performance, the goddess Puṣpavatī herself spoke these words to the portion of Kṛṣṇa: "Who were you in your previous birth?"
Having heard this, the heroic Udaya laughed and spoke these words:
"O beloved, I am King Candradāsa from my previous birth.
Since childhood, I have experienced suffering ordained by fate."
I performed the worship of the Śālagrāma stone every single day; by the power of that merit, I indeed became a sovereign emperor.
When the anniversary of my death arrived, I fixed my mind upon the Śālagrāma.
By the grace of Brahmā himself, I attained union with Hari;
yet Viṣṇu, the Supreme Lord who is the soul of time, being entreated by Kali,
caused me to be cast out from his own body and take birth upon the earth.
Whenever there is indeed a decline of Dharma, O beloved,
I manifest myself for the sake of establishing the boundaries of the age's dharma;
through truth, however, mental worship is the cause of satisfaction for the gods.
In the Tretā age, the worship of the sacrificial fire and rites such as sacrifice and charity [are preferred];
in the Dvāpara, the worship of the physical forms (mūrti) of the gods is indeed dear to them;
but when the terrible Kali age has arrived, the supreme worship of Brahman is [the best].

In the Satya Yuga I am Haṃsa; in Tretā, I am Yajñapuruṣa; and in Dvāpara, O beloved, I am Hiraṇyagarbha, the bestower of happiness. When Kali arrives, I indeed become the Śālagrāma for the satisfaction of the gods.
O beloved, all the sages, all the deities, as well as the hosts of ancestors,
all attain satisfaction through the worship of the Śālagrāma.
This worship with sandalwood paste and other offerings should be performed by the twice-born and those of the three castes.
For Śūdras, worship with a spirit of devotion is sufficient through mere bathing;
for Mlecchas, even the sight [of the Śālagrāma] is meritorious when performed with humility and a spirit of devotion.
The Śālagrāma is itself Brahman, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss.
"By the mere sight of him, impurities will indeed go to their destruction.
Thus, O Goddess, I have described to you the supreme boundary of the Yuga.
Tell me truly and without delay: in the past, whose daughter were you?"
Puṣpavatī said:
"In a previous birth, I was a courtesan known as Candrakānti;
I performed singing, dancing, instrumental music, and other arts before the Lord."
By the power of that merit, she ascended to the heavenly world;
there, though sought after by the gods, she who was endowed with beauty and youth did not abandon her vow of celibacy, even in the realm of heaven.
By the power of that merit, I became Uṣā, the daughter of Bāṇa;
Aniruddha himself, who is Brahmā, took my hand in marriage. My lord, the God, was entreated by Kali for his own sake.
Having reached the Arcāvatāra and gone to Mārkaṇḍeyasthala,
he indeed demonstrated there the greatness of his own grace;
for even here lies the boundary of the residence of my Lord in his wooden form.
"O Lord, by his command I became the daughter of that Jambuka;
endowed with a divine form, my name was Vijayaiṣiṇī.
My own death was brought about by your brother Balakhānin."
Having become the sister of Makaranda, I have come to you as my husband;
because of that transgression, your brother has undergone intense torment within the very palace of King Innagatha, in the abode of Gajapati himself.
Having spoken thus, she observed a vow of silence and rejoiced joyfully with her husband. When the time of Holi arrived, Malanā, distressed by affection,
beheld her beautiful daughter Candrāvalī at the end of a dream.
At night, distressed by affection for her own son, she wept in sorrow;
then the great hero Udaya, having learned the cause of the weeping,
set out together with ten thousand brave men and abundant wealth.
The hero went alone to the house where Candrāvalī resided;
the king, her enemy, having understood the supreme reason for this,
followed after him for the sake of his purpose— he who was a portion of Duryodhana.
In the village known as Balīṭhāṭha, which was protected by the Yādavas,
there lived King Vīrasena, endowed with an army of three hundred thousand.
He had eight sons who were distinguished by their beauty and youth.
Kāmasena, Prasena, and likewise Mahāsena;
Sukhasena, Rūpasena, Viṣvaksena, Madhuvrata,
and Madhupa were born in succession as Yādavas from portions of the Yādava.
Having gone there, the high-minded Kṛṣṇāṃśa, that lion among men,
prostrated himself like a staff before King Vīrasena in the assembly hall and presented the letter inscribed by Malana to the monarch.
He further had ten *bhāras* of gold woven into cloth;
having eaten various delicacies together with the Yādavas,
he approached Candrāvalī and inquired after her welfare.
Longing with love and distressed, the sister said to the portion of Kṛṣṇa:
"O hero, you were then two years of age, while I was already married;
since then twenty years have passed, and you have been forgotten by your father and mother."
O hero, by you, who are so capable, my sister herself has been remembered.
Today my birth has become fruitful, and my life as well;
by the mere sight of my kinsman, everything of mine has become successful.
There, with a serene mind, he spoke humbly to his sister:
"The entire house has been plundered by a powerful jackal;
because of him, the king is terrified day after day."
Through great hardship, Vijaya obtained safety from the jackal;
however, the powerful Mahīrāja besieged my city.
My brother was married by me to the daughter of Brahmā.
Furthermore, we went to Siṃhaladvīpa for the sake of Jayantī;
indeed, many such miseries befell our father.
Therefore, O sister, we are well-pleased with you and are your servants.
Hearing those gentle words, Candrāvalī, overwhelmed with love, then joyfully led him to her own home. In the meantime, the cunning king arrived.
In the assembly hall of Vīrasena, having been honored by that very king,
the lord of the earth, upon finding another opportunity for conversation, said to him:
"All those wicked men, Ahlāda and the others, have been expelled by the king."
The treasury of the king was plundered by those of low birth who possessed great strength;
then, all of them, rendered powerless, resided in the city named Śirīṣa.
But that portion of Kṛṣṇa who perceives vulnerabilities has come to your house.
"Having taken up the swing for Candrāvalī, he will go;
O King, I speak the truth, my word shall not be otherwise.
Having heard this and understood the cause of its truth, Vīrasena [acted accordingly].
Having summoned his son Kāmasena, the husband of Candrāvalī, he spoke these words: "O son, bind him indeed.
Hearing this, Kāmasena took up a terrible poison.
Then Candrāvalī, having learned of this, gave [the food] to her for the sake of a meal;
she approached her brother, took the vessel, and departed.
And Kāmasena, becoming enraged, seized a cane staff.
Seeing him, he struck his own beloved wife and became enraged;
seizing him by the arms, he prepared to bind him.
When his son had been brought into bondage, the exceedingly powerful Vīrasena [acted].
He commanded his sons for the purpose of capturing him.
In the meantime, the hero, quickly taking up his swing (dolā),
arrived in the midst of the army and waged a great battle.
Ten thousand on one side and three hundred thousand on the other fought for a day and night in a fierce battle that made the hair stand on end;
one hundred thousand mighty and powerful great heroes were slain by Udayana.
All the remaining Yādavas fled,
overcome with fear upon seeing their army defeated; then the seven sons of great strength, mounting their own elephants, furiously besieged the portion of Kṛṣṇa.
That hero, mounted upon Bindula and having placed the elephants upon the ground,
severed their weapons and bound them, proud of his strength.
Having heard this, Virasena, who was solely devoted to the worship of the Sun, [acted].
Taking up the Saura weapon, he set his army ablaze.
By that very weapon, the portion of Kṛṣṇa along with his horse fainted upon the ground.
Vīrasena, however, having bound him, released his sons and his daughter-in-law.
Having quickly returned to his own home, he played various musical instruments.
Then those heroes, their anger subsided, departed in all directions;
they related everything from the beginning to Parimala regarding the cause [of the incident].
Perceiving the lord of the earth to be a great rogue, the king said this:
"Go, O son of Malanā, accompanied by an army of one hundred thousand;
having bound your sister's husband, quickly release your own kinsman."
Having heard this, that powerful son, accompanied by Lakṣasena,
went quickly to the city and besieged it in a fit of rage.
When the two forces were engaged in battle, Vīrasena, the best of kings, [advanced].
Taking up the Saura weapon, he prepared himself for the purpose of burning [the enemy].
When that weapon was ready, the mighty Brahmānanda,
in a fit of rage, warded off that arrow with the Brahmāstra itself.
Seeing him, the king was filled with fear and sought refuge in him alone.
But Brahmānanda, remaining fearless, spoke these words to the king:
"O King, by the words of a rogue, my kinsman has been oppressed by you."
"A woman is always exempt from being killed, yet your son struck her;
therefore, O King, give me your own son along with his sister.
Having heard these words, the king, with a humble mind, spoke.
"My daughter is not at home; O sir, take Kāmasenā.
Having said this, Vīrasena, with a gracious heart, gave his son and Candrāvalī to him and saw him off on his journey.
Brahmānanda also, powerful and endowed with a portion of Kṛṣṇa,
went to Mahāvatī together with an army of eighty thousand.
Seeing her own son, Malanā trembled, overwhelmed with love.
Having bathed him with streams of tears, he gave wealth to the twice-born.
Thus, O Brahmin, I have related to you the auspicious life-story of Kṛṣṇāṃśa; it destroys the sins of the Kali age for those who hear it. I shall indeed relate it again.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the *Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, in the *Pratisarga Parvan*, within the *Kaliyuga Itihāsa Samuccaya*—also known as the *Caturyuga Khaṇḍa*.
Sūta said:
When the powerful portion of Kṛṣṇa had reached his twenty-fourth year...
On the tenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, the king held a great festival;
having fed the best of the twice-born and given them sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā),
he likewise bestowed wealth upon his own servants in due order and according to their merit.
On the auspicious full moon day of Kārttika, Kṛṣṇāṃśa, endowed with strength,
joined by Indule, and accompanied by Devasiṃha,
set out with ten thousand brave warriors and tens of thousands of gold pieces.
She went to the city of Barhiṣmatī, which was filled with various kings.
In the meantime, the goddess Citrarekhā arrived there,
surrounded by her seven companions, having worshipped Citragupta.
In the middle of the Gaṅgā, she created a most delightful vehicle made of illusion,
filled with great curiosity and endowed with many riches.
Kings arrived there from various places, eager for a sight of it.
Then Udaya, accompanied by Devayuta and joined by Jayaṭa as well as by hundreds of heroes, arrived for the purpose of seeing her.
Citrarekhā, the exceedingly beautiful daughter of the Vāhīka king, [was there].

She beheld his beautiful and lovely face, which was like the moon and possessed the splendor of the moon; it was by that face that she had enjoyed delightful happiness with him in the midst of her dream.
Recognizing him as the son of Āhlāda, the daughter of Abhinandana rejoiced.
Having fashioned a net composed of delusion, as white as a parrot and as fine as a moonbeam,
he took her away at the beautiful self-choice ceremony through the power of supreme bliss;
then, having withdrawn that illusion, he returned to his own home with joy.
Then Kṛṣṇāṃśa, having realized this, did not see his own child;
having awakened Devasiṃha, he asked, "Where has the child gone?
Devasiṃha, though he knew the times, was himself deluded by that wondrous illusion.
The child was not recognized by him; "Where has he gone, or by whom has he been taken?
Seeing the Lion of the Gods thus bewildered, the powerful Kṛṣṇāṃśaka then wept loudly and intensely, deluded by that wondrous illusion.
Hearing his weeping, the wicked king went quickly with a composed mind to where Āhlāda himself was staying;
having wept there deeply, he spoke these words with a humble heart.
Your brother named Udaya, having deluded those two with intoxication,
slew the god Indulama and impaled him upon a pillar;
this was indeed witnessed by me as it was performed by that hero.

"Having given me a hundred gold pieces, Devasiṃha was restrained by him with humility; yet, through his own wit, he did not realize what he had done. Having heard these words, he could reach no certain conclusion.
In the meantime, those two heroes arrived, intent on weeping due to their separation from him. Then the portion of Kṛṣṇa (Āhlāda) prepared to abandon his own body.
Āhlāda, having understood the king's resolve and his speech, [acted accordingly].
He struck Kṛṣṇāṃśa with whips and leather-cutting tools.
His mother, wife, and sister, distressed by love for him,
awakened Āhlāda, who was deluded by the deceptive magic of the rogue.
At that time, the hero, deluded by a wonderful illusion, was not awakened.
Then Queen Puṣpavatī, distressed by her husband's suffering, saw him tormented by his brother and went there quickly, herself afflicted by grief for her husband.
"Though innocent, the portion of Kṛṣṇa has incurred great censure;
therefore, the Brahmins learned in the Vedas have declared that joy is supreme.
Know that killing and abandoning are equal; consider what is appropriate with your intellect."

Thus addressed, that Turīyātman, distressed by grief for his son, summoned the Cāṇḍālas and said: "Bind this slayer of my son and, together with his wife, deliver him to them; execute the punishment without delay."
"Having plucked out his eyes, show them to me together," he said.
Hearing this, they indeed went into the dense forest inhabited by tigers.
Then Devasiṃha, having gone there and given them great wealth, [departed].
Having reached the forest from the Cāṇḍālas, the heroic couple went there;
and the wife of Balakhāna, Gajamuktā, a devoted wife,
joyfully protected the couple in her secret dwelling.
Those Cāṇḍālas, having gathered together, gave him [the deer] to her who had eyes like a doe's.
Then Devasiṃha, arriving there with a mind full of wrath, said to him:
"Fie on you, O sinful one of wicked conduct! By you my friend has been killed."
"Your son is alive on earth; for the sake of searching for him, I shall travel through various kingdoms. I speak the truth, the absolute truth.
Having said this, the hero departed for the auspicious city named Śirīṣa.
Having obtained permission for the elephant's pearls and having secured the couple, he became fearless and arrived at the beautiful city of Mayūra during the terrible night.
But the powerful Makaranda, having understood the entire cause of the matter, [acted accordingly].
With love, he settled his sister’s husband and his own sister within his heart;
he propitiated Dharma through various kinds of sacrifices and hymns.
And the pleased Dharmarāja spoke to Makaranda:
The daughter of King Abhinandana was Citraprapūjinī;
her friend Kesariṇī was the daughter of Nāṭya and was skilled in deceit.
Kutuka, assuming the form of a guru, should be known as the preceptor of Kesariṇī.
By him, an illusion was spread over a distance of a hundred yojanas;
the ground became impassable for enemies, turning them into stones.
Through the power of Citragupta, the king himself became fearless.
Citrarekhā, the daughter of the king, captivated Jayanta;
he assumed the form of a man at night and the form of a boar during the day.
Indula remained there in misery, deluded by Citramāyā.
And you, O Lord, as an incarnation of a portion of Kṛṣṇa, together with Sūryavarman and filled with joy,
having taken the mechanical weapons given by me,
go to Citrarekhā and perform dances and other arts along with them.
Having deluded that goddess and recited that auspicious mantra,
he said, "Return quickly indeed and once again form your army.
Having spoken thus, the god vanished, and the king was filled with wonder.
He described the portion concerning Kṛṣṇa as it has been spoken according to the Dharma:
when the month of Phālguna had arrived, those three, who were experts in dance and song and possessed the forms of yogis, went to the beautiful Innagaṭa.
Then the heroic Lord Makaranda,
an incarnation of Kṛṣṇa who enchants all beings, holding a mṛdaṅga drum on his lap and a lute (vipañcī), performed dance and song;
having thus enchanted the city as well as the king, the lord of elephants.
Delighted, the king spoke these words to him along with his family and army:
"O yogin, tell me what you desire. Having heard this, he replied with a humble mind:
"Give me your own son, Sūryavarman, for the sake of my task."
"Having quickly accomplished my task, I shall give back your son;
for Dharma was ordained by the Creator through kings for the protection of the world.
Having heard this, the lord of elephants gave his own son to them.
The king returned to his own queen; those others, intent on their task,
joyfully proceeded toward the city of Bāhlīka within a mere fortnight,
taking with them the machines bestowed by Dharmadatta to reach the enemy's palace.
Those who knew the essence of the art of dance arrived, intent on enchanting the king;
all the citizens and hosts of warriors also came there with joy.
And they were all captivated by those experts in song and dance.
The king, born of the Tomara lineage, gave them great wealth;
taking them with him, King Abhinandana returned to his own home and,
desiring to perform a domestic dance, had it performed once again.
Then the powerful Makaranda, the son of Bhīṣma, took up the lute and the drum;
Sūryavarman took up the anklets, and Kṛṣṇāṃśa took up the singing and dancing,
and they delighted the most excellent multitude of women.

Having seen them herself, Citrarekhā employed her power of illusion (māyā) for the purpose of deluding them; yet that illusion became fruitless in an instant. Deluded by them, the goddess spoke to them with great joy.
"Tell me your desire, O hero," Kṛṣṇāṃśa said to that bride.
"Give me the parrot; if you do not, I shall cast a curse upon you.
Hearing this, Citrarekhā’s mind became overwhelmed with grief.
He said to the yogi Kṛṣṇāṃśa, "Tell me the truth, who are you?
By that [illusion] created by me, all the gods beginning with Indra were deluded in a mere moment; yet you have not been deluded by me."
"Whether it be the god Nārāyaṇa, Dharma, or Śiva himself," having been addressed thus, that portion of Kṛṣṇa spoke these words fearlessly:
"O Queen, this excellent lion among gods is named Udaya."
This fish-kinsman Makaranda, as well as Sūryavarman, is of that same nature;
due to separation from Indulekhā, we have attained the state of ascetics (yogins),
and my preceptor likewise became insane and agitated because of her absence.
"O Mahāmāyā, give me Śuka, or else give me Indula!
Having said this, she wept aloud: "Alas, Indula of great power!
Show yourself to me quickly; otherwise, I shall give up my life."
To the hero who was speaking thus, the most excellent Citrarekhā, feeling bashful, spoke again: "O sir, take me as your wife and accept my son;
assume a human form that is lovely and beautiful in every way."
Having fallen at his feet, the couple wept aloud;
and seeing them in such a state, Kṛṣṇāṃśa, filled with joy,
took the excellent letter written by Indula.
By the power of the *dharmayantra*, Sūryavarman went to Mayūranagara; honored by Makaranda, he returned home,
while the powerful Devasiṃha took the excellent letter.
Mounted upon his desire, he went to where Āhlāda was filled with grief;
"Who are you? he asked him, for he appeared like one possessed by a great madness. "Know me to be Devasiṃha, intent on searching for your son."
"O hero, take this letter written by his son.
Having heard this, Āhlāda attained supreme joy;
for he understood the entire cause of the matter: that his son had been taken away according to the prescribed rite.
Having summoned the lord of the earth, he of humble intellect spoke these words:
"O King, tell me the truth: was my son slain by a portion of Kṛṣṇa?
He replied: "O hero, I have heard exactly how he was slain by a portion of Kṛṣṇa."
Having spoken thus and laughed, Ahlāda— his eyes copper-red with rage— swiftly achieved his purpose; seizing him by the hair with joy,
he repeatedly struck him with his own hand using reeds.
Upon hearing this, King Parimala arrived together with his wife and greatly delighted the portion of Rāma who had assumed many forms. "O rogue, O great sinner! My kinsman has been slain by you!"
"I shall lead you, along with your family, to where my life has gone.
Then the king, sorrowful and sighing, remained silent;
fixing that sin within his heart, he experienced great agony.
In the meantime, the heroic Balakhāni arrived;
having released his deceitful maternal uncle,
he consoled his elder brother and indeed made preparations for the marriage of his nephew.
King Netrasiṃha arrived accompanied by an army of one hundred thousand;
Tāraka also came toward him along with thousands of heroes;
and Vīrasena himself arrived together with ninety thousand warriors.
Then Tālana arrived accompanied by an army of one hundred thousand; likewise Sūryavarman arrived accompanied by an army of one hundred thousand;
and Brahmānanda himself arrived joined by a force of three hundred thousand.
And Āhlāda, overcome with grief and accompanied by an army of a hundred thousand, cried out, "Alas, brother!
Where have you gone, abandoning me, the lowest of men?
Having spoken thus, the hero departed, his mind agitated by sorrow.
But Balakhāni, powerful and accompanied by an army of a hundred thousand,
went toward Bāhlīka together with Devasiṃha;
indeed, he traveled for one month on the road, measuring a day and a night.
On the fifth day of the dark fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, he reached the village of Vāhlīka.
A battle array for his own troops was formed by Balakhānin:
a single chariot stood at the front of the battle, and behind it were stationed the elephants.
Fifty of those [elephants] in succession, and one hundred horses for each of them;
following them in sequence, ten foot soldiers are stationed. That is to be known as one *senā*; I shall now state its measurement.
There was one chariot, all fifty elephants, and five hundred horses; likewise, five thousand *śataghnīs* are recorded in the army,
and fifty thousand foot-soldiers are recorded in the entire host.
Such were those sixteen armies of Balakhāṇi;
ten thousand elephants, intoxicated with rut, marched forth separately.
In this battle, the number of heroes who strike down their enemies was indeed calculated thus.
The Mlecchas, who follow the ways of the Piśācas, belong to King Abhinandana;
three hundred thousand are mounted on horses, one hundred thousand are elephant-riders,
and one hundred thousand are foot-soldiers armed with *bhuśuṇḍīs* and iron clubs.
Indeed, millions of Kṣatriyas belonging to the Tomara lineage arrived there on elephants at the place where the great army of Āhlāda was stationed.
Between those two, there occurred a great, tumultuous battle that made the hair stand on end.
Intoxicated with pride, they all entered the battle without fear.
The battle of those skilled in combat lasted for seven days and nights;
and half of Bāhlīka’s army was brought to destruction by those kings.
All one hundred thousand were slain by Balakhāni and his army commanders;
when the enemy host was crying "Alas! Alas!", terrified, and fleeing in all directions, Balakhāni and the others were filled with joy and spoke these words to Durgā: "Victory!"
Having witnessed the destruction of the army, the seven princes—
the Kaurava portions— those great chariot-warriors, namely Mahānanda, Nanda, Parānanda, and Upanandaka, departed for the place where he was born.
Sunanda, Surānanda, and Prānanda were born in succession;
those great heroes, stationed upon elephants, born of the Tomara lineage,
struck the army of the high-souled Balakhānin with sharp arrows.
Terrified, they all approached Balakhāni.
Seeing his army defeated,
the mighty Balakhāni then, mounted upon a pigeon, rushed forward with great speed in a fit of rage.
The god Tālana [attacked] Nanda and Parānanda;
Sūryavarman [attacked] Upananda; Tāraka [attacked] Sunanda;
Netrasiṃha [attacked] Surānanda; and the Yādava [attacked] Praṇanda.
Fighting with one another and seeking each other's death,
that battle, which caused the destruction of many heroes, lasted for half a day.
Then those mighty sons of Bāhlīka were defeated.
Having abandoned the battle, those cowards fled home before Balakhānin.
Upon seeing their formidable strength,
King Abhinandana summoned Kutuka, as well as Nāṭyā and Kesīraṇī.
Having heard the reason for the defeat as told by the king,
Kutuka comforted that monarch and reflected upon the illusory power of sorcery (*śāmbarī māyā*) created by Mahādeva.
She bewildered that army, which became like stone and devoid of consciousness.
Then, having bound the eight mighty ones by means of the Kesariṇī dance,
she approached the king's side, gave them over, and returned to her home.
And Bāhlīka, his mind serene, having bound them with firm shackles and plundered their wealth, cast it into the treasury;
for by the boon of the Goddess, that lion among men was overcome by fear.
Having arrived at Mahāvatī, he informed Svarṇavatī;
and the goddess Svarṇavatī, who was proficient in all branches of knowledge,
assuming the form of Śyenī, went toward Puṣpavatī.
Seeing Makaranda staying there in the house with his wife,
he wept and related how his defeat had occurred;
then Kṛṣṇāṃśa, filled with grief, spoke these words to Makaranda.
"Go, O hero, with me; my guru has fallen into captivity.
A great sin lies in the destruction of one's family, as was well said by the ancient sages.
O my beloved, rescue those submerged in the ocean of suffering."
Having heard this, his brother-in-law, accompanied by ten thousand heroes,
cast off his disguise and, equipped with sword and shield,
mounted a horse with a portion of Kṛṣṇa’s splendor and hastened toward Bāhlīka.
Then the goddess Svarṇavatī, accompanied by Puṣpavatī,
assumed the form of a hawk and went to where Mahāraṇa was;
having dispelled Śambarī’s illusion, she alerted her own soldiers.
He besieged the city of that high-souled Bāhlīka;
and seeing them joined by their enemies, Kutuka, together with her,
again dispatched the Śāmbarī illusion against them.
Having cut through all that illusion and bound those two who resembled Daityas,
she caused the city of that king to be burned by means of her own magic power;
yet he who had undergone the burning was not truly burnt, and he who had become ashes was not truly reduced to ash.
A wonderful feat was performed by Svarṇavatī herself through her divine power;
then the goddess Puṣpavatī, having angrily slain the lioness,
gratified the vultures, jackals, and crows with its flesh.
And having likewise slain Kutuka,
Svarṇavatī herself liberated the heroes who were held in the iron prison;
then that goddess of auspicious countenance returned once more along with her.
Where Makaranda stood, accompanied by a portion of Kṛṣṇa,
all those great heroes were filled with wonder upon realizing they had been deluded by the Goddess; overcome with anger, they advanced for battle.
Once again, a battle took place between those two armies in the fray.
Mahānanda went against Balakhāni, Nanda went against Āhlāda,
Parānanda went against the god Tāraka, and Upanandana went against [the other].
Sunanda and Netrasimha, Surānanda and Tālana,
Prānanda and Vīrasena, and Brahmānanda—
the king [and his sons] were all mounted upon elephants and intent on a battle with bows.
A tumultuous battle took place between them for a day and a night in succession;
in the meantime, during that night, Citrarekhā arrived,
having indeed observed her own people to be so distressed and in such a state.
Then, having meditated upon Citragupta, he performed a wondrous illusion;
at that time, his kinsmen were there, offering many kinds of praise.
Seeing them, everyone was struck with amazement and, overcome by fear, fled.
Having abandoned the battlefield, their minds agitated by grief,
those mighty warriors traveled five yojanas and established their camp there; when the twilight had turned to darkness, they remained there devoid of energy.

"Alas, O portion of Kṛṣṇa, O mighty-armed one, O you who are compassionate toward those who seek refuge! This prince Indulata has been snatched away by Citrarekhā. Deluded by her, we heroes have come to you for protection."
Having spoken thus, they wept: "O high-minded one, where have you gone?
Then there arose a great clamor from those powerful men as they wailed;
having reproached Āhlāda, they fell senseless upon the ground, overwhelmed with grief.
But Āhlāda, hearing this, was himself struck as if by a thunderbolt;
becoming like one deranged, he then struck [him] on the chest.
In the meantime, the yogi who was a portion of Kṛṣṇa, an emanation of the Blessed One—
At moonrise on the eighth day, falling on a Saturday,
Śūra himself arrived accompanied by ten thousand troops and Makaranda;
he then awakened that army which was being protected by Balakhānin.
Having conquered all those kings and seized vast wealth,
he returned and roared at his kinsman who was established in the five sounds.
By that roar, the portion of Śeṣa was awakened by the powerful one.
Beholding an auspicious omen, the valiant one raised his arms and placed the portion of Kṛṣṇa, who appeared in the form of a yogi, upon his own lap;
overwhelmed with love, he bathed that portion of Kṛṣṇa with streams of tears.
Having given [gifts] to the foremost of the twice-born, he described the cause; Kṛṣṇāṃśa, too, with a gracious soul, having related his entire story exactly as it had happened,
returned once more to Bāhlīka.
Having personally created the painting and had it painted by Citrarekhā,
he bound King Abhinandana along with his son and ministers,
and caused the marriage of Jayanta to take place with her.
But Bāhlīka, with a delighted soul, having given away abundant wealth,
joyfully bestowed his daughter Citrarekhā upon Jayanta;
he also gave him a hundred elephants and thousands of horses accompanied by riches.
He personally gave a hundred male and female servants to Jayanta;
he then caused the high-souled Balakhāni to set forth.
They all arrived at Mahāvatī in the month of Śrāvaṇa.
All the kings, honored and filled with joy, departed for their respective homes.
Thus, O Brahmin, I have narrated to you this life-story which destroys the Kali age;
it removes all sins for those who hear it, and I shall indeed tell it again.

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Compendium of Histories of the Kali Age," within the Kali-yuga section of the Pratisarga-parvan, which is an alternative designation for the Caturyuga-khaṇḍa, in the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said: When Kṛṣṇāṃśa had arrived at his home and Indula was married...
The lord of the earth was constantly distressed and went toward the threshold;
having related the account before the king, that Tāraka was struck with great wonder regarding the deeds of Kṛṣṇa’s portion.
In the meantime, the noble-minded minister Candrabhaṭṭa spoke these words to Bhūmirāja: "Listen, O best of kings!
I have propitiated the Goddess Vaiṣṇavī, the creator of the universe."

At the end of three years, she became pleased, the bestower of boons and the remover of fear. She granted me auspicious knowledge that destroys poor intellect. Then, O King, having become possessed of knowledge, [I turned] toward the portion of Kṛṣṇa.
He described his life story, which destroys all impurities.
Having spoken thus, that pure-souled one recited this auspicious work composed in the vernacular language,
proclaiming the greatness of those devoted to the Goddess, to the assembly.
Upon hearing that, the king of the earth was instantly struck with wonder;
then the lord of the land, proud of the strength of his divine horses, spoke:
"Who is this powerful man named Udaya, whose story has been described in such a manner?"
"Those four divine steeds— those that move on water, on land, and those that fly through the air—
quickly gather them together and become a powerful king yourself!
Having heard this, that king [addressed] the one skilled in explaining the scriptures.
Having summoned Kundanamala, he dispatched him with haste.
Arriving at Mahāvatī, that messenger spoke these words with affection to the king regarding the lord of the earth, the monarch.

"O King, those four horses of yours are indeed divine in form and possess auspicious radiance. My daughter, named Velā, is your bride; she has summoned these horses for the sake of seeing you. Give them to her and cast aside your astonishment."
"If not, all the army commanders will perish by the fire of their own impatience.
Having heard these terrible words, the king, overcome with fear,
summoned Āhlāda and the others and spoke these words with a humble mind.
"Give me your respective horses with joy; carry out my command.
Hearing this, Āhlāda meditated upon Śivā, who is identical with all things, and spoke these sweet words: "Listen, O King, beloved of Śiva!"
"Wherever our vital breaths are established, there you, O Victor, are also established.
We shall not give [it up], O King; this is the truth, the truth, and not otherwise.
Having heard these words of his, the powerful King Parimala—
He uttered a terrible oath in the hearing of those powerful men:
"May my food be the flesh of a Brahmin, my drink like the blood of a cow,
my bed like that of my own mother, and my assembly hall like the slaughter of a Brahmin."
"And by your dwelling in my kingdom, a great sin has been committed.
Upon hearing this curse, Devakī, overcome with grief,
wept bitterly along with the members of her household.
When he had reached his twenty-fifth year, devoted to yoga and a portion of Kṛṣṇa,
those intent on dharma departed from his home on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada for Kānyakubja, which was protected by Jayacandra.
Accompanied by Svarṇavatī, Puṣpavatī, and Citrarekhā,
Indula set out quickly with forces of ten thousand horses;
his father, moreover, mounted the horse Karāla and the chariot Pañcaśabda.
The portion of Kṛṣṇa, mounted upon a peacock, followed after Devakī.
Abandoning that king’s village, which was endowed with every prosperity,
they stayed for three days on the road and then approached Jayacandra.
Having bowed to that king with affection and explained the entire cause,
they stayed at the Śītalā shrine and worshipped Ambikā.
King Jayacandra, meanwhile, was described by Devasiṃha.
And Bhūmā did not grant them a livelihood by the command of Parimala.
Devasiṃha, however, being frustrated, went to the supreme portion of Kṛṣṇa;
having related the entire cause, he heard [the response] and gave way to anger.
Quickly mounted upon Bindula and surrounded by five hundred horses,
he plundered that city protected by Lakṣaṇa.
Seeing him, the heroic Lakṣaṇa took his seat upon the back of an elephant.
He struck Kṛṣṇa’s heart firmly with an arrow,
but the shaft, impelled by the Viṣṇu-mantra, became fruitless.
Astonished, the king descended from his mount to the ground.
Having bowed at his divine feet, which were adorned with the thunderbolt and other marks,
Lakṣaṇa prostrated himself like a staff and praised him with a faltering voice.
Lakṣaṇa said:
"Know me, O Lord, to be a Vaiṣṇava, devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu.
I know you, O mighty-armed one, to be an incarnation of Kṛṣṇa’s power.
For who else on earth besides you could render my arrow fruitless?"
"Forgive my wickedness, O Lord; this was brought about by your own illusory power.
Having spoken thus, he went together with him to King Jayacandra and informed him how he had met with defeat.
The king, for the sake of testing those two who had been deluded by the shadow,
abandoned the two elephants, Kuvalayāpīḍa and Uccaiḥśravas, on a cool spot;
then, with ease, he seized those two heroes who were experiencing a surge of joy.
They dragged the two elephants by their tails with force for a distance of one krośa again and again.
Seeing that Kuvalayāpīḍa and his companion were dead, the king, overcome with fear yet clear-minded, gave the village of Rājagṛha for their sake.
When the month of Āṣāḍha had arrived, the powerful one named Lakṣaṇa,
accompanied by those such as Tāla and others, set out swiftly at the king’s command for the conquest of the quarters,
together with an army of seven hundred thousand.
Having reached the city of Vārāṇasī, he then besieged the city;
and King Rudravarman, the glory-maker of the Gauḍa dynasty,
arrived for the sake of battle together with his own armies numbering fifty thousand.
Having conquered him in a mere watch of the night, he obtained from the sixteen-year-old a tribute consisting of ten million gold coins and presented it to Jayacandra.
Then, having again defeated the Lord of Magadha, named Vijayakārin, he [conquered him].
Having obtained a revenue of twenty years, he offered it to his own king; then,
accompanied by those [revenues], the hero Lakṣaṇa went again with five crores of silver coins to the lord of the lands of Aṅga and Vaṅga.
Having defeated that excellent king Kālīvarman, who possessed an army of one hundred thousand,
in a great battle within a single day and night,
Lakṣmaṇa then received a tribute of twenty years' revenue and ten million pieces of gold.
With great joy, he dispatched [a message] to King Jayacandra;
the hero went to the land of Uṣṭra, which was protected by those mighty forces.
There, King Dhoyīkavi was accompanied by an army of one hundred thousand.
By the command of Jagannātha, he arrived together with them for the sake of battle;
between those two there occurred a great, tumultuous, and hair-raising combat,
at the end of which the king was defeated by the portion of Kṛṣṇa after the duration of a day and a night.
Having obtained everything for twenty years along with ten million pieces of gold, he sent it indeed to the lord of Kānyakubja;
then the hero Lakṣaṇa, exceedingly powerful, went to the Puṇḍra country.
Having defeated the king named Nāgapati, who was endowed with the strength of fifty thousand [soldiers], in a single day, he seized ten million gold coins (koṭimudrā). Then,
having gone to Mount Mahendra and bowed to that sage Bhārgava, he remained there.
Having returned from Nanda’s [village], they all went to the city of Netrapāla.
Then, O Bhārgava, Yogasiṃha arrived and gave ten million gold coins (koṭimudrā) to that portion of Kṛṣṇa and had him reside there for seven nights.
Those heroes, exceedingly intoxicated with pride, went to Vīrasiṃhapura;
from atop Himatuṅga, they besieged the entire city,
which was protected by the yogi named Gorakha for the sake of his devotees.
The younger brother of the king, a pre-eminent hero accompanied by ten thousand troops,
waged a fierce battle against the army of Lakṣmaṇa;
every day that powerful warrior slew thousands of brave men.

Having reached his home in the evening, he worshipped that yogin. Through that worship, the yogin became pleased in spirit; having revived the king's army and bestowed the strength of elephants upon them, he indeed resumed his yoga practice once more.
Half a month passed there while those powerful warriors were fighting;
then, losing their enthusiasm, they said to that lion among gods:
"O King, how shall we achieve victory? Tell us the truth before us."

Having heard this, he said: "Listen, O portion of Kṛṣṇa, to my words. After you have defeated the one named Gorakha—who dances with pride among the yogins—engage in battle once more; then indeed you shall obtain victory."
Having been addressed thus, Kṛṣṇa and the others assumed bodies composed of yoga; having stationed their army, which was protected by Lakṣmaṇa, in the field of battle,
they went at dawn to the abode of that yogin.
Kṛṣṇāṃśa was a dancer, expert in the playing of the flute;
Devasiṃha was rich in the mṛdaṅga drum; and Tālana held the lute.
Then Āhlāda, holding the cymbals, sang the eternal song.
Keeping that purpose in his heart, Gorakṣa, the master of all yoga, said to them, "Choose a boon. Having heard that, they spoke these words:
"We pay homage to you; if a boon is to be granted by you..."
"Grant the Saṃjīvinī lore for the delight of this great-souled one.
Having heard this and meditated upon it in his heart, he, with a gracious mind, said to them:
"The Saṃjīvinī lore shall belong to you for only one year."
After that, having become formless, he will come into my presence.
O hero, from this day forward, this world has been abandoned by me;
I shall go where Bhartṛhari is my disciple and there indeed I shall rest.

Having spoken thus, the yogi vanished; they then proceeded to the front of the battle. Having defeated Pravīrasiṃha as well as Vīrasiṃha, and having slain his army of ten thousand, they plundered his palace.
Having made the king a servant, Lakṣaṇa departed with joy;
arriving in the country of Kośala and defeating its monarch,
he compelled Sūryadhara and ten thousand soldiers to pay tribute.
Having joyfully obtained sixteen years of life and ten million crores of mudrās,
they arrived at the Naimiṣa forest and dwelt there, intent on ritual bathing.
On the beautiful day of Holi, Lakṣaṇa became exceedingly powerful.
Having bestowed gifts upon the Brahmins, he held a great festival;
at that time, we sages were established in meditative absorption, as was the king,
when that Lakṣaṇa arrived at the supreme Naimiṣa forest.
Having bathed in all the sacred fords (tīrthas) and having offered libations to the twice-born and the gods,
they went to the city of Kānyakubja on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Caitra. Thus, O Brahmin, has been told to you how the conquest of the quarters occurred.
Listen, O Brahmin, to this delightful story of how the mighty Balakhāni, the king of the earth, died on the seventh day of the dark fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa; how,
at the command of Mahīpati, he fearlessly spoke to his vassal.
"I have heard that your son has become arrogant due to the boon of Śaradā and has attained the state of Raktabīja; give him to me, have mercy!
When he had spoken thus, that feudal lord was honored by the king as if he were the king himself.
Having summoned his son named Cāmuṇḍa, he spoke this:
"O son, you who are fond of battle, always perform the king's business.
Having heard his father's words, he indeed spoke to the king.
"O King, give me your command; you shall quickly attain victory.
Having heard this, the exceedingly powerful Balakhānin said:
"Having cut down my Śirīṣa forest, take this excellent kingdom!"
"Established in your home, fearless, possessed of great strength, and with senses subdued—
if you indeed defeat Balakhāni and hand him over to me,
or else slay him and bring his entire kingdom to you, then you shall remain [in power]."
Having spoken thus, he summoned his own army and gave seven hundred thousand [soldiers] to that Raktabīja; having received them, the latter departed with joy.
After traveling for three days on the road, he arrived at the place named Śirīṣa.
He besieged the entire city of the high-souled Balakhāni.
Upon hearing of Cāmuṇḍā’s arrival, the mighty Balakhāni,
having worshipped Mahāmāyā and given manifold gifts, [prepared for battle].
Accompanied by an army of one hundred thousand, he marched out from the city.
His younger brother, the great hero Sukhakhāni, together with his forces,
mounted that female elephant and attacked the enemy host.
Balakhāni, stationed upon a pigeon, having destroyed the enemy's force of one hundred thousand troops,
approached Cāmuṇḍa with great joy;
between the two of them there occurred a great battle that caused the destruction of their respective armies.
The Kṣatriyas slain in battle by the measure of day and night were left behind;
then, when morning had arrived, those two heroes, experts in the bow and arrow, performed their ritual acts such as bathing and proceeded to the field of battle.
Balakhāni, standing upon his chariot, and Cāmuṇḍa, mounted on the back of an elephant,
waged a tumultuous and terrible battle that caused wonder among men.
Having cut down arrows with arrows, those two, devoted to the Goddess, fought with joy.
Having slain one another with their mounts,
the two heroes, bearing swords and shields, fell to the ground and fought each other;
as many drops of blood as were produced from the limbs of Raktabīja...

An equal number of men were born, possessing the prowess of Raktabīja. O best of the Bhṛgus, Balakhāni was besieged on all sides by those heroes who were intoxicated with pride, and he sought refuge with Śāradā.
In the meantime, the heroic younger brother Sukhakhanis took up an Agneya arrow and incinerated the Raktabijas;
formerly, Sukhakhanis had indeed gratified the god Pāvaka with sacrificial offerings.
Then the Lord himself, being pleased, worshipped him for five years;
with a gracious soul, he gave him a beautiful arrow of fire that destroys enemies, and by means of it, he became victorious.
But Bālakhāni, seeing the destruction of his enemy and that Cāmuṇḍa had been defeated, bound,
and brought home, assumed the guise of a woman out of fear of the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Having placed him upon a swing, the powerful one dispatched him to the enemy;
then, having gone to Dehalī, he reported the news of how the great battle had occurred to the remaining five hundred thousand troops.
And seeing Cāmuṇḍā in the guise of a woman,
that powerful lord of the earth, overcome with anger, spoke to the king:
"How will victory be mine, and how shall I live happily?"
Having heard this, the lord of the earth said: "Act through a stratagem.
Her mother should be known as Brāhmī; she alone is pure and devoted to her husband.
O sir, having learned the reason through female messengers, wage war once again."
Having heard this, the king of the earth summoned those female messengers, who were experts in stratagems,
and dispatched them toward the residence of Balakhāni.
Having then assumed the guise of Brahmin women, they went to Balakhāni’s house.
Having quickly praised her along with her daughter, they, filled with humility, asked:
"By good fortune, your two sons are great heroes who bring about the destruction of their enemies;
how might their death come to pass so that they may live for a hundred autumns?"
Then Brāhmī spoke these words: "The auspicious arrow of Pāvaki (Agni) brings life to Sukhakhāni and strikes down Balakhāni.
Having understood this, those female messengers set out toward Dehalī.
Having spoken thus before the king and received their wealth, they went home.
But Mahīrāja, having heard that, joyfully performed the worship of Mahādeva, the Lord of Umā, along with other kings for a thousand days.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Compendium of Histories of the Kali Age," within the *Caturyugakhaṇḍa* (also known as the *Pratisargaparvan*) of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
Listen now to how [the events] occurred when the portion of Kṛṣṇa was in his twenty-sixth year.
O Sage, there is a place named Bindusaras situated in the southern direction.
On its shore lived a village extending for one yojana, known by the name Bindugaḍha; it was a fortress that promoted the duties of the social orders.
In that village lived a king born of the lineage of Viṣvaksena,
named Śāradānandana, who was devoted to meditation upon Brahman;
by the power of his celibacy, his vital energy (vīrya) remained fixed in his head.
To him was born a son renowned on earth by the name Kāmapāla.
He worshipped Prajāpati, the eldest of the gods, with sacrifices;
and as soon as he had partaken of the sacrificial portions, the queen conceived a child.
Born within ten months, she was a maiden who was an abode of all virtues;
renowned by the name Padminī, she was endowed with every beauty.
Upon reaching the age of twelve years, that woman of excellent complexion became truly radiant.
Padmākara, the son of the king and a follower in the footsteps of the great monarch,
quickly summoned the kings at his father’s command and joyfully conducted the *svayaṃvara* for his sister.
Kings from various lands, accompanied by their foremost heroes,
set out at the command of their father along with the four heroes, including Lakṣmaṇa and Ahaḷāda. They went to the village of Bindugr̥ha, where a great festival was being held.
But the powerful Mahīrāja, seeing that the auspicious signs had appeared,
stationed his army for the protection of all the kings.
In the meantime, Queen Padminī was with her female companions.
Having quickly observed all the kings, she approached the one who possessed the ultimate marks:
a dark-limbed youth endowed with every auspicious characteristic,
and forty or fifty years of age.
Seeing him— broad-chested, firm-shouldered, ageless, free from disease,
resembling her own self, and protected by joy and other [emotions]—
Padminī gave a victory garland to Lakṣaṇa.
Then that heroic Lakṣaṇa, taking her excellent hand and mounting his own chariot, went forth with joy into the midst of the kings;
likewise Pṛthvīrāja and all the rulers of the earth accompanied by their armies.
They hemmed in the powerful hero Lakṣmaṇa from all sides.
Tālana, born from a portion of Bhīmasena, joyfully grasped an iron club and, stationed upon Siṃhinī, began to fight the armies.
Mounted upon a five-toned elephant and armed with a *tomara* spear, Cāhrāda,
born from a portion of Balabhadra, tore asunder his enemies.
Bindula, an incarnation of a portion of Kṛṣṇa, mounted a horse and took up an excellent sword.
Having cut down the kings in many ways, he wrought a great slaughter;
mounted upon his chariot of desire, the god took up a terrible spear,
and having struck the army in many places, he roared again and again.
Taking up his bow and once again aiming the Vaiṣṇava weapons,
Lakṣmaṇa swiftly struck down the generals of Mahīrāja’s army.
The battle between them continued for the duration of a watch (three hours).
Then, having abandoned the battle along with all the kings, Mahīrāja,
the delighter of Śāradā, went to the village of Dehalī; there he erected an auspicious pavilion and performed the marriage rites.

He gave his daughter away according to the prescribed rites, providing her with wealth, grain, and other possessions. In the meantime, the lord of the earth arrived and spoke to that prince Padmākara, who was accompanied by an army of a hundred thousand.

"O friend, O great hero, what kind of disposition has come to you? You were indeed born into the lineage of Viṣvaksena as the best of Kṣatriyas; yet you are now devoid of dharma and joined with the confusion of castes."
"And those heroes, Āhlāda and the others, born of the Ābhīra mother—
those who know the Dharma must certainly abandon their dwelling together with them.
Having heard this, Padmākara, who was skilled in all forms of illusion, [acted accordingly].
Having employed the Śāmbarī illusion and bound those very invincible ones,
he placed them in a stone prison within his own home;
and then, by the boon of the Goddess, that lion among gods [remained] at night.

Having abandoned that which consisted of illusion and delusion, she went to Kānyakubja. After Indulā had related everything to him, he, who was skilled in divine illusions, joined with her and quickly reached Bindugadha.
But Padmākara, having heard that and employing the Śāmbara illusion,
exerted himself there to bewilder [the enemy], just as a cloud [obscures] the sun in the sky;
and Indula then fixed an excellent arrow upon his bow.
By the weapon of desire (*kāmāstra*), her illusion was reduced to ashes in an instant.
Then, all those mighty ones were awakened by the weapon of desire;
having pierced the iron net as well as the firm door-panel, they emerged.
The enemy armies, having come forth from outside, were destroyed;
five thousand kṣatriyas died and went to the city of Yama.
King Śāradānandana, arriving there, bowed down before them.
And the king joyfully gave his own daughter to that high-souled Lakṣaṇa,
as well as various kinds of foods and excellent ornaments to all those thousands at that time.
Perceiving that his own daughter was intent on weeping profusely,
Kāmapāla indeed settled her in his own house;
then Lakṣaṇa arrived at the home on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha.
Upon seeing Lakṣaṇa, Jayacandra was overwhelmed with affection;
he gave a hundred villages to them, including Tāla and others.
Having bestowed those, he then gave other gifts, such as cows, garments, and ornaments.
He gave [gifts] to the Brahmins and celebrated a great festival. Sūta said:
The King of the Earth obtained a boon from Śaṅkara by means of worshipping the king of kings.
Having assembled a host terrifying to his enemies in the month of Phālguna,
he went to the city named Śirīṣa accompanied by seven hundred thousand [soldiers].
And by the king's command, Cāmuṇḍa again besieged the city.
Then Sukhakhāni, enraged and accompanied by an army of one hundred thousand,
came out from the city and wrought a great slaughter;
the powerful one, having slain ten thousand with the fire-weapon (pāvakāstra), [continued his destruction].
Approaching the king of the earth, he spoke these words fearlessly:
"Today I shall slay you, or you shall be the slayer of me in battle. O King, employ your own magic arts; otherwise, you will surely meet with destruction."

Having heard this, the king of the earth took up the Raudra weapon upon his bow; from that weapon, a terrifying and great fire manifested. Then Sukhakhāni aimed the Āgneya weapon for its pacification.
And by the fierce fire, Sukhakhāni, along with his arrows, was dissolved;
having accomplished that task, that weapon returned to Śiva’s quiver.
But upon hearing this, Balakhāni, overcome with fear, arrived there.
Taking up enmity toward his brother, he struck down the enemy's forces;
then, having meditated upon the goddess Śāradā, he approached Bhūmirāja.
But Bhūmirāja, seeing him, was bewildered by the superiority of that [new] strength.
He spoke these words with affection: "O Balakhāna, listen!
Within the distance of a single *krośa*, twelve pits have been prepared by me;
they are guarded by twelve hundred heroes who are skilled in battle."
"Having conquered and leaped over the twelve pits,
O best of strong men, take my entire kingdom as your half-share.
Having heard these pleasing words spoken truly by the king, [Bali replied:]
Mounting a pigeon-colored horse and with sword in hand, he went to the forest;
having seen the pits, that great hero, mighty-armed and self-controlled, slew hundreds upon hundreds of warriors and proceeded through the twelve pits.
Then Cāmuṇḍa, that lowest of brahmins and a practitioner of deceit, arrived accompanied by ten thousand arrows and besieged the hero from all sides; meanwhile,
Balakhāni struck down his vast army.
Having approached Cāmuṇḍa, he roared again and again;
[he saw] the thirteenth secret pit, covered with grass and earth,
its opening obscured by great, poison-washed arrows.
And that hero, deluded by fate, fell along with the pigeon into a most terrible and deep darkness extending for about one *krośa*. There, indeed, the lotus-like foot of Vatsaja was torn asunder.
With great difficulty, that horse emerged from the pit and struck the army of Mahīrāja with its hooves;
then Cāmuṇḍa arrived and indeed struck off the head of Balakhāna.
Having cut down that army, he struck it down until it was leaderless and filled with cries of "Alas! Alas!
Then Gajamuktā, hearing of this, ascended the funeral pyre and, being a virtuous wife, had her husband's limbs cremated along with his own.
Then Brahmā, having arrived there together with his own wife,
summoned Sukhakhāni and cremated that body;
indeed, that king reduced the now-desolate city to ashes.
Endowed with great enthusiasm, he went quickly to Dehlī.

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter in the *Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, in the *Pratisarga Parvan*, within the *Kaliyuga Itihāsa Samuccaya* (also known as the *Caturyuga Khaṇḍa*), during the time of the narrative of Vikrama.
Sūta said:
When the month of Śrāvaṇa arrived, the king—
who was always fond of quarreling— set out for Dehlī for the sake of the Nāga festival.
Having seen the Nāga festival there, accompanied by song and dance, he...
Having paid homage to the great king, he, with a humble mind, spoke these words:
"O King, in the village of Mahāvatī, situated in the midst of the ocean of fame,
there is an exceedingly great festival of Vāmana, accompanied by barley and rice."
"Go there and do exactly as I say.
Having heard this, the king of the earth, accompanied by Dhundhukāra,
joined by a force of seven hundred thousand, and attended by Cāmuṇḍa, [set out].

Having arrived at the Śirīṣa grove, he took up residence there. Then the king, that deceitful man skilled in illusion, bowed to the monarch of the Lunar dynasty and, though himself sorrowful, spoke these words.
"O King, a great sovereign has arrived and stands before you seeking battle;
having worshipped the divine liṅga, he will forcibly seize your daughter Candrāvalī and your son Brahmānanda."
"Therefore, O high-minded one, together with me and your own forces,
defeat him through a stratagem and dwell happily in this city.
Having heard this, the powerful King Parimala, subject to the power of fate, [acted accordingly].
Accompanied by four hundred thousand troops, he arrived at midnight;
having slain five thousand brave Kṣatriyas who were lying asleep,
he unleashed the wrathful Śataghnī weapon, which destroys many heroes.
Then the king of the earth rose up, hurriedly girding his loins;
regarding him as a supreme enemy, he waged a great battle.
While the two armies were fighting there, Malinī, longing for her son, [intervened].
Having approached Śāradā with reverence, he worshipped her with devotion:
"O Goddess of goddesses, O Great Goddess, O destroyer of all suffering!
Remove all my afflictions and quickly awaken the portion of Kṛṣṇa within me."
Having recited this mantra ten thousand times, and having performed the fire-oblation, the libation, and the ritual purification,
Śivā herself, being pleased, slept in that house; she said,
"Do not grieve, for the great affliction in Malana shall go to its destruction."
Having spoken thus, the goddess Śāradā approached the portion of Kṛṣṇa and said:
"O son, your mother Earth is being oppressed by Mahīrāja;
she will soon go to ruin, therefore you must rescue her."
Having heard these words of the goddess, that hero was filled with wonder;
he approached Devakī and explained the reason.
She, however, having heard those terrible words, was accompanied by Svarṇavatī.
Distressed and lamenting in many ways, the virtuous woman wept bitterly.
Then Kṛṣṇāṃśa, sorrowful, spoke to Devasiṃha:
"O hero, what must I do? Give me your command in this terrible danger."
Having heard that, accompanied by him and endowed with auspicious marks,
the noble-minded general Tālana— an incarnation of Bhīmasena— set out for Mahāvatī under the pretext of a world conquest.
Accompanied by seven hundred thousand [soldiers], he proceeded without joy;
having reached Kalpakṣetra, those [followers] then became yogins,
and he caused the army to encamp there in that dreadful forest.
The god Tālana, a portion of Kṛṣṇa and possessed of great strength,
took up the implements of dance and arrived at the battlefield.
A battle between the two, which increased the prospect of death, took place for seven days.
On the seventh day, those heroes arrived at the forefront of the battle;
on that day, O illustrious one, a great war took place.
Seeing his army defeated, the powerful King Parimala—
Standing in his chariot and taking up his bow, he approached the King of the Earth;
and then the Yādava, the husband of Candrāvalī, mounted upon an elephant,
challenged Dhundhukāra and engaged him in a duel with bows.
Mounting his golden elephant, the mighty Brahmānanda challenged his enemy Tāraka and engaged him in a battle of archery; likewise,
Raṇajit, established in his glory, fought against Prince Mardana.
He struck him with his own arrows and slew his son;
indeed, Rūpaṇa, mounted upon a horse, went toward Saradana.
The powerful Madana was born as the son of an Ābhīrī woman.
Śaṅkhāṃśa went against Nṛhara and the prince;
and in those battles, Cāmuṇḍa, the commander of ten thousand troops,
having heeded the words of the lord of the earth, returned to the city.
The hero, devoted to the worship of the Goddess, beheld the beautiful city, filled with people of the four castes and abounding in wealth and grain;
for the king was indeed a rogue who had arrived at the gate of the fortress.
Accompanied by Cāmuṇḍa, the sinner approached the royal palace.
Seeing her brother, Malanā spoke these words in distress:
"Today is the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada, and barley and rice are stored in the house."
The great sinner Mahīrāja did not reach the supremely meritorious Kīrtisāgara, situated by the water; having come to the festival of Vāmana,
he experienced great misery instead of joy, for he was devoid of the portion of Kṛṣṇa.
When this was said, the mighty Brahmin laughed and said:
"This man has come from Kānyakubja, dispatched by a portion of Kṛṣṇa;
his name is Devīdatta, and he will accomplish your task."
Having heard this, Queen Candrāvalī, adorned with all her ornaments,
beheld the Brahmin Cāmuṇḍa who was tormented by the fire of desire;
approaching her mother, she spoke these words with great intensity.
"O mother, this Brahmin is a rogue; he will surely carry me away.
Who is this hero? I do not know him. How can I go [with him], being a devoted wife?
Having heard these words of hers, the lord of the earth was filled with shame.
Accompanied by Cāmuṇḍa, he arrived at the place where that great battle was taking place.
In the meantime, those [enemies] led by Brahmā, having been defeated by them,
abandoned the fight and returned home with their three hundred thousand troops.
Having made the door very secure, they fell into great anxiety.
But the powerful Mahīrāja,
supported by the king of the earth and accompanied by a force of sixty lakhs, arrived at the pleasure grove.
There, the powerful one guarded [the city] for the sake of a festival of honor;
meanwhile, the four [brothers], Tāla and the others, went to the city named Śirīṣa. Seeing that village had become dry land, they were filled with wonder.

Deprived of happiness, they proceeded and beheld the sage Himada. Overcome with grief, they bowed and said: "O Sage, where has the powerful Balasva gone, along with those who boast of battle and his wicked followers?"
Having heard that the yogi Himada had been destroyed by the king of the earth through deceit,
and that Balakhāni had also perished and this beautiful woman was his wife,
Kṛṣṇāṃśa, hearing these terrible words, became overwhelmed with grief.
There he lamented bitterly: "Alas, my brother, portion of Dharma!
Without you, dwelling upon this earth is exceedingly terrifying to me.
Grant me your sight quickly; otherwise, I shall give up my life."
Thus addressed, his brother Balakhāni, who had gone among the Piśācas,
arrived together with his wife and wept profusely; he related the entire account of how his own slaughter had occurred exactly as it happened.
Having ascended a divine celestial chariot, he went to the delightful heaven;
at that time, not even a sixteenth part of Balakhāyin’s power remained in Yudhiṣṭhira.
Then, that sorrowful portion of Kṛṣṇa offered a handful of sesame seeds as a libation for his brother.
Having arrived at Mahāvatī, he approached the royal palace;
there Kṛṣṇāṃśa, the deluder of people, danced to the sound of the flute. And Tālana, assuming the form of a yogin, sang while playing the lute.

The Lord Lakṣaṇa played the mṛdaṅga drum and the bell-metal cymbals, and sang there with a beautiful voice; hearing this, the king was utterly enchanted. Then Queen Malanā, having witnessed that festival of Vāmana—
Having wept, she spoke these words: "Where has my beloved gone—Kṛṣṇāṃśa, along with his kinsmen—who abandoned me, unfortunate as I am?
Deprived of you, this land has been plundered by Mahīrāja."
Seeing Malanā thus addressed, the partial incarnation of Kṛṣṇa, distressed by affection, spoke these words with a humble soul: "O Queen, please do as I say.
We are yogis, O Princess, and experts in all forms of combat."
"Having performed this entire task for you, we shall indeed go to Naimiṣa. Taking all the barley and rice grains that are stored in your house, let all the women go to the edge of the ocean."
"But we shall provide protection for you with an army of yogis.
Having heard these words of his, his daughter, a devoted wife, spoke these words to her mother: "This is a portion of Kṛṣṇa; he is no mere dancer."
His eyes resemble lotuses and his dark-limbed form is beautiful;
O Mother, who on earth is capable of protecting him without a portion of Kṛṣṇa? Even the invincible King of the Earth was utterly defeated by a portion of Kṛṣṇa.
Having heard those words, Malanā, overwhelmed with love,
removed the barley and rice and placed them in the hands of the women;
all those women then sang of the auspicious deeds of Kṛṣṇa’s portion.
Lakṣaṇa, arriving swiftly, had his soldiers dressed in the garb of yogis;
having prepared them and stationed himself there, he remained well-protected by drummers and others.
Then those heroes, arrogant in their strength, approached Kīrtisāgara.
The women stationed there, numbering ten thousand, wept on all sides.
But the king, realizing that the descendant of Kṛṣṇa— the scion of the Lunar dynasty—
had arrived as one who would destroy his lineage, wept along with his son upon his approach.
O Great King, all the women were plundered by those yogis; Malanā was seized there, as was Candrāvalī, the daughter of Mahīrāja. Those soldiers of Mahīrāja arrived there disguised as yogis.
Having heard these terrible words— "He has given his daughter, my own sister, to Mahīrāja, the son of Tāraka"— the mighty Brahmānanda,
filled with rage, set out for that place accompanied by an army of one hundred thousand.
But Mahīrāja, accompanied by his ten thousand sons and protected by Kāmasena as well as Raṇajit,
advanced; and a great battle took place between those two armies upon the earth.
Tāla, disguised as a yogi, attained the bliss of Brahman;
while Lakṣaṇa and Śūra,
having conquered and bound King Devasiṃha, returned joyfully along with Kāmasena.
Then the god Lakṣmaṇa bound Kāmasena and Raṇajit;
those two heroes, who caused the destruction of the enemy army, remained there bound.
In the meantime, the powerful Brahmā indeed bound Tālana.
Having reached the target, he engaged in a duel with bows;
then, having bound the target once more while his bow was broken,
that one of great strength approached Devasiṃha and rendered him unconscious.
When the army of yogis had become wailing "Hā! Hā! and fled in every direction, the dark-complexioned portion [of Viṣṇu], with a humble mind, spoke these words to all the women:
"This is the bliss of Brahman that has arrived, which brings about the destruction of my army."

"Therefore, you all must go quickly with me toward him. Having said this and taking them along, Brahmā approached Naranārāyaṇa; and between those two, Nara and Nārāyaṇa, there occurred a great battle.
