Then the powerful portion of Kṛṣṇa, traveling through the path of the sky toward him,
approached him as he stood in his chariot and bewildered him with a sword.
When he had thus fainted, [Kṛṣṇa] joyfully released those women.

Accompanied by his army, the yogi became intent on fleeing from the battle. When the yogi’s army was defeated, the exceedingly powerful Brahmānanda took those women and set his mind upon returning to his own home.
But Mahīrāja, having arrived with the approval of the lord of the earth,
that powerful one who had received a boon from Śiva, besieged the women on all sides.
Nṛhara, Abhaya, Śūra, Mardana, and Rūpaṇa [also joined him].
Madana was indeed slain by Saradana, and Tāraka slew Brahmānanda;
Cāmuṇḍa caused a bow-duel with Kāmasena.
Then the great hero Abhaya shook his enemy, Nṛhari.
Having severed his bow, he approached and engaged in a sword-fight.
Deprived of his sword, Nṛhari turned away from the battle.
Abhaya, enraged and intent on fighting, spoke these words to him:
"You are indeed the nephew of Mātṛṣvasrīya and the son of Mahīrāja;
why do you wish to destroy the supreme dharma of the Kṣatriyas?
Having heard this, Nṛhari, seizing a mace in his wrath, [advanced].
He struck him on the head, and being slain, he went to heaven;
that portion of Kṛtavarman indeed dissolved back into Kṛtavarman.
And the powerful Saradana, having killed Madana who was born as a cowherd, departed.
Having again struck the enemy's force, he uttered a loud cry of victory;
that is to be known as the northern portion, and Madana is dissolved in the north.
Then Rūpaṇa, having arrived and caused a swoon, performed the crushing.
Reaching Punassaradaṇa once more, he engaged in a sword-fight.
The powerful Brahmānanda, having bound Tāraka with fury,
proceeded to the end of Mahīrāja and engaged in a bow-fight.
Then Nṛhara, who delighted in battle, having encountered Raṇajit, angrily struck the auspicious son of Mahīrāja with his own arrow.
He was indeed a portion of Duḥśāsana, and he died when they met in that encounter.
When his kinsman Nṛhari was slain, Mardana, intent on wrath,
struck Satyaki’s supreme portion with his own arrows;
but that hero, victorious in battle and born of Parimala, cut them down.

With his own crescent-headed arrow (bhallena), he struck off Mardana’s head from his body. When the heroic Mardana was slain, the powerful Saradana then struck that hero in the chest with his own crescent-headed arrow.
Having encountered great hardship, he who was born from the crushing of the conquerors in battle severed the head of his enemy from the body with his own sword.
When Tribandhu had been slain in the fight, Tāraka was overwhelmed with rage.
Standing upon his chariot, he struck the one standing on the enemy's chariot with arrows;
having cut down the opponent's arrow and likewise his bow,
Raṇajit struck Karṇāṃśa Tāraka in the heart with three shafts.
Overcome by indignation like a serpent struck by a staff,
he meditated upon the god Śaṅkara and again fixed an arrow washed with poison;
having aimed it and issued a threat, he struck the throat of his enemy.
By that arrow, Raṇajit abandoned his body and went to heaven. When that one of great heroism was slain, Brahmānanda was distressed;
out of fear of Mahīrāja, Brahmā placed the women at the forefront.
When the time of twilight had arrived on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādra,
he firmly bolted the door with sixty thousand troops,
entered his home, and sought refuge with Śāradā.
The powerful Mahīrāja, distressed by grief for his son,
made a terrible resolve in the hearing of all the kings:
"Just as the beautiful city named Śirīṣa has been rendered desolate by me," so shall it be with this world.
"Likewise, the entire Mahāvatī, along with Brahmānanda and the others—
all those of the Lunar dynasty— shall meet their destruction by my arrows.
Having spoken thus, the king indeed challenged Dhundhukāra.
"O dear one, come quickly with five hundred thousand troops!
Having heard this, Dhundhukāra went swiftly to the threshold,
stayed there for seven days, and then arrived at the battlefield.
Then the mighty Mahīrāja, accompanied by his eight hundred thousand [followers],
joined with Tāraka and advanced for battle.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter in the *Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, in the *Pratisarga Parvan*, within the section titled *Caturyuga Khaṇḍa*— also known as the *Kaliyugīya Itihāsa Samuccaya*.
Sūta said:
When the twenty-seventh year had arrived for that portion of Kṛṣṇa who is the source of all auspiciousness,
on the tenth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada, Malanā became overwhelmed with grief.
Distressed, she summoned her father-in-law and spoke these words:
"O you who belong to the region of Kacchapa and are born of the lineage of Gautama,
mount the horse Harināgara and go now to Kānyakubja."
Having summoned her son Āhlāda, who was accompanied by his younger brother and intent on doing what was pleasing to her,
she reflected again in her heart upon these words she had heard and spoke to the sorrowful Mālinī: "That Lord will not come."
Thinking that these words of King Parimala alone were so deeply distressing,
the virtuous Malanā wept upon hearing them;
she fell into a swoon on the ground, intent on giving up her life.
"Alas, O mighty-armed portion of Rāma! O handsome child, portion of Kṛṣṇa!
Where have you gone, along with Devakī, having abandoned me, unfortunate as I am?
Then Parimalā’s son, seeing the queen in such a state, [fainted].
Having consoled him in many ways, the powerful one went to the city of Kānyakubja.
The sages said:
"The Lord of Beings was described by you as the son of Parimala."
"O Romaharṣaṇa, tell us: who was this person, and what did he do?
Sūta said:
"I have already mentioned Pradyota, who resided in the city of Indraprastha."
O Sage, the father of Parimala was a minister of King Anaṅga. To him was born a daughter named Parimalā, who,
being born from a portion of Duḥśalā, was as delicate as Rambhā.
For the sake of that marriage, her father himself made preparations for a *svayaṃvara*.
Her son, the king of Kacchapa named Kamalāpati,
having married her according to the prescribed rites, joyfully departed for his own home.
From their union was born this son, a leader of men,
devoted to the science of archery, a hero skilled in sword-fighting;
having conquered by force the kings dwelling on the shores of the ocean, that valiant one became a ruler.
Having taken a sixth share as tribute, he presented himself before the kingdom of the Pitṛs.
Once, however, Mahīrāja, surrounded by his own army,
arrived at the land of Kaccha and presented himself for the purpose of collecting tribute.
A great battle took place between those two, the leader of men and the king;
at the end of a month, the one of the solar dynasty was defeated by Mahīrāja. Abandoning his kingdom along with his family, he arrived at Mahāvatī.
Then King Parimala gave him an auspicious village;
he established his residence there, which became renowned on earth by his own name.
That man from the Kacchapa country indeed departed at the command of Parimala.
Then that king of the earth, approved by his sovereign lord,
quickly summoned Cāmuṇḍa, who was accompanied by an army of a hundred thousand;
the king issued a command to him for the purpose of capturing [the enemy].
When he reached the banks of the Netravatī with an army of one hundred thousand,
that commander of the host besieged the supreme leader of men, a scion of the Solar dynasty.
Then, taking up his sword, that hero of mighty arms and self-controlled senses—
Having slain a hundred heroes there, he ascended the path of the sky;
he seized the crown from the head of the army commander as he stood upon his elephant.
Humiliated, that Cāmuṇḍa, with a bowed mind, spoke these words:
"You are my provider of livelihood, for you are indeed a Kṣatriya to a Brāhmaṇa.
O hero, give me your crown; live long and be happy.
Having heard this, he humbly gave him auspicious wealth.
Protected by Vāmana, the hero arrived at the city of Kuṭhāra;
there, exhausted by extreme fatigue, he beheld the shade of a banyan tree and slept fearlessly in that pleasant spot.
Then Vāmana, having learned the reason for that through his own messengers,
arrived there, covered the divine horses with garments, and took them away. When those divine horses had been taken, the Leader of Men awoke.
Having fallen into great anxiety, he wept profusely;
but upon seeing the mark of a horse's hoof and reaching Vāmana, he became fearless.
With a humble spirit, he spoke these words to the king born of the Gaura lineage:
For among Kṣatriyas, laughter is always a source of fear upon this earth.
You are a knower of royal policy; therefore, give me back my horse and be happy.
Otherwise, the portion of Kṛṣṇa will surely destroy you along with your city.
Having heard these words, Vāmana, born of a noble lineage,
being terrified and having made his decision, gave the golden whip,
adorned with various jewels, to Harināgara.
Out of greed, the king, who had sworn a false oath, did not give it up.
Then Parimala’s son, being frustrated, said to the monarch:
"O King, because of your greed for the goad, this fortress shall go to ruin."
Having spoken thus, the hero departed for the most excellent city of Kānyakubja.
Lakṣaṇa, seated upon his female elephant, spoke these words with pride:
"Who are you, O best of Kṣatriyas, who have arrived here fearlessly mounted on a horse?"
He said: "O Great King, beloved of those who seek refuge, I have been sent by the descendant of the Lunar dynasty and have arrived in your presence.
And the powerful Mahīrāja, along with his family, [has sent me] to the descendant of the Lunar dynasty."
"And he shall slay them with fierce weapons, approved by the lord of the earth.
Therefore, O Great King, go, go now together with your own forces and accompanied by Āhlāda and the others; restore the dead to life!"
Thus addressed by him, Lakṣaṇa bowed to Jayacandra and related everything exactly as the king of the earth had come.
Jayacandra, having heard that, summoned his father.
With a mind filled with rage, he spoke these words: "Listen, O descendant of Gautama's lineage!
The cruel King Parimala has abandoned me, his own sovereign, and has instead formed an alliance with my enemy, the Lord of Dehalī."
"Thinking him to be a dear relative, the protectors were abandoned by him;
he must now experience on earth the fruit of his own actions.
Having heard these words, the partial incarnation of Kṛṣṇa, with a humble mind, spoke.
"O King, Śuddhaparimala is the reciter for the lord of the earth;
therefore, having indeed abandoned you, he has come under the power of Bhūmirāja. Since you are truly a knower of all dharma, please forgive this offense."
"Give us your command, O Great King; we shall dwell in your presence.
Having heard these words, King Jayacandra said to the portion of Kṛṣṇa, "O hero, give me the price for my sustenance."
"Go quickly with your family; otherwise, you ought not to go.
Hearing this, the portion of Kṛṣṇa who deludes all beings laughed and said:
"The entire conquest of the quarters, which strikes fear into cowards, has already been accomplished by me."
"Therefore, O King, give me that which is to be given; accept this payment for my sustenance.
Thus addressed, the protector of the earth, abashed by the partial incarnation of Kṛṣṇa, commanded his army of seven hundred thousand great warriors.
Then indeed, the heroic Sakula, full of joy and endowed with auspicious marks,
stood before the king, paid his respects, and departed with delight.
Having reached the city of Kuṭhāra, he besieged the king's fortress.
Having realized this, King Vāmana joyfully gave him the whip.
Then the powerful Lakṣaṇa, placing the king— who was accompanied by ten thousand troops—
behind him, quickly proceeded to the excellent bank of the Yamunā.
Having crossed the waters of the Yamunā,
the hero Lakṣaṇa, who was exceedingly powerful, reached the field of Kalpa; placing King Gaṅgasiṃha, accompanied by sixty thousand [soldiers], at his head, he marched forth.
Having reached the delightful river Vetravatī with their forces,
those heroic Kṣatriyas, equipped with all weapons and missiles, took up residence there.
In the meantime, the hero Cāmuṇḍa, the commander of a hundred thousand troops, arrived.
He stationed the terrifying Śataghnīs, which destroy enemies;
and between those two positioned for battle with the Śataghnīs, there occurred a great conflict.
And at the end of the assault, the hero saw that army defeated.
The powerful Raktabīja, mounted upon an elephant, arrived swiftly and struck the army protected by Tālana with his arrows;
some heroes were slain in the battle, while others there were defeated.
Terrified by fear and oppressed by Cāmuṇḍa, they fled;
seeing his own army broken, Tālana, armed with an iron club,
struck the elephant with it, and Cāmuṇḍa fell to the ground.
The hero Lakṣmaṇa, intent on sword-fighting, defeated Tālajaṅgha, who was armed with a mace,
and then proceeded further as the destroyer of the enemy host. Having gone quickly, Lakṣmaṇa struck that foe with his own crescent-headed arrow.
He struck them with his two arms, and then they became many;
a thousand Raktabījas appeared, swords, spears, and double-edged blades in their hands, shouting "Stay! Stay! at the Kṣatriyas who were intoxicated with the pride of battle.
Those heroes, Āhlāda and the others, being distressed by the fear of Raktabīja,
all abandoned the battle and went to the mighty Brahmānanda.
Seeing them, Brahmānanda then went toward his own father.
O Sage, he related the account of Lakṣmaṇa’s arrival;
upon hearing it, King Parimala, overwhelmed with love and his voice choked with emotion,
approached Āhlāda and wept intensely in great distress.
Then Queen Devakī, with a sorrowful yet pleasant countenance, spoke to the king who was intent on her with love: "We are yours, devoted to you;
yet, abandoned by you, we shall wander among other kings."
"Forgive my wickedness, born from the ripening of the fruits of my previous births.
Having heard this, the king was filled with supreme joy and gladly bestowed his ministerial authority upon the portion of Rāma.
His own army of one hundred thousand was urged on by its commander;
then, at the end of five days, Mahīrāja arrived and,
emboldened by the strength of Cāmuṇḍa’s forces, besieged the entire city.
A terrifying great battle between the two lasted for exactly one month.
When the clear dawn had arrived, Lakṣasainyapa, a portion of Kṛṣṇa,
approached Cāmuṇḍā and dispatched a thousand of his own kinsmen.
And he severed the heads of those Cāmuṇḍas one by one. When their heads were cut off, they all became Lakṣavīras;
then that army, tormented by those Cāmuṇḍas, was thrown into utter confusion.
O Sage, at that time the portion of Kṛṣṇa, filled with wonder and terrified by fear,
praised the goddess Śāradā, the bestower of all auspiciousness.
The portion of Kṛṣṇa said:
Salutations to you, O Mother Śāradā, who dwells in the world of Brahmā!
By you this entire universe is pervaded, consisting of nothing but uninterrupted sound.
O you who assume the form of Cāmuṇḍā for the destruction of Raktabīja!
"Salutations to you, divine Cāmuṇḍā! Protect me, who have come to you for refuge.
Having heard this hymn, the Goddess, the giver of boons and the accomplisher of all things, approached his sword and indeed consumed Raktabīja with it.
When the enemy of Lakṣa had been reduced to ashes, Cāmuṇḍa came to the earth;
that portion of Kṛṣṇa bound him, and he went to the presence of Brahmānanda.
Hearing this, the King of the Earth, overcome with fear, arrived there.
Then the king spoke these words to King Parimala, who was compassionate and overwhelmed with affection: "Forgive my misdeed;
a great fear has come upon me at the word of the lord of the earth."
"From this day forward, O hero, my beloved quarreling has been abandoned;
you are now my kinsman, and we are indeed your servants.
Having heard this, Parimala spoke thus to the king:
"Go for refuge to the son of Ratnabhānu, renowned by the name Lakṣaṇa; he is a protector, a devotee of Viṣṇu, and supremely compassionate.
Having heard this, the powerful king of the earth, assuming the form of a brahmin, [proceeded].
He prostrated himself on the ground before Lakṣaṇa like a staff with all eight limbs.
Then the heroic Lakṣaṇa, having shown affection toward the king,
proceeded to Kānyakubja together with his seven hundred thousand troops.
When the month of Phālguna arrived, they all went to their respective homes. Balakhāni, remaining steadfast, performed the Śrāddha ceremony at Gayā;
then, having reached his own residence in the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra.
He fed a thousand Brāhmaṇas who were devoted to the Vedas.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Compendium of Histories of the Kali Age," in the Caturyuga-khaṇḍa (also known as the Pratisarga-parvan) of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
When his twenty-eighth year had arrived, during the most powerful portion of Kṛṣṇa,
on the full moon day of Kārttika, under the influence of the Moon, in the constellation Kṛttikā and the Vyatīpāta yoga,
Kṛṣṇāṃśa, accompanied by an army of ten thousand and joined by Svarṇavatī, [set forth].
With joy,
he went to the sacred Lotus Forest (Utpalāraṇya), frequented by the sage Vālmīki,
on the bank of the Gaṅgā— a supreme pillar of Brahma— to renounce his very marriage crown.
Having gone there, that pure-souled one, accompanied by Puṣpavatī,
gave a thousand cows to the Brahmins with a serene mind upon his bath.
In the meantime, those born of the Mleccha race arrived.
A most beautiful and exceedingly charming courtesan named Śobhā beheld the Supreme Person, Kṛṣṇa, who was supremely delightful;
she became instantly bewildered by the sight of Him and was overcome with agitation.
Beholding her unconscious, Kṛṣṇāṃśa, the deluder of all,
returned to his own abode, summoned the brāhmaṇas, and asked:
"By whom were the eighteen Purāṇas spoken, and what is their fruit?"
"Speak to me, O best of the wise, you who are devoted to the Vedas and the Shastras.
Having heard these pleasing words, the learned scholars, experts in the scriptures,
spoke these delightful words to the one who is a portion of Krishna and the source of all dharma.
The Purāṇa composed by Parāśara has Viṣṇu as its presiding deity;
the Skānda was composed by Śiva; the Pādma originated from the mouth of Brahmā;
the Bhāgavata was proclaimed by Śuka; and the Brāhma was indeed made by Brahmā.
The Gāruḍa was proclaimed by Hari; these six indeed arise from the quality of goodness (sattva).
The Matsya, Kūrma, Nṛsiṃha, Vāmana, and Śiva—these Purāṇas were indeed composed by Vyāsa under the inspiration of Vāyu.
O Hero, six Rājasa Purāṇas, consisting of the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa), are remembered on earth:
the Mārkaṇḍeya and the Vārāha, which was composed by Mārkaṇḍeya;
and the excellent Āgneya, which Aṅgiras brought forth.
Furthermore, in the auspicious Liṅgabhāṇḍa composed by Taṇḍi,
the future was beautifully described by Mahādeva for the sake of the world.
Six [Purāṇas] are considered to be Tāmasa by the wise, being devoted to the dharma of Śakti.

And among all the Purāṇas, the Bhāgavata is remembered as the most excellent. When the terrible Kali age had arrived upon the earth, a king named Vikrama came from Kailāsa to this world and summoned all the sages.
Then all those sages dwelling in the Naimiṣa forest urged Sūta to speak so that they might hear it;
for eighteen Upapurāṇas had already been proclaimed by Sūta.
Having heard these words, the portion of Kṛṣṇa who is devoted to righteousness,
having heard that most excellent Bhāgavata scripture on the seventh day,
gave gifts consisting of cows and gold to the Brahmins.
He fed a thousand Brahmins devoted to the Vedas;
at that time, however, a woman named Śobhā, intoxicated with pride, having assumed the form of a beggar, employed her magic power upon reaching the place where the portion of Kṛṣṇa was situated.
Having meditated upon the hero Mahāmada, the Piśāca servant of Rudra,
she brought forth a Māyā capable of turning everything into stone.
Seeing that Māyā arising from Śobhā, the goddess Svarṇavatī [reflected].
Having cut [the hair] and comforted the woman of beautiful limbs, that prostitute, overcome with grief, prepared to go to her own home;
meanwhile, she [the woman] beheld her husband’s exquisite and charming ornament,
set in a golden casket and valued at a hundred thousand pieces of wealth.

Having withdrawn [the people] through her illusory power, that rogue woman went to the land of Vāhlīka. Having arrived at Kalpakṣetra, she became deeply distressed upon learning that my passion had been stolen by a courtesan who was born from Netrasiṃha.
He spoke these words to Kṛṣṇāṃśa: "Go, go, O one of great strength!
Taking my ornaments, return quickly to me.
O hero, this pill was prepared by me; [take] it with your mouth."
"For the destruction of Dhūrtamāyā and for the sake of your welfare.
Having heard this and acting accordingly, the one who deludes all, an expansion of Kṛṣṇa,
arrived at Śūkarakṣetra and beheld the courtesan there.
That courtesan, seeing that hero who was like the god of love, again employed her magic and approached his side; then,
having become unsuccessful, she wept piteously and profusely.
Beholding her weeping, he, compassionate and clear-minded, took all his ornaments and spoke these words fearlessly:
"O noble lady, why do you weep? Tell me the truth without delay."
"My brother named Sahasra, as dear to me as my own life, has met his death along with five thousand dancers.
Therefore, O illustrious one, I weep; I have come to you for refuge."
Having spoken thus, that deceitful woman, devoted to her own purpose, used her magic to create corpses of outcastes and showed them to him;
then, weeping once more, she prepared to give up her life right there.
The compassionate portion of Kṛṣṇa spoke these piteous words to her:
"O beautiful one, tell me quickly, how will they bring you back to life? She replied, "O hero, there is an auspicious pill resting within your mouth."
"O hero, give it to me out of compassion; they will thus restore my life.
When addressed thus by her, the hero gave that wealth to her.
Then that cunning woman, being pleased, assumed the form of a parrot.
Taking Kṛṣṇāṃśa, who was confined in a cage, she, overwhelmed by passion,
arrived at the auspicious city of Sāraṭṭa in the Bāhlīka country;
having assumed a divine form, she herself dwelt in his house.
When midnight had arrived, she, afflicted by passion, embraced that portion of Kṛṣṇa who was skilled in dharma and appeared in human form.
Seeing her in such a state, that portion of Kṛṣṇa [addressed] the Mother of the World.
The wise one, with a humble mind, praised her mentally with the Rātrisūkta. Then she, becoming agitated, abandoned that excellent portion of Kṛṣṇa,
transformed it back into a parrot, and climbed the ciñciṇī tree once more.
Then the goddess Svarṇavatī, awakened by the illusory power of Viṣṇu (Viṣṇumāyā),
assumed the form of a female hawk and went there filled with joy;
she beheld the portion of Kṛṣṇa who had become a parrot, intent upon yoga.
In the meantime, the courtesan, having again assumed an auspicious form as a man who was a portion of Kṛṣṇa, spoke these words with a humble mind:
"O dear lord, beloved of my life, accept me, who am overwhelmed by desire."

"Protect me with the gift of pleasure; you are always a knower of dharma. Thus addressed, he said to her: "Listen, O beautiful one, I am established on the path of the noble and am devoted to the way of the Vedas."
He who does not approach his own auspicious, married wife during her fertile period is a sinner who goes to hell; this is remembered as leading to birth in the wombs of animals.
Therefore, the enjoyment of another's wife should be known as granting rebirth in hell.
Having heard this, she replied to the wise Viśvāmitra:
"O highly intelligent one, in the past Śṛṅgin also engaged in union with a courtesan; yet no one fell into hell because of that. Therefore, enjoy me, your beloved."
Furthermore, that portion of Kṛṣṇa said:
"By the power of my asceticism, my sin has been severed by those two sages; for at present, I am indeed incapable of sexual intercourse, especially as a woman constitutes but half the body of a man."
I am a noble man, and you are a courtesan who enjoys many pleasures.
The word *Ṛc* was born from her eastern mouth; it is the eternal *Ṛgveda*.
And the word born of yoga from her southern mouth became the *Yajus*.
Any word ending in a *taddhita* suffix, as well as that which is born from the western [Veda],
and those words which have become *chandas*— all these are dear to the Brāhmaṇas.
Furthermore, a word consisting of a single phoneme alone is traditionally held to be born from the Atharva.
Those words that arise from the fifth month which cause worldly existence—
all those should be known as belonging to Prakṛti, divided into four hundred thousand varieties.
Indeed, having abandoned those, he who is of pure soul is devoted to the four Vedas.
Having indeed abandoned the forest of worldly existence, he goes to the state that is free from affliction.
He should not speak the vulgar tongue even when his life-breaths have reached his throat;
nor, even while being tormented by elephants, should he go to a temple of non-Jinas.
Thus indeed were the words of the Smṛti recited by the Sage:
"How can I abandon this Dharma which bestows happiness upon all the worlds?
Having heard this, that prostitute, born from a portion of Mlecchā, [reflected].
The woman named Śobhanā, whose thighs were like plantain stalks, became greatly enraged;
having struck him with reeds and then turning him back into a parrot herself,
she indeed refused to give any food, even the fruit-diet intended for the parrot.
Then the goddess Svarṇavatī, having assumed a female form,
reduced that hero to the size of a mosquito and vanished right there;
then, assuming the form of a hawk, she prepared to depart from that region.
Having placed Maśaka upon his back, he went to Mayūranagara. The powerful Makaranda, however, seeing that daughter of Netrapāla named Svarṇavatī accompanied by a portion of Kṛṣṇa, [acted].
Having clasped her feet, he caused her to dwell in his own home. Śobhanā, having regained consciousness, approached the interior of the cage;
she did not see the beautiful parrot, and falling into a swoon, she collapsed upon the ground.
"What shall I do? Where shall I go without that supreme lover?"—having lamented thus in many ways, she went to the city of Madahīna.
There she found a Piśāca dwelling, who was skilled in the arts of illusion and intoxication.

Having worshipped Mahāmada, she prepared to renounce her own body. But Mahāmada, being well-pleased, went to the temple of Śiva and praised the Liṅga known as Marusthaleśvara in the language of the Ṛṣis.
Then the gracious Lord spoke these words to his servant:
"The hero, a portion of Kṛṣṇa who abides in noble dharma, has been carried off by Svarṇavatī.
Come with me toward the city of Mayūra."
Thus addressed by him, the Paiśāca, accompanied by five thousand actors and joined by Sahureṇa, departed quickly with her;
and Indula and Āhlāda were likewise awakened by the illusory power of Viṣṇu.
Endowed with three hundred thousand troops and accompanied by Devasiṃha,
he reached Mayūranagara and approached Makaranda.
At that time, however, the courtesan Śobhanā was there together with Sahura and his forces.
He manifested the Bhairavī illusion, which causes terror to all enemies;
a wind arose from every direction accompanied by great clouds,
and meteors fell in many ways, intent on raining down gravel.
Seeing that terrifying illusion pervading everything with darkness,
the powerful Makaranda himself arrived standing upon his chariot;
the one of great strength reduced that illusion to ashes with a Śani-arrow.
Having seized the rogue Sahura along with his forces, he brought him to his home.
Then, the beautiful woman employed the power of her desire;
many courtesans, skilled in song and dance, were present there.

All the Kṣatriyas were deluded; they fainted from the sight of the dance, and except for Devasiṃha, who was a portion of Kṛṣṇa, they fell into a state of stupor. At that time, the goddess Svarṇavatī, Kāmākṣī, remained intent on meditation.
Having raised them all up again and seized that beautiful [city],
he approached Mayūradhvaja and bound them with fetters.
But Mahāmada, having learned of this, became intent on meditation upon Rudra.
He performed the Śāmbarī illusion, which produced various kinds of creatures:
tigers, lions, boars, monkeys, gadflies, and men;
snakes, vultures, and likewise crows devoured him from all sides.
Then the goddess Svarṇavatī, intent on meditating upon Kāmākṣī,
created an illusion born of Smara that destroys that [enemy’s] illusion in battle.
From it were produced Tārkṣyas and mighty Śarabhas.
They devoured lions and other beasts, and slew them by the thousands.
When that army had fallen into utter woe and was fleeing in all directions,
the illusory maidservant Śobhanā became the servant of Svarṇavatī.
Together with those joyful dancers, he was overwhelmed by delight; their streams of blood flowed and spread across the earth.
And thus, O tiger among sages, the battle continued for four months.
When the month of Vaiśākha had arrived, those heroes returned home.
Thus has it been told to you, O Brahmin; what else do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Compendium of Histories of the Kali Age," in the Kaliyuga section of the Pratisarga-parvan, which is another name for the Caturyuga-khaṇḍa, within the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
The sages said:
O great sage, regarding that maiden named Kinnarī whom you mentioned—where was she born and how did she come to be? Please tell us all of that out of compassion.
Sūta said:
Formerly, in the region of Caitraratha, frequented by various people,
when the spring season had arrived, the dwellers of heaven used to sport there.
And Mañjughoṣā, a celestial courtesan, arrived at the place where Śuka was;
seeing that beautiful youth, she prepared herself to enchant him.
Overwhelmed by desire, she performed songs, dances, and amorous gestures.

Having joined his palms in reverence and bowed down, he again praised that sage. Then the venerable Śuka, having heard those auspicious verses of praise, with a heart full of grace, said to him, "Choose a boon."
Having heard those auspicious words, she spoke with a gentle voice:
"O Lord, you who are compassionate toward those who seek refuge, become my husband!
Having heard these words, he did as she requested and remained with her.
That tiger among sages, Śuka, who was skilled in higher knowledge, took his delight;
from those two, a son named Muni was born,
and that powerful youth performed austerities with great effort for twelve years.
Then Kubera, together with Rudra, joyfully gave him the daughter of Svarṇadeva as his wife; that sage,
with a delighted soul, took pleasure with her, and from them was born an excellent son.

A goddess renowned as Kinnarī, born on the heights of the Himalayas and endowed with beauty and youth, performed austerities. Then the Blessed Lord Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, became pleased.
He gave that lady of radiant countenance to the wise Makaranda.
Then the sage said to Śaṅkara, "O God of gods, salutations be unto you!
Grant a boon for my daughter that shall cause the supreme increase of the kingdom."
Having heard this, Śiva said: "Upon the earth, at the end of Guruṇḍa, in the Middle Country (Madhyadeśa), there shall be a kingdom that bestows happiness upon you;
after a duration of thirty years, it will then go to ruin."
Having heard this, that sage who dwells on Himatuṅga made his residence there together with Makaranda.
Thus it has been told to you, O Brahmin; now hear again this auspicious narrative.
When he reached twenty-nine years of age, the portion of Kṛṣṇa [the Buddha] became the cause for war;
perceiving that the city of Netrapāla was adorned with various minerals,
the Buddhist king Nyūnapati besieged that auspicious city.
The king, a lion among Buddhists endowed with great strength and accompanied by seven hundred thousand [troops],
waged war together with those joined by three hundred thousand forces.
A terrifying battle between the armies took place for seven days and nights.
Yogasiṃha, Bhogasiṃha,
and the mighty Vijaya slaughtered the enemy army protected by Bauddhasiṃha;
meanwhile, those from the region of Śyāmajāpaka arrived.
All the Buddhists were deceitful, yet they were honored and worshipped by the world.
Then, for one month, a great battle broke out between those two once again.
By the command of Netrapāla, all those who were portions of Kṛṣṇa and others arrived.
Kṛṣṇāṃśa was mounted upon a spotted deer, while the god [Brahmā] was seated on his own horse; Indula was on a fierce horse, and Maṇḍalīka was stationed upon an elephant;
and Gautama arrived, mounted upon a green elephant.
And Tālana arrived, stationed upon Siṃhinī;
Dhānyapāla, the oil-presser, was born from a portion of Yuyutsu;
and the powerful Lallasiṃha was born from a portion of Kuntibhoja.
Tāmbūlīyakajātīya departed with the permission of Lakṣaṇa;
then Netrasiṃha, surrounded by seven hundred thousand troops and protected by eight heroes, arrived for their destruction.
Terrified by fear, those Buddhists fled from the region in all directions;
having reached the land of China, they established a battlefield there.
Following that, they indeed proceeded toward Hūhānada.
When the month of Māgha arrived, the battle broke out once again;
a hundred thousand from the Śyāma country and likewise a hundred thousand reciters (jāpaka),
along with ten million from the land of China, stood ready for combat.

Kṛṣṇāṃśa was endowed with a hundred thousand troops; the god [Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa] was accompanied by a hundred thousand; Netrapāla was enriched by a hundred thousand and endowed with the enjoyment of yoga;
and Maṇḍalīka, along with Indula, was accompanied by a hundred thousand soldiers.
Dhyānapāla Lallasiṃha stood there accompanied by a hundred thousand troops;
Jananāyaka himself also stood there joined by a hundred thousand troops;
and Tālana, enriched with a hundred thousand soldiers, arrived for the battle.

There, O best of sages, a terrible battle took place between the Buddhists and the Āryakas for half a month, increasing the population of the realm of Yama. Seven hundred thousand Buddhists were slain, and two hundred thousand were born in the land of the Āryas.
Then, terrified by fear, they abandoned the battle and went home;
having fashioned an army of wood through the power of mechanical contrivances,
there were ten thousand elephants made of wood, each with a hero upon it.
One hundred thousand were mounted on horses, and thousands of wooden figures were intent on battle;
a thousand were mounted on buffaloes, a thousand rode upon the backs of boars,
a thousand were mounted on lions, and a thousand had swans as their vehicles.
Likewise, there were separate groups mounted upon crows, jackals, and vultures;
seven thousand camels accompanied by brave men, eager for battle;
and thus, humans with wooden armies numbering one hundred and twenty-five thousand.
Two hundred thousand [soldiers], well-protected by Kṛṣṇāṃśa and others, met their destruction;
then the army raised a cry of "Alas! and that host of the Āryas perished.
Seeing that wonderful and delightful spectacle, Jayanta, skilled in warfare, [advanced].
Taking up a fiery arrow, he discharged it at the wooden armies;
they were all reduced to ashes and perished right there. Three hundred thousand kṣatriyas remained, facing Jayanta, who was skilled in battle.
They raised shouts of victory there and praised him again and again.
Then the powerful Chinese Buddhists, having prepared twenty thousand iron figures mounted on horses, dispatched them.
The mighty Yogasiṃha, mounted upon an elephant and bearing a bow and arrows, [advanced].
Then he struck those heroes, whose knees were made of iron, upon their necks;
afflicted by the arrows of Yogasiṃha, five thousand of them died.
At that time, the heroic Bauddhasiṃha, having witnessed his prowess, [was amazed].
Having fashioned a lion out of iron, he crushed the Lion of Yoga;
by the fall of that iron lion, the hero met his death. Then the Lion of Enjoyment, mounted upon a horse, departed.
Having slain that lion with his own arrow, he indeed roared there.
Then, the tiger was incited there by the lion of the Buddha; and both Sahaya and Bhogasiṃha met their death by his very hand.
Seeing his two maternal uncles fallen under the power of death, the son of Svarṇavatī mounted his formidable horse and approached the Lion of the Buddhists;
he quickly took up an auspicious arrow named Sammohana.
Having deluded the enemy force accompanied by the Lion of the Buddhists,
and having bound those ten thousand kings including the Lion of the Buddhists,
he crushed the Kalayantra machine and approached Kṛṣṇā for peace.
Then, all of them, filled with joy, crushed [the inhabitants] and went to the city;
having forcibly plundered that palace, which was one yojana in extent and endowed with every prosperity, they all approached the king's fortress.
Then the lion of the Buddhists arrived and was released by Jayanta;
he joyfully gave his own daughter, named Padmaja, to Jayanta,
as well as ten crores of gold for his delight.
And all the assemblies of Buddhists there took an oath:
"We shall never go to the Noble Land for the sake of the kingdom.
Having said this and bowed to them, they quickly set out on their journey.
Accompanied by three hundred thousand, they indeed went to the house of Netrapāla.
The sages said:
"O Sūta, why was no living being made there by Indula?"
"O wise one, tell us about Supriyā, Yogasiṃha, and the others.
Sūta said:
"Indeed, some living beings have returned from the world of Yama to this earth."
Then, distressed, the god approached Mahendra.
"O King of the Gods, salutations to you, who brings pleasure to all the gods!
Jayanta, having reached the earth, himself revives those who are dead."
"Therefore, a violation of the boundaries of the world is seen upon the earth.
Having heard these words, Mahendra, through divine illusion,
brought forth the nectar from the mare's head and likewise restored her to the path leading to heaven.
He rejoiced together with the gods over his own son, Jayanta;
meanwhile, Indula, being sorrowful, worshipped Śāradā, the all-auspicious one,
according to the prescribed rites, and became intent on yoga and meditation.
Thus it has been told to you, O Brahmin; listen again to this auspicious narrative:
The powerful Netrapāla, who had many sons, was overcome with grief;
he gave ten crores of gold to them, all in equal shares.
He caused eight powerful ones to set out;
they, accompanied by an army of two hundred thousand, departed joyfully for their own homes.

Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter in the Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, in the Pratisarga Parvan, within the section titled Caturyuga Khaṇḍa, which is an anthology of histories pertaining to the Kali Yuga.
Sūta said: O Brahmin, when they were staying in the land of China, Lakṣaṇa— who was indeed a partial incarnation of Nakula— was summoned by King Kāmapāla.
"O illustrious Jayacandra, listen attentively to these words:
at the break of day on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, this very moment has arrived.
Therefore, the heroic Lakṣmaṇa shall surely encounter me alone."
"Having taken my daughter, he will go into your presence;
but when the mighty king of the earth learns that he is accompanied by an army, he will defeat him and seize him. Therefore, my words are appropriate."
Having reflected upon these words from that place, the king, with a clear mind,
summoned Lakṣaṇa— who was accompanied by a hundred heroes and seated upon a female elephant—
and dispatched him to the wise Kāmapāla.
Having stayed on the road for five days, O hero, he went to that house.
Then his brother-in-law, Padmākara, recognizing that Bhūmirāja had arrived based on his physical marks, summoned him and engaged him in battle.
Lakṣaṇa and Nakulāṃśa, seeing the enemy approaching,
gratified the mighty king of kings with their own arrows;
the powerful one, having rendered the king of the earth unconscious, slew five hundred [of his followers].
Having approached Kāmapāla and bowed to him, he took up residence there.
Then the king of the earth, rising and going toward Padmākara, spoke these words seeking his purpose: "Listen, friend, to my words."
"A great enemy with auspicious marks has come to your house;
if you deliver him bound, I shall make you my own body.
Having heard this, that greedy-souled man gave him the *hālāhala* poison.
Having bound that hero Lakṣmaṇa, they delivered him to the King of the Earth;
and having slain those hundreds of warriors, they ensured that no news of it reached anyone.
Upon learning this, the lotus-eyed woman was deeply distressed and lamented most bitterly.
She worshipped Caṇḍikā for the sake of her husband’s welfare.
Then that goddess, the bestower of boons and the source of all auspiciousness, being pleased,
consoled the lotus-eyed woman and approached Lakṣmaṇa.
In a dream, that goddess said to him: "Recite *hrīṃ phaṭ gheghe*;
by the power of this mantra, all obstacles shall perish.
Having understood this, the hero Lakṣaṇa recited that mantra.
When the month of Āṣāḍha had arrived, Kṛṣṇāṃśa and the others went home;
accompanied by those two, Tālana approached Kalyakubja.
The heroic Lakṣaṇa, the beloved of Jayacandra, was not seen.
Having understood the cause of that, they assumed bodies composed of yoga:
Dhānyapāla, Kāṃsyadhārī, Vīṇādhārī, Tālana, Lallasiṃha, and Mṛdaṅgāṅka; they indeed went to Mahāvatī.
Having gone to the assembly hall of Parimala, all those beings in the form of yogis, filled with joy, sang songs; they were all overcome by enchantment.
Then the king, being pleased, [offered] a pearl necklace from his own neck.
Out of affection, he gave two golden rings to Tāla and Nāga;
then they all, filled with joy, approached the portion of Kṛṣṇa.
And that portion of Kṛṣṇa, having recognized them, assumed a body composed of yoga.
Accompanied by Tālanāda and others, the hero went to Bindugadha;
having arrived in the midst of the marketplace and performed an auspicious rāsa festival,
they went to the house of Padmākara and danced there with joy.
In the meantime, all the women arrived there and repeatedly beheld the hero, a portion of Kṛṣṇa, surrounded by the music of flutes;
enchanted by his singing and rendered motionless, they bestowed wealth upon him.

Then the woman Padminī, endowed with all auspicious marks, recognizing him as a portion of Kṛṣṇa, wept for a long time in great distress. And after lamenting, she quickly said: "My husband was the powerful Lakṣmaṇa."
"I have been forcibly confined in prison by the heroic Mahīrāja;
I am a woman and you are a yogi—how will our purpose be accomplished?
Having heard this, the king quickly raised his arm.
Having comforted the lotus-like woman, they went toward the threshold;
having reached the palace gate, that portion of Kṛṣṇa danced.
The powerful King Mahī, pleased by his playful charm, [welcomed him].
"Tell me your desire, O portion of Kṛṣṇa; I shall grant you everything, O lord of yoga.
Hearing these words of the king, he laughed and said to him:
"O King, a prison made of iron, suitable for a monarch, is what I require."
"O crest-jewel of kings, show us truly your own [form] quickly!
Having heard this, that king, enchanted by the play of Kṛṣṇa,
showed them [the form] for a moment and then gave them wealth once more.
Then all those yogis, having reached Mahāvatī and bowed to King Parimala, explained the entire cause;
and by the king's command, Āhlāda prepared his own army.
Five hundred thousand from Mahāvati were stationed mounted on horses;
seven hundred thousand Tālana troops arrived after being summoned.
Thus, there were twelve hundred thousand Kṣatriyas, fierce in battle.
And they all arrived at the threshold, equipped with every kind of weapon.
In the meantime, the minister Cadrabhaṭṭa,
who was highly learned, skilled in the meaning of all the scriptures, and a worshiper of the Vaiṣṇava power, [arrived].
Having approached the great king, he spoke these words: "Listen, O Lord!
By the grace of the Goddess, I indeed witnessed a secret play there;
and therein Udaya, a portion of Kṛṣṇa, attained the state of the Full Brahman."
With a serene soul, he spoke these words: "Listen, O you who are the embodiment of goodness!
Today I shall go to the threshold of the house for the destruction of the lineage of Agni;
having slain the Kauravas and their factions, I shall establish Kali upon the earth."
"Having returned to your presence once more, I shall engage in secret dalliance with you.
Having spoken thus, that hero, mounted upon a drop (*bindu*), approached you.
Thus, O King, did I perceive through yogic sleep (*yoganidrā*) that he was a portion of Kṛṣṇa.
Having heard these words of his, the king was filled with wonder;
terrified by fear, he quickly summoned thousands of heroes,
gave them rewards, and spoke these words to them:
"Go quickly to King Padmākara, show him my marks,
and then return to me immediately and tell him the reason for this.
Having heard this, all those mighty warriors of the Vahni lineage [prepared to depart].
Having gone there and acted accordingly, they approached Mahīrāja;
and Bhagadatta, the leader of those thousands, spoke these words to Mahīrāja: "Hear that which was spoken by them, O King."
"O King, Padminī is my sister, an expert in secret sciences.
In the past, she perfectly propitiated the Lord, the Master of Sacrifice (Yajñapati).
He granted her a most delightful and supreme boon consisting of the power of invisibility."
"She will cause that beloved mark to disappear"—
hearing this, the king attained supreme joy.
In the meantime, the mighty ones headed by Kṛṣṇāṃśa arrived.
They blocked the entire threshold of the palace protected by the King of the Earth.
Then that King of the Earth, having taken many ornaments,
gave them to all with affection and, with a humble mind, spoke these words.
"The king named Lakṣaṇa is certainly not in my prison;
if he were in my city, your anger would be such as this.
Having said this, she showed him the house that was a portion of Kṛṣṇa.
Out of fear, the king had made a solemn oath to Mahādeva;
thereupon Udaya, considering the king's word to be true, became deeply distressed and arrived at the auspicious village of Bindugadha along with his own people.
Having heard of the arrival of Kṛṣṇāṃśa, the powerful Kāmapāla quickly took many offerings and went for refuge to Kṛṣṇāṃśa;
bowing down with palms joined in reverence, the timid one spoke these words.
"A lotus-like woman, endowed with all auspicious marks, was born to me;
not knowing where she has gone, we have been searching. I speak the truth, the absolute truth. Having heard these words, the partial incarnation of Kṛṣṇa, together with his own forces, [set out].
Having arrived at Kānyakubja, he said to Jayacandra:
"O King, I have ascertained in many ways that your brother's son, endowed with the marks of a lotus-woman (Padminī), is not in the house of Kāmapāla."
I do not know where the king, who is as dear to me as my own life on this earth, has gone.
O King, if I do not see you, I shall truly give up my life.
Alas, son of Ratnabhanu, devotee of Vishnu, bringer of auspiciousness!
"Having abandoned me, your own friend, in which direction have you gone?
Having spoken thus, he who is a portion of Kṛṣṇa and beloved of Vaiṣṇavas fell into a swoon.
Then the goddess Svarṇavatī, together with her maidservant Śobhā, [approached].
Assuming the form of a parrot and arriving there, she remained within her own body; then,
sent by her, a radiant splendor skilled in the illusions of the Mlecchas approached Jayacandra and assumed a divine form.
There she spoke these words: "Listen, O crest-jewel of kings!
Know me to be Māyāvinī, renowned by the name Śobhanā. It was I who indeed caused your husband and wife to be seized and taken away."
There I shall go, accompanied by Mahāmada;
and the hero Indula, the powerful deity Tālana,
and all those protected by a portion of Kṛṣṇa— we shall all go there, O lord of the earth.
Having spoken thus, the beautiful courtesan assumed a body composed of yoga,
mounted the great mada, the piśāca servant of Rudra,
and set out, placing at her front those of great strength who were disguised as yogins.
Āhlāda was indeed mounted upon an elephant, while Indula was mounted on Karāla; Tālana was seated upon a lioness, and Devasiṃha was in his chariot.
Kṛṣṇāṃśa, mounted upon Bindula, caused that horse to dance.
Capable of assuming any form at will and traveling a hundred yojanas,
those powerful men reached every region, house by house and person by person; yet,
though they searched for his physical marks, they did not find that king there.
Again, Śobhanā, accompanied by them, went to Mayūranagara;
searching for that king among the people there, she did not find him.
Then again, Śobhanā went to Innagaḍha village, among the crowds of people.

She sought for the auspicious marks but did not find them there. Having gone to the city of the Bāhlīkas accompanied by those [maidens], she, being beautiful, beheld that best of kings but saw no auspicious marks upon him; thus she remained distressed.
Returning once more to her own country, she went to Bāhlīka, a land inhabited by Mlecchas,
where she spoke there to the forest-dwelling lord Markaṭeśvara;
and having worshipped him, that courtesan became devoted to singing and dancing.
That god, having emerged from the midst of the earth, filled with joy and honored by the mlecchas, bowed down to the portion of Kṛṣṇa and said:
"I have been well-planted by Kālāgnirudra within a pit in the earth."
"Know me to be powerless; go, O hero, as you please.
Having heard this, Śobhā herself then became despondent.
Reaching Svarṇavatī once more, she told everything from the beginning.
When thirty years had passed and the bright fortnight of Caitra arrived during the portion of Kṛṣṇa,
Suvarṇāṅgī, having consoled them, worshipped Caṇḍikā;
she spent the nine nights without food or clothing.
At the end of the night, when darkness had fallen, the Mother of the World went and said:
"The woman named Padminī, who was indeed the beloved of Maṇideva,
has been born in the house of Kāmapāla, having been slighted during a sacrifice."
He is indeed remembered as Maṇideva, the commander-in-chief of Kubera;
for he was previously slain by Bhīmasena in battles with the Yakṣas. Then that lotus-born woman [approached] the God of gods, the Lord of Umā.
And being fasting, she praised her husband: "O Śaṅkara, grant [my wish]!
After a hundred years had passed, the god Mahādeva said to her: "Indeed, in the Kali age, during the time of Vikrama, near the twelfth century..."
Having obtained a portion of Nakula and enjoyed great happiness with him,
you will then cast off this lotus-scented body through separation from him;
and having regained your own husband, you shall return once more to Kailāsa.
Then the goddess Śāradā will bestow the beautiful city of Mahāvatī upon Rāṣṭrapāla; meanwhile, Maṇideva, your husband,
will be appointed by her to the earth, intent on the protection of the villages.
Having reached you, O Padminī, this woman will return to Kailāsa.
Therefore, O Svarṇavatī, go quickly to Kailāsa, the abode of the Guhyakas, and having reached Padminī there, awaken her and deliver my words.
Having heard this, Svarṇavatī went toward Padminī; having related the account before her, she, overcome with compassion,
reached the house of Kāmapāla and took up residence there.
Then Svarṇavatī also quickly arrived at Mahāvatī. When she had entered the house, King Parimala, filled with joy, read the auspicious letter written by Padminī.
Come with your army, O most powerful portion of Kṛṣṇa;
having conquered our kinsman Padmākara, quickly release my husband.
King Lakṣaṇa stands upon the earth, afflicted by the distress caused by Padmākara.
Knowing this, the portion of Kṛṣṇa, with an army of twelve hundred thousand,
besieged the entire city protected by Kāmapāla;
the powerful Kāmapāla, however, was joined by a force of three hundred thousand.
By his daughter's command, he indeed went to battle with Padmākara;
then a great battle took place between those two armies for the duration of a day and night, and the king’s army was defeated.
Having sought refuge with Padminī, her brother and father remained there;
she quickly ensured their victory as it was destined,
and for their sake, she gave them a leaf of invisibility.
Having become invisible there, the two of them, intoxicated with pride, struck ten thousand of the enemy's forces with their respective swords; then they [the enemies] were filled with amazement.
Tāla and the others, abandoning the battle, sought refuge with Kṛṣṇa and Aṇa.
Then Kṛṣṇāṃśa, also distressed, meditated upon Śivā, who pervades all;
having thereby attained divine vision, he fought with Kāmapāla, who was stationed in the sky,
as well as with King Padmākara.
Having bound [the horse] there, filled with joy and having attained auspicious marks, he became fearless;
having placed that goddess upon the swing, he went happily toward his own home.
Having indeed given those two, the husband and wife, to King Jayacandra—
Having seen Lakṣmaṇa and Padminī, Jayacandra then felt his purpose was fulfilled; and the powerful king, seeing his own wife and husband at home,
gave gifts to the twice-born and fully liberated the monarch.
"In the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, Kṛṣṇāṃśa came to his home.
Thus, O Brahmin, I have related to you the auspicious life-story of Kṛṣṇāṃśa;
I shall tell you further what was indeed seen through the power of yoga.

Thus ends the thirtieth chapter in the *Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, in the section on the secondary creation (*Pratisargaparvan*), within the sub-section titled the *Caturyugakhaṇḍa*, specifically the compendium of histories of the Kali Age.
Sūta said:
"Listen, O highly fortunate Brahmin, Candrabhaṭṭa himself then..."
The moon-like [prince] approached that great king who was seated in the assembly hall.
Beholding him arrived, the king, overcome with grief, spoke these pleasing words: "Listen, O lord, best of ministers."
"Great heroes such as Kṛṣṇāṃśa and others have brought fear to my village;
when will those terrible thorns of mine perish?
Having been addressed thus, that pure-souled one meditated upon Śivā, who pervades all.
He spoke these words to the king: "O crest-jewel of monarchs, Brahmānanda, born from a portion of Jiṣṇu, has arrived at Mahāvatī.
That most excellent one, accompanied by a portion of Kṛṣṇa, is ever devoted to her welfare."
"And when Malanāputra abandons his body and departs,
then all those portions of the gods from which he came shall likewise depart. To the minister who was speaking thus with such wisdom, the lord of the earth [replied]:
With a humble soul, he spoke these words: "A certain matter has been contemplated by me.
Having summoned the supreme king Brahmānanda—a great hero who was alone—the lord of the earth [has sent me] for the purpose of his second arrival."
"Having caused him to be killed by means of a stratagem, he will have accomplished his purpose.
When this was said, Mahīrāja, with a clear mind, spoke to the king:
"Listen to my words, O friend; go quickly to Mahāvatī."
Having approached Mālanā and awakened her himself,
he came into my presence and said, "Live long and be happy.
Having heard these words, the lord of the earth bowed to him.
At night, O best of sages, the fearless Malana spoke to her:
"O great queen, your daughter-in-law named Velā, who is beautiful,
endowed with youth, auspicious-faced, and worthy of her husband, has arrived."
Moreover, it has been heard by the high-souled king that Kujāti is a portion of Kṛṣṇa;
therefore, your daughter was not sent to your wise son.
Thus, taking my word to heart, perform what is pleasing to you.
Together with me, your son, the mighty Brahmānanda,
having reached the city on earth accompanied by my army,
will approach King Mahīrāja and swiftly obtain his wife.
"If she does not abandon her beloved at my command, she shall die.
Having heard this, the queen, deluded by divine illusion,
approached the king and [reported] her brother's excellent words.
Having heard everything, he related it all; and the king said this:
"The lord of the earth is a great rogue, intent on my destruction.
His news is not pleasing to me; a deception has been devised by him."
Having heard this, Malanā spoke these words to the king who was filled with anger: "O King, I am indeed like a kinsman to you.
Do as I say, O King; otherwise, I shall give up my life."
When she had spoken thus at night, King Parimala,
that son who was devoted to his mother, honored his mother’s command and, accompanied by his maternal uncle, bestowed the bliss of Brahman upon him.
Having reached Mātulagrāma during the night, he was filled with joy;
and when morning arrived, having set out for Harinagara,
he, deluded by the god, went alone toward the beautiful Dehalī.
When evening had arrived at the palace of Mahīrāja,
Agamā appeared, showing herself in a beautiful form with a divine body;
and upon seeing her, Agamā experienced supreme joy.
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, the fearless Brahmānanda beheld seven women with beautiful faces among his brothers-in-law:
three widows and four who were accompanied by their husbands.
Filled with joy, they spoke these words, which were like arrows of Brahmānanda:
"O illustrious Brahmānanda, listen attentively to our words.
Your wife is Kālī herself, who has taken the form of Velā in the guise of a quarrel."
"He has withdrawn his suitors, but we remain deeply distressed.
Let there be co-wifehood for her; O Manohara, accept us!
O hero, abandon those other suitors and become our husband with joy."
Having heard their words, the immensely powerful Brahmānanda spoke these sweet words, consistent with the Śruti and Smṛti:
"In former times, during the Satya Yuga, there was a woman who was most excellent and devoted to her husband."
In the Tretā age, women were middling; in the Dvāpara, they were inferior;
but in the Kali age, women are indeed base, enjoying the company of other men. Therefore, in the Kali age, the remarriage of widows is indeed forbidden.
Śubhā was proclaimed by Devala, and Asitā herself is mentioned in the Smṛti; Satī was declared to exist in the Kṛta age, while in Tretā she was one whose husband was smeared with ashes;
she was called Madhyamā in Dvāpara, and in Kali she is a virtuous widow.
"In the Kali age, it should be known that devotion to celibacy is the highest; there is no vow of fidelity for women.
Therefore, you three should enjoy pure happiness together with me. Having heard these pleasing words, those three widowed women—
Having fashioned ornaments and forms of exquisite beauty in every way,
and having attained the bliss of Brahman, they were intent on embracing one another.
Seeing them, the fearless son of Malanā spoke these words:
"I shall not accept you from now on—neither those husbands abandoned by you, nor those slain by my kinsman;
I speak the truth, the absolute truth.
Having heard these terrible words, which were yet tinged with irony, the women...
Having approached the great king, they wept, deeply afflicted by grief:
"O King, the lord of the shore is a rogue; he truly abandons his duty toward me.
Inflict punishment upon this rogue, or else I shall give up my life."
Having heard this, the king of the earth summoned Brahmānanda Mahābala and spoke these words: "You are the lowest of the royal lineage!
He who enjoys another man's wife goes to the abode of Yama."
"O beloved of your son, this very day you shall enter prison!
Hearing these terrible words, the mighty Brahmānanda cast aside his sword and rushed toward Mahīrāja.
Seeing this, the king, overcome with fear, approached Cāmuṇḍā;
having firmly closed the door, he took up residence there.
The sages said:
Tell us in detail the truth regarding how their marriages took place;
from where did they come, what were their portions, and how indeed were they perceived by you through yoga?
Sūta said:
O best of sages, in the land of Aṅga there was a king named Māyāvarman.
Having worshipped the power (Śakti) of darkness that deludes all beings,
he was granted by her an excellent armor that struck fear into all creatures.
Having taken her, that king set out upon the earth.
His wife, named Pramadā, gave birth to ten sons at the end of a year;
they were portions of the Kauravas, O illustrious one—now hear their names from me.
Matta, Pramatta, Unmatta, Sumatta, Durmada,
Durmukha, Durdhara, Bāhu, Suratha, and Viratha were their names in order;
they had a sister, a younger daughter, who was lovely-eyed and possessed of a beautiful name.
Seeing her truly beautiful form, with eyes rolling from intoxication,
the Daitya named Kitava fell into a state of infatuation;
approaching Māyāvarman with a humble mind, he spoke these words.
"If you give me your own daughter, for me who am afflicted by desire, then I shall accomplish all your purposes; of this there is no doubt.
Having heard this, the king then gave his daughter to him.

A gambler, dwelling in a cave, having approached the king’s palace at night while it was enveloped in terrible darkness, feasted there, overwhelmed by passion. But at dawn, having abandoned her, he retreated to the interior of the mountain cleft.
When Varmadeva’s son was born,
King Madātura summoned his domestic priest, provided him with a hundred thousand pieces of wealth,
and dispatched him to Mahīrāja; he then chose Tāraka as his son-in-law.
The powerful Mahīrāja, commander of sixteen lakhs of troops,
accompanied by a hundred kings,
arrived at the end of the month when the fifteenth part of the dark fortnight had arrived and [the king] was intent upon his vow.
And Tāraka brought many kings for the sake of the marriage. Seeing Tāraka accompanied by those kings, the powerful Māyāvarman spoke these words: "O King of Kings, listen to my speech."
There is a clever gambler named Kitava, who brings glory to the lineage of the Daityas.
By him my young daughter was tormented at night while shrouded in thick darkness;
and the princes who had gathered for the sake of my daughter were slain.
Devoured by that Daitya, they went to the abode of Yama;
and having plundered their wealth in many ways, he, intoxicated with pride, gave it all to my daughter. Therefore, you must slay that son of Diti.
Having heard this, the king of the earth, accompanied by his entire army,
summoned Kitava and engaged him in a great battle.
That deceitful Kitava, however, having conquered all those of great strength, [prevailed].
Having gathered Tāraka, he arrived at the cave.
Then Tāraka, distressed, meditated upon the supreme Śaṅkara;
by the grace of Mahādeva, he indeed became like stone and departed.
In the meantime, ten thousand Kṣatriyas residing in Mahāvatī, protected by the portions of Kṛṣṇa and others, arrived there.
Upon seeing them, Mahīrāja [confronted] the exceedingly powerful Balakhāni.
Afflicted by grief for his son, he spoke these words with affection:
"Tāraka has indeed been slain by that very same deceitful Diti-son.
If you will give me my son, I shall give you ten million pieces of gold."
Having heard this, those wise ones— the portion of Kṛṣṇa, Devasiṃhaka,
and the two sons of Vatsa— approached and forcibly restrained the gambler.
A battle ensued between them and him for a full day and night.
But Kitava, overcome with rage, having deluded Devasiṃhaka Kṛṣṇāṃśa and Balakhāni, roared again and again;
then the hero Sukhakhāni [confronted] the exceedingly powerful Kitava.
Having severed his own head with his sword, he approached the king;
those three having become happy and having praised the mine of happiness,
he gave that deceptive head, Tāraka, to the great king of the earth.
Then the princess, the queen, closed her eyes in blissful sleep.
Thereupon the lord of the earth arrived and, having awakened his lotus-eyed daughter with various words of persuasion, the king returned to the end of the earth.
The marriage of Tāraka with her took place joyfully.
Having received ten million gold pieces from the king, the exceedingly powerful Balakhāni departed for the auspicious city named Śirīṣa along with his kinsmen.
Sūta said:
In Gurjara there was a king named Mūlavarmā, who was possessed of great strength.
His daughter was Prabhāvatī, who was the youngest of ten brothers.
Bala, Prabala, Subala, Balavat, and Bali;
Sumūla, Mahābhūla, Durga, Bhīma, and Bhayaṅkara—
these were indeed the Yakṣas named Karabha, who were servants of King Lalla.
Beholding Prabhāvatī, he, overwhelmed by passion, lost his senses;
when five years had passed, that maiden was enjoyed by him.
Then Mūlavarmā summoned Mahīrāja along with his army.
With a humble soul, he spoke these words: "O King of Kings, do as I say;
I shall give my auspicious daughter Prabhāvatī to Nṛhari. Having said this, he summoned his son Nṛhari to his own palace.
And according to the Vedic injunctions, he gave his daughter to Nṛhari. Within the space of a fortnight, a Yakṣa named Karabha arrived there;
having defeated all the lords of the earth, he began to harass the royal couple.
Then the great king, distressed, summoned the two very powerful sons of Vatsa;
having spoken before them, the mighty and strong monarch wept.
The compassionate and heroic sons of Vatsa approached the one who had reached the end of his life.
Having gazed upon the camel, he vanished right there;
having bound the couple with a serpent-noose, he tormented them.
Having heard this, that portion of Kṛṣṇa [addressed] the camel, the servant of the Yakṣas.
Having bound them by the power of yoga alone, he released the couple;
having approached those two brothers and cut the serpent-noose with his sword,
the powerful one rejoiced and took ten million pieces of gold.
The king of Bhūmi, with a serene soul, went joyfully to Dehalī.
Sūta said:
And in Kaśmīra there was a king, renowned by the name Kaikaya.
He had ten sons and one daughter, Madanāvatī:
Kāma, Prakāma, Sakāma, Niṣkāma, Nirapatrapa,
Jaya, Vijaya, Jayanta, Jayavat, and Jaya.
That king, having summoned Bhūmirāja, spoke these words:
"Your son Saradana is indeed worthy to obtain my daughter;
let the Gandharva named Sukala take my daughter of auspicious countenance."
Having gathered [his forces] during the moonlit night, he indeed sports with her;
and having arrived on the full moon day, he who is dear to Citraratha is present today on the auspicious eighth day of the dark fortnight of Vaiśākha.
"O best of kings, carry out the execution; you ought to go to Dehalī.
Having heard this, the king of the earth, accompanied by an army of one hundred thousand, quickly took the couple and went to the city of Dehalī.

On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, when Sukhajātā was born, a valiant Gandharva named Sukala, out of wrath, besieged the city with ten thousand followers. Those heroes who had been born outside the city were intoxicated with pride.
Having swiftly killed them, Sukala indeed caused great sorrow to the king.
Terrified by fear, the lord of the earth meditated upon Śivā, who consists of all things;
the pure-souled king slept at night, and the Mother of the Universe became pleased.
Having awakened Kṛṣṇāṃśa and the others, he joined them;
then a great battle took place between them and the Gandharva on that day.
And the powerful Balakhāni fought with the excellent Śatagandharva.
At the end of three days, having gathered together, Sukhakhāni did the same;
then the enraged Sukala created a Gandharvī,
and those many Gandharvas indeed rushed forward along with them.
Then, all of them, terrified by fear, sought refuge in Rāma’s portion. Āhlāda, with a serene soul, praised Śāradā, the source of all auspiciousness, with the Divāsūkta; then Śivā appeared.
Having quickly bewildered the Gandharvas, Śāradā put them to flight;
and when the Gandharvas were defeated, Kṛṣṇāṃśa, the deluder of people,
approached Mahīrāja and took ten million pieces of gold.

And when the sixteenth year had arrived, during the portion belonging to Kṛṣṇa, while the worshipper of the Goddess was engaged in his rites, and when the month of Mārgaśīrṣa had begun, Mardana was married. Sūta said:
In the land of Puṇḍra, there was a mighty great king named Nāgavarman,
who was devoted to Takṣaka and righteous upon the surface of the earth.
His auspicious wife was Nāgavatī, the daughter of Takṣaka.
Born from the curse of her father, she became the daughter of the King of Kaliṅga;
he had ten sons and one daughter of auspicious countenance,
renowned by the name Suvelā, endowed with beauty and youth.
Having summoned his domestic priest, he dispatched him to Mahīrāja;
having gone there and spoken before him, [he said], "Mardana has been slain by me.
Upon hearing this, Mahīrāja, accompanied by an army of three hundred thousand, set out.
Having gone to the auspicious Nāgapura, she caused the auspicious rites to be performed.
Suvelā said to her father: "Give me the ornaments of the Nāgas;
for I shall perform my marriage, otherwise I shall give up my life."
Having heard this, Nāgavarman went into the presence of Mahīrāja and described Suvelā’s intention in detail.
Thus addressed, that King Mahīrāja was both amazed and deeply distressed.

He dispatched a letter to the place where Āhlāda and the others were stationed. Having learned this, Āhlāda, surrounded by five hundred heroes and accompanied by the sons of Kṛṣṇāṃśa, arrived there at the end of the day.
In the second watch of the night, there were swift horses capable of traveling a hundred yojanas;
their prowess reached a thousand yojanas by day and by night. These horses were born from a mere fraction [of his power], while the Vājins themselves were born directly from Hari.
A portion of Ratnāśva was Kapota, who became Haraṇībhava;
he who became the Gāyatra horse was the setter-in-motion of the wheel of time (Kālacakra).
From a portion of that [Gāyatra] was born Ravidatta, the Papīhaka.
That power of Hari, named Hariṇī, descended to the earth from a fraction of His portion;
she is the mine of happiness residing in the letter *pa*, the mine of strength residing in the letter *ba*,
the delight residing in the letter *ka*, and the digit of Hari residing in the bindu.
Having gone and bowed to Mahīrāja, they proceeded to the lofty throne.
That gracious Mahīrāja, with a humble mind, spoke these words:
"My three heroic sons have been married by you."
"O hero, marry Mardana in that very same way and be happy.
Having heard this, Āhlāda went to the excellent earth and the famous Rasātala, and fearlessly spoke to the Nāginī.
"For your husband Puṇḍarīka, O lady of auspicious countenance, is asleep.
Awaken him quickly, O Great Queen; have mercy on us, the serpents.
Thus addressed, she said to that hero, "And Puṇḍarīka is my husband."
"Filled with rage, that powerful one might even burn your body.
Hearing this, she laughed and said, "We have no fear of your husband.
Having spoken these words, she struck his tail with her two feet.
Then the king, possessed of great strength and valor,
awoke and produced a garland of flames from his own body.
Seeing that blazing poison, he meditated upon Sarvamangalā.
The powerful Puṇḍarīka, devoted to the worship of the Goddess and tranquil in soul, quickly gave that excellent serpent-ornament, complete with all its ornaments, for the delight of Nāgabhūṣaṇa.
Āhlāda, mounted upon his horse, gave [the bride] to the King of the Earth;
he performed the marriage according to the prescribed rites for weddings.
Having received ten million gold pieces from the king, he took them and departed quickly.
Mounted upon their horses, those five hundred heroes, all skilled in horsemanship, arrived at the house; they were all known to have come home together with their steeds. Sūta said:
In the Madra country, there was a very powerful lord of the Madras who worshipped the two best of gods, the physicians of heaven, for five years.
And by virtue of the boon granted by them, ten sons were born to him.
A daughter named Kāntimatī was born, endowed with beauty and youth.
The Lord of Madra summoned Mahīrāja, who was accompanied by an army of three hundred thousand, and according to the prescribed rites, gave his daughter to Sūryavarman.
Then Sūryavarman took his newly-wedded wife and,
the king of the earth, departed quickly for his own home with his forces.
Karvura, the powerful son of Vibhīṣaṇa, was a master of illusion.
A Rākṣasa arrived there and, seeing the auspicious Kāntimatī—
the daughter of the lord of the Madrakas, endowed with divine splendor—
he abducted her while they were looking on and went to the Sahya mountain range.
Then the King of the Earth, deeply distressed, lamented repeatedly and intensely;
having returned to his palace, he summoned a messenger with great haste and dispatched him as an emissary to Kṛṣṇa’s portion. Having arrived there, he described everything that had occurred.
Having learned this, those five hundred brave warriors, mounted on horses and surrounded by their followers, arrived at the Sahya mountain toward Karbura, the son of Kṛṣṇa;
and being fearless, he spoke these words: "Listen, O best of Rākṣasas!"
Vibhīṣaṇa is the king of devotees, and you are his beloved son;
therefore, you must not commit a sin that would bring ruin to your lineage.
It is known to you how Sītā was formerly abducted by Rāvaṇa.
Having heard this, he said: "Formerly, this beloved and dear daughter of a Gandharva was mine; she has come to the earth due to a sage's curse.
Therefore, because of separation from her, I have abandoned the great city of Laṅkā."
Having reached the kingdom of the Madrakas, out of fear of the Madraka king,
I did not carry off my beloved, though she was charming; having stayed there for many days,
that auspicious woman named Kāntimatī has today come under my power.
"Having defeated me, seize her quickly; we are always capable.
Hearing this, that portion of Kṛṣṇa engaged in a sword-fight.
Having defeated him in seven nights, he obtained the auspicious Kāntimatī.
Then, having reached Dehalī, he went as far as Mahīrāja;
the king gave ten million gold pieces to the high-souled Kṛṣṇāṃśa,
and that hero, together with his kinsmen, went to Pramadāvana.
Sūta said:
In the city named Paṭṭana, there was a powerful king named Pūrṇāmala;
he joyfully propitiated the Vasus for a period of five years.
Then those gods, being pleased, granted him an auspicious boon;
and by virtue of that granting of the boon, ten sons were born to the lord of the earth,
and a daughter named Vidyunmālā was born, endowed with beauty and youth.
Having summoned the mighty King Mahīrāja for the sake of that marriage,
he gave his daughter to his son along with seven hundred thousand troops.
Having obtained a beautiful wife, Bhīma, the son of Mahīrāja, [was filled with joy].
Having arrived home, he rejoiced upon the threshold together with them.
At that time, King Sahoda, residing in the land of the Piśācas,
was prepared for the sake of Vidyunmāla along with ten thousand Mlecchas.
At the command of the Daitya Bali, he arrived at the auspicious site of Kurukṣetra;
having pierced through the forms of the gods, he turned the water of the sacred ford red with their blood.
Then, the powerful one inscribed a letter for the righteous King Mahī.
Having heard that his own messenger had been dispatched by him, the king said this:
"You are the king of the Mlecchas, exerting yourself for the sake of Vidyunmāla; know me to be a marksman who hits by sound alone, the leader of the realm of thieves."
Having spoken thus, he arrived at Kurukṣetra with three hundred thousand [followers].
Between the two of them there occurred a great and terrifying battle for a day and a night.
When midnight had arrived in the month of Jyeṣṭha, which was filled with darkness,
Bali, accompanied by ten thousand Daityas,
emerged from Pātāla and swiftly struck down the king’s army, devouring them again and again.
Then the king, terrified with fear, sought refuge in Śāradā.
In the meantime, O Sage, the immensely powerful gods, headed by Kṛṣṇāṃśa,
arrived there on foot in a mere moment;
having slain thousands of Daityas, they approached the Daitya Bali.
Deśaja, Vatsaja, Vīra, and likewise Devasiṃha,
gratified the mighty king of the Daityas with their respective swords;
then the powerful king of the Daityas, Bali himself, became pleased.
"Choose a boon," he said to them; and having heard that, they spoke these words:
"Let those Daityas not come with you to the land of the Āryas;
rather, having always reached the land of the Mlecchas, devour those who follow the Mleccha dharma."
Having heard these terrible and unpleasant words,
Bali himself approached the portion of Kṛṣṇa who had arisen and praised him with a supreme voice.
Then the portion of Kṛṣṇa, being pleased and fearless, spoke these words.
"As long as I remain a dweller on earth, so long should you dwell in your home;
after that, having come to the earth, O sir, act as is appropriate.
Having heard those words, Sahoda, accompanied by Nīla, [departed].
He went again to the Paiśāca region and reached Rasātala;
then Bhūmirāja, with a gracious soul, gave him ten million gold pieces.
Mounted upon elephants, those five then departed for Mahāvatī.
Sūta said:
Vardhana, the son of Bhūmirāja, was the most excellent of all;
having reached the age of five years, he praised Śrīda with devotion.
And during the rainy season, the Blessed One bestowed every auspicious treasure;
by virtue of that entire wealth, the royal treasury became completely full on all sides with gold through the power of the King of Kings.
The maiden celebrated as Kinnarī was given by Kubera to that dear Vardhana;
thus, O sage, the entire account of the marriage has been told to you.
The great hero Dhundhukāra, accompanied by an army of one hundred thousand,
approached Brahmānanda and challenged him for battle when Kṛṣṇāṃśa had reached his thirty-first year and was exceedingly powerful.
Seeing the army approaching, Malanāputra remained alone;
fixing the Brahmāstra upon his bow, he incinerated half the host.
Those fifty thousand heroes, overcome with fear, fled in all directions.
Dhundhukāra, having abandoned the battle, approached Bhūmirāja.
Then Bhūmirāja, distressed and terrified on all sides,
summoned Mahīpati and Candrabhaṭṭa and spoke to them.
"How shall my victory come about? Consult quickly on all this!
Then the lord of the earth said, "Listen, O crest-jewel of kings!
Having assumed the female guise of the powerful Cāmuṇḍā..."
And perceiving the right time, entrust that swing to Brahmānanda.
Your four heroic sons, joined by Dhundhukāra,
being powerful, shall cause him to be slain through deceit and with their own weapons.
Having heard this, the king of the earth was delighted with divine bliss;
having acted accordingly, he gave the palanquin protected by the five heroes.
When evening had arrived on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha.
Velāvaṃśa and Cāmuṇḍa attained the bliss of Brahman;
having forcibly driven the trident into the belly of the enemy by means of a stratagem,
that powerful hero wept, and those heroes assembled there approached him.
Tāraka struck him in the heart with arrows, Sūryavarman with javelins, Bhīma with a mace, Vardhana then with a sword,
