and Dhundhukāra struck the enemy on the head with a broad-headed shaft.
Fainting and falling to the ground, the mighty Brahmānanda,
wounded by a great blow, took up his own sword there;
likewise, he [severed] the head of Bhīma from his body, as well as that of Vardhana.
Having likewise cut through the earth's center,
Tāraka, Dhundhukāra, and Cāmuṇḍa arrived;
then, abandoning that Brahman-bliss, they went as far as the King of the Earth.
When those sons were slain, the king of the earth, overcome by fear and deeply distressed,
went to the shore of the sea and wept profusely.
Hearing this, the Sea-goddess (Velā) then quickly ascended her swing.
He quickly attained the bliss of Brahman and beheld him in a swoon;
then, by the power of the shore through the nectar-like presence of Kaniṣṭhā,
he rose and saw the beautiful woman weeping.
"Who are you, whose beautiful daughter are you, that have approached me in battle? O noble lady, give me water; do this very pleasing favor.
Having heard this, Velā, filled with grief, then gave him water.
She spoke these words at night: "Listen, O son of Malanā!
I am Velā, the daughter of a lord of the earth, and I have come before you.
You, O wise one, are my husband, though you were deceived by those who acted under a disguise."
"Live your life, O Indra among kings, and enjoy pleasures with me.
Thus addressed, he said to her: "Now that the Kali age has arrived, death is better than living; therefore, do as I say."

"O lady of auspicious countenance, having mounted a golden elephant and traveled with me to beautiful sacred fords (tīrthas), I shall cast off this body. Having spoken thus, the two of them mounted it and first went to the vicinity of Kapila.
Having gone there and bathed according to the prescribed rites, they then proceeded joyfully;
having bathed separately for the sake of their sons and offered gifts,
they went to the southern end of the Setubandha and toward Dvārakā in the west.
Having bathed at the northern site of Badarī, they proceeded to the sacred fords;
having arrived at Gandhamādana, the exceedingly powerful Brahmānanda addressed these words to Velā on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada.
"O Queen, I shall cast off my body; slay Tāraka on the earth!
Hearing this, she said: "My lord, do as I say;
you must indeed go to Kurukṣetra together with me."
Remaining there with an equanimous mind, you should worship Sarvamangalā.
Having reached Mahāvatī and likewise having slain Tāraka, I shall indeed return once more to Dehalī and come into your presence.

Thus addressed, he replied, "So be it," and became intent upon meditation on Brahman. Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Compendium of Histories of the Kali Age," within the *Caturyugakhaṇḍa* (also known as the *Pratisargaparvan*) of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
And when the thirty-second year had arrived, belonging to the portion of Kṛṣṇa, a virtuous woman named Velā, who was the embodiment of Yoga and resided in Harinagara,
came to Mahāvatī and entered that assembly hall.
In the meantime, the mighty Kṛṣṇāṃśa and the others arrived;
having bowed to King Parimala, Velā spoke these words,
considering the lord of the earth to be dear to Kṛṣṇāṃśa, O King, yet disagreeable to her.
By you my husband, the mighty Brahmananda, was slain along with the powerful sons of Mahiraja, the rogues Tāraka and the others.
And Cāmuṇḍā was made to assume the guise of a woman by Dhundhukāra;
having approached their master, they went away under that deceptive pretext.
"The Lord is situated at Kurukṣetra, overcome by a great swoon;
therefore, you ought to go toward him along with me.
Having heard these most terrible words, they were all filled with grief.
"Fie on the king! Fie on Malana! By those two, our friend has been slain!
Having spoken thus, the mighty Kṛṣṇāṃśa and the others wept aloud and dispatched messengers to their respective kings.
Then, at that time, filled with wrath, he wrote a formidable letter,
dispatched it to King Mahīrāja, and returned to the palace of Malana.
King Mahīrāja, having read that letter according to the prescribed ritual, [acted accordingly].
Having understood all the causes of that situation and having heard it, the lord of the people fell into a state of anxiety and destroyed his peaceful sleep; then,
summoning all the kings, he became intent upon a terrible war.
Accompanied by twenty-four lakhs of heroic warriors and joined by the king,
the one born from a portion of Dhṛtarāṣṭra went swiftly to Kurukṣetra;
likewise, King Parimala, commander of sixteen lakhs of troops, [proceeded].
The descendant of Drupada went quickly with his own kinsmen along the shore;
he established his camps at the holy site of Syamantapañcaka,
where Brahmānanda remained, intent upon meditative absorption.
And all those mighty Kaurava factions, desiring victory, established various colorful camps on the banks of the Gaṅgā;
having performed their ritual baths at the full moon of Kārtika, they bestowed numerous gifts.
On the second day of the dark fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, they arrived at the battlefield.
King Laḥara, the sovereign of Viṣvaksena, arrived there,
as did the sixteen exceedingly powerful sons of the Kaurava faction.
In this world, they are humbly addressed by the names they bore in their previous births:
Dussaha, Duḥśala, Jalasaṃdha, Sama,
Saha, Vinda, Anuvinda, Subāhu, and Duṣpradharṣaṇa.
Durmarṣaṇa, Duṣkarṇa, Somakīrti, Anūdara,
Śala, Sattva, and Vivitsu— these should be known as the mighty ones in order.
The lord of Bāhlīka, a king born of the Tomara lineage, has also arrived.
And with an army of three hundred thousand, the king [departed] along with his seven sons—
Citropacitra, Citrākṣa, Cāru, Citra, Śarāsana,
Sulocana, and Savarṇa— who were the Kauravas in their previous birth.
Their portions were born in succession from the body of Abhinandana:
Mahānanda, Nanda, Parānanda, Upanandaka,
Sunanda, Surānanda, and Prananda, who was a portion of Kaurava.
The mighty King Māyāvarman of the Parihāra dynasty arrived accompanied by a hundred thousand troops and ten sons:
Durmada, Durvigāha, Nanda, and Vikaṭānana.
Citravarma, Suvarma, Sudurmocana,
Urnanabha, Sunabha, and Upananda were the Kauravas;
their portions were born in succession as the sons of the Lord of Anga.
Matta, Pramatta, Unmatta, Sumatta, Durmada,
Durmukha, Durdara, Vāyu, Suratha, and Viratha—
these kings of the Śuklavaṃśa dynasty, along with Mūlavarmā, arrived in succession.
Accompanied by an army of one hundred thousand and joined by his ten sons, the powerful Ayobāhu—
also known as Mahābāhu, Citrāṅga, Citrakuṇḍala,
Citrāyudha, Niṣaṅgī, Pāśī, and Vṛndāraka— set forth.
Dṛḍhavarman and Dṛḍhakṣatra were Kauravas in their previous birth; their portions were born upon the earth in the house of Mūlavarman as Bala,
Prabala, Subala, Balavat, and Bali.
With deep roots and great foundations, formidable, terrifying, and fearsome,
the Kaikaya king of the Lunar dynasty arrived at Kurukṣetra for the great battle, accompanied by a hundred thousand troops and ten sons.
O Kauravas, in his previous birth Jarāsandha was known as Bhīmavega, Bhīmabala, Balākī, Balavardhana,
Ugrāyudha, Daṇḍadhara, Dṛḍhasandha, and Mahīdhara,
as well as Satyasandha.
Their portions were born in the auspicious house of Kaikaya:
Kāma, Prakāma, Saṃkāma, Niṣkāma, Nirapatrapa,
Jaya, Vijaya, Jayanta, Jayavat, and Jaya.
Nāgavarman, the king of the Nāga lineage,
arrived accompanied by a hundred thousand troops and ten sons;
on this earth, the Kauravas bear the same name as he did in his previous birth.
By the command of Śiva, ten sons were born to the lord of the Puṇḍra country:
Ugraśravas, Ugrasena, Senānī, Duṣparāyaṇa,
Aparājita, Kuṇḍaśāyin, Viśālākṣa, and Durādhara.
Dṛḍhahasta and Suhasta were the sons of Nāgavarman;
Madrakeśa, born of the Tomara lineage,
arrived accompanied by a hundred thousand troops and joined by ten sons.
Vātavega, Suvarcas, Nāgadanta, Ugrayājaka,
Ādikeśu, Vakśī, Kavacī,
Krātha, Kuṇḍa, and Kuṇḍadhāra were the Kauravas in their previous birth.
Born on earth with that very name in the palace of Madrakeśa,
the king of Magadha— belonging to the Śārdūla lineage, endowed with a hundred thousand troops, pure and complete, and accompanied by ten sons— set forth.
Vīrabāhu, Bhīmaratha, Ugra the wielder of the bow,
Raudrakarman, Dṛḍharatha, Alolupa, Abhaya,
Anādhṛṣṭa, and Kuṇḍabhedin were the Kauravas in their previous birth.
In the house of Pūrṇāmala, there was a birth on earth by his name;
he was a lord of the earth named Maṅkaṇa, a Kinnara, in the land of Rūpa.
The wise know that the land of Rūpa lies beyond the borders of the land of Cīna.
A man of Kinnara lineage named Priyadarśana lived there;
then Maṅkaṇaka arrived, accompanied by ten thousand Kinnaras and his eight sons, at the place where all the kings were stationed.
Virāvī, Prathama, Pramāthī, Dīrgharomaka,
Dīrghabāhu, Mahābāhu, Vyūḍhoras, and Kanakadhvaja—
by these names they were known on earth among the Kinnaras according to the names they bore in their previous birth.
And the portion of Viraja who was born as the Kinnara named Maṅkaṇa—
Netrasiṃha arrived accompanied by a hundred thousand troops;
he is to be known as the portion of Śalya, born from the lineage of Śārdūla.
Then King Gajapati, accompanied by an army of one hundred thousand, arrived;
he was an incarnation of Śakuni who had left his own sons at home.
Mayūradhvaja likewise arrived, accompanied by an army of one hundred thousand.
Having left Makaranda at home, Virāṭāṃśa arrived;
Vīrasena also came there accompanied by Kāmasena,
along with Lakṣasena, who was born from a portion of Ugrasena.
And Lakṣaṇa arrived, accompanied by seven hundred thousand troops;
the king, having abandoned the woman Padminī with great difficulty,
as did Tālana, Dhānyapāla, and likewise Lallasiṃha.
The portions of Bhīma and Yuyutsu arrived in succession with Kuṃtibhoja; and the heroic Āhlāda also arrived, endowed with a portion of Kṛṣṇa,
accompanied by Jayanta and a powerful force of one hundred thousand troops.
The leader of the world himself, accompanied by ten thousand heroes,
arrived— born of the lineage of Gautama and being a portion of Bhagadatta—
as did other minor kings, numbering in the thousands, each separately.
Overwhelmed by intoxication, they marched toward Kurukṣetra, that supreme place.
King Mūlavarmā, accompanied by his son and leading a hundred-thousand-strong army,
joined the lord of Dehlī upon reaching King Parimala.
King Kaikaya himself, accompanied by his son and possessing an army of one hundred thousand,
arrived at King Parimala and stood ready for battle.
And the heroic King Netrasimha, the commander of a hundred thousand troops, [also arrived].

Mayūradhvaja, endowed with a hundred thousand [soldiers], was also there; Lakṣaṇa, of the lunar lineage; Vīrasena, enriched by a hundred thousand and accompanied by his son, who took the side of the mountain-king;
and Lakṣaṇa, enriched by seven hundred thousand, arrived for the purpose of battle.
Āhlāda, rich with one hundred thousand troops, was on the side of the Lunar dynasty;
King Candravaṃśa, accompanied by two hundred thousand, stood ready for battle.
Thus, Parimala stood in the fray, augmented by sixteen hundred thousand.
Lahara, the best of kings and commander of a hundred thousand troops, arrived with his son and approached Mahīrāja, standing ready for battle;
Abhinandana likewise, accompanied by his son and commanding a hundred thousand troops, [did the same].
King Māyāvarman arrived with his son, commander of a hundred thousand troops;
Nāgavarman arrived with his son, commander of a hundred thousand troops;
and the lord of the Madrakas, with his son and a hundred thousand troops, stood facing the battle.
Pūrṇāmala was there with his sons, as were Lakṣapa and Pakṣaga;
Maṅkaṇaka, known as Kinnara, was also stationed there with his sons. Then Gajarāja arrived, for Lakṣapa indeed went to Mahīrāja.
Dhundhukāra himself arrived, the lord of five hundred thousand [troops];
and Bhagadatta, the son of Kṛṣṇakumāra,
arrived accompanied by three hundred thousand forces, [joining] Mahīrāja, the lord of the earth.
And Balavāhana’s son, accompanied by ten cowherds,
arrived there; Aṅgada, the beloved of Devakī,
having approached Mahīrāja, stood ready for battle.
King Kaliṅga arrived, as did Trikoṇa;
likewise King Śrīpati and Śrītāra arrived.
Also present were Mukunda, Suketu, Ruhila, and Guhila.
Induvāra, the powerful Jayanta, and others of like sort—
all numbering ten thousand— presented themselves before Mahīrāja;
and on the side of Mahīrāja were a thousand minor kings.
Those kings, endowed with armies of a thousand, approached the lord of the earth;
and from among them, he dispatched two hundred monarchs along with their forces toward Dehali for the purpose of protecting his kingdom.
Thus that King Dehalī, possessing twenty-four lakhs [of troops],
engaged in battle for eighteen days, resulting in the total destruction of all.
O best of the Bhṛgus, listen to the delightful account of the war in great detail.
On the second day of the dark fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the mighty Mahīrāja,
free from fear, summoned King Lahara and spoke these words:
"You, along with your sons and your vast army, are protected by Dhundhukāra."
"O best of men, you ought to go to battle accompanied by Cāmuṇḍa.
Having heard this, Parimala went quickly to Kurukṣetra for the great war,
indeed [to face] Mayūradhvaja himself.
Having summoned him, he spoke these words: "Listen, O best of kings!
Protected by Jayanta, the lion among gods, who is a portion of Kṛṣṇa, you may indeed go to battle, accompanied by an army of one hundred thousand."
Having heard these words, Mayūradhvaja himself,
accompanied by an army of one hundred thousand, advanced against King Lahara;
and a great battle took place between those two armies on the field.
The army of Lakṣavīra in that battle is thus proclaimed:
one chariot, five hundred elephants,
five thousand horses, and ten times as many foot soldiers should be known to be present in that conflict.
These men are to be known as soldiers; now hear, O sir, about the commanders of the troops:
the lord of ten *pañcaras* is called a *pattipa*, and the lord of five horses is called a *gulmapa*.
And the lord of five elephants, named Gajādhipa—
this chariot-warrior is to be known as being with these [allies] in this terrible battle of the Kali age. Furthermore, forty messengers mounted on camels are recorded in his army.
There, among them, were thousands of *śataghnīs* each;
thirty-six of them indeed moved on foot. Listen to me regarding their functions:
ten were the providers of the balls (*golaka*), and ten were those who nourished them.
Among those, ten were indeed Ārdrakaras, three of whom were givers of fire;
three were to be known as Dṛṣṭikaras, each distinct from the others within these triads.
The remaining ones were Śūdras, devoted to the heroic duties of armies.
And thus, an army of a hundred thousand heroes was proclaimed to be there;
therein occurred a tumultuous battle between the two armies, fought according to the rules of righteousness on all sides, beginning from the morning until midday.
After that, for the duration of one watch, the army commanders arrived for battle;
following them, the great heroes, Dhundhukāra and the other forces,
stood at the front of the fray for one watch to fight.
Cāmuṇḍa fought with Kṛṣṇāṃśa, and Dhundhukāra with Indula;
indeed, the god Bhagadatta engaged in a supreme battle.
When evening arrived, all the heroes met their destruction.
There, the powerful Kṛṣṇāṃśa, having conquered Cāmuṇḍa, swiftly slew the sixteen sons of Lahirā within a mere ghaṭī. With a serene mind, he blew his conch shell and arrived at the end of Lakṣaṇā.
Cāmuṇḍa and Dhundhukāra, along with Bhagadatta joined by hundreds,
approached Mahīrāja and slept fearlessly during the night. Indula and Devasiṃha, accompanied by thousands, arrived there with joy.
Having approached King Parimala, the two then slept during the night.
When the morning of the third day had arrived, which was terrifying,
the powerful Mahīrāja summoned King Gajapati.
He spoke these words: "O King, you are well-protected by the three heroes and by your own hundred thousand troops; indeed, you ought to go to the battlefield.
Then King Parimala [addressed] King Netrasiṃha.
He ordered them to go forth to battle, well-protected by Kṛṣṇa, Aṃśa, and the others.
Then a great battle ensued between those two armies in succession;
horses met with horses and perished, and likewise elephants with elephants.
O best of sages, in the afternoon, the exceedingly powerful Netrasimha went with his chariots against the enemy chariots and with his *śataghnīs* against the *śataghnīs*,
and having approached the great elephant, the lord of elephants, he engaged him in battle.
Then, deprived of their chariots and with their bows shattered,
they both reached the ground sword in hand and waged a fierce battle.
Having slain one another, they both departed for the heavenly realm.
Having conquered Indulasta, Cāmuṇḍa, and likewise Dhundhuka,
as well as King Bhagadatta— who was a portion of Kṛṣṇa—
they returned to Lakṣmaṇa together with those five hundred remaining heroes.
Defeated, they all departed together with their thousands.
When morning had arrived, the mighty king of the earth,
free from fear, summoned Māyāvarman and spoke these words.
"O best of men, you, accompanied by ten heroic sons and an army of one hundred thousand,
ought to go for the destruction of all enemies.
Having heard this, that king caused musical instruments to be sounded and set forth.
Seeing that Māyāvarman had arrived, King Parimala summoned Jagannāyaka and, free from fear, spoke these words:
"You, together with ten thousand [soldiers] and accompanied by those three..."
"You ought to go forth to battle quickly; bring about my victory.
Having heard this, he went swiftly to the great encounter between the two armies.
O best of sages, a terrifying battle took place for the duration of a single watch (yāma).
Those ten thousand, well-protected by the portions of Kṛṣṇa and others, were slain;
and all those inhabitants of the Aṅga region blew their conchs.
In the meantime, the wise ones—the four beginning with the portion of Kṛṣṇa—[acted].
Within just one watch (yāma), they then struck down the enemy's army by the hundreds of thousands.
In the afternoon, the great king Māyāvarman, together with his sons,
approached the Lord of the World, Devasiṃha, who was a portion of Kṛṣṇa.

Then the very portion of Kṛṣṇa himself, the heroic Vīravara, the subduer who was born from a single digit of Madhusūdana, swiftly mounted his horse and quickly approached the King of Aṅga along with his ten sons. Thereupon, the King of Aṅga struck him on the head and on both sides with exactly three arrows.
The powerful king, unable to endure [the insult], was struck by the king's forces like a serpent swiftly killed by a staff;
then, leaping onto his horse, he approached that monarch standing in his chariot at the edge of the beautiful lotus-lake.
With the trampling of his horse, he deprived the king of his chariot, while the king himself took up a sword.
Having made his own sword the arrowhead for the shaft of his body, he spoke these words to Kṛṣṇāṃśa:
"The waves of your illusion have been brought forth for your destruction; you have conquered the foremost kings.
Only then will my fame quickly arise, and by slaying you, I shall become happy."
Having spoken thus to the great king, he severed his head with his own sword.
When King Aṅga was slain, his ten sons, who were partisans of the Kauravas, rushed toward him in battle;
but Indule, filled with wrath, then killed five of those who had arrived with his arrows.
There, the god slew both princes with a perfected broad-headed arrow;
Gautama himself having slain the eldest son, he struck down those two who were portions of Kṛṣṇa.
Blowing their conchs, those men of radiant faces went to their camps at the time of nightfall.

Exhausted, they slept during the night; rising at dawn and performing their respective duties, they went to the assembly hall, bowed to the king, and spoke these words: "Listen, O scion of the Lunar dynasty!
Who indeed shall be our commander-in-chief this very day? O King, command us so that we may guard him."
Having heard this, King Vīrasena, accompanied by Kāmasena and joined by his own forces, said:
"O heroes, before long he will wage war; therefore, protect yourselves well from the enemies.
Having bowed to the king, that Vīrasena marched forth for battle with hundreds of thousands of his own troops.
Then that powerful King Mahīrāja, the Tāpī, spoke to Nāgavarmā:
"O best of kings, go quickly to battle accompanied by your sons and a hundred thousand of your own troops;
for having slain the most terrible enemy, the great hero Vīrasena, in combat, O hero."
Having spoken thus to the king, the hero then indeed saluted him and blew his conch;
a great battle then swiftly took place between those two, both leaders of armies engaged in a tumultuous conflict.
Within the span of three watches (nine hours), all were slain, and having ascended their celestial chariots, they went to heaven.
When all his sons had been slain, Nāgavarman spoke to the Yādava king:
"You are without an army, and so am I; you are with your sons, and so am I.
Remembering the code of righteousness (*dharma*), engage in battle immediately. Thereupon, standing upon his chariot and seizing a mighty bow, [the king prepared for combat].
Having cut those arrows with their own arrows on the ground, those two foremost of kings became deprived of their chariots;
likewise, having severed sword with sword, they ascended celestial vehicles and indeed went to heaven.
Then that Kāmasena slew his enemy’s eight sons with his arrows.
Then the two elder brothers, filled with wrath and grasping their swords, rushed toward him;
with fierce speed, they struck off the head of the enemy, while Kāmasena remained as a mere headless trunk.
Having slain those two enemies, they then united and ascended celestial chariots to go to heaven.
Then, all those three, beginning with Cāmuṇḍaka, being filled with hatred, united together and obstructed the Lord of the World;
they struck him and his horse, the noble steed of Hari, with their harsh arrows.
Then that divine horse, spreading its wings, quickly went through the sky toward the enemy.
Having struck down the elephant of Puṃdhūkāra and crushed the elephant of Cāmuṇḍaka,
and having pulverized Bhagadatta’s chariot upon the ground, he swiftly ascended into the sky.
Blowing his conch shell, the Leader of the World approached a portion of Kṛṣṇa and recounted the events.
Having passed the night, the leaders of the world and the others rose at dawn and went to the battlefield.
Then Mahīrāja, along with Aśukārī and the Kinnara king Kaṇaka together with his son, said:
"O King, listen; these very powerful enemies of mine are the Kinnaras."
"O slayers of powerful enemies, quickly destroy these men in battle along with the gods!
Having spoken thus, King Maṅkaṇaka departed with his son and ten thousand troops.
Seeing that he had arrived there, the king commanded his own warriors.
Manoratha, the leader of the world, having seized Tālana,
and Jayanta, stationed at Karāla, having taken up his bow, proceeded with speed;
and Rūpaṇa, situated upon a Papīhaka bird, went forth accompanied by a portion of Kṛṣṇa.
Lallasiṃha, mounted upon an elephant in rut, and Dhānyapāla, having ascended his horse,
destroyed the formidable army of Kinnaras on all sides with secret daggers.
As the three-thousand-strong host was being destroyed, that lord of the Kinnaras advanced with speed.
Having meditated upon Kubera, he took up his bow and became subtle, moving through the sky;
remaining invisible, he let out a terrible roar and struck everyone with his harsh arrows.
While all the heroes were lamenting, Jayanta quickly went against the enemy.

Having meditated upon Maheṃdra and bound Kaṇaka, he approached Kṛṣṇāṃśa and bowed at his feet. Then, hearing that their own lord Kaṇaka had been bound amidst an army of thousands of enemies, they raised a terrible outcry and besieged everyone; the Māyāvins then unleashed the Guhyaka weapon.
Thus, for seven days and nights, the battle continued on all sides with them;
when those seven great heroes were exhausted and all their [opponents] had been slain, they fell asleep.
Then Kaṇaka, having meditated upon Kubera and obtained a boon, quickly severed his bonds.
Rising up at midnight, he engaged in battle with seven heroes who were asleep;
having conquered those six by the power of his boon, he then fought a duel with Induleva alone.
Having slain them both as they wandered upon the earth, sword in hand and intoxicated by the horrors of war, he then moved on.
Accompanied by the gods at their side and being praised by the best of the deities, the two went to heaven.
Then, when the clear morning had dawned, that portion of Rāma—
endowed with noble lineage and surrounded by all his attendants— wailed and lamented, O Lord of Sages, being tormented by his sinful fates.

He mounted his elephant Pañcaśabda and swiftly advanced with an army of three hundred thousand. Hearing this, Mahīrāja cried out, "Go this very day and join me! and together with five hundred thousand powerful and heroic warriors, he quickly hemmed in the enemy's army.
As they roared at one another for the sake of battle, a most terrible combat quickly ensued;
within the span of three watches, all those on both sides, though they were powerful, were slain.
Then Mahīrāja indeed arrived, accompanied by his retinue, taking up his bow.
Then Dhundhukāra approached Lakṣaṇa, the fierce hero, who was stationed upon his chariot;
at that time, Udaya, the son of King Bhīṣmaka, went toward Bhagadatta and Cāmuṇḍaka.
Mounted upon an elephant that produced fivefold sounds, he indeed proceeded swiftly to the king.
Then the king, grasping a swift, formidable, and terrifying bow,
spoke these words to the fierce, intoxicated elephant given by Śiva, the destroyer of joy:
"O foremost of intoxicated lordly elephants, O hero, O you bestowed by Śiva, grant me victory!"
"That king is a ruler of the earth, intoxicated by war, and an incarnation of Rāma known as Āhlāda.
Therefore, O elephant, protect me quickly from that immensely powerful Kālarasmi, the hero.
Being addressed thus, the elephant spoke these words to the king: "O King, listen at once to my speech!"
"As long as I indeed bear this body and life, may you remain a source of fear to your enemies.
To the intoxicated elephant who had spoken thus, Pañcaśabda then,
with his own four tusks, tore open the mouth of his enemy and roared terribly, O Mahendra-datta.
And that elephant Rudradatta, intoxicated and filled with rage, rushed swiftly toward the lordly elephant;
he dug his feet into his enemy, struck him with his frontal globes, and prodded him with the staff of his trunk.
Then, amidst the fivefold sounds, that king of elephants quickly fell into a swoon before the monarch.
Having inflicted a wound upon his own body with a javelin and slain the fierce lord of elephants with his sword,
that crusher of enemies went on foot to where Indula, the wielder of the formidable bow, was stationed.
He then approached his son and his wife, who was lamenting for him, and raised her up.
Then the two elephants, though intoxicated, cast off their swoon and once again engaged in combat.
Lakṣmaṇa, having severed the enemy's arrows with his excellent sword, fixed his own Vaiṣṇava weapon upon his bow after consulting with Sumantreya,
and incinerated the elephant Dhundhukāra.

When that chief kinsman was slain, King Sabhūmi, seizing his bow and standing there in a most terrifying position, struck Lakṣaṇa with a fierce arrow. He fainted; then the Sun rose over the Śukla clans, and indeed Bhagadatta [arose] as well.
Having fainted, he departed quickly to where the peerless hero Lakṣaṇa stood. Beholding him filled with fear, the king swiftly fled from Raktabīja.
Then Raktabīja, having conquered Sudeva who was joined by a portion of Kṛṣṇa, departed.

Having quickly rendered him unconscious with an arrow, and having again rendered the god unconscious, the swift-acting Lakṣmaṇa then went there, intent on binding him. Fixing the Vaiṣṇava weapon upon his bow, he discharged it at Raktabīja.
Then that powerful son of a vassal, having abandoned the battle and quickly observed the twilight,
departed in fear accompanied by his own men to where the kings stood in anger;
and having sighted the enemy, the son of Ratnabhanu, joined by his followers, likewise went toward the camps.
Having heard of his own victory, that king of the Lunar dynasty fell asleep along with them;
and at dawn, that king of the Lunar dynasty, seeing the descendant of Śukla, spoke to the king:
"O Mūlavarmā of the Gurjara country, together with your sons..."
"Accompanied by an army of one hundred thousand, you should indeed proceed," he said;
thus addressed,
that powerful king named Pūrṇāmala arrived at the battlefield at the command of Mahīrāja.

Accompanied by ten sons and joined by a hundred thousand troops in battle, a great conflict ensued between those two for the duration of two watches. When all of them, including the kings and their powerful sons, had been slain, [the survivors fled].
Having engaged in battle anonymously, they both went to the realm of Yama.
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, at dawn when the sun was bright,
Kaikaya, accompanied by an army of one hundred thousand and joined by his compassionate son, [arrived].
Having been summoned by the challenge of the signs,
the king of the Madrakas, accompanied by ten sons and a hundred thousand troops, arrived at that terrifying battlefield where the combat was taking place.
At the end of the day, all those kṣatriyas were slain by one another in battle.
Again, at the clear dawn, the mighty Bhagadatta,
joined by an army of three hundred thousand, roared at the head of the fray.
Seeing him, the heroic Lakṣaṇa, joined by an army of three hundred thousand,
raised a tumultuous and terrible fray with his own forces.
Then, in the afternoon, all the soldiers of both kings were slain.

Enraged himself, Bhagadatta, standing upon his chariot, advanced against Lakṣaṇa. Having mounted his chariot, Lakṣaṇa, having pierced the king who was the enemy of his father with three arrows, struck him with a broad-headed shaft.
Then Bhagadatta, enraged, deprived him of his chariot;
and Lakṣaṇa, sword in hand, having slain that fierce and angry enemy’s horses as well as his charioteer, approached Bhagadatta himself.
Having crushed that hide and cut away the armor produced from it,
the powerful Lakṣaṇa divided Bhagadatta’s son into three pieces at twilight. When he had been slain, Lakṣaṇa was filled with haste.
Alone, he reached the camp and stood atop an elephant.
When Bhagadatta had been slain, that king, overwhelmed with rage,
[summoned] all his own kings together with Cāmuṇḍa.
On the day he set out on his journey, he dispatched them for battle:
Aṅgada, Kaliṅga, Trikoṇa, Śrīpati,
Śrītāra, Mukunda, Ruhila, and Guhila.
Those nine kings, including Suketu, endowed with the strength of ninety thousand troops,
played musical instruments during that great festival of battle.
Seeing them along with their own kings, the heroic Lakṣaṇa—
Having thus arrayed his enemies with their weapons, he went forth to battle;
and King Rudravarman, regarding Aṅgada as an adversary, fought alongside him with ten thousand brave warriors.
Kālīvarmā, together with ten thousand [soldiers], marched against Kaliṅga; Vīrasiṃha, together with ten thousand, marched against Trikoṇa.
Then his younger brother, Pravīra, along with ten thousand, [advanced] against Śrīpati.
King Sūryadhara, a hero endowed with ten thousand [soldiers] and powerful in battle,
having encountered King Śrītāra, engaged him in a great war.
Accompanied by ten thousand Vāmanas, he then marched against Mukunda.
The powerful Gaṅgasiṃha went toward Mahila accompanied by his followers;
Lallasiṃha went toward Guhila along with his own men.
Then, three thousand kings, each with an additional thousand, set out individually.
Three hundred minor kings arrived,
and having fought a terrifying battle, they were all slain by one another.
Then Cāmuṇḍa, seeing all those kings dead, [acted].
Having reached the end of his life-span, Lakṣaṇa indeed engaged in a great battle;
yet, knowing that Raktabīja was esteemed by the Brāhmaṇas,
he did not discharge the Vaiṣṇava weapon at him, though he was afflicted by him.
When evening had arrived, Lakṣaṇa, mounted upon an elephant,
reached the camp alone and approached King Cāmuṇḍa.
And on the morning of the second day, Kṛṣṇāṃśa, accompanied by the gods, [arrived].
Accompanied by ten thousand heroes,
Tāraka, together with Cāmuṇḍā and joined by a force of two hundred thousand,
arrived at the battlefield along with two hundred kings, ready for combat.

Placing all the kings at their front, those two exceedingly powerful heroes, accompanied by their armies, stood behind them in battle; there a great conflict ensued. Within the span of a single watch (yāma), those two heroes slew all the lords of the earth.
Having likewise slain hundreds of thousands of troops, the two stood there exhausted by fatigue;
then the rogue Cāmuṇḍa and Tāraka arrived, seeking an opportunity for attack. And with those two who were overcome by weariness, they engaged in an equal battle.
A great battle took place among them for only three watches of the night;
then, as evening arrived, the valiant portion of Kṛṣṇa, being unarmed,
rendered his enemy unconscious with a blow of his palm.
In the meantime, the heroic Tāraka, having slain the horse Manoratha— the lion among gods— then blew his conch shell. From that sound, the mighty Cāmuṇḍa abandoned his swoon.
Having swiftly severed the head from the body of Kṛṣṇāṃśa and grasping the heads of those two, he approached Mahīrāja.
Upon seeing them, Mahīrāja was filled with supreme joy.
Having given gifts to the twice-born, he held a great festival.
At that time, a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose within Lakṣaṇa’s army.
Hearing their clamor and learning that those two had been slain, the king [acted].
Then Brahmānanda, having abandoned his swoon, said to Velā:
"O beloved, go quickly to the battlefield mounted upon the elephant of Hari;
assuming my auspicious form, slay Tāraka without delay."
Having heard this, Velā, accompanied by Rāmāṃśa and joined by a thousand Śūras, went to the field of battle. Having heard it, the heroic Lakṣaṇa, together with Tālana, [also set out].
Accompanied by ten thousand troops, Tāraka, the exceedingly powerful one, approached Mahīrāja; and on the morning of the third day,
regarding him as the bliss of Brahman, he engaged in a great battle.
And Raktabīja Cāmuṇḍa, a portion of Rāma who was exceedingly powerful,
engaged in a fierce battle during that encounter of heroes;
within a single watch (yāma), the portion of Rāma slew his great elephant.
Having likewise cut those weapons asunder, he engaged in a wrestling match.
Then, when the evening had arrived after only three watches of the night,
he crushed the slayer of his brother, and that hero died.
Then Velā, having severed the weapons of the exceedingly powerful great enemy Tāraka with her own sword, struck off his head from his body;
and that daughter of Drupada, the goddess, having prepared a funeral pyre according to the prescribed rite, [performed the cremation].

Having paid homage to the bliss of Brahman, she ascended onto his funeral pyre. Along with her husband, that pure woman, by the command of her father-in-law, joyfully recounted the story of their seven births and then entered the flames.
And having placed her husband Indula, who was exceedingly powerful,
upon that funeral pyre, she cremated her own body along with him.
At night, King Parimala, endowed with auspicious marks, [remained there].
Having approached the King of Mahī, he waged a great war;
then the remaining mighty forces of three hundred thousand, who had survived the slaughter,
stood ready to fight together with those remaining from his own side, numbering three hundred thousand.
Dhānyapāla killed a hundred kings, Lakṣaṇa likewise a hundred, and Tālana a hundred kings; having slain them, he approached the king. Then Mahīrāja, distressed, meditated upon Rudra Maheśvara.
When midnight had arrived, he joined with those who remained after the slaughter;
mounting an elephant alone, he went toward that most terrifying place.
Having slain King Parimala with an arrow bestowed by Rudra, he departed.
Having likewise slain Dhānyapāla and the exceedingly powerful Tālana,
he reached Lakṣaṇānta and engaged in a great battle;
by means of the terrible weapons of Mahīrāja, all the troops were brought to destruction.
Lakṣaṇa aimed the Raudra missile at Mahīrāja;
then the heroic Lakṣaṇa aimed the Vaiṣṇava missile.
By that missile, Mahīrāja’s arrow was destroyed.
By the power of that weapon, the king experienced great agony;
having meditated upon Rudra Mahādeva and abandoned his Vaiṣṇava lore,
the lord of the earth severed his own head from his body with his own arrow.

Then the female elephant, enraged, went to fight the most terrifying bull-elephant; having fought for a moment, she ascended to heaven. And when the time of dawn arrived, Malanā [approached] her excellent husband.

Having placed him upon that pyre, he cremated his own body. Then Devakī, having offered clarified butter and other substances along with the *tāla* and other musical instruments, cremated her own body, which was pure and possessed of most excellent marks.
When the pure dawn had appeared on the fourth day, a Tuesday,
having likewise offered oblations and performed the *tilāñjali* for them,
he meditated upon the Goddess who consists of all things and remained himself steadfast.
In the meantime, Kali, accompanied by his wife,
arrived there having obtained his desired fruit, and praised [the deity] with gentle words.
Kali said:
Salutations to the Great Delight, the bestower of all bliss;
to the Lord of Yoga, the pure one, who dwells in Mahāvatī.
O mighty-armed one, you are a portion of Rāma, intent upon my protection.
Having arrived at one time, the burden of the earth was removed by you;
having slain those five thousand kings of the lineage of Agni, who were endowed with the power of asceticism, as well as numerous minor princes.
Seated in the midst of yoga, salutations to that Great Soul!
O Hero, six million soldiers of theirs have been slain by you in succession.
O highly fortunate one, choose a boon, whatever resides in your mind.
Having heard these words, that Āhlāda spoke fearlessly:
"O Lord, you must establish my fame among every person;
furthermore, O Sir, listen, I shall perform an incomparable task for you."
And Mahīrāja, the righteous soul devoted to the worship of Śiva, said:
"My two eyes must be made pure by you, yet appearing blue in form;
for Nīla is always dear to you, and likewise, he is dear to me."
"O Lord, you who bring suffering to the gods and increase the joy of the Daityas"—
having spoken thus, that portion of Rāma mounted his elephant with speed and,
approaching Mahīrāja, engaged him in a great battle.
Rudradatta’s elephant quickly approached Pañcaśabda; having mounted Padmadanta, they fought with one another. Having thus struck each other down, both elephants ascended to heaven.
Then, overcome by fear, the king abandoned that terrifying battle and fled with great speed; thereupon, the powerful portion of Rāma pursued him and swiftly seized the lord of the earth by his hair.
Because of that [act], he placed a great sapphire given by Kali upon his eyes;
from that time forward, Śambhu, considering the king to be impure despite being dear to him, abandoned him and went to his abode on Kailāsa, the dwelling place of the Guhyakas.
Āhlāda, together with Kali, went to an excellent plantain grove on Mount Gandhamādana and quickly entered into a state of yogic union.
Seeing that portion of Rāma in such a state, Kali was filled with joy.
Having approached the side of Bali, he described everything in detail.
That very Bali, the king of the Daityas, having set forth with tens of thousands of followers and arrived at the Gauradeśa, spoke to Uḍḍīna.
"Go, O hero, with your forces at night while protected by me;
having slain King Mahīrāja Vidyunmāla, seize him, my friend!
Having heard these words of his, sixteen years passed by.
With an army of one hundred and fifty thousand, he marched toward Kurukṣetra;
having conquered the daughter of Mahīrāja, summoned Mahāvatī,
and dispatched the lord of Mahī, he plundered her wealth.
That king exerted himself for the sake of the Liṅga in that ocean of fame;
however, not having attained it, the king then departed for his own home.
Having performed one hundred thousand Caṇḍīs, he attained supreme bliss.
Having heard that, Jayacandra, overcome with grief for his son,
became a mendicant who abstained from food and died; having fought a terrifying battle with Uḍḍīna, that king went to the city of heaven.
In just seven days and nights, he fell under the power of the Mleccha king;
though slain with great effort, Mahīrāja did not die at all. Then the Mleccha, leaping up together with him, placed him in confinement.
There, at the king’s command, Candrabhaṭṭa struck Jyotirūpa with a sharp-edged arrow (kṣurapra) and indeed cremated him in fire; meanwhile,
that Mleccha took Vidyunmālā along with much wealth.
Having left his own servant there, he arrived by means of a miraculous flight out of curiosity.

Thus ends the thirty-second chapter in the *Kaliyugīyetihāsasamuccaya* (Compendium of Histories of the Kali Age), which is an alternative title for the *Caturyugakhaṇḍa* within the *Pratisargaparvan* of the glorious *Bhaviṣyamahāpurāṇa*.
Thus, the third section is completed.
Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
Victorious is Śrī Rādhāvallabha.
Vedavyāsa said:

Thus, at the end of the Dvāpara twilight, the narrative of the lineages of the Sun and the Moon was described by Sūta; that has been recounted by me to you. Furthermore, having gone to Viśālā, it was composed by Vaitāla.
The Sūta will recount that compendium of histories;
all of that has been told by me, which bestows merit upon the most excellent of men.
Furthermore, there shall be a recitation by King Vikrama.
Having reached the Naimiṣa forest, he will indeed cause the story to be heard;
those very eighteen Purāṇas which were repeated [in the past],
as well as the Upapurāṇas, shall exist in the Kali age.
And of those Upapurāṇas, the twelfth chapter is the most excellent;
it is declared to be the very essence, a compendium of histories,
which has been joyfully narrated by me to you, O Hṛṣīkeśa.
At the conclusion of the Vikrama-narrative, there was an incarnation of Hari by a portion (kalā);
that indeed was the Śakti-incarnation of Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa upon the earth.
The venerable Sūta, residing in the Naimiṣa forest, [related] its story.
He will indeed cause eighty-eight thousand sages to hear that which has been joyfully narrated by me to you, O best of the senses (Hṛṣīkeśa). Furthermore,
Śaunaka and the others, having performed their ritual acts such as bathing and so forth, [will listen].
The inhabitants of the Naimiṣa forest shall go to the side of the Sūta;
O sir, listen to that which was spoken by the Sūta when questioned by them.
The sages said:

O Blessed One, we have heard the life-story of Kṛṣṇa as narrated by you. Now I wish to hear, in due order, the lineage of those kings born from the four fires; for our curiosity regarding this is indeed great.
"He is said to be present during three ages; how then was he born in the Kali age?
Sūta said:
"O best of sages, I shall answer your excellent question."
Listen now in detail to the history of the kings of the Agnivaṃśa lineage.
King Pramara established himself in the southern direction;
for that Pramara, Ambā constructed a divine and auspicious city.
The powerful king, devoted to the Sāmaveda, made his residence there;
he ruled for six years, and from him was born Mahāmanas. Devāpi ruled for three years and became his son.
The kingdom was made equal to that of his father, and thus he became a messenger of the gods.
O Sage, hear the reason why the kingdom was made equal to that of his father:
when that mighty Buddhist king, Aśoka, had been slain.
Kali, intent on meditation, propitiated the Sun with austerity;
at the end of five years, the Sun,
pleased by his devotion, joyfully bestowed upon Kali a person named Śaka.
Then, being pleased with the high-souled Śaka, Kali,
his mind filled with joy, affectionately gave him the city of Taittira. There, the mighty one subdued the cowherds and the bands of robbers.
Having repeatedly exerted himself for the destruction of the noble land, he slew the kings with his arrows; therefore, they were short-lived.
And King Gandharvasena, the powerful son of Devadūta, [was likewise slain].
Having established his rule for fifty years, he returned once more for the sake of asceticism.
Then, by the command of Śiva, his son Vikrama became king;
having ruled for a hundred years, he subsequently became a devotee of the gods.
The kingdom was ruled by the wicked Śakas for ten years and then fell into ruin;
Śālivāhana himself, the son of one devoted to the gods,
conquered the Śakas, ruled for sixty years, and then departed for heaven.
Śālihotra, his son, having ruled for fifty years,
then attained the heavenly world; his son was Śālivardhana,
who ruled a kingdom equal to that of his father and subsequently became the slayer of the Śakas.
Suhotra became the son who ruled the kingdom equal to his father; from him was born Havirhotra, who likewise ruled the kingdom equal to his father;
from him was born Indrapāla, who likewise ruled the kingdom equal to his father.
Having made the city Indrāvatī, he ruled his kingdom there.
His son, named Mālyavān, established a kingdom equal to that of his father;
having made the city Mālyavatī, he attained a status equal to his father's.
Thereupon, a great drought occurred lasting for four years.
Then, afflicted by hunger, the king prepared dog-dung mixed with grain— an act otherwise held in contempt—
and offered it to the Śālagrāma stone within his palace.
Then the Blessed One, being pleased, took up the words uttered from the sky and granted him a boon; listen to it, O best of sages:
"O best of kings, as many kings as shall exist in your lineage,"
There shall be no drought in your excellent kingdom for so long.
Mālyavanta had a son named Śambhudatta, who was dear to Hara;
having ruled the kingdom equal to his father, he then became Bhaumarāja.
The kingdom was governed like that of his father, and thus he became Vatsarāja;
the kingdom was governed like that of his father, and thus he became Bhojarāja;
the kingdom was governed like that of his father, and thus he became Śambhudatta.
He ruled a kingdom that was diminished by ten [provinces], equal to that of the father of King Bhoja.
Then Bindupāla became the son of Śambhudatta;
having established the kingdom of Bindukhaṇḍa, he lived in happiness.
O sage, that knower of the Vedas ruled the kingdom equal to his father;
from him was born Rājapāla, the son of Bindupāla,
who likewise governed the kingdom as his father had done, and from him was born Mahīnara.
Having ruled a kingdom equal to his father's, Somavarman became king; having ruled a kingdom equal to his father's, his son Kāmavarman became king;
and thereafter Bhūmipāla ruled a kingdom equal to his father's.
Bhūsarastena excavated a city and established a splendid one there;
he ruled a kingdom equal to that of his father, and thus became Raṅgapāla.
King Bhūmipāla, however, having conquered numerous monarchs, [ruled].
Thereafter, he became renowned on the earth by the name Vīrasiṃha;
having consecrated Raṅgapāla in his own kingdom, he departed for the forest.
Having performed austerities, he ascended to heaven through the grace of the God of gods.

Then Kalpasiṃha was born from Raṅgapāla, the best of kings; for that childless monarch established him in a position equal to his own father. Once, he went joyfully to the waters of the Jāhnavī for the purpose of bathing.
Having bestowed gifts upon the twice-born, he attained Kalpakṣetra;
and beholding that holy land as well as the desolate site,
he joyfully caused a city to be built there.
It became famous on earth by the name of Kalāpanagara.
He established his kingdom there, and from him Gaṅgasiṃha was born.
Having lived for ninety years, he went to war without having any offspring.
Having abandoned his life-breaths at Kurukṣetra, he attained the heavenly world;
O Brahmin, the auspicious lineage of Pramara came to its end.
Thereafter, those Kṣatriyas who remained in that lineage [followed].
O Brahmin, from that [union] among women there arose a mixture of castes;
all of them, adopting the livelihood of Vaiśyas, became like Mlecchas upon the earth.
Thus, O Brahmin, has the lineage of the southern king been described to you.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the Pramara Dynasty," in the *Kaliyuga-itihāsa-samuccaya*, which is another name for the *Caturyuga-khaṇḍa* within the *Pratisarga-parvan* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
Vayohāni was the ruler who established his own domain in the Middle Country (*Madhyadeśa*).

Having taken it, he settled Ajamera, which was fashioned by Brahmā. Because it is the abode (mā) of the unborn (aja) Brahmā and because Lakṣmī (ramā) has gone there, that beautiful city is remembered as Ajamera, the unborn.
He ruled the kingdom for ten years; his son was Tomara.
He worshipped Maheśvara for one year with offerings from various kings.
Being pleased, Śiva gave him the city of Indraprastha.
And those born in his lineage are known as the Tomara Kṣatriyas.
The younger brother of Tomara was the auspicious Cayahānisuta,
who was named Sāmaladeva and became renowned on the earth for his humility.
Mahādeva then reigned for seven years; thereafter Ajaya became king and ruled a kingdom equal to that of his father. Then Vīrasiṃha became king and ruled a kingdom equal to that of his father.
He ruled for fifty years, after which Bindusura became king;
that high-souled one ruled for half his father’s duration in the Middle Country (Madhyadesha). From him was born a pair of sons: Vira and Virihataka.
In accordance with Vedic injunctions, his father joyfully bestowed his own kingdom, situated within the Madhyadeśa region, upon his heroic son Vikrama.
Māṇikya became his son, who ruled a kingdom equal to that of his father.
Mahāsiṃha ruled for fifty years;
thereafter Candragupta ruled, equal to his father's reign. His son, Pratāpavān, ruled for half as long as his father.
Mohana became his son and ruled the kingdom equal to his father;
he ruled for thirty years, after which Śvetarāya became king.
He too ruled a kingdom equal to his father, after which Nāgavāha became king.
Having ruled a kingdom equal to his father’s, Lohadhāra was born;
having ruled a kingdom equal to his father’s, Vīrasiṃha was born;
having ruled a kingdom equal to his father’s, Vibudha became his son.
Candrarāja then ruled for fifty years;
he administered the kingdom equal to his father, after which Harihara became king. Vasantasena, his son, likewise ruled the kingdom equal to his father.
Having ruled a kingdom equal to his father’s, Balāṅga became his son;
having ruled a kingdom equal to his father’s, Pramatha became his son;
and having ruled a kingdom equal to his father’s, Aṅgarāja was born thereafter.
Viśāla was his son, and he ruled the kingdom equal to his father;
from him came Śārṅgadeva, who likewise ruled the kingdom equal to his father;
and from him arose Mantradeva, who also ruled the kingdom equal to his father.
Having made his kingdom equal to that of his father, Jayasiṃha then arose;
all the noble lands were conquered by that great-souled one,
and with their wealth, he caused a sacrifice to be performed that yields abundant fruit.
Then indeed, a son named Ānandadeva was born, who possessed a beautiful countenance.
The wise Jayasiṃha ruled the kingdom for fifty years,
and his son likewise ruled over the earth for a period equal to that of his father.
Someśvara was his son, a truly great hero.
Anaṅgapāla’s son married Kīrtimālinī, the eldest [daughter],
according to the prescribed rites, and begot sons upon her.
Dhundhukāra was indeed the eldest, residing in the kingdom of Mathurā;
the middle son, named Kumāra, occupied his father’s position;
and the powerful third son, Mahīrāja, became the lord of Dehalī.
Having fallen under the power of King Sahoddīna, he met his death;
and having eclipsed the lineage of Capahāni, he went to heaven.
In his dynasty, however, there were kings whose wives were possessed by Piśācas.
Having been enjoyed by the Mlecchas, they became a mixture of castes;
they were neither truly Āryas nor truly Mlecchas—namely the Jaṭṭas, who by birth are Mehanas.
The Mehanas are known to be of Mleccha origin, while the Jaṭṭas are considered to be of Ārya nature.
"And those remaining Kṣatriyas who were scattered here and there, having lost their power.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Pramara Lineage," in the *Kaliyuga Itihāsa Samuccaya* within the *Pratisarga Parvan* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:

I shall proclaim the lineage of Śukla; listen, O best of Brahmins, from the beginning. When Kṛṣṇa himself, having abandoned his own station as Brahmā on earth, departed for the divine and beautiful Vṛndāvana, at that time—
Knowing the arrival of the Kali age, the barbarians (mlecchas) remained in the middle of the island;
indeed, the various men dwelling on those islands, who were devoted to the Vedas,
became corrupted by Kali in the guise of friendship.
O best of sages,
from this day forward, the time of the onset of the Kali age has indeed begun;
for sixty thousand years he ruled the kingdom of the island-continent.
That Kali, devoted to the worship of the Sun, arrived together with the Mlecchas;
thereafter, Kali came to the land of Bhārata along with the Mlecchas,
having seen that land of Bhārata protected by the world-protectors.
Terrified and filled with haste, that Kali, who brings glory to the Gandharvas,
propitiated the Sun and became absorbed in meditative concentration.
Then, at the end of a hundred years, the Sun, being well-pleased, arrived.
Having heated the world with his rays, he caused a great rain to fall.
O best of sages, four thousand and four hundred years have passed; from this day forward, let us converse.
Then the land of Bhārata-varṣa became fully established on all sides;
indeed, the world was filled by that Yavana named Nyūha.
When the Kali age of a thousand years had arrived, Mahendra himself, the king of the gods, [appeared].
He sent Kāśyapa to the most excellent Brahmāvarta;
there, Devaśakti, the noble lady of Āryāvatī, joyfully accepted his hand.
Having begotten ten sons, that twice-born man returned to Miśra.
Having joyfully subdued ten thousand Mlecchas born in the land of Miśra,
he returned to his own country and made them his disciples;
and when the seven cities had perished, [he established] the most excellent Brahmāvarta.
He lived there in the region between the Sarasvatī and the Dṛṣadvatī rivers.
Having summoned his son Śukla, the best of the twice-born whose wealth was asceticism,
and having instructed him regarding Mount Raivataka, he himself went once more to perform penance.
That righteous king, who followed the dharma of Manu, caused his nine sons as well as his disciples to hear the eternal dharma of Manu.
Śukla, too, having approached Raivata, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss—
He propitiated Vāsudeva, the Lord of the World, through his ascetic penance. Then the powerful Lord, the leader of the Dvārakā folk, being pleased,
took that Brahmin by the hand and went to the edge of the ocean.
He showed him Dvārakā, endowed with divine splendor.
When two thousand years had passed and a little more had elapsed, O best of the Bhṛgus,
that Śukla departed for Mount Arbuda by way of the fire-gate.
Having defeated the Buddhists along with the twice-born and his other three kinsmen,
he indeed caused Dvārakā to be built through the grace of Hari.
Dwelling there joyfully, the king became intent on meditation upon Kṛṣṇa.
In the western region of Bhāratavarṣa, he established his rule for ten years;
by the grace of Nārāyaṇa, Viṣvaksena became his son.
Jayasena then ruled the kingdom for twenty years.
Viṣeṇa ruled for thirty years, and his son [Kṛta] ruled for fifty years; Mithuna was his son, and [his sons were] Pramoda and Modasiṃha. Vikrama gave his own daughter to him.
Viṣeṇa, out of affection, gave his excellent kingdom to his son;
his son Siṃdhuvarmā established a kingdom equal to that of his father,
having abandoned that paternal station on the banks of the Sindhu.
Consequently, the region became famous on earth by the name Sindhudeśa. King Siṃdhuvārman ruled the kingdom equal to his father;
his son was Siṃhudvīpa, who likewise maintained the position equal to his father.
Śrīpati, his son, having obtained Kācchapī as his queen— a woman born of the Gautama lineage— went to the region of Kaccha;
having conquered the Pulindas and Yavanas, he established a kingdom there.
There was indeed a country on the banks of the Sindhu named Śrīpati;
Bhujavarmā ruled the kingdom there like his father,
and having conquered the Śabaras and Bhillas, he established his realm therein.
From him was born Bhujadeśa, who became famous upon the earth;
his son was Raṇavarman, who ruled the kingdom equal to his father;
his son was Citravarman, who likewise ruled the kingdom equal to his father.
Having built the city of Citranagarī in the midst of the forest, that best of kings,
Dharmavarman, became a son equal to his father;
Kṛṣṇavarman, his son, likewise ruled a kingdom equal to that of his father.
Having established a beautiful city named Udayapura in the midst of the forest, that best of kings ruled a kingdom equal to his father's; his son was Udaya.
Having ruled a kingdom equal to his father's, Vāpyakarma became his son.
That righteous-souled king indeed caused various ponds, wells, tanks, and palaces to be constructed for the sake of dharma within that city. In the meantime, a monarch named Balada arrived there.
Accompanied by an army of one hundred thousand, that hero stood firm in great intoxication;
with him, there was a battle for King Vāpyakarman.
Having conquered the Piśāca Mlecchas, he held a festival for Kṛṣṇa.
He ruled the kingdom equal to his father; his son was Guhila.
He ruled the kingdom equal to his father; his son was Kālabhoja.
He ruled the kingdom equal to his father; from him was born Rāṣṭrapāla.
Having abandoned his paternal abode, he attained the power of Viṣṇu;
through penance, he propitiated Śāradā, the source of all auspiciousness.
Then, being pleased, that Goddess caused a city to be built.
Having resided for ten years in Mahāvatī, a most delightful city protected by Maṇideva,
the wise king obtained a kingdom;
two sons were born to him, namely Vijaya and Prajaya.
Leaving his parents behind, Prajāyu went to the bank of the Gaṅgā;
there, for twelve years, he worshipped the goddess Śāradā with ascetic penance—
the goddess who exists in the form of a maiden and is intent upon playing the flute.
Having mounted her horse, she approached and said to the lord of the earth with a smile:
"O prince, for what purpose have you propitiated Śivā?
You shall indeed obtain the fruit of that penance from me very quickly."
Having heard this, he said to the maiden of sweet voice, "O Goddess, build a new city for me; salutations to you.
Having heard this, that goddess gave him an auspicious horse.
Having become a musician and come from the southern direction,
that king mounted his horse, covered his eyes, and arrived;
then that king came again from behind, from the western direction.
Then he proceeded to where the king of birds, Arkaṇa, was previously located;
terrified by him, the king opened his eyes and beheld a beautiful city, auspiciously constructed for the maiden.
To its north was indeed the Gaṅgā, and to the south was the Pāṇḍurā;
to the west was the river of Īśa, and to the east was the Markaṇa river.
That village became humpbacked and is known as Kānyakubja.
For ten years, Jayapāla indeed held that position;
a son was born to him, and from his playing of the flute he was named Veṇuka. That king Veṇu [married] Manoharā, who had been given by Devī.
Having married a maiden named Kanyāvatī as his wife, he shone resplendent.
From her were born seven sons who were auspicious portions of the Mothers,
as well as the daughters known as Śītalā, Pārvatī, and Puṣpavatī.
Govardhanī, Sindhurā, and Kālī are proclaimed by name;
likewise Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī,
Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, and Cāmuṇḍā appeared in succession.
Once, while the king’s wife was affectionately tying a clay pot with a cord into the well just as she had done before,
she saw many women adorned with various ornaments.
Clad in but a single garment, she herself fell into a state of mental exhaustion.
At that very moment, the jar did not reach the ground along with its contents.
Seeing this, Queen Kanyāvatī went home, deprived of the jar.
At that time, however, the seven maidens remained in the house as stone;
hearing this, Veṇu arrived, rebuked his beloved,
abandoned his vow of celibacy, and took pleasure with the woman.
From that king, by Queen Vīravatī, a son named Yaśovigraha was born;
he was powerful, righteous, and himself became the lord of Āryadeśa. That king ruled over the earth for twenty years.
Mahīcandra was his son, who established a position equal to that of his father.
Candradeva was his son, and he ruled the kingdom equally with his father.
From him was born a son, the lord of the earth named Mandapāla.

In the time of that king, all the kings from every direction abandoned that weakling Maṇḍapāla and remained in their homes provided for by him. Then Kumbhapāla became the ruler of a kingdom consisting of half of his father's realm.
And the city of Rājanīyā was situated in the realm of the Piśācas;
its ruler was Mahāmoda, who followed the dharma of the Mleccha-Piśācas.
Having conquered many lands and plundered vast wealth, he—
Since Kumbhapāla stood there, he became a follower of the Mleccha religion.
But when Kumbhapāla saw him, O King, created by Kali,
that wise man was filled with great joy and bowed down to him.
Then the heroic lord of the Mlecchas, having given him much wealth,
reached the city of Rājanīyā and Mūrtikhaṇḍaka;
the wise Kumbhapāla ruled the kingdom for twenty years.
His son, Devapāla, having married Candrakānti, the daughter of King Anaṅga, according to the prescribed rites,
reached the palace of Kānyakubja together with her after defeating numerous kings.
The kingdom was made equal to that of his father; he had two sons, Jayacandra and Ratnabhānu. Having conquered the eastern and northern quarters of the Āryadeśa, the Vaiṣṇava attained sovereignty.
And the son of Ratnabhānu, renowned by the name Lakṣaṇa,
having encountered battle at Kurukṣetra and cast off his life-breaths, went to heaven.
Thus the lineage of the wise Vaiśyapāla came to its end.

The kings born in the lineage of Viṣvaksena— namely Kuṃbhapāla, Śauklya, and Rakṣaka of the Vaiśyas— are known as the Viṣvaksenas. Those born in the family of Visena are known as the Visena Kṣatriyas.
Those born in the lineage of Guhila are indeed the Kṣatriyas known as the Gauhilas;
those born in the lineage of Rāṣṭrapāla are remembered as the Rāṣṭrapāla kings;
and [those born] in the family of the wise Vaiśyapāla, the son of Kumbhapāla.
Those Kṣatriyas indeed became Vaiśyapālas in many ways;
when death arrived for Lakṣaṇa, the upholder of the Śukla lineage,
all those principal Kṣatriyas met their dissolution at Kurukṣetra.
But the remaining minor kings were born of the intermixture of castes;
they became corrupted by the Mlecchas and were established in the terrifying kingdom of the Mlecchas.

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of the Pramara Lineage," in the *Kaliyuga Itihāsa-samuccaya* (Compendium of Histories of the Kali Age), which is an alternative section of the *Caturyuga-khaṇḍa* within the *Pratisarga-parvan* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
O best of the Bhṛgus, listen indeed to the lineage of Parihara;
having defeated the Buddhists, Parihara became devoted solely to the Atharvaveda.

Having meditated upon the eternal Śakti who consists of all things, he became absorbed in love. Then that Goddess, being pleased, created on Mount Citrakūṭa a city half a yojana in extent, which was invulnerable to the Kali age.
Since Kali was bound in this city, O beloved of the gods,
it became famous on the earth by the name Kaliñjara.
He ruled for twelve years in the eastern region.
Gauravarman was his son; having ruled a kingdom equal to that of his father,
he joyfully installed his younger brother Ghoravarman there and,
arriving in the Gauḍa country, established his rule there.
From Gauravarman there arose a king named Suparṇa;
he ruled the kingdom equal to his father. His son was Rūpaṇa, who likewise ruled the kingdom equal to his father. His son was Kāravarmā.
Then the king named Śaka [worshipped] the eternal Mahālakṣmī;
and at the end of three years, that goddess, assuming the form of Kāmākṣī,
made her residence there for the sake of protecting her devotees.
Kāmavarman ruled for fifty years;
he begot a twin pair with Bhogavatī, for she was indeed Bhogavatī.
The king gave his daughter Bhogavatī to Vikrama alone.
And he bestowed his own kingdom upon his son Bhogavarman;
his son Kālivarman ruled a kingdom equal to that of his father.
That king also performed a great festival for Mahākālī.
To him, Kālī herself appeared, gracious and ready to grant boons;
out of her own joy, she transformed those buds into many flowers,
and from them the enchanting city of Bhava was produced.
The city known by the name Kalikātā became famous upon the earth. Kauśika was his son, and he attained a station equal to that of his father.
Kātyāyana was his son, and he likewise attained a station equal to that of his father.
His son was Hemavata, who attained a position equal to his father;
Śivavarman was his son, and he too attained a position equal to his father;
and Bhavavarman was his son, who likewise attained a position equal to his father.
Rudravarmā, his son, ruled the kingdom equally with his father;
and Bhojavarmā, his son, having indeed abandoned his paternal station,
that heroic man established the Bhoja kingdom in a forest region.
King Govarman ruled a kingdom equal to that of his father;
King Vindhyavarman likewise ruled a kingdom equal to that of his father,
and having bestowed his own kingdom upon his younger brother, he departed for Vaṅga.
He ruled the kingdom equal to his father, and thus Sukhasena came to be;
he ruled the kingdom equal to his father, and Balāka was his son.
He ruled the kingdom for ten years, and Lakṣmaṇa was his son.
Mādhava ruled the kingdom equal to his father;
his son was Veśava, who also ruled the kingdom equal to his father;
from him was born Surasena, who likewise ruled the kingdom equal to his father.
He ruled the kingdom equal to his father, and thereafter Nārāyaṇa became king;
Śāntivarmā was born as his son, who likewise ruled the kingdom equal to his father.
That wise man established the city of Śāntipura on the bank of the Gaṅgā.
The king made his residence there, having established a position equal to that of his father.
His son was Nadīvarman, a powerful man who had received the boon of Gaṅgā;
he built a beautiful city named Nadīhā within the Gauḍa kingdom.
Then Gaṅgā herself summoned that wise Vidyādhara,
and by him alone was the city, devoted to the Vedas, protected.
That high-souled king ruled the kingdom for twenty years.
From him was born the Gaṅgavaṃśa, which became renowned upon the earth.
His son was Śārṅgadeva, a powerful devotee of Hari who,
having gone to the Gauḍa country, became intent on meditation upon Hari.
Gaṅgadeva, his son, ruled the kingdom for ten years;
Cāṇaka, his king, ruled for twenty years;
and his son was the powerful lord of the Gauḍa country.
He ruled the kingdom equal to his father, and thus became a lord of kings;
he ruled the kingdom equal to his father, and Nṛsiṃha became his son; he ruled the kingdom equal to his father, and Kalivarmā became his son.

Having arrived in the kingdom and conquered its king, the powerful one took up residence in the beautiful city of Mahāvatī and lived in happiness. His son Dhṛtivarmā became the ruler of a kingdom equal to that of his father.

His son, a lord of the earth, ruled a kingdom equal to that of his father. By the command of King Jayacandra, the monarch caused the city known as Āyāminī to be built on the earth and established his residence there.
When all the Kṣatriyas of the Lunar dynasty had been slain at Kurukṣetra,
the king Mahīpati then became the sovereign of Mahāvatī.
He ruled the kingdom for twenty years together with Uddīna.
Those who were portions of Suyodhana met their death at Kurukṣetra.
King Ghoravarmā was indeed the son of Parihāra;
he established his kingdom in Kaliñjara, and Śārdūla became his son.
And in his lineage, those kings who are celebrated as the Śārdūlas,
their kingdom— born of the Śārdūla dynasty—
became manifold throughout the earth by the grace of Mahāmāyā.
Thus, O Brahmin, I have related to you the lineage of the kings of the line of Pāvaka,
which destroys all sins just as [the lineage] of the Moon and Sun does;
I shall now further relate how Hari himself was born.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the *Pratisarga Parvan*, in the section titled *Caturyuga-khaṇḍa*, which is also known as the *Kaliyuga-itihāsa-samuccaya*.
Sūta said:
When midday had arrived for Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest...
Immediately after the appearance of the eye, a great wind arose;
by its power, Mount Hemādri trembled again and again,
just like a tree, and because of that very trembling, the entire region shook as well.
Then, O tiger among sages, as [the fire] reached the earth from the sky, the ground trembled; it became destructive to all the worlds. The seven continents and the oceans turned into water.
Then Śeṣa became the Lokāloka mountain together with its northern range; during the dissolution at the end of the Manvantara, the earth reached a state of absorption,
and within a thousand years, the earth came to lie amidst the waters.
Then that Blessed Viṣṇu, together with Bhava and Vidhi,
took all the stars and planets according to the prescribed rule and established the auspicious Śaiśumāra wheel in the sky.
The Blessed Grandfather established [the world] according to its proper order.
Once again, the entire earth was dried up by the circles of the luminaries;
at the end of ten thousand years, it became dry land and became visible once more.
Then the Blessed Brahmā produced from his mouth Soma,
the king of the twice-born, who was highly wise and proficient in all the Vedas;
and with his two arms, the Blessed Brahmā produced the Kṣatriya king, who possessed great strength.
And he brought forth Sūrya, who is devoted to the science of statecraft;
from his two thighs, the Supreme Lord Pitāmaha created the King of Vaiśyas, the Ocean, the lord of rivers, and the mine of jewels.

And from his two feet, Viśvakarman produced the supreme Dakṣa by name, who was skilled in all arts, a king of the Śūdras, and a performer of good deeds. Indeed, the Brāhmaṇas were born from Soma, and those born of the royal lineage (Kṣatriyas) were born from Sūrya.
From Samudra the Vaiśyas were born, and from Dakṣa the Śūdras came into being.
Manu Vaivasvata himself was born from the solar disc;
his sovereignty encompassed all living beings dwelling in the world.
And that which is to be known as the seventy-one divine yugas—
then the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, the manifestor of the universal form,
was born from the first half as Viṣṇu, and from the latter half, Vāmana himself.
In the Satya Yuga, the eternal Lord Viśvarūpa was a child;
at that time, the maximum lifespan of human beings was four hundred years.
In the Tretā Yuga, Hari attained youth, having manifested from the first half [of his life].

The lifespan of humans is proclaimed to be three hundred years in the Dvāpara age; in the Tretā age, O Lord, it is two hundred years for men. But in the Kali age, Viśvarūpa Hari himself has met his death.
The lifespan of men is one hundred years for some who are endowed with righteousness; [but] from beyond a parārdha ago, the divine Vāmana, Hari, the younger brother of Mahendra,
four-armed and deep dark-blue in complexion, was seated upon Garuḍa.
For the sake of the welfare of the universe in its manifold forms, he manifested as the Triyugī;
from the half of Vāmana, Nārāyaṇa himself was born as the Triyugī.
In the Satya-yuga, Hari is white in form, the Lord himself known as Haṃsa.
In the Tretā age, the Lord himself appeared in a red form known as Yajña; in the Dvāpara age, Hari himself appeared in a yellow form as Svarṇagarbha;
and when the Kali age arrived, during the twilight of the Dvāpara yuga—
A portion of Viṣṇu, as well as a portion of Vāmana,
became unified and was born as Viṣṇu himself from Devakī in the beautiful house of Vasudeva in Mathurā, O gods.
Then Brahmā and the others praised the Lord, the supreme, eternal Brahman.
Thereupon, the Blessed One was pleased and spoke auspicious words to the gods,
for the sake of the welfare of the gods and for the destruction of the Daityas.
O best of gods, in the Kali age I shall manifest in many forms;
there, in the divine and beautiful Vṛndāvana, which is subtle yet situated upon the surface of the earth,
I shall perform secret pastimes during the Kali Yuga.
In the terrible Kali age, all the Vedas will become cowherd girls everywhere;
having abandoned the earth at that time, they shall indeed sport with me.
This was when I was entreated by Rādhā at the end of the Kali Yuga.
And having concluded my secret sports,
O best of gods, when the Satya age arrives, I shall become Kalki; having brought about the dissolution at the end of the Yuga and again assuming a dual form, I shall establish the true Dharma.
Having heard this, those gods vanished right there.
Thus, in age after age, is the play of Hari, whose deeds are wondrous.
Indeed, only those who are devotees of Viṣṇu know him who pervades the universe.
O Brahmin, just as the servants of a king understand the gravity of their own sovereign's task and no others do, so too do the servants of Hari himself;
for it is the eternal Viṣṇu-māyā that acts according to the will of Viṣṇu.
Having fashioned various worlds, Mahākālī indeed came into being;
having made the entire world, including all that moves and is stationary, consist of Time (Kāla),
she shall afterwards become Mahāgaurī after devouring them.
"Salutations to that Mahākālī; salutations again and again to Viṣṇumāyā!
O Mahāgaurī, salutations to you; protect us who are filled with fear.

Thus ends the fifth chapter in the *Kaliyugīyetihāsasamuccaya* (The Compendium of Histories of the Kali Age), which is another name for the *Caturyugakhaṇḍa* within the *Pratisargaparvan* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
The sage said:
O best of sages, who were the kings of the earth?
Tell us of them, O illustrious one, for you are always all-knowing.
Sūta said:
The Paiśāca demon, exultant with curiosity, took possession of Dehalī-rājya—
the most beautiful city of Valīgaḍha, which was protected by the Yādavas.
Accompanied by ten thousand heroes, that Piśāca went there;
having conquered Bhūpasena, the grandson of Vīrasena and best of kings, who was stationed in the village of Dehalī, he remained there, exultant with curiosity.
In the meantime, kings from various lands arrived;
having been defeated by them, that Uddīna was expelled from his own country.
Hearing of this, Uddīna returned once more to Dehali.
Having conquered the kings, the best of the Daityas then divided his form into fragments.
Subsequently, many Mlecchas arrived here from all sides and,
having ruled for five, six, or seven years, they met their destruction.
"O best of sages, from this day forward, within a hundred years in this land,
there will arise short-lived and dull-witted Mleccha kings who destroy the gods and sacred fords; therefore, you must depart with me."
"You ought indeed to go quickly to the auspicious city of Viśālā. Having heard these words, they all departed from Naimiṣa out of sorrow and went to Viśālā on the Himavat, the best of mountains.
There, all those established in meditative concentration meditated upon Hari, who consists of everything;
at the end of a hundred years, they all departed from their meditation for the abode of Brahmā.
Vyāsa said:
Thus, everything should be meditated upon swiftly through the power of yoga practice.
I have described this to you; what else do you wish to hear?
Manu said:
O Blessed One, knower of the truth of the Vedas, bringer of auspiciousness to all the world:
I am born from Māyā, while you are born from the Veda upon this earth.
And by ignorance, my entire knowledge has been taken away.
Therefore, having taken various births, I have come to this world;
yet, out of compassion, the Supreme Brahman himself, seeing me so unfortunate,
assumed the form of Vyāsa and has arrived to deliver me.
Salutations to that lord of sages, Vedavyāsa, the witness;
salutations again and again to the one who protects from the states of ignorance and delusion.
O Sage, tell me further: what else was done by Sūta and the others?
"O Lord, you ought to explain all of that now out of compassion.
Vyāsa said:
"All the worlds that exist within the cosmic egg (Brahmāṇḍa) reside within this body."
For the ego (ahaṃkāra) is indeed the individual soul (jīvātman); it is all-pervasive, yet devoid of millions [of parts]. It is ancient, subtler than the subtlest, the eternal sixteen-fold self.
These consist of the senses, the mind, and the five objects of the senses.
The individual soul (jīva) in this body is bound by the qualities of the Lord;
for the Lord is indeed eighteenfold—Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the individual soul.
These consist of the intellect, the mind, the objects of the senses, and likewise the sense organs.

Mahādeva, the eternal, is indeed the lord of the ego; Nārāyaṇa is the individual soul (jīva) himself, who was deluded by Śaṅkara. Bound by the fetters of the three qualities (guṇas), he who is one became manifold.
The Lord Īśa, whose nature is Time, is the embodiment of the Great Kalpa (Mahākalpa).
These are the Śivakalpa, the Brahmakalpa, and Viṣṇukalpa as the third;
these indeed are the eyes of Īśa, while the Bandhakalpa is the fourth.
The Vāyukalpa, the Vahnikalpa, the Brahmāṇḍa, and the Liṅgakalpaka—
these five faces of Īśvara have indeed been described by the knowers of reality;
likewise the Bhaviṣyakalpa and the Garuḍakalpaka.
The Kalpa, Bhāgavata, Mārkaṇḍeya, Kalpaka,
Vāmana, Nṛsiṃha, Varāha, Matsya, and Kūrma—
these ten should be known by the wise as the arms of Maheśa, whose nature is knowledge.
Within eighteen days alone, all eighteen Kalpas of Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest, are to be known by the wise in reverse order.
Among them, the Kūrma Kalpa is the first, and the Matsya Kalpa is the second.
