The third is to be known as the Śvetavārāha Kalpa by the ancients. The Lord Brahmā is twofold: subtle and gross, devoid of qualities (aguṇa) and possessed of qualities (guṇin). He who possesses qualities is named Virāṭ, born from the navel of Viṣṇu.
He is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), of imperishable form, unmanifest in birth, self-existent, and self-born.
The lifespan of the qualified Brahman is one hundred years as determined by time;
this consists of one lakh and nineteen thousand human years.
By these years, a day of Virāj, the self-existent Brahmā, is to be known.
He is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), his birth is unmanifest (avyakta), and he is the supreme Lord of all, transcending time.
The Unmanifest (avyakta) is to be known as Prakṛti; from that indeed proceed the twelve limbs.
The senses, the mind, and the intellect are indeed said to belong to the Unmanifest;
beyond the Unmanifest is Brahman, that imperishable, subtle light.
When he has himself reached the Manifest, he is remembered as having his birth from the Unmanifest.
He who remains continuously established in samādhi for a hundred years,
becoming subtle like the mind-wind, shall indeed go to the station of Brahmā;
that is to be known as Satyaloka, the eternal realm attainable through yoga.
In that place, all the sages entered into meditative absorption;
having dwelt there for a hundred thousand years— which was but a mere moment from the perspective of the earthly realm—
they then attained the state of dense being, consciousness, and bliss within their very bodies.
And when the second day had arrived, they opened their eyes and saw all men as being like animals— subtle in form,
possessing a lifespan of sixty years, and standing at a height of two and a half cubits, appearing truly formidable.
In various places, the castes remained, appearing as if their boundaries were blurred;
all became barbarians and heretics, existing in many forms.
At that time, they abandoned the entire earth, including all sacred fords and the Vedas.

Having become *gopīs*, they celebrated a great festival together with Hari. Various types of heretics (*pāṣaṇḍas*), who show various paths and were created by Kali, remained on earth having deceived the social classes (*varṇas*).
Having seen this, the sages will go into the presence of Romaharṣaṇa; then, with palms joined in reverence,
they will praise Sūta there as he enters the eternal yogic sleep.
"He will speak to the sages, setting aside the narrative of the Kalpas;
listen to that, O best of kings, exactly as it was described by Sūta.
Sūta said:
I shall proclaim the narrative of the Kalpa as it was seen by Yoganidrā;
listen to that, O best of sages, as it occurred at the end of a hundred thousand years.
A barbarian king named Piśācaka, born of the Mukula lineage, [will arise].
Known by the name Timiraliṅga, he arrived in the Middle Country;
assuming the form of Time itself, he conquered both Āryas and Mlecchas and then carried out a great slaughter in the midst of the city of Dehlī.
Having summoned all the Brahmins residing in the Āryadeśa, the wise one spoke these words: "You are worshippers of images;
by whomsoever an image was fashioned, it is considered equal to his own daughter."
What is her pure worship? It consists of the Śālagrāma stone.
And as for the god Viṣṇu mentioned by you, he is certainly not Hari.
Therefore, all your Vedas and various scriptures [are contradicted].
"Those things were performed in vain by the sages for the sake of deceiving the world!
Having said this, he seized them by force and cast them into a blazing fire;
likewise, all those Śālagrāma stones, which were highly worthy of worship by them, he also cast in.
Having taken them and loaded them onto the backs of camels, he went home;
having arrived at the region of Taittira, he established a fortress there and performed the consecration of the Śālagrāma stones upon their respective seats.
Then all the gods, being distressed, spoke in many ways to their lord Vāsava, the god of gods and husband of Śacī:
"O Blessed One, we have all taken refuge in the Śālagrāma stone."
Having abandoned all our forms, awakened by a portion of Kṛṣṇa,
we dwell joyfully within the Śālagrāma stones.
O Lord, all our stones originate from the region of Śāla.
"And they have indeed been made to ascend his own throne by the Mleccha king.
Having heard these words of the gods, the Blessed Lord Svarāṭ,
knowing everything that had been done by Bali and that the worship of the gods had been cast aside, [acted accordingly].
Lord Indra, whose vehicle is the clouds, became enraged toward the Daityas;
seizing his incomparable weapon, the thunderbolt which destroys the Daityas,
he dispatched Taittiri to the region inhabited by the Mlecchas.
At his voice, all the lands, though divided into many parts, [were moved];
then that barbarian met his death along with all the people of the assembly.
Then the wise ones took up all the Śālagrāma stones.
Having cast [them] into the Gaṇḍakī, they departed for the heavenly world.
Then Mahendra, together with the gods, spoke to the one worshipped by the gods:
"O Blessed One, when the Kali age has arrived upon the surface of the earth, there will be the most excellent Dānavas."
"Having utterly transgressed the Vedic dharma, they are intent on my destruction;
therefore, O Blessed One, protect me along with the gods in the Kali age.
Jīva said:
O Mahendra, your most excellent wife named Śacī was granted a boon by Viṣṇu: "In the Kali age, I shall become your son.
And by your command, that goddess [established] the auspicious city of Śāntimayī.
Having returned to the banks of the Gaṅgā in the land of Gauḍa,
he will become a twice-born man and accomplish his purpose;
you indeed, becoming a Brāhmaṇa, must fulfill the task of the gods.
Having heard these words of the Guru, Vāsava, together with the eleven Rudras,
the eight Vasus, and the two Aśvins,
approached Prayāga, the king of holy fords, which is dear to the Sun.
In the month of Māgha, when the sun was in Capricorn,
Bṛhaspati propitiated the Sun-god; having arrived there, he recited the twelve chapters that describe the supreme majesty of the Sun to Indra and the other gods.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Pramara Lineage," in the *Kaliyuga-itihāsa-samuccaya*, which is an alternative section of the *Caturyuga-khaṇḍa* within the *Pratisarga-parvan* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
The sages said:
"But the venerable sage Bṛhaspati [addressed] the gods who were assembled..."
"And what did he proclaim regarding the majesty of the Sun situated within the mandala?
O Brahmin, out of compassion, tell all of that to us who are eager for it.
Having heard these words of theirs, Sūta spoke this speech:
To Bṛhaspati, who was seated there in the form of Jīva, the abode of all virtues,
Mahendra, staying at Prayāga together with the gods, spoke:
"O highly fortunate one, tell us the supreme majesty of the Sun."
"By what [means] heard today might the Lord Ravi himself become gracious?
Bṛhaspati said:
"A certain twice-born man named Dhātṛśarman, for the sake of offspring, [approached] Prajāpati."
Remaining in the city of Barhiṣmati, he propitiated [the Lord] through austerity;
and in the fifth year, the blessed Prajāpati, being well-pleased, granted him three offspring:
a daughter and two sons.

Having fathered three offspring within a year, that best of the twice-born, Dhātṛśarman, attained supreme joy through the fondling of his sons. He then reflected: "How shall their most excellent marriages be brought about?"
Thus filled with anxiety, the Brahmin propitiated Tumburu, the lord of the Gandharvas,
by means of oblations according to the prescribed rites for one year.
Then Tumburu, having arrived, fulfilled his heart's desire.
Then the Brahmin, being delighted upon seeing his daughter-in-law and son-in-law with joy, and observing their sporting together, fell once more into anxiety regarding the ornaments,
garments, and various kinds of wealth.
"How will it be for those who are destitute, O my impure one?
Having become sixty years of age, he, being intent upon it, duly worshipped the Lord of Wealth with sandalwood and other offerings for the duration of one year.
Then the Lord, being pleased, joyfully gave him much wealth and a beautiful Yakṣa-vidyā that bestows five gold pieces;
he who recites it a thousand times, having performed worship and an oblation consisting of one-tenth of that number.
Having performed libations and purificatory rites, he attained his desire; thus,
as he lived in this manner, a great deal of time passed by,
and the arrival of death occurred for him, accompanied by disease.
Afflicted by pain and deprived of strength, the brahmin praised Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, with hymns in the form of the Vedas;
after only a month, the Blessed Lord Hara himself bestowed knowledge upon him.
Having obtained that [instruction], Dhātṛśarman, with a humble mind, propitiated Bhāskara— the destroyer of delusion— there through vows observed on Sundays.
After five years, the Lord Sūrya, who is affectionate toward his devotees, [appeared] out of devotion.
On the full moon day of Caitra, he spoke these words to him again and again: "Choose a boon.
Having heard that, Dhātṛśarman, bowing low with humility, praised Bhāskara, the destroyer of delusion, with a voice of supreme devotion.
Dhātṛśarman said:
Both activity (pravṛtti) and cessation (nivṛtti) are dear to this mind within the body;
activity takes the form of night, while cessation takes the form of day.
Born from Your splendor as the cause of bondage for the world,
Your divine and subtle energy remained unmanifest;
salutations to that essence of light which, having become threefold, exists for the sake of the universe.
The Lord Brahmā is known as the master of that intellect which is characterized by rajas;
salutations to you, Vidhi, who were born from his splendor.
The Lord Hari is the master of that intellect within the body which is characterized by sattva.
Salutations to that Hari from whom you were created as a being; salutations again and again to Him, for you were born of Śiva himself, the lord of that delusive, dark-minded intellect,
through you who had become [overcome by] darkness.
"O Blessed One, grant me liberation; O beloved of consciousness, salutations, salutations!
Bṛhaspati said:
"Thus was the Blessed One praised by that Dhātṛśarman."
Mahendra spoke these words to that twice-born man, who was skilled in knowledge:
"O Brahmin, liberation is fourfold: Sālokya, which arises from austerity;
Sāmīpya, which is born of devotion; and Sārūpya, which results from meditation."

Sāyujya (union) is to be understood through knowledge; their Lord is the Supreme Person, who is to be known as both with attributes (saguṇa) and without attributes (viguṇa), and as bliss for those seeking liberation in due order.
And as for those liberations that have returned again within the bodies of the gods—
That which, once reached, one does not return from—that is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
O best of Brahmins, by his grace, you shall attain union with me;
and for as long as the time it takes to utter the syllable "ma," your liberation shall be established.
Having spoken thus, the god vanished, and by him that twice-born man was liberated.
Sūta said:
To Vāgīśa who had spoken thus, Divākara [spoke] in the month of Caitra.
The eternal God of gods revealed his true form:
"Listen, all you gods who have assembled here;
I shall accomplish the work of the gods by producing a portion of myself in the land of Vaṅga."
Having spoken thus, the Sun-god produced light from his own mouth and bestowed it upon Sukanyā, the wife of the twice-born, who was his devotee;
for that very Brahmin Dhātṛśarman had attained liberation in the Sun.
Born indeed by his splendor in the abode of the author of the Kāvya,
he became renowned as Īśvara, the self-possessed lord who dwelt at Purīśadvāra;
having conquered brahmins devoted to the Vedas, he attained great fame.
Thus, O Brahmin, I have related to you that which was spoken by Jīvana.
Now listen again to the delightful story concerning the gods as told by Jīvana.
Bṛhaspati said:
In Māyāvatī, there was a certain brahmin renowned as Mitraśarman;
he was constantly devoted to the science of poetry, a connoisseur of aesthetic flavor, and beloved by women.
When I arrived at Gaṅgādvāra in the zodiac sign of Aquarius, there was a great festival.
It was caused to be performed by many kings devoted to sacred pilgrimage sites;
at that festival, men and women adorned with many ornaments arrived, filled with supreme bliss, for the sake of beholding it.
Mitraśarman, having obtained the auspicious daughter of King Kāmasena— a twelve-year-old girl endowed with poetic skill and the arts,
the daughter of a southern monarch with a sweet countenance— [remained there].
Upon seeing that fawn-eyed woman, he fell under her sway;
she, however, seeing that excellent man named Mitraśarman— Citriṇī by name— was overcome with fainting, for the form of a Brahmin remained fixed within her heart.
Having returned to her own home, Citriṇī worshipped the Lord Bhāskara every day with great reverence; meanwhile,
Mitraśarman remained in that place on the charming bank of the Gaṅgā.
Having bathed in the morning and become pure, staying in the midst of the water during the month of Vaiśākha, he,
devoted to the Sun, recited the Ādityahṛdaya hymn;
every day, with twelve repetitions, he propitiated the Maker of Light.
At the end of the month, the Blessed Sun indeed granted him that boon.
Having obtained the boon, that brahmin returned once more to his own home;
Citriṇī, for her part, had received the desired boon from the Sun, the light of the world.
Then those two parents, awakened by Bhāskara in a dream,
summoned Mitraśarman and chose him for their daughter;
and Kāmasena also took up residence in the hearts of the couple.

Filled with joy, those two fashioned that solar deity’s disc and its yantra according to the prescribed rites, inscribing it upon a copper plate; having undertaken a vow dear to the Sun, they worshipped him daily with red flowers.
"Both of them, possessing bodies that last for a hundred years, are free from decay and devoid of fatigue;
being healthy, they attain death and reach the proximity of the Sun.
Having heard this verse of the Sun, the King of the Gods himself [spoke] on the full moon day of Vaiśākha.
He beheld the god Bhāskara in person, accompanied by the deities.
Seeing the gods bowed down in devotion, the Blessed One, the dispeller of darkness,
spoke these beautiful and auspicious words concerning the purpose of the gods:
"O best of gods, a son shall be born on earth from my portion.
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus, [he cast] a mass of splendor from his own form in every direction.
Having been born in Kāśī, he became Rāmānanda;
he was the son of the brahmin Devala of Kānyakubja. From his very childhood, he was a man of wisdom, devoted solely to the name of Rāma.
Abandoned by his father and mother, he went to Rāghava for refuge;
then the Blessed Lord Hari himself, possessing fourteen kalās,
the husband of Sītā, joyfully made his dwelling within his heart.
"Thus, O Brahmin, I have told you how Rāmānanda, who was powerful and born from the grace of Hari, arose from a portion of the deity Mitra. Bṛhaspati said:"
Listen, O Śakra, to this delightful narrative concerning the sun in the month of Jyeṣṭha.
In ancient times, during the Satya Yuga, there was indeed a brahmin named Aryaman,
who was a knower of the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, and was devoted to the treatises on dharma.
The wife of that king Śrāddhadeva was Pitṛmatī,
a most virtuous daughter; she gave birth to seven sinless sons who were devoted to the scriptures of dharma, just like Aryaman himself.
Once, that wise brahmin, having reflected deeply within his heart,
desiring wealth, praised the god Bhāskara with many forms of worship;
at dawn, he honored him with white flowers, sandalwood paste, and other offerings.

At midday, for the propitiation of the ancestors, he worshipped the Sun according to the prescribed rites with red and yellow flowers for the duration of one month. In the month of Jyeṣṭha, the Lord Sūrya indeed granted him an auspicious gem.
And by the power of that jewel, it produced a prastha measure of gold every day; with that, he accumulated merit by constructing ponds,
wells, tanks, and palatial mansions upon the earth.
Seeking righteousness, he caused it to be built through the grace of the god Sūrya;
having become a thousand-year-bodied being, free from decay and free from affliction,
he cast off his beautiful body and attained the world of Sūrya.
Having dwelt there for a hundred thousand years, he indeed became the very form of the Sun.
Thus has the majesty of Bhāskara himself been recounted by me;
therefore, O Śakra, together with the gods, worship Ravi as he resides within his orb.
Having heard this, those gods, out of love, gratified him with verses concerning the Sun; and in the month of Jyeṣṭha,
that very Sun appeared there before the eyes of the gods, and with a gracious mind, he spoke to them.
At the end of the Dvāpara age, Sudarśana, commanded by Kṛṣṇa, will be born;
known as Nimbāditya, he will remove the decline of dharma.
Sūta said:
Listen to the life-story of that great-souled Nimbārka,
whom the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa addressed, saying: "Perform my work by my command on the auspicious bank of the Narmadā, on the southern side of Mount Meru."
In the beautiful land of Tailaṅga, frequented by gods and the best of sages,
descend there and, by my command, propagate on earth the true Dharma which has almost vanished, having received it from Nārada, the seer of the gods.

"O sinless one, you must reside in Mathurā, the Naimiṣa forest, Dvāravatī, my own hermitage, Sudarśana’s hermitage, and other such places. Having received this command with the words "Om," the Lord Śrīsudarśana departed.

The direct bestower of the desires of his devotees has descended upon the surface of the earth in the meritorious land of Tailaṅga; he is a noble-minded and eminent brahmin born of the lineage of Bhṛgu in the sacred hermitage of Sudarśana.
Known by the name Āruṇa, he was a master of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences;
together with his wife Jayantī, he assumed the form of a sage.
By him, the concentrated splendor originating from the discus of Viṣṇu was [received].
The goddess Jayantī, devoted to her husband, conceived [the child] in her mind;
she shone with that splendor like the stainless quarter of the sky with the moon.
Then, at a most beautiful time endowed with every excellence—
In the bright fortnight of Kārttika, on the full moon day,
when the moon was in Taurus and the constellation Kṛttikā, while the entire circle of planets was in their exaltations;
at the time of sunset, with Aries as the ascendant at the beginning of the night.
On the day of Jayantī, which is of the nature of victory, the Lord of the Universe was born;
by him this entire universe was established in the Vedic dharma.
Once, Viriñci [Brahmā] was at that auspicious hermitage of Iṃbārka.
Having approached, he said, "O Brahmin, I have arrived overcome by hunger;
as long as the sun remains in the sky, so long do feed me, O twice-born one.
Hearing this, he replied, "So be it," and gave him food.
Then, as the blessed sun was approaching the western mountain,
that sage,
the seer, established his own splendor— the essence of light known as Sudarśana— within an auspicious neem tree by means of his own power.
Seeing that splendor resembling the sun, the Creator, filled with wonder,
prostrated himself on the ground like a staff before the young sage who was dressed as a mendicant, like another sun; for he had been gratified by the sage's ascetic power.
He spoke these pleasing words, honoring him by saying, "Excellent! Excellent!
"You shall become renowned on earth as Nimbāditya.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of Rāmānanda and Nimbārka," in the *Kaliyugīyetihāsasamuccaya* (Compendium of Histories of the Kali Age), within the *Caturyugakhaṇḍa* (Section on the Four Yugas), which is part of the *Pratisargaparvan* (Section on Re-creation) of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Bṛhaspati said:
O Śakra, in former times, during the Tretā Yuga, there was a twice-born man named Śakraśarman in Ayodhyā; he was highly fortunate and devoted to the worship of the gods.
Having worshipped the Aśvins, as well as the Rudras, Vasus, and Sūryas individually with mantras consisting of the Yajurveda, the twice-born one, with a serene mind,
gratified those gods with sacrificial offerings every day.
By virtue of that state, the thirty-three gods, accompanied by their minor hosts,
granted him his heart's desire— which was difficult to obtain but now made easy—
so that for ten thousand years he remained free from old age and free from affliction.
Afterwards, having cast off his body, he became the Sun;
thereafter, he exercised authority over that orb for a hundred thousand years.
Then, by the grace of all the gods, the Brahmin went to the world of Brahmā.
"Having beheld that supreme state within the maṇḍala for eight thousand divine years, he attained the Sun through recitation and worship.
Having heard these words, Mahendra, together with the gods, [acted accordingly].
With a humble mind, he worshipped the god Bhāskara in the month of Āṣāḍha.
And on the full moon day of Āṣāḍha, that god appeared visibly there upon the surface of the earth; listen to what he said to the gods.
In the most delightful Vṛndāvana, during the terror of the Kali age, I shall take birth;
that twice-born one, in the form of the Sun, will accomplish the work of the gods.
He will become the son of the twice-born Mādhava.
"The illustrious one named Madhu is devoted to the path of the Vedas.
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Sun, intent on accomplishing the purpose of the gods, [proceeded].
Having generated splendor from his own body, he sent it forth toward Vṛndāvana;
having subdued those who were averse from all sides with sweet words,
he bestowed upon them the Vaiṣṇava power that grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
He became renowned on the surface of the earth as Madhvācārya.
Jīva said:
And in the Dvāpara age, there was indeed a most excellent brahmin named Meghaśarman.
Possessed of knowledge and wisdom, a righteous man devoted to the path of the Vedas,
he was constantly intent on the work of agriculture; with a tenth part of that wealth,
he, full of devotion, daily worshipped all the gods.
Once, when King Śantanu was five years old,
a drought occurred in his kingdom;
indeed, that entire field was watered by the rain-cloud for only the distance of a krośa.
The price of a *droṇa* measure of grain was fixed at a single coin;
thus Meghaśarman became possessed of wealth and grain,
while other people, being oppressed, went for refuge to the king.
Then, the distressed king summoned Meghaśarman:
"O best of the twice-born, salutations to you; be my beloved preceptor.
O Brahmin, instruct me so that there may be no drought."
To the king who spoke thus, Meghaśarman addressed these words:
"When the month of Śrāvaṇa has arrived,
having personally invited twelve Brahmins devoted to the Vedas, [one should perform] exactly one hundred thousand [recitations] for the Sun."

Having caused the *sumanas* flowers to be offered with a devout mind on the full moon day while observing that vow, and having had the twice-born perform ten parts of the oblations of *sūrya-mantras* into the fire according to the prescribed rite,
you shall have fulfilled your duty; be happy.

Having heard this and acting accordingly, he fed those who were versed in the Vedas. Then the Sun, whose nature is Parjanya, being well-pleased, covered the earth and all directions and, as the Lord, caused rain to fall everywhere.
Then King Śāntanu, being devoted to the vow of the Sun,
became a most meritorious and excellent monarch through that vow; indeed,
whomever the aged king touched with his hand became young again.
By the power of Sūryadeva, Meghaśarman indeed became thus:
he possessed a lifespan of five hundred years, was free from old age, and was without affliction;
having cast off his life-breaths, he became the Sun and went to the world of the Sun.
"Having reached the earth after a hundred thousand years, he shall go to the world of Brahmā.
To Jīva, who was speaking thus, the blessed Lord Parjanya-Ravi,
having arrived at Prayāga, revealed his true form.
Murāri said: "With a serene soul, I shall come to Vṛndāvana in the Kali age within the kingdom of the Mlecchas and accomplish the work of the gods. Sūta said:
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Sun went to the auspicious Vṛndāvana;
there he became the renowned son of Vedaśarman, named Śrīdhara,
who was an expert having thoroughly studied the scripture of the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam.
Śrīdhara composed this auspicious and radiant work for the benefit of the learned;
that scripture, the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, was produced by him as a pinnacle above all Purāṇas.
Jīva said:
Formerly, when the Kali age had arrived, there was a brahmin named Prāṃśuśarman who was constantly devoted to the Vedas and the Shastras, a regular worshiper of the deities and guests,
truthful, highly virtuous, and free from theft and violence.
Constantly devoted to the life of a mendicant yet supporting his wife and son,
once, as that king was walking along the road for the sake of alms,
the rogue Kali, a performer of illusory deceptions, came within his sight.
Having constructed a garden that was enchanting due to its gifts, Kali spoke to him, assuming the form of a tall brahmin: "Listen to my words;
this beautiful garden is mine, so go there and be happy."
Having heard these words of the brahmin, Kali arrived at that garden;
having gone into the middle of the garden, the great rogue Kali plucked some delicious fruits and gave them to him for the sake of his meal.
Bowing with palms joined in reverence, he spoke to Prāṃśuśarman:
"O Brahmin, eat the auspicious fruit of the Kaliṅga tree together with me.
Thus addressed, he laughed and replied to him in a sweet voice.
The wise maintain that the Kali age is found in the *bibhītaka* tree and likewise in the fruit of the *kaliṅda*; therefore, I do not accept it.
If this fruit has been offered today with devotion by you, a servant of the twice-born—
Having indeed offered the *prasāda* to the Śālagrāma, I partake of it;
for the Śālagrāma is Brahman itself, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*).
By the mere sight of it, that which is unfit to be eaten certainly becomes fit to be eaten.
Having heard this, Kali became ashamed and despondent there;
the twice-born man, taking that fruit, went to the village of Bhūmi.
Then the king, arriving there with a gracious mind, spoke to the twice-born man.
"O Brahmin, what have you taken? Show it quickly; do what is pleasing.
Hearing this, Prāṃśuśarman, the best of the twice-born, was struck with wonder; he took that fruit—which was like a calf's head—and presented it to the king.
Then King Kali, who was a friend to justice, having beaten that brahmin with cane whips,
cast him into an iron prison.
When the sun had risen at dawn, Prāṃśuśarman became deeply distressed.
He praised the divine Bhāskara with hymns originating from the Ṛgveda.
Then the blessed, eternal Ravi, being pleased,
spoke these words into the ears of the brahmin, as they were conveyed through the sky.
Listen, O highly fortunate Brahmin: Hari himself, in the form of Time (Kāla), created the four ages for the sake of protecting the universe and other purposes;
likewise, he fashioned the Kali age for the destruction of the multitudes of beings.

"Therefore, when the terrible Kali age has arrived, dwell joyfully in the city of Kaliñjara, which was created by the Māyā of Viṣṇu. Having spoken thus and having provided protection for that brāhmaṇa, Bhāskara [departed].
And he sent that twice-born man to the city of Kaliñjara.
Living there for one hundred and twenty-five years, the twice-born man,
together with his wife and son, propitiated Ravi and attained the world of Ravi.
Having become the sun for ten thousand years in the month of Bhādrapada,
he subsequently reached the city of Brahmā and attained supreme bliss;
thus, O Brahmin, has been told to you how the Jīva spoke to him.
The divine Bhāskara, having arrived on the full moon day of the month of Bhādrapada when the twenty-eighth Kali age had begun,
was himself born in Kaliñjara as the son of Śivadatta, renowned by the name Viṣṇuśarman.

O Brahmin, that righteous-souled Viṣṇu, the Lord of all and Hari, who was well-versed in the Vedas, scriptures, and arts, a devotee of Viṣṇu, and a worshiper of the gods, summoned men of the four castes to the temple of Hari and spoke these words.

Listen to the cause of that, O disciple: the Lord Saccidānanda, the creator of the cause of the universe, who possesses the twenty-four principles, created the gods for the sake of the worlds; therefore, he became the Lord of all.
"For first a pure man, having worshipped all the gods,
should afterwards worship Viṣṇu, just as servants [serve] a king.
Having heard this, they all praised him in many ways.
Delighted, they spoke of him by the name Viṣṇusvāmī.
Thus, O Brahmin, I have told you how Viṣṇusvāmī came to be;
now hear again the delightful story as uttered from the mouth of Bṛhaspati.
The Jīva said:
Formerly, in the region of Caitraratha, there was a twice-born man named Bhagaśarman; on earth, he had two sons, Muni and Medhāvin, by the celestial courtesan Mañjughoṣā.
Abandoned by his father and mother, that boy, endowed with faith,
propitiated the Sun for a hundred years through austerity.
The deity named Sāvitrī, who dwells in the center of the solar orb, [appeared].
The eternal maiden, the mother of all the suns, indeed manifested from his orb,
pleased by his ascetic penance;
in the month of Āśvina, she made the king a twice-born within that orb.
For a hundred thousand years, month after month during the month of Āśvina, that Brahmin made himself manifest and was honored by the inhabitants of the world.
"O Lord of the Gods, worship the Sun; he will accomplish your purpose."
Having heard this, in the month of Āśvina, that Sun-god appeared there in person through the worship of the gods and spoke these words to the deities:
"In the auspicious land of Kānyakubja, I am known as Vāṇībhūṣaṇa."
"I shall become the auspicious son of the brahmin Satyadeva.
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Sun was born in the auspicious city of Kānyakubja.
Having defeated the heretical Brahmins who were intent on eating meat, he,
who was beloved by the gods, composed a *Chandoga* text in his own name.
Those Brahmins [who had been defeated] were eaters of fish and meat, as well as eaters of deer, sheep, and goats.

Having united and assembled together, those twice-born ones established the formidable meaning of the scriptures. Protected by Kali, the friend of unrighteousness, they defeated that brahmin and Matsyaketu in his own house.
Then, by his power, that twice-born one, beloved of Viṣṇu, performed a rite of immobilization;
having invoked the Vaiṣṇavī energy, he brought to life the fish devoured from his own mouth and showed them to them, and upon seeing this, they were then struck with wonder.
And having become his disciples, they indeed attained the Vaiṣṇava doctrine.
Jīva said:
Once, on the bank of the Sarayū, there was a twice-born man named Devayājī.
Constantly devoted to all the gods and dedicated to the recitation of the Vedas,
his son met his death at birth, indeed in a most cruel manner;
then that twice-born man, having heard of it, propitiated the Sun-god.
By his grace, he lived and became known by the name Vivasvān;
possessing a body of sixteen years and being proficient in all branches of knowledge,
he was blessed with offspring, devoted to dharma, and dedicated to the worship of the Sun.

When the day of Śivarātri arrived, his wife, known by the name Suśīlā and fond of ornaments, came there for the sake of serving her husband. Seeing that woman with a sweet face, the observer of the vow [beheld] the god Rudra.
Having seized her by force at night, he, overwhelmed by passion, enjoyed her;
yet, due to the very fault of that sexual act, he suffered from a great case of leprosy,
his penis fell off, his anus became displaced, and he experienced great bodily pain.
Following a certain instruction,
he performed the vow of Sunday for twelve months with devotion, abstaining from food and restraining his senses.
By the power of that vow, all afflictions were brought to an end.
Then, having gained faith in the Sun, that best of the twice-born recited the Ādityahṛdaya every day and became able to assume any form at will.
Previously reviled by women, he was now entreated by them with desire.
Having undertaken the vow of celibacy, he became devoted to the meditation on Brahman;
becoming a hundred-year-old Brāhmaṇa, possessed of knowledge and free from disease,
he cast off his life-breaths and, becoming the Sun, entered the center of the solar orb.
"In the month of Kārtika, you made the sky radiant for a hundred thousand years;
therefore, O Mahendra, quickly worship that Sun along with the gods.
Sūta said:
Having heard this, Mahendra worshipped the Sun according to the prescribed rites for exactly one month; then, on the full moon day, he beheld him.
The Sun said to Śakra, "I shall perform the work of the gods."
The Bhaṭṭas—those rogues consisting of mere learning—have corrupted the recitation of the Sūtras;
they have taught a distorted Dhātupāṭha with erroneous meanings and phonetics.
Having conquered those heretical Bhaṭṭas, O friend, I shall restore the Veda.
Having spoken thus, he went to the house of Vedaśarman in Kāśī;
born into the lineage of initiated priests, he became known by the name Kāryaguṇa. Having attained the physical form of a twelve-year-old, he became a master of all the śāstras.
He propitiated Śiva, the Lord of the Universe, who is dear to Pārvatī.
At the end of three years, the Blessed One bestowed upon him great knowledge;
by the power of that knowledge, he perceived the supreme, manifest, and unmanifest.
Then, that which is known by the very quality of its effect within the heart of the initiated one—

when the intellect (*buddhi*) resides in the unmanifest— is the twelve-limbed *vidyā*. And when it resides in the manifest, consisting of the ego (*ahaṃkāra*) and the elements, that intellect should be known by the wise as the Unborn (*ajā*).
Ignorance (avidyā) is renowned as having the nature of sixteen limbs;
the Unmanifest is the Supreme Brahman, while the Manifest is remembered as consisting of sound.
Indeed, the Ego (ahaṃkāra), which creates the world, is manifest and possesses eighteen limbs.
The chief one, bearing the form of a bull, is remembered by the wise as Nandīyāna;
that bull has four horns, three feet, two heads,
seven hands, is bound in three ways, is eternally pure, and stands at the mouth.
The nominal stem, the verbal root, the primary derivative (kṛdanta), and likewise the indeclinable—
these two each are known as the two horns on the head of Naṇḍiyāna. Furthermore,
the past, the future, and the present are indeed its three feet.
Conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) and etymological-conventional meaning (*yogarūḍhi*) are the two heads of that Bull;
the agent, the object, the instrument, the recipient,
as well as the relation and the qualification, are indeed its limbs.
A sentence is to be known as that which is endowed with accents, and a word is traditionally defined as ending in a case-ending.
O Lord of Nandi, salutations to You, the Bull who is bound by those two;
situated eternally above Him is that which is unmanifest, in the form of a *liṅga*.

"Having realized within his heart this knowledge— that he himself was Hari, Nārāyaṇa, the sixteen-fold self, possessing many forms yet formless, born from the two marks of a Vṛṣala— he then [composed] the Siddhāntakaumudī."
Having quickly defeated the Bhaṭṭas, Bhaṭṭoji became renowned.
Jīva said:
Formerly, in the beautiful city of Kāñcī, there was an excellent Brāhmaṇa who was an astrologer.
Once, the wise court astrologer said to King Satyadatta, who was devoted to the Vedas:
"This moment called Abhijit is conjoined with the Puṣya asterism."
"O Great King, now provide sustenance that grants many means of livelihood!
Having heard this and having acted accordingly, he caused the proclamation to be made throughout the city with the sound of drums;
O best of gods, listen as he commanded the men.

"Whatever goods have not been purchased in this marketplace by those skilled among the Vaiśyas, know that they have been purchased by me; this word of mine is the truth. Hearing this, the Śūdra people brought various kinds of wealth.

At that time, everything was purchased by the Vaiśyas, for it had indeed become a great market of gold (hāṭa). Once, a blacksmith, having turned his poverty into the form of iron, approached the market and begged for a hundred coins.
The king, having learned that the poor man had not been purchased,
bought him for a hundred coins and brought him home. Then, the poor man was stationed by the king in the treasury.
At midnight, when darkness had arisen, while he was thus looking on, Karma and Dharma emerged from the king's house and departed;
following after them, the Satyapuruṣa spoke this to the king.
O protector of the earth, where there is poverty, one is certainly not devoted to ritual action;
and dharma devoid of ritual action does not remain stable upon the surface of the earth.
Fortune devoid of dharma never shines at all.
"I shall never remain bereft of Lakṣmī.
Having said this, as he wished to depart, the king took him by both hands, bowed low, and spoke these words: "Listen to my truthful and pleasing speech."
"O Lord, you must not be abandoned by me; you ought to command me.
Having heard these words, Satyadeva went home.
Thereafter, Lakṣmī herself prepared to go to his house.
The steadfast king said to her, "O Goddess, you are always fickle;
O Mother, become steady and then enter my palace.
Having heard this and granted the boon, she then went to the king's residence.
Having summoned that family priest and the astrologer, the best of kings gave him a hundred thousand pieces of gold after explaining the entire reason;
for at the time of his son's birth, wealth had indeed arrived for him.
Having spent all his wealth, he nourished the boy;
thus, on an auspicious day in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, he was born under the name Pūṣan.
That son, devoted to the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra), propitiated the Sun.
But Sūrya attained liberation through the grace of the God of gods;
therefore, O Indra of the gods, you too should worship the Sun during the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
Sūta said:
Then, having been honored by the Lord of the Gods, Sūrya himself approached and,
under the name Pūṣan, spoke these words in a sweet voice to the gods:
"O gods, I shall go to Ujjayinī, to the abode of Rudra’s sacrificial animal."

"And by name he shall be Mihirācārya, the founder of the science of astrology. Having spoken thus, the Blessed One Pūṣan was indeed born as the son of the twice-born in the auspicious conjunction of Abhijit, within the region of Mūlagadānta.
As soon as that son was born, his father took him in a wooden basin,
cast him into the middle of the river at midnight, and set it adrift;
the son went to the ocean, protected by rākṣasīs.
Having arrived at Laṅkā, he studied the science of astrology right there—
the Jātaka, the Phalitajyotiṣa, and likewise the Mūkapraśna— from the very beginning;
and having completed his studies, he approached Vibhīṣaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas.
"O King of devotees, obeisance to you, O Vibhīṣaṇa, beloved of Hari!
Having been seized by the Rākṣasīs, I have come to you for refuge.
Hearing this, that king [addressed] the excellent Vaiṣṇava brāhmaṇa.
Having reflected thus, we dispatched him to that land of his birth,

where the Vedic auxiliary science of astronomy— the movement of the celestial bodies— had been destroyed by the Mlecchas; it was by him that this eternal science, which had become divided into three parts, was once again restored.

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origins of Madhvācārya, Śrīdharācārya, Viṣṇusvāmī, Vāṇībhūṣaṇa, Bhaṭṭojidīkṣita, and Varāhamihirācārya," in the Kali-yuga History Compendium, which is an alternative section of the Caturyuga-khaṇḍa within the Pratisarga-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
Having thus spoken of the supreme majesty of the Sun, the Lord Jīva...

Then, at Prayāga, the Lord of Speech spoke again to the gods: "O best of gods, listen to this: in ancient times, at the end of the Tretā Yuga, Sūrya was born in the beautiful city of Pratiṣṭhāna by the command of Hara."
At the end of the Tretā age, there was a king named Parīkṣit in Siṃhaladvīpa;
he was constantly devoted to the Vedic dharma and a worshiper of the gods and guests. His daughter was Bhānumatī, who was entirely dedicated to the vow of the Sun.
With a spirit of devotion, the Lord himself ate every day at her house the auspicious food prepared by her at midday. Once, on a Sunday, that Nalinī went toward the ocean.
Then, as a maiden had come for the purpose of bathing, Nārada arrived;
seeing the beautiful young girl alone in the midst of the water,
he fearlessly seized her garment and spoke these words.
"O fair-browed one, take my hand; I have come under the sway of your glance.
To the sage who had spoken thus, the maiden, with her neck bowed, replied:
"Listen, O divine seer, I am a maiden and you are a bestower of sons."
You are sought after by celestial nymphs in the realm of heaven;
where indeed are Menakā and Rambhā, and where am I, born from a human womb?
Within this body with its nine gates, foul odors always reside.
"Indeed, [such beauty] does not exist even on the bodies of celestial nymphs; therefore, salutations again and again to you.
Having heard these words of hers, Nārada was then ashamed;
he approached Mahādeva and related the entire matter.
Seeing the sage afflicted with leprosy, Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world,
praised the divine Bhāskara; then the Lord appeared,
assuming the auspicious body of Nārada, and spoke to Śiva.
"Give me your command, O Mahādeva; I shall fulfill your wish.
When he had spoken thus, Śiva said to him, "Become a brahmin on earth and take the king's daughter"; and so it was done by Ravi.

Having performed penance daily together with Bhānumatī, Savitṛ has once again attained the solar realm; he is the bringer of light in the month of Pauṣa. O Mahendra, worship him quickly and accomplish the work of the gods.
Sūta said:
Having heard these words of his preceptor, Mahendra, together with the gods,
praised the Sun in the month of Pauṣa with auspicious offerings.
Then the blessed Lord, being pleased, spoke these auspicious words to the gods:
"Today I myself shall become Dhanvantari by name in Kāśī;
[I shall heal] the people on earth who are afflicted by diseases created by the Kali age."

"Having stayed there, I shall bring peace; thus the work of the gods will be accomplished. Having spoken thus, the Blessed Sun arrived at the city of Kāśī, having become the son of the Brahmin Kalpadatta upon the surface of the earth.

Having made the prince Suśruta, accompanied by aged brahmins, his disciple, he, with a serene mind, caused this Kalpa to be composed. This is known by the wise as the Kalpa concerning the body wasted by diseases.
His knowledge is recorded in this tantra as the Kalpavedha;
that Blessed One became renowned as Dhanvantari in the Kali age,
by the mere sight of whom diseases perish instantly.
Having studied that Kalpaveda composed by Dhanvantari, which consists of one hundred chapters, Suśruta composed that treatise known as the Sauśruta-tantra. Bṛhaspati said:

Formerly, in the beautiful city of Paṃpā, there was a brahmin named Helī who was proficient in the sixty-four arts and devoted to the worship of the Sun. Having abandoned the practice of accepting gifts, he adopted the profession of an artisan.
Having mastered the arts of weaving cloth, metallurgy, painting,
and the crafting of images from metal, as well as all other crafts,
he became a master artisan by purchasing these skills for five thousand coins.
Within the span of a single month, he constructed it by himself;
with that wealth, he indeed worshipped the god Ravi with sacrifices during the month of Māgha.
Viśvakarman is Ravi himself, the illuminator in the month of Māgha.
The Lord, daily gratified by sacrifices abundant with clarified butter,
has himself arrived there in the form of light, most beautiful, at the excellent pillar erected upon the lovely Pampā lake.
Having eaten the food offered at midday by the Sun, which is dear to the deities, that Lord,
who is Hari composed of all the gods, sustains the three worlds month after month, O Divākara.
Having become a twice-born man with a lifespan of a thousand years, the Sun himself gave up his life-breaths;
having become so, he sat in the midst of the solar orb and propitiated [the Lord] during the month of Māgha.
O Indra, worship that Sun, and he will accomplish your purpose.
Sūta said:
Having heard these words of his preceptor, Vāsava, together with the deities,
propitiated Sūrya, the supreme Viśvakarman.
Then the blessed Tvaṣṭṛ, pleased and bringing satisfaction to the people, spoke these delightful words to the gods: "O best of gods, listen!
I shall be born in the village of Bilga in the land of Vaṅga as an author of etymological treatises."
"He shall indeed be known as Jayadeva, the crest-jewel among poets.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Sun arrived in the land of Vaṅga;
he was born in the house of a ball-playing Brāhmaṇa upon this earth.
Having become five years of age, he was devoted to his father and mother;
for twelve years, he performed great service to them there. When both parents passed away, he gratified them with the funeral rites.
Indeed, through the Gayā-śrāddha performed by Jayadeva, those two went to heaven.
Then Jayadeva, having become a detached brahmin on this earth,
made his dwelling in that most delightful and sacred forest.
Then, when his twenty-third year had arrived, a certain Brahmin offered a beautiful and auspicious maiden to Jagannātha.
At the conclusion of the worship, the eternal Lord Aniruddha appeared.
The Brahman made of wood spoke to him directly with his own voice:
"Listen, O Satyavrata! Jayadeva is my very body;
by my command, offer your daughter Padmāvatī to him."
Having been addressed thus, the twice-born man, seeing him who embodied dispassion toward worldly existence, quickly established his own daughter there and departed for his home with joy.
That maiden Padmāvatī, however, considering him to be her handsome husband—
Filled with joy, she performed service to him for many years;

he, moreover, composed the Nirukta and the Vedic auxiliary sciences (Vedāṅgas) through meditative absorption. [He explained that] there is the addition of a letter in words such as *gaveṃdra*, and the transposition of letters in the word *siṃha*.
In words such as *pṛṣodara*, there is both a modification and the loss of a phoneme at the beginning of the sixteenth [vowel].

That which is a connection with a verbal root through both the modification and the loss of a phoneme to a superior degree is called by the wise *mayūra-vipulā* (the peacock-expansion) and similar forms.
Thus, these five types of etymological explanations (niruktas) are indeed remembered;

however, in the Kali age, they were corrupted by Śūdras and those of the Nāga lineage. Having defeated the ignorant authors of the Prakrit languages who are fond of the Kali age, [the true meanings were recovered].
Pāṇini indeed composed this pure treatise for the benefit of the gods.
Once, however, the rogue Kali— who dwells in the hearts of those who commit theft—
plundered a great deal of wealth belonging to a brahmin that had been granted by the king.
Thinking Padmāvatī to be unchaste, he abandoned her and went home;
meanwhile, Kali, along with the thieves, cut off the hands and feet of the brahmin.
Then the distressed queen [saw] her husband situated in the middle of a pit.

Having dragged him out, he spoke many harsh words, squeezed him with his hand, and carried him away. One day, the king went out for the purpose of hunting and beheld the sage Jayadeva, who was without hands or feet.
Questioned by him right there, he said:
"O Great King, I am one deprived of hands and feet;
I have arrived here through my own karma; indeed, it was not done by anyone else."
Having heard this, King Dharmapāla placed that best of the twice-born,
along with his wife, upon a palanquin and went to his own home;
having received his initiation, the king had a hall of righteousness constructed for him.
Once, those thieves created by Kali, having become devotees of Viṣṇu,
reached the house of Dharmapāla and spoke thus to the king:
"We are indeed experts in the scriptures, and we have come to your home."

"O best of kings, behold this: the food prepared by us is consumed daily with affection by Viṣṇu himself, who has become a stone image. Having said this, those devotees of Kali [showed him] the four-armed form of Viṣṇu.
They showed the king their own selves, who had been fed by his illusory power (*māyā*).
Astonished, Dharmapāla said to Jayadeva:
"O Guru, Vaiṣṇavas devoted to Viṣṇu have arrived at my palace."
"They have seen Hari manifest before their very eyes; therefore, you must return quickly.
Having heard this, the twice-born man arrived, and the king was likewise struck with wonder.
Then those heretics, laughing, spoke to the king.
O King, that brahmin was once a cook residing in the Gauḍa country; out of greed for wealth,
that man in the guise of a heretic mixed poison into food for him.
Having recognized that brahmin, the king indeed impaled him upon the middle of a stake.
In the meantime, O King, we arrived there;
perceiving the twice-born man to be an offender, we bestowed many [magical] sciences upon him.

Having extracted him from the stake, the king cut off his hands and feet. As soon as these words were spoken— "For the king has become our disciple and was enlightened by us"— she became distressed and torn with grief.
Indeed, she placed those thieves, protected by the gods, in the netherworld (Pātāla).
When Jayadeva saw the thieves thus transformed into spirits, he wept;
as that twice-born man was crying out, his hands and feet returned to their natural state.
He described the entire cause to the astonished king there.
Having heard what issued from the mouth of Jayadeva, the king, with a serene soul,
attained liberation after quickly reciting the *Gītagovinda*.
Thus has it been told to you, O Brahmin, how Jayadeva came to be;
now hear how the life of Kṛṣṇacaitanya arose.

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of Dhanvantari, Suśruta, and Jayadeva," in the *Kaliyugīyetihāsasamuccaya* (the Compendium of Histories of the Kali Age), which is a section of the *Caturyugakhaṇḍa* within the *Pratisargaparvan* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Jīva said:
In ancient times, there was a certain Brahmin named Viṣṇuśarman who had mastered the Vedas;
with a tranquil mind, he worshipped Viṣṇu, who embodies all the gods.
Through his worship of Hari, he became honored by other deities as well;
though he was constantly devoted to the life of a mendicant, he had a wife but was without sons. Once, a certain observer of vows arrived at his house.
Seeing the wife of a twice-born man— alone, humble with devotion, and impoverished— the illustrious one, rich in touch and devoted to compassion, said:
"By means of this touch-stone, even iron ore becomes gold."
"Therefore, O great virtuous lady, accept him for three days.
After bathing in the Sarayū, I shall joyfully come to your side.
Having spoken thus, the Brahmin departed, and the Brahmin woman [received] much gold.
Having completed his task and attained prosperity, Viṣṇuśarman then arrived;
seeing his wife accompanied by much gold, he, the beloved of Hari, said:
"Go, O woman reeling with intoxication, to where there are indeed people who are connoisseurs."
"I am devoted to Viṣṇu and always wretched, for I am perpetually afraid of thieves;
how indeed am I able to take you, who are intoxicated with honey, upon this earth?
Having heard these terrible words, the devoted wife became afraid of her husband.

Having given him a touchstone together with gold, he became intent on serving him. The twice-born man also forcibly cast that wealth into the middle of the Ghargharā river. At the end of three days, that ascetic arrived there filled with joy.

He said to the distressed Brahmin woman, "Why was gold not made by you? She replied, "O sir, my husband, having taken the touchstone, threw it into the Ghargharā river in anger; therefore, I am one who must be cooked in fire."
"O Guru, from that time forward, the Brahmin has lived free from greed.
Having heard these words, the ascetic was filled with wonder;
at the end of the day, standing there, he spoke to the Brahmin, rebuking him severely.
"You are a poor beggar, deluded by fate;
give me my ring quickly, otherwise I shall give up my life.
To the ascetic who had spoken thus, Viṣṇuśarman then replied:
"Go to the bank of the Ghargharā river; there indeed is your tester.
Having said this, he took many thorns along with the ascetic and showed those thorns to the ascetic as if they were testers.
Then that ascetic, bowing with a humble mind, said to the brahmin:
"Indeed, for twelve years I have properly propitiated Śiva;
consequently, by the sight of Him, this auspicious jewel has been obtained by me."

"O twice-born one, through my greedy nature, I experienced many forms of touch. Having spoken thus, Viṣṇuśarman attained auspicious knowledge and reached liberation after dwelling upon the surface of the earth for a thousand years.
Having propitiated the Sun according to the prescribed rites, that twice-born man attained liberation from Viṣṇu; indeed, having assumed the Vaiṣṇava splendor in the month of Phālguna, he,
the lord devoted to the work of the gods, scorched the three worlds.
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Jīva spoke again to the husband of Śacī:
"By propitiating that Sun-god in the month of Phālguna, may you become happy."
Thus addressed by his preceptor, the Lord meditated upon Hari, who pervades all things,
and worshipped the God of gods with various forms of offerings.
Then the Blessed One became pleased and emerged from the solar disc.
Indeed, with four arms and a red body, he was exactly like a yakṣa;
while all the gods were looking on, he entered the body of Śakra.
Then, by his splendor, Śakra caused his own body to dissolve within it.
Having become a twice-born man through improper means, Śacī the goddess likewise became so;
then, joined as a couple and tormented by the Vaiṣṇava fire,
they took their pleasure for a year on the bank of the Gaṅgā in the great forest.
Then the goddess Śacī, appearing in the form of a twice-born woman, conceived the embryo. On the twelfth lunar day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, on a Thursday, within the Brahma-maṇḍala,
Viṣṇu himself, Hari, manifested, assuming all his divine attributes.
He had four arms and a red body, with a luster equal to the sun and a water-pot;
then the Rudras, Vasus, Viśvedevas, Maruts,
Sādhyas, Bhāskaras, and Siddhas praised that Eternal One.
The gods said:

O Lord, we bow to Your foot, which bears the splendor of the thunderbolt, banner, lotus, mace, and goad, adorned with magnificent ornaments; which is the delight of the sages and joined by Brahmā and Śiva; and which removes the fear of worldly existence.
Bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, you are the destroyer of the formidable bodies of the enemies of the gods;
you are the support for the worlds of moving and unmoving beings, yet restless, the annihilator of the wicked, and the performer of the work of the gods.
Salutations to you, O bringer of joy to the son of Śacī, the remover of the difficult-to-eradicate torment of great sins.
Having swiftly slain the enemies of the gods, O Sustainer of the World, you have struck away millions of limbs of sin through your own devotion.
You must truly uphold the Truth in the form of a swan, and you must protect the Veda in the form of the sacrifice.
Indeed, you shall become the sustainer of the world in the form of the sacrifice—the son of Śacī, Śakra, who is intent upon the welfare of all beings.

Having long ago descended into the Kali age out of compassion to bestow upon us the splendor of his own devotion— exalted and radiant in essence— the Son of Śacī, though his beauty is surpassed by the clusters of light from Lord Hari, may he forever shine within the cave of our hearts. You, O Lord, having protected men on earth with compassion, now release them so that they may be led to your own supreme abode, which is higher than the highest.

O Great Lord, O Kṛṣṇa Caitanya, Son of Śacī! Lift up those submerged in the ocean of the afflictions born of the Daityas in this Kali age. With the sweetness of honey, you whose face is fragrant like a forest of golden lotuses, who are nourished by the cascades of the nectar of compassion, and who are the golden mountain of true love—O God, who bears the victorious and unshakable seven-hooded serpent as the garment of the cloud of devotees, the Lord Kṛṣṇa Caitanya Hari reigns supreme as our family deity.
Oppressed by the people who are enemies of the gods and born of unrighteousness, this earth has quickly shrunk; alas, even this body remains only as a seed for the sake of the Kali age.

By your name alone, the enemies of the gods have been shattered, those dwelling in the netherworld are tormented, and the barbarians have become devoted to dharma and intent upon bowing to the Lord of the Gods; salutations to that all-pervading One!
Sūta said:
Having thus praised the Supreme Person, the Lord of Sacrifice, and the Lord of Śacī,
the gods approached Bṛhaspati and spoke these words:
"O highly fortunate one, here are we, the Rudras, as well as these Vasus and the two Aśvins."
"By what respective portions shall we be born upon the surface of the earth?
O Lord, it behoves Your Honor to tell us all that out of compassion.
Bṛhaspati said:
I shall tell you; listen, O best of gods!
In a former birth, there was once a hunter, the lowest of the twice-born, who constantly carried a bow and arrows and harassed brahmins on the road.

Having killed the twice-born ones, that great fool, the wicked one, playfully seized their sacred threads (yajñopavīta); a great outcry was raised by them. And whatever wealth belonged to the Brāhmaṇas, which was unsurpassed and like nectar—
Knowing that honey is the food of the Kṣatriya, food equal to rice for the Vaiśya,
and blood for the Śūdra,
the wicked twice-born man slew many Brāhmaṇas of the three castes.

Terrified on all sides by the destruction of the twice-born, all the gods approached the Supreme Lord (Brahmā) and recounted the cause of their distress. Having heard this, Brahmā was grieved and spoke to the world-traversing Seven Sages.
"O best of the twice-born, go there yourself and give him instruction.
Having heard this, Marīci, accompanied by Vasiṣṭha and the others,
went there and all remained in the forest of the hunter.
But the powerful hunter, seeing them while bearing his bow and arrows, spoke these terrible words: "I shall indeed kill you all today.
Marīci and the others laughed and said, "For what purpose are you prepared to kill us?"
"O one of great strength, speak quickly for the sake of your family or for your own benefit.
Thus addressed, the twice-born man said to them: "For the welfare of my family and myself, I shall kill you along with your wealth, and especially the Brahmins."
Having heard that, those brahmins said to him: "O wielder of the bow, go quickly! Consider this: who would endure the sin committed by the killing of a brahmin?
Having heard this, his soul became terrible, yet he was purified by their gaze.
Having gone there, he said to the members of his lineage, "I have accumulated great sin;
that sin must be accepted by you just as wealth is.
But having heard him, they said to the twice-born man, "We are not partakers of sin."
"This earth is an immovable witness; this supreme sun is a witness.
Having heard this, the hunter, with palms joined in reverence, said to the sages:
"You ought to command me so that my sin may go to destruction."
Thus addressed by him, they said: "Listen to this supreme mantra.
O Rāma, that which is known as your name must be understood as the destroyer of the entire flood of sins. Until we arrive at your side, you should recite this most excellent mantra."
Having spoken thus, those brahmins departed from one sacred ford to another;
meanwhile, he muttered "mara-mara-amara" for a thousand years. By the power of that recitation, the forest became filled with blue lotuses.
That place became famous on earth as Utpalāraṇya. Then the Seven Sages arrived and, seeing that pure brahmin who had been cast out from the anthill, they spoke to him, filled with wonder.
"Since you have emerged from an anthill (*valmīka*), therefore, O brahmin, O high-minded knower of the three times, your supreme name shall be Vālmīki.
Having spoken thus, they departed for their own world, while the sage [remained] to compose the *Rāmāyaṇa*.
Indeed, he composed that pure work, consisting of one hundred crores of verses and eighteen thousand chapters, which destroys the entire flood of sins;
thereafter, having become Śiva himself, he took up residence there.
"Even today the eternal Lord remains established as the Deer-hunter (Mṛgavyādha). And listen, all you gods, to his life-story, which is dear to Hara.
When the Vaivasvata Manvantara had arrived, during the auspicious first age, the Satya Yuga..."
Brahmā, having arrived at Utpalāraṇya, performed a sacrifice there.
Then the goddess Sarasvatī, having become a river, arrived;
upon seeing her, Brahmā himself [produced] an auspicious Brāhmaṇa from his own mouth.

From his two arms the powerful one begot the Kṣatriya, from his two thighs the excellent Vaiśya, and from his two feet the Śūdra of auspicious conduct. Likewise, the king of the twice-born was Soma, the Moon, known by the name Dvija.
In this world, the sun is the most scorching; for he protects the energy of Kaśya.
Indeed, that second one is Kaśyapa, and from him Marīci arose.
He who is truly the mine of jewels is known as Ratnākara.
He who sustains the worlds with his riches is indeed called Dharma by name;
he possesses a treasury as profound as the lord of rivers.
He who protects the worlds through his deeds is Dakṣa, the Lord of Creatures.

They were born from a limb of Brahmā; therefore, they are indeed remembered as Brāhmaṇas. By virtue of their specific duties (varṇadharma), they all gradually became the very essence of the social orders (varṇas).
Then, five hundred daughters were born from the mind of Dakṣa.
Through the power of Viṣṇu’s Māyā, they remained on earth as partial incarnations.
Then the Lord Brahmā bestowed upon Soma the excellent group of twenty-seven constellations for the prosperity of the world.

That great sage gave the group of thirteen beginning with Kaśyapa, who were of the kṣatriya form, to Dharma; and he gave Kīrti and the others as well. Various kinds of created beings came into existence during the Vaivasvata interval.
By the command of Brahmā, Dakṣa became their lord upon this earth;
there, devoted to sacrifice, Dakṣa himself made his dwelling,
and indeed all the hosts of gods move about after paying homage to Dakṣa.
The Great God, the Lord of Beings, never bowed down [to Dakṣa].
Then, becoming enraged, Dakṣa himself did not offer a portion to Śiva.
Śiva, the Hunter of the Deer, grew angry and became Vīrabhadra.
Then Triśiras, who had three heads, three eyes, and three feet, arrived there;
by him alone were the gods, sages, and ancestors tormented.
At that time, the Lord of Sacrifice (Yajñapuruṣa) was terrified on all sides.
Having become a deer, he fled swiftly; seeing him, the hunter became auspicious.
Pierced in his limbs by Rudra as the hunter, that deer indeed fell.
Then the Lord Brahmā praised him with sweet voices.
And the satisfied hunter caused the sacrifice to be completed;
while the sun was situated in the zodiac sign of Libra, Brahmā himself, having installed that Rudra within the lunar orb, [performed it] over a period of twenty-seven days.
Indeed, that Rudra, possessing the form of the Moon, departed for the seven worlds.
Having heard this, Vīrabhadra, his mind filled with joy,
manifested a portion of himself from his own body and dispatched it to the house of the twice-born.

Having gone to the house of the Brahmin Bhairavadatta, that Śiva indeed became his son in this terrible Kali age, renowned by the name Śaṅkara. Even as a child, he was virtuous, learned, and lived as a celibate student (brahmacārī).
Having composed the Śaṅkarabhāṣya, he revealed the path of Śiva;
the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), the rosary, and the auspicious five-syllabled mantra—
brought forth by Śaṅkarācārya— are the bringers of welfare for the devotees of Śiva.

Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "Description of the Birth of Kṛṣṇacaitanya and Śaṅkarācārya," in the Kali-yuga Itihāsa-samuccaya, which is an alternative section of the Caturyuga-khaṇḍa within the Pratisarga-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa.
Now begins the eleventh chapter:
"Description of the Birth of Ānandagiri, Vanaśarman, and Purīśarman."
Bṛhaspati said:
Formerly, in the Naimiṣa forest, there was a brahmin who had become a python;
he was proficient in the Vedānta scriptures, possessed of knowledge, and a worshipper of Śambhu.
Within twelve years, Rudra became pleased by his worship of the earthen image;
then, having arrived, he bestowed upon him knowledge, and [the king] attained liberation while living.
By propitiating Saṅkarṣaṇa through that knowledge, the best of the twice-born—
He praised the Supreme Lord with abundant hymns of praise.
The python said: "The divine Pradhāna is the supreme form of light, formless, unmanifest, eternal bliss."
That [Prakṛti] has become threefold, distinguished by the unity of its three attributes: the male is of the nature of *sattva*, the female is of the nature of *rajas*.
That which remains of those two is indeed of the nature of *tamas*; therefore, salutations to you, O Śeṣa, salutations, salutations!
And *māyā* is the primordial state of the quality *rajas*, while the male is the intermediate state of the nature of *sattva*.
Likewise, you are the internalized neuter state, ever like darkness; O Lord of Nagas, salutations to you!
You are the support of men, the creator of time, the attractor of men, and indeed Saṅkarṣaṇa.
The lords of sages rejoice in you, the abode of Brahman; salutations to you, salutations again to you, let there be salutations to you once more!
"Indeed, that Śivā who is remembered as the foundational support within the limbs of men is your own power, Yoganidrā.
The Jīva said:
"Thus praised by the twice-born, the Lord [spoke] to the serpent."
Rudra united him with his own body, and he indeed became a serpent,
possessing a thousand hoods, fair-limbed and fair-bodied;
his abode was the ocean of milk, which is a mine of virtues.
Having returned personally to that Great Rudra named Sarpa,
while the Sun was situated in the sign of Capricorn and the Moon in the sphere of the constellations,
the Self-born Lord himself established that Rudra there, and he became the Moon.
Having heard these words spoken by the venerable Guru, Śeṣanāga,
with a delighted soul, generated a splendor from his mouth and brought it forth on the Vindhya mountain in the house of the brahmin Devadatta.
That brahmin Giriśarman, having defeated the assemblies of the learned,
arrived at the city of Kāśī and indeed became a disciple of Śaṅkara.
Thus, O brahmin, has been told to you how Rudra came to be.
Listen again, O Brahmin, to the story as told by Jīva.
Jīva said:
"In ancient times, there lived at Prayāga a Brāhmaṇa who was a devotee of Hari."
Afflicted by poverty and ill-fated, he was known by the name Nairṛta.
At the end of each day, he obtained alms from that very person only with great hardship.
Day after day, Nairṛta remained oppressed by poverty along with his wife and son.
Once the yogi Nārada, who is dear to the Vaiṣṇavas, arrived;
having been honored by that brahmin, he departed for the world of Viṣṇu. Having beheld the god Nārāyaṇa, he prostrated himself before him again and again.
With a humble soul, he who was ever dear to the Blessed One spoke these words:
"O Blessed One, all the gods are always devoted to your worship;
and those on earth who are your devotees are endowed with wealth and grain."
"O Lord Janārdana, salutations to you! Tell me, for what reason are your devotees on this earth always seen by me to be afflicted by poverty?
Thus addressed by Nārada, the Blessed One, who is affectionate toward his devotees, [replied].
He spoke these pleasing words to him; listen to them, O best of gods:
"The Lord Brahmā, my devotee, having seen the people dear to Nārāyaṇa and having brought them under his own control, indeed performs the work of the world."
By him, Dharma was created; that Dharma is remembered as consisting of the Vedas.
By that wise one, the seven worlds were fashioned:
Bhūr, Bhuvar, Svar, Mahar, Jana, and Tapas.
Truth likewise bestows happiness upon men in a progressively doubling manner.
Adharma on earth is devoid of the Veda and is produced by those other than the authors of the sacred words;
for those words which have been corrupted by the Great Speech (Mahāvāk) are indeed prevalent among the people.
Those things other than the Vedas, consisting of evil and always increasing the power of the Daityas,
are to be known as unrighteousness (adharma); indeed, the seven worlds were created by the Ordainer within the cavities of the earth as sources of pleasure for that [unrighteousness].
Aṭala, Vitala, Sutala, Talātala,
Mahātala, Rasātala, and Pātāla, which was born of another dharma;
for that other dharma is indeed adharma, and those others who were gods are now the asuras.

The gods are to be known as those belonging to the side of Dharma, while the Asuras are born from other forms of Dharma. That Dharma which is devoid of both of them, corrupted by gods and Daityas alike, is to be understood as Vidharma; therein, the worlds are distressed and agitated.
Tāmisra, Andhatāmisra, Kumbhīpāka, Raurava, Mahāraurava, as well as Mūrti, Ayas,
Ikṣuyantra, Śālmalī, and likewise Asipatravana.

The Creator has fashioned this universe consisting of twenty-one worlds as an object of knowledge; beyond that is My supreme abode. Those who are truly My devotees on this earth go to that supreme state.
Those worlds which are devoted to the gods go to the seven worlds;
whereas those worlds which are characterized by darkness (tāmasa) and intent on the worship of the Daityas, they go to the nether regions such as Bhūrloka, Bhuvarloka, and so forth.
The lower world (adholoka) is proclaimed to extend for one hundred thousand yojanas down from Pātāla;
those worlds are devoted to unrighteousness, and indeed, people go there to a downward state.
Therefore, my devotees who have fallen away from the prescribed rule become poor.
Those who are my devotees, having first worshipped the gods and then worship me,
should be known as prosperous ones, devoted to both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
At Prayāga, there was a Brahmin named Nairṛta who, having abandoned the gods dear to me, [worshipped me].
Because he worships with undivided devotion, he is indeed poor;
for whatever wealth is given by the gods must always be enjoyed by people,
but as for the object given by me, O Nārada, it does not exist within the entire universe.

"Therefore, O Brahmin, at my command, grant him an auspicious boon. Thus addressed by Hari, the creator of the universe, the yogi Nārada went to the house where the brahmin’s wife was staying and spoke these words.
"Choose a boon, O virtuous lady, whatever is desired by you in your heart.
She said, "O Lord, grant me this boon: may I become the queen of the king of the earth.
Having spoken these words there, she assumed a divine form.
The king arrived there and, taking him, went to his home. When evening had set in, the twice-born Nārada arrived there and spoke these words to him: "Listen, O Brahmin, you who are dear to Hari."
"Because of that boon, your wife indeed exists as the queen of the earth.
What object do you desire from me? Having obtained it, be happy.
Hearing these words, he, subject to fate, spoke with anger:
"May she become my wife, a female jackal; O Brahmin, grant me this boon.
Having spoken these words, by his command that beloved of the twice-born became a female jackal. In the meantime, her son, a worshiper of his preceptor, arrived.
Having heard all the reasons for that, he spoke these words to Nārada:
"O Lord, may my mother likewise quickly obtain a boon.
Thus was this attained by those three, who were deluded by the illusory power of destiny (daivamāyā).
Then Nārada, filled with sorrow, spoke these words to the Nairṛta:
"This universe is composed of the gods, and Bhava is its Great Lord (Maheśvara).
Therefore, worship Bhava immediately; he will accomplish your purpose."
Having spoken these words, the brahmin praised that Lord with supreme devotion through offerings to the sovereign for the duration of one year;
then the Blessed Maheśa, who is compassionate toward his devotees, was pleased.
He gave him great, divine wealth equal to that of Kubera. With that wealth, the brahmin indeed performed acts of righteousness;
he became renowned upon the surface of the earth by the name Puṇyajana because of his riches.

By the power of devotion to Śiva, having obtained wealth free from obstacles and having lived for a thousand years, he cast off his life-breaths and went to heaven when the sun was situated in the sign of Taurus,
like King Soma [the Moon] in the presence of Candra.

"Renowned as Nairṛta, Rudra is beloved by all people. Having heard these words spoken by his preceptor, O best of the Bhṛgus, Nairṛta descended to the surface of the earth from his own portion and went to the forest on Mount Girināla.
The son of that forest-dwelling yogi, who was perfected in Sāṃkhya,
became renowned as Vanaśarman; devoted to the Vedas and the Śāstras,
he reached the age of twelve and, having defeated many learned men, [attained preeminence].
Having arrived at Kāśī, Vanaśarman, seeking the ultimate truth, bowed down to the supreme Śaṅkarācārya and became his learned disciple. Bṛhaspati said:
In ancient times, there was a certain twice-born man named Vasuśarman in the city of Māhiṣmatī.
Constantly devoted to the vows of Śiva and desiring a son,
that wise man worshipped the Lord of the Earth for twenty-four years.
O gods, although much time passed there, Śiva did not become pleased.
Then the distressed brahmin, having kindled a terrible fire,
offered his own body’s flesh into it, starting from the mouth down to the feet.
Rudra did not become pleased; then the brahmin, overcome with grief, took an excellent ram and, having purified himself, performed the consecration.
Accompanied by that ram, he approached the blazing fire.
The blessed Lord Rudra, having arrived there accompanied by his attendants, revealed his own form, as beautiful as pure crystal.
He spoke these words to the excellent Vasuśarman: "Choose a boon."
Having heard that, his soul purified, he bowed to the beloved of Pārvatī; becoming humble with modesty, he spoke these words to Śaṅkara:
"O Lord, you who are compassionate toward those who seek refuge, grant me a son."
Thus addressed by him, Śaṅkara smiled and said to that twice-born man:
"Brahmā himself is the giver of sons and the creator of destiny, higher than the highest;
yet for a hundred lifetimes, he has not granted you a son."
"Therefore, O Brahmin, I shall grant you a son from my own portion.
Having said this, Maheśvara withdrew his splendor from his mouth and caused [it] to be born from Vasuvarman through his wife.
Within ten months, a handsome-faced son was born;
one foot was like that of Aja (the Unborn), while the second was like that of a man. Consequently, he became renowned on the earth as Ajaikapād (One-footed Aja).
When his beloved son had reached the age of four hundred years,
the Lord Death arrived, accompanied by hosts of diseases;
indeed, a battle then took place between him and Ajaikacaraṇa.
Having conquered all of them in a mere year,
that man, fierce in the arena of wrestling, became renowned on the surface of the earth by the name Mṛtyuñjaya (Conqueror of Death).
The Lord Death was distressed, having been defeated by that brahmin.
Having approached the Supreme Lord, he related the cause.
Then the Blessed Brahmā, accompanied by all the hosts of gods,
[beheld] the king situated within the lunar orb while the divine sun was in the pitcher (Kumbha) sign.
And he quickly transformed that twice-born man into the form of Rudra, the dispeller of fear.
Sūta said:
Having heard this, Mahādeva and that brahmin then recited the mantra.
The Lord, who effects the purification of the Kali age, arrived at the city of Māhiṣmatī.
Known as Purīśarman, he was indeed the son of Yatidatta;
having become sixteen years of age, he conquered those devoted to the Vedas.
Having approached Śaṅkarācārya, he indeed became his disciple.
Thus, O Brahmin, has been told to you how he became Mṛtyuñjaya.

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of Ānandagiri and Vanaśarman Purīśarman," in the Kaliyuga History Compendium, which is another name for the Caturyuga-khaṇḍa within the Pratisarga-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
Listen again to this delightful story told by Jīva at Prayāga.
In ancient times, there was a Dānava named Hiraṇyākṣa, who was a thorn to the worlds.
Born of the lineage of Nikumbha and possessing prowess equal to Śakra,
he performed austerities for a thousand years and truly tormented the gods.
Then Brahmā, the Lord of the Worlds, exerted himself for the sake of protecting the worlds.
"Choose a boon," he said to the lord of the Danujas.
Having bowed to the Creator, he, with a humble mind, spoke these words:
"O Lord, O All-maker, if a boon is to be granted by you, my master, O All-pervading One..."
"May death not come to me, even by all moving and non-moving beings created by you!
Having been addressed thus, he replied, "So be it," and departed for the world of Brahmā. That fierce-natured Dānava, however, having conquered the inhabitants of heaven—
Having summoned the Dānavas and Daityas from their lairs, he of serene intellect caused them to dwell in heaven; those gods were thus brought down to the surface of the earth,
and all the deities endured supreme calamities for a hundred thousand years.
Once, the wise Nārada, whose soul was absorbed in yoga, seeing the gods who had come before him, spoke these words: "Worship the benefactor of the world;
he is the god Mahādeva, the lord of the universe, and the remover of calamity."
Having heard these words, those gods were filled with wonder;
they honored the God of gods, the Lord of Umā, with earthly offerings.
And eleven years passed for those who were performing that worship.
Then the blessed Maheśa, the benefactor of the world, being pleased,
assumed the form of a *jyotirliṅga* and completely consumed the three worlds;
