yet those who were devoted to the gods and the rest remained amidst that great terror.
Others, however, were reduced to ashes along with the Dānavas. In the meantime, Brahmā, together with Viṣṇu, was filled with joy and praised Mahārudra with hymns originating from the Sāmaveda.
"When the Lord of Day was situated in Gemini, he [Brahmā] created Hirbughna and Mahārudra for the sake of the gods, as well as the Moon, the Maṇḍala, and the Bhūpati.
Having heard this, that Hirbughna prepared himself for the purpose of the gods' mission.
On the delightful Himalaya mountain, there was born a son of Sādyakarman,
known as Bhāratīśa, who was like the Lord of Beauty and proficient in the arts;
having conquered the Vṛndas, he arrived at the city of Kāśī.
Having approached Śaṅkarācārya, he became his disciple and was defeated by him.
Bṛhaspati said:
"The son of Maya, known as Māyī, performed a terrible penance."
Standing on one foot upon the sun for a thousand years with great effort,
he scorched the inhabitants of the worlds with his ascetic heat.
Then the Lord Parameṣṭhin, the Grandfather, was pleased.
For the sake of his beloved, he indeed created three villages in succession:
a golden city, sixteen yojanas in extent, resembling heaven;
and beneath that, at a distance of one yojana, a silver city belonging to Bhuvarloka.
And at the end of a yojana below that, there was an iron realm like the earth;
thus, the wives of the Daityas dwelling in those cities lived with joy,
while hundreds of millions of righteous-souled Daityas resided there.
Having received their sacrificial portions, they became equal to the gods.
Then the gods, rendered powerless and afflicted by hunger,
praised the Lord, the Blessed Mahāviṣṇu, with supreme speech.
O Lord, O Master, groups of years consisting of four yugas remain in the celestial realm devoid of their authority;
even within the period of darkness (tāmasa), there are sixteen such sets of four yugas.
"O Mahāviṣṇu, many [ages] have passed while we, practitioners of illusion, have been experiencing suffering.
Having heard these words of theirs, and having observed in the refined discourse that the Daityas were devoted to righteousness, the Blessed Lord Madhusūdana [spoke].
When the terrifying Kali age arrived, Janārdana himself was born in the form of a Buddha; having become the son of the twice-born Ajina,
the heroic one deluded the brahmins who were devoted to the Vedic dharma.
Devoid of discernment and devoid of ritual action, those of the three castes became characterized by darkness during the interval [of the Kali age].
When the sixteenth [cycle], the Kali age, arrived, they became bereft of sacrifice;
then all the Daityas dwelling in Tripura were possessed by wrath.
They oppressed human beings who were devoid of sacrifice and bereft of the Vedas;
all men went to their destruction, devoured by the Daityas at the end of the kalpa.
Then, when the Satya Yuga arrived once more, [the gods resided] on Kailāsa, the abode of the Guhyakas.
Worshipped by the gods, Śambhu, the bringer of auspiciousness to all the worlds,
assumed the form of a *jyotirliṅga* and remained there, appearing formidable. In the meantime, the gods became gratified within that darkness.
Having taken the essence of the earth, they fashioned a chariot according to the prescribed rules;
likewise, having taken the essence of the moon and the sun, they made the two wheels;
and having taken the essence of Mount Sumeru, they indeed made it the banner of the chariot.
He gave that great vehicle in the form of a chariot to Śiva.
Then Brahmā himself arrived and became the charioteer;
and the Vedas indeed became the horses for the chariot of the God of gods.
The essence of the Lokāloka mountain became the bow of that great-souled one;
it was a formidable bow, renowned by the name Ājagava.
The Blessed One strung that great and rigid bow.
The bow of the God of gods indeed broke asunder out of his wrath.
Then the Lord Viṣṇu, filled with wonder at that essence of heaven,
quickly seized the divine Pināka bow and strung it.
The great bow, which was born strung by Rudra and had become full of vigor,
was then praised in their minds by the gratified Brahman-sages;
and thus Maheśvara became renowned by the name Pinākin.
The string of that bow was indeed Śeṣa, and Śakra became the arrow;
Agni and Vāyu were the two feathers of the shaft, and the eternal Viṣṇu was the barb.
By that arrow, tens of millions of Daityas were slain in the sky.
Śiva caused Tripura, which was protected by a master of illusion, to be consumed by fire; when that terrible city had been reduced to ashes, Vidhi, the Lord of the Worlds,
[praised] Mahārudra, the wielder of the Pināka bow, while the sun was situated in the zodiac sign of Pisces.
He made him the king of the lunar disc itself;
then, during that period of darkness, the gods regained their respective domains.
Sūta said:
Having heard this, the wielder of the Pināka bow produced from his own mouth an excellent portion of himself and established him at the gateway of Hara on the snowy peak;
there he became a yogi named Macchanda, devoted solely to Śambhu.
The splendor from the mouth of Gorakha’s guru entered there; indeed, the celestial courtesan named Rambhā, capable of assuming any form at will,
became overwhelmed by passion and, having brought Macchanda under her control, enjoyed him.
From them was born a son of radiant countenance, renowned as Nāthaśarman; he became a learned man of the highest excellence. Having defeated scholars on the earth, he arrived at the city of Kāśī.
He had a disciple who was indeed conquered by Śaṅkarācārya.
Bṛhaspati said:
When the twelfth Dvāpara Yuga of the Cākṣuṣa Manvantara had arrived...
The Tālajaṅghīya Kṣatriyas, having seized vast wealth, destroyed the Brāhmaṇas born of the Bhṛgu lineage at Kurukṣetra;
those powerful and most base partisans of the Daityas then enjoyed [the spoils].
The wife of a certain sage, pregnant and filled with fear, approached Himavat; there,
that goddess, whose form was knowledge through asceticism, bore that child born of the sage for a hundred years.
Having split his mother’s thighs, the son was born upon the surface of the earth;
by the splendor of that son, the entire world was reduced to ashes.
Then all the gods, placing Prajāpati at their head, [approached him].
And the Vaitālas, established like adamant, arrived there, overcome with fear;
the child had been commanded by the Pitṛs and the deities on the Himālaya mountain.
He then cast that splendor, which was capable of destroying the world, into the midst of the water.

And the goddess Jaladevī, having become a mare and drunk that supreme energy, vomited it right there, being oppressed by that fierce radiance. Then Brahmā himself came to the mountain Trikuṭa where that [energy] was located.
The protector of the world established him beneath the terrible ocean;
when the sun had entered Aries, the Supreme Lord Pitāmaha quickly made that Rudra dwell within the lunar disc.
He who was born from the thighs is remembered as Vaurva, the burner [of the world] at the end of the cosmic dissolution;
that lord, born from the mouth of the mare, is named Vāḍava.
Sūta said:
Having heard these enchanting words of his preceptor,
the Fire-god generated his own splendor from his mouth and created Kurukṣetra;
indeed, that Śiva was born in the house of the Brahmin Sārasvata.
There was one renowned as Kṣetraśarman, the most excellent among the learned.
Having approached Śaṅkarācārya and become his disciple, he was defeated [in debate];
remaining a celibate student (brahmacārī) in Kāśī, he remained devoted solely to Śambhu.

Bṛhaspati said: In ancient times, when the world had become a single ocean and all moving and unmoving things had perished, when a hundred years of Brahmā— who is born from the unmanifest and dwells in the worlds— had elapsed.
Having joyfully drunk all the waters, the unmanifest Prakṛti, known as Māyā,
herself became Mahākālī, whose form is that of darkness;
she alone remained there in that primordial state, formidable at the end of the kalpa.
During that terrible dissolution lasting for sixty million times ten million cycles of the four yugas, time passed away;
yet at that time, the Goddess Prakṛti remained eternally pure and eternal.
And by her own will, Śivā assumed her own unsurpassed form, which was intensely white, five-faced, ten-armed, and three-eyed;
with the eye on her forehead, that Mother beheld a subtle radiance.

Then the Supreme Brahman, which is void-like, eternal, unchanging, and stainless, pervaded all directions. At that time, Prakṛti, as she had been before, desired to seize it with her own arms, but she was truly unable to do so.
The mother Prakṛti, filled with wonder, praised the eternal one who is higher than the highest for a long time with supreme devotion;
she used verbal roots originating from the eastern face and suffixes originating from the southern face.
She is the stable one through words consisting of case-endings (*suvibhakti*) produced from the mouth and the west;
she is the eternal one through joy by means of words consisting of verbal suffixes (*tiṅvibhakti*) produced from the mouth and the north;
and she is the stainless one through sounds consisting of vowels (*varṇa*) and measures (*mātra*) produced from the sky and the mouth.
The eternal, perfect Brahman, a mass of truth, consciousness, and bliss, was pleased; that omniscient one entered into five faces. Brahman became the Puruṣa, and his name became Svayambhū.
He is indeed remembered as having an unmanifest birth, for he was born from the unmanifest Prakṛti.
For his sake, the Goddess herself, the bestower of boons who assumes the form of the world,
Mahālakṣmī, was born from his eastern half, possessing sixteen abodes.
Her eighteen arms were intent upon protecting the world;
seeing that wondrous form, the Self-Existent One (Brahmā) was filled with amazement.
Having entered [her] and become manifold, he did not reach her end.
Because of his greatness and manifold forms, he is renowned by the name Brahmā.
Having performed his labors, the blessed Lord Brahmā, established in Satyaloka,
praised Śaṅkara with the Vedas emerging from his mouths.
For a long time, indeed, rivers and streams arose from his body;
then everything became a single ocean, and the Lord himself lay there.
Having dwelt there for the duration of a thousand yugas, he, whose nature is unmanifest, remained himself.
Having ascended to Satyaloka, he indeed performed creation once more;
infinite creations arose, each distinct and in the form of hosts of attendants.
Through them, the entire manifest world became composed of Mahālakṣmī.

Seeing the vastness of the created beings, the eternal Mahālakṣmī was filled with wonder and approached the Blessed Lord, the Master of All. Having bowed down, she spoke these charming words to Kṛṣṇa, the unmanifest source of auspiciousness: "O Blessed One, O eternally pure-souled one, men have indeed become exceedingly great."
"And how should their enumeration always be performed by me?
Having heard these words of hers, that imperishable one became twofold;
from his upper half he was red-limbed, and from the other half he possessed a fair form.
He has four arms, red limbs, and a fair complexion; he is the four-armed Lord Bhava, the master of all the hosts of creation. He is renowned by the name Gaṇeśa and is celebrated as Īśvara.
He who is indeed the four-armed one, the stainless one to be meditated upon by yogis—
that Śiva, the beloved of Pārvatī, was once born according to the ordinance;
he worshipped Gaṇeśa with great effort for a thousand years.
Then the blessed Lord Gaṇeśa, the worshiper of Śarva, being pleased,
said to Hara who was accompanied by Pārvatī, "Choose a boon. With a humble mind, Bhava himself, his soul delighted, offered praise.
Śiva said:
Salutations to Gaṇeśa, whose nature is Viṣṇu, the Supreme Self;
who has four arms, who is red in hue, and whose hands are full of sacrifice.
Salutations to you, the destroyer of obstacles, the sustainer of the world, the bestower of all bliss, the lord of supernatural powers (siddhis), and the lord of treasures.
Be gracious, O Lord of Gods; become my beloved son.
Having heard this, Gaṇeśa, the first worshipful one and lover of his devotees—
who had arisen from the mass of splendor issuing from Pārvatī’s entire body—
then [spoke] on the peak of Kailāsa in the presence of all the gods, including Indra.
They arrived at the temple of the God of gods for the sake of auspiciousness,
and there was a great festival there that brought happiness to all the worlds.
In the meantime, Śani himself, the son of the Sun, [arrived] there.
The one with a cruel gaze, the very embodiment of Time, arrived at the pavilion of the gods;
by the mere sight of him, that boy became headless, and a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose on Kailāsa, the abode of the Guhyakas.
And that head indeed shines upon the earth for twenty-seven days when the sun is situated in Libra in the world of the moon;
there, Saturn, censured by the deities, brings fear to the people.
Having severed the head of the elephant, which possessed a single tusk that was the very form of passion,
the one born of the Sun placed it upon the neck of his son amidst the blood.
Then Brahmā, praised by the elephant-birth, [severed] the head of the crab.
But having placed him [within her], that womb became a crab and was deprived of its head;
thus Gaṇeśa himself was born with the face of an elephant.
Sūta said:
Having heard these excellent words of his preceptor,
Gaṇeśa raised his shoulder from his own mouth;
he was born in Kāśī as the son of a twice-born astrologer, possessing an auspicious countenance.
Thereupon, he became famous on the earth by the name Ḍhuṇḍhirāja;
having composed the astronomical treatise on results known as the *Jātakābharaṇa* for the sake of protecting the Vedas, he approached Śaṅkarācārya.
Having become a disciple with a serene soul, he became devoted to the service of his guru.
Thus, O Brahmin, has been told to you how Ḍhuṇḍhirāja came to be.

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of Ḍhuṇḍhirāja at the Sacred Site of Gorakhanātha in Bhārata," in the *Kaliyugīyetihāsasamuccaya* (Compendium of Histories of the Kali Age) within the *Caturyugakhaṇḍa* (Section on the Four Ages), which is part of the *Pratisargaparvan* (Section on Re-creation) of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the thirteenth chapter:
A Description of the Birth of Hanumān Bhairava of the Aghora Path, the Greatness of Rudra, and the Origin of Bālaśarman.
Bṛhaspati said:
When the sixteenth year of Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest, had arrived,
he dwelt within the lotus and remained intent upon the task of creation. In the meantime, Śāradā emerged from his mouth.
Seeing her two divine limbs so beautiful, Brahmā was overcome by passion;
seized by the god of love, he forcibly took hold of the maiden and said, "O you who reel with intoxication, grant me pleasure! Save me, who am overwhelmed by desire!"
Having heard this, the mother spoke in anger to the Grandfather:
"This inauspicious five-faced one is not fit for your neck;
rather, the four-faced one, who is composed of the Vedas, is fit for you, the Lord of All."
Having spoken thus, the Mother vanished; Brahmā became filled with wrath.
By the fire of his anger, the water on earth became parched.
When that anger was pacified, the terrifying Rudra was born.
The one renowned as Bhairava, whose nature is Time and who has seven mounts,
having cast off that fifth head with his own claws which resembled those of a man-lion,
the powerful Rudra, Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, roared aloud.

Then Brahmā, terrified with fear, went for refuge to Bhairava. "O Lord, [protect] us who have become sinful; [salutations to] Him who shall impel our intellects. Having heard this, the Blessed One Bhairava, world-renowned, [responded].
"O Lord, I have come to you, who have become Brahman, the most excellent one.
We meditate upon that excellence of the divine Savitṛ, which is his splendor.
He wept intensely and loudly, and immediately drops of tears fell from his eyes.
Then trees grew forth, each consisting of individual rudrākṣa beads.
Fearing the sin of killing a brāhmaṇa, Śiva took that skull;
thus Bhairava became renowned by the name Kapālī.
Having quickly visited all those sacred sites and shrines that exist throughout all the worlds, Śivaṅkara did not become purified.
Once, the Blessed Lord Hara was stationed among those trees.
Then, having cast far away the sin of killing a Brahmin,
Śambhu, from that time forward wearing the supreme Rudrākṣa,
arrived at the city of Kāśī; by him, the skull was liberated.
The sacred ford named Kapālamocana, which destroys all sins, came into being.
In the meantime, Brahmā, accompanied by all the gods,
arrived and praised Mahādeva with hymns and eulogies.
When the Lord of Day was situated in Capricorn, the Blessed Vidhi created the auspicious Īśvara Śaśin, the Skull-bearer Mahārudra. Sūta said:
Having heard these words of the Guru, Bhairava Śiva, the bearer of the skull (Kapālī), produced a portion of himself from his own mouth; he was indeed born in Kāśī, not from a womb.
Having emerged from the Kuṇḍa known as Kapālamocana onto the surface of the earth, [he remained there].
The renowned ascetic Bhairava, a treasure-house of the Vedas,
exhorted his disciples toward the formidable and rigorous path;
having approached Śaṅkarācārya, that Bhairava became his disciple.
He indeed composed the tantra named Ḍāmara, which is the essence of mantras;
by it, those mantras that were obstructed were set free.
Bṛhaspati said:
Mandodarī, the daughter of Maya and sister of the lord of Tripura,
remained hidden when Tripura was destroyed; then that goddess, filled with devotion, praised the eternal Mahāviṣṇu every single day.
Then, having attained the most excellent yoga with Hari through the state of devotion,
she vanished right there in that formidable cave of the Vindhya mountains.
Two hundred cycles of four yugas passed for her while she remained in meditative absorption.
When the Vaivasvata interval had arrived, specifically during the twelfth Kṛta Yuga,
Viśravas, the son of Pulastya and grandson of Brahmā, was born from his wrath;
that sage named Viśravas performed austerities for a hundred years.
Then Pulastya, who was Viśravas, having joyfully married Kaikasī, the daughter of the Daitya Sumālī, according to the prescribed rites,
dwelt in the delightful Kadalī grove on Mount Gandhamādana.
The venerable sage Viśravas took his pleasure with her, and from them were born two Rākṣasas:
Rāvaṇa and Kumbhakarṇa.
Of these, Rāvaṇa was devoted to his mother, while his younger brother was devoted to his father.
Seeking boons, the two of them performed severe penance for a thousand years.
Then the Lord Parameṣṭhin, the Grandfather, was pleased and granted them a delightful boon, one that could not be overcome by gods or dānavas.
Having obtained their boons, those two heroes, filled with rage, seized the supreme aerial chariot Puṣpaka by force and fought one another;
by them the gods were utterly defeated and abandoned heaven, the bestower of happiness.
Residing on Kailāsa, they worshipped Śiva with earthly offerings;
having propitiated the Lord of Girijā for eleven years,
those gods obtained a boon from Śaṅkara and then became free from fear.
And Śiva, too, was born from his own left half on Mount Mānasottara,
where the goddess born of Gautama’s body resides—
the one renowned by the name Añjanā, who is the mother of monkeys, lions, and serpents.
Then a fierce and terrible radiance entered the mouth of the lion;
yet the lord of monkeys, afflicted by love, consumed that woman of auspicious countenance.
In the meantime, Vāyu entered the body of the lord of monkeys.
He forcibly took pleasure with the radiant Añjanā, who was his desired object;
thus, twelve years passed while the couple remained in union. Thereafter, having conceived the embryo, she indeed carried it for one full year.
A son was born who was passionate in nature; he was Rudra with the face of a monkey.
Because of his ugly form, he was then cast down from the mountain by his mother.
Coming there by his own power, the mighty one saw that the sun had appeared.
Having drawn [the figure], the Lord Rudra arrived there;
even though struck by the thunderbolt, he did not then abandon the Sun.
Then, terrified with fear, the tall one cried out, "O Sun, save me!"
Hearing those words of distress, Rāvaṇa, the "Roarer of the World," seized that monkey by the tail and engaged him in a fist-fight.
Then the son of Kesari, filled with rage, abandoned the sun.
He engaged in a most terrible hand-to-hand struggle for the duration of a year;
there Rāvaṇa became exhausted and terrified on all sides,
intent on flight as he was struck by the Rudra-like monkey.
In the meantime, the venerable sage Viśravas arrived;
with hymns consisting of the Vedas, he praised the God with a supreme voice.
Then Rudra, being pleased, [addressed] Rāvaṇa, the one who makes the worlds cry out.
Having abandoned his dwelling on the shore of Lake Pampā, the powerful one remained there like a pillar; because he stood there like a pillar, he thereafter became known by the name Sthāṇu.
Meanwhile, Rāvaṇa, the "roarer of the worlds," continued to strike down the chief gods.
He who strikes with his fists and is not renowned as Hanumān—that monkey’s ascetic power has pleased the Lord Brahmā. With a humble mind, he spoke these words: "Listen, O Rudra, treasury of penance!"
When the Vaivasvata interval has arrived, in the twenty-eighth yuga,
during the first quarter of the Tretā age, Rāma will manifest in person.
Having attained devotion to him, you shall have fulfilled your purpose.
Having spoken thus, he gave him the moon that illuminates the month of Bhādra;
and according to the ordinance, Mandodarī, his beloved and beautiful wife, was given to Rāvaṇa.
And Rāvaṇa became the guardian of the quarter of the Nairṛtas.
"Having met with death due to a short lifespan at the hands of Rāma in the form of a monkey," Sūta said:
"Having heard this, Hanumān, who was not born from a womb, [remained] in the Kadalī forest."
Having become incarnate on earth, he became renowned as Bālaśarman;
he arrived at the city of Kāśī where Maṇikarṇikā is located.
In the tradition of Rāma he is Bālaśarman, but in the tradition of Śiva he is Śaṅkara.
For the duration of a single month, there was a most excellent debate on the meaning of the scriptures between those two;
Bālaśarman was defeated by the ascetic Śaṅkarācārya,
and having become his disciple, he remained right there, devoted to the service of his guru.
"He who composed the Tantra-mantra consisting entirely of discourses on the castes.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Birth of Aghora-patha, Bhairava, and Hanumān, and the Origin of Bālaśarman, along with the Greatness of Rudra," in the *Kaliyuga-itihāsa-samuccaya*, which is an alternative section of the *Caturyuga-khaṇḍa* within the *Pratisarga-parvan* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the fourteenth chapter.
Description of the Greatness of Rudra.
Bṛhaspati said:
When this visible world did not exist—neither being nor non-being, nor that which consists of both;

That splendor consists of the syllable, its form is all-pervasive and inconceivable; it is neither gross nor subtle, neither cold nor hot, and is supreme. It is devoid of beginning, middle, and end, and is not characterized by even the slightest form.
The supreme, eternal object of vision for the yogi is the Void (śūnya), which is higher than the highest.
Indeed, Māyā is the single primordial nature (prakṛti); the line situated below that is known as consisting of the Great Principle (mahattattva). And below that are the upward-pointing lines.
Consisting of *rajas*, *sattva*, and *tamas*, it is well-characterized by the syllable *Om*.
That supreme Brahman, known as *Tat-Sat*, is to be realized, reaching which there is no rebirth.
And after some time, His desire was fulfilled.

From that, ego (ahaṅkāra) was born; from that, the subtle elements (tanmātras); and from those, the five gross elements (pañcabhūtāni). Furthermore, because of the distinction between cognition (jñāna) and consciousness (vijñāna), the all-pervading Lord, who consists of His own will, beheld the twenty-two insentient entities.
Having become dualized and endowed with qualities, He arrived as the intellect (buddhi) and the individual soul (jīva).
From the first half [of the syllable], he who possesses qualities (saguṇa) arose; from the second half, he who is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa).
From those two, all that was grasped became consciousness (caitanya);
thus the eternal living being (jīva), known as Virāṭ, was born.
From the navel of Virāṭ was born a lotus extending for a hundred yojanas;
from that lotus was born a supreme flower one yojana in width,
and from that lotus-flower was born Virañci, whose seat is the lotus.
The Lord Brahmā, who has two arms, four faces, and two feet, should be known as having his seven limbs extended; he attained great contemplation, wondering:
"Who am I? From what cause? Whence have I come? Who is my mother? Who is my father?"
Reflecting thus in his heart upon that Lord, he spoke with words imbued with great significance:
"Austerity must indeed be practiced for the removal of doubt.
Having heard this, Viṣṇu himself performed most intense penance.
Having meditated with effort for a thousand years upon the eternal Viṣṇu—
the four-armed one, accessible through yoga, devoid of qualities yet the expansion of all qualities—
the Lord Brahmā, seated upon the lotus, became established in profound meditative absorption (samādhi).
In the meantime, Viṣṇu, having become a four-armed child with a dark-complexioned body,
powerful and adorned with divine ornaments,
Hari stood upon the lap of Brahmā, just as a son himself stands upon his father's lap.
Then, having awakened and seeing him, Brahmā was overcome with delusion. With a serene mind, Brahmā spoke the words, "O child, O child! Then Viṣṇu, smiling, said, "O Brahmā, I am your father."
While they were thus disputing, Rudra was born, composed of darkness;
he was a fiery *liṅga* that inspired fear, extending for infinite *yojanas*.
At that time, Brahmā took the form of a swan and the Lord, the Master, took the form of a boar.
Having been born one after the other, one above and one below, for a hundred years with great effort, they returned filled with shame; then, having approached him with joy, they praised him.
Praised by them, Hara, the manifest Bhava, appeared before them in person.
Having made Kailāsa his abode, he became established in meditative absorption. Five divine yugas passed there while Rudra remained in yoga. In the meantime, the terrible Dānava Tārakāsura appeared.
Having performed austerities for a thousand years, he obtained a boon from Brahmā:
"A son born from the seed of Bhava shall bring about your death.
Thinking thus, he conquered the gods and then became Mahendra.
Those gods, having gone to Kailāsa, offered praise to Rudra.
Then Śiva said to the gods, "Choose a boon.
Having heard this, they bowed with their necks bent and spoke these words.
"O Blessed One, a boon was indeed granted by Brahmā to Tāraka:
'A son born from the seed of Śiva shall be your death.
Therefore, O Blessed One, protect us; O Śaṅkara, perform the marriage."
Formerly, in the Svāyambhuva Manvantara, there was a Prajāpati named Dakṣa. From him were born sixty daughters, among whom Satī was the most excellent.
For one year, she worshipped you with earthly offerings.
A boon was granted by you to her, and she became your beloved. Because of the censure directed at her by her father, whose vision was clouded by ignorance,
the virtuous goddess Satī abandoned her own body.
Then a divine and terrible splendor belonging to Satī descended upon the Himālaya;
afflicted by it, the king of mountains became overwhelmed by passion.
With his mind agitated by desire, he praised the Lord of the Pitṛs.
Then Aryaman, being pleased, gave him his own daughter,
Menā, who was enchanting and pure; seeing her, he became filled with joy,
having assumed a beautiful human form that was god-like and dear to her.
He sported with her for a long time in the great forest;
then a beautiful and excellent embryo was conceived, which reached maturity at the end of nine years.
Then a daughter was born, fair-browed, fair-complexioned, and virtuous.
As soon as she was born, that girl became nine years of age;
she had propitiated you, Lord Śaṅkara, with penance for a long time.
She remained submerged in water for a hundred years and stayed within the fire for a hundred years.
For a hundred years she remained in the wind, for a hundred years she remained in the sky;
for a hundred years she remained in the moon, and for a hundred years in the solar orb;
and for a hundred years that virtuous Girijā remained within the womb of the earth.
Having entered the Great Principle (mahattattva) for a hundred years by the power of yoga,
she beheld you, the pure Śaṅkara, there and has remained until today;
thus three hundred years have passed since then, therefore [seek] Pārvatī, the auspicious Śivā.
"O Mahādeva, grant a boon with a gracious soul; salutations be unto you!
Having heard these pleasing words, Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, then spoke these words to the gods: "Indeed, your request is an improper word."
Those Rudras who are my elder brothers, who observe the vow of celibacy (kumāra-vrata),
and who are the principal ones such as Mṛgavyādha and others born from the ten lights— I am their younger brother, named Bhava, the sovereign of yoga.
How can I accept this auspicious woman, who is a form of illusion and the giver of the world?
This goddess is the woman herself; by her all this is pervaded. She should be known as the Mother-form to the yogis dwelling in the world.
"I am a yogi; how could I possibly restrain a woman, even my own mother?
Therefore, for your sake, I shall deposit my seed.
Upon receiving that seed, the Lord Fire will accomplish the task."
Having spoken thus, the Lord bestowed his unsurpassed seed upon Agni;
the Blessed Lord Hara himself then became absorbed in meditative concentration there.
At that time, Śakra and the other gods departed together with Agni.
Having arrived at Satyaloka, they all spoke to Prajāpati.
Upon hearing the entire reason for that, the four-faced Svayambhū,
having offered salutations to the Supreme Brahman, became intent on meditating upon Kṛṣṇa.
Having traveled by way of meditation to the supreme state of Brahmā,
the Blessed One described the cause exactly as it had been spoken by Śaṅkara;
having heard this, the Blessed One smiled and emitted a supreme radiance from his own mouth.
Then, having been produced from that, a man with a beautiful face was born;
the splendor that indeed resided in the cosmic egg became the body of that great-souled one,
and the name Pradyumna became renowned for him.
Then Brahmā, having regained his own body together with him,
gave to them that Puruṣa Pradyumna, the tormentor of Śambara.
By the splendor of that god, men and women on all sides [were transformed].
Afflicted by passion, all beings in the three worlds became united;
even the immobile and gentle creatures, tormented by the fire of desire,
came together with rivers and creepers.
Śiva, the Lord of the Cosmic Egg, was Rudra himself, resembling the fire of universal destruction;
producing radiance from his third eye, he quelled that agony.
Then, becoming enraged, he whose body was dark blue took up his flowery bow.
To his kinsman Mahādeva, he offered five divine and terrible arrows:
by the arrow of eradication (*uccāṭana*), the benefactor of the world departed;
by the arrow of subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*), Śiva became subject to women.
By the act of paralyzing, Mahādeva became motionless at the side of Śivā; by the act of attracting, the Lord became intent on drawing Śivā toward him;
and by the very arrow of slaying, Maheśvara fell into a swoon.
In the meantime, the auspicious Goddess, who was established in the principle of Mahat,
vanished on the spot upon seeing Śiva unconscious.
Then, having risen, Mahādeva lamented repeatedly and intensely.
"Alas, my beloved with a moon-like face! Alas, O auspicious one with pot-shaped breasts!
Alas, O Umā of beautiful luster! Protect me, who am overwhelmed by passion.
Grant me your vision, O lady with thighs like plantain stalks; I have now become your slave."
While he was thus lamenting, the Yoginī Girijā herself approached; and Śaṅkara, having bowed to his beloved, spoke these words to him:
"O Blessed Lord, O God, I am a maiden who follows the will of my mother and father."
"O Blessed One, accept my hand from their presence!
Thinking "So be it," Śiva, though tormented by Pradyumna’s arrows, dispatched the Seven Sages; they, having gone to the Himālaya mountain, [spoke].
Having addressed him, they joyfully performed the rites of marriage.
Maheśvara is the lord of all those gods who reside within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa);
when his marriage arrived, all the gods assembled there.
Then Himācala, the king of mountains, seeing Ananta, the Gaṇas, and the gods,
himself sought refuge with Girijā and stood there.
At that time, the goddess Pārvatī [beheld] the treasures and the Siddhis all around her.
There, the eternal one assumed many forms by the millions.
Seeing this, the gods, along with Brahmā, were struck with wonder and, filled with joy,
praised the goddess Pārvatī, the eternal jewel among women.
The gods said:
O Umā, you are indeed perceived as Lakṣmī in many forms;
therefore, your name is Umā. Salutations to her, salutations again and again!

O Auspicious One, within this cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), you alone are to be known as Kātyāyanī; salutations to her, salutations again and again. Because of your fair complexion you are Gaurī, and because of your dark complexion you are Kālikā.
To her who is red in color, Haimavatī, salutations to her, salutations again and again!
You are indeed Bhavānī, the beloved of Bhava, united with Rudra;
you are Durgā, difficult for even yogis to attain—salutations to her, salutations again and again!
"We could not reach the end of them; she is indeed renowned by the name Caṇḍikā. You are our Mother, our very source of being; salutations to her, salutations again and again.
Having heard this hymn of theirs, the granter of boons, the embodiment of all auspiciousness, [spoke].
She said to the gods with joy, "I shall remove your fear of the Daityas;
being well-pleased by this hymn on the surface of the earth, I shall grant my favor.
Having spoken thus, she departed for Kailāsa, the abode of the Guhyakas, accompanied by Śambhu.
Having united in the cave, he indeed sported for a thousand years.
In the meantime, the gods, fearing the destruction of the worlds,
placed Brahmā at their head and praised the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain.
Then, filled with shame, the two of them felt remorse;
great anger arose within them, and because of it, the gods indeed fled.
But the powerful Pradyumna remained there, as immovable as a mountain.
Burned by the fire of Rudra’s wrath, Pradyumna then became exceedingly powerful; having abandoned his physical form which was composed of ashes,
he attained a subtle body and became renowned as Anaṅga.
The omnipresent Lord Smara assumed a body exactly as he had before;
the goddess Rati, in her gross form, propitiated Śaṅkara— the beloved of the Daughter of the Mountain— for a hundred years through meditation and vows.
Then the eternal God granted a boon to her for the sake of Rati:
"O Goddess Rati, listen; you shall indeed be born within the hearts of people when they have reached the age of youth, through their bodies, longing for their own husbands."
"You shall enjoy half of me, Pradyumna, who is born from Kṛṣṇa.
The period of the Svārociṣa Manvantara has passed,
and now the Vaivasvata Manvantara has arrived during its twenty-eighth Yuga."

And at the end of the Dvāpara age, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa will be born in person. Then, you shall worship his divine son Pradyumna for a long time with ease upon the summit of Mount Meru, in the delightful Nandana grove.
In other ages ending in Dvāpara, he indeed exists on earth as the Lord with a golden womb (Svarṇagarbha), being born just like Kṛṣṇa;
this occurs at midday and at the twilight of Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest.
"In every kalpa, Hari himself shall manifest as the auspiciousness of all beings.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Śambhu vanished on the spot;
the King became Rudrāṇī, and Bhava became the beloved of Girijā.
Sūta said:
Having heard this, Bhava himself then produced his own supreme portion from his own mouth and became manifest on earth at the Godāvarī.
A son named Bhavānśaka was born in the house of Ācāryaśarman;
he indeed became the younger brother of Rāmaśarman by name.
Once, Rāmaśarman, established in the system of Patañjali, [spoke].
Having traveled from one sacred ford to another, he reached the city of Kāśī, beloved of Śiva.
Accompanied by a hundred disciples, he approached Śaṅkarācārya; there, Kṛṣṇapakṣa, who was dear to Hari, engaged in delightful discussions on the meaning of the scriptures.

Defeated by Śaṅkarācārya, the timid one returned to his own home at night feeling ashamed, as if struck by the arrows of Śaṅkara. But Rāmānuja, who was learned in all the scriptures, having heard that, [acted].
Accompanied by his brothers and disciples, he arrived at the city of Kāśī. A debate on the Vedānta scriptures took place between those two great souls:
Śaṅkara was the proponent of the Śiva-pakṣa, while that twice-born one was indeed the proponent of the Kṛṣṇa-pakṣa.
Within just one month, Hari was indeed revealed by him in the Vedānta;
He whose name is Vāsudeva is the embodiment of Being, Consciousness, and Bliss.
Vāsudeva is to be known as such because He shines with a portion of the Vasus.
Vāsudeva is indeed Hari himself, the eternal one worshipped by Śiva, who is remembered as the very essence of that which belongs to Vasudeva, namely Brahmā. It was there,
in the context of the Bhāṣya-śāstra, that Śaṅkara became ashamed.
Śiva indeed described [the Lord] for only one fortnight with auspicious threads;
there, in that very commentary (*bhāṣya*), Hari was revealed by Rāmānuja.
He is the renowned Govinda, the deity of grammar.
Because he finds the supreme cow (gāṃ parāṃ vindate), Hari is indeed named Govinda;
Girīśa, however, is not Govinda, for he is the lord of mountains (girīṇām īśvaraḥ).
Gopāla, moreover, is certainly not Rudra, as he is proclaimed to be mounted upon a cow.
"Paśupati is to be known as Śambhu; Gopati is not at all renowned. Śaṅkarācārya was put to shame when he encountered the Mīmāṃsā scripture.
For ten days, a great debate on the scriptures took place between the two of them.

That very Yajñapuruṣa, who was dear to the doctrine of Rāmānuja, was indeed severed by Śaṅkara; having become a deer, he was defeated. Dharma, which originates from right conduct, was established by Yajñadeva.
"Then, at the sacrifice of the Prajāpati Dakṣa, a lapse in proper conduct occurred.
Having heard these words, Rāmānuja, with a humble mind, spoke:
"The sacrifice was performed for the sake of the protection of the universe."

Know that the origin of karma is Brahman, and that Brahman originates from the Imperishable (akṣara). This Imperishable is Śiva himself, who is established within the Śabdabrahman (the Veda as the Word-Brahman). He is to be known on earth as the Ancient Person (Purāṇapuruṣa), the Sacrifice, and the creator of the Imperishable.
He is indeed superior to the Imperishable (Akṣara), the eternal Supreme Self;
he was not satiated by the Imperishable during the sacrificial rite,
and thus he is renowned in the Veda and in the world by the name Yajñapuruṣa, the Person of Sacrifice.
Then, seeing the prosperity of his great-grandson, Śiva became filled with rivalry;
having become a deer, that Rudra gratified him with divine arrows. Recognizing that this Śiva was his preceptor, the capable Lord of Sacrifice [Yajñapuruṣa] understood the situation.
Having become intent on flight, Dharma was made great by him.
Śaṅkarācārya, feeling ashamed, entered into the Nyāya-śāstra;
he is to be known as Bhava because he exists (bhavati), and indeed as Mṛḍa because he gladdens (mṛḍati).
The God who sustains the worlds is indeed the creator, Bharga himself;
he is to be known as Hara because he takes away [evil], that Rudra who is the destroyer of sin.
Śiva himself is the creator, he himself is the sustainer, and he himself is the destroyer.
"From Śiva, Viṣṇu attained the earth, and from Viṣṇu, the lotus-born Brahmā.
Having heard these words, Rāma’s younger brother then said:
"Blessed is this Lord Śambhu, whose supreme majesty is such as this!"
"Truly, truly, this is my command: Śiva is the doer and the cause of action.
Since the name 'Rama' is supreme and eternal, how could Śambhu ever chant the name of Hari?
For it is by his splendor that all infinite creations have arisen."
"Ananta is Śeṣa; indeed, yogis delight in that Śeṣa. And he is truly the abode of my Lord, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss.
Having heard these words, Śaṅkara then became ashamed.
In the Yoga-śāstra, the Supreme Lord Kṛṣṇa was revealed by him;
he is the Lord Kṛṣṇa, the soul of time, the master of yoga, and devoted to yoga.
And in the Sāṅkhya-śāstra, Kapila was revealed by him; it was to him that [the teaching] was shown.
He who protects the power (vīrya) is indeed Kapi, and he who takes that [power] is also Kapi.
He is to be known as Kapila; Kapi is proclaimed to be Rudra.
The Blessed Lord Viṣṇu is Kapila, the omniscient one who possesses all forms.
Then Śaṅkarācārya, feeling ashamed and with his neck bowed,
became a wearer of white garments named Govinda; with a pure heart, he became a disciple of Rāmānuja and indeed chanted [the mantra] "Nirmala" within his mind.
Thus, the majesty of Rudra has been described by you even incidentally;
whoever hears this shall become wealthy, possessed of sons, and eloquent.
Thus ends [the section] in the *Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, in the *Pratisarga Parvan*, within the sub-section known as the *Caturyuga Khaṇḍa*.
The fourteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Rudra and the Subsequent Account of the Birth of Rāmānuja.
Now begins the fifteenth chapter:
"In the Glorification of Vasu, the Account of the Birth of the Vaiśya Trilocana."
Sūta said:
O most excellent and illustrious Bhṛgu, listen to this account of Jīva,
the purifying majesty of Vasu, which bestows happiness upon all things.
Bṛhaspati said:
When the Vaivasvata interval had arrived, in the auspicious first age, the Satya-yuga,
Ilvalā, who was of the nature of darkness (tāmasī), became the beloved wife of the sage Viśravas.

That virtuous woman propitiated Śiva with offerings of earth. In the meantime, there was born a great rogue named Yakṣaśarman, born into a family of initiated priests, who was devoted to the worship of Yakṣiṇīs.
His friend's daughter-in-law, who had beautiful eyebrows, was enjoyed by that sinner;
because of that transgression, this brahmin then became afflicted with leprosy.
Abandoning the twice-born man who had become a leper, the Yakṣiṇī, who was devoted to the mantra, departed.
The goddess went to the world of Śiva, to Kailāsa, the abode of the Guhyakas; meanwhile,
Yakṣaśarman, afflicted by hunger during that most excellent Śivarātri,
performed worship as he had been instructed by the women.
When morning arrived, the twice-born man took his meal;
however, the leper met his death right there in the temple of Śiva. By the power of that merit, he became a king in Karṇāṭaka.
There was a provincial king known as Rājarāja;
that mighty Rājarāja caused the auspicious worship of Śiva to be performed by Brāhmaṇas day after day in every house.
That high-souled king ruled the earth for a hundred years;
he then entrusted the authority of the kingdom to his eldest son.
Thereafter, having reached the city of Kāśī, he propitiated Śiva with acts of worship.
At the end of three years, Mahādeva indeed became a *jyotirliṅga*;
Śiva himself became renowned by the name Rājarājeśvara.
Purified by that [liṅga], the king then himself gave up his life.
Having entered the womb of Ilvalā, a son endowed with auspicious marks was born;
since he was born at an ill-omened hour at night, shrouded in terrible darkness,
his name became famous on earth as Kubera.
That boy gratified the Supreme Lord with his ascetic penance;
then the Lord Brahmā, having come there, caused a beautiful and auspicious city named Laṅkā,
fashioned of gold, to be built and gave it to him.
It is recorded that there were thirty million yakṣas devoted to the affairs of the world;
their lord was indeed the one renowned as Yakṣarāja.
There were also kiṃnaras of many forms who dwelt under his command.
Then the Lord of the Kinnaras himself, along with the Guhyakas who had assumed human forms and were adorned with divine, priceless ornaments, worshipped him with offerings;
for he was indeed the blessed Kubera himself, their master.
Having taken many jewels from the mountains for the sake of the world,
he sent them by means of Rākṣasas to every house and to every person.
As for those men who perform righteous deeds and are devoted to the Vedas—
Their treasuries were filled by that very one who possesses human nature;
but as for those men who are devoted to greed, rogues, and hoarders,
the Lord King, the sovereign of the Rākṣasas, is the giver of wealth to them.
"Those men who have become corpses and have been cremated in the fire-rite,
the Rākṣasas always consume their flesh through the gateway of the fire.
Seeing him endowed with such splendors, the powerful Rāvaṇa— "

Having conquered him and expelled him from Laṅkā, Kubera himself became the king. Thereupon, Kubera, filled with grief, sought refuge with Śaṅkara, the destroyer of suffering and the worthy protector; then the Blessed Lord Hara appeared.
He established a beautiful friendship with Kubera.
The city named Alakāvatī was constructed by Viśvakarman;
having obtained that auspicious city, Kubera attained great joy.
Having heard this, his younger brother Rāvaṇa, the one who makes the world cry out,
went to Mount Kailāsa; there the son of Pulastya beheld Nalakūbara’s consort and touched that sweet-faced woman.
Then the devoted lady Suprabhā spoke to him with anger:
"O evil-souled one, O terror of the world, I live here like your daughter-in-law;
therefore, by that offense, let there be a terrible leprosy upon your body."
"Since you have seized the Puṣpaka chariot belonging to my eldest brother,
let it become as fruitless as wealth stolen by thieves.
Thus cursed, the hero became so and was deeply distressed.
He propitiated Śiva on Kailāsa with offerings of earthly substances. As he performed that worship for twelve years, Rudra did not become pleased; consequently, Rāvaṇa was filled with grief.
The man-eater offered his heads one by one into the fire;
he then surrendered his entire gross body to Rudra.
Having been reduced to ashes, the Rākṣasa did not die, owing to the boon of Brahmā.
Having obtained another beautiful body born from fire,
the powerful one again offered his own limb to Śiva, who is in the form of wind;
and that Rāvaṇa was devoured by Piśācas in the form of wind.
The formidable body born of Vāyu did not die by virtue of the boon;
having seized it, he offered it to Rudra, who had become the ether.
Then that Rāvaṇa was devoured by the terrible hosts of Mothers.
By virtue of a boon from Brahmā,
that Rāvaṇa did not meet his death; having regained his body, which had arisen from the ether and become as empty as space, he offered it once again for the sake of Śiva, who is the true Being.

Then the blessed Lord Rudra, the deity of the ego-principle (ahaṅkāra), became pleased; he became a friend to Kubera as well as to Rāvaṇa. With each single head, he came to possess millions upon millions of heads.
By the grace of the God of gods, his body became like adamant;
thus did that terrible Rāvaṇa become arrogant due to the boon.
[He seized] the women of the gods, Daityas, humans, and serpents.
Newlywed brides were enjoyed by that Rākṣasa throughout the universe; consequently,
the eternal Vedic dharma, though inherently delightful,
became broken for everyone in all the worlds by that Rākṣasa.

He was eternally free from hunger and thirst, being constantly satiated by Śaṅkara himself; whereas the other gods became hungry even without performing sacrifices. Placing Brahmā at their head, they reached the Ocean of Milk in a state of distress.
Having united as one, all the gods praised the Supreme Lord.
Then the blessed Hari, who is both with attributes and without attributes, being pleased,
spoke to all the gods who were bowed in devotion and whose senses were restrained.
In the Śvetavārāha Kalpa, there was no such Dānava as this Rāvaṇa, the one who makes the worlds cry out. Likewise,
in the ancient Mārkaṇḍeya Kalpa, there were indeed Niśumbha and Śumbha.
Just as [I was] at birth, so too were the terrible Kumbhakarṇa and Rāvaṇa;
there have been many Rāvaṇas, but none such as this Rāvaṇa.
I am Brahmā and likewise Rudra, from whom we eternal ones were born.
She is indeed that primordial nature, Māyā, who brings about millions of universes.
The King of the Gods himself is capable amidst the terrible perils facing the gods;
when an obstacle arises for Śakra, the Blessed Lord Hara is capable.
In the midst of a terrible crisis involving the Rudras, I am always capable on this earth;
when a crisis has befallen me, the Lord Hara is capable;
and in the supreme suffering of Brahmā, the Supreme Prakṛti is capable.
In ancient times, two world-renowned Dānavas named Madhu and Kaiṭabha were born.
Because of them, Brahmā was filled with distress and praised the Mother of the Universe.
Then, by her power, I slew Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
"Therefore, by my command, all of you, having sought refuge in the eternal Viṣṇumāyā, who is the source of shelter, perform what is beneficial for the world.
Having heard this, those gods praised the Supreme Prakṛti.
Then the gracious goddess Śivā, consisting of the light of Brahman,
became twofold and descended to the earth as Sītā and Rāma, the supreme and the non-supreme.
Sītā, the mother of the three Liṅgas, was herself further divided into two by her.
Once created, those two became divided into two: sound and meaning, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
Rāma, the eternal one, is the lord of all collections of mere sounds;
he who is neuter, Lakṣmaṇa, is the master of all collections of mere meanings.
He whose vigor is like a diamond and whose celibacy is likewise firm—he alone is a man;
others than him are indeed eunuchs, even though they be monkeys. But Sītā is their supreme nature, the one who bestows auspiciousness upon them both.

Indeed, she has emerged from the midst of the earth; though not born from a womb, she is the creator of wombs. For that wise person by whom the mantra "Rāma, Rāma" has been recited a thousand times under the name of Sītā, it should be known that his fruit is equal to that [of the former].
Having become the source [of his birth], those two gods went to the house of Rādheya;
at that time, when this visible world did not exist, the tamasic nature,
consisting of the entirety of the imperishable beings, was born of its own accord through its threefold will.

Rāma is indeed Śeṣa in the beginning; Lakṣmaṇa is the neuter (klība) in the middle. The two others were born from the former as the male and the neuter, the supreme lords. The subsequent portion, however, is that Goddess, the eternal Yoganidrā.
In other kalpas, O gods, Hari himself reclined upon the ocean of milk;
he is to be known as Rāma, while Śeṣa is Lakṣmaṇa in the form of Rudra.
Sītā, the divine Lakṣmī, was born as the daughter of Janaka.
Sudarśana was Bharata, and Śaṅkha was his younger brother;
then, in the Śveta-Vārāha Kalpa, Rāma, who is higher than the highest, was born.
Pradyumna should be known as Bharata, and the Lord Aniruddha, the slayer of enemies, [was Śatrughna].
By them all the Rākṣasas, headed by Rāvaṇa, were utterly crushed;
having established his own purifying fame throughout the worlds,
the Lord then restored the Puṣpaka aerial chariot to Kubera.
Having ruled for a thousand years—the number of Rudras—he departed for the supreme state.
Sūta said:
Having heard this, Kubera, the first of the Vasudevas, [acted accordingly].
Having produced a portion of himself from his own mouth, he was indeed born into the womb of a Vaiśya;
having become the son of the Vaiśya Dharadatta on the surface of the earth,
he came to be known by the name Trilocana in Mathurā.
Having spent all his wealth at various holy places with great joy,
Trilocana arrived at the city of Kāśī; there, having bowed down to the Vaiṣṇava Rāmānanda, he became his disciple and devoted himself to him.
Having returned to his own home by the command of his guru,
that Vaiśya became devoted to the worship of Rāma and intent upon serving the virtuous;
at that time, the Blessed Lord Rāma became a servant in his house.
Remaining in the thirteenth month, he, the granter of all desires,
personally bestowed jewels, gems, gold, and various garments, as well as diverse items suitable for seasoning, upon the Brahmins.
Bestowing whatever is desired by the Vaiṣṇavas and the ascetics, the Blessed One, the destroyer of Rāvaṇa’s distress, then spoke to Trilocana:
"I am Rāma; I am certainly not your servant, though I am captivated by your devotion."
"Devoted to your pleasure and welfare, I have made my dwelling in your home;
from this day forward, O Vaiśya, I shall dwell within your heart.
Having spoken thus, the Lord vanished, and that Vaiśya was filled with joy.
Having abandoned his wife and son and attained intense detachment,
he dwelt on the banks of the Sarayū and became absorbed in meditation upon Rāma.
Thus ends [the section] in the Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, in the Pratisarga Parvan, within the sub-section known as the Caturyuga Khaṇḍa.
In the *Kaliyugīyetihāsasamuccaya*, within the section on the Greatness of Vasu, the fifteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Origin of the Vaiśya Trilocana," is concluded.
Now begins the sixteenth chapter: "Description of the Origin of the Vaiśya Raṅkaṇa."
Bṛhaspati said: Formerly, in the Svāyambhuva Manvantara, there was a king named Prācīnabarhis, born of the lineage of Dhruva, who was a performer of sacrifices.
Following the instruction of Nārada, he abandoned the sacrifice characterized by violence;
having become a wise devotee of Viṣṇu, he begot ten sons named Pracetas,
who were all identical in form.

Placing their father’s command foremost, they plunged into the midst of the waters of the ocean, the mine of jewels, seeking to perform penance. The four-faced Self-born One, gratified by their asceticism, [appeared].
Having established those seven sons in the seven oceans,
that sovereign of the world made his eighth son the lord of the Jewel-Mine (Ratnākara), his ninth on Mount Mānasottara,
and his tenth on the branch of Meru, and thus he rejoiced.
He who carries the waters in the world is known as Āpava;
the second is named Varuṇa, the lord of aquatic creatures and the master of the waters.
Then Brahmā gave him a noose for the purpose of binding the Daityas.
From that, the one named Pāśī was born to the high-souled Varuṇa.
In a previous birth, he had been a Brāhmaṇa named Āpava, renowned as a worshiper of Śakti who was devoted to drinking Vāruṇī liquor.
A beloved devotee of Bhadrakālī, constantly intent upon her worship,
took a red garland woven with various red flowers and smeared with red sandalwood paste, while remaining joined with the mantra.
Having quickly offered oblations to Bhadrakālī, he became intent upon the nine-syllable mantra;
having worshipped Mahālakṣmī, the eternal Bhadrakālī, with incense, lamps, food offerings, betel, and seasonal fruits.
Having himself offered oblations of sesame seeds mixed with sugar and honey through the medium of the fire,
he praised the Mother of the Universe,
reciting the middle narrative of the Goddess composed by Lord Viṣṇu.
Devoted to the daily recitation of that very nine-syllable mantra,
three years passed as he performed worship in this manner.
Then the Goddess Sarvamaṅgalā, the bestower of boons, became pleased with him.
"Choose a boon," he said to that best of the twice-born.
Hearing these pleasing words, the brahmin Āpava, his mind bowed in humility,
prostrated himself like a staff and offered praise to the eternal Bhadrakālī.
Āpava said: "In a former Viṣṇu-kalpa, there was a Dānava named Mahiṣāsura,
who was accompanied by thousands of crores upon crores of chariots, horses, and elephants."

Having brought the three worlds under his control, Mahendra then became the sovereign; thus the period of the Svārociṣa Manvantara passed while he was exercising his rule. Thereafter, the Blessed Viṣṇu, accompanied by all the gods, [appeared].

Having emitted fire from her mouth, she became garlanded with flames; then, by her own will, you, O Goddess, were born on earth from that fiery liṅga as the slayer of Mahiṣa— salutations again and again to that Goddess!
Long ago, in the Raudra Kalpa, it was heard from the mouth of Rudra-Śambhu in heaven that Rāvaṇa,
the demon who roars throughout the universe, was born with a thousand faces;
he was powerful and terrible, dwelling below the Lokāloka mountain.
The devourer of gods, demons, and humans dwelt there;
by him, during the sixth Manvantara, the entire universe was brought under his sovereignty.
Then, when the Vaivasvata Manvantara had arrived and the twenty-eighth Tretā Yuga had begun, the Lord [reappeared].
Born in the house of the Raghavas as Rāma himself, who is Saṅkarṣaṇa, he assumed a body sixteen years of age and went to the abode of Janaka; there,
that wise one broke the terrible bow of Ājagava.
Then the gods, headed by Brahmā, having recognized Rāma as the eternal one,
described the cause of the thousand-faced one's [manifestation].
Having heard that, he mounted his swan-vehicle together with Sītā.
Having reached Mount Lokāloka, he engaged in a terrible battle.
Hanumān, the monkey, was stationed upon the banner of Haṃsayāna;
the Vedas were the horses there, and the eternal Brahmā was the driver.
A terrible battle took place for a divine year with that Rākṣasa.
Then Rāvaṇa, enraged, with his two thousand arms,
rendered those two brothers, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, unconscious.
The powerful one roared with a terrible sound that caused the universe to resound.
O Brāhmaṇas, you are the Mother praised as the embodiment of Brahman;
Sītā is eternally composed of peace, and by her, the universe was made to roar.
Salutations to her who has destroyed him; salutations to her, salutations, salutations!
Long ago, in the Brahmakalpa, there was a great Daitya named Mura, born of the lineage of Tālajaṅgha, who was arrogant because of his strength against Brahmā.

Having defeated Mahārudra, the lord of the cosmic egg (Brahmāṇḍeśa), who was accompanied by Mahendra and the other gods, he became the presiding authority on the seat of Rudra. Together with the gods, Mahādeva [approached] Mādhava, who reclines upon the ocean of milk.
Having gone there, Viṣṇu, filled with wrath, announced [the matter];
then, mounted upon Garuḍa, he went to where the Daitya Mura was stationed. A fierce battle took place between that god and him.
Seeing that she had been born after a thousand years had passed, Brahmā was filled with fear;
he then praised the supreme, eternal Prakṛti with gentle words.
Then the goddess, a maiden of seven years, became pleased.
Having become four-armed and equipped with weapons, she said to the Daitya:
"This Blessed One has indeed been defeated by you, O King of the Daityas;
but I am my own beautiful Victory, and I have never been defeated by anyone."
Unmīlinī, Viñculī, Trispṛśā, Pakṣavardhinī,
Jayā, Jayantī, and Vijayā— year after year, in due order,
these eleven daughters of Viṣṇu, who follow auspicious conduct, are mine.

"I am indeed always renowned as Ekādaśī within the Vedas. Therefore, having conquered me, who am powerful, take my beautiful hand— she who is Vijayā, the mother of Viṣṇu— and you shall become worthy of worship by all."

Having heard this, the Daitya Mura, infatuated by her beauty, fought with her; in half a moment, he met his destruction. Seeing that Mura had been slain, his younger brother, the Asura Naraka, [advanced].
She created a most terrible illusion of the Daityas that was destructive to the gods;
then Ekādaśī herself, as Māyā, having slain him along with Naraka by a mere *huṃ* sound, roared, O Mother of the World.
Their most terrible splendor entered into the midst of the foods;
that food became a wicked spirit, bestowing fear of disease upon men.
And seeing this, the one named Ekādaśī spoke to Ravi and Śukra.
"May you two, who are world-renowned, remain pure within yourselves.
Having acted accordingly by his command, O Lord, they became worthy of worship.
Thus, O Mother, everything was accomplished by you; salutations again and again to her!
Having heard this divine hymn consisting of sacred narratives, the goddess Bhadrakālī spoke to Āpava, the Brāhmaṇa well-versed in the Vedas,
at the time when the dissolution had arrived and all things mobile and immobile had perished.
"In the past, during the single vast ocean, you indeed became happy through my grace. Being well-pleased by this hymn, I am always a granter of boons to men.
Having spoken thus, the Goddess vanished, and that brahmin became Varuṇa.
Sūta said:
Having heard these words of his preceptor, the second Vasu,
Varuṇa, produced fiery energy from his own mouth onto the surface of the earth.
He was indeed born at the threshold in the house of Dharmabhakta;
his daughter, though a widow, herself conceived a child from Hari. Knowing this, Dharmabhakta rejoiced at the birth of his son.
Known as Nāmadeva, devoted to Sāṅkhya and Yoga,
he realized and beheld that the entire world, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, is pervaded by Viṣṇu; having done so, he went to Kāśī to meet Rāmānanda, the beloved of Hari.
Having bowed and attained discipleship under him, he made his residence there.
Skandagupta, the lord of the Mlecchas, established himself in the kingdom of Dehlī;
having summoned Nāmadeva and thoroughly tested him, he was then at ease.
Kalipriya gave him wealth amounting to fifty million;
with that wealth, Nāmadeva indeed caused an excellent, all-white Gaṅgā-rohaṇa to be constructed at Kāśī, made entirely of stone.
That master of yoga restored to life ten Brahmins, five kings, five Vaiśyas, and a hundred cows that had become corpses. Bṛhaspati said:
In former times, there was a Brahmin named Viśvānara, well-versed in the Vedas;
being childless, he propitiated the Creator with many offerings.
After only a year, the Lord Parameṣṭhin, the Prajāpati, [appeared].
Having approached, he spoke these words: "O best of the twice-born, choose a boon.
Hearing this, he said: "O Blessed One, salutations, salutations to you!
By your grace, may I have a son who is beyond primordial nature (prakṛti)."
Having heard this, Brahmā was then amazed and said to that twice-born one:
"Prakṛti, indeed, is Māyā alone; she herself is the mother of the three genders. By her, the entire visible world was produced by herself."
That which is indeed beyond primordial nature is the Supreme Self, and it is immutable.
Though devoid of intellect, it is devoted to awakening; though without ears, it truly hears.
Being bodiless, it touches this world; though without eyes, it sees by itself.
He eats food without a tongue; he smells without a nose.
He is a speaker of the Vedas without a mouth, and a performer of ritual acts without hands.
Indeed, he moves without feet; thus, being without marks, he does not enjoy the pleasures of women.
For the Unhidden (Aguhya) indeed creates this [universe], which is identical with reality and whose nature is secret.
To that Brahman— who is the Brahman of Sound, consisting of Touch, the Brahman of Form whose essence is Taste, and the supreme Brahman of Smell to be known— I pay homage.
Know that both Prakṛti and Puruṣa are indeed beginningless;
know also that the transformations and the qualities (guṇas) arise from Prakṛti.
These two are identical in purpose, identical in name, and identical in form, possessing eternal bodies.
Devoid of beginning, middle, and end, eternally pure and eternal—
she who gives birth to males, females, and neuters should be known as the supreme Prakṛti.
And the Puruṣa is the seer, subtle, immutable, possessed of knowledge, and supreme.
"One who is unborn attains birth; born by me, he possesses birth.
How can that Puruṣa be eternal and yet become your son?
Therefore, O Sage Viśvānara, Hari himself has become a manifestation of Māyā."
"Janārdana shall attain the status of your son by my boon.
Having spoken thus, the god Pāvaka vanished;
and by virtue of that boon, this Pāvaka indeed became the lord of the eight Vasus.
The lord Svāhāpati became renowned as Vaiśvānara;
in a former birth, in a previous kalpa, that god was the fire-god Agni. Just as King Nala was a wise Brāhmaṇa of Niṣadha, so too was he.

When the king had fallen into distress, the devoted wife Damayantī reached her father’s house and began to search for the monarch. At that time, Nala, the lord and husband of Damayantī, encountered a brahmin.
Seeing him, the beautiful-faced Damayantī fell into a state of delusion.
In the meantime, an incorporeal voice spoke there:
"This is not Nala, your husband; this is a Brahmin who has been utterly deluded."
He became renowned by the name Anala due to the words of the gods;
deluded, he praised the goddess Mahāsarasvatī,
and by the power of his merit, he became the son of Viśvānara.
Sūta said:
Having heard these words of his preceptor, the lordly and powerful Pāvaka produced a portion of himself from his own mouth; from that, Vasu was born.
There was a famous man named Raṅkaṇa, the son of Lakṣmīdatta,
born of the Vaiśya caste in the city of Kāñcanapura. His wife was named Yaṅkaṇā, and she was devoted to her husband.
Having exhausted all their wealth for the sake of religious duties,
the husband and wife brought wood and sold it to support one another.
Rāmānanda was the preceptor of that noble-souled Raṅkaṇa.

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of the Vaiśya Raṅkaṇa," within the *Vasumāhātmya* of the *Kaliyugīyetihāsasamuccaya*, which is an alternative section of the *Caturyugakhaṇḍa* in the *Pratisargaparvan* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Bṛhaspati said:
"The two sons of Diti were most terrible; [they were slain] by the powerful Viṣṇu."
Perceiving that they had united, Diti honored Kaśyapa; then,
after twelve years, the venerable ṛṣi Kaśyapa said to his wife, "O fair-faced one, choose a boon."
Having heard this and offered her salutations, she spoke with joy:
"The goddess Aditi is my co-wife; she possesses sons, while I am known to have only two sons. She has twelve children, whereas I have but two."

"O Lord, those two terrible sons of yours were not destroyed by Viṣṇu, the protector of the gods; therefore, I am deeply distressed. O Master, grant me a son who shall bring about the destruction of the twelve Ādityas."
Having heard these terrible words, he spoke to Diti, deeply distressed:
"In this world, Dharma and Adharma, the higher and the lower, were created by Brahmā.
Those men in the world who belong to the side of Dharma are dear to Brahmā."
But those men who sided with unrighteousness were his enemies;
therefore, his two sons, who had taken the side of unrighteousness, met their death.
For this reason, O lover of dharma, that mighty one made it pure.
"A wise son shall be born to you, long-lived and dear to you.
Having heard this from Kaśyapa, the goddess Diti, being of virtuous conduct, conceived that most excellent embryo and became observant of religious vows.
While her son was in the womb, Mahendra became filled with fear;
at the command of the preceptor Diti, he remained in the house as a servant.
When the fetus had reached the seventh month, Śakra, deluded by his illusory power (māyā), [acted].
The goddess Diti, being impure, fell asleep in her own palace;
the Lord Mahendra, the size of a thumb and armed with the thunderbolt,
entered into the middle of her womb and divided the embryo into seven parts.
Seeing those seven great enemies, who were exceedingly powerful and had become his very life-force,
Mahendra then divided each one of them into seven parts.
And seeing that he was humbled, Mahendra became joined together with them once more.
Having approached through the vaginal opening, he then bowed to Diti;
she, being pleased, gave those gods to Mahendra.
And all those hosts of Maruts became renowned as the servants of Śakra.
In a previous birth, he was born as a world-renowned Brāhmaṇa named Ila, a knower of the Vedas, who later became King Ila. Once, that powerful King Ila, the son of Manu, himself—
Alone, he mounted his horse and went to the forest of Meru.
At the foot of Meru lies a region called Svarṇagarbha, beloved by Hari;
there he established an excellent kingdom and made his dwelling.
O gods, because that region was indeed made surrounded by Ilā, it became the continent known as Ilāvṛta, which is dear to the wise. Those people who were situated in Bhārata arrived in Ilāvṛta.
Indeed, that Meru mountain was fashioned by the Creator out of wood;
upon it, men constructed an auspicious ascent made of gold.
Having ascended it step by step, the world reached the realm of heaven.
Seeing those men arrived in the celestial realm with their physical bodies,
all the gods were struck with wonder and sought refuge in Maheśa.
Knowing this, the blessed Lord Rudra, Śaṅkara, together with Bhavānī, [acted].
He took delight with her in the beautiful Ilāvṛta forest.
In the meantime, the great son of Vaivasvata,
the highly wise one named Ila, arrived seeking Śiva while out hunting.
Seeing her standing there naked, he remained with his eyes closed;
then, beholding Girijā thus ashamed, Lord Hara cursed her:
"In this region, women shall always exist without me."
When these words were spoken by him, all those noble ladies became pregnant; O King, Ilā became a daughter who captivated the hearts of men,
and for a long time she performed great penance on the peak of Mount Meru.
For Ilā, who had become established in meditative absorption, twenty-seven cycles of four yugas passed.
Then, during the middle of the Tretā Yuga, Ilā gave birth to a daughter;
having made the divine Budha, born of the Moon, her husband, she gave birth to the Lunar dynasty (Candravaṃśa).
When the illustrious lord of Ayodhyā arrived at Yavelāvṛta,
his queen, named Madavatī, offered praise to Pārvatī.
At that time, the brahmin Ila arrived, infatuated by her beauty.
Deluded by passion, he touched Queen Madayantī.
In the meantime, an incorporeal voice spoke there:
"O Ilā, this is not a woman; this is a twice-born man, infatuated by your beauty."
In that very place, there was a brahmin well-known by the name Anila.
Afflicted by the fire of desire, that brahmin praised the Fire-god;
having repeatedly cut off his beautiful head, it grew back for him again and again.
Having given [the bow], he praised that god, and Dhanañjaya became delighted. He said:
"You shall produce forty-nine varieties;
likewise, having become my friend, I shall grant you desires equal in number to those."
"Just as the Blessed Kubera is the beloved friend of Varuṇa in twenty-six ways, so indeed am I your friend in forty-nine ways.
When these words were spoken, O best of the twice-born, [the fetus] was in the womb of Diti.
"He was indeed born as Vāyu, the dear friend of Pāvaka.
Sūta said:
"Having heard these words of his preceptor, he who was born of the Vaiśya caste—"
In the house of Dhānyapāla, there was a son born from a low-caste woman;
abandoned by his father and mother, he was then in the Vindhya forest at Kāśī.
A Mleccha named Alika arrived at that place.
Childless Vastrakārī, having obtained a son, went home;
that son, sweet-faced, became renowned as Kabīra. Having reached the age of seven years, he was devoted to drinking cow's milk.
Regarding Rāmānanda as his guru, he became intent on meditating upon Rāma.
Having prepared the food with his own hands, he offered it to Hari;
for the sake of pleasing Him, Hari himself became the granter of all desires.
Bṛhaspati said:
In ancient times, Uttānapāda had a son named Dhruva who was a Kṣatriya.
Abandoned by his father and mother, he was but a five-year-old child.
Having reached Govardhana Hill at the instruction of Nārada,
that observer of great vows performed meditation on the Lord for six months.
Then the Lord Viṣṇu, the master Nārāyaṇa, became pleased.
In the circle of the sky, he affectionately bestowed upon him a station consisting of the ether itself.
Beholding his beautiful face, which by its power of illusion pervaded the ten directions,
and perceiving their Lord to be eternal, they became bowed down with devotion.
The Lord Dhuva himself became visibly worthy of all worship;
he is to be known as the lord of the quarters, the lord of the constellations themselves,
the lord of the sky, the maker of time, and indeed the lord of Śiśumāra.
Indeed, Māyā consists of the five elements, and she herself is the Mistress of Prakṛti. From her was born upon the Earth the great planet named Bhauma;
from the Goddess of Water (Jaladevī) was then born the great planet named Śukra.
Then I was born there as the great planet from Vahnidevī;
from Dhruva, I was born as the great planet named Ketu through Vāsudevī.
Having become a planet, I remained there, having originated from Nabhodevī.
Likewise, the terrible great planet Rāhu, along with his subordinate planet,
[arose]; from him was born the elephant Airāvata in the eastern direction,
and from him the elephant Puṇḍarīka appeared in the south-eastern direction.
Vāmana, Kumuda, and Puṣpadanta were the elephants in due order;
Sārvabhauma and Supratīka were their sons in the directions of the sky and the quarters. Abhramu, Kapilā, and the one named Piṅgalā followed in sequence.
Tāmrakarṇī, Śubhradaṃtī, Aṅganā,
and Añjanāvatī became the female elephants in the various directions of the earth as his beloveds;
likewise, [the other daughters] became his sister, mother, daughter, and daughter-in-law.
For men born from animal wombs, those women are always considered their sisters; for men born from divine wombs, she is remembered as their wife;
and for men born of the lineage of Manu, women born of other [lineages] are likewise [regarded].
Thus has Dharma been declared by me as spoken by the Creator;
for you gods, it should be known that the Pole Star (Dhruva) is twofold—above the earth and likewise below.
It possesses the quality of goodness (Sattva) in the form of day, and the quality of darkness (Tamas) in the form of night.
Below the Pole Star (Dhruva), there is perpetual night; indeed, the denizens of hell reside there.
Above the Pole Star, it is eternal day; in the middle region of heat (Tapa), there is both night and day.
In the worlds of Mahas, Jana, Tapa, and Satya, it is traditionally held that it is always day.
Raurava, Andhakūpa, Tāmisra, and Tamomaya—
in these, night is eternally remembered by the learned as being equal in measure to a kalpa. In his previous birth, he was a brāhmaṇa devoted to Mādhava.
For sixty years, that brahmin Mādhava, beloved of Mādhava, performed his morning ablutions at all sacred fords. By virtue of the merit of those holy sites,
he entered a womb in Sunīti and, having become Dhruva, shone forth with splendor.
Having ruled for thirty-six thousand years, Dhruva became steadfast.
Sūta said:
Having heard these words of his preceptor, that Dhruva, the fifth Vasu, [proceeded].
Having come to the land of Gurjara, he was born into the Vaiśya caste;
known by the name Naraśrī, he was indeed the son of Guṇavaiśya. Kusīdaguṇagupta and Naraśrī were both deeply affectionate toward their sons.
Having cast off his life-breaths, that son of a Vaiśya, Dhruva, went to heaven;
every day, by the grace of Śiva, he beheld the manifest pastimes of Hari in the most excellent Vṛndāvana and attained great joy.
At whose son’s wedding the Blessed Lord, who is affectionate toward his devotees and the granter of desires, arrived together with the Yādavas; he himself,
the King of the Lords of Men and Fortune, came to the city of Kāśī.
Rāmānanda had a disciple who was an expert in the Viṣṇu-dharma.
Bṛhaspati said:
Once, the venerable Atri was on the bank of the Gaṅgā with Anasūyā.

Performing great penance together, he became intent on meditation upon Brahman. Then Brahmā, Hari, and Śambhu, mounted upon their respective vehicles, those eternal ones, spoke these words to him: "Choose a boon."

Having heard these words of theirs, the sage who is the son of the Self-born remained established in the Supreme Self and did not utter a single word in reply. Perceiving his state of being, the three eternal gods—
Having approached his wife Anasūyā, they spoke these words:
"Rudra himself stands with a linga in hand; Viṣṇu, the nourisher of that essence, stands there;
and Brahmā, whose power over desire and sacred knowledge has vanished, has fallen under her control."
"Give us pleasure, O you who reel with intoxication; otherwise, I shall give up my life.
Hearing these inauspicious words of theirs, Anasūyā, devoted to her husband, said nothing at all to the gods, fearing their wrath.
Deluded there by that illusion, those gods seized her by force and then made an effort for sexual union.
Then Satī, the beloved of the sage, became enraged and indeed cursed them.
"You shall become my sons, deluded by desire.
Indeed, the linga of Mahādeva, the great head of this Brahmā,
and the feet of Vāsudeva must always be worshipped by men."
"O best of gods, this will become a supreme mockery.
Having heard these terrible words and having paid homage to the beloved of the sage, they,
bowed down with devotion, offered praise with divine hymns composed of the Rig Veda.
Then Anasūyā said, "O sirs, you are my little sons;
having cast off my curse, you shall attain satisfaction.
When these words were spoken, Brahmā and the Moon then indeed became so.
Dattātreya was Hari himself, and the venerable Durvāsas was Hara;
for the sake of removing that sin, they became endowed with yoga.
In the meantime, the Goddess Prakṛti, the upholder of all dharma, appeared.
She, whose form consists of the qualities (guṇas), created Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara as well as others.
Consequently, a Manvantara was born from those who were engaged in union;
and the three gods, being delighted, came together toward them.
He spoke these pleasing words for their auspicious sake:
"Candramas shall become Soma, the sixth Vasu, beloved of the gods;
Durvāsas, who is a portion of Rudra, shall be Pratyūṣa, the seventh Vasu."
The yogi Dattātreya and Prabhāsa were the eighth Vasu.
Having heard their words, those three became Vasus.
Sūta said:
Having heard these words of the Guru, the three Vasus were filled with joy;
for the sake of purifying the Kali age, they went to the surface of the earth by means of their own portions.
They took birth in the Vaiśya caste in the royal city of Dakṣiṇāpatha.
At that time, Soma, the son of Sudeva, was known as Pīpā;
he established a royal seat in that city just like a king.
He became a disciple of Rāmānanda and arrived at Dvārakā.
