Having obtained from Kṛṣṇa a golden image of Hari’s mudrā, which destroys the very essence of the state of being a ghost (preta), that king indeed gave it there to the Vaiṣṇavas. And Pratyūṣa was born in the Pāñcāla country from a mother of the Vaiśya caste.
The son of Mārgapāla was the renowned Nānaka;
having approached Rāmānanda and become his disciple,
that Nānaka indeed subdued the Mlecchas and showed them the subtle path.
Prabhāsa was indeed born in Śāntipura into the Brahmin caste as the son of Śukladatta; he is known as Nityānanda.
Thus, O Śaunaka, the majesty of Vasu has been described by me to you.

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of Vasu, Kabīra, Nara, Śrī Pīpā, Nānaka, and Nityānanda," within the *Vasumāhātmya* section of the *Kaliyugīyetihāsasamuccaya*, which is an alternative designation for the *Caturyugakhaṇḍa* in the *Pratisargaparvan* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus to those gods, the Lord, the Blessed One, the Master of the Great, [departed].
And having beheld the two Aśvins, he described their history:
"Formerly, in the Vaivasvata Manvantara, Viśvakarman, the creator of wonders,
beheld the splendor of Citragupta as it had been fashioned by Citralekhā."

Competing with Mahāmāyā, he praised her with many offerings. Then that goddess was pleased; she who had been born from her own portion as his wife Citrā was herself remembered as Saṃjñā, the bestower of all knowledge.
When Saṃjñā reached the age of sixteen, her father,
seeking happiness and desiring her marriage, invited all the gods to the summit of Mount Meru.
The twenty-six lords of the Yakṣas, headed by Kubera, also assembled there.
Ten lords of aquatic creatures arrived there as suitors;
forty-nine fires (pāvakas) and likewise the winds (vāyus) are recorded to have come;
two poles (dhruvas) arrived in person, and sixteen moons (somas) were present right there.
And thirteen Pratyūṣas have arrived as the protectors of the universe;
and three hundred and sixty Prabhāsas are the protectors of the day.
And the Rudras, beginning with Bhava, are the protectors of the lunar orb.
All the Ādityas were present at the svayaṃvara of Saṃjñā;
the eighty-four Dānavas led by Vipracitti arrived,
as did the Daityas led by Prahlāda and the Pannagas led by Vāsuki.
Then the Nāgas, headed by Śeṣa, and the Garuḍas, headed by Tārkṣya, arrived;
all having gathered for the svayaṃvara, a great tumult arose.
In the meantime, the Goddess, accompanied by celestial maidens, [arrived].
Then, Saṃjñā appeared visibly in heaven before the gods.
Beholding her, the powerful Bali, deluded by passion,
took her by the hand and departed while all the archers looked on.
Then the gods, afflicted by anger, obstructed that best of Daityas;
having gratified him with various weapons and missiles, they engaged in a great battle.
And then the Dānavas and Daityas, mounted upon various vehicles, [joined the fray].
The gods joyfully waged a great and tumultuous battle with the Dānavas;
the gods were slain by the Dānavas, and the Daityas were destroyed by the gods.
With their bodies becoming corpses, the earth in Ilāvarta became impassable.
For a full fortnight there was a divine battle between the Dānavas and the gods.
[The combatants were] Pāñcajanya and Dhātṛ, Hayagrīva and Mitraka,
Aghāsura and Aryaman, as well as Bala and Śakra.
Bakāsura and Varuṇa, Śakaṭa and Prāṃśu,
Vatsāsura and Bhaga, Vivasvat and Bali himself,
as well as Pralamba and Pūṣan, Gardabha and Savitṛ [were slain] in battle.
Viśvakarman, Maya, Kālanemi, and Hari himself,
all desiring victory, fought with one another;
and those defeated Daityas fled, abandoning the battle.
Then Vivasvat, having taken Saṃjñā as she sat upon his chariot,
approached Viśvakarman and, with a gracious mind, gave her to him.
Seeing Vivasvat, the best of the gods, Saṃjñā spoke these words:
And may you, my lord, become a god who always accomplishes what must be done.
O Blessed One, since I have been won by you from Bali, who acted against your will,
there shall never be any fault in me for taking my brother as a hostage.
A woman who is always enjoyed by heroes is remembered by the sages as a jewel among women.
The Goddess Prakṛti is fourfold, differentiated by the qualities (guṇas) yet one in her essence.
She is that single, eternal Mother, Prakṛti, due to the equilibrium of the qualities.
She who is the sister in the form of *sattva*, the housewife in the form of *rajas*,
and the maiden in the form of *tamas*— salutations again and again to that Goddess!
There are indeed many persons who are devoid of qualities and uniform in form.
In this world, those endowed with consciousness and ignorance are born of *prakṛti*;
in the otherworld (*aloka*), all are born of sin, arising from the gods and Brahman.
But whichever auspicious man a woman consisting of knowledge chooses, [he shall be her husband].
A certain son becomes her father, and he also becomes her brother and her husband;
Brahmā took his own daughter, the god Viṣṇu took his own mother,
and the blessed Śambhu took his own sister, and yet they attained preeminence.
Having heard these words consisting of the Veda,
Vivasvat, the son of Aditi, took Saṃjñā, the sister of his brother, and became preeminent.
From those two were born sons and daughters, as well as Manu Vaivasvata.
Yama and Yamunā were also endowed with divine splendors.
Then Saṃjñā, being virtuous, and perceiving her husband to be a personification of light,
produced Chāyā and went to the forest for ascetic penance.
Sāvarṇi Manu, Śani,
and Tapatī were likewise born from Chāyā; however, perceiving that woman to be a mere illusion due to her harsh gaze toward Vivasvat, he was filled with wrath.
The divine Sun, Vivasvat, reduced her to ashes.
Then Śani and Sāvarṇi, perceiving that Vivasvat was filled with rage,
their own eyes copper-red with anger, fought with one another.
After some time, having been defeated by Vivasvat,
they reached the Himācala mountain and performed supreme penance.
At the end of three years, that goddess Mahākālī arrived.
And being honored by them, she, who was affectionate toward her devotees, granted them a boon;
yet they both returned and fought with Vivasvat,
and Vivasvat, terrified by fear, abandoned the battle and fled.
Residing there in the most delightful Kurukhaṇḍa, the beloved Saṃjñā, assuming the form of a mare, was performing severe penance.
Having gone there, the Blessed One beheld Saṃjñā, who was engaged in awakening [him].
Becoming a horse overcome by desire, he took his pleasure there with her.
Within five years, Saṃjñā herself conceived a child from him,
and two sons were born, endowed with divine forms and prowess.
Beholding their father’s suffering, those two of wicked conduct, having themselves conquered their kinsmen with a cruel gaze, went to the solar orb; then,
having bound them, the two sons of Vaḍavā arrived at the side of their father.
Seeing that his two enemies had approached, the blessed Lord Vivasvat struck them with terrifying iron clubs until they became crippled;
then the Sun-god abandoned the two sons of Chāyā.
Beholding the two sons of Aśvinī, he joyfully spoke these words to them:
"Just as Jīva and Īśa, or as Nara and Nārāyaṇa are friends,
so shall you two, being pleased by this single name, become the Nāsatyas."
The goddess Iḍā, the power of Soma, shall become the elder wife;
Piṅgalā, the power of Sūrya, shall become the younger wife.
He shall indeed be named Iḍāpati, and the second shall be Piṅgalāpati.

For the twelfth sign of men, Saturn will cast a cruel aspect; Jyeṣṭha shall be the one who pacifies that [aspect] upon the earth. And for the second sign of men, Sāvarṇi will be the cause of confusion.
On earth, Piṅgalāpati shall be his pacifier;
for the goddess Tapatī, who dwells in the zodiac sign of his birth and is the performer of his rites,
both Iḍā and Piṅgalā shall become her pacifiers.
Having heard his words, the two physicians of the gods became Sāvarṇi, Śani,
Rāhu, and Ketu, who scorches heaven;
and for the sake of their avoidance, the two Aśvins were born as the Dasras.
Sūta said:
Having heard these words of the preceptor, the two best of gods became pleased;
praised by the Sun, they were born on the surface of the earth from their own portions within the womb of a Śūdra woman.
Born in the house of a caṇḍāla as the husband of an iḍā who killed goats, he was famous by the name Sadhana; devoted to his father and mother,
he sold goat meat as if it were equal to the śāligrāma stone.
Having approached Kabīra and become his disciple, he indeed shone forth.
That treasure-house of truth, having previously undertaken ascetic penance for Brahmā,
showed the cow, who was terrified with fear, to a Cāṇḍāla there.
Therefore, the hand of that wealthy man entered the royal palace;
he was born in the house of a leather-worker as the second husband of Piṅgalā. Mānadā’s son became renowned as Raidāsa.
Having arrived at the city of Kāśī, he defeated Kabīra— who was devoted to Rāma— through a debate on their respective doctrines; then, having encountered Śaṅkarācārya,
a dispute arose between them concerning different philosophical views for a full day and night.
Having bowed to that best of the twice-born, Raidāsa, who had been defeated,
approached Rāmānanda and became his disciple. Thus, O Brahmin, I have told you how those who were portions of the gods came to be.

"The play of those who show the path is that which purifies the Kali age. Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of Sadhana and Raidāsa," in the *Aśvinīkumāra-avatāra* section of the *Kaliyuga-itihāsa-samuccaya*, within the *Caturyuga-khaṇḍa* of the *Pratisarga-parvan* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the nineteenth chapter.
The Description of Viṣṇusvāmī and Madhvācārya.
Sūta said:
Having thus spoken, the Blessed Lord Jīva [described] the supreme majesty of the God.
Having produced a portion of himself from his own mouth, he came into being at Brahmayoni.
He was the son of Gurudatta in the beautiful city of Iṣṭikā;
he was renowned by the name Ropaṇa and was a guide to the path of Brahman.

In the Kali age, having placed a rosary made of thread and a mark (*tilaka*) made of water upon every person while reciting the mantra "Vāsudeva," and having approached Kṛṣṇacaitanya and his blanket by his command—
Having taken [the child] and reached his own city, he became absorbed in meditation upon Kṛṣṇa. O sage, listen hereafter with joy to the life-story of Hari,
by hearing which a person shall never experience fear even in the terrible Kali age.
In the fifth year of Kṛṣṇacaitanya, while Yajñāṃśa was performing a sacrifice,
a Brahmin from the land of Vaṅga named Īśvara— beloved of Śāradā and emboldened by the grace of the Goddess of Speech—
arrived at the village of Śāntipura.
Having performed a world-conquest among the virtuous and being proficient in all the scriptures,
that twice-born one composed and recited a divine hymn on the banks of the Gaṅgā;
in the meantime, Yajñāṃśa arrived there.
He spoke these pleasing words to the Lord who was offering praise:

"That which you have stated in your hymn—that merit, public works, and even the very essence of the Vedas are but debt—is indeed so; yet, tell me what fault there is in this, for it is actually an ornament."
Thus the wise Īśvara said, "No defect whatsoever is seen.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One declared, "No ornament whatsoever is seen.
Good action is remembered as Dharma, and the act of construction (pūrta) is called consciousness (caitanya)."

"Arṇa" and "vīrya"—these three should be known as the essence of the Vedas. 'This is a defect in the water of the Gaṅgā; this is an ornament in the body'—having heard this, that mendicant, who was fond of sacred speech, was indeed struck with wonder.

Seeing her own people ashamed, Śāradā, who is all-auspiciousness, laughed and said this to Īśvara: "Kṛṣṇa, who is known as Caitanya. Having heard that, his disciple, a worshiper of the Kṛṣṇa-mantra, [acted accordingly].
He became a preeminent Vaiṣṇava and a servant of Kṛṣṇacaitanya.
Sūta said: There was a famous Brāhmaṇa named Śrīdhara who was a worshiper of Śiva.

In that beautiful city of Pattana, the king had the Bhāgavata performed for seven excellent days with abundant wealth. Having received these gifts, the brahmin Śrīdhara went to his father-in-law’s house.
Having stayed there for exactly one month with his wife, the twice-born man set out on the road toward his own home; however, seven thieves encountered him there,
and having sworn an oath by the name of Rāmadeva, they proceeded along with him.
When the beautiful forest had been cleared, they then killed the brahmin Śrīdhara and seized his ox-cart, along with his wealth, his wife, and himself.
In the meantime, Rāma, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss—
Having slain those seven with his arrows and then restored that twice-born man to life,
the Blessed Lord, the Master, sent him away to Vṛndāvana.
From that time forward, O Brahmin, the Śrīdhara became a Vaiṣṇava.
In his seventh year, having gone to the auspicious city of Śāntipura,
he attained knowledge of Brahman from Yajñāṃśa and became his disciple.
A commentary on the Bhāgavata was composed by that great-souled one.
Sūta said:
The wise brahmin Rāmaśarman, devoted to the worship of Śaṅkara, resided in Kāśī at the site of Avimukteśvara on the night of Śivarātri.

Remaining alone, vigilant, and meditative, he chanted the auspicious five-syllabled mantra. Then the Blessed Lord Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, being pleased, spoke these words to that best of the twice-born: "Choose a boon."
Having bowed to Śiva, Rāmaśarman, with a humble mind, spoke these words: "O Lord, by your grace, may that God in whose samādhi you abide and who is supreme in your meditation dwell within my heart."
When he had spoken these words, Maheśvara laughed and said:
"Indeed, Māyā is the one primordial nature (prakṛti), which, though consisting of the essence of Brahman, is threefold;
having determined it to be of the nature of the void, it is the half-luminous state of the Puruṣa."
Having taken them up, the Mother of the World gave birth to two sons, a male and a female.
The male was Nārāyaṇa himself, fair-complexioned and endowed with eight arms;
the Blessed One, the protector of the universe, manifested in three forms by his own will.
Viṣṇu, wearing a forest garland and possessing four arms, is indeed half of that splendor;
he is the milk-reclining Āditya himself, the deity of the true qualities. That very same splendor, divided into two parts, constitutes the two sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
That Jishnu is indeed to be known as Vishnu on Mount Gandhamadana. Sankarshana is manifestly the neuter (klība) form; thus the form of Brahmā became threefold.
From the first half [of the body] came Gaurī and Śeṣa, and from the second half came Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.

At the end of the Dvāpara age, that very Balabhadra himself shall remain as Gauraśeṣa. You must always perform meditation upon Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa and the worship of Balabhadra; having attained that, may you be happy.
Having spoken thus, the Lord vanished; and there appeared Kṛṣṇacaitanya, twelve years of age, who, having approached Rāmānanda,
remained there as his disciple, a worshiper of Kṛṣṇacaitanya.
By his command, that auspicious *Adhyātmarāmāyaṇa* was composed by him.
Sūta said:
That brahmin Jīvānanda was indeed endowed with Rūpānanda.
Having heard the life-story of Caitanya, he went to the city of Śāntipura. When Caitanya was sixteen years old, the two of them bowed to him and remained there;
they said to Kṛṣṇacaitanya, "What is it that you consider to be the essential teaching?"
Laughing, Caitanya said: "O twice-born ones, I am a Śākta and a worshiper of Śakti; I am a Śaiva and always observe the vows of Śaṅkara for the sake of the world;
I am a Vaiṣṇava, devoted to meditation upon the God of gods and full of devotion."

"Having drunk the intoxication of devotion, I, intent on sacrifice, have offered the auspicious oblation of the sinful man into the fire of knowledge for the sake of [attaining] power at the conclusion of the homa. Having heard this, those two brahmins became his disciples.
Having followed the path of right conduct, they both became worthy of all worship.
By their command, Jīvānanda indeed composed the *Ṣaṭsandarbha*.
That wise devotee of Kṛṣṇacaitanya resided there.
Placing the command of his guru before him, the great sage Rūpānanda composed the *Kṛṣṇakhaṇḍa*, a ten-thousand-verse limb of the Purāṇa;
having resided there, he was rich in service to his guru and a worshiper of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa.
Sūta said:
That brahmin Viṣṇusvāmī went to the auspicious city of Śāntipurī;
when he was in his nineteenth year, having performed a sacrifice, that twice-born one bowed to him and spoke.
"Who among all the gods is worthy of worship within the scope of the universe?
Having heard this, the Blessed One said to that best of the twice-born:
"Mahādeva, who bestows grace upon his devotees, is the one worthy of worship by all."
Viṣṇvīśvara, Rudreśa, Brahmeśa, and the Lord Hara— indeed,
all these objects of worship are fruitless without one who worships them.
Those who are devotees of Viṣṇu and intent upon the worship of Śaṅkara [attain success].
Through the grace of Śiva, supreme devotion to Viṣṇu is easily attained; yet,
having become a Vaiṣṇava man and having come to this land of action (Karmabhūmi), one who does not worship Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, is a denizen of hell.
Having heard that [name], Viṣṇusvāmī became his disciple through his virtues;
having worshipped the mantra of Kṛṣṇa, he became a worshipper of Śiva,
and by his command, a Vaiṣṇava Saṃhitā was composed by him.
Having stayed there, that devotee of Viṣṇu and worshiper of Kṛṣṇacaitanya—
Sūta said:
Madhvācārya, who was supremely devoted to Kṛṣṇa, recognized that the portion of the sacrifice was most excellent.
Having gone to the beautiful city of Śāntipurī and bowed down to Him, that twice-born one said:
"This Kṛṣṇa is the Lord Himself; others are the creators of the universe.
The gods, such as Dhātṛ and the rest, should be known [as His parts]; what then is the use of worshipping them?"
"O Brahmins devoted to the path of Śakti, you vainly worship the gods on this earth with sacrifices consisting of senseless violence, such as the horse sacrifice (Aśvamedha) and others.
Having heard this, the son of Śacī, who partakes in the portions of the sacrifice, laughed and said:
The Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa is not directly this one, for he is born of Tamas and produced from Śakti;
he is a thief, an enjoyer of all things, a violent man, and an eater of meat;
indeed, he who would consort with another's wife shall go to the abode of Yama.
A thief, and especially one who takes life, goes to the abode of Yama;
but he who is devoid of these characteristics is the Blessed One, beyond primordial nature (prakṛti). He whose intellect is Brahmā and whose ego (ahaṅkāra) is indeed Śiva—[he is the Lord].
Gaṇeśa is the subtle element of sound, Yama himself is the subtle element of touch,
Kumāra is indeed the subtle element of form, and the King of Yakṣas is the subtle element of taste.
Viśvakarmā is the subtle element of smell, and the Lord Śani is the sense of hearing.
The wise one is to be known as his skin, and the eternal Sun is his eye;
having conquered him, the venerable Śukra became his sense of smell, and the two sons of Aśvinī his nose.
The venerable Jīva is his mouth, and the King of the Gods (Indra) is his hand.

Kṛṣṇa is his feet, Dakṣa Prajāpati is his organ of generation, and the Lord Mṛtyu is his anus; salutation to that Blessed One! And through sacrifices involving violence, may that Blessed One attain satisfaction.
And that sacrificial animal, through its transformation into Brahman within the fire, attains liberation;
by the power of that liberation, one obtains great merit.
But the man who, devoid of the prescribed rites, performs a sacrifice involving violence is a sinner.
Due to that fault, one shall dwell for a long time in the Andhatāmisra hell;
for great merit and great sin reside in sacrifices involving violence.
Therefore, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa [prohibited] the sacrifice involving violence in the Kali age.
Having completed [his duties] in the month of Kārttika, on the first day of the bright fortnight,
he established a sacrifice consisting of a mountain of food upon the earth.
At that time, the King of the Gods (Indra), distressed and enraged toward his younger brother, [acted].
Then Kṛṣṇa submerged the eternal Vajrī into Prakṛti and praised her for the sake of the world’s welfare;
then that Mother, Prakṛti, [assumed] her own former divine form.
Having assumed a vast form as Rādhā, she entered the heart of Kṛṣṇa;
by her power, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa held up Mount Govardhana and became the god Giridhara, worthy of worship by all.
"Lord Rādhākṛṣṇa is the eternal, perfect Brahman;
therefore, Kṛṣṇa alone is not the Lord, but Rādhākṛṣṇa is the supreme Master.
Having heard these words of his, Madhvācārya, the beloved of Hari, [replied].
Having become a disciple, he remained there as a worshiper of Kṛṣṇacaitanya.

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Accounts of Balabhadra, Viṣṇusvāmin, Madhvācārya, and Others—Disciples of the Sacrificial Portion of Kṛṣṇacaitanya," in the *Kaliyugīyetihāsasamuccaya* (Compendium of Histories of the Kali Age), which is a section of the *Caturyugakhaṇḍa* within the *Pratisargaparvan* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the twentieth chapter.
Description of the Majesty of Jagannātha.
Sūta said:
And that Bhaṭṭoji was pure-souled and devoted solely to the worship of Śiva.
Having approached Kṛṣṇacaitanya and offered obeisances, he spoke these words:
"Mahādeva is indeed the Guru; he is Śiva, the Self of all embodied beings.
Viṣṇu and Brahmā are his servants; therefore, what is the use of worshipping them?"
Having heard this, Yajñāṃśa, who was twenty years of age, laughed and said to Bhaṭṭoji: "This is not Śambhu, the Great Lord;
for is the Lord Śambhu not capable of being the creator of embodied beings?"
Without Viṣṇu as his sustainer, this Sadāśiva cannot be the destroyer;
they have arisen as a single form in three ways: Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.
According to the Śākta path, the Lord Brahmā is the bestower of liberation.
Viṣṇu, by way of the Vaiṣṇava path, is the bestower of liberation upon living beings;

Śambhu, by way of the Śaiva path, is the giver of liberation to embodied souls. The Śākta is the true householder of the stages of life, the enjoyer of sacrifice, and the one who goes to the ancestors and the gods.
The forest-dweller (vānaprastha) who is indeed a Vaiṣṇava, subsisting on bulbs and roots;
the ascetic stage (yatyāśrama), which is always fierce, devoid of qualities, and pure in form;
and the stage of celibate studentship (brahmacaryāśrama)—among these, the great stage follows after them.
Having heard these words of his guru, that twice-born man became a disciple and expounded the third limb of the Vedas composed by Pāṇini;
and by his command, he indeed composed the Siddhāntakaumudī.
Having stayed there, the wise devotee of Kṛṣṇacaitanya was initiated.
Sūta said:
That wise Varāhamihira was devoted solely to the Sun.
And in his twenty-second year, while he was engaged in a sacrifice, the Sun himself approached him and spoke these words:
"O Blessed One, I am the Sun from whom the three gods have arisen:
Brahmā in the morning, Viṣṇu at midday, and Sadāśiva in the evening."
"Therefore, what is the use of the auspicious worship of the Sun through the sacrifice to the three deities?
Having heard this, that portion of the sacrifice laughed and spoke these auspicious words:
"Nature has become twofold: the lower (apara) and likewise the higher (para)."

The supreme primordial nature (prakṛti) is to be known as eightfold: as the subtle element of name, the subtle element of flower, the subtle element of that [tanmātra], the subtle element of sound, the subtle element of touch, the subtle element of form, the subtle element of taste, and likewise the subtle element of smell.
The other [nature], which is the life-force, eternally pure, and identical with the universe, is to be known as the eightfold lower *prakṛti*:
earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, intellect,
and ego.
Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Mahādeva, Gaṇeśa, Yama, Guha, Kubera, Viśvakarman, and the supreme deity Prakṛti;
Sumeru, Varuṇa, Vahni, Vāyu, and Dhruva as well.
Soma, Ravi, Śeṣa, and the other deities of primordial nature (prakṛti)—
therefore Rudra is the lord of Soma, Ravi is the lord himself, Brahmā is the lord of Ravi,
and Hari is directly the lord of Śeṣa; salutations to them, salutations again and again!
Having heard this, the brahmin then became a disciple of that guru;
by his command, he composed the fourth limb, the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra),
namely the Varāhasaṃhitā and indeed the Bṛhajjātaka.
Having composed various minor tantras and others as well, he lived there.
Sūta said:
Vāṇībhūṣaṇa himself was likewise devoted solely to the worship of Śiva.
Approaching Kṛṣṇacaitanya with a humble mind, he spoke these words:
"Viṣṇumāyā, the sustainer of the world, is that one supreme Prakṛti;
by her this universe was born, and from the universe the God [Viṣṇu] arose."
That Puruṣa, born of Śakti, became manifold as the Viśvedevas;
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara, as well as the gods, are born of Prakṛti.
Therefore, the Blessed Goddess is to be worshipped; what then is the use of worshipping them?
Having heard this, that portion of the sacrifice laughed and said to the best of the twice-born:
"Indeed, the Blessed One is not the foremost; she is insentient in form and composed of the qualities (guṇas).
She is that single Prakṛti, Māyā, capable of fashioning the worlds."
O twice-born one, this story is well known in the scripture of the Devībhāgavata, which is like that of a woman with her male companion;
it tells how once the Goddess Prakṛti, by her own will, indeed [created] this world.
That created being, though insentient, was then awakened in many ways;
yet, O Brahmins, consciousness did not arise, and Nature was then struck with wonder.
Then Consciousness gratified the Person, who had become as empty as space.
The Blessed One entered the sphere produced by the illusion of Māyā;
like a dream, he himself became born, and the world became consciousness.
Therefore, that Blessed One is the supreme Puruṣa, beyond all qualities (nirguṇa).

Born from Prakṛti by his own will, he then assumed the form of a Liṅga. Born from the masculine Prakṛti, this eternal one is of the masculine gender; born from the feminine Prakṛti, this eternal one is of the feminine gender.
Born from the neuter nature, that Lord indeed has the form of a eunuch;
born from the immutable nature, this Adhokṣaja is devoid of qualities.
Salutations to that Blessed One, whose form is emptiness, the witness.
Having heard those words, that twice-born man indeed became a disciple;
in his twenty-third year, during a portion of a sacrifice, he made his residence there. Furthermore, the *Chandograntha*, an auxiliary of the Veda (*vedāṅga*), was composed by him under his own name.
Having chanted the supreme name of Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa, he attained great joy.
Sūta said:
There was a twice-born man named Dhanvantari who was devoted to the worship of Brahman.
Having approached Kṛṣṇacaitanya and bowed down, he spoke these words:
"You are the supreme person, eternally pure and eternal;
that Māyā is insentient, yet you, the Blessed Lord, are yourself capable."
"Perpetual, unmanifest, supreme, and subtle—Prakṛti arises from that; therefore, that Blessed One is to be worshipped. What is the use of worshipping Prakṛti?
Having heard this, the Lord of Sacrifice, who is conversant with all scriptures, laughed and said:
This Supreme Person is not possible without Prakṛti;
this auspicious narrative is well-known in the ancient Vārāha Purāṇa:
"Once, the eternal Puruṣa, by his own will, existed as a mere name."
There, the Supreme Person himself became manifold, just like a ghost;
being unable to fashion the worlds by his own power,
he praised the Goddess Prakṛti, the eternal one, for a long time.
Then the Goddess, having attained that Mahat-tattva, brought it forth;
from Mahat was born Ahaṅkāra, and from that the Tanmātras. From those, moreover, arose the Mahābhūtas, and by them this world was produced.

"Both of these are eternal, yet primordial nature (prakṛti) is superior to the person (puruṣa), and the person is indeed superior even to primordial nature; therefore, salutations again and again to those two. Having heard this, Dhanvantari became a disciple of that guru.
Having resided there, he indeed composed the Kalpa-veda, which is an auxiliary of the Vedas.
Other disciples of Dhanvantari besides Suśruta are also recorded.
Sūta said:
Indeed, the Brahmin Jayadeva, who was devoted to the Buddhist path,
approached Kṛṣṇacaitanya when he had reached the age of twenty-five; having bowed down, that most excellent one, the husband of Uṣā, spoke these beautiful words.
From whose navel there arose a lotus from which Brahmā emerged;
therefore, he is celebrated in the Sāmaveda by the name Brahmasū.
Viśva-Nārāyaṇa himself is stationed upon his banner.
Viśvaketu, Ratnākara, Aniruddha, and Aniruddhaka;
Brahmavelā was his wife, as were the eternal Uṣā and Mahottamā.
He indeed descended in the form of an image for the sake of the welfare of the world.
Having heard this, Yajñāṃśa laughed and said to that best of the twice-born:
"The Veda is Nārāyaṇa himself; it is always to be worshipped by men.
From that comes Time, from that comes Action, and from that Dharma proceeds."
From Dharma was born Kāma, and Rati herself became the wife of Kāma.
From Kāma and Rati was born the deity named Aniruddha;
Uṣā was his sister, having come into being together with him.
He who is indeed Time is Kṛṣṇa, and Rādhā is his uterine sister;
he who is in the form of action is Brahmā, and Niyati is his uterine sister;
Mahādeva is in the form of Dharma, and Śraddhā is his uterine sister.
How is it that Aniruddha has been described by you as the eternal Lord?
Furthermore, the creation within the cosmic egg is threefold: gross, subtle, and causal.
For the sake of the gross creation, the Lord Nārāyaṇa himself manifested.

Nārāyaṇa and his Śakti—between those two, Śeṣa was born from the water; he indeed arose from the water, and they both rested upon him. While the divine Nārāyaṇa was asleep, an excellent lotus emerged from his navel.
From that, Vidhi (Brahmā) arose, extending for infinite yojanas;
from Vidhi came the gross creation consisting of gods, animals, humans, and so forth. From him was born Aniruddha, the lord of Uṣā, for the sake of the subtle creation.
Then, from that seed, water was produced upon the summit of the cosmic egg;
from that seed, Śeṣa was indeed born, and he remained stationed above it.
From his navel arose Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds.
From that, the subtle creation was born, which is seen even in a dream. For the sake of the causal creation, Nārāyaṇa himself manifested as the Vedas.
From the Vedas came Time; from that, Action; and from that, Dharma and the rest are remembered to have arisen.
"O twice-born ones, my guru, the Lord of the World, resides in the land of Uḍra;
I must go there this very day along with my disciples.
Having heard these words, the servants of Kṛṣṇacaitanya—
Having summoned their respective disciples,
those twelve hosts of Śaṅkara then departed and approached Rāmānuja;
there, the seven hosts led by Nāmadeva and others also assembled.
Having paid obeisance to Rāmānanda, his servants remained there;
then Ropaṇa arrived, surrounded by many of his own disciples,
and having approached Kṛṣṇacaitanya and paid obeisance, he himself stood before him.
Intent on devotion, they indeed proceeded to the city of Jagannātha;
there, the treasures (Nidhis) and the supernatural powers (Siddhis) arrived for the sake of their service,
along with all ten thousand Vaiṣṇavas, Śaivas, and Śāktas.
Placing their share of the sacrifice before them, they went to the city of the Lord of the World.
There, the Blessed One Aniruddha, the husband of Uṣā, was present as an incarnate image (arcāvatāra). Upon seeing their arrival, the sage assumed the form of a twice-born brahmin.
Jagannātha himself arrived where the portions of the sacrifice and others were present.
Having beheld him, the portion of the sacrifice bowed down and spoke these words:
"What do you intend, now that the terrifying Kali age has arrived?"
"Please tell me all of that; I wish to hear it according to its true nature.
Having heard these words, Hari himself, the Lord of the World, spoke these beautiful words for the sake of the welfare of the world.

The Mlecchas born in the land of Miśra were indeed governed by Kāśyapa; having been refined by the Śūdra caste, they attained the status of the Brāhmaṇa caste. Having assumed the topknot and the sacred thread, and having studied the supreme Veda.
They worshipped the God of gods, the Lord of Śacī, with sacrifices.
Distressed, the blessed Indra went to Śvetadvīpa and awakened me with hymns of praise for the sake of the gods' welfare.
Once awakened, the speech addressed me: "Listen, O Lord, O ocean of compassion!
A twice-born man ought not to eat food prepared by a Śūdra;
likewise, I shall not attain satisfaction through sacrifices performed by Śūdras."
When Kāśyapa had passed away and the King of Magadha had ascended the throne,
my enemy, the Daitya Bali, having joined the side of Kali,
prepared to act in such a way that I would indeed be deprived of my splendor.
Born in the land of Miśra, that Mleccha refined the Sanskrit language;
that language led to the destruction of the gods and the prosperity of the Daityas.
Furthermore, he indeed corrupted the Prakrit language among the Āryas.
"Therefore, O Blessed One, protect me who have come to you for refuge.
Having heard this, I then spoke to the King of the Gods:
"O twelve Ādityas, you ought to go to the surface of the earth."
"For the sake of the welfare of the world, I shall be born in the Kali age—
proficient, skillful, wise, dexterous, accomplished, and happy;
likewise, well-versed, learned, omniscient, and a Sugata."
And likewise, the awakened and the enlightened are the Suns (Ādityas) who arise in succession:
Dhātṛ, Mitra, Aryaman, Śakra, Megha, Prāṃśu, Bhaga,
Vivasvat, Pūṣan, Savitṛ, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Viṣṇu.
Having come to the land of Kīkaṭa, those gods were born in due course;
setting aside the censure of the Vedas, they composed Buddhist scriptures.
Taking the Vedas from them, the gods bestowed them upon the sages.
By the power of their disparagement of the Vedas, those gods became afflicted with leprosy;
approaching Lord Viṣṇu in his Buddhist form, they offered hymns of praise.
Hari, through the power of yoga alone, eradicated their leprosy.
Due to those faults, the Buddhist became naked through his splendor;
from the first half [of the lineage] came Neminātha, and from the latter half came the Buddhist himself.
To destroy the Buddhist kingdom, he assumed the form of wood and stone.
I was born on the shore of the ocean for the sake of the world's welfare;
and King Indradyumna, having arrived from the heavenly realm,
constructed a temple there, and I have come to that very place.
And remaining here, he established this great place, which bestows the grace of sacrificial portions,
grants all desires in the world, and bestows liberation;
for here there is neither the duty of the social classes (varṇadharma) nor indeed the duty of the Vedas (vedadharma).
And here, within this circle of sacrificial portions, there is no vow [to be kept] even within the distance of a yojana.
Whoever has spoken the Yavana language and whoever has looked upon a Buddhist—great sin has been incurred by him; I stand here as the remover of that evil.
"Upon beholding me, a man shall become pure in the Kali age.

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Jagannātha," within the *Kṛṣṇacaitanyacarita* of the *Kaliyugīyetihāsasamuccaya*, which is a section of the *Caturyugakhaṇḍa* in the *Pratisargaparvan* of the glorious *Śrībhaviṣyamahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the twenty-first chapter.
Description of Kṛṣṇacaitanya.
Sūta said:
Having thus heard the words of that wise Jagannātha, [he spoke].
Kṛṣṇacaitanya himself, with a gracious mind, spoke to him:
"O Blessed One, O Sage, tell me in detail that account of the welfare of living beings which was mentioned by you, and how the Buddha came into being."
Jagannātha said:
When the Kali age had arrived after a thousand years, a preeminent sage named Kaṇva, the son of Kaśyapa, came to the land of action, Bhārata.
The noble Āryāvatī, the celestial maiden and beloved wife of Kaṇva,
arrived at the bank of the Śaradā together with her husband by the command of Śakra;
she was the Sarasvatī in the form of a river, dwelling in Kurukṣetra.

With a humble mind, Kaṇva praised her with hymns composed of the four Vedas. Within the span of a single year, the Goddess appeared before him in her grace and granted him an auspicious boon for the prosperity of the noble creation.
Ten sons were born to them, for they indeed brought about noble wisdom:
Upādhyāya, Dīkṣita, Pāṭhaka, Śukla,
Miśraka, Agnihotrī, Dvivedī, Trivedī, and Pāṇḍu.
As their names were proclaimed as "Caturvedīs," so too were their qualities;
with bowed necks, they indeed praised the goddess Sarasvatī.
Then, from those who were twelve years of age, the goddess [bestowed knowledge] according to her own power.
Having performed the rites, the mother Śāradā, who was devoted to her children, gave away the girl.
She was successively known as Upādhyāyī, Dīkṣitā, Pāṭhakī, Śuklikā,
Miśrāṇī, and the sixth was Agnihotriṇī.
Likewise, Dvivedinī is to be known as the eighth, and Trivedinī as the ninth;
Pāṇḍāyanī is the tenth, and Turyavedinī is the eleventh.
From their respective husbands, sixteen sons were born to each of them.
They should be known as the founders of the lineages; hear their names from me:
Kaśyapa, Bharadvāja, Viśvāmitra, Gautama, Jamadagni, Vasiṣṭha, Vatsa, and Gautama.
Parāśara, Garga, Atri, Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras,
Śṛṅgin, Kātyāyana, and Yājñavalkya were likewise their sons in succession;
thus all these sixteen sons should be known by their names.
By the command of Sarasvatī, Kaṇva went to the land of Miśra; there, having addressed ten thousand Mlecchas in Sanskrit and brought them under his control,
he himself arrived at the most excellent Brahmāvarta.
They all praised the goddess Sarasvatī with ascetic fervor.
Within five years, the goddess Sarasvatī manifested herself;
she then reduced those Mlecchas, along with their wives, to the status of Śūdras.
All of them became practitioners of the artisan's craft and had many sons;
among them, two thousand were Vaiśyas.
Among those, there was a teacher named Pṛthu, a servant of Kaśyapa.
And for twelve years he propitiated that great sage with ascetic penance;
then the blessed Kaṇva, the best of gods and the most excellent of givers, being pleased,
made them his king and bestowed upon him the city of Rājapura.
His wife, named Rājanyā, then gave birth to a son, Māgadha.
Kaṇva bestowed upon him a village called Māgadha in the eastern direction.
Then that sage, the son of Kaśyapa, returned once more to the heavenly world.
When the brahmin Kāśyapa had ascended to heaven, those Mlecchas of the Śūdra caste worshipped the God of gods, the Lord of Śacī, with sacrifices;
thus the Blessed Indra, along with his kinsmen, became sorrowful upon the surface of the earth.
Desiring to retrieve the Vedas, they were born from the womb of Brahmā;
there was a certain twice-born man named Jina, and his wife was known as Jayanī.
They were both born in the land of Kīkaṭa from portions of Kaśyapa and Aditi.
Born from those two for the sake of the world, the Ādityas resided at the city known as Bodhagayā on the banks of the Karmanāśā river;
there, enriched by the Buddhist scriptures, they established the supreme meaning of the teachings.
Having recovered the Vedas from the Śūdras, they went to the city of Viśālā;
there, having personally roused all the sages who were absorbed in meditation, they returned them.
From that time forward, all the gods departed for heaven, leaving the surface of the earth.
The Buddhists became Mlecchas, while others remained devoted to the Vedas;
through the power of Sarasvatī, many of them became Āryas,
and by them, the sacrificial offerings (havya) and ancestral oblations (kavya) were presented to the gods and the ancestors.
The thousands of noble gods became satisfied when two hundred and twenty-seven years of the Kali age had passed on earth. Then,
sent by Bali, the great asura Maya arrived upon the earth.
The teacher Śākyasiṃha, who incited many deceptions, was known by the name Gautamācārya; he was a promoter of the faction of the Daityas, and indeed,
it was by him alone that magical diagrams (yantras) were established at all sacred fords (tīrthas).

Those among them who had gone down below and were Buddhists all around became outcasts (varṇasaṅkara), devoid of the top-knot and the sacred thread. Ten crores of noble ones are recorded as having become followers of the Buddhist path.

Then, five hundred thousand remained; by the power of the four Vedas, those kṣatriyas born of the lineage of Agni ascended to the mountain peak. Forty warriors were left by them, and by them the Buddhists were utterly cast out.

Having refined those noble ones who had been established on the southern slopes of the Vindhya mountains, they settled them there in all directions according to their castes and forms. That region is the sacred land of Āryāvarta; those residing there number five hundred thousand.
Sūta said:
Having heard these words, the Lord Hari, the recipient of the sacrificial portions,
became a disciple of the Lord of the World, devoted to the path of the Vedas.
The son of Śukladatta, the excellent twice-born Nityānanda,
having bowed at the feet of Jagannātha and become his disciple, shone with splendor.
Then the Lord Aniruddha, the husband of Uṣā, was pleased.
He performed the consecration on their foreheads with the principle of Mahat;
from that time forth, the status of Mahat was established upon the earth.
The preceptor and his kinsmen, being well-pleased, joyfully spoke to their own disciples:
Whoever beholds here the face of Jagannātha, the lotus-navelled Lord of Uṣā, and having reached this place,
whoever partakes with reverence of the grace (prasāda) of that deity, shall indeed attain heaven.

Having bathed in the great ocean at Indradyumna-saras, one beholds Kṛṣṇa at Mārkaṇḍeya-vaṭa; such a person shall become a Brahmin for ten million births, a worthy recipient of the Vedas, and immensely wealthy,
and he never undergoes rebirth again.
"Whoever indeed hears this verse, endowed with faith and devotion,
shall quickly obtain that merit and fruit which comes from going to Purī.
Having heard these words of Yajñāṃśa, that Avatāraka [acted accordingly].
Having said, "So be it," to the Vaiṣṇavas, he vanished right there.
In the meantime, O Brahmin, Bali, being entreated by Kali,
summoned the Daitya Maya and spoke these words in distress.
"Sukandara, the lord of the Mlecchas, is always intent on my prosperity;
O Lord of Daityas, by my command, quickly provide him with assistance.
Having heard these words of Bali, he [the Lord] was accompanied by a hundred Daityas.
In the land of action (Karmabhūmi), Maya, who was proficient in the arts and sciences,
taught the excellent science of calculation by lines (rekhāgaṇita)— the twenty-first chapter of the Kalaveda— to wicked men of barbarian (mleccha) origin.
Then the Mlecchas, endowed with arts and proficient in the sciences of the arts,
caused machines to be constructed within those very seven cities.
All those people who had gone below them subsequently became Mlecchas.
A great clamor arose among the noble ones who were filled with grief;
hearing this, all those Vaiṣṇavas, the servants of Kṛṣṇacaitanya,
recited the divine mantra of their Guru and proceeded toward the city.
A disciple of Rāmānanda indeed arrived in Ayodhyā;
having reversed that mantra, he caused those Vaiṣṇavas to adopt the mark of the trident on their foreheads, which then became white and red.
With a garland of *tulasī* on their necks and their tongues made of Rāma,
those barbarians indeed became Vaiṣṇavas through the power of Rāmānanda;
they should be known as *saṃyogins*, established in the doctrine of Rāmānanda.
The noble and preeminent Vaiṣṇavas resided in Ayodhyā. The wise Nimbāditya, accompanied by his disciples, went to the city of Kāñcī;
there he beheld a mechanical device of the Mlecchas situated on the royal highway.
Having reversed the mantra of his own guru, he resided there;
a line like a bamboo leaf upon the forehead and a garland around the neck—
the Gopīvallabha mantra indeed shone upon their faces.
Those worlds situated below became Vaiṣṇavas;
the Mlecchas are to be known as Saṃyogins, while the Āryas are the Vaiṣṇavas of that path.
Viṣṇusvāmī, surrounded by his own followers, went to Haridvāra.
There, he indeed caused that great machine which was situated there to turn in reverse.
All those worlds that had been below it became Vaiṣṇava;
there, the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) appeared like two lines with a supreme dot in its center.
A *tulasī* bead remained upon their necks,
and the mantra of the Holy One stayed in their mouths, bestowing benefit.
Then Madhvācārya, the beloved of Hari, arrived in Mathurā.
He turned the machine situated on the royal road upside down;
those worlds situated beneath it that belonged to his faction became Vaiṣṇava.
He placed an auspicious tilaka, resembling a karavīra petal, upon his forehead.
A garland of *tulasī* remained upon their necks at the tip of the bridge of their noses,
and the auspicious name "Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa" was on their mouths;
even Śaṅkarācārya himself became devoted to the path of Śiva.
By the command of Rāmānuja, he arrived at the city of Kāśī accompanied by his attendants;
having reversed that yantra, the Śaivas stood beneath it,
with the *tripuṇḍra* mark upon their foreheads and rosaries of rudrākṣa beads around their necks.
And the Govinda-mantra was present in their mouths there.
Then Rāmānuja arrived happily at Totādri,
where there is a subtle yellow line between two vertical lines.
Likewise, on his forehead and throat was a beautiful garland of *tulasī*.
When the virtuous Varāhamihira arrived in Ujjayinī,
he rendered that [astrological] instrument useless and made the men there devotees of Śiva.
With funeral ashes on their foreheads and garlands of rudrākṣa beads around their necks,
the auspicious name "Śiva" became theirs there.
Indeed, Vāṇībhūṣaṇa himself arrived at Kānyakubja.
There, a sectarian mark (puṇḍra) in the shape of a half-moon and a garland of red sandalwood appeared;
moreover, the pure name of the Goddess was revealed there to them.
And Dhanvantari, having gone to Prayāga, [found] that supreme yantra.
There, those men who had gone below performed the rite in reverse;
a red half-tilaka with a dot was prescribed for their foreheads,
and a garland made of red sandalwood appeared upon their necks.
The wise Bhaṭṭoji went to the excellent Utpalāraṇya forest.
There, they bore the triple sectarian mark (tripuṇḍra) and red sandalwood paste, as well as garlands of rudrākṣa beads around their necks;
and the mantra "O Viśvanātha! indeed became theirs there.

Having reached the city of Iṣṭikā, he found that very machine rendered useless; having done so among the people there, he beheld the path of Brahman. Jayadeva himself, a devotee of Viṣṇu, arrived at Dvārakā.
That machine became fruitless for those men who had gone beneath it; however,
a streak of red remained on their foreheads,
and a rosary of lotus seeds with the mantra "Govinda" appeared upon their necks.
Thus, those Vaiṣṇavas, Śaivas, and Śāktas became manifold.
The Śāktas are to be known as *nirguṇa* (without attributes), while the Vaiṣṇavas are remembered as *saguṇa* (with attributes).
Furthermore, those who are both *nirguṇa* and *saguṇa* are to be understood by the wise at that time as Śaivas.
The gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three became meritorious through their abiding in samādhi.
Hari is Nityānanda in Śāntipurī, at Nadīhāpattana;
Kabīra is in the land of Māgadha, and Raidāsa is in Kaliñjara.
Accompanied by his disciples, he became absorbed in meditative concentration in the Naimiṣa forest;
even today, O Brahmin, that great host of Vaiṣṇavas remains established there,
and a vast increase in sacrificial portions has arisen upon the summit of Mount Meru.
Thus, O Brahmin, I have related to you this auspicious account of the conduct of the sacrificer’s portion,
hearing which men and women shall attain great merit.
Today, the Daityas, rendered fruitless by me, have approached the presence of Bali.

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Life of Kṛṣṇa Caitanya," in the *Kaliyugīyetihāsasamuccaya* (Compendium of Histories of the Kali Age), which is an alternative section of the *Caturyugakhaṇḍa* within the *Pratisargaparvan* of the glorious *Śrībhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the twenty-second chapter:
"A Description of the Monarchy of Guruṇḍa."
Sūta said:
Having thus heard of the great victory of the gods,
the Daitya Bali summoned the lord of the Daityas named Roṣaṇa and spoke these words.
"You are well-known by the name Sutastimiraliṅga;
indeed, having gone there, you must accomplish the great task of the Daityas.
Having heard this, that Daitya was filled with rage in his heart.
Established at the threshold, he destroyed those who stood upon the path of the Vedas.
His son, Bābar, ruled for five years;
his son, Homāyu, ruled for twenty years.
Blinded by intoxication, he disregarded the deities through his sacrificial rites; those gods then praised Kṛṣṇacaitanya, who was staying in the grove on the riverbank,
in many ways, and upon hearing this, Hari himself became enraged.
And by his own splendor, he indeed rendered that kingdom an obstacle;
his sacrificial fires were extinguished by the people produced from that army.
Then, in that place, the Mahārāṣṭras established themselves, subsisting on the remains of vegetables.
In the beautiful city of Dehalī, a Mleccha indeed ruled the kingdom;
he performed righteous deeds for five years.
There was a celibate student named Mukunda, born of the lineage of Śaṅkarācārya.
While performing austerities at Prayāga accompanied by twenty disciples,
he was then deprived of his divine powers by the deceitful barbarian king Bābara;
realizing this, he indeed offered his body into the fire.
His disciples entered the fire for the purpose of destroying the Mlecchas.
Having drunk the hair that was in cow's milk along with that milk,
the sage Mukunda was born in the womb of a Mleccha due to that fault.
While Homāyu was residing in Kashmir, a son was born to him. As soon as that son was born, an incorporeal voice spoke:
"By good fortune, this son has been born; he is endowed with all auspicious fortune."
On this terrible path of the Piśācas, there has never been, nor will there ever be, anyone like him;
therefore, he shall be known by the name Akabara, the son of Homāyu,
[and] Śrīdhara, Śrīpati, Śambhu, Vareṇya, and Madhuvratī.
Vimala, Devavān, Soma, Vardhana, Vartaka, Ruci,
Māndhātṛ, Mānakārī, Keśava, Mādhava, Madhu,
Devāpi, Somapa, Śūra, and Madana were his disciples.
"That illustrious Mukunda, a twice-born, has by fate come to your house.
Hearing these words from the sky, Homāyu, with a serene mind,
gave gifts to those afflicted by hunger and protected his son with love.
When his son was ten years old, he came to the land of Dehlī;
having defeated Śeṣaśāṅka, he indeed became king. He ruled the kingdom for one year, and his son became the monarch.
When the kingdom had come into the possession of Ekabara, his seven beloved disciples—
those who were the principal ones in their previous birth— approached the king:
Keśava, Gānasena, Vaijavāka, and Mādhava.
And they are remembered there as Mlecchas; among them were Haridāsa and Madhu.
Born in the lineage of Madhvācārya, he was a Vaiṣṇava who understood all forms of devotion.
In a previous birth, he had been Devāpi, and he became Vīrabala.
There was indeed a Brāhmaṇa from the western region, proud of the boon granted by the Goddess of Speech;
and Somapā Mānasiṃha, born of the lineage of Gautama,
who served as the commander-in-chief for the king, that crest-jewel among noble monarchs.
A twice-born man named Sūra was born, who was both skillful and learned;
he was also known by the name Bilvamaṅgala and was a friend of that king.
He was an expert in distinguishing the various types of heroines (nāyikās) and had mastered the ways of courtesans.
Madana was born as a Brāhmaṇa from the eastern region, and he became a dancer;
he was renowned by the name Caṇḍāla and was skilled in secret amorous play.
As for their other disciples, thirteen of them had gone to foreign lands.
The son born of Anapāyī was Śrīdhara, who was known as a conqueror of enemies;
the celebrated poet Tulasīśarman, skilled in the Purāṇas,
having received instruction from Nārī, arrived at Rāghavānanda.
Having become a disciple in Kāśī, he remained steadfast in the doctrine of Rāmānanda;
that Śrīpati became blind, yet remained firm in the doctrine of Madhvācārya.
He is to be known as Sūradāsa, the poet who brings forth the divine play of Kṛṣṇa.
Śambhu was indeed born in the lineage of Candrabhaṭṭa;
he was dear to Hari, established in the doctrine of Rāmānanda, and devoted to the glory of his devotees.
That most excellent one, named Ugrabhuñ, remained steadfast in the doctrine of Rāmānanda.

Constantly devoted to knowledge and meditation, a poet who composed works on prosody, he was born as Madhuvratī; he is renowned by the name Kīlaka. Wise and a performer of Rāma-līlā, he remained steadfast in the doctrine of Rāmānanda.
He was indeed born as Vimala, and by name alone he was Divākara;
he was the wise Sītālīlākara, established in the doctrine of Rāmānanda.
Devavān was born as Keśava, established in the doctrine of Viṣṇusvāmī.
Having composed works such as the *Kavipriyā*, he fell into the state of a *preta*;
but having composed the *Rāmajyotsnāmaya* treatise, he ascended to heaven. He was born as Soma, indeed that very Vyāsa, who stands firm in the doctrine of Nimbāditya.
Having composed a work consisting of secret amorous sports, he departed for heaven.
He was indeed born as Vardhana, known by the name Caraṇadāsaka;
having composed a work consisting of a garland of knowledge, he followed the path of Raidāsa.
And Vartaka was born, who remained adhering to the opinion of Ropaṇa;
he is to be known as Ratnabhānu and the author of the Bhāṣā commentary on Jaimini’s work. And Ruci was born as Rocana, who remained adhering to the opinion of Madhvācārya.
Having performed divine sports consisting of various forms, he departed for heaven.
That king named Māndhātṛ became a Kāyastha.
Madhvācārya composed the auspicious Bhāgavata in the vernacular language.
Mānakāra, having abandoned his male state, entered a female body;
he became known by the name Mīrā, the auspicious daughter of a king,
whose beauty was such that it shone upon her person and whose gait was indeed like that of an elephant.
And that Mīrā is declared by the wise to be established in the doctrine of Madhvācārya. Thus, O Brahmin, I have related to you this type of literary work in the vernacular,
a composition that brings auspiciousness in this terrifying age of Kali.
That king named Akabara, having made his kingdom free of thorns,
went to the abode of Vaikuṇṭha along with fifty disciples.
His son was Salomā, who ruled the kingdom equally well as his father.
Khurdaka was his son, who held the position for ten years;
he had four sons, of whom Navaraṅga was the middle one. Having conquered both his father and his brothers, he ruled the kingdom.
In a previous birth, this one was the famous Daitya named Andhaka;
by the command of the King of the Daityas, he went to the land of action (Karmabhūmi) as a portion of himself.
By him alone, many forms were cast down in every direction.
Seeing this, the gods arrived and said to Kṛṣṇacaitanya:
"O Blessed One, a portion of the king of the Daityas has been born as a sovereign of the earth;
having caused the gods and the Vedas to fall, he is increasing the faction of the Daityas."
Having heard this, that portion of the sacrifice, remaining on the bank of the river in the grove,
cursed that man of evil conduct so that his lineage might perish;
for forty-nine reigns had been established by that wicked soul.
There was a king named Sevajaya, who increased the side of the gods.
A Brahmin from Maharashtra, skilled in the science of warfare,
slew that man of wicked conduct and bestowed his position upon his son.
Having given [the kingdom], Devavivardhana departed for the southern country;
his son, named Alobha, held that position for five years.
Thereafter, O Sage, he met his death through the pain of an abscess.
O Brahmin, when one hundred and seventy years of Vikrama’s reign have passed, it should be known that seven years later, when Loma has met his death,
a powerful Mleccha named Phalaruṣa will be born into the lineage of Tālaṇa.
Having destroyed the lineage of Mukula, he himself indeed ruled the kingdom;
that king governed the earth for ten years before meeting his death at the hands of enemies and proceeding to the world of the Daityas.
Mahāmada, his son, held power for twenty years;
then, in that kingdom, a Daitya named Nāda arrived in the country,
and having slain the noble ones and conquered the gods, he went to the land of Khuraja.
Mahāmatsya, the son of Mada, seized the throne of his father and ruled the kingdom for five years;
that wicked man, born of the Tāla lineage, was slain by the Mahārāṣṭras.
Indeed, Mādhava ruled the kingdom in the city of Dehalī for ten years;
at that time, the Mleccha Ālomā obtained the sovereignty. Many kings born in their own country subsequently arose in that realm.
Many village chiefs became kings in various regions;
thus, the title of *maṇḍalīka* became imperishable upon the earth.
From that time on, for thirty years, this occurred in every village and among every king.
Then all the gods approached Kṛṣṇacaitanya;
and Hari himself, having directly perceived the suffering upon the earth and his own share of the sacrifice,
entered into meditation for a moment and spoke these words to the gods:
In the past, the wise Rāghava, having conquered the Rākṣasa Rāvaṇa,
restored the monkeys to life on all sides with showers of nectar:
Vikaṭa, Vṛjila, Jāla, Varalīna, and Siṃhala.
And those small monkeys, Javassumātra by name, spoke these words to Rāmacandra: "O Lord, grant us our desire.
The glorious Rāma, son of Daśaratha, having understood their intention, [acted accordingly].
Having given those maidens born of celestial nymphs to them from Rāvaṇa, the one who makes the world cry out, Hari himself, being delighted, spoke these words:
"And those islands fashioned by Jālandhara shall bear your names."
Among them, O sirs, there will be those who act for the king's benefit.
From the bull Ruṇḍa and the cow Nandinī, indeed, the fearsome Mlecchas were born;
their progeny, the Guruṇḍas, have always remained among them.
"Having conquered those Guruṇḍas, indeed, establish an excellent kingdom!
Having heard this and bowed to Hari, they departed joyfully for the islands.
The Guruṇḍas, born of the Vikaṭa lineage, had the faces of monkeys.

The Gauruṇḍas, followers of the Buddhist path, have come here for the sake of trade; they are established in the doctrine of Īśaputra. Their supreme heart is devoted to truth, has conquered desire, is free from anger, and is intent upon the Sun.
"Having stayed there, perform the work for humanity without delay.
Having heard this, those gods respectfully undertook the Ārcika;
prepared and diligent, they established it in the city of Calcutta.
In the western island of Vikaṭa, his wife Vikaṭāvatī performed the king’s counsel according to the eightfold path of skill;
her husband, Pulomārcis, resided in the city of Kalikātā.
When one hundred and eighteen years of the Kali age had passed since the departure of Vikrama’s kingdom,
and in the fortieth year thereafter, a king indeed arose.
In his lineage, seven kings known as the Guruṇḍas appeared.
Having ruled for sixty-four years, they went to their destruction. When the eighth king, Guruṇḍa, had arrived and was ruling with justice,
Bali, the Daitya, [slew] the great Asura named Mura on the side of Kali.
Having ascended, he dispatched [him] to the most excellent region of the gods;
having brought King Muru Vārḍila under his control while remaining established within his heart,
he indeed set his mind upon the destruction of the noble Dharma.
Then all the gods, assuming physical forms, went to him who partakes in the sacrificial portions;
having paid their respects, they all said: "The asura Mura has arrived.
Having learned this, the portion of Kṛṣṇa cursed the Guruṇḍas, the followers of the Buddhist path.
"All those who have fallen under the power of Mura shall go to their destruction.
When these words were spoken,
the wicked Gurundas, impelled by Time (Kāla), met their end along with their own armies within the space of a single year.
All thirty thousand of them proceeded to the abode of Yama;
and by means of verbal punishments, that king Vārdila met his destruction.
The ninth was Guruṇḍa, who reached [the state of] the powerful one named Bhekalaka.
He ruled the kingdom with justice and diligence for twelve years;
while he governed according to justice, that kingdom flourished in the land of the Āryas.
There was a famous man named Laḍila, a Guruṇḍa who was deluded by the ten [vices].
That righteous king ruled the kingdom for thirty-two years.
When Laḍila had passed away, the noble ones born of the Makaranda lineage— known as the Maunas— then arrived from their residence on Himatuṅga.
Brown-colored, with subtle minds, round in shape, and long-headed—
such were the followers of the Buddha who arrived at the threshold in their hundreds of thousands.
Indeed, a king named Ārjika was their ruler there.
His son, Devakaṇa, performed severe penance for twelve years on the summit of Mount Gaṅgotra for the sake of increasing his kingdom; then,
by the power of that wise man's austerity, the blessed Gaṅgā [appeared].
Having attained his own true form by his own will, he went to the world of Brahmā.
Then Kubera arrived and, having bestowed upon him a great station as the sovereign of the circle of noble ones,
vanished right there.
Maṇḍalīka Devakarṇa became the protector of the realm;
that king ruled over the earth for sixty years. In his lineage, eight kings arose who were worshippers of the gods.
Having held the throne for two hundred years, they departed for the heavenly realm.
And he who was the eleventh, known as Mauna Pannagāri,
having diligently ruled the kingdom for forty years, [departed].
The king went to the heavenly world, having met his death at the hands of the serpents.
Thus was the kingdom on the surface of the earth ruled by those born of the Maurya lineage.

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Gurunda and Mauna Kingdoms," in the Kali Age History Compendium, which is an alternative section of the Caturyuga-khaṇḍa within the Pratisarga-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the twenty-third chapter,
titled "A Description of the Collection of Histories from the Kali Age.
Sūta said:
O Sage, when two hundred and sixty-four years of the Vikrama era had passed, King Bhūtanandin then [ruled]. From the Kubera-yakṣas, he obtained silent [attendants] endowed with wealth and grain.
Having conquered those combatants with terrible battles lasting for a hundred and fifty thousand kalpas,
he himself established a kingdom over Kilkilā along with the Naga lineages.
In the south-eastern direction, there is a famous city built by Puṇḍarīka.
In that city named Kilakilā, there was once a king;
while he was ruling the kingdom, the Nāgas beginning with Puṇḍarīka became objects of worship for all people in every household.
Svāhā, Svadhā, and Vaṣaṭkāra, who perform worship to the gods upon the surface of the earth,
abandoned the gods and, having approached, took their stand upon the summit of Meru.
By the command of Śakra, Kubera [placed] awned grain all around.
The Lord, having taken a sixth portion from the Yakṣas, bestowed it upon the gods;
furthermore, whatever items such as jewels and gold were given in the kingdoms of Maunī,
the Lord placed those back into the treasuries.
That ruler of the mandala was honored by Bhūtanandin.
After him, King Śiśunandi reigned for fifty years;
he placed the worship of the Nāgas foremost, thereby setting aside the gods on earth.
Then his younger brother Yaśonandin,
who was devoted to the worship of the Nāgas, ruled the kingdom for twenty-one years; having himself attained the throne of his brother, he governed for twenty-five years.
Then his son, Pravīraka, became king.
That kingdom is celebrated as lasting for eleven years on this land of action (karmabhūmi).
Once, he arrived in Bāhlīka accompanied by his army.
There, a battle took place between them and the fierce Piśāca Mlecchas;
within the span of a single month, the Mlecchas reached the number of one hundred thousand in death,
and likewise sixty thousand devotees of Nāga met their end.
The king named Bādala, who was immensely powerful and resided in Romaja,
summoned Yaśonandin and gave him his daughter Jālavatī.
Having taken the daughter of the Mleccha king, he returned to his home.
Then a powerful son was born from her as an embryo;
he became famous by the name Bāhlīka, devoted to the worship of the Nāgas. Thirteen kings known as the Bāhlīkas were born in his lineage.
Having ruled for four hundred years, they passed away;
while Ayomukha was governing the kingdom here in Bāhlīka,
all the hosts of ancestors then approached Kṛṣṇacaitanya.
Having bowed, they spoke these words there: "O Blessed One, hear my words.
We are the hosts of Pitṛs who have been excluded by the kings born of the Naga lineage.
By them, we have always been deprived of the rites of Śrāddha and Tarpaṇa."

From the increase of the ancestors comes the increase of Soma; from that, the gods increase. From the increase of the gods comes the increase of the worlds; therefore, Brahmā Prajāpati increases. From the increase of Brahmā, there is supreme joy in every house and among every person.
"Therefore, O Blessed One, protect us; preserve these eternal subjects.
Having heard these words of theirs, the Blessed Lord Hari, who partakes in the sacrifice, [established] Puṣyamitra, the supreme devotee of Dharma and the increaser of the lineage of the Āryas.
As soon as he was born, that boy indeed attained the age of sixteen;
having conquered and expelled those born from wombs who were preceded by iron-faced warriors,
he himself took possession of the kingdom.
Just as the king named Vikrama, born from a portion of Śiva,
became worthy of worship after conquering the Śakas, Gandharvas, and birds;
so too [he conquered] the kings of the Naga faction and the terrifying Golakāsyas.
Having then conquered [the world], Puṣyamitra became honored by all on earth; his reign, which had lasted for one hundred and seventy-two years since the time of Vikrama,
came to an end at that point.
When Puṣyamitra attained the position of kingship,
he then held that royal office for a hundred years as a righteous soul.
[The sacred cities were] Ayodhyā, Mathurā, Māyā, Kāśī, Kāñcī, and Avantikā.
By that king, the city of Dvāravatī was restored,
as well as the various sacred fields (kṣetras) of Kuru, Sūkara, and Padma;
and on the surface of the earth, the forest-fields of Naimiṣa, Utpala, and Vṛnda were likewise raised up.
By him alone were various holy places established on all sides.
Then that Gandharva Kali, the defiler of gods and ancestors,
assumed the form of a Brahmin and approached Puṣyamitra.
Having bowed, he spoke these pleasing words: "Listen, O King, you who are devoted to compassion!

In the land of the Āryas, the hosts of ancestors are worthy of worship through śrāddha rites and libations. Know this: that which is the worship of the ancestors on earth is [the remedy for] ignorance."
Those men who have died on earth, following the power of their past karma,
become embodied beings in eighty-four hundred thousand ways; thus,
by the god Maya, the worship of the ancestors was fashioned through artifice.
"The labor of men is in vain, their ritual acts are in vain, and so too is the worship of the ancestors.
Having heard these terrible words, the lord of the earth laughed and said:
"You are a fool, a great deluded one; you do not know the supreme fruit."
Those radiant ones who are not seen in the Bhuvarloka and have become like the void—
those indeed are the hosts of ancestors (pitṛgaṇas) who travel in celestial chariots in the form of funeral cakes (piṇḍa).
And as for the offering of the funeral cake performed according to the prescribed rite by virtuous sons;
That celestial chariot, born from the sky, bestows all forms of bliss;
for those whose forms consist of the essence of the funeral cake (piṇḍa), their stay there lasts for one year.
[This is achieved] through the eighteen chapters of the Gītā and the life-stories of the Saptashatī.

That funeral cake (piṇḍa) which has indeed been offered remains for three hundred years. Those men who are seen on earth devoid of the śrāddha and water-libations (tarpaṇa) should all be known as inhabitants of hell, along with one hundred and one generations of their lineage.
"The Śrāddha rite is a great dharma; this Śrāddha is the cause of all [attainments].
Having heard this, that Gandharva, the king of Kali, with a cheerful countenance, bowed and spoke to that best of kings regarding embodied beings.
"O King, may you always quickly become mine; I am your servant.
May you always be Kalimitra and Puṣyamitra on this earth, just as you were the friend of King Vikrama and of the Vetāla."
"I shall indeed accomplish all your tasks; of this there is no doubt.
Having spoken thus to the steadfast king and taking him with him, that Kali traversed the seven continents, the various regions, and numerous paths through the sky.
The valiant one showed it to the king who stood upon his own back;
that king, having established the noble dharma— which had perished— in the Kali age,
gave up his life in a portion of the sacrifice, and his splendor entered into him.
A powerful king named Sugata, born in the land of Āndhra,
having seen that country without a ruler, established his reign there; he held the throne for twenty years, and thus the Land of Action was honored by him.
In his lineage there were sixty kings who followed many paths;
during the reign of Puṣyamitra, three hundred and ten years passed.
At that time, those residing in the land of the Āndhras met their destruction.
Then, for fifty years, the earth was indeed without a king.
At that time, men became base and greedy, plundered by fierce thieves;
they fell into terrible poverty, and the earth was devoid of gold.
Furthermore, the Blessed Lord, being entreated by the gods, spoke to them:
"In the land of Kosala, there shall arise a lord of the earth born from a portion of the Sun,
renowned as Rākṣasāri, who is devoted to the path of the gods."
"By my command, he shall indeed become the king upon the surface of the earth.
Having spoken thus, Viṣṇu vanished and returned to the world of the gods.
The enemies of the Rākṣasas then installed him as king in Ayodhyā.
Whatever wealth had been gathered by the Rākṣasas in the kingdom of Āndhra,
he conquered those Rākṣasas and distributed that wealth village by village;
he caused gold worth eight times the value of a pearl to be produced on the earth.
A hundred-fold value was indeed made from silver by him;
a fivefold value was made from copper and likewise from lead;
and a fivefold value from tin was fashioned upon the earth by that very same person.
Copper is more purifying than lead, and tin is even superior to that.
Tin is worth one hundred times the value of iron; thus it is highly esteemed.
Having enjoyed the earth for fifty years, he went to the world of the Sun.
In his lineage, sixty kings devoted to the Vedas were born;
when seven hundred years had passed since the kingdom was established by Puṣyamitra,
the kings born of the Kauśala dynasty ascended to heaven.
Then, for fifty years, the earth was without a sovereign ruler;
O Bhārgava, petty kings enjoyed the land in various regions.
Following that, there was a king from the Vaidara country named Viśārada.
Having arrived in the noble land accompanied by an army of one hundred thousand,
he brought the petty kings under his control and became a sovereign ruler (*maṇḍalika*). Through various arts, he performed diverse deeds upon the surface of the earth.
In village after village, men brought about the intermixture of castes.
The caste consisting of Brahmins and Kṣatriyas was seen in name only;
noble men were mostly Vaiśyas, and those who performed the duties [of the twice-born] were mostly Śūdras.
In that kingdom, men were worshippers of the gods in name only;
by him, the status of the land of action was honored for sixty years.
Then six kings of his lineage obtained the earth.
When the kingdom had passed to Puṣyamitra, sixteen hundred years [had elapsed]; in that terrifying Kali age, the Vaidūras met their destruction,
and for four hundred years the earth took on a wretched form.
After him, King Kālamālī became the ruler of the Niṣadha kingdom;
having brought minor kings under his control, he indeed became the sovereign himself.
By Yama’s command, Tvaṣṭṛ built a city on the bank of the Yamunā upon this earth.
A woman named Kālakālī, renowned for her magical powers, was created there;
she became the honored queen among the kings of that noble land.
Disregarding the gods and the ancestors, she established the worship of the *preta*s among every person.
And Kālamālī, established in the kingdom of Niṣadha, ruled for thirty-two years; that reign was a source of oppression to the people.
Following him, sixty kings of his lineage arose who were worshippers of the spirits of the dead (Pretas).
The kingdom of those rulers of the Niṣadha region lasted for a hundred years;
thereafter, for a thousand years, the earth was indeed filled with petty kings.
Only the worship of the gods, the Vedic path, and the mere hearing of the scriptures were seen.
When the kingdom had passed to Puṣyamitra and three thousand one hundred and thirty-two years of the Kali age had elapsed, the gods were then distressed;
approaching Kṛṣṇacaitanya and bowing down, they spoke these pleasing words.
O Blessed One, in this Kali age today on the surface of the earth, the four castes have fallen from their proper conduct; they are like hungry ghosts, living for only fifty years,
and disregarding the gods and ancestors, they indeed worship only the Piśācas.
In village after village on this earth, images of Kūṣmāṇḍas are seen by us today being worshipped by men; yet those men are themselves exceedingly distressed,
along with the hosts of bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, ḍākinīs, and śākinīs.
Blinded by intoxication from their own worship, they revile the gods and the ancestors;
therefore, know us—the weak ones—to be the powerful leaders of beings.
O Lord, you who are compassionate toward those who have come for refuge, protect us with mercy!
Having heard this, that Yajñāṃśa, while staying in a grove on the bank of the river,
spoke to the gods who had become humble; he was the lord of the earth in Māgadha,
Purañjaya, devoted to Brahman, and his wife was Purañjanī.
"By my command, a son shall be born to them— one of great strength,
renowned as Viśvasphūrji, devoted to the path of Brahman, and endowed with virtue.
When he had spoken these words, Purañjanī conceived a fetus.
Within ten months, the immensely powerful Viśvasphūrji was born. As soon as that son was born, an incorporeal voice spoke:
"Just as Puṣyamitra was the promoter of the duties of the social orders (*varṇadharma*),"
Thus this child has been born, powerful and devoted to the path of Brahman;
he will bring the Kalingas,
Yadus, and Madrakas under his supreme rule, and that one of firm resolve will establish the subjects as being preeminent in Brahman.
Hearing these words from the sky, "The energetic one, having destroyed the Kṣatriyas, will indeed [conquer] the city of Padmavatī," King Purañjaya,
together with his retinue, gave gifts to hungry guests.
O Sage, when the Kali age arrived, eight thousand and eight hundred years had then passed in this land of action. At that time,
King Viśvasphūrji was a man of great intelligence and great strength.

Having brought the petty kings and all classes of men under his control, O Brahman, he then established them in the Brahmin class, which is devoted to the Supreme Brahman. The Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, Piśācas, and those of mixed castes were likewise established.
The Guruṇḍas and other Mlecchas became Brāhmaṇas;
they performed various rites such as the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā), libations (tarpaṇa), and the worship of the gods according to Vedic injunctions, while maintaining the custom of eating together.
O Sage, he ruled the kingdom for sixty years and governed it perfectly;
thereafter, thousands of kings renowned throughout the earth arose in his lineage,
living for ten thousand years and remaining devoted to the path of Brahman.
And the portions assigned by them according to the ritual rules in the midst of the sacrifice arrived in forms identical for both the Daityas and the Suras;
and all the gods, being astonished, sought refuge in the sacrificial portion itself.
Having understood that cause, the son of Śakra said to them:
"The Veda is Nārāyaṇa himself, the discerning one in the form of a swan;
he indeed established the distinction of castes for men according to the differences of the Yugas."
The Brāhmaṇa caste possesses the quality of *sattva*, while the Kṣatriya possesses the quality of *rajas*.
Likewise, the Vaiśya possesses the quality of *tamas*, and the Śūdra arises from the equilibrium of the qualities (*guṇasāmya*).
Through Brāhmaṇas, the hosts of ancestors attain satisfaction; through Kṣatriyas, the gods.
The Yakṣas and Rākṣasas were created from Vaiśyas, and the Daityas and Dānavas from the low-born;
thus, within a single caste, there are four castes, for he is indeed the Kāyastha.
The Bhūtas, Pretas, Piśācas, and others are always gratified by the Kāyasthas.
At present, the four castes are established within the Brahman-caste;
for previously, O Dānavas, this was the caste of Brahmā and Śaṅkara.
After that, they shall become half-satisfied inhabitants of heaven.
"Therefore, O gods, in this terrible Kali age, for your sake I shall go to the house of the King of Saurāṣṭra on the surface of the earth by means of a portion of myself.
Having spoken thus, that Somanātha, who is a portion of the sacrifice, [remained] with one part.
In that house there was one named [Kṣattravarmā], who, residing in a city of Saurāṣṭra,
conquered kings and joyfully established his own kingdom on the shore of the ocean.
At that time, in the Kali age, the earth became composed entirely of the Kṣatriya caste.
That Somanātha indeed gratified all the gods with sacrifices;
by the grace of the gods, he ruled for a hundred years,
and his reign became renowned throughout the world.
