In his lineage there were one hundred and fifty kings who were beloved by the gods;
they bestowed happiness for a period of slightly more than ten thousand years.
When the Kali age arrived in this land of action (Karmabhūmi), three tens of thousands of years passed.
Then, after that time had passed, the distressed Daityas said to Kali:
"Formerly, Maheśvara was propitiated by us through austerities for a hundred years;
he then truly granted us his favor."
"O Lord, half of your beautiful body is composed of diamond and half is tender;
protect us who are suffering in this age.
Having heard this, Kali, the enhancer of the faction of the Daityas, [acted].
Having taken birth from a portion of himself in the terrible land of Gurjara during the Kali age,
he entered the womb of a wicked cowherd woman named Siṃhikā, who was a devourer of lion-flesh; there he became known as Rāhu.
Just as Rāhu, the terrible devourer of the moon, moves through the path of the sky,
so too was this Rāhu, a portion of Kali born upon the earth, a tormentor of the gods. As soon as that son was born, a great earthquake occurred.
All the planets, having become adverse, produce great fear;
out of fear of that, all the gods, abandoning their forms on every side,
went for refuge to Mahendra on the summit of Mount Sumeru.
For that purpose, Lord Śakra praised the Mother of the World;
the Goddess, who brings auspiciousness and consists of the form of a maiden, spoke to the gods:
"O gods, by the sight of my body, you shall forever be free from hunger and thirst."
"And therefore, you all must remain intent upon beholding me.
Having heard this, those gods became filled with joy.
Rāhu, the son of the Ābhīrī, having ruled for a hundred years—
Having renounced his life-breaths, that best of sages became absorbed in the Kali age.
Within one hundred and fifty thousand years of his lineage,
the terrible and great doctrine of Mada was destroyed after a long period of time.
Furthermore, by them it was uprooted from the earth, and all became Mlecchas;
in the Kali Yuga, neither the Vedas, nor the gods, nor the social classes (varṇas) were seen,
nor were any boundaries observed in that lineage during the Kali Age.
Thousands of remnants of the twice-born [reappeared] upon the summit of Arbuda;
they were capable of propitiating the gods with great effort for twelve days.
And from Arbuda was born a kṣatriya, bearing a sword and a shield.

Having conquered the invincible Mlecchas, he indeed became known by the name Carvabali. For the sake of his own expansion, that pure king established a territory measuring five yojanas, which is remembered by the name Carvapurī.
Gradually, the noble lineage flourished there once again;
with great effort, he ruled that vast kingdom for fifty years.
O Sage, one hundred and fifty kings then reigned in that dynasty.
At the end of ten thousand years, there will be fierce barbarians (mlecchas), friends of the barbarians, and those of mixed caste;
they will marry barbarian girls, be terrible, and follow the path of the Aryas in name only.
Then, by the hundreds of thousands of barbarians residing in the land of Malaya—
A hair-raising battle took place with the Ārvudas and the Āryas.
Within the span of a single year, the mighty Mālavas were defeated; and having been released on all sides by the Āryas along with the infantry of the regional lords, they departed.
For forty thousand years on the surface of the earth,
there were hundreds of Mleccha kings who lived for very short spans of life;
the total number of those monarchs was twenty-five thousand.
But those meritorious rulers of the earth who arose from the ascetic penance of previous births—
their deeds have been proclaimed by the sages in the Purāṇas.
All others, however, are makers of various eras, mere Piśācas, and corrupters of dharma.
"Ninety thousand years have passed in the Kali Yuga;
the earth has become filled with Mlecchas, and misfortune has arisen among every person.
Thus [ends] the Pratisarga Parva of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, in the section on the Fourth Age (Caturyugakhaṇḍa).
The twenty-third chapter, titled "A Comprehensive Description of the History of the Kali Yuga.
Now begins the twenty-fourth chapter:
A Comprehensive Description of the History of the Kali Yuga.
Sūta said: Then all those Daityas, preceded by Kali,
constructed water-vessels and proceeded toward Harikhaṇḍa.
In Harikhaṇḍa, men who were equal to gods and possessed great strength fought with them using mighty weapons; living for ten thousand years,
they were all defeated within ten years by means of illusory battles.
The inhabitants of Harikhaṇḍa went for refuge to Mahendra.
Then the blessed Śakra spoke to Viśvakarman:
"This lathe and this bending machine are situated within the seven oceans."
O dear one, by your power, men on this earth do not go to other continents; yet that very machine was caused to fall by your illusory brother Maya,
along with the Mlecchas, from every side.
"Men who are my enemies shall go to the seven islands;
therefore, protect our boundaries established by you in the midst of the earth.
Having heard this, Viśvakarman fashioned a divine machine.
By the power of that machine, they were set into motion;
from that rotating machine, a great wind arose which was the destroyer of the Mlecchas.
From that wind there was born a son, Vātya, who originated from the whirlwind.
Having conquered the Daityas, Yakṣas, and Piśācas, the powerful one, who consists of knowledge,
honored the three castes— the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas.
By his might, the exceedingly powerful Vātya made the Mlecchas conform to the [caste] system.
He occupied the position of a sovereign ruler on earth for fifty years;
thereafter, thousands of kings appeared in his lineage during the Kali Yuga.
For sixteen thousand years, they were followers of Vāyu, endowed with the three social orders (varṇas).
Brahmā himself was born from Vāyu; indeed, that Hari was born from Vāyu;
Mahādeva was born from Vāyu. The entire world consists of Vāyu.
Without Vāyu, all are dead; by means of Vāyu, all live upon the earth.
Thinking thus, those people gratified Vāyu;
then, once again, the terrible Kali bowed to Bali, the lord of the Daityas,
and informed him, whereupon Bali became distressed.
Having approached Vāmana accompanied by Kali-mitra,
that king bowed and spoke to Janārdana, the God of gods:
"O Best of Gods, Kali has been bestowed upon me by you, who are well-pleased."
The Kali age was repelled from the land of action (Bhārata) by the Vātya brāhmaṇas;
only one quarter of this lordly Kali has passed, and it is slightly diminished.
By me, through the illusory power of the Lord of Devas, the earth has indeed been fully enjoyed.
When the Kali age arrived, the surface of the earth was enjoyed by me for a thousand years;
thereafter, the celestial realm was enjoyed by the gods for one thousand five hundred years, and slightly more than that.
For the sake of all the world, I have enjoyed this land of action;
thereafter, for one thousand five hundred years, this excellent [land] was enjoyed by the gods together with me.
Since then, it has been held by me for slightly less than one thousand five hundred years.
The earth was enjoyed for thirty-three thousand years by the gods and likewise by the Daityas;
again by the Daityas and then by the gods, and likewise by the gods and the Dānavas.
O God, destroyer of the Kali age, this Kali age has indeed been granted to me by you.
"O Lord, no formal request was made; this is the truth, O You who are devoted to truth and capable of enduring it.
Having heard these words of Bali, the Blessed Lord Vāmana Hari, who increases the faction of the Daityas, arrived upon the surface of the earth as his own partial incarnation (aṃśa).
Then the brahmin Kāmaśarman, staying on the bank of the Yamunā,
diligently praised Hari in his mind for twelve years.
Then the glorious Vāmana spoke these words to that best of the twice-born:
"Choose a boon, O best of the twice-born, whatever resides in your heart.
Having heard this, Kāmaśarman praised him with gentle words.
Kāmaśarman said:

Homage to the Great God; homage to you, who are worthy of all worship. Homage again and again to the one who loves dharma, to Dharma itself, the creator of gods and demons, the sustainer of men who are subject to fate, and the performer of actions.
Those gods are dependent on fate, and those Dānavas transgress fate;
to that God who is their sustainer and, in due course, their destroyer, I offer my salutation.
O Lord Hari, become my son and make my desire fruitful.
Having heard this, Hari himself, who had become Vāmana as the protector of Bali,
manifested from his own upper body through his wife Devahūtī;
thus appearing in two forms, they were born with divine limbs and divine bodies upon the earth.
Bhogasiṃha, Kelisiṃha, Devapa, Daityapa, and Hari—
having conquered the kings born of the Vātya lineage, they arrived at the field of Kalpa.
There is a city named Rahaḥkrīḍāvatī, built by Maya.
Having stayed there, those two powerful ones took up the burden of the Kali age.
This wife of theirs is eternal, the very essence of all dharmas;
those noble men born of her, who are devoted to their husbands, are beloved by the gods.
Thinking, "All men born from a corrupted woman are a mixture of castes," the Blessed Lord Hari assumed a body composed of desire and enjoyed thousands of women day after day.
Having conceived, they all gave birth with joy to twins.
Those uterine brothers took delight with that sister of their own womb.
And thus was their progeny multiplied in many ways during the Kali age.
Having consumed those three kinds of food produced previously day after day,
they grew in the land of action like birds upon a tree;
at the end of two thousand years, the former human beings were thus nourished by them.
Then the second foot of Kāla descended upon the earth;
at present, the news of the Kinnaras is on the ground.
The men there are known to be two *kiṣkus* in height, and they are composed of the nature of Daityas.
"Just as birds that live for forty years are devoid of karma, so too are those who dwell upon the earth; indeed, O sirs,
no distinction whatsoever is seen among them today by you on this terrestrial plane— neither Kinnaras nor humans."
And indeed, at the end of the second quarter, it shall be exactly thus:
there will be no marriage, no king, no exertion, and no performance of ritual action for them at the conclusion of that second quarter.
"O twice-born ones, from this day forward for a period measured by one hundred and fifty thousand years,
those born of the lineage of Bhogakeli will appear upon the surface of the earth.
Therefore, O best of sages, you shall remain here together with me."
"Having approached Kṛṣṇacaitanya, we shall depart by his command.
Vyāsa said: Having heard this, the sages residing in Viśālāpurī—

"O Lord, salutations to you! All the best of sages, having bowed down to the Lord who is the embodiment of sacrifice and the recipient of the sacrificial portions, will go toward their shares with joy and speak these words:
'O Blessed One, O Master, grant us your command.'"
"We shall go to Indra’s world, to the enchanting midst of heaven. Having heard this, Yajñāṃśa, accompanied by all his disciples and beloved by the gods,
will go to the celestial realm together with them all.
Then Kali, together with the Daityas, will frequent the surface of the earth.
What else do you wish to hear, O Hṛṣīkeśa? Tell me that.
Manu said:
"O Blessed One, tell me in detail about the conduct of worldly enjoyments and amorous play; O Lord, describe how human beings will be in the Kali age.
Vyāsa said:
When Bhogasiṃha and Kelisiṃha, born from a portion of Vāmana,
had conquered the Daityas on earth— both those consisting of men and those arising from the wind—
they approached the portion of Vāmana and became filled with joy.
Then the distressed gods, abandoning their forms on all sides,
approached Kṛṣṇacaitanya and, bowing with necks bent low,
said: "O Blessed One, by Your grace, [we have attained] the first step of the Kali age."
"O Lord, having conquered those who worship the Daityas, the earth has thus been enjoyed;
what should be done regarding the portion of the sacrifice? Salutations to you, O Compassionate One!
Having heard this, Hari said: "Listen then, O best of gods."
"I shall go to heaven with you, filled with joy;
therefore, all you gods, quickly rouse the men from the lineage of the gods, and having come together, proceed to the third heaven."
When Sūta had thus spoken to the sages regarding Sumaṇḍala,
O mind, the gods then took their celestial chariots and set out for that place,
having mounted them along with Sūta and all the other sages.
Then, at that river-side grove, they shall receive their share of the sacrifice:
the yogi Ahlāda, Gorakṣa and the others,
as well as Śaṅkara and the other Rudras who are portions of Rudra, and King Bhartṛhari.
Others, who are established in yoga and bestow welfare, shall also go;
with them, Kṛṣṇacaitanya will go to the world of the gods.
Then, those two portions of Vāmana will appear in the second part of the Kali age.
While he dwells in the Kalpa-field, having attained the perfection of yoga and established himself in meditative absorption,
all the Daityas will then be filled with joy and, through those men,
will repeatedly expand their subterranean abodes, such as Pātāla and others, in every direction.
When the third quarter of the Kali age has arrived, those Kinnaras will gradually go to destruction on earth from all sides;
this shall occur when twenty-six thousand years of the third quarter have passed.
By the command of Rudra, the sage Bhṛṅga, taking the side of the spirits (bhūtas), shall depart;
his wife, named Saurabhī, shall give birth to men of great strength,
born of the Kaula lineage, who are terrible and devourers of all kiṃnaras.
At that time, in the Kali age, they will be twenty-six years of age;
together with the Kinnaras, they will seek refuge in the portion of Vāmana. Then, Bhoga-siṃha and Keli-siṃha will engage in a great battle with them.
He shall rule for ten years, and then, defeated by those Daityas,
the portion of Vāmana will go to Pātāla along with them;
at that time, in the Kali age, there will arise a most terrible creation of Bhṛṅga.
Those sons of the maternal aunt will indeed be men in the form of cattle;
blinded by lust, they will eat with pleasure and procreate many sons.
When the third quarter of the Kali age has concluded, those creations [will prevail].
In the Kali age, those who possess the nature of animals will become fierce;
and when the fourth quarter of the Kali has arrived,
men will die at the age of twenty, destined for hell.
Just as aquatic beings and forest-dwellers subsist on roots, tubers, and fruits, so shall men become in the Kali age. Then,
those regions renowned for their light, such as Āloka and others, will become terrifying places of darkness.
All of them will be filled by men born in the land of action (karmabhūmi),
just as the Satyaloka is filled in the first quarter of the Truth (satya-yuga),
the Tapoloka in the second, and the Janaloka in the third.

In the first quarter of the Tretā Yuga, the fourth heaven (Svargaloka) was filled by those born in the land of action; just as that heaven is remembered to have been filled by those men, so too was Bhuvarloka— the abode of the earth— filled in the first quarter of the Tretā Yuga.
In the second [age], the world of the sages (ṛṣiloka); in the third, the realm of the planets (grahaviṣṭapa);
and in the fourth, the Bhuvarloka was filled by men born of their karma.
When the first quarter of the Dvāpara age is completed, that Puṣkara island comes into being.
In the second [quarter], Śālmaladvīpa; in the third, Krauñcadvīpa, which is the last of the islands;
and in the fourth quarter, Jambūdvīpa is recorded by the sages. And in the first quarter of the Kali age, the world was filled from below to above.
In the second [layer] there is the seventh netherworld (saptapātāla), and in the third, the realm of spirits (bhūtaviṣṭapa);
these are filled with humans born in the land of action (karmabhūmi).
From that time on, all those who are not destined for hell will come to fill them completely with those men.
Thus, O Manu, everything that I was asked by you has been told to you.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Compendium of Histories of the Kali Age," in the Caturyuga-khaṇḍa (also known as the Pratisarga-parvan) of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa.
Now begins the twenty-fifth chapter,
titled "A Description of a Collection of Histories from the Kali Age.
Vyāsa said:
Those born under the twenty-first [asterism] in the fourth quarter will suffer from indigestion and go to hell, to the abode of Yama.
Homage to you, O Dharmarāja, who brings us satisfaction.
"O Omniscient One, hear our words; our birth has become undigested.
O Best of Gods, act in such a way that we may return to our original nature.
Having heard this, Dharmarāja, accompanied by Citragupta, [acted accordingly].
And in the Kali age, they shall go to Brahmā at the time of twilight;
having seen the four Yamas, the Supreme Lord Pitāmaha,
knowing for himself what was uttered by them, will depart toward the Ocean of Milk.
Having worshipped the Lord of the World, the God of gods, Vṛṣākapi, he will fully praise the Supreme Lord with hymns consisting of the Sāṅkhya scriptures:
"Victory! Victory! Victory! O Attribute-less One who assumes attributes, O Supporter of the world, O Source of the principles of the universe, O Bringer of auspiciousness!"
He constructs the gods from the principles consisting of essential, virtuous qualities, and protects them through the qualities of *sattva*;
salutations, repeated salutations to Him, the mass of qualities, who manifests as Kṛṣṇa within the hearts of the hosts of gods,
and who swiftly creates men upon earth from the principles consisting of *rajas*.
"O Lord, you who protect and strike down those who are arrogant, upon whose head the burden of the world rests—
protect us, O Protector, O destroyer of demons, O you who shine with the qualities of your playful pastimes born of Time!
Having heard these words of theirs, the Lord [responded] as if instantly swallowing the earth.

Listen quickly with a focused mind to how that Lord will be born: Viṣṇu, having bowed to those who were themselves bowed down in devotion, will speak these delightful words to them for the sake of the world’s welfare:
"O gods, this Kaśyapa shall be born in the village of Sambhala."
Known by the name Viṣṇuyaśas, his beloved wife will be Viṣṇukīrti;
she will cause those men to hear this book consisting of the pastimes of Kṛṣṇa.
Then, becoming joyful and gathering together from all sides, they will assemble.
Having seized that twice-born Viṣṇuyaśas and bound him with firm fetters along with his wife,
all those great rogues, as cruel as hell-beings, will cast him into a strong iron prison.

On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, at midnight when darkness has arisen, that Blessed One, Nārāyaṇa Hari, the Great Viṣṇu who brings auspiciousness to all the worlds, will be born from Viṣṇukīrti, becoming complete.
Bringing auspiciousness to the universe, he will manifest as the gods:
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, Gaṇeśa, Vāsava, Guru,
Vahni, Pitṛpati, Pakṣa, Varuṇa, and Vibhīṣaṇa.
Citra, Vāyu, Dhruva, Viśva, Ravi, Soma, Kuja, Budha,
Guru, Śukra, Śani, Rāhu, and Ketu shall go there;
with each verse, those gods will praise the Supreme Lord.
Your unborn power, consisting of form, is most great; from her I was first produced as his [Brahmā’s] progenitor in the beginning.
By me, this entire universe has always been pervaded; therefore, salutations to that Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
From the power of the Unborn, I was produced in the beginning as Viṣṇu, the authority who brings about the great dissolution.
That [universe] was always pervaded by me with my own name; thus, salutations, salutations to you!
From the western face of the Unmanifest, I, Śiva, was born as the first creator of the principles of existence (*suratattva*).
By your command, O Lord, I hold the Great Kalpa in my hand; this is the third [manifestation]; salutations, salutations to you!
From the northern face of Pradhāna, I was indeed born first as Gaṇeśa, the creator of the Kalpa;
by me this entire universe has always been pervaded—to that supreme compassionate one, I offer salutations.
From the face of Ardhanārīśvara, I was born first as Mahendra, the lord of the Maruts and the maker of the great Kalpa.
By my own power, O Lord, this entire universe was pervaded by me according to your command; salutations, salutations to you!
Born from the eye on the forehead of Pradhāna, I am known as Guha, the maker of the great kalpa;
this universe was fashioned by me according to your command, O Protector—salutations, salutations to you!
Born first from the mouth of the Unborn (Aja) and having preceded [all others], I am the Fire that brings about the Great Kalpa;
by me indeed this Egg of Brahmā was pervaded—for the sake of the Brahmāṇḍa-kalpa, salutations, salutations to you!
Born first from the right arm of the Unborn, I am the one who brings about the Great Kalpa, endowed with righteousness.
I was created by you together with the gods; salutations, salutations to you, the one known as the Liṅga-kalpa!
From the western arm of the Unborn (Aja), I was first born as that Sacrifice (Yajña) who brings about the Great Kalpa;
by me this entire universe has been pervaded—salutations, salutations to you, the one known as the Matsya-kalpa!

O Lord, I was first born from the northern arm of Pradhāna as Pracetas, the creator of the Mahākalpa; by Your command, this world was pervaded by me for the sake of the Kalpa known as Karma—salutations, salutations to You!
Born from the darkness of the cosmic egg, I am Your servant, Vibhīṣaṇa.
By me the three worlds have been pervaded; salutations to you who take the form of Manu.
Born from the excellent qualities of the cosmic egg, I am Citta, the creator of Manu.
By me the three worlds have been pervaded; O Svāyambhuva, let there be salutation to you.
O Lord, the wind was born from the dust of the cosmic egg and has pervaded the Manvantara;
salutations to You, O Master, who appear in the form of Manu Svārociṣa.
I, Dhruva, the maker of the Manu-period, was born from the mind of the cosmic egg.

The *Mayottama* has been composed; salutations be unto you. By your command, I, the Lord Viśvakarman, was born from hearing the *Brahmāṇḍa*. By your command, O God, the *Raivata* has been spread by me; salutations to you.
Born from the body of the Cosmic Egg, I am the Sun who bestows sight;
by Your command, the universe is pervaded—salutations to You in the form of Manu.
Born from the eye of the Cosmic Egg, I am indeed the Moon, and by me the universe is pervaded.
Salutations to you in the form of Manu, the delightful Vaivasvata interval; salutations to you who have assumed the form of Manu.
Born from the tongue of the Cosmic Egg, I am delusion itself, the creator of Manu.
Salutations to you in the form of Manu, by whom this Sāvarṇika period has been extended.
O Lord, born from the nostril of the Cosmic Egg, I am Budha, your servant;
O Father, I have created Brahma Sāvarṇi—salutations, salutations to you!
Born from the mouth of the Cosmic Egg, I am Jīva, the progenitor of Manu.
Indeed, by me was Dakṣasāvarṇi created; salutations, salutations to you!
Born from the hand of Brahmāṇḍakara, I am Śukra, your servant. By me was Rudrasāvarṇi fashioned for you; salutations, salutations to you!
Born from the Brahmāṇḍa-pada, O Lord, I am Mandu, your follower;
salutations again and again to this Dharmasāvarṇa at dawn.
Born from the Brahmāṇḍa-liṅga, I am Rāhu, your beloved.
O Lord, I have performed the *bhauma* [rite]; salutations to You who take the form of Manu.
Born from the secret of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), I am Ketu, Your follower.
The *bhauta-manvantara* has been created; salutations to You, that Divine One.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these praises of theirs, the Lord will speak to the gods,
and then Manu will address him in turn with the words, "Choose a boon."
Having done this, those gods, having themselves bowed down to Hari in the form of a child, will speak of his desire for the sake of the worlds:
"Who is this? Tell us; who is he that arises in every kalpa for the sake of the worlds?"
"Likewise, we wish to hear about the Manvantaras. Kalki said:
"Eighteen Mahākalpas reside within the body of Prakṛti."

The first is the Great Kalpa of Brahmā; therein resides Brahmā, the Supreme Person. From his first half were born the thirty-three deities, and from his latter half arose the Lord Brahmā, the stainless one who is the object of meditation for yogis.
In that kalpa, however, the divine play (līlā) which is recorded by the Brahmanical Paurāṇikas has an extent of one hundred crores;
indeed, at the end of the Purāṇa-Puruṣa, a great kalpa (mahākalpa) is remembered by the wise.
A *kalpa* at the dissolution of the universe consists of one thousand divine *yugas*.
Eighteen such *kalpas* are renowned; hear their names from me:
the Kūrma-kalpa, the Matsya-kalpa, and the Śveta-vārāha-kalpa.
The Nṛsiṃha-kalpa, as well as the Vāmana-kalpa;
the Skanda-kalpa, the Rāma-kalpa, and likewise the Bhāgavata-kalpa;
the Mārkaṇḍeya-kalpa, and likewise the Bhaviṣya-kalpa.
Likewise, the Liṅgakalpa is to be known, as well as the Brahmāṇḍakalpa;
the Agnikalpa, the Vāyukalpa, and likewise the Padmakalpa;
and then in sequence the Śivakalpa, the Viṣṇukalpa, and the Brahmakalpa.
A great aeon (*kalpa*) is recorded as consisting of two thousand such cycles;
the lifespan of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) is proclaimed to extend for a thousand such yugas.
This Virāj was born from that which is remembered by the name of the aeon.
Among the fourteen Manus, that Kalpa possesses its own specific duration of time. Whatever cycle of four Yugas arises within the interval of Svāyambhuva Manu,
listen now to how the lifespan of all men is diminished during that cycle of four Yugas.
In the Satya Yuga, the lifespan is indeed one hundred thousand years; in the Tretā, ten thousand years;
in the Dvāpara, one thousand years; and in the Kali, the lifespan is one hundred years.
In each intermediate period (antara), beginning with the Svārociṣa Manvantara, a cycle of four yugas (caturyuga) arises.
Listen to that: the lifespan of men in the Satya Yuga is eighty thousand years;
in the Tretā, it is half of that; in the Dvāpara, it is half of that again;
and in the Kali Yuga, the lifespan of men is proclaimed to be two thousand years.
In the Satya Yuga of the Auttama Manvantara, the lifespan is sixty thousand years;
in the Tretā, it is half of that; in the Dvāpara, half of that again;
and in the Kali, the lifespan of men is proclaimed to be one thousand five hundred years.
In the interval between the Tāmasa ages, the lifespan of humans is thirty-six thousand years; in the Satya Yuga it is that same amount, in the Tretā it is half of that,
in the Dvāpara it is half of that again, and in the Kali age it is one thousand years.
In the Raivata interval, during the Satya Yuga, the lifespan is thirty thousand years;
in the Tretā, it is half of that; in the Dvāpara, half of that again;
and in the Kali, the lifespan of men is proclaimed by the Vedas to be eight hundred years.
In the Satya Yuga, the lifespan of humans is proclaimed to be four thousand years;
in the Tretā, three thousand years; in the Dvāpara, two thousand years;
and in the Kali Yuga, it is one thousand years.
In the Vaivasvata Manvantara, during the Kṛta age, the lifespan of men is said by the Ayurvedic scriptures to be four thousand years;
in the Tretā age, three hundred years; in the Dvāpara age, two hundred years;
and in the Kali age, one hundred years.
O God, during the Sāvarṇika interval, the lifespan of men in the Kṛta age is twenty thousand years; that half (ten thousand) is proclaimed for the Tretā,
half of that (five thousand) for the Dvāpara, and half of that (two thousand five hundred) indeed for the Kali age.
In the Satya Yuga of the Brahma-Sāvarṇika Manvantara, the lifespan of men is ten thousand years;
in the Tretā, it is half of that; in the Dvāpara, half of that again;
and in the Kali, the lifespan of men is proclaimed to be half of that as well.
In the Caturyuga of Dakṣasāvarṇika, the lifespan is likewise one thousand years;
in Rudrasāvarṇika, it is eight thousand years in the Kṛtayuga;
in Tretā it is half of that, and in Dvāpara it is half of that again.
In the ancient past, the lifespan of men in the Kali age was known to be half of that;
likewise, in the Dharma-Sāvarṇika Manvantara,
the lifespan in the four ages was such that in the Satya Yuga of the Bhauma Manvantara, it was four thousand years.
In the Tretā age, the human lifespan is three thousand years; in the Dvāpara, half of that;
and in the Kali age, half of that again—this is the lifespan of men as agreed upon by the sages.
Furthermore, during the Bhautamanvantara, in the Satya age, it is four hundred years.

In the Tretā age, the lifespan of men is declared to be three hundred years; in the Dvāpara, it is half of that; and in the terrible Kali age, it is half of that again. Furthermore, regarding the kings who existed throughout the four ages within each Manvantara according to their respective names:

And kings were born with their respective names, and their exploits were distinct. Thus it should be understood elsewhere as well: in each Manu of the fourth age, there are the lineages of that Manu for the duration of seven divine yugas.
The dissolution of the land of action (Karmabhūmi) at the end of a Yuga is indeed known as a Kalpa;
the dissolution of the entire earth at the end of a Manvantara is likewise a Kalpa.
Furthermore, that which occurs at the end of a day of the Ancient Puruṣa is indeed the [Great] Dissolution.
That indeed should be known as the primary cycle (mukhyakalpa), which brings about the destruction of all worlds;
for that which is remembered as a great cycle (mahākalpa) consists of twenty-six thousand kalpas.
When the Ancient Person (Purāṇapuruṣa) is situated in the zodiac sign of Aries (meṣarāśi)...
Then Brahmā, together with the gods, went to King Svāyambhuva; at that time,
when the Ancient Puruṣa had arrived in the form of a boar,
he indeed became Vārāha upon the earth in the midst of Svāyambhuva Manu.
When the Ancient Puruṣa departed from his own lion-form by his own will at the end of the Svārociṣa Manvantara,
he indeed became Nṛsiṃha upon the earth;
when the Ancient Puruṣa was situated in the sign of Taurus.
Then, in the midst of Uttama Manu, Rudra appeared on earth with his attendants. When the Ancient Puruṣa was situated in the zodiac sign of Pisces,
at the end of the Tāmasa period, that eternal one indeed became the Fish upon the earth.
When the Ancient Person (Purāṇapuruṣa) was situated in a dual sign during the interval of Vaivasvata Manu, that Lord became Kṛṣṇa on earth;
when the Ancient Person was situated in the sign of Cancer.
At the end of the Raivata [Manvantara], he was indeed the eternal Tortoise on earth;
when the Ancient Puruṣa was situated in the sign of Virgo,
at the end of the Cākṣuṣa [Manvantara], he became Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, on earth.
When the Ancient Puruṣa arrived there by his own will at the beginning of the Vaivasvata Manvantara,
he indeed became Vāmana on earth;
when the Ancient Puruṣa was situated in the zodiac sign of Libra.
In the interval of Vaivasvata Manu, I have come as one named Kalkī;
when the Ancient Puruṣa is situated in the zodiac sign of Aquarius,
he will indeed appear on earth at the beginning of the Sāvarṇika Manvantara under the name Buddha.
When the Ancient Puruṣa was situated in the sign of Sagittarius,
Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, appeared on earth during the interval of Vaivasvata Manu;
when the Ancient Puruṣa was situated in the sign of Capricorn—
Indeed, there shall never be an incarnation worthy of all worship [other than these].
For in this Caturyuga, O gods, three incarnations of the Ancient Puruṣa have been declared; likewise, there is no other [incarnation] in the Caturyuga.
In the first quarter of the Tretā age, the lord Rāma, son of Daśaratha, appeared on earth;
likewise, Kṛṣṇa with Śeṣa appeared during the Dvāpara age;
and at the end of the Kali age, I indeed appear for thirty-two thousand years.
Therefore, this Khaṇḍa is pure and the destroyer of the sins of men.
Whoever reads or causes others to hear this Khaṇḍa throughout the four Yugas, his sins from birth onwards shall perish; it is not otherwise.
Thus, O gods, has this account of the Great Kalpa been told to you;
that which is the second Great Kalpa is indeed known as the Viṣṇu-kalpa. O gods, this narrative of it should be recited by men who are well-versed in the Purāṇas of Viṣṇu.
The Viṣṇu Purāṇa indeed extends to one hundred crores [of verses].
In that very work is the Great Kalpa (Mahākalpa) concerning the birth from the navel of Viṣṇu;
from the eastern half [of that lotus] arose the Lord Brahmā, accompanied by all the gods.
From the first half of the Parārdha, the Lord Viṣṇu, the Ancient Puruṣa, indeed [appeared];
that which was the third Mahākalpa is remembered as the Śivakalpa.
From the first half of the Śiva-kalpa, Viṣṇu was born, and from him, Brahmā himself [was born].

The fourth great aeon (mahākalpa), which is remembered by the Śiva-paurāṇikas as having an extent of one hundred crores [of years], is indeed known as the Padma-kalpa. Therein, the Lord Gaṇeśa was seated upon the throne of the Ancient Puruṣa.
From Gaṇeśa was born Rudra; from Rudra came Viṣṇu, the supreme among gods.
From the navel of Viṣṇu arose Parameṣṭhin, the Grandfather (Brahmā).
In every Kalpa, in the beginning, the gods were produced in this sequence and in their entirety.
The fifth great aeon (mahākalpa) is indeed remembered as the Vāyukalpa.
There, the blessed Mahendra was seated upon the seat of the Ancient Puruṣa.
From Mahendra, [the power] was obtained, and from Mahendra the sense-faculties (indriyāṇi) arose.
And from the sense organs [arose] those gods; hear their names from me:
Śani, Budha, Ravi, Śukra, Viśvakarman, Bṛhaspati, Indra, Viṣṇu, as well as Brahmā, Rudra, and Soma are recorded in this order.
He is indeed Brahmā, the creator, born from the linga and the senses;
he is indeed Viṣṇu, the protector of creation, born from the station of the avatāras. In every kalpa, he proceeds as the Lord over the twenty-four principles.
Sanatkumāra, Haṃsa, Vārāha, and likewise Nārada;
the two Nārāyaṇas, Kapila and Ātreya, Yajña, Aśva, and Kaṇṭaka;
Vṛṣabha, Pṛthu, Matsya, Kūrma, and likewise Dhanvantari.
Mohinī and Nṛsiṃha, Vāmana and Bhārgava,
Rāma, Vyāsa, Balarāma, Kṛṣṇa, Buddha, and Kalki who has attained his own true nature;
Guhyajanman, Mahādeva, the creator and destroyer of the Daityas.
Thus were three gods born during the fifth great aeon (mahākalpa);
that which was the sixth great aeon is indeed remembered as the Vahni-kalpa.
Therein, the Blessed Lord Skanda sat upon the seat of the Ancient Puruṣa.
From the imperishable Puruṣa, Skanda was emitted; from him [was born] Mahārcis.
From that great radiance which had the form of the Sun, Hari himself was born;
from that great radiance which had the form of Fire, the Grandfather (Brahmā) was born.
He who was born from that great radiance, which had the form of the moon, is indeed Hara.
From the Grandfather (Pitāmaha) were born the sages, the seers, the social orders, and the worlds; as well as the Ādityas, the Viśvedevas, the Vasus, the Tuṣitas, the Bhāsvaras, and the Anilas.
The Mahārājikas, the Sādhyas, and the gods born from Viṣṇu; the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Gandharvas, Piśācas, Kinnaras, and others;
as well as the Daityas, Dānavas, and Bhūtas—these are of the nature of Tamas and are born from Rudra.
In every eon, thus arising within the sphere of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa),
there is a seventh great eon (mahākalpa) which indeed constitutes the kalpa of the cosmic egg;
therein, the Lord Pāvaka sits upon the seat of the Ancient Puruṣa.
From that Puruṣa of inconceivable splendor, fire was produced;
from him the great ocean was born, and from that, the cosmic egg (virāṭ) came into being. From every single hair of his, millions of cosmic eggs were manifested.
From the cosmic egg (Brahmāṇḍa) was born Brahmā, the grandfather of all the worlds;
from him was born the pervasive Viṣṇu, and from him was born Hara himself.
[This is recounted] in the Purāṇa known as the Brahmāṇḍa, which extends to one hundred crores [of verses].
The three-eyed, five-faced, and ten-armed Bhava,
along with Vāyu, is indeed remembered by the Vedic seers as the duration of eighteen kalpas.
In the Mahākalpa, all [beings] were twice a thousand [in number], and they have gone to their destruction.
The eighth great kalpa is indeed known as the Liṅgakalpa.
Therein, at the seat of the Ancient Puruṣa, the Lord Dharma was born— the eternal Dharma, whose form is inconceivable and unmanifest.
From Dharma, Kāma was born; from Kāma, the Liṅga became threefold:
the masculine gender, the neuter gender, and the feminine gender, O best of gods.
From the masculine gender Viṣṇu arose, and from the feminine gender Mahendrā (Indrāṇī) arose.
That Śeṣa indeed arises from the neuter gender, and he stands upon him;
from those three consisting of darkness (tamas), the world was born as a single ocean.
While the god Nārāyaṇa was asleep, there appeared from his navel an excellent lotus.
Therefore he is indeed Brahmā, and from him this Virāj was born;
this supreme essence has been sung before the Creator as a narrative from the Liṅga Purāṇas, spanning hundreds of millions of verses.
The ninth great aeon (mahākalpa) is indeed known as the Matsyakalpa.
Therein, the Lord Kubera was seated upon the seat of the Ancient Puruṣa;
likewise, a vast mass of dust arose from the Imperishable One.
From that dust-like state, Kubera was born;
from Kubera was born the fish, who was the embodiment of the Vedas and possessed of excellent qualities.
From the belly of the fish was born Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, Hari.
From the navel of Viṣṇu was born Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds.
From Brahmā arose the divine [Prajāpati], and from that deity the gods were born. Indeed, the twenty-four principles (tattvas) were produced by those very gods.
In age after age, he thus caused the names of the Kalpas to arise in succession.
In the Matsya-kalpa, however, the Fish was born from the Great Fish;
from that Fish, the Lord Viṣṇu appeared, and from him, Brahmā was born.
In the Kūrma-kalpa, the Tortoise was born from the Great Fish;
that Tortoise [became] Viṣṇu the Blessed One, from him Brahmā, and from him the Virāṭ.
And in the Śvetavārāha-kalpa, Viṣṇu’s manifestation arose from the Boar.
And from the navel of Viṣṇu, that Brahmā was born as this Virāj;
thus indeed all kalpas everywhere should be understood by the wise.
That which is the tenth great kalpa is known as the Kūrma-kalpa.
There, upon the seat of the Ancient Puruṣa, the Lord was indeed without consciousness;
for he who is beyond primordial nature (prakṛti) is the Fourth (turīya), the immutable.
From that which had become void, the conscious Lord himself was born.

From that, the great ocean was born; therein the Lord slept, he who is known as Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Waters himself. From half of that, the Great Tortoise arose, and from that, the Great Śeṣa came into being.
That Śeṣa indeed became threefold: Bhūman, Śeṣa, and Bhaumanī.
That Bhūman is to be known as Virāṭ, and he is situated upon Śeṣa.
And Bhaumanī is Mahālakṣmī; she is established in the heart of Bhūman.
Born from the Abundant One (Bhūman), he is indeed Brahmā, the creator, sustainer, and destroyer;
that very Brahmā possesses three forms, appearing in succession in every Kalpa.
That which was formerly the seat of the Ancient Puruṣa is a cloth-like state, like one who has entered deep sleep.
Having gone there, the senses themselves attain satisfaction and indeed perish;
then the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), having arrived and deceived the consciousness residing in the mind, again creates the world through its own play.
She who is to be known as the fourth power, the eternal Mahākālī,
and by all those Vedas, her body is remembered as the Great Kalpa;
salutations to that Mahākālī, my mother, salutations again and again.
For from whence the ancient beings come into existence and dissolve;
O gods, ten great kalpas have indeed passed away here. And that which is now current is the one known as the Bhaviṣyaka (Future) Mahākalpa.
O gods and hosts of seers, hear from me the origin of that:
that which is inconceivable, imperishable, the fourth state, eternally abiding;
having gone to which, men do not return—that very state.
The various arrangements of creation exist solely as His sport;
even the gods do not know His end, so how indeed could humans know it?
O Brahmin, every great kalpa that has occurred has been seen by you as described by Him.
Those who are to be cultivated [as future Buddhas] do not indeed always know [the duration of] the great aeons (*mahākalpa*).
Some Vedas proclaim thirty-three great aeons;
eighteen great aeons have been described separately by name.
"Eleven great kalpas have been declared by certain ancient sages.
Therefore, O gods, I am certain today that this shall be so in the future kalpas;
the word of the Vedas is truth and can never be otherwise."
From that Imperishable One (Avyaya) was born the eternal Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa;
the unified body of the two is remembered by the wise as Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa.
He performed supreme austerity for the duration of a thousand yugas.
Then He became divided into two, Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, each separately;
for the duration of a thousand yugas, they performed supreme austerity.
From their bodies arose a moonlight that dispels all darkness.
By those moonlights, the auspicious and divine Vṛndāvana was brought forth.
Twenty-one primordial natures (prakṛtis) are said to exist at every yojana;
thus, the divine Vṛndāvana extends for eighty-four yojanas.
O Lord, hear from me concerning that most delightful liṅga, one krośa in extent:
the ten groups of the ten senses,
as well as Gokula, Vārṣa, Nanda, Bhāṇḍīra, and likewise Māthura.
And [he described] Vraja, the venerable Yamunā, the auspicious Gopikā, in due order;
likewise, the origin from the ten primary elements (prakṛtis) which constitute the mother; and the delightful Daśavana—listen to me as I recite their names.
Vṛndāvana, Gopavana, Bahulāvāna, Madhuśṛṅga, Kuñjavāna, Dadhivāna,
the beautiful Rahaskrīḍāvāna, and Veṇupadmavāna follow in succession.
The great Govardhana mountain was born from the mind of Prakṛti;
upon seeing the divine Vṛndāvana, he attained supreme bliss.
From Kṛṣṇa arose thirty million cowherds, whose nature consists of the [divine] qualities.
Śrīdāmā and others were born as *sāttvika*, Arjuna and others as *rājasa*,
and Kaṃsa and others as *tāmasa*, all manifesting divine pastimes.
From the limbs of Rādhā, three crores of gopīs were likewise born in succession.
Lalitā and others were of the nature of goodness (sāttvika), Kubjā and others were of the nature of passion (rājasa),
and Pūtanā and others were of the nature of darkness (tāmasa); they displayed various playful gestures and deeds,
and their divine play continued for a thousand yugas.
Then, having gathered them together, the two of them performed penance once more. That Kṛṣṇa indeed became twofold, and the goddess Rādhā likewise became twofold;
he is the Puruṣa with a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet.
He was indeed born from the first half, and Kṛṣṇa himself from the latter half;
she who has one head, three eyes, two feet,
and two thousand [attributes] was born from the first half as the goddess Rādhā, while [the other half] was from the latter half.

Both Puruṣa and Prakṛti performed supreme austerity for the duration of a thousand yugas in the auspicious, divine Vṛndāvana. Through that austerity, they both increased in power; He was indeed named Ananta, and she was Anantaka.
After that, having become one, they stood together with a desire for sexual union;
from the pores of their bodies, millions of cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas) came into being,
each measuring half a crore yojanas in extent and existing individually.
O gods, this entire universe has arisen from the hair-pores on his chest;
and Brahmā, born from that universe, is seated upon a lotus flower.
That lotus, extending for a yojana, is situated within the sphere of the earth.
O gods, that lotus-lake from which the lotus of Brahmā was born is indeed the famous Puṣkara-kṣetra; it is that very lotus-lake. Then the four-faced Brahmā, in his human form, was filled with wonder.
For every stalk he passed through, a hundred divine years elapsed;
yet he did not reach the end of the lotus, and Brahmā returned there,
weeping many times, deluded by that illusion.
"From weeping, Rudra was born, and he is the one who provides security for that [tear].
Why do you weep, O illustrious one? Is your Lord within your heart?
Having heard these words, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, [replied].

Having become absorbed in meditation, he remained in his heart for a long time according to his own will. Then, at the end of a hundred divine years, Hari himself appeared and the Blessed One spoke these words with a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
O Brahmā, this is the land of action (karmabhūmi), which ends with the living beings and causes them to live;
it extends for a thousand yojanas within the entire terrestrial sphere.
To its north lies the Himālaya mountain, and to its east is the great ocean.
The western ocean is Ratnākara, and the southern is Vaḍavābdhika;
from these shall arise all the worlds above as well as below.
This eternal Puṣkara stands at the center of the land of action (Karmabhūmi).
"From me, you shall obtain the Vedas and perform an auspicious sacrifice.
From that sacrifice, the gods will arise, divided threefold according to the three qualities (guṇas):
the Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and Cāraṇas are the threefold Sāttvika [deities]."
The Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas, who dwell in the mountains, are characterized by passion (rājasa).
The Piśācas, Guhyakas, and Bhūtas, who move downwards, are indeed characterized by darkness (tāmasa).
Likewise, O Creator, the sacrifices consisting of *svadhā* offerings are threefold, as are the classes of ancestors (pitṛgaṇa).
They will become delightful like the gods, resembling celestial chariots in the sky;
those who move in the sky are fair-complexioned, while those of the *sattva* nature are known to be dark-complexioned.
Those of the *rajas* nature are delightful, consisting of mountains and islands, and taking the form of lakes.

O Creator, those who dwell on the surface of the earth will become the three classes of Pitṛs. Those who exist in the subterranean realm (bila) and those who consist of the torments of hell will be the Tāmasa Pitṛs in the lower regions of the earth.
Those worlds, consisting of increase, middle state, and decrease, are subject to decay in succession;
yet this earth, O highly fortunate one, is eternal and always abiding.
Indeed, Meru and Nameru, as well as the continents, do not exist [as they appear].
The regions such as Ilāvarta and others do not exist anywhere at all;
rather, O Creator, there are worlds consisting of stars that resemble celestial chariots (vimānas),
which will act according to their own will and be protected by the performance of sacrificial rites.
O Creator, when there is no sacrifice on earth,
then those hosts of stars shall move as obstacles, constantly deviating from their courses and moving in retrograde or exceeding speeds.
And the land of action (karmabhūmi) should be known as Gaurī, who is the embodiment of the Vedas and pervades the entire world.
O Brahmin, he who protects her is renowned as Gopa;
he is indeed the power of Gopa, the protector of cowherds, and Hari is the worshiper of the cowherds. Thousands of millions upon millions of all these cowherds are portions (kalās) of Hari.
There are exactly as many cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas) proclaimed under the name of Gopa;
likewise, above the land of action (karmabhūmi), the sun is at a distance of one hundred thousand yojanas,
and from there the moon is of the same measure, and further above that is the sphere of the stars (bhamaṇḍala).
Two hundred thousand yojanas from there is the terrestrial [world] of that same kind;
from the terrestrial world, Budha is to be known as being likewise situated; from Budha, Bṛhatāmpati (Jupiter);
from Guru, Śukra is of the same measure; and from Śukra, Sauri (Saturn) is likewise positioned.
Just as [the orbit of] Śani is to be known, so too is that of Rāhu; and Ketu likewise moves above it.
The sphere of the Seven Sages (Saptarṣimaṇḍala) is to be known as measuring seven hundred thousand [yojanas] from Ketu.
All of them extend for eleven hundred thousand [yojanas], and above that is the abode of Dhruva.
One hundred thousand yojanas above that is the great realm;

one should know that it extends for one hundred thousand yojanas. One hundred thousand yojanas above that is the abode of Janaloka; one should know that the station of Tapoloka is likewise one hundred thousand yojanas above that.
And thus, the land of action (Karmabhūmi) extends for fifty million yojanas.
Below the land of action, there are seven intermediate netherworlds (Pātālas);
they should be known as extending for one hundred thousand yojanas each, situated further down from that.
The hells are to be known as extending sequentially from the earth for half a *koṭi* yojanas;
beyond that, to the north of the land of action (*karmabhūmi*), there are eight regions.
Then follows the salt ocean, then an island, and indeed then the milk ocean.
From that [mountain] comes an island, from that a river, from that another island, and from that the ocean;
each extending by fifty thousand *koṭis* of *yojanas*,
O Creator, you yourself should know that the great mountain Lokāloka marks the limit of the land of action (*karmabhūmi*).
The Lokāloka mountain indeed extends to the south and the west;
likewise, there is a Lokāloka of the same kind to the east of the land of action (Karmabhūmi).
This entire collection of these [elements] is proclaimed to be the Brahmāṇḍa (the Cosmic Egg).
"O Creator, from you indeed shall it come forth until the end of the kalpa.
'Om'—the single-syllable Brahman; from that, Viṣṇu became threefold.
Today he is Viṣṇu, he is indeed Kṛṣṇa here, and he is indeed the Virāṭ."
Thus, he is to be known as Viṣṇu, the ancient Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
The Ancient Person (Purāṇapuruṣa) is to be known as the Primordial Brahmā, whose lifespan lasts for many ages.
Two thousand divine yugas are proclaimed to be his single day and night.
"Within the pores of Viṣṇu’s skin, millions of cosmic eggs have come into being.
Today, O Brahmā, I am Viṣṇu, the destroyer of your obstacles on this earth.
Having spoken thus, Viṣṇu vanished; Brahmā then carried out the work of creation.

He declared: "That which is to come is indeed known as a Mahākalpa; it shall be celebrated by the name Bhaviṣya, with a lifespan of two thousand births. It consists of the first half and the second half of the Ancient Puruṣa."
Eighteen thousand kalpas have passed in the first half;
the second half is now to be known, and two days of it have already occurred.
Today, I am Kūrma and Vāhana is proclaimed as Matsya.
O gods, the third day of that Kalpa belongs to Śvetavārāha; indeed, it is currently midday. In the great Kalpa named Bhaviṣya, there shall be a narrative told by people of the future.
It was recounted in the presence of Brahmā with an expansion of one hundred crores; the Great Purāṇa,
endowed with ten characteristics and an expansion of one hundred crores,
is said to be the ancient Purāṇa consisting of five characteristics.
And thirty-six thousand verses were proclaimed in each Kalpa;
the Purāṇa named after the Kalpa was composed by Mahādeva.
Eighteen Purāṇas were thus created by the one whose self is Śiva.
And at the end of the Dvāpara age, the Blessed Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī,
brought those very same [Vedas] forth for the sake of the welfare of the world.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of Kalki, those gods, filled with wonder and greatly rejoicing,
will pay their respects and depart for their respective abodes.
Thus ends [the section] in the Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, in the Pratisarga Parvan, within the sub-section known as the Caturyuga Khaṇḍa.
The twenty-fifth chapter, titled "A Comprehensive Description of the History of the Kali Age.
Now begins the twenty-sixth chapter:
A Comprehensive Description of the History of the Kali Age.
Vyāsa said: Then that Blessed One Kalki, born from the Ancient Puruṣa,
mounted his divine horse, armed with a sword, clad in armor, and bearing a shield.

Having slain those Mlecchas who have become Daityas, he will attain Yoga. Then, scorched by the fire of his Yoga, the land of action (Karmabhūmi) will be reduced to ashes, devoid of life, and remain so for sixteen thousand years.
Then, having been produced as a cloud that brings about dissolution,
it will cause that earth to go into the midst of the waters at the onset of the dissolution.
At that time, the terrible Kali Yuga will go to the side of Bali.

When the terrible Kali age has arrived, Hari will once again make the land of action beautiful by turning it into solid ground, and he will worship the gods with sacrifices. Having received their sacrificial portions, those gods, joined by their forces, [will prevail].
Having gone to Vaivasvata Manu, they will explain the reason:
"The Brāhmaṇa caste indeed arose from the mouth of Kalki;
the Kṣatriya from his arms, the Vaiśya from his knees, and the Śūdra caste from his feet."
The Brāhmaṇas and the other castes shall be fair, red, yellow, and dark-complexioned respectively;
having received the power of the Goddess, they shall procreate many sons.
Those men, who are embodiments of righteousness, will measure twenty-one cubits in height.
When, following the law of their birth, they joyfully sacrifice to the gods,
then the wise son of Vivasvat (Yama), having bowed to that Kalki Hari,
will, by his command, establish him in the royal position in Ayodhyā.
By training under him, he shall indeed become his son, that very Ikṣvāku;
honoring his father’s kingdom, he will rule upon the earth for a hundred divine years,
and having lived for a hundred divine years, he will cast off his body and depart.
But when the Blessed Kalkī shall perform the Brahma-thread ceremony (brahmasūtra), then the four Vedas, together with their auxiliary limbs, will arrive there in personified form,
along with the eighteen Purāṇas, full of joy.
They shall praise the god Kalki, who is a portion of the Ancient Puruṣa,
on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, on a Thursday.
From the sacrificial fire-pit, that most excellent Person shall emerge.

By name, it is to be known as the Satya Yuga, the indicator of the path of truth. Having beheld that beautiful Person, the gods beginning with Brahmā will then describe that lunar day of Manu as that which brings about the destruction of karma.

On this lunar day, whatever gods a person joyfully worships on the bank of the Dhātṛ tree, those gods shall remain under his control. This ninth day is indeed called Akṣaya-navamī, for it is the ninth day of the beginning of the Yuga.

Those who joyfully establish Mālatī and Tulasī at the base of the Dhātṛ tree according to the Vedic injunctions and worship the Śālagrāma stone— she is the bestower of auspiciousness upon the world and the destroyer of all sins.

They should be known as liberated while living (jīvanmukta), for they bring satisfaction to the ancestors. Whoever performs a śrāddha ceremony at the foot of the Dhātṛ tree shall indeed obtain the supreme fruit of a thousand Gayā-śrāddhas.
"He who performs such a fire-sacrifice (homa), which is equal to a thousand sacrifices (sahasrāsya), shall,
upon death, attain heaven along with his family and his retinue.
When these words had been spoken by them, the divine Kalkī was filled with joy.
"‘So be it,’ he will say to the gods.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Kalki, while the gods in their celestial forms were watching,
vanished on the spot and entered a state of deep sleep.
When that Blessed One has departed, the land of action will become deeply distressed;
being filled with the fire of separation, it will cause those seeds to perish.
At that time, the great Daityas dwelling in the depths of Pātāla—
Placing Prahlāda at their head, they will go forth against the gods,
mounted upon donkeys, camels, vultures, buffaloes, and crows;
some are mounted on lions, tigers, and wolves, while others have jackals and hawks for their vehicles.
Seizing spears, pattiśas, swords, bhuśuṇḍīs, iron clubs, and other weapons, they will roar again and again with great speed;
then the gods, headed by Śakra, along with the thirty-three hosts, will rejoice.
Quickly seizing their own weapons, they will engage in a great battle;
a terrible war lasting for a divine year will take place among them. Bhārgava will restore to life the Daityas who have died one after another in the fray.

Then the gods, overcome by exhaustion, will abandon the battle on all sides and go to the Ocean of Milk, where Hari himself is personally present. By their hymn of praise, that Blessed One [will appear] for the sake of the auspiciousness of the gods.
The eternal one will manifest his own form as Svapūrvārddha;
he is the swan, Hari himself, possessing a splendor equal to a hundred suns,
and he will scorch Śukra and those led by Prahlāda with his brilliance.
Then the defeated Daityas, having abandoned the earth and being exceedingly distressed,
will go to the netherworld (Vitala), protected by Mahādeva.
Furthermore, all those gods shall be fearless and free from affliction.
And they shall consecrate the son of Vaivasvata as king upon the earth;
that Ikṣvāku shall have a divine lifespan of one hundred years,
while the measure of human life shall be four hundred years.
Thus, O Mānasa, I have related to you everything that I was asked by you:
the history of the four yugas and the deeds of the kings individually.
For the Dharma has four quarters: knowledge, meditation, tranquility, and self-restraint.
Self-knowledge is indeed true knowledge; meditation is the contemplation of the inner self.
Steadiness of mind, tranquility, self-restraint, and the subduing of the senses [constitute this path].
It lasts for exactly four hundred and thirty-two thousand years.
For by that same number, one quarter of Dharma is proclaimed;
it consists of the morning, midday, and evening— the three junctions (*trisandhya*)—
and through each of these parts, he dwells upon the earth as Virāj.
When the Dharma has increased, then life itself increases.
Indeed, seven thousand verses have been narrated in this section;
therefore, O Manu, listen as I describe the Uttara-khaṇḍa.

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Compendium of Histories of the Kali Age," in the Caturyuga-khaṇḍa (also known as the Pratisarga-parvan) of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Thus ends the third section, the Caturyuga-khaṇḍa (also known as the Pratisarga-parvan), of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Description of Vyāsa’s Arrival.
Homage to Śrī Gaṇeśa. Homage to Śrī Sarasvatī.
Oṃ, salutations to the Blessed One Vāsudeva!
May Gaṇapati grant you auspiciousness—he, when displeased, causes even Brahmā to falter in his ability to accomplish even the most trivial task.

By repeatedly resorting to whose lotus-feet, the Goddess Lakṣmī herself attained renown in the world through the dawning of her fortune and good luck, surpassing even the prosperity of the Lord of the Gods.
May that Goddess of Speech herself, who eternally sits upon the lion-throne of the tongue of Puṇya-hiraṇyagarbha, bestow upon you abundant blessings;
for by the moonlight of the nails upon her pure and tender toes, the ocean of the nectar of the Word-Brahman is stirred, so that it sports unrestrainedly within the minds of the wise.

Salutations to that Śiva, the primordial cause of the creation, dissolution, and preservation of the universe; to Him whose feet sever the flood of afflictions and who is saluted by the lotus-like devotees; to Him who assumes vast bodies for His play, manifested with intense spontaneity; and to Him who establishes the state of one’s own true essence, which is beyond even the path of the speech of the three Vedas. May that Lord of the Gaṇas protect us—He upon whose cheeks shines a pure row of bees like a stainless rosary. Oṃ, salutations to Vāsudeva, who holds the Śārṅga bow and the banner.
Salutation after salutation to Him who possesses the mace, the discus, and the conch;
salutation to Śiva, the embodiment of the moon, together with His attendants, His son,
His bull, His trident, His skull-bowl, and the moon-god.
Having meditated upon Śiva, praised Hari, and bowed to Parameṣṭhin,
and having saluted Citrabhānu and Bhānu,
one should recite this treatise concerning Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, who knows the dharma and was consecrated with the royal parasol.
The supreme sages Vyāsa and others arrived joyfully to behold [him]:
Mārkaṇḍeya, Samaṇḍavya, Śāṇḍilya, Śākaṭāyana,
Gautama, Gālava, Gārgya, Śātātapa, and Parāśara.
Jāmadagnya, Bharadvāja, Bhṛgu, and Bhāguri;
Uttaṅka, Śaṅkha and Likhita, Śaunaka, and Śākaṭāyani;
Pulastya, Pulaha, Dālbhya, Bṛhadaśva, and Lomaśa.
Nārada, Parvata, Jahu, Apāva, and Supārāvasu—
seeing those ṛṣis who had arrived, masters of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, he,
full of devotion, together with his brothers and preceded by Kṛṣṇa and Dhaumya, [welcomed them].
Yudhiṣṭhira, greatly delighted, rose and offered salutations;
he himself presented them with water for the hands, water for sipping, water for the feet, and seats.
When those ascetics were seated, Yudhiṣṭhira [proceeded].
Bowing down with humility, he addressed these words to Vyāsa:
"O Blessed One, by your grace, a great kingdom has been obtained by me;
having displayed my prowess, Suyodhana has been slain in battle along with his followers."
Just as the enjoyment of one who is diseased does not bring happiness even when obtained, so too,
having slain my kinsmen, this kingdom does not appear as happiness to me. That pure joy which belongs to those who subsist on forest roots and fruits is true contentment.
O Grandfather, having conquered the earth and slain our enemies, there is no one who is our kinsman,
teacher, protector, constant source of happiness, and armor—
Bhīṣma— who has been struck down by me, a sinner, out of greed for the kingdom.
"I shall bear my lack of discernment; my mind is mired in sin.
Having washed it with the water of your words, which reveal manifold truths, I have heard the Purāṇas and the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs, O Lord."
Reveal to me today the entire essence of the Dharma with the lamp of wisdom;
these sages, the protectors of the true Dharma, have assembled here to drink from the lotus of your face with the bees of their eyes.
Whatever treatises on statecraft and whatever treatises on dharma there may be—
all the scriptures have been heard from Bhīṣma, the son of Bhagīrathī.
Now that Śāntanu’s son has gone to heaven, you, Kṛṣṇa the Yādava, [are the authority].
"Because of his friendship and because of our kinship, no one else is a better instructor for me.
The son of Satyavatī will truly speak the truth to Dharmarāja regarding all the specific duties of the sages without exception."
Vyāsa said:
O sinless one, that which was to be told has been told to you by me, by Bhīṣma,
by Mārkaṇḍeya, by Dhaumya, and by the great seer Lomaśa.
For you are a knower of dharma, wise, virtuous, and the best among the intelligent;
there is nothing unknown to you regarding the determination of what is dharma and what is adharma.
With Hṛṣīkeśa Keśava, the slayer of Keśin, standing by your side.
The tongue falters when attempting to describe him who is the creator,
protector, and destroyer of the worlds, who is identical with the universe,
and who perceives everything directly; he will declare the duties to you.
Having thus instructed what was to be done, the Blessed Bādarāyaṇa,

honored by the sons of Pāṇḍu, departed for his own forest hermitage. When the author of the Mahābhārata had departed after conversing with them, those tranquil sages, their minds agitated by curiosity, [spoke].

"What does he ask, the one who has extinguished the grief of the world and its burdens? What will the Blessed One, the hero of the Yadu lineage, say here? Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of Vyāsa’s Arrival," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
[This is followed by] the "Description of the Origin of the Brahmāṇḍa."
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Whose foundation is it said to be? What is the cause? What is the ultimate resort?
Into what does this world dissolve, and from what is it produced?
"How many are the continents and oceans? How many indeed are the principal mountain ranges? What is the measurement of the earth, and how many are the worlds?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O sinless one, this ancient subject about which you have questioned me has been both heard and personally experienced by me as I wandered for a long time through saṃsāra.
[I offer salutations] to the unborn one, whose form is the universe, who is devoid of qualities yet the soul of all qualities.
Salutations to that Blessed One, Vāsudeva, the Creator!
O Pārtha, listen as I describe here to you this ancient account:
how the Lord of the luminaries was addressed by the radiant sage Yājñavalkya regarding the future.

O Yudhiṣṭhira, I shall relate to you this Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa, which bestows wealth, fame, and long life, and destroys all inauspiciousness— whatever answer the Rishis received when questioned, as I have heard it.
The single-souled source of the three deities, possessing four or five auspicious characteristics,
is demonstrated as both existent and non-existent through the distinctions of qualities, time, and so forth.
The one alone, the womb of the universe, is established within every individual womb.
He is seen as one and indeed as many, like the moon reflected in water.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva—the bull-bannered god—are considered the three deities by the wise;
they are differentiated by differences of name and differences of function, but not by their own self.
The primary process (prakriyā), the secondary consequence (anuṣaṅga), the introductory context (upoddhāta), and the conclusion (upasaṃhāra)— this is proclaimed as the fourfold division. Furthermore,
there is reasoning (tarka), re-absorption (pratisarga), genealogy (vaṃśa), and the periods of the Manus (manvantara).
The history of the dynasties and the Purāṇa with its five characteristics—
this subject matter appears to me to be very vast. Nevertheless, O sinless one, I shall speak to you concerning the primary creation (sarga) by way of brief indication.
The world— consisting of the principles from Mahat down to the specific elements (viśeṣas), possessing various forms and characteristics,
comprising five means of valid cognition, and containing six categories— is presided over by the Puruṣa. From the Unmanifest (avyakta) arises the Intellect (buddhi), which is also known as Mahat.

The ego (ahaṃkāra), however, is said to be composed of the three qualities (guṇas) and is derived from the Great Principle (mahat). They say that the five subtle elements (tanmātras) arise from the sattvic ego, and from those [subtle elements] the gross elements (bhūtas) are born; and from the gross elements, the world of moving and non-moving beings arises.

When Viṣṇu, whose form consists of water, had dissolved all moving and non-moving beings, there arose that great cosmic egg (aṇḍa), composed of the elements, resting upon the waters. Through the power of creation, that egg was split asunder into two parts.
The earth became its skull, and the sky was its second [skull];
Mount Meru became its membrane, and the mountains are known as its placenta;
the rivers became its veins, and moisture became the water pervading everywhere.
Established sixteen thousand yojanas below,
with a height of eighty-four [thousand], and thirty-two [thousand] in width at the top,
Mount Meru is called the pericarp (karṇikā) of the earth-lotus.
Because he is the primordial deity, Āditya exists there as the embodiment of the three qualities (guṇas):
in the morning he is Prajāpati, at midday he is held to be Viṣṇu, and at the time of afternoon he is Rudra; thus, he alone is threefold in his abodes.
In the morning, nine sages, the sons of Prajāpati, were born:
Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Bhṛgu, and Vasiṣṭha—these eight; Nārada is remembered as the ninth.
"There are nine Brahmās"—this is the conclusion recorded in the Purāṇas.
From the right thumb of the Lotus-born One, Dakṣa was born;
from the left thumb, the female offspring arose, and those two became husband and wife.
The sons born of those two, the Haryaśvas,
were destroyed by the high-souled Nārada while they were intent upon creation.
Seeing his sons diminished, Dakṣa begot daughters.
The fifty daughters renowned as Satī were remembered by their names;
he gave ten to Dharma, thirteen to Kaśyapa,
and twenty-seven, who are engaged in the guidance of time, to Indu.
The Lord of the moving and unmoving gave two daughters to Bāhuputra and two indeed to Kṛśāśva; four daughters, endowed with beauty and youth, he gave to Ariṣṭanemi;
and one to Bhava, the son of Bhṛgu—he gave them to those [sages].
O tiger among men, there came into being the fourfold collection of beings;
moreover, on the summit of Meru, there are three peaks known by name as Vairāja, Vaikuṇṭha, and Kailāsa, which are the abodes of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
By virtue of their sequential arrangement toward the eastern direction,
the sides and fronts of those [mountains] are known to belong to Indra and the other world-protectors, endowed with divine celestial characteristics.
They are Himavat, Hemakūṭa, Niṣadha, and Meru itself.
In Jambūdvīpa, there are the Kulaparvatas known as Nīla, Śveta, and Śṛṅgin.
That [continent], measuring one hundred times the size of Jambūdvīpa and multiplied by a thousand,
is further divided into nine regions according to its various Varṣas, O Bhārata.
Jambū, Śāka, Kuśa, Krauñca, Śālmala, Gomeda,
and Puṣkara are declared to be the seven islands, surrounded by seven oceans:
those of salt water, milk, sugarcane juice, wine, curd, and clarified butter.
Filled with sweet water and increasing twofold at each stage,
O Pārtha, the seven abodes of the gods are said to be Bhūrloka, Bhuvarloka, Svarloka, Maharloka, Janaloka, Tapoloka, and Satyaloka.
Mahātala, Bhūmitala, Sutala, Vitala,
then Rasātala, and the seventh to be known as Talātala;
there dwell the lords of the Dānavas, such as Hiraṇyākṣa and others, along with great serpents.
O Kaunteya, the Siddhas and the Rishis dwell within these;
first was Svayambhuva Manu, then followed Svārociṣa,
Uttama, Tāmasa, Raivata, and Cākṣuṣa— these are the six.
This present Manu, the son of Vivasvat, is now the supreme sovereign;
by his sons and grandsons this earth has been divided.
Likewise, the Ādityas, the Vasus, the eleven Rudras, and the two Aśvins [are his progeny].
Three Uṣas are proclaimed to have existed during the interval of the Vaivasvata Manu.
Among them were Vipracitti and Hiraṇyākṣa, the most excellent of the Daityas and Dānavas;
in their lineage, moreover, there were many other preeminent Daityas and Dānavas.
The measurement of the earth, consisting of seven continents and oceans, is recorded as being fifty times ten million yojanas in extent;
and in total thickness, it is seventy thousand [yojanas] within the midst of the waters.
This vast earth shines like a cow and does not dissolve;
it is the Lokāloka mountain, most distant and of immense height.
It is fixed as the dual object even for the rays of the sun.
Dissolution is to be known as fourfold: occasional, elemental, absolute, and the fourth is eternal—time, which is the constant destroyer.
Whatever arises of its own accord dissolves back into that very same source.
And it is the certain conclusion regarding living beings that they are preserved by another Person;
just as at the transition of seasons, the various signs of the seasons are seen to be exactly the same as before, so too are all things at the beginnings of the Yugas.
When all beings had become latent,
that Great Lord, having awakened, first fashioned the entire world from the very words of the Veda—
[beings] violent and non-violent, gentle and cruel, characterized by righteousness and unrighteousness, truth and falsehood.
Deprived of that [earth], they again enter into those very same karmas;
earth is enveloped by water ten times its size, and that [water] by fire;
fire is enveloped by wind, and wind by ether, each with its own quality.
Likewise, space is enveloped by the *bhūtādi*, and the *bhūtādi* is enveloped by the Great One (*mahat*);
that Great One is enveloped by the imperishable Puruṣa.
In this manner, there are hundreds and thousands of such cosmic eggs (*aṇḍas*).
Arising and perishing, yet cultivated by the Great-Souled One, this entire world—comprising gods, humans, serpents, and siddhas—is known to reside within the treasury of Vaikuṇṭha.
Pure sages behold it both externally and internally; for the Teacher of the moving and the unmoving, there is as it were another, distinct Māyā.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of the Cosmic Egg," within the Uttara Parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
[Now follows] the description of the manifestation of Māyā.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, what is that Māyā of Viṣṇu, whose splendor is immeasurable,
by which this entire world of moving and non-moving beings is deluded?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
On that island where Viṣṇu formerly dwells, the wielder of the discus and mace—
Vāsudeva, together with Garuḍa, his discus, and Śrī;
he who is dark as the petal of a blue lotus and adorned with two earrings.
He shone with his crown, radiant armlets, and forest garland;
then Nārada, the best of sages, arrived to behold him. Having prostrated before the God and offered hymns of praise, he spoke these words, filled with wonder.
I ask you about my doubt, O Blessed One; you should explain it to me:
What is illusion? Of what nature is illusion? What is its form, and from where does it arise? O Supreme Person, show me the true form of that illusion.
She who deludes the entire three worlds, including all that is moving and unmoving,
from Brahma down to a blade of grass, along with gods, asuras, and humans—
O Vaikuntha, O Vasudeva, you ought to show favor.
Thus addressed by the sage, Janārdana, the God of gods,
laughed and said, "O celestial sage, you should not employ such illusion.
Yet he once again deluded Nārada by means of an eclipse of the moon.
Nārada also, O great king, spoke this again and again:
"O Lord, show me your illusory power (māyā); there is no other purpose.
Then that Viṣṇu, having risen, went back once more to Śvetadvīpa.
Having seized Nārada, the bull among sages, by the tip of his finger,
he then assumed the form of a twice-born on the path;
Viṣṇu himself, resembling the Ṛgveda, stood there appearing as Brahmā.

The doubt of that best of the twice-born was no small matter; he assumed the form of an aged brahmin, bearing a tuft of hair, a water-pot, a deer-skin, and a sacred thread. That lord then gave himself the name Yajñaśarman.
Having fashioned a sacrificial purifier (*pavitraka*) from the tips of *kuśa* grass,
he arrived upon the surface of the earth and wandered through Jambūdvīpa.
He reached the auspicious city named Vaidiśa on the banks of the Vetravatī river.
In that [place], he was constantly devoted to exertion, possessing an abundance of wealth and grain;
he subsisted by cattle-rearing, which was filled with cows, buffaloes, and goats;
and he was an irreproachable member of the Vaiśya caste, dedicated to the work of the plow and the taming of bulls.
Devoted to his household duties, he was known as Sīrabhadra.
Hari himself came into his presence accompanied by Nārada;
they were both received with due honor and provided with seats by him.

"By whom was this said? What is it that you seek to achieve? Is food not being prepared for you? Or does our food not please you? Then Hari, the best of the twice-born, laughed and granted him a great boon.
Raising his face, he spoke with a voice praised by the gods:
"May you have many sons whose minds are intent on the management of fields,
who are devoted to cattle, bonds, and home, and who possess fifty thousand troops and vehicles."
"May their sons and grandsons increase through agriculture and prosperity;
and may you, surrounded by your own kin, always flourish with hundreds of means of livelihood.
Having spoken thus, Vāsudeva, the Lord of the World, together with Nārada, departed.
And the two of them saw a brahmin named Gosvāmin in that field—
poor, distressed by the labor of plowing, and afflicted by the yoke and other farming implements—
on the beautiful bank of the Bhāgīrathī near the village of Veṇikā.
Anxious for his field covered with grass, shrubs, and creepers,
that Brahmin was entreated by the two of them and gave them some food, saying:
"Having arrived from afar, you have come into my presence as guests."
Thus addressed, that best of the twice-born, having performed that labor with the plow,
returned quickly and with great haste to his home along with the two of them;
and he himself, out of devotion, showed them honor by offering the rites of hospitality, beginning with a seat.
Having performed the washing of his feet and likewise having applied well-prepared oil massage there,
he, together with his wife and son, partook of food and enjoyed the meal.
Having finished eating, they slept happily during the night, and at the end of the night, they arose.
As they departed, they granted this excellent boon to that twice-born man:
"O master of cows, may you never again have to plow;
O best of the twice-born, by my grace, may you never lack grain or the fruits of sacrifice."
Having spoken thus, they departed quickly; then Nārada questioned him again:
"Tell me, O Lord of Gods, why was this curse-like boon granted by you to Bhadra Gosvāmin, and likewise such a one to the Vaiśya?"
Thus addressed, the Lord of Gods said: "Listen, Nārada, to my words.
I shall proclaim for you the supreme truth that cuts through doubt:
whatever sin a fisherman might commit in a single year..."
On that day, who would perform the plowing? There is no doubt in this matter.
For this reason, the plowman goes to hell because of his agricultural labor;
without it, there would be no ritual observance (kalpa), and through that [observance], liberation in me is certain.
"O Nārada, what difference does it make to him whether I eat or am pleased?
If neither heaven nor liberation were to be attained thereby, that would be in vain.
Now, Sīrabhadra is occupied with the plow and its impurities through his activities."
Through the consequence of many sins, he will go to a terrible hell;
his wealth has been taken from his house by me, along with his sons, grandsons, and lineage.
It was neither enjoyed nor rested upon by me, but was instead rested in the house of a brahmin.
"That twice-born one as well, O best of sages, shall cross over the cycle of existence.
Speaking thus, they both proceeded along the excellent path;
near Kānyakubja, they beheld a preeminent lake.
