It was filled with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks, adorned with *cakravāka* birds,
and covered with lotus ponds featuring water-lilies, white and red lotuses, and blue lotuses;
it was also strewn with lotus leaves and inhabited by fish and aquatic tortoises.
Its banks were adorned with lovely, dense trees and clusters of *ketakī* plants;
the shores were beautified by *lakucha* trees fragrant with the scent of *ketakī* blossoms,
and the area was teeming with water-hens, peacocks, *bhāruṇḍa* birds, *cakora* partridges, and others.
It was made delightful by kurava birds and cātaka birds, resounding with the cries of peacocks,
filled with the songs of water-fowls, graced by swans and cranes,
and adorned by jīvañjīvaka, hārīta, and cakora birds.
The place renowned by the name of the sage Vasiṣṭha is Śrī Mahodaya; today, great people of discernment must enter it.
They should stand before those [deities], and therefore one should perform the ritual bath.

Having spoken thus, Keśava first bathed in those waters which are renowned throughout the world as a sacred ford (*tīrtha*); having bathed, he took his place upon the bank. During the watch of Vāsudeva, Nārada also, filled with joy, [arrived].
Having rinsed his mouth,
the noble-minded sage reached the sacred bathing place and bathed; but as soon as he rose from the water,
he had attained womanhood— by whom can Nārada be described?
Her eyes were wide, her auspicious face was like the moon;
her ears resembled the noose of the God of Love, and her cheeks shone like gold;
her nose was like the flower of a sesame plant, and her eyebrows were like the bow of Kāma.
His teeth are like diamonds, his auspicious lower lip has the luster of coral,
and the arrangement of his hair is like a peacock's plumage;
the region of his neck shines with three lines like those on a conch shell.
Her auspicious arms were as beautiful as the *mādhavī* creeper;
her hands, joined with the luster of red lotuses, possessed fingers with reddened nails;
and her breasts, firm, full, elevated, and slender-waisted, resembled jars.
Her breasts are firm, smooth, and resemble a pair of ruddy geese;
her waist is so slender it can undoubtedly be grasped by a single fist.
Who can describe the depth of her navel-circle or her exquisite loveliness?
Her waist was adorned with three folds and graced by a line of hair;
her two eyes were as beautiful as those of a doe,
and her hips, shaped like the fruit of the *bimba* tree, were a lovely abode for the God of Love.
Her thighs, resembling a pair of *raṃbhā* plantain stalks, were firm and served as the very bowstring for the arrows of Love;
they were capable of enduring the weight of exhaustion from the exertion of inverted sexual union,
and were joined together with a fastening as straight and elegant as the core of a fresh *kunda* creeper.
O Great King, his pair of shanks and likewise his pair of hidden ankles,
as well as his pair of lotus-feet— red, well-settled, and adorned with creeper-like fingers, palms, nails like moons, and blood-red soles.
At that moment, that woman, honored with all auspicious marks,
became in an instant a captivator of the world,
appearing like another Lakṣmī emerged from the churning of the Ocean of Milk.
Having been seen, Madhusūdana vanished through his illusory power (māyā); and she,
who was like the night that devours the end of time, having reached him,
remained there alone, bewildered, casting her gaze in all directions.
Then the king named Tāladhvaja arrived at that place,
surrounded by his armies like Purandara by the immortals;
he was accompanied by the best of men mounted on elephants, horses, and chariots.
Surrounded by women of the inner apartments seated in pairs of celestial chariots,
and by armies dense with banners and parasols,
he suddenly beheld that lotus-eyed woman.
In a mere moment, he became afflicted by the arrows of Kandarpa.
"Who is she? Whose is she? From where has she come? Is she a goddess or a human?
She is some goddess who has arrived, her form unseen even by the Apsarases."

"A man within the range of Surūpā’s gaze becomes like one who desires death through delusion, as if struck by a poisoned arrow. Having reflected thus in his heart, King Tāladhvaja [spoke] in her presence.
He said to that charming woman, "Listen to my words, O auspicious one:
who are you, whose are you, and from where have you come to this land, O lady of radiant smiles?
When he had spoken thus, she, with beautiful limbs and shedding tears, replied to me, "Know me to be one not born from a womb."
Having learned that she was without father or mother, still a young maiden,
and destitute of refuge, the king then became afflicted by love;
he placed her upon the back of a horse and returned home.
Then, having led her away, he married her according to the rites prescribed in the scriptures.
He took delight with that fair-complexioned woman upon a couch on the pinnacle of a palace,
in the beautiful grounds of gardens, and on the sandy banks of rivers.
On the slopes of mountains, at waterfalls, and in caves; in blooming clusters of lotuses and in beautiful lakes;
at holy fords such as Prayāga and in the hermitages along the rivers.
O King, O Bhārata, for as many as twelve years the monarch dwelt on the shores of the sea in delightful celestial dwellings, even for a single day;
then, in the thirteenth year, a great embryo was formed within her.
When this womb was fully developed, long gourd-like beings were born. From the germination of seeds in jars struck by the breaking of those gourds,
men arose who were indeed devoid of physical elements (dhātus), yet possessed the intense strength of divine bodies.
Numbering fifty, they were born free from all calamities;
all the sons had reached the prime of youth and were skilled in warfare.
Their sons and grandsons, O best of gods, became preeminent.
Blinded by rage like the Kauravas, they fought with volleys of arrows, discuses, spears, swords, and battle-axes; on other horses and other elephants,
they swiftly met their destruction in battle against the Pāṇḍavas.
Accompanied by foot-soldiers and elephant-riders, along with their inner apartments and according to their desires,
they perished upon reaching the ocean like the currents of rivers;
though they possessed the expansion of swords and strength, were full of pride, and were exceedingly tall.
Beholding her entire family, which was like the world of Indra, destroyed in an instant during that battle, she— possessing the nature of Nārada’s daughter—
weeping with emotions filled with affection, spoke with a voice choked with distress.
"Alas, Fate! Alas, Ordainer! O sinful one! O Kṛtānta, you who are worshipped [by all]!
Having shown me this arrangement, you have now taken away my eyes!
Having spoken thus, she, being deeply afflicted by grief, struck her own chest with her hands.
Having fallen to the ground in a swoon, she regained consciousness;
that king too, despondent and weary in an ocean of grief,
fell upon the earth and wept, overwhelmed by intense sorrow.
Despondent and filled with profound grief, he sat together with his ministers;
in the meantime, Viṣṇu arrived accompanied by brahmins,
disguised in the attire of a brahmin, and sat upon a comfortable seat.
Then, stepping forward, he presented a vision of the Dharma and its purpose:
"What is the use of this excessive weeping that only causes you both distress?
Listen: this is the illusory power of Viṣṇu, comparable to wealth seen in a dream."
O Śobhanā, the grief you have felt in this ocean of saṃsāra is natural;
for all living beings, such is the nature of transformation. Thousands of Purandaras and hundreds of universal monarchs [have likewise passed away].
They were extinguished in time, like a lamp by the wind—
even those who are capable of drying up the ocean teeming with sea-monsters,
or who could reduce Mount Meru to powder upon the earth with their two hands.
In order to lift up the earth and seize the moon and the sun,
they entered at that time the mouth of Kṛtānta;
for them, Mount Trikūṭa was the fortress, the oceans were the moats, the Rākṣasas were the warriors, and the wealth of Kubera was their treasury.
And that Rāvaṇa, for whom the mantra was composed by Uśanas, is despondent due to the power of fate.
Even in battle crowded with elephants and horses, or in fire, or having entered a cave, or in the great ocean,
or even while living together with all those whose anger is aroused— destruction is never possible for him.
Let him enter the underworld, let him go to the realm of the lord of the gods, or let him ascend Sumeru, the king of mountains;
let him provide protection with mantras, herbs, and weapons—whatever is destined to be, that shall come to pass, O Lord, for I am now disillusioned.
Then someone else wept, overwhelmed by a profound sorrow that washed his face with tears.

Even one with deformed feet dances, while another, whose body is composed of dharma and other virtues, sings most melodiously with a wide, long lower lip, captivating the heart and overflowing with bliss; this is the essence: this very person is like a dancer upon the stage, possessing the form of a drum.
Having thus taught the Dharma regarding the activities of worldly existence, Viṣṇu became silent; immediately thereafter, those best of the twice-born said:
"Arise, bathe, and perform the funeral rites for your sons."
"Do not grieve; this is a Māyā of Viṣṇu, created by Viṣṇu himself.
Having been addressed thus, she who was beautiful in all her limbs became an immovable man;
at that very moment, he became Nārada, possessing a form identical to his own.
Then that king, together with his ministers, his domestic priest, and his entire harem, beheld all this as being like a momentary illusion of Indra;
he saw Nārada, the tiger among sages, formidable with the weight of his matted locks.
He was fair-complexioned, blazing, and resplendent with the splendor of Brahman;
he bore a topknot and a water-pot, and likewise held the neck of a lute in his hand;
he was adorned with a bright sacred thread and a loincloth for covering.
Standing on his sandals at the edge of the lake upon the seat of Brahmā,
Hari, having grasped them with the tips of his hands,
vanished from that region along with the gods in the sky, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Then, having reached Śvetadvīpa, O King, the Lord spoke to the sage:
"O celestial sage, regarding that which you previously asked about the narrative of Māyā—
what kind of Māyā it is, what its essential nature is, and what its constituent essence is."
"O Brahmin, that Vaiṣṇava illusion of mine has been displayed to you.
Having spoken thus to the best of sages, Janārdana, the God of gods,
immediately vanished while that celestial seer was looking on.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Vision of Māyā," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira;
[it also contains] the description of the defects of worldly existence.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
By what karma does a person attain the state of a god, the state of a human, or the state of an animal? By what [karma] does one enter the most dreadful dwelling in a womb?
And while staying in the womb, what does one eat, and how is one born again?
How does one cross over the difficult-to-traverse faults such as being abandoned or cast out? How is nourishment attained during childhood? By what action does one become a youth?
By what does one become of noble birth, handsome, and wealthy?

How does one obtain a wife and a home endowed with all virtues? How does one become a wise man, possessed of sons, generous, and free from disease? How does one die in happiness, and how does one experience the fruits of good and evil deeds?
"O one of stainless intellect, everything indeed appears dense and impenetrable to me.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"Through auspicious deeds one attains the state of a god; through mixed deeds one goes to the human state."
Through impure actions, a living being is born among the animal species.
In this matter of determining dharma and adharma, scripture alone is the authority:
sin arises from sinful action, and merit from meritorious action.
When consumed during the period favorable for conception, that [semen] remains free from defect;
then, touched by the wind, it attains oneness with the woman's blood.
At the time of the emission of semen, the living soul (jīva), joined with its instruments (karaṇas), [enters].
The servant, impelled by his own past actions, enters the womb;
that semen and blood, united in one place, become an embryo (kalala) in a single day.
In five nights, the embryo attains the form of a bubble (budbuda).
After seven nights, the bubble becomes a mass of flesh;
after fourteen days, that mass becomes a peśī, firmly endowed with blood and flesh.
From the peśī, like sprouts from a seed, [limbs] emerge after twenty-five nights.
Within just one month, five parts arise again:
the neck, the head, the shoulders, the spinal column, and likewise the abdomen;
within two months, all these gradually come into being.
In three months, the limbs, fingers, and joints are produced along with their constituent substances;
in four months, the fingers are produced in their proper order;
and in five months, the mouth, nose, and ears are formed.
Furthermore, the rows of teeth, the private parts, and the nails are produced;
within six months, the ears with their openings, as well as the anus,
the penis, the generative organ, and the navel also come into being.
The joints that form within the limbs are produced over seven months;
then, complete with major and minor limbs, endowed with a head and hair,
and with distinct parts fully developed, it becomes robust over an eighth month.
Endowed with the five elements, it remains fully developed;
it subsists through the sixfold potency of the mother's food. By means of that essence, O bull of the Bharatas, the child grows day by day.
I shall explain that to you, O subduer of enemies, exactly as I have heard it:
by means of its connection to the cord of the navel, that [embryo] grows day by day;
then, when this body is fully formed, the individual soul (jīva) regains consciousness.
One experiences pleasure and pain, as well as sleep and dreams resulting from past actions.
"I have died and been born again; having been born, I have died again.
Indeed, thousands of various wombs have been seen by me."

Now that I have just been born and have already received the sacraments, I shall perform that which is most beneficial, by which I will not again take recourse to a womb. While still within the womb, I shall meditate upon the Lord; once emerged from the womb, I shall continue my practice.
"I shall study the four Vedas which turn one away from the cycle of rebirth.
Thus, that living soul (jīva), intensely tormented by the great suffering of the womb,
remains there under the power of karma, contemplating the means to liberation.
Just as someone oppressed by a great mountain remains in pain,
so the embodied soul, constrained by the fetal membrane, remains in suffering and agitation;
just as one who has fallen into the ocean remains overwhelmed by miseries.
With his limbs drenched by the amniotic fluid, the person remains there in great distress;
just as someone cast into an iron cauldron is cooked by fire,
so too is that creature, whose belly is constricted, cooked while dwelling within the womb.
The suffering that would arise from being continuously pierced by needles as hot as fire becomes eightfold within the womb;
there is no dwelling anywhere more painful than dwelling in the womb.
O King, for embodied beings, this suffering of the womb is indeed most terrible and exceedingly perilous;
thus has the suffering of living beings— of all things, both moving and stationary— been fully described according to their respective wombs.
For the embodied being who is about to be born, as he is squeezed by the machine of the womb while in a state of fainting, there arises suffering ten million times greater than that in the womb;
he is tormented on all sides as if by a machine, like an arrow being compressed.
As he is struck on the head with the hammer of sin,
and as he is shaken from the womb by the powerful winds of birth,
a most great suffering arises for him who finds no protection.
Just as sesame seeds and sugarcane become devoid of essence when pressed by a machine,
so too is the body rendered insubstantial when crushed by the machine of the womb;
it is constrained by the binding of bones, marrow, skin, flesh, and sinews.
It is joined with clay of blood and flesh, smeared with the fluids of feces and urine,
covered with hair, body-hair, and grass, a sick abode of diseases,
having one great door which is the mouth, adorned with the teeth and lips.
With the two lips as its door-panels and the teeth and tongue as its bolted bars,
with the flow of the channels as its sweat and overflowing with phlegm and bile,
it is beset by old age and sorrow, situated within the fire of the wheel of time.
Overcome by desire and anger, crushed by calamities,
afflicted by the thirst for enjoyment, deluded, and subject to the power of passion and hatred;
with its major and minor limbs constricted and enveloped by the fetal membrane.
Having emerged through the narrow and impure birth canal,
its limbs drenched in feces, urine, and blood, and arising from filth and hair—
thus is described the house of the body belonging to the eternal Self, which is itself impermanent.
The impure body of the pure [soul] is produced by the bondage of karma;
since the body arises from the union of semen and blood,
and is eternally filled with feces and urine, it is therefore remembered as impure.
Just as a pot may be pure on the outside yet filled with filth within,
so too this body remains impure even when diligently cleansed,
despite obtaining here purifying substances such as the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and sacrificial offerings.
What else is there but drops of matter that become impure in an instant?
Even when the body is thoroughly cleansed with the five products of the cow and water infused with kuśa grass,
it does not attain purity, just as charcoal does not become clean even when scrubbed.
How can that body ever be purified, from which streams of phlegm, urine, feces, and so forth flow constantly like those from a mountain?
For this body, which is a repository of all impurities, no purity exists.
It is said that even a single spot, though pure, becomes foul when filled with excrement;
likewise, the body, though refined with effort by means of fragrant incenses and the like,
does not abandon its own inherent nature, just as a dog’s tail does not straighten when bent.
Just as that which is black by birth cannot become white through any means,
so too the physical form would not become pure even while being thoroughly cleansed;
for one continues to smell one's own foul odor and see one's own impurity even while looking.
This world does not become dispassionate even when its nose is being tormented!
Oh, the greatness of delusion, by which the entire world is utterly infatuated;
smelling and seeing it, one does not become dispassionate toward the defects of one’s own body.
Thus, this body is indeed inherently impure by its very nature;
it is certainly devoid of essence, having only skin as its substance, and is like the pith of a plantain tree.
The memory that the being possessed while dwelling in the womb perishes upon birth.
For that embodied being who has fainted from the pain of being crushed by the mechanism of the womb,
as soon as he is touched by the external wind known as "delusion," a terrible fever arises.
By that great fever, a state of great delusion arises;
for one who is utterly bewildered, a loss of memory quickly occurs once again.
And from that loss of memory, due to the power of his past actions in this world—
Attachment arises quickly for a living being in that very same birth. This world, being deluded and impassioned, engages in what ought not to be done;
it does not know itself, nor does it find the Supreme.
The highest good is not heard when there is an eye, yet one does not see;
walking slowly on a level path, one stumbles at every step.
When the intellect is present, one does not understand, even when being enlightened by the wise.
Driven by the power of passion and greed, one is afflicted in saṃsāra;
because of the absence of recollection of the womb, the great sages have declared that the scripture is for the purpose of crushing that suffering and for the attainment of heaven and liberation.
That those who exist in this supreme knowledge— which accomplishes all desires and goals—
do not effect their own welfare, is a great wonder here.
Furthermore, there is great suffering in childhood because the functions of the senses have not yet manifested.
Even though he desires it, he is unable to perform or speak acts of hospitality;
likewise, there is great suffering during the eruption of teeth due to innate disease,
as well as affliction from various childhood ailments and even from infantile seizures.
With his body overcome by thirst and hunger, someone stands there crying out piteously;
out of delusion, even a child might commit the act of eating excrement and urine.
Through the piercing of the ears in childhood and through the beating by his parents, [he suffers].
For men, there is suffering from the study of letters and from the commands of a teacher;
the activity of the senses is troubled by the affliction of desire and passion;
and for one constantly overwhelmed by disease, how can there be happiness even in youth?

Through envy and delusion, great suffering arises for one who is attached; like the redness of an inflamed eye, passion leads only to misery. Tormented by the fire of anger, one finds no sleep at night.

Even by day, where is there happiness for one whose body is exhausted by women, due to the constant anxiety of acquiring wealth? Those drops of semen should not be considered sources of pleasure; they are like drops born of perspiration.
For one afflicted by worms, for a leper, and likewise for a lustful man,
that which arises from the heat of the fire of scratching women is indeed the same as the pleasure one finds upon the emergence of a boil.
Such [pleasure] should be understood as existing among women; nothing more than that is found in them.
Just as the pain of a boil ceases once it has burst, so too should it be understood regarding women: there is no happiness in reality.
The pleasure that arises from the discharge of feces and urine—
such is the nature of those [pleasures] to be understood; yet they are imagined otherwise by the deluded,
regarding women who are impure and the abodes of all defects.
Upon reflection, not even a particle of happiness exists in this way:
honor is countered by dishonor, union by separation, and youth is swallowed by old age; what happiness is there that is free from affliction?

The fresh beauty of men and women, which was formerly dear to one another, [now] has its form rendered feeble by wrinkles, gray hair, and baldness; it is incapacitated for all activities and worn out by old age.
That very same body, when seized by old age, is no longer dear to either of them.
What person other than one devoid of consciousness could feel attachment while seeing oneself transformed by old age, as if becoming something entirely new?
A man overcome by old age is treated with contempt by his wife, sons, and other kinsmen,
as well as by servants who behave poorly because he has become powerless;
for one who is aged can no longer pursue dharma, artha, kāma, or mokṣa.
Therefore, one is able to accomplish this body of the self.
The imbalance of wind, bile, phlegm, and so forth is called disease;
thus, this body of the self should be known as consisting of disease.
Since diseases and the cage [of the body] are not distinct from wind and the other humors,
those manifold bodily sufferings caused by various kinds of illnesses—
which are each to be known by one's own self— what else shall I say?
One hundred and one deaths reside within this body;
among them, one is associated with Time (Kāla), while the rest are known as adventitious.
Those which are declared here to be adventitious are pacified by medicines.
Death by time cannot be stilled by recitations, fire-offerings, or gifts;
nor, even if death were not to occur, would one fearlessly consume poison.
Therefore, there are no fears of untimely death for that person.
Various diseases, weapons, creatures such as serpents,
and poisons originating from mobile sources— these are the gates of death for embodied beings;
even Dhanvantari himself cannot protect one who is afflicted by all these maladies and the like.
Neither medicine,
nor austerity, nor charity, nor mantras, nor kinsmen are able to restore to health or protect a living being who has reached the time of death; no one can save a person afflicted by Time.
Even death at its appointed time is overcome by wise and high-souled men who have attained perfection through yoga, elixirs, austerities, and recitation; it is not overcome by idle men.
There is no suffering equal to death, and there is no fear equal to death.
There is no terror equal to death for any embodied beings whatsoever.
Death cuts asunder all— virtuous wives, sons, friends, kingdoms, sovereign power, wealth, and even unrequited enmities.
O people, do you not see that even in the midst of a thousand men,
there are only five who live to a hundred years, and even they may or may not exist? Some men perish at eighty, and some at seventy.
The maximum lifespan is established at sixty thousand years, yet that too is uncertain.
Whatever lifespan may belong to embodied beings due to their past karmas,
half of that lifespan is taken away by night in the form of death.
Due to childhood, delusion, or likewise due to old age and decay,
twenty years pass for men devoid of virtue, pleasure,
and wealth, beset by various adventitious fears, diseases, and sorrows.
Even there, half is devoured, and that which remains lives on;
at the end of its life, it meets a most terrible death,
and having died, it is born again under the power of karma through tens of millions of births.
The separation of men from their bodies due to the exhaustion of karma is designated as death; it is not otherwise in the ultimate sense.
This occurs for one who has entered the Great Tapas while his vital organs are being severed.
The suffering that a living being experiences at death has no comparison anywhere in this world.
Crying out thus in agony, "O father! O mother! O beloved!", a person is swallowed by death just as a frog is seized by a serpent.
Embraced by his kinsmen and surrounded by those dear to him,
he sighs long and hot breaths as his mouth becomes parched;
he cries out and tosses repeatedly upon his bed.
Utterly deluded, he tosses his hands and feet about excessively;
from the bed he longs for the floor, and from the floor again for the bed, while on the ground,
helpless and stripped of shame, he is smeared with urine and excrement.
With my throat, lips, and palate parched, begging for water while thinking of wealth— wondering whose these will be when I am dead—
I am dragged by the noose of Time as five pits are being dug for me.
While people are looking on, the living being, making a gurgling sound, dies;
like a water flea moving from one blade of grass to another, it enters body after body in succession.
Having attained a subsequent body, it indeed abandons its former one.
For the discerning person, the suffering born of longing is indeed greater than the suffering of death;
the suffering of death is momentary, whereas that produced by longing is infinite. Even Viṣṇu, the Lord of the worlds, became a dwarf because of his state of being a petitioner.

What other thing could be more excessive than that which does not lead to lightness? Now I have understood this: that which is considered "heavy" by you is precisely what I have realized. One should not further solicit from another; craving is the cause of heaviness.
Suffering at the beginning, suffering in the middle, and terrible suffering at the end—
such is the succession of sufferings for all beings by their very nature.
These are the sufferings that are present and those that have passed.
Ignorant men do not cultivate [the path], nor do they become dispassionate because of that.
From over-eating comes great suffering, and from fasting, even greater;
life weighed in the balance is thus miserable—how then can there be happiness?
Hunger is considered the most excellent of all diseases;
it is pacified for a mere moment by the application of the medicine of food. Yet, this disease of hunger is equal to the pain of any other ailment, utterly destroying one's entire strength.
Overcome by that [taste], one does not die as one would from other diseases;
for even that flavor, whether through desire or otherwise, remains upon the tip of the tongue,
but in that very instant, it reaches the throat and returns with the onset of old age.
Thus, food is remembered as being like medicine for those tormented by the disease of hunger;
it should not be considered a source of happiness by the wise in the ultimate sense.
For one who is like the dead, having abandoned all worldly activities, would view it [only as medicine].

And even there, how can there be happiness for one whose self is shrouded in darkness? Even upon awakening, how can there be happiness for one whose self is afflicted by labors such as agriculture, cattle-rearing, trade, service, and travel?
Living beings are oppressed by urine and excrement in the morning, by hunger at midday,
by desire when they are satiated, and even by sleeplessness;
there is suffering in the acquisition of wealth, and likewise in the preservation of what has been acquired.
In acquiring wealth there is suffering, and in its loss there is suffering; from riches, whence can there be happiness?
For those possessed of wealth, there is constant fear—from thieves, from water, from fire, from their own kin, and even from the king—just as for living beings there is constant fear of death.
Flesh carried into the sky is devoured by birds; on the earth, it is devoured by beasts of prey;
and in the water, it is devoured by fish—so too is the man of wealth devoured everywhere.
Prosperity deludes him, while adversity torments him.
For when they are being acquired, wealth causes distress; when, indeed, do riches bring happiness?
For the master of wealth is anxious, whereas he who is indifferent to all wealth is at ease; since the master of wealth is miserable, while he who is indifferent to all wealth is happy.
In winter there is suffering from the cold, in summer from the harsh heat, and in the rainy season from wind and rain; thus, even in the proper seasons, where is there any happiness?
There is suffering in the elaborate preparations for marriage, and again in the carrying of that fetus.
There is suffering from the birth of offspring and the defects of children, and suffering from painful labors; alas, what shall I do with this misery caused by my son’s toothaches and eye ailments?
The cows are lost, the cultivation is ruined, and the bulls have fled somewhere away.
"These guests have arrived at my house at the very time my food supply is exhausted;
moreover, my wife is pregnant with her first child—who will do the cooking?
And what kind of groom might there be for my daughter at the time of her giving away?"
Thus, for householders overwhelmed by such anxieties, whence can there be happiness?
For a man agitated by concerns for his family, his learning, his character, and all his virtues—
like water poured into an unbaked clay pot— perish along with his very body.
Even in kingship there is great suffering due to the constant anxiety over peace and war; where there is fear even of one's own son, what kind of happiness can there be?
Indeed, for almost all embodied beings, death at the hands of their own kin is the common lot.
Like dogs competing for the same piece of meat,
no king on earth was renowned for possessing invincible strength; for there was none who, having overcome everyone, could dwell in happiness and fearlessness.

"O King, I have described to you that this body of yours, consisting of suffering from birth onwards, is composed of karma. By performing acts of charity, fasting, and religious observances, men here partake in the happiness of all enjoyments. Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Faults of Saṃsāra," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira. [This is followed by] the description of the classification of sins.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
The downward descent of men is proclaimed as "adhaḥ-karma" (downward action);
suffering within the terrible oceans of hell is called "pāpa" (sin).
The varieties of unrighteousness (*adharma*) are to be understood through the distinctions of the fluctuations of the mind;
they are gross, subtle, and extremely subtle, divided into many millions of types.
Among these, those accumulations of sin which are gross are the causes for rebirth in hell.

These are briefly described as the means of action pertaining to mind, speech, and body. Now, mental action is fourfold: intention toward another's wife, thinking of what is undesirable with the mind, and intentness upon what should not be done.
Idle chatter, that which is untrue and unpleasant,
slandering others, and backbiting— these are the fourfold vocal actions. Furthermore, eating what is unfit to be eaten, violence, and the pursuit of false desires [are the mental actions].
The appropriation of others' property is the fourfold physical action;
thus, these twelve types of action have been declared along with their means.
I shall now further describe their divisions, the fruits of which are infinite.
Those who hate Mahādeva, the savior from the ocean of saṃsāra,
being possessed of all sins, go into the fires of hell;
even the slayer of a Brahmin, the drinker of liquor, the thief, and the violator of the guru’s bed.

These are the perpetrators of great sins (mahāpātakin), and the fifth is one who associates with them. Those who kill a Brāhmaṇa out of anger, hatred, fear, or greed— those who commit such a mortal transgression are proclaimed to be slayers of a Brāhmaṇa (brahmaghna).
Having summoned a Brahmin who is destitute and begging,
if one subsequently tells him "there is nothing," he is likewise considered a slayer of a Brahmin (brahmahā). Furthermore,
he who constantly triumphs over other twice-born men out of pride in his own learning [is also such].
Even he who sits in the midst of the assembly is proclaimed a slayer of a Brahmin;
he who by force elevates himself through false virtues,
and he who acts in opposition to his gurus, is likewise remembered as a slayer of a Brahmin.

He who creates an obstacle for Brahmins whose bodies are tormented by hunger and thirst and who desire to eat, him they call a slayer of a Brahmin. A slanderer of all people is one who is intent upon searching for their faults.

He who causes agitation and is cruel is likewise considered a slayer of a Brahmin. He who creates an obstacle for cows overcome by thirst as they approach for water is likewise considered a slayer of a Brahmin.

He who, having recognized a fault, whispers it into the ear of a king, is a wicked, base slanderer; he is indeed considered a slayer of a Brahmin. Furthermore, he who seizes land previously enjoyed by gods, twice-born men, or cows [is likewise a sinner].
They say that even after time has passed, such a person is called a slayer of a Brahmin.
In the theft of a twice-born man’s wealth—even if it was acquired through lawful means—the sin is to be known as equal to the killing of a Brahmin; there is no doubt in this matter.
The abandonment of the *agnihotra* and other sacrificial rites;
the desertion of one's mother and father; giving false testimony; the killing of a friend;
and setting fire to a cow-path, a forest, a city, or a village.
Thus, these terrible sins are equal to the drinking of liquor:
the theft of one's own property, as well as the theft of men, women, elephants, and horses;
and the theft of cows, land, silver, gems, medicinal herbs, and gold dust.
The theft of sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, musk, sugar-candy, or fine garments,
when placed in one's hand, is recorded as equal to the theft of gold. Likewise, the failure to give daughters who are marriageable to a suitable bridegroom is considered a grave offense.
Sexual intercourse with one’s son, friend, or wife, as well as with one’s sisters,

the heinous violation of a maiden, consorting with women of the lowest castes, and sexual intercourse with a woman of a different caste— these are recorded in tradition as equal to violating the teacher’s bed.

Those sins which have been described as equal to the great transgressions (mahāpātaka) are designated as "pātaka"; likewise, I shall now describe the minor transgressions (upapātaka). Furthermore, he who promises wealth for the sake of a twice-born man but does not give it;
Therefore, O Lord of Men, the seizure of a Brahmin’s property and the transgression of established boundaries are minor sins equal to obstacles;
as are excessive anger, pride, hypocrisy, and ingratitude.
Excessive attachment to sense objects, miserliness, supreme envy,

the abduction of another's wife, the defilement of a virtuous maiden, being the elder brother whose younger brother marries before him (parivitti), being the younger brother who marries before his elder (parīvettṛ), and the woman by whom he is so superseded;
The giving away of these two [parents] and the daughter, as well as officiating at their sacrifices;
likewise, in the absence of a son, friend, wife, or master,
there is renunciation for the learned ones and for those ascetics who are born together with them.
There shall be the failure of religious duties and the destruction of one's companions;
one must not inflict even the slightest suffering upon those residing in the hermitage,
nor upon one's own circle of servants, nor upon the cattle, grain, and wealth.
The theft of base metals, grain, or cattle; begging from those who should not be asked; and the sale of cows, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, women, or Śūdras—especially so—is [a minor offense].
Likewise is the sale of sacrificial implements, groves, tanks, or one's wife and children.
They subsist on the wealth of women, being utterly conquered by them; they neglect the observances of pilgrimages, fasts, vows, and temple rites;
they fail to protect their wives, and they consort with women who drink liquor.
Not repaying debts, living off the interest on grain, accepting wealth from a censured person, selling goods that should not be sold,
employing spells for malevolent purposes, and the practice of root-magic (mūlakarman).
Deliberation on the rite of eradication (*uccāṭana*), the practice of causing paralysis (*gara*) and inciting hatred (*dveṣaṇa*),
and undertaking one's own ritual actions for the sake of enjoying the tongue— these are [forbidden]. Furthermore, he who teaches for a fee and those who study for a fee [are likewise excluded].
The state of being a *vrātya* consists of the abandonment of religious vows, the consumption of all kinds of food, approaching the wives of others, resorting to fallacious reasoning,
and the censure of the gods, the sacred fires, virtuous men, virtuous women, cows, and Brahmins.
Whether in the presence of kings or in their assemblies,
those who are immoral, nihilistic, sinful, and proponents of universal emptiness—
whether during festival times or by day— engage in sexual intercourse with women of improper species or with animals.
Those who engage in sexual intercourse with women in their menses or within the womb; those who cut off the food portions of women, sons, and friends;
those who speak unpleasantly to people; rogues; and those who violate established agreements.
He who destroys tanks, wheels, bridges, and chariots,
and he who causes a breach in the cooking of those standing in a single row— by these sins, men are known as secondary offenders (upapātakin).

Those who are joined with minor sins less than those [previously mentioned] are considered even more sinful. Those men who create a rift in matters of business between cows, Brahmins, maidens, masters, friends, or ascetics, are known as hell-beings.
Those who burn with envy at the prosperity of others, those who point out the wealth of others,
those intent on the affairs of others, those who defile the wives and men of others,
and he who always causes suffering to a twice-born man by many means— [these go to hell].
The twice-born who serves a Śūdra woman, or who intentionally smells liquor;
those cruel men who are addicted to drinking, and those men who, for the sake of wealth, perform acts such as giving gifts and sacrifices; [these fall from their status].
In cow-pens, near fires, in water, on roads, in the shade of trees, in hermitages,
and in pleasure gardens and temples, men constantly discharge impurities;
these men are perpetually devoted to drinking liquor and addicted to singing and instrumental music.
And those who, like serpents in their play, are intent on seeking out vulnerabilities;
who obstruct the paths with bamboo, *kāśa* grass, wood, or even auspicious stakes; and who carry off the wives of others.
Those who carry forged edicts, those who delight in fraudulent acts,
those who engage in treacherous combat with weapons, and those who deal in deceptive transactions;
and he who is the maker or the seller of bows, arrows, and missiles.
He who is exceedingly merciless toward his servants and a tamer of animals;
he who listens slowly to the words of one speaking falsely;
he who betrays his master, friends, and teachers; and who is deceitful, fickle, and treacherous.
Those who afflict with hunger their wives, sons, friends, children, the elderly, the emaciated, the sick, their servants, guests, and kinsmen;
and he who eats sweet food himself while giving something else to a Brahmin— [such a person is condemned].
One should know that such a person is a futile cook, despised among those who discourse on Brahman:

those who, having personally undertaken the observances, abandon them because their senses are unsubdued; those who live as renunciants and yet reveal secrets; and those who break the rules of secrecy.
They strike them with force and curse them again and again;
they do not nourish those who are weak, but instead make them carry [loads] once more.
They oppress them with excessive burdens and make them carry loads even when they are wounded.
Those who eat after the midday hour has passed,
and those who do not diligently protect their own cattle— whether they be joined with others or afflicted by broken limbs, wounds, or disease— from hunger, such men are the guardians of hell.
Those who cause the most wicked of bulls to shed their semen,

those who drive a cow fit for slaughter, and those who do not provide hospitality to one who has arrived at their hermitage, afflicted by hunger, thirst, and fatigue— they are remembered as destined for the great hells.
Those who do not honor a guest surely go to hell;
those fools who do not show compassion for the helpless, the disabled, the miserable, the child, the aged, or the emaciated and afflicted, go to the ocean of hell.
One who keeps goats and sheep, one who keeps buffaloes, one who lives by the sea, the husband of a Śūdra woman,
and one who follows the livelihood of a Śūdra, Vaiśya, or Kṣatriya— such a lowest of the twice-born shall go to hell.
So too shall artisans, craftsmen, physicians, goldsmiths, actors, and [other] twice-born men [who follow such forbidden trades].
Likewise, others are recorded as hell-beings who wear armor made of iron;
he who, having transgressed what has been enjoined, seizes taxes according to his own will,
and he who takes pleasure in inflicting punishment, shall be cooked in hell.

That king whose subjects are oppressed by bribe-takers, officials, and thieves, and who is thus provoked to anger, is cooked in the hells. Those twice-born men who accept gifts from a king who behaves unjustly [share in his guilt].
They too go to terrible hells, there is no doubt;
whatever sin belongs to adulterers and thieves, that same sin accrues to a king who fails to protect his subjects; therefore, accepting gifts from him is dreadful.

If a king, without investigation, should execute one who is not a thief as if he were a thief, or one who is a thief as if he were not a thief, he shall go to hell. [He should likewise avoid confiscating] ghee,
oil, food, drink, honey, meat, wine, and spirits.
Molasses, sugarcane, alkaline substances, vegetables, curd, roots, and fruits;
grass, wood, flowers, leaves, medicinal herbs, and bronze vessels;
sandals, umbrellas, carts, seats, beds, and clothing.
Copper, lead, tin, glass, and items derived from water such as conch shells; household utensils made of wood or bamboo and the like;
and those produced from wool, cotton, silk, hemp, and fine cloth.
Those who, out of greed, steal coarse or fine garments,
as well as various other such articles,
will certainly go to the hells— whether they be men or women; of this there is no doubt.
"Having stolen even a single mustard seed of another's property—whatever it may be—a man goes to hell; there is no doubt about this.
By such sins as these, immediately after the departure of the soul (utkrānti), [the deceased suffers]."
The body shall assume its former shape for the purpose of undergoing torment;
by the command of Yama, he shall go to the world of Yama in that very body,
being led by the most terrible messengers of Yama and experiencing extreme suffering.
For those among the bodies of animals and humans whose souls are devoted to unrighteousness,
Dharmarāja is remembered as the teacher who disciplines them through various most terrible executions;
likewise for those endowed with disciplined conduct who have stumbled due to negligence.
The Guru is the teacher of atonement, and Yama is not seen by them;
for adulterers, thieves, and those who act unjustly,
the king is the punisher, and for those who are concealed, the King of Dharma (Yama) is the judge.
Therefore, one should perform the expiation for the evil that has been committed;
otherwise, there is no destruction of what has not been experienced even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
He who performs an action himself, or causes it to be done, or approves of it—
Through body, mind, or speech, the downward course is his fruit.
Thus, the various types of sins along with their means have been briefly described;
now the diverse destinies of men who perform sinful deeds are told.

"O Moon among the lords of men, through various actions produced by speech, body, and mind—which are divided into many types and serve as the causes for the arising of auspicious and inauspicious fruits—human beings attain the radiant realm of the Lord of the Gods or numerous hells.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Different Types of Sin," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
This is the description of the teaching on the fruits of auspicious and inauspicious deeds.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Now, by these four kinds of sins, all embodied beings, rendered helpless, go to the world of Yama, which is terrible and produces great terror.
By those dwelling in the womb, by those being born, by children, youths, and middle-aged persons,
by men, women, and eunuchs, and by the elderly— all living beings must understand that therein the auspicious and inauspicious fruits of embodied beings are deliberated.
By Citragupta and the other members of the assembly, who are impartial and all-seeing:
"There are no living beings here who do not go to the abode of Yama;
for the karma performed must necessarily be experienced as it has been ordained."
In that regard, those men who perform auspicious deeds, whose minds are gentle, and who are endowed with compassion,
travel by a pleasant path to the abode of Yama;
this applies to him who gives sandals or wooden shoes to the best of the twice-born.
With a great, excellent horse, he goes happily to the abode of Yama;
by the gift of an umbrella, embodied beings go as if under an umbrella;
and those who give clothing go wearing divine garments.
By the gift of a palanquin and horses, one shall then proceed happily;
by the gift of beds and seats, they go happily to the abode of Yama.
The planter of groves shall proceed happily in the cool shades.
Those who donate flower gardens travel by means of the Puṣpaka chariot; likewise,
the builder of a temple for the gods, a hermitage for ascetics,
or pavilions for the destitute, travels sporting in magnificent mansions.
Those men who worship the gods, the sacred fire, their gurus, the brahmins, and their mother and father,
proceed happily by the path of their desire while being honored themselves.
Those who give lamps go forth illuminating all the directions.
By the gift of shelter, they go to their own home in comfort;
those who give cows travel by a path enriched with all desired objects.
Those who commit no sins go there satisfied, and not otherwise.
Those who provide medicine for the afflicted go to happiness free from agitation;
those devoted to the service of their elders proceed with ease, finding rest;
and by providing water for washing the feet, one travels upon a cool path.
He who provides foot-massage shall travel upon the back of a horse;
by the gift of gold and jewels, he goes forth crossing over difficulties;
and by the gift of vehicles and mounts, he travels by means of a human carriage.
One whose self is fulfilled with all desires goes [to Yama’s abode] by the gift of land;
one who drinks and eats goes there by the gift of food and drink.
By such gifts as these, people go happily to Yamakṣaya.
O best of men, they obtain vast enjoyments even in heaven.
Of all gifts, the gift of food is remembered as supreme;
it provides immediate gratification, is divine, and increases strength and intelligence.
For all three worlds, water is indeed considered life itself;
it is pure, immortal, divine, stainless, and a panacea for all things.
Food, drink, cattle, clothing, land, bedding, umbrellas, and seats— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly at "āsanaṃ". The translation reflects the portion given.]
In the world beyond, eight types of gifts are especially praised;
among them, the gift of food is preeminent. Since men go to the city of Dharmarāja with ease by means of it, one should therefore practice righteousness.
Furthermore, those who are of cruel deeds, sinful, and devoid of charity go by a terrible southern path to their own abode;
having traversed eighty-six thousand yojanas.
The city of Vaivasvata is to be known as being established in various forms;
it appears as if close at hand to men of auspicious deeds,
yet it remains exceedingly distant for those who travel by the terrible path.
It was filled with sharp thorns and strewn with gravel;
it was covered with fierce stones resembling the edges of razors;
in some places there was great mud, and in others, ditches difficult to cross.
In some places they travel along paths covered with darbha grass resembling iron needles; in others,
they go along a road filled with heated coals, obstructed by mountains with precipitous slopes and crowded with trees, while they are deeply distressed.
In some places it was filled with uneven pits, in others with very slippery clods of earth, with heated sands, and likewise with sharp spikes; in some places,
a bamboo forest was pervaded by various widespread torments.
In some places it was covered with sand, making entry possible only with great difficulty;
in some places it was filled with hot water, and in others with fires of dried cow-dung;
in some places it was infested with lions and wolves, as well as with biting insects and dreadful vermin.
In some places there were great leeches, and in others pythons;
in some places there were fierce flies, and in others serpents of virulent poison;
and there were herds of rutting elephants, intoxicated with strength and intent on destruction.
With great bulls whose sharp horns were goring the path,
with buffaloes possessing massive tusks, with rutting camels and scavengers,
with fierce ḍākinīs, and with terrifying rākṣasas;
Afflicted by most terrible diseases, they proceed while being struck by a fierce,
violent wind mixed with thick dust,
and by a rain of massive stones, left utterly without refuge.
In some places they go along being torn apart by the falling of lightning;
in others, they are pierced on all sides by a great rain of arrows,
and by the falling of masses of thunderbolts and terrible meteors.
Scorched by a rain of blazing embers, they flee;
filled by a rain of scalding dust, they weep;
and they are terrified again and again by the terrible roars of great clouds.
Surrounded by men and being crushed by a rain of sharpened weapons,
they flee as they are drenched by streams of great caustic water;
and they are assailed by a wind that is intensely cold, piercing, and harsh.
Being oppressed on all sides, they wither and shrink;
thus, by that terrible path— devoid of travelers,
without support, impassable, and waterless on every side.
Without rest, through great [suffering], without refuge,
in the form of darkness, painful, and the locus of all miseries—
all embodied beings who are deluded and performers of evil deeds are led away.
Then, by the most terrible messengers of Yama who carry out his commands, they are forcibly taken—
solitary, dependent on others, and deprived of friends and kinsmen—
mourning their own deeds and weeping again and again.
Some men appeared like hungry ghosts, naked, with their throats, lips, and palates parched;
their limbs were emaciated, they were terrified, and they were being consumed by the fire of hunger.
Some were bound with iron chains, lying on their backs with their feet upward.
Being dragged and rubbed by the exceedingly powerful messengers of Yama,
some men are dragged with their faces turned downwards,
while others, bound by their masses of hair with ropes, are dragged along in extreme agony.
Embodied beings, pierced by sharp goads on their foreheads, are dragged along;
some lie face up, wailing, while others are led along a path of glowing coals.
Their hind legs, arms, and shoulders are bound together, and they are tormented in their bellies.
Bound with chains and their hands pinned together,
they are cast here and there by means of a half-moon-shaped collar around their necks;
and having been tied by a leather rope to their penis and testicles, they are led away.
Others have their bellies split open and are dragged by means of heated chains;
others have their ears pierced and their chins split.
Some have their hands and feet cut off, while others have their ears, lips, and noses severed.
With their penises and testicles severed and their joints and limbs mangled and split apart,
being pierced here and there by spears and arrows,
they run about while being torn asunder, crying out in distress with no refuge.
Struck repeatedly with mallets and iron clubs,
and with various terrible whips possessing a radiance like blazing fire,
they are pierced by *bhindipāla* missiles, streaming with pus and blood.
Wounded by worms in their flesh, these men are led along helpless;
they beg for water while being tormented by hunger,
and they long for shade while suffering from the cold due to the fierce wind.
Thus do those men who are devoid of charity and turn their faces away from it depart;
however, those who have taken the provisions of charity set out for the abode of Yama with ease.
Having thus reached the city of Yama by that most arduous path, they then proceed.
Then, having been pointed out by the messengers, they are ushered into the presence of Yama.
There, Yama honors those who have performed virtuous deeds with a welcome,
the offering of a seat, water for the feet, and a respectful oblation, treating them with affection.
Blessed are you, O great-souled ones, who act for your own welfare,
since you have performed meritorious deeds for the sake of divine happiness.
Having ascended this celestial chariot, adorned with the enjoyments of divine women—
Go to the incomparable heaven, which is endowed with all objects of desire.
Having enjoyed great pleasures there until the exhaustion of your merit,
you shall again experience here whatever small amount of evil remains.
And those men, by the power of their merit, behold the King of Dharma with a gentle countenance, as if he were their own father;
whereas those who have committed evil deeds see him as terrifying.
Those whose vision was unpurified by sin and whose intellects regarding the self were perverted [beheld him] with a face made terrifying by fangs, eyes crooked with a frown,
hair standing erect, and a great beard with his upper and lower lips quivering.
Eighteen-armed and wrathful, resembling a mass of black collyrium,
with hands raised holding various weapons and threatening with the staff of Brahmā,
he is mounted upon a great buffalo, his eyes like a blazing fire.
Wearing red garlands and garments, as lofty as Mount Meru,
with a roar like the clouds at the dissolution of the world, he seemed to be drinking up the ocean,
swallowing the worlds, and vomiting forth fire.
And Death stood near him, with a radiance like the fire of cosmic destruction;
Time was like collyrium in hue, and the Terrible End was fearsome.
Also present were the fierce Mārī, Mahāmārī, and the most dreadful Kālarātri.
Various painful diseases, bringing fear in many forms, [appeared]—fierce beings bearing spears, tridents, and goads; holding nooses, discs, and swords;
wielding thunderbolts and staffs; and carrying small quivers and bows.
Innumerable, of great prowess, cruel, and with the luster of collyrium,
these terrifying messengers of Yama have their hands raised with all manner of weapons;
he was surrounded by this most formidable retinue.
The most sinful see Yama and the terrifying Citragupta, who are excessively reviling Yama, the benefactor of the virtuous;
and the lordly Citragupta, awakening them with words of dharma.
"O you of evil deeds, stealers of others' property,
arrogant in your beauty and prowess, violators of others' wives!
Whatever action is performed by oneself, that very same thing is experienced again by oneself."
"Why have you committed this evil deed for the sake of destroying yourselves?
Why do you now feel remorse while being tormented by your own actions?
Experience your own karma; there is no fault here belonging to anyone else."
And these guardians of the earth have arrived in my presence,
brought by their own terrible deeds— foolish and arrogant in their strength.
O kings of wicked conduct, you who bring destruction upon your subjects!

For the sake of a kingdom lasting but a short time, what evil deed was committed? O kings, now reap the fruit of that [deed] by which the subjects were oppressed through greed for sovereignty, or through delusion, force, or injustice.
The kingdom and the wife for whose sake you committed evil deeds—all that has been utterly abandoned; now you stand here alone.
Behold that power of yours by which the subjects were devastated!
"Being beaten by the messengers of Yama, what will it be like now?
Thus rebuked by Yama with many such words,
O King, they remain silent, grieving over their own deeds.
Having thus instructed the kings in the Dharma, the King of Dharma (Yama) spoke these words once more for the sake of purifying them from the mire of their sins:
"O Caṇḍa and Mahācaṇḍa, seize these kings!"
"Cleanse yourselves from sins gradually within the fires of hell!
Then, rising up swiftly, seize the kings by their feet,
whirl them with great speed, and having grasped them, hurl them upward."
With all their great strength, they violently strike the intensely heated stone surface with speed, as if with a thunderbolt against a massive tree;
then, shattered, it flows with streams of blood.
Then that embodied being becomes unconscious and motionless;
thereafter, touched by the vital wind, he gradually returns to life once more.
Then, for the sake of purifying his sins, he is cast into the ocean of hell.
There are exactly twenty-eight crores of hells beneath the earth,
situated at the end of the seventh layer in terrible darkness;
and a hundred hells, beginning with Raurava, are recorded.
The great circle of hells consists of forty [eight] divisions,
wherein sinful men are intensely cooked according to their respective deeds,
by various tortures until the exhaustion of their karma.
Just as metals are cast into fire until their impurities are exhausted,
so too are sinners purified in the fires of hell through the destruction of their sins; there,
men are firmly bound by very tight hands and heated chains.
They are suspended from the high branches of great trees by the servants of Yama;
then, cast into serpent-machines, they are swung back and forth by the servants.
Being swung with extreme velocity, they become unconscious for the distance of a yojana.
Then, while they remain suspended in the intermediate space, hundreds of loads of iron are bound to their feet by the mighty messengers of Yama;
by that great weight, those men are intensely tormented.
Reflecting upon their own deeds, they stand silent and overwhelmed;
those evildoers are struck on all sides by the terrible servants with fire-colored flames and thorny iron rods.
Then, having been mangled and their limbs shattered, they are smeared on all sides with blazing caustic, even more so than fire; and then,
their bodies are torn open again, starting from the head and proceeding in sequence through the limbs.
They are cooked like eggplants in cauldrons of boiling oil;
then they are cast into a well filled with excrement, and thereafter into a pool teeming with swarms of worms, which is full of fat,
skin, and pus.
They are devoured by sharp-witted worms and by crows with iron beaks;
they are also eaten by dogs, gadflies, fierce wolves, tigers, and even monkeys.
Furthermore, they are cooked like meat upon heaps of blazing coals.
Men who, by their own sinful deeds, have been impaled upon sharp spikes,
are likewise crushed like sesame seeds in the hell named Cakra, being trampled by the terrible fruits of their own actions as if they were masses of sesame.

Furthermore, the tongues of those who spoke falsehoods and pleasant words that were untrue are split in many ways upon iron frying pans and beds; they are repeatedly crushed many times over in cauldrons filled with boiling oil.
They are crushed at the feet with a pair of tongs that are intensely heated;
and the tongue of the double-tongued one who proclaims false scriptures,
having emerged to a span of half a krośa in width, is tormented by sharp plows.
Those cruel ones who revile their mother, father, or teacher—
their chests are filled with owls, and their mouths are attended by them;
thereafter, they are repeatedly [scorched] with blazing molten copper and caustic lye.
That mouth is excessively filled with boiling oil;
furthermore, having been violently filled from all sides,
the man who stole gold is struck by excrement and by worms.
He embraces the most fierce and blazing iron śālmali tree;
he is struck on the back again with sharp, massive mallets,
and with a powerful, jagged, and highly curved saw.
From head to foot, they are devoured by their own offspring through terrible deeds; they eat their own flesh and drink their own blood—
those fools by whom food and drink were neither given nor even approved.
Their heads crushed, they are squeezed like sugarcane;
in the terrible Asitalavana forest, they are cut into pieces.
With all their limbs pierced by needles, they are impaled upon glowing spikes.
Being oppressed and rendered helpless, they suffer and do not indeed die;
their flesh is torn from the body and their bones are shattered with mallets,
while their vision is swiftly dragged away by the exceedingly powerful messengers of Yama.
Cast down and breathless, they remain certainly in hell;
covered by sands as if by a mouth, they constantly gasp for breath with their sighs. Wailing in Raurava, they are tormented by various arrows.
In the vicinity of that hell, amidst the great torments of Mahāraurava,
they are driven into the feet, the mouth, the anus, the sides, the chest,
and the head with thick, sharp, and intensely heated iron spikes.
They are rolled back and forth upon sand that is intensely heated;
cast into a scorching mire of lac, they cry out loudly and at length.
In those very forms [of their victims], they mock the adulterers.
They are made to embrace tightly a blazing woman fashioned of iron,
and likewise a man blazing on all sides with his former form. Women of evil conduct embrace them closely and speak [these words].
"Why do you flee with such speed? There is no escape for you now.
Since you have transgressed against your husband, you must now suffer the consequences of that sin.
Thus, you shall be cast into an iron cauldron by those who perform the rites, little by little."
Then, by their own sins alone, men are cooked over a mild fire;
weeping, they are cast into mortars and upon grinding stones;
they are thrown into blind wells and bitten violently by bees.
With all their limbs torn apart by worms and shattered in hundreds of ways,
those sinners are thereafter cast into pits of extremely sharp alkaline liquid;
and in the Mahājvāla hell, they shriek aloud.
They run here and there, being scorched by its flames;
having brought their two shanks behind [the neck] and placed them upon the shoulders,
they are dragged through the middle of those two with great force by the back of the arms.
Having bound them all together very firmly with strong ropes,
the bees made of sharp iron, highly enraged,
torment those who were formerly proud and wrathful due to their transgressions.
For sinful men, it is rubbed upon them in hell like sandalwood paste;
it is a terrible torment that enters within the bodies of the young.
This is known as the "Bond of the Body" (piṇḍabandha) inflicted by Yama, consisting of agonies amidst great conflagrations.
With their limbs bound by ropes and smeared with mud,
they are roasted in fires of dry cow-dung and yet do not die;
they are also cast upon pebbles and rocks and scorched by water as caustic as sharp alkali.
Until their sins are exhausted, the wicked are rubbed down like sandalwood;
men are intensely devoured by numerous worms with sharp mouths that have entered within their bodies until the destruction of the physical frame.
Cast into heaps of worms and piles of putrid flesh,
they remain with agitated hearts, crushed between two mountains;
their bodies are smeared with a coating of intensely heated vajra.
With their faces downward and their feet upward, they are held and tormented in fires;
they eat a mass of highly heated iron placed within their mouths,
while, rendered subject to another's will, they are beaten with mallets.
Those most sinful men who assault temples of Śiva, gardens, ponds, wells, monasteries, and courtyards, and those who dwell therein,
[are reborn as] those who [subsist on] physical exertion, ointments, massages, baths, drinking parties, and meals.
Those who practice sport, sexual intercourse, gambling,
and revelry are cooked in the fires of hell along with various terrible torments, such as being crushed in sugarcane presses, for as long as the moon and stars endure.
The ears of those who listen to the censure of their guru are filled with iron spikes the color of fire, with molten copper and other metals, as well as with tin,
lead, brass, and the like, and furthermore with caustic lye and lac.
Gradually the ears are filled, and in the hells these tortures occur in succession throughout all of them on every side;
likewise, through sin, the tortures of all the sense organs occur in due order.
Terrible torments arise individually within the body as a result of that [act]:
those fools who, out of greed for touch, violate another’s wife,
have their skin intensely filled with needles glowing like fire.
Then their bodies are smeared with all kinds of caustic substances and the like,
and they suffer great agony in all the hells—
those men who cast a frown upon their guru or look at him with a cruel eye.
Those who, being greedy, look upon the wives of others with a lustful eye,
have their eyes filled with needles glowing like fire;
and they undergo all manner of torments throughout their bodies, beginning with caustic substances and so forth, in succession.
Those who eat without first offering food to the gods, the sacred fire, their gurus, and the brahmins,
have their tongues and mouths filled with hundreds of glowing iron spikes;
thereafter, they are successively filled with caustic lye, blazing oil, copper, and other such substances.
And upon their bodies there shall be most terrible and varied torments of hell for those of deluded minds who,
out of greed, take the flowers from the groves of Śiva with their hands, smell them, or wear them upon their heads.
Their heads are filled with intensely heated iron spikes,
and their noses are repeatedly pierced many times with caustic substances and the like—
those who revile the Great-Souled One, the Teacher and instructor of Dharma.
And for those fools who [speak ill] of the devotees of Śiva and the eternal Śiva-dharma,
[the Lord shall plant His foot] upon their chest, throat, tongue, the junctions of their teeth,
the palate, the hollow of the mouth, the nose, the head, and the joints of all their limbs.
Red-hot iron spikes, glowing like fire and possessing three points,
are driven deep into these various spots many times over with mallets;
thereafter, they are further treated with caustic lye, molten copper, and tin.
They are filled on all sides with everything from boiling oil to other substances;
furthermore, they are repeatedly burned by blazing alkaline copper and the like.
In all the hells, their bodies undergo various forms of torment.
Many painful afflictions arise from the hands and feet of those wicked people who,
somewhere within the precincts of a temple of Śiva or in a grove sacred to Śiva,
discharge excrement or urine.
Their genitals, along with the testicles, are crushed with iron hammers;
then they are filled again with needles glowing like fire,
and a massive iron staff, likewise blazing like fire and covered in thorns, is thrust [into them].
Their anus is excavated until it emerges from their head;
thereafter, the anus and the penis of those embodied beings are intensely filled with molten copper and tin, along with a great caustic substance.
Since the mind is said to be the activator of all the senses,
therefore, through the suffering of the senses, it becomes intensely distressed.
Those who, despite possessing wealth, do not bestow gifts due to craving—
Those men who, while in the householder stage of life, treat a guest who has arrived at the proper time with contempt,
are bound at the iron archway; with their hands and feet beaten and their limbs torn asunder, they remain there for a hundred years, wasting away.
Their hands, feet, and foreheads were pinned with iron spikes;
their mouths were constantly covered and pierced by two stakes.
They were tormented by worms, fierce creatures, iron rods, and crows.
Then, they are tormented by various kinds of calamities and by serpents with gaping mouths;
moreover, being bound by chains at the roots of their tongues,
they remain suspended, oppressed by loads of iron.
Furthermore, when his testicles were moistened and bound, two loads of iron remained suspended from them,
weighing four times as much as the load itself;
then, having cut off his own flesh in pieces the size of sesame seeds, he offered it.
Food is given to them, mixed with blood, on the tip of a needle; and when, after a long time, they have once again become fleshless,
their bodies are then smeared with blazing caustic alkali.
They are drenched by showers of rain and then dried by the wind;
they are drenched on all sides with boiling oil that has been heated intensely. Afterwards, they are again slowly scorched by fire situated at a distance.
Furthermore, they are tormented in succession by every kind of torture:
by intense hunger, by fainting, by extreme thirst,
by excessive heat, by extreme cold, and by the slaughter of the sinful.
Thus, those who commit evil deeds undergo such extremely terrible torments in each and every hell by the hundreds and thousands; indeed,
in all the hells, the various torments are manifold for each individual.
Alas! Even for a hundred years, it is difficult for all those in hell to endure [their suffering];
and these various evildoers, the most sinful performers of wicked deeds, though driven by diverse and terrible karmas, do not die at all.
Known as Mahāghorā and Abhighorā, they are comparable to the fire of cosmic destruction;
upon hearing these most terrible names, those of weak minds die.
Therefore, the sinners mentioned here go there of their own accord.
When merit has been performed for the sake of sons, friends, and wife,
one is burned by it alone and does not see them;
likewise, the evil deed committed by oneself must certainly be experienced by oneself.
"O fool, why have you committed this sin for the sake of harming another? Thus rebuked by the messengers, they then ask again:
"For how long a time, and on account of what sin, does a man remain here?"
Through the destruction of the property of the gods and through acts such as treachery toward one's guru,
all who are sinful are cooked in all the hells until the great dissolution;
and even those who have committed the most heinous crimes (mahāpātakins) [suffer] here in all the hells.
Until the moon and stars cease to exist, those who have committed great sins and others are tormented by various forms of slaughter in tens of millions of ocean-like hells;
they are cooked for half a *kalpa* amidst diverse tortures in the fourteen [worlds].
Men who have committed minor offenses (upapātakin) go there for half that duration,
and those with remaining sins for half of that time as well.
Therefore, one should not commit sin while life remains so fickle.

For by their own evil deeds, men certainly go to the hells; the soul of that man who commits sin is surely displeased with him. The fruit of sin in this world is suffering, and that must be experienced here by the self itself.
How do those men, devoted to evil, lie down during the nights—
those for whom there is the intense torment of hell, separated from them only by death?
Thus are they both afflicted and purified by their remaining karma.

Then, having reached the earth, embodied beings are born again as various kinds of immobile things, distinguished by the differences of grasses, shrubs, and so forth. Having experienced miseries there, they are born among the species of insects.
Having emerged from insect wombs, they are then born as birds;
remaining closely attached to the state of birds, they become [beings] among deer and the like.
Having transcended that path of suffering, they are born into the wombs of animals.
Gradually reaching the womb of a cow, human beings are born again;
thus, having passed through all wombs in succession,
they eventually attain the exceedingly rare human state by the power of time.
Human birth is attained even by skipping over other stages through the sphere of merit;

for the destinies are said to be diverse according to the gravity or lightness of karmas. He who, having reached human birth—which is the means for accomplishing heaven and liberation— [should not neglect it].
He who fails to accomplish the welfare of both [gods and men] suffers for a long time after death.
Human birth is extremely difficult to attain for all the gods and asuras;
having attained it, one should engage in [meaningful] discourse so that one does not go to hell.
If one is not resolute in striving for the attainment of heaven and liberation,
one should protect with effort that human birth which is the root of heaven.
Having obtained this human state, which accomplishes all goals through the root of dharma, [one should strive for the highest].
If you have no concern for gain, then protect your root with diligence.
Having attained this extremely rare human birth and the status of a Brahmin,
who else is more senseless than he who does not work for his own ultimate welfare?
Of all regions, Madhyadeśa is remembered as the most excellent;
from here, men attain heaven, liberation, and fame.
Having obtained this transient human birth in this meritorious land of Bhārata, [one should strive for the highest goal].
He who performs what is for his own welfare has himself protected;
he who does not perform what is for his own welfare has himself deceived.
Heaven is considered the land of enjoyment, while this world is regarded as the land of action.
Whatever action is performed here is experienced in heaven.
Practice dharma while the body is healthy;
for when one is unwell, even with great effort, one will not have the desire to do anything at all.

For he who seeks to accomplish the impermanent by means of an impermanent body has surely lost what was permanent, and his impermanent gains are utterly destroyed. Pieces of your life-force fall before you like fragments of a crumbling wall.
Why do you not understand by means of the instruction regarding day and night?
Since it is not known when or for whom death will occur,
who could find any stability when death is so sudden?
When you must inevitably depart alone, having abandoned everything,
why do you not give this wealth for the sake of provisions for the journey?
Those who take the provisions of charity travel the great path with ease.

Otherwise, a living being suffers on the path like one devoid of provisions for the journey. But for those whose vessel, carried by the best of the twice-born, proceeds full of its contents toward the city of the heavenly realm, there is gain at every step.
Knowing this, a person should perform meritorious deeds and avoid sin;
through merit one attains divinity, while from demerit one goes to hell. Those who have sought refuge even slightly with Śiva, the Lord of Gods, [attain liberation].
Those men do not behold the terrible mouth of Yama; however,
due to their most horrific sins, they remain as kings of the pretas for a certain period by the command of Śiva, and thereafter they go to the abode of Śiva.
Furthermore, those who have practiced with their whole being toward Maheśvara are not smeared by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
Therefore, a wise person should constantly increase their devotion to the Lord.

O Pārtha, through reflection on its majesty and through detachment from the defects of worldly existence, these five sins— which truly bestow suffering for a very long time in the world of the ancestors—
along with other terrors that endure for a long duration, are indeed beyond description, even though they are perfectly clear.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Results of Auspicious and Inauspicious Actions," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira;
followed by the description of the greatness of the Śakaṭa-vrata. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
This profound ocean of hell which has been described to you is easily crossed by means of the boat of vows, fasts, and restraints;
for having attained this human birth, so difficult to find and as fleeting as a flash of lightning, one must strive.
