In this manner, one should compose oneself so that one does not fall away again;
for that embodied being who possesses fame here in this world consisting of charity and vows,
he is recognized even in the next world as one who increases his kin.

"A man who is devoid of vows and Vedic study gains no renown here or in the hereafter, O tiger among men; therefore, one should be devoted to vows. In this regard, I shall relate to you an ancient history."
Indeed, there was a conversation with a Siddha concerning a Brahmin in Avanti.
A certain Siddha, fully perfected through the attainment of yogic power, wandered the earth having assumed a deformed and most terrifying body.
With his teeth swallowed, protruding lips, tawny eyes, and thin hair;
with one ear torn off, a foul complexion, tattered clothes, and a massive belly;
with flattened eyes, cracked shanks and calves, and emaciated elbows.
Delighted, he looked in all directions and wandered about like one whose mind was bewildered.
He was seen and questioned by the Brahmin Mūlajālika: "Who are you?
When did you arrive from heaven? For what purpose have you come? Tell me."

"Have you seen Rambhā, who illuminates the quarters of the sky, who infatuates the minds of the gods, and who is the singular beauty among them? Having gone there, she must be addressed in my name as follows: 'She is beyond description by those who perceive her faults.'"
The best of brahmins from Āvantī asked after your welfare;
that accomplished and renowned sage, filled with wonder, said this to him:
"How was I clearly recognized by you as having returned from heaven?"
Then the Brahmin said to him: "I have recognized you as you truly are;
therefore, I shall explain it to you—listen, for the flood of your sins has been exhausted.
Your three bodies would be deformed, or perhaps one of them would remain in its natural state."
Having seen your deformity in every limb, you were then recognized by me:
"The nature of things is truly difficult to overcome; it must manifest itself through direct experience.
A change in one's nature is perceived by people in every way."
Having heard these words of the Brahmin, he gradually vanished from sight. After some days and nights, he returned to that city.
Questioned by the Brahmin Mūlajālakā, he spoke of Amarāvatī.
Having gone there, I questioned Rambhā, who causes alluring confusion,
as she was returning to her own home after the occasion for Śakra had concluded. I delivered your message to her, and she said, "I do not know him."
"By means of knowledge, a portion [of merit], human effort, religious vows, or austerity, a mortal man is known for a long time in heaven.
Then the Brahmin said to her: "Foolish woman! You have been burnt by the fire!"

"I do not eat a cart because of this vow; he knows me by this. Having heard these words of his, that Siddha of perfectly pure intellect laughed, took leave of that Brahmin, and vanished once more from sight.
And once, while she was sporting with him, she happened by chance to see Rambhā on the path to heaven;
having seen her, she reported everything exactly as it had been told by the twice-born one. Rambhā said:
Who does not know that brahmin who observes the Śakaṭa vow,
who subsists on roots and creepers, and who dwells in the Mahākāla forest?
[He is known] by sight, by conversation, by his acts of assistance, and by sharing a seat.
A fourfold attachment arises excessively in men;
yet for me, there has never been a sight or a conversation with him.
Even by the mere hearing of his name, a great affection is manifested.

Having spoken thus, the elephant-gaited Rambhā, her thighs like plantain stalks and her eyes wide with wonder, went into the presence of the Slayer of Jambha (Indra). Having arrived, she reported his conduct characterized by affection and religious observance.
With her heart obstructed by the presence of the wise Brahmin before her,
Śakra spoke to the lady of beautiful limbs, who was so pleasing to the hearts of the gods:
"Shall I bring that Brahmin of excellent vows into your presence?"
Having placed him upon an excellent celestial chariot, adorned with divine garlands and garments, and anointed with divine unguents, he showed him [the world] once more.
Remaining there, that twice-born man enjoyed himself together with Rambhā, the mistress of pleasures.
Thus has this greatness of the Śakaṭavrata been declared by me to you.

One attains royal splendor in this world, to be enjoyed by all people, as well as residence in the abodes of Indra, Śiva, and Keśava. There is nothing in the universe unattainable for those of firm vows; therefore, a man should always be devoted to the observance of vows.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Narration of the Greatness of the Śakaṭavrata," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[Now follows] the Description of the Tilakavrata.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Madhusūdana, the vows of Brahmā, Īśa, Keśava, and others, as well as those of Gaurī, Gaṇapati, Durgā, Sūrya, Agni,
and Soma, which are seen in other scriptures and have entered your intellect—
O God, O delighter of the gods, tell me all of those;
for whichever lunar day (tithi) is ordained by the sequence of its progression, proclaim in their entirety what ritual duty must be performed for that particular deity on that day.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: In the spring, on the first day of the bright fortnight, which is as beautiful as the Kiṃśuka and Aśoka trees, one who is intent upon his observances should perform a ritual bath.
O Indra among kings, whether a woman or a man, having gratified the ancestors and the gods on the bank of a river,
by a lake, or in their own home, being self-restrained,
should carve the figure of a person out of *piṣṭātaka* for a year.
Then, one should worship with sandalwood powder, flowers, incense, and so forth;
one should also perform worship for a year with lamps and food offerings (naivedya).
Afterwards, one should worship using the names of the months and seasons, joined at the end with the word "namas" (salutation).
The wise man should honor the Brāhmaṇas with auspicious mantras declared in the Vedas:

"Thou art the Saṃvatsara, thou art the Parivatsara, thou art the Iḍāvatsara, thou art the Abhivatsara; may thy dawns prosper, may thy days and nights prosper, may thy half-months prosper, may thy months prosper, may thy seasons prosper, may thy year prosper.
Having thus worshipped them with garments, he should thereafter wrap him [the image] around with them.
With seasonal roots, fruits, and sacrificial offerings such as sweetmeats (modaka) and the like,
one should thereafter stand before him with palms joined in reverence and pray:
"O Blessed One, by your grace, may this year be auspicious for me."
Having spoken thus, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brahmin according to one's ability;
then, one should apply a mark (tilaka) made of sandalwood paste upon the surface of the forehead. From that time forward, day after day, one’s face should be adorned with such a mark.
It should be maintained for as long as a year, like the sky by the moon;
in this way, whether a man or a woman, one should observe this vow.
O tiger among men, such a person always enjoys pleasures upon this earth.
Bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and the irresistible seizing spirits (grahas) who act as enemies—
all these become useless the very moment they behold that tilaka.
Formerly, there was a victorious king named Śatruñjaya.
Her wife was named Citralekhā, adorned with virtuous conduct.
In the month of Caitra, she undertook this vow in the presence of a brahmin;
having worshipped for a year while holding Janārdana in her heart, she completed it.
One who approaches with malice or a desire to revile her goes before her,
while one who does her a kindness passes by with his face cast down upon seeing her countenance;
she is the remover of the pride of rival wives and has brought the surface of the earth under her control.
She lived happily and without anxiety, beloved by her husband and full of joy;
meanwhile, her husband was overcome by his hand (elephant), and their son,
suffering with a headache, met his end, bringing grief to his friends.
At that very moment, O great king, the servants of Dharmarāja, who strip away all beings of their merit,
arrived at his gate, seeking to enter the palace immediately.
Led by Kālamṛtyu, they had come to bring Śatruñjaya;
however, upon seeing Citralekhā standing nearby, her face adorned with a tilaka,
their resolve vanished and they turned back and departed once more.
When they had departed, O Bhārata, that king, free from disease, enjoyed with his son the auspicious pleasures acquired by his previous actions.
This vow of great prosperity has thus been described to you, O highly fortunate one.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, this was previously recounted to me by Śaṅkara:
"This supreme vow, which is the ornament for the forehead of the tilaka of the three worlds and the remover of all suffering, has been described to you.
That mortal who performs it in this manner, having lived happily, goes to the abode of the Lotus-born [Brahmā] even in times of calamity."

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Tilaka Vow," in the Uttara Parva of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira; followed by the description of the Aśoka Vow. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
On the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja, at the break of dawn,
one should worship the Aśoka tree with its burgeoning, auspicious sprouts,
using sprouted seeds of the seven grains, along with fragrant and auspicious sweetmeats.
O sinless one, on that day one should likewise worship the Aśoka tree with divine fruits produced in season, such as coconuts and pomegranates, as well as with flowers, incense, and other offerings;
O best of the Pāṇḍavas, he shall never encounter sorrow anywhere.
"O Aśoka, you who pacify grief, be the quencher of sorrow for our fathers, brothers, husband, mother-in-law, and father-in-law, and likewise throughout our entire family.
Having uttered this, one should then offer the *arghya* water with faith.
Having adorned her with banners and covered her with auspicious garments,
Damayantī shall become as beloved to her husband as Svāhā and the virtuous Vedavatī, by virtue of this Aśoka vow.
While walking in the forest, Sītā demonstrated the true dharma;
O Pārtha, seeing an Aśoka tree in the woods with its canopy adorned with young shoots,
she placed her husband and brother-in-law nearby and honored them with sesame seeds and unbroken grains of rice.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, having worshipped that red Aśoka tree with offerings of lamps, ornaments, food, incense, garlands, and fruits,
he made his request with palms joined in reverence before Maithilī, while Rāghava listened.
"May my aged father-in-law, the lord of Kosala, live long;
may my husband and my brothers-in-law, Bharata and the others, also live;
and may I behold Kausalyā still living," thought Maithilī.
The illustrious lady, having circumambulated that tree whose prayers are always fulfilled, made her request to it; then they departed once more.
Likewise, any other woman on earth who should worship that mountain [shall obtain her desires].
O son of Kuntī, having propitiated the tree with sesame, rice, barley, wheat, and mustard seeds mixed together, and having bowed to the root of that tree with red sprouts,
a devoted wife should worship it with this mantra.
"O great tree, O great-branched one, abode of the dolphin-bannered god! I entreat you, O illustrious ornament of the forest and its groves!
Having thus addressed that tree and having given the sacrificial fee to the Brahmin, [he departed].
Accompanied by her friends, that virtuous woman should then return to her own home.
Those young women who worship the Ashoka tree— the destroyer of grief— with flowers, unbroken grains, incense, and lamps,
shall attain incomparable happiness born of a husband on this earth and, being filled with joy, shall again reach the state of Gauri.

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Aśoka Vow," in the Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, in the Uttaraparvan, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira. Now follows the description of the Karavīra vow.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
On the first day of the bright fortnight in the month of Jyeṣṭha, at the break of dawn,
one should worship a charming Karavīra flower born in a divine garden,
clothed in red thread and adorned with perfumes, incense, and ointments.
Having sprinkled [the area] with water containing unbroken rice and grains, along with sprouted seven types of grain, oranges,
citrons, divine guṇakas, ghaṭakas, and beautiful coconuts,
one should ask for forgiveness with this mantra.
O Karavīra, abode of poison, salutations to you, the beloved of the Sun! O excellent jewel that adorns the crown, salutations to you, the lord of the hair!
Moving with the dark dust, establishing both the immortal and the mortal...
The god Savitṛ comes on his golden chariot, beholding all beings.
Having thus worshipped with devotion and given a sacrificial fee to a Brahmin,
and having performed a circumambulation, one should then go to one's own home.
O highly fortunate one, this vow was undertaken out of a desire to propitiate the Sun by Anasūyā, Kṣamā, Sāvitrī, Satyabhāmā,
Damayantī, Sarasvatī, Gāyatrī, and likewise by Gaṅgā.
O Pārtha, this Karavīra vow, which bestows the fruit of all happiness, has been performed by other women as well in the world of mortals.
Having worshipped the Karavīra tree, whose every branch is adorned with jewel-like flowers and whose body is covered with dark green leaves;

"Having enjoyed on earth all desirable pleasures according to his heart's desire, O best of the Bharatas, he finally goes to the abode of the Sun. Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Karavīra Vow," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira. [Now follows] the description of the Kokilā Vow.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O best of gods, tell me of that vow for noble women so that they may possess great affection for their husbands.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Formerly, on the bank of the Yamunā, there stood the auspicious city of Mathurā. In that city, there was a king named Śatrughna, established by Rāma.
His wife was Kīrtimālā, who was renowned throughout the world.
Having prostrated before the Blessed One, Vasiṣṭha, the bull among sages, she asked:
"O best of sages, how is happiness produced?
Tell me of the supreme vow connected with sesame seeds."
Thus addressed by Kīrtimālā, the wise and self-controlled Vasiṣṭha meditated for a moment and then proclaimed the supreme Kokilā-vrata.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
When the time of twilight has arrived on the full moon day of Āṣāḍha, she should form this resolve: "Beginning tomorrow, for one month during the month of Śrāvaṇa,
remaining self-controlled and established in celibacy, I shall perform my ritual bath."
"I shall eat only at night, sleep upon the ground, and practice compassion toward all living beings.
Having thus made this resolve, whether a man or a woman, and having obtained permission from a Brāhmaṇa, one should then, at dawn, be equipped with all the necessary materials.
O Pārtha, on the first day of the lunar fortnight, a person observing the vow should first clean his teeth and then go to a river,
a pond, a lake,
or a mountain torrent to perform his bath with fragrant *āmalaka* fruits and sesame seeds.
Then, for eight days thereafter, one should again grind all the medicinal herbs individually,
and furthermore, having ground eight parts of *vaca*, one should massage the hair.
Then, having bathed, meditated upon the Sun, and paid homage to the ancestors;
Having gratified the cuckoo in her bird-form with sesame flour,
one should worship the sweet-voiced goddess with auspicious flowers born of the *caṃpaka*,
or with its leaves, incense, food offerings, lamps, red lac, and sandalwood.
Having worshipped with sesame seeds, rice grains, and tips of dūrvā grass, one should ask for forgiveness daily, O Pāṇḍava, as a devotee observing the sesame vow, with this mantra:
"O you who are accompanied by sesame, O you who are the bliss of sesame, O you who have the color of sesame, O you who are fond of sesame!"
"O Kokila, grant me good fortune, wealth, and sons; salutations to you!
Having uttered this, O Pārtha, he should thereafter enter his home with self-restraint, take his meal, and sleep until the month has come to an end.
At the end of the month, one should present to a Brāhmaṇa a cuckoo made of sesame paste in a copper vessel, with eyes of jewels and wings of gold; this may be offered on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa,
accompanied by garments, wealth, and molasses, or alternatively, as earrings.

Or she may give it to her mother-in-law, her father-in-law, or their kin, or to an astrologer, a domestic priest, or Vyāsa; by those observing the vow who desire auspiciousness, it should be bestowed in this manner.
Thus, the woman who performs the Kokilā-vrata with devotion—
For seven births, she attains extensive good fortune on this earth,
having obtained a noble husband who is free from rivals and full of affection;
then, upon death, she goes to the city of Gaurī by means of a celestial chariot radiant as the sun.
This vow was formerly proclaimed by the sage Vasiṣṭha;
and it was likewise performed in its entirety, O Pārtha, by Kīrtimālā.
And for her, everything here was accomplished through the word of Vasiṣṭha.
O son of Kuntī,
whatever woman shall likewise perform the Kokilā-vrata with devotion, she will certainly attain good fortune, honor, and the destruction of her enemies, born of divine grace.
Those who offer to the twice-born a cuckoo— sweet-voiced, with a melodious throat, and made of sesame flour mixed with clarified butter—
shall roam at will in the Nandana and other celestial groves, and upon returning to the mortal world, they become possessors of sweet speech.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Cuckoo Vow," in the Uttara Parva of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the Vow of Great Penance.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Now I shall describe the unsurpassed Bṛhad-vrata, which removes all sins.
Listen to the rite by which [this] is difficult even for gods, demons, and sages to attain:
at the end of the month of Āśvayuja, on the full-moon day,
one of purified soul should eat milk-rice mixed with ghee at night, or boiled rice accompanied by sugarcane juice.
Having sipped water and become pure, and having used a tooth-stick made of *bilva* wood,
one should bow to Mahādeva and utter this:
"I desire to perform this eternal vow of the gods."
"O Mahādeva, act so that this may be accomplished according to your command.
Having made this resolve, for sixteen years he followed the sequence of lunar days (tithis),
beginning with the first day (pratipad), thinking, "I shall observe them in due order."
Then, on the first day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa,
having asked his preceptor for permission to fast and repeatedly remembering Mahādeva,
he bathed, worshipped the deity, and lit lamps at night.

Having bowed to Yamunā and Mahādeva, one should subsequently invite Brahmins devoted to Mahādeva who observe vows along with their wives— either sixteen, eight, four, or even one, according to one's capacity. Having invited them and returned to one's own home, one should remain on the ground while remembering Mahādeva.
Having spread out clean garments and remaining without food, he should sleep at night.
Upon the rising of the sun, having bathed and taken up lamps,
one should go to the temple of Śiva with offerings, water for bathing, flowers, and incense.
Having massaged the Lord of Gods, one should dry him with astringent decoctions;
immediately thereafter, one should bathe him with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), then with milk,
and again with ghee, honey, curd, meat-broth, and milk.
Then, having bathed [the image] with sesame-water, one should bathe it with warm water.
Afterwards, one should smear it thickly with camphor, agallochum, and sandalwood.
Having worshipped with flowers, a golden lotus should be placed upon its head.
One should offer a pair of garments, a five-colored banner, a canopy,
incense, a lamp, and a bell to the deity according to one's capacity;
thereafter, having presented the food offering and offered praise, one should return to one's own abode.
Then, having kindled the fire well, one should worship Jātavedas;
likewise, one should feed those observing the vow as well as the preceptor and married couples,
and seek their forgiveness by giving gifts of gold, clothing, and other items according to one's ability.
Having thus dismissed all those people along with his own kinsmen,
and having himself partaken of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), he should joyfully eat while remaining silent.
Having performed the ritual in this very manner, one who is poor may become wealthy.
According to one's financial capacity, this should be performed every month in its entirety; however,
one who lacks wealth may perform all of this repeatedly through the ritual of flower worship with faith.
Having thus observed the fast every month until the end of the month of Kārttika,

O Pārtha, one should clearly perform the concluding rite (pārayaṇa) with the oblation according to the prescribed procedure for the commencement. Then, on the fifteenth day of the second [fortnight], the lord of men should observe the night-meal (nakta).

If that [first] lunar day falls on the second tithi, the wise man should observe the fast on it; from then on for the duration of the year, he should observe the second tithi when it is bright (śukla),
and likewise complete the vow on the second tithi according to the rules for the commencement.
Having performed two fasts, one should then begin the third;
by this sequential method, it continues until the year is completed.
Having done so for sixteen years, one should be prepared on the full moon day.
Having worshipped the deity as before, and having gratified the sacrificial fire,
one should indeed give a cow with golden horns, silver hooves, bells,
and a bronze milking vessel to a twice-born man who has been initiated for Mahādeva.
The observer of the vow should, according to his capacity, honor sixteen pure Brahmins who are devoted to Śiva with gifts of clothing and ornaments;
he should also feed other Brahmins according to his means.
And one should give gifts according to one's desire to others who are afflicted by hunger;
this great vow of austerity indeed dries up the sins of those who have slain a Brahmin and other such evils,
and bestows abundant enjoyments upon men in the worlds of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and the rest.
Standing like a staircase to heaven for all four castes,
he who does not perform [this] upon obtaining wealth is robbed and deprived of his senses.
It is auspicious, bestows long life, is meritorious, and increases beauty and good fortune.

This ancient vow has been prescribed for both women and men; it should be observed by a widow as well, for the sake of further ensuring her non-widowhood, and it should be observed by a married woman too,
for the sake of avoiding separation from her husband.
Having observed the fast every month, O son of Pāṇḍu, one should eat together with Brāhmaṇas—
either one, two, three, or four, according to one's own capacity— at the end of each period, one should perform the concluding rite according to the procedure for the commencement, using gold.
Seeking the accumulation of merit, O Great King, one should pass [the time] until reaching the abode of Śiva; however, if by some chance a hindrance to the vow should arise through fate,
then other lunar days (tithis) equal in number to that [deficiency] must be observed as fasts for the sake of completion.
Now, O King of Kings, if someone is more swiftly intent on performing the vow, he should observe two lunar days according to this procedure:
at the end and at the beginning of the years, following the rules for the commencement.
Now, O Yudhiṣṭhira, if someone should die while the vow has been commenced but before it is completed,
he too obtains its fruit by the power of the truthful commencement;
this applies to both the reciters and the listeners of this vow.
Through the power of meditation upon Śiva, they become embraced by sons.
Those who, devoted to their own duty, perform this meritorious and great penance— the vow— with reverence for sixteen years,
pierce the impenetrable, inconceivable, and primordial solar orb and go to the base of the feet of the Moon-crested Lord.

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of the Vṛhattapas Vow," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira. [Now follows] the description of the Bhadra-upavāsa vow.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Lord of Gods, it is my conviction that the state of remembering past births is difficult to attain. Therefore, I wish to know by what action it is obtained—
whether through the granting of boons by the gods, or by the service of the sages?
"O Lord, [is it attained] by bathing at sacred fords (tīrtha), or by austerity, fire-offerings, and vows?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O King, four auspicious days should be observed with diligent effort."
O King, by the power of that [vow], a man will certainly become a rememberer of his past births.
Formerly, on the bank of the Yamunā, there was a Vaiśya named Śubhodaya;
he performed this vow, and in due course of time, he died.
A son was born to Sañjaya, renowned as Svarṇaṣṭhīvī;
through the power of his vows, he knew his past births, yet he was struck down by thieves.
By the power of Nārada, however, he was restored to life once more.
He remembered his entire previous history according to the rules of his vow.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"How did Sañjaya have a son, and how did he come to be named Svarṇaṣṭhīvī?"
"How was he led to death by the Dasyus, and how indeed did he return to life?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O lord of men, there was a king named Sañjaya in Kuśāvatī."
The celestial sage Nārada and Parvata were always his friends;
once, they arrived at Sañjaya’s house by chance,
and he honored them with hospitable rites such as offering them seats and other courtesies.
Then, while they were seated and discussing their previous history,
the youthful daughter of Sañjaya arrived in the presence of her father.
Parvata said to the king, "This maiden is of excellent complexion."
Her ankles were concealed, her thighs were firm, and her hips and breasts were full;
her eyes, nails, and palms had the luster of lotus petals and lotus filaments;
and she possessed hair that was curled, soft, glossy, unthinned, and dense.
Her gait is playful like that of an elephant, her nose is well-formed, and her voice is like that of a cuckoo.
Oh, what beauty! Oh, what fortitude! Oh, what supreme loveliness!
Her nose is as prominent as a blooming sesame flower; her form is truly remarkable.
"Whose daughter is this auspicious Bhadrā, who so deeply captivates my heart?
To the Brahmin speaking thus, his eyes wide with wonder,
the king said, "O Parvata, this maiden is my own daughter."
Then the wise Nārada, his senses agitated, said to the king:
"O King, I desire to marry; let this maiden be given to me.
I shall grant you a boon desired by you, one that is difficult for mortals to obtain."
Thus addressed by Nārada, Sañjaya, his soul filled with joy,
spoke these words with palms joined in reverence, his eyes wide with delight:
"Let my son be given to me quickly— he whose gold-mine is inexhaustible."
"Whatever urine, feces, or phlegm he casts upon the ground,
let all that indeed become stable gold.
"So be it," O King, Nārada replied to him.
"O you of noble vows, I give to you a son who spits gold.
Having spoken thus, Nārada, his mind filled with joy, married that slender-waisted maiden, who was adorned with ornaments, to him.
Seeing that deed of his, Parvata was overcome with anger;
with eyes blazing and lips quivering, he spoke to Nārada out of rage:
"Since she was previously sought by me, yet has been married by you..."
Therefore, you shall by no means go to heaven with me.
O Nārada, that son who was granted to him by you through the granting of a boon will also be struck down by thieves and meet his death.
Thus addressed by Parvata, Nārada spoke with a troubled mind:
"O you of evil intent, you do not understand dharma at all; you are a fool.
O observer of vows, a maiden belongs in common to all living beings."
The learned do not see any fault in obstructing her in this world;
you have not served the elders, and for that reason you curse me in anger.
The completion of the marriage mantras occurs at the seventh step.
"Since you curse me, who am innocent, without understanding this,
therefore, alas, you too shall not go to heaven without me.
If Sañjaya’s son should meet his death because of this curse,"
"Nevertheless, I shall bring him back from the realm of Yama; of this there is no doubt.
Having thus cursed one another, those two celestial sages, having been honored by Sañjaya, then departed for their own hermitages.
Then, in his seventh month, a son was born to that king;
the father gave him the name Svarṇaṣṭhīvī, which was truly appropriate for him,
as he remembered his former births, possessed a body like that of the god of love, and was the cause of the production of gold.
Through the fruit of his auspicious vows, he became one who understands the cries of all beings here; furthermore,
by the grace of Nārada, whatever he cast upon the ground— be it urine, phlegm, excrement, or anything else— all turned into gold.
Surrounded by various Brahmins, that king performed sacrifices such as the Rājasūya according to the prescribed rites and with abundant sacrificial fees;
he constantly maintained his dependents and nourished his kinsmen and guests.
He constructed temples for the deities, as well as lakes and groves;
surrounded by guards, he likewise protected his son with affection.
From this son of the king, there arose heaps of gold.
Then, having heard of that gold mine,
certain Dasyus from the south— intoxicated with pride and greedy for wealth— attacked it.
When that [king] was destroyed, everything arising from the boon of the gods was lost.
Not seeing that gold, they perished one after another.
Seeing his son struck down by bandits, the king was deeply distressed;
with a distracted mind, he lamented, fainted, and fell to the ground.
Seeing him lamenting, Nārada said to Sañjaya:
"O King, do not despair; listen to these words of mine.
Having spoken thus, he related the deeds of those of great splendor.
Having heard of the deeds of those distinguished lords of men, of ascetics who bestow sacrificial fees, and of other high-souled kings,
that king was suddenly freed from his grief and returned to his natural state.
Nārada also swiftly brought the dead son of the king from the abode of Yama, exactly as he had been slain.
Seeing and touching that son, the king’s heart was filled with supreme satisfaction.
Ashamed and amazed, with palms joined in reverence, he then said:
"O Nārada, what a marvel! By you, who are so gracious, such a son was given to me—one who has been slain by bandits."

At the end of six months, he indeed remembered his entire former life and all past events resulting from the breaking of his fasts during auspicious occasions. All this has been narrated to you, which causes the recollection of one's previous births.
What other vow superior to this vow, most excellent, shall I tell you?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"Both Brāhmaṇas and Śūdras [attain] birth in a great family."
One may be a donor, patient, wealthy, eloquent, and handsome—endowed with these auspicious qualities.
O King, these four blessings each have four constituent parts;
they are beset by many obstacles and are difficult to attain for those who have not disciplined themselves.

O King of kings, the first [observance] is in Mārgaśīrṣa, the second likewise in Phālguna, the third in Jyeṣṭha, and the last is renowned for Bhādrapada. O lord of men, one should perform it for three months beginning from the start of the bright fortnight of Phālguna.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, that which is known as Tripuṣpa is the supreme practice of austerity; performed for three months at the beginning of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha,
it is renowned as Trirāma, bestowing truth and valor.
O son of Pāṇḍu, for three months beginning with the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada,
it is known as Triraṅga, which bestows manifold knowledge. And for three months beginning with the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, O lord of men—
That is called the station of Viṣṇu, the bestower of all dharmas.
These auspicious acts have been described in brief, O Bhārata;
they should be performed by men, women, or those authorized by a Brahmin.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O God of gods, Lord of the universe, tell me in detail about the foundation of auspicious observances as well as the primary observances.
The Blessed One said: Listen attentively, O King, to the supreme expansion of auspicious things,
which I shall relate to you— never before told by me to anyone.
In the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, at the beginning, four lunar days are excellent:
the second, the third, the fourth, and likewise the fifth.
On the first day (pratipad), one who has conquered the senses should remain seated, eating but once a day.
On the morning of the second day, having performed what was to be done,
when more than three *praharas* have passed, the wise man should perform his bath,
taking up earth and cow-dung while reciting these mantras.
I shall, however, impart to you the supreme procedure for the mantras;
listen as I tell you who they are to whom they should be given and to whom they should not be given—
those Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who are pure and stainless.

The mantras should indeed be given to them, but not to those of mixed character. A woman who, though separated from her husband, remains endowed with virtuous conduct and auspicious, may receive the mantras along with her husband by his permission.

Bathing in a river, a pond, a large tank, a well, or even at home, the fruit is known to increase tenfold; indeed, it is greater when performed with mantras. Having taken earth with a mantra, one should smear it over all the limbs.
"O soft earth, you who are saluted by the gods along with the Daityas who have slain their enemies—even by me you are saluted with devotion; therefore, make me pure. This is the mantra for the clay.
Having thus recited the mantra while applying clay with the tips of his own hands without uttering mantras,
the knower of Dharma, having drawn the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), should immerse himself in water;
[and he should scatter] white mustard seeds, black sesame, vacā, and all medicinal herbs in sequence.
O you who consist of the universe, you are the origin of all the gods and of all worlds;
salutations to the Lord of beings, of plants, and of the essences.
[I offer] the water born from the Gaṅgā and the ocean, as well as that from the Puṣkara and the Narmadā.
"May the presence of the Yamunā and the Sāṃnihitya be here with me.
This is the mantra for bathing.
Having first performed the touching of the body with clay, cow dung, and water, [one should proceed].
Having thus bathed, immersed himself, and sipped water, he stands upon the bank;
having put on two bright garments, pure and with a restrained mind,
he should offer libations to the gods, the ancestors, and human beings with great concentration.
Having thus undertaken the vow and being pure in his observances, he should go home;
having sat down, he should not speak until the appearance of the moon.
Then, having bathed, on the fourth day following the third, he should utter the name [of the deity].

One should worship the Lord Acyuta on the four days beginning with the second, reciting "Namaḥ Kṛṣṇāya," "Acyutāya," "Anantāya," and "Hṛṣīkeśāya" respectively. On the first day, the prescribed worship is of the feet of the wielder of the discus (Cakrapāṇi).
On the second day, men should perform the worship of the navel according to the prescribed rites;
on the third day, one should place the worship of the Enemy of Mura upon the chest;
on the fourth day, one should arrange the worship of the Creator of the World upon the head.

Having worshipped Viṣṇu, the Lord of the Universe, according to the prescribed rite with flowers, ointments, incense, water for honor, ornaments, food offerings, and the offering of lamps with devotion, the observer of the vow— |||
Then, at the end of the day, when the muhūrta has passed,
a person, permeated by that state of being, should devoutly offer an *arghya* oblation to Soma,
reciting the names Śaśin, Candra, Śaśāṅka, and Indu in succession.

Having proclaimed the names of the Moon on the third and subsequent lunar days, one should present the *arghya* offering. Now, listen to me, Yudhiṣṭhira, as I shall fully explain to you what kind of *arghya* is to be given by those possessed of prosperity as well as by others.
With sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, curd, dūrvā grass, unbroken rice, and other such items;
with gems produced from the ocean and others such as diamonds, lapis lazuli, and pearls;
and with flowers and fruits appropriate to their season, including dates and coconuts.
O King, this procedure is prescribed for one who is endowed with goodness and prosperity, possessing garments, coverings, cattle, grain, land, gold, and elephants;
for another, however, it is performed according to one's ability with fruits, flowers, unbroken grains, and water.
Salt, jaggery, ghee, oil, jars of milk, and sesame seeds—these are recommended for the offerings (arghya);
one should increase them in proportion to the waxing of the moon.
O best of men, one should increase the offering every day in accordance with the growth of the moon.
In this manner, the arghya should be offered; listen now to the sequence of the mantra ritual:
"Being born again and again at the end of every month, you are ever new.
Indeed, united with the three fires, you nourish the oblation for the gods."

O younger brother of Ramā, who are the lamp of the courtyard of the sky, born from the churning of the ocean of milk, and who illuminate the expanse of the quarters with your radiance— salutations be unto you!
Having offered the *arghya* to the Moon, the king of the twice-born, one should present it to that Brahmin.
Having completed this sequence for the offering of water (arghya), one should then eat while restraining one's speech,
using the earth as a vessel, covered with lotus leaves,
Madhuka leaves, or other beautiful leaves, or upon a stone surface.
Having touched the goddess Earth with this mantra, the knower of mantras says:
"O Goddess, source of all flavors, desiring to eat upon your surface,
for the sake of favoring me, make it delicious, like nectar."
Having thus recited [the mantra] and eaten vegetables of excellent quality that have been cooked,
one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), touch the sense organs, and remembering Soma, sleep upon the ground.
On the second day, however, one should eat sacrificial food (havis) that is free from pungent substances and salt.
On the third day, the food of sages (munyanna) is prescribed; on the fourth, products of the cow (gorasa) are best; on the fifth, rice mixed with sesame and ghee is always recommended;
and in all auspicious rites, śyāmāka grains are always praised.
The female attendant [should offer] cow's ghee and unasked-for wild fruits;
then, having performed her morning bath and having gratified the ancestors and deities,
she should devoutly feed the Brahmins and dismiss them after they have been given their gifts.
Afterwards, he should eat at his pleasure together with his servants and kinsmen.
Thus, for all these auspicious three-month periods, the man who,
free from envy, performs this with devotion for one year—
Prosperity and victory shall always attend her, and the Moon will be pleased with her.
Whatever maiden performs this rite obtains an auspicious husband;
she becomes fortunate, virtuous, and forever free from widowhood.
"One who desires a kingdom obtains a kingdom; one who desires wealth obtains wealth;
and one who desires sons obtains sons," so said Prabhākara.
[He further described] those things delightful for the marriage of women from noble or humble families, adorned with beds, food, vehicles, couches, and seats.

"Having obtained auspicious things born of wealth, sons, and wife, one who performs auspicious deeds becomes a rememberer of past lives, O Bhārata. Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Vow of the Auspicious Fasting (Bhadropavāsa)," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira; it is a description of the greatness of the second vow.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Pārtha, there are other well-known lunar days (tithis), such as the second and so forth;
and for four months during the bright fortnights of the rainy season, there are four [observances] that remove all fatigue.
They have always been kept secret in the world and were never spoken of by me anywhere;
yet now, O Pārtha, I shall reveal them to you—listen to all of them as they are told by me.
One is in the month of Śrāvaṇa, and another likewise in Bhādrapada.
In the month of Āśvayuja there is the fourth [tithi]; in Kārttika it is the Caturthī; in Śrāvaṇa it is named Kaluṣā; in Proṣṭhapada it is Gīrmalā;
in Āśvina it is Pretasaṃcārā; and in Kārttika it is remembered as Yamā.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Why is she called "the turbid"? Why is she considered "stained with speech"? Why is she "frequented by the departed spirits"? And why is she proclaimed as "belonging to Yama"?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Long ago, when the slaying of Vṛtra had occurred and Purandara had regained his kingdom,
the horse sacrifice was undertaken for the purpose of dispelling the sin of Brahman-slaughter.
Out of anger, Indra struck down the sin of Brahman-slaughter with his thunderbolt;
it was divided into six portions and cast into a tree, water, the surface of the earth,
a woman, a Brahmin-slayer, and fire, respectively.
That sin was cast off on the second day of the month of Śrāvaṇa at the break of dawn;
it was purified upon coming into contact with a woman, a tree, a river, the earth, fire, or a slayer of a Brahmin. For this reason, she is remembered as "Kaluṣā" (the Impure).
In ancient times, the earth was called Medinī because it was immersed in the blood of Madhu and Kaiṭabha;
it is pure to the depth of eight finger-breadths, yet the menstrual flow of women is its impurity. All rivers are impure with their silt, and the crest of smoke is the impurity of fire.
Because impurities move within her, she is considered *kaluṣā*.
She is called *gīḥ*, *girā*, *bhāratī*, *vāṇī*, *vācā*, *medhā*, and *sarasvatī*.
Since she carries the impurity of speech (*gīr-mala*), she is considered the second [form], *gīr-malā*.

Those who revile the deities, sages, ancestors, and the Dharma—atheists and rogues—their speech is a heap of impurity; for that reason, their second [type of] speech is foul. They teach and recite the scriptures during times when study is forbidden.

The Grammarians, Logicians, and Vedic scholars—these are the "Malas" (impurities) arising from correct and incorrect words; they are arrayed in the second [chapter], and therefore that speech is also called "Mala. The deceased ancestors are called "Pitṛs," and their movement occurs therein.
And in the second world, by him [is reached] that path frequented by the departed;
there are the Agniṣvātta, Barhiṣad, Ājyapa, and Somapa ancestors,
along with the paths frequented by fathers, grandfathers, and the departed— hence it is called Pretasaṃcara.
Well-honored by sons, grandsons, and daughters' sons with *svadhā* mantras,
and satisfied by *śrāddha* offerings and sacrifices,
those wandering as spirits depart from there on the second day of the bright fortnight of Kārtika, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Formerly, Yama was feasted by Yamunā in her own home;
then, on the second day, during the great offering, those belonging to the hells were gratified.
Released from their sins, they were all liberated and freed from their bonds.
Having been whirled around and made to dance, they all remained contented by chance;
a great festival occurred among them that brought happiness to the realm of Yama.
Therefore, O Yudhiṣṭhira, it is called "Yamadvitīyā" in the world.
Therefore, O Pārtha, one should not eat in her own home;
rather, out of affection, one should eat from the hand of a sister, for it increases nourishment.
Furthermore, gifts should be bestowed upon sisters according to the prescribed rites.

O Yudhiṣṭhira, on the first day, all sisters should be honored with gold ornaments, garments, and the like, as well as worship, hospitality, and food; in their absence, those who are next in order of seniority should be honored, beginning with the paternal uncle’s sister.
O King, on the second day, one should eat from the hand of the maternal uncle’s daughter;
on the third day, from the hands of one’s father’s sister and mother’s sister;
and thereafter, from the hand of one’s own sister.
One should eat strength-increasing food from the hands of all one's sisters;
it is auspicious, conducive to fame and longevity, and increases virtue, desire, and wealth.
Out of affection, I have explained this entire matter to you, including its secret.
On that lunar day on which the god Yamarāja was fed by Yamunā out of her affection for living beings in this world,
he who eats here from the palm of his sister’s hand obtains wealth as well as unsurpassed food.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Yamadvitīyā Vow," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the Greatness of Aśūnyaśayana.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Blessed One, you have described the excellent means for achieving dharma, artha, and the other goals."
That state of householdership belongs to a husband and wife who are mutually affectionate;
for a man devoid of his wife, or likewise a wife separated from her husband,
O Madhusūdana, there can be no accomplishment of dharma, kama, or artha.
Therefore, O Lord of the gods, tell me that vow by which a woman does not become a widow,
and by which, O Govinda, a man is never separated from his wife.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen to me regarding the second [vow], named Aśūnyaśayanī,
by fasting upon which a woman, O Yudhiṣṭhira, never incurs widowhood,
nor does a man ever become separated from his wife.
When indeed Viṣṇu, the Lord of the World, lies down together with his consort,
that lunar day is to be observed as Aśūnyaśayana (the Non-Empty Bed). This should be done by means of fasting, eating only at night, or likewise by eating only what is unasked for.
O best of kings, on the second day of the dark fortnight of Śrāvaṇa,
one who is self-restrained, having performed his bath in a river, a pond, or at home,
and having devoutly offered libations to the ancestors, humans, and gods, [should proceed].
Then, one should have a square altar made of clay;
having there worshipped with devotion Śrīdhara, the Lord of Śrī, together with Śrī,
using food offerings, flowers, incense, and other auspicious fruits produced in season.
Having prostrated before the Lord of the Universe, one should recite this mantra:
"O Bearer of the Śrīvatsa, O Beloved of Śrī, O Abode of Śrī, O Imperishable Lord of Śrī!
May my householder life—which bestows dharma, artha, and kāma—not come to ruin."
May the sacred fires not perish; may the deities not perish;
may the ancestors not perish from me through the separation of husband and wife. O Kṛṣṇa, just as you are never separated from Lakṣmī, so may it be for me.
Likewise, O Lord, may my connection with a wife never perish;
O Giver of Boons, just as Your bed is never empty of Lakṣmī,
so may my bed also be never empty in birth after birth.
Having thus propitiated and performed worship for Lakṣmī and Hari,

at the rising of the moon, one should first bathe with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brahmin according to one's means, accompanied by fruit offerings.
By this procedure, O King, for four months,
one should perform the previously described rite on the second day of the dark fortnight.
Then, when the month of Kārttika has arrived, [one should offer] a bed together with the Consort of Śrī.
One should give to a twice-born man a vessel together with its accessories, along with a water-pot and food.
And every month, one should offer the *arghya* to Soma accompanied by mantras,
using curd, unbroken rice, roots, fruits, jewels, and golden vessels.

O younger brother of Ramā, salutations to you, who are the lamp of the courtyard of the sky, born from the churning of the ocean of milk, and who illuminate the expanse of the quarters. The man who performs this correctly for four months—

For three lifetimes, no destruction of his home shall occur; he shall have an unfailing bed and accomplish virtue, pleasure, and wealth. Such a man becomes possessed of unimpeded sovereignty—of this there is no doubt.
And that woman, O Pārtha, who knows the dharma and performs this vow according to the prescribed rules, does not become an object of grief for her circle of kinsmen; nor does she suffer widowhood,
misfortune, or abandonment by her husband, O best of men.
O descendant of the Pāṇḍu lineage, she does not undergo three more births;
for this second lunar day, O King, is known as Aśūnyaśayanā (the Unempty Bed), which removes all impurities and is peerless.
Whatever man or woman observes this, they shall attain a preeminent bed fit for the enjoyment of the most noble.

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Majesty of the Aśūnyaśayana Vow," in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira within the Uttara Parvan of the glorious *Śrīmad Bhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*.
[Now follows] the description of the Madhūka-tṛtīyā vow. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
On the third day of the dark fortnight of Phālguna,
having fasted and remained in celibacy from the morning, adorned with a crown of matted locks,
she beheld the Goddess seated upon a chariot drawn by iguanas, entirely devoted to meditation upon Rudra.
One should worship her with perfumes, flowers, lamps, lac, sandalwood, saffron, sweet substances, and with offerings of gold and rubies. Om! Bhūṣikā, Devabhūṣā, Bhūṣikā, Lalitā, Umā.
May Gaurī, who delights in the forest of asceticism, grant me good fortune; may she,
with a mind ever well-pleased, pacify my misfortune and bestow upon me the birth of a woman never widowed within her family in a future life.
"May Gaurī grant me auspicious fortune, bestowing upon every limb, every subsidiary part, and every joint the nectar that consists of pleasant sight, touch, and taste.
Having thus recited these mantras, the virtuous woman, possessed of the knowledge of women, [proceeded].
The newly married woman should worship with mantras spoken by Brahmins,
using cumin, pungent herbs, salt, molasses, and ghee;
with heart-pleasing fresh fruits, gold, and beautiful flower garlands.
With flowers, saffron, perfumes, kāleya, aguru, and sandalwood;
with exceedingly red vermilion, various auspicious garments,
eyes produced from many regions, cakes, sesame seeds, and rice.
Having worshipped the great tree with such offerings as Aśoka flowers, Viguṇaka fruits, and sweetmeats filled with ghee,
one should then perform a circumambulation and give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brahmin.
Whatever daughter performs this supreme third-day vow (Tṛtīyā-vrata), she shall thereafter attain Śrīdhara, who is difficult to reach even in the three worlds.
This vow has been proclaimed by me; those who observe it shall dwell in eternal years.
Kaśyapa first explained this supreme vow of Rukmiṇī;
all those women who shall perform it will become free from disease,
beautiful in every limb and member, and enchanting to the eyes of the world.
Having remained there for a hundred years, they will then go to the auspicious city of Rudra by means of a swan-vehicle resounding with the tinkling of small bells;
there they shall delight their own husbands for many years.
Enjoying divine pleasures, joyful, and endowed with the eight supernatural powers (siddhis),
a woman who offers to the Madhupa tree an offering (argha) rich with precious gems, saffron, and filaments, accompanied by garlands, fragrances, and the humming of swarms of bees,
and joined with fruits and unbroken grains (akṣata)— becomes honored in this world like Gaurī.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Madhūka-tṛtīyā Vow," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[Now follows] the description of the Meghapālī-tṛtīyā vow.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, when is the Meghapālī-vrata ever performed by men? What is its merit, what is its ritual procedure, and how is that creeper described?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
On the third day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja, O Yudhiṣṭhira,
an offering (argha) consisting of sprouted wheat combined with the seven grains should be devotedly presented by women and men alike to Meghapālī.
Those desiring merit should offer it with balls made of sesame seeds and rice.
With joints resembling those of betel leaves, the red creeper, adorned with clusters of blossoms,
has grown up in garden enclosures, on village paths, and even upon the mountains.
In Meghapālī, people who live by trade even set up stalls for grain, oil, molasses, saffron,
and gold; greedy for wealth and desiring profit, they acquire results by committing sins through a mixture of truth and falsehood.
Having offered the *arghya* to Meghapālī, they destroy [the sins] here in an instant;
whatever sin has been committed anywhere during one's birth through measures of honor or dishonor,
all that goes to destruction by means of this vow, O Pāṇḍava.
The Meghapālī has arisen in an auspicious place and a favorable region;
she is to be worshipped by excellent women with fruits, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata), as well as with dates,
coconuts, pomegranates, and oleanders.

Having covered it with perfumes, incense, lamps of curd, sprouted grains, heaps of rice, and red cloths, and having adorned it with flour-paste (piṣṭātaka), an offering (arghya) should be presented with this mantra, O Bhārata: [The mantra follows: "Obeisance to you, O Goddess, who are the embodiment of all the worlds, who are the source of all prosperity, and who are the supreme power of the three worlds. Accept this arghya, O Mother of the Universe, for the sake of the welfare of all beings. Thus, O descendant of Bharata, the arghya should be offered with this mantra.
"A learned twice-born man should offer that [gift] to her according to what is declared in the Vedas.
Having thus worshipped that Meghapālī,
O tiger among men, whether a man or a woman, one attains supreme prosperity.
Having remained for a hundred years in the mortal world, which abounds in happiness, prosperity, and pride,
one attains the realm of Viṣṇu at the end of the body while seated in a celestial vehicle;
one leads seven generations of one's own lineage from the netherworld to heaven.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, you should have no doubt in this matter:
he who, out of fear of hell, offers arghya water along with fruits and other offerings to Meghapāla,
destroys the sins committed through cheating in measures and weights, just as the sun destroys the sprouts of darkness.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Meghapālī Tṛtīyā Vow," in the Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the Uttaraparvan, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[Now follows] the description of the Rūpārambhā Vow.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Tell me that auspicious vow by which women in the mortal world attain a beautiful home and, moreover, possess supreme love for their husbands. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:

Once, Pārvatī and Śambhu were staying on the delightful peak of Kailāsa, which was variegated with various minerals, filled with diverse trees and creepers, and adorned with many kinds of flowers; they were surrounded by sages and gods.
In that place resounded by throngs of sages and kinnaras and filled with song and dance,
Śaṅkara said to Pārvatī: "O lady of excellent complexion, what virtuous vow have you performed, since you have become so exceedingly dear to me in this form as Vāmā?"
"Come, O beloved, and with a very gracious mind,
tell me everything exactly as it happened, O Pārvatī, all that was done by you.
Thus addressed, the auspicious Gaurī bowed down and spoke to Śiva.
"In the past, on the third lunar day, I performed the auspicious Rambhā-vrata;
by that merit, O Śaṅkara, you, the captivating Manohārī, have been obtained as my husband.
Furthermore, I am the sovereign of women, having taken half of your body."
Īśvara said:
"O blessed Pārvatī, tell me with care what that vow is which bestows all happiness, and which was observed by you in the presence of your father."
Gaurī said:
"O Lord, formerly I dwelt as a maiden in my father's abode,
in a delightful cave of the Himavat, surrounded by a circle of female companions."
Then I was addressed by Menā and by my father, Himādri:
"O daughter, observe the noble Rāmavrata, which increases one's excellence and good fortune;
by the mere commencement of which everything shall be accomplished for you."

"O Mother, I shall indeed bring about good fortune, sovereignty over hosts of women, and likewise the status of a Great Goddess; for you previously told me that by whatever means my heart desires, I shall attain Śaṅkara."
Menā said:
"Today, on the third day of the bright fortnight, having bathed and being intent upon your observances,
place five blazing fires around yourself."
The Gārhapatya fire, the Dakṣiṇāgni, another, the Āhavanīyaka,
and the fifth, the splendor of the Sun— these are the five fires.
Standing for a long time in the midst of these, face the east.
Visualize the Goddess facing you, four-armed and absorbed in meditation, seated upon two lotuses,
her breasts covered by a deer-skin, wearing matted locks and bark garments,
yet adorned with all ornaments.
She is Mahālakṣmī, Mahākālī, Mahāmāyā, and Mahāmati;
she is Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sindhu, Śatadu, Narmadā, and Mahī;
she is Sarasvatī and Vaitaraṇī—she alone is declared to be the Greatly Virtuous One (Mahāsatī).
And let her be intent on gazing at him, illuminated by his very being.
Let self-controlled Brahmins perform the fire-oblation (homa) in every direction;
thereafter, the worship of the Goddess should be performed with flowers, incense, and other offerings.
One should place various kinds of food offerings before the Goddess, including offerings cooked in ghee, as well as separate items for good fortune (*saubhāgya*):
cumin, *kaḍuhuṇḍa*, cakes, and flowers.
Having prepared salt, sugar, and jaggery— which are more purifying than even the *nipā* plant—
one should construct a pavilion of flowers scented with fragrant blossoms; there,
one should remain seated in the lotus posture (*padmāsana*) until the sun has set.
Then, having prostrated before Rudrāṇī, one should utter this mantra:
"In the Vedas and in all the Śāstras, in heaven, on earth, and upon the surface of the world,
this hymn has been seen and heard many times, free from any doubt."

"You are Śakti, you are Svadhā, you are Svāhā; you are Sāvitrī and Sarasvatī. Grant me a husband, grant me a home, grant me wealth; salutations be unto you! Thus one should propitiate the Goddess, prostrating again and again.
Out of devotion, give me a beautiful house, wonderful and many-storied, adorned with covered doorways, courtyards,
and pigeon-cotes; richly endowed with walls, pillars, and windows, featuring archways embellished with jewels and decorated with rubies, sapphires, diamonds, and lapis lazuli.
Having honored a glorious Brāhmaṇa together with his wife according to the ritual for the gift of a house, and having provided it with all necessary furnishings,
that food offering dedicated to the Sun should be given to married women.
Having performed [the rite] according to this procedure, one should afterwards atone for any faults.
On the fourth lunar day, couples should be fed with sweet flavors.
Thus was the supreme Rambhā-vrata described by Umā, and it was practiced by Hara.
At the conclusion of her vow, she gave a beautiful and excellent house to the sage Agastya;
his beloved wife Lopāmudrā was honored in that residence.
By virtue of that merit, O God Śaṅkara, you have been obtained as my husband.
O son of Kuntī, those women or even men who, while staying at Ardhāṅka, shall perform this famous Raṃbhā-vrata on earth,
for them there will be sons, a home, enjoyments, and the prosperity of their lineage.
It bestows upon women cleverness and good fortune, fulfilling all desires of domestic life;
it increases the beauty and charm of girls, the elderly, and those in their prime;
it shatters the pride of rival wives and is the supreme means of subjugation.
Having been born in a beautiful dwelling within the charming land of Āryāvarta, situated between the Himavat and Vindhya mountains, in a family possessing ancestral wealth,
one who dies goes to the city of Śakra and from there proceeds to the city of Viṣṇu.

Then, according to the words of Vyāsa, one goes to the city of Śiva. Indeed, that vow which removes fear was practiced by Rambhā, and also by Gaurī while she resided in the abode of the Himālaya mountain; she who is devoted to that vow and intent on righteousness shall obtain the Lord of Brahmā, Īśa, and Keśava, the bestower of happiness.

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Vow of Rambhā-tṛtīyā," also known as "The Practice of the Five Fires," within the *Śrīkṛṣṇa-Yudhiṣṭhira-saṃvāda* of the *Uttara-parvan* of the glorious *Śrīmad-Bhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*.
[Now follows] the description of the Gopa-padatṛtīyā-vrata. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Pārtha, every year on the third or the fourth lunar day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada, at the break of dawn,
one should undertake the vow known as Gopada by means of fasting.
Having bathed, whether a man or a woman, one should worship with flowers, incense, ointments,
curd, unbroken grains, garlands, flour-cakes, and a forest garland;
and one should anoint the horns, the hooves, and even the tip of the tail of the cows.
One should devotedly give daily fodder to those cows in both the forenoon and the afternoon.
One should eat food not cooked with fire, avoiding oil and alkaline substances.
O Bhārata, one should always follow the cows as they go out and as they return.
O Pāṇḍava, the knower of mantras should offer the *arghya* oblation at the city gate, or in a cow-pen, or upon the hoof-prints of a cow that has recently calved, using this mantra:
"She is the mother of the Rudras, the daughter of the Vasus, the sister of the Ādityas, and the navel of immortality."
"I have spoken to the discerning people: 'Do not kill the cow, the sinless Aditi'—this is the mantra for cows.
May cows be before me; may cows be behind me."
"May cows abide in my heart; I dwell in the midst of cows.
Having thus worshipped and offered the *arghya* water, he should then proceed to his household.
On the fifth day, free from anger, he should eat cow-products such as curd.
Having eaten rice-paste, fruit, vegetables, sesame,
and excellent food, O Indra among kings, one should sleep that night with self-restraint. At dawn, having given a golden cow's footprint to a Brahmin, [one should proceed].
One should seek forgiveness from Govinda, the Lord of cows, who has Garuḍa as his banner.
Just as the cows are honored here, so too is Mount Govardhana.
Having bowed down with Acyuta in mind, hear what fruit one may obtain.
A devotee of cows, having performed the cow-vow with devotion and according to his capacity,
attains good fortune, beauty, and charm upon the surface of the earth;
in brief, he obtains a home filled with cows, calves, and herds.
Endowed with wealth and grain, and possessing an abundance of rice, sugarcane, and juice,
one obtains honored progeny and thereafter becomes an immortal in heaven,
assuming a divine form, wearing garlands, and adorned with celestial ornaments.

Served by Gandharvas with song and instrumental music and by hosts of Apsaras, he shall dwell there for a hundred divine yugas; having completed that time, he shall then go to the city of Viṣṇu. He who performs this Gopada-vrata for three nights and worships cows, through the worship of cow-products, [attains this].
"By bowing to Govinda, the Primal Person, one who possesses the splendor of the sun attains the supreme light, the purifier of cows.

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Vow of Goṣpadatṛtīyā," within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*. This concludes the description of the Harikālī vow.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: On the third day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada,
one should worship her who is covered with all kinds of grains, sprouted, and possessed of green grass.
Having gratified Harakālī, the goddess of gods, Gaurī, the beloved of Śaṅkara,
with perfumes, flowers, fruits, incense, and food offerings such as sweetmeats,
and having clothed her in a radiant ruby;
Having kept a vigil at night with the sounds of bells and musical instruments, auspicious songs, and divine narratives, she should be led by married women at dawn, when the sun has risen,
into the middle of a sacred body of water.
In that [place], O Pārtha, one should offer oblations to Harakālī, the beloved of Hari.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Blessed One, who is the goddess called Harakālī on this earth?"
"Why is she worshipped by women with moist grains?
What does she grant when worshipped here? Tell me everything, O Keśava.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen to this divine story from me, which removes all sins.
There was a daughter of Dakṣa, a maiden named Kālī;
she was dark in complexion, with the luster of a fresh blue lotus.
And she was given to Tryambaka, the great god Śūlin;
she was wed according to the prescribed rites amidst the sounding of conchs and trumpets,
accompanied by the arrival of the gods and the chanting of the Brahmins.

Once the marriage had been performed, the Three-eyed Lord sported with her in various enjoyments that increase the delight of the mind. Then, on one occasion, that bull-bannered god, who was equal to a deity, [proceeded].
Accompanied by Viṣṇu,
the Destroyer of Tripura sat in a beautiful assembly hall; staying there, he called out in jest to Kālī, who was dark as a blue lotus and surrounded by hosts of Gaṇas and Mothers.
"Come, come here! Who are you, endowed with black collyrium? O Kālasundarī, sit down by my side, you who are fair.
Thus addressed with a mind intent on abduction, the goddess became enraged in her heart.
The copper-eyed maiden consoled him with a voice faltering with tears;
standing there, her lower lip quivering, the young woman wept aloud.
"By what stroke of fate," she said, "are you called Tāmra, Gaurī, and Gaurī?"
"O Śaṅkara, since you have given me this comparison,
calling me 'Harakālī'— I who am served by hosts of gods and sages—
therefore I offer this dark body as an oblation into the blazing fire."
Having spoken thus, though being restrained, Harakālī, filled with rage,
released her green-shaded luster upon the green meadow;
she cast her malice into the blazing fire of passion.
Furthermore, she became Gaurī in the abode of the King of Mountains;
established as half the body of Mahādeva, she is worshipped by the gods. Thus, she exists as Harakālī, the consort of the Lord of Gaurī.
O Pāṇḍava, the Great Goddess is to be worshipped with this mantra:
"O you who have arisen from the deeds of Hara, whose body is Hara, who are beloved by Hara;
O you who abide in the form of the Lord, protect me! To you who are bowed down to, salutations again and again!"
Having thus performed the worship, O Pāṇḍava, one should offer the food oblation (naivedya) to a Brahmin;
and in the morning, one should dismiss her with this very mantra into beautiful water:
"O Goddess, you have been worshipped by me with devotion; go now to the abode of the gods."
"O Śiva, O Gaurī, [grant this] for my return at the time of Hara's departure.
O King, that auspicious woman or man, O best of the Pāṇḍavas, who performs the Harakālī vow in this manner according to the prescribed rite year after year, [attains her goal].
O lord of men, hear what fruit she obtains:
she shall dwell for a long time in the world of mortals, free from all diseases,
endowed with every enjoyment, and proud of her good fortune and strength.

O great sage, having enjoyed pleasures upon the earth for more than a hundred years, surrounded by sons, grandsons, friends, allies, nephews, and granddaughters' sons, she then, at the end of her bodily existence, attained the knowledge of Śiva.
Cirabhadra, Mahākāla, Nandīśvara, and Vināyaka—
all these servants of his command, by the grace of Mahādeva—
[praised] her, the daughter of the Himālaya mountain, known as Harakālikā, whose [fields] were filled with crops grown from the seven suns and their hosts.
"Those women who, having performed worship with songs and music that are not arrogant, keep a vigil here, become beloved by their husbands.

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Vow of Harakālī-tṛtīyā," in the Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, Uttara Parvan, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira; [this is followed by] the description of the Lalitā-vrata.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "Now,
O Blessed One, I ask about the vow lasting twelve months known as Lalitārādhana, whether it is performed month by month or in its entirety."
Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen attentively, O Pāṇḍava, to the ancient account of how it occurred—
the dialogue between Śaṅkara and the Great Goddess, O best of the Kurus.
On the delightful peak of Kailāsa, abounding in many flowers and fruits,
shaded by mango trees and adorned with campaka and aśoka blossoms,
where bees were captivated by the fragrance of kadamba and bakula flowers.
Resounding with the cries of peacocks, adorned by royal swans,
and filled with deer, bears, elephants, lions, and troops of monkeys;
it was frequented by Gandharvas, Yakṣas, celestial sages, Siddhas, Kinnaras, and Pannagas.
Having bowed down to Mahādeva— who was being served on all sides by highly fortunate ascetics, who was seated comfortably, surrounded by hosts of beings,
and encircled by Apsarases— Umā spoke this.
Umā said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods, wielder of the trident, whose banner is the bull;
O Maheśāna, tell me of the supreme vow of the third lunar day.
"By which a woman obtains good fortune, wealth, sons, cattle, happiness,
heaven, auspicious beauty, health, and supreme prosperity.
Thus was he addressed with affection by his beloved wife.
Smiling, Śaṅkara said: "O beloved, what is the use of a vow for you?
Whatever desires there may be in the three worlds—whether celestial, terrestrial, or born of the waters—all of them are already under your control, since I, your husband, am subject to your will."

Umā said: "O Lord of the Gods, this is true; when you, the ornament of the expanse of the three worlds, who are adorned by the moon, are beheld, nothing is difficult to obtain. For women, O God, recite their good and evil deeds to me with devotion."
Some who are ugly are easy to find; some have no sons, while others have many.
Some who are virtuous through asceticism are greatly tormented by their mothers-in-law;
and those endowed with purity and proper conduct do not please anyone at all.
Thus, being tormented by many kinds of dreadful sufferings,
they sought refuge in me; therefore, filled with compassion,
I [bestowed upon them] that wealth of beauty and grace, which consists of the enjoyment of happiness.
"O best of gods, may they be endowed with sons, good fortune, and floods of wealth;
therefore, tell me in truth that most excellent of vows among all vows.
Īśvara said:
On the third day of the bright fortnight in the month of Māgha, those who are firm in their vows,
having washed their faces, hands, and feet with concentrated minds,
undertake the observance of fasting preceded by the cleansing of the teeth.
Then, at midday, one should bathe with auspicious *bilva* and *āmalaka* fruits;
having bathed in the pure water of a sacred ford and put on two clean garments,
one should adorn oneself with fragrant flowers and abundant saffron and other unguents.

O Goddess, you who are affectionate toward your devotees, they always worship you with devotion using camphor and other substances, as well as incenses, food offerings such as sugar, and with incense,
lamps, and other articles of worship obtained according to their means.
Then, having invoked the goddess Īśānī by name, he should wait for one ghaṭikā;
meanwhile, having placed a brāhmaṇa together with gold into a pure copper vessel mixed with water and unbroken rice (akṣata), he should do so with mantra and meditative concentration.
Meditating upon her heart's desire, she should pour water over her head;
she is the goddess who has come from Brahmāvarta, emerged from the womb of Brahmā,
the auspicious Bhadreśvarā, and the beloved Lalitā of Śaṅkara.

O beloved of Hara, having reached Mount Kailāsa from Gaṅgādvāra, purified by the waters of the Gaṅgā, you have come for the sake of good fortune, health, sons, and wealth. O auspicious one, wait for a single ghaṭikā; salutations, salutations!
Having given gold to him, she should drink water infused with *kuśa* grass; then,
having sipped water and become pure,
she should spend the night on the ground upon a bed of green barley, meditating on the divine Umā.
Then, having bathed on the second day and likewise worshipped Pārvatī,
and having honored the twice-born according to one's ability, one should eat while restraining speech.
In this manner, O Kālikā, you are to be worshipped in the first month.
In the second [kalpa] you were named Pārvatī; in the third, Śaṅkarapriyā; then in the fourth, Bhavānī; in the fifth, Skandamātā;
in the sixth, the daughter of Dakṣa; and in the seventh, you are remembered as Mainākī.
Kātyāyanī [is worshipped] in the eighth month, while Himādrijā is in the ninth;
in the tenth month, the goddess is renowned as Saubhāgyadāyinī;
Umā is in the eleventh month, while Gaurī is the supreme one in the twelfth.
Kuśa-water, milk, clarified butter, cow-urine, cow-dung, fruit,
neem leaves, kaṇṭakārī, water from a cow's horn, and curd—
these are the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), as well as vegetables; these are the substances for consumption in successive order.
Thus, remaining devoted to fasting month after month,
she faithfully gives these— safflower, clarified butter, salt, cumin, and molasses— to an excellent Brahmin who recites [the scriptures].

"O beloved, you who abide in the sun are pleased by these gifts offered; you who abide in the sun are indeed gratified. In every month, O Goddess, the mantra consisting of twelve syllables beginning with the letter 'ga' is proclaimed to be preceded by the syllable 'oṃ' and ending with a salutation."
O beloved, when you are worshipped with these mantras, you are pleased by virtue of the vow;
being satisfied, you grant one's desired wishes with affection.
When that vow has been completed, [one should honor] a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas.
Having honored him together with his wife with auspicious perfumes, flowers, and other offerings,
and having made the twice-born man Maheśvara and his wife likewise Umā,
he should give food along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) as well as two white garments.
O beloved of Hara, one endowed with faith should give a pair of red garments to a Brahmin, dedicating them to you; hear now the fruit of that act:
having attained the supreme and lower worlds for ten thousand years.
She rejoices together with her husband, just as Śacī does with Indra; and having attained human birth once again, she,
endowed with fortune, enjoys happiness in a virtuous family along with her own husband, free from disease.
For as long as seven births, she shall not experience widowhood;
she shall obtain sons, enjoyments, beauty, good fortune, and health,
and as a devoted wife, she shall become dearer to her husband than even his own life.

Whoever listens with devotion to this Lalitā-vrata as it is being recited by me out of affection shall also partake in its fruit. Having worshipped Lakṣa-lalitā, whose limbs are as graceful as a slender vine, one should pour upon one's head a jar of fragrant water that is like nectar.
Having ascended to heaven as the most distinguished ornament among the graceful goddesses, she attained a king as her husband and enjoys the earth.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Majesty of the Lalitā-tṛtīyā Vow," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira;
herein is the description of the Aviyoga-tṛtīyā vow.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O best of men, tell me how a woman, having attained union here with her husband and kinsmen, may go to the abode of Śiva.
And even as a widow, she shall not be separated again in the next world;
that beautiful woman becomes endowed with an abundance of happiness and good fortune.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Having obtained with great effort that nectar of playful speech concerning both [states],
and having seen the mass of great good fortune of the Goddess, you— whose birth was separated from Dakṣa’s wrath by the Great-Souled One— [attained this].
Listen to what was told by Vasiṣṭha when questioned by Arundhatī:
"When the month of Mārgaśīrṣa has arrived and the moon is waxing, O lady of pure smiles,
having reached the second lunar day, she should eat milk-rice at night."
Having sipped water and become pure, one should prostrate like a staff before Śaṅkara.
Having joyfully offered salutations and informed the Supreme Lord,
one should take a straight stick of Udumbara wood and use it as a tooth-stick.
On the second day,
or on the following day, one should worship Gaurī and Śambhu,

having fashioned auspicious male and female forms out of rice-flour paste, using a piece of wood from the northern direction that is more than a span long, with its bark intact, free from blemishes, and beautiful.
Having placed [the image] in a vessel and worshipped it, one should observe a vigil at night;
having worshipped Śaṅkara according to the rules while reciting his praises, one should sleep;
then, in the morning, having taken those [images], one should present them to the preceptor.
With devotion to Śiva, one should feed the best of the twice-born with delicious food;
one should also feed married couples there according to one's capacity. Restrained, one should perform this every month according to that prescribed rule.
Then, at the end of the month of Kārttika, one should exert oneself in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa;
I shall proclaim his names in sequence for each month— listen—
for the purpose of worship and recitation, and for the sake of his spiritual accomplishment.

Thus, when the month of Pauṣa has arrived, the wise man, having worshipped Giriśa as well as Pārvatī on the fourth lunar day, should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). This is prescribed as the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) for that which pertains to the path at the beginning of Mārga.
