Nor is any other supreme purifier, such as the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), traditionally remembered [as superior to this].
One should worship Bhava and Bhavānī in the month of Māgha;
however, in Phālguna, one should worship Mahādeva together with Umā.
Then, one should worship the goddess Lalitā and the god Śaṅkara in the month of Caitra;
in the month of Vaiśākha, one should indeed worship Sthāṇu, accompanied by Lolanetrā;
and in Jyeṣṭha, the god Vīreśvara, together with Ekavīrā.

In the month of Āṣāḍha, one should worship the Lord of Beasts (Paśunātha), the Three-eyed One (Trilocana), together with Śakti; in Śrāvaṇa, one should worship the god Śrīkaṇṭha accompanied by his daughter;
and in the month of Bhādrapada, one should sacrifice to Bhīma together with Durgā.

In the month of Kārttika, one should worship Īśāna together with the goddess Śivā for the sake of recitation, meditation, and worship. O King of excellent vows, when these names are remembered according to the prescribed rule, the perfection of the vow will certainly be attained.
I shall now describe in due order those flowers which, when employed in worship each month, truly bring immediate satisfaction;
first, the blue lotus (*nīlotpala*) should be used, or in its absence, others as well.
One should devoutly employ purifying and fragrant flowers in the worship:
the *karavīra*, the *bilva* leaf, the *kiṃśuka*, the *kubja-mallikā*,
the *pāṭala*, the lotus, the *kadaṃba*, the *tagara*, the *droṇa*, and the *mālatī*.
O King of kings, these [offerings] should be performed with devotion throughout all twelve months in the very order described, for the sake of pleasing Śiva and Śivā;
and at the end of the year, one should offer a canopy and the wafting of incense along with a bell.
One should offer a banner, a lamp, and a pair of garments to Śaṅkara;
having bathed and anointed him, one should place a golden lotus upon his head and set down a pair of cakes made of rice-flour before him.
Having offered food-oblations according to one's ability and having prostrated before Śiva according to the prescribed rite,
one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for Śambhu and then go to one’s own home.
Having gone there, one should cause a triangle and a square to be drawn.

In a triangular [enclosure], a Brāhmaṇī should be fed; in a quadrangular one, the best of the twice-born. Afterwards, O Pāṇḍava, one should feed twelve excellent Brāhmaṇas who observe vows, as well as an equal number of couples, according to one's capacity and with devotion.
Having caused a very beautiful golden image of Umāmaheśvara to be made, one should place sixty-four pearls, as many corals,
and as many topazes upon a copper vessel.
Having wrapped it in cloth, one should worship it with perfumes and incense; then,
provided with these materials, one should present it to the preceptor,
O Bhārata, as well as to the Brahmins observing vows and to married couples.
Having given gold and garments, one should ask for forgiveness while prostrating.
Then, one should give forty-eight water-pots, along with an umbrella and sandals, all accompanied by gold, unbroken rice grains, flowers, and water.
On that day, [these gifts] should be distributed to the poor, the blind, and the suffering, or at least set aside for them.
One should arrange for the gift of food while considering one's own capacity;
it may be made less or more according to the measure of one's wealth. One should fulfill the requirement through such planning and must not practice stinginess regarding one's resources.
This practice of the vow, properly extracted from the Purāṇas, bestows non-separation [from loved ones], grants beauty, good fortune, and wealth,
bestows long life and sons, leads to heaven, and grants the world of Śiva;
it is the essence of the practice of the vow belonging to the Heart of the Teacher of the Moving and the Unmoving.

Having performed the worship according to the prescribed rules, a virtuous woman does not suffer separation from her husband, sons, kinsmen, or wealth. Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Vow of the Aviyoga-Tṛtīyā," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
[This section contains] the description of the Umā-Maheśvara vow.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: By what dharma, by what vow, and by what observance do women attain supreme good fortune and many auspicious sons?
He obtains wealth, grain, gold, and various garments,
and he attains constant, never-ending union with his sons and grandsons.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Pārtha, I shall proclaim the most excellent of vows,
by performing which a woman becomes fortunate and gives birth to many children,
as well as abundant wealth, grain, gold, and numerous male and female servants.
I shall tell you that by which it arises in the home;
formerly, Umāmaheśvara was performed by Apsarases,
as well as by Vidyādharas, Kinnaras, and the daughters of the sages.
O Pārtha, this vow, the best of all vows, was performed by Rūpiṇī, Rambhā, Sītā, Ahalyā,
Rohiṇī, Damayantī, Taptā,
and Anasūyā.

It bestows the fruits of good fortune and health, and destroys poverty and disease. Furthermore, those women in the mortal world who are unfortunate, devoid of beauty, childless, destitute, and bereft of all enjoyments— [for them it provides these].
O Pārtha, for their benefit, the Umā-Maheśvara vow was brought down by Pārvatī in ancient times; inferior women do not know it. Formerly, in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, a woman devoted to dharma—
On the third day of the bright fortnight, having fasted and subdued her senses,
she should bathe and worship Lalitā, who dwells upon half of Hara’s body; then,
at the time of dawn, she should bathe again in natural water.
Having performed [the rites] and having gratified the goddesses, one should utter this speech:
"Obeisance, obeisance to you, O Lord of Gods, who bear half of Umā’s body!
O Great Goddess, obeisance to you, who dwell in half of Hara’s body!"
Having placed Śiva in her heart, she should mutter the mantra until she has reached home;
then she should worship the Lord Īśāna with flowers produced in season—
Umā the goddess on the left side and Maheśvara on the right.
Afterwards, she who has been well-prepared should burn incense or even guggulu resin;
she should offer an oblation according to her ability, consisting of food cooked in ghee.
She should indeed perform the Vaiśvadeva rite, well-consecrated with sesame seeds and clarified butter.
Then, having consumed the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) for the purification of one's own body,
and having thus worshipped Maheśvara for twelve months,
one should then perform the concluding rite (udyāpana) with a joyful inner soul.
Having fashioned Śiva out of silver and Umā likewise out of gold,
both mounted upon a silver bull and adorned with all ornaments;
having anointed Śiva with sandalwood paste and Pārvatī with saffron.
Thereafter, one should worship with fragrant and most captivating flowers;
one should clothe Śiva in a white cloth and Pārvatī in a red one. Then, a woman, permeated by a spirit of devotion, should burn incense.
One should feed devotees of Śiva and Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas.
To the devotees, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given with devotion, free from deceit.
Then, having performed a circumambulation, the wise person should recite this:
"May the two gods Umā and Maheśvara, the grandfathers of all the worlds,
be forever well-pleased with me by means of this vow.
Having spoken thus to the brahmin, who had conquered anger and was a master of the Vedas, [the king departed].
One should devoutly announce the vow to the reciter or to one endowed with virtuous qualities.
Having performed this vow, a woman whose mind is dedicated to Maheśa goes to the supreme abode where the god Maheśvara dwells.
He shall dwell in the world of Śiva for as long as fourteen Indras reign;
surrounded by Apsarases and likewise by Kinnarīs,
when he returns to the human state, he is born into a pure family.
Endowed with beauty and youth, blessed with many sons, and devoted to her husband,
she dwells for as long as she lives in a delightful home— abounding in wealth and grain, adorned with gold and jewels— with her senses unimpaired.
She shall never experience separation from her husband, friends, sons, and others;
having died, she goes to the city of Śiva by the grace of Śiva and Gaurī.
[One should worship] Umā made of gold and Maheśa made of a mass of silver, both seated upon a beautiful silver bull.
"By worshipping [the two deities] covered with a pair of red and white garments, a woman becomes one who is not widowed and is endowed with the happiness of sons.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Umā-Maheśvara Vrata," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[Now follows] the description of the Rambhā-Tṛtīyā Vrata.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: I shall now describe the Raṃbhā-tṛtīyā, which destroys all sins,
bestows the fruits of sons and good fortune, and wards off all diseases.
It removes all evils, is meritorious, and likewise bestows all happiness;
it crushes the pride of rival wives and brings about sovereignty—
the auspicious one (Śivā) which was formerly proclaimed by Śaṅkara out of a desire to please Pārvatī.
Listen to this, O protector of the earth, for the welfare of all beings.
On the third day of the bright fortnight in the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa, O lord of men,
having risen in the morning and performed the cleansing of the teeth;
"O Goddess, filled with devotion, she should undertake the vow of fasting for as long as a year; having fasted on the third lunar day,
she will perform the breaking of the fast on the following day every month."
"O Pārvatī, by your grace, may that [merit] of mine proceed without obstacle.
Having thus made this resolve according to the rules, O son of Kuntī,
a man or a woman, firm in their determination, should perform the bath with devotion and without sloth.

Whether at a river, a pond, a well, or in one's own home, the self-controlled person should worship her by the name Pārvatī at night after consuming water infused with *kuśa* grass. In the morning, the wise man should especially feed those devoted to Śiva.

One should give gold and salt as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for them; being purified and self-controlled, one should feed Gaurīśvara according to one's capacity. O King, by this procedure, one should perform [this rite] in the month of Pauṣa.
One should consume cow’s urine at night and feed the twice-born at dawn; thereafter,
one should cause gold and cumin to be given according to one's capacity,
and having presented them with *kaḍuhuṇḍa* and gold, one should bid them farewell.
One obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya and Atirātra sacrifices without a doubt;
one shall dwell in the world of Śakra for a kalpa and thereafter proceed to the city of Śiva.
On the third day of the month of Māgha, one should worship the goddess named Sudevī.
She should consume cow dung at night and then sleep alone.
In the morning, she should give safflower and gold to the twice-born according to her means.
Having dwelt for a long time in the world of Viṣṇu, she attains equality with Śiva.
On the full moon day of Phālguna, one should give the name "Gaurī" [to the image] and cause [the devotee] to consume cow's milk at night.
At dawn, the wise man should feed the devotees of Śiva and married women;
having given them a *kaḍuhuṇḍa* vessel along with gold, he should bid them farewell.
One obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya and Atirātra sacrifices without a doubt.
In the month of Caitra, she who is intent on devotion should worship Viśālākṣī;
having consumed curd, she should sleep, and in the morning, she should give gold along with saffron.
One attains great good fortune through the grace of Viśālākṣī;
on the third day of Vaiśākha, one should worship her by the name Śrīmukhī,
consume clarified butter at night, and then sleep alone.
Having fed Śiva-devoted twice-born men in the morning as much as they desire,
and having given them betel-leaf and salt, one should bow down and dismiss them.
By giving according to this rite, one obtains excellent sons.
Having bowed to Mādhavī in the month of Āṣāḍha, one should consume water mixed with sesame seeds.
In the morning, one should feed the Brahmins; for the ritual fee (dakṣiṇā), jaggery along with gold is prescribed.
Indeed, such a person attains auspicious worlds; of this there is no doubt.
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, having worshipped Śrī and honored the devotees of Śiva, one should drink water produced from a cow’s horn and offer gifts of gold along with fruits;
thus, becoming the lord of all worlds, one shall attain all desires.
On the third lunar day of the month of Bhādrapada, one should worship Haratālī;
by drinking buffalo milk, one shall obtain incomparable good fortune.
Having enjoyed happiness in this world, at the end one shall go to the city of Śiva.
On the third day of the month of Āśvina, one should worship the Daughter of the Mountain (Pārvatī).
Having consumed rice-water in the morning, one should also worship the Brahmins.
Gold along with sandalwood is prescribed as the sacrificial fee.
Having obtained the fruit of all sacrifices, one is honored in the world of Gaurī.
In the month of Kārttika, one should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) after arising from the lotus;
one should keep a vigil at night and feed the twice-born at dawn.
One should honor those devoted to Śiva who are accompanied by their wives and are of virtuous conduct with garlands, garments, and ornaments; one should also feed young maidens.
O King, at the conclusion [of the rite], one should have a golden image of Umā and Maheśvara fashioned.
According to the extent of one's wealth, one should provide a five-colored canopy,
auspicious food, a white umbrella, a water-pot,
sandals, shoes, and pairs of divine garments, O Pāṇḍava.

Having installed and worshipped Umāmaheśvara according to the prescribed rites— with yellow sacred threads, with lamps blazing like eyes, and beautifully adorned with conch shells, mother-of-pearl, and mirrors—
With various fragrant leaves, flowers, and fruits,
as well as food offerings cooked in ghee, rows of lamps,
sugar, coconuts, pomegranates, and citrons.

One should worship the Lord of the gods with cumin, salts, safflower, and saffron, using divine waters mixed with juices in vessels of pure copper; immediately thereafter, one should ask for forgiveness.
With the sounding of conch shells accompanied by the chanting of the Vedas—
if this is performed, the fruit that shall arise cannot be described by me;
one shall partake of the fruits previously mentioned and be honored by all the gods.
For as long as a hundred crores of kalpas, one shall obtain all desires;
at the end of that time, one attains union with Śiva—of this there is no doubt.
Since this was formerly performed by Raṃbhā, it is known as the Raṃbhā-vrata.
"I am she who is known as Gaurī, and she who is Gaurī is Maheśvara.

Thinking thus, O Great King, go for refuge to Pārvatī. This beloved of the Daughter of the Snowy Mountain, having assumed her third form as Rambhā on earth by his own act—by fasting upon her while reciting the multitude of names uttered by those who have tasted the truth, a woman obtains many desired fruits.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Vow of Rambhā-tṛtīyā," in the Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the Uttaraparvan, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira;
followed by the description of the eightfold auspiciousness (saubhāgyāṣṭaka). Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
In the same way, I shall proclaim another [rite] that bestows the fruit of all desires,
known by those who know the Purāṇas as "The Bed of Good Fortune" (saubhāgya-śayana).
Long ago, when the worlds— Bhūr, Bhuvas, Svar, Mahas, and the rest— had been consumed by fire,
At that time, the auspicious fortune of all the worlds became concentrated in one place;
and having reached Vaikuṇṭha, it remained upon the chest of Viṣṇu.
Then, O King, after a long period of time, during the process of creation once again—
When the world was shrouded by egoism, yet endowed with both Pradhāna and Puruṣa,
and when a rivalry had arisen between the Lotus-seated One and Kṛṣṇa,
a tawny-colored flame then emerged from his chest.
That [nectar] issued forth from the chest of Hari as he was scorched by her; having taken refuge in Viṣṇu’s chest, it attained its state of auspiciousness, and then,
in the form of liquid essence, it reached the surface of the earth.

Thrown up into the sky by the wise son of Brahmā, it was drunk by Dakṣa as soon as it reached him; thereby, great strength and splendor were produced in Dakṣa, the son of Parameṣṭhin, as the cause of his beauty and charm.
The remainder that fell upon the earth was produced in eight forms:
sugarcanes, salt, flat beans, chickpeas, and grain;
as well as cow’s milk and its derivatives, safflower, and saffron.

And salt is the eighth therein; this is called the "Eightfold Saubhāgya. It was drunk by the son of Brahmā, who was a knower of yoga and knowledge; from that, a daughter was born to him, who is known as Satī.
Because she transcends the worlds through her gracefulness, she is called Lalitā.
The wielder of the Pināka bow married this lady, who is the most beautiful in the three worlds,
who embodies the auspiciousness of the triple universe, and who bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
"O King, what woman does not attain [her desires] by worshipping Umā with devotion?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Janārdana, how is the worship of her, the Mother of the World, performed?"
"O Lord of the World, tell me all the rules for that [vow].
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, having reached the month of Vasanta, on the third lunar day..."

In the forenoon of the bright fortnight, one should perform a bath with sesame seeds. On that day, it is said, that goddess of excellent complexion, being the soul of the universe, is to be married with the mantras used for taking the hand in marriage.
Likewise, on the third lunar day, one should worship the Lord of Gods together with [the consort],
accompanied by various kinds of fruits, along with incense, lamps, and food offerings;
and every month, one should likewise perform the rite with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and scented water.
Having snapped [the flowers], one should worship Gaurī together with the Moon-crested Lord;
one should worship Pāṭalā together with Śambhu at the feet,
and Triyugā together with Śiva on both the ankles.
A wise person should worship Vijayā together with Bhadreśvara upon the pair of knees; Īśānī and Harikeśa on the hips;
and Koṭanī and Śūlin on the belly, along with Maṅgalā conjoined with Śarva.
O King, one should worship Nandin and Rudra on the belly;
one should worship Ananta and Tripuraghna in the two breasts; one should worship Bhava and Bhavānī on the neck, and likewise Gaurī and Hara on the face.

With his whole being, accompanied by his attendants, he should worship Lalitā above his head with these mantras preceded by "Oṃ" and joined at the end with "namas," together with devotion, using perfumes, garlands, and unguents.
Having thus worshipped according to the rules, one should place before [the deity] the eight auspicious items (saubhāgyāṣṭaka):
steamed flat beans, safflower, milk-cumin,
tavarāja, sugarcane, salt, saffron, and likewise the eighth item.
Because good fortune (*saubhāgya*) has been bestowed, it is called the "Eightfold Good Fortune" (*saubhāgyāṣṭaka*). Having thus offered all that for the pleasure of Śiva and Śivā,
O subduer of enemies, one should consume the water from a horn in the month of Caitra and sleep upon the ground.
Then, having risen at dawn, purified and having performed breath-control (prāṇāyāma),
he should worship a Brahmin couple with garlands, garments, and ornaments,
along with the eight auspicious items (saubhāgyāṣṭaka) and a pair of golden feet.
"May Lalitā be pleased here"—thus one should offer it to a Brāhmaṇa.

In this manner, O King, for as long as a year, on the third lunar day (Tṛtīyā), always [perform the rite]. Now learn from me this specific distinction regarding the consumption of the food and the mantra containing her name.

In the first month [Kārttika], one should consume cow-horn water; in Vaiśākha, cow-dung; in Jyeṣṭha, Mandāra flowers; and in Āṣāḍha, Bilva leaves is prescribed. In Śrāvaṇa, curd is to be consumed, and in Nabhasya (Bhādrapada), Kuśa-water.
Likewise, one should consume milk in Āśvayuja; in Kārttika, ghee mixed with coagulated milk (pṛṣadājya);
in Mṛgaśīrṣa, cow’s urine; in Pauṣa, clarified butter;
in Māgha, black sesame seeds; and similarly, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) in Phālguna.
At the time of giving the gift, one should recite: "May Lalitā, Vijayā, Bhadrā, Bhavānī, Kumudā, Śritā,
Vāsudevī, Gaurī, Maṅgalā, Kamalā, Satī,
and Umā be pleased."
The mallikā, aśoka, kamala, kadamba, utpala, mālatī,
the bud of the karavīra, the bāṇa, the unfading saffron (kuṅkuma),
and the sinduvāra are prescribed in succession for all the months.
Flowers of the *japā*, safflower (*kusumbha*), jasmine (*mālatī*), and the hundred-petaled rose (*śatapatrikā*),
as well as the oleander (*karavīra*), should always be offered according to their availability.
Having thus observed the fast according to the prescribed rule for the duration of a year, a man—
A woman or a maiden, having worshipped Śivā according to her ability during the night,
should at the conclusion of the vow give a bed equipped with all its furnishings,
as well as a golden image of Umā and Maheśvara along with a bull and a cow.
Having placed [the image] upon the bed, one should present it to a Brāhmaṇa;
likewise, other couples according to one's ability, along with garments and the like,
grains, ornaments, gifts, and other accumulations of wealth.
Free from stinginess regarding wealth and devoid of pride, one should perform the worship. He who thus properly observes the Saubhāgya-śayana-vrata attains all desires and enjoys the infinite state.
O King, he who performs the Saubhāgyaśayana vow for twelve years shall not be deprived of good fortune, health, beauty, long life, clothing, ornaments,
and decorations for three hundred thousand years.
He who performs [this] seven or eight times shall be properly worshipped by Śrīkaṇṭha and Bhuvaneśvara for as long as thirty thousand kalpas.
O Lord of Men, whether it be a woman or a maiden who performs this, [the same result follows].
She too, cherished by the grace of the Goddess, attains that fruit;
and whoever should hear this, or give it away, or even direct their mind toward it,
he too, having become a Vidyādhara, shall dwell for a long time in the heavenly world.

This was the conduct formerly desired here by Madana; this was indeed the vow observed by Śaśabindu. This was practiced by the Lord of the Gods, by Dhanada, by the Wind-god, by Soma, by Karuṇa, and by Bandin.

Those gifts which were given here in the past by kings, which bring about merit, wealth, and fame—he, truly a virtuous man, takes them back again, making them like discarded flower-offerings before an image.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Vow of Saubhāgyāṣṭaka-tṛtīyā," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
[Now follows] the description of the Rasakalyāṇinī-vrata.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Janārdana, please tell me of some vow that bestows the fruits of good fortune and health, causes the destruction of adversaries, and grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
That which the God, the slayer of Asuras, formerly spoke to Umā when the narrations concerning the propitiation of Lalitā had commenced—
that I shall now proclaim, for it bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Now listen attentively to this unsurpassed means of propitiating both men and women, which destroys all sins:
whether in the month of Nabhasya, Vaiśākha, or again in Mārgaśīrṣa.
On the third day of the bright fortnight, having bathed with genuine white mustard seeds,
one should apply a tilaka on the forehead consisting of yellow orpiment, excellent cow urine, musta grass, cow dung, curd, and sandalwood, all mixed together.

That which bestows good fortune and health, and is always dear to Lalitā, should be worn after being tied on every third lunar day of each fortnight; or else, one should wear garments of yellow cloth,
or flowers that are red and yellow.
A widow, a devoted woman, or a maiden dressed in white garments should then bathe the image of the Goddess with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), then with milk alone,
and likewise with honey, flowers, and scented water.
One should worship with white flowers and various kinds of fruits,
as well as with coriander, cumin, salt, molasses, milk, ghee, and so forth.
Whoever always worships Lalitā, she who is to be honored with white unbroken rice grains and sesame seeds—
One should perform the worship of Gaurī correctly and concisely, beginning from the feet:
"Salutation to Varadā" for the two feet; likewise, "Salutation to Śrī" for the two ankles;
"Salutation to Aśokā" for the two shanks; and likewise, "Salutation to Bhavānī" for the two knees.

Salutations to the thighs for Māṅgalyakāriṇī, and likewise to the waist for Kāmadevī; salutations to the belly for Padmodbhavā, and to the chest for Kāmapriyā. Salutations to the hands for Saubhāgyavāsinī, and to the arms for Śaśimukhaśrī.
Salutations to Pārvatī, the abode of Kaṃdarpa, for her face; likewise to Gaurī for her smile. Salutations to Sunetrā for her nose, and to Tuṣṭi for her forehead; likewise to Kātyāyanī for her head.
Salutations to Gaurī, salutations to Sṛṣṭi, salutations to Kānti, salutations to Śrī;
salutations again and again to Raṃbhā, to Lalitā, and to Vāsudevī.
Having thus worshipped according to the prescribed rite, one should draw a lotus in front.
One should place [the lotus] provided with twelve petals and a pericarp made of saffron;
first, one should install Gaurī, and after that Aparṇā;
likewise Bhavānī in the south, and after that Rudrāṇī.
One should place Madanavāsinī in the west,
Pāṭalāvāsā in the northwest, and then Umā in the north;
[and likewise] Lakṣmī, Svāhā, Svadhā, Tuṣṭi, Maṅgalā, Kumudā, and Satī.
Having placed Rudrāṇī in the center and Lalitā upon the pericarp,
one should install them with flowers, unbroken grains, and white offerings, accompanied by prostrations;
and having caused auspicious songs to be sung, one should honor the married women.
One should worship them with red garments, red garlands, and red unguents;
one should apply vermilion and bathing powder upon their heads,
since vermilion, saffron, and bathing are always desired by Satī.
In the month of Nabhasya (Bhādrapada), one should worship Gaurī with blue lotuses; likewise in Āśvayuja with bandhujīva flowers, in Kārttika with śatapatra flowers,
in Mārgaśīrṣa with kunda flowers, and in Pauṣa indeed with saffron.
In the month of Māgha, one should worship the Goddess with devotion using *siṃduvāra* flowers;
in Phālguna, O son of Pāṇḍu, Pārvatī is to be worshipped with *jāti* flowers.
In Caitra, she is worshipped with *mallikā* and *aśoka*, and in Vaiśākha with fragrant *pāṭala* flowers.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should worship Umā with lotuses and mandāras; in Āṣāḍha, with campakas and water-lilies; and in Śrāvaṇa, with kadambas and mālatīs.
[One should also offer] cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, kuśa grass, and water.
One should always consume, in sequence, bilva leaves, arka flowers, water from a cow's horn, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and bilva fruit.
This is declared to be the ritual consumption that begins with the month of Bhādrapada.
O lady of beautiful countenance, I have declared the counter-measure for the second [day]:
having envisioned a Brāhmaṇa and a Brāhmaṇī as Śiva and Gaurī,
one should feed them and worship them with devotion using garments, garlands, and ointments.
Having given yellow garments to the man and safflower-dyed clothes to the woman,
one should give to the woman flat beans, cumin, salt, and a stalk of sugarcane endowed with its fibers; and to the man, a fruit together with a golden lotus.
Just as the Lord of the Gods does not depart, leaving you behind,
so may my husband not go elsewhere, completely abandoning me.
O Kumudā, Vimalā, Anantā, Bhavānī, Vasudhā, and Śivā!
"Lalitā, Kamalā, Gaurī, Satī, Rambhā, and Pārvatī—
may they be pleased during the months beginning with Nabhasya (Śrāvaṇa).
At the conclusion of the vow, one should give a bed accompanied by gold and a lotus.
One should worship twenty-four pairs, or half of that [twelve], at once;
then, during the Cāturmāsya, one should worship eight pairs each time.
Likewise, one should also diligently honor the preceptor as the Guru.
Where the Guru is not honored, all ritual actions there are fruitless.
This third [form] of Ananta has been described; she always bestows infinite fruits.
She is the Goddess who removes all sins and increases good fortune and health.
One should never neglect this [observance] out of stinginess regarding wealth;
whether it be a man or a woman, one falls downward through such parsimony.
Furthermore, [one should avoid crossing water] at night when a woman is pregnant, has recently given birth, is a maiden, or is afflicted by disease.
When one has faith, then one should have it performed by another.
He who observes this third [lunar day], which bestows infinite fruit,
is honored in the world of Śiva for more than a hundred crores of kalpas.

Even one devoid of wealth should perform fasts for three years according to the prescribed method of flowers and leaves; he too shall obtain that fruit. Likewise, whether it be a woman, a maiden, or a widow who performs them, [she shall obtain the same].

She too, being imbued with Gaurī’s grace, attains that fruit. Whoever thus recites or hears this vow of the Daughter of the Mountain, or even forms a thought of it, shall dwell in the world of the Moon; he too shall be honored by the gods, the celestial damsels, and the *kiṃnaras*.
(Thus ends the Ananta-Third-Day Vow.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
I shall now describe another third-day vow as well, which destroys all sins.
Those who know the ancient ritual manuals recognize this rite by the name Rasakalyāṇinī.
Having reached the third day of the bright fortnight in the month of Māgha,
one should perform a bath in the morning with cow’s milk and sesame seeds.
One should bathe the Goddess with honey as well as with sugarcane juice.
Worship should be performed again, either with jasmine or with saffron.
Having worshipped the right limbs, one should then worship the left limbs.
One should worship the feet with "Salutation to Lalitā," and likewise worship the ankles;
the shanks and knees with "Salutation to Satyā," and the chest with "Salutation to Śrī"; the hips with "Salutation to Madanālasā," and the belly with "Salutation to Madanā."
One should worship the two breasts with "Madanavāsinyai" and the neck with "Kumudāyai";
the arms and the tips of the arms with "Mādhavyai," and the private parts with "Kamalāyai"; the eyebrows and forehead with "Rudrāṇyai," and likewise the curls of hair with "Śaṅkarāyai."
I offer the crown to Viśvavāsinī, and likewise the locks of hair to Kānti;
the eye to Cakrāvadhāriṇī, and the face again to Puṣṭi;
salutations to the throat for Utkaṇṭhinī, and the neck to Anantā.
To Rambhā, [he should offer] the left arm; and salutations to Viśokā, the supreme [deity].
To Manmathādityā, the heart; repeated salutations to Pāṭalā.
Having thus worshipped according to the rules, he should honor a Brahmin couple.
Having fed [the recipient] with sweet food-gifts free from envy,
one should give a vessel of water along with sweets (laḍḍukas), a pair of white garments,
and a golden pitcher; then one should worship [the recipient] with perfumes and garlands.
"May Kumudā be pleased here; she shall observe the vow of abstaining from salt.
According to this rite, one should worship the Goddess month after month.
One should avoid salt in the month of Māgha, and likewise, molasses in Phālguna."
Likewise, one should avoid *tavarāja* in the month of Caitra, and honey in Mādhava (Vaiśākha);
one should avoid *yāraka* in the month of Jyeṣṭha, and similarly, cumin (*jīraka*) in Āṣāḍha;
one should avoid milk in Śrāvaṇa, and likewise, curd in Bhādrapada.
Likewise, one should avoid ghee in the month of Āśvayuja, and majjikā [oil] should be avoided as well;
coriander (dhānyaka) in Mārgaśīrṣa, but sugar (śarkarā) is to be avoided in Pauṣa.
At the conclusion of the vow, a vessel full of these [substances] should be offered month by month.
At the time of the two twilights, one should offer white-colored rice grains together with a vessel for food,
as well as saṃyāva cakes, honey-filled pūrikās,
ghārikās, ghee-filled pastries, maṇḍakas, milk, and vegetables.
One should place these six kinds of offerings— curd-rice, *bhiṇḍī*, and vegetable-sticks—
successively upon the water-pot (*karaka*) starting from the month of Māgha:
Kumudā, Mādhavī, Gaurī, Rambhā, Bhadrā, Jayā, and Śivā.

Likewise, one should recite "May Umā, Śacī, Satī, Maṅgalā, and Rati-lālasā be pleased" for all [months] starting from Māgha in due order. Chewing and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) is declared to be the ritual consumption (prāśana).

One should always observe the fast; if unable [to do so], one should place sugar upon the right hand. Then, having obtained [the gift] again during the month of Māgha, one should fashion a golden iguana over the water-pot (karaka), endowed with five jewels.
Having given Umā a water-pot made of a thread of nectar measuring only the size of a thumb,
and likewise a pair of cows, entirely golden-faced and white,
along with garments and vessels, one should say: "May Bhavānī be pleased."
Whoever performs the Rasakalyāṇinī vow according to this procedure is liberated from all sins at that very moment;
for thousands of billions of births, he shall never again be born into suffering anywhere.
Whatever fruit is obtained by a thousand Agniṣṭoma sacrifices, that she shall attain—
whether it be a woman, or a maiden, O Yudhiṣṭhira,
or even a wretched widow; she too shares in that fruit.
Endowed with good fortune and health, she is glorified in the world of Gaurī.

Whoever thus recites this, or whoever hears it even incidentally, being freed from all impurities, goes to the world of Pārvatī. And he who gives even his thought for the sake of others shall become an unfailing leader of wise men.

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Rasakalyāṇinī Vrata," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
The Description of the Vow that Brings Moisture and Bliss.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Likewise, I shall describe another third-day vow (tṛtīyā) which destroys all sins.
This vow, renowned throughout the worlds by the name Ārdrānandakarī,
should be undertaken auspiciously whenever the third lunar day of the bright fortnight coincides with the asterism Āṣāḍhā, Rohiṇī (Brahma), or Mṛgaśīrṣa.
Then one should properly perform the ritual bath with darbha grass and fragrant water;
wearing white garlands and garments, and anointed with white perfumes,
one should worship Bhavānī with devotion using fragrant white flowers.
To Vāsudevī, who is seated upon an excellent throne together with Mahādeva, salutations to her feet; to Śaṅkara, who is the feet of Hari, salutations;
to the shanks of the Goddess who destroys sorrow, salutations to the Lord Ānanda.

One should worship the thighs with "To Rambhā" and for Śiva, the wielder of the Pināka bow; the waist of the trident-bearer should be worshipped with "To Ādityā," and likewise the navel with "To Mādhavī" and for Śambhu, with "To Bhava."
Salutations to the breasts that cause bliss for Śaṅkara, who bears the moon;
salutations to the throat of Hara, which causes longing for the one who wears the crescent moon; and salutations to the hands of the Lord of the World, Rudra, which bear the blue lotus.
He offered his arm to Pariraṃbhiṇī and to Nṛtyaśīlā, the beloved of Hari;
his face to Vilāsinī and to Vṛṣeśa, the Lord;
his smile to Sasmaraśīlā and to Viśvavaktra, the All-pervading Lord.
The eye [is offered] to Madanavāsinī; to the Trident-bearer, the Abode of the Universe; the two eyebrows to Ratipriyā and to the Lord of Tāṇḍava, O All-pervading One;
the forehead to the Goddess Indrāṇī and to the All-pervading One, the Bearer of Oblations.
I bow to the crown of the Goddess Svāhā, and indeed to the five arrows of the Lord;
I praise the auspicious Pārvatī and Parameśvara, who possess universal forms and supreme universality, whose feet and hands are the universe itself, and whose faces are serene.
Having thus worshipped according to the rules before the two Śivas,
one should again have lotuses and water-lilies made in various colors,
as well as a conch, a discus, bracelets, a svastika, and a vardhamānaka.
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, water with *kuśa* grass;
likewise water from a horn, water with *bilva* leaves, and water from a jar; similarly, water with *uśīra* root, and then water with barley powder.
Having obtained water mixed with sesame seeds, one should sleep during the months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa;
on the second day of each fortnight, the consumption [of this mixture] is prescribed.
In all cases, white flowers are recommended for the worship of Śiva.
On all occasions of giving, one should recite this mantra:
"May Gaurī be ever pleased with me for the destruction of sin; may Maṅgalā be for my welfare; may Lalitā Bhavānī be for good fortune and for the attainment of all perfections."
At the end of the year, one should prepare salt, a jar of jaggery,
sandalwood, an eye-cloth, and a pair of white garments;
likewise, a golden image of Umā and Maheśvara, accompanied by sugarcane and fruits.
One should offer a bed covered with a grass mat and provided with a pillow to a Brahmin together with his wife, saying, "May Gaurī be pleased with me.
This third eternal [vow] is named Ārdranandakarī.
By fasting on this day, a person goes to that supreme abode of Śambhu;
in this world, he attains such bliss as comes from the accumulation of wealth,
becomes endowed with long life and health, and shall experience no grief whatsoever.
Whether it be a woman, a maiden, or likewise a widow,
she too— cherished by the grace of the Goddess— obtains that same fruit,
provided she fasts on every lunar fortnight according to the prescribed ritual for mantra worship.

Such a person attains the world of Rudrāṇī, from which there is no return. Any man who constantly hears this or causes it to be heard is honored in the world of Śakra along with the Gandharvas for three hundred years.
"The chaste wife who duly observes this third lunar day (Tṛtīyā), which bestows bliss and removes all suffering,
shall experience hundreds of joys in her own home and, thereafter, go joyfully to the city of Gaurī together with her husband.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Vow of Ārdra-Ānandakarī-Tṛtīyā," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the months of Caitra, Bhādrapada, and Māgha.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
[Tell me of that which] bestows beauty, fortune, and sons in the months of Caitra, Bhādrapada, and Māgha.

O Kṛṣṇa, why has this triad of the third [chapter] not been proclaimed to me? Am I a man devoid of devotion, one who has strayed from the path of the three Vedas? This is well known throughout the world; for what reason has it been concealed?
"It is my conviction that you are omniscient and favorable toward all purposes.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "This vow is well-known in the world; it was not disclosed by him to you, and therefore it was not told to you by me."
If you have the inclination to hear it, O son of Pāṇḍu, then listen!
Who else in this world on earth is a listener equal to you?
Jayā and Vijayā are indeed the two attendants of Umā.
Having arrived, they were questioned by the daughters of the sages out of a desire for their desired fruit:
"O ladies, you are indeed always knowers of the movements of the Goddess's mind;
by what ritual observance and on which day does Pārvatī [grant her favor]?"
When worshipped with certain mantras, O fair-faced one, she attains satisfaction.
Having heard their words, Jayā spoke respectfully:
"Listen; I shall declare that which bestows the fruit of all desires."

On the third day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, preceded by the cleansing of the teeth, a man or woman, filled with devotion, should undertake the vow of fasting— a delightful observance accompanied by festivals.
Saffron, betel with areca nut, vermilion, and two red garments—
even for a widow observing a fast— constitute the supreme means for ensuring she does not become a widow.
A widow travels by the [prescribed] path, whereas a maiden goes according to her own will.
One should perform the rite of worship; now hear the power of the mantra.
One should have a beautiful cloth pavilion constructed with silk scarves and fine fabrics, adorned with divine ornaments and the fragrance of flowers.

One should have a canopy fashioned in front, adorned with clusters of hanging coral, with a divine cloth spread within, wherein full water-pots are placed and Brahmins are seated upon excellent pedestals; and one should have a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) made, measuring one cubit in size and provided with a girdle (mekhalā).
Then, having bathed and anointed herself, and having put on two beautiful garments,
she should worship the gods and the ancestors, and thereafter proceed to the temple of the Goddess.
Gaurī, the beloved of the Lord of Cows, should be worshipped with her eight names.

Having anointed [the image] with saffron and with flowers produced at that time, which are fragrant and crowded with *bakula* blossoms, and having likewise worshipped according to the rules with camphor, agallochum, and sandalwood,
one should consecrate it with excellent incense.
Pārvatī, Lalitā, Gaurī, Gāndhārī, Śāṅkarī, Śivā,
Umā, and Satī— this is the eightfold name-list proclaimed by me.
[One should worship with] sweetmeat balls, sugar-coated sweets, small candies, and lion-manes.

One should please Umā with pleasing food offerings that captivate both the sight and the senses— consisting of *somālaka*, *kokasara*, and various kinds of *khaṇḍakhādyaka* sweets, cooked in ghee, prepared with well-ripened fruits.
One should place before [the deity] pieces of ginger, cumin, saffron, salt, fresh ginger, stalks of sugarcane, sugarcane products, turmeric,
and fresh [vegetables], as well as coconuts, emblic myrobalans, citron fruits, and pomegranates.
One should offer pumpkins, cucumbers, melons, oranges, jackfruits,
and other fruits that appear in season;
as well as the house, the mortar, the grinding stone, and the winnowing basket, along with prostrations.
One should offer collyrium sticks for the eyes, chickpeas for the nails,
a mirror, and bamboo vessels to Bhavānī,
accompanied by the sounding of conchs and trumpets and the resonant chanting of auspicious songs.
With devotion, one should worship the Goddess, the beloved of Śiva, according to one's own capacity.
Then, at the time of the sun’s setting, young maidens,
filled with joy, should perform a ritual bath with fresh handfuls of water for the increase of good fortune and health.
At the end of every watch (yāma), bathing and the worship of the Goddess should be performed;
with those very names, an oblation of sesame seeds and clarified butter is highly recommended.
Seated in the lotus posture, the virtuous woman, while still wearing that same wet garment, [should perform the rite].
Intent on beholding the face of Gaurī, she should pass that night.
Some play musical instruments with great joy, some dance with delight,
and others relate stories of the Goddess during that great festival.
In the city of the Goddess, some women with arched eyebrows danced, accompanied by song and rhythm, neither arrogant nor agitated;
Hara rejoices in the dance, while Gaurī is satisfied by the song.
Or else, through their sincere devotion, all may attain supreme joy.
Betel, saffron, and flowers should be given to the married women, as well as to those who keep the vigil and others; something should also be given to everyone else.
Accompanied by actors, jesters, and warriors, as well as theatrical performances and festivities,
and together with her friends, she should spend the night singing and dancing.
Thus, at the time of dawn, having bathed and worshipped Pārvatī, [she should proceed].
Then she should indeed ascend that arch adorned with garments and ornaments;
while seated there, she should be weighed against jaggery, salt,
saffron, or— as far as her means allow— camphor, agallochum, and sandalwood.
Some wise men even desire [the construction] with fragments of mountains;
one should adorn that very place with the materials for the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and the pavilion (maṇḍapa), and with mantras.
Indeed, the self is weighed against salt or against molasses.

By some woman devoted to worship, incomparable good fortune was attained. Having thus prostrated before the noble Goddess and asked for her forgiveness, one should enter the home after taking leave of those learned in the scriptures who have mastered the rules of right conduct.
Having fed the married women with food that is mostly sweet,
he himself should eat together with his kinsmen and wise friends;
and whatever was offered before the Goddess as *naivedya*, that he may eat according to his desire.
With a mind free from confusion, one should divide everything and lead it all back home;
then, having fulfilled the duty, one should give [the remainder] to householders. This same procedure, which bestows great beauty, is also prescribed for the month of Bhādrapada.
One should worship Umā, who embodies the seven types of grain, upon a winnowing basket;
because of the consumption of cow's urine here, it is known as "Gomūtra.
Now, listen to the special observance for the third day of the month of Māgha.
Having performed everything previously mentioned, at dawn one should weigh out a bed of barley grass and worship it with *kunda* flowers;
for this reason, the fourth day is designated by the name *Kundā*.
I have now related to you this third [chapter], which is the cause of all things,
just as it was formerly proclaimed by Jayā to the daughters of the sages.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
In the city of Vidarbha, there was a courtesan who was beautiful in every limb.
By the word of a Brahmin, she performed all this in the past;
having enjoyed pleasures upon the surface of the earth, she gave gifts according to her desire.
O lord of men, when her time had come,
that daughter of the king, who was exceedingly beautiful and beyond thought,
named Avantīsundarī— more beautiful even than the gods— met her death.
Even if one were somehow to possess a thousand times a thousand mouths,
it would still be impossible to fully describe that beautiful-eyed woman;
through the greatness of the third day of the month of Caitra, she became Prabhāvatī.
Most beloved to her parents, disciplined, and dear to other people,
she was obtained by Kṛṣṇa of unwearied deeds just like the one born from the ocean;
thereafter, that virtuous woman joyfully enjoyed pleasures together with her husband.
The ornaments such as bracelets and the like that she gave to the Brahmins—by their power she obtained good fortune; what could be greater than that?
And she gave birth to sons whose prowess was equal to that of Viṣṇu and Indra.
Skilled in all missiles and weapons, and having mastered the rites prescribed in the Vedas—
having thus attained such great fortune and the excellence of sons,
that devoted wife met her death at the end along with her husband.
Having traversed the abodes of the world-protectors, beginning with Śakra, in due order,
and having reached the world of Brahmā, she attains identity with Śiva. Thus, whatever auspicious vow a woman performs in this manner, [she obtains the same fruit].

Having obtained beauty, good fortune, and sons, she is honored in heaven. No daughter in her family shall be unfortunate, nor shall there be a son who is ill-behaved, nor a servant who acts unfavorably.

Neither poverty nor disease arises in that house where that virtuous woman, possessing the luster of molten gold, dwells; and so it shall be for any other women who observe this vow with the permission of the Brāhmaṇas.
Having honored the reciter with devotion through ornaments, garments, and other offerings,
O best of the Kurus, those women shall become endowed with all happiness and their desires shall remain unfrustrated; salutations to that Goddess.

In the month of Māgha, women worship the beloved of Śambhu, whose footstool is adorned with highly precious gems; in Caitra, her limbs are smeared with heaps of various flowers; and in Nabhasya (Śrāvaṇa), she consists of fresh grain sprouting from winnowing baskets. By thus worshipping her, women attain prosperity. Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Vows of the Third Tithi of Caitra, Bhādrapada, and Māgha," in the *Uttara-parvan* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[Now begins] the description of the subsequent vow of the third lunar day (*anantarā-tṛtīyā-vrata*).
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Many third days of the bright fortnight have been proclaimed;
tell me of the Ānantarya-vrata associated with both [fortnights].
For the welfare of all beings, and especially for women,
[one should worship] with name-recitation, the tasting of offerings, and food-oblations, month by month, individually.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen to the unprecedented vow of Ānantarya, as it was described by the foremost of gods, beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa;
one should perform this vow at the outset in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
On the second day, she should perform the rite at night; on the third day, having fasted,
she should worship the goddess Umā with flowers, perfumes, and other offerings in due order,
and after prostrating herself, she should offer a sugar figurine according to her means.
Having consumed curd at night, she should sleep free from envy;
in the morning, the wise man should devoutly feed a couple according to the prescribed rites.
He obtains the full merit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice; of this there is no doubt.
Likewise, on the third day of the dark fortnight, having observed a fast and subdued her senses,
she should mutter the name "Kātyāyanī" and offer a coconut.
Having consumed milk at night, she should sleep while remaining free from desire and anger.
One shall obtain an auspicious marriage, enjoyable food, and the fruit of a cow-sacrifice.
On the first third-day (tṛtīyā) of the month of Pauṣa, having fasted and subdued the senses,
one should worship the goddess named Gaurī and offer sweetmeat balls (laḍḍukas).
Having consumed clarified butter at night and renounced all desire before it, one should sleep;
in the morning, a couple should be fed, and the fruit of a human sacrifice (naramedha) shall be attained.
In this manner, one should worship Pārvatī on the third day of the dark fortnight.
One should offer cooked rice and fried cakes, and at night one should cause [the couple] to consume cow dung;
by feeding the husband and wife various kinds of food, one obtains the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
Having fasted on the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, [one should perform this].
Having worshipped the Goddess of the Gods, one should offer a piece of bilva fruit.
Then, having consumed water mixed with kuśa grass, she should sleep on the ground with her senses subdued.
At dawn, she should devotedly feed a married couple with sweet food.

Having asked for forgiveness and paid obeisance at the conclusion, one thus obtains the fruit of gold. Furthermore, thereafter, during the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha, she who is pure in her vows should worship the goddess named Āryā and then offer various kinds of edible foods.
Having consumed honey, she should sleep at night, free from desire and anger;
having fed a married couple, she shall obtain the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
Thus indeed, in the month of Phālguna, she who observes the fast and maintains pure vows [attains this merit].
Then, having worshipped the goddess named Bhadrī, one should offer a pool [of water].
Having consumed sugar well, one should sleep at night free from envy.
In the morning, a couple should be fed; one shall obtain the fruit of the Sautrāmaṇi sacrifice.
Furthermore, O Bhārata, on the third day of the dark fortnight of Phālguna itself,
having worshipped Viśālākṣī, one should offer *pūrikās*.
Having offered rice grains with water, the wise woman should sleep upon the ground.

One should feed a married couple in the morning; thus one obtains the fruit of an Agniṣṭoma sacrifice. On the first third-day (tṛtīyā) of Caitra, being pure and having conquered the senses, one should worship the goddess Śrī with devotion and offer her *vaṭaka* cakes.
Then, having consumed a bilva leaf, she should sleep devoted to meditation.
Rising in the morning, the wise woman, with devotion to Me, should worship a couple;
having prostrated and asked for forgiveness, she shall obtain the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
Furthermore, having fasted properly on the third day of the dark fortnight of Caitra,
one should worship the goddess named Kālī, consume flour (piṣṭa), and sleep at night; then,
having offered cakes (pūpaka), one should keep a vigil during the night.
And by feeding couples, one obtains the fruit of an Atirātra sacrifice.
Thus, in the month of Vaiśākha, she who has fasted and subdued her senses should worship the goddess Caṇḍikā and offer honey-nectars (madhuka).
Having smeared herself with śrīkhaṇḍa sandalwood paste, she should sleep on the ground before the Goddess;
and by feeding a married couple, she obtains the fruit of the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
Likewise, on the third day of the dark fortnight, she who is free from envy and observes a fast [attains the same].

One should worship Kālarātri with perfumes, flowers, and lamps; having offered well-prepared barley gruel, one should eat sesame seeds and sleep at night. In the morning, a couple should be fed, and one shall obtain the fruit of the Atikṛcchra penance.
On the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha,
one who observes a fast should worship the auspicious goddess and offer mangoes;
having consumed an *āmalaka* fruit at night and meditated upon Gaurī, one should sleep comfortably.
Then, having risen at dawn and fed the beautiful couple according to the prescribed rite, one obtains the fruit of a pilgrimage to sacred sites.
Furthermore, on the third day of the dark fortnight, a married woman should observe a fast.
Having worshipped Skandamātā, one should offer [the oblation] to Iḍā;
then one should consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and sleep before the Goddess. In the morning, having fed a couple, one obtains the fruit of giving a daughter in marriage.
When the month of Āṣāḍha has arrived, one should worship Yaśodhana;
one should offer *karañja* as the food offering (*naivedya*) and drink water from a cow’s horn at night.
In the morning, a couple should be fed, and one shall obtain the fruit of giving a maiden in marriage.
Likewise, on the third day of the dark fortnight, one should worship Kūṣmāṇḍī according to one's ability;
one should offer before her parched grain flour mixed with jaggery and clarified butter.
Having consumed water infused with Kuśa grass, she should sleep at night with her senses subdued.
At dawn, having fed a couple, one obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows. In the month of Śrāvaṇa, observing a fast, one should worship Caṇḍā-Ghaṇṭā;
boiled grain (kulmāṣa) is the offering there, and one should drink water infused with flowers.
At dawn, one should provide food for a married couple according to one's ability;
one obtains the fruit of the gift of fearlessness—of this there is no doubt.
Likewise, on the third lunar day of the dark fortnight, one should worship Rudrāṇī with her names.
One should likewise cause divine, perfected *piṇḍas* to be offered as a food-oblation (*naivedya*).
Having consumed the oil-cake (*piṇyāka*), one should sleep at night free from envy.
By honoring a Brahmin couple, one obtains the fruit of both sacrificial rites (*iṣṭa*) and charitable works (*pūrta*).
On the third day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, one should worship the Daughter of the Snowy Mountain (Pārvatī).
Having offered an oblation of wheat-based food, one should consume white sandalwood paste.
Then, having consumed perfumed water, one should go to sleep together with one's female companions.

At dawn, a couple should be fed, and one shall obtain a hundred *mārgapālī* fruits. Likewise, on the third day of the dark fortnight, one should worship the divine Durgā and offer divine cakes made of flour filled with molasses and clarified butter.
Having consumed cow's urine with a tranquil mind, one should sleep;
then, having fed a couple in the morning, one shall always obtain the fruit of a sacrifice performed with all its components.
And in the month of Āśvayuja, one should worship the goddess Nārāyaṇī with devotion.
Observing a fast, she should offer an oblation of sugar-cakes;
she should consume red sandalwood paste and sleep free from envy. At dawn, she should feed a married couple, whereby she obtains the fruit of the Agnihotra sacrifice.
Likewise, on the third day of the dark fortnight, one should worship the deity named Svasti.
Thereafter, one should offer as an oblation boiled rice mixed with jaggery.
Having consumed safflower seeds, one should abandon all desire and sleep during the night.

By feeding a couple in the morning, one obtains the fruit of a daily gift of cows. On the third day of the month of Kārttika, one should worship the goddess named Svāhā and offer her an oblation of milk mixed with sugar and ghee.
Having conquered anger, one should eat saffron filaments at night and sleep;
in the morning, a couple should be fed, and one shall obtain the fruit of eating only one meal a day.
Likewise, on the third lunar day of the dark fortnight, one should worship the goddess named Svadhā.
Having offered rice mixed with mung beans and consumed clarified butter, one should sleep at night;
in the morning, having fed a couple, one obtains the fruit of the Nakta vow.
By performing this for a year, one becomes purified and freed from sin.
On the third day of the bright fortnight, fasting and free from ailment,
she quickly recognized Umā with devotion through the understanding of the meaning of the scriptures;
and then, having drawn a nine-centered mandala that bestows boons.
One should have the Lord fashioned in gold together with Umā.
Pearls and sapphires should be placed for their eyes;
coral should be given for their lips, and jeweled earrings for their ears.
The sacred thread (upavīta) belongs to the God, and likewise a necklace upon the chest belongs to the Goddess.
One should worship the Goddess, who wears red garments, and Maheśvara, who wears white garments,
after having anointed them with the four-fold mixture (catuḥsama) and with flowers and incense.
Having performed worship in the maṇḍala, one should then perform the fire-oblation (homa) for the preceptor.
Then, one should worship the goddess named Aparājitā right there.
After consuming a portion of clay, one should keep a vigil throughout the night.
One should recite with devotion throughout the night until the sun rises, accompanied by delightful songs, instrumental music, festivities, lutes, and auspicious recitations;
[seated] upon a couch exquisitely adorned with cotton mattresses and bolsters.
Having lifted the deity from the mandala, one should place him upon a throne,
provided with a canopy, banners, garlands, bells, and a mirror;
it should be covered by a pavilion of flowers and perfumed with incense and guggulu resin.
In front of him, one should devotedly feed couples according to one's own capacity,
gratifying them with various kinds of food, both hard and soft, as well as with sweet and auspicious cooked dishes.
Then, having placed unbroken rice grains (akṣata) in their hands, one should offer betel leaf (tāmbūla).
"May Śiva, the beloved of Umā, together with Pārvatī, be pleased with me.
Having thus purified the remnants and sprinkled water all around,
[one should offer] a cow that is red in color, of good character, beautiful in form, and yielding abundant milk.
With its two horns adorned with gold and its hooves joined with silver,
equipped with a bronze milking vessel and draped in red cloth,
it is enriched by the beauty of bells and ornaments, standing before the God and the Goddess.
Having circumambulated three times, one should offer everything to the Guru, including sandals, shoes, an umbrella, food, and vessels;
[and] the deity Umāmaheśvara, who is inseparable and worshipped by the gods.
"May that which is unbroken and well-pleased be mine here.
Having prostrated with his head upon the ground, he should say to the Guru, "Forgive me.
In this manner, the undertaking of the Ānantarya-vrata for the Goddess is completed.
Listen to the fruit of merit for that man or woman who performs [this]:
they shall go to the worlds of the Gandharvas and Yakṣas, the Vidyādharas and Mahoragas,
the world of the Ṛṣis, Siddhas, and immortals, and the eternal world of Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
Having enjoyed all pleasures without exception, accompanied by twenty-one generations of his lineage,
mounted upon a jewel-chariot and surrounded by secret apsarases,
he goes to the abode of Śiva, attended by gods, vidyādharas, and yakṣas.
Having enjoyed great pleasures there, he enjoys many more like Śiva himself.
When his time has come and his enjoyment of those pleasures ends due to the exhaustion of his merit,
he returns to earth and becomes a sovereign ruler of the entire world.
Any woman who practices this becomes a Great Goddess;
like the goddess Umā, she enjoys uninterrupted pleasures,
and like Rudra, the lord of the three worlds, she enjoys them together with him.
Just as Manu with his great divine power, or Śakra with his ease,
she enjoys uninterrupted happiness together with her husband;
just as Arundhatī dwells with the Sage, or Lakṣmī resides in the heart of Viṣṇu.
In that way, great happiness and indeed constant continuity arise between them;
just as Sāvitrī is to Brahmā and Gaṅgā is to the ocean,
so too shall their affection remain uninterrupted in birth after birth.
Now, if this vow is performed on a day other than her birthday,
she shall never suffer separation from that very husband;
she shall become beautiful and reside within a mandala extending for ten thousand yojanas.
Abounding in offerings, fortunate, virtuous, and adorned with sons and grandsons—
thus has this entire Ānantarya-vrata been described by me. It should be told to a devoted and well-disciplined person, and not otherwise.
This third [day], specifically ordained and declared, has been loudly proclaimed by widows as the *Anantarī* (the day without interval).
By fasting on this day according to the rules through the conjunction of the first lunar day (*pratipad*), one never encounters a separation from sons, friends, or kinsmen.

Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Anantara-Tṛtīyā Vow," in the *Uttara-parvan* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the Akṣaya-tṛtīyā Vow.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
What is the use of speaking much here, or of a long string of syllables?
Listen, O Pāṇḍava, to [the account of] that single third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha:
whatever bathing, giving, recitation, fire-offering, Vedic study, or libation to the ancestors is performed on this day,
all of it shall be inexhaustible in this world.
Because this occurred at the beginning of the Kṛta Yuga, it is called the "commencement of the age" (yugādi);
it pacifies all sins and bestows all happiness.
In the city of Śākala, there was a certain merchant named Dharma.

Priyaṃvada was devoted to truth and a worshiper of the gods and Brahmins. He had previously heard it being recited that when the third lunar day (Tṛtīyā) coincides with the Rohiṇī asterism and is joined by Mercury, it yields great fruit.
"Whatever is given there, all that becomes inexhaustible.
Having heard this, he offered libations to the ancestors and the gods in the Gaṅgā;
then, returning home, he took water-pots filled with food and water.
Then, one should gradually place water-filled jars in the house until they are completely exhausted;
likewise, barley, wheat, chickpeas, flour, curd,
boiled rice, products of sugarcane and milk, along with gold, according to one's ability.
Pure, with a purified mind, the merchant gave to the Brahmins even though he was being restrained by his wife due to her anxiety over the household; meanwhile,
he remained established in goodness, considering everything to be perishable.
Then, after a long time, being capable in the pursuit of dharma, artha, and kāma,
he passed away while repeatedly remembering Vāsudeva;
thereupon, that kṣatriya was born as a lord of men in Kuśāvatī.
And his prosperity, won through righteousness, became inexhaustible.
He performed great sacrifices accompanied by excellent sacrificial fees;
day and night he bestowed gifts of cattle, land, gold, and other riches.

He enjoyed pleasures according to his desire, satisfying people who were poor and distressed; nevertheless, that wealth of his, which had been given with faith on the third lunar day even without great means, did not undergo depletion, but remained inexhaustible.
I have described this vow; now hear the procedure for it:
one should provide water-pots together with water-jars filled with all bathing-ingredients and perfumes.
In this case, the gift of all summer crops is highly praised.
The gift of an umbrella and sandals, as well as cows, land, gold, and clothing—whatever else is most dear to one—that should be given without hesitation.
All this has been explained to you; what else do you wish to hear?
"I have nothing that remains unspoken; may it be well with you, O sinless one!
On this lunar day, what is offered in sacrifice or given in charity reaches its end; therefore, the sages have declared this third day to be inexhaustible (Akṣayā).
Whatever is performed by men on this day in honor of the gods and ancestors, O Bhārata, all of it becomes entirely inexhaustible."
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Akṣayyatṛtīyā Vow," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Now follows the description of the Aṅgāraka-caturthī vow.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
It bestows beauty, good fortune, and happiness; it is dear to men and women alike; it removes sins and yields abundant fruit; it is easy to perform and involves excellent fasting;
it brings about prosperity and intelligence, leads to heaven, confers fame, and grants all desires.
"Therefore, tell me some vow, O Mādhava, if you are pleased with me.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"Listen, O Pārtha, to this supreme secret which has never been told by me before."
Long ago, while you were dwelling in the forest, I shall now declare that which occurred:
from the great joy of Śiva and Śivā, a drop of blood fell upon the earth;
it was then carefully caught by the Earth, who was endowed with fortitude.
Born from that [fire], this youth is red and originates from the red;
"aṅga" is well-known here, and it is called "vega.
Because he was born with impetuosity from the limb (aṅga) of Śiva, he is therefore called Aṅgāraka.
Because he possesses the luster of glowing embers (*aṅgāra*) and is born from the limbs and minor members (*aṅga-pratyaṅga*), and because he bestows good fortune and health, he is known as Aṅgāraka.
Any woman who, with single-minded devotion and endowed with faith, diligently worships him on the fourth lunar day by means of a night-fast (*nakta*), [attains her desires].
Being pleased with him, he shall grant that which you have described—
a form endowed with beauty, captivating to both men and women.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Lord of Gods, tell me this auspicious rite for Aṅgāraka,
including the placement of the *sahomamantra* according to the procedure for perfuming (*adhivāsa*).
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Having previously made his resolve and bathed in the external water, he should,
while standing in the water, take up earth for the purpose of bathing with mantras:
"O Earth, you were indeed praised of old by Kṛṣṇa as he lifted you up."
"By this, burn away the flood of my evil that has been accumulated by me in the past.
Reciting this mantra, O Pārtha, one should show it to the Sun;
[the body] heated by the rays of the Sun and sprinkled with drops of Ganges water.
Having first placed that clay upon his head and applied it to the joints of his limbs,
he should then perform his bath within the water while reciting the mantra:
"O Waters, you are the source of all Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas."
Salutations to the Lord of the essences born from sweat and those produced from the earth.
I have bathed in all sacred fords and in all springs;
may my bathing take place in those rivers and in those natural pools of the gods.
Meditating upon this mantra, one should then perform the ritual bath;
having bathed and become pure, one should return home and not touch anything,
nor speak, nor look at anyone who is indeed most sinful.
The knower of mantras, having touched dūrvā grass, the aśvattha tree, and the śamī tree, as well as me, with the mantra;
and [having offered] even the dūrvā grass present there along with the joined mantra:
"O Dūrvā, you are born of the nectar of immortality and are saluted by all the gods."
"O Goddess, I bow to you; may all that evil deed which was committed by me be burnt away. (This is the mantra for dūrvā grass.
"You are the purifier of purifiers; you are called Kāśyapī in the Vedas.
O Śamī tree, pacify that sin which was poorly performed by me."
(Thus ends the Śamī mantra.
Learn from me this mantra for obtaining the branch of the Aśvattha tree:
[it wards off] the twitching of the eyes, the twitching of the arms, bad dreams, and evil thoughts.
"And O Aśvattha, pacify for me the rising of my enemies. (Thus is the mantra for the Aśvattha.
Then one should give a cow to the Goddess along with her calf and a ritual fee (pradakṣiṇā).
Having touched [the tree] with the mantra, one should utter this mantra:
"O Goddess, you who consist of all the gods, you are well-worshipped by the deities;
therefore, I touch you and I bow to you—being thus saluted, be the destroyer of my sins. (This is the mantra for the cow.
O Pārtha, reciting this mantra while being imbued with a spirit of devotion, [one should proceed].

Whoever performs a circumambulation upon seeing a cow of excellent color has, by that act, circumambulated the entire earth; of this there is no doubt. Having thus approached in silence, one should salute those worthy of salutation and then go home.
Having washed his feet with earth, he should enter the house of one who maintains the sacred fires;
there he should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) with these excellent words and mantras:
"To Śarva, to the son of Śarva, to the son of Pārvatī, and to the son of the Cow."
To Kujā, the red-limbed one, and to Aṅgāraka, the lord of the planets,
he indeed offers oblations again and again,
having repeatedly poured them out with mantras preceded by the syllable *oṃ* and joined at the end with the word *svāhā*.
One hundred and eight times, O Pārtha, or half of that, or even half of that again;
with these mantra-words, out of devotion, according to one's capacity, or for the sake of a specific desire,
[one should offer oblations] with fuel-sticks of *khadira* wood, clarified butter, milk, sesame seeds, and barley.

Having offered oblations according to his capacity with various kinds of edible foods and other offerings, O Pārtha, the knower of mantras who has gained control [of the deity] should then install the god upon the ground. Some desire a ceremonial bath [of the image] in a copper vessel containing molasses.
It may be made of gold, or red-colored wood,
or likewise of black agalloch,
or fashioned from sandalwood; it should be worshipped with saffron filaments in either a golden or a silver vessel.

O Pārtha, O King, one who possesses wealth, being imbued with devotion, should worship with red flowers, auspicious garments, fruits, and various jewels according to his capacity and with a devoted heart,
as long as he is able to direct his mind toward it.
For as long as men worship with red flowers, saffron filaments, and the like in a vessel made of copper, bamboo, or even clay, the merit of the donor increases a hundred-thousandfold.
(Oṃ, homage to Aṅgāraka on the head;
Oṃ, homage to Kujā on the face;
Oṃ, homage to Bhauma on the two shoulders.)
Oṃ, salutation to Maṅgala on the two arms;
Oṃ, salutation to Rakta on the chest;
Oṃ, salutation to Lohitāṅga on the hips.
Oṃ, obeisance to Ārāya, on the shanks;
Oṃ, obeisance to Mahīdhara, on the feet. This is the eight-flower offering.
Having fashioned a figure of a man within the vessel, one should worship Kuja with mantras;
there, with concentrated mind, one should offer incense consisting of guggulu mixed with clarified butter and black agallochum, or else incense made from excellent substances.
One should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) with the previously mentioned mantras known as auspicious.
Having thus prostrated before the Lord of Devas, one should present [the image] to a Brāhmaṇa;
or, according to one's capacity, one should give a meal of flat beans (niṣpāvaka) along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
For one who practices stinginess regarding wealth shall not partake in the primary fruit.
Having made the earth his vessel, he should eat silently;
first, however, he should consecrate it with this mantra—listen as I declare it.
"In this abode of the essence of all herbs, which grants everything at all times, I desire to eat beneath you; may that which is eaten become nectar.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:

"O Yādava, tell me: when the fourth lunar day (Caturthī) coincides with the day of Aṅgāraka (Mars), how many such days are there that should be observed as fasts with eating only at night? Is it only one? Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Whenever the fourth lunar day (Caturthī) coincides with a Tuesday,
one should observe a fast on that very day and worship Mars (Kuja) according to the prescribed rite.
Those who are destitute of wealth wait until they have acquired some means.
And on each fourth day, O Pāṇḍava, hear the injunction:
having fashioned an artificial image of Aṅgāraka in a golden vessel,
it should be made of ten gold pieces as the best, or even half of that, or half of that again.

O Pārtha, the vessels should weigh twenty palas, or twenty-five palas, or twenty karṣas; one should not have them made less than this. Having established Mars with mantras, it should be completely wrapped in cloths.
Having constructed a divine flower-pavilion perfumed with excellent incense,
one should there worship the God according to the prescribed rites with the original mantras,
with devotion, and with various kinds of food, fruits, and oceanic jewels.
With garments, coverings, vehicles, beds, sandals, and excellent seats;
with umbrellas, flowers, and the finest perfumes— according to one's ability and in accordance with one's wealth—
one should then, O Brahmin, examine [the recipient] for his possession of vows and purity.
One who is perfected in the study of the Vedas, knowledgeable in the scriptures, free from egoism,
and who correctly understands according to the treatises the ritual for the embers,
as well as the procedure for invocation, the mantras, the fire-oblation, the worship, and the dismissal;
Having worshipped him with garments and ornaments, that best of Kuja-s should be given to him.
Just as he has been heard of and just as he has been known, so indeed, having fasted with devotion, [one should say]:
"O Bhauma, O Bhavodbhava, be pleased with me according to the extent of my wealth."
Reciting this supreme mantra, he should present it to the Brāhmaṇa;
and that learned Brāhmaṇa, in turn, should utter this mantra:
"I accept this auspiciousness; may there be auspiciousness for both of us."
"May there be well-being and health for both the giver and the receiver"—
this is the mantra for the recipient.
Thus, when the fourth [period] has arrived, no acquisition of wealth occurs.
Then, devoted to the worship of the mantra, one should perform this again until the fall of the body, thereby becoming a partaker of the fruit as described;
one with little wealth should perform all of this according to one's capacity.
Having given a garment made of sesame fibers on a Thursday coinciding with the fourth lunar day,
according to this procedure, one shall partake of the aforementioned fruit.
Likewise, he who observes the fast on the fourth day with devotion when it is conjoined with Mars [shall obtain the same].
Listen, Yudhiṣṭhira, to the fruit of that merit:
having remained here for a long time, surrounded by the prosperity of sons and grandsons,
at the end of his bodily existence, he becomes possessed of divine vigor, anointed with divine perfumes and unguents.
Surrounded by a host of celestial women and seated upon an excellent celestial chariot,
he goes joyfully to the city of the gods, greeted with acclaim by the deities. There, like the Lord of the Gods himself, he enjoys himself for a long time together with the deities.
After thirty-six cycles of the four yugas, at the end of that period of time,
he returns here and is born again into a great family—
handsome, wealthy, eloquent, charitable by nature, and devoted to compassion.
And a woman who is endowed with beauty, fortunate, and possessed of noble birth,
surrounded by sons and grandsons, shall rejoice for a long time together with her husband.
Having rejoiced for a very long period, she shall again attain the state of heaven.
Thus has this procedure, along with its secret, been told to you, O King;
it is difficult for men and even for gods to attain. May prosperity be yours!
Indeed, the fourth lunar day of the bright fortnight when conjoined with Mars is recommended for the ritual worship of the gods and for the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍas) to the ancestors.
"O scion of the Kuru lineage, those who worship Kuja on that day upon the earth become recipients of great auspiciousness.

Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Aṅgāraka-caturthī Vrata," within the Caturthī Vrata section of the Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Yudhiṣṭhira Saṃvāda in the Uttara Parva of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*.
[Now begins] the description of the Vināyaka-snāna Caturthī Vrata.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Mādhava, for what reason do the undertakings commenced by the best of men fail to succeed? Being questioned by me, please tell me this."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Vināyaka was appointed by Rudra and likewise by Brahmā for the sake of accomplishing the goals of the world and for the leadership over the Gaṇas.
Learn now the symptoms of one who is afflicted by that [demon]:
in a dream he plunges excessively into water, sees shaven-headed men,
those dressed in saffron robes, and mounts upon carnivorous beasts.
He dwells together with outcasts, donkeys, and camels;
