likewise, while walking along, he considers himself to have been overtaken by others.
Dejected and with his undertakings frustrated, he sinks into despair for no apparent reason.
O King, a sinner is characterized by a loss of luster and signs of pallor;
he perceives himself as mounted upon a camel, or likewise upon a buffalo or a donkey,
and sees his vehicle as being occupied by demons near a cremation ground.
O tiger among the Kurus, at the end of the dream he shall behold his own body moist with oil and adorned with oleander flowers;
possessed by that [spirit], the prince will not obtain the kingdom— of this there is no doubt.
A maiden does not obtain a husband, nor does a woman obtain offspring or a fetus;
a learned Vedic scholar does not attain the status of a teacher, nor does his pupil obtain instruction;
a merchant does not gain profit, and a farmer likewise does not reap the fruits of agriculture.
His ceremonial bath (snapana) should be performed according to the prescribed rites on an auspicious day;
while he is covered with a cloth,
his head should likewise be anointed with all medicinal herbs and all fragrant substances, using a paste of white mustard seeds.
On the fourth day of the bright fortnight, or on a Thursday,
under the Puṣya constellation and the Vīra nakṣatra, O King,
while he is seated upon an auspicious throne, benedictions should be recited by virtuous brahmins in his presence.
Then the four [sages] devoted to the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas,
having worshipped Vyomakeśa, as well as Pārvatī and Bhūmija,
and then the white incarnation who is the father of Kṛṣṇa.
O Bhārata, [one should worship] Dhiṣaṇa, Kledaputra, Koṇa, Lakṣmī,
Vidhuntuda the son of Bāhulā, and Dhārin of Nandaka;
[these are to be taken] from a horse-stable, an elephant-stable, an anthill, a confluence, and a lake.
One should place earth, yellow pigment (rocanā), gems, and guggulu resin into the water.
Having brought this from a lake by four men of a single caste using jars,
one should likewise place a *bhadrāsana* upon the red hide of a bull.
The thousand-eyed, hundred-streamed [water], made purifying by the seers—with that I sprinkle you; may the purifiers purify me.
Om! May King Varuṇa grant you fortune, may Sūrya and Bṛhaspati grant you fortune.
May Indra and Vāyu grant you fortune, and may the Seven Sages grant you fortune. Whatever misfortune is in your hair, at your parting, or on your head;
whatever is on your forehead, in your ears, or in your eyes—may the waters destroy it forever.
Having bathed, one should offer mustard oil with a ladle made of udumbara wood into the head [of the image], while holding the wood-shavings in the left hand; namely,
Mita, Sammita, and likewise Śālakaṭaṅkaṭa.

At the end, having spread *kuśa* grass everywhere upon a winnowing basket at a crossroads, one should offer the bali-oblation with the names "Kūṣmāṇḍa" and "Rājaputra," accompanied by the word *svāhā*, the mantra for the offering, and a salutation.
Rice grains both prepared and unprepared, as well as rice mixed with meat broth, raw fish, and likewise meat— just this much;
along with fragrant flowers and the three kinds of liquor.
One should offer radishes, fried cakes, bread, as well as garlands of *uṇḍeraka* flowers,
rice with curd, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and sweetmeats wrapped in molasses;
then one should worship Ambikā, the mother of Vināyaka.
Having offered a full handful as the *arghya* oblation consisting of *dūrvā* grass, mustard seeds, and flowers, [one should pray]:
"Grant me beauty; grant me victory; grant me fortune, O Bhavānī; grant me sons; grant me wealth; and grant me all my desires."
O Goddess, make my power exceedingly strong, arising from the renown of my strength.
Wearing white garlands and garments, and anointed with white perfumes and unguents,
one should feed Brahmins and give a pair of garments even to the preceptor.
Having thus worshipped Vināyaka and the planets according to the prescribed rule,
one obtains the fruit of one's actions and attains unsurpassed prosperity;
likewise, one should always perform the worship of the Sun and apply the *tilaka* of one’s own lord.

By performing the rites for Mahāgaṇapati, one shall attain success. For men endowed with discipline and courage, bathing at Vaināyaka is highly praised here as it destroys obstacles. Those who perform this rite according to the prescribed rules, their undertakings will undoubtedly yield their desired fruits.

Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Vow of the Vināyaka-Snāna-Caturthī," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira;
herein is the description of the Vināyaka-Caturthī vow. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Now, O King, I shall describe to you a vow that causes no obstacles,
by the proper performance of which no impediment arises here in this world.
This vow should indeed be undertaken on the fourth lunar day of the month of Phālguna.
O King of kings, it is prescribed that one should eat sesame and rice as the breaking of the fast after eating only at night;
that very same food should be offered into the fire, and it should likewise be given to a Brāhmaṇa.
[Salutations] to the Hero, to the Valiant, to the Elephant-faced One, to the Pot-bellied One, and indeed to the Single-tusked One.
Having thus performed the worship, the observer of the vow should again perform a fire sacrifice (*homa*) for the sake of destroying obstacles.
Having likewise observed the vow during the four months (*cāturmāsya*), he should then, in the fifth month,
have a golden elephant-faced image made and cause it to be given to a Brahmin.
O King, these should be accompanied by four copper vessels filled with milk-rice (pāyasa),
and a fifth vessel made of clay containing sesame seeds, presided over by Gaṇeśa.
One who lacks wealth, however, may have the vessels made of clay.
In the same manner, one should cause a silver image of Heramba to be given according to this rite.
By performing this vow in this way, one is liberated from all [obstacles] by means of the Brahmins.
Long ago, when an obstacle arose for the horse-sacrifice, Sagara [acted thus].
Having observed this very vow, he recovered the horse once more.
Likewise, in the past, when the god Rudra was destroying Tripura, he performed this very same rite; therefore, Tripura was destroyed by him.
While entering the ocean, I observed this very vow;
by that means, the earth, together with its mountains and trees, was raised up once again.
In former times, other rulers of the earth as well performed this very same act.
O scorcher of foes, for those seeking the fruits of austerity so that their sacrifices may be accomplished without obstacle,
by the mere performance of this [rite], one is liberated from all [sins] along with all the Brahmins;
upon death, one goes to the city of Rudra, according to the word of Varāha.
No obstacles ever arise in the home of one who,
performing the rite at night on the fourth lunar day, worships Vighneśa— the end of all impediments— who possesses the form of a crescent moon on his seventh digit.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Vināyaka Caturthī Vow," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Thus ends the fourth ritual manual.
Description of the Śānti Vow. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
I shall now proclaim the vow of peace; listen with a focused mind.
By its performance, there shall always be peace for householders.
O King, on the fifth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Kārtika—
Having undertaken this for one year, he should eat food devoid of sour substances at night,
after worshipping the Lord Hari seated upon Śeṣa;
[he should worship] the feet with "To Ananta" and the hips with "To Dhṛtarāṣṭra."
One should worship the belly for Takṣaka, the chest for Karkoṭaka,
the ears for Padma, the pair of arms for Mahāpadma,
the breast for Śaṅkhapāla, and the head for Kulika.
In this manner, one should worship Viṣṇu, who is omnipresent, as if he were distinct;
with speech restrained, one should perform a ceremonial bath for Hari using milk.
In his presence, the wise practitioner should offer oblations of milk along with sesame seeds.
Thus, at the end of the year, the wise man should provide a feast for Brahmins; having fashioned an image of Acyuta out of gold,
he should also give a cow with its calf, a pair of garments, a brass vessel, and milk-porridge.
And one should bestow gold upon a Brāhmaṇa according to one's ability.
O lord of men, for him who performs this vow with devotion in this manner,
there shall be constant peace and likewise freedom from fear of the Nāgas.
Having worshipped the Lord of the King of Birds, the Sacrificial Person (Yajñapuruṣa), who reclines upon the coils of the serpent Śeṣa and whose birth is beyond union (Ayogasūti)—
for those who worship Him with sweet offerings on the bright fifth days (Śukla-pañcamī), no fear arising from serpents shall approach them.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Vow of Peace" (Śāntivrata), in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the Sārasvata Vow.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Madhusūdana, by what vow does one's speech become sweet?
O Keśava, by what means do people attain good fortune, excellence in the sciences, skill in the arts,
inseparability between husband and wife as well as with their kinsmen,
and a long life?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O King, you have asked well; listen now to the Sārasvata vow, by the mere glorification of which Sarasvatī becomes pleased in this world.
Whatever devout man should perform this unsurpassed vow,
he should first worship it with a Brahmin at the beginning of the year and then practice it accordingly;
furthermore, on a Sunday, when the planets and stars are in a favorable position.
Having fed them milk-rice (pāyasa), one should perform the recitation by Brahmins;
one should also give white garments along with gold according to one's ability,
and worship Gāyatrī with devotion using white garlands and unguents.
Having first recited these mantra-words with palms joined in reverence, [he said]:
"O Goddess, grant this boon so that the Blessed One Brahmā, the great grandfather of the worlds, may never remain apart from you."
O Goddess, may those perfections (siddhis) be mine which were mastered by you— the entire corpus of the Vedas and Shastras, as well as dance, song, and the rest—
just as Lakshmi, Medha, Vararishthi, Gauri, Tushti, Prabha, and Mati.
"O Sarasvatī, protect me with these eight forms.
Having thus worshipped Gāyatrī— who holds a lute and a rosary of beads,
and who carries a water-pot and a book— with unbroken grains (akṣata) during the bright fortnight out of devotion;
One who knows the Dharma should eat in silence at both morning and evening;
and on the fifth day of each fortnight, having honored married women,
one should offer a *prastha* of rice along with sesame seeds and a vessel of clarified butter.
"May the Gāyatrī be pleased with this milk and gold.
Then, during the twilight (saṃdhyā), one should observe silence and perform that vow;
one must not eat in between until thirteen months have passed.
Upon the completion of the vow, one should give a meal with white rice,
a full set of two fine garments, a cow, and a meal to a Brahmin;
and to the Goddess, an awning, a bell, and a white-eyed cloth.
One should also worship the preceptor, the guru, with devotion, offering sandalwood, a pair of garments, and curd-rice topped with mountain-shaped mounds,
free from stinginess regarding wealth, and with cloths, garlands, and ointments.
Whoever performs the Sarasvata vow according to this procedure becomes possessed of learning, endowed with wealth, and possesses a melodious voice;
by the grace of Sarasvatī, he becomes a poet like Vyāsa.
Any woman who performs it likewise partakes in that fruit;
she shall dwell in the world of Brahmā for as long as thirty thousand kalpas.
Whoever hears or even recites this Sārasvata vow—
He too shall dwell in the city of the Vidyādharas for thirty thousand kalpas.
Those who worship Sarasvatī, the mother and progenitor of the world, with this excellent vow for one year,
become sweet-voiced, endowed with beauty, and skilled in many arts.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Sārasvata Vow," in the Uttara Parva of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[Now follows] the description of the Nāga-pañcamī vow. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O King, the fifth lunar day increases the joy of the Nāgas;
indeed, on the fifth day there is a great festival for the Nāgas.
Vāsuki, Takṣaka, Kālika, and Māṇibhadra [participate in it].
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Raivata, Karkoṭaka, and Dhanañjaya—
these grant fearlessness to living beings who subsist by their very lives. Those men who bathe the Nāgas with milk here on the fifth lunar day [attain this merit].

They always grant fearlessness to living beings within their families. When the Nāgas were cursed by their mother and were burning day and night, they were extinguished by the milk of cows; from that time forth, cows have been beloved.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Janārdana, how were the Nāgas cursed by their mother, and for what purpose and cause? And how did the destruction of that curse come about?"
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"The king of horses, Uccaiḥśravas, is white in color and born from the nectar of immortality.
Seeing him, Kadrū, the mother of the serpents, spoke to her sister."
"Behold, behold this white jewel of a horse, born of the nectar of immortality!
Why do you look upon these black children as if they were all white today?
Vinatā said.
"This excellent horse is entirely white; it is neither black nor red.
Why do you see it as black? Vinatā said this to her sister. Kadrū replied:
"I see the young Kṛṣṇa accompanied by one eye;
you, however, have two eyes, O Vinatā, yet you do not see him—make a wager!
Vinatā said:
"O dark-haired one, I shall become your slave once you have revealed [the snakes];
if you do not reveal them, O Kadru, you will become my slave.
Having thus concluded their bargain, she departed filled with rage.
While everyone was fast asleep and free from faults, Kadrū thought a crooked thought;
having summoned her sons, she said, "Becoming small, stay upon the excellent horse in the gambling hall; I shall defeat Vinatā, who is greedy for victory."
Procustes and the Nāgas, having seized that crooked-minded Kadrū, said:
"This is a great unrighteousness; we will not carry out your command.
Enraged, Kadrū cursed them: "The Fire shall consume you!"
When a great deal of time has passed, O Janamejaya, that Pāṇḍava will indeed perform a snake sacrifice on earth, which is very difficult for others to accomplish;
and at that sacrifice, the fire-god Tigmāṃśu will consume [the snakes].
Having thus cursed [her], Kadrū then said nothing in reply.
Cursed by his mother, the Naga Vāsuki, tormented by grief, fell to the ground in a swoon. He did not know what ought to be done.
Seeing Vāsuki distressed, Brahmā spoke to him consolingly:
"Do not grieve excessively, O Vāsuki; hear my supreme words.
There is a twice-born man named Jaratkāru, born in the lineage of the Yāyāvaras."
At that time, there will be one of great splendor, a treasury of asceticism;
you shall give your sister Jaratkaru to him,
and he will have a son renowned as Astika.
The sage, having honored the king, will indeed suppress with his words that great and flourishing sacrifice which causes fear to the Nāgas; therefore,
this sister of yours, endowed with beauty, nobility, and virtue, [should be given].
"Jaratkāru must indeed be given to Jaratkāru without hesitation.
Whenever he is entreated in the forest and says anything whatsoever,
that must be carried out in its entirety if one desires one's own welfare."
Having heard the words of the Grandfather and having prostrated before Vāsuki,
he applied himself with supreme effort and acted exactly as he had been told.
Hearing that, all the serpents had their eyes wide open with great joy.
The best of serpents considered themselves as if born again;
for those submerged in the terrible ocean of the sacrificial fires from which there was no raft,
Āstīka will there become a boat that grants them fearlessness.
Having heard this, that King Agni, immediately thereafter, will cause the priests to desist from the sacrifice which is supremely enchanting to the Nāgas;
and on the fifth day, Brahmā spoke thus to Lelihāna.
Therefore, O Great King, this fifth auspicious beloved was formerly given by Brahmā to the Nāgas, who produce joy for them; indeed,
it was given after first providing food to the Brāhmaṇas according to their desire.
Having released them, let all the nāgas who dwell upon the surface of the earth,
those who reside on the Himālayas, those situated in the atmosphere or in heaven,
those great nāgas in the rivers, and those who frequent the lakes, be pleased.
Having offered salutations to all those serpents and brahmins at the step-wells and tanks, and having dismissed them according to the proper rite,
one should thereafter eat together with one's servants, O lord of men.
One should first eat sweets according to one's desire, and thereafter [eat other food]. Listen to me regarding the fruit obtained by one who observes this rule:
upon death, he goes to the city of the Nāgas, being honored by hosts of Apsarases.
Mounted upon an excellent celestial chariot (vimāna), he enjoys himself for as long as he desires.
Having returned here, this king shall become the most eminent among all kings;
he is born endowed with an abundance of all jewels and possessed of many vehicles.
In every Dvāpara age, this king shall be born for five lifetimes,
free from mental and physical ailments, and accompanied by his wife and sons;
therefore, the Nāgas should always be worshipped with ghee, milk, and other offerings.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, what becomes of that man whom serpents, filled with rage, bite? O Hari, tell me in detail."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O King, a man bitten by a snake who meets his death goes downward;
having gone downward, he becomes a snake devoid of venom—of this there is no doubt.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Tell me, what should be done if one's father, brother, mother, friend, son, sister, daughter, or wife has been bitten by a snake?"
"O Govinda, O tiger among the Yadus, tell me what gift, vow, or fast he should perform for the sake of liberation, by which he may attain the heavenly realm. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O King, the fifth lunar day (pañcamī) should be observed as a fast; it increases the prosperity of the nāgas.
O Indra among kings, listen to the procedure for this, which should be performed for one year.
O Lord of the Earth, it occurs during the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada.
And that [day] is declared most meritorious; it should be observed by those desiring a happy rebirth.
O bull of the Bharatas, the Pañcamīs should be known to occur at the end of twelve years.
On the fourth day, however, a single meal is prescribed, while on that [fifth day], eating only at night is proclaimed.
O King, listen: having fashioned a five-hooded serpent made of silver, or else of gold,
or even of wood, or perhaps of clay,
one should worship the serpent with devotion on the fifth lunar day.
Having worshipped the best of serpents with *karavīra* flowers, lotuses, beautiful jasmine blossoms,
fragrant flowers, and offerings of food (*naivedya*),
one should afterwards feed the Brahmins with ghee, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and sweetmeats (*modaka*).
The Nārāyaṇa-bali rite should be performed for a living being bitten by a snake;
one should satisfy the Brāhmaṇas with gifts and the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍas). O King, the release of a bull (vṛṣotsarga) should be performed once a year has passed.
Having performed his ablutions, he should offer water, saying: "May Kṛṣṇa be pleased here.
O King, [the serpents are] Ananta, Vāsuki, Śeṣa, Padma, Kambala, as well as the Nāga Takṣaka and the Nāga Aśvatara.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Śaṅkhapāla, Kāliya, Takṣaka,
and the great nāga Piṅgala are proclaimed [as the presiding deities] month by month.
At the end of the year, there shall be the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) and the feeding of great brāhmaṇas.
O King, according to the one learned in the Itihāsas, a serpent should be fashioned out of gold;
likewise, a reddish-brown cow with her calf and a bronze milking vessel should be given.
O Pārtha, this is the rule for the breaking of the fast proclaimed by the wise.
When that most excellent vow is performed, even those kinsmen who have fallen into a low state— those bitten by the fangs of venomous serpents— attain a good rebirth.
Those who shall practice this supreme vow with devotion for one year [shall likewise attain such a state].
The danger from fanged creatures will be released for them, and they shall attain an auspicious state.
Whoever should constantly hear this or recite it, endowed with devotion,
there shall never be any fear of serpents anywhere within their family.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Likewise, in the month of Bhādrapada, on the fifth lunar day,
a man endowed with faith who paints serpents using black and other colors—
One should worship with perfumes, flowers, clarified butter, guggulu resin, and milk-rice;
then Takṣaka and the other serpents will attain satisfaction toward him.
For seven generations of his lineage, there shall be no fear from the Nāgas.
Therefore, a wise person should worship the Nāgas with every effort.
Likewise, O descendant of Kuru, on the fifth day of the month of Āśvayuja,
having fashioned Nāgas out of Kuśa grass, one should worship them along with Indrāṇī.
O Lord of the People, having bathed [the image] with ghee, water,
and milk, one who is pure and endowed with devotion should offer various kinds of food— such as wheat soaked in milk and diverse edible delicacies— to the various deities on this day.

One should worship them, O tiger among the Kurus; for him, O King, Śeṣa and the other Nāgas become pleased in this world, and he attains auspicious peace. Having reached the world of peace, he rejoices for eternal years.
Thus, O Hero, has this supreme Pañcamī vow been described.
In this regard, the mantra that wards off all defects is now declared:
(Oṃ Kurukulle hūṃ phaṭ svāhā).

Those who, with devotion, worship the serpents on the Pañcamīs of the month of Śata with offerings of flowers, in their homes the serpents always grant fearlessness; indeed, they become eternally full of supreme joy and radiant splendor. Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Nāga-Pañcamī Vow," in the Uttara Parva of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the Śrīpañcamī Vow.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
How is that prosperity attained which is difficult to obtain in the three worlds?
"Whether by charity, or by austerity, or by vow, or by restraint;
or by recitation, oblation, salutation, or by various other purificatory rites—
tell me this, O best of the Yadus, for you are considered by me to be all-knowing."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: It is heard that in former times, the auspicious Śrī was born to Bhṛgu from Khyāti;
she was given by the sage to Vāsudeva for the increase of the human race.
Vāsudeva, too, having obtained her— whose breasts were full and elevated,
whose large eyes were like lotus petals, whose face resembled the full moon,
and who illuminated the expanse of the quarters like the very radiance of the sun in person.
O King, he took delight with her, whose hips possessed great splendor, who moved with the gait of an elephant in rut, and whose mind was agitated by amorous play;
and she [took delight] with Viṣṇu, the conqueror of the world, the lord of the three realms.
Having attained her goal, she who regarded honor, fame, and wealth as her only treasure considered herself fulfilled;
the entire world became joyful and nourished by her radiant presence,
and the surface of the earth indeed became filled with bliss, as if gazed upon by the Goddess Lakṣmī herself.

The world became secure, well-supplied with food, free from disease, without lamentation, and undisturbed; likewise, it was free from agitation and its calamities were stilled. In heaven, the gods rejoiced, as did the Dānavas and Daityas who had arrived there.
And the serpents in the subterranean realm have expanded the full extent of their hoods;
in the heart, the oblation is consumed by the Brahmins in the sacrificial fire;
and the four castes, remaining unmixed, are protected by kings, O Pārtha.
Having seen this, Virocana and the other foremost Daityas,
self-restrained, began to perform austerities while taking refuge in the sacred fire;
they did so through sacrifices such as the Somasaṃsthas, the Havissaṃsthas, the Pākayajñas, and others.
The world was gradually pervaded by those who were devoted to virtuous conduct, who undertook what was desired by those longing for their own welfare,
who were preeminent in righteousness, and whose souls delighted in the study of the Vedas.
Through their prowess, they took possession of the world step by step.
The pride of the gods arose from the power of the play of Lakṣmī;
through that pride, their character, purity, and truthfulness were instantly destroyed.
Then, having abandoned those fickle gods who were bereft of truth and purity, [Lakṣmī departed].
Out of devotion to his family deity, he went to the clan of the Dānavas; there,
those whose bodies were permeated by the goddess Lakṣmī, yet who were arrogant in mind and haughty with pride,
began to conduct themselves unjustly.
"We are the Vedas, we are the sacrifices, we are the sciences, and we are the world.
We are all the inhabitants of heaven, including Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śaṅkara, and the rest.
Having recognized those best of Dānavas as being deluded by egoism, [he spoke].
Then, her mind bewildered, that daughter of Bhṛgu entered the ocean;
with her gone into the midst of the milk-ocean, the three worlds became depleted of their accumulation of wealth, devoid of joy, and stripped of their splendor.
Then, considering himself to have lost his fortune, the slayer of Śambara asked the brahmin Aṅgiras: "Tell me of some vow by which prosperity may be attained,
and once obtained, shall not waver again."
O Sage, even if she is steadfast, she becomes available for enjoyment by friends and allies;
yet that prosperity should not be considered one's own, for she is like a maiden kept in the house who is enjoyed by friends,
allies, and servants for the sake of others.
Having heard these words of Śakra, the noble-minded Bṛhaspati reflected and recounted the auspicious Śrīpañcamī vow,
which was formerly declared by someone as the most excellent of all vows.

He then related that [matter] to him in its entirety, including all its secret mysteries. Having heard it, the Lord of the Gods, along with the gods, Daityas, Dānavas, Gandharvas, and Yakṣas whose impurities were destroyed, began to perform it.
Together with Siddhas of celebrated conduct, with the all-powerful Viṣṇu, with Brāhmaṇas who know the reality of Brahman, with capable kings,
and with some characterized by a sattvic nature and others by a rājasic nature—
Likewise, O Lord, some performed this vow characterized by darkness (tamas). When that vow was mostly completed with supreme devotion,
a fierce battle then ensued between the gods and the dānavas.
"Having churned the ocean, the lord of rivers, by the strength of our arms,
let us recover the nectar for the welfare of the dwellers of heaven.
Having made this agreement, they churned the abode of Varuṇa.
Having made Mount Mandara the churning stick and Vāsuki the rope,
the radiant moon of cool rays was born from the waters as they were being churned;
immediately thereafter, Lakṣmī emerged from the midst of the Ocean of Milk.
Having looked upon all those foremost among the Daityas and Dānavas,
she beheld them and quickly went to the auspicious chest of Viṣṇu;
for by that very rite, the vow performed by Viṣṇu, she was born from the ocean.
Remaining within his body, she became one whose eyes were whirling with confusion;
moreover, because this was performed by Śakra through his *rājasa* nature,
he thereby attained the great prosperity of sovereignty over the three worlds.
It was indeed practiced by the Daityas and Dānavas whose minds were shrouded in darkness;
consequently, their sovereignty became as if seen and then lost.
Thus, the world—including gods, asuras, and humans—became possessed of prosperity.
O best of the worlds, by the power of this vow, old age shall not afflict you.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Kṛṣṇa, how is this vow performed by men, and when?
"O best of the Yadus, tell me everything that is undertaken and brought to completion.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, at the rising of the sun..."
O protector of the earth, one should quickly establish a vow for the fast in the heart of a friend;
one should have an image of the goddess Lakṣmī made of gold, silver, brass, copper, clay, or wood, or depicted upon a painted cloth.

[One should meditate on] Padmā, who holds a lotus in her hand, whose complexion is like a lotus, and whose eyes are like lotus petals; she is being bathed by the lords of the elephants of the quarters with excellent golden jars. Then, when three watches of the night have passed, [one should perform the rite] either at a river or in one's home.
One should perform the bath without agitation, with the same ritual care as that shown toward Śakra.
Having satiated the gods and the ancestors, one should then proceed to the temple of the deity.
There, one should worship the Goddess with flowers appropriate for that season.
Salutations to Capalā for the feet; salutations to Cañcalā for the knees;
salutations to Kamalavāsinī for the hips; repeated salutations to Khyāti for the navel; salutations to Manmathavāsinī for the breasts; and salutations to Lalitā for the two arms.

One should worship the throat with "Salutation to Utkaṇṭhitā," the facial orb with "Salutation to Mādhavī," and the head with "Salutation to Śrī"; then, one should respectfully present the food offering,
as well as fruits according to availability and heaps of sprouted grains.
Then the married woman (suvāsinī) should be honored with flowers and saffron;
one should feed her sweet food, prostrate before her, and bid her farewell.
Thereafter, a prastha measure of rice, accompanied by a vessel of ghee, [should be given].
"It should be given to a Brahmin with the words, 'May Śrīśa be well-pleased.
Having completed that in its entirety, one should then eat while remaining restrained in speech.
O Bhārata, this should be performed month after month according to this rite."
O King of kings, month by month, one should recite: "May Śrī, Lakṣmī, Kamalā, Saṃpat, Umā, Nārāyaṇī, Padmā, Dhṛti, Sthiti, Puṣṭi, Ṛddhi, and Siddhi be pleased," in due order.
Then, when the twelfth month has arrived and the fifth day,
having prepared a pavilion of cloth perfumed with flowers and incense,
one should place Lakṣmī upon a bed, accompanied by all necessary ritual implements.
Adorned with eight pearls, her breasts veiled by a silken cloth,
accompanied by the seven grains and endowed with the [six] flavors and minerals,
she is graced by sandals, shoes, an umbrella, a vessel, and a seat.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite, he should give [the image] to a Brahmin who maintains a family,
or to Vyāsa, a knower of the Vedas, or to whomever he himself chooses;
having given the cow along with its appurtenances and her calf, he should ask for forgiveness.
O Goddess, who arose from the churning of the ocean of milk, whose abode is the chest of Viṣṇu, and who grants all desires—bestow prosperity upon me; salutations be unto you!
Then, having honored married women with auspicious garments and ornaments, [one should proceed].
Having fed [the guests], he should afterwards eat himself along with his kinsmen.
O Pārtha, for him who thus performs the Śrīpañcamī vow with devotion,
prosperity shines in his home for twenty-one generations.
A woman who performs this rite, having obtained permission from her own husband,
becomes fortunate, beautiful, and the mother of many sons.
This Śrīpañcamī vow, beloved by Murāri, she performs with devotion while worshipping the daughter of Bhṛgu.
Having enjoyed his own kingdom on earth—the pleasures to be experienced by auspicious beings—he goes to the world of Madhusūdana.

Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Śrīpañcamī Vow," within the *Pañcamīvrata-kalpa* of the *Śrīkṛṣṇa-Yudhiṣṭhira-saṃvāda* in the *Uttara-parvan* of the glorious *Mahāpurāṇa Bhaviṣya*.
Thus concludes the *Pañcamī-kalpa*.
Description of the Viśoka-Ṣaṣṭhī Vow.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Janārdana, please tell me now the rules for the Ṣaṣṭhī vow.
"The pacification of all diseases and the bestowal of the fruits of all actions—
I have heard that the Sun, when worshipped, grants everything.
Therefore, O Keśava, tell me how to propitiate the Maker of Day."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O best of men, I shall describe the incomparable Viśoka-Ṣaṣṭhī;
by fasting upon it, a person never experiences grief again in this world.
Having bathed with black sesame seeds on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha,
and having taken food [on the previous day], one should perform the preliminary cleansing of the teeth for the sake of emaciation; then,
having undertaken the vow of fasting, one should remain celibate during the night.
Then, having risen at dawn and performed his ablutions, being thus purified,
he should fashion a golden lotus and worship it with the thought,
"This is the Sun," using a red oleander flower and a pair of red garments.
"Just as your abode is always free from sorrow by you alone, O Āditya,
so may I possess freedom from sorrow, and may devotion to you remain with me in birth after birth.
Having thus worshipped on the sixth lunar day, one should worship the twice-born according to one's ability.
Having slept and consumed cow's urine, and having risen with firm resolve,
he should worship with a Vedic mantra and, accompanied by a vessel of jaggery,
present a pair of very fine garments to a Brāhmaṇa.
Having eaten food without oil or salt on the seventh lunar day while observing silence,
one who desires prosperity should thereafter listen to the Purāṇas.
By this procedure, everything [is accomplished] during both fortnights.
One should continue this until the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha.
At the conclusion of the vow, one should donate a water-pot accompanied by a golden lotus,
as well as a bed with its furnishings and a milch cow of the Kapila breed.
Whoever performs the Viśoka-ṣaṣṭhī according to this rite, free from stinginess regarding wealth, attains the supreme goal;
for as many as a hundred and ten million plus one thousand births, he shall remain [in that state].
Free from disease and misfortune, he does not encounter sorrow so long as he obtains in abundance whatever desire he may pray for;
but he who performs [this rite] without desire goes to the Supreme Brahman.
Whoever recites or even hears this "Sixth" [chapter] which destroys sorrow,
he too attains the world of Indra and is never born into suffering anywhere.
Those who, having observed a fast, worship and bow down to Bhāskara, the maker of day, with oleander flowers (karavīra), [attain the same].

Free from suffering and grief, they shall dwell together with their friends upon the earth and then attain the world of the Sun. Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Viśoka-Ṣaṣṭhī Vow," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira; herein is the description of the Kamala-Ṣaṣṭhī Vow.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
I shall likewise describe another auspicious Padmaṣaṣṭhī;
by fasting on this day, a person becomes liberated from sin and attains heaven.
In the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa, on the fifth lunar day, one who is firm in his vows should fast on the sixth day, have a lotus made of fine gold,
and give it, together with sugar, to a Brāhmaṇa who maintains a household.

Having fashioned an image of gold, the knower of Dharma, having performed his ablutions, should offer a single fruit in the morning, saying, "May Bhānu be pleased with me. Having honored the Brahmins with devotion on the seventh lunar day, he should partake of a meal of milk.
Having performed [the rite], one should renounce the fruit; and as for that which is the Kṛṣṇasaptamī,
having fasted on this day according to the rule and in this very sequence,
one should indeed give that golden fruit accompanied by gold lotuses.
O Great King, having fasted on both the sixth lunar days for a full year, one should give [the gift] accompanied by a vessel of sugar, cloth, and garlands; then,
one should gradually recite the mantras of the Sun.
"Bhānu, Arka, Ravi, Brahmā, Sūrya, Śukra, Hari, Śiva,
Śrīmān, Vibhāvasu, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Varuṇa— may he be pleased.
Thus, one should recite each name individually on the seventh lunar day of every month.
One should perform this practice by effecting the abandonment of the result through its counteragent.
At the conclusion of the vow, one should honor a Brahmin couple with garments and ornaments,
and give a jar of sugar accompanied by a golden lotus and fruit.
O Ravi, just as the month of Phālguna is always [fruitful] for your devotees,
so may there be the attainment of infinite fruit in birth after birth for whoever observes this Phala-ṣaṣṭhī,
which bestows infinite fruit.
Freed from all sins, he is glorified in the world of the Sun.
Whatever [evil], such as the drinking of liquor, has been committed here or in the hereafter, all that goes to destruction; he goes to the world of the Sun.
He who hears or even reads this shall deliver twenty-one generations of men—both those born and those yet to be—and he too shall become a partaker of auspiciousness.

Having fasted on the sixth lunar day according to the rules, one should give a golden fruit together with a lotus and a water-pot to an eminent brahmin; having bowed to the Sun, whose feet are rubbed by the crest-jewels of gods and demons, that mortal attains the perfection of his desires.
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Kamala-Ṣaṣṭhī Vow," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[Now follows] the description of the Mandāra-Ṣaṣṭhī vow. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:

Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the meritorious sixth lunar day known as Mandāra, which destroys all sins, grants all desires, and is auspicious. On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, a man should eat light food.
Then, having used a tooth-stick, the wise man should fast on the sixth lunar day;
having duly honored the Brahmins, he should consume a mandāra flower at night.
Then, having risen at dawn and performed his ablutions, he should again [honour] the twice-born.
Having fashioned eight mandāra flowers, one should feed [the guests] according to one's ability;
likewise, one should fashion a very beautiful golden image of Puruṣa with a lotus in his hand.
Having made an eight-petaled lotus out of black sesame seeds in a copper vessel, [one should place it there].

One should worship with mandāra flowers in the eastern petal with the mantra "To Bhāskara," and likewise with a prostration in the southern petal with "To Sūrya"; similarly, one should worship in the south with "To Arka" and in the southwest with "To Aryaman."
In the west, one should worship Vasudhātṛ; in the northwest, Caṇḍabhānu; and in the north, Pūṣan. Beyond that, one should worship Ānanda.
Then, upon the pericarp (karṇikā), Puruṣa should be worshipped with the mantra "Sarvātmane."
Having wrapped it in white cloths and honored it with various foods, garlands, fruits, and so forth,
he should then give all of that to one who knows the Vedas.
The householder, restrained in speech and facing the east, should eat [the remainder] without oil or salt.

By this procedure, one should perform everything every month on the seventh lunar day for as long as a year, free from any stinginess regarding wealth. At the conclusion of the vow, however, one should place this very [image] upon a water-pot.
One desiring prosperity should give [this] together with cows to one who is radiant.
Homage to the Lord of Mandāra and to the abode of Mandāra!
And may you indeed deliver us from this mire of saṃsāra.
The mortal who performs the Mandāraka vow according to this rite becomes free from sin, happy, and rejoices in heaven for a kalpa.
This [vow] is a true lamp that serves as a wick to dispel the darkness of the mass of clouds of sins.
A man walking through the night of saṃsāra will not stumble if he holds onto this;
whoever reads or even hears this celebrated Mandāra-Ṣaṣṭhī, which bestows the fruits of desired objects, is also liberated from sins.

Having fasted on the sixth lunar day and worshipped the Sun upon the pericarp of a sesame-lotus with flowers from the celestial tree (*suravṛkṣa*), men attain that state which they could never reach even by gifting cows, land, gold, or sesame seeds. Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Mandāra-Ṣaṣṭhī Vow," in the *Uttara-parvan* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the Lalitā-Ṣaṣṭhī Vow.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Yudhiṣṭhira, on the sixth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada, O auspicious one—
A beautiful woman, well-attired and captivating to all the world,
having performed her morning bath in a great river and gathered sand,
should go home without weariness, carrying it in a new bamboo vessel.
Observing a fast with great care, she should worship the Goddess there;
having constructed a beautiful cloth pavilion covered with lamps, curtains, and nets,
and having installed the Goddess therein, she should worship her with fresh flowers.
Having meditated upon Lalitika Gauri, who dwells in the forest of asceticism,
one should worship her with this mantra and with the most beautiful flowers of the *campaka*,
as well as the *karavīra*, *nemāli*, and *mālatī*.
Having taken blue lotuses, ketaki flowers, and likewise tagara,
one should take eight hundred or twenty-eight buds of each with unbroken grains; with these, one should worship the Goddess.
Having bathed at Gaṅgādvāra, Kuśāvarta, Bilvaka, and the Nīla mountain, and having reached Lord Hara after bathing at the Kanakhala tīrtha, one should proceed,
O Lalitā, O Lalitā Goddess, bestower of happiness and good fortune!
"Salutations again and again to that Goddess who has arisen from good fortune.
Having thus worshipped according to the prescribed rite, one should place the food offering (naivedya) before her,
consisting of *kūṣmāṇḍa* gourds, *karkaṭī* cucumbers, *karkoṭa* pumpkins, and *kāravella* bitter melons.
With unbroken grains of rice marked with circular designs on the limbs, along with lamps, incense, and alaktaka dye;
together with incense mixed with molasses, sohalaka, and karaṃbaka;
with flowers dipped in molasses, ear-ornaments, modakas, and mukhamodakas.
Having thus worshipped according to the prescribed rites, she should then keep a vigil at night;
accompanied by her friends, that virtuous woman should pass the night in great splendor with songs, instrumental music, dancing, parasols, and beautiful spectacles.

A woman should not close her eyes for the four watches of the night; by closing her eyes, she may become unfortunate, miserable, or barren. Having thus performed the vigil on the seventh day, she should lead [the image] to a river.

Then, having worshipped with perfumes and flowers accompanied by song and instrumental music, that [offering], as well as the food offering (naivedya) and so forth, O best of men, should be given to the eminent brahmin. Having bathed and returned home, one should duly offer oblations into the sacred fire (vaiśvānara).
Having worshipped the gods, the ancestors, and human beings, as well as a married woman,
young maidens, and fifteen Brahmins should be fed with various kinds of foods and drinks; and liberal sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) should be given to them.
Having said, "May Lalitā be pleased," one should dismiss them.
Listen to the fruit of the merit of whoever performs this Lalitikā vow with devotion— whether a man or a woman.
There is nothing in the world of men that cannot be attained by her;
endowed with happiness and good fortune, she shall reach the realm of Gaurī.
She who, on the sixth lunar day, having gone into the water, takes sand in an excellent bamboo vessel and worships it in due order, [attains these rewards].
Having kept a vigil at night with songs and dances performed without agitation, she indeed shines like Lalitā in the three worlds.
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Lalitā-Ṣaṣṭhī Vow," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira;
followed by the "Description of the Worship of Kārttikeya."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O best of the Bharatas, this sixth lunar day (Ṣaṣṭhī) in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa is meritorious,
a destroyer of sins, auspicious, blessed, peaceful, and dear to householders.
Having slain Tāraka on the sixth lunar day, Guha shone like the king of stars;
therefore, that lunar day is beloved by the Lord of Kārttika. Any rite performed on that day, such as bathing and giving gifts, is said to be inexhaustible.

In that [tithi], those who behold the son of Gaṅgā (Bhīṣma) residing in the southern region are liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin; of this there is no doubt. Therefore, on this day, one should observe a fast and [worship] Kumāra made of gold.
O Great King, one should have [the image] made either of silver or even of clay;
then, having bathed in the afternoon and sipped water, being restrained in one's vows,
one should remain in meditative absorption (samādhi), seated in the lotus posture (padmāsana) and contemplating the son of Gaṅgā (Bhīṣma).
Then the learned Brāhmaṇa, taking a new water-pot,
should pour a stream [of water] upon his head while facing south—
a stream purified by the ashes of Śiva and consisting of the lunar orb.
"O Lord of the World, this Gaṅgā, the daughter of the Mountain, has fallen upon your head.
Having thus bathed and worshipped the Sun, the lord of the universe,
with flowers, incense, and other offerings, one should thereafter worship the son of the Kṛttikās."
"O Lord, O General Skanda, Kārttikeya, Bhavodbhava,
Kumāra, Guha, Gāṅgeya, O wielder of the spear— salutations be unto you!
Having worshipped him with these names, one should present the food offering (naivedya).
One should worship fruits, sacrificial fees, food, and sandalwood produced from the Malaya mountains;
one should also honor two goats and two cocks standing at the sides, who are dear to the Lord,
as well as a peacock with its tail-feathers complete, and the daughter of the Snowy Mountain (Pārvatī) in person.
Having worshipped Skandavallabha at the side of Kṛttikākaṭaka,

one should perform a fire-oblation with sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter using those very names. Having thus completed the rite according to the rules, O Yudhiṣṭhira, the fruit is indeed as follows.
Having eaten these, one should sleep on the ground upon a well-spread bed of *darbha* grass.
One should likewise consume coconut, citron, orange,
jackfruit, lime, pomegranate, grapes, and other heart-pleasing mango fruits.

O King, one who is self-restrained and firm in his vows should eat the *śrīphala*, the *āmalaka*, the cucumber, and the plantain fruit in that order. If these are unavailable, he should, being vigilant, eat the fruit of the *kalakālaugha* tree.
In the morning, one should present to a Brahmin a goat or a cock fashioned of gold, saying, "May Senānī be pleased.
And he who was born in the army as Guha, the six-faced son of Krauñca’s enemy, [is that Senānī].
Gāṅgeya, Kārttikeya, Svāmī, Bālagrahāgraṇī,
Chāgapriya, Śaktidhara— these are remembered as the twelve door-keepers.
One should recite their names in order during each month, saying, "May they be pleased."
Having first fed the Brahmins, he should afterwards eat while restraining his speech.
Thus, at the end of the year, in the auspicious month of Kārttika,
having worshipped Kārttikeya with garments along with ornaments, [he should proceed].
Gāṅgeya and Kārttikeya likewise should perform this once;
having completed the annual rite accompanied by recitation and fire-offerings,
O King of kings, he should give it to a Brahmin, especially to one who is a reciter.
These Brahmins are known as divine; other twice-born ones are of the earth.
O Pārtha, when this vow is observed, one shall be crossed over from the ocean of worldly existence.
Thus, whether it be a man or even a woman, whoever performs this with devotion—
Having obtained his auspicious desire in this world, he goes to the same world as Indra.
O lord of the earth, Kārttikeya is always to be worshipped;
indeed, it shall be declared that no one other than Kārttikeya is to be honored by kings.
The hero who worships the son of Kṛttikā while going to battle conquers everything,
just as Indra conquered the Dānavas in war;
therefore, one should worship the son of Śaṅkara with every effort.
When worshipped with true devotion, he grants all desires.
O best of the Bharatas, the man who observes the *nakta* fast on the sixth lunar day shall be liberated from all sins and always go to the son of Gaṅgā.
Having heard this, one who is endowed with faith should go to the southern month and,
having reached the temple of Śiva, worship the Lord of the Gods—
the primordial deity Skanda, Guha, born from the Śara-reed forest, the son of Śambhu and the beloved of the Daughter of the Mountain King.
"He experiences unimpeded pleasures in heaven and becomes a commander-in-chief, bearing the burden of sovereignty.

Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Tārakavadha-Kārttikeya-pūjā-Ṣaṣṭhī Vrata," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[Now follows] the description of the Vijaya-saptamī Vrata.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Lord, when is the seventh lunar day (Saptamī) to be worshipped, and by what duration of time? What is its fruit, and what is the specific rule? Tell me, O son of Devakī.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: When the seventh lunar day (saptamī) of the bright fortnight falls on a Sunday, that saptamī is named Vijayā; whatever is given on that day yields great fruit.
Bathing, giving gifts, recitation, fire-offerings, and likewise fasting—
all these on Vijayā-saptamī destroy even the greatest sins.
He who performs circumambulation of the Sun with fruits and flowers [attains great merit].
He obtains an unsurpassed son endowed with all virtues.
The first [offering] is made with coconuts, the second with red ginger,
the third with citron fruits, and the fourth with plantains.
The fifth [offering] is with excellent kūṣmāṇḍa fruits; the sixth with ripe *teṃduka* fruits;
the seventh should be offered with eggplants (*vṛntāka*), numbering one hundred and eight.
Likewise, [offerings may be made] with pearls, rubies, sapphires, and *karketana* gems.
With one hundred and eight gems of gomedaka, vajra, and vaiḍūrya;
with akṣoṭa, badara, bilva, karamarda, and sabarbara fruits;
and with the fruits of āmra, āmrātaka, jaṃbīra, jaṃbu, and karkoṭikā.
On the Vijayā-saptamī day, one should perform circumambulation of the Sun with flowers, incense, fruits, leaves, modakas, auspicious guṇakas,
and other desirable fruits, as well as with sugar-cane products that are free from knots.
One should perform circumambulation of the Sun; one should predict the fruit according to the fruit [of the circumambulation].
One should not enter, nor converse, nor say anything at all.
With single-mindedness, one offers [the mind] for the contemplation of the Sun.
A stream of wealth (vasordhārā) should be offered with cow’s ghee to the Sun;
one should fasten a moon-shaped parasol adorned with small bells for victory.
Having anointed [the image] with saffron, one should worship it with flowers and incense.
Having offered the auspicious oblation, one should thereafter ask for forgiveness:
"O Bhānu, Bhrāskara, Mārtaṇḍa, Caṇḍaraśmi, Divākara!
Grant me health, long life, victory, and a son; salutations be unto you!"
This Jayasaptamī, which is observed by one engaged in religious vows through fasting, eating only at night, or likewise eating only what is unasked for,
liberates the sick from disease and enables the poor to attain prosperity.
A sonless man obtains a son, and knowledge shall come to one who seeks it.
O Pārtha, when the seventh lunar day (Saptamī) falls during the bright fortnight along with the Sun,
one should spend seven such Saptamīs subsisting on mung beans at night.
Having bathed on the ground upon palāśa leaves and having offered oblations according to the prescribed rite, one should,
upon the completion of the vow, give a golden [image] mixed with mung beans to an excellent brahmin,
especially to the reciter.
On the seventh [tithi], O best of men, when joined with the Sun,
one who knows all should fast according to this rule and perform the worship and the consumption of the mantra using the six-syllabled mantra.
A man should perform worship and fire-rituals one hundred and eight times; then,
upon the completion of the vow,
O Pārtha, he should have a beautiful golden image of the Sun fashioned, placed within a vessel of refined gold.
One should give red garments, saffron-dyed cloth, and perfume along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a brahmin of the twice-born caste for the successful completion of the rite, using this mantra:
"Oṃ, salutations to you, Bhāskara, the noble deity, the bestower of glory."

Be the bestower of my desired objects today; salutations again and again! One who desires eternal satisfaction for the ancestors and the gods should offer gifts, houses, beds, and ancestral rites (śrāddhas).
A journey is auspicious for travelers and for kings seeking victory;
then, victory is certain for ascetics and men alike. For this reason, it is forever renowned in the world as Vijaya-saptamī (the Seventh Day of Victory).
Thus, O Pārtha, this lunar day (tithi) bestows desires upon men in this world;
it is auspicious, granting happiness in the hereafter and leading to the world of the Sun.
One who gives on this day becomes an enjoyer of pleasures, clever, long-lived, free from disease, and happy.
Having come here, one becomes a king possessed of elephants, horses, wealth, and jewels;
or if it is a woman who performs [this rite], she too becomes a sharer in that merit.
O Pārtha, you should never entertain any doubt in this matter.
That which leads to heaven, bestows the fruits of desired happiness and wealth, and is sought after by the foremost of sages as the most excellent among lunar days—
that Vijayā always grants victory to those men who are intent upon worshipping the lotus feet of the Sun.
Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Narration of the Vijayā-Saptamī Vow," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the Ritual for the Solar Orb.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Now I shall tell you yet another gift that brings about supreme welfare.
The so-called Ādityamaṇḍala, which destroys all that is inauspicious,
should be made with white barley flour or wheat flour;
it should be well-baked, resembling the orb of the sun, and filled with molasses, cow-products, and clarified butter.
Having worshipped the Sun with devotion, one should prepare an auspicious mandala before him,
made specifically of red sandalwood or, preferably, saffron.
Having established the mandala there, it should be well-honored with red cloths.
"O Pāṇḍava, it should be given to a Brāhmaṇa with this mantra:

'O Brahmin, may you accept this excellent silver object, produced from the splendor of the Sun and fashioned according to the prescribed rites, for my spiritual welfare. (Thus ends the mantra for the gift.)"

"O King, I accept this mandala, which grants desires, bestows wealth, is righteous, grants sons, and grants happiness; it is offered for the propitiation of Āditya. (This is the mantra for acceptance.
Having given [this] thus, O King, a man shines in heaven like the Sun.

One who has achieved all desires shall become the sovereign of the mandala. O Great King, beginning from the seventh day of victory, one should offer [worship] to the Sun day by day, according to one's ability and with a purified heart.
Having fashioned a solar disc (*ādityamaṇḍala*) made from wheat flour or barley flour, filled with unbroken jaggery and other sweets,
he who bestows it upon a twice-born man according to the prescribed rite becomes adorned with an immeasurable orb upon the earth.

Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Solar Disc," in the *Uttara Parvan* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the Vow of the Seventh Day to be Avoided on the Thirteenth [Tithi].
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
By fasting on which [day] does a man obtain the desires cherished in his mind?
"O Lord, tell me that one seventh [tithi] which bestows wealth and happiness.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "When the sun is in its northern course (uttarāyaṇa) and the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa) of the day has passed..."
One should undertake the Saptamī vow under a lunar mansion named after a male deity.
One should avoid rice, barley, sesame, mung beans, kidney beans, wheat, meat, honey, sexual intercourse, and vessels made of bell-metal.

On the sixth day, for the sake of success, one should strictly avoid ointments, collyrium, and powders ground on stone slabs. Having gratified the gods, sages, and the hosts of ancestors with water-offerings, and having worshipped those who have been "eaten by the hand" in the courtyard of the sky; and having offered into the fire many oblations of sesame and barley soaked in clarified butter, one should sleep upon the ground while keeping that sacred thread (or the sun) in one's heart. By avoiding those thirteen substances which are forbidden to people here, and by observing this for sixty-two years, O Bhārata, one attains happiness and whatever is desired by the mind for the duration of one year.

Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Vow of the Thirteenth-Excluded Seventh Day," in the *Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the *Uttara Parvan*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira;
followed by the description of the *Kukkuṭī* and *Markaṭī* vows. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
In former times, O Yudhiṣṭhira, a brahmin-sage named Lomaśa went to Mathurā;
he was honored there by Vasudeva and Devakī,
and having sat down, he recounted sacred and captivating stories.
Then he began to relate this story once more:
"When Kaṃsa was slain, your sons died; yet sons were born again and again.
Devakī, you have been one whose children have died, distressed by the sorrow for your sons."
Just as the girl Candramukhī, who had lost her son, became radiant with light and later,
having observed her vows, regained her child unharmed;
even so, O Devakī, you shall become [the mother of the Lord], of this there is no doubt.
Devakī said:
O Brahmin, who was that moon-faced woman who had many daughters? What was the excellent vow she performed that caused her to have such a large progeny?
The performance of virtuous deeds for the sake of the good increases fortune and health.
Lomaśa said:
In ancient times, there was a famous king in Ayodhyā named Nahuṣa.

In former times, that king had a chief queen named Candramukhī, and he also had a wife named Mānamānikā who was the wife of his very priest. Between them there existed a firm and enviable mutual affection.
Then those two friends also arrived at the waters of the Sarayū for the purpose of bathing,
and many women of the city likewise reached that very spot;
having bathed, they fashioned images of their husbands in manifest form within a mandala.
Having had an image of Śiva, the peaceful Śaṅkara, together with Umā, inscribed,
and having worshipped it with devotion according to the prescribed rites using perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata),
those men and women, desiring to depart after bowing down, were questioned by the two of them.
They said: "Śaṅkara has been worshipped by us together with Pārvatī;
our very selves have been offered to Śiva as threads made of golden thread.
This [body] shall consist of a stream [of life-force] only so long as the vital breaths are maintained."
Having heard their words, O Bhārata, those two friends of hers also bound him there with their arms as if with cords, according to that very agreement;
then they departed for their own homes, surrounded by their companions.
O King, after a long time had passed,
that vow of Candravatī was indeed forgotten by her while she was distracted;
and having died after some days and nights, she became a female monkey.
The proud one was born as a hen and generally roamed nearby;
likewise, the two who were friends were born [as herons] with memories of their former lives, and having come together, they again made an agreement as they had done before.
When that same time had arrived again on that very day, they did not die;
rather, they were born right there in that region of Mātṛka, endowed with cowherds (Gokula),
as the wives of the king, the lord of the earth.
The queen named Īśvarī was famous and beloved by the lord of kings.
Agnimīlā, the wife of the twice-born man named Bhūṣaṇa, became the priest’s wife;
in time, she became a hen that produced many offspring.
O King, she remembered her past lives, held a lotus in her hand, and had eight sons; yet, their offspring had died. Then, once again, an uninterrupted affection arose between the two of them.
There, Īśvarī gave birth to a single son who was afflicted with disease.
But at nine years of age, O Yudhiṣṭhira, he met his death.
Thereupon, grieving for her son, she— out of friendship and excessive affection— set out together with all her sons to see that Bhūṣaṇā.
Seeing that auspicious woman, who was always adorned by her very nature without needing ornaments and was blessed with a son, the mistress blazed up in rage; then,
filled with intense jealousy, she sent her friend back home.
During that night, she reflected upon the killing of her son:
"Though slain again and again, her sons live on, free from harm.
Then, having summoned her friend Bhūṣaṇā, who stood before her, she spoke.
The Goddess said: "O friend, what meritorious deed have you performed, by which your slain sons have been restored to life and we no longer have fear?
How is it that you, who have many sons, whose children are living, and whose ornaments are not yet removed?"
"O blessed lady, you shine exceedingly, like the lightning of the clouds.
Bhūṣaṇā said:
"O blessed one, on the seventh day of the month of Bhādrapada, at a reservoir of water..."
Having bathed and having drawn a Śiva-maṇḍala together with Ambikā,
one should worship it with devotion and, having bound a thread around the wrist, make this pledge:
"As long as I live, my very self is offered to Śiva."
Having thus made this agreement, from that time forward she should wear a cord made of gold or silver upon the fingers of her hands;
she should give a *maṇḍaka* or a *veṣṭikā* to a member of her mother-in-law’s family or to a Brahmin.
And you yourself, O friend, must not eat them for fear of breaking your vow.
Having placed silver and gold rings all around upon a copper vessel, O Yudhiṣṭhira, one should present them to a Brāhmaṇa.
One should offer auspicious brass vessels and eat from them oneself; having fully worshipped the mandala, the dwelling, the wealth, Śiva together with Śakti,
and the female companion (sakhi)— nothing difficult to obtain exists even throughout the three worlds.

Thus, O friend, that agreement which was previously made by me with you has been faithfully observed by me; therefore, I am well-established. But that agreement was broken by you out of pride, and the two bodies were abandoned.
Because of that, even while possessing a kingdom, she was miserable, her lineage having been severed.
Thus have I described to you the power of this vow.
O lady of excellent vows, I shall grant you half of that merit.
"Accept this out of friendship; there is no need for hesitation here.
Having said this, she then accepted the fruit of the gift of the vow.
That virtuous lady became a mother of noble offspring, and the queen of the gods attained liberation.
"By the power of this vow, O Devakī,
you shall have a son who will become the lord of the three worlds.
Having spoken thus to her, Lomaśa, the best of sages, [departed].

O Pārtha, he departed through the sky; this has also been told to you by me. O Yudhiṣṭhira, those men who shall practice this auspicious vow known as the *Kṛkavākuprasaṅga*, which is the life-story of Devakī, [shall attain their goal].
The continuity of their lineage shall never be interrupted.
And those women who practice this vow which bestows sons,
having dwelt in happiness in the mortal world, shall go to the abode of Śiva.
"She who, having placed the Teacher of the Moving and the Unmoving within her heart, performed the excellent *Kukkuṭī* vow together with the *Plavagī*,
she— whose song is beautiful and whose offspring is virtuous— explains that protection which destroys the flood of impurities for you both.

Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the *Kukkuṭī* and *Markaṭī* Vows," in the *Uttara-parvan* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the Vow of Both Seventh Days.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Hereafter I shall proclaim the most excellent ritual procedure for the seventh day (Saptamī-kalpa).
O Yudhiṣṭhira, beginning from the month of Māgha during the bright fortnight,
on the seventh day, O King, perform the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for the vow throughout the day and night;
having worshipped with the mantra "Varuṇa," one should then partake of the *brahmakūrca*.
On the eighth day, one should feed Brahmins sesame flour and rice with jaggery;
such a person obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
On the seventh day of the month of Phālguna, one should worship the Sun.

On the seventh day of the month of Caitra, one who worships Vedāṃśu with devotion obtains the merit equal to the Uktha sacrifice and the Vājapeya sacrifice, as previously described. A devoted man attains that same religious merit.

On the seventh day of the month of Vaiśākha, one should worship Dhātṛ; by doing so, a person fully obtains the merit of a sacrifice involving the immolation of animals. On the seventh day of the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should worship Indra.
Having worshipped the Sun on the seventh day of the month of Āṣāḍha, one obtains the difficult-to-attain fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice;
one obtains the abundant fruit of the Bahuvārṇa sacrifice.
On the seventh day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, one’s mother should also be honored;
by doing so, a person properly attains the auspicious fruit of the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice. On the seventh day of the month of Prauṣṭhapada, one who is pure should worship the Sun.
A person obtains the fruit of the tulāpuruṣa gift by worshipping the Sun on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja;
such a person obtains the fruit of the gift of a thousand cows.

On the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, the meritorious soul who worships the Sun, the seven-horsed Lord of Days, attains the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice. Having worshipped Bhānu according to the prescribed rite during the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, he likewise gains great merit.
Having worshipped the Sun according to the prescribed rites during the month of Pauṣa, one shall enjoy a tenfold fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice;
one obtains the abundant fruit of the Naramedha sacrifice.

On that very Kṛṣṇa-saptamī, O Yudhiṣṭhira, a wise man should diligently worship the Name while observing a fast for one year. Afterwards, when the vow has been completed, he should perform a sacrifice to the Sun.
Being pure, one should smear a level area on the ground with red sandalwood paste;
it should be one cubit, two cubits, or even four cubits in size.
Then, one should draw the solar disc using vermilion and red ochre.

Having worshipped with red flowers, lotuses, and incenses such as kunduraka and others, one should offer a diverse food offering cooked in ghee. One should place jars before [the deity] together with honey and rice.
Then one should perform the fire-ritual (agnikārya) after sprinkling the sacrificial fire with water;
using the mantra "Ākṛṣṇena," one should offer one thousand oblations with fuel-sticks produced from the Arka tree, along with sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter and molasses.
Then, O Yudhiṣṭhira, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given to the Brāhmaṇas;
having fed them, one should have them clothed in red garments or even white ones. In this rite, they praise twelve auspicious cows provided with garments.
One should cause an umbrella and a pair of sandals to be given to each individual brahmin.
Having thus dismissed those brahmins, one should eat oneself while maintaining silence.
O Pārtha, he who performs this most excellent Saptamī vow in this manner—

One who observes a fast on the seventh lunar day beholds the face of the Sun; such a person is born free from disease, endowed with beauty, eloquent, and long-lived. Those who behold the face of the Sun while fasting on that day are liberated from all sins and shall attain the world of the Sun.
"O Great King, this vow destroys all that is inauspicious,
pacifies all evils, and brings about physical health;
it bestows the world of the Sun at the end— thus spoke the sage Nārada."

Those who observe the fast on the seventh lunar day of both the bright and dark fortnights, and worship the sun—the possessor of rays—with the syllables of his name, become forever free from all diseases and happy; having thus become so, they remain for a very long time as attendants of the Sun.

Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Vow of Both Seventh Days," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the Kalyāṇasaptamī Vow.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Blessed One, [please describe] that which effects the crossing over the difficult ocean of saṃsāra.
"Please describe some vow that bestows heaven, health, and happiness.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "When the seventh lunar day of the bright fortnight falls on a Sunday,"
Then that highly meritorious day is called Vijayā.
On this day, one should perform a bath with cow's milk in the morning;
wearing white garments, one should fashion a lotus out of unbroken grains (akṣata).
Facing east, one should place an eight-petaled lotus in the center with a variegated pericarp;
then, on all the petals starting from the east, one should assign [the mantras] in sequence:
"Salutation to Tapanāya" and "Salutation to Mārtaṇḍāya" in the east.
In the south, [one should worship] with "To Divākara"; in the southwest, to Vidhātṛ;
in the west, to Varuṇa; in the northwest, to Bhāskara;
in the north, to Varuṇa; and on the eighth petal, to Ravi.
At the beginning, at the end, and in the middle, let there be salutation to the Supreme Self;
having thus worshipped with mantras illumined by concluding salutations,
[one should worship] with white garments, fruits, edibles, incense, garlands, and unguents.
One should worship with devotion upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) using jaggery and salt;
then, having distinguished the best of the twice-born by means of the oblation of the Vyāhṛtis,
one should satisfy them according to one's ability with devotion through jaggery, milk, clarified butter, and other offerings.

One should present a vessel of sesame seeds and gold to the preceptor. Having thus performed the observances and bathed, the man, having risen in the morning and completed his ritual bathing and recitation of mantras, should, together with the Brahmins, [partake of] rice-milk porridge with ghee.
And having eaten with those learned in the Vedas who are free from the "vow of the jackal," O King,
having thus performed all this at the end of the year,
one should perform the concluding rite (udyāpana) according to one's ability, while remembering the Sun-god within the heart.
One should present a vessel of clarified butter along with a water-pot and a water-jar;
or, even if one is destitute of wealth, one who is free from envy should give at least one milch cow adorned with garments and ornaments and having a golden face.
One should not practice stinginess regarding wealth; otherwise, one falls downward due to delusion.
Whoever performs the Kalyāṇa-saptamī according to this rule, or hears of it, or even recites it, is also liberated from sins.

And whoever should worship with flowers, incense, and ointments the Sun, the remover of the nine afflictions and the vessel of auspiciousness, within the pericarp of an eight-petaled lotus on the day following the sixth [tithi], that living being indeed becomes a recipient of prosperity.
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Kalyāṇasaptamī Vow," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the Śarkarāsaptamī Vow. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
I shall describe the Śarkarāsaptamī, which destroys all impurities.
By means of this [rite], infinite longevity, health, and sovereignty are produced.
On the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mādhava, one endowed with faith,
having bathed in the morning, [should worship] with pure sesame seeds, white garlands, and unguents.
Having drawn a lotus with a pericarp upon the sacrificial ground using saffron,
one should offer fragrance and flowers upon it with the mantra "Oṃ namo savitre. One should also place a water-pot together with a vessel of sugar.
Having well-adorned him with red garments, white garlands, and unguents,
one should worship him— yoked to a golden horse— with this mantra:
"Since he is composed of the Viśvedevas, he is recited as the proclaimer of the Vedas."
"You alone are the essence of all nectar; therefore, O Eternal One, protect me!
One should remain standing while reciting the Saura-sūkta or by listening to the Purāṇas.
When day and night have passed, on the eighth lunar day, having performed the daily obligatory rites,"
One should present everything to a Brahmin who is learned in the Vedas;
one should feed the Brahmins according to one's ability with sugar, ghee, and milk-rice (pāyasa).
Then, remaining silent, one may eat oneself, but without oil or salt.
By this rite, one should perform everything month after month;
at the end of the year, being composed in mind, one should again give to a Brāhmaṇa a bed covered with cloth and accompanied by a jar of sugar.
One should give a milch cow together with all its utensils,
as well as a house endowed with every kind of household implement according to one's means; one may give it even after providing for it a thousand or a hundred gold coins.
Out of devotion, a golden horse should be given with ten, two, or three *niṣkas*, or even half of that; the recitation of the mantra is to be performed as before.
One should not practice stinginess regarding wealth; by doing so, one incurs faults.
As the nectar-drinking Sun drank from his mouth, drops of nectar fell;
these, having risen up, are known as rice, mung beans, and sugarcane. Furthermore, sugar is considered to have originated from the juice of sugarcane.
Therefore, sugar is auspicious for the Sun and is meritorious for offerings to the gods and the ancestors;
this Śarkarā-saptamī bestows the fruit of a horse sacrifice (vājimedha).
Indeed, all [obstacles] attain pacification through it, and it further increases one's progeny.
He who performs this with supreme devotion goes to the Supreme Brahman;
he shall dwell in heaven for one kalpa and thereafter proceed to the highest station.
O sinless one, whoever hears this, remembers it, or recites it here in this world shall [attain] the realm of the Lord of the Gods.
"He who bestows even his counsel upon people is worthy of worship by the wives of the immortals and the Kinnaras.
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Śarkarā-saptamī Vow," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[Now begins] the description of the Kamalā-saptamī vow.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Hereafter, I shall describe the Kamala-saptamī,
by the mere glorification of which the Sun-god becomes pleased in this world.
Having bathed on the stainless seventh day (Amalāsaptamī) during the spring season,
one should place a golden lotus in a vessel of sesame seeds,
wrap it in a pair of garments, and then worship it with perfumes and flowers.
Salutations to you, O lotus-handed one; salutations to you, the sustainer of the universe.
O Maker of Day, salutations to you; O Maker of Light, let there be salutations to you.
Then, at the time of the two watches [of the day], accompanied by a water-pot—
Having honored a Brahmin with garments, garlands, and ornaments, one should give [the gift] to him;
then, when a day and night have passed, on the eighth day, one should feed the twice-born according to one's capacity. Afterwards, one should eat meatless food, free from oil.
By this procedure, on the seventh day of the bright fortnight month after month,
one should perform everything with devotion, free from stinginess regarding wealth.
At the conclusion of the vow, one should give a bed accompanied by a golden lotus.
He should give a milch cow, adorned with gold, according to his capacity;
he should also give desired articles such as vessels, seats, lamps, and other household utensils.
Whoever performs the Kamala-saptamī vow according to this rite, [attains the supreme goal].
Having attained infinite prosperity, he rejoices in the world of the Sun;
likewise, in kalpa after kalpa, having gone separately to each of the seven worlds surrounded by celestial nymphs, he then attains the supreme goal.
Whoever beholds this, hears it for even a moment, or recites it with devotion, bestowing their good will,
shall likewise attain unshakable prosperity in this world and go to the realm of the Gandharvas and Vidyādharas.
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Kamalā-saptamī Vow," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the Śubhasaptamī Vow. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
I shall now describe another auspicious vow, the Śubhasaptamī.
Having fasted on which [day], a man is liberated from disease, grief, and suffering.
Having performed his ablutions in the auspicious month of Āśvayuja and being pure with milk,
he should then cause the Brahmins to recite [the prayers] and commence the Śubhasaptamī rite.
One should worship the tawny cow with devotion using perfumes, garlands, and ointments:
"I bow to you, who were born from the Sun, the abode of the entire universe;
I bow to you, whose body is auspicious and blessed, for the sake of all spiritual accomplishments."
Then, having brought a prastha of sesame seeds together with a copper vessel,
