as well as a golden bull provided with cloth, garlands, and molasses,
one should give them at the hour of twilight, saying, "May Aryaman be pleased."
Having consumed the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), he should sleep on the ground free from envy.
Then, when morning has dawned, he should devoutly gratify the twice-born.
By this rite, a man should always offer [these gifts] month after month.
One should likewise worship two garments, a bull, and a golden image;
at the end of the year, one should provide a bed accompanied by sugarcane stalks and molasses, along with pillows, a place for repose, a vessel, and a seat.
One should give a copper vessel, a *prastha* measure of sesame seeds, together with a golden bull, to one who knows the Vedas, saying: "May the Soul of the Universe be pleased.
O King, he who performs the auspicious *Saptamī* according to this rule—
In birth after birth, he shall possess pure fortune and fame;
being honored by hosts of Apsarases and Gandharvas in the abode of the gods,
he shall dwell as a lord of the Gaṇas until the dissolution of all beings.
Having descended from that kalpa, he shall become the sovereign of the seven continents; indeed,
this auspicious Saptamī, once performed, brings about the destruction of a thousand killings of Brahmins and a hundred killings of embryos.
Whoever should recite this, hear it for even a moment, or behold it being given away even through association,
he too, having cast off his body after experiencing some distress here, attains the status of a leader of the Vidyādharas.
Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Śubhasaptamī Vow," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the Snāna-saptamī Vow.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
What rite should be performed out of distress, and by what is misfortune destroyed?
"What is desired in rites concerning those who have miscarried their offspring and in the case of bad dreams?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, sins committed in the past bear fruit here [in this world]."

I shall now describe the "Seventh-Day Bath" (Saptamī-snāna), which destroys the afflictions of disease and brings constant auspiciousness; it wards off poverty, miserable rebirths, physical deformities, and likewise the frustration of one's desires.

Where the drinking of milk is praised for the death of infants, I shall likewise describe here what is required for the pacification of the death of children, and so forth, whether they be old, diseased, or even in their youth.

O Great King, when this very Vaivasvata Manvantara of the Varāha Kalpa had arrived, during the Kṛta Yuga, there was a Haihaya named Rūpavardhana, whose mind was filled with wonder, agitation, anxiety, and distraction.

In former times, O descendant of Bharata, there was a most excellent king named Kṛtavīrya, who was possessed of great majesty. He protected the entire earth with its seven islands for seventy-seven thousand years.
It is said that as soon as he was born, his hundred auspicious sons met their destruction long ago due to the curse of a Yavana; however,
Kṛtavīrya, having propitiated the thousand-rayed Sun-god, attained his goal.
O Bhārata, through divine fasts and vows and by means of Vedic hymns,
he revealed himself to the radiant Kṛtavīrya.
Being questioned by Kṛtavīrya, Bṛhaspati spoke this:
O lord of men, through great hardship your son shall become long-lived; however, for the destruction of his impurities,
perform the ritual bathing on the seventh lunar day in a pond to eradicate his sins.
O King, for a woman who has given birth to a stillborn child in the seventh month,
a wise man— having obtained the strength of the house and stars and having performed the recitation by Brahmins—
should avoid that lunar day which corresponds to the birth asterism of the child.
Thinking, "Let this be performed for the virtuous, the elderly,
and the sick," he, with a one-pointed mind, [prepared it] upon ground smeared with cow dung,
using red śāli rice grains mixed with the milk of the varuṇā plant.
One should offer oblations according to the rules to Sūrya with the two *Udgāt* verses and also to the Mothers.
One should recite the hymn dedicated to the deity Sūrya and offer oblations of clarified butter into the seven-flamed fire.
Likewise, O Bhārata, one should offer oblations to Rudra with the *Rudrasūkta*.
In this case, fuel-sticks made of *arka* or *palāśa* wood should be offered there;
furthermore, a fire-oblation (*homa*) of one hundred and eight barley grains and black sesame seeds must be performed.
Having offered these, the wise man should perform a bath with Ganges water in the midst of the rite.
Having had a Brahmin learned in the Vedas, with darbha grass in hand,
duly place four beautiful jars in the four corners,
and a fifth one in the center, adorned with unbroken rice grains (akṣata).
One should place [the image] covered by a mirror, consecrated by the Seven Sages,
filled with water from the solar Tīrtha along with the *pūrṇacandra* flower,
and provided with all medicinal herbs and the water of the five *bhaṅgas*.
Having brought very pure earth from places associated with the five jewels, as well as from branches entwined [with creepers], from elephant and horse paths, from royal gates, from anthills,
from ponds, and from cow-pens— one should place it into all the jars, including the middle one which contains the gems. Furthermore, one should place it into all four jars that contain the gems.
Having taken hold of the Brahmin there, one should recite the solar mantras;
and here, seven women adorned with earrings should be fed according to one's capacity with garlands, garments, and ornaments.
And the consecration of the woman who has miscarried must be performed by Brahmins, [with the prayer]:
"May this child be long-lived, and may she become a mother of living sons;
[may he live] as long as the sun and moon, and the entire circle of planets and constellations."
May Śakra together with the world-protectors, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—
may these and all other gods always protect the young boy. May there be no fear of lightning, no fear of fire, and may there never be any danger from child-seizing spirits anywhere.
"May they not cause suffering to the child, nor indeed to the mother or the father.
Then, wearing white garments and accompanied by their husbands,
the women should devoutly worship the Seven Mothers with flowers, perfumes, and auspicious fruits.
Then, having fashioned a golden image of Dharmarāja and placed it upon a vessel of sesame seeds, one should present it to the preceptor,
along with garments, heaps of gold and jewels, and various foods including milk-rice mixed with ghee.
In the same way, one should honor the Brahmins and avoid stinginess regarding wealth. After eating with the Guru, this sequence of mantras should be recited:
"May this child have a long life and remain happy for a hundred years."
Whatever evil he possesses has been cast into the mouth of the boar.
May Brahmā, Rudra, Viṣṇu, Skanda, Vāyu, Śakra, and Hutāśana protect him from all wicked beings; may they always go forth as bestowers of boons.
While speaking such words and others, one should honor the gurus;
having given a tawny cow according to one's ability, one should bow down and dismiss them.
And having bowed to the Sun and Śiva along with her son, she should offer the *caru* oblation.
Then, having brought the remains of the oblation, one should offer it with the words, "Salutation to you, O Āditya.
This indeed is a wonderful yoga, and it is praised among wondrous rites.
At that time, during the birth of the trees, one should worship the gods.
"By performing this on the seventh day of the bright fortnight for the sake of peace, one does not come to grief.
O best of men, having spoken of this meritorious, purifying, and life-prolonging 'Seventh-Day Bath' (Saptamī-snapanam) of the Sun, the Sun-god vanished right there."
And by this ordinance, King Kārtavīrya Arjuna ruled this earth for ten thousand years.
One may seek health from the Sun; one may seek wealth from the Fire-god.
One should seek knowledge from Śaṅkara and seek liberation from Janārdana;
the knowers of the Vedas declare that this destroys even the greatest sins and is inexhaustible.
The sages say that perfection belongs even to him who hears this with undivided mind.
Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Snapanasaptamī Vow," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[Now follows] the Description of the Acalāsaptamī Vow.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:

O delighter of the Yadus, what is the fruit of this transient body, even if it is well-cooked, if it is deprived of the Māgha bath? Behold the bodies of embodied beings who are unable to perform the morning ablution.
Tell me, O best of the Yadus, what should be done by one who fears cyclic existence during the month of Māgha? For women do not endure physical hardship;
likewise, the delicacy of their bodies and their lack of stability [are obstacles].
And how may they be beautiful, fortunate, and likewise blessed with good offspring?
For all this is the fruit of merit well-performed here in this world,
by which very great merit is attained with little effort.
"O Ramādhava, tell me the truth regarding the ritual bath for women during the month of Māgha.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"Listen, O best of the Pāṇḍavas, to this secret spoken by the sages."

O best of the Kuru lineage, I have not told this Acalasaptamī vow to anyone. There was once a courtesan named Indumatī, endowed with beauty, generosity, and virtue, who was the beloved mistress of the King of Magadha.
Slender-waisted, with beautiful hips and full, elevated breasts,
her limbs were perfectly proportioned and her face resembled the full moon;
her beauty and delicacy were extolled by Kāma.
Merely by the sight of her, one becomes overcome with desire;
her form, like that of the moon, brings joy to the eyes,
and she is as captivating to all the world as the science of subjugation.
One morning, O King, as she sat with a serene countenance,
she reflected in her heart upon the instability of worldly existence,
having seen this entire world submerged in the ocean of the body within sense-objects.
No one perceives that the crocodiles of birth, death,
and old age are fashioned by the artisan Creator from the vessel of the elements, yet remain uncooked;
enveloped by the fuel of one's own karma, it is cooked by the fire of ignorance.
Those days which pass for men devoid of virtue, desire,
and wealth never return here again, unlike those men who are devotees of Hara.
[For them], bathing, charity, austerity, fire-offerings, Vedic study, and libations to the ancestors [bear fruit].
That day on which [this practice] is not performed is wasted for men;
for the minds of sons are indeed attached to their wives and homes. Like a she-wolf seizing a lamb, death approaches the door.
Having reflected thus, the courtesan Indumatī,
who moved with the gait of an elephant, then went to the holy hermitage of Vasiṣṭha;
there, having bowed with humility to the seer Vasiṣṭha as he sat, she [proceeded].
With palms joined in reverence, she spoke these words:
Indumatī said:
"An oil-presser is equal to ten slaughterhouses; a tavern-keeper is equal to ten oil-pressers."
A prostitute is equal to ten banners, and a king is equal to ten prostitutes. By me, nothing was given, no oblation was offered, no fast observed, nor was a vow performed;
Śambhu was not worshipped with devotion, nor was a single wealthy man sought as a refuge.
"Tell me now of some vow pertaining to the present time, by which I may cross over the ocean of worldly existence, with its flood of sins and waters of suffering.
Having heard this from her many times, the scorcher of foes [replied]: [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the portion available.]
The sage Vasiṣṭha, who is possessed of great compassion, spoke:
Vasiṣṭha said:
"On the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, [one should perform that which] bestows the fruit of all desires."
O fair-faced one, having performed this bath which generates austerity and good fortune, you should eat but a single meal on the sixth day; then, on the seventh day, while the water remains still,
you should move it at the end of the night after placing a lamp upon your head.
O King, on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, I moved Mount Acala;
yet, among all those things pure as water, not even one was moved.
Having heard these words of Vasiṣṭha on that day, O ruler of the earth.
Cakrāndumatī performed every rite of bathing and giving according to the prescribed rules.
By the power of bathing for three days, and having enjoyed all desired pleasures,
she attained the status of a leading Apsaras among the throngs of celestial nymphs in the world of Indra.
O Lord of the People, the ritual bath on Acalāsaptamī has been described;
it pacifies all sins and increases happiness and good fortune.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"The greatness of the seventh-day bath has been heard by me, yet not in detail. Now I wish to hear the procedure accompanied by its mantras.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Having worshipped the Sun-god while observing a single meal on the sixth lunar day,
one should go in the morning on the seventh day to a very deep body of water—
whether it be a confluence of rivers, a pond, or even a natural lake excavated by the gods.
One should perform one's bath as long as the water— which is easy to enter, unpolluted by wicked beings,
and undisturbed by beasts, birds, aquatic creatures, fish, and tortoises—
remains still.

Salutations to you who possess the form of Rudra; salutations to the Lord of the essences. Salutations be to Varuṇa; salutations be to you, O dweller in the waters. Whatever sin has been committed by me throughout seven lifetimes, from birth until now—
May that Saptamī, the mother of all beings, who dwells within the solar disc, destroy my disease and my grief, O seven-times-seven Saptamī! O Goddess, remover of all ailments, salutations to you!
Having bathed at a lamp situated on the water and having offered libations to the deities,
one should draw an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp using sandalwood paste. One should worship Śarva together with his consort in the center with the syllable *praṇava*.
Having worshipped Bhānu in the eastern petal, one should worship Ravi in the southeastern petal;
one should worship Vivasvat in the southern petal and Bhāskara in the southwestern petal;
Savitṛ is to be worshipped in the western petal, and Arka is to be worshipped in the northwestern petal.

To the north, one should worship the Thousand-rayed One (Sahasrakiraṇa), and to the remainder [the directions], the All-Self (Sarvātman). These should be worshipped preceded by the syllable Om (Praṇava) and joined with the word of salutation (Namaḥ) at the end.
Having covered the Sun with flowers, fragrant incense, and cloth—
Afterwards, one should dismiss them, saying, "May you go to your own abodes.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, one should place sesame powder, along with ghee and molasses, in a very wide vessel made either of copper or clay.
Having fashioned a golden palm tree and placed it upon sesame powder that has not been sprinkled with water,
one should worship it with red cloths, flowers, and incense.
Then, having offered that palm tree to a Brāhmaṇa while reciting the mantra, one should give it away.
By the grace of Āditya, one shall obtain the fruit of bathing at dawn.
I have bestowed this seal against evil, misfortune, and suffering;
having applied that seal, one should present it to a Brāhmaṇa.
"May this sun be pleased with me, together with my sons, cattle, and servants.
Then, one should worship the instructor of the vow with garments, cows, and sesame seeds;
having worshipped other Brahmins according to one's ability, one should return home.
Thus has been described to you this rite which brings about beauty and good fortune:

the bath on Acalāsaptamī, which bestows the fruit of all desires. He who thus recites this, or hears it even incidentally—this bath on Saptamī which removes the impurities of the Kali age—and he who, even incidentally, offers his intellect to it, shall, upon reaching the abode of the gods, be honored by the hosts of deities.

Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Acalā-saptamī Vow," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Now follows the description of the Budhāṣṭamī vow.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Pāṇḍava, listen once more as I describe the Budhāṣṭamī vow,
by the performance of which a man never beholds hell.
In ancient times, at the beginning of the Kṛta Yuga, there was indeed a king named Dṛḍha.
Surrounded by many servants, friends, allies, and ministers, he went to the side of the Himalayas; however, being forbidden by Mahādeva, he was told:
"Whoever else enters this earth shall certainly become a woman."
Following after the deer, that king entered that forest of trees alone with his horse; in an instant, he attained womanhood.
With full and elevated breasts, she wandered through the empty forest.
She did not perceive anything at all, such as "From where have I come?
The wise planet Budha beheld her, gentle and endowed with the qualities of beauty and nobility;
for on the eighth lunar day falling on a Wednesday, the planet Budha was pleased with her.
Pleased by the beauty of Ilā, he placed the embryo within her womb;
he brought forth a son who became known as Purūravas,
the king who founded the Lunar dynasty and was the first of all sovereigns of the earth.
From that time forward, O venerable Dharmarāja, the eighth lunar day (Aṣṭamī) joined with Wednesday pacifies all sins and destroys all calamities. Now, I shall tell you another narrative as well.
There was a king of the Videhas in Mithilā who was slain by his enemies in battle; that hero’s wife, a poor woman named Ūrmilā,
wandered the earth accompanied by her young son.
Having reached the region of Avanti, she stayed in the house of a Brahmin;
for the sake of filling her belly, she performed the tasks of husking and grinding daily.
Then, having stolen a few wheat grains, she gave them to the two children.
Out of compassion and maternal affection for those two who were tormented by hunger,
that virtuous and auspicious woman passed away after a long time.
Her son, having gone to Videha, ascended the throne of his father.
Seated there, he ate the cow with composure through his mastery of inner strength.
Having sought out the daughter of the Mithila lineage for the King of Dharma, she was wedded;
devoted to her husband, that great lady became his principal consort.
A woman of beautiful limbs named Śyāmalā is renowned and heard of in the sacred scriptures.
To that lady of noble hips, his beloved, Dharmarāja himself said:
"O Śyāmalā, you must carry out all the affairs within my household."
"O daughter of Videha, bestow gifts upon your kinsmen and servants as you desire;
however, these seven cages, firmly secured with stakes,
must never be opened by you."
Saying "So be it," she also performed her own duty.
Once, when the Lord of Dharma had become distracted,
the daughter of Videha opened [the door] first and saw her own mother.
Being cooked while crying out, she is bound by the terrifying servants of Yama and cast with ease into boiling oil again and again;
likewise, having been struck with a palm-staff, that high-minded woman was filled with shame.
In the second cage, she likewise saw her own daughter being plastered with lime by means of a stone slab and brick;
and in the third cage, she similarly saw her own mother.
In the fourth enclosure, she is split open on the head with saws attached to hands as large as clubs,
by those with terrifying and cruel faces;
being devoured by beasts of prey, she wails again and again.
In the fifth [hell], she is placed on the ground and crushed at the neck with the foot;
in rage, she is torn apart with pincers and blows from forest trees.
And in the sixth, she is placed within a sugarcane press and struck on the head with a mallet.

Seeing his mother thus situated in the seventh cage— constantly being crushed like a very firm piece of sugarcane, her voice choked with weeping, and reeking of a foul odor— he was himself dragged down by grief.
Dark-complexioned and with a dejected face, the beautiful woman said nothing at all.
Then Śyāmalā, filled with rage, spoke to her husband Yama as he arrived:
"O King, what very cruel thing has been taken from me by my mother?"
"Yama, seeing his beloved, said: 'O blessed lady, these seven cages by which you were being struck in many ways with various blows have indeed been opened by you;
for you were previously forbidden by me.'"
"O auspicious lady, do you not know that those wheat grains which were indeed taken by your mother out of affection for her son have provoked my anger?
For the property of a Brahmin, when consumed out of friendship, burns the family unto the seventh generation."
And that very [debt] burns him in the form of theft as long as the moon and stars exist;
these beings are wheat-grains in the form of most dreadful worms,
which were formerly stolen from the house of a Brāhmaṇa for your sake by this woman.
Śyāmalā said:
"I know all that was done to me by my mother in the past;
nevertheless, having obtained you, a virtuous son-in-law, she [is now at peace]."
"You shall be released from being a mass of worms; now, do that.
Having heard this, Dharmarāja remained for a long time absorbed in thought, and then spoke to his beloved wife, the mistress of his life and wealth, as she sat beside him.
Furthermore, in the seventh birth prior to this one, you were a virtuous Brāhmaṇī;
through association with your friends,
you observed the Budhāṣṭamī vow perfectly, which bestows the fruits exactly as described.
"Make a vow before me that you shall give her the fruit of that merit;
by that, your mother shall be liberated from the perilous hell of her sins.
Having heard this, she quickly bathed and gave away the merit she had performed.
Śyāmalā, her own mother, was pleased by that and attained liberation;
the auspicious Ūrmilā, endowed with beauty, assuming a divine body,
mounted an excellent celestial chariot, clothed in divine garlands and garments.
Even today, she is seen by people in the sky near her husband and near King Mithi,
beside Budha,
shimmering by the power of the eighth day of Budha, O Great King.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, if this Budhāṣṭamī is indeed such an excellent lunar day,
then tell me its ritual procedure, O Lord, if you are pleased with me."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen attentively, O Pāṇḍava, to the auspicious procedure for the Budhāṣṭamī;
whenever the eighth day of the bright fortnight falls on a Wednesday.
On each such occasion, she should be worshipped by men who eat but a single meal;
having bathed in a river in the forenoon, they should take a new pitcher filled with water,
containing ritual substances and accompanied by a vessel of fullness.
It should be performed eight times according to distinct rites:
the first should be done with sweetmeats (modaka), the second likewise with cream cakes (pheṇaka);
the third with ghee-filled cakes (ghṛtapūpa), and the fourth with fried dumplings (vaṭaka), O King.
The fifth [day] is with *śubhrakāra* sweets; likewise, the sixth is with *sohālaka*;
the seventh is with white *aśokavarti* confections combined with sugar-candy;
and the eighth is with fruits and flowers, as well as pure, unbroken *pheṇikā* cakes.
In this manner, one should gradually proceed with friends, kinsmen, and relatives;
having performed the rites together, one should eat while remaining composed in mind.
This is the best method for those observing fasts, as they should speak very softly.
Having heard the greatness of the Wednesday eighth lunar day (Budhāṣṭamī), one should renounce food;
indeed, one must not eat at all until the narrative is completed.
Likewise, having eaten in the presence of Budha, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) again and again.
Speaking thus, one should bestow it upon a Brahmin learned in the Vedas—
a beautiful image made of gold, accompanied by unbroken grains and gold,
and honored with various flowers, fragrant incenses, and lamps.
One should worship Budha, who has the form of the son of Soma and is clothed in yellow garments,
with one *māṣaka* of gold, or half of that, or even half of that again.
*Oṃ budhāya namaḥ*.
Oṃ, homage to the son of Soma! Oṃ, homage to the destroyer of evil intellect! Oṃ, homage to the bestower of noble intellect!
Oṃ, homage to her who is born from Tārā! Oṃ, homage to the gentle planet! Oṃ, homage to the bestower of all happiness! These are the mantras for worship.
But when the eighth lunar day is full, O best of royal sages,
one should feed eight Brahmins and give a cow along with its calf,
adorned with all kinds of garments, ornaments, and various decorations.
Having worshipped Budha together with his wife, O son of Kuntī, one should give [the offerings] such as earrings and finger-rings while performing the rite in this manner, reciting this mantra:
"May this Budha accept it; he himself is present here in this substance."
"It is given to the King of the Wise; may the Wise One be pleased with me.
(This is the mantra for the gift.
Budha is gentle, the son of Tārakā, the prince, and the lord of Ilā.
The prince who was the father of Purūravas, the king of the twice-born—
(this is the mantra for receiving [the gift]). And may the wise one, the son of the Moon, having destroyed the suffering born of my evil thoughts, grant me happiness and mental well-being.
Having recited this and taken [the object], one should give it accompanied by the mantra.
O King of kings, having been born for seven lifetimes, one shall become a rememberer of past births (jātismara);
endowed with wealth and grain, one’s sons and grandsons shall increase.
Having enjoyed a long life and vast pleasures upon the surface of the earth, and then,
having meditated upon the all-pervading Lord Nārāyaṇa while facing death at a sacred pilgrimage site,
that man, equal to Indra, attains heaven upon dying.
It remains thus until the end of creation, until the dissolution of all beings.
In this way, I have declared to you this supreme vow among all vows.
And thus, O Pārtha, I have explained to you this secret Budhāṣṭamī.
Having heard this, even a killer of a Brahmin or a killer of a cow is liberated from all sins.

Whoever, having reached the eighth lunar day conjoined with Mercury, worships the son of the Moon (Mercury) with devotion while he is situated upon the back of a ram, and beholds him with offerings of cooked food, vessels, and garments of various colors, shall never see the city of Yama. Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Budhāṣṭamī Vow," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of Janmāṣṭamī.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Acyuta, tell me in detail about the vow of Janmāṣṭamī."
"At what time did it arise? What is its merit? What rite is prescribed?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "O Yudhiṣṭhira, when the wicked demon Kaṃsa had been slain in Mathurā,"
Devakī, having embraced me and placed me upon her lap,
wept right there amidst the festival of the people gathered on the platforms at Raṅgavāṭa,
where the ancient wrestling match had taken place and the Kukuras and Andhakas had assembled.
Surrounded there by his own kinsmen, relatives, and affectionate friends along with their wives,
Vasudeva also wept out of paternal affection;
drawing him close and embracing him, he cried, "O my son, my son!"
With a faltering voice, dejected, and eyes clouded with tears, he embraced both Balabhadra and me again with joy, saying:
"Today my birth has become fruitful; my life is truly well-lived."
The union that had arisen from both of these excellent sons thus became joyful and flourishing for the couple throughout the year; indeed,
all the people, having prostrated themselves before them, were filled with great delight.
Having seen such a great festival, all the people said to me:
"O Lord, let grace be bestowed upon this world through your favor.
O Lord of the Universe, on the very day that Devakī gave birth to you..."
"O Vaikuṇṭha, grant it this very day; we shall build it here, salutations again and again!
O Keśava, bestow your grace upon us who have fully surrendered through devotion.
When the multitude of people had spoken thus, Vasudeva was greatly amazed.
Having looked at Balabhadra and me, she wept;
"So be it," she said, "tell the people exactly as it is.
Then, by her father's command, she likewise observed the Janmāṣṭamī vow.
O Pārtha, in Mathurā, before the multitude of people, this was fully revealed by me:
"Let the citizens,
beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, celebrate my birthday as Punarjanmāṣṭamī every year."
Kṣatriyas, those of the Vaiśya caste, Śūdras, and others who were righteous,
[perished] when the sun had entered the zodiac sign of Leo, while the sky was filled with clouds,
on the eighth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada at midnight.
When the moon was situated in the sign of Taurus and conjoined with the Rohiṇī asterism,
I myself was born to Devakī by Vasudeva, O people. Thus has this Janmāṣṭamī vow been fully described in the world.
O King, after that great festival of many forms by the side of the Blessed One,
it shall thereafter attain fame in the world as "Mathurā. May there be peace, may there be happiness, and may the people be free from disease.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Lord, what kind of vow is that which is observed by all the worlds?
O Puruṣottama, it is the sacred vow known as Janmāṣṭamī."
"O Lord of the worlds, O imperishable one, tell me by what means you attain satisfaction;
O Blessed One, Madhusūdana, please speak this to me out of grace.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:

O Pārtha, when that day has arrived, one who is filled with devotion should perform the cleansing of the teeth first and then take the vow of fasting. O descendant of Kuru, by performing this single fast alone, [one attains great merit].

One is liberated from all sins committed throughout one's entire life; of this there is no doubt. That which consists of dwelling with virtuous qualities after having turned away from sins, and which is devoid of all worldly enjoyments, is to be understood as true fasting (upavāsa).
Then, having bathed at midday in pure water such as that of a river,
one should construct a most beautiful maternity chamber for the goddess Devakī,
adorned with rubies and lotus petals, and anointed with auspicious substances.
The beautiful forest grove, adorned with protective gems and garlands,
should be made entirely like Gokula, crowded with the community of gopīs,
and provided with the sounds of bells and mṛdaṅga drums, songs, and auspicious water-pots.
Having tied up barley half the way along with walls adorned with svastikas and crowded with conchs and musical instruments,
and having bound the asuras with iron swords while providing them with beloved goats;
and having placed a pestle upon the grain, it was guarded by watchmen.
With offerings of various kinds made complete by the sixty goddesses, and so forth, the lying-in chamber (sūtikāgṛha) should be prepared in its entirety.
In the center of this, she [the goddess] is to be installed; she is remembered as being of eight types.

The ear-ornament (karṇikā) may be made of gold, silver, copper, bell-metal, clay, wood, or even precious gems; it may be engraved or painted. Endowed with all auspicious characteristics, she lies half-asleep upon a couch.
Resplendent like molten gold, that ascetic woman, having set out with me,
gave birth at that very moment and was filled with joy; meanwhile,
I remained on the couch with the infant sleeping, nursing at her breast.
With the Śrīvatsa mark upon his chest, full and possessing the luster of the petals of a blue lotus,
Yaśodā also gave birth right there to an excellent daughter. There, the gods, Nāgas, Yakṣas, Vidyādharas, and men [were present].
The gods and asuras stood with their hands extended at the tips of flower garlands, bowing down;
they seemed to move through the sky amidst the ever-rising ramparts.
Vasudeva also stood right there, bearing sword and shield.
Kaśyapa was born as Vasudeva, and Aditi as Devakī;
the serpent Śeṣa became Balabhadra, and Yaśodā was born from Aditi.
Prajāpati Dakṣa became Nanda, and the four-faced Brahmā became Garga.
O Indra among kings, this is their incarnation: Kaṃsa here is born from Kālanemi.
And all those various Dānavas appointed by Kaṃsa, bearing diverse weapons, are the guards who have fallen asleep, stupefied by slumber.
His divine cows, herds of elephants, and Dānavas with weapons in their hands [attend him];
the Apsarases dance joyfully, and the Gandharvas are intent on singing;
and there, in the very pool of the Yamunā, Kāliya is to be depicted.
Having thus performed this delightful rite, O Pārtha, one should worship Devakī, who has recently given birth, with devotion using perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains, fruits,
pumpkins, coconuts, dates, and pomegranates.

O Yudhiṣṭhira, having meditated upon the previously described incarnation, one should worship with citron fruits, betel nuts, lakuca fruits, trapusa fruits, and likewise with handfuls of flowers produced in the appropriate season and place, using this mantra.
Constantly surrounded by Kinnaras and others singing, attended by lords of sages holding censers, mirrors, water-pots, and fly-whisks, and served by the sounds of flutes and lutes—
she who sits perfectly upon a well-spread couch with a most joyful mind, a mother of sons, that goddess Devakī, the mother of the Divine, of lovely form and beautiful countenance, is victorious.
Near the feet of Devakī, Śrī was massaging her feet.
Seated upon a lotus, she is to be worshipped with the mantra: "Obeisance to the Goddess.
Oṃ, obeisance to Devakī; Oṃ, obeisance to Vasudeva;
Oṃ, obeisance to Balabhadra; Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
"Oṃ, obeisance to Subhadrā; Oṃ, obeisance to Nandā; Oṃ, obeisance to Yaśodā.
Having thus recited these names individually, all the twice-born should perform the worship. For women and Śūdras, however, it is to be done without mantras.
Some excellent twice-born ones desire another ritual procedure here:
at the rising of the moon, one should offer the *arghya* oblation to the Moon while remembering Hari—
the sinless Vāmana, Śauri, Vaikuṇṭha, and Puruṣottama.
Vāsudeva, Hṛṣīkeśa, Mādhava, Madhusūdana;
Vārāha, Puṇḍarīkākṣa, Nṛsiṃha, the beloved of the Brāhmaṇas;
Dāmodara, Padmanābha, Keśava, whose banner bears Garuḍa.
Govinda, Acyuta, Kṛṣṇa, the infinite and unconquered;
Adhokṣaja, the seed of the universe, the cause of creation, preservation, and destruction;
Viṣṇu, without beginning or end, the Lord of the three worlds, Trivikrama.
Nārāyaṇa, four-armed, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace;
eternally clad in yellow garments and adorned with a forest garland;
marked with the Śrīvatsa, the bridge for the world, the bearer of Śrī, the Lord of Śrī—Hari.

Salutations again and again to Govinda, the Lord of Yoga, who has arisen from Yoga, the Master of Yoga. (This is the mantra for bathing. Salutations again and again to Govinda, the Lord of Sacrifice, who has arisen from Sacrifice, the Master of Sacrifice.
This is the mantra for the application of unguents, the offering of water (arghya), worship, and incense.
Salutations again and again to Govinda, the Universe, the Lord of the Universe, who has arisen from the Universe, the Master of the Universe.
(Thus ends the mantra for the food offering.
Salutations again and again to Dharmeśvara, the Lord of Dharma, the source of Dharma, Govinda.
(Thus ends the mantra for the seat of the lamp.)
O you who were born from the Ocean of Milk, O you who arose from the eye of Atri,
O Moon, lord of the stars, together with Rohiṇī, accept this water offering from me.
One should then install the deity upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), as well as Rohiṇī accompanied by the Moon.
By worshipping Devakī, Vasudeva, Yaśodā, Nanda,
and likewise Baladeva, one is liberated from all sins;
at midnight, one should cause a stream of wealth (vasordhārā) to fall with jaggery and clarified butter.
Then, the celebration of my birthday, the naming ceremony on the sixth day, and so forth, should be performed by me at that very moment during the night; and on the morning of the ninth day,
a great festival for the Goddess should be conducted just as it is for me.
One should feed the Brahmins according to one's capacity and give them a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),
such as gold, silver, cows, garments, and flowers;
whatever is most dear to oneself, one should offer with the thought, "May Kṛṣṇa be pleased with me."
Salutation to that Self of Brahman, whom the goddess Devakī bore from Vasudeva for the protection of the earthly Brahman;
salutation to Vāsudeva of noble birth, who acts for the welfare of cows and Brāhmaṇas.
Having said, "May there be peace; may there be auspiciousness," one should dismiss [the deities].
O son of Dharma, my devotee who performs such a great festival for the Goddess Devakī year after year for the Blessed One, [attains the highest reward].
Whether a man or a woman, one shall obtain the aforementioned fruit:
a lineage of sons, health, wealth, grain, and other excellent household goods,
as well as a most beautiful district filled with rice, sugarcane, and barley.

In that kingdom, the lord enjoys long life and all things desired by his heart; there is no fear of enemy armies in that realm, O Pāṇḍava. The rain-god shall shower according to wish, and there shall be no fear of calamities.
O son of Pāṇḍu, in whichever house this Devakī-vrata is observed,
there shall be no exit of the deceased, nor miscarriage of the fetus;
furthermore, it is my conviction that there shall be no fear of disease there.
There is no association with physicians, nor even quarreling in the home;
whoever performs the Janmāṣṭamī vow, even through mere contact [with it],
O Pārtha, he too attains the world of Viṣṇu— of this there is no doubt.
The Janmāṣṭamī, which delights the minds and eyes of people, instantly destroys sins, and brought joy to the cowherd Nanda—
by worshipping Devakī along with her consort on this day here, one obtains sons and attains the abode of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Janmāṣṭamī Vow," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
The Description of the Dūrvāṣṭamī Vow.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Yudhiṣṭhira, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, [one should observe this vow].
Whoever, endowed with faith, performs the meritorious vow of Pūrvāṣṭamī,
his progeny for seven generations shall never suffer decline;
his lineage shall always rejoice and flourish, just as it was before.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
From where did this dūrvā grass originate, and why is it long-lived?
And why is it pure? O Lord of the World, tell me this.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Formerly, when the Ocean of Milk was being churned by Viṣṇu in his quest for nectar, Mount Mandara was supported by him with his arms and thighs.
As he was indeed whirled about with great speed, his body hairs were raised up;
these very hairs, tossed up from that ocean by the waves of water,
became beautiful, auspicious *dūrvā* grass and lovely green meadows.
Thus was this dūrvā grass produced, its body as slender as the moon;
and upon it was placed the supreme churned nectar by the gods,
dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, and vidyādharas.
There too, drops of the flowing nectar from the vessel of immortality fell;
as soon as she was touched by them, this dūrvā grass became delicious, ageless, and immortal— venerable,
pure, and formerly saluted and worshipped by the gods.
On the eighth day, with fruits and flowers— namely dates, coconuts, grapes,
walnuts, wood-apples, barbaras, lakucas,
oranges, jambukas, mangoes, bījapūras, and pomegranates— [one should worship].
With curd, unbroken rice, beautiful flowers, incense, food offerings, and lamps—
O King of Kings, listen with an attentive mind— to this mantra:
"O Dūrvā grass, you are born of nectar and are praised by both gods and demons."
Having bestowed good fortune and progeny, become the accomplisher of all my purposes.
Just as you have spread across the surface of the earth with branches and sub-branches,
so too grant me a lineage that is free from old age and death.
Thus, O Pārtha, this [Goddess] was formerly worshipped by the best of the thirty gods,
as well as by their wives, daughters-in-law, and sisters;
she was honored and praised with words, O King, by Gaurī and likewise by Śrī.
In the world of mortals, [he was attended] by Vedavatī, Damayantī, and Sītā;
by Sukeśī, Ghṛtācī, Rambhā, and Sukeśā; by Sahajanyā, Kāmakandalyā, Menakā, Urvaśī, and others.
Durva grass, when worshipped by women alone, bestows good fortune and happiness;
having bathed, wearing clean garments, and accompanied by female friends and well-wishers,
one should give gifts to the Brahmins, offer fruit, and worship the Lord.
O Pāṇḍava, those women who, having eaten sesame paste, wheat, and the seven grains, shall perform this ancient vow among their friends, companions, relatives, and kinsmen; |||

Known as Dūrvāṣṭamī, it is meritorious and brings about progeny. Having remained for a long time in the mortal world with all those [benefits] such as happiness, good fortune, sons, and grandsons, they then go again to heaven.
Rejoiced there by the gods along with their husbands and kinsmen,
they dwell in delight until the dissolution of all beings.

That auspicious eighth lunar day (Aṣṭamī) in the month of Nabhasya, which bears fruit when the sky is covered by clouds and at the edge of green forests— if a woman honors it with dūrvā grass, fruits, unbroken rice, and sesame seeds, she attains growth through sons and friends, just like the dūrvā plant itself.
Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Dūrvāṣṭamī Vow," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[Now follows] the description of the Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī vow. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Pārtha, listen to the vow of Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī, which removes the fear of sin,
generates righteousness in the world, and is supremely pleasing to Rudra.
When the month of Mārgaśīrṣa has arrived, one should first perform the cleansing of the teeth.

Whether it be the fast (*upavāsa*) or the eating at night (*nakta*), one should observe the prescribed rule. Having gone outside from his home, the wise man, having consulted his teacher, should perform this for one year on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, according to his capacity or incapacity.
A celibate practitioner who has conquered anger and is devoted to the worship and recitation for Śiva,
having bathed in a river at the time of afternoon with a purified mind,
should worship the Śivaliṅga with fragrant flowers.
Having burned auspicious *guggulu* resin, one should present the most excellent food offering (*naivedya*).
Then, the preceptor (*guru*) should perform a fire sacrifice (*homa*) with sesame seeds before the deity.
In the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should worship [the Lord] saying, "To Śaṅkara!"
Having consumed cow urine, one should then sleep on the ground during the night;
such a person obtains the fruit of the Atirātra sacrifice.
Likewise, having worshipped Maheśvara by the name Śambhu under the Puṣya asterism, [one attains the same].
By consuming clarified butter on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, one shall partake in the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
In the month of Māgha, one should worship the deity named Māheśvara on the eighth day of the dark fortnight;
by drinking cow’s milk at night, one obtains the merit of eight horse-sacrifices (Gomedhas).
In the month of Phālguna, having worshipped Mahādeva, one should consume sesame seeds;
one shall enjoy eightfold the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
And in the month of Caitra, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, one should worship Śiva under the name Sthāṇu.
By subsisting on barley for a year, one obtains the fruit of the Aśvamedha sacrifice;
however, by worshipping the one named Śiva at night during Vaiśākha and drinking water infused with *kuśa* grass,
one enjoys ten times the fruit of the Puruṣamedha sacrifice.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, having worshipped Paśupati, one should drink water from the horns of cows;
such a man shall obtain the fruit of donating a hundred thousand cows.
And in Āṣāḍha, having worshipped the deity named Ugra and having consumed cow-dung, [one obtains the same merit].
For more than a full million years, he is glorified in the world of Rudra.
Having worshipped the Sun by the name of Śarva at night during the month of Śrāvaṇa,
a man shall obtain the fruit of a sacrifice involving much gold.
On the eighth day of the month of Bhādrapada, one should worship the deity named Tryambaka;
having consumed a bilva leaf at night, one shall obtain the fruit of the initiation into the eating of food (annadīkṣā).
In the month of Āśvina, the deity Bhava is to be worshipped; one should consume rice-water (taṇḍulodaka).
One shall enjoy a hundredfold the fruit of the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice.
By worshipping the one named Rudra in the month of Kārttika and consuming curd,
a human being obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
At the end of the year, one should feed Brahmins who are devoted to the worship of Śiva,
offering milk-rice mixed with honey and thoroughly saturated with ghee.
According to one's means, one should devoutly present them with gold and garments.
Twelve black water-pots filled with sesame seeds and accompanied by various kinds of food and edibles should be offered here, along with an umbrella and a pair of sandals;
one should also present a black, milch cow to the Rudras.
Listen to the meritorious fruit of that man who, with devotion, observes the Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī vow in this manner continuously for one year:
he shall be liberated from all sins and endowed with all forms of sovereignty.
He rejoices eternally like a king in the world of mortals for a hundred years.
By this very method, all the gods attained godhood;
the Goddess attained the state of being a goddess, and Guha attained the state of being Skanda.

Indeed, I, having become Brahmā, attained the state of Brahmahood; Viṣṇu attained the state of Viṣṇuhood; Indra attained the kingship of the gods; and Gaṇeśa attained the status of the leader of the Gaṇas.
Whether a woman or even a man, by performing the vow of Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī, [attains these states].
O Great King, one obtains unbroken and unsurpassed merit [by this]. One travels in celestial chariots that shine like ten million suns, fulfilling all desires,
crowded with the daughters of Rudra, and accompanied by swans and cranes.
Accompanied by dances and musical instruments resounding with sublime sounds,
fanned by yak-tail whisks, and praised by gods and asuras,
he was three-eyed, wielder of the trident, and endowed with the sovereignty of Śiva.
He remains in the city of Śiva for as long as eight kalpas.
Thus, O Pārtha, I have fully described to you the Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī vow;
by hearing this, one is liberated from all sins—of this there is no doubt.

Having fasted on this Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī vow with truthful speech and uttering the names [of the deity] as they arise, one whose soul is purified by Śiva gives away black jars filled with sesame seeds; such a person goes to the supreme abode of the Moon-crested Lord.
Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī Vow," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the Anaghāṣṭamī Vow. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
There was a great ṛṣi named Atri, the son of Brahmā, who possessed immense splendor.
His wife, O fortunate one, was the devoted Anasūyā. In the course of time, a son of great asceticism was born to them;
he was the great yogi named Datta, an incarnation of Viṣṇu upon the earth.
In this world, there was one renowned as the second [son], known by the name Anagha. His wife was named Nadī, who accompanied him;
she had eight sons, all of whom were living, and she herself was endowed with every Brahmanical virtue.
Of these two, Viṣṇu was born in his form and Lakṣmī is remembered as the river.
Thus, while he was devoted to the practice of yoga together with his wife,
the gods, oppressed by the demon Śumbha, came to him for refuge.
O King, O descendant of Bharata, having swiftly gone to Amarāvatī through the grace obtained from Brahmā,
he found it besieged by the Daitya Jambha for a hundred divine years;
then, arriving from Pātāla amidst the alliance of Daityas and Dānavas, he [intervened].
His army was innumerable, consisting of Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas.
By him, the gods—including Indra, Candra, and the hosts of Maruts—were utterly destroyed;
deprived of their own abodes, they abandoned them and fled in the ten directions.
At the front, the gods led by Indra, afflicted by fear, were heading toward their destruction;
behind them followed the Daityas, with Jambha at their head,
fighting with volleys of arrows, maces, clubs, and mallets.
Roaring, some mounted on bulls, others riding buffaloes,
and some hurrying along on śarabhas, gaṇḍakas, tigers, and impetuous monkeys, they went forth discharging stones, śataghnīs, tomara-spears, and arrows.
They reached the hermitage precincts on Mount Vindhya,
where the sinless Anagha and Anadī lived as a couple;
those men, seeking refuge, arrived in their presence.
Then Anagha, having effortlessly entered within those gods along with Indra, said,
"Stay here, free from all anxiety.
Having replied, "So be it," they all attained great satisfaction.
The Daityas also arrived swiftly, striking their enemies with weapons;
they spoke these fierce and terrible words: "Seize the Brahmin woman of the sage!
Quickly cast down the trees laden with flowers and fruits!"
Then, having placed the sinless one upon their heads, the Daityas went to his hermitage;
at that very moment, the Goddess of Fortune (Śrī) came to reside upon the heads of the Daityas.
But they were seen by Dattaka and, in an instant, were destroyed by the fire of his meditation.
Deprived of their luster, shorn of their splendor, and bereft of their pride and learning,
those Daityas were seized by the gods in the battle for plunder;
wailing and groaning, these thorns of Brahmā became motionless.
By means of spears, swords, tridents, trishulas, and heavy iron clubs,
those asuras met their destruction through the power of that sage at that time;
they were conquered by Indra with a multitude of divine weapons and slain.
All the gods also remained in their own realms as they had done before;
even by the gods, the greatness of that sage, the celestial seer, was acknowledged.
Thereupon, he remained ever intent upon the welfare of all the worlds.
Performing only auspicious deeds through action, mind, and speech,
with arms raised high like wood, a wall, or stone,
that one of great austerity practiced the penance known as Brahmottara with perfectly restrained vows.
Having fixed his unblinking eyes and gazing at the space between his eyebrows,
he remained there for three thousand divine years; so indeed we have heard concerning him as he stood with his vital energy drawn upward and his gaze unwavering.

The lord and sovereign Arjuna Kārtavīrya, the king of Māhiṣmatī, having arrived swiftly from there in a single day, performed service and humble attendance with tireless devotion day and night for the sake of his effort in the practice of yoga.

When her vow was fully completed, he, filled with firm satisfaction, granted her four excellent boons that were nourishing and possessed of great splendor— namely, the massaging of his limbs and worship performed even when merely conceived in the mind.
First, he chose as his boon a thousand arms;
second, protection from the virtuous against unrighteousness when it was being practiced;
and third, the conquest of the earth through righteousness and its preservation likewise through righteousness alone.
"Having won many battles and slain thousands of heroes,
may my death occur at the hands of Hari while I am fighting in combat;
by that gift, a kingdom has been granted to me upon this earth."
O son of Kuntī, for Kārtavīrya, the practice of yoga was explained in detail,
as well as the status of a universal monarch endowed with the eight supernatural powers;
by him, too, the entire earth with its seven continents and mountains [was ruled].
The earth, together with its oceans and forests, was conquered by him through righteous means;
indeed, by the power of that wise one, a thousand arms appeared through his majesty,
and from his sacrifice, a chariot and a banner emerged through his illusory power.
O Pāṇḍava, ten thousand sacrifices were performed without obstruction in those seven islands by him himself;
all those sacrifices, O mighty-armed one, were well-conducted and accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
All [the sacrificial grounds] possessed altars of gold and all were adorned with golden sacrificial posts;
they were graced by highly fortunate deities stationed in celestial chariots,
and were eternally embellished by gandharvas and apsarases.
At his sacrifice, the Gandharvas and Nārada sang this verse,
beholding the conduct and majesty of that lion among kings:
"Surely no other monarchs shall ever attain the state of Kārtavīrya."
By means of sacrifices, gifts, austerities, valor, and sacred learning,
he indeed roamed across the seven continents, armed with sword, shield, and bow; like a hawk, he would observe his prey from afar or nearby.
His wealth was never lost, and he experienced neither grief nor exhaustion;
by his power and through righteousness,
the king of the earth protected his subjects for eighty-five thousand years.
He became a universal monarch (cakravartin) upon the earth girt by the oceans;
he himself became a cowherd, and he himself was a guardian of the fields.
Through his mastery of yoga, he became Arjuna, who brings rain through the agency of Parjanya.
Indeed, with his thousand arms, the skin of which was hardened by the striking of bowstrings,
that one of great splendor moved about while the great ocean was being agitated by his thousand rays;
for neither by *nāgas* nor by humans could he be approached on the banks of the Mahīmatī.
Having conquered the sons of the serpent Karkoṭaka, he settled them in that city.
Intoxicated with pride, he sported with the lotus-eyed daughter of the ocean during the rainy season and even caused the waters to flow upstream.

As he sported playfully, the Narmadā river— garlanded with the rippling of its fruits— became apprehensive, as if her waves were frowning brows, thinking, "He will swallow me. Thus was the great ocean agitated by his thousand arms.
The great Asuras dwelling in the netherworld became cowed and motionless;
O illustrious one, the high-minded [Rāvaṇa], having silenced them,
made the ocean— whose lofty waves were agitated— with his thousand arms.
The great serpents, their heads rendered motionless,
became like plantain groves struck down by a thunderbolt at the close of day;
and all the archers were conquered by him with five well-aimed arrows.
Having forcibly deluded Rāvaṇa along with his army, the lord of Laṅkā,
he conquered him, brought him under his control, and bound him in Māhiṣmatī.
Then Pulastya, having arrived there, sought to appease Arjuna.
He released the Rākṣasa descendant of Pulastya, who was followed by another descendant of Pulastya.
From that thousand arms, there arose the sound of bowstrings being struck.
Once, he was requested by the hungry Fire-god (Citrabhānu).
He offered this earth, consisting of seven islands, as alms to the Resplendent One (Citrabhānu).
Consequently, the Lord Hari is seen even today reclining upon the sacrificial pit (Kuṇḍeśaya),
and Nimbāditya remains visibly present, ever awake, in his abode.
On account of his daughter, he remained thus even until today;
such was King Arjuna on earth, endowed with these virtues,
O Pāṇḍava, by the grace of the sinless teacher of yoga.
Therefore, this sinless Aṣṭamī, celebrated in the world of mortals, was set in motion by the yogi Kārtavīrya who had obtained boons.
In the world, "agha" is understood as sin, and that is also said to be threefold.
Because it destroys evil (agha), it is therefore known as Anaghā.
Its eightfold sovereignty is manifested for the sake of diversion:
atomization (aṇimā), magnification (mahimā), extension (prāpti), fulfillment of desires (prākāmya), and lightness (laghimā).
Mastery, self-control, and the power to resolve all desires—
these eight perfections of one accomplished in yoga are the characteristics of liberation. Having arisen in Dattaka, they serve as signs of realization in this world.

Upon the completion of the pilgrimage, having gathered whatever sins [there may be], or likewise [having purified them], one should make the entire world sinless; therefore, O twice-born, I am sinless. A twice-born man in this world who has offered his life to me and is my own portion is like a dead man [to the world of sin].
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Lotus-eyed One, what kind of vow did that King Arjuna perform in the three worlds, and with which mantras and under what conditions?
"At what time, on which lunar day, and for whom was this [performed]? Tell me this, O Keśava.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, a husband and wife made of darbha grass..."

O Yudhiṣṭhira, having bathed, one should likewise worship with fragrant flowers Anagha and Anaghā, who were formerly rendered auspicious and peaceful by Kṛtī, and who stand together with many sons upon a blessed plot of ground.
A Brahmin, having meditated upon Viṣṇu as described in the verses of the Ṛgveda— Viṣṇu who is born from my own portion,
the sinless Vāsudeva, the sinless Lakṣmī, and the body of Vraja,
along with the group of sons beginning with Pradyumna, exactly as declared in the Harivaṃśa— [should worship].
Oṃ! May the gods protect us from that place whence Viṣṇu strode forth across the seven stations of the earth.
Viṣṇu strode across this [world]; he established his foot in three places.
He has trodden upon the dust with his foot;
Viṣṇu, the infallible guardian, strode out three steps,
thereby upholding the sacred laws.
Behold the deeds of Viṣṇu, through which he has made his vows manifest;
he is the close companion and friend of Indra.
The wise ever behold that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Like an eye fixed in the sky,
the wise, ever-vigilant and full of praise, kindle that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
He who, endowed with devotion, worships with fruits produced in the world, bulbs, auspicious *śṛṅgāra* berries, *badara* fruits,
wealth, grains, flowers, perfumes, incense, and lamps,
is liberated from all sins.
Then one should feed the twice-born, as well as friends, relatives, and kinsmen.
At the conclusion of the vow, a certain single man should undertake the vow;
among them, those who are firm and have successfully completed their blameless vows should perform it.
If this [practice] involves the destruction of life, it must indeed be observed according to the established rule for one year; thereafter, you may act as you wish. This is your sinless vow.
In that regard, you should remain indifferent toward actors, dancers, and singers.
At dawn on the ninth day, one should release that [effigy] into the midst of the water.
He who performs this pilgrimage year after year with joy,
endowed with devotion and faith, is liberated from all sins.
The family of him with whom Viṣṇu is pleased prospers;
he attains health for seven births and thereafter reaches the supreme goal.

O son of Kuntī, I have now described to you for your benefit this sinless Aṣṭamī, which pacifies the multitude of sins. Those who observe it with undistracted minds for the increase of their own glory attain prosperity equal to that of the son of Kṛtavīrya.
Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Vow of Anaghāṣṭamī," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[Now follows] the description of the Somāṣṭamī vow. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Now I shall proclaim another vow, supreme and conducive to the highest good—a meritorious rite that bestows the world of Śiva; learn it from me according to the prescribed rule.
On the Monday coinciding with the eighth day of the bright fortnight, one should worship Soma.
Having obtained this moon-adorned [image] according to the prescribed rite, the observer of the vow,
having meditated upon Hari in the southern half and the Lord in the center all around,
should install the deity with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and other offerings.
One should smear the right half with sandalwood paste mixed with moon-essence;
the portion belonging to Hara should be blue and red, and above Śiva’s [portion] there should be pearls.
Afterwards, one should worship with flowers—white and unsurpassed red ones.
One should again perform the *nīrājana* rite with twenty-five lamps;
then, one should present an offering (*naivedya*) of auspicious, consecrated foods.
Having thus observed the fast, at dawn one should worship Śiva as previously described.
Having performed worship, one should offer oblations of clarified butter mixed with sesame seeds into the sacred fire.
Afterwards, having fed the Brahmins who observe the vow according to the prescribed rule,
one should feed married couples and honor them according to one's ability.
O you of noble vows, having turned [the wheel] and honored the two parents according to that rite,
learn from me everything that must be performed at the end of the year.
According to the previously mentioned procedure, one should worship the pair of white and yellow [discs].
One should offer a canopy, as well as banners, a water-pot,
incense, perfumes, and an exceedingly beautiful lamp-tree;
such items as these should be employed, and one should perform the offering of food as previously described.
Then one should have a mandala made, both square and triangular;
one should meditate on Pārvatī within the triangle and Maheśvara within the square.
Having thus consecrated a Brahmin couple with garments and ornaments, [one should proceed].
Having worshipped according to one's ability, one should perform the auspicious *nīrājana* rite with twenty-five lamps; then, having fed [the recipient], one should bid them farewell.
The man who performs this for five years, or even for a single year, [attains the fruit].

Having attained both worlds, he shall go to the state that is free from all ailment. He who performs this constantly until the fall of his body is perceived here on earth as Hari himself in human form.
Calamities do not touch him, nor does he ever become miserable;
he is never afflicted by fevers, planetary influences, or other such ailments.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:

Alternatively, one should know that the eighth day of the bright fortnight occurs on that path; having reached it during the conjunction with the Sun, one should practice according to the previously mentioned procedure.
However, the wise man should worship the Sun situated within the Dakṣiṇatantra.
Having anointed Pārvatī with divine ruby and gold,
and likewise Śiva with saffron and sandalwood;
in the absence of all these gems, one should employ gold everywhere.
The seed-syllable of Rudra is supremely pure and always dear to Rudra.
[One should offer] red garlands and garments, and an oblation cooked in ghee. The remaining details of the ritual procedure should be performed according to the previously established rules.
O sinless one, when the lunar day is full, one should perform the breaking of the fast with products of the cow.
Having performed this for one year, and likewise for five years, and having first established [the ritual],
one shall enjoy pleasures in the worlds of the Sun and other deities, and then proceed to the Supreme.
One shall be as majestic as a moth [in its brilliance], undepressed, and beloved by the people;
in this [state], disease shall not afflict him, and he shall possess wealth and sons.
O scion of the Kuru lineage, if the eighth lunar day (Aṣṭamī) should ever coincide with the moon or the sun, one should fast upon it.
"Accompanied by me, he shall worship Hara, who is marked with the crescent moon; through devotion, he attains the state that is the goal of long life—the abode of the Enemy of Tripura.

Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Somāṣṭamī Vow," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira. [Now begins] the description of the Śrīvṛkṣa-navamī Vow.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: In ancient times, when the jewels had emerged from the churning of the Ocean of Milk,
Janārdana manifested as a woman for the purpose of deluding the Daityas.

Exhausted, Kamalālayā rested for a moment under a bilva tree; thus they spoke to one another, while the gods and dānavas continued to fight. O Pārtha, in former times, all were conquered in battle by Kṛṣṇa, the wielder of the discus.
The Daityas were sent to the netherworld (pātāla), while Śrī herself returned;
because she was made to dwell there, it is therefore known as the Śrīvṛkṣa.
Therefore, O best of the Kurus, [one should perform this] during the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada.
On the ninth day, at the slight break of dawn, one should worship with devotion the mountain Śrīvṛkṣa (the Bilva tree) with various flowers, fruits not cooked by fire,
rice-paste mixed with sesame, wheat, incense, perfumes, garlands, and garments.
O King of kings, when the surface of the sky has been turned a deep copper-red by the slightly rising rays of the sun,
one should feed the Brahmins with this mantra;
thereafter, observing silence and avoiding oil and alkaline substances, one should eat.
O Pārtha, whatever man or woman performs the worship of the Śrīvṛkṣa in this manner— placing auspicious curd, flowers, and fruits in an earthen vessel without cooking them over fire—
is liberated from suffering and grief; of this there is no doubt.
For seven successive births, she shall be endowed with happiness and good fortune;
auspicious, fruitful, and blessed, she is glorified in the world of mortals.
One who, on the ninth lunar day, offers an unblemished fruit-bearing Bilva tree, adorned with food offerings, flowers, fruits, garments, and various grains—
Worshipful at the time of dawn, he is dear to Puruṣottama; men attain that which is venerated by the lords of men.

Thus ends the sixtieth chapter, titled "Description of the Śrīvṛkṣa-navamī Vow," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira. [Now follows] the Description of the Dhvaja-navamī Vow.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
After Mahiṣāsura had been slain by the Goddess,
many battles were waged by the great asuras, who recalled their former enmity.
Assuming various forms, the Goddess descended again and again;
for the sake of establishing the Dharma, she struck down the foremost of the Daityas.
Then there was a great Asura named Raktāsura, the son of Mahiṣa.
He performed austerities for six hundred thousand years;
Caturvaktra (Brahmā) granted him sovereignty over the entire circle of the three worlds.
Having obtained this boon, he then assembled the sons of Danu.
Having gone to Amarāvatī, he began a battle with Śakra;
seeing that Dānava army equipped and with their banners raised high,
he fought together with the gods led by Śakra against the Dānavas.
There a river began to flow, its waves consisting of floods of blood;
it had swords for fish, maces for crocodiles, and Vasunandaka spears for turtles;
terrifying to both gods and asuras, it flowed toward the realm of the ancestors.
Then the Asura Raktāsura, out of rage, fought with the gods. Being struck down by Raktākṣa in that great battle,
those gods abandoned their weapons and swiftly fled, leaving heaven.
They reached the city of Karacchatrā, where dwells the beloved of Bhava—
Durgā together with Cāmuṇḍā, accompanied by the nine Durgās;
first among them is Mahālakṣmī, as well as Nandā and Kṣemakarī.
Śivadūtī, Mahāruṇḍā, Bhrāmarī, Rudramaṅgalā,
Revatī, and Harasiddhi— these nine are thus proclaimed.
With their faces bowed in prostration, the gods offered praise to them.
Victorious is Durgā, whose lotus-feet are kissed by the crowns of the lords of the immortals, who generates happiness for the entire world,
who is praised by the Lord of the Universe, who is whole yet stainless and partless;
she whose hands hold a sword wounded and smeared with blood from her own mangled nails, teeth, ornaments, and flesh.
Victorious is Caṇḍī, who consumes human heads, flesh, and wine;
whose moon-jewel shines within her formidable matted locks that conceal her flock of peacocks.
Victorious is Mahālakṣmī, the sovereign of Siddhavaṭa, adorned with the directions as her garments.

Victorious is the goddess Nandā, who brings relief to those who bow before her; she possesses the splendor born from her lotus-like hands, her face is fixed in the lotus posture (*padmāsana*), and a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) rests in her hand. Clad in the directions as her garment, with a distorted face, she fills the expanse of the quarters with the forceful howling of jackals.
Victorious is she of the formidable body, the bestower of security, abiding in a fierce state;

victorious is Śivadūtī, the primordial power of Śiva, whose roar of "huṃ" resounds through the mouths of the foremost gods within the belly of the crying universe, and who holds a rutting elephant by the trunk.
Victorious is Mahātuṇḍā, whose ears are adorned with the jewels of the lords of serpents, who terrifies the entire circle of the quarters with her unbearable and fearsome loud laughter,
and whose limbs are made to dance by the resonant sounds of sharp-sounding ḍhakkās, murajas, mardalas, and jhallaris.
Victorious is the goddess Bhrāmarī, who has the form of a honey-bee and is a lioness to the Daityas;
she is peaceful, with a tranquil countenance, the best of lions, and established in the yoga of meditation.
Victorious is the goddess who possesses a four-armed body, who is a digit of the moon and resides within the lunar orb.
Victorious is the many-formed Revatī Bhadrā, who holds a sharp trident in her hand and has crushed various hosts of enemies with the blows of her wings and beak;
she wanders joyfully through the world and in the dwellings of the cremation grounds, accompanied by yoginīs.

"Victory to her named Harasiddhi, the Siddhi of Hara, who is saluted by the Siddhas! Having thus composed this incomparable hymn to the Nine Durgās in Āryā meters, Aparārka, together with the gods, spoke this: "Protect us from all fears!"
Bowing again and again, they said to Bhavānī, who rides upon a lion:
"O refuge for those terrified by fear, be our protection!
Having heard those words of the gods, she then granted them freedom from fear.
In former times, mounted upon a lion and accompanied by the Durgās,
she emerged and fought with the Dānavas in a great battle like a tempestuous storm;
the twenty-armed Kumārī was like a flash of lightning amidst thick clouds.
Those fierce Asuras, possessing the form of Rudra, had also arrived there;
they were all heroes who had obtained boons and had likewise performed intense austerities,
endowed with the prowess of great sea-monsters for the destruction of wicked illusionists.
From his own rising desire for a non-Brāhmaṇa woman, both by name and deed,
Indramārin was born; and from that same source came Asatkleśa, Pralamba, Naraka,
Kuṣṭha, Puloman, Śarabha, Śambara, Dundubhi, and Khara as sons.
Ilvala, Namuci, Bhauma, Vātāpi, Dhenuka, Kali,
Māyā, Vṛtra, the two Balas, Bandhu, Madhu, Kaiṭabha, Kāla-jit,
Rahu, Pauṇḍraka, and other lords of the Daityas are proclaimed here primarily by name.
All the people were equipped with quivers, and their banners stood before them;
those banners, described according to their forms and colors, each distinct from the others,
appeared, O king of kings, like blazing fires.
Golden, with golden supports, adorned with golden garlands, and endowed with auspicious marks, banners were raised, decorated with various plumes;
they were blue, yellow, white, red, and black— possessing five colors.
There, the flames, adorned with silken cloths and garlands, variegated with bubbles,
and possessing the beauty of banners, shone like beautiful dancing girls;
then those foremost of Dānavas raised a tumultuous roar.
They beat the paṇavas, bherīs, jharjharas, and gomukhas; others sounded conchs, ḍamarus, and ḍiṇḍimas.
Thus those Daityas and Dānavas fought against Bhavānī.
They struck one another with arrows, spears, iron clubs, javelins, and lances;
with *karṇakas*, *īṣaṇas*, darts, *śataghnīs*, mallets, and hammers.
Striking out with pride and rage, they blazed forth even more intensely in the battle.
Mounted upon a lion, the goddess swiftly rushed into the midst of the battle;
with fury in that protectorless conflict, she forcibly tore away the emblems and various kinds of banners from the Daityas.
Pleased, the swift-moving goddess gave tokens to the gods,
which were accepted by the deities as they cried out, "Victory to the Goddess!
Ambikā, being exceedingly gratified, brought about their destruction in an instant.
Like the goddess Mārī, she descended as the Night of Doom for the Dānavas;
that delighter of the gods seized the lives of the Daityas.
Then, seizing Raktāsura by the throat, she cast him down upon the ground.
The goddess struck him violently in the sky with her sharp trident;
his heart pierced, he was subsequently dashed against the ground there. Although already slain by the goddess, he fell and died.
Having conquered those asuras and reached the enemy's city,
the gods beheld great banners hanging at the edge of the battlefield;
filled with joy, they performed a procession marked by the banners on the ninth day.
Even now, O Pāṇḍava, this day is observed here by kings who have been honored out of a desire to attain victory, as well as by devoted men and women alike.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Lord, tell me what the procedure for that ninth [day] is,
along with its secret and its mantras, by which Caṇḍikā is pleased.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
On that day well-known as the ninth of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa,
having bathed, one should worship the auspicious sister of Hari with beautiful flowers—
the maiden goddess, the fortunate one, who travels in a lion-drawn chariot.
Having fashioned various kinds of banners, one should worship her in front with *mālatī* flowers, lamps, perfumes, incense, and ointments;
and with offerings consisting of pure animals, as well as liquor, meat, blood, and garlands.

O son of Kuntī, with curd, sandalwood powder, and unbroken grains that have not been cooked by fire, one should worship the auspicious, divine, dark-complexioned goddess who is the benefactress of the entire world, using this mantra— or even that of Brahmā.

I have sought refuge in you, O auspicious Night, who brings rest, who restrains all, and who is garlanded with planets and stars; O Blessed One, bring my vow to completion! [Protect me] from all spirits and piśācas, and from all living beings and reptiles.
"Protect me always from fears of gods and men.
Then the king should cause her to be placed in the temple of the goddesses;
he should feed the young maiden, prostrate before her, and ask for her forgiveness.
One should perform [this worship] by means of fasting or else by eating but one meal;
O King, devotion is superior to [mere] ritual service.
Those men who thus worship the Blessed Lady with banners—

For them, Bhavānī, the source of all auspiciousness, constantly provides protection on difficult paths, amidst the perils of thieves, serpents, and fire, in battle, in the royal court, in the home, in the midst of combat, and when situated in water.
On this ninth day, O son of Pāṇḍu, victory was achieved;
therefore, this ninth day is always dear to the Blessed Goddess.
It is auspicious, meritorious, a destroyer of sins, and a dispeller of all calamities.

This should be performed with diligence by those desiring all their wishes. That man whose mind is intent on the worship of the Goddess who, on the ninth day, offers a golden garland and an excellent banner— having obtained all the enjoyments desired by his heart to his full satisfaction— he leaves his body and attains the world of heroes.
Thus ends the sixty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Dhvajā-navamī Vow," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[Now follows] the description of the Ulkā-navamī vow.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O King, listen as I describe the ninth [tithi] known as Ulkā,
which was proclaimed by Kaśyapa as the destroyer of Tāraka’s affliction;
it is the world-renowned ninth day in the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja.
Having bathed in the river and duly worshipped the ancestors and the goddesses,
he should thereafter worship the goddess Cāmuṇḍā, the beloved of Bhairava,
with flowers, incense, food offerings, meat, fish, wine, and spirits.
Having performed worship, a person should offer praise with this mantra, placing his joined palms upon his head while kneeling upon the ground:
"O slayer of Mahiṣa! O Great Illusion! O Cāmuṇḍā, garlanded with severed heads!"

"O Goddess, grant me wealth, health, and victory; salutations be unto you! Afterward, one should feed young girls, having adorned them with fresh blue garments, fine silk cloths, undergarments, and ornaments, and then ask for their forgiveness—either seven, five, or even just one, according to the disposition and means of one's heart and wealth.
"The Goddess is pleased by faith"— this is the instruction of the Vīras.
Having sprinkled the area and prepared a mandala with cow dung, one of pure smile should sit upon a provided seat and place the vessel before him.
Then, one should serve all that food which has been well-prepared;
one should also place milk-rice (pāyasa) with ghee near the vessels. Taking sixty blades of grass as well as a bellows, one should proceed.
Then one should ignite the food as long as the fire continues to burn. When the fire has subsided, having abandoned the food and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) with a clear mind,
one should meditate upon Cāmuṇḍā in the heart and become intent on household duties.

By this procedure, one should perform everything month after month. Then, at the end of the year, having fed young maidens and honored them with garments and ornaments, one should prostrate and ask for their forgiveness.

One should give gold according to one's ability and a beautiful cow to a Brahmin. O Pārtha, the king who performs this Navamī vow in such a manner shall have no enemies, no suffering, and his thieves shall be destroyed.
Spirits, ghosts, and demons do not produce fear in our home; even when weapons are raised, there is no slayer to be found. Caṇḍikā, ever-vigilant, protects him in all calamities.
Whether a man or a woman, whoever should observe this vow,
he or she shall always remain blazing in the hearts of rivals like a firebrand.
[One should meditate upon her] with a mouth like a dry well, possessing prominent fangs, wearing a garland of skulls, and carrying a severed head.
