"Among those who have observed the prescribed vows, for whose heart does Caṇḍī not bring auspiciousness when she is worshipped on the ninth lunar days?
Thus ends the sixty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Ulkā-navamī Vow," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[Now follows] the description of the vow concerning the deeds of the ten incarnations.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Formerly, at the beginning of the Kṛta-yuga, there was a most virtuous wife of Bhṛgu,
who dwelt in the beautiful Divyārāma hermitage and was solely intent upon her domestic duties.

She was always one who fulfilled the desires of Bhṛgu’s heart. Having entrusted the Agnihotra sacrifice to her— a task fraught with the protection of the family from the fear of Viṣṇu and the Dānavas— the sage of great splendor departed.
Having released [the king] who stood ready for battle at his side and entrusted everything as a deposit to the divine lady, that bull among sages, possessed of great ascetic power,
went in secret to the slopes of the Himalayas to propitiate Hara.

For the sake of the Saṃjīvanī herb, the family priest of the king of the Dānavas constantly drank smoke face-downward by means of grains for the sake of victory. When he had departed, Hari, mounted upon Garuḍa, arrived.
Having approached, he engaged in speech with him whose head had been severed by the discus;
then, seeing the entire army of the asuras slain by Viṣṇu— drenched in flowing blood and resembling a vast ocean of crimson— he [spoke].
Divyā, her eyes clouded with tears, was about to utter a curse against Viṣṇu;
but before she could speak a word, he severed her neck with his discus and struck down her head, adorned with earrings.
Having acquired the Saṃjīvanī lore, as soon as that sage returned, he did not see the Daityas; instead, he beheld [his son] struck down.
With his face contorted by a frown of rage, he cursed Hari.
Because you have slain the Daityas— who were destined to exist inevitably and who were the cause of harm to the universe— having been accepted by Brahmā as my own,
therefore you shall go to the world of men for ten incarnations.
For this purpose, and for the protection of the rulers of the earth,
I have taken various forms of incarnation again and again in the world of men. O Pārtha, it is for the reasons previously mentioned that I have descended upon the surface of the earth.
"For those men who shall worship me, their dwelling shall be in Triviṣṭapa.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, tell me in detail the vow known as the Daśāvatāra."
[This is] together with its mantras and secret doctrines, the destroyer of all sins.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
On the tenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Proṣṭhapada, one should remain self-controlled and pure.
O best of the Kuru lineage, having bathed in a clear body of water and performed the libations for the ancestors, gods, and others,
a person returning home should take three handfuls of grain flour.
One should gradually purify that [deity] known as Puṃs, supported by ghee, on that specific day every year for ten years:
in the first year, *pūrikās*; in the second year, *ghṛtapūrakas*.
In the third year, white sweetmeats; in the fourth, auspicious *modakas*;
in the fifth year, *sohālakas*; in the sixth year, *khaṇḍaveṣṭakas*;
in the seventh year, *kokarasas*; and likewise in the eighth, cakes (*apūpas*).
In the ninth [month], one should give ear-rings; in the tenth, auspicious small ornaments.
At the tenth day, O bull of the Bharatas, one should cause ten cows to be given to ten Brahmins after having consumed [the food] in the prescribed order.
One should likewise grind half of that half for a twice-born man;
having gone to a beautiful body of water, one should eat half by oneself.
After worshipping the ten incarnations with flowers, incense, and unguents, [one should proceed].
With this mantra, the wise one, having sprinkled Hari with water,
[worships] the Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, Narasiṃha, Trivikrama,
Śrī Rāma, Rāma Kṛṣṇa, Buddha, and Kalki.
I have gone for refuge to the Lord Hari Nārāyaṇa;
I bow down to the Master of the World—may that Viṣṇu be gracious to me.
May Janārdana, born through devotion, cut asunder the Māyā of Viṣṇu.
"Lead us to Śvetadvīpa and offer us unto your own self.
O Pārtha of noble vows, listen to the meritorious fruit for him who performs this according to the prescribed rite known as the *Daśāvatāra-nāma*.
It is heard that Hari cuts through these ten stages of men when he perceives them; there is no doubt that Hari [rescues] me as I am sinking there in the terrible ocean of saṃsāra.
"May he, gratified by this vow, lead you quickly to Śvetadvīpa.
What could not be attained in this world for one with whom Janārdana is pleased?
O King, I am that very Janārdana, appearing in the form of Time (Kāla), the son of the Earth."
O Pārtha, in this world of mortals, for the purpose of relieving the burden of the earth,
whatever woman shall perform this vow proclaimed by me, O Pārtha,
she shall be endowed with unshakable prosperity and accompanied by her husband and sons.
Having dwelt for a long time in the mortal world, he is glorified in the realm of Viṣṇu;
from the realm of Viṣṇu, he goes to the realm of Rudra, and thence to the supreme state—
those men who worship the ten incarnations of Puruṣottama, beginning with the Fish, on the tenth lunar days.

"Having enjoyed happiness throughout all ten stages of life, those mortals ascend a celestial vehicle and go to the worlds of the Lord of the Gods. Thus ends the sixty-third chapter, titled "The Vow of the Deeds of the Ten Incarnations," in the *Uttara-parvan* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira; followed by the description of the *Āśā-daśamī*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Pārtha, listen attentively as I describe to you the Aśā-daśamī vow, which causes the lotus-faces of the multitude of kings to bloom with joy.
O lord of the earth, there was formerly a king among the Niṣadhas named Nala;
we have heard that he was defeated in his kingdom by his brother Puṣkara at dice,
O Indra among kings, and departed together with his wife.
Having entered that terrifying, empty forest resounding with the chirping of swarms of crickets,
he went there day and night, subsisting on water alone,
and beheld birds with the luster of gold dwelling in the midst of the forest.
O King, desiring to seize them, he covered them with his own garment;
but the birds, taking that beautiful cloth, quickly flew into the sky. Having lost his garment, he waited for some time in great distress.

Having recovered Damayantī, who had then been carried off by sleep, he departed out of sorrow; yet, by the power of destiny, he first reached the Lord of Wealth. When the King of Niṣadha had gone, the daughter of Bhīma awoke with her face cast down in dejection.
Not seeing the heroic Nala in the forest, the daughter of Bhīma wandered here and there, crying out "Alas! Alas! repeatedly;
overcome by pain and grief, she longed intensely for the sight of Nala.
After some days, she reached the city of the King of Cedi quite quickly;
surrounded by children who were filled with curiosity, she appeared like one intoxicated.
She was seen by the mother of the Cedi king, amidst the throng of people.
Like a crescent moon fallen upon the earth, illuminating the quarters of the sky,
she was taken to her own palace and asked, "Who are you, O lovely-faced one?
Damayantī replied with modesty, "Know me to be a *sairandhrī*."
"I shall not wash my feet, nor shall I eat the remnants of another's meal;
if anyone should request [these things], he would now deserve punishment.
O Goddess, by this vow I shall remain in your residence."
"Let it be so," said the faultless-limbed queen to her.
Thus, for some time, she dwelt blamelessly in that palace;
and when the period had passed, it is said, O twice-born one, she lived on half of the king's own provisions.
Joyfully, he brought Damayantī to her father’s house;
there she was reunited with her mother, father, sons, and brothers.
Nevertheless, Damayantī remained in sorrow, being deprived of the King of Niṣadha.
Summoning them, he spoke with a troubled mind: "Tell me of some vow or even a gift by which I might have a reunion with my beloved. Thereupon, a wise Brahmin skilled in ancient lore replied:
"O blessed lady, observe the Āśā-daśamī, which grants the fulfillment of all desires.
Then the slender-limbed woman did everything exactly as it had been previously described by Damanaka, the priest who was learned in the Purāṇas and the traditional narratives.
"O best of men, by the power of this vow,
Damayantī has attained a most blissful reunion with her husband.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Govinda, when and how is this tenth stage of hope performed?
Explain all of this to me; you are omniscient, O Yādava.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
The prince [strives] out of a desire for sovereignty; the farmer for the sake of cultivation;
the merchant’s son for the sake of a wife; likewise, the pregnant woman for the sake of a son;
and the maiden of the world, seeking a bridegroom, for the complete attainment of dharma, artha, and kāma.
An excellent twice-born man desiring to perform a sacrifice, a sick person seeking the removal of disease,
and a wife whose beloved husband has been long away— all these, and others as well, should always observe this Āśā-vrata, being wise in maintaining fortitude through time.
When someone is afflicted by distress, they should indeed observe this vow.
Having bathed on the tenth day of the bright fortnight and worshipped the deities,
one should then worship the quarters at night with flowers, lac-dye, and sandalwood.
Having drawn [the deity] in the courtyard of the house with barley or with flour-paste,
and having offered an oblation (naivedya) smeared with ghee, one should again present this prayer:
"May all directions be ever auspicious, and may all desires be fulfilled."
"By the grace of you ladies, may there always be well-being.
Having thus worshipped and given a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brahmin, one should eat.
One should perform this in the prescribed manner month after month.
Once his desire is fulfilled through subsequent exertion—
whether after one month, six months, a year, or two years—
he should have banners made of gold, or of silver and plaster.
Having bathed together with kinsmen and relatives and being properly adorned,
one should worship [Indra] in the courtyard of the house while meditating with these collections of mantras:
"O Śakra, saluted by gods and asuras, you are present here."
Salutations to the deity of the eastern direction, who is accompanied by the Moon;
O Noble Lady, because you encompassed the fire, you are recited as the goddess of the south-east.
You are the supreme power consisting of light; O Goddess of the South-East, grant us boons!
Having approached the King of the Gods, this world restrains itself;
therefore, you go to Saṃyamanī, and in the realm of Yama, become a granter of desires. You, O exceedingly deformed one, have been brought as an offering to Nairṛti along with a sword.
For that reason, Maghavan has always designated you by the name Nairṛtī.
Varuṇa, the lord of aquatic creatures and the support of your abode, resides within you;
therefore, become the daughter of Varuṇa for the sake of accomplishing your desired purpose.

Since you are presided over by Vāyu, the life-breath of the world, therefore grant us constant peace, O Vāyavyā; salutations again and again! Because you dwell with Kubera, you are known as the gentle and auspicious Uttarā.
O Goddess, you are adorned by Śambhu, the Lord of the World, in the northeast;
therefore, O Śivā, grant me the presence of Śiva—salutations to you!
Though you are served by the entire lineage of the eight serpents, you remain below.
Accompanied by the wives of the Nāgas, be ever a benefactor to us.
Since you are always auspicious, encompassed by the seven worlds,
and surrounded by Sanaka and the other [sages], O Brāhmī, drive away those who are crooked.
May all the constellations, as well as the planets and the star-planets,
the Mothers of the Constellations, and the spirits, ghosts, and Vināyakas—
may they all remain forever bowed in devotion for the sake of the accomplishment of my desired goals.

Having worshipped with these mantras using flowers, incense, and so forth, and having established [the image] with garments, one should present fruits. This should be done amidst the sounding of musical instruments and auspicious melodies for the journey.

One should spend that night in happiness with excellent women dancing, [provided] with intense saffron powder, gifts, honors, and the like. At dawn, one should bestow all of that upon a knower of the Vedas.
Having performed everything according to this procedure and having prostrated,
one should eat together with friends, well-wishers, and kinsmen.
O Pārtha, he who thus observes the Daśamī vow with devotion—
That man obtains every desire wished for by his mind; indeed,
O Yudhiṣṭhira, this vow should especially be performed by women,
since women are light-minded and always devoted to their desires.
O Great King, I have described to you this unsurpassed vow, which brings merit, fame, and long life, and bestows the fruit of all desires.
O bull among men, those men who, desiring their heart's wishes, always worship the ten directions on the tenth lunar days.
For those in whose hearts these [observances] have been specifically established, their hopes bear fruit abundantly; enough said at great length.
Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Āśā-daśamī Vrata," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[This is followed by] the description of the Tāraka-dvādaśī Vrata.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"I am a sinner who has committed an offense and have caused the destruction of the earth;
having bowed at your feet, O Govinda, I question you."
"Tell me some unsurpassed vow, more secret than the most secret,
by which I may cross the ocean of the slaughter of Bhīṣma and Droṇa, which is a flood of sins.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
In Vidarbha, there was a king named Kuśadhvaja,
who ruled his kingdom with vigilance, accompanied by his harem and sons.
Once, while out hunting, he killed an ascetic through negligence.
Thinking him to be a deer in the great forest, the Brahmin was deluded by fate;
by the ripening of that karma, he went to hell at the end of his life.
There, having experienced terrible torments, he was exceedingly afflicted.
Therefore, having come here to the mortal world, he became a fierce serpent.
O king of kings, he too bit a Brahmin on the foot out of anger;
having attained death along with that twice-born man, he departed.
Then, having perished there, he became a most terrible lion in his second birth;
with a gaping mouth, violent, and a source of fear to various creatures,
he again slew an eminent kṣatriya who had gone out hunting.
Thereafter, struck down by many weapons from the royal hosts,
he became a tiger again in his third birth as well; there, having destroyed herds of deer with the blows of his sharp claws and talons,
he was himself brought to his death by a merchant in a certain part of the forest.
He was reduced to a heap of worms by people through being dug up and cast down;
yet he became a great bear, causing pain to creatures struck by his claws.
He killed a child, and from this act of killing, he shall meet his death at the hands of a *caṇḍāla*.
In the fifth month, a most terrifying makara was born in the ocean;
it then killed a young woman who had come to bathe at night during a lunar eclipse in front of Śaṅkara at dawn.
There too, having been caught on a hook, he was deprived of his life by people;
then, in his sixth birth, he was born as a flesh-eating *piśāca*—
cruel, intent upon finding vulnerabilities, base, and a depriver of human life.
Having descended, he dragged the limb of a certain man;
having summoned him with a perfected mantra, the man was rendered lifeless by the physician.
In his seventh birth, he was born again with an exceedingly hideous body that was difficult to behold.
With cruel fangs and a terrifying mouth, a consumer of flesh and blood,
naked and dwelling in desert lands, this Brahmarākṣasa of Vasiṣṭha’s lineage rendered the entire kingdom withered and desolate through poisons and other means.
Having been attacked by King Bhīmadāsa, the enemy of the Rākṣasas,
he was struck down in battle with the Brahmāstra after the king had strung his bow;
yet he once again became equal to a tiger upon his eighth birth on earth.
Kruddhāṅga, who was among the forest-dwellers, met his death at the hands of a brahmin;
thereafter, both the elephant and the bear were slain by a bow-wielding Mātaṅga.
Furthermore, Pāñcāla was formidable even amidst the cycle of existence during the eleventh [birth].
With hair standing erect, blood-red eyes, short in stature yet sturdy,
he was a wicked demon wearing the banner of righteousness; though bearing garlands abandoned by the gods,
he was indeed suspended from the tip of a tree by the very officer with the staff and noose.
In his twelfth birth, having become a vessel for abundant afflictions, he entered a pit out of greed for food and was struck down by a hunter. Yet,
in that previous life as well, he had performed the Tārakadvādaśī vow.
Although born again and again in evil wombs due to its power,
he quickly met his death within the ocean of worldly existence;
then once more he became a most righteous king in Vidarbha.

Furthermore, he observed the auspicious Tārakadvādaśī fast; behold the greatness of this vow! Having been born again and again, he enjoyed a kingdom free from all obstacles in this world through the power of that vow.
He attained a station in the city of Viṣṇu that lasts until the dissolution of all beings.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, how is this vow to be performed by the best of men?"
Whether by the women themselves or at the word of their husbands, [they perform] bathing, giving, recitation, and so forth.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Having undertaken the vow of Dvādaśī in the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa...
One should perform a bath in natural water during the afternoon;
then, having bowed to the Sun and likewise performed the worship of the deities,
the fire-oblation (homa) should be maintained until the sun has set.
Then, having eaten fruits, flowers, perfumes, incense, and ointments,
and having prepared water with unbroken grains and gold along with auspicious fruits,
he knelt upon the ground with his knees touching the earth over a beautiful copper vessel.
Facing the east at the beginning of the evening, having placed the vessel for the *arghya* offering upon his head and having drawn a mandala on the ground with cow dung together with stars,
he should indeed delineate it with sandalwood paste while looking upward toward the firmament.
O best of the Kurus, with the *Sahasraśīrṣā* mantra, one should oneself slowly and unweariedly offer water for honor (*arghya*) to the stars upon the ground according to one's capacity; then,
having sprinkled water around and raised incense smoke, one should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to a Brahmin.
Having prepared all the foods in due order, one should eat them at the arrival of night:
in Mārgaśīrṣa, candied sweets; likewise in Pauṣa, *sohālaka*;
in Māgha, sesame and rice; and in Phālguna, cakes with jaggery.
In the month of Caitra, one should offer modakas; in Vaiśākha, sweets made with sugar-candy; in Jyeṣṭha, vessels filled with roasted flour (saktu); in Āṣāḍha, guḍapūrikas;
in Śrāvaṇa, honeyed rice-pudding (madhuśīrṣa); and in Nabhasya, milk-rice (pāyasa).
O King of kings, having fed the twice-born with *ghṛtaparṇa* leaves in the month of Āśvayuja and with *kāṃsāra* leaves in Kārttika, in this manner for twelve years,
one should eat oneself with devotion; thereafter, one should ask the deity for forgiveness.
Upon the completion of the vow, having fashioned a silver cluster of stars—
or having beheld them according to the previous rite— one should worship them and ask for forgiveness.
Twelve water-pots filled with water and containing sweetmeats (modaka) should be given as gifts.
For the Brahmin woman, there is the lower garment and a ruby with its casing;

for the Brahmin, a forehead ornament of *vallī* flowers adorned with a hundred thousand blossoms, as well as a sacred thread and a flower from the *cālaka* tree; having offered these, one should ask for forgiveness.

O best of the Bharatas, whether a man or a woman who performs this vow according to this rule with a heart full of devotion goes to the world of the stars by means of a celestial chariot radiant as the sun.
Honored in the heavenly world by hosts of Apsarases, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Vidyādharas, and gods,
as well as by thousands of sun-like lords,
he shall dwell there for ten thousand kalpas and then go once more to the city of Viṣṇu.
In the past, this vow was performed by Queen Śacī, by Lakṣmī,
by Sītā, Damayantī, Rukmiṇī, and Satyabhāmā;
and in heaven, by Menā, Rambhā, Urvaśī, and Devadattā.
O Pārtha, this vow— which destroys all fear of sin— has been observed by other women as well as by various kinds of men;
it removes even those evils committed in previous births, for it burns them away day after day through the application of merit.
"That twelfth day (Dvādaśī) in this world is named Tāraka; there is nothing that it does not accomplish when performed by men.
Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Vow of Tāraka-Dvādaśī," in the *Uttara-parvan* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[Now follows] the description of the Araṇya-Dvādaśī vow.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Blessed One, tell me correctly about the vow of Araṇyadvādaśī,
together with its prescribed food, its fast, its secret rites, and its mantras."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O son of Kuntī, that vow which was formerly performed by Sītā while she resided in the forest— by the command of Rāghava— is praiseworthy and free from all defects.
In the abode of Lopāmudrā, the virtuous wives of the sages, who had many offspring,
were fed and satisfied by everyone with all kinds of food that fulfills every desire,
served upon broad lotus leaves along with fresh side dishes.
With various foods to be chewed, eaten, licked, and sucked, according to his desire—
listen now with a one-pointed mind, O Pārtha, to this Araṇyadvādaśī.
On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, at the break of dawn:
Having bathed and observed a fast, a man should perform worship to Janārdana with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains, incense, and lamps, spending the night in vigil; then,
at dawn, he should go to the forest and approach those who have mastered the Vedāṅgas.
Having fed [the Brahmins] with food consisting mostly of fruit, he should eat himself while remaining silent.

O Yudhiṣṭhira, having first consumed the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) on that very day, and having completed the auspicious vow for one full year, he should perform the concluding rite (pāraṇa).
When worshipped in the months of Śrāvaṇa, Kārttika, Māgha, or Caitra, [the deity is pleased] with side dishes,
leafy vegetables, sesame cakes (śaṣkulikā) and the like, as well as with sweetmeat-filled pastries (apūpa), sugar-coated sweets (khaṇḍaveṣṭa), black pepper, and siṃhakesara.

The wise man should satisfy [the deity] with dust-covered roots, nectar-like fruits, auspicious and sweet-tasting stalks, cool *arka* flowers, and beautiful *mālaka* blossoms; and he should offer worship with hands bearing curds, milk, and clarified butter, adorned with the four aromatic spices (*cāturjātaka*).
Having gone to a forest abounding in many trees— filled with excellent, sweet jackfruit pierced by *karpūra* and *nakha* [spices]— and reaching a pure, auspicious place with very sweet water,
they sat upon comfortable seats, being pure and facing either the east or the north.
He should feed ten or two sages dwelling in the forest—
both those who carry a single staff and those who carry three— as well as householders of excellent vows,
and various types of Brahmin women, seven of whom are devoted wives faithful to a single husband.

Those limbs of the Sun-god, beautiful in every part, honored, bathed, and radiant in all their members, should be worshipped with fine garments, bodies anointed with saffron, and adorned with fragrant flowers;
or else, those very deities of the Sun should be fed with offerings.
Vāsudeva, Janārdana, Dāmodara, Madhusūdana;
Padmanābha, Kṛṣṇa, Viṣṇu, Govardhana, Trivikrama;
Śrīdhara, Hṛṣīkeśa, Puṇḍarīkākṣa, and Ādivārāha.
Having offered incense and cloth along with sandalwood paste separately for each of these twelve mantras joined with the word of salutation (*namaskāra*),
and having fed them with auspicious foods, one should give them a generous sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Having bowed down, he should pray with devotion, "May Viṣṇu be pleased with me.
Then, he should eat together with his servants, dependents,
guests who have arrived, friends, relatives, and kinsmen.
O son of Kuntī, the man who thus observes the Araṇyadvādaśī vow,
at the end of his body, seated upon a celestial chariot and surrounded by divine maidens,
goes to Śvetadvīpa, the city of Hari, accompanied by his kinsmen.
There, the worlds consist of beings with yellow garments and dark bodies, four-armed,
with beautiful hands holding the conch, discus, mace, and lotus; they possess the Kaustubha gem,
are seated upon Garuḍa, and are adorned with ornaments, crowns, and prominent earrings.
Their chests adorned with garlands of profuse blue and red lotuses,
possessing the hue of clouds and bearing the goddess Lakṣmī, they remain— adorned with bracelets upon their elbows— possessing the common attributes of Viṣṇu, until the dissolution of all beings.
Therefore, having come from there, those of great splendor, honored by kings upon the earth,
become the best of men, renowned in the world of mortals;
thereafter, they go to the supreme abode, the auspicious and blessed path of liberation.
Having gone there, they do not grieve nor do they wander in saṃsāra—
those who fast on the twelfth lunar day known as "Araṇyā" in the month of Vaiśākha, and who then feed the best of the twice-born in the forest;
for virtuous women adorned with good conduct, Viṣṇu attains great favor and grants them liberation.
Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Aṇyadvādaśī Vow," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[Now follows] the description of the Rohiṇī-Candra Vow.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
When the excellent god is shrouded by clouds and the rainy season has arrived—
disturbed by the cries of peacocks and filled with the croaking of frogs—
to whom do noble women offer food? Who is the deity here?
"What is the renowned vow, O Kṛṣṇa, and on which lunar day does its food take place?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"When the month of Śrāvaṇa has begun and the dark fortnight has arrived..."

O King of kings, having become pure on the eleventh day, one should consume indurika made from the flour of black gram with auspicious waters containing all medicinal herbs; likewise, one should eat five very clean sweetmeats (modaka) cooked in ghee.
Then,

having gone to a reservoir of water that is free from wicked crocodiles, filled with pure water, and abounding in aquatic plants, one should prepare a pleasant spot on its bank, consecrated with food offerings and smeared with cow dung and other substances.
Having prepared a circular mandala adorned with flour-paste and other materials,
anointed with perfumes and flowers, and made radiant with incense, lamps, and unbroken grains of rice,
one should there draw the Lord Moon together with Rohiṇī.
And, being purified by this mantra, he should indeed worship [the tree] together with his wife:
"O King Soma, homage to you; homage again and again to Rohiṇī.
O great chaste one, O great goddess, fulfill my desire."

Having thus performed the worship, one should offer consecrated food (naivedya) before it; right there, one should give it to a Brāhmaṇa with the words, "May Soma be pleased with me," and "May the Goddess,
together with her beloved Rohiṇī, be pleased with me."
Having recited thus and offered [the oblation],
one should then enter the water up to the neck, the waist, or the ankles;
and then one should meditate in the mind upon Soma together with Rohiṇī.
Once that entire meal has been consumed and he has finished eating, he should stand on the bank of the river.
Having restrained those who dwell there, he should then provide a meal for a Brāhmaṇa along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),
and he should make a firm resolve regarding his speech.

O King, O son of Pṛthā, whatever man, woman, or maiden performs this Rohiṇī vow according to the prescribed ritual every year— with devotion, according to their capacity, and in accordance with their heart and wealth— [attains the fruit].
Having remained for a long time in this world, which abounds in wealth and grain,
and having attained an auspicious lineage of sons, grandsons, and so forth within the householder stage of life,
one should then meet death at a sacred pilgrimage site and thereafter proceed to the City of Brahmā.

"Therefore, O Pārtha, from there one goes to the auspicious city of Rudra. Rohiṇī is esteemed and beneficial in the sky; hear, O lord of men, the reason why I declare it to you. The fruit of eating *indurikā* made of ground black gram with jaggery and ghee while looking at the moon in water is this very thing. Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Rohiṇī-Candra Vow," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
The Description of the Aviyoga Vow.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O delighter of the Yādavas, tell me about the Aviyoga vow.
"What is its procedure, what is its merit, and who is the deity here?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"Listen attentively, O Pāṇḍava, as it is being told in its entirety."
The vow known as Aviyoga-vrata is the most excellent among all vows.
Having risen early on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Prauṣṭhapada,
one who wears white garments should first bathe in a body of water.

On a charming and delightful terrace of the palace, one should have Hari drawn within a mandala made from flour ground from wheat; Lakṣmī should be depicted at his side. In that very place, Hara and Gaurī, as well as Sāvitrī together with Brahmā, should also be drawn.
O King of kings, one who observes the vow of non-separation should worship the Sun, the illuminator of the three worlds, together with his queen,
according to one's ability, with perfumes, flowers, incense, and food offerings,
using this mantra.
Whether woman or man, having formed a firm resolve never to be separated,
meditative and silent with devotion, one should worship the divine couple.
[They are] the thousand-headed Puruṣa, Padmanābha, Janārdana.
Vyāsa, the teacher Kapila, the Blessed One Puruṣottama,
Nārāyaṇa, Madhuliṭ, Viṣṇu, Dāmohara, Hari,
Mahāvarāha, Govinda, Keśava, and Garuḍadhvaja.
Śrīdhara, Puṇḍarīkākṣa, Viśvarūpa, Trivikrama,
Upendra, Vāmana, Rāma, Vaikuṇṭha, Mādhava, Dhruva,
Vāsudeva, Hṛṣīkeśa, Kṛṣṇa, Saṅkarṣaṇa, and Acyuta.
Aniruddha, the great yogi, Pradyumna,

and Nanda— may he, who is eternally auspicious, joyful, and endowed with Śrī, the one with matted hair and the trident, the lord of Umā, the blue-throated one, Sthāṇu, Śambhu, and the destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes, be ever pleased with me.
Īśāna, Bhairava, Śūlin, Tryambaka, Tripurāntaka, Kapardīśa, Mahāliṅgin, Mahākāla, Vṛṣadhvaja,
Śiva, Śarva, Mahādeva, Rudra, and Bhūtamaheśvara.
May Śaṅkara, the bestower of happiness, together with Pārvatī, be my source of well-being for a long time.
May he be Brahmā, Śambhu, the Lord, the Creator, Puṣkarin, the Great-Grandfather,
Hiraṇyagarbha, the knower of the Vedas, Parameṣṭhin, and Prajāpati.
May the four-faced creator, the self-born one seated upon the lotus,
Virañci, and the lotus-born— may he always be the granter of boons to me.
May Āditya, Bhāskara, Bhānu, Sūrya, Arka, Savitṛ, and Ravi [grant this].
Mārtaṇḍa, Maṇḍaladhyoti, Agni, Aṃśu, Janeśvara,
Prabhākara, Saptasapti, Taraṇi, Saraṇi, Khaga,
Divākara, Dinakara, Sahasrāṃśu, and Marīcimān.
May the Lotus-awakener, the Sun, the Rayed One, the Ornament of Meru,
Nikumbha, Varṇabha, and the God— be forever well-pleased with me.
May Lakṣmī, Śrī, Saṃpadā, Padmā, Mā, Vibhūti, and Haripriyā [grant their grace].
Pārvatī, Lalitā, Gaurī, Umā, the beloved of Śaṅkara;
Gāyatrī, Prakṛti, Sṛṣṭi, and Sāvitrī, who is considered the intellect of Brahmā; Rājñī, Bhānumatī, Saṃjñā, Nityabhā, and the beloved of the Sun.
Thus, having worshipped Padmanābha, Śaṅkara, Pitāmaha, Arka, and the others together with their consorts,
and having given gifts— or even if not giving— after eating, one should go home at the conclusion.
A man who performs this vow on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī), permeated by devotion, [attains success] in the world.
He becomes a partaker of fame and wealth, possessed of progeny, and free from all affliction.
Having enjoyed vast pleasures in the worlds of Hari, Hara, Hiraṇyagarbha, and the Sun in due order, the yogi then attains final liberation.
"Whether a couple, or a man alone,
or a woman performs this vow, having observed it, they go to the abode of Viṣṇu.

Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter, titled "The Vow of the Non-Separation of Hari, Hara, Hiraṇyagarbha, and Prabhākara," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the Govatsadvādaśī Vow.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Eighteen akṣauhiṇīs have been destroyed for the sake of the kingdom of Madra.
Because of that sin, a profound sense of revulsion dwells within my mind;
for therein were slain Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and others— Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kaliṅga, Karṇa, Śalya, Suyodhana, and the rest.
"The sin resulting from their slaughter cuts into my vital organs.
O Lord of the World, tell me of some dharma that may wash away this sin.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O Pārtha, O mighty-armed one, bearer of the burden of the Pāṇḍavas, there exists the Govatsadvādaśī vow, which generates very great merit. Yudhiṣṭhira said:
What is this known as Godvādaśī, and what is its ritual procedure?
How did it originate, and at what time, O Janārdana?
Tell me all of this, O Hari; protect me from the ocean of hell.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Pārtha, formerly in the Kṛta Yuga, ten million sages assembled on a mountain; observing the vow known as Nāma-vrata, they performed extensive penance.
Filled with great joy and longing for a vision of the Divine,
they went to the highly meritorious Jambūmārga, adorned with various sacred fords (tīrthas),
to the delightful Tāṇḍulikā hermitage on Mount Pāriyātra, which was a vessel for the perfected ones (siddhas).
O King, on the celebrated and supreme peak known as Taṇṭāvi,
there is an incomparable forest of ascetics adorned with divine groves,
frequented by Vasiṣṭha, Śukra, Aṅgiras, Kratu, Dakṣa, and others.
The hermitage circle of Bhṛgu was clothed in bark garments and deerskins;
it was frequented by various herds of wild animals and accompanied by troops of monkeys; lions and deer there were perfectly peaceful; and trees stood everywhere throughout the site.
It was a dense, delightful, and secluded forest, thick with the spreading of creepers;
it was frequented by lions, tigers, elephants, deer, Śabaras, and hares,
and it was graced on all sides by wonderful boars and large bears.
O Lord of the Earth, while those sages were performing austerities there, desiring a vision of him,
the one with four eyes (Śiva) assumed a disguise;
he became an aged Brāhmaṇa whose hair was white with old age.
With her skin wrinkled and loose, humpbacked, trembling, and holding a staff in her hand, Umā too assumed the form of a cow; hear now, O Pārtha, what kind of cow she was.
She was one of those born from the waters of the Ocean of Milk during the ancient churning for the nectar of immortality.
O Pārtha, there are five auspicious cows, the mothers of the five worlds:
Nandā, Subhadrā, Surabhī, Suśīlā, and Bahulā.
These exist for the benefit of the world and for the gratification of the gods.
Then Jamadagni, Bhāradvāja, Vasiṣṭha, Asita, and Gautama accepted the five cows granted by the gods as fulfillers of desires;
[the five products] of the cows being cow dung, yellow pigment, urine, milk, curd, and clarified butter.
The six limbs are pure and effect complete purification.
The glorious Bilva tree, beloved of Śiva, arose from cow dung;
because the goddess Śrī, holding a lotus in her hand, resides there, it is known as the Śrīvṛkṣa (the tree of fortune).
The seeds of blue and red lotuses are born again from cow dung;
gorocanā is auspicious, purifying, and effective for all accomplishments.
Fragrant guggulu resin, pleasing to behold, is produced from cow urine.
The food of all the gods, and especially that of Śiva,
is to be known as originating from milk— whatever seed there is of the universe. All beings who have been born offer auspicious gifts for the attainment of their goals.
From clarified butter (ghṛta) was produced nectar (amṛta), which is the cause of satisfaction for the gods.
Brāhmaṇas and cows constitute a single family divided into two parts:
on one side reside the mantras, and on the other resides the sacrificial oblation (havis).
In cows the sacrifices proceed; in cows the gods are established;
in cows are engraved the Vedas, together with their six limbs, word-for-word commentaries, and phonetic recitations.
At the base of the horns of cows, Brahmā and Viṣṇu are eternally stationed.
All holy places, both stationary and moving, reside at the tips of the horns;
in the middle is Śiva Mahādeva, the cause of all causes;
Gaurī is situated on the forehead, and the Six-faced One (Kārttikeya) is on the bridge of the nose.
The two Nāgas, Kambala and Aśvatara, reside in the nostrils;
the two divine Aśvins are in the ears; the Moon and the Sun are in the eyes;
all the Vasus are in the teeth; and Varuṇa is stationed in the tongue.
Sarasvatī is in the hollow of the throat, Yamayakṣau are in the two cheeks;
likewise, the two twilights are in the two beloved ones (the ears), and Purandara is in the neck.
The Rakṣases are on the hump, and Dyaus is situated in the heel.
The entire Dharma with its four quarters always resides in the shanks;
the Gandharvas are in the middle of the hooves, and the Pannagas are on the tips of the hooves;
the Rākṣasas are established at the rear part of the hooves.
The eleven Rudras reside on his back; Varuṇa is in all his joints;
the Pitṛs are situated on the slopes of his hips; and the Manusyas are in his cheeks. Śrī is always in the drinking vessel of the cows, and Svāhā has taken refuge in his ornaments.
The rays of the sun exist as hairs gathered together into a mass;
Gaṅgā herself resides in the cow’s urine, and Yamunā resides in the cow dung;
thirty-three crores of gods reside within the pores of the skin.
The entire earth, with its mountains, forests, and groves, is within her belly;
the four oceans are said to be the udders of the cows;
Parjanya is in the streams of milk, and the clouds are established as the drops.
The Gārhapatya fire resides in the stomach, the Dakṣiṇāgni fire is situated in the heart;
the Āhavanīya fire is in the throat, and the Sabhya fire is situated in the palate. The mountains are established in the bones, and the sacrificial rites reside in the marrow.
The Ṛgveda, Atharvaveda, Sāmaveda,
and Yajurveda are established within the colors of the cows— red, yellow, black, and so forth.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, having meditated upon the form of Umā, one should contemplate those fragrant cows.
Recalling that moment, Gaurī desired a body similar to his;
listen, O Dharmarāja, as the Goddess fashioned herself:
she was six-fold elevated, five-fold depressed, with eyes like a frog and a beautiful tail.

Having touched that mistress in the form of a cow, who had copper-colored udders, a silver-colored belly, beautiful hooves, a lovely face, and was white in color; who was of excellent character, full of affection for her calf, yielding abundant milk, and possessed of fine teats; and who was accompanied by her young calf—[he touched] Umā herself in the form of a cow.

O Pārtha, while on his way in the morning, the great god Mahādeva, delighted in his heart and assuming the form of a brahmin, proceeded slowly toward the great hermitage. Having approached the presence of Bhṛgu, the lord of the clan, he presented that cow to him.
O Pāṇḍava, that ascetic of great splendor, having guarded her for two days as a trust, gave that cow to all of them,
saying: "Until I have bathed here and crossed over to Jambūmārga."
"Once the sages have promised to protect this Surabhi,
the god vanished; he became a tiger once again,
with claws like thunderbolts and wheels, and eyes blazing tawny-red, facing the goddess."
With a tongue and a mouth formidable, and terrifying with his tongue-like tail,
he approached the hermitage and, stationed in the quarters of the sages, O Lord, terrified that cow together with her calf.
Even the sages, being overwhelmed, let out cries of distress;
some cried out "Hā! Hā! loudly, while others uttered "Huṃ" sounds.
Seeing the exceedingly terrifying tiger, some clapped their hands.

O Yudhiṣṭhira, that tawny cow, afflicted by fear of the tiger, leaped up with her calf and let out a lowing cry; as she fled into the midst of the rocks, her four hooves remained momentarily imprinted there.
There, the Vyāghra and Vatsaka [shrines] are saluted by gods and kinnaras;
even today, that quartet is seen very clearly. There is a Śiva-liṅga with water, and that is the supreme tīrtha of Śambhu.
O Indra among kings, he who touches it dispels the sin of cow-slaughter.
O lord of men, having bathed there at that great sacred ford on the Jambūmārga, one is liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin; of this there is no doubt.
Then those sages, filled with rage, struck the loud-sounding bell given by Brahmā and presented by the gods— a bell that filled the mountain caves—
with which even a tiger, hearing that sound, released the cow together with her calf.
The sages there gave it the name Ḍhuṇḍhāgiri; so says the tradition.
O Pārtha, those who behold him become Rudras themselves—of this there is no doubt. Then, the supreme Lord Maheśvara appeared before their very eyes.

The wielder of the trident, the destroyer of Tripura, the slayer of Kāma, seated upon his bull; accompanied by Umā, the bestower of boons, together with his Lord (Śiva), Vināyaka, Nandi, Mahākāla, Śṛṅgin, and Manohara— Hara.
And Vīrabhadra and Cāmuṇḍā were surrounded by Ghaṇṭākarṇa and others,
by the Mothers, by hosts of spirits, by Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Guhyakas,
and by gods, Dānavas, Gandharvas, sages, Vidyādharas, and serpents.

Having prostrated before the God of gods, Umā, together with her wives, was worshipped by the celibate students; likewise, the cow in the form of a calf was worshipped. On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, the Nandinī vow is observed.

From that time forward, O Indra among kings, it has descended upon the surface of the earth. Listen now to how this vow was performed by Uttānapāda. There was a kṣatriya named Uttānapāda, O lord of the earth.
He had two wives, renowned as Ruci and Śūghnī.
To Śūghnī was born a son named Dhruva, who was lame in his left foot and indolent.
[His mother said: "O friend, this Dhruva has been entrusted to Ruci; let him be protected by you."
"I myself shall always personally perform service for my husband. Ruci constantly prepared delicious food in the house every day;
Śūdrī, devoted to her husband, performed service for her husband daily.
Once, out of anger and envy, she displayed her co-wifely malice;
having herself struck that child with a pestle, she cut him into pieces. Thus, he was thoroughly cooked and prepared in a frying pan and a cooking pot.
At the time of eating, she gave it to him in the king's vessel;
indeed, that wicked woman intended to devour him along with the food containing meat.
Then, at the time of the meal, he chose his life and obtained it.
In that very manner, laughing, the child emerged from his mother’s lap.
Seeing that great marvel, Ruci was struck with wonder and asked:
"Tell me, what is this? What is the account of this? Whose is this supreme manifestation?"
"What vow have you observed, what gift have you given, or what oblation have you offered—
truly, truly, and again truly— that which has caused your son to live?
For seven times was he pierced by my arrows and torn to pieces."
Cooked by himself in a vessel together with side dishes and main courses,
and being served once again— how did he regain his life?
Have you mastered the auspicious and great science of reviving the dead?
"O highly fortunate one, tell me the truth, the absolute truth; you are my sister. What is this jewel, this gem, this great treasure, this magical collyrium, and this great medicine?
When she had spoken thus, Ruci explained to her the Vatsa-govrata vow.
Just as it was performed of old on the twelfth day of the month of Kārttika,
by the power of this vow my son shall live again;
my calf, though dead at the hour of milking, shall regain its life.
And there shall be a reunion even with those who have gone abroad due to their vows;
this Godvādaśī vow has been explained to you exactly as it is.
If it pleases you, all of that will become auspicious and dear to you.
When this had been said, Ruci performed the vow; her sons obtained happiness and wealth, and at the end of their lives, they were established in the abode of Dhruva.
Ruci lived together with her husband, who was the creator Brahmā.
The Pole Star (Dhruva), joined with ten constellations, is visible even today. When the world beholds the Pole Star, it is liberated from sins.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Janārdana, tell me what that ritual procedure was,
which you performed out of affection at the request of Śughni, O scion of the Yadu clan. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O best of the Kurus, when the month of Kārttika has arrived, during the bright fortnight,
on the twelfth day, having bathed in a sacred body of water,
a man or a woman should observe a single meal.
Then, at the time of midday, O Lord of the women of the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, he saw a cow with her calf— well-behaved, affectionate, white, tawny, and red-hued.

O Pāṇḍava, having worshipped her in due order with perfumes, flowers, water, unbroken grains of rice, saffron, red lac, lamps, auspicious cakes of black gram, and vatsaka flowers, one should worship with this mantra.
"Oṃ! She is the mother of the Rudras, the daughter of the Vasus, the sister of the Ādityas, and the navel of immortality.
I have declared this to the wise person: do not slay the cow, the sinless Aditi! Homage, homage, Svāhā!
Having thus worshipped the cow and questioned her, he should afterwards ask for her forgiveness.
Oṃ! O Goddess who embodies all the gods, O bringer of auspicious joy to the worlds!
O Mother, O Nandinī, make my desire bear fruit.
Thus one should worship a single cow; for this indeed constitutes the daily rite for cows (gavāhnika).
Having sprinkled water with devotion and bowed to Surabhi,
one should then avoid food cooked on a griddle and food cooked in a pot on that day;
sleeping on the ground while observing celibacy, one shall obtain the fruit [of the vow].
O descendant of the Kuru race, for as many years as there are hairs on the bodies of cows, he dwells in Goloka; of this there is no doubt.
[Furthermore,] the eight cities of Meru, belonging to Indra, Agni, Yama, and the Rakshasas, are delightful.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, Goloka is situated above the realms of Varuṇa, Vāyu, Yakṣas, and Rudra; there that observer of the cow-vow goes.
Those who, on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika, worship a cow with her calf using flowers and delicious sweetmeats (vaṭaka), [attain that state].
"Those who dwell for a very long time among mortals, enjoying all pleasures, happiness, and opulence,

and possessing many living calves," thus ends the sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Vow of Govatsadvādaśī," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira;
followed by the description of the Devaśayanotthāpanadvādaśī vow.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Pārtha, I shall describe the vow of Govinda-śayana (the lying down of Govinda),
the gift of the mat, the ritual for rising [from the vow], and the sequence of the Cāturmāsya vow.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
What is this so-called "lying on the waters," and why does that god sleep?
For what purpose does the god sleep? Tell me always what the procedure is.
"What are the mantras, what are the observances, the vows, and what is the ritual action?
What is to be accepted and what is to be eaten while the Lord Janārdana is asleep?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
When the thousand-rayed sun is situated in Gemini, one should install Madhusūdana;
when it has entered the zodiac sign of Libra, one should again raise him up for the vow. This same sequence of ritual procedure applies even when an intercalary month (adhimāsa) occurs.
One should not install the deity otherwise, nor should one cause Hari to be awakened [from sleep].
Having fasted on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha,
a devoted person should install Viṣṇu, who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, [one should meditate upon] the gentle one wearing yellow garments, seated upon a beautiful,
well-spread couch covered with white cloth and provided with a pillow—
[that] man who knows the Itihāsas and Purāṇas and is also a devotee of Viṣṇu.
Having bathed [the image] with water consisting of curd, milk, ghee, and honey,
and having anointed it with auspicious perfumes, incense, and garments,
one should worship it with saffron and other offerings while reciting this mantra, O Pāṇḍava.

"O Lord of the World, when you are asleep, this entire world becomes asleep; when you awaken, the whole world, including all things mobile and immobile, awakens. Having thus installed that image of Viṣṇu, O Yudhiṣṭhira...
Then,

in the presence of that very deity, a devotee of mine— whether woman or man— who is firm in his vow for the sake of dharma, should personally undertake the observances for the four months of the rainy season until the time of the deity’s awakening.
One should undertake these observances, beginning with the cleansing of the teeth;
I shall describe their respective fruits for those who perform them.
By abstaining from jaggery, a man becomes a king with a sweet voice.
By abstaining from oil, O Pārtha, one is born with beautiful limbs;
by renouncing pungent oil, one attains the destruction of enemies;
and by the abandonment of honey-plant oil, one shall possess incomparable good fortune.
By renouncing the enjoyment of flowers and other such things, one becomes a Vidyādhara in heaven;
he who practices yoga shall attain the state of Brahman.
[One should avoid] pungent, sour, bitter, sweet, alkaline, and astringent [tastes].
He who avoids [these] shall avoid deformity and shall never encounter misfortune.
By abstaining from betel, one becomes an enjoyer of pleasures and possesses a resonant voice.
Through the renunciation of ghee, one attains great beauty, and furthermore, all perfections (siddhis) shall arise.

By renouncing fruits, an intelligent man becomes the father of many sons; by subsisting on leafy vegetables he becomes free from disease, and by eating uncooked food he becomes pure. O King, by abandoning the anointing of the feet and the anointing of the head, [one attains these benefits].

A man who observes the discipline of curd, milk, and buttermilk becomes a radiant Yakṣa, a performer of brilliant deeds, and a lord of wealth; by abstaining from cooked rice prepared in a single pot (sthālīpāka), he attains the status of Indra's guest and reaches Goloka.
By abstaining from eating food cooked by heat, one obtains a long lineage;
by sleeping on the bare ground, one becomes an attendant of Viṣṇu.
By always avoiding honey and meat, one is forever a sage and forever a yogi.
By abstaining from wine and intoxicants, one becomes free from disease, painless, and full of vigor.
O son of Dharma, through the renunciation of such things as these, one's merit increases;
by fasting on every other day, one is glorified in the world of Brahmā.

For one who maintains their nails and hair, performs daily ablutions in the Ganges, and observes the vow of silence, his command shall remain unimpeded. He who always eats upon the ground shall become the lord of the earth.
For one who recites "Namo Nārāyaṇāya," the fruit is that of fasting;
by bowing at the feet of Viṣṇu, one obtains the fruit of gifting a cow;
and by contact with the water from Viṣṇu’s feet, a person becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done.

Whoever performs the smearing and worship at the temple of Viṣṇu shall become a king who endures for an eon; of this there is no doubt. Furthermore, he who performs a hundred circumambulations while reciting hymns of praise [attains the same].
He shall go to the city of Viṣṇu by means of a celestial chariot yoked with swans;
one who provides song and instrumental music for Viṣṇu shall attain the world of the Gandharvas;
and he who constantly awakens people through the delight of the scriptures [shall likewise attain that state].
That Lord in the form of Vyāsa shall go to the city of Viṣṇu at the end;
having performed worship with flower garlands and other offerings, he shall go to the city of Viṣṇu.
That man who bathes daily does not see hell.
He who conquers his appetite for food obtains the merit of the Pauṣkara bath;
having performed a divine spectacle, he shall obtain a kingdom of apsarases;
and by eating only what is unasked, he attains the same fruit as that of constructing a large and small reservoir.
By eating only at the sixth mealtime, a man becomes an eternal resident in heaven;
the man who eats from leaves obtains the merit of Kurukṣetra;
by eating daily from a stone slab, one’s bath is equivalent to that performed at Prayāga.
By abandoning water for two watches [of the night], one is not overcome by diseases;
O Pārtha, through such vows as these, Keśava, the Lord of the World whose banner is Garuḍa, becomes pleased with the devotee when he is asleep.
O Bhārata, all the ritual activities of the four castes cease:
marriage, the binding of vows, the consecration of living beings, initiation,
sacrifices, the entering of houses, and the rites established since the gift of the cow.
One should avoid all those ritual acts that are worthy of worship; indeed,
one should avoid the intercalary month (māsa) in rites for the gods and the ancestors,
as well as the impure month (malimluca), which is devoid of the sun’s transit (saṃkrānti).
When the month of Bhādrapada has arrived, on the eleventh day of Hari,
the offering of a bed for Viṣṇu should take place, and one should perform the great worship. Listen now to the reason why this very [day] is called Śayana (the Bed).
Formerly, having gratified the omnipresent Hari by the power of his asceticism,
he honored my body at my request;
and then the gods, seeing their own chest obstructed by Lakṣmī, [were filled with envy].
My arms were obstructed by the conch, discus, sword, and other weapons, as was my chest;
below my navel, I was blocked by the bird Vainateya;
my head was hemmed in by his crown, and my ears by his two earrings.

Then, being pleased, I respectfully granted her a place in my eyes for the four months of the rainy season; thus, Yoganidrā shall not remain there during that time. Even she, having heard this auspicious ancient majesty, [remained].
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, she made her dwelling in my eyes for this very purpose;
and I, having meditated upon that high-minded lady,
honor her while remaining on the couch of Śeṣa as Yoganidrā, the Great Sleep."

And at that time, he who casts four months into my devotion— whether at the Ocean of Milk or on the peak of the Vindhya mountains, with feet washed and mind composed, his two feet being massaged by the stainless lotus-hands of Lakṣmī.
O best of the Pāṇḍavas, by means of various vows and observances, a human being shall dwell for a kalpa in the world of Viṣṇu; of this there is no doubt.
Thereafter, he awakens as the glorious Lord who bears the conch and the mace.
Listen separately, O King of kings, regarding the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Kārtika: on that day,
the twice-born should awaken the God with this mantra,
"Viṣṇu strode across this," while [the deity] is upon his own seat, O King.
O Viṣṇu, when he has arisen, one should then set all ritual activities in motion;
at night, amidst the sound of great trumpets, one should cause him, seated upon his chariot, to be paraded.
When the Lord of the Gods of gods has arisen, the king himself [should do so] in the city.
O King of kings, on that path which provides intense illumination and is crowded with people dancing and singing,
whatever Dāmodara— the upholder of the earth— beholds as he stands there,
all that should be given; it conduces to heaven for everyone.
During the night vigil on the eleventh day (Ekādaśī) in a temple of the gods,
one should bathe at the clear dawn on the twelfth day (Dvādaśī) and worship Viṣṇu;
one should also offer oblations into the sacrificial fire with clarified butter and other suitable materials.
Then, having bathed, the sacrificer— contented and free from haste or laughter— should feed auspicious Brahmins with abundant food,
including ghee, curd, honey, and the like, along with molasses, incense,
and sweetmeats.
O best of the Kurus, one should honor eleven, ten, eight, five, or even two of the most excellent brahmins with sandalwood paste, incense, flowers, and perfumes;
O Pārtha, a fortunate man should feed these ascetics according to the rules prescribed in the scriptures with faith.
Then, once they have sipped water (ācamana), he should offer whatever he possesses as a gift—
leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth— as desired by his own mind and expressed by his own words.
This applies to whoever has undertaken a specific vow for the four months of the rainy season.
Having spoken thus to the twice-born, he should give it to them with devotion along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Having given it, he should dismiss the Brahmins and then eat himself.
He should maintain the practice of that which was renounced during the four months.
O Pārtha, he who practices in this manner shall attain infinite merit;
at the conclusion, O Indra among kings, he shall go to the city of Vāsudeva.
O King, for him whose Cāturmāsya vow is completed without obstacles, [this reward is assured].
He would indeed have accomplished all that was to be done and would not be born again as a mortal,
O Pārtha, who observes the month-long period of the Lord’s sleep and likewise His awakening,
for he shall attain the world of Hari.

O Pārtha, that man who hears, meditates upon, praises, offers oblations to, or proclaims the supreme devotion to Viṣṇu shall indeed go to the station of Viṣṇu. On the day when the Lord Ananta sleeps upon his couch in the milk-ocean, or on the day when he awakens, the Lord who reclines upon the body of Garuḍa grants a blessed state to those men who observe a fast with undivided minds.

Thus ends the seventieth chapter, titled "Description of the Vow of Devaśayanotthāpana-dvādaśī," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[Now follows] the description of the Nīrājanā-dvādaśī vow.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
In former times, there was a royal sage known as Ajapāla. Being entreated by his subjects for the removal of all their suffering, he said:
"O Lord of Men, effect the alleviation of the suffering of those who are afflicted by disease."

Having been addressed thus, he meditated for a long time and, having made the multitudes of subjects free from disease, he protected them with joy; thus he became Ajapāla. By him was this propitiation created among the people, known by the name Nīrājanā.
O best of the Pāṇḍavas, listen as I describe its characteristics to you;
it is to be performed according to the prescribed rites by the king together with his domestic priests.
At that time, there was Rāvaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas.
Residing in Laṅkā, he appointed the hosts of gods to their respective duties;
he made the moon, with its unbroken orb,
his royal parasol, appointed Indra as his commander-in-chief, and Vāyu as the sweeper of dust.
He appointed Varuṇa, who was established in the performance of his bounden duties, as the giver and protector of wealth;
Yama, for the restraint of enemies; and Manu for counsel. The clouds overspread the king amidst rows of tree blossoms and the like.
The seven sages, devoted to peace, were stationed together with Brahmā;
the Gandharvas, intent on song, were the sentries in the middle courtyard;
a host of Apsarases was in the viewing gallery, and the Vidyādharas surrounded the outer perimeter.

The Gaṅgā and other rivers reside in his drinking water; the sacrificial fire resides in his domestic hearth; Viśvakarman resides in the preparation of his food; and Yama resides in his employment of artisans.
All earthly beings stand before him, performing service.
They were seen, radiant with brilliant jewels and magnificent ornaments;
beholding them, Rāvaṇa spoke to his excellent doorkeeper:
"Tell me, who has arrived here to perform service in my presence?"
Having prostrated before him, the night-stalker Daṇḍapāṇi said: "This is Kakutstha, Māndhātṛ, Dhundhumāra, Nala, Arjuna,
Yayāti, Nahuṣa, Bhīma, this Rāghava, and Vidūratha."
"These and many other kings sit here like clouds; Ajapāla has not come to your presence. Enraged, Rāvaṇa spoke thus and quickly dispatched a messenger.
When this was said, a messenger named the Rākṣasa Dhūmrākṣa was dispatched:
"Dhūmrākṣa, go and speak to Ajapāla on my command:
'Perform service and come [to me], for King Kabandha is his sovereign.'"
"Otherwise, with my sword Candrahāsa, I shall turn you into a headless trunk like Rāvaṇa.
Thus addressed by Rāvaṇa, Dhūmrākṣa, like Garuḍa,
reached that beautiful city and went to the royal palace.
He saw that very same man, the single cowherd surrounded by goats—
his hair disheveled, his armpits exposed, with one foot bare and the other covered by a sandal,
carrying a staff upon his shoulder, covered in dust, and encircled by diseases.
Having inscribed his name upon the earth— which slays the tiger-like enemies and destroys all calamities— he destroyed the host of his foes;
he was like a sage who, having bathed and eaten in an auspicious place, has fulfilled his purpose.
Having seen this, Dhūmrākṣa, with a joyful mind, repeated what Rāvaṇa had said;
Ajapāla, however, having replied with a reproach and citing another reason,
dispatched Dhūmrākṣa and then attended to his own task.
Having summoned the Fever, the lord of the earth spoke these words:
"Go to the abode of the Lord of Laṅkā and perform what is appropriate. O King, thus commissioned by Ajapāla, the Fever departed.
Having arrived, he caused the lord of the Rākṣasas and his entire retinue to tremble.
But Rāvaṇa, recognizing that it was an exceedingly terrible fever, said:
"Let the king remain; I have no need for him."

Thereupon, the King, the younger brother of Dhanada, became free from his fever. This peace-chant (*śānti*), which pacifies all diseases and destroys all calamities, was composed by that wise Ajapāla.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, at the beginning of the night,
when the Lord Dāmodara had arisen and was free from sleep,
he sat upon a beautiful altar adorned with garlands and encircled by lovely strings of jewels.
Having generated a new Viṣṇu and offered oblations with mantras by the best of the twice-born,

and having worshipped the sacrificial fire with lamps made from the wood of the *vardhamāna* tree, the great multitude, together with all [the participants], should slowly perform the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*) for Hari.
The God was worshipped with flowers and anointed with sandalwood paste;
likewise with jujube fruits, variegated berries, cucumbers, and sugarcane;
and honored with perfumes, flowers, ornaments, garments, and jewels.
Then, with his permission, one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for Lakṣmī, Brahmā, and Caṇḍikā;
likewise for Āditya, Śaṅkara, Gaurī, the Yakṣa, Gaṇapati, the planets,
the mother, the father, and all the Nāgas.
One should perform the *nīrājana* rite for the cows and the circular procession (*maṇḍala*) for the buffalo-cow and others;
one should cause them to be whirled around and terrified by means of trumpeting, ringing bells, and waving cloths.
Those cows, adorned with garlands, clusters of flowers, and ornaments, proceed forth having been milked.
With the tips of their horns adorned with vermilion,
accompanied by calves and herdsmen, they follow you, driving your wealth;
their limbs are smeared with the blood from the slaughter, and they wear red, yellow, and white garments.
When such a clamor had arisen during the Nīrājana festival of the cows,
[the king] brought forth from the courtyard of his own palace all the royal insignia, as well as horses endowed with auspicious marks and well-adorned elephants.
The king, together with his domestic priests, ministers, and attendants,
seated upon the throne amidst the sounding of conchs, trumpets, and other instruments,
should worship [the deity] with perfumes, flowers, garments, lamps, and ointments.
Then, either a courtesan endowed with the marks of a woman or a noblewoman should wave a wooden vessel over the head of the king,
saying: "May there be peace and prosperity through the brahmins and one's own kin."
Then, O gentle one, one should perform the *nīrājana* ceremony for the army crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots.
Thus is this great propitiation (*mahāśānti*) known among people as the *nīrājana*,
which, O son of Pāṇḍu, is performed in their kingdom, city, or village.
Their diseases come to an end, and then there is an increase in abundance;
through the performance of *śānti* and *nīrājana* rites, one dispels all diseases in the world.
Having caused the worlds to flourish, he is like a preeminent protector of goats.

"Desiring the welfare of these living beings when they are afflicted by diseases and other misfortunes, one should perform the propitiatory rite of *nīrājanā* every year. Those who perform the *nīrājanā* for Hari— who resembles a fresh cloud— as well as for cows, Brahmins, chariots, elephants, and the insignia of kings;
"By the word of Ajapāla, those who are free from all diseases and honored by kings shall become like Indra in splendor upon the earth.

Thus ends the seventy-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Nīrājanadvādaśī Vow," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[Now follows] the description of the Bhīṣmapañcaka Vow.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"This incomparable merit, this supreme vow among all vows,
the Bhīṣmapañcaka, must be performed with great effort during the month of Kārttika."
"O best of the Yadus, tell me by your grace what the procedure for that is and what its fruit, for the sake of the benefit of these sages who desire it.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
I shall proclaim this meritorious vow, the most excellent of all vows;
how it is to be performed according to the rules, and its fruit as it has been declared. This was told by me to Bhṛgu, and Bhṛgu gave it to Uśanas.
For Uśanas [taught it] to the Brahmins and to the wise Prahlāda;
just as fire is among the radiant, the wind among those that move swiftly,
a Brahmin among those worthy of honor, and gold among gifts.
As the earthly realm (bhūloka) is among all worlds, as the Ganges is among sacred fords (tīrtha),
as the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha) is among sacrifices, as Mathurā is for those desiring liberation,
as the Veda is among scriptures, and as Acyuta is among the gods; [so is this].
Likewise, among all vows, the Bhīṣmapañcaka has been declared the best.
They say that the Bhīṣma-vow is difficult to perform; it is said here that it is not possible for anyone else.
O King of kings, he who performs it has accomplished everything.
It was practiced by Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, Bharga, and others during the Kṛta Yuga and other ages;
it was practiced by Nābhāga, Aṅga, Ambarīṣa, and others during the Tretā Yuga and other ages;
and it was practiced by Vaiśyas such as Sīrabhadra, by Śūdras, and by others in the Kali Yuga.
These five days are to be honored; this great vow has been performed by Brāhmaṇas through celibacy, recitation, fire-offerings, and other rites,
and likewise by Kṣatriyas according to their capacity, being devoted to purity and vows.
The supreme burden must be borne through celibacy and steadfastness;
by men who have renounced liquor, meat, sexual intercourse, and sinful speech,
who are devoted to a diet of vegetables, and intent on the worship of Kṛṣṇa.
It should be performed by women at the word of their husbands for the increase of happiness;
it should also be performed by widows for the sake of the growth of sons, grandsons, and so forth,
O Pāṇḍava, as well as for the fulfillment of all desires and even for the sake of liberation.
One should constantly perform ritual bathing and giving of gifts until the full moon day of Kārttika;
having bathed according to the prescribed rite in the morning and likewise at midday,
the observer of the vow should apply cow dung at a river, a mountain stream, or a pool.
With barley, rice, and sesame seeds, he should diligently and properly satisfy the gods, the sages, the ancestors, and others who move at will;
having performed his bath and observed silence, the man of firm vows shall wear washed garments.
Then one should worship the god Hari, the remover of all sins;
and with devotion, one should bathe Acyuta with honey, milk, and ghee,
as well as with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and water scented with sandalwood.
One should smear Keśava, whose banner is Garuḍa, with fragrant sandalwood and saffron mixed with camphor and uśīra;
one should worship him with beautiful flowers accompanied by perfumes and incense.
One should devoutly burn guggulu resin mixed with clarified butter for Kṛṣṇa;
one should also offer a lamp day and night for five days. One should present the food offering of the God of gods consisting of *paramānna* (sweetened milk-rice).
One who observes the vow should mutter "Oṃ namo vāsudevāya" one hundred and eight times;
then, he should offer oblations of sesame seeds and rice grains smeared with clarified butter,
accompanied by the six-syllable mantra and the utterance of "svāhā."
Having performed the evening twilight devotions (saṃdhyā), having bowed to the one whose banner is Garuḍa (Viṣṇu),
and having recited the mantra as before, the man should sleep on the ground.
Indeed, this entire ritual procedure must be carried out for five days.
One should lie down upon this blanket; first, listen to me regarding the sequence of the days.
On the first day, a person should worship the feet of Hari with lotuses;
on the second day, one should worship the region of the knees with bilva leaves.
And on the third day, one should worship the navel with the juice of the *bhṛṅga* plant;
then, in the middle, with *bilva* and *jayā* flowers; thereafter, one should worship the shoulders;
and then one should worship the head with fresh *mālatī* blossoms.
On the full moon day of Kārttika, having worshipped Hṛṣīkeśa— the God of gods— with devotion and a mind fixed upon Him, one should, being composed on the eleventh day,
properly consume cow-dung while reciting the mantra and observe a fast.
Having consecrated cow urine with mantras, the observer of the vow should consume it on the twelfth day;
milk on the thirteenth day, and likewise curd on the fourteenth day. Having consumed these for the sake of purifying the body, he should fast for four days.
On the fifth day, however, having bathed and worshipped Keśava according to the prescribed rites,
one should devoutly feed the Brāhmaṇas and give them sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
Likewise, one should honor the instructor as well with garments and ornaments.
Then, one should eat at night, preceded by the consumption of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
In this manner, one should properly complete this supreme vow,
known as Bhīṣmapañcaka, which is meritorious, renowned, and the destroyer of all sins.
A drinker of intoxicants who abandons liquor from birth until death obtains a fruit even greater than that, provided he observes the Bhīṣmapañcaka,
having practiced the most formidable lifelong vow of celibacy.
By performing the Bhīṣmapañcaka, one attains great merit; yet by abandoning even this single Bhīṣmapañcaka,
and instead indulging in oil massage for the limbs, oil massage for the head, honey, meat, and sexual intercourse,
one falls from the world of Brahmā.
Whatever merit is gained in a full year, and whatever merit may arise from the month of Kārttika—
whatever fruit has been declared for Kārttika, that same fruit is obtained during the Bhīṣmapañcaka.
This vow is observed by the gods, the Siddhas, the Kinnaras, the Nāgas, and the Guhyakas.
Having obtained the desired fruit and having worshipped Janārdana,
one should fashion an image of sin, O King, with a fierce face and extremely terrifying,
with a sword in hand, highly deformed, and consisting of all the worlds.
Placed upon a measure of sesame seeds and wrapped in black cloth,
adorned with a crest of karavīra flowers and swinging golden earrings,
she should be given to a Brāhmaṇa with the words, "May Kṛṣṇa be pleased with me."
Having given whatever wealth was desired even to others,
one who has fulfilled his duty should become steadfast, dispassionate, and self-controlled;
with a peaceful mind and free from affliction, he shall attain the supreme state.
Dark as the petal of a blue lotus, with four fangs and four arms,
possessing sixty-eight eyes, spike-like ears, and a great roar;
wearing matted hair, having two tongues, dark as the night, and clad in a tiger-skin garment.
"Mahādeva, whose form is not known, is to be meditated upon.
This was told to me by Bhīṣma while he lay upon his bed of arrows.
That very same practice, the difficult-to-perform Bhīṣmapañcaka, has now been fully explained to you.
And there is the vow, O tiger among kings, known as the preeminent Bhīṣmapañcaka; for whomever one pleases with devotion during that time, Acyuta bestows liberation upon them—
whether they be a celibate student, a householder, a forest-dweller, or a renunciant.
By properly performing the Bhīṣmapañcaka, one attains the abode of Viṣṇu;
even a killer of a Brahmin, a drinker of intoxicants, a thief, or one who violates the teacher’s bed—
provided he is of good character— is completely liberated from sin by performing the Bhīṣmapañcaka just once.
There is no vow more meritorious than this Vaiṣṇava vow;
for when Viṣṇu is propitiated by means of it, he becomes the bestower of liberation upon men.
Having heard this sacred Bhīṣmapañcaka being recited, [one attains the highest goal].
Or the reciter is liberated from sins and becomes a partaker of the world of Viṣṇu.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, this great vow is auspicious, meritorious, and a destroyer of sin;
it is celebrated on earth as the Bhīṣmapañcaka, restricted to the five days beginning with the eleventh and ending with the fifteenth.
"O Pāṇḍava, by virtue of abstaining from food on this day, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow bestows the desired fruit.

Thus ends the seventy-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Bhīṣmapañcaka Vow," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[Now begins] the description of the Malladvādaśī Vow.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O wielder of the conch, discus, and mace; O you who bear the Śrīvatsa mark and have Garuḍa as your seat;
O son of Devakī, tell me the ritual procedure for the Malladvādaśī.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
When I dwell at the Yamunā’s bank beneath the Bhāṇḍīra banyan tree,
in the midst of the cowherds with the calves, I am eight years old by way of my divine play.
Then, for the sake of slaying the demon Kaṃsa, he went to a grove on the outskirts of Mathurā in the form of a child; having met with the powerful cowherd wrestlers from his childhood,
he joined them in the forest along with the strength of the wrestler Gopa.
They clapped their hands and danced like the gods in heaven;
Surabhadraka, Maṇḍalīka, Yogavardhana, Yogada,
Yakṣendrabhadra, and others were their names in Gokula.
Learn from me also the names of the gopīs according to their prominence:
Gopālī, Pālikā, Dhanyā, Viśākhā, Dhyānaniṣṭhikā,
Ilvānugandhā, Subhagā, and Tārakā as the tenth.
Thus, while I was comfortably seated upon an excellent throne,
I was honored by the gods with flowers, curd, milk, and unbroken grains;
three hundred and sixty wrestlers likewise worshipped me.
And with wrestling matches, wine, meat, the singing and dancing of Aṅgaja women,
various kinds of outdoor wrestling by prominent champion fighters,
as well as with foods, edibles, drinks, curds, milk, ghee, and fermented liquors;
Through gifts of cows and gifts of bulls, through the worship of Brahmins with faith,
through gatherings of women abounding in mutual affectionate conversation—
thus, twelve Dvādaśīs should be observed according to one's desire.
My kinsmen, in turn and individually for each of the wrestlers,
worship my body month by month with devotion using twelve names, beginning in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa and ending in Kārttika.
At each meal, one should give small bowls to a twice-born man, saying:
"Salutations again and again to Keśava, Nārāyaṇa, Mādhava, Govinda, Viṣṇu, Madhusūdana, Trivikrama, Vāmana, Śrīdhara, Hṛṣīkeśa, Padmanābha, and Dāmodara.
One should likewise honor him with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and by keeping a vigil at night.
"Through songs, instrumental music, dances, wrestling, lion-roars, and hand-to-hand combat,
and by gifts of clarified butter and gifts of milk, may Kṛṣṇa be pleased with me.
Thus, O King, this ritual has been proclaimed for the twelve months.
This twelfth day, which even today increases the joy of my mind,
is called Malladvādaśī because it was inaugurated by the Mallas;
O Yudhiṣṭhira, such is the knowledge regarding those supreme Mallas.
In the cow-pen, there were many cattle, buffaloes, goats, and sheep;
and by my grace, O son of Dharma, strength, fame, glory, and wealth [increased].
In this same way, other men as well, and even women, [attain these] by observing the Malladvādaśī.
"To those devotees of mine who shall perform this, I will grant that which is in my heart:
health, strength, sovereignty, and the eternal realm of Viṣṇu.
[This was said] by the great wrestlers, most powerful and possessing unassailable arm-strength, who had gathered at the foot of the Bhāṇḍīra tree."
On whichever lunar day he was thus honored, that twelfth day (dvādaśī) became well-known by the name *Vratamalla*.

Thus ends the seventy-third chapter, titled "Description of the Vratamalla-dvādaśī Vow," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[Now follows] the description of the Bhīmadvādaśī vow.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
