In former times, there was a glorious and highly righteous lord of Vidarbha;
he was formerly the father of Damayantī and the father-in-law of Nala on this earth.
He was habituated to speaking the truth, devoted to protecting his subjects,
intent on the duties of the Kṣatriya, illustrious, and unconquered in battles. While he was ruling the kingdom according to the conduct prescribed by the scriptures,
The illustrious and highly fortunate Pulastya, the son of Brahmā and a treasury of all knowledge, arrived in the course of his pilgrimage. Then,
seeing that sinless one born of Brahmā arrive, he [perceived him].
Rising up, the king offered him his own desired seat;
he himself personally presented him with water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), and whatever else was required.
Joining his palms in reverence, he offered even his own kingdom along with himself.
Permitted by him, he sat down upon an excellent seat; he then inquired after his welfare regarding his asceticism and his Vedic studies. Having replied "So be it," the sage addressed the king.
Pulastya said:
"O King, is all well with you regarding your treasury, your realm, and your city? O Monarch, does your mind always abide in righteousness?"
Bhīma said:
"O Brahmin, all is well with those for whom you desire our welfare;
and I have been purified by your arrival, which is like the water of the Ganges."
Having thus reached an agreement and conversed with one another,
they both took delight in recounting their past adventures and stories to each other.
Then, O King of kings, at the conclusion of the conversation, he was filled with wonder regarding Pulastya.
For the welfare of all the world, the Lord of the Universe asked:
"O Blessed One, all living beings situated in the midst of the ocean of saṃsāra are seen being tormented day and night by various sufferings."
In hell and in the womb, through diseases and likewise through birth,
as well as through the sufferings of painful separations and those arising from poverty—
many who live off the oppression of others lament thus.
O bull among sages,
O giver of honor, having seen these many such sufferings of living beings and creatures upon this earth, my mind is deeply afflicted by them.
"Out of a desire to favor me, please tell me that which brings benefit;
O Blessed One, a very great fruit is produced with little effort.
Pulastya said:
Listen, O King, I shall proclaim the most excellent of vows—
that by fasting upon which a person does not become a vessel for miseries.
In the month of Māgha, during the bright fortnight, the twelfth day is remembered as purifying.
Having fasted on that day while wearing wet clothes, one shall become a partaker of happiness.
Bhīma said:
O tiger among sages, how is that Dvādaśī to be observed as a fast?
"O best of Brahmins, tell me by what procedure this is performed; explain it to me in due order.
Pulastya said:
"Listen attentively, O King, to the vow that destroys all sins."
Because of your service, this must also be told to me; of this there is no doubt.
It should never be given to one who is uninitiated, nor to one who is not a disciple. Indeed, it is for one devoted to Viṣṇu, who is peaceful and firmly established in dharma.
"O Great King, this must be told by you to no one else:
a slayer of a Brahmin, a killer of a guru, likewise a slayer of children or women, an ungrateful person,
a betrayer of friends, a thief, a base man, and likewise one who has broken his vows."
O King, one is liberated from all sins by means of this vow.
Then, on a pure lunar day and at an auspicious hour, one should have a pavilion constructed,
measuring ten cubits in size and sloping toward the north-east.
In the middle of that, one should construct an altar five cubits in size;
having carefully prepared the ground of the altar white and well-smeared,
one should draw a maṇḍala there with five colors according to the prescribed rule.
A Brāhmaṇa endowed with Vedic knowledge, devoted to Viṣṇu, with senses conquered,
knowing the twenty-five principles (tattvas), and likewise delighting in his own proper conduct,
should fashion there either eight or four sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas).
Among them, one should employ auspicious Brahmins learned in the four Vedas; and then,
in the center of the mandala, upon the pericarp,
one should place the god Janārdana, facing westward, with four arms, O subduer of enemies.
The wise preceptor should worship him according to the ritual prescribed in the scriptures,
with perfumes, flowers, incense, and various kinds of food offerings.
Having thus worshipped the Lord of Gods together with the Brahmins, the preceptor—
Afterwards, standing there, one should place two pillars provided with wooden beams facing the deity; there,
one should prepare a pedestal (pīṭha) that is thirty-six finger-breadths in size, square, and equal on all sides.
There, having fastened a well-rounded, very firm, and new carrying-net (śikya), one should place the jar upon it; hear from me what kind of jar it should be:
made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay.
One should prepare one hundred or one thousand [rope-loops], endowed with all the required characteristics, firm, and free from defects;
or else, according to one's skill, only a single loop with a single opening.
Then, in that vicinity, he should provide water for the purification of the cloth;
he should also prepare auspicious fuel-sticks of *pālāśa* wood for the sake of the fire-oblation,
as well as sesame seeds, clarified butter, milk, and indeed *śamī* leaves.
On the northeastern portion of the altar, one should prepare the pedestal for the planets;
there, all the planets are to be worshipped according to the ritual procedure for the sacrifice to the planets (grahayajña).
In the eastern direction, one should diligently perform the worship of Śakra.
One should offer oblations with fruits and unbroken grains (akṣata) to Yama in the south, to Varuṇa in the west,
and likewise to Kubera in the north. Having thus prepared the necessary materials, one should likewise wear white garments.
Having anointed him with auspicious fragrances, the best of the twice-born, with darbha grass in hand and free from sloth, should cause the sacrificer to ascend the pedestal.
The sacrificer also, being self-restrained and pure, should stand facing the deity.
Having sat down, one should recite the mantra; listen to this which is declared in the Purāṇas:
"Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods; salutations to you, O Sovereign of the world.
Protect me by means of this vow, O Supreme Self; obeisance be to you!"
Then, with his inner self absorbed in that [deity], he should silently bear those streams of water upon his various limbs, holding them with his head. Thereafter,
the Brahmins, intent on that rite, should perform the fire-oblation (homa) in all directions.
They should recite the chapter on pacification (śāntikādhyāya) and those [hymns] known as Viṣṇu-saṃjñā,
accompanied by the sounding of musical instruments, the resonance of conch shells and songs,
and the proclamations of "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha) and "Victory" (jaya), all blended with the sound of the Vedas.

One should cause that great festival to be celebrated with auspicious hymns joined with praises. An excellent Brahmin should recite the entire account of Keśava, the God of gods and the Great Ascetic, including the Harivaṃśa and other such works.
Then, those skilled in exposition should, without weariness, recite the narrative of Suparṇika and the narrative of the Mahābhārata;
by this method, they should spend that entire night, which increases joy.
The wise sacrificer should lead [the rite] until sunrise;
and the Brahmins, O lord of the earth, should pass that night offering oblations into the sacred fire with divine Vaiṣṇava mantras.
O King, one should cause a stream of *vāsu* (wealth) to fall upon the head of Vāsudeva,
using either milk or clarified butter, which bestows all perfections.
Then, at the time of dawn, the patron of the sacrifice, together with the twice-born, [should perform the concluding rites].
O best of kings, one should perform a bath in a river or a lake;
or, if the patron is lacking in strength, he may bathe with warm water.
Then, having donned white garments and being firm in his vows, he should proceed.
Having offered the *arghya* to the Sun according to the prescribed rite, one of serene mind should worship Puruṣottama with flowers, incense, and food offerings. Then,
having offered oblations into the fire with devotion, he should subsequently offer the final *pūrṇāhuti*.
One should honor all the Brāhmaṇas who have been appointed as Hotṛ priests for the sacrifice with beds,
food, gifts of cows, garments, and ornaments; moreover,
O Bhārata, the Ācārya should be honored here even with one’s entire wealth.
Or rather, he by whom his satisfaction is found, for the Guru is equal to a god;
provided he is free from stinginess regarding wealth and endowed with devotion and power.
The poor, the helpless, the distinguished, and bards have all assembled there.
One should give them food and gold with a pure mind;
having thus honored the Brahmin and fed him as desired,
one should afterwards eat oneself, restrained in speech and according to the extent of one's wealth.
Food fit for oblation is offered with sacrifice, as are sesame seeds fit for oblation;
thus, O great king, has this sacrifice been proclaimed and fully described to you.
Even the most sinful are liberated from all their sins—of this there is no doubt.
Those who perform the Vājapeya and Atirātra sacrifices for a hundred years—
all of them are not worth even a sixteenth part of the Viṣṇu sacrifice.
For seven births, they shall possess good fortune, long life, health, and prosperity.
By fasting according to the prescribed rules on this twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī), one attains it;
upon death, such a person goes to the city of Viṣṇu and rejoices with Viṣṇu,
remaining there for thirty-two cycles of the four ages, assuming the form of Viṣṇu himself.
O King, he remains in the world of Rudra for twelve yugas;
likewise, in the world of Brahmā for three, and in the world of the Sun for [three] yugas. Upon the exhaustion of his merit, returning here to this world, he becomes a righteous king.
The illustrious lord of the earth, victorious over his enemies and possessed of great majesty—
this very vow was formerly observed by the high-souled Sagara,
by Aja, Dhundhumāra, Dilīpa, and Yayāti.
And by other protectors of the earth who have guarded the entire surface of the world;
by women, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras always desiring righteousness, O King;
and by all the sages headed by Bhṛgu, as well as by Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas.
O lord of men, having been questioned by you, I have told this to you;
from this day forward, it shall attain renown upon the earth as "Bhīmā-dvādaśī," and thus, O Bhārata, one shall have fulfilled their purpose.
This was narrated by the sage Pulastya, O descendant of Kuru.
Whoever, having meditated upon this as it was told, should perform it with a spirit of devotion,
shall be liberated from all sins and honored in the world of Viṣṇu.
O Pārtha, even a poor man should avoid stinginess regarding wealth;
this [vow] should be performed by a devotee of Viṣṇu who is terrified by the fear of saṃsāra.
Indeed, it was formerly observed by Bhīma on the night when a steady stream of water mixed with excellent sesame seeds was poured from a jar.
He who, being properly observant of the vow, practices that Dvādaśī which he has heard from the mouth of the Ten-faced One (Rāvaṇa), goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the seventy-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Bhīmadvādaśī Vow," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[Now follows] the description of the Śravaṇadvādaśī Vow.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: O Puruṣottama, O sinless one, tell me of that single twelfth day which is meritorious for those who are always unable to observe fasts.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: In the month of Bhādrapada, the twelfth day of the bright fortnight conjoined with the Śravaṇā nakṣatra is meritorious, bestowing all desires; it yields great fruit through fasting.
Having bathed at the confluence of rivers and fasted on the twelfth day (dvādaśī),
one effortlessly obtains the fruit of twelve dvādaśīs. On a twelfth day falling on a Wednesday and under the Śravaṇa asterism, one should likewise remain self-restrained.
On that [day], everything performed becomes exceedingly great and indeed inexhaustible.
O Bhārata, when the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) is joined with the Śravaṇa asterism,
by bathing at the confluence of rivers, one obtains the fruit arising from bathing in the Gaṅgā and other sacred waters.
One who observes a fast attains [the fruit]; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Likewise, a wise man, having placed [the image] in a jar filled with water, provided with the five jewels, accompanied by a sacred thread, and well-worshipped;
Having placed a well-crafted golden image of Janārdana upon his shoulder— adorned with a conch and the Śārṅga bow according to his means—
and having bathed it according to the prescribed rite and anointed it with white sandalwood paste;
Covered with a pair of white garments and provided with an umbrella and a pair of sandals,
one should worship the head of Hari with "Oṃ namo vāsudevāya";
likewise, the face with "to Śrīdhara," and the throat again with "to Kṛṣṇa."
Oṃ, salutations to the illustrious one; [salutations] to the chest and arms, to the bearer of all weapons;
salutations to the pervasive one on the belly, and salutations to Keśava on the stomach;
salutations to the progenitor of the three worlds—in this manner, one should worship Hari.
"Salutation to the Lord of All for the shanks; salutation to the Soul of All for the feet.
O King, with this procedure one should worship with flowers and incense.
Then, an offering of food cooked in ghee should be presented before him.
The wise man should offer new water-pitchers according to his ability;
having thus worshipped the Giver of Cows, he should observe a vigil there.
At the clear dawn, having bathed and worshipped the One whose Banner is Garuḍa (Viṣṇu), [he should proceed].
With offerings of flowers, incense, and the like, along with food, fruits, and beautiful garments,
one should then form a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali) and utter this mantra:
"Obeisance, obeisance to you, O Govinda, known by the names Budha and Śravaṇa."
"Having brought about the destruction of the flood of sins, become the bestower of all happiness.
Having thus worshipped Govinda,
one should then worship a Brāhmaṇa who has reached the further shore of the Vedas and Vedāntas.
One should especially cause [the gift] to be bestowed according to the rules upon one who knows the Purāṇas.

On the twelfth lunar day joined with the Śravaṇa asterism and endowed with the entire solar disc, having bathed at the confluence with a water-pot, [one should say]: "May Janārdana be pleased with me."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O protector of the earth, listen to this ancient history which they cite even here; hear that which occurred in a vast forest.
There is a country named Daśārṇaka; in its western region lies a certain desert land that strikes terror into all living beings,
where the ground consists of scorching sand and there dwell wicked great serpents.
Thick with trees providing scant shade and crowded with dead creatures,
it is filled with *śamī*, *khadira*, *pālāśa*, *karīra*, and *pīlu* trees;
there, O Pārtha, stand formidable trees variegated with firm thorns.
O King, wherever the earth is seen strewn with multitudes of burnt creatures,
there the clouds do not provide food or water;
indeed, even at times, birds are seen wandering about [in vain].
O King, the best of birds are seen there with their lives cut short, along with thirsty young ones constantly staying among the trees;
and deer, afflicted by thirst, suddenly arrive at the sandy bank.
Just as things perish in sands that resemble water-sands,
so too in such a region, a certain merchant, by the power of fate,
having strayed from his caravan, entered a desert wilderness.
The best of merchants saw Piśācas— filthy, fierce, fleshless, and terrifying to behold— wandering here and there;
his heart was bewildered as he wandered himself, exhausted by hunger, thirst, and delusion.
"Where is the village? Where is the water? Where shall I go? he did not know.
Then he saw ghosts whose senses were agitated by thirst, their feet consisting of bones bound together with sinews, looking here and there.
He beheld one ghost mounted upon the shoulder of another ghost.
He saw him approaching calmly, surrounded on all sides by many spirits (pretas),
preceded by the sound of weeping;
descending from the shoulders of the spirits to the ground, he drew near to his presence.
Having seen him, the eminent merchant then spoke these words:
"How is it that you have come to this waterless region?
The wise merchant replied to him: "I am one who has indeed strayed from my caravan."
My entry here was brought about by the conjunction of fate and my past actions;
yet thirst afflicts me excessively, and hunger likewise torments me intensely.
My vital breaths have reached my throat, and my speech seems to fail me.
"In this matter, I see no means by which I might live by any means whatsoever.
Kṛṣṇa said:
When he had spoken thus, the ghost addressed these words to the merchant.
"Resorting to this *puṃnāga* tree, wait for a moment;
having been offered hospitality according to what is available, you shall depart at your ease.
Thus addressed, that merchant, tormented by thirst, did accordingly.
When midday had arrived,
he came to that place from a Punnāga tree carrying a water-pot as beautiful as a stream of water,
containing curd-rice and accompanied by a *vardhamāna* vessel.
When he had arrived, the merchant then gave it to the guest;
having eaten the food and drunk the water, the merchant attained satisfaction,
and in an instant he became free from thirst and relieved of his distress.

Then, indeed, he gave curd-rice with water to the host of hungry ghosts who were desirous of eating; the hungry ghosts attained supreme satisfaction. Having thus gratified the guest and the entire realm of the hungry ghosts, [he departed].
Then he himself ate the remains of the meal at his pleasure;
once he had finished eating, the food and the water were completely exhausted.
Then the merchant, being satiated, spoke these words to the Lord of the Dead:
"This appears to me as a supreme marvel in this forest:
from where do you obtain such excellent food and drink?
And yet, with so little food, you support so many people individually."
"How is it that these [beings] are so utterly satiated, yet devoid of flesh and with their bellies torn open?
Furthermore, how is it that here,
in this desolate forest, you have arrived as one who provides me with a hand to grasp?"
"And how are you satisfied with a mere morsel, O observer of auspicious vows?
Who are you that has made your home in this most terrible forest? Cut through this doubt; my curiosity is great."
Thus addressed, that preta who had been a merchant spoke these words:
"Listen, O blessed one, I shall describe my own evil deed. In the beautiful city of Śākala, I was a man of very wicked mind."
O sinless one, in the past my time was spent devoted to trade;
and there, once, out of greed for wealth and being heedless,
I did not give alms to a mendicant who was tormented by thirst.
And there lived in my neighborhood a virtuous Brāhmaṇa.
On the occasion of Śravaṇa-dvādaśī in the month of Bhādrapada,
he once went with me to the river named Toṣā.
And at that place was the holy confluence with the Candrabhāgā;
the Candrabhāgā is the daughter of Soma, while the Toṣā is the delight of the Sun. The meeting of their cool and warm waters is exceedingly beautiful.
Having reached that excellent holy site, that neighboring brahmin bathed and observed a fast on the occasion of Śravaṇa-dvādaśī,
using new and sturdy water-vessels from the Candrabhāgā and the Tōṣā rivers.
Together with full *vardhamānaka* vessels filled with curd-rice,
he offered an umbrella, a pair of shoes, a garment, and an image of Hari according to the prescribed rites,
along with curd-rice provided by a fisherman from the Candrabhāgā river.
Having done this, I returned home; then, after some time,
having met my death through atheism, I entered the state of a preta,
O sinless one, just as you have seen me here in this terrible forest.
These sinners, who seized the property of Brahmins, have come to the state of ghosts;
some were devoted to the wives of others, others were intent on betraying their masters,
and some were intent on betraying their friends, in this most dreadful region.
These have entered into my service for the sake of food and drink.
The Blessed Kṛṣṇa is the imperishable, eternal Supreme Self;
whatever is given with him as the intended recipient is proclaimed to be inexhaustible.

"Deprived of me, how will these [monkeys] endure the most cruel suffering born of their past actions in this exceedingly dreadful forest? O highly fortunate one, out of a desire to show me favor, you must [protect] them."
Take many names and lineages by means of writing;
let your auspicious casket remain within your armpit.
Having thus reached the Himavat mountains, you will find a treasure there.
"Then, O high-minded one, go to Gayāśīrṣa and perform the Śrāddha ceremony,
offering it individually for each deceased person as you please.
While he was speaking thus, that being, possessing the luster of molten gold, [vanished].
Having ascended an excellent celestial chariot, he departed from here for the heavenly realm.
When the lord of the departed had gone to heaven, that merchant man, by means of his power,
took their names and lineages and set out for the Himalayas.
Having reached that place, he went there, deposited [the treasure] in his own house,
and taking a portion of the wealth, he went to the banyan tree at Gayāśīrṣa.
There, day after day, he performed the śrāddha rites for the deceased ancestors in due order.
On whichever day that merchant performs the *Gaya-śrāddha*,
he always appears in his dreams in his own form and says:
"O illustrious one, O sinless one, by your grace..."

"I have abandoned the state of a preta and have attained the supreme goal. Having thus performed the rites for the pretas out of greed for wealth, the merchant went to his own home during that month of Bhādrapada.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, having worshipped Janārdana on the conjunction of the Śravaṇa asterism and the twelfth lunar day (Śravaṇadvādaśī),
and having given gifts to the Brahmins while fasting and with senses subdued,
one should do so every year at the confluences of great rivers.
He performed the gift-giving according to the prescribed rites, and then, having met his end,
he attained the supreme abode that is difficult for men to reach—
a place where the trees bear fruits that grant all desires and the rivers have mud made of milk-rice (pāyasa).
Having reached that region of enchanting lotus-pools filled with cool, pure water, the high-souled merchant— his limbs adorned with refined gold—
rejoiced eternally in heaven for the full duration of a kalpa, always delighted in the company of beautiful women.

Thus ends the seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Śravaṇa-dvādaśī Vow," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Now follows the description of the Vijaya-śravaṇa-dvādaśī vow.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Yudhiṣṭhira, the rite for the twelfth day in the month of Śrāvaṇa has been described to you;
it pacifies all sins and bestows all happiness.
When that Ekādaśī is conjoined with the Śravaṇa asterism, [it is especially auspicious].
That lunar day is declared to be Vijayā, bestowing victory upon devotees.
There was a powerful and unconquered Daitya named Bali, possessed of great strength;
by him all the hosts of gods were deprived of their celestial abode.
Then the gods, having approached Mahāviṣṇu, spoke these words:
"You are the refuge of all the gods; quickly deliver us from this distress!
O mighty-armed slayer of Bala, kill the Daitya Bali."
Having heard those words of the gods, which gave rise to compassion, Viṣṇu,
who knows the proper time and desires the welfare of the gods, spoke these words:
"I know the Daitya Bali, the son of Virocana, who is a thorn to the three worlds."
For him whose self is purified by austerity, who is tranquil, self-controlled, and has conquered his senses;
who is my devotee, whose life is dedicated to me, who is true to his word, and possessed of great strength—
for him, the end of his austerity shall not come for a very long time.
"When I come to know at some time that he is perfected in discipline,
I shall gather what is pleasing to him and bestow it upon the denizens of heaven.
Aditi, desiring a son, has indeed sought refuge with me for the sake of a son."

"O gods, I shall accomplish what is beneficial for you; of this there is no doubt. That which is for the welfare of the gods will all be detrimental to the enemies of the gods. Therefore, go forth free from anxiety and await a certain time."
Having been addressed thus, the gods departed; Viṣṇu then reflected upon his task.
After reflecting for a long time on how the Goddess might descend into a womb, he said to Aditi, "My desire shall be fulfilled."
Then, after a long time had passed, she became pregnant;
in the ninth month, she gave birth to a son, Vāmana Hari—
a child with short feet, a small body, and a large head.
Seeing Nārāyaṇa Hari himself as Vāmana, with his hands, feet, and belly emaciated,
she was about to speak;
however, her speech was obstructed, and she was unable to say anything at all.
O best of men, on the eleventh day of the month of Bhādrapada under the asterism Śravaṇa,
when Vāmana had become Trivikrama, the earth trembled;
fear arose among the Daityas, and joy arose among the gods.
The wise Kaśyapa, the lord of progeny, himself performed for him the purificatory rites beginning with the birth-ceremony; he did so unwearied,
wearing his girdle, carrying his staff, and having donned the sacred thread.
Carrying kuśa grass and carrying pure water, adorned with a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu),
he went to the extensive sacrifice of the powerful Bali.
Upon seeing Bali, Vāmana approached him at that very moment and spoke.
Then he said: "O Lord of Sacrifice, let my land be given to me;
for you stand here for the purpose of recitation, measuring out three paces.
Bali replied to that best of the twice-born: "Whether it be given or not given by me, [it is yours]."
Then the dwarf, whose prowess was infinite, began to expand;
having placed his feet upon the earth and encompassed heaven and earth with his head,
he [covered] the worlds beginning with that of Indra with those two, and the station of Brahmā upon his forehead.
He did not obtain a third step; then the dwellers of heaven roared.
Seeing that great marvel, the Siddhas and the celestial rishis, filled with joy, praised the Lord of Gods, saying, "Excellent! Excellent!"
Then, having conquered all the hosts of Daityas and brought the three worlds under his control, the Subduer said to Bali:
"Go now to Sutala, followed by your own forces.
There, protected by my arm, you shall enjoy all desired pleasures."
"At the conclusion of this Indra's term, you yourself shall become Indra.
Having been addressed thus, Bali departed after bowing to the best of men;
then, having dismissed Bali, he spoke to all the gods.
"Go to your own abodes and remain there free from anxiety.
Thus addressed by the God, the deities departed, joyful after having worshipped Vāmana.
Having accomplished the work of the world, the God vanished right there.
All this occurred on the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī), O lord of men;
therefore, that day is always the victorious lunar day (Vijayā) for the worship of the God of gods.
This indeed, O King, occurs in the month of Phālguna in conjunction with the Puṣya asterism.
The virtuous declare that Vijayā is superior by millions upon millions of times.
On the eleventh day, one who has fasted should worship Hari at night,
using either a silver vessel, a golden vessel, or even one made of wood or bamboo.
One should place the water-pot (kuṇḍikā) at the side, as well as the umbrella and the sandals;
likewise, the auspicious Vaiṣṇava staff, the sacred thread, and the water-vessel (kamaṇḍalu).
Having covered the vessel with cloths and also with very beautiful fruits—
With the scent of deerskin from the path, or with devotion using a deer-skin;
a wealthy person [should offer] a *droṇa* of sesame seeds, or a *prastha*, or a *kuḍava*;
or it may be done with rice, wheat, fruits, or white sesame seeds.
One should worship Hari with flowers, perfumes, incense, lamps, and cooked foods;
with various kinds of offerings, both solid and soft, such as rice mixed with jaggery.
According to one's own means, one should also perform the rite accompanied by gold.
Through mantras, the merit is a hundredfold; through devotion, it is a hundred-thousandfold superior;
and for one endowed with devotion and virtuous qualities, it is many millions of millions of times superior.
With these mantra-words, one should worship the one whose banner is Garuḍa there.
Having become pure and composed, O best of men, offer these oblations:
"Oṃ! Salutations to you, O Puruṣottama, whose body resembles the water-born lotus, whose face is like the lotus, who holds the conch, and whose very nature is the mass of waters."
"Salutation to the one whose navel is a lotus; salutation to you who recline upon the waters;
salutation to you, O Keśava, Ananta, Vāsudeva; let there be salutation to you.
Thus is the mantra for bathing.
"Produced in the Malaya mountains, rich in fragrance and most enchanting, I offer this to you; accept it, O Supreme Lord.
This is the mantra for sandalwood. "Produced from the lord of the forest, rich in fragrance and most enchanting..."
"O Supreme Person, accept this flower offered by me.
This is the mantra for the flower.
"Homage to the one whose pure garment is yellow like the filaments of a lotus!"
"To the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, who holds the discus upon his shoulder and possesses a body that captivates the mind"—this is the mantra for worship.
[The incarnations are: Matsya, Kūrma, Varāha, Nārasiṃha, and Vāmana.
"Rāma, Rāma, and Kṛṣṇa"— by these names,
one should perform the worship of each individual limb starting from the feet, and then the worship of the head;
thus is the worship of all the limbs.
"O Lord of the gods of gods, bearer of the conch, discus, and mace; O Acyuta, Ananta, Govinda, Vāsudeva, salutations be unto You! Thus is the incense mantra.
"You alone are the earth, light, wind, and space;
you alone are the light of lights. May this lamp be accepted.
Thus is the mantra for the lamp.
O Supreme Lord, be gracious! This fourfold food, endowed with the six flavors and provided with various kinds of edibles and consumables,
is Prajāpati, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Indra, the Moon, and the Sun.
"May Tvaṣṭṛ, Yama, and the imperishable Agni take away my sin"—

this is the mantra for the food offering (naivedya). "May Janārdana, the beginning of the world, whose form is the world, who is without beginning, the end-maker of the world, the reservoir of waters, and the source of the world, be pleased with me."

Thus is the mantra for propitiation: "I bow to Mādhava, the slayer of Madhu, who dwells in Mathurā, who destroys the bondage of manifold karmas, and who reclines upon the waters. Salutations to the one in the form of Vāmana; salutations be unto you, O Trivikrama."
"Salutations to you, O Maṇibandha; salutations be to you, O Vāsudeva.
This is the mantra of salutation.
"Salutations, salutations to you, O Govinda, O Lord Vāmana, O Trivikrama!"
"Having brought about the destruction of the flood of sins, be the granter of all desires"— this is the mantra of petition.
"The omnipresent one, the Lord of all gods, the bearer of Śrī, the abode of Śrī,
the Sovereign of the Universe, Viṣṇu, and the one who reclines upon Śrī— salutations again and again"— this is the mantra for the reclining.
O best of kings, having thus performed worship on the eleventh day (Ekādaśī),
one should keep a vigil there at night with the sounds of singing and musical instruments.
And that twelfth lunar day (Dvādaśī) which is conjoined with the Śravaṇa asterism is the supreme occasion.
And having bathed at that confluence, one is liberated from all sins.
Having thus worshipped with diligence when the morning has become clear,
a gift should be given according to the mantras to a Brāhmaṇa who is learned in the scriptures.
And the Brāhmaṇa should accept [the gift] with the mantra, reciting the mantra:
"Vāmana is the recipient; salutations again and again to Vāmana.
(Oṃ in the secret place; Oṃ on the head; Oṃ on the feet; Oṃ on the navel; Oṃ on the two arms; Oṃ on all limbs; salutations to the Soul of All.)
Having fasted on the Ekādaśī day, a person should, according to the prescribed rule, offer flowers, fruit, and food offerings— all these with the appropriate mantras. Then,
in the morning, following the previously mentioned ritual, one should partake of a meal consisting of *pṛṣadājya* (clarified butter mixed with curds).
Having first given to the Brahmins, one should afterwards eat while restraining one's speech;
O Indra among kings, this rule is prescribed for every occasion, even when repeated again and again.
Now, O King, learn from me the merit that accrues when the vow is completed.
O Indra among kings, having spent seventy-one cycles of four yugas in the city of Viṣṇu, O King, he sports there for eternal time; then,
returning here, he becomes a king who brings about the destruction of his adversaries.
One who gives elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, and who enjoys them without envy,
shall be endowed with beauty and good fortune, long-lived, and free from disease;
surrounded by sons, that living being shall live for a hundred autumns.

I have already declared to you the fruit of this Ekādaśī; likewise, the Dvādaśī conjoined with the Śravaṇa asterism has been fully described. Having fasted on the Ekādaśī, one should subsequently fast on the Dvādaśī as well.
And in this case, there shall be no omission of the prescribed rule, for Hari is the deity of both [Ekādaśī and Dvādaśī].

(The meaning is that when either Ekādaśī or Dvādaśī is joined with the Śravaṇa asterism, the fulfillment of both vows occurs simply by fasting on the one joined with Śravaṇa; thus, the "omission of the rule"—which would otherwise occur if one were to fast on a different lunar day before completing the previous vow and then fast again on another—is avoided because both share the same deity.
A Dvādaśī conjoined with Mercury and the Śravaṇa asterism is like water at a sacred confluence.

The gift is curd-rice, and truth is the supreme rule for the fast. O Indra among kings, this Dvādaśī vow was indeed performed by Sagara, Kakutstha, Dhundhumāra, Gādhi, and by these and others as well.

"That twelfth day (Dvādaśī) in the month of Nabhasya (Bhādrapada), when conjoined with Wednesday and the Śravaṇa asterism, is declared by the sages to lead to victory. By fasting upon it with devotion, O Pārtha, a man attains immortality endowed with the qualities of *aṇimā* and the rest.

Thus ends the seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Vijaya-Śravaṇa-Dvādaśī Vow," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[Now follows] the description of the Samprāpti-Dvādaśī vow.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: The Dvādaśī vow begins in the dark fortnight of the month of Pauṣa;
its breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) at the end of six months is traditionally held to occur on the full moon day of Jyeṣṭha.
First, the name Puṇḍarīkākṣa is sung for Kṛṣṇa;
second, the one called Mādhava; then Viśvarūpa in Phālguna; then the one called Puruṣottama, and thereafter the one named Acyuta in the fifth month.

In the sixth month, O Lord of Gods, the secret name "Jaya" is proclaimed. During the months previously mentioned, sesame seeds are used for bathing and consuming; however, from Āṣāḍha onwards, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) are prescribed.
Bathing and the consumption of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) are both prescribed;
one should worship the Lotus-eyed Lord with those very names.
And month by month, O Lord of Gods, having performed the worship according to the rules, [one should proceed].
One who is faithful should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to a Brahmin with devotion;
O Lord of Gods, one should perform the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*) with devotion so as to please Him,
since worship is performed with a spirit of true devotion toward Govinda.
One should always eat only at night, avoiding oil and alkaline substances;
having fasted on the eleventh day, or likewise on the twelfth day,
thus at the end of the year, whatever is desired by oneself [should be attained].
"Wealth, goods, gold, grain, vessels, a seat, or a bed—one should give these to a Brāhmaṇa, saying: 'May Keśava accept this.
Having fasted according to the prescribed rite on this [day], one should be intent upon the propitiation of Viṣṇu."

One obtains all desires whatsoever that one wishes for in the heart; therefore, this [day] has indeed become renowned in the worlds as "Dvādaśī. When performed with longing, observed, and undertaken by those devoted to righteousness, it fulfills every wish.
Whether remembered day after day, she fulfills all desires. O best of men, those devotees of Viṣṇu who, desiring the attainment of their goals, fast and recite this mantra,
to them she eternally grants the fruits of their wishes through the grace of the Lord, so that they dwell in the abode of the Lord of the Gods.
Thus ends the seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Vow of Saṃprāptidvādaśī," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira;
it is a description of the Govinda-dvādaśī vow.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Likewise, O Govinda, I shall tell you of another Dvādaśī; listen.
By its proper performance, one obtains the desired fruit.
Having fasted on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Pauṣa, [one attains the goal].
Having properly worshipped Govinda, the god Adhokṣaja,
by name with offerings of incense, flowers, and food, he should,
with a concentrated mind and his thoughts fixed upon Him, mutter the name "Govinda."

O lord of men, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a brahmin according to one's ability; having awakened oneself, one should recite, "I am weighed against Govinda. One should also avoid conversation with heretics and those who follow forbidden occupations.

For the sake of self-purification, one should consume cow’s urine, or cow dung, or curd, or even milk— each produced from the milking of a cow. On the second day, having bathed again and likewise worshipped Keśava, one should proceed as before.

Having worshipped [the deity] with that very name and given a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brahmin, he should then eat during the time it takes to milk a cow, consisting of what has been produced from that [offering]. In this very manner, having fasted throughout all the months, being self-restrained and pure—
A wise man should give daily fodder for a cow every month according to his ability;
and upon the completion of the year, he should worship Govinda together with Lakṣmī, saying:
"May Govinda always be pleased with me through this vow."
Furthermore, O King, one should especially give the daily provision for cows on that day with supreme devotion; hear now what fruit one shall obtain:
[one should give] a bull of excellent quality with horns of gold and hooves of silver, along with a hundred cows.
Whatever fruit one enjoys by giving [gifts] to the twice-born for an entire month,
one who has properly observed this vow obtains all of that;
and he attains that world where Govinda dwells.
Having fasted according to the prescribed rites on this Govinda-dvādaśī,
people are seen shining even today like the moon;
for they worship Govinda while subsisting on cow-products (gorasa), delight the cows, and likewise provide daily sustenance for them.
"O King of the Kurus, he who observes a fast on the twelfth lunar days (dvādaśī) attains the world of the gods, free from sorrow.

Thus ends the seventy-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Govinda-dvādaśī Vow," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[This is followed by] the description of the Akhaṇḍa-dvādaśī vow.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O high-minded one, tell me what kind of ripening results for one who has committed a deficiency in the vow of fasting or in the practice of giving."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O lord of men, hear from me what kind of deficiency in results arises from the deficiency of sacrifices, fasts, and vows.
Listen now to how they indeed incur deficiency even without observing the fasts:
men who have lost their sovereignty and become impoverished live again,
having obtained only a superior form due to the fault of incompleteness in their vows.
Men become one-eyed, hunchbacked, eunuchs, or blind;
likewise, a man who observes the fast and a woman who obtains a husband—
both shall suffer separation through a deficiency in their vows and attain misfortune.
Those who do not give when wealth exists, nor kindle the sacred fire when food is available;
those who dwell in a family of bad character or low birth despite their commitment to virtue;
and those who, though possessing great beauty, are devoid of clothing, ointments, and ornaments.
And those who were of deformed appearance, yet endowed with the qualities of a practitioner—
all of them attained a deficiency of fruit due to a deficiency in their vows. Therefore, that deficiency in the vow is indeed a deficiency in the sacrifice.
"Due to deficiency, the fruit of that which is to be performed by fasting becomes deficient.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"If, somehow, a deficiency should occur in the fasting and other observances..."
"Tell me, what must be done there so that it becomes free from flaw?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"Indeed, this Akhaṇḍa-dvādaśī is [the most important] among all religious rites."

Listen as I speak: one's deficiency comes to rest. On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, being self-restrained and pure, and having observed a fast, one should worship Janārdana, the Lord of Gods.
Having bathed, one should say "Nārāyaṇa"; likewise, while eating, "Nārāyaṇa"; while walking, to the god "Nārāyaṇa"; and again, while sleeping, "Nārāyaṇa.
Having bathed with the water of the five products of the cow, one becomes pure in soul and has conquered the senses.
Having devoutly given a vessel made of barley and rice to a Brahmin,
one should thereafter recite this before the Lord Hari:
"Whatever incomplete vow has been performed by me throughout seven births,"
O Blessed One, by Your grace, may that [vow] remain unbroken for me here;
just as You alone are the entire universe in its entirety, O Supreme Person,
so indeed may all my vows be unbroken.
The first breaking of the fast is prescribed after four months;
thereafter, one should perform the propitiation of Hari once the fast has been completed.
Furthermore, during the months beginning with Caitra, the breaking of the fast occurs at intervals of four months.
There too, one endowed with faith should give vessels of barley meal;
the breaking of the fast occurs during the months beginning with Śrāvaṇa and ending with Kārttika.
There also, one should give vessels of ghee and sacrificial fees to a Brahmin.
A vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or clay is prescribed;
O King, one may also have it made of *palāśa* wood according to one's own capacity.
Thus, at the end of the year, he who has conquered his senses [should honor] the Brāhmaṇas.
Having invited twelve Brahmins, one should feed them with ghee and milk-rice (pāyasa),
and after bowing down, one should ask for their forgiveness by giving gifts of clothing and ornaments.
One should also worship the preceptor who provided the instruction here according to the prescribed rite.
Thus, having fasted properly and according to the rule for the unbroken Dvādaśī, a person enjoys the fruit of that unbroken vow;
whatever deficiency of the vow was committed at any time throughout seven births [is thereby rectified].
Indeed, that Akhaṇḍa-Dvādaśī accomplishes everything in its entirety.
Therefore, O observer of noble vows, men and women who desire the fruit should properly observe the fast of Akhaṇḍa-Dvādaśī with great effort.
"By that [observance] which, concerning the supreme limb of the month known as the Akhaṇḍa-Dvādaśī-vrata,
causes whatever partial vows have been well-performed by men to attain completeness through the grace of Hari.

Thus ends the seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Akhaṇḍa-Dvādaśī Vrata," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the Manoratha-dvādaśī Vow.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Having fasted on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Phālguna, [one should observe the vow].
Whether a man or a woman, having worshipped the Lord of the Universe,
O Yudhiṣṭhira, one should utter the name of Hari with devotion and a focused mind;
rising and even while sleeping, one should indeed glorify Hari alone.
Then, when another day had arrived— the twelfth— he, being self-restrained, bathed and properly worshipped Hari; having given a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brahmin,
he performed the rite of a ghee-oblation in the fire dedicated to Hari.
Having prostrated before the Lord of the World, one should utter these words:
"May that Vāsudeva, who, having propitiated the Earth situated in the netherworld (Pātāla), obtained all his heart's desires, grant my own heart's desires."
Having worshipped him, the Lord of the World, Indra attained all his desires in heaven;
and having been deprived of his kingdom,
it was by worshipping him that he regained his new and heart-stealing wishes.
Having thus worshipped and completed the ritual adoration of Hari, O son of Pāṇḍu, one should then eat pure vegetarian food with self-restraint;
this applies during the months of Phālguna, Caitra, Vaiśākha, and Jyeṣṭha, O best of men.
The completion of these four months should be accomplished with four *pāraṇas*.
One should perform worship with red flowers for the four months;
one should burn *guggulu* incense and consume water used for washing a cow's horn.
The food offering should consist of sacrificial grain (haviṣya), as should one’s own meal.
Furthermore, O Pārtha, listen now to the rite that is performed at the beginning of Āṣāḍha:
jasmine flowers and incense made from sāra-juice are recommended, O King.
Having consumed darbha-water, he should offer śāli rice as the oblation;
he himself should eat that very same food and perform the remaining rites as before.
In the months beginning with Kārtika, cow-urine serves for the purification of the body.
If one desires fragrance, one should offer incense and perform worship with a water-vessel;
the food offering here should be made of bell-metal, and one should indeed eat that oneself.
Furthermore, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should likewise be given to a Brahmin every month.
The breaking of the fast is intended for the purification of Viṣṇu’s own desire; thus, the breaking of the fast is considered holy.
One should act according to one's capacity and according to what is pleasing, avoiding any stinginess regarding wealth, because Govinda is pleased only when worshipped with sincere devotion.
At the conclusion of the fast, O King, when Hari has been bathed and worshipped according to one's ability,
He, being gratified, grants those desired and imperishable boons.
At the end of the year, having caused a beautiful and pleasing image to be fashioned, [one should perform the final rites].
One should present to a Brāhmaṇa a [liṅga] adorned with a conch and a Śārṅga bow, covered with a pair of garments and flowers, according to one's ability by means of a goldsmith;
having fed twelve Brāhmaṇas there, one should ask for their forgiveness.

O descendant of Bharata, twelve jars filled with food, water, and unbroken grains (akṣata) should be given here, along with pairs of umbrellas and sandals, and with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā). This auspicious Dvādaśī is the destroyer of sins for those who desire its fruit.
O best of kings, she grants all desired objects;
because she fulfills all their heart's desires through devotion,
this twelfth day is therefore renowned in the worlds as Manoratha-dvādaśī.
In ancient times, by fasting on this day, Indra indeed obtained the three worlds;
the Ādityas were made his sons, and likewise Dhanva [obtained] the wealth of Uśanas. Through Dhaumya, mastery of the Vedas was attained, and others likewise achieved their desired fruits.
Whether by royal sages, brahmins, women, men of pleasure, or śūdras on this earth,
whatever desire one contemplates while observing this vow,
intent upon the worship of Viṣṇu, one obtains that very thing without doubt.
One without a son obtains a son; one without wealth obtains wealth;
one overcome by disease obtains health; and a maiden obtains a virtuous husband. By fasting on this [day], even those living abroad obtain reunion with their loved ones.

One obtains all desires and, upon death, rejoices in heaven. By observing this vow, even a mortal woman or a Śūdra is born as one who is neither sonless, nor destitute, nor lacking an eldest brother, nor devoid of virtue.
Having enjoyed desired pleasures here and there according to his wish for thousands and tens of thousands of years in the heavenly world,
he is born here among meritorious men who are wealthy and possessed of modesty.
O King, he is born in a household free from all diseases. How can those who do not fast on the twelfth lunar day known as Manoratha, who do not worship Puruṣottama, the primordial God,
and who neither bow to nor honor cows and Brāhmaṇas, ever attain their heart's desire?

Thus ends the eightieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Manoratha-dvādaśī Vow," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[Now follows] the description of the Ulkā-navamī vow.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Blessed One, O Lord, you should tell me that by which sin may be pacified with little effort or with small wealth. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Pārtha, to the supreme, meritorious Dvādaśī that destroys all sins,
by fasting upon which one endowed with faith attains the highest merit.
This occurs when the month of Māgha has arrived and the moon is in the constellation Āṣāḍhā.
On the twelfth day of the dark fortnight, one who is firm in his vow should undertake this rite which yields meritorious fruit; listen to its procedure from me.
Having bathed well and become pure and restrained, he should worship the God of gods.
O high-minded one, having worshipped [Kṛṣṇa] by the name "Kṛṣṇa" on the eleventh day,
and having fasted, one should again worship Keśava on the following day,
praising him repeatedly with that very name called Kṛṣṇa.

One should give sesame seeds to a Brahmin, saying, "May Kṛṣṇa be pleased with me. Then, O King, one should consume those auspicious black sesame seeds once the annual fast is concluded and the mantra for propitiating Viṣṇu has been recited.
Black water-pots, together with sesame seeds, cooked food,
umbrellas, pairs of sandals, and garments— filled with grain within and provided with these items—
should be given to Brāhmaṇas according to the number of months, in the prescribed manner.
O King, for as many thousands of years as there are sesame seeds produced from a single sprout, one is honored in the heavenly world; moreover,
that person is born perpetually free from disease in birth after birth.
By observing this twelfth day known as Tiladvādaśī, a man shall not become blind, nor deaf, nor afflicted with leprosy, nor loathsome;
by this rite, O Pārtha, he becomes a giver of sesame seeds— of this there is no doubt.
A human being is liberated from all sins without effort;
for the pacification of every sin, there is the gift, the ritual, and likewise the śrāddha ceremony.
O best of kings, there is neither great expense nor physical exertion required for the body.

On the tenth day, one who is devoted to all enjoyments should perform a bath with sesame seeds, offer sesame, eat sesame, and give sesame to an excellent Brahmin; having worshipped Virājaketu, that mortal attains the station of Viṣṇu. Thus ends the eighty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Ulkā-navamī Vow," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the Virtuous Vow of Dvādaśī.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Tell me of that deed performed for the sake of the next world which does not lead to suffering for men."
O best of the Yadus, tell me that which leads to the destruction of sin;
indeed, describe here, O mighty-armed one, the power of fasting for those who desire to worship Kṛṣṇa, for I am not yet satiated by your speaking.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Pārtha, to that which you have asked us out of curiosity;
that which pertains to the world beyond leads neither to suffering nor to glory.
O best of men, O most excellent of kings, I shall relate to you exactly as it occurred in the past the power of the fast for those desiring to worship Kṛṣṇa.
There is a famous city named Vaidiśa, O best of monarchs.
In that place, there was formerly a Vaiśya known as Sīrabhadra,
who was accompanied by his wife— who was his mother’s daughter— as well as his sons and grandsons;
he possessed a large retinue of servants and engaged in many business enterprises.
His mind and his very thoughts were entirely absorbed in the maintenance of his sons, grandsons, and others;
he never once turned his mind toward the next world.
Thereafter, he acquired wealth day after day through both righteous and unrighteous means.
Elsewhere he was devoid of affection for everyone, yet he was overwhelmed by love for his son;
he did not offer oblations at the prescribed time, nor did he give gifts due to excessive greed,
and he became utterly intent on the maintenance of his son and others.
Overwhelmed by craving, O King of kings, and having abandoned the maintenance of his own kin, he neglected his obligatory and occasional duties through his own actions. As time passed,
he eventually died on the slopes of the Vindhya forest.
O King, during the summer season, there was a preta bearing a body of torment;
the illustrious brahmin named Vipīta, a knower of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas but a hater of them, beheld him while mounted upon a divine vehicle.
He was being scorched by the extremely fierce and blazing rays of the sun;
afflicted by thirst, he was greatly tormented amidst the midst of scorching sands,
his throat emaciated by hunger, his mouth parched, and his eyes rolled back.
With tongues protruding from its limbs, covered everywhere with boils,
overwhelmed by the exhaustion of labored breathing, and with a distended belly,
it was bound by its own karma and rendered unable to move.
Then, O King of kings, having seen such a sight, the great sage Gardabhiya,
filled with compassion, spoke these words,
even though he already knew that the fruit arising from the performance of that rite would come to pass as it had.
As if gladdening that creature from every side for its benefit,
Vipīta said:
"On the road, by the many dust particles heated from below by the rays of the sun..."
Afflicted above by the sharp rays of the sun and oppressed by thirst and wind,
and further tormented by other terrible, unbearable, and most cruel instruments of protection,
tell me here according to the truth: how is it that you burn alone?
Having heard these words of Vipīta, Sīrabhadra,
afflicted by pain and tormented by that sensation, sighed with difficulty and spoke softly.
Sīrabhadra said:
O Brahmin, what was previously contemplated will how come to pass at the end?
Because I possess the notion of permanence regarding that which is impermanent, I, the evil-minded one, am consumed by grief.
"I shall do this," "and having done this, I shall do that again."
Thus, having mounted upon a hundred desires, I, the evil-minded one, am consumed by them.
Out of greed, I have endured the inauspicious suffering born of cold, heat, rain, and the like;
yet that very thing was not for the sake of dharma, and therefore I, the evil-minded one, am consumed.
For those who have passed away without having given to the ancestors, gods,
and humans, they have neither gone [to a higher state] nor do they remain; here, I alone, a fool whose mind is captivated by attachment to son, field, and wife, am consumed by grief.
I, a person of evil mind, have performed many unwholesome deeds; therefore I burn with remorse.
When I am dead, those handsome men will enjoy that wealth which was always acquired through unjust means; here, I alone, of evil mind, burn.

I did not honor those best of the twice-born when they departed from my home; therefore, my mind is consumed with desire for my own kin here. Since the gods were not honored by me, I have instead nourished only my family.
I burn there all alone; those sons of mine have gone elsewhere.
The daily rites, the occasional rites, and the ancestral offerings for our forefathers were not performed;
therefore, I burn alone, while they have departed to enjoy the fruits.
"Wife, sons, and servants were supported by me with a sinful intent;
therefore, I burn alone, while they have gone away to enjoy the fruits.
Wife, sons, and servants were for my sake, and the accumulation of wealth was for their sake."
I am being burned here for what was done by them; those whom they consumed have gone elsewhere.
The sin incurred has been experienced by me, while that karma was accumulated by others.
I alone am burning excessively, while they, who were the enjoyers of the fruit, have departed.
Whatever evil has been accumulated by me, overcome by the sense of "mine," that belongs to no one else; it is my own misdeed alone.
Consumed by internal suffering, I burn outwardly as I contemplate this.
"O best of sages, this fresh suffering is but a single evil situated in two ways;
therefore, effect your deliverance from it, so that you may behold the ocean of nectar and I too may attain joy."
Vipīta said:
"I perceive doubt regarding your deliverance from this short period;
your sin has been exhausted to this extent, and you possess supreme virtuous conduct."
In his tenth birth,
having fasted on Bhadradvādaśī with the desire to worship Acyuta, he obtained the victory of virtuous deeds; yet, by her grace, even the most invincible sin was not [left behind].
In a few days, her sin was utterly exhausted like water in an unbaked clay vessel; for her power is exceedingly rare,
as it brings about the destruction of evil and the victory of meritorious deeds.
"For this [twelfth day] indeed bestows the fruit of an action performed only once; therefore it is known as Dvādaśī.
Since you, O afflicted one, have lamented in this manner, he said to him:
'In this matter I have a doubt; O Lord, why do you grieve?'"
"O Bhadra, evil committed here results in torment after death;
likewise, merit brings joy to men who perform meritorious deeds in this world.
Having thus consoled Sīrabhadra, the great sage departed.
He too attained liberation from that state in a very short time. O best of men, I have thus described to you the power of fasting,
by which even great sin was brought to destruction in just a few days.
Therefore, a person should strive for merit and not for sin;
one who desires their own welfare should always observe fasts.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Now, O best of beings, tell me of that liberation which is eternally experienced by men dwelling in hell as the ripening of their grievous sins. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Men who are endowed with victory are always performers of virtuous deeds;
that twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) known as Jayā is praised for men of meritorious actions.
Having fasted on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Phālguna, [one should proceed].
O best of the twice-born, on the twelfth day one should worship Madhusūdana;
rising on the eleventh day while chanting the names of Viṣṇu,
one should eat with a well-composed mind during the worship of Vāsudeva.
One should avoid lust, anger, greed, pride, and delusion;
one should avoid malice and all other defects arising from the intoxication of wealth.
Furthermore, a devotee of Viṣṇu should cultivate a sense of dread toward worldly existence and likewise recognize its lack of essential substance.
One who has thus cultivated the mind and desires the welfare of living beings should say "Namo Nārāyaṇāya" while sleeping at night.
O King, in the same manner, on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī), one should break the fast with the name [of the deity] after having fasted from hunger.
O Pāṇḍava, one should first offer vessels made of gold, copper, or even clay,
as well as vessels of barley, for four months;
O high-minded one, one should then conclude the second [period] starting from Āṣāḍha.
There too, endowed with faith, one should give vessels of ghee during the months beginning with Kārttika and ending with Māgha; likewise,
having fasted each month, one should give sesame seeds and a vessel to a Brahmin.
Reciting the three names in their entirety for two days every month,
one should likewise offer barley and other grains month by month;
having prostrated before Hṛṣīkeśa and performed worship, one should seek His grace.
O Viṣṇu, salutations to you, the progenitor of the universe; salutations, salutations to Śrī Vāsudeva!

May he who is named Nārāyaṇa and meditated upon by those who bow before him make me a mass of eternal merit. Be gracious, O Viṣṇu; may merit attain victory, and may merit attain the prosperity of Śrī Vāsudeva.
Let it go either to the state of sovereignty or to total destruction; let my mind never turn elsewhere from your lotus feet.
O Viṣṇu, may there be for me the arising of merit; may Vāsudeva grant me auspiciousness.
May Nārāyaṇa be my dharma; destroy all evil without remainder.

May the merit produced throughout many births—during childhood, youth, and old age—increase; and may sin go to its destruction. [May this apply] to space and the other elements, to sound and the other objects of sense, to the ear and the other organs of perception, and to the Mahat and the other principles.
In Prakṛti, in Puruṣa, and even in Brahman—
that Lord Vāsudeva alone, whose nature is Dharma, is established.
By that truth, may my sin, which brings the agony of hell, come to an end.
"May my merit increase day by day;
may there be the destruction of my sin and the most excellent growth of my virtue.
Having uttered this, one should give to the Brahmin that which has been described to you.
Having fulfilled his duties, he should eat when the time for breaking the fast has arrived;
at the conclusion of the fast, O King, lord of gods, he should offer propitiation according to his ability and avoid conversation with all heretics.
Thus, at the end of the year, having worshipped a golden image of Hari with garments, flowers, and vessels filled with ghee, one should,
endowed with faith, give a cow along with its calf to a Brahmin.
If one should worship other deities after having previously delayed [the rite],
then on that day, food should be given without restriction;
thus has this meritorious [observance] been described, which brings victory through good deeds.
O Pārtha, he who fasts on the twelfth day does not behold hell;
neither fires, nor weapons,
nor birds with iron beaks do those denizens of hell afflict him whose mind is fixed upon Janārdana.

Merely by the utterance of Viṣṇu’s name, the accumulation of sins is destroyed; when sin is annihilated, how could there be a fall into hell? One who glorifies [him] saying, "Obeisance to Nārāyaṇa, O Hari, O Vāsudeva," [is liberated].
A mortal whose every sin has been completely exhausted does not go to hell;
therefore, by observing this Dvādaśī while avoiding the company of heretics,
a man, through the accumulation of merit, does not go to hell.

"It destroys evil, increases merit, bestows prosperity, and restrains all defects; why then do those of deluded minds not observe this Dvādaśī, which is so highly beneficial in this world? Thus ends the eighty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Sukṛta-Dvādaśī Vow," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[Now follows] the description of the Dharaṇī Vow.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
That which is recited as this supreme secret in all the Vedas is that very god,
the lotus-eyed one, Nārāyaṇa himself, Hari.
O best of the Yadus,
that eternal Supreme Lord is somehow attained through various sacrifices and vows performed with abundant wealth by officiating priests who have mastered the Vedas.
Even with good companions, those most difficult tasks are accomplished only when undertaken together;
yet, O Kṛṣṇa, it is not possible to give a gift without wealth. Even when wealth exists, one whose mind is attached to family has no inclination to give.

O Kṛṣṇa, how may liberation be attained? Hari, the eternal Lord, is difficult to reach in every way; tell me briefly that by which He may be obtained with little effort, and what that might be for all social classes.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
I shall tell you the supreme secret, a mystery fashioned by the gods,
concerning that which was done previously by Dharaṇī as she was sinking into the surface of the earth.
O King, in ancient times, the earth first came into contact with the waters;
when she was joined by that water, the earth sank down into the netherworld (rasātala). That auspicious earth, the sustainer of all beings, thus entered the depths of the netherworld.
The goddess propitiated the omnipresent Lord Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme,
through fasts, vows, and various kinds of observances.
After a long time, the one whose banner is Garuḍa became pleased with her.
The Imperishable One (Acyuta) lifted it up and established it in its place;
when the month of Mārgaśīrṣa arrived, on the tenth day, he who was self-restrained bathed,
performed the worship of the gods, and carried out the fire-ritual according to the rules.
Clad in clean garments and with a serene mind, having eaten very little well-prepared food, one should perform the five-fold prostration and again cleanse the feet; then,
taking a piece of wood eight finger-breadths long produced from a milk-exuding tree, one should proceed.

One should chew the tooth-stick and then, having carefully performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), touch and perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the mantras; then, after meditating for a long time upon Janārdana—
holding the conch, discus, and mace in his hands and clothed in yellow garments— one should attend to other duties.
At that time, O one of great splendor, he should utter these words:
"O Lotus-eyed One, having remained without food on the eleventh day, I shall partake of food on the following day; O Acyuta, be my refuge."
Having spoken thus, O God, one should then, in the presence of the God of gods,
recite "Nārāyaṇāya" according to the prescribed rule in that form. Then, at the clear dawn, one should go to a river that flows into the ocean.
Or else, a man of self-restraint, having brought pure earth from another place, from a pond, or from his own house, [should perform the rite] with this mantra:
"O Goddess, the supporting and nourishing of all beings always proceeds from you."
"O you of excellent vows, protect me by means of that being; release me from evil.
This is the mantra for the clay.
"The holy waters within the belly of the Cosmic Egg have been touched by your hands, O Sun."
"Beings arise from the existent; one should again take hold of the clay.
This is the mantra for beholding the Sun.
Having thus placed the clay before the Sun, one should then apply it to oneself.
Having drawn the entire sacrificial pit three times in the water with the *mṛdvī* mantra,

a man who has bathed properly and possesses the honors of a universal monarch should perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), attend to his necessary duties, and then proceed once more to the temple of the deity.
Having propitiated that Lord Nārāyaṇa, the Great Yoga, [one should worship him thus]:
"Salutation to Keśava for the feet; to Dāmodara for the hips;
to Nṛsiṃha for the pair of thighs; and to the bearer of the Śrīvatsa for the chest."
The throat to the Lord Kaustubha, the chest likewise to the Lord of Śrī;
the arms to the Conqueror of the Three Worlds, and the head to the Self of All;
the discus to the Wielder of the Chariot-Wheel (Cakra), and the lotus to Śaṅkara.
Saying "Obeisance to the Profound One" and "Obeisance to the One of Peaceful Form who Grants Fearlessness," having thus worshipped the Lord of Gods, the divine Lord Nārāyaṇa,
the wise man should again place four water-pots before Him.
Filled with water, adorned with garlands, smeared with white sandalwood paste,
covered with four vessels of sesame seeds, and endowed with jewels—
these four are proclaimed to be the jars representing the oceans.

In their midst, one should place a pedestal covered with cloth. Upon that, having prepared a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or likewise wood, and filled it with water, one should then set it down in the center.
O King, having fashioned the divine Janārdana in the form of a fish out of gold—
endowed with the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, adorned with the Śrutis and Smṛtis,
and beautified by various kinds of edible foods, fruits, and flowers— [one should worship Him].
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rites with perfumes, incenses, and the most excellent mantras, [I pray]:
O Keśava, just as the Vedas were recovered by you from the subterranean realm (rasātala) while you were in the form of a fish, even so, deliver me from worldly existence.
Having recited this, one should cause a vigil to be held there before him.
According to the extent of one's wealth, one should also offer oblations repeatedly.
Furthermore, one should cause four water-pots to be given to four Brahmins.
One should first give [the vessel] to a Bahvṛca, and likewise the southern one to a Śaṃdoga;
to one belonging to a Yajurvedic branch, one should give the excellent western jar.
One may give the northern one according to one's preference, following the specific rule for that region.
May the Ṛgveda be pleased in the east, and the Sāmaveda in the south;
likewise, let the Yajurveda be in the west by name, and the Atharvaveda in the north.
One should have jars prepared, covered with full vessels containing sesame seeds.
Then, O highly fortunate one, he should indeed give that [image] contained in a water-vessel to a brahmin who maintains a family; thereafter,
the householder should feed the brahmins with milk-rice (pāyasa) and afterwards eat himself.

One should eat together with one's dependents, restrained in speech and with senses controlled. O King, best among the truthful, listen to the fruit of the merit of that man who passes the twelfth day according to this rule.
O high-minded one, even if one were to possess thousands of mouths in age after age, and if one’s lifespan were equal to that of Brahmā,
it would still not be possible to calculate the total measure of its fruit; indeed, one could not contain it.

O King, he who observes this Kṛṣṇa-dvādaśī according to this rite attains the world of Brahmā; of this there is no doubt. Even sins such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa committed in other lifetimes [are destroyed].
Whether unintentionally or intentionally, they perish without a doubt;
likewise, by means of the month of Pauṣa, the nectar was churned by the gods,
and that became the Lord Kūrma himself, Janārdana.
This lunar day is prescribed for Hari in his tortoise form;
having reached the month of Pauṣa, on the twelfth day (dvādaśī) conjoined with the bright fortnight,
one should perform the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) as before, along with the morning bath and other rites.

Having completed his duties, O best of kings, one should worship Janārdana— the God of gods and Teacher of the world— on the eleventh day of the night with pleasing mantras. First, one should well-worship the feet of Hari with "Kūrmāya," and the waist with "Nārāyaṇāya."
One should purify the abdomen with "To Saṅkarṣaṇa," and the region of the throat with "To Purojava.
O son of Pāṇḍu, the two arms should be worshipped with "To Subāhu," and the head with "To Sarvātman.
Furthermore, one should worship the conch and discus with their respective mantras, and the mace with the mantra dedicated to salutation.

Having worshipped the God with these mantras, with fragrant flowers, incense, various food offerings, lamps, and fruits, one should place a water-pot before Him, adorned with garlands, ointments, and the like. Then, having filled that pot— which contains jewels— with highly fragrant water, one should [place] a golden [image] therein according to one's means.
One should place the Lord of the Gods (Viṣṇu), who has the form of a tortoise and is as vast as Mount Mandara, upon an auspicious vessel filled with ghee and situated at the front of the water-pot;
one should worship Him with vigils, dances, and songs. Having worshipped the Brahmins, one should first offer them ghee and milk-rice (pāyasa) to the most excellent of the twice-born.
Having performed everything according to the prescribed rites, he should then eat with a contented mind along with his dependents.
When this is done, he shall dwell in heaven for many intermediate *kalpa* ages, with all his desires fulfilled.
Having swiftly abandoned the wheel of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*), he attains the ancient realm of Hari in this world.
Sins quickly go to destruction, and one becomes endowed with prosperity and truth-dharma.
Through devotion, the sins accumulated over many lifetimes perish for a man;
he obtains the aforementioned fruit and immediately attains residence in Nārāyaṇa.

O King, most righteous supporter of the earth, listen now to another [account] regarding the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, concerning Varāha. One should perform the ritual bath and the formal vow (saṃkalpa) according to the procedure previously described.
Having worshipped the deity with focused concentration on the eleventh day,
and having honored Him again with incense, food offerings, and perfumes,
the man should thereafter place a water-filled jar before Him.

One should worship the feet with "Salutation to Varāha," the waist with "Salutation to Mādhava," the belly with "Salutation to Kṣetrajña," the chest of Hari with "Salutation to Viśvarūpa," the throat with "Salutation to Pūrvatra," and the head with "Salutation to Prajāpati."

He should worship the two arms with "Salutation to Pradyumna," the Sudarśana discus with "To the Wielder of Divine Weapons," the conch with "To Him Born from Nectar," and likewise the mace with "To the Mace-Wielder";
having thus worshipped, the wise man should also place these within that pitcher.
A wise person, having placed a vessel made of gold, silver, or copper according to his wealth and capacity, and having filled it with all kinds of seeds,
should then have a golden image of Varāha fashioned there according to his means.
Lifting the earth, together with its mountains, forests, and trees, by the tip of his tusk—
Mādhava, the slayer of Madhu, who has assumed the form of a boar—
[he stands] upon a jar containing jewels, which rests on vessels filled with all kinds of seeds.

One should install the supreme deity Hari, made of gold, covered with a pair of white garments; however, in the absence of copper, he may be installed in a vessel of bamboo. One should worship him with perfumes, flowers, various food offerings, and fruits.
Having constructed a pavilion of flowers, one should perform a vigil there;
the wise man should recite and cause others to sing of the divine manifestation of Hari.
Thus, for him who observes these restraints, when the sun has risen at dawn—
O Indra among kings, one should especially cause this to be given to one who is learned in the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (vedāṅgas), who is of virtuous conduct, wise, and a devotee of Viṣṇu.
Having thus given [the image] along with the water-pot, [one should worship] Hari in the form of the Boar.
Listen to me regarding the fruit that accrues to a Brāhmaṇa:
in this very life, O King, a man obtains good fortune, prosperity, beauty, and nourishment, as well as whatever else he may desire.
Even a single [observance] of this, when performed according to the rules, bestows the highest nectar;
how much more so, O descendant of Kuru, if it is practiced for an entire year!
And this [day] is the twelfth day (dvādaśī) of the bright fortnight in the month of Phālguna.
Having observed the fast according to the previous procedure, the wise person should worship Hari:
the feet with "Salutation to Narasiṃha," the belly likewise with "To Govinda," the waist by worshipping "To Viśvasṛj," and the chest of Hari with "Aniruddha."

One should worship the throat with "Salutation to Śitikaṇṭha," the head with "Salutation to Vainateya," the face with "Salutation to Asuradhvaṃsana," and [the conch] with "Salutation to the Self of Water.
Having thus worshipped the conch with perfumes, flowers, and fruits, [one should proceed].
Having placed a water-pot before that [image], provided with a pair of white garments,
one should place a golden Nṛsiṃha upon it in a copper vessel— or, according to one's means, in a golden, wooden, or bamboo vessel.
Having placed it within a vessel made of precious gems and worshipped it with devotion,
a person should present it on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) to a Brāhmaṇa who is learned in the Vedas.
This Dvādaśī, which destroys sins and is worthy of veneration, has been described by me.
It has been described with effort and heard by you as desired.
O tiger among men, having thus resolved upon this twelfth day of the month of Caitra,
one should fast and thereafter worship Janārdana, the God of gods.
One should place a water-pot (kuṇḍikā) at the side, as well as a small umbrella and sandals;
having established the stainless Vāmana there, along with a grass mat and a bronze vessel,
one should [offer] fruits, flowers, and fragrances to a virtuous twice-born man at dawn.
One should cause [the gift] to be given, saying, "May Viṣṇu, in his short form, be pleased. Here, the manifestation should be joined with the name of the month according to the prescribed rule.
The injunction "May he be pleased" is proclaimed to apply everywhere.
One without a son shall obtain a son; one without wealth shall acquire wealth;
one who has lost his kingdom shall regain his kingdom; and having died, he shall go to the city of Viṣṇu.
After sporting there for a very long time, he shall return here to the mortal world.

"The wise son of Nahuṣa, Yayāti, became a universal monarch (cakravartin) by performing this very rite in the month of Vaiśākha after making a formal resolve according to the rules; likewise, a man should perform his bath with clay in that same manner and then proceed to the temple of the deity."
