"O Kṛṣṇa, who is this person spoken of by you as the one renowned as Ananta?
Is he the serpent Śeṣa, or is Ananta considered to be Takṣaka?"
"Is he the Supreme Self (Paramātman), or the Infinite (Ananta), or is he called Brahman?
Who indeed is this one known as Ananta? Tell me the truth, O Keśava.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O Pārtha, know that 'Ananta' is my name.
He is the Time that arises during the days of the week, beginning with Sunday,
possessing a body composed of days and nights, and consisting of units such as kalās, kāṣṭhās, and muhūrtas."
O best among the upholders of dharma, this time— consisting of fortnights, months, seasons, years, and so forth, arranged according to the system of yugas and kalpas— which I have described to you,
is that very same Time (Kāla) who has descended here for the purpose of removing the burden of the earth.
Know me, O Pārtha, to be the one born in the lineage of Vasudeva for the destruction of the Dānavas— know me as Ananta, Viṣṇu, Jiṣṇu, Hara, Śiva,
Brahmā, Bhāskara, Śeṣa, the all-pervading Lord.
"I have declared myself to be that Great-Souled One of universal form, the cause of creation and destruction, for the sake of your conviction; O Pārtha, I am He, there is no doubt.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O best among the wise, tell me the procedure for the greatness of the Ananta-vrata.
What is its merit and what is the fruit for those men who perform it?
By whom was it first practiced in the past, and by whom was it revealed in the world of mortals?
"O Hari, having thus explained everything in detail, tell me of the Ananta-vrata.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"In former times, during the Kṛta-yuga, there was indeed a twice-born man named Sumantu."

Born in the lineage of Vasiṣṭha and being handsome, he then married that daughter of Bhṛgu named Dīkṣā according to the rites prescribed in the Vedas. In time, a daughter endowed with infinite auspicious marks was born to her.

That girl named Śīlā, being of excellent character, grew up in her father’s house. In time, her mother, afflicted by the fever of love for Hara, perished on the riverbank; having died, she went to the city of heaven.
Furthermore, Sumantu duly married another daughter of Dharmapuruṣa,
known by the name Karkaśā;
yet she was ill-behaved, harsh, fierce, and constantly quarrelsome.
O Lord, Śīlā too, devoted to the worship of the household deities in her father’s home, adorned the walls,
pillars, lintels, doorways, arches,
and other parts with paintings of the four castes, using yellow, blue, white, and black pigments.
Repeatedly worshipping with svastikas, conchs, and lotuses,
she was seen by her father Sumantu, who, observing that she possessed the marks of a woman and had reached her youth, reflected, "To whom should Śīlā be given by me? and became deeply distressed.
On an auspicious day, the father gave [his daughter] to Kauṇḍinya, the lord of sages;
he then performed the marriage according to the rites prescribed in the Smṛtis and the Śāstras.
Having completed all the wedding ceremonies, the twice-born man spoke to Karkaśā.
"A small amount of wealth and other gifts should be given as a reward for the son-in-law.
Hearing this, Karkaśā became enraged; she threw open the house pavilion, firmly bolted the door, and said, "You may go!"
She prepared provisions for the journey from the remains of the food powder.
Kauṇḍinya, having married her, traveled slowly along the road,
taking his bride Śīlā— who was possessed of excellent character— in a bullock cart.
At midday, at the time for eating, Śīlā, having stepped onto the bank of the river, saw a multitude of women dressed in red garments,
each individually worshipping the deity with devotion on the fourteenth day of the lunar fortnight.
Approaching slowly, Śīlā questioned the group of women:
"O ladies, tell me, what is this? What is the name of such a vow?
All those women replied: "There is one renowned by the name Ananta."
She said, "I too shall likewise observe this supreme vow.
What is the procedure for it? What is the gift to be given? Whom is one to worship?
The women said:
Of the well-prepared cooked food belonging to one who is firm in virtue and named Puṇya,
half should be given to a Brahmin and half should be eaten by oneself on the bank of a river,
after having heard this narrative of Hari.
Having worshipped the Infinite-infinite [Lord] within the mandala with perfumes, lamps,
incense, flowers, and food offerings, along with four hundred yellow lac-dyed threads,
one should place before Him a firm cord and a beautiful wrist-thread smeared with saffron.
O King of kings, one who possesses fourteen knots— on the left for a woman and on the right for a man— should wear it with this mantra until the year is completed:
"O Vāsudeva, lift up those who are submerged in the great ocean of endless saṃsāra!"

"O you whose self is engaged with infinite forms, salutations again and again to you who possess infinite forms! Having bound this cord and meditated upon the god Nārāyaṇa, who is infinite and possesses the form of the universe, one should eat with a tranquil mind."
Having eaten, he should go home at the end; thus has this vow been described to you.
Śīlā, having heard it, performed the vow after tying an excellent thread-bracelet.
Her husband, arriving there, saw her possessed of great wealth.

Having given the remainder of her provisions to a Brahmin and likewise partaken of them herself, she returned joyfully to her own hermitage by means of the ox-cart. Together with her husband, she proceeded slowly; and in that very instant, he became visible before her eyes.
By that infinite power, his household life became filled with auspicious cattle and wealth; endowed with prosperity and possessed of riches and grain,
it was bustling yet orderly, delightful, and everywhere characterized by the honoring of guests.
She too, adorned with jeweled girdles and pearl necklaces,
draped in divine garments, became like an image of Sāvitrī. Once, while seated, he saw a beautiful thread-bracelet tied [upon her].
At the base of Śīlā’s hand, he angrily tore it off with a violent jerk.
Due to the ripening of that karma, his fortune came to an end;
his wealth of cattle was carried off by thieves, and his house was consumed by fire.
Whatever comes into the house perishes right there;
quarrels with one's own kin, discord with friends, and likewise with other people;
due to the fault of endless insults, poverty has fallen upon the home.
No one in the world spoke with him, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Thereupon Kauṇḍinya, out of despondency, went into a forest thicket, meditating in his mind upon the Infinite One: "When shall I behold Keśava?"
Having undertaken a vow of fasting and observing celibacy while chanting the name of Hari,
Pārtha, overwhelmed with emotion, went to a forest devoid of people.
There he saw a great tree, laden with both fruit and flowers.
He asked him: "O great tree, has Ananta been seen by you? Tell me that.
He replied: "O twice-born one, I do not know Ananta.
Thus questioned by him, he beheld a cow with her calf.
O Pāṇḍava, as she was running hither and thither among the grass,
he said to the cow, "O little cow, tell me if Ananta has been seen by you.
The cow then replied, "O Kauṇḍinya, O Lord, I do not know Ananta."
Then he went into the forest and saw a bull standing on a grassy meadow;
having seen it, he asked, "O master of the herd, has Ananta been observed by you?
The bull then said to him, "Ananta has not been seen by me."
Then, proceeding further, he saw before him two beautiful lotus ponds,
adorned with the mutual splashing of water-waves,
covered with white and red water-lilies, and decorated with night-blooming and blue lotuses.
Frequented by bees, swans, ruddy geese, ducks, and cranes, those two lotus ponds asked the twice-born Ananta: "O twice-born one, was Ananta not perceived by you both?
They replied to him: "O twice-born one, we did not recognize Ananta."
Then Brahmā saw before him a donkey and likewise an elephant;
they too were addressed by Sumantu, and he informed him that Ananta had not been seen by either of them. Having heard that, he sat down.
At that moment, out of compassion, the infinite Lord himself became manifest before Kauṇḍinya, the best of sages and foremost of brahmins;
appearing in the form of an elderly brahmin, he said to him, "Come here."
Having led him into his own home and taken him by the right hand,
he showed him that city filled with divine women and men;
there, O King, he saw himself seated upon an excellent lion-throne.
He revealed to the brahmin the previously described universal form (viśvarūpa), adorned with conch, discus, sword, mace, and Garuḍa at its sides—
the infinite Supreme Lord, who is infinitely manifold through His various manifestations.
Upon seeing him, the twice-born one spoke with supreme joy:
"I am a sinner, I am a doer of evil, I am evil-minded, and I am born of sin.
Protect me, O Lotus-eyed One; become the remover of all my sins."
Today my birth has become fruitful and my life well-lived. [Tell me] who is the mango tree and who is the bull; what is the cow and what are the two lotus ponds;
and who are the donkey and the elephant—O Lord, tell me these according to the truth.
Ananta said:
"That brāhmaṇa was indeed a mango tree; he was a learned man who was arrogant of his Vedic knowledge.
Because he did not provide the gift of learning to his disciples, he became a tree."
That cow, the earth, whom you beheld, has been seen by you as fruitless;
that bull, joy, whom you chose for the sake of gain, has been seen;
and those two lotus ponds are the establishment of dharma and adharma.
"The donkey you saw was anger; the elephant was the destroyer of dharma.
That brahmin was I, the infinite one, within the cave of the worldly existence (saṃsāra).
O brahmin, I have told you all this; go back home."
"Practice the vow of truth for fourteen years;
then, being pleased, I shall grant you the supreme station among the stars.
Having enjoyed all vast pleasures and every desire as wished,"
"Surrounded by sons and grandsons, you shall thereafter attain liberation.
Having granted this boon, the Lord vanished on the spot.
Kauṇḍinya also returned home and performed the excellent vow of Ananta.
Having enjoyed delightful pleasures together with Śīlā,
that righteous soul eventually went to heaven and became the constellation Punarvasu;
existing for the duration of a kalpa, he is seen blazing even today.
O Kaurava, when the dharma of the Ananta-vrata has been properly performed,
this supreme of all vows has been described to you, O Pārtha;
by performing it, one is liberated from all sins— of this there is no doubt.
O best of men, those who constantly hear this being recited shall all be liberated from evil and go to the supreme goal.
O scion of the Kuru lineage, those of pure essence who desire to sport with great ease within the cavern of the ocean of saṃsāra— [for them, this is intended].
"Having worshipped the Lord of the three worlds, the infinite God (Anantadeva), they tie the auspicious thread (varadoraka) upon my right hand.

Thus ends the ninety-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Ananta-Caturdaśī Vow," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira. *Śabdakalpadruma*— (Note: The term *varadoraka* refers to the sacred thread or wristband bestowed as a blessing; *anantadeva* refers to the deity of infinity, Viṣṇu; and *tribhuvaneśa* means the Lord of the three worlds.)
King Yudhiṣṭhira, the self-controlled one, having dwelt in the forest retreat,
was met there by Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul and Lord of the three worlds;
a conversation, both pleasant and serious, took place between them.
And Yudhiṣṭhira questioned Govinda specifically;
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Lord of Gods, by what vow is the desired fruit obtained?"
All people become free from sin, birth after birth.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: There exists a vow named Ananta, which was performed in the abode of the gods.
Listen as I relate that which was told by Indra and the other guardians of the world:
on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada,
by the mere performance of its observance, all sin is destroyed.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Kṛṣṇa, who is this one described by you as being designated by the name Ananta?
Who is this Śeṣa and the Nāga known as Takṣaka? What is remembered as Ananta?
"Is it the Supreme, or even the Most Excellent, or is it called Brahman? Who indeed is this one known as the Infinite? Tell me that, O Janārdana.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"I am Ananta, O Pārtha; understand that form of mine which exists as Time, presiding over the forms of the sun's movement,
through the arrangement of days and nights, and by means of the divisions of kalās, kāṣṭhās, muhūrtas, and so forth."
Through the divisions of fortnights, months, seasons, years, yugas,
and kalpas, I am that very Time who have descended to remove the burden of the earth and for the destruction of the Dānavas, born from the body of Vasudeva.
Know me, O Pārtha, as the infinite— Kṛṣṇa, Viṣṇu, Hari, Śiva, Brahmā, Bhāskara, Śeṣa, the all-pervading Lord.
For the sake of conviction, O Pārtha, behold that universal form revealed by me.
"O mighty-armed one, [you have previously described] that which is the unsurpassed object of meditation for yogis.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O best among those who know the ordinances, [tell me] the greatness of the Ananta-vrata and its ritual procedure."

O Lord Nārāyaṇa, tell me all of this in great detail: what is its merit, what is its fruit, and what is its performance? By whom was it performed in the past, and by whom was it revealed in the world?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: In former times, during the Kṛta-yuga, there was indeed a twice-born man named Sumantra,
born of the lineage of Vasiṣṭha, who was learned, virtuous, and had his senses fully subdued.
His wife was Dīkṣā, a virtuous woman established in truthful vows,
endowed with good conduct and character, beautiful, and born of the lineage of Bhṛgu.
In time, a daughter endowed with all auspicious marks was born to her.

That woman named Śīlā, being well-behaved, grew up in her father’s house. In the course of time, her mother was afflicted by the burning heat of a fever; she went to the waters of a river and, having died, went to the city of heaven.
Sumantu performed for her whatever rites pertain to the world beyond.
Then, having gradually abandoned his grief and sorrow, Sumantu reflected:
"Indeed, a householder who lacks a wife is never able to perform his religious duties."
Having reflected thus in his mind, with a heart eager for marriage,
he married the daughter of the sage Devala, Karkaśā.
That Karkaśā was of extremely wicked character and always spoke harshly.
She is irritable, antagonistic, shameless, and fond of quarreling;
she is unskilled in household duties but clever at the act of eating;
she finds satisfaction in strife and is angry toward her kinsmen.
That Śīlā, having grown day by day in her father’s house,
engaged in unsurpassed childhood play with her companions upon the floors,
doors, thresholds, archways, and other parts within the home.
Adorning the svastika, the lotus, and the conch again and again with colors of four kinds— red, yellow, white, and black— the young girl daily performed the worship of the deities and guests.
Always skillful in her domestic duties and exceedingly dear to her father,
after some time the Brahmin, seeing that she had reached the bloom of youth,
became filled with anxiety, wondering, "To whom should I give this daughter?"
Then, by the power of fate, Kauṇḍinya arrived there—
the most excellent sage, highly fortunate, of noble lineage, and devoted to dharma.
Sumantu, the wise one of great asceticism, reflected thus in his mind.
Thinking, "By the power of destiny, Śīlā must be bestowed upon him with great effort," the Brahmin gave his daughter on an auspicious day;
he gave the virtuous Śīlā, adorned and with a face like the moon.
Then, according to the Vedic rites prescribed in the Gṛhyasūtras, he performed the marriage ceremony;
thereafter, having completed the rites such as the fire-oblation at the proper time, the sage Sumantu said to Karkaśā, "Give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to your son-in-law."
"Make my gift fruitful, O beloved born of the lineage of sages,
for a ritual act devoid of a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) becomes fruitless.
Hearing those words of his, Karkaśā became enraged.
She rebuked her husband Sumantu with harsh words;
having taken her own ornaments and her binding cord,
she placed them in a secret spot and went to the house of Karkashā.
Then Sumantu, his soul deeply dejected and filled with shame,
brought whatever articles were suitable for the purpose and gave them as a dowry to his son-in-law; the Brahmin served him again and again.
Then, having completed the wedding, Kauṇḍinya placed Śīlā upon a bullock-cart and set out for his own hermitage;
meanwhile, on the road, Śīlā, whose face was like the moon, continued her journey.
At midday, at the time for eating, having ascended to the riverbank,
Śīla beheld a multitude of women observing vows and likewise a group of men there, seated upon garments of red and yellow.

Seeing a multitude of women worshipping Ananta individually with devotion on the fourteenth day, the virtuous Satī, bowing down in humility and prostrating before the Lord of the Gods, questioned them with respect.
"What is this task being performed by you? Let it be told.
The women said:
"In the month of Bhādrapada, during the bright fortnight, when the banner of Vāsava has arisen..."
When Mahendra has been propitiated and the flagstaffs have been erected,
he who, having bowed and bathed in the lake, should begin the worship of Ananta,
having fashioned an image of the deity out of darbha grass and provided it with water and sacrificial grain;
[He saw] the infinite Lord of the gods, four-armed and wearing a crown,
resembling the flax flower (atasī) in hue, adorned with golden armlets,
bearing the conch, discus, mace, and the Śārṅga bow, and wielding various other weapons.

"Come, come, O Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa; your sacrifice is now proceeding. Then, one should offer the infinite Blessed One into the water-vessel. In the mandala, one should present flowers, food offerings, incense, garments, and ointments.
And having given it, one should worship with devotion the infinite one who possesses universal forms.
For the sake of the flour, there should be rice powder or that of barley or wheat;
whatever is obtained from these should be taken in the measure known as a *prastha*.
Half [of the offering] should be given to a Brahmin, and half one should apply to oneself;
likewise, having worshipped the God with perfumes and flowers in due order,
and having heard His story, [one should receive] a beautiful bracelet smeared with saffron.

A woman should place [the rosary] with fourteen knots on her left hand, while a man should place it on his right arm; then he should worship Ananta. Having completed the worship of the deity and eaten the cake, one may enjoy oneself as is pleasant.
Having dismissed them, given them a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), and bowed as they pleased,
Śīlā, having heard their words exactly as they were uttered by them,
undertook a vow, binding an excellent cord upon her arm.
Having prepared a measure of cakes and likewise having eaten them,
she returned once more on that very same ox-cart;
by his infinite grace, she reached her home, which was crowded with wealth of cattle.
Then that hermitage was endowed with splendor, filled with wealth and grain,
crowded with various guests, and adorned with many jewels; it was provided with excellent horses, rutting elephants, buffaloes, and herds of cattle.
Adorned with girdles of gems and ornaments of pearls,
her limbs divine and perfected by virtue, she was like the goddess Sāvitrī herself.
Once, while seated, she approached the sacrificial fire-pit.
Kauṇḍinya, having seen the endless cord fastened with great effort at the base of Śīlā’s hand, entered [the house] out of anger;
with his face contorted by a frown, he questioned her with words of wrath.
"What is this cord tied to your hand that you stand here as my wife?
O evil-minded one, tell me quickly: for which god are you an object of worship?
Śīlā said:
The auspicious cord of the God of gods is infinite and immeasurable; listen to my words, O Lord, regarding how it is bound upon the hand according to the prescribed rite,
by whose grace one enjoys very abundant wealth.
“O Lord, how is it that you do not know this, O Sovereign of the World?
Having heard these words of Śīlā, Kauṇḍinya became enraged:
“Who indeed is this one named Ananta? He has never even been heard of, O fair-faced lady!”
Having spoken thus, the enraged [king] violently pulled the endless arm from his beloved and, after rebuking her in many ways, cast it into a fire filled with flames.
Then, out of agitation, Śīlā cried out "Alas! Alas! and ran away.
Having taken the thread from the fire, she then threw it into the midst of milk;
thereafter, she tied that beautiful bracelet back onto her left wrist.
Due to the fault of casting [the thread] into the infinite [ocean], poverty fell upon her home.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, that brahmin was not described by anyone among the people;
filth had settled upon his limbs, and likewise his eyes were overcome by sleep.
The houses appeared empty, and in some places they were burnt by fire.
Having gazed upon his own city, the Brahmin reflected in his mind:
"Now Śīlā, pale and distressed by her husband's fault,
wanders through the entire city, which is filled with empty houses."
Then, the supreme understanding arose in the brahmin Kauṇḍinya:
"I too have committed evil deeds, or perhaps I have done something censurable;
because of the fault of my endless transgressions, my destiny is likewise such as this."
"Wherever I see Ananta, there I shall go," thought the dull-witted one; then Kauṇḍinya went to a forest infested with tigers and other beasts,
in order to search for the vow and likewise to behold the feet of Hari.
Agitated, he went along a path devoid of people and living beings;
there he saw that tree, endowed with fruits and flowers,
yet shunned by flocks of birds and especially by insects.
He asked him, "O great tree, have you ever seen Ananta anywhere?
And that great tree replied, "O twice-born one, I do not know Ananta.
Then, proceeding further, he saw before him, amidst some grass, a cow with its calf.
Running among the grass, she neither ate nor smelled it.
"O Great Cow, tell me, have you seen Ananta? She, along with her calf, then replied to him: "O Brahmin, I do not know Ananta."
Then, proceeding further, he saw before him an excellent bull standing in the forest.
This brahmin asked it, "Has Ananta been seen by you?
The bull spoke these words to that dejected brahmin:
"If I were to know the infinite, then my state would be such as this.
Then, while proceeding, he saw before him a donkey and likewise an elephant,
both wandering with various guiles and arrogant with the roar of rut.
Having seen him, the twice-born man asked, "Did you see Ananta? He gave this reply: "O twice-born one, I did not see Ananta. Then, proceeding further, he saw before him two beautiful lotus ponds.
It was adorned with waves formed by the mutual collision of waters,
beautified by auspicious white and red water-lilies, and graced by lotuses and blue lilies;
it was filled with bees, ruddy geese, swans, and kāraṇḍava ducks.
The twice-born Ananta asked him, "Have you two observed anything?
The two lotus-ponds replied, "We do not know Hari anywhere.
Then the brahmin fell to the ground, crying out "Alas! Alas! and weeping.

"What shall I do? Where shall I go? How may I behold that All-pervading Lord? Then, at that very moment, the Blessed Viṣṇu—the compassionate-hearted Lord of Gods, worshipped by the gods—appeared before the eyes of the twice-born.
In the form of an aged brahmin, he spoke these words to the twice-born: "Arise, arise, O chief of brahmins! Abandon your sorrow and become happy.
I shall show you Ananta, Kṛṣṇa, Viṣṇu, Hari, and Śiva."
Taking that Brahmin by way of the path to Pātāla, he showed him that city; then the twice-born one vanished. Kauṇḍinya beheld that city, which is difficult to find even in the three worlds.
There Kauṇḍinya beheld the God of gods, Ananta, accompanied by divine women and men, adorned with jewels and gems, entirely fashioned of gold, and encircled by Takṣaka and other [nāgas].
[He beheld] the Lord of the World, whose form is the universe, four-armed and wearing a crown,
bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, with Garuḍa as his banner;
on his right was the radiant Lakṣmī, and on his left, the playful Sarasvatī.

Having seen the Lord of the World in such a form— endowed with seven hoods and seated upon a divine throne— he approached Ananta and, with devotion, offered praise while bowing his head to the ground.
Salutations to the Infinite One, who possesses a thousand forms, a thousand feet, eyes, heads, thighs, and arms;
salutations to the eternal Puruṣa of a thousand names, the sustainer of thousands of millions of ages. O Lord, whatever sinful deed has been committed by me through ignorance, [may it be forgiven].
"Out of compassion, tell me all of that; forgive me, O Madhusūdana.
Then, having heard the praise of the brahmin Kauṇḍinya, the blessed Lord Janārdana, the god Ananta who assumes infinite forms, was pleased.
"O Brahmin, how was it that my beloved [son] was told to come here?
Ananta replied:
"I am pleased, O best of Brahmins, especially by your devotion."
"Accept a boon, O best of Brahmins; I am pleased, so cast away your astonishment.
Kauṇḍinya said:
"Whatever womb I enter through the experience of the fruits of my own actions,"
O Hṛṣīkeśa, may my devotion to Hari be firm in each and every one of those [lives].
Whatever evil deed has been committed by me through extreme negligence or delusion—O Lord, may that transgression be forgiven; I bow down to you again and again.
Having heard those words, Ananta granted him three boons:
the destruction of poverty, righteousness, and likewise the imperishable world of Viṣṇu.
Kauṇḍinya said:
"O Lord, my heart's desire is fulfilled today, especially for me.
O Lord of Gods, I ask something; tell me that, O Master of the World!
Who is the mango tree? Who is the bull? What is the cow? And what are those two lotus ponds?"
"Who is the donkey, who the elephant, or who is the best of the aged brahmins?
O Lord, please tell me out of compassion: whom did I see on the road today?
Śrī Ananta said:
Indeed, that brahmin who was seen as an *āmra* tree— proud of his learning because he did not impart knowledge to a student who had approached him—
remains there having attained the state of a tree as the ripening of that karma.
That bull whom you saw previously was one who performed acts of greed;
because he gave stale food and ate delicious things himself,
he has attained the state of a bull and now remains in this desolate place.

Having given to a Brahmin land that is fruitless and devoid of crops, he, having attained the state of a cow, runs about in the midst of grass. One should understand that righteousness and unrighteousness are those two lotus-pools.
"The donkey was possessed of ignorance, and the elephant was arrogant with rut;
that Brāhmaṇa you showed me, O Sage, was none other than myself.
All this has been told to you; go now, O Brāhmaṇa, to your own hermitage."
"Furthermore, O Brahmin, prosperity shall be yours; of this there is no doubt.
Having enjoyed abundant pleasures, you shall attain the supreme state.
Having granted him this boon, he vanished on the spot.
Having returned home, the righteous Kauṇḍinya observed for fourteen years the supreme vow known as Ananta, which brings great merit;
together with Śīlā, that virtuous soul enjoyed his heart’s desires in happiness.
Having reached the abode of Viṣṇu, she shone together with Śīlā.
O King, by the very completion of this vow called Ananta,
those who are liberated from all sins shall go to the supreme goal.

In this very way, O King, by the power of the Ananta-vrata, women necessarily attain the world of Viṣṇu for as long as the moon and sun endure, having enjoyed their heart’s desires and being endowed with sons, grandsons, and wealth.
Thus ends the Ananta-vrata in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa. [Now begins] the Śravaṇikā-vrata.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"In the world, deities known as Śrāvaṇīs are heard of.
Who are they, what do they do, and tell me their religious duty.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Pāṇḍava, there exist meritorious deities named Śrāvaṇīs,
created by Brahmā at the very beginning, to whom he assigned this duty:
"Whoever in this world speaks, whether auspiciously or inauspiciously," [they shall hear it].
For the Brāhmaṇa women quickly proclaim that sphere of their ritual activity;
O Lord of Creatures, those born [into it] are indeed worthy of worship throughout the three worlds by virtue of their observances.
They possess the power of hearing from afar and the range of vision from afar.
They possess here that inconceivable power which cannot be fathomed by logic or reasoning;
for they hear whatever is spoken by men who are satisfied regarding what ought and ought not to be done,
O Pārtha, because it is held that they are not merely those who hear with their ears alone.
Just as the gods, the Daityas, the Vidyādharas, and men;
just as the Siddhas, Gandharvas, Nāgas, Kimpuruṣas, birds,
Rākṣasas, and Piśācas— the eight classes of beings born from the gods.
In the same way, these women of virtuous names are remembered as venerable recipients of offerings;
men and women here should perform [the rite] with them in mind.
However, their vow at that time is indeed most formidable and requires great self-restraint.
Having smelled the incense, the cooked food, and even water that is odorless,
the meal for breaking the fast should be given again to other women. O Pāṇḍava, if death should occur in the interval before this is done, [the rite is incomplete].
Then, seized by the planets at the ascendant,
those low-born and miserable people are devoured from above the ascendant with fierce, frothing mouths.
Indeed, O Pārtha, it is heard that in ancient times there was a king on earth named Nahuṣa.
His wife, O Bhārata, was the great queen named Jayaśrī;
she was endowed with manifest beauty, most lovely to behold, and auspicious,
with full thighs and breasts, of dark complexion, and soft, curly hair.

Her speech was faltering like the sound of a bell, her gait was like that of an elephant in rut, and her conduct on this earth was consistent with her beautiful form; she was a virtuous woman whose actions were true to her nature.
Once, she went to the Ganges to bathe at the hermitage of a sage.
Then he saw Vasiṣṭha’s virtuous wife, Arundhatī,
feeding the wives of the sages with various kinds of food;
having prostrated before her, the goddess questioned that great chaste lady.
"O Blessed One, worthy of worship, tell me: what is this vow that is being described?
Arundhatī said:
"O Jayashrī, listen to this vow known by the name Śrāvaṇikā."
This was fully explained by my husband, the great seer Vasiṣṭha—
the secret essence of all the Brahman-sages, auspicious, and concerning the vow of a devoted wife.
Whether you go or stay, O Queen, I shall perform the rites of hospitality for you.
Thus addressed, Jayaśrī, having been offered that food by chance,
ate right there, though she was made somewhat bashful by Arundhatī.
Having eaten and sipped water for purification, she then departed for her own city, the supreme abode.
In the course of time, she forgot that vow of his and his meal.
Then, when the appointed time was fulfilled, the great lady Jayaśrī, as she was dying, made a gurgling sound with her throat choked with emotion as she prepared to depart.
Vomiting froth from her mouth, which was fouled with saliva,
she remained for fifteen days, loathsome and with a dreadful countenance.
Then, when the sixteenth day arrived, Arundhatī herself—
Having entered the inner quarters and beheld the queen,
he related to Nahuṣa what had been said regarding the Śrāvaṇī vow.
Upon hearing that, King Nahuṣa quickly prepared food for her.
Having given whatever was desired, including that which Arundhatī had mentioned,
and having offered eight water-pots (karakas) dedicated to Jayaśrī,
she met her death in an instant due to the offering of those water-pots.
She departed for the realm of Śakra in a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun,
being fanned by yak-tail whisks and praised by the gods and goddesses.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Pāṇḍava, during all twelve months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa,
the acquisition of materials and devotion at the time of giving is highly praised.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, having eaten at a sacrifice on the fourteenth or the eighth lunar day, [one should perform the rite].
Having bathed in the forenoon in pure water at a river or similar site,
the observer of the vow should invite eleven women who are of the nature of Gaurī—
women who are of disciplined conduct, well-attired, and either Brāhmaṇas or born of his own lineage.

There, one should give everything according to the prescribed rite, preceded by the washing of the feet, to twelve Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (Vedāṅgas), who are knowers of mantras and histories, who are tranquil, and whose senses are subdued.
One should adorn them with fragrant sandalwood, as well as flowers, incense, and the like,
and with necklaces, threads, vermilion, and saffron.
Furthermore, twelve *vardhanī* vessels should be placed before them.
They should be without cracks, filled with water, well-rounded, and wound with thread; covered with *sauhālaka* grass and other materials, adorned with flower garlands,
anointed with sandalwood paste, and each accompanied by gold.
In the midst of that, he should place a single *vardhanī* vessel upon his own head;
then, standing in the center of the mandala, the patron himself [should reflect]:
"Whatever was done in childhood, in youth, or even in old age..."
May all that [sin] of the ancestors, gods, sages, and men go to destruction.
O Svarṇa, deliver me from this ocean of worldly existence;
today I desire to go to the unsurpassed abode of Viṣṇu.
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, all those women should say, 'So be it.
Then, having summoned a Brāhmaṇa, the sacrificer should say this:
'Tell me, O Brāhmaṇa, that by which my sin may go to destruction.'"
Having completed the month of Śrāvaṇa, now cause [the people] to cross over;
let the Brāhmaṇa and the *vardhanī* vessel cross over by means of the mantra.
Having fasted and crossed over the trees growing at the head of the Goddess, [one should proceed].
"Or [climb] the bitter neem tree, and from there ascend the madhuka tree;
from there go to Mahādeva at Śravaṇa, the most excellent of sacred sites.
This is the mantra for raising the water-pot (*vardhanikā*).
Having thus spoken these words of agreement and bestowed their blessings,
they should present that *vardhanikā* to the Brahmin in private;
then, taking the water-pots, the women should depart for their own homes.
The sacrificer, too, when they have departed, may act according to his desire as he pleases.
O Pārtha, he who thus observes the Śrāvaṇī vow with devotion,
when his time has arrived, meets death with ease.
Free from disease and pain, possessing enjoyments, he shall dwell happily for a hundred years;
having experienced mortal pleasures through the abundance of sons, grandsons, and the like,
he attains the world of Rudra and goes to the world of Soma.

Even one who is inferior, if he observes the vow, shall attain the fruit of the vow equally with women when the Gaurī-bhojya offerings are given eleven times; O Pārtha, he obtains that same fruit by means of even a single Śrāvaṇika-vow.
"By means of devotion, they go to those worlds, having dwelt there happily with reverence.
Thus ends the ninety-fifth chapter, titled "The Śravaṇikā Vow," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira;
herein is the description of the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Now listen, O Pāṇḍava, to the rule for the night fast (naktopavāsa),
by the mere knowledge of which a person shall attain liberation.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight in whichever months those [observances] occur,
one should feed a Brāhmaṇa and then commence the vow.
In every month there are two eighth days and two fourteenth days.
Devoted to the worship of Śiva and with his mind solely intent on the meditation of Śiva,
he should take the earth as his vessel and eat his meal at night.
Begging for alms is superior to fasting, and not begging is superior to begging.
A night-meal (*nakta*) is superior to food obtained by begging; therefore, one should feed [the guest] with a night-meal.
The gods eat in the forenoon, likewise the sages at midday, the ancestors in the afternoon, and the Guhyakas and others at twilight.
Transcending all worldly ways, he should always be one who eats only at night;
his food should consist of sacrificial offerings (haviṣya), he should bathe, speak the truth, and practice moderation in eating.
Indeed, performing the fire-sacrifice and sleeping on the ground, he should always be one who eats only at night.
Thus, at the end of the year, when the vow is complete, one should place a full water-pot upon clarified butter and worship it, O beautiful lady;
one should then install a clay image of Śiva using the five products of a tawny cow (kapilā-pañcagavya).
Fruit, flowers, barley, milk, curd, and likewise sprouts of *dūrvā* grass— these,
mixed with water in those jars, are called the eightfold *argha*.
Having placed one's knees upon the ground and holding [the vessel] with the head, one should offer it.
One should offer fragrant flowers to Mahādeva in the proper sequence;
having presented an oblation of edible foods and water and bowed to the Supreme Goddess,
one should give a cow as a sacrificial fee, or even a bull capable of bearing the yoke.
Listen to the fruit of merit for him who gives with devotion to Śiva a gift to one who is learned in the Vedas, poor, and conversant with the ritual observances:
a celestial chariot resembling the sun, adorned and drawn by swans.
Mounted upon it, he goes happily to the abode of Rudra to the songs of the Apsarases.
Having stayed in the residence of Rudra for three hundred million years,
O best of kings, he shall become the lord of a hundred thousand villages in this world.

And he who observes the *nakta* fast on the auspicious eighth and fourteenth lunar days according to the injunctions seen in the scriptures, ascends a celestial chariot resounding with the sweet warbling of heavenly nymphs and proceeds happily to the world of the Lord of the Gods. Thus ends the ninety-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Śiva-Caturdaśī Vow," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen attentively, O King; I shall describe the vow of Maheśvara, renowned throughout the three worlds by the name Śivacaturdaśī.
On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, O King, a man who eats but once [a day] should not act in this manner during other months, O Pārtha; rather,
having fasted on the fourteenth day and worshipped Maheśvara, he should proceed.

"Having given a golden bull, I shall eat on the following day. Having thus made this vow and slept, that man, having risen in the morning and performed his ablutions and recitations, [should worship] Śaṅkara together with Umā.

One should worship with white flowers, perfumes, incense, and ointments. One should worship the feet with "Obeisance to Śiva," the head with "Obeisance to the Soul of All," the forehead with "To the Three-eyed One," and the eyes with "Obeisance to Hari."

The wise one should worship the face with "To the Moon-faced One," the belly likewise with "To Īśāna," the two sides with "To Ananta-dharma," the waist with "To Jñāna-rūpa," and the two thighs with "To Anantya-vairāgya" and the two knees.

One should worship the shanks with "Salutation to Pradhāna," the two ankles with "Salutation to Vyomātman," and the back with "Salutation to Him whose form is the essence of the ether of space. One should also worship Pārvatī with "Salutation to Sṛṣṭi" and "Salutation to Tuṣṭi."

Then, one should present to a Brāhmaṇa a golden bull accompanied by a water-pot, adorned with white garlands and garments, embellished with five jewels, and provided with various kinds of edible foods.
"May the God of gods, Sadyojāta, the wielder of the Pināka bow, be pleased here.
Having consumed the speckled butter (pṛṣadājya), he should sleep on the ground facing north.
Then, on the fifteenth day, he should perform all of this again in the morning.
Having then gratified auspicious Brahmins with food according to his capacity,
he should afterwards eat while restraining his speech, accompanied by his friends and foot-soldiers.
Then, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should perform all of this in the same manner.
On all fourteenth days, one should perform worship as previously described.
Now learn here, in due order, those specific rites that occur in each month;
during the months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa, while sleeping, one should recite these [mantras].
Salutations to you, Śaṅkara; salutations to you, Karavīraka.
Salutations to you, Tryambaka; and beyond that, to Maheśvara. Let there be salutations to you, Mahādeva; and after that, to Sthāṇu.
Salutations to Paśupati, O Lord; salutations to you, Śambhu.
Salutations to you, Supreme Bliss; salutations to the bearer of the crescent moon.
Salutations to Bhīma and Ugra; I have come to you for refuge.
One should duly consume the five products of the cow— cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, and clarified butter— as well as water from *kuśa* grass, along with *bilva*, rice gruel, milk, and water,
and black sesame seeds, as prescribed.
It is prescribed that on the fourteenth day of every month, one should consume a single morsel [of food] with mandāra,
mālatī, and likewise dhattūra flowers,
as well as sinduvāra, aśoka, mallikā, kubjaka, and pāṭala flowers.

O King of kings, Maheśvara should be worshipped with *arka* flowers, *kadaṃba*, *śatapatra*, as well as *utpala*, and *karavīra*. On the fourteenth day of the lunar fortnight, one should worship the Lord of Pārvatī with each of these individually.
Furthermore, when the month of Kārttika arrives, a man should gratify the twice-born with various kinds of food,
edibles, garments, garlands, and ornaments;
having performed the rite of releasing a dark bull according to the procedure prescribed in the Śruti.
One should present a golden image of Umāmaheśvara along with a bull and a cow,
accompanied by eight pearls, covered with a white eye-cloth,
upon a bed provided with all necessary furnishings.
Likewise, having placed it together with a water-pot and rice grains of the *śāli* variety,
it should be given to a peaceful Brahmin who is devoted to Vedic vows and knows the *Jyeṣṭha-sāman*; yet they do not do so anywhere.
Having honored him who is free from physical defects, gentle, and ever-performing auspicious deeds,
together with his wife, with garlands, garments, and ornaments,
one should not practice stinginess regarding wealth; for by acting out of greed, one falls downward.
The person who observes the Śivacaturdaśī according to this rite obtains the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices;
whatever sin has been committed here or in the hereafter, such as the killing of a Brahmin, [is likewise purified].
All that [sin] shall perish, whether committed by fathers or mothers.
Here, there is long life, health, and the increase of one's lineage; and elsewhere, imperishable four-armed divinity.
Having dwelt in heaven for ten million kalpas as a lord of the Gaṇas, one attains the station of Śambhu.
Neither Bṛhaspati, nor Indra, nor even the Grandfather (Brahmā) is able to describe the fruit of this [work];
nor is even a Siddha endowed with [supernatural] qualities capable of it, much less I, even if I possessed ten million tongues in my mouth.
He who reads, remembers, or even constantly listens to this work—which liberates one from all sins—becomes beloved by the immortals, provided he is free from envy.

On this Śivacaturdaśī, millions of celestial nymphs praise it joyfully in heaven; what then can be said of one who observes it always? O Pārtha, that woman who, with great devotion, having consulted her husband or a virtuous elder, performs this rite, she too, by the grace of the Supreme Lord, the wielder of the Pināka bow, attains the supreme state.

Thus ends the ninety-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Śiva-Caturdaśī Vow," within the Dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious *Śrīmad Bhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*.
[Now follows] the description of the Phalatyāga-Caturdaśī Vow.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Likewise, O Bhārata, hear of the majesty of renouncing all fruits [of action],
which is imperishable in the other world and bestows the fruit of all desires.
Having undertaken a vow on the fourteenth day of the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa, [one should act as follows].
Having performed the recitation for the Brahmins at the beginning of the bright fortnight,
O best of men, one should also worship the twice-born with milk-rice (pāyasa) and sacrificial fees according to one's ability on the eighth day of other months as well.
Except for fruits and roots, one should avoid the eighteen types of grains for one year while performing the medicinal rite according to the prescribed rules.
Then, at the end of that year, on the fourteenth and eighth lunar days, [one should proceed].
And one who is unable to perform the vow is instantly liberated.
One should have an image of Rudra made of gold, as well as that of Dharmarāja,
and likewise of a kūṣmāṇḍa, a mātuluṅga, a vṛntāka, and a panasa.
Mango, hog-plum, wood-apple, *kaliṅga*, and eggplant;
*bilva*, banyan, holy fig tree, citron, and plantain;
jujube and pomegranate—these sixteen items should be offered according to one's ability.
Radish, myrobalan, rose-apple, lotus, karamarda,
udumbara, coconut, grape, the two types of bṛhatī,
kaṅkālī, kākatuṇḍīra, karīra, kuṭaja, and śamī.
One should have these sixteen fruits fashioned out of silver according to one's capacity;
or one may make the palmyra fruit out of copper, as well as the agasti fruit,
the piṇḍīraka, the date palm, and the sūraṇa tuber.
The jackfruit, the lakuca, the karkaṭa, and likewise the tamarind; similarly, the fruit of the citrā-vallī and the fruit of the kūṭa-śālmalikā;
the madhūka, the kāravella, the vallī, the gudapattraka, and the paṭola.
The wise man should have these sixteen fruits prepared according to his capacity.
He should place two water-pitchers upon a cloth,
provided with two side-vessels and accompanied by [the images of] Yama and Rudra.
On an auspicious day, having honored a peaceful Brahmin who maintains a household and is accompanied by his wife, one should present [the gift] together with a cow;
for just as all tens of millions of immortals reside within all fruits, so do they dwell within this.
Likewise, through the renunciation of all fruits [of action], may I always possess devotion to Śiva;
and just as Śiva and Dharma always bestow infinite fruits,
may they both become the granters of boons to me by bestowing the fruits associated with that [devotion].
Just as there is always the fulfillment of desires for one devoted to Śiva,
may there be the attainment of infinite fruit in birth after birth;
and may I never perceive any difference between Śiva, Viṣṇu, Arka, and Padmaja.
"May the Universal Soul, Śaṅkara, the bestower of happiness, always grant me happiness. Having uttered this and having adorned all of that with ornaments,
one who is able should give a bed provided with all necessary furnishings.
But one who is unable [to perform the full rite] should, according to the prescribed rule, give the aforementioned fruits,
as well as two golden images of Śiva accompanied by water-pots,
to a Brahmin, and then eat food free from oil and alkaline salts.
One should also feed other eminent brahmins according to one's ability.
If one is unable to give away all the fruits, then,
having set aside just one, one should present them in this manner.

O best of kings, those who know the Vedas consider this vow of renunciation— namely, the abandonment of all fruits— to be prescribed for Vaiṣṇava yogis who seek the Supreme Cow; and it should be performed by women according to their capacity.
O best of sages, there is no other vow in this world or the next that yields such fruit as the gift of food. As many atoms as there are within vessels of gold, silver, and copper—
O best of kings, as long as the fruits continue to be crushed,
one is honored in the world of Rudra for that many thousands of yugas.
O lord of men, may this [gift], which removes all the impurities of people, be available for their livelihood at all times.
Even in other births, he does not suffer the pain of losing sons or wife; rather, he attains that very abode frequented by Purandara (Indra).

Or, whether it be a man of little wealth who hears this, or a Brāhmaṇa in the houses of the righteous, even he, O King, being freed from sins, attains in the hereafter the supreme and bliss-bestowing city of Murāri (Viṣṇu). Thus ends the ninety-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Phalatyāga Caturdaśī Vow," in the Uttara Parva of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the Paurṇamāsī Vow. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O great king, the full-moon day (Paurṇamāsī) is the beloved lunar date of Soma.
Because the full moon occurred on that day, it is remembered as Pūrṇamāsī;
and on that Pūrṇamāsī, a battle characterized by victory arose between Soma and his enemies, causing terror to all living beings.
The Moon was attached to Tārā, and Bṛhaspati was her husband.
In ancient times, a great battle occurred between the two of them on account of their wife.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Whose daughter was Tārā, and why did he, the slayer of the enemies of the gods, become enraged? Why did the wielder of the discus and mace engage in battle with Soma?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Prajāpati had a daughter named Tārā, the younger sister of Vṛtra;
he gave her, the most beautiful woman on earth, to Bṛhaspati. She became the wife of the preceptor of the gods, a woman of such indescribable beauty.
By means of these two forms, she remained beautiful;
yet at times she attended upon Bṛhaspati just as other women do.
He beheld her, with long-cornered eyes, slender-limbed, and sweetly smiling.
The cool-rayed moon fell under the sway of desire merely by seeing her;
he spoke sweetly, "Tārā, come, come, do not delay!
Tārā, skilled in discerning gestures and facial expressions, understood the intention of Soma.
Then, perceiving his purity, the slender woman spoke these sweet words:
"O gentle one, you are the son of the sage Aṅgiras and a king of the moon-like sages.
O hero, I am the daughter-in-law of the sage Aṅgiras; this is not appropriate for you."
O Moon,

do you not remember how, in ancient times, Aṅgiras established you in sovereignty over the gods, asuras, and rākṣasas, together with that great and wonderful conjunction with Saumya which has now been accomplished?
"How is it that today you, O Lord of the Night, have been afflicted by the bodiless one?
Therefore I say this: I desire your success; do what must be done.
I am under the power of another—blessings be upon you—I am not to be approached, O best of the wise."
Having been addressed thus, he did not do so;
instead, Soma, overcome by the power of love, seized her and drew her toward himself.
Bṛhaspati, however, perceiving this, censured that Soma.
"She will send my wife to me herself.
Having realized this after a long time, the noble-minded Bṛhaspati,
his lower lip quivering with rage, did not approach his own wife.
He related all of this conduct of Soma to Indra.
Indra then summoned the gods and the hosts of sages;
Soma did not take them into account, and thereupon the king of the gods became aware of it.
Having summoned all the gods, he reported the deeds of Candra.
Upon hearing this, the gods and Gandharvas, blinded by rage and agitated in mind,
took up their weapons and mounted their respective chariots.
Soma, too, having learned that the gods were diligent and resolved upon righteous action,
assembled the Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas and took his stand;
then, mounting his excellent chariot, he set his mind solely on battle.
A truly great battle commenced with arrows, javelins, and lances;
it was a conflict between the *kauṇapa* demons and the earth-dwellers (*kṣmāsura*) using spears, a slaughter that tore asunder both gods and *dānavas*.
Having engaged them in that immense combat, the Lord of the Host of Stars (Rāhu) departed.
The maker of night shattered the gods, including Indra, with a rain of gold;
having conquered the gods and Gandharvas, O best of kings,
Soma was endowed with supreme splendor, such as no other consumer of oblations possessed.
The gods were conquered by that Soma of immeasurable splendor;
they went for refuge to the God who is the protector of the dwellers of heaven.
Indra related all such conduct of Soma.
Hearing this, Hṛṣīkeśa became enraged; mounting Garuḍa with fury and seizing his most excellent weapons, he set his mind on battle alone.
Bearing the discus, the Śārṅga bow, and the mace, he prepared to wage a truly great war.
Enraged, he went forth together with the gods toward Soma;
and Soma, perceiving that Viṣṇu had arrived along with the hosts of Daityas,
stood ready for battle, full of martial indignation, having blown his conch shell.
Having conquered the host of gods, including Indra and led by Vāyu,
he was joined by Viṣṇu with weapons and missiles that consume life;
yet when he did not desist from fighting along with Viṣṇu, [he continued].
Then Viṣṇu, filled with wrath, seized his discus in anger.
Thereupon Brahmā spoke to the imperishable Viṣṇu, the unconquered Lord of gods:
"Listen to that which I say concerning him whose limbs are nourished by the clouds."
"O sinless one, there is no one in the three worlds who can be slain by this discus of yours.
Soma has been consecrated by me in the sovereignty over the twice-born.
Therefore, let whatever is appropriate for this task of the gods be performed."
Then the Blessed Viṣṇu spoke in the presence of the gods and the celestial sages:
"In her named Sinīvālī and Kuhū, the maker of night (the moon) was lost;
though he has perished, he will obtain birth once again—of this there is no doubt."
Having obtained the consent of Rākā and Anumati, his growth shall increase;
nourished by the ancestral funeral cakes (piṇḍas) accompanied by mantras as prescribed in the Śrutis,
he will cause the Brāhmaṇas to deliver the offerings to the gods (havya) and the ancestors (kavya).
There was no further increase for him even after being born by Kṛṣṇa;
such indeed was the decree seen by me, that his nourishment would be exactly so.
There shall never be any failure of the infallible [Kṛṣṇa].
Soma has been cursed by Dakṣa, and he will certainly become so;
likewise, Sudarśana’s affection will be exactly as it is now.
"Let it be so," O Lord of Gods, for that which you declare shall indeed come to pass.
Brahmā spoke to Soma, who stood before him in a humble manner:
"Return the preceptor’s wife; such an act must never be repeated.
Thus addressed, he brought Tārā back and gave her to Bṛhaspati.
The Moon spoke clearly again in the hearing of the gods:
"This embryo within her is mine; whatever offspring she bears shall belong to me alone.
Then Bṛhaspati said: "The embryo was conceived by me."
And since he has been born in my field, he is therefore my son.
For it has been said by the seers who know the Vedic scriptures and perceive the Dharma:
"The seed that is sown and carried away by the wind, in whose field it sprouts..."
"The seed belongs to the owner of the field; the sower of the seed shall not be the one to enjoy the fruit.
You have not spoken correctly; the Moon, who knows the truth, has said:
"The mother is but a bellows; the son belongs to the father by whom he was begotten; he alone is his own."
Thus spoke the Puranic sages, who possess the eye of political wisdom.
Then, having restrained the two disputants, Brahmā led that bride aside in private and said to her softly: "Tell me, whose child is this? Speak."
Thus addressed, Tārā said nothing out of shame;
in an instant, she released the fetus, which illuminated the abode of the gods.
Then Brahmā said to him: "O son, whose son are you?"
"O Brahmin, I have spoken the truth when I said, 'I am the son of Soma.
This Budha is the foremost among those who know all branches of knowledge," so said the gods.
Taking his son, Soma went to his own abode.
The Guru, taking his own wife, slowly returned to his home;
Soma too, having regained his son, was his mind overwhelmed with joy. That night was celebrated as Paurṇamāsī, for her every desire had been fulfilled.
"A son has indeed been obtained by me through her, and likewise victory has been gained.
Therefore, being devoted to my vows, I shall attend upon her according to the prescribed rite.
Thus, another [son] was born who had his purpose fulfilled, whose portions were complete, and whose characteristics were perfect.
"Whoever shall worship me with devotion according to the prescribed rites on this lunar day (tithi) of Māmakī, I shall indeed be well-disposed toward him through my grace and grant all his desires.
Thus, O Pārtha, is this auspicious lunar day beloved of Soma."
It is declared to be the Paurṇamāsī because the month becomes full. Having bathed in its stream on that day and having satiated the ancestors and the deities,
one should draw the powerful Soma together with the constellations within a mandala.
One should worship with pleasing flowers and offerings cooked in ghee;
having worshipped with white unbroken rice grains and white garments, one should ask for forgiveness.
Restrained in speech, one should eat at night, subsisting on vegetables and the food of sages.
O Moon, friend of spring, cool-rayed one, grant us well-being!
O Moon, the ruby of the ocean of the sky, Lord of the daughters of Dakṣa!
This procedure is proclaimed to be performed on every full moon night throughout each fortnight.
Even for anyone who, possessing faith, observes this vow during the dark fortnight,
this same procedure is prescribed as the bestower of all happiness.
This lunar day of the new moon (āmāvāsyā) is always beloved to the ancestors.

Whatever austerity is performed or whatever gift is given on this day shall become inexhaustible for the ancestors. O Great King, by those who have observed the fast with diligence on the new moon day, what is given to the ancestors becomes imperishable; it is the most excellent of sacred sites.
Whoever performs the rites of offering funeral cakes and water for the ancestors at that place,
that meritorious soul delivers twenty-one generations of men;
his worlds, frequented by the ancestors, shall become inexhaustible.
But when, at the end of time, his arrival here occurs—
being a Brāhmaṇa devoted to his ancestors and proficient in all branches of knowledge—
he shall likewise be endowed with wealth in that birth, O Indra among kings.
Thus, at the end of the year, having fashioned a very beautiful golden image of Soma together with the constellations, one should present it to a Brahmin. Furthermore,
the man who provides instruction to that performer of the vow [should also be honored].
Having honored [the deity] with garments and ornaments, one should offer this petition with the mantra:
"O Lord of Men, this is the procedure for this vow month after month;
for one who is unable to perform it continuously, or even for a fortnight."

The wise man should perform the concluding rite (*udyāpana*) after fasting for even a single day. O Pārtha, the man who performs this Full Moon vow (*paurṇamāsī-vrata*) is liberated from all sins and shines in heaven like the moon.
Endowed with sons, grandsons, and wealth, having performed sacrifices, being a donor, and speaking kindly,
one who attains extensive progeny and meets death at Prayāga thereafter reaches the imperishable worlds frequented by the gods.
Served by Gandharvas and praised by gods and demons,
he remains with all his limbs complete for as long as thirty thousand kalpas.
Those who worship the Moon on the fifteenth days of the bright fortnight and the Pitṛ-gaṇas on the dark fortnights with offerings of water and funeral cakes [attain this state].
"O King, by the ordinance of Fate, their houses become filled with the prosperity of wealth, grain, sons, and so forth.

Thus ends the ninety-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Vijayā-Paurṇamāsī Vow," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[This is followed by] the description of the vows for the full-moon days of Vaiśākha, Kārttika, and Māgha.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O best of the Yadus, tell me of those lunar days throughout the year that are characterized by merit and yield great fruit through bathing and giving gifts."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O son of Pāṇḍu, the lunar days of Vaiśākha, Kārtika, and Māgha are exceedingly sacred; they must not be passed by those who fail to perform ritual bathing and charity.
At that time, bathing at sacred fords (tīrtha) and giving gifts according to one's wealth is commended, O best of the Pāṇḍavas. Vaiśākhī is considered the most excellent of illuminations;
Puṣkarāraṇya is remembered [as the best] on the full moon of Kārttika, and Vārāṇasī on the full moon of Māgha.

By means of ritual bathing and the offering of water, one delivers even those who have committed evil deeds. By giving jars filled with pure water, accompanied by gold and food, on the full moon day of Vaiśākha after performing the vow, a Brāhmaṇa does not grieve.
One should duly present vessels radiant with gold, filled with sweet foods and juices, along with cows, land, gold, and garments;
likewise, on the full moon of Māgha and under the Maghā asterism, one should satiate the ancestors and the deities.
Vessels of sesame seeds should be given, as well as sesame and rice mixed with meat;
in this very context, the gift of cotton and the gift of sesame are commended.
Blankets, skins, jewels, and the two "mocakas"—the liberators from sin—are also to be offered.
The gift of sandals is taught right here as the bestower of all desires.
Whether at this place or any other, bathing and giving according to one's wealth are praised for overcoming everything arising from the Kali age, O son of Pāṇḍu.

O best of the Kuru lineage, on the full moon day of Kārttika, one should perform the ritual release of a bull, a marriage characterized by auspicious marks, as well as the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for Hari; furthermore,
one should give gifts of elephants, horses, and chariots, as well as cows made of clarified butter and other such offerings.

Those various fruits that exist— fragrant and sweet, such as nutmeg (*jātīphala*), *kaṅkola*, clove (*lavaṅga*), and *lavalī* fruit— should be offered by those who perform meritorious deeds after having mentally conceived them as deities.
Dates, coconuts, and plantains; pomegranates, citrons, and cucumbers; likewise trapusa gourds, eggplants, and kāravella;
bimba fruits, pumpkins, and variegated melons.
O Bhārata, those whose sacred days pass away without giving are born on earth as men afflicted by disease and poverty;
indeed, giving is praised not only for Brāhmaṇas, but for everyone.
A gift given to sisters, nephews, maternal uncles, paternal aunts,
and poor kinsmen yields a merit ten million times greater. So too does a gift to a friend of noble birth who has fallen into distress, or to a relative suffering from poverty.
A guest who has come from afar out of hope is a bridge to heaven;
yet when Rāma had set out for the forest with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa,
[Bharata] came from his maternal grandfather’s family with a pure inner soul.
When that daughter of Kośala was thus addressed by Bharata and many others,
yet the princess of Kośala did not in any way regain her composure,
then, with a pure heart, the lunar days (tithis) were recounted once more.
"The full-moon days of Vaiśākha, Kārtika, and Māgha are honored by the immortals;
they pass away for one who gives no gifts, yet he has gone with the consent of his noble mother.
Upon hearing this, Kauśalyā was suddenly filled with conviction.
Having brought Bharata onto his lap, he consoled him who was filled with grief.
This greatness of the lunar days has been recounted by me at great length;
what more, O high-minded King, shall I tell you?

"Furthermore, on the full moon day of Vaiśākha, Kārtika, and Māgha— which is marked by the full orb of the moon— a man who gives water, food, gold, clothing, and an umbrella goes to the world of Indra. Thus ends the one hundredth chapter, titled "The Description of the Vows of Vaiśākhī, Kārtikī, and Māghī," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the Greatness of the Vow on the Yugādi Lunar Days.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Lord of Gods, speak again to me, whose soul is purified by devotion to you.
I desire to hear here the great and auspicious teaching on the Dharma,
wherein even that which is given or chanted by men, though it be as small as an atom, becomes exceedingly great.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:

Listen, O Pāṇḍava, I shall tell you a secret ordained by the gods, which I have never spoken to anyone, O Bhārata, even to one who is very dear. It is the third day of the month of Vaiśākha and that ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika.
The thirteenth and fifteenth days of the dark fortnight of the month of Nabhasya,
the third day of Vaiśākha which is equal to the Kṛta age,
and the ninth day of Kārttika which has attained the status of the Tretā Yuga— these are the times.
The thirteenth day of the month of Nabhasya is joined with the Dvāpara age;
O King, the fifteenth day of Māgha is said to be the beginning of the Kali age.
O Indra among kings, these four days are like the origins of the Yugas.
These Yugādis are likewise proclaimed by all the wise; whatever is performed—
be it fasting, austerity, charity, recitation, fire-offerings,
or any other act— it shall all become ten millionfold in merit.
On the third day of the month of Vaiśākha, you should worship Nārāyaṇa, the Teacher of the World, together with Śrī, with flowers, incense, and ointments,
as well as with garments, ornaments, various offerings, and diverse food oblations.
Then, O best of the Kuru lineage, a cow should be made for him from one āḍhaka of salt, and a calf from a fourth part of that,
having placed it upon a goat skin and prepared according to the prescribed rite.
One should present it to a Brāhmaṇa according to the sequence prescribed in the scriptures, saying:
"May Śrīdhara, the Lord of Śrī, the Auspicious One, the Master of Śrī, be well-pleased.
O Bhārata, having given the cow to the Brāhmaṇa by this rite, [one attains the fruit].
In this world, he undoubtedly obtains the merit of ten thousand cows;
likewise, a man who eats only at night on the ninth day of the month of Kārttika,
having bathed in rivers, ponds, or natural pools dug by the gods.

Then one should worship Śiva, the auspicious Śaṅkara, who is accompanied by Umā, the bestower of boons, and the blue-throated one, with blameless offerings of flowers, incense, and food. One should give a cow made of sesame seeds according to the procedure prescribed in the Purāṇas.
One should reflect: "May the eight-formed, blue-throated Lord be pleased.
O Pārtha, by whom can the merit obtained here be described?
By giving a cow made of sesame seeds, one attains the world of Śiva.
On the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Nabhas,
one should worship the ancestors with offerings of milk-rice (pāyasa), honey, and ghee;
and with devotion, one should feed Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.
O Great King, a young, prolific cow with a brass milking vessel and her calf should be given in honor of the ancestors;
for the father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather are [as if] visibly present.
Saying, "May [the deity] be pleased by this gift of a cow," one should release [the animal] after it has been given.
O King of kings, who could possibly describe the merit obtained by men through performing this, even in hundreds of millions of years?

By worshipping the Grandfather (Brahmā) on the fifteenth day of the month of Māgha, a person obtains sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons, as well as highly desired wealth in this world, and an auspicious state in the hereafter.
One should present to a Brāhmaṇa the deity accompanied by the Gāyatrī, adorned with the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (Vedāṅgas),
along with a cow made of fresh butter, provided with various kinds of fruits,
together with gold and her calf.
One should proclaim: "May the lotus-born Grandfather be pleased here.
Whatever is in heaven, whatever is in the netherworld, and whatever is very difficult to obtain in the mortal world—that one undoubtedly attains through the grace of the lotus-born.
And whatever other gifts have been given, O Great King, even in great abundance during the beginnings of the Yugas, they indeed become inexhaustible;
for even one who is destitute, if he should give even a very small amount, [that gift likewise becomes inexhaustible].
All that shall become inexhaustible on the days marking the beginning of the Yugas; of this there is no doubt.
Whether one is wealthy or even a king, having understood his own means, he should act according to his wealth through an inconceivable state of meditative absorption.
Land, gold, a house, clothing, beds, and seats,
as well as umbrellas and pairs of excellent sandals, should be given to the twice-born.
Having thus given according to one's ability, one should also feed the twice-born.
Thereafter, with a joyful mind and restrained speech, one should eat together with one's kinsmen.
Whatever sin there may be— whether mental, physical, or verbal—
all that comes to destruction through the worship performed on the lunar day marking the beginning of a Yuga.

Being sung of by Gandharvas and praised by gods and asuras, he rejoices in the heavenly world for an inexhaustible period of time; of this there is no doubt. Whatever is given [in charity] becomes ten-million-fold, and they say that bathing, recitation, and self-restraint all become entirely inexhaustible.
"O King, on the first lunar days of the Yugas, Vyāsa and other eminent sages declare that [the merit] shall be inexhaustible.

Thus ends the one hundred and first chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Vow of the First Days of the Yugas," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[Now begins] the Description of the Vaṭasāvitrī Vow.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Hṛṣīkeśa, I remember that which was never spoken by you at any time;
please show me compassion and tell me about that Sāvitrī vow."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Yudhiṣṭhira, I shall describe the great good fortune of noble women,
just as that excellent vow was performed by Sāvitrī, the princess.
Among the Madras there was a righteous king named Aśvapati, devoted to the welfare of all beings and beloved by the people of both the city and the countryside;
he was a lord of the earth, patient, truthful, and one who had conquered his senses.
Accompanied by his wife, that king himself observed this vow,
which— when perfected through the Sāvitrī-vrata— bestows all desires. O King, Sāvitrī, the beloved of Brahmā, became pleased with him.
"O King, this goddess Bhūrbhuvaḥsvaḥ stands here visibly personified,
holding a water-pot and possessing a serene face and eyes;
she said, 'A daughter shall indeed be born to you.'"
Having spoken thus, Sāvitrī vanished once more. In time, O King, that daughter of divine form was granted by the pleased Sāvitrī when she had been recited.
The Brahmins and her father gave her the name Sāvitrī;
that princess grew up like a housewife, endowed with beauty. Sāvitrī, whose limbs were delicate, reached the prime of youth.
Seeing her— slender-waisted and broad-hipped, like a golden statue—
the other people thought she was surely a celestial maiden descended to earth;
for she, with eyes like lotus petals, seemed as if blazing with splendor.
And she performed the Sāvitrī-vow as it was proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
Then, having fasted and bathed her head, and having approached the deity,
she offered oblations into the fire according to the rules and caused the Brahmins to recite blessings on the lunar festival day.
Having received the remaining flowers from them,
the princess, virtuous and devoted to her husband, approached like Devaśrī incarnate;
she saluted her father’s feet and first presented the remnants to him.
With palms joined in reverence, the beautiful woman stood by the side of the king.
Seeing her, who had attained youth, was pure, and possessed a celestial form,
the king consulted with his ministers and spoke for the sake of recollection.
"The time for her bestowal has arrived; therefore, let someone choose her.
Having reflected, I shall look for a suitor equal to that high-souled one, so that she may not have to be spoken of as having been obtained from the gods and others; act accordingly."
"O daughter, being enlightened by me regarding the treatises on Dharma, go to him.
For that maiden who, remaining uninitiated, beholds her menses in her father's house, there the sin of killing a Brahmin falls upon the father; such a maiden is declared to be a *vṛṣalī*."
"Therefore, my daughter, send for him; hold a *svayaṃvara*.
Accompanied by your aged ministers, go quickly and bring him here.
"So be it," said Sāvitrī, and having spoken thus, she departed from his presence.
She went to the delightful penance groves of the royal sages;
there she performed the ritual foot-washing for the venerable elders,
and then visited all the sacred fords and hermitages.
Sāvitrī returned home with her ministers;
there she saw the celestial sage Nārada seated on a throne before her father. Having bowed to the brahmin, she spoke with a smile.
She related all of that exactly as it had occurred in the forest.
Sāvitrī said:
"Among the Śālvas there was a righteous-souled Kṣatriya, a lord of the earth."
He who was known as Dyumatsena was formerly Devadatta.
Nārada said:
"Alas! O King, a great hardship has been undertaken by Sāvitrī."
Because of her childhood nature, she did not make King Satyavat true to his name;
yet his father speaks the truth and his mother speaks the truth:
the powerful son of Dyumatsena is endowed with all virtues.
"He has but one fault and no other: from this day forward he shall speak only the truth;
in one year, his life-span being exhausted, he will cast off his body.
Having heard Nārada's words, the king spoke to his daughter:
"Daughter Sāvitrī, go now and choose another as your husband;
he will give up his life after one year because of his short lifespan.
Sāvitrī said:
Kings speak but once; the wise speak but once;
a daughter is given in marriage but once—these three things happen only once.
Whether he be long-lived or short-lived, virtuous or even devoid of merit.
"My husband has been chosen by me once; I shall not choose a second.
Having made this resolution with my mind, it is then expressed by speech, and afterwards acted upon through deed; my mind is always my authority."
Nārada said:
"If this is desired for your daughter, then let it be performed quickly;
may there be no obstacle at the outset in the giving away of your daughter Sāvitrī."

Having spoken thus, Nārada flew up and departed for the celestial realm. Then the king performed all the marriage rites for his daughter at an auspicious moment, with Brahmins well-versed in the Vedas standing by his side.
Having obtained the boon of her heart’s desire— a husband— Sāvitrī too,
that slender-limbed woman, rejoiced exceedingly, like a doer of meritorious deeds who has attained heaven.
Thus they dwelt in that hermitage with mutual affection.
O Bhārata, as Sāvitrī remained performing austerities day and night, a certain period of time passed; meanwhile,
the words spoken by Nārada remained fixed in her mind.
Then, after a long time had passed,
one day that beautiful woman, reflecting that her time had come and she would die,
[prepared herself] at the beginning of the night on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Proṣṭhapada.

Keeping the words spoken by Nārada in her heart, Sāvitrī observed a three-night vow, remaining apart from him day and night. Then, having completed those three nights and bathed, she offered libations to the deities.
Thinking, "I must die on the fourth day," the beautiful-smiling lady prostrated at the feet of her mother-in-law and father-in-law. Then Satyavān set out for the forest, taking his axe.
Sāvitrī also followed behind her husband as he went.
Then her husband said to her, "Inquire after the welfare of your own parents-in-law.
Saying "So be it," she bowed at the feet of her mother-in-law and inquired after them.
And her parents-in-law said, "O sinless one, you must not go!
O child, you are extremely timid; how will you go to the forest?
With great earnestness, she replied, "The forest must be seen by me."
Then her two fathers-in-law said to that sweet-smiling woman, "Go!
Thereupon, quickly gathering fruits, flowers, sacrificial fuel, and kusha grass,
she collected them as if they were dry wood and prepared a load of firewood.
Then, as he was splitting the wood, a pain arose in his head. "O young woman, O beautiful one, this agony afflicts me; I wish to sleep.
"Rest, O mighty-armed one," the sorrowful Sāvitrī replied.
"Afterwards I shall go to my own hermitage, which destroys all fatigue.
While he was sitting on the ground with his head resting upon her lap,
Sāvitrī beheld a man who was dark-brown in complexion.
To him, who wore a crown and yellow garments and appeared like the sun itself risen, Sāvitrī then bowed and spoke to that honey-tawny one:
"Who are you? Are you a god or a daitya who has come to overpower me?"
"And I cannot be displaced from my own duty by anyone,
O best of men, nor can I be touched, just like a blazing crest of fire.
Yama said:
"I am Yama, the Restrainer, who strikes fear into all the worlds.
O devoted wife, this husband of yours has reached the end of his lifespan; I am leading him away.
He could not have been led by my servants, which is why I have come here in person."
Having spoken thus, Yama forcibly extracted from the body of Satyavat a person the size of a thumb by means of his coils of nooses;
then he began to travel along the path frequented by the ancestors.
Sāvitrī, the lady of beautiful limbs, followed behind him.
Then Yama spoke to that devoted wife who was thus exhausted:
"Turn back, Sāvitrī, go to your own home; you have come far enough here."
"O large-eyed lady, this path is not followed by anyone.
Sāvitrī said:
"Neither fatigue nor exhaustion ever arises within me."
For those women who follow their husbands, there is no fatigue or other such suffering. For the virtuous, there is no other refuge; for women, the husband is always the refuge.
The Veda is the refuge of the social classes and stages of life, and the teacher is the refuge of disciples.
