"The surface of the earth is the dwelling place for all living beings;
for human women, the husband alone is their refuge, and there is no other.
With these and various other words consistent with dharma and artha,"
The son of the Sun was pleased and said this to Sāvitrī:
"I am gratified with you; may prosperity be yours! Choose a boon, O beautiful lady.
Sāvitrī, her face bowed low in modesty, chose her boons.
The recovery of his sight, as well as the kingdom of his high-souled father-in-law,
a hundred sons for his father, a hundred sons for himself,
the life of her husband, and eternal perfection in dharma.
Having granted the boons, Dharmarāja then sent her away. Then Sāvitrī, having rejoined her husband with a joyful heart, went to the hermitage together with him, free from all anxiety.
"O King, since this vow was observed on the full moon day of the month of Bhādrapada,
its entire majesty has been recounted by me.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:"
O Lord, what was that vow which Sāvitrī performed? What kind of prepared food did she consume during that month of Bhādrapada?
O Master, tell me according to my desire: who was the presiding deity in that vow?
"O Hṛṣīkeśa, speak in detail of the eternal dharma.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"Listen with reverence, O best of the Pāṇḍavas, to the Sāvitrī vow."
O Yudhiṣṭhira, how did that virtuous woman perform it?
O Bhārata, on the thirteenth day of the month of Bhādrapada, preceded by the cleansing of the teeth, a three-night vow of fasting should be observed.
If, however, he is unable [to fast], one who has conquered his senses should take a single meal at night on the thirteenth day;
on the fourteenth day, he should eat food obtained by begging, and complete the full moon day with a fast.
He should bathe daily in a great river, a pond, or a mountain spring.

There is a special distinction regarding the full moon day: one should bathe with mustard seeds, clay, and water. Having taken a measure (prastha) of sesame seeds in a vessel, O Yudhiṣṭhira, or else having taken grain such as barley, rice, sesame, and so forth.
Then,
having fashioned an image of Sāvitrī, beautiful in all her limbs—
either made of gold, clay, or silver according to one's means— one should wrap it in a pair of cloths within a vessel made of bamboo.
One should likewise offer a pair of red garments to Sāvitrī and to Brahmā;
thus, one should worship Sāvitrī together with Brahmā with devotion,
using perfumes, fragrant flowers, incense, food offerings, and lamps.
With full *kośātaka* gourds, edible *kūṣmāṇḍa* pumpkins, and *karkaṭī* cucumbers;
with coconuts, dates, *kapistha* fruits, and pomegranates;
as well as with *jambū*, *jambīra*, oranges, *karkaṭa* fruits, and jackfruits.
With cumin, pieces of ginger, jaggery, and salt;
with sprouted grains of the seven types of grain arranged in bamboo vessels;
and with auspicious saffron filaments worn as necklaces by noble women.
Sāvitrī, who is thus the one who brings [the soul] down, is dear to Brahmā;
a Brāhmaṇa himself should worship that Sāvitrī with her mantra.
For others, the mantra mentioned here is that which is declared in the Purāṇas.

"O Goddess, preceded by the syllable Oṃ, who hold the lute and the book, Mother of the Vedas, salutations to you; grant me freedom from widowhood. Having worshipped her in this manner according to the prescribed rite, one should then observe a vigil.
One should pass the night with the sounds of singing and instrumental music, accompanied by groups of eight female dancers, with dances and laughter, and with stories told behind one's back;
or else, one should have the best of the twice-born recite the narrative of Sāvitrī.
He should continue with song, accompanied by the aesthetic flavors of emotion, until the time of dawn.
Then, when the pure hour of dawn has arrived at morning,
he should offer the Sāvitrī to a Brāhmaṇa who is learned in the Vedas.

O son of Kuntī, having prostrated according to the prescribed rite with this mantra before one who knows the Sāvitra-kalpa, one who recites the narrative of Sāvitrī, an astrologer, one who subsists by gleaning, a poor man, or an Agnihotrī— |||
Facing the eastern direction, mixed with *darbha* grass, unbroken rice, and sesame seeds,
the wise and excellent brahmin, O brahmin, preceded by the syllable *oṃ* and the word "svasti," [should say]:
"This great, virtuous Sāvitrī is given by me along with gold."
"For the sake of pleasing Brahmā, O Brāhmaṇa, please accept this.
Having thus given [the image] to that best of twice-borns, O Yudhiṣṭhira, one should lead Sāvitrī,
along with all the offerings such as the *naivedya*, to the Brāhmaṇa’s own home.
He himself should walk ten paces and then re-enter his own house;
having there eaten sacrificial food (haviṣya) together with Brahmins and kinsmen,
he should then dismiss the Brahmins with the words, "May Sāvitrī be pleased."
Likewise, on the fifteenth day of the month of Jyeṣṭha, a great chaste woman,
having fasted for three nights,
should worship Vaṭaka according to this rite together with Satyavat, offering fruits, food-oblations, and lamps.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, having made a silk cloth his support for carrying a load of wood,
and having kept a vigil at night preceded by dance and song,
that best of men should, at dawn, perform the rites according to the previously mentioned procedure.
One should give all of that to a Brāhmaṇa, prostrating and asking for his forgiveness.
Thus has this vow been described by me to you according to the rules;
those who shall practice it in this world, accompanied by their sons and grandsons, [shall attain the highest state].
Having enjoyed pleasures on earth for a long time, they shall go to the abode of Brahmā.
This merit-bestowing, sin-destroying, auspicious rite, which destroys evil dreams,
belongs to those who recite or listen to the Sāvitrī-vrata with devotion.
Having observed a fast for three nights, she should worship here the Mother of the Vedas and Smṛtis together with Śambhu’s consort;
like Sāvitrī, she shall deliver her father’s lineage as well as her own husband, and she shall enjoy happiness for a long time through the grace of the Lord.

Thus ends the one hundred and second chapter, titled "The Description of the Vaṭasāvitrī Vow," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
The Description of the Kārttika-Kṛttikā Vow.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Formerly, in the Kṛta Yuga, there was a Kṣatriya woman who had many sons.
Named Kaliṅgabhadra, she was endowed with beauty and charm;
possessing full breasts and lotus-like eyes, her gait was like that of a swan or a lordly elephant.
She was perfect in the qualities of auspiciousness, with a face resembling the orb of the moon.
In the region of Vṛṣasthala in the Middle Country, there was a city completely filled with wealth and jewels;
there dwelt that queen, the wife of the high-souled King Dilīpa,
the noble Kaliṅgabhadrā, who was graceful and endowed with great virtues.
Considering it a great favor,
the great virtuous woman bestowed gifts upon the Brahmins with great respect;
in terms of renunciation, enjoyment, and good fortune, no second person was ever her equal.
O best of men, just as was the manner of Dilīpa, so too for women;
having reflected in her mind upon this vow undertaken in the month of Kārttika, she observed it for the duration of six months.
She has completed almost everything, yet a mere fraction remains;
whether it be at the conclusion of one fast or another, O best of the twice-born who knows the Purāṇas,
that beautiful woman passes her time while preparing for the final concluding rite (udyāpana).
Once, while sleeping with her husband at midnight,
she was bitten by a fierce serpent and perished in an instant.
Due to that fault, the young woman was born from the womb of a goat.
A forest-dweller devoted to dharma, firm and remembering her former births,
she had undertaken the Kṛttikā vow through that very same previous practice;
separated from her herd and wandering alone, she remained steadfast in her fast.
While wandering into another's field, the goat trampled the grain;
on the full moon day of Kārttika, she was tied by the neck by a village boy and remained there for a long time.
That illustrious woman was seen by Atri, who remembered his former birth.
Having understood the cause and having realized that [truth] together with Kālindī and Bhadrā,
that virtuous woman— who was devoted to perseverance— was liberated from her bondage by the cowherds while she was performing the Kṛttikā vow, though she remained bound by jujube fruits.
Having reached the Badarī leaf and drunk the water of the Puṣkariṇī pond, she,
saying "This is mine," remained undisturbed and completed that vow.
Then, having bestowed Yoga upon her, Atri departed for the penance grove.
She too, having become a mistress of yoga and having censured her own birth,
abandoned her life-breaths through yoga and departed; for she became the daughter of the sage Gautama, Ahalyā, beautiful as the womb [of her conception].
Known by the name Yogalakṣmī, that maiden, endowed with a multitude of virtues,
was given by her father like a sacred lore to the great seer Śāṇḍilya;
she shone as his constant companion to him, whose wealth was austerity and who was ever self-controlled.
Radiant with the splendor of Brahman, she was like the personified Veda and Smṛti;
she was like Sarasvatī, Svāhā, Śacī, and Arundhatī;
likewise she was Gaurī, Rājñī, Lakṣmī, and the supreme and virtuous Gāyatrī.
Likewise, O King, Mahālakṣmī shone in the house of Śāṇḍilya,
constantly devoted to the service of the ancestors, the gods, and human beings. Then, Atri saw her in his house once again, pregnant with child.
Offering alms with devotion to the blameless Brahmins,
she was addressed by the Blessed One, who had recognized her through his yogic power, as before, in a gentle voice:
"O Yogalakṣmī, O highly fortunate one, how many Kṛttikās are there?"
That great virtuous woman, remembering her past lives, spoke to the Blessed One:
"O Great Yogin, six [of us] remain, while one is under the control of another.
Hearing that, the Blessed One, with a heart full of compassion, addressed her.
The vow was granted and likewise the mantra, by which she went to heaven;
having enjoyed pleasures here for a long time, surrounded by the prosperity of sons and grandsons,
she then attained that state from which a return is difficult to find.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, Janārdana, what is that vow like, and what is the mantra?
Tell me the procedure for the Kṛttikās and the proper time for it."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: When the Moon itself is in the constellation Kṛttikā, and Bṛhaspati is also in Kṛttikā on a Monday, that is remembered as Mahākārtikī.
Such an occasion is obtained only after many years and through great merit;
therefore, if one desires one's own welfare, it should not be spent in vain.
O Pārtha, even another Kārttikī should be observed with fasting according to the prescribed rules.
O Indra among kings, listen with a one-pointed mind to its procedure:
on the full moon day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, at the break of dawn,
one should undertake the vow for the night-meal (nakta), preceded by the cleansing of the teeth.
Or, according to one's ability, having observed a fast and then bathed in a body of water at Kurukṣetra, Prayāga, Puṣkara, or Naimiṣa,
as well as at Śālagrāma, Kuśāvarta, Mūlasthāna, or Sakuntala;
Whether at Gokarṇa or the holy Arbuda, or likewise at Amarakaṇṭaka;
in a city or a town, or even in a village, a cowherd settlement, or a port-city;
wherever it may be, a man or even a woman should bathe there.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, having performed the worship of the gods, sages, and ancestors, and having offered the oblation (homa),
then when the time for sunset has arrived, one should prepare a vessel completely filled with cow’s ghee or milk, and provided with jaggery and fruit.
Just as one would place the constellation Kṛttikā and the cart [of Rohiṇī] in the sky with six measurements,
O son of Pāṇḍu, one should fashion the six images of the Kṛttikās out of gold and silver, filled with jewels, according to one's own capacity.
The first was made of gold, the second of silver;
the third was fashioned from jewels, and the fourth from fresh butter.
The fifth was slightly smaller than a *kaṇikā*, and the sixth was made of flour.
The six Kṛttikās, having fashioned their forms, were adorned with threads of lac;
they contained jewels within, were smeared with saffron, possessed clusters of flowers at their backs,
were anointed with vermilion and sandalwood paste, and were well-honored with jasmine blossoms.
O King of kings, one should present [the gift] to a twice-born man with this mantra:

"Oṃ! These wives of the Seven Sages, who are the beloveds of Agni and are protected by Brahmā, being the Mothers of Kumāra according to their true nature—may they be satisfied and likewise most highly pleased with me; Svāhā!"
Having spoken thus, O King, the Kṛttikās should be given to the Brahmin;
and the Brahmin, O Pāṇḍava, should accept them with this mantra:
"May these Mothers of the Nakṣatra be givers of dharma and fulfillers of desires."
"May the Kṛttikās deliver our lineage from the difficult cycle of existence.
Having given [the gift] according to this rite and having beheld them stationed in the sky,
one should dismiss the Brāhmaṇas with devotion and follow them for six steps.
Having turned back from worldly discourse, one should listen [to this teaching] and obtain its fruit:
having traveled to the circle of the stars by means of a sun-colored celestial chariot,
one shall be endowed with a divine body, adorned with garlands and sandalwood paste.
Surrounded by hosts of celestial women, he indeed enjoys bliss free from all affliction;
fanned by yak-tail whisks, he shines resplendent with rows of jewels,
and is graced by the radiant splendor of *pārijātaka* and *mandāra* flowers.
Having accomplished her purpose, she remains with her desires fulfilled until the dissolution of all beings;
or, having performed the stars at the conclusion of her vow, that virtuous woman goes to heaven with her husband and rejoices fearlessly, endowed with every enjoyment.
O Pārtha, whether it be a woman or a man, whoever listens to this with devotion and concentration is liberated from all sins.
Having fashioned the six Kṛttikās out of gold, silver, gems, cow-butter, and flour mixed with sesame seeds, [one should worship them].
Having placed [the offerings] in a vessel and worshipped with flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), incense, and lamps, mortals do not enter the thicket of rebirth.

Thus ends the one hundred and third chapter, titled "The Description of the Kṛttikā Vow on the Full Moon of Kārttika," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[Now follows] the description of the Pūrṇamanoratha Vow.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O best of men, on the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Phālguna, [one should avoid] heretics,
the fallen, and likewise those of the lowest castes.
One should never converse with atheists, those of broken conduct, or sinners;
for a man whose mind is fixed on Nārāyaṇa has indeed conquered his senses,
whether he is standing, walking, stumbling, or even eating, he remains focused on Janārdana.
And at the time of performing the rite, O Lord of the Earth, one should recite [the mantra] seven times;
one should worship Janārdana, the Lord endowed with Lakṣmī,
as well as Hari, the Supreme Lord, who is the very form of the moon at the conclusion of the twilight prayers.
And at night, having meditated upon Lakṣmī, one should worship her properly with the arghya offering:
"O Vāsudeva, Lord of the World, you who are the very form of the moon, O God, fulfill my heart's desire; obeisance, obeisance!"
Having offered the *arghya* to the God of gods with devotion using this mantra,
one should eat at night, not at will, avoiding oil and alkaline substances.
It is the same in the months of Caitra, Vaiśākha, and Jyeṣṭha, O best of kings.
And one should worship as prescribed on that day month after month;
O Pārtha, one breaking-fast (pāraṇa) should be performed according to one's ability. O best of men, I shall now describe to you the second breaking-fast as well.
When the months of Āṣāḍha, Śrāvaṇa, Bhādrapada, and likewise Āśvayuja have arrived,
one should worship Śrīdhara together with his beloved;
then, having offered the water of honor (arghya) to the Moon, one should eat according to the prescribed rite.

This second [rite] has been declared; now hear the third, the breaking of the fast. Having likewise worshipped Keśava during the months beginning with Kārttika, one should offer [the gift] together with prosperity to the Moon at night.
And one should eat as prescribed; now hear about the third breaking of the fast.
Having honored them, one should then give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the Brāhmaṇas.
I shall also describe the monthly consumption for the purification of the body.
For the first four months, the consumption of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) is prescribed;
likewise, for another four months, water infused with kuśa grass is enjoined.
Similarly, water heated by the rays of the sun is declared to be a purifier of the body.

One should cause songs, instrumental music, and so forth, as well as auspicious narrations of Kṛṣṇa, to be performed at night. When the fast is concluded, one should first worship Janārdana together with his consort.
Likewise, in the third month, Saśrīka and Śrīdhara; and in the fourth, Bhūti and Keśava.
These, O Bhārata, are the names of Kṛṣṇa for each month.
Having observed a fast and bathed well, one should worship Janārdana.
Uttering this, a man proceeds according to his destination and according to his happiness.
Thereafter, he should indeed give to a Brahmin a water-pot along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),
as well as a pair of sandals, a pair of garments, an umbrella, and gold.
Whatever month it may be, one should indeed proclaim, "May [the Lord] named after this month be pleased.
Thus, one should worship Keśava in Mārgaśīrṣa, Nārāyaṇa in Pauṣa,
Mādhava in the month of Māgha, and Govinda in Phālguna.
Likewise, one should worship Viṣṇu in the month of Caitra, Madhusūdana in Vaiśākha;
Trivikrama is to be known in Jyeṣṭha, and Vāmana in Āṣāḍha;
similarly, Śrīdhara in Śrāvaṇa, and Hṛṣīkeśa in the following month.
Rāma is praised in the month of Bhādrapada by those desiring merit;
Padmanābha in Āśvayuja, and thereafter Dāmodara. By praising the Lord of the gods in Kārtika, one overcomes misfortune.

Thus, at the end of each month throughout the year, as prescribed in due order, if one is unable to give [the gift], one should indeed give it all at once. Furthermore, a special rule is stated here: having fashioned a golden image of the Moon.
Having worshipped with fruits and garments, one should present them to a Brāhmaṇa;
praising Him according to this procedure, one should worship the Lord at the breaking of the fast.
For as many lifetimes as there are [offerings], one does not experience the unhappiness born of separation from beloved ones.
Having attained composure right here, and then recollection at the time of death,
one reaches my abode and is glorified in the heavenly world;
thereafter, having regained human birth, one becomes free from distress and devoid of fever.
Birth in a prosperous family of virtuous lineage, abounding in wealth and grain, is well-deserved.

O King, those who offer an *argha* on this full-moon day of the month of Śrīśarvarī (Kārttika)—mixed with sandalwood paste, sesame seeds, unbroken rice, and flowers—certainly become ones whose desires are completely fulfilled. Alas, even the Lord Moon himself [is born] in that honey-like month!

Thus ends the one hundred and fourth chapter, titled "The Vow for the Fulfillment of Desires," in the *Uttara-parvan* of the glorious *Śrīmad Bhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira;
followed by the description of the "Viśoka-Pūrṇimā" vow. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Now hear from me as I speak of another, the Aśoka-pūrṇimā,
by fasting on which men never again encounter sorrow.
O best of men, it falls on the full moon day of the bright fortnight of the month of Phālguna.
Having bathed with clay and water, and having applied clay to his head,
the man should then consume a portion of the clay; then,
having fashioned a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) out of clay and worshipped the mountain by its name with flowers and leaves.
One should likewise invoke the goddess Dharaṇī as Aśokā:
"O Dharaṇī, just as Janārdana made you free from sorrow,
so do you release me from all sorrows, O bearer of all."
Just as you are established as the support for all beings,
so grant me freedom from sorrow through the manifestation of all my desires.
O Earth, you know how Viṣṇu attains composure through mere meditation.
"Likewise, O Sustainer of Beings, grant me peace of mind.
Having praised her thus, having worshipped her accordingly, and having offered the *arghya* oblation to the Moon,
one should either observe a fast or eat at night, avoiding oil.
In this very manner, O King, the four months beginning with Phālguna are to be observed as fasts; the first breaking of the fast is prescribed [at the end].
Likewise, in the months beginning with Āṣāḍha, one should perform ablutions with clay and water.

In the same manner, there is the consumption [of the fast], worship, and likewise the honoring of the Moon; and the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) is prescribed for the other four months beginning with Kārttika. Indeed, the Cāturmāsika vow is said to consist of these three instances of breaking the fast.

Special worship, charity, and likewise keeping vigil at night must be performed with particular care during each fast until the breaking of the fast has passed. In the first month, O Earth, [the vow] is named after you for four months.
On the second day, Medinī should be invoked; on the third, Vasundharā.
O Pārtha, at each breaking of the fast, one should worship pairs of twice-born brahmins, as well as the goddess Dharaṇī and the god Keśava, with their respective mantras.
In the absence of cloth, one should likewise worship the Earth with a thread;
in the absence of ghee, milk or water is recommended for Hari.
Thus, at the end of the year, a cow with her calf should be given to a twice-born man.
The goddess Earth, together with garments and ornaments, should be given as a gift;
this great vow was performed by the goddess residing in the netherworld (Pātāla).
Through her devotion to Keśava, Dharaṇī subsequently attained exaltation.
Long ago, the Earth was addressed by the Lord in the form of a boar:
"O auspicious one, you have uplifted me from the netherworld while devoted to the vow of fasting;
I have been fully gratified by this vow of yours."
Therefore, O virtuous lady, I grant you incomparable favor,
since you perform such a beautiful worship for me with devotion;
likewise, O auspicious one, whoever shall bow down to you will receive the same.
Having undertaken this vow and performed the concluding rite (pāraṇa) according to the rules,
one shall be liberated from all afflictions even throughout future births;
free from sorrow, he will undoubtedly become a vessel for all auspiciousness.
Just as you yourself, O Earth, have attained the state of ultimate bliss,
so too shall that man obtain supreme happiness in the world beyond.
Thus is this [act] of great merit, which grants the pacification of all sins.
Perform that supreme vow known as Viśoka, a great observance.
O King of fame equal to Manu and Mahendra, I have fully explained to you the Pūrṇimā which brings about the end of sorrow.
O bull among the Kurus, for that man who performs this with diligence, no grief shall arise even within his lineage.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifth chapter, titled "The Vow of Viśoka-Pūrṇimā," in the Uttara Parva of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira;
followed by the description of the Ananta-vrata. Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Having propitiated Janārdana through many various means, one obtains all desires, whatever else one may wish for in one's heart, O Kṛṣṇa;
for all men and women alike, there is no other cause of sorrow.
Indeed, in this life, nothing exists that is superior to offspring.
Childlessness is a great sorrow, and having a wicked son is an even greater sorrow;
in my view, a virtuous son is the cause of all happiness.
Blessed are those who have obtained a son who is free from all suffering,
capable, tranquil, strong, and who has attained supreme peace;
one who is constantly devoted to his own duty and dedicated to the gods and the twice-born.
One who knows the scriptures, who knows all dharmas, who has compassion for the poor and the helpless,
who has completely conquered the wealth of all enemies, who delights the minds and hearts [of others],
who is endowed with favor from the gods, and who is possessed of perfect virtue.
"O high-minded one, there is no one on earth more fortunate than that son who attains supreme Nirvana through the honor bestowed by friends and kinsmen;
such as I am, I desire to hear about such a deed."
"By what means is such a son obtained by men on earth?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O highly fortunate one, it is exactly so; this concerns the birth of sons and the absence of sons."
Suffering does not come to an end here by any means other than through a son.
In this regard also, O Sage, hear the account of what occurred in the past at the birth of the high-souled Kārtavīrya of the Haihaya lineage.
In ancient times, there was a protector of the earth named Kṛtavīrya of the Haihaya lineage.
He had a wife of excellent complexion named Śīladhanā,
who was the foremost among his thousands of wives and whose ornament was her virtuous character.
Being childless, that illustrious lady questioned Maitreyī,
who had taken her seat for the sake of obtaining a virtuous son;
then, being thus properly questioned by her, Maitreyī, the expounder of Brahman, replied.
The ascetic woman spoke of the supreme and great vow known as Ananta,
which is the cause for attaining the fruits of all desires and the destroyer of sins,
for the sake of that princess obtaining a virtuous son.
Maitreyī said:
Whatever desire a man or a woman of excellent complexion may wish for,
by propitiating that omnipresent Lord Janārdana, they obtain it from him.
On that day in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa when the constellation Mṛgaśiras and the day of Bhīma (the fourteenth) coincide,
one should drink cow’s urine after bathing with a restrained mind,
and then worship with devotion using flowers, incense, perfumes, and fasting.
O lady of excellent complexion, one should worship the left foot of Ananta.
May the Lord Ananta grant the fulfillment of all desires and bestow infinite fruit, both now and again in another birth.

"O Supreme Person, perform for me this great vow, which is infinite and an accumulation of endless merit, so that I may obtain my heart's desire. Having spoken thus and having worshipped Him according to the prescribed rule, the man—
Having become composed in mind, one should first prostrate and give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brahmin, uttering the words, "May Ananta be pleased.
Then, at night, one should eat a meal free from oil.
Then, in the month of Pauṣa, under the Puṣya asterism, one should likewise worship the Blessed One’s left hip with devotion; thereafter, one should consume cow’s urine and further recite:
"Ananta [is the fulfiller] of all desires."
Likewise, one should feed the Brahmins and have them recite blessings according to the prescribed rite;
and during Maghā in the month of Māgha, one should worship the arm of the God.
And during the two Phālgunī constellations in the month of Phālguna, O beautiful lady, one should worship my shoulders.
O daughter of a king, one should cause these four to consume cow’s urine;
likewise, one should give sesame seeds and gold to a Brāhmaṇa.
In the month of Caitra, under the Citrā constellation, one should worship the right shoulder of the God.
In that same manner, the consumption of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) is prescribed here;
one should give barley for four months to a Brahmin who acts as the reciter.
And in the month of Vaiśākha, under the Viśākhā asterism, having worshipped the right arm—

In the same manner, one should offer other [offerings] and perform the act of eating at night. During the month of Jyeṣṭha, O observer of auspicious vows, one should perform the worship of the hips under the Jyeṣṭhā asterism;
likewise, during the month of Āṣāḍha, O auspicious lady, one should perform the worship of the feet under the Āṣāḍhā asterism.
One should worship the two feet during the month of Śrāvaṇa;
ghee should be given to a Brahmin and consumed according to the prescribed rite.
During the months beginning with Śrāvaṇa, there is both the consumption [of the offering] and the giving [of it].
This has thus been fully explained; one should likewise worship the deities.
One should worship Guhya during the conjunction with Proṣṭhapadā in the month of Bhādrapada.
Similarly, Hṛdaya is to be worshipped during the conjunction with Aśvinī in the month of Āśvayuja.
With a concentrated mind, one should perform the bath, the ritual sipping of water,

and the worship on the day of the Kṛttikā constellation during the month of Kārttika; and on whichever specific day the worship occurs, it should be performed on that very day for the sake of Anantaśiras.
The name of Ananta should be recited when one has sneezed, stumbled, or committed other such lapses.
O delighter of the family, for the first four months beginning with Caitra, one should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) with ghee and śāli rice, dedicating it to Ananta.
In the months of Śrāvaṇa and the others, the oblation should be performed with milk for four months;
feeding on sacrificial food (haviṣya) is recommended in all months.
Thus, O auspicious lady, there are three breaking-fasts (pāraṇā) over the course of twelve months.
At the conclusion of the vow, one should have an auspicious, infinite golden image made;
one should also place a silver pestle and a plough at its sides.
Worship should be performed according to the prescribed rules with flowers, incense, and other offerings, including food oblations.
Upon the copper seat, one should worship with these mantras of Hari in their proper order:
"Salutation to Ananta" for the head; "Salutation to the Soul of All" for the feet;
"Salutation to Śeṣa" for the pair of knees; and "Salutation to Kāma" for the waist.
Homage be to Vāsudeva;

one should worship the side of Hari with "To Saṃkarṣaṇa," the belly with "To the Sustainer of All Life-Force (Prāṇa)," the neck with "To the Lord Śrīkaṇṭha," and the face with "To the Moon-Faced One."
The wise man should worship the plow and the pestle by their own names;
having thus worshipped Govinda, adorned with white garments,
provided with an umbrella and sandals, and likewise decorated with garlands and wreaths.
The deities of the lunar mansions and the lunar mansions themselves should be worshipped in every respect,
as well as Soma, the king of the lunar mansions, the month, and likewise the year.
Here, one should prepare twelve jars filled with water and provided with food.
Having thus worshipped Janārdana, the God of gods, according to the prescribed rites,
and having honored a Brāhmaṇa with garments and ornaments— who is peaceful, self-controlled, and has conquered his senses— with sacred ear-rings and finger-rings;
To one who knows the Purāṇas, who is constant in dharma, free from physical defects, and speaks pleasantly—
to him all this should be given with the thought, "May Ananta be pleased by this.
To other Brāhmaṇas as well, gifts should be given according to one's ability and as desired.
By this method, O Pārtha, this vow is completed;
and when it is fulfilled, one attains all one's heart's desires—
those seeking sons, those desiring wealth, and those longing for servants and wives.
O highly fortunate lady, those who desire health, fruits,
and prosperity in this mortal world [should observe] this meritorious vow which bestows well-being;
it is indeed known as the Ananta-vrata, the destroyer of all sins.
"Therefore, O Goddess Śīladhanā, if you desire a son, perform that supreme and most excellent vow which is honored by all the world. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Having heard these auspicious words of Maitreyī, Śīladhanā,
with her mind fixed upon Viṣṇu, undertook this excellent vow. O observer of noble vows, for her who desired a son, by means of this vow—
Viṣṇu was pleased, and when Viṣṇu was satisfied, she gave birth to a son. As soon as he was born, a pure breeze blew; the sky became free of dust, and the entire world attained joy.
The celestial drums resounded and a rain of flowers fell;
the gods and gandharvas sang, and the hosts of apsaras danced. O Pārtha, the minds of all people in the world became fixed upon righteousness.
His father gave his son the name Arjuna;
and because he was the son of Kṛtavīrya, he became known as Kārtavīrya.
By him also, the Blessed Viṣṇu, appearing in the form of Dattātreya, [was worshipped].
O Pārtha, the Lord of the World was propitiated by that king through exceedingly great austerity;
being pleased with him, he bestowed upon him supreme sovereignty as a universal monarch (cakravartin), as well as wealth in the form of heroism and all his divine weapons.
And he chose this boon: "O God, let my death come from you.
Furthermore, [he requested] supreme remembrance and knowledge that destroys the suffering of those who are afraid;
O Lord of the World, may there be the quality of benefiting this world through such remembrance.
The Lord of the Gods, whose eyes resemble lotuses, said to him:
"O highly fortunate one, all this shall happen for you once again;
and whatever man shall glorify you both at dawn and at night."

And whoever shall utter the words, "Homage be to Kārtavīrya," that person shall obtain the merit of giving a prastha of sesame seeds; furthermore, by the chanting of your name, there shall be no loss of one's wealth.
Having said, "He shall become a protector of the earth," Hari departed from him;
and that king, having obtained the boon from the gracious Garuḍa-bannered Lord,
ruled over the earth with its seven continents.
By him various sacrifices were performed with excellent sacrificial fees;
having conquered the entire host of enemies, the subjects were protected according to dharma;
and by the greatness of the Ananta-vrata, he obtained that son.
O Lord, there was not even the slightest suffering for the father arising from the birth of his son.
Thus has this vow called Ananta been described to you,
by performing which that queen gave birth to Kārtavīrya.
Any person, whether man or woman, who hears this account of the birth of Kārtavīrya shall not experience suffering arising from offspring for seven lifetimes;
they shall instead attain unimpeded sovereignty, supreme discernment, and many sons who cause distress to the hearts of their enemies.
"By performing this vow, one obtains the name 'Ananta' through the grace of the All-pervading Lord, whose own glory is infinite.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ananta-vrata," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira. [Now follows] the description of the Sāṃbarāyaṇī-vrata.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:

O best of men, men do not suffer such pain from the non-attainment of sovereignty and other such things as they do from their own various desires; indeed, these bring about manifold suffering for human beings.
Just as men would have no fear of suffering if their desires were fulfilled,
so too one who has fallen from sovereignty, from his lineage, from the world of the gods,
or from any other desired state, finds atonement for his sin [through this].
Whether it be a man or a woman, by the accumulation of merit one attains [this state]. Tell me that, O Blessed One, by which one does not undergo a fall.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O illustrious one, it is true that he who is intent upon the rise of power and the happiness of his circle of kinsmen undoubtedly encounters suffering. Therefore,
O Pārtha, listen to how one may avoid falling away from what is desired."

O King of kings, for virtuous people who observe fasts correctly, heaven and other rewards arise; O monarch, one should duly worship Acyuta during those twelve lunar mansions that occur each month, using the names corresponding to them.
O best of kings, beginning with the month of Kārttika and starting from the constellation Kṛttikā, one should worship with flowers, incense, water, and other desired offerings;
during the first four months, the food offering (naivedya) here should consist of kṛśara.
Thereafter, one should offer saṃyāva (flour-cakes) starting from the month of Phālguna;
from Āṣāḍha onwards, one should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) to the God.
With that very food, O King of kings, the wise man should feed the Brāhmaṇas.
One becomes pure by bathing in water mixed with the five products of the cow and by consuming that same mixture.
O King of kings, having properly worshipped that very Puruṣottama and having bowed down,
one who is purified and has bathed according to the rules should pray to Viṣṇu.
Salutations, salutations to you, O Acyuta! May my sin be destroyed and may my merit reach full increase.

Likewise, may my sovereignty, wealth, and so forth be inexhaustible, and may my progeny never come to an end. Just as you, O Acyuta, are beyond the beyond, having become Brahman, the Supreme Self beyond the supreme; [so may I be].
O Acyuta, make my desire fulfilled; O Immeasurable One, likewise take away my sin.
O Acyuta, Ananta, Govinda, be gracious! O Immeasurable Self, O Supreme Person, make that which is desired by me inexhaustible.
Having thus worshipped and likewise prayed for the welfare of Śiva,
one should personally consume the food offering (naivedya) at night once Acyuta has been fully honored.
Then, at the end of the year, when Acyuta has risen from his pleasant sleep—
One should present a copper vessel filled with clarified butter to a Brāhmaṇa;
one should give a sacrificial fee according to one's ability, saying, "May Acyuta be pleased.
Then, at the end of the seventh year, the wise man should perform the concluding rite (udyāpana).
O King, an image of Acyuta should be fashioned out of gold according to one's means;
before it, an elderly Brāhmaṇa woman of the Sāṃbhara lineage should be installed—
a great chaste lady, made of silver, equal in status, and accompanied by her deity.
Then, O King of kings, having worshipped those two with garlands, garments, and unguents, and having prostrated according to the prescribed rule with this mantra,
if one gives a copper vessel to a twice-born man every year;
One should give that very same [gift] with ease, accompanied by gold and a horse;
and having performed worship, one should give cows along with their calves and brass milking vessels.
Or, according to one's capacity, one should give even a single cow with devotion; for thus Keśava is pleased.
Having given jars designated as auspicious vessels, filled with food and radiant with water,
together with an umbrella and a pair of sandals, one should bid them farewell;
likewise, one should give a bed with a cotton mattress and a house equipped with household utensils.

One should worship Viṣṇu together with Śrī and adorn the Lord with garments and ornaments; having prostrated, one should ask for forgiveness. By performing this, O King of kings, a human being does not suffer a fall from his station.
Likewise, through the worship of the months and lunar mansions, a person does not fall away from sovereignty over their lineage, wealth, heaven,
and so forth, nor from whatever else is desired;
therefore, one should strive with every effort in these rites.
One who desires imperishability should always worship Puruṣottama.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
In this regard, a certain perfected woman of great vows is heard of in heaven.
Having become a woman rich in asceticism, she became renowned as Sāṃbharāyaṇī;
for she was the remover of all doubts and a constant dweller in the heavenly realm.
Then, after some time, Śatakratu, the king of the gods, [arrived].
O King, he asked Bṛhaspati this concerning the conduct of the former Indras:
"O best of the Aṅgirases, I desire to hear the history of those lords of the gods who existed before the former Indra."
Thus addressed by that lord of the gods, the supreme rishi Bṛhaspati, the best among the upholders of dharma and possessed of stainless luster, replied:
"O King of the Gods, O Lord of the Suras, I do not know the ancient lords of the gods."
"O Lord of the Gods, know him to be a contemporary of yourself.
Then the King of the Devas asked: "O highly fortunate one, who is this bull among sages who has been questioned by us, and who has made his dwelling here in heaven since the beginning?"
Having reflected for a long time, Bṛhaspati then said to the Lord of Śacī:
"Ask this illustrious ascetic woman, Sāṃbharāyaṇī.
Thus addressed by him, the Lord of the Devas was filled with curiosity.
She went to where the highly fortunate ascetic lady sat properly;
seeing Indra, the king of the gods, and Bṛhaspati approaching together,
that woman of excellent vows honored them duly with the arghya offering and, having prostrated herself, spoke.
Homage be to the King of the Gods, and likewise homage to Aṅgiras! O highly fortunate ones, let whatever task you have be stated here in its entirety;
if it is possible for me to perform, I shall do it after due reflection.
Bṛhaspati said:
"We two have come here to question you, who are so highly discerning. O illustrious lady, tell us what we have asked regarding our task."
"If you indeed remember, O auspicious one, the former deeds of Indra, then tell them, O highly blessed lady, for the curiosity of the Lord of the Gods. Sāṃbharāyaṇī said:
I indeed know all those who were prior to the Lord of the Gods, and he who was the very first among them;
I know him who is even more ancient than that, and him who was the first even before him;
and I know all those who were more ancient than them.
O best of the Agiras, I know their entire conduct,
as well as many Manvantaras and the creations of the inhabitants of heaven;
I know the many Saptarṣis and the kings who were the sons of the Manus.
Having spoken thus, Sāṃbharāyaṇī, greatly delighted,
duly related to them the great former history of Indra:
who he was during the Svāyambhuva Manvantara, and who he was during the Svārociṣa Manvantara.
To Sāṃbharāyaṇī, that ascetic woman then related exactly as it happened the conduct of those who had been the lords of the gods during the Uttama, Tāmasa, Raivata, and Cākṣuṣa Manvantaras.
And he related that marvel, which I shall also tell you:
at that time, the Daitya Śaṅkukarṇa became exceedingly invincible;
having defeated the world-protectors along with the gods in battle, he [prevailed].
Having reached Indra’s palace, he entered it quite fearlessly;
seeing him suddenly arrived, Śakra rolled upon his bed,
and afflicted by the fear of Śaṅkukarṇa, he suddenly sought to protect himself.
The Dānava sat down upon that bed of Śakra;
Indrāṇī, likewise terrified, went to the house of Vācaspati.
Then the gods, out of fear, assembled to see the enemy of the gods.
Seated upon Śakra’s throne, preceded by prostrations,
Vāsudeva also arrived there to see that thorn of the gods.
Seeing Kṛṣṇa had arrived, the Dānava spoke with joy.
"I am blessed, I have fulfilled my purpose, for Keśava, whose banner bears Garuḍa, comes to visit me while I am seated upon the bed of Śakra. Then, taking him by the hand, he led him toward the bed.
Delighted, he embraced his kinsman as if with affection;
then Kṛṣṇa, suddenly seizing him with both arms, slowly but firmly squeezed him while laughing and letting out terrible roars.
That lord of the Dānavas died, his skeletal frame shattered by force.
Then Śakra emerged from the foot of the bed with his head hanging down and praised Hari, who was seated there, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.
"O Śakra, this was seen by me while I was dwelling in the abode of the gods.
Then, filled with curiosity, the king of the gods said to that ascetic woman:
'O Sāṃbharāyaṇī, how do you know these [sages]? "
Sāṃbharāyaṇī said:
"Indeed, all these lords of the gods who dwell in heaven and are the masters of immortality have existed; I know their conduct by that very means."
"I have heard of their conduct and have likewise seen it.
Indra said:
"Tell me, O knower of dharma, what was done by you so that this [merit] is inexhaustible?"
Dwelling in the heavenly world has been attained by him as it could not be by anyone else.
Oh, among all vows, this fast is indeed wonderful;
it is considered the most preeminent and the ultimate bestower of residence in heaven.
Thus addressed by that Lord of the Gods,
the highly fortunate Ambhārāyaṇī, a woman of great austerity, replied appropriately:
"O Lord of the gods, the infallible God indeed dwells month by month within the lunar mansion of each month."
Having been properly worshipped for seven years by her who observed the prescribed vows,
this is the fruition of that deed of mine— the propitiation of Acyuta:
my descent from the desired station of the king of the gods to the world of the gods.

A man desires the sovereignty and majesty of the lord of heaven, as well as progeny and immortality; therefore, the Lord must be propitiated in this manner. Thus, I have related to you the entire account of the former lord of the gods.

O Lord of the Thirty-three, O Ruler of the Gods, as you have asked, I have duly explained to you, O Deva, how the imperishability of one's residence in heaven is attained through the worship of the lunar mansions and the planets; and likewise,
O Sovereign of the Wise, the attainment of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, which are all desired.
"There is no cause for supreme accomplishment other than the propitiation of Viṣṇu.
Having heard those words of hers, Devarāja and Bṛhaspati said to that virtuous woman, "So be it," and they performed that vow as well.
Therefore, O Pārtha, with effort and a concentrated mind, you should always remain intent upon the worship of Acyuta according to the lunar mansion of each month.
Those wise ones who, for seven years, conduct themselves according to the rules in this vow consisting of the narrative and conduct of Sāṃbarāyaṇi—
Having reached their own world and established their residence there, they do not fall even for hundreds of millions of tens of thousands of kalpas.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Sāṃbharāyaṇī Vrata," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[Now begins] the description of the Nakṣatrapuruṣa Vrata.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: O best of the Yadus, by what action is the handsome appearance of men and women produced? You should explain that to me.
O best of the Yadus, some men possess beautiful forms, graceful limbs, and excellent attire;
yet, due to either deficiency or excess, there may be a limb that does not develop properly,
even when all other limbs are beautiful.
Men and women are born one-eyed, hunchbacked, or with severed ears;
tell me first, O stainless one, by what karma such things occur, and how the beauty of all limbs comes to be for both men and women.
O Great-minded One, when beauty is present, gracefulness, speech,

and gait— indeed all supreme qualities combined— produce an exceeding splendor. However, a gait that is merely graceful through the refinement of speech and charm becomes nothing but a mockery for those who are ugly.
"One should strive through action that serves as the cause for form;
therefore, explain to me that beautiful action which bestows beauty.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O King, you have indeed asked this correctly regarding the fast.
I shall relate it to you exactly as it was spoken by the most excellent Great-Souled One—
by the twice-born Vaśiṣṭha, the preeminent among the Seven Sages, as he sat [in meditation]."
When Arundhatī was thus questioned by you, she asked what this was;
and as she questioned him, that best of sages spoke. Listen, O son of Kuntī, to all of this as I relate it to you.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Listen, O woman of excellent complexion, to that which I have been asked by you— namely,
how beauty arises for men and for women alike.
Without having worshipped Govinda and without having propitiated Keśava,
by what other action can qualities such as beauty and the rest be obtained?
Therefore, O illustrious lady, Viṣṇu alone must first be propitiated.
O auspicious lady, he who desires to attain excellence of form, sons, and other blessings in the world beyond,
and who seeks a beautiful form with all limbs lovely, should worship the Nakṣatra-puruṣa while knowing the Dharma, having conquered anger and subdued his senses.
Whether a woman or a man, he who, having bathed well and being restrained in diet, worships Acyuta with devotion, is born with a beautiful body. Indeed,
for a woman desiring supreme beauty, the Lord of the World [is the means].
That very Janārdana, whose body consists of the stars, is the one to be propitiated first.
Arundhatī said:
"The Blessed One, the Supreme Person, is worshipped in the form of the constellations."
"O Sage, you ought to explain to me the procedure by which [this is accomplished].
Vasiṣṭha said:
"Beginning from the month of Caitra, one should perform the worship of Viṣṇu’s feet."
Listen now to the truth of how one should act for the sake of attaining a [divine] form:
having bathed and properly observed a fast, the wise man should worship each individual lunar mansion as a limb of the Nakṣatra-Puruṣa.
One should worship the two feet at the root [of the tree], as well as the shanks under Rohiṇī;
the knees under the conjunction of Aśvinī; the thighs under Āṣāḍhā;
the private parts under the two Phālgunīs; and likewise the hips under Kṛttikā.
One should worship the two sides with Bhādrapadā, the two ankles with the two Pūrvabhādrapadās, and the two flanks with Revatī; the chest with Anurādhā, the back with Dhaniṣṭhā,
the pair of arms with Viśākhā, and the two hands with Hasta.
One should worship the fingers under Punarvasu, likewise the nails under Āśleṣā;
one should worship the neck under Jyeṣṭhā, and likewise the ears under Śravaṇa;
one should worship the face under Puṣya, and the teeth under Svāti.

One should worship the mouth with devotion during the conjunction of Śatabhiṣaj, and the nose during the conjunction of Maghā; one should worship the eyes during the auspicious conjunction of Mṛgaśiras;
the forehead during the conjunction of Citrā, and likewise the head during the conjunction of Bharaṇī.

During the Ārdrā asterism, the hair should be honored by the wise. O auspicious lady, a man who has fasted must diligently avoid bathing preceded by an oil massage; that is declared to be destructive of one's beauty.
One should worship that constellation and the deity of the constellation;
the wise man should honor Soma, the king of constellations, with his own mantras.
Furthermore, in conjunction with each individual constellation, the most excellent of the twice-born should be fed.

One should give a gift according to one's ability to a Brahmin who knows the lunar mansions. If an obstacle arises caused by birth-impurity or ritual defilement, one should fast and wait until another lunar mansion appears, and then proceed with the recitation.

In this manner, at the conclusion of the month of Māgha, the completion of the vow is finalized. When the vow is finished, one should give according to one's capacity a golden image of the Nakṣatrapuruṣa (the Constellation-Man), provided with all its accessories, and worship it there according to one's means.
One should honor both the Brahmin and the Brahmin woman with garments, ornaments, and decorations; they should be seated upon a bed provided with perfumes, garlands, and ointments;
and one should offer the seven types of grain as available, along with a milch cow accompanied by her calf.
One should present an umbrella, a pair of sandals, and likewise a vessel of ghee to a virtuous Brahmin with this mantra:
"Just as no sin whatsoever ever arises for the devotees of Viṣṇu..."
Likewise, may there be for me here in this world beauty, health, happiness, and prosperity,
just as your bed is never empty of Lakṣmī, O Janārdana;
so too, may my bed be never empty in birth after birth.
Having thus reported all of that, one should prostrate and ask for forgiveness.
One who is lacking in means, however, should give a cow together with a vessel of clarified butter.
This rite known as Nakṣatrapuruṣa has been described to you exactly as it is.
It removes the sins of virtuous people who possess right faith;
moreover, O illustrious lady, his limbs and secondary members, beginning with the feet,
are born beautiful in all future births.
May there be auspicious limbs, supreme health of the body,
progeny, joy of the mind, and exceedingly beautiful form;
likewise, sweetness of speech, splendor, and whatever else is desired.
The Person of the Constellation (Nakṣatrapuruṣa) bestows gifts when worshipped, as does Janārdana;
all this has been reported to you exactly as it was told by Vasiṣṭha.
This vow, named Nakṣatrapuruṣa, is the most excellent among all vows.

"O son of Kuntī, those who, having conquered anger and mental fluctuations, worship the beautiful-bodied Puruṣottama by assigning [the limbs] to the heart, arms, knees, eyes, thighs, and hips with their right hands, indeed become possessed of handsome bodies. Thus ends the one hundred and eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Nakṣatra-puruṣa Vrata," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the Vows Named after the Lunar Mansions.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"For one who is unable to fast but still desires the fruit of it at that very time..."
If, due to a lack of practice or because of yoga,
one has devotion toward Śiva rather than the Sun,
tell me: how should that person perform the vow known as Nakṣatra?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
For those who are unable to observe fasts, eating at night (nakta) is prescribed.
Listen now to how even this [eating at night] becomes great and inexhaustible within this vow.
The Śiva-nakṣatra-puruṣa, who bestows devotion to Śiva,
is that conjunction of constellations which those learned in the Purāṇas describe as occurring when the asterism Hasta arises during the bright fortnight of the month of Phālguna.
Then one should undertake the vow and worship Śiva with an offering of food at night.

O Pāṇḍava, during the Citrā constellation, the feet are considered most worthy of worship; the ankles are to be worshipped with the mantra "Śivāyai namaḥ," and the two ankles are to be worshipped with "Namaḥ Śaṅkarāya."
O bull among men, one should worship [the deity] with the mantra "to Bhīma" under the asterism Svātī;
one should worship the two thighs under Viśākhā with the mantra "to the Three-eyed One";
and the genitals under Anurādhā with the mantra "to the Destroyer of the Limbs of Anaṅga."

One should likewise worship the hips with the *Jyeṣṭhā* [mantra] and with "Obeisance to Surajyeṣṭha. The navel of the Wielder of the Trident is to be worshipped with the mantra called "Dāna" and with the *Mūla* [mantra].
The Lord of Pārvatī is indeed to be worshipped on the two sides during the pair of *Pūrvāṣāḍhā* and *Uttarāṣāḍhā*.

O Pārtha, one should worship the two sides with the name *Kukṣi* during the asterism Śravaṇa, and likewise the head with the name *Kapālī*. One should worship the chest with the name *Sadyojāta* during Dhaniṣṭhā,
and the heart with the name *Vāma* during Śatabhiṣā.
In the Pūrvottara-yuga, one should worship the two arms with "Obeisance to the bearer of the Khaṭvāṅga";
likewise, in the Revatī asterism, the two hands are to be worshipped;
and in the Aśvinī conjunction, the nails are to be worshipped with "Obeisance to the bearer of the crescent moon."

Then, on the Bharaṇīs, [one should worship] the back, saying: "Obeisance to you who have the bull as your emblem. Likewise, on the Kṛttikās, [one should worship] the nape of the neck, saying: "To the one clad in animal skin.
In conjunction with Rohiṇī, speech is to be worshipped, saying: "Obeisance to Vācaspati."

O Yudhiṣṭhira, under the asterism Ārdrā, the two lips are to be worshipped with the mantra: "Salutation indeed to Bhairava on the head of the best of deer. Furthermore, under Punarvasu, the nose is to be worshipped with the mantra: "To the destroyer of the teeth of Pūṣan."
Under the asterism Puṣya, the three eyes are to be worshipped with: "Salutations to You, the All-Seeing!

Under Āśleṣā, the forehead is worshipped with: "Repeated salutations to Tryambaka! And under Maghā, the mass of matted hair (jaṭājūṭa) is to be worshipped with: "Salutations to the Destroyer of Andhaka!"

Salutations to the bearer of the moon, who resides in the pair of Pūrvāphālgunī and Śravaṇa; salutations to Śiva, the root cause of the destruction of Gajāsura, Anaṅga, Dhūrjaṭi, Andhaka, and others, who holds the noose, goad, lotus, trident, skull-bowl, serpent, moon, and bow.
One should worship the head [of the deity] and then offer incense and ointment.
Thereafter, one should eat at night, avoiding oil and alkaline substances;
[the meal should consist of] a *prastha* measure of *śāli* rice accompanied by a vessel of clarified butter.
O best of kings, one should give [gifts] to a Brahmin during all *nakta* observances;
there is no fault if one lacks the capacity, and if one gives more, the fruit is greater.
When two lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) coincide, one should perform the pair of *nakta* observances.
If, however, the impurity of birth or death (sūtaka-āśauca) occurs, one should fast again on another day.
When the time for breaking the fast (pāraṇa) arrives in this sequence, as on the Pāṇḍava and other such days,
one should devoutly feed Brāhmaṇas with jaggery, milk, ghee, and other such offerings.
One should have the god Śaṅkara fashioned out of gold together with Umā;
having prepared an auspicious bed, free from discordant knots,
provided with pillows for rest, and covered with beautiful rugs and cloths.

Having placed that deity, endowed with all virtues, upon it— adorned with a vessel, sandals, an umbrella, chowries, a seat, a mirror, ornaments, fruits, garments, and unguents— Please provide the text you would like me to translate. I am ready to assist you.
One should give away a tawny cow, covered with cloth, pure in character, and yielding milk;
one with horns adorned with gold and hooves with silver, accompanied by her calf and a bronze milking vessel,
during the forenoon, using the prescribed mantra, and should not let the proper time pass by.
Just as your bed, O Lord, is never empty of the mountain-born [Pārvatī] in her conduct and her lineage,
so may my spiritual attainments be likewise.
Just as there exists nothing else anywhere, O Lord, that is superior for the sake of the highest good.
"Likewise, lift me up from the entire ocean of saṃsāra, which is full of suffering. Then, having circumambulated [the image] and prostrated,
one should bid it farewell and lead the bed, the cow, and all those other items to the house of a twice-born man.

This vow of the Moon-crested Lord must not be revealed to one who lacks moral conduct, nor to a hypocrite, nor to one corrupted by fallacious reasoning, nor to a slanderer; nor should it be given to one whose inner self is afflicted by greed. It should be bestowed by those devoted to Śiva upon one who is faithful, self-controlled, and endowed with virtuous qualities.

Those who know the Vedas declare that this [rite] brings inexhaustible merit even to men who have committed great sins. Furthermore, a woman who, with supreme devotion, relies upon her husband or upon a virtuous preceptor,
shall suffer no separation from kinsmen, sons, or wealth, nor shall she experience sorrow arising from friends.
This was performed in ancient times by Vasiṣṭha, Arjuna, Kubera, and Indra.
By the mere recitation of this, all sins are destroyed and obstacles do not arise; there is no doubt in this matter.
Whoever thus reads or hears this account of the person of Śiva shall become beloved of Indra.
"Furthermore, he who performs this here leads all his ancestors, even those gone to hell, to the abode of Śiva.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Śivanakṣatrapuruṣa Vrata," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira; herein is the complete description of the vow.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, if one is unable to perform the vow associated with the lunar mansion (nakṣatra) or any other excellent vow that has been rashly undertaken,"
"By means of which that which was previously unpracticed becomes fully accomplished?
Grant me your grace; you ought to tell me this secret matter.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"Excellent, excellent, O mighty-armed Yudhiṣṭhira, King of the Kurus!
I shall tell you the secret of secrets, the most excellent of vows,
known as Sampūrṇa, which bestows its fruit perfectly."

Whatever has been performed by men and women that results in a complete fulfillment [of the vow] must certainly be performed again by those who desire its fruit not to diminish. Even if something has become slightly broken due to negligence, it remains a duty for those established in their vows.
O Pāṇḍava, through this vow all that may have been broken—
whether by various calamities, or out of pride and delusion, O King,
or by Brahmins and Vināyakas— shall become entirely complete.
O Pārtha, that [liṅga] shall become complete; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.
A goldsmith should have it fashioned from gold or silver;
for the deity whose vow has been broken, one should have his form well-constructed.
Indeed, whatever form of a man or woman had been commenced during the vow was not yet fully completed; however, by the power of destiny, it all arose in that manner:
two-armed, seated upon a lotus, with a gentle and smiling countenance.
Having completed it through the process of craftsmanship day by day,
when that same month arrives once again, the Brāhmaṇa should bathe the image in his house according to the prescribed rite with milk, curd, ghee, milk-essence, and water.
One should smear [the vessel] with fragrant sandalwood paste, flowers, saffron, and so forth;
then, having placed the water-filled jar upon the ground with sandalwood paste,
one should worship it with incense, lamps, unbroken grains (akṣata), garments, jewels, and various offerings.
And one should offer the *arghya* with his name, O Pāṇḍava, using this mantra:
"O Lord, show compassion today toward me who have approached you, who am miserable, who have joined my palms for atonement, and who have sought refuge."

"Obeisance to you, O Lord of the World; I bow to you, O Infinite One. Grant favor to me, who am terrified by the fear of the next world and whose vow has been broken and fragmented. May my vow be made complete; may it be fulfilled for me.
Whatever flaw there is in my austerity, whatever flaw in my vow, and whatever flaw in this broken vow—"
O Lord of Gods, by your grace may everything be free from defect for us. Svāhā!
(Salutation to [Name] Deva. To the east, south, west, and north, and in the intermediate directions, above and below—to the guardians of the quarters, salutations again and again.
"This is the water for honor (arghya), this is the water for the feet (pādya), and this is the food offering (naivedya) for you; salutations, salutations!
Having spoken thus, one should then touch the feet, knees, waist, head, chest, belly, eyes, back, arms, shoulders, and hair.
One should worship that deity and thereafter ask for forgiveness:
"O Supreme among Gods, you have been worshipped according to my ability; salutations be unto you!
O Lord, grant me the accomplishment of my goals in this world and the next."
Having thus asked for forgiveness according to the prescribed rite for one in the form of a deity,
O son of Kuntī, he should then present it to the twice-born who knows the ritual.
Standing facing the east, the brahmin should receive it with darbha grass in his hand.
O son of Kuntī, the donor, having fasted and being diligent, should place [the gift] into the hand of the Brahmin while facing north, with this mantra:
"O twice-born one, this vow was previously performed by me in a fragmented manner."
"O Blessed One, by your grace, may that vow of mine be fulfilled here.
The Brāhmaṇa should also accept that vow with this mantra:
"May your vow be complete in speech, complete in mind, and complete in bodily observance."
By the grace of the Perfect One, may you have your desires fulfilled.
For that which the Brahmins proclaim, the deities indeed approve;
the Brahmins embody all the gods, and their word cannot be otherwise.
The ocean was brought to salinity, fire to the state of consuming all things,
and even Indra, the thousand-eyed, was reduced to such a state by high-souled Brahmins;
yet, by the mere word of Brahmins, the sin of killing a Brahmin (brahmahatyā) is utterly destroyed.
One obtains the full fruit of the horse sacrifice; there is no doubt about this.

By the words of Vyāsa and Vālmīki, by the words of the Brāhmaṇas, and by the words of the sages beginning with Garga, Gautama, Parāśara, Dhauṃya, Aṅgiras, Bāṣṭhi, and Nārada, may your vow be fulfilled.
Having undertaken it according to such a procedure, the Brāhmaṇa should depart.
He himself should send that gift to the house of a Brāhmaṇa;
thereafter, he should perform the five great sacrifices (mahāyajñas) and provide food and other offerings.
He who performs this vow even once with devotion in this manner—
That vow which was previously undertaken attains completion for him;
even a fragmentary portion reaches fulfillment when the presiding deity of the vow is pleased.
Having thus made it complete, the practitioner of the vow becomes one whose body is perfected by the rite.
Possessing enjoyments, worthy, with radiant fame and his desires completely fulfilled,
he shall remain in the mortal world for a hundred years and thereafter become an immortal in heaven;
acting according to his own will, he shall be honored by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra.
"Having remained in the heavenly world for a long time, one shall again attain liberation.
This expiation was proclaimed to me in the past by Garga, O Lord;
it was observed by me while still a child in Gokula, which is filled with herds of cows."

In this same way, O son of Kuntī, you too should observe the vow in its entirety. Those vows which were broken by a man under the influence of pride and delusion, even if undertaken in other births, become before one who is intent on complete worship and grant the fruit of fulfillment. Thus ends the one hundred and tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Complete Vow," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
The Description of the Vow of the Courtesan Kāmadānavī.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"I have heard in the Purāṇas the origin of the social classes (varṇas) and stages of life (āśramas)."
I wish to hear in truth the customary conduct of courtesans.
Who, O Kṛṣṇa, is their deity; what is their vow, and what is their fast? And by what dharma will they attain the unsurpassed heaven?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Pāṇḍava, I have sixteen thousand wives who are endowed with beauty, generosity, and virtue; they are auspicious and like temples of the god of love.

In that place, which was adorned by those women who were deeply engaged in unrestrained drinking parties during the springtime— a season filled with flocks of cuckoos and swarms of bees, on the banks of lakes where lotuses bloomed amidst flowering groves— [the Lord sported].
The illustrious Sāmba, conqueror of enemy cities, whose eyes were like those of a deer and who wore a garland of *mālatī* flowers as his crest-ornament, was traveling nearby along the path,
manifest in the form of Kandarpa himself and adorned with every ornament.
Gazed upon with longing by those women tormented by the arrows of the bodiless god of love,
the passion of desire increased within them, causing a trembling throughout their entire bodies.
Observing all that transformation with my eye of wisdom, I [perceived it].
"Enraged, all these bandits will carry you off here without exception once I have attained heaven, for you will be deluded by passion.
Having heard these words, their eyes became clouded with tears.
They said to me, "Speak, O Govinda! How will this come to pass—
that you, the unconquered Lord of the worlds, shall become our husband,
and [attain] a city of divine splendor and houses filled with jewels?"
"O Blessed One, how shall we, all the youths of divine form who dwell in Dvārakā, become objects of enjoyment for the entire world? And furthermore, how shall we come to the state of being slaves?"
"What is the Dharma? What is the proper conduct? How will our livelihood be?"—thus lamenting with eyes clouded by tears, those young women were addressed by me: "Let this grief be abandoned."
Formerly, during your sporting excursions in water at Lake Mānasa, Nārada approached you while you were full of pride. All of you were formerly Apsarases, the daughters of Agni.
Being asked with arrogance by one who would not bow, that knower of yoga instructed him,
saying, "How might Nārāyaṇa become our master?
From that, there formerly arose both the granting of a vow and the pronouncing of a curse.
By the gift of two beds during the months of Madhu and Mādhava,
and by the offering of golden utensils on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight,
her husband will surely become Nārāyaṇa in another birth.

"Because I did not offer you salutation out of envy for your beauty and good fortune, I have been asked by him [the Lord] to depart; therefore, there will soon be separation from you all. You shall all be carried off by thieves and attain the state of prostitutes."
Thus, due to the curse of Nārada and my own curse, you should not feel any agitation at present; you shall become my servants. O fair-faced ones, listen now to what I shall say even regarding this.
Formerly, in the war between the gods and the asuras,
when the hosts of dānavas, asuras, and rākṣasas had been slain by the hundreds and in various places,
there remained hundreds and thousands of their women.
The Lord of Gods, the best among speakers, declared regarding all those who had been married or indeed those who had been enjoyed by force:
"From now on, you must conduct yourselves according to the profession of courtesans within the royal palace."
Then those women of beautiful hips, full of devotion, stayed in the temples of the gods;
and the kings, their lords, the praised ones, and the highly learned Brahmins—
stay in their houses as well, for their birth-impurity (sūtaka) is equal to that.
Good fortune shall belong to all of them according to their capacity;
yet one should not place affection in a man who is devoid of wealth. He who pays the bride-price should always be honored and propitiated like a god.
Whether he be handsome or ugly, the wealth is the purpose there;
one must not transgress that [rule], for one would incur the sin of killing a Brahmin. Nor should those with crooked minds ever become drinkers of intoxicants.
Whoever shall come to your house taking a dowry,
all that must be taken back from him without guile and free from deceit;
nor should any transgression ever be committed against your husband.
Furthermore, any woman who, out of pride in her beauty and youth or through greed for wealth,
becomes a servant and commits adultery, that most sinful woman goes to a most sinful downward state along with her husband.
When an auspicious day for the deities and the ancestors has arrived,
cows, land, gold, and grain should be given according to one's ability;
O lady of beautiful hips, the words of the Brahmins should also be heeded.
Furthermore, I shall correctly instruct you in another vow according to its true nature;
that must be practiced by all without hesitation. Those who know the Vedas understand that this alone is sufficient for crossing over the cycle of worldly existence.
When the day of the Sun arrives, if the asterism Puṣya or Punarvasu should occur,
a woman should properly perform a bath with all medicinal herbs;
then even the God of the Five Arrows will come into her presence.

One should worship the lotus-eyed Lord; one should offer praise even to Anaṅga (the bodiless one). Having worshipped the feet for the sake of Kāma, one should worship the shanks for the sake of Mohakārin (the deluder);
the penis for the sake of Kadarpanidhi (the treasure-house of desire), and the waist with "Salutation to Prītiyuja" (the one joined with love).
The navel to the Ocean of Bliss, likewise the abdomen to the Dwarf; the heart to the Lord of the Heart, the two breasts to the Source of Delight;
the throat to Longing, and the mouth to the Born of Bliss.
One should worship the left shoulder for the sake of the Flower-Bow, and the right for the sake of the Flower-Arrows;
one should worship the crown for Ananta, and the banner for Vilola;
likewise, one should worship the head of the deity as the Soul of All.

Salutations to the Lord of Śrī, who bears the banner of Tārkṣya and the goad; salutations to the wielder of the mace, the one clad in yellow garments, the bearer of the conch, and the wielder of the discus. Salutations to Him who is Nārāyaṇa, and salutations to Him whose very self is Kāmadeva.
Salutations to Śānti, salutations to Prīti, salutations to Rati, salutations to Śrī;
salutations to Puṣṭi, salutations to Tuṣṭi, and salutations to the bestower of all goals.
Having thus worshipped Govinda, the Lord whose essence is Ananga (the God of Love), [one should proceed].
Then, O beautiful lady,

having invited a Brahmin who knows the Dharma and has mastered the Vedas— one whose limbs are free from deformity— and having honored him with perfumes, garlands, incense, food offerings, and likewise with scents and flowers; |||
She should give that best of brahmins one *prastha* of śāli rice accompanied by a vessel of ghee, saying, "May Mādhava be pleased";
and she should provide that same excellent twice-born with as much food as he desires.
Having resolved in her mind, "This is Kāmadeva for the sake of pleasure," the playful woman should do whatever that best of Brahmins desires;
speaking with smiles, she should offer herself to him with her whole being.
In this manner, she should always perform that vow on Sundays,
giving a *prastha* measure of rice for twelve months.
Then, when the thirteenth month has arrived, his beautiful wife—
One should give to a Brahmin an extraordinary bed, equipped with all necessary furnishings—
auspicious, provided with pillows for rest, covered with fine sheets and a canopy,
and accompanied by a lamp, sandals, an umbrella, wooden shoes, and a seat.
Having adorned the [image of] Kāmadeva together with his consort with golden neck-chains, finger-rings,
fine garments, bracelets, incense, garlands, and ointments,
[one should place them] upon a jar of molasses.
Seated upon a copper vessel as a throne, covered with a golden eye-cloth,
accompanied by a bronze bowl and provided with a stalk of sugarcane—
one should give this, along with a single milch cow, while reciting this mantra.
O Viṣṇu, O Keśava, just as I never perceive any difference between Kāma and you, so may there always be for me the attainment of all desires;
just as [Kāma] never departs from the body of a woman, O Keśava, [may you likewise remain ever with me].
"Nevertheless, O Lord of Gods, make my husband reside within my body.

In that same manner, the best of the twice-born, taking hold of the golden image of the god, should recite the Vedic mantra: "Who is this? Who has given it? To whom has he given it? Desire has given it to desire; desire is the giver, desire is the receiver. I enter the ocean of desire—this is that!"
Reciting the mantra "ko'dāt" while meditating on Mādhava in his heart,
he should then circumambulate the eminent Brahmin and bid him farewell;
he should then lead all the items, such as the bed and the seat, to the Brahmin's home.
From that time forward, whoever else has come to the house for the sake of pleasure should be properly honored according to one's desire, like [the worship performed] on a Sunday.
In this way, [one should honor] even a single twice-born man who is peaceful, learned in the Purāṇas, and discerning.
One should always worship that [deity], or another by its command;
then one will never encounter obstacles arising from childbirth or impurity,
whether they be divine, human, or caused by an eclipse.
One should complete [the task] according to one's ability, like a lost animal that is common property.
Thus has all this dharma of courtesans been told to you in its entirety;
it was proclaimed by Indra to the Danavas, and from him it was received by me.
And this entire vow has been revealed to you all;
it pacifies all sins and bestows infinite fruit.
It has been told to you auspicious women; therefore, O fair-faced ones, perform it.
O Pārtha, this ancient scripture, the essence of all dharma which bestows happiness upon the people of the courtesans, was previously revealed by me to the gopīs.
That auspicious woman who performs this entire work without interruption shall reside in the world of Mādhava.
"Worshipped by all the hosts of gods, she goes to the place of Viṣṇu which bestows bliss.

Thus ends the one hundred and eleventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Kāmadānaveśyā Vrata," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira;
followed by the description of the rules for the Vṛntāka Vrata.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual procedure for the eggplant (*vṛntāka*).
One should not eat it for one year, six months, or three months.

Then, having observed a fast for one night under the asterism of Bharaṇī or Maghā, one should invoke the gods upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) and worship them with perfumes, incense, flowers, food offerings, lamps, and so forth.

Holding *darbha* grass in hand, one should invoke them with fragrant water, saying: "I invoke King Yama; I invoke Kāla; I invoke Nīla; I invoke Citragupta; I invoke Vaivasvata; I invoke Mṛtyu; I invoke Parameṣṭhin. Thereafter, having established the sacred fire, one should offer oblations of sesame seeds and clarified butter.

"Oblation to King Yama, svāhā! Oblation to Kāla, svāhā! Oblation to Nīla, svāhā! Oblation to Citragupta, svāhā! Oblation to Vaivasvata, svāhā! Oblation to Mṛtyu, svāhā! Oblation to Parameṣṭhin, svāhā! Having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the verse "Agnirmūrdhā," having performed the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, and having offered the expiatory oblations (*prāyaścitta*), a Brāhmaṇa performs them himself; for others, the teacher does so.
Then, he should present a golden eggplant (*vṛntāka*) to a Brāhmaṇa and give a black bull and a cow.
One should give earrings, finger-rings, an umbrella, sandals, a pair of black garments, and a black woolen blanket.
Having fed the Brāhmaṇas, one should cause them to pronounce blessings;
thus, one obtains the fruit of the Pauṇḍarīka and Aśvamedha sacrifices.
