"One is honored in the vault of heaven for seven thousand crores [of years];

for as long as seven births, one does not behold the realm of Yama," so said the Blessed Baudhāyana. "He who, having observed the vow for one year or one month, gives to a twice-born man a vṛntāka (eggplant) that has been perfected by gold within it and accompanied by ghee and buttermilk—such a person never beholds the city of Yama."

Thus ends the one hundred and twelfth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Vṛntāka Vow," in the Uttara Parva of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Now follows the description of vows dedicated to the planets and constellations. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully declare this supreme secret,
by which prosperity, happiness, and nourishment arise,
and by which all the planets always become auspicious, O Pāṇḍava.
On a Sunday, the wise man should first take hold [of the plant] with his hand;
then, according to the prescribed rite for eating at night (*nakta*), he should perform the entire worship of the Sun.
Having performed these seven *nakta* observances in person, the man becomes devoted to the Lord.
Then, when the seventh [day] has arrived, a person should perform the recitation by Brahmins;
having carefully fashioned a golden image of the Sun out of pure gold,
he should place it in a copper vessel and worship it with red flowers.
Covered with a pair of red garments and provided with an umbrella and a pair of sandals,
one should perform a bath with ghee, offer sweetmeat balls (laḍḍukas),
and present it to a learned Brāhmaṇa while reciting this mantra:
O Primordial God, homage to you, O seven-horsed Sun!
O Ravi, deliver us from this ocean of saṃsāra.
By performing this, O King of Kings, there shall be supreme health.
The experts in the Purāṇas know this as "the attainment of wealth and sons";
it is unfailing for men and bestows peace and prosperity.
Likewise, on a Monday falling during the Citrā constellation, the wise man should collect [the substances].
Then, when the seventh [day] has arrived, having provided a feast for the Brahmins,
one should place King Soma— wrapped in white cloth— into a vessel made of bell-metal, silver, or gold.
Having given to a Brāhmaṇa a peak of curd-rice accompanied by sandals, shoes, an umbrella, a vessel, and a seat,
one should present it with this mantra; O King of kings, listen as I speak it to you.
"O Śrī Mahādeva, you who are as white as jasmine flowers and cow's milk;
O Soma, be gentle toward us, always the most excellent of the excellent.
When this is done, O Great King, Soma will bestow satisfaction.
When the son of Atri (Budha) is pleased, all the planets become favorably disposed. Having taken up a Tuesday under the asterism Svāti, one should observe a fast by eating only at night.
Then, when the seventh [Tuesday] arrives, [the substance] should be placed in a copper vessel.
Covered with a pair of red garments and anointed with saffron,
having worshipped it with offerings, the *haṃtakāra* food, incense, unbroken grains (*akṣata*), and so forth,
one should give it to a householder Brahmin with this mantra:
Although you were born of an ignoble birth, you are recited as auspicious by the wise;
having swiftly destroyed inauspiciousness, always bestow auspiciousness!
Having observed the vow of Mercury under the asterism Viśākhā, one should then perform seven nights of eating only at night (nakta).
Having fashioned an image of Mercury out of gold and placed it in a bronze vessel,
covered with a pair of white garments and adorned with white garlands and unguents,
one should present an offering of rice cooked with jaggery to a Brāhmaṇa.
O Budha, who generates true wisdom and bestows enlightenment upon men at all times, grant me the realization of reality; O Prince, salutations, salutations!
Furthermore, during the asterism Anurādhā, one should worship the Preceptor (Bṛhaspati), who is honored by the gods, with devotion.
Following the sequence previously described, one should then perform seven night-vows (naktas).
Having placed an image of Bṛhaspati made of gold in a vessel made of gold,
it should be covered with a pair of yellow garments and provided with a yellow sacred thread.

Having worshipped with heaps of flowers, lamps, incense, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), and so forth, as well as with offerings of sweetmeats and snacks, one should present [the sandals] along with an umbrella, a staff,
and a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) to a twice-born man.

O knower of the Dharmaśāstras and Arthaśāstras, you who have reached the further shore of theoretical and practical knowledge; O Teacher of the Gods, whose depth of intellect is unfathomable—salutations be to you!
Having gathered semen under the asterism Jyeṣṭhā, one should consume it while fasting during the night.
Having performed the gratification of the twice-born according to the previously mentioned sequence and method,
when the seventh [day] arrives, one should have a beautiful golden image made,
or alternatively, place the son of Bhṛgu in a silver vessel or a bamboo vessel.
Having worshipped with supreme devotion using white garments and unguents,
one should offer milk-rice mixed with ghee before him.
A wise person should give it to a Brāhmaṇa while reciting this mantra:
"O Bhārgava, son of Bhṛgu, O Śukra, you who are skilled in the traditional sequence:
having destroyed the afflictions caused by the planets, become the bestower of long life and health!
O bull among the Bharatas, having seized the son of the Sun (Saturn) with the Mūla [mantra],"
On that day, O King, one should reverently worship the triad of planets—
Saturn, Rāhu, and Ketu— in their proper order.
A knower of mantras should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with sesame seeds and ghee, using the name of the house as the mantra.
The sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh) for each [deity] in order are: Arka, Palāśa, Khadira, Apāmārga, Pippala, Udumbara, Śamī, Dūrvā, and Kuśa;
there should be one hundred and eight or twenty-eight of each.
One should offer oblations of honey and ghee, or curd, or milk-rice.
Then, when the seventh [day] of the Sun’s son has arrived,
O King, three auspicious images of the planets should be made out of metal.
At the conclusion of the vow, O King, one should have these [images] made of gold from all parts;
one should present a pair of black garments to each one in succession,
having anointed them with musk and offered *kṛśara* (rice and sesame).
At the conclusion of the oblation, one should present all of that to a Brāhmaṇa:
"O Śanaiścara, obeisance to you; likewise, obeisance to Rāhu.
Obeisance to you, Ketu; be the bestower of all peace."
O Lord of Men, learn what happens when this is performed:
even if Mars, Saturn, the Sun together with Rāhu,
and Ketu— all these afflictive planets— should stand upon one's head.
By the mere performance of this, all calamities are pacified.
O King, for one who always performs it thus, endowed with devotion,
all [the deities], being favorably disposed toward him, grant victory and happiness.
Whoever hears this ritual manual of the planets, or even recites it, all [the planets] will bestow grace upon him and grant peace; it shall not be otherwise.
One should place Saturn, Rāhu, and Ketu in vessels made of iron.
Black aloe-wood is prescribed as incense, and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given according to one's means.
Having worshipped the Sun, the Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn, together with the lunar mansions beginning with Hasta, in their order of rising,
and having presented [images of them] fashioned from gold to an eminent brahmin, a man is not afflicted here by the host of planets.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Vows of Planets and Constellations," in the *Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the *Uttara Parvan*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira; followed by the "Description of the Vow of Śanaiścara.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Long ago in the Tretā Yuga, O Pārtha, Indra, the subduer of Pāka, did not send rain. Due to the king’s misconduct, it did not rain anywhere throughout his kingdom.
Consequently, the kingdom became exceedingly terrible, overwhelmed by hunger.
Overcrowded with locusts and rats, and agitated by the fear of thieves and serpents—
in that terrible and chaotic time, Kauśika, together with his wife and children, abandoned his own home and slowly went to a foreign kingdom.
Then, as that great seer Kauśika was traveling along the road,
he abandoned that single infant and his family, who were difficult to support;
at that time, moreover, the stores of grain and medicinal herbs had become especially depleted.
Having performed that most cruel deed, the sage Kauśika departed.
That boy, weeping and distressed, stood on the path looking toward the quarters;
then, rising up, he began to eat the fruits beneath a *pippala* tree.
He drank water from the well daily within that very circle of hermitages;
having established himself there properly, he performed intense and extensive penance.
Then the blessed Nārada, who had mastered the Vedas, arrived.
Seeing that young brahmin boy with a dejected face and afflicted by hunger,
he performed for him out of compassion the rites of initiation, including the binding of the girdle of muñja grass,
and taught him the Vedas along with their secret doctrines and the methods of *pada* and *krama* recitation.

And he bestowed upon him the Vaiṣṇava mantra consisting of twelve syllables. To this Pippalāda, who was devoted to the study of the Vedas and intent on the meditation of Viṣṇu, Viṣṇu became directly manifest every day.
Mounted upon Vainateya, possessing the luster of a blue lotus petal,
four-armed, clad in yellow garments, and bearing the conch, discus, and mace— he,
being pleased, then said: "Choose whatever boon you desire."
Having heard that and looking toward the face of Nārada, the child then,
being permitted by Nārada, requested knowledge and wisdom; and [Nārada],
having given him knowledge along with its instructions and pure practice of yoga, [departed].
Viṣṇu, whose gait is like that of a lion among elephants, vanished right there.
Then, O King, that great sage of vast knowledge, while still a child, questioned Nārada: "O Sage, by whom have I been afflicted?"
Seized by a spirit that had taken possession of him, though appearing as a mere child, he cried out in distress:
"Neither my father nor my mother is mine; I live only through great suffering!
O best of the twice-born, Brahminhood has been granted to me by you through destiny."
Having heard these words of the child, Nārada said:
"Indeed, you are afflicted by the cruel planet Śanaiścara (Saturn),
and this entire region is also oppressed by that slow-moving one."

"Therefore, this fruit has been obtained by you; this is that very Saturn, the son of the Sun, blazing with excessive pride as if flickering in the vault of the sky. Thus addressed, the boy blazed up in anger like a fire.
Having observed him, he caused Śani to fall from the sky to the earth;
falling from the peak of a mountain, he was broken and became lame.
Seeing the son of the Sun fallen upon the ground and distressed, [he took pity on him].
With his heart filled with joy, Nārada danced with the gestures of his arms;
then, out of delight, he summoned the gods and showed them Śani.
Thereupon, the gods—Brahmā, Rudra, Indra, and Agni—arrived in that manner.
Gradually calming themselves, they said this to that Ṛṣi:
"May it be well with you, O illustrious one, Pippalāda, great sage! May prosperity be yours; here your name was bestowed by the great Ṛṣi Nārada."
"O best of Brahmins, your life is truly meaningful because of this act of nourishing;
O Sage, since you have been restored to life by eating the *pippala* fruits,
you shall therefore attain fame in the world as 'Pippalāda'."
And those who, having bathed and being filled with devotion, shall approach you, the great seer, in this hermitage with flowers while you are in this form—
they shall have their lineage of sons and grandsons follow them for seven future births.
For them, the affliction of the planet will not truly be an obstacle.
And those who here remember you by the name Pippalāda,
for them the suffering caused by Śanaiścara shall have no power.
"Forgive him, O highly fortunate one; this leader of the planets is faultless.
Moving slowly through the tree, he bestows both auspicious and inauspicious fruits.
These planets whose *sādhya* [vitality] has been struck down never become [effective] at any time."
When worshipped with offerings, oblations, and prostrations, they bestow peace;
therefore, on this day, a bath preceded by an oil massage should be performed,
and oil should be given to the Brahmins for the purpose of anointing.
But that man who, for the duration of a year, whenever a Saturday arrives,
gives oil to Brahmins according to his capacity and to others as well,
then, when the end of that year has come and that day arrives once again—
One should cast an image of the Sun, fashioned from iron, into the midst of oil;
it should be placed within an iron vessel, covered with a pair of black cloths,
accompanied by the gift of a black cow, and laid upon a black woolen blanket.
Having bathed with sesame oil and performed a thorough worship with black flowers,
black perfumes, black incense, kṛśara-rice, and sesame-rice,
one should worship the Son of the Sun and present it to a Brāhmaṇa.
O Brahman-sage, one who is devoted should [use] this mantra, "śanno devī," for [the propitiation of] others;
now hear the mantra for the other castes, O best of the twice-born:
"Whatever angry planet, by the power of its cruel gaze, shall destroy the world..."
May Saturn, the son of the Sun, protect you—he who, being pleased, bestows wealth, gold, and happiness;
he who, it is said, formerly gave his own mantra, which grants the fruit of all desires, to Nala when his kingdom had been lost. Listen to that mantra.

I bow to Śanaiścara, whose chest resembles blue collyrium, who wears a garland of the same dark-blue hue, and who is born from the shadow of the Sun. Salutations to the son of the Sun, to Śanaiścara, who is as dark as frost and blackened collyrium.
Having heard this secret, O Son of the Sun, become the fulfiller of my desires for existence and the bestower of its fruits.
Homage be to the King of the Departed, homage indeed to the one with the dark body;
homage to Śanaiścara, the fierce one, who bestows pure intellect.
"I become pleased with whoever praises me with these names;
for him, fear of me shall not exist even in a dream.
Thus Śani spoke in the past; therefore, one should offer it to a Brāhmaṇa.
O Brahmin, those men who shall observe this vow for the duration of one year,
even during the most stationary period [of the planet Saturn],
shall not suffer from the affliction of Saturn, nor shall such suffering occur in their country.
Having spoken thus, all the gods returned as they had come;
Śanaiścara also, established among the planets in the sky, remained in his own place. Pippalāda too, the knower of Brahman, continued to abide by the command of Brahmā.
Having worshipped Śanaiścara, he praised him with palms joined in reverence:
"May the one who dwells in the corner, the tawny, the brown, the black, the fierce, the Ender, Yama,
the son of Sūrya, Śanaiścara, the Joyful— may this best of planets be pleased with me."

Having thus praised Śanaiścara, the great sage Pippalāda was seen even today by human beings, blazing in the sky while seated in his celestial chariot. Those who listen with a concentrated mind to this narrative of Śanaiścara—

O best among the excellent Kurus, Saturn shall not cause them affliction. Whoever, having placed an image of the King of Planets fashioned from black iron into a vessel of metal filled with sesame oil, devoutly gives it to a Brāhmaṇa along with the Sun-son (Saturn), him no affliction caused by Śanaiścara shall ever trouble.

Thus ends the one hundred and fourteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Vow of Śanaiścara," in the *Śrībhaviṣyamahāpurāṇa*, within the *Uttaraparvan*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira; followed by the "Description of the Rule for the Night-vow on Sunday.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Govinda, tell me of that vow which brings about health for men, which bestows infinite fruit, and which destroys all sins. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
That which is the abode of the Universal Self, the supreme, eternal Brahman,
exists in the world in three forms— as the sun, fire, and the moon.
O descendant of Kuru, what is there that a person does not attain by worshipping Him?
Therefore, one should always eat only at night on Sundays.
When perpetual devotion toward the Sun arises,
from that time forward, one should always observe the practice of eating only at night on Sundays.
Having honored the best of the twice-born according to the previously mentioned rite, one should then,
at the time of the sun’s setting, draw a twelve-petaled lotus with red sandalwood paste and worship it, beginning from the east with the mantra "Sūrya."
Likewise, one should place Divākara in the southeast, and beyond that, Vivasvat;
the god Bhaga in the southwest, and Varuṇa on the western petal;
Mahendra in the northwest petal, and likewise Āditya in the north.
One should place Śānta in the Īśāna direction with a salutation.
One should place the horses of the Sun on the eastern petal of the pericarp;
Yama by name in the south, and Mārtaṇḍa on the western petal.
To the north of the god Ravi, one should place Bhāskara upon the pericarp;
then, O Pārtha, one should offer *arghya* consisting of red sandalwood with sesame seeds,
along with fruit and unbroken rice, and likewise recite this mantra:
You are the soul of time, the soul of all beings, the soul of the Vedas, and the one whose face is turned everywhere;
since you possess the forms of both fire and the moon, protect us, O Maker of Light!
I praise Agni; salutations to you, O Sun, for the sake of food and vigor.
"O Agni, come hither, O giver of boons; salutations to you, O Lord of lights!
Having offered the *arghya* and performed the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*), one should then eat at night—avoiding oil—with a purified mind, repeatedly recollecting the Sun.
On the previous day, and on a Saturday, one should avoid an oil massage.
At the end of the year, having caused an excellent golden lotus to be made,
one should likewise have a two-armed male figure fashioned according to one's means.

Having placed upon a full copper vessel filled with jaggery a highly precious tawny cow with golden horns, silver hooves, and a bronze milking-pail, together with her calf, one should then place a lotus upon it. Having thus prepared the cow and a man together with the lotus, one should present them to the leader of many vows.
Salutations be to you who possess an unimpaired form, who have conquered the senses, who are a householder, pure, and free from arrogance;
salutations to the knower of the Ṛg, Sāma, and Yajur Vedas, to the awakener of the lotus, the creator of the world;
salutations again and again to you, who consist of the three Vedas, whose self is the three qualities (guṇas), and who are the Lord of the three worlds.
By this procedure, the man who observes a fast at night on Sundays for one year shall become free from disease;
he will be endowed with wealth and grain, and blessed with sons and grandsons.
Having remained in the mortal world for a long time, he shall attain the realm of the Sun.
Upon the exhaustion of his karma, the king— freed from grief, suffering, fear, and disease—
shall become like the very death of his enemies' clans, an embodiment of dharma endowed with immeasurable splendor.

And she who is devoted to her husband, her guru, and the gods, who observes the vow of the Veda-form day and night—she too goes to the world honored by the Lord of the Immortals, as does one who honors the Sun; of this there is no doubt. Furthermore, the man who recites this, or hears it, or sees it thus, or even rejoices in it [attains the same].
He too is praised by the celestial dwellers in the abode of Śakra for one hundred million kalpas.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Rules for the Day of the Sun and the Night-Vow," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira; followed by the "Description of the Concluding Rite for the Saṃkrānti."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Now I shall tell you another thing as well— the fruit of the concluding rite (udyāpana) for the Saṃkrānti festival—
which the poets of the Purāṇas know to be supreme and inexhaustible in this world.
One should commence the Saṃkrānti vow either at the equinox (viṣuva) or at the solstice (ayana).
On the day preceding it, one should eat only a single meal after first cleansing the teeth.
When the day of the Saṃkrānti arrives, a bath with sesame seeds is prescribed.

One should draw an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp upon the ground using sandalwood paste; therein one should invoke the Sun. One should place Sūrya Āditya in the pericarp, and then [the other deities] starting from the east.
Salutation to Agni, the seven-rayed; and to the circle of disease in the south.
Salutation to Savitṛ in the southwest; one should worship Varuṇa in the west.
And in the northwest, one should worship the Lord of luminaries, the seven-horsed Sun.
One should place Mārtaṇḍa on the northern petal and Viṣṇu on the northeast petal;
thereafter, one should worship him upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with perfumes, garlands, fruits, and edible offerings.
Having offered the respectful oblation (argha) with sandalwood water and flowers, one should then place [the deity] upon the ground.
"Salutations to you, whose form is the universe, the sustainer of the universe, the self-existent one!
Salutations again and again to you, O giver of boons, Lord of the Ṛg, Sāman, and Yajus!
O best of men, having offered the *arghya* to the Sun according to this rite,"

O best of men, having caused a water-pot, a vessel of ghee, and a golden lotus to be made according to one's capacity, one should offer them to a twice-born man; this rite should be performed month after month according to this procedure.
O son of Kuntī, all of this should be performed according to the rules by men eating but one meal [per day],
either on a single day or at the end of the year;
having worshipped the fire with ghee and milk-rice (pāyasa), it should be offered to an eminent brahmin.

One who is afflicted by poverty should further offer twelve water-pots accompanied by twelve cows, along with one auspicious vessel, to an eminent Brāhmaṇa; and he should give a golden earth [model] together with crops, or according to his capacity, one made of silver, copper, or flour; if he is unable, he should fashion the earth [model] out of flour.

One should give [this] together with a golden sun; a person should not practice stinginess regarding wealth here. By doing so, one goes downward as long as the lords of the gods headed by Mahendra endure, as long as the earth remains with its mountains, and as long as the sun, wind, fire, and moon exist.
O descendant of Bharata, he is honored by all the hosts of Gandharvas in the vault of heaven for that long;
thereafter, upon the exhaustion of his merit, he shall be born into a noble family as the sovereign of the seven continents,
endowed with a body possessed of divine features, together with his wife, and surrounded by a circle of sons, descendants, and kinsmen.
Whoever recites or hears this entire meritorious rite with great devotion during the solar transits (saṃkrāntis),
or even bestows their attention upon it, shall, upon death, be honored by the gods headed by Indra, the lord of the immortals.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Conclusion of the Saṃkrānti Vow," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the Viṣṭi Vow.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Kṛṣṇa, who is this that is called "Viṣṭi" and "Bhadrā" by all people?
"Whose daughter is she, what is her form, and how is she worshipped by people?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"In ancient times, she was born from the shadow (chāyā) of the god Mārtaṇḍa."
The sister of Śanaiścara, born of the same womb, was exceedingly terrifying;
as soon as she was born, she began to seize the world—
black, with a gaping mouth, white fangs, and hair standing erect.
If someone standing before him creates an obstacle for another who is departing on business, or for one who is sleeping, eating, or standing still—
she is a fierce bringer of obstacles to sacrifice and a destroyer of assemblies and festivals.
Fierce and causing constant agitation, she destroys the world.
Seeing her thus addicted to wicked conduct, the divine Sun thought: "To whom shall I give this woman of slender waist?"
In this world, due to the misconduct of a maiden, her father is held accountable for the fault;
thereafter, it falls upon the husband of the young woman. Therefore, having reflected thus, one should lead a virtuous daughter to the house of whichever man he intends to give her to.
In an instant, those gods, rākṣasas, and kinnaras bowed down;
yet at the commencement of the pavilion, it would break and terrify the people.
Vivasvān was overcome with anxiety: "To whom shall this be assigned?"
"Though she is ugly, wicked-hearted, and one who acts and dwells according to her own whims,
she will not cause any fault whatsoever here even if she is given away.
While the Lord Indra, the master of the day, remained reflecting thus, [the gods arrived].
Meanwhile, the entire world was assailed by that wicked woman;
then Brahmā, born from the cosmic egg,
came to the side of the Sun and reported the wickedness of Viṣṭi in its entirety.
Then Bhāskara spoke to Brahmā, the Lord of the World:
"You are both the creator and the destroyer; why then do you speak thus?
Being addressed in this way by Bhāskara, Brahmā of immeasurable luster then [replied].
Having summoned Viṣṭi, he said: "Listen, O auspicious one, I shall speak.
Abide with the Karaṇas—Bava, Bālava, and Kaulava—and when the seventh half-day arrives, perform whatever you desire."
For the sake of journeys, entries, auspicious rites, agriculture, and trade,
devour those men who go against you or travel on wrong paths. Indeed, people must not cause us agitation for three days.

"O noble lady, you shall be worshipped by gods and asuras for half a day. O auspicious one, those men who proceed fearlessly, transgressing you—quickly bring about their destruction; thus, O noble one, may you be at peace."

Having spoken thus, Brahmā departed, and Bhadrā too wandered through the three worlds with a bewildered heart, terrifying both gods and demons. In this manner, Viṣṭi was born, the destroyer of desired objects.
O son of Kuntī, this has been declared to you; therefore, one should avoid her.

Having the color of a dark cloud, with a long nose and fierce fangs, a broad jaw and skull, and shanks swollen like a calf's leg, vomiting forth hundreds of thousands of fires from all sides, Viṣṭi falls upon the middle of the earth for the destruction of undertakings.
The daughter of the Sun, born before the hundred Ketus, she is black, ill-formed, and always poorly clothed.
The *viṣṭi* yoga, which exists for the purpose of performing actions as appointed by the gods, must be avoided in all circumstances.
Five *ghaṭikās* are always situated in the mouth, two in the throat,
eleven are said to be in the heart, and four in the region of the navel.
Five lines on the hips should be known [as auspicious], while three on the tail bring victory;
one on the face leads to the destruction of undertakings, one on the neck destroys wealth,
one on the heart should be known as life-taking, and one on the navel brings about quarrels.
At the waist there is loss of wealth; at the tail of Viṣṭi, victory is certain.
Whatever tasks there are on earth, whether auspicious or inauspicious, they all succeed at the tail of Viṣṭi—of this there is no doubt.
Dhanyā, Dadhimukhī, Bhadrā, Mahāmārī, Kharānanā,
Kālarātri, Mahārudrā, Viṣṭi, Kulaputrikā,
Bhairavī, and Mahākālī, who brings about the destruction of the Asuras.
Whoever, having risen early in the morning, recites these twelve names alone, shall suffer no disease; the sick shall be liberated from illness,
all planetary influences shall become favorable, and no obstacles or the like shall arise.
In battle, in the royal court, and at the gambling table, such a man shall be victorious everywhere.
For the person who constantly worships according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures,
there is no doubt that the accomplishment of all his goals occurs in this world.
I shall describe to you that very rite of fasting and vow by which the illustrious goddess, when worshipped, attains satisfaction. O Bhārata, on whichever day Bhadrā occurs, on that very day—
Whether it be a woman or a man, one should observe the rules for fasting;
if there is an *viṣṭi* (an inauspicious lunar division) at night, one should eat only once on two days,
for by that means the fast is accomplished— such is the scriptural tradition of the Purāṇas.
When Viṣṭi occurs after the first watch (prahara), one should observe a fast for three watches;
otherwise, a single meal (ekabhakta) should be taken.
Furthermore, one should bathe with all medicinal herbs and water, as well as with fragrant Āmalaka fruits.
Bathing in a river, a pond, or at home is recommended in all circumstances.
Having gratified the gods and the ancestors, one should then fashion an auspicious image out of *darbha* grass and worship it with flowers, incense, and food offerings.
Having performed the *homa* with one hundred and eight oblations of *viṣṭi*-seeds,
he should then eat after giving sesame seeds and milk-rice (*pāyasa*) to a Brahmin;
having eaten the *kṛśarā* mixed with sesame, he may thereafter eat as he desires.
O Goddess Chāyā, daughter of the Sun, you who are Viṣṭi and the bestower of desired objects, you have been worshipped according to my capacity; O auspicious one, be the granter of prosperity.
Having fasted according to this rite for seventeen days in due order, [one attains the fruit].
Then one should perform the concluding rite (udyāpana) as before, having worshipped the beautiful lady;
having placed her upon an iron seat and offered her *kṛśara* rice,
and having clothed her with a pair of black garments, one should praise her again with the mantra.
Furthermore, one should give iron, oil, and sesame seeds to a Brāhmaṇa;
likewise, a single black cow with her calf and a single black blanket.
Having given a sacrificial fee according to one's ability, one should bid farewell to Bhadrā.
O Pārtha, for that man who thus correctly performs the Bhadrā-vrata,
no obstacle shall ever arise at the commencement of his undertakings;
nor shall Rākṣasas, Piśācas, Pūtanās, Śākinīs, or Grahas cause him harm.
No afflictions torment that mortal who observes the Bhadravrata;
nor shall there be separation from what is dear, nor does any loss occur for him.
At the end of the body, he goes to the abode of the Sun, without a doubt.
The sister of Saturn, beloved by the Sun, who wanders through the mortal world as an *atiratha* in the sequence of the *karana*s—
by fasting on that day when her face shines black, even an ignorant man attains the fulfillment of his desired aims.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventeenth chapter, titled "Description of the Viṣṭi Vow," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the Agastya Vow. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
There is another vow, the Agastya Vow, which destroys all sins.
"Listen to that, O sinless protector of the earth, as it is being told by me.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"I am listening; tell me, O Kṛṣṇa, of the deeds of that celestial sage."
[Regarding] his birth, the offering of the *arghya*, and the time of his departure—
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"In former times, these two, Mitra and Varuṇa, were the foremost among the gods."
Near Mount Mandara, they performed extensive austerities;
to disturb them, Vāsava dispatched the excellent Apsaras Urvaśī, who was endowed with the qualities of beauty and nobility.
Merely by the sight of her, those two best of gods were agitated;
perceiving the transformation of their minds, they both discharged their seed into a jar.
From that, due to the curse of Nimi, the venerable sage Vasiṣṭha was born.
Immediately thereafter, the divine Agastya, whose wealth was his asceticism, was born;
in a certain region of the Malaya mountains, together with his wife and surrounded by brahmins, he performed most difficult penance according to the Vaikhānasa injunctions.
In ancient times, at the beginning of the Kṛta Yuga, there were two wicked Daityas named Ilvala and Vātāpi,
who were thorns to the gods and brahmins.
One of them became a ram, while the second was the provider of food.

In this manner, by means of that very sequence of *śrāddha* rites, many twice-born ones were destroyed. Then, on another day, the Daitya invited Agastya to a meal together with Brāhmaṇas born of the lineages of Bhṛgu and Garga.
Agastya also became the leader at the śrāddha, filled with righteous indignation;
he too, having slain Vātāpi who was in the form of a ram, cooked him in the fire.
While the offerings were being served, he spoke to the motionless Dānava.
The venerable Agastya, becoming enraged, said, "Give me everything!
Thereupon, the furious Ilvala gave him that human flesh;
having consumed it, the great sage became healthy and free from all affliction.
Then, appearing radiant, Ilvala spoke slowly to Vātāpi:
"Come forth, having burst through the body of the sage; why do you delay?
Hearing that, the brahmin Agastya also produced a loud belch.
"From where did he emerge? He has been eaten by me again! This Vātāpi, a thorn to the Brahmins, has been digested and turned to ashes.
Ilvala, his anger flaring up, was then stared down by Agastya.
In an instant, everything was reduced to ashes, and the world then appeared tranquil.
Because of that enmity, those wicked Dānavas were destroyed, with none remaining.
Having consulted together on Mount Meru and reached a decision, they then approached Agastya.
Desiring to increase the splendor of this sage,
the denizens of heaven said to Agastya, "O Brahman-sage, dry up the ocean indeed.
Having heard that, the brahmin Agastya assumed the meditative concentration (*dhāraṇā*) of fire.
Even the ocean was drunk by her, its waves and tortoises bewildered;
and when the waters of the ocean had been drunk, the Dānavas were all brought to destruction in an instant by the enraged gods, as they wailed again and again.
By the grace of the sage Agastya, all in the world became secure.
Then, when the ocean was once again filled with the waters of the river Gaṅgā,
they made Mount Mandara the churning-stick and Vāsuki the rope.
All the Daityas and Dānavas together churned the ocean;
then the moon, the Kaustubha jewel, and the elephant arose from the mass of gems.
As they churned the ocean, the reservoir of waters, with excessive greed, [the nectar appeared].
Then the great and terrible Kālakūṭa poison arose, blazing fiercely; by it, that host of gods was as if made to reel. Having entered the ocean, they emerged night after night.
Having emerged, they slaughtered the sages who were celibate ascetics;
they shattered the sacrificial vessels and hid themselves by day within the waters of the ocean,
remaining unknown even to Brahmā, Nārāyaṇa, and Hara.
Vāyu, Kubera, all the Vasus, and all the gods including Indra were there;
then, by means of mantras, Śaṅkara consumed a portion right there.
In an instant, that mantra was burnt away, and Hara was turned blue-throated.
Even Brahmā, having regained his composure, spoke words of protest:
"There is no one in this world capable of drinking the poison;
the great sage Agastya resides in the southern region at the base of Laṅkā."
"Therefore, O highly fortunate ones, go to him for refuge, for he is always [our protector].
Having been addressed thus, the gods went to the southern region of Agastya's hermitage;
and seeing those gods, Agastya, the best of sages, was filled with joy.
By means of meditation, he neutralized the poison which had entered the Himalaya—
the serpents' necklaces within the groves on the mountain peaks—
at which time a small residue of the poison remained clinging to the trees and other plants.

O Pāṇḍava, that poison was ground up by the wind from the Unmattakara, Karavīra, Arka, and Stalabhūmi trees, as well as by water; thus, it was instantly neutralized by that wind, which was as pure as a cool breeze from the Himalayas.
Various kinds of diseases arise among humans on earth;
and those, intense with poison, circulate for three and a half months.
Starting from the transit of the Sun into Taurus (vṛṣasaṃkrānti) until the end of Leo, the poison subsides.
And by its power, O Pārtha, there shall be the removal of the defects of disease;
thus, after a long time, when this world had become densely populated with hosts of beings, O Pārtha, it became free from illness and devoid of disease.
In the continuous world of mortals, as [the sage] stood with arms outstretched upward,
powerful Death, embodied and driven by the indication of smoke, wandered about;
destroying all creatures, he arrived before the great sage at the appointed time.

Enraged, Death appeared in person before him; when gazed upon by him, he was reduced to ashes. Subsequently, for the sake of Brahmā’s happiness, another Death was created, accompanied by a multitude of diseases.
Likewise, another excellent king named Śveta in the Daṇḍaka forest, while eating his own flesh, entreated a sage out of despondency:
"O Blessed One, everything else has been given away; the kingdom alone was not given by me."
Neither food, nor water, nor even a funeral offering (śrāddha) had been given by that man of evil intent.
Thereupon, out of compassion, Agastya performed a śrāddha with precious gems.
When the śrāddha was completed, he suddenly assumed a divine body, endowed with splendor.
And he attained the supreme state through the grace of the sage Agastya.
Then the great mountain Vindhya began to grow out of anger toward the Sun, thinking:
"Why does he not circumambulate me as he does Mount Meru?"
Seeing him growing in size, the gods, together with Indra,
went as one to the hermitage and, having praised that preeminent divine sage,
spoke to Agastya: "O Blessed One, [subdue] this one who obstructs the path of the sun."
"Restrain this Vindhya yourself and establish the mountain in its place.
Agastya, having gone quickly, spoke thus to the Vindhya mountain:
"O best of mountains, know me to have set out on a pilgrimage to the sacred fords."
"Stay here for as long as it takes for me to return.
Having spoken thus, he departed and has not yet returned;
he is seen blazing in the sky, illuminating the southern quarter.
He whose feet are worshipped by the three worlds and who was accompanied by Lopāmudrā—
Lopāmudrā also spoke to that celestial sage, who is honored by the gods,
when the time of her season had arrived there at the hermitage site.
Desiring happiness, I wish to enjoy the objects of the senses with you,
provided that there may be a delightful home adorned with all kinds of jewels,
filled with elephants and chariots, and furnished with beds and excellent seats.
"O Sage, with graceful movements and eyes like fine silk garments, I shall unite with you; fulfill what you have intended.
Having heard this, the sage was delighted and in an instant summoned the Giver of Wealth (Kubera).
He caused a residence to be built, filled with heaps of jewels;
there the venerable Agastya dwelt happily in his own hermitage.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, offer the guest-offering (arghya) to that sage who acted in this manner.
O Pāṇḍava, through faith and devotion you shall obtain wealth;
when the sun has entered the sign of Virgo, on the seventh day from now. Whoever turns back when the sun has reached Virgo—
At the time of dawn, at the rising of the moon, the wise householder should perform his bath at night with white sesame seeds; likewise, wearing white garlands and garments,
he should place a flawless water-pot adorned with garlands and cloth.

Having fashioned a very beautiful golden vessel according to one's means, it should be provided with the five jewels, joined with a vessel of clarified butter, accompanied by various kinds of food, and endowed with the seven grains.

He was a sage in human form, tranquil, wearing a rosary and a sacred thread; holding a water-pot in his hand, he was surrounded by disciples and deer; he was the destroyer of death, a bearer of poison, and held darbha grass, akṣa beads, and a staff.
Then, one should place [the image] firmly fixed in that position with sandalwood paste;
it should be bathed and anointed with fragrant sandalwood,
worshipped with pleasing flowers, and perfumed with incense.
Thereafter, the *argha* offering should be presented; hear from me which substances are required for it:
dates, coconuts, pumpkins, and also trapusa gourds;
as well as karkoṭaka, karelā, karcūra, and bījapūraka fruits.
With eggplants, pomegranates, oranges, and plantains;
with sprouts of dūrvā grass, kuśa grass, and kāśa grass, as well as lotuses and blue water-lilies;
with various kinds of edible foods, cows, garments, and auspicious juices.
With seven kinds of grains that have sprouted, placed within a bamboo vessel—
or in a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or bamboo—
held upon his head while bowing down with both knees upon the surface of the earth.
Facing the south, O delighter of the Kauravas, one should offer the water for honor (*arghya*), the water for the feet (*pādya*), and so forth, with virtuous conduct, a focused mind, and devotion—
O you who resemble the *kāśa* flower and were born from Agni and Māruta.
O son of Mitra and Varuṇa, O pot-born one, salutations be unto you!
O cause of the growth and decline of the Vindhya mountains, O remover of the poison of the waters of the ocean,
O red-colored one, beloved of the gods and sages, O dweller of Laṅkā, salutations be unto you!
Salutations to you, the glorious husband of Lopāmudrā, by whom Vātāpi was devoured and the oceans were dried up in ancient times;
by whose rising even sins and diseases go to their destruction.
Salutation to that Agastya, together with his disciples and his virtuous sons.
A Brāhmaṇa should offer the *arghya* with a Vedic verse, saying: "Salutation to you!
Agastya, while digging, constantly desired the *bali* offering belonging to Prajāpati."
"Both castes, for the sake of favoring the rain, observed a fast; Satyadeva went forth without a tuft of hair.
Having thus offered the guest-water (arghya), O son of Kuntī, and having honored him with flowers, one should dismiss Agastya and bestow [the merit] upon a Brahmin.
To him who speaks of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, appearing in the form of a divine sage Vyāsa—
to such a one, he who performs the worship of Agastya with devotion shall offer a single fruit, grain, or even a vessel for residence, and then depart.
When that year is complete, O Pāṇḍava, one should again begin another [year],
offering the *arghya* for seven years in this sequence;
listen now with a one-pointed mind as to what fruit a man obtains thereby.
A Brāhmaṇa becomes learned in the four Vedas and proficient in all the scriptures;
a Kṣatriya obtains the entire earth girt by the oceans;
and even a Vaiśya attains long life, wealth in cattle, and rejoices.
For the Śūdras, there shall be wealth, health, and great honor;
for women, sons shall be born, and their good fortune shall increase with prosperity and growth;
and for widows, O son of Pāṇḍu, great merit shall increase.
A maiden obtains a husband, and one who is suffering is freed from disease;
in those regions where the worship of the sage Agastya is performed by people, the rain-god Parjanya becomes a showerer of rain according to desire.
Calamities are pacified and diseases likewise perish for those who recite or others who listen to the narrative of the sage Agastya;
they all become liberated from sin and, after dwelling long upon the earth, [attain their goal].

O best of men, mortals who so desire go to heaven by means of a celestial chariot yoked with swans; they obtain a home endowed with supreme prosperity, a healthy body for enjoyment, and abundance of cattle and sons—all that is dear to them—during the rising of the sage [Vallabha], if they offer what is highly precious along with other costly fruits, garments, and wealth. Thus ends the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa.
The one hundred and eighteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Gāstya Arghya Ritual Vow.
Description of the Abhinava-candra Arghya Vow.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Pārtha, O King, you who are like the moon to the lotus-faces of divine women,
listen now to the supreme ritual for offering libations (*arghya*) upon the rising of the new moon.
If the sun is seen in the western quarter (*vāruṇī*) divided into twelve parts, [then this rite should be performed].
O Pārtha,

at the time of dusk on the second day of the bright fortnight, when the twilight has arrived, one should offer an *arghya* oblation to the Lord; if the newly risen moon is seen upon the earth, [one should perform the rite].

Having prepared a mandala with cow dung and beautifully adorned it with sandalwood paste, one should worship the God— who is accompanied by Rohiṇī and who possesses the fragrance of the white water-lily—
with flowers, sandalwood, incense, lamps, unbroken grains (akṣata), and auspicious water.
O King of kings, with dūrvā sprouts, excellent jewels, curd, and white garments,
the Kṣatriya, together with his family priest, [should perform the rite] with this mantra:
"At the end of each month, being born again and again, you are ever new."
"O King Soma, be nourished; come together, salutation after salutation!
O Kunteya, he who, being composed, bestows a teacher who grants the fruit of all desires according to this rite month after month, [attains his goal].
That man on earth shall be blessed with renown, fame, and splendor;
surrounded by sons and grandsons, and abounding in cattle, grain, and wealth,
he shall remain in the mortal world for a hundred years and thereafter go to the city of Soma.

There, O best of kings, he dwells with a divine body, enjoying pleasures together with excellent women until the dissolution of all beings. If you desire righteousness and incomparable prosperity, then perform my word here month after month.
"O joy of the Lunar dynasty, with incense and flowers, offer the *arghya* to the newly risen Soma with your knees bent.

Thus ends the one hundred and nineteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Abhinavacandrārghya Vrata," in the *Uttara-parvan* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[This is followed by] the "Description of the Worship and *Arghya* Offering to Śukra and Bṛhaspati."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Now, therefore, O protector of the earth, listen to [the rites] for the pacification of an adverse Venus (pratiśukra),
whether at the commencement of a journey, during a departure, or upon the heliacal rising of Venus here on earth.

The worship of Śukra must be performed; listen to its essence. It should be conducted in a vessel made of silver, gold, or even bell-metal, adorned with white flowers and white garments, and filled with white rice.
Having placed a silver vessel containing pure semen together with pearls, he should present it, along with a cow and its calf, to a Brāhmaṇa, saying:
"Salutations to you, O Lord of all gods; salutations to you, O delight of Bhṛgu."
"O Kavi, for the sake of the accomplishment of all goals, accept this water offering; salutations be unto you!
Having thus presented the arghya, O son of Kuntī, one should prostrate and dismiss him, provided that the auspicious worship of Śukra has not been performed by the Sauhālakas.
O descendant of Bharata, for the sake of attaining their desires and wealth, women should not give gifts of *vaṭaka* cakes, *pūrikā* pancakes, wheat, or even chickpeas during his [the Moon's] rising,
nor should they undertake journeys and other such activities when he is thus exalted.
One shall obtain all harvests and indeed attain all desires;
likewise, O Yudhiṣṭhira, I shall describe the worship of Vācaspati.
[One should place] the priest of the Lord of the Immortals in a golden vessel, made of gold.
Having dressed [the deity] in yellow flowers and garments, and having bathed [him] with mustard seeds,
with fragments of palāśa and aśvattha wood, and with water consisting of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
one should then perform a ghee oblation for the one adorned with yellow unguents and garments.
Having prostrated, one should present [the image] along with a cow to a Brāhmaṇa, saying:
"Salutations to you, O Lord of the Aṅgirases, O Bṛhaspati, Lord of Speech!
Be our source of immortality for those afflicted by cruel planets."
Having thus worshipped the Preceptor of the Gods (Bṛhaspati) and prostrated before him, one should ask for his forgiveness;
by doing so at the time of a solar transit, at sunrise, or at sunset, one shall attain all desires.
Alternatively, [one may offer] pearls that are perfectly round and large.
Having meditated upon Bhārgava and Aṅgiras, one should bestow those very [mantras];
O joy of the Kurus, by the devout gift of pearls thus given,
the deformity of men's eyes during pilgrimages and festive occasions [is removed].

One who performs worship of Bṛhaspati is never born again [into this world]. O Bhārata, for those partakers of merit who, upon the rising of Venus, perform worship of Aṅgiras with garments and flowers with undivided minds, no obstacle arising from the retrograde motion of Śukra occurs in their homes as they enter them.

Thus ends the one hundred and twentieth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Arghya-Worship of Śukra and Bṛhaspati," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira;
followed by the description of the eighty-five vows. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Bhārata, I shall describe the eighty-five vows which have not been mentioned by any sages who perceive dharma,
though they are described in the Bhaviṣya, Matsya, and Mārtaṇḍa Purāṇas.
O Pāṇḍava, having taken up the Vārāha [Purāṇa], those [other Purāṇas] are recounted;
yet that collection of dharma which was not told to Sumitra, his disciple, and his son— what is the use of that which merely dwells in the belly?

O best of the Kurus, I shall tell you that which has been ascertained by me from the Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇas; for to whom else could this be taught? Having bathed at the morning twilight and having taken hold of a Pippala branch...
He who gives sesame vessels shall not grieve on account of that deed;
for this is the best of vows, the destroyer of all sins. Known as the "Vow of the Vessel," it has not been told by me to anyone else.
He who, on an auspicious day proclaimed by a Brahmin, joyfully gives pure gold along with a pair of yellow garments to one of perfectly pure gold—
this is the vow of Vācaspati, which bestows strength and intelligence.
Formerly, it was told by the Guru to the slayer of Vṛtra— that which grants all desires:
salt, pungent and bitter substances, cumin,
black pepper, asafoetida, ginger, and likewise all kinds of condiments.
On the fourth day, having eaten only one meal and having given food once to a householder,
O Bhārata, he should always provide stone-slabs at seven houses;
this is known as the Śilā-vrata, which bestows the world of Lakṣmī.
One should here diligently perform that which produces eloquence of speech:
having subsisted on food only at night for one year along with a cow,
one should give a golden discus and trident, as well as two garments, to a Brahmin householder.
Having bowed with devotion to the two lords of gods, may Śiva and Keśava be pleased.
This very vow, named *Eka-bhukta*, destroys even the greatest sins.
Having observed it for a year by eating but one meal a day, at the end of the year, one should offer according to one's ability a golden bull along with [other gifts].
One should give a cow made of sesame seeds, complete with all its necessary appurtenances;
this is known as the Rudra-vrata, which destroys both sin and sorrow.
O King, the man who performs this attains the state of Śaṅkara.
Having bathed with water infused with all medicinal herbs on the fifth lunar day, the householder who worships the five [implements] and makes the gift of the seven household articles— namely,
the mortar, the winnowing basket, the grinding stone, the cooking pot, and the fifth, the ladle— [attains great merit].
The water-pot, the hearth, and whatever else belongs to these [household items]:
that woman who, having established these in the home of the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), maintains them, never comes to grief.
O son of Pāṇḍu, this is known as the Gṛhavratam, which bestows all happiness; it was indeed narrated by Atri to Anasūyā. He who [offers] a golden blue lotus together with a vessel of sugar—

Endowed with faith, he who gives to a Brāhmaṇa householder attains the station of Viṣṇu; this is remembered as the Līlā-vrata. During the four months beginning with Āṣāḍha, a man should avoid the application of oil for anointing his body.

Furthermore, at the conclusion, one should give a new jar of sesame oil, as well as food consisting of milk-rice and ghee; such a person goes to the abode of Hari. This is called the Prīti-vrata, which brings joy to the world.
He who, during the month of Madhu, avoids honey and instead gives curd, milk, ghee, and sugarcane juice,
along with a pair of fine garments accompanied by vessels of flavorful liquids,
and honors a Brahmin couple while saying, "May Gaurī be pleased with me," [attains great merit].
This is known as the Gaurī-vrata, which bestows the world of Bhavānī.
A man who, having observed a fast at night on the thirteenth lunar day,
continues it for a year or on that same day, shall be free from obstacles.
One should give a golden Aśoka tree, draped with a pair of fine garments and accompanied by wealth, to a Brahmin, saying, "May Pradyumna be pleased.
O King, having remained in the abode of Viṣṇu for a kalpa, one shall thereafter be free from sorrow.
This is known as the Kāmavrata, which destroys all sorrow.
For the four months beginning with Āṣāḍha, one should avoid cutting one's nails;
likewise, one should consume eggplants and offer jars filled with honey and clarified butter.
On the full moon day of Kārttika, however, one should present a golden [image] to a Brāhmaṇa;
he attains the world of Rudra—this is remembered as the Śiva-vrata. Having thus observed the fifteenth day with a single meal, the man [attains this result].
Having worshipped the goddess Pūrṇimā and having drawn her image with sandalwood paste and other substances,
one should then present five jars filled with milk, curd, ghee,
honey, and sugar-candy to a Brāhmaṇa.
Fulfill my desires, for you are indeed the full moon;
through the gift of the five jars, may there be satisfaction for all beings.
Having thus paid homage to the twice-born, one shall attain all desires.
This vow, known as Pañcaghaṭa, bestows prosperity.
One should observe the vow during the Hemanta and Śiśira seasons while avoiding flowers;
and having offered three flowers on the full moon of Phālguna, one should then offer gold according to one's capacity.

One should indeed give [these gifts] at the proper time; may Śiva and Keśava be pleased! By performing this supreme Saugandhya-vrata—which produces fragrance for the head and grants eternal bliss to men—one attains the highest state.
He who avoids salt on the third lunar day starting from Phālguna,
and at the conclusion of the vow offers a bed along with household utensils in his home,
having honored a Brahmin couple [with the prayer], "May Bhavānī be pleased," [attains great merit].
By performing the supreme Saubhāgyavrata, a man shall dwell in the world of Gaurī for a kalpa. Having observed silence during the twilight prayers, upon its completion, he should offer a pot of ghee,
a pair of garments, and a bell to a Brāhmaṇa.
One goes to the station of Sarasvatī, from which a return [to this world] is difficult to obtain.
This is known as Sārasvata, which bestows beauty and knowledge.
Furthermore, on the fifth lunar day falling within the month of Lakṣmī, a man should observe a fast.
Upon its completion, one should present a golden lotus together with a cow;
he indeed goes to the abode of Viṣṇu, and Lakṣmī shall be his in birth after birth.
This is known as the Lakṣmī-vrata, which destroys suffering and grief.
But that woman who drinks water while causing a stream of water to fall,
should give a new *vartikā* lamp filled with a full measure of ghee.
This is known as the *Dhārā-vrata*, the supreme remover of all diseases.

Having installed Rudra accompanied by Gaurī, Janārdana together with Lakṣmī, and Sūrya accompanied by his queen, according to the prescribed rites— one who generates beauty and good fortune and destroys the pride of rival wives.
He who, having worshipped with white flowers, gives a beautiful bell together with a vessel and accompanied by the offering of incense to the best of the twice-born,
and having provided it with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and bowed down, should then bid them farewell.
This is known as the Devavrata vow, which bestows a divine body.
Having performed the anointing of Śambhu and Keśava,
one should maintain this vow until its completion and then offer a cow accompanied by water.
For ten thousand births he shall be a king, and thereafter he shall dwell in the city of Śiva.
Having heard this vow, which brings about manifold auspiciousness,
one should, with speech restrained, bow down to the Aśvattha tree, the Sun, and the Gaṅgā.
A man free from envy should observe the vow of eating once a day for eight months and one day;
at the conclusion of the vow, having honored a Brahmin couple along with three cows,
he should give a golden tree, and he shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
Abiding in a celestial chariot in heaven, he is served by hosts of apsarases.
This is known as the Kīrtivratam, which bestows the fruits of prosperity and fame.
Having performed the ceremonial bathing of Śambhu or Keśava with clarified butter, [one attains these rewards].
A Brāhmaṇa should fashion a lotus out of unbroken grains (*akṣata*) upon a circle of cow-dung for either the Sun, Gaurī, or Lambodara (Gaṇeśa). Having completed this,
he should present a golden lotus accompanied by a sesame-cow (*tiladhenu*).

One should give a pure [vessel] measuring eight finger-breadths; one is glorified in the world of Śiva. By singing the Sāmans, this is called the Sāma-vrata here. Having taken a single meal on the ninth lunar day, one should [feed] maidens according to one's ability.
Having fed [the Brahmins], one should present them with golden garments and cloths;
and by giving a golden lion to a Brahmin, one shall go to the city of Śiva.
For a hundred million births, he shall be handsome and remain unconquered by his enemies.
This is known as the Vīravratam, which bestows happiness upon women.
Whoever begins this vow on the fifteenth day while observing the milk-fast, should,
upon its completion, devoutly give five milch cows.
He who gives ochre-colored garments along with water-pitchers goes indeed to the world of Viṣṇu and delivers a hundred ancestors;
at the end of the kalpa, he shall become a king of kings— this is remembered as the Pitṛvrata.
Whether it be a woman or a man, whoever regularly offers betel-leaf along with areca nut and lime at the proper time,
then, at the end of the year, having had a golden image fashioned together with its fruit—
She who offers the three types of powder made of pearls shall experience neither misfortune nor foul odor of the mouth;
this is known as the "Leaf Vow" (patravrata), which produces supreme fragrance.
O son of Pāṇḍu, one should subsist on water obtained by begging for four months beginning with Caitra;
or for the month of Jyeṣṭha or Āṣāḍha, or even for a fortnight.
At the conclusion of the vow, one should give a water-jar accompanied by food and clothing.

Likewise, one who offers a vessel of sesame seeds accompanied by ghee and endowed with the seven grains, as well as gold, is glorified in the world of Brahmā; at the end of the kalpa, he shall become a king of kings. This is here called the Vow of Water (vārivrata).
Having performed the ceremonial bathing of Viṣṇu and Śiva with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), one should,
at the end of the year, again give a cow accompanied by the five nectars. By giving gold and a conch to a Brahmin, one attains the state of Śaṅkara.

At the end of the kalpa, he becomes a king; this is here called the *vṛttivrata*. Indeed, having avoided violence for a month or likewise for a year, at the conclusion of the vow, the wise man should, according to his ability, fashion a golden deer.
Likewise, one should give a cow together with its calf; such a person shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
This vow of non-violence bestows peace upon all men.
Having performed the ritual bath at dawn during the month of Māgha, one should honor a married couple.
Having fed [the Brahmins] according to one's ability and honored them with garlands, garments, and ornaments,
one attains great good fortune and supreme physical health;
one shall dwell in the world of the Sun for a kalpa— this is known as the Sūryavrata.
During the four months beginning with Āṣāḍha, a man should bathe every morning;
he should provide a meal to a Brahmin and, on the full moon day of Kārttika, become a donor of a cow.
Then, by giving a pitcher of ghee, he shall attain all his desires.
This is called the Vaiṣṇava vow; by it one attains the world of Viṣṇu.
One should abstain from honey and clarified butter from one solstice until the next. At the conclusion of that period, one should give meritorious gifts together with a cow made of ghee.

Having given [this], one goes to the state of Śiva; indeed, having given ghee and milk-rice (pāyasa), this is called the vow of moral conduct (śīlavrata), which bestows the fruits of virtue and health. He who offers the twilight lamp should avoid meat and oil.

Upon completion, one should offer a lamp before a golden discus and trident, as well as a pair of garments to a Brahmin; he shall certainly become radiant. This is known as the Dīpavrata, which always bestows splendor.
He who worships Gaurī for seven days by eating but one meal a day,
having worshipped Pārvatī with devotion using perfumes, flowers, and ointments,
should then anoint two married women with saffron.
One should smear her with flowers and with camphor, agallochum, and sandalwood;
having offered excellent betel-leaf as well as a coconut fruit,
one should say, "May the goddess Kumudā be pleased," and after prostrating, bid her farewell.
One should worship each goddess for as long as seven days;
then, when the seventh week is complete, one should invite those same seven.
Having fed them with food of the six tastes, one should honor them with ornaments according to one's ability.
Having adorned them with garlands, garments, earrings, and rings,
Kumudā, Mādhavī, Gaurī, Bhavānī, Pārvatī, Umā,
and Kālī should each present a mirror in their hand.
Having honored a single Brāhmaṇa, one should say to him: "May there be abundant food for you.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, this vow is named Saptasundaraka;
it makes the body beautiful and bestows supreme good fortune.
He who avoids perfumes and ointments during that month,
and having given a conch shell filled with fragrance and two white garments to a Brahmin,
should also give a sacrificial fee according to his ability; he attains all desires.
One attains the state of Varuṇa; this is indeed the Varuṇa-vrata.
Having restrained one's vows by avoiding salt during the month of Vaiśākha, one should then, at the end of the month, give a cow along with its calf to a twice-born man.
Having remained thus for a kalpa at the foot of Viṣṇu, one shall thereafter become a king here on earth.
This is the vow known as Kāntivrata, which bestows beauty and fame.
Having fashioned a golden Brahmāṇḍa placed upon a drona-measure of sesame seeds, [one should offer it].
Having observed the vow of sesame for three days, he should gratify the fire and a brahmin;
having honored a brahmin couple with garlands, garments, and ornaments,
he should say according to his ability, "May the Soul of the Universe be pleased," offering at least three palas of gold.
On an auspicious day, he who gives [this gift] attains the Supreme Brahman and is not born again.
This is known as the Brahma-vrata, which bestows the fruit of liberation upon men;
and so too for one who gives a "two-faced" cow accompanied by abundant gold.

He who observes the milk-vow for a day attains the supreme state. Having remained for three days on the milk-vow, he should offer gold, a wish-fulfilling tree, and rice of excellent quality, weighing more than a pala, according to his capacity.

Having given [a cow] covered with excellent garments and adorned with flower garlands, one shall dwell in heaven for a kalpa; this is remembered as the Kalpa-vrata. Furthermore, he who gives a beautiful young heifer adorned with neck-ornaments...
One should place upon its back a well-saddled, comfortable-to-touch elephant adorned with a bit,
provided with a vessel of sweetmeats and water and accompanied by betel;
it should be covered and placed there, with ice upon its tusks.
On such an occasion as this— during a *vyatīpāta*, an eclipse, or at either solstice—
one should remain without soliciting anything and then give [gifts] to a twice-born man.
This is known as the *Vāravrata*, which destroys the exhaustion of the journey.
It removes the supreme exhaustion and fatigue encountered on the journey to the other world;
one who eats only at night on the eighth lunar days for a year and gives eight cows at its conclusion attains the station of Indra—
this is called the Sugati-vrata.
O King, he who provides fuel during the winter and the cool season,
and offers a cow of clarified butter, goes to the Supreme Brahman;
it generates physical health and bestows luster and radiance.

The vow known as Vaiśvānara destroys all sins. O Pāṇḍava, he who, eating only at night on the eleventh lunar day, should offer a golden discus and likewise a conch shell during the Citrā constellation in the month of Caitra, [attains the supreme goal].
He who performs this with devotion shall attain the abode of Viṣṇu.
This is known as the Viṣṇu-vrata; at the beginning of the Kalpa, it brought about the attainment of sovereignty.
One who observes the milk-vow on the fifth lunar day and, at the conclusion of the vow, gifts a pair of cows [attains the same].
One shall dwell in the world of Lakṣmī for a kalpa; this is known as the vow of the Goddess (Devīvratam).
On the seventh lunar day, one who eats only at night should, upon completion, give a milch cow;
he attains the world of the Sun; this is here called the vow of Bhānu.
On the fourth [lunar day], one who eats only at night should give eight cows and perform the fire-oblation;
this is the vow named Vaināyaka, which destroys all obstacles.
He who, having renounced great fruits, [observes this] during the four months for the sake of a twice-born man—
In the month of Kārttika, a person should give golden [images] along with a pair of cows,
a pair of white garments, and jars filled to the brim;
this is known as the Phalavrata, which always brings about the attainment of fruits.

And he who, having observed the fast on the seventh day at the end of the year, should give a golden lotus and cows with their calves along with bronze milking vessels according to his means— O King of kings, he should devotedly present these to a Brahmin who is a reciter.
This is known as the Saura-vrata, which bestows the world of the Sun.
He who, having fasted for twelve Dvādaśīs while engaged in the consumption [of specific foods],
at the end of the year offers jars filled with water along with garments, [attains that goal].
Twelve [cows] should be given here for the fulfillment of all desires;
this is known as the Govinda-vrata, which bestows the state of Govinda.
He who, on the full moon day of Kārttika, performs the release of a bull and observes the *nakta* fast, [attains the goal].
He attains Goloka; this is remembered as the Vṛṣavrata.
At the conclusion of the vow, a cow should be gifted, and furthermore, food should be provided according to one's capacity.
This Prājāpatya vow has been described here for the Brahmins.
One who eats only at night on the fourteenth day and gives a pair of cows at the end of the year attains the state of Śiva; this is to be known as the Tryambaka-vrata.
Having fasted for seven nights, one should give a jar of ghee to a twice-born man.
They say this is the Brahma-vow, which bestows the world of Brahmā. At the end of the month, he should give a cow; at the conclusion, a milch-cow.
He shall dwell in the world of Śakra for a kalpa; this is remembered as the Śakra-vow.
O lord of men, on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika,
a wise man, having fasted, should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) at night;
[specifically] the urine of a tawny cow and likewise the dung of a black cow.
O King of kings, having taken the milk from a white cow, the curd from a red one,
and the clarified butter from a brindled cow,
one should mix them together along with water infused with *kuśa* grass, while reciting the mantras prescribed in the Vedas.
Then, at the time of dawn, having bathed, offered libations to the deities,
and caused the Brahmins to recite auspicious prayers, he should eat while remaining pure and restrained in speech;
for this is the Brahmakūrca vow, which destroys all sins.
Whatever was done in childhood, in youth, and even in old age—
all that perishes in an instant through the Brahmakūrca fast.
Furthermore, the man who eats food not cooked by fire on the third lunar day [attains great merit].
By giving a cow, one attains Śiva, from whom there is no return.
This is known as the Ṛṣivrata, which brings about all auspiciousness.
A golden chariot weighing more than two palas, yoked with a pair of horses, [should be given].
Having fasted and offered a white garland together with a pair of garments upon a measure of sesame seeds, one shall dwell in heaven for a hundred kalpas; at the end of that time,
one shall become a king of kings— this is remembered as the Agnivrata.
Having fashioned an excellent golden chariot weighing more than two *pala*s, joined with two couches and equipped with all necessary implements,
a man shall dwell in Satyaloka for a thousand kalpas and then become a sovereign of the earth.
Having fasted and given this auspicious Karivrata, one should abstain from mouth-perfumes;
at the conclusion of the year, one should become a giver of a cow.
One attains the Lord of the Yakṣas; this is called the Sumukha-vrata.
Having stayed in water during the night, one should become a giver of a cow at dawn;
he attains the world of Varuṇa, and this is called the Varuṇa-vrata.
Furthermore, he who performs the Cāndrāyaṇa penance should offer a golden moon.
This is declared to be the Candra-vrata, which bestows the world of the Moon. In the month of Jyeṣṭha, one who performs the penance of the five fires at evening and gives a golden cow goes to heaven.
Furthermore, on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days, this is remembered as the Rudra-vrata.

He who applies anointment in a temple of Śiva on the third lunar day goes to heaven like a giver of cows; this is called the Bhavānī-vrata. On the seventh lunar day at night during the month of Māgha, one should wear wet clothes and become a giver of a cow.
Having performed the Tāpana vow and observed the fast, one shall dwell here in heaven for a kalpa and then become a king;
having given [the gift], one shall dwell in heaven for a hundred kalpas,
and at the end of that, one shall become a king of kings— this is known as the Aśva-vrata.
Likewise,

O best of men, having fasted for three nights, one should give on the full moon day of Phālguna a golden chariot, equipped with all its furnishings and yoked to two elephants, as well as a beautiful mansion, for a duration of two kalpas.
He attains the world of the Sun, honored by gods and demons;
he reaches the celestial realm, a dwelling endowed with the power of his vows.
By worshipping a married couple at the three junctions of the day while observing a fast and adorning them with ornaments, he attains this state.
On the full moon day, one attains liberation here through the Indu-vrata; likewise,
O King of kings, by giving on the second day of the bright fortnight a meal of salt to the Moon,
along with a bell-metal vessel, clothing, and a sacrificial fee.
At the end of the year, the giver of a cow goes to the abode of Śiva;

at the end of the kalpa, he becomes a king of kings—this is remembered as the Somavrata. On the first lunar day (pratipad), one who eats only a single meal and, at the end of the year, gives away a tawny cow (kapilā).
He goes to the city of Vaiśvānara; this is called the Āgneya vow.
On the eleventh day of the month of Māgha, and on the fourteenth and eighth days as well, he who gives young goats and antelope skins while subsisting on a single meal [attains this result].
O Great King, a wise man who, according to his capacity, gives sandals, blankets, umbrellas and the like, as well as saws and other tools in the month of Caitra,
shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice from the Brāhmaṇas.

This is known as the Saukhya-vrata, which bestows all happiness. Having eaten only one meal on the tenth day, at the end of the year-long period, one should give ten cows and golden images of the quarters (the cardinal directions) in the form of women, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
One who stands upon a drona-measure of sesame seeds becomes the sovereign of the cosmic egg (Brahmāṇḍa).
This is known as the Viśvavrata, which destroys even the greatest sins.
Having worshipped on the seventh lunar day of the bright fortnight, he who [offers] seven measures of grain to the Sun...
He who, eating only at night, gives salt to a twice-born man,
delivers seven or eight generations of his lineage as well as himself.
This is known as the *dhānyavrata*, which bestows wealth and grain.

He who, having fasted for a month, gives a beautiful cow to a Brahmin, goes to the abode of Viṣṇu; this is remembered as the Bhīma-vrata. He who, having fasted for a fortnight, gives two tawny cows to a Brahmin...
He attains the world of Brahmā, honored by the best of the gods;
having fashioned a golden earth weighing more than thirty palas, he should give it along with the principal mountain ranges and accompanied by sesame seeds and garments.
Having placed [the image] upon a drona-measure of sesame seeds and given it to a householder Brahmin, one should observe a milk-vow for a day; such a person is honored in the world of Rudra.
This is declared to be the Mahī-vrata, which endures through seven kalpas.
In the month of Māgha or Caitra, one should become a giver of a cow made of molasses;
observing the vow of molasses on the third lunar day, provided with all necessary utensils,
one attains the world of Gaurī and is honored by hosts of celestial nymphs.

This Umā-vrata is proclaimed as the constant bestower of bliss. By eating only one meal a day for a year and giving vessels of food and water, one shall dwell in the world of Śiva for a kalpa; this is remembered as the Prāpti-vrata.

Having consumed cow’s urine and barley-gruel on the third lunar day of the month of Kārttika and so forth, one shall dwell in the world of Gaurī for a kalpa; thereafter, one shall become a king here in this world.
This is known as the Rudra-vrata, which brings about great auspiciousness.
He who, having fasted for three nights during the month of Caitra and bathed in a river,
gives five milch goats to a Brāhmaṇa householder,
is never again born in the world of the living.

This is declared to be the vow of the goat, which destroys all diseases. Furthermore, he who performs the gift of a maiden in marriage and he who causes the wedding to be performed goes to the world of Brahmā, accompanied by twenty-one generations of his lineage.
There is no gift superior to the giving away of a daughter in marriage;
O King, for those who shall perform this, there is an imperishable world in heaven.
Having fashioned an elephant out of sesame paste and adorned it with gold—
In the same manner, one should fashion an image made of *kuśa* grass, provided with a rider,
accompanied by a garland of constellations, bearing a chowrie and a crest-ornament,
with eyes fixed upon the tips of its teeth, and endowed with a pair of red garments.
Having offered a portion of cooked rice or prepared sweetmeats in a copper vessel,
one should give them to a Brahmin couple after honoring them with garlands and ornaments. Then,
free from impurity, one should enter waist-deep into water.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, this was indeed spoken by the Maker of the Forest;
it restrains even evildoers within the difficult terrains of the forest,
both in this world and in the next— of this there is no doubt to be made.

Those men who perform the Pauraṃdara vow on this auspicious day shall attain the world of Indra until the dissolution of all beings. Furthermore, by observing a milk-vow on the fifth lunar day and giving a serpent [image] to a twice-born man, one attains the same reward.
No fear arising from serpents shall befall those who,
having fasted on the eighth day of the bright fortnight, present a bull covered with white cloth and adorned with bells and ornaments.
One shall dwell in the world of Śiva for a kalpa, and thereafter become a king here on earth.
This is proclaimed as the Vṛṣavrata, which bestows all dharmas. When the northern solstice has arrived, he who [worships] Hari with a prastha of ghee...
O King, he who, having bathed, bestows a mare upon a Brāhmaṇa,
shall dwell in the world of the Sun, endowed with all desires and accompanied by his sons and brothers; this is here called the Rājñī-vrata.
On the ninth day of the lunar fortnight, one should worship the Goddess dwelling on the Vindhya mountains with a single meal,
and then offer a golden cage adorned with parrots, along with flowers and incense,
to a peaceful Brahmin; that man shall become eloquent.

This is declared to be the Āgneya vow, which bestows the station of Agni. By giving a meal consisting of meat and sugarcane juice to a Brahmin on the twelfth lunar day for the sake of the Guhyakas, one goes to the abode of Hari.

A man who delights in even one of the yogas beginning with Viṣkambha performs this vow known as Āgneya, which bestows the station of Agni. He who gives, in due order, clarified butter, oil, fruit, and sugarcane juice during these [yogas], [attains the same reward].
Barley, wheat, chickpeas, niṣpāva beans, and śāli rice;
salt, curd, milk, and cloth; gold, as well as blankets, a cow, a bull, an umbrella, and a pair of sandals.
Camphor, saffron, sandalwood, and flowers,
as well as iron, gold, copper, and silver— O Yudhiṣṭhira,
