one who has bathed according to the rules with these substances to the best of one's ability is liberated from all sins.
One does not suffer separation; this is known as the vow of Yoga.
On the full moon of Kārttika, one should eat only at night and give a ram; in Mārgaśīrṣa, a bull;
and in the months beginning with Pauṣa and Māgha, indeed all [the animals] should be made of gold.

Gradually, all the zodiac signs (rāśis) were adorned with garments and garlands on every full moon day, O son of Kuntī, accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees. This is known as the Rāśivrata, which destroys all calamities.
Likewise, it fulfills all desires and bestows the world of Soma.
O son of Pāṇḍu, these eighty-five vows have been recounted to you;
by hearing which, even a killer of a Brahmin, a killer of a cow, or likewise a killer of a father or mother [is purified].
One is liberated at that very moment from major sins as well as minor offenses.
O King, I have described to you these eighty-five vows which bestow great happiness and wealth.
For one who performs, hears, or recites this, the world of the Lord of the Gods remains as if held in the palm of his hand.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Eighty-five Vows," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira;
followed by the description of the rules for the Māgha bath. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
The Kṛta age is declared to belong to the Brāhmaṇas, while the Tretā age belongs to the Kṣatriyas.

They say the Dvāpara age belongs to the Vaiśyas, and the Kali age is remembered as belonging to the Śūdras. O King, in the Kali age, there is laxity among men regarding the performance of ritual bathing.
Nevertheless, under the pretext of the month of Māgha, I shall speak to you; listen.
He whose hands, feet, speech, and mind are well-restrained, and who possesses knowledge, austerity, and renown—he enjoys the fruit of the sacred fords.
One who lacks faith, one whose soul is sinful, an atheist, one whose doubts are not severed, and those who rely solely on reasoning— these five do not partake in the fruit of the sacred fords,
even if they reach Prayāga, Puṣkara, or Kurukṣetra.

"Wherever one may bathe, one should do so constantly during Māgha; such is the Vedic revelation. Any rivers that do not flow to the ocean yield the fruit of three nights; those flowing to the ocean yield the fruit of a fortnight; and the Lord of Rivers (the ocean) yields the fruit of a month."

Bathing near dawn, during the twilight, or when the sun has risen, is equal to the Prājāpatya penance and destroys even the greatest sins. That brahmin who, having risen in the morning, always performs his morning bath [attains this merit].
Freed from all sins, he attains the Supreme Brahman.
Bathing in warm water is in vain; recitation that is non-Vedic is in vain;
a Śrāddha performed for one who is not learned in the Vedas is in vain; and a meal eaten without witnesses is in vain.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, those who know the rules of bathing have declared that there are four kinds of baths;
listen now to each separately: the Vāyavya, the Vāruṇa, the Brāhma, and the Divya.
The Vāyavya bath consists of the dust raised by cows, while the Vāruṇa bath takes place in oceans and other such bodies of water.
The Brāhma bath is that which is prescribed by the Brāhmaṇa mantras; the Divya bath is that involving clouds, water, and the sun. Among all baths, the Vāruṇa is the most distinguished.
This applies to the student (brahmacārī), the householder (gṛhastha), the forest-dweller (vānaprastha), and the mendicant (bhikṣuka).
All these—
children, youths, the elderly, men, women, and eunuchs—
always praise bathing during the month of Māgha; having bathed in a sacred ford during the auspicious Māgha, they obtain their desired fruit.
For the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas, bathing accompanied by mantras is prescribed;
however, O descendant of Kuru, for Śūdras and women, it is performed silently.
In the month of Māgha, when the sun has slightly risen, the waters proclaim: "Blessings! (raṭanti).
Whether one is a slayer of a Brahmin or a drinker of liquor, we purify that very person.
There, the palaces are made of gold and the women are like Apsarases;
there, rivers flow with streams of curd and have mud of milk-rice for their banks.
There they go and immerse themselves— those who, like ascetics, travel the path in silence, free from malice, at sunrise during the month of Māgha,
if they desire abundant enjoyments and houses as radiant as the moon and sun.
Between the months of Pauṣa and Phālguna, a man should become one who bathes at dawn;
beginning from the full moon and the new moon,
he should perform his ablutions for thirty meritorious days while the sun is situated in Capricorn.
Having risen there, one should undertake the observance according to the prescribed rule,
making a mental resolve with the thought: "Throughout this entire month of Māgha, I shall install the god Mādhava here at this holy ford which always possesses cool water."
He who, with his body uncovered, performs a difficult bath,
obtains at every step the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice;
O youth, having bathed there in that auspicious tīrtha and having applied earth to his head, he attains this merit.
O King, one should offer the arghya to the Sun according to the rites prescribed in the Vedas;
having satiated the ancestors while remaining there, and then descending from that water,
one should bow to one's chosen deity and worship Puruṣottama.
One should worship the god named Mādhava, who bears the conch and the discus;

having offered oblations into the fire according to the prescribed rite, one should thereafter eat but a single meal. Sleeping on the ground and observing celibacy, the capable practitioner should perform the ritual ablution.
For one who is incapable but wealthy, that [bathing] is said to be performed according to his own will.
"The ritual bath in Māgha must certainly be performed"—such is the sacred revelation (śruti).
According to the Lord's desire, dharma follows after strength.
One who bathes with sesame seeds, one who rubs oneself with sesame, one who eats sesame, one who offers water with sesame,
one who performs oblations with sesame, and one who gives sesame— this "sixfold sesame" person does not perish. Oil and *āmalaka* fruits should always be offered at a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*).
Likewise, he should kindle the fire for the sake of providing a windless place for the twice-born.
Thus, at the conclusion of the bath, food should be offered without restriction;
one should feed a Brahmin couple and honor them with garments and ornaments.
Blankets, skins, and jewels, as well as various garments,
divine tunics, and likewise bedspreads;
and a pair of sandals, along with hidden sweetmeats that liberate one from sin.
By this rite, one should give [the gift], saying, "May Mādhava be pleased.
One is liberated from the sins of approaching those who should not be approached, theft, and the acquisition of forbidden property—
even if committed in secret— provided one performs the ritual bath.
Together with his fathers, grandfathers, and likewise great-grandfathers;
together with his mothers, maternal grandfathers, and likewise maternal great-grandfathers—
having enjoyed desired pleasures along with twenty-one generations of his lineage.
Having bathed at dawn during the month of Māgha, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
That man who performs his ablution at dawn in the month of Māgha, when the river's beautiful current is reddened by the rays of the sun—
having delivered seven generations of ancestors on both the paternal and maternal sides— he departs for heaven, bearing a stainless body.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Māgha Bath," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[Now follows] the description of the ritual for daily bathing.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Purity and the purification of one's being are not possible without bathing;
therefore, for the sake of purifying the body, bathing is prescribed at the outset.
One should perform the bath with water that is either gentle or forceful.
The wise knower of mantras should prepare the sacred site (tīrtha) with the root mantra.
"Obeisance to Nārāyaṇa" is declared to be the root mantra.
Holding darbha grass in his hand, the learned one, having sipped water according to the rule, should remain pure and self-controlled.
Having fashioned a square measuring four cubits on all sides, the wise practitioner should invoke Gaṅgā with these mantras:
"Oṃ! You are born from the foot of Viṣṇu; you belong to Viṣṇu, and Viṣṇu is your deity."

"Protect us from that sin from birth until the end of death. Vāyu declared: "O Jāhnavī, there are thirty-five million sacred fords (tīrthas) in heaven, on earth, and in the intermediate space; they are yours."
Your name among the gods is Nandinī, and also Nalinī;
you are remembered as Kṣamā, Pṛthvī, Vihagā, Viśvakāyā, and Śivā;
likewise, you are Vidyādharā, Suprasannā, and Lokaprasādinī.
One should recite these auspicious names at the time of bathing: Kṣemyā, Tathā, Jāhnavī, Śāntā, and Śāntipradāyinī. By doing so, Gaṅgā, who flows through the three paths, becomes present there.

O King, having consecrated water seven times with the mantra, one should place it upon the crown of the head while joining the palms together; one should perform the bath with clay in the same manner, having consecrated it according to the rule three, four, five, or seven times.
O Earth, trodden by horses, trodden by chariots, and trodden by Viṣṇu;
O Clay, take away all that evil deed which has been committed by me!
You were lifted up by the boar Kṛṣṇa with his hundred arms.
"Salutations to you, O upholder of the life-breath of all worlds, O lady of excellent vows!
Having bathed in this manner and thereafter having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the rules,
one should rise and put on two fine, white garments."
Thereafter, one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) for the nourishment of the three worlds:
"The gods, yakṣas, as well as nāgas, the hosts of gandharvas and apsarases;
all the cruel ones, the suparṇas, the hyenas, the birds, and the sky-dwellers."
For the sake of the nourishment of those Vidyādharas, those who dwell in the clouds, those who move through the sky,
those living beings who are without support, and those who are devoted to sinful deeds—
for them this water is offered by me.

Having placed the sacred thread over the left shoulder for the gods, one should thereafter wear it around the neck (nivītī) and satisfy the humans with devotion, as well as the sons of Brahmā and the sages:
Sanaka, Sananda, and Sanātana as the third; |||
May Kapila, Āsuri, Voḍhu, and Pañcaśikha likewise—
may they all always attain satisfaction through the water offered by me.
[And may] Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu [attain it].
One should satisfy Pracetas, Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, and Nārada,
as well as all the divine and brahminical ṛṣis, with water and unbroken grains (akṣata).
Then, having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya) and resting the left knee upon the ground, one should proceed.
One should devotedly satisfy the Agniṣvātta, Barhiṣad, Haviṣmat,
Uṣmapa, Sukālita, Bhauma, Ājyapa,
and Somapa ancestors with water mixed with sesame seeds and sandalwood paste.

Holding *darbha* grass in his hand, he should duly offer libations according to name and lineage (*gotra*) to the ancestors beginning with the father, as well as to the maternal grandfathers; having offered these libations according to the rule and with devotion, he should recite this mantra:
"May all those who are my kinsmen or not my kinsmen, and those who were my kinsmen in another birth, as well as whoever desires [offerings] from me— may they all attain complete satisfaction.
Then, having sipped water according to the rule, one should draw a lotus in front.
One should diligently offer the *arghya* oblation together with unbroken grains (*akṣata*), flowers, sesame seeds, and red sandalwood, while reciting the names of the Sun:
"Salutations to You who possess the universal form; salutations indeed to the friend of Viṣṇu."
Salutations always to you, the thousand-rayed one, the embodiment of all splendor;
salutations to you whose body is everything, salutations to you who possess all power;
O Lord of the World, adorned with divine sandalwood, may there be salutations to you.
O Padmanābha, salutations to you who wear earrings and armlets;
salutations to you, O Lord of all worlds, who are worshipped by all the asuras.
You always know perfectly both good deeds and evil deeds.
"O Satyadeva, salutations to you; O Sarvadeva, let there be salutations to you!
O Divākara, salutations to you; O you who consist of the three Vedas, let there be salutations to you!
Having thus paid homage to the Sun and having performed the circumambulation three times, [one should proceed].
Having touched a twice-born man, a cow, or gold, one should then proceed to the temple of Viṣṇu.

Indeed, daily bathing has been declared by the lords of sages to be the remover of sin, the cleanser of impurity, and always bestowing happiness. Therefore, with a mind intent on dharma, this should be performed here by a man either in rivers, in houses, or in tanks.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Rules for Daily Bathing," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the Ritual for the Rudra-Bath.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Janārdana, tell me the procedure for the ritual of the Rudra-bath.
It pacifies all evils and bestows all peace upon men.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
[I praise] Skanda, the invincible commander-in-chief of the gods and son of Rudra.
Agastya, the tiger among sages, spoke to him as he sat comfortably:
"O Kumāra, by the grace of Śaṅkara you are indeed omniscient;
tell me, for whom and how does the bath according to the Rudra-vidhāna take place?"
Rudra said:
For a woman whose children have died, one who is unfortunate and childless, one who has lost a son,
one who has only daughters, or one who is barren— for these, the performance of this bath is prescribed.
Devoted to fasting on the eighth or the fourteenth day,
she should perform the rite at the confluence of two rivers— especially of two great rivers— on the fourth day of her pure menstrual period, or when it falls on a Sunday.
Then, in a temple of Śiva, a cow-pen, or a secluded courtyard of his house,
he should request a twice-born man who maintains the sacred fires, who is tranquil, knows the Dharma, is devoted to truth,
and is skilled in fierce rites, to perform the ritual bathing for the deity.
Then one should construct a square pavilion sloping toward the north,
adorned with garlands of sandalwood and smeared with cow-dung.
In its center, one should draw a lotus flower completely filled with white powder.

One should install Mahādeva in the center upon the pericarp (karṇikā). One should place Śakti and the others upon the petals according to the fourfold ritual procedure, and one should assign the world-protectors (lokapālas), beginning with Indra, to the other petals.
One should install the Goddess and Vināyaka at his side;
having offered the arghya, along with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and rice mixed with jaggery,
one should present various kinds of edible foods and diverse fruits.
O Brahmin, one should place a water-pot adorned with *aśvattha* leaves in each of the four corners, filled with all medicinal herbs;
thereafter, one should offer an oblation to the spirits in the four directions of the pavilion.
In the south-eastern direction, near the pavilion,
the fire-rite (agnikārya) should be performed in an auspicious pit (kuṇḍa) adorned with flowers and leaves;
[the oblation consists of] salt mixed with mustard seeds, along with ghee and honey.
One should perform the oblation with the *mānastoka* mantra when the homa for the nine planets has been completed.
Appoint a second Brāhmaṇa to perform the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*),
and an *ācārya* who recites the *Rudra* hymns and is anointed with white sandalwood paste.
Clad in white garments, wearing a white garland, and auspicious,
adorned with bracelets, necklaces, earrings, and finger-rings,
one who stands near the mandala should recite the Rudra hymns, free from envy.
One should recite those [mantras] once more until eleven have been reached.
A second auspicious mandala should be prepared like the mandala of the deity. In its center, that woman should be adorned with white flowers.
Covered in white garments and anointed with white perfumes,
while she sits upon a comfortable seat, the preceptor, meditating on Rudra,
should then consecrate her with water from the hollow of a *nāgakeśara* leaf.
With sixty-four varieties of Rudra and eleven [recitations],
one should employ seven hundred and four flawless *mantras* for the purpose of bathing.
Having brought earth from a horse stable, an elephant stable, an anthill, a confluence, a lake, a courtesan’s quarters, a royal palace,
and a cow-pen, as well as all medicinal herbs, yellow pigment (rocanā), and waters from river-tirthas;

Having condensed these [substances] into a well-worshipped jar designated as "Śiva," a certain woman of virtuous character should smear them all over the body of the lady, specifically from the soles of the feet to the hair, and especially upon her belly.
Then, one should bathe her with a water-pot over which the Rudra-mantra has been recited; subsequently,
she should be bathed with eight water-filled pots filled with *aśvattha* leaves,
positioned in every direction, along with fruits and unbroken grains (*akṣata*).
Having bathed in this manner, one should give a cow and likewise gold to the bath-attendant.
Herein, the reason is also specified: the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is a milch cow.
O son of Pāṇḍu, [this applies] to the Brāhmaṇas as well as others, according to one's own capacity.
Having given a calf, gold, and other such gifts, one should ask forgiveness for everything.
O King of kings, by performing this Rudra-bath, a beautiful woman becomes fortunate,
endowed with happiness, and possessed of many sons.
For indeed, among all months, this is auspicious and esteemed by the Brahmins;

therefore, it must certainly be performed by one who desires the welfare, prosperity, and happiness of their sons. O Bhārata, that woman who, endowed with faith and with her body bowed low, performs the bath known as the "Rudra" bath with the approval of the best of the twice-born, destroys all defects from the parts of her own body and becomes beloved by her husband, possessing living children.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Bath of Rudra," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[Now follows] the description of the ritual for the bath during lunar and solar eclipses.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"I wish to hear about that bath which is prescribed during lunar and solar eclipses, and regarding the substances and food, primarily. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
I shall now describe the ritual bath, accompanied by mantras and medicinal herbs, for one who encounters a total eclipse occurring over his own birth asterism.
Having encountered a lunar eclipse, one should perform the recitation by Brahmins.
Having first honored four Brahmins with perfumes, garlands, and ointments,
and having brought together medicinal herbs and other substances prior to the eclipse,
one should place four jars before them, thinking of them as the oceans; [filling them] from an elephant, a horse, a carriage-track, an anthill, a confluence, a lake, and a cow-pen.
Having brought earth from the vicinity of the king’s gate, one should cast it into the jars;
likewise, one should place the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and the five gems (pañcaratna) therein,
along with yellow pigment (rocanā), a lotus, and a conch shell, together with the five-fold medicinal herbs (pañcabhaṅga).
Having placed all of these— crystal, white sandalwood, water from sacred fords, mustard seeds, ivory, saffron, as well as ushira and guggulu— into the jars, one should invoke the deities.
May all the oceans, rivers, sacred fords, rain-clouds, and lakes come to the patron of the sacrifice, bringing about the destruction of his misfortunes.
He who is the wielder of the thunderbolt, the god regarded as the lord of the Ādityas—
May Indra, the thousand-eyed, dispel my suffering here;
may the lord of the hosts of Rākṣasas, who is manifest as the wind of universal destruction and is exceedingly terrifying with sword in hand, dispel the affliction caused by the Rākṣasas.

May that Śaṅkara— the creator of the drop, the Bindu, the wielder of the Pināka bow, whose vehicle is the bull— destroy the sins of the lunar eclipse. Whatever beings there are in the three worlds, both stationary and moving, [may he destroy their sins].
"May those [vessels], joined with Brahmā, Arka, and Viṣṇu, indeed burn away my sin!
Thus addressed, the pitchers, filled with water and accompanied by the [four] Yugas,
were honored with the mantras of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, and with white garlands and unguents.
One should honor the Brahmins, who are one's chosen deities, with gifts of clothing and cows.
O best of men, having inscribed these very mantras upon golden plates, they should then be placed upon the head of the patron.
When the occasion of an eclipse has arrived, one should prepare water-pots filled with ritual substances;
once the lunar eclipse has ceased,
having performed the auspicious rite of *godāna* and bathed, one should present a white cloth to a Brāhmaṇa.
Whoever performs this ritual bath along with the planetary offerings shall suffer no affliction from the planets, nor shall there be any loss among their kinsmen;
they attain supreme perfection, from which a return to worldly existence is difficult to find.
During a solar eclipse, one should always recite the name of the Sun within the mantras.
O descendant of the Kuru lineage, it is said that the bath should be performed with those very same materials.
Any person who would constantly hear this, or even cause others to hear it, [attains great merit].
Freed from all sins, he is glorified in the world of Śakra.

O King, during a lunar eclipse or a solar eclipse, the man who recites me while consecrating auspicious water with these mantras and performs his bath according to the rule— him no affliction caused by the planets shall ever again torment.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for Bathing during Lunar and Solar Eclipses," in the *Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the *Uttara Parvan*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[Now follows] the description of the Sāṃbharāyaṇī vow.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"When death has arrived, how does a householder give up his life?
Tell me this, O Govinda, for my curiosity is great.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
The wise have declared that there is no other austerity superior to fasting;
I shall describe its characteristics, that which is to be chanted by one about to die,
and the form in which the Blessed Lord Janārdana is to be meditated upon.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, knowing that his own time has arrived, the wise man—
having shaken off the stain of impurity, bathed, and with a restrained mind—
should then worship Hṛṣīkeśa with flowers, incense, and other offerings.
One should worship with prostrations, praises, meritorious acts, perfumes, and incense;
having given gifts to the Brahmins and to those who are disabled or otherwise needy,
one should also offer to the Brahmins whatever is required for the worship of the deity and other such purposes.

O King of kings, one should repeatedly turn away from the sense of "mine" regarding relatives, sons, wives, fields, grain, wealth, and so forth, as well as the circle of friends. One should likewise regard friends, enemies, neutrals, others, and one's own kin again and again [with equanimity].
One should not think of [the world] with excessive malice, nor with [excessive] favor;
therefore, O King of kings, being self-restrained, one should perform the renunciation of all actions, both auspicious and inauspicious, and utter this speech:
I renounce all enjoyments; I abandon all my friends. Indeed, I have cast aside my food, my ointments, my garlands, ornaments, and the like, as well as my songs, gifts, and even my seat.

Sacrifices and the like performed for the sake of others, those rites that have come down as daily obligations, as well as occasional and optional rites, and the duties of ancestral offerings and so forth—
these are abandoned; likewise, the duties pertaining to the stages of life (āśrama-dharma) and the duties pertaining to the social classes (varṇa-dharma) are renounced.
Moving about on my feet and hands, performing actions and bearing burdens,
may I commit no sin against anyone; may all living beings be righteous and free from fear—
those who dwell in the sky, those in the water, and those upon the earth.
Those who dwell in crevices of the earth, those within the hollows of stones,
and those among grains, clothes, beds, and seats—
they shall awaken by themselves; I have granted them freedom from fear.
I have no kinsman whatsoever except for Viṣṇu, the teacher of the world;
and Viṣṇu is on my side as a friend— below, above, and likewise again on my flanks, my head, my heart, my two arms, and my two eyes.
"In all [senses], beginning with the ears, Viṣṇu is established as my [Self].
Having thus renounced everything and holding onto Acyuta, the Lord of All, one should incessantly chant the name of the God: "Vāsudeva."
O Indra among kings, he lies upon darbha grass with its tips pointing south, with his head toward the east or toward the north, meditating on the Lord of the World—
Viṣṇu, the Victorious, Hṛṣīkeśa, Keśava, and Madhusūdana.
Nārāyaṇa, Nara, Śauri, Vāsudeva, Janārdana; Vārāha, Yajñapuruṣa, Puṇḍarīkākṣa, Acyuta;
Vāmana, Śrīdhara, Kṛṣṇa, Nṛsiṃha, and Aparājita.
Padmanābha, the Unborn, the Lord of Śrī, Dāmodara, Adhokṣaja, the Lord of all lords, the Pure, the Infinite, the one whose form is the universe;
the wielder of the discus, the wielder of the mace, the Peaceful, the wielder of the conch, whose banner is Garuḍa.
I bow to the imperishable one who wears the crown and the Kaustubha gem.
O Lord of the Universe, I am here; dwell within me swiftly.
Let there be no difference between us, just as there is none between the wind and space.
"This is Viṣṇu, this is Śauri, this is Kṛṣṇa before me—dark as the petal of a blue lotus, with eyes as broad as lotus petals. Let this Lord look upon me; I behold Adhokṣaja."

Thus, with a one-pointed mind, remembering Hari, the Lord of All, he should recite this while remaining equanimous amidst pleasure and pain, as well as toward friends and enemies. He should constantly recite: "Oṃ, obeisance to Vāsudeva."
In whatever manner the desire may arise, one should recite the name accordingly;
and one should meditate upon Viṣṇu, the Lord of the gods of gods, whose form is enchanting,
with serene eyes and eyebrows, and who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace.

Having made the mind single-pointed in resolve, one should meditate upon the form of Kṛṣṇa together with his consort— his chest adorned with the Śrīvatsa mark, possessing a beautiful countenance and four faces, wearing a crown, clad in yellow garments, and bearing lovely armlets.
Or whatever form the mind fixes its steadiness upon that of the Wielder of the Discus—
one should contemplate that very form and proclaim, "Vāsudeva.
Thus, constantly chanting and remembering the essential nature of the Supreme Self, [one attains liberation].

O bull among men, even a person burdened with every sin attains dissolution in Acyuta— the Lord of the gods of gods, the most worthy of praise— provided he possesses supreme magnanimity regarding his life-force and has his mind and ultimate refuge fixed upon Him.
Just as fire, when joined with the wind, consumes masses of grass,
so too does the resolve for fasting undoubtedly destroy the sins of men.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
At the time of the departure of the elements, the mental faculties of living beings become deluded;
how much more so for those afflicted by the defects of disease, let alone those free from old age and sickness?
One who is utterly consumed by extreme age and tormented by disease [is likewise overwhelmed].
If one is unable to remain on the ground upon a bed of darbha grass,
is there any other means for the practice of fasting by which one does not incur deficiency? Tell me that, O Janārdana.
"You have mentioned meditation, O Blessed One; tell that to me according to its true nature. Describe the entire essence of meditation, O Janārdana.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
In this matter, neither the ground, nor the kusha grass, nor even one's own bedding is the cause;
for one who has made the forest his home, the mind alone is the cause—
whether standing, eating, sleeping, walking, or running hither and thither, Vishnu himself is the cause here.
At the time of departure, by remembering Govinda, one becomes absorbed in Him.
Whatever state of being one remembers when casting off the body at the end,
to that very state one goes, O son of Kuntī, for one is always permeated by that state of being.
Therefore, the primary mantra is the meditation upon Vāsudeva.
Whatever meditation you have asked about, that very thing I shall describe to you.
O Pārtha, this was previously told to me by the wise Mārkaṇḍeya.

When, due to delusion, excessive desire and longing arise for the enjoyment of sovereignty, beds, seats, and vehicles, as well as for women, perfumes, garlands, jewels, garments, and ornaments, those who know the truth declare that this is the meditation known as *ārtadhyāna* (painful meditation). When compassion does not arise in one's heart toward beings undergoing cutting, burning, beating, and torment, nor toward those subjected to blows, subjugation, and mutilation, those who know the truth declare that this is the meditation known as *raudradhyāna* (cruel meditation).

The virtuous proclaim that *dharmya-dhyāna* consists of the investigation of the meaning of the Sūtras, the cultivation of the Great Vows, reflection on the causes of bondage, liberation, rebirth, and transmigration, as well as the pacification of the five senses and the attainment of tranquility.

But the Siddhas proclaim that *śukla-dhyāna* belongs to one whose senses are not distracted by objects, who is free from the fluctuations of conceptualization born of mental construction, and whose heart is fixed solely on reality, with an inner self that is perfectly composed.

In the first [type of meditation], there is certainly rebirth as an animal or in the lower realms; however, in fierce meditation, the result is always hellish, while in righteous meditation, the auspicious fruit is birth among the gods. Oh, in the pure [meditation], there is the destruction of rebirth! Therefore, a wise person should exert effort in that most excellent meditation which is white—wholesome, which removes the disease of birth, sustains one through saṃsāra, and crushes the dust of passion. Indeed, [the fruits last] seven thousand years in water, eleven in fire, and sixteen in wind.
"Sixty [cows] in the house of cows, eighty in battle, and at the time of fasting, O Bhārata, there is imperishable destiny.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Sāṃbharāyaṇī Vow," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira;
followed by the "Description of the Ritual for the Consecration of Wells, Ponds, and Tanks."
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "O God, best among those who know the ordinances, O highly blessed one, son of Devakī, tell me the procedure for the inauguration of a tank."
What mantras are proclaimed for the waters of the ponds and wells?
Who are the officiating priests here, and what sacrificial posts (yūpas) are to be prepared in the sacrificial pit and pavilion?
What gift is prescribed here, and what offerings (balis) are proclaimed?
"At what time and in what manner should one perform it? Tell me all of this.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"Excellent, excellent, O mighty-armed one, that you question me thus!"
I shall describe to you the consecration of tanks, ponds, and wells:
when they are completed, their embankments secured, free from all fissures,
provided with rows of steps, and lined on all sides with stones.
In that [reservoir] filled with water, especially during the month of Kārttika,

the ritual for a pond (taḍāga) should be performed when there is a conjunction with a fixed asterism (sthiranakṣatra). Some sages maintain that it should be done after the sun has passed the winter solstice (uttarāyaṇa).
For in this matter, there is no fixed rule regarding time, since the water is the authoritative standard.
One should cause an auspicious mandala to be constructed at the edge of the dam of the pond,
measuring ten or twelve cubits and very spacious with four gates.
Furthermore, wise men should construct four archways in the four directions made from the branches of the Aśvattha, Udumbara, Plakṣa, and Vaṭa trees;
they should also arrange banners of various colors all around them.
In the center, a magnificent great banner of five colors should be fashioned.
There should be an altar four cubits in size, or perhaps five cubits, in the middle;
it should be adorned in the center with a sacrificial post (yūpa) according to the measurement of the patron.
A sacrificial post made of *kadaṃba*, *aśvattha*, *pālāśa*, or *vaikaṅkata* wood is prescribed as auspicious for this Brāhmaṇa by those learned in the Vedas;
for Kṣatriyas, one born from *nyagrodha* or *bilva* is declared, as well as one made of *khadira*.
The sacrificial post (yūpa) of a Vaiśya is made of Udumbara wood originating from Madhvarjuna;
that of a Śūdra is prescribed as being made of Bibhītaka, Udumbara, Śāka,
or Śālmali wood, or alternatively, of heartwood.
There, one should delineate the eight world-protectors with colored powder:
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Kamalā, and Ambikā;
likewise, Sāvitrī should be fashioned together with them, and one should then worship them with flowers and incense.
The wise man should construct four sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) in the four directions,
each measuring one cubit on all sides and provided with three girdles (mekhalās).
Sixteen or eight officiating priests (hotṛs), adorned with golden ornaments, should be appointed.
The officiating priests (sthāpaka) appointed here were clothed in unwashed garments, adorned with garlands and sandalwood paste; they had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences,
were conversant with the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, were pleasant of speech, and free from envy.

Vessels made of clay and those of copper, as well as the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, should be prepared; likewise, the side dishes, the sacrificial fuel (*samidh*), and sesame seeds must be ready for the fire oblation (*homa*).
A wise person should perform the *homa* according to the prescribed rules for the sacrifice to the planets (*grahayajña*).
And for the deities who have been consecrated upon the altar, a fire-oblation (homa) is prescribed;
likewise, with mantras dedicated to Varuṇa, one should offer oblations that increase prosperity.
This is done for the world-protectors, Indra and the others, according to the sequence starting from the east.
One should offer the bali-oblation with mantras bearing those specific characteristics for the accomplishment of all aims.
At the gates, one should place water-pots containing gold and sprouts;
auspicious garlands of sandalwood should be made from the sprouts of the Aśvattha tree.
One should have a tortoise made of gold, likewise a crocodile of copper;
a fish of silver, and likewise a frog of tin;
and one should have a porpoise and a leech made of silver alone.
One should place all of them in a copper vessel according to their respective positions;
one should consecrate them with the mantra "This is the installation (pratiṣṭhā).
Thereafter, the installation of the sacrificial post (yūpa) must be performed according to the procedure prescribed in the Vedas.
Having anointed [the image] with saffron, one should worship it with flowers and incense;
having honored it with a pair of garments, one should present the food offerings and so forth in due order.
Then, the most excellent of the twice-born, having cooked fresh *caru* rice, [should proceed].
Then one should offer oblations into the fire in the sequence of "bhūḥ," "bhuvaḥ," and "svaḥ.
Thereafter, one should invoke the god Varuṇa, the lord of rivers,
with the sounds of musical instruments, songs, perfumes, garlands, and ointments.
One should wrap the head with a white cloth alone;
then, taking a copper vessel while preceded by the chanting of the Veda (*brahmaghoṣa*),
one should go to a body of water of immeasurable extent and offer it to Varuṇa.
One should cause it to flow into the middle of the water with the mantra "tvaṃ varuṇa.
Whatever else there may be—clothes, seeds, and so forth—all that should be submerged in the water.
Then, one should cause a cow to cross over and proceed toward the north from the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
A wise man should wrap his head with a cloth if one is available;
then, taking the tip of the plow and descending into the water,
the performer, accompanied by his kinsmen and his wife, should immerse himself.
Then, having descended from the water and given that cow to a Brāhmaṇa,
one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one's ability and thus dismiss the Brāhmaṇas with these words:
"This water has been given by me in common to all beings."
Having thus offered the ceremonial handful of water (jalāñjali), one should worship the Mothers of Water (Jalamātṛs).
All laborers should be gratified, and one should worship the spades.
For three days, the materials should be given away without restriction, preceded by the recitation of mantras.
And for one day, according to his ability, he should not practice stinginess regarding wealth;
[he should give] a thousand cows, or half of that, or even half of that again,
or a hundred, or fifty, or even twenty-five.
In the absence of these, one should give a cow with its calf and a bronze milking vessel.
O King, this procedure for a pond has been fully described to you;
now I shall likewise explain the rules for constructing large and small wells.
One should perform the preparation of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), the pavilion (maṇḍapa), the ornaments, the coverings, and so forth;
as well as the installation of the sacrificial posts (yūpa) and the crossing over [of the water], according to the procedure for the construction of a tank (taḍāga).
One should cause jars with Akālamūla plants to be placed at the corners of the pond.

Having cooked the sacrificial oblation (caru) there according to the prescribed rite, in quantities as required, he should offer those [pots] filled with water from sacred fords (tīrtha), smeared with white sandalwood paste, covered with pairs of white garments, adorned with garlands, and containing precious gems.
One should offer four oblations in sequence with "Bhūḥ," "Bhuvaḥ," and "Svaḥ.
One should perform the oblation to the planets (grahahoma), which increases peace and prosperity.
One should also present an offering (bali) to Varuṇa and to the guardians of the world (lokapālas).
The best of the twice-born should recite the hymns dedicated to Varuṇa.
In the center of the altar, a lotus mandala is recommended;
in its midst, one should worship Śambhu, as well as Brahmā and Keśava.
One should consecrate the fish, tortoise, and frog in the center of the sacrificial altar with the mantra:
"You are the friend of all beings, the giver of wealth to those who desire wealth;
you are the physician for those overcome by disease, and the refuge for those seeking protection."
With this very mantra one should dismiss Varuṇa;
at the outset, one should especially invoke the deity with this same mantra:
"Salutation to you, the protector of the universe; salutation, O Viṣṇu, Lord of the waters."
"O Lord of Gods, manifest your presence here just as you do in the ocean.
Then, O King, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given to the Brahmins;
a cow should be given to the consecrator (sthāpaka), and food should be provided without restriction."
This ancient rule applies to all:
water that has come from a river is traditionally considered the first choice;
however, water situated in a watering hole or a pond shall also be pure.
The first water found in a large pond, a well, or a tank becomes entirely undrinkable; that water is equal to the water of a woman who has recently given birth.
For even the ocean, O son of Kuntī, is a divine source and the lord of waters.
One should not rashly touch the Unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) even with the tip of a blade of kusha grass.
"Agni is the heat within your body; may he be gracious. Viṣṇu, the depositor of seed, is the navel of immortality.
Speaking these words of truth, O Pāṇḍava, one should then plunge into the Lord of Rivers.
When the month of Vaiśākha has arrived, as well as the asterism presided over by Varuṇa,
one should devotedly offer an oblation (arghya) to the great ocean at that time,
having bathed in the sea according to the rules with the sacred mantras, being composed in mind.
One should offer the arghya with fruits, roots, unbroken grains (akṣata), and edible foods. Even the sin that a man commits throughout a thousand births—
he is liberated from all those sins by bathing in the salt waters.
This must be performed by a Brāhmaṇa who knows the ritual rules according to the prescribed injunctions;
both the performer and the one who causes it to be performed shall go to heaven. However, he who performs it while ignorant of this rule, being deluded regarding his purpose, [attains no such merit].
Both the one who performs the work and the one who causes it to be performed go to hell.
He who does not cause peace to be established through works such as the construction of tanks and the like— everything he undertakes is fruitless for him, like seed sown in barren soil.
The performer of meritorious deeds ascends a divine celestial chariot composed of all kinds of jewels, possessing a radiance like that of the sun and moon and endowed with splendor.
Someone drinks that water from a watering place, and then offers a handful of it.
Whether it be a Brahmin, an ascetic, or a cow, by which means the performer does not suffer;
once the rite is completed and his purpose fulfilled, a well-wisher should perform a great festival.
For eight days, the patron should provide a grand feast and a great offering.
Furthermore, those men who are the agents of the work, such as the master builders and others,
indeed go to heaven by virtue of their merit consisting of *iṣṭāpūrta* (sacrificial rites and charitable works).
As for those living beings that perish while a portion of the earth is being excavated, [they too attain a higher state].
Or, O best of men, for the sake of a painted image of Devakūṭa, they all go to the third heaven; indeed, for as many hair-pores as there are on the cow here,
for that many thousands of years and hundreds of millions of years [they dwell there].
The builder of a pond shall dwell in heaven for a thousand million yugas; O Lord of the Earth, if any of his ancestors have fallen into hell,
he delivers them all as well as himself.
"The ancestors clap their hands and the great-grandfathers leap for joy, thinking:
'Will one born in our family build a tank?
O son of Kuntī, provide water accessible to the land even at the cost of your entire wealth."
One may save seven generations of one's lineage where there is a cow that quenches thirst;
yet even by staying for a hundred years in the Kṛttikā forest,
it is better to dwell for a single month in the house of Ceta, for wealth perishes in a mere moment.
When these four— a pond, a temple, a step-well, and a grove of densely leafed trees—
are constructed, one obtains a fourth part of the merit;
just as a son describes his own character through his own virtues to his mother.
Likewise, through the taste [of the water], all the merit and demerit of the maker [accrues to him].
Therefore, one should cause substances obtained through merit to be poured into tanks and the like.
Having reached a tank adorned with trees, travelers [find relief] for the fortunate man.
Having drunk the water, they rest and delight at the foot of the trees;
with hands whose tips are formed by waves stirred by the wind, the wise man has prepared this lotus-adorned pond for the arrival of guests.
By that excellent son, through whom water from the earth was offered to all beings, both families were delivered;
for he manifested the form of the naturally perfected and desired [deity] as revealed by mantra.
O King, through the performance of sacrifices and works of public utility, a man becomes one who has fulfilled his purpose;
yet, O Pārtha, it is by him whose fame— whether high or low— has been made manifest that his mother becomes truly possessed of a son, for he is a moon to the three worlds.
One who constructs a pond on the earth, O Lord, or one who builds a temple for the gods, should lead the three [classes of beings] to humility and the three [qualities] to the highest exaltation;
in this world, his fame shall become stainless.

He alone truly lives; he alone becomes free from old age and death. Even though others may attain heaven by performing boundless rites, his body, consisting of glory, remains forever free from affliction.
A person of meritorious deeds rejoices in heaven for as long as their fame remains imperishable;
likewise, they dwell in the celestial realm of Tilā until that merit is exhausted.
There, they behold a cluster of lotuses adorned with stalks whose tips are darkened by the beaks of swans.
Blessed are those who behold their own lake being drunk by great throngs of villages;
for what else can be described of that [lake] from which all living beings drink its water with jars, cupped hands, mouths, or the hollows of their palms?
It is said that a lake arises near the edge of a city for a fortunate person;
the accomplishment of wealth is seen for both the maker and the people,
provided that their temple is completed upon the shore of that lake.
O Pārtha, what can be said of those who have constructed temples for their chosen deity?
As long as the structure— whether it be a small shrine or one as vast as a valley— is not leveled with the earth,
the builder is honored in heaven.
A well dug in the house of one who enjoys its fruits, containing sweet water and equipped with a strong rope,
purifies the family up to the seventh generation;
for people constantly drink the sweet water from that well.
What merit has not been performed by him who benefits all sentient beings, he who constructs beautiful temples for the deities? His fame wanders extensively through the paths of his lineage;
and the builder always enjoys divine pleasures. Having experienced immeasurable happiness, he shall once again become a universal monarch upon the earth.
For them there are ponds with abundant water, wells, sacrificial posts, and shelters;
they are exempt from the declarations of Yama regarding the gift of food and sweet speech.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Consecration of Ponds, Wells, and Tanks," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the Ritual for the Completion of a Tree Planting.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O son of Devakī, tell me of the greatness of planting trees.
And [he taught] the procedure for the concluding rite (udyāpana), along with its secret teachings, in brief.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"Five excellent trees are those that grow from the earth; ten are those that grow from the wood of mountain trees."
With many sons born of the dead, who are devoid of dharma and purpose, they perform the libations for their ancestors with leaves, flowers, fruits, and roots;
yet it is better to have a single tree by the roadside where people may find rest.
The excellent trees, thick with foliage, gladdened living beings with their shade, bark, and sprouts; they gratified the gods with flowers and the ancestors with fruits.
[They provided] flowers, leaves, fruits, shade, roots, bark, and wood.
Blessed are those trees whose branches do not pass by fruitless for those who seek them;
whereas sons may or may not perform the ancestral Śrāddha at the end of the year,
trees indeed produce nourishment and welfare for others every single day.
A son born of a wife does not bring such happiness as an agnihotra sacrifice,
nor even as a tree planted by the roadside that provides dense shade;
for a grove of trees is blessed when it possesses both shade, flowers, and fruit.
Like a noble wife, she follows her husband into both worlds;
like a woman scattering the fruits of the *aśoka* tree, her face is adorned with *tilaka*; and like a courtesan, this garden is always full of aesthetic delight, providing every enjoyment.
He who plants a tree is always a pilgrim, he always bestows gifts, and he always performs a sacrifice. One *aśvattha*, one *picumanda*, one *nyagrodha*, and ten *ciñciṇīkā* trees.
One who plants a triad of *kapittha*, *bilva*, and *āmalakī* trees, or five mango trees, shall not behold hell.
He who offers to a twice-born man a tree rich in flowers, fragrant with abundant fruit,
shall indeed obtain a home resembling a celestial chariot (*vimāna*), filled with many jewels and abounding in women.

Since you have rested there without weariness, seeking shelter, consider this: what desired fruit was not obtained by one who is hungry? Reflect upon this: were trees not planted for the sake of the next world?
Were lotus-pools not dug, and were great trees not grown?

What has been gained by that son who was born as a thief of his mother’s youth? Great trees provide shade for others, yet they themselves remain in the heat; they bear fruit for the sake of others, not for their own sake.
Henceforth, O Pārtha, I shall proclaim the ritual for the consecration of a tree,
which pacifies all sins and increases all renown;
[this was performed] in ancient times on Mount Mandara by Pārvatī, who was childless.

Aśoka, the quencher of grief, was adopted as a son. O wise Yudhiṣṭhira, listen now to those rites for him, such as the birth-ceremony and others, as they are indeed described in the Caraka and Tripurāṇa.
Then, a young tree— possessing thick leaves at its base, with spreading shade and tender shoots, and capable of enduring cold, wind, and heat— should be consecrated;
provided it is not thorny, nor named after a woman, nor stunted, nor infested by insects or scorpions, nor hollow within.
O Pārtha, a tree that is not approved by the virtuous should not be planted; rather,
having cleared that spot where a well-constructed, auspicious, and enclosed square water-basin has been prepared, one should then have it planted in a well-guarded manner.
O Pārtha, the concluding rite (udyāpana) for trees is always highly praised.
On an auspicious day declared by a Brahmin and endowed with favorable planets and constellations,
one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) of the tree, adorned with banners, on the preceding day.
Having covered it with red cloths, one should wrap it with a red thread;
one should sprinkle the tree with flour-paste and all medicinal herbs.
A wise person should place full water-jars in the four directions.
All the trees in their vicinity should be decorated with sprouts, smeared with white sandalwood paste, draped in pairs of white garments, filled with jewels within,
and adorned with banners.
Flasks placed at the base and wrapped with red threads,
smeared with beautiful red, yellow, and white powders,
and [adorned] there with fifteen or ten fruits made of gold.
One should consecrate the straight *sarala* sticks together with their seeds in a copper vessel; then,

amidst the sounding of musical instruments and auspicious music, the preceptor who knows the mantras should scatter the sacrificial offering (*bali*) in the four directions for Indra and the other world-protectors, as well as for the spirits (*bhūta*).
Then, at the clear dawn, having prepared a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with its surrounding girdle,
one should commence the rite of pacification (śāntikarma) according to the procedure for the sacrifice to the planets (grahayajña).
Having selected Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas and adorned them with gold ornaments, [one should proceed].
One should honor four or eight [deities] with garments according to one's ability;
furthermore, an oblation of sesame seeds and clarified butter should always be performed, as it brings about satisfaction and nourishment.
Having first established the Mother [Goddess], one should worship her with flowers and unbroken grains of rice.
Having properly cooked the sacrificial oblation (caru), overflowing with milk-rice and other offerings,

and having bathed the tree with water from sacred fords while reciting mantras— beginning from the fire-oblation and the birth-rite, and continuing up until the rite of hair-cutting (godāna)— one should proceed.
One who knows the ritual procedure should perform the birth rite, the naming ceremony, and the first feeding of solid food; he should pierce the ears with a golden needle,
and there, the tonsure ceremony should be performed in due order using a razor made of gold.
One should tie on a girdle made of muñja grass and cause [the initiate] to put on the garment.
Then the sacrificer, having bathed, wearing white clothes, and being pure,
should approach with a handful of flowers and utter this mantra:
May those trees— the ornaments upon the peaks of mountains, those who have established their dwellings in the Nandana groves and other forests,
and those who grant the desires of gods, humans, serpents, and *kiṃnaras*— be the dispellers of the afflictions of my misfortunes as I bow before them.
While these twice-born ones offer oblations into the fire according to the prescribed rites, may that sun, stationed in the sky, behold this.
"O tree, you have been chosen by me with the thought that you are my son; therefore, you must always perform for me the duties of a son.
Having spoken thus and caressing that tree again and again, he should look at his own face reflected in a vessel of ghee and utter a blessing.
"You are born from limb after limb; you are produced from the heart.
You are indeed the self (ātman) named 'son' (putra); live for a hundred autumns!
Then, with joyful minds, sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) should be given to the Brāhmaṇas.
Having given an auspicious cow to the officiating priest, one should perform a great festival;
food should be provided without restriction to the poor and the helpless,
and those others should be given wine and liquor with a joyful heart.
One should eat at will together with one's own kinsmen and relatives;
all servants and laborers should be honored according to one's ability.
O Pārtha, he who thus performs this great festival for trees—
One attains all desires both in this world and in the next;

yet without sons, men cannot attain an auspicious state, for with wicked sons there is likewise the destruction of both worlds. Having reflected on this, the wise man, after protecting the trees, should beget sons according to the ancient injunctions.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Concluding Ceremony of a Tree," in the *Uttara-parvan* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[Now follows] the description of the ritual for the worship of the gods. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Those men who construct abodes for the forms of the Thirty-three Gods, which are enchanting to the eyes of virtuous people,
possess a body made of fame that wanders through the world after their physical body, consisting of the supreme reality, has perished.
He who causes to be built for the gods a temple white as a lofty mansion, with a gateway as pale as white clouds—
Having attained happiness in heaven within a palace as white as the moon, he comes to enjoy the glory of sovereignty on earth endowed with wisdom.

Those who cause images of the deities to be made in divine temples out of gold, silver, iron, stone, or copper, shine upon their thrones wearing armlets and crowns, honored by rays from the crest-jewels of tributary kings.
Those who consecrate the best of gods with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) are themselves consecrated by the hosts of gods upon the summit of Mount Meru.

Those who anoint the faces of the gods with sandalwood from the Malaya mountain, the king of mountains, and with excellent saffron, shall attain the lordship of the gods for a divine kalpa and again obtain an incomparable royal consecration.

With bodies fragrant with divine perfumes and fine garments, they rejoice in the Nandana groves together with the Apsarases. Those who daily worship the gods with fresh flowers—divine blossoms such as the richly scented Jāti, Kamala, and Utpala—shall attain the status of a king and before long reach the perfection that is white as a Kunda flower. Those men who incense even the foremost of the gods with fragrant incenses of Himālaya turuṣka shall delight in a celestial abode in heaven, filled with palaces and delightful with the exquisite scent resembling a mass of camphor.

He is fanned by excellent whisks adorned with golden handles and beautified by lovely white earrings; having performed worship with celestial garments, garlands, and unguents, and with the very air of the abode of the Lord of the Gods as his offering, he shines brilliantly in a golden celestial chariot suffused with the luster of rubies glowing like the sun. Surrounded by divine women and enchanting to the eye, he illuminates the palace of the gods with a stainless lamp.

He who keeps vigil, beloved by the foremost of gods, on festival days such as those of Caitra, accompanied by the sounds of trumpets and songs sung with sweet voices from lutes and flutes by slender-waisted Kinnarīs— he dwells in heaven. Those who, full of devotion, perform the cleansing of the temple of the foremost of gods with fine stones and mineral pigments,
they dwell in heaven upon a floor of lapis lazuli, variegated with golden inlays and adorned with strings of pearls.

And he who, endowed with supreme devotion, offers to the gods a bell, a canopy, an excellent chowrie, and a parasol; adorned with armlets, necklaces, jewels, and earrings, that lord of gems dwells as a sovereign of the entire earth. One should worship with various flowers those whose lotus feet are praised by the God of Gods;
bowing with a joyful mind and devotion, they become gods who have attained the fruits of the greatness of Bhūr, Bhuvar, and Svar.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for Worshipping the Deities," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[Now follows] the description of the ritual for offering lamps.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Blessed One, by what austerity, vow, or discipline,
or by what kind of gift, does one become radiant in the world—
possessing such great, blazing splendor, shining with rays like those of the sun?"
"You ought now to tell me that by which the body is produced.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O Pārtha, in former times in Mathurā, there was an ascetic named Piṅgala."
He arrived and was honored by my wife Jāmbavatī;
when questioned regarding this very matter, he spoke exactly as it happened.
She, too, related all of that to me, and I shall tell it all to you.
Whenever, O best of kings, an auspicious time arrives—
during the transit of the sun, a solar eclipse, a lunar eclipse, a parvan, or the Vaidhṛti yoga;
when the northern solstice has arrived, or likewise during the southern solstice and the equinoxes.
On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight, on the fourteenth at the end of the day,
or on the seventh or eighth, a man or woman devoted to the vow, having bathed with purified limbs,
should offer [the gift] to the gods of the earth (the Brahmins).
With a jar of ghee as a lamp, [he saw] a lamp burning brightly.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Madhusūdana, that which was spoken by you—that they are called 'the gods of the earth' (bhūmideva)—"
"What is this curiosity of mine? You ought to sever my doubt.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"In ancient times, at the beginning of the Kṛta Yuga, there was a king named Triśaṅku."

O best of men, he desired to go to heaven in his physical body; however, he was reduced to the state of a caṇḍāla by the high-souled Vasiṣṭha. Thereupon, Triśaṅku related everything to the wise Viśvāmitra.
Under the sway of wrath, he also performed a sacrifice after summoning the deities;
they did not accept the oblation, whereupon the son of Kuśa,
Viśvāmitra, became enraged and by his power created other supreme gods.
Out of anger, the sage released Śṛṅgāṭakas, Nālikeras, Pacanas, Ānājauḍakas, Medhārathas, Dvārtākas, Tārikūṣmaṇḍakas, Kodravas, Uṣṭras, Manujadevas, and others.
He created seven other supreme gods as the Ṛṣis for each month.
Then Śakra, having approached Viśvāmitra and propitiated him, restrained the creation; yet those who had already been created remained as they were.
And all those gods in the world of mortals, as well as in the divine abodes,
were bound by mantras and remained within the ritual cakes (piṇḍīs), bearing their respective forms—
namely Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and whatever other hosts of deities there may be.
Having descended to the mortal world for the benefit of the worlds,
they remain eternally within their images and enjoy perpetual delights;
they grant boons to their devotees— this is the secret that has been declared.

Before them, a blazing lamp should be offered to the Sun, with a full wick saturated in ghee and wrapped in a red cloth; one should cause it to be presented, burning brightly with four *prasthas* of ghee, while reciting this mantra:
“The wise ever behold that supreme abode of Viṣṇu,
like an eye stretched across the sky.
[Salutations] to Kṛṣṇa with the yellow garment, and to the Trident-bearer with the white garment.
One should cause [a lamp] to be offered for Gaurī with a rich safflower-dyed cloth;
for Durgā, one should kindle a full wick dyed with lac;
and for Kāma and Gaṇanātha, [one should offer] with a blue cloth and [fuel] made of khadira wood.
One should offer a black cloth to the Nāgas, reeds for the planets, and weapons for the deities;
one should awaken the *pitṛvarti* for the ancestors.
Listen to the specific detail: for the Sun, a full wick (*pūrṇavarti*) is prescribed.
For Śivā, there was the Īśvaravarti; for Janārdana, the Bhogavarti;
for Viriñca, the Padmavarti; for Gaurī, the Saubhāgyavarti;
for the Nāgas, the Nāgavarti; and for the Planets, O Yudhiṣṭhira, the Grahavarti.

O King of kings, listen to this Vedic mantra with which one should awaken Lalitā after she has been honored and worshipped with a cloth for her eyes, honey, and ghee in a vessel of honey. *Oṃ namo bhagavatyai lalitāyai madhuparkam arpayāmi svāhā.* || 1 || *Oṃ namo bhagavatyai lalitāyai madhu ghṛtaṃ ca arpayāmi svāhā.* || 2 || *Oṃ namo bhagavatyai lalitāyai madhukuṇḍakam arpayāmi svāhā.* || 3 || *Oṃ namo bhagavatyai lalitāyai pūjitāyai carcitāyai ca prabudhyasva svāhā.* || 4 ||

“O Agni, at the beginning, with a song born of longing, they have sung all those songs to you— those who dwell in fair abodes, each separately— singing for the sake of desire within the beloved domains of Agni.”
"Kāma is the sovereign ruler of what has been and what is to be; he alone shines forth. To both of them, Svāhā!
In this manner, whoever offers a lamp according to this rite, placed within a large and wide vessel filled with a jar of ghee—
They go to the abode of Brahmā by means of a celestial chariot with the splendor of the sun;
they remain there, radiant, until the dissolution of all beings.
For indeed, in a place where there is a lamp, the eyes possess great power.
Likewise, O King, those who give lamps become possessed of fruitful vision;
just as the flame of a lamp always moves upward,
so too does the beautiful upward path of the giver of lamps come to be.
O King, a lamp should be offered with ghee or else with oil;
it should never be offered with fat, marrow, or similar substances. A lamp made with oil should be used, but never one made for ritual purposes by one who understands the law.
Extinguishing a lamp and its destruction are both censured;
by performing such an act, one becomes "Flower-Eyed" (Puṣpitekṣaṇa).
A stealer of lamps becomes blind, while the one who extinguishes it becomes one-eyed.
By offering a wick made from lotus fibers ignited with scented oil,
a person becomes free from disease and endowed with good fortune;
likewise, by lighting a lamp with camphor for the God of gods.
One obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and uplifts one’s entire lineage.
O moon of the Kuru dynasty, I have thus described to you in its entirety the fruit of offering lamps.
Having heard this, you should indeed constantly offer lamps in the dwellings of Brahmins and the abodes of the gods, exactly as prescribed.
In this regard, they cite this ancient history,
O sinless one, concerning what was formerly attained by Lalitā through the gift of a lamp.
There was a lord of the earth named Citraratha in the land of Vidarbha.
To that king were born one hundred and fifteen sons;
he had only one daughter, known by the name Lalitā,
who was endowed with all auspicious marks and possessed a beauty unparalleled on earth.
The King of Kāśī gave that Cārvaṅgī to Cārudharman;
Cārudharman had three hundred other wives,
and among them, Lalitā became his chief queen.
In the temple of Viṣṇu, she would daily light a thousand lamps,
burning them without ceasing day and night,
during the dark fortnight of Āśvayuja and the bright fortnight of Kārttika.
A lamp lit for her was auspicious when placed in a high position;
at that time, as well as always in the Brāhmaṇa’s dwelling,
she would be busy in the evening, intent on sending out the lamps.
At crossroads, on main roads, and in temples;
at sacred trees, in cow-pens, and on the summits of mountains;
and on the sandy banks of rivers and at the bases of wells, O Pāṇḍava.
Then her co-wives, having gathered together, respectfully asked her this:
"O Lalitā, may you be blessed; speak words that are pleasing, for neither in offerings of food and flowers nor in the worship of the twice-born was she so devoted."
"Your great effort in lighting this lamp is such that it excites our utmost curiosity, O Lalitā.
We believe you must have certainly heard of the fruit of giving lamps."
Lalitā said:
"I am not envious, O auspicious ones, nor am I defiled by passion and the like;
you virtuous women, devoted to a single husband, have bestowed honor upon me."
May those who practice the Dharma without deviation listen to my words: by me,
this fruit of the gift of a lamp is enjoyed according to my desire—
a wife beloved for her gold and a sublime daughter of the King of Mountains.
In the land of the Madras, that best of rivers is known as Umādevī;
she was indeed brought down by Brahmā for the sake of compassion toward human beings.
Have you heard of that Devikā, the destroyer of sins?
By bathing even once in that river, one attains the status of Gaṇapati.
Furthermore, in that very place is the tīrtha named Nṛsiṃha, which destroys all impurities;
it is there that Hari, in his form as Nṛsiṃha, performed his ablutions in ancient times.
In former times, Maitreya was the priest of the King of Sauvīra. He caused a temple of Viṣṇu to be built on the bank of the Devikā,
where he performed daily service with flowers, incense, and ointments.
There, that twice-born man indeed performed [rites] with offerings of lamps and other such acts.
Once, on the full moon day of Kārttika, he offered a lamp there;
at night, while devoted to the worship of the deity, it was nearly extinguished.
I lived in a temple, O fair-faced ones, where I too was a mouse; having set my mind on stealing the wick of a lamp,
I then seized the wick, and the jackal-dog howled.
Then, terrified by that cat, I fled;
while looking at him with the corner of my mouth, I pushed the lamp,
and it blazed up again in that temple with its former brilliance.

Having died, I was born again as a princess in the land of Vidarbha; remembering my past lives, I became the queen of King Cārudharman. Such is the auspicious power of the lamp offered in the month of Kārttika.

This supreme splendor belongs to Viṣṇu, the recipient of that gift, at whose shrine this dawn has broken. This fruit is now being enjoyed by me for that act of urging on Keśava which I performed as a mere child, even though it was not intentionally planned.
"For this reason, I offer these lamps day and night in the temple of Hari, so that its great fruit may accrue to him.
Having spoken thus, she, devoted to the offering of lamps, [proceeded] together with her co-wives.
She always resided in the house of Keśava, the god of gods;
then, after a long time, having met her death along with the high-souled king,
that bestower of honor attained the world of Viṣṇu.
Having reached that world together with the king, that queen, whose eyes possessed the luster of lotuses,
rejoiced with joy alongside the protector of the earth, freed from all afflictions by her gift of lamps.
Indeed, the wise declare that the gift of a lamp is even more meritorious when offered in the courtyards of the dwellings of Brahmins, fires, cows, and the families of gods.
"Then, by means of a body illuminated by that gift, a man walking in the darkness of the road never falls nor stumbles.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirtieth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for Giving Lamps," in the *Uttara-parvan* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[Now follows] the description of the ritual for the release of a bull (*vṛṣotsarga*).
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Yudhiṣṭhira, this [vow] may be undertaken on the full moon day of Kārttika, or Māgha,
or on the third day of Caitra, or on the twelfth day of Vaiśākha.
One should fashion Khaṇḍanīla, Śaṅkhapāda, Sapauṇḍra, and Dhautapuṣpaka,
together with four cows; listen to the ritual procedure,
O sinless Pāṇḍava, which Garga spoke of long ago in Gokula.
I shall now declare to you that procedure enjoined by Garga:
having first established the Mothers, one should worship them with flowers and unbroken grains (akṣata);
thereafter, one should perform the Śrāddha for the Mothers, which always brings about prosperity.
There, the wise man, having performed his recitation, should place a water-pot with its base turned upward and adorned with *aśvattha* leaves, enshrining the deity Rudra within it;
then, he should thoroughly kindle the fire while preceded by the fire-mantras.
Then one should offer oblations to it with six separate mantras designated as *āhuti*s; thereafter, having offered into the fire according to the prescribed rule,
[one should select] a horse that is either of a single color or two colors, whether reddish-brown or white.
The food of a cow that has a living calf and abounds in milk is beautiful in every limb;
it is further adorned by four young heifers.
A Brahmin should whisper into their ears: "May your husband be strong and auspicious."
Having come together with him, play with joyful minds.
Then, one should draw a trident on the left and a discus on the right;
it should be marked with a conch and a discus and sprinkled with flowers and other offerings.
One should release a powerful bull, its neck adorned with a garland of flowers and covered with white cloths, accompanied by young blue calves,
either at a temple, in a cow-pen, or at the confluence of rivers.
When the sage Garga had thus spoken regarding the ritual for the release of the bull, [he described] that blessed woman who releases a bull—
the lord of cattle, possessing a hump, beautiful, proud, roaring,
and roaming at will.
I shall declare its fruit; listen to it as I speak.
By the rite of releasing a bull (vṛṣotsarga), one purifies ten preceding generations and ten subsequent ones.
Whatever water he touches after emerging from the water onto the earth, [he purifies those who touch it].
The release of a bull for the ancestors is declared to be inexhaustible;
and whatever water they touch with their tails and other limbs at the end,
all that becomes inexhaustible for their ancestors— of this there is no doubt.
Whatever furrows the bull incessantly draws upon the earth with its horns or hooves,
those become inexhaustible streams of honey for its father; indeed, a tank dug even to the depth of a thousand palms does not yield such merit according to the sacred tradition.
Whatever satisfaction the ancestors might obtain, a bull surpasses that;
for he who gives sesame seeds mixed with other grains, or sesame seeds alone, at the time of the Śrāddha rite,
or honey, or blue sugar-candy— all of that becomes truly inexhaustible.
One should desire many sons, so that at least one might go to Gayā,
or perform the horse sacrifice, or release a dark-colored bull;
for he who does not perform the rite of releasing a bull, nor offers a handful of water at a sacred ford, [is deficient].
A son who does not bestow [his wealth] upon his father is indeed nothing but excrement.
Whether he scratches the earth with his horns and hooves in delight, or whether he challenges rival bulls upon seeing them,
every fragment of that action brings satisfaction to the one who performed his marriage, even when he has reached the assembly of Śakra.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Release of a Bull," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[Now follows] the description of the vow (vrata) on the full moon day of Phālguna.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Janārdana, for what reason does a festival take place in every village and every city at the end of Phālguna, on the full moon day?
And for what reason do children in every house speak so much on that occasion?
Why does the Holi festival blaze forth? What is said at the end of Phālguna? What is the meaning of the name "Aḍāḍā"? What is meant by "cold and heat"?
Which deity is worshipped in this rite, and by whom was it brought down?
"O Kṛṣṇa, what is to be done regarding this? Tell me this in detail.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O Pārtha, in the Kṛta Yuga there was a lord of men named Raghu."
A hero endowed with all virtues, speaking kindly and deeply learned,
he conquered the entire earth and brought the lords of men under his sway; then,
according to dharma, he protected his subjects like his own biological sons.

While that king was ruling, there was neither famine nor disease, nor was there untimely death; nor did the citizens take delight in unrighteousness. Indeed, as he thus governed the kingdom, being devoted to the duty of a Kshatriya, [all these things ceased].
All the citizens gathered together and cried out, "Save us! Save us!
The citizens said: "In our house, there is indeed a certain Rākṣasī named Ḍhuṇḍhā."
Meeting by day and by night, she oppresses children by force;
O lord of men, she cannot be restrained by guards, even by stakes, nor by medicines,
nor by those masters of mantras who are supreme teachers.
Having heard the words of the citizens, Raghu was struck with wonder;
his heart filled with amazement, he then spoke to the family priest.
Raghu said:
"O best of the twice-born, who is this Rākṣasī and what is her power?
How is she, a doer of evil deeds, to be restrained by me?
A king is called 'Rakṣan' (the Protector) because of his protection, and a 'Pati' (Lord) because of his guardianship of the earth."
"A king who fails to protect the earth becomes a sinner.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"Listen, O King, to this supreme secret which has never been told by me before."
There was a Rākṣasī named Ḍhauṃḍhā, the daughter of Mālin.
In former times, she propitiated Śambhu with fierce ascetic penance.
Pleased, the Blessed One said to her: "O lady of virtuous vows, choose a boon."

"I shall grant you whatever your heart desires without hesitation. Ḍhuṇḍhā said to Mahādeva, "O Śaṅkara, if you are personally pleased with me, let me not be subject to death at the hands of gods or humans."
O Lord of the three worlds, make me likewise [immune] to weapons and missiles;
O Maheśvara, by your grace may I always have fearlessness during cold, heat, and the rainy season, by day and by night, and whether outside or within a house.
Śaṅkara said:
"So be it," having thus spoken to her, the wielder of the trident spoke again:
"Fear shall arise for you from madmen and from children."
"O highly fortunate one, do not harbor distress in your heart at every season.
Having thus granted her this boon, the Blessed One, the destroyer of Bhaga's eyes,
vanished on the spot, just as the object of her desire had been obtained in her dream.
Having thus obtained the boon, that Rākṣasī, who could assume any form at will, constantly tormented children, remembering the words spoken by Hara;
as a housewife, she would seize them by uttering the perfected mantra: "Aḍāḍaya!"
Because of that, she is called "Aḍāḍā" in the world among households.
All this account of Ḍhauṇḍhā’s life has been narrated by me to you;
now I shall explain the means by which she is destroyed.
"O lord of men, today is the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna;
the winter season has departed, and tomorrow morning the summer will begin.
O Supreme Person, let the gift of fearlessness be granted to the worlds."
Just as people delight and laugh when they first suspect [a battle],
let the children go forth full of joy like warriors eager for combat, taking pieces of wood in their hands.
He should cause a pile of dry wood and stones to be prepared;
there, having offered oblations into the fire according to the rules with extensive mantras that destroy demons,
he should then [proceed] with shouts of joy and charming sounds of clapping hands.
Having circumambulated that fire three times, let the people sing and laugh;
let them chatter as they please, without hesitation, according to whatever opinion each holds.
By that sound and by the oblation, that sinful woman was cast out.
"By means of unseen blows, the Rākṣasī shall bring about the destruction of the children.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O son of Pāṇḍu, having heard the words of that Ṛṣi, that king..."
The wise man performed everything exactly as it had been prescribed,
and by that fierce deed, the Rākṣasī met her destruction.
From that time forward, she became known in this world as Aḍāḍā.
O Pārtha, because the Homa sacrifice— which removes all evils and brings peace from all diseases— is performed by the twice-born on this day, it is considered Holikā.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, this [night] was formerly the most essential of all things in the world.
Because it is the essence, this [night] is called *phalgu*, and it bestows supreme bliss.
O Pārtha, at the arrival of this night, children must be protected within the house;
