specifically in the courtyard of the house, which has been smeared with cow dung and provided with a central square (*catuṣka*).
One should visualize men resembling children, with swords held firmly in their hands;
they protect the children by touching them with pieces of wood and singing humorous songs. To them, one should give molasses and cooked food.
Thus, as soon as he is sought out, that affliction shall subside.
Therefore, children must be protected when night falls.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"At dawn, O Lord, what should be done by those desiring happiness when the month of Mādhava has begun and the sun has risen on the first day of the lunar fortnight? Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Having performed his necessary duties and having gratified the ancestors and the deities,
he should worship the ashes of Gholikā for the pacification of all evils,
in the courtyard of the house which has been decorated, smeared with plaster, and well-swept.
One should have an excellent four-square diagram made with auspicious, unbroken grains of various colors;
in its center, one should place a pedestal covered with a white cloth,
and in front of it, one should place a full water-pot adorned with sprouts.
O Bhārata, before the water-pot, one should offer a pair of excellent sandals and fine garments, accompanied by unbroken grains, gold, and anointed with white sandalwood paste,
while the donor is seated upon a seat amidst the chanting of the Vedas.
A woman with unimpaired limbs and auspicious marks should grind sandalwood;
she should be draped in a cloth superior to a ruby and adorned with excellent garments.
Upon the tip of her head, she should hold a stream of wealth (vasudhārā) accompanied by curd, dūrvā grass, and unbroken rice grains.
Having applied sandalwood paste for the increase of longevity and health,
the wise man should thereafter consume a mango blossom with sandalwood;
this is the worship of the Mind-born (Kāmadeva) as demonstrated by the sages.
Those who drink mango blossoms mixed with sandalwood at the onset of spring truly and swiftly achieve the fulfillment of their heart's desire.
Immediately thereafter, [he honored] the foremost of the twice-born, as well as the sūtas, māgadhas, and bards.
One should give a gift according to one's ability, thinking, "May Kāma be pleased with me.
Then, at the time of the meal, one should first consume that cooked food which was prepared on the previous day,
and thereafter eat as one desires.
O Pārtha, for one who thus performs the Phālguna festival as prescribed in the scriptures,
all their heart's desires are fulfilled without effort;
mental anxieties and physical ailments likewise perish, without a doubt.
Endowed with sons and grandsons, a person dwells in happiness.
Auspicious, purifying, bestowing victory, and destroying all obstacles—
this most excellent of lunar days has been described to you, O Pārtha.
"When the winter season has passed, on the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight, at dawn when the spring season has arrived,
he who has consumed mango blossoms together with sandalwood— truly, O Pārtha, that man dwells in happiness.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Full-Moon Festival of Phālguna," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the Method of Swinging.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Having abandoned even the soft flowers that have been pecked by swarms of bees...

O wise one, sun to the lotus-like Yādavas, tell me how the leaders of heaven are worshipped by the worlds through Damanaka; describe the greatness of swinging on the swing (dolāndolana) and the great festival of the chariot procession (rathayātrā).
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O King, you who are a noble tree for those seeking the son of Pṛthā, and an abode of forgiveness—
listen as I speak to you regarding that which you have asked.
Formerly, on Mount Mandara, the abode of the gods, which possesses beautiful caves,
the Damana tree was born, licked by the Gandharva Kulālī;
having smelled its fragrance, which is beyond the reach of ordinary scent, the celestial women [were captivated].
Overpowered by the intoxication of passion, they sang and laughed;
abandoning their religious observances, the sages fled toward their homes.
Indeed, they found no delight in the study of the Vedas nor in meditation.
O beloved, the supreme pride of haughty women, which had been shattered by an offense, was restored once again by the fragrance. Seeing the world agitated by that fragrance, Brahmā spoke to him:
With his lower lip quivering in anger, Brahmā spoke in a voice created by his power of self-control:
"Since you have subdued the world, you have truly been born as Damana by me."
Why do you cause the world to reel? This action is not worthy of you, for it is the kind that virtuous men do not approve of—devoid as it is of all excellence.
A man should practice that action in which there is no cause for distress among the wise.
He who commits an injury against even a single person is the lowest of men;
what then can be said of one who is intent upon harming many? An action that subverts the perceived good must never be performed under any circumstances.
Regarding the unseen [dharma], there is doubt; that is what we infer.
Consequently, he will himself take part in rites for the gods and ancestors, and for the sake of enjoyment, he will become one who cannot be excluded from the three worlds.
Damanaka said:
"O Brahmin, this was undertaken by me out of necessity, not out of anger nor for the sake of wealth. O Lord, this is my very nature, created by you in the past."
Whatever the nature of a living being may be, whether auspicious or otherwise,
he finds delight in that very thing— be it evil or good.
If, for one who acts according to his own nature, you have uttered a curse against me;
"Since he has been given away, what can I do? This duty does not fail; it is the one who commits the offense.
Hearing these words spoken by Damanaka, which were full of sound reasoning, the Lotus-born Lord, with a pleased soul, said: "I shall do what is truly dear to you."
In that season, when the people were turned golden by the mango blossoms,
and in the forest rich with the beauty of flowering aśoka trees and filled with male cuckoos— at that time, having effortlessly stepped upon the heads of the lords of the gods—
If you remain for even a single day, as is ordained for your welfare,
those men who shall install you with offerings of gifts and honors will always be happy among the gods.
"Always beloved by Śiva, meritorious, and the remover of the fear of sin,
the fourteenth day known as Damanā will attain renown in the month of Madhu.
Having spoken thus, Brahmā went to Mount Mandara to fetch the damana plant.
Having perfumed the entire world with the excellence of his fragrance,
Damanaka dwelt upon that divine mountain— the abode of the Lord of Mountains— which resounds with songs and whose golden slopes are strewn with jeweled raiment;
there he remained, having internalized both the curse and the boon of Śambhu within his heart, his inner self fully subdued.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Dharmarāja, learn of this great festival of the swing,
which is attended by men and women and made beautiful by the chanting of the fifth note.
Accompanied by Ārdrā, like one in the Nandana grove,
he wandered about with eyes smiling with wonder, exhaling fragrance and intoxicating many hosts of Vidyādharas in that holy forest.
During the spring season, he who is worshipped by hundreds of gods and demons caused some women— who were dancing and entwined with *mādhavī* creepers grown from the *saṃtāna* and *pārijāta* trees—
to swing while embracing them as their breasts grew firm.
The celestial women, mounted upon the swing, sang that song which even produced love within the God of Love himself;
seeing him, Bhavānī, who resembles gold, spoke to Śaṅkara.
"O Śaṅkara, O Lord, curiosity has arisen within me; behold!
Have a swing fashioned for me, beautifully adorned, so that I may swing together with you, O Three-eyed One."
Having heard those charming words of Gaurī, the bull-bannered Lord summoned the great Asuras and caused a magnificent swing to be constructed;
having erected two firm pillars consisting of his meritorious works of public utility and charity (iṣṭāpūrta).
And he fashioned the excellent wood Satya as the upper part;
having bound Vāsuki, who shone like molten gold, in the place of the staff,
he made his jeweled hood the central pedestal adorned with gems.

Having fashioned that wonderful swing, which was wrapped in new garments of silk, cotton, and fine cloth, its edges adorned with hanging garlands and crests of gems and pearls, and covered with a layer of cloth and deerskin,
he respectfully presented it to the perfected Siddhaguru.
Mounted there, that gentle one adorned with the moon,
together with his attendants standing at his sides, caused Mount Mandara to sway;
Vijayā was on his left side, while Jayā was on the right.
His two arms, occupied by chowries, were fanned by them as they embraced him;
together with Pārvatī, who was swinging [the chowries], he uttered words of praise,
by which the women of both gods and demons became filled with joy.
The lords of the Gandharvas sang and the hosts of Apsaras danced;
the Cāraṇas played their rising cymbals and musical instruments.
All the principal mountain ranges shook, and the seven oceans were agitated.
When the Lord had mounted the swing, winds accompanied by thunderclaps blew.
Beholding the world thus agitated, the gods, led by Śakra,
approached, prostrated themselves, and spoke to him who is the supreme remover of all sins.
"Cease, O Blessed One, from this sport of yours,
by which the world is being afflicted and the ocean is agitated. Thus addressed with the words of the gods, Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, was delighted.
With eyes wide open in great joy, he leapt up from the swing and spoke these words, O Pārtha, while the assembly of gods looked on—
words full of compassion, exquisitely graceful, and with syllables and phrases of perfectly clear meaning.
Śrī Mahādeva said:
"From this day forward, those who shall cause the swing-sport (dolākrīḍā) to be performed on the bank of the Puṣkariṇī pond during the spring season, when the courtyard of the gods has been adorned,"
It was covered with silk curtains and fine cloth, adorned with rubies,
provided with a parasol, and set with golden rods;
it illuminated the intermediate quarters of the sky with the luster of its various ornaments.
[He saw] a garland, beautiful with flower-garlands whose variegated parts were as peaceful as stars,
held by Vidyādharas, with mirrors suspended at its intervals,
covered with umbrellas and chowries, and adorned according to his capacity.
Then, having performed the fire-ritual (agnikārya) and offered the oblation to the quarters (diśāṃ bali), one should cause the deity to ascend that [swing], surrounded by beloved and joyful people.
The mounting of the swing for the deities is said to be performed with the root-mantra (mūlamantra);
or a learned Brāhmaṇa standing nearby may recite the supreme mantra.
Amidst the deep, resonant sounds from within and the voices of women,
along with words of praise and auspicious chants, the place was perfumed with flowers, incense, and fragrant offerings.
In that interval, a woman was brought to the milking shed for milking.
One should cause [the image] to enter, rich with saffron, together with those dear to her through play and color;
for whom would the water falling upon the body—not variegated by the rays of her smiling teeth—be a giver of happiness? This was declared by Suvarṇaśṛṅgin.
The entire multitude of courtesans became resplendent, their garments moistened with water and adorned with girdles; they were graced by conch-like necks and embellished with saffron powder,
betel, and flower garlands.
Abandoning that water-sport, his mind was set upon no other;
even though struck by the impact of the cold water he had drunk, a certain person felt only happiness—
this must surely be the power born of the God of Love.
Thus, those men who shall go by the path that has been traversed will become free from disease and happy for a hundred autumns;
they will be endowed with sons and grandsons, and possessed of wealth and grain.
Having dwelt there in the perfection of happiness, they shall thereafter go to my city.
Those who, when the spring season arrives, emulate the swinging festival of the best of gods,
obtain the fruits of the tree of human birth on this earth and deliver even hundreds of their lineages from the ocean of suffering.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Swing," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira; followed by the description of the great festival of the Damana, the Swing, and the Chariot procession. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Yudhiṣṭhira, I shall describe to you the procedure for the chariot procession;
remain steadfast and understand this, for you are the best among those who know the embodied forms [of the gods].
In the month of Caitra, on the great mountain named Malaya, which was born from the Third Eye [of Śiva],...
At that very time, while the clusters of creepers were being swayed by the sound of the blowing wind,
Nārada, wandering at his own pleasure, arrived from the world of Śiva, which is as beautiful as the autumnal moon.
Having seen Śiva, who was peaceful and surrounded on all sides by the lords of the gods,
the brahmin bowed and sat down before Keśava and Īśa.
Observing him seated there, the Blessed One, the destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes, [spoke].
With his mind obscured, he asked, "From where have you come again?
Śrī Nārada said:
"O best of the gods, know that Śiva’s desire has indeed been burnt; do not grieve."
There is this certain one called Spring, the beloved friend of Kāma;
by him, joined with the Malaya breeze, the entire world has been brought under his sway,
having mounted the great elephant that is the mango tree and sounding the drum that is the cuckoo.
In every city, he nourished the victory of Manmatha.
"Who is this moon-crested one? Who is this wielder of the conch and mace?
Who is this rogue, or is it Brahmā? Or is Kāma the lord of the three worlds? [Thus they asked.]

Generally, the world is devoted to play; moreover, at the sound of the spring, people dance with arms raised, their feet moving in time with the rhythm. Those who withdraw into the depths of the forest do not apply themselves to any exertion.
Singing and greatly delighted, they too come and go; the cowherd women have reached the boundary, while the guardians of the sacred field sing,
dance, and laugh, their eyes fixed on the Star of Remembrance.
When struck, the drum resounds with a deep, rumbling tone;
unchaste women regard the rogue as a scholar fit for their pursuits;
and flowers [are offered] to the excellent performance of song, dance, and instrumental music.
Thus is the consensus of people in these three worlds:
even an old woman dances upon seeing a girl with swaying, pendulous breasts. This is the power of spring; some unprecedented force unfolds itself.
The lakes possessed wondrous lotuses, the flower gardens were in full bloom,
and the trees were crowded with hundreds of birds; the gods had their faces covered in fragrance, and the wind— composed of the three qualities— caused the hems of their garments to flutter.
O Spring, you have manifested a great presence never before seen in the three worlds;
yet the children speak with mouths full of insults, and the elders have their teeth fallen out.
Both alike are tormented—behold this play of desire!
The birds dance with the flapping of their wings, the rivers with their lofty waves,
and the trees, filled with joy, with their hundreds of sprouts;
having heard these words of Nārada, the moon-crested Lord [replied].
Agitated by curiosity, he quickly ascended his own chariot;
with his golden-bodied vehicle and the foremost of birds as its banner,
the lotus-eyed Lord, bearing the conch, discus, and mace, set forth.
Mounting a chariot resembling a pigeon and composed of the four Vedas,
Brahmā, praised by Brāhmaṇas, set forth joyfully,
accompanied by sages, Apsarases, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and great serpents.
Surrounded by his chariot, Bhāskara, the stealer of the waters,
set forth on a vehicle possessing the splendor of the sun and bearing a banner with the head of Śailaja.
Kātyāyanī also moved forward, accompanied by a five-faced emblem as her standard.
Laṃbodara, holding a golden lotus in one of his hundred hands,
set forth mounted upon his own chariot, having brought together the entire Karṇa clan;
thus was the Lord, the Blessed One whose banner bears the bull, surrounded by them.
Mounted upon his chariot, the Lord of Gods, with an undeluded mind, descended to the world of mortals; and as much as he beheld there, all that was imperishable,
exactly as it had been described by Nārada.
Just as Narada had described it— filled with the bliss of the universe—
Paśupati, together with the gods, gazed on in wonder; at that very moment, his own attendants beheld the perfect reality of the Supreme Brahman.
Some sang with longing, while others rolled about in great joy;
some played instruments contentedly, and some laughed loudly.
Some groups of attendants played musical instruments in one way, while others sang in another.

Others dance in various ways; wonderful indeed is the activity of Caitra! Even the gods, with eyes as beautiful as blue lotuses and shimmering outer corners and pupils, engage in playful delights and commence conversations.
Perceiving the agitation of the gods, the Blessed One whose banner is the bull reflected:
"A very great conjunction of circumstances has indeed arisen;
likewise, there is a calamity that has emerged, and those people who exist for its destruction [must be considered]."

Those who, due to extreme foolishness, lead themselves into calamities are overcome by them; whereas those who dwell in devotion to their master are honored. When the spring season arrives, the people are full of passion, and I must protect them while accomplishing my own twofold task.
Having reflected thus, Śaṅkara summoned Vasanta and said:
"You have been summoned; you must remain here for one month.
This bright fortnight is your companion, bestowing happiness upon all beings."
A truly great joy arises especially for the inhabitants of heaven.
Whosoever has ascended his chariot and come here to behold [him],
he shall return year after year in that very same form.
"Those mortals who shall cause the great festival of the chariot procession to be performed will become enjoyers of divine pleasures and free from disease.
Having spoken thus to Vasantaka and the gods, the Blessed One—
Having been thus praised and bowed to, he then departed for his own abode.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Of what nature should the chariot be made, and how should the expedition be conducted?"
"O Lord of the World, tell me how one should place the gods upon the chariot.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"A chariot made of excellent wood, most wonderful and beautifully adorned..."
It had very firm axles, a solid frame, excellent wheels, and a sturdy pole;
alternatively, it was constructed of bamboo, covered with a cloth blindfold for the eyes,
adorned with hundreds of stars as its variegated parts, and decorated with garlands of flowers.
One should place [the chariot] in the courtyard of the house, yoked with a pair of white oxen, bearing the five-arrowed banner, and adorned with the splendor of the parasol and chowries;
thereafter, one should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite according to the procedure for the sacrifice to the planets.
O Brahmin, the knower of mantras should mount the deity upon the chariot with four-footed mantras that bring peace and prosperity, using the root mantra;
[the chariot] which has been perfumed with scents and incense and is adorned with Vedic and Puranic hymns.
Standing on the chariot, the skillful charioteer leads the horses forward wherever he desires.
Marvel at the greatness of the reins; from behind, the traces follow them.
Amidst the sounds of conchs and kettledrums, and the blare of trumpets—
With blazing hand-lamps and the clamor of cymbals and drums,
let him delight in the night's pleasures preceded by female messengers;
then, amidst the weight of a great festival, he should cause the chariot to be paraded all around.

One should provide betel leaves along with flower garlands for the chariot; furthermore, one should distribute these to the onlookers without restraint. To whichever house the chariot is driven by the charioteer, [there he should go].
Whosoever he may be, he should be honored with flowers, incense, unbroken grains, and other offerings;
even an ordinary person should be honored when he arrives at the house of householders—
how much more so the Lord of the worlds, the Great Sovereign of all beings?
If at any time there should be a breakage of the axle, or perhaps a breakage of the flagstaff,
or if the yoke should break in the middle, or if the fastening should snap,
the wise man, having honored the Brāhmaṇas there, should perform a fire-oblation (homa).
With sesame seeds, clarified butter, and milk, by whatever means happiness is attained;
and having caused the excellent chariot to be circumambulated with songs and spectacles,
one should station it within the city and hold a great festival there.
By means of seizing the ends of swings, whirling on circular swings, and likewise with *ḍamaruka* drums,
the conduct of the Vidyādharīs is displayed by the other women.
O Pārtha, he who thus performs this joy-bestowing chariot festival—
In that very manner, O Pārtha, a man devoted to fasting should perform the worship;
he shall be free from all diseases and live happily for a hundred autumns.
He who, having caused an excellent chariot to be made of gold or silver, [performs this rite...]
Whoever offers to the Sun-god a beautiful image made of wood, painted with colors, or fashioned by their own hand,
shall enjoy happiness for a very long time in the world of mortals.
Having caused the Sun, who stands upon his chariot, to revolve according to the previously described rite,
one should establish him in every direction while songs are sung preceded by instrumental music.
Then, on the second day, one should lead the chariot toward the southern quarter.
There too, one should keep a vigil with instrumental music, singing, and beautiful hymns.
On the third day, during the afternoon, one should install the excellent chariot.
One should pass that night in the diversion of spectacles.
On the fourth day, one should station the chariot in the north;
there, one should perform the great procession (mahāyātrā), wherein miraculous events may occur.
When the fifth day arrives, the Sun is situated within the city.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rules, one should lead [the image] to its abode on the sixth day. In connection with the chariot procession, the Rathasaptamī has been described;
it is meritorious and removes all sins. Listen now to something else from me.
On the third day, Gaurī is to be worshipped; on the fourth, the Lord of Obstacles (Gaṇeśa);
on the fifth, one should worship Sarasvatī who holds a lotus in her hand;
on the sixth, Skanda who bears the spear; and on the seventh, the Sun-god.
On the eighth and the fourteenth [lunar days], the moon-crested Lord (Śiva) is to be worshipped;
on the ninth, one should worship Caṇḍī, Cāmuṇḍā, who wears a garland of severed heads.
On the tenth, all the peaceful sages, with Vyāsa at their head, [are to be honored].
One should worship Cakrapāṇi on the eleventh day (Ekādaśī) or the twelfth day (Dvādaśī).
On the thirteenth day (Trayodaśī), one should worship Him whose form is pacified by the fire arising from the third eye.
The full moon day (Paurṇamāsī) is traditionally remembered as common to all.
Indeed, during swings, the festival of Madana, and chariot processions,
the sequence of lunar days may even be transposed due to the importance of the occasion;
for this springtime procession is supremely conducive to mental well-being.

"In a palace of the gods whitened with excellent lime, adorned within with fine cloths and variegated with jewels, pearls, and gifts; having performed the procession there with betel, areca nuts, and courtesans—he shall become the Lord of Bhārata.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Great Festival of the Damanaka, the Swing, and the Chariot Procession," in the *Uttara-parvan* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira. [This concludes] the description of the Great Festival of Madana.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Having married Gaurī, Hara,
the Lord of Umā and Master of Creatures, undertook the Pāśupata vow and became absorbed in meditation.
Having consulted with Brahmā and the other gods for the sake of obtaining a son,
and being delighted by Gaurī’s desire to fulfill her heart's wish,
they dispatched Manmatha, deeming him capable of causing agitation.

Then Māra, Smara, and Kāma arrived at that hermitage, accompanied by Rati, Prīti, Mada, Unmāda, and the splendor of Spring; surrounded by the treasures of wine, pride, and the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra);
adorned with a crown of mango and aśoka blossoms, and wearing a crest of mālatī flowers.
He has the lute, the drum, music, and the cuckoo as his messengers;
he has the sounding jhallarī cymbals as his treasurer and scribe;
he is mounted upon women intoxicated by drink, and possesses the swing as his marvelous minister.
Rich with the fragrance of the southern breeze and raining down side-long glances,
Smara— the Great King of Kings— approached the presence of Hara;
drawing his flower-bow, he took up an arrow capable of intoxicating with passion.
He hurled it at the Destroyer of Tripura in order to break his meditative absorption.
Perceiving that intention of his, Rudra, blazing with wrath,
emitted fire from the third eye on his forehead.

Kāma was gazed upon by him and was reduced to ashes at that very moment. Seeing Smara burnt, Rati and Prīti remained there in constant grief, lamenting piteously; everything else had fled in all directions.
Then Gaurī, her heart afflicted with grief, said to Rudra:
"O Blessed One, for our sake you have utterly consumed that Kāma;
therefore, look at these two women of Kāma—how can they weep?"
"O Lord of Gods, O Bull-bannered One, show favor for the sake of Rati’s joy!
O Śambhu, restore Smara to life and make him manifest once again.
Hearing that, Mahādeva was delighted and spoke to Pārvatī.
The entire world is overwhelmed by the embodied god of love;
how could there be a return of Kama, who was burnt by me?
Nevertheless, O beloved, honoring your words, I shall make them fruitful.
In this spring season, on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight,
O Goddess, on this very day the Mind-born One shall become embodied.
By him, acting as the seed, the entire world shall be brought forth.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, having thus granted this boon to Manmatha,
the beloved of Pārvatī went to Mount Kailāsa on the peak of the Himavat.
O King, all this history of Smara has now been narrated to you.
I shall describe another method of worship; listen to it.
Having bathed on this thirteenth day, one should draw a tree called Aśoka with limbs fashioned from vermilion, filled with great affection.
O Great King, [one should worship] Kāmadeva, who dwells in the springtime, who has the face of a horse, whose banner bears a fish,
who is golden, or wooden, or even variegated;
he who moves with playful grace, who is full of pride, and who is accompanied by a host of Apsarases.
Filled with the sounds of gandharvas singing and playing instruments, and crowded with spectacles, it was joined by vidyādharas who took delight in the playful sports of the Nandyāvarta dance;
at midday, one should devoutly feed [the deities] with various foods, incenses, garlands, and garments.
O son of Kuntī, a man accompanied by a woman, with this mantra:
"Salutations to Vāma, to Kāma, to the God of gods, to the Embodiment,
who indeed causes agitation to the minds of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Indra."
Having thus performed [the rites] and worshipped the God of gods, the Mind-born (Anobhava),
one should then offer before him sweetmeats that delight the mouth and various kinds of edible foods, saying: "May Kāma be pleased with me."
Then, having given a pair of garments along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), she should dismiss the Brahmins;
and with a joyful inner self, reflecting "This is Kāma," the woman should honor her husband with clothes, garlands, and ornaments.
In that temple of Manmatha, the sacrificer, surrounded by friends,
should perform a night vigil so that it may become a "Happy Night" (Sukharātri),
using camphor, saffron powder, perfumes, betel, and incense.
One should hold a great festival at night with various kinds of foods,
with the lighting of lamps, dances, performances, and spectacles.
O Pārtha, he who thus performs this great festival year after year—
When the spring season arrives, the king is joyful and content within his city;
for as long as that year, the people are liberated from diseases.
There is abundance of food, security, health, fame, prosperity, and supreme happiness.
In that kingdom, the rain-god Parjanya pours down rain according to desire;
the god who has twelve, five, and two eyes is exceedingly pleased,
as are Kāma, Viṣṇu, and Prajāpati Vasantaka.
All the planets, beginning with the moon and the sun, as well as the Brahman-sages,
Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Dānavas— all of them are pleased with him;
so too are the Asuras, Yātudhānas, Suparṇas, birds, and trees.

When pleased, they grant happiness to that performer; of this there is no doubt. During the festival of Caitra, by worshipping Kāma—the abode of the hearts of all people—accompanied by Rati and aided by the Malaya mountain breezes, a man and an excellent woman shall always be endowed with good fortune, beauty, progeny, and happiness.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Great Festival of Madana," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira. [Now follows] the description of the festival of Bhūtamātṛ.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Bhūtamātā!"— thus exulting, in every village and in every city,
the entire world runs about in all directions, singing and dancing;
like one intoxicated, it prattles on the ground, and like one drunk, it falls down.
Like one possessed by anger, he runs from the city; like one intoxicated, he drags things outside; like one seized by wind, he distorts his face and limbs in the world;
and like one possessed by a spirit, he plunges his body, covered in ashes, into the mud.
"Is this the path prescribed by the scriptures, or is it merely worldly? My mind is bewildered, O Kṛṣṇa; you ought to explain this to me.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Pārtha, I shall tell you whatever is in your mind;
it is my conviction that you are both a believer and full of faith.
Accompanied by Pārvatī, O Pārtha, [I dwell] on Mount Mandara with its beautiful caves.
The Teacher of the World, Hara, sat playing with joy, provided with divine playthings;
he beheld Gaurī, delighted, possessing the lofty gait of a swan, her two breasts radiant like beautiful jars,
and her fine girdle tinkling.
And though his passion was consumed, Hara’s desire blazed up;
Śiva desired her who had emerged from him onto a costly couch.
When a hundred divine years had passed while the two remained engaged in sexual union, [the gods grew anxious].
Then, due to the obstruction of the goddess’s upward growth,
a woman emerged from the urine and water outside; she arose with her belly torn open,
dark-complexioned, with a terrifying face, tawny eyes, and disheveled hair.
Adorned with a garland of skulls, with her hair tied in a topknot and a mass of matted locks,
she is auspicious, bearing a khaṭvāṅga staff and holding the Time (Kāla) in her hand, her hands marked by ritual gestures (mudrās).
She wears a garment of tiger skin, and her girdle is adorned with tinkling bells.
The ḍamaru drums resounded with a *ḍama-ḍḍama* sound, filling the sky with their blast;
other young women at her side, following the rhythm of song and instrumental music,
danced and laughed with rapid beats of their hands.
Carrying skull-topped staffs and khaṭvāṅgas, and draped in elephant hides,
a man was likewise born from Śaṃkara, possessing that same form and ornaments,
followed by many most terrifying spirits.
Seeing Bhavānī and the Lord born of Bhava united in an instant by those [beings] with faces like lions and tigers, whose teeth scraped the very sky,
the God, his mind delighted, spoke to the greatly astonished Goddess.
"O auspicious lady, look, look at these two born from your own body!
Bearing weapons that are both loathsome and wonderful, yet possessed of supreme beauty—
O Goddess, in my opinion, these two are like brothers and playthings."
Due to a slight resemblance, Hara caused the distinction between man and woman to appear;
having bestowed these three names— Bhrātṛbhāṇḍā, Bhūtamātā, and likewise Udakasevikā— upon them, he then granted a boon.
Those who, having eaten, shall serve with devotion this goddess who has arrived and is seated at the foot of an ancient tree, using water-filled jars,
and who shall anoint her with sandalwood paste and worship her with flowers and incense;
One should feed [the guests] quickly with kṛsara, cakes, and milk-rice (pāyasa).
O Goddess, he who performs this, purified by a spirit of devotion,
shall obtain an increase in sons and cattle, as well as physical health.
Neither Śākinīs, nor Piśācas, nor Rākṣasas cause affliction in his house; his children grow up free from disease. Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O tiger among men, when should the worship of Bhūtamātā be performed by those men who desire happiness? You ought to tell me that.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
This Blessed Lady, who brings benefit to children, is worshipped everywhere through various names, various rites, and at various times,
from the first lunar day (pratipad) of the month of Jyeṣṭha until the fifteenth day (pañcadaśī).
For that long, worship should be performed with incitements and spectacles;
the exposition of the fruits of forbidden actions and the humiliation of the Pāṇḍavas are displayed by men intent on laughter through their wondrous gestures.
Out of greed for the wealth of a trusted friend, he was slain on the road at twilight;
indeed, he does not see one who does not look upon his ascent to the tip of a stake.
You have seen him, full of joy, insulting those on the other shore.
Having cut [the fruit] with his own hands, the Lord gave the finest modaka;
the children were delighted by the garland, even as it was broken into fine pieces upon a leaf,
and having placed their faces toward the west, they took mouthfuls of the testicles.
"O people, do you not see this supreme traitor to his master,
who, having been torn apart by saws with gushing streams of blood,
has now arrived as a spy for the Asuras, causing the greatest terror to all?"
Struck by blows from a staff, this thief is led away by the staff-bearers; surrounded by onlookers, he cries out, utterly bewildered. But this fool, his eyes clouded with cruelty, is led away bound.
"Do not look at that twice-born man with white hair, white beard, and white garments, who is being struck with blows and slaps like a monkey.
O slut, come out of the house; even though he is old, he still belongs to a woman."
This fool does not provide for his own maintenance and nourishment;
behold these lamps of darkness, who, adorned with Bhairava ornaments and wearing serpents as sacred threads, perform the steps of the *tāṇḍava* dance.
Disgust for the world dwells not at all in his heart;
for even as a child, he has undertaken this great vow.
Do you not see that Śabara, whose body is black like a crow with bloodshot eyes?
Having cut down the young parrots dwelling within the hollows of the trees and having enclosed them with many compartments,
he was shattered by volleys of arrows;
behold him, his pride in his great blows now abandoned along with his drum.
Behold this woman with a face half-black, adorned with vermilion,
her hair disheveled, dancing like a yoginī;
she has been awakened by the deep sound of musical instruments and performs a circular tāṇḍava dance.
Having thus performed the spectacle, one should lead her beneath a tree.
When this is done, there shall be neither poverty nor suffering for men.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Bhūtamātṛ Festival," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the Binding of the Protective Thread. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Now, therefore, O King, I shall fully explain the ritual for the protective thread of Bali.
Listen with a one-pointed mind to that which has been related by me in brief:
formerly, in the war between the gods and the asuras, the dānavas, defeated by the gods, went forth placing Śukra before them; then Śukra said to him:
Śakra said:
"You should not despair; such is the course of actions.
Through destiny, at the appointed time, victory and defeat come to all beings."
Let an alliance with Śakra be formed for two years;
the Lord of Śacī has been rendered invincible by Śacī against all enemies.
By the power of the *rakṣābandhana* (protective binding), the great lord of the Dānavas was conquered.
"Wait for one year; thereafter, prosperity will come to you.
Having been addressed thus by Bhārgava, those Dānavas, their fever of anxiety dispelled, remained waiting for the time exactly as instructed by their preceptor.
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, this power of the protective rite has been described to you;
it bestows victory, happiness, sons, health, and wealth.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Supreme God, by what rite is the binding of the protective thread performed?
On which lunar day and at what time, O Lord? You ought to tell me this.
For indeed, in whatever manner the Blessed One speaks of these diverse matters, [it is so].
"In that same way, I am never satiated while hearing your many meaningful stories.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O Pārtha, when the sky is covered with clouds and the surface of the earth is like a lush green meadow..."
When the full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa has arrived at the break of dawn,
a wise person should perform his bath according to the injunctions of the Śruti and Smṛti;
thereafter, he should offer libations to the gods and the ancestors with the most excellent water.

Brāhmaṇas should perform the rites prescribed by the Vedas, such as the *upākarma*, as well as the libations (*tarpaṇa*) for the sages; they should also perform the *śrāddha* ceremony dedicated to the gods according to their capacity.
For Śūdras, bathing accompanied by mantras and the giving of gifts are commended.
Then, during the afternoon, one should have auspicious protective amulets prepared with unbroken grains,
excellent *siddhārtha* seeds, and adorned with gold;
they should be wrapped in various cloths made of cotton or linen, free from any impurity.
One should place [the vessels] tied with very beautiful threads upon the ritual vessel.

For the protection of the house and for the pacification of all misdeeds, one should perform the rite using well-rounded *kuṇḍūka* seeds free from cow dung, accompanied by *dūrvā* grass and colored powders.
In the center of a well-smeared house, one should place an auspicious seat upon a four-legged stool.
Thereon the king shall sit, together with his ministers, his domestic priest, and his friends,
accompanied by courtesans and amidst auspicious sounds, pleasant laughter, and auspicious signs.
The binding of the protective thread (rakṣābandha) for the king should be performed amidst the sound of propitiatory chants.
First, one should honor with respectful offerings (arghya) the gods, the twice-born, and virtuous women who have been praised.
Thereafter, the domestic priest shall bind the protection upon the monarch while reciting the sacred mantra.
With that same [power] by which the mighty King Dānavendra, possessed of great strength, was bound, with that I bind you, O Rakṣas; do not move, do not move!
By Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and other human beings.
One should perform the binding of the protective thread after worshipping the twice-born with devotion.
Whoever performs the binding of the protective thread according to this rite shall be free from all defects and remain happy for a year.
O King, that man who performs the ritual for protection during the month of Śrāvaṇa when the cool waters flow,
shall dwell in supreme happiness, alone yet accompanied by all his sons, grandsons, and surrounded by his friends.
Thus ends the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira in the Uttara Parva of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa.
The one hundred and thirty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for Tying the Protective Thread on the Full Moon of Śrāvaṇa.
Now begins the one hundred and thirty-eighth chapter,
"Description of the Mahānavamī Vow."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"The Mahānavamī is a meritorious lunar day, the most excellent among all lunar days. It should be observed by all the gods, and especially by the protectors of subjects."
"O Pārtha, you should cause Bhava to arise for the sake of happiness for a year,
for the pleasure of the bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas, or for the sake of a festival.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:

From what time has this ninth day (Navamī) come to be associated with the word "festival" (maha)? O Blessed One, from what beginning did the ritual for the Navamī originate? Does the procession commence from the birth from the womb of Yaśodā?
Or was it already so in the Kṛta, Tretā, and other ages? Regarding those living beings whom some people in this world intend to kill or do kill— what is their destiny in the world beyond?
"O Keśava, you ought to explain this doubt of mine to me first: regarding those who kill themselves, those who cause others to kill, and likewise those who approve of such acts. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Pārtha, she who is the supreme power, infinite and world-renowned; the primordial, all-pervading, pure, accessible through devotion, and enchanting;
Kālī, the first eighth digit, and the second, Sarvamaṅgalā.

Māyā, Kātyāyanī, Durgā, Cāmuṇḍā, and Śaṅkarapriyā—those devoted to yoga meditate upon her; she is the Goddess, the Supreme Sovereign. Bhavānī, the auspicious Śivā, is worshipped through various forms and various names.
On the eighth and ninth days, she is worshipped by gods, dānavas, and rākṣasas; by gandharvas, uragas, yakṣas, kinnaras, and men.
She was manifested at the beginning of other ages as well, prior to creation.
This goddess was worshipped in ancient times by those even more ancient than them.

On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja, when it is conjoined with the Mūla asterism— that which is known as Mahānavamī— is exceedingly rare to find even throughout the three worlds.
When the sun has entered Virgo, that eighth day of the bright fortnight which is conjoined with the Mūla asterism is known as Mahānavamī.
On both the eighth and the ninth days, one should worship Ambikā, the Mother of the World.
Having worshipped her in the month of Āśvina, one becomes free from sorrow and conquers enemies.
Threatening with "huṃ" sounds and with swords and other weapons day and night,
the Goddess, when worshipped on the ninth day, bestows the ninth fruit.
She is meritorious, she is pure, and she is the bestower of the bliss of Dharma;
therefore, Cāmuṇḍā, who wears a garland of severed heads, should always be worshipped. If living beings such as buffaloes and others are employed for her [sacrifice], [it is for her sake].

All those who [sacrifice] go to the heavenly realm; no sin is found in killing [them]. Neither by the offering of oblations, nor by flowers, incense, and unguents, is Vindhyavāsinī so well-pleased in this world as she is by buffaloes.
O son of Kuntī, those creatures who are slain here according to the prescribed rite for the sake of Durgā go to heaven, even though they are killed out of devotion;
O Yudhiṣṭhira, the same applies to those whose lives have departed in the courtyard of Bhavānī.
Their residence in heaven is certain; they are beloved by the Apsarases.
O descendant of Kuru, throughout all the Manvantaras and Kalpas, this ninth [day] has been honored since ancient times in all of them.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhavānī, who is renowned as being without beginning or end, is worshipped year after year by the gods through repeated incarnations;
she has always descended upon the earth eternally as the destroyer of the Daityas.
She maintains the stability of heaven, the netherworld, and the mortal realm;
furthermore, this Great Goddess, born from the womb of Yaśodā,
shall place her foot upon the head of the demon Kaṃsa and deprive him of his life.
From that time forward, having installed her who bestows fame and joy upon the worlds on the Vindhya mountain, worship was once again established.
Although her greatness had already increased previously, it was further enhanced by her sister.
For the sake of benefiting all on earth and for the pacification of all calamities,
thus [it is said] regarding one who fasts at Vindhya during the nine nights (Navarātra),
whether by fasting for a single night, by eating only at night, or by eating only what is unasked for, according to one's own capacity.
In every place, in every city, in every house, in every village, and in every forest, the gods were served through sacrifices performed by those devoted to worship;
there were bathed, joyful, and delighted Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and kings.
O tiger among the Kurus, listen to this procedure for Vaiśyas, Śūdras, Mlecchas, and other men, as well as for women, who—
desiring victory— should perform it starting from the first day of the lunar fortnight in due order.

One should cause the ritual of the iron-strike (lohābhihārika) to be performed up to the eighth day. On ground sloping toward the northeast, one should have a divine pavilion constructed, measuring nine or seven cubits, and adorned with banners.
In the southeast, one should cause a very beautiful pit to be made, measuring one cubit,
provided with three girdles and a yoni shaped like an ashvattha leaf;
[therein should be placed] all the royal insignia and whatever weapons and missiles there may be.
Having brought all those [materials] into the pavilion, one should perform their consecration (adhivāsana).
Then, a Brāhmaṇa who has bathed, is pure, and wears white garments,
should offer clarified butter into the fire with mantras preceded by the syllable Om and characterized by the appropriate lingas.
Formerly, there was a very powerful Dānava named Loha;
he was cut into many pieces in battle by the enraged gods,
and all that iron which is seen on the earth today originated from his limbs.
One should offer milk-rice mixed with clarified butter while reciting mantras for weapons and missiles;
one should present the remnants of the oblation to the horses and elephants.
Because of this, this rite is remembered by the sages as the *lohābhihārika* (the iron-attracting) ritual.
And he should constantly cause it to be paraded through the city, adorned with elephants and horses, preceded by the sounding of joyful drums;
every day, the king, having bathed and worshipped the ancestors and the gods, [should perform this].
One should worship the royal insignia with fruits, garlands, and unguents;
the remnants of the oblation should be given to a twice-born man who officiates at the initiation ceremony.
It is declared that through the presentation of these to him, the king attains victory.
I shall proclaim to you the worship mantras spoken in the Purāṇas,
by which, when worshipped, [the deities] bestow fame, longevity, glory, and strength;
just as a cloud covers this earth for the sake of Śiva’s welfare.
"Thus, cover the king for the increase of victory and health. (This is the mantra for the umbrella:
"Born of the lineage of the Gandharvas, may you not be a defiler of your family!
By the truthful word of Brahmā, and of Soma and Varuṇa..."
And by the power of the sacrificial fire, grow strong, O horse!
By the splendor of the sun, by the asceticism of the sages,
by the celibate discipline of Rudra, and by the strength of the wind.
Remember that you are a prince; remember the Kaustubha gem!
Consider the fate that awaits the killer of a Brahmin, as well as the killer of a father or a mother, one who speaks falsehood for the sake of land, and a Kshatriya who turns his back in battle.
O horse, if you undergo a transformation on the path of battle, that indeed would be a sin; for neither the sun and moon, nor the wind and fire, shall quickly reach that destination where you go.
"Having conquered your enemies in battle, may you be happy together with your master.
(Thus ends the mantra for the horse.
"O banner of Indra, of great prowess, Suparṇa has presented himself before you."
The king of birds, Vainateya, likewise the banner of Nārāyaṇa;
he is to be known as the son of Kaśyapa, the immortal, the enemy of the serpents, and the vehicle of Viṣṇu;
he is immeasurable, invincible, and the destroyer of the enemies of the gods.
Garuda, possessing the speed of the wind, is present and stationed within you;
protect our weapons, armor, missiles, warriors, and ourselves, and consume our enemies.
(Thus ends the mantra for the banner.)
Kumuda, Airāvaṇa, Padma, Puṣpadanta, Vāmana,
Supratīka, Añjana, and Nīla— these eight are of divine origin.
Their sons and grandsons have taken refuge in the eight [directional] powers.
The Bhadra, the Mandra, the Mṛga, the Gaja, and the Saṃkīrṇa—
these great elephants, born in forest after forest from the elephant-womb,
may they protect you! May the Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, and the hosts of Maruts protect you!
"O King of Serpents, protect your husband while observing your agreement.
For they have indeed attained victory in battle; may you have a safe journey as you depart.
Your splendor comes from Soma, your strength from Viṣṇu, your brilliance from the Sun, and your speed from the Wind."
May the serpents protect you in battle— the steadfastness of Mount Meru, the victory of Rudra, and the glory of Indra, the subduer of cities; may the quarters of the sky along with their deities,
and the two Aśvins together with the Gandharvas, protect you always from every side.
(Thus ends the elephant-mantra:
The fire-gods, the Vasus, the Rudras, Vāyu, Soma, and the great sages;
the nāgas, kinnaras, gandharvas, yakṣas, hosts of bhūtas, and the grahas.
May the Pramathas along with the Ādityas, Bhūteśa together with the Mothers,
Skanda the general of Śakra’s army, and Varuṇa— having taken refuge in you—
burn all enemies, and may the king attain victory.
Those offensive weapons which were deployed by your enemies from all sides have been destroyed by your splendor—
just as they were in the battle for the slaying of Kālanemi and in the destruction of Tripura.
In battle after battle with Hiraṇyakaśipu, as well as in the war between the gods and the asuras,
you were thus resplendent; likewise, being radiant today,
may the enemies of the king perish this day upon seeing this blue and white [banner].
Defeated in battle by various terrible diseases and weapons,
they instantly became healthy when cleansed by your wind.
She who is known as Pūtanā, Revatī by name, and remembered as Kālarātri—
"O Banner, having swiftly destroyed all enemies, you have come to me.
(Thus ends the mantra for the banner.
The sword is the slayer of enemies, a blade of sharp action, and difficult to withstand.
Śrīgarbha, Vijaya, and likewise Dharmadhāra—
these eight names of yours were spoken by Brahmā himself.
Your lunar mansion is Kṛttikā, and your presiding deity is Maheśvara.
"Gold is your body; the god Dhātṛ, Janārdana, is your father and grandfather. O God, protect me at all times.
(Thus ends the mantra for the sword. "O armor made entirely of iron, you are the bestower of protection in battle."
"Protect me, protect me; I am worthy of your protection, O Varmān!
Salutations to you! (Thus ends the Varma-mantra.
"O Dundubhi, by your sound you cause the hearts of my enemies to tremble!"
O King, may you be the increaser of victory for your armies just as excellent elephants rejoice at the thundering of clouds;
likewise, let our joy, brought by your voice, be a source of delight for us.
"Just as terror is produced among women by the sound of a thundercloud, so may our enemies tremble at your sound in battle. (This is the mantra for the drum.
O great sovereign of all weapons, O slayer of the enemies of all the gods!
"O bow, protect me always along with your most excellent arrows. (Thus is the mantra for the bow.
"O conch, you are holy, the most auspicious among all auspicious flowers."
"May you, who are eternally upheld by Viṣṇu, grant peace to my mind.
(This is the mantra for the conch. "O beloved of the gods and immortals, white as the rays of the moon and as pale as snow-foam, quickly dispel all evil!"
(Thus ends the mantra for the fly-whisk.
You were fashioned first among all weapons by the wielder of the Pināka bow,
having been extracted from his trident-weapon and shaped into the form of a handle to be grasped in the fist.
You have been bestowed upon Caṇḍikā, O destroyer of all the wicked;
likewise, you have been expanded and presented to the gods.
You have become the very limb of all living beings, O warder-off of all that is inauspicious.
"O Churikā, protect me always; grant me peace; salutations be unto you!
(Thus ends the mantra of the Churikā. "You were fashioned by Brahmā for the expulsion of the wicked, for the gathering of the virtuous, and for the establishment of worldly conduct."
Bestow glory, bestow happiness, and be the victor for the king!
Strike down all enemies quickly; O Golden Staff, salutations to you!
(Thus ends the mantra of the Golden Staff.)
Vijaya (Victorious), Jayada (Bestower of Victory), Jetṛ (Conqueror), Ripughātī (Slayer of Enemies), Priyaṅkara (Doer of Good),
Duḥkhaha (Destroyer of Suffering), Dharmada (Giver of Dharma), Śānta (Peaceful), and Sarvāriṣṭavināśana (Destroyer of All Calamities)—
because these eight mighty lions are present here with you.
Therefore, O Brāhmaṇa, you are celebrated as "Siṃhāsana" in the Vedas;
Śiva himself resides in you, as does Śakra, the lord of the gods;
the god Hari resides in you, and for your sake he performs austerities.
Salutations to you, O Sarvatobhadra; be auspicious to the lord of the earth. O Lion-throne, the very essence of victory over the three worlds, let there be salutations unto you.
(Thus ends the mantra for the lion-throne.)
Having performed this rite of offering iron preceded by mantras,
with fruit offerings, flowers, incense, lamps, and unguents;
having bathed on the eighth lunar day, one should perform the ritual ablution in the forenoon.
(Now, in prose:

Having fashioned an image of Durgā—whether of gold, silver, copper, wood, or bronze—from the month of Caitra onwards, and having placed it in a beautiful spot before him, adorned with various wooden arches; having positioned the Goddess in the center of a variegated house, bathed, her limbs anointed with saffron, sandalwood, perfumes, and the four-fold unguents, and draped in fine silken cloths; and having worshipped her with flowers, the King himself, accompanied by many twice-born men whose fame is being celebrated and who have been made joyful, [should perform the rite] during the day.
One should present [the offering] to the Blessed Lady together with the family priests, using a *bilva* leaf for worship and with this mantra:
"Victorious one! Auspicious one! Kālī! Bhadrakālī! Kapālinī!
Durgā! Śivā! Kṣamā! Dhātrī! Svāhā! Svadhā! Salutations be unto you! (Thus ends the prose section.)
The Bilva tree, born from nectar, is always dear to Mahādevī;
O Sovereign of the Gods, I offer this pure Bilva leaf to you.
And on that day, Durgā is to be worshipped with Droṇa flowers.
And she is beloved by the Lord of the Gods (Śiva), as well as by those whose wounds have been healed.
Then, having paid homage to the sword that crushes the pride of enemies,
O King, one who desires victory for oneself, a kingdom, and abundance of food, should [worship it].
Having prostrated again and again, one should then meditate upon Śivā in the heart—
the auspicious maiden who slays Mahiṣa, possesses many arms, rides a lion,
threatens the Dānavas, and holds a raised sword in her hand.
[One should meditate upon] Durgā, who stands at the commencement of battle, wearing a bell, a rosary, and a garland;
then, with cries of "Victory! Victory!", one should thereafter offer this hymn:
"O auspiciousness of all that is auspicious, O Śivā, the accomplisher of all goals!"
O refuge, O Tryambakā, O Gaurī, O Nārāyaṇī, salutations be unto you!
O Durgā, who are anointed with saffron, smeared with sandalwood paste,
and adorned with a garland made of bilva leaves, I have come to you for refuge.

Having performed the worship in this manner, O Kauravya, one should hold a great festival at night on the eighth day with dancing, acting, and singing. Having thus passed the night joyfully, at dawn when the sun rises, [one should proceed].
One should cause buffaloes and rams to fall before [the Goddess] with their necks bowed,
numbering a hundred, or fifty, or twenty-five, according to one's desire;
and one should satisfy the Supreme Goddess with jars filled with wine and spirits.
O son of Kuntī, that [wealth] should be given to the Kāpālikas by means of male and female servants; likewise, having divided everything among friends, relations, and kinsmen,
[one should then proceed] at the time of afternoon on the ninth day to her who is seated upon a chariot.
The king himself, accompanied by his army, should cause Bhavānī to be paraded through the kingdom;
or else, with thousands of well-trained men mounted on chariots,
he should do so slowly, with lamps blazing with increasing brilliance.
With heroes who had drawn their swords, with elephants drenched in the blood of their bodies,
with conchs and drums resounding, with troops of women dancing,
with adorned ladies, and with children beautifully decorated.
One should offer a bali-oblation to the spirits with this mantra, consisting of meat,
blood, water, and cooked rice, combined with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains.
One should cast the bali three times each toward the cardinal and intermediate directions using the trident.
May the gods— the Ādityas, the Vasus,
the Maruts, the Aśvins, the Rudras, the Suparṇas, the Pannagas, and the Grahas— accept this offering;
as well as the Asuras, the Yātudhānas, the Mātṛs, and the Piśācas.

May Brahmā and the other great sages, the bringers of peace to the worlds,
pacify my obstructed sins; may my adversaries be stilled,
and may the spirits and departed ones become gentle, satisfied, and sources of happiness.

In this manner, O Pārtha, one should cause the goddess Durgā, seated upon a chariot or in a palanquin, to be paraded through the kingdom; thereafter, one should bring the rite to completion without obstacles. Furthermore, when obstacles have arisen, one should perform the propitiation of the spirits (bhūtaśānti).

By this means, no obstacles arise and the journey reaches completion. Those kings and other men who perform such a pilgrimage on the Mahānavamī day, under the Nandā constellation, with joyful minds, shall obtain sons.
All of them, liberated from sin, go to the city of the Bhāgavatas;
neither their children, nor fire, nor thieves,
nor Vināyakas cause obstacles for those, O King of kings, with whom the Great Goddess is pleased.

Devotees of the Blessed Goddess become free from disease, happy, enjoyers of pleasures, and devoid of fear; what more need be said? Thus has this great festival of the goddess Durgā been fully described to you.

It destroys all that is inauspicious for those who read it and those who hear it. Having worshipped on the ninth day Durgā— who stands upon the back of the demon Mahiṣāsura pierced by the tip of her trident, whose beautiful arm-staff is adorned with an armlet carved from the marrow extracted from his body, and who is followed by the Five-faced One— mortals cross over even the most difficult and impenetrable thickets.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Mahānavamī Vow," in the *Uttara-parvan* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya-mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira; followed by the "Description of the Great Festival of the Banner of Mahendra.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O King, in ancient times during the war between the gods and the asuras, the staff of Mahendra’s banner was established by the immortals, beginning with Brahmā, for the sake of victory;
it was set up upon the summit of Mount Meru by the Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and Uragas.
That goddess was indeed constantly honored and adorned with her own ornaments,
along with her own parasols, bells, caskets, and clusters of tinkling bells;
seeing her, the Dānavas were destroyed and slain in battle out of sheer fear.

The Daityas went to the netherworld (rasātala) and the gods remained in heaven. From that time forward, O Yudhiṣṭhira, all those gods and all the hosts, joyful and satisfied, worshipped that divine Indra-staff.
Therefore, having gone to heaven by the power of his abundant merit,
the illustrious King Vasu dwells in the world of Indra, highly honored by the Vasus.
Let this sacrificial staff of Vasu, granted to him by Mahendra, be accepted.
Having performed worship, O highly fortunate one, for the sake of dispelling all the Daityas,
Vasu brought [the image] down during the rainy season and, together with all the kings,
worshipped it upon the earth; he celebrated a festival for Indra.
Delighted by the festival, Maghavat granted a holy boon to Vasu:
"In those regions where men, preceded by a spirit of devotion,
shall worship the great banner given by me at the end of the year," [they shall attain the highest merit].
In those regions, the subjects will be joyful and free from disease;
they will have abundant food, be endowed with righteousness, and celebrate great festivals such as the Vṛṣamedha.
They will be well-dressed, eloquent, and beautifully adorned.
Having heard these words, King Vasu, the best among the possessors of wealth,
thereafter celebrated a great festival with increasing splendor year after year.
He would establish a staff at Śravaṇa, having worshipped it with ritual baths and garments.
The king himself should diligently install a beautiful staff made of solid wood, twenty cubits in length,
in that previously designated place of Indra known as Indramātṛka, where he shall reside.
It is clothed in various garments and likewise adorned with *piṭikās*. O Great King, I shall now describe to you the sequence of those *piṭikās*:
first is that called Lokapāla, which is square and possesses a central pericarp (*karṇikā*).
Then there was a second beautiful circular arena, smeared with red powder, joined by Yama, Indra, Kubera, and Varuṇa;
and a third auspicious octagonal arena, white and variegated, containing a pit.
The fourth is a circle surrounded by *indragopāla* [red insects];
the fifth is an eight-cornered [figure], white and variegated with minerals;
the sixth is a circle with a black pericarp, adorned with bubbles.
The seventh is an eight-cornered, pure [mandala] joined with the Vidyādharas;
the eighth is a circular Piṭaka encircled by leather straps and threads;
and the ninth is radiant, joined with the nine planets, and accompanied by Caṇḍikā.
The tenth is situated in Śiva, accompanied by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa;
O Yudhiṣṭhira, the eleventh is Kṛṣṇa, circular and joined with Yama;
the twelfth is white and has a parasol; and the thirteenth is long like a banner.
Having bound the pillar with ropes at intervals marked by the moon's positions, and having adorned it with kusa grass, garlands of flowers, bells,
and chowries, O Pārtha, one should slowly raise it after men have offered oblations to the fire and to the twice-born brahmins.
Having honored [the deity] with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) and offerings of molasses, milk-rice porridge, and cakes,
the king should hold a great festival for nine or seven days,
accompanied by spectacles, great gifts, actors, songs, and narrative recitations.
With the mounting and lowering of swings and carousels, with crabs, and with wrestling matches;
with courtesans, joyful men, and great festivals of gambling;
and with gifts of camphor and garments, and mutual honors.
One should diligently remain awake at night for the sake of protection,
so that there may be no landing of crows, owls, or pigeons;
for from a crow comes famine, and from an owl, the king perishes.

From a dove, there is the destruction of the subjects; therefore, one should always remain vigilant to protect against it. If, due to negligence or laxity, the Indra-banner is lowered by the mountain-dwellers, one must not raise the Indra-banner again in that region.
As long as the Indra-banner is led from another location,
if the raising of the Indra-banner has not been performed due to negligence,
then it must be done in the twelfth year, and not again in the interim.
If, by some chance, an obstacle should arise, understand indeed my ripening [of karma]:
when the parasol breaks, the parasol is destroyed; when the banner [falls], the kingdom perishes;
when there is an interruption of the mantra at the head, there is a destruction of the principal force in the mouth.
One should predict suffering from the staff-like arms and danger to the digestive fire from the belly;
from the leather thong comes the loss of friends, and from the pillars come foot soldiers who go to their destruction, O King of Kings; therefore, one should diligently worship Indra.
Having raised it, one should worship it with devotion day and night, remaining untiring.
If the Indra-dhvaja should fall due to negligence, break, or split in two,
one should fashion a new one out of gold or silver and raise the banner whole once again.
Having performed rites for peace and prosperity, one should cause food to be given to the twice-born, as well as cucumbers,
eggplants, coconuts, wood-apples, citrons,
oranges, and various kinds of edible foods.
Having worshipped with offerings of food and other gifts, one should satisfy [the deity] with this mantra:
"O wielder of the thunderbolt, slayer of the enemies of the gods, many-eyed Purandara!
For the sake of the welfare of all the world, please accept this worship."
O Pāṇḍava, having performed the worship according to the prescribed rules from the constellation Śravaṇa until Bharaṇī, one should dismiss Indra at night with this mantra:
"O Purandara, O Śatakratu, together with the hosts of gods and asuras!"
"O Mahendradhvaja, take this offering and depart.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, for him who thus performs the procession of Indraketu, Parjanya shall rain according to his desire in that kingdom; of this there is no doubt."
Calamities do not arise, nor does the fear caused by death;
having conquered enemies in battle and brought the earth under his control,
he enjoys the kingdom for a long time and is glorified in the world of Indra.

"O Pārtha, in whatever kingdom, town, or city a festival for the sake of the Lord of the Gods (Indra) is performed by the people of the king, gathering together, no fear whatsoever shall arise there from evil portents or from the armies of enemies. Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Great Festival of Mahendra’s Banner," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the Dīpālikā Festival.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: In ancient times, having requested this earth in the form of Vāmana, [he gave it to Bali].
At the sacrifice of Bali, Hari traversed everything with his three strides;
having made the lord of the Daityas dwell in Pātāla, O King, he gave the kingdom to Indra and established Bali as an inhabitant there for another day and night.
O best of men, I shall now tell you that very secret concerning the *balirājya* [the kingdom of Bali], which is marked for the purpose of enjoyment alone.
On the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight of Kārttika, at the onset of night—
"The Daityas act as they please, and their kingdom is upon the earth.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Hṛṣīkeśa, O Lord, tell me about Kaumudī in its entirety."
For what purpose is a gift given on that day, and who is the deity presiding over it?
What indeed should be offered to her, and to whom should one give, O Janārdana?
What joy is prescribed here, and what sport is proclaimed in this context?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika, at the break of dawn,
those who fear hell must certainly perform their ritual bath.
Or one should wave above the head sprouts of the *apāmārga* plant,
together with clods of earth from a furrow (*sītā*) and leaves possessing thorns, [reciting]:
"O *apāmārga*, as you are being waved again and again, take away my sin!"
"O Apāmārga, remove my misfortune and sin entirely;
salutations to you, purify my body. (This is the mantra for the circling of the Apāmārga plant.
Thereafter, the libation (tarpaṇa) should be performed for Dharmarāja by means of his names.
Having worshipped the deities, a lamp should be offered to Yama, the King of Dharma, Death, the Ender, Vaivasvata, Time, and the Destroyer of all beings, as well as to Naraka.
Then, at the time of dusk, one should offer delightful lamps in the temples and monasteries of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others,
as well as in gabled chambers, shrines, assembly halls, and along rivers.
In the walls, gardens, and ponds; in the main streets and pleasure groves; in the temples of Siddhas, Arhats, Buddhas, Cāmuṇḍā, and Bhairava;
and indeed in secluded stables and elephant sheds.
Thus, O lord of men, at the time of dawn on the new moon day,
having bathed and having worshipped and bowed with devotion to the gods and the ancestors,
he performed the Pārvaṇa Śrāddha with curd, milk, ghee, and other offerings.
Having fed the Brahmins with various kinds of foods and having asked for their forgiveness, the king then, at the time of afternoon, should proclaim throughout the city:
"Today the world belongs to Bali; let it enjoy itself as it pleases."
And the world would rejoice in the next life, as every courtyard was whitened with lime, every house adorned with sandalwood trees and garlands,
and all was made enchanting by men and women intoxicated with the pleasures of gambling and wine.
Resounding with dancing and musical instruments, with lamps brightly aflame,
where the people were thrilled by the mutual joy of sharing gifts,
their faces delighted by betel-leaf and anointed with powdered saffron.
In a setting adorned with garments of fine *dukūla* silk and ornaments of gold and rubies,
where wonder was evoked by marvelous, heroic, and amorous displays,
and where young women moved about resplendent in bright attire amidst the throng.
In the delightful evening, crowded with garlands of lamps that dispel the mass of darkness— free from faults yet auspicious as the arrival of the night—
rice grains were scattered by maidens whose faces were like the full moon.
The *nīrājana* rite should be performed with lamps upon the branches of trees;
as the lord of men walks along, bowing his head,
he should proceed while avoiding the sight of those lamps placed on the tree branches.
Therefore, this *nīrājana* rite is proclaimed here as bestowing victory;

for that reason, it should be performed by people during processions, excursions, and travels, while shouting "Victory! and "Live long!", in order to dispel the fear of the defects caused by *rakṣas* demons.
In a city free from minor calamities, abandoned by fear of kings and thieves,
and filled with the affectionate love of friends, kinsmen, relatives, and well-wishers—
the king himself should then proceed to the city at the hour of midnight.
To behold the beautiful city, he should proceed slowly on foot;
with the great sound of musical instruments and blazing hand-lanterns,
he should view the city adorned and protected by his own men.
Having beheld that great wonder and his own auspicious supernatural power (*ṛddhi*),
as well as the joy of Bali’s sovereignty, he would then return to his own home when midnight had thus passed and the people's eyes were moist with sleep.

Then, while the entire populace was awake and a great festival had commenced, Alakṣmī was driven out from the courtyards of her own homes by the women of the city playing upon śūrpas and ḍiṇḍimas with joyful hearts.
With garlands and lamps in hand, her eyes overflowing with affection,
that playful courtesan, bestowing blessings and auspiciousness,
went from house to house offering foot-massages.
While they were intent on kneading flour and applying unguents, busy with service to their elders,
devoted to saluting the twice-born, and gazing upon the blissful kingdom;
and while gifts were being bestowed at will upon married women.
Just as at the time of dawn one should bring forth those worthy of a king,
so too should the virtuous, the gods, and the twice-born be satisfied with sincerity alone;
others with food and drink, and the learned with the gift of kind words.
With gifts of garments and betel, with flowers, camphor, and saffron; with various kinds of snacks and foods, he gratified the women of the inner apartments;
and with villages, grants of territory, and fuel for the neighboring kings.
The king himself should personally satisfy his own infantrymen, who were adorned with necklaces and bracelets,
by honoring each of those people and servants individually;
and having satisfied them according to their merit, he then [honored] the wrestlers, actors, and soldiers.
Mounted upon a platform, he himself beheld bulls and buffaloes fighting with their rivals,
as well as elephants, horses, warriors, and well-adorned foot soldiers;
and he watched the actors, dancers, and wandering minstrels.
Then one should cause cows, buffaloes, and so forth to be agitated and brought forward;
with a joyful air, one should engage in conversation regarding the task at hand, speaking words of light and response.
Then, O Bhārata, during the afternoon hour in the eastern direction—
One should tie a divine path-fence made of kuśa and kāśa grass, surrounded by many [branches], to a lofty pillar or a tree;
having worshipped the elephants and horses when three watches of the night have passed.

When the homa has been performed by the best of the twice-born, one should receive the Mārgapālikā [offering] consisting of cows, bulls, and decorated buffaloes, as well as water-pots overflowing with liquid;
and with the food of the kingdom, one should offer a thousand or a hundred streams [of water].
Or, according to his own capacity, he may offer food with the left hand;
he who gives the *mārgapālī* gift delivers his mother’s family, his father’s family, and himself along with his kinsmen— all of them— to the further shore.
And at that very place, the *nīrājana* ceremony should be performed for the king to grant him victory.
Thus, along the path of the *mārgapālīs*, horses, cows, elephants, bulls,
kings, princes, Brahmins, and those of the Śūdra caste [should pass].

Having completely crossed over the path of the Mārgapālī, one shall be free from disease and always happy. Having performed all this here, a man should perform the worship of Bali, the lord of the Daityas, directly upon the ground in a prepared mandala during the night.
Having painted Bali, the lord of the Daityas, with five-colored pigments—
fully adorned with all ornaments and seated together with Vindhyāvalī,
surrounded by Kūṣmāṇḍa, Bāṇa, Jaṅgha, Uru, and the Dānava Muru.
Having himself fashioned the king of the Daityas with a fully joyful face, wearing a crown and prominent earrings, and possessing two arms,
the king should then worship him in a spacious hall in the middle of his house.
Accompanied by his brothers, ministers, and people, he was gratified and praised by bards;
[he was honored] with lotuses, water-lilies, flowers, kahlāras, and red lotuses,
as well as with perfumes, incense, food offerings, sacrificial oblations, unbroken grains, and molasses cakes.
O King of Kings, together with his ministers and his domestic priest, he should offer wine, meat, liquor, linctuses, lamps, wicks, and oblations while reciting this mantra:
"O King Bali, obeisance to you, O Lord, son of Virocana!"
"O future Indra, enemy of the gods, please accept this worship.
Having thus performed the worship, the king should then observe a vigil at night,
engaging in spectacles and the like, such as performances by actors and storytellers.
And the people, having placed King Bali upon a bed at the edge of their house with white rice, should worship him with fruits and flowers.
O descendant of Kuru, gifts are given in honor of Bali.
Those things which they call inexhaustible have been thus fully demonstrated by me:
whatever gift is given on this [day], whether it be small or great,
all of it becomes inexhaustible and is supremely pleasing to Viṣṇu.
The earth was recovered by Viṣṇu and given back to Bali out of his favor;
he granted a great festival for the Asuras that brought them benefit.
From that time forward, O King of kings, the Kaumudī festival was once again established.
She who drives away all calamities, destroys all obstacles,
removes the grief of the world, is desirable, and brings about the increase of wealth and happiness;
by the word *ku* the earth is to be known, and *mud* thereafter signifies joy.
Because it was known by those who understand the elements and those who know the conventions of society, it is remembered as Kaumudī.
Since people rejoice with one another through various states of being—
joyful, satisfied, and established in happiness— it is therefore remembered as Kaumudī.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, because *kumuda* flowers are offered to Bali on this day for the sake of wealth, O Pārtha, it is therefore known as *Kaumudī*. Thus,
O Lord of the People, there is but one such day and night in every year.
For that king who bestows [this gift] upon the King of the Dānavas as if it were a mirror upon the earth, from where could there be fear of disease in his kingdom?
From where could there be fear of calamities there? There is no fear caused by death.
O King, by means of this Kaumudī festival, there shall be abundance of food, security, health,
and all the highest prosperities upon this earth; all people shall be free from disease and devoid of every calamity.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, whatever state of mind one maintains during this [period]—whether in the form of joy, dejection, or otherwise—the rain follows that very state.
If one weeps, the rain weeps; if one is joyful, the rain rejoices.
In the enjoyment [of this day], one becomes a consumer for a year; being healthy, one shall remain healthy.
Therefore, the Kaumudī festival should be celebrated by men who are joyful and contented.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, this lunar day belongs to Viṣṇu, to the Dānavas, and to the ancestors.
May this auspicious day of the festival of lamps, which is like the *Rāmāyaṇa*— wherein Meghanāda was subdued, Daśānana was set ablaze, and Rāma was delighted— remove your misfortune.
