It is made delightful by the offering of *kūṣmāṇḍa* gourds and brings prosperity through clusters of blue water-lilies.
May the day of lamps, which is like autumn when sleep has departed from the eyes of Hari, remove your misfortune.

O King, for those who, with a devout mind, perform the worship of King Bali during the Festival of Lamps—which generates joy for all people—their year passes here in delight, filled with hundreds of increases in the happiness of giving and enjoyment. Thus ends the one hundred and fortieth chapter, titled "Description of the Dīpāvalī Festival," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the Ritual for One Hundred Thousand Homas for the Nine Planets.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O illustrious one, please tell me, for you are indeed omniscient, O Yādava."
"How is the rite for the attainment of all desires, as well as the rites for pacification (śāntika) and nourishment (pauṣṭika), performed?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"One who desires prosperity or one who desires peace should undertake the sacrifice to the planets (grahayajña)."
Whether desiring long life, prosperity, or likewise performing rites of exorcism,
I shall now proclaim the pacification of the planets (*grahaśānti*), as spoken in the Purāṇas and the Śrutis, having examined all the scriptures and abridged their voluminous extent.
On an auspicious day declared by the Brahmins, having performed the *brāhmaṇavācana* rite and having installed the planets and their presiding deities, one should commence the *homa*.
The sacrifice to the planets (*grahayajña*) is said to be threefold by those learned in the Purāṇas and the Śrutis.
The first is the *ayutahoma* (ten-thousand oblation), after which follows the *lakṣahoma* (hundred-thousand oblation);
the third is the *koṭihoma* (ten-million oblation), which bestows the fruits of all desires.
A sacrifice to the nine planets (*navagrahamakha*) is prescribed with ten thousand oblations.

I shall now describe its procedure as declared in the Purāṇas and the Śrutis: to the northeast of the pit, one should construct an altar according to the rules, measuring two vitastis in width and one vitasti in height.
For the establishment of the gods, one should prepare a square altar that floats upon water;
having performed the rite of bringing the fire (agnipraṇayana), one should invoke the deities upon it.
There, twenty-twelve (thirty-two) deities are to be installed.
The Sun, the Moon, the Son of Earth (Mars), Mercury, Jupiter,
Venus, Saturn, Rāhu, and Ketu— these are declared to be the planets that bring benefit to the world.
[Their images should be made] from copper, crystal, red sandalwood, gold, and silver.
These planets should be fashioned respectively from silver and iron:
one should know the Sun to be in the center, Mars to the south,
Jupiter to the north, and Mercury to the northeast.
One should know that Bhārgava is in the east and Soma in the southeast;
one should establish Ketu in the northwest using white rice grains.
O Great King, one should then establish the kings and ministers with rice grains.
One should know Īśvara to belong to Bhāskara (the Sun), and likewise Umā to Śaśin (the Moon);
Skanda to Aṅgāraka (Mars), and likewise Hari to Budha (Mercury);
one should know Brahmā to belong to Guru (Jupiter), and the Lord of Śacī (Indra) to Śukra (Venus).
One should worship Yama for Śanaiścara, Kāla likewise for Rāhu, and Citragupta for Ketu; these are the presiding deities for all of them.
Fire, Water, Earth, Viṣṇu, and Indra are the deities of the golden [vessels].
Prajāpati, Sūrya, and Brahmā are the presiding deities (pratyadhidevatās).
Likewise, Vināyaka, Durgā, Vāyu, and Ākāśa;
as well as Sāvitrī, Lakṣmī, and Umā together with her husband.
One should invoke the two Aśvin-kumāras with the vyāhṛtis;
one should likewise visualize the Sun as red, accompanied by Aṅgāraka (Mars),
Soma and Śukra as white, and Budha and Jīva as tawny.
Mandara and Kṛṣṇa are likewise known as smoke-colored, possessing the quality of Ketu.
The colors of the planets should be applied to their garments, flowers,
perfumes, offerings, and incenses, beginning with guggulu.
One should offer rice with jaggery to the Sun, milk-porridge with ghee to the Moon, wheat-cakes to Mars, sixty-day rice with milk to Mercury,
curd-rice to Jupiter, and rice with ghee to Indra.
One should offer krisara (rice cooked with sesame) to Śanaiścara and goat meat to Rāhu;
to Ketu, variegated rice (citraudana). Then, one should worship all [the planets] with various edibles.
To the northeast of that [central area], one should place [an offering] adorned with curd and unbroken grains (akṣata).
One should place a flawless water-pot (kumbha) provided with mango sprouts, a pair of garments, the five jewels, and likewise the five types of grain; therein one should install the deity Varuṇa.

O King of kings, having brought earth from all the rivers including the Gaṅgā, from oceans and lakes, from elephant and horse tracks, from anthills, from confluences, and from ponds and cow-pens, together with all medicinal herbs and water;
There, the knower of dharma should place [the vessels] for the sake of the bath of the patron:
"May all the oceans, rivers, lakes,
and springs come here to bring about the destruction of the misfortunes of the patron."
Having thus invoked them all, O best of kings,
one should commence the fire-offering (*homa*) with clarified butter, barley, rice, sesame seeds, and so forth;
[the wood used should be] from the *arka*, *palāśa*, *khadira*, *apāmārga*, and *pippala* trees.
Fuel sticks of udumbara, śamī, dūrvā, and kuśa grass should be offered in sequence—
either one hundred and eight or twenty-eight of each—
with honey, clarified butter, curd, or milk-rice (pāyasa).
Faggots a span long, straight, forked, and auspicious,
are always prescribed by the wise for all rites;
even for all the gods, the knower of the supreme truth performs [the offering] in a whisper.
The fuel sticks (samidhs) should be offered separately with their respective mantras, as follows in order:
"ākṛṣṇena," "imaṃ devāḥ," "agnirmūrdhā divaḥ," and "udbudhyasva" for the Bodhya fire. Thus they are cited according to their sequence.
The *bṛhaspate atiyat asti*, likewise the *parisruta* from food,
the *śanno devīḥ*, and the *kayā naścitra ābhuvat*—
with these, one should offer clarified butter, sacrificial porridge (*caru*), or even edible foods.
Having offered ten oblations with the mantras, they should then perform the homa with the vyāhṛtis.
The eminent brāhmaṇas, facing either north or east,
should prepare the sacrificial carus for each deity accompanied by their respective mantras.
One should begin the bali-homa for Rudra with "apo rājā";
for Umā with "āpo hi ṣṭhā"; likewise for the Lord (Śiva) with "śyena";
for Viṣṇu with "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ"; and for Svayambhū with "svam iccha".
For the deities beginning with Indra, one should again offer oblations to Indra;
the oblation for Yama is proclaimed to be performed with the mantra "navā yamasyāyaṃ gauḥ.
For Kāla, the mantra "brahmajajñānam" is highly recommended.
The wise knowers of the Purāṇas understand this to be the birth of Citragupta.
The mantra beginning with “agniṃ dūtaṃ vṛṇīmahe” is declared for Agni,
while the mantra beginning with “indraṃ yamaṃ varuṇam” is proclaimed for Yama.
In the Vedas, it is recited that from the earth [came] the atmosphere;
and the Puruṣa with a thousand heads is cited as Viṣṇu.
Likewise, Varuṇa, Pavana, the Lord of Wealth, and Śiva [are mentioned].
May Śeṣa together with Brahmā and the guardians of the quarters protect you always.
Kīrti, Lakṣmī, Dhṛti, Medhā, Puṣṭi, Śraddhā, Kriyā, Mati,
Buddhi, Lajjā, Śānti, Puṣṭi, Kānti, and Tuṣṭi are the Mothers.
May these lawful wives, assembled here, consecrate you;
may the Sun, the Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn—
may these planets, as well as Rāhu and Ketu when propitiated, consecrate you.
Gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and pannagas; sages, Manus, cows, and the mothers of the gods;
the wives of the gods, trees, nāgas, daityas, and the hosts of apsarases.
Missiles, all weapons, kings, vehicles,
medicinal herbs, jewels, and whatever are the constituent parts of Time;
rivers, oceans, mountains, sacred fords, clouds, and streams.
"May these [deities] consecrate you for the attainment of all desires and goals.
Then, wearing white garments, anointed with white perfumes,
endowed with all fragrances, having bathed, and filled with faith—
The sacrificer, free from pride, should diligently honor those who have attained perfection along with their wives,
being composed in mind, by means of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās).
He should give a tawny cow to the Sun and likewise a conch shell to the Moon.
One should give a red bull with prominent humps to Bhauma (Mars);
gold to Budha (Mercury); two yellow garments to Guru (Jupiter);
a white horse to the preceptor of the Daityas (Śukra, Venus); and a black-limbed cow to the son of the Sun (Śani, Saturn).
One should give an iron image to Rāhu and an excellent goat to Ketu.
The sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be made equal in value to gold by the sacrificer;
or alternatively, he may give to all of them, or whatever by which the Guru is satisfied.
All sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) for all purposes should be given with this auspicious mantra:
"O Kapilā, you are worthy of worship by all the gods;
since you consist of sacred fords and deities, therefore grant me peace."
O Śaṅkha, you are the merit of merits and the most auspicious of all auspicious things;
since you are eternally held by Viṣṇu, grant me peace.
O Dharma, in the form of a bull, you are the bringer of joy to the world.
Since you are the abode of the eightfold form [of Śiva], grant me peace.
Since you are the golden seed within the womb of Hiraṇyagarbha and the essence of fire,
which yields the fruit of infinite merit, grant me peace.
One should offer a pair of yellow garments, which are dear to Vāsudeva;
by the gift of these, may Viṣṇu grant me peace.
Since Kapila, in the form of a horse, was born from the nectar of immortality (amṛta).
Since you are the constant vehicle of the moon and the sun, grant me peace.
Since you are the entire earth, the cow known as Kṛṣṇā,
and the eternal remover of all sins, grant me peace.
Since all iron implements, such as ploughs and weapons, are always under your control, therefore grant me peace.
Since you, O goat, are established as an essential constituent of sacrifices, [grant me peace].
Since you are the eternal womb of the fire-god Vibhāvasu, therefore grant me peace.
Since the fourteen worlds abide within the limbs of cows,
may there be auspiciousness for me in this world and in the next.
Since the bed of Keśava and Śiva is never empty,
may my own bed likewise be never empty in birth after birth;
just as all the gods are established within all jewels.
Likewise, may the gods grant me peace through this gift of jewels,
such that other gifts do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of gifting land;
indeed, for me, peace arises from the gift of land more than from any other gifts.
Thus one should worship with devotion, free from stinginess regarding wealth,
using garments, gold, heaps of jewels, garlands, perfumes, and ointments.
Now listen to me as I describe the incomparable forms of the planets.

For one who has surrendered with a spirit of devotion, the following description shines forth: Ravi (the Sun) should always be visualized as having two arms, seated upon a lotus throne, holding a lotus in his hand, possessing a splendor like the interior of a lotus, possessing seven horses, and having seven reins.
Śaśin should be depicted as white, wearing white garments, with ten horses, and adorned with white ornaments;
he has two arms, holds a mace in his hand, and grants boons.
[Agni] wears red garlands and garments, and possesses a luster equal to that of the Karṇikāra flower.
The son of the Earth (Budha) should be depicted holding a sword, a shield, and a mace;
wearing yellow garlands and garments, and anointed with yellow sandalwood paste,
the wise one always shines upon a divine golden chariot.
Likewise, the two preceptors of the gods and the Daityas should be depicted as yellow and white, four-armed,
holding staffs, granting boons, and carrying rosaries and water-pots.
The wielder of the trident, possessing the luster of a sapphire, should be shown granting boons and mounted upon a vulture.
The son of the Sun (Saturn) should always be depicted holding arrows and a bow;
he has the face of a tiger, carries a sword, wears armor, holds a trident, and grants boons.
Seated upon a blue lion-throne, Rāhu is thus praised here.
All [the banners] should be smoke-colored, two-armed, wielding maces, and having deformed faces;
they should always be seated upon vultures and be granters of boons. All the planets, which bring welfare to the world, should be depicted wearing crowns.
All of them should then be one hundred and eight finger-breadths in height according to one's own cubit. O son of Pāṇḍu, this nature of the planets has been explained to you;
having understood this, the wise should perform their worship with great effort.
The man who undertakes the worship of the planets according to the prescribed rule attains all his desires and is glorified in heaven after death. However,
if there is a planet that constantly causes affliction to him, whether through his garlands or his wealth—
Having honored that [deity] with great effort, the wise man should also worship the others:
the planets, cows, kings, and especially Brahmins. When honored, these [beings] honor him in return; when treated with contempt, they consume him utterly.
Therefore, one who desires prosperity should not perform [the rite] deficient in sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā);
for when the dakṣiṇā is complete, even a single [deity] is satisfied. This sacrifice to the nine planets (navagrahamakha) is always remembered as the Ayutahoma.

O Great King, this *ayutahoma* has been described for the purpose of removing obstacles during marriages, festivals, sacrifices, consecrations, and other rites, as well as in times of distress and portents;
now hear about the *lakṣahoma*.
Since the wise know that the *lakṣahoma* leads to the attainment of all desires,
and since it is beloved by the ancestors and bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation,
one should obtain the strength of the planets and stars and perform the *brāhmaṇavācana*.

A wise man should have a pavilion constructed to the northeast of the house, or on the ground of a temple of Rudra; it should be square and face the north. He should construct it according to the rules, measuring ten or eight cubits.
A person should diligently have the ground sloping toward the northeast;
having reached the northeastern portion of the pavilion's site,
he should have a beautiful sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) constructed, duly endowed with the prescribed characteristics.
Because it would be deficient in measurement, unpraiseworthy, and a source of many fears,
a perfectly complete *śānti-kuṇḍa* is prescribed.
For a *lakṣahoma*, the Self-born One (Brahmā) has declared that the dimensions should be ten times this.
With offerings made with diligence and likewise with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās),
the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) for a Lakṣahoma should be two cubits wide and four cubits long;
it should have a yoni-shaped opening and three tiers (mekhalās).
For the establishment of the gods, it is surrounded by three ramparts;
the first rampart is declared to be two finger-breadths in height,
and the two ramparts above it are each endowed with a height of one finger-breadth.
The width of all [the lines] therein is said by the wise to be two finger-breadths.
Above that, the wall of the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) should be ten finger-breadths high.
Upon that, one should invoke the deities as before with flowers and rice grains.
All the subordinate deities (pratyadhidevatās) should be installed facing the sun;
O best of sages, they must not be placed with their backs turned toward one another.
One who desires prosperity should worship Garuḍa there as the preeminent deity.
"O vehicle of the Supreme Lord (Brahmā), whose body is perfectly full,
you who constantly remove the poison of sin, grant me peace.
Having addressed the water-pot as before, one should likewise perform the fire-oblation (homa).

Having again offered a hundred thousand oblations along with the prescribed number of fuel-sticks and so forth, he should then fashion a sacrificial ladle (*sruk*) made of moist *udumbara* wood, free from crooks or hollows, and measuring one cubit in length; thereafter, upon two pillars—
One should likewise cause a continuous stream of clarified butter to fall properly over the fire;
one should cause the recitation of the Āgneya, Vaiṣṇava, Raudra, and Aiṃdava Sūktas,
as well as the Mahāvaiśvānara Sāman and the Jyeṣṭha Sāman.
The bath for the patron is performed as before, with the recitation of mantras;
the patron, free from desire and anger and possessing a tranquil mind, should give separate sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the officiating priests as previously prescribed.
In the sacrifice to the nine planets, four Brahmins who are knowers of the Vedas should be employed;

or else, two peaceful and highly learned officiating priests (ṛtvij) alone should be engaged for the ten-thousand-fold oblation (ayutahoma), so that one does not become entangled in excessive elaboration.

And likewise, for the Lakṣahoma as well, ten or eight officiating priests (ṛtvij) should be appointed according to one's capacity; or else four, provided they are free from envy. In the sacrifice to the nine planets (Navagrahamakha), everything is the same as in the Lakṣahoma, with the addition of ten.
And the best of the Pāṇḍavas, being devoted, should also give ornaments according to his ability;
he should present beds, garments, golden bracelets,
and earrings and finger-rings as sacred offerings.
A person should not perform a rite devoid of the sacrificial fee through stinginess regarding wealth;
by failing to give out of greed or delusion, one brings about the ruin of one’s lineage.
One who desires prosperity should give the gift of food according to one's ability.
Since a vow lacking food yields the fruit of famine,
one deficient in limbs destroys the kingdom, while one deficient in mantras destroys the officiating priests;
one without sacrificial fees destroys the patron— there is no enemy equal to such a sacrifice.
Furthermore, a man with meager wealth should never perform a Lakṣahoma anywhere;
therefore, one should worship with devotion according to the rules that specific planet which constantly causes affliction, or two, or three.

One should worship even a single Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas with devotion and with great effort through sacrificial fees; or, if one possesses abundant wealth, one may worship many. Furthermore, if there is wealth in every house, a Lakṣahoma should be performed.
For by performing [this] according to the injunctions, one attains all desires and is honored in the world of Śiva by the Vasus, Ādityas,
and hosts of Maruts for eight hundred kalpas; thereafter, one shall attain liberation.
He who, possessing a specific desire, performs this Lakṣahoma according to the prescribed rule, attains that desire and enjoys an eternal state.
One seeking a son obtains a son; one seeking wealth obtains wealth.

One desiring a wife shall obtain a beautiful wife, and a maiden a virtuous husband; likewise, one who has lost his kingdom shall regain his kingdom, and one desiring prosperity shall attain prosperity. Whatever desire one prays for, that one obtains in its full measure.

He who performs [the rite] without desire attains the Supreme Brahman. O King, he who duly performs the Lakṣahoma with many eminent brahmins brings about peace consisting of the pacification of the nine planets, the quelling of misfortunes, security, abundant food, incomparable prosperity, and the increase of one's lineage; indeed, wherever he performs the Lakṣahoma, such blessings abide there.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Lakṣahoma of the Nine Planets," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira. Now follows the description of the ritual for the Koṭihoma.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
In former times, the illustrious King Saṃvaraṇa, powerful and skilled in the meaning of the scriptures, dwelt in the supreme city of Pratiṣṭhāna;
he was devoted to Brahman, dedicated to his ancestors, and a worshiper of the gods and the Brāhmaṇas.
Then, while he was ruling the kingdom and properly protecting his subjects,
Sanaka, the son of Brahmā and a great yogi, arrived.
Having offered him a seat, the king likewise bowed his head in salutation.

Having honored him with offerings of water for the hands and feet and other rites, and having offered himself, he— being a knower of things as they truly are— related various stories from the Itihāsas and Purāṇas,
as well as the life-stories of ancient royal sages.

Then, during the course of conversation, the high-minded king, endowed with humility, asked the master of yoga about a matter that had been dwelling in his mind for the benefit of the lords of the earth, as well as for the world and himself.
Saṃvaraṇa said:
"O Blessed One, when there occurs a great portent, an earthquake,
a thunderclap, a rain of dust, and likewise the collapse of a house— "
During afflictions caused by one's birth star, in times of fear of drought,
during fevers, afflictions by planets, famine, or civil war;
when diseases have arisen, or when the body is excessively tormented.

When great affliction has arisen, what should be done by the best of men? O best of the twice-born, tell me that which is the means for attaining heaven, as well as that which bestows fame and wealth, and likewise grants health to human beings.
Sanatkumāra said: Listen, O King, I shall proclaim the unsurpassed rite of pacification known as the Koṭihoma; it is incomparable and bestows the fruit of all desires.
I shall describe the procedure by which sins such as the killing of a Brahmin are destroyed in that very instant,
portents are pacified, and great happiness is attained;
listen and be attentive.

One who desires his own welfare should perform [this rite] in a temple, on a riverbank, in a forest, in a dwelling, or even on a mountain; and it should be done during an auspicious conjunction of constellations, on a day endowed with the previously mentioned qualities.
One should perform the Koṭihoma rite for the benefit of the patron,
having diligently honored a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas with garments,
ornaments, perfumes, garlands, and ointments.
Having prostrated before him according to the prescribed rite, one should offer oneself:
"You are our refuge, father, and mother; you are our goal and our supreme resort.
By your grace, O brahmin-sage, may everything that is in my heart be attained."
"Perform for me the unsurpassed sacrifice for liberation from calamity—
an incomparable *koṭihoma* for the sake of peace and the fulfillment of all desires.
Then the wise priest, pure and wearing white garments, [prepared].
Accompanied by Brahmins who are well-versed in the Vedas, meritorious, and composed,
he should first cause them to pronounce an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) after having honored the Brahmins well on a level, pure plot of ground that slopes toward the east and the north.
Then, the Brahmin, being honored, should construct an auspicious pavilion—
excellent if one hundred cubits in size, middling if half of that,
and inferior if half of the latter, depending upon his capacity, the time, and other factors.
Furthermore, the wise man should construct a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in the center of the pavilion,
measuring eight cubits in length as well as in width;
its three tiers (mekhalā) should each be twelve finger-breadths in breadth.
With a well-concentrated mind, one should fashion the womb (yoni) to be of that same measurement.
O King, the wise practitioner should construct an altar (vedi) in the eastern part of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa),
measuring four cubits square and exactly one cubit in height.
The wise man should diligently prepare that site for all beings;
then, having smeared the ground near the pavilion,
he should place fourteen water-filled jars there.
One should decorate [the pavilion] with sprouts from the Aśvattha, Plakṣa, Cūta, and other trees,
and arrange a canopy above the pavilion. The wise person should then set up archways (toraṇas) in all directions.
When the preparations have been thus completed, O subduer of enemies, the priest, being well-composed,
should commence the rite of oblation with the proclamation of "Auspicious Day" and "Victory. Having established the deities to be mentioned hereafter upon the altar, he should proceed.
One should place the Brāhmaṇas in the eastern part, Janārdana in the middle,
Rudra in the west, and likewise the Vasus in the north;
all the planets in the northeast, and the Maruts in the southeast.
O best of kings, having thus established the world-protectors in their respective places— Vāyu in the north, Saumya (the Moon) in the northeast, and the others in due order—
one should worship those deities according to the rules with garments, perfumes, garlands, and ointments.
With mantras declared in the Vedas, those containing their specific names, and those spoken in the Purāṇas, each separately—
[he worships] the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, the guardians of the world, as well as the planets;
Brahmā, Janārdana, and the trident-bearer who destroyed the eyes of Bhaga.
May all those present here partake in happiness;
may you all accept this worship offered by me with devotion;
and may you all, being composed, perform auspicious acts for the sake of the sacrificial rite.
Having thus worshipped those gods with diligence and a pure mind,
with various offerings of food, edibles, fruits, and likewise leaves,
he then, together with those twice-born brahmins, performed the ritual for the sacrificial pit according to the prescribed rules.

One should perform the purificatory rites as prescribed by those who contemplate the Vedas. Then, O best of kings, one should summon the fire known by the name Ghṛtārcis and appoint a hundred Brahmins there.
But if many are not available, he should employ as many as are available—
those who are advanced in learning, advanced in age, householders with restrained senses,
devoted to their own duties, possessed of knowledge and virtuous character, and tranquil, the best among the twice-born.
O King, one should meditate there upon the Lord of Gods, the five-faced Fire;
his four faces and seven tongues, O Ruler of the Earth,
and then that single tongue which is remembered as the granter of all desires.
When the mind is merely smoldering, oblations should not be offered in vain; they should be offered when the fire has truly blazed.
Oblations with the Ṛg verses should be performed facing east, with the Yajus verses facing north, with the Sāman verses facing west, and with the Atharva verses facing south.
Having first offered the two libations (āghāra) and the two portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga), the wise one should then strew grass around the fire and likewise prepare the seats;
having first [invited] the Brahman priest, he should perform all of this subsequently.
Everything there is prescribed by means of the *vyāhṛtis*;

one should offer oblations to all the deities who have been prepared upon the altar with those [mantras] beginning with the *praṇava*, possessing their respective characteristic marks, and joined with the *svāhākāra* at the end.

In this manner, one should perform the supreme sacrifice known as the Koṭihoma. In the Koṭihoma, black sesame seeds smeared with ghee and mixed with a small amount of barley should be offered as oblations, along with fuel-sticks made from Palāśa wood.
When each thousand [oblations] is complete,

O King, one should offer an auspicious *pūrṇāhuti* into its mouth during the fifth [round], for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals. These *pūrṇāhuti*s are declared to be required in a *koṭi-homa*, O lord of men.
O best of kings, ten thousand Brahmins learned in the scriptures, who discourse upon the Veda, must remain present from the day of commencement along with the sacrificer,
or else together with the family priest.
"O Indra among kings, the sacrificer who desires to attain the coveted worlds of heaven must strive diligently to avoid defects such as anger and greed.
Saṃvaraṇa said:

O Brahmin, because of the vastness of ritual action, a crore of oblations is extremely difficult to perform; it can only be accomplished with great difficulty over a long period of time. Indeed, it is my view that such a feat is difficult to achieve even through religious observances or celibacy.

O Brahmin, the cessation [of activity] for Brahmins during the *bhṛśayyā* and other such periods is difficult to perform, because it is heavy due to its obligatory nature and because it depends on specific times such as the lunar festivals (*parvan*). This is understood, O Brahmin, if it is stated in the scriptures.
"O Brahman-born one, tell me the summary of the *koṭihoma*.
Sanatkumāra said:
"It may have a hundred faces, ten faces, two faces, or likewise a single face."
O Great King, the Koṭihoma is prescribed as being of four kinds. Having understood the gravity of the task at hand, one should never perform it on an improper occasion.
Listen now to how the Koṭihoma is to be performed in brief.
Having constructed one hundred divine sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) as prescribed, each measuring one cubit,
he should then appoint one hundred Brahmins at each pit;
however, in the Sadyah-pakṣa rite, a thousand Brahmins are prescribed.
When the fire has been established in a single location and thoroughly consecrated on all sides,
all the twice-born should perform the oblation as prescribed in each individual pit,
just as in the great Rājasūya sacrifice where there is a multiplicity of pits.
Moreover, no multiplicity of fires is prescribed there in that sacrifice;
likewise, even here when a hundred fire-pits are spread with ghee-flames,
the sacrifice shall be considered as one alone— the Koṭihoma— without a doubt.

Thus, when that which is normally performed [in a long time] is quickly done by those who are distracted due to the weightiness of their duties, it should be known as the *śatānana* *koṭihoma*; of this there is no doubt.
It may be performed in a few days, even during the rainy season or other such times.
At that time, a wise person should perform a Koṭihoma ten times greater;
there, one should employ two hundred Brahmins, having distributed [the offerings] well among them,
who should be learned in the Vedas, observant of vows, and masters of their senses.
O King, having prepared two sacrificial pits and divided the fire between them,
the twice-born should perform the oblation again after consecrating it according to the prescribed rites;
indeed, one hundred Brahmins should be employed there, duly distributed.
Whether after a month or two months, when the proper time has arrived,
the wise should thus perform the Koṭihoma with two openings;
however, when the sacrificer wishes to conclude the sacrifice at his own will.

O King, at that time, it may be performed in many ways according to the occasion, or it may be performed with a single entrance. The fire, situated in a single hearth, is tended by wise Brahmins who are concentrated in mind, possessed of knowledge and good conduct, and remain content with whatever they obtain.

O best of men, there is no restriction here regarding the number of Brahmins, nor is there any restriction regarding the time; it is called a sacrifice performed according to one's own will. Through repetition, it fulfills all desires, like the ritual of the Cāturmāsya.
If that [prolonged performance] is not possible, this sacrifice must be performed at all times.
O King, this sacrifice has but a single entrance; over a long period of time it may become fraught with many obstacles. Therefore, one should perform it in an abbreviated form.
Since the mind, wealth, and even life itself are always unstable,
it is therefore praised that one should perform the duties of dharma in brief.
Then, once the sacrifice is completed, one should cause a great festival to be held.
Then, amidst the sounding of conchs and trumpets and the resonance of Vedic chants,
the king, filled with faith, should initiate the Brahmins and the Hotṛ priests,
O King, with gifts of gold coins, bracelets, and various kinds of earrings.
At that time, one hundred cows and a hundred horses should be given,
and one should cause a thousand pieces of gold to be bestowed upon all.
One should also honor the family priest with villages, elephants, chariots, and horses.
One should honor all the poor, the blind, and the wretched with clothing and other gifts.
Then, one should perform the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) using those previously prepared jars,
while reciting the mantra prescribed for the Lakṣahoma sacrifice, which always brings victory.
O best of kings, for one who thus concludes the auspicious Koṭihoma sacrifice,
there arises health, as well as the increase of wealth, sons, and kingdom; indeed,
the destruction of all sins occurs.
Fear of drought, fear of portents,
famine, and affliction by the planets— all these shall be pacified upon the earth.
This merit is a destroyer of sins and bestows the fruits of all desires.
To inform the king, the sage Sanatkumāra declared:

"Those men who, whether in their home or in the forest, perform the *nṛpakohoma*—which pacifies all calamities—shall obtain all the enjoyments desired by their hearts to their full satisfaction; then, with their being utterly purified, they go to the abode of Śakra."

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Koṭihoma," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[Now follows] the description of the ritual for the Great Peace (Mahāśānti). Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
I shall proclaim the Great Peace (Mahāśānti), spoken by Mahādeva for the benefit of kings, which enables one to cross over what is otherwise most difficult to traverse;
it should be performed at the time of a king’s consecration and during the king’s military expedition.
In the event of bad dreams or ill omens, when there is an affliction caused by malevolent planets;
upon the falling of lightning or meteors; on one's birth star or the day presided over by the planetary deity; when a comet has appeared, or during a thunderclap or an earthquake.
In the case of childbirth occurring during the Mūla or Gaṇḍa asterisms, or upon the birth of twins;
when umbrellas or banners fall to the ground from their own positions;
and likewise, when crows, owls, or pigeons enter the house.
When malefic planets are in retrograde motion,

especially during birth and other such [auspicious] occasions; and when Jupiter, Saturn, and Mars, as well as the Sun specifically, are situated in the first, twelfth, fourth, or eighth houses from the birth [ascendant].
If, during a battle, all the planets appear with the sun and moon as their stakes,
or if there is the destruction of clothing, weapons, cattle, horses, jewels, and hair,
and likewise if a rainbow is seen in the sky at night;
In the event of the collapse of a house, the miscarriage of fetuses, or the birth of mules from mares,
as well as during eclipses of the sun and moon, the performance of a Great Peace (mahāśānti) rite is highly recommended;
by this means, all ill omens are entirely pacified.
Five Brahmins, endowed with noble lineage and virtuous conduct, should perform that rite,
O Pāṇḍava— those who know the four Vedas, the three Vedas, or even two Vedas;
specifically those of the Atharva-veda, as well as the Rig-veda and the Yajur-veda.
Pure, endowed with Vedic learning, and devoted to the recitation of mantras and burnt offerings,
having purified their bodies through penances such as the Kṛcchra, Pārāka, and Naktā,
they should first propitiate [the deity] with mantras and thereafter commence the ritual action.
One should have an auspicious pavilion constructed measuring ten or twelve cubits;
in its center, one should make an altar measuring four cubits,
and in the southeast, one should construct a very beautiful sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one cubit.
O twice-born ones, [the sacrificial post] should be joined with three girdles and adorned with a yoni;
it should be bound with a garland of sandalwood and likewise decorated with an archway,
within a pavilion smeared with cow dung.
Having bathed, wearing white garments, and adorned with white garlands and unguents,
one should then place five water-pots upon that altar—
four in the corners starting from the southeast (āgneya) and the fifth in the center.
Upon an eight-petaled lotus adorned with mango sprouts,
one should prepare the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) according to the rite of the *brahmakūrca*.
[One should also include] medicinal herbs, the five gems, yellow pigment (*rocanā*), and sandalwood.
White mustard seeds, śamī, dūrvā grass, kuśa grass, rice, and likewise barley;
apāmārga, the fruit-bearing [branch], as well as nyagrodha and udumbara;
plakṣa, aśvattha, and kapittha, along with priyaṅgu and the sprouts of the mango tree.
One should place elephant-tusk earth into the corner-pitchers (koṇakumbha);
likewise, one should place water from sacred fords (puṇyatīrtha), food, grain, and products of the cow into the central pitcher.
With the mantra "vācam" and "iti," one performs the consecration (abhimantraṇa) of the fire-pitcher.
With the mantra "Āśuḥ śiśānaḥ," one should consecrate the vessel for Vāyu;
with the "Īśāvāsya" mantra, the fourth vessel;
and the mantras beginning with "Bhavodbhava" should be recited over the central Rudra-vessel.
One should perform the worship of the water-pot (kumbha) with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), garments, food offerings cooked in ghee,
fruits such as coconuts, and lamps;
and immediately thereafter, one should cause the recitation of the Svasti-vācana to be performed.
By this sequence, one should gradually perform the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*).
One should first establish the fire with the mantra "Agniṃ dūtam" (Fire, the messenger). Then, with the mantra "Hiraṇyagarbhaḥ samavartata," one should appoint the seat for Brahmā.
One should perform the ritual with the well-proclaimed mantra of Kapota;
having performed the protection of the fire as well as the consecration of the clarified butter (ājya),
one should then procure the materials according to the requirements for the purpose at hand.
Then, the cooking of the milk-rice (pāyasa) should be performed with the Puruṣasūkta. Once it is cooked, one should sprinkle it with clarified butter and place it upon the ground.
Then, one should offer eighteen fuel-sticks made of Śamī wood, measuring the prescribed length.

One should cause seven fuel-sticks of *pālāśa* wood to be offered, likewise seven by seven; having performed the two *āghāra* libations and the two *ājyabhāga* portions according to the previous procedure,
one should offer seven oblations with the verse beginning "O Jātavedas."
One should offer oblations from the *sthālīpāka* again with the *jātavedas* [mantra];
then one should offer four oblations with the *taratsamandī* hymn;
and thereafter, one should offer seven other oblations ending in "svāhā" with the mantra beginning "yamāya."
Then, O King, one should offer seven oblations with the mantra "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ";
thereafter, twenty-seven oblations with "svāhā to the constellations";
and then one should again offer the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation with the mantra "yatkarmaṇeti."
Then the oblation for the planets (graha-homa) should be performed with sesame seeds drenched in clarified butter;
having offered the expiatory rite (prāyaścitta), one should complete the ritual of the oblation.
Thereafter, amidst the sounding of trumpets and the blasts of horns and conchs, [the ceremony proceeds].
Indeed, the consecration of the sacrificer must be performed by the best of the twice-born. Having placed him upon an auspicious seat made from the *kāśmarya* tree,
situated in the center of the altar, for the sake of pacifying ill omens.
With five full jars, one should perform the rite with these mantras in due order:
first with "sahasrākṣeṇa," then with "śatāyuṣā," then with "sajoṣasā ca indra," and finally with the Ṛgvedic verse beginning "viśvāni."
Then, with concentrated minds, they should bathe [the image] while reciting "May there be Truth" (*ṛtam astu*).
Thereafter, one should offer a ritual oblation (*bali*) to the quarters of the world, consisting of various kinds of food, while uttering the mantra:
"Homage to all beings" (*namo 'stu sarvabhūtebhyaḥ*).
All the Brāhmaṇas, having bathed, should recite the supreme peace-mantra (śānti).
Having caused a stream of the water of peace to fall from all sides,
and having performed the declaration of the auspicious day (puṇyāhavācana), one should complete the rite of peace.
Free from envy, one should give land, gold, garments, beds, and seats as sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to Brahmins according to one's ability;
one should also cause gifts to be given to the poor, the helpless, the distinguished, and those learned in the Vedas.
By giving excellent food, everything thereafter becomes successful;
one obtains a long life and conquers enemies in an instant. One's difficulties are resolved, and one obtains auspicious sons.
Just as armor serves as a defense against the blows of weapons,
so does propitiatory rite serve as a defense against the afflictions of fate.
For one who is non-violent, self-controlled, and whose wealth is earned through righteousness, [there is no fear].
For one endowed with compassion and courtesy, all the planets become benevolent;
they facilitate his goals, increase his merit, fulfill his desires, and grind away his evil.
Thus, a man of tranquil heart should always cause this capable peace-making rite, which removes every affliction, to be performed.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual for Great Peace," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira; followed by the description of the peace rite for Gaṇanātha.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Lord of Gods, O All-pervading One, tell me the peace-mantra (śānti) of Gaṇanātha, by performing which every human being crosses over all difficulties. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Indra among kings, I shall declare the supreme Śānti, beloved of Gaṇanātha,
by the mere performance of which all misfortunes are destroyed.
Understand Vināyaka for the sake of accomplishing one's undertakings without obstacle.
In his dreams, he plunges deeply into water and sees shaven-headed men; he sees those clad in saffron robes and ascends upon carnivorous beasts;
he stands together in one place with Rudras who are headless corpses.
Even while walking, he imagines himself followed by enemies;
dejected and with his undertakings fruitless, he desponds without apparent cause.
Possessed by him, the prince does not obtain the kingdom.
A maiden does not obtain a husband, nor does a pregnant woman obtain offspring;
likewise, a learned Brahmin does not attain the status of a teacher, nor does a student succeed in teaching.
A merchant does not gain profit, nor does a farmer succeed in his cultivation.
His ceremonial bath (snapana) should be performed according to the prescribed rites on an auspicious day;
he should first be rubbed with a paste of white mustard seeds mixed with clarified butter,
and likewise his body and head should be anointed with fragrant saffron.

Having seated [the image] upon an auspicious throne and having had the virtuous twice-born recite benedictions, one should cast into the waters earth from a horse-stable, an elephant-stable, an anthill, a confluence of rivers,
and a lake, as well as yellow pigment (rocanā), perfumes, and guggulu resin.
When these have been taken from the lake with jars by means of single-syllable mantras;
Having placed the auspicious throne upon a red bull-hide, [I perform this rite].
The speech uttered by the Sage is thousand-eyed and hundred-streamed;
with that I consecrate you—may the purifying verses (pāvamānyas) cleanse you.
May King Varuṇa grant you fortune; may Sūrya and Bṛhaspati grant you fortune;
may Indra and Vāyu grant you fortune, and may the Seven Seers grant you fortune.
Whatever misfortune is in your hair, at your parting, or upon your head—[may it be removed].

May those waters on your forehead, ears, and eyes always destroy [your misfortunes]. Having bathed, one should offer mustard oil with a ladle made of udumbara wood upon the head, while grasping kusha grass with the left hand.
Mita and Samita, as well as Sālakaṭaṅkaṭa, Kūṣmāṇḍa, and Rājaputra— at the end [of their names], accompanied by the word *svāhā*,
with offerings (*bali*) and mantras joined with salutations.
At a crossroads, having spread kuśa grass everywhere upon a winnowing basket,
one should offer both husked and unhusked rice, as well as rice mixed with sesame paste,
cooked fish and likewise raw fish, and meat in that same measure.
Having offered variegated and fragrant flowers, the three kinds of liquor,
radish, *pūri*, cake, as well as a garland of *uṇḍeraka* flowers,
*dūrvā* grass, and all types of blossoms, he should present the full *arghya* in a circular vessel.
Then one should worship Ambikā, the mother of Vināyaka:
"Grant me beauty, grant me fame, grant me fortune, O Bhavānī;
grant me sons, grant me wealth, and grant me all my desires."
Then, wearing white garments and adorned with white garlands and unguents,
one should feed the Brahmins and give a pair of garments even to the preceptor.
Having thus worshipped Vināyaka and the planets according to the prescribed rite, [one should proceed].
One obtains the fruit of one's actions and attains supreme prosperity;
likewise, by performing the worship of the Sun, the tilaka of one’s Lord,
and that of Mahāgaṇapati, one shall attain perfection.
Furthermore, that Mahāgaṇapati who is fashioned from the root of a white Arka tree,
being complete with all auspicious characteristics, is remembered as a bringer of success;
when he is recited over in a pure place, there is indeed no obstacle for the embodied soul here.

One should always worship the Supreme with perfumes, garlands, wreaths, and other offerings. Even a man whose fortune is exhausted becomes a lord of men when he is thus honored; he attains all perfections and is ever victorious.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Peace Rite for Gaṇanātha," in the Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, in the Uttaraparvan, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira;
followed by the "Description of the Ritual for the Nakṣatra Homa. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
While [the sage] was seated comfortably during the Agnihotra sacrifice, Garga questioned Kauśika:
"In cases of bondage, confinement, the affliction of limbs, or the onset of diseases, how may his liberation be achieved? Tell me what is curable and what is incurable."
Questioned by Garga, Kauśika spoke these words:
"If a disease arises for one during the time of conception, at the birth asterism, or at the signs of death, it leads to suffering and even to death."
If someone contracts a disease under the asterism Kṛttikā, there will be suffering for nine nights; under Rohiṇī, for three nights;
under Mṛgaśīrṣa, for five nights; and under Ārdrā, it is fatal.
A seven-night period is prescribed under Punarvasu and Puṣya;
likewise, a nine-night period under Āśleṣā, and until the end of the cremation ground (the Śmaśāna) under Maghā.
Under the two Phālgunīs it lasts for two months, and under the Uttarās for three fortnights.
In Hasta, it may be seen for a short time; in Citrā, for half a month;
likewise, in Svātī, for two months; in Viśākhā, for twenty days;
in Anurādhā (Maitra), for ten days; and in Jyeṣṭhā, for half a month.
Liberation arises through Mūla; during Āṣāḍhā, it lasts for fifteen days;
through the nine [days] of Uttarā, it lasts for two months; through Śravaṇa, [one month];
during Dhaniṣṭhā, half a month; and during Vāruṇa (Śatabhiṣaj), ten days.
If one dies under the constellation Bhādrapadā, it lasts for nine days; under the three Uttarās, for fifteen days;
under Revatī, for ten nights; and likewise under Aśvinī, for a single day and night.
One will certainly be deprived of life [during these periods], O Garga; there is no doubt in this matter.
The origin of diseases caused by the constellations has been instructed by Kauśika;
furthermore, the astrologer must know the constellation of one's birth.
One should offer oblations of fuel-sticks from a milk-tree into the fire dedicated to the deity of the horse (Aśvadevata).
One should offer sesame seeds soaked in honey to Yama; barley alone to Agni as the deity;
for Prajāpati, one should offer the *baka* bird, which produces edible seeds;
*priyaṅgu* grains to Soma; and [an offering] combined with ghee and meat to Rudra.
And for Āditya, one should diligently offer white rice smeared with ghee,
together with milk and clarified butter; for Bṛhaspati as the presiding deity,
[the offering is made] with cultivated herbs and banyan leaves, along with clarified butter, for the serpent-deity.
The Homa sacrifice of *priyaṅgu* seeds is prescribed under the constellation presided over by Yama;
under the constellation of Savitṛ, there is a curd-offering (*dadhi-homa*), while under that of Tvaṣṭṛ, the oblation is variegated rice (*citraudana*).
One should offer barley with clarified butter in the fire of Rudra, but milk-rice (*payodana*) in the fire of Agni.
Then, with the Maitra mantra,
one should perform a sesame oblation (tilahoma) in the southwest (nairṛtya), in the unmanifest fire, and in the fire of the deity of the year;
furthermore, one should cause the Vaiśvadeva rite to be performed with śāli rice seeds.
Red rice grains should be offered as oblations to Viṣṇu;
for Varuṇa, an oblation of Pārijāta flowers is prescribed.
Under the Nakṣatra Ajaikapād, it is equal to that performed under Prajāpati.
Under the constellation Āhirbudhnya, one should perform the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice;
red rice grains should be offered as oblations to the deity Viṣṇu.
In the month of Pauṣa, one should offer one hundred and eight unbroken fruits.
In ancient times, Brahmā proclaimed a single *sāvitrī-homa*,
which pacifies all fevers and is the supreme immediate remover of fever.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Nakṣatra-Homa," in the *Uttara-parvan* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
The Description of the Vow for a Hundred Offenses.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Furthermore, O King, I shall tell you of another vow that yields great fruit.
"Listen to that by which even a hundred offenses go to destruction.
Ikṣvāku said:
Tell me what that vow is, and tell me what that offense is."
"Who indeed is worshipped therein, and when is it performed by men?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
"Listen, O mighty-armed King, to the vow of a hundred offenses."
The Lotus-born One declared that by the mere performance of this, a woman may obtain both desire and liberation; all expiations performed for the removal of every sin shall become as if unperformed.
Even a very heavy sin is burned away like a heap of cotton.
O King, listen as I speak of a hundred offenses:
that a man, out of delusion, does not perform this vow day after day.
Not belonging to any stage of life (āśrama), being without sacred fires, failing in vows,
not giving gifts, impurity, cruelty, covetousness,
intolerance, harming others, and deceitfulness— these are inauspicious.
Breach of vows, atheism, reviling the Vedas, harshness, untruthfulness, violence, theft, the derangement of the senses,
lack of restraint of the mind, anger, envy, and malice— these are [the defects].
Hypocrisy, deceit, thievery, harsh speech, negligence,

the abandonment of one's wife, mother, sons, and others, the worshiping of those unworthy of worship, the omission of ancestral rites (śrāddha), the forsaking of recitation (japa), and the neglect of the five great sacrifices (pañcayajña).
The omission of the twilight libations and fire-offerings, the extinction of the sacred fire,
sexual intercourse at improper times, O Pārtha, as well as sexual intercourse on sacred festival days (parvan),
backbiting, adultery with another's wife, giving gifts [to the unworthy], and frequenting prostitutes.
Giving to those who are unworthy, eating roots and bulbs in small quantities, sexual union with outcastes, abandoning one's mother, deserting one's father,
lack of devotion toward one's parents, engaging in disputes, and the neglect of the Purāṇas and the Smṛtis.
Eating forbidden food, treachery toward one's husband, lack of discernment, engaging in agricultural labor, taking a wife,
failure to conquer the senses, deceitfulness, and likewise the forgetting of sacred knowledge.
Abandoning the sacred scriptures, debt, painting, washing the private parts,
the sale of one's wife, sons, daughters, and so forth, sexual intercourse with animals,
cutting down trees for firewood, and filling in a hole with water and such— these are [forbidden acts].
The occurrence of coming to a pond, the act of selling knowledge,
the loss of livelihood, O protector of the earth, being a beggar, having bad friends,
the killing of a woman, the killing of a cow, officiating as a domestic priest, and the killing of a friend.
Feticide, eating the food of others, and the consumption of a Śūdra’s food; for a Śūdra, performing fire-rituals, lack of scriptural injunction, and having a bad son;
begging from the learned, talkativeness, and the acceptance of gifts.
The deficiency of Vedic sacraments, the failure to protect those in distress,
the killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, the theft of gold, and thereafter, sexual intercourse with the wife of a guru as well as association with such persons.
O sinless one, these hundred offenses have been recounted by me to you;
there are many others as well, but these have been mentioned primarily.
Even if one were to have thousands of mouths and hundreds of tongues in each mouth, [one could not fully enumerate them].
Nevertheless, these cannot be fully described because they are infinite;
yet thousands, lakhs, and hundreds of crores of offenses truly perish in that very instant through the worship of Satyeśa.
The worshipful Lord, who has accomplished his purpose and conquered [all],
stands here upon the banner of Truth together with Lakṣmī, the Lord of the World. Vāmadeva is stationed to the east, and Nṛsiṃha is stationed to the south.
Kapila is at the western face, while Vārāha is situated in the north;
Acyuta is to be known as the upward-facing one—this indeed is the group of five Brahmas.
O King, one should always worship that Lord of Truth who is thus established.
Seated upon the pericarp of a lotus situated within the half-moon of the Ocean of Milk,
he holds the weapons— the lotus, the mace *kaumodakī*, the conch, and the discus—
on the lower left, the upper right, the rear, and the lower [right], O King.
The Gaṅgā, ever purified by men, flows forth from beneath his feet;
likewise, there is another group of eight Śaktis—listen to their names from me:
Jayā, Vijayā, Jayantī, and Pāpanāśinī.
Unmīlinī, Vañjulī, Trispṛśā, and Vivardhanā—
Śiva is endowed with these Śaktis, yet he is devoid of the guardians of the world-quarters (Lokapālas).
He wears white garments, is serene, and possesses a joyful countenance.
One should worship with diligence Hari, who is enriched by the splendor of all ornaments and who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation; hear now the procedure by which this is done,
always during all twelve months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa.

Having observed a fast on the twelfth, the new moon, or the eighth day of both the bright and dark fortnights, one who is pure in soul should perform the vow without sloth. Thus, during both fortnights, I shall worship Janārdana.
Having thus made this resolve, preceded by the cleaning of the teeth,
he should then go to a pond, a lotus-pool, or even to his own home;
having bathed there, he should perform his daily (nitya) rites and then his occasional (naimittika) ones.
One should perform everything with diligence, exactly and in due order.
One should have an image of the God made of gold, possessing the form as previously described,
accompanied by the eight Śaktis and joined by Lakṣmī, who is seated upon a lotus throne.
This entire [image] should be executed in detail according to the measure of one *pala* of gold.
Upon a vessel of milk, one should fashion a golden lotus;
upon its pericarp is the deity, accompanied by the multitude of his powers (*śaktis*).
Thereafter, impelled by the teacher’s mantra,
wearing pure white garments and established in the ritual requisites for the mantra,
one should worship according to the prescribed rule upon this ocean of divine milk, when the moon has appeared in the lotus.
There, O Lord of Truth, remain present together with Satyā.
O destroyer of sins, bathe in the waves of the Ocean of Milk by means of this drop of water offered for the sake of the past and the future.
O Lord Janārdana, take away all my misfortune;
O Lord of Truth, bring me auspiciousness through this pure gift of cloth.
You are always declared to be the purifier in sacrifice, yoga, and likewise in Sāṃkhya.
By the gift of the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), make me pure of all sins.
All that is smeared by action is not truly real by anyone;
O you whose limbs are anointed with sandalwood, become the remover of all smearing for me.
O Satyanātha, salutations to you whose nature is both manifest and unmanifest;
O Vāsudeva, known as Nṛsiṃha, Kapila, and the divine mountain;
O Varāha, Acyuta, Lord of Sacrifice, Beloved of Lakṣmī, and Sovereign of Kings.
"O enemy of sin, O stainless one, grant me cattle and a son!
O Saṃkarṣaṇa of great heroism, O Lord of all of immeasurable prowess!
O Aniruddha, Indra, Govinda, you who hold the discus—salutations be unto you!"
(Thus is the mantra for worship:
O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, O Lord; O Rāma, Rāma, O all-pervading Kṛṣṇa, O Hari!
O Mādhava, together with Ramā, protect me from all sufferings.
"And this worship has been offered by me, O Grandfather, Teacher of the World;
accept it, O Lord of the Universe, Nārāyaṇa, salutations be unto you!
O Protector of the Earth, [accept] this secret wealth for the removal of all sins."
O Great King, one should offer a gift to a single Brahmin for the duration of a year; however, if one is unable due to lack of resources,
this most excellent vow must be performed every fortnight.
Then, when the year is complete, the wise man should perform the concluding rite (udyāpana).
He should worship the deity as before with extensive preparations of many materials. He should request permission from the Brahmins, saying: "May there indeed be the destruction of my sins."
And the twice-born man should say, "May there be the constant destruction of your evil.
Then, having offered everything to the Brāhmaṇa, one should ask for his forgiveness.
O King, when this vow is performed, there shall be the arising of great fruit.
Whatever fruit is found in all the Vedas and whatever fruit is found in all the sacred fords—
that fruit is multiplied ten millionfold by the practice of this vow.
In this world, there shall be wealth, grain, sons, friends, happiness, and so forth.
O best of kings, a person duly obtains the weapons of knowledge, health, and the arts,
as well as dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa;
there is no doubt in this, for it is according to the word of Brahmā.
Whoever reads or even hears this is liberated from all sins;
whoever indeed performs this again shall partake of infinite fruit.
Whether one is incapable or capable, provided one is free from stinginess regarding wealth.
A man performing this vow with devotion attains the eternal state.
Indeed, when it is performed during the Kṛta age, the performer shall obtain its fruit;
by means of this vow, he shall destroy a flood of sins consisting of hundreds of offenses.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Vow for a Hundred Transgressions," in the Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, in the Uttaraparvan, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira. Now follows the description of the Kāñcana-vrata.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
To Vāsudeva, the God of gods and Lord of the universe, seated comfortably on Śvetadvīpa— the Master of the world who effects its maintenance and withdrawal,
the ancient and supreme immutable Creator of all things high and low.

O King of kings, having prostrated before the primordial God, the Lord of the universe, the cause of the world, the Great God Hari— the teacher of all that is moving and unmoving— Lakṣmī, while engaged in massaging his feet, spoke.
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, compassionate toward devotees,
O best among those who know how to answer questions, I wish to ask something that ought to be asked;
please do so, O highly fortunate one, by showing mercy toward me.
"Tell me of some vow that bestows beauty and good fortune,
the most excellent among all vows for all castes,
by the performance of which, O Lord of Gods, the fruit of all sacred pilgrimage sites may be obtained."
Viṣṇu said:
"Just as the householder is among the stages of life (āśramas) and the Brāhmaṇa is among the social classes (varṇas),
so is the Jāhnavī renowned throughout the world among all rivers."
As the ocean is the best among lakes, as Viṣṇu is the highest among gods,
and as Lakṣmī is the foremost among women, so too is this vow the most excellent.
Neither the Gaṅgā, nor Kurukṣetra, nor Kāśī, nor Puṣkara [is its equal].
O illustrious lady, this supreme vow is purifying,
just as it was formerly performed by the goddess Gaurī and by the high-souled Śaṅkara;
and in ancient times, it was performed by Rāma together with Sītā after he had regained his kingdom.

O blessed lady, this vow which bestows heaven and liberation was performed by Nala during his separation from Damayantī, and likewise by the Pāṇḍavas while dwelling in the forest together with Kṛṣṇā, O son of Pṛthā.
This auspicious vow was performed by Rambhā, Menā, Paulomī, Satyabhāmā,
Śāṇḍilī, Arundhatī, Urvaśī, and Devadattā,
out of a desire for good fortune and happiness.
In the netherworld (pātāla), this most beautiful [work] was created by the daughters of the nāgas,
by Gāyatrī, Sarasvatī, and Sāvitrī— the wife of Brahmā—
and by all other women who desired the fruits of every wish.

Therefore, I shall proclaim to you that which destroys all sins, which brings delight to the Vasus, and is beautiful—the supreme among vows; listen. Even a killer of a Brahmin, a drinker of intoxicants, or a stealer of wealth is liberated from sin.
One who approaches the wife of a guru, one who associates with these [sinners],
one who uses false weights and measures, one who lives off a daughter, one who observes the vow of cattle,
one who has sexual intercourse with a woman who should not be approached, one who eats meat, and the husband of a *vṛṣalī*.

He who eats from the sacrificial fire-pit (kuṇḍa), as well as he who steals land—by all these great sins one is liberated; there is no doubt in this matter. This supreme vow should be performed by men and women through these [means].
Therefore, I shall describe the procedure; attend to this injunction.
There is a city named Kāñcanā, and a vow renowned throughout the three worlds.
O Goddess, whatever man or woman performs it endowed with devotion, [attains the fruit].
His sons and grandsons shall obtain abundant wealth.
O beautiful one, this vow must be observed in that month;
and in that month, the auspicious city named Kāñcanā must be constructed.
O highly fortunate one, on the third lunar day of either the bright or dark fortnight, on the eleventh, on the full moon,
on a solar transit (saṃkrānti), on the new moon (kuhū), or on the eighth lunar day—
indeed, on all other such festival days (parvan)— the city made of gold should be given as a gift.
Having bathed in the forenoon in pure water such as that of a river, O lady of virtuous vows, one observing the vow should perform the application of earth with this mantra:
"As you were formerly uplifted by Viṣṇu in the form of the Boar."
For the sake of benefiting the worlds, you grant success and fulfill desires through salutation;
therefore, being thus saluted, take away my sin born of many lifetimes.
(Thus ends the mantra for the clay.)
"For the waters are indeed the womb of the universe, created by Viṣṇu himself;
therefore, my presence must now be established here together with the sacred fords.
(This is the mantra.)
Having bathed according to this procedure, the sacrificer, being composed and pure in soul, should return home without speaking to slanderers,
heretics, those engaged in improper acts, rogues, gamblers, or cheats.
Having washed his hands and face, he should then perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
He should then undertake the vow of fasting or, alternatively, the vow of eating only at night.
Taking an excellent conch shell adorned with gold and filled with water, [he should proceed].
One should consecrate that water with the twelve-syllable mantra;
having returned home, he should drink it and mutter the syllables "Ha-ri.
There should be an altar made of *śamī* wood, provided with four pillars.
They should be made very beautiful with a measurement of four cubits;
the pillars should be wrapped in cloth, adorned with an excellent canopy,
provided with flower garlands, and perfumed with divine incense.
In the center, however, a mandala called "Lotus" should be fashioned with beautiful colors,
O Goddess of Gods, by the sight of which the destruction of all sins occurs.
Indeed, in the middle of the mandala, there should be a most splendid auspicious throne.
Having placed there a soft seat covered with cloth,
one should install upon it the Lord Janārdana, accompanied by Lakṣmī.
In front, however, a beautiful water-pot filled with water should be prepared.
That [vessel] should be diligently designated as the "Ocean of Milk.
A wise person should wrap it with cloth and cover it with wealth consisting of the five jewels; he should then place a jar completely filled with water upon it.
Having established upon it the auspicious city named Kāñcana—
excellent if it measures four palas, middling according to tradition if two palas,
and common if made of one pala— it should be provided with water-pots (kalaśas). One should place divine sweetmeats (modakas) of beautiful form all around it.
In front of that, one should construct an archway with plantain pillars;
O beautiful lady, having invited Brahmins versed in the four Vedas there,
one should perform its consecration with the most auspicious Vedic mantras.
In its center, one should place Viṣṇu, made of gold and accompanied by Lakṣmī.
His eyes should be fashioned from jewels, his teeth adorned with diamonds,
and one should provide him with ornaments made of pearls.
The body [of the deity] should be fashioned from gold, bearing the conch, discus, and mace as weapons.
Having bathed the omnipresent Lord Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Gods, with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta),
one should worship Him alone with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings while reciting the mantra.
A Brāhmaṇa should worship Madhusūdana with Vedic mantras;
the remaining castes [should worship] with those spoken in the Purāṇas—listen to them from me, my dear.
One should worship the feet for Vāsudeva and the ankles for Saṃkarṣaṇa.

One should worship the knees of Hari with "To the progenitor of the three worlds," the secret parts with "To the Lord of the three worlds," and the hips with "To the one consisting of knowledge. One should worship the belly with "To Dāmodara" and the heart with "To the one whose form is the universe."

O Goddess, one should always worship the chest with the words "to the bearer of the Śrīvatsa," the throat with "to the Lord of the Kaustubha," and the face with "to the mouth of sacrifice. One should worship the arms with "to the destroyer of the Daityas" and the weapons with their own respective names.
O Goddess, one should worship the head of the God of gods with the mantra of the Universal Self (Sarvātman).
One should worship the goddess Śrī with the various specific mantras of the goddess.
The worship of the world-protectors, beginning with Indra, should be performed in their proper sequence.
A fire-oblation (homa) for the nine planets must be performed to destroy obstacles;
likewise, worship of Gaṇapati should be performed along with a fire-oblation according to the prescribed rules.
First, one should cause an incomparable food offering (naivedya), cooked in ghee, to be presented.
One should offer milk-rice, ghee-filled cakes, sweetmeats, and *pūrikās*,
as well as offerings such as *sohālīkā*, *pheṇikās*, and sugar;
one should likewise present fruits produced in accordance with the specific region and season.
One should offer ten lamps with red wicks to the ten directions;
O large-eyed one, one should cause them to be given while reciting this root mantra,
having prepared them adorned with sandalwood and provided with garlands of flowers.
Having consecrated [the items] with effort using the mantras known as the *Viṣṇustabaka*,
and while the most excellent Brāhmaṇas recite the *Sahasraśīrṣa* and other mantras,
he should then worship sixteen [Brāhmaṇas], together with their wives, according to the prescribed rite.
One should adorn him with beautiful garments as well as ornaments and the like;
considering him to be Viṣṇu, the twice-born man is worthy of worship, and considering her to be Lakṣmī, the Brāhmaṇa woman is likewise worthy of honor.
One should also offer an umbrella, sandals, and finger-rings.
Fruits, seven types of grain, and whatever food is desired should be given to one accompanied by his wife, with the thought: "May Kṛṣṇa be pleased with me.
Furthermore, a bed complete with its furnishings should be carefully covered with a cloth.
Likewise, a beautiful woman should prepare [the image] according to her wealth and capacity;
when the vow is completed, a cow should be given along with all its appurtenances.
One should first have a city fashioned, diligently covering it with cloth.
One should act with such effort that the performer does not see;
O beloved, one should bring lamps that have been lit there into the sacrificial pavilion,
while the eyes of the sacrificer are covered with a white cloth.
The wise preceptor, learned in the scriptures, possessed of great intelligence, and having brought about the destruction of all his sins, should bind the eyes of the disciple and say this to him:
"Behold this city named Kāñcana, which grants all desires."
Adorned with excellent garments, beautiful, and the destroyer of suffering and misfortune—
having been addressed thus, O fortunate one, he should remove the cloth from his eyes,
cast a handful of flowers upon the Guru, and behold that auspicious city.
O Goddess, having seen that city, the sacrificer, being composed,
should take a vessel made of gold, silver, or even copper;
or else, O beautiful one, he should take a conch shell if no other vessel is available.
One should place the five jewels, water from the Ganges, and fruit into the vessel;
first, white mustard seeds, unbroken grains, yellow pigment (rocanā), and curd;
then, the arghya offering should be presented to the powerful Kṛṣṇa.
The divine couple Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, who bestow the fruits of all desires—
by the gift of this city of gold, grant me my wish!
O Nārāyaṇa, Hṛṣīkeśa, O stainless one, whose nature is both knowledge and the object of knowledge!
"O Beloved of Lakṣmī, Lord of the World, accept this arghya; salutations unto you. (This is the mantra for the arghya.
Having thus offered the arghya to the all-powerful Viṣṇu, the arghya for the Goddess should then be presented with a mind full of devotion.
Having knelt upon the ground, one should utter this mantra:
"The Goddess who is worshipped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śaṅkara;
Lakṣmī who is worshipped by Pārvatī, Skanda, and Vaiśravaṇa."
And I have worshipped you, O Goddess, with the desire to conquer through Dharma.
Grant me good fortune, sons, wealth, and honored grandsons.
Accept this *arghya* offered by me, O Goddess, and bestow happiness upon me.
Having thus presented [the offerings] before you according to the previously mentioned procedure,
one should perform a vigil at night with a mind endowed with devotion,
through the diversion of song and dance, and by means of Vaiṣṇava narratives.
By whatever means possible, one should ensure that sleep does not arise;
he who remains awake and vigilant shall obtain the fruit of a hundred sacrifices. Having bathed at dawn in clear water and having worshipped the ancestors and the deities, he attains this merit.
Having clothed the Brahmins together with their wives, one should feed them;
and having bestowed sacrificial fees according to one's ability, one should ask for their forgiveness.
One should satisfy all those who are miserable, blind, deaf, and lame.

If one has observed the fast, the breaking of the fast (pāraṇaka) should be performed afterwards with sweet food mixed with milk, together with friends and kinsmen. O lady of pure smiles, this vow should be observed in this manner on the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī).
On the third lunar day of either the bright or the dark fortnight,
or on the day of a solar transit (saṃkrānti), or during the Vyatīpāta or Vaidhṛti yogas—
whenever wealth and the inclination of the mind arise, O lady of excellent complexion.
Having brought a cow, she should be given away with the words, "May Kṛṣṇa be pleased with me.
The merit obtained when this is done cannot be fully described,
even in a thousand years or by hundreds of thousands of generations.
Having reached the world of Brahmā for thousands of millions and hundreds of millions of kalpas, one rejoices together with Brahmā; thereafter,
one reaches the worlds of Brahmā, Ka, and Rudra, and finally the presence of Viṣṇu.
One who observes the vow of the world-protectors, beginning with Indra, shall attain their world.
Then, having enjoyed pleasures, O beautiful one of the three worlds, being pure and illustrious,
he shall become a sovereign emperor on earth, devoted to Brahmanas and likewise a devotee of Viṣṇu.
Whoever should constantly hear this, or recite it everywhere,
shall uplift seven generations of their lineage and attain the world of Viṣṇu.
This very vow, known as Kāñcanapurī, was performed by you in the past.
"By that merit, I have obtained you as my husband, who is worshipped by the three worlds.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Kāñcanapurī Vrata," in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Viṣṇu Saṃvāda* within the *Uttara Parva* of the glorious *Śrīmad Bhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*.

Now follows the description of the gift of a daughter (*kanyādāna*). [Note: The provided source text contains a fragmentary title for the chapter and then abruptly transitions to the next topic, the gift of a daughter.]
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
He who bestows a maiden given as a gift to a Brāhmaṇa after adorning her,
delivers seven ancestors and seven descendants— those seven men in his own lineage.
By that gift of a daughter, he undoubtedly delivers [his ancestors] and likewise attains the worlds of Dakṣa Prajāpati;
through the Prājāpatya rite, he shall uplift himself as well.
One attains great merit and goes to the heavenly world; yet,
by giving gifts of land, cattle, horses, and likewise elephants to one who is devoid of caste,
one sinks into terrible darkness.
For many thousands of years, he shall eat excrement like a crow;
and by giving a daughter for a bride-price (śulka), one shall attain a terrible hell.
Likewise, such a man shall consume impurities for many thousands of years.
One should give a maiden of equal caste to men of equal caste according to the prescribed rule;
having given her to one of superior caste, he should likewise give double [the usual fee] even if he is devoid of merit.
Furthermore, he who performs the sacramental rites for the son of a twice-born man who is without a protector, or for one destitute through his actions, [attains great merit].
By performing the rites of tonsure (cūḍā), initiation (upanayana), and others, he shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
By giving away a maiden who is without a protector, one is glorified in the heavenly world.
And gold given together with a maiden is as if offered at the root of the sacrificial fire.
The ancients have declared that the fruit of this is double the entire [merit].
O best of men, by the gift of a daughter one attains the world of Dakṣa;
through the honoring of that daughter, there arises merit equal to the worship of Viṣṇu.

"Having acquired a celestial chariot (vimāna) that is enchanting to the mind and delightful with the playful songs of divine damsels, one attains the world of the highest gods through the gift of a daughter; of this there is no doubt. Thus ends the one hundred and forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Gift of a Daughter," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the Rules for Serving Brāhmaṇas.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
On earth, the Brāhmaṇas are the deity; in heaven, the Brāhmaṇas are the deity.

There is nothing superior to the Brahmins; there is no being in the three worlds greater than them. They could make a non-god a deity, and they could make a deity a non-god. For the highly fortunate Brahmins, these twice-born ones, are constantly worshipped.
The traditional teaching (smṛti) states that the gods were first produced from the Brāhmaṇas;
since the entire world [originated] from the Brāhmaṇas, the twice-born are most worthy of worship.
It is through their mouths that the deities as well as the ancestors eat.
O knower of dharma, what being is greater than those sages and nāgas? At the very moment a man bestows [gifts] upon the Brāhmaṇas with devotion, he obtains [the fruit thereof] in birth after birth.
By means of the breeze from palm-leaf fans, by massaging those who are fatigued, by the rubbing of the limbs, as well as by the fanning of the body,
by providing water for washing the feet, and by sprinkling the feet;
O best of the twice-born, by serving [the preceptor] according to one's desire alone,
even without performing sacrifices, one attains the eternal world of heaven;
having performed what is auspicious for the Brahmins, one is glorified in the celestial realm.
"What the Brāhmaṇas, being satisfied, declare regarding the perceptible gods—that which concerns the imperceptible gods—is surely auspicious for that man; therefore, one should constantly serve them.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Rules for Serving Brāhmaṇas," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the Ritual for Bestowing a Bull.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Janārdana, as I listen to this nectar of your words, I am truly gratified.
I do not attain satisfaction, for curiosity has indeed arisen within me:
