Govinda is indeed renowned throughout the three worlds as the Lord of Cows;
by the gift of a bull, he causes the three worlds to rejoice.
"Therefore, O Acyuta, please tell me the procedure for one who is like a bull among men.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"Listen as I describe to you the meritorious fruit of the gift of a bull."
It is purifying, sanctifying, and likewise the best of all gifts. A single bull capable of bearing the yoke is equal to ten cows;
indeed, that one alone excels the gift of ten cows.
O son of Pāṇḍu, he who is a bearer with beautiful limbs, free from disease,
young, auspicious, well-behaved, and devoid of all faults—
he alone, as a leader, establishes a great lineage.

He becomes a savior from saṃsāra; there is no need for deliberation on this point. Having adorned a peaceful bull with a silver tail-tip, one should present it to a Brāhmaṇa when an auspicious day has arrived.
O Indra among kings, listen to this mantra which I shall speak to you:
"You are Dharma in the form of a bull, the cause of joy for the world;
O Eternal One, protect me, for you are the abode of the eightfold forms."
Having thus given the gift accompanied by a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and prostrated, one should dismiss [the recipient].
Whatever sin has been committed during seven lifetimes through the actions of speech, mind, and body—
all that goes to dissolution by the merit of the gift of a cow.
Having ascended a divine, blazing, and most beautiful vehicle yoked with bulls that moves at will, he ascends to the heavenly world;
O Lord of the Earth, as many hairs as there are on that bull...
For that many thousands of years he is glorified in the world of cows;
then, having descended from Goloka to this world, he becomes an excellent twice-born man,
a performer of sacrifices, possessed of great luster, and honored by all Brahmins.
"O Great King, you have indeed asked to whom this best of bulls should be given;
I shall tell you that as well, regarding the worthy recipient who provides protection to men:
those whose ears are always filled with sacred learning, who have conquered their senses, and who abstain from the slaughter of living beings."
Those householders who are restrained in accepting gifts are capable of delivering others;
by giving a bull that is sturdy, well-nourished, capable of bearing burdens, possessed of fine horns, and endowed with every excellence—
equal to ten cows— those who give become partakers of its fruit upon this earth, for they are the embodiment of truth.

Thus ends the one hundred and fiftieth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Gift of a Bull," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira. Now follows the description of the ritual for the vow of gifting a visible cow (and other various gifts).
Yudhiṣṭhira said:

O Acyuta, by your grace I have previously heard the subject matter of the Purāṇas; having realized the worthlessness of worldly existence, I have also heard the detailed exposition of religious observances. Now, I desire to hear further about the supreme majesty of giving.
"O Kṛṣṇa, tell me what is given, when it is given, and by what means;
for it is my conviction that there is nothing superior to giving. Whatever wealth belongs to the wealthy cannot be taken away by kings or thieves."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Wealth that is not secured as a deposit, wealth that is not lent out and thus increases,
and wealth that is not spent travels the path [of depletion] when it is placed in the hands of Brahmins.

What is the use of a body that is well-nourished, strong, and long-lived, if that life does not serve to benefit sentient beings? Why is even half a morsel, or even a single morsel, not given to those who seek it?
When will anyone possess wealth that accords with their desires?
When even a single day has passed devoid of giving,
one who has been plundered by thieves grieves both by day and by night.
He whose days come and go devoid of the three aims of life does not truly live, even though he breathes like a blacksmith’s bellows.
Those by whom nothing has been given, no oblation offered, and no death met at a sacred ford—
Gold, food, and water were not offered to the Brahmins; consequently,
O Great King, they are seen being born again— miserable, starving, emaciated, with begging bowls marked upon their hands.

Wealth, acquired through hundreds of labors and held dearer than life itself, has but one true course: giving; all other uses lead to ruin. Prosperities are not diminished by enjoyment, nor are they exhausted by acts of charity.
Due to the exhaustion elsewhere of merits previously acquired,
even one who has not perceived the supreme reality should bestow wealth upon worthy recipients;
for that [wealth] does not exist for the deceased, and therefore it is better to give while there is still uncertainty [as to its survival].
O sinless one, I shall describe to you various kinds of gifts that were formerly recounted to me by Vyāsa, Vālmīki, Manu, and others. Whichever vow is performed, the Three-eyed Lord is worshipped.
And that which is given to the Brahmins is the fruit of this tree of birth.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
For the sake of pleasing the Brahmins, as well as Keśava and Śiva—
O best of the Yadus, please describe those gifts which are to be given,
and by what procedure a gift brings merit and happiness,
securing attainment in this world and the next, and is never destroyed.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "They say there are three supreme gifts: cows, land, and knowledge. These three purify [the donor] up to the seventh generation through their milk, their labor as beasts of burden, and their teaching."
I shall first describe the gift of a cow (godāna) according to the sequence of direct observation,
by which very procedure it is neither deficient nor excessive in its detail.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:

"O King, what are the characteristics of the cows that should be given? Which ones are to be avoided? To what kind of person should they be given, and to what kind indeed should they not be given? Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
A cow that is young, endowed with beauty, well-behaved, and prolific;
acquired through righteous means, accompanied by her calf—such a cow should be given to a learned Brahmin (*śrotriya*).
[One should not give] one that is old, diseased, deficient in limb, barren, wicked, or whose offspring have died.

A cow that is far away or obtained through unjust means should never be given as a gift. Yet, when given to a *śrotriya* who maintains the sacred fires, who is fond of guests, self-controlled, and preeminent in virtue, it shall indeed remove his sin.

A cow must never, under any circumstances, be given to one who is of low birth, to a fool, to a greedy person, to a slanderer, or to one who is excluded from offerings to the gods and ancestors. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Then, having reached an auspicious day, and having bathed and likewise offered libations to the ancestors,
and having performed the consecration with ghee and milk for Viṣṇu and Śiva,
one should worship them duly with flowers and other offerings in the proper sequence.
Having positioned a milch cow that has calved for the first time, facing either northward or eastward,
together with her calf, covered with a cloth, wearing a white sacred thread,
having horns adorned with gold and hooves with silver, and provided with a bronze milking vessel;

According to one's capacity, one should present [the image] to a Brāhmaṇa along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). A black antelope skin (kṛṣṇājina) should be given at the tail; a cow at the tail; an elephant at the trunk; a horse always at the right ear; or a female slave should be caused to be given at the head.
"May cows be before me; may cows be behind me;
may cows be in my heart; I dwell in the midst of cows.
Then, having performed a circumambulation of that cow for the best of the twice-born, [he should give it].
"And accept this cow given by me to you.
Having spoken thus, one should regard that Brahmin as the Lord of Gods.
And as he departs, O lord of men, one should follow him for eight steps.
The man who, according to this rite, bestows a cow upon a Brahmin,
goes to the heavenly world with his soul enriched by the fulfillment of all desires;
that person [delivers] seven ancestors, seven descendants, and himself as well.

O Lord of the Earth, it liberates a person from the sins committed in seven lifetimes; at every step, O King of kings, such a man obtains the fruit of a horse-sacrifice and the merit of giving a hundred cows—
thus did Hari speak to Dakṣa.
O King, she shall be the granter of all desires at all times;
she becomes the destroyer of sins for as long as the fourteen Indras endure,
even for all sins committed knowingly by those who understand.
This expiation has been declared, augmented by remorse;
the fruit of all gifts indeed persists for a single lifetime,
[to be attained] by Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and other human beings.
O King, by giving this according to the prescribed rite, one attains worlds that grant all desires.
Those learned in the scriptures declare that there is no other purifying gift in this world superior to that of cows;
therefore, those who desire the prosperity of the gods should always give them according to the rite to the best of the twice-born.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Vow of the Gift of a Visible Cow," in the *Śrībhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, in the *Uttaraparvan*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira. [Section:
Description of the Ritual for the Vow of the Gift of a Cow.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Now, therefore, O King, I shall fully explain the preparation of cows,
as well as those which, according to specific rites, are to be given by those desiring the fulfillment of their wishes.
Whatever gift is given with a specific desire brings that entire wish to fruition.
However, that which is incomplete leads to harm both in this world and the next.
Therefore, O Great King, one who desires the full fruit should not give a gift that is devoid of a priestly fee (dakṣiṇā) or likewise deficient in its prescribed ritual procedure.
Otherwise, that which is given results only in self-conceit;
it would be a visible loss of wealth, or it might not yield its fruit at all.
O best of kings, listen as I describe the gift of a sesame-cow.
Formerly proclaimed by Vārāha, this [teaching] destroys even the greatest of sins;
by giving it away, even a slayer of a Brahmin, a killer of cows, a patricide,
one who violates the teacher’s bed, an arsonist, a poisoner, or even one devoted to every kind of evil, is purified.
One who is burdened with great sins (mahāpātaka) and associated with minor sins (upapātaka) is indeed liberated from all evils and goes to the heavenly world,
provided he is on the surface of the earth smeared [with ashes] and covered with a black antelope skin (kṛṣṇājina).
Having fashioned a cow made of sesame seeds and having strewn darbha grass all around, one should cause the entire cow to be made from white sesame,
black sesame, sesame the color of cow-urine,
and various other kinds of sesame.
One should provide for Droṇa a calf and a cow yielding four āḍhakas of milk;
she should have horns of gold, hooves of silver, and be endowed with fragrance and color.
Her tongue should be made of sugar, her mouth of molasses, and she should be covered with a woolen blanket.
One should fashion a beautiful cow with legs like sugarcane, a copper-colored back, eyes like pearls and mother-of-pearl, ears like excellent leaves, teeth like fruit,
a tail like a garland of flowers, and udders like fresh butter.
Having fashioned [the image] endowed with such a form— one whose head is draped in white cloth, whose body is covered with white mustard seeds,
and who is provided with charming fruits, food, jewels, and pearls—
one should act while filled with faith.
One should give a cow with a bronze milking vessel when the auspicious occasion has arrived:
"That Goddess who is the prosperity of all beings and who indeed resides among the gods— may she, in the form of this cow, dispel my sin."
Then, having performed a circumambulation, having worshipped, and having prostrated,
one should dismiss [the deity] by saying, "Together with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), it has been given by me to you.
O lord of men, having given a sesame-cow according to this rite, [one attains the fruit].
Freed from all evil, he attains the supreme Brahman;
so too does he who receives it according to the prescribed rite with joy,
and those whose minds are delighted who praise it as it is being given.
They too, freed from all defects, go to the world of Brahmā;
by giving a cow made of sesame seeds to one who is peaceful, well-behaved, and devoted to Vedic vows, one does not grieve over what has been done or left undone.
O King, he who subsists on sesame for three nights, or gives a sesame-cow,
or even for a single day with a focused inner self—
through that gift, O monarch, there is purification from sin for that meritorious man.
The consumption of sesame seeds is said to be superior even to the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
it purifies whatever sin was committed in childhood, youth, or old age,
whether accumulated through speech, mind, or physical action.
As well as in spitting water, bathing naked,
when a mace is raised, or when a Brahmin is suspended;
likewise for sexual intercourse with a *vṛṣalī* woman, or for one who approaches the wife of his guru.
Whatever sin arises from drinking liquor or from eating forbidden food—
all that goes to destruction for those who give sesame-seed cows.
On the most terrible path of Yama, there is said to be the river Vaitaraṇī.
There is a place of sand where sinners are cooked;
there are crows with iron beaks and terrifying dogs that,
being hungry, tear off the flesh of the sinners and devour it.
Having crossed over the Forest of Sword-leaves (Asipatravana), the Iron-thorned Silk-cotton Tree (Lohakaṇṭakaśālmalī), and all these [other hells],
he would then proceed to the city of Yama in a divine golden celestial chariot adorned with jewels and gems.
Having ascended it, that best of men goes to the supreme goal.
It should not be given to one devoid of virtues, nor should it be given to a lord of wealth;
it must never be given to a *kuṇḍa*, a *gola*, or to one who is greedy.
"O Pārtha, it was declared of old by the sages that one [gift] should be given to each individual;
this was announced by Nārada in the Naimiṣa forest.
I shall now fully describe that to you, which bestows a thousandfold fruit."
This merit is purifying, auspicious, and increases one's fame;
by reciting it to Brahmins during a Śrāddha ceremony, one enjoys infinite fruit.
A cow, a house, a bed, and women should not be given away to many people.
If these [gifts] are divided, they cause the donor to fall downward;
but if she (the cow) is sold, she burns the family down to the seventh generation.
By the power of the gift of her, one obtains a celestial chariot that fulfills all desires.

Having ascended it, a man goes to where the Lord Hari himself resides. This [gift] should be bestowed with a disciplined inner self on the full moon day of Māgha and likewise on the full moon day of Kārttika, O Bhārata.
During an eclipse of the moon or sun, at the equinoxes and solstices,
at the commencement of the six-aśīti periods, and always during the vyatīpāta yoga;
on the full moon day of Vaiśākha or Mārgaśīrṣa, and indeed during the gajacchāyā conjunctions.
This gift of a sesame-cow has been described to you by me, O sinless Pārtha.
O bull among kings, for as many hairs as there are on the body of that cow,
for so many thousands of years one is glorified in heaven.
He who receives according to the prescribed rite, he who witnesses her being given,
and he who indeed rejoices in it— all of them go to heaven.
O Lords of Wealth, those wise ones who give a cow made of sesame seeds measured by four *āḍhakas* according to the Magadhan standard;
Having performed the arrangement as prescribed and having provided the calf with its beautiful mother, those who give her away on earth become liberated from sin.
"O Goddess, I accept you for the maintenance of my family;
O Cow, you are always indeed capable of granting our desires through your compassion."

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Vow of the Gift of a Sesame-Cow," in the *Uttara-parvan* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira. [Now follows] the description of the ritual for the vow of the gift of a Water-Cow.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:

I shall now describe the water-cow (jaladhenu), by the gift of which Hṛṣīkeśa, the god of gods, the creator of all beings, is pleased when worshipped. O tiger among men, having established a well-worshipped water-pot,
Having placed that [image] within a jewel-casket (ratnagarbha) filled with cultivated grains,
covered with a pair of white cloths, adorned with sprouts of dūrvā grass,
and provided with kuṣṭha, māṃsī, pura, uśīra, vālaka, and āmalakī;
[One should worship] the silver [image], accompanied by four [attendants], wearing a white sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) made of *priyaṅgu* leaves,
provided with sandals and an umbrella, seated upon a seat of *darbha* grass,
and surrounded in the four directions by vessels of sesame seeds.
The mouth [of the vessel] should be covered with a curd-pot filled with ghee and honey;
having established a cow together with her calf, adorned with cow-dung,
one should provide her with a garland, a tail-tassel, and a copper milking vessel.
Then, having worshipped the all-pervading Vāsudeva, the eternal one,
with offerings of flowers, incense, and food according to his own means,
and having consecrated a water-cow and that water-pot, he should perform the ritual recitation over them.
"May she who is Lakṣmī upon the chest of Viṣṇu, and Svāhā of the Fire-god,
and the power of Soma, Śakra, and the Sun— may she exist for me in the form of this cow.
Having thus addressed her according to the rules, [one should offer] the fruitful cow together with its calf.
Having worshipped Govinda, the infallible one who reclines upon the waters, with devotion—
wearing white garments, peaceful, free from passion, and devoid of envy—
one should give [a gift] to a Brahmin, O King of kings, for the sake of pleasing the one who reclines upon the waters.
"May the glorious Keśava, who reclines upon the serpent Śeṣa, who is adorned with the Śārṅga bow,
who rests upon the waters, and who is the source of the universe, be pleased with me.
Having uttered this, one should present that [image] to a brāhmaṇa as the Lord of the World.
On that day, one should observe the cow-vow (gograta) endowed with supreme faith.
O lord of men, by giving a water-cow according to this rite,
one obtains all enjoyments, whether they be divine or human.

Incomparable physical health and perpetual tranquility—indeed, all desires—come to men when [this gift] is bestowed; of this there is no doubt. In this regard also, O King, it is heard that by the high-souled Mudgala:
It is said that in former times, having returned here, Jātismara sang this:
"In the past, the sage Mudgala, a brahmin who had gone to the world of Yama,
beheld many torments of men who had committed sinful deeds."

O bull among men, there are terrifying places consisting of blazing fires and sharp instruments, as well as those filled with boiling decoctions and oils; there are falls into rivers of hot alkaline water,
the infliction of caustic on wounds, and the great abodes of the Kumbhīpāka hell.
Seeing those torments, the Brahmin felt supreme compassion;
through his mercy, those sinners then experienced joy.
Seeing him, some of the denizens of hell remained there, gazing intently at him.
Then, beholding the circle of hell-beings in that state, the sage questioned Dharmarāja regarding the cause for their pacification.
O king of kings, Vaivasvata Yama then explained it to him.
O Best of Men,
O Best of the Twice-born, this supreme joy has arisen for all those in hell through the power of your gift; hear from me the cause of that joy.
"O foremost of the twice-born, in a former birth you worshipped the Lord of the Universe, the Master of All who reclines upon the waters, and you duly gave a water-cow as a gift.
Therefore, in the third birth following that one, O twice-born one— "
This is the joyful fruition of that gift of yours:
those men who see you, hear you, and meditate upon you;
and those whom you, O best of Brahmins, hear of, meditate upon, and behold.
For them, cessation is the supreme state, bestowing all joy;
it occurs instantaneously—do not, O twice-born one, feel astonishment at this. O chief of Brahmins, there is no other cause for producing such delight.
O twice-born one, for those who give a water-cow, no defect, no fever, no affliction, and no exhaustion arises for nineteen lifetimes; indeed,
even throughout a thousand births, no such thing occurs for the givers of the water-cow.
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, go and take half from me;
for those who have placed their refuge in Kṛṣṇa cannot be restrained by me.
Those by whom Kṛṣṇa has been worshipped, and those who have fasted for the sake of Kṛṣṇa—[they are not to be punished].

O Brahmin, those by whom Kṛṣṇa is constantly remembered do not come within my domain; nor do those who, with hearts imbued with devotion, have uttered the names "Kṛṣṇa, Acyuta, Ananta, Vāsudeva," come within my domain.
O Brahmin, those who, while giving gifts, say "May Acyuta be pleased" with faith as their guide, do not fall within my domain;
for he alone is the Lord of all, and we act only under his command.
"I am the restrainer of people, and Hari is my restrainer.
Having heard these entire words spoken by Yama,
all those denizens of hell, terrified of fire, weapons, and the sun, spoke.

Salutations to Kṛṣṇa, to Hari, to Viṣṇu, and to the Victorious One; salutations to Hṛṣīkeśa, to Keśava, to the Sustainer of the World, and to Acyuta. Salutations to the Lotus-eyed One, and salutations to the One whose navel is a lotus.
Salutations eternally to Janārdana, the Lord of Śrī, the Sustainer of Śrī, who is clothed in yellow garments; salutations to Govinda, and salutations to him who reclines upon the ocean;
salutations to the lotus-eyed one, to Nṛsiṃha, the Roarer.
Salutations to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, who bears a sharp sword and carries the conch, discus, and mace; salutations to the one in the form of Vāmana, who traversed the three worlds;
likewise, salutations to the one in the form of the Boar, who assumes the limbs of sacrifice.
Salutations to you, Vāsudeva, the Supreme Self who pervades all the quarters of space and is infinite; salutations to the slayer of Kaiṭabha;
salutations to Keśava, O Rāma, O upholder of the earth, may there be salutations to you.
When "Namo'stu Vāsudevāya" was thus uttered by them,
their weapons became blunt, the fire turned cold,
the garments were torn asunder, and iron-tipped arrows flew upward.
The dried-up rivers of alkaline water were crossed, and the silk-cotton tree fell;
from that hell, light was born along with the sunbeams,
and then a wind blew, fanning the forest of sword-leaves.
The servants of Yama became devoid of energy and dull-witted;
the rivers carrying the waters of the Gaṅgā became streams of pus and blood;
and likewise, the divine wind became fragrant and pleasing to the mind.
Sounds delightful to the mind, accompanied by the music of flutes and lutes, were heard there.
Then, perceiving them to be such, Yama, the son of Vivasvat,
honored those whose threefold sins had been exhausted with water for the feet and respectful offerings.
Having worshipped them, O lord of men, Dharmarāja, with a composed mind and palms joined in reverence, spoke to Kṛṣṇa:
"O Viṣṇu, O God, O Sustainer of the world, O Janārdana, O Lord of the universe!"
Homage again and again to those who even offer salutation to him! Homage again and again to those who offer salutation to Acyuta, the immeasurable one, who assumed the illusory form of Vāmana!
Salutations to Vāsudeva, the wise one of meritorious fame;
salutations again and again to those who offer prostrations to him.
[Salutations] to that Viṣṇu, the Sacrificial Boar of immeasurable splendor.

Having thus praised Hṛṣīkeśa while Dharmarāja looked on, the denizens of hell ascended an excellent celestial chariot and went to heaven. O King, the highly intelligent Mudgala also witnessed all of this.
That great sage, a Brahmin of the Kaṇva lineage, possessed the memory of his past lives;
having recollected the words of Yama as well as the majesty of Viṣṇu and the greatness of the water-cow, he sang this.
Oh, how difficult it is to cross this most profound illusion of Viṣṇu!
By it, the mind being deluded, the individual soul (jīva) does not know the Supreme Lord;
it goes to the state of a worm, or to the wombs of lice and bugs.
Therefore, after passing through the womb of trees, creepers, and the like, and from there that of birds,
and then having attained the state of a beast, one desires the human condition;
having then attained humanity, the man [seeks] the womb of those who have perfected their selves.

Having attained that supreme prosperity, a person deluded by Māyā finds that very Māyā— which is otherwise difficult to overcome— easily mastered; for that enchanting power of Kṛṣṇa exists only as a vain attachment of the mind toward Madhusūdana.
Having thus attained the state of a householder and having likewise attained that which is beyond it,
one whose mind is offered to Keśava cuts through the Māyā of Viṣṇu;
enjoying sense objects without conflict, he takes refuge in Viṣṇu.
Having partaken of this, a person crosses over this most difficult-to-traverse illusion of Viṣṇu.
Devotion to Keśava, the sustainer of all, yields such manifold fruit;
yet, deluded by the illusion of that very God, people do not practice it.
In vain was the drinking of nectar spoken of, for that exertion was indeed futile;
in vain was that birth which perished where Hari was not worshipped.
For when worshipped by men, He bestows the fruit of both this world and the next.
The Blessed Lord, the God, bestows [all things]; who would not worship Him? Those years, months, and days have been fruitless for those men blinded by sensual objects who have not worshipped Hari.
Who would not worship that Lord, who is satisfied by the heart alone, and not by wealth, prosperity, power, garments, or ornaments?
Having heard such greatness as this of the water-cow (jaladhenu), O men!
For those who do not practice self-restraint here, where indeed can their discernment abide?
For a human birth on this land of action,
which yields the fruits of heaven and liberation, is attained by men only rarely, even after tens of thousands of births.
Those people by whom Viṣṇu was not propitiated with the gift of water-cows have fallen from their births and been deceived by His Māyā;
O sirs, with arms uplifted I cry out, for I have seen both worlds.
Worship Govinda and offer a water-cow;
the fire of hell is unbearable and the torment is unendurable.
Having realized this, take refuge in Kṛṣṇa and become steadfast.
He is indeed the guide and instructor on the path of Yama, so difficult to traverse;
having reflected upon this truth, let the mind be fixed upon Kṛṣṇa.
What is the use of a hundred desired sacrifices, which are exceedingly difficult to perform and involve great hardship, or of meritorious observances and vows?

"Even a single cow made of water, when given to a twice-born man who has gone to the abode of the King of the Ancestors (Yama), brings forth great happiness. Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Vow of Giving the Water-Cow," in the *Uttara-parvan* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[Now follows] the description of the vow for giving the Ghee-Cow (*ghṛtadhenu*). Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
I shall now describe the ghee-cow; listen to it, O best of men. Hear the procedure by which it is given and the form in which one should have it fashioned:
jars of cow’s clarified butter, adorned with perfumes and garlands, provided with bronze milking vessels, and wrapped in white cloths.
The legs should be made of sugarcane and the hooves likewise of silver;
the two eyes should be made of gold, and the two horns of aguru wood;
the sides should consist of the seven types of grain, and there should be a blanket of woolen cloth.
One should fashion the nose from *turuṣka* and camphor, the breasts from fruit,
the tongue likewise from sugar, and the mouth from molasses and milk;
the tail from linen thread and the body hairs from white mustard seeds.
Endowed with faith, one should fashion a back made of a copper vessel.
O lord of men, having thus conceived the form of the ghee-cow, one should likewise,
through that same mental conception, fashion its calf.
O Indra among kings, having worshipped her with this mantra, the wise man [should know]:
"Clarified butter (ājya) is declared to be splendor; clarified butter is the supreme remover of sin;
clarified butter is the food of the gods; everything is established in clarified butter."
"And you, O Goddess, have indeed been fashioned by me as this ghee;
for the removal of all sins and for my happiness, be so, O beautiful lady!
And that illustrious Brahmin [I shall satisfy] with the very flame of the clarified butter in my mind."
Having thus fashioned it, one who is self-restrained should then present it to him:
"O best of the twice-born, please accept this auspicious cow made of clarified butter, accompanied by a sacrificial fee, for my benefit."
Having recited this, one should present that cow to a Brahmin;
having given it and stayed for one night, subsisting on ghee and restrained in his vows,
one should [fashion] an auspicious image made of fresh butter according to this rite.
O King, a cow free from defects of deficiency or excess should be given as a gift.
Listen, O mighty-armed Pārtha, to the supreme fruit of such a gift:
there, great rivers of clarified butter and milk flow, with mud made of milk-rice (pāyasa).

Those who give a cow with ghee go there, fully satisfied by their desires. O King, he leads those seven ancestors of his who are above, as well as those who are below, into those worlds, freeing them from all impurity.
O best of kings, this prosperity has been described for those with desires;
those who give a cow of ghee without desire attain a state free from all taint.
Ghee is Agni, ghee is Soma, and all the deities consist of that.
All the deities become terrified of those who bestow clarified butter (ghṛta). Oh,

those possessing great merit cross the shoreless ocean of worldly existence— whose waters are illusion (māyā), whose rows of great waves are sons and wives, and which is treacherous with the fierce poison of greed— by clinging to the tail of a cow offered with ghee, even if their bodies are submerged.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Vow of Gifting a Cow of Clarified Butter," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[Now follows] the description of the vow of gifting a cow made of salt.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, O mighty-armed one, you who are learned in all the scriptures!
Tell me here that which is proclaimed as the most excellent of gifts—
that gift by the giving of which all other gifts indeed become [fulfilled].
"May there be the fulfillment of all desires and the destruction of all sins;
tell me that means of purification through expiation, O you of noble vows.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O King, I shall proclaim the most excellent of all gifts,
known as the salt-cow (*lavaṇadhenu*), which grants all desires to men;
by giving it, even a slayer of a Brahmin, a killer of cows, a patricide, or one who violates the teacher’s bed [is purified].
Even one who betrays trust, is cruel-minded, or is devoted to every kind of sin,
is liberated from this— of this there is no doubt— and he goes to the world of Śiva.
He becomes fortunate, endowed with wealth, long-lived, and unconquered.
A man is born in this world endowed with all his desires.
O Indra among kings, I shall now describe the ritual procedure for the preparation of salt here:
it should be placed upon a bed of *darbha* grass spread over ground smeared with cow dung.
Having spread out a sheepskin and stood facing the eastern direction,
the wise man, having covered it with a cloth, should fashion a cow;
he may do so with one *āḍhaka* of [flour], whether he possesses great wealth or little.
One should fashion [the cow] with golden horns, silver hooves, sugar-cane legs, and fruit for udders;
likewise, the tongue should be made of sugar and provided with scent for the nostrils.
One should fashion its two ears from oyster shells born within the belly of the ocean.
One should place a blanket around its neck with a silk thread and likewise a small bell; on the two horns, two pieces of sandalwood wood; on both eyes, two pearls;
on the cheeks, two balls of roasted flour; and one should cause barley grains to be placed in its mouth.
One should devoutly place sesame seeds at the sides and likewise wheat;
in this manner, one should arrange the seven grains according to availability.
On the back, one should place a copper vessel, and at the anus, a ball of jaggery.
One should offer a blanket upon the tail, grapes at the region of the udders,
honey at the region of the vulva, and all kinds of objects and fruits.
Having thus properly established the cow, who is composed of the essence of all flavors,
A person should set aside one calf, which is one-fourth the size [of the cow];
having thus worshipped the cow with garlands, garments, and ornaments,
and having bathed, performed the worship of the deity, and honored the Brahmins.
Having circumambulated the cow, O King, accompanied by his son and wife,
he should give her with great devotion and preceded by mantras to a virtuous Brāhmaṇa endowed with good conduct on all festival days.
"In salt indeed reside all tastes; in salt dwell all the deities.
O Goddess, who consist of all the gods, salutations to you who are named Salt!
Having thus recited this mantra, one should present it to the Brahmin.
O King, descendant of Bharata, by performing a complete circumambulation accompanied by a sacrificial fee, one has effectively performed a circumambulation of the entire earth;
all gifts have been bestowed by him, and the fruits of all sacrifices have been attained.
All flavors, all food, and everything moving and unmoving;
good fortune, supreme intelligence, health, and all riches—
these undoubtedly come to men who have given a cow of flavor (rasadhenu).

And his residence in heaven shall be certain until the dissolution of all beings. Having given to a twice-born man according to the rules this "flavor-cow" (rasadhenu) named Lāvaṇā— which has a leaf and a woolen blanket for its neck, and whose udders are made of salt— with fruits for her teats, he shall enter the world of cows, endowed with every happiness.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Vow of the Gift of the Salt-Cow," in the *Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, in the *Uttara Parvan*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Now follows the description of the vow of the gift of the Gold-Cow.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Henceforth, O King, I shall describe the golden cow;
by giving her away, one is liberated from all sins—of this there is no doubt.
Whether one is a drinker of spirits, a slayer of a Brahmin, a killer of a cow, a coward, or even one who has broken his vows.
One who has killed his guru, one who has had sexual intercourse with his sister, and one who is devoted to the wives of others—
such a person is liberated from all sins by giving a beautiful golden cow made of fifty palas of purified gold.
Or one should fashion it with half [the size], or according to one's capacity, O best of kings;
the sacrificial pot (ukhā) should be placed in the western part, with its belly and breasts clearly visible,
its limbs well-proportioned, its hips beautiful, and its base (karṇikā) most charming.
One should have a beautiful, tawny cow fashioned, its limbs adorned with all kinds of jewels;
one should provide a calf for it consisting of a fourth part [of the image's size],
and having placed it within a silver vessel, it should be wrapped in silk cloth.
One should likewise fashion a cow with copper horns and a blanket made of lapis lazuli;
its eyes should be made of pearls and its tongue of coral.
Upon a black antelope skin, one should place a prastha of molasses and have an auspicious image situated thereon.
It should be provided with eight water-pots, endowed with various fruits,
as well as eighteen types of grain, a parasol, a pair of sandals,
a vessel, clothing, and a copper milking pail.
Having honored a Brāhmaṇa with garments and auspicious ornaments, one should give him a lamp along with food, salt, sugar, and coriander seeds; then,
having bathed and circumambulated a cow complete in all its limbs.
Having invoked her with the mantras prescribed for the *guḍadhenu* (sugar-cow) and having worshipped her thoroughly:
"O You who are the ornament of the abode of all the hosts of gods; O You who are the ocean of the triple-pathed Ganges for the Lord of the Universe and for the mountains;
You whose flood of sins has been shattered by the sharp waters of faith—I bow to You, who bestows supreme and unsurpassed bliss."

"O Goddess who bestows the fruits desired in this world, what mortal here could possibly be subject to fear after having approached you? For those learned in the Vedas call you the 'Cow of Plenty' (*kāmadhenu*) because you pacify the sufferings of *saṃsāra* for those who are free from desire.
Having thus addressed that cow, one should present her to the Brahmin.
Having prostrated before her along with the sacrificial fee and the ritual implements, one should ask for forgiveness.
O Lord of Men, hear now of those gods, sacred fords, and sages who dwell within her body at the time of the gift.
The sun and moon are in her two eyes; Sarasvatī is in her tongue;
the Maruts are in her teeth; likewise, the Aśvins are in her two ears;
and the two gods Rudra and Pitāmaha are always at the tips of her horns.
The Gandharvas and Apsarases are established upon his hump;
the four oceans are in his belly, and the river that flows through the three paths is in his womb.
The sages reside in the pores of his skin, and the earth is situated in his anus.
The Nāgas are to be known as residing in the intestines, and the mountains are situated within the bones.
Dharma, Kāma, Artha, and Mokṣa are fully established in the feet;
the four Vedas are in the syllable *huṃ*, and the Rudras are stationed in the throat.
Meru stands at the back, and Viṣṇu pervades the entire body;
thus the Goddess, who consists of all things, is purifying and universal in form.
A cow fashioned from gold is traditionally held to consist of all the gods.
He who gives such a cow is indeed a giver of all gifts;
for among mortals in this land of action, this gift is very difficult to obtain.
Therefore, one should give this according to one's ability, as it destroys all impurities.
It is purifying, a means of deliverance, as well as bestowing fame and peace;
a man who performs it goes to the heavenly world for more than a hundred crores of years,
and even a woman is honored by the gods, seated upon an excellent celestial chariot.
Being sung of by Gandharvas adorned with garlands of flowers,
endowed with all ornaments and freed from all dualities,
he remains in heaven for a long time and is thereafter born in the mortal world.
Freed from mental and physical ailments, handsome and pleasing to behold—
whether a man or a woman who gives this gift on earth—
obtains all desires as they are born again and again.
He who, having invited a Brahmin endowed with noble lineage, character, and virtue, should bestow this golden cow,
attains the station of the Moon-crested Lord (Śiva), which is frequented by perfected sages, Kinnaras, and gods, and is surrounded by hundreds of maidens.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Vow of the Gift of the Golden Cow," in the *Uttara-parvan* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the Ritual Procedure for the Vow of the Gift of a Jewel-Cow.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe another gift that is very difficult to obtain.
This rite, renowned as "The Jewel Cow," bestows the fruit of Goloka upon men. Having reached an auspicious day, O Great King, one should smear the ground with cow dung and fashion a cow there.

One should fashion a cow made of jewels, preceded by the respective formal resolve (saṃkalpa). A wise person should place eighty-one rubies in the mouth of the cow and arrange one hundred topazes upon her feet.
On the forehead is a golden tilaka; on the two eyes, a hundred pearls;
on the pair of eyebrows, a hundred corals; on the two ears, two pearl-oyster shells are prescribed;
there are golden horns, and the head consists of a hundred diamonds.
A hundred *gomedaka* gems should be placed on the neck and in the sockets of the eyes;
a hundred *indranīla* gems on the back; a hundred *vaidūrya* gems on the sides;
the belly should be made of crystal; and a hundred *saugandhika* gems on the waist.
The hooves should be made of gold, and the tail of strings of pearls; the two stones,
sūryakānta and indukānta, should be placed on the nostrils, while the hair should be made with camphor, sandalwood,
and saffron, and one should have the navel made of silver.
In the same manner, one should imagine a hundred *gārutmata* gems in the *apāna*;
likewise, one should place other jewels in all the joints.
One should fashion the tongue out of sugar and the cow-dung out of molasses.

One should provide cow urine with clarified butter, as well as curd and milk in their natural forms; one should place a chowrie on the tip of the tail and a copper milking vessel at the two udders. In this very manner, one should fashion the calf using a fourth part [of the materials].
Having carefully arranged various fruits at the sides and performed the worship,
one should invoke [the deity] as in the case of the Guḍadhenu and then recite this:
"Rudra, Indra, Candra, Brahmā, and Vāsudeva praise you, saying, 'You are the abode of all the hosts of gods.'"

"Therefore, O Goddess, who possess a body encompassing the entire three worlds, protect me immediately as I am submerged in the ocean of existence. Having thus addressed that cow, one should present her to a Brahmin who knows the ritual rules and has mastered the Vedas, after honoring him with garments and ornaments.
Then, having given the sacrificial fee and prostrated, one should ask for forgiveness.
O Pārtha, listen to the fruit of merit for him who performs it in this manner:
he shall dwell happily in the world of Śiva for more than a hundred crores of kalpas.
Then, after a long time has passed, he shall become a king of kings here on earth, enriched with all his desires and the destroyer of the host of his enemies.
Thus, the knower of all rites bestows the gift of the jewel-cow; having obtained a brilliantly shining celestial chariot, he departs.
"Indeed, freed from all impurities and accompanied by his kinsmen, sons, and grandsons, he who resembles Madana attains the abode of Śambhu.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Vow of the Gift of the Jewel-Cow," in the *Uttara-parvan* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[Now begins] the description of the vow for the gift of a cow with two faces (*ubhayamukhī-godāna-vrata*).
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O knower of dharma, when should a cow that is about to calve be given to an eminent Brāhmaṇa? By what rite should it be given, and what is the fruit of such a gift?"
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O best of kings, a cow is obtained through the accumulation of most meritorious deeds;
only certain men, whose store of merit is vast, attain her.
As long as the feet are within the womb and the head is still visible,
so long is the cow to be known as the Earth, provided she does not release the fetus. O Bhārata, this remains true until the cow turns her face away.
Then that earth, together with its mountains, forests, and groves, should be known as such;
the merit that is obtained by men, O King, through giving the "two-faced" cow,
cannot be described by anyone using even a single mouth.

O best of beings, what is the use of many sacrifices you have performed, or the gifts you have bestowed? Give me a single cow that is currently giving birth. For one alone protects from hell, and one alone can bring about happiness.
O descendant of Bharata, even a single cow given with two faces becomes [equivalent to] many cows;
O King, having adorned her with golden horns, silver hooves, and a tail decorated with pearls,
and providing a bronze milking vessel, one should give her to an excellent Brahmin.
By giving a cow that is in the process of calving, one obtains a great fruit of merit;
for as many hairs as there are on the cow and its calf, O lord of men,
for so many thousands of years is one honored in the heavenly world.
One who bestows abundant sacrificial fees undoubtedly delivers his fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers from hell. There,
rivers flow with ghee and milk, and their mud consists of curds and milk-rice.
There they go to where there is a tree that grants all desired objects;
O King, Goloka and Brahmaloka are easily attained by him who gives [the image] along with much gold and a beautiful woman.

O King, a weak cow should not be given as a gift, nor one accompanied by meager sacrificial fees; for this prescribed rite is intended for those desiring specific results, and it yields fruit when performed according to the rules. Furthermore, women with faces like the moon and complexions like refined gold [are attained].
"Women with large hips and slender, rounded waists, possessing eyes like lotuses, serve [him] incessantly.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Gift of a Cow with Two Faces," in the *Śrīkṛṣṇa-Yudhiṣṭhira Saṃvāda* within the *Uttara Parvan* of the glorious *Mahābhārata*, the *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*. [Next:
Description of the Ritual for the Gift of a Thousand Cows.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Janārdana, tell me the procedure for the gift of a thousand cows;
at what time should it be bestowed, and how should it be given?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Cows are the purifiers of the worlds; cows alone are the ultimate refuge.
O Lord of Creatures, when Brahmā created the worlds, he did so for the sake of providing a means of livelihood.
Cows were created first out of a desire for the welfare of the three worlds;
by their urine and dung even the abodes of the gods became pure— what, then, could be more excellent than that?

The auspicious cow-dung, containing all the gods, is the root of every desire-driven sacrifice; that it contains the goddess Lakṣmī is sufficient proof of this. Brahmins and cows constitute a single family, divided into two parts.
In one place the mantras abide, and in another the sacrificial oblation abides.
O Lord of the Earth, hear now the rules for the giving of those [cows] by whose sons the worlds and all the deities are supported.
Even a single cow, endowed with excellent qualities—
a young female who is beautiful, perfected in character, well-provided with milk,
accompanied by a fine calf, easy to milk, and free from disease— delivers the entire family.
One who gives such [land] according to the prescribed rule delivers his entire lineage;
how much more so one who gives ten, or a hundred, according to the ritual?
As for one who would give a thousand, what indeed can be said of him in this world?
In former times, a thousand cows were given by King Nahuṣa;
he, as well as the high-minded Yayāti, went to the abode of Brahmā.
A great gift was also made on the bank of the Gaṅgā by Aditi out of a desire for sons.
He obtained as his son the sinless Nārāyaṇa, the lord of the three worlds.
O King, listen to those verses sung by the ancestors, which are thus heard:
"If someone in our lineage should cause a thousand cows to be given [in charity]..."

We shall attain the supreme perfection brought about by meritorious deeds. Or, if any daughter in the family gives a thousand cows, she will provide a staircase to a happy rebirth; of this there is no doubt.
Henceforth, I shall describe the sacrifice that fulfills all desires. A man should then give a thousand cows according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures.
He should cause an auspicious pavilion to be constructed at a sacred ford, in a cow-pen, or even in his own home.
It should be ten or twelve cubits in size, four-faced, and provided with archways; in its center, one should have a matchless altar constructed,
measuring one cubit in height and beautifully adorned with one cubit [in width].
One should prepare the altar for the planets in the north-eastern direction;
there, one should worship the planets in due order according to the ritual procedure for the planetary sacrifice.
Indeed, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are to be worshipped first of all.
Sixteen, eight, or four excellent officiating priests (ṛtvij) should be appointed,
O Great King, with the preceptor as the fifth;
they should be adorned with all ornaments, including earrings and finger-rings.
Adorned with umbrellas and provided with two copper vessels,

one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) and present the sacrificial offerings according to the procedure prescribed for the sacrifice to the planets. On the north-eastern portion of the altar, one should establish the Śiva-pit (śivakuṇḍa).

O best of the Kuru lineage, one should place two jars at the doors along with the five gems and sprouts; thereafter, one should commence the fire sacrifice (homa) and offer the oblation to the world-protectors (lokapāla-bali) as prescribed for the Tulāpuruṣa gift.
Having extracted ten cows with their calves from among a thousand cows,
one should set aside garments, garlands, and ornaments for those [ten].
Then, having brought those ten back inside, one should honor them with garments and garlands.
It was equipped with golden bells and provided with copper milking vessels;
it was adorned with a golden tilaka-mark, its hooves were decorated with silver,
its horns were made of gold and jewels, and it was graced with chowries.
Some sages desire a golden Nandikeśvara;
one should also have that fashioned with devotion on the peak of Lavaṇadroṇa.
For some, the gift of a single actual bull is desired.
Having fully worshipped the planets and the gods with garlands, garments, fruits, and unbroken grains (akṣata),
and having adorned the temples of the deities with banners,
one should arrange all of this according to a tenth part even of a hundred cows.
If cows possessing all the highest qualities are not available,
one should carefully honor ten [cows] and arrange for the others; then,
with flowers, musical instruments, songs, and the sounds of auspicious proclamations, [the ceremony should proceed].
Having bathed with water containing all medicinal herbs and being consecrated by the best of the twice-born,
he should, holding a handful of flowers, recite this mantra:
"Salutations to you who possess universal forms and who are the mothers of the universe."
Salutations again and again to the Rohiṇīs who dwell within the worlds!
Twenty-one universes abide within the limbs of cows, as do the gods beginning with Brahmā; may these mothers, the Rohiṇīs, protect us.
May cows be before me; may cows be behind me;
may cows be on all sides of me; I dwell in the midst of cows.
Since you are the eternal Dharma in the form of a bull—(according to another reading: since you are the eternal one)—
"O Eternal One, protect me, for you are the abode of the Eight-formed Lord (Śiva).
Having thus addressed him, he should then give Nandikeśvara to the Guru,
provided with all necessary implements and especially accompanied by a cow.
One should give a hundred cows, or even one each, or half of that, or twenty;
or ten, five, or a hundred, according to the permission of the [donor], when giving to many.
A single cow must not be given to many; the giver would become a perpetrator of a fault.
Many [cows] should indeed be given to one person for the increase of prosperity and health.
Then, the giver of a thousand cows should remain for one day observing the milk-vow;
likewise, he who desires abundant prosperity should remain a celibate student (brahmacārī).

A cow that is weak, one that yields little milk, one that is diseased, one that is aged or has worn-out hide, or one whose consciousness is fixed on her calf, should not be given away. He who bestows a thousand cows according to this rule [attains the highest merit].
Completely liberated from all evil and attended by Siddhas and Cāraṇas,
he is honored by the gods in the world of all the World-Guardians, traveling in a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun, adorned with garlands of networks of tinkling bells.
By giving a thousand cows according to the prescribed rite, one rescues seven ancestors, seven descendants, and seven more beyond them— both preceding and succeeding generations.
Likewise, whether it be a man fallen from the heavenly world or a woman devoted to the supreme goal, [they are likewise saved].

For seven births, O Queen, she shall be praised again and again. However, this [act] is not merely praised as a gift; rather, the recipient, the time, the specific type of cow, and the ritual procedure are also essential. Therefore, these cows, adorned with all ornaments, provided with milk, and given at the proper time to a worthy recipient according to the injunctions— [The verse continues: "By giving them, one attains the world of the sun, the moon, and fire; by giving them, one obtains the worlds of Prajāpati and Brahmā. By giving them, one attains the worlds of Indra and Viṣṇu; by giving them, one reaches the highest state of Śiva. Thus it is said: "One who gives a cow, well-adorned and accompanied by a bull, along with gold, garments, and grain, goes to the world of the Sun. Furthermore: "A cow that is gentle, yielding much milk, adorned with a bell, and accompanied by a calf, bestows heaven upon the giver for as many years as there are hairs on her body. And: "One should give a cow that is young, beautiful, and endowed with all auspicious marks, having first honored her with perfumes, flowers, and fine garments. In this manner, the gift of a cow, when performed with devotion and according to the prescribed rules, yields inexhaustible merit. Thus concludes the discourse on the gift of cows.
"Even a single cow, possessing many virtues, when given according to the prescribed rites to a virtuous recipient, purifies the lineage of the donor for three generations.
O King, it is impossible for me to describe the fruit obtained by one who bestows a thousand cows here with faith.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Vow and the Rite for the Gift of a Thousand Cows," in the *Uttara-parvan* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
The Description of the Vow of Giving a Bull.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Janārdana, as I listen to this nectar of your words, I am [delighted].
I do not attain satisfaction, for curiosity has indeed arisen within me:
it is said that Govinda, renowned throughout the three worlds as the Lord of Cows,
rejoices in the gift of a bull.
"O Acyuta, tell me the fruit of that gift of a cow and a bull.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"Listen, I shall tell you the meritorious fruit of the gift of a bull."
It is purifying, sanctifying, and indeed the most excellent among all gifts.
A single bull capable of bearing the yoke is equal to ten cows;
for that one alone excels the gift of ten cows.
O son of Pāṇḍu, he who is joyful, possessed of very well-nourished limbs, free from disease,
young, auspicious, virtuous, and devoid of all defects—
he alone, as a leader, establishes a great lineage.

He becomes a savior in saṃsāra; no doubt should be entertained in this matter. When an auspicious time has arrived, one should decorate a peaceful bull, provide it with a silver tail, and present it to a Brāhmaṇa.
O Indra among kings, listen to this mantra; I shall speak it to you:
"You are Dharma in the form of a bull, the bringer of joy to the world.
You are the foundation of the eightfold form [of Śiva]; therefore, protect me, O Eternal One!"
Having thus given the gift accompanied by the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and having prostrated, one should dismiss [the recipient].
Whatever sin has been committed over seven lifetimes through the actions of speech, mind, and body—
all that goes to dissolution by the merit of the gift of a cow.
Having ascended a divine, brilliantly shining, and most beautiful vehicle yoked with bulls that travels at will, he ascends to his own world.
O Lord of the Earth, as many hairs as there are on that bull...
For as many thousands of years as there were cows given, he is honored in the world of cows (Goloka).
Having descended from Goloka, he becomes a twice-born man in this world,
a performer of sacrifices, possessed of great splendor, and honored by all Brahmins.
As it has been said by you, O Great King: "To whom should this best of bulls be given?
I shall now declare to you who is a worthy recipient, a source of protection for men:
those who are patient and self-controlled, whose ears are filled with sacred learning, who have conquered their senses, and who abstain from the slaughter of living beings.
Those householders who are restrained in accepting gifts are those Brāhmaṇas capable of delivering others across the ocean of existence.
Those who bestow a bull that is vigorous, capable of bearing burdens, firm-necked, and endowed with every excellence— truly,
they become partakers on earth of that merit which arises from the gift of ten cows.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixtieth chapter, titled "Description of the Vow of the Gift of a Bull," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[Now follows] the description of the greatness of the gift of a Kapilā cow.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Lord of the World, tell me the greatness of the gift of a Kapila cow— that merit which is superior to all gifts and the destroyer of all sins. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
I shall now fully declare to you that gift of a Kapila cow which was formerly told by Vinatāśva; listen to it, O high-minded one.
Vinatāśva said:

Hereafter, O Great King, I shall briefly describe that ritual which was formerly told by Varāha to Dharaṇī, as well as the fruit of the merit arising from it, for those who are foremost among the fearless.
Dharaṇī said: O Lord, that cow named Kapilā who was formerly produced by you is always meritorious as a sacrificial cow, the very source of the manifestation of sacrifice.
How indeed should she be given to the Brahmins, on which day as well?
To what kind of Brahmin should she, who possesses auspicious marks, be given?
And how many types of tawny cows (kapilā) were proclaimed by the Self-Existent One himself?
"O Mādhava, what merit would arise from giving them with great effort?
O Madhusūdana, I wish to hear this in detail.
Varāha said:
Listen, O blessed lady, to this truth that is purifying and destructive of sin;
by performing it, one is liberated from all evils—of this there is no doubt.
O lady of beautiful countenance, [one should give] a tawny cow for the sake of the *agnihotra* sacrifice and for the sake of the [great] sacrifice.

Having extracted all splendors, she was created by Brahmā in the past; O fair-faced one, the Kapilā cow is the most sacred of the sacred, the most auspicious of the auspicious, and the highest merit among merits.
Austerity is indeed the foremost of austerities, the highest vow among vows, and the supreme gift among gifts; for when performed according to the prescribed rule, it is imperishable.
So too are all the sacred fords on earth and the secret shrines.
O Vasundharā, in all the worlds, the purifying and meritorious Agnihotra sacrifices must be offered by the twice-born at dawn and at dusk,
using either the ghee or the milk of a Kapila cow.
Those who constantly perform the agnihotra sacrifices with various kinds of food,
who honor guests, and have attained supreme devotion—
their destination arises by means of celestial chariots with the luster of the sun.

In the center of the solar disc, O beautiful lady, all the sacred fords (tīrthas) were created by Brahmā in ancient times; by the command of the Grandfather, they dwell there eternally within the head and neck of Kapilā.
That mortal who, having risen at dawn, devoutly receives upon his head the water flowing from the tip of the hump of a tawny cow (kapilā)—
endowed with that merit, he is instantly freed from all sin.
The sin committed over twenty years is consumed like fire consuming fuel by that mortal who,
rising at dawn, performs their circumambulation;
O Vasundharā, the entire earth has been circumambulated by him.
O Vasundharā, when a single circumambulation has been performed, the sin committed over ten years is destroyed; of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, he who is pure in his vows should bathe with the urine of a tawny cow.
That man becomes as one who has bathed in the Ganges and other sacred fords;
by that single bath,
a person is liberated from worldly existence and is released at that very moment from the sins committed throughout his entire life.
The Grandfather (Brahmā) declared in the world of Brahmā in ancient times that a man who gives a thousand cows, or even a single tawny cow (kapilā), gains equal merit;
yet, if a man who acts as a rope-maker should kill even a single tawny cow, [he incurs great sin].
By that act, a thousand cows are effectively slain; of this there is no doubt in this world.
One should provide for the sustenance of cows and must not defile cow-products such as clarified butter.
For as long as one increases the supply of cow-products, for that long is one purified of sins.
Scratching the cows and likewise protecting them are equal to the gift of cow-ghee; so too is the protection of them from fear, disease, and other perils.
Furthermore, one should provide land and other necessities for the sake of the cows' consumption of grass and such.
The best of men obtains the divine fruit of dwelling in heaven;
ten types of *kapilā* cows have been described here by the Self-born One himself.
That man who gives one to a *śrotriya* goes to heaven.
Honored by various divine celestial chariots and celestial maidens,
and served by Gandharvas, they shine like blazing fires.
The first is golden-brown (kapila) and the second is pale yellowish-brown (gaurapiṅgalā).
Āśā is the third, and Agnijvālā is the fourth;
the fifth is Juhuvarṇā, while the sixth is Ghṛtapiṅgalā;
the seventh is Śvetapiṅgā, and the eighth is Kṣīrapiṅgalā.
The ninth is to be known as Pāṭalā, and the tenth is Puṣpapiṅgalā;
these ten, O Vasuṃdharā, are declared to be Kapilās.
Indeed, all of these are highly fortunate and deliver [beings], of this there is no doubt.
They are praised at confluences and are the destroyers of all sins.
Thus, O Vasundharā, these Kapilā cows are slayers of sin;
and she who is called Āśā possesses the brilliance of fire and has fire within her womb.
With peaks blazing like flames of fire, with eyes like glowing coals,
with fiery flowers and fiery hair, and likewise another possessing the splendor of fire—
one should always offer her in the southeast to a Brāhmaṇa, and never to others.
If a Śūdra, out of desire, should take a Kapilā cow and drink her milk,
that man shall eternally become an outcaste, equal to a Caṇḍāla;
therefore, one should never accept a brindled cow under any circumstances.

A tawny cow (kapilā) must be avoided at the doorway by those other than the twice-born; in this world, those who consume the milk of a tawny cow are the most foolish. Those sinful Śūdras are fallen and are not to be spoken to.
As long as they drink the milk of a Kapila cow, so long do their ancestors consume impure matter; therefore, one who is not a twice-born should not subsist upon it.
[This applies to] their ghee, milk, or even butter.
Those Śūdras who subsist [on the products] of Kapilā cows go to the abode of Yama;
all Śūdras who live by [the trade of] Kapilā cows go to Raurava. Having dwelt there for hundreds of millions of years, they experience suffering in Raurava.
Released from there, they are born in time into the wombs of dogs;
released from the womb of dogs, they enter the wombs of worms in excrement. And those most sinful ones remain constantly in excrement itself, amidst perpetual foul odors.
Furthermore, there is no deliverance for those who are born there again;
O Goddess, from the moment a Brāhmaṇa accepts gifts from them,
his ancestors lie in that impure place.
One should not converse with that brahmin, nor sit upon the same seat as him;
indeed, that lowest of brahmins must always be avoided from afar.
Any twice-born man who converses with him must perform a penance.
A thousandth part of the merit of a single gift of a cow is not equaled by other gifts, however numerous they may be, even if they extend to tens of millions in number—
when given to a learned Vedic scholar who is poor, of virtuous conduct, and a maintainer of the sacred fires.
By giving a single tawny cow, one is liberated from all sins.
One who desires to give should wait for a cow to bring forth her calf during the month;
indeed, those who fear hell must never keep such a cow for their own sake.
A tawny cow that has half-born her calf should indeed be given to a twice-born man;
as long as the face of the calf being born is visible at the birth canal,
for that long she is to be known as the Earth, until she releases the fetus.
O Vasundharā, for as many thousands of years as there are hairs on a cow with her calf,
as many grains of dust upon the earth, and as many stars and constellations in the sky— for that long shall he be honored by Brahmā, Śiva, and the other gods.
He who gives even a single tawny cow dwells in the world of Brahmā;
he who, having fashioned a cow with golden horns and silver hooves and duly honored it,
places gold and silver in the hand of a Brāhmaṇa [is likewise rewarded].
Then he should place the son of Kapilā into the hand of the Brahmin;
having poured water into his hand, he should cause him to recite according to his ability,
using four, three, or even two pieces of gold.
If one desires one's own welfare, one should not give [the earth] deficient by even a single [village];
for there is no doubt that the earth, when given, becomes as if filled with jewels, together with its oceans and forests, its mountains, woods, and groves.
By this gift, which is indeed equal to the gift of the earth,
a man is delivered and goes with his ancestors to that supreme station of Viṣṇu.
Even one who has seized the property of a Brāhmaṇa, a killer of cows, a destroyer of an embryo, or a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa [is purified].
One who has committed evil deeds should offer a two-faced cow adorned with pure gold;
on that day, he should pass the time restrained and subsisting only on milk.
Then, having smeared a mandala with cow dung according to the prescribed rite, he should proceed.
The wise practitioner should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with the mantra prescribed in his own Vedic branch.
First, he should offer oblations with the Vyāhṛtis, and likewise with the five Vāruṇa mantras,
or again with the verses beginning "irāvatī," "dhenumatī," and "devasya tvā."
With the mantra "Syonā pṛthivi," a new cow together with her calf becomes a cow that grants all desired fruits; she is Surabhi, the delighter.
Likewise, the goddess Sarasvatī and the Earth were [established] by Viṣṇu.
Having uttered "Gaurī Viṣṇupadam," one should recite it during rites for peace.
As long as the two feet and the head of the calf are visible,
so long is the earth to be known as belonging to her, until she releases the fetus.
At that time, O Earth, it should be given to a Brāhmaṇa:
a cow with horns tipped in gold, hooves of silver, a brass milking vessel, and adorned with copper;
provided with cloths and bells as ornaments, and decorated with perfumes and flowers.
Having worshipped it with garments and unbroken grains (akṣata), one should present it to a Brāhmaṇa,
O beautiful lady, [valued] at a thousand gold pieces, or half of that,
or even half of that again according to one's capacity, or even half of that once more.
One should give according to one's capacity, free from stinginess regarding wealth;
having placed gold or even silver in the hand [of the recipient], say:
"Accept this great cow; quickly become my brother indeed."
Having brought about the destruction of all sins, be forever a bringer of well-being.
After that, [I shall give you] the Irāvatī, the Dhenumatī, and the Jāhnavī;
I will specifically give you a cow for the sake of your family.
"May there be constant well-being for you, and likewise unsurpassed happiness.
This divine Earth has been given by you; please accept it.
And this mantra, "Who indeed gave it? should be recited by the twice-born.
Having dismissed the Brāhmaṇa, he too should lead that cow to his own home.
O Vasundharā, he who gives a cow that is thus giving birth [to her calf] shall possess this earth,
complete with its oceans and forests, its mountains, groves, and woodlands.
There is no doubt that the earth filled with jewels would be given [in comparison];

for the gods constantly serve a tawny cow (kapilā) who possesses a complexion like refined gold, large haunches, a slender and rounded waist, who has recently calved, and who has two faces, and who is of excellent character.

That man who, having risen early in the morning, becomes self-controlled and pure, and then recites this *Dhenukalpa* with devotion on this earth; and he who recites it at the three periods of the day— [he destroys] the sin produced over a hundred years.
Just as dust is destroyed by the wind in a single moment,
so too the ancestors eat the consecrated food of that wise man who recites this supreme purifier at the time of a śrāddha ceremony.
If a learned man recites this before the twice-born on the new moon day,
his ancestors remain satisfied for a full hundred years;
and whoever hears this merit-bestowing account with an inner self fully absorbed in it, [attains the same reward].
One is liberated from the sins committed throughout a year at that very moment.
O King of kings, this secret emerged from the mouth of the Boar;
it was previously told to the Earth and destroys all sins.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Gift of a Kapilā Cow," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira; followed by the description of the ritual procedure for the vow of gifting a buffalo-cow. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Yudhiṣṭhira, I shall describe the greatness of the gift of a buffalo-cow;
it is meritorious, destructive of sin, conducive to long life, and grants all desires.
[It should be given] during the auspicious eclipses of the moon or sun, on the full moon day of Kārttika, or likewise at the solstices.
O joy of the Kurus, when on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, on the day of the sun’s transit (saṃkrānti), or whenever the thought and the means arise,
then indeed should the queen be given by one who fears the terrors of saṃsāra.
Abounding in the beauty of excellent udders, possessing beautiful horns and beautiful hooves,
having calved for the first time, young, of good character, and free from defects;
adorned with golden horns and forehead-marks, and decorated with ornaments of bells.
Covered with red cloth, beautiful, provided with a bronze milking vessel,
accompanied by a basket of oil-cake, and endowed with gold according to one's means,
it should be given along with seven kinds of grain to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas.
Likewise, it should be given to one who recites the Purāṇas and to one who knows the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra);

it must never be given to one devoid of Vedic knowledge nor to one who follows evil vows. On an auspicious day, accompanied by these materials, it should be offered according to the prescribed ritual.
O Indra among kings, one should give [the gift] with the mantra recited in the Purāṇas:
"May she who is the auspicious queen of the world-protectors, beginning with Indra,
grant all my desires through the greatness of this gift of a buffalo."

"May she, whose son is established in the service of Dharmarāja, and who is the mother of Mahiṣāsura, be a granter of boons to me. (This is the mantra for the gift. Having circumambulated her, one should give that milch cow to a Brāhmaṇa.
The Self-born One ordained that its acceptance should take place on her back.
Having given it in this manner according to the rule, O joy of the Kurus, one should lead it to the house of a Brahmin,
honoring it with devotion through garments and ornaments.
"I have prepared this for you; be satisfied with me, O twice-born one.
Having given a buffalo to an eminent brahmin according to this rite, one obtains all desires in this world and in the next.
She who gives a buffalo shall become a queen;
O King, a man shall become a great king, according to the word of Vyāsa. A Brahmin shall become a performer of sacrifices, and a Kṣatriya shall be victorious.

A Vaiśya would indeed become wealthy, and a Śūdra would be endowed with all prosperity. Therefore, a man who desires his own welfare for the sake of his sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons should give a buffalo-cow when he has the means.
"O King, Nārada has declared a buffalo to be equal to ten cows;
Vyāsa [declared it] equal to twenty cows, and Ravi [declared it] the best of all gifts.
By Sagara, Kakutstha, Dhundhumāra, and Gādhi,"
Having honored the Brahmins, buffaloes that grant all desires were given as gifts.
That man who always hears the greatness of the gift of a buffalo is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of Śiva.

"Having given to an eminent brahmin a buffalo that yields abundant milk, which has the hue of a water-bearing cloud, is adorned with a fine cloth tied about its neck, possesses a beautiful hindquarters, and is marked with a golden tilaka—one conquers both worlds. What wonder is there in this?

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Vow of Giving a Buffalo," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the Rules for the Avidāna Vow. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Pārtha, to the supreme gift that destroys all sins.
By giving [her], the threefold sin immediately goes to destruction—
[giving] one with golden hair, made of gold, or a truly beautiful living one,
adorned with a golden tilaka and decorated with all ornaments.
She is clothed in silk, adorned with divine sandalwood paste,
offered with divine flowers, and endowed with all mineral pigments;
likewise, she is provided with the seven kinds of grain and possesses fruits and flowers.

One should have it made of gold with care, using a hundred [pieces] or according to one's capacity; one must not practice stinginess regarding wealth. This should be done during the solstices, the equinoxes, and during the eclipses of the moon and the sun.
Upon seeing a bad dream, on one's birth star, during the death of a parent,
or whenever wealth arises accompanied by a mind full of faith— that indeed is the time for giving, for life is truly impermanent.
One should give [the gift] at a sacred ford, in one's home, or wherever the mind finds delight;
having installed there Śaṅkara, the Lord of Gods, together with Umā,
as well as Brahmā with Gāyatrī, and likewise Śrīdhara accompanied by Śrī.
Having likewise worshipped Anaṅga along with Rati, as well as the world-protectors and the planets, according to the prescribed rite with offerings of perfumes and flowers,
one should perform a fire-oblation (homa) before them with sesame seeds and clarified butter, O Lord of the Earth.
Having adorned the peaceful brahmin and honored him with garments,
an oblation (homa) should be performed in the kindled fire with mantras corresponding to his [the deceased’s] signs. Then, that [image] situated within a jar of sesame seeds and placed upon salt—
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite, one should utter this mantra:
"O Earth, you have always flourished for the world through all your resources, such as hair, skin, flesh, marrow, and so forth; therefore, I pray to you who remain steadfast."
"Whatever evil deed has been committed by me through speech, mind, or body—
may all that go to dissolution through this gift offered to you.
Having spoken thus, one should give it to a Brāhmaṇa who maintains a family.
One should not speak to him after giving [the gift], nor should one look at his face;
a Brahmin who accepts from a wicked person becomes a sinner, struck down by that evil acceptance.
One should not give a gift devoid of a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā); it must be given according to the prescribed rule.
A gift devoid of the prescribed ritual for the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) brings about suffering and grief. In the past, this gift was given by Gaurī out of a desire for Śaṅkara;
by that means, she obtained Śambhu as her husband, who is saluted by all the gods.
Having given a hundred golden-haired cows according to the prescribed rites to Indrāṇī,
she rejoices even today having obtained as her husband the lord of all the gods.
Indeed, after giving this kingdom to Nala, he departed for heaven.
I have obtained Rukmiṇī as my husband, as well as incomparable good fortune;
by the power of this gift, one obtains sons endowed with great strength.
One who is childless obtains a son, and one who is poor obtains wealth.
Having bestowed gifts that grant auspicious luster and abundant prosperity,
whoever should constantly listen to this unsurpassed ritual manual on giving (Dānakalpa) is liberated from the sins committed during a day and night; of this there is no doubt.
"A ewe that removes specific impurities is highly praised when given as a gift; it should always be accompanied by mercury, minerals, and grain.
O joy of the Kurus, bestow it with reverence, for by giving it you shall shine like the sun, its darkness of sin having been dispelled.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Aviddāna Vrata," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the Gift of Land. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "I shall now describe the gift of land, which destroys all sins."
Those who bestow the gift of land, along with a sacrificial fee,
upon a learned Brahmin who is poor and devoted to the *agnihotra* sacrifice,
become themselves satisfied in soul by all desires and adorned with every kind of jewel.
Completely liberated from all sins and shining like the sun,
