he goes to the world of Viṣṇu by means of radiant, divine celestial chariots, which are adorned with musical instruments and banners and illuminated by the splendor of the rising sun.
There, served by celestial women, moving at will and assuming any form at will, he sports in inexhaustible bliss as long as the worlds,
originating from the sprouts of the earth, endure.
For that long, the giver of land is indeed honored in the world of Viṣṇu;
for there is no gift whatsoever that excels the gift of land.
The one who seizes it favors the ten directions, and the one who takes it destroys those same ten.
O bull among men, other gifts perish with time;
however, the exhaustion of the merit from the gift of land never occurs.
Indeed, all sins are exhausted through the progressive course of time.
O Indra among kings, for one who seizes land, there is no end to suffering.
But that man who, having given land to a virtuous Brāhmaṇa,
does not make use of it himself, shall attain great merit.
Having ploughed the earth, sown it with seed, and made it garlanded with crops,
one is honored in heaven for as long as the world exists by the light of the sun.
Wealth, grain, gold, jewels, and ornaments—
O Indra among kings, by giving the earth, one gives all gifts;
by giving the earth, one gives oceans, rivers, mountains, the level and the uneven, all fragrances, tastes, and oils.
He who gives land gives herbs rich in milk, laden with various flowers and fruits, and clusters of lotuses and water-lilies;
he performs the Agniṣṭoma and other sacrifices accompanied by ritual fees.
And those men who,
having given land to a Vedic scholar (śrotriya), do not take it back, shall attain that merit which is obtained from the gift of land; for them, heaven shall endure as long as the worlds persist.
The ancestors of one who bestows land filled with crops upon a Vedic scholar remain satisfied until the dissolution of all beings;
whatever sin such a person, distressed for a livelihood, might commit—
A man is purified even by the gift of land the size of a cow-hide.
Whatever merit is proclaimed to result from a thousand pieces of gold,
a man shall obtain that same fruit by the gift of land the size of a cow-hide.
O best of men, the fruit that a man obtains by giving food to thousands of tawny cows is attained by a person through a piece of land measuring only the skin of a cow,
according to the calculation of Vyāsa for a man of medium stature.
By giving thirty staff-lengths of land as a *gocarma*, one is glorified in heaven.
The earth has been enjoyed by many kings, beginning with Sagara;
for whomsoever the land belongs at any given time, to him alone accrues the fruit thereof.
The servants of Yama, the punishments of death, the forest of sword-leaves and the like,
the terrible nooses of Varuṇa, and the hells such as Raurava and the unbearable Kumbhīpāka— none of these approach the giver of land.
And likewise, the agonizing torments do not approach the giver of land;
Citragupta, Kāla, Kṛtānta, Mṛtyu himself,
and even King Yama pay homage to the giver of land.
Rudra, Prajāpati, Śakra, and likewise the hosts of gods and asuras,
as well as I myself, with supreme affection, honor here the giver of land—
to one who performs the six duties, who is of good conduct, who is destitute, and who seeks what is dear.
O tiger among men, land should be given so that there may be inexhaustible merit;
O lord of men, land should be given to a learned Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires, whose family is suffering, who is established in righteous conduct, and who is poor.
Just as a mother always nourishes her son with milk,
so does the earth satisfy the giver of land with all his desires;
just as a cow supports her calf and yields milk.
Likewise, the earth, endowed with all flavors, sustains the giver of land;
just as seeds sown upon the ground sprout when moistened by water,
so do the desires of the giver of land flourish day by day.
Just as the thousand-rayed sun dispels all darkness,
so too does the gift of land dispel all evil.
But he who should ever injure land given by another...
Bound by the nooses of Varuṇa, he is cast into pus and blood. That man who seizes land given by himself or given by another suffers in a terrible hell until the end of the dissolution of the world.
He who causes the loss of livelihood for those who weep falls into hell and is cooked there for as many thousands of years as there were drops of tears;
when the field of Brahmins is seized, the family of the thief is destroyed for three generations.
If, after having given land to a Brahmin, one should later harm it,
that evil-minded person is cooked head-downwards in the Kumbhīpāka hell.
At the end of a thousand divine years, having emerged from Kumbhīpāka, he is released.

O King Yudhiṣṭhira, best among rulers, one shall indeed possess sovereignty in this world for seven births; therefore, with effort, protect land given by yourself or by another. O foremost of kings, the preservation of what has been given is superior to the act of giving.
Those men who steal the property of Brahmins are born as black snakes dwelling in dried-out hollows within waterless forests.
Having thus given away the earth, O King, with a joyful inner soul, [one attains the highest state].
A person obtains all desires conceived by the mind;
there is no greater happiness in the hereafter than the gift of land,
nor is any other sin said to be more grievous than the seizure of land.
Those best of the twice-born who bestow well-ploughed land upon a worthy recipient go to the abode of Śakra with perfectly purified bodies;
however, those who seize it by excessive force out of desire and greed do not emerge from the most profound Raurava hell.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Gift of Land," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the Ritual for the Gift of Land.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"The gift of land is appropriate for Kṣatriyas, but not for others."
For they are indeed capable of acquiring, giving, and protecting [it] as prescribed.
O Yādava, tell me of anything else equal to the gift of land that can be accomplished by those who have acquired wealth and who are terrified by the fear of saṃsāra.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:

Having fashioned an auspicious golden earth according to the prescribed rites, complete with its mountains and trees, and bestowing it upon Brahmins, that [gift] is declared to be equal to [the gift of] the actual earth.
Listen with a one-pointed mind, O best of men, as I shall explain the great gift along with its ritual procedure and the fruit that arises from it with effort:
during an eclipse of the moon or sun, at one's birth star, and likewise at the equinoxes.
It should be given at the beginnings of the Yugas and during the solstices according to the prescribed rules; furthermore,
it should be given by men on earth at other auspicious times when wealth has been accumulated, either for the destruction of sin or for the sake of fame.
It is prescribed that one should make [the image] with a hundred palas of gold, or even with half of that according to one's ability;
even one who is incapable, if possessed of devotion, should make it with at least five palas.
One should have a golden earth made, resembling the continent of Jambudvīpa.
It possesses boundary mountains and is centered by Mount Meru;
it is endowed with the eight world-protectors and joined by Brahmā and Viśveśa;
it is filled with various mountains and adorned with ornaments of jewels.
Having prepared such a ground— one whose surface is variegated with all kinds of grain and perfumed with all fragrances— one should then have a pavilion constructed,
measuring ten or twelve cubits and provided with four archways, O Four-faced One.
In the center, one should construct an altar measuring one bow-length in height; then,
having adorned the abodes of the deities with banners, one should establish the assembly hall in the northeast and the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in the southeast.

The world-protectors and the planetary deities should be worshipped with garlands and unguents; the twice-born, peaceful, auspicious, and learned in the four Vedas should perform the fire-oblation (homa),
adorned with ornaments, dressed in fine garments, and decorated with garlands and sandalwood paste.
Having first performed the ritual installation of the fire there,
O King, the twice-born should then bring the earth forward, preceded by the chanting of the Veda,
accompanied by the sounding of conchs and trumpets, and the resonant sounds of auspicious songs.
Having covered the altar with sesame seeds, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) there.
Then, one should place eighteen kinds of grains, liquids such as salt and others,
as well as eight auspicious full water-pots all around it.
Having prepared a canopy of silk, various fruits,
diverse fine garments, and pieces of sandalwood,
he performed the preliminary consecration for her in this manner.
Then, at the conclusion of the fire oblations, when all the rites for pacification have been completed,
the patron himself, wearing white garlands and garments,
shall circumambulate the earth and take a handful of flowers.
Then, having reached an auspicious time, one should recite these mantras:
"Salutations to you, for you alone are the abode of all the gods;
you are the sustainer of all beings, therefore protect us, O Vasundharā!"
Since you sustain wealth (*vasu*) which bestows all happiness, you are therefore born as Vasundharā; protect us fully from fear.
O Immovable One (*acale*), even the Four-faced One cannot reach your end.
Salutations to you, O Infinite One; protect me from the mire of saṃsāra.
You alone are Lakṣmī in Govinda, and as Śivā you abide as Gaurī;
you are Gāyatrī at the side of Brahmā, Jyotsnā in the moon, and Prabhā in the sun.
Buddhi is renowned as residing in Bṛhaspati; Medhā is established among the sages.
Because she stands pervading the entire universe (viśva), she is therefore considered Viśvambharā.
She is Dhṛti, Kṣiti, Kṣamā, Kṣoṇī, Pṛthivī, Vasudhā, and Mahī.
"O Goddess, protect me from the ocean of saṃsāra with these forms.
Having uttered this, one should present that goddess to the Brāhmaṇas;
one should bestow half a dharana or a fourth part upon the preceptor.

The wise man who, according to this rite, bestows the goddess Earth when an auspicious occasion has arrived, attains the station of Viṣṇu. If he is unable to perform the extensive ceremony on a holy day, [he should do so in a condensed form].
Having established it in a beautiful place, one should cause the earth itself to be given as a gift;
having gone to the city of Nārāyaṇa by means of a celestial chariot (vimāna) with the color of the sun and garlanded with clusters of tinkling bells, one shall dwell there for three kalpas.
Having come here when his merit is exhausted, he becomes a righteous king—
victorious, a subduer of enemies, with a vast retinue of servants and attendants;
a hero and lord of a hundred crores, a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) of great power.

"By the greatness of this gift, one shall obtain sovereignty for seven births. Having fashioned a golden earth, variegated with the islands and oceans, according to the rules—like the divine earth situated amidst the Vindhyas, and joined with the lords of the world, Śambhu, Śiva, and Keśava—O Pārtha, you have bestowed it. What more need be said? Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual for the Gift of the Earth," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the Ritual for the Gift of a Row of Horses.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Hereafter, I shall describe to you a most wonderful gift.
O Indra among kings, by giving this, one becomes a bestower of all gifts;
it pacifies all sins, bestows all happiness,
and when offered with a line of ploughs, it yields the fruit of every possible gift.

A row of ten ploughs is declared a *paṅkti*; a single plough consists of four oxen. The wise say that the ten ploughs should be made of solid wood, bound with golden bands, adorned with jewels, and auspicious.
One should yoke auspicious, unbroken bulls— youthful, strong, handsome, free from physical defects,
well-adorned with garments, gold, and flowers, and with their heads anointed with sandalwood paste—
to those ploughs.
One should have halters made that are joined in pairs and provided with bulls;
it should be equipped with goads, stakes, bindings, and all necessary implements. In this manner, one should construct a row of plows joined together by such plows.
One should provide a tortoise, a shield, or even a village garlanded with crops,
or perhaps a hundred nivartanas of land, or even half of that;
one should give such a gift at the time of a festival with a disciplined mind.
One should cause [the gift] to be bestowed on the full moon day of Kārttika or Vaiśākha, or likewise during the northern solstice, on one's birth star, during an eclipse, or at the equinox;
[to] Brāhmaṇas who are perfected in the Vedas, free from physical defects, and well-adorned.
One should invite learned Vedic scholars who are humble and as many as the number of ploughs [to be used].
A wise man should have a pavilion constructed measuring ten cubits;
it should be very beautiful, with one or two walls on the eastern side, each measuring one cubit.
There, those best of the twice-born should perform the fire-oblation with the *vyāhṛtis*.
A wise man should worship Parjanya, Āditya, and the Rudras with milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
In that rite, the fuel-sticks should be of *palāśa* wood, along with clarified butter and black sesame seeds.
Having accepted that auspicious row situated amidst the grain,
the sacrificer, having bathed, dressed in white garments, and being pure and composed, then yokes the row of ploughs in the presence of everyone.
Amidst the sounds of musical instruments and conchs, and with abundant recitations of the Veda,
one who has taken handfuls of flowers in both hands should utter this mantra:
"Since all the hosts of gods always reside here, O Hala..."
Since they are ever-present in the one whose shoulders are like a bull, may my devotion be directed toward Śiva alone;
and since other gifts do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of a gift of land, may my devotion to Dharma always remain firm.

When this has been said, the best of the twice-born should then urge the row [of plowmen] forward with seeds, all kinds of gems, gold, and silver. Afterwards, the [donor] himself, having taken hold of the plow, should scatter [the offerings] into the hands of the Brahmins.
The wise man should proceed until he reaches the point of return and then desist;
having performed a circumambulation and presented gifts to the Brahmins according to the prescribed rite,
he should prostrate and bid them farewell along with the ritual fees.
Whoever bestows this gift according to this rite is honored in the heavenly world together with twenty-one generations of his lineage;
for seven births, he shall be free from poverty, misfortune, and diseases.
And he does not see the ground; likewise, he becomes its sovereign.
Having seen this gift being given, O Yudhiṣṭhira, one is liberated from the sins committed since birth; of this there is no doubt.
Indeed, this gift was bestowed by Dilīpa,
Yayāti, Śibi, Nimi, and the wise Bharata;
by the power of this very gift, they even now rejoice in heaven.
Therefore, O best of kings, this gift should be given with every effort by one endowed with devotion, whether a woman or a man;
even if no formal row is available, it may be given to five or four [persons].
Even a single ploughshare should be given according to the prescribed rite by the wise.
As many particles of dust as arise from the tip of the plough, and as many hairs as there are on the oxen that bear its yoke—
for so many *tri-yugas* shall a man who performs this gift of a row [of ploughs] remain in the city of Śaṅkara.
"Those virtuous ones who, on an auspicious day, bestow upon the foremost of the twice-born this row of ploughs joined with exceedingly powerful bulls,
together with land and accompanied by provisions, shall become noble kings after reaching the earth.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Gift of the Row of Ploughs," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the Ritual for Cooking and Giving.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Lord of Gods, tell me that by which, when given, a human being [attains the goal].
He is born with many sons, much wealth, and many servants.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O Bhārata, in former times there was a king in this lineage named Havyavāhana."
By him, the kingdom inherited from his father and grandfather was obtained free of thorns;
in his reign there was no destruction, nor any fear born of enemies,
nor any great disease arising from the body that could bring about his end.
While he was ruling his kingdom in this manner, due to the unwholesome karma acquired in previous lives,
there was no servant capable of bearing the burden who could sustain the entire weight of the realm;
there was no son who acted with affection, nor any minister of sweet speech.
He was not a friend capable of performing a service, nor likewise a well-wisher;
when the time for food arrived, there was no meal providing every desire,
nor betel-leaf joined with areca nut, nor even clothing.
Neither wealth nor a hoard of jewels creates a connection with people;
for him who acts in this manner, the kingdom remains unimpeded and effortless. Then, one day, the highly renowned Brahmin Pippalāda arrived.
The great yogi of immense splendor came into the presence of the king.
Seeing that the sage had arrived, the queen Śubhāvatī honored him in every way by offering water for his feet, the guest-offering, and a seat.
Then, at the conclusion of a certain conversation, Śubhāvatī said to him:
"O Blessed One, O twice-born one, why is it that this kingdom of ours— devoid of all afflictions—
is [bereft] of servants, sons, ministers, friends, and the like?"
"And the attainment of enjoyments is not such as to surpass all the world.
Pippalāda said:
"Whatever has been previously ordained by him, that is the natural fruit."
O Queen, this is the field of karma; you ought not to grieve for this.
Neither kings, nor heirs, nor enemies, nor kinsmen, nor friends can do that which was not performed by oneself in the past.
"Therefore, that excellent kingdom which was given by you has been obtained;
but the relationship with servants, friends, and others was not given—how could it be obtained?
Śubhāvatī said:
O brahmin-sage, why is that not taught to me this very moment— that by which I may indeed have many sons, wealth, and servants?
Is it a mantra, a perfected yoga, a vow, a gift, or a fast?
"O one of pure intellect, tell me that by which happiness is attained.
Thereupon, Pippalāda, the best of the twice-born,
spoke of the great gift known as Āpāka, which bestows all prosperity.
"O tiger among the Kurus, whether it be a woman or a man, by giving that [gift] with faith one becomes the recipient of many fortunes.
Having heard this, the king bestowed the supreme gift known as Āpāka.
He obtained sons, cattle, servants, ministers, friends, and well-wishers.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Yudhiṣṭhira, I shall now describe the great gift known as Āpāka.
By giving that which makes a man a vessel for the fulfillment of his desires,
one should worship the auspicious Bhārgava after obtaining the favorable strength of the planets and stars; with garments, ornaments, flowers, agallochum, and sandalwood.
One should show him such honor that he becomes truly satisfied.
"Prepare for me vessels, both heavy and light;
bright water-jars and other such items, as well as most beautiful cooking pots."
"O highly fortunate one, fashion jars, water-pots, neck-ornaments,
earrings, bowls, and many other kinds of vessels and utensils;
for you alone are indeed Viśvakarman."

The descendant of Bhṛgu, being wise, should also with great effort prepare a thousand auspicious and divine vessels, complete with various implements, using the ritual procedure prescribed by the rules. Having arranged those one thousand vessels, he should proceed with diligence.
Having kindled the fire at the time of twilight, one should offer oblations;
then, one should keep a vigil at night with the sounds of songs and auspicious chants.
Then, when the morning has become clear, one should know that the fire has been gradually extinguished.
Having covered it with red cloths, one should worship it with flower garlands.
Then the patron, having bathed, pure and wearing white garments,
[should offer] vessels made of gold, silver, copper, and iron.
Having placed those sixteen [offerings] all around according to his ability,
and having worshipped them with diligence, performed a beautiful circumambulation,
honored the Brahmins, and carefully worshipped Bhārgava;
Having brought together the women there who are not widows and having honored them, one should then perform a circumambulation and worship them with this mantra:
"O cooking vessel, you are the form of Brahmā; these pots are living beings."
"By this gift, may there be prosperity for my progeny and may heaven be mine forever.
May all these vessels and forms that have indeed been prepared by me here become excellent recipients and attend upon me."
This is the mantra for giving.
Then, whatever vessel each woman takes up, she should cause that to be given to her;
let her take it according to her own will, and no one should be restrained.
O King, he who bestows this gift according to this rite shall have Viśvakarman pleased for three lifetimes;
and a woman, having given it, attains incomparable good fortune.

One shall obtain a house endowed with all virtues, surrounded by servants and friends, never separated from one's master, and a form of unsurpassed beauty. O sinless one, this gift of land has been described to you according to its proper method.
O Lord of Men, this stage [of life] is divided into many sub-divisions.
Just as an excellent woman here, having diligently prepared a great heap of vessels, experiences joy from their completion until they are finally given away;
so too, having enjoyed the increase of sons, grandsons, and cattle, she remains forever happy after death in the company of her husband.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for Gifting Food," in the Śrīkṛṣṇa-Yudhiṣṭhira Dialogue within the Uttara Parvan of the glorious *Śrīmad Bhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*.
[Now follows] the description of the ritual for gifting houses. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:

"O knower of the true essence of the meaning of all scriptures, O master who has reached the further shore of knowledge and realization, O best among the wise, tell me the greatness and the ritual procedure for the gift of a house.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
There is no dharma higher than that of the householder; there is no gift greater than the home;
there is no sin greater than falsehood; and there is none more worthy of worship than a Brahmin.
[The home] is filled with wealth and grain, and crowded with wife and children.
A house filled with herds of cattle, elephants, and horses is superior to heaven;
for just as all living beings exist by depending upon their mother,
so do the other stages of life (āśramas) subsist by depending upon the householder.

Dharma, artha, and kāma, as well as friends and renowned fame— O Pārtha, the householder stage of life should always be pursued by men who have attained their desires; for without the home, there is no dharma, no artha or kāma, and no happiness.
Neither worldly status nor fame is attained even by the gods of the thirty-three;
it is found neither in heaven nor in liberation—how can it be compared to anything?
It is the bliss of those who, at night, sleep in their own homes with their feet stretched out.
"The days are not counted for him, nor do they call him a glutton;
even for one cooking only vegetables in his own home, there is supreme happiness.
Thinking thus, O Great King, he had [the hall] made most beautiful.
A Brahmin desiring auspicious prosperity should have a dwelling constructed for a worthy recipient;
it should be built with sturdy pillars and made of fine, baked bricks,
beautiful like the back of a tortoise, and illuminating the quarters of the sky with its radiance.
One should provide a shelter plastered with lime, well-protected, and adorned with comfortable halls,
which yields infinite fruit for Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, and Yogic practitioners;
provided that such a spacious residence is constructed along with abundant water.
What could not have been accomplished for the sake of the poor, the helpless, and those seeking water?
[He saw houses] provided with walls and gateways, secured with doors and bolts,
whitened with plaster, beautiful, possessing spacious courtyards and gardens,
with facilities for entry and exit, and situated near reservoirs of water.
Filled with iron implements, provided with copper implements, enriched with the splendor of golden implements, crowded with silver implements,
endowed with gem-studded implements, and adorned with bell-metal implements.
[He saw houses] made of brass, tin, and lead, devoid of furnishings;
some crowded with bamboo utensils, others augmented by wooden implements;
some filled with earthenware vessels, and others provided with cloth articles.
Adorned with the equipment and requisites for dharma, such as hempen and bark garments; shining with grass and stones, yet decorated with every kind of utensil;
and whatever vessels made of the seven metals that originate from precious gems.
[He saw] leather goods, wooden items, and large vessels made of new materials;
likewise, [he saw] herds of cows, buffaloes, horses, bulls, servants, and groups of courtesans;
as well as desirable, auspicious, and excellent mansions situated near fields, groves, and water.
It was completely filled with all kinds of grains, such as ghee, oil, and molasses;
with sesame, rice, śāli rice, sugarcane, mung beans, wheat, and mustard; and with flat beans, adāka beans, chickpeas, horse gram, peas, and lentils.
[He should prepare] vessels rich with rice, mung beans, barley, and the like, filled with stalks of potherbs, and provided with salt, fresh ginger, dates, grapes, cumin, coriander,
asafoetida, saffron, camphor, bathing substances, and sandalwood.
With incense-burners, scattered cotton, bolsters, and pillows; with hearths, chopping-blocks, churning-sticks, auspicious seats, and flower-clusters;
with cooking-pots, mortars, basins, winnowing-fans, mirrors, and metal plates.
With pestles, swords, spears, arrows, staffs, bows, and mallets;
with houses, fences, ladles, stone mortars, clods of earth, and hands;
with whisks, silken cloths, iron implements, and blazing churning-sticks and the like.

One should give houses filled with such things as a grain-pounding mortar, a grinding stone, a hearth, a water-jar, a broom, a chest, a cupboard, a couch, and blankets made of wool; thus one should bestow these upon the twice-born.

The time for giving is praised when it occurs on an auspicious day declared by a Brahmin, endowed with the strength of the moon and joined with a fixed asterism (sthira-nakṣatra). Having thus gathered all the necessary materials, the patron himself [should address] the twice-born.
One should invite those endowed with noble lineage and good character, numbering according to the household;
those who have studied the Vedas, who know the Shastras, who have mastered the Puranas and Smritis;
those devoted to the duties of a householder, who are peaceful, self-controlled, and have conquered their senses.
Then, having adorned them along with their wives with garments, one should worship them;
having made them wear fragrant garlands, one should employ them in the rite of pacification (śāntikarma).
One should have a single sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) constructed in the courtyard of the house, provided with a girdle (mekhalā).
A sacrifice to the planets (grahayajña) should always be performed to bring about satisfaction and nourishment;
thereafter, the Brahmins should recite the hymns that destroy demons (rākṣoghnasūktas).
The worship of Vāstu should be performed, and one should offer oblations to the spirits (bhūtabali) in all directions.
Then, with the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*),
the wise patron, pure and wearing white garments, should have those Brahmins enter those houses and seat them, together with their wives, upon couches.
Whatever has been previously ordained for him, that one should bestow upon him:
"Accept this house, furnished with all its utensils;
O Brahmin, by your grace, may my desired fruit be attained."
Having thus given each gift one by one, he should prostrate and ask for forgiveness.
The Brahmins, being honored, should say, "May there be well-being! and "Who has given? The sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be equal to the household utensils, excluding the house itself.
The great sages should consult their teacher, for he is the root [of their knowledge];
having personally honored them, they should then return to their own abodes.
According to this rite, one should give a single house, or even many.
No fixed rule regarding the number [of recipients] should be observed; here, capacity is the determining factor.
By giving even a grass hut that protects against cold, wind, and heat, one attains desired objects and is honored in heaven after death.
What need is there for much more to be said? Having bestowed his beloved Brahmapurī, adorned with every kind of utensil and ornament, out of an extreme longing for happiness,
[he attained the fruits of] gifts of cows, land, and gold, as well as the restraints and observances of Yama.
O Kaunteya, they do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of the gift of a house.
He who causes to be built a city for the twice-born—possessing very firm mansions, highly precious, inhabited by the virtuous, and enjoyed by noble people;
whose mental disposition is gladdened by divine apsarases—he attains the unsurpassed state of the Moon-crested Lord.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Gift of a House," in the *Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the *Uttara Parvan*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira;
followed by the "Description of the Greatness of the Gift of Food.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:

O sinless Yudhiṣṭhira, I shall describe to you the greatness of the gift of food, as it was proclaimed by the sages of old; listen to this with a focused mind. "Give food! Give food! Give food! [is the command].
What gift from another in this world could bring you such immediate satisfaction?
I shall relate to you that which was spoken long ago by Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, while he was dwelling in the forest out of despondency regarding his own younger brother.
"O son of Sumitrā, although the earth is filled with food, we still long for more; surely it must be that no oblation was offered by us into the mouth of a Brāhmaṇa.
For whatever is spoken of as the seed of action, its fruit must inevitably be reaped by men."
"O Lakṣmaṇa, we have obtained nothing; no food has been offered into the mouth of a Brahmin.
That which is obtainable through learning or through human effort has not been obtained by us.
This popular proverb is true: what is not given does not come to one."

The gift of food, through its consumption, brings about the highest welfare. O Bhārata, while there are other types of edible gifts and other kinds of giving, the gift of food alone is supreme; truthful speech is the supreme state.
Intelligence is surpassed by greed, and contentment is the supreme happiness.
For men who have bathed, been anointed with unguents, and adorned with ornaments,
there is neither pleasure nor contentment without food.
In ancient times, there was a sovereign ruler of the earth named Śveta.
He performed many sacrifices, conquered numerous battles,
bestowed gifts, and protected the earth according to righteousness.
Having enjoyed vast pleasures and stood at the head of his enemies,
O King, he abandoned royal splendor according to the rules for forest-dwellers;
having done so, he went to heaven, honored by the hosts of Maruts.
Filled with joy, he ascended a celestial chariot resembling the sun;
there he dwelt, sporting happily together with the Vidyādharas. He was praised by renowned Siddhas and served by hosts of Apsarases.
He is sung of by joyful gandharvas and followed even by Śakra;
wearing divine garlands and garments, adorned with celestial ornaments,
he constantly descends from the foremost of canopies to the surface of the earth.
O son of Kuntī, he eats his own flesh after first casting off his body;
yet that body remains exactly as it was, preserved by his past karmas.
Once, he approached Brahmā, the Lord of the Gods.
Having bowed down with palms joined in reverence, he spoke these words out of world-weariness:
"O Blessed One, by your grace, the happiness of heaven has been attained by me;
O bull among the gods, you are worthy of worship even by all the deities."
"But, O Lord, even though I am situated in heaven, hunger afflicts me excessively,
such that I must eat my own flesh in the absence of food.
Brahmā said:
O Śveta, endowed with a pure lineage, listen to my words:
you have studied, performed oblations, given gifts, and satisfied your gurus;
O lord of men, you have bestowed destruction upon the twice-born.
This fruit of the gift of food is being enjoyed by you;
therefore, there is nothing other than the gift of food that brings about the health of the body.
Apart from food, there is no other life-sustaining medicine for human beings.
"O Great King, having gone to the earth, carry out my word.
Bestow it upon one who is endowed with austerity and Vedic study, who is learned in the scriptures, and whose senses are subdued—
by which, O Lord of the Earth, your inexhaustible satisfaction shall be attained."
Having gone to the surface of the earth with haste at the word of Viriñci,
O best of the Bharatas, he fed Agastya with devotion.
Having fed him, his sins being exhausted, he then gave him a sacrificial fee.

Then, having removed a radiant single-string necklace from his own neck and having given food along with sacrificial fees, Śveta— honored by the best of the gods with the sound of kettledrums and being fully satisfied— went to heaven.
After Paulastya had been slain and the conflict between the gods and the dānavas had subsided,
Agastya, with supreme joy, bestowed the Ekāvalī upon Rāma.
I shall now describe to you another aspect of the greatness of this food.
And nothing more truthful than this has been spoken by me to you:
food is indeed the life-breath of living beings; food is vigor, strength, and happiness.
For this reason, the virtuous have declared that the giver of food is the giver of life.
Who else is a man equal to him, at whose house those who have come from afar with hope and hunger depart satisfied?
An initiated priest, one who maintains a sacrificial fire for cows, a king, a mendicant, and the great ocean— [these are likewise unsurpassed].
These [guests] purify merely by being seen; therefore, one should look upon them constantly.
For one who is unable to provide food for even a single guest, what is the fruit of his dwelling at home with its undertakings and hardships?
It is possible to live for a long time even on difficult tasks,
but it is not possible to survive for long without food.
He who, having eaten in the house of a householder, indulges in sexual intercourse [is likewise unable to endure].
"The wise say that the sons belong to him whose food they eat;
for the evil deeds of men persist by depending upon their food.
Whoever eats the food of another, he eats that person's misdeeds."
If one eats the food of another while the Soma juice has entered the trees, the merit accumulated by that person over a month goes to the giver.
Why is [merit] not constantly given? Why is food not given?
He who eats without having given alms, or abundant food, or even a mere morsel to a twice-born man— of whom such an attainment of fruit has been described by the ancient sages— incurs sin.
O Pārtha, in former times there was a merchant living by his shop in Vārāṇasī who, having fed ten thousand or a thousand twice-born men, had surely built a small hut near the house of a Brāhmaṇa.
There was a man known as Dhaneśvara, a worshiper of the gods and Brahmins.
While he had set down an egg of pale luster in one part of his shop, a serpent emerged from it; seeing this, the merchant became alarmed.
Then that egg was seen by the merchant, who was possessed of a compassionate mind;
from that time forward, he guarded it and nourished it every day.
After some days, a young serpent emerged, having broken through the eggshell.
The merchant reared him with services such as feeding him milk;
he licked pots of ghee, sniffed heaps of perfumes,
rolled in piles of dust, and wandered about in the midst of water.

Protected by the merchant out of affection, he went there again day after day; a very long time passed, and this [period] became terrifying. Then, one day, he went to the Gaṅgā, which flows through the three worlds, to bathe.
Having stationed his son, who was as wise as a merchant, in the marketplace to oversee the goods,
the merchant began to conduct business with the intelligent merchant’s son;
he gave and received ghee, oil, barley, and sugarcane products.
Due to the distraction of his business dealings, the serpent moved between the merchant's feet out of restlessness; thus, the merchant fell into a state of agitation,
even though he was aware of what had happened, owing to the power of destiny at its root.
Out of fear, he threatened the foot-traveler with his strength;
rising up from the earth and lowering his head,
that lowest of serpents spoke these most cruel words.
"Why do you kill me, O evil-minded one, when I have come to you for refuge, was nurtured by your father, and acted for your pleasure? How will you escape with your life?
Immediately thereafter, a great clamor arose from the men who were weeping.
The son of Dhaneśvara, bitten by a serpent and greatly distressed,
cried out, "Acyuta, Ananta, Govinda, Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa!
Then Dhaneśvara himself arrived and spoke with an agitated voice.
"O ascetic, what displeasure has my son caused you,
that he has been encircled by your own body upon your head?
For one who is of low birth, even if he be a friend or a close relative, is indeed a fool."
He who makes charcoal embers with his own hand drags them back again;
and that serpent spoke to him in a voice faltering with tears:
"I, innocent of any offense, have been struck by your son."
"Therefore, O lord of men, while you look on, I shall now bite this [serpent] so that there may never again be any fear for living beings from it.
Dhaneśvara said:
Who can restrain one who has departed, bypassing the path of the virtuous— one for whom there is no limit to affection, who performs service and observes vows with devotion?
Wait but a moment, until my child [returns].
She herself performed the funeral rites for herself.
Having been told this, she went home and fed a thousand ascetics and celibate students with meals of milk-rice mixed with ghee.
Then all the Brahmins, their minds filled with joy, rose up and scattered flowers and unbroken grains of rice upon the head of the merchant’s son, saying:
"O merchant’s son, live long! May your enemies be destroyed!"

"May you attain the fulfillment of your desired fruit by the command of the Brahmin. Then that evil-natured serpent, resembling a mountain, struck by the thunderbolt of the Brahmin’s words, fell down and died.
Seeing the fallen serpent, the Lord of Wealth, his eyes filled with terror, cried out, "Ah! What is this? and fell into the deepest despair:
"This child was nourished by me, protected, and likewise cherished."
The wind-eater has met his death because of my transgression.
What merit is there in the goodness of one who is good toward those who help him?
He who is good toward those who do him harm—he is considered truly good by the virtuous.
Having thus resolved, his mind tormented by sorrow,
he neither ate nor slept that night due to his agitation.
Then, at dawn, having bathed in the Gaṅgā and offered libations to the deities, he departed.
He again fed a thousand twice-born brahmins;
and being gratified by those brahmins who had eaten and attained their desired success, the merchant said:
"My wish is that this serpent may come back to life."
Then, sprinkled with the waters released by the best of the twice-born,
that noble man of sound limbs rose up suddenly;
seeing him standing before him, he experienced incomparable joy.
Seeing his limbs restored to youthfulness and his lips repeatedly licking with joy, a great cry of "Well done!
arose; all the inhabitants of the city, their eyes wide with wonder, praised the Lord of Wealth.
The greatness of feeding a thousand has been told to you, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
What else shall I tell you concerning one who is endowed with perfect faith?
Those of pure mind who daily give food to the foremost of the twice-born who have arrived in great numbers—
Having dwelt for a very long time among mortals together with their friends and kinsmen, they depart after death to the abode of Murāri, filled with joy.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Gift of Food," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira;
followed by the "Description of the Gift of a Cooking Pot."
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"In connection with the gift of food, something has also come to my memory;
that I shall relate to you exactly as it was heard and seen by me."
O Blessed One, our wealth and kingdom were taken from us by means of a game of dice.
Having been summoned by deceitful gamblers skilled in the casting of dice,
we have all been sent away to the forest, clothed in garments of bark and deerskin.
O Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by Draupadī and [the presence of] Karṇa, Duryodhana, and the others,
all the self-controlled Brahmins, having learned that we had gone to the forest,
came to see us, and the citizens also followed them.
Seeing us suffering out of affection for him, the best of Brahmins, as well as the citizens and the laborers, spoke these words out of despondency:
"He whose life is lived such that Brahmins, friends, and kinsmen live [for his sake]..."
His life is fruitful; for who does not live for their own sake?
Yet, having abandoned visiting guests, friends, and family, the sinful person who merely fills his own belly is dead even while living.
Having thus reflected, I spoke again to those sages:
"O great seers, you who have reached the further shore of knowledge and realization, all of you are knowers of the three periods of time; you have assembled here for my sake."
"Tell me some means regarding my departure, sirs:
how may I go forth into the empty forest for these twelve years together with all of you— servants and brothers alike?"
Then Maitreya said to me: "Listen, O son of Kuntī, to my words.
I shall relate an ancient account seen by me with divine vision.
There was once a certain Brahmin woman, a celibate practitioner, in a forest of asceticism."
Unfortunate, fallen into misfortune, she sought to propitiate the twice-born through her suffering.
Satisfied by her purity, humility, and self-restraint, the sages said: "Speak, O large-eyed one; what may we do for you, O lady of noble vows?"
She said to them: "What is that vow or even what gift should I perform?
Tell me so that I may indeed become a partaker of fortune and happiness, the support of all beings, possessed of many offspring, and beloved by my husband."
Desirable to the three worlds and the source of the fruits of the three aims of life,
Vasiṣṭha then said to her: "Listen, I shall tell you of that gift which bestows honor upon men and grants all desires."
Having fashioned a copper vessel weighing five hundred palas,
one who is unable to do so may instead make one of half that weight, or even a quarter;
and one who is entirely destitute of means may have it made of clay.
It had a firm handle and a deep,
hollow belly; it was quickly filled with well-steamed, perfectly formed mung-bean rice,
accompanied by side dishes and water, and provided with a vessel of ghee.
Having placed her— whose sides and ears have been washed and who is anointed with sandalwood paste—
within a mandala, one should then worship her with garments, flowers, and incense.
This should be done on a Sunday, during a solar transit (saṃkrānti), or on the fourteenth or eighth lunar days.

On the eleventh or the third lunar day, one should present [the gift] to a Brahmin. Just as there can be no successful preparation of food for living beings without a cooking pot— even with watered rice grains placed beside a blazing fire— [so too is the gift ineffective without a worthy recipient].
You are the accomplishment for those desiring accomplishment; you are the nourishment for those seeking nourishment.
Therefore, I bow to you; quickly make my word come true regarding my circle of kinsmen, relatives, friends, brahmins, and likewise my servants.
"O Giver of Boons, you should not eat while I have not yet eaten.
Having spoken thus, the pot should be presented to the eminent Brahmin by one who desires all their wishes and seeks contentment and nourishment for themselves.
Having heard the words of Vasiṣṭha, she did exactly so;
she gave the vessel to the Brahmin along with many sacrificial fees.
And she, O Pārtha, is this very Draupadī who became your beloved wife.
By the power of that gift, she shall never have empty hands;
she is Satī, Śacī, Svāhā, Sāvitrī, Bhūḥ, Arundhatī,
and Śrī— wherever she dwells, nothing there is difficult to obtain.
"O Kunteya, with this very pot that has been filled, you shall feed this entire world; what need is there for these brahmins?
Having heard this from Maitreya, his mind was filled with great joy.
"O lotus-eyed one, previously in the forest I fed many brahmins;
in connection with that gift of food, this gift of a cooking vessel was mentioned by me. It should be forgiven by you without resentment."

"O Kṛṣṇa, for those who give to the twice-born a large-mouthed vessel filled with rice and made of sweet copper, even while it is being consumed by their friends, kinsmen, and Brahmins, that gift does not go to ruin. Thus ends the one hundred and seventieth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Gift of a Vessel," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
The description of the ritual for the gift of female and male slaves.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O destroyer of enemies, I shall now describe to you the gift of female and male slaves.
Out of devotion and affection for you, whatever has been said by anyone anywhere—that among the four stages of life the householder is indeed declared the best;
that the home is better than the householder; and that excellent women are superior to the home—[is true].
That house where women with faces like the orb of the full moon and full, uplifted breasts— women adorned by their virtuous character— are seen;
where sisters-in-law are honored, there the gods rejoice.
That house where these women are not honored will quickly perish;
those households which the female relatives curse when they are not properly worshipped go to ruin instantly, as if struck by a magical spell.
By whom were women created? They are like jars of nectar, like heaps of happiness, and like treasuries of delight.
Dark-complexioned, with slow and graceful gait, they possess full and elevated breasts.
In every house there are no noble wives nor excellent women;
there is no gold, no female slaves, little food, no clarified butter, and no milk products.
The home of those who live as misers is but another form of hell.
A village without a magistrate, a house without female slaves,
and food without ghee— such things are, in my opinion, in vain.
A house that is attended by female slaves adorned with wealth and ornaments [is truly a home].
There dwells Lakṣmī, the lotus-handed one who resides in the Ocean of Milk;
yet that house where there is no purity, no happiness born of worldly conduct, or even a single servant,
is always unsettled.
Where there is no female servant who always performs all tasks,
even a hundred male servants cannot achieve that same degree of auspiciousness,
which a single female slave hired by the householder can accomplish.

For one whose intellect is occupied with the Dharma, what cause for agitation can there be in a mind that is already agitated by the world? For him whose village is crowded with many people, whose house is filled with male and female servants,
and whose household duties are efficiently managed by wives who are devoted to their service— what anxiety remains?
Servants who are ever intent on exertion are seen there [in that state], and the sacred tradition declares:
"Whatever is most desired in this world, that should be given.
Having reflected upon this in one's heart, a female slave should be given to a twice-born man.
Sages praise the time for giving when the moon is conjoined with a fixed asterism (sthira-nakṣatra) and accompanied by benefic planets, or again on a festival day (parvan);
having adorned [the recipient] according to one's ability with garments and ornaments.
O Kaurava, she should be given to the Brahmin with this mantra:
"O Blessed One, this slave girl is offered by me to you;
she is to be employed for work or fed as you wish. May it be well with you."
Having given [the gift], one should afterwards ask the Brahmin for forgiveness with gold;
having followed him as far as the door of his house, one should then bid him farewell.
According to this procedure, one should give [the gift] after having marked it in the temple of the deity.

O Great King, what fruit is obtained by men, O Pārtha, when they give a young woman endowed with beauty who performs all household tasks, whether at a famous sacrifice or in a shelter? How could that even be described?
He who, having observed a maidservant who is highly skilled in household duties, gives her to a Brāhmaṇa of noble birth and virtuous character,

becomes honored even by hundreds of lords of the Vidyādharas and goes to the world of the Apsarases who delight the three worlds. Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-first chapter, titled "Description of the Rules for the Gift of a Maidservant," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the Ritual for Providing Water-Sheds.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O son of Devakī, tell me the greatness of providing water-sheds.
"How should it be given? When should it be given? And what is the fruit of that gift?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"When the month of Phālguna has passed and the great festival of Caitra has arrived..."
On an auspicious day proclaimed by the Brahmins, endowed with the strength of the planets and the moon,
the wise man should have a beautiful pavilion constructed, providing dense shade,
either in the center of a city, on a road, or in a waterless wilderness.
In a temple of the deities, or even at the foot of a sacred tree (caityavṛkṣa),
one should cause a magnificent pavilion to be constructed— exceedingly cool, delightful, provided with various seats, sturdy, and capable of withstanding cold winds.
In the midst of that, one should devoutly place beautiful gems and jars,
as well as *akālamūla* and *karakā* fruits wrapped in cloths; then,
a Brāhmaṇa endowed with good character, having been given his appropriate livelihood, [should perform the rite].

One should establish a water-station (prapā) provided with many attendants and sons, wherein one causes men to drink water without weariness. Having constructed such a water-station on an auspicious day according to the prescribed rites, [one attains great merit].
O best of men, at the commencement, one should feed the twice-born according to one's ability;
thereafter, the man should dismiss the Brahmins with this mantra:
"This water for drinking is offered as common to all beings."

"By the giving of this, may the fathers and grandfathers be satisfied. Therefore, water must be offered without fail for four months, or for three fortnights, O Great King; it is the supreme sustenance for living beings."
One should offer [the water] rich in fragrance, delicious, and cool, placed in a beautiful vessel;
it should be given without hesitation, while not looking at the face [of the recipient].
One should cause the feeding of Brahmins to be performed daily for her, according to one's ability.
Listen now to the fruit of merit for him who, according to this rite, gives excellent water that destroys the parching heat of summer:
whatever merit exists in all sacred fords (tīrthas) and whatever fruit exists in all acts of giving.
He attains the fruit of that merit, highly honored by all the gods;
having ascended a celestial chariot (vimāna) resembling the full moon,
he goes to the city of the Lord of Gods (Indra), being worshipped by hosts of apsarases.
For twenty million years, served by yakṣas and gandharvas, he remains there;
then, upon the exhaustion of his merit, having come here, he becomes a twice-born master of the four Vedas.
Thereafter, he attains the supreme state from which a return is difficult to obtain.

By one who is unable to provide a water-station (prapā) but especially desires to attain merit, a "Dharma-pitcher" (dharmaghaṭa)— filled with cool, pure water and its mouth wrapped in a cloth— should be carried daily to the house of a Brāhmaṇa.
O best of men, O descendant of Kuru, the concluding rite (udyāpana) for that very vow should be performed month after month,
dedicated to Śaṅkara, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā, with maṇḍakas, veṣṭikās, and cooked foods that fulfill all desires.
Having sprinkled water with this mantra, the person [should say]:
"This vessel of Dharma (dharmaghaṭa), whose essence is Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, has been given;
by its gift, may my desires be fulfilled."
(Thus ends the mantra for the gift of the Dharma-jar.
Whoever bestows the Dharma-jar according to this rite obtains here the fruit of providing a water-station; of this there is no doubt.
If a person is unable even to give the gift of a Dharma-vessel,
he should daily water the root of an Aśvattha tree with a self-controlled mind,
saying: "May the Blessed Janārdana, who exists in the form of the Aśvattha, be pleased with me."
Having uttered this and offered salutations, whoever daily performs the watering at the root of the tree for four months as a destroyer of sins,
he too attains that same fruit; such is the eternal Vedic revelation.

"He whose water-station (*prapā*)—containing sweet, cool water that dispels fatigue—is situated at the edge of a city on a road frequented by throngs of travelers, and which is enjoyed by all people; indeed, such a person lives as one preeminent in righteousness (*dharmottara*) in this world of living beings.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-second chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Gift of a Water-Station," in the *Uttara-parvan* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the Rules for Giving the Agniṣṭikā:
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
How should the agniṣṭikā be given during the winter by those who fear the cold?
With minds made compassionate for the sake of benefiting all beings, Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O Pārtha, I shall describe the Agniṣṭikā; learn it from me."
In accordance with the ritual procedure by which it bestows happiness upon all sentient beings,
one should first, on an auspicious day in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa,
have a beautiful and pleasant fire-altar constructed, provided with a comfortable seat.
In a temple courtyard, on a path, in a house, or in a spacious square,
having piled up a heap of wood until it is thoroughly dry at both twilights,
one should then kindle the fire, making oblations with the Vyāhṛtis in their proper order.
Having offered oblations according to this rite, one should thereafter kindle the fire every day.
If anyone should be there seeking food, one should provide him with nourishment;
thus the person sitting there becomes comfortable, free from cold, and likewise free from fever.
O Pārtha, those stories that one tells cannot possibly be recounted by me—
whether they be news of kings or news of common folk— if some person, sitting at ease, should speak them according to his own desire, no one can prevent him.
O King, listen to me as I describe the meritorious fruit for that man who, according to this rite, should offer an *agnīṣṭikā* fire-altar:
he shall ascend a magnificent celestial chariot, resplendent like the sun.
For sixty thousand and sixty hundred years,
he is honored in the world of Brahmā, exceedingly joyful and supremely happy;
and when he descends to this world, he becomes a twice-born man learned in the four Vedas.
Free from disease, a performer of sacrificial sessions (*satrayājī*), and endowed with splendor like fire itself—

those who provide a beautiful fire-pit (*agnīṣṭikā*) rich in fuel at a sanctuary, a temple courtyard, an assembly hall, or a dwelling, obtain for themselves a kindling of the bodily fire that brings comfort to people during the winter and early spring seasons. Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-third chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for Giving Fire-Pits," in the *Uttara-parvan* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the Ritual for the Gift of Knowledge.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O learned one, I have heard from you about the many kinds of gifts, including the gift of cows."
The greatness and the ritual procedure for the gift of land have been understood.
Now, O tiger among the Yadus, I desire to hear that which is the ritual procedure for the gift of knowledge; tell me that, O Janārdana.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O descendant of Kuru, I shall now describe to you, exactly as it is, the procedure for the gift of knowledge (vidyādāna), how it should be given, and what fruit is obtained by its bestowal.
On an auspicious day declared by the Brahmins, one should have a beautiful, divine mandala made with cow dung, square on all sides,
covered with a profusion of flowers, and adorned with svastikas and other designs.
Having placed the book there, one should worship it with perfumes and flowers.
A golden pen should be prepared, along with a silver ink-pot.
After honoring the scribe, the wise person should cause the commencement of the writing.
From that time forth, the scribe was disciplined and vigilant;
he wrote with the correct measures and nasalizations, accompanied by the proper division of words,
with even characters, uniform heads, and well-rounded, thick strokes.
One should have the letters written here with an inner self absorbed in that [task],
having completed that scripture— whether it be Śaiva or Vaiṣṇava.
Once it has been completed, the scribe is then to be honored with garments and ornaments.
Having honored that scripture, it should then be given to one who possesses virtuous qualities,
to one who knows the true essence of the scripture, and to a reciter who speaks pleasantly.
One should present the book wrapped in a pair of garments.
Or else, one should establish it as common property for all people in a monastery.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, listen as I declare to you the fruit that a man obtains by giving according to this rite.
Whatever merit is gained from a pilgrimage to sacred fords, and likewise whatever merit belongs to those who perform sacrifices—
a man obtains that merit multiplied ten millionfold through the gift of knowledge.
Whatever fruit results from the perfect donation of a thousand tawny cows (kapilā), [that too he obtains].
The giver of a book attains that very fruit. O Pārtha, who can describe the fruit that one obtains by giving away a Purāṇa, the Bhārata, or even the Rāmāyaṇa?

Who is as meritorious as he who, having risen at dawn, diligently instructs his disciples in the Vedas, the Shastras, dance, and song? That person who provides a livelihood for his teacher while teaching him is truly blessed.

What could possibly remain ungiven by that man who perceives the goals of Dharma, Artha, and Kāma? By providing students with food, oil for massage, clothing, or even alms, a person attains all desires; of this there is no doubt.
Discrimination is long life; it is the perfection of virtue, pleasure, and wealth.
By providing nourishment for students, one has effectively given everything.
Whether it be scripture, the arts of weaponry, or craftsmanship—whatever one wishes to acquire [is obtained through this].
O Pārtha, one’s mind should always be intent upon performing acts of service for him.
There is no doubt that through the gift of knowledge one obtains the same fruit as that which results from a thousand Vājapeya sacrifices properly performed.
In a temple of Śiva, a house of Viṣṇu, or likewise in a shrine of the Sun,
that righteous-souled person who always causes the recitation of books to be performed [shall gain merit].
Cows, land, gold, garments, beds, and seats—
O bull of the Bharatas, by that [gift], daily offerings are made on his behalf;
for a man devoid of knowledge does not distinguish between righteousness and unrighteousness.
Therefore, one who is ever righteous should be devoted to the gift of knowledge.
The three worlds, the four castes, and the four stages of life separately;
all the deities beginning with Brahmā— O Indra among kings, these are established upon the gift of knowledge throughout the seventy-one cycles of the four yugas.
He shall dwell for a kalpa in the city of Viṣṇu, being honored by the best of the gods;
or, returning to earth at the end of time, he becomes a righteous king,
rich in gifts of elephants, horses, and chariots, a donor, an enjoyer, and free from envy.
Endowed with beauty and good fortune, one shall be long-lived and free from disease;

surrounded by sons and grandsons, one shall live for a hundred autumns. In this world, there is no gift that yields such exceptional fruit as knowledge—which dwells within the lotus of the mouth—apart from that. O Pārtha, what is there in this world that would not be considered given by those who bestow upon others all things, including cows, land, gold, elephants, horses, and chariots? If they give that [knowledge], everything else has already been given.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Procedure for the Gift of Knowledge," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira. [Now follows] the description of the procedure for the gift of the *Tulāpuruṣa*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
In ancient times, King Priyavrata, the son of Svāyambhuva Manu,
protected the earth like another Prajāpati;
having ruled this earth for thirty thousand years.

Having divided the seven islands among his sons, that powerful lord bestowed them upon his children; having established his seven sons in the kingdoms over the seven islands and withdrawn from all worldly objects, he went to the forest for asceticism.
Having heard that the king of supreme luster had gone to the forest of asceticism,
high-souled sages, desiring to see him, gathered there.
Seeing those sages who had arrived, their impurities washed away by austerity—
The wise one honored them with rites prescribed by rule—
offering water for the feet, the arghya, and water for sipping, along with pleasant inquiries and replies—
and then, when those high-souled Brahmins had taken their seats.
The highly effulgent Pulastya, the son of Brahmā, arrived;
blazing with great splendor like a second sun (or fire).
Seeing him, all the sages and that king, the great chariot-warrior, [stood there].
Then they all rose up, filled with wonder, their eyes wide open;
having conversed with him and performed the appropriate rites according to tradition,
they offered him a seat, as well as water for his feet, the arghya offering, and water for sipping.
Then all the sages, seated at their ease,
joyfully engaged in various discourses based on the teachings of the Vedas. Then, at the conclusion of one such discourse, those sages, together with the king, [proceeded].
Desiring the welfare of the worlds, the sages questioned the son of Brahmā.
The sages said:
"O Blessed One, by what gift, by what vow, or by what observance [does one attain this]?"
"O best of sages, both men and women attain a good state of existence;
we wish to hear this from you, as does this king who is firm in his vows.
Pulastya said:
Listen, all you sages, to this secret that destroys sins;
I shall declare to you the collection of all supreme gifts,
by giving which even a slayer of a Brahmin, a killer of a cow, a murderer of a father, or one who violates the teacher’s bed [is purified].
An ungrateful person and a false witness are both liberated from their sin;
they immediately attain divine bodies, as do women likewise,
through penances such as the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa, and those known as the Tulāpuruṣa.
Desiring the station of Brahman, one should purify the body through vows;
O best of sages, vows such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* are for Brāhmaṇas, forest-dwellers, mendicants, and widows alike.
Those [perfections] are certainly not accomplished by bodily mortification among householders;
nor is dharma ever praised as being achievable through hardship for those people who possess great wealth, such as kings and those partaking in jewels.
That which is called "wealth" consists of these vital breaths that move externally;
therefore, the wise should always unite the Self with the externally moving breaths.
In this world, gold is the best of all substances, as it fulfills all desires.
The eldest son of Vibhāvasu, the chief of the gods, is thus; he who,
being self-restrained, weighs himself against him with the wise,
shall instantly cast off all sins and become possessed of a divine body.
"O best of kings, this was related by the sage Pulastya to the ṛṣis and to the kings; and from them, O best of men, it was heard by me. Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Supreme Lord, O Illustrious One, out of compassion for me, your devotee, please describe the procedure for the gift of the Tulāpuruṣa.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen attentively, O King,
as I describe to you the procedure for the gift known as the Tulāpuruṣa, O best of monarchs:
during a Vyatīpāta yoga, at the solstices, on the full moon of Kārtika, and likewise at the equinoxes.
O best of kings, this should be given whenever there is an eclipse of the moon or sun, or on the full moon day of Māgha;
likewise during planetary afflictions at one's birth star, upon seeing an evil dream,
or whenever wealth happens to arise.
"Since life is impermanent and the body is exceedingly fickle,
one should practice the Dharma while still being seized by the hair by Death.
Therefore, O Lord, at whatever moment faith toward giving may arise," so it was said.
At that very moment, it should be the time for giving, for that is my purpose.
Whether at a sacred ford, in a temple, in cow-pens, or even in the courtyard of one's home,
a wise and learned man should have a pavilion constructed with four auspicious faces.
One should cause a divine, firm pavilion to be constructed, provided with fresh branches, sloping toward the east and north,
measuring sixteen cubits in size, and adorned with banners;
in its center, one should have a beautiful altar made, one cubit in height.
It should be square, measuring seven cubits on all sides, and very beautiful.
In its center, the wise man should install a divine scale according to the prescribed rite; he should bury two cubits [of it] and have it rise four cubits high.
O Great King, one should firmly establish two new pillars.
Sandalwood, Khadira, Bilva, Śāka, and likewise Iṅguda;
Tiṇḍuka, Devadāru, and Śrīparṇa is remembered as the eighth.

Thus, these eight types of trees are proclaimed as suitable for pillars; otherwise, there may be other trees as well, provided they are known to have core wood and are fit for sacrifice. Then, having made it perfectly steady, one should place a horizontal beam upon it.
One should place a beam of that same species, measuring four cubits in length;
one should then firmly attach a balance of the same species in its center.
The divine iron hook should be complete, measuring ninety-six finger-breadths.
One should also fashion two ears for it made of black iron;
in the middle, there should be a man fashioned as the one known as Tulāpuruṣa.
Having thus constructed the balance adorned with various jewels, [one should proceed].
Her limbs were anointed with sandalwood paste, and her body was adorned with garments and ornaments;
the two pillars were likewise draped in cloth, hung with flower garlands,
their surfaces anointed with sandalwood and decorated with various jewels.
One should have four fire-pits constructed here, provided with wombs (yonis) and measuring one cubit in size, each possessing three girdles (mekhalās).
To the northeast, a very beautiful altar (vedi) measuring one cubit should be made.
And there, O King, worship of the planetary deities of the world-protectors (lokapāla) is prescribed;
likewise, the honoring of Viriñci and Acyuta,
as well as the ritual for Śaṅkara, should be performed there with garlands, garments, fruits, and unbroken grains (akṣata).
Toranas should be constructed from the wood of milk-exuding trees (kṣīravṛkṣa).
At the four gates, water-pots (kumbhas) should be placed, adorned with garlands and sprouts,
filled with the five jewels (pañcaratna), and set upon heaps of the seven grains (saptadhānya).
One should appoint two reciters of the Ṛgveda at the eastern pit;
those learned in the Yajurveda at the southern; those versed in the Sāmaveda at the western;
those of the Atharvaveda at the northern; and the ninth, the teacher of Dharma, [at the center].
On this very occasion, some sages maintain that sixteen officiating priests (ṛtvij) should be invited;
a pair of copper vessels and a seat should be given to each one,
as well as all materials for the fire-oblation (homa), namely sesame seeds, clarified butter, and sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh).
Sruva-ladles, sruc-ladles, ritual weapons, grass seats, and flowers; golden Lokapālas and auspicious banners all around;
and one should fasten a great five-colored banner and a canopy.
Having gathered all this together on an auspicious day, the wise architect,
an expert in all crafts, should, along with the Brahmins,
show the completed sacrificial pavilion to the patron.
Then the wise sacrificer, pure and wearing white garments,
should cast the offering for the world-protectors with these auspicious mantras, accompanied by the sound of conchs and trumpets and the resonance of Vedic chanting.
Come, come, O Lord of the Immortals, wielder of the vajra, praised by all the gods, siddhas, and sādhakas!
Being fanned by a host of apsarases, O Blessed One, protect our sacrifice; homage to you!
(Oṃ, homage to Indra).
Come, come, O bearer of oblations for all the immortals, with a heart gladdened by the foremost of sages;
together with the radiant host of worlds, protect my sacrifice, O Sage—salutations to you!
(Oṃ, obeisance to Agni.)
Come, come, O Vaivasvata, King of Dharma, you whose divine form is worshipped by all the immortals!
O Lord of those who experience the joy of good and evil deeds, protect my sacrifice; O Blessed One, salutations to you!
Om, obeisance to Yama.
Come, come! You are the leader of the hosts of *rakṣasas*, together with vast multitudes of *vetālas* and *piśācas*.
Protect my sacrifice, O Lord of the *piśācas*; you are the Sovereign of the World, O Blessed One, homage to you!
*Oṃ nirṛtaye namaḥ*.
Come, come, O Parjanya, together with the host of ocean-dwelling aquatic creatures and the Apsarases!
O Blessed One, praised by the lords of the Vidyādharas and the immortals, protect us; salutations to you!
(Oṃ, salutations to Varuṇa.)
Come, come to my sacrifice for its protection, mounted upon your deer, together with the hosts of Siddhas!
O Lord of Life, ally of Kālakavi, accept this worship; O Blessed One, salutations to you!
(Oṃ, obeisance to Vāyu.)
Come, come, O Lord of Sacrifice! Perform the protection of the sacrifice together with the host of constellations.
Together with all medicinal herbs and the ancestors, accept this worship; O Blessed One, salutations to you!
(Oṃ, salutations to Soma.)
Come, come, O Lord of All, whose form is the universe, together with the world that bears the trident and the skull-topped staff!
O Lord of Beings, accept this worship for the success of the sacrifice; O Blessed One, salutations to you!
(Salutation to Īśāna.)

Come, come, O Ananta, Lord of the Earth and the Netherworld, whose praises are sung by the wives of the Nāgas and the Kinnaras; together with the hosts of Yakṣas, lords of serpents, and the gods, protect our sacrifice! (Oṃ, obeisance to Ananta.)
Come, come, O Lord of the Universe, Sovereign of Sages, Lord of the World, together with the ancestral deities!
Enter the conclusion of this sacrifice for eternal auspiciousness; you are the Grandfather, and I bow to you eternally.
(Oṃ, salutation to Brahmā.)
Whatever beings there are in the three worlds, both stationary and moving— may they, together with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, grant me protection.
May the gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and pannagas [likewise protect me].
"May the sages, the Manus, the cows,
and the divine mothers all joyfully provide protection for my sacrifice.
Having thus invoked the deities, one should give neck-ornaments to the officiating priests (ṛtvij).
One should give double to the preceptor: golden earrings, threads, bracelets, as well as finger-rings, garments, flowers, ornaments, coverings, and so forth.
Having first offered the two *āghāra* libations and the two *ājyabhāga* portions,
the wise one should perform the oblation for the deities established herein; this oblation is said to consist of their own names preceded by the syllable *praṇava* (*om*) and ending with *svāhā*.

An oblation (homa) should be performed according to one's desire for the planets, the world-protectors (lokapālas), as well as for Śiva and Keśava; for the lords of the forest (vanaspati), and for Brahmā.
Then, accompanied by auspicious sounds and Vedic benedictions, [the image] is installed.
Having circumambulated three times from left to right and holding a handful of flowers, and having put on white garlands and garments, he should consecrate that scale with the mantra:
"Salutations to you; you are the power of all the gods, established in truth."
O Sustainer of the World, you were created by the Source of the Universe as a witness;
you have been established for the welfare of the world in the midst of those who uphold dharma and adharma, with all truths on one side and hundreds of falsehoods likewise on the other.
O Tula, you are proclaimed here as the standard of measure for all beings;
weighing me, lift me up from this cycle of existence—salutations to you!
He who is the Lord of Reality, the God, the Puruṣa, the twenty-fifth principle—
O Goddess, he alone is established in you; therefore, salutations, salutations!
Salutations, salutations to you, O Govinda, known as Tulāpuruṣa!
O Hari, deliver us from this ocean of saṃsāra.
Then, having reached an auspicious time and performed this preliminary consecration (adhivāsana),
the wise man, having bowed with supreme devotion,
should ascend that scale while clad in a coat of mail made of leather and adorned with all his ornaments.
Then, taking Dharmarāja together with the golden Sun,
he sat gazing at the face of Hari with his two hands clenched in fists;
likewise, holding Yama on his left and the Sun on his right.
Then, O lord of men, other eminent brahmins should place upon the other side of the scale as much extremely pure gold as equals or exceeds [the weight of the body].
One who desires prosperity, however, should have it placed upon the ground.
Having remained there for a mere moment, one should then utter this again:
"Salutations to you, the eternal witness of all beings;
O Goddess, you were created by the Grandfather, the Supreme Lord."
"The entire world, together with all things mobile and immobile, has been uplifted by you.
O you who abide as the self of all beings, salutations to you, the sustainer of the universe!
Then, having descended, one should offer half of everything to the preceptor."
He should give the other half to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), preceded by the pouring of water;
or, having obtained their permission, he may likewise cause it to be given to others as well. He should honor the poor, the helpless, the distinguished, and so forth, together with the Brahmins.
A wise person should not keep gold that has been consecrated by sprinkling in his house for long,
because its presence brings fear and may cause painful diseases; yet,
by taking possession of another's property for a single night, one attains unsurpassed prosperity.

By this very same procedure, some desire it to be made of silver; likewise, certain eminent brahmins desire it to be made of camphor. Similarly, on the third day of the dark fortnight, women whose good fortune is increased [should perform it].
They offer [the gift] with saffron, salt, and molasses;
in this case, there are no mantras nor any fire-oblation (homa). One should cause it to be given in this very manner.
Whoever, being composed, should give this gift according to this rite—
O King, listen as I describe the fruit of his merit:
whether it be a woman or even a man, having ascended an excellent celestial chariot crowded with throngs of Apsarases and resembling a city of the Gandharvas, he shall travel.
It was delightful, crowded with various trees, and perfumed with diverse fragrances;
its body was inlaid with many jewels and hung with strings of pearls;
it was filled with couches and seats and adorned with banners.
Having ascended such a celestial chariot— which resounds with the ringing of a hundred bells, is provided with yak-tail fans,
grants pleasure in all seasons, is delightful, and is free from all suffering—
one shall go to the world of the Sun.
Having gone there, O Indra among kings, he remains free from disease for one kalpa;
likewise for a kalpa in the world of Viṣṇu, and similarly in the world of Śiva,
as well as in the city of the King of Gods, the Lord of all the gods.
Having dwelt in the city of Dharmarāja, as well as in that of Varuṇa and in the city of Dhanada,
for a hundred times ten million kalpas,
a man returns again to the human state and becomes a righteous king.
He who is a performer of sacrifices, a lord of charity, wise, and the destroyer of the enemy faction—
he who hears this glorification of great gifts with devotion shall also be liberated from the threefold sin; of this there is no doubt.
There is no one superior to Brahmā, Śiva, and Keśava to be worshipped; there is no sacrifice equal to the Aśvamedha;
there is no sacred ford (tīrtha) in the three worlds equal to the Gaṅgā; and there is no other gift here equal to the Tulāpuruṣa.
