Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Tulāpuruṣa Gift," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the Hiraṇyagarbha Dāna Vow.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of all beings, saluted by all beings!"
For the benefit of the worlds, tell me something further:
O Lord of Gods, tell me that gift or even that vow by which one becomes equal to you in longevity, fame, and prosperity.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O King, I shall declare for the sake of your desire for the welfare of the world that means by which human beings on earth may become equal to Me.

This world of mine, which is difficult even for the gods to attain, is not reached by means of vows or fasts, nor by pilgrimages to sacred sites, nor by deaths on the Great Path (Mahāpatha) and the like, nor by sacrifices, nor by Vedic learning.
"O illustrious one, out of affection for Pārtha, I shall tell you what is for your benefit:
that wise man who meets death for the sake of cows and Brahmins,
or who practices fasting at Prayāga, or who worships Śaṅkara," [shall attain the highest goal].
One attains the same world as Brahman; this is the eternal Vedic revelation.
Hereafter, I shall tell you that by which one attains equality with Me.
Listen to me as I describe the gift known as Hiraṇyagarbha.
Gold is declared here to be the first offspring of Agni;
it is the purifier of all beings, the supreme and great means of purification. Its universal synonym is said to be *hiraṇya*.
Having entered the womb of the waters and being born again upon the earth,
he who gives that [gift] to a Brāhmaṇa is indeed born equal to me.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Lord of Gods, O Eternal One, tell me its ritual procedure; O Supreme Lord, what is its measure and how it is to be given?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Mahāmati, this gift should be bestowed on auspicious festival days (parva),
during the solstices, at the equinoxes, during the eclipses of the moon and sun,
during the Vyatīpāta yoga, on the full moon day of Kārttika, or on one's own birth star, O best of men.
Indeed, upon seeing an evil dream, or when afflicted by the influence of the planets,
one should go to Prayāga, Naimiṣa, Kurukṣetra, and Arbuda;
likewise to the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, and the confluence of the Sindhu and the ocean.
And in this act of giving, meritorious rivers are undoubtedly praised;
O King, whether it be in one's own house, in a temple,
in a grove, by a pond, or in any pure place according to the prescribed rite.
There, one should perform the purification of the ground, which should be auspiciously sloping toward the east and north.
A very beautiful pavilion measuring twelve cubits should be constructed,
provided with charming pillars and appropriately fitted with moist branches.
In the center of that, one should construct an altar five cubits in size and well-adorned;
above it, a canopy should be suspended with garlands of flowers.
On the first day, one should fashion the Hiraṇyagarbha image in its midst.
I shall describe its measurement and the form arising from the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila).
First, one should worship the artisan with garments and ornaments;
afterwards, one should cause the Brāhmaṇas to recite benedictions, and then one should commence the rite.
A wise person should have it fashioned from well-purified gold according to their capacity;
its length is proclaimed to be sixty-four finger-breadths,
while at the mouth it is reduced by one-third, and at the base its width is half that.
It should be circular, shaped like a lotus seed-vessel (karṇikā), and free from beautiful knots;
a lid should be made above it, exceeding [the base] by one finger-breadth.
One should fashion ten weapons, a stalk, and a solar disc out of gold.
One should provide a sickle with a ribbon and all necessary implements, as well as needles and razors— all these made of gold;
one should place a golden staff and a water-pot by its side.
Having fashioned a pair of small parasols and sandals adorned with diamonds and lapis lazuli,
and having thus endowed the interior with these characteristics, the wise man [should perform the rite] with a great sound of Vedic chanting and the resonance of conchs and trumpets.
O King, having prepared an elephant, a cart, or a brahmin’s chariot, one should bring [the image] to the pavilion, circumambulating it without weariness; then,
placed upon a drona-measure of sesame seeds in the center of the altar, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana).
Having again anointed everything with fragrant saffron,
he should then clothe him in two bright silken garments.
The wise man should then worship him with devotion on all sides with garlands of flowers.
Having thoroughly perfumed it with incenses, one should utter this mantra:
"The worlds, beginning with Bhūrloka, are situated within your womb;
likewise are the gods, headed by Brahmā. Salutations to you, O Source of the Universe!"
Salutations to you, O support of the worlds; salutations to you, O Lord of the worlds.
Salutations to Hiraṇyagarbha, within whose womb resides the Grandfather (Brahmā). Having thus worshipped them, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) for that night.
One should arrange sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) on all four sides of the altar;
four of them should be square, and within them the fire-oblation (homa) is prescribed.
There, four Brahmins who have mastered the mantras should serve as the officiants.
All of them, having conquered their selves and observing silence, should perform the fire sacrifice (homa).
Adorned with all ornaments and all wearing new garments,
they should be provided with two copper vessels and worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
On the north-eastern portion of the sacrificial altar (vedī), one should prepare the altar for the planets (grahavedī).
There, one should worship the planets, the world-protectors (lokapālas), and Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—
represented by images fashioned of gold— with flowers, incense, and unguents.
Having adorned the pavilion with banners as well as archways,
one should place two jars filled with jewels at the entrances;
and with the mantras of the Tulāpuruṣa rite, one should offer the bali-oblation to the world-protectors (Lokapālas).
In that rite of oblation, fuel-sticks of *pālāśa* wood are recommended;
likewise, there should be *caru* dedicated to Indra, sesame seeds, and cow’s ghee.
First, a man should offer these with his own specific mantras and with the *vyāhṛti* syllables.
The wise have declared that the number of oblations for the fire-sacrifice is twenty thousand.
Then, having bathed, wearing white garments, and being pure,
the sacrificer should worship Hiraṇyagarbha with devotion at the time of the festival.
Salutations to Hiraṇyagarbha, salutations indeed to the Womb of the Universe;
salutations to you who have become the abode of the world of moving and unmoving beings.
O best of Asuras, I was previously born from Māyā and am subject to the nature of mortals.
"By the birth of your offspring today, I shall become possessed of a divine body.
Having uttered this and having himself performed a circumambulation with devotion,
the wise man should enter that womb which is filled with milk, clarified butter, and curd.
Then, having placed a golden image of Dharmarāja in his left hand and the Sun-god in his right, and having carefully formed a fist,
he should place his head between his knees with a concentrated mind.
One should remain for five breaths meditating on Śiva with the mind.
Then those eminent twice-born ones should perform for Hiraṇyagarbha the rites of conception (garbhādhāna), the rite for a male child (puṃsavana), and the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana).
They should perform the birth-rites and the other sixteen ceremonies.
Then, having risen and departed, he should again perform a circumambulation.
O best of kings, until then, he must not look upon the face of anyone.
Until the golden earth has been seen with clear eyes,
one should then perform a ritual bath preceded by the chanting of the Vedas (*brahmaghoṣa*).
Eight twice-born men, their limbs adorned with gold, [should do so] with auspicious golden jars.
With jars made of silver, or of udumbara wood, or of beautiful clay—
possessing limbs variegated with curds and unbroken grains, adorned with mango sprouts,
their necks encircled by flowers, and being firm and free from cracks.
Having established an excellent, unblemished pedestal in the center of the fourfold area,
O highly fortunate ones, the best of the twice-born should place the patron there and perform his consecration with the mantra "devasya tvā."
"Today we shall consecrate the limbs of you who have been born;
with this divine body, may you live long and be happy.
Having thus performed the consecration, the sacrificer remains composed.
One should offer that Hiraṇyagarbha with the hand itself while holding water;
having honored them with devotion, or by his command to many others,
one should present all the sacrificial implements to the Guru.
Sandals, shoes, an umbrella, a fly-whisk, and a vessel— these,
as well as gifts specifically for other Brahmins who are members of the assembly there, should be bestowed.
One should give all that is desired to the poor, the blind, and the miserable;
a food-charity (annasatra) should be established for as long as the acceptance of gifts continues.
He who bestows this gift according to this rule—
He shall deliver his entire family and go to the world of the gods,
having ascended an excellent celestial chariot five yojanas in width,
adorned with ponds, wells, lakes, and other reservoirs of water.
It was filled with hundreds of gardens, frequented by lotus ponds,
crowded with hundreds of palaces, and attended by hundreds of excellent women;
that great city resounded, filled with the sounds of lutes, flutes, and drums.
O Indra among kings, its floors were divine, auspicious, and made of jewels;
it was adorned with variegated altars and possessed the radiance of the sun;
well-constructed by Viśvakarman, it was supported by a thousand pillars.
Adorned with various colorful banners and vajras,
he ascends that foremost of celestial chariots accompanied by hosts of vidyādharas;
he goes to the world of Śakra and rejoices together with Śakra.
When a hundred manvantaras have passed, he is born on the land of action (karmabhūmi);
possessing divine prowess, he enjoys the entirety of Jambūdvīpa.
He is righteous, truthful in character, devoted to Brahman, and affectionate toward his gurus.
For ten births, that king is born free from disease;
and whoever hears this secret, which destroys sin, with devotion,
he too is honored in the world of the gods for more than a hundred years.
Having duly entered the golden womb, his body consecrated by the purificatory rites, he emerges from it once again;
having offered that to the best of the twice-born with devotion, he shines in a divine body like the sun in the sky.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Gift of the Golden Womb," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the Ritual for the Gift of the Cosmic Egg (Brahmāṇḍa).
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"In ancient times, Agastya proclaimed this supreme procedure for gifts."
Listen, O tiger among kings, as I now relate that by which,
when given, O lord of kings, one dispels every sin—
whether mental, verbal, or physical, and however difficult to overcome.
Auspicious, auspicious, meritorious, and the best among all gifts;
it is conducive to wealth, fame, and long life, and it removes the fear of the next world.
Having fashioned a golden Brahmāṇḍa endowed with all auspicious characteristics, [one should offer it].
It was joined by gods, asuras, and humans, as well as by gandharvas, uragas, and rākṣasas;
it was likewise filled with rivers, oceans, and mountains,
adorned with hundreds of millions of celestial chariots and the finest of apsarases.
O King, one should conceive of the fourteen worlds upon the body of that [liṅga], which is joined by the eight elephants of the quarters, has four faces situated in the center,
and is endowed with Śiva, Acyuta, Ārkaśikhara, Umā,
and Lakṣmī.
One should fashion it with a length and width of one hundred finger-breadths (vitasti-aṅgula),
made of two pieces joined together in the form of a hollow vessel (puṭa), well-fitted, out of twenty palas up to a thousand, according to one's devotion.
Since this universe, which grants all desires, was fashioned by the artisan [Viśvakarman],
one who is endowed with faith and wealth should [worship] during the solstices, the equinoxes, lunar and solar eclipses, and indeed at other times as well.
Having constructed a pavilion of flowers, the wise man should install [the image] there,
placed upon a drona-measure of sesame seeds, smeared with powdered saffron,
covered with a pair of garments, and perfumed with flowers and incense.
In all directions of that [site], he should place full jars;
furthermore, he should bring eighteen others, each measuring one *droṇa*.
The wise man should install them either in the house or in the pavilion.
One should have it provided there with sandals, shoes, an umbrella, a vessel, a seat, and a mirror,
as well as a milch cow; and one should likewise have a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) made,
measuring one cubit, according to the prescribed rule.
There, the best of the twice-born, well-bathed, wearing clean garments and adorned with all ornaments, should perform the fire-oblation in four turns; the brahmins,
accompanied by their preceptor, should proceed there.
Likewise, the royal priest is ordained as the sixth;
however, the others, five in number, should perform the sacrifice without weariness.
According to the ritual procedure for the sacrifice to the planets, the worship of the planets is thus prescribed.
O King, one should offer sesame seeds into the fire in the names of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva;
thereafter, one should perform ten thousand oblations with the Mahāvyāhṛtis.
Immediately following that, the twice-born should perform the recitation of the Rudra-mantra.
Then, when everything has been completed, having bathed and being pure, clad in white garments, one should worship the Brahmāṇḍa with devotion while holding a handful of flowers:
"Salutations to the foundation of the universe; salutations be to You, the abode of all."
O Creator of the auspiciousness of the universe, become the source of welfare for me who am immersed in the depths of speech;
may all those beings whatsoever that dwell within the belly of the universe always grant me incomparable satisfaction.
May Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, as well as the guardians of the world, the planets,
the lunar mansions, the serpents, the sages, and the Maruts—
all of them remain satisfied with me for seven future births.
Having uttered this, one should then present the Brahmāṇḍa, which grants all desires;
having provided it with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), one should satisfy the twice-born with wealth.
O best of men, whatever merit may arise from giving according to this rite—

I shall relate that to you; listen as I speak, O Bhārata. In the first age, there was a king named Sudyumna, glorious and possessing the strength of ten thousand elephants, who maintained a vast retinue of servants and attendants.
Having ruled a kingdom free from thorns for thirty thousand years,
the king then installed his son upon the throne and departed for the forest.
Having entered the formidable forest, he indeed performed intense austerities.
Having mastered the reality of the internal state and having cast aside the ritualistic section of the Vedas,
the king in former times met his destined end after a long time;
he ascended a divine celestial chariot resounding with the noise of various musical instruments.
Having passed beyond the world of Śakra and other realms, he went from here to the world of Brahmā.
Then Brahmā, surrounded by hosts of gods and asuras, offered him a seat that was divine,
with limbs variegated with gold and a form adorned with jewels.
Thus, O best of kings,
he remained delighting in that supreme world day after day, yet devoid of divine enjoyments;
as that king lived there, his body was tormented with heat.
O best of men, being thus afflicted by hunger and extreme thirst, he addressed Brahmā with palms joined in reverence:
"O Blessed One, this world of Brahmā is free from all defects."
"O Lord, even as I remain here, hunger and thirst afflict me.
By the ripening of what karma does this hunger not depart from me? Even though I have gone to the world of Brahmā, you ought to sever my doubt."
Brahmā said:
"O King, while you were ruling the kingdom, your limbs indeed flourished;
however, being devoted to self-praise, you did not give anything in abundance."
"Considering that giving is of the nature of bondage, you did not give [anything] from that [wealth].
Through knowledge, the state of Brahman was attained; yet due to the lack of giving, hunger afflicts me.
The King said:
"O Blessed One, O Supreme Lord, how may my thirst be dispelled? You should show favor by granting me instruction.
Brahmā said:
"O King, having gone further, bestow upon the foremost of the twice-born the entire earth, which fulfills all desires; by that, you shall attain satisfaction.
Thus addressed, the lord of the earth returned properly to the world of mortals.
Having bestowed the cosmic egg upon the Brahmins according to the prescribed rite,
he returned once more to heaven and attained eternal satisfaction.
Thus, I have explained to you all the fruit that results from this great gift.
He who gives the Brahmāṇḍa has given the entire world of moving and non-moving beings;
by giving it, he delivers his kinsmen— seven generations below, seven above, and seven both above and below— and likewise those yet to come, of this there is no doubt.
He is glorified in the world of Brahmā for thirty-six Manvantaras;
returning once more to the human state, he is born into a righteous family.
He shall experience neither poverty, nor disease, nor even separation from his loved ones.
Whether it be a woman or a man, by the power of this gift,
whoever hears this with devotion or causes it to be heard by devotees, they too attain a good rebirth; how much more so for one who actually bestows it?

Having given two halves of the Cosmic Egg (Brahmāṇḍa), together with the mountain ranges, the oceans, the lakes, and the regions of the quarters inhabited by Siddhas, to the most excellent of the twice-born who possess the virtues [of the directions] according to the number of the directions, a person attains the station of Pitāmaha (Brahmā). Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Gift of the Cosmic Egg," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the Ritual for Bestowing the Kalpavṛkṣa.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
In former times, the Lord Śaṅkara was married by me.
Delighting with her, he remained for many groups of years;
then all the hosts of gods fell into great terror and,
out of fear for their offspring, went to him alone for refuge.
The gods, with Vaiśvānara at their head, [praised] the three-eyed Mahādeva;
and the three-eyed one became gracious toward those deities.
Īśvara said:
"Why are all the thirty gods afraid? What boon shall I grant you? O wise ones, when I am pleased, there is indeed nothing that is difficult to obtain.
The gods said:

O Blessed One, O Śaṅkara, through union with Pārvatī, let [our offspring] be fruitless, O Lord of Gods; we are afraid of your son. And may you remain forever childless, O Lord of Gods, O Master of Beings.
"We are all powerless to sustain your vital energy.
The Blessed Lord said: "From this time forward, O gods, I shall remain established as one whose seed is drawn upward (a celibate)."
"And I shall remain standing like a pillar, and this shall indeed be my name.
Thereupon, Umā became enraged and spoke these words to those gods:
"O Suras, you have rendered my happiness regarding my son futile."
"Therefore, you too shall not procreate sons.
From that time forward, O King, the gods were no longer born.
Having thus bestowed the curse, the Goddess then spoke to Śaṅkara regarding the gods.
"O Lord of the world, I have not yet obtained the birth of a son;
for this Vedic scripture is heard: 'There is no destination for one who is sonless.
Therefore, O illustrious Lord, command that which is beneficial for both worlds."
The Blessed One said:
"O Daughter of the Mountain, whatever man or woman is childless must give a golden Kalpavṛkṣa tree endowed with all virtues."
Or he may adopt even an artificial child, such as a tree or an immobile being; or a son whose father has already died may designate another as his son.
By that act, O Goddess, he attains the worlds of those who possess sons; of this there is no doubt.
The Kalpavṛkṣa (wish-fulfilling tree) should be fashioned from pure gold;
it should have many branches, beautiful golden limbs, and be endowed with numerous flowers.
It should possess the form of a massive trunk, its body adorned with jewels.
One should fashion its fruits as divine and made of gold; O best of kings, one should make them weighing more than twenty palas, or according to one's capacity.
This gift should be bestowed, and likewise, an excellent silver one may be given.
One should fashion four golden trees at the four corners, covered with coral sprouts and draped with strings of pearls;
O fair-faced one, I shall now describe the measurement for the gold.
With a thousand, or half of that, or again half of that [number of bricks], one should have a pavilion constructed there—
either on the bank of a river, in a house, or likewise in a temple—
in a location sloping toward the northeast.
With a measurement of ten cubits, there should be ten altars (vedikās);
and with a measurement of one cubit, one very beautiful sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be constructed in the southeast, O King, along with its girdle (mekhalā) and plastering.
In that regard, Brahmins who recite the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas should be employed;
the instructor himself should be the third or the fifth among them.
They should be adorned with all ornaments and provided with two copper plates.
Anointed with sandalwood paste and adorned with garments, garlands, and other ornaments,
one should place a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpapādapa) upon a prastha measure of jaggery;
it should have five branches, be accompanied by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, and include the Sun-god.
One should place Kāmadeva together with his wife below;
Saṃtāna with Gāyatrī to the east upon salt;
and Mandāra with Śrī likewise to the south on clarified butter.
In the west, however, there is the Pārijāta tree together with Umā;
likewise, on the sesame seeds is Haricandana accompanied by Surabhi,
provided with silken garments and endowed with sugarcane, garlands, and fruits.
Likewise, one should arrange eight full water-pots all around;
having performed the rite of bringing forth the fire and consecrated the trees,
one should likewise arrange all kinds of grain all around.
One should present there all kinds of various foods as an offering;
one should light diverse rows of lamps on all sides,
having employed them with the mantra spoken by me, O lady of beautiful countenance.
"For you are the granter of desires to the gods; therefore, you are remembered as the wish-fulfilling tree (Kāmavṛkṣa).
Being worshipped by me with devotion, fulfill my heart's desires.
Having thus worshipped according to the prescribed rite, one should observe a vigil there.
The Brahmins, with their inner selves absorbed in me, should perform the fire-oblation accompanied by the sounds of conch-trumpets blended with the resonance of the Vedas;
the wise one, having first offered the two libations of clarified butter (āghāra) and the two portions of ghee (ājyabhāga).
Then, one should nourish the deities installed by means of their respective *liṅgas* through oblations (*homa*).
After that, they should perform the *homa* with the *mahāvyāhṛtis*.
O lady of excellent complexion, success in the sacrifice shall be attained by ten thousand [oblations].

Then, having risen at dawn and bathed, being pure and clad in white garments, one should offer a Kalpavṛkṣa (wish-fulfilling tree) along with a sacrificial fee near a festival day. Having performed three circumambulations, one should utter this mantra:
Salutations to you, the wish-fulfilling tree who bestows all desired objects;
salutations to you, the divine sustainer of the universe, whose form is the universe itself.
Since you alone are the soul of the universe—the Brahman, Śiva, and the Sun.
"O Eternal One, protect me from this seed which is both manifest and unmanifest.
Having thus addressed him and having seen that wish-fulfilling tree for the preceptor,
one should likewise bestow upon the four officiating priests (ṛtvij) the neighboring lands and other such gifts.
O Goddess, listen as I describe the fruit of merit for him who bestows this gift according to this rite:
having ascended a preeminent celestial chariot, radiant with a splendor equal to the sun’s brilliance, he shall depart.
Crowded with throngs of Apsarases and garlanded with networks of tinkling bells,
he goes to the world of the Lord of the Gods, which is free from all afflictions;
then, returning to the earth of karma, he is born into a family of Vedic scholars.
"A man who has performed sacrifices, who is brave and learned, becomes righteous;
furthermore, in the end, he shall indeed attain the world of the Lord who bears the Śārṅga bow.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Gift of the Kalpavṛkṣa," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the Ritual for Bestowing the Kalpalatā.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of all beings, honored by all the worlds!"
For the benefit of the worlds, tell me something further:
that by which one becomes free from sin through longevity, fame, and prosperity;
tell me that, O Lord of Gods—whether it be a gift or a vow.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O King, I shall speak out of a desire for the welfare of the world;
by what means men on earth become fortunate.
This world of mine cannot be attained through vows, nor by fasts, nor even by pilgrimages to sacred fords;
it is not reached by deaths on the Great Path (Mahāpatha) and the like, nor by sacrifices, nor by Vedic learning—
even though it is difficult to reach even for the gods.
O illustrious Pārtha, out of affection for you, I shall declare what is beneficial for you.
I shall describe the auspicious gift of the Kalpalatā according to the prescribed ritual;
one should perform all the preliminary rites therein as ordained in the Tantra.
There, the wise practitioner should offer the *bali* oblation to the guardians of the quarters according to the prescribed ritual;
having first performed the two *āghāra* libations and the two *ājyabhāga* portions,
he should then perform the *grahayajña* sacrifice with the *vyāhṛti* mantras.
The completion of the fire sacrifice (homa) here is said to be by means of ten thousand oblations.
Then, having bathed, wearing white garments, and being pure,
one should worship in the presence of all [the deities] with flowers, incense, cloths, fruits, and unbroken grains (akṣata).
Then, having circumambulated [the directions], one should utter these mantras:
"Salutations, salutations to the quarters, who destroy all sins, who protect the lords of the worlds within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa),
who bestow fruits exceeding hundreds of desires, and who are like celestial wish-fulfilling creepers."
"Whatever supreme power has been ordained for that best of gods in the Veda and the Purāṇa—that I worship here with the highest devotion; may she grant me auspiciousness; to her I bow.
Having uttered this, one should offer all of those [images] to the Brāhmaṇas.
Having mentally conceived those various ten directions with supreme devotion,
one should then ask forgiveness from the Brahmins after prostrating before them and offering ritual fees (dakṣiṇā).
Whoever bestows this gift according to this procedure—
O King, listen to me as I describe the fruit of his merit:
in this world, he shall be victorious, wealthy, and possessed of sons;
upon death, he shall dwell in the city of the Lord of the World for the duration of every Manvantara.
O King, having subsequently come from the netherworld (rasātala) surrounded by great powers,
he shall become a universal monarch (cakravartin) on earth who has conquered all rulers of the earth;
and whatever woman, O Great King, bestows this gift, [she too attains the same].
She gives birth to a son who is a powerful universal monarch (cakravartin).
Whoever sees it being given away, whoever approves of it once it has been given,
or whoever hears it as it is being recited— he too is liberated after death.
"Those who hold in their hands the thunderbolt, fire, the staff, and the noose, and who possess the powers of Vāta, Indu, Rāja, Śiva, Keśava, and Śambhu—

having worshipped those ten Kalpalatās, give them to the twice-born if you have the intent to conquer the three worlds. Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual for Giving the Kalpalatās," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
The description of the rules for the gift of elephants, chariots, and horses.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Blessed One, by brave Kṣatriyas who have acquired their wealth through their own prowess..."
O Kṛṣṇa, what gifts should be given that are purifying and auspicious— gifts which may be offered by other men who are terrified by the fear of unrighteousness,
tormented by the afflictions of the planets, or oppressed by evil dreams and the like?
"In this world and indeed in the next, you have described that which bestows all desires. O Great-minded One, please speak further regarding the specific injunctions for giving.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O protector of the earth, may it be well with you; I shall describe the unsurpassed dharma of giving, which is especially for the benefit of kings, of this there is no doubt.
Gifts are of many forms and are proclaimed in various scriptures.
O Indra among kings, gifts such as the gift of cows are preeminent, there is no doubt;
however, O Bhārata, I shall describe to you one supreme gift,
which Śukra proclaimed in its entirety to Vairocana, O Bhārata.
Śukra said:
Listen, O Lord of the Daityas, to the gift that destroys all sins;
it [removes] mental anxieties, physical diseases, and even the most terrible afflictions caused by the planets.

By giving this, one's sins are destroyed and one attains supreme merit. This gift should be bestowed on the full moon day of Kārttika, during the solstices, during lunar and solar eclipses, at the equinoxes, and during the sun’s passage into a new zodiac sign.
Then, having reached an auspicious day, with his anger conquered and his senses subdued,
he established a divine chariot made of wood, adorned with golden bands,
possessing excellent wheels, axles, and supports, and equipped with a yoke and traces.
Adorned with a golden banner and white and black flags,
[the chariot should be placed] on auspicious ground sloping toward the northeast, strewn with heaps of flowers;
or else on a riverbank, in a cow-pen, or in a variegated courtyard of a house.
Having constructed an unsurpassed altar on the front part of the chariot,
one who is learned in the Purāṇas and Vedic sciences and endowed with humility and proper conduct should install upon it the gods beginning with Brahmā; I shall describe them to you.
Having installed Brahmā in the center, one should worship him with the Praṇava;
Viṣṇu should be established to the north, and one should worship him with the Puruṣasūkta;
Rudra should be worshipped in the south with the Raudra hymn.
One should likewise worship the planets, headed by the Sun,
according to the prescribed rites with flowers, perfumes, fruits, edible offerings, and rows of lamps.
One should worship them with fragrant blossoms, white garments, and sandalwood paste.
One should cause a great festival to be celebrated with the sounds of conchs, kettledrums, and clay drums that resound everywhere,
mingled with the chanting of the Vedas;
and having constructed a sacrificial pit according to the rules, measuring one cubit in size.
O Indra among kings, one should worship the Brāhmaṇas there in the south-eastern direction—
four wandering Brāhmaṇas adorned with the ornaments of Brahman,
or four, eight, or even a single preceptor, O great king.
Having gathered all the implements for the fire sacrifice (homa), including sesame seeds and clarified butter (ghṛta),
one should then perform the fire ritual (agnikārya) correctly according to the prescribed rules;
having offered the two Āghāra libations and the two Ājyabhāga portions as previously described.

The oblation for the planets is prescribed with auspicious mantras previously mentioned for Viṣṇu, the blue-throated one (Śitikaṇṭha), as well as those recited in the rite of the planetary sacrifice (grahayajña). Having thus performed the sacrificial procedure together with the twice-born brahmins, the patron of the sacrifice (yajamāna) [should proceed].
One should yoke to the chariot two well-trained elephants endowed with auspicious marks,
their bodies covered in variegated cloths, possessing beautiful girth-straps and fine bells,
and adorned with golden bands, exquisite tassels, conch shells, and chowries.
Covered with divine pearls, equipped with divine goads,
accompanied by mahouts, and adorned with all ornaments—
having thus prepared that chariot along with the elephant, the man [should proceed].
Then, one should place upon it a Brāhmaṇa of celebrated vows,
adorned with necklets, bracelets, earrings, and finger-rings,
and provided with a cloak, an umbrella, garments, and weapons.
With his quiver fastened, bow in hand, and adorned with many skins,
his body bound by a scabbard and decorated with necklaces—
then the wise patron, pure and wearing white garments, [should approach].
Having circumambulated the chariot and holding a handful of flowers,
one should recite this mantra, which destroys all sins:
"Kumuda, Airāvaṇa, Padma, Puṣpadanta, and Vāmana."
Supratīka, Añjana, and Sārvabhauma— these are the eight divine origins.
May those two, born of their lineages and endowed with strength and beauty,
grant me boons by means of the gift of a chariot equipped with them.
"This chariot is the Person of Sacrifice; here, O Brāhmaṇa, Śiva himself is present.
By this gift of my chariot, may Śiva and Keśava be pleased.
Having spoken thus, O highly fortunate lady, and having worshipped [them] again and again—
Then, one should install upon it a Brāhmaṇa who has observed his vows,
who is devoted to his own wife, who is tranquil, who has mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas,
who honors the five fires, who is free from physical defects, and who is devoid of disease.
Having circumambulated once more that best of the twice-born seated in his chariot,
he should follow him as far as the gate, and after prostrating, enter his own home.
Then, at the conclusion of the sacrifice, [he should provide for] the poor, the blind, the dull-witted, and the emaciated.
One should worship with various gifts, such as clothing, the gift of cows, and food;
having thus resolved according to this very procedure, one should prepare an excellent chariot, along with the sacrificial pit,
the pavilion, the necessary materials, ornaments, coverings, and so forth.
The sacrificial materials for the oblation are indeed those same ones, and the mantras for the oblation are likewise those very same ones.
O King, listen as the specific details regarding the horse-chariot are being told:
there are two horses endowed with auspicious marks, their faces adorned with bits.

Adorned with various garments and decorated with neck-ornaments, and joined with a beautiful ring, these two should be offered by the donor during that supreme rite. Having circumambulated it clockwise, he should utter this mantra:
Salutations to You, the horse of the Vedas, whose essence consists of the three Vedas and who is composed of the three qualities (guṇas).
Salutations always to You, the bearer of the horse, who are a vessel for the easy drinking [of nectar] upon the most difficult path.
This chariot is Savitṛ himself, and these horses are the Vedas.
Having uttered, "May this Aruṇa Brāhmaṇa grant me happiness," he should then cause that best of Brāhmaṇas to ascend the chariot and follow him as far as the door of his house.
O wise one, listen to the fruit of the merit of that person who, according to this rite, gives a chariot with horses:
he shall be liberated from all sins and freed from all diseases; his reward is a kingdom with its horses and chariots.
For as long as a hundred Manvantaras, endowed with all enjoyments,
he shall dwell in heaven— possessing divine pleasures, glorious, moving at will— in a celestial chariot (vimāna) radiant as the sun and crowded with throngs of Apsarases.
Having returned here from the exhaustion of his merit, he becomes a righteous king,
endowed with sons and grandsons, long-lived, and hospitable to guests;
such is a certain king designated as "Gajaratha" (Elephant-Chariot) by means of a single elephant.
Those who speak according to the Vedas describe a horse-chariot as being made with even a single horse;
the mantras for such a gift are the same, though the fruit thereof is said to be greater.
Those who give an excellent chariot, well-equipped with poles, axles, and wheels, or one yoked to powerful elephants or horses—
"Adorned with all its furnishings and with its pole decorated with golden bands, they travel by means of that chariot to the city of the King of the Gods.

Thus ends the one hundred and eightieth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Gift of Elephants, Chariots, and Horse-Chariots," in the *Uttara-parvan* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[Now begins] the description of the ritual for the gift of the *Kālapuruṣa* (the Person of Time).
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Kṛṣṇa, best of the Yadus, tell me of other gifts that are auspicious,
purifying, and destroyers of all sins.
"O Mādhava, you are the cause for crossing over the ocean of saṃsāra;
in the full comprehension of dharma and adharma, there is no one else here besides you.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
I have described to you various kinds of gifts;
if you still have curiosity, I shall speak of them once more—
both those already told to you and those yet to be told.
When performed with great purpose, they succeed and bestow a great fruit;
O Pārtha, the ritual of giving for the sake of specific desires, when carried out with diligence,
has been declared by the sages to lead to results, whereas its opposite leads to fear.
One hundred gold coins (niṣkas) should be known as the supreme rule for all gifts;
that which is half of that is middling, and half of that again is recorded as the lowest.
This applies likewise to the tree-chariot, the lordly elephant, the cow, and the black antelope skin.
Even for one who is incapable, this procedure involving five gold coins has been prescribed.
O lord of men, if anyone should give a great gift (mahādāna) with less than that,
or if one should accept it, it will bring about suffering and grief for him.
First, I shall describe to you the personification known as Time (Kāla-puruṣa),
the gift of the seven oceans, the jar of the great elements (Mahābhūta-ghaṭa),
the offering of the arghya water as prescribed by mantra, and likewise the representation of oneself.
The sixth is remembered as the gift of a golden horse, and another is the chariot with golden horses;
O King, the black antelope skin is the best of all gifts and is the eighth;
the ninth is the Viśvacakra, as well as the golden elephant-chariot.
O best of kings, I know this tenfold path of giving;
O most excellent of men, give and cause others to give with a virtuous mind.
For one who possesses wealth, there is no other benefit greater than giving.
For when it is given away, it does not diminish; rather, it increases all the more. Even as a well is being dug out, it becomes possessed of abundant water.
Then, having reached an auspicious day, on a level and pure plot of ground, [one should proceed].
O son of Pāṇḍu, on the fourth lunar day, or the fourteenth, or during the Viṣṭi yoga,
an effigy of a man should be fashioned from black sesame seeds, with silver teeth and golden eyes,
holding a raised sword in his hand, with gaping wounds, and adorned with Japā flower earrings.
Wearing red garments and adorned with garlands and a rosary of conch shells,
his hips were broadened by a bow of sharp sword-blades; indeed,
he was equipped with a pair of sandals and had a black blanket draped at his side.
Likewise, having fashioned a man holding a lump of meat in his left palm,
and having thus prepared him while holding a handful of flowers,
one should worship him with perfumes and flowers and present an offering of food (naivedya).

There, one should offer oblations of sesame seeds and clarified butter with the mantra "Tryambaka," performing one hundred and eight offerings according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Gṛhya-sūtra. With a tranquil mind, the patron should utter this mantra:
Because you reckon everything, you are called Time (Kāla).
O observer of noble vows, you are unassailable even by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others.
You have been worshipped by me with devotion, and likewise, I have prayed for my well-being.
"O Lord, do that which you have spoken; salutations, salutations to you!
Having thus worshipped him, one should present [the image] to a Brāhmaṇa.
First, having worshipped Brahmā with garments and ornaments, [one should give the image].
One should give a sacrificial fee according to one's ability, prostrate, and then dismiss [the officiant].
For whoever bestows this gift according to this rule,
there is no fear of untimely death, nor any fear arising from disease.
He becomes one whose sovereignty is unimpeded and who is free from all afflictions;
at the end of the body, having pierced the solar realm, he goes to the supreme state. Upon the exhaustion of his merit, returning here, he becomes a righteous king.
Endowed with continuous prosperity and accompanied by sons and grandsons,
having duly worshipped Kālapuruṣa and given [the image] to a twice-born man— one who is the cause for the arising of the fruits of both auspicious and inauspicious deeds—
the embodied soul, even amidst diseases consisting of all manner of defects, does not fall into a state of being subject to slaughter by their power.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Gift of the Kālapuruṣa," in the Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the Uttaraparvan, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[Now follows] the description of the ritual for the gift of the seven oceans. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the unsurpassed gift of the Earth (Pārthadāna),
known as the Seven Seas, which destroys all sins. Having reached an auspicious day, such as the beginning of a Yuga or an eclipse, [one should perform it].
A wise person should have seven sacrificial pits made of gold,
measuring either one span (prādeśa) or one cubit (ratni) in size;
he should perform [the rite] from seven hundred up to a thousand [repetitions], according to his capacity.
All these [materials] should be placed upon a black antelope skin and sesame seeds.
First, the wise one should fill the pit with salt;
likewise, the second with milk, and the third again with clarified butter.
The fourth [offering] should be with jaggery, and the fifth with curd;
likewise, the sixth with sugar and the seventh with water from a sacred ford.
At the end of the salt [offering], one should place a beautiful golden image of Brahmā.
One should install Keśava in the midst of milk, Maheśvara in the midst of ghee,
Bhāskara in the midst of molasses, and the Lord of the Gods (Indra) in the midst of curd;
one should install Lakṣmī in sugar and Pārvatī in the midst of water.

O best of men, one should place all kinds of jewels and grains everywhere, according to what is available and as is convenient. Then, on the eve of a festival, the householder, having bathed and wearing white garments, [should proceed].
Having circumambulated three times clockwise, one should utter these mantras:
"Salutations to you, the eternal foundations of all rivers;
salutations again and again to the oceans that grant life to living beings."
All of you are indeed full with salt, milk, ghee, sugarcane juice,
curd, sugar, and likewise with the waters of sacred fords;
therefore, O givers of honor, effect the destruction of my flood of sins.
"May misfortune be pacified, and may prosperity dwell in my home.
Having uttered this, O Yudhiṣṭhira, one should give those [gifts] to the Brāhmaṇas;
or, having thus honored even a single one with flowers, garments, and ointments.
This has been prescribed for many or for a single person;
or rather, that which is to be given should be common to all, according to the nature of the ritual and the Brahmins.
O King, he who bestows this gift known as the "Seven Seas" [attains great merit].
Fortune does not depart from his house for as long as eight generations;
being honored by hosts of gods, Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and serpents,
he does not fall from the world of the gods for seven Manvantaras.
And then, through the refinement of the Vedas, he attains the Supreme Brahman.
Thus, having given here oceans filled with nectar and ambrosia— pure, wonder-inspiring, and composed of fire,
gold, and jewels— he reaches the abode of Hari, which is encompassed by Ramā.
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, having reflected with a mind fixed in meditative concentration, it has been declared by the Brāhmaṇa that this gift is preeminent and exceedingly superior.
By fashioning the seven oceans out of gold and bestowing them according to your capacity, you shall attain all your cherished desires.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Gift of the Seven Oceans," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the Gift of the Jar of the Great Elements.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Now, therefore, I shall describe to you another excellent gift.

Having reached an auspicious lunar day, one should have a golden pitcher, filled with great jewels, fashioned in a well-smeared courtyard of the house; this is called the "Pitcher of the Great Elements," which destroys even the most heinous sins.

O best of men, one should fashion it according to measure from one span up to a hundred finger-breadths; and according to one's capacity, its weight should be from five palas upwards to a hundred. Having filled it with milk and clarified butter, it should be provided with a Kalpavṛkṣa tree.
There, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara were seated upon lotus-thrones;
the world-protectors and the great Indras were mounted upon their respective vehicles;
and the Ṛgveda was present with his rosary, as was the Yajurveda with his lotus.
The Sāmaveda should hold a lute, while Atharvaveda is adorned with a beautiful garland;
Purāṇaveda, the bestower of boons, holds a rosary, a water-pot, and a staff.
A wise man should place seven kinds of grain before them according to his capacity.
Having thus duly prepared sandals, shoes, an umbrella, chowries, a pre-eminent seat, and weapons,
a person should then worship the jar of the great elements,
which is filled with molasses and essence, with garlands and cloths.
Then, having bathed near the junction of the lunar phases (parvan) with a restrained mind,
and having performed three circumambulations, one should utter this mantra:
"Since there is nothing whatsoever that exists apart from the great elements..."
And since this [image] is composed of the great elements (mahābhūta), may it grant me peace.
The gods present here, established by Viśvakarman—
may they, being honored with a spirit of devotion, bestow peace upon me.
Having thus worshipped the jar of the great elements,
and having honored a Brāhmaṇa with ornaments, clothing, and other gifts,
a man who is firm in his vows should present the jar of the great elements at the time of a festival.
Having circumambulated that Brahmin once more, he should ask for his forgiveness.
Whoever bestows this gift according to this rite goes to the world of Śiva accompanied by twenty-one generations of his lineage.
Having come here from the exhaustion of his merit, he becomes a righteous king,
invincible by hosts of enemies, possessed of great strength and prowess,
devoted to the dharma of the Kṣatriyas, learned, and a worshiper of the gods and Brahmins.

Having fashioned a stainless, eight-sided (aṣṭāpada) excellent jar, joined with Brahmā, Īśa, and Keśava, along with the world-protectors (lokapālas), and containing a cavity filled with milk and clarified butter, bow down with devotion and give it to a Brahmin. What is the use of your other hundreds of gifts? Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Gift of the Great Elemental Jar," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the Ritual for the Gift of a Bed.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O scion of the Pāṇḍu lineage, I shall now describe to you the ritual for the gift of a bed.
The best of the twice-born always offer gifts of beds, thinking: "Having given this, one shall partake in happiness both in this world and the next;
since life is impermanent, who else will provide it after [the donor] has passed?"
O Bhārata, he is a kinsman and he is a father only so long as he lives;
once he is dead, knowing him to be dead, affection ceases in an instant.
Therefore, one should personally provide the bed, food, water, and other necessities.

Reflecting thus in one's mind that "the self alone is indeed the friend of the self," who else could be more beneficial than the self for one who does not honor their own self with gifts and enjoyments? Who will worship it hereafter?
Therefore, having approached a bed made of solid wood, firm,
adorned with ivory carvings, beautiful, decorated with sheets of snow-cloth,
covered with swan-down feathers, auspicious, and provided with pillows;
Upon that [bed], which is provided with a covering cloth and perfumed with fragrant incense,
one should place a golden image of Hari accompanied by Lakṣmī;
and one should arrange a water-pot placed at the head of the bed.
O Pāṇḍava, the wise should always consider betel-leaf—
along with powdered saffron, camphor, agallochum, and sandalwood;
as well as lamps, sandals, umbrellas, chowries, seats, and food— to be equivalent to sleep.
One should place the seven types of grain according to one's capacity at the sides; furthermore,
whatever else is useful for one lying on the bed—
such as water-pitchers and so forth, flowers, and a canopy of five colors— should be provided.
Having prepared such a bed, one should cause it to be presented to a Brāhmaṇa together with his wife on an auspicious day, according to the prescribed ritual, after having honored him:
"Salutations to you, O Lord of all gods; this gift of a bed has been made by me."

Therefore, grant me the fruit of peace; salutations to you, O Puruṣottama! Just as the bed of Kṛṣṇa is never empty of the daughter of the ocean, so may my own bed also be never empty [of you] in birth after birth.
Having thus provided a pure bed and prostrated, one should bid them farewell;
this same procedure is proclaimed for the eleventh day as well.
If a man gives [the bed] for the sake of dharma when a kinsman has died, [he attains merit].
Furthermore, O Indra among kings, listen to me as I describe the specific distinction regarding that which was previously enjoyed by him while he was in his home— whatever object,
as well as whatever touched his body, including his clothes, vehicles, and vessels.

Whatever was desired by him, all that one should provide; likewise, one should place a golden image of that very person at its end. Having worshipped it, the death-bed (mṛtaśayyā) should be given as prescribed.
By the power of giving a bed, that living being dwells happily in heaven, in the abode of Purandara, or even in the residence of the Son of the Sun;
the terrifying-faced messengers of Yama do not torment him.
That man is never oppressed by heat or cold;
even if he was joined with sin, he is honored in the heavenly world,
mounted upon an excellent celestial chariot and served by throngs of apsaras.
Free from sin, one shall remain until the dissolution of all beings;
this stainless gift of a bed, proclaimed by the son of Pāṇḍu, is a treasury of all happiness.
He who bestows it according to the rules himself shines truly in heaven upon a celestial couch, free from all conceptual duality.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Gift of a Bed," in the *Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the *Uttara Parvan*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira; followed by the "Description of the Ritual for the Gift of Oneself.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
I shall now fully explain to you that gift called the "Self-Image," as it was described to someone in the past; it increases one's honor.
The sages have proclaimed that the time for its giving is always appropriate.
O Pārtha, such a meritorious day is attained through merits and not merely by living;
O King, having fashioned for yourself an auspicious image made of iron,
mounted upon a desired vehicle and adorned with beloved ornaments.
Accompanied by her beloved husband and provided with all necessary utensils,
she was then covered with silk cloths and fine fabrics, adorned with jewels,
her limbs anointed with saffron and scented with camphor and agallochum.

If it is a woman who gives [the gift], she herself should cause it to be placed upon the bed while lying there. Whatever is most beloved to her, all that she should set at his side— whatever may be beneficial to women and whatever pertains to her own body.
Having reflected upon all this within his own mind, he should set it all aside;
then, having gathered all these things and placed them each in their respective positions,
he should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas), the houses, the Goddess, and Vināyaka.
Then, having bathed and dressed in white garments, the wise man, holding a handful of flowers,
should recite this mantra in front of the Brahmin:
"This is my own image, provided with all necessary implements."
O Brahmin, this [offering] endowed with all jewels has been presented by you;
Śambhu, Śiva, Śauri, and Śakra, surrounded by the hosts of gods, are the Self.
Therefore, by the gift of my own self, may my soul be well-pleased.
Having uttered this, O Yudhiṣṭhira, one should then give [the gift] to a Brāhmaṇa;
and the Brāhmaṇa should receive it while reciting, "May [this] give [me].
Then, having circumambulated him and prostrated, one should dismiss him.
O King of kings, whatever man or woman bestows this gift according to this rite, or even hears of it, shall obtain its fruit:
surrounded by the gods, they shall dwell for more than a hundred divine years in the heavenly world.
Indeed, by granting desired fruits, one becomes a partaker of those desired fruits;
for wherever a living being is born again when his karma is exhausted,
there that king becomes a partaker of the fruits of all his desires.
O King, a man never experiences separation from his beloved kinsmen; he attains heaven and enjoys eternal bliss.
Furthermore, he who has fashioned a golden image of himself seated upon a noble vehicle, surrounded by wealth and grain—
"He who gives [an image] along with its furnishings to an excellent Brahmin with devotion shines in heaven like the moon and the sun; indeed, he becomes a king of kings.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Gift of One’s Own Image," in the *Uttara-parvan* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[Now begins] the description of the ritual for the gift of a golden horse.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Now I shall fully describe the supreme ritual of the golden horse,
by the grace of which a person enjoys eternal fruit.

Having attained an auspicious day, or even a recipient of superior merit, O best of men, one should have a golden horse fashioned according to one's means, weighing more than three palas but not exceeding a hundred,
its face adorned with a bit.
One should place [the image] in the center of the altar upon a black antelope skin and sesame seeds— [the image] having a loud voice, uplifted shoulders, firm knees, and a tail,
clothed in silk garments and anointed with saffron.
Having worshipped with white flowers and offered chickpeas (*caṇaka*),
and then, near the full-moon day (*parvan*), holding a handful of flowers while restrained by his vow,
he should recite this mantra spoken in the Purāṇas:
Salutations to you, O Lord of all gods, you who are intent upon bringing forth the Vedas!
In the form of a horse, protect me from this ocean of saṃsāra.
You alone, having become sevenfold in the form of the meters, [illuminate] the Sun.
"Since you sustain the worlds, therefore protect us, O Eternal One.
Having uttered this, O King, one should present it to the Brahmin;
then, having performed a circumambulation and prostrated, one should bid him farewell.
O King, by giving a decorated golden horse according to this rite,
one attains the eternal world of the Sun through the destruction of sins;
on that day, one should eat food devoid of oil and alkaline substances.
Likewise, one should cause the hearing of the Purāṇas to take place after the meal.
O Lord of Men, he who performs this rite of the Golden Horse on a most auspicious day,
having attained great merit and being liberated from sin, reaches the city of Murāri, which is honored by the Siddhas.
The king who thus recites this account of the gift of a golden horse, being liberated from all impurities,
shall travel to the world of the Sun in a golden celestial chariot drawn by horses, and there he is honored with the enjoyments of palaces by the wives of the Lord of the Gods.
Furthermore, the man who hears this, or remembers it, or rejoices at the gift of a golden horse being given, [attains the same reward].
He too, with his body purified and his sins destroyed, goes to that place frequented by Indra and Maheśvara.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Gift of a Golden Horse," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira. [This is followed by:
"Description of the Ritual for the Gift of a Golden Horse-Chariot."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Now, therefore, O best of the Pāṇḍu lineage, I shall fully describe to you the meritorious [vow] named Hemaratha, which destroys even the greatest of sins.

On an auspicious day declared by a Brahmin, having smeared the courtyard of the house with unguents and spread out a black antelope skin and sesame seeds, O highly fortunate one, he should place a golden chariot there—
quadrangular, four-wheeled, and equipped with a pole.
Placing Brahmā at its head, it was adorned with auspicious reins held fast,
joined with a banner in the form of an emerald pitcher,
accompanied by the eight guardians of the world, and endowed with petals of ruby.
There should be four full jars and eighteen types of grain;
above, it is covered with silken cloth and a canopy;
in the center, it is provided with fruits and accompanied by a man.
The man should be joined with yoga, and one should cause him to dwell there;
having thus worshipped him with garlands, perfumes, and ointments,
both Viśva and Kumāraka are to be made his protectors of the wheel.
Then, having reached an auspicious time, bathed, and worshipped the deities,
and having performed three circumambulations while holding a handful of flowers,
one wearing white garlands and garments should utter this mantra:
Salutations, repeated salutations, to the destroyer of sins, the soul of the universe, the divine steed;
to the creator, the lord of the gods, the source of both existence and non-existence—grant me peace through the gift of this chariot.
You alone are the sustainer of the Vasus, Aṣṭakas, Ādityas, and the hosts of Maruts; you are the supreme treasure.
"May my heart, through the destruction of the flood of sins, turn toward the singular focus on Dharma from whatever direction it may come.
He who performs this gift of horses and chariots— which is a mantra that destroys the fear of worldly existence—
his body being liberated from the layers of impurity, attains the supreme state of the wielder of the Pināka bow.
With his resplendent body, having surpassed the power of the circle of the fierce-rayed sun,
he dwells for a long time together with the Lotus-born Lord (Brahmā), whose lotus-face is being drunk in by the pair of eyes of the Siddha women.
Whoever reads or hears this account of the gift of the golden-horsed chariot in this [context], [attains the same merit].
"He shall never go to the city of hell; he goes again to the abode of the Enemy of Hell (Śiva).

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Gift of the Golden Horse-Chariot," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[Now follows] the description of the ritual for the gift of the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*).
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O sinless one, tell me the rule and the proper time for the gift of a black antelope skin, and describe the Brāhmaṇa [to whom it should be given]; for in this matter I have a great doubt.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: At the beginnings of the Yugas, during eclipses, at the transit of the sun, at the end of the day,
on the full moon of Māgha, during afflictions by the planets, upon seeing bad dreams or portents, [one should perform this rite].
O King, this great gift should be given when wealth has been acquired;
it should also be given to a twice-born who maintains the sacred fires, who has mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences,
who is devoted to the Purāṇas, and who is skillful.
Listen as I describe the procedure by which it is performed:
O lord of men, having first spread out a beautiful woolen cloth upon a pure place smeared with cow dung.
Its horns should be made of gold and its teeth likewise of silver;
its tail should be adorned with a string of pearls and likewise covered with sesame seeds.
Having fashioned the head out of sesame seeds, O King, the wise man should cover it with a cloth.
One should surround it with gold and especially adorn it;
one should worship it with flowers, perfumes, fruits, and food offerings.
Likewise, one should place jewels according to one's ability in its various directions.
One should place four bronze vessels upon them in due order;
having thus offered ghee, milk, curd, and honey according to the prescribed rite,
one should then recite this mantra in the presence of all.
O God, you are black, with black impurities, and likewise the best of black antelopes' skins;
may you, who dispel my sins through your gift, be pleased with me—salutations again and again!
You are established as the foundation of the thirty-three gods.
"O black antelope skin, you are Kṛṣṇa incarnate; salutations be to you!
Having thus circumambulated it and prostrated again and again, [he should honor] the Brahmin who accepts it, one who has mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
Having bathed, covered with a pair of garments, and adorned according to his means,
the Self-born One himself declared that the acceptance [of the gift] should take place at the tail-end;
for a Brahmin consumed by the fire of accepting such gifts, O Bhārata, [this is the remedy].
One should not look at his face afterwards, nor should one speak to him.
By giving the black antelope skin according to this procedure,
a person obtains the complete fruit of a gift of land.
Those who, having provided a black antelope skin, sesame seeds, gold, honey, and clarified butter,
bestow them upon a Brahmin, are indeed not to be pitied;
having ascended to the sky, they traverse all worlds, moving according to their will.
Until the final dissolution of all beings, they undoubtedly attain heaven;
there is no gift in the three worlds equal to the black antelope skin (kṛṣṇājina).
Those who know the Vedas understand that even the acceptance of such a gift is highly sinful.
Whatever has been acquired in the three states of existence in its threefold manner—
all that perishes in an instant by giving a black antelope skin.
Having given the skin of the black deer to a preeminent brahmin with a concentrated mind, one attains the vision of Kṛṣṇa.
As it has been said: "One should not grieve over this death; one attains the desired fruit of the mind.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Vow and Ritual for the Gift of a Black Antelope Skin," in the *Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, in the *Uttara Parvan*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[Now follows] the description of the ritual for the gift of a golden elephant.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O great king, I shall describe to you the gift of the golden elephant-chariot,
by the giving of which a human being goes to the abode of Viṣṇu.
Having reached a festival day, or during a solar transit (saṃkrānti) or an eclipse,
one should construct a chariot in the form of Indra’s chariot, adorned with jewels,
provided with four wheels, and featuring variously decorated gables.
It should be yoked to four golden elephants and adorned with gold;
one should place Garuḍa upon the banner and Vināyaka at the front of the pole.
It should be endowed with the eight world-protectors (Lokapālas) and joined by Brahmā, the Sun, and Śiva.
In the center, one should place a chariot accompanied by Nārāyaṇa and joined with Lakṣmī and Puṣṭi;
having prepared a heap of black antelope skins and sesame seeds, one should station that chariot there,
with a canopy above it adorned with various fruits.
O best of men, one should have [the image] clothed in silk garments and adorned with unfading flowers, weighing more than five palas but no more than a hundred. Then,
having bathed and worshipped the ancestors and the gods according to the prescribed rite, [one should proceed].
Having circumambulated three times clockwise and holding a handful of flowers,
one should recite this mantra which bestows all happiness:
"Salutations, salutations to Śaṅkara, Padmaja, Arka, the Lords of the Worlds, Vidyādharas, and Vāsudeva."
You are served by the Vedas, Purāṇas, and sacrifices; you are indeed our splendor. O Chariot, protect us from that!

That which is the most supreme secret, the ancient state, the cause of bliss, and free from the bonds of the multitude of forms—that reality which sages, whose minds are fixed solely on Yoga, perceive in Samādhi—you are that, O Lord, mounted upon your chariot.

"Since you alone are the vessel for the drink held within the jar of bliss for those submerged in the ocean of worldly existence, therefore, O Mādhava, show favor by quelling the multitude of my sins through the gift of a golden elephant-chariot. Having thus prostrated, he who causes the gift of a golden elephant-chariot to be made shall have his body liberated from all sins.
He attains that state beyond the senses of the Moon-crested Lord, which is frequented by hosts of Vidyādharas, gods, and lords of sages.

Furthermore, one who has given gifts of elephants and chariots leads his kinsmen— fathers and grandsons— even if they have caused a mass of sins or have distressed their bodies through the service of the sacrificial fire and the sun, from the entirety of the Raurava hell to the eternal abode of Viṣṇu.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Gift of the Golden Elephant-Chariot," in the Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, in the Uttaraparvan, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Now follows the description of the ritual for the gift of the Viśvacakra (the Universal Wheel).
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
I shall further proclaim for you a most wonderful gift,
renowned as the Viśvacakra, which destroys all sins.
One who is pure in soul should then have it fashioned out of refined, pure gold.
The best [Viśvacakra] is made with a thousand palas, the middling with half of that,
and the smallest is said to be half of that again.
Likewise, even one who is unable may offer it with twenty palas or more.
Then, one should visualize a sixteen-spoked wheel surrounded by eight revolving rims,
with Viṣṇu situated upon a lotus at its hub; he is four-armed, established in yoga,
with the conch and discus positioned at his sides, and surrounded by the eight goddesses.
In the second enclosure, likewise, [one should worship] Jalaśāyin in the east;
then Atri, Bhṛgu, Vasiṣṭha, Brahmā, and Kaśyapa;
and the Fish, Tortoise, Boar, Narasiṃha, and Vāmana.
Rāma, Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, Buddha, and Kalki—these are the ten;
in the third enclosure is Gaurī, joined by eight Manūs;
in the fourth are the twelve Ādityas and the four Vedas.
In the fifth [enclosure], one should cause the five elements and the eleven Rudras to be fashioned;
in the sixth, the eight world-protectors as well as the elephants of the directions;
and in the seventh, all the weapons and auspicious objects.
Furthermore, one should place the deities within the intermediate spaces at the eighth [stage]; then,
having constructed a pavilion ten cubits in size, provided with banners and arches,
one should have it made along with a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and covered with cloth.
In the center of that [altar], one should place an altar (vedi) measuring four cubits;
upon it, according to the prescribed rite, one should place a universal wheel (viśvacakra) resting on a black antelope skin (kṛṣṇājina),
as well as the eighteen grains and the flavors, such as salt and the rest.
Likewise, one should place eight full water-pots adorned with cloth and garlands,
and offer fruits at the sides; then, having spread a canopy of five colors,
one should consecrate the wheel and subsequently perform the fire sacrifice (homa).
There, four Brahmins belonging to the four Vedic schools, self-controlled and adorned with garments and ornaments,
equipped with the materials for the oblation and with ladles (*sruk* and *sruva*) and copper vessels, should perform the fire-sacrifice (*homa*).
For deities established upon a *cakra*, a fire-oblation (*homa*) is prescribed;
one should offer oblations with mantras bearing their specific characteristics for the pacification of all calamities.
Then, having bathed and wearing white garments, the householder [should proceed] amidst auspicious sounds.
At the conclusion of the fire-offering and the consecration (adhivāsana), having taken handfuls of flowers and having performed three circumambulations while reciting this mantra:
"Obeisance to the Sustainer of the Universe; obeisance to the Soul of the Universal Wheel."
O You whose nature is supreme bliss, protect us from the mire of sin!
Since the wise always behold this world as consisting of light,
I bow to that wheel of the universe within the heart which transcends the qualities (guṇas).
The discus is situated in Vāsudeva, and Mādhava is in its center;
I bow to these two as they stand here in a state of mutual support.
Since this universal wheel of Hari removes all sins, [I worship it].
"May the weapon and the consecrated garment therefore grant me peace.
Having thus addressed [the deity], he who, free from envy, gives the Viśvacakra discus,
being liberated from all sins, is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Having reached the realm of Vaikuṇṭha, which is surrounded by four-armed Naras,
he is served by throngs of Apsarases and shall remain there for three hundred kalpas;
or else, he who bows down after having fashioned the Viśvacakra every day [attains the same].
His lifespan increases greatly and his prosperity shall become vast.
Therefore, men should always have a discus made and kept in their own home—
either of gold, or silver, or, in the absence of those, of copper.
Thus, he who bestows this golden sixteen-spoked [discus], the abode of the gods of the entire world, reaches the realm of Hari;
there, having been approached for a long time by hosts of Siddhas and Apsarases, he is honored with prostrations.
Furthermore, it brings about the state of being "Sudarśana" (the auspicious to behold) for his enemies, and the state of being "Madanasudarśana" (the one whose beauty intoxicates) for women.
He, who is worthy of Keśava of the beautiful Sudarśana, whose sins were burnt away by the gift of the golden Sudarśana,
and who— though having committed heavy sins against his guru— attained a most excellent form through the bestowal of the sixteen-spoked discus of Murāri,
repeatedly overcomes the worldly existences arising from *bhava* by breaking through *bhava* on every side within the world.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninetieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual for the Gift of the Universal Discus," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira; followed by the "Description of the Foundation of the World.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Madhusūdana, by what gift is eternal stability attained,
as well as most wonderful fame in this world and the next,
and so that all one’s fathers and grandfathers likewise attain a virtuous state?
"O delighter of the Yadus, how may one’s lineage remain inexhaustible in this world and one’s prosperity also become abundant through the installation of all the gods?
O illustrious one, tell me that— whether by means of a gift or by means of a religious observance."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O King, you have asked well; it is beneficial for the worlds.
Listen with a one-pointed mind to this supreme and most excellent secret."
I shall describe to you in brief the foundation of the worlds:
the gods, asuras, nāgas, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, pretas, piśācas, and bhūtas are all established therein; of this there is no doubt.
On an auspicious moment favorable to the performer, during a victorious and propitious hour,
on a meritorious lunar day, in a sacred field, and on a day conjoined with benign planets,
one should prepare a square cloth measuring seven cubits, well-woven and firm.
O King of kings, one should have all the worlds depicted upon that [disc], which has unbroken parts, is firm, pure, and possesses the luster of pure crystal;
having brought together the four castes for the variegated work of painting.
Having diligently honored a young, healthy, auspicious,
and skilled painter with divine garments and ornaments,
one should employ him in that task while the best of the twice-born recite [the appropriate mantras].
Then, with the sounding of conchs and kettledrums, the resonance of auspicious songs,
and the proclamations of "Auspicious Day" and "Victory," one should honor the Brahmins;
likewise, one should fully worship the preceptor with garments and ornaments.
O King, one should cause the commencement of the work on that cloth as it has been described;
and in the center, O King, one should depict Jambūdvīpa in detail.
Meru stands in its center, and above Meru are the deities.
In front of the world-protectors in the various directions stood eight [deities] accompanied by gods;
likewise, the earth consisting of seven continents, the seven great mountain ranges,
the seven oceans, as well as the rivers, lakes, and ponds were all present there.
Right here are the seven netherworlds (pātālas) and the seven splendors of the heavens;
likewise, the worlds of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others in their proper order;
and the path of the Pole Star, as well as the sun, accompanied by the planets and the hosts of stars.
The gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and pannagas;
the ṛṣis, munis, cows, and the divine mothers;
the birds such as the suparṇas, and the nāgas such as Airāvata and others.
One should have the eight elephants of the quarters, adorned with rut, painted right here on this very [canvas].
O King, having had such a beautiful cloth prepared,
it should be completely surrounded by water in ten successive layers.
That [fire] is further enveloped on all sides by the fierce Great Principle (mahat);
that fire is enveloped by air, and air is enveloped by space;
likewise, space is enveloped by the origin of the elements (bhūtādi), and the origin of the elements is likewise enveloped by the Great Principle.
The Great Principle (mahat), characterized by purity, is indeed pervaded by the Unmanifest;
the Unmanifest is pervaded by Darkness (tamas), and Darkness likewise by Passion (rajas);
Passion is completely pervaded by Goodness (sattva)—this threefold nature is called Prakṛti.
O King, thus the entire cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa),
possessed of its coverings, is entirely pervaded by the Puruṣa both internally and externally. Having made all of this into a painting situated upon a cloth, the wise man [should proceed].
On the full moon day of Kārttika, at the solstice, the equinox, or during an eclipse,
listen to me briefly regarding the procedure by which one should perform the worship.
A wise person should have a variegated pavilion constructed in front of it.
There, one should have four square sacrificial pits constructed; in each of these, one should appoint two Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas,
who are provided with the implements of sacrifice, and adorned with garments and ornaments.

All of them, having conquered their selves and observing silence, should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) with mantras preceded by the syllable Oṃ for the deities stationed upon the cloth. Then the patron, having bathed and adorned himself with all ornaments, [should proceed].
One should perform worship together with the preceptor in front of the cloth painting (paṭa). Having honored it thoroughly with flowers and garments, one should utter this mantra:
"The fourteen worlds existing within the interior of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa)..."
May these [deities], being present here, be honored for my sake.
May Brahmā, Viṣṇu, as well as Rudra, the Ādityas, and the Vasus,
being honored, remain perpetually well-established for me.
Having thus worshipped that cloth-painting and performed circumambulation,
one should cause various kinds of edible foods to be offered as a sacrificial oblation there. Then, with the sounding of conchs and trumpets, one should arrange for a vigil.
With various sounds of Vedic chanting and the auspicious resonance of songs,
having bathed again at the clear dawn and being pure and adorned,
he should once more worship that cloth-painting according to this previously mentioned procedure.
Then, having performed the worship of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), the wise man should give a hundred cows,
or else a pair of well-adorned cows to each one;
likewise, he should give sandals, an umbrella, and household utensils.
