Whatever is most beloved, the wise man should give all of that;
then he should provide a decorated vehicle yoked with elephants,
or, if those are unavailable, one yoked with horses and adorned with banners and flags.

Having given a thousand as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), the wise man should then have the cloth-painting mounted; or else, he should have a Brahmin carry it in a chariot to the temple. Having brought it there, he should install it and honor it with perfumes, flowers, and incense.
There too, one should offer food oblations and celebrate a great festival; O King, in whichever temple his consecration is performed,
a grand worship must also be conducted there by one who desires prosperity.
O King of kings, the wise man, constrained by reverence for his guru, should cause a moon-shaped parasol, a bell, a banner, and other such items to be given according to his capacity;
having honored the brahmins with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), he should then dismiss them.
On that day, food should be given without restriction to the poor, the blind, and the wretched, as well as to friends, kinsmen, and relatives. He who,
being faithful and having conquered his senses, performs this according to the prescribed rite—
Whether it be a man or a woman, whoever performs this installation that is honored by all the world,
by him the three worlds, including all things moving and stationary, are established;
and by that virtuous son, O Yudhiṣṭhira, his entire lineage is delivered.
As long as the cloth-painting remains worshipped in a temple,
so long his imperishable fame spreads throughout the three worlds;
and for as long as his fame is sung in the mortal worlds because of his generosity.
For that many thousands of years he is honored in the heavenly world;
being sung to by Gandharvas and attended by hosts of Apsarases,
he shall dwell in heaven with a joyful mind for as long as the reigns of fourteen Indras endure.
Having returned here from the exhaustion of his merit,
O Indra among kings, he is born again and again for ten lifetimes as a righteous king, endowed with sons and grandsons, illustrious, long-lived, and exceedingly virtuous.
It is heard that in ancient times there was a king named Raji, possessed of great strength;
he was a universal monarch (cakravartin) of firm resolve, who had conquered his enemies and mastered his senses.
By him, in a battle of old, the earth was given to the King of the Gods.
Having conquered the entire host of Daityas,
O illustrious one, he restored heaven to Mahendra, entirely cleared of all thorns.
Once, while that lord of the earth was seated in the midst of his assembly hall—
Then Pulastya, the illustrious son of Brahmā, arrived there surrounded by his disciples who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences;
having been offered the arghya water by him, he sat down upon an excellent seat. (Alternative reading: *dattārdhastu*)
He shone with supreme splendor like a second Grandfather (Brahmā).
Then, having first honored him with the *madhuparka* offering, the king,
endowed with humility, asked that monarch for an account of his own origins.
"O Blessed One, O Knower of Dharma, by what gift, austerity, or observance has this prosperity come to me, as well as unimpeded splendor on earth,
strength, nourishment, wealth, grain, and excellent sons and grandsons?"
"Tell me all of this, for you are omniscient, O best of the twice-born.
Pulastya said:
"Listen, O King, to this most enchanting story of your own."
Listen to this story, which increases one's sovereignty, as it is being told by me correctly regarding your seventh birth;
O best of men, you were indeed born into the Vaiśya caste in Vārāṇasī.
Surrounded by many servants and attendants, endowed with wealth and grain,
righteous, devoted to truth, and always intent on the duties of a merchant—
there indeed you heard the teachings while engaged in the recitation of the Dharma.

O Indra among kings, you have heard through incidental discourse about the various bases of giving and the diverse types of vows; and you have also heard, according to the prescribed rites, of the installation of divine images which bestows abundant merit.
By that fruit, you have been born as a lord of the earth for seven lifetimes;
your fame is renowned in the world, and your strength is likewise great.
For another seven births as well, you shall be a king.
"Afterwards, having become part of the family of yogis, you shall attain nirvāṇa.
All this that you asked me has been told to you;
whether it be a woman or a man, whoever [seeks] the earthly foundation..."
"By performing this according to the prescribed rite, the wise man shall have accomplished his purpose.
Having spoken thus to the king there, that sage of celebrated vows,
resembling the sun or fire, vanished from sight.
It increases righteousness, brings fame, bestows hundreds of boons, fulfills desires, and removes sin.
This devotion of yours to charity has now been proclaimed by me; there is nothing that this foundation of the world does not accomplish.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Foundation of the World," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the Ritual for Giving Gifts on the Lunar Mansions.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Lord of Ramā, by your grace, the entire procedure for giving gifts has been heard by me.
"Now, tell me the ritual procedure for the gift of constellations.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"In this regard, they cite this ancient history."
Devakī,

who perceives the dharma, then asked this very question of Nārada, the seer of the gods, who had come to Dvārakā after having a vision of the deity and was engaged in conversation with the celestial sage Nārada.
Then, as she was questioning him, the celestial sage Nārada explained everything to her according to the rules; listen to that, O lord of the people.
I shall describe the conjunction of the lunar mansions (nakṣatrayoga), which destroys all sins.
O highly fortunate one, by gratifying virtuous Brahmins with milk-rice mixed with clarified butter under the constellation Kṛttikā, one attains unsurpassed worlds;
O best of the Pāṇḍavas, [likewise] under Rohiṇī, with meat, food, and clarified butter.

Having satisfied virtuous Brahmins, one attains unsurpassed worlds; for the sake of discharging one's debt, a gift of milk and food should be given to a twice-born man on the lunar mansion presided over by Soma (Mṛgaśīrṣa), specifically a milch cow together with her calf.
Having given [this], situated in a divine celestial chariot, one attains unsurpassed heaven.
By giving *kṛśara* mixed with sesame seeds under the constellation Ārdrā while composed in mind,
a man, O best of men, crosses over all difficulties whatsoever.
Having given well-cooked cakes filled with ghee under the constellation Punarvasu,

one is born into a family as a person of renown, endowed with beauty, and virtuous. Furthermore, by giving gold— whether fashioned or unfashioned— under the constellation Puṣya, one attains these same qualities.
In worlds devoid of light, he shines like the moon;
likewise, he who gives a beautiful silver image under the constellation Āśleṣā is liberated from all fears and is born learned in the scriptures.
By giving vessels filled with sesame seeds under the Maghā constellation,
a man is born possessed of cattle and sons. Under the Pūrvaphalgunī constellation, O bull among the twice-born, one should give a mare.
Having given [a gift], one attains the worlds of the merit-makers, which are served by the gods.
By giving a golden lotus during the conjunction of Uttaraphalgunī,
one reaches the world of the Sun, freed from all afflictions.
Having given an elephant made of gold according to one's means in the constellation Hasta,
one goes to the abode of Śakra, mounted upon the back of a noble elephant.
By giving a bull in Citrā, one attains the highest merit among all merits.
He wanders in the world of the Apsarases and rejoices in the Nandana grove;
and by giving wealth during the Svāti constellation for whatever is desired by oneself here,
one attains auspicious worlds and great fame in this world.
O Great King, by giving a cart adorned with draft animals, complete with its equipment, filled with grain, and covered with cloth under the asterism Viśākhā,
one pleases one’s father and enjoys infinite rewards after death.
And that man does not encounter difficult realms such as Raurava;
having given what he desires to the Brahmins, he goes to his desired destination. By giving blankets and coverings under the constellation Anurādhā, he attains the same.
Having given black śāka vegetables along with their roots to Brahmins, a mortal dwells for more than a hundred years in heaven surrounded by hosts of gods;
he attains seniority over his brothers and goes to his desired destination.
Having offered roots and fruits to the Brahmins with a concentrated mind at the root [of the tree],
he gratifies all his ancestors and attains the unsurpassed goal. Furthermore, if a man offers vessels of curd under the Pūrvāṣāḍhā stars...
By giving [a gift] to a Brahmin who is endowed with noble lineage and conduct and has mastered the Vedas, one is born after death in a family possessing great enjoyments;
surrounded by sons and grandsons, one likewise becomes possessed of cattle and wealth.
By giving a stirred drink (udamantha) mixed with ghee, honey,
and molasses under the Uttara-āṣāḍhās, one shall obtain all desires;
likewise, by giving milk saturated with ghee and honey under the portion of Abhijit.
Constantly devoted to the Dharma, that merit-sharing man dwells in heaven among the wise;
he who here gives an excellent book for the purpose of hearing it travels by his own will in a celestial vehicle to all the worlds— of this there is no doubt.
A person who gives a pair of oxen to a Brahmin under the asterism Dhaniṣṭhā attains honor everywhere,
wherever he may be born in this world;
likewise, by giving sandalwood with aloe-wood under the conjunction of Śatabhiṣaj.
After death, one attains the world of the Apsarases and beautiful fragrances.
Under the conjunction of Pūrvabhādrapadā, one should cause king-māṣa beans to be given;
endowed with all kinds of food and fruits, such a person indeed becomes happy after death.
He who gives fine clothing during the Uttara-yoga pleases all the ancestors and enjoys infinite rewards after death;
he who gives a cow with a bronze milking vessel under the constellation Revatī [obtains the same].
Having departed this life, he approaches the donor, taking with him his desires.
O best of men, by giving a chariot yoked with horses under the asterism of Aśvinī,
one is born into a family abounding in elephants, horses, and chariots, and becomes endowed with splendor.
By giving a sesame-cow to the twice-born under the asterism Bharaṇī,
a man indeed obtains abundant cattle and likewise glory after death.
Thus has been declared this section on the southern quarter in connection with the lunar mansions.
This [mantra], which pacifies all sins and destroys all calamities, was told to Devakī by Nārada and by me as well;
herein there is no restriction of time, nor likewise any sequence of lunar mansions.
Wealth and faith, O Indra among kings, are said to be the causes in this matter. Whatever gift has been proclaimed by the Blessed One, the son of the Lotus-born, having carefully examined the Vedas—
if one gives that while possessing wealth to those of virtuous conduct, what is there in this world, O Pārtha, that has not been accomplished by him?

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-second chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for Giving Gifts on the Lunar Mansions," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[Now follows] the description of giving gifts on the lunar days (tithis). Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Now, O Yudhiṣṭhira, I shall describe to you the gift of the lunar day (tithidāna),
which pacifies all sins and destroys all obstacles;
whatever evil there may be, whether mental, verbal, or born of action.

O Pāṇḍava, through this gift, everything attains complete pacification. Beginning from the bright fortnight of the months of Śrāvaṇa, Kārttika, Caitra, Vaiśākha, and likewise Phālguna, that which increases merit should be given.
Wealth, a companion endowed with faith, and likewise the arrival of a worthy recipient—
the seers of truth have declared these to be the constant time for giving here in this world.
Whether at a sacred ford, in a temple, in a cow-pen, or in one's own home, one who is self-restrained [should give].
Whatever that best of men gives becomes conducive to infinity.
Having honored the twice-born on the first lunar days (pratipad), and having worshipped Prajāpati,
he should have a golden eight-petaled lotus fashioned.
Having placed [the lotus] in a vessel made of udumbara wood filled with fragrant ghee,
and having worshipped it with flowers and incense, one should present it to a brahmin. By giving a lotus— the abode of Lakṣmī— according to this rite, [one attains the fruit].
One who is free from desire attains identity with Brahman; one who has desires obtains those desired objects.

Having worshipped the Fire on the second lunar day with the sequence "bhūḥ bhuvaḥ svaḥ," and having offered a hundred oblations of sesame and clarified butter, one should then offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
O King, one should place a golden image of Vaiśvānara upon a copper vessel filled with molasses and clarified butter, which rests atop a water-filled jar;
having worshipped it with garments, garlands, and various kinds of foods and edibles.
Then one should give it to a Brāhmaṇa, saying, "May Agni be pleased with me.
One is liberated from the sins committed throughout one's life; there is no doubt about this.
Having died, one goes to the city of Agni; thus spoke the sage Nārada.
On the third day, O Great King, having placed an auspicious golden image of Rādhā upon a copper vessel, one should set it down over salt; one should then cause cumin,
black pepper, and molasses to be offered at the side-posts.

O Pārtha, who can describe the fruit that one obtains by giving to a twice-born man a [cow] covered with a pair of red cloths, adorned with saffron, and having worshipped her with flowers, incense, and food offerings?
Where there are palaces made of gold and rivers with mud of milk-rice,
and where Gandharvas and Apsarases dwell— to that place those men go. Having returned from heaven to this world of transmigration, they become handsome and fortunate.
The donor shall become a consumer of abundant wealth, endowed with sons and grandsons;
or, in this world, a woman shall likewise be possessed of those same qualities—of this there is no doubt.
On the fourth lunar day, one should offer a very beautiful golden elephant weighing more than a pala.
Having meditated upon Gaṇeśa as holding a goad, one should place him upon a drona-measure of sesame seeds;
having worshipped him with garments and flowers and offered the food-oblation (naivedya),
one should then give [the image] to a Brāhmaṇa, saying, "May Gaṇeśa be pleased."
In all undertakings, no obstacle shall arise for him.
For seven births, he shall have elephants intoxicated with rut;
mounted upon a lordly elephant, he shall be a conqueror of the three worlds.
On the fifth lunar day, one should have a serpent fashioned out of a single piece of gold;
having worshipped it while placed in the midst of milk, clarified butter, and leaves, one should present it as a gift.
After honoring the twice-born with garments and prostrating before him, one should ask for his forgiveness.
In this world and in the next, this gift brings happiness;
it dispels the afflictions caused by serpents and destroys all that is evil.
Likewise, Śambhu has declared this to be the expiation for one bitten by a serpent.
On the sixth [lunar day], having had Kumāra fashioned together with Śakti, mounted upon his peacock,
and adorned with a golden garland according to one's means,
one should then worship him with devotion on a peak using rice grains and cloths.
On the sixth day, having fashioned a golden image of Skanda according to one's ability,
and having worshipped him with perfumes, flowers, incense, and food offerings,
one should then bow down and give it to a Brāhmaṇa who maintains a family.
Having attained supreme prosperity in this world, one is glorified in heaven after death;
a Śūdra attains the status of a Brāhmaṇa, and a Brāhmaṇa attains the world of Brahmā.
By worshipping the Sun on the seventh lunar day, and by honoring Brāhmaṇas and an excellent horse, [one gains these rewards].
One should give [a horse] with its neck adorned, equipped with a saddle, and accompanied by a sacrificial fee;
such a person attains the world of the Sun and rejoices together with the Sun.
When a well-adorned horse is given, the Gandharvas attain satisfaction.

On the eighth day, one should bow to a Brahmin and give a white bull— possessing unimpaired limbs, capable of bearing the yoke, covered with a pair of white cloths, and adorned with bells and ornaments— saying, "May the Bull-bannered Lord be pleased."
Then, having performed a circumambulation, one should follow [the bull] as far as the door.
O King, by this gift, the world of Śiva is not difficult to attain;
for upon the shoulders of the bull, the fourteen worlds are established.
Therefore, by the gift of a bull, the goddess Bhāratī becomes as if bestowed.
On the ninth lunar day, having had a golden lion fashioned according to one's means,
adorned with eight pearls and draped in blue cloth;
One should give [this gift] while recollecting the Goddess, the destroyer of wicked Daityas;
by thus bestowing it upon the most excellent of the twice-born, one attains all desires,
even when on a path through wildernesses, forest fastnesses, or infested with thieves and beasts of prey.
By the power of this gift, those who would harm him do not harm him;
upon death, he goes to the city of the Goddess, being honored by gods and asuras. When his merit is exhausted, returning here to this world, he becomes a righteous king.
On the tenth day, O tiger among kings, ten directions made of gold were established upon salt,
molasses, milk, niṣpāva beans, sesame seeds,
the three products of the cow, rice grains, and mung beans.

Having worshipped with garments, flowers, and other offerings, one should present it to a twice-born brahmin. O Indra among kings, listen to the fruit of the merit of that man or woman who, by this very rite, performs the ritual extinguishing (nirvāpaṇa).
In this world he shall be a lord of the earth, and after death he is glorified in heaven.
All his hopes, whatever desires are cherished by his mind, are fulfilled.
Then, returning from that heaven to this world, he is born into a great family.
On the eleventh day, having caused a golden Garuḍa to be fashioned and worshipped according to one's means upon ghee in a copper vessel,
[one should give it] especially to a Brahmin who is devoted to the five fires and is particularly learned in the Purāṇas.
Having given these— what is the use of saying more— one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu:
a cow, a bull, a buffalo, gold, the seven types of grain, goats and sheep,
a mare, all kinds of sugarcane juices, as well as many fruit-bearing trees.
Having gathered various flowers and many diverse perfumes according to one's ability, one should cover them with new cloths;
on the twelfth lunar day (Dvādaśī), these twelve items should be presented to Brāhmaṇas.
Or rather, O Great King, listen to the fruit of that single act:
having attained supreme fame in this world and enjoyed pleasures as desired,
he then goes to the city of Viṣṇu, being attended by throngs of celestial nymphs.
Having returned here upon the exhaustion of his karma, he becomes a righteous king;
he performs sacrifices, is a lord of charity, and lives for a hundred autumns.
Furthermore, on the thirteenth lunar day, he should bathe thirteen Brahmins here.
Having clothed them in new garments, one should then worship them with perfumes and flowers;
one should feed them excellent food and present a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) consisting of pieces of gold according to one's ability, saying, "May the Righteous One (Dharma) be pleased."
To Dharmarāja, Kāla, Citragupta, Daṇḍin, Mṛtyu, Kṣayarūpa, Antaka, Yama,
Pretanātha, Raudra, and likewise to Vaivasvata.
Having pronounced these thirteen names here for the God who stands upon the buffalo,
one endowed with faith should prostrate and then dismiss Him.
O Great King, whoever performs this delightful worship, [attains the highest state].
Having lived happily in the mortal world, free from disease,
that man who has followed the path of Yama does not subsequently encounter suffering;
he does not behold the face of a preta, but goes instead to the realm of the ancestors.
Having returned here from that state due to the exhaustion of his merit, he shall become happy and free from disease.
On the fourteenth lunar day, one should offer a very beautiful buffalo and a water-pot filled with milk,
accompanied by a plowman, adorned with gold and fine garments.
O best of men, he who gives a bull— adorned with the beauty of bells and ornaments and accompanied by a cow— to a Śiva-devoted Brāhmaṇa who maintains a household,
is glorified in the world of Śiva after having given that bull.
Having remained there for a long time, he eventually returns to the surface of the earth and is born into a great family endowed with health and wealth,
for the sake of fulfilling all desires, for as long as three hundred lifetimes.
Having performed the ritual release of a bull according to the prescribed rules on the full moon day,
one should worship with fragrant flowers and offerings of food a beautiful image made of silver or moonstone using a single fruit.

O King of kings, having made a formal resolve (saṃkalpa), one should give [the gift] to a brāhmaṇa along with garments, ornaments, and decorations, using this mantra as it has been declared; listen to that:
"O you who arose from the Ocean of Milk, O illuminator of the courtyard of the three worlds!"

"O King, grant auspiciousness to the Lord of Umā, the crest-jewel upon his head; salutations again and again! By this gift, O monarch, you shall shine like the moon in heaven, surrounded by celestial nymphs (apsarases) until the dissolution of all beings."

Those of pure being who bestow these gifts upon the most excellent of the twice-born according to the prescribed rules and in due order, having enjoyed happiness in the worlds of Brahmā and Viṣṇu, go to oneness with Śiva; of this I have no doubt.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-third chapter, titled "Description of Gifts on Specific Lunar Days," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the Ritual for the Gift of a Boar.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Yudhiṣṭhira, I shall now describe to you the gift of the Primordial Boar (Ādivārāha).
That which was formerly proclaimed by me to the Earth while in the form of a boar—
meritorious, purifying, life-prolonging, the most excellent of all supreme gifts,
the destroyer of faults such as great sins, and honored by the best of the righteous— [is this].
Gifts should be given during the transit of the sun, during eclipses, on the twelfth lunar days,
at sacrifices, festivals, and weddings, or upon seeing an evil dream or a portentous marvel;
and whenever wealth arises that is accompanied by a mind full of faith.
At that very moment, it should be the time for giving, since life is uncertain;
whether at sacred sites such as Kurukṣetra and others, at rivers such as the Gaṅgā and others, in holy cities, or in wildernesses and forests.
Whether in a cow-pen, a temple, on a chariot, or in the courtyard of one's own home,
O Pārtha, it should be given to a Brāhmaṇa who maintains a family, according to the ancient rite,
after having strewn it with Kuśa grass consecrated by the syllable Om (Praṇava).
Above them, one should fashion a boar out of sesame seeds;
it should be filled with four *drauṇas*, or else half of that, or even with one *āḍhaka*. One should not practice stinginess regarding the wealth expended.
The face should be made of gold, and the two arms equipped with the discus and mace. One should have the tusk made of silver and adorned with a ruby;
one should place a conch at the side and a golden forest garland.
The wise man should likewise have the two feet fashioned out of silver with flowers;
he should have the auspicious earth depicted as clinging to the tips of the tusks, made of gold,
endowed with all kinds of grains and liquids, and its form adorned with garments.
Having covered the Lord of Gods, Varāha, who grants all desires, with garments,
and having fashioned a line of hair with *kuśa* grass, one should then worship him with perfumes and flowers.
A sacrifice to the nine planets (*navagrahamakha*) should be performed, and an oblation (*homa*) with sesame seeds is prescribed here.
Having thus established [the deity] according to the prescribed rite, one should then recite this hymn:
"O Lord Varāha, crush, crush all wicked things and the fruits of every sin! O Great-Tusked One, adorned with radiant golden earrings!"

"Salutation to the one who holds the conch, discus, and sword in his hands; to the destroyer of Hiraṇyākṣa; to the one who lifted up the earth with his tusks; salutation to the embodiment of the three Vedas. Having uttered this and having paid obeisance, one should follow [the deity] by circumambulating.
Then one should give that [gift] to a Brahmin, adorned with garments and ornaments;
the supreme sages have declared that its formal acceptance consists of grasping the [donor's] feet.
Having given it according to this rite, one should prostrate and ask for forgiveness.
O Lord of the Earth, O Pārtha, by whom can that fruit be described which one obtains after thus giving a boar that grants all desires?
Whatever merit exists in all gifts, and whatever fruit exists in all sacrifices— [that fruit one attains].
One obtains that fruit by giving to the god Janārdana;
having rescued the Earth according to one's ability, just as she was raised up by Varāha,
one is honored in the world of Viṣṇu after having delivered one's own lineage.

This gift is common to Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, women, and the Śūdra class, as well as to the Yogins of Śiva and Viṣṇu. Having given to a Brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas an image of Nṛsiṃha made of sesame seeds, *amalaka* fruit, and gold, along with clothing—
Having rescued his ancestors along with his wife and friends, he attains the realm of the Siddhas, which is frequented by gods and Siddhas.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Procedure for the Gift of the Boar," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[Now begins] the description of the procedure for the gift of the Mountain of Grain (Dhānyaparvata).
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Blessed One, I wish to hear about the supreme majesty of giving—
that which is inexhaustible in the next world and honored by the hosts of gods and sages."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O best of the Kurus, listen to that which was formerly spoken by Rudra to the high-souled Nārada, and likewise by the Fish [incarnation] to Manu.
I shall describe to you once more the tenfold gift of Meru,
by which a donor attains the higher worlds honored by the gods;
[a gift] found in the Purāṇas, the Vedas, the sacrifices, and the sacred studies.
One does not obtain here that fruit by studying or performing [other rites] which one experiences through this;
therefore, I shall describe the ritual procedure for the mountains in their proper order:
first is the mountain of grain (dhānya-śaila), and second is the mountain of salt (lavaṇācala).
The third is Guḍācala, while the fourth is Hemaparvata;
the fifth shall be Tilashaila, and the sixth Kārpāsaparvata;
the seventh is Ghṛtaśaila, and likewise the eighth is Rasashaila.
Likewise, the ninth is made of gold, and the tenth is a mountain of sugar;
I shall describe the ritual procedure for these in due order and according to the rules, on the auspicious occasion of the solstice, the equinox, the Vyatīpāta yoga, or the day of the new moon.
On the third day of the bright fortnight, during an eclipse, or at the waning of the moon;
or on the twelfth day,
or again on the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight, or primarily under an auspicious constellation.
One who understands the scriptures should give gifts such as the mountain of grain (dhānyaśaila) and others according to the sacred texts,
whether at a sacred ford (tīrtha), a temple, a cow-pen, or even at a confluence of rivers.
With devotion, one should have a square pavilion constructed facing the north.
There, on ground sloping toward the northeast, or facing east according to the prescribed rule,
having smeared the ground with cow-dung or having strewn kuśa grass upon it,
one should fashion a mountain in its center, accompanied by the supporting mountains (viṣkambhaparvatas).
With a thousand *droṇas* of grain, the best mountain here should be made;
the middling one with five hundred, and the smallest should consist of three hundred.
The Meru, made of great rice, should be joined with three trees of gold in its center.
It should be joined with pearls and diamonds on the south, with *gomedaka* and *puṣparāga* gems;
it should possess *gārutmata* and sapphire gems on the north, and with *vaiḍūrya* and ruby;
it should be surrounded by pieces of sandalwood and provided with coral creepers, and its surface should be of pure stone.
Then Brahmā, the Lord Viṣṇu, Purāri (Śiva), and Divākara (the Sun) shall also be here, golden-hued;
likewise, with their necks slightly raised, there shall be streams of ghee and water flowing in all directions.
Another divine mountain, clad in white garments, shall be in the east, while those in the south shall be black.
One should place garments behind [the central deity], then filaments, and red petals to the north.
Likewise, one should install the eight world-protectors (lokapālas), headed by Mahendra, in their proper order, made of silver.
There should be a row of various fruits all around, along with beautiful garlands, ointments, and other offerings.
And above, one should place a canopy of five colors, adorned with unfading flowers, or white;
having thus established the celestial mountain, the Unmanifested One (Unmanā) should then, in due order,
arrange the groups of supporting pillars (viṣkambha-gaṇas) in the four directions using a fourth part [of the space], along with flowers, ointments, and other offerings.
To the east, one should fashion Mount Mandara, which is frequented by many fruits and marked by clusters of shining golden *bhadra* trees;

it should be resplendent with a golden form, richly adorned with flowers, garments, and ointments. Furthermore, it should shine with the Kṣīroda and Aruṇoda lakes and with a silver forest fashioned from *śakti*-metal.
To the south, Mount Gandhamādana should be situated here, composed of wheat or made of gold.
One should fashion the entire first mountain out of gold, with its lord, the king of birds, holding Mount Mānasa;

and thereafter, one should cause the Tilācala mountain to be made, endowed with many fragrant flowers, a golden *pippala* tree, and golden swans, likewise provided with a forest of silver flowers. Having established that vast mountain, one should then place to its north the Supārśva mountain, made of black gram and possessing beautiful slopes.
One should fashion [the image] from flowers, with the form of a golden *vaṭa* tree adorned with all kinds of jewels, and made radiant by a golden cow;
likewise, having prepared it with the collection of honey, auspicious juices, silver, and shining essences,
one should then perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) with these four [substances] by means of eminent Brahmins who are knowers of the Vedas and Purāṇas, irreproachable and of excellent appearance.
Having fashioned a sacrificial pit here with its opening facing the east, one should perform the rite with sesame seeds, clarified butter, fuel sticks, and *kuśa* grass.
At night, a vigil should be kept with gentle songs and musical instruments; now I shall describe the invocation of the mountain deities:
"O abode and treasure-house of all the hosts of gods, O divine mountain, quickly destroy all obstacles within our homes!"
Bestow security and grant us supreme peace; being fully honored by us who possess the highest devotion, grant it to us.
You alone are the Blessed Lord, the Ruler, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the Sun;
you are the manifest, the unmanifest, and the supreme seed—therefore, protect us, O Eternal One!
Since you are the abode of the world-protectors, of Viśvamūrti,
and of Keśava, Arka, and the Vasus, therefore grant me peace;
since your head is never empty of the immortals and the Gandharvas.
Therefore, lift me up from this entire ocean of suffering and saṃsāra!
Having thus worshipped that Meru, one should also worship Mandara,
because it is [adorned] with Caitraratha and the most excellent Bhadrāśva.
O Mandara, you shine forth; quickly become a bringer of satisfaction! Since you are the crest-jewel of Jambudvīpa, O Gandhamādana, may my fame be sung by Gandharvas and Apsarases.
Since you possess Ketumāla and the Vaibhrāja forest,
and because your rocks are made of gold, therefore grant me peace.
Since you possess the Uttarakurus and the Sāvitra forest, [grant me peace].

"O Supārśva, you shine eternally; therefore, may there be for me the protection of prosperity. Having thus addressed them all, at the clear dawn, he should bathe and give the middle of the best of mountains to his preceptor.
O King, he should give those remaining five to the officiating priests in due order.
O Bhārata, thirty-four cows should be given, or ten;
or, according to his capacity, seven or eight—thus should one who lacks sufficient means give.
Even a single tawny cow that yields excellent milk should be given to the preceptor;
this same rule is prescribed for all mountains without exception. Whatever mantras are used in the worship, those very same ones are to be used for the ritual accessories as well.

For all the planets, the world-protectors, Brahmā and the others, along with their mounts, it is recommended that the fire-oblation (homa) be performed upon the mountains using their respective mantras. One should always observe a fast; however, if one is unable, eating only at night is prescribed.
Listen, O Bhārata, to the procedure for all mountains in due order,
as well as the mantras to be used at the time of the gift and the fruit obtained from the mountains.
Since food is declared to be Brahman, and since the vital breaths are established in food.
From food all beings arise; the world grows by means of food. Since food itself is Lakṣmī and food itself is Janārdana, therefore protect me, O best of mountains, in the form of a mountain of grain.
Whoever gives a mountain made of grain according to this rite is honored in the world of the gods for more than a hundred manvantaras,
in a place resplendent and crowded with hosts of Apsarases and Gandharvas.
Served by sages, he travels upon the back of heaven in a celestial chariot;
when his merit is exhausted, he obtains the sovereignty of kings in this world—of this there is no doubt.
[He who gives] a mountain of grain, resplendent with golden trees, joined by the supporting mountains, and frequented by gods and Siddhas.
"Those wise ones who, having prostrated before the Brahmins, bestow [this gift], attain the pair of supreme lotus feet of Parameṣṭhin.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Gift of the Mountain of Grains," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Purāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[Now follows] the description of the ritual for the gift of the Mountain of Salt.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the excellent mountain of salt (lavaṇācala),
by the gift of which a person attains the world united with Śiva.
The best salt-mountain (lavaṇācala) should be made with sixteen droṇas;
the middling one should be half of that, and the lowest is recorded as half of that again.
One who lacks wealth should have it made according to his ability, even down to half a droṇa.
One should construct the various regions and mountains separately using a fourth part [of the area];
one should always perform the ritual procedure for Brahmā and the others as previously described;
likewise, one should fashion all the golden trees and the abodes of the world-protectors.
In the same manner, one should place Kāmadeva and the others there upon their heads;
one should also keep a vigil here—learn from me the mantras for the gift:
"Since this essence of salt is produced from the juice of good fortune..."
And as one whose essence is charity, protect me from evil, O best of mountains!
Therefore, all the flavors of food are not superior without salt;
it is eternally dear to Śiva and Śivā, so be the bestower of peace.
Since it arose from the body of Viṣṇu and increases one's health,
and since you exist in the form of a mountain, protect me from the ocean of saṃsāra!
He who gives a mountain of salt according to this rite—
One shall dwell in Umā’s world for a kalpa, and from there go to the supreme goal.
Upon the exhaustion of merit, returning here to this world, one becomes a righteous king;
surrounded by sons and grandsons, he shall live for a hundred autumns.

Those who perform the gift of a mountain of salt attain a very great celestial chariot (*vimāna*) in heaven. There, served by hosts of Apsaras and honored by gods and demons, they remain with joyful minds, increasing in prosperity in the celestial realm.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Gift of a Mountain of Salt," in the *Uttara-parvan* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[Now begins] the description of the ritual for the gift of a mountain of jaggery (*guḍācala*).
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Hereafter I shall describe the most excellent mountain of jaggery (guḍaparvata),
by the gift of which a man attains heaven, which is honored by the gods.
The best [image] is made with ten bhāras, the middling with five, and the lowest with three bhāras; that which is half of that is considered the smallest.
Likewise, one should perform the invocation, worship, and the veneration of the golden tree and the deities.
There, one should perform the rites for the supporting mountains (*viṣkaṃbha-parvata*), the lakes, and the forest deities;
likewise, the fire-oblation (*homa*), the ritual vigil (*jāgaraṇa*), and the consecration of the world-protectors (*lokapālādhivāsana*).
One should act as in the case of the mountain of grain (*dhānyaparvata*) and recite this mantra:
Just as Janārdana is the supreme soul among the gods,
the Sāmaveda among the Vedas, Mahādeva among yogis,
the Praṇava among all mantras, and Pārvatī among women; so too [is he]...
Likewise, sugarcane juice is always considered the best among all liquids;
therefore, O Mountain of Jaggery, grant me supreme prosperity.
[I bow] to all the gods and demons, as well as the Nāgas, Yakṣas, Ṛkṣas, and Garuḍas.
And since there was even the destruction of Pārvatī, therefore protect me always!
He who gives a mountain made of jaggery according to this rite,
being honored by Gandharvas, is glorified in the world of Gaurī.
Furthermore, at the end of a hundred kalpas, he shall become the sovereign of the seven continents,
endowed with long life and health, and unconquered by his enemies.
There was a highly fortunate queen named Sulabhā, who was devoted to her vows.
The beloved wife of Marutta was endowed with beauty and youth;
that high-souled king had seven hundred wives,
who always carried out her commands as if they were maidservants.
The king was intent on looking at her face, and she was his beloved.
Then, after a long time, Durvāsas, the best of sages,
arrived in her presence while wandering about at will.
Then, having performed hospitable rites for him and having offered the *arghya* according to the prescribed rule,
Sulabhā questioned the sinless Brahmin Durvāsas.
Sulabhā said:
"By what merit, O Blessed One, does my king Priyaṅkara remain always under my control, intent on looking upon my face? And by what merit,
O Brahmin, do my co-wives always delight in what is dear and beneficial to me?"
"Tell me this, O Blessed One; my curiosity is great.
Durvāsas said:
"Listen attentively, O fair-browed one, to the ancient account of your own past lives."
"O fortunate one, I know your entire history in its entirety.
In former times, you were the queen of the Vaiśya king in the city of Girivraja; you were righteous, truthful in character, and devoted to your husband."
In that regard, O child, you previously heard the entire procedure for making gifts from the presence of the Brahmins while standing near your husband;
specifically, the mountain of jaggery was described there by the Brahmins.
O daughter, having gathered [the materials] at that time, you also gave [it] according to the prescribed rites;
by the majesty of that gift, O lovely-faced one,
you have enjoyed a kingdom free of rivals and undisturbed for four births.
For seven other births, you shall possess sovereignty, incomparable good fortune, beauty, and health; and all this,
born of the gift of the mountain of jaggery, will surely come to pass.
"O lady of excellent limbs, tell me your story; may you become pregnant with a son.
Therefore, this gift should be given by one desiring the highest fruit;
[by so doing] one obtains eternal progress, as well as good fortune and beauty."
O King, they especially praise this gift for women;
having obtained the previously mentioned fruit, one is born having accomplished all that was to be done.
[This place] is filled with the sound of water flowing from the beautiful caves of Kṛṣṇeṣṭa and is frequented by hundreds of Gandharva and Siddha women.
"O Bhārata, by one who acts according to the prescribed rules, Gaurī always attains satisfaction through the gift of a mountain of jaggery (*guḍācala*).

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Gift of a Mountain of Jaggery," in the *Uttara-parvan* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[Now begins] the description of the ritual for the gift of a mountain of gold (*hemācala*).
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Now I shall describe the supreme Suvarṇācala, which removes all sins,
by the grace of which a human being goes to the abode of Vairiñca.
The best [image] weighs one thousand palas, the middling five hundred; the lowest is half of that.
Likewise, even one of small means should give according to his ability;
a wise man should give more than one pala, as far as his capacity allows.
O best of kings, one should perform everything just as in the case of the mountain of grain;
likewise, having fashioned the supporting mountains, one should utter the mantra:
"Salutations to you, the seed of Brahman; salutations indeed to the womb of Brahman."
Since you bestow infinite fruit, therefore protect me, O mountain;
since you are the offspring of Agni and the embryo of the Lord of the World,
therefore protect me, O best of mountains, in the form of the Golden Mountain.
Whoever gives a mountain of gold according to this rite goes to the supreme abode where the Lord Maheśvara dwells;
he remains there for a hundred years and thereafter attains the highest goal.

There is no gift superior to that of a mountain of gold found anywhere else. He who is capable and bestows here a golden mountain of the Earth, endowed with hundreds of jeweled peaks, accompanied by the eight guardians of the world and the lords of sages, shall dwell in the world of Gaṇeśa for a kalpa, O bull among the Kurus, just like Kumāra. Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Gift of a Mountain of Gold," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the Ritual for the Gift of a Mountain of Sesame Seeds.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Hereafter, I shall describe the ritual for the mountain of sesame seeds according to the prescribed rules.
By the gift of which a man goes to the unsurpassed world of Viṣṇu:
sesame seeds are an incomparable purifier and the most sanctifying among all purifiers;
born from the body of Viṣṇu, they have therefore attained the state of excellence.
In ancient times, there were two sons of Diti named Madhu and Kaiṭabha;
there, Viṣṇu engaged in incessant combat with Madhu for a thousand years,
yet the Dānava did not survive.
Then, O descendant of Kuru, as the wielder of the mace grew enraged, there was a great sweat upon him;
and when he fell upon the surface of the earth, sesame seeds, beans,
and kusha grass rose up in fragments and particles.
And Madhu, the best among the strong, was slain in battle by Hari;
at that time, the entire earth was colored by his fat,
and thus she obtained the name Medinī, the bearer of mountains.
Then, when the foremost of the Daityas had been slain, the gods attained supreme satisfaction;
having praised him greatly with hymns of praise, they spoke to the bull among the gods.
The gods said:
O Lord, the world is sustained by you and likewise created by you;
O Master, everything dissolves into you alone, O Madhusūdana.
Therefore, let these sesame seeds born from your own body be for the welfare of the world.
And may they always protect the offerings to the gods and the ancestors, O Lord of Gods;
they should be constantly employed by men devoted to them in rites for the gods and the ancestors.
For neither Daityas nor Piśācas, O Bhārata, ever act as officiating priests for a Brāhmaṇa.
"Wherever sesame seeds are employed, let that be done quickly.
Having heard those words of the gods, Viṣṇu said this to them:
"Let there be sesame seeds for the protection of even the three worlds."

Having bathed and being endowed with faith, one should offer water with sesame seeds to the gods during the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa), and to the ancestors (pitṛs) during the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa);
the handful of water should be presented with seven or eight sesame seeds.
The gods and the ancestors, being satisfied, bestow auspiciousness upon him.
Whatever has been defiled by dogs or crows, or even by outcasts and the like, shall all become pure when sprinkled with sesame seeds; of this there is no doubt.
Whoever, having fashioned an excellent mountain out of these crushed sesame seeds,
should bestow it as a gift upon a preeminent brahmin, his gift shall become inexhaustible.
An excellent mountain is considered to consist of ten *droṇas*, while a middling one is held to consist of five.
O Indra among kings, the smallest sesame-mountain is proclaimed to consist of three [loads];
everything else, such as the supporting mountains and so forth, is as previously described.
O best of monarchs, I shall now duly explain the gift of food.
Since sesame seeds, *kuśa* grass, and black gram (*māṣa*) originated from the sweat of Viṣṇu’s body during the slaying of Madhu, may they grant us peace here;
and since it is with sesame seeds alone that consecration is performed for offerings to the gods (*havya*) and the ancestors (*kavya*).
"O Lord of Mountains, O Tilācala, lift me up from worldly existence; salutations be unto you!
Having thus addressed [the deity], he who gives this unsurpassed mountain of sesame seeds indeed attains the station of Viṣṇu, from which a return to this world is difficult to find.
One attains long life in this world and the next;
honored by the ancestors, gods, and gandharvas, one shall go to heaven. Upon the exhaustion of merit, returning here, one becomes a righteous king.
Or his wife shall be a woman endowed with beauty and good fortune,
skillful, born of a noble lineage, and possessed of sons and grandsons;
having heard this ritual procedure, one should perform it according to the rules, filled with faith.
One shall obtain a fruit equal to the merit of the gift of a Kapila cow.
Having reflected with the intellect upon the collection of scriptures, consider whether there exists any other gift equal to a mountain of sesame seeds;
for those by whom the rites for the ancestors are abandoned and the fire-oblation is not performed, what gift can possibly grant them happiness in this world?

Thus ends the one hundred and nineteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Gift of a Mountain of Sesame," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[Now follows] the description of the ritual for the gift of a mountain of cotton. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Hereafter, I shall describe the supreme mountain of cotton (kārpāsācala),
which is the most excellent of all gifts and is dear to all the inhabitants of heaven.
Having secured the proper place and time, as well as wealth and faith, one should proceed with diligence.
This great gift (mahādāna) should be given for the sake of uplifting one's lineage;
having performed everything without exception according to the previously mentioned procedure,
one should there fashion a mountain out of cotton according to the rules.
The wise should construct the best mountain out of twenty *bhāras*;
the middling is said to consist of ten, and the lowest is considered to be five.
One of modest means should give it with one *bhāra*, avoiding any stinginess regarding wealth.
O bull among kings, having prepared everything just as in the case of the mountain of grain,
one should perform the vigil in that same manner and likewise the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana).
Then, when the night has turned to dawn, one should utter this mantra:
"Since you alone are always an obstacle for people here in this world,
O Karpāsa Mountain, therefore become the destroyer of the multitude of our sins.
Thus, whoever should give the lordly Karpāsa Mountain on the occasion of a festival, [attains the supreme goal].

One shall dwell in the world of Rudra for a kalpa, and thereafter become a king here on earth—handsome, fortunate, eloquent, illustrious, and of incomparable valor. Or, for five births, one shall be born as a woman; of this there is no doubt.
Since the sole kinsman of the world, who is endowed with excellent garments, is devoid [of this gift] when one bows down,
therefore, for the sake of quelling the multitude of sins and for eternal happiness, it should always be given by a man free from envy toward the Lord of Men (the King).

Thus ends the two-hundredth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Gift of the Cotton Mountain," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the Ritual for the Gift of a Mountain of Ghee.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the unsurpassed gift of a mountain of ghee.
Divine, consisting of fiery nectar, and the destroyer of great sins,
the "Mountain of Ghee" (Ghṛtācala) made from fifty jars of ghee is considered the best;
that of half that size is middling, and half of that again is known as the lowest.
One with limited wealth, however, should perform the rite according to his capacity and the prescribed injunctions;
likewise, he should fashion the supporting mountains (viṣkaṃbha-parvatas) using one-fourth of that amount.
He should also arrange jars filled with śāli rice.
One should have them constructed closely joined, not too high, and according to the rules for aesthetic beauty.
One should wrap them with white cloths and adorn them with sugarcane stalks, fruits, and so forth.
The remaining procedure here is recited as being the same as that for the mountain of grain (*dhānyaparvata*).

Having first performed the ritual acceptance (*adhivāsana*), he should likewise perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) and the worship of the gods. When the night has turned to dawn, with a tranquil mind, he should present the supporting mountains (*viṣkaṃbha-parvata*) to the preceptor and the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
O son of Kuntī, listen to this mantra which I shall speak to you:
"Since ghee was produced from the union [of milk] for the sake of immortal splendor,
therefore may Śaṅkara be pleased with me by means of this mountain of ghee."
Therefore, Brahman, consisting of light, is eternally established in ghee;
O Supporter of the Earth, protect us by means of this mountain of ghee.
According to this ritual, one should offer this unsurpassed mountain of ghee.
Even one joined with great sins attains the world of Śaṅkara,
traveling in a celestial chariot yoked with swans and cranes, garlanded with networks of tinkling bells, and surrounded by Apsarases, Siddhas, and Vidyādharas.
Those mortals who here bestow a mountain of clarified butter, attended by beautiful women with swaying earrings, shall dwell together with their ancestors until the dissolution of all beings;
they shall attain heaven, the abode of the Lord of the Gods, or the presence of Śiva, and all these things shall remain unshakable through the bond of affection.

Thus ends the two hundred and first chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Gift of the Mountain of Ghee," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[Now follows] the description of the ritual for the gift of the Mountain of Jewels. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the unsurpassed Mountain of Jewels (Ratnācala),
by the gift of which a man goes to the worlds inhabited by the Seven Sages. With a thousand pearls, the mountain becomes unsurpassed.
The medium [image] is five hundred [units] in size, while the inferior is remembered as three hundred;
one with little wealth, however, should make it with a hundred pearls.
The supporting mountains (viṣkambha-parvatas) should be on all sides, equal to a fourth part [of the main image].
To the east, Gandhamādana should be fashioned by the wise with vajras and gomeda stones; to the south, it should be joined with sapphires and topazes;
to the west, Vipulācala, the mountain of Sāvitra, should be made of lapis lazuli and coral.
One should also place a ruby together with gold to the north.
One should arrange the remainder here just as in the case of the mountain of grain (dhānyaparvata). Likewise, having performed the invocation for the trees and the golden deities.
One should worship with flowers and food offerings, and at dawn perform the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*).
As before, the preceptor and the officiating priests should recite these mantras:
"Just as all the hosts of gods are established within all jewels..."
And since you are eternally composed of jewels, O Great Mountain, protect us;
for Janārdana attains satisfaction through the gift of jewels—
therefore, protect us always with the offering of jewels for worship.
He who gives a mountain made of jewels according to this rite goes to the world of Viṣṇu, which is honored by the Lord of the Immortals;
having dwelt there for a full hundred kalpas, O lord of men, he returns here.
Endowed with beauty, health, and virtue, one shall become the sovereign of the seven islands.
Whatever sin, such as the killing of a Brahmin, has been committed here or in the hereafter,
all of that goes to destruction like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt.

"Having offered to the best of the twice-born a mountain of jewels, variegated with patterns of pearls, gold, and coral, and endowed with a mass of shimmering rays from great gems— one who possesses such radiant splendor shall surpass the world of the gods. Thus ends the two hundred and second chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Gift of the Jewel Mountain," in the *Uttara-parvan* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the Ritual for the Gift of the Silver Mountain.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Hereafter, I shall describe the unsurpassed gift of the silver mountain.
O best of men, by the gift of which a person goes to the world of Soma:
a silver mountain weighing a thousand palas is considered the highest;
one of five [thousand] is declared middling, and half of that is remembered as the lowest.
If one is unable [to do so], one should always devoutly have [the mountains] made beyond twenty [yojanas].
Likewise, one should fashion the supporting mountains (viṣkaṃbha-parvatas) with a fourth part [of that size].
One should construct Mandara and the other mountains out of silver according to the previous rule and the prescribed ritual.
In that same manner, O King, one should have the world-protectors fashioned from silver—namely Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others. Here, the pedestal (nitaṃba) should be made of gold;
whereas for all others, that which would otherwise be silver should here be made of gold.
Having performed the remaining rites as before, including the fire-oblation and the night vigil,
one should likewise present a mountain of silver to the preceptor at dawn.
One should also give the mountains of the supporting peaks to the officiating priests and honor them with ornaments.
Reciting this mantra, one who is free from envy and holds *darbha* grass in his hand should offer silver;
for since it is beloved by the ancestors and brings auspiciousness to Śaṅkara,
may it therefore protect us from the terrible ocean of saṃsāra.
The person who, having thus dedicated it, gives this excellent silver mountain,
obtains the fruit of giving ten thousand cows;
he dwells in the world of Soma together with hosts of Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and Apsarases.
The wise man shall dwell there, being honored, until the dissolution of all beings.

O King, those virtuous ones who bestow the silver mountain— covered with rows of golden stones, accompanied by lakes of clear water, stainless, and free from sorrow— go, O King, to the world of Soma, cleansed of all impurities.

Thus ends the two hundred and third chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Gift of the Silver Mountain," in the *Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the *Uttara Parvan*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira. [Now follows] the Description of the Ritual for the Gift of the Sugar Mountain.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the supreme mountain of sugar (śarkarācala),
by the gift of which Viṣṇu, Arka, and Rudra are always pleased.
With eight loads of sugar, the great mountain becomes excellent.

The middling [size] is declared to be with four *bhāras*, and the inferior is remembered as being with two *bhāras*. One who has little wealth should make the supporting mountains (*viṣkaṃbha-parvata*) with one *bhāra* or even half a *bhāra*, using a fourth part [of the size of the main mountain].
Having prepared everything according to the ritual for the Mountain of Grain (Dhānyaparvata), including the addition of the six flavors, one should likewise place three golden trees upon Mount Meru:
the Mandāra, the Pārijāta, and the third, the Kalpapādapa.

One should place these three trees upon the summit of all [mountains]. The *haricandana* and *saṃtāna* trees are to be established on the eastern and western sides respectively on all mountains, especially on the Śarkarācala mountain.
One should place Kāmadeva at the foot of Mount Mandara;
Garuḍa should be fashioned at the foot of the Jambū tree on Gandhamādana;
and on Vipulācala, there should be a golden image of Haṃsa facing the east.

Those seeking prosperity should fashion a fragrant golden [cow] facing the south. Having performed everything— including the invocation and the sacrifice— just as in the case of the Mountain of Grain,
one should then present the central, most excellent mountain to the preceptor.
To the officiating priests (ṛtvij), he should recite these mantras over the four mountains:
"This supreme essence of the nectar of good fortune is combined with sugar;
since you cause delight, O Lord of Mountains, may you be so forever."

O Śarkarācala, you have arisen from those droplets that fell upon the earth as the gods were drinking nectar; protect us! For it is from the center of the bow of the Mind-born [Kāma] that this sugar-grain was produced.
O Great Mountain, you are composed of that [essence]; protect me from the ocean of saṃsāra!
The man who gives a mountain of sugar according to this rite, being liberated from all sins, goes to the abode of Śiva.

Mounting a vehicle resembling the moon and other luminaries, he shall set out together with his attendants; he shall dwell in the sky at the station of Viṣṇu. Then, at the end of a hundred kalpas, he shall become the sovereign of the seven continents.
Endowed with long life and health for as long as thirty thousand births,
one should, free from envy, give food according to one's ability on all mountains;
or, with his permission, one may personally consume alkaline salt.
One should cause all the mountain-apparatus to reach the abode of the Brāhmaṇas.
Formerly, in the Brahmakalpa, there was a lord of men who was the very embodiment of Dharma;
he was a friend of Śakra, by whom thousands of Daityas were slain.
By whose splendor the moon, the sun, and others have become lusterless;
by whom even hundreds of kings have been defeated;
and who, though a mere human, is unimpeded and assumes any form at will.
His wife was named Bhānumatī, the most beautiful woman in the three worlds;
in beauty she was like Lakṣmī herself, having surpassed even the celestial beauties.
She was the chief queen of that king, dearer to him than his own life.
He shone like Śrī in the midst of ten thousand women and was never abandoned by ten million kings. Once, while seated in his place, he questioned his own domestic priest.
With his heart filled with wonder, he asked Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages:
"O Blessed One, by what dharma does my unsurpassed prosperity arise? And why is there always such vast and supreme splendor in my body?"
Vasiṣṭha said:
In ancient times, there was a courtesan named Līlāvatī who was devoted to Śiva. On the fourteenth lunar day, she gave a mountain of salt to her preceptor.

Then, in accordance with the prescribed rites, a goldsmith of the Śūdra caste named Śauṇḍa became a servant in the house of Līlāvatī along with the gods of the Hemavṛkṣa grove; by him, golden objects were fashioned.
O King, having brought together trees and the foremost of the immortals,
who were endowed with great beauty and filled with faith,
and having understood their intention toward righteous deeds, he did not by any means accept [the gift] into his heart.
O King, the golden celestial trees were ignited by her wife,
and Līlāvatī herself performed service at her side;
with great joy, the two of them attended to the twice-born Brahmin and carried out all his needs.
O King, after a long time, that courtesan Līlāvatī,
completely liberated from all sins, went to the abode of Śiva;
and as for that goldsmith, though he was poor, he was possessed of great fortitude.
You have not yet paid the price for her here;
you have now become the lord of the seven islands, possessing a splendor equal to ten thousand suns—
by whom [trees] fashioned of gold and golden deities were provided.
This wife of yours, Bhānumatī, has been properly kindled;
by this kindling, her naturally noble form has become radiant, as has her sovereignty over this world.
Therefore, that preparatory rite for the salt-mountain was performed during the night by the two of you with humility.
"And because of that, you shall be unconquered in the worlds, as will Lakṣmī, endowed with health and good fortune.

Therefore, you too should here perform the ten types of mountain offerings, such as the Mountain of Grain (dhānyācala), according to the prescribed ritual. Having honored these words of Vasiṣṭha, who was the very embodiment of Dharma, he gave them all [to him].
Having offered the mountain of grain and the others in due order, he went to the world of the Ancient One (Śiva), being honored by the immortals.
Furthermore, that man devoted to dharma who, though poor, beholds here the gift of Meru being given,
or hears of it with supreme devotion and without negligence— he too, cleansed of sin, goes to heaven.
While this king of mountains, which shatters the fear of worldly existence for men, is being recited, even a bad dream comes to an end;
what then need be said of that creature who, with a perfectly tranquil mind, performs [this rite] here before the bull among kings—he goes to the city of Hari and Hara.

Thus ends the two hundred and fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Gift of the Sugar-Mountain," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Description of the Dharma of Righteous Conduct.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"The detailed exposition of the lunar days (tithis) according to their sequential order has been heard."
Together with its secret portions and mantras, along with the commencement and concluding rites,
everything pertaining to the fire-offering (homa) from the sacrifice to the nine planets has been determined;
the sequence of ablutions is known, and the festivals have been understood by me.
The entire doctrine of giving has been heard by me as revealed for all purposes;
the ritual for the dedication of tanks is known, as is the festival for trees.
Yet, O Madhusūdana, my mind remains thus deluded.
O Kṛṣṇa, son of Devakī, by describing those various vows while taking refuge in those respective deities,
you have demonstrated the diversity among the gods;
and by explaining the sequence of lunar days, the worship, the mantras, and the consecration.
By all the sages, such as Vyāsa and others, who were devoted to the yoga of meditation,
only this one God— the omnipresent and immutable— has been pointed out here.
Why has the dharma of the conduct pertaining to the castes and stages of life not been demonstrated in this work?
"These great sages are satisfied and desire to hear your words.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O King, this mere fragment of the merit of vows and gifts has been recounted to you."
And Sarasvatī is especially able to declare:
"Everyone overcomes difficulties; everyone beholds auspicious things.
This is proclaimed as the dharma common to all classes and stages of life.

This selection of vows, which I have declared for the sake of the gods, is the ultimate truth; that very deity has been described, so comprehend him. He who is Brahmā is said to be Hari, and he who is Hari is Maheśvara.

Maheśvara is remembered as the Sun; the Sun is said to be the Purifier (Agni). That Purifier is Kārttikeya, and Kārttikeya is Vināyaka. Gaurī, Lakṣmī, and Sāvitrī are proclaimed to be the various manifestations of Śakti.
The man who performs a vow dedicated to the God and the Goddess should not perceive any distinction therein, for the world is composed of Śiva and Śakti.
The earth has many varieties, as do the distinctions of fire, wind, and water.
When considered from the perspective of ultimate truth, no distinction appears.
O Pārtha, someone may take refuge in a particular deity and perform some vow; even in that case, the sole cause is conformity with the dharma of the three Vedas.
Furthermore, that supreme rite of giving for the observance of vows which has been described by me to you should be understood as fruitful only for virtuous people who possess good conduct.
The Vedas do not purify one who is devoid of good conduct, even if they have been studied together with the six auxiliary sciences.
At the time of death, the Vedas abandon him, just as birds with grown wings leave their nest.

Just as water in a skull or milk in a dog-skin bag becomes tainted by the defect of its container, so too does even that which is auspicious become defiled when it rests in one devoid of right conduct.
One should protect one's conduct with effort, for wealth comes and goes;
he who is lacking in wealth is not truly lost, but he who is lacking in conduct is utterly destroyed.
Thus, O King, conduct is the root of both dharma and family lineage.
For a creature fallen from right conduct is neither of noble birth nor righteous;
what is the use of proclaiming the vast lineage of the wicked?
Do worms not arise even within fragrant flowers?

Even one born of a low caste, if endowed with purity and right conduct, skilled in all matters of dharma and worldly affairs, is well-born and the best among the virtuous. They do not say that lineage is what constitutes a noble family; it is conduct that is said to constitute a noble family.
"O King, one who is skilled in right conduct rejoices both in this world and the next.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, I wish to hear about eternal and virtuous conduct."
"Everything consists of dharma; what here is proclaimed as right conduct (sadācāra)? Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"Dharma originates from conduct, and the virtuous are characterized by conduct."
The conduct of the virtuous is called "righteous behavior" (sadācāra).
Therefore, one who desires their own welfare in this world should practice such conduct;
for even in the case of one with a sinful body, righteous conduct destroys inauspicious marks.
He makes dear to himself that person who practices righteousness, performs his own duties, and knows the Veda— which is unseen and unheard—
while those who are atheists, nihilists, and transgressors of their gurus and scriptures [he does not].
Those who are ignorant of dharma and of evil conduct have their lifespans diminished.
However, even a man who is devoid of all auspicious marks, if he is of good conduct,
full of faith, and free from malice, shall attain all his desires.
One should wake during the *brāhma-muhūrta* and reflect upon dharma and artha.
One should never urinate toward a Brahmin, fire, the sun, or the north;
by day or night, one should discharge waste facing north, but at night, facing south.
Having risen and sipped water, he should remain composed during the morning twilight (pūrvā saṃdhyā).
In the same manner, he should attend to the evening twilight (uttarā saṃdhyā) with his speech restrained. He must never look at the sun as it rises, nor when it sets.
The sages attained long life through long-term austerity; yet those twice-born ones who perform only the morning twilight ritual and not the evening one—
the righteous king should employ all of them in the labor of Śūdras.
When afflicted by illness, one may void urine and feces as desired;
however, one must cover the earth with grass and do so with the head covered,
away from villages, dwellings, sacred fords, fields, and paths.

One should not perform the consecration of urine in a ploughed field nor in a cow-pen. One should avoid five types of earth: that from within water, from a dwelling, from an anthill, from a mouse-hole, and that which remains after one has already performed purification.
Likewise, one should avoid [earth] for rites such as the worship of the gods and for saluting one's teacher.
Having sipped water properly, one should likewise perform the ritual for eating food.
With care, using clear water that is free from foam, sound, and foul odor,
one who is self-restrained should sip water correctly while facing either the east or the north.

Whatever must always be accomplished by a wise man for the attainment of the three aims of life (trivarga), that is achieved here and in the next world through the presence of a householder. One quarter of one's efforts should be directed toward the next world, and one quarter should be set aside for accumulation.
O King,

the wise should always exert effort in the acquisition of wealth, for by its successful attainment, dharma, desire, and other goals are accomplished— including daily, occasional, and final rites performed with half of that wealth.
Grooming the hair, looking into a mirror, brushing the teeth,
and the worship of the deities should be performed only in the forenoon. One should void urine at a distance from one's dwelling, and likewise, the washing of the feet should be done at a distance.

One who desires his own welfare should always discard food remnants at a distance. That man who crushes clods of earth, cuts grass, or bites his nails is perpetually impure and creates confusion; he does not attain a long life in this world.
One should not look at another man’s naked wife, nor should one look at one’s own excrement. One should avoid seeing or touching a woman in her courses, nor should one converse with her.
One should not void urine or feces in water, nor should one engage in sexual intercourse therein.
One should not stand upon excrement, urine, hair,
ashes, potsherds, chaff, charcoal, bones, fragments, ropes, garments, and the like.
A wise man should not bow down to those who carry such things, nor should he offer them a seat.
A wise man should bow to Brahmins and offer them a seat;
he should attend upon them with palms joined in reverence and follow behind them when they depart. He should not sit on a broken seat, and he should avoid broken bronze vessels.
One should not eat with disheveled hair, nor should one perform a bath naked;
one should never sleep naked, nor should one lie down while still impure from food. While impure, one must not touch the head, for all the vital breaths (prāṇas) are dependent upon it.
One should avoid seizing the hair and striking the head;
however, O son, the use of a whip for flogging is traditionally permitted for no one other than a son or a disciple.
One should not scratch one's own head with both hands joined together.

Men should not bathe their heads frequently without a specific reason. Bathing at night is forbidden, except during an eclipse of the moon. One should also not bathe immediately after a meal, nor in a deep body of water.
One should bathe the head with oil, but not touch any other part of the body;
one should not eat sesame paste, for in this way one's lifespan is not diminished.
One should not commit an offense against the guru, and if he is angry, one should appease him.

One should not listen to the slander of others even when they are speaking; one should always remain unharmed and likewise consume auspicious medicinal herbs. A self-restrained man should also wear gems associated with Garuḍa.

A man should always have hair that is very glossy and clean, be fragrant, wear beautiful clothing, and carry pleasant white flowers. He should not take even the slightest thing belonging to another, nor should he speak even the smallest unpleasant word.
A lord of men should not speak what is pleasant if it is untrue, nor should he proclaim the faults of others;
likewise, he should not take pleasure in enmity directed against another. He should not mount a defective vehicle, nor should he seek shelter in the shade of a riverbank.
[One should not associate] with those who are hateful, fallen, insane, or beset by many enemies;
nor with those who are eunuchs, the husbands of eunuchs, the base, or speakers of falsehood;
likewise, not with those who are profligate, devoted to slander, or deceitful.
A wise man should not practice loving-kindness [toward the unworthy], nor should he travel alone on a road; O Lord of Men, he should not plunge into the force of a rushing torrent,
nor enter a burning house, nor climb to the very top of a tree.
One should not utter the sound "huṃ," nor should one handle a corpse, for the odor of a corpse arises from Soma.
One should not grind one's teeth, nor should one twitch the nose.
One should not speak with the mouth uncovered, and one should avoid [making] sounds of snoring or coughing.
A wise man should not laugh loudly nor emit sound while passing wind;
he should not make his nails clink, nor cut them, nor scratch the earth with his nails;
he should neither bite his beard nor crush clods of earth.

One should not step over a foot, nor should one lead a venerable person toward oneself; one should never sit on a high seat in the presence of a guru. Therefore, one should always be devoted to right conduct and must certainly not act according to one's own whims.
One who desires merit in both worlds is honored in heaven after death; furthermore,
one should always avoid at night crossroads, sacred trees, cremation grounds, groves, and the company of wicked women.

During the summer and rainy seasons, he should carry an umbrella and observe silence at night while in the forests. He should likewise avoid from afar hair, bones, thorns, impure things, sacrificial offerings, ashes, chaff, as well as the earth when wet from bathing.
The way must be yielded to Brahmins, to kings, and to women; likewise to one superior in learning, to a pregnant woman, to one oppressed by a burden, to one of great stature,
and to those who are mute, blind, or deaf, as well as to the intoxicated and the insane.
One should not wear shoes, clothes, or garlands that have been worn by others;
for there is nothing in this world so detrimental to longevity as a man's pursuit of another's wife.
One should not practice jealousy toward women; one's wife must be protected with great effort.
Jealousy shortens one's lifespan; therefore, one should completely avoid it.
[This applies especially to those who are] fools, the insane, the addicted, the deformed, and likewise the arrogant.

One should not insult those who are deficient in limbs, those with redundant limbs, or those lacking in learning. O Great King, the ritual use of water at night, as well as curd and barley-meal, and all acts of eating, must be avoided at midnight.

A wise man should stand for a long time with his knees raised upward and should not be intent on secrecy; likewise, he should not sit down while treading upon his seat with his foot. Nor should he wear excessively dyed garments, nor those that are variegated or black.
One should not act with perversity regarding clothing nor regarding ornaments;
one who desires to live a long life should not despise a woman, even if she is emaciated.
One should treat every Brāhmaṇa and Kṣatriya with respect, for all are like venomous serpents.
An enraged venomous serpent kills only as far as it touches with its fang;
a kṣatriya, when angry, may burn others with his splendor only as far as he sees them;
but a brāhmaṇa can destroy an entire lineage through his mere meditation and even by a single glance.
One should not travel too early in the morning, nor too late in the evening, nor likewise at midday.
One should not travel with unknown persons, nor alone, nor with many.
One should not be a wounder of others' vitals, nor a speaker behind their backs, nor one who is insolent toward his elders.
A forest burnt by fire or struck down by an axe grows back again;
but the word spoken wickedly and loathsome does not grow back, even in a hundred years.
Atheism, reviling the Vedas, and contempt for the deities—these do not heal.
One should completely avoid hatred, arrogance, pride, and impotence. One should not revile a Brahmin, nor point out the lunar mansions (nakṣatras),
nor speak of the lunar days (tithis) of the fortnight, so that his life may not be harmed.
Having spat out his impurities and put on fresh clothes, the wise man should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
A king who has conquered his enemies, who is powerful and devoted to his duties—
