therein a wise man, having accomplished his purpose, should always dwell happily under that ruler.
Where the citizens are well-united and always abide by justice;
where the women are free from envy—there residence brings about happiness.
In that kingdom where the farmers for the most part do not speak excessively.
A wise man should dwell where all medicinal herbs are found;
but, O King, one should never reside where these three things are ever present:
a desire for conquest, ancient enmity, and people whose festivities have ceased.
In that regard, O King, one should not dwell where these four things are absent:
a lender of loans, a physician, a learned Vedic scholar, and a river with water.
Furthermore, a mirror covered in grime should not be looked upon by those who are most wise.
And at night, O Great King, one who desires a long reign should not eat food in the house of a goldsmith, nor should he place his trust in him;
nor should he ever make a goldsmith his friend.
A broken vessel, a bedstead, a dog, and likewise a cock—
these four are inauspicious, as are trees that bear thorns.
An offering is generally made upon a broken vessel, while the bedstead is certainly used for this purpose here.
The ancestors do not eat from that [offering] where there are a dog or a cock;
at the foot of a tree is the dwelling place of all the Piśācas. Therefore, eating beneath them, one consumes pus and blood.

One should personally consume unrefined food consisting of urine and the like produced by children and others; however, one should first feed a newly married woman, a pregnant woman, an elderly woman, and children who are ill with refined food, and only afterwards eat oneself.
He who eats while the elder brother is looking on, yet does not give him food, eats only sin; he incurs the guilt of one who has stolen a bound ox or vehicle.
Thereafter, he should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite, offering oblations in their proper sequence.
One should give the first portion to Brahmā, then to Prajāpati;
the third to the Guhyas, and likewise the next to Kaśyapa. Then one should offer it to Anumati, and thereafter, having given the domestic oblation (gṛhabali).
That which was previously explained by me to you regarding the procedure for the performance of daily rites:
one should then offer three water-jars to the [guardians of the] quarters;
furthermore, one should cast the oblation (bali) for Indra and the others according to the sequence starting from the east.

Having performed the *apasavya* rite for Brahmā, the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), Sūrya, and in due order for all the gods (*viśvedevāḥ*) and all beings (*viśvabhūtāni*), one should offer the portion for Vāyu with the words: "O Yakṣman, this is offered to you."
Then, having set aside the first portion prepared as an offering for the *hantakāra*,

one should present it to a Brāhmaṇa according to the rules and in the proper manner. Having given [the remainder] to the deities, the ancestors, the teachers, and the learned physician (*suśruta*), [one may then eat].
O Lord of Men, wearing fragrant garments and bearing garlands, one should eat while dressed in many clothes;
O King, one should not eat with wet feet.
With a pure face and a joyful heart, one should eat, but never facing the south.
Facing either east or north, and with his mind not distracted by anything else,
a householder should eat after first giving food to the learned, the hungry, and that which has been killed by a contemptible person, or is loathsome and unrefined.

O King, a ruler should eat from vessels that are praised and pure, without being agitated. O Lord of Men, he should not eat from a vessel placed on a stool, nor in an improper place, nor at an improper time, nor in a very crowded place; and the man on earth should first offer the first portion [to the gods].

Becoming absorbed in that [food], one should eat first the sweet flavor; thereafter, the salty and pungent; then the bitter, sharp, and so forth. Indeed, a person eating should consume soft food at the beginning and hard food in the middle.
Furthermore, at the end, a man who eats liquid food is released from disease.
Alakṣmī dwells in *dhānā* grains by day and in curd-mixed barley meal by night; she always makes her home in *kovidāra* trees.
One should always eat blameless food, restrained in speech and not disparaging it;
having eaten properly and sipped water for purification (ācamana), facing either the east or the north,
one should again perform ācamana correctly after carefully washing both hands.
A person should also perform the remembrance of their chosen deity:
"May there be unimpeded happiness for me today, and may there be nourishment from food for my prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna breaths."

"May Agasti, Agni, and the submarine fire digest all that I have eaten; may Vāsudeva grant me the health resulting from its digestion. Having spoken thus, he rubbed his own hands and likewise his belly.
One should perform one's duties with vigilance so as not to cause weariness.
O Bhārata, if some traveler arrives at the time of twilight,
one should honor him with a humble bow, by offering water for washing his feet and a seat, and by uttering words of welcome.

Furthermore, O King, when the sun has entered the mouth of the swan (the month of Māgha), any single sin that might occur by turning one's back on a guest during the day or on a sacred lunar day through the failure to provide food and a bed—
that very same sin becomes eightfold for men.
O King, one should go to a bed that is made of wood and not cracked;
nor should one occupy a bed that is too narrow, broken, uneven, dirty, or made of animal skins, except in times of distress.

O Lord of the Earth, for men who always sleep with their heads toward the eastern direction or even toward the southern direction, it is auspicious; however, the opposite [orientation] brings disease. O King, approaching one's co-wife during her fertile period is indeed recommended.

During an auspicious lunar mansion and at a favorable time, sons are conceived on even nights. One should not approach a woman who has not bathed, nor one who is pregnant, nor one who is menstruating;
nor one who is undesirable, nor one who is angry, nor one who is ill-omened, nor one who is diseased.
One should not [engage] with a woman who is unwilling, nor one who desires another, nor one who has no desire, nor the wife of another; nor one who is excessively emaciated or has eaten too much.
One should do so oneself when endowed with these same qualities:
having bathed, wearing fragrant scents, being confident, and neither fatigued nor hungry.
A man, full of desire and passion, may engage in sexual intercourse;
however, on the fourteenth, the eighth, and the fifteenth days of the lunar fortnight— on these festival days—
he should avoid oil massages, sensual enjoyments, and women.
O Bhārata, after the performance of a razor-rite, at the conclusion of a ritual, and after sexual intercourse with a woman,

one should bathe while wearing clothes in the morning; likewise, having approached the cremation ground, one should bathe, as well as after contact with a guru, devoted wives, or those engaged in sacrifice and austerity.
One should not engage in slander, O Bhārata, even in jest;
a wise man should not carry water and fire at the same time.
Likewise, one should not stretch out one's feet toward a teacher or toward the gods.
One should not point out a cow suckling her calf; one should not drink water with the hollowed palms;
one should not expose oneself to wind and sun, and one should avoid regret. One should not, when angry, curse a servant, nor should one be envious toward all kinsmen.
The virtuous man who provides consolation to the frightened attains heaven as his imperishable fruit.
A man should not wander about looking upward at the gateway of the city;
rather, a man should walk looking ahead upon the surface of the earth for only the distance of a yoke.
Even regarding the remaining days, for one who, with a self-controlled mind, casts off the remnants [of food],
not even the slightest loss of virtue, wealth, or pleasure occurs.
One should not eat meat in vain, nor likewise the meat from the back.
One should avoid abuse, quarreling, and slander.
One should not prepare for one's own sake *saṃyāva*, *kṛśara*, meat, *śaṣkulī*, or milk-rice (*pāyasa*); rather, one should offer these to the deities.
One should not drive goats [into the village], for they cause harm from the outside;
one should not wear red garlands, but white ones should be worn by the wise.
O Lord, with the exception of the lotus and the blue water-lily, these are to be avoided here.
Red [garments] should be worn on the head, and likewise even those used for drinking;
a garland made of gold is never defiled. O best of men, the clothing used upon the bed should be entirely different.
The food offered to the gods in their images is one thing, and that which is served in assemblies is another;
likewise, the *pippala*, the *vaṭa*, the withered *śleṣmātaka*,
and the *udumbara*— a man seeking his own welfare should not eat these, O Supreme Being.
One should avoid conversation with outcasts at the end of a discourse, as well as any form of association;
O King, a man becomes an outcast by associating with outcasts.
Furthermore, one should honor an elder, a kinsman, a friend, or anyone who is poor in this world.
Those who desire the prosperity of their home should keep these birds in their house:
pigeons are auspicious, as are parrots along with mainas;
however, these [other] birds are sinful, as indeed are the *tilapāyika* insects.

One should always keep in the house fresh cow dung, sandalwood, a lute, a mirror, honey, clarified butter, water, and fire; this is the established rule. Furthermore, O lord of men, one should constantly apply effort to the science of archery.

O Indra among kings, apply yourself diligently to riding on the backs of elephants, on the backs of horses, and indeed to the maneuvers of chariots; for one who possesses statesmanship prospers in happiness.
Furthermore, O King, one who is devoted to the protection of his subjects does not find rest.
Having mastered the science of sacrifice and the science of grammar, O Bhārata,
one should understand the science of music and the arts, O Bhārata;
likewise, the Purāṇas, the Itihāsas, and whatever other narratives there may be.
This brief enumeration of the characteristics of proper conduct has been proclaimed to you; the remainder, O lord of men, should be learned from the elders and internalized.
Conduct generates prosperity; conduct increases fame.
For through right conduct life is prolonged, and right conduct destroys inauspicious marks.
Indeed, among all the scriptures, right conduct is said to be the most excellent.
Right conduct is the supreme dharma; through right conduct wealth increases.
This great merit, which brings fame, long life, and heaven, and which is a source of well-being,
has been proclaimed by me for the sake of compassion toward all social classes.
O bull among men, it is conduct alone that, when practiced, yields the fruits of dharma, artha, and kāma for human beings in this world.
Therefore, O King, a wise man should always be vigilant; for the duty proclaimed in the scriptures must indeed be observed daily.

Thus ends the two hundred and fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Dharma of Right Conduct," in the *Uttara-parvan* of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
[This is followed by] the description of the ritual procedure for the *Rohiṇī-candra-śayana-vrata*.
Nārada said: "O moon-crested Lord, tell me that vow of yours which, when properly observed, enables a man to be endowed with long life, health, prosperity of his lineage and so forth,
and to be possessed of virtues in birth after birth."
The Blessed Lord said:
This which you have asked is indeed correct; it brings about imperishability in the hereafter. I shall declare to you this secret, which those who know the Purāṇas understand.

There is an excellent vow here called Rohiṇī-candra-śayana; on that occasion, one should worship the image of Nārāyaṇa with the names of the Moon. Whenever the fifteenth lunar day (Pañcadaśī) happens to coincide with a Monday, [one should perform this vow].
Alternatively, O Brahmin, when the constellation Rohiṇī arises on the full moon day,
a man should perform a bath with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and white mustard seeds;
furthermore, the learned man should recite the mantra "Āpyāyasva" one hundred and eight times.
Even a Śūdra, with supreme devotion and avoiding the conversation of heretics,
having performed his prayers, should say: "Salutations again and again to Soma, the giver of boons, and to Viṣṇu," and then return to his own home to [worship] Madhusūdana.
One should worship with fruits and flowers and recite the names of Soma:

"Salutation to Soma, the Peaceful," at the feet; "Salutation to the one named Ananta," at the knees; "Salutation to Vṛkodara," at the two thighs; and one should worship the genitals with "Salutation to Anaṅgabāhu."
Salutations again and again to the bestower of the pleasure of desire; the waist is to be worshipped as that of the Moon.
Likewise, the belly is for the one whose belly is nectar, and the navel is well-worshipped as that of the Eye of Brahmā (Viṣṇu).
Salutations be to the Moon; having worshipped the face, the jaw is to be worshipped as the Lord of the twice-born (Brahmā).

I bow to the face of the Moon, the beloved of the night-lotus groves; to His lips, the Lord of forest herbs; and again, to His eyebrows that bestow joy. I bow to His two eyes, the lover of the blue water-lily, and to His chest, dark as a blue lotus, which holds the hand of Lakṣmī.
Salutations to the destroyer of the Daityas, whose two ears are worshipped at all sacrifices;
the forehead is for the beloved of the ocean (the Moon); the hair is to be honored as belonging to the Lord of Suṣumṇā.
Salutations to the Moon for the head; salutations to the Enemy of the Asuras, the Lord of the Universe, for the crown.

Having worshipped the Goddess, the consort of the Moon, with fragrant incense, food offerings, flowers, and other articles— addressing her as "O Padmapriye, O Rohiṇī, O Lakṣmī, the savior who bestows the nectar of fortune and happiness"— and having bathed again after rising from the ground where he had prostrated, he should provide a Brahmin with an offering of sacrificial food (haviṣya).
In the morning, that pitcher of water with gold should be given away for the destruction of mental sins.

Having consumed cow’s urine and food that is meatless and non-alkaline, one should then fast for twenty-eight mouthfuls; thereafter, having eaten food mixed with milk and ghee, one should listen to an Itihāsa for a muhūrta.
The kadamba, blue lotus, ketaka, jasmine, red lotus, and śatapatrikā;
the amlāna, kubjā, and sinduvāra flower; furthermore, the nārada and mallikā;
the muktā and karavīra flower for Viṣṇu, and the śrīcampaka for the Moon—these are to be offered.
In the months beginning with Śrāvaṇa, these [offerings] should always be made in sequence;
in whichever month the vow begins, one should worship Hari with flowers.
Having fasted according to the rules for the duration of one year, the man [attains the fruit].
At the conclusion of the vow, one should give a bed accompanied by a mirror and household utensils.
Having fashioned a golden pair consisting of Rohiṇī and the Moon,
the Moon should be made six finger-breadths in size and Rohiṇī four finger-breadths.
Adorned with eight pearls, covered with a white cloth and eye-bandage,
and placed upon a jar of milk together with a bell-metal vessel containing unbroken rice grains,
as well as śāli rice, sugarcane, and fruit, one should offer it in the forenoon while reciting the mantra.
Then, having adorned a white cow with a golden face and silver hooves,
provided with a cloth and a vessel, as well as a beautiful conch shell,
he should likewise honor a virtuous Brahmin couple with ornaments.
One should imagine that this Moon, in the form of a brahmin together with his wife,
does not leave the bed of Rohiṇī, O Kṛṣṇa; likewise,
may there be non-difference between you, who possess the form of Soma, and my own forms.
"Just as you alone are the bestower of supreme bliss and liberation to all,
so may there be for me firm devotion toward you in this sacrifice— both worldly enjoyment and liberation—
for I am afraid of saṃsāra and desire release, O sinless one."

O Sage, this alone is the unsurpassed provider of beauty, health, and long life; it is always beloved by the ancestors as well. Having become the sovereign of the three worlds for three hundred times one hundred kalpas, [one shall remain so].
One attains the world of the Moon, from which return is difficult to find;
likewise, a woman who observes the Rohiṇī-vrata or the Candraśayana-vrata also obtains that same fruit, from which return is difficult to find.
Whoever thus recites or hears this worship of the Slayer of Madhu accompanied by the praise of the Moon,
and even one who merely directs their mind toward it, shall, upon entering the abode of Śauri, be honored by the hosts of immortals.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Rohiṇī-Candra-Śayana Vow," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira, and the conversation between Nārada and Maheśvara.
The Description of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s Arrival at Dvārakā.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O King, the vows, the gifts, and indeed your religious duties have been revealed."
Since this [world] has its root in dharma, therefore be devoted to dharma.
O Pārtha, although I knew them, I did not reveal desire and wealth;
for the world here proceeds of its own accord—why should they be further described?
Describing desires to one who is lustful, or describing greed to one who is greedy—
what fruit does such a man obtain, other than falling like a blind man into a well?
This *Bhaviṣyottara* has been told to you, O son of Pāṇḍu.
O Bhārata, this collection of vows and gifts for men of virtuous conduct— which is seen in the Itihāsas and Purāṇas and is connected with the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences—
is all presented here.

O best of men, one should not place any reliance on that which is spoken in contradiction to worldly custom and the Vedas, for that is remembered as mere idle chatter. I have uttered this to you out of great affection.
O Pārtha, before sages even speech becomes dull;
for this must not be disclosed to the hypocrite or the rogue,
nor to the atheist, nor to one whose mind is set elsewhere, nor to one afflicted by fallacious reasoning.
When this is narrated to one who is of virtuous conduct, self-controlled, and devoted to truth and integrity, it shall indeed produce an auspicious destiny.
O moon among kings, this is common to the best of the gods as well as to those of the various castes and stages of life.
Out of friendship for you, O Pārtha, I have related to you this Purāṇa known by the name Bhaviṣyottara.
You yourself, O son of Pṛthā, are Dharma here on earth; you are a knower of dharma and worldly purpose, and you have perceived both the higher and the lower.
Therefore, being questioned, I speak of dharma, and this shall be all the more worthy of faith by the people.
"I shall go to Dvāravatī, and I will return for the sacrifice and the great festival;
for knowing that everything is under the sway of Time, you should not feel any regret in this matter.
Having spoken thus, the high-souled one, desiring to depart, was honored by the sons of Pāṇḍu and departed with a joyful heart.

Having inquired after all his friends and kinsmen, Kṛṣṇa departed after bowing down to the Brahmins. Indeed, when the venerable Vasiṣṭha was questioned by the sage Yājñavalkya, he gave a reply in many ways; and that which had been ordained for the son of Pāṇḍu by Vyāsa was carried out, O wonder, by that bull among sages.
Victorious is Vyāsa, the son of Parāśara and the delighter of Satyavatī’s heart,
from whose lotus-like mouth the world drinks the holy honey of speech.

Thus ends the two hundred and seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Conclusion and the Departure of Śrī Kṛṣṇa for Dvārakā," in the Uttara-parvan of the glorious *Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
The Statement of the Table of Contents (Now, the narrative accounts): First, the following of Vyāsa, and then the origin of the Brahmāṇḍa.
Because of Vaiṣṇavī Māyā, there is the proclamation of the defects in saṃsāra; from that follows the classification of sins, and from that, the determination of what is auspicious and inauspicious.
[Then follow] the greatness of the Śakaṭa-vrata, the glorification of the Tilaka-vrata, the vow known as Aśoka and Karavīra, and from that, the Kokila-vrata.
The vow known as Bṛhattapovrata, the fasting of Rudra, the greatness of the second lunar day vow, likewise the Aśūnyaśayana; the third lunar day vow called Kāmākhyā, and also the Meghapālīvrata.

The practice of the five fires is delightful; it is the supreme third-day vow (Tṛtīyāvrata). There is also the three-night vow named Goṣpada, as well as the Harakālī vow, the one called Lalitā-tṛtīyā, and another known as Yoga.
The vow known as Umāmaheśvara, likewise the third lunar day with Rambhā, that called Saubhāgya, and Ārdrānandakarī—
these are declared to be the Tṛtīyā vows for the months of Caitra, Bhādrapada, and Māgha.
The third is Anaṃtarī, as well as the Gaṇaśānti-vrata;
the fifth is called the Sārasvata-vrata.
Likewise, the sixth is named Śrī-pañcamī, which destroys grief.
Now the Phala-ṣaṣṭhī and the Mandāra-ṣaṣṭhī vow are described;
likewise the Lalitā-vrata-ṣaṣṭhī, the Ṣaṣṭhī known as Kārtika,
the Mahattapa-saptamī, and the Vibhūṣā-saptamī.
The Ādityamaṇḍapa-vidhi, the Trayodaśī, and the Saptamī; the Kṛkavāku-plavaṅgā, and likewise the Abhaya-saptamī;
the one named Kalyāṇa-saptamī, and the Śarkarā-saptamī-vrata.
The seventh is called Kamalā, and likewise another, Śubhasaptamī;
then there are the Snapanavrata-saptamī and the Acalasaptamī;
furthermore, the vow known as Budhāṣṭamī and the Janmāṣṭamī-vrata.
The Dūrvā-observance is proclaimed, as well as the Aṣṭamī-vow;
then the Aṣṭamī of the Sun (Arkāṣṭamī), the Vṛkṣa-navamī-vow,
the Navamī called Dhvaja, and likewise the Navamī called Ulkā.
Then follows the Daśāvatāra-vrata, as well as the Aśādaśamī-vrata; next is the Rohiṇī-hari-śambhu-brahma-sūryāviyoga-vrata,
and after that, the vow known as Govatsa-dvādaśī is declared.
The Nīrājanadvādaśī, the Bhīṣmapañcaka,
the one called Mallikā-dvādaśī, the excellent Bhīmā-dvādaśī,
the one named Śravaṇa-dvādaśī, and the Saṃprāpti-dvādaśī-vrata.
Thereafter, the vow named Govindadvādaśī is declared;
after that, the one named Akhaṇḍadvādaśī; after Tiladvādaśī, the one named Sukṛtadvādaśī, and also the Dharaṇīvratadvādaśī.
The vow known as Viśokadvādaśī is the Vibhūtidvādaśī-vrata;
likewise, there is Puṣyarkṣadvādaśī, Śravaṇarkṣagā-dvādaśī,
Anaṅgadvādaśī, and the Aṅgapāda-vrata.
Then come the Nimbārka and Karavīra observances, as well as the Yamā, Darśa, and Trayodaśī;
also Anaṅgadvādaśī, the Pālī and Rambhā vows,
the Caturdaśī vow, and thereafter the Anantacaturdaśī.
The Śrāvaṇī-vrata, the Nakta-vrata, and the observances on the fourteenth and eighth days;
the Śiva-caturdaśī-vrata, the Phalatyāga-caturdaśī,
and the Vaiśākhī, Kārtikī, and Māghī— this is the series of vows that follows.
The Kṛttikā-vrata is prescribed for the full moon of Kārttika when the moon is in conjunction with the Kṛttikā constellation;
on the full moon of Phālguna, however, is the Pūrṇamanoratha-vrata,
as well as the one known as Aśoka-pūrṇimā and the Ananta-vrata.
Indeed, there is the Sāṃbharāyiṇya vow, the Nakṣatrapuruṣa vow,
and by means of the perfected Śivanakṣatrapuruṣa, one is liberated;
also the vow named Kāmadāna and the ritual procedure for the eggplant (vṛntāka).
The fruit of a solar transit (saṃkrānti) occurring at night during the day of the Sun,
the Bhadrā-vrata, the offering to Agastya (agastyārgha), the vow of the new moon and sun,
the offering to Venus and Jupiter, and the eighty-five vows— [all yield the same merit].
The Māgha bath, the daily bath, the procedure for Rudra baths,
the bath during lunar and solar eclipses, the rules for the consumption of food,
the consecration of ponds, wells, and tanks, and the ritual planting of trees.
Likewise, there is the procedure for the worship of deities, the offering of lamps, and the release of a bull;
then the festival known as Phālguny-utsava, as well as another, the Sadanotsava;
and Bhūtamātā on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa, along with the rite of binding the protective thread (Rakṣābandha).
Likewise, the ritual for the ninth day, as well as the great festival of the Moon;
the fire-oblation on Dīpālikā, and likewise the procedure for the hundred-thousand oblations (lakṣahoma);
the ten-million oblations (koṭihoma), the Mahāśīti, and the propitiatory rite (śāntikā) of Gaṇanātha.
Likewise, the fire-offering for the constellations (*nakṣatra-homa*), the rite for the gift of a cow (*godāna-vidhi*),
the vows of the molasses-cow, the ghee-cow, and the sesame-cow,
as well as the prescribed rite for the water-cow and another for salt.
"The cow known as Kāryā, another known as Navanīta,
and likewise the Suvarṇadhenu— these are for those desiring to perform rites for the gods.

Thus ends the two hundred and eighth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Concise Table of Contents," in the Uttara Parvan of the glorious Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Thus ends the fourth concluding section.
This work, the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa, is complete. [The section on] the Ananta-vrata.
From the *Śabdakalpadruma*: King Yudhiṣṭhira, who had dwelt in the forest and possessed self-mastery,
was met by Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul and Lord of the three worlds.
A conversation concerning matters both pleasant and unpleasant arose between the two there;
and Yudhiṣṭhira, in particular, questioned Govinda.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Lord of Gods, by what vow is the desired fruit obtained,
such that all people become free from sin throughout every birth?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:

There is a vow named Ananta which was performed in the abode of the gods by Indra and the other world-protectors; listen as I describe it. It is observed on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada.
By the mere performance of it, all sin is destroyed.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Kṛṣṇa, who is this one described by you as being designated by the name Ananta?
Who is this one known as Śeṣa, the Nāga Ananta, and Takṣaka? Is he the supreme and most excellent, or is he called Brahman? Who indeed is this one named Ananta? Tell me that, O Janārdana.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"I am Ananta, O Pārtha; understand that form of mine.
It is the Time that arises, presiding over the movement of the sun."
Through the arrangement of days and nights consisting of *kalās*, *kāṣṭhās*, *muhūrtas*, and so forth;
and through the arrangement of fortnights, months, seasons, years, *yugas*, and *kalpas*—
I am that very Time who has descended for the purpose of removing the burden of the earth.
Know me, O Pārtha, as the one born from the body of Vasudeva for the destruction of the Dānavas— Ananta, Kṛṣṇa, Viṣṇu, Hari, Śiva,
Brahmā, Bhāskara, Śeṣa, the all-pervading Lord.
"O Pārtha, for the sake of your conviction, behold that universal form (viśvarūpa) which,
O mighty-armed one, is the unsurpassed object of meditation for yogis, revealed by me even before now.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O best among those who know the ordinances, [tell me] the greatness of the Ananta-vrata, its procedure,
what its merit is, what its fruit is, and what its performance consists of;
by whom was it performed previously, and by whom was it revealed in the world?
"O Lord Nārāyaṇa, relate all of that in great detail.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"In ancient times, during the Kṛta-yuga, there was indeed a twice-born man named Sumantra."
Born of the Vasiṣṭha lineage, he was a learned man of virtuous character who had conquered his senses.
His wife was Dīkṣā, a chaste woman established in truthful vows;
she was born of the Bhṛgu clan, beautiful in form and endowed with excellent conduct and virtue.

In time, a daughter endowed with every auspicious mark was born to her; named Śīlā, she was virtuous and grew up in her father’s house. But in the course of time, her mother became afflicted by a burning fever.
Having come together at the river water, she died and went to the city of heaven.
Sumantu performed for her whatever rites belong to the world beyond;
thereafter, Sumantu gradually abandoned his grief and sorrow once again.
"A householder without a wife is never fit to perform his religious duties.
Having reflected thus in his mind, with a heart eager for marriage,
he married Karkaśā, the daughter of the sage Devala.

She was harsh and extremely ill-behaved, always speaking with cruelty; she was irascible, antagonistic, shameless, and fond of quarreling. She was incompetent in domestic duties, yet skilled only in the act of eating.
Content with quarreling and angry toward her kinsmen,
that Śīlā, having been raised day by day in her father’s house,
engaged in unsurpassed childhood play together with her friends.
Within the interior of the house, on the ground, at the doorways, on the thresholds, and upon the arches,
she repeatedly decorated them with the four colors— red, yellow, white, and black—
forming svastikas, lotuses, and conch shells.
Daily performing the worship of deities and guests,
always skilled in domestic duties, and exceedingly dear to her father,
the Brahmin saw her after some time as she had reached the bloom of youth.
He became filled with anxiety, wondering, "To whom should I give my daughter? Then, by the power of destiny, Kauṇḍinya arrived there—
a most excellent sage, highly fortunate, of noble lineage, and devoted to dharma.
The wise Sumantu, a performer of great penance, reflected in his mind:
"By the power of destiny, Śīlā must be bestowed upon him with great effort.
Having thus resolved, the brahmin gave his daughter on an auspicious day.

Then, according to the rites for marriage prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras and the Vedas, he performed the wedding of the maiden, who was virtuous, well-adorned, of excellent character, and whose face was like the moon. Thereafter, having completed the ritual acts such as the fire-oblation at the proper time, the sage—
Sumantu spoke harshly to Karkaśā: "O beloved, born of a lineage of sages, give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to your son-in-law and make my gift fruitful;
for a ritual act devoid of a sacrificial fee becomes fruitless."
Having heard those words of his, she became harsh and enraged;
she rebuked her husband Sumantu with harsh words,
and having brought her own ornaments and her binding cord, she spoke.
Having deposited [the items] in a secret place, he went to another house;
Sumantu, his soul deeply dejected, was then filled with shame,
having brought whatever wealth was suitable for the purpose as a dowry.
The Brahmin, having served her again and again, gave her to his son-in-law.
Then, having completed the wedding, Kauṇḍinya also took Śīlā, placed her upon a bullock-cart, and departed for his own hermitage.
Then, as she was traveling on the road, Śīlā, whose face resembled the moon, having descended at midday during the time for eating onto the bank of a river,
saw a multitude of women observing religious vows.
Seeing there a multitude of men, seated on red and yellow cloths, each individually worshipping Ananta with devotion on the fourteenth day, Satī respectfully questioned that group of women.
The virtuous woman, bowed down in humility, prostrated before the Lord of the Gods and said,
"Tell me, what is this task that is being performed by you? The women replied:
In the month of Bhādrapada, during the bright fortnight,

when the banner of Indra has been raised and Mahendra has been propitiated, he who bows down and bathes in the lake and then begins the worship of Ananta upon the flagstaffs shaped like banners— [attains the supreme goal].
Having fashioned an image of the God made of darbha grass, provided with water and sacrificial grain—
an infinite Lord of the lords of gods, four-armed and wearing a crown,
resembling the *atasī* flower, and adorned with golden armlets—
[One should worship Him] bearing the conch, discus, mace, and the Śārṅga bow, and holding various other weapons.
"Come, come, O Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa; your sacrifice is now proceeding.
Likewise, one should employ the Blessed Ananta upon the water-vessel.

Having offered flowers, food offerings, incense, garments, and unguents upon the mandala, one should worship with devotion the infinite one who possesses universal forms. For the sake of the flour, one may use rice powder or that of barley or wheat.
That which is obtained from these is designated as a *prastha* and is to be divided;
half is to be given to a Brahmin, and half one should apply to oneself.
Likewise, having worshipped the deity with perfumes and flowers in due order, [one should proceed].
Having heard his story, a woman should place the well-prepared thread-scarf, smeared with saffron and provided with fourteen knots, upon her left hand;
a man, however, should place it on his right arm and then worship Ananta.
Having performed the worship of the Lord, having eaten the cake as she pleased,
and having dismissed him after giving the priestly fee and bowing according to custom,
Śīlā heard the words they had spoken.
She undertook a vow, binding an excellent cord upon her arm;
having prepared a prastha of cakes and consumed them accordingly,
she returned once more, accompanied by that very same ox-cart.
By that infinite faith, his home became crowded with herds of cattle;
his hermitage was endowed with splendor, provided with wealth and grain,
filled with various guests, and adorned with many kinds of jewels.
It was filled with excellent horses, rutting elephants, buffaloes, and herds of cattle;
she was adorned with silken garments, jeweled girdles, and ornaments of pearls;
possessing a divine form and perfected in virtue, she was like the goddess Sāvitrī herself.
Once, while she was seated, she approached the fire-pit;
Kauṇḍinya also entered out of anger upon seeing the endless cord tied with great care at the base of Śīlā’s wrist.
With words of anger, his face contorted by a frown, he asked:
"What is this cord tied to your hand? Why do you stand here as a wife?
O evil-minded one, tell me quickly—to which god are you subject?"
Śīlā said: "O Lord, listen to my words: the auspicious cord of the God of gods is infinite and immeasurable; it has been bound upon the hand according to the prescribed rite."
"By whose grace you enjoy such vast wealth,
how is it, O Lord, that you do not recognize him as such, the Sovereign of the World?
Then, having heard these words of Śīlā, Kauṇḍinya became enraged.
"Who indeed is this one called Ananta? He has never even been heard of, O fair-faced one!
Having said this, he became enraged, seized the serpent Ananta by its arm, and after rebuking his beloved in many ways, hurled it into a fire filled with flames.
Then Śīlā, in great agitation, cried out "Alas! Alas! and ran forward; taking the thread from the fire, she cast it into the midst of the milk.
Then she tied that beautiful bracelet once more upon her left wrist.

O Yudhiṣṭhira, due to the fault of endless profligacy, poverty fell upon that brāhmaṇa’s house; he was no longer described by anyone in the world. Filthiness came over his body, and likewise, sleep took hold of his eyes.
Seeing his own city with its houses empty and some burnt by fire, the brahmin reflected in his mind. Then Śīlā, pale and distressed due to her husband's fault, [remained there].
He wandered through the entire city, which was filled with empty houses.
Then, a supreme thought arose in the mind of the Brahmin Kauṇḍinya:
"I too must have committed an evil deed, or perhaps something censurable has been done by me."
"By the fault of endless entanglement, my own fate is likewise such:
I, a fool, shall go wherever I perceive the infinite.
Thereupon Kauṇḍinya departed for a forest teeming with tigers and other beasts.
Agitated, he went along a path devoid of people and living beings in order to seek out his vow and likewise to behold the feet of Hari;
there he saw that tree, endowed with fruits and flowers.
It was devoid of flocks of birds and especially of insects.
He asked him, "O great tree, has Ananta been seen by you anywhere?
And that great tree replied, "O twice-born one, I do not know Ananta."
Proceeding from there, he saw before him, in the midst of the grass, a mother cow with her calf;
though they were running through the grass, neither would eat nor smell it.
"O great cow, tell me: has Ananta been seen by you?"
Then she, along with her calf, said to him, "O twice-born one, I do not know Ananta.
Thereupon, as he was proceeding, he saw before him an excellent bull standing in the forest.
That brahmin asked him, "Has Ananta been seen by you?"
The bull said this to the dejected brahmin:
"If I knew Ananta, then my state would be such as yours.
Then, as he was proceeding, he saw ahead of him a donkey and likewise an elephant.
Seeing him wandering with various illusions, arrogant with a lion’s roar, that brahmin asked, "Have you seen Ananta?
He replied with this answer: "O brahmin, I do not know Ananta."
Then, proceeding further, he saw before him two beautiful lotus ponds,
adorned with waves that dashed against one another,
and graced by auspicious white and yellow water-lilies, as well as by red and blue lotuses.
Filled with bees, cakravākas, swans, and kāraṇḍava ducks, the twice-born Ananta questioned them; and they, having been observed by him, said to him: "We do not know Hari anywhere."
Then the brahmin fell to the ground, crying out "Alas! Alas! and weeping:
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? How may I see that Lord?
Thereupon, the Lord of Gods, worshipped by the gods, whose heart was compassionate, [appeared].
At that very moment, Lord Viṣṇu appeared before the twice-born man in the form of an elderly brāhmaṇa and spoke these words to him:
"Arise, arise, O best of brahmins! Cast off your sorrow and become happy."
"I shall show you the infinite Kṛṣṇa, Viṣṇu, Hari, and Śiva. Having taken that Brāhmaṇa by way of the path to Pātāla, he showed him that city; thereafter, the twice-born one vanished.
Kauṇḍinya beheld that city, difficult to find even in the three worlds, filled with divine women and men, adorned with jewels and gems;
it was entirely fashioned of gold and surrounded by Takṣaka and other [nāgas].
There Kauṇḍinya beheld the God of gods, the infinite one;
the Lord of the world in his universal form, four-armed, wearing a diadem,
bearing the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus, and having Garuḍa as his banner.

Having beheld the Lord of the World in such a form— resplendent with Lakṣmī on his right and playing Sarasvatī on his left, seated upon a divine lion-throne provided with seven hoods— he offered praise with devotion.
He went upon the ground before Ananta with his head bowed, [saying]:
"Salutations to Ananta, who possesses a thousand forms;
salutations to the eternal Puruṣa, whose name is a thousandfold, who sustains thousands of millions of yugas, and whose feet, eyes, heads, thighs, and arms are a thousand in number."
"O Lord, whatever evil deed has been committed by me through ignorance,
please graciously declare all that and forgive me, O Madhusūdana.
Then, having heard the praise of the brahmin Kauṇḍinya, Janārdana—
The blessed Lord Ananta, who assumes infinite forms, was pleased and said, "O Brahmin,
how did you tell my beloved that I should come here?
Ananta replied:
"I am pleased, O best of brahmins, especially by your devotion. Choose a boon, O lord of sages; I am satisfied, so cast aside your astonishment.
Kauṇḍinya said:

O Hṛṣīkeśa, in whatever womb I may enter through the experience of the fruits of my own karma, may my devotion to Hari remain firm in each and every one of them. Whatever evil deed has been committed by me through extreme negligence or delusion—
"O Lord, may that offense be forgiven; I bow down to you again and again.
Having heard those words, Ananta granted him three boons:
the destruction of poverty, the practice of righteousness, and likewise an imperishable place in the world of Viṣṇu.
Kauṇḍinya said:
"O Lord, my heart's desire has been fulfilled today, especially so.
O Lord of Gods, I ask something; tell me that, O Master of the World."

"O Lord, please tell me out of compassion what was seen by me today on the road: what was that mango tree, what was the bull, what was the cow, what were those two lotus ponds, who was the donkey, who was the elephant, and who was that most excellent aged brahmin?"
Śrī Ananta said:
"That mango tree which was seen, O Brahmin, was indeed one who was arrogant in his learning;
for that reason, he did not impart knowledge to a disciple who had approached him."
By the ripening of that karma, he remains having attained the state of a tree.
As for that bull which was seen by you, it was produced in the past by the karma of greed;
because you gave stale goods and ate delicious food yourself.
Having attained the state of a bull, he then remains in a desolate place;
having given to a Brahmin land that is fruitless and devoid of crops,
he therefore assumes the form of a cow and runs among the grass.
One should understand that the two lotus ponds represent dharma and adharma;
the donkey is one endowed with ignorance, while the elephant is one intoxicated with pride.
O Sage, this Brāhmaṇa whom you have shown me is the infinite Self.
"All this has been told to you; go now, O Brahmin, to your own hermitage.
Prosperity shall be yours again, O Brahmin, there is no doubt.
Having enjoyed abundant pleasures, you shall attain the supreme state."
Having thus granted him the boon, he vanished on that very spot. Kauṇḍinya, having returned home, performed for fourteen years the supreme vow known as Ananta, which yields great merit.
Having enjoyed his heart's desires together with Śīlā,
the righteous-souled one reached the realm of Viṣṇu and shone there in her company;
O King, this was because the vow known as Ananta had been completed here on earth.

Completely liberated from all sins, they shall go to the supreme state. O King, in this very way, by the power of this rule, women who observe the Ananta-vrata, endowed with sons, grandsons, and wealth, shall enjoy their heart’s desires.
"They attain the world of Viṣṇu for as long as the moon and sun endure.
Thus ends the Ananta-vrata in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa.
